en: Now begins the section on vowel-sandhi (*acsandhi*).

(48) *iko yaṇ aci* [Pāṇini 6.1.77]. "The *ik* vowels are replaced by *yaṇ* before an *ac* vowel. Here, "*ika*" is in the genitive case. Therefore, according to the rule "the genitive denotes the element to be replaced," it signifies the locus of substitution.

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "in the place of" (*sthāne*), the meaning "in the place of" is obtained. It has been stated that "place" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). Since it is impossible for one phoneme (*varṇa*) to be the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of another phoneme, the term *aci* is a locative absolute (*satisaptamī*).

By the technical rule "when [something] is specified by the word 'in that' (*tasmin*), [the operation applies] to what precedes," [the term *aci* refers to] a vowel (*ac*) uttered immediately after [the cause of substitution] without being intervened by another phoneme.
The phrase "of what precedes" (pūrvasya) is understood. Likewise, the meaning "when followed by a vowel" (aci parataḥ) is obtained.
The term "in saṃhitā" (saṃhitāyām) is the governing heading (adhikṛtam). Consequently, the absence of an interval exceeding half a mora (ardhamātrā) is obtained.
Thus, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "of the place of iK," and so forth. And this—

In accordance with the essence of the ancient views that follow the literal words of the Sūtras, however, in the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra "saṃhitāyām," the governing scope (adhikāra) of *saṃhitā* is rejected by taking the locative case *aci* in the sense of immediate proximity (*sāmīpika*)— that is, as a point of contact (*upaśleṣika*)— in relation to the word *tasmin*. For it is stated there as follows:
Commentary: This *yoga* (rule) can be explained. How so?

A locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is of three kinds: pervasive (*vyāpaka*), contiguous (*upaśleṣika*), and objective (*vaiṣayika*). But what other connection could there possibly be between one word and another, other than contiguity (*upaśleṣa*)? [As in the rule: *iko yaṇ aci*.

Regarding the phrase *acyupaśliṣṭasya*: in that context, even without the explicit mention of *saṃhitā*, it will apply only within *saṃhitā*. "Adherence" (*upaśleṣaḥ*) means proximity or connection; the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) produced by that is "adherent" (*auvaśleṣika*), which is to say, "proximate" (*sāmīpika*). Thus...

And thus it results that [the term *saṃhitā*] refers to an *ik* vowel situated in proximity. Proximity, moreover, consists in the absence of any intervention, whether by time or by phoneme. Consequently, since the absence of *yaṇ*-substitution is established in the case of non-*saṃhitā* simply because the aforementioned proximity is lacking, the heading (*adhikāra*) for *saṃhitā* need not be formulated; such is the meaning of the Bhāṣya. And so it is.
In the rule "tu syanyāyasmin" (P. 1.1.66), when it is specified that [an operation applies] "in this," the locative case is used in the sense of an *aupaśleṣika* locus (a locus of proximity).

Consequently, in the rule "acīti" (P. 6.4.77) and others, when a sound such as 'a'—which is the referent of the locative ending—is uttered, [the preceding element is affected] by virtue of the relationship of proximity (*sāmīpya*).

The meaning is that the effect would belong to a preceding [element] that is present. It bears fruit. However, since [the effect] does not [bear fruit] when [the cause] is uttered without immediate succession, the qualification "immediate" (*avyavahita*) must be applied to the term "uttered" (*uccārite*); for this is obtained by the locative case itself being used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpikādhikaraṇa*). And in that context, proximity is in terms of time.

And because it consists in the absence of intervention (*vyavadhāna*) with respect to color (*varṇa*), the term *nir* need not be included there for the sake of meaning "immediacy" (*nairantarya*). This is clearly stated by Kaiyaṭa on the sūtras *snukramoḥ* and *tatra ca dīyate*. However, the threefold nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is as follows:

This will be clarified under the section on *kāraka*s in the rule *ṭhādhāro'dhikaraṇam*. Regarding the word *sudhī*: from the root *dhyai* (meaning "to think"), by the rule *dhyāyateḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*, the suffix *kvip* is applied;
the *yakāra* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, becoming *ikāra*, followed by the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi and the lengthening of the vowel by the rule *halaśca*, resulting in the word *dhī*.

They are called *sudhiyaḥ* because they meditate well (*suṣṭhu dhyāyanti*). Alternatively, they are *sudhiyaḥ* because their intellect (*dhī*) is very beautiful (*su-śobhanā*). The analysis of the compound is: "he whose form is by means of those with good intellect" (*sudhībhiḥ rūpa asya*). The compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. The case ending of the instrumental plural (*bhisaḥ*) is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. [Thus: *sudhī*.

The grammatical connection is as follows: *upāsya* being established [as the subject], there is the substitution of *y* for the vowel *ī*. The application of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the objects denoted by those [substitutes] in the case of *pratyāhāras* has been explained in detail in the rule *na-j-ja-lau*. The vowel *ī* was cited as an example to illustrate that point. Now, one might ask: why should the vowels *va*, *ra*, and *la* not also be substitutes for *ī*?
To the objection that [the substitution] would follow from the lack of distinction [between the sounds], he says: "On account of position and proximity.

Because of the similarity in having the palate (*tālu*) as their place of articulation, by the rule "in place of [a sound], the most similar [sound] in its own place," it is the *yakāra* itself that occurs in place of the *īkāra*;
it is not the *varalas* (the semi-vowels *y*, *r*, *l*, *v*), because they have different places of articulation—this is the meaning. For this very reason...
Regarding the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "The designation follows the order of enumeration for those that are equal": "What is the example here?

'iko yaṇ aci' [Pāṇini 6.1.77]. As in 'dadhy atra' and 'madhv atra'. This is not correct, because this is already established by the rule 'sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ' [Pāṇini 1.1.50]. Thus [ends the discussion of] "sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ".

In the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, however, it is stated: "What is the example here? [The rule] *iko yaṇ aci*. [As in] *dadhy atra*. This is not [the case]. This is established even by the principle of corresponding enumeration (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). The meaning is that this is accomplished by the rule regarding corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhyasūtra*).
Now, one might object: "But here, by the word *yaṇ*, there are four [sounds]: the non-nasalized *ya*, *va*, and *la*, and the letter *ra*."
[The sounds] are not included because, due to their being subject to modification (*bhāvyamānatva*), they do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).
Even though the qualities (*guṇa*) do not differentiate [the phonemes], seven [sounds] are included: the six [nasals] *ya, va, la*, and *ṛ*.
However, by the word *ik*, sixty-six [sounds] are included; thus, since the numbers are unequal, how can this be so?
If it is argued that the rule for sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyasūtra*) applies here, we say no;

for [the vowels] are made equivalent by being subsumed under the categories of *ik*, *aC*, *yaṇ*, and so forth. Now, if thirty [substitutes] were presented individually for each of the *ṛ* and *lṛ* sounds, then there would be the substitution of *r* for the *lṛ* sounds and [the substitution of *l*] for the *ṛ* sounds.

If it is argued that since there is also the contingency of substituting *l* [for *ṛ*], the matter cannot be resolved by the rule of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*), listen: from the rule of respective order it is understood that *r* occurs in place of what is delimited by the property of being *ṛ* (*ṛtva*), and *l* occurs in place of what is delimited by the property of being *lṛ* (*lṛtva*). Furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) of being *ṛ* does not exist in the *lṛ*-sounds.

Furthermore, the class-property of *ṛt* does not reside in the *ṛ*-vowels. Due to the force of the rule establishing the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the *ṛ* and *ḷ* vowels, the property of being *ṛt* is superimposed upon the *ḷ* vowel, and the property of being *ḷt* is superimposed upon the *ṛ* vowel, for the sake of grammatical operation. Thus, by taking the actual properties of *ṛt* and *ḷt*, the application of the "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) here proceeds without obstruction; let this suffice.
To that extent:
(49) *anaci ca* [Pāṇini 8.4.47]. When *sudhÂ y* is established, this connects with what will be stated later: "there is doubling of the letter *dh*."

To the question "By which sūtra?", he says: *anaci ca*. From the previous rule *ṭhyaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā*, the word *ṭhyaraḥ* ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and the word *vā* are carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve*, the word *acaḥ* ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) and the word *dve* are carried over. *Anac* means "not a vowel" (*na ac*).

In that context, *anaci* is not a *paryudāsa* (exclusion); for if it were so, then according to the maxim "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* refers to something other than or similar to [the excluded object]," the meaning would be "in a consonant (*hal*) other than a vowel (*aj*). If that were the case, he would have simply said "in a consonant" (*halī*) for the sake of brevity. Furthermore, doubling would not occur in cases such as *rāmād* where there is a final *e*sāna.

Therefore, the statement "it does not occur when *ac* follows" is another sentence intended as a prohibition, based on an *asamartha-samāsa*. This is what he says with the words beginning "of what follows after *ac*" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the letter *dh*":
the meaning is that by this rule, the letter *dh* is pronounced twice. [This occurs] because of the letter *dh* following the vowel *u*.
The sense is that [the substitute] is subsequent and lacks the status of being non-subsequent.
(50) *sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau* (P. 1.1.56). Now, in the case of *sudhy*, regarding the *y* which is the substitute for the *ī*:

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since the substitute (*ādeśa*) possesses the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is a vowel (*actva*) and followed by a vowel (*acpara*), how can there be doubling of the letter *dh*?—the author states the sūtra that establishes that status of the original for the substitute: "A substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*). This applies to that which occupies the position of the guru.
In the world, it is established that when someone takes the place of a teacher’s son or similar person, they acquire his attributes;

and in the Vedic tradition, this is established by the rule regarding *kuśa* grass and so forth being substituted for *śara* grass and so forth. However, in this present treatise, because of the statement "the word's own form [is the meaning]," the attributes of the substituendum (*sthānin*) would not apply to the substitutes (*ādeśa*).

For the sake of attaining that [result], the rule *sthānivadādeśaḥ* (P. 1.1.56) has been commenced. It has been stated that "sthāna" means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). That for whose place another is prescribed is the *sthānin* (the original element). That by which, being prescribed, another [element] that was occasioned is replaced is the *ādeśa* (the substitute). That which is equal to the *sthānin* is *sthānivat*. By that...

The suffix *vati* [in the word *tulya*] has the sense of "like. An *ādeśa* (substitute) appears as equal to its *sthānin* (original element); that is to say, it possesses the properties (*dharma*) of the original element. *Al* is a synonym for "phoneme" (*varṇa*). A *vidhi* is that which is prescribed;

it refers to a grammatical operation (*kārya*). An *alvidhi* is an operation dependent on a phoneme (*alāśraya-vidhi*); *analvidhi* means that which is distinct from an operation dependent on a phoneme (*alāśrayabhinnē*).

The meaning understood as "when an operation dependent on *al* (a phoneme) is to be performed" results in the conclusion that [the substitute] does not behave like the original (*sthānivat*) when an operation dependent on *al* is to be performed. Because the term "dependent on *al*" (*alāśraya*) is stated in general terms, it includes all cases:

an operation concerning *al* itself (*alo vidhiḥ*), an operation concerning what follows *al* (*alaḥ parasya vidhiḥ*), an operation concerning *al* [as the locus of the operation] (*alo vidhiḥ*), and an operation concerning *āL* [a suffix beginning with a vowel] (*Āli vidhiḥ*). Thus, everything is subsumed.
In a rule concerning what follows an *al* (vowel or consonant), as in *vyūḍhoraskena*:

here, although the substitution of *s* for the *visarga*—by the rule "the *visarga* becomes *s*" (*visarjanīyasya saḥ*)—would otherwise trigger the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule "there is *ṇ* when preceded by *aṭ*," such *ṇ*-substitution does not take place. In a rule concerning what follows an *al*, as in *dyauḥ*: [this is explained] by the rule "for *div*, there is *Au*" (*diva āṬ*).
Because the *āṬ* vowel in place of the letter *va* is considered to possess the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is treated as a consonant (*hal*);

consequently, the elision of the nominative suffix *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* does not apply. This is according to the principle that when a rule is prescribed with reference to an *al* (phoneme), [the substitute] is not like the original; for example, in *dyaukāmaḥ*, the *u* in place of the *v* of *div* is not treated as a consonant due to *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *diva u*.

Because of the presence of the letter *va*, the elision [of *y*] that would otherwise be required by the rule *ṭh-lopo vy-or vali* does not take place. As an example of a rule applied when a vowel (*al*) follows: *ka iṣṭaḥ*. This is derived from the root *yaj* with the suffix *kta*. Here, although the substitution of the semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for *yakāra* results in an *ikāra*, the status of that substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) causes it to be treated as a *haś* (a consonant). Consequently, the substitution of *u* (by the rule *haśi ca*) does not occur.

It occurs as follows: here, the term *al* refers both to that which has become the substituendum (*sthānin*) and to a portion of that substituendum. Consequently, the result is that when a rule is conditioned by an *al* that is either the substituendum itself or a portion of the substituendum, the substitute does not behave like the original (*na sthānivat*). In that regard, concerning a rule conditioned by an *al* that has become the substituendum:
The example "vyūḍhoraskeṇa" has already been cited. Or, for instance, consider the root *dhivi* in the sense of "pleasing.

When the suffix *laṭ* is applied, and the first-person plural ending *jhi* is replaced by *anti*, the augment *ukāra* of the *vikaraṇa* is changed to *yaṇ* (the vowel *u*) according to the rule "dhinvikṛṇvyora ca. Because of the status of that [substitute] as a *sthānivadbhāva*, it possesses the nature of an *ārdhadhātuka*.
The addition of the augment *iṭ* does not occur here because the root belongs to the *balādi* class;

for the augment *iṭ*, which applies by depending on the *vakāra* as its substitute for the *ukāra* that constitutes the original element (*sthānin*), is dependent upon the original element (*sthāny-al*). This is according to the principle: "In a rule based on an original element (*sthānin*) or a part thereof... as follows:

In *pratidīvya*, the augment *iṭ*—which would otherwise be required because the substitute *ya* (of *ktvā*) is treated as the original by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, thereby making the suffix *lyap* one beginning with a *val* sound and thus an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix—is not applied. This is because, regarding the condition of beginning with a *val* sound for the application of *iṭ*, [the *ya*] depends upon the *l* which is a constituent part of the original (*sthānin*). This is what he states: "The substitute..."

"It shall be as if it were the original (sthānin), but not in a rule that depends on the *al* (vowel/consonant) of the original. In the phrase "not in a rule that depends on the *al* of the original," what is the purpose of the word "original" (*sthānin*)? [Consider the example: *rāmāya*. Here, although the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule *supi ca* depends on the *su*-affix beginning with *yañ*, and thus depends on the *al* (the *y*) belonging to the substitute, nevertheless— [The answer follows: In this case, even though the lengthening depends on the *al* belonging to the substitute, it does not depend on the *al* of the original. Therefore, since the condition for the exception—that the operation depends on the *al* of the original—is absent, the substitution of *e* for *as* by the rule *ato guṇe* would apply. To prevent this, the word "original" (*sthānin*) is included in the rule. Since the lengthening here depends on the *al* of the substitute and not on the *al* of the original, the prohibition does not apply, and the substitution of *e* for *as* takes place. Thus, *rāmāya* is correctly formed.

In the case of what is to be done, the status of being a *supt* (inflectional suffix) indeed occurs for the substitute by virtue of its being *sthānivat*; furthermore, although the long vowel (*dīrgha*) depends on the form of the letter *y* residing in the substitute, it does not depend on the original phoneme (*al*) of the *sthānin*, because that [long vowel] lacks dependence on the *al* of the *sthānin*.

Nor is there [an issue] regarding the substitution of *ai* for the *aikāra* when the root *nī* takes the suffix *ṇvul*, resulting in the form *nai-aka* after the application of the *vṛddhi* substitute.

It should not be argued that the substitution *āy* would not occur because, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would possess the properties of the vowel *ī*, and since the vowel *ī* lacks the substitution *āy*, [the rule would not apply]. For in this context, only that grammatical operation (*kārya*) which is prescribed by the rules (*śāstrīya*) and is occasioned by the original element (*sthānin*) is extended [to the substitute]; and the absence of the substitution *āy* in the case of the vowel *ī* is not such an operation.

Let it suffice to say that, because [the substitution] is prescribed by the technical rules (*śāstra*), there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the property of the *ī* vowel to the *ai* vowel which takes its place;

this is the sense of the phrase "by this. By the aforementioned *sthānivat* rule, in the case of *iha ucyate*, the *y* which takes the place of the *ī* vowel is treated as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāvena*).

The meaning is that one should not suspect a prohibition of doubling for the letter *dh* by means of the rule *anaci*, which—by the sense that "there is no doubling when *ac* follows"—is based on the fact that [the substitute] does not perform the function of the original (*akāryakāritva*). Why not? To this he says: "Because of the prohibition of that [substitute] under the rule *analvidhau*. This means: because of the prohibition of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

The meaning is that the prohibition of doubling the *y*— which operates by relying on the *y*-sound for the vowel-ness (*actva*) residing in the *i*-vowel that constitutes the original locus (*sthānin*) of that *y*-substitute— is based on the original element (*sthānyal*).

(51) *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* [Pāṇini 1.1.57]. Now, one might object: "In the case of *sudh-y*, let there be no substitution by virtue of the rule *sthānivad ādeśo na...* [1.1.56]; however, by the subsequent rule (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) would certainly still apply."
Anticipating this doubt, he states the subsequent sūtra: *acaḥ parasmin*.
To the question, "Since this is already established by the rule *sthānivad ādeśo ‘nalvidhau*, for what purpose is this sūtra?

he replies: "For the sake of rules not involving an *al* (*alvidhyartham*). The meaning is that it is intended to ensure the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) even in the case of a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) based on an *al* (a vowel or consonant).

By this, *vavraśca* is established. [The root] *ṭhu vraścū* means "to cut. In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], with *tip* and *ṇal*, there is reduplication. By the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *ṛ* in the reduplicated syllable. This becomes the vowel *ṛ*. Then the *pūrvarūpa* [sandhi] applies. Next, *urat* [substitution] applies. Then *rapara* [substitution]. Finally, by *halādiśśeṣaḥ*, all other consonants are elided.

In that case, there is no further *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *v* during the process of repetition (*abhyāsa*), because the substitution of *u* (the *uratva*) for the letter *ñ* is considered a *samprasāraṇa* by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*,

and is thus prohibited by the rule "there is no *samprasāraṇa* in place of a *samprasāraṇa*" (*na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam*). However, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies here according to the preceding rule.
It is not possible—the sense being that the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* depends upon the original element (*sthānyal*) [which has been replaced].

From the preceding rule, the phrase "an *ādeśa* is like the *sthānin*" (*sthānivadādeśaḥ*) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here. The word *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") connects with the word *ādeśaḥ* ("substitute"), thus forming "the substitute of a vowel" (*aca ādeśaḥ*). The term *parasmim* ("when another follows") is in the locative case (*sati-saptamī*). And therefore:

The term *paranimittaka* (conditioned by what follows) is understood; and this is a qualifier of the substitute (*ādeśa*). Thus it says: "a substitute for a vowel (*aj*) conditioned by what follows. The word *vidhi* means that which is prescribed, i.e., an operation (*kārya*). A rule concerning what precedes is a *pūrvavidhi*. Although "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) is relative—since there are three [possibilities: preceding, following, or simultaneous]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]

And here, there are three factors: the original element (*sthānin*), the substitute (*ādeśa*), and the external cause (*paranimitta*). Among these, the original element cannot serve as the limit (*avadhi*), because it is removed by the substitute. Nor can the substitute serve as the limit, nor can the external cause, as in the case of the word *vaiyākaraṇa*.

Because, when the substitution of *āy* for *ai* (by the rule *na yvābhyām*) is to be applied following the vowel *ā*— which itself follows the cause for the substitution of *yaṇ* in place of *ik*— the *yaṇ* substitute would, by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, incur the property of being a vowel (*actva*). Nevertheless, in this context, "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) is determined solely in relation to the original element (*sthānin*).

This is intended [to mean]: even though the original element (*sthānin*) has been replaced by a substitute (*ādeśa*), its status as preceding [the vowel] is possible by way of its former existence. This is what he says:

"by virtue of being prior to the vowel that constitutes the original element," and so forth. In this context, whatever occurs when the original element is present also occurs when it is replaced by the substitute.

It occurs; and since that which does not occur [in the original rule] does not occur even when there is an extension (*atideśa*), thus there is an extension of the absence of an operation even for that which is non-grammatical (*aśāstrīya*). Regarding this, the first case has already been illustrated by *vavraśca*, because in that instance the operation of prohibition—namely, "there is no *samprasāraṇa* when there is a *samprasāraṇa*"—is itself grammatical (*śāstrīya*).

In the second [example], however, "gaṇayati" is cited as an illustration. The root *gaṇ* meaning "to count" belongs to the curādigaṇa (the tenth class) and ends in the letter *a*. From that [root], the suffix *ṇic* is added. By the rule *ato lopaḥ*, the final *a* is elided. Then the suffixes *tip* and *śap* are added, and by the rule *ṇer guṇaḥ*, *guṇa* substitution occurs; this results in the replacement by *ay*. Thus, the form "gaṇayati" is established. Here, when *ṇic* follows, [the *guṇa* substitution applies] to that which has become the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel.

The rule "gakārādakārasya ṭhata upadhāyāḥ" does not apply, because by the present sūtra, the elision of 'a' (allopa) is treated as if it were the original element (sthānivadbhāva). Since 'a' remains as the substituendum (sthānin), the status of the preceding vowel as an *upadhā* (penultimate) is destroyed; consequently, the *upadhā*-vṛddhi cannot take effect.

Even though the absence of *vṛddhi* is not prescribed by the rules (*aśāstrīya*), [the rule for] *vṛddhi* applies because it is extended (*atideśa*) to the case of elision (*al-lopa*). Nor does the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-vṛddhi*) fail to apply here due to the loss of the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva-bhaṅga*) of the vowel *a* following the letter *g*;
for even though the absence of *vṛddhi* is not prescribed by the rules, [the rule for *vṛddhi*] is extended to the case of elision. Nor is there [an obstacle] here...

It should not be argued that the letter *a* [in *an*] is not "preceding" the letter *a* [in *āp*] because it is separated from the substitute letter *a* by the letter *ṇ*; for here, "precedence" applies generally to both cases—whether there is an intervening element or not—as is indicated by the prohibition regarding vowels in the subsequent sūtra. That point will become clear in that very place, so let this suffice. Thus.

Regarding the word *yaṇi*: by this sūtra, when the prohibition of doubling for the letter *dh* in the form *sudh-y* is to be applied, there arises the possibility of treating the *y*—which is the substitute for the vowel *ī*—as if it were the original (*sthānivat*).
It is for the purpose of prohibiting that [application] that this sūtra is commenced.

(52) [The term *sthānin*] is not designated by the word *pratyaya* in the rules concerning: (a) the end of a word (*padānta*), (b) doubling (*dvirvacana*), (c) the substitution of *vār* for *ya*, (d) elision (*lopa*), (e) accent (*svara*), (f) homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), (g) the nasal dot (*anusvāra*), (h) lengthening (*dīrgha*), (i) the substitution of the unaspirated voiced stops (*jaś*), and (j) the substitution of the unaspirated voiceless stops (*car*).
Pāṇini 1.1.58.

"Not [the substitution] at the end of a word, nor reduplication. The phrases "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) and "when something follows" (*parasmin*) are understood from the previous rules. The syntactic connection is: "A substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) caused by a subsequent element is not like the original. [The exceptions are: at the end of a word (*padānta*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), before *vare* (the suffix *vara*), elision of *ya* (*yalopa*), a vowel (*svara*), and a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*).

*Anusvāra*, *dīrgha*, *jaś*, and *car*: this is a *dvandva* compound. The term *teṣāṃ vidhayaḥ* means "the rules for them"; the genitive case is used here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). Consequently, it is understood that these apply when [the positions] at the end or beginning of a word (*padāntādiṣu*) are the objects of the rule.
By the word *vara*, the substitution of a vowel (*ajādeśaḥ*) occurring in place of a *vṛddhi* vowel (*vare*) is intended. The *dvandva* is an archaic (Vedic) formation.

And there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*). The word "vidhi" (rule/operation) is connected with each [term]—namely, "in a rule concerning the end of a word" (*padāntavidhau*), "in a rule concerning reduplication" (*dvirvacanavidhau*), and so forth. The "end of a word" (*padāntaḥ*) is the final constituent part (*caramāvayavaḥ*) of a word (*pada*).

"In the formulation of a rule concerning the end of a word" (*padāntasya vidhāne*) means in a formulation whose object is the end of a word (*padāntakarmake vidhāne*). [This refers to] when an operation (*kārya*) is to be applied to the final constituent part of a word.

And this applies until an operation such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) takes place; thus he says: "of the final [element] of a word," and so forth. However, it is not explained as "in an operation prescribed for the position of the end of a word," because if that were the case, forms such as *eṣo yan hasati* would remain unestablished. To explain: the analysis is *eṣaḥ yan*. [This refers to] the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *iṇ*.

In the case of the suffix *śatṛ* with the augment *śap*, when the *śap* is elided, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *i* occurs by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*. Here, the elision of the *su* (the nominative singular ending) by the rule *etattadoḥ* does not take place, because that rule is prescribed only when a consonant (*hal*) follows; and in this instance, since that elision is to be performed, the *y* which occupies the place of the *i* is not considered a vowel (*ac*) due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*. Nor...

The prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.58], "not at the end of a word" (*na padānte*), need not be raised as an objection; for that prohibition applies only to that which, when prescribed, becomes the final constituent part (*caramāvayava*) of a word. In this case, however, the elision of *su* (*sulopa*), which is what is being prescribed, does not constitute a constituent part of the word. This remains true even under the interpretation that the rule applies "to that which is prescribed in place of the final element of a word. For here—

The status of *yakāra* as a *sthānivadbhāva* would not be established, because the elision (*lopa*) occurs in place of a *sakāra* that is at the end of a word (*padānta*). In this case, when the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* is to be applied, *yakāra* does not behave as a *sthānin*, because the *ukāra* being prescribed constitutes a final element of the word (*padacaramāvayava*). Thus...

The phrase "and in the case of a rule regarding the end of a word" (*padāntavidhau*) provides an example for the scope of the *utva* (the substitution of *u*) in the rule *eṣo 'śvaḥ*, whereas it serves as a counter-example for the scope of the elision of *su* (*sulopa*). This is clear in the *Bhāṣya*. It is even more explicit in the *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota*. What [rules] are there that concern the end of a word?

The example beginning with *santi* will become clear immediately following in the root text. The example for *dvirvacane* (in the case of reduplication) is *sudhy-*. One might object: "Even if there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the letter *y* when reduplication is to be performed here, would there not still be the status of a substitute in the prohibition [of that reduplication]?"

It must be stated that, because the doubling [of a consonant] by the rule *anaci ca* is unconditional (*anaimitika*), the status of *yakāra* as a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original) is not required in its scope; therefore, since the prohibition of that [status] in that context would result in being purposeless, the term "doubling" (*dvirvacana*) here refers specifically to the prohibition of doubling by the rule *aci na*.
The intended meaning is that it is because [the suffix] is intended to be expressed. For example, as in *yāyāvara*:

from the root *yā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffix *varac* is added by the rule "after a root ending in *yaṅ*, [the suffix] *varac*. By the rule "doubling occurs after *san* and *yaṅ*," there is doubling. In the stage *yāyāya vara*, the vowel *a* of *yaṅ* is elided by the rule "elision of [the *a* of] *yaṅ*. Then, by the rule "elision of *v* and *y*," [the *y* is elided].

There is the elision of the letter *y*. Here, with reference to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādya*), when the elision of the *ā* [of *yā*] is to be performed by the rule "the elision of *at* before an *it*-marked suffix" (*ato lopa iṭi ca*), the elision of *al* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Regarding the elision of *y*: from the root *yā*, we derive *yātiḥ*. From the root *yā*, there is the *yaṅ* suffix; reduplication; the suffix *ktic*; and thus we have *yāyāya ti*.

When [the suffix] *stha* is present, there is elision by the rule *ato lopaḥ*. Then, there is elision of *y* by the rule *lopo vyor vali*. Because the elision of *a* is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *ā* is elided by *āto lopaḥ*. Then, there is elision of *y* by *lopo vyor vali*. Thus, the form *yāti* is established. In this case, when the elision of *y* is to be performed, the elision of *a* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Nor...

It should not be argued that in the case of *vāyvoh*, when the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is to be applied by the rule *lopo vyor vali*, there would be a prohibition of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) regarding the substitution of the vowel *u* for the consonant *v*; for the Vārttika provides an exhaustive enumeration stating that among the operations of vowel-substitution, lengthening, and elision of *y*, it is only the elision (*lopa*) that is not treated as "as if the original. And this is indeed the case here.
Because the letter *va* does not consist of an elision (*lopa*). Regarding the rule for vowel [accentuation], as in *cikīrṣakaḥ*:
from the desiderative base *cikīrṣa*, the suffix *ṇvul* is added; there is the substitution of *ak* (for the *u* of *ṇvul*); then, by *ato lopaḥ*, the *a* of the suffix *san* is elided.
Here, when the acute accent (*udātta*) is to be applied to the *ī* by the rule *vitī* (Pāṇini 6.1.197), the elision of the *a* (*allopaḥ*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.

Although there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule here— since the vowel *ī* is not immediately preceded by the *a* that serves as the substitute for the elided *ā*— nevertheless, by virtue of this very indicator (*jñāpaka*),
in the preceding sūtra, "preceded-ness" (*pūrvatva*) applies to both immediate and non-immediate [elements]. The purpose of this, however, is...

This has already been stated in the previous sūtra. Regarding the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), for example: *śiṇḍḍhi*. This is derived from the root *śiṣ* belonging to the Raudhādika class, in the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*). [The suffixes are: *sip*, *śnam*; thus: *śinaṣ* + *si*.

*hitvam* (doubling). *dhitvam* (the substitution of *dh*). *ṣṭuatvam* (the substitution of *ṣṭu*). For the *ṣ*, there is *jaśtva* (substitution of a voiced unaspirated stop), which is the letter *ḍ*. [The form becomes] *śinaḍḍhi*. By the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*, there is elision of the *a*. By the rule *naścāpadāntasya*, there is an *anusvāra*. By the rule *anusvārasya yayi*, its *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the following) is the letter *ṇ*. Thus, the form is *śiṇḍḍhi*. In this case, regarding the *parasavarṇa*:

In a case where an operation is to be performed, the elision (*allopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. However, in reality, this is not an example regarding rules concerning homogeneous vowels (*savarṇavidhi*). Here, the elision of the letter *m* in *śnam* is a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*).
That which occupies its place is precisely the letter *m* of *śnam*. Since that [elision] exists, there is no possibility at all for the nasalization (*anusvāra*) of the letter *n*.

Furthermore, since the *anusvāra* has never been observed to precede its original vowel (*sthānin*), when the *parasavarṇa* substitution is to be applied, the prohibition [of *sthānivadbhāva*] is unnecessary; for the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57) does not apply to the elision (*alopa*) in this case. As for what is stated in the *Tattvabodhinī* regarding the *anusvāra*:

It has been stated that since the letter *n*, which serves as the original element (*sthānin*), is perceived as preceding the letter *m* of the suffix *śnam*, the *anusvāra* that replaces it is also perceived as preceding it, because precedence is accepted even by way of the original element. This being the case, [in the derivation of] *titaumācaṣṭe*:

In the form *titāpayati*, the augment *puk* would not occur. [The derivation is as follows: the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*) or "he describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*). Due to the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, there is the elision of the final vowel (*u*) by the rule "of the suffix *ṭi*" (*ṭer iti lopah*). By the rule "vṛddhi for a vowel before a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (*aco ñṇiti*), the vowel following the *t* is replaced by its *vṛddhi* substitute, which is *ā*. Then the augment *puk* is added. From the form *titāpi*, the present tense suffix *laṭ* is applied.

*tip*, *śap*, *guṇa*, and the substitution of *ay*. Thus, the form is *titāpayati*. Here, when the augment *puk* is to be applied to the long *ā* obtained through the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), if the status of the elision of *u* were treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), there would be an intervention by that *u*.

In the *Siddhāntaratnākara*, it is argued that the augment *puk* would not apply because the suffix is not preceded by a *niṣṭhā* [ending]; for although the letter *u*—which is the original locus (*sthānin*) of the elision of the vowel *ā*—does not itself possess the property of being "preceded" [by a *niṣṭhā*], this property exists through the medium of its substitute (*sthānin*). This point is refuted in the commentary on the *Prakriyākaumudī* (the *Prakriyāpradīpa*).
In the *Śabdaratna*, it is explained that [the root] *pā* expresses "to go" (*ācaṣṭe*) as *pādayati*; from that, by the suffix *kvip*, we have *pāt*.

In examples such as *hasati* (he laughs), when the rule *jhayo haḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.62) is to apply to produce a homogeneous substitute for the preceding sound, this rule in the present sūtra is intended to prohibit the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) which would otherwise be obtained through the analysis of the fifth case compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*), according to the principle that "an operation applies to what follows what precedes."
The inclusion of the term *savarṇa* has been explained in detail. As an example in the rule for the substitution of *anusvāra*: *śiṃṣanti*.
From the root *śiṣ*, there is the suffix *jhi* in the present tense (*laṭ*). By the rule *jho'ntaḥ*, *jhi* is replaced by *anta*. By the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*, the *a* of *śnas* is elided.
Then, by the rule *naścāpadāntasya*, an *anusvāra* is substituted [for the *n*]. Thus we have *śiṃṣanti*. However, in this case, there is no substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*).

Because there is no *yay* substitution for the phoneme *ṣ*. Here, when an *anusvāra* is to be applied, the elision (*allopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. In this case, regarding the rule for long vowels (*dīrghavidhi*), as in *pratidīvnā*: when the lengthening of the vowel *i* following the letter *d* is to be applied by the rule *hali ca*, the elision (*allopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. Regarding the application of the *jaś* sounds...
For example: *sagdhiśca me*. [The root] *ad* in the sense of eating takes the suffix *ktin*. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the substitution of *ghasl* for *ad*.
By the rule *ghasibhasor hali ca*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule *jhalo jhali*, there is the elision of the suffix *s*.
By the rule *jhaṣas tathordho'dhaḥ*, the *t* is changed to *dh*. By the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, there is the change to the *jaś* sound.

The letter *ga* is the substitute for *gha*. *Sagdhiḥ* means "eating together"; [it is derived from] *samāna* + *gdhiḥ*. By the rule *samānasya chandasi*, there is the substitution of *saṃ* [for *samāna*]. Here, when the substitution of a *jaś*-sound is to be applied, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. As an example of the application of a *cari*-rule: *jakṣatuḥ*. [This is formed from] the root *ghas* with the suffix *atus* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). There is reduplication; then by the rule *halādiśśeṣaḥ*, [the *gh* is replaced by *j*], and by the rule *abhyāse*... [the *g* is replaced by *k*].
In *carca*, the substitution of *ja* occurs [by *coḥ kuḥ*]. By the rule *ṭhkuhoścuḥ*, the letter *j* is substituted.
By the rule *ṭhgamahana*...*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule *ṭhkhari ca*, the substitution of *c* (the *cartva*) results in the letter *k*.

By the rule *ṭhśāsivasī*..., the letter *ṣ* is substituted. Here, when the *cartva* operation is to be applied, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.

In the Bhāṣya, however, relying on the principle that "when a preceding rule is not established, [the subsequent] does not behave as the original (sthānivadbhāva)," the rules concerning doubling (dvirvacana), homogeneous vowels (savarṇa), lengthening (dīrgha), and the substitution of *jhaś* for *cara* have been rejected. Furthermore, following the rule "long [vowels are substituted] according to the teachers," there is the rule: "The *parasavarṇa* is substituted for *anusvāra* before a *yay* [consonant]," or [alternatively, it is optional].

The sequence of rules as accepted in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *halo yamāṃ yami* is the reading of five sūtras beginning with *padāntasya*, *ṭhkhari ca*, *vāvasāne*, *aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*, and [the rule under discussion]. In this way, there is no possibility of the application of *parasavarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound) in the form *śiṇḍḍhi*. Regarding *parasavarṇa*:
Since the *jaś*-substitution (of *ṣ* to *ḍ*) in the case of what ought to be done is considered *asiddha*, there is an absence of a following *yaṇ*;
therefore, in any case, "śiṇḍḍhi" cannot be cited as an example for the rule regarding homogeneous vowels (*savarṇavidhi*). Let this matter rest for now.

The phrase "iti sthāni" means that by this sūtra, when the prohibition of doubling (dvitvaniṣedha) is to be applied in the case of *sudh-y-*, there is a prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* status of the letter *y*. The sense is that, since the condition of being followed by a vowel (*acparakatva*) is thus absent, the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *anaci ca* does not apply; consequently, the doubling of the letter *h* is unimpeded. And so it is.
It remains as *sudh* by [Pāṇini 6.1.66].

(53) *Jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* [Pāṇini 8.4.53]: "In place of *jhal* sounds, *jaś* sounds occur before a *jhaś* sound. This is clear; that is, in place of *jhal* sounds, *jaś* sounds shall occur when a *jhaś* sound follows.
Thus, it has a clear meaning; the sense is that there is nothing further to be explained therein, because no other word follows. "Of the letter *dha*" means:
of the first *dha*. "The letter *da*" is used because of proximity in terms of place of articulation (*sthāna*).

(54) *Adarśanam lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.1.60. Regarding the form *sudhī*, he states the rule for the technical designation *lopa* in order to raise the possibility of the elision of the final *y* by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*: "Non-appearance is *lopa*."
Since this is an introduction to the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), "seeing" (*darśana*) here is intended to mean the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of words.

"Non-seeing" (*adarśana*) is the absence of seeing; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of absence. From the rule "that which is most similar [to the original] takes its place" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*), the term *sthāna* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. It has been stated that "place" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). This is according to the technical terminology of the science (*śāstra*).
The meaning is that when there is the occasion for hearing some sound, its non-hearing constitutes what is termed *lopa* (elision).
(55) *Saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23): [There is elision of a consonant cluster at the end of a word.]

He says this with the words "of that which is applicable" (*prasaktasya*). In that context, since the elision (*lopa*) consisting of non-hearing (*aśravaṇa*) has been prescribed, it follows by implication that there is no utterance even for the purpose of hearing. What [is meant by] "of that which is applicable"?
In cases such as *dadhi*, the elision consisting of the non-hearing of the suffix *kvip*—by resorting to the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)—[applies to] the short vowel.
"piti kṛti tug bhavati. [The suffix *kṛt*] followed by a *pit* [suffix] takes the augment *tuK*. "There is elision (*lopa*) of that which ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
This is governed by the heading "of a word" (*padasya*). The analysis of the compound is: "that of which a conjunct consonant is at the end. The syntactical connection is:
"there is elision of a word that ends in a conjunct consonant. And it is not the case that there is elision of the entire word.
However, by the paribhāṣā "alontyasya" (P. 1.1.52), it applies only to that which ends in [the specified element].
Thus he says: "ending in a conjunct consonant," and so forth. Here, the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) is for the sake of clarity alone;

for since the *saṃyoga* (conjunct) functions as a qualifier of the *pada*, the status of being "that which ends in" is obtained by the very rule "yena vidhis tadantasya" (P. 1.1.72). As for [the objection]...

The inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is for the sake of obtaining the analysis (*vigraha*) "that which has [two] conjuncts at its end. Otherwise, in the case of *sudṛṣat-prāsāda*, there would be the elision of the *t* preceding the *p*;
however, that is not so, because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) functions as a collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).

In the *Śabdaratna*, it is explained in detail that the description of the purpose for including the term "ādi" (and so forth) would be futile if one did not accept its individual application (*pratyekavṛttitva*).
Thus, regarding the rule "elision of *y*" (*yalopa*): when *sudh-ya* occurs, the elision of the letter *y* would [otherwise] apply by this very rule.

The prohibition of that [deletion] is now commenced. "A prohibition regarding *yaṇ* must be stated" means that a prohibition of the deletion of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) for a *yaṇ* sound must be formulated.
By this *vārttika*, the remainder is that the deletion of the final consonant cluster for the letter *y* does not occur. This *vārttika* is found in the original source (*ākara*).
[The objection] is rejected.

Now, since the *y* here is neither followed by a vowel (*ac*) nor preceded by a vowel, the doubling [of the consonant] prescribed by the rule *anaci ca* does not apply; therefore, he states the rule for doubling: "The *m* following a *yaṇ* should be doubled. By this [rule],...

The grammatical connection is that there is doubling of the letter *y* by means of the *vārttika*. Now, one might object: if *yaṇaḥ* is in the ablative case and *mayaḥ* is in the genitive case, then it would follow that there is doubling of a *m* or *y* that follows a *yaṇ*. However, in the present instance, the letter *y* is neither followed by a *yaṇ*, nor is it itself a *m* or *y*. Therefore, how can this *vārttika* apply to it?

To address the question of duality [of interpretation], he says: "by the word *maya*. By the phrase "in one alternative" (*pakṣe*), it is indicated that both types of explanation are intended; the sense is that there is no decisive reason (vinigamanā) to prefer one over the other.
Here too, in the Vārttika, the term "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule "a nasal may optionally follow a semi-vowel" (*yaro'nunāsika*) is understood to carry over.
And then he states the result: "Therefore, here... [The word] "tat" (that) is to be supplied.
The meaning is that by this much of the composition which has been elaborated, four forms are produced in the word *iyatsudhi* due to the optional doubling of the letters *y* and *dh*.

"Ekadham ekayam": that which has one *dhakāra* is "ekadham"; likewise for "ekayam. The meaning is that when there is no doubling (*dvitva*) of either the *dhakāra* or the *yakāra*, the first form consists of a single *dhakāra* and a single *yakāra*. "Dvidham dviyam": that which has two *dhakāras* is "dvidham."

The same applies to the pair [of *dha* and *ya*]. When both the letter *dha* and the letter *ya* are doubled, the second form consists of two *ya*s and two *dha*s; this is the meaning. Regarding "two *dha*s and one *ya*" (*dvidhamekayam*): when the letter *dha* is doubled but the letter *ya* is not doubled, the third form consists of two *dha*s and one *ya*; this is the meaning.

"Ekadhaṃ dviyam": this means that when there is no doubling of the letter *dh*, but there is doubling of the letter *y*, it is the fourth form, namely "ekadhaṃ dviyam. Regarding "suddhyupāsya," the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule "na bhūsudhiyoḥ" does not apply here, because that rule applies only before a *sup* suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*).
Because of the specific rule [Pāṇini 6.1.102]. Nor does [the rule] *iko yaṇ aci* apply, because that is prohibited by the rule *na samāse*.

As for *maddhv-ari*: Madhu is the name of a particular demon; his enemy (*ari*) is *maddhv-ari*. The meaning is "Hari. Here, [the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs] in place of the vowel *u* following the letter *dh*.

The letter *va* [is the substitute] either by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*) or by the technical rule of "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhyaparibhāṣā*). Nor should it be argued that there is no similarity of place (*sthānasāmya*) here because the letter *va* possesses an additional dental place of articulation; for even though the requirement for homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) consists in a complete identity of places of articulation, in the case of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), even a partial similarity of place is sufficient.

Because it is the cause [of the doubling]. Otherwise, in cases such as *cetā stota*, there would be no occurrence of the single substitute *e* for *i* and *a*. Regarding the term *dhātraṃśa*: it will be stated immediately below in the rule *aco rahābhyām* that here the doubling applies to the letter *t* alone, and not to the letter *r*. [The example is] *lākṛtiḥ*.

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose form (*ākṛti*) is like the form of the vowel *ḷ*. Here, when the vowel *ā* follows, the letter *l* replaces the vowel *ḷ* because of the commonality of their dental place of articulation (*sthāna*). Nor should it be argued that, due to this common dental place of articulation—and because there is no reason to bypass the first [corresponding letter]—the letter *v* alone should replace it.

It should not be argued that "some degree of similarity of position" (*sthānasāmya*) serves as the determining factor for proximity, because this was already stated in the commentary on *madhvariḥ*. For here, four *yaṇ* sounds—*ya*, *va*, *ra*, and *la*—are to be prescribed; among these, the prescription of *va* applies to the vowel *ū*.

Because of the similarity in their place of articulation—the lips—it would follow that [the substitute] *la* is without a rival and has scope there; however, since *la* is not applicable because its place of articulation is different, being the teeth, in the case of the form *lākṛtiḥ*, both *va* and *la* would be applicable to the vowel *ḷ*. In this matter, one must rely on the rule of "subsequent application" (*paravipratiṣedha*) regarding words.

The rule for *l* (the substitution of *l* for *ṛ*) prevails over the rule for *v* because it is both subsequent and an exception (*apavāda*). For if, due to the absence of a reason for skipping the first [rule], *v* were to occur here as well, then the rule for *l* would be entirely without scope (*niravakāśa*). Therefore, in this case, the *ṛ*-vowel is replaced by *l*.
Let this matter rest for now. (56) *nādiny-ākrośe putrasya* | Pāṇini 8.4.48.
[The sūtra reads: *nādiny-ākrośe*. The terms *dve* and *yara* are understood by anuvṛtti from the previous rules. *Ākrośaḥ* means censure or reproach.

The word *ādinī* is a form ending in *ṅī* (feminine suffix) with the locative case elided. The meaning is that when the word *ādinī* follows, there is no doubling of the *yaT*—that is, the letter *t*—which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *putra*, provided that an insult (*ākrośa*) is implied.
This is what [the author] expresses by the words "of the word *putra*" and so forth; the meaning is "of a constituent part of the word *putra*."
"O wicked woman, you are a devourer of sons!"—the term *putrādinī* means one whose nature (*śīla*) is to eat sons.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule *supy ajātau*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*. "O wicked one (*pāpe*), you are a devourer of sons"—this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). The meaning is "you are a killer of sons. Such an insult is generally...

Haradatta maintains that because [the word] occurs only in the feminine, the form *ādinī* in the Sūtra is intended to be in the *ṅīp* (feminine) suffix. Mādhava also holds this view. In this case, the doubling of the letter *t* following the vowel *u*—which would otherwise be required by the rule *anaci ca*—is prohibited; however, for the letter *r*, there is no such doubling anywhere.

The consequence of [the rule] resulting in two [separate operations] will be stated immediately below. Regarding the question "What is the purpose of [the mention of] *ākrośe* (in the case of abuse)?":

the meaning is, "What is the utility of this term *ākrośe*? Amara states in his list of indeclinables: "*kiṃ* [is used] in the sense of inquiry and in the sense of loathing. This should be understood in the same way for similar cases that follow.

Regarding the phrase "in the statement of the actual fact": when one speaks of the actual state of affairs—that a woman whose sons die of their own accord is called *putrādinī* (one who devours her sons)—there is no prohibition of the dual number, because in that case no censure (*nindā*) is perceived. And [the rule applies] when it follows that; this is a Vārttika. That word *ādinī* follows [the noun].

Because he is intent on that: the meaning is that when the word *putra* follows [the word *putra*] and the word *ādinī* follows [the word *putra*], there is no doubling of the *yar* (consonant) which is a constituent of the word *putra*.
