It does not occur when followed by another [word], because of the intervention of the word *putra* as a second member. Therefore, this rule is commenced because the prohibition of doubling was not obtained by the preceding sūtra. *Vā hatajagdhayoḥ*:
when the words *hata* or *jagdha* follow, there is optionally doubling of the *yar* (consonant) belonging to the word *putra*.

The meaning is "it may be. Regarding the form *putrahatī*: it is derived by doubling the letter *t*. The analysis of the compound is "she by whom a son has been killed" (*putro hato yayā*). Some maintain that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *ṭh-svāṅga-pūrva-padāt*.

However, in reality, because the phrase *jāti-pūrvāt* (from a word preceded by a genus-term) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) there, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied on account of [the word] belonging to the *gaurādi* group.

This is correct. Since the crime of murdering one's son occurs only among women, the feminine gender alone has been cited as the example: *putraghātī*. This is the form when there is no doubling (*dvitva*).
Likewise, *putrajagdhī* and *putrajagdhī* [are formed]. Since the doubling is already established by the rule *anaci ca*, [the present rule serves to restrict it].

They say that this Vārttika is for the purpose of restricting the application of the word *putra* when ending in a *kta*-suffix, such that it occurs only with *hata* and *jagdha*, and only in the sense of abuse (*ākrośa*).
(57) *Triprabhṛtiṣu śākaṭāyanasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.50).

According to Śākaṭāyana, when three or more consonants (*hal*) are conjunct, there is optional doubling (*dvitva*) of the *yar* (semivowels and spirants) following the first vowel, according to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana; however, in other opinions, this does not occur. Thus, in the word *indra*, there is an option for the doubling of the letter *n*; and in the word *rāṣṭram*, [there is an option] for the doubling of the letter *ṣ*.
The option regarding doubling:

(58) *sarvatra śākalyasya* | Pāṇini 8.4.61. "In all cases, according to Śākalya. The term *ne* is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule]. Wherever doubling has been prescribed, in those instances—

In that regard, according to the opinion of the sage Śākalya, there is no doubling [of a consonant]; this is the meaning. Regarding the rule *dīrghād ācāryāṇām*: the term *ṭhne* is understood to follow.

According to the opinion of certain teachers, there is no doubling of a *yar* (consonant) following a long vowel; however, according to other opinions, it does occur. [This applies] when a non-vowel (*anaci*) follows.
In this regard, Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary on the sūtra *nājjhalau* that the word "or" (*vā*) from the preceding rule is understood here. Thus,

since the optionality of doubling is established by the rule *anaci ca* alone, it is concluded in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* that the three subsequent sūtras beginning with *triprabhṛtiṣu* need not have been composed.
Due to the contradiction with these three sūtras, it appears reasonable that the mention of *vā* ("optionally") should not be carried over (*anuvartate*) to the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47).
(59) *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (Pāṇini 8.4.46): [A consonant] following *ra* or *ha* is doubled after a vowel.

"Two [are substituted] after *a* and *ra-ha*. From the rule *yaro 'nunāsike*, the term *yaraḥ* (in the genitive case) and *vā* (the word "optionally") are understood to carry over. The term *acaḥ* is in the ablative case used in connection with direction (*digyoge*). The phrase "after those following" (*parābhyām*) is the ellipsis.
The term *rahābhyām* is also in the ablative case; the phrase "of what follows" (*parasya*) is the ellipsis. Thus he says: "after a vowel... (*acaḥ*).
By the rule beginning with *parābhyām* and so forth: "haryanubhavaḥ" (the experience of Hari). The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is "hareḥ anubhavaḥ" (the experience of Hari).

When "hari-anubhavaḥ" is established, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs for the vowel *i* following the letter *r*. That [substitution] is then doubled. Next, he provides an example following the letter *h*: "nahyasti" (for it does not exist). When "naha—asti" is established...

The *yaṇ* [substitution] of the vowel *i* following the letter *ha* occurs; that [substituted *y*] undergoes doubling (*dvitvam*). Here, in both cases, doubling—which would otherwise not apply because the *y* is neither preceded by a vowel nor followed by a vowel—is prescribed. In this context, doubling does not occur for the letters *ra* and *ha* by virtue of the rule *anaci ca*. This is because, within the section on doubling, there is the rule *rahābhyām*.

Because the status of being a cause is directly heard (*śruta*) for the letter *repha* and the letter *ha*, this subverts their participation in the grammatical operation (*kārya*) indicated by the word *yar*. This is according to the maxim: "Between that which is directly heard and that which is inferred, the directly heard is stronger. Thus, there is the experience of *har-y-ya* and not *nah-y-ya*.
When [the preceding rule] has been established: (60) *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* | P.
8.4.64. He states the rule for the elision of the first *y* in both cases: *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*.

The term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is carried over from the rule *ṭhjhayo ho'nyatarasyām*. This is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that functions as a substitute for case endings and signifies the sense of "or. The plural number in *yamām* refers to the multiplicity of usages; for in each individual usage, there may be many [consonants].

Because of the impossibility of [the elision of] *yam*. In the rule *hal*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of direction (*digyoga*). The word "of what follows" (*parasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

Thus he says: "of a *yama* following a *hal*, etc. By this sūtra, when the first *yakāra* is elided in both examples, they result in a form consisting of a single *yakāra*. In the alternative case where there is no elision:

[The form] becomes one consisting of two *y* sounds. Now, it might be argued that the rule *ṭh-alo yamām* need not have been formulated for this purpose; for since the doubling of *y* by the rule *aco rahābhyām* is optional, there would be a form with two *y*s when doubling occurs, and a form with one *y* when doubling does not occur.
Anticipating the objection that [the rule] is already established, he states that this sūtra has no purpose here: "iti lopa" (in the case of elision).
Then, he asks what the fruit of this sūtra is and replies: "lopārambha" (the initiation of the elision).
[This refers to the rule: "dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ" (after *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, and words ending with these as the final members of a compound, the suffix *ṇya* is applied).

Thus, from the word *āditya*, which ends in the suffix *ṇya* with the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of a deity (*devatā*). When the form *āditya-ya* is established, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the vowel *a* following the letter *y* is elided; then, by this present rule, the letter *y* following the letter *t* is elided. Only when that [second *y*] has been elided is the form *ādityam*, containing a single *y*, established.

Not otherwise. Therefore, the intention is that the commencement of the Sūtra is not fruitless. Here, the elision [of the final *a*] by the rule "ṭhāpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti" does not apply, because since it has the sense of "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth, it lacks the status of being a descendant (*apatya*).
The intention here is that this particular Sūtra has been cited because it is more appropriate [in this context]. But even so—

In the sense of "the state of a great-souled one" (*mahātman*), when the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied according to the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*, and with the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) and the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening, one obtains *māhātmyam*. In this case as well, there would be the elision of the letter *m* after the letter *t*, because that [letter *t*] is a *yam* sound and because it is followed by a *yam* sound in the form of *y*. To address this, he says: "of the *yam*s."

"From the *yathāsaṃkhya* rule": that by which something is known is "knowledge" (*vijñāna*), according to the *sūtra*. Amarasimha states: "Knowledge [is used] in the sense of craft and science. Thus, the meaning is: from the *yathāsaṃkhya* rule;
and so, since the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *m* is obtained only when another *m* follows, there is no elision when the letter *y* follows.

(61) *eco'yavāyāvaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.78. The analysis of the compound is: *ay* and *av*, *āy* and *āv*. From the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the term *aci* is carried over by anuvṛtti. According to the paribhāṣā on "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhyaparibhāṣā*), *ekāra* is replaced by *ay*.

It is understood that *okāra* becomes *av*, *aikāra* becomes *āy*, and *āṬkāra* becomes *āv*. Thus it is said: "of the *ec* vowels, in order. However, according to the method of the Bhāṣya on the rule regarding "correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya*), the determination here should be understood through the *paribhāṣā* concerning "the most similar" (*antaratama*) alone. Here, [the rule] "before a vowel" (*ico'ci*)...
It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as *yaṇaya-vāyāvaḥ*.
(62) *tasya lopaḥ* | 1.3.9 | When these substitutions [are applied], the *yakāra* and *vakāra* [of the original] receive the designation *it* by the rule *halantyam*.
He states the apprehension regarding elision (*lopa*): "There is elision of that. This sūtra occurs at the end of the section on the technical designation *it*.
In that context, the word *tat* refers back to the immediately preceding *it*. Thus he says: "of that" (*tasya*).
The meaning is that by this sūtra, one should not suspect the elision of *y* and *v*. Why? [From here follows the reason.]

He says: "Regarding the mention [of *ya* and *va*]. The sense is that if there were elision (*lopa*) of *ya* and *va* here, then they would not have been mentioned at all in the Sūtra, according to the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. If that is so, then what is the purpose of assigning the technical designation *it* to these two? To this he replies:

He says: "And thus. The meaning is that when there is no elision (*lopa*) in the manner described, the designation *it* also does not apply here to the letter *ya* or the letter *va*, because there is no result [for such a designation]. He provides examples in sequence, beginning with "haraya" and so forth.
When the forms "hare-e," "viṣṇo-e," "nai-akaḥ," and "pau-akaḥ" have been established:
The vowels *ay* and so forth [are substituted] for *e* and so forth, respectively.
(63) *vānto yi pratyaye* | 6|1|79|. "In the suffix *yi*" (*yi*): this is in the locative case. By this, it means "when [the suffix] begins with *y*."
It is obtained from the Vārttika: "When there is a mention of 'a' [in a rule], that which has the rule applies to what begins with that.

In this context, *yasmin* (in which) is intended as being in the locative case (*saptamyanta*). *Al* is a synonym for *varṇa* (phoneme). The meaning is: when a phoneme is mentioned in the locative case, whatever rule is prescribed should be understood to apply to that phoneme at its beginning. By...
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule (*vidhi*). That which has "va" at its end is called *vānta*.

The substitution of *ava* and *āva*, introduced by the previous sūtra, is intended here. When there is an expectancy as to for which [sounds] these two substitutions occur, the meaning "of *o* and *au*" is obtained by implication, since those two alone were mentioned in the previous sūtra.
Because both [the *au* of *gaurī* and the *a* of *ava-*] are established as substituends (*sthānin*), he says this with the words "in the case of *yakāra* and so forth.

Regarding the form *gavyam*: when *go-ya* is situated, since the vowel *o* is not followed by another vowel (*ac*), the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* does not apply; therefore, the substitution of *ava* occurs here.
It is prescribed. And since there is the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*) for *yu* here, he says: "In the case of *go* and *payas*, *yat*" (*gopayasoryat*).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "by this rule, the affix *yat* is applied after the word *go* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). [The example is] *nāvyam*; [it is derived from] *nau-ya*.

Since the vowel *au* is not followed by a vowel (*ac*) when [the suffix] *yat* is present, the rule *eco'yavāyāvaḥ* does not apply; therefore, the substitution of *ava* is prescribed here. Furthermore, since *yat* possesses the status of a suffix (*pratyayatva*) in this instance, he says: "by the rule *gopayasoryat*" (Pāṇini 4.3.160). By this sūtra—

The remainder [of the rule] is: "from the word *go*, the suffix *yat* is added in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). Regarding the form *nāvyam*: when *nau-ya* is established, since the vowel *au* is not followed by a vowel (*ac*), the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* does not apply; therefore, this statement is made. Furthermore, he states that *ya* here indeed possesses the status of a suffix: "*nauvaya*."

In the cases of *gavyam* and *nāvyam*, the elision of the letter *v*— prescribed by the rules *lopaḥ śākalyasya* and *hali sarveṣām*— does not occur; for those two rules apply specifically to word-final positions (*padānta*), whereas here, the status of being a *bha*-stem subverts the status of being a word (*pada*).

An addition [to the rule] should be made regarding the word *yūti* in the Veda (*chandas*). The author of the Sūtra is instructed that an additional statement must be formulated: "In the Veda, when the word *yūti* follows, the substitute *vānta* (i.e., *au*) optionally takes the place of the vowel *o* which is a constituent part of the word *go*, provided it is followed by a vowel. [Example: *ṭhā no*.
"O Mitra and Varuṇa, sprinkle the pasture with clarified butter"—this is the illustrative example.

*Gavyūti* means "the land for cattle to roam. According to the Vedic commentary (*Vedabhāṣya*), it is derived from the root *yu* (to mix) with the suffix *ktin* in the locative sense, meaning "that in which cows are mixed or gathered."
Bhaṭṭabhāskara: Here, because the word *yūti* is not an affix (*pratyaya*), the rule "before an affix beginning with *y* that ends in *v*" does not apply; therefore, this statement [is made].
And even when a specific measure of distance—that is, a particular measurement of a path—is to be understood, [the substitution occurs] when the word *yūti* follows.

The meaning is that an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made [to the rule] for the substitution of *vānta* (*au*) for the vowel *o*, which is a constituent of the word *go*, when followed by *avi*. This is also for the sake of obtaining the correct form in common usage (*loka*). Although the previous Vārttika should have been introduced only in the context of Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*), [it is included here].
Nevertheless, it is introduced here for the sake of facilitating the understanding of its recurrence. Regarding "gavyūti":
the distance over which the word *go* (cow) is uttered, perceived, or heard is a *gavyūti*, which is two *krośas*. Amara states: "A *gavyūti* is feminine and equals two *krośas*."

The suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *yudh* in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). To the question, "How is there lengthening of the vowel in the root *yudh* here?", he says: "*ūti-yūti-..."*. The intention is that the lengthening occurs precisely by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). An irregular derivation (*nipātana*) is the mention of a form whose grammatical formation has already been established. [Objection: But in cases such as *gavyam* and *nāvyam*, because they possess the status of a *bha*-stem...

Due to the sublation of its status as a *pada* by the rule "the elision [of *y*] according to Śākalya" (*lopaḥ śākalyasya*), and because of the absence of elision by the rule "before a consonant for all [grammarians]" (*hali sarveṣām*), there would still be an elision in the word *gavyūti*; this is because, by relying on the intervening case-ending, it retains the status of a *pada*, and since the word *yūti* lacks the suffixes beginning with *yaj* or those beginning with *su*.
Because there is no existence [of the vowel] subsequent to that [consonant], he says:

"In the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*," and so forth. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*, a *v* is elided (*praśliṣyate*) before the *v* [in *vāntaḥ*], and in the rule *goryūtāvupasaṃkhyānam*, a *v* is elided before the *cch*. If that is so, then [the form is] *v-vāntaḥ*, i.e., *v*.

To the question, "Why is the letter *v* not heard [in the word *chandasi*]?", he says: "by the elision (*lopa*) according to the rule *lopo vyor vali*. The word "concealed" (*antarhita*) is the remainder [of the thought]. Now, one might ask: "What follows from this *praśleṣa* (the doubling of the vowel)? To this he says: "by that," [referring to] the letter *v* in the sūtra *vānte yi*.

In the previous rule (*prāg-viti*), that which is being compounded is a qualifier of "ending in *va*" (*v-anta*). Because it is a qualifier, when the rule of "application to what ends in that" (*tad-anta-vidhi*) applies, the meaning "ending in *v*" is obtained. In that context, by the force of stating again that the substitute "ends in *va*," it is understood that the substitute ending in *v* must contain a *v* that is being elided (*lupyamāna*).

The word "syāt" (it may be) is obtained. In the rule *goryūtau*, this very mention of *vānta* (the substitute *au*) is understood to carry over; thus, there too it is understood that the substitute *vānta* must contain the audible letter *v*.
Furthermore, in the rule *goryūtau*, even though [the word] is elided (*praśliṣyamāṇa*) before the letter *c*, it is still understood.

The meaning is that since the term *vānta* (ending in *va* or *au*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra as a qualifier, the status of being "ending in *va* or *au*" is obtained through the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application to what ends with that); however, by the force of stating again that [the substitute] is "consisting of *va* or *au*" (*vān*), it is understood that the substitute itself must consist of *va* or *au*.

Now, one might object: "Even if the statement that the vowel *v* is heard in the form *gavyūtiḥ* after the substitution of *ava*, the suspicion regarding its elision (*lopa*) has not yet been dispelled. To this, he says: "The meaning of 'the vowel *v* is not elided' is equivalent to saying 'the vowel *v* is heard. Thus, the mention of the vowel *v* being heard serves to convey the sense that the vowel *v* is not elided.

The meaning is that it has reached its conclusion; the point is that the word *lopa* (elision) signifies precisely the non-hearing [of a sound]. Although, in the rule *vānto yi* (Pāṇini 6.1.79), the inclusion of the letter *v* [as *v-v-anta*] serves no purpose in its examples such as *gavyam* and *nāvyam*, because in those cases, due to their status as *bha*-pratyayas, they do not possess the status of a *pada*.

Because the previously mentioned elision (*lopa*) does not apply due to [the subsequent rule] *bādha*. In cases such as *lavyam*, the elision does not apply because there is no status as a word (*padatva*) by its very nature. Even in the case of *gavyati*—derived from *gām icchati* with the *kyac* suffix—there is no possibility of the elision of the *vakāra*, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "not before *kyac*" (*na kye*).

Because it lacks the status of being a *pada*. Nevertheless, there is indeed a purpose for its recurrence in the Vārttika "goryūtau," namely in the case of *gavyūti*. And thus, it is not appropriate to include that [anusvāra] within the Vārttika itself. It is precisely because of this lack of conviction (*asvarasa*) that it was stated "or from the letter ś. In reality, however, it is the letter *va*...

The elision (*praśleṣa*) is untenable; for if that were the case, it would follow that the elided element would be heard in both the *sūtra* and the *vārttika*. Nor can it be argued that it is not heard because of the elision by the rule "ṭhlopo vyoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.66), since the mention of the letter *va* [in the rule] is not for the sake of providing an example for the elision of *va*.

This is because it would contradict the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *lopo vyor vali*, which states that [the elision] must be performed. Therefore, in this case, the elision of the coalesced *v* must be described as being purely Vedic (*chāndasa*). However, in the *Prakriyāprakāśa*, it is stated that because of the rule "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory" (*saṃjñāpūrvako vidhir anityaḥ*), there is no [elision] in the word *avyūti*.

It has been stated that there is the elision of the letter *va*. Others, however, say that based on the authority of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, where it says "the *va* is indicated as elided in the case of *ato lāntasya*," there is sometimes an elision of the letter *va*.

(64) *Dhātoḥ tannimittasyaiva* || 6.1.80 || Now, one might raise the objection that in forms such as *oyate* and *āuyate*, the substitution of *vānta* (i.e., *au*) for the *okāra* and *āūkāra* would apply by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* [6.1.79]. Anticipating this doubt, the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*...

It restricts [the substitution] to that which has that very [suffix] as its cause: namely, the *ec* vowels. The terms *ecaḥ* and *vānto yi pratyaye* are carried over [from previous rules]. That suffix beginning with *ya* is its cause; thus, it is "that which has that as its cause.
When a suffix beginning with *ya* follows, the substitution of *vānta* (the sounds *au*, *ai*, and *auk*) for the *ec* vowels of the root occurs.
The meaning is that the *ec* vowels [are substituted] only when there is an affix beginning with *ya*, and not otherwise.

He states this with the words "when the affix begins with *ya*" (*yādau pratyaye*), and so forth. Regarding the form *lavyam*: from the root *lūñ* (to cut), the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat*.
By the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, the *ū* vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution, becoming *o*. Of that...
The substitution of *vānt* (i.e., *au*) occurs because it is a constituent part of a verbal root (*dhātu*) and because it is not caused by suffixes such as *ya* and others.

Regarding the form *avaśyalāvyam*: the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *lū* by the rule *ṭhorāvaśyake*; the vowel *ū* is replaced by the vṛddhi vowel *au* according to the rule *aco ñṇiti*; and *avaśyam* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. The elision of *m* occurs by the rule *ṭhlumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye*. Here, because the vowel *au* is a constituent part of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and is caused by a suffix beginning with *y*, the substitution of *vānta* (i.e., *au* for *av*) takes place. Now, one might object: in cases such as *lavyam* and *avaśyalāvyam*, the substitution of *vānta* is already established by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* alone.
Therefore, the established position is that this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction, namely, that [the suffix] occurs only when that [specific condition] is the cause.
He asks what the purpose of this restrictive rule is: "Why 'only when that is the cause'? The meaning is:
what is the purpose of the restriction? It is said: *oyate*—from the root *veñ*, meaning "to weave" (*tantusantāne*).
The *laṭ* suffix is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). The *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *bāvakarmaṇoḥ*. The *yak* affix is added.

By the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnām*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *v* following [the root], resulting in the vowel *u*; this undergoes *pūrvarūpa* (merger with the preceding vowel).
By the rule *ṭhakkṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, the *u* is lengthened. [Finally,] there is the merging of the *u* with the prefix *āṅ*.

By the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitute is *o*. Although this *o* is a constituent of the verbal root (*dhātu*) by virtue of its status as the initial element of the subsequent item (*parādivadbhāva*), the substitution of *vānta* (i.e., *au*) does not occur, because it is not caused by an affix beginning with *ya*.
Now, one might object that according to the perspective of the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra concerning the elision of a verbal root (*na dhātulopa-*), the *guṇa* in *ādguṇaḥ*...

Because the *o*-sound depends on two words (*padadvayāpekṣatva*), it is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*); thus, when the substitution of *vānta* (the *au* sound) is to be applied, the *o*-sound is non-existent due to its being treated as unestablished (*asiddhatva*), and consequently, there is no possibility for the substitution of *vānta*.
Stating this because of such an underlying lack of conviction, he says: "*āṬyateti*. [This refers to the rule] that from the root *vaiñ* alone, in the sense of the object (*karmani*).

*Tat* [is the root]. The *ātmanepada* endings and so forth are as before. By the rule *āḍajādīnām*, the augment *āṭ* is added. By the rule *āṭaśca*, there is *vṛddhi*, resulting in the vowel *au*. Although this [augment] is a constituent part of the verbal root by virtue of its status as a subsequent element (*parādivadbhāva*), because it is not caused by an affix beginning with *ya* (such as *yat*), the substitution of *vānta* does not apply. Not here...

The substitution of *vṛddhi* is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it does not depend upon two words. Since the establishment of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) is achieved by the maxim "the formulation [of a rule] when something is already established serves for restriction," the particle *eva* in the phrase "only that which is caused by it" is intended to exclude the possibility of a contrary restriction.

For, in the absence of the particle *eva*, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) would also be understood as: "If a substitute ending in *vānt* (i.e., *au* or *av*) is prescribed for an *eC* vowel conditioned by an affix beginning with *ṭh* and so forth, then it must be an *eC* vowel belonging specifically to a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, in the word *bābhravya*, the substitution of *vānt* would not occur; [yet it is required], since *bābhravyaḥ* means "the descendant of Babhru."

By the rule *madhubarbhvor brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied. By the rule *orguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitute for the vowel *ū* is *o*. Since this [substitute] is caused by the suffix beginning with *y* (*yañ*) and does not constitute a part of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution of *va* for *vānta* (the final *au* sound) would not occur. Therefore, [this sūtra] is intended to establish the desired result.
The particle *eva* [in the rule] serves to restrict [the application] to that very cause.
(65) *Kṣayya* and *jayya* [are used] in the sense of "possible. Pāṇini 6.1.81 states: *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe*. The words *kṣayya* and *jayya* function as denotators in the sense of "possible."
This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: "Is there not some specific action to be enjoined here that is not perceived?

To this he says: *yānteti*. *Nipātana* is the mention of a word-form whose grammatical derivation is already established, even without a specific individual injunction (*prātisvikavidhi*). Consequently, when a suffix beginning with *y*—such as *kṣi*, which has the sense of "possible" (*śakya*)—follows, [the rule applies].

The rule here bears fruit as follows: for the verbal roots *kṣi* (to perish) and *ji* (to conquer), the replacement *yā* should occur in place of the vowel *e*. The intention is that this is a specific irregular derivation (*nipātana*), because the individual rules stating "for *kṣi* and *ji*, *yā* [is substituted] in the sense of possibility" would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, we have *kṣayyam*. This occurs under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "kṛtya suffixes."

From the verbal root *kṣi*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat*. This suffix has the sense of "possibility" (*śakya*) according to the rule *ṭhśaki liṅ ca*. The meaning of that rule is that the optative (*liṅ*) may be used in the sense of possibility, as well as the gerundive suffixes (*kṛtya*).
By the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, the *ik* vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution, resulting in the vowel *e*.
Since there is no following of *añ* or *ac*, the substitution of *ay* (for *e*) does not apply; therefore, it is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) here.
*Jayyam* is also explained in the same manner as before. Regarding the question "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'in the sense of possibility' (*śakyārthe*)?":
this is the question asking what the function of the phrase "in the sense of possibility" is. Regarding "to be sown" (*kṣetum*), etc.: that which is fit to be sown is *kṣeyam* (the sin).

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "the mind (*manaḥ*) is that which is fit to be conquered (*jetum yogyam*)," i.e., that which is to be conquered (*jeyam*). The suffix *yat* is applied here by the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* ("the kṛtya suffixes and *tṛc* are used in the sense of fitness"). However, since that [suffix] does not have the meaning of "capability" (*śakya*), there is no substitution of *ya* for the final vowel [of the root] in this case; such is the meaning. (66) *krayyaḥ tadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.1.82).

The word *krayya* is for that purpose. This [sūtra] is also for the sake of prescribing the substitution of *y* [for the final letter]. He explains the term *tadartha*—namely, "for that"—as follows: in the word *krayya*, that which is the root *krīñ*, which serves as the base for the suffix *yat*, its meaning is the signified object.

Purchase (*kraya*) consists in the exchange of substances; that is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), and it is what is intended by the word "that" (*tat*). "For that" (*tadartham*) means for the purpose of that [purchase]; thus, the result is that when a thing intended for purchase is to be understood, the suffix *yat* follows the root *krī*. Therefore, [the rule] "after *krī*, the suffix *yat* is added when it is for the purpose of that" is established.

Thus, due to the gravity of the rule, the formation [of the word] by means of nipātana (irregular derivation) has been resorted to. Furthermore, he states—beginning with "buyers" and ending with "what is to be bought"—that what is intended here as the purpose of buying is that which actually brings about the result.

The point is that if one were to take the mere sense of fitness [as the purpose], then the phrase "for that purpose" (*tadarthe*) would fail to serve as a differentiator. [This concerns] the root *krī*.

In the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "ṭhaco yat. By the rule "sārvadhātuke," there is *guṇa*, resulting in the vowel *e*. Here, because the vowel *e* is not followed by a vowel (*ac*), the substitution of *ay* (the *ayādeśa*) is prescribed by this [rule]. "Other things to be purchased" means grain and so forth collected in the house and elsewhere for the purpose of food and the like. [The suffix] *arha*...

Regarding the rule *kṛtyatṛcaśca*: here, the substitution of *ay* does not take place, because in that case there is no connection with a result (*phalopadhāna*) for the purpose of purchasing. This is the meaning. (67) *lopaḥ śākalyasya* 8.3.19.

In the examples *hare ehi*, *viṣṇo iha*, *śriyai udyataḥ*, and *gurau utkaḥ*, after the sequential substitution of *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* for the *ec* vowels (*e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*), the treatise prescribes the optional elision of the *y* and *v* sounds with the rule:
*lopaḥ śākalyasya*. This is understood to apply to the *y* and *v* that follow a vowel other than *a* (by the rule *bho-bhago-*) and to those not followed by *ś* (by the rule *aśi*).
And it follows [from the previous rule]. From the rule "vyor laghuprayatne" (Pāṇini 6.1.70), the word "vyoḥ" is understood to follow.
This means "of the letters *v* and *y*. Furthermore, the term "apūrvasya" (preceded by something other than *a*) is a qualifier of "vyoḥ.
That which has an *a*-vowel (*avarṇa*) preceding it is called "apūrva. Thus, [the meaning is] "of a *v* or *y* that is preceded by something other than *a*."
The singular number is used with the intention of referring to each [consonant] individually.

The term "of the word" (*padasya*), which is the subject under discussion, is qualified by the letters *y* and *v* that do not have a vowel *a* preceding them. Because these are qualifiers, the status of being "ending in those" (*tadanta*) is obtained for *vyoḥ*. Consequently, that *y* which is preceded by a vowel *a*—
The meaning is that the *va* and *ya* [substitutes] are elided when they occur at the end of a word followed by a vowel (*aś*) other than *a*.
By the rule "of the final [alophon]," it is understood that this applies to the end of such a word.
Because of the mention of Śākalya, it is understood that in other opinions this does not occur. And therefore—

He states the result with the words "before *a* and *ava*," etc. Although the term "*vyaḥ*" is understood from the previous rule, the expression "*ya-va-yoḥ*" is used because the letter *ya* occurs first in the traditional sequence of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*). Nor is this elision of *ya* followed only by persons belonging to the lineage of Śākalya and not by others.

It should not be asked why the mention of Śākalya is not intended merely for the purpose of establishing a restriction based on the distinction between individuals; for in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *na veti vibhāṣā*, having introduced the topic with the statement "and when one emulates the region of a teacher, that [region] becomes the scope [of the rule]," it says: *iko hrasvo'ṅyo gālavasya*.
In rules such as *ṭhprācām avṛddhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.160), the mention of teachers such as Gālava and others,

as well as the mention of specific regions such as "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) and "of the Northerners" (*udīcām*), serves solely to provide an unrestricted option; it does not, however, intend to establish a restriction on usage based on belonging to those respective lineages or residing in those specific regions.

Because this has been established as the settled conclusion (*siddhānta*). Now, an objection: in the case of *hare ehi*, when the substitution of *ay* occurs and the letter *y* is elided, would there not be the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule "before *ṭha*, *m*, or *āṅ*" (*ṭhāmāṅeśca*)? Similarly, in *viṣṇo iha*, *śriyai udyataḥ*, and *gurau utkaḥ*, when the substitutions of *av*, *āy*, and *āv* occur and the letters *v* and *y* are elided, would there not be the substitution of a single *guṇa* vowel by the rule "the *guṇa* substitute [occurs] for *ā* followed by *a*" (*ādguṇa*)?

To address this, he says: "as before. Since the elision (*lopa*) of the letters *va* and *ya* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), they remain separated by those letters; thus, because the condition of being followed by a vowel (*ac-paraka*) is absent, the vowel-sandhi (*acsandhi*) that was suspected does not occur. This concludes the description of the *ik-sandhi* and the *ec-sandhi*.

Anticipating the objection that this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in both cases, he provides the resolution with the words beginning "Which ones... (*kāni*). Although the words *yadi* and *tathāpi* must be supplied, the syntactical connection is as follows: although the substitution of *yaṇ* and *āv* would have been applicable in the questions "which are they? (*kāni santi*) and "who are they? (*kau staḥ*), nevertheless, they do not occur. Now, one might object here...

Since the vowels *i* and *ū* are followed by *s* and not by a vowel (*ac*), how can there be the possibility of *yaṇ*-substitution? To this he says: "by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) of the elision (*al-lopa*) of the root *as*.
The form *santi* arises from the root *as*, belonging to the second class (*adādi*), in the present tense (*laṭ*), first person plural.

In the dual number of the third person, however, the form is *staḥ*. In both cases, the established rule is that the initial *a* of the verbal root is elided by the rule "elision of the *a* of *śn* and *as*" (*śnasorallopaḥ*).
Regarding that elision of *a*:

The meaning is that, by virtue of being *sthānivat*, the short *a* and the long *au* would undergo the substitutions of *ay* and *āv* respectively because they are followed by a vowel (*ac*). Nor is it the case that the status of being *sthānivat* is impossible here on the grounds of the rule *sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau*; for the original locus (*sthānin*) of the elision (*al-lopa*) is [the vowel].

It should not be argued that because the two rules prescribing *yaṇ* and *av* substitutions proceed by depending on the vowel *a* as their cause (*nimitta*), they depend upon the original substituendum (*sthānin*) which is an *al* (vowel), [and thus the substitution would not apply];

for the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is established by the rule "when a subsequent element intervenes, [the preceding] is treated as the original in a prior operation. This applies to the elision of the *a*.
When an operation is prescribed with respect to a following *kṅit* suffix, because that [suffix] is a cause situated after [the substitute],

the *iK* vowels (*i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*)— which are perceived as preceding the *a* that serves as the original locus (*sthānin*) for that substitute— are subject to the rule prescribing *yaṇ* substitution; this is established by the principle "when something follows *ṭhaC*" (*ṭhacaḥ parasmin*).
The meaning is "because of the occurrence [of the rule].
(68) *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84). To the question, "In that case, why do the *yaṇ* and *av* substitutions not occur here?", he says: *na padānta...* (Pāṇini 6.1.86).
The meaning is that because the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.58] prohibits that [substitution] when a rule applies to the end of a word (padāntavidhi),

the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to the elision of the *an* (*añ-lop*)— which is a substitute for an *ac* (*ajādeśa*) caused by a subsequent element— when the substitutions *yaṇ* and *āv* are to be applied in place of the *i* and *u* sounds that have become word-final (*padāntabhūta*), since they then constitute the final members of a word (*padacaramāvayava*).

Now, in order to define the euphonic combination (*ekādeśasaṃdhi*), he says: "having taken as the governing rule [the sūtra] *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*. The meaning is that this sūtra, consisting of two words, is recited here for the purpose of being carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) into subsequent rules, and thereupon several combinations will be prescribed.

(69) *ādguṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.87. *ādguṇaḥ*: The word *āt* is a locative case ending (*pañcamī*), not a marker indicating the length of the vowel (*taparakaraṇa*). The governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is understood here. Thus he says [the commentary]: "after a vowel of the *a*-class, before a vowel," and so forth. For example: *upendra*.

When *upa* and *indra* stand together, the *a* following the *p* and the *i* [of *indra*] undergo a single *guṇa* substitute, namely *e*, which has the same place of articulation (*sthāna*)— namely, the throat and the palate— for both the preceding and the following sounds, due to their closest internal similarity (*āntaratamya*). Now,
in order to recall the definition stated regarding the pratyāhāras when they denote their own expressed meanings:

He provides an example of a long vowel: *rameśa*. When *ramā-īśa* is situated, in place of the letter *ā* and the letter *ī*, there is a single *guṇa*, the letter *e*, as before. In the case of *gaṅgodakam*, when *gaṅgā-udakam* is situated, [in place of the letter *ā* and the letter *u*...]

In the same way, the single *guṇa* vowel *o* belongs to both the throat and the lips as its places of articulation (*sthāna*). In the case of *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*, when it stands as *kṛṣṇa ṛddhiḥ*, the rule *ādguṇaḥ* would apply. Here, there are two substituends (*sthānin*), namely the vowel *a* and the vowel *ṛ*; for these two, [the corresponding substitutes are] *e*, *ai*, and *o*.
All three *guṇa* vowels would be applicable [to the substitution of *a*], because there is no distinction in their similarity of place of articulation (*sthāna*) with the letter *a*.
(70) P. 1.1.51: *uraṇ raparaḥ*.
However, the substitute *ṛ* possesses no similarity of place of articulation with any original (*sthānin*); therefore, which *guṇa* [should apply]?

When there is an expectation as to what [is meant by] "it occurs," this is commenced: *uraṇ raparaḥ*. It is said [that this was stated]—the remainder [of the sentence] being "in the sūtra *aṇuditsavarṇasya ca pratyayaḥ*. *Uḥ* is the genitive singular of *ṛ*. By the paribhāṣā *ṣaṣṭhī sthāne*, the word "in place of" (*sthāne*) is understood. In the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Even when that technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is not present, the term *sthāne* (in place of) is carried over from there.

Thus he says: "that *aṇ* which is in its place. From the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P. 1.1.50), the term *sthāne* is also carried over. It has been stated that *sthāna* means *prasaṅga* (occasion of application).
The intended meaning is "in the state of *prasaṅga*. Thus he says: "being [the letter] *ra*, it proceeds as such.

Here, the *pratyāhāra* "ṛ" is intended. Consequently, it is understood that [the letter *la*] proceeds preceded by the letter *ra* and preceded by the letter *la*. [Now follows] their systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*).

He demonstrates this with the word "tatra" (therein). In the cases of *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ* and *tavalkāraḥ*, the application is such that *ar* occurs in the former and *al* in the latter, both being preceded by the letters *repha* (ṛ) and *lakāra* (l). To the question "Why is this the established rule?", he replies:
"Because of proximity (*āntaratamya*). When the three *guṇa* vowels are applicable, [the substitution of] *a* for the vowel *a* (*aṇ*)...

Because it is headed by the letter *r*—that is, because its nature consists of *ar*, *al*, and so forth—in the portion consisting of the vowel *a*, there is identity of place with the substitute *a*; in the portion consisting of *r*, with the original *ṛ*; and in the portion consisting of *l*, with the original *lṛ*. Thus, in place of *a* and *ṛ*, *ara* occurs; and in place of *a* and *lṛ*, [the corresponding result follows].
It occurs in its own place (*sthāne*). However, *e* and *o* do not become *guṇa* substitutes at all;

the meaning is that this is because they lack similarity of place (*sthāna-sāmya*) with *ṛ* and *lṛ*. Nor should it be asked how *e* and *o* could not be followed by *r* (i.e., become *rapara*), for [the rule] is already established by the preceding [sūtra].
For here, by the letter *ṇ*, the suffix *ān* is understood, as indicated by the rule *praśāstṛṇām* and others; enough of this.

Regarding "optionally doubling" (*pakṣe dvitvam*): from the root *ṛdh*, with the suffix *ktin*, the substitution of *dha* for *ta* according to the rule *jhaṣastathordho 'dhaḥ* results in the form *ṛddhiḥ*, which naturally contains two *dh* sounds. In that case, when the *ār* substitute is applied, [the doubling occurs] after the *r*.
The meaning is that, according to the rule *aco rahābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.46], the letter *dh* may sometimes undergo doubling.
(71) *jharo jhari savarṇe* [Pāṇini 8.4.65]: A *jhara* sound is optionally elided before a following *jhara* sound when they are homogeneous (*savarṇa*).

The term *anyatarasyām* is carried over from the rule *ṭhjhayoho'nyatarasyām*. From the rule *ṭhhalo yamā'm*, the terms *hal* and *lopa* are also carried over. Therefore, he says: "of that which follows a consonant," and so forth. Thus, three forms are produced here; he states this as "the absence of doubling."

By the phrase "and so forth," the meaning is that when the *ṛ* following the letter *r* is at the end of a verbal root, the doubling (*dvitva*) of the letter *dh* is absent by the rule *ṭhaco rahābhyām*, and the letter *dh* is then elided by the rule *ṭhjharo jhari*, resulting in a form containing only a single *dh*. The word "asati" (in the absence) draws in the phrase "in the absence of doubling."

The meaning is as follows: when there is no doubling of that very *ṛdhi*’s *dh* and it is not elided, the form consists of two *dh*s; likewise, when there is doubling of that very *ṛdhi*’s *dh* and it is elided, the form likewise consists of two *dh*s. Regarding the word "satī" (when it exists): [it refers to] when there is doubling of that very *ṛdhi*’s *dh*.
The meaning is that the form [of the word] is threefold, whether the elision occurs or does not occur. Although, according to the view of two *dhakāras*,

the first *dhakāra* becomes a *dakāra* by virtue of the rule "ṭhjhalāñjaś jhaśi" (Pāṇini 8.4.53), and according to the view of three *dhakāras*, the middle *dhakāra* likewise becomes a *dakāra*, nevertheless, this is stated with reference to the process of derivation (*prakriyā*) by way of its prior state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).
Or, there is no fault in [the rule] being twofold or threefold. Now, regarding the word *tavalkāra*, he says "yaṇaḥ" (after a semi-vowel).

The meaning is that when explained as "doubling of a *may* following a *yaṇ*," there is doubling of the letter *k*, while for the letter *l*, there is doubling according to the rule "anaci ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.47). By that...

The meaning is that there is an option regarding the doubling of both the letter *l* and the letter *k*. "Doubling of *l* alone" means that when there is doubling of the letter *l* but no doubling of the letter *k*, the first form consists of two *l*s and one *k*. "Not of both" means [not doubling] both the letter *l* and the letter *k*.
The meaning is that in the absence of doubling (dvitva), the third form consists of a single *la* and a single *ka*.

"Of both as well" means that when both the *la* and the *ka* are doubled, the fourth form consists of two *la*s and two *k*s. Regarding "in *tavalkāra* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) [includes other examples].
The mention of *ma*, *l*, *k* (*ādiṅgrahaḥ*) [is for the sake of the subsequent rules].
(72) *vṛddhir eci* | P. 6.1.88.
Regarding *vṛddhir eci*: from the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, the word *āt* ending in the fifth case is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). *ekaṛ*...

The phrase "of the preceding and the following" is understood [from the previous rule]. This is stated by [the sūtra] beginning with *ādeci*. The term "exception to the *guṇa* [rule]" means that this [new rule] is commenced because the *guṇa* rule (*ādguṇa*) would otherwise apply.
Regarding "the oneness of Kṛṣṇa": it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "the oneness belonging to Kṛṣṇa."

The prohibition regarding the *pūraṇa* group is stated to be non-permanent (*anitya*) in that very same root text. Others maintain that *kṛṣṇa* ending in the vocative case is a separate word. In this instance, there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), the diphthong *aikāra*, in place of both the vowel *a* and the vowel *e*, which share the same place of articulation—the throat and the palate. [As in] *gaṅgā-ogha*.

This being the case, in place of the vowel *ā* and the vowel *o*, which have the throat and lips as their points of articulation (*sthāna*), there occurs the corresponding diphthong *au*. This is likewise the case in expressions such as *devaiśvaryam* and *kṛṣṇautkaṇṭhyam*. In reality, however, we shall explain later that words such as *saṅkhyā* (number) and the like are not adjectives (*guṇavacana*).

(73) *etyedhatyūṭhasu* | Pāṇini 6.1.89. The analysis of the compound is: *eti* (the root *i*), *edhati* (the root *edh*), and *ūṭh*. The forms *eti* and *edhati* are indicated by the suffix *śtip*, according to the rule "when indicating a verbal root, the suffixes *ik*, *śtip*, and *p* [are used]. Thus, it refers to the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*).

The two verbal roots *edh* and *vṛdh* are intended here. The term *ecī* (in a vowel beginning with *e* or *o*) is understood from the previous rule. By the principle "a rule applies to that which begins with [the specified element]," it is obtained that the condition is "when [the root] begins with an *ej*-vowel. And this qualifies only *eti* and *edhati*, not the augment *uṭ*, because such an augment is impossible in their case. [This is established by] *ekaḥ*.

The phrase *pūrvaparayoḥ* (of the preceding and the following) is understood from the governing context. From the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, the word *āt* (from *a*), ending in the ablative case, is carried over (*anuvartate*). This is what he states with the words "after an *a*-vowel," and so forth. Regarding the form *upaiti*: it is the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *iṇ*; *tip* [is the personal ending], and *śap* is elided (*luk*); [the substitution of] the vowel *i* [for *ya*] occurs by the rule *sārvadhātuka*.
The *guṇa* substitute is *e*. When [the form] *upa-eti* is established, *vṛddhi* is applied by this rule, resulting in *upaiti*. Regarding *upaidhata*:

it is the present indicative (*laṭ*) of the root *edh*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the substitution of *ta*, the suffix *śap*, and the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the *ātmanepada* endings according to the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānām*. When [the form] *upa edhate* is established, *vṛddhi* is applied by this rule.

Regarding the word *praṣṭhauhaḥ*: it is called *praṣṭhavāṭ* because it carries (*vahati*) the side-horse (*praṣṭham*). The suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *ṭhvahaśca*. There is the elision of *v* by the rule *ṭhverapṛktasya*. Then, by the rule *ṭhata upadhāyāḥ*, there is vṛddhi [of the penultimate vowel]. Subsequently, when the suffix *śas* follows, the term *saṃprasāraṇa* is supplied from the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, and by the rule *vāha ūṭh*, [the substitution of] *ūṭh* occurs.

The *ūṭh* which bears the technical designation *saṃprasāraṇa* undergoes the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) by the rule "from *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*samprasāraṇācca*). When *praṣṭha-ūhi* is established, the vowel *au* is substituted [for *pra* + *ū*] by this very rule [of *vṛddhi*]. Now, one might object that the mention of *eti* and *edhati* here is redundant, because in cases such as *upaiti* and *upaidhate*, the *vṛddhi* can occur even without this rule, by the rule "the *vṛddhi* [is substituted] for *ai* and *au*" (*vṛddhireci*).

The inclusion of *ūṭh* is also redundant, since [the desired form] is established by the rule *vṛddhireci* alone. As for the inclusion of *ūṭh* in the rule *vāha ūṭh*, it is purposeless because [the substitution] has already been effected by *samprasāraṇa*. However, the *guṇa* [substitution] occurs because [the condition] is characterized by the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Thus says the author of the *Vārttika*: "The *vṛddhi* [occurs] because of the inclusion of *ej*."

Because it has been stated in that very way, the mention of *ūṭh* need not be made. Let the rule simply be "vāha. Let only the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) be prescribed as "there shall be *saṃprasāraṇa* for the [final] *vāh* of a *bha*-stem. Consequently, when the *v* is replaced by *u* through *saṃprasāraṇa*, and the resulting form is *uh* due to the application of the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) rule; [the desired form is achieved].

The meaning of the Vārttika is that, by relying on the characteristic of being a condition (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), when the suffix *ṇvi* follows, the substitution of *o* for the *u* of the penultimate light vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) occurs; thus, when *praṣṭhauhi* is established, the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88) applies the *vṛddhi* substitution.
Therefore, [the opponent argues] that the sūtra "etyedhatyūṭhsu" (Pāṇini 6.1.89) is redundant; to this, [the author] replies:
"An exception to the rule regarding the single substitute of the form of the subsequent element" means that this [rule] is an exception to *etyedhatyoreṅi parataḥ* (P.

6.1.89) and *ādguṇaḥ* (P. 6.1.87). For if only the *samprasāraṇa* of *vāh* were prescribed and not the *ūṭh*, then once the *samprasāraṇa* of *v* had been effected as *u*, the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute of the preceding and following vowels) would apply.

When that [substitution] is to be performed, the *laghūpadha-guṇa* (the strengthening of a light penultimate vowel) does not occur, because the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form of the preceding vowel and the semivowel) is dependent upon the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization), which in turn depends upon the designation *bha*—which itself depends upon the external suffix *śas*.
Thus, due to its being *bahiraṅga* (external), it is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of this rule. Consequently, in the absence of the *guṇa*, we have *praṣṭha-u-āhi*.
If *praṣṭha-ūh* were established [by the rule *ūḍha*], and then, with *praṣṭha-uh* established, the substitution of *o* by *guṇa* (P.

6.1.87) applied, the form would be *praṣṭhoḥ*. However, when the rule for *ūṭh*, which bears the technical designation *saṃprasāraṇa*, is applied, the sequence becomes *praṣṭha ū āh*; since the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) is not applicable here, [the form remains as intended].
Since the vowel *o* is absent and only the vowel *ū* exists, the rule *vṛddhireci* (Pāṇini 6.1.88) does not apply; rather, *ād guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) would prevail.

However, since the rule *etyedhatyūṭhasu* (Pāṇini 6.1.89) prescribes *vṛddhi*, the form *praṣṭhauhaḥ* is established. Therefore, the inclusion of *ūṭh* in the rule *vāha ūṭh* (Pāṇini 6.4.132) is necessary—this is the Vārttika cited in that sūtra.
Let it rest for now that [this] has been refuted in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the word *upeta*: from the root *iṇ*, the suffix *laṭ* is applied, followed by *tas*, and then *śap* is elided (*luk*).

Because of the rule "sārvadhātukam apit," the suffix *tas* is treated as having an indicatory *ṅ*; consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *i* before this suffix. Here, because the root *iṇ* does not begin with the letter *e* (ej-ādi), there is no [guṇa] substitution before it.
[The form] *vṛddhiḥ* [is derived as follows]. [In the example] *mā bhavān predidhat*, there is the suffix *ṇic* after the root *edh*. Then the *luṅ* [tense marker], followed by *tip*.

By the rule "ṅtiḥ is always [substituted for tip]," there is the elision of the *ikāra* (the *i* of *tip*). Then, by the rule "after roots ending in *ṇi*, *śri*, *dru*, or *sru*," there is the *caṅ* [substitution for *liṭ*]. By the rule "when *caṅ* follows, the penultimate vowel is shortened," the penultimate vowel is shortened. By the rule "when *caṅ* follows, the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel," there is reduplication of the syllable *dhi* (from *edh*), which is the second syllable beginning with a vowel.
In *carcā*, the substitution of *jaś* occurs according to the rule *ṭhabhyāse carcā*. There is no augment *āṭ* due to the rule *na māṅyoga*.

The first person is used for the two instances of the word *bhavat* because they follow a verbal root; this will become clear in the section on the governing rule for *tiṅ*-endings (*tiṅantādhikāra*). When *pra-aididhat* is established, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *etyedhatyūṭsu*.

Because the root *edh* does not begin with the vowel *e*. If the qualification "beginning with *e*" were absent there, then *vṛddhi* would occur here as well. Nor should it be argued that when the single *e* is shortened to *i* by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*, this is no longer the root *edh*, because a form modified in one part remains identical [to the original]. Herein lies the proof (*māna*).
The form *aididhat* is not cited as a counter-example because [the root] has been abandoned.

If that were the case, with the augment *āṭ* by the rule *āḍajādīnām* and the subsequent *vṛddhi* by the rule *āṭaśca*, the form would be *aididhat*. In that situation, since the root *edh* begins with a vowel (*ej-ādi*), *vṛddhi* is indeed desired there. However, the word *bhavat* has a doubtful purpose. Now, [one might object]: [The text continues: "But surely..."

When *ā ehi* and *ava ehi* are present, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, the single substitute *e* (the *guṇa*) is treated as if it were the end of the preceding element and the beginning of the following element (*antādivacca*). Furthermore,

by the principle of "designation as possessing [the properties of] what precedes and follows" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), according to the rule *ādyantavadekasmin*, because the root *iṇ* begins with *i* when that [substitute *e*] follows, [the conditions for the application of the following rule are met].

In the case of *ṭheṅpirarūpam*, if one were to override the rule for *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) by applying the rule *etyedhatyūṭhṣu vṛddhiḥ*, the desired form *avaihī* would not result. Nor can it be argued that this is resolved by the rule *omāṅośca*, which prescribes *pararūpa*; for the *vṛddhi* prescribed by *etyedhatīti* applies only when *e* or *ai* [follows].

The rule *pararūpam* is an exception (*apavāda*), and likewise, the rule *omāṅośca* is also an exception; this is because they share the same logical status according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*. Therefore, he says: "prior" (*purastāt*). The maxim is: "Exceptions stated earlier sublate the immediately following rules, not those further removed. Thus, exceptions read earlier [sublate subsequent rules].
The meaning is that [these rules] sublate only those subsequent rules that are immediately following, but not those that are separated by others.
In the present context, after reciting several sūtras following "etyedhatyūṭhasu," and then having recited "eṅi pararūpam," and again after reciting several more sūtras—

The rule *omāṅośca* is recited [in the sūtra]. Therefore, by the aforementioned logic, through the application of the *vṛddhi* substitution in *ṭheḍeṣatī*, only the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) prescribed by *ṭheṅ pirarūpam* is sublated, but not the *pararūpa* prescribed by *omāṅośca* as well; this is the intended meaning. In reality, however, the *vṛddhi* substitution in *etyedhatī* is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *omāṅośca*.
In cases such as *upaiti*, even though that [condition] has not yet been reached, the rule for *vṛddhi* (as taught in *ety-edhaty-ūthsu*) is initiated.

Therefore, this is not a case for the maxim "exceptions [operate] before the rules they supersede" (*purastādapavādāḥ*). Consequently, in *ava-e-hi*, the rule *omāṅośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.95) applies by virtue of its posteriority, superseding the rule *ety-edhaty-ūthsu*.

It is only proper to say that it is "correct" (nyāyya). For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states: "When *eṅ* [the rule for] *pararūpa* has not yet applied, it is only proper to say that, having set aside *etyedhatyūthsu*, the *pararūpa* [prescribed] by *omāṅośca* is correct because it is subsequent. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states: "When *eṅ* [the rule for] *pararūpa* has not yet applied..."

The rule *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1), which begins with the words *eti* and *edhati*, is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [substitution]. It has been stated quite clearly: "Since the substitution of the single substitute *pirarūpa* applies both when [the condition for] *vṛddhi* has already been reached and when it has not yet been reached, the *vṛddhi* being introduced [by the subsequent rule] is not an exception to that. As for the alternative view mentioned in the Bhāṣya—"Or rather..."—it is as follows:

"Exceptions occurring earlier subvert the immediately following rules; thus, by the rule *ety-edhaty-ati vṛddhiḥ*, the single substitute *ai* (vṛddhi) subverts only the *pararūpa* [single substitute] prescribed by *eṅi pararūpam*, but not also the *pararūpa* prescribed by *om-āṅ-śca*.
However, that is not so, because both the *vṛddhi* [substitute] from *ety-edhaty-ati vṛddhiḥ* and the *pararūpa* [substitutes] from *eṅi pararūpam* and *om-āṅ-śca*...

This is merely a statement of provisional acceptance (*abhyupagamavāda*) because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to two preceding rules, or it is based on not considering the general category of what is to be sublated (*bādhyasāmānya*); enough of this prolixity.
[The rule] *akṣād ūhinyām upasaṃkhyānam* (an addition concerning *ūhinī* after *akṣa*) follows from the words *āt*, *aci*, and *vṛddhiḥ*.

And [the rule] "ṭhekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.84) applies. The root *ūh* means "to infer" (*vitarka*). Inferring is *ūha*; that which possesses this is *ūhinī*. The meaning is that when the word *akṣa* is followed by the word *ūhinī*, there shall be a single substitute *vṛddhi* for both the preceding and following vowels. Thus: *akṣauhiṇī*.

The suffix *ini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Because it ends in *n*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The analysis of the compound is "that which carries (*ūhinī*) the *akṣas*" (dice).

An army characterized by a specific measure is called an *akṣauhiṇī*. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs according to the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. When the form *akṣa-ūhinī* is established, although *guṇa* would normally apply, this Vārttika prescribes *vṛddhi* instead.

*svādīreriṇoḥ*: When the word *sva* is followed by the word *īra* or the word *īrin*, there shall be a single substitute *vṛddhi* for the preceding and following vowels. This is the meaning. In the form *svaira*, the root *īra* means "to go. The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which moves according to its own will" (*svena cchandena īraḥ*). [The compound is formed] by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*.

The compound is *bahulam*. When *sva-īra* is established, although *guṇa* would normally apply, this *vārttika* prescribes *vṛddhi*. Thus, *sveneritum*. In the sense of "one whose nature it is to move about (*saṃcarituṃ*) by one's own will (*svena icchayā*)," the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*.

The meaning is "one who acts according to his own will. It is a *upapada* compound (*upapadasamāsa*). When *sva-īrin* is established, although *guṇa* would normally apply, by this [rule] *vṛddhi* is substituted.
[This applies] in the presence of *prāt*, *ūha*, *ūḍha*, *ūḍhi*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*. After the prefix *pra*, there are the forms *ūha*, *ūḍha*, *eṣa*, and *eṣya*.
The meaning is that, among these subsequent [rules], a single substitute *vṛddhi* occurs in place of the preceding and following vowels.
Regarding *prauha*: the root √ūh means "to infer" (*vitarka*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), resulting in a *gati-samāsa*.
When *pra-ūha* is established, the *vṛddhi* substitution is applied by this Vārttika, resulting in *prauḍha*. The root √bāh means "to convey" (*prāpaṇe*); the suffix *kta* is applied.

By the rule *vacisvapi* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). The preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied. By *ho ḍhaḥ* (8.2.31), *h* becomes *ḍh*. By *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (8.2.40), *t* becomes *dh*. Then *ṣṭutva* is applied. By *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* (8.3.13) and *ḍhralope* (6.3.111), the long vowel is substituted. When *pra-ūḍha-* is established, although *guṇa* would have been applicable, by this [rule] *vṛddhi* is substituted. Even in the case of *proḍhavān*, when the suffix *ktavatu* is added to the root *vah*, the forms *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, elision of *ḍha*, and lengthening occur, resulting in the stage *pra-ūḍhavat*. At that point, the rule *prādūhoḍhe* would require vṛddhi;
however, even there, because the word *ūḍha* is heard as the subsequent member [of the compound], [the rule does not apply]. Therefore...

He says: "meaningful" (*arthavat*). The meaning is that when it is possible to grasp a word that possesses meaning, there is no grasping of a word that lacks meaning. This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is established by the mention of the term *rūpa* ("form") in the rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68); this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on that very sūtra. By the word "thereby" (*tena*), [he refers to] the meaningful [word].

The meaning is: "by way of the restriction of inclusion. Regarding the phrase "only that which ends in *kta*": the suffix *kta* indeed possesses meaning, because it is prescribed for the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). The suffix *ktavatu*, however, is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*).
Therefore, since the portion *kta* within it is devoid of meaning, it is not included by the mention of *ūḍha* in the rule *prādūhoḍhait*.
It does not occur; therefore, in that case, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution for the subsequent [vowel], but rather only *guṇa*.

Regarding the word *prauḍhi*: it is derived from the root *vah* with the suffix *ktin*. [The changes] are the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*, *ḍha* for *dha*, *ṣṭu* for *ṭu*, the elision of *ḍh*, and lengthening.
When *pra-ūḍhi-* is established, this rule causes *vṛddhi* to take effect, overriding *guṇa*.

Regarding "iṣa icchāyām" and so forth: in all three groups, these roots have a short vowel as their penultimate (upadhā). The genitive case in "teṣām" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). When the suffix *vvan* or *ṇyat* is added to any one of them, and the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel has been applied, the forms *eṣa* and *eṣya* are established. Thus: *pra-eṣa*, *pra-eṣya*.

This being the case, *vṛddhi* is applied by this rule, overriding the *pūrvarūpa* [substitution] of *eṅ*. By this, the argument that the mention of *evaiṣaiṣya* in the rule *vṛddhireci* was redundant is refuted. Now, if this is so, how are the forms *preṣaḥ* and *preṣyaḥ* derived? To this he says: "But as for... (*yastu*).

Because these two roots have long vowels as their penultimate letters (*dīrghopadha*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for a vowel followed by *la*, *ru*, or *ū* as their penultimate; thus, the forms *īṣa* and *īṣya* are established.

However, since these two are not included in this particular *vārttika*, when *vṛddhi* does not occur before them, the form *preṣaḥ* and *preṣya* are also possible due to the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule "ṭhādguṇaḥ. This is the meaning.

By virtue of its association with the word *eṣa*, the word *eṣya* is also understood here as being exclusively a form ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Consequently, there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] when it is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) or ends in the suffix *lyap*. For example: *agnaye preṣya dūtam* (having sent a messenger for Agni), *preṣya gataḥ* (having gone after sending).
And [there is no *vṛddhi*] in the case of the word *ṛta* in a compound with a third-case term (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). That is, when the word *ṛta* follows an initial *a* in a third-case compound.

The meaning is that there shall be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) for both the preceding and following vowels. The analysis of the compound is shown as "sukhenartta" (*sukhena* + *ṛta*). The root *ṛ* means "to go. The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72).
The third case ending is used because it belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*. The compound is formed by the rule *sup-supā*. When the form *sukha-ṛta* is established...
When a *guṇa* is obtained, the vowel *ā* is substituted [by the rule of *vṛddhi*]. When *ra* follows, the form becomes *sukhārtaḥ*.

Since the counter-example for the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) has essentially been shown by the very analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) cited, he asks about the purpose of the portion "by the third case" (*tṛtīyā*): "Why 'by the third case'? [The example is] *paramārtaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]. "Parama" and "ṛta" form a *karmadhāraya* compound. By the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, [the result is] *paramarta*. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). The meaning is that when the word *ṛṇa* follows these—namely *pra*, *ṛt*, *vatsatara*, *kambala*, *vasana*, *ṛṇa*, and *daśa*—there shall be a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) consisting of the *vṛddhi* vowel for both the preceding and following vowels.

Regarding the term *prārṇam*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) as "that from which debt has departed" (*pragatam ṛṇam*), there is a *gati*-compound according to the rule "prefixes [such as *pra*] form compounds with a word in the first case when they have the sense of 'departed' and so forth. When *pra-ṛṇam* is established, this *vārttika* applies *vṛddhi* (the vowel *ā*) instead of *guṇa*. This is followed by the substitution of *r* for the final element (*raparatvam*). A *vatsatara* is a calf that is very young; of that...

The analysis of the compound is "debt" (*ṛṇam*). Debt that is incurred either with reference to a young bull (*vatsatara*) or for the purpose of obtaining one is "debt for a young bull" (*vatsatarārṇam*). The same should be understood for the subsequent cases as well. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "debt for a blanket" (*kambalārṇam*), "debt for clothing" (*vasanārṇam*), and "debt for a fringe" (*daśārṇārṇam*) are included. In all instances, this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
To the question, "How can there be a connection of the word *ṛṇa* when another word *ṛṇa* follows?", he says: "of the debt" (*ṛṇasya*).

To the question, "How does the word *daśārṇa* apply to a specific country and a specific river?", he says: "the word *ṛṇa* [means] difficult terrain. Thus, a country in which there are ten *ṛṇas*, that is, ten difficult terrains, is called *Daśārṇa*.
A specific place. The analysis of the compound is: that river in which there are ten kinds (*daśavidhāni*) of water (*ṛṇāni*) is called *Daśārṇā*.
[This is governed by the rule: *upasargād ṛti dhātau* Pāṇini 6.1.91.

In the rule *upasargād ṛti*, the word *āt* (from the previous rule *ād guṇaḥ*) follows as a fifth-case ending (*pañcamyanta*). That [word] qualifies *upasarga*; therefore, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends with it (*tadantavidhiḥ*). Thus, "ending in the vowel *a*" is obtained.
The word *ṛti* is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*). By the principle *yasmin vidhis tadādau*, this results in an application of the rule regarding that which begins with it (*tadādividhiḥ*).
It is understood that [the rule applies] when preceded by *ṛ* and so on. From the rule *vṛddhireci*, the word *vṛddhiḥ* is carried over (*anuvartate*).
The governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is also in force. Thus he says: "from one ending in an *a*-vowel," and so forth.
Regarding the term "single substitute" (*ekādeśa*), the remainder is "of the two vowels, the preceding and the following. Otherwise, [the rule would apply to] the prefix...

And there shall be a universal substitution for the *dhātu* [root]. In the forms *upārcchati* and *prārcchati*, when *upa ṛcchati* and *pra ṛcchati* have been established, and the *guṇa* substitution would otherwise apply, this rule effects the *vṛddhi* substitution followed by the replacement of the vowel with its corresponding short form (*aparatva*).
(75) *Antādivacca* (6.1.85): [The substitute] is treated like the final element of the preceding and the initial element of the following.

Now, in order to establish that the *repha* [the sound *r*] is at the end of a word—so as to raise the possibility of applying the *visarga* prescribed for the end of a word—the author says: "And like the end and the beginning" (*antādivacca*). The rule "one [substitute] in place of the preceding and the following" (*ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*) is understood to carry over. By the paribhāṣā concerning "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyaparibhāṣā*), the phrase "like the end and the beginning" [is interpreted as follows].

The application is sequential. Consequently, it is established that the single substitute occurring in place of both the preceding and the following [sounds] is treated as if it were the final part of the preceding and the initial part of the following. Although the single substitute has two constituent sounds as its substituenda—the preceding and the following—and of those two sounds...

Since each [substitute] is a single unit and indivisible, the statement that the single substitute (ekādeśa) is like the final letter of the preceding element or the initial letter of the following element in relation to them is inconsistent; nevertheless, when a single substitute occurs in place of both the preceding and following sounds, it belongs to the composite whole formed by the first constituent.

The meaning intended is as follows: that which is the final element (*anta*) of the preceding [element] becomes the substitute for the first position (*prathamasthānin*), performing its grammatical operation;

and that which is the initial element (*ādi*) of the subsequent aggregate (*samudāya*) containing the second position (*dvitīyasthānin*) becomes the substitute for the second position, performing its grammatical operation. In this regard, concerning the status of being "as if the final element of the preceding" (*pūrvāntavat*):

In the case of *kṣīrapeṇa*: when *kṣīra-pa-ina* is established, the single substitute *e* (the *ekādeśa*) occurs by the rule "ṭādguṇaḥ. Therein, because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), namely *pe*, is treated as ending in the preceding element (*pūrvāntavat*), it possesses only one vowel (*ekāc*);

thus, by the rule "ekājuttarapade ṇaḥ," the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* takes place. In this instance, the rule regarding the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original) does not apply to the single substitute.
This is because, by relying on the vowel *a* as being situated in one part of the sequence *pe*,

the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) which operates on the basis of *pe* having a single vowel (*ekāj*) as its subsequent member (*utarapada*), depends upon an *al* (phoneme) that constitutes the original element (*sthānin*).
Even though the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* primarily relies upon the condition of having a single vowel as the subsequent member, [it nevertheless depends on the phoneme *a*].

Although the *ala* [the letter *a*] in the word *adakāram* relies upon the *ac* [the vowel *a*] which serves as a qualifier for its substituendum (*sthānin*), nevertheless, the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning *al*" (*analvidhau*) certainly applies here;
for what is intended there is simply the reliance on an *al* that is the substituendum in any way whatsoever. Otherwise...

In the case of *pratidīvya* (from *prati-dīvy-ktvā*), when the substitution *lyap* takes the place of *ktvā*, there arises the impossibility of the prohibition by the rule *analvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56) regarding the introduction of the augment *iṭ*, because [the substitute] is based on the fact that the original element (*sthānin*) possesses the quality of being a root (*dhātuka*) starting with a *val* sound. This is because, in that context, the *val* sound is not relied upon as the primary factor. By this [argument],...

The claim that this sūtra is redundant because its purpose is already served by the *sthānivat* sūtra is refuted. Regarding the treatment as "like the subsequent" (*parādivat*), consider the example: *khaṭvā*. Here, from the word *khaṭvā*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*. A long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) results in the form *ākāra*. By virtue of being treated as "like the subsequent," this [long] *ā* is considered to have the nature of *ṭāp*; consequently, the case-ending *su* following it is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*.

This too cannot be resolved by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), because the author himself will state later that the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* etc. (*halṅyādi-lopa*) here depends upon an original *al* (vowel) as its cause. And this being so, in the case of the root *yaj*, in the *laṅ* [aorist], first person singular, after the addition of *iṭ*, *śap*, and *āṭ-guṇa*, with the augment *aṭ*, we have *ayaje*.

Regarding the word *indram*, it might be argued that because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) vowel *i*—which is a quality (*guṇa*)—is treated as the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādivattva*), it is identical to the letter *i*; therefore, when this *i* follows [the preceding *e*], a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) should occur. However, it must be stated that in this context, only the properties of the collection of phonemes (*al-samudāya-dharmāḥ*)—such as being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*), being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subantatva*), and being an affix (*pratyayatva*)—are extended by analogy (*atidiśyante*), and not [other properties].

Properties such as *atva* (the quality of being *a*) and *hrasvatva* (shortness) belong solely to the phoneme (*varṇa*). And it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, not so, because there is no extension (*atideśa*) of that form. The meaning is that in cases such as *ayaja indram*, since there is no extension of properties residing solely in the final or initial phonemes, the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) and the like do not occur.
Enough with this excessive detail.

[The rule] "The *visarjanīya* occurs in place of the *repha* before a hard consonant (*khaR*) or a pause" (Pāṇini 8.3.15) applies here. In the case of *upārcchati*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *ār* is treated as if it were the final element of the preceding member (*pūrvāntavat*), [the *repha* is not elided].

The connection with what follows is: "when the letter *repha* (r) is at the end of a word (*padānta*), the substitution of *visarga* would [otherwise] occur. To the question, "How is the occurrence of *visarga* obtained? he says: "in the case of a consonant (*khara*) or a pause (*avasāna*). From the rule "ro rī" (*Pāṇini 8.3.14*), the word "ra" in the genitive case is understood by anuvṛtti. And that [genitive] qualifies the term "of a word" (*pada*), which is the governing topic (*adhikṛta*). By which...

The term *vidhi* (rule) is understood here as referring to that which ends in the letter *r*. The meaning is that the *visarjanīya* shall replace the final *r* of a word when followed by a *khari* sound or at the end of a sentence (*avasāna*). By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, this substitution applies to the final [sound].
And although the "end of a sentence" (*avasāna*) is essentially a non-entity, its status as being "subsequent" (*paratva*) is established through mental construction.

He states the result: "and at the end of a word" (*khar-avasāne ca*). Regarding "at the end of a word" (*padānte*), the words "of that which exists" (*vidyamānasya*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
