If, however, the designation *avasāna* (pause) were applied to the final phoneme itself, then the application [of the rule] would be in the phrase "the pause is *avasāna*" (*avasānam*), as stated in the rule "the cessation [of sound] is *avasāna*" (*virāmo'vasānam*). Thus ends the section on the *visarga*. [This applies] in examples such as *upārcchati*, etc., by means of this [rule].
The meaning is that when the occasion for *visarga* arises, its avoidance is now stated. Regarding the term "antavat" (having an end):

the meaning is that *visarga* does not occur for the letter *r* which has reached the status of being a word-final (*padānta*) by virtue of having an end. To the question "Why?", he says: "In both types of *ṛk*s. Otherwise, there would have been an explicit mention of *visarga* even in those cases.
[This is] the state of being. [Objection: But here, the mention of "in a verbal root" (*dhātau*) is redundant;

for by the very mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*), the status of being "in a verbal root" is already established, since the designation "prefix" is prescribed only when there is a connection with an action (*kriyā*). Nor is it the case that in the example *uparkāraḥ* (derived from *upagata ṛkāraḥ*), because the connection with an action exists and because it is a prefix, the rule for *vṛddhi* substitution would apply.
It must be stated that the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) here is for the purpose of excluding that [undesired application], because by the *paribhāṣā*—"prefixes (*pra-*, etc.

have the designations 'motion' (*gati*) and 'preverb' (*upasarga*) only with respect to that action which they are connected to"—they possess the status of a preverb only with respect to the implied action of going; and in the present case, it is precisely the status of a preverb caused by the vowel *ṛ* [that is intended].

Anticipating the objection that [the root] is already intended [to be included], he says: "By the mention of the prefix alone," and so forth. The syntactical connection is as follows: since the root is implied by the very mention of the prefix through the principle of *arthāpatti* (presumption based on the impossibility of otherwise), the further statement "in the case of a root" (*dhātau*) is for the purpose of a re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*). How so?

Regarding the attainment of a further rule, he says: "by means of the division of the *yoga*. The word *yoga* is a synonym for the word *sūtra*. The *sūtra* "upasargād ṛti" and "dhātau" is divided [into two].
Therein, in the preceding *sūtra* "upasargād ṛti," the word "dhātau" is understood by implication from the context.

The meaning already stated is obtained. Even in the subsequent sūtra, "dhātau," the preceding sūtra, "upasargād ṛti," is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Thus, this sūtra becomes identical in meaning to the preceding one;
the sense is that there is an acquisition of a restatement (*punarvidhāna*). For what purpose is this?
Regarding the term "re-enactment" (*punarvidhāna*), he says: "by that" (*tena*). This means "by means of re-enactment.
[In the rule] *vā supyāpiśaleḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.92), it is stated that [the *prakṛtibhāva*] does not occur. Even though the *prakṛtibhāva* is subsequent, it is set aside by the force of the re-enactment.
This is the meaning. In the rule *vā supi*, the preceding sūtra *upasargād ṛti dhātau* is carried over (*anuvartate*).

From *ād guṇaḥ* and *vṛddhir eci*, the terms *āt* and *vṛddhiḥ* are respectively carried over. By the term *āt*, the word *upasargāt* is qualified; thus, this is a case of *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element).
By the *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), the word "sup" is intended to mean a verbal root whose base form ends in a case-ending (*subanta*).

Furthermore, the rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" (one [element] replaces both the preceding and the following) is also governing this context. This is what he states with the words beginning "from that which ends in an *a*-vowel," etc.
Regarding the term "in a *subdhātu*": the meaning is "when a verbal root having a base ending in a case-ending follows"; [it does not refer to] the case-ending itself.

Because it is impossible for [the word] to be a verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the term "single substitute" (*ekādeśa*), the remainder of the rule is *pūrvaparayor acor ari* ("of the preceding and following vowels, when followed by a vowel").

Although it is possible for forms such as *ṛccha* (from the root *ṛcch* 'to go') in its *kvip*-derived state to possess both the status of a verbal root and the status of being a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), nevertheless, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *tusyāsya*, examples such as *upārkārīyati* are given as illustrations of this very point.
Since this is stated in the Bhāṣya, the interpretation that [the suffixes] have *subanta* (inflected nominal stems) as their base is indeed appropriate.
Now, one might object: "Since the desired result is already established by the very mention of the word *vā* (optionally), the mention of Āpiśali is redundant.
To this he says: "The mention of Āpiśali... This point is also accepted by the teacher Āpiśali.

The meaning is "for the sake of obtaining" [a bull], etc. Regarding *prārṣabhīyati*: in the sense of "he desires a bull for himself," the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*; then, by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, it acquires the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). By the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*). Finally, by the rule *kyaci ca*, the substitution of *ī* occurs [for the final vowel of the stem].

*laṭ*, *tip*, *śap*. [By the rule of] *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form), when *pra ṛṣabhīyati* is established, *vṛddhi* (the substitution of *ā*) occurs by this [rule]. Then there is the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. Thus: *prarṣabhīyati*. In the alternative case where *vṛddhi* does not occur, there is *guṇa* (the substitution of *ar*) by *ādguṇaḥ*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. [The phrase] "due to homogeneity" (*sāvarṇyāt*) refers to the rule *ṛlṛvarṇayoḥ*.

The meaning is that by the rule *sāvarṇyād ṛti*, there is also the inclusion of *ḷ*. In the form *upālkārīyati*, the sense is "he desires *ḷ* for himself"; *kyac* and so on are applied as before, with the specific distinction being the substitution of *l* for *r*.
In *upalkārīyati*, because there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution], there is *guṇa* here, and the substitution of *l* for *r* applies.

Regarding the phrase *taparatvāt*: because the vowel *ṛ* is marked with a following *t* (i.e., *ṛt*), only that [vowel] of its specific duration is grasped; therefore, when a long *ṛ* (*ṝ*) follows, this optional *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur, but rather only *guṇa* substitution takes place.
This is the meaning. The form *ṛkārīyati* is derived from the sense "he desires the vowel *ṛ* for himself" by adding *kyac* and so forth.

As before; because there is no *vṛddhi*, there is only *guṇa* here. (78) *eṅi pararūpam* | 6|1|94|. *eṅi pararūpam*. The [terms] "from a prefix" (*upasargāt*) and "in a verbal root" (*dhātau*) are carried over [from previous rules].
The term *ādityanuvṛtam* (followed by *āditya*) is an adjective qualifying *upasargāt* (from a preposition); thus, there is an application of the rule for [an element] ending in that [term].

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "in a rule where [something] is prescribed, that which begins with it is also included," there is the inclusion of what begins with that [term]. Furthermore, the governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* ("one [substitute] in place of the preceding and the following") is also in force. This is what he states with the words beginning "from that which ends in an *a*-vowel" (*avarṇāntāt*), and so forth.

Regarding "ekādeśa" (single substitute): the phrase "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder of the rule. In the case of *prejataḥ*: the root *ejṛ* means "to tremble. When *pra-ejate* is established, this [rule] provides the single substitute *e* (the *pararūpa*), overriding the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhireci*. However, the root *ejṛ* meaning "to shake" is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. Regarding *upoṣati*: the root *uṣ*...

In the case of *dāhe* (in the sense of burning): *laṭ*, *tip*, *śap*. The *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) applies. When *uṣa* + *oṣati* is established, this rule [Pāṇini 6.1.97] effects the substitution of *o* instead of [the usual] *vṛddhi*.
Now, consider *eḍakaḥ* (a ram); one who desires that for himself is *eḍakīyati*.
When *upa* + *eḍakīyati* is established, by this rule [Pāṇini 6.1.94], there would invariably be the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpam*).
But an increase [of the vowel] is also desired—as in *upaiḍakīyati* and *upaiḍakīyati*. To this he says: "In this case," etc.

In the rule *eṅi pararūpam*, the phrase *vā supi* ("optionally before a *sup* suffix") is understood to carry over. However, that [phrase] does not connect as part of a single syntactical unit [with the current rule].
For if it were so connected, then when a *sub*-suffix follows a verbal root beginning with *eṅ* after a preposition ending in an *a*-vowel...

The meaning would simply be that the single substitute (ekādeśa) might be the subsequent form (pararūpa). This being the case, in forms such as *prejate* and *upoṣati*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would not necessarily occur. Therefore, it must be explained by splitting the rule into two distinct statements. The first statement is: "In place of iṭ and eṅ, the subsequent form [occurs]."

The meaning of that [first rule] is: when a vowel beginning with *e* or *o* follows a preposition ending in a non-vowel, there shall be a single substitute of the form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*) before a verbal root beginning with *a*. The second sentence is "vā supi" (Pāṇini 6.1.92). Therein, "eiṅ pararūpam" is understood from the previous context, as are the conditions "dhātau" and "upasargāt". And therefore:
It is understood that when a *sub*-ending stem (*subdhātu*) follows, the single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) may optionally occur in the scope of the previously mentioned rule.

This is what is meant by the word "thereby" (*tena*). According to the aforementioned method, by resorting to a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the single-substitute form is optional when the *sub*-ending begins with *eṅ*, whereas it is obligatory for other stems; such is the meaning. Thus [ends the section].
And [this applies] except when there is *niyoga*. He explains the word *niyoga*: "niyoga is restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

Restriction is the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). When the word *eva* occurs in that other sense [of restriction], provided it follows the letter *a*, there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) consisting of the form of the subsequent [element] for both the preceding and following sounds.
The meaning is "it might be. Regarding "kveva bhokṣyase" (where indeed will you eat?), the meaning is that we do not ascertain "here.
Since "kva-eva" is established, by this Vārttika the single substitute *e* (ekāra) occurs, overriding the rule for *vṛddhi*.
Regarding "anavaklṛptau," the meaning is "in the sense of non-determination. Regarding "tavaiva," the meaning is "of you alone, and not of another."

In this very context, because the word *eva* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), there is no substitution of a single substitute (*pararūpa*) when that [vowel] follows. Now, in order to prescribe the substitution of a single substitute for *ṭi* in certain cases, he states the technical designation *ṭi*: "The last vowel among the vowels is called *ṭi*" (*aco 'ntyādi ṭi*). In the expression *aco 'ntyāt*, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*). That which exists at the end is *antya*; *antya-*...
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose beginning is [the same as] its end. He states the resulting meaning: "in the midst of vowels.

Regarding the rule *śakandhvādiṣu*: the meaning is that for the sake of establishing such forms within the category of *śakandhu* and others, it must be stated that the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs for both the preceding and following sounds. Consequently, in the case of words such as *śaka* and so forth—

When *ṭi* follows, the meaning obtained is that a single substitute in the form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*) occurs in place of both the *ṭi* and the following vowel (*ac*). This is because, despite the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *āt*, forms such as *sīmanta* and others within the *śakandhvādi* group would otherwise remain unestablished. Thus he says: "And that [is taught] by the rule *ṭeḥ*."

He recites the *śakandhvādi* group, beginning with "śakandhu" and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "the well (*andhu*) of the Śakas," referring to a specific region. When *karka-andhu* is established, the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) applies. Regarding *kulaṭā*: the root *aṭ* means "to go"; the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* class, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied.

The analysis of the compound is *kulānām aṭati* ("she wanders among families"). A woman who wanders from house to house for the sake of alms or for the sake of sexual misconduct is called a *kulaṭā*. However, if the analysis were *kulāny aṭati*, then by the rule *karmaṇy aṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), the suffix *aṇ* would be applied; subsequently, by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would be added. Thus, with the form *kula-aṭā* established, the substitution of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*) would apply.

Regarding the rule *sīmantaḥ keśaveśe*: this is a *vārttika* included within the *gaṇa*. "Arrangement of hair" (*keśaveśaḥ*) refers to a particular mode of arrangement of the hair. When that [meaning] is to be understood, the meaning of the rule is that there is a single *pararūpa* substitute in place of both the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the word *sīman*—which is not necessarily fixed—and the vowel *a* of the word *anta*. However, if the term *āditya* is supplied from the preceding context...
This would not be established [by the rule].
"Another boundary" (*sīmānta*) means the region at the edge of a village. Regarding the term *manīṣā*:
the analysis of the compound is *manasa īṣā* (the desire of the mind). Here, by the suffix *ṭhañ*, in place of the final vowel (*ṭi*) and the letter *ī*, [the substitution of *ai* occurs].
The subsequent form is *īkāra* (the vowel *ī*). From the root *īṣ* meaning "to go," the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

According to Amara, *buddhiḥ* and *manīṣā* are synonyms. Regarding *halīṣā*: according to Amara, *īṣā* means "the shaft of a plow. The analysis of the compound is *halasya īṣā* (the shaft of the plow). This is a tautology, similar to the term *karikalabha* (an elephant-calf).

It should be corrected. When this quality is attained, the *pararūpa* (single substitute of the form of the subsequent vowel) applies. The same applies in the case of *lāṅgalīṣā*. Regarding *patañjali*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he in whom the hands are joined (*añjali*) while falling (*patan*), because he is worthy of salutation.
Here, by the rule *ṭha'd*, the single substitute *akāra* takes the place of both the final syllable (*ṭi*) and the initial *akāra*. Some, however, [hold otherwise].

According to tradition, [the sage] emerged from the joined palms (*añjali*) of a certain seer at the time of his twilight devotions in the region called Gonarda; thus they analyze the term as *añjaleḥ patan* ("falling from the palms").
It is a compound by virtue of belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class. Furthermore, [the word] *sāraṅga* refers to both animals and birds. This too [is so].

This is a *vārttika* included within the *Gaṇapāṭha*, as it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*. The word *sāra* means "excellent. According to Amara: "The word *sāra* [is used] in the sense of strength, the solid part, and what is right; it is neuter, and in the masculine it means 'sky' (*ambara*).
The analysis of the compound is: "one whose limbs (*aṅga*) are *sāra* (excellent). Thus, we have *sāra-aṅga*. At this stage—

When the rule for lengthening a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise apply, this [rule] effects the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). According to the *Anara* lexicon: "The word *sāraṅga* denotes a *cātaka* bird or a deer in the masculine, and something variegated in the three genders. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. The meaning is that this class of words is to be determined by its general form—that is, by the nature of its constituent members.
The meaning is that words of this kind should be included in this group precisely according to common usage.

He states the result of this: "mārtaṇḍa. One whose *maṇḍa* (essence) is dead is *mṛtaṇḍa*, a certain sage. When *mṛta-aṇḍa* is formed, by this [rule], the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels) is superseded.

The subsequent form (*pararūpa*). When the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), [the word] *mārtaṇḍaḥ* is formed. In the Vedic passage "He mounted the supreme *mārtāṇḍa*," however, the long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) is due to the Vedic style (*chāndasa*). Regarding the rule *otvoṣṭhayoḥ*:
when the word *otu* or the word *oṣṭha* follows an *a*-vowel, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) takes the place of both the preceding and following sounds (*racau*).
The meaning is that it must be stated. Regarding "sthūlotuḥ": according to Amarasimha, "otuḥ" means "biḍālaḥ" (cat) or "mārjāraḥ" (cat).
When "sthūla-otuḥ" is established, the optional *pararūpa* (single-substitute form) applies, overriding the rule for *vṛddhi*.
Regarding "bimboṣṭhaḥ": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose lips are red in color like the bimba fruit."

(79) *omāṅośca* | Pāṇini 6.1.95. The analysis of the compound is *om* and *āṅ*. The words *āt* (from the previous rule), *pararūpam* (the single substitute is the latter form), and *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (a single substitute takes the place of both the preceding and the following) are understood here. This is what he states with the words beginning "omīti" and so forth.
Regarding "śivāryo namaḥ": here, setting aside the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution], the *pararūpa* (single-substitute form) applies. Regarding "śivahī":

when *āḥ* and *ihi* are present, the *guṇa* [vowel substitution] results in the form *ehi*. Then, when "śiva-ehi" is present, setting aside the *vṛddhi*, the *pararūpa*—the single vowel *e*—applies. And it is not the case that, when "śiva-aḥihī" is present...

It should not be argued that the mention of *āṅ* is redundant because the form *śivehi* is established by first applying the rule for long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) and subsequently applying the rule for *guṇa*; for, according to the maxim "an operation between a root and a prefix is internal (*antaraṅga*)," the *guṇa* would apply first, resulting in *śiva-ehi*, at which point the rule for *vṛddhi* would be applicable.

Because it is for the purpose of excluding that [substitution]. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is established that the mention of *āt* (the long *ā*) is for the purpose of excluding the *savarṇadīrgha* [substitution] in cases such as *ā ṛśyāt*, *guṇaḥ arśyāt*, *adya-arśyāt*, and *adyarśyāt*.

(80) *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta iti* Pāṇini 6.1.98. The phrase "the subsequent form" (*pararūpa*) is understood [from the previous rule]. "Indistinct" (*avyakta*) refers to a sound produced by the falling of trees and the like, in which the distinction between phonemes (*varṇa*) is not clear.
The imitation of that [sound] is a word similar to it which expresses it, having indistinct phonemic distinctions (*aparisphuṭavarṇavibhāga*).

The meaning is that when the word *iti* follows, the single substitute (*pararūpa*) occurs in place of the vowel *a* (denoted by *at*) and the vowel *i* (denoted by *añc*) which are its constituent parts. Here, in the word *iti*, that which is the first...

It should be explained as "the letter *i* [is substituted] when that [suffix] follows. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the entire word *iti* being replaced. He states this with the words beginning "dhavaneḥ" and so forth.

In this case, the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*) does not apply, because of the principle: "there is no application of the rule for the final [element] when [the substitute] is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lo'ntyavidhiḥ*).

Because of the prohibition. "paṭat-iti" is an illustration of the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*). One should not, however, be deluded into thinking that this is the form when there is no substitution of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*), for in this case, the substitution of the subsequent vowel is obligatory. Alternatively, it is an indication [of the form] when there is no *saṃhitā*. "paṭiti" is an example. "vṛkṣaḥ" [is another].
The words "fallen" (*patita*) and so forth are to be supplied [from the context].
Here, he summarizes the meaning of the *vārttika*—"the mention of 'more than one vowel' (*anekāc*) must be made"—as follows: "not for that which has a single vowel.
That which has one vowel (*ac*) is "single-voweled" (*ekāc*); for such an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the previously mentioned substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) does not apply.
The meaning is "no. Regarding the term *aditi*: here, because it consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule does not apply. Now, one might object:
in the case of *paṭat-paṭat iti*, the form *paṭat-paṭeti* is desired;
however, if the *pararūpa* rule from the sūtra *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau* were to apply there, the result would necessarily be *paṭat-paṭiti*.

(81) *Nā'mreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* [Pāṇini 6.1.99]. Regarding this, he says: *nā'mreḍitasya*. The rules *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau* [Pāṇini 6.1.98], *pararūpam* [Pāṇini 6.1.94], and *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.84] are understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).

In the case of an imitative sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) that is reduplicated (*āmreḍita*), the single-substitute *pararūpa* shall not occur for the vowel *a* which is a constituent part of that sound when followed by the word *iti*. However, it may optionally occur for the final [vowel]. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. The meaning is that the single-substitute *pararūpa* may optionally occur for the final *t* and the *i* [of *iti*] alone, but not for the *a* as well.

He says this with the words beginning "of that which is reduplicated, as previously stated," and so forth. Now, one might ask: how is there reduplication in *paṭat-paṭat*? To this he says: "in the case of *ḍāc*. The grammatical connection is: "in the case of *ḍāc*, reduplication occurs diversely (*bahulam*). Now, [one might further object]: according to the rule "after an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) consisting of two or more syllables, when followed by *anit*, [the suffix *ḍāc* is added],"...
One might ask: "How can there be the occurrence of the suffix *ḍāc* here [in the word *ḍāci*], since there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of it when the word *iti* follows?

To this he says: "Because of the mention of *bahula*. Without having stated "or" (*vā*), the mention of *bahula* is for the purpose of providing various rules; it is called *bahula* because it takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) many meanings.
The meaning is that this is due to the understanding of that [rule].

(82) *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (Pāṇini 8.1.2). And those who are proficient in grammar say: "In some cases there is application; in some cases there is non-application; in some cases there is an option (*vibhāṣā*)."

In some cases, it is indeed otherwise; this should be understood in common usage by following the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), provided there is frequent occurrence [of such usage]. Now, what is called *āmreḍita*?
To that he says: "The subsequent [word] of that is *āmreḍita*. This sūtra follows immediately after the rule "sarvasya dve" (Pāṇini 8.1.1).
It is recited [in the rule]. Consequently, by the word "tasya" (of that), "of the reduplicated form" is understood.
Precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the genitive case is used in connection with the word "para" (subsequent), which denotes a part [of the reduplication].
Thus he says: "of the reduplicated," and so forth. *paṭat-paṭetīti* means *paṭat paṭat iti*.
When [the word] *paṭat* stands, there is the single substitute *ikāra* for both the *takāra* and the *ikāra* by the rule of *pararūpa*. Then, by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, [the result is *paṭit*].

(83) By the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* (Pāṇini 8.2.39), in the alternative case where *pararūpa* does not apply—namely, in the case of *paṭat-paṭat iti*—there is the substitution of *dakāra* for the *takāra*.
The rule *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte* is prescribed. The term *padasya* (of a word) is understood [from the governing context]. Therefore, it says "at the end of a word" (*padānte*).
Regarding the example *paṭat-paṭat-i*: the meaning is that, due to the equality of place of articulation (*sthāna-sāmyāt*), the letter *t* is replaced by *d*, which is a *jaś* sound.
Here, since there is no prohibition of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule for the word *ac-chabda*, [the substitution applies] to the letter *t* alone.

It should be noted that when there is an option regarding the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa-ekādeśa*), in the alternative where that subsequent form does not occur, the subsequent form would apply to the word *at* by the preceding rule, resulting in *paṭatpaṭiti*. (84) *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* | P. 6.1.101. When a vowel homogeneous (*savarṇa*) to a short or long *ak*-vowel (*akaḥ*) follows, a single long substitute takes the place of both. For example, *daityāriḥ* (*daitya-ariḥ*), *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ* (*khaṭvā-ārūḍhaḥ*), *hotṛkāraḥ* (*hotṛ-kāraḥ*), *tātṛkāraḥ* (*tātṛ-kāraḥ*). The term *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to indicate the sense of "substitution" (*sthāne*); it is understood as "in the place of *ak*" (*akaḥ sthāne*). The word *dīrghaḥ* is used in the nominative case (*prathamā*) to indicate the "substitute" (*ādeśa*); it is understood as "a long [vowel] is the substitute" (*dīrgha ādeśo bhavati*). The word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case (*saptamī*) to indicate the sense of "when following" (*pare*); it is understood as "when a homogeneous vowel follows" (*savarṇe pare*). In this context, the term *savarṇa* refers to those vowels that possess the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*). This is because the definition of *savarṇa* is given as "those which have the same place of articulation and effort" (*tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam*). Furthermore, the word *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case to express the sense of "substitution," and the word *dīrghaḥ* is used in the nominative case to express the sense of "substitute. The word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case to express the sense of "when following. [Counter-examples: *dadhi atra*, *madhu atra*—here, because the *i* and *u* are not homogeneous with the preceding *a*, the long substitute does not occur. *Khaṭvā indraḥ*, *hotṛ udakaḥ*—here, although the *ā* and *u* are homogeneous, they are not homogeneous with the preceding *a*, so the long substitute does not occur. *Daityāriḥ*, *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ*, *hotṛkāraḥ*, *tātṛkāraḥ*—here, because the *a* and *ā* are homogeneous, the long substitute occurs. Regarding the phrase "a single long substitute": since the word *eka* is used, it is understood that a single substitute occurs in the place of two sounds (*dvayoḥ sthāne eka ādeśaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "homogeneous vowel": since the word *savarṇa* is used, it is understood that the substitute is a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa eva ādeśaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in the place of *ak*": since the word *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case, it is understood that the substitute occurs in the place of an *ak*-vowel (*akaḥ sthāne*). Regarding the phrase "when a homogeneous vowel follows": since the word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case, it is understood that the substitute occurs when a homogeneous vowel follows (*savarṇe pare*). Thus, the meaning is: "When a homogeneous vowel follows an *ak*-vowel, a single long substitute occurs in the place of both. [Application: *daityāriḥ* (*daitya-ariḥ*), *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ* (*khaṭvā-ārūḍhaḥ*), *hotṛkāraḥ* (*hotṛ-kāraḥ*), *tātṛkāraḥ* (*tātṛ-kāraḥ*). [Objection: If this were the case, then in *khaṭvā-indraḥ*, *hotṛ-udakaḥ*, etc., the long substitute would also occur because the *ā* and *u* are homogeneous with each other. [Response: No, because the word *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case to express the sense of "substitution," and the word *dīrghaḥ* is used in the nominative case to express the sense of "substitute," while the word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case to express the sense of "when following. Therefore, the meaning is: "When a homogeneous vowel follows an *ak*-vowel, a single long substitute occurs in the place of both. Since the *ā* and *u* in *khaṭvā-indraḥ* and *hotṛ-udakaḥ* are not homogeneous with the preceding *a*, the long substitute does not occur. [Objection: Even so, in *dadhi-atra*, *madhu-atra*, etc., the long substitute would occur because the *i* and *u* are homogeneous with the *a*. [Response: No, because the word *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case to express the sense of "substitution," and the word *dīrghaḥ* is used in the nominative case to express the sense of "substitute," while the word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case to express the sense of "when following. Therefore, the meaning is: "When a homogeneous vowel follows an *ak*-vowel, a single long substitute occurs in the place of both. Since the *i* and *u* in *dadhi-atra* and *madhu-atra* are not homogeneous with the preceding *a*, the long substitute does not occur. [Objection: Even so, in *khaṭvā-indraḥ*, *hotṛ-udakaḥ*, etc., the long substitute would occur because the *ā* and *u* are homogeneous with each other. [Response: No, because the word *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case to express the sense of "substitution," and the word *dīrghaḥ* is used in the nominative case to express the sense of "substitute," while the word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case to express the sense of "when following. Therefore, the meaning is: "When a homogeneous vowel follows an *ak*-vowel, a single long substitute occurs in the place of both. Since the *ā* and *u* in *khaṭvā-indraḥ* and *hotṛ-udakaḥ* are not homogeneous with the preceding *a*, the long substitute does not occur. [Objection: Even so, in *dadhi-atra*, *madhu-atra*, etc., the long substitute would occur because the *i* and *u* are homogeneous with the *a*. [Response: No, because the word *akaḥ* is used in the genitive case to express the sense of "substitution," and the word *dīrghaḥ* is used in the nominative case to express the sense of "substitute," while the word *savarṇe* is used in the locative case to express the sense of "when following. Therefore, the meaning is: "When a homogeneous vowel follows an *ak*-vowel, a single long substitute occurs in the place of both. Since the *i* and *u* in *dadhi-atra* and *madhu-atra* are not homogeneous with the preceding *a*, the long substitute does not occur. [Objection: Even so, in *khaṭvā-indraḥ*, *hotṛ-udakaḥ*, etc., the long substitute would occur because the *ā* and *u* are homogeneous with each

*akaḥ savarṇe*. The word *ṭhakaḥ* is in the ablative case. From the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci*, the term *aci* is understood by anuvṛtti (carrying over). The governing rule *ṭhekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is also in force. Thus he says: "When a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) follows a short *a*-vowel (*akaḥ*), [the single long substitute occurs] in place of both," and so forth.
In the case of *daityāriḥ*: when *daitya-arir* is established, one long vowel replaces the two *a*-vowels.
The *ākāra* [is substituted] due to the similarity of position (*sthāna*). When *śrī-īśa* is present, one of the two *ī*-sounds becomes a single *ī*.

When *viṣṇu-udaya* is present, one of the two *u*-sounds becomes an *ū*. He asks—“What is the purpose of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aci*?”—by asking, “Why [specify] *aci*? [The answer is: as in *kumārī śete*.

If the term *aci* were not carried over [from the previous rule], then because the vowel *ī* and the consonant *ś* share the same place of articulation (the palate) and the same open effort (*vivṛta-prayatna*), they would be considered homogeneous (*savarṇa*); consequently, a long *ī* would result as a single substitute for those two.
To prevent this, it is intended that the term *aci* must be carried over. Now, one might object:

Although there is equality of place (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*) between the vowel *ī* and the consonant *ś*, they do not share the property of being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*), because of the prohibition in the rule "nājjhalau" (Pāṇini 1.1.10).

Therefore, since the application of the rule "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.101) is impossible in the example "kumārī śete," the continued reference to the term "ac" (vowel) [in the subsequent sūtra] would be redundant; to address this, he says: "because of the prohibition nājjhalau."

The prohibition of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) by the rule *nājjhalau* applies only to those vowels and consonants included in the phonetic inventory (*vārṇasamāmnāyika*), and not even to the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels; for it is understood from the rule *ādirantyena sahetā* that only those [sounds] in the phonetic inventory are denotable by the term *ac*. Therefore...
The meaning is that because there is phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ī* and the consonant *ś*, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur in the case of "kumārī śete";
therefore, the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aci* is necessary. Now, one might object:
even if only those sounds enumerated in the *vārṇasamāmnāya* are denoted by the word *ac*, [the rule still holds].

By virtue of the rule *aṇudit*, there is also the inclusion of the short, long, and protracted forms (*hrasva-dīrgha-pluta*) by means of the letters *a* and so forth presented by the word *ac*. Consequently, since there is no possibility of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the letter *ī* and the letter *ś*, the non-continuance (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aj* would be useless; therefore, he says: "by the [term] *grahaṇaka*."

For the *grahaṇaka-sūtra* "aṇuditsavarṇasya... is only capable of functioning in rules such as "ṭhasya cvau" once it has acquired its own existence; however, at the stage when the rule "nājjhalau" is in operation, this *grahaṇaka-śāstra* has not yet acquired its own existence. Indeed, that [latter rule]...

Because it is composed of words denoting homogeneous phonemes (*savarṇa*), its existence is only established after the meaning of those words has been understood. And although the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (Pāṇini 1.1.9), which prescribes the technical designation of homogeneity, conveys its own general meaning,
it finds its final application only outside the scope of the exception *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10).

It attains the capacity for its own function. And it has been said: "The general rule applies after setting aside the scope of the exception. Thus, there is the operation of the sūtra *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (Pāṇini 1.1.9) together with the prohibition *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10), which pertains to the sūtra *aṇuditsavarṇasya...* (Pāṇini 1.1.69).

Because [the vowel *i*] has not yet acquired its own status as a technical term (*prāgalbhyātmatā*), the long and protracted vowels are not included by the mention of *ac* in the rule *nājjhalau*; consequently, since there is no prohibition of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ī* and the consonant *ś*, homogeneity does exist. Thus, in the case of *kumārī śete*, the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* would apply.

The meaning is that, for the purpose of excluding that [undesired application], the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *aci* must be resorted to. This very point was explained in detail during the commentary on the passage beginning with "Even though there is the prohibition of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) by the rule *na-aj-jhalau*. [Furthermore, one might argue that] it would be easier to simply state "a long vowel replaces a short *a* before a short *a*" (*ako 'ki dīrghaḥ*). And in this way, the mention of the term "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) need not be made at all.
[The principle of] brevity [is applied]. However, in the case of *dadhyukāra*, there is no over-extension because the rule relies on the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṃkhya*).
Consequently, the intention is that the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aci* need not be resorted to.
Regarding the Vārttika "In the case of *ṛ*, [the substitute] is optionally *ṛ*," the word *savarṇa* is carried over from the rule "A vowel homogeneous with itself... (*akaḥ savarṇe*).

Having applied [the rule], he recites: *ṛti savarṇe ṛ vā*. The term *akaḥ* is understood from the previous context, as is the principle *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*. The meaning is that when a vowel (*akaḥ*) is followed by a homogeneous *ṛ*-sound (*ṛti*), there shall be a single substitute *ṛ* for both the preceding and the following sounds. For example: *hotṛkāraḥ*.

When "hotṛ-ṛkāra" is established, by this [rule], in place of the two *ṛ* sounds, there arises a certain phoneme possessing two *repha*s (visargas), which is distinct from the *ṛ* sound and possesses a dual nature like that of Nṛsiṃha. He shows the form in the absence of this [application]: "hotṛṛkāra."
By the rule *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe*, a long vowel [is substituted].

Regarding *lṛti savarṇe lṛ vā*: the meaning is that when a homogeneous *lṛ* follows a vowel (*akaḥ*), there is optionally a single substitute *lṛ* for both the preceding and the following sounds. Thus, *hotṛ-lṛkāraḥ* becomes *hotlṛkāraḥ*.

This being the case, in place of the *ṛ*-vowel and the *lṛ*-vowel, there arises a certain phoneme consisting of two *lṛ*s, which has the nature of being between the word *nṛ* and *siṃha*. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*):
in the alternative view where such a phoneme having the nature of being between the two does not exist, there is simply the *a*-vowel in place of the *ṛ*-vowel and the *lṛ*-vowel.

The meaning is that when [the rule] *savarṇe* prescribes a long vowel, because of the mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*, only the long *ṛ* occurs, since there is no long form for the sound *ḷ*. For this very reason, in the case of *hotṛ-lṛkāra*, the *Bhāṣya* provides *hotṛṛkāra* as the example under the alternative view of the long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrgha*). Now, [regarding the rule] *ṛti ṛ vā*.

In the rule *ṭh-lṛ-ti lṛ-ve*, he distinguishes the nature of the phonemes to be prescribed: "In both cases, the two phonemes to be prescribed are each of two morae (*dvimātra*). He establishes this very point with the words "in the middle of the first" and "one mora. This is because, since consonants consist of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), each individual *repha* (the letter *r*) consists of half a mora.
The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "abhito'jbhakteḥ," after the word "abhitaḥ," the words "rephayoḥ" (of the two *repha*s) are to be supplied.
The singular number in "ajbhakteḥ" is used with a general intention. The meaning is that there is another *mātrā* for the short *ṛ*-portion existing both before and above the two *repha*s.

Regarding the phrase "of the second": the word "of that which is to be prescribed" (*vidheyasya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "The rest is as before" means that one *mātrā* belongs to the two *lakāra*s, and another *mātrā* belongs to the two portions of *lṛkāra* situated on either side of them. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the *Tulyāsyaprayatna* sūtra. By this...

The statement in the ancient treatises that "when a long vowel is obtained, a short *ṛ* or *ḷ* is prescribed here" is refuted. "Optional" (*pākṣika*) means alternative. "Prakṛtibhāva" (the state of being the original form) means remaining in one's unmodified nature; that is to say, the absence of *saṃdhi*.

(85) *eṅḥ padāntādati* | Pāṇini 6.1.109. From the rule *ami pūrvaḥ*, the word *pūrvaḥ* is understood to carry over. The governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is also in force. Thus he says [the sūtra] with the words "from the end of a word" (*padāntāt*), etc. Example: *hare-ava*.

In the case of *sthite*, the single substitute *e* (ekāra) occurs by overriding the substitution of *ay*. In the case of *viṣṇo-ava*, the single substitute *o* (okāra) occurs by overriding the substitution of *āv*.
(86) *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.122.

The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies everywhere. The phrase *padāntāt* (from the end of a word) is understood from the previous rule. From the rule *ṭhprakṛtyāntaḥpādam*, the term *prakṛtyā* (by its original form) is also understood. This means that [the vowel] remains in its original nature (*prakṛtyā*), that is, in its own state without modification. [This is understood] from the rule *yajuṣyuraḥ*.

The term *yajuṣi* is understood from the preceding context. To indicate this, the word *sarvatra* ("everywhere") is employed; by this, both "in common usage" (*loke*) and "in the Veda" (*vede*) are obtained. Thus he says: "In common usage," and so forth. "Original state" (*prakṛtibhāva*) means remaining in one's own nature. And thus, there is neither the substitution of the former vowel (*pūrvarūpa*) nor the substitution of *ava*.

The form *go'gram* arises through the application of the *prakṛtibhāva* rule; otherwise, by the rule of *pūrvarūpa*, it would be *go agram*. Here, the term *eṅ* also continues to apply [from the previous rule]. Consequently, by the maxim that "that which is modified in one part is not treated as something else," there is no over-extension of the rule to the case of *citragvagram*. Furthermore, [the rule] does not apply to *he citrago'gram* either.

There is no preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), because the rule applies only to the *eṅ* vowels specified by their actual wording (*pratipadokta*). In the present case, however, the vowel *o* in the word "go" is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical operation) by the rule "the guna of a short vowel. Thus, in the stage "go as," since the *o* of "go" does not occupy the end of a word (*padāntatva*), there is no preservation of the original form.

Nor should it be argued that, because [the vowel] is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*), the *pūrvarūpa* substitution prescribed by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* would also be impossible; for it is precisely for this reason that the *pūrvarūpa* is introduced there by the rule *ṅsiṅsośca*. (87) *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya* 6.1.123.

"avaṅ is substituted [for the final vowel of *go*] according to the opinion of Sphoṭāyana. The word "at" (from Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.93) has ceased to apply; the remainder is from 6.1.76 (*ṭheṅḥ padāntāt*), as is understood from the commentary. The words "padāntāt," "goḥ," and "aci" are carried over [from previous rules]. According to the view of the sage Sphoṭāyana, *avaṅ* is substituted; for others, however, it is not. Consequently:

The alternative interpretation is established. Thus he says, beginning with "before a vowel" (*aci pare*), etc. [This refers to] the substitution of *avaṅ* for the final syllable ending in *ṅ*. In the case of *gavāgram*, when *go-agram* is situated, the *avaṅ* replaces the *o* following the *g*.
When *gava-agram* is situated, there is a long vowel by rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). Nor is there an *ac* (vowel) in the word *agra*.

It should not be argued that since the *avaṅ* substitution has proceeded by depending upon [the preceding vowel] as being "other" (*para*), how could it then trigger the *savarṇadīrgha* (homogeneous long vowel) rule which destroys that very condition, due to a conflict with the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the destruction of the cause)?
For the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* will be explained later in the case of *rāmāya*.
Regarding *gavi*: when *go* remains as *g-o*, since the vowel *o* lacks the status of being a word-final (*padānta*), *āvaṅ* does not apply.
Nor do the two preceding rules apply to produce either the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) or the subsequent form (*pararūpa*); rather, the substitution *ava* takes place.
However, if the term *ati* were continued [from the previous rule], forms such as *gaveśa* would not be established. Thus, [the rule] is restricted.
In some cases, only the portion "it exists" (bhavati) applies; in others, only the portion "it does not exist" (na bhavati);

and in yet others, both apply. Thus, the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) that functions according to a fixed rule (*vyavasthayā*) in accordance with the specific objects of application is what is intended by the term *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* in the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ*. Consequently, [the form] *gavākṣa* [is established].

In this context, the meaning is that *avaṅ* is obligatory. And this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yaṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.32): "And in the case of the application of *devatrāta*, *aṭhagala*, and *aṭhgrāha*, the rule [for *avaṅ*] applies always; they are not optionally applied to one another, as in *gavākṣaḥ* and *saṃśitavrataḥ*. Regarding *gavākṣa*:
The analysis of the compound is *gavām akṣīva* ("like the eye of cows"). [The suffix] *ac* is applied after *akṣi* by virtue of the rule *akṣṇo 'darśanāt*.
Its masculine gender is established from common usage. Amara states: "A window is called *vātāyana* or *gavākṣa*.
(88) [The suffix *ac* is also applied] after *indra*, [forming *aindra*]. Pāṇini 6.1.124.
And with regard to *indra*: the [sūtras] *ṭhgoḥ*, *ṭhavaṅ*, and *ṭhaci* are understood to follow. Thus he says: "of *go*" (*goriti*).
This is for the purpose of excluding the optionality [of the previous rule]. In the case of *gavendra*, when *go-indra* is situated [as the state of the base], *avaṅ* is applied;
then *ādguṇaḥ* [applies].
It is finished.
Now begins the section on *ad* and other suffixes.
(252) *ṛterīyaṅ* | P. 3.1.29. Regarding *ṛterīyaṅ*: since *ṛti* is not seen in the Dhātupāṭha, he says—"*ṛti* is a word from the Sūtra"—in its own sense (*svārthe*).

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that because no specific meaning is indicated, this verbal root is specified as ending in *takāra* (t), and not as ending in *ikāra* (i). For if it were *idanta* (ending in *i*), the form would be established by the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) alone;
consequently, the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *ī* in the rule *īyaṅ* would be redundant. Nor, even if it were *idanta*, would the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ* apply.

Thus, one should state that *yaṇ* [substitution] would occur; even so, once the *ṅī* suffix is applied by the rule "ṛterṅyaḥ," the desired form is already established by the lengthening rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ," and therefore the prescription of *iyaṅ* would be redundant. The word "eke" means "others. The form "ṛtīyate" [is cited].

Because *īyaṅ* ends in a vowel, there is a single-substitute (*pararūpa*) form before the suffix *śap*. Thus: *ṛtīyāñcakre*. By the rule *kāspratyayād*, the suffix *ām* is added: *ṛtīyitā*. [Future: *ṛtīyiṣyate*. [Imperative:
*ṛtīyatām*. [Imperfect: *ārtīyata*. [Optative: *ṛtīyeta*. [Precative: *ṛtīyiṣīṣṭa*. [Aorist: *ārtīyiṣṭa*. [Conditional: *ārtīyiṣyata*. [Periphrastic perfect: *ānarta*.

From the root *ṛ*, ending in *takāra* (the letter *t*), in the *liṭ* tense with the suffix *ṇal*: after doubling, the substitution of *urat* (short *u*) occurs; then *rapara* (the substitute is followed by *r*); then *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant); then by the rule *ṭhata ādeḥ*, the long vowel is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Then, by the rule *ṭhtasmānnuḍdvihalaḥ*, the augment *nuṭ* is added.
Regarding the prescription of *nuṭ*, the *repha* (the letter *r*) which is a portion of the *ṛ*-vowel is treated as a *hal* (consonant).

The sense is: because of the statement "ityukteḥ. [Regarding the root] *ṛ*: [the forms are] *ānarta*, *ānṛtuḥ*, *ānṛtuḥ*. Since this root is not listed among the *aniṭ* (unaccented) roots, there is invariably *iṭ* in the *thali* (perfect tense suffix). Thus: *ānartitha*, *ānṛtathuḥ*, *ānṛta*, *ānarta*, *ānṛtiva*, *ānṛtima*.
[Future: *artitā*. [Periphrastic future: *artiṣyati*. [Benedictive: *ṛtyāt*. [Aorist: *ārtīt*. In the case of *ārtīt*, there is elision of the *sic* suffix by the rule "*ṭhiṭa īṭi*" (Pāṇini 6.4.62).

The augment *āṭ* is applied. [Thus we have] *ārtiṣyat*. Now, he begins to describe the roots that lack a conjugational suffix (*lugvikaraṇa*): *ada* in the sense of eating. This root is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). (Pāṇini 2.4.72) *adi-prabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ*: [There is elision of the suffix *śap* after the roots beginning with *ad*.]
Intending that the word *luk* (elision) is understood from the rule *ṭhṇyakṣatriyārṣañitaḥ*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "there shall be elision" (*luk syāt*).
The result is that there is elision of *śap* following roots beginning with *ad*. Regarding the example *atīti*: since *śap* has been elided...

The letter *t* is substituted for the suffix *dasya* (the suffix *si* in the second person singular). The same applies to *ataḥ* (the suffix *asi*). [The rule] "they eat" (*adanti*) is for that very purpose; otherwise, in the rule "ṭhjho'ntaḥ," a substitute beginning with the vowel *a* would have been required. Thus: *atsi*, *atthaḥ*, *attha*; *admi*, *advaḥ*, *admaḥ*.
(254) *liṭaḷnyatarasyām* | 2|4|40| The rule *liṭaḷnyatarasyām* follows from *ada* in the rule *ado jagdhir lyapti kiti*, and from *ghaslṛ* in the rule *luṅsanorghaslṛ*. Therefore, he says— *ada*.

Thus [it is said]. In this substitute, the letter *ḷ* is the *it*. Here, the substitute *ghas* is without the augment *iṭ*. Regarding the form *jaghāsa*: the sense is that because the suffix is not *kit*, there is no elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule *gamahana* (Pāṇini 6.4.98). When the form *jaghas atus* is established, he says:
"there is elision of the penultimate vowel by *gamahana*. The sense is that because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5), [the elision applies].

When *jaghÂs atus* is established, anticipating that he will explain the substitution of *c* for the letter *gh*, [the author] raises the doubt regarding the status of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) as being *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element) and says: "tasya" (of that). This means "of the elision of the penultimate vowel.
When *jaghÂs atus* is established, since the *s* does not belong to either a substitute (*ādeśa*) or an affix (*pratyaya*), he says: [the following].

Regarding *śās*: by the rule "krādiniyamāt," *iṭ* is obligatory; for the prohibition [of *iṭ*] stated in "ṭhupadeśe'tvataḥ" applies only to those roots that are invariably *aniṭ* (without *iṭ*) in the *tās-* form. However, in the case of *ragh*, [the augment] does not exist at all in the *tās-* form;
how then could it be considered *aniṭ* in the *tās-* form? For the rule states: "that which exists in the *tās-* form and is *aniṭ*..."

The commentary says this: "From *ghas*, [the suffix] *tās* and *iṭ*" (*ghasestāsāviti*). Thus: *jaghasitha*; *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*; *jaghāsa*, *jaghasa*; *jakṣiva*, *jakṣima*. Regarding the alternative view where the substitution of *ghas* does not occur, it says: "By the rule *ādeta*" (*ādeti*). Since the option for *iṭ* by the restriction of Bhāradvāja applies to the suffix *thali*, [the form is] *āditha* by the rule *iḍatyartīti*; [and] *ādathuḥ*.

*Ad*, *ād*, *ādiva*, *ādima*. Regarding *atā*: it is that which will eat (*atsyati*); it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). *Das* becomes *tas*. [The forms] *atu*, *atāt*, *atām*, *adantu*. When *ad-hi* is situated, since the rule *jhayo ho’nyatarasyām* allows for the optional substitution of the preceding homogeneous sound (*pūrvasavarṇa*) for the letter *ha*, there arises the possibility of optionally substituting *dha* for *ha*.

(255) *hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.101. [The rule states: "In place of *hi*, there is *dhi* after roots ending in *ha* or those beginning with a *jhal* consonant. The meaning is that because [the term *jhal*] qualifies the stem (*aṅga*), the designation of "ending in" (*tadanta*) applies; thus it refers to stems ending in a *jhal* consonant. Since [the substitute *dhi*] consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is a complete replacement (*sarvādeśa*).

However, this does not apply in the case of *rudihī*, as is clear from the Bhāṣya: "The augment *iṭ* is not added to the *hi* that is actually specified [by the rule], because it is separated [from the root]; moreover, the *hi* accompanied by *iṭ* is not what is specified. Regarding *atāt*:

the substitution *ātām* (*tātaṅ*) occurs because it is subsequent to the substitution of *dhi*. Even though *dhi*-ness would apply again due to the status of the substitute being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it does not do so.

This is because of the maxim: "In the case of a conflict between two rules, that which is once superseded is superseded forever. Thus, *ata* becomes *ata*. Regarding *adāni*: the augment *āṭ* is applied by the rule *āḍajādīnām*. The very purpose of pronouncing the long vowel in this *āṭ* is for this reason; such is the intention. *Adāva*, *adāma*. When *lah* [the substitute for the endings] is replaced by *āt*, the form stands as *ād-t*.

(256) *adaḥ sarveṣām* | 7|3|100|. The word *adaḥ* [is the subject] "of all [substitutes]. The form *adaḥ* is in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). By the metarule *tasmādityuttarasya*, the meaning "of the following" is obtained. From the rule *guṇo'pṛkte*, the term *apṛkte* [is understood].

From the rule "ṭh-tu-ru-stu-śam-yamaḥ," the term "sārvadhātuke" is also carried over (anuvartate). The two locative cases are converted into genitive cases. From the rule "ah gārgya-gālavayor ito'ḍ," the word "aṭ" is carried over.
The term "sarveṣām" is used to ensure the continuation [of the rule] for Gārgya and Gālava, while excluding it for others.

This is what he states with the words "adaḥ parasya," etc. Because it has the marker *ṭ*, it is the first member of the compound. This is what he states with "ādaditi. Regarding "ātām": the sense is that the augment *āṭ* does not apply because of the mention of the term "apṛkta. [This refers to] the optative (*vidhi-liṅ*).

He states the form *rūpa*—namely, *adyāt*. The intention is that because the *śap* affix has been elided (*luk*), there is no *ataḥ* (the letter *a*) preceding it; therefore, the rule *ato yeyaḥ* does not apply. In the case of *mip*, when *ami* follows with *yāsuṭ* and the *s* is elided, and after the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), we have *adyām*. Similarly, *adyāva* and *adyāma*. Having taken for granted the form *adyāt* as established in the optative (*āśīr-liṅ*), he says *adyāstām*. In the aorist (*luṅ*), [it is] *id*.
This being the case—(257) *luṅ-sanoḥ ghaslṛ* | Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.37:
*luṅ-sanoḥ ghaslṛ*. From the rule *ad-ghoḥ* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.36], the term *ad-* is understood to carry over.

He says this with the word "adaḥ. He states the purpose of its being marked with the *lṛt* indicator: "because it is *lṛdit*. The root *han* is neither *iṭ*-nor *niṭ*. In the form *praṇihanti*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*; the nasal undergoes *anusvāra* and then *parasavarṇa*; and by the rule "ṭhnergade," the substitution of *ṇ* occurs.

(258) Pāṇini 6.4.37: *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnāmanunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti*. The elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) occurs for those roots taught with an anudātta vowel, as well as for *van*, *tan*, and others, when followed by a *jhal* consonant or an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. [The term] "taught with an anudātta vowel" refers to those roots included in the list beginning with *ūḍṛdantaiḥ*.
The roots taught with an *anudātta* accent include *vanati* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, while the *tanotyādi* group will be listed under the rule beginning with "√tan vistāre" (DhP 8.1).

The understood meaning of the rule is that the nasal of these [roots] is elided before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant that has *k* or *ṅ* as an *it*. This being the case, in forms such as *mukta*, etc., [the nasal is dropped].
The elision of the *m* sound and so forth would also apply to [roots] such as *muc*. To this he says: "the word *anunāsika* (nasal) has its genitive case ending elided.
Even so, because the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was, he says: "it is a qualifier for the others, excluding *van*."

The meaning is: "of those taught with an anudātta [accent] and of the roots beginning with *tan*. And thus, because they function as qualifiers, by the rule of "specification of that which ends in [the qualifier]," there is elision of the final letter of those ending in an anunāsika, of those taught with an anudātta, of those beginning with *tan*, and of *van*.
Because the meaning "it may be" (syāt) is obtained, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *mukta*.

He states this with the words "of those ending in a nasal" (*anunāsikāntānām*), etc. However, the verbal root *van* is not qualified [by the term "ending in a nasal"], because it does not deviate from that condition; this is the intended meaning.
Here, he shows those that have anudātta vowels as their upadeśa and end in an anunāsika: *yam, ram, nam*, etc.
The meaning is that among those taught with anudātta vowels, only these six end in an anunāsika.
Next, he shows those ending in an anunāsika such as *tanoti* and so forth: *tanu, ku, kṣiṇu*, etc.

The phrase ending with "ṭhmanu" is the nominative singular of a collective dvandva compound; the meaning is that these eight roots beginning with *tan* end in a nasal. The ten verbal roots starting from "ṭhtanu vistāre" (to expand) up to "ḍu kṛñ karaṇe" (to do/make) are the "roots beginning with *tan*" (*tanotyādayaḥ*).

In this context, the root *kṛ* is not included because it does not end in a nasal; nor is the root *sā* (from *ṣo*) included here, because its substitution with *ā*—as in *san*—will be explained by the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sanjhaloḥ*. Furthermore, the root *vanu* "to beg," which is listed in the *tanādi* group, is also not included here because it takes the *u*-vikaraṇa and is marked with an *u*-diacritic (*udit*).

Because it is not included by the mention of *vanati*, there is a separate mention of the root *van* even though it is read in the *tādi* (roots beginning with *t*) group. Since that *van* belonging to the *tādi* group ends in an *u*dit vowel (*u*), the suffix *iṭ* is optional after the suffix *ktvā* by the rule *udito vā*.
Consequently, when the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied, *iṭ* is absent by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, resulting in the examples *vataḥ* and *vatavān*.

As for the root *van* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, because it lacks the marker *u*, even though the *niṣṭhā* suffix would be *seṭ*, the example is given as *vatī* [from *ktin*]; this is because the prohibition of *iṭ* applies there by the rule "in the case of *titu-vrata-thasisu-saraka-seṣu*. Enough of this. Regarding *hataḥ*: [this is from] *tasi*.
The *n* is elided because the root ends in a nasal and is taught with an *anudātta* accent; furthermore, the suffix *tas* is marked with *ṅ*, as indicated by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*.

In the form *ghnanti*, the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule *gamahana-* because the suffix begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) and is marked with *ṅ*; then, by the rule *ho hanteḥ*, the *h* is changed to *gh* due to the presence of a *has* (a sibilant or *h*). In *hasi*...
*hathaḥ hatha-* (259). *vamorvā* |8|4|23|.

After *va* or *ma*, [the substitution of *ha* for *tha*] is optional. From the rule "after a prefix, even when not in a compound" (*upasargādasamāse’pi*), the word *upasargāt* ("after a prefix") is carried over [to this sūtra].

The rule *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* is understood to follow here. From the rule *ṭhhanteratpūrvasya*, the word *ṭhhanter* is carried over. Thus he says: "after a cause [in the form] of a prefix (*upasarga*) ending in *ṇ* or *ṛ*. Regarding the form *jahāna* in the *ṇal* suffix, he says: *ho hanteḥ*. This is because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the requirement of the rule *abhyāsācca*.

The intended meaning is "because it is logical. Regarding the form *jaghnatuḥ*: due to the elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule *gamahana-* and the substitution of *k* for *h* by the rule *ho hanteḥ*, the form becomes *jaghan-tha*. At this stage, because of the optionality of the augment *iṭ* according to the restriction of Bhāradvāja, and because there is neither a following *ñ-ṇit* suffix nor a following *n* sound, [the rules do not apply].
In the absence of the substitution of *k* by the rule *ṭhho hanteḥ*, [the following applies]:
(260) *abhyāsācca* | Pāṇini 7.3.55.
[The sūtra] *abhyāsācca* follows from *ṭhho hanteḥ*. [The phrase] *ṭhcajoḥ ku-* [is understood].

And the mention of *ku* is carried over from the rule *ghinn-yatoḥ*. Thus he says: "after the reduplication," and so forth. *Jaghanitha*, *jaghantha*: in the absence of *iṭ*, there is the substitution of *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* for *n*. *Jaghnathuḥ*, *jaghna*, *jaghāna*—or *jaghana*;
*jaghniva*, *jaghnima*. In the *lṛṭ* [future] with *syap*:

Anticipating the objection that this [substitution] would be prohibited, he says: "of *ṛ* and *han*" (*ṛdhanoh*). When *han* is present as *hi*, the substitution of *dh* [for *t*] by the rule "after *hu*, *jhal*, and *bha*" (*hujhalbhyaḥ*) would apply;
however— (261) *hanter jaḥ* | 6.4.36 | [The substitute *ja* takes the place of the final phoneme of the root *han* when followed by an affix beginning with *dh*.]

Regarding *hanterjaḥ*: intending that *hau* is carried over from the rule *ṭhśā hau*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "when *hau* follows. Having raised the objection that once the substitution of *j* for *han* has been made, the elision of *hi* would apply by the rule *ato heḥ*, he replies: "because it is *ābhīya* (non-antaranga). Thus: *jahīti*, *hatāt*, *hatam*, *hata*.

"He shall kill" (*hanāni*): because the suffix *āṭ* is *pit*, the *hitva* (substitution of *ha* for *han*) does not apply, and thus there is no elision of the penultimate vowel; this is the intended meaning. "He killed" (*ahan*): after the *laṅ* suffix *tip*, the *ikāra* is elided by the rule *itaśca*, and then the *takāra* is elided by the rule *saṃyogāntasya*;
or rather, the elision of the consonant and following vowels (*halṅyādi-lopa*) occurs because it is more logical. "I killed" (*ahanam*); [and] "we two killed" (*ahanva*).

*ahanma*. Because there is no following *jhāl*-beginning suffix, the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) does not occur. In the potential mood (*vidhiliṅ*), [the forms are] *hanyāt*, *hanyātām*, and so forth. Stating that he will explain the substitution for *hi* in the benedictive mood (*āśīrliṅ*), he says:
(262) *ārddhadhātuke* || 1.2.4.35 ||

"Under the governing heading 'before an ārdhadhātuka suffix'—" this is the context. The remainder [of the sentence] is: "rules such as 'jadhi replaces han' will be stated. He states the sūtra situated within that governing heading: (263) *hano vadha liṅ* 2.4.42.

The word *hanaḥ* is a nominative with its case-ending elided, meaning "of *han*" (*vadhe*); the sense is that the substitute *vadh* shall take the place of *han* in an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix when the sense is the precative (*liṅ*). (264) *luṅ ci* 1.2.44. [The augment *ciṇ* is added after *han* in the *luṅ* tense.]

What is the rule? The meaning is clear: "In the *luṅ* [aorist], there should be the substitute *vadh* for *han*. That the substitute *vadh* ends in a vowel (*adanta*) means that the vowel *a* after the letter *dh* is not for the sake of ease of pronunciation; rather, its purpose will be explained immediately below in the example *avadhīt*. Now, when the form *hanyāt* is established for the *āśīr-liṅ* (precative):

Since the substitute *vadh* has been applied [to the root *han*], and because it does not end in the vowel *a* at the time of its introduction (*upadeśa*) into the *ārdhadhātuka* domain, one might ask how the elision of *a* (*allopa*) can occur in forms such as *vadhyāt*. To this, he says:
"It is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Thus, when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix is intended, [the substitution occurs] even prior to its actual application.

The result is that once the substitution of *vadh* has been applied, the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes come into operation. Consequently, because the substitute *vadh* ends in the vowel *a* during the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, the elision of the penultimate *a* (*allopa*) occurs without obstruction. This is what he means by saying "by that" (*tena*). Thus, in the form *avadhīt*, once the elision of *a* has been effected in the *sic* suffix, [the substitute *vadh* remains].

Although it consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*) because it ends in the letter *dh*, the augment *iṭ* is applied to the root *sac* because it is not a single-vowel root at the time of its formal instruction (*upadeśa*). Furthermore, the rule "vṛddhi for [a short] *a* followed by a consonant" (*ato halādeḥ*) does not apply, because the elision of the *a* (*allopa*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule "that which follows an *ac* is [treated as if it were] in the original position. It is precisely for this purpose...

For it is based on the fact that the substitute *vadh* ends in a long vowel (*ā*). [The rule] "svariteṭ" results in [the designation of these roots] as "ubhayapadin" (verbal roots used in both voices). Regarding *dviṣ* in the sense of "displeasure": it is *aniṭ*. In *dveṣṭi*, because it has a *pi*t suffix, there is an absence of *ṅ*ttva; thus, by the rule for the *guṇa* of a light penultimate vowel, [the form is derived]. [The forms are: *dviṣṭaḥ*, *dviṣanti*; *dvekṣi*, *dviṣṭhaḥ*.

*dviṣ* (to hate): *dviṣṭe*, *dveṣmi*, *dviṣvaḥ*, *dviṣmaḥ*. He cites an example for the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings—namely, *dviṣṭe*. Because of the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* [strengthening]. [The forms are: *dviṣāte*, *dviṣate*; *dvikṣe*, *dviṣāthe*, *dviḍḍhve*; *dviṣe*, *dviṣvahe*, *dviṣmahe*. Thinking that the change of *ṣ* to *k* occurs by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* [Pāṇini 8.2.41], he says: *dvekṣyati*. [The form] *dviḍḍhe*.

*dhṛṣṭiḥ*: the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ* by the rule of *jaśtva*, and *ḍh* by the rule of *ṣṭutva*. *dviṣṭāt*, *dviṣṭam*, *dviṣṭa*. *dveṣāṇi*: because the augment *āṭ* is *pit*, it lacks the status of being *ṅit*, so there is no *guṇa*; and because it follows a *ṣ*, there is *ṇatva*. *dveṣāva*, *dveṣāma*. *dviṣṭām*, *dviṣātām*, *dviṣatām*.

*dviṣ-tas* becomes *dviṣṭas*; *dviṣ-athaḥ* becomes *dviṣāthām*; *dviṣ-anti* becomes *dviḍḍhavam*. In *dvaiṣe*, because the augment *āṭ* is *pit*, it lacks the *ṅtva* designation; thus, there is no *guṇa* substitution—this is the intended meaning.

In *adveṭ*: the suffix *tip* of the *laṅ*; *guṇa* substitution; elision of the vowel *i*; elision by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*; and finally, by the rules *vāvasāne* and *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*.
The intention is that [the suffix] *jhas* is replaced by *at*. Regarding *adviṣṭām*:
(265) *dviṣaśca* | 3.4.112|. From *dviṣaśca*, the rule *jherjus* and *laṅḥ śākaṭāyanasya* are also understood as continuing in application.
Intending this, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "laṅi jheḥ" (in the *laṅ* [aorist], for *jhi*).
Thus: *adviṣat*, *adviṣṭām*, *adviṣan*; *adviṣaḥ*, *adviṣṭam*, *adviṣṭa*; *adviṣam*, *adviṣva*, *adviṣma*.
Regarding the optative (*vidhiliṅ*) in the parasmaipada, he says: *dviṣyāt*, *dviṣyātām*, *dviṣyuḥ*.
And so forth. Regarding *taṅ* (the middle voice): *dviṣīta*, *dviṣīyātām*, *dviṣīran*, and so on.
Regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*): *dviṣyāstām*, and so on. Regarding *taṅ* in the precative (*liṅ*): *dvikṣīṣṭa*, *dvikṣīyāstām*, and so on.
Because of the rule "the suffixes *liṅ* and *sic* are *kit* when used with the *ātmanepada* endings," there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Thus: *dvikṣīyāstām*, and so on.

The author states in the *luṅ* (aorist) *parasmaipada*: "advikṣat. [This is derived] by the rule "śala igupadhāt," which prescribes the suffix *ksa*. [The forms] "advikṣatām," "advikṣan," and so forth, follow. Regarding the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and so on, because the meaning of "excellent filling" (*prakṛṣṭapūraṇa*) is not understood, he says: "prapūraṇam means the absence of filling (*pūraṇābhāva*). [The form] *ūdhaḥ*.

The meaning is "the state of being contrary to filling," that is to say, "in the act of drawing out from the udder. Now, one might ask: from where does this meaning of the word *prapūraṇa* derive? To this he says: "A certain [prefix] subverts the root-meaning. That is, a certain prefix, having set aside the well-known root-meaning, [conveys] another meaning.

*nayatīrtthaḥ* (the crossing point of leading). Regarding *dogdhīti*: by the rule *dāderghaḥ*, the *h* becomes *gh*; by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*, the *t* becomes *dh*; and by the rule for *jaś*-ness, the *gh* becomes *g*. Similarly, *dugdha* is also formed. *duhanti*. Regarding *dhokṣīti*: the *h* becomes *gh*, which by *ca*-ness becomes *k*, and then there is the substitution of *ṣ*; such is the intended meaning. *dugdhaḥ*.

In the *laṭ* (present tense), the *ātmanepada* forms are as follows: he says "dugdhe. [The roots] *ghas*, *dagh*, and *duh*. [For the second person dual: *duhāte*, *duhate*; [for the second person singular: *dhukṣe*. Here, *h* becomes *gh*; by the rule *bhaṣ*, *d* becomes *dh*; by the rule *ghas* [becoming *k*], *gh* becomes *k*; and there is the substitution of *ṣ*. [For the second person dual: *duhāthe*; [for the second person plural: *dhugdhve*. Here, *h* becomes *gh*; [by *bhaṣ*], [the final consonant becomes *dh*]; and by the rule *ghas*, *gh* becomes *g*.
*duhvahe*, *duhmahe*; *dudoha*, *duduhatuḥ*, *duduhuḥ*.
Because it ends in a vowel and lacks the letter *a*, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory by the rule for roots beginning with *krī*. [Second person singular: *dudohitha*, [second person dual:
*duduhathuḥ*, [second person plural: *duduha*; [first person singular: *dudoha*, [first person dual: *duduhiva*, [first person plural: *duduhima*. [Middle voice: *duduhe*, *duduhāte*.
They have milked; you have milked; you two have milked; you all have milked—[you] have milked.
He has milked; she has milked; we two have milked; we have milked.
He will milk; she will milk. Let him milk; let them milk; let her milk. Let [her] milk.

*herdhiḥ*: by *ghatva*, *jaśtva*, and *cutva*, [it becomes] *dugdhi*. *dugdhat*: [by *jaśtva* and *cartva*]. *dugdham*, *dugdha*: [by *jaśtva* and *cartva*]. *duhāthām*: by *ṣatva*. *dhugdhvam*: *ha* becomes *gha*; by *bhaṣ*; *gha* becomes *jaś*. *dohai*: the intention is that because *āṭ* is *pit* and the *aṅga* is *aṅt*, there is *guṇa*. *dohāvahai*.
We shall explain the *doh* root in the *parasmaipada*. [The form] *adhok* is derived as follows:

after the elision of the *i* of *tip*, there is the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes; *h* becomes *gh*; *d* becomes *bhaṣ*; and for *gh*, there is an optional substitution by the *car*-class sounds.
Thus: *adugdhām*, *aduhan*; *adhok*, *adugdham*, *adugdha*; and *adoham* (as well as) *aduhva*.
Regarding the *laṅ* [aorist] tense, he says: *aduh* (they milked). Here, *h* becomes *gh*, *t* becomes *dh*, and *gh* becomes *g*.
[The forms are: *aduhātām*, *aduhata*; *adugdhāḥ*, *aduhāthām*; *adhugdhvam*. By the rule "*ṭhksasyā'ci*" [Pāṇini 7.3.97], [the forms are: *adhukṣātām*, *adhukṣanta*; *adhukṣathāḥ*, *adhukṣāthām*.

*adhukṣadhvam*, *adhukṣi*, *adhukṣāvahi*, *adhukṣāmahi*. Regarding the rule *lugvā*: when these four suffixes beginning with dentals—*ta*, *thās*, *dhvam*, and *vahi*—follow, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the *ksa* affix according to the rule *lugvā duheḥ*. This means that in the case of elision, the forms are the same as those of the *laṅ* (imperfect). Thus, for example: *adugdha*, *adugdhāḥ*, *adhugdhvam*.
The resulting forms are *taduhvahi* and so forth. *Adhokṣyat*, *adhokṣyata*. The root *diha* means "to increase";

here, "increase" (*upacaya*) means growth. It is *aniṭ*. [In the form] *praṇidegdhi*, there is the substitution of *ṇa* by the rule *nergade*. The forms are like those of the root *duh*. The root *liha* means "to taste."

[The root *lih*] is *aniṭ*. [In the present indicative: *leḍhi*. When there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*, there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍh*. [In the future: *lekṣīti*. In the case of the *sip* suffix, *ha* becomes *ḍha*. The intention is that by the rule *ṭh-ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, *ḍha* becomes *ka*. [The past passive participle: *līḍhaḥ*, *līḍhavān*. [First person forms: *lehmi*, *lihvah*, *lihmaḥ*. Regarding the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings in the present indicative (*laṭ*), he says: *līḍhe*. [Dual: *lihāte*, *lihate*. [Second person singular: *likṣe*.
Thus [ends the section on] *ḍhakṣā*. "They lick" (*lihanti*) is easy to understand. Regarding "they have licked" (*līḍhāve*):
there is the substitution of *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, the elision of *ḍha*, and lengthening. [The forms are: *lihe*, *lihvahe*, *limahe*. [The future active is: *leḍhā*;
[the future middle is: *lekṣyati*, *lekṣyate*. Regarding "let them lick" (*leḍhāvu*): [the forms are] *līḍhāt*, *līḍhām*, *lihantu*. [The imperative middle is: *līḍhai*.
*dhīḍh* [is substituted]. Through the application of the rules for *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍh*, followed by lengthening, [we obtain] *līḍhāt*, *līḍham*, *līḍha*.

[In the first person singular imperative] *lehāni*; the intention is that because the augment *āṭ* is marked with *p* (indicating it is not *ṅ*), there is no absence of *ṅ*-status, and thus [the substitution of *ī* for *e*] occurs as *guṇi*.
[The forms are] *lehāva*, *lehāma*. [In the third person plural imperative] *līḍhām*, *lihātām*, *lihatām*. [In the second person singular imperative] *likṣva*, *lihāthām*, *līḍhvam*.

*lehati*, *lehāvahti*, *lehāmahti*; *aleḍhi*. [In the case of] *laṅ* as well, due to the elision (*luk*) of *śap*, the elision of the vowel *i*, and the elision of [the suffixes] beginning with *hal* and *ṅ*, there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*. The meaning is that there is an option regarding the change to *ca* (the substitution of *ṭa* for *ta*). [The forms are: *alīḍhām*, *alihant* (3rd pl.); *aleṭ*, *alīḍham*, *alīḍha*; *aleham*, *alihva*, *alihma*; *alīḍha* (3rd sg.).
*alihātām*, *alihata*; *alīḍhāḥ*; *alihāthām*, *alīḍhvam*;
*alihvahi*, *alihmahi*. Regarding *alikṣit*: in the *luṅ* [aorist], the suffix is *ksi*. [Examples: *alikṣatām*, *alikṣanta*;
*alikṣathāḥ*—which becomes *alīḍhāḥ*; *alikṣāthām*, *alikṣadhvam*—which becomes *alīḍhvam*; *alikṣi*.
Considering the option of elision (*lug-vikalpa*) as in "ṭhlu-g-vā du-he," he says: *alikṣāvahi*, *alihvahī*;

and *alekṣyat*, *alekṣyata*—these being the forms in the conditional (*lṛṅ*). Thus, the four roots beginning with *dviṣ* have been explained as having a circumflex accent (*svarita-ita*). Now, *cakṣiṅ* [is taught] in the sense of "articulate speech" (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*), for the purpose of making its hidden meaning clearly understood.

The meaning is "in the Vivaraṇa. This [is] also in the case of the *darśana* (vision/philosophical system). In the Śruti, for example: "Moving one before and the other behind by means of their creative power (*māyā*), these two children play as they go around the sacrifice; one beholds all beings, while the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again," and so forth. Thus [it is].

Nor can it be said that [the *ṅ*] is for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) conditioned by the property of being unaccented (*anudāteta*), because that is established by the property of being marked with *ṅ* alone; therefore, he says: "The vowel *i* is unaccented for the sake of *yuj*.
Nor can it be said that it is for the sake of the middle voice conditioned by the property of being unaccented, because [that is already established] by the property of being marked with *ṅ*.

To establish that, he says: "The vowel *i* is unaccented (*anudātta*) for the sake of the suffix *yuc*. The meaning is that this serves as the basis for the suffix *yuc*, which is an exception to [the rule for] *lyuṭ* by the sūtra "ṭhanudātetaśca halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.149). Furthermore, the pronunciation of the vowel *i* while bypassing the vowel *a* is intended to convey that the *i* lacks the status of being a mere phonetic utterance (*uccāraṇārthatva*).

Since the addition of the augment *num* would be required if this were merely a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), he says: "But *num* does not [apply]. Why not? To this he says: "At the end, when marked with *it*.
The intention is that in the rule *idito num dhātoḥ*, the word "at the end" (*ante*) is understood from the preceding rule *goḥ pādānte*. Now, regarding the letter *ik*...

Anticipating the objection that since the requirement for the anudātta accent and the designation as *it* is necessary for the sense of "joining" (*yuj*), the atmanepada suffixes can arise from those alone and thus the utterance of the marker *ṅ* is redundant, he says:
"But the marker *ṅ*... The marker *ṅ* is for the purpose of ensuring the obligatory atmanepada.

However, the ātmanepada [ending] conditioned by the fact that [the root] is marked with an *anudātta* vowel might not occur at all; therefore, the letter *ṅ* is pronounced. For this very reason, it is understood that "the ātmanepada conditioned by the *anudātta* status is non-mandatory. As for *sphāyan*, although the root *sphāyī* (meaning "to grow") is also marked with an *anudātta*, [it takes parasmaipada].

The meaning is that there is a substitution of *śatṛ* for the present suffix (*laṭ*), but not the substitution of *śānac* for the ātmanepada. However, in reality, since [the rule] has already served its purpose by preventing the singular number at the end, how can the pronunciation of the letter *ṅ* be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the stated meaning? Furthermore, this has not been stated as such in the Bhāṣya. Therefore, it must be understood through the assumption of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

They say that *sphāyan* is somehow to be established. Regarding *caṣṭe*: there is the elision of the *k* by the rule *skoḥ*, and the change of *ṣ* to *ṭ* (ṣṭutva), such is the intention.
