(304) *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* 7.2.76. From the roots beginning with *rud*, etc. Considering that the phrase *iḍ valādeḥ* is to be supplied, he says: "from a consonant-initial [suffix] (*valādeḥ*)". [Thus, the form] *rudita*.

Thus: because of the *ṅ* designation, there is no *guṇa*. They weep (*rudanti*). You weep (*rodiṣi*), you two weep (*rudithaḥ*), you all weep (*ruditha*). I weep (*rodimi*), we two weep (*rudivaḥ*), we all weep (*rudimaḥ*). He wept (*ruroda*), they two wept (*rurudatuḥ*), they wept (*ruruduḥ*). You wept (*ruroditha*), you two wept (*rurudathuḥ*), you all wept (*ruruda*).
I wept (*rurodaṃ*), we two wept (*rurudiva*), we all wept (*rurudima*). He will weep (*roditā*), he will weep (*rodiṣyati*).

[The forms] *roditu*, *ruditāt*, *ruditām*, and *rudantu* [are derived from the root *rud*]. When *rudi hi* is established, one might suspect the substitution of *hi* for *dhi* by the rule *hujhalbhyo hedhiḥ*; therefore, he says: "Because *hi* is subsequent [to the rule *dhi*]. Thus, *rudihī*. Since *hi* is not marked with *p* (apit), it is treated as having the marker *ṅ*; consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). [The forms] *ruditāt* and *ruditam* [are likewise derived].
*rudita*, *rodāni*, *rodāva*, *rodāma*.

(305) *rudaśca pañcabhyaḥ* |7|3|98|. [The rule] *rudaśca* [is applied]. By the rule *nābhyastasyāci pitsu sārvadhātuke* [6.4.122], the substitution of *ta* for the final vowel of an abhyasta [reduplicated stem] occurs before a sārvadhātuka affix beginning with a vowel; and by the rule *uto*... [the substitution of guṇa occurs].
From the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 1.1.1), the word "halī" (after a consonant) is understood; from "guṇo 'pṛkte" (Pāṇini 7.3.91), the word "apṛkte" (in an unreduplicated [affix]) is understood;

and from "bruva īḍ" (Pāṇini 7.3.93), the word "īḍ" is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). The word "rudāt" is in the ablative case. Intending to express "from rud and the others," he completes the remainder of the sūtra with the words "hal-ādeḥ" and so forth.

(306) Aḍgārgyagālavayoḥ | 7|3|99 | According to the opinion of Aḍgārgya and Gālava, there shall be the augment *aṭ* after the five roots beginning with *rud*, before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that begins with a consonant, is marked with *P*, and consists of a single phoneme (*apṛkta*).
The meaning is clear. Regarding *arodīt*: it should also be understood as *aruditam* and *aruditā*.

Regarding *arodam*: it should also be understood as *arudiva* and *arudima*. Now, one might object: when the suffix *liṅ* takes the ending *tip*, since the augment *yāsuṭ* is superseded by the subsequent rule *ṭhaḍ gārgyagālavayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.112), and [the rule] *rudaśca*... [is applied].

Regarding the statement "from five [roots]," he says "prakṛtipratyaya... because both *aṭ* and *iṭ* augment would otherwise apply. It should also be understood that this is in view of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes beginning with a consonant (*hal*) which have an indicatory *p*, as well as those that are *apṛkta*. Regarding the case where *aṅ* applies by the rule "luṅ-laṅ-luṅ-ḷṅ-kṣv aṅ" for roots ending in *ṛ*, he says "arudit. In the alternative case where *aṅ* does not apply...

He said to you: "He wept" (*arodīt*). Here, the augment *īṭ* is applied by the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*. However, the rule *rudaśca pañcabhyaḥ* does not apply here because it is intervened by the suffix *sic*. [The root] *ñi ṣvap* means "to sleep. This is a root taught with an initial *ṣ*.
It is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. [The form] *svapiti* is derived by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ*.
*svap* (to sleep): *svapiti*, *svapanti*; *svapiṣi*, *svapithaḥ*, *svapitha*;

*svapimi*, *svapivaḥ*, *svapimaḥ*. Regarding *suṣvāpa*: when there is reduplication, the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs by the rule *liṭ-abhyāsasya*, followed by the formation of the single substitute vowel (*pūrvarūpa*). The idea is that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because the substitute is a *sakāra*. *Suṣupatuḥ*.

The meaning is that after the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) has been applied by the rule *vacisvapī*, reduplication (*dvitva*) and so forth follow. One should also know the form *suṣupuḥ*. [In the second person singular], *suṣvapitha* or *suṣvaptha*; the meaning is that according to the *bhāradvājaniyama*, there is optionally *iṭ* in the *thal* suffix. *Suṣupathuḥ*, *suṣupa*; *suṣvāpa*—*suṣvapa*, *suṣupiva*, *suṣupima*.
[The word] *su* is included by [the rule] *supi* for the root *svap* which has undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*;

[the word] *sūti* refers to the word *sūti* ending in a *kṛt* suffix; [the word] *sam* also refers to the word *sam*. The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. [This is understood] from [the rule] *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*.

The word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is understood [from the previous rule]. The term *mūrdhanya* (retroflex) is the governing topic (*adhikṛta*). Thus he says: "after these, when preceded by *su*, etc. Examples are *suṣuptiḥ*, *suṣūtiḥ*, and *suṣamaḥ*. Here, because the root *svap* is included as having undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*, there is no retroflexion (*ṣatva*) in the case of *sukhapraḥ*.

Commentary: Now, this being the case, how is there the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* in *suṣvāpatus*? For the substitution of *ṣ* applies to the root *svap* when it has undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*. In that regard, if we have *svap* + *atus*, and after reduplication has first taken place, [the rule] "vacisvapi... subsequently applies...

In that case, when the *halādiśeṣa* [removal of all consonants except the first] occurs, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* applies only to the subsequent portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*), and not to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). This is because the *atus* suffix is separated from the *kit* affix by the subsequent portion, and because of the prohibition: "there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* for what has already undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*. Consequently, [the form becomes] *su sasvap*.
In the word *atusī*, since the preceding portion (*atu*) has not undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*, how can there be the substitution of *ṣ*?

Furthermore, since the following portion (*sī*) is not immediately preceded by the prefix *su*, how can the substitution of *ṣ* occur by this rule? [The opponent argues that] the substitution of *ṣ* must occur even before the application of the doubling [of the *s*] according to the rule "after *iṇ* and the *ka*-class [consonants]."

It must be stated [that this is so], yet that is not tenable. This is because, according to the *paribhāṣā*—"first the verbal root is joined with its suffix, and afterwards with a prefix"—the connection with the prefix *su-* does not apply prior to reduplication. Thus, there is *sup* (the suffix) after the semivowel has undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*, but before the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*) has taken place.

In this case, when there is reduplication, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] would apply only to the latter portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) because of the rule "the suffix beginning with *ṭh* is *ṣ*" (*ṭhādeśapratyayaḥ*),

and not to the former portion (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*), due to the prohibition "not after *sa*, nor at the beginning of a word" (*sātpadādyoḥ*). Once the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the initial consonant) has been applied, the former portion is no longer of the form *su*, and thus the rule "after *su*, *vi*, *ni*, and *dur*" (*suvinirdurbhyaḥ*) does not apply.

Thus, this [rule] also does not apply. Nor should it be suspected that a form modified in one part (ekadeśavikṛta) is not subject to grammatical operations, because even so, since the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would be meaningless, the substitution of *ṣ* would not apply there by virtue of the paribhāṣā "that which is meaningful" (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*). Therefore, in the case of *suṣuṣupatuḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs in the first member (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*).
Anticipating the objection that this is difficult to establish, he says: "First the root," and so forth.

Here, in accordance with the requirements of the examples (*lakṣya*), it is accepted that "first the root is joined with a prefix (*upasarga*), and afterwards with an inflectional suffix (*sādhana*). Consequently, [the doubling occurs] precisely after the prefix has been applied.
Since the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs first due to its higher priority, the form *su*—derived from *sup*—is taken as being preceded by the prefix *su*.

Once the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) has been applied, one might ask: "How can there be doubling (*dvitva*) of the form *ṣu*, which already possesses the *ṣatva*, given that when doubling is to be performed, the *ṣatva* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent)? To this, he says:

Regarding the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*: one might object that, in that case, the sound *ṣṭ* would also be heard in the first half of *susuṣvāpa*. To this he says: *piti tu*. Because there is no *kit* status when the suffix *ṇal* follows a *pit*, the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* does not apply; thus, after reduplication has occurred, [the rule] *liṭyabhyāsasya* [applies].

There is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the first part. When *su*, *sup*, and *svap* are present, because the substitution of *ṣ* [by the rule] *su-vi-ni-dur-bhyaḥ raḥ* is considered asiddha, the meaning is that *halādi-śeṣa* applies.
And "because of its constancy" means that *halādi-śeṣa* applies whether the substitution of *ṣ* has been performed or not.

The state [of the suffix]. Regarding "tataḥ" (from that): it should be understood that because of the state of beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi-bhāvāt*), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. [Imperative forms: *svaptā*, *svapsyati*;
*svapitu*, *svapitāt*, *svapitām*, *svapantu*; *svapihi*, *svapitāt*, *svapitam*, *svapita*; *svapāni*, *svapāva*, *svapāma*. [Optative form from the *laṅ* stem: *supyāt*.

The intention is that there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) by the rule *vacisvapi...* [Pāṇini 6.1.15]. Thinking that *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) applies by the rule *suvinirdubhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.88], he says: *suṣupyāt*. Regarding *asvāpsīt*: because it is not marked as taking the augment *iṭ*, there is no elision of the *s* of the *sic* suffix; this is the intention. As for the root *śvas* in the sense of "breathing": it takes the augment *iṭ* before *ārddhadhātuka* affixes beginning with a consonant (*valādi*), but before *sārvadhātuka* affixes...

In the case of the *luṅ* [aorist], considering that the augment *iṭ* applies by the rule "after roots beginning with *rud*" (*rudādibhyaḥ*), and that the augment *īṭ* applies by the rule "also after *rud*" (*rudaśca*) and the augment *aṭ* applies by the rule "in the *laṅ* [imperfect] for Gārgya" (*aḍ gārgyasya*), he says: *aśvasīt*, *aśvasat*.
Having taken for granted that *śvasyāt* is established in the *liṅ* (optative) used for injunction or benediction, he says: *śvasyātām*.
"May he breathe tomorrow," [it is said]. "And *an*"—the meaning is that even the root *an* is used in the sense of breathing.

This [root] is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*). Since there is also an *iṭ* after roots beginning with *rud* when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*val*), considering the *liṅ* [augment] and the *īṭ* [augment], he says: *ānīt*, *ānat*.

(307) *aniteḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.19. Regarding *aniteḥ*: the phrase *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]. From the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi*, the word *upasargāt* is also understood. Therefore, he says: "from that which stands in an upasarga. Since [the *n*] would not otherwise be subject to the rule due to being situated in a different word (*bhinnapadasthatvāt*), [this sūtra is stated].
The verbal root *jakṣ* is marked with the *seṭ* designation. Even before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant other than *y*, it is *seṭ* by the rule "after *rud* and the others.
(Pāṇini 7.1.4) *adabhyastāt*: [The substitution of *at* for the final vowel of the stem occurs] after a reduplicated (*abhyasta*) root ending in *a*.
The meaning is that because of the continued application (anuvṛtti) of the rules "adabhyastāt" [3.4.114], "jhasya" [6.1.7], and "jho'ntaḥ" [7.1.3].

Regarding the form *jakṣati*: the meaning is that the designation "abhyasta" (repeated) is applied by the rule "jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ" [6.1.6]. Having taken for granted the forms *ajakṣīt* and *ajakṣat*—which are established by the addition of *iṭ* and *āṭ* after the *tip* suffix of the *laṅ*—he says: "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca" [3.4.109].

The suffix *jus* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ad*. [The rule] "ending in a semivowel (*antastha*) and beginning with one" means that it begins with a palatal semivowel (*tālavya*). The word *babhrāma* is used because, in the Upaniṣad passage "eating, playing, rejoicing," the fact that it begins with the third letter of the *ca*-class is beyond dispute; such is the intention. [The root] *jāgṛ*...

The root *jāgṛ* ends in the vowel *ṛ* and is *seṭ*. Regarding *jāgarti*: after the elision (*luk*) of *śap* by *tip*, the *ṛ* vowel undergoes *guṇa*, and *ra* replaces it by rule. Regarding *jāgṛtaḥ*: because the suffix is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa*. Regarding *jāgrati*:
since the designation *abhyasta* applies by the rule "jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ," the substitution of *ad* for *jhi* occurs by the rule "ad abhyastāt."
The intention is that when the prohibition of *guṇa* applies due to the presence of *ṅ*, the *yaṇ* substitute occurs for the *ṛ*-vowel. [Thus we have: *jāgarṣi*, *jāgṛthaḥ*, *jāgṛtha*;

*jāgarmi*, *jāgṛvaḥ*, *jāgṛmaḥ*. Regarding the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, since the suffix *ām* would necessarily apply by the rule "after a root ending in *kāsa* or having more than one vowel," he says: "after *uṣ*, *vid*, etc., *ām* is optional. Thus, *jāgarām* [is formed] with *ām*.
The meaning is that there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ṛ*, followed by the substitution of *ra* in place of the final element. Regarding the absence of *ām*, he says: *jagāgāra*.
Since *kit* status would prohibit *guṇa* in forms such as those ending in *atus*, [the following rule applies]:
(309) *jāgro'viciṇṇalṅitsu* | Pāṇini 7.3.85. [In the case of the root *jāgr*, *guṇa* is substituted before endings other than *vi*, *ciṇ*, and *ṅit*.]

The word *jāgroḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). From the rule *miderguṇaḥ*, the term *guṇaḥ* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Therefore, he says: "There shall be *guṇa* for *jāgarti*.
The analysis of the compound is *avi-ciṇ-ṇal-ṅt-su*. It is a *dvandva* of these: *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, and *hit*.

This is a negative compound (nañ-samāsa). Thus he says: "other than [those ending in] *vici*, *ṇiṅ*, *ṅt*, and *ṅ*. Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *ciṇ* and *ṇal*, this [suffix] applies even in cases where *vṛddhi* would otherwise occur. Because of the exclusion of *ṅt*, it applies even in cases where there is a prohibition of *guṇa*.
Thus it says: "and in the case of *vṛddhi*. Regarding *jajāgatuḥ*: here, despite the presence of the *kit* suffix, there is *guṇa*.

[The forms are: *jajāgaruḥ*, *jajāgaritha*, *jajāgarathuḥ*, *jajagāra*, *jajāgāra*—*jajāgara*, *jajāgariva*, *jajāgarima*. However, in the case of *vic*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, and *luṅ*, there is no *guṇa*. [Examples: *vi*-[suffix] *jāgṛviḥ*.

In the case of *ciṇ*: *ajāgāri*. In the case of *ṇal*: *jajāgāra*. In the case of *ṅti*: *jāgṛtiḥ*. Regarding the scope of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening): as in *jāgarakaḥ* with the suffix *ṇvul*. Regarding the scope of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*): as in *jajāgaratuḥ*. Even when there is *kitva* (the suffix being marked with *k*), there is *guṇa* (vowel shortening/strengthening); this and other cases are to be inferred accordingly. [Future forms: *jāgaritā*, *jāgariṣyati*. [Imperative: *jāgartu*, *jāgṛtāt*.

The imperative forms are: *jāgṛtām*, *jāgratu*; *jāgṛhi*—*jāgṛtāt*, *jāgṛtam*, *jāgṛta*; *jāgarāṇi*, *jāgarāva*, *jāgarāma*. Regarding the *laṅ* (imperfect): it says *ajāgarat*. [In this form], after the elision of the *ik* vowel by the rule *tipa ikāralopaḥ*, there is the elision of the *takāra* by the rule *halṅyādinā talopaḥ*, and the *repha* (*r*) becomes a *visarga*; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding the point that since [the root] is reduplicated (*abhyasta*), the substitution of *jhi* for *laṅ* would result in *ad*, he says: "because it is reduplicated, *jus* [is substituted]. The intention is that this is by the rule "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca. It is reduplicated because it belongs to the class beginning with *jakṣ* (Pāṇini 6.1.6). When the form *ajāgṛ us* has been established, [the rule] "sārvadhātukamapit" [applies].
Since the rule "before *ṅ*, *tu*, etc., *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṅt* [and *si*]" (*aṅgasya*) would not apply because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and since *guṇa* would otherwise not be obtained, he says:
*Jusi ca*. The term *aṅgasya* is understood from the context. From the rule "*miderguṇaḥ*" (*mid* takes *guṇa*), the word *guṇaḥ* is also understood.

This [rule] continues [from the previous sūtra]. By the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "guṇa and vṛddhi replacements occur in place of iK," the term "iK" is supplied; because this qualifies the "aṅga" (stem), there is an application of the "tadanta-vidhi" (the rule that the qualification applies to what ends with that). By the term "acī" (in the presence of a vowel), which is supplied from the [previous rule] "jus syāt parasmaipadeṣu madhyame bahuvacane ksaḥ," the term "jus" is qualified; because of this, there is an application of the "tadādi-vidhi" (the rule that the qualification applies to what begins with that). Thus he says:

By the phrase "not beginning with a vowel" (*ajādau*) and so forth; [the forms] *ajāgaruḥ*, *ajāgaḥ*, *ajāgṛtam*, *ajāgṛta*; *ajāgaram*, *ajāgṛva*, *ajāgṛma*. In the potential mood (*vidhiliṅ*), because the augment *yāsuṭ* has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. [The forms are] *jāgṛyāt*, *jāgṛyatām*, *jāgṛyuḥ*. Regarding the rule *ṭhjusi ca*: *Note:* This passage discusses the conjugation of the root *jāgṛ* (to wake). It explains the formation of the aorist (*luṅ*) and the potential (*liṅ*). In the aorist third person plural, the suffix *jus* is applied, and the rule *ṭhjusi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.83) applies, which mandates *guṇa* for the root vowel before this suffix. In the potential, the augment *yāsuṭ* is added, and due to its *ṅ*-marker, it prevents the *guṇa* substitution of the root vowel. The examples provided illustrate these grammatical operations.

The intention is that there is no *guṇa* substitution because it has been stated [in Pāṇini 1.1.5] "not before *a* and so on. He demonstrates the sequence for the application of *yaṇ* and other operations in the case of the root *jāgṛ* when followed by *luṅ*, *is*, and *iṭ*: "In the form *jāgṛ is*... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "when that has been done":

once *guṇa* has been applied by the rule "for *jāgr*, [there is *guṇa*] except before *vi*, *ciṇ*, and *ṇal*" (*jāgro'viciṇṇal*), and *ra* has been substituted for *ar*, the form *ajāgar īt* is established.

The meaning is "it being so. Regarding the phrase "so they say," the word "the elders" (*vṛddhāḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject. Forms such as *ajāgariṣṭām* and *ajāgariṣuḥ* are easy to understand. The root *daridrā* ends in a long vowel (*ā*) and is *seṭ* (taking the *iṭ* augment). *Durgatiḥ* means becoming destitute, i.e., the state of being deprived of wealth. *Daridrāti* means "he becomes deprived of wealth."

(311) *iddaridrasya* | Pāṇini 6.4.114. The short vowel in *daridra* is Vedic (*sautra*). From the rule *gamahana...* [Pāṇini 6.4.98], the phrase *kṅiti* is understood to carry over. From *ī halyaghoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.113], the word *hali* is understood; and from *ata ud...* [Pāṇini 6.4.110], the term *sārvadhātuke* is understood. Thus he says:
Regarding *daridrāteḥ*: this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of *ā* prescribed by the rule *śnābhyastayoḥ*.
By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, the final vowel [of the root] is replaced by *i*; thus, we have *daridrita*. Regarding *daridritaḥ*:
because the suffix *tas* is marked with *ṅ* (indicating that it is treated as having an indicatory *ṅ*), the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* applies, and the *ā* of the verbal stem is replaced by *i*.

(312) *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.112. Regarding *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*: from the rule *gamahana...* [P. 6.4.98], the word *lopaḥ* (elision) is understood; from *ata ud...* [P. 6.4.110], the word *sārvadhātuke* (before an affix of the *sārvadhātuka* class) is understood. Thus he says: "of these two," namely, of the *śnā* affix and...

And the meaning is "of that which is reduplicated. Regarding the form *daridratīti*: because it belongs to the class beginning with *jakṣ* and is thus reduplicated (*abhyasta*), the substitution of *ad* for *jha* occurs by the rule *adabhyastāt*, and there is the elision of the long *ā*. [The forms are: *daridrāsi*, *daridrithaḥ*, *daridritha*;
*daridrāmi*, *daridrivaḥ*, *daridrimaḥ*. Now, regarding the *liṭ* [perfect tense]...

"Because [the root] has multiple vowels (*anekāctvāt*). This is clear from the commentary on the rule *kāspratyayādām amantre liṭi*. Regarding the form *daridrāñcakāra*, there is a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* (P. 6.1.101) before the suffix *ām*. He states Kaiyaṭa’s opinion: "After *ā*" (*āta iti*). In the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* (P. 7.1.34), since there is no reason to skip the first [vowel], it is indeed the letter *o* that is intended.
It is proper to enjoin [the substitution of] *au*. For, as established by such rules as "In the case of *vṛddhi*, [the substitute] is that much [only]," and so forth;

therefore, the injunction of *au* results in the hearing of the vowel *au* in the form *dadaridrau*, because when the suffix *ṇal* follows the root *daridrā*, the rule "The elision of *daridrā* should be stated before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix" applies, resulting in the elision of *ā*. Thus, the purpose of the *au*-injunction is achieved.

However, since the substitution of *ok* is prescribed [for the root *dṛ*], and because *vṛddhi* is impossible when there is elision of *ā*, it is understood that the suffix *ām* applies to the root *daridrā* in the *liṭ* tense. The meaning is that once *ām* is present, the suffix *ṇal* is simply not applicable.
This has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *vasvekājādghasām* and clarified by Kaiyaṭa.
"That [suffix] is indeed rootless. *dadaridra*, *dadaridrau*, *dadaridruva*, *dadaridrima*.

Regarding the phrase "when an ārdhadhātuka suffix is intended": the elision of the *ā* of the root *daridrāti*—occurring by the rule "there is elision of the *ā* when *iṭ* follows"—takes place before an ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with a vowel, whether that suffix has a *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*kṅit*) or not. And that...

The meaning is that it should be stated that [the substitution] occurs even before the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is intended to be applied. By this, from the root *daridrā*, one forms *daridraḥ*; once the elision (*āllopa*) of the long vowel is effected, the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is established. However, if the elision of the long vowel were to apply only when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix follows, then the suffix *ṇa*—prescribed by the rule "after roots ending in *śyai*, *vadi*, and *vadhi*"—would have to be applied instead.

Furthermore, if the suffix *ṇa* were applied first, it would subvert the elision of the long *ā* (āllopa), and by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, the augment *yuk* would be inserted, resulting in the form *daridrāya*. However, when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is intended, the elision of the long *ā* (āllopa) occurs even before that [suffix is added].
Since the root does not end in a dental consonant (*adanta*), the suffix *ṇa* is absent; consequently, the suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādi*) is applied without obstruction.
This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the rule *luṅ vā*: the meaning is that the elision of the vowel *ā* (*āllopa*) is optional when the suffix *luṅ* follows.
This is a summary of the meaning of the Vārttika: "It should be stated that [the elision] is optional in the case of the *adyatanī* (imperfect tense)."

By the phrase "in the *adyatani* [tense]," the *luṅ* suffix prescribed for the meaning of the past occurring on the current day (*adyatanabhūta*) is intended, because that alone is cited as an example in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the rule "not in *san*, *ṇvul*, or *lyuṭ*," the meaning is that it must be stated that the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) does not occur for the root *daridrāti* in these [suffixes]. For example, in *ṇvul*: [Example follows]

The word *daridrāyakaḥ* [is formed] by the suffix *yuk* after [the root] *ā*. As in the case of the suffix *lyuṭ*: *daridrāṇaḥ*. When no substitute is applied, there is no elision of the long *ā*, and thus a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) occurs. As in the case of the desiderative suffix (*san*): *didaridrāsati*.
By the maxim "of that which is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya*), this prohibition applies only to the elision that would otherwise be obtained by the Vārttika.

Therefore, regarding the statement "the addition of *daridrāṇān* [is required] for the case of *ṭh* and *stan*" (Pāṇini 6.4.123), when the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied to the root *daridrā*, the elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule "there is elision of *ā* when *iṭ* follows" (Pāṇini 6.4.64); thus, one forms *didaridriṣati*. When the suffix *tāsi* is present with the augment *iṭ*, the elision of *ā* occurs according to the aforementioned Vārttika. This applies to the rule "there is elision of *ā* when *iṭ* follows."
Even though it is possible [to derive it otherwise], the *vārttika* is presented here because it is the logical course. [The forms of the root *daridrā* (to be poor) are as follows:
*Daridriṣyati* (he will be poor). Imperative: *daridrātu*, *daridritāt*, *daridritām*, *daridratu*;
*daridritam*, *daridrita*; *daridrāṇi*, *daridrāva*, *daridrāma*. In the *laṅ* (imperfect): *adaridrāt*, etc.

Having considered this, he says: "adaridritām" (they have not become poor). Regarding "adaridruḥ" (they have not become poor): because [the root] belongs to the *jakṣityādi* group, it is treated as an *abhyasta* (repeated) stem, and thus the suffix *jus* is applied—this is the intended meaning.
[The forms are: *adaridrāḥ*, *adaridritam*, *adaridrita*; *adaridrām*, *adaridrava*, *adaridrima*. [The optative form is: *daridriyāt*.
The intention is that because it is sārvadhātuka, the *it* augment [is applied] by the rule *vidhiliṅ*. Regarding the optative in the sense of benediction (*āśīrliṅ*), he says:
*daridryāt*. The intention is [the application of] *āto lopaḥ*. Regarding the aorist (*luṅ*) in the alternative where there is elision of the *ā*, he says:
*adaridrīt*. [The forms] *adaridriṣṭām* and so forth follow. However, in the alternative where there is no elision of the *ā*, he says: [the following].

Regarding *iṭsakau*: [the form] *adaridriṣyat*. Regarding *cakāsṛ* in the sense of "shining": it is marked with *ṛt* (ṛdit) and takes the augment *iṭ*. Having taken for granted that [the forms] *cakāsti* and *cakāstaḥ* are established, he says: "for *jha*, *at*" (*jhasya at*). The intention is that because [the root] belongs to the class beginning with *jakṣati*, it is *abhyasta* (repeated). [The forms are: *cakāsatī* (third person dual), *cakāssi* (second person singular), *cakāsthaḥ* (second person dual), *cakāstha* (second person plural).

*cakāsmi*, *cakāsvaḥ*, *cakāsmaḥ*; *cakāsāñcakāra*—the reason for the suffix *ām* is that the root has more than one vowel (*anekāctvāt*). [The forms] *cakāsitā*, *cakāsiṣyati*; *cakāstu* (or *cakāstāt*), *cakāstām*, *cakāsatu*. When *hi* is substituted for the imperative suffix, the form *cakās dhi* results; then, by the rule *dhica*, there is elision of the *s*.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding this, he states another opinion: "Some say [the elision] is only of *sic*. This means that some consider the elision [prescribed by the rule] *dhi ceḥ* to apply only to *sic*. Their intention is based on the Vārttika: "When there is the letter *dh*, the elision of *sic* occurs; the purpose [of this rule] is [to account for forms such as] *cakāddhi*. In this view, [the elision applies] to the letter *s*.

The letter *d* becomes *j* by virtue of being *jaś*. Thus he says: "from *cakādhi*. The phrase "in some [manuscripts]" (*eke*) indicates the presence of a lack of conviction (*asvarasa*). The reason for this is that, having rejected the Vārttika "there is elision of *sic* before *dh* and *s*" (*dhisakāre sico lopaḥ*), [the author] maintains the rule "and before *dhi*" (*dhi ca*) as applying to the letter *s* alone.
There is acceptance of its elision. Thus he says: "The Bhāṣya states simply 'cakādhi'. When *cakās* follows [the suffix] *tāt*, it becomes *caṭakāstam*;
[in the present], *cakāsta*. [In the first person singular,] *cakāsāni*, [in the dual,] *cakāsāva*, [and in the plural,] *cakāsāma*. When the *laṅ* [suffix] follows, the form stands as *acakāst*.
(313) *tipyanasteḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.73. *tipyanasteḥ*: "not being *asti*" is *anastiḥ*; this is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound.
The term *padasya* ("of a word") is understood by context. From the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*, the word *ante* ("at the end") is carried over (*anuvartate*).
From the rule *sasajuṣo'r*, the word *saḥ* (in the genitive case) is understood to follow.

From the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ*, the word *daḥ* (meaning the substitute *d*) is understood. He states this by saying "of that which ends in a pada," and so forth. What is the purpose of the condition *anasteḥ*? [Consider: *salilam idaṃ sarvam ā*. [The word *ā* is used here.]

Thus, from the root *as* (to be), in the *laṅ* tense with the suffix *tip*, after the elision of the vowel *i*, there is no insertion of *īṭ* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" and the rule "astisicaḥ"; then, after the elision of the consonant by the rule "halṅyādi," the form [is *ās*]. In the present case, however, from the root *cakās* (to shine), in the *laṅ* tense with the suffix *tip*, after the elision of the consonant by the rule "halṅyādi" and the substitution of *d* for *s*, [the form *cakād* arises] by the rule "vāvasāne."
Intending to show the forms in the *cartvijaś* (the *liṭ* perfect tense), he says: *acakāt*, *acakāt*; and *acakāsuḥ*.

The sense is that the suffix *jus* is applied by the rule "after *sij*, when followed by an affix with an indicatory *b* or *ṅ*, there is *jus*" (*sijabhyastayor ātaḥ*). (314) *sipi dhāto rurvā* | Pāṇini 8.2.74. [In the *sip* (second person singular *parasmaipada*) ending, the substitution of *ru* for the final letter of a verbal root is optional.]

[This is] from the root *sip*. "Of a word" (*padasya*) is the governing rule (*adhikṛta*). From "jhalām jaśo'nte," the word "at the end" (*ante*) is understood by anuvṛtti. From "sasajuṣo'r," the word "sa" follows with its sixth case ending elided. Thus he says: "of that which is at the end of a word. [The phrase] "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*)...

The intention is that this [suffix] follows from the rule "ṭhvasusraṃsvi" (Pāṇini 8.2.72). Since the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is never absent in the case of *sip*, the mention of "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is for the sake of subsequent rules. Examples: *acakāsīt* and *acakāsiṣyat*.
The root *śās* is marked with the indicatory letter *u* (*udit*) and is *seṭ* (taking the augment *iṭ*).

(315) *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.34. Regarding *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*: from the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*, the phrase *upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* is understood to carry over. Thus, [the meaning is] "of the *śās* [root], of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)". As for *śāsti*: because it belongs to the *jakṣādi* group...
The intention is that [the substitution] does not apply because [the root] has already been applied [elsewhere]. *śāssi*, *śiṣṭhaḥ*, *śiṣṭha*; *śāsmi*, *śiṣvaḥ*, *śiṣmaḥ*.

However, in the case of *ṭhā-śāste*, the long vowel (*ī*) does not occur, as it is clear from the Bhāṣya that only the root *śās* which takes the augment *aṭ* and is conjugated in the Parasmaipada is intended to be included there. *śaśāsa*, *śaśāsitha*; *śāsitā*.
He will instruct. When *śās* followed by *hi* is present, he says:
(316) *śā hau* | 6.4.35 | *śā hau*. The term *śā* here has its nominative case ending elided. [The rule] *śāsa idaṅtyitaḥ* applies to *śās*.

This [word] continues [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of the root *śās*. This is an exception to the substitution of *it*. Now, one might object: since the *ś* of *śās* is replaced by *ś*, there is no *jhal* (a consonant) following it; therefore, how can *dhi* replace *hi*? To this he replies: "because that [substitution] is considered as if it were not having taken effect (*abhīyatvena*). Although the form *śādhi* is established by the elision of the *hi* according to the rule "dhi ca," [the objection remains valid regarding the application of *dhi*].

Nevertheless, because the elision of *l* (*salopa*) is considered asiddha, the substitution of *i* by the rule "śāsa id" would apply; they say that the prescription of *śā* is for the purpose of preventing that. Regarding the *laṅ* [aorist], he says: *aśāt*. The intention is that, according to the rule "tipyanaste," there is the substitution of *d*, and then the optional application of *c* (the retroflex *ṣ*). Regarding *aśāsuḥ*: the intention is that the suffix *jus* is applied because the root is abhyasta (repeated). *Aśāḥ*.
*aśāt*—the intention is that there is an option regarding the substitution of *r* and *t* by the rule *sipi dhātoḥ*. *aśiṣṭam*, *aśiṣṭa*;

*aśāsam*, *aśiṣva*, *aśiṣma*. *śiṣyāt*—the intention is that after the substitution of *i* for *śāsa* by the rule *śāsa it*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *śāsivasīṣu*. *aśiṣat*—the intention is that *aṅ* is substituted [for *luṅ*] and *it* is added.

The root *dīdhīṅ* ends in the vowel *ī*. Because it bears the marker *ṅ*, it is conjugated in the Ātmanepada. "These five [roots] and so forth"—this is stated in accordance with Mādhava; however, the true state of affairs will be explained later. Due to its inclusion in the group beginning with *jakṣ* (Pāṇini 6.1.6), it is classified as *abhyasta* (repeated); consequently, the substitute *at* is applied to the suffix *jha*. Thus: *dīdhyate*; *dīdhīṣe*; *dīdhyāthe*.

*dīdhīdhve*. Regarding the substitution of *i* for the *laṭ* [present tense marker], he says: (317) *yīvarṇayordīdhīvevyoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.53. "In the case of *dīdhī* and *vevī*, when *yi* or an *ivarṇa* [follows]. *Yi* and *ivarṇa* form a *dvandva* compound, from which the locative case [is derived]. *Yi*.
In this context, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. From the rule "tāsastyoḥ," the word "lopa" (elision) is understood to follow.
By the rule "alo'ntyasya," the elision applies to the final [letter]. Thus he says: "of these two," and so forth.
In the examples "ādīdhyagataḥ" and "āvevyagataḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *ī* before the suffix *lyap*. This occurs when an *i*-vowel follows.

An example will be stated. Regarding the phrase "thus [regarding] elision": in the case of *dīdhī* where *i* is the substitute for *laṭ*, although elision would apply because of the rule "elision occurs before a vowel" (*yīvarṇayoḥ*) due to the subsequent *ivarṇa*, that elision—which is a subsequent rule—is set aside by the substitution of *it* for the final *ṭi*, because the latter is a permanent (*nitya*) rule. This is because the substitution of *etva* (the replacement of the penultimate vowel with *e*) operates whether the elision has taken place or not.
The sense is that when that [substitution] has been performed, there is no elision because of the absence of a following *y*-vowel.
Regarding "the prohibition of *guṇa*": the meaning is that once *dīdhī-ām* is established, the *guṇa* substitution—which would otherwise apply by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*—is prohibited.
Regarding the form *dīdhīta*: the intention is that once the augment *iṭ* is applied, the long vowel *ī* is elided because it is followed by the vowel *i*.
[The forms are: *dīdhītām*, *dīdhyātām*, *dīdhyatām*; *dīdhīṣva*, *dīdhyāthām*, *dīdhīdhvam*; *dīdhyai*, *dīdhyāvahai*, *dīdhyāmahai*; [and in the imperfect: *adīdhīta*, *adīdhyātām*.
*adīdhyata*; *adīdhīthāḥ*, *adīdhyāthām*, *adīdhīdvam*; *adīdhi*, *adīdhīvahi*, *adīdhīmahi*. [Optative: *dīdhīta*, *dīdhīyātām*. [Precative:
*dīdhiṣīṣṭa*, *dīdhiṣīyāstām*, *dīdhiṣīran*. [Aorist: *adīdhiṣṭa*. [Conditional: *adīdhiṣyata*. However, in reality, this is according to the Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Because these five [roots] follow what is observed, it is improper to describe their forms according to worldly usage. "The roots *vevīṅ* and *veti* are equal [to *vī*]"—thus their forms are like those of *dīdhī*.
Thus [end] the group beginning with *jakṣ*. "The roots *ṣasa* and *ṣasti* mean 'sleep'"—these two are taught with an initial *ṣ*. Second [section].
Thus it is said. Therein, he provides examples for the root *ṣas*: *sasiti* (he lies down), *sasantī* (they two lie down).

The intention is that because [the root] is not yet considered reduplicated (*anabhyasta*), there is only the substitution of the final letter [with *s*]. Thinking that the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication apply, he says: *sesatuḥ* (they two have lain down), *sesuḥ* (they have lain down). [The forms are: *sasitha*, *sesathuḥ*, *sesa*; *sasāsa*—*sasasa*, *sesiva*.

*sasima*, *sasitā*, *sasiṣyati*. Regarding *sastu*—from *sas tu*: after *sas* [is established], when *hi* is substituted for *hi* by the rule *herdhi*, considering the elision of *s* by the rule *dhi ca*, he says *sadhi*.
In that case, because the substitute *dhi* is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the doubling [of the consonant] occurs by the rule *ato heḥ*.

Anticipating the objection regarding the elision (*luk*), he says: "In the previous [section]. *Sasta* means *sas-tāt sas-tam sas-ta*. *Sasāni*, *sasāva*, *sasāma*. Regarding the *laṅ* [he says]: "It was not" (*asad*). The sense is that when *as-as-ta* is established, the *takāra* is elided by the rule *halṅyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), and then the *sakāra* is changed to *dakāra* by the rule *tipyanasteḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.73). [The form] *asastām* [is derived similarly].

It should also be understood that *asasan* [is the form]. However, when the *sip* [suffix] of the *laṅ* follows, the sequence *asas s* arises; then, by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, there is elision of the *t* [of *sip*], and by the rule *tipyanasteḥ*, there is the substitution of *d* for *s*. Thus, the sense is that [the form becomes] *asastaḥ*. It should also be understood that *asasan* [is the form]. However, when the *sip* of the *laṅ* follows, the sequence *asas s* arises.
When *sip* follows, by the rule "after a root [comes ru]," *ru* optionally replaces it; in the alternative case, *da*. Then, by the rule "elision of *hal*, *ṅ*, etc.," [the suffix is dropped].
Thus he says: *asaḥ*, *asad*. [The forms] *asastam*, *asasta*; *asasam*, *asasva*, *asasma*. Regarding the *liṅ* (optative), he says: *sasyāt*, *sasyātām*, *sasyāstām*, and so forth.
The *Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara* says: "It was not" (*asāsīt*). The intention is that there is an optional *vṛddhi* by the rule *ato halādeḥ*. [In the future tense: *asasiṣyat*.
Now, he gives examples from the root *ṣas* (to destroy): "they are" (*santi*). Because it is marked with the *idit* indicator, *num* is added.
Because it is marked with the *idit* indicator, *num* is added. When the form *saṃs t ti* is established by the rule *naśca*, [the following applies].

The meaning is that when the *salopa* (elision of *s*) is applied by the rule *ṭhskoḥ*, and the *parasavarṇa* (substitution of the following sound) is applied, then by the rule *jharo jhari*, there is an optional elision of the first *t*; thus, the forms are either *ekataṃ* or *dvitaṃ*. Regarding *saṃstanti*:
the meaning is that because it is not an *abhyasta* (repeated) root, only the final substitution (*antādeśa*) applies. When *sip* is added, the form stands as *saṃst si*.
By the rule *ṣṭuan*, when the *s* is elided, the *anusvāra* is replaced by its homogeneous nasal (*parasavarṇa*), which is *n*.
Because there is no following homogeneous sound (*savarṇa*), the *t* is not elided by the rule *jharo jhari*. [The forms are:
*santsi*, *santhaḥ*, *santha*; *saṃstmi*, *saṃstvaḥ*, *saṃstmaḥ*; *sasasta*, *sasastatuḥ*.

*sasaṃstitha*, *sasaṃstiva*, *sasaṃstima*; [future] *saṃstiṣyati*; [imperative] *saṃstu*—*saṃstāt*, *saṃstām*, *saṃstantu*. When *saṃst hi* is established, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs; by the rule *skoḥ*, the *s* is elided; with the subsequent *savarna* (homogeneous) replacement, *saṃst dhi* is established; then, by the rule *jharo jhari*, the *t* is [elided].

Elision; euphonic combination (*sandhi*). In the absence of elision, when the *jaś*-substitution applies to the letter *t*, [we have] *saṃddhi*—*santāt*, *santam*, *santa*; *saṃstāni*, *saṃstāva*, *saṃstāma*. When the suffix *tiP* of the *laṅ* follows, resulting in *asaṃst t*, there occurs elision by the rule *halṅyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), elision of the initial member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*), and elision of a word-final conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) (Pāṇini 8.2.23)—thus: *asan*.
*asantām*, *asantaḥ*; *asan*, *asantam*, *asantaḥ*; *asaṃstam*, *asaṃstva*, *asaṃstma*;

*saṃstyāt*; *asaṃstīt*; *asaṃstiṣyat*. He states another opinion: "of many," etc. "Relying on this," etc.; thus, in the present case, when the *laṭ* [present tense] has taken the suffix *tip*, resulting in *saṃst ti*, and [the condition of] a *jhal* [consonant] follows...

The meaning is that because of the combination of the three—*anusvāra*, *s*, and *t*—the pair *s-t* lacks the designation of a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant); consequently, by the rule *ṣṭuan iti lopaḥ*, there is no elision, and thus forms such as *saṃsti* and so forth are to be inferred. [Regarding the root] *vaś* in the sense of "desire": "desire" means longing; it is *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment).

Regarding *vaṣṭi*: by the rule *vraśca*, the *ś* of *śas* becomes *ṣ*, and the *t* becomes *ṭ* by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭu*. Regarding *uṣṭa*: the form is derived through vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā* when a *ṅit* affix follows; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *uvāśa*: in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], vocalization occurs for the reduplicated syllable by the rule *liṭabhyāsasya*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *ūśatuḥ*.

The intention is that, because [the root] is subsequent [to the rule *grahijyā*], semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is performed; then, after doubling and the application of the *halādi-śeṣa* rule, a long vowel is substituted for the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). Thus: *uvaśitha*, *ūśathuḥ*, *ūśa*; *uvāśa*—*uvaśa*, *ūśiva*, *ūśima*. By the form *vaśitā*, its status as having an augment *iṭ* (*seṭ*) is indicated. [The future forms are: *vaśiṣyati*; *uṣṭām*.

The form *uśant* should also be understood [as an example]. From *uḍḍhaīti*: when *vaś* + *hi* is established, by the rule *dhica* (Pāṇini 6.1.112), since it is not marked with *p*, the semivowel is replaced by a vowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). Then, by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), the *ś* becomes *ṣ*. By the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the *dh* becomes *ḍh*.
And by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*. This is the intended meaning. [The forms] *vaśāni*, *vaśāva*, and *vaśāma* [are derived similarly].

The author says "avaṭ" etc. The intention is that after the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the *ś* becomes *ṣ*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*, and for that [ḍ], there is an option regarding the substitution of *c* (by Pāṇini 8.4.55). Regarding "āṬśan": *avaṭ āṬṣṭam* and *āṬṣṭa*. Regarding "avaśam": the intention is that because it has a *pi*t marker, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization). [Examples: *āṬśva*, *āṬśma*. In the *vidhyāśīrliṅ* (the optative used for injunctions and blessings), [we have] *uśyāt*.
Taking them for granted, he says: *uśyātām*, *uśyāstām*. [The aorist forms are] *avaśīt*, *avrāśīt*;

[the conditional is] *avaśiṣyat*. Thus, Mādhava and others maintain that these five roots—*dīdhī*, *vevī*, *ṣasa*, *ṣasti*, and *vaś*—are exclusively Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding this, in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*...
The *Bhāṣya* states: "Because *dīdhī* and *vevī* have the Veda as their domain. Regarding the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ*, the *Bhāṣya* says:

"*ṣas* and *vaś* are Vedic. From this very *Bhāṣya*, it is understood that the root *ṣasti* is not included here [in the list of six]. For this very reason, [the root is given as] "*ṣasa* [meaning] to sleep."

Kaiyaṭa states that because there is no difference in meaning, the repetition of the reading [of the root *vaś*] is due to the mention of the suffix *stip* in the rule for the admission of the reading (*pāṭhābhyupagama*).

In this regard, the statement that the root *vaś* is Vedic (*chāndasa*) is merely general; for it is said: "Bhāguri [teaches] the elision of *a* [after *vaś*], as in 'the gods desire Senānī for victory'."
Let us leave it at that for now, as we have seen such usage in examples like these. Regarding the term *carkarītam*: this is a metrical rule (*gaṇasūtra*) within the Dhātupāṭha.

The designation *carkarītam* is an established convention among the ancient teachers for that which ends in the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*). Thus he says: "That which ends in *yaṅluk* belongs to the *adādi* class. By this...

Only the *vikaraṇa* suffix *śap* is elided after a stem with the *yaṅ*-luṅ (reduplication with elision), and not another suffix such as *śyan*. Because the section begins with "for the *parasmaipada*," that which ends in *yaṅ*-luṅ is exclusively *parasmaipada*. The root *hnuṅ* means "to remove"; it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). Thus: *hnute*.

*hnuvāte*, *hnuvate*, and so forth. *juhnuve*; *juhnuvāte*, *juhnuvire*—the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *krī*. *juhnuviṣe*; *juhnuvivahe*. *hnotā*. *hnoṣyate*. *hnutām*. *hnuṣva*. *hnavai*, *hnavāvahai*. *ahnuta*—having thus treated these as established forms.

He states the optative in the injunctive sense (*vidhiliṅ*) with "hnuvīta"; he states the optative in the benedictive sense (*āśīrliṅ*) with "hnoṣīṣṭa"; and he states the aorist (*luṅ*) with "ahnoṣṭa. Thus ends the section on the *lug-vikaraṇa* in the *Bālamanoramā*.
(176) *arthavad adhātu-pratyayaḥ prātipadikam* | 1.2.45 | That which possesses meaning, excluding roots and suffixes, is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Now, by means of the sūtras *sv-au-ja-sam-auḍ* and so forth, he will explain the suffixes beginning with *su*. In this context, the rule *ṅy-āp-prātipadikāt* is understood as a governing heading (*adhikāra*). When there arises the desire to know what that *prātipadika* is, he says: *arthavad adhātuḥ*. That which possesses meaning is "meaning-bearing" (*arthavat*).

Following the neuter gender [of the compound], the substantive "the form of the word" (*śabdasvarūpam*) must be supplied. "Not a root" (*adhātuḥ*) and "not an affix" (*apratyayaḥ*) are its qualifiers. "Non-root" (*adhātuḥ*) is a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*). According to the rule "the gender of the latter member [prevails] in *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds," the masculine gender [would otherwise apply]; however, here it remains neuter.
The term "ṭapratyaya" (the suffix ṭ) recurs [in the rule]. What is intended is that which is distinct from a suffix and distinct from that which ends in a suffix.

The masculine gender is as before. The prohibition regarding the "formulation of a technical name" (*saṃjñāvidhau*) applies specifically to cases where the suffix itself is the technical name; this is the sense. Thus he says: "the root, the suffix," and so forth.

Words such as *ḍittha* and others, whose meanings are not conventionally established, serve as examples here. Why [is it specified] "meaningful" (*arthavat*)? So that in cases such as *danaṃ* (curd) and *vanaṃ* (forest), the designation of *prātipadika* does not apply to each individual phoneme. For if the designation *prātipadika* were applied to each phoneme, the addition of case-endings (*sup*) would occur for every single phoneme.

Furthermore, even in the absence of number and grammatical relation (*kāraka*), the nominative singular suffix *su* is unavoidable; for it has been established as the final doctrine (*siddhāntita*) in the Bhāṣya that the nominative case does not depend upon a *kāraka*, and thus the singular number functions even when no number is understood. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there is no harm even if the *su* suffix arises for each individual letter due to its elision by the rule *halṅyādi*, because even so, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would be unavoidable, and furthermore, *ru*-hood and the visarga would result from the vowel *a*. Enough of this. What is the purpose of the restriction "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*)? [Consider: the *liṅ* suffix after the verbal root *han*.

In the case of *ahan*, after the elision of *ti* and *śa*, the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *itaśca*, the addition of the augment *aṭ*, and the elision of the final consonant by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, the form *ahan* is produced. Here, when the designation of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is superseded by the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), the suffix *tiṅ* is introduced; once that [suffix] has been elided, the designation of "nominal stem" [remains].

There would be no elision of the *naL* because that which arose previously has not departed. Nor should it be argued that, by relying on the rule of "characterized by an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not apply simply because of the exclusion of what ends in an affix; for even so, the status of being a nominal stem that had already occurred previously has not departed. Nor, even in this case, [is there a solution] under the view that the time of application is determined by the time of the operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*).

It should be stated that when the designation *prātipadika* is being applied for the purpose of [the suffix] *nalopa*, the designation *prātipadika* would not apply to that which ends in a suffix by virtue of the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*. If that were so, then even in the case of "he rājan," there would be an absence of the *prātipadika* designation because it ends in a suffix by virtue of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*.

Otherwise, since the elision of the *n* would not even be applicable, the prohibition "not [before] *ṅsi* or the vocative" (*na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ*) would result in being purposeless. Nor can it be argued that the word *rājan*, ending in the *uṇādi* suffix *kanin*, falls under the category of "kṛt or taddhita derivatives" (*kṛtaddhita*).

It should not be argued that the prohibition "na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.6) is meaningful because the elision of *n* would otherwise apply due to its being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); for under the view that Uṇādi derivatives are unanalyzed (*avyutpatti*), the rule "kṛttaddhita-samāsāś ca" (Pāṇini 1.2.46) does not apply. And thus, from this very [fact],...

It is understood that because of the prohibition [of the suffix], the exclusion (paryudāsa) "not ending in a suffix" does not apply by resorting to the definition of a suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa). And thus,
in the case of *ahann*, since it does not end in a suffix, the status of being a nominal stem (prātipadika) would result.
The mention of "not being a root" (*adhātu*) is for the purpose of excluding that [case]. Why say "not being an affix" (*apratyaya*)?
In the case of *hariṣu* and *karoṣi*, since the *sup* and *sip* endings possess meaning and do not end in another affix, they would otherwise incur the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*);
therefore, to exclude that, the term "not being an affix" serves as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of affixes. And this is not the case here...

It should not be argued that since *sup* and *sip* would lose their status as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) due to the application of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), whereby they possess a suffix, and since this very possession of a suffix would suffice to exclude them by means of the exclusion of items ending in suffixes, what is the purpose of the separate exclusion of suffixes?

Because of the paribhāṣā rule stating that "when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with it and ends with it," the entire aggregate of base and suffix alone possesses the status of "ending in a suffix" (pratyayānta);
consequently, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the simple suffixes *sup* and *sip* cannot be obtained. [This is why the term] "not ending in a suffix" (*apratyayānta*) is used.

Why? [So that] in *hariṣu* (*haribhyaḥ*), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—which would otherwise apply to both the base and the suffix as a whole because they are distinct from the suffix and possess meaning—does not occur. (177) *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46).

*Kṛttaddhita*: The analysis is "the *kṛt* [suffixes] and the *taddhita* [suffixes], as well as compounds (*samāsa*). From the preceding sūtra, the term "*prātipadika*" (nominal stem) is carried over by anuvṛtti; this is modified to have a plural ending. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* includes that which ends with them (*tadanta-grahaṇa*).

Thus he says: "ending in kṛt or taddhita suffixes. Since words ending in kṛt or taddhita suffixes are already included by the previous rule because they end in suffixes, the explicit mention of "kṛt" and "taddhita" is for the purpose of excluding them from the application of the preceding rule. Because there is no need for the technical designation (saṃjñā) when applied to kṛt and taddhita suffixes alone, the prohibition stated as "in the formulation of a technical designation" applies here.

It does not apply. For this very reason, even in the formulation of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) in the preceding sūtra, the suffix-final form is obtained through the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*); thus, there is an exclusion of that which ends in a suffix. Some, however, maintain that by carrying over the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) from the previous rule, one obtains the rule for suffix-final forms through its force. [This applies] to *kṛt*-derived words.

For example: "the agent" (*kartā*), "the sustainer" (*bhartā*), and so forth. In the case of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), for example: "descendant of Upagu" (*aupagava*), and so forth. In the case of compounds (*samāsa*), for example: "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*), and so forth. [Objection: But the mention of "compound" is redundant, since in a compound such as "king's man" [the rule applies]. [Response: Indeed, the mention of "compound" is redundant, since in a compound such as "king's man"...

This is because the status of words such as *ityādi* as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is already established by the preceding rule itself. Nor should one suspect that the exclusion of items ending in suffixes (*pratyayānta-paryudāsa*) applies here by relying on the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) with respect to the suffix that has been elided after the second member of a compound; for even though the second member alone ends in a suffix, [the entire compound is not thereby considered to end in a suffix].

Because the aggregate [of sounds] does not end in a suffix, and because when a suffix is mentioned, only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed is understood, the exclusion of what ends in a suffix—by relying on the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle—does not apply; thus [it is stated]: "not before a *ṅi*, a *si*, or the vocative."

Since it has already been explained in detail in the preceding sūtra that [the nature of the word] is made known through negation, he says "by the preceding sūtra," etc. He demonstrates the actual form of the restrictive rule (niyama) with the words "where... The statement "the prior portion is a word" is an elliptical indication; it also implies "but the subsequent portion is not an affix."

This must be observed. Otherwise, in examples such as *janmavān*, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not apply, because the preceding portion would possess the status of a word (*pada*) by virtue of the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*.

Nor can it be argued that the status of being a nominal stem is possible here solely by the force of the inclusion of the term "secondary derivative" (*taddhita*) in the rule *kṛttaddhita* [Pāṇini 1.2.46].
This must be stated [as a definition], because the mention of "taddhita" (secondary suffix) in rules such as *dākṣi* has its purpose fulfilled there;

for in those cases, the initial portion is not a *pada*, since it is sublated by its status as a *bha* (stem). If it were not stated that "the preceding portion is a *pada*," then in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) would not apply.

With the phrase *īṣadasamāptau* (when there is slight incompleteness) continuing [from the previous rule], by the sūtra *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāttu*, when the suffix *bahuc* is added before the nominative plural ending *paṭavaḥ*, the resulting form *apaṭavaḥ* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because it possesses meaning; consequently, the case-ending *jas* belonging to that constituent part is elided, as indicated by the rule *citaḥ*.

In the case of *bahvajartha*, when the vowel *u* following the letter *ṭ* becomes acute (*udātta*) by the rule for the accent of a *cit* suffix, and then *jas* is added, the form *bahupaṭavaḥ* results. Here, the established state is that the vowel *a* following the letter *ṭ* is acute. Prior to the suffix *jas*, when the *bahuc* suffix is applied, it belongs to the entire aggregate *bahupaṭavaḥ*.

If, however, there were no status as a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*), then another suffix *jas* would not arise after that [base]. Nor is this an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because if that were the case, since the *jas* belonging to the base of the *bahuc* compound would lack the status of being a constituent part of a nominal stem, the rule "sup [suffixes] are elided after verbal roots and nominal stems" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*) would apply.

Because the suffix *jasi* has been elided, the term *bahupaṭavaḥ* is derived from the base ending in *jasi*; consequently, the *cit-svara* (acute accent) prescribed for a *cita* suffix would apply only to the vowel *ā* of *jasaḥ*. However, it is desired that the accent fall on the syllable following the *ṭ*-marker, namely the entire word-group *bahupaṭavaḥ*.

The meaning is that since the *luk* elision of *jas* occurs because it is a part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the word *paṭu* itself serves as the base for the suffix *bahuc*; thus, when the acute accent (*citsvara*) applies to the syllable following the letter *ṭ*, the form *bahupaṭavaḥ* (with the re-appearance of *jas*) is stated without any contradiction. He states the result of this restriction with the words "by that" (*tena*).

The meaning is "according to the stated rule. Otherwise, even a sentence such as *devadatta gām abhyāja śuklāṃ daṇḍena* would incur the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and consequently, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) would occur.
Nor should it be argued that a sentence cannot be a nominal stem simply because it ends in an affix (*pratyaya*).
The sense is that when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is the inclusion of only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed.

The particle *ca* in the rule *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca* serves the purpose of collecting what has not been previously mentioned. Consequently, the Vārttika stating "the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) must be stated for a meaningless particle" becomes redundant.
(178) *Pratyayaḥ* | 3|1|1 | *Pratyayaḥ*. This is the first sūtra of the third chapter. From here onwards...
The meaning is that from the completion of the fifth chapter onwards, the word *pratyaya* is employed as a technical term (*saṃjñā*).

However, substitutes (*ādeśa*) and augments (*āgama*) such as those in the rules "and for *han*, *vadha*" (*hanaśca vadhaḥ*), "and for *khan*, *ī*" (*ī ca khanaḥ*), and "the suffix *kuk* after *naḍa* etc. (*naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca*), do not receive the technical designation of *pratyaya*.
Because it creates a great designation.
(179) "And the subsequent [term]" |3|1|2|. This is the second sūtra of the third chapter. This one also is likewise.

The meaning is that this rule of application (*adhikāra*) also extends up to the completion of the fifth book (*pañcamaparisamāpti*). Regarding the determination of its limit, however, the commentary itself is the sole refuge. (180) *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* 4.1.1.

*ṅy-āpprātipadikāt*. This is the first sūtra of the fourth chapter. *Ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika* form a collective dvandva compound. *Ṅī* is a general term for the inclusion of *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *ṅīṅ*; *āp* refers to *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp*.

[The word] "grahaṇa" [is used]. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (pratyaya-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā), there is the inclusion of that which ends in it (tadanta-grahaṇa). He states this with the words "from that which ends in a ṅī" (ṅyantāt) and so forth. However, as for the restrictive rule (avadhi-niyama) "up to the fifth [case-ending]," the only recourse is the [traditional] commentary itself. Now, one might object: "Let the sūtra simply be formulated as 'from a nominal stem' (prātipadikāt)."

The mention of *ṅyāp* need not be made; for by the paribhāṣā "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included," suffixes such as *su* and others can occur even after words ending in the suffix *ūṅ*, such as *daṇḍinī*, *ajā*, and *khaṭvā*, just as they do after the word *śvaśrū*. Therefore—

He says: "When a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. This means that which is qualified by suffixes such as *ṅīp* and others which convey feminine gender. "So that it may be so" (*yathā syāt*): the word "so that" (*yathā*) here denotes fitness (*yogyatā*). It is only from a stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp* that the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is fit to occur; that [is what is intended].

The meaning is that [the rule] would apply only when there is the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*. He shows what is to be excluded: "lest it should occur before *ṅī* and *āp*. Consequently, forms such as *lohinikā* and *āryakā* are established.
For instance, the word *lohita*, being a [color] term...

By the *phiṭ-sūtra* "taṇatinitāntānām," the first syllable is udātta; consequently, the vowel *o* is udātta. According to the rule "anudātaṃ padamekavarjam" (a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]), the remaining vowels *i* and *ñ* are anudātta. Thus, by the rule "varṇādanudātātopadhāto naḥ" (the suffix *naḥ* is applied after a color-word that is anudātta and has an anudātta vowel as its penultimate).

From the existing word *lohita*, when the feminine gender is intended, the suffix *ṅīp* is applicable, as is the substitution of *na* for the *ta* by virtue of its co-occurrence (*tatsaṃniyoga*). Furthermore, the suffix *kan* is applicable as a *svārthika* (denotative) suffix by the rule "after *lohita*, [the suffix *kan* is added] when referring to a gem. In that case, because it is a *svārthika* suffix, *kan* is both internal (*antaraṅga*) and subsequent (*para*).

It would not operate by setting aside the *ṅīp* suffix prescribed as being invariably associated [with the root]; consequently, there is no occasion for the *ṅīp*. This is because, since it has a *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), it lacks the property of having a *t* as its penultimate letter (*topadha*). Therefore, from the word *lohitaka*, after the application of *ṭāp* by the rule "ṭhājadyataḥ," and the subsequent substitution of *ī* by the rule "pratyayasthāt...," the form is simply *lohitikā*.
It would be [the form] *lohinī*, but not *lohinikā*; however, both forms are desired.

But in the rule *ṅy-āp-prātipadikāt*, since the term *ṅīp* is explicitly mentioned, by virtue of that, even though it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) suffix, it sets aside the suffix *kan* (which follows) and applies the feminine suffix *ṅīp* as prescribed in conjunction with the substitution of *n* for the final letter.

From the word *lohinī*, when the suffix *kan* is applied and the vowel is shortened by the rule "ṭhke'ṇaḥ," the form *lohinikā* results. However, since the rule "varṇādanudātā... is optional, in the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* which is prescribed in conjunction with the substitution of *n* for the final letter, the suffix *kan* is added to the word *lohita*; then, after the vowel is shortened, [the form *lohitakā* arises].

By applying the rule *pratyayasthāt* for the substitution of *it*, the form *lohitikā* is also established as *kāntāṭṭāp*. Similarly, from the word *ārya*, when the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*), since it is possible to indicate femininity by the *ṭāp* following the entire complex, the *ṭāp* is applied after the element ending in *kan* alone— following the maxim of reduplication of a single syllable (*ekājdvirvacananyāya*)— and thus [the form] *āryakā* is derived from *kan*.

Previously, because the suffix *ṭāp* was absent, there was no *at* (short *a*) in place of *āt*; consequently, since the optional substitution of *it* by the rule "of the Northeners (*udīcām*), in place of *āt*" did not apply, the rule "from a suffixal [element]" (*pratyayasthāt*) would have necessitated a compulsory *it*, resulting only in *āryikā* and never *āryakā*. However, both forms are desired.

In the rule *ṭhṅyāpprātipadikāt*, however, because of the inclusion of the term *āp*, the suffix *kan*—which is svārthika—is set aside by *ṭāp*. Then, after *ṭāp*, *kan* is added; subsequently, the vowel is shortened by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*.
Finally, *ṭāp* is added again after the form ending in *kan*, and by the rule *udīcāmātaḥ sthāne*, there is an optional substitution of *ī* for the final vowel, resulting in two forms.
It is established. In reality, however, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* need not be made;
the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) arises from that which already ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), and *ṅī* and *āp* operate precisely before the case-suffixes.

This is because the grammatical operations triggered by self-meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), case-role (*kāraka*), and censure (*kutsā*) occur in a sequential order.
For instance: the meaning of the word itself consists of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which serve as the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Knowledge of that [genus, etc.

arises first, because knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*). Following that, there arises knowledge of its substratum (*āśraya*), because it is primary as the substantive (*dharmin*) and because it is what is required by the inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth. After that—
From that, there arises the cognition of gender, because it depends solely upon its own substrate.

From that, there arises the cognition of number, which depends upon a category of entities belonging to the same class, as opposed to the dependence [of gender] upon a *kāraka* associated with an action of a different class. From that—

There is a dependence on the meaning of the case endings that express the grammatical relations (*kāraka-rūpa-vibhakti-artha*). It is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kutsitaḥ* that the cognition of contempt and so forth occurs when those [case endings] have ceased [to apply]. This has also been refined in the *Śabdaratna*.
(181) *svaujasamauṭchśaṣṭābhyāmbhisreḍbhyāmbhyasṅsibhyāmbhyasṅsosāmṅyossup* || 4.1.2 || *s-au-ja-sam-au-ṭ*, *am-au-ṭ-ś-as*, *ṭā-bhyāṃ-bhis*,
*re-ḍ-bhyāṃ-bhyas*, *ṅ-si-bhyāṃ-bhyas*, *ṅ-s-os-ām*, *ṅ-y-os-sup*.

The twenty-one suffixes beginning with *sva* (the case endings) consist of the group starting with *ṅi* and ending with *sup*. This is either a collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva compound or a copulative (*itaretarayoga*) dvandva; if the latter, the singular number used in the sūtra is for metrical reasons.
Furthermore, the rules "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *ṣ*," "it is an affix (*pratyaya*)," and "it follows [the stem]" apply as appropriate.

And it is modified [by the following rule]. Thus he says, beginning with "from that which ends in *ṅ*" (*ṅyantāt*), etc. Regarding the phrase "of *su*, *ṅsi*": the *u* and *i* of *su* and *ṅsi*; the *ja* and *śa* of *jas* and *śas*; the *ṭ* of *āṬ* and *ṭā*; and the *ṅ* of *ReĀ*, *ṅsi*, *ṅs*, and *ṅ*.

The meaning is that the letter *p* in *sup* and these [other letters] are to be understood as having the technical designation *it*. The remainder [of the explanation] is by means of the rules: "In the original instruction (*upadeśa*), an *anunāsika* vowel is *it*," "The letters *c* and *ṭ* are *it*," "The letters *l*, *ś*, and *k* are *it* when not followed by a *taddhita* suffix," and "The final letter in a root, suffix, or augmen is *it*. Furthermore, when there is the designation *it*, there is elision (*lopa*). The purpose of pronouncing them [as *it*] is found therein.
Regarding this, it will be stated: (182) *vibhaktiśca* 1.4.104.
Now, [the rule] *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* and so forth is useful for this purpose.

He states the technical name *vibhakti*: "And *vibhakti*. From the preceding rule, the mention of *sup* is carried over, and from the rule "tiṅstrīṇī" (Pāṇini 5.4.11), the mention of *tiṅ* is also carried over by virtue of the convention that a word marked with a circumflex (*svarita*) applies to a single portion [of a compound]. Thus he says: "*suptiṅau*. The particle *ca* (and) [is used for conjunction].

The purpose of using the designations "puruṣa" (person) and "vacana" (number) is for the sake of their simultaneous application (*samāveśa*). Therefore, even though they fall under the jurisdiction of the single designation rule (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), they do not function as synonyms (*paryāyatva*). Otherwise, in forms such as *rāmebhyaḥ* and *bhavāmaḥ*, since the designation "vibhakti" (case-ending) would be absent, the prohibition *na vibhaktau* would not apply.

But how is it that [the rules] such as "the first case ending occurs when there is mere expression of the nominal stem-meaning, gender, measure, and number; the second case ending in the sense of the object; the third case ending for the agent and the instrument; the fourth case ending in the sense of the recipient; the fifth case ending in the sense of the point of departure; the sixth case ending in the sense of the residual relation; and the seventh case ending in the sense of the locus" are established?
Since the technical designations "first" (*prathamā*) and so forth were not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras, Pāṇini, [the commentator] says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). This means:
"among those," namely, among the suffixes beginning with *su*. The phrase "of these and so forth" (*ityādīnām*) refers to this.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādinā*), there is the inclusion of [the suffixes] *am*, *āṬ*, *śas*, and others. Regarding the phrase "of the ancients" (*prācām*):

the grammatical connection is that in the treatises of the teachers prior to Pāṇini, such as Sphoṭāyana and others, technical designations (*saṃjñā*) beginning with "first" (*prathamā*) and ending with "seventh" (*saptamī*) were established. To the question "What are those?", he says: "by means of them" (*tābhiḥ*).
The meaning is that by means of those designations, such as "first" (*prathamā*) and so forth, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is possible here too— in this grammatical system of Pāṇini— as well.
*sup*: This is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term) for the case endings; it refers to the singular of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-ekavacana*).
The rule *tāny ekavacanadvivacanabahuvacanāny ekaśaḥ* follows [from the previous sūtra], with the word *tāni* being elided. *Ekaśaḥ* means "one by one" (*ekaikam*).

By the rule "ṭhsaṅkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām" [Pāṇini 5.4.43], the suffix *śas* is applied. Since the repetition (*vīpsā*) is already expressed by the suffix *śas* itself, there is no doubling (reduplication) according to the rule "ṭhnityavīpsayoḥ" [Pāṇini 8.1.4]. This point will be explained in detail during the commentary on the sūtra "ṭhsaṅkhyaikavacanācca."
From the rule "ṭhhtiṅstrīṇi trīṇi" [Pāṇini 1.4.102], the phrase "trīṇi trīṇi" is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "supastrīṇi," etc.
(184) *dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane* [Pāṇini 1.4.22].

Regarding the rule *dvayekayoḥ*: the mention of *dvayekayoḥ* is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; otherwise, it would have been *dvayakeṣu*. With this intention, he explains: "in the case of duality and singularity. (185) *bahuvacanaṃ bahuṣu* | 1.4.21 || [The plural number is used for many.]

Regarding the word *bahuṣu*: in order to avoid a lack of symmetry with the preceding sūtra, he states that here too the word *bahu* refers to plurality (*bahutva*), saying "in plurality. One should not raise the objection: "Even if the word *bahu* in this sūtra refers to plurality, since plurality is a single entity, how can there be the plural form *bahuṣu*?"
This is because [the term] "plurality" is established by superimposing the plurality residing in the substance that possesses the number "many" onto the quality of plurality itself.
And plurality is a specific property that pervades numbers beginning with three and four up to the highest number (parārddha), but it is not—

It is established in the *Kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa* of the first chapter of the eleventh book [of the *Tantravārttika*], as well as in its *bhāṣya* and *vārttika*, that "one of the three or more" is intended; for it is stated there: "Because all [birds] would be included by the plural number, there would be an option.
This has been elaborated by us in the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti*. And thus, "much rice..."
Thus, because the word *bahu* expresses abundance (*vaipulya*), it does not necessarily denote the plural number;

for, by the force of common usage such as "in the case of two or one," what is intended here is a specific plurality determined by a particular number. This applies even to a single individual, such as a woman.

In expressions such as *dārāḥ*, however, the plural number is used because the multiplicity of parts is superimposed upon the whole, by virtue of the authority of lexicons and the usage of elders; this is sufficient [to explain]. Regarding "the substitution of *r* and *visarga*":
when the first-case singular suffix *su* follows the word *rāma*, the vowel *u* is replaced by *it*.
The meaning is that when [the final *s*] is elided, *ru* is substituted by the rule "sasajuṣo ruḥ," and then a *visarga* is substituted by the rule "kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ.

However, the mention of *saḥ* (with the vowel *u*) is for the purpose of qualifying [the word] in rules such as "arvaṇastrasau. For if it were simply stated as *asi*, the meaning would be "when beginning with the letter *s*"; consequently, [the rule would not apply] in cases such as *vājamarvatsu*.

The rule *arvaṇas-tṛ* would not apply. Nor should it be argued that here, because the *ru* [of *arvan*] is not a *suptiṅanta* (an inflected word), its final member lacks the status of a *pada*, and thus the *repha* (the letter *r*) does not occupy the end of a *pada*—so how could there be a *visarga* here?
For by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), the *ru* retains the status of a *sup*. And this *sthānivadbhāva* applies when...
It should not be suspected that the *ru* (the substitute for *visarga*) belonging to a *traipādika* rule is *asiddha*,

because by the inclusion of the term "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) in the rule *ṭhidudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*, it is indicated that there is no status of being *asiddha* when the designation of *sthānivadbhāva* applies. For in that context, the mention of "not a suffix" is intended to prevent [the application of] *agni* [to the example].

In examples such as *kavibhiḥ kṛtam*, the purpose is to exclude the visarga. For if the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* were to apply, and since the substitute *ru* is considered *asiddha*, there would simply be no visarga at all in that position; thus, its [the prohibition's] redundancy is quite evident. Enough said. Regarding *rāma*: "Yogins rest in the infinite, true bliss, the conscious Self. Thus [it is said].
"He is designated as the Supreme Brahman by the word 'Rāma'"; such is the Śruti. [The formation of the word is as follows:

under the governing rule "karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.117), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root under the rule "halaś ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.121). By the rule "kṛttaddhitasamāsāś ca" (Pāṇini 1.2.46), it attains the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Alternatively, it is an unanalyzed technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*). Likewise...
Since it possesses meaning, it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). (186) Pāṇini 1.2.64: "Of words that have the same form, only one remains when they occur with the same case-ending.
Now, when there is a desire to express duality and so forth residing in the meaning of the nominal stem, [the suffixes] of the nominal stem...

This [sūtra] is commenced because it applies to cases where two, three, or more [identical words] are employed: *sarūpāṇām*. The phrase *ekavibhaktau* (in one case-ending) connects with *sarūpāṇām* here. Those whose form (*rūpa*) is the same are "those having the same form" (*sarūpāṇi*).
The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule beginning with *jyotir-janapada-*. This is a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The word *vṛddha-*...]

The word "eva" (only) is drawn down from the subsequent sūtra [P. 1.2.64]. "Śiṣyate" (is left remaining) is the understood sense; it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karman*). The compound "ekaśeṣa" is a *pūrvakālaika* (prior-time-singular) compound, meaning "one that is the remainder. The result is this: when a single case-ending follows, only one is left remaining from among those identical forms that were observed [together].

Thus he says: "When there is a single case-ending. What is the purpose of the word *eva* (only)? The word *mātṛ* signifies both "mother" (the progenitor) and "measurer" (one who measures).
