In forms such as *mātṛbhyām*, although there is similarity in some respects, because dissimilarity is observed in forms like *āṬ* and *as*—namely, *mātarau* versus *mātārāv*—there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

Although there is indeed observation of similarity between the two words *mātṛ* when they appear in certain case-endings (*vibhakti*), nevertheless, the intended meaning is that [the two words] are not seen to be dissimilar even when following a single case-ending. It is precisely for the sake of illustrating this that the phrase "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) is used here.

Regarding the mention of *ṭhekā* (the singular marker): some maintain that the mention of *eka* alone is for the sake of clarity, intended to state the established meaning resulting from the extraction of the particle *eva*. However, the inclusion of the single word *ekaśeṣa* is for the purpose of ensuring that the elision (*śeṣa*) does not apply to two or more [words]. If the word *śeṣa* were not included...

In the place of [two] words that are identical in form (*sarūpa*), there should be a single substitute. Consequently, in the place of "aśvaś ca" and "aśvaś ca"—both of which possess two udātta accents—there would be a substitute possessing two udātta accents. To prevent this, the term *śeṣa* ("the remainder") is included. The phrase "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for identity of form; it does not mean "only when in a single case-ending."

The explanation that "the *ekaśeṣa* [retention of one] occurs from the subsequent [element]" is appropriate, as otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *ekaśeṣa* between the words denoting "mother" and "one who cuts," and so forth,
as elaborated in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*. Here, [the rule] "in a *dvandva* compound of lunar mansions, [the singular is used for] Tiṣya and Punarvasu" applies.

Carrying over the term *dvandva* from the preceding sūtra, it should be explained as "when a *dvandva* is applicable. Consequently, there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) in cases such as *devadattayajñadattau* or *rājarājau*. The result is that *ekaśeṣa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *dvandva*. Although this *ekaśeṣa* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it is not dependent on a specific cause and thus precedes the production of case-endings (*sub*), [it is superseded by *dvandva*].

It would indeed apply even earlier; nevertheless, this is specifically an exception (*apavāda*) to the *dvandva* compound. For if the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) did not exist, the case-ending (*sup*) would arise [after each word], and the *dvandva* would optionally occur. But when it exists, because there is an absence of multiple words ending in case-endings (*aneka-subanta*), the non-application of the *dvandva* is established as the result. [Example: *ghaṭaś ca ghaṭaś ca ghaṭaś ca*.

The phrase "the collection of those" refers to the scope of a collective dvandva compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), but this [rule] does not apply there because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Furthermore, one should not explain that "once a dvandva has been formed, there is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*)," for if that were so, in examples such as *ṛk-pathānaḥ*, the suffix prescribed by the rule *ṛk-pūrabdhūḥ* etc. would erroneously apply. Also, in examples such as *karau*, the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām* would apply.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule] *prāṇitūrya-* and so forth. Furthermore, since the term *dvandva* is understood here from the previous sūtra, the mention of *ṭhidita* in the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ* serves as an indicator (*liṅga*).
In this context, *idit* refers to that whose *it* (the letter *i*) is designated as having the technical name *it*. Here, the two words ending in *ic* [refer to those] in the same case-ending.

Even though there is similarity of form (*sārūpya*), there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) because it does not fall under the scope of a *dvandva* compound; otherwise, there would have to be an *ekaśeṣa* even in that case—enough said on this point. With *rāma au* established, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) by means of the rule beginning with *prathamayoḥ*, [resulting in] *vṛddhi*.

When the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would have applied, he says: "not after *at* or *ci*" (*nādici*). The meaning is that once that [substitution] is prohibited, the form *rāmau* results through the application of the *vṛddhi* rule.

The logic of "the killer of Devadatta being killed" (devadatta-hantṛ-hata-nyāya) does not apply here, as was explained in detail under the *svādi-sandhi* rules in the case of *manoratha*. When *rāma* + *jas* is situated [in the derivation], [the rule] *cuṭū* [applies].
From the rule *ṭhupadeśe'janunāsika it*, the word *it* is carried over (*anuvartate*). And that...

It is transformed into the dual number. Having carried forward the term "beginning with ṭ" (*ṭhādi*) from the rule "ṭhādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ," it is likewise transformed into the dual number. The phrase "of the affix" (*ṣaḥ pratyayasya*) is also carried forward. Thus he says: "the first letters of the affixes," and so forth. This refers to [the case ending] *jas*.
The elision [of the *t*] occurs by the rule "itsaṃjñāyāṃ tasya lopaḥ" (P. 1.3.9). The letter *j*, however, is for the purpose of excluding *śas* in rules such as "jas-śasoḥ śiḥ" (P. 7.1.20).
(188) P. 1.3.4: "In a case-ending (*vibhakti*), [the letters] *t*, *u*, and *m* [are not *it*]."

Now, fearing that the *sakāra* of *jas* would be elided because it is designated as *it* by the rule "the final letter of a *thak*, a *hal*, or an *it* [is called *it*]," he says: "Not [before] a case-ending.

Here, *tu* and *sa* are in a *dvandva* compound with *ma*. The term "final" (*it*) is understood from the previous rule and is modified to have the form of a plural ending. Thus he says: "Those situated in a case-ending," and so forth.

(189) *ato guṇe* | 6|1|97|. Now, when *rāma* and *asi* are situated [in sandhi], the author states *ato guṇe* in order to propose *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent form) as an exception to the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel for homogeneous vowels) taught by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*. [The word] *eṅi pararūpam* is supplied from that [preceding rule].
The term *pararūpa* (the subsequent form) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
From the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ*, the phrase *apadāntāt* (not being at the end of a word) is understood to carry over.
The governing heading is *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (one [substitute] in place of the preceding and the following). The word *ataḥ* is in the ablative case.

He says this with the words beginning "apadāntāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.93). "Thus [the objection] arises" means that [the objection arises] because of the rule for *at* (6.1.97), since an exception (*apavāda*) is stronger than a subsequent [general rule]. The phrase "because of being subsequent" means that the rule "pūrvasavarṇa of the first two [vowels]" (6.1.102) is subsequent to the rule "guṇa in place of [a vowel] followed by *a*" (6.1.97). Now, one might object:

Since this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*), one might ask: why does it not also supersede the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the lengthening of the preceding vowel to its homogeneous long vowel), just as it supersedes the *savarṇadīrgha*?

To this, he says: "By the rule *ato guṇaḥ*, etc. [The term] "immediate" (*anantarān*) means "unseparated" (*avyavahitān*). [The term] "subsequent" (*uttarān*) means "separated" (*vyavahitān*). [This refers to the rule] *ato guṇaḥ*.

Having read the rule beginning with *avyaktānukaraṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.98), [the sūtra] *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102) and *ṭhprathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.103) are subsequently recited. Consequently, this rule of *pararūpa* (substitution by the subsequent form) subverts only the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening by homogeneity), but not even the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (lengthening by the preceding homogeneous vowel) which is intervened by that [first rule].
This is the state of affairs. In reality, however, this is not the domain of the maxim regarding subsequent exceptions (*purastādapavādanyāya*).

For this subsequent single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) is not an exception to the preceding homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*); for even in cases such as *bhavanti*, where the preceding homogeneous long vowel would otherwise apply, this subsequent single-substitute form is introduced. Enough of this. [Now follow] the *ru*-substitution and the visarga.
He says [the following], taking it for granted that [the form] is established: "rāmā" (190).
[The rule] "The singular number [is used] in the vocative" (Pāṇini 2.3.49) applies.
When "he rāma" is situated [there], he intends to prescribe the elision [of the *s*] by the rule "after a short vowel, the *s* of the vocative is elided" (*heṅhrasvātsaṃbuddheḥ*).

He states the technical term *saṃbuddhi*: [the suffix] *su*. From the rule *prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātre prathamā*, the word *prathamā* is understood and is transformed into the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
From the rule *saṃbodhane ca*, the word *saṃbodhane* is understood. Thus he says: "in the sense of address" (*saṃbodhane*). [The suffix] *su*.
It is more appropriate to say simply "saṃbuddhau. Due to the continued application of the mention of the nominative case (*prathamā*), there is no inclusion of the seventh-case plural (*sup*) suffix.

Nor should one suspect that the rule for the inclusion of the suffix itself (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) would lead to the inclusion of the word ending in that suffix here; for [the rule] "hrasvasya guṇaḥ" [applies].

Because of the rule for the substitution of *guṇa* in the case of the suffix following a *saṃbuddhi*, and because of the prohibition of the "rule of extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*),
this refutes the claim that the mention of the singular number (*ekavacanagrahaṇa*) is intended to prevent the application of that technical name to what ends with it.
(191) *eṅhrasvātsaṃbuddheḥ* |6|1|69|.

[The word] *eṅhrasvāt*: the term *eṅhrasva* is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem), and thus the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. From the rule *sutisyapṛktam hal* [1.2.41], the word *hal*, which is in the nominative case, is carried over (*anuvartate*).

And that [word *lopa*] connects with "from the *aṅga*" (*aṅgāt*) here—namely, "after the *aṅga*, *ha* is elided" (*ha-l-lopaḥ*). From the rule "the elision of *vyoḥ*" (*lopo vyoḥ*), the word "elision" (*lopaḥ*) is carried forward (*anuvartate*).
And that connects in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "ha. That which is elided is "elision" (*lopaḥ*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

In the rule *saṃbuddheḥ*, the genitive case expressing a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) connects with the word *hal*. Consequently, the resulting meaning is: "That which is a constituent part of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*), when following an *aṅga* ending in *eṅ* or a short vowel, is elided. This is what he states by saying "ending in *eṅ*" and so forth. Now, [an objection]:

Since the rule *eṅhrasvāt* does not reside within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the "stem" (*aṅga*), how is it that the stem is obtained as the qualificand? Or what would be the purpose of that? Let it simply be stated: "A *ha*-sound that is a constituent of the vocative suffix following an *eṅ* or a short vowel is elided."

Regarding this, he says: "of that which is projected by a *saṃbuddhi*," and so forth. Since *saṃbuddhi* is a suffix (*pratyaya*), it follows by implication that its base (*prakṛti*) is the stem (*aṅga*). And because that [stem] is qualified by *eṅ* and a short vowel (*hrasva*), according to the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*), the *h* is elided when it follows a stem ending in *eṅ* or a stem ending in a short vowel.
The meaning is that, for the sake of obtaining this specific result, there is no elision [of the case-ending] here. He states the substantive for the word "here" (iha) as:
"O, which one among the families? (he katarat kulam iti). The word *kula* is used to clarify the neuter gender of the word *katara*.
From the neuter gender of the word *katara*, the vocative suffix *su* is applied; then the substitution of *ṭād* occurs, and the letter *ḍ* [is added].
Because of the force of the *ḍit* designation, even though the suffix is not *bha*, there is elision of the vowel *a* following the *repha* (r) by the rule *ṭeḥ*;

then, by the rule *ṭhV-āvasāne*, the substitution of *c* occurs, resulting in the form *katarat*. If, in the rule *eṅhrasvāt*, the *aṅga* were not the thing to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), then in the case of *katarat*...

Because the *takāra* follows a short *a* that is a consonant (*hal*) and because it is a constituent of the vocative case ending (*saṃbuddhi*), its elision would necessarily follow [by P. 6.1.68]. However, there is no fault if the *aṅga* (stem) is the thing being qualified (*viśeṣya*). For in this case, after the elision of the *ṭi*, the *aṅga* is *katar-* ending in *repha*; that, however, does not end in a short vowel.

However, that [suffix] is not part of the stem (*aṅga*), because the letter *a* following the *repha* (the *r*) is a constituent of the substitute *ḍā*, and as such, being a constituent of an affix, it is not included within the portion of the base (*prakṛti*). But is it not the case that the recurrence of the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) here is redundant, since [the rule applies to] what follows a stem ending in *eṅ* or ending in a short vowel?

Let it be explained simply that there is elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*). Or, even if the term *hal* (consonant) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], why not explain it thus: "A consonant (*hal*) which is a constituent part of a vocative suffix following an *aṅga* (stem) ending in a *ṭh*-class letter or a short vowel is elided"? If this were the case, [in the example] *he...* [The text ends here.]

Otherwise, it would not be established. This will become clear from the root text itself during the derivation (*prakriyā*) of the word *jñāna* under the section on neuter stems ending in vowels (*ajanta-napuṃsaka-liṅga*). [Examples: *he hare*, *he viṣṇo*.
From the words *hari* and *viṣṇu*, the vocative case suffix *su* is applied. [By the rule] *hrasvasya guṇaḥ*...

This is the purpose of the *guṇa* [substitution]. When the forms *he hare* and *he viṣṇo* are established, the elision of the case-ending *su* would not occur because it is not preceded by a short vowel; therefore, the mention of *eṅ* is necessary. Now, one might object that prior to the *guṇa* substitution, at this very stage—namely, in the forms *he hari s* and *he viṣṇu s*—[the elision should apply].

Since the elision of *su* (the nominative-accusative dual ending) is possible simply because it follows a short vowel, the mention of *eṅ* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "In this case. Compared to the elision of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), this *guṇa* substitution is subsequent and is also obligatory, because it applies even when the elision of the vocative has not yet occurred, as well as when it has already occurred.

Because that [substitution] operates by relying on the characteristic of being an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), even when the elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhilopa*) has already occurred, it would still operate by relying on the characteristic of being an affix; therefore, if the *guṇa* substitution for the short vowel were made prior to the elision of the vocative suffix, then because the condition of "following a short vowel" (*hrasvāt paratva*) would no longer exist, the elision of the *su* suffix would not take place. Hence...
The meaning is "the inclusion of *e*.
Now, regarding the second case ending (*dvitīyā vibhakti*): when *rāma am* is situated [in the derivation], the *m* is not subject to the substitution of *it* by the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*.

(192) *ami pūrvaḥ* |6|1|107|. Having set aside [the rule] *ṭhakaḥ savarṇe*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by *ṭhato guṇaḥ* would have been obtained; having set that aside, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) by *ṭhprathamayoḥ* would have been obtained—

"Preceded by *am*. From the rule "A long vowel replaces [the preceding and following vowels] when followed by a homogeneous vowel" (*ṭhakaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), the word "of *ak*" (*akaḥ*) is understood as being in the ablative case. The phrase "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) is supplied from the governing context. From the rule "The *yaṇ* substitute replaces *iK* before a vowel" (*ṭhiko yaṇ aci*), the word "before a vowel" (*aci*) is understood. Thus he says: "Of *ak*, before *am*, not before a vowel" (*ako'myacīti*). That which exists in *am*...

The meaning is "when that vowel (ac) follows. In the word *rāmam*, there is a single *pūrvarūpa* (the preceding form) for both the vowel *a* following the letter *m*, and the vowel *a* which is a constituent part of the suffix *am*.

Since the term *aci* is understood from the previous rule, it is established that "when a vowel (*ami*) follows, there shall be a single substitute in the form of the *pūrvarūpa* for both the preceding and the following sounds."

If that were the case, there would be a *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) of "ama" together with the letter "m. To prevent this from occurring, the term "aj" is carried over [from the previous rule]. Thus, "rāmāu. When "rāma" and "āṬ" are situated thus, by the rule "halantyam," the letter "ṭ" receives the designation *itsaṃjñā*, and its elision occurs. The "ṭ" of "āṬ" is for the purpose of forming the *pratyāhāra* "suṭ."

(193) *laśakvataddhite* | 1.3.8 | When *ṭhrāma-śas-* is established, the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* prevents the substitution of *it* for the letter *s*. Since the letter *ś* is not at the end of that [suffix], the rule *halantyam* does not apply; therefore, he says: *laśakvataddhite*.

*ṭhlaśaku* is a collective dvandva compound. From the rules *upadeśe 'janunāsika it*, *ādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ*, and *ṣaḥ pratyayasya*, the terms *it*, *ādiḥ*, and *pratyayasya* are carried over [as governing words]. In the expression *ataddhite*, the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive.

The meaning is that for a suffix other than a *taddhita*, the group beginning with *l*, *ś*, and the *ka*-varga (the gutturals) bears the designation *it*. Thus it is said: "except for *taddhita*. Why say "except for *taddhita*"? [Consider:
*ṭhkarṇalalāṭātkanalaṅkāre* (Pāṇini 4.3.65). *Karṇikā*. Here, [the *k*] of the *kan* suffix...

Because it is a constituent part of a *taddhita* suffix, the substitution of *ī* does not occur. If that were present, there would be *vṛddhi* by the rule "before a *ṭit* or *kit* [suffix]" and so forth.

By this, the argument that the mention of "not being a *taddhita*" (*ataddhita*) is redundant—on the grounds that the substitution of *ī* simply does not occur in *laśādi* *taddhita* suffixes due to the absence of any purpose—is refuted. Thus ends the section on the *śas* [suffix].

When the letter *ś* receives the technical designation *it*, its elision occurs according to the rule "there is elision of that (*tasya lopaḥ*"). However, the explicit pronunciation of the letter *ś* is for the sake of distinguishing its scope in rules such as "jas becomes *śī*" (*jasaḥ śī*) and "the *n* replaces [the final *s*] of *śas* after that" (*tasmāc chaso naḥ*). When the form *rāma as* is established, the rule "a long vowel replaces [a simple vowel] before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) is set aside, and the rule "guṇa replaces [a simple vowel] before a short *a*" (*ato guṇaḥ*) applies.
When the rule *prathamayoḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.102] has applied the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the form *rāmāḥ* is established.

Then, by the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* [Pāṇini 6.1.103], the *śas* [ending] following that [feminine stem] becomes *naḥ*. This is because the preceding sūtra was formulated as *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*.

The long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa* rule is referred to by the word "tasmāt" (from that). This [ablative case] is used in connection with a word denoting direction (*dik-śabda*). Therefore, the word "parasya" (of what follows) must be supplied. In the term "śasaḥ," the genitive case denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*); and that part is qualified by its position as being subsequent. That...
And the "part" (avayava) refers, by implication, to the letter *s* alone, because no other [letter] is possible.

Thus he says: "[The word] *kṛtapūrva* etc. What is the purpose of saying *kṛtapūrva*? If it were stated that [the substitution occurs] for a part of *śas* following a long vowel, then in the example "ṭhetān gāḥ paśya," [the rule would apply] even to the *s* of *śas* after the word *go*.

But there is no undesirable consequence. Therefore, [the rule states] "after what has been formed by the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). In the case of *gāḥ*, the single substitute is the vowel *ā* according to the rule *āṬt-aṃśasoḥ*; it is not the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Consequently, the following [suffix] does not undergo the substitution of *ṇ*. Why [specify] "after *śas*"? Consider *rāmāḥ*. And when the substitution of *ṇ* applies in the present context, [we get] *rāmān*.

*rūpam* | (195) *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye'pi* | Pāṇini 8.4.2. Regarding this, he says—*aṭkupvāṅ*—in order to raise the doubt that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* might occur here [due to the presence of *ṭ*, *ra*, or *ṣa*]. *ṭhraṣābhyām*...

The preceding rule, *no ṇaḥ samānapade*, is understood to carry over here. In that rule, *na* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). By that rule, the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed for a *n* that follows immediately after *ra* or *ṣ*. This applies even in cases such as *rāmeṇa*, where there is an intervention by [the augment] *aṭ* and so forth.

This [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of obtaining [the desired result]. *aṭ* refers to the *aṭ* pratyāhāra; *kuḥ* refers to the *ka*-group (*kavarga*); *puḥ* refers to the *pa*-group (*pavarga*).
Even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*, *ku*, *pu*, *āṅ*, or *num*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* following *ra* or *ṣ* shall not occur.

Therefore, it should be explained that [the rule applies] even when there is an intervention by the letters *aḍ* and so forth, whether individually or combined as far as possible. And in this way, the inclusion of the word *kṣubhna* in the sūtra prohibiting *ṇatva*, namely *kṣubhnādiṣu ca*, becomes meaningful; likewise, the grammatical indications such as *sarūpāṇām* and others become logically justified.

Thus he says, beginning with "aṭ-kavarga-etc. On the occasion of the commentary (*vivaraṇa*), the use of indeclinable expressions such as "aṭ kavarga-" and so forth is not to be faulted, because such usage is frequently observed in the *Bhāṣya*. "In the same word" (*samānapade*) means "in a single word" (*ekapade*). It is indeed indivisible (*akhaṇḍam*).
The word *pada* is intended here [in its technical sense]. Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *rāmanāma*.
As for the justification of the substitution of *ṇ* in *mātṛbhogīṇa* and similar forms, it will be explained in the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).
An example [of the rule] regarding separation by a *aṅga* is *paryāṇaddham*. If the mention of *aṅga* were absent here, however—
In the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi*, because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that [previous rule], the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur.
Now, one might object: "The substitution of *ṇ* will occur here by the rule *aḍvyavāya* alone; what is the purpose of including the mention of *āṅ*?
To this, he says: "The mention of *num*. By the mention of *num*, the nasalization (*anusvāra*) is indicated.

The meaning is "in accordance with the application [of the rule]. And thus he says—"And that"—meaning that the mention of *num* is to be rejected. Now, one might ask: in the absence of the mention of *num*, how can the *anusvāra* indicated by it be obtained? To this he replies: "Of the *ayogavāhas*. No.

Those which possess a connection (*yoga*) within the traditional enumeration of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*) are "non-connected" (*ayoga*). This means they are not explicitly taught, or rather, they are not grasped by those that are explicitly taught. They are called "carriers" (*vāha*) because they carry or bring about grammatical usage (*prayoga*). Thus, "non-connected carriers" (*ayogavāha*) refers to the *anusvāra*, *visarga*, and so forth.
The meaning is that this was stated during the discussion on *hal-sandhi* (conjunction of consonants) regarding the recitation of the *aṭ* augment as taught [in the rule *aṭ kuṅtiṅaḥ*].
This is clear from both the *bhāṣya* and the *vārttika* on the *hayavaraṭ* sūtra. Furthermore, it is stated in the *bhāṣya* on this very sūtra:
"There is no need for the mention of *num*; once the *anusvāra* has been applied, the rule 'when there is an intervention by *aṭ*' (*aḍ-vyavāya*) will suffice here."

"The substitution of *ṇ* is established. Regarding "the substitution of *ṇ*": this means that when the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* which is a constituent of the suffix *śas* would otherwise apply, [the following rule intervenes]. (196) *padāntasya* | 8|4|37|.

[The rule] "of a word-final [n], after ṭ or raṣ" (ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ) is understood from the previous sūtra, as is "not [after bhā, bhū, pū]" (na bhābhūpū), and from that [latter], "not [after e]" (ne).
Therefore, he says: "of a word-final [n]. Now, the third case-ending (tṛtīyāvibhaktiḥ).
Therein, regarding the suffix *ṭā*, the letter *ṭ* is subject to elision because it receives the technical designation *it* by the rule "cuṭū". As for the pronunciation of the letter *ṭ*, however—
[The mention of] *ṭh*, *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, *ṅs*, *ām*, *ṭā*, *bhyām*, *bhis*, etc., is for the purpose of qualification [in rules such as P. 1.4.15].
(197) "That from which a suffix is prescribed, beginning with that, is called an *aṅga* (base) when a suffix follows.
[P. 1.4.13] With *rāma-ā* established, [the author], intending to prescribe the operations pertaining to the *aṅga*, states the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the *aṅga*:

"From which there is the prescription of an affix (*yasmāt-pratyaya-vidhiḥ*). The phrase "from which" means "from that which has become the base (*prakṛti*). Regarding the phrase "which affix" (*yaḥ pratyayaḥ*), the supply of the word "which" (*yat*) from another [sentence] is obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And that [supply] is for the purpose of obtaining the meaning: "when there is a prescription of a certain affix from a certain [base], then that [base] beginning with it is designated as an *aṅga* (stem) with respect to that affix."

That which has that as its original form (prakṛti) at its beginning is "that-beginning" (tadādi). Because of the neuter gender, the word "word-form" (śabdarūpa) is to be supplied [as the subject]. Thus he says: "the word-form beginning with that. And in the present context, the status of being "beginning with that" belongs to the word *rāma* in its form as a base (prakṛti) alone.
From the root *bhū*, the suffix *laṭ* [is applied]. Then *mip* [is applied]. By the rule "kartari śap," the augment *śap* is added, which is designated as a *vikaraṇa*.

The *guṇa* and *āveśa* substitutions [apply], and by the rule "ato dīrgho yañi," the long vowel is substituted for the stem ending in *a*, resulting in the form *bhavāmi*. Similarly, from the root *bhū*, *lṛṭ* and *mip* [are applied]; then, by the rule "syātāsī lṛluṭoḥ," [the suffixes *syat* and *tās* are added].

The suffix *sya* is designated as a *vikaraṇa*. [The augment] *iṭ* is applied, followed by *guṇa* and the substitution [of *av* for *u*]. Then *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) occurs. By the rule "a long vowel is substituted for *at* before a suffix beginning with *yañ*," there is a lengthening of the stem in "bhaviṣya. Thus, the form "bhaviṣyāmi" is obtained. In this context, if the mention of "beginning with" (*ādi*) were absent, then when the suffix *mip* follows, the substitution would apply to the entire base "bhū" alone.

There would be the designation "aṅga" [of the base] only from the word *bhū* itself, because the suffix *mip* is prescribed for that, and not for *bhava* or *bhaviṣya*, which are qualified by their respective verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*), since the suffix *mip* is not prescribed for them. Consequently, when the suffix *mip* occurs, the rule "ato dīrgho yañi" [Pāṇini 7.3.101] applies.
Otherwise, the lengthening would not apply to the subsequent [element]. Therefore, the meaning is that the word "beginning" (ādi) is included.

As for the question "What is the purpose of the term 'rule' (vidhi)?": since it is already established by the mere statement that "the verbal form beginning with that which is heard as a suffix following [something] receives the designation 'base' (aṅga) with respect to that suffix," the inclusion of the word "rule" serves a specific purpose.

The question is: "For what purpose? [The answer is: "A woman is of such a measure. In the sense that "this is her measure," the suffix *vatup* is applied after the word *idam* by the rule "ṭhkimidaṃbhyāṃ vo ghaḥ"; *va* is replaced by *gha*. For this [suffix], there is the substitution of *iy*. By the rule "idaṃkimoḥ," *idam* becomes *ī*; because it is marked with the *ś* indicatory letter (*śit*), it is a replacement for the whole [stem].

When *ī-iyat* is established, the elision of the vowel *ī* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Thus, only the suffix *iyat* remains. By the rule *ugitaśca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in the form *iyatī*. In this context, if the term *vidhi* (prescription) were not included [in the rule], then in the case of *strī-iyatī*, the *ī* following the *r* would [be subject to the rule] *striyāḥ*.

In this case, *iyaṅ* would be the result of the substitution for the *aṅga*. This is because the suffix *iyat* is heard [as the replacement] immediately following the word *strī*, due to its position as a subsequent element. Nor is it the case that *iyaṅ* does not apply here because the elision of the *y* (by *yasyeti ca*) is considered *asiddha* by virtue of being an *abhīya* rule, which would prevent the suffix from being followed by an *ac*-beginning affix; for [the elision] is not *asiddha* in this context.

It must be stated that [the term] "attainment" (*prāpti*) is intended; for when an operation (*kārya*) is to be performed upon a locus (*āśraya*) that is neither deficient nor excessive and is identical, the *ābhīyāna-asiddhatva* (non-validity of what is internal) indeed applies. And in the rule *stryāḥ* (P. 4.1.3), there is a requirement for the additional word *strī*, in comparison with the rule *yasyeti ca* (P. 6.4.148). However, once the mention of *vidhi* (prescription) is made, [the objection is resolved].

The substitution *iyaṅ* does not occur here; for since *batu* is prescribed specifically for this [stem] *idam*, when that [suffix] follows, the word *strī* lacks the status of being a *aṅga*. Nor should one suspect that the elision of *y* (by *yasyeti lopa*) would undergo the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* when *iyaṅ* is to be applied, because [the rule *acaḥ parasmin*] is restricted to operations concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*).

Because that [designation] is prohibited. Even though the word *strī* is well-established as an *aṅga*, the designation *iyaṅ* does not apply here; for its application occurs when the word is established as an *aṅga* relative to a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), based on proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

Regarding the question "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'in a suffix' (*pratyaye*)?": the meaning is that it would suffice merely to state, "That from which a suffix is prescribed is the initial element of the *aṅga*."

Lest there be [the application of the term *aṅga*] to that which is qualified by the suffix, or even to something greater than that—when there arises the expectation as to how much of this word-form beginning with that [suffix] constitutes the *aṅga*, since no distinction is specified, either the form qualified by the suffix or even something greater than that would become the *aṅga* without limit. And it is not the case that [the rule applies] "from which the suffix... [is elided].
It should not be argued that because the suffix (*pratyaya*) is explicitly heard [in the rule], the status of being an *aṅga* (auxiliary) will apply only up to the limit of that suffix;

for the mention of the suffix in that rule has already fulfilled its purpose by providing the meaning "that which begins with what is specified by the suffix. Consequently, if the status of being an *aṅga* belonged to that which is qualified by the suffix, then in the case of *vavraśca*, [the following would occur].

If the *aṅga* were qualified by its conditions (*pratyaya-viśiṣṭa*), then the substitute *ur* (as in *uraḍ*) would not obtain the status of having a subsequent element as its cause; consequently, since the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (P. 1.1.57) would not apply, the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* by the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam* (P. 6.1.37) would not take effect. Furthermore, if the *aṅga* were [qualified] by something additional, then in the case of *devadat...* [the following would occur].

In examples such as *odanam apākṣīt*, because the portion up to the *luṅ* suffix is an *aṅga* (base) with respect to the *sup* (case-ending) following words like *devadatta*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the augment *aṭ* appearing even before the word *devadatta*, since it is followed by a *luṅ* suffix; this is due to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "base" (*aṅga*).

Because the meaning "of that which has been defined as an *aṅga* by [the rules for] *luṅ* and so forth" is difficult to obtain due to the absence of a cause for such a designation, whereas if one says "in a suffix" (*pratyaye*), there is no fault whatsoever; enough of this. (198) *ṭāṅsiṅsām ina ātsyāḥ* | 7|1|12|

In the rule *ṭāṅsiṅbhyo ṅayi*, the term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which was previously governed [by the fifth case], is modified [to the seventh case]. From the rule *ṭhato bhisa ais*, the word *ataḥ* (from *at*), ending in the fifth case, is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) as a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*). This involves the application of the rule regarding that which ends in such [a suffix] (*tadantavidhiḥ*). Thus he says: "from a stem ending in the vowel *a*."
The word "of others" (*pareṣām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "In order" (*kramāt*) is obtained from the rule concerning numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyasūtra*).

"Of *ṭā* and so forth" means of *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, and *ṅs*. "Inā and so forth" means these: *ina*, *āt*, and *sya*. When *rāma-in* is established, *ādguṇaḥ* (P. 6.1.87) applies. Regarding "nasalization" (*ṇatvam*), [the following applies].

The meaning is that the *ṇ* replaces the *n* according to the rule *ṭh-ṭha-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi*. When *rāma-bhyām* is established, the *m* does not become nasalized (*itva*) by the rule *na vibhaktau*.
(199) *supi ca* | Pāṇini 8.3.102.
And regarding *supi*: the rule "a long vowel [is substituted] for [the final of] what ends in *ṭha* before *yañ*" is understood to follow. The term "*yañ*" is also understood to follow.

By this "*yañ*" [rule], "*sup*" is qualified. Since there is the principle "in whatever [context] a rule is prescribed, it applies to that which begins with it," he says: "before one beginning with *yañ*. [This refers to] "of the stem ending in *at*."

The meaning is "of a member [of a compound] that does not end in a dental. When *rāma-bhis* is established, the *s* is not changed to *ī* by the rule *na vibhaktau*. (200) *ato bhisa ais* | Pāṇini 7.1.9. [When the word *rāma* ends in short *a*, the case-ending *bhis* is replaced by *ais*. Thus, *rāmair*.

Therefore, *bhis* becomes *ais*. The word *ataḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). The governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is modified to the ablative case by attraction; *ataḥ* is its qualifier. Because it is a qualifier, the rule of "application to that which ends in [the qualifier]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus he says: "from that which ends in the vowel *a*. [Then follow] the substitution of *ru* and the visarga.

He states [the rule] as if it were already established: "by the *rāma*s" (*rāmair iti*). Although forms such as *rāmair* are established even when *vṛddhi* is applied after the suffix *asi*, one should not suspect that the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) prescribed by the rule *ato guṇe* would apply;
for that is impossible precisely due to the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *e*. Otherwise, he would have simply prescribed *i* alone.

Nevertheless, because there is no distinction between *e* and *ai* regarding their having two morae (*dvimātra*), and for the sake of brevity in grammatical procedure (*prakriyālāghava*), this rule applies to *ai*.
Anticipating the objection that, by the rule *alo’ntyasya*, the substitution should apply only to the final letter, he says: "because it consists of more than one phoneme" (*anekāltvāt*).

Now follows the fourth case ending (*caturthīvibhakti*). In that context, regarding the suffix *ReĀ*, the *ṅ* is elided because it falls under the technical designation *it* according to the rule *laśakvet*.
The utterance of "tat" (in *taduccāraṇam*) is for the purpose of [indicating] *gher ṅti* and so forth. When *rāma-e* is established, [the rule] *ReĀryaḥ* [applies].
In *ReĀryaḥ*, the term *heḥ* is the genitive singular ending from that which ends in the vowel *e*; it is not the *ṅi* [case-ending].
This is the singular locative case, as established by the commentary. From the rule *ato bhisa ais*, the word *ataḥ* (ablative) is understood to carry over;
by this, the term *aṅgasya* (genitive), which is the governing heading, is modified into the ablative case. Thus he says: "from that stem (*aṅga*) ending in *at*."
The meaning is "from a toothless [source] part by part. Having considered that the lengthening occurs by the rule *supi ca*, he says "to Rāmāya. Now, one might ask:

since the substitute *yā* lacks the status of being a *sup* (case-ending), how can there be lengthening by the rule *supi ca* when this [substitute] follows? To this he replies: "In this case... Now, one might ask: here, because of its having the form of a *yañ*-beginning suffix and its being a *sup*, the substitute *yā*— [...is treated as such... (Note: The source text appears to be an excerpt from a grammatical commentary discussing the formation of the dative singular of *rāma*. The final sentence fragment suggests a discussion regarding the application of rules for lengthening vowels.)

It operates by taking something else as its cause (paranimittīkṛtya). And since that [cause] does not depend on the element *y* (the *yaṇ*), how can there be the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the substitution of *y* when that [element depending on *y*] is to be performed? If you argue that this is because it is prohibited by the rule "not in the case of an operation concerning an *al*" (*analvidhau*), that is true—but here, regarding the long vowel...
Even though [the substitution] is based on the *al* (phoneme) in the form of the letter *y* which has replaced [the *su*],

when that [substitution] is to be performed, the status of being a *sup* (case-ending) still exists due to the *sthānivadbhāva* (treatment as the original) of the *yādeśa*; for although the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is based on the *al* in the form of the letter *y* which has replaced it, it lacks the quality of being based on the *al* of the original (*sthānin*).
However, the rule "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25), though subsequent, is not introduced here;
for by the force of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the phrase "ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ," that [lengthening] applies only when there is no *sup* suffix.

They say it is for the sake of the grammatical operation (*pravṛtti*). This might be so; however, there is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) which states: "A rule characterized by a conjunction [of phonemes] is not the cause of that conjunction's destruction.
Here, *saṃnipāta* means "conjunction" or "contact," and *lakṣaṇa* means "characterized by" or "conditioned by"; thus, a rule whose condition is such a conjunction is called *saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*.

*Vidhi* means "that which is to be done" (*kārya*). *Tadvighāta* refers to the obstruction of that [action]. It is called *tadvighāta* because it obstructs the conjunction of those [factors] (*tanu-saṃnipātam vihanti*).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the agent when the object (*karman*) is the upapada, according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. The substitution of *t* for *han* occurs by the rule *hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ*. The change to *gh* (the *kutva* substitute) occurs by the rule *ho hanteḥ*.

The meaning is that it is not the cause (*nimitta*) of that which destroys the *saṃnipāta* (the coalescence of conditions). That is to say, that which depends on something else does not destroy that upon which it depends. And in the present case, how could the substitution of *y* (*yādeśa*), which operates by depending on the connection with a final short vowel (*adanta-sambandha*), be the cause of a long vowel (*dīrgha*) that destroys that very connection with a final short vowel?
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "characterized by conjunction" (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
He says "from the two *rāma*s" (*rāmābhyām*), taking the lengthening as established, just like the dual ending of the third case (*tṛtīyādvivacana*).
[Pāṇini 7.3.103 states: "In the plural, when followed by a consonant (*jhal*), there is *e*. (202)
By the rule *bhyasi na vibhaktau*, the substitution of *it* for *s* does not occur. When the rule *supi ca* would have required a long vowel, [the following applies]:

in the case of a plural ending (*bahuvacana*) that begins with a *jhal* sound, [the final vowel] becomes *e*. From the rules *ato dīrgho yañi* and *supi ca*, the word *ataḥ* (from "at") and *supi* are respectively understood as governing the present rule. By the term *jhalī*, [the condition of the suffix being a *jhal*-beginning one is specified].

The term "sup" is specified [as the condition]. By the rule "a prescription applies to that which begins with [the element specified]," it refers to the beginning of that [element]; thus he says: "when preceded by a *jhal* sound. "Of the *aṅga*" means "of an *aṅga* ending in *at*. When the *etva* (substitution of *e*) has occurred, the *rutva* (substitution of *r*) and *visarga* follow.

He states [the rule] as if it were already established: "to those ending in *rāma*. Regarding the term *rāma*: since the *visarga* is included among the *ayogavāha*s both above the vowel *a* and among the *śar* consonants, it possesses the status of a *jhal*. Consequently, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, it also possesses the status of a *sup* suffix; thus, when this [suffix] follows, the substitution of *e* for *o* would be applicable. This remains so even though the *rutva* and *visarga* substitutions are considered *asiddha*.

Rāma—[The substitution does not apply] in the state of *siti* (before a *sit* suffix) because of the condition that a *jhal*-beginning suffix follows. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "plural" (*bahuvacana*) is for this purpose. [The example] "rāmasya" [is given] as another purpose for including the term "plural": when the genitive singular suffix *ṅsi* undergoes replacement by *syā*, [the rule would otherwise apply].

The meaning is that because [the suffix] would otherwise undergo *etva* (the substitution of *e*) due to its being *suptva* by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, and also because it is inherently *jhalādi*, the mention of the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is for the purpose of preventing that *etva*. They say, however, that the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* does not apply in the rule prescribing *etva*, on account of the indication (*nirdeśa*) in the form "sarveṣām. [This applies] when a *jhal* [follows].

"What is [the purpose]?"—this is the question. One could have explained it simply by carrying forward "after *hal*" from the rule *ṭhuto vṛddhir luki halī* and stating that *etva* occurs before a *sup* suffix beginning with *hal* in the plural; for by that much alone, the *etva* would be excluded in plural forms beginning with vowels such as "rāmāḥ. [The answer is: "rāmāṇām."
If it were stated that "there is *etva* (the substitution of *e*) before a *sup* [ending] beginning with a *jhal* consonant in the plural," then *etva* would also occur in the form *rāmāṇām*.

The purpose of including the term *jhal* is to prevent this. Even though, in this case, by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*, the rule would have applied by depending upon the presence of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in a short vowel [which is destroyed when *etva* occurs].

Since it is impossible for the substitution of *e* (etva) to have the *nuṭ* augment as its cause—because that *nuṭ* would destroy the very conditions for the *e*-substitution—the *e*-substitution will simply not occur;

nevertheless, the mention of *jhal* in this rule is for the purpose of making known that the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical occasion) does not apply here. Consequently, by the citation in the rule *hali sarveṣām*, the word *sarva* [is included].

Even when *etva* (the substitution of *e*) is not established, *etva* occurs in cases such as *viśveṣām* and so forth. In *pacadhvam*, although the suffix *dhvam* begins with a *jhal* consonant and is plural, it lacks the status of being a *sup* (case-ending); therefore, the rule for *etva* does not apply when it follows.

Nor can it be argued that the rule *bahuvacane jhalīk* (Pāṇini 7.3.103) should suffice; for [if that were the case], due to the *kit* designation, the *antāvayava-ādeśa* (substitution of the final element) would apply, and subsequently, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), the *guṇa* substitution would take place.
It should not be argued that this is established by the rule *ṭhrāmebhyaḥ* and so forth; for if that were the case,
then in the subsequent rule *osi ca*, which prescribes the augment *iK*, the *num* augment would undesirably apply in the form *jñānayoḥ* by the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau*.
Now begins the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-vibhakti*). In this context, according to the rule *ṭhupadeśe 'janunāsika it*, the letter *i* in *ṅsi* is an *it*.

Its elision occurs. The letter *ṅ*, however, by the rule *laśakvataddhite*, is an *it*; its elision occurs. The letter *ṅ*, however, by the rule *laśakvataddhite*, is an *it*; its elision occurs. The purpose of pronouncing both [the *i* and the *ṅ*] is as follows:
The forms *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, and *ṅs* [are mentioned] for the purpose of [applying rules such as] *ṭāṅsiṅsām* and *gherṅtī*. From *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, and *ṅs*, the suffix *āt* is applied;

this results in a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). Regarding "the substitution of the *jaś* sounds": by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*, the substitution of *jaś* sounds would necessarily apply. The meaning is that the optional substitution of *car* sounds is now being introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

(203) *vāvasāne* |8|4|56|. From the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the term *jhalām* is carried over; from the rule *abhyāse carc*, the term *car* is also carried over. Therefore, he says: "at the pause (*avasāne*). Regarding the form [of the doubled consonant], it is as follows.

The meaning is that there are four forms: two resulting from the doubling of the *takāra* and *dakāra* by the rule *anaci ca*, and two where such doubling does not occur. Among these, in the case of *cartva* (the substitution of *cakāra*), there is a form with two *takāras* and a form with one *takāra*.
In the case of *jaśtva* (the substitution of *dakāra*), there is a form with two *dakāras* and a form with one *dakāra*. [Thus we have: *rāmābhyām* and *rāmebhyaḥ*.
The meaning is that the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) is easy to understand, as in the case of the fourth case-ending (*caturthī*).

Now, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*): for the *ṅ* of *ṅsi*, there is elision (*lopa*) due to the rule "ṭhlaśakvataddhite" (Pāṇini 1.3.8), which prescribes *it* (the substitution of *i*). However, the pronunciation of the *ṅ* is for the sake of [triggering] rules such as "ṅiti hrasvaśca" (Pāṇini 1.4.6). [This is established by] the rule "ṭāṅsiṅsām" (Pāṇini 7.1.12).
Taking the elision (*lopa*) as established, he says: "of Rāma" (*rāmasya*). Now, one might object:

if there were doubling of the *s* by the rule *anaci ca*, and if the preceding *s* were replaced by a *t*—which is the closest in terms of place of articulation (*sthāna*) according to the rule *khari ca*—then the form would have to be *rāmatsya*. To this, [he replies]: [The text continues: ...because [the doubling] occurs only when a vowel or a semivowel follows, and because the *s* here is followed by a consonant, the doubling does not take place. Furthermore, since the *s* is not followed by a *khar* (voiceless consonant), the substitution of *t* by *carkhara* does not apply. Therefore, the form remains *rāmasya*. Thus, it is established that the genitive singular of *rāma* is *rāmasya*.
He says: "In the case of the doubling of the *sa*. "That very one" means the letter *sa* itself.

He states what is excluded by the word "only": "but not the letter *ta*. Now, an objection might be raised: since the internal effort [of place] and the external efforts consisting of dental position, breath, voicelessness, and openness are no different in the case of the letter *ta* as well. To this [he replies]:
He says: "Because of having few breaths. The letter *sa* is a place-holder (*sthānin*) that possesses great breath (*mahāprāṇa*), whereas the letter *ta* possesses few breaths (*alpaprāṇa*).
Therefore, due to this difference in external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*), the letter *ta* does not [replace] it. This is an illustration;
it should be understood that the letter *ta* also replaces the letter *sa* due to a difference in internal effort (*ābhyantaraprayatna*). Hence...

The meaning is as follows: in the case of the root *vas* (meaning "to dwell") in forms such as *vatsyati*, the substitution of *t* for the *s* is prescribed when another *s* follows; however, if the substitution of *t* for *s* were already to occur by the rule *tra khari ca*, then that specific prescription would be rendered purposeless.
(204) *osi ca* | Pāṇini 7.3.104. When the form *rāma os* is established, and the rule for *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) would otherwise apply, [the present sūtra] states *osi ca*.
From the previous rule *ato dīrgho yañi*, the word *ataḥ* (of *at*) is understood to carry over. The governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is also in force.
From the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*, the term *e* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "when *osi* follows.

Regarding *ato 'ṅgasya*: this means "of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a*. When *rāme os* is situated, having taken for granted the substitution of *ay* (*ayādeśa*) as well as the *rutva* and *visarga* [changes], he says: *rāmayoḥ*. [The form] *rāma*...

When *ām* is established, the substitution of a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise apply; however, [the rule] *hrasvanadyāpaḥ* applies. Here, *hrasva*, *nadī*, and *āp* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*), and the ablative case is used in connection with the word *para*. The word *parasya* ("of the following") is to be supplied as an ellipsis. The term *aṅgasya* ("of the stem"), which is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*), is modified into the ablative case and qualified by *hrasva* and the others.
Therefore, this is a rule concerning the final letter (*tadanta-vidhi*). From the rule "ṭhāmi sarvanāmnaḥ," the word "ṭhām" is carried over (*anuvartate*).

And by the maxim "when both [terms] are mentioned, the ablative mention is stronger," that [word ṭhām] becomes a genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), according to the principle "after that [which is in the ablative], the following [is affected]."

(205) *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* [Pāṇini 7.1.54]. He says this with the words "from that which ends in a short vowel," etc. It is clear in the Bhāṣya that here *ṭhām* is specifically the genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvacana*), and not the *ṭhReĀrām* prescribed by other rules. In the augment *nuṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is an *it*.
The letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, it becomes the initial constituent [of the suffix]. (206) *nāmi* | Pāṇini 6.4.3.
When *rāma-nām* is established, [the rule] *nāmi* applies. The phrase *ḍhralopaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.9) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).

By the rule *dīrghaśrutyā ca ṭhacaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhac* is brought to mind; by that, the base (*aṅga*) is qualified. Therefore, there is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the designation applies to that which ends with the specified element). Thus he says: "of that which ends in a vowel" (*ajantasya*). It was not formulated as *ṭhnuṭi*.
[This is because] in the word *bhṛṅga*, which ends in the Uṇādi suffix *gan* according to the rule *bhṛñaḥ kinnuṭ ca*, the vowel *ṛ* [would otherwise be subject to lengthening].
In *dīrghāpateḥ*, however, there is no lengthening; nor is there lengthening in cases such as *ṭhaṅgānāṃ* or *pāmanām*.

This is because, by the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), only a meaningful *nāman* is understood. Thus, when the suffix *naP* (conditioned by the *pāmādi* group) is applied, followed by *ṭāP* and then the second-case singular ending *am*, all three suffixes [are considered meaningful].

Even though each individual [element] possesses meaning, the aggregate as a whole lacks meaning. Now, one might object: let there be no inclusion of the letter *n* in the term *nām*; rather, let the rule be formulated simply as *ṭh ami*. And it cannot be argued that, in the state of *rāma-ām*, once the long vowel (*dīrgha*) has occurred, the condition of ending in a short vowel (*hrasvāntatva*) is absent, and thus the rule *ṭh hrasvanadyāpaḥ* would not apply.

If it is argued that *nuṭ* should not occur [in this case], we reply: no, because by the force of the rule "after a word ending in a short vowel, *nuṭ* [is added]," even when the long vowel has already been substituted, the addition of *nuṭ* is justified by resorting to the consideration of its prior state (*bhūtapūrvagati*).

If it is further objected that the mention of the letter *n* (in the rule *san-ka-ra-nirdeśasya*) [is intended to prevent *nuṭ*] in the rule "the penultimate vowel is lengthened" (*nopadhāyāḥ*), [we reply...]

This is because [the word *ām*] is for the sake of what follows. For if only *ām* were stated, then in the subsequent sūtra, "ṭhnopādhāyāḥ," the word *ām* alone would also carry over. Consequently, the rule would simply yield that there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of a stem ending in *n* when *ām* follows; in that case, [the form] *carmaṇām* [would not be obtained].

In cases such as *ṭhvarmaṇām*, there would also have to be a long vowel; therefore, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that the mention of the letter *n* in the term *nāmī* is for this very purpose. Enough of this digression. Taking the substitution of *ṇ* (by the rule *aṭkupvāṅ*) as already established, he says: *rāmāṇām*. [Objection: But surely, because it is subsequent in order, the lengthening by the rule *supi ca* should apply here?

This is how it should be presented; however, one might object: "The long vowel [in 'nāmī'] is not [to be applied], because even the absence of a specific result follows from the very operation of the grammatical system in accordance with logical principle, as has been explained at length in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *iko jhal*. To this, he replies: "Even though the lengthening by *supi ca* is subsequent..."

He refutes [the objection] with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*). Regarding the term *sannipāta*: the sense is that it is impossible for the augment *nuṭ*—which operates depending upon the conjunction (*sannipāta*) of a short vowel at the end—to serve as the cause for the long vowel [prescribed] by the rule *supi ca*, which destroys that very short vowel. Now, one might object: even if the long vowel [prescribed] by *nāmī* were to apply here...

Since the contradiction with the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* would be equal [in both cases], he says: "But by this [rule] *nāmī*... If the long vowel were not prescribed here by the rule *nāmī*, then its formulation would be purposeless. Consequently, because it would otherwise have no scope of application, the long vowel by *nāmī* in forms such as *rāmāṇām* would [by necessity] override the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.

It operates by setting aside [the rule]. However, as for the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *supi ca*, since it finds its scope of application in forms such as *rāmābhyām* and so on, it is not able to set aside the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* when *ām* follows—as in *rāmāṇām* and so on. Therefore, in cases such as *rāmāṇām*, where *ām* follows, the lengthening does indeed take effect.

The introduction of the term *nāmī* [in the rule *nāmi*] is for the purpose of overriding the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. But is it not improper to say that the lengthening by *nāmī* overrides the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* because it is without scope (*niravakāśa*)? For in cases where the suffix *nuṭ* applies without depending at all on the combination of a short vowel [with a following consonant], [the lengthening would indeed have no scope].

Because the application of the long vowel *ī* in forms such as *katīnām* has its own scope, precisely by not being overridden by the prohibition concerning the *sannipāta* (the loss of the cause for the application of a grammatical operation). For instance, in the case of *katīnām*, the augment *nuṭ* applies by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaḥ*;
that is to say, the augment *nuṭ* occurs after *ām* when it follows words designated as *ṣaṭ* (six) and the word *catur* (four).
If it is argued that this is for the sake of that [specific rule], then, such being the case, the rule should have been formulated simply as *katernāmī*.

The meaning is that the general rule *nāmī*—intended to mean "there is lengthening of a stem ending in a vowel before *nām*"—need not have been composed at all. Otherwise, [the formation of] *mudgaudaṇ* would be untenable; so says Kaiyaṭa.

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, there is complexity (*gaurava*) due to the inclusion of the additional word *kati*; for there is simplicity (*lāghava*) because the prohibition of lengthening in the *nām* [vowel]—as in the rule "not in *tisṛ* or *catasṛ*"—is not formulated. Thus, instead of stating "of *kati* in the *nām*," [the author] says simply "in the *nām*."
By the force of the commencement of the general rule (*sāmānyasūtra*), it is logical that even in cases such as *rāmāṇām*, the long vowel *ām* (by P.
7.1.54) applies, overriding the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*.
Thus, the statement in the root text, "by the force of the commencement," is also appropriate; for it does not say "after *katṛ*" (*katernāmī*), but rather simply "after *nāman*" (*nāmī*).
This must be explained by the force of the commencement of the general rule (*sāmānyasūtra*); enough with further elaboration.

Therefore, the seventh case ending (*saptamīvibhakti*) is applied. Since the letter *e* is the *it* (the marker), when "rāma-i" is established, considering [the rule] "ādguṇaḥ," he says: "rāme. As for "rāmayoḥ," it is like the dual of the sixth case.

The meaning is: "when *itva* has been applied," that is, when the *itva* [of the suffix] has occurred, followed by its elision (*lopa*), and then the *itva* prescribed by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* has been applied. (207) *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.55.

When *rāme-su* is established, intending to prescribe the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, he says: "of that which is not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*). "Cerebral" (*mūrdhanya*) means having the palate as its place of articulation (*mūrdhasthānaka*). This sūtra is recited in the middle of the third quarter of the eighth chapter. From here...
The meaning is that this [rule] is governed from its commencement until the conclusion of this section.
Regarding the phrase "having governed *iṇkoḥ*": the intention is that it continues to apply to the rules that follow.
*Iṇ* and *ku* form a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*). The masculine gender is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).

In the case of a copulative compound (*itaretarayogadvandva*), the singular number is also an archaic usage. *Ṭhi* refers to a pratyāhāra consisting of the letter *ṇ* followed by the letter *i*. *Kuḥ* refers to the guttural class (*kavarga*).

(209) *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* |8|3|59|. Now he states the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṣ*: *ādeśa*. It is in the genitive case; the meaning is that the letter *s* was specified in the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*. And that [letter *s*] is referred to here.

Having been modified into the dual number, it is connected with the rule *ṭhādeśapratyayayoḥ*. Consequently, [the rule applies] to those [sounds] which follow the letters *ṭ* and the *ka*-group (*ṭh*), provided they are not at the end of a word and consist either of a substitute (*ādeśa*) or a portion of an affix (*pratyaya*).
The meaning is that when the sounds *s* and *k* occur [in contact], a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) sound shall take their place.

He states the resulting conclusion with the words "by *im*, the *ka*-class," and so forth. However, in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa* (the *Prakriyā-kaumudī*), it is held that although the genitive case in *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* is a single one, in the context of suffixes (*pratyaya*), it signifies the sense of being a constituent part (*avayava*).

And in the domain of substitution (*ādeśa*), it signifies non-difference; thus, it is understood as referring to both the substitute and the *s* which is a constituent of the suffix, so that the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) was stated without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, it is accepted that this is a Vedic-style copulative compound (*dvandva*) even in the absence of a desire to express co-occurrence (*sahavivakṣā*). However, if...

Even in the domain of an *ādeśa* (substitute), there might be a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), such that [the rule] would mean "the *ṣ* of the *s* which is a part of the substitute. If that were so, there would be a fault in forms such as *tisraḥ* and *tisṛṇām*. Nor can it be argued that in the case of *tricaturoḥ striyām*, the substitution does not undergo *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) due to the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *s* in the substitute; for [if that were the case], the same logic would apply here as well.

In the case of *tisraḥ*, [the rule] has already served its purpose by prohibiting *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) through the rule *ṭhna raparasṛpisṛjispṛśispṛhisavanādīnām*; furthermore, in cases such as *viṣam* and *viṣam*,
since the *s* would be a constituent part of the substitute, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṣatva* applying to it.
This is because it will be stated later that the doubling (dvirvacana) prescribed by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4) is of the nature of a substitute (*ādeśa*).

If, however, one were to explain [the rule] as "that which is the letter *s* belonging to an affix (*pratyaya*)," then [the suffixal *s*] would apply only in cases such as *jigīṣu*, but not in cases such as *rāmeṣu*. Therefore, it is both a substitute and a constituent part of an affix.

That which is the letter *s* has been explained by the word "its" (*tasya*). Furthermore, in the rule *ṭhali sarveṣām*, the mention of *ṭha* is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for [the fact that] the letter *s* is a constituent part of the suffix. Regarding the phrase "of the unvoiced open [articulation]," the quality of being a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) is common to the letters *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣ*.

The meaning is that for the letter *s*, which possesses the internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) of being open (*vivṛta*) and the external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*) of being voiceless (*aghoṣa*), there arises only the letter *ṣ*, which consists of both [efforts]. The first qualification is for the purpose of excluding the letter *ṭ*; the second is for the purpose of excluding the vowel *ṛ*. [In the example] "rāmeṣu," [one might object]: "But surely... [su]...

If it is argued that, by virtue of being treated as the principal element (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the form *supi* would possess the status of a *pada* due to its ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), and thus the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would apply—this is not so; for when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, only that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed is understood. Enough of this. Regarding *supisau*: [the root is] *pis*.
The suffix *kvip* occurs after a verbal root. The intention is that this *sakāra* belongs to the verbal root itself; it is neither a substitute (*ādeśa*) nor a constituent of an affix (*pratyaya*).
Therefore, intending to prescribe the operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma-kārya*) for words beginning with *sarva*, etc., [the author] proceeds as follows:
He states the technical designation *sarvanāman* [pronoun]: "The words beginning with *sarva*.
Those for which *sarva* is the beginning—that is, the first member—are the *sarvādīni*. Here, the word *sarva* refers to its own form.
(Pāṇini 1.1.27: "The words beginning with *sarva* are pronouns (*sarvanāman*)."
By virtue of the neuter gender, the substantive "word-forms ending in *ṭh*" must be supplied;

thus he says, "beginning with *sarva*. Now, since a *bahuvrīhi* compound has as its primary referent an external object (*anyapadārtha*), and given that the word *sarva*— [The text continues: —is [the first member of the compound], [one might ask how it can denote the entire class].

If it is argued that because the word *viśva* and others function as members of a compound (*samāsavarti*), they lack the status of being the "referent of another word" (*anyapadārtha*), and since the words *viśva* and so forth alone are understood through the *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *sarva*, the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāmasaṃjñā*) would apply to those [words like *viśva*] but not even to the word *sarva* itself— then it is said in reply: [the compound is analyzed as] "that collection of which *sarva* is the first."
[The opponent states: "The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: the meaning of a compound (*samāsa*) is a collective whole (*samudāya*) composed of all its constituent words.

Now, the designation 'pronominal' (*sarvanāman*), which applies to that collective whole, would—by the maxim 'that which applies to a whole descends to its parts when it would otherwise be purposeless or redundant'—descend to the individual members [of the compound] even when that whole is not being employed."

Because there is no distinction, this also applies to the word *sarva*. Thus, in this context, the word *sarva* functions as the meaning of the constituent member (*vartipadārtha*) by way of its own form, whereas it enters into the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) by way of being a collective whole (*samudāya*). Nor is there any inconsistency in using the plural number in the rule *sarvādīni* if the collective whole constitutes the meaning of the external referent.

[The compound] is to be suspected [of being a bahuvrīhi], because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is a collection (*samūha*) composed of all the words [in the compound] and possessing the intended number of members. This is precisely the meaning of Kaiyaṭa’s statement: "A collection whose constituent parts are not [individually] manifested is the meaning of the compound. Therefore, it is not [the case that...].

The use of the plural number [in the rule *hali sarveṣām*] would otherwise be untenable; thus, this very interpretation is supported by the citation of forms such as *hali sarveṣām*. If the word *sarva* lacked the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), then in examples such as *sarveṣām*, the operations specific to pronouns—such as the addition of the suffix *suṭ*—would not apply. And so it is.

The term *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound. In this compound, the "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) which take the form of the members of the compound (*vartipada*). A *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* is that [compound] in which there is a "cognition of those qualities" (*saṃvijñāna*), meaning their cognition as being connected to the action, even though they are not the primary referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*).

[Now,] *vyatpatti* [is as follows]: where the meaning of the constituent members (*varti-pada*) is construed with the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) through either the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), that is generally a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (retaining-the-quality) *bahuvrīhi*.
For example: "Devadatta, who has two garments, eats," or "Feed the one with hanging ears," and so forth.
For in the case of "those two whose clothes and ears are blue" (*nīla-vasana-karṇau*), even though there is no connection with the act of eating,
it is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* compound by virtue of mere proximity; and in the present case,
the word *sarva* [functions] within the collective which is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*).

Because the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*)—which is superimposed and included within the sense of *samavāya* (inherence)—exists [in such compounds], they are *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (those in which the qualities of the members are understood). However, when the meaning of the constituent words is connected with the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) through relationships such as that of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*), it is an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* *bahuvrīhi*. For example, in expressions such as "bring the man with brindled cows" (*citragumānaya*). Enough of this. Now, since words like *sarva* and *viśva* are listed in the *sarvādi* group only in their simple forms, how can words such as *paramasarva* be called pronouns (*sarvanāman*)? To this [it is replied]: [they are so because]...
He says: "Even that which ends in such [a word]. Regarding the rule *dvandve ca*:

by this rule (*dvandve ca*), the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) is prohibited for a *dvandva* compound whose final member is a word beginning with *sarva*, as in examples such as *varṇāśrametarāṇām*. If [the prohibition applied] only to isolated [words],...

Let the status of being a *sarvanāman* (pronoun) belong only to those words listed in the *sarvādi* group when they are used alone, and not to those ending in them; for the operations pertaining to *sarvanāman*, such as "for a *sarvanāman*, [the suffix] *smai*" (*sarvanāmnaḥ smai*), reside within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), and according to the rule "in the governing headings of *pada* and *aṅga*... (*padāṅgādhikāre*).

And because of the *paribhāṣā* "and that which ends with it," [the forms] such as *paramasarvasmai* are established; therefore he says "by that. The meaning is: by the force of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of that which ends with it.
The meaning is that it is established. By the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *tasil* is also included, according to the rule *pañcamyās tasil*.
Nor should it be argued that this is established by the fact that the pronoun resides in the constituent parts [of the compound];

for, according to the perspective of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *kutsite* (Pāṇini 5.3.74), since the full meaning [of the pronoun] is understood to connect with another [word] through number and case-role (*kāraka*), it is understood that the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) arises precisely from the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

The point is that when there is a desire to express contempt or the like regarding the meaning of a *subanta* (inflected nominal) whose base is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the rule results in the application of *akac* before the final phoneme of the pronoun; since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronoun" would then not apply to the whole [compound] due to the absence of that designation for the [final] element ending in it, the desired form would remain unestablished.
(211) *jasaḥ śī* | Pāṇini 7.1.17.

When the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would have been obtained for the case-ending *jas* after the word *sarva*, [the rule] *jasaḥ śī* applies. From the rule *ato bhisa ais*, the term *ataḥ* is understood to carry over; and from the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ smai*, the term *sarvanāmnaḥ* is understood to carry over.

This [term] continues [to apply]. Thus he says, beginning with "from that which ends in a short vowel" (*adantāt*). The long pronunciation of *śī* is for the sake of the subsequent rule, "and after a neuter [stem]" (*napuṃsakācca*); by this, the form *vāriṇī* is established. [The phrase] "because it consists of more than one phoneme" (*anekāltvāt*) means that the status of being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*) here is not caused by the fact that [the suffix] is marked with *ś*. Now, [one might object]:...

There is a *paribhāṣā* stating: "The property of having more than one phoneme (*anekāltva*) is not caused by an *anubandha*. The meaning is that the status of having more than one phoneme resulting from an *anubandha* does not serve as a cause for a universal substitution (*sarvādeśa*). Consequently, in the case of the element *śī*, since the letter *ś* has the technical designation *it* according to the rule *laśakvataddhite*, how [can it be considered to have more than one phoneme]?

The property of having multiple phonemes (*anekāltva*) is caused by that [the *śit* designation]. For this very reason, in the rule "ṭhavarṇastrasāvanañaḥ," the substitute *tṛ* does not possess the property of having multiple phonemes, because it is taken as having the measure of the *ṛ*-vowel;
otherwise, it would follow that it too would be a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśa). Therefore, in this case, [the substitution] is governed solely by the property of being marked with *ś*.

Having raised the objection that it is appropriate to rely on [the rule] *sarvādeśatva* (being a substitute for the whole), he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*) and so forth. The connection is as follows: as in the case of *arvaṇas tṛ* and similar rules, there is no "having more than one phoneme" (*anekāltva*) caused by an *anubandha*; thus, [the condition for a whole-stem replacement] does not apply. [The word] *śī* refers to the phoneme *ś*.

It must be stated that [the letters] *ṭ*, *h*, *l*, *ś*, *k*, and *v* receive the designation *it* when they occur in a *taddhita* suffix. By that rule, the designation *it* is prescribed for the groups of letters *l*, *ś*, *k*, and *v* when they constitute the beginning of a suffix. In the present case, however, because the element *śī* does not reside within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "suffixes," it does not inherently possess the status of a suffix; rather—

Because it is a substitute (*ādeśa*), its status as an affix (*pratyayatva*) must be stated by means of the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). And this *sthānivadbhāva* applies to the element *śī*, which has undergone the state of being a substitute.
Thus, prior to the establishment of its status as a substitute—at the stage when the rule for the substitute is being formulated—the *ś* of *śī* [is subject to the relevant operations].

Because the *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it") is not established [for the whole substitute], the status of having multiple phonemes (*anekāltva*) remains unimpeded. For this very reason, the argument that "[the substitute] is a replacement for the whole because it is marked with *ṭ* or *ś*" is also refuted. However, in the case of the substitute *tṛ*, since the *ṛ*-phoneme already possesses the *itsaṃjñā* prior to the occurrence of the substitution, [the aforementioned objection does not apply].
Intending to resolve the objection that there is an inequality because the [substitution] is applied to multiple *al* sounds, he replies:
"Because it is a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatvāt*) prior [to the application of other rules]. When the substitution of *śī* has occurred, the form *sarva ī* is established;
taking the formation of the *guṇa* vowel by *ādguṇaḥ* as already accomplished, he says: "sarve."

(212) *sarvanāmnaḥ smai* | Pāṇini 7.1.14. When the rule *ṛḍreḍbhyo ṅasiṅyoḥ smāt* [sic; actually *ṛḍreḍbhyo ṅasiṅyoḥ smāt* is not the source, but rather *ṛḍreḍbhyo ṅasiṅyoḥ smāt* is a misinterpretation of *ṛḍreḍbhyo ṅasiṅyoḥ smāt* which is not in the Aṣṭādhyāyī; the correct source for the *smai* ending in the dative singular is *sarvanāmnaḥ smai*] would apply to the dative singular of the word *sarva*, [the sūtra states: *sarvanāmnaḥ smai*. From the rule *ato bhisa ais*, the word *ataḥ* is carried over (*anuvartate*). And from the rule *ṛḍreḍbhyo ṅasiṅyoḥ smāt*, the word *ṅeḥ* is also carried over. Thus, when the dative singular suffix *ṅe* follows a pronoun, *smai* is substituted for it.
Thus he says, beginning with "therefore, all...
(213). Regarding the rule *ṅsiṅyoḥ smātsminau* (Pāṇini 7.1.15):
when the suffixes *ṭā*, *ṅsi*, and *ṅs* follow the word *sarva*, the rule *ṭāṅsiṅsām* would otherwise apply; however, for the case endings *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, [the following applies].

The term *ṅsiśca ṅśca* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. From the rule *ato bhisa ais*, the word *ataḥ* is understood; and from the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ smai*, the word *sarvanāmnaḥ* is also understood. Thus he says: "from this [stem] *sarva-*, etc. The phrase "of these two" means of *ṅsi* and *ṅi*. The phrase "these two" means *smāt* and *smin*.

Thinking that because the substitute *smāt* possesses the status of the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is a case-ending (*vibhakti*), and therefore the rule *na vibhaktau* prohibits the substitution of *īt* for the letter *t*, he says: *sarvasmāt*.
(214) *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* | Pāṇini 7.1.52.
When *sarvā-ām* is established, the *nuṭ* augment would apply by the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ*. However, [the following applies]: *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ*.
