Here, the word *āt*, which is understood from the previous rule *aj-jas-erasuk* and ends in the ablative case, qualifies the governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which has been transformed into the ablative case; thus, the rule of "specifying that which ends in" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies.

The word "of what follows" (*parasya*) must be supplied. By the maxim that "in the case of a mention of both [the antecedent and the subsequent], the mention in the ablative case is stronger," the technical rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* causes the locative form *ām* to be understood as a genitive. Furthermore, the term *sarvanāmnaḥ* is a qualifier of what is prescribed. Consequently:

The meaning is that the augment *suṭ* is applied to the *ām* prescribed after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) following a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *a*-vowel. This is established; thus he says [the rule] beginning with "ending in an *a*-vowel" (*avarṇāntāt*).
After "ending in an *a*-vowel," the word "stem" (*aṅgāt*) is to be supplied as a remainder.

However, if one were to explain [the rule] as "of *ām* prescribed after a pronominal ending in the letter *ṭh*," then in forms such as *yeṣām* and *teṣām*, the augment *suṭ* would not occur; for in those cases, *ām* is prescribed after a word ending in the letter *d*. But it has not been explained as "of that which follows a pronominal."

This being the case, the [objection] that "the [term] *varṇāśrametarāṇām* is unestablished" will become clear later in the root text itself. Regarding the terms *etva* and *ṣatva*: the substitution of *e* occurs by the rule *bahuvacane jhaly et*;
however, the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* does not apply here, as it is stated [in the commentary] regarding the plural number (*bahuvacane*).
This was stated under the rule *jhalyed* (Pāṇini 7.3.102). Regarding the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the *suṭ* augment as well;

the point is that because it is an integral part of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is included by the mention of that suffix, according to the principle: "The augments of those [elements] are included by the mention of those [elements].
As for the word *sarveṣām* ("of all"): [an objection is raised] "But [the rule] says *āmī*..."

If it is argued that, by the force of the locative case designation (*saptamīnirdeśa*), the rule "from this [stem], for what follows" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*) does not apply, and therefore the augment *suṭ* is properly attached to the base itself when *ām* follows—this is not so; for the intention is that the locative designation is necessary for the sake of the subsequent rule, "trayas for *treḥ*" (*trestrayaḥ*). This is because the mention of the locative case is required for the following statement.
Taking the substitution of *smin* for *su* as already established, he says: "in all" (*sarvasmin*). Regarding "the remainder" (*śeṣam*):

it is called "remainder" (*śeṣa*) because it remains (*śiṣyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The rule "words ending in *ghañ* or *ac* are masculine" is, however, merely general; this is the intended meaning. "In the same way" means: like the word *sarva*.

Nor should it be argued that the plural number alone is logical because the word *sarva* has as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the specific property of "allness" (*sarvatva*), which pervades plurality; for the word *sarva* refers to a collection (*samudāya*) composed of many parts. In that case, when the collection is intended without its parts being manifested, the singular number is used, as in "the whole world" (*sarvo lokaḥ*). Here, "non-manifestation" means that the number [of parts] is not intended to be expressed. However, when two collections with non-manifested parts are intended, then the dual number is used.

As in the case of *sarvau vyūhau* (both arrays). But when there is a collection of manifested parts (*udbhūtāvayavasamudāya*), then the plural number is used, as in *sarve janāḥ* (all people). Now, what are those words beginning with *sarva*, and how many are they? To this he says: "The words beginning with *sarva* are thirty-five. This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "five and thirty," or alternatively, a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "thirty exceeded by five" according to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*. The suffix *ḍac* (which would yield *-ka*) as a compound-ending is not applied here, because of the rule stating that the suffix *ḍac* is added to a *tatpuruṣa* numeral compound only when the word *adhika* ("exceeded by") is elided elsewhere.

Regarding the rule *pūrvaparāvareti*: this is a sūtra included within the *gaṇa* (list). Its meaning is that the seven words beginning with *pūrva*, when not used as technical names (*asaṃjñāyām*), should be understood as belonging to the *sarvādi* group.
As for their designation as pronouns (*sarvanāmasaṃjñā*), it is established by the very rule: "The words beginning with *sarva* are pronouns" (*sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*).
The two *gaṇasūtra*s, "ṭha-svam-ajñāti" and "antaraṃ-bahiḥ," are to be applied in exactly the same manner.
Words such as *vyavasthā* and so forth will be explained in the very root [section] of the *agni*.
The word "iti" serves to indicate the completion of the *sarvādi* group. In that regard, the word *viśva* also...

It is exactly like the word *sarva*. Regarding the word *ubha*, however, he states a distinction with the words "therein" (*tatra*). This means: among the [words] beginning with *sarva*. "For this very reason" means: precisely because it denotes a specific duality. "Always" (*nityam*) means:
it always ends in the dual number alone, and never in the singular or plural; such is the sense. By that—

The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are not excluded. Now, if this is the case, since the operations prescribed for sarvanāman— namely, *jas* being replaced by *śī*, *sarvanāmnaḥ smai*, *ṅsi-ṅyoḥ smāt-sminau*,
and *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ*— do not occur in the dual, what is the purpose of including the word *ubha* in the *sarvādi* (all-inclusive) group?

To show that [the objection] is futile, he says: "tasyeha" (of that, here). The meaning is as follows: the inclusion of that word *ubha* in this list, namely the *sarvādi* group, is for the purpose of the *akac* suffix, as prescribed by the rule "avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ svamor akac prāk ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.71), which applies in forms such as *ubhakau*. Now, one might object: let there be no inclusion of the word *ubha* in the *sarvādi* group.

Let there be no status as a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*), and let there be no *akac* suffix triggered by that status; for even when the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*) to the word *ubha*, the form *ubhakau* is established. Nor should a difference in accent between *ka* and *akac* be suspected, because [the accent] would be determined either by the rule "the accent of a taddhita suffix" (*taddhitasya*) due to the accent of the suffix itself, or by the rule "that which has a *cit* marker, along with its base" (*citaḥ saprakṛteḥ*).

Or, because there is no difference [in the result] regarding the final acute accent (*antodātta*) when [the suffix] *citsvara* is applied; and as it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "What is the difference between *ka* and *kak*? To that, he replies: "Not so" (*na ca*). The connection is that the desired form *ubhakaḥ* is not established by means of the suffix *kap*. Why? To this he says: "Because of the dual number" (*dvivacana*).

In the absence of the condition of being followed by a dual ending (*dvivacanaparatva*), the suffix *ayac* is prescribed after the word *ubha*. However, when the *akac* suffix is present, by the maxim "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing," the word *ubhaka* is also included under the term *ubha*. And of that [word], in the state *ubhaka-āṬ*:

Because it is followed by a dual suffix (*dvivacana*), the *ayac* affix does not occur. However, when the *kap* affix is present, since it is prescribed after the word *ubha*, the rule of "inclusion within the interval" (*tanmadhyapatitanyāya*) does not apply;
consequently, the word *ubhaka* is not included under the term *ubha*, and thus the word *ubha* is separated from the *kap* affix.

Because of the absence of being followed by a dual ending (*dvivacana*), [the form] would be *ubhayakau* in the case of the *ayac* suffix. The meaning is that just as there is no *ayac* suffix in the cases of *ubhayataḥ* and *ubhayatra* because of the absence of being followed by a dual ending, so it is here. That which was stated—that the *ayac* suffix does not occur when a dual ending is present—is [explained] by the rule *ubhayo 'nyatra*.

The meaning is that it was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* while speaking [of this]. He explains the term "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) as follows: "elsewhere means when there is an absence of being followed by a dual ending. In the cited *Vārttika*, the intended meaning of the word "elsewhere" is "when something other than a dual ending follows," for there is an absence of "other" (*anya*) [in that case].

The meaning is that, because the previous Vārttika [P. 1.1.27] mentions only the dual number (*dvivacana*)—as in the phrase "because it is the domain of the dual number and the *ṭāp* suffix"—the mention of *ṭāp* there is not intended to be significant; this is clear from Kaiyaṭa and others. Consequently, for the sake of the *akaC* suffix, which is triggered by the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*), the word *ubha* [is treated as such].

It is established that [the word *ubhaya*] is recited among the words beginning with *sarva*. Regarding this, what needs to be said will be stated in the section on secondary derivation (*taddhita-prakriyā*) under the rule *ṭhūbhādudāto nityam*. Now, he states the specific detail concerning the word *ubhaya*: "of the word *ubhaya*" etc. That whole (*avayavin*) which has two parts (*ubhau avayavau*) is *ubhaya*.

Regarding the word *maṇi*: by the rule "after *ubha*, [the suffix] *ayac*," the suffix *ayac* is applied. The meaning of that rule is: "the suffix *ayac* shall occur after the word *ubha*, which expresses a number when used in the sense of a part, provided it refers to a whole (*avayavin*). Thus, the meaning is "a gem composed of two parts. Since the gem, as a whole, is singular, the form is *ubhayo maṇiḥ* (a single gem consisting of both), using the singular number; and [the word] *ubhaya*.

Even when there is an intention to express two jewels (*maṇi*) composed of two parts—namely "both" and "both"—the dual number does not occur as *ubhayau maṇī*; for it is understood from the cited Vārttika, *ubhayo 'nyatra*, that the word *ubhaya* is prescribed for use only other than in the dual number. Nor is there [an exception] in that case...
It must be stated that in the Vārttika, only the word *ubhaya* ending in the svārthika suffix *yaC* is intended for inclusion,
because that Vārttika proceeds precisely by taking up the word *ubha* ending in the svārthika suffix *yaC*;
as seen in the commentary on this Vārttika, in the examples "the *ubhaya* jewel" (*ubhayo maṇiḥ*) and "both gods and humans" (*ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*).
Since the Bhāṣya cites [the word *ubhayá-*] as an example, it is understood that the suffix *-āyan* (which has the same meaning as *-tayaP*) is also included therein.
With this very intention, the status of *ubhaya* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) under the rule "A taddhita suffix is an indeclinable when it does not take all case-endings" does not apply;
for although it does not take all case-endings due to the absence of the dual number, [it is excluded] by the rule "The suffixes beginning with *tasil*... [and so forth].

Kaiyaṭa has stated that [the suffixes] are enumerated as follows: "those ending in *pāśap*," "those beginning with *śas* up to before the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*)," "*am*," "*ām*," "the *kṛtvas*-artha suffixes," "*tasivatī*," and "the two, *nānā* and *añ*. He says this, namely Kaiyaṭa. And thus: *ubhayaḥ*, *ubhaye*; *ubhayam*.
The forms are as follows: *ubhayau*, *ubhayena*, *ubhayaiḥ*; *ubhayasmai*, *ubhayebhyaḥ*; *ubhayasmāt*, *ubhayebhyaḥ*;
*ubhayasya*, *ubhayeṣām*; *ubhayasmin*, *ubhayeṣu*. Thus it is established that there is no usage of the dual ending, such as *ubhayau* and so forth. — Haradatta.

This is the presentation of the underlying dissatisfaction (*asvarasa*). The seed of that [dissatisfaction] is precisely the contradiction with the previously cited *Vārttika* and *Bhāṣya*, which state "both [words] elsewhere" (*ubhayo 'nyatra*); this has been explained in detail elsewhere. [In the case of *ubhaya*], when the suffix *jas* follows, the mandatory designation as a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*)—which would apply by the rule *sarvādīni*—is set aside by the subsequent [rule].

Anticipating the possibility that the designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) might optionally apply by virtue of the rule "the first, the last, few, half, and *katipaya*, as well as *nema*," he offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
That is to say, because of that word *ubhaya*, when the suffix *jas* is present, although the optionality of the rule "the first, the last... would otherwise apply...
The meaning is that the designation (saṃjñā) remains permanent; the phrase "by this [rule] ‘sarvādīni’" is to be supplied as the remainder. Now, one might ask:

since the word *ubhaya* is not included among the words beginning with *prathama* and *carama*, how can it have the suffix *tayap*? To this he replies: "by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the substitute *ayac*. This refers to the rule *ubhādudāttaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *saṅkhyāyā avayave tayap*, two views are established in the Bhāṣya: first, that the substitute *ayac* is applied to the suffix *tayap* prescribed after the word *ubha*; second, that *ayac* is an independent suffix, without following the mention of *tayap*. Here, [the term is used] according to the first view.

One should be aware of the doubt regarding the optional application (*vikalpa*) of the designation *sarvanāman*. Now, one might ask: since the option provided by the rule *prathamacarama-* is subsequent (*para*), how can the designation *sarvanāman* be considered here as strictly obligatory (*nitya*) by the rule *sarvādīni*?
To this, he says: "Because it is internal (*antaraṅga*)."

To demonstrate this very point—namely, "by virtue of being independent of case-endings": the optional rule [Pāṇini 1.1.33], *prathamacarama*, which applies when the suffix *jas* is present, is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on a case-ending (*vibhaktyapekṣatva*) by virtue of depending on *jas*.
However, the rule for the permanent technical designation (*saṃjñā*) [Pāṇini 1.1.27], *sarvādīni*, is *antaraṅga* because it does not depend on that [suffix].

This is according to the maxim: "That which depends on fewer factors is more internal (antaraṅga). Therefore, here, setting aside even the subsequent optional rule "prathamacarama" (Pāṇini 1.1.33), the designation [of *sarvanāman*] occurs invariably by the rule "sarvādīni" (Pāṇini 1.1.27), because the internal is stronger than the external; such is the intended meaning. And thus, the substitution of *śī* [for the dual ending *au*] occurs.

He says "both" to show that [the suffix] is eternal (*nitya*). Now, since the words *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are not observed to be used anywhere [independently], for what purpose are they recited? To this he says: "*ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are suffixes. [The rule states: "After *kim*, *yad*, and *tad*, when there is a selection from among two, the suffix *ḍatarac* [is added]; or..."

In the case of questioning regarding many births (*jāti*), the suffix *ḍatama* is applied. The suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) by the rule "after [words] ending in *eka* and those preceded by [the word] *pra*, etc.

This is because their prescription occurs under the heading "the suffix *ṭha*. Therefore, by the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), through the mention of *ḍatara*, [the mention of *ḍatama* is also understood].

The intention is that words such as *katarad* and others would also be included. He raises an objection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). Regarding the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam*: if the paribhāṣā concerning the inclusion of suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) were to apply even in the formulation of a technical definition (*saṃjñāvidhi*), then the sūtra would have been formulated simply as *suptiṅ padam*.

Since the meaning "ending in a *sup* or *tiṅ* affix" is obtained by the very *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it is understood that the *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of an affix does not apply in the formulation of a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*). And thus,
in the present case, in the rule prescribing the name "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*), when the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are mentioned...
The objection is: "How can there be a reference to that which ends in [the suffix], since the technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding the mention of a suffix does not apply here?

He answers: "Even so..."—meaning that although in other rules prescribing technical names (*saṃjñā*) there is no reference to that which ends in [the suffix] when a suffix is mentioned, in this rule prescribing the name "sarvanāman," there is such a reference because of the mention of *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*.
The meaning is that there is indeed the inclusion of the end [of the base]. Why? To this he says: "of the two alone.
According to the maxim, "A base should not be used alone, nor should an affix be used alone," since the use of the affixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* alone is improper, [the rule applies] to those two.

The meaning is that there is no result [of applying] the technical designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal). Therefore, it is established that by the mention of the suffixes *-tara* and *-tama*, words such as *katara* and *katama* are included here. Now, an objection: since the inclusion of the word *anyatara* in the list of *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) is already accomplished by the mention of the suffix *-tara* alone, its recitation in that list is redundant. The same applies to the word *anyatama*.

Because they end in the suffixes *ḍatam* and *ḍatama*, there would be the undesirable consequence [of these words] being treated as pronouns (*sarvanāman*); therefore, he says: "The words *anyatara* and *anyatama* are un-derived (*avyutpanna*).
This means that, like words such as *ḍittha*, they are devoid of any division into base and suffix. [This applies] to the group beginning with *kim*, *yat*, and *etad*.

The meaning is that this is because [the suffixes] *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are prescribed [only for such cases]. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, how is the discernment of two or many [entities] understood from the words *anyatara* and *anyatama*?
To this he says: "By their very nature. And thus, there is no [need for further rule] regarding the word *anyatama*.
He states that [these] possess the nature of pronouns (sarvanāmatva) by saying "therein" (tatra). The meaning is: "between these two.

The intention is that this is because the suffixes -ḍatara and -ḍatama are prescribed for the word *anyatara*. Now, one might ask: if this is so, how is the determination of two or many understood from the words *anyatara* and *anyatama*? To this [he replies]:

He says: "By its very nature. And thus, he states that the word *anyatama* does not possess the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) by saying: "In that case," which means "between these two. As for the word *anyatara*, however, even though it lacks the suffix *-ḍatara*, [it is a pronoun] precisely because of its inclusion in the *sarvādi* (the list beginning with *sarva*) group.

That they are pronouns has already been largely stated. Therefore, in order to prevent the misconception that "tva" and "tve" constitute a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and because their meaning is not well-known, he explains:
"Both *tva* and *tva* are neuter stems ending in *a*, and are synonyms for 'other' (*anya*). The meaning is that they have the same sense as the word *anya*.
To avoid the redundancy of reading either one of the two [forms] when both end in a dental, he says: "Some say" (*eka iti*).

This means that certain authors of commentaries (*vṛttikṛt*) and others hold this view. [This refers to] the acute accent (*udātta*) in "etaṃ tvaṃ manye" and the grave accent (*anudātta*) in "uta tvaḥ paśyan," and so forth.

The sense is that this is because it is seen in the *Ṛgveda*. Regarding the phrase "one ending in -t": the meaning is that others hold the view that, based on the division "tvat" in the *saṃhitā* recitation, the first [word] ends in -t and the second ends in -a. Otherwise, one would recite it only once, either with monotonous intonation (*ekaśruti*) or devoid of accents.

For by that alone both [meanings] are obtained, and because of the Phiṭ-sūtra: *ṭhvattvasamasimetyanuccāni*. Furthermore, in the Vedabhāṣya on the occasion of explaining the Ṛgveda verse "starīru tvadbhavati, sūta u tvat," it says: "*tva'diti*."

This is because it has been stated that "this [term], which is listed as the first of all [pronominal bases], is anudātta and is a synonym for *anya* (other/another)," and also because of the usage by Jayadeva in the verse: "drinking the honey sweeter than your lower lip" (*tvadadharamadhuramadhūni pibantam*).
For in that instance, the word *tvat* is a synonym for *anya*; the analysis of the compound is *tvataḥ adharaḥ* (the lower lip of another). It refers to the lower lip of another woman.

This is the meaning. However, "your lip" (tavādharah) is not intended [as the referent], because that would result in an inconsistency with the connection to the preceding sentence: "He sees you in secret in every direction. *Nema* means "half" (*ardhe*). The word "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is based on the Vedic verse: *pra nemasmin dadṛśe somo antaḥ*.

The sense is: "because it is seen to be so. Regarding the word *sama*: the meaning is that the word *sama* is listed in the group beginning with *sarva* (the *sarvādi* gaṇa) as having exactly the same meaning as the word *sarva*. Regarding the phrase "but a synonym for *tulya*":
the meaning is that it has the same meaning as the word *tulya*. Regarding the phrase "by way of an indicator (*jñāpaka*)": otherwise, in that case...

The intended meaning is that one should specify "of all these. Now, an objection may be raised: in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, the rule *antaraṃ bahiryogopasaṃvyānayoḥ* (1.1.36), which prescribes the optional designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) in the nominative plural (*jasi*), is accompanied by a reading of the *vārttika* found in the *Mahābhāṣya*: *apuri iti vaktavyam*.

Thus, although the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronominal) is prohibited for the case-ending *jas* in the rule "evam cāntarāḥ puryaḥ," in the instance "antarāyāṃ purī" (the city within), that prohibition would not apply due to the optionality provided by the rule "anyatarasyām. To address this, he says:
"in the *gaṇasūtra*. Even though this *vārttika* belongs to the section prescribing optional rules for *jas*.

Nevertheless, this [statement] "antaraṃ bahiḥ" is a supplement (śeṣa) specifically to the *gaṇasūtra* that reads "antaraṃ bahiḥ," and not a supplement to the rule "antaraṃ bahiḥ" read in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* which prescribes [the substitution of] *jas*.

This is because, in the rule "jasaḥ śī," the word "ataḥ" is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), and thus there is no possibility of its application to a stem ending in *ṭāp*. Consequently, [the point remains as follows]:

The meaning of this Vārttika is that the word *antara* does not receive its place in the *sarvādi* group when it qualifies the word *puri*. Consequently, it is established that, except for the case of the nominative plural (*jasaḥ*), the word *antara* does not function as a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) when qualifying *puri*. Therefore, in the case of *antarāyām*...

Intending to show that in forms such as *purī* the operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) applies, while the suffixes *syāt*, *ḍāp*, and so forth do not, he provides the example: *antarāyāṃ purī*. Although it is the word *antara* itself that is listed in the *sarvādi* group, and not its feminine form ending in *ṭāp*, nevertheless, by the principle of "the qualified [form] includes the gender-distinctive" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), [the rule applies].

The attainment of the status of a *sarvanāman* (pronominal) should be understood as occurring either by way of a technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) or because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*). Furthermore, the word *sima* is well-known in the lexicon (*kośa*) in the sense: "The word *sima* occurs in the senses of 'entirety,' 'power,' and 'that which is bounded by a limit' (*maryādā*)."
(215) *pūrvaparāvaradakṣiṇottarāparādharāṇi vyavasthāyām asaṃjñāyām* | 1|1|34|.
Now, [we shall explain] that sūtra recited in the Aṣṭādhyāyī which is identical in form to the three sūtras contained within the *sarvādi* group.

He explains the three sūtras beginning with *pūrvapara* while dispelling the suspicion of redundancy: *pūrvapara*. The [sūtra] *sarvanāmāni* and *vibhāṣā jasi* are understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of these. This means: of the seven beginning with *pūrva*. [The word] *gaṇa*...

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is "in the *sarvādi* group. Regarding the phrase "which was obtained": the meaning is that by the rule "*sarvādīni*," the designation (*saṃjñā*) was obtained as obligatory (*nityā*). By this, the sūtra *pūrvaparāvaradaksinaottarāparādharaṇi svam adese* (Pāṇini 1.1.34), as recited in the *gaṇa*-list, serves to provide the obligatory designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) for *jas* (the nominative-accusative plural) and other cases. However, that which is recited in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*...
It has been indicated that there is no tautology because [the term] is used for the purpose of its conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*). Regarding the phrase "its own denotation" (*svābhidheya*):

*apekṣa* means that which is expected (*apekṣyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, words such as *pūrva* (eastern, etc. necessarily function with a meaning that depends upon a limit (*avadhi*) with respect to their own [denoted] direction.

The result is that there is an option regarding the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "sarvanāman. As for the question "What [is the purpose] in the case of *vyavasthā*?"—the question arises because words such as *pūrva* (eastern) exist only in a sense that necessarily depends upon a limit (*avadhi*). Regarding the example "southern singers" (*dakṣiṇā gāthakāḥ*), the point is that here the word *dakṣiṇa* does not depend upon a limit.
Regarding the phrase "the singers situated on the right side," there is indeed an expectation for a limiting term (*avadhi*) as to why they are so designated; therefore, he says:
"the meaning is 'skilled'.
Although proficiency (*prāvīṇya*) also requires a limiting term as to why it exists, nevertheless, [it is understood] from such expressions as "capable in both question and answer."
They say that this should be understood as a counter-example. As for the question "What is meant by 'not being a name' (asaṃjñāyām)?":

since it will be stated later that "those which have become names or secondary members (upasarjana) are not [included among] the *sarvādi* group," the question arises because the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) does not apply in the case of a name. The example given is "the Northern Kurus" (*uttarāḥ kuravaḥ*). Here, the word *kuru*...

The term *nityam* [in the rule] refers to the plural ending when there is a specific fault (*doṣaviśeṣe*). There is indeed a fixed convention (*vyavasthā*) here, in that the word *uttara* (northern) is applied with reference to Mount Sumeru as the limit. However, because it is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*), it does not possess the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*). As for the words *pūrva* (eastern) and so forth, since their conventional designation (*saṅketa*) regarding the directions is beginningless, they [do possess the status of pronouns].

These are technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*). It is considered that because the word *tūtara* is a modern convention for the Kuru region, it is a technical term. However, some say that if the rule *asaṃjñāyām* were not present [to negate the application of the suffix], then for words such as *pūrva*, there would be an optional application (*aprāptavibhāṣā*) only when they function as technical terms.

(216) *svam ajñāti-dhanākhyāyām* | 1|1|35 | The word *svam* [is a pronoun] except when it denotes a kinsman (*jñāti*) or wealth (*dhana*). Here too, the terms *sarvanāmāni* and *vibhāṣā jas-i* are understood from the previous rules. "Kinsman and wealth" is *jñātidhane*; the expression for those two is *jñātidhanākhyā*; [it is not a pronoun] when it is such an expression.

"Called kinsmen's wealth" means not called kinsmen's wealth; in that case—namely, in the case of "not called kinsmen's wealth"—the neuter gender is used with reference to the form of the word itself. Thus he says: "kinsmen's wealth and so forth. Regarding *sveṣvā*, because it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is the substitution of *śī*.

The meaning is: "In the absence of that, there is the absence of that. The word *sva* has four meanings: self (*ātman*), what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). As Amarasimha states: "The word *sva* [is used] for kinsmen and the self; as a neuter, it means one's own (*ātmīya*) in three genders, and as a masculine, it means wealth. Here, "the word *sva* [is used] for kinsmen and the self" constitutes a single sentence.
The meaning is that the word *sva* is masculine when it denotes a kinsman or the self (*ātman*).

The second statement is: "In the three genders, *sva* [means] one's own (*ātmīya*). The meaning is that the word *sva*, when denoting what belongs to oneself, conforms to the gender of the noun it qualifies. The third statement is: "In the neuter, *sva* [means] wealth (*dhana*). In this case, the word *sva* [denotes wealth].

The meaning is "masculine and neuter. The *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *svaḥ* occurs in the masculine in the senses of 'self' and 'kinsman'; in the three genders [it means] 'one's own'; and in the feminine, it means 'wealth'. Since the senses of "kinsman" and "wealth" are excluded there, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) applies to the senses of "self" and "one's own," with the optionality [of the suffix] *jas* being prescribed.

Intending this, he explains: "the meaning is 'one's own'; or 'oneself'. He states the purpose of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of kinsmen and wealth: "but [in the case] of those denoting kinsmen and wealth...
Because of the exclusion of the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) for those denoting kinsmen and those denoting wealth, [the form] *svāḥ* occurs in the *jas* [case-ending].

The meaning is "of such a form. Nor should it be argued that even in the case of "kinsman" (*jñāti*) and "wealth" (*dhana*), the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) would not apply when they are presented as "one's own"; for, by the force of the inclusion of the term *ākhyā* ("name/designation"), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) operates only when [the kinsman or wealth] is presented specifically as a "kinsman-ness" or "wealth-ness."
(217) *antaraṃ* [is used] in the sense of connection with (*yoga*) what is outside (*bahiḥ*) or what is worn as an upper garment (*upasaṃvyāna*). 1|1|36.

The word *antaraṃ* [is mentioned]. Here too, the two rules *sarvanāmāni* and *vibhāṣā jasi* are understood to carry over. *Bahiḥ* means an uncovered space; that which has a connection (*yoga*)—that is, a relation—with that is [the referent of *antaraṃ*].

*Bahiryoga* means an object existing outside. *Upasaṃvyāna* refers to that which is wrapped around or put on; it is the lower garment (*antarīya*). He states this with the words beginning "external" (*bāhyā*), etc. [Pāṇini 2.3.29]:
*pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* ||7|1|16|| (The suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* [genitive] is optionally used after the nine words beginning with *pūrva* when they denote external objects).
The rule "ṭāṅasiṅsām inātsyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.12) continues [into this context], as he says: "from these.
By "these," the words beginning with *pūrva* intended in the three sūtras starting with "pūrvapara" (Pāṇini 1.1.34–36) are meant.
The words beginning with *tyad* will be explained under the section on consonantal stems. The word *eka* refers to the number one.

However, in other senses, the dual and plural numbers also occur. Regarding the word *eka*, the lexicon (*kośa*) states: "The word *eka* is used in the sense of 'another,' 'principal,' 'first,' 'alone,' 'common,' 'equal,' 'small,' and also in the sense of 'number. This might be the case—[as in the examples] *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* ("having you as father") and *matkapitṛkaḥ* ("having me as father").

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The colloquial analytical sentences (*laukika-vigraha*) are "he whose father is *tvakam*" and "he whose father is *ahakam*. "Colloquial" (*laukikatva*) means fitness for usage.
When the suffix *akac* is added to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the sense of "unknown" and so forth—by the rule *avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ svamo 'tṛtīyā-asthāne* [Pāṇini 5.3.71]—it becomes *yuṣmakad*.

This being the case, when *ami* is applied by the rule "ṬhReĀ prathamayoḥ," and when the substitutes *tvā* and *ahā* are applied by the rule "tvāhau sau," followed by the elision of the final *s* by the rule "śeṣe lopaḥ," and finally by the rules "ato guṇe" and "ami pūrvaḥ," the forms *tvakam* and *ahakam* are produced. [The stems] *yuṣmad* and *pitṛ* [follow].
"asmad-pitṛ-s—" is the non-linguistic (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).

The established rule is that "non-linguistic status" (*alaukikatva*) means unfitness for actual usage. In that regard, in the state of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* or *matkapitṛkaḥ*, the suffix *kap* does not occur.
Because *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would be subject to the suffix *akac* due to their status as pronominals (*sarvanāman*), [the following rule is stated]:
(219) *na bahuvrīhau* 1.1.29. In that regard, this is commenced: "not in a *bahuvrīhi*. [The class of words beginning with] *sarva*, etc., [is defined].

The term "sarvanāmāni" (pronouns) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. The meaning understood is that, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, words beginning with "sarva" (sarvādi) would not be pronouns. This being the case, this sūtra would be redundant, because [the designation of] words beginning with "sarva" occurring within a *bahuvrīhi*, such as in "priyasarvāyai," [would already be excluded by the general rule].

Since the prohibition of its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is already established by its being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) due to its primary function of conveying a meaning transferred from its own referent, and because it will be stated later that "those [words] which have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or subordinate elements are not [included among] *sarva* and the others," he therefore explains: "in the intended [bahuvrīhi]," namely, in the bahuvrīhi compound.

This meaning is obtained by resorting to the locative case in the sense of "object" (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Thus, when a *bahuvrīhi* compound is about to be formed, this prohibition is meaningful precisely before that stage, in the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*), because the semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*)— which constitutes the capacity for composition (*sāmarthya*)— exists only at the stage of the compound itself, and not in the analytical sentence.

The meaning is that, due to the absence of that [subordinate status], the subordinate status (*upasarjanatva*) previously mentioned is absent at that time. Now, while demonstrating the colloquial analytical sentence (*laukika-vigraha-vākya*), he shows the *bahuvrīhi* which serves as the object of observation (*lakṣya*), beginning with "one whose father is you" (*tvakampitṛkaḥ*) and so forth. Because it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the suffix *kap* is applied.

By the rule *ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca*, the forms *tvatkaḥ* and *matkaḥ* arise through the substitution of *tva-* and *ma-*. Now, one might object: since the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) is prohibited in the non-standard analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*) prior to the application of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, how can there be the form *tvaṃ pitā*?
To demonstrate the non-locative compound sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*), he says: "here" (*iha*).

This means in this sūtra, *na bahuvrīhau*. Regarding "in the analytical sentence" (*prakriyā-vākya*): the meaning is that it occurs only in the non-locative analytical sentences such as *yuṣmad-s-pitṛ-s*, *asmad-s-pitṛ-s*, and so forth.

However, this prohibition does not apply to the non-technical (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), because a *bahuvrīhi* compound— being already established in its own meaning— is fit for independent usage; thus, there is no intention to form a *bahuvrīhi* in that context, as it occurs only within the analytical sentence which constitutes the non-technical stage of derivation (*prakriyāvākya*).
Because it is intended to be so. How this is so will be explained in the analysis of compound words (*samāsa*).

[Objection: "Let there be no prohibition of the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) in the non-grammatical analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*); what is the fault? To this, he says: "Otherwise," meaning that the rule *na bahuvrīhau* applies to the non-grammatical analytical sentence.
The meaning is: "provided there is no prohibition. Regarding the phrase "there too":

the meaning is "even in the non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*). Now, [one might object]: even if *kac* occurs in the non-ordinary analytical sentence, what of it? Even when *kac* is present, its...
Because there is no sublation [of the rule] due to its being unfit for application, he says "And that" (sa ca).

The sense is that there is a rule of hearing [the word] in the non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*), as well as in the ordinary analytical sentence and in the compound (*samāsa*). This rule applies in both cases.

He states two examples, beginning with *atikrānto bhavakantam* and so forth. Because the word *bhavat* is listed in the *sarvādi* group, it possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*); consequently, in the stage of the non-worldly analytical compound (*alaukika-vigraha*), the suffix *akac* is applied. Thus, the non-worldly analytical compound sentence results as *bhavakat-am-ati*. In that context, [the rule] *atyādayaḥ...* [applies].

When the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs in the sense of "surpassed" (*krānta*, etc. and a compound (*samāsa*) is formed, the case-ending suffix (*sup*) is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*.
Thus, from the word *atibhava* in the nominative singular, the form *atibhavakān* arises.

In the alternative view where there is no compound (*samāsa*), the non-technical analytical statement (*laukika-vigraha*) is "one who has transcended *bhavaka*. In that context, although the meaning of the word *bhavat* is subordinate (*upasarjana*) during the stage of compounding—because its own meaning has been subsumed by another primary meaning—it is not subordinate during the stage of the non-technical analytical statement. Consequently, since it retains its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the suffix *akac* is applied; this suffix persists both in the non-technical analytical statement "one who has transcended *bhavakan*" (*atikrānto bhavakantam*) and in the compound *abhavakān*. This is because, according to the aforementioned reasoning, the word *bhavat* is not subordinate during the stage of the non-technical analytical statement.

Even though that [stem] is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) in the compound, there is no factor to prevent *akac* from applying, because it was triggered during the pre-compositional, non-grammatical analytical stage (*alaukika-vigraha-daśā*) which serves as its source. Nor can it be argued that although the status of being non-subordinate exists during the pre-compositional analytical stage— as in "bhavat-am"— it will be destroyed upon reaching the stage of the compound.

Because it is on the verge of destruction, according to the technical definition of "that which has not yet formed its compound," even in the non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*), it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*); therefore, the suffix *akac* is difficult to obtain. Consequently, one might ask: how could *akac* be applicable in the ordinary analytical sentence "one who has transcended *bhavakaṃt*" (*atikrānto bhavakantam*) or in the resulting compound *atibhavakān*?

It should not be said that the example is unestablished; for in a non-worldly (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) of this kind, when a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is applied, the maxim regarding the non-application of grammatical operations once they have been completed (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*) does not apply, because that maxim is non-eternal (*anitya*).
And as for its non-eternality, the very sūtra *na bahuvrīhau* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Likewise...

For— were the paribhāṣā "akṛtavyūha" universal, then even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, [the condition of] being a non-subordinate (*anupasarjana*) would apply to words such as *yuṣmad* and *pitṛs* in ungrammatical analytical sentences (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*).

Since the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) does not apply because [the word] is already prone to destruction at the time it becomes a *bahuvrīhi*, the rule "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīhau*) need not have been formulated. This is because the paribhāṣā "the non-application of a grammatical operation once a configuration has been formed" (*akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*) would operate there; thus, the quality of being a non-subordinate (*anupasarjanatva*) is already prone to destruction at the time it becomes a *bahuvrīhi*.

Since the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) does not apply in the non-ordinary syntactical derivation (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*) that precedes it, the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīhau*) is meaningful as a negation of that [status]. Nor should it be argued that the absence of the pronoun status in the aforementioned *bahuvrīhi* subject should be based solely on the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that what has not been formed remains unformed) within the non-ordinary derivation, rather than by the rule "not in a *bahuvrīhi*. For if that were so, forms such as *atikrānto bhavakantam atibhavakaḥ* ("one who has surpassed Bhavakanta") would not be established.

If, by the prohibition regarding *akṛtavyūha*, the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) were absent even in its non-technical (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), then the suffix *akac* would not apply; consequently, there would be no audible occurrence of *atibhavakān* both in the technical analytical sentence such as *atikrānto bhavakantam* and in the resulting compound.

And thus, since the prohibition of *sarvanāman* status is established by assuming that the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* does not apply in the non-locus (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) regarding *bahuvrīhi*, it is understood that the *sarvanāman* status applies even in the non-locus analytical sentences regarding other types of compounds, because the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* does not apply there either. It is for this very purpose that the rule *na bahuvrīhau* exists; the details are explained elsewhere. The word "pratyācakhyau" means "he rejected" or "he refuted."

Anticipating the objection that there might be an option (vikalpa) between the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya since both are equally Smṛti, he says: "according to the later" (yathottaram). The sense is that this is the established doctrine of the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇasamaya): that among the sages, the authority of each subsequent work increases while the authority of each preceding one decreases—namely, the Vārttikakāra has greater authority than the Sūtrakāra, and the Bhāṣyakṛt has greater authority than both of them.

Nor should it be said that this sūtra is intended to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the maxim *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* according to the method already stated; for the groundlessness and fruitlessness of the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* will be explained in the discussion of the word *sedivas* under the rule *halantādikāre*, and also in the section on *samarthānāṃ prathamādre*. Regarding the phrase "those which have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*)," a modern convention is a *saṃjñā*. That which presents its own meaning as a qualifier of another is an *upasarjana*. The phrase "not [included among] *sarva* etc. means that they are not recited in the list of words beginning with *sarva*.

Regarding the term "great designation" (*mahāsaṃjñā*): by the power of creating a designation based on its etymological meaning— namely, that these are the names of all [words] rather than being treated as single-syllable designations like *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so forth— it possesses, as its primary characteristic, the capacity to denote all its own referents.

The meaning is that because it is understood that [the word] possesses the status of being the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of all pronominal terms, one infers that only such words are included in the *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*) list. By the phrase "when [a thing] is presented as primary," there is an exclusion of the subordinate (*upasarjana*). When it is stated that "[it is the capacity to denote] all objects presented as primary,"...

Because there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of words such as *pūrva* and others, [the author] says "in its own [meaning]. By the phrase "in all meanings," words that function as proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*) are excluded, because proper names refer to individual specific instances (*vyakti*). "The operation of a name" means the grammatical operations associated with the designation "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*), such as the substitution of *śī*, *smāy*, and so forth.

Regarding the term *antargaṇa*: a group (*gaṇa*) that is included within the *sarvādi* group is an *antargaṇa*. The meaning is that its grammatical operations include such rules as "uṭhaḍḍḍatarādibhyaḥ" and "tyadādīnām aḥ. In the example *sarvāya dehi*, because it is a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*), the substitution of *sam* does not take place.

Regarding *atikataram*: in the expression *atikataram* (meaning "which family has surpassed [another]"), the word *katara* does not undergo the substitution of *ādḍ* because it functions as an *upasarjana* (secondary member of a compound). Regarding *atitad*: in the expression *atitad* (meaning "a Brāhmaṇa who has surpassed him"), the substitution of *at* for the initial of *tyadādi* stems occurs, and the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau* (where *s* replaces *t* and *d* after a vowel before the nominative singular suffix *su*) does not apply.

(220) *Tṛtīyāsamāse* 1.1.30. Regarding the rule *Tṛtīyāsamāse*: intending that the term *sarvanāman* ("all-name") is carried over from the rule *sarvādīni* and the word *na* ("not") is carried over from the rule *na bahuvrīhau*, he says "here" (*iha*).
Regarding the example *māsopāvya*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is *māsena pūrvaḥ*. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
By the rule *pūrvasadṛśa...*, this forms a *tṛtīyā-tatpuruṣa* compound. The meaning is "that which exists prior to a month.
Since the term *samāsa* (compound) is understood to carry over from the rule *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau*, [this is a compound].

The repetition of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of including even the secondary compound (*gauṇasamāsa*) consisting of a non-technical analytical sentence (*laukikavigrahavākya*) based on a third-case compound. Consequently, he states the resulting conclusion: "having the sense of a third-case compound," and so forth. And [this applies] to the copulative compound (*dvandva*) as well.

From the rule *sarvādīni* [P. 1.1.27], the term "all pronouns" (*sarvanāman*) is carried forward; from the rule *na bahuvrīhau* [P. 1.1.29], the word "not" (*na*) is also carried forward. (221) *dvandve ca* [P. 1.1.31].

Thus he says: "In a *dvandva* compound, it is stated [that they are not included]. The meaning is that the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronoun) does not apply. Regarding the example "varṇāśrametarāṇām": this is from the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, which states, "Tell us, without omission, the duties (*dharmas*) of the castes (*varṇa*), the stages of life (*āśrama*), and others (*itara*). Here, there is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "castes," "stages of life," and "others. In this context...

Because they lack the status of being *sarvanāman* (pronominal), the augment *suṭ* does not apply by the rule *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ*. [The phrase] "only of the aggregate" means that it is not the case that those items beginning with *sarva* which exist within a *dvandva* compound would cease to be *sarvanāman*; for such an interpretation would involve the unnecessary burden (*gaurava*) of supplying an unstated verb like "exist. Rather, [the meaning is simply] "in a *dvandva*..."

The meaning is that the designation *sarvanāman* does not apply; thus, the connection is with the very action of negation (*na-kriyā*), which is the primary element, as the basis for the *dvandva* compound. The literal sense is: "the designation *sarvanāman*, which has the *dvandva* as its substratum, does not occur. The resulting conclusion is: "the *dvandva* compound does not have the designation *sarvanāman*."
The state of being a *dvandva* compound belongs to the entire aggregate such as "varṇāśrametara" and not to its individual constituents.

Thus, the factual position is that the prohibition of the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) applies only to the aggregate "varṇāśrametara" and so forth, and not to its constituent parts. Now, [one might object]: what about the constituents of the *dvandva*?

In the absence of the prohibition against its being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), because the word *itara* would be a pronoun within the compound *varṇāśrametara*, the augment *suṭ* would be applied to the *ām* following it, resulting in the form *varṇāśrametareṣām*.
However, the rule for the application of *suṭ* prescribes it only after a pronoun whose stem ends in an *a*-vowel. Therefore, [the prohibition is necessary].

Even though the entire compound *varṇāśrametara* is excluded from being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) because it is a *dvandva*, the word *itara* which constitutes its member remains a pronoun. Consequently, since it follows a stem ending in that [pronoun], the augment *suṭ* would have to be applied before the case-ending *ām*. This is not the case, however, because the prohibition applies to the *dvandva* as a whole. As for the word *itara* itself—

It bears the designation *sarvanāman*, yet the suffix *ām* is not prescribed after it, because *ām* is prescribed only after the entire composite form. Therefore, the sense is that *suṭ* is not applied. However, if one were to explain the rule as "the suffix *suṭ* is added to *ām* prescribed after a *sarvanāman* stem ending in the vowel *a*," there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yeṣām* and *teṣām*.
Therefore, it should be explained that *suṭ* is added to *ām* prescribed after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) that follows a stem ending in a vowel other than *a*.
(222) *vibhāṣā jasi* 1.1.32.

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā jasi*: the mention of "sarvanāma" (pronoun) and "dvandva" (copulative compound) is carried over [from previous rules]. The term "jasi" is a citation without a case ending (*avibhaktika*). "Jaśiḥ" means the substitution of *i* for *jas*. This is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*) where the locative case ending is elided. The word "i," being followed by the vowel *i*, denotes the suffix "śī. Consequently, this refers to the substitution of "śī" for "jas."
The result is that the substitution of *śī* must be applied; this is what he states with the words "having *jas* as its basis" (*jasādhāra*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *jas* as its substratum," i.e., having *jas* as its locus. Now, one might ask: why is it not explained simply as "when *jas* follows, the designation *sarvanāman* may optionally apply to a *dvandva*"?
Therefore, he says: "Only with regard to the substitution of *śī*, etc. For if *akac* were present, then because it would not act as an intervention, the substitution of *śī* would result.
But when the suffix *kap* is present, there is no such fault because of the intervention by that [suffix]; thus he says: "The *varṇāśrametara*s. And [this is so] even when *akac* is present.

It should not be argued that even in the absence of an option (*vikalpa*) regarding what ought to be done, why the permanent designation (*nitya-sarvanāma-saṃjñā*) "sarvādi" would not apply here; for its permanent prohibition is established by the rule "dvandve ca.
Nor can it be said that the prohibition "dvandve ca" applies only to the individual members [of the compound] according to the method previously stated.

It should not be argued that because the suffix *akaC* is unavoidable in the compound *varṇāśrametara*, since the pronoun *itara*— as a member of that collective aggregate— retains its status as a pronoun due to the absence of any specific application (*pravṛtti*), [just as in *dvandva*s]; for, just as adjectives such as "beautiful" do not apply to a mere member of a *dvandva* compound, there is likewise an absence of any intention to express contempt or the like regarding the individual member.

When there is a desire to express that [defect] with respect to the aggregate, since the defect belonging to the parts is also understood through the suffix following the aggregate, the meaning has already been expressed; therefore, the suffix does not arise separately from the individual parts. Otherwise...
Because the suffix *ka* would otherwise apply individually to each member of the compound. With this very point in mind, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"In the word *varṇāśrametara*, the suffix *akac* does not occur. And thus, when a *dvandva* compound is formed with the word *itara*, and then the application of contempt is expressed as "the castes, stages of life, and others are contemptible" (*kutsitā varṇāśrametarāḥ*).
When the suffix *kap* is applied, the form is simply *varṇāśrametarakāḥ*. However,

when *itara-* is treated as contemptible— forming *itaraka-* by adding *akac*, and then a *dvandva* compound is formed as "the castes (*varṇāḥ*), the stages of life (*āśramāḥ*), and the contemptible other (*itarakaḥ*)"— then there would indeed be an option regarding the substitution of *śī*.

(223) *prathama-carama-taya-alpārdha-katipaya-nema-aś-ca* | 1|1|33 | The terms *prathama* and *carama* [are included]. The rule *vibhāṣā jasi* is understood [from the previous sūtra], as is *sarvanāmāni*.
Thus he says: "these. This means *prathama* and so forth. "Receive the aforementioned designation" means they receive the technical name *sarvanāman* (pronoun).

This is the meaning. In that regard, the designation of *sarvanāman* for the word *nema* in the *jas* case-ending is permanently applicable due to its inclusion in the [Pāṇinian] list; here, its optionality is prescribed. However, for words such as *prathama* and others, distinct from the word *nema*, the designation of *sarvanāman* is not even applicable in the *jas* case, because they are not included in that list.

It is prescribed by way of an option (*vikalpa*). Therefore, he states—*the remainder is like Rāma*—that for words such as *prathama* and others, other than those [ending in] *nema*, there is no operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) except after the suffix *jas*.
He states that the word *taya* is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by saying: "the suffix *tayaP*. [Regarding] "of a number..."
The word "śeṣaḥ" (remainder) refers to the rule stating that the suffix *tayap* is prescribed [after a word denoting a part]. Regarding the word "tataḥ":
because of that reason—namely, the fact of being a suffix—the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the mention of a suffix applies;

thus, the meaning is that those ending in it—that is, words ending in *tayap*—are to be understood. In the forms "dvitaye" and "dvitayā," the suffix *tayap* is used in the sense of "that which consists of two parts."

Although the aggregate of parts constitutes the whole (*avayavin*), and since that [whole] is a single entity, the singular number alone would be appropriate; nevertheless, when the aggregate has its internal distinctions among the parts manifested, it constitutes the referent of the word, and "manifestation" consists in possessing the specific number intended by the speaker.

In that case, there is no fault, as the plural number is intended either to refer to the multiplicity of parts or to the non-difference of the parts from the whole. And in this regard, the very mention of the suffix *tayaP* is the proof; otherwise, since the nominative plural *jas* would not occur after a word ending in *tayaP*, what would be the purpose of it? [Examples: *carame*, *caramāḥ*; *alpe*, *alpāḥ*; *ardhe*.

The forms *ardhāḥ*, *katipaye*, and *katipayāḥ* are to be illustrated in the same manner as the word *prathama*. However, the word *ardha* denoting a single part (*ekadeśa*) is masculine; when it denotes an equal portion (*samāṃśa*), it is neuter, according to the lexicon which states: "In the masculine, *ardha* [is used] for a half, and *ardham* for an equal portion."

"The rest is like [the treatment of] all [words]"— this is the sense, because the word *nema* is included in the *sarvādi* (all-beginning) group. "In the section on optionality" refers to the statement that within the governing rule *vibhāṣā jasi*, the designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) is prescribed for words ending in the suffix *-tīya* when followed by the case-endings *ReĀ*, *ṅsi*, *ṅsu*, *ṅi*, and *ṅas*.

The meaning is "that which is to be done. Regarding *dvitīyasmai* and *dvitīyāya*: that which completes a pair is *dvitīya*. By the rule *dvestīya*, the suffix *tīya* is applied in the sense of ordinal number. "And so forth" means: *dvitīyasmāt*, *dvitīyāt*;
*dvitīyasmin*, *dvitīye*, and so on. Likewise for *tṛtīya*.
Thus [it is said]. The remainder is "the forms ṭhṅt-sū-dāhāryi" should be cited.

Regarding the word *tṛtīya*, the suffix *tīya* is applied in the sense of ordinal number (*pūraṇa*) by the rule "ṭhreḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca" (Pāṇini 5.2.51). There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *r*, resulting in the vowel *ṛ*. By the rule "saṃprasāraṇācca" (Pāṇini 6.1.108), the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is substituted. Now, one might object: since the suffix *jātīyar* is prescribed by the rule "prakāravacane jātīyar" (Pāṇini 5.3.69) after the word *paṭu*, [how can it be formed otherwise?]
The word *jātīya* ends in the suffix *tīya*; since it also ends in *tīya*, there would be an option regarding its being a sarvanāman by virtue of the suffix *ṅtsu*.

To this, he says: "that which has meaning" (*arthavat*). By the paribhāṣā "in the case of the mention of that which has meaning, that which is meaningless is not [included]," the *tīya* ending here is understood as one that possesses meaning. However, in the case of the suffix *jātīyar*...

The meaning is that only the whole (samudāya) possesses semantic significance, and not its individual parts. "Nirjaraḥ" means one who has emerged from old age (*jarā*). The compound is formed according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*; the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule *gostriyoḥ*. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "one from whom old age has departed."

(224) *jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 7.2.101. He states this to show the specific distinction of the word *nirjara*: *jarāyāḥ*. The term *vibhaktau* is understood from the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (7.1.21), and *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (7.2.100) is also understood.

Therefore, [the word] *jarā* is qualified by the term *ṭhaci*, which is carried over [from the previous rule]. By the principle "a rule applies to that which begins with [the element specified]," this is a rule concerning the initial [portion]. This is what he states with the words beginning "of the word *jarā*," etc.
Now, one might ask: how can the substitution of *jaras*, which is prescribed for the word *jarā*, apply to the word *nirjara*? To this [he replies]:
He says: "In the section on *pada*. The meaning is that whatever is prescribed under the heading of *pada* and under the heading of *aṅga* applies to that [stem] itself and to that which ends in it.
And this substitution of *jaras* applies to the word *jarā* because it occurs within the heading of *aṅga*, as well as to that which ends in it.
In examples such as *jarasā* and so forth, however, one should understand that the status of being "ending in that" (*tadantatva*) is established through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva*.

Although the rule for "ending in that" is already established because *jarāyāḥ* functions as a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*), there is no fault here, as this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is an elaboration of the principle *yena vidhis tadantasya*. Therefore...

In the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, it is stated that "the word-base (*pada*) and its member (*aṅga*) are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), and by means of the qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*), the rule of 'application to what ends with that' (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Now, an objection is raised: since the substitution of *jaras* is prescribed for that which ends in the word *jarā*, it would apply to the entire word *nirjara* because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). Having raised this objection:
He explains: "Because it is not the occasion" (anokālatvāt).

Regarding the phrase "of that which is being pointed out" (nirdiśyamānasya), the meaning is: "only of that which is being directly pointed out. By this paribhāṣā, the substitution of *jaras* applies only to the word *jarā*; for in this context, the word *jarā* itself is the substituendum (*sthānin*).

It is directly specified [by the word *jarā*]. The intention is that the mention of that which ends with the word *jarā*, however, is inferential (*ānumānika*), because it is obtained through the rule of "specification by the end" (*tadantavidhi*).
Furthermore, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is intended merely to state the meaning established by the sūtra *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*; thus, it is discussed in that very [sūtra].

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: since the word *nirjara* does not end in the word *jarā*, how can the substitute *jaras* apply here? To this he says: "by the principle of being a part" (*ekadeśa*). The sense is that it is according to the maxim: "Even when its tail is cut off, a dog remains a dog, neither a horse nor a donkey. Thus: *nirjarasā*, *nirjarasaḥ*.

The forms for the dual and plural of the first and second [cases] are as follows: for the *ami* ending, one should cite the example *nirjaras-am* by means of the rule *in-ābhyāṃ nirjarasaḥ*. Now, in the case of the third singular and the fifth singular, when *nirjara-ā* and *nirjara-as* have been established, [the rule] *in-ātoḥ* applies.

When *jaras* has been substituted [for *as*], the forms *nirjarasina* and *nirjarasāt* are obtained; likewise, in the singular dative and the singular genitive, when *nirjara e* and *nirjara as* have been established,
[the rules for] the substitution of *y* and the substitution of *sy* apply respectively.
Since the case endings *sat* and *jasi* are absent, the substitution *jaras-* does not occur; thus, one might expect the forms *nirjarāya* and *nirjarasya*.

To this, he says: "ina-ādi" (ina, etc.). Because they are subsequent rules, the substitution *jaras-* overrides the substitutions *ina*, *ya*, *āt*, and *si*, as well as the augment *nuṭ*. Consequently, because the final vowel is no longer *a*, the suffixes *ina* and the others do not apply.
The meaning is "it becomes.
*Nirjarasā* is the singular instrumental case. *Nirjarase* is the singular dative case. *Nirjarasaḥ* is the singular ablative case.

And this is the form in the sixth case singular (*ṣaṣṭhy-ekavacana*). One should also cite *nirjarasoḥ*, *nirjarasām*, and *nirjarasi*. "In the alternative" (*pakṣe*) means in the alternative where the substitution of *jaras* does not occur.
Regarding "and before a consonant-initial [suffix]" (*halādau ca*): when *ais* is substituted for *bhis*, the form is indeed *nirjaraiḥ*, and not otherwise.

Regarding the substitution of *jaras* [for *jara*], as in the form *nirjarasaiḥ*: since the suffix *ais* is applied based on the assumption that the stem ends in *a*, it cannot—by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the destruction of a grammatical occasion)—be the cause for the substitution of *jaras*, which would destroy that very occasion.
Therefore, the author of the commentary (*vṛtikṛt*) restates another opinion he has devised in order to refute it.

The passage beginning with *tv ityādinā* and ending with *kecid* in the phrase *pūrvavipratiṣedhena ityādi kecit* is a portion of the *Vṛtti*. The connection of the sentence is as follows: the author of the *Vṛtti*, however, stated that when *in* and *āt* have been applied and *jaras* has been substituted, the form is *nirjarasāt* and not *nirjarasaḥ*, according to some.

Now, one might object: "Since the substitutes *in* and *āt* would override the substitution of *jaras* by virtue of being subsequent rules, once *jaras* has been applied, the stem would no longer end in *an*, so how could *in* and *āt* apply?
To this, he says: "By means of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). A prior conflict occurs where there is the application of the preceding rule.
That [rule] is understood; the meaning is by means of that sūtra, "In the case of a conflict (vipratiṣedha), the subsequent operation prevails.

In that context, having relied on the fact that the word *para* signifies what is desired (*iṣṭa*), it amounts to accepting the application of the prior operation in certain instances of conflict. Now, [one might object]: "But not for *inātoḥ*..."
Since the substitution of *jaras* would apply when [the suffix] *bhis* has already been applied, which would contradict the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*, he says:

"of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*. "In that way" means that when *ais* is substituted for *bhis*, in the alternative where the substitution of *jaras* does not occur, the form is *nirjaraiḥ*. [This is] due to the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*.

The meaning is that because it is the final [element], when *jaras* is applied, the alternative form *nirjarasaiḥ* is stated. "By those who follow that" means by those who have stated forms such as *nirjarasina*. "Only *nirjarasya*" is said by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

When the substitution *syā* (for *su*) has been applied, there is no replacement by *jaras* because the case endings beginning with *ac* (*ajādi-vibhakti*) are absent. Since a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of application) is resorted to for the forms ending in *in* and *āt*, it is appropriate to resort to *pūrvavipratiṣedha* even in the domain of the *syā* substitution, as both rules are contained within the same sūtra. Therefore, the form is simply *nirjarasya*.
The meaning is that [the form] is *rūpam*, but not even *nirjaras*.

As for the phrase "and this": it refers to the view of certain [grammarians] conceived by the author of the Vṛtti, as well as the view following that [conception]. "Contrary to the Bhāṣya" means that [the rule] *ṭāṅsiṅsāminātsyāḥ* [prescribes] the substitute *nā*.

In this case, only *ad* should be prescribed; let there be no mention of the vowel *i*. Likewise, only the substitution of *ad* should be prescribed, and not the long vowel *ād*. As for the *e* in *rāmeṇa*, it occurs through a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*); for it is stated:
"In the plural, when followed by a *jhal* [consonant], *e* [is substituted]"; "also after *osi*"; "and also after *āṅ*"; and "also in the vocative."

The sequence of the sūtras is as follows: In that context, a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is made for the rule beginning with *āṅ*. Thus, there should be the substitution of *ekāra* (e) for *aiṅ* [in the case of *āṅ*]. For example: *rāmeṇa*. Then, the sequence of the sūtra is: "After [a stem ending in] *āp*, and also in the vocative (*saṃbuddhau*). In that context, a *yogavibhāga* is made for the rule beginning with *āṅ*. Thus, there should be the substitution of *ekāra* (e) for *āṅ*. For example: *rāmeṇi*. Another [rule] is: "After [a stem ending in] *āp*, and also in the vocative."
The *yoga* [is as follows]: the form *ekāraḥ* (the vowel *e*) occurs in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) and before the affix *osi*. Thus: *he rame*, *ramayā*, *ramayoḥ*.

Regarding the substitution of *at* for the case-ending *ṅsi*, it is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭāṅsiṅsām* that, by virtue of the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *a*, the rule *ato guṇe* does not apply to produce a single substitute (*pararūpa*), and so forth. [Thus we have] *nirjarasina*.

If *nirjarasāt* were the correct form, the inconsistency with this Bhāṣya would be quite evident; for here, since both the phonemes *i* and *ā* are heard, it would be necessary to pronounce the *i* when applying the substitute *in*. Furthermore, Gonardīya says: "It must necessarily be *atijaraiḥ*, because of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*."

Thus it is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭh-ja-rā-yā jaras anyatarasyām*. If one were to accept the form *nirjarasaiḥ*, this [view] would be clearly inconsistent. Therefore, the meaning is that the alternative opinion beginning with "by means of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*) and so forth is incorrect.
(225) *paddanno*...
[sūtra 6.1.63]. Now, in order to show the specific modification of the word *pāda* before suffixes beginning with *śas*, he says: *paddanno*.

The compound *pad-dat-nas-mās-hṛd-niś-asan-yūṣan-doṣan-yakan-śakan-udan-āsan* is a collective dvandva. The term *śas-prabhṛti* (beginning with *śas*) is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi, meaning "those for which *śas*, the second case plural ending, and so forth are the beginning. From the rule *ṭhanudātasya cardupadhasyānyatarasyām*, the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood to carry over. The meaning is that when *śas* and the following endings follow, the substitutes beginning with *pada* may optionally occur. By these substitutes beginning with *pada*, their corresponding original bases (*sthānin*) are implied.

He says this with the words beginning "from the foot" (*pādāt*) and so forth. According to the rule of corresponding order (*yathāsaṅkhyaparibhāṣā*), the substitutes beginning with *pada* are to be understood as applying respectively to [the forms] beginning with *pāda*. The phrase "that is due to negligence" (*tatprāmādikam*) means that it is rooted in error. The point is that in the mantra "offering oblations in the mouth" (*havyā juhāna āsani*) and in passages such as "they spoke of the breath in the mouth" (*āsanyaṃ prāṇamūcuḥ*), the word is seen to have the meaning of "mouth" (*āsya*) alone. As for the word *danta*, when followed by the suffix *su* (nominative singular), it is like *rāma*. When followed by the suffix *śas* (accusative plural), there is the substitution of *dad* according to the rule *paddannomāshṭap* (*paddanniti dadādeśaḥ*).

When *dat-as* is established, one might suspect that the *jaś*-substitution (the replacement of a consonant by a voiced unaspirated stop) prescribed for the end of a word by the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo'nte* would apply to the letter *t*. To address this, he will state the sūtra defining the technical term *pada*: *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*. (Pāṇini 1.4.17) [The sūtra continues: *suḍanapuṃsakasya* (1.1.43).
In that context, since it is asked what constitutes a *sarvanāmasthāna*, he says: *suḍanapuṃsakasya*. [And the following rule: *śi*...

From the rule "sarvanāmasthānam," the term "sarvanāmasthāna" is carried over [as an *anuvṛtti*]. The meaning is: for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is not neuter—that is, distinct from the neuter gender—the suffix *suṭ* shall be designated as a "sarvanāmasthāna. In this context, because the word *suṭ* has an unfamiliar meaning, he explains it: "*suṭ*" [refers to the augment *s-*].

Regarding the term *pratyāhāra*: in the word *su*, the remainder is "by the letter *ṭ* of *āṬ*" (*āṬṭaṣṭakāreṇa*), and not by the letter *ṭ* of *ṭā*, because there is no reason to bypass the nearest [preceding] element. (227) *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* 1.4.17.

This is what he says: "svādi-pañca" (the five beginning with *su*). [The rule] "asaḥ svādau" (P. 7.2.83) applies to the case endings beginning with *su*. The singular number used here for the plural is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*), as in the rule "asarvanāmasthāne" (P. 1.1.42). Regarding the phrase "up to the suffix *kap*": this means those [suffixes] that have as their limit the suffix *kap* prescribed at the end of the fifth chapter. And in that regard, there is only the explanation itself [to be provided].

[This is] the refuge. And thus, in the case of *dat-as*, although the word *dat* lacks the status of a *pada* because it is not a form ending in a *sup* suffix, this sūtra would nevertheless grant it the status of a *pada*; consequently, the objection is indicated that by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte*, the *jaś*-substitution (i.e., *d*) would apply to the letter *t*.

(228) *yaci bham* | 1|4|18|. To provide a solution for the fact that the substitution of *jaś* does not occur because the designation *pada* is superseded by the designation *bha*, he states the rule for the *bha* designation: *yaci bham*. [The compound] *yac* is a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva* consisting of *ya* and *ac*.
The term *asarvanāmasthāne*, which is understood from the previous rule (*ṭhsvādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*), is qualified by the word *yacī*.

According to the principle *yasminvidhistadādau* (a rule [applies] when [a certain sound] occurs, it applies to that which begins with it), this refers to a suffix beginning with *ya*. Thus he says: "in those beginning with *ya*" and so forth.
And so, in the case of *dat-as*, because the designation *bha* supersedes the designation *pada* for the element *dat*, [the substitution does not occur].

The intended meaning is that there is *jaś*-ness [of the final consonant]. Now, one might ask: why should there not be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *pada* and *bha* here? Nor should it be argued that, according to the rule "in the case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails," the designation *bha* alone would apply because it is the subsequent one; for a "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*) occurs only when there is a contradiction.
(229) "Up to *kaḍāra*, there is only one designation" (Pāṇini 1.4.1).

For there is no contradiction here in the coexistence of two designations, since we observe the coexistence of designations such as *kṛt*, *kṛtya*, and *pratyaya* in the case of suffixes like *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar*. Therefore...

He says: "Up to *kaḍāra*. He states that *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*)—namely, "the *kaḍāra* words [are optionally compounded] in a *karmadhāraya*. Here, *āṅ* does not signify inclusion (*nābhividhi*). This is because there would be no purpose for including the word *kaḍāra* itself. Furthermore, in the rule "prior to *kaḍāra*" (*prākkaḍārāt*), the word *kaḍāra* is not the upper limit. [The rule begins: "*kaḍārāḥ*..."

In the rule "karmadhāraye," because the word *kaḍāra* serves as the subsequent limit (*uttarāvadhi*), there is an additional benefit. This is because, following the rule "prākkaḍārāt," both *tatpuruṣa* and *dvigu* are mentioned;

the particle *ca* (and) is indeed intended to effect the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of these two designations. In that case, since the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding a single designation does not apply...

What is the use of that? [Objection: Let there be only one designation here; nevertheless, how is it established that it must be the designation *bha*, given the absence of any decisive factor (*vinigamanā*)? To this, he says: "That which is subsequent," and so forth. [This refers to] the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*), because there is no contradiction [between the two].

The sense is this: even though the principle that "the particular is stronger than the general" does not apply here, since it is observed elsewhere that "priority" (*paratva*) and "being without scope" (*niravakāśatva*) are stronger, it is appropriate here as well to determine the matter by means of those two. Between two [conflicting rules] that both have scope, the later designation prevails.

It is powerful; however, it should be understood that when one [rule] is left without scope, that very [rule] prevails. In this regard, an example of the subsequent [rule] is as follows: in the expression "he pierces with a bow and arrows," since the bow—which serves as the point of departure (*apādāna*) for the separation of the arrows—is also the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for the act of piercing, it would otherwise be designated as the *apādāna* case.
And when both [the designation of] *karaṇa* and another [designation] would apply, the other designation alone prevails.

For example, in *atatakṣat*: here, because the vowel *a* following the *t* is subject to the designation *guru* by the rule *saṃyoge guru*, that designation alone occurs due to its lack of occasion (*anavakāśatva*), and not the designation *laghu*. Of that...

Because it has already served its purpose (*caritārthatvāt*) with respect to what follows when there is no conjunction (*asaṃyoge*), the rule *sanvallaghuni* does not apply there. "By that" means by virtue of having no other occasion (*anavakāśatvena*). "Hence" means that because of the absence of *padatva*, the substitution of *jaś* does not occur. Regarding "the substitution of *jaś*," as in *dat-bhyām*.

Because [the word *dat*] is a word-final (*padānta*) by virtue of the rule *ṭh-svādiṣv-asarvanāmasthāne*, there is the substitution of a *jaś* sound [for the dental *t*] by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte*. This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): words such as *dadbhiḥ* and *date* are the meaning of the word "etcetera. By the rule *khari ca*, there is the substitution of a *car* sound [for the dental *t*], resulting in *datsu*. In the alternative case, it is like *rāma*.
