Regarding "māsa": when the word *māsa* is followed by the suffix *śas*, it takes the substitute *mās* according to the rule *ṭhpaddanna*; thus, *māsa* is the form. *Māse* is the singular instrumental case. Regarding "ru-tva" (the substitution of *r*): when *mās-bhyām* is established, because it is a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*, the *r* is substituted [for the *s*] by the rule *sasajuṣoḥ*. By the rule *bho-bhago-*, that [substituted *r*]...

The meaning is that when the letter *ya* is elided by the rule "sarveṣām" (Pāṇini 7.1.51), the forms become *mābhyām* and *mābhiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to forms such as *mābhyaḥ*. When *mās-su* is established, after the application of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) and the visarga by the rule "kharavasānayorvisarjanīyaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.15), the rule "vā śari" (Pāṇini 8.3.36) applies.
The conceptualization of a sentient being (*satvavikalpa*). *Māssu* and *māḥsu*.
(230) *Bhasya* | 6|4|129|. The term *bhasya* is clearly established as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*). The word *yūṣa* denotes a broth (*maṇḍa*).

It is well known in the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*) that "the broth of mung beans and *āmalaka* is digestive, appetizing, and carminative," and so forth. When the word for that [broth], *yūṣaḥ*, undergoes the substitution of *paddanaḥ* (i.e., *yūṣan*), the form *yūṣan-as* results.

(231) *allopo'naḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.134. In the rule *allopo'naḥ*, the word *at* is a separate item with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīkam*). The word *anaḥ* ends in a genitive denoting a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Therefore, it is a qualifier [of *at*]: "of that *a*-sound which is a constituent part of *an*."

[The word] "lopaḥ" [is understood]. Here, the term "aṅgasya," which has been previously introduced as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*), is taken in the sense of a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). That [term] connects with "anaḥ"—meaning, "there is elision of the vowel *a* which is a constituent part of that *an* which is itself a constituent part of the stem (*aṅga*).
Thus, the term "aṅgasya," which has been previously introduced as a governing heading, is here taken in the sense of a partitive genitive; and that [term] [connects with "anaḥ"].

In this context, [the word] "aṅga" (stem) is connected as follows: the phrase "the elision of the *akāra* which is a constituent part of that which is a constituent part of the *aṅga*" connects with the governing term "bhasya" (of a *bha*-ending stem) by means of the term "anaḥ" (of *an*).
Consequently, the condition of being followed by a non-*sarvanāmasthāna* case ending beginning with *ya*, etc., or by a *su*-beginning case ending, is obtained.

He says this with the words "aṅgāvayava" and so forth. According to the explanation of the ancients—that "there is elision of the *a* of a *bha*-stem *aṅga* ending in *at*"—there would be the undesirable consequence of eliding even the *a* following the *t* in *takṣṇā*. [The correct view is: "There is elision of the *a* of a *bha*-stem *aṅga*... according to the ancients...
In the explanation [of the rule], however, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the vowel *a* following the *t* in the word *takṣṇā*.

If, on the other hand, the rule were explained as "the *a* of an *an* belonging to a *bha*-stem is elided," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *anasā* and *manasā*. To avoid this, one must repeat the term "an" and [interpret it as] "that which ends in *an*."

If one were to explain [the rule] as "there is elision of the letter 'a' which is a member of the *bha* stem," then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *ṭhanastakṣṇaḥ*. Therefore, the explanation given above alone is correct; this is explained in detail elsewhere. In the case of *yūṣan-as*, when the letter 'a' following the letter 'ṣ' is elided, the form stands as *yūṣn-as*.

(232) *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ samānapade* [Pāṇini 8.4.1]. *Raṣābhyām*: The ablative case in *raṣābhyām* indicates direction (*digyoge pañcamī*). The word "of what follows" (*parasya*) is to be supplied. The term *samāna* is a synonym for "one" (*eka*). For example, in the phrase "we are from the same village" (*samānagrāmā vayam*), it refers here to indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatvam*). In a single word-form (*samānapade*), when a *ṇa* is to be substituted for a *na*, it occurs after a *repha* (r) or a *ṣakāra* (ṣ). For instance, in *praṇamati*, the *na* is changed to *ṇa* because it follows the *repha*. Similarly, in *viṣṇuḥ*, the *na* is changed to *ṇa* because it follows the *ṣakāra*. This rule applies provided the *ṇa* and the preceding *r* or *ṣ* belong to the same word (*samānapada*). If they belong to different words, such as in *mātṛṇām* (where *mātṛ* and *ṇām* are separate words), the substitution does not take place. Thus, the rule ensures that the change occurs within the boundaries of a single lexical unit.

This is intended [to be understood], since the point is established by the word *pade* alone; however, by the force of the inclusion of the term *samāna*, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of *ṇatva* (nasalization) in examples such as *rāmanāma* according to the rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅ* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), because that very term *samānapada* is also understood to recur there. As for the *ṇatva* in *mātṛbhogīṇaḥ*, however...
This will be explained in the section on secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
Regarding the form *yūṣṇaḥ*, it is the nominative plural (*śas*); regarding *yūṣṇā*, it is the singular instrumental (*tṛtīyaikavacana*).
One should not suspect that, due to the status of the elision (*allopa*) as being "as if it were still there" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *n* would not be followed by a *ṣ*.

Regarding the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām*, when the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* following *ṣ* is to be applied, the status of *al-lopa* as a *sthānivat* is not required; rather, it is required for the absence of that *ṇ*-substitution. And since the absence of *ṇ*-substitution is not prescribed by any grammatical rule (*aśāstrīya*), it cannot be extended [to the substitute] by means of *atideśa*. For an operation applies only when the original element (*sthānin*) is present.

For that very [property] which exists [in the original element] is extended by the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. However, we have already stated in the discussion on the *sthānivadbhāva* rule that the absence of an operation— namely, "that which does not occur when the original element (*sthānin*) is present does not occur when its substitute (*ādeśa*) is present"— is not extended, because such an absence is not something prescribed by grammatical rules (*aśāstrīya*).
Although it was stated that even the absence of an operation not prescribed by grammar (*aśāstrīya*) is extended [by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*], nevertheless, this rule does not apply here.
This is because that rule applies only to the prescription of something that was previously observed as standing before the vowel which serves as the *sthānin*. In this case, however...
The point is that the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed only for what follows the short vowel *a* which has become a *sthānin*.

Now, an objection might be raised: in the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57), the view that "an *ādeśa* is like its *sthānin* with respect to what precedes the *sthānin* vowel" is also established in the *Bhāṣya*. And if that were so here...

Regarding the question of how *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) can occur when the rule for *ṇatva* applies to the *n* following the *ṣ*, given that the *ṣ* is preceded by the vowel *a* which is the substitute (*sthānin*) for the elision (*lopa*), and thus there is an intervention by the *a*—which would mean the *ṣ* is not directly followed [by the *n*]—the author says:

"from the preceding" (*pūrvasmāt*). This indicates that the intervention is not considered an obstacle because the elision is treated as if it were its original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus, since the *ṣ* remains immediately followed by the *n*, the condition for *ṇatva* is satisfied.

By the words "But in the alternative" (*pakṣe tu*) and so forth, the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of this position is indicated. For this very reason, the use of *pravigaṇayya* in the Bhāṣya is appropriate. In the *curādigaṇa*, there is a root ending in *ṇ*—namely *gaṇa* in the sense of "counting" (*saṅkhyāna*). [The suffix] *ṇic* is added; then there is the elision of the *a* (by *ato lopaḥ*); and [then] the elision of the *a* (by *allopasya*).

Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no *vṛddhi* by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ. After a causative (*ṇyantāt*) root, when *lyap* follows *ktvā*, the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi* occurs by the rule "lyapi laghupūrvāt," overriding the elision of *ṇi*. If the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* were absolute regarding a rule applied after what precedes [the *sthānin*], then here, in the case of *lyap*—

The substitution of *ay* for the *ṇi*-affix would not occur after a light-pūrva (laghupūrva) vowel. This is because, when the rule prescribing the *ay* substitution for the *ṇi* following an *at* that stands in the place of the elided [vowel] is applied, the elision (*al-lopa*) would be considered as still present by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*. Consequently, the *ṇi* would be separated from the preceding *at*, and thus it would not follow immediately after a *ṇakāra* with a light-pūrva vowel.

Therefore, it is understood that in the rule *tasmādacaḥ parasmim* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitutional identity) regarding an operation on what follows an *ac* is non-permanent (*anitya*). In this way, from the word *go* in the vocative case, when the vowel *o* is treated as having a *ṇit* marker, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs, and the form *he gauḥ* is established. Otherwise, [if the rule were permanent], the *āṬ* (the long *ā*) would [not be substituted].

It is clearly stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that, because of the status of the substitute as the original (sthānivadbhāva), when the *sambuddhi* [vocative case ending] following the *ga* which precedes the *o* that has become the locus (*sthānībhūta*) is elided, the elision of the *sambuddhi* would occur since it follows an *eṅ* vowel (namely, the *o*).
The phrase "only when there is no intervention by a consonant" means that [the rule] applies solely by the sūtra *ṣṭuan kupvoṅ*.

As for the examples illustrating the prescription of *ṇatva* for a *n* that is not separated from a *ṣ* by more than one intervening element, they should be understood as *puṣṇāti* and so forth. In reality, however, even in those cases, the result is established by the rule *ṣṭuan* itself.

The inclusion of the word "ṣa" (in the rule *ṣapūrvah*) is for the sake of what follows; this is clear from the original source (*ākara*). Now, one might object: how can there be the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) when the substitution of *ṇ* is to be applied, given the prohibition that "that which is not established in the preceding [rule] does not behave as a substitute"? This is because the substitution of *ṇ* falls under the category of "not established in the preceding. To this, he says: "In the preceding... [and so on].

When the elision of the initial member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*) and the substitution of *l* (*latva*) are to be applied, there is no fault—that is, no subversion—of the rule "that [which is replaced] is not like the original when something precedes" (*tasya pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivad*). This means that the rule does not apply.
For example, regarding the elision of the initial member of a conjunct consonant: *cakrayatra*. Here, by the rule "when a subsequent element follows," the *yaṇ* substitute [is applied].

Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position), there is no elision of the letter *k* by the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca*. Regarding the substitution of *l* (*latva*), for example: *nigālyate*. Here, because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of *ṇi*, the substitution of *l* occurs by the rule *aci vibhāṣā*. Regarding the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*), for example: *māṣavapanī*. [This is derived from] the root *vap* with the suffix *lyuṭ*.

There is no specific instruction [regarding the elision]; because of the presence of the *ugit* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. By the rule "when *yasya* follows" (*yasyeti ca*), there is the elision of the letter *d* after the letter *n*.

Here, due to the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) regarding the elision of the vowel *a*, the letter *n* does not qualify as being at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); therefore, the rule "in the case of a nominal stem-final, *num*, or a case-ending" (*prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca*) does not apply.
It is not so. When *yūṣan-bhyām* remains, [the following applies]:

(233) *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* | 8|2|7|. There is elision of *na*. The word *na* is a separate word ending in the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti); the genitive suffix is elided by Vedic license (*ārṣa*).

The meaning is that there should be elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n*. The word "of the end" (*antasya*) is an adjective qualifying the letter *n*. For this very reason, because *n* requires an adjunct (*viśeṣaṇa*), no compound is formed with the word "elision" (*lopa*), due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). When the expectation arises as to "the end of what?"—
The term "of the word" (*padasya*), which is supplied as a governing rule, connects with the genitive ending of the member [of the compound];

that is, there is elision of the *n* which is the final member of the word. When the question arises as to what kind of word is intended, the term "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*)—with its genitive case ending elided—connects [to it]: [the meaning is] "of that word which bears the designation of a nominal stem."
This means that there should be elision (*lopa*) of this *nakāra*, which is the final member [of the compound]. For this very reason, *prātipadikāntasya* is not a single, unified word;
for since it is construed with the word *pada*, it lacks syntactic connection (*asāmarthya*) with the word *anta*. Thus he says: "not."

Regarding the phrase "and [the word] *prātipadika* is elided": it means "of that which ends in it. The meaning is: of that syllable *n*, which is a final constituent of that word (*pada*). Why is there the mention of *prātipadika*? [To exclude cases like] *ahan*; it does not apply to that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). Why is there the mention of *pada*? [To exclude cases like] *ahan*; it does not apply to that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

What is the purpose of mentioning the word *pada*? [Consider the forms] *rājānau*. [Objection: But when the *n* is elided (*nalopa*), in the case of *yūṣabhyām*, there would be lengthening by the rule *supi ca*; and in the case of *yūṣabhiḥ*, there would be the substitution of *ais* by the rule *ato bhisa ais*; and in the case of *yūṣabhyaḥ*, there would be the substitution of *et* by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*.

To address this, he says: "because the elision of *n* (nalopa) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) refers to forms such as *yūṣṇe*, *yūṣṇaḥ*, *yūṣṇoḥ*, and *yūṣṇām*. When the stem *yūṣan* is followed by the suffix *ṅi*, the elision of *an* (*allopo'naḥ*) would apply invariably; however—

(234) *vibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ* |6|4|136|. "Optionally (*vibhāṣā*) [the elision of *ṭhak*] after *iṅ* and *śyā*. The phrase "elision of *ṭhak*" (*ṭhillopaḥ*) from the preceding rule is understood here. The governing terms "of the member" (*aṅgasya*) and "when it is a *bha*-stem" (*bhasya*) are also supplied. And by the term "when it is a *bha*-stem" (*bhasya*),...
When followed by an *asarvanāmasthāna* suffix beginning with *j*, or by *svādi* (case-endings), the substitution of *an* is obtained as before.
Thus he says: "being a constituent part of the *aṅga*. Regarding "after *ṅś* and *ī*": the analysis is *ṅci* and *śī*.
Here, only the *śī* prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakācca* is understood, and not the *śi* substituted for *jaś* and *śas*.

Because that [substitution] is impossible when [the word] is in the *para* (nominative) case. "In the alternative" (*pakṣe*) means: in the alternative where the substitution of *yūṣan* does not occur.
Now, in order to establish the substitution of *pad-ādi* even in cases other than after *ch*, *sa*, and so on, he says: "By the rule *paddanno...*". "Manner" (*prakāra*) means similarity; and that...

It should be understood as having the sense of "condition" (*pratyayatva*). He shows the evidence for the fact that the inclusion of the word *prabhṛti* (and so forth) has the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) with the words "for this very reason. The meaning is: precisely because the inclusion of *prabhṛti* has the sense of "manner.
This is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Mahādeva asks for [the sacrifice] together with the hump and the shoulder-blade."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the substitution of *doṣan* occurs when the suffix *śī*—which has become part of the *āṬṅ* augment—is subsequent, the example cited is therefore consistent. Regarding the word "tena" (by that): the meaning is "by the inclusion of the term *prabhṛti*, which signifies 'and so forth'.
In the expression "padaṅghri," the form "pad" is the nominative singular; in the expression "svāntaṃ hṛd," [the same applies].
The word *hṛt* means "it gathers" (*saṅgacchate*). By the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of "night" and other such things is intended.

Regarding the phrase "the breath in the mouth" (*āsanyaṃ prāṇam*) and "they spoke of the breath in the mouth" (*āsanyaṃ prāṇam ūcuḥ*), the syntactical connection is that for this very reason [the word *hṛt*] "gathers.

He dispels the misconception that the word *āsana* undergoes the substitution *āsanna*—namely, that it means "that which occurs in the vicinity"—by stating: "that which exists in the mouth" (*āsye bhavaḥ*).
The intention is that this very etymology [is intended] because of its co-occurrence with the word *prāṇa*.
According to the rule *śarīrāvayavācca*, the suffix *yat* is applied to the word *āsya* in the sense of "occurring therein" (*bhavārtha*), and *āsanna* is the substitute for *āsya*.
By the rule *ye cābhāvākarmaṇoḥ*, the base form remains as it is (*prakṛtibhāva*), and by the rule *nastaddhite*, the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) does not take place.

The point is that if the inclusion of the word *prabhṛti* were not intended to signify "and so forth" (*prakāra*), then the substitution of *āsanna* would not occur here for the suffix *yat*, because *śas* and the other case-endings (*sup*) are not included [in the category of *prabhṛti*]. Now, one might object:
the neuter usage in the Bhāṣya, "doṣaṇī," is untenable, since [the word] "doṣam" [is masculine].

Since the masculine gender alone is observed in usage in such instances as "tathāvidhasya" and so forth, he says: "dor" is the second case singular of the word "doṣ. The intention is that if it were in the masculine, it would have been "doṣam."
Now, one might object that according to the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the word *doṣ* should necessarily be neuter; to this he says:

"bhujeti. The meaning is that, according to the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "the arm, the upper arm, the forearm, and the *doṣ*," it is also masculine. But is this lexicon [applicable] to the word *doṣ*?
Since it is also appropriate [to apply this] in the neuter gender, he says "due to association" (*sāhacaryāt*).

The meaning is: due to association with words such as *bhuja* which are masculine. The intention is that this is established by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stated in the lexicon: "and in some cases, due to association. This applies to the word *doṣ*.

He shows the fruit of establishing masculinity with the words "the fault of that... [Śrīharṣa writes]: "Taking the fault of that such-like bow as it bends, yet grasping its string. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: taking the hand (or the defect) of the bow as it bends, and grasping its string (or its excellence). "Fault" (*doṣam*) refers both to the hand and to a defect; "string" (*guṇam*) refers both to the bowstring and to excellence.

In this context, *doṣam* is the masculine singular accusative form of the word *doṣ*. Although one would have expected the rule to state *sup-prabhṛtiṣu* (in the case of *su* and so forth), the fact that it says *śas-prabhṛtiṣu* (in the case of *śas* and so forth) indicates that the substitution of *padādi* (the beginning of a word) occurs only in certain instances even within the domain of *sup* suffixes. Regarding *dvayor ahnoḥ*: this is a compound formed according to the rule *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51).

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *kālāt ṭhaṭhañ*. There is elision (*luk*) by the rule *dvigor lug-anapatye*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *rājāhaḥ-sakhibhyaṣ ṭac*. The substitution of *ahna-* for *ahan* occurs by the rule *ahno 'hna etebhyaḥ*.
The forms are like those of the word *rāma*.

(235) *saṅkhyā-visāya-pūrvasyāhnasyāhan anyatarasyāṃ ṅe* [Pāṇini 6.3.110]. He states a specific rule regarding the locative case (*ṅi*): *saṅkhyā-visāya*. The analysis of the compound is as follows: *saṅkhyā* (numeral), *vi* (the word *vi-*), and *sāya* (the word *sāya-*) are *saṅkhyā-visāyāḥ*; that which has these as its prior members is the analysis of the compound.

Intending this, he says: "by number," and so forth. He illustrates that which is preceded by a number: *dvyahni*, *dvyahnī*; these are the forms when there is elision (*alopa*) and when there is no such elision. *Dvyahne* is the form when there is no substitution of *ahan*. Thus...
He cites an example with *vi-* as a prefix: *vigatam* ("gone away"). This is a compound formed according to the rule *prādayo gatādyarthe prathamayā*;
the substitution of *ah* for *ahan* occurs as before. He cites an example with *sāyam* as a prefix: "the evening of the day," and so forth.
By this very indication (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that this is an *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compound). [The example] is *viśvapāḥ*.

There is no elision of *su* because there is an absence of the suffix *āp*. This is precisely the point: even though the term "long" (*dīrgha*) is present in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], the explicit mention of *āp* is for this very purpose. In the sense of "he protects the universe" (*viśvaṃ pāti*), although the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.3] would apply, by the principle of *vāsarūpa* (optionality regarding dissimilar suffixes), [the suffix *ka* is applied].

In the rule *manin-kvanip-vanip-śa-c*, the suffix *vic* is included by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*). Although the term "in Vedic [usage]" (*chandasi*) follows from the previous rule *ṭhvidupeśchandasi*, nevertheless, *kvip* is applied by this rule in the Veda, whereas in common usage (*loke*), *vic* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*. Others, however, interpret it as *kvip-ca*.

They say that the suffix *kvip* is used by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.178]. However, the substitution of long *ī* (as in *pī*) does not apply here, because of the Vārttika: "The prohibition of the substitution of *ī* applies when *vakāra* follows. This is necessary for the form *pāvān* (from *pā-kanip*). But as for *kvip*, it [is applied] after roots ending in long *ā*.

It is clearly stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that there is simply no application [of the suffix] for those *kvip* suffixes not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* refutes the *Vārttika* which states, "it should be stated that the substitution of *ī* occurs before a suffix beginning with *v* or *y*," by relying on the derivation of the form *pāvānaḥ* through the suffix *vanip*. Consequently...

In the case of *viśvapāḥ*, it is exactly like *vij* [in the nominative plural]. When *viśvapā-āṬ* is established, the rule "the preceding [vowel] is homogeneous with the following in the first two cases" would apply; however, this is superseded by: (236) *dīrghāj jasi ca* | Pāṇini 6.1.105.

In the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca*, the terms *pūrvasavarṇa* (from *ṭhprathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*) and *na* and *icī* (from *nādicī*) are carried over by *anuvṛtti*. This is what [the author] expresses with the words beginning with *dīrghāt*. Now, one might object: this sūtra is redundant, since the desired form is already established by the rule *nādicī* alone.

He raises an objection with the words *yadyapīha* ("even though here"). [Objection: Surely this sūtra is necessary to prohibit the long vowel resulting from the "homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) rule when *jasi* follows, as in the form *viśvapā-as*;
for in that case, the rule *nādici* does not apply. To this he replies: *jasi tu* ("but in the case of *jasi*..."). Let it be so.

The prohibition of the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is [unnecessary]. For even if the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* were applied, the form "viśvapāḥ" is established when *jas* follows; and even if that [long vowel] were prohibited, the form "viśvapāḥ" is still established by applying the rule "a long vowel is substituted for *ak* before a homogeneous vowel. Therefore, the meaning is: what is the purpose of that prohibition?
He refutes this with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): by the word "etcetera," examples such as *lakṣmyau* are included.
The point is that since the rule *nādici* would not otherwise apply there, its prohibition is necessary. Now, if the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* were intended solely for cases such as *goryau*, then...
Since it would have been more appropriate to introduce that [rule] at the very point of defining the word *gaurī* within the section on stems ending in *-ī*, he says:
"here too" (*ihāpi*). In the case of *viśvapau*, both the rule *nādici* and the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* apply;
however, by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* [prevails].
The meaning is that it is appropriate to introduce this very [sūtra]. [By the rule] "ṭhami pūrvaḥ" [the form is] *viśvapām*.

(237) "āto dhātoḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.140]. After the augment *āṬ*, [we have] *viśvapau*. When *śas* follows, [the form] *viśvapā as* remains; then, by the rule for the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), [it becomes *viśvapān*].

When [the word] *prāpte* occurs, the governing rules (*adhikṛta*) are *aṅgasya* and *bhasya*. The term *dhātoḥ* is qualified by *ātaḥ*, which ends in the genitive case; therefore, the rule of "specification of that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
From the rule *allopo'naḥ*, the word *lopaḥ* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "that which ends in the vowel *ā*..."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding *alo'ntyasya*: the remainder of the rule is "there is elision (*lopa*) of the final *a*. Regarding *viśvapābhyām*: the intention is that because it does not end in *abha*, there is no elision of the *ā*. "And so forth" refers to:
*viśvapābhiḥ*, *viśvape*, *viśvapaḥ*, *viśvapoḥ*, *viśvapām*, *viśvapi*.

In *viśvapoḥ* and *viśvapāsu*, it is the same as in *śaṅkhadhmādayaḥ*. One who blows a conch shell (*śaṅkha*) with a [wind-instrument] is a *śaṅkhadhmāḥ*. [The root] *dhmā* is used in the senses of "making sound" and "contact with fire. As before, there is either the suffix *vic* or *kvip*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *somapā* and others is intended. One who drinks *soma* is a *somapāḥ*.

One who drinks *kīlāla* is a *kīlālapaḥ*. According to Amara’s lexicon, among the synonyms for water, it says: "milk (*payaḥ*), *kīlāla*, and nectar (*amṛta*) [are synonyms]. One who drinks honey is a *madhupaḥ*, and so forth. [The objector asks: Why is the word "dhātoḥ" (from a verbal root) used? [The answer is: Let the rule simply be formulated as "ato 'nāpaḥ" (the short *a* of a verbal root is replaced by *ā* when followed by *ap*, except in the case of *āp*); with just that much, the desired result is achieved.
The question is raised: "Why is there an exclusion of elision (*lopa*) in cases such as these? [The answer is: *hāhān*.

When the long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) has been applied, the substitution of *n* occurs by the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ*. This word *hāhā* is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) denoting a specific type of Gandharva.

According to Amara: "Hāhā, Hūhū, and others such as these are the Gandharvas who dwell in the third heaven. In the case of *suṭ* [the augment], it is like *viśvapā*. In the case of *śas*, in the form *hāhā-as*, there would also be the elision of *ā* by the rule "āto 'nāpaḥ"; therefore, the mention of the word "dhātu" (root) is for this purpose. Regarding "ṭā-savarṇa-dīrghaḥ": [this refers to] *ṭā*.

Thus, the mention [of the case endings] without their specific vibhaktis (inflectional markers) is not faulty during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). The meaning is that in the third case singular, there is a long vowel by way of *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence). This should be applied similarly in what follows as well. Regarding "ReĀ vṛddhiḥ": when *hāhā-e* is situated [as the base], the meaning is that there is a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) by the rule "vṛddhir eci. Regarding "ṅsiṅsoḥ": [the meaning is that there is elision].

In *hāhā-as*, the meaning is that there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). In *hāhā-os*, the meaning is that there is a *vṛddhi* [vowel] by the rule "there is *vṛddhi* before *ec*" (*vṛddhireci*). In *hāhā-i*, the meaning is that there is the *guṇa* vowel *e* by the rule "there is *guṇa* for *ā* and *i*" (*ādguṇaḥ*). *Ktvā* and *śnā* are suffixes (*pratyaya*).
The two forms ending in *ā* are like *viśvapā*. Now, one might ask: since this is not a verbal root (*dhātu*), how can there be the elision of *ā* (āllopa) here?
To this, he says: "by the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.140] *ātaḥ*. In the rule *āto dhātoḥ*, the word *ātaḥ* is separated [into its own independent rule].
The meaning is that there is elision of the final *ā* of a nominal stem (*bha*) which is a member of a word (*aṅga*). By this, [the forms] *ktvaḥ* and *śnaḥ* [are explained].
Thus the form *śasi* is established. The rule *dhātoḥ* is another *yoga*.
Its meaning is: there shall be elision (*lopa*) of that *bha*-affix which ends in a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in long *ā*, provided it is part of a stem (*aṅga*).
This [rule] is intended to exclude stems ending in *ā* (such as feminine nouns) and to exclude words like *hāhā* and others. [The word] *ātaḥ* [is used]...

The *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) in [Pāṇini 6.4.52] *ktvo lyap*, *śnaḥ*, etc., is for the purpose of avoiding the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) in certain instances. Now, consider the form *mālāḥ* derived from *mālevācarati* ("he behaves like a garland"). Here, after the *kvip* suffix denoting the agent following a root ending in *kvip* used in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra-kvip*), the case endings (*sub-utpatti*) arise. Even if the term "root" (*dhātu*) were included [in the definition of what undergoes elision], the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) would still be unavoidable before suffixes such as *śas* and others, because [the rule] *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.32] applies.

This is because [the word *nābhi*] is a verbal root (*dhātu*) and ends in the vowel *ā*. Nor should one suspect that the rule *allopo 'naḥ* does not apply to words ending in *ā* on the basis of the Vārttika "it should be stated that [the elision applies] after *ṭhan* and *āp*"; for, as explained above, the Vārttika "after *ṭhan* and *āp*" is accepted in the Bhāṣya by means of a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

If it is argued that [the suffix *kvip*] is prohibited, it is not so; for it has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that, precisely by the authority of this *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya*, it is understood that there is no occurrence of the *ācārakvip* suffix after words ending in long *ā*.

[The form] *hariḥ*: from the word *hari*, the nominative singular suffix *su* is added; then the substitution of *ru* and the replacement by a visarga (*visarjanīya*) occur. Nor is there [any rule] regarding the visarga...

It might be suspected that, by means of an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) following the rule for *akāra*, there would be a *yaṇ* substitution for the vowel *r* (repha) when it follows that [vowel], because the *visarjanīya* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the *yaṇ* substitution is to be applied.
Regarding the rule *prathamayoḥ*: when *hari-āṬ* is situated [in the derivation], once the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* has occurred by this [rule], [the form] becomes *harī*.
This means "the form is *rūpa*. When *jasi* follows, resulting in the sequence *hari-as*, the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would apply;
however, [this is blocked by] *jasi ca* 7.3.109.

And in this case, the rule "guṇa of a short vowel" (Pāṇini 7.3.108) is understood to carry over. The term "of the aṅga" (Pāṇini 6.4.1), which is the governing heading, is qualified by the word "short" (hrasva). Consequently, there is an application of the rule regarding the final element of that which ends in [the short vowel]. Thus he says: "of that which ends in a short vowel," and so forth. In the example *harayaḥ*, by the paribhāṣā concerning the final letter (alo'ntyaparibhāṣā), the guṇa substitution applies to the final [vowel], namely the *i*-sound.

The vowel *e* arises from the similarity of their palatal place of articulation (*tālusthāna*). The substitution of *ay* occurs; the intention is that this results in the *ru*-augment and the visarga.

(239) *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108). When *he hari s* is the state [of the word], the *guṇa* substitution for the short vowel applies. This is because of the rule *sambuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106).
The term "in the vocative" (*sambuddhau*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says, beginning with "of the short vowel," etc.

By this, there is *guṇa* substitution—namely, the vowel *e*—for the vowel *i* following the letter *r*. As for the phrase "elision of the vocative suffix" (*sambuddhilopa*), the intention is that it occurs because of the subsequent presence of *eṅ*.

For in this case, there is no status of being "after a short vowel," since the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative suffix takes precedence due to its higher rank and its obligatory nature (*nityatva*).

In the case of *kṛte*, [the substitution] does not occur because it lacks the property of being subsequent to a short vowel (*hrasva*). Regarding *harim*: when the case-ending *am* follows, the form results from the application of the *pūrvarūpa* rule. Regarding *harīn*: after the application of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the substitution of *n* occurs by the rule "after that [long vowel], *śas* becomes *n*" (*tasmācchasaḥ*). (240) *Śeṣo ghy asakhi* 1.4.7.

When *hari* + *ā* remains in the third case singular, the author, intending to state the grammatical operations (*ghikārya*) applicable to a *ghi* stem, declares the designation *ghi*: "The remainder" (*śeṣo*). From the rule "feminine stems ending in *ī* and *ū*" (*hyū stryākhyau*), the term "*hyū*" is understood by anuvṛtti. This refers to *ī* and *ū*—that is, vowels with the phonetic qualities of *i* and *u*. [This applies] from the rule "before an affix beginning with *ṅ*, and when short [vowels follow]" (*ṅiti hrasvaśca*).
The term *hrasva* (short vowel) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. And that applies to each of the two [feminine suffixes] *yū*.
"The remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to anything other than that which has been designated by the technical term *nadī*; and that also applies to each of the two *yū*.

The phrase "the form of the word itself" (*śabdasvarūpam*) must be supplied, and it qualifies the two *yū*. This is a case of the rule regarding endings in *tadanta* (i.e., it applies to words ending in those suffixes).
He says this with the words beginning "those not designated as *nadī*," etc. The question "What is the purpose of *śeṣa*?
asks for what reason the qualification "not designated as *nadī*" is included.

[The example given is] *matyai*; for, in the absence of the mention of *śeṣa*, even under the alternative where it is treated as a *nadī* by the rule "before a suffix marked with *ṅ*, there is shortening of the vowel" (*ṅiti hrasvaśca*), [the form would be different].

The designation *ghi* would apply [to *mati*]. Consequently, after the addition of the augment *āṭ* by the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* [would occur], and then by the rule *gher ṅti*, the substitution of *guṇa* followed by the replacement with *ay* would result in the form *mataye*. This is the intended meaning. Even in the absence of the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder), the designation *ghi* does not apply to *matyai*, because the rule *ā kaḍārād ekā saṃjñā* ("from *āṅ* up to *kaḍāra*, there is only one designation") is without scope [for the *ghi* designation in this case].
Because there would be an obstruction [to the application of the rule] due to the designation *nadī*, he says: "by the single designation. Regarding the example *vātapramye*:

in the absence of the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*), when *vātapramī-e* is established, the designation *ghi* would apply even to that which ends in the long vowel *ī*. Consequently, by the rule *gher ṅti*, there would be *guṇa* and the substitution of *ay*, resulting in *vātapramaye*.
It might be so; therefore, the intention is that the mention of "short" (hrasva) is necessary. Regarding the word *mātre*:

in the absence of the rule *yū*, when *mātṛ-e* remains, if the term *ghi* were applied even to a stem ending in *ṛ*, then by the rule *gher ṅti*, there would be *guṇa* substitution for the vowel, resulting in the letter *a*;
with the subsequent substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*, the form would become *mātare*. Therefore, the intention is [to include] *i* and *u* [in the definition of *ghi*].

In reality, however, the mention of *idūt* is entirely redundant; for if the status of being a *ghi* were granted to that which ends in *ṛ* even in the case of *mātre*, then the desired *guṇa* would be established by the rule *gher ṅti*, so what is the purpose of that [mention]? (241) *āṅo nā'striyām* | Pāṇini 7.3.120.

Regarding "after *ghi*": the intention is that the term *ghi* is understood from the rule "and *ṭā* after *ghi*" (*ṭa-cca gheḥ*). In the word *hariṇā*, the substitution of *ṇa* occurs by the rule "ṇatva [occurs] after *ṭh*, *k*, *p*, *ūṣman*, and *aṅ*. Now, one might ask: since the substitution of *nā* is prescribed for *āṅ*, how could it apply to *ṭā*? To this, he says: "*āṅ-tī-iti*. (The meaning is that the substitute *nā* applies to *āṅ* when it is identical with *ṭā*.)

The meaning is that this is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) according to the treatise of the Eastern teachers. Regarding *matyā*: since the word *mati* ends in the suffix *ktin*—according to the rule "the suffix *ktin* occurs in the feminine"—it is feminine; therefore, the intention is that the substitution of *nā* [for the final vowel] does not apply.
[Thus we have] *haribhyām*, *haribhiḥ*. When *hari-e* is in the state of being established...

(242) *Gher ṅiti* | Pāṇini 7.3.111. From the rule *supi ca* [7.3.102], the term *supi* is understood; from the rule *hrasvasya* [6.1.71], the term *guṇa* is understood. Thus he says: "of that which bears the technical designation *ghi*, etc. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *yaṇ*-substitution. [Example: *haraye*.

Thus [it is said]. There is the substitution of *ā* for the vowel in a *guṇa* [context]. Why [is the condition] "in a *sup*" stated? Consider the example *paṭvī*. Here, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭhvoto guṇavacanāt*. Although that [suffix] ends in *ṅ*, because it lacks the status of being a *sup*, the *guṇa* substitution does not take place when it follows [the stem]; this is the meaning. Nor should the sūtra be formulated simply as *gheṅī*; the mention of *id* is not [superfluous].

It should not be argued that [the rule] must be applied because the meaning "before a *sup* beginning with *ṅ*" is obtained through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "in which there is an injunction" (*yasmin vidhiḥ*). For if that were the case, then even in the rule *āṇ nadyāḥ*, since only *ṅī* would be carried over [from the previous rule], *āṅ* would be prescribed for *ām* beginning with *ṅ*; and consequently...

In the case of *ṭhmatyām*, there would not be the substitution of *ām*. This is because *ām* lacks the marker *ṅ*. Nor should it be suspected that *ām* acquires the status of having the marker *ṅ* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original). This is because it is not a rule conditioned by an *al* (phoneme). Since the original element (*sthānin*), the vowel *ā* [of *ReĀRÇĀ*], has been removed by the assignment of the technical name *it* and its subsequent elision, the *ām* which replaces it does not possess the status of being an *al*.

Because the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are not invariably present [in all forms]. Even in the view that they are invariably present, an indicatory letter is not included by the mention of *al*; this is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) found in the rule "anekāl-śit sarvasya" [Pāṇini 1.1.55], where the mention of *śit* would otherwise be redundant. Otherwise, in rules such as "idama iś" [Pāṇini 5.3.3], the *śit* markers...

Since [the substitution] is already established by the fact that [the element] has multiple *al* sounds due to being accompanied by the suffix *ś*, what is the purpose of that [specification]? For this very reason, the status of being *pit* and so forth is established for the substitutes *tiP* and others.
For this very reason, in the rule "ṭh-s-e-r-hy-ap-it-ca," the term "ap-it" is meaningful; otherwise, it would be redundant.

Since the *pit* designation of the element *hi* is not applicable here because the *alvidhi* status [of the operation] precludes the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule itself, what is the point of its prohibition? This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara* under the *sthānivat* sūtra. Regarding the phrase "guṇe kṛte" (when the *guṇa* substitution has been made), it refers to the rule *ṅsiṅsor at*.

The remainder [of the rule]. When *hare-as* is established, because it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*), the substitution of the single substitute of the form of the preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*) prescribed by "ṅṇoḥ kuṅiḥ" does not apply; rather, the substitution of *ay* would apply. [To prevent this: (243) *ṅsiṅsośca* | Pāṇini 6.1.110.
Regarding the rule *eṅaś ca*: from the rule *ṭheṅaḥ padāntād ati*, the words *ṭheṅ* and *ṭhati* are carried over (*anuvartate*).

From the rule *ami pūrvaḥ*, the word *pūrva* is carried over. The rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is the governing heading (*adhikṛtam*); thus he says: "of *eṅ* [before] *ṅsi* and *ṅsu*. As in *harer* (from *hareḥ*), by means of the *pūrvarūpa* [substitution].

The forms *rut* and *visarga* are the shapes of both the singular of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and the singular of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Although there are two [suffixes] for the genitive singular—*ṅsi* and *ṅs*—and two for the dative singular—*eṅ* and *ai*, nevertheless, a correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended here.

This is because one accepts the division of the rule as: "A designation according to order applies when the elements are equal in number" (*yathāsaṃkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām*) and "by means of the circumflex accent" (*svaritena*).

It is clear from the commentary on the *yathāsaṅkhya* (correspondence) sūtra that wherever the svarita accent is promised, the understanding of correspondence occurs precisely there; this is also evident from such grammatical indications as "ṭhacca gheḥ" and "upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ. Regarding the form "haryoḥ": it is the form resulting from the substitution of *yaṇ* in the genitive dual.

Regarding "harīṇām": the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ*; the lengthening is by the rule *nāmī*; and the substitution of *ṇ* is by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye*. (244) *acca gheḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.119].
When "hari i" is established, the rule "gher ṅti" would require a *guṇa* substitution; however, [the rule] "acca gheḥ" applies.

From the rule "ReĀrām," the term "ReĀ" is carried over (*anuvartate*). The rules "idudbhyām" and "āṬt" are also carried over. Thus he says: "from *it* and *ut*" (*idudbhyām*). This refers to a final substitute (*antādeśaḥ*).

This is obtainable through the paribhāṣā *alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*. Regarding "vṛddhi": when *hara-āṬ* is situated, by the rule *vṛddhireci*, the vṛddhi [substitution] occurs, resulting in the form *harau*; such is the meaning. Regarding *hariṣu*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. Now, from the word *sakhi*, [the suffix] *su* is added: *sakhi-su*.
When [the word] *sakhi* is present:
(245) *anaṅ sau* | Pāṇini 7.1.93. *Anaṅ sau*: the phrase *sakhyurasambuddhau* is understood to follow. The governing term *aṅgasya* is also supplied.

He says this with the words "of the friend's body" (*sakhyuraṅgasya*), and so forth. The term *sau* is the nominative singular, not the locative plural, because of the exclusion [implied] by the rule "except in the vocative" (*asambuddhau*). The element *anaṅ* has *ṅ* as its *it*-marker; the vowel *a* after the *n* is for the sake of pronunciation.
Fearing that [the substitution] would apply to the whole because it consists of more than one letter (*anekāltvāt*), he says: "ṅc" [in Pāṇini 1.1.53].

(246) *alo'ntyātpūrva upadhā* [Pāṇini 1.1.65]. Having established *sakhan-s*, and intending to explain the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to the penultimate letter (*upadhā*), he states the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the penultimate: *alo'ntyāt*.

The word *ṭhalaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *antyāt*. The term *al-* is a synonym for "phoneme" (*varṇa*). Since they belong to the same class (*sājātya*), the preceding [phoneme] is also understood as *al*; this is stated by the phrase beginning with *antyādalaḥ*. [Question: Why [is the condition] *alaḥ*? [Answer: In the word *śiṣṭa*, [it refers to] the *ās* [portion] within the verbal root *śās*.

The letter *ś* preceding a cluster does not function as an *upadhā*. Otherwise, by the rule *ṭhśāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the letter *ś* being replaced by *i*. Why is the mention of the individual letter (*varṇagrahaṇa*) necessary?
[To show that] in the verbal root *śās*, the entire cluster *śā* does not function as an *upadhā*. Otherwise, [the rule] *ṭhśā...* [would apply].

The *ik* [vowel] should belong to the entire group (*samudāya*). Nor should it be argued that, by the rule regarding the final letter (*alontyaparibhāṣā*), the *ik* would apply only to the long *ā*, because that is prohibited by the rule: "A rule concerning the final letter does not apply when [the element to which it refers] is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ*).

(247) *sarvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau* |6|4|8|. [The word] *sarvanāmasthāne* [is the context]. The rule *nopadhāyāḥ* is understood [to follow]. The word *na* is a term with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhī*). By that, the word *aṅgasya* is qualified as having a genitive of part-whole relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

This is a rule concerning the final element of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*). From the rule *ṭhḍhralope* [Pāṇini 6.3.111], the word *dīrghaḥ* ("long vowel") is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of that which ends in *n*" and so forth. (248) *apṛkta ekāl pratyayaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.2.41. A suffix consisting of a single phoneme is called *apṛkta*.

The word *sakhi* being present as *sakhān s*, the author—about to explain the grammatical operation (*kārya*) pertaining to the *apṛkta* (uncombined) suffix—states the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the *apṛkta*: "The *apṛkta* [is that which consists of a single phoneme]. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which has one phoneme" (*ekāl*). Here, the word *eka* signifies "having no companion. As Amarasimha states: "The words *mukhya*, *anya*, and *kevala* mean 'alone' (*eka*). Thus, when the technical designation *apṛkta* is applied to the element *s*.

(249) *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktam hal* 6.1.68. The compound *halṅyābbhyaḥ* is a *dvandva* consisting of *hal*, *ṅī*, and *āp*. The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of direction (*digyoga*). The word *param* (following) is to be supplied. Even though they are parts of a compound, [the rule applies] specifically to *ṅī* and *āp*.

The qualification "from a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) applies [to the base], not to the consonant (*hal*), because [the latter] is impossible. And thus, in the case of doubling, the singular number in "from a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). This is because the rule *ṭh-ḷ-ṅ-y-ābbhyo dīrghāt* functions as a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*) implied by the suffixes *sū*, *ti*, and *si*, and by the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*).

This is an *anta-vidhi* (a rule concerning the final element). Consequently, it is understood that [the suffix] follows what ends in a consonant (*hal*) as well as what ends in a long vowel (*dīrgha*) or the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*.

The term *sutisi* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The word *apṛkta* and the word *hal* are construed in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). When the *u* and *i* have been elided, the remainder [is the suffix].

The *sakāra* and *takāra* are intended here by the rule *sutisi*. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) established by the rule *hal*. From the rule *ṭhlopoḥ vyoḥ*, the term *lopa* is carried over (*anuvartate*). And here, that [term] is understood as a passive derivative (*karmasādhana*): it is that which is elided (*lupyate*) is the *lopa*.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of "stepping" (*kramaṇi*). Thus he says: "after a word ending in a consonant," and so forth. [The question] "Why [specify] 'after a consonant, a long vowel, or the feminine suffixes *ī* and *ā*? is asked because there is no fault in forms such as *rāma*, since they do not end in a long vowel. [The example] *grāmaṇīḥ*: the analysis is "one who leads the village" (*grāmān nayati*). [The root] *ṇīñ* is used in the sense of "leading."
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs according to the rule *agragramābhyāṃ nayater ṇo vācyaḥ*.
Since the word does not end in a *hal*, a *ṅī*, or an *āp* vowel, there is no elision of the nominative suffix *su*. Regarding the question "Why 'from a long vowel' (*dīrghāt*)?":
since the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is invariably present in both *ṅī* and *āp*, the question asks for what purpose the qualification "long" is stated.

In the examples *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* and *atikhaṭvaḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "gone out from Kauśāmbī" and "having transcended the bed. In these cases, the compound is formed by the rules: "nir-ādayaḥ with words meaning 'gone over' [are compounded] with a word in the fifth case" and "ati-ādayaḥ with words meaning 'gone over' [are compounded] with a word in the second case. [The feminine suffix is dropped] by the rule "gostriyoḥ... [when the final member is a feminine noun ending in -ī or -ū].

Shortness (*hrasvatva*). For here, because of the shortness of *ā* and *p*, there is no elision of *su*. Regarding the form *abhaitsīt*: this is from the root *bhid* with the suffix *luṅ* and the augment *sic*. Here, there is no elision of the *s* following the *t*, because it lacks the status of being any one of *su*, *ti*, or *si*; such is the meaning. Now, [one might object]: "But surely this is simply the *s* of *sic* itself... To this [it is replied]:

He says: "tip. The meaning is that because only that which has the form of an inflection (*vibhakti*) co-occurring with *tip* is understood, there is no inclusion of the suffix *sic*. As for the example *bibharti*: here, the entire cluster *tī* does not possess the status of a consonant (*hal*).
Although the letter *t* is indeed a consonant (*hal*) that is a constituent part of *ti*, it nevertheless lacks the status of being an *apṛkta* (a single-consonant suffix).

In reality, however, when the *u* and *i* have been elided, the remaining *s* and *t* are included by the rule *sutisī-* because of their coreferentiality with the word *hal*; this has already been stated. There is no elision of the *i* here. Therefore, by the very mention of *hal*, [the rule applies] in the case of *vibharti*.
This is not a counter-example for the mention of "apṛkta," because the non-occurrence of elision (*lopābhāva*) is not established.
He asks about the purpose of the second mention of *hal*: "Why *hal*?
[The example is] *bibheda*. [It is derived from] the root *bhid* with the suffix *liṭ*, *tip*, and *ṇal*; because the vowel *a* of *ṇal* lacks the status of being a *hal*, [the rule does not apply].

[The rule states: "There is elision [of the final consonant]. [The questioner asks: "Why [specify] 'the first consonant'? This is the question, based on the reasoning that when *rājan* + *s* is situated, the form *rājā* and so forth is already established by the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) and the elision of the final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). [The objector replies: But how can this *rājā* serve as a counter-example, since it is established by the elision of the final conjunct alone?
Because [the substitution] would be otherwise established, he says: "The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and so forth would not occur.
The sense is that when the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) has taken place, the elision of *n* would not occur.

In the example "abhino 'tra," the change to *u* (*utva*) is what is meant by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). [This is derived from] *bhid* with the suffix *laṅ*, followed by *is*, and then [the rule] "from *it*" (*itaśca*).

There is the elision of the *t* (of *at*). By the rule "ru for the root-final before *sip*," there is the substitution of *r*. There is the elision of *s*. In this case, the substitution of *u* by the rule "for *at* and *ror*, when not followed by a protracted vowel" would not apply. Why? To this he says: "because the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered asiddha (non-existent) [for the purposes of that rule]. However, the elision [of the final *t*] by the rule "hal-ṅy-ādi... [does apply].

The meaning is that it is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it occurs within the sixth chapter and the first quarter (*pāda*). It is clear in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that in some manuscripts, the textual portion beginning with "dīrghāt kimaḥ" is presented here. Regarding the word *sakha*: when the *su*-suffix is elided, the *n* is dropped by the rule "na lopaḥ."

One should not say here that, because *anaṅ* is applied depending on the sound *su*, the elision of *su* (*sulopa*) cannot occur depending on the sound *n* due to a conflict with the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*; for by the rule "the agent is independent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*),
etc., the elision of *su* occurs depending on the *n* of *anaṅ*.
They say that this is because the rule regarding simultaneous occurrence (*sannipātaparibhāṣā*) does not apply when an operation is to be performed. Regarding the form *he sakhe*:

in the rule *anaṅ sau*, since the term *asambuddhau* (except in the vocative) is understood to follow, there is no substitution of *anaṅ*. Consequently, after the *guṇa* substitution [of *i* for *e*], the suffix *su* is elided by the rule *eṅhrasvāt sambuddheḥ*, resulting in the form [he sakhe].

(250) *sakhyurasambuddhau* | Pāṇini 7.1.92. When the form *sakhi-āṬ* is established, intending to state the vowel-vṛddhi substitution as a *ṇit*-operation, he demonstrates its treatment as if it were a *ṇit*:
*sakhyurasambuddhau*. In the term *sakhyuḥ*, the ablative case is used in the sense of separation (*digyoge*).
The word *ṭhaṅ* is governed [by the previous rule] and is transformed into the ablative case (*pañcamī*). The word *para* is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*).
From the rule *itaḥ sarvanāmasthāne*, the term *sarvanāmasthāne* is carried over (*anuvartate*).
The term *asambuddhau* connects [with the previous rule] without distinction. From the rule *goto ṇit*, the term *ṇit* is carried over.

The word ending in the nominative case is carried over [from the previous rule]. By virtue of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that, the locative case in *ṭhasambuddhyoḥ* and *sarvanāmasthāne* is interpreted as a nominative. This is what he states by saying "after the base *sakhi*, etc. The term *ṇidvat* means "as if it were marked with the *ṆI* augment."

The meaning is that [the suffix] should perform the operation (*kārya*) of a *ṇit* [suffix]. The intention is that the word *ṇit* is for the purpose of extending (*atideśa*) those operations. (251) *aco ñṇiti* | Pāṇini 7.2.115.
Regarding *aco ñṇiti*: *añṇau* refers to *ñ* and *ṇ*; that which has these two as its *it* (indicatory letters) is called *ñṇit*.

From the rule "of *mṛj*" (*mṛjer*), the term "vṛddhi" is understood to carry over. The term "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*), which is the governing heading, is qualified by the vowel [of the suffix]; consequently, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). This is what he expresses with the words "of that which ends in a vowel," and so forth. Due to the correspondence of place of articulation (*sthānasāmya*), the *vṛddhi* substitute for the vowel *i* is *ai*; for that, the substitution of *āy* (*āyādeśa*) applies.

Intending this, he says "sakhāyau" (two friends). Likewise: *sakhi-āsu* becomes *sakhāyaḥ* (friends); *sakhi-am* becomes *sakhāyam* (a friend); *sakhī-au* becomes *sakhāyau* (two friends). In the case of the *śas* ending, the form is like that of *hari* (the horse/god Hari), because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending and lacks the marker *ṇit*, there is no *vṛddhi* [strengthening]. This is because there is an absence of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "ghi. This is due to the exclusion of the word "friend" (*asakhī*) in the rule *śeṣo ghyasakhī*.
The intention is that it is because of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). "Not that effect" means that the grammatical operation conditioned by a *ghit* suffix does not apply.

Regarding *sakhyā*: when *sakhi-ā* is situated, since there is no *ghit*-ness, the rule *āṅe nā'striyām* does not apply; thus, in the absence of the substitution of *nā*, the form is derived through *yaṇ*. Regarding *sakhye*: when *sakhi-e* is situated...
Because it is not a *ghi* stem, there is no application of the rule "gher ṅti" (Pāṇini 7.3.111), and thus no *guṇa*; consequently, by *yaṇ*-substitution, the form is [sakhya].
When the forms *ṅsi* and *ṅsas* follow, the situation is *sakhi-as*, and since it is not a *ghi* stem, there is no *guṇa* by "gher ṅti"; with *yaṇ*-substitution, the form stands as *sakhyas*.

(252) *khyatyāt parasya* |6|1|112|. Regarding the rule *khyatyāt parasya*: the forms *khya* and *tya* are technical designations (*nirdeśa*) for *khikhī* and *titī* respectively when the semivowel substitution (*yaṇ-ādeśa*) has taken place. [The vowel *a* follows the *y*.]
The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). From the rule *ṭheṅḥ padāntā’d*, the word *at* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*).

And that [word *at*] is transformed into a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the following [element]. From the rule *ṅsiṅsośca*, the term *ṅsiṅsoḥ* is understood as a carry-over. This is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Consequently, from the rule *ṭhṅsiṅsor avayavasyātaḥ*, the word *ataḥ* is obtained. From the rule *ṭhṛt u’d*, the word *ud* is carried over (*anuvartate*). However, the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is excluded because of the force of the mention of the word *para*. Otherwise, since the word *khyatyād* is indicated by a fifth-case (ablative) construction, [the desired result would follow] even without it.
If it is already established, what is the purpose of that? He says this with the words "by the two words *khi* and *ti*" and so forth. Regarding the word *sakhyuḥ*:
when *sakhyas* is situated [in the sandhi], the vowel *a* after the letter *y* is replaced by *u*, and then the *ru*-substitution and the visarga occur. (253) *ĀṬ* 7.3.118.

When *ṅai* is present as *sakhi i*, because it lacks the designation *ghit*, the rule *ṭhacca gheḥ* does not apply, and thus *savarṇadīrgha* (the long vowel of the same class) would be expected. [To prevent this, the rule] *āṬt* applies; the sūtra *ṭhidudbhyām* is understood to carry over, as is *ReĀḥ* from the rule *ReĀrām*. Thus he says: "from *idudbhyām*," and so forth. Now, [an objection]: *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "nanu".)*

In words designated as *gh* such as *harika* and *kavi*, the rule "ṭā-cca gheḥ" applies; however, in words designated as *nadī*, the preceding rule "ṭā-si-d-d-bhyām" applies. Therefore, it is clear that the scope of this [present] rule consists exclusively of the words *sakhi* and *pati*, which fall outside the scope of those two rules. And thus:

He says "ukāra" because the recurrence of the vowel *u* would otherwise be purposeless. The meaning is that the recurrence of *u* is for the sake of its recurrence in the subsequent rule, "acca gheḥ. Regarding *sakhyau*: the sense is that the form arises through the substitution of *ReĀr* (the diphthongs *ai* and *au*) and then the application of *yaṇ*. Regarding *susakhā*: this is a *prādi*-compound (a prepositional compound). [The rule] "rājāhaḥ... [applies].
The suffix *ṭac* does not apply after the word *sakhi* by virtue of the rule *sakhyaṣṭaḷj*, because of the prohibition *na pūjanāt*.

[In the nominative singular] there is the substitution of *anaṅ*, lengthening of the penultimate vowel, elision of the final consonant according to *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* etc., and the elision of the *n* according to *nalopaḥ*; such is the intended meaning.

In *susakhāyau*, *susakhāyaḥ*, and so on, there is the status of being *ṇit* (as if marked with Ṇ), which results in vṛddhi; this is the intended meaning of the substitution of *āy*. Now, one might ask: if the status of being *ṇit* and the substitution of *anaṅ* are prescribed for the word *sakhi* itself, how could they apply to the word *susakhi*? To this, he says: "because of *anaṅ*, etc. This is because [the rule] resides within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning "bases" (*aṅga*).

The meaning is that, by the *paribhāṣā* "in the section concerning the members of a compound" (*ṭhpadāṅgādhikāre*), the rule applies even when the word *sakhi* occurs at the end [of a compound]. Now, one might object: if this were the case, then in the word *susakhi*, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not *sakhi*" (*asakhi*), there would be no doubling, and consequently, the substitution of *ā* and so forth would not occur; to this, he says: "of the whole [compound]."

Nor should it be argued that even though the word *susakhī* lacks the form of the word *sakhi*, the exclusion of words ending in *sakhi* (by Pāṇini 6.4.150) would still be unavoidable because it ends in the word *sakhi*;
for the reason is that [the rule] "the remainder is *ghi*, except for *sakhi*" (*śeṣo ghyasakhī*) occurs within the governing context of *pada* and *aṅga*.
Regarding *susakhi-nā*: by the rule *gher ṅti*, the form is *annātve*. Regarding *susakhye*:

by the rule *gher ṅti*, the *guṇa* [substitution] occurs, and then the *ayādeśa* [is applied]. Regarding *ṅsi*: the connection is that once the *guṇa* has been applied to the *ṅsi* and *ṅs* cases of the stem ending in *ghi* by the rule *gher ṅti*, the substitution of *utva* (the change to *u*) does not occur by the rule *khyatyāt*. Why? From this [it follows].

He says: "Because there is an absence of the substitution of *yaṇ*. The meaning is that, by the mention of "that which has undergone the substitution of *yaṇ*" (*kṛtayaṇādeśa*) in the rule *khyatyāt*, the substitution of *u* occurs only where the substitution of *yaṇ* has taken effect.
Regarding *susakheḥ*: this is the form [of the word] in the *ṅsi* and *ṅs* cases. Regarding *susakhau*: [this is the form] with the suffix *au*. *Acca*...
The substitution of *au* occurs by the rule "gheḥ. "In this way" means as in the word *susakhī*. *Atisakhā*:
this is a *prādi*-compound; the suffix *ṭac* is not applied because of the prohibition "not after words denoting honor.
In reality, however, the designation *ghisaṃjñā* does not apply at all to the cited words *susakhī* and *atisakhī*.

In the rule *śeṣo ghyasakhī*, the term *asakhī* is indeed a qualifier of *śeṣa*. This involves the application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that). Thus, it is understood that a remainder (*śeṣa*) ending in the word *sakhi*, provided it is not [the word] *sakhi* itself, is designated as *ghi*. For this very reason, regarding the question "What is the example for the elision of the vowel *i* when followed by the vowel *i* according to the rule *yasyeti ca*?"—the example is the word *sakhī*.

In the rule "sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, resulting in the elision of the vowel *i*. Nor can this be resolved by applying the rule for long vowels from homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*). [For example: "one who has surpassed a female friend" is *atisakhiḥ*; this is a *prādi* compound (with the prefix *ati-*). By the rule "gostriyoḥ," the final vowel is shortened. In the phrase "atisakher āgacchati" ("he comes from the one who has surpassed a female friend"),...

Because there would be no elision of the *ik* vowel, the rule for long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) would apply; since that single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as part of the preceding element, it would be included under the term "sakhi. Consequently, because the prohibition of the *ghit* designation applies to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the word "asakhi," the *ghit* designation would undesirably result. However, when the elision of the *ik* vowel occurs, and the shortening of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* has been applied, this is no longer the word "sakhi."

The *Bhāṣya* statement, "because the *ṅīṣ* suffix does not have that [suffix] as its constituent part," is thus consistent; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the example *paramasakhā*: because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and lacks the status of a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* is not applied.

Among these, he first derives it by means of the passage beginning with "vātapramīḥ," etc. Immediately after the word "kiṃ," [the text states] "it is irregularly formed" (*nipātyate*).

This is the remainder [of the analysis]. With *vātam* as the upapada (governing word), from the root √mā in the sense of the agent, with the suffix *ī*, because it is *kit*, there is elision of the *ā* by the rule "elision of *ā* when *iṭ* follows"; then, in the compound formed by "the upapada is compounded with a non-finite verb," after the case-ending (*sup*) has been produced, the form *vātapramīḥ* appears in the nominative singular. Because it ends in a consonant (*aṅ*), [the feminine suffix] does not apply.

There is elision of the *su* [case-ending]. This is the intended meaning: that it is precisely for this purpose that the mention of *ṅīp* is included in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* even though the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is already present there. Regarding the word "from a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*): when *vātapramī-āḥ* is established, the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is prohibited by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca*; consequently, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*.

The meaning is that the form is *vātapramyau*. [In the vocative] "he *vātapramī*," because it ends in a long vowel, the rule "guṇa for a short vowel" (*hrasvasya guṇaḥ*) does not apply. Regarding *amī*: when *vātapramī-am* is situated, by the rule "the preceding form before *ami*" (*ami pūrvaḥ*), the resulting form is *vātapramīm*; this is the meaning. [Regarding the rule] "for a root with more than one vowel" (*eranekācaḥ*).
Thus, *yaṇ* [substitution] does not apply here, because that which ends in the *ī*-suffix lacks the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding *vātapramīn*:
after the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇa-dīrgha*, the substitution of *n* occurs by the rule *tasmāc chasaḥ*. Regarding *vātapramyā*:
because it is not a feminine (*aghitvāt*), the substitution of *nā* by the rule *āṅe nā'striyām* is absent, and thus *yaṇ* applies. [In the dual, it becomes] *vātapramye*.

Because [the vowel] is long, there is no *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *aṅitvān heṅsiṅsu ṭhgherṅtī*. Thus, the form is *vātapramyām*; this is the form resulting from the *yaṇ* substitute for the *ām* ending. The intention is that because it is long, the *nuṭ* augment does not apply, due to the inclusion of the term "short" (*hrasva*) in the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ*. Regarding the form with the *ṅi* ending: when *vātapramī-i* is situated [in the sandhi process], [the following applies].

By overriding the *yaṇ* substitution due to its subsequent status (*paratva*), the *savarṇadīrgha* [vowel lengthening] applies, resulting in the form *vātapramī*. Furthermore, because it does not end in *i* or *u* (as required by the condition *idudantatva*), the rules *acca gheḥ* and *āṬt* do not apply.
In fact, according to the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe*, that which ends in *ī* or *ū* in the locative case [is treated as a single word].

It does not exist in common usage. Therefore, it is stated clearly in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*— which cites "somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ" and "māmakī tanū" as examples from the Veda alone— it is inferred that the word *vātapramī* ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) has no usage in common parlance.

Regarding the word *yāpau*: this refers to the *uṇādi* sūtra, *ṭhpāpoḥ kid voṣace*. The meaning is that the suffix *ī* is added to the roots *yā* and *pā*, and it is *kit*; furthermore, there is reduplication of those two which constitute the base. Because the suffix is *kit*, by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, there is elision of the final *ā*. There is also shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding the term *vāta*: some claim that the word *vātapramī* is derived from the root *māṅ* (in the sense of "measuring") with the suffix *kvip* in the agentive sense, followed by the substitution of *ī* for *ā* according to the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām...* [Pāṇini 6.4.66].

This is incorrect, because it contradicts the Vārttika rule stating that "the substitution of *ī* occurs when *ava* or similar prefixes follow" (*ītvam avakārādau*). [The correct derivation is] from the root *mīñ* (in the sense of "injuring").
However, when the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *mī*, the form *vātapramī* is unobjectionable. This is because the *yaṇ* substitution—which will be explained later—applies here;

it prevails over the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute elision) in the nominative plural (*am*), the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same class) in the accusative plural (*śas*), and the *savarṇadīrgha* in the dative singular (*ṅe*), due to its higher status as a subsequent rule. The intention is that this occurs because the verbal root ends in the vowel *ī*.

Regarding the example *pradhīvat*: "one who meditates intensely" (*prakṛṣṭaṃ dhyāyati*) is *pradhīḥ*. By the rule *dhyāyateḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *y* into *i*. By the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is substituted. By the rule *halaḥ*, there is lengthening. And because this [word] ends in the vowel *ī* (as a verbal root), [the case endings] *am* and *ṅsi* [are applied].

In *ṅai*, the substitution of *yaṇ* applies by the rule "ṅai ca ṭheranekācaḥ. Regarding *bahvayaḥ*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "bahvādibhyaśca. Regarding *śreyasyaḥ*: the meaning is "those who are most excellent. The suffix *īyasun* is applied by the rule "dvivacanavibhajyopapade. The substitution of *śra-* for *praśasya-* occurs by the rule "praśasyasya śraḥ. The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ugitaśca."

Regarding the term *bahuśreyasī*: the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) occurs by the rule *ṭhstriyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskād anūṅ*. However, the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by *ṭhgostriyor upasarjanasya* does not take place here, because that is prohibited by the statement: "It should be stated that [shortening] does not occur after the suffix *īyasun* in a bahuvrīhi compound. Once *bahuśreyasī-s* is established, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), stating: "Because it ends in a long vowel followed by a ṅ-letter."

Is it not the case that the word *śreyasī* itself ends in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, since when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), the rule applies only to that which begins with the element from which that suffix is prescribed? Nor should it be argued that the restriction to what begins with that element does not apply here because of the prohibition stating, "In the case of a feminine suffix, there is no restriction to what begins with that [element]," for that prohibition applies only when the suffix is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*).

If it is argued that there is a prohibition [of the application of the feminine suffix] because, in the case of a feminine derivative (*strīpratyaya*), there is no restriction that the suffix must apply to the beginning of the word, whereas here, due to its status as a secondary member (*upasarjana*), such a restriction certainly exists— let it be granted then that only the word *śreyasī* (ending in the feminine suffix) possesses the feminine suffix,
and not the word *bahuśreyasī*. Nevertheless...

The elision [of the case-ending] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* is here unimpeded, because the status of being subsequent (*paratva*) to the word *śreyasī*, which ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*), remains intact. Nor is it a qualifier of that which is prescribed by the rule *na hiṭhhalṅyābbhyaḥ*, as there is a lack of evidence for such a view; furthermore, this would result in over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *yā sā kā*. In that instance:

Because there is an absence of being prescribed after a word ending in *s* or *uṣṭan*. As for *yat*, *tat*, and *kim*, they [are derived] from words ending in *hal*.

When the substitution of the long vowel identical with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is prohibited, the *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs: *bahuśreyasyau*, *bahuśreyasyaḥ*.

(263) *yū stryākhyau nadī*: The two vowels *yū* (the feminine suffixes *ī* and *ū*) denoting a female are called *nadī*. When *he bahuśreyasī* is established, the operation pertaining to a *nadī* applies.

Intending to state the technical designation *nadī*, he says: "The [vowels] *yū* termed *strī* (feminine) are called *nadī*. *Yū* refers to both *ī* and *ū*. [The dual form *yū* is derived from *y* + *u* with] the long vowel resulting from the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). The absence of the prohibition [of the nominative-accusative plural case-ending *jas*] by the rule "after a long vowel, *jas* is not elided" (*dīrghāj jasi ca*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Due to the explanatory context (*vyākhyāna*), only the long vowels are understood here. Those which denote a feminine are termed *stryākhyau*.
The term "two sounds" (*śabdau*) is understood from the sense of the context. The word *yū* is a qualifier for that [pair], and therefore the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
Although the form would be established by the rule *striyām* alone, the inclusion of the word *ākhyā* is for the purpose of obtaining the status of being exclusively feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*).
In the case of duality, the singular number in *nadī* is Vedic. This is what he states with the words beginning "ending in *i* or *u*" (*idūdantau*), etc. *Yū*.
What [is the result]? In the case of *mātre*, the rule "ṭāṇnadyāḥ" does not apply. Why [specify] "feminine gender"? [Consider] *vātapramye*. Why [specify] "always"? [Consider] *grāmaṇye*.
Now, since the word *bahuśreyasī* in the present context is masculine, how can it have the designation "nadī" (feminine noun ending in long ī)? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "And the first apprehension of the gender. This is a *vārttika*.

The meaning is that the feminine gender—which has already functioned prior to the operation of a compound (*samāsa*) or other derivative formation (*vṛtti*)—must be included in the rule "feminine genders are called *strī*" (*ṭhyūstryākhyau*). But if this were the case...

Fearing that words such as *gaurī* would not possess the status of a river-name (*nadītva*) in the absence of compound formation (*samāsa*) and other such operations, he provides an explanation by supplying the word "also" (*api*) and stating "prior," etc.:
[it refers to] that which exists as feminine prior to the occurrence of compound formation and the like.

The meaning of the *vārttika* is that even though the feminine gender is absent because [the word] is subordinate (*upasarjana*) in its state as a member of a compound (*vṛtidaśāyām*), it must still be stated that it possesses the status of a river-name (*nadītva*). This is the intended sense. [The rule: "Shortening for words denoting 'mother' and for river-names" (264). *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ* | 7|3|107|.

"Of those words meaning 'mother' (*ambārthānām*)" means "of synonyms for mother. "Of those ending in *nadī*"—because this occurs within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the "stem" (*aṅga*), it is understood as a rule concerning that which ends in such [stems].
Due to the same underlying logic, it should be understood that the rule concerning "those meaning mother" also applies to words ending in such [synonyms].
Regarding the phrase "in the case of a vocative singular" (*sambuddhau*): the intention is that this [condition] is carried over from the rule *sambuddhau ca*.

However, in words such as *ambā* and *gaurī*, the shortening [of the final vowel] should be understood as occurring because they end in [a feminine suffix] by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). In the example *he bahuśreyasi*, once the shortening has occurred, [the rule] *eṅhrasvāt* applies.
