There is the elision of the *sambuddhi* [vocative case-ending]. However, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the short vowel; for it is clear from the Bhāṣya that, rather than stating "there is a short vowel for words ending in *ambā*, *arthanadī*, and *nadī*" (*ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ*) for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation, one should instead state "there is *guṇa* for words ending in *ambā*, *arthanadī*, and *nadī*" (*ambārthanadyorguṇaḥ*), because of the force of the rule prescribing the short vowel. [Examples: *bahuśreyasyau*; *bahuśreyasyaḥ*. [This applies] by the rule "also after a long vowel before *jas*" (*dīrghāj-jasi ca*).
When the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is prohibited, the *yaṇ* [substitution] applies. In the case of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, the preceding form is used:

*bahuśreyasīm*, *bahuśreyasyau*, *bahuśreyasīḥ*. The intention is that if the homogeneous long vowel were applied, the rule "after that [e], the *s* of *śas*" would cause the substitution of *n* for *s*. [In the instrumental singular: *bahuśreyasyā*; because it does not end in *ā*, there is no substitution of *ābh* [for *as*].

No; rather, there is the substitution *yaṇ*. [In the forms] *bahuśreyasībhyām* and *bahuśreyasībhiḥ*, when *bahuśreyasī-e* is present, because of the absence of the status of being a *ghit* (a stem ending in a vowel other than *a*), that grammatical operation [of *gher ṅiti*] does not apply. When *yaṇ* is applied, the form *bahuśreyasye* is obtained.

(265) *āṇ nadyāḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.112. The term *aṅgasya*, which is supplied as a governing rule (*adhikṛtam*), is modified into the ablative case. It is qualified by the word *nadyāḥ* in the ablative; thus, the rule applies to that which ends in *nadī*. [The rule continues] from *gher ṅti*.
The term *ṭhṅtī* is understood [from a previous rule] and is modified to the genitive case; this is what is expressed by the phrase beginning with *nadyantāt*.
(266) *āṭaśca* | Pāṇini 6.1.90. Because it has the marker *ṭ*, it is the initial constituent. When *bahuśreyasī* + *ā* + *e* is situated [in the derivation], [the rule] *āṭaśca* applies.

From the rule "ṭhikoyaṇaci," the term *aci* is carried over; from the rule "ṭhvṛddhireci," the term *vṛddhiḥ* is carried over; and the phrase "ṭhekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" is also governing the context. Thus he says [the sūtra] beginning with "āṭo'ci. Regarding the form *bahuśreyasyai*: it is derived from *bahuśreyasī* + *ā*.

The intention is that when [the suffix] *ṅasi* is present, the form is derived through the application of the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 6.1.88) for the vṛddhi substitute, followed by the substitution of *yaṇ*. Although the desired form would be established by the rule "vṛddhir eci" alone, nevertheless, the rule "māṭaśca" (Pāṇini 6.1.90) is cited here as well because it is more appropriate for cases such as "aikṣata. [The example] "bahuśreyasyāḥ" [is formed] with the suffix *ṅasi*.

When *bahuśreyasī* + *ā* remains, the sense is that the form is derived by applying the *vṛddhi* vowel [ā] according to the rule *ṭhāṭaśca*, followed by *yaṇ* [e]. However, this is also established by the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality). Nevertheless, the *vṛddhi* [ā] is applied according to the rule *āṭaśca* because it is the more logical [application], since the word *śreyasī* follows after a stem ending in *nadī*.

Because it is a feminine noun ending in *ī* and is always feminine, it is treated as a river-name (*nadī*) due to its having many vowels; thus, when a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise apply— (267) *ReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ* 7.3.116.

Regarding the rule *reĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ*: because [the suffix] *reĀ* is a member of a word (*aṅga*) and by virtue of the paribhāṣā concerning the inclusion of that which ends in a suffix, he says "from that which ends in a nadī-suffix" and so forth, intending the application of the rule for what ends in such a suffix. The form *reĀḥ* is the locative singular, as established by the commentary. Now, one might object: once the case-ending *ām* has been applied, the augment *nuṭ* would be inserted by the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ*.

Anticipating the objection that, by the maxim *yadāgamāḥ*, the augment *āṭ* would apply because the name [of the suffix] is included within the mention of "ā" (in the rule *āṇnadyāḥ*), he says: "In this case, due to its posteriority. Nor should it be argued:
"Even if the augment *āṭ* has been applied, why should the augment *nuṭ* not still occur?"—for [the latter is precluded] by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
The intended meaning is that according to the maxim "what has been sublated remains sublated," [the rule does not apply].

Regarding the phrase "ending in the suffix īp": the point is that since the word *vātapramī* also lacks a verbal root ending in an *i*-vowel, the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule "ṭeranekācaḥ" would not apply in the cases of the *ām*, *śas*, and *ṅi* endings.
The word *lakṣmī* is derived from the verbal root *lakṣ* with the suffix *ī*, and by the rule *lakṣermuṭ ca*, the augment *muṭ* is added to it.
In the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "one who has surpassed Lakṣmī," the compound is formed according to the rule *ṭyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*.

Because it does not end in a feminine suffix (*astrīpratyayāntatvāt*), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*nopasarjanahrasvaḥ*). This is because [the word] ends in a semivowel (*aṅyantatvāt*).

The intention is that [the suffix] ends in an *āṬṇādika* pratyaya. "The rest is like *bahuśreyasī*"—the meaning is that it possesses the status of a *nadī* (feminine noun) because of the rule "and the mention of the original gender. Now, when the word *kumārī* has attained the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*) and is in the masculine gender, its distinction from the word *śreyasī* is as follows:
In order to demonstrate this, he says: "desiring a maiden," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from that which ends in *kyac*":

in the sense of "desiring a maiden for oneself" (*kumārīm ātmana icchati*), the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*. The *kac* portion is elided. Since that which ends in *kyac* is a verbal root (dhātu) according to the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, the case-ending *am* belonging to the *sup* that is a constituent part of it [is replaced].

There is elision [of the case-ending] by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ. Then, by the rule "kvip ca," the suffix *kvip* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The *k* and *p* are for the sake of pronunciation; the *i* is for the sake of articulation. There is elision of the *a* by the rule "ato lopaḥ," and elision of the *y* by the rule "lopo vyoḥ. There is elision of the *v* by the rule "verapṛktasya. Thus, the form "kumārī" is obtained.

*Rūpam* [is derived as follows]: from the root *ācar*, followed by the suffix *kvip*. In the sense of "he acts like a girl" (*kumārīvācarati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *kvip* may optionally be added after all nominal stems. The *k* and *p* are elided. The *v* is elided by the rule *verapṛktasya*. Since it is a verbal root by virtue of the rule *sanādyantāḥ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

And for that [suffix], as before, there is total elision (*kṛtsnalopa*). Thus the form is *kumārī*. Nor should one suspect a shortening by the rule *gostriyoḥ* on the grounds that the word *kumārī* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) with respect to the meaning of the *kvip* suffix;
for in the rule *gostriyoḥ*, only a technical (*śāstrīya*) subordinate member is intended.

Because between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the natural (*akṛtrima*), it is the artificial that is understood [by the rule]. Thus, in the case of *halṅyābbhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], there is the elision of the nominative suffix *su*.

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be elision of *su* after a form ending in *kyac*, since by the rule of *pūrvavidhau* [Pāṇini 1.1.57], the elision of *al* would be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present)? For [the rule] states: "That which is elided in *kvip* is not [treated as *sthānivadbhāva*]."
The intention is that [the substitution] is prohibited by the rule *sthānivadbhāva* (P.
1.1.56). (268) *aci śnu-dhātu-bhruvāṃ y-v-or iyaṅ-uvaṅau* (P.
6.4.77). When *kumārī + āṬ* is in this state, [the rule] *iko yaṇ aci* (P. 6.1.77) applies.

Fearing that one might suspect an exception regarding *yaṇ*, he says: "before *ac*, [the substitution of] *śnu*. *Yū* refers to *i* and *u*; the meaning is "before *i* and *u* vowels" (*ivarṇa* and *uvarṇa*). *Śnu*, *dhātu*, and *bhrū* form a *dvandva* compound. By the paribhāṣā governing the mention of suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), what is intended is that which ends in the suffix *śnu*.

The term *ṭhyvoḥ* is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself; therefore, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to it. However, because *śnu* and *bhū* invariably end in the vowel *u*, the term is not a qualifier of them. Furthermore, because [the roots *śnu* and *bhū*] cannot possibly end in the vowel *i*, the term is not a qualifier of them either. For it is said: "A qualifier is meaningful only when there is both possibility [of its application] and deviation [from its scope]."
By logical necessity (*nyāya*). Since "of the [verbal] root" (*dhātoḥ*) is the governing rule (*adhikṛtam*), it follows that [the operation occurs] when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows.
The term *aci* is its qualifier. This is a rule of "application to what begins with that" (*tadādividhiḥ*).
Thus he says: "of that which ends in the suffix *śnu*" and so forth. Why [mention] *yvoḥ*? [Consider] *cakratuḥ*. [The rule applies] when *aci* [follows].
What [is it that one would obtain]? One would obtain [the entire stem].
Fearing that *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* might be substitutes for the whole [stem] because they consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), he says:
"By the rule *ṅc*, these are substitutes for the final [phoneme]. Nor [does this conflict with] the rule "for *śnu*, verbal roots, and *bhrū*, when followed by *i* or *u* vowels..."
It should not be said that "let this be explained in such a way, but let this [suffix] not be applied," for if that were the case,

there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in examples such as *kṣipati*. Nor can it be argued that this is avoided by the rule "when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows," because the status of being followed by a suffix is a qualification of the stem (*aṅga*) as implied by the term "stem" itself.

Enough with this, as it has already been raised. Regarding "due to internal similarity" (*āntaratamyāt*): the meaning is that for the *ivarṇa* which has the palate as its place of articulation, there is *iyaṅ* of exactly that same nature; and for the *uvarṇa* which has the lips as its place of articulation, there is *uvaṅ* of exactly that same nature.
This being the case, when *iyaṅ* would [otherwise] apply—as in examples such as *kumārī + au*—[the rule *aci nudhātu...* applies]. This is the remainder of the sense.

(269) *eranekāco 'saṃyogapūrvasya* | Pāṇini 6.4.82. *eranekācaḥ*: The term *yaṇ* is understood to carry over from the previous rule *iṇo yaṇ*. *Eḥ* is in the genitive case; it means "of that which has the vowel *i*. Although in the preceding rule there was a compound enumeration (*dvandva*) as *śnudhātubhruvām*, [the word *eḥ* here refers specifically to the final *i* of a verbal root].

The term *dhātoḥ* (of the root), having been separated [from the previous rule], is carried forward as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) ending, but not *śnu* and *bhrū* as well, because the vowel *i* is absent in those cases. Furthermore, the term *dhātoḥ* which has been carried forward is repeated:
one instance is in the genitive denoting a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), while the other is in the genitive denoting a locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). And the term *eḥ* is also [governed by] *dhātoḥ*.
This is a qualifier of the genitive ending; from that, there is an application of the rule *tadanta* (pertaining to what ends with that). The meaning is "of a verbal root ending in an *i*-vowel.

This genitive ending denoting a part, namely *dhātoḥ* ("of a verbal root"), connects with the portion concerning *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) in the rule *ṭhasaṃyogapūrvasya*. [Thus, it means] "that from which a consonant cluster belonging to a part of the verbal root precedes."

"Preceded by the conjunction of stem-constituent parts" (*dhātvavayavasaṃyogapūrvaḥ*); "different from that" (*tadbhinnaḥ*) means "not preceded by such a conjunction. The word "of that" (*tasya*) is a qualifier for the *i*-vowel. The term "of the base" (*aṅgasya*), which is supplied as the governing rule (*adhikṛtam*), is qualified by the root ending in the genitive case; this is a case of the "rule of inclusion of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhiḥ*). "That which has more than one vowel" (*anekāca*) refers to that [base] which possesses multiple vowels.
Thus, this [rule] pertains to that which follows a stem (*aṅga*). From the rule *ṭhaci śnudhātubhrāvām*, the term *aci* is understood to carry over.

That [term *aci*] qualifies the affix implied by the word "stem," and thus there is an application of the rule *tadādividhiḥ* (the operation applies to what begins with that). This is stated by the words "part of a verbal root" (*dhātvavayava*) and so forth. [This is necessary] for the sake of preventing the substitution of *yaṇ* in examples such as *hariṃ* and *harīn*.

The term "dhātoḥ" (of the root) is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem). Otherwise, as in the case of *pradhyam* and similar forms, the *yaṇ* substitution would occur, overriding the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) rule and others. However, the purpose of qualifying the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) with "being a part of the root" (*dhātvavayava*) will be explained in the root text during the analysis of the word *unnī*.
This will become clear [later]. It would be easier to state simply: *anekācaḥ asaṃyogāt*.

The term *yvoḥ* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning obtained is: "that which ends in an *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel which does not follow a conjunct consonant that is part of the verbal root. However, as for the rule *oḥ supi*:

The purpose is restrictive (*niyamārtha*): [the rule applies] that *yaṇ* occurs for the vowel *u* only before a case-ending (*sup*). Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *luluvatuḥ*, and so forth; this suffices. Thus ends the section on *yaṇ*. In the cases *kumāryau* and *kumāryaḥ*, the meaning is that *yaṇ* serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to *iyaṅ* by the rule "er anekācaḥ. Now, [one might object] regarding the internal *sup*...

Since the word *kumārī*, ending in the suffix *aṅ* (amāpyajanta), possesses the status of a *pada*, the rule "ṭhiko'savarṇe" would cause the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). If it is argued that even though the elision of *a* (*allopasya*) is treated as if it were in its original position (*sthānivadbhāva*), the aforementioned difficulty remains unavoidable by relying on that very fact—this is not so; for by the rule "naḥ kye," [the prohibition applies] only when the stem ends in *n* before the *kyac* suffix.
Because of the restriction regarding the status of being a *pada* (a word-form), [the rule] "before *ami* and *śas*" applies.

Since *iyaṅ* would apply—barring both the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) before *ami* and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same class as the preceding) before *śas*—the rule "for a stem ending in *ṭh*, if it has more than one vowel," provides the *yaṇ* substitute as an exception to that.
Thus, the forms are *kumāryām* before *ami* and *kumāryaḥ* before *śas*. [This is further governed by] the rule "after that [stem], before *śas*."

But it is not so in your case, because there is an absence of what follows a previously formed *savarṇa-dīrgha* (long vowel by class-similarity). Thus, the point is that, in comparison with the word *bahuśreyasī*, there is a difference in form only for the [accusative] endings *am* and *śas*.

Regarding *pradhī*: *pradhīḥ* means "one who meditates intensely" (*pradhyāyati*). The suffix *kvip* is applied [to the root *dhyai*] according to the rule: "There is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the root *dhyai*."
The *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *y* is the vowel *i*. By the rule "after a *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*saṃprasāraṇācca*), the single substitute is the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*).
By the rule "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*), there is lengthening. Because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus the case endings (*sup*) arise.

Since it does not end in an *aṅga* [ending in *a*], there is no elision of the nominative singular *su*. In all cases beginning with vowels, by the rule "for a word with more than one vowel," the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.

Because it is not feminine, the grammatical operations pertaining to the *nadī* (feminine) class do not apply. Thus: *he pradhīḥ*, *pradhyau*, *pradhyaḥ*; *pradhyaṃ*, *pradhyaḥ*; *pradhyā*; *pradhye*;

*pradhyoḥ*; *pradhyi*. However, in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "one whose length is excellent" (*prakṛṣṭā dīrghasya saḥ*), because the word *dī* is invariably feminine, [the rule] "and the mention of the gender of the first [word]" (*prathamaliṅgagrahaṇaṃ ca*) applies.

Because it is treated as a river-name (*nadī*), it takes the grammatical operations prescribed for rivers. Because it ends in a long vowel (*aṅ*), there is no elision of the case-ending *su*. *pradhīḥ* (the wise one). The remainder is like the previously cited *kvip*-derived form *kumārī*. *he pradhi* (O wise one); *pradhyau*; *pradhyaḥ*. *pradhyam*; *pradhyau*;
*pradhyaḥ*. *pradhyā*; *pradhyai*; *pradhyā* (instrumental dual); *pradhīnām* (genitive plural).
In *pradhyām*:

[the form] *unnīḥ*. By the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc., the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *ud*. There is the arising of a *sub*-ending. Because it ends in a non-conjugational (*aṅ*) affix, there is no elision of the *su* ending. However, when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows...

By the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ*, *yaṇ* [substitution] applies. Now, one might ask: "Since the vowel *i* here is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), how can *yaṇ* apply here? To this, he says: "by the root" (*dhātunā*). The *yaṇ* substitution is excluded only for those vowels preceded by a conjunct that is part of the root (*dhātu*). The point is that in this case, the conjunct is not a part of the root. [Thus it becomes] *he unnīḥ*.

The point is that because it is not feminine (*astrī*) and not a river-name (*anadī*), the grammatical operations applicable to a *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long ī or ū) do not apply by the rule beginning with *ambārtha*.
As for *unnyaṃ*: the point is that the *yaṇ* substitution is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of *pūrvarūpa* (vocalization of the preceding vowel). As for "O *unnī*" (*he unnī*):
the point is that because it is not feminine and not a river-name, the grammatical operations applicable to a *nadī* do not apply by the rule beginning with *ambārtha*. [As for] *unnyaṃ*.

The meaning is that there is an exception to the *pūrvarūpa* (the substitution of the preceding vowel with the following one) by the rule *yaṇ*. In the case of the suffixes beginning with *śas*, [we have] *unnyaḥ*, *unnyā*, *unnye*, *unnyaḥ*, *unnyoḥ*. Regarding the rule *ReĀrām*: even though the status of being a *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long *ī* or *ū*) does not apply here, the suffix *ām* occurs because the word *nī* is mentioned separately in the sūtra *ReĀrām*; and since it is part of a nominal stem (*aṅga*), it applies even after a word ending in the root *nī*.

That which comes into being is called *bhāva*. Similarly, there is the word *grāmaṇīḥ*. One who leads (*nayati*) or guides (*niyacchati*) a village is a *grāmaṇīḥ*. The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule: "The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *nī* is prescribed after the words *pra* and *agrama*. [Question: Why [is the condition] "having more than one vowel" (*anekācaḥ*) stated? [Answer: This is the remainder [of the context] from the rule "the suffix *ṭhaN* after a root having more than one vowel" (*eranekācaḥ*). [Example: *nīḥ*—from the root *nī*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied as in the previous case (*pūrvavat*). Because there is no absence of multiple vowels (*anekāctva*), *yaṇ* does not occur; rather, by the rule "ṭhaci śnudhātu," *iyaṅ* is substituted. The point is that this alone constitutes the difference between this word and the word *unnī*.
Regarding *suśriyau*: from the root *śriñ* (in the sense of "service"), the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "kvibvacī" and so forth.

And [the vowel] *prakṛti* is long. [In the word] *suśrīḥ*, meaning "he who performs well" (*su śrayati*) or "he whose prosperity is beautiful" (*śobhanā śrīr asya*), the *yaṇ* substitution does not occur when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows. The point is that the *i*-vowel is preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) that is part of a verbal root (*dhātu*). [In the example] *yavakriyau*, [it refers to those who] perform barley-work (*yavān*).

"Yavakrīḥ" means "one who buys barley" (*krīṇāti yavān iti yavakrīḥ*). This is the form derived from the root *krī* with the suffix *kvip*. Here too, the sense is that the *yaṇ* substitution does not occur because the root contains a *saṃyoga* (a cluster of consonants) as its initial element.
Regarding this, there is a *vārttika* on the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ* which states: "It is desired [that the substitution applies] only when preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*."

Having read [the rule], he summarizes its intent with the words *gatikāraketara-* (Pāṇini 6.2.139). For if one were to follow the literal wording [of the sūtra], the *yaṇ* substitution would not occur in the example word *kumārī*, which ends in a *kvip* suffix. Regarding the phrase *śuddhadhiyau*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "those whose intellect (*dhī*) is pure (*śuddhā*). In this context, [the role] of the word *śuddha*...

The meaning is that *yaṇ* does not occur for [a word] preceded by a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or anything other than these. However, in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one meditates on pure Brahman" (*śuddhaṃ brahma dhyāyati*), *yaṇ* would indeed occur—resulting in forms such as *śuddhadhyau*.
[Question: How then? [Answer: If *yaṇ* is excluded only when preceded by a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or something other than these...

However, in the case of a word preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, the *yaṇ* [substitution] is mandatory; therefore, the syntactical connection is: "how then [could there be forms such as] *durdhiyaḥ* (one of evil intellect) or *vṛścikamiyaḥ* (one who fears the scorpion)? By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), forms such as *durdhiyau* and *vṛścikabhiyau* are included. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those whose intellect (*dhī*) is ill-situated (*duḥsthitā*). Or, according to the rule *ṭhprādibhyo dhātujasya vā*, [the substitution is optional].

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule "cotarapadalopaḥ," involving the elision of the latter member. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "fear from a scorpion" (*vṛścikād bhīḥ*). Here, because *duḥ* functions as a *gati* and because the scorpion is the source of the fear (*apādāna*), [the rules apply].

The objection is that, since the status of being a *gati* (preverb) is prior to the status of being a *kāraka* (case-role), and in the absence of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the substitution *yaṇ* would be unavoidable here as an exception to *iyaṅ*. It is said: [this is] the "resolution" (*parihāra*).

The remainder [of the sentence] is "the status of being a *gati* simply does not exist. This refers to the fact that [terms like] *pra* and so on [are designated as] *upasargas* when in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*) and as *gatis* [only] under those same conditions.

In the context of verbal action (*kriyānvaya*), the designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) have been prescribed. Furthermore, the word *dhī* denotes the quality of intellect (*buddhiguṇa*) and is not a denoter of action. Therefore, *duḥ* does not function as a motion (*gati*) in relation to it;

thus, due to the absence of being preceded by a motion, the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply here, but rather the rule for *iyAṄ* and *uvaṄ* applies—this is the meaning. [Objection: But what of that which has been elided?

Since a word denoting a state (sthitāśabda) indeed possesses the status of a motion (*gati*) with respect to that which serves as the cause for the commencement of an action, he says: "by whatever action" (*yatkriya*). The meaning is that prepositions (*prādayaḥ*), when joined with whatever action, are designated as *gati* and *upasarga* only with respect to that very word which expresses that [action].

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, since the word *sthitāḥ* has been elided, the word *duḥ* possesses the status of a prefix (*gati*) by virtue of being preceded by a verb, and thus the word *dur-dhaḥ* indeed has the quality of being preceded by a verb; for the status of being a prefix (*gati*) or an upasarga belongs only with respect to that which expresses the very action with which the prefixes like *pra* and others are connected.

This is because it is intended that the operation of a prefix (upasarga) applies only to that which expresses an action (*kriyā*) of such a kind; this is obtainable through the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) as expressed in the rule *yatkriyāyuktāḥ*. As for the word *vṛścika*, the status of the scorpion as the point of departure (*apādāna*) is not intended here.
And the phrase "those connected with the action" (*yatkriyāyuktāḥ*) is obtained through the principle of proximity. Regarding the word *vṛścika* ("scorpion"):

the connection is that the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) for the word *vṛścika* is not intended here. Why? To this he says: "produced by the intellect" (*buddhikṛtam*). The meaning is "superimposed. For the status of being an *apādāna*...

The state of being the limit of separation (*viśleṣāvadhitva*). For in the case of "the leaf falls from the tree," the tree alone possesses the status of the limit of separation regarding the leaf; however, in the case of "fear [comes] from the scorpion," the scorpion does not possess the status of the limit of separation regarding fear, because—just as the leaf has no prior contact with the tree—the fear likewise lacks any prior contact with the scorpion. This is because separation...

Because it is preceded by a connection (*saṃśleṣa*). And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "The case-relations (*kāraka*) are [determined] according to what is intended to be expressed. In the present case, since the superimposition (*āropa*) of the status of an ablative (*apādānatva*) upon the scorpion depends on the speaker's intention (*vaktradhīnatva*), and since such a superimposition is not made here, one resorts to the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) with the view of expressing a mere relationship (*sambandhamātra*), as in "of the scorpion" (*vṛścikasya*).

In the case of the compound *bhī-ṛti*, the derivation of the word *vṛścikabhī* is accepted as being based on a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound. Consequently, because it is preceded by something other than a *kāraka*, the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply here; this is the intended meaning. Nor [should it be argued] that in examples such as *vṛścikād bhīḥ*, the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative point) is assumed solely on the basis of a mental construction (*buddhikṛta*).

It should not be argued that the rule *bhītrārthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.25) is redundant because of the occurrence of the fifth case (*pañcamī*); for that rule has been rejected in the Bhāṣya, and thus its application is desired—enough of this. He states another solution: "connected with a scorpion" (*vṛścikasambandhinī*). [He says] "of the second member" (*uttarapada*).

The meaning is that in the compound *vṛścikasambandhinī*, there is an elision (*lopa*) of the word *sambandhinī* in the latter member of the first constituent, because it belongs to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva*. The word *sudhī* is formed from the analysis *suṣṭhu dhyāyati* (he meditates well) or *su-śobhanā dhīr yasya* (one whose intellect is very beautiful). In this case, when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows, [the rule] "of a polysyllabic stem ending in /ṭhi/" applies.

Thus, when *yaṇ* would [otherwise] apply—(270) *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* | P. 6.4.85. "Not for *bhū* and *sudhī*. From the rule *iṇo yaṇ* [P. 6.4.81], the word *yaṇ* is understood; from the rule *thoḥ supi* [P. 6.4.84], the word *supi* is understood.
The word *supi* [is understood], and from the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci*, the word *aci* also carries over.

Thus he says, "of these two," and so forth. "Of these two" refers to the roots *bhū* and *sudhī* mentioned in the sūtra. "In *aci*" means "before a vowel-initial [suffix]. When the *yaṇ* [substitution] is prohibited...
Intending this, he says: "by the wise" (*sudhiyā*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is a comprehensive inclusion of all [suffixes] beginning with *ajādi*.
The forms are like those of *pradhī*; this alone is the distinction. The fact of the matter is that it occurs before a vowel (*aci*);

for there is no possibility of *yaṇ* substitution before a suffix beginning with a consonant (*anaj-ādi*). Why say "before a case-ending" (*supi*)? Consider: *sudhībhir upāsyaḥ* (to be worshipped by the wise) becomes *sudhyupāsyaḥ*.

In reality, however, *sūp* should not be carried over [from the previous rule]. For there is no possibility of the application of *yaṇ* here by the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ*, since that [rule] prescribes *yaṇ* before an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi-pratyaya*), and the word *upāsya* is not an affix. However, the rule *iko yaṇaci* does indeed apply, according to the principle *anantarasya* ("that which is immediately preceding").

According to the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ* and because the prohibition [of *yaṇ*] applies only to that which has already undergone the *yaṇ* replacement by the rule *ṭhoḥ supi*, [the substitution does not occur here]. However, in the case of *sudhyupāsyaḥ* (to be worshipped by the wise), although the prohibition *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* would apply to the *yaṇ* [substitution] based on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), the word *upāsyaḥ* [remains as it is].

Thus, relying on this [rule], the *yaṇ* substitution indeed occurs by the rule "ṭhiko yaṇ aci," because there is no prohibition of that [substitution] here according to the maxim "anantara-sya" (the operation applies to what is immediately preceding). Enough of this.
Regarding the form *sakhīyati*: when the suffix *kyac* is applied to the word *sakhi* by the rule "supa ātmanaḥ," [the following occurs].

By the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayor dīrghaḥ*, the form *sakhīyati* is produced. From that, [the suffix] *kvip*: the meaning is that from the word *sakhīya*, which is designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*) by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvip ca*. Then, by the rule *allopo 'naḥ* and *lopo vyor vali*, [the *a* and *y* are elided]. By the rule *ato lopaḥ*...

The meaning is that by the rule "lopaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *a* following the letter *y*, and by the rule "lopo vyoḥ," there is the elision of *y*. When the elision of *y* (yalopa) is to be performed, the elision of *a* (allopa) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original), because the status of being *sthānivat* is prohibited for the elision of *y* by the rule "na padānte. [The phrase] "due to *sthānivatva*" refers to the rule "acaḥ... [etc.].

The phrase "by this [rule]" is to be understood as referring to *parasmin* (in the presence of another). Regarding the statement "when *yaṇ* is about to occur," the ellipsis is: "of the vowel *ī* following the letter *kh*, by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*. Nor should one suspect a prohibition based on the rule *na padānte* ("not at the end of a word"), because the status of being a word-final (*padāntatva*) is precluded by the internal *sup* suffix; furthermore, in the case of the *kyac* affix—as in the rule *naḥ kye*—it is only that which ends in *n* [that is affected].

Because it is a word (*padatvāt*). Regarding the phrase "when *kvip* is elided" (*kvau lupte*), this refers to the Vārttika on the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58), which states: "An addition [should be made] regarding the elision of *kvip*, the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), the *aṅ* augment, the shortening of a vowel (*paranirhrāsa*), and the substitution of *ku*."

This is the explanation of the portion "ṭhkvilugiti. In that context, it is clear from the Bhāṣya itself that by "ṭhlu" (the suffixes ṭhak and luk), elision (*lopa*) is intended. The word "luptam" is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). The meaning is that an elision occurring when followed by a *kvip* suffix is not treated as if it were still present (*na sthānivat*). And therefore—

The point is that because the vowel *ī* following the letter *kh* is not preceded by a vowel (*ac*), the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply. Although in the rule *na padānte*, the principle *kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat* ("that which is elided before the suffix *kvip* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*") was rejected,

and it was instead accepted that *kvau vidhiṃ prati na sthānivat* ("before the suffix *kvip*, a substitute is not *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to an operation"), nevertheless, [this applies] in the case of *gomatyateḥ* with the suffix *kvip*.

It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that, based on the commentary stating "one who possesses cows" (*gomān*), there are cases where what is elided by *kvip* is not treated as if it were present (*na sthānivat*). Consequently, in the sense of "desiring a friend," the form *sakhī*, ending in long *ī*, is established; from that, the case endings (*sub*) arise.

Regarding the phrase "anaṅṇitve" (the substitution of *anaṅ* and the *ṇi*-mark): the remainder [of the meaning] is that [these two rules] apply by virtue of both "ṭhanaṅ sau" and "sakhyurasambuddhau. One might ask: since the substitution of *anaṅ* and the *ṇi*-mark is prescribed for the word *sakhi* ending in short *i*, how could they apply to the word *sakhī* ending in long *ī*? To this, he says: "by means of a portion," as in the example "he sakhīḥ."

Because it ends in a verbal suffix (*aṅg*), there is no elision of the *su* case-ending. Due to the absence of femininity and the consequent absence of the designation *nadī*, the grammatical operations specific to *nadī* do not apply.
Regarding the phrase "when *yaṇ* is about to occur": the remainder of the sense is that this would occur by the rule *ṭeranekācaḥ*.
Regarding "the *yaṇ* [substitution] in the presence of *śas*": the *yaṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).

The sense is that because the long vowel *savarṇadīrgha* (resulting from the previous rule) has not been applied, the substitution of *n* does not occur. [The forms are: *sakhyā*, *sakhye*, *sakhyuḥ*, *sakhyoḥ*, *sakhyau*. [The etymology is: "together with *kha*"; *kha* means either the sky (*ākāśa*) or the letter *kh*.
The compound is a *bahuvrīhi* according to the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge*. [The form is derived] by the rule *vopasarjanasya*.
It is the essential nature (*sabhāva*). "One who desires that" means "one who desires happiness for oneself"; in this sense, the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ*.
By the rule *kyaci ca*, there is the substitution of long *ī* (for the short *u* of *sukha*), and because it is a verbal root by the rule *sanādyantāḥ*, the suffix *kvip* is added;
following the elision of the *a* and the *y*, the word *sakhī* is formed. The words *sukhī* and *sutī* are formed in the same manner.

Regarding the word *sakhī*: because it ends in a short vowel (*aṅ*), there is no elision of the case-ending suffix (*su*). Thus we have *sakhyau*, and so forth. The intention is that when a vowel-initial suffix follows, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs according to the rule "for a polysyllabic stem ending in *ṭh*. [The form] *sakhyam* [is derived from *sakhi-am*]. [In the dual] *sakhyaḥ* and [in the instrumental] *sakhyā*. [In the dative] *sakhye*. Regarding the phrase "even for the long [vowel]": the intention is that the mention in that rule (*Pāṇini 6.1.108*) is made using a form where the *yaṇ* has already been applied, precisely for this purpose.

In *sakhyām* and *sakhyi*, the same applies to the words *sukhī* and *sutī*. Regarding *lūnīḥ*: it is derived from the root *lūñ* (meaning "to cut") with the suffix *kta*; by the rule *tvādibhyaḥ*, there is the substitution of *na* [for *n*]; in the *kyac* formation, there is the substitution of *ī*; because it is not treated as a verbal root (*aṅyantratvāt*), there is no elision of the *su* [of *sukham*]. Regarding *kṣāyaḥ*: it is derived from the root *kṣai* (meaning "to perish") with the suffix *kta*; by the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śitī*, there is the substitution of *ā*; [then] by the rule *kṣāyo...* [there is the substitution of *ī*].

The substitution of *ma* [for *m*] is indicated by "maḥ. The suffixes *kyac* and so forth are applied as before. Regarding the form *prastīmi*: the root is *ṣṭyai* or *ṣṭyaḷ*, meaning "to sound" or "to collect. The suffix *kta* is added; by the rule "ādeca upadeśe'śiti," there is the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel. By the rule "prastyo'nyatarasyām," the substitution of *ma* [for *m*] occurs. Then, by the rule "styaḥ prapūrvasya," there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
The *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) is applied by the rule *samprasāraṇācca*; the lengthening is applied by the rule *halaḥ*.

The forms beginning with *kyac* are as before, such as *sakhī*, *sutī*, and so on. Regarding the form *yaṇ* for the cases *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, the remainder [of the explanation] is "by the rule *eranekācaḥ*. Immediately after the phrase "because of being *asiddha*,"...

The phrase "because it follows that [rule]" is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Regarding *śuṣkīyate*: this is a reference by means of the *śtip* affix, according to the rule "the suffixes *ik*, *śit*, and *tap* are used when referring to a verbal root. From the root *śuṣ*, the suffix *kta* is added, resulting in *śuṣkaḥ*.
The substitution of *ka* for the final letter occurs according to the rule "for *śuṣ*, [substitute] *ka*. In the sense of "one who desires *śuṣka* for oneself," [the suffix *kyac* is applied].
The meaning is that from the root *śuṣkīy*, which ends in a *kyac* suffix, the form *śuṣkī* arises through the application of the *kvip* suffix;

because it does not end in an *aṅ* suffix, there is no elision of the case-ending *su*. The word *śuṣkī* is like words such as *sakhī* and *sutī*. In forms such as *śuṣkiyau*, there is no *yaṇ* substitution because of the preceding conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), but rather the *iyaṅ* substitution—this is the distinction.

Such is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). Regarding the rule *ṅsi-ṅsoḥ śuṣkiya*, one should not suspect that the substitution of *u* (by *khyatyāt parasya*) applies because the substitution of *k* (*katva*) is considered *asiddha*; the point is that once the substitute *iy* has occurred, the condition for the application of the *yaṇ*-substitution no longer exists. Thus end the words ending in long *ī*. [The word] *śambhuḥ* is like *hariḥ*.

In that context, the long vowel *ū* arises from the rule of "prior homogeneous lengthening" (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), while the *o* vowel arises from "guṇa" substitution; the specific exceptions such as *av-ityādi*, however, are connected through their internal proximity (*āntaratamya*). [This is derived] from the root *kruś* in the sense of "calling out" or "weeping," by the rule: *sitanigamimasisacyavidhāñkruśibhyastun*.

Thus, with the suffix *tun*, the letter *ś* of the root *kruś* becomes *ṣ* by the rule *ṭh-vraśca*, and subsequently becomes *ṭ* by the rule *ṣṭuan*; hence the word *kroṣṭu*. With the suffix *tṛc* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) applied to the root *kruś*, however, the word is *kroṣṭṛ*. Both [words] denote the jackal (*sṛgāla*).

(271) *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.95. Since the application of both [forms] would otherwise occur everywhere without distinction, he states this to show the specific rule: *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*. By the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the term "tṛc" [is understood].
The form ending in *tṛc* is understood [as the base]. The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the third case by the rule *tena tulyam*.
From the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne*, the term *sarvanāmasthāne* is carried over (anuvartate);
and from the rule *sakhyurasaṃbuddhau*, the term *asaṃbuddhau* is also carried over.

Thus he says: "By [the rule] *kroṣṭus-tṛjantena*," and so forth. As it is said: "Effect, form, cause, purpose, treatise, identity, and designation—these seven are declared to be the extensions (*atideśas*). Among these, there are seven such extensions. In that regard:

Here, by virtue of its predominance, only the form ending in *tṛc* is extended [by analogy]; and that is not forms such as *kartṛ* or *bhartṛ*, but rather specifically the form *kroṣṭṛ* that is extended. This is intended because the root *kruś* is present [in the mind] and because of semantic proximity (*ārthata āntarya*).

He states the result: "in place of the word *kroṣṭu*. We shall, however, demonstrate the examples for the causes (*nimitta*) and so forth in their respective places. When *kroṣṭu-s* is established, [the rule applies]:
(272) *ṛto ṅsirvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110).

From the rule *ṛto ṅ*, the term *guṇa* is understood from the preceding rule *ṭhhrisvasya guṇaḥ*. The governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is qualified by *ṛtaḥ* (of that which ends in ṛ), and thus there is an application of the "designation of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*). He states this as *ṅavi* (in a word ending in a ṅ-suffix).

(273) *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasāṃ ca* | 7|1|94 | The [words] *ṛt*, *uśanas*, *purudaṃsas*, and *anehas* [are mentioned]. From the rule *sakhyurasaṃbuddhau*, the term *asaṃbuddhau* ("except in the vocative singular") is carried over;
and from the rule *anaṅ sau*, the term *anaṅ* is carried over.
The term "of the stem" (*ṭhaṅgasya*), which is the subject under discussion, is qualified by "clay and so forth" (*mṛdādibhiḥ*). Thus he says: "of those ending in *ṛ*.

It should be understood that the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) applies even to words such as *uśanas* and others. *Anaṅ* is [the substitute] with the marker *ṅ*; the vowel *a* after the *n* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By the rule "when *ṅ* follows," there is an internal substitution (*it*); thus, when *kroṣṭan* followed by *s* is established, [the following operations apply].
(274) *aptṛntṛcsvasṛnaptṛneṣṭṛtvaṣṭṛkṣattṛhotṛpotṛpraśāstṛṇām* || 6.4.11 || Regarding *aptṛn*: from the rule *ṭhnopadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* is understood to carry over.

The phrase "except for [the word] *cāsaṃbuddhau*" from the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau* continues [into this context]. Thus he says: "of *ab* and so forth. Here, in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are prescribed in the sense of the agent by the rules *tṛn* and *ṇvultṛcau*. Likewise...

Having prescribed the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* by means of the two rules—"In the *uṇādi* [section], *tṛn* and *tṛc* are added after roots such as *śaṃs*, *kṣā*, and *dā*, provided they form proper names (*saṃjñā*) and are not subject to the augment *iṭ*; [this applies] diversely (*bahulam*) in other cases as well"—the forms *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *mātṛ*, *pitṛ*, and *duhitṛ* are established as *nipātana*s (irregularly formed words) by the rule "naptṛ-neṣṭṛ-tvaṣṭṛ-hotṛ-potṛ-bhrātṛ-jāmātṛ-mātṛ-pitṛ-duhitṛ. Consequently, the established position is that these proper-name words ending in *tṛn* and *tṛc* belong to the *uṇādi* class. In that regard, since the forms would be established simply by virtue of ending in *tṛc*, the inclusion of *naptṛ* and the others [in the rule] would be redundant; therefore, he says: "The mention of *naptṛ* and the others... [is for the purpose of...]
He states the body of the restrictive rule (*niyama*)—namely, "in the *uṇādi* [list]": by that [rule].

The sense is that among the *uṇādi*-derived forms, the long vowel occurs only for the seven beginning with *naptr*, which end in *tṛn* and *tṛc*; by this very restriction, others such as *pitṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, and so on, do not have the long vowel. Nor [does this apply to] the word *praśāstṛ*.

One should not be deluded into thinking that [the word *naptr̥*] is not derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes; for even this technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) belongs to the *uṇādi* class by virtue of its inclusion in the *śaṃsi-kṣadādi* group. Here, by the statement in the root-text, "in the view of derivation," [it is implied that] in the view of non-derivation, the seven [terms] beginning with *naptr̥* [are established].
Since the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are absent, the rule would not otherwise apply; thus, the inclusion of *naptr* and others in the list is purposeful.

It is indicated that for other words such as *pitṛ* and *mātṛ*, which belong to the *uṇādi* group and are considered *avyutpanna* (irregularly formed), there is no lengthening precisely because they lack the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*. Now, if this is the case...

One might ask: since the word *udgātṛ* is a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*) derived from the *uṇādi* class under the rule for roots beginning with *śaṃs* and *kṣad*, and since it is not included among the seven suffixes beginning with *nvi* and *tṛc*, how can there be lengthening of the vowel?
To this, he says: "of the word *udgātṛ*. However, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, it is stated:
It has been explained that one should simply say *ṭhaptṛ* and omit the mention of both *tṛn* and *tṛc*.

However, in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the rule *ṭhtṛn*, it is stated that in the prescription of *tṛn*, it should be added: "after [roots] ending in *ṛ* and after *ṛtvij*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix. Examples are *hotā* (priest) and *potā* (purifier). Why "not preceded by a prefix"? Consider *praśāstā* (director).

*Pratihartā*: This word ends in the suffix *tṛc* according to the *āuṇādika* [list]. Regarding the root *ṇī*, it should be stated that the suffix *tṛn* is applied and there is the augment *ṣuk*. Thus: *neṣṭā*. Regarding the root *tviṣ*, it should be stated that the suffix *tṛn* is applied when referring to a deity, and that the penultimate vowel becomes *a* and the root is treated as non-*iṭ*. Thus: *tvaṣṭā*. Regarding the root *kṣad*, it should be stated that the suffix *tṛn* is applied when it is connected with the sense of "fitting" or "suitable. Thus: *kṣattā*.
Thus, the words *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, and *kṣattṛ* have been derived as being formed with the suffix *tṛn*.
According to that view, however, the inclusion of these five here is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).
The inclusion of *naptṛ* and *praśāstṛ* is for the purpose of stating the aforementioned restriction; this is explained in detail elsewhere. [The example] *kroṣṭṛ*.

When *kroṣṭan* is established, because the partially modified form is not different [from the original], it is treated as ending in *-tṛ*; thus, the long vowel [is applied]. Then, by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*, there is the elision of the case-ending *su*. There is also the elision of the *n*. Although the lengthening is established here even by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, nevertheless...

Because it is subsequent, the long vowel is more logical [to apply] only when *aptṛ* is present, as in *kroṣṭārau*. When *kroṣṭu-a-āṬ* is situated, there is the substitution of *tṛjvat* (the form of the agentive suffix *tṛc*). When *kroṣṭu-a-ā* is situated, [the rule applies]:
(275) *vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣv aci* | Pāṇini 7.1.97. [In the case of *kroṣṭu*,] the substitution of *tṛjvat* is optional before vowels beginning with the third case-ending.
The third case [ending] is under discussion. The rule *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.95) is understood to follow here.

The term *aci* is a qualifier for the case endings beginning with the third case; it is a *tadādividhi* (a rule that applies to what begins with that). Thus he says: "in those beginning with vowels. Regarding *kroṣṭrā*: when the substitution of *tṛjvat* has occurred, resulting in the form *kroṣṭṛ-ā*, the *ṛ*-vowel is replaced by its *yaṇ* substitute, which is *r*.
Similarly for *kroṣṭu*: in the absence of the substitution of *tṛjvat*, [the forms are] *kroṣṭunā* and *kroṣṭave*, like *śambhu*. (276) *ṛta ut* 6.1.111.

When *kroṣṭﬁa* remains in the form *kroṣṭﬁa-as* after the application of the rule *ṛjvat* [Pāṇini 7.1.94], the rule *ṛta ut* [Pāṇini 6.1.111] applies. From the rules *ṭheṅḥ padāntādati* [Pāṇini 6.1.109] and *ṅsiṅsośca* [Pāṇini 6.1.110], the words *ati* and *ṅsiṅsoḥ* are carried over (*anuvartate*). In the expression *ṅsiṅsoḥ*, the genitive case denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and it connects with the word *ati*.
The term *ṭhaṅ* is the subject under discussion, and it is qualified by the word *ṛta*.
Consequently, by means of the rule for [specifying] that which ends in [a particular element], he states "from that which ends in *ṛ*" and so forth. Regarding the expression *raparatvam*:
it refers to the substitution of the vowel *u* in place of both the vowel *ṛ* and the vowel *a*.

The meaning is that the status of being the substitute for the vowel *ṛ* is not lost. The addition of the *tapara* marker (*u*) in the rule *ud* is for the purpose of excluding the two-mora (*dvimātra*) vowel. One should not argue that this exclusion is already established by the principle that "a vowel being taught as a substitute does not include its non-homogeneous counterparts" (*bhāvyamāno 'savarṇān na gṛhṇāti*); for that principle is not universal, and thus the possibility of a two-mora vowel would still arise here.

Because it serves to exclude that [other possibility], its non-eternality (anityatva) is indicated by this very use of *ta* as a *tapara*. Consequently, Kaiyaṭa states in the commentary on the sūtra *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*: "When followed by *y*, *v*, or *l*, the *y*, *v*, and *l* are optionally nasalized," which implies that for the letter *m*, only nasalized substitutes occur. As for the mention of *taparatva* in the rule *ḍhralope dīrgho'ṇaḥ*, [it is merely for the sake of clarity].

[The claim] that [the term *dīrgha*] is for the sake of preventing lengthening (*dīrghanivṛttyartha*) is incorrect; for it would contradict the usage in the Bhāṣya on the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, which reads: *ṭhū-raḥ paraḥ*. [Consider also: "The arrows, well-feathered and swift, like blazing serpents, were discharged from the chest of Nairṛta like the rays of the sun."
And because it would contradict the performance [of the rules] in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, enough [of this discussion].
(277) *rātsasya* | Pāṇini 8.2.24. When *kroṣṭu-ar-s* is established, [the rule] *rātsasya* applies; otherwise, by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, [the final consonant] would simply be elided.

He says "of that very [word]" (*tasyaiva*) to indicate that this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), even though [the result] is already established. By this, there is no elision of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) in cases such as *ūrk*.

"The visarga of the letter *r*" means that the visarga occurs by the rule "before a vowel or at the end of a word" (*kharavasānayoḥ*). "Because it is subsequent" means that because it is subsequent, the augment *nuṭ* is superseded, and the substitution of the form of the suffix *-tṛc* (*tṛjvat*) takes place.

The meaning is that, after *nuṭ* has been applied and the lengthening by the rule *ṭh-nām-i* has occurred, once *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) has been effected, the form would be *kroṣṭṝṇām*. Nor should it be argued that *nuṭ* is obligatory, because once the substitution of *tṛjvat* has taken place,
*nuṭ* becomes difficult to obtain due to the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the destruction of the cause).

Regarding *num acireti*: *acire* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). The *repha* (the sound *r*) prescribed by the rule *aci ra* is intended here. However, the principle that "an imitation behaves like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇaṃ bhavati*) is not universal. Consequently, even though *aci-re* enters into a compound, there is no elision (*luk*). As for *kroṣṭūnām*, the substitution of the *tṛc*-stem applies.
When the augment *nuṭ* has been applied and the lengthening by the rule "ṭh-nāmī" has occurred, the form is [kroṣṭrī].

As for *kroṣṭari*: when *tṛjvat* has been applied, leaving *kroṣṭu-a*, the form arises through the substitution of *guṇa* by the rule "ṛto ṅī" followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*. As for *kroṣṭroḥ*: when *tṛjvat* has been applied, the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *ṛ* is the letter *ra*.

Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): this means in the alternative view where there is an absence of *tṛjvat* (the substitution of the masculine form ending in *-tṛ*) before vowels beginning with those of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) onwards. Now, one might object that the three rules—"*tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*," "*striyāṃ ca*," and "*vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣvacī*"—are redundant, since the two words *kroṣṭṛ* and *kroṣṭu*, which denote a jackal, are independent [words].

If it is argued that [the form *kroṣṭā*] exists because of its presence [in the sūtras], listen: the three sūtras [Pāṇini 7.1.95–97] are for the purpose of restriction, stating that "the word *kroṣṭṛ* ending in *ṛt* is used only before neuter nominal suffixes (*sarvanāmasthāna*) and in the feminine; however, before the third case and those beginning with *aj*, both forms are used; and before the suffix *śas* and those beginning with a consonant (*hal*), only the form ending in *ud* is used. Thus end the words ending in *ud*.

Now, those ending in long *ū*: *hūhū*. This is an uninflected nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a specific type of Gandharva. [The forms] *hūhvā*, *hūhvaḥ*, and so forth, follow. In the case of the nominative plural (*jasi*), there is a prohibition of the "long vowel homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) by the rule "dīrghāj jasi ca. The form is derived through the *yaṇ* substitution by the rule "ṭhiko yaṇ aci. [The vocative singular is] *he hūhūḥ*.

*hūhūm*, *hūhvau*, *hūhūn*, *hūhvā*; *hūhve*; *hūhvaḥ*; *hūhvoḥ*; *hūhvām*; *hūhvi*. Regarding the word *aticamū*: one who has surpassed the army (*camū*) is *aticamūḥ*. The compound is formed according to the rule: "*ṭhatyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*" (Pāṇini 2.2.18).
Because it does not end in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), the shortening prescribed by the rule *go-striyoḥ* does not occur.
"The operation of a *nadī* [term]"—the sense is that this follows from the statement: "And there is the inclusion of the original gender (*prathamaliṅgagrahaṇam*).
Regarding *khalapū*: [it is derived] as *khalaṃ punāti* with the suffix *kvip*. Thus, we have *khalapū-āṬ* and *khalapū-as*.
When *ṭhac* is present, *u* is obtained by the rule "śnudhātubhruvām yvoḥ iyaṅuvaṅau.
(278) *oḥ supi* | 6.4.83. Regarding *oḥ supi*: the rule "ṭer anekācaḥ" is understood, with the exception of the word *eri*. [This applies] when *ṭhac* is present.
From the rule *anudhātu*, the term *aci* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*). By that, *supi* is qualified.

This is a rule concerning the initial element of the following word (*tadādividhiḥ*). From the rule *ṭhiṇo yaṇ*, the term *yaṇ* is carried over. He states this with the words "being a part of a verbal root," and so forth.

Regarding "gatikāraka": the intention is that this *vārttika* also applies here. [Thus we have] *khalapv-au*, *khalapvaḥ*. The intention is that the *yaṇ* substitution occurs here because it is preceded by a *kāraka*.
[The vocative is] *he khalapūḥ*. [The accusative is] *khalapvam*, *khalapv-au*, *khalapvaḥ*. [The instrumental is] *khalapv-ā*. [The dative is] *khalapve*. [The ablative is] *khalapvaḥ*.

*khalapvaḥ*, *khalapvoḥ*, *khalapvi*. Here, in forms beginning with vowels, the rules "ṭh for a stem with more than one vowel" (*anekācaḥ*) and "yaṇ for ṭhu before a case-ending" (*supi*) apply everywhere as exceptions to the rules for *pūrvarūpa* and *savarṇadīrgha*. In the same way, [the forms of] *sulū* and others are derived. One who cuts well is *sulūḥ*; because it is preceded by a motion [as a prefix], here too—

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), forms such as *kedāralūḥ* are included. Regarding *kaṭaprūḥ*: from the root √*pru* meaning "to move," the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvibvacipracchi...* etc., and there is lengthening of the vowel *u*. Regarding *paramaluvau*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is both supreme (*parama*) and a cutter (*lūḥ*). Because it is preceded by something other than a *gati* or a *kāraka*, the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply.

Regarding "luluvatuḥ": although the element *lulū* contains more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), the rule for *yaṇ* substitution does not apply because it is not preceded by a case-ending (*sup*). Regarding *svabhūḥ*: the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of "one who arises from himself" (*svasmād bhavati*).
Since the word is preceded by a *kāraka* (a participant in action), the rule for *yaṇ* would have applied; therefore, he says: "not in the case of *bhū* or *sudhī*" (*na bhūsudhiyoḥ*).

*Varṣābhūḥ* means "that which exists in the rains"; that is, it is produced during the rainy season (*varṣartu*). The word *varṣa* is always feminine and plural. This is because the author of the Sūtras stated in the section on gender under the heading of feminine nouns in the *Liṅgānuśāsana*: "There is plurality for the words *ap*, *sumanas*, *samāsi*, *katā*, and *varṣā*."

According to Yādava, "varṣābhū" means a male frog (*dadura*). Although the prohibition [of the substitution of *u* for *o*] applies by the rule "not after *bhū*, *su*, or *dhi*" (Pāṇini 6.4.85), [the following sūtra applies]:
(279) "And [the substitution of *u* for *o* occurs] in *varṣābhū*" (Pāṇini 6.4.84).
"And *varṣābhvaḥ*. The [sūtra] *ṭhoḥ supi* is understood to follow. From *ṭhaci śnudhātvi*, *ac* is understood; and from *ṭhiṇo yaṇ*, *yaṇ* is understood. Thus he says: "of this" (*asya*).
This means "of the word *varṣābhū*. Regarding *dṛbhati*: the root *dṛbhī* [meaning] "to weave" belongs to the *tudādi* class.
Because the suffix *śavi* is treated as having the marker *ṅ* by the rule "sārvadhātukam apit," there is no *guṇa* substitution. Regarding the statement "it is a nipātana":
the meaning is that here the suffix *ku* is introduced along with the augment *num*.
By the rule "naścāpadāntasya," an *anusvāra* is substituted [for the *m*], and by the rule "anusvārasya yayi," that *anusvāra* is replaced by a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*).

The letter *m* [is the final element]. And here, the vowel *ū* is not a constituent part of the verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, neither *uvaṅ* nor the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule *ṭhoḥ supi* applies. Rather, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs solely by the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci*. And this [application of *yaṇ*] is set aside by the rule *ami pūrvaḥ*. With this intention, he says: "dṛmbhūm. In the case of the *śas* ending, [the form is derived] by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca*.

Intending to show that the *yaṇ* substitution [prescribed by] "ṭhiko yaṇaci" is superseded by the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) due to the non-application of the prohibition, he says: *dṛmbhūn*. [The forms are: *dṛmbhvā*, *dṛmbhave*, *dṛmbhvaḥ*, *dṛmbhvaḥ*, *dṛmbhvoḥ*, *dṛmbhvām*. But here, in the case of *dṛnkāra*, the *yaṇ* does not apply.

This occurs because in that [previous rule], only the meaningful word *bhū* is taken, whereas here the word *bhū* is meaningless. For the indeclinable *dṛn*, ending in *n*, signifies "injury" (*hiṃsā*). When this is the upapada, the root *bhū* takes the suffix *kvip*; thus, *dṛn* means injury.

The analysis of the compound is *bhavate upāpnoti* (he approaches the state of being). Regarding *dṛnbhūḥ*: it is a specific type of tree; others say it is a specific type of serpent. Here, the nasal *n* is purely phonetic (*svābhāvika*).

Because it is at the end of a word (*padānta*), the rule *naś cāpadāntasya jhali* does not apply to change it to an *anusvāra*. For this very reason, there is no substitution with the following sound (*parasavarṇa*).
When the prohibition "not after *ṭh*, *bhū*, or *sudhī*" has been reached—[the author says] *dṛnkara-punaḥ* [and] *dṛnbhvam*.
The meaning is that the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute short vowel) is set aside by the *yaṇ* [substitution]. [And] *dṛnbhvaḥ*:

the meaning is that the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel resulting from the same preceding and following vowels) is set aside by the *yaṇ* in the case of the [ending] *śas*. [The compound] *karabhava* means "that which exists in the hand" (*kare*) or "from the hand" (*karāt*).
Intending to say that *karabhū* is like *dṛnbhū*, he says: "karabhvam, karabhvaḥ.
Regarding the statement in the cited Vārttika, "dṛnkare," there is another opinion that the word *kāra* with a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is read therein;
to that he says: "dīrgha... [and] "svārthikaḥ. *Svārtha* means the meaning of its own base (*prakṛti*); in that regard—

The suffix *bhava* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). According to the rule "from *adhyātma* etc., [the suffix] *ṭhañ*" and the rule "*aṇ* after *prajñā* etc.," the intention is that the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after words beginning with *prajñā* in their own sense.

In the long-vowel reading (*dīrghapāṭha*), there is only the substitution *uvaṅ* for the vowel preceding *kara*; in the short-vowel reading (*hrasvapāṭha*), there is only the *yaṇ* substitution for the vowel preceding *kara*.

Commentary: [The term] *punarbhū* means "one who becomes again" (*punarbhavati*). Now, since the lexicon states, "A *punarbhū* is a remarried woman (*didhiṣū-rūḍhā*)," and because the word *punarbhū* is feminine, it would be more appropriate to define it only within the section on feminine genders; to this he replies: "The etymological (*yogika*) sense of *punarbhū* applies to the masculine as well."

The meaning is that the word *punarbhū*, which is derived from the action of "becoming again" (*punarbhavati*), also possesses a masculine gender. Regarding *dṛgbhū*: it is one who "becomes [the object of] sight" (*dṛśo bhavati*), hence *dṛgbhūḥ*.
Regarding *kārābhū*: it is one who "exists in a prison" (*kārāyāṃ bhavati*), hence *kārābhūḥ*; *kārā* refers to a place of confinement. It is like *svayambhū*.

The point here is that the substitution *yaṇ* is prohibited by the rule *ṭhna bhūsudhiyoḥ*, and there is no counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to it. Thus end the words ending in *ū*. Now, those ending in *ṛ*: "dhātā" etc. [The root] *ḍudhāñ* [is used in the sense] of supporting and nourishing; in this case, the suffix *tṛn* may optionally take the form *taj*. Like the word *kroṣṭṛ*, there is the substitution of *anaṅ* and lengthening [of the vowel].

There are elisions of *su* and *upana*. In the form "he dhātaḥ," there is no *anaṅ* substitution because the word "except in the vocative" (*asaṃbuddhau*) is understood to follow in the rule *ṛduśanas-puru-daṃśo’naṅ*.

By the rule *ṛto ṅī*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by the *guṇa* vowel *a*; this is followed by *rapara* (substitution of *r*), the elision of the final consonant and following vowels according to *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, and finally the *visarga*. This is based on the rule *aptṛn*.

But it is not long [vowel], because of the continued application of the rule *asaṃbuddhau*. [In the forms] *dhātār-au*, by the rule *ṛto ṅī* [applied to] the *ṅi* and the *sarvanāmasthāna* case endings, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* as the *guṇa*; then there is the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, and by the rule *aptṛn*, there is the lengthening of the vowel. [Thus we have] *dhātāraḥ*. [The accusative singular is] *dhātāram*. [The nominative dual is] *dhātārau*. Now, with the *śas* ending...

The long vowel resulting from the previous *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* is replaced by *Añ* (ā), and *N* is not substituted. *Dhātṛn*. [In the instrumental singular: *ṭā* is replaced by *yaṇ* (*i*), yielding *dhātrā*. [In the dative singular:

*ReĀ* is replaced by *yaṇ* (*e*), yielding *dhātre*. [In the genitive singular: By the rule *ṅsiṅsoḥ-ṛta ut*, *ut* is substituted; then *raparatva* applies, followed by the elision of *s* (*salopaḥ*) and the substitution of *visarga*—yielding *dhātuḥ*. [The same for the second genitive singular: *dhātuḥ*. [In the genitive dual: *dhātroḥ*, *dhātroḥ*. [In the genitive plural: By the rule *āmi ṭhhrasvanadyāpaḥ*, [the suffix *N* is added].
The suffix *nuṭ*. By the rule *nāmī*, there is lengthening [of the vowel]. Since the letter *n* is not followed by the letters *r* or *ś*, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) does not apply.
[To remedy this, it is said: "After a vowel of the *ṛ*-class (*ṛvarṇa*), the *n* [is replaced by *ṇ*]. This means: "after that which follows a vowel of the *ṛ*-class. However, this is a Vārttika.

It is supplementary to all the sūtras prescribing the *ṅit* [affixes]. In the case of *ṅai*, by the rule "ṛtaḥ ṅī," the *guṇa* vowel *a* is substituted, followed by *raparatva*. Thus: *dhātari*, *dhātṛṣu*. Nor is there any issue here with the word *dātṛ*, because it is derived from the root *dā* (to give) via the *tṛn* or *tṛc* suffixes under the *auṇādika* group beginning with *śaṃsi-kṣad-ādi*. It is not a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*) for Hiraṇyagarbha.

One might ask: "How is there a long vowel in *aptṛn*? It should be replied that this is due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that among the words ending in the *uṇādi* suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*, the long vowel occurs only for these seven: *naptr*, etc. However, the point is that the word *dhātṛ* is not derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes, because there is no evidence for assuming that the root *dhā* belongs to the class beginning with *śaṃs* and *kṣad*. Thus it is. Similarly...

"Regarding *naptrādayaḥ*": the meaning is that the words *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣattṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ* are like the word *dhātṛ*. Although the word *udgātṛ*—ending in the suffixes *tṛn* or *tṛc* according to the *āuṇādika* [list]—is not included among the *naptrādi* group, it appears as *udgātāraḥ* in the *samarthasūtra*.

It was stated previously that [the vowel] is long precisely because of its usage in the Bhāṣya. He brings this very point together with the example *udgātārau*. Regarding *pitā*: like *dhātṛ*, there is no *aṅ* substitution.
However, in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending], by the rule *ṛto ṅī*, the *guṇa* substitute is the vowel *a*, followed by *rapara* (substitution of *r*). [The suffix is] *aptṛn*.

Thus, [the author] says "no" regarding the lengthening [of the vowel], stating "by derivation" (*vyutpatti*). [The word] *pitā* means "he protects" (*pāti*); the suffix *tṛc* is applied, and the augment *iṭ* along with the elision of the vowel *ā* should be understood as the derivation. However, in the view that [words] are not derived [from verbal roots] (*avyutpattipakṣa*), since it is not included among [the group of suffixes] beginning with *aptṛ* and *tṛj*, there is no suspicion of lengthening at all; this is the intended meaning. [The dual form is] *pitarau*.

The forms *pitaraḥ*, *pitaram*, *pitarau*, *pitṝn*, and so forth, follow the pattern of *dhātṛ*. Likewise for *jāmātṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, and others. This is because they are listed among the *uṇādi* derivatives in the rule:
*ṭhnaptṛneṣṭṛtvaṣṭṛhotṛpotṛbhrātṛjāmātṛmātṛpitṛduhitṛ*.

In the Sūtra, the words *pitṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, and *bhrātṛ* are derived. Among them, the derivation of the word *pitṛ* has been stated. As for *bhrātṛ*: from the root *bhrāj*, with either the suffix *tṛn* or *tṛc*, there is the elision of the *ja*. Thus, *bhrātā*. As for *jāmātṛ*:
[it is derived] from the sense "he measures (māti) his wife (jāyām)," thus *jāmātā*. There is the suffix *tṛn*; alternatively, by the rule *tṛjvat*, there is the elision of the *ya*.
The meaning is that even for these two [words], because they are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes and are not included among the *naptr*-type words, there is no lengthening of the vowel.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *mantṛ* and *hantṛ* is intended; for those two are cited in the *uṇādi* section under the rule "tṛn-tṛcau śaṃsi-kṣadādibhyaḥ," specifically within the sub-rule "bahulam anyatrāpi" (the suffixes tṛn and tṛc are applied diversely elsewhere as well).

No. The word *nṛ* denotes a human being. From that [root], the suffix *su* is applied. By the rule *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso’naṅ*, the substitution *anaṅ* occurs. Since it is not included within the *aptṛn* group in the rule *aptṛn*, the lengthening of the vowel caused by the status of having *n* as its final member—by the rule *tadantatve sarvanāmasthāne ca*—does not apply. There is elision of the final consonant and the following vowel according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. After the elision of *n*, the form is *nā*. In the dual, it is *narau*. In the plural, it is *naraḥ*.

In *nṛbhiḥ*, by the rule *ṛto ṅī* [Pāṇini 7.3.110], there is *guṇa* substitution, with *ra* following (*rapara*). Because it is not included among the group beginning with *aptṛn* (Pāṇini 6.4.11), and because it lacks the suffix *n* at the end, there is no long vowel. Thus: *he naḥ*. In *nṛbhiḥ*, by the rule *ṛto ṅī*, there is *guṇa* substitution, with *ra* following; then, by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [Pāṇini 6.1.68], there is elision of the case-ending, and the *visarga* is applied. *Naram*, *narau*. In the *śas* [case]:

The long vowel *ā* (āṅkāraḥ) results from the rule of prior homogeneous lengthening (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), and there is no substitution of *n* (natvam); thus, *nṛn*. When a vowel follows beginning with *ṭ*, the *yaṇ*-substitution yields *repha* (the letter *r*);

thus, *nr̥* or *nrē*. In the case of the endings *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, the *ṛ* is replaced by *ut* (short *u*), followed by *rapara* (with *r* as the subsequent element), there is elision of *s* (*salopaḥ*), and the visarga; thus, *nuḥ* or *nuḥ*. For the dual *nroḥ*. Regarding the plural *ām*, the augment *nuṭ* is added; although a constant lengthening (*nitya-dīrgha*) would have been required by the rule "nāmī," [it does not apply here].

(280) *nṛ ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.6. *nṛ ca*: The word *nṛ* here has its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). The rule *nāmī* is understood (*anuvartate*) from the previous context. From the rule *ḍhralope*, the word *dīrghaḥ* is understood (*anuvartate*). [This is also understood] from the rule *chandasyubhayathā*.

The phrase "in both ways" (ubhayathā) is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "nṛtyetisyā" and so forth. Regarding *nṛṇām* and *nṛṇām*: the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "after a vowel ending in *ṛ*, there is *ṇ* for *na*. In the dative singular (*ṅai*), the substitution of *guṇa* [by the rule] "for *ṛt*, there is *ṅī*" is followed by the substitution of *ra* [as the *apṛkta*]. [The forms are: *nari*, *nroḥ*, *nṛṣu*. These are the words ending in *ṛ*. Now, those ending in *ṝ*.

They are analyzed by the words *kṛ* and so forth. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the case of the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the two roots *kṛ* and *tṛ*, there is the substitution of *i* (by Pāṇini 6.1.98) and the replacement of the semivowel by a vowel (*raparatva*). [The roots are] *kṛ* "to scatter" and *tṛ* "to swim or cross.
When imitation is performed by means of these two sounds, *kṛ* and *tṛ*, [the following applies] to those two which have become the imitations.

The two roots *kṛ* and *tṛ* as recited in the *dhātupāṭha* are intended here. For this very reason, the meaning of an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is the object being imitated (*anukārya*). Furthermore, it is established in the commentary on the sūtra "ṭhmatau cchaḥ" that the object being imitated is distinct from the imitation, even when there is a transposition of the sequence [of sounds].
That "the capacity to bring an object to mind arises from similarity to the expressive word" is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary and in the Bhāṣya on the rule *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ*. Consequently,

because the two instances of the suffixes *kṛt* and *tṛc* [in the forms *kṛt* and *tṛc*] which constitute the imitation possess meaning through their similarity to the two suffixes *kṛt* and *tṛc* which are the objects of imitation...

Because they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the case endings (*sup*) arise. Now, one might object: since these two [words] are imitations (*anukaraṇa*), they denote the very form of the word being imitated (*anukārya*); thus, lacking the expression of an action (*kriyā*), they lack the status of verbal roots (*dhātu*). Consequently, how can there be *it*-substitution (the change of *ṛ* to *i*) by the rule "ṛta id dhātoḥ"? Nor should it be argued that the status of being a verbal root applies to these imitations because of the metarule "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*); for if that were so, the status of being a nominal stem would be untenable due to the exclusion of verbal roots in the rule "that which is not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*). To this, he says: "Regarding the statement 'an imitation is like its original'..."

The meaning is as follows: by the rule *yatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe* (Pāṇini 5.2.39), since there is a mention of a case-ending (*vibhakti-nirdeśa*) in reference to the imitation of a verbal root (*dhātvanukaraṇa*), the principle *prakṛtivadanukaraṇam* (an imitation is treated like its original) applies optionally. Consequently, by adopting the state of transfer (*atideśa-bhāva*), there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* according to *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) because of its status as a verbal root (*dhātutva*). By adopting the absence of transfer, however, there is no status as a verbal root; rather, because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*), the subsequent arising of case-endings (*sub-utpatti*) is not contradicted. Regarding *kīḥ*: this means the verbal root *kṛ*. When the vowel *a* [of the suffix *kvip*] is replaced by *i*, and *i* is subsequently replaced by *ra* (by *uraṇ raparaḥ*), the long vowel is applied by the rule *ṛt-voḥ samprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.4.14). Then, the elision of the case-ending *su* occurs by *hal-ṅy-ādi-lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), followed by the visarga.

*Kirau*—because it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*), there is no lengthening by the rule *ṭhrvoḥ*. *Tīḥ*—this means the root *tṛ*. *Gīrvad*—this means the forms are like those of the word *gīr*.
*Kiraḥ*, *kirau*, *kiraḥ*; *kirā*, *kīrbhyām*, *kīrbhiḥ*; *kire*, *kiraḥ*, *kiroḥ*.
In *kīrṣu*, the lengthening occurs because of its status as a *pada* by the rule "in the case of *ṭha*, *su*, etc., when not in a *sarvanāmasthāna*.

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of *it*": this means that since the maxim "an imitation is like the original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*) is not universal, the imitation does not possess the nature of a verbal root (*dhātu*); thus, the *it* substitution prescribed by the rule "the vowel *i* is substituted for the final of a root ending in *ān*" does not take place.

"Not [the vowels] lacking the quality of *a*" (anaṅguṇau na). It should be understood that even the substitution of *u* in "ṛta ud" does not apply here because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*). For this very reason, the grammatical indications such as "gro yaṅi" are consistent. "Kṛṛ" means the verbal root *kṛ*. In forms such as *krauḥ* and *kraḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. "And so forth" refers to *kraḥ*, *kraḥ*.

*kroḥ krām* | *kri* and so on end in *ṛ*; *ata* and so on end in *ḷ*. *gamlṛ*—that is, *gamlṛ* in the sense of "going" and *śaklṛ* in the sense of "ability"—are roots ending in vowels (*ajantau*). Regarding *anaṅ*: the remainder [of the rule] is "by this [sūtra], *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso’nehasām*" (Pāṇini 7.1.94). [This applies to] the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*.

The intention is that [the substitution occurs] because of their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*). Regarding the phrase "but in the domain of *guṇa*": in the case of the feminine suffix *ṅī* and the *sarvanāmasthāna* endings, the *guṇa* substitute for *ṛ* is the vowel *a*; the meaning is that it is followed by *l*. This is because the term *rapara* is employed in the rule "ṭhuraṇraparaḥ. As for "gamṛn": [this refers to] the *ṛ*-vowel and the *ḷ*-vowel.

Because a long vowel is absent, there is only the short *ṛ* sound. The intention is that [the substitution of] *n* occurs by means of the "long vowel homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) rule.
Regarding "but in the case of *ṅsi* and *ṅs*": when *gamlṛ* and *as* are in combination, *ut* is substituted [for the *ṛ*], and since *l* follows, it is *lapara*.
When *gamul* and *s* are in combination, by the rule "there is elision of a final conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*), the form *gamul* results. "And so forth" refers to this.
*gamlṛ-bhyām*, *gamlṛ-bhiḥ*, *gamlṛ-bhyaḥ*, *gamlṛ-bhyaḥ*; but in the case of the *ām* [genitive plural], *gamṛṇām*;

*gamali*, *gamloḥ*, *gamlṛṣu*. However, in reality, regarding the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, since it should have been stated as *ajiti* (when an *ac* follows), the fact that *aṇ* was specifically mentioned indicates—according to what was stated in the Bhāṣya—that [the substitution] occurs only by the preceding rule (*aṇ*).

If the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *ḷ* were *l*, then, because the subsequent mention of *aṇ* would necessarily have to include *l* in order to account for its being "followed by *l*" (*laparatva*), the aforementioned inconsistency would be quite evident.
Therefore, they say that the usage of such types of forms is not approved by the Bhāṣya. Thus [ends the section].
Those ending in *lṛ*. Now, those ending in *e*: *in*. [The example is] *aḥuviṣṇuḥ*; his descendant is *iḥukāmaḥ*. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied after a vowel (*ata iñ*).
By the rule "and that which begins with *ya*" (*yasyeti ca*), there is the elision of the vowel *a*. In the sense of "together with *in*" (*inasaha*), [the suffix] *tena saha* [is applied].

The term *tulyayoga* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the rule *vopasarjanasya*, the *s* is changed to *ṣ*. By *ādguṇaḥ*, the form *se* is obtained. From that, the suffix *su* is added, followed by the application of *rutva* and *visarga*, resulting in *seḥ*. Similarly for *smṛteḥ*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *smṛta-i-ukāmaḥ* as "one by whom the desire for *i* (fire) is remembered," the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* applies.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
