Nor should one suspect that because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the final element of the preceding word, and since *se-* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffix would be elided by the rule "after an indeclinable, *āp* and *sup* suffixes are elided" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*). This is because the technical designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) applies only to those words whose meaning is not connected with gender and so forth. [In this case,] there is the substitution of *ay* for the vowel at the beginning of the following word.
Thinking thus, he says: *sayaḥ sayaḥ*. By the rule *ṭhehrahrasvāt*, there is elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*). [Thus we have] "he se.

But if this were the case, then in the example "he hare," the elision of the vocative suffix would not occur; for the elision of the *su* (the vocative suffix) would strike at the very vocative suffix upon which the dependent condition for the application of *guṇa* was based.

Because, according to the definition of *saṃnipāta* (immediate proximity), it is impossible for [the vowel] to be the cause [of the elision]. If it is argued that, this being the case, the mention of *iṅ* (the vowel *i*) is redundant because it already serves its purpose in the example *he se*, listen: in the example *he hare*, [the rule applies] to that which has the form of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*).

There is no destruction of the quality (guṇa) that serves as its own basis; for even if that [quality] were lost, the vocative case-ending (saṃbuddhi) would still exist by resorting to the rule of "treatment as if the suffix were present" (pratyayalakṣaṇa), and by that, the quality remains unimpeded. Some, however, argue that because the rule states "eṅ hrasvāt" rather than saying "guṇāt saṃbuddheḥ," [the quality is not destroyed].

They say that even after setting aside the prohibition regarding the *saṃnipāta* (the loss of a condition), the elision of the *sambuddhi* suffix still takes effect. Furthermore, how is it that [the form] *sayas* occurs in the *jas* case? For, by means of the intervening case-ending, the element *ṭhse* becomes a *pada*; thus, it would set aside the *ayādeśa* (the substitution of *ay*) and, by the rule *eṅḥ padāntādati*, result in the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*).

This must be stated, because of the prohibition: "And when there is a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), [the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule does not apply] in an operation concerning what is not the beginning of a word.

For its meaning is that when the status of being a word (*padatva*) is to be applied to the subsequent word or to that which contains it, there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule for the internal case-ending. [This applies to] the *se-* occurring within words such as *senā* (army) and *sevaka* (servant).

Or let there be an imitation of this [form]. In that case, since the substitution of *ay* before the suffix *jas* is unimpeded, [the forms] ending in *it* and *et* are accounted for. Now, those ending in *ot*: when *go* + *s* remains, [the rule applies:

Regarding *goto ṇit*: the mention of *gota* with a long vowel (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of clarity. From the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne*, the term *sarvanāmasthāne* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and is transformed into the nominative case.
Thus he says: "from the word *go*, etc. [The suffix] should be like a *ṇit* [suffix]. That is, when a *ṇit* [suffix follows].

The meaning is that one performs whatever action others perform. Regarding *gaur*: when the suffix is treated as having the marker *Ṇ* (*ṇit*), there is a *vṛddhi* substitution of the vowel *au* by the rule *aco ñṇiti*; the intention is that this results in the forms *gaur* and *gāvaḥ* through the application of *rutva* and *visarga*. Regarding *gāvau* and *gāvaḥ*: when the suffix is treated as having the marker *Ṇ*, there is a *vṛddhi* substitution followed by the replacement of the final vowel with *ā*; this is the intended meaning. In the vocative *he gauḥ*, once the *vṛddhi* has occurred, [the rule *eṅhrasvāt* applies].

Because of the absence of the quality of being "other" (*paratva*), there is no elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*). When *ami* follows *go*, the form *go am* results; at this point, since the suffix is marked with *Ṇ*, the rule for *vṛddhi* substitution would apply.
However, [this is blocked by] the rule: (282) *āṬto'mśasoḥ* | P. 6.1.93. [This prescribes *āṬ* in place of *am* and *śas* after a stem ending in long *ā*.]

"āṬto'mśasoḥ": the analysis is *ā-ota* (ā + ota); the sense is that this is based on the commentary. In the term *ota*, the *t* is used as a *tapara* marker; the meaning is "from [a stem ending in] the vowel *o*. The compound *amśasau* is analyzed as *am* and *śas*; the phrase refers to those two. This is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The rule continues with] *iko...* [etc.]
The term *aci* is understood from the rule *yaṇ aci*; the governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is also in force.

This is what he states with the words beginning "from the vowel *o*," and so on. Here, only the nominal suffix *śas* (the accusative plural) is intended, and not the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *śas* [meaning] "much" or "little," because of the continued application of the condition *aci*, and because a secondary derivative suffix...

Because *śas* cannot follow a vowel beginning with *a*, as there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *taddhita* suffixes in the rule *ṭhlaśakvataddhite*. Now, consider the root *ciñ* (to pile) in the *laṅ* [mood]: the augment *aṭ* is added, the third person plural ending *mip* is applied, *mip* is replaced by *am* according to the rule *tasthasthamipām*, and the *śnu* vikaraṇa is added.

By the rule "sārvadhātukārghadhātukayoḥ," there is guṇa, resulting in the vowel *o*. When *acinavaḥ* is established, the substitution of *av* occurs, yielding the form *acinavam*. In that context, when *acinavaḥ* becomes *acinava am*, the substitution of *ā* by the rule "āṬtaḥ amśasoḥ" supersedes the substitution of *av*, resulting in *acinām*.
To this he says: "It may be so"—namely, that the rule *gām* applies. Regarding the word *parā*, the *Vārttika* states:

"The *vṛddhi* [substitution] prescribed by the rule *ṭhañcauṇitī* does not occur here. The intent of the *Bhāṣya* is that because the substitution of *ātva* (the replacement of the final vowel with *ā*) has no other scope of application, it serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to that *vṛddhi*. For there is no occurrence of *ātva* anywhere outside the domain of *vṛddhi*; such is the underlying meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *āt* for the final vowel of the word *dyauḥ* before the case-ending *am* has its own scope [and thus does not require the present rule], because the *ṇit*-character of the suffix prescribed by the rule *goto ṇit* would not apply there, resulting in no possibility of *vṛddhi*.
For, based on this very Bhāṣya, the *ṇit*-character of the suffix [in *dyām*] will be stated under the rule *oto ṇit*. Therefore, that [substitution of *āt*] also...

The meaning is that [the vowel] is the object of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). Regarding *gāḥ*: because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* case ending, there is neither the status of being a *ṇit* nor *vṛddhi*.
The meaning is that there is the substitution of *āt* by the rule "āṬtaḥ am-śasoḥ.
Thinking of the substitution of *āv* for the vowels beginning with the fourth case (*ṭā*), he says—*gavā*, *gave*. Regarding *goḥ*: [this is derived from the stem *go*].

The intention is that [the form] *dyoḥ* is derived by applying the rule for the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* (the preceding vowel) according to the rule *ṭhṅsiṅsośca*. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): its meaning refers to forms such as *gavoḥ*, *gavām*, and *gavi*.
The word *dyo* ends in the vowel *o* and is feminine; as Amara states:
"The words *suraloka*, *dyo*, and *div* both mean heaven and are feminine. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *suśobhanā dyaur yasya* ("one whose heaven is very beautiful"), [the same applies].

[The word] *puṃliṅgaḥ* [is masculine]. Regarding forms such as *sudyauḥ* in the case of sarvanāmasthāna suffixes, since [the rule] *gotaḥ ṇit* would not apply, it should be stated that "after an *o*, there is a *ṇit* [suffix]. Thus, having removed the letter *g* from *gotaḥ*, one should say "after an *o*, there is a *ṇit*."
The meaning is that it must be stated. The proof for this has been stated immediately below. However, this is not the Vārttika.
In that [sūtra], the vowel *o* is followed by *t* (i.e., *ota*) for the purpose of indicating length; thus, it is understood that a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following the vowel *o* is a *ṇit*.

"Prescribed" (*vihita*) means that one must rely on the qualification "prescribed by *ot*" for the rule stating that a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix] following an *okāranta* [stem] is *guṇa*-strengthened;

that is to say, the phrase "following *ot*" must be taken as a qualifier of what is prescribed. "By that" means by the statement "following *ot*," having removed the letter *g* from "following *got*. "In *sudyām*, etc. refers to such cases.
The meaning is that the forms are like those of the word *go*. Regarding the phrase "O Bhāno":

according to the explanation that "a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following an *o*-vowel is marked with *Ṇ*," when the vocative singular of the word *bhānu* undergoes *guṇa* substitution by the rule "there is *guṇa* for a short vowel," resulting in the vowel *o*, the suffix *su* (the case-ending) follows this *o*-vowel; thus, it is treated as having the property of *Ṇ*.

In the case of the augmented form *āṬ* (āḥ), because the condition *eṅ* is absent due to its subsequent application, there is no elision of the nominative suffix (*sulopa*), and consequently, after the application of *rutva* and *visarga*, the form would be *he ṭhbhānau* (he bhānau). Therefore, the meaning is that [the rule] must be qualified by what has been prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇam*). Now, one might object:
in the rule *ehhrasvātsambuddheḥ*, by the very force of including the term *eṅ*, [the desired result] in *he bhāno*...
The suffix *ṇit* and the *vṛddhi* substitution caused by it do not occur. Otherwise, one would have simply stated "after a short vowel ending in *ṭha* or *eṅ*" (*ṭheṅhrasvāt*).
Therefore, because the qualification of the prescribed [suffix] would otherwise be redundant, the author states "he bhānavaḥ" out of dissatisfaction [with that view].
In that case, when the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *a-u*] has occurred by the rule "also before *jas*" (*jasi ca*), the form stands as *bhāno as*. Then, from the *ot*...
If [the rule] were applied after the substitution of *paratva*, the substitution of *ṇit*, the *vṛddhi* increment, and the replacement by *āv*, the form would have to be *bhānāvaḥ*.

Therefore, the intention is that the rule is a qualification of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇam*). In reality, however, by the maxim of "that which is taught by a specific rule versus that which is taught by a general characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa-pratipadokta-paribhāṣā*), [the forms] *he bhāno* and *he bhānavaḥ* [are established].
Since the absence of the state of being a *niṣṭhā* is logically established, resorting to the interpretation of it as a qualifier of the enjoined [element] is indeed redundant.

Regarding "uḥ śambhuḥ": *śambhuḥ* is an explanation (*vivaraṇa*) of *uḥ*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "by whom *uḥ* is remembered," it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word *smṛta* is placed first according to the rule *ṭhniṣṭhā*.

[The rule] "ṭhādguṇaḥ" [applies]; thus, the form is *smṛtaḥ*. From that, when case-endings (*sup*) arise, the forms are like those of the word *go*. However, in reality, as a supplement to the sūtra "goto ṇit," the Vārttika "vṛddhir vaktavyā dyośca" is seen in the Bhāṣya. [The rule] "āṬt-amaśasoḥ" [applies].

In this context, however, the rule "oto ṇit" is not observed; therefore, they say that there is no other nominal stem (prātipadika) ending in the vowel *o*. Thus end the words ending in *o*. Now, those ending in *e*: the word *rai* denotes wealth. As Amarasimha states: "The words *ṛtha*, *artha*, and *vibhava* also [denote wealth]."

(283) *rāyo hali* | Pāṇini 7.2.85. This sūtra shows a specific rule regarding that [stem] in case-endings beginning with a consonant: *rāyo hali*. The word *rāyaḥ* is the genitive singular of the word *rai*. From the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the particle *ā* is understood here.
The phrase "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) also carries over [from the previous rule]. By the term *hal* ("consonant"), "in a case-ending" is qualified;

consequently, there is an application of the rule regarding the beginning of that [element]. Thus he says: "of the word *rai*. Because of the mention of *hal*, the substitution of *āt* does not occur before a vowel (*ac*), but rather only the substitution of *āya*; therefore he says: "before a vowel (*aci*). When *āt* is substituted for *rāḥ*, the rules for *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) and *visarga* apply. Before a vowel (*aci*).
They cite the substitution of *ā* for *i* as follows: *rāyaḥ*, *rāyaḥ*. And so on: *rābhiḥ*;

*rāye*, *rābhyām*, *rābhyaḥ*; *rāyaḥ*, *rābhyām*, *rābhyaḥ*; *rāyaḥ*, *rāyoḥ*, *rāyām*; *rāyi*, *rāyoḥ*, *rāsu*. The *Bhāṣya* states that the word *rai* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It occurs only at the end of a *kyac*-derivative.
"Chāndasa" (Vedic) is another alternative view. Thus end those [stems] ending in *ai* and *au*.

Now, those ending in *āu*: the word *glau* denotes the moon; as Amara states: "The moon is *glau*, *mṛgāṅka*, and *klānidhi*. In that case, there is no modification before a consonant-initial suffix, but before a vowel, the substitution of *āv* occurs.
Having considered this, he said: *malaur glāvau glāva iti* (the forms *glāvaḥ*, *glāvau*, *glāvaḥ*). [The declension is as follows: *glāvam*, *glāvau*, *glāvaḥ*;
*glāvā*, *glābhyām*, *glābhiḥ*; *glāve*, *glābhyām*, *glābhyaḥ*; *glāvaḥ*, *glābhyām*, *glābhyaḥ*; *glāvaḥ*, *glāvoḥ*, *glāvām*.

*glāvī*, *glāvaḥ*, *glauṣu*. Now, one might object: since the term *o* in the rule *āṬtaḥ am-śasoḥ* includes the vowel *au* by virtue of their being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*), why would the substitution of *ā* not apply to the word *glau* before the suffixes *am* and *śas*? To this, [the author replies]:

He says: "The rule *āṬto'm-śasoḥ* does not apply here. As for the passage beginning with *aiāṬj*, it has already been explained in the section on technical definitions (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*). Similarly, from *jan* (to produce), one forms *janauḥ*. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied; then by the rule *jvaratvara-*, *ūṭh* is substituted; and by the rule *etyedhaty-*, *vṛddhi* is applied. Thus we have *janāvau*, *janāvaḥ*, and so forth.
Thus end those ending in -au.
Thus ends the section on masculine nouns ending in vowels in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on feminine stems ending in vowels.

She delights, or she is delighted, thus she is *ramā*. [The root] *ṛm* is used in the sense of "playing" (*krīḍā*). By adding the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* class) and then the suffix *ṭāp* (by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*), the form *ramā* is derived.

Although it is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) because it ends in a suffix, the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) are still applied—either because the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned separately in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, or by the maxim regarding words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*).
By the rule *ṭh-ḷ-ṅ-y-āp-iti sulopaḥ*, there is elision of the suffix *su*.
Then, by the rule *āṬ ṅ-āpaḥ* 7.1.18, when *ramā* and *āṬ* remain, [the rule] *oṅ āpaḥ* applies. Here, *āpaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*).

By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a *pratyaya*, that which ends in *ā* (ābanta) is intended. The word "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) from the rule beginning with *ṭhaṅgasya* is modified to the ablative case. "Of *ṭā* and *ṅi*" (*ṭāṅḥ*) is in the genitive. From the rule *jasaḥ śī*, the word *śī* is understood by *anuvṛtti*. Thus he says: "from that which ends in *ā*."

Because the meaning of the word *āṬ* is not well-known, he says: "*āṬtīti*" (meaning "the substitute *āṬ*"). He says "*saṃjñā*" (it is a technical name). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "in the grammar of the Easterners. Regarding "*rame*" (in the case of *ramā*): when the form *ramā āṬ* is established, the substitution of *śī* occurs; because that [substitute] is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is a suffix (*pratyaya*). Consequently, by the rule "*llaśakvataddhite*" (Pāṇini 1.3.8), the letter *ś* receives the designation *it*.

By the rule "lope ṭhādguṇaḥ," the *ekāra* [e] is substituted. However, elision by the rule "yasyeti ca" does not occur, because [the preceding element] is not an *ab*. Regarding the *jas* ending, he says "ramāḥ," considering the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrgha*) according to the rule "akaḥ savarṇe. But the long vowel of the preceding homogeneous class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) does not apply; it does not occur, because of the prohibition "dīrghāj jasi ca."
When *ramā* + *as* has been established, [the rule] applies:

(285) *saṃbuddhau ca* | 7|3|106|. Regarding *saṃbuddhau ca*: from the rule *bahuvacane jhalye'dit* [6.1.105], the word *edit* is understood; and from the rule *āṅ cāpiḥ* [6.1.129], [the word *āt* is understood].
The word "ṭhāp" (the suffix *ṭāp*) also carries over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says, beginning with "āpaḥ," etc.; the meaning is "of that which ends in *ā*.

[By the rule] "ṭh-lo 'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54), when "he rame s" is established, he demonstrates the grammatical process (*prakriyā*) by saying "eṅhrasvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.69). However, the elision [of the final vowel and consonant] by the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt... (Pāṇini 6.1.68) does not apply here.

The point is that once *etva* (the substitution of *e*) has been applied—both because it is taught later in the order of rules (*paratvāt*) and because it is taught as a specific rule (*pratipadoktatvāt*)—the elision prescribed by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68) does not apply;
rather, the elision prescribed by *ṭeṅhrasvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) is more appropriate due to its superior status (*nyāyyatvāt*).

Regarding *ramām*: the form *pūrvaḥ* (from *ami pūrvaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.107) applies the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute of the preceding vowel). Regarding *āṬṅḥ*: when *śī* replaces *āṬ*, *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) applies.
He says "ramā" with this in mind. Regarding the phrase "because it is feminine": when *śas* follows *ramā*, the form becomes *ramā-as*.

Although the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the substitution of a single long vowel for two homogeneous vowels) occurs first, the rule *tasmāc chasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.103), which prescribes the substitution of *n* for the final *s* of the stem, does not apply because the stem is feminine. Thus, the form remains *ramā-ā*.

(286) *āṅ cāpiḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.105. The rule *āṅ cāpiḥ* [is explained as follows]: The phrase *osi ca* is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. The word *āpaḥ* is in the genitive case; because the term *aṅgasya* is supplied [by context], there is an application of the principle of inclusion of that which ends in [the specified element] (*tadantavidhi*). This is further understood from the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*.
The word *edit* (e-t-i) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. He states this with the words "āṅ oisi ca" (*āṅ* and *osi* are treated as *e*), and so forth.

Regarding the statement "āṅ," the Prācīnas have declared that it is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the suffix *ṭā*. Since the substitution of *et* applies to the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*), he says "ramayā.
As for "ramābhiḥ," because of the inclusion of the vowel *a* in the form *tapara* in the rule "ato bhisa ais," the substitution of *ais* does not apply here. Thus, we have *ramā-e*.
In the case of [the suffix] *yaṅ*:
(287) *yāḍāpaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.113. *yāḍāpaḥ*. The word *āpaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). From the rule *dherṅtī*, the term *ṅti* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtta*).

The sixth [case-ending] is transformed. This is stated by the words "āpaḥ parasya" and so forth. Because it is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, it becomes the initial constituent. By the rule "vṛddhireci," when "yā-e" remains, the sense is that the single substitute *aikāra* takes the place of both the vowel *ā* and the vowel *e*. Regarding the term "savarṇa": [in the case of] *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, [we have] *ramā as*.

This being the case, when the *yāṭ* augment is applied, the intention is that there is a long vowel by the rule "a long vowel is substituted for a homogeneous pair" (*savarṇadīrgha*). It would be more appropriately stated as *ṭhyaḍ*. However, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule "guṇa is substituted for [a final *at*] before a guṇa" does not occur, due to the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*. Regarding the phrase "of *ra* and *ma*": [this refers to] "and the augment *āṅ* after *api*."

The intention is that there is the substitution of *ay* for *i* in the *āt* case-ending. Regarding *ramāṇām*: the inclusion of the term *āp* in the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.54] is intended to trigger the addition of the augment *nuṭ*; then, by the application of the rule *nāmī* [Pāṇini 6.4.3], the vowel is lengthened, and finally, by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* [Pāṇini 8.4.2], the *ṇatva* (nasalization) of the *n* occurs. Regarding *ramāyām*: [the form arises from] *ramā-i*.

The sense is that when [the case ending] *ṬhRē* is present, the substitution of *ām* occurs by the rule "ṭhReĀrāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ," and then the augment *yāṭ* is applied, resulting in a long vowel by the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). By the rule "na vibhaktau," the *m* of the case ending does not become *it*. From the word *sarva*, with the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form *sarvā* is derived; this also generally follows the paradigm of *ramā*. When the case endings *ṅ* and *su* follow, although the rule "yāḍāpiḥ" would have applied, [it is blocked].

(288) *sarvanāmnaḥ syāḍḍhrasvaśca* [Pāṇini 7.3.114]. The suffix *syāṭ* is added after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*). From the rule *ṅyāḍāpaḥ*, the word *āpaḥ* is understood as being in the ablative case;
this qualifies the term *sarvanāmnaḥ*. This is an application of the rule regarding endings containing a specific element (*tadantavidhiḥ*).

From the rule *ṭhgherṅtī*, the portion *ṅtī* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and is transformed into the genitive case. Consequently, the meaning is: "The suffix *syāṭ* shall be applied after a feminine noun ending in *āp* that is a pronominal (*sarvanāman*).

Because it is marked with the *ṭ* indicator (*ṭit*), it becomes an initial constituent [of the stem]. There is another sentence, *hrasvaśca*; [the word] *āp* [is understood from the previous context].
Thus, the preceding [word] recurs and is transformed into the genitive case. That [genitive] connects with the word "hrasva" (short). Its meaning is: "In place of *āp*, a short vowel occurs.

This is what he states by saying "from that which ends in *ā*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *yāṭ*, according to the maxim "that which applies when something else is not already applicable" (*yena nāprāptinyāya*).

The meaning [of the rule] is as follows: when *sarvā-e* is established, *syāṭ* is applied. The vowel following the letter *v* becomes short; this is the meaning of "vṛddhi" (in this context). Thus, *sarvasyāḥ*.
When *ṅsi* and *ṅs* follow, *sarvā-as* is established; then *syāṭ* is applied, the *ā* of *āp* becomes short, and there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous combination (*savarṇadīrgha*).

[This is] the state of being. Now, one might ask: since the word *sarvā* ending in *āp* (the feminine suffix) is not included in the list of words beginning with *sarva* (*sarvādigaṇa*), how can it possess the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*)? To this he says: "of the single-substitute" (*ekādeśasya*). The meaning is: of that *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneous combination) which is the single substitute for the vowel *a* following the *v* [of *sarva-ā*] and the suffix *āp*. Now, [one might object: what of that which is produced by a single-substitute?

If the *ākāra* were considered its initial portion (*pūrvānta*), its status as ending in *ā* (*ābanta*) would be contradicted because the property of being *āpt* (ending in *ā*) would not be sublated. Nor can it be argued that it retains its status as ending in *ā* by virtue of being treated like the subsequent portion (*parādivattva*), for there is a prohibition against this when both [the preceding and following elements] are relied upon, according to the rule: "In the case of relying on both, there is no application of the rules regarding what precedes the end or what follows the beginning" (*nāntādivat*). If this is [your objection], then:

By the maxim *satyam-liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*, that which ends in *āp* (the feminine suffix) possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*). However, they say that its status as ending in *āp* is due to the principle of *parādivadbhāva* (treating it as if it were the beginning of the subsequent element). Regarding the form *sarvasyām*: when *ṅi* follows *sarvā*, resulting in *sarvā-i*, the augment *ām* is applied by the rule *ReĀrām*. Since this is further, it applies after having set aside the augment *suṭ*.

And it is short. By the principle of "once [occurred, no more]," *suṭ* does not apply again. "In this way" means that words such as *aviśva*, which are listed in the *sarvādi* group, attain the status of having the feminine suffix *āp*, just like the word *sarvā*.
That which lies between the northern and eastern directions is *uttarapūrvā*.
The compound *ṭhdiṅnāmanyantarāle* is a specific type of *bahuvrīhi*.
(289) *Vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau* | 1.1.28. To show the distinction therein, he says: *vibhāṣā diksamāse*. [This is] from the rule *sarvādīni*.

The term "sarvanāma" (all nominal stems) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "here. This means: in a compound of directions (*dik-samāsa*). Some hold that this is for the sake of providing an option (*vikalpa*) where a permanent prohibition (*nitya-niṣedha*) would otherwise apply by the rule "not in a *bahuvrīhi*," based on the ungrammatical analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*). Others hold that this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) because [the application] would not otherwise occur due to the secondary (*gauṇa*) status [of the word].

He provides examples for the view that it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*): *uttarapūrvasyai*. Here, the augment *syāṭ* and the short vowel [of the feminine suffix] are applied. For the view that it lacks the status of a pronoun: *uttarapūrvāyāḥ* (with *yāṭ*) or *uttarapūrvasyāḥ*. [In the plural: *uttarapūrvāsām* or *uttarapūrvāṇām*.

In the case of *uttarapūrvasyām*, it is [the form] *uttarapūrvāyām*. According to the rule "in all simple compounds (*vṛti*), there is the substitution of the masculine form for a pronoun," because of the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) [in the rule], the first member of the compound takes the masculine form even though it is not currently a pronoun. Now, one might object: having gone to the northern direction, [one has a city] whose eastern direction is [reached] through delusion.

That [compound] is *uttarapūrvā*. It is a *bahuvrīhi* according to the rule "anekam anyapadārthe. Here too, because it is a compound containing a word denoting direction (*dikśabda*), there is an option regarding its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāma*); thus, two forms would result: *uttarapūrvasyai* or *uttarapūrvāyai*. Furthermore, the augment *syāṭ* [is applied].

It is not accepted. Regarding this, he says: "The names of the directions" (*diṅnāmāni*). The term *diṅnāmānyantarāle* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound that is specifically prescribed as a directional compound (*diksamāsa*), because it is ordained after the utterance of a word denoting a direction.
It is not, however, a *bahuvrīhi* formed by the rule *anekamanyapadārthe*. And therefore...
The meaning is that, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "that which is taught as a specific term" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*), it is not included here. Regarding the words *yatarā* and so on:

the words *yataḥ* and *tataḥ* are used to indicate the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *utarā* and the word *pūrvā*. In the absence of such coreferentiality, [the compound would be formed] by the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24).
Because a *bahuvrīhi* compound is impossible here, according to the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* should be stated [only] for words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the term *unmugdhāyāḥ*: by this, the doubt as to how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the contradiction between the preceding and following [words] is dispelled. Now, [one might object]: "In the case of a directional compound (*dig-samāsa*), it is optional (*vibhāṣā*)."

"Let it be so; the mention of *bahuvrīhi* need not be made, because by virtue of being explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*), the term 'names of directions' (*diṅnāmāni*) will necessarily refer only to the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
To this, he replies: "The mention of *bahuvrīhi* is for the sake of clarity. [This refers to] the meaning "to Bāhyā."

The meaning of *antar* is given by the lexicon (*kośa*) as: "interval, space, limit, clothing, disappearance, division, purpose, hole, one's own, without, outside, opportunity, middle, and inner self.
The point is that because [the word *antar*] here has the sense of "another object" (*arthāntara*), it lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and therefore [the suffix *ṣyaṅ*] would not occur.

Regarding the statement "because it is said [to be] non-feminine" (*apurītyukteḥ*): the remainder of the sentence is "according to the *gaṇasūtra* 'the word *antara* [is feminine] when used in connection with the external'.
(290) *vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyābhyām* | 7|3|115|.
The word *vibhāṣā* [is understood]. From the rule *gher ṅti*, the term *ṅti* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) and is transformed into the genitive case.

From the rule "ṭhyāḍāpaḥ," the term "āpa" is understood; from the rule "sarvanāmnaḥ syāṭ," the term "syāṭ" is understood; and "hrasva" also carries over. This is what he states with the words beginning "ābhyām. As for "idam":
the meaning is that the sūtra "vibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyābhyām" need not be formulated. Why?

To this he says: "of that which ends in *tīya*. The meaning is that, within the section concerning the option (*vibhāṣā*), there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) for words ending in the suffix *tīya* when followed by case-endings marked with *ṅ* or *su*. Nor should it be argued that the very extension of the status of a pronoun for words ending in *tīya* before endings marked with *ṅ* or *su* should be abandoned; for [it is necessary] for the sake of the masculine and neuter genders.

Because that [shortening] is necessary. Regarding the rule *ambārtha-*: this has been explained under the section on masculine stems ending in /i/ and /u/. There, examples were given for the case of *nadī* (feminine) stems; now he gives examples for words meaning "mother" (*ambārtha*)—namely, *he amba*, etc. The rest is like *ramā*. Here, the Bhāṣya states: "A prohibition must be stated for those [stems] containing the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ḍlak*: *he ambāḍe*."

"O Ambāle! O Ambike! Having stated that this *vārttika* should not be composed, it was established that "only for a word meaning 'mother' (*ambārtha*) consisting of two syllables is there shortening. His intention was that, if the *vārttika* were taken literally as it stands, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in the case of "O Alle! (addressing a girl).

He states the result of this here: "asaṃyuktāḥ" (uncombined). Because the rule "there is shortening for words meaning *ambā* that consist of two syllables" (*dvyackānām ambārthānāṃ hrasvaḥ*) is a governing rule (*aṅga*), there is an extension of the application (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, in the word *jagadambā*, shortening occurs because it ends in *ambā* consisting of two syllables. Regarding *jarā*: [it is derived from] the root *jṛṣ* in the sense of "decline of age."

The suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *ṭhṣidbhidādibhyaḥ*. By the rule *ṛdṛśo'ṅī*, there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by *raparatvam* (the replacement of the vowel by the corresponding semivowel). Because the stem ends in *a*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; then *su* is applied, and the *su* is elided by the rule *halṅyādinā*. This is the intended meaning. Regarding *jarasau*: by the rule *jarāyā jarasanyatarasyām*, the substitute *jaras* occurs for *jarā* before vowels and so forth.

[The opponent] says: But surely, once the substitution of *śī* has been applied, since that [substitution] was triggered by depending upon the co-occurrence (*sannipāta*) of the suffix *āp*, it is impossible—by virtue of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*—for it to be the cause for the replacement of *jaras* which would destroy that very status of ending in *āp*; thus, there would be an absence of the *jaras* replacement.

One might think that by the rule *ādguṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.87), the form would simply be *ṭhjare*; therefore, he says: "because of the absence of *śībhāva*. The intention is that once the substitution of *jaras* has been applied, *śībhāva* does not occur because the condition for it (*āb*) is absent. [The forms are: *jarasaḥ*, *jarasam*, *jarasau*, *jarasaḥ*.
[In the instrumental case: *ṭā*-jarasā. And here, when the form *jarā + ā* is established, the substitution of *jaras* does not apply, as it would be superseded [by other rules].
It should not be argued that because the rule "paratvāt ṭhāṅ cāpiḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.35] applies later, the substitution of *ay* for *e* (resulting in *jarayā*) is more appropriate;

for even after the substitution of *ay* has occurred, the *jaras* replacement— which was already applicable by the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*)— is mandatory and therefore necessarily takes effect, since a mandatory rule is stronger than a subsequent one.

In the case of *āpaḥ*, the *yāṭ* augment prescribed for the *sup* [case endings] beginning with *ṅti* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on many factors; therefore, [the rule *ṅsiṅsoḥ* applies]. From *ṅsi* and *ṅs*: *jarasāḥ*. Here too, as before, there is no *yāṭ*.

From *ṅsi* and *ṅs*: *jarasoḥ*. Because it is *nitya*, *jaras* replaces [the final vowel] by overriding the substitution of *e* [by P. 7.3.103]. From *ām*: *jarasām*. But surely, in the case of *ām*...

Since the suffix *nuṭ* has been applied, there is an absence of case-endings beginning with *aj* (vowels); how then can the substitution *jaras* occur? To this, he says: "after *ām*, *nuṭ*. Thus, in the form *ṅai*, the substitution *jaras* occurs. Even though the augment *ReĀ* and the augment *yāṭ* follow later, they are respectively set aside by *jaras* due to its being both obligatory (*nityatva*) and internally conditioned (*antaraṅgatva*). In the alternative case, when a consonant-initial [suffix] follows, [the form remains as *rāmābhyām*].
"And like *ramā*" means that in the alternative view where the substitution of *jaras* does not occur, it remains "like *ramā*" even before suffixes beginning with a consonant (*hal*).
He restates another opinion in order to refute it, beginning with the words "here, *pūrva*," etc.
The syntactic connection is as follows: "In this case, when the word *ajarā* is present as *ajarā + āṬ*, some say *jarasī* by resorting to the substitution of *śī*."
Immediately after the word "āśritya," the phrase "when the substitution of *jaras* has been made" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Now, one might object:
since the substitution of *jaras* is subsequent (*para*), it is more logical that it should indeed supersede the substitution of *śī*;
to this, he replies: "by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). This refers to the rule "in a conflict (*vipratiṣedhe*), the subsequent [rule prevails]."
The meaning is that, by relying on the fact that the word *para* denotes "desired," in some instances the operation of the preceding [element] is resorted to.

Now, an objection: since the substitution of *śī* (for *au*) has proceeded by depending upon the co-occurrence (*saṃnipāta*) with the stem ending in *ā*, it cannot—by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*—be the cause for the substitution of *jaras*, which would disrupt that very co-occurrence with the *ā*-stem.
Since it is not possible [for that to occur], he says: "and also the non-eternality of the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*.

Regarding the phrase "that is without foundation": because the recourse to a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction) does not apply to cases not enumerated in the Bhāṣya, the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* [is considered non-eternal].
The point is that there is no evidence for assuming universal impermanence.

This might be argued: in the forms *jarasau* and *jarasām*, let the substitution of *jaras-* take effect because it is subsequent to the rules "ṭāṅasiṅsṅām ātaḥ" and "hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ"; and let there likewise be *jarase* in the case of the [suffixes] *Re*, *Aṅ*, *Si*, and *ṅsi*.

In the case of *jarasaḥ*, the substitution *jaras* prevails by overriding *yāṭ* due to its being antaranga; and let it be that in *ṅe* [the form] *jarasi*, the substitution *jaras* prevails by overriding both the nitya *ām* and the antaranga *yāṭ*.
Nevertheless, by virtue of that substitution *jaras* being *sthānivadbhūta*, one relies upon its being an *ābanta* [stem].

Why would the substitution of *et*, the change to the feminine form (*śī*), the augment *yāṭ*, and the augment *nuṭ* not occur? Furthermore, by this very principle, the substitute *jaras* would [otherwise] override the substitution of *et*, the change to the feminine form (*śī*), the augment *yāṭ*, and the augment *nuṭ* in the case of the words *nāsikā*, *niśā*, and *pṛtanā*. Nevertheless...

One might raise the objection—beginning with "Even though" (*yadyapi*)—that because the substitute *aujas* is treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), it would end in the vowel *ā*; and relying on that *ā*-ending, the rules for *etva*, *śībhāva*, *yāṭ*, and the *nuṭ* augment would consequently apply.
He refutes this with "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*): these rules are dependent upon the original form (*sthānin*) which ends in *ā*.

The rules for *et* and so forth apply; therefore, when those [rules] are to be applied, the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) cannot belong to the substitutes such as *jaras*, because that is prohibited by the rule *analvidhau*.
Consequently, since the substitutes such as *jaras* do not acquire the status of ending in long *ā* (*ābantatva*), the rules for *et* and so forth do not take effect—this is the meaning.

Indeed, a rule (*vidhi*) that operates by taking as its basis a substitute (*sthānin*) on the grounds of properties such as *akāratva* (the property of being the phoneme *a*), which are not coextensive with *altva* (the property of being any vowel), is an *al-vidhi*; it is not any rule whatsoever that takes an *al* as its basis. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of the lengthening [of the vowel] in *rāmāya* by the rule *supi ca*. For in that case, the lengthening...

In the case of *yā* and so forth as well, [the suffix] is prescribed by another rule. Furthermore, the status of being a *suptiṅ* (an affix) for the substitute *yā* is obtained through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. Moreover, the substitute *yā* has the vowel *e* as its original element (*sthānī*). Consequently, because the long vowel [of *yā*] depends on that portion of the *suptiṅ* status which constitutes its own cause, the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning an *al*" (*analvidhau*) applies, and thus [the substitution] occurs in the long vowel.

If the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* were absent for the substitute (*ādeśa*) when an operation was to be performed, then because it would lack the property of being a *suptiṅanta* (an inflected word), the long vowel would not occur when that [substitute] follows. However, there is no fault if one adopts the view that an "operation concerning an *al*" (*alvidhi*) is an operation that proceeds by taking as its basis a substitute *al* through the mediation of properties such as being the letter *a*, which are subsumed under the general property of being an *al*.

For the long vowel [ā], which is the substitute (y-ādeśa), does not rely on its original element (sthānin) as being the phoneme *e* (*ekāra*), but rather solely as being a case-ending (*sup*). Furthermore, the property of being a case-ending (*suptva*) is not coextensive with (*avyāpya*) the property of being an *al*-phoneme (*altva*), because it exists even in forms such as *bhyām*. Consequently, since the substitution of the long vowel is not a rule concerning an *al*-phoneme (*analvidhi*), when that [substitution] is to be performed, the substitute *y-ādeśa*...

Since the status of being a *suptiṅanta* (an inflected word) is possible through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is unimpeded. In the present case, however, rules such as those for *etva* (the substitution of *e*) are applicable by virtue of the fact that the forms ending in *ā* and *ī* constitute the substituenda (*sthānin*) for the *jaras* replacement. Furthermore, the property of being an *āp* (a nominal stem ending in *ā*) is a characteristic of the entire complex, not merely of the letter *ā*.

Furthermore, anticipating the objection that since the rules for *et* and so forth are not *analvidhi* (rules where the substitute is not like the original), the status of having an *ā*-stem (*ābantatva*) for the substitute *jaras* would be unavoidable when those rules are to be applied due to its being a *sthānivadbhāva* (treated like the original), he says "ā āp" and so on.
In rules such as "āṅ cāpiḥ," one should understand the form "ā āp" by compounding it through *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous sounds).

The substitution of *et* (and other such changes) is prescribed by taking recourse to that which ends in the long vowel *ā*. Consequently, since those [substitutions] also take recourse to the form of the property of being *ākāra*, they are not *al-vidhi*s (rules concerning phonemes).

Therefore, when those [substitutions] are to be applied, because of the status of *jaras* as a *sthānivadbhāva* (behaving like its original), the state of ending in *ā* (*ābanta-tva*) is not possible. And thus...
The meaning is that rules such as those concerning *et* and so forth do not apply here. He states "in this way" (*evam*) by way of a digression:
just as in rules such as "āṅ cāpiḥ," there is a *praśleṣa* (splitting) of *ā* and *āpi*, so too in the rule "halṅyābbhyām," there is a *praśleṣa* of *ṅī* and *ī*, and *ā* and *āpi*;
thus, by means of the long vowel resulting from *savarṇadīrgha*, the long vowel is included [in the technical name].

The construction [of the rule] is that [the suffix] must be rejected. Now, one might object: if there were no mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in that [rule], then in forms such as *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, there would also be elision of the case-ending *su*.
For instance, the word *khaṭvā* ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; thus, one who has surpassed a bed is *atikhaṭvaḥ*. [In this derivation,] "words beginning with *ati*"...

The compound is formed according to the rule *krāntādyarthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). The city established by Kuśāmba is *Kauśāmbī*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tena nirvṛtam*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. One who has departed from Kauśāmbī is *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā*.
This is a compound. In both cases, by the rule *gostriyoḥ*, there is shortening of the long vowel *ā* (in *āp*) and the long vowel *ī* (in *ṅīp*);

thereafter, the case endings (*sup*) are produced—this is the established position. Here, because the status of ending in *āp* (in the form of the vowel *ā*) and the status of ending in *ṅīp* (in the form of the vowel *ī*) are not lost due to the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of the case ending *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* would otherwise apply.

Therefore, he says that the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) is indeed necessary for the sake of excluding those cases, stating: "for the purpose of establishing forms such as *atikhaṭvaḥ* and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. The underlying intention is this: if there were a *praśleṣa* (splitting of a vowel) such that *ṅī* and *ī* are taken together, and *ā* and *āp* are taken together, then one would have to rely upon both the form *āt* and the form *īt* as the bases for the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*.

The application of *sulopa* (the elision of the nominative suffix) must be stated; furthermore, because the rules for *ītvā* and *ātva* possess properties that are subsumed under the property of being vowels (*altva*), and because the rule for the elision of *su* applies by taking those [properties] as its primary consideration, it is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). Therefore, [the substitution] does not function as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Since there is the status of being a *ṅyāp* [ending], there is no elision of *su*. And thus, since the purpose of including the term "long" (*dīrgha*) is accomplished by means of the *praśleṣa* (the inclusion of the long vowel), the inclusion of the term "long" in the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* need not be made;
this is explained in detail elsewhere. It might be argued that in the rule *ṭhyāḍāpaḥ*, [the compound] is *ā-āp*.
Even if there were *praśleṣa* (the elision of the final vowel of the first member), the suffix *yāṭ* would be unavoidable in the case of *atikhaṭvāyāḥ*.

[The derivation is as follows: *atikhaṭvaḥ* is derived from "one who has surpassed the bed" (*khaṭvām atikrāntaḥ*). Through the compound formation governed by the rule *atyādayaḥ*, and the shortening of the feminine stem by the rule *go-striyoḥ*, this form is obtained. Then, when the replacement by *ReĀP* occurs, [the rule] *supi ca* applies.
The form is *dīrghe atikhaṭvāyāḥ*. In that case, the suffix *yāṭ* would apply by the rule *ṭhyāḍāpaḥ*.

This is because, given the presence of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), the property of having the vowel *ā* (*ākāratva*) exists by virtue of its being treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor [can it be argued] that because the property of being the vowel *ā* (*ākāratva*) is a sub-property of the property of being a phoneme (*altva*), it cannot be taken into account.

It should not be argued that because the rule for *yāṭ* is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*), the long vowel [of *ākāra*] does not possess the status of being an *ā* by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*; for the application of *yāṭ* is based on an *ā* whose form is precisely *ākāra*. In that regard, the fact that it has the form of *ākāra* is established for the long vowel by its very nature.

That [quality] cannot be obtained through *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). Rather, it is only the property of *āptva* (being the augment *āP*) that is obtainable through *sthānivadbhāva*.

And *āptva* is a property of the entire complex (*samudāya-dharma*), not a property subsumed under *altva* (the property of being an *al* [phoneme]). Therefore, even though it depends on the original *al* (*sthānyalāśrayatva*) in its form as such, because it is not a rule concerning an *al* (*alvidhi*), *sthānivadbhāva* applies in the rule for *yāṭ*.

Having raised the objection that [the rule] would be difficult to block, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not). "Evam api" means even though there is the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā* in the rule "ṅy-āḍ-apah.
"Svāśrayam" means that whose locus (*āśraya*) is its own (*sva*), namely the vowel *ā*, is the locus of the property of being *ā* (*ākāratva*). That is "svāśrayam."

The meaning is that [the suffix] *siddha* is established by the *stava*. The textual passage beginning with "even so" (*evamapi*) and ending with "it would be" (*syāt*) is intended to express a doubt. The syntactical connection is: "and thus it should not be said. To the question "Why?", he says: "when a stem ends in *-āp*" (*ābantam yadaṅgam*).
For in the rule "*yāḍ apaḥ*," the mention of *-āp* (by means of the term *āp-grahaṇena*)...

By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), that which ends in *ā* (an *ābanta*) is understood. The term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) serves as its qualifier. Consequently, *yāṭ* is prescribed for the *ṅit* [suffix] following a stem ending in *ā*.
This applies to that which has as its initial constituent the form of the word from which the suffix was ordained.
The meaning of the subsequent technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is that there is the inclusion of a composite whole whose final constituent member is of the nature of an affix (*pratyaya*).
The resulting meaning is that when an affix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of the entire composite consisting of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the affix.
And in the present case, namely *atikhaṭvāyā*, [this applies].

Since the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is prescribed after the word *khaṭvā*, which ends in a short vowel (*a*), the form *khaṭvā* itself is that which ends in *ṭāp*. However, with respect to the case-ending *ṅti* (the nominative singular), this [form *khaṭvā*] is not a stem (*aṅga*), because the suffix *ṅti* is prescribed only after the word *atikhaṭvā*.
As for the fact that *atikhaṭvā* is a stem, it does not end in *ṭāp*; therefore, by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), it possesses the status of *āp*.

The sense is that even though [the condition] exists, the suffix *yāṭ* does not apply. Now, since it was stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇam* that "in the case of a feminine suffix which is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*),
the restriction [that the name *aṅga* applies] to what begins with that [suffix] is prohibited"— and thus when [a form] ending in that [suffix] is taken, by that [rule], the *aṅga*...

It should not be argued that because the term "aṅga" (base) is qualified [by the word "ṅy-āp-antam"], the meaning becomes "that base which ends in a feminine suffix marked by ṅ or ā," and thus the aforementioned fault remains intact in the case of *atikhaṭvāyai*— for we rely on the qualification of the base itself (*aṅgasya*). For this very reason,
the opinion of the author of the Vārttika is that "when there is the mention of ṅī, āp, and ghu, a substitute that is not long does not behave as a *sthānin*."

The author of the Bhāṣya has refuted [the objection] by stating: "Since there is an absence of the result (*phala*) when the word is short, the status of being a *sthānin* does not apply; how, then, could that status be obtained for the long vowel in place of it? Now, he states the specific rule regarding the word *nāsikā*: *paddan...* [Pāṇini 6.1.63]. Thus, in the *śas* case, we have *nasaḥ*; in the *ṭā* case, *nasā*; and in *nobhyām*, etc.

In the case of *nas-bhyām*, since the condition for being a *pada* is met by the rule *svādiṣu*, the substitution of *ru* occurs by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*. Then, by the rule *haśi ca*, the vowel *u* is substituted [for the *r*], and after applying the *guṇa* [vowel] change, the forms *nobhyām*, *nobhiḥ*, and so forth, are produced; this is the meaning.
Regarding *nassu*: "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*) means in the alternative where the substitution of *naś* does not occur before suffixes beginning with *śas*. Now, regarding the word *niśā*:

He shows the specific [application]: "of *niś* before *niś*" (*niśāyā niśiti*). The remainder [of the rule] is supplied by the sūtra *ṭhśasādau ṭhpaddanno* (Pāṇini 6.1.63). When *niś-bhyām* is established, [the following applies:
(291) *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājaccchaśāṃ ṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.36.

*braśca-bhrasj-*: these seven roots beginning with *vraśc* [are the subject]. *Ch* and *ś* are the two phonemes; by means of them, taking the word-form as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in those sounds (*tadantavidhi*). From the rule *ṭhjalo jhalī*, the term *ṭhjhalī* is carried over (*anuvartate*). *Padasya* (of a word) is the governing heading (*adhikṛtam*). [The rule continues: *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyor ante*.

The word "at the end" (ante) is understood from the preceding context. Thus he says: "of *vraśc* and so forth. That it is a substitute for the final letter is obtained from the rule *alo'ntyasya*. Regarding the phrase "by the *jaś*-ness of *ṣ*": when *ś* has become *ṣ* by the present rule, that *ṣ* becomes a member of a word (*padatva*) by the rule *svādiṣu*, and consequently, [it becomes *j*] by the rule *jhalāñ jaśo'nte*.
The meaning is that because of the similarity of place (*sthāna-sāmya*) due to the *jaś*-ness [of the dental *s*], the form becomes *niḍ-bhyām* and so on when there is the letter *ḍ*.
Regarding "in the case of *sup*" (*supi*): when *niś-su* is situated, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ṭvraśca*; then, by the *jaś*-ness of that [ṣ], it becomes *ḍ*;
and by the rule *ṅsi dhuṭ*, the augment *dhuṭ* sometimes occurs. Regarding "the change to *c*" (*cartvam*): [this refers to the subsequent substitution].

The phrase "ṭh-ḍh-dh-ay-oh" is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Due to similarity of place of articulation (*sthāna-sāmyāt*), *ḍ* becomes *ṭ*, and *dh* becomes *t*. Regarding the word "tasya": it means "of the *cartya*" (the substitution of *c*). Regarding "ṭhathau na": this means that in the alternative where *dhuṭ* is absent, *ṭ* does not become *ṭh*; and in the alternative where *dhuṭ* is present, *t* does not become *th*. This is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṭh-nādiny-ākrośe". Regarding the term "cayaḥ"...

Since the reading "dvitīyā" is observed, the *cartva* (the substitution of *ra* for *repha*) is subsequent (*para*) with respect to that. Now, having raised the objection that the letter *ta* might become *ṭa* by virtue of the rule *ṣṭuan*, he says: "not after a word-final [consonant].
It should be understood that the status of being a "word" (*padatva*) applies here because of the rule *svādiṣu*. The form *niṭtsu* is the form when the *dhuṭ* augment is present.
But in the alternative where that [dhuṭ] is absent, we have *niṭsu*.

(292) *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ saki* (Pāṇini 8.2.41). There, in the alternative where *dhuṭ* is absent, when *niṭ-su* is established, by the rule *vraśca-* (8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ* for [the final consonant], and of that...

Before the application of *jaśtva* to the letter *ṣ*, he states [the following] to address the potential objection regarding the letter *k*: *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *ṣa* and *ḍha*. The term *si* is in the locative case. Thus he says: "of *ṣa*" and so forth.
"But this does not occur" means that the letter *k* does not replace the letter *ṣ*; rather, *jaśtva* [applies].

"Because it is not established for the present case. The sense is that, in comparison with the rule *jhalāñ jaśo'nte*, the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* is subsequent (and thus takes precedence). In the case of the absence of the substitute *niś* in the forms beginning with *śas*, and also in the locative singular (*suṭ*), it is like *ramā*. Regarding the rule *vraścādi*, he states another opinion: "Some, however... [referring to] *ekāco vaśaḥ*.

The sense is that because the term *dhātoḥ* (of a root) is carried over from the subsequent sūtra, it is appropriate for it to be carried over even into the middle [sūtra]. And this carried-over term *dhātoḥ* is a qualifier only of *ch* and *ś*, as in the case of *vraśca* and others.

Because of the non-deviation from being a verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the phrase "by way of being a *jaś* sound": in forms such as *niṣṣyām*, since *niśit* lacks the status of a verbal root, there is no application of the rule for *ṣatva*. Consequently, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte* ("the *jaś* sounds replace [the *jhaś* sounds] at the end of a word"), the letter *ś* is replaced by *j* due to the similarity of their place of articulation (*sthāna*). This is the meaning in the case of *nijbhyām*.

Anticipating the objection regarding the substitution of *k* (*kutva*), he says: "But there is no *kutva*," because the substitution of *j* (*jaśtva*) is not established [at that stage]. The phrase "with respect to *kutva*" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Regarding *nicśu*: when *niśsu* is present, the *ś* is replaced by *j* through *jaśtva*; that *j* is replaced by *ś* through *ścutva*; and the *j* is replaced by *c* through *cartva*. [Then] the *ś*...
This is the *cchatva*-substitution.

The meaning is that for the words *māṃsa*, *pṛtanā*, and *sānu*, the substitutes *māṃs*, *pṛt*, and *snu* should be stated [respectively]. This is a *vārttika* on the rule *paddanno* (Pāṇini 6.1.63). Therefore...
Thus he says: "or in the case of *śas* and so on. The sense is that this is because the rule *paddan* applies optionally.

Since the words *māṃsa* and *sānu* are not feminine, he cites *pṛtanā* alone as an example for the substitution of *pṛt* before *śas* and so on—namely, *pṛtaḥ*. The phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*) refers to the alternative in which the substitution of *pṛt* does not occur.

This is the meaning. Regarding the example *gopā viśvapāvat*: because the word does not end in the suffix *āP*, there is no elision of the *su* (nominative singular ending); this is the meaning. Thus end the words ending in *ā*. Now, those ending in *i*. Regarding the word *prāyeṇa*: the word *prāya* is a synonym for *bahula* (frequently/mostly). Amara states, "The word *prāya* [is used] in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*). However, in this context, it denotes a slight deficiency (*īṣadūnatva*).

The third case ending [instrumental singular] is applied because [the word *mati*] belongs to the group beginning with *prakṛti*. The meaning is that the word *mati* is to be understood as being slightly deficient (*īṣadūna*) in its sense of "lion" (*hari*). He states the specific rule regarding the nominative plural (*śas*): "Due to its feminine gender, there is an absence of *natva*.
The intention is that *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *s*) is prescribed by the rule "tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi" only when [the stem] is masculine. In the instrumental singular...

Fearing that the substitution of *n* for *na* might not apply, he says: "not *nā*, nor *na*. The intention is that in the rule prescribing the substitution of *n* for *na*—namely, *āṅe nā'striyām*—the phrase "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*) functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion).
(293) *ṅiti hrasvaśca* | Pāṇini 1.4.6.

Since the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) would not apply here because [the stems] are called *yū* and *strī*, he says—intending to show the optional application of the suffixes *ṅ* and *su*—“*ṅiti hrasvaśca*” (before a suffix marked with *ṅ*, there is also the short vowel). Here, due to the word *ca* (“also”), there are two sentences. For it follows from the previous rule: “*yū stryākhyau nadī*” (the *yū* [stems] and those called *strī* are *nadī*). *Yū* refers to *ī* and *ū*. From the rule “*dīrghāj jasi ca*”...

The absence of the prohibition of the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). The term *stryākhyau* means "those two which denote only a female"; that is to say, they must be invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*).
The rule *neyaṅvaṅsthānāvastrī* follows [from the previous], with the negative particle (*nañ*) excluded. [This refers to] *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.

The analysis of the compound is: "those two whose positions are *sthāna* and *sthiti*. This means they are eligible for the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. From the rule "vāmī," the word "ve" (the suffix *vāp*) is understood to carry over. Consequently, [the term refers to] long vowels (*ī* and *ū*) that are not the word "strī," which are always feminine and occupy the positions for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.

The phrase "or they are termed *nadī* when followed by a *ṅit* [suffix]" constitutes one complete rule. Furthermore, the term *ṭhyū* (the *yū* following *ṭhi*) is carried over [by *anuvṛtti*]. *Yū* refers to both *i* and *u*. The term *hrasva* (short vowel) applies there to each of them individually.
The term *stryākhyau* (denoting feminine) is also carried over; however, for that term, only the sense of "feminine gender" (*strīliṅgau*) is relevant here.

The intended meaning is that there is not a single sentence such as "the vowels *ī* and *ū*, being feminine by nature, are designated as *nadī* when followed by a *ṅit* [suffix]. Furthermore, the term *ṭhyū* is carried over [from the previous rule]. *ī* and *ū* together form *yū*. There, the term *hrasva* (short) applies to each one individually. [The term] *stryākhyau* (denoting feminine) [is also carried over].

And [the word] *anu* follows. Of that [word], only this much is intended to be expressed: "feminine gender," and not "invariably feminine gender," according to the commentary. From the rule *vāmī*, the word *vā* also follows. Consequently, short *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels that are feminine are designated as *nadī*.
Thus, the two rules "vā sto ṅiti" merge into a single statement.

This is what he means by saying "those that have *i* or *u* as their *sthāna*. Furthermore, in the second statement, although the feminine gender is qualified by the term "nitya" (constant), this applies to words such as *iṣu*, *aśani*, and *araṇi*, which possess both genders.

It should be understood that for words such as *paṭu* and *mṛdu*, which possess all three genders (*triliṅga*), there would otherwise be no optionality regarding their being treated as *nadī* when followed by an affix marked with *ṅ*. In this regard, since the status of *nadī* is already established for the short vowels (*hrasva*) and is precluded for the long vowels (*dīrgha*) by the rule "ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ" and "neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī," this [present] rule provides an optional alternative (*vibhāṣā*) for the application of *nadī*-status.

Regarding the view that it is a *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long ī), he says: *āṇ nadyāḥ*. When *mati-e* is established, after applying *āṭ* [augment] and *vṛddhi*, and then *yaṇ* [substitution], he states the resulting forms: *matyai* and *mataye*. In the alternative view where it is not a *nadī*, because it is a *ghi* by the rule "the remainder is *ghi*, except for *sakhi*," there is *guṇa* by the rule *heḥ ṅti*, and with the substitution of *ay*, the form is like that of the word *hari*.
In the case where [mati] is treated as a *nadī*, when the suffixes *ṅsi* and *ṅs* follow, there is *vṛddhi* (resulting in *ā*), followed by *yaṇ* substitution:

*matyāḥ*. In the absence of *nadī*-status, it is *mateḥ*. Regarding the suffix *ām*, even though *nadī*-status is absent, because the stem ends in a short vowel, *nuṭ* is inserted, resulting in the long vowel: *matīnām*. He states the specific rule for the suffix *ṅi*: "In the case where [it is treated as] a *nadī*. In the case where it is treated as a *nadī*...
Because [the word] has been replaced by *ghi*, the substitution of *au* (as prescribed by *ṭā-cca gheḥ*)—which is taught as being conditioned by the presence of *at*—does not occur.
Rather, *ReĀrām* would have applied; however, having set that aside, when *āṬ* alone is about to apply by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), this is the meaning.

(294) *idudbhyām* | Pāṇini 7.3.117. From the rule *ReĀrām*, the term *nadī* and the expression *ReĀrām* are carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "from those [stems] designated as *nadī*" and so forth. The phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*) refers to this.

The meaning is that in the case where [the word] does not possess the status of a *nadī*, the *aut* substitution (for the final vowel) is taught as being conditioned by the presence of *atva* in the rule "ṭā-ṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ" (*Pāṇini 7.3.112*).

[The forms] *matyām* and *matau* are the forms when there is the status of a *nadī* and when there is its absence. In *matyām*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs because the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Similarly for *śruti* and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
The inclusion of *smṛti* and so forth.

(295) *tricaturoḥ striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ* |7|2|99|. [The rule begins with] *tricaturoḥ*. For these two, these forms [are substituted]: for *tri* and *catur*, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* [are substituted]. *tricaturostisṛ catasṛ*.

The meaning is "these two. Regarding the phrase "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*): the intention is that this is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "of *aṣṭan*, [the substitution of] *āt* before a case-ending" (*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*). When *jaś* and *śas* follow, the form *tisṛ-as* is established.
Then, by the rule (296) *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (P. 7.2.100): "Before a vowel, *ra* is substituted for the final *ṛ* of *tisṛ*."

*aci* and *ṛtaḥ*: From the preceding sūtra, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are carried over (*anuvartate*). This is understood here as having its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). Thus he says, beginning with "tisṛ," etc. Now, one might object that the result is already established by the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci*; to this he replies: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *guṇa*, *dīrgha*, and *utva*. [The rule applies to] *ṛtaḥ*.

The meaning is that *ratva* (the substitution of *r*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa* [substitution] prescribed by "ṅī" (Pāṇini 7.3.110), to the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same class as the preceding) prescribed by "prathamayoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.102), and to the *utva* (substitution of *u*) prescribed by "ṛta ud" (Pāṇini 6.1.111). Regarding the form *tisraḥ*: this is the form for the case-endings *jas* and *śas*.

Among these, in the case of *jas*, *ratva* is the exception to the *guṇa* [substitution] prescribed by "ṛto ṅī"; however, in the case of *śas*, [it is the exception to the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* prescribed by] "prathamayoḥ."

Thus, the substitution of *ra* (by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Regarding the form *tisṛ-ām*: when *tisṛ-ām* is established, the substitution of *ra* by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* would apply, superseding the augment *nuṭ*. However, since the rule *numaciratṛjvadbhāvaguṇebhyo nuṭ pūrvavipratiṣedhena* states that the augment *nuṭ* takes precedence over the addition of *num*, the substitution of *ra* would result in *tisrām*. [To prevent this, the following applies: The substitution of *ra* is an exception to the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Regarding *ām*: when *tisṛ-ām* is established, the substitution of *ra* by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* would result in *tisrām*, as it would supersede the augment *nuṭ*. However, according to the principle "the augment *nuṭ* [takes effect] by prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over the addition of *num*, the substitution of *ra*, the treatment as *ṛju*, and the *guṇa*," the substitution of *ra* would occur. [Therefore, the following rule is required: The substitution of *ra* is an exception to the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Regarding *ām*: when *tisṛ-ām* is established, the substitution of *ra* by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* would result in *tisrām*, as it would supersede the augment *nuṭ*. However, because of the rule "the augment *nuṭ* [takes effect] by prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over the addition of *num*, the substitution of *ra*, the treatment as *ṛju*, and the *guṇa*," the substitution of *ra* would occur. [To avoid this, the following is stated: The substitution of *ra* is an exception to the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).
