The meaning is that [the rule] *nuṭ* is set aside.
(297) *na tisṛcatasṛ*. When *tisṛnām* is established, the long vowel [prescribed] by the rule *nāmī* would apply; hence, *na tisṛcatasṛ*.

The word "tisṛcatasṛ" is a compound in which the genitive case ending has been elided. From the rule "ḍhralope," the term "dīrgha" (long vowel) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*, and the sūtra "nāmī" is also understood. Thus he says, beginning with "tisṛ" and so forth. In the form "tisṛṇām," the substitution of *ṇ* occurs according to the rule "ṛvarṇānnasya. Now, [one might object]: "In the presence of an *ac* [vowel], *ra*..."

If it is argued that the substitution of *rat* [for *tisṛ*] cannot be an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ut* by the rule "ṛta ud" because the substitution of *ut* applies only to the cases of the nominative-accusative singular (*ṅsi-ṅsoḥ*),

and because the words *tri* and *catur* always end in the plural number and thus lack the *ṅsi-ṅsoḥ* endings— [we reply: no, for that [substitution of *ut*] occurs in Bahuvrīhi compounds such as *priyatisra*.

And that will be explained immediately below. Now, one might ask: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *priyatri*, meaning 'one who has three beloveds,' why should the substitution of *tisṛ* not occur? To this, he says "in the feminine," and so forth. For it is the word *priyatri* that is feminine, not the word *tri*.

Regarding the term *striyām* ("in the feminine"): it is a qualifier of *tri* and *catur*, but not of their compounds (*tadanta*), as there is no evidence for such a claim. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the compounds is obtained through the status of being a *prakṛti* (base); for even so, since *tri* and *catur* themselves are directly heard in the text, it is more appropriate that *striyām* be a qualifier of those two alone.
The meaning is as follows: having considered the optional application of the designation *nadī* (feminine stem) by the rule "ṭhṅiti hrasvaśca," he says "like the word *mati*.

As for the phrase "but in the case of *ām*": the intention is that in the genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvacana*), because the substitution of *traya-* [for *tri-*, as prescribed by the rule "ṭhtrestrayaḥ"] is a *prakṛty-aṅga* (an operation affecting the base), it applies even when that [substituted form] ends in the suffix. And thus, regarding the term "in the feminine" (*striyām*).

If [the rule] were qualified by "having three or four as specific members," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *priyatri*, which contains the masculine/neuter gender word *tri*; therefore, it is established that the qualification "only for *tri* and *catur* in the feminine" must be applied. Now, [the discussion continues:]

Thinking that the term *striyām* ("in the feminine") is a qualifier of *tri-* and *catuḥ-* alone—and not of those [stems] ending in them—in order to avoid the charge of non-application (*avyāpti*) in a bahuvrīhi compound containing the feminine word *tri*, he says "one who loves three" (*priyatisra*), etc. Regarding *priyatisā*: when the compound is formed, there is elision (*luk*) of the intermediate case-ending.

Upon the elision of the *t* and the cessation of the substitution of *tisṛ*, the suffix *su* follows the word *priyatri*. Here, although the word *priyatri* is masculine, the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs because the word *tri* is feminine.
By the rule *ṛduśanas-puru-daṃsa-sunvanta-tamām-ṇyaḥ*, the suffix *anaṅ* is applied. By the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, there is lengthening of the vowel. Then, the *n* is elided.
The point is that if the term *striyām* were a qualifier of the base (*aṅga*) ending in three or four suffixes, there would be an instance of under-extension (*avyāpti*) here.
Now, one might object: "Even if it is a qualifier of the base ending in three or four suffixes, there is no under-extension here, because [in the case of] *priyāstisraḥ*..."

If it is argued that because the substitution of *tisṛ* for *tri*, which operates in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "yasya," can also be understood to carry over into the compound, this is not so; for the worldly sentence (*laukikavākya*),
being already finalized, is not the source (*prakṛti*) of the compound, but rather the non-worldly sentence (*alaukika*) alone is.

This is the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*). Consequently, in the non-worldly analytical sentence (*alaukikaprakriyāvākya*) "priyā as tris," when the compound (*samāsa*) is about to take effect, the elision (*luk*)—being external (*bahiraṅga*)—overrides the substitution of *tisṛ* by means of the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "An external [operation] overrides even internal rules. Thus, after the elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktiluk*), [the form is established].
When the suffix *su* is produced after the compound *priyatris*,

the word *tri* undergoes the substitution *tisṛ* by the paribhāṣā rule "substitutions apply to that which is explicitly indicated," because *tricatur-*, etc., functions as an *aṅga* (stem) even under the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*). And that [substitution] applies to the form *stirāyaṃ*.

If [the word] were a qualifier of three or four constituent members (*aṅga*), it would not be possible, because the constituent member *priyatri* is masculine. Furthermore, even if the substitution of *tisṛ* were to occur here, the suffix *kap* would not apply by the rule *nadyutaśca*. For that suffix, being a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), ought to apply to the unanalytic (extraordinary) compound sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*) just as it does to the compound itself.

And at that time, because the final member of the compound, the word *tri*, does not end in the vowel *ṛ*, the suffix *kap* is not applied; furthermore, since the intervening case-ending has been elided by *luk*, there is no application of the rule regarding the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and thus the substitution of *katisra-* conditioned by *jas* does not occur. Nor [is it applied] when the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) has not yet been formed, even if *kap* were present.
When the case-ending suffix (*sup*) is produced after the word *priyātri*, and the substitution of *tisṛ* has occurred, the addition of the suffix *kap* might be suspected.

However, since the status of being a compound (*samāsatva*) cannot be established until the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) has been applied, it is impossible for the case-ending suffix to arise from that [word with the *tisṛ* substitution]; let this matter rest for now. [The form] *priyatisrau* [is derived by applying] the *guṇa* [vowel substitution].

The substitution of *ratva* (the replacement by *r*) occurs by setting aside [the application of] *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*. Thus, in *priyatisraḥ*, *ratva* sets aside the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* that would otherwise apply before the case-ending *jas*.
In *priyatisram*, *ratva* sets aside both the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form) and the *guṇa* (vocalic strengthening) that would apply before the case-ending *am*.
The phrase "an exception to *guṇa*, *dīrgha*, and *utva*" is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the *pūrvarūpa* as well.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth": *priyatisrau*, *priyatisraḥ*, *priyatisrā*, *priyatisre*.

In the forms of the genitive singular (*ṅsi*) and ablative singular (*ṅs*), it remains simply *priyatisraḥ*; here, the substitution of *u* (by the rule *ṛta ut*) is superseded by the substitution of *r*.

[In the dual genitive/ablative: *priyatisroḥ*. In the case of the genitive plural marker *ām*, since the substitution of *tisr-* applies after superseding the substitution of *tray-* due to its higher priority, [the form is *priyatisṝṇām*].
Having set aside *ratvam*, the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "ṭh-num-aciraḥ. Thus: *priyatisṛṇām*, *priyatisraḥ*.
By the rule "ṛto ṅī," *ratvam* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa* substitution. Thus: *priyatisroḥ*. Now, one might ask:
how is it that a family which has three beloved women is called *priyatṛ*? [This is because] of the word *tri*.

Because the form *tisṛ* would apply due to its feminine gender, he says: "by the elision of *su* and *am*. The meaning is that since *su* and *am* are elided by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, there is an absence of the designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by the rule *na lumatā*, and consequently, because it is not followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the substitution of *tisṛ* does not occur.

Regarding the phrase "because of its being non-eternal": it will be stated in the section on neuter nouns that the rule *na lumatā* ("there is no substitution when a *lumat* suffix follows") is non-eternal, because of the inclusion of the term *aj* in the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau* ("for *ik*, before an *ac*-beginning case-ending").

Since the rule *daci raḥ* ("*raḥ* is substituted for *daḥ* before an *ac*-beginning case-ending") is more powerful than the *num* augment prescribed by *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* ("*num* is added after a neuter stem ending in *jhal* or *ac*") with respect to case-endings beginning with *ac*, [the former prevails].
Fearing that *ratvam* (the substitution of *ra*) might apply [to the word *ṛtaḥ*], he says: "Because of *katvam*"—this is a fifth case (*pañcamī*) used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
The meaning is that by the rule of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *num* is applied, overriding *ratvam*. Thus, *priyatisṛṇī*:
having overridden *ratvam*, *num* is applied, and then *ṇatvam*. *Priyatisṛṇi*: [here] *śi* replaces *jas* and *śas*.

The augment *num* occurs by overriding the substitution of *ṇ*. Because [the stem] ends in *n*, it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*; thus, there is the lengthening of the vowel characterized by ending in *n*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. This is established by resorting to a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior counter-exception) on the basis of the examples given in the Bhāṣya for the rule *ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca*: namely, *priyatisṛṇī* and *priyatisṛṇī*.

It should be understood that there is the substitution of *rat* [for *ṛt*]. Regarding *priyatisṛṇā*: this is the form with the *num* augment when the *ṭā* case-ending is present and the option of *puṃvat* (masculine-like treatment) does not apply.

Regarding *pritatisrā*: here, because of the *puṃvat* treatment, there is no *num*, and thus the substitution of *rat* occurs. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), forms such as *priyatisre* and *priyatisṛṇe* are to be understood. Regarding "the substitution of *rat* for *dvi*": [this refers to the rule concerning the dual].
The meaning is that when a case-ending follows the word *dvi*, the substitution of *yat* for *tyadādi* occurs, and then by the rule "ṭāb-aj-ādya-taḥ," the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
Thus, "dve" and so forth; once *ṭāp* has been added, through the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*), the forms of the word *dvā* are identical to those of *ramā*.
These are the words ending in short *i*.

Now, those ending in *ī*: [the word] *gaurī* [is derived] from the word *gaura* by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule for the *gaurādi* group, and then the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "and that which is marked with *ṭh*" (*ṭhyasyeti ca*). From that [base *gaurī-*], the nominative singular suffix *su* is added; the intention is that [the final *ī*] is elided by the rule "after a consonant, *ṅ*, or *ī*, etc. (*halṅyādilopa*). Regarding *gauryau*: the substitution *yaṇ* occurs because the rule "prohibition of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding" (*dīrghājjasi ca*) applies here.

The meaning is as follows: regarding "gaurīṣu," the intention is that the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel resulting from the same preceding sound) is prohibited by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca*, and thus the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. Regarding "nadīkāryam" (the operations pertaining to a *nadī* [feminine stem ending in long ī or ū]), the meaning is that it refers to what is prescribed by the rules: *ambārthanadyor hrasvaḥ* (shortening for words meaning "mother" and *nadī* stems), *āṇ nadyāḥ* (the suffix *āṇ* after a *nadī* stem), *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (the insertion of *nuṭ* after short vowels, *nadī* stems, and *āp*), and *ReĀrāmnībhyaḥ* (the substitution of *ReĀ* for the case endings beginning with *ā* after feminine stems ending in long vowels, *nadī* stems, and *ām*). [The text continues with: *yū...*

The designation "nadī" (feminine noun) applies by the rule *stryākhyau*. It is like *bahuśreyasī*. Similarly, there are forms such as *vāṇī* and *nadī*. [Regarding *vāṇī*: from the root *vaṇ* (meaning "to sound"), it is derived as *vaṇyate* or *śabdyate* ("it is sounded"). The suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *iñvapādibhyaḥ*. Then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. [Regarding *nadī*: it is listed among the roots beginning with *pac* by the rule *nadaṭ*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after [stems ending in] *paṭhita*, *aṭṭita*, and so on; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), forms such as *katrī* and *daṇḍinī* are included.

Regarding the form *sakhī*: according to the rule "In the spoken language, [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* is added after *sakhi* and *śiśu*," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to the word *sakhi*, and after the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule "and that which is designated as *yasya*" (*yasyeti ca*), the word *sakhī* is formed.

He raises the doubt that for [the word] *sakhi*, there might be the application of the augment *anaṅ* by the rule *ṭhanaṅ sau* and the status of being a *ṇit* by the rule *sakhyurasambuddhau*—this is what is meant by "prātipadika... etc. This point is addressed in the Bhāṣya on both the rules *vibhaktau liṅgaviśiṣṭāgrahaṇam* and *yuvoranākau*, as well as on the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*.

The *paribhāṣā* has been recited. Its meaning is that when an operation conditioned by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is to be performed, if there is a mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is no inclusion of the form qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*). Thus, the intention is that [the substitution of] *anaṅ* and the status of being a *ṇit* do not occur.

Regarding "sakhī": because it ends in a *ṅ* (long vowel), there is elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*). Regarding "sakhya- etc.": the meaning is that its forms are exactly like those of *gaurī*. The word *lakṣmī* is derived from the root *lakṣ* with the suffix *ī* and the augment *muṭ* according to the rule "ṭhlakṣermuṭ ca. He states its specific distinction: "because it does not end in a *ṅ*" [referring to the rule] "kṛdikārādaktinaḥ."

Thus, when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, the elision of the final vowel (*sulopa*) indeed occurs. The remainder is like *gaurī*. Regarding the word *strī*: [the root] *styai* means "to sound" and "to collect. She is called *strī* because the semen and blood coagulate (*styāyataḥ*) and come together within her. The suffix *ḍraṭ* is added to the root *styai*; both *ḍ* and *ṭ* are indicatory (*it*). By virtue of the presence of the *ṅ*, even though it is not a nominal stem (*abha*), [the feminine suffix is applied].
There is elision of the *ṭi* (the final syllable). There is elision of *y* by the rule *lopo vyoḥ*. Because it has the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

The intention is that [the subsequent] elision occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Thus, we have *he stri*. By the rule *ambārthanadyorhrasvaḥ*, the vowel is shortened. When *strī* is followed by *āṬ* (the vocative singular ending), since it is not a verbal root (*adhātu*) and does not end in *ik* or *ar*, the substitution *iyaṅ* prescribed by the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām yvoḥ* would not apply.

(298) *striyāḥ* |6|4|79|. The word *striyāḥ* [is the subject]. From the rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām yvoḥ iyaṅuvaṅau* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the terms *aci* and *iyaṅ* are carried over [by *anuvṛtti*]. Thus he says: "of the word *strī*" and so forth. *Striyau*, *striyaḥ*—these are the forms in the dual (*au*) and the nominative-accusative plural (*jas*).
Regarding the forms *ami* and *śas*, since the rule "striyāṃ striyāḥ" prescribes *iyaṅ* invariably for the feminine, [the following applies]:
(299) *vā'mśasoḥ* |6|4|80|. The analysis of the sūtra is *vā-am-śasoḥ*. From the word *striyāḥ*, [the suffix] *iyaṅ* [is applied].
And it follows [the previous rule]. Thus he says: "In *ami* and so forth. Regarding *striyam*:
this is the form with *iyaṅ*. Regarding *strīm*: in the absence of *iyaṅ*, there is *ami-pūrvaḥ* (the preceding vowel is substituted).
Regarding *striyau*: this is the form with *āṬ*. Regarding *striyaḥ* and *strīḥ*: in the case of *śas*, by the rule "*vāmśasoḥ*" and in the absence of *iyaṅ*, [the forms are derived].

*rūpam* (form): *strī* + *i* → *iyaṅ*, resulting in *striyai*. *strīyai*: by the rule *ṭāṅasiṅasām-āṭ*, the augment *āṭ* is added; then *vṛddhi* and *iyaṅ* apply. *striyāḥ*: by the rule *ṅsiṅsorāṭ*, the augment *āṭ* is added; then *vṛddhi* and *iyaṅ* apply. *striyāḥ*: in the case of the suffix *osi*, *iyaṅ* applies. Regarding the statement "because *nuṭ* is subsequent": in the case of *ām*, the rule *striyāḥ* [prescribing *iyaṅ*] overrides [the application of *āṭ*].

The augment *nuṭ* occurs because [the word *strī*] is followed by a case-ending (*paratvāt*). Regarding the example "of women" (*strīṇām*): once *nuṭ* has been applied, there is no longer a case-ending beginning with a vowel (*ajādi-vibhakti*), and thus *iyaṅ* does not apply.

Regarding the example "in a woman" (*striyām*): *ReĀrām* becomes *iyaṅ*. Now, as an incidental digression, he shows the specific forms of the word *strī* in the masculine and neuter genders—namely, "one who has surpassed a woman" (*atistrī*).

The compound is formed by the rule *ṭhatyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe* ("*ṭha*, *ati*, etc., [form compounds] with words meaning 'gone beyond,' etc."). By the rule *gostriyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), there is shortening of the vowel. Because it does not end in a long vowel (*dīrgha*), nor because it does not end in a feminine suffix ending in *ī* (*īkāranta*), the elision of the case-ending prescribed by *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68) does not occur. Thus we have *atistriyau*. [In the formation of *atistriyaḥ* from *atistriyām*, the rule] *striyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.79) [applies].

The intention is that because this [substitution] is an ancillary (*aṅga*) operation, it applies even at the end of the word by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), resulting in *iyaṅ*. Now,
in the case of the suffixes *jas*, *ṭā*, *ReĀ*, *ṅsi*, *ṅs*, *ām*, and *ṅī*, the word *strī* undergoes the substitution *iyaṅ*.

He summarizes this with the verse beginning "guṇanābhāva... and so forth. The syntactical connection is as follows: it should be understood that, due to its superior status, the *iyaṅ* substitution for the word *strī* (in the nominative plural) overrides the absence of *guṇa*, the absence of *nābhāva*, and the addition of *auṅ* in the masculine, as well as the addition of *num* in the neuter. Furthermore, there is *guṇa* by the rules "jasi ca" and "gher ṅti".

The meaning is that these [rules]— namely, the substitution of *n* by "ṭhāṅe nā'striyām," the substitution of *au* by "ṭhacca gheḥ," the addition of *nuṭ* by "ṭhhrasvanadyāpaḥ," and the addition of *num* by "ṭhiko'ci vibhaktau"— are subsequent to the *iyaṅ* substitution. Following the rule "jasi ca," the phrase "iti guṇaḥ" (the *guṇa* substitution) is to be understood as the remainder.

Regarding *atistri*: having set aside *iyaṅ* by means of *guṇa*, the form [is derived] through the substitution of *ay*. In *he atistre*, the *guṇa* is applied by the rule "guṇa for a short vowel," and then the elision of the vocative suffix is applied by the rule "eṅ and a short vowel.

In *atistrīn*, *iyaṅ* is applied by the rule "vāmśasoḥ" (in place of the feminine suffix ī when followed by the accusative plural ending -n). In the absence of *iyaṅ*, there is the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).

By the rule *tasmāc chasaḥ*, there is no substitution of *n*. In the case of the feminine suffix *ṭā* (i.e., *ā*), *nā* replaces it by the rule *āṅe nā'striyām*, which takes precedence over *iyaRṃĀ*. In the forms beginning with *bhyām*, there is no modification. In the case of *ReĀ* (the dative singular), the rule *gher ṅtī* applies; this causes the *guṇa* substitution, resulting in the replacement by *ay*. The form *atistrīṇi* is thus established. **Note on Feminine Singular:** The singular forms *atistriḥ* and *atistriḥ* are derived from the base *atistri* + *su* (the nominative/accusative singular feminine suffix). In *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, because the rule *ṭhgherṅtī* (Pāṇini 7.3.111) for *guṇa* is subsequent, it applies first;
then by *ṅsiṅsośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.110), the single-substitute *pūrvarūpa* occurs: *atistriyoḥ*. [In the case of the genitive plural *ām*: *iyaṅ* is superseded by *iyaRṃĀ* (Pāṇini 7.1.94).

Because the *nuṭ* augment is subsequent, it applies, and then by *nāmī* (Pāṇini 6.4.3), the vowel is lengthened, followed by *ṇatva*: *ati-strīṇām*. [In the case of the locative plural *su*: *iyaRṃĀ* [applies].
Because it is subsequent, the rule "ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.12) supersedes [the previous rule], and thus [the form] is *atistriau*. [The forms are: *atistriau*, *atistriyoḥ*, *atistriṣu*.

Now, regarding the masculine gender, he summarizes the very matter already established in the preceding verse by means of a more concise method for the sake of easy understanding, beginning with the words "and when there is *osi* and *aukāra*" (*osyaukāre ca*). This refers to the state of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) in the masculine.
The substitution of *iy* for the existing word *strī*, as prescribed by the rule *striyāḥ*,

would necessarily apply in the dual forms of the sixth (genitive) and seventh (locative) cases (*osi*), as well as in the dual forms of the first and second cases (*au*), but it would apply optionally (*vibhāṣā*) in the singular forms of the accusative (*am*) and nominative/accusative plural (*śas*).
The construction is as follows: "In all other cases than the four mentioned, the substitution of *iy* shall occur everywhere before a vowel.
Regarding the neuter, however, there is the augment *num*; the remainder of the rule is "it (*num*) subverts *iyaRṃĀ*. Thus, *atistri*.
[This means] a family that has surpassed the woman—*atistri*. The *su* suffix is elided by the rule "after a neuter [stem], *sva* and *ām* [are elided]."

Regarding *atistriṇī*: when *atistri-āṬ* is established, by the rule *napuṃsakācca*, the *auṅ* case-ending is replaced by *śī*. This replaces the *iyaṅ* substitution because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Then, by the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau*, *num* is inserted. Since this is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending, there is no lengthening. The *ṇatva* (nasalization) is applied. Thus we have *atistrīṇi*. By the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*, the *śi* replacement occurs for the *jas* and *śas* endings.

In the case of the word *strī*, the augment *num* is applied, overriding both the rule for *guṇa* substitution (*iyaRṃĀ jasi ca*) and the rule for the long vowel (*śi sarvanāmasthānam*). Because it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the long vowel is applied, followed by the substitution of *ṇa*.
With the suffix *ṭā*, the form is *atistriṇā*; here, the substitution of *nā* overrides both the *iyaRṃĀ* and the *num*.

Regarding the phrase "in *reĀ*, *prabhṛti* (and so forth), and *avajādi*": since it will be stated later that there is *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) when these— *reĀ*, *ṅsi*, *ṅs*, *ām*, *iṅ*, and *os*— are pronounced as beginning with the third case (*tṛtīyā*) onwards, then in the alternative where *puṃvadbhāva* applies, the form is like that of the masculine word *atistri*.

In the case where the masculine form (*puṃvat*) does not apply, the form is like *vāri* due to the presence of the *num* augment; this is the meaning. Regarding the *ṭā* case-ending, however, whether the masculine form applies or not, there is no difference in the resulting form because of the substitution of *nāt*; therefore, it was stated [in the rule] "starting from the *ReĀ* [case-endings]. As for *atistriye*: when the masculine form applies, by the rule *gher ṅti*, there is the *guṇa* substitution, which is the replacement with *ay*. Thus: *atistriṇe*.

Thus [it is said]. In the absence of *puṃvat* (masculine-like treatment), the form is produced with the *num* augment. Here, in both cases, *iyaṅ* is superseded by the *guṇa* and the *num*. Regarding *atistreḥ*: in the case of *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, when *puṃvat* applies, there is *guṇa* by the rule *gher ṅti*, and then the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) by the rule *ṅsiṅsośca*. Regarding *atistriṇaḥ*: [the same applies].

In the case where *ṅsi* and *ṅsoḥ* do not undergo *puṃvat* (masculine stem) substitution, the form is derived with the *num* augment. Here too, in both instances, *iyaṅ* is superseded by *guṇa* and *num*. Thus we have *atistriyoḥ* and *atistriṇoḥ*.
When there is no *puṃvat* substitution, *num* applies; when there is *puṃvat* substitution, *iyaṅ* applies. And so forth. Regarding *ām*, when *puṃvat* substitution occurs...

And in the absence of that [the feminine suffix], *nuṭ* alone is applied, overriding *iy-aṅ*, and not *num*, because of the rule "num-acira-". The lengthening occurs by the rule "nām-i". Thus: *atistrīṇām*. [The forms] *atistrau* and *atistriṇi*;
*atistriyoḥ* and *atistriṇoḥ*. Such is the case for the word *strī* when it is an upasarjana (secondary member).
Having demonstrated the forms regarding masculine and neuter [nouns], he returns to the subject at hand with the words "striyāṃ tu" (but in the feminine).

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who has surpassed a woman," the compound is formed by the rule "ṭatpratyādayaḥ," and when the shortening occurs by the rule "gostriyoḥ," the word *atistri* is obtained. Of that [word], for the most part...
The meaning is that these are the forms of the word *atistri* in the masculine gender as previously cited. In the case of the *śas* [instrumental/ablative plural], the form is *atistrīḥ*.

This is because, although the substitution of *iyaṅ* applies by the rule "vāmśasoḥ" and the preceding long vowel [pūrvasavarṇadīrgha] would also apply, the substitution of *n* [natva] by the rule "tasmāc chasaḥ" does not occur due to its being in the feminine gender. This is the point. [The form is] *atistriyā*.
Because it is feminine, there is no substitution of *nāt* (the long vowel *ā*), and thus *iyaṅ* applies. Regarding the phrase "ending in a short vowel":

in the rule *ṅiti hrasvaśca*, the first part of the statement is: "The vowels *ī* and *ū* that do not belong to the word *strī*, which are always feminine and occupy the place of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, optionally receive the technical designation *nadī*."

The second sentence is: "Short vowels that are *i*-colored (*ivarṇa*) or *u*-colored (*uvaṇa*) are optionally designated as *nadī* when they belong to a feminine [stem]. In this context, the meaning is that by virtue of the second sentence, there is an option regarding the *nadī* designation for the word *atistri* before the case-endings beginning with *ṅ* (i.e., the dative through the locative). Now, one might ask: since the term *astrī* ("not feminine") is understood here from the rule *neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī*, how can this [designation] apply here?
To address the [possible] misconception that this refers to the status of being a *nadī* (feminine noun), he says: "But 'not feminine' (*a-strī*)...

This exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the status of being a *nadī*—as prescribed by the first rule, "those having *iy*, *uv*, or *aṅ* as their substitutes" (*iyaRuvaṅsthānau*)—applies only to that specific case, and not to others.
The meaning is that this applies even to the status of being a "nadī" (feminine noun) prescribed by the second rule beginning with *ṭhhrasvāc ca*. Why?
To this he says: "Because only that which is connected to it [the first rule] is carried over.
(Pāṇini 1.4.4): *neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī*.

From the rule "iyaRuvaṅsthānau," it must be stated that the term "not feminine" (astrī) is carried over [from a previous rule]. Consequently, wherever the phrase "iyaRuvaṅsthānau" is connected, it is appropriate for the term "not feminine" associated with it to be carried over as well. And thus, in the rule concerning short vowels and so forth—

The intention is that because the phrase *iy-aRu-vaṅ-sthānau* does not recur [in the subsequent rule], the phrase *a-strī* also does not recur there. Thus, for *atistriyai*: when the "river" (*nadī*) designation applies, *āṬ* is substituted and *vṛddhi* occurs.
For *atistraye*: when the "river" designation does not apply, because it is a *ghi* stem, the rule *gher ṅti* applies.

In the case of the *guṇa* [substitution], there is the replacement by *ay*: *atistriyāḥ*, *atistreḥ*. When the designation *nadī* applies, there is *āṭ*; in its absence, there is *guṇa*. By the rule *ṭhṅsiṅsośca*, there is the formation of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). Thus: *atistriyām*. In the alternative where the designation *nadī* applies, there is *ReĀrām* and *āṭ*: *atistrāu*. In the alternative where the designation *nadī* does not apply, there is *acca gheḥ*.

Regarding the word *śrī*: it is called *śrī* because "they resort to her" (*śrayantyetām*). The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṭhkvibvacipracchiśrisrudruprujvāṃ dīrgho'saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*, whereby there is both the *kvip* suffix and lengthening of the stem vowel. From the word *śrī*, the nominative case ending *su* is added. Because it ends in a long vowel (*aṅ*), there is no elision of *su*. Thus we have *śriyau* and *śriyaḥ*. [The rule *dīrghājjasi ca* applies here.]

Regarding the prohibition of the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* [substitution], when the *yaṇ* [substitution] prescribed by the rule *ṭhiko yaṇ aci* would otherwise apply, the *iyaṅ* [substitution] occurs by virtue of the root ending in the vowel *i* according to the rule *śnudhātubhruvām yvoriyaṅuvaṅau*.

Because the word consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*) and because it is preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyogapūrvaka*), the *yaṇ* substitution does not take place. This is according to the rule *ṭhyū stryākhyau*.

Since [the words] are *nadī* (feminine stems), the shortening prescribed by the rule "in the sense of *ṭhaṃbha*" would apply; however, this is precluded by the rule *neyaRuvaṅ*. From the rule *yū stryākhyau nadī*, the terms *yū* and *nadī* are carried over (*anuvartate*). The word *sthāna* is derived from the root with the suffix *lyuṅ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those two for which *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are the *sthāna*, i.e., their position."

The meaning is that these two [forms] are eligible for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Thus it says: "by the rule *iyaṅuvaṅeḥ*" and so forth. Regarding the form *he śrī*: because it is eligible for *iyaṅ* due to beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*), the prohibition of the designation *nadī* applies;

consequently, by the rule "*ambārthanadyor-hrasvaḥ*," the shortening [of the final vowel] does not occur—this is the intended sense. Regarding the form *śriyam*: in the case of the accusative singular ending *am*, *iyaṅ* replaces the stem, overriding the rule for the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form).

*Śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*: as before, due to the rules for *āṬ* and *śas*. *Śriyā*: by *ṭā*. *Śriyai*: by *ṅe*; when the *nadī* designation applies because of the rule "before a *ṅit* [ending], there is also the short vowel," *āṬ* is applied and there is *vṛddhi*. *Śriye*: when the *nadī* designation does not apply, there is *iyaṅ*. *Śriyāḥ*: by *ṅsi* and *ṅs*; when the *nadī* designation applies, *āṬ* is applied and there is *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the word *śriyaḥ*: in the alternative view where it does not belong to the class of *nadī* (feminine stems ending in long ī), the substitution of *iy* and *uv* applies; however, because it lacks the designation *ṅīp*, the rule "āmi ṅiti hrasvaśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.54) would not otherwise apply. Therefore, [the sūtra] states:
(301) *vāmi* (Pāṇini 1.4.5).

The phrase *vā āmi* [is the rule]. The term *nadī*, defined as "feminine stems ending in *ī* or *ū*," is understood from the preceding context. The negation (*nañ*) from the rule *neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī* is also understood. The analysis is *vā* (or) *āmi* (in the case of *am*).
This is because there is no application of the *nadī*-rules in the presence of *am*. Thus he says: "those which occupy the place of *iy* and *uvaṅ*," and so forth.
Regarding the forms *śrīṇām*: in the view that it is a nadī-stem, the augment *ṇuṭ* is applied by the rule "ṭhhrasvanadyāpaḥ. Regarding the form *śriyām*:
in the absence of nadī-status, however, only *iy* is substituted [by "vāmśasoḥ"]. [The forms] *śriyoḥ* and *śrīṣu* follow accordingly. Regarding the word *pradhī*:

in the sense of "one who meditates" (*pradhyāyati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *dhyai*, with the rule "ṭhdhyāyateḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca" causing the semivowel *ya* to undergo vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

When the semivowel (saṃprasāraṇa) *i* undergoes the substitution of the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*) by the rule "saṃprasāraṇācca," and the lengthening by the rule "halaḥ" is applied, the word *pradhī* is formed. According to the views of the author of the Vṛtti and Haradatta, its forms are like those of the word *lakṣmī*;
for in that case, the *iyaṅ* substitution is superseded by the *yaṇ* substitution according to the rule "eranekācaḥ."

The meaning is that because they do not have the status of being *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutes, the prohibition of *nadī* status by the rule "neyaṅuvaṅsthānau" does not apply; thus, since the status of *nadī* is constant by the rule "dyū stryākhyau," the operations pertaining to *nadī*—such as those beginning with "ambārthā"—take effect. In that regard, [this applies] when *ami* and *śas* follow.
The distinction is that *yaṇ* alone occurs, overriding both the *pūrvarūpa* rule and the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Now, one might object:
[what about] the word *pradhī*, derived from the root *dhyai* with the suffix *kvip*, which functions as a term for "one who meditates intensely" (*prakarṣeṇa dhyātṛ*)?

Since it is common to all three genders, it lacks the status of being eternally feminine and thus lacks the designation "nadī" (feminine noun); how then can it undergo the grammatical operations (*nadī-kārya*) associated with feminines? To this, he says: "even without another word. This means that even in the absence of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with another word, a term which conveys a meaning that is feminine in form [is treated as such].
What is intended here is "that which is always feminine. For this very reason, the form *ādhyai* was adopted for the word *ādhi* when applied to a Brāhmaṇī woman in the Bhāṣya;
otherwise, if one were to accept the definition that "only that which occurs exclusively in the feminine is 'always feminine,'" the inconsistency of that [Bhāṣya statement] would be quite evident.

Since the word *ādhi* is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*), it possesses all three genders; therefore, its status as "always feminine" (*nityastrītva*) consists simply in its occurrence in the feminine even without another word [in apposition]. However, the form *ādhyai* for the word *pradhī* is maintained in the Bhāṣya. Only that which occurs exclusively in the feminine [is considered always feminine].

However, if one were to accept [the definition] as "always feminine," that would be clearly inconsistent, because the word *ādhī* is a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*) and thus possesses all three genders. Therefore, "always feminine" simply means existing in the feminine gender even without another word [in apposition]. This, however, applies to the word *pradhī*.
It is indeed possible, because the application [of the term] to a woman is possible by taking the excellence of being a meditator as the cause.
However, when "pradhīḥ" is uttered, since there is the possibility of understanding it as referring to either a man or a woman, the word "brāhmaṇaḥ" is used to exclude one or the other.

The expectation of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words such as *brāhmaṇī* is required. However, this much does not mean that its denotation of a female (*strī*) disappears in the absence of co-occurrence with other words. Therefore, the meaning is that since the word *pradhī* possesses an inherent feminine gender (*nityastrīliṅga*), the grammatical operations pertaining to the "nadī" designation apply without obstruction. [Regarding the phrase] "in another gender" (*liṅgāntare*).

Kaiyaṭa’s opinion is that "eternal femininity" (*nityastrītva*) consists precisely in not denoting anything other than the feminine gender. His intention is based on the *Bhāṣya* under the rule *yū stryākhyau*, which states that only those two vowels (*yū*) which refer exclusively to females receive the technical designation *nadī*.

Regarding the phrase "the form is like that of the masculine": since the word *pradhī*, as cited, possesses all three genders (*triliṅga*), it lacks the status of being exclusively feminine (*nityastrītva*); therefore, the intention is that—just as in the masculine—it is not an *anadī* (non-river-name) in the feminine either.
Regarding the example *prakṛṣṭā dhīḥ*: when analyzed as such, the compound *pradhī* is formed through a *prādi-samāsa*.
The meaning is that, according to both systems of thought, because it is eternally feminine, its form is like that of *lakṣmī*. Regarding the rule "before *am* and *śas*" (*ami śasi ca*):

in the analyses *pradhyāyati* (she meditates intensely) and *prakṛṣṭā dhīḥ* (excellent intellect), from the word *pradhī*, before the endings *am* and *śas*, the rules for *pūrvarūpa* and *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* are set aside by the rule "of a stem with more than one vowel" (*ṭeranekācaḥ*).

The meaning is that this much is the distinction [of the word *lakṣmī*] with respect to the word *lakṣmī*. According to Kaiyaṭa’s view, however, the usage in the Bhāṣya, "brāhmaṇyām ṭhādhyai," should be understood as referring to a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For this very reason, they say that the suffix *kap* (as prescribed by the rule "nady-utaśca") does not apply here on the basis of the Bhāṣya. [The example is: "suṣṭhu dhīrasyāḥ" (she who possesses excellent intelligence).

In both analyses— *suṣṭhu adhīr yasyāḥ* ("she whose intellect is excellent") and *suṣṭhu dhyāyati* ("she meditates well")— the term *sudhī* is considered to have a permanent feminine gender (*nityastrīliṅga*) because it exists in the feminine without requiring another word, according to the opinion of the author of the Vṛtti; thus, by the rule *ṭh-neyaRuvaṅ-sthānau*, [the feminine suffix ṅīp is applied].
The forms should be understood to be like those of the word *śrī*, because the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rules "ṭhnṅiti hrasvaśca" and "vāmī.

The intention is that, due to the prohibition of *yaṇ*-substitution by the rule "na bhūsudhiyoḥ," only the *iyaṅ* substitution takes effect. However, according to another opinion, it follows the masculine form.
According to Kaiyaṭa’s view, however, that which does not denote another gender is "eternally feminine" (*nityastrī*);

thus, because [the word *sudhī*] lacks the status of a *nadī* due to its being tri-gendered (*triliṅga*), its form is exactly like the masculine. Now, one might object: since the word *dhī* is eternally feminine prior to the application of the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the word *sudhī*, [it should be a *nadī*].

If it is argued that, by the rule *ṭhprathamaliṅgagrahaṇaṃ ca*, the status of being a *nadī* (feminine noun ending in long ī or ū) would be unavoidable [in the case of *dhīmatī*], this is true; however, the status of being a *nadī* is extended even when there is the state of being a subordinate term (*upasarjana*) for that word which was previously seen to have the status of a *nadī* prior to its composition (*vṛtti*).
And here, since the word *dhī* alone, prior to composition, consists of only one vowel (*ekāc*), the substitution of *yaṇ* does not occur.

Let us leave it at that for now: because the status of being a *nadī* (feminine noun) is prohibited by the rule "the [stems] *iy*, *u*, and *ū* are not *nadīs* when they occupy the place of *ṭā*, *ne*, or *ṅi*," there is no extension of that status even in the case of *vṛtti* (compound). However, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of *suṣṭhudhīḥ*, it is exactly like *śrī*. The point is that in both views, it is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*). *Grāmaṇīḥ*.

Regarding the rule *puṃvat*: the word *striyām* (in the feminine) is to be understood as the remainder [of the context]. Now, one might object: since the word *grāmaṇī*—meaning "one who leads or restrains a village"—functions in the feminine even without another word [to qualify it], just like the word *pradhī*, and since it possesses the status of a *nadī* (a term for certain feminine nouns requiring specific grammatical operations) due to its being invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), how can it be said that it is *puṃvat* (treated like the masculine)? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "Of leading [someone] to the village. In common worldly usage, leading someone to a village is generally (*utsargataḥ*) a duty of a man (*puṃdharma*), meaning it is an action to be performed by a male;
thus, without the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of another word such as "Brāhmaṇī," the feminine gender is not perceived. This remains true even according to the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*.

The meaning is that because there is an absence of an inherently feminine gender (*nityastrīliṅgatva*), the designation "river" (*nadī*) does not apply. In this way, it is established by general rule (*autsargika*) that actions such as sweeping, cooking, weaving mats, and digging ditches are normally to be performed by a male. Therefore, words such as *khalapūḥ* (a female sweeper) and *kaṭaprūḥ* (a female mat-weaver) [also] [apply] to a woman.

Even according to the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti*, there is no permanent feminine gender [for these words]. Therefore, the meaning is that their form is exactly like the masculine. Thus end the words ending in long *ī*. Now, those ending in *ū*: "The word *dhenu* is like *mati*"—the intention is that the specific details, such as the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel *o* for the letter *ū* and its subsequent replacement by *av*, are easily understood.

(302) And in the feminine: Pāṇini 7.1.96. Now, he states the specific rule for the word *kroṣṭu* in the feminine: "And in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ca*). The phrase "like one ending in *tṛc*" (*ṭhṛjvatkroṣṭuaḥ*) is understood from the previous rule. It has been stated that this is an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*).

Thus he says, beginning with "denoting a female," and so forth. Consequently, it follows that the word *kroṣṭṛ* does not exist in the feminine with the suffix *-ud*; rather, it exists only as ending in *-ṛ*, namely as *kroṣṭṝ*.
[Pāṇini 4.1.5: *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* ("The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after words ending in *ṛ* or *n*").

The rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* is a compound consisting of *ṛtaḥ* and *naḥ*. The term *striyām* is the governing heading (*adhikṛtam*). From the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, the word *prātipadikāt* is carried over (*anuvṛttam*) and is qualified by the [elements] *ṛt* and *nakārānta*.

Therefore, he states the rule regarding the final element with the words "from those ending in ṛ," and so forth. [The suffixes] ṅī and āP are applied. When *kroṣṭu* + *ī* is established, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs, and the case-endings (*sup*) arise from the word *kroṣṭrī*.
He says that the forms are like those of *gaurī*: *kroṣṭrī*, etc. Thus end the words ending in *ṛ*. Now, the words ending in *ū*.

"Vadhūḥ" is like "gaurī. By the rule *vaho dhaśca*, the suffix *ū* is applied, and *h* is replaced by *dh*. Since there is no vowel *o* as a constituent of the root, *uvaṅ* does not occur. The specific details, such as the substitution of *v* for the *ū*-vowel via *yaṇ* replacement, are easy to understand—this is the intended meaning. "Bhrūḥ" is like "śrī. [This is derived] from the rule *bhrameśca ḍūaḥ*.
Thus, this [word] ends in the suffix *ḍū*. The intention is that the specific application of *uvaṅ* by the rule *ṭhaci śnudhātubhruvām* is easily understood.
She whose eyebrows (*bhrū*) are beautiful (*su*) is *subhrūḥ*. This is because it does not end in a feminine suffix (*strī-pratyaya*).

The short vowel [substitution] does not occur by the rule "ṭhgostriyoḥ. Because of the prohibition regarding the words *bhrū* and those ending in it—namely, "neyaRuvaṅsthānāvastrī"—the status of being a *nadī* (feminine noun) does not apply. Consequently, intending that the operations of a *nadī*, such as those beginning with "amvārthe," do not apply, he says: "he subhrūḥ. [The questioner asks: "How then? If...

The meaning is: if the grammatical operations pertaining to a feminine noun (*nadī*) were not to apply to the word *subhrū*, then how could Bhaṭṭi have said, "Alas, O father! Where are you? O fair-browed one (*he subhru*)"? This is Rāma’s lamentation after Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa; the sense is: "Alas, O fair-browed one, I have been abandoned by you through the power of fate."

The word *hāpita* means "caused to be abandoned. Regarding the term *pramāda*, the sense is that the short vowel was employed in the sense of the suffix *am*. As for the word *bahavaḥ*, some have offered a tentative explanation by resorting to the neuter gender in the sense of a general plurality (*sāmānye*). Regarding *khalapūḥ puṃvat*: [this refers to] the sweeping of a threshing floor (*khalapavana*) as the general rule.

The point is that because [the word *punarbhū*] lacks the status of a masculine dharma—since it does not exist in the feminine without another word [to qualify it]—it lacks the quality of being eternally feminine (*nityastrītvābhāva*), and thus the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) does not apply. Regarding *punarbhū*: according to Amara, "A *punarbhū* is a woman remarried (*didhiṣū*) after having been previously wed. For that [word], [the rule] "neyaRuvaṅ" [applies].
Anticipating an objection, he says: "By *dṛnkara*.

Thinking that *yaṇ* applies by the rule *dṛnkara*, overriding both the *pūrvarūpa* and the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* rules for the [nominative] endings *ṭham* and *śas*, he says: *punarbhvam*, *punarbhvau*. [The genitive is] *punarbhvām*.

When the augment *nuṭ* is applied due to the word ending in *nadī*, and the lengthening (*dīrgha*) has occurred, the form *punarbhūnām* is established. At this point, since the letter *n* is situated in a separate word from the letter *r*, the rule *ṭhakupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (8.4.2) would require the substitution of *ṇ* for the following *n*. However, this is precluded by the rule: (304) *ekājuttarapade ṇaḥ* | 8|4|12| [When the first member of a compound consists of a single vowel, the substitute *ṇ* is applied to the *n* of the second member.]

The suffix *ṇa* [is applied] when the final member (*uttarapada*) consists of a single vowel. Since the word "final member" (*uttarapada*) is conventionally understood here as referring to the entire compound, it follows that "compound" (*samāsa*) is what is intended. That which has a single-vowel (*eka-ac*) final member is "that whose final member is a single vowel" (*ekāc-uttarapada*). The phrase "in that compound" is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*.

The rule "ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.1) is understood to carry over. From the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 8.4.3), the term "pūrvapadāt" (from the preceding member) also carries over. That which has a preceding member is called "pūrvapada.
The singular number is not intended to be significant; thus, the meaning obtained is "from [the letters] ṭha and raṣa situated in the preceding member."

The phrase *ṭhprātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* is understood [from the previous rule]. The word *vidyamānasya* (of that which exists) is the ellipsis. Thus he says: "when the subsequent member consists of a single vowel," and so forth. Now, one might object that the inclusion of the letter *ṇ* here is redundant, since its recurrence is already established from the rule *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ*. Nor...

It should not be said that the re-mention of *ṇ* is for the purpose of removing the optionality [implied] by the rule *ṭhprātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca*; for its obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is established by the very force of its initial formulation. To this he says: "By the formulation... [and] "the *yaṇ*. This means the *yaṇ* [substitution] prescribed by the rule *dṛnkara*.

Regarding the term *punarbhūnām*: the substitution of *u* for the letter *r* (as prescribed by the rule *ṛt-ṣaṭ-k-at-saṃyogādyoḥ*) does not apply here, because that rule specifically prescribes it only for the word *ru*. Thus, we have *punarbhvām* (in the dual). Regarding the word *varṣābhū*, he states the specific rule—namely, *bhekā-*—which provides the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *bahvādibhyaś-ca*.

Due to its optional nature (*vaikalpikatvāt*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is absent, resulting in the form *varṣābhūḥ*. This word is of two genders (*dviliṅga*) when referring to the species of frog. As Yādava states: "In the sense of a female frog (*bhekyām*) or the plant *punarnavā*, it is feminine; in the sense of a male frog (*dardure*), it is masculine. Here, *dardura* means a frog. Thus, according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, [the term] does not denote a different gender.

The meaning is that because it lacks the status of being exclusively feminine, it does not possess the designation of *nadī*; consequently, since the short vowel [of the penultimate] is not applied by the rule *ṭāṅasiṅasām-in-ṅyo-yāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.12), the form is *he varṣābhūḥ*. Regarding "but according to another view": this refers to the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti* and others, who hold that the quality of being feminine exists even without the presence of another word [expressing gender].

Since the word *varṣābhū* is understood to denote only the feminine gender when referring to the species of frog (*bhekajāti*), one might ask why it does not have "eternal femininity" (*nityastrītva*) even according to Kaiyaṭa's view; to this he says: "in the case of female frogs" (*bhekyām*).
The intention is that, in accordance with the *Yādava-kośa*, the mention of the word "feminine" (*strī*) in the *Amara-kośa* is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively:

Even according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, let there be permanent femininity (*nityastrītvam*) following the rule for *amarā*. When the rule "for [stems] with more than one vowel, [the substitution of] *yaṇ* occurs before endings beginning with vowels" would apply, and the prohibition "not for *bhū* and *sudhī*" would have been reached, the counter-exception "and also for *varṣābhū*" was stated regarding the *yaṇ* substitution. He recalls that [rule] with the words: "and *varṣābhvaḥ*. *Svayambhūḥ* is neuter.

Since the word *svayambhū* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to the four-faced Brahmā, and since it does not apply to the feminine gender without another word when used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), it does not possess "inherent femininity" (*nityastrītva*) according to Vṛttimat. However, according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, because it possesses multiple genders, it lacks inherent femininity; this is the intended meaning. Thus end the words ending in /ū/. Now, those ending in /ṛ/.

In the word *svasṛ*, the suffix *ṛn* is applied to the root *as* when *su* is the upapada; thus, the word *svasṛ* denotes a sister. (305) *Na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.10. [The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after the six [numerals] nor after *svasṛ* and others.]

When the suffix *ṅīp* would have been applicable by the rule "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp," [the author states] "not for the six" (*na ṣaṭ*). He says "from those having the technical name *ṣaṭ*" because by the word "six" (*ṣaṭ*), those items designated as *ṣaṭ* are understood. Regarding "the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṭāp*": the intention is that *ṅīp* is carried over from the rule "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp" and *ṭāp* is carried over from the rule "ṭāvṛci."

He recites *svasṛ* and the others with the words *svasā tisraḥ* and so forth. Now, the reading of the two terms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* need not be performed; for the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is established by the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the prohibition of lengthening in the *nām* [vowel] case, namely, *na tisṛcatasṛ*. Thus, according to the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*...

In the *Sūtra*, Kaiyaṭa [comments]: "She does not rejoice (*na nandati*) is *nanāndā*. By the rule "after *nand* with the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *ṛn* [is applied] and there is *vṛddhi*," [the form is derived]. Amara [states]: "But *nanāndā* is the husband’s sister. She milks (*dogdhi*) is *duhitṛ*. [This is derived] by the rule: "The forms *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *pitṛ*, and *duhitṛ* [are formed with the suffix *ṛn*]."

The suffix *tṛc* is prescribed after the root *duh*, and the absence of *guṇa* is also enjoined by rule. That which is honored or revered is called *mātā*; the root *mān* means "to honor. After the suffix *tṛc*, there is also the elision of the nasal (*n*). That which exerts itself is called *yātā*; according to the rule "after *yat*, there is *ṛn* and vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel," the suffix *ṛn* is applied and the penultimate vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*. [The wives] of the group of brothers are... [the term *bhāryā* is derived from *bhrātṛ*].
"Those who are sisters to one another," says Amara. Regarding the form *atṛn*: from the word *svasṛ*, the suffix *su* is applied;

by the rule "ṛduśanas," *anaṅ* is substituted [for the final syllable]. Although it does not end in the suffix *tṛn*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs because of the specific mention of *svasṛ* in the rule "aptṛn. The phrase "like mother and father" refers to the rule "aptṛn."

The intention [of the author] is that, according to the *sūtra*, among those words ending in *tṛn* and *tṛc* derived from the *āṬṇādika* [section], it is specifically for *naptr* and others that the long vowel is restricted. Thus end the words ending in *ṛ*. Now, those ending in *o*: "Heaven (*dyauḥ*) is like 'cow' (*go*)," because of the extension of the status of being a *ṇit* by the rule "*oto ṇit*" [Pāṇini 7.1.90]. Consequently, there is *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule "*aco ñṇiti*" [Pāṇini 7.2.115]. [The forms are] *dyauḥ* and *divau*.

"Abhraṃ means 'cloud' in the feminine," according to Amara. Thus end those [words] ending in *ai*. Now, those ending in *ai*: "rāḥ is like the masculine. By the rule "rāyo halī," there is the substitution of *ā* [for *ai*]. The sense is that this word is also feminine, based on Kṣīrasvāmin’s statement: "Some say *rāḥ* is feminine. Thus end those ending in *ai*. Now, those ending in *o*.
"A ship like a cow. According to Amara: "In the feminine, *nauḥ*, *taraṇiḥ*, and *tariḥ* [mean ship]. Thus end those ending in long *au*.
Thus end the feminine stems ending in vowels in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on neuter stems ending in vowels.

(306) *ato 'm* | Pāṇini 7.1.24. When the suffix *su* [the nominative singular] follows the word *jñāna*, its elision (*luk*) would otherwise apply by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*. To prevent this, the rule *ato 'm* is applied.
Here, *ataḥ* is in the ablative case. The governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which is supplied from the context, is modified to the ablative case [to become *ataḥ*].
By the word "ṭha," the [base] is specified. Therefore, the rule of "application to that which ends in this" (tadantavidhi) applies.

The phrase "of the neuter, after *su* and *am*" (*svamornapuṃsakāt*) is understood to follow. Thus he says: "after a base ending in *at*. This means "after a base ending in the letter *a*. As for the example "jñānam": when *am* is substituted for *su*, [the form becomes *jñānam*].

The sense is that this is the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute form). However, the prescription of *am* is for the purpose of preventing the elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṭhsvamornapuṃsakāt*. Now, one might object: let the analysis be simply *ato'm*; since *jñānam* is established by the substitution of *m* for *su*, and by the rule *ami cādeḥ parasya*, the *a* [of the suffix] would be replaced.

If it is argued that the knowledge [of the form] *jñānam* is established simply by the elision of the final *m* through the rule for the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), we say: not so. For if that were the case, the long vowel in *jñānam* would result from the rule *supi ca*. Nor can it be maintained that the substitution of *m* (for *as*) operates by depending on its co-occurrence with a stem ending in *a*.

It should not be argued that its status as a long vowel caused by a factor (*nimitta*) that destroys that very [condition] is impossible due to conflict with the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*, for it has already been stated that the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* does not apply when the lengthening prescribed by the rule *supi ca* is to be performed; so, enough of this.

Regarding "he jñāna": when *jñānas* is established, the case-ending *su* is replaced by *am*, and after the application of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitution of the preceding vowel), the *m* is elided by the rule *ṭeṅhrasvāt*. Thus, the form becomes *he jñāna*. Now, one might object that in the rule *ṭeṅhrasvāt*, it is more appropriate for the term [implied] by *saṃbuddhi* to be construed with *saṃbuddhi* itself; and therefore...

It is understood that the *hal* (consonant) which is a constituent of the vocative case (*saṃbuddhi*) following a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *eṅ* or a short vowel (*hrasva*) is elided. Consequently, in the present instance, once the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute sandhi) has been applied, the stem *jñāna-* is considered to end in *at* by virtue of its being the final element of the preceding form; therefore, no vocative follows it.
This is because the *makāra* alone does not constitute a vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), whereas the *ām* ending with a preceding *su*-suffix is indeed a vocative;

furthermore, since there is partial modification, the maxim of "modification in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) does not apply here. Nor should it be argued that the rule *ṭeṅhrasvāt* might apply prior to the formation of the *pūrvarūpa*, for...

Because the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute replacement) occurs first due to its priority, and because the *pūrvarūpa*—being the final element of the preceding member—is included within the *aṅga*, the *aṅga* ends in /a/ as in "jñāna-"; furthermore, since "am" begins with a subsequent sound, it possesses the status of a vocative (*saṃbuddhi*). Thus, relying on this, [the rule applies] to the consonant that is a constituent part of that [vocative].

It should not be argued that the elision of the *m* alone [in *sam*] by the rule "after *eṅ* or a short vowel" (*eṅhrasvāt*) is unimpeded; for that is prohibited by the rule "when both sides are relied upon, it is as if it were neither the end nor the beginning" (*ubhayata āśrayaṇe nāntādivat*). Therefore, he says:

"the elision of the mere consonant by the rule 'after *eṅ* or a short vowel'"; for once the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) has been applied, what remains of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) is merely the *m*.

The remainder of that [sūtra] means that there is elision by the rule *ṭeḥ hrasvāt*. Due to the requirements of the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*), the stem (*aṅga*) implied by the vocative does not connect with the vocative case itself; rather, it connects only with the *hal* (consonant) that is a constituent part of the vocative. And therefore—

It is understood that the *hal* which is a constituent of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) following an *aṅga* ending in *eṅ* or a short vowel (*hrasva*) is subject to elision (*lopa*). In the present case, even after the formation of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels), the *hal* consisting solely of the letter *m*, which is a constituent of the vocative, remains immediately after the *aṅga* ending in a short vowel; thus, by the rule *ṭeḥ hrasvāt*, [that *m* is elided].
The elision [of the case-ending] is unimpeded; this is explained in detail elsewhere. (307) *napuṃsakācca* |7|1|19|.
From the rule *napuṃsakācca*, the word *śī* is supplied from the rule *jasaḥ śī*, and the word *āṅ* is supplied from the rule *āṅ āpaḥ*.

And it follows accordingly; thus he says: "from the neuter" (*klībāt*). It has been stated that *oṃ* is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the case-ending (*vibhakti*) ending in *u*. When [the form] *jñāna* is followed by *ī*, [the rule] applies:
(308) *yasyeti ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.148.

Regarding the phrase *yasyeti ca*: the analysis of the compound is *yasya-ītīti*. *Yaṃ* is the collective term for *i* and *a*; thus, it means "of that which has the vowel *i* or the vowel *a*" (*yasya ṭuivarṇasya avarṇasya ca*). The term *bhasya* is supplied as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*). From the rule *nastaddhite*, the word *taddhite* is understood to follow. This is what he states with the words beginning with *bhasya*. Thus, there is the elision of the letter *a*.

Regarding the word *prāpte*: the sense is that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule *suḍanapuṃsakasya*, the substitution of *śī* is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*; therefore, when it follows, [the preceding stem] is considered a *bha* [by P. 1.4.18].
Regarding *āṬṅ śyām*: when the substitute *śī* for *āṬ* follows, by the rule *yasyeti ca*...

The meaning is that a prohibition of the elision must be stated. From the very mention of *śyām* [in the rule], its permanent feminine gender is to be understood. However, the mention of *ṭhāṬṅ* is indeed redundant; for in cases such as *sarvāḥ*, the exclusion of the rule *jasaḥ śī* is already established by the presence of the letter *ā*. [The example] *jñāne* is *jñāna ī*.
This being established, the intention is [to apply] the rule *ād guṇaḥ*.
(309) *jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ* | 7|1|20|. Regarding *jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ*: from the preceding rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, the word *napuṃsakāt* (from a neuter [stem]) is understood to carry over.

He says this [in the rule]: "from *klība* etc. When *jñāna-śi* is established, because it is a suffix by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the letter *ś* becomes an *it* by the rule *laśakvataddhite*.
(Pāṇini 1.3.8) Then, by the rule *śi sarvanāmasthānam* (1.1.42), the suffix *śi* is designated as a *sarvanāmasthāna*.
"Śi is a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Regarding the phrase "that which has been given the designation": the meaning is "that which bears the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*.
Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of neuter nouns by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.43], the designation *sarvanāmasthāna* would not otherwise apply to the suffix *śī*; therefore, this statement is made.

(311) *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.72. "Of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*). [The compound] *jhal-ac* is a collective dvandva consisting of *jhal* and *ac*. By this, the term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which is the governing heading, is qualified. This is a rule of *tadantavidhi* (application to that which ends in...). [This follows] from the rule *ṭhidito num* (Pāṇini 7.1.58).

The term *num* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of that which ends in a *jhal* consonant," and so forth. Because of its *mit* designation, [the augment] follows the final vowel. Regarding the phrase "lengthening of the penultimate (*upadhā*)": this means that when *jñānan-i* is situated [in the form], the lengthening occurs by the rule "also before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. "Again, in the same way" refers to the forms in *am*, *auṭ*, and *śas*: *jñānam*, *jñāne*, *jñānāni*.

The meaning is that the forms [are produced] in this sequence. "The remainder is like Rāma" (*śeṣaṃ rāmavat*). "Remainder" (*śeṣa*) means that which remains (*śiṣyate*); it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The rule "those ending in *ṭha*, *ghañ*, and *ac* are masculine" (*ṭh-ghañ-ac-abantāḥ puṃsi*) is, however, merely a general tendency (*prāyika*), such is the intention. (312) *adḍ ḍatarādibhyaḥ pañcamyaḥ* Pāṇini 7.1.25.

*adḍḍatarādibhyaḥ*. The analysis of the compound is *ṭha-adḍ-ḍatarādibhyaḥ*. Kaiyaṭa maintains that the substitution of *ḍa* for *da* by virtue of the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), as well as the elision of the final *ḍa* due to the rule on the elision of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*), have not been applied here for the sake of understanding the actual form of the substitute. The suffixes *ḍatara*, *ḍatama*, *anya*, *anyatara*, and *itara* constitute the group known as *ḍatarādi*.
These are read in the *sarvādi* group. Here, the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* are involved; therefore, there is a reference to words ending in those suffixes.
The rule *ṭh-svamornapuṃsakāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.23) is understood to apply here, which is why he says "from these," and so forth.
The letter *ḍ* is the *it*. When *katara* is present [as a stem], [the rule] *ṭeḥ* applies. From the rule *ṭhallopo’naḥ*, the word *lopaḥ* is carried over;
from the rule *viṃśaterṅtī*, the word *ṅtī* is carried over as *ḍitī*;
and the term *bhasya* is supplied as a governing heading (*adhikṛtam*). He states this with the words beginning "when followed by a *ḍit*," etc., in the case of *katara-aḍ*.

There is the elision of the letter *a* after the letter *r*. [The author] recalls the optional application of *cartva* (the substitution of *t* for *d*) by citing the rule *vāvasāne*. Now, one might ask: since the form *ṭhkataraḥ* is established by means of the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent vowel) rule, what is the purpose of making the augment *adḍ* marked with the indicatory letter *ṭ* (*ḍit*)? To this, he says: "Because of the elision of the final syllable (*ṭi*). Because the final syllable (*ṭi*) has been elided, the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel homogeneous with the preceding) does not apply.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the form] "bhavati" results. The intention is that in the absence of the *ḍit* designation, the rule "ṭe" (Pāṇini 6.4.143) would not apply; consequently, the substitution of the single preceding form (*pararūpa*) would be set aside, and the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would result.
Now, one might object: "To prevent the occurrence of the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*, let the substitute be the letter *d* itself. To this, [the author replies:]...

He says: "Regarding *eṅhrasvāt* and so forth: if there were the substitution of *s* for [the final syllable], then by virtue of its being *sthānivadbhāva*, it would possess the status of a vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), and because it would follow an *aṅga* ending in a short vowel, its elision (*lopa*) would result.
However, when there is the substitution of *adḍ*, after the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the resulting *aṅga* is *katara*; that does not end in a short vowel."

As for the form *ṭhkatara*, which ends in a short vowel, that is not the *aṅga* (stem); because the letter *a* following the *repha* is a constituent part of the suffix, the element ending in it lacks the status of being followed by a suffix, and thus it does not possess the status of an *aṅga*. Therefore, the intention is that the rule prescribing the substitute *adḍ* is for the purpose of applying *ṭilopa* (elision of the final phoneme). "Again, in the same way" means this.

The meaning is that it is like the first [form], not the second. "The remainder is like the masculine" means it is like *sarva*. Regarding the word *anyatama*, however, because it is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) and lacks the suffix *-ḍatama*, the substitution of *adḍ* does not occur there.

Regarding the rule *ekācca prācām iti*, which prescribes the substitution of *adḍ* for the nominative and accusative singular endings (*svam*) after the word *ekatara* ending in *-atarac*, the author says:

*ekatarāt*. The meaning is that a prohibition of the substitution of *adḍ* for the *svam* endings following the word *ekatara* must be stated. [This applies] in the analysis of the compound: "that family which has no old age" (*avidyamānā jarā yasya kulasya*).

In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *nañ-asty-arthānām*, after the elision of the word *vidyamāna* and the shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule *go-striyoḥ*, the word *ajara* is formed. He demonstrates its grammatical derivation [with the words] "of *su*" (*sor*). Once the substitution of *am* for *su* has been made, the connection is *ajaram*.

Anticipating the objection regarding the substitution of *jaras*, he says: "in the case of *saṃnipāta*. The meaning is that the substitution *jaras* cannot serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for the elision of the final vowel of *am*—which depends upon that very [final] vowel being short—since it would destroy its own condition. Thus, *ajarasī*: when the formative suffix *śī* is applied by the rule "also after neuter nouns," and the substitution *jaras* occurs, this is the resulting form. *Ajare*.

Thus, this is the form when there is no substitution of *jaras*. To demonstrate the form in the *jas* case, he says: "Because it is subsequent. When *ajara-s* is established, the substitution of *śi* by the rule "jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ" is superseded by the subsequent application of *jaras*; thereafter, because the stem ends in a *jhal* consonant, *num* is added once the substitution of *śi* has occurred—this is the meaning.

Thus say some. However, this view is to be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the rule *jarāyā jarasi*, which states that in the case of *ajarāṃsi*, where both the *num* augment and the substitution *jaras* would apply, the latter prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Furthermore, the substitution *jaras* applies precisely before the substitution of *śi*.
For if [the substitution of] *jaras* were to apply first, then because the case ending *jas* would no longer be a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the application of *num* itself would be impossible;

thus, that [Bhāṣya] passage would clearly be inconsistent. However, if one relies on the principle of "priority of the preceding" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) and assumes that the substitution of *śi* occurs prior to [the substitution of] *jaras*, then that Bhāṣya is consistent. And so, regarding *jaras*:

Since the substitution of *śi* has already been applied previously, and because that [substitute] is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, both *num* and *jaras* would apply when it follows; however, between these two, *jaras* applies by virtue of its priority over *num*. Thereafter, *num*—characterized by the condition of being a *jhal*-ending base—applies. This is precisely how it should be explained. For if, prior even to the substitution of *jaras*...

The augment *num*, characterized by its position at the end of a word, would apply; then, with *ṭhajaran i* established, by the maxim "substitutes take the place of that which is specifically indicated," when *jara* is substituted for *jaraḥ*, the form *ajaras na* results. Since there is no *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) following the final *s*, the rule *ṭhsānta mahataḥ* applies.

The [substitution] of *dīrgha* (long vowel) as will be mentioned later would not occur, and so forth; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara* during the analysis of the word *nirjara*. Furthermore, in both cases, when the form *ajaran s* is established, since it lacks the status of ending in *n*, the rule "before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix" (*sarvanāmasthāne ca*) does not apply to effect the long vowel substitution.

(314) *sānta-mahataḥ saṃyogasya* || 6.4.10 || The [words] *sānta* and *mahataḥ* [are the bases]. From the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau* and from *nopadhāyāḥ*, the word *na* is understood with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka-padam*). [This applies] when there is the elision of *ḍh* or *r* (*ḍhralope*).

From the previous rule, the word "dīrgha" (long vowel) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. Thus, it is obtained that there is lengthening of the penultimate (*upadhā*) *n* sound. The term "saṃyogasya" (of a conjunct), ending in a genitive denoting a part, is construed with the *n* sound. "Sānte" is a separate word ending in the genitive; here the genitive case-ending is elided in the Vedic style (*ārṣa*). Thus, "sāntasya" (of that which ends in *s*) is obtained.

And that [word *mahat*] connects with "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) non-differently—as in "the conjunction which is preceded by *s*. For this very reason, due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), there is no compound of it with the word *mahat*. Furthermore, the word *mahataḥ* also ends in a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*); and that [genitive] connects with the letter *n*.

He says this with the words "of a saṃyoga ending in a sibilant," and so forth. Regarding the word *ajarāṃsi*: when the vowel is lengthened, the anusvāra is applied by the rule *naśca padāntasya*. Here, the term *upadhā* is an indicator for "that which precedes" [the final consonant], because the technical definition of *upadhā* (as the penultimate letter) is impossible in this context. Now...

To show the form in the second case singular, he says: *ami luk*. When *ajara-am* is established, *suk* is applicable by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*; that being set aside, its exception, the substitution of *am* by *ataḥ*, would apply; and that being set aside, [the rule] *vipratiṣedhe*...

In the word *paraḥ*, the substitution *jaras* occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Regarding *ajarasam*: this is a statement of the actual state of affairs (*vastusthiti*). Now, one might ask: since the substitution *ām* (which is an exception to elision) has been superseded by the substitution *jaras*, why does elision (*luk*) not occur again for *ām* according to the maxim: "When an exception is negated, the original rule (*utsarga*) stands"? *Paraḥ* means "because it is subsequent. *Ajarasam* is a description of the actual state of things. Now, an objection is raised:

since the substitution *ām*—which is an exception to elision (*lug-apavāda*)—has been set aside by the substitution *jaras*, why does elision (*luk*) not take place again for *ām* according to the principle: "When an exception is negated, the original rule stands"?
To this he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). The syntactic connection is "therefore not elision" (*tato na luk*).
The meaning is that after the substitution of *jaras*, elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *am* does not occur. Why? To this he says:

"By the principle of *saṃnipāta*" (*saṃnipāteti*). This refers to the fact that once *jaras* has been applied by depending upon the presence (*saṃnipāta*) of the ending *am*, [that ending] cannot subsequently be elided.

The sense is that [the substitution] does not occur because it lacks the status of being a cause (*nimitta*). The remainder follows the masculine form. In the neuter: *ajarasā* / *ajareṇa* (instrumental singular) *ajarase* / *ajarāya* (dative singular) *ajarasaḥ* / *ajarāt* (ablative singular) *ajarasaḥ* / *ajarasya* (genitive singular) *ajarasoḥ* / *ajarayoḥ* (genitive/dative dual) *ajarasi* / *ajare* (locative singular) The words *hṛdaya*, *udaka*, and *āsya* take the augment *suṭ* when followed by case-endings beginning with a vowel.
Like *jñānavat*. He states the specific rule regarding [stems ending in] *śas* and so on: *paddan...* etc. Regarding *hṛndī*:
from the word *hṛdaya*, when *śas* is replaced by *śi*, the substitute *hṛd* is applied; then, by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the augment *num* is added after the vowel *ṛ*;
then, by the rule *naśca padāntasya*, the *anusvāra* is substituted for the *n*; and finally, the *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous sound) is substituted for that *anusvāra*.
The form *nakāra* [is derived] as follows: *ityādi*. [In the case of *hṛd*:

*hṛde*, *hṛdaḥ*, *hṛdaḥ*, *hṛdoḥ*, *hṛdām*, *hṛdi*, *hṛdoḥ*, *hṛtsu*. In the alternative where *hṛd* does not occur, it is like *jñāna*. The word *udaka* is like *jñāna* in the nominative singular (*su*). Regarding the specific forms beginning with the accusative plural (*śas*), he says: "Now, *udāt*"—that is, when the *ś* of *śas* is replaced by *śi*, there is the substitution of *udan*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*; however, the elision of the final *a* (by *allopo'naḥ*) does not apply here, because the suffix *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Regarding *udnā*: when *udaka-ā* is in the state of being established, the substitution of *udan* occurs, followed by the elision of the final *a*.
Regarding *udbhyām*: when the substitution of *udan* has occurred, the elision of the final consonant of the nominal stem (*prātipadikāntasya*) applies by the rule *na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*.

There is elision of *n* because [the word] has the status of a *pada* by the rule "in the case of suffixes beginning with *su*, except for the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes]. Regarding the phrase "and so forth":

*udge*, *udgaḥ*, *udgaḥ*, *udgoḥ*, *udani*—*udgi*, *udgoḥ*. In the alternative where the form *udan* does not occur, it is like *jñāna*. The word *āsya* is like *jñāna* when followed by *su*; in the case of *śas* and the following suffixes...
He states the distinction: "āsāni," and so forth. The forms are like those of *udán* (water). Regarding "and so forth":

*āsne*, *āsnaḥ*, *āsnaḥ*, *āsnoḥ*, *āsni* (or *āsani*), *āsnoḥ*, *āsasu*. In the alternative where there is no *āsanna* (proximity), they are like *jñāna*. The word *māṃsa* (flesh) also follows *jñāna* when *suṭ* is applied.

In the presence of suffixes beginning with *ś*, such as *śas* and others, the substitute *māṃsa* is applied for [the word] *māṃsa-pṛtanā-sānu*. Here, the mention of *nakāra* (the letter *n*) is made after it has undergone *anusvāra* by the rule *naścāpadāntasya*.
For this very reason, he says "mānbhyām. When the substitute *māṃsa* is applied, there is the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the letter *s*.
When the *anusvāra* has ceased due to the removal of its cause (*nimitta*), the form [is established].

Because the elision of a final consonant in a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered non-established (*asiddha*), the elision does not occur. Now, he says "in reality" (*vastutas tu*) in order to establish the substitution of *hṛd* and so forth even for *suṣṭhu*. "Thus it was stated" refers to the example "kakud-doṣaṇī."

The meaning is that, in the section on masculine stems ending in vowels (*ajanta-puṃliṅga*), it has been stated by [the author] himself that the inclusion of the word "starting from" (*prabhṛti*) in the *Bhāṣya* indicates the sense of "and so forth" (*prakāra*). Now, even if the inclusion of "starting from" indicates the sense of "and so forth," if one intends to express similarity based on being a suffix (*pratyaya*), then in the nominative singular, [the form would be] *hṛt*.
