The application [of the rule] is untenable, because since that [suffix] has been elided by *luk*, there is an absence of even the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); furthermore, there is no evidence for resorting to the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of that [rule]. Therefore, he says: "These very [cases]," etc. Regarding *māṃspacanyā*: it is called *pacanī* because "it is cooked in this pot"; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*), with the substitution of *an*.

Because it ends in a *ṭi* vowel, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The term *māṃsasya pacanī* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Here, because the genitive case ending (*ṅsi*) has been elided by *luk*, there is an absence of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations as if the suffix were present); consequently, due to the absence of a suffix following [the stem], the substitution of *māṃsa-* would not occur. Therefore, in the rule prescribing the substitutions for *hṛdaya-* and so on, the phrase *na lumatā* [is invoked].
The meaning is that the non-eternality (anityatva) of the prohibition is relied upon. Now, one might object:
in the case of *māṃsapacanyāḥ*, by relying on the elision of the internal genitive suffix (*ṅs*), the portion *māṃs* possesses the status of a word (*padatva*);
for the designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*), defined as "that which ends in a sup or tiṅ," is a property of both base and suffix.
Because there is an absence of being a mere constituent element (*kevalāṅga*) here, the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.63] beginning with *ṭh na lumatā* does not apply.

Otherwise, how could there be elision of the *n* in "rājapuruṣa"? Consequently, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would be unavoidable here; therefore, he says: "Because it is a nominal stem (*bha*), there is elision of the final consonant cluster."

"No. [Objection: But surely, since the designation *bha* is prescribed when suffixes such as *yajādi* and *svādi* follow, it is a property solely of the *aṅga*; therefore, when that suffix is elided by *luk*, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule is prohibited—so how can there be the designation *bha* here?
To this, he says: "By virtue of being included among the *ayasmaya*-type words."

The meaning is that because *māṃsādi* is listed in the *ayasmayādi* group, it possesses the status of a *bha* [stem] according to the rule *ayasmayādīni chandasi*. Consequently, the objection is raised that its mention is appropriate only within the context of Vedic grammatical derivation (*vaidika-prakriyā*). He answers this with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), referring to the rule *paddanno* [Pāṇini 6.1.63].

Even though the inclusion of the term *cchandaḥ* (Vedic) continues [from the previous rule], the connection is "also in some cases in common usage" (*loke 'pi kvacit*). To the question "Why is there usage even in common usage?", he says: "In *apo bhī* etc. This refers to the rule *apo bhī*. The meaning is that the letter *t* should replace the final *p* of the word *ap-* when followed by a suffix beginning with *bh*. In that context, there exists [the following].

The Vārttika states: *māsaś chandasi*. Its meaning is that the substitution of *t* for [the *s* of] *mās* occurs when followed by a suffix beginning with *bh*, provided it is in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). An example from the Ṛgveda is the mantra beginning with *mādbhiḥ śaradbhiḥ*. If [the rule] *paddan...* were restricted solely to the Vedic language...

In that case, since the substitution of *māsi* would pertain exclusively to Vedic literature (*cchandomātra*) and would thus be non-worldly (*alaukika*), the mention of "Vedic" (*cchandas*) in the rule prescribing the replacement of *s* by *t*— namely, *māsaś chandasi*— would be redundant. Therefore, [the substitution] occurs in some instances even in common worldly usage (*loke*).

According to the view expressed by Kaiyaṭa, the meaning is that the substitutes for *pada* and so forth are fit to be employed even in common usage, having accepted the application of the rule "ṭhpaddannitis" even in the world. Thus end the words ending in short *a*. (315) *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* [Pāṇini 1.2.47]: "A short vowel is substituted for the final vowel of a neuter nominal stem."

Now, those ending in vowels: the word *śrīpa*—meaning "one who protects prosperity" (*śriyam pāti*)—is either formed with the suffix *viC* or the suffix *kvip*, like the word *viśvapā*. Regarding its neuter gender, he states the rule for the short vowel: "The [final vowel] is short in the neuter.
By the mention of "short" (*hrasva*), the term *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") is brought to mind, [referring] to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

He states that the rule of "extension to what ends with [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies because of the qualification, beginning with the words "in the neuter" (*klībe*), etc. Nor should it be argued that in the case of *kule* (dual),
a short vowel would result because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as part of the preceding element (*pūrvāntatvena*), thereby making the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) end in *a*.

Since the term *prātipadika* is understood from the rule *arthavad adhātuḥ* (P. 1.2.45), the repetition of the word *prātipadika* here serves to indicate that the status of being a *prātipadika* does not apply by virtue of the principle of "behaving as the final element" (*antavadbhāva*), thereby making it known that the short vowel [of the suffix] is absent. As for the example *jñānavat*: because of the prescription of the short vowel, the [suffix] conditioned by the state of having a long vowel at the end [is excluded].

The sense is that there is no distinction whatsoever. [In the case of] *śrīpāṇi*, the form is derived from the rule "jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ. Even though the words are situated in different *pada*s, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the application of the rule "ekāc-utarapade ṇaḥ. In the case of *śrīpeṇa*, when the substitute *in* is applied and the *guṇa* [vowel] is formed, because that [substitute] is treated as the final element of the preceding part (*pūrvāntatva*), the subsequent member (*utarapada*) consists of a single vowel; therefore, the substitution of *ṇ* would indeed occur.
[The change to] *ṇatva* [occurs]. Regarding *śrīpāya*: after the word *śrīpā*, by the rule "there is shortening in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*), there is shortening;

then, with the substitution of *ReĀ* [for the feminine suffix], and by the rule "also before *sup*" (*supi ca*), there is lengthening, resulting in the form [śrīpāya]. As for the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship), it was previously stated that it does not apply here because of the citation of the form *kaṣṭāya*. Now, if [one objects] regarding this shortening...

Even when the substitution of *ṭha* has been applied, by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is not lost; consequently, once the lengthening (*dīrgha*) has occurred, because the word ends in the vowel *ā*, the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) would apply by the rule "āto dhātoḥ.

Furthermore, since the substitute *yā* is inherently headed by *y* and, by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, is treated as a suffix beginning with *s* (i.e., *svādi-pratyaya*), [the aforementioned rules would apply] when that [substitute] follows.

Since the state of being a *bh* (the substitute for *bha*) also exists [in this case], he says: "In this matter, by the *saṃnipāta*-paribhāṣā. Now, it is understood from the *saṃnipāta*-paribhāṣā that that which destroys what it depends upon (*upajīvya*) does not become the cause (*nimitta*) for that which depends upon it (*upajīvaka*).

But in the present case, how is it that the substitution of *y* (*yādeśa*), which operates depending on a stem ending in *a*, does not [become the cause] with respect to the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*)?

If it is argued that there is no obstacle to the substitute *yā* being the cause (*nimitta*) for the elision of the vowel *ā*, because its application does not depend upon the existence of that *ā*-vowel, we say:
do not speak thus. For the substitute *yā* operates by depending upon a short *a*-vowel; such is the rule for its prescription.

This is because of the continued application [of the rule]. Consequently, the combination of shortness (*hrasvatva*) and being of the *a*-vowel class (*avarṇatva*) constitutes the basis upon which the substitution of *y* depends. In that regard, by means of the citation "kaṣṭāya," the long vowel is applied even after setting aside the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā*; nevertheless, only the aspect of shortness is withdrawn.

The portion consisting of non-*avarṇ* (i.e., *e* and *o*) is indeed subject to recurrence. If that too were to be removed by the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*), there would necessarily be a subversion of what it depends upon (*upajīvyavighāta*), and thus there would certainly be a conflict with the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*.
Therefore, it is resolved in the *Kaustubha* that the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) does not occur [in this case], on the grounds of the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi replace *iK*" (*iko guṇavṛddhī*).

In this regard, according to the principle that "between what is taught by a rule and what is taught as a specific word-form (lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā), the specific word-form is preferred," in the rule *āto dhātoḥ*, only a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the vowel *ā* that is taught as a specific form is understood. However, here, when the short vowel of the root *pā* is replaced and subsequently lengthened, the resulting form *pā* is merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*); therefore, it is not [governed] by that [rule].
Let the mention of "grahaṇa" rest for now. Thus end those [words] ending in vowels.
(316) *svamornapuṃsakāt* | P. 7.1.23. Now, in order to demonstrate the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) of the word *vāri*, he says: *svamornapuṃsakāt*. From the six [cases]...

From the word *luk*, the term *luk* is understood to carry over. Thus he says, "from a neuter [stem]," and so forth. Regarding *vārī*: this is the form resulting from the elision (*luk*) of both the nominative suffix *su* and the accusative suffix *am*. Nor should one raise the objection that, by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("of the subsequent [element], [the elision applies] to the initial [sound]"), only the vowel *a* of *am* would be elided and not the consonant *m* as well; for [that rule does not apply here].

Indeed, the elision (*lop*) of an affix is precisely what is termed *luk*. Here, the entire cluster *am* is the affix, and not merely the letter *a* which constitutes a part of it; therefore, the *luk* of *am* is a substitution for the whole (*sarvādeśa*).

(317) *iko'ci vibhaktau* | Pāṇini 7.1.73. Regarding *iko'ci*: from the rule *ṭidito num dhātoḥ*, the word *num* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the word *napuṃsakasya* (of the neuter) is understood as a carry-over.

In the rule beginning with *ṭhaṅi*, the vowel *i* is qualified; consequently, the rule of "specifying that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. This is what he expresses by saying "ending in an *i*-vowel," and so forth. "In a case-ending beginning with a vowel" (*aci vibhaktau*) means "in a case-ending whose initial sound is a vowel. It would have been easier to state it simply as "*iko'ci supi*" (for an *i*- or *u*-vowel before a case-ending beginning with a vowel). Why specify "in a case-ending"? [To exclude forms such as *dadhi atra*.]

*Madhu* means wine; its derivative is *mādhava*. When the suffix *aṇ* follows, after the insertion of *num* and the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel), the form would be *mādha*. Regarding *vāriṇī*: when *vāri* and the dual ending *au* stand together, the substitution of *śī* occurs, followed by the insertion of *num*; then, by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*, the *n* is changed to *ṇ*, resulting in the form. Regarding *vārīṇi*: when the dual endings *jas* and *śas* are replaced by *śi*, the insertion of *num* occurs.

In the form [vāriṇi], the long vowel is produced by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, and then the substitution of *ṇ* occurs. Regarding the form *he vāri su*, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) when the suffix *su* is elided, stating: "in one alternative" (*pakṣe*). This means that the guṇa substitution caused by the vocative case ending (*sambuddhi*), according to the rule *hrasvasya guṇaḥ*, may sometimes take place. Now, here...

One might ask: since the suffix *sambuddhi* has been elided by *luk*, and because the rule "when an affix is elided by *lumat*, the operations conditioned by that affix do not take place" (*na lumatāṅgasya*) prohibits the application of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an element as if its affix were present), how can there be *guṇa* substitution?

To this, he says: "Because the prohibition *na lumatā* is non-universal (*anitya*). And in this regard, the mention of the term *aci* in the rule *ṭhiko'ci vibhaktau* serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because even though [the case endings] *bhyām* and so forth begin with consonants (*hal*), [the rule would still apply].

Since the elision of the *n* at the end of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is possible by the rule "numi ṭhna lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya," the mention of "in a vowel" (*aci*) would be redundant. Nor can it be argued that the mention of the vowel (*aj*) is for the purpose of excluding the vocative (*sambuddhi*), because if *num* were present there, the prohibition "na ṅsimbuddhayoḥ" would apply, resulting in the undesirable consequence of hearing the sound of the *n*. This is not so.

Because the *sambuddhi* [case ending] is elided by *luk*, there is an absence of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix); consequently, since there is no possibility at all for the occurrence of *num* in that position, the mention of *ac* [in Pāṇini’s rule A 7.1.70] would be purposeful only if the prohibition "not when there is an elision (*na lumatā...*)" were considered non-universal (*anitya*),
as it would then serve to block the *num* that would otherwise be obtained through the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* in the *sambuddhi*.

They say that the inclusion of the term *aj* [in Pāṇini’s rule] is a mark (*liṅga*) of the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule *ṭhna lumatā*. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *iko 'ci* [provides the example] *he trapo*, and the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *eṅ hrasvāt* provides *he trapu*; thus both are consistent. As for [the prohibition] "not after *āṅ*": although there is no difference in the resulting form, [the rule applies].
The sense is that, in comparison with *num*, the application of *abhāva* (non-existence) alone is more logical because it is subsequent.

He states the distinction between the *ṅsi* and *ṅs* [cases] with the words "of a *ghi*" (*gher*). The meaning is that, having set aside *num*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply because it is subsequent.

"Vṛddhyautve" is a Vārttika. Regarding the respective scope (*avakāśa*) of *vṛddhi* and the others: [the forms] *gāvau* and *harau* and *kroṣṭrā* and *haraye* are the scope for *vṛddhi* and so on; the scope for *num* is [the form] *vārīṇi*.
In the case of *atisakhīni*, because the suffixes *jas* and *śas* are treated as having the *ṇit* designation by the rule "sakhyurasambuddhau," *vṛddhi* occurs.

In the case of *vāriṇī*, the substitution of *au* (by the rule *ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ*) would apply, overriding the addition of *num*. In *priyakroṣṭūni*, the substitution of the *tṛc*-stem form (*tṛjvat*) would apply for the cases of *jas* and *śas*.
In the case of the word *vāri* followed by feminine suffixes (*ṅī* etc.), the *guṇa* substitution would apply. Here [in these instances]...

The meaning is that, due to the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the rule of priority), only *num* [is applied]. Thus, *vāriṇe*: having set aside the *guṇa* [substitution] by the *ṅi* case-ending, *num* is inserted, and then *ṇatva* [nasalization] occurs, resulting in this form. *Vāriṇaḥ*: having set aside the *guṇa* [substitution] by the *ṅsi* and *ṅs* case-endings, *num* is inserted, and then *ṇatva* occurs, resulting in this form. *Vāriṇoḥ*: having set aside the *yaṇ* [substitution] by the *osi* case-ending, *num* is inserted, and then *ṇatva* occurs.
Regarding the form *vāriṇa*: having set aside the *guṇa* substitution for the case endings *ṅsi* and *ṅs*, the form is derived by applying *num* and then *ṇatva*.
Regarding the form *vāriṇoḥ*: having set aside the *yaṇ* substitution for the ending *osi*, the form is derived by applying *num* and then *ṇatva*.
Regarding *vāri-ām*, since *num* would apply there by priority, overriding *nuṭ*, he says: "by the rule *numacira-*."
Regarding the term *nuṭ*: since one might ask what the difference is between *num* and *nuṭ*, he says, "the long vowel by [Pāṇini 6.4.3] *nāmī*.
The intention is that if *num* were present, because it is a part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*), the lengthening by *nāmī* would not occur.
In the case of *vāriṇī*, even though the substitution of *au* (by *ṅer ām nady-āmnoḥ* and *auto 'śas*) is subsequent, it is set aside.

By the rule "ṭhvṛddhyautve" (Pāṇini 1.1.3), the augment *num* applies by way of prior precedence (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). That which has no beginning (*ādi*)—that is, no origin (*utpatti*)—is "anādi," such as Īśvara. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is anādi. Brahman is anādi. This word is tri-gendered and follows the gender of the noun it qualifies (*viśeṣyanighna*). When it is neuter, the forms for the first and second cases are like those of the word *vāri*.

(318) *Tṛtīyādiṣu bhāṣitapuṃskaṃ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskasya* [Pāṇini 7.1.74]. Regarding the suffixes beginning with *ṭā*, he states a specific rule concerning vowels: "In the case of the third case and those following. That by which a male [referent] is expressed is *bhāṣitapuṃska*; that which possesses such [a cause of application] is [called] *bhāṣitapuṃska*, [formed] with the suffix *ac* according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*.

The nature of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). This means that [the gender] is based on a single basis for application (*ekapravṛttinimittaka*), whether in the masculine or neuter. [The term "neuter" is supplied] from the rule *iko'ci vibhaktau* as "*iko'ci*" and from the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* as "*napuṃsakasya*."

And it follows [from the previous rule]. The genitive case is also transformed into the nominative. Thus he says: "when there is identity of the cause of application," and so forth. Regarding "as in the masculine" (*puṃvat*): the intention is that this is due to the mention of Gālava.
Regarding "in a vowel" (*aci*): the meaning is "in a vowel-initial [suffix]. When the masculine form is applied, the absence of the short vowels *u* and *m* results as the fruit.

It is beyond dispute that words such as "pot" and "cloth" denote their respective individual instances precisely through the forms of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), cloth-ness (*paṭatva*), and so forth, and not through the forms of substance-ness (*dravyatva*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), and so on. Consequently,
whatever qualifier these words— such as "pot"— place foremost when they are applied to those respective individual instances [is that which constitutes their primary denotation].

The qualifier of that [referent] is called the *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for the application of the word); that is to say, it is the delimitor of the denotable object (*vācyatāvacchedaka*). And thus, that form of a word which has one and the same delimitor of the denotable object across both the neuter gender and other genders is intended by the term *bhāṣitapuṃska*.

Furthermore, the word *anādi*—taking as its primary basis the state of being beginningless (*anāditva*) consisting in the absence of origination—is a designator of feminine, masculine, and neuter genders, as well as of their respective individual instances (*vyakti*). Thus, when its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is one and the same, it possesses the quality of being "not-neuter" (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). Therefore, in relation to that [word], before a vowel beginning with *ṭa*...
Intending to illustrate the optional application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva-vikalpa*), he provides the example: *anādaye*, *adādine*.

The point is that when the masculine form applies, the augment *num* does not occur, and by the rule *dherṅtī*, a *guṇa* substitution takes place. However, in the absence of the masculine form, *num* is applied. "And so forth" includes: *anādeḥ*, *anādinaḥ*.

In the case of *anādyoḥ*, it means *anādinoḥ*. But in the case of *āmi*, it is simply *anādīnām*. "The rest is like *vāri*" means that for the first and second cases, as well as for the forms beginning with *bhyām* and before consonants (*hal*), it is like *vāri*.
He says "the tree is a *pīlu*" in order to demonstrate the purpose of the rule "identity of the ground for application" (*pravṛtinimitaikya*).
When the specific tree is denoted by the word *pīlu*, the word *pīlu* is masculine;
when the fruit produced by the *pīlu* tree is denoted by the word *pīlu*, this [word] is neuter.
By the rule "ṭhphale luk," there is elision of the suffix *aṇ*. Here, the meaning is that when the fruit is to be expressed, the masculine form (*puṃvattva*) does not apply.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

*Pīlutva*—which consists of a specific genus (*jāti*) subordinate to "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*)—is the ground for application when a particular tree is to be expressed. However, when a particular fruit is to be expressed, [it is the ground].

The meaning is that the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is *pīlutva* (the state of being a *pīlu*), which consists of a specific genus pervaded by the state of being a fruit; thus, there is a difference in the grounds for application. As it has been said: "A *pīlu* is a tree; the fruit is a *pīlu*.
[One says] 'for a *pīlu*,' but not 'for a *pīlava* (fruit). In the case of the tree, the ground is *pīlutva*; in its fruit, it is the state of being born from that."
Furthermore:
(319) *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaṅ udāttaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.75. For *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the forms are optionally like those of *vāri* in the first and second cases.

He states a specific rule regarding [stems ending in] *as* when followed by vowels beginning with those starting with *ṭ*: *asthidadhi*. The words "in the third case and beyond" (*tṛtīyādiṣu*) and "when a vowel follows" (*aci*) are carried over from the previous rule. Thus he says, "of these," and so forth. This is an exception to *num*. In *anaṅ*, the letter *h* is for the sake of pronunciation (*it*), while the letter *a* is for the sake of articulation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because of the marker *ṅ*, it is a substitute for the final letter (*antādeśaḥ*). Examples: *dadhani*, *dadhni*.

The intention is that there is an option regarding the elision of *ā* by the rule "vibhāṣā ṅśyoḥ. [The phrase] "of that which ends in it" means because it is a stem (*aṅga*). [The example] "atidadhnā": that family which has surpassed the curd is "atidadhi. Here too, the word "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) is connected [to the rule]. Consequently, from the root *dhā*, [the suffix *kvin* is added] by the rule "ādṛgamahan... [etc.].

When the suffix *ki* is applied, the word *dadhi* takes the masculine gender, resulting in *dadhinā* alone. The term "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*), being explicitly stated, connects only with the group beginning with *asthi*; by this, forms such as *atidadhnā brāhmaṇena* are established. Thus end the words ending in short *i*.

Now, those ending in *ī*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *sudhī* as "one who meditates well" (*su dhyāyati*) or "one whose intellect (*dhī*) is beautiful (*su-śobhanā*)", the short vowel is applied by the rule "the [final vowel] is short in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*).
Thus, he states that its forms are like those of *vāri*: *sudhi*, *sudhinī*, and so forth. Because it is subsequent, *iyaṅ* takes precedence over *num*.
The sense is that [the word] is subject to restriction. Regarding *sudhiyā* and *sudhinā*:

because the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—namely, being a wise person (*sudhyātṛtva*) or possessing excellent knowledge (*śobhanajñānavatva*)—is the same in both the masculine and the neuter, there is an option regarding the masculine form (*puṃvat*). The word *pradhī* is likewise. In that regard, [the rule] "not after *nabhas* or *sudhī*" (*nabhūsudhiyoḥ*) applies.
By the rule "niṣedhā'bhāvāderanekāca," *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs. Thus end the words ending in *ī*. Now, those ending in *u*:
*madhu*. According to the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "madhu means liquor and flower-nectar" and "madhu means spring and the month Caitra," the word *madhu* is both masculine and neuter.

There is no option for the masculine form (*puṃvat*) because of the difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as being an intoxicant (*madyatva*) or being spring (*vasantatva*).

However, the distinction is that the word *madhu*, when denoting a modification of the grape (*bhṛdvīkāvikāra*), is invariably neuter and thus does not take the masculine form. Regarding the word *sānu*, it is optionally *snus* according to the rule *paddan* (Pāṇini 6.1.63).
The remainder [of the rule] is: "By the Vārttika ‘In the case of *māṃsa*, *pṛtanā*, and *sānu*, the forms *māṃs*, *pṛt*, and *snab* should be stated [as substitutes].
Regarding *snūni* and *sānūni*—these are the forms in the *śas* case, because the prescription for *snu* applies only from the beginning of the *śas* case onward.
Since the mention of *prabhṛti* (beginning with) has the sense of "in the manner of," *snu* also occurs in the *su* case. And this [term] is *snu*.

Regarding the word *prasthaḥ*, since it is listed among the "masculine-neuter" (*puṃnapuṃsaka*) words ending in *-an* that have been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), there indeed exists an option for its treatment as masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*). Thus, we have *priyakroṣṭu-a* and *priyakroṣṭu-anī*. The analysis of the compound is *priyakroṣṭā yasya* ("one for whom a beloved jackal exists"). Because the following suffix is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the substitution of *tṛjvat* (treating the stem like *tṛc*) does not apply. Now, [considering] the case endings *jaś* and *śas*:

When the *śi* suffix is present, since it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, it would block the application of *num* and, by virtue of being subsequent, cause the substitution of *tṛjvat* (the form of the agentive suffix *tṛc*) to apply; therefore, he says: "on account of the *tṛjvadbhāva*. The intention is that this follows from the Vārttika: "The [substitution of] *vṛddhi* and *aut* [occurs].
Thus, we have *priyakroṣṭūn*. When *jaś* and *śas* are present, upon the application of the *śi* suffix and the addition of *num* in the *sarvanāmasthāna* state...

The form [of the word] is *ce'ti* with a long vowel. Nor should it be argued that since *num* is established by its very permanence (*nityatva*), what is the use of the "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)? For even if *num* were applied due to its permanence, by the maxim "augmentations [are like the original element]" (*yadāgamāḥ*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of including the form qualified by *num* under the rule *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*.

Furthermore, regarding the occurrence of *tṛjvat* (the substitution of the suffix *tṛc* for the feminine suffix): although one might assume that by relying on the rule of priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *tṛjvat* would override [the application of] *num*, once *num* has been applied, *tṛjvat* does not apply again. This is because of the maxim: "In a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*), that which has been overridden remains overridden. Enough of this. Regarding the alternative view (*pakṣa*) of *puṃvat* (masculine-like treatment): there too—

The meaning is: "in the alternative view where [the stem] is treated like *tṛc*. *Priyakroṣṭrā*: this is the form when there is both *puṃvat* (masculine treatment) and *tṛjvat* (treatment like *tṛc*). Because it is not neuter, *num* does not occur. *Priyakroṣṭranā*: this is the form when there is *puṃvat*, and in the absence of that, when there is no *tṛjvat*. Even in the alternative view where *puṃvat* does not apply, *num* [does not occur].

Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], *nātva* (the substitution of *nā*) alone prevails. Thus, *priyakroṣṭre*. When there is *puṃvat* (masculine-like treatment), there is *tṛjvat* (treatment like the suffix *tṛc*), and consequently *yaṇ*.

Since it is not neuter, *num* does not occur. *Priyakroṣṭave*: this is the form when there is *puṃvat* treatment and the absence of *tṛjvat* treatment. "Elsewhere" means in the alternative case where *puṃvat* treatment does not apply.
*Priyakroṣṭuanā*: this is the form when there is an absence of both the *puṃvat* (masculine) and *tṛjvat* (as if ending in *-tṛ*) substitutions. Likewise, there are three forms in the *ṅi* case:
*priyakroṣṭau*, *priyakroṣṭvi*, and *priyakroṣṭvani*. Similarly for the *ṅsi* and *ṅs* cases:
*priyakroṣṭuaḥ*, *priyakroṣṭoḥ*, and *priyakroṣṭunaḥ*. [In the genitive dual: *priyakroṣṭroḥ*, *priyakroṣṭvoḥ*, and *priyakroṣṭunoḥ*. In the locative plural: *priyakroṣṭuṣu*.
In the case of the *bhyām* and subsequent [case endings] beginning with a consonant (*hal*), it is like *madhu*. Thus end those words ending in *u*. Now, those ending in *ū*:

*sulū*—[this is derived from] *suṣṭhu lunāti* (he cuts well), with the suffix *kvip*; the shortening occurs by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake*. *Sulunī*—here, the *num* augment applies because it is subsequent, overriding the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by the rule *oḥ supi*. *Sulvā*.

The capacity for performing the act of cutting well (*śobhana-lavana-kartṛtva*) is one basis for the application [of the feminine form]; thus, there is an option regarding the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvat*).

In the case of masculine-like treatment, because there is no short vowel (*hrasva*), it is not *aghi*, and therefore the substitution of *nā* does not occur, nor does the absence of *num*. Consequently, by the rule *ṭhoḥ supi*, the *yaṇ* substitution takes place. However, in the alternative case where masculine-like treatment is absent, *num* applies, overriding the *yaṇ* substitution.

In the case of *reṅ* and so forth, however, when there is no *puṃvat* (masculine) treatment, by the prior application of the rule "vṛddhyautve" (Pāṇini 1.4.3), the *num* augment is applied, resulting in the form *sulune*; whereas, when *puṃvat* treatment applies, the forms are *sulve*, and so on—thus ending those words whose stems terminate in *ū*. Now, for those ending in *ṛ*: *dhātṛ*. [It is derived from] *dadhāti* ("he places").

Regarding *dhātṛ*: because of the prohibition [by the rule] *ṭhna lumatā*, the augment *anaṅ* does not apply. Thus, *dhātṛṇī*. In this case, after the application of *num* by the rule *ṭhiko'ci*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *ṭhṛvarṇānnasya*. Regarding *dhātṛṇī*: when *jaś* and *śas* are replaced by *śi*, *num* is applied, and then lengthening occurs by the rule *ṭhsarvanāmasthāne ca*, followed by the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. [This is also governed by] *ṭhna lumatā*.
Because the prohibition is not universal (*anityatva*), there is optionally a *guṇa* substitution for the short vowel when caused by the vocative case-ending; thus he says:

*he dhātaḥ*, *he dhātṛ*. Since the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—the state of being the agent of supporting (*dhāraṇakartṛtva*)—is identical, there is an optional application of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) before vowels beginning with *ṭā*.
Thus he says: *dhātrā*, *dhātṛṇā*; *dhātre*, *dhātṛṇe*; *dhātuḥ*, *dhātṛṇaḥ*;
*dhātroḥ*, *dhātṛṇoḥ*. By the rule *ṭhnumacite’ti nuṭ*, [we have] *dhātṛṇām*.
*dhātari*, *dhātṛṇi*. Thus end those ending in *ṛ*.

(320) *eca igghrasvādeśe* | 1.1.48 | Now, regarding words ending in *o*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *pradyuḥ*, meaning "one for whom the sky (*dyau*) is excellent," the substitution of the short vowel prescribed by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake* would apply to the word *pradyoḥ*. However, because the *ec* vowels (*ai*, *au*, *e*, *o*) lack a short form, and because they occupy two places [in the alphabet], [the substitute] is *a*.

Since there is no "most similar" (*antaratama*) correspondence for these short vowels— *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ*— due to the absence of similarity in their internal [articulatory] positions, this rule is commenced to ensure that, among the *avarṇa* (vowels *a* and *ā*) and the others, the substitution occurs according to a specific restriction or alternately as required: *eca ik*.

That which is pointed out (*ādiśyate*) is an *ādeśa*. The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). There is a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word "short" (*hrasva*); the inversion of the order, placing the qualifier first, is a Vedic archaism (*ārṣa*). The locative case in "in the *ādeśa*" (*ādeśe*) is a locative of specification (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*). The singular number is used according to Pāṇini’s rule (the *sautra* usage). He states this with the words "among those being pointed out," etc., [meaning] "in the midst."

This is a faulty reading (*apapāṭha*), because when that [term] is joined, the genitive case alone is appropriate. "Only *ik*"—the sense is that by this, the exclusion of the vowel *a* results. Although there are four *ik*s and likewise four *ec*s, nevertheless, there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) between the substituends (*sthānin*) and the substitutes (*ādeśa*). For this is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

But this is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*). A restriction is applied only to that which has already been established. For in these [vowels], the first part resembles *a*, while the second part resembles *i* and *u*. Thus, the similarity of the first part exists in the *a*-vowels. And when that [similarity] is excluded by the mention of *ic* (*iggrahaṇa*), [the rule applies].
By taking merely the similarity to the *ivarṇa*, the status of the *ekāra* and *aikāra* as *ivarṇa* is established;

and by the similarity to the *uvarṇa*, the status of the *okāra* and *aukāra* as *uvarṇa* is established. This arrangement follows from logical necessity (*nyāyaprāpta*). Since that which is already obtained is simply being regulated, there is no correspondence according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Consequently, in the word *pradyoḥ*:

Intending that the short *u* is the substitute for the [long] *ū* of *okāra*, he provides an example: *pradyau*, etc. Now, one might ask: since the efficient cause (*pravṛttinimitta*) for both the masculine and neuter genders is indeed the same—namely, the state of possessing an excellent heaven (*prakṛṣṭasvargavatva*)—why is there no optional application of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) before endings beginning with *ṭā*? To this, he says: "In this case, there is no masculine form. Why?
To this he says: "yadigantam" (if it ends in -i). The word *pradyo* ending in *-o* is masculine;

however, the word *pradyau* ending in *-au* is neuter. Thus, although the word *pradyo* is one that has been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) when in the masculine, the word *pradyau* in the neuter is distinct from it and therefore lacks the status of being *bhāṣitapuṃska*. Consequently, [the rule does not apply].

The meaning is that it takes the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Some, however, say: "The word *pradyoś* ending in *o*, which was masculine, is now neuter; even though it has become short-voweled at the end, because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole, the option of taking the masculine form certainly remains. This applies to the following cases as well: *prari*, *sūvu*.

The meaning is "and so on. Thus end [the words] ending in *i*. Now, those ending in *e*. As for an example of a word ending in *ekāra* (e): one by whom desire (*kāma*) has been remembered is "smṛteḥ";
that which possesses a beautiful memory is "susmṛti"—these and others should be understood in this way. Regarding *prarī*:
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *prarāudhanaṃ yasya*, the word is *praraiḥ*.

Due to the shortening of the neuter [final vowel], there is the vowel *i*. When the suffix *su* is present, it is like *vāri*. Because the suffix *su* has been elided, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ṭhrāyo halī* does not apply;
furthermore, in the case of vowels beginning with the *ṭā* suffixes, there is an option for the masculine form, as in the word *pradyauḥ*. In the case of *bhyām* and so on...
He states a specific rule regarding the ploughman (*halin*): "In *rāyaḥ* and *halī*, there is substitution by *ā*. Now, one might ask:
since the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for the word *rai*, which ends in *ai*, how can it apply to [the form] ending in *i*?
To this he replies: "Because that which has undergone a modification of a single part is not different [from the original]. Regarding the suffix *ām*:

He states the distinction: "numacira... etc. The connection is that when *nuṭ* is applied, there is the substitution of *ā* by the rule "rāyo halī" (Pāṇini 7.2.85), resulting in *prarāṇām*. Now, one might object: when the form *prari-ām* is established, since *num* is subsequent (*para*), it would supersede *nuṭ*; and because *num* is a part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*), the suffix would not begin with a consonant (*halādi*). Therefore, how can the substitution of *ā* occur? To this [he replies]:...

He says: "numacireti. The sense is that, by means of the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction), *num* is set aside, and thus the application of *nuṭ* and *ḷtva* remains unimpeded. [He says: "saṃnipāteti. The sense is that it is impossible for *nuṭ*—which operates depending upon the state of having a short vowel at the end—to serve as a cause (*nimitta*) for *ātva*, which would destroy that very condition upon which it depends. [Objection: But surely...

In that case, how can the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by the rule *nāmī*—which subverts the *nuṭ* augment applied on the basis of the word ending in a short vowel—be considered a cause for that very *nuṭ*? To this he says: "But the long vowel in *nāmī*... The phrase "it has been stated" implies the remainder of the context: "in the section concerning the word *rāma*. Thus end the words ending in *ai* and *au*. Now, those ending in *āu*.

In the analysis of the compound *suśobhanā nauḥ* (a very beautiful boat) as a *bahuvrīhi*, thinking that the vowel *u* becomes short according to the rule "the [final] vowel is shortened in the neuter," he says *sunu*. Thus end those [words] ending in *au*.
Thus end the nouns ending in vowels in the neuter gender in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on compounds where elision does not occur (*aluk-samāsa*).
(942) *Alug-uttarapade* [Pāṇini 6.3.1]: Elision (*luk*) does not take place when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows.

Now, the *aluk* compound is defined: "The *aluk* [non-elision] occurs when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). This is not a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *rājapuruṣa*, and because rules such as *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* must be initiated. Rather, two words are here taken as the governing topic (*adhikāra*). Of this...
He states up to what limit this application continues: "The section on non-elision (aluk-adhikāra) extends prior to ānaṅ.

This means it extends prior to the rule "ṭhānaRﬁĀtaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.173]. Regarding "in the subsequent member" (uttarapade): this is the first sūtra of the third quarter (pāda) of the sixth book (adhyāya). #ti.
The meaning is that from this point up to the completion of the section on subsequent words (*uttarapada*) is the governing heading for subsequent words.
Regarding the rule for the governing heading of subsequent words in these various instances, the *Bhāṣya* itself is the authority.
(943) *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ* | P. 6.3.2. [The ablative case-ending is not elided after the words *stoka*, etc.]

Regarding the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*: the meaning is that the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *supo dhātu* should not apply to the ablative case (*pañcamī*) that follows words such as *stoka* and others. Regarding the term *uttarapade*:

the word *uttara* is conventionally used to denote the final member of a compound; for if the word *pade* alone were sufficient [to mean "in a following word"], the inclusion of the word *uttara* would be purposeless.

Regarding the phrase *stokānmuktaḥ*: it means "freed from a small amount. The compound is formed by the rule *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena* (Pāṇini 2.1.39). In this case, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*). The word "thus" (*evam*) implies that terms such as *antika* and others, which are included in the rule prescribing compounds, are also understood here.

"Come from nearby," "come from close by," "come from afar," "come from a distance," "come with difficulty. Regarding *niḥstoka*: the compound is formed according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyām* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Here, because the word *stoka* is not followed by another member of the compound (*uttarapada*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*).

In examples such as *stokānmuktaḥ*, the purpose of the compound is the accentuation of the compound (*samāsasvara*) and the absence of connection with qualifiers such as "released from everything slightly" (*sarvasmāt stokāt muktaḥ*). Furthermore,
in cases such as *staukāmuktiḥ*— meaning "the offspring of one released slightly"— [the compound serves its purpose].

And there is the derivation of secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes from a collective compound. It is clear in the *Bhāṣya* that there is no compound with words ending in dual or plural numbers, such as *stokānmuktau* or *stokānmuktāḥ*, because of the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhānāt*). [Furthermore,] there is an extension of the rule for the word *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*.
Regarding the statement "there is an addition [of the suffix] for *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*," the remainder is that the suffix *aluk* applies after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*).

But how can there be a fifth case when the meaning is "he recites the *brāhmaṇas*"? For it is by the word *brāhmaṇa* that the prescriptive sentences are meant; as the *Kalpasūtra* states: "The *brāhmaṇas* are the injunctions of ritual action."

Furthermore, because Jaimini has designated the term *brāhmaṇa* for that portion of the Veda distinct from the *mantra*— in the rule "The word *brāhmaṇa* [applies] to the remainder"— and because no recitation (*śaṃsana*) of such a *brāhmaṇa* portion is prescribed anywhere in the Śrutis (such as "He recites the *ṛc*s" or "He recites the *nivids*"), he says: "In the *brāhmaṇa*."

Regarding the term *śastra*: a collection of *ṛc* verses and *nivid*s constitutes a *śastra*. "By way of metaphor" (*upacārāt*) means by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the accusative": it means that, precisely by virtue of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) concerning the non-elision (*aluk*) of the ablative case, the ablative is used in the sense of the accusative.

(944) *ojaḥ-saha-ambhas-tamasa-stṛtīyāyāḥ* | 6|3|3| The compound *ojaḥ-saha-ambhas-tamasaḥ* is a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of the words *ojas*, *sahas*, *ambhas*, and *tamas*.
The meaning is that there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) following these [words] when they precede a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in a compound.

Regarding *ojasākṛtam*: the compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). According to Amara, *ojas* means "splendor" (*dīpti*) and "strength" (*bala*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth": examples include *sahasākṛtam*, *ambhasākṛtam*, and *tamasāvṛtam*. However, *tamovṛtam* is certainly incorrect [according to this specific rule]. Alternatively, the compound may be formed with the genitive case of the *śeṣa* relation.

Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] for *añjas*": the meaning is that there is an addition [to the rule] for the non-elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending after the word *añjas*.

As in the example *añjasākṛtam*, the word *añjas* occurs in the sense of "straightforwardness" (*ārjava*), as is seen in such usages as "the Knower of the Field leads straightforwardly" (*kṣetrajño 'ñjasā nayati*).
Thus he says: "by means of straightforwardness" (*ārjavena*). [The commentary continues:

"Puṃsānujaḥ" and "januṣāndhaḥ. [Regarding] *puṃsānujaḥ*: the remaining point is that it is grammatically correct because there is no elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending. Regarding *yasya* ("of whom"): [it refers to] him.
The man was the elder; "by reason of the man" means he was the younger or junior.

Regarding the word *januṣā*: according to Amara, "janu, janana, and janman" all mean birth. Thus, "by birth" means by way of his birth, i.e., he was blind. He states the conclusion: "blind from birth."
The meaning is "blind from birth," being equal to those of the *brāhmaṇa* caste and so forth; that is to say, blind from the very moment of birth.

(945) *manasaḥ saṃjñāyām* | 6|3|4|. [The rule] *manasaḥ saṃjñāyām* means that there shall be no elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending of *manas-* when it is followed by another word in a compound, provided the resulting form is a name.
*Manasāguptā*: this is the name of a certain woman. However, in the absence of such a specific name, it would be *manoguptā*.

[Pāṇini 4.1.14] Regarding [the rule] "and in the sense of one who commands" (6.3.5): the word "in the sense of one who commands" (*ājñāyin*) is also included. The meaning is that the word "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) indeed continues to apply.

The meaning is that there shall be no *aluk* (non-elision) of the third case ending of *manas-* when followed by *ājñāyin*. This is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *saṃjñā* (technical names). Regarding *jñātum*: the meaning is "to impel. In *manasājñāyī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau* ("after a verbal root ending in a case-ending, when not denoting a genus..."), and *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yukciṇkṛtoḥ*. In this context: [The following applies: The elision (*luk*) of the third case ending occurs after *manas-* when followed by *ājñāyin*. This is stated to exclude cases where it is a *saṃjñā*. As for *jñātum*, the sense is "to urge" (*prerayitum*). In *manasājñāyī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule *supyajātau*, and *yuk* is added according to the rule *āto yukciṇkṛtoḥ*. Here:
In the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, the Vārttika "And for the word *ātman*, there is an addition [to the rule] when it means 'filling'" is recited:
(947) *ātmanaśca* | Pāṇini 5.3.6. Therein, in order to explain the portion *ātmanaśca*, he sets it forth separately: "And for the word *ātman*."
He says that by the word "ca" (and), the rule "there is no elision [of the case-ending] of the third case" is also drawn in—namely, "there is no elision of the third case of *ātman*.

The phrase "when a subsequent member follows" is the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [this applies] when a *pūraṇa* [word follows]," the word *pūraṇa* is not taken here in its literal sense; rather, it is understood through the force of the *svarita* accent.

Intending that the rule "ṭhapratyayagrahaṇe" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) applies the principle of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with the specified element) because the suffixes prescribed for ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*) are being taken here, he says: "ending in an ordinal suffix. In the expression *ātmanāpañcamaḥ*, the meaning is "the self is the fifth. The instrumental case is used in the sense of the nominative according to the rule *prakṛtyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.18). Alternatively:

The meaning is "one who has himself as the fifth. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). By including the action of "doing" (*karoti*), the compound *tṛtīyā-tat-kṛta* is formed according to the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.30].
Both of these two positions are established in the Bhāṣya. Now, [one might ask: what of the three, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha?
The arrays of Viṣṇu: it is established in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts that Janārdana is the controller of these. Regarding this, the Paurāṇikas say: "Janārdana, however, is the fourth self.
In that case, since there is no elision (*luk*) of the third case ending, it ought to be "ātmanā caturthaḥ" (the fourth by means of the self); therefore—
He says: "It is *janārdana*. [Regarding] "it is a *bahuvrīhi*": the meaning is that it is a *bahuvrīhi* based on the analysis (*vigraha*) "that which has the Self as its fourth.

The sense is that, even though [the Self] is one, one must intend to express both its status as the referent of the constituent members (*vṛtti-padārthatva*) and its status as the referent of the whole compound (*anyapadārthatva*), by postulating a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*). This very point...
This is clear in the Bhāṣya.
(948) *vaiyākaraṇākhyāyāś caturthyāḥ* |6|3|7|. Regarding the phrase *vaiyākaraṇākhyāyām*: the word *ātmanaḥ* indeed continues [from the previous rule]; this is the meaning. And not...

If it is asked how this [vārtika] can be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) here into the sūtra when "ṭhātmanaśca" is itself a vārtika, the answer is that it is possible, just as the vārtika "kāmye roreveti vācyam," which is read in the sūtra "so'padādau," is carried over into the sūtra "iṇaḥ ṣaḥ. [The word] *vyākaraṇe* means "belonging to grammar."
"Vaiyākaraṇī" means that which is called "vaiyākaraṇa"; the meaning is that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) when it occurs in that [term]. Regarding "ātmanebhāṣe":
this is a technical name for the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) created by former teachers, well-known in the *dhātupāṭha*.
Regarding the statement "the dative case is used in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that)": thus, the meaning of *ātmane* is "for the sake of the self" (*ātmārtham*).

The intention is that this [dative] is generally prescribed when the fruit [of the action] accrues to the self. Now, one might ask: since there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra*) here, how can there be a compound with the dative of *tādarthya*? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "The fourth [case-ending] occurs due to a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). The commentary on the *Paspasāhnika*—specifically the statement, "A restriction for the sake of merit is 'dharmaniyama'"—serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here.
And regarding the word *para*: the meaning is that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the dative case ending even for the word *para* when it is used as a designation for a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
(950) Pāṇini 6.3.9: "After a word ending in a consonant or the letter *a*, the locative case ending is not elided when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is formed.
[Example: *tvacisāra*. Precisely because of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), [the compound] consists of words in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇapada*).
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding the word *tvaksāra*, Amara states: "The words *tvaksāra*, *karmāra*, *tvacisāra*, *tṛṇa*, and *dhvaja* [are used] in the sense of *vaṃśa* (bamboo).

Now, he will provide another example of a word ending in *hal* (a consonant): *yudhiṣṭhira*. Here, the word *sthira* is derived from the root *sthā* with the suffix *kirac* according to the *uṇādi* sūtra: "ajira, śiśira, and sthira."
[The word *vyutpāditaḥ*] has been explained.

(951) Pāṇini 8.3.95 states: *gaviyudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ*. In that case, although the rule for *ṣatva* [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] would apply by the rule *ṭhādośapratyayayoḥ*, it is prohibited by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*.

Now this [sūtra] is commenced: *gavi-yudhibhyāṃ sthiraḥ*. *Gavī* and *yudhī* are imitations of the locative case. The word *sthiraḥ*, though in the nominative, functions as a genitive. From the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*, the word *saḥ* is understood as being in the genitive case. [The rule *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* applies.]
This is the subject under discussion. He says this with the words "by these two.

Now, one might object: according to the paribhāṣā, "An external elision (luk) subverts even internal rules," the elision of *ReĀ* would apply before the substitution of *av*, and since the word would then not end in a consonant (*hal*), how can there be non-elision (*aluk*) here? To this, he replies: "In this case..."
"Gavī" and "Yudhiṣṭhira. [In the latter case], from the verbal root *yudh* (to fight), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), resulting in the word *yudh*.

From this word *yudh*, the seventh case singular ending is added. Because it ends in a consonant (*hal*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending, and the change to the retroflex *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) also occurs.
This is the name of the son of Dharma, one of the Pāṇḍavas. Thus, having explained the absence of elision (*aluk*) after a word ending in a consonant, [the author proceeds].

He provides an example of the elision of *luk* after *adanta* [stems]: "araṇyetilakāḥ" (wild sesame plants). Now, one might ask: since the word *tilaka* is not included in the *śauṇḍādi* group, how can there be a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*) with it? To this he replies: "In this case, it is by virtue of the rule *atra saṃjñāyām*" (Pāṇini 2.1.44).

"And from *hṛt* and *dyu*. This means that the elision (*aluk*) of the seventh case ending should be stated after the words *hṛt* and *dyu*. This is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] technical names (*saṃjñā*). For example, in *hṛdispṛk*: by the rule *paddannomās—*, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs before the neuter nominative singular ending *ṅi*.
The meaning is "it touches the heart. Regarding *divispṛk*, the meaning is "it touches heaven.
In both these cases, the commentary states that the locative case is used for the object precisely by virtue of the rule prescribing the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative.
This [non-elision] is not established by the rule *ṭhamūrdhamastakāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.129), because in that [rule],...
Because of the continued application of the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.3] "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*).

(952) *Kāranāmni ca prācāṃ halādau* [Pāṇini 6.3.10]: "And when it is the name of a tax (*kāra*), according to the Easterners, before a suffix beginning with a consonant. Regarding "when it is the name of a tax": where there is the name of a tax, as in *kara*, which is a portion to be taken by the king, that very thing is called *kāra*.

The meaning is that it expresses a specific instance of that [general category]. "For the sake of restriction" means: for the sake of three types of restrictive rules—namely, "if [the suffix] occurs after a place-name of the easterners (prācām) beginning with a consonant, it must be [only] when it is a name of a cause (kāra-nāman)"; "if it is a name of a cause beginning with a consonant, it must be [only] after [a place-name] of the easterners"; and "if it is a name of a cause of the easterners, it must be [only] when beginning with a consonant. This is the meaning.

Regarding *avikaṭoraṇa*: the suffix *kaṭac* is applied after the word *avi* when it does not denote a collection; thus, *avikaṭa* means "a sheep. Regarding *nadyām*: in the case of crossing a river, the milk is to be given as a temporary fee (*tātkālika-doha*). (953) [Pāṇini 6.3.11] *madhyādgurau*. *madhyam* is derived from *madhya* with the suffix *ap*, and the final vowel is lengthened by *gurau* (Pāṇini 6.3.11). Thus, *madhyama* means "middle" or "central. The word *madhyama* is used here to indicate that the milk is to be given at the time of crossing the river. This is an example of a temporary obligation (*tātkālika-doha*) rather than a permanent tax (*nitya-bhāga*). The rule *madhyādgurau* (Pāṇini 6.3.11) prescribes the substitution of the long vowel *ā* for the final short vowel *a* of *madhya* before the suffix *ap* when the resulting form refers to something "heavy" or "great," which in this context applies to the significance of the crossing. The term *avikaṭoraṇa* illustrates the formation of a specific compound where the sheep is the object of the action, while *nadyām* illustrates the specific circumstance under which the milk is offered. Regarding "madhyādgurau": when the word *guru* follows, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending of the word *madhya*; this is for the purpose of excluding its use as a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). (1) Also [there is no elision] after the word *anta*.
"And after [a word ending in] /ant/. This means that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending when followed by *guru*.

(954) *amūrdhastakātsvāṅgādakāme* 6.3.12. "Not from *mūrdhan* or *mastaka*": [the rule applies] to a word denoting a limb of the body (*svāṅga*), excluding the words *mūrdhan* and *mastaka*, when it ends in the locative case.
The meaning is that [the elision] occurs when there is no *luk* elision, but not when the word *kāma* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

Here, the term "in a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is understood to carry over from the previous rule. For this very reason, the explicit mention of *hṛt* in the rule *ṭhṛddyaubhyāṃ ca* is purposeful. *Kaṇṭhekālaḥ*: a name of Śiva. *Urasilomā*.
It is the name of someone. For this very reason, based on this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), there exists a *bahuvrīhi* compound with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*).
(955) *bandhe ca vibhāṣā* | Regarding "and in the case of *bandha*, optionally": he explains the sūtra by supplying the remainder [of the rule], namely: "after a consonant or a final *a*."

Regarding the term *bastebandha*: this is a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound by virtue of the rule *saṃjñāyām*. Here, it is connected with the phrase "in a tatpuruṣa," whereas *bandha* ends in the suffix *ghañ*; however, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that elsewhere there is a prohibition [of the suffix] by the rule *nen-siddhe*.

(956) *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* | 6|3|14| In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the elision of the case-ending] of a locative case is frequently not applied before a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix when it is the second member, provided it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This is the meaning. For example: *stamberamaḥ*. Here, *stamba* means a clump of grass.
"He delights in that" is *stamberama*, meaning an elephant (*hastī*). Regarding *karṇejapa*:
he whispers into the ear (*karṇe japati*), that is, he reveals another's faults in a low voice; thus, *karṇejapa* means a slanderer (*piśuna*).
[The suffix] *ac* is applied by the rule "after *stamba* and *karṇa*, the roots *ram* and *jap*" (*ṭhstambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ*). This is an *upapada* compound. In some cases, however, it is not so.
The intention is that this is due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"). Regarding the example *kurucara*:

by the rule *careṣṭaḥ*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied when a word denoting a location (*adhikaraṇa*) is used as an *upapada*. This forms an *upapada-samāsa*. Although this result is already established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *haladantāt*, nevertheless, since it is established precisely by the inclusion of *bahulam*, the mention of *haladantāt* [is not strictly necessary].
The sense is that [the suffix] should not be applied.
(957) *prāvṛṭ-śarat-kāla-divāṃ je* | 6|3|15|. [The rule states: after *prāvṛṭ*, *śarat*, *kāla*, and *div*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending when followed by the suffix *ja*.
Thus: *prāvṛṭ*, *śarat*, *kāla*, *div*. For these, there is no elision of the case-ending in a compound.

The meaning is that [the substitution] occurs when followed by the word *śabda* in a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Now, one might ask: since the rule *haladantāt* alone would suffice, for what purpose is this stated? To this he says: "This is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding [rule]. The meaning is that it is a detailed expansion. (958) *vibhāṣā varṣakṣaraśaravarāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.16).
The term *vibhāṣā* means "optionally. He explains the Sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "from these [words], in the seventh case (*saptamī*).
(Pāṇini 2.3.44) *ghakālataneṣu kālanāmnaḥ*. Regarding *ghakālataneṣu*, he explains the Sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "in the seventh case. The word *gha*...

This is an illustration indicating that *gha* follows [the suffixes mentioned]. "The suffixes *ṭh*, *tara*, *tama*, and *p* are called *gha*" (*ṭhtaraptamapau ghaḥ*). In the example *pūrvāhṇetaraḥ*, the suffixes *tara* and *tama* are used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*) after a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*).
For this very reason, it is understood that *tara* and *tama* follow words ending in those respective case endings. As for the word *kāla*: [it refers to the time of action].

This is an indication of an example: *pūrvāhṇekāle*. For this very reason, even in the case of a compound with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, it is only those words ending in specific case-terminations that are compounded. *taneti*:
this is an indication of an example: *pūrvāhṇetane*. [The rule] *vibhāṣā*...
By the rule *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām*, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ayuṭhayul* [are applied], along with the augment *tuṭ*.

(960) *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt* 6.3.18: when *śaya*, *vāsa*, and *vāsin* follow, [the seventh case-ending] after a word other than one denoting time [is replaced by these suffixes]. *śaya*, *vāsa*, *vāsin*: when these follow, [the suffixes are applied] after a word other than one denoting time, provided it ends in the seventh case.
The meaning is that there shall be an *aluk* [elision].
[In the rule] *apo yoniyanmatuṣu*:
when the word *yoni*, the suffix *yat*, or the suffix *matup* follows the word *ap* [in the locative case], there is [an *aluk*].

The meaning is that there shall be an *aluk* [elision]. In the case of *apsavya*, the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group; then, by the rule "ṭhorguṇaḥ," the *guṇa* substitution occurs, and by the rule "vānto yi pratyaye," the *av* replacement takes place. Regarding *apsumantau*: those two specific ritual portions (*karmaviśeṣau*) known as the *ājyabhāgau* are called *apsumantau* if the word *apsu* exists within their respective mantras.

(961) *nen-siddha-bandhu-ādiṣu ca* | 6|3|19|. [The word *baddha*] is also [used in a compound with a word ending in the seventh case] when preceded by *ni*, *siddha*, *bandhu*, and so forth. For example, *cakrabaddhaḥ*. This is a compound of a word ending in the seventh case with a word ending in *kta* according to the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā*.
(962) *sthe ca bhāṣāyām* |6|3|20|.

Regarding *sthe ca bhāṣāyām*: by the maxim "the prohibition applies to what follows immediately," this is a prohibition specifically of [the rule] *tatpuruṣe kṛti*. For this very reason, [the rule] *anekam anyapadārthe* [is not affected].

In the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, during the explanation of the Vārttika rule "saptamyupamānapūrvapadasya," the analysis "kaṇṭhesthaḥ kālo yasya" (one whose time is situated in the throat) is presented; this is consistent provided that one accepts the compound status of the word *kaṇṭhestha* and then proposes the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). However, when...

If this prohibition were to apply even to the word *āditya* when it follows *ṭhamūrdhan* and *mastaka*, then there would be an inconsistency, because the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] would be required by rule Pāṇini 5.4.111. (963) Pāṇini 6.3.21: *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe*. (The genitive case ending is not elided after a word denoting a limb of the body when used in a term of abuse.)
Regarding the sixth case [genitive]: "In the sense of reviling; there is elision of the genitive suffix when the following word follows" is the remainder [of the rule]. Reviling means censure.
(1) Regarding *vāg-dik-paśyadbhyo yukti-daṇḍa-hareṣu*:
after *vāc*, *dik*, and *paśyat*, there is non-elision (*aluk*) of the following genitive case.
The meaning is: when these words—*yukti*, *daṇḍa*, and *hara*—occur as subsequent members [of a compound] in their respective order.

*Vācoyuktiḥ* means "the employment of words. *Diśodaṇḍaḥ*: here, the genitive case is used because there is an intention to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). *Paśyatoharaḥ*.
The meaning is that one seizes while disregarding what is being seen. The genitive case is used here according to the rule "ṣaṣṭhī cānādare" (the genitive is also used in the sense of disregard).
Regarding the forms *āmuṣyāyaṇa*, *āmuṣyaputrika*, and *āmuṣyakulika*: this is a Vārttika; these words are thus derived as irregular formations (*nipātita*). [The base form is] *amuṣya*.

The meaning is as follows: for the sense of "the son of so-and-so" (*amuṣya apatyam*), the suffix *phañ* is applied by the rule *ṭhañ-ṇaḍādibhyaḥ phak*. After the substitution of *āyan* [for *phañ*], the initial *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel] occurs. Because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix, it becomes a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) which would otherwise apply because it is a member of that [stem] is prohibited. Then, the change of *n* to *ṇ* occurs, resulting in the form *āmuṣyāyaṇa*. Thus, [the compound] *āmuṣyāyaṇa-putraḥ* means "the son of so-and-so."

In a *vigraha* (analytical statement) involving a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) where the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not elided (*aluk*), there is the word *amuṣyaputra*. To express the sense "the state of being the son of such-and-such a person" (*amuṣyaputrasya bhāvaḥ*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule *dvandvamanojñādibhyaśca*;

following this, the substitution of *ak* occurs, the case-ending (*sup*) after the word *putra* is elided, the initial vowel is strengthened (*vṛddhi*), and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added due to its feminine gender.

The meaning is that when the *it* (the long vowel *ī*) is substituted for the final vowel by the rule *ṭhpratyayasthāt* [Pāṇini 7.3.44], the word *āmuṣyaputrikā* is formed. Regarding the phrase "in the same way":

in the case of the genitive compound *amuṣya kulam*, when the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not elided (*aluk*), the suffix *buñ* and so forth are applied to the word *amuṣyakula* as before; this is the meaning.
And the term *devānāṃpriya* refers to a fool. [The analysis is: *devānām*. This is a *vārttika*. A fool (*mūrkha*) is one who is ignorant (*ajña*). [From the root] *divu* "to play";
thus, *devāḥ* are fools addicted to play. He who is dear (*priya*) to them is indeed a fool.
"Because it is necessarily foolishness [to be] dear to a fool"—thus says Kaiyaṭa on the rule *ṭhāj-ij-vī*. Regarding the rule *śeṣa-puccha-lāṅgūleṣu śunaḥ*:
"śeṣa-puccha" refers to this Vārttika. The remainder is that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*).

Regarding the term *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name): the *Bhāṣya* states *ṣa śunaśśepaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose tail (*śepa*) is like that of a dog (*śunaḥ*). [The word *śepa* is derived from] *meḍhra-mehana-śepasī*; there is also the word *śepha*, as seen in the Vedic formula *śepāya svāhā*. [The example] *śunaḥpucchaḥ* means "one whose tail is like that of a dog."
The analysis of the compound is *pucchaṃ yasya* ("that which has a tail as its [defining] member"). Similarly, there is also *śunolāṅgūla*.
These are proper names (*saṃjñā*) of specific sages.
[Also, the word *diva* takes the suffix *aṇ* before the word *dāsa*: *divodāsa*.]

"And after *div*, [the suffix] *dāsa*. This is a *vārttika*. The remainder is that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*). *Divodāsa* refers to a certain royal sage (*rājarṣi*).
(964) "After *putra*, optionally" (Pāṇini 6.3.22).

Regarding the rule *putre 'nyatarasyām*: the phrase "in the sense of censure" (*nindāyām*) is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "in the sense of abuse" (*ākrośe*). This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *ānaṅ ṛt-aḥ*. (965) *ṛto vidyāyonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ* 6.3.23.
*Ṛt* is present. The plural number is used for the singular.

[The rule] "the taking of that as the prior or subsequent member [occurs] after words denoting relations through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*)" applies here. Thus it says: "after a word ending in *ṛt* which denotes a relation through learning or a relation through birth. There is no elision (*aluk*).
It may be so. The remainder of the rule is "when a subsequent word follows.
He provides an example denoting a connection with knowledge: *hotur-antevāsī* ("the pupil of the Hotṛ").
The *hotṛ* is the performer of specific rites prescribed by the Ṛgveda; therefore, the word *hotṛ*...
The meaning is that [the designation] is caused by the occurrence of a relationship through learning. "The son of the Hotṛ" is another example of a term expressing a relationship through learning.
Now, he provides an example of a term expressing a relationship through birth: "the pupil of the father. "The son of the father."
And: [Objection] But would there not also be non-elision (*aluk*) in cases such as *hotṛdhana* and *pitṛdhana*?
To this he says: "In the case of relations of learning (*vidyā*) and of birth (*yoni*), there is the inclusion of both the preceding and the following words.
Regarding the phrase "from relations of learning and of birth," [it refers to] those two which express the relation of learning and the relation of birth.
The meaning is that there is a mention of both the preceding and the following words.
The intention is that it is intended for both the preceding and the following words to denote either a connection through knowledge (*vidyā*) or a connection through birth (*yonisambandha*).
In the examples "the wealth of the *hotṛ*" (*hotṛdhana*) and "the wealth of the father" (*pitṛdhana*), [it refers to] the following word.

The point is that there is no *aluk* (non-elision) of the genitive case-ending because [the word *hotṛ*] does not denote either a connection through knowledge (*vidyā-sambandha*) or a connection through birth (*yoni-sambandha*).
Precisely because the intention is to express one or the other of these two types of connection, forms such as *hotuḥ putraḥ* ("the son of the Hotṛ") are established.
(966) *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* | 6|3|24|.

[The rule] *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* [is stated]. [The phrase] "ending in /ṛ/" [is understood]; the remainder [of the context] is "denoting either a relationship of learning (*vidyā-sambandha*) or a relationship of birth (*yonisambandha*)". And therefore—
There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *bhoktṛsvasṛ* [in the rule *mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ svasā*].

(967) *mātuḥpiturbhyāmanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 8.3.85). Since the previous rule would have made the elision compulsory, this [present rule] provides an option. In the alternative where there is no elision (*alukpakṣe*), [the form is *mātṛpitṛsvasṛ*].

He states the specific rule: *mātṛpitṛbhyām anyatarasyām*. From the preceding sūtra, *svasṛ* is understood [by anuvṛtti]. This is in the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive. [The rule] *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* [applies].

From this sūtra, the word "sa" (that), ending in the genitive case, is understood to carry over. The governing rule "ṭhapadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ" (the cerebral [substitute occurs] for a non-final ṭh) is also in force.

Thus he says: "by these two. This means by the two genitive forms "mātuḥ" and "pituḥ. Regarding the phrase "in a compound": this refers to the rule "samāse 'ṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ" (in a compound, [ṣ replaces s] after aṅguli when followed by saṅga).

The meaning is that this is because of its recurrence [in subsequent rules]. The forms *mātuḥṣvasā* and *pituḥṣvasā* are derived with the suffix *ṣatva* (retroflex sibilant) when there is no elision (*aluk*). The forms *mātuḥsvasā* and *pituḥsvasā* are derived without *ṣatva* when there is no elision.
Regarding the phrase "but in the case of elision," the remainder of the sentence is "the specific distinction will be stated."

(968) *mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ svasā* || 8|3|84 || [The word] *svasā* [is added] after *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*. Regarding the form *svasuḥ*: the intention is that in the sūtra, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, we have *mātṛṣvasā* and *pitṛṣvasā*. In the alternative where there is elision (*luk*), the substitution of the sibilant (*ṣatva*) is necessarily constant. [This applies to the] substitute [form].

Since the condition of having *sakāra* as a suffix (*pratyaya*) is absent, this rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would not otherwise apply; thus, it is prescribed here. He demonstrates the purpose of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule for *ṣatva* by stating: "but in a non-compound" (*asamāse tu*). The meaning is that even the optional *ṣatva* does not occur in a sentence (*vākya*).
Thus ends the section on compounds with elision (aluksamāsa) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on the derivation of patronymics (*apatya*) within the rules for secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
(1055) *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā* | Pāṇini 4.1.82. "From among words that are semantically connected, [the suffix is added] optionally after the first [word]."

Having thus explained the extensive treatment of compounds (*samāsa*), he begins the section on secondary suffixes (*taddhita*): "Of [words] that are semantically capable (*samartha*), [the suffix is applied] optionally after the first [word]. Considering that this is not an independent rule because no thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is seen, he says:
"These three words are introduced as a governing heading. The underlying intention is that this is due to the force of the formal declaration of the *svarita* accent.

He states the upper limit of the governing scope (*adhikāra*): "up to *prāgdiśaḥ*" (Pāṇini 5.3.1). The meaning is that the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1) is the upper limit. In the phrase *samarthānām*, the genitive case denotes selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). And its priority [in the governing scope] is established in various specific rules such as *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92).

"Being uttered first" means "among those that are semantically connected (*samartha*), [the suffix is applied] after that which is uttered first. It would be more appropriately stated as *samarthāt prathamād vā* ("after a semantically connected word, optionally after the first"). However, some maintain that by virtue of the plural number [in the rule], this [suffix] applies only when there is a collection of multiple semantically connected words; and thus, [the rule] *prāgdiśaḥ*...

They say that this [paribhāṣā] does not apply to rules for suffixes with an inherent meaning (*svārthika-pratyaya*) such as these, because it will be stated that *taddhita* suffixes are produced from words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*); thus, since the rules for *taddhitas* are "word-based rules" (*padavidhi*), they are already governed by the paribhāṣā:
"A rule concerning words applies only to those that are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*).
Since the term "capable" (*samartha*) would be redundant here because it already possesses the capacity consisting of the state of having a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), he says:
"Capacity is the state of being fully established. "Capable," "clever," and "powerful" are synonyms.
And the state of being capable is the fitness for the production of an effect. And [this applies] to the word...
The function [of words] is precisely the communication of meaning. And that capacity [to communicate] is possible only when the operations of *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) have been performed.
Thus, in this context, "capacity" ultimately results in nothing other than the state of having undergone the operations of *saṃdhi*.
Therefore, he says: "the state of having undergone the operations of *saṃdhi*."

(1056) *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* | Pāṇini 4.1.83: *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*. Here, the word *dīvyañ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the single constituent part *dīvyati* from the rule *tena dīvyati khanati jayati jitam*. And by that...
That [term] is observed to be formed with that suffix. Thus he says: "before [the rule] 'one who plays with that' (Pāṇini 4.1.21).
And so, in subsequent rules such as "his offspring" (Pāṇini 4.1.92), when they are not connected with a specific suffix to be prescribed, what [is the status]?
When there is the expectancy "what comes into being?", it is understood that "the suffix *aṇ* presents itself.
When there is the expectancy "from what does it come into being?", the specific base is understood as "from a capable [word] in the nominative case.
However, where a specific suffix to be prescribed is heard, there [the suffix] is *aṇ*.
It does not apply [to the suffix], because the general rule (*utsarga*) is set aside by the specific rule (*vaiśeṣika*) beginning with *iñ*.
(1057) *aśvapatyādibhyaś ca* |4|1|84|.
From *aśvapati* and others. By the word "and" (*ca*), the rule "*ṭhprāgdīvyato 'ṇ*" is drawn back [into this sūtra].
Thus he says: "The suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after these. *Prāgdīvyat* means "prior to *dīvyati*.

This is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "after *ṭha*, *apara*, *pari*, *bahis*, and *añcu*, when [governed] by the fifth case-ending. The suffix *ṭac* is not applied here because it is only optional. Those who exist prior to *dīvyati* are *prāgdīvyatīyāḥ*. [The suffix] *cha* is applied by the rule "after a *vṛddha* [stem], *cha*."

However, [the form] *avyayātya* does not occur, because when an *avyayībhāva* compound is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it is included in the specific enumeration [of cases where elision applies]: "The purposes [of being an indeclinable] are the elision of the final vowel, accent, and metaphorical usage. For this very reason, the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix of indeclinables before any *bha*-ending" also does not apply here. Now, one might ask: since the desired form is already established by the rule *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*, what is the purpose of this [present rule]?
Regarding the sūtra, he says: "of that which is to be stated.

The meaning is that it is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *ṇya*, which would otherwise be applied due to the condition of having "pati" as a subsequent member (as prescribed by the rule *dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ*).
