It must be stated that [the *gotra* designation] is set aside by the *yuvan* designation, because the *yuvan* designation sublates the *gotra* designation. Nor should it be argued that its cessation is possible due to the restrictive rule "only one [suffix occurs] in the *gotra*," because the *yuvan* designation sublates the *gotra* designation. Furthermore, even if there were a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), [it would not follow that] "there is no *yuvan* suffix in the feminine."
It should be stated that [the objection] is refuted because the term "yuvan" (descendant) is expressed by means of the *gotra* suffix;

enough of this. Regarding the example "gargasya": from the word *gārgya*, which ends in the *yañ* suffix denoting a *gotra*, when the *phañ* suffix is added to denote a *yuvan* descendant in the fifth generation or beyond, one obtains "gārgyāyaṇa."

The meaning is "form" (rūpa). He demonstrates the purpose of the prohibition of the technical designation *yuvan* for a feminine by saying "in the feminine" (*striyām*). Because the fifth and subsequent female descendants lack the designation *yuvan*, they possess the status of a *gotra*. By the restrictive rule "only one [is designated *yuvan*] in the *gotra*," the form is simply *gārgī*, and not—

The meaning is that the form is *gārgyāyaṇī*. The intention is that if one were to rely on the meaning "only after a *gotra* [stem], when a young descendant [is to be expressed] other than a female," then the *gotra* designation would be superseded by the *yuvan* (young descendant) designation; consequently, since the rule *eko gotre* ("only one suffix in the *gotra*") would not apply, there would result an infinite series of suffixes (*pratyayamālā*).

(1078) *ata iñ* | Pāṇini 4.1.95. The term *ataḥ* (from "a") qualifies the governing term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem); thus, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in [the specified element].
Therefore, it says: "that nominal stem which ends in 'a'. The phrase "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) is understood as a carry-over from the previous rule.

And [there is the rule]: "From a capable [word], two [suffixes] after the first. From this, it is understood that [the suffixes follow] the nominal stem (prātipadika) indicated by the word *tat* when uttered first.
Furthermore, because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that taddhita suffixes arise from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is understood that they follow a *subanta*.

Because it is most proximately present, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) alone is intended; thus, it is understood as "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the genitive. Although a nominal stem does not itself end in the genitive—since, by the *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyaya*), the entire complex of base and affix is what is obtained—nevertheless...

The intended meaning is "from a base noun ending in the genitive case. Thus he says: "from that which has it as its base, ending in the genitive. Regarding *dākṣi*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of Dakṣa.
[The suffix] *iñ* is applied; there is initial *vṛddhi*, and by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the letter *a* is elided. Let it be given.

The form *dāśarathāya maithilī* is Vedic (ārṣa), as explained under the rule *tasyāpatyam*. If the term *prātipadika* were not understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it would follow that the suffix applies after a genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) ending in *at*;
in that case, the form *dākṣiḥ*, meaning "the offspring of Dakṣa" (*dakṣayoḥ apatyam*), would not be established—this is the intended point.

(1079) *bāhvādibhyaśca* |4|1|96|. From [the group] beginning with *bāhu*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied]. The remainder [of the rule] is "when *apatya* [is to be expressed], *iñ*. Thus, *bāhavir iti*. There was a certain seer named Bāhu; then, under the heading "seers," [it is stated]: "Bāhavir, Gārgya, Gautama."

This is because it is seen thus in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of Bāhu. By the rule *iñi orguṇaḥ*, the guṇa substitution occurs. Thus we have *ĀṬḍulomi*. The analysis is "the offspring of Uḍuloman.

By the rule *ṭhnastaddhite*, there is elision of the final *ṭ* (the *m* of *man*). There is initial vṛddhi; however, since [the base] does not end in *a*, the [usual] application [of the vṛddhi rule] would not otherwise have occurred.

(1080) *sudhātur akaṅ ca* | 4|3|97 | The rule *sudhātur akaṅ ca* means that after the word *sudhātṛ* ending in the genitive case, the suffix *iñ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), and the substitute *akaṅ* is substituted for the base. The letter *ṅ* in *akaṅ* is an *it*, while the letter *a* [is for euphonic purposes].
The purpose is for pronunciation. By the rule *ṭhṅcci*, there is the substitution of the suffix *in*. Thus he says: "Saudhātaki.
It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after Vyāsa, Varuḍa, Niṣāda, Caṇḍāla, and Bimba.
Regarding "Vyāsa": from Vyāsa, Varuḍa, Niṣāda, Caṇḍāla, and Bimba, the suffix *iñ* [is applied].
The meaning is that it is a portion of the *prakṛti* (base).
(1081) *na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyāmaic* | 7|3|3|.
[The rule begins with] *na yvābhyām*. The analysis of the compound is: *y* and *v* are *yvau*; the vowel *a* after *v* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Regarding this, he says: "by the letters *ya* and *va*. The word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*) is to be understood through ellipsis. "There is no *vṛddhi*"—the intention is that this follows from the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "there is *vṛddhi* for *mṛj*" (*mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*). He states that the word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of indicating a distinction, saying: "however" (*kiṃ tu*). "By those two" (*tābhyām*).
The meaning is "by means of the letters *y* and *v*. "The two preceding" means the two preceding constituent parts (*pūrvāvayava*).
By this, their status as augments (*āgama*) is obtained. Thus he says: "The diphthongs *ai* and *au* are augments. *Aic* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviation).
According to the respective order, *aikāra* follows after *y*, and *aukāra* follows after *v*.

Regarding the term *Vaiyāsaki*: he who "unfolds" (*vyasyati*) or "expands" (*vivadhamasyati*)—that is, divides—the Vedas by means of different branches (*śākhā*) is called Vedavyāsa. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule for the formation of nouns denoting an action (*karmaṇyaṇ*). Here, there is the mention of a part of the name [to denote the whole]. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the offspring (*apatyam*) of Vyāsa. The suffix *iñ* is applied, and the substitution of *aka* for the base occurs. In this context...

The letter *ya* stands at the end of a word (*padānta*). Consequently, for the vowel *ā* following it, the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) does not apply—despite the general rule of grammatical operation proceeding like rain (*parjanyavat*)—but rather the augment *ai* is inserted before the *ya*.
Thus, the form is *vaiyāsaki*. In the case of *sauvaśviḥ*, meaning "the descendant of Svaśva," [the same principle applies] after the letter *va*.

There is no *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), but rather the vowel *au* occurs before that. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is redundant— since the absence of *vṛddhi* is already established because the *aij* substitutes (*ai* and *au*) are exceptions to *vṛddhi*— because the *aij* substitutions apply only in those cases where there would otherwise have been a potential application of *vṛddhi* following the letters *y* and *v*.
Because it serves the purpose of specifying the object [of the rule],

this prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies— by the principle of "that which was not otherwise applicable" (*yena nāprāptinyāya*)— only to the initial *vṛddhi*. Therefore, in the case of *dvyāśītika*, meaning "hired for two eighty-year periods," the [rule] *saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṅkhyasya...* [does not apply].
And thus, the vṛddhi of the subsequent syllable indeed occurs. Varuḍa and others are specific castes.
[The derivatives are] vāruḍakiḥ, naiṣādakiḥ, cāṇḍālakiḥ, and baimbakiḥ.
(1082) Pāṇini 4.1.98: *gotre kuñjādibhyaś-cphañ*. [The suffix cphañ is applied after the words beginning with kuñja when forming a patronymic.]

*Gotre* means "in the sense of a lineage. This is clear. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ*. *Cphañ* and *iña* are elided. (Pāṇini 4.1.95). (Pāṇini 5.3.113): *brātacphañor astriyām*. [The analysis is as follows:
*brāta-cphañoḥ* refers to *brāta* and *cphañ*; this is a *dvandva* compound, and by transposition (*vyatyayena*), it functions in the sense of the ablative case.

The sixth [case ending]. Thus he says: "after words denoting a *vrāta*. The suffix *ñya* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). The word "*ñya*" is carried over from the rule "after a *pūga* [name] not preceded by the name of a *grāmaṇī*, [the suffix] *ñya*.
And that [suffix] is *svārthika* (denotative), because it is enumerated among the *svārthika* suffixes in the rule "those beginning with *ñya* up to *vuñ*."
The meaning is "descendant. Regarding *kauñjāyanya*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatyam*) of Kuñja.

When the suffix *cphañ* is applied, *cañ* and *it* are elided; there is the substitution of *āyan*, initial *vṛddhi*, and then the suffix *ñya*. The letter *ñ* is an *it*; by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the vowel *a* is elided. [He says] "because it belongs to that class" (*tad-vāja-tvāt*); for "the *ñya*-suffixes and so forth are *tadrāja* [suffixes]."

The sense is that this is because of the aforementioned statement. "The elision (luk) will be stated" refers to the rule "tadrājasya bahuṣu" (Pāṇini 2.4.62); this is the ellipsis. Regarding *brādhnāyanya*:
the analysis of the compound is "the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) of Bradhna. The suffix *cphañ* and so forth are as before.

He states the purpose of the rule *vyavidhāv astriyām*: "In the feminine, *kauñjāyanī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the female descendant of Kuñja. The point is that because it denotes a feminine, the suffix *ñya* is not applied here.

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *ṭāp* might apply here because the word ends in the letter *a*, he says: "by virtue of being a *gotra* (clan name). However, once [the suffix] has been applied...

The intention is that when the suffix *ñya* is applied, since the word ends in *y*, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule for generic names (*jāti*)—is not used, and instead the suffix *ṭāp* occurs.
He states the purpose of including the term "clan" (*gotra*) in the rule prescribing the suffix *cphañ*: "In the case of a descendant of an immediate [son], it is *kauñjiḥ*."

(1084) *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* |4|1|99|. The suffix *phak* is added after [words beginning with] *naḍa*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ*. Regarding the example *anantara-nāḍiḥ*: since the immediate descendant (*anantarāpatya*) does not possess the status of a lineage (*gotra*), the suffix *phak* is absent; thus, the meaning is that only *iñ* is applied.
(1085) *Haritādibhyo 'ñaḥ* |4|1|100|. The rule beginning with "from *harita* and others, the suffix *añ*" is clear. (1086) *YaÑ-iñoś ca* |4|1|101|.

Regarding the phrase *yañiñośca*: the term *gotre* (in the sense of a lineage) is a qualifier for *yañ* and *iñ*, and not a qualifier for the suffix *phak* which is being prescribed, according to the explanation. Thus he says: "those two suffixes *yañ* and *iñ* [occurring] in the sense of a lineage. By implication, this refers to the suffix *yaūn*. For there is no further lineage-suffix (*gotra-pratyaya*) following a lineage-suffix, as [stated in the rule] *eko...* [P. 4.1.93].
Because of the restriction "in [denoting] a *gotra*. Regarding "anātī": *gargasya gotram* (the lineage of Garga) is *gārgyaḥ*.

By virtue of belonging to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is applied. In the sense of "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of Gārgya," when *phañ* is added after the stem ending in *yañ*, the substitution of *āyan* for the final portion occurs.
Due to the exclusion by the rule "anātī," the elision of *y* prescribed by "ṭhāpatyasya ca" does not take place; thus, through the application of *ṇatva*, we arrive at the form.

The meaning is that the form is *gārgyāyaṇa*. Regarding *dākṣāyaṇa*: *dakṣi* is the descendant in the lineage (*gotra*) of Dakṣa [formed with] *iñ*; the young descendant (*yuvan*) of *dākṣi* is *dākṣāyaṇa*, [formed with] *phak* after a stem ending in *iñ*.
Why "in the lineage" (*gotre*)? [Consider: in the sense of "not far from Sutaṅgama," [the suffix is applied] according to *sutaṅgamādibhyaḥ*...
The suffix *phak* is not applied [after the word] *sautāṅgami*, which means "the descendant of Sutaṅgama.

(1087) *Śaradvat-śunaka-darbhād bhṛgu-vatsāgrāyaṇeṣu* [Pāṇini 4.1.102]. [The author] explains the sūtra by supplementing it with the phrase "the suffix *phaṅ* is used in the sense of a gotra (lineage). The first two [names] are...
Regarding the term *vidādī*: the words *śaradvat* and *śunaka* belong to the *vidādi* group;

therefore, the meaning is that [the suffix] *añ* is an exception (*apavāda*) in regard to both of them. However, in the case of *darbha*, it is quite clear that it is an exception to the suffix *iñ*. *Darbha* refers to a certain sage (*ṛṣi*). Although the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed for sages] would have applied, *iñ* is used instead because [the name] belongs to the *bāhvādi* group.
Regarding the phrase "if [it is] Āgrāyaṇa": *Agra* is the name of a certain ṛṣi. This word ends in the suffix *phak* according to the rule beginning with *naḍa*.
(Pāṇini 4.1.99) "Optionally after *droṇaparvata* and *jīvantī*" (Pāṇini 4.1.103):
*droṇaparvata*. Regarding the term "having no beginning" (*anādi*): it refers to the father of Aśvatthāman who appears in the Mahābhārata.
The meaning is that he is a different, beginningless Droṇa than the one well-known at the start of the Kali age.
Regarding "in Aśvatthāman": the usage "Drauṇāyana" refers to Aśvatthāman, the immediate descendant of the teacher Droṇa; this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *bāhvādibhyaśca*.

(1089) *anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.104]. Regarding *anṛṣyānantarye*: the word *anṛṣi* contains an elided ablative case ending (*luptapañcamīkam*). The phrase *bidādibhyo’ñ* recurs twice. Thus, it is understood as: "after the *bidādi* group, when there is no immediate succession from a seer (*anṛṣyānantarye*), the suffix *añ* is applied."

The entire [first] sentence is one: "ṭhbidādibhyaś cāñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.104). A second sentence is: "ṭhbidādibhyo 'ñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.105). Therein, he explains the second sentence: "ebhyo 'ñ gotre" (from these, the suffix añ is used when a lineage [gotra] is intended to be expressed). The meaning is that when a lineage is intended to be expressed, the suffix añ shall occur after the words beginning with ṭhi and bi.

Now, he explains the first statement, which constitutes the entire sūtra, with the words "But those who... (ye tu). The literal meaning is that the suffix *añ* is applied after [names of] non-ṛṣis such as Vida and others, when forming a descendant in the immediate generation.
For in the list beginning with Vida, both ṛṣis and non-ṛṣis are recited; therein, the suffix *añ* is applied after those who are non-ṛṣis for the sake of the immediate descendant.
The meaning is that [the suffix] has been applied. Now, one might ask: since the word *ānantarya* (immediacy) is heard [in the rule], how can it be [derived as] *anantara*?

To this he says: "In the sūtra, the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). The remainder [of the sentence] is "from the word *anantara*. The intention is that [it belongs to] the group beginning with *caturvarṇa*. [For example: Baida is the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*) of Bida. Of Bida...

The meaning is that, because of the status of being a *ṛṣi*, the suffix *añ* is applied specifically to the *gotra* [lineage]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*. There is a difference regarding the accent (*svara*). Now, one might ask: "If the suffix *añ* does not apply to the immediate descendant (*anantarāpatya*), then the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* would be more appropriate as its exception; why then is the immediate descendant called 'Vaidi'? To this, he says: "Because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group."

He provides an example of the suffix *añ* after a non-ṛṣi word belonging to the *bidādi* group, namely: *pautraḥ* (grandson) and *dauhitraḥ* (daughter’s son). The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the immediate offspring of a son" and "the immediate offspring of a daughter," respectively.
In each case, the suffix *añ* applies as a specific exception (*apavāda*) to [the general rule for] *aṇ*.

(1090) *Gargādibhyo yañ* | Pāṇini 4.1.105. From the group beginning with *garga*, the suffix *yañ* is applied. For example: *gārgyaḥ*, *vātsyaḥ*. The analytical explanations (*vigraha*) are: "the descendant in the lineage (*gotrapatya*) of Garga" and "the descendant in the lineage of Vatsa. Similarly: *rāmaḥ jāmadagnyaḥ* ("Rāma, the son of Jamadagni"), *pārāśaryaḥ* ("the son of Parāśara").
Regarding examples such as *vyāsa*, they say that the suffix *yañ* is applied because the status of a *gotra* (lineage name) is superimposed upon the immediate descendant.
(Pāṇini 2.4.64) *yañañośca*. This sūtra belongs to the second quarter of the fourth chapter (*dvitīyacaturthapāda*), but this [example] does not.

The fourth [section] pertains to the domain of *apatya* (descendants). Therein, by the paribhāṣā rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there is the inclusion of that which ends with it. The sūtra "tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivā'striyām" follows [from the previous rules], with the exception of the word "tadrājasya. From the sūtra "ṇyakṣatriya... onwards, the word "luk" [is understood].
[The rule] "from *ṭhyaṣka* and so forth, in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*) follows from that [previous rule]; thus he says: "that which [is applied] in the sense of a lineage.
"Of these two" means "of *yañ* and *añ*. The intention is that *luk* is defined as the non-appearance of a suffix.
"Caused by that" means, in other words, when there is plurality residing in the meaning of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ*.

"Gargāḥ" [is formed as follows]: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the descendants of Garga," and so forth. "Priyāgārgyaḥ" [is formed as follows]: the analysis is "those for whom a Gārgya is dear. The point here is that because there is no plurality residing in the meaning of the suffix *yañ*, there is no elision (*luk*). "Dvaipyāḥ" means "those who exist on an island"; [this is derived] by the rule "dvīpāt anusamudram."

Regarding the term *yañ*: *āṬtsā* means "those born of *utsa*. [The suffix] *añ* is applied according to the rule *ṭhutsādibhyo'ñ*. The point here is that in both cases, there is no elision (*luk*) because *yañ* and *añ* do not denote a *gotra* (lineage). [Objection: But then, in the case of *pautrāḥ* and *dauhitrāḥ*, there would also have to be elision of the *añ* suffix prescribed by the rule for non-*ṛṣi* names beginning with *vidādi*. And it is not [the case that this happens].

The point is that there is no elision (*luk*) because that [suffix] does not denote an immediate descendant. Now, one might object: even in cases such as *pautrāḥ* and *dauhitrāḥ*, there would be elision of the suffix *añ* by virtue of the rule for descendants of non-seers (*anṛṣi*) beginning with *vidā*. Nor should it be said that there is no elision because that [suffix] denotes an immediate descendant and lacks the sense of a "grandson" (*gotra*).

Since it has been established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the *Sūtrabhāṣya* on the rule *ṭhyūni luk* that, outside the section concerning offspring (*apatya*), only the worldly (*laukika*) lineage (*gotra*) is understood, he says: "In the *Pravara*...
[The lineages are: Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Gautama, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha.

The meaning is that here, by "gotra," the Bhārgavas and others well-known from the *Pravarādhyāya* of Bodhāyana and others—according to which it is stated, "These seven are remembered as the sages; whatever is their offspring is called a gotra"—are intended. Kaiyaṭa [states] that "the worldly gotra is what is being grasped."

The sense is that [the rule] has been explained in exactly the same way by taking the *Bhāṣya* as the authority. And thus, in cases such as *pautrāḥ* and *dauhitrāḥ*, since the words *pautra* and *dauhitra* do not denote a lineage (*gotra*) of that specific kind, the elision (*luk*) does not occur; this is the established conclusion. A detailed discussion, however, should be sought in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

(1092) *madhubabhvror brāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.106. Regarding *madhu-babhvvoḥ*: he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion—namely, "in the sense of a gotra [descendant], the suffix *yañ* [is applied]. From the words *madhu* and *babhru*, the suffix *yañ* shall optionally be applied in the sense of a gotra descendant, provided the person is a Brāhmaṇa or a Kauśika.
The meaning is that [the suffixes] should be applied according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). "The effect of *lohita* and so forth" means the suffix *ṣpha*.
The intention is that *lohita* and the others belong to the sub-group (*gaṇa*) within the *gargādi* group. Regarding *bābhravyāyaṇī*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the female descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatyam*) of Babhru. From the word *bābhravya*, the suffix *yañ* [is applied] because it belongs to the *gargādi* group.

By the rule "ṣpho 'sarvatra lohitādikatantebhyaḥ," the suffix *ṣpha* is applied; there is the substitution of *āyan* [for the final vowel and consonant of the stem], and because the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added—this is the intended meaning. (1093) *kapibodhād āṅgirase* 4.1.107.

"From *kapi* and *bodha*, [the suffix] *yañ* [is applied] when the lineage (*gotra*) is [that of] Āṅgirasa. This is a supplement to the rule. The meaning is that the suffix *yañ* is applied after the words *kapi* and *bodha* when the lineage understood is that of Āṅgirasa. Regarding the example *kāpeya*: here, because the lineage is not that of Āṅgirasa, the suffix *yañ* does not occur.

The suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule "ṭhitaścāniñaḥ. Regarding *baudhi*: here too, because he is not an Āṅgirasa, the suffix *yañ* does not apply; rather, setting aside the *ṛṣyaṇ* suffix, the intention is that the suffix *iñ* applies due to his inclusion in the *bāhv-ādi* group. Although *kapi* is read in the *garga-ādi* list, its mention there is for the purpose of restriction, namely that he is an Āṅgirasa only. [This applies] to him in the *garga-ādi* list.

The reading [of the sūtra], however, is for the purpose of [including] *lohitā* and others as derivatives. [The form] *kāpyāyanī* [is derived from *kapya*]. From the word *bodha*, the rule applies where it was not previously established. (1094) *vataṇḍācca* 4.1.108.
[The suffix] *vataṇḍī* [is formed] from *vataṇḍa*. Since *vataṇḍa* is listed both in the *garga* group and the *śiva* group, both *yañ* and *aṇ* would be applicable;
this rule is for the purpose of restriction, stating that when it belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras, only *yañ* is used.
(1095) *luk striyām* | 1.4.109. [In the feminine, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix.]
Regarding the phrase "in the case of a female (*luk striyām*)," it refers to that which is prescribed by the rule *vataṇḍācca*. The word *ṭhyañaḥ* is the remainder [of the context].
The form *vataṇḍī* is analyzed as: "the female descendant (*gotrāpatyam*) of Vataṇḍa, belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras.
The sense is that when the suffix *yañ* is elided (*luki*), the initial *vṛddhi* is also removed, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. The form *vātaṇḍyāyanī* is derived from the suffix *añ*.

The intention is that when there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel, the suffix *ṣpha* applies according to the rule for words beginning with *lohita*; because it has the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* follows.

He states the purpose of [the suffix] prescribed by the rule "after *vataṇḍa*" as follows: "but when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, it is *vātaṇḍī*. Because it belongs to the *śiva*-class, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; since it denotes a lineage (*gotra*), it is a genus (*jāti*), and thus the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies by the rule for genera. Of that *aṇ*—
The point is that even though [the suffix] is prescribed after *vataṇḍa*, there is no elision (*luk*) because it is not prescribed by the rule "after *vataṇḍa*" (Pāṇini 4.1.108).

Now, one might object: if the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *vataṇḍa*, then the suffix *ṣyaṅ* would apply to it according to the rule to be stated later, "of non-Vedic *aṇ* and *iñ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.78); to this he says: "because of being a seer" (*ṛṣitvāt*).

(1096) *aśvādibhyaḥ phañ* | Pāṇini 4.1.110. "From *aśva* and the others. The word "in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*) is supplied here to complete the sense; "in the case of the descendant of Aṅgiras" (*āṅgirase*) is no longer applicable. For example: *āśvāyanaḥ*. The analysis is: "the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatyam*) of *aśva*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iñ*.

*phañ* | "In the sense of 'born' (*jāta*), [it is used] in the masculine" (*puṃsi jāte*)—this is a *gaṇasūtra*. It is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). The meaning is: *phañ* is applied after the word *jāta* when it exists in the masculine sense, provided it denotes a lineage (*gotra*). Regarding *jāteya*:
[the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after feminine bases.
(1097) *bhargāt traigarte* | Pāṇini 4.1.111. Regarding *bhargāt traigarte*: this is also a *gaṇasūtra*. Trigarta was the son of Bharga.
His descendant is Traigarta, formed with the suffix *aṇ* [by 4.1.114]. In that lineage, the suffix *phañ* is applied after *Bharga*.

(1098) *śivādibhyo’ṇ* |4|1|112|. The meaning is that [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after [words beginning with] *śiva*. This is because it has been stated in both the *Vṛtti* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary that [the application of *aṇ*] is restricted. However, in the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *yūni lūg* [Pāṇini 4.1.90], [the discussion] extends up to the rule defining the technical term *gotra*.

The heading "Gotrādhikāra" (the section on lineages) is understood here. Some say that this is a different opinion; however, it is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that this [latter view] alone is correct.
(Pāṇini 4.1.113): "After names of rivers and female humans that do not have an initial *vṛddhi* vowel, [the suffix *cha* is applied] provided they are used as proper names."

"[The suffix ṅīp is applied] after [names of] rivers that are non-vṛddha. Regarding the feminine form "after non-vṛddha [names]," it depends on the words "river" (nadī) and "human female" (mānuṣī). However, in reality, it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as "after non-vṛddha names of rivers and human females"; thus he explains with the words "after non-vṛddha," and so forth. Now, [an objection]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

Since the form would be established by the single rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), for what purpose is this [present rule] stated? To this he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ḍhak*.
*Cintitā* is the name of a certain human woman. Regarding *vāsavadatteya*:
*Vāsavadattā* is the name of a certain human female; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "her offspring. Because she bears the designation *vṛddha*, the suffix *aṇ* does not apply.
The sense is "instantly. Regarding "Vainateya": the analysis of the compound is "the offspring of Vinatā.
The sense is that Vinatā is the mother of Garuḍa; she is neither a human nor a river.
Regarding "Śaubhaneya": the sense is that this word "Śobhanā" is not the name of a river or a human woman.

(1100) *ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca* | Pāṇini 4.1.114. Regarding *ṛṣi*, *andhaka*, etc.: those from whom the Vedas, having become lost, flow forth—that is, are recovered—by the power of their asceticism (*tapas*), are called *ṛṣis*. Thus it is heard in the Taittirīya Śruti: "The Vedas, indeed, [were lost]... [and so on].
"Upon the *pṛśni*s performing austerity, the self-existent *Brahman* descended [into them]; they became the *ṛṣis*;
that is the *ṛṣi*-hood of the *ṛṣis*. The *ajāḥ* are eternal; the *pṛśnayaḥ* are white—that is to say, pure.
Upon those *pṛśni*s performing austerity, practicing penance, the self-existent *Brahman*, the beginningless Veda, [descended]."

"He approached" (*abhyānarṣat*). [The root] *ṛṣ* means "to go. He attained [the Vedas] by facing toward them. According to the *Vedabhāṣya*, they became denotable by the word *ṛṣi* because of their approaching (*arṣaṇa*) of the Veda: "At the time of the beginning of all things, the great seers (*maharṣis*), being authorized, first obtained the Vedas along with the Itihāsas through austerity (*tapas*)."
This is well known in the Purāṇas and is made clear by the work titled *Sarvānukramaṇikā* composed by Kātyāyana.
Thus it says: "The seers (*ṛṣis*) are the perceivers of the mantras. By the words "Andhaka" and "Vṛṣṇi"...
By the word *kuru*, those belonging to the lineages of Andhaka and others are intended.
The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after words denoting specific sages as well as after words denoting the lineages of Andhaka and others, to form a patronymic (*apatya*).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iñ*. He provides examples from the sages: *bāsiṣṭhaḥ* (descendant of Vasiṣṭha) and *vaiśvāmitraḥ* (descendant of Viśvāmitra).

Regarding the phrase "to those belonging to the Andhaka lineage": the meaning is that examples are cited from words denoting members of the Andhaka dynasty. Regarding "Vāsudeva": the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is "the descendant of Vasudeva. Regarding "Āniruddha": the analytical derivation is "the descendant of Aniruddha.
Now, one might object: there was a certain person named Śūra belonging to the Vṛṣṇi dynasty; his descendant would be *Śauri*.

To address how there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (*aṇ-prasaṅga*) [of the suffix *aṇ*], he says: "But as for *śauriḥ*, etc. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "It is to be resolved by means of the suffix *iñ* because [the word *śūrasena*] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. Regarding "from the Kurus":
the meaning is that examples are cited from words denoting those belonging to the Kuru lineage. Nakula and Sahadeva are well-known.
One might object: "In the sense of 'the offspring of Atri,' since the suffix *ḍhak* applies by the rule *ṭhaki cāniñaḥ*, how is the form *Ātreya* derived?
For it would be more appropriate that *ḍhak* also be sublated by the *ṛṣyaṇ* suffix, just as *iñ* is. To this, he says: "of *iñ* alone. The meaning is: but not of *ḍhak*.

(1101) *māturutsaṃkhyāsaṃbhadrapūrvāyāḥ* |4|1|115|. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word] *mātṛ*, when preceded by the numeral *dvi*, or by *saṃ* or *bhadra*. [Example: *dvaimāturaḥ*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "the offspring of two mothers.

This is a compound formed under the rule *taddhitārtha* ("in the sense of a secondary derivative"). The suffix *aṇ* is applied; the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *u*; and *ra* is substituted for the final element of the stem (*raparatva*). Thus...
Regarding *ṣāṇmāturaḥ* and *sāṃmāturaḥ*: *saṃmātā* means a good mother;
the offspring of *saṃmātā* is *sāṃmāturaḥ*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied, followed by the substitution of *r* for the final vowel (*raparatva*). Regarding *bhādramāturaḥ*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she who is both auspicious (*bhadrā*) and a mother (*mātā*). The application of *aṇ* and so forth is as before. Now, [one might object]:...

Since the form would already be established by the rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), the prescription of *aṇ* is indeed superfluous; therefore, he says: "The statement is for the purpose of an *ādeśa*.
This means it is for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *ud-* in conjunction with *aṇ*. Now, one might ask:
why should the mother not also be included for one who measures grain? And thus...
In that case as well, one might reach the conclusion that [the term] refers to *dvaimātura* and so forth;

therefore, he says: "The designation in the feminine gender is dependent on the meaning. Having superimposed the femininity residing in the mother onto the word, it is designated by the rule *saṅkhyā-sambhadra-pūrvāyāḥ*. Thus, regarding the feminine gender—
The meaning is that the word *mātṛ* is taken here as denoting a biological mother (*jananī*). Therefore, [the form] *dhānyamātuḥ* [is not included];
the intention is that in this case, the word *mātṛ* denotes a measurer (*paricchetṛ*) and is masculine.
Regarding *saumātra*: in the sense of "the offspring of Sumātṛ," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyāpatyam*.

The meaning is that this [suffix] is not *aṇ* because it lacks the prefix "saṃkhyā-sambhadra-"; nor is it *iñ*, because it is taught as being conditioned by that very [prefix]. Now, one might ask: how is the form *dvaimātreya* derived, given that since it is preceded by a number, the substitution of *u* for *a* (by *aṇ*) would be unavoidable? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "Because it belongs to the *śubhra* group. The meaning is that the form is derived by adding the suffix *ḍhak* according to the rule *śubhrādibhyaśca*.

(1102) *kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca* [Pāṇini 4.1.116]. [The word] *kanyāyāḥ* [is used]; *ka* [is the substitute]; and *kanīna* is [the form] with the nominative case ending elided. [The word] *ḍhak* [is understood from the previous rule]. [From the rule] *strībhyo*... [the suffix *ḍhak* is applied].

The meaning is "of that which is prescribed by [the suffix] ḍhak. And regarding the statement "there is the substitution of *kanīna*," the word "in the present context" (*prakṛte*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
It is well known in the *Mahābhārata* that Vyāsa and Karṇa were the sons of a maiden (*kanyā*). Now, one might object:
since a maiden has not manifested her youth and thus lacks union with a male, how can there be a connection with offspring?
Therefore, he says "of one who is unmarried" (*anūḍhāyāḥ*). This means "one who has not obtained marriage. And this is clear in the Bhāṣya.
(1103) *Vikarṇa-śuṅga-cchagalāt vatsa-bharadvāja-atriṣu* [Pāṇini 4.1.117].

Vikarṇa: By the words *vatsa* and so forth, those belonging to their lineages are intended. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *vikarṇa*, *śuṅga*, and *cchagala* when the descendant belongs to the lineage of Vatsa—meaning in the lineage of Bharadvāja or the lineage of Atri.
By this, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to *vikarṇa*, *śuṅga*, and *cchagala* when [the descendant] belongs to the lineage of Vatsa and the others.
The meaning is "in the descendant of Vatsa," "in the descendant of Bharadvāja," and "in the descendant of Atri"; that is to say, in the offspring [of these lineages].

By this, the objection that because Vatsa and the others are the *mūlapuruṣas* (founder-ancestors), they cannot possibly be the offspring (*apatya*) of Vikarṇa and the others, is refuted. [This is done] for the purpose of establishing the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that the suffix *ṛṣya-aṇ* applies only to the descendants of Vatsa and the others when derived from Vikarṇa and the others.
The Sūtra states: (1104) *pīlāyā vā* |4|1|118|.
Regarding *pīlāyā vā*: the remainder [of the rule] is that the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatye*). *Pīlā* is the name of a certain human woman.

Regarding the phrase "tannāmikāṇam": in the absence of the mention of the word "vā" (optionally), this *aṇ* suffix would invariably supersede the *ḍhak* suffix. Nor should it be argued that because the *aṇ* is optional by virtue of the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), the *ḍhak* suffix occurs when the *aṇ* is absent; for according to the Great Option, once an exception (*apavāda*) is prohibited, the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply.
Because it makes [the suffix] known.
(1105) *Ḍhak ca maṇḍūkāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.119).
Otherwise, forms such as *śaivaḥ* and *śaiviḥ* would result; however, there is also the suffix *ḍhak*. Maṇḍūka was the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*).
Regarding the rule *pakṣe iñ*: the intention is that the word *vā* ("or") is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
(1106) *strībhyo ḍhak* | 4.1.120. Regarding *strībhyo ḍhak*: by the term *strī*, the feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others taught in the fourth chapter are understood.
But other words denoting women are not included [in this rule], because of the explanation; thus he says: "from those ending in feminine suffixes.

*Vinatā* is the mother of Garuḍa; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of her. Why is there mention of the "suffix" (*pratyaya*)? [Consider: *Darad* was a certain Kṣatriya; his female offspring is *darat*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "dvyañmagadha... [Pāṇini 4.1.170]. By the rule "ataśca" [Pāṇini 2.4.69], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. His offspring is *dāradaḥ*.
Here, although the word *darat* is feminine, the suffix *ḍhak* does not apply because it is not a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).
But how is it that the offspring of Sumitrā is *saumitriḥ*, and the offspring of Sapatnī is *sāpatnaḥ*?

Since there is the possibility of [the application of] the suffix *ḍhak*, he says: "because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group," and so forth. It has already been stated that in the word *sāpatna*, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) does not apply.
(1107) *dvyacaḥ* | 4|1|121 | [The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a word ending in *a* which consists of two syllables.]

[The suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after a word consisting of two syllables. Now, one might ask: since the rule "ḍhak after feminine stems" (*strībhyo ḍhak*) would already suffice, for what purpose is this [separate rule] stated?
To this he says: "tannāmikā-". In the example *dāteyaḥ*, the analysis is: "the offspring of a certain human female named Datā. But then, how is it that the offspring of Pṛthā is called *pārthaḥ*?

Because the suffix *aṇ* would be superseded by that [suffix] and the suffix *ḍhak* would consequently apply due to the rule "ṭhdvyacaḥ" [Pāṇini 4.1.121], he says: "in the case of *pārtha*. Others hold that because [the word *pṛthu*] belongs to the *śivādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* applies only in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*).
(1108) "And after this [suffix *iñ*], except for *aniñ*" [Pāṇini 4.1.122].

And for this reason, [the suffix] *iñ* does not apply. This is intended to cover cases where the word ends in a suffix other than a feminine one; for example, *duliḥ* and *nidhiḥ* (a certain treasure).

Regarding *Ātreya*: *Atri* is well-known. The point is that, because it is subsequent in the order of rules, this [suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*] also supersedes the *ṛṣyaṇ* suffix. (1109) *Śubhrādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.123).
"And after *śubhra* and others. The word "the suffix *ḍhak* shall be used" completes the rule; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *iñ* and others.
The meaning is that since [the suffix *iñ*] would not apply because [the word *śubhra*] is not feminine, *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of "the descendant of Śubhra.
(1110) After *vikarṇa* and *kuṣītaka*, [the suffix *ḍhak* is used] when [the descendant is] Kāśyapa. Pāṇini 4.1.124.

*Vikarṇa* and *kuṣīta*: [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied in the sense of offspring; this is a completion of the rule's requirements (*śeṣapūraṇam*). The separate recitation [of these two] from the *śubhra* group is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), meaning that only *kāśyapa* [is formed]. (1111) *Bhruvo vuk ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.125).

"bhuvo vuk ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.124) and "cāḍḍhak" (Pāṇini 4.1.125). From the word *bhrū*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), and there is the augment *vuk* for the base. In *vuk*, the letter *k* is *it* (indicatory), and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is *kit*, it is an internal constituent (*antāvayava*). Thus, *bhrauveya*. [This refers to] a certain woman named Bhrū; her—

The analysis of the compound is *apatyam* (offspring). When the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, the substitute *ey* is introduced; with the elision (*luk*) of the base [suffix], there is the initial *vṛddhi* [vowel change].

In the absence of *vuk*, however, when *vṛddhi* is applied to the vowel *ū*, the substitute *āv* occurs, resulting in *bhrāveya*. (Pāṇini 4.1.121) [Note: The commentary addresses the formation of *bhrātr̥ya* from *bhrātṛ* via *ḍhak*. (Pāṇini 7.3.28) *pravāhaṇasya dve*: [In the name] *pravāhaṇa*, [the first syllable] is doubled.
[The rule applies] to *pravāhaṇa*. The phrase "of the second member" (*uttarapadasya*) is understood as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*).

From the rule "in the case of taddhita suffixes, [vṛddhi is substituted] for the first among the vowels" (*taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*), the phrase "for the first among the vowels" (*acāmādeḥ*) is carried over (*anuvartate*).

From the rule "vṛddhi [is substituted] for *mṛj*" (*mṛjervṛddhiḥ*), the word "vṛddhi" is carried over; and from the rule "of a measure [ending] in *ardha*, but of the preceding [member]" (*ardhātparimāṇasya pūrvasya tu*).
"Or from that, or from the preceding"—thus he says: "of the word *pravāhaṇa*.
[The form] *prāvāhaṇeyaḥ* is derived as *pravāhaṇena īyaḥ*. By virtue of its inclusion in the *śubhra*-group, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied;
there is optional initial *vṛddhi* for the first member and obligatory *vṛddhi* for the second member. The purpose of the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *ā* in the second member is as follows:

In the case of *pravāhaṇeyībhārya*, there is indeed a prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "and [the feminine ending is not elided] when [the word] has a cause for Vṛddhi" (*vṛddhinimitasya ca*). Furthermore, [the same applies] to the suffix that causes that [Vṛddhi]. (Pāṇini 7.2.29).

And regarding that suffix: everything that was carried over from the previous sūtra is also carried over here; by the word *tat*, the suffix *ḍha* is referred to. Thus he says: "of that which ends in the suffix *ḍha*.
[The examples are] *prāvāhaṇeyiḥ* and *pravāhaṇeyiḥ*. [In these cases,] the suffix *iñ* follows a word ending in the *ḍhak* suffix from the *śubhra* group. Now, [one might object]:...

Since this would already be established by the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), [the author] says "bāhye" (external) to show that it is not redundant: the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) prescribed by the rule "taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ" is compulsory when caused by the *iñ* suffix that occurs outside of a word ending in the *ḍhak* suffix. The phrase "by means of the *ḍha*-basis" refers to the *ḍhak* suffix.

The meaning is as follows: it cannot be sublated by such an alternative option for *vṛddhi* prescribed by a subsequent rule, because their causes (*nimitta*) are distinct. For the preceding rule, indeed, assumes the suffix *ḍha* at the end of a word ending in the suffix *ḍha* as its subsequent cause (*paranimitta*).

It is logical that this [rule] should supersede the initial *vṛddhi* caused by the suffix *ḍhaṅ*, but it does not [logically] supersede the constant (*nitya*) initial *vṛddhi* caused by the suffix *iñ*. Therefore, the meaning is that this sūtra is intended to supersede that [initial *vṛddhi*] as well. Both of these rules for *vṛddhi*...

It would have been more appropriate to state [the rule] right here in the sūtra *ṭhaśubhrādibhyaśca*. [The example is: *kalyāṇyāḥ* (of a beautiful woman). The suffix *inaṅ* is added with the marker *ṅ*, which causes the feminine suffix (*ṅīp*) to be elided.
(1114) *kalyāṇyādīnāminaṅ* 4.1.126. [The example is: *kālyāṇineyaḥ*. The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is: "the offspring (*apatyam*) of *kalyāṇī*. [Another example is: *bāndhakineyaḥ*.

The analysis of the compound is "the offspring of a *bandhakī*. In this list (*gaṇa*), only those words ending in feminine suffixes are recited. From these, the suffix *ḍhak* is already established; however, the suffix *inaṅ* is specifically prescribed [in place of it].
(Pāṇini 4.1.127) *kulaṭāṭā vā*. [This means: after the word *kulaṭā*, either *ḍhak* or *inaṅ* may be applied.
"Or [the suffix] *inaṅ* for a *kulaṭā*. The intention is that this is based on the [author's own] commentary.

"By the previous rule alone" means by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*. A *kulaṭā* is one who wanders (*aṭati*) among houses (*kulāni*, i.e., homes); the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) is according to the *śakandhvādi* group. Regarding the word "here": [it refers to the rule for] *kulaṭā*.

The word "ve" means "in the sūtra. The phrase "in the alternative, ḍhrak" means that the suffix *ḍhrak* also occurs at times. Regarding the form *kaulaṭera*: when *ḍhrak* is applied to *kulaṭā*, the *ḍha* is replaced by *ey*; then, by the rule "the *ya* and *va* are elided," the *ya* is dropped—this is the intended meaning.

(1116) *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca* | Pāṇini 6.3.97. [The rule states: "In compounds ending in *hṛd*, *bhaga*, and *sindhu*, [the substitution of *ṣat* for the final consonant of] the preceding member [is optionally applied], and by the word *ca* ('and'), it is drawn over from the previous rule that the substitution applies to the subsequent member as well. The meaning is: in compounds ending in these—namely *hṛt*, *bhaga*, and *sindhu*—the substitution is optional. By the force of the word *ca*, the phrase "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*) is carried over.

Thus he says: "of the preceding and following words," and "in *sauhārda*. In the suffix *aṇ*, there is vṛddhi of the initial vowel of both words; for the vowel *ṛ*, however, the substitute is *ā*, followed by *r*. In *saubhāgineya*, the intention is that because [the word] belongs to the *kalyāṇī*-class, the suffix is *ḍhak*, which becomes *inaṅ*, and there is vṛddhi of the initial vowels of both words.

This sūtra has been introduced here precisely because of this context. In the phrase "for great fortune" (*mahate saubhagāya*), however, the suffix *añ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) due to its inclusion in the *udgātrādi* group; the absence of *vṛddhi* in the initial syllable of the second member is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
As for the word *sindhavaḥ*, it means "horses."

(1117) *caṭakāyā airak* |4|1|128|. The meaning is that the suffix *airak* is applied after the word *caṭakā* to denote offspring (*apatya*). Now, one might object that because the feminine gender is specified [in the rule], the suffix would not apply to the masculine form; therefore, he says: "from *caṭaka*. [This is stated] in the Sūtra.
The meaning is that, having removed "ṭhcaṭakāyāḥ," one should state "ṭhcaṭakāḥ.
If that were so, [the suffix] would not occur after a feminine [stem]; therefore he says: "liṅge" etc.
[The rule is: the elision (luk) should be stated for the feminine offspring.

"Even from a feminine [word]" means that [the suffix] occurs even after a word in the feminine gender. "Of those two" means of the male sparrow (*caṭaka*) and the female sparrow (*caṭakā*). Now, one might ask: how is it *caṭaka* [without a feminine marker], since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply because it denotes a genus (*jāti*)? To this he says: "because it belongs to the *ajādi* group."

(1118) *godhāyāḍhrak* |4|1|129|. The suffix *ḍhrak* is applied after the word *godhā*. Thus, *gaudhera* [is formed]. The analysis is: "the offspring (*apatyam*) of a *godhā*. When *ḍhrak* is applied, the letter *ḍh* undergoes the substitution *ey*; then, by the rule *ṭh-lopo vyoḥ*, there is the elision of the *y*.
The intention is that there is vṛddhi [substitution] for the initial vowel because of the presence of the suffix *kit*.

The meaning of "ārag for the Northerners" is that the suffix *ārañ* may optionally be applied to the word *godhā* by those belonging to the Northern schools. [The word] "from another [source]" (*anyataḥ*)...
The meaning is that [the suffix] other than one ending in *ā* is one ending in *a*; the purpose of this rule is to prescribe it even after such a form in certain instances.
For example, *jāḍāra*. The point is that in the rule prescribing the suffix *ra*, the vowel *ā* would not be heard [as part of the stem].
*Paṇḍa* means a eunuch; his offspring (*apatyam*) is so called because he was born from the wife (*kṣetra*) of another, and so forth.

(1120) Or from words meaning "low" (*kṣudra*). [Pāṇini 4.1.131] "Or from words meaning 'low'": *aṅgahīnāḥ* ("those deficient in limbs") means those lacking some parts such as the eyes and so forth. *śīlahīnāḥ* ("those deficient in conduct") means those lacking virtuous behavior.
"Those who move about with whichever man they please," that is to say; "those who have no fixed husband or those who are deformed are called *kṣudrāḥ* (low)," so says the Bhāṣya.
(1121) [Pāṇini 4.1.132: *pitṛṣvasuś chaṇ*. (The suffix *chaṇ* is applied after the word *pitṛṣvasṛ* [to form a feminine noun denoting a descendant]).
The suffix *chaṇ* is applied after *pitṛṣvasṛ* [to form a patronymic]. Thus, *paitṛṣvastrīyaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring (*apatyam*) of the father’s sister (*pitṛṣvasṛ*).
When *cha* is replaced by *īya*, there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel. By the rule *karārādṛkārasya yaṇ*, the semivowel *y* replaces the vowel *ṛ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.133:
*ḍhaki lopaḥ* ("There is elision [of the final vowel and consonant] when the suffix *ḍhak* follows").

There is elision (*lopa*) by means of *ḍhak*. The term "of the father's sister" (*pitṛṣvasuḥ*) is understood from the previous rule. By the metarule regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*), there is elision of the final [letter]. Thus he says: "there is elision of the final [letter] of *pitṛṣvasṛ*. Now, one might object: since the suffix *ḍhak* is difficult to obtain after *pitṛṣvasṛ* when forming a descendant (*apatya*), how can it occur when that [suffix] follows?

To address the point that this is a rule for elision (*lopavidhi*), he says: "For this very reason. Others hold that the suffix *ḍhak* is applied because [the word *pitṛṣvasṛ*] belongs to the *śubhra* class.

Regarding the form *paitṛṣvaseya*: when *ḍhak* is added, there is elision of the final vowel *ṛ*, and the initial vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ svasuḥ*.

(1123) *mātṛṣvasuśca* |4|1|134|. [The suffix] *chaṇ* is also applied after *mātṛṣvasṛ*; by the word *ca* ("and"), *ḍhak* and the elision (*lopa*) are also drawn in. Thus he says: "that which was stated regarding *pitṛṣvasṛ* [is also applicable here]."

(1124) *catuṣpādbhyo ḍhañ* | Pā. 4.1.135. From words denoting quadrupeds [the suffix] *ḍhañ* is applied. Quadrupeds are animals. The meaning is that *ḍhañ* is applied to denote offspring (*apatya*) from words expressing specific types of quadrupeds.
(1125) *ḍhea lopo’kardvāḥ* | P.

6.4.147. Regarding the rule *ḍhea lopo’kardvāḥ*: the term *bhasya* is supplied as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*) from the preceding rule *ṭhorguṇaḥ*. This [term *bha*] is qualified by the word *oḥ*, which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from that rule in its genitive form. There is thus an application of the rule regarding the final element of a compound (*tadantavidhi*).

Regarding this, he says: "of that which is different from *kadrū*. By the rule *alo’ntyasya*, there is the elision of the final letter. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *orguṇa* rule. In the case of *kāmaṇḍaleya*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of *kamaṇḍalu*.

When the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, it is replaced by *eya*; then, after the initial vowel-vṛddhi, the letter *u* is elided. Now, [one might ask] regarding that which is denoted by the word *kamaṇḍalu*:
"How can there be a connection with offspring for a water-vessel, which is insentient?

To this he replies: "The word *kamaṇḍalu* [denotes] a specific species of four-footed [animals]. The intention is that for this very reason, the statement in the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*, "He places [the fire] upon the *kamaṇḍalu*," is consistent.
(1126) *gṛṣṭyādibhyaśca* |4|1|136|.
From *gṛṣṭi* and others. [The suffix] *aṇ*. These are *gṛṣṭi*, *hali*, *bali*, *kuṭhi*, *agasti*, and *mitrayu*;
these are the *gṛṣṭyādi* group. Here, because the last two [names] refer to sages (*ṛṣi*), the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise be required by rule 4.1.104.

The distinction is that from other [bases], the suffix *ḍhak* would otherwise apply by the rule "ṭhitaścā'niñaḥ. A *gṛṣṭi* is any female, such as a human woman, who has given birth once, not only a cow. Consequently, there is no application of the rule "catuṣpādbhyaḥ" [to this case].

(1127) *kekaya-mitrayu-pralayānāṃ yāder iyaḥ* || 7.3.2 || The words *kekaya* and *mitrayu* [are mentioned]. From the rule *taddhiteṣv acām ādeḥ*, the term *taddhite* (in a taddhita suffix) is understood to carry over. From the rules *aco ñṇiti* and *kiti ca*, the terms *ñṇiti* (after a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ) and *kiti* (after a suffix marked with K or Ṅ) are understood.
Regarding this, he says: "of these. In the substitute [form], the letter *a* after *y* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

*Kaikeyī* is the female descendant of Kekaya; the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule "from words denoting a country" (*janapadaśabdāt*). He praises [her] by means of Maitreyikā. In the sense of "the state of being of two friends," the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule "from lineage names and Vedic schools" (*gotracaraṇād*).

*Prāleyam* means "that which has come from *pralaya*. [The suffix] *āṇ*. In all these cases, there are examples where the substitution of *iy* occurs for the initial [of the suffix]. Regarding *prāpte*: when the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied to form a descendant of *mitrayu*, and the substitution of *ey* has occurred, resulting in the form *mitrayu-eya*, the substitution of *iy* for *yu* takes place, overriding the *guṇa* rule for *o*.
The meaning is that when *maitreyeya* is obtained by applying the rule *ād guṇe* [Pāṇini 6.1.87], [the following applies]:
(1128) *dāṇḍināyana-hāstināyana-ātharvaṇika-jaihmāśineya-vāśināyani-bhrauṇahatya-dhaivatya-sārava-aiṅkṣvāka-maitreya-hiraṇyamayāni* [Pāṇini 6.4.174].

*Dāṇḍināyana*: these are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). The offspring of Daṇḍin and Hastin is *Dāṇḍināyana* and *Hāstināyana*. The suffix *phak* is applied because they belong to the *naḍādi* group;
due to the irregularity (*nipātana*), the elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*) does not occur. Furthermore, the text proclaimed by Atharvan is metaphorically called "Atharvan."

One who studies that [text] is an *ātharvaṇikaḥ*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied because it begins with the word "vasanta" etc.; by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).

The offspring of *jihmāsina* is *jaihmāśineyaḥ*. The suffix *ḍhak* is applied because it belongs to the *śubhra* group; by irregular derivation, there is no elision of the *ṭi*. The offspring of *vāśin* is *vāśināyaniḥ*. The suffix *phiñ* is applied according to the rule "of the Northerners, after a word ending in a long vowel."

Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is no elision of the *ṭi* suffix. For the words *bhrūṇahan* and *dhīvan*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, the substitution of *ta* for the letter *na* is also prescribed by irregular derivation. One should not suspect that this substitution of *ta* is already established by the rule *ṭhano'to 'ciṇṇaloḥ*; for [the rule] states: "An operation prescribed for a verbal root applies when that same suffix follows."

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "bhavati," the substitution of *t* for *th* (as prescribed by the rule *ṭhano'staḥ*) occurs only when a suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) follows; this very substitution of *t* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this *paribhāṣā*, as is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*. Consequently, in the word *vārtraghna*, the substitution of *t* does not take place.

In *sarayvām bhavam*, [the word] *sāravam* means "water. For the root *aṇi-yū*, the substitution of *va* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). *Aikṣvākaḥ* is the descendant of Ikṣvāku. The suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule "from a word denoting a country, when it refers to a Kṣatriya.
The elision of the letter *u* is prescribed as an irregularity. However, in the plural, because it is a *tadrāja* suffix, there is elision (*luk*), resulting in *ikṣvākavaḥ*.
One who exists among the *ikṣvāku* people is also called *aikṣvāka*. [This is derived] by the suffix *aṇ* after a word ending in the letter *k*, with the elision of the vowel *u*.

In the rule regarding *aikṣvāka*, both forms ending in *añ* and *aṇ* are included. In the plural, because it belongs to the class of royal designations (*tadrāja*), there is elision of the suffix *añ*, but not of *aṇ*; this is the distinction. That which is a modification of gold is *hiraṇmaya*.

In the suffix *mayaṭ*, there is the elision of the initial *ṇakāra* and the vowels *i* and *a*. Thus, regarding "elision of *yu*": when *mitrayu-eya* remains, the intention is that the elision of *yu* occurs by way of a formal exception (*nipātana*). In the form *maitreyī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
(1129) *yaskādibhyo gotre* [Pāṇini 2.4.63]. This rule does not belong to the section on *apatya* (descendants), but rather to the second chapter (*dvaitīyīka*).
Therefore, by the word *gotra*, what is intended here is specifically that *gotra* which is well-known from the *Pravarādhyāya*.

Because it has been established as a settled doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the *bhāṣya* on the sūtras "ṭhyūni luk" and "strīpuṃsābhyām," stating that "except in the context of the office of a village headman (*ṭhapatya*), only the worldly lineage (*laukika-gotra*) is taken";
and because "su" is understood from the rule "ṇyakṣatriyārṣe... [down to] "tadrājasya bahuṣu...".

The rule *tenaivāstriyām* ("by that very [suffix], provided it is not feminine") follows after the section excluding the *tadrāja* suffixes. Thus he says: "after these, the suffix denoting offspring [is elided]. Regarding *mitrayavaḥ*: the meaning is "the male descendants of the Mitrayus. When the *iḍhak* suffix is elided according to the *gṛṣṭy-ādi* list, the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is also removed.

(1130) *Atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhagotamāṅgirobhyaśca* | 2|4|65 | [The suffix *yañ* is applied after the names] Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, and Aṅgiras. [In the rule *atribhṛgu...*,] from the previous sūtra, the term *gotra* [is understood]; whatever was carried over there is all carried over here as well. Thus it says: "after these, [the suffix *yañ* is applied] when denoting a *gotra*. [Examples: *ātreyaḥ* (descendant of Atri), *bhārgavaḥ* (descendant of Bhṛgu).

The analytical resolutions (*vigraha*) are: "the male descendants of Kutsa," "of Vasiṣṭha," "of Gotama," and "of Aṅgirasa. In that regard, for *Atri*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule "ṭhitaścāniñaḥ," and its elision (*luk*) occurs by this [present] rule.
For the others, however, it should be understood that the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied. Upon elision (*luk*), the initial *vṛddhi* is also removed.

(1131) *bahvaca iñaḥ prācyabharateṣu* | 2|4|66| [The suffix] *iñ* [is elided] after a word with many syllables [denoting a descendant], when the patronymic belongs to the Easterners (*prācya*) or the Bharatas. He gives an example for the Easterners: *pannāgārāḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the descendants of Pan-nā-gā-ra. Consequently, there is elision (*luk*) of *iñ*. [This applies] to a lineage of the Bharatas.

He provides an example: *yudhiṣṭhirāḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of Yudhiṣṭhira. Here, the suffix *ṇya*, which would normally apply by virtue of [Yudhiṣṭhira] belonging to the *Kuru* class, is set aside; instead, the suffix *iñ* is applied because he belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group. That suffix is then elided (*luk*). However, when plurality is expressed, the form is *yaudhiṣṭhirāḥ*.

(1132) *na gopavanādibhyaḥ* | P. 2.4.67. [The suffix *phak*] is not [added] after [the group beginning with] *gopavana*. This is a sub-group (*antaḥgaṇa*) within the *bidādi* group; therefore, the intention is that the elision (*luk*), which would otherwise apply by the rule *añaḥ ṭhyañañośca*, does not take place.

(1133) *tikakitavādibhyo dvandve* |2|4|68|. [The suffix *phiñ* is applied after the words *tika*, *kitava*, and so forth, when they form a *dvandva* compound. For example: *taikāyanayaś ca kaitavāyanayaś ca* (the descendants of Tika and Kitava). This is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the *dvandva* compound. The resulting form is *tikakitavāḥ*. Because the rule specifies the locative case in the word *dvandve*, the suffix *phiñ* is applied even from both members of the compound.
*luk* | (1134) *upakādibhyo 'nyatarasyām advandve* | 2.4.69. [The author], having supplied the word *ca*, says: "and in the case of a *dvandva*. And thus:

Since the rule would have been established even without the recurrence of the term *dvandva* from the preceding sūtra—simply because it lacks the *svarita* accent—the inclusion of the term *advandva* is for the sake of clarity alone. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition "not in a *dvandva*" (*dvandve na*) might apply here; for even *dvandva* compounds are included in the list [of words to which the rule applies].

Indicating this very point, he cites an example of a *dvandva* compound: *bhrāṣṭrakakapiṣṭhalāḥ*. [In this case,] there is optionally a *luk* elision of the suffix *iñ*. He cites an example of a non-*dvandva* (singular) formation: *lamakāḥ*, *lāmakāyanāḥ*. There is an optional *luk* elision of the suffix *aśvādiñ*. Examples such as *aupakāḥ*, *aupakāyanāḥ*, and so forth, should also be cited.

(1135) *Āgastyakauṇḍinyayor agastikuṇḍina-c* [Pāṇini 2.4.70]. [The forms] *āgastya*, *agastayaḥ*, and *kuṇḍināḥ* [are derived as follows]: from the word *agastya*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*; the base is replaced by the substitute *agasti*. The word *kauṇḍinya* ends in the suffix *yañ* belonging to the *garga*-class; [the substitution occurs] in the plural.

The suffix *yañ* is elided (*luk*), and there is the substitution of *kuṇḍina* for the base. From "after *yaska* and others in the sense of a lineage" (*yaskādibhyo gotre*) up to "of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*" (*āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ*) constitutes the second [section]. Now follows the original [section] belonging to the fourth [chapter]: *yaño luk | prakṛteḥ kuṇḍinādeśaśca | ṭhyaskādibhyo gotre' ityārabhya ṭhāgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ' ityantaṃ dvaitīyīkam | atha prakṛtaṃ cāturthikam-*

(1136) *rājaśvaśurādyat* | Pāṇini 4.1.137. The meaning is that the suffix *yat* is applied after the words *rājan* and *śvaśura* to denote offspring. This is, respectively, an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*.

It should be stated: "Only for the king, when [the word] denotes birth. That is to say, "only for the king, when [the word] denotes birth" means provided that "birth" (*jāti*) signifies a collective whole. (1137) *Ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.168).

"And those ending in *abh*. The word "from the preceding sūtra" (*pūrvasūtrāt*) is supplied. From the rule "a single vowel by its own nature" (*prakṛtyaikāj*), the term "by its own nature" (*prakṛtyā*) is carried over. The suffix, obtained through the governing context of the *aṅga*, is specified by the letter *y*. This is a rule concerning that which begins with it (*tadādividhi*). Thus he says: "in that which begins with *y*" (*yādau*). For example, *rājanya*. [This is derived from] "from a *kṣatriya* [patronymic], in the case of a *kṣatriya* woman... (*kṣatriyāt kṣatriyāyām*).

It is well known in the *Dharmaśāstras* that "one born of one's own wife is a *rājanya*. Because of the suffix *yat*, there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) due to the rule of *prakṛtibhāva*. Regarding the phrase "among Śūdras and so forth," the meaning is: one born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother, or from another [lower caste] woman who has not been married. The form *rājanaḥ* is derived from the suffix *aṇ*.
In that context, when the elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the suffix] is about to occur by the rule "ṭhanas-taddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144)— (1138) *an* 6.4.167. The term *an* [is prescribed].
From the rule "inaṇyanapatye" (Pāṇini 5.4.15), the word *aṇ* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). From the rule "prakṛtyaikāj" (Pāṇini 6.4.163)... [the word *prakṛtyā* is understood].

And [the word] *prakṛtyā* [is used]. He says this with the word *aṇi*. [The word] *rājyam*: [it is derived from *rājan*] by the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*, which prescribes the suffix *ṣyañ*; there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
(Pāṇini 6.4.166) *saṃyogādiśca*.

"And *saṃyoga* etc. [is mentioned]. Regarding "by the base (*prakṛtyā*)," the intention is that this follows from the recurrence of the rules "in the sense of a descendant other than a grandson (*inaṇyanapatye*)" and "one vowel by the base (*prakṛtyaikāj*). As for "cākriṇaḥ," there is no application [of the rule] because of the exclusion of the non-descendant (*anapatye*) in the rule "in the sense of a descendant other than a grandson (*iṇyapatye*)."

(1140) *Na mapūrvo 'patye 'varmaṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.170. "Not [is there] the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for a word preceded by *m*, when the suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of offspring, provided it does not end in *varman*. For example: *bhādrasāmaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the offspring of Bhadrasāman. When the suffix *aṇ* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion (*sām-a*). Because the word ends in *an* and is preceded by *m*, the preservation of the original form does not occur. [The result is] *saunvaḥ*.
Thus: the analysis of the compound is *sutvana-apatyam* (the offspring of Sutvan). Because it is not preceded by *m*, there is *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form).
Regarding *cārmaṇaḥ*: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *ṭh parivṛto rathaḥ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the *an* portion).
Because the *aṇ* does not denote offspring (*apatya*), there is *prakṛtibhāva*.
Or it should be stated as "vā hitanāmnaḥ" (or [the suffix is added] after *hitana*).

Regarding "vā hitanāmnaḥ," the remainder [of the rule] is that there is a prohibition by the rule "na mapūrvaḥ. (1141) *brāhmaṇāt* [the suffix *ṭhak* is added] when not denoting a genus (*ajātau*). 6.4.171.

[The word] *brāhmaṇa* [is derived] from the [word] *brāhma*. From the word *brahman*, by adding the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), the prohibition of the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) by the rule "na mapūrvo 'patye" results in the meaning that this [prohibition] applies only when [the derivative denotes] a genus (*jāti*). This being the case, [the form] *brāhmaṇaḥ* as "the offspring of Brahmā" would not be established for the specific genus [of Brahmins], because of the rule "na mapūrvaḥ."
Because, when the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prohibited, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule "ṭhnastaddhite" would be unavoidable.

Furthermore, the derivation of "brāhmaṃ haviḥ" (an oblation for which Brahmā is the deity) would not be established; for the prohibition of *prakṛtibhāva* by the rule "na mapūrvam" is restricted to cases where a genus (*jāti*) is expressed, and [the word *brahman* here] does not denote a genus.
Because the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is impossible due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), he says: "by means of a split in the rule" (*yogavibhāga*).

The word "brāhma" constitutes one separate rule. In that context, the term "in the non-derivative sense of the suffix *aṇ*" (*anaṇyanapatye*) is understood from the previous rule; thus he says: "the form *brāhma* is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*)."

Regarding the rule *anapatye ñaṇī*: likewise, since the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *brahman* when no secondary derivative (*apatya*) is intended, and since the substitution of *ani* for the base has been set aside, the elision of the final vowel (*iṣṭilopa*) results; with this in mind, he provides the example: *brāhmaṃ haviḥ*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "that which has Brahman as its deity" (*brahmā devatā asya*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sāsya devatā*.

Regarding the phrase "tato jātau": the meaning is that the rule *jātau* must be formulated as a separate sūtra from the sūtra *tato ṭhañ brāhmaṇe*. Here, from the sūtra *na mapūrvo 'patye 'varmaṇaḥ*, the word *apatye* is carried over, and from the sūtra *prakṛtyaikāj*, the word *prakṛtyā* is also carried over. Thus he says: "in the sense of offspring (*apatye*)."

Regarding the term *jātau* ("in the sense of birth"): *brāhmaṇaḥ* means one born from *brahman* (the Veda/Brahmā) in a wife of the same caste (*sajātīyā*). This analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is clear in the Bhāṣya.
(1142) *āṬkṣamanapatye* 6.4.173. [The suffix *āṬk* is applied after a word ending in *an*, provided that the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) is not intended.]
*Āuksam*. He explains the sūtra by completing the remainder: "The elision of *ṭi* is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity) when *aṇ* follows.

The intention is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) which would otherwise apply due to the suffix *ṭhan*. Regarding *āuksam*: it is the form resulting from the elision of *ṭi*. Regarding *āuṣṇa*: the intention is that when *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*), there is no elision of *ṭi*, and thus the elision of *aL* (the penultimate vowel) occurs.

(1143) *ṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñāmaṇi* | P. 6.4.135. Now, one might object that due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), the elision of *a* [prescribed by P. 6.4.134] would not occur; therefore, he says: *ṣapūrvahan*. The rule *allopo’naḥ* (P. 6.4.134) is understood to carry over. The governing term *bhasya* (in a *bha*-stem) is also in force; thus he says: "preceded by *ṣ*" (*ṣapūrva*).

Regarding *tākṣṇa*: by the rule "the addition of *aṇ* after *takṣan*," the suffix *aṇ* (which otherwise has the sense of an agent) is an exception [to other rules]. Regarding *tākṣaṇya*: by the rule "after words ending in *senā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kārin*, [the suffix] *ṇya* [is added]," the suffix *ṇya* is applied.

(1144) *kṣatrāddhaḥ* |4|1|138|. [The rule] *kṣatrāddhaḥ* [is stated]; the word *apatye* ("in the sense of offspring") is understood as a remainder. Thus, *kṣatriyaḥ* [is derived]. When *gha* is replaced by *iy*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. [The term] *kṣātriranyaḥ* means one born from a *kṣatra* [man] and a *śūdrā* woman.

(1145) *kulāt khaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.139. From *kula*, the suffix *kha* [is applied]. The remainder [of the rule] is "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*). Thus, *kulīnaḥ*. For *kha*, the substitute *īna* is applied.

Now, one might object: since the prohibition against extension to the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*) applies to rules concerning compounds and suffixes (*samāsa-pratyaya-vidhau*), [the form] *āḍhyakulīnaḥ* [should not be formed].
To the question "How so?", he says: "even from that ending in -anta. Regarding the example *āḍhaḷkulīna*:
the suffix *kha* is applied here after the *karmadhāraya* compound *āḍhaḷkula*. The result here is the comprehension of wealth (*ādhyatva*) within the family.
However, when [the suffix] is applied to the word *kulīna* as a *karmadhāraya*, that [wealth] is not comprehended; this is the distinction.

(1146) *Apūrvapadād anyatarasyāṃ yaṅ-ḍhakau* |4|1|140|. "From a word that does not have a preceding member, optionally. This means that after the word *kula*, when it lacks a preceding member, the suffixes *yaṅ* and *ḍhak* are optionally used to denote offspring; in the alternative case, [the suffix] *kha*.

This means: in the case where the suffixes *yaṅ*, *ḍhak*, and *kañ* are absent. In the word *bahukulya*, the suffix *bahuc*—by virtue of the rule *vibhāṣā supaḥ*—is not a *pada*. Therefore, because it lacks a preceding member (*pūrvapada*), the suffixes *yaṅ*, *ḍhak*, and *kañ* indeed occur; this is the meaning.

(1147) *mahākulādañ-khañau* |4|1|141|. [The sūtra] "from *mahākula*, the suffixes *añ* and *khañ*" follows. Otherwise, within the scope of the *mahāvibhāṣā* (general option), once an exception (*apavāda*) has applied, the general rule (*utsarga*) would not apply; as in the case of *pīlā*.

The intention is that because [the suffix] *ve* has been prescribed here, the suffix *kha* mentioned in the preceding sūtra would not apply. Thus he says: "In one alternative, *kha*. The intention is that, this being the case, the initial vṛddhi does not occur. (1148) *duṣkulāḍ ḍhak* | 4.1.142 | [This sūtra prescribes the suffix] *ḍhak* after the word *duṣkula*.

The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after [a word denoting] a low family (*duṣkula*). "As before" means that the option (*anyatarasyām*) and the mention of the suffix *ār* continue to apply; this is the intended sense. (1149) Pāṇini 4.1.143: *svasuśchaḥ*. The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *svasṛ* ("sister").

The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *svasṛ* (*sister*). The phrase "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) is understood as a remainder [of the rule]. Thus, *svastrīyaḥ* ("sister's son"): *cha* is replaced by *īya*, and the vowel *ṛ* undergoes *yaṇ* substitution. (1150) *bhrātuṣṭhañ ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.144).
And [the suffix] *vyat* is used after the word *bhrātṛ*. It should be understood that the letter *t* is for the purpose of the accent, according to the rule *titsvaritam*.

(1151) *vyat-sapatne* [Pāṇini 4.1.145]. Regarding *vyat-sapatne*: [the suffix] *apatya* [is applied]; by the suffix, "offspring" (*apatya*) is expressed. However, the meaning of the word *bhrātṛ* is...

It is not intended [to be taken literally]. Thus, it is clear in the Bhāṣya that when the word *bhrātṛ* (brother) precedes, the meaning of the suffix *vyat* is "enemy. Now, one might ask: how can it be said "by the evil enemy (*pāpmanā bhrātṛvyeṇa*)", since evil (*pāpman*) cannot be a descendant? To this he says: "figuratively" (*upacārāt*).
The meaning is that [the term] is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) due to its association with the quality of being harmful.
(1152) *Revatyādibhyaṣṭhak* |4|1|146|.

From "Revatī" and the others, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. The phrase "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) is understood as the remainder. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] *ḍhak* and other such suffixes.

(1153) *ṭhasyekaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.50. *ṭhasyekaḥ*. The term *aṅgasya*, which is supplied from the governing context, is modified here to the ablative case. Thus it is said: "of the *ṭha* following an *aṅga*. This means "of the letter *ṭha*. For example: *raivatikaḥ*.
The analysis of the compound is "the offspring of Revatī. In the suffix *ṭhak*, the letter *k* is an *it* (indicatory), and the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.

For the letter *ṭh*, there is a substitution of an *ik* vowel ending in *ā*. Why [is it said] "from a stem" (*aṅgāt*)? In the case of *karmaṇaḥ* [in the rule *karmaṇaṣṭhañ*], the substitution does not occur for the letter *ṭh*. In this regard, in the *Bhāṣya*, when explaining [the word] as "of the *ṭha* suffix connected with a stem," in the example *karmaṭhaḥ*...

Since the word *karmaṭha* is a base (*aṅga*) with respect to the suffix *sup*, the substitution of *ik* for its *ṭha* occurs; and since the *ṭha* that serves as the cause for the technical designation of the base (*aṅgasaṃjñā*) is the one for which this *ik* substitute applies, such a *ṭha* must be a suffix (*pratyaya*). However, it has been established that in this instance, the *ṭha* is not a suffix. Therefore:
In the suffix *ṭhak*, the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; it is understood that the suffix is simply *ṭhak*.

It is also established in the *Bhāṣya* that "the mention of *ṭhasya* refers to the entire cluster. On this view, the letter *a* in *ṭhak* is not for the purpose of pronunciation; rather, the entire cluster is the suffix, and the letter *a* [is present] in place of *ik*.
It suffices to say that it serves the purpose of mere pronunciation.
(1154) *Gotrastriyāḥ kutsane ṇa ca* [Pāṇini 4.1.147]. Regarding *gotrastriyāḥ*: the suffix *ṇa*, with its nominative case ending elided, is drawn forward from the rule *cāṭ ṭhak*.

He says this with the words "the lineage (gotra) which is a woman," and so forth. "By implication" means that the intention is based on the restrictive rule (niyama): "only one [descendant] is formed in the lineage" (*eko gotre*). Regarding "the offspring of Gārgī": Gārgī is a female descendant in the lineage of Garga.

The suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule "from Garga and others" (*gargādibhyaḥ*), and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "after *yañ*" (*yañaśca*). [The elision of the final vowel and consonant of the base is then applied] by the rule "of that which [ends in a vowel]" (*yasyeti*).

There is the elision of the letter *e* by the rule *cē’tyakāralopaḥ*. There is the elision of the letter *ya* by the rule *ṭhhalastaddhitasya*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the young descendant (*apatyam yuvā*) of Gārgī. The designation by the mother due to ignorance of the father is a form of disparagement (*kutsanam*). Although, when the suffix *ṇa* is applied and the substitution of *ika* for *ṭhak* occurs, there would be the elision of the final vowel by the rule *yasyeti ca*, resulting in *gārga* or *gārgikaḥ*.
Even though it is established [by other means], he states the actual state of affairs with the words "as in the case of *bhū* and so on" (*puṃvadbhū-ādi*).

Having accepted that the rule "before a *bha*-affix which does not begin with a vowel" (*bhasyāḍhea*) applies when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is intended to be expressed, he says "from the word *gārgya*. And that [point] is addressed in the section on collections (*samūha*), specifically under the rule "the suffix *aṇ* after *bhikṣu* and others" (*bhikṣādibhyo 'ṇ*).
This will become clear. [Example: What about a feminine stem? *aupagaviḥ*—the youthful descendant of *aupagava*.

The contempt is to be understood from the context or other factors. Why "of a *gotra*"? [Counter-example: The fact that the suffix *ṇa* is marked with the indicatory letter *ṇ* is for the sake of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in cases such as *glau cukāyanaḥ*, which is the youthful descendant of *glucukāyanī*.

(1154) *vṛddhāṭ ṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam* ||4/1/148|| The suffix *ṭhak* follows a *vṛddha* [patronymic] stem when denoting the Sauvīra tribes. From the preceding sūtra, the term *gotre* (in the sense of a lineage) is understood as an elided portion (*anuvartate*). *Sauvīreṣu* is a qualifier of the base [stem]. Thus he says: "after a *vṛddha* [stem]."

The phrase "of that which has a *vṛddhi* vowel as its initial among its vowels" means [a word] designated by the technical term *vṛddhi*.
