The mention of *ṭhak* is for the purpose of terminating the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *ṇa*. Regarding "Bhāgāviti": Bhāgavita’s descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) is Bhāgāviti; in the sense of "his descendant in the younger generation" (*yuvāpatya*), when the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, there is the substitution of *ik*.

The form *bhāgavittika* means "the form [ending in] -ika. In the alternative case, it is *phak*; the words "by this rule" (*anena*) are to be supplied as the remainder, referring to the rule *ṭhyañiñośca*.
(Pāṇini 4.1.149) *pheścha ca*.
And [regarding] *pheśccha ca*: the term *ṭhche* has its nominative case elided. Regarding *yamundasya*, *yamunda* was a certain person in the land of Suvīra. As for *yāmundāyaniḥ*:

since there is no censure (*kutsanā*) in the sense of "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of Yāmundāyani," the suffix *chaṭhak* does not apply; instead, by the rule *tasyāpatyam* ("his descendant"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
The meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe*. Regarding *taikāyani*:
in the sense of "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of Taikāyani," because he is not a Sauvīra, the suffix *cha* is absent;
then, by the rule *tasyāpatyam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. The meaning is that there is elision of that [suffix *aṇ*] by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe*.

*Taikāyaniḥ*: In the sense of "the young descendant (yuvan) of Taikāyani," because he is a Sauviira, the suffix *chaṭhac* is absent; then, by the rule *tasyāpatyam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. The intention is that this *aṇ* undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṇyakṣatriye*.
(1156) *Phāṇṭāhṛtimimatābhyāṃ ṇa-phiñau* [Pāṇini 4.1.150].

*Phāṇṭāhṛtiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "among the Sauvīras," this is a supplement to complete the sense; it means "from the *gotra* of the Sauvīras. The analysis is as follows: *phāṇṭāhṛtiḥ* is the descendant of the *gotra* Phāṇṭāhṛta, formed with the suffix *iñ* after the word *phāṇṭāhṛta*; [the form] *phāṇṭāhṛtiḥ* denotes his younger descendant (*yuvan*). Regarding *maimataḥ*, it is the descendant of Mimata.
[This is] the analysis [of the compound]. In the word *mimataḥ*, the phrase "from the Sauvīra lineage" (*sauvīragotrāt*) does not apply;
the sense is that this is because of the explanation [in the commentary] and because it lacks the status of being a lineage (*gotratvābhāvāt*).
(1157) *kurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.151.

The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [words] such as *kuru*. "In the sense of offspring" (*apatye*)—this is a supplement to the rule. "Among the Sauviras" is no longer applicable here. In the example *kauravyā brāhmaṇāḥ*, *kuru* is the name of a certain Brāhmaṇa; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of him. When the suffix *ṇya* is applied, the *guṇa* substitution of *o* occurs.

There is the substitution of *ava*. There is the initial *vṛddhi* [vowel]. As for the suffix *ṇya* that will be taught by the rule "ṭhkurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ," because it is a *tadrāja* suffix, there is elision (*luk*) when applied to many [members of the group], resulting in "ṭhkuravaḥ kṣatriyāḥ" (the Kuru kṣatriyas).
It is precisely for the sake of indicating this that the plural number is used, and the qualifier "brāhmaṇāḥ" (brahmins) has been cited as an example.

Regarding *vāvadūkyāḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the descendants of a *vāvadūka*. Regarding *samrājaḥ kṣatriye*: this is a sūtra from the *kurv-ādi* group; the word "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) is to be supplied as the remainder. This is for the purpose of restriction, meaning [the suffix applies] only when it is a *kṣatriya*. Regarding *sāmrājo 'nyaḥ*: [this refers to the rule] "from *samrāj*, when it is a *kṣatriya*."

This is a sūtra from the *kurv-ādi* group. The word "in the sense of offspring" (*apatye*) is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. This is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that [the suffix] applies only to a *kṣatriya*. Regarding the phrase "other than a *samrāj*": the meaning is one born from a *samrāj* who is a *śūdra* or the like.

(1158) *senāntalakṣaṇakāribhyaśca* || 4.1.152 || [The suffix *ṇya* is applied after words ending in *senā*, as well as after those denoting marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and makers (*kārin*). "From these"—that is, from words ending in *senā*, and from those denoting marks and makers.
This statement is made because [the word *hariṣeṇa*] does not belong to the *kurv-ādi* group. Regarding *hāriṣeṇya*: there was a certain person named Hariṣeṇa.

The suffix *ṭha* is used here in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), and by the rule "ami," there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Because that [substitution] is considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*), the suffix *ṇya* is applied due to the word ending in *senā*. Regarding the form *lākṣaṇya*: the analysis is "one who possesses a *lakṣaṇa* (mark/definition) is *lakṣaṇaḥ*"; this is formed with the suffix *ac* from the *arśa-ādi* group. Then, the analysis is "the offspring (*apatyam*) of that.
He explains the word *kārin* with the words "a *kārin* is an artisan (*śilpī*). From that [he derives the following].

The meaning is that [the suffix] *ṇya* occurs when expressing a specific agent (*kāriviśeṣa*). Regarding *tāntuvāyya*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the offspring of a weaver (*tantuvāya*). Regarding *kaumbhakārya*:
the analysis is "the offspring of a potter (*kumbhakāra*). Regarding *nāpitya*: [the analysis is] "the offspring of a barber (*nāpita*)."
The section on compounds (*vigraha*). (1159) *udīcām iñ* | Pāṇini 4.1.153.
Regarding *udīcām iñ*: the meaning is that, according to the opinion of the Northern grammarians (*udīcām*), the suffix *iñ* shall be applied after words ending in *senā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kārin*.
"Because it is subsequent, [the suffix] phiñ alone [is applied]"—the remainder of the sense is "by the rule *udīcāṃ vṛddhād añ*.
"The addition of *aṇ* after *takṣan*" means "the addition of *aṇ* after *takṣan*"; the remainder of the sense is "in the opinion of the Northerners (*udīcām-mate*). Thus, [the form] is *tākṣṇaḥ*.

Because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*. However, the elision of *ṭha* occurs by virtue of the rule "ṭhṣapūrvahann" (Pāṇini 6.4.153). In the alternative view, the form is *tākṣṇya*; according to the opinion of the Eastern grammarians (*prācām*), this means the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the characteristic of *kāritva*. Because of the *prakṛtibhāva* prescribed by the rule "ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.168), there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*.

(1160) *tikādibhyaḥ phiñ* | Pāṇini 4.1.154. From *tiki* and the others, the suffix *phiñ* is applied. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iñ*. For example, *taikāyaniḥ*. If *phañ* were used instead, there would be the substitution of *āyan* for the final vowel and following consonant.

(1161) And [the suffix] after *kausalya* and *kārmārya*. [The forms] *kausalya* and *kārmārya* are derived from the ultimate base itself; that is to say, the suffix *phiñ* is applied after *kosala* and *karmāra*, and for that [suffix], *yuṭ* is substituted. This is clear in the Bhāṣya.
Also for *chāga* and *vṛṣa*.

Regarding the phrase "also for *chāga* and *vṛṣa*": the meaning is that it should be stated that [the suffix] *phiñ* applies, and that for this [suffix], *yuṭ* is also added. (Pāṇini 4.1.156) *aṇo dvyacaḥ*. (Note: This rule prescribes the addition of the augment *yuṭ* after the suffix *phiñ* when it follows a base ending in *aṇ* that consists of two syllables.)

"From a *dvyañ* [stem] ending in the suffix *aṇ*, [the suffix] *phiñ* is applied for a descendant. This is a supplement to the rule (*śeṣapūraṇa*). The meaning is: "The suffix *phiñ* is applied after a stem ending in the suffix *aṇ* that consists of two syllables (*dvyañ*) to denote a descendant. Regarding *kārtrāyaṇi*: a student of Kṛta is *kārtta*. By the rule "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. The descendant of *kārtta* is *kārtrāyaṇi*.

In the case of the suffix *phiñ*, there is the substitution of *āyan* and the application of *ṇatva*. Thus, *dākṣāyaṇa*: the offspring of Dakṣa is *dākṣi* (by the rule *ata iñ*). The offspring of *dākṣi* is *dākṣāyaṇa* (by the rule *ṭhyañiñośca*, which prescribes the suffix *phak*).
The point is that because it does not end in the suffix *aṇ*, the rule *na phiñaḥ* does not apply. [The example] *aupagaviḥ* is as follows.
The offspring of Upagu is Aupagava. His [i.e., Aupagava’s] offspring who is a youth is Aupagavi.

The point is that because there is no occurrence of two vowels (*dvyactva*), the suffix *phiñ* does not apply. However, regarding the offspring of a *kartṛ* (agent), it is included in the *kurv-ādi* group.
It should be understood that [the suffix] -ṭhañ alone [is applied].
It should be stated that for words beginning with *tyad*, the suffix *phiñ* is optionally used. "Tyādāyaniḥ" or "tyādaḥ"—thus it appears in some manuscripts.

This is seen [in some manuscripts], but it is erroneous; for since the pronouns beginning with *tyad* are "vṛddha" according to the rule *tyadādīni ca*, the desired result is already established by the rule *udīcāṃ vṛddhāt*. Furthermore, this Vārttika is not found in the Bhāṣya. (1162) *udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt* | Pāṇini 4.1.157.

"Vṛddha for those of the North": the meaning is that according to the opinion of the Northerners (*udīcām*), the suffix *phiñ* should be applied after a word designated as *vṛddha* which ends in a non-*gotra* secondary suffix (*apratyaya*). For example, *āmraguptāyaniḥ*; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the descendant of Āmragupta.

Regarding "but for the Easterners" (*prācām tu*): the word "in the opinion [of the Easterners]" (*ṭhmate*) is to be supplied. Thus, *āmraguptiḥ* (with the suffix *iñ* applied after the short vowel *a*).
Regarding "ĀṬpagavi": Upagu’s descendant in the lineage is ĀṬpagava; his young descendant (yuvan) is ĀṬpagavi.
Since ĀṬpagava belongs to the *gotra* category, the point is that when deriving a term for a young descendant (*yuvan*) from him, the suffix *phiñ* does not apply, and thus only *iñ* is used.

(1163) *vākinādīnāṃ kuk ca* | Pāṇini 4.1.158. Regarding the rule *vākinādīnām*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing words: "the suffix *phiñ* may optionally [be applied] in the sense of offspring. The intention is that, due to the particle *ca*, the terms *udīcām* and *phiñ* are understood as being carried over from previous rules. And thus:

The result is that after words such as *vākin* and others, the suffix *phiñ* may optionally be applied, and the augment *kuk* is added to the base forms; (1164) [and] after a word ending in *putra*, it is optional. 4.1.159.
*putrāntād anyatarasyām*: this is clear.

(1165) *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam* | 4|1|160|. The meaning is: after the names of the Easterners (*prācām*) that are not designated as *vṛddha*, the suffix *phin* is diversely (*bahulam*) applied in the sense of offspring (*apatye*).
The mention of "prācām" (of the easterners) is for the sake of honor. Regarding *glucukāyani*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the descendant of Glucuka.
Why [is it said] "from a non-vṛddha [stem]"? Consider *rājadantiḥ*. Because of the mention of "bahuvrīhi," it does not apply here: *dākṣiḥ*.
(1166) [Añ and yatya are the suffixes after the word *manu* when denoting a genus, and there is also the augment *ṣuk*. 4.1.161.

Regarding *manorjātau*: after the word *manu*, these two suffixes—*añ* and *yat*—occur, and when they follow, there is also the augment *ṣuk* for the word *manu*; the meaning is that this occurs when the genus (*jāti*) is to be understood by the combination of both base and suffix. Thus he says: "The genus is the collective meaning."

The intention is that the term "apatya" (offspring) is not connected here; otherwise, in the case of "mānuṣāḥ," there would be elision (*luk*) by the rule *yañañośca*. (1167) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.168] From a word denoting a country, when it refers to a Kṣatriya, the suffix *añ* is applied.
"From a word denoting a *janapada*. A *janapada* is a country; a word expressing that is a *janapadaśabda*. The meaning is: from such a word as one that denotes a *kṣatriya*.
He states the conclusion: "of the *janapada* and the *kṣatriya*. For example, *Aikṣvāka*: [the son] of the one named Ikṣvāku.

The place and the king. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "the offspring of that king," the suffix *añ* is applied, which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. There is a distinction in accent. By overriding the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *u*, the elision of the final *ṭi* (the *u*) occurs due to the specific rule (*nipātana*) in the sūtra "dāṇḍināyana-. Thus, [we get] *aikṣvākāḥ*. However, in the plural:
The sense is that this will be explained later. Regarding the phrase "kṣatriyasamāna":

a compound word denoting a country is [here] synonymous with a word denoting a Kṣatriya; therefore, the meaning is that suffixes applied in the sense of a descendant (apatya) occur after a word ending in the sixth case when used in the sense of a Rājanya.
He states that this Vārttika is intended to explain the meaning established by the Sūtra, saying: "tadrājam" (that which denotes a king).

The designation *tadrāja* has been prescribed for the suffixes such as *añ* and others ordained by rules beginning with "from a word denoting a country" (*janapadaśabdāt*). The status of being a *tadrāja* for these suffixes is secondary (*gauṇa*), because it consists in their denoting that [king]. And thus...

The term *tadrāja* (denoting that king) is a designation based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*), and not devoid of constituent meaning like [the technical markers] *ṭi*, *ghu*, or *bha*. Consequently, it is understood that the suffixes beginning with *añ*, when designated as *tadrāja*, also denote "king"; thus, even when the word "king" (*rājan*) is to be expressed, [the rule applies].
The meaning is that they are understood to be so. Regarding the term *pañcālānām*:
this is the name of a specific region ending in the plural number, as such usage is observed in the Bhāṣya.
In the Bhāṣya on the rule *dvyañmagadha*, it says: "This is a country named Neṣa."

It should be understood that even when denoting a country (*deśa*), the singular number is used after a word expressing a region (*janapada*). Why [is it specified] "after a word for a region"? Consider: *drauhyavaḥ*, the descendant of Druhyu. Here, only the suffix *aṇ* is applied; because it does not denote a *tadrāja* (a title of a king), there is no elision (*luk*) in the plural. Thus: *drauhyavāḥ*. Why [is it specified] "after a word for a Kṣatriya"? Consider: a certain Brāhmaṇa named Pañcāla.
His offspring is *pāñcāliḥ* or *vaidehiḥ*. Regarding *pūroḥ aṇ vaktavyaḥ*:
since the word *pūru* does not denote a country (*janapada*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to it] in the sense of "belonging to that" (*prāgdīvyatīya*).

The statement is made for the purpose of establishing the technical designation *tadrāja* [for the suffixes]. However, if it denotes a country (*deśa*), it is already established by the rule "dvyañ-magadha" [Pāṇini 4.1.170].
[In the case of] Pāṇḍu, the suffix is *aṇ*.

"Pāṇḍoḍaḷ" [is formed]; the word "should be stated" (*vācya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Here, there is no inclusion of *pāṇḍu* when it denotes the quality of whiteness or when it denotes Yudhiṣṭhira’s father, because of the statement "from a janapada," and because that [father] lacks the status of being the king of the Pāṇḍu country. Thus, "pāḍaḷ."

The meaning is "the offspring of Pāṇḍu" or "the king of the Pāṇḍu country. (1168) *Sālveyagāndhāribhyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 4.1.169]. [The examples are] *sālveya* and *gāndhāri*. Now, one might object: "But the words *sālveya* and *gāndhāri* are underived (*avyutpanna*)."

Since the suffix *iñ* would already be established by [Pāṇini 4.2.128] for both words denoting a country (*deśa*) and a kṣatriya when followed by a word signifying a people (*janapada*), for what purpose is this [rule] stated? To this he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ñyaṅ*. (1169) Pāṇini 4.1.170: *dvyañ-magadha-kaliṅga-sūramasādaṇ*.

"Dvyañ-magadha" means "an exception to añ. The meaning is that it is an exception to the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule "janapada-śabdāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.167). Regarding "dvyañ": the word "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Suhma—these are names of countries consisting of two syllables (*dvyaca*) which denote Kṣatriyas.

The analysis of the compound is *aṅgasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of Aṅga"). Similarly, regarding the king of that [land], the analysis is *aṅgādideśasya rājā* ("the king of the region beginning with Aṅga").

(1170) *vṛddhetkosalājādāñ ñyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.17): [The suffix] *ñyaṅ* is applied after a word denoting a country (*janapada*) that begins with a *vṛddhi*-strengthened vowel, as well as after *ut*, *kosala*, and *ajada*.

*vṛddhetkosalā*: From a word denoting a country or a Kṣatriya that is designated as *vṛddha* (containing a *vṛddhi*-strengthened vowel), from *kosala*, and from *aja*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). Regarding "from a *vṛddha* [word]": this means it is illustrated [by examples]. *Āmbaṣṭhyaḥ*, *sauvīryaḥ*: the words *āmbaṣṭha* and *sauvīra* [are examples].

The two terms *janapada* (country) and *kṣatriya* (warrior-noble) are both denotative. The word *id* [in the sūtra] is for the purpose of indicating the examples that follow. Regarding *āvantya*: the word *avanti* denotes both a country and a king. Regarding *kausalya*: the word *kosala* denotes both a country and a king. Regarding "the offspring of Ajāda": this applies when [Ajāda] is a denoter of a king.
This is the analytical exposition (*vigraha*). However, when [the term] denotes a place, the analysis is "the king of the Ajādās.
(Pāṇini 4.1.172) *Kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*: after the word *kuru* and after those beginning with *na*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied. From the word *kuru* and from those beginning with *na*.

The meaning is that the suffix *ṇya* occurs after words denoting a country (*janapada*) or a *kṣatriya* when the derivative refers to a descendant (*apatya*) or a king (*rājan*). For example, *kauravya*: the analysis is either "the descendant of Kuru" or "the king of the Kurus. *naiṣadhya*: the word *niṣadha* denotes both a country and a king. Regarding the term *śaiṣika*: it is by means of the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).
The remainder [of the rules].

(1172) *sālvāvayavapratyagrathakalakūṭāśmakādiñ* |4|1|173|. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied after [words denoting] parts of the *sālva* country, as well as *udumbara* and so forth. [Examples: *udumbarāḥ*, *tilakhalāḥ*, *madrakārāḥ*.

The Yugandharas, Bhūliṅgas, and Śaradaṇḍas are known by the designation "parts of the Sālva" (sālvāvayava); this is the established tradition. However, in the Mahābhāṣya's rule *dvyañmagadhe*, the Budhas, Ajamīḍhas, and Aḍakrands are also included.

(1173) *te tadrājāḥ* | 4|1|174 | "Those are called *tadrāja*. By the word "those" (*te*), the suffixes *añ* and others—prescribed starting from the rule beginning with "from words denoting a country" (*janapada-śabdāt*)—are referred to. Thus he says: "the suffixes *añ* and others."

(1174) *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivā'striyām* || 2.4.62 || The word *tadrājasya* [is understood]. From the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe'tya-to luK*, the word *luK* is carried over (*anuvartate*). After the word *tenaiva*, the phrase *kṛte bahutve* is supplied (*adhyāhāraḥ*). Thus he says: "in the case of many" (*bahuṣu*).

Regarding the phrase "tadarthakṛtabahutve" (when plurality is produced by that meaning): the meaning is "when plurality resides in the meaning of the base ending in suffixes such as *añ* and so forth. What is the purpose of [specifying] "by that" (*tena*)? [Consider the example: "priyavāṅgāḥ," meaning "those for whom a dear limb (*priya-vāṅga*) exists. In this case, because the plurality resides in the meaning of the *anyapada* (the external referent), the suffix does not follow from the word *vāṅga*.

*Luk*. Although the plurality residing in the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*)—which is qualified by the meaning of the *varti* member—also resides in the meaning of the *varti* member itself, nevertheless, because it does not reside solely in the meaning of the base (*aṅga*) ending in the suffix *añ*, there is no *luk* elision. It is for this very purpose that the particle *eva* is included [in the rule]. Examples: *ikṣvākavaḥ*, *pañcālāḥ*.
Thus [it is said]. By prescribing [the suffix] *añ* through the rule "janapada-śabdāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.167), when there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix, the initial *vṛddhi* [vowel] is also removed.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": examples such as *aṅgāḥ* and *vaṅgāḥ* should be understood. How then [is it formed]? In the case of *kauravyaḥ*, there is the suffix *ṇya*; and in the case of *pāṇḍayaḥ*, there is the suffix *ḍyaṇ*.

The meaning is that, because they are *tadrāja* (patronymic) suffixes, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of elision (*luk*) when applied to many [descendants]. Regarding the phrase "they are correct" (*sādhava iti*):

from the words *kauravya* and *pāṇḍya*, when the suffix *yat* is added by the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Since the suffix *yat* is not a *tadrāja* suffix, there is no elision (*luk*). This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Since the words *raghu* and *yadu* do not denote a country (*janapada*), the suffix *aṇ* would not apply in the sense of 'belonging to that' (*tadrāja*) according to the rule for derivatives beginning with *prāgdīvyatīya*; how then can there be elision (*luk*) of that suffix when it refers to many? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the resolution: "Of the Raghus," etc. [He says] "by means of figurative indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*), and "in usage" (*prayoge*).

The remainder [of the rule applies]. Consequently, the intention is that this [term] does not end in a secondary suffix (*apatyapratyaya*). However, the basis for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) should be understood as having the same application (*samānavṛttikatva*) as in the case of *raghu* and *yadu*. *Kambojālluk*. The term *tadrāja* (which was previously understood as a genitive case ending) is here transformed into a nominative. The meaning is that there shall be elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix following *kamboja*. This rule is for the purpose of excluding the plural number. he will explain later that where one's ancestors have dwelt, that is *abhijana*. Regarding *sindhutakṣa* and so forth:
the intention is that the word *kamboja* is included in the list beginning with *sindhu*.

(1176) *Striyām avantikuntikurubhyaś ca* | Pāṇini 4.1.176. Regarding the feminine gender, [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after the words *avanti*, *kunti*, and *kuru*. Thus, one forms *avantī* and *kuntī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "a female descendant of Avanti" or "a queen of Avanti," and likewise for Kunti. By this rule, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ñyaṅ* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhet kosale yañ*. Since [the final vowel] is now *it*, [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added].

In *manuṣyajātiḥ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. In *kurūḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṇya* by the rule *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.177) *ataśca*. (Note: The rule *ataśca* [4.1.177] provides that when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* follows a stem ending in short *a*, the final *a* is also elided.)

And for this reason [it is stated]: "of the *tadrāja* [suffix] that is *a*. Here, "that" (*ataḥ*) is a qualifier of the *tadrāja* suffix; the meaning is "of the *a* that constitutes a *tadrāja* suffix. Regarding *śūrasenī*: when the suffix *añ* is elided, by relying on the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix), it ends in a suffix denoting lineage (*apatya*); thus, because it is a genus (*jāti*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. [The rule] "not... [is not applicable].
The prohibition [of the feminine suffix] does not apply to *lumat* because the rule for *ṅīṣ* is not an operation (*kārya*) pertaining to the base (*aṅga*). Thus, *madrī*.

(1178) *na prācyabhargādiyaudheyādibhyaḥ* |4|1|178|. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after [words denoting] non-Easterners (*aprācya*), but not after [the group beginning with] *bharga* nor [the group beginning with] *yaudheya*. (Pāṇini 4.1.178).

"Not from the Easterners" means "from these"—that is, from the Bhargas and others, and from the Yaudheyas and others. "These are Easterners": the word "Kṣatriyas" is to be understood as the remainder [of the definition]. According to the respective rules, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *añ* and *aṇ*. He cites examples of the Bhargas and others: Bhārgī and Kārūśī.

Regarding "Kaikeyī" and the relationship of "progeny and progenitor": what needs to be said on this matter has already been stated under the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*. Now, he says "Yudhā, Śukrā," etc., in order to demonstrate the prohibition of elision (*luk*) for [patronymics derived from] *yaudheya* and others. As for "ḍhak": [the meaning is] the offspring of Yudhā.

In the analysis of the compound *śukrāyā apatyam* ("the offspring of Śukrā"), the suffix *aṇ*—which would apply by the rule *tannāmikāṇ*—is set aside; instead, by the rule *dvyacaḥ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, which undergoes the substitution *ey*. Then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel *ā* is elided, and the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is applied.
From the word *yaudheya* and from the word *śaukreya*, [the respective suffixes are applied] by the rule *pārśvādi-yaudheyādibhyo 'ṇ-añau*.

Thus, when the suffix *añ*—which bears the technical name *tadrāja* and is added in the fifth case (denoting descent)—is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*), the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*.
Then, by the rule *ṭhśārṅgaravādyañaḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīn* is added, resulting in the forms *yaudheyī* and *śaukreyī*; this is the intended meaning.
Now, one might object: even if the suffix *añ* is elided here by the rule *ṭhataśca*, the form *yaudheyī* would still be derived by adding the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhea*.

Since the mention of *yaudheya* and others here would be redundant because [the desired form] *śaukreyī* is already established, he says: "And therefore," and "but in the case of elision (*luk*. Regarding "the removal of the acute accent (*udātanivṛtti*)," by the rule "and where there is the elision of an acute accent, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is acute," the *ṅīp* would be acute. In the final view (*siddhānta*), however, because it ends in *añ*, the suffix *ṅīn* applies.
The sense is that the initial syllable is acute (*ādyaudātta*).
(1179) *Aṇ-iño-r-anārṣayor-guru-potamayoh-ṣyaṅ-gotre* [Pāṇini 4.1.78].
Regarding *aṇ-iñoḥ*: the sense is that, according to the Bhāṣya, the last among three or more [syllables] is called "the penultimate" (*utama*). Of that...
"Nearby" (*samīpam upotamam*)—the sense is that this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of proximity.
The analysis of the term *guru-upotamam* is "those two which are near to the highest (*utama*).
The base form (*prātipadika*), which is the subject under discussion, is modified by the genitive dual.
It is understood that [the rule applies] to the nominal stems *upotama* and *guru-varṇaka*.

By the rule *ṭhaṇ-iñoḥ*, through the technical maxim regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there is the inclusion of those [stems] ending in the affixes *aṇ* and *iñ*. The term *gotre* (in the sense of lineage) follows after *aṇ* and *iñ*. "Not prescribed for a seer" (*ṛṣer-avihitau*) means *anārṣau* (not belonging to a seer). This also [is understood].

This is a qualification of *aṇ* and *iñ*. The term "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is the governing rule (*adhikṛta*). This is what he expresses by saying "the *aṇ* and *iñ* which [occur] in the sense of a lineage," and so forth. The phrase "it shall be a substitute" (*ādeśaḥ syāt*)—the status of being a substitute is obtained because of the indication using the genitive case of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Now, one might object: "Since this substitution of *śyaṅ* for both *aṇ* and *iñ* consists of more than one letter (*anekāl*), it ought to be a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*).
To this he says: "Of that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasya*). Thus, the intended meaning is that this substitution applies only to *aṇ* and *iñ*.
However, it is not correct to say that it is a replacement for the final letter (*anta*) by the rule "ṅcci," because [the substitute] *ṣyaṅ* possesses the marker *ṅ*.
Because [the rule] has its application in cases such as *samprasāraṇam* and so forth. Regarding *kumudagandheḥ*:

the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose scent is like the scent of a water-lily" (*kumudagandha*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* should be stated for a word preceded by a locative case, with the elision of the final member of the compound. Thus, in the first part [of the compound], there is elision of the final member.
There is also elision (*lopa*) of the word *gandha* in the latter member. By the rule *ṭhupamānācca*, the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final vowel of the first member].

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "the female descendant of Kumudagandhi," the suffix *aṇ* is applied. There is elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *yasyeti ca*, followed by initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), resulting in the form *kaumudagandha*. In that form, the vowel *a* of the suffix *aṇ* follows the letter *dha*.
The *utama* [the highest vowel] is the letter *a* following the letter *ga*. This is because it is stated that "a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) is heavy.

Nor should it be asked how the letter *a* can be situated immediately after *ga* when it is separated by the *anusvāra* and the letter *dha*; for the principle holds that "whatever does not constitute an actual separation [is considered contiguous], even if there is an intervention [by other sounds]."

According to the logic [of the rule], the intervention by *hal* vowels is not a defect; for indeed, there is nowhere a heavy syllable (*guru*) that is not intervened [by a vowel] when followed by an *aṇ* suffix. And thus, the word *kaumudagandhī*, which ends in the *aṇ* suffix and is the base form (*prātipadika*) with a heavy penultimate vowel, becomes the word *kaumudagandhyā* even after the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* for the case-ending *am* (accusative singular) and the subsequent substitution of *āp* for *ṣyaṅ* by the rule *ṣyaṅaśca*.
This is the meaning. He provides an example ending in *iñ*: "vārāhyā" (the female descendant of Varāha). The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the female offspring of Varāha.
[The suffix] *iñ* is applied after [the word ending in] *at*. There is elision of the vowel *a*. The word "vārāhī" results; therein, the vowel *i* is the penultimate (*upadhā*).
The vowel *ā* following the *repha* is heavy (*guru*) and situated immediately before the penultimate. By the rule "cāu," there is the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* for the *i* of the suffix *iñ*.

The state [of being]. "Vāsiṣṭhī" and "Vaiśvāmitrī"—these two end in the suffix *aṇ* derived from a seer's name (*ṛṣyaṇ*). "ĀṬpagavī"—even though it ends in *aṇ*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* does not apply because it lacks the condition of having a heavy vowel as the penultimate syllable (*gurūpotama*). Regarding the definition of a genus (*jāti*):

according to the rule "A lineage (*gotra*) is a genus when associated with Vedic schools (*caraṇa*"), it possesses the status of a genus. "Āhicchatrī"—here the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "born there" (*jātārtha*), and not otherwise.

The suffix *ṣyaṅ* does not apply in the sense of *gotra*. Nor should it be asked why the suffix *ṣyaṅ* itself is not prescribed [in this context]; for if that were the case, in the analysis "the female descendant of Udamegha," the form *Audameghī* would be derived by applying both *ata iñ* and *ṣyaṅ*, and consequently, the form *Audamegheya*—meaning "her male descendant"—would not be established.
It is stated clearly in the Bhāṣya that because this [term] lacks the status of being a *apatya-pratyaya* (a suffix denoting offspring), the elision of *y* does not apply.
(1180) *gotrāvayavāt* |4|1|79|. Regarding *gotrāvayavāt*: he explains the word *gotrāvayava*—[the term] *gotrāvayava*.

Regarding the term *gotrābhimatāḥ*: the analysis of the compound is "those by whom the lineage (*gotra*)—that is, the family (*kula*)—is intended (*abhimata*), meaning renowned. The sense is that they effect the renown of the family; in other words, they effect the designation of the family. Thus he says: *kulākhyāḥ* ("named after the family"), meaning those by whom the family is named or designated.
*Kulākhyāḥ* means names of clans (*kulanāmāni*). For it is by words such as *puṇikā* and others that a clan is designated—as in "we are the Puṇikas," "we are the Bhuṇikas," and so forth.
[The word is derived] from the root *yu* meaning "to mix," preceded by the prefix *ava*, which, by virtue of the prefix, carries the sense of being well-known.

The word *avayava* is derived from the root *pac* with the suffix *ac*; the sense is that a "part of a family" (*kula-avayava*) is understood as a "representative word of the family. Now, one might ask: since this is already established by the preceding rule, for what purpose is this stated? To this he replies: "for the sake of [denoting] a descendant who is not preceded by a heavy syllable. That which is separated from the *gotra*—that is, unmixed with it—is the immediate offspring (*anantara-apatya*).

That this is for that purpose (*tadartham*) is also clear from the Bhāṣya. Thus, even though it falls outside the governing topic of *apatya* (offspring) in the preceding sūtra, the natural inclination of the Bhāṣya is that only the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense of *gotra* is intended to be understood here. Regarding *pauṇikyā*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "the female offspring of Puṇika," [the suffix] *ata*...

After a stem ending in *iñ*, the suffixes *ṣyaṅ* and *cāp* are applied. For example: *evīmauṇikyā*. When it is a personal name, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied after the *tannāmika-aṇ* [secondary suffix]. (Pāṇini 4.1.80: *krauḍy-ādibhyaś-ca*. "And after *krauḍi* and others."

Regarding the rule *krauḍyādibhyaśca*, he says "the suffix *ṣyaṅ*" by relying on an alternative view stated in the Bhāṣya: "this is a rule for the introduction of the suffix *ṭh*. To the question, "Since this is already established by the preceding rule, what is the purpose of this [present] one? he replies: "It is for the sake of those [names] where the penultimate vowel is not heavy (*agurūpotama*), and for the sake of those that do not end in *anaṇ* or *niñ*."

*Krauḍī*: In the analysis *kroḍasyāpatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Kroḍa"), the suffix *iñ* is applied after the stem ending in *at*, followed by the feminine suffixes *ṣyaṅ* and *cāp*. Here, because it is stated that "for *try* and so forth, the last vowel is the *upottama*," the penultimate vowel is not heavy (*gurūpotamatva*).
However, if it is a proper name of a human, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. The word *gaukakṣya* ends in the suffix *iñ* from the *gargādi* group; of that—
Even though it does not end in *ana* or *ni*, there is the suffix *ṣyaṅ*. Regarding the phrase "of *sūta* and *yuvati*": this is a *gaṇa*-sūtra.

The meaning is that the word *sūta* takes the suffix *ṣyaṅ* when referring to a young woman (*yuvati*). Thus, *sūtreyī*; the meaning is "one who has attained youth. But in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), it remains simply *sūtī*. [The word] *bhoja* refers to a Kṣatriya; this also...
Gaṇasūtra:
(1182) *daivayajñi-śaucivṛkṣi-sātyamugri-kāṇḍeviddhi-bhyo 'nyatarasyām* 4.1.81. [The patronymic suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied after these names.]

Regarding *daivayajñī*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "the female descendant of Devayajña," the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is optionally applied after a stem ending in *iñ*. Regarding "and so forth": the female descendant of Śucivṛkṣa is *śaucivṛkṣyā*—or *śaucivṛkṣī*. In the sense of "one whose fierce [nature] is truth," there is *satyamugraḥ*.

The suffix *mum* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The female descendant of Satyamugra is Sātyamugrī or Sātyamugrī. One pierced by an arrow is Kāṇḍeviddha; the vowel *e* is substituted here by irregular derivation. The female descendant of Kāṇḍeviddha is Kāṇḍeviddhyā or Kāṇḍeviddhī. "Kaṇṭheviddhī" is an alternative reading.
Thus ends the section on offspring (*apatya*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the suffixes used in the sense of "worthy of" (*ārhīya*):
(1657) *prāgvateṣṭhañ* | Pāṇini 5.1.18. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied before the word *vati*.

Now, the *ārhīya* suffixes. [The rule] "before *vati*" (*prāgvateḥ*). The word *vati* refers to the sūtra containing that term. Thus he says: "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*). This means that in those sūtras prior to "equal to that," only the meanings are specified, but not the suffixes; in those cases, the suffix *ṭhañ* is understood to apply.

(1658) *Ārhād ago-pucchasaṅkhyā-parimāṇāt ṭhak* [Pāṇini 5.1.19]. "From *ārhāt* onwards" means: the word *arhati* occurring in the sūtra *tadarhati* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of one part [of that word], and it refers to the sūtra containing that [word]; the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*).

Because of the explanation. Thus he says: "it deserves that" (*tadarhati*). "Pervading this" (*ityetadabhivyāpya*). This sūtra also applies when no specific suffix is heard. Here, because number (*saṅkhyā*) and measure (*parimāṇa*) are mentioned separately, number is not measure. And so:
The Vārttika states: "Unmāna is indeed measurement by height; parimāṇa is measurement from all sides; pramāṇa would be length; and saṅkhyā is external [calculation] in every respect.
That by which the weight of a substance is determined after it has been placed upon a scale is [unmāna].

That is measurement (*unmāna*), consisting of the *guñjā*, *māṣa*, *niṣka*, *suvarṇa*, *pala*, and so forth; it is that particular vessel made of wood or other materials, which is long, wide, and high,
by means of which grains such as rice are measured according to the length, width, and height contained within that vessel.

Dimension (*parimāṇa*) refers to the *prastha* and so forth; extension (*āyāma*), meaning length, is that by which something is delimited, such as the *aratni*, *prādeśa*, and so forth. Number (*saṅkhyā*), however, is external to and distinct from the aforementioned triad [of dimension, extension, and shape], meaning it consists of oneness, duality, and so forth.

(1659) *asamāse niṣkādibhyaḥ* |5|1|20|. Regarding *asamāse*: this means up to that point, specifically up to the rule *tena krītam* [Pāṇini 5.1.37]. Regarding *ṭhak*: the intention is that this suffix is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Regarding *ārhīyeṣu* ("in the case of derivatives denoting 'worth' or 'price'"): [this refers to the scope of the application].
The phrase "up to *tadarhati*" (it deserves that) means [in the context] of the meanings such as "bought with that" (*tena krītam*) and so forth, which have been enumerated.

Regarding *naiṣkikam*: it means "bought with a *niṣka*. The connection with the meanings of "bought," etc., occurs according to the specific application. However, in a compound, only the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied]; this means [it is applied] after words such as *paramaniṣka*.

(1660) *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ* | 7|3|17| This sūtra belongs to the section concerning the initial *vṛddhi* [strengthening] under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of the second member" (*uttarapadasya*). He explains it by supplying the missing words: "there shall be *vṛddhi* of the second member. [The meaning is: In a compound ending in a word denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*), provided it is not a name (*asaṃjñā*) and does not end in *śāṇa*, there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel of the second member.
The meaning is that there shall be *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel of the second member (*uttarapada*). "In the presence of *ñit*, etc.
means in the presence of *ñit*, *ṇit*, and *kit* suffixes. "Paramanaiṣkika" means "purchased for a supreme *niṣka*.
Because it is a compound (*samāsa*), the suffix *ṭhak* is absent, and the general suffix *ṭhañ* applies by default. There is a difference in accent (*svara*).
[Objection: Since the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed only after [the specific items] such as *niṣka*, it cannot possibly apply after a compound ending in those;

therefore, the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa*) is redundant. Nor can it be argued that because the mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is governed from the beginning up to the end of the fifth chapter, there is a possibility of *ṭhak* applying even after a compound through the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) by way of qualifying the nominal stem—given the prohibition that "there is no *tadantavidhi* with a nominal stem that possesses [a specific] suffix, just as with the mention of *ṭ*. Furthermore, since *niṣka* and the others are specifically mentioned, they possess [the suffix], and thus the prohibition applies. To this, he says: "The mention of 'non-compound'... [Example: *sugavyam*.

*Sugauḥ* (an excellent cow): because of the prohibition "not after a word of worship" (*na pūjanāt*), the suffix *ṭac* is not applied by the rule "after *go*, when no *taddhita* suffix with elision follows" (*gor ataddhitaluki*). From the rule "after *go* and others" (*ugavādibhyaḥ*), the suffix *yat* is added to a word ending in *go*. Regarding *yavāpūpyam*: because it ends in *apūpa*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "optionally after sacrificial offerings and *apūpa* and others" (*vibhāṣā havir-apūpādibhyaḥ*). Now, one might object: since there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the mention of "non-compound" (*asamāsa-grahaṇa*), why should there not be an application of the rule to that which ends in [the word] *ūrdhva*?

Furthermore, regarding the rule "he performs the *pārāyaṇa*," one might think that the suffix *ṭhañ* would apply here as well—just as in the case of "he performs the *pārāyaṇa*, *turāyaṇa*, or *cāndrāyaṇa*"—and so he says: "But from this point onward... This is a *vārttika*. Now, even if this were so, one might still object that the suffix *añ* (by the rule "after *śūrpa*, *añ* optionally") would apply even after a word ending in *dviśūrpa*; therefore, he says: "And that [occurs] when there is no elision (*aluk*). The meaning is that what was stated previously—that "from this point onward, the inclusion of the final member applies to compounds preceded by a numeral"—does not hold when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix.

This also is merely a *vārttika*. Regarding the term *dviśūrpa*: this is a *dvigu* compound according to the rule "taddhitārtha... (Pāṇini 2.1.51). The word that serves as the base for the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) does not end in a *luk*-elision. Therefore, from this word ending in *śūrpa* which has a numeral as its prior member, the suffix *añ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule "śūrpādañ anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.1.26)—is subject to elision (*luk*) by the rule "adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug" (Pāṇini 5.1.28). Thus, the word *dviśūrpa* ends in a *luk*-elision. Consequently, the suffix *añ* prescribed by "śūrpādañ" (Pāṇini 5.1.26) does not apply when the sense is "bought with that," because once the *luk* has occurred, there is no longer a mention of that [base] as the final member of the compound. This is the meaning.

Regarding the term *dviśaurpika*: by the rule *tena krītam* ("bought with that"), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; then, by the rule *parimāṇāntasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ*, there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). However, the elision (*luk*) of this *ṭhañ* does not occur, because it is not caused by a *dvigu* compound.

(1661) *ardhātparimāṇasya pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.26): "After *ardha*, [vṛddhi] of a measure-word occurs; but for the preceding [member], it is optional. This sūtra follows from the previous rule *parimāṇāntasya*.

Regarding *ardhadrauṇikam-ardhadrauṇikam*: although the word *droṇa* belongs to the class beginning with *niṣka*, the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply because of the inclusion of the term "non-compound" (*asamāsa*). Instead, only the suffix *ṭhañ* applies.
(Pāṇini 5.1.1662) *nātaḥ parasya*. (Pāṇini 7.3.27) [The final vowel of the first member is not lengthened when followed by a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ.]

"Not beyond this" means "of the vowel *a* that constitutes the measure. This means: of the vowel *a* which is a constituent part expressing a measure. "But optionally for the first member" means: but for the initial vowel of the first member, there is optionally *vṛddhi*. "Half-a-kuḍava" (*ārdhakauḍavika*) means: purchased with half a *kuḍava*.

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "bought with that," as in *tena krītam*. Here, because the initial vowel of the word *kuḍava*, which denotes a specific measure, is not the letter *a*, there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi*. Rather, the intention is that *vṛddhi* occurs in the final member (*uttarapada*) by the rule "of a measure following *ardha*" (*ardhātparimāṇasya*). [Question: Why is the *tapara* (the *a* followed by *p*) specified?

The question is: since there would be no result in prohibiting the *vṛddhi* of a long vowel (*dīrgha*), it is established that [the prohibition applies] to a short vowel (*hrasva*). Regarding the example "ardhakhārī": the point is that the prohibition would not apply, because in the alternative where the first member (*pūrvapada*) does not undergo *vṛddhi*, it lacks the status of being a cause conditioned by the result with respect to that *vṛddhi*.

However, in the alternative where *vṛddhi* is applied to the first member (*pūrvapada*), since the cause for *vṛddhi* is indeed present as being conditioned by the result (*phalopahita-nimittatva*), there would necessarily be a prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvattva*) even when the *vṛddhi* of the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is prohibited.
The section beginning with "of that which ends in a measure-word" (*parimāṇāntasya*) and ending here belongs to the seventh book (*sāptamika*). Now, [we return to] the subject at hand.
[The suffix] *pañcamika* [is formed].

(1663) *Śatācca ṭhanyatau 'śate* (Pāṇini 5.1.21). [The rule] "from *śata*" means that in the sense of "worth" (*ārhīya*), the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭhañ* are applied after *śata*, but not when the meaning is "a hundred" (*śata*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *kan* suffix prescribed by the subsequent sūtra. The meaning is that [the suffix] *kan* applies by the subsequent sūtra. It should not be argued that this is already established by the shortening of the *upasarjana*; for if the rule ordaining *it* were absent, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would be removed by the rule *suk-taddhita-lukī*, and consequently, because the stem would end in a long *ā*, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply instead.

This is because it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of applying the rule] even to "pañcagoṇi" and so forth. As stated clearly in the Bhāṣya: suffixes expressing the sense of "bought" (krīta) occur only after a word denoting the original substance ending in the third case, and not in the sense of "bought by Devadatta," because such usage is not sanctioned by linguistic convention (anabhidhāna).

(1680) *tasya nimittaṃ saṃyogotpātau* |5|1|38|. "The cause of that" (*tasya nimittam*). The meaning is that when the sense is "the cause of that is either a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or a portent (*utpāta*)," the suffixes *ṭhañ* and others, as prescribed, shall be applied after a word ending in the genitive case. For example: *śatyaḥ* or *śatikaḥ*.

The meaning is "for the sake of a hundred. [The suffixes] *yat* and *ṭhan* are applied by the rule *śatācca*. Regarding the phrase "in connection with the Lord of Wealth" (*dhanapati-saṃyoge*), the meaning is "contact through officiating at sacrifices, service, and so forth. He provides an example for the sense of "an omen":
"the throbbing of the right eye is a *śatyaṃ* or a *śatikaṃ* [omen]. The meaning is "it is an omen for a hundred."
The intended meaning here is that being indicative (*sūcakatva*) itself constitutes the causal condition (*nimittatva*). Regarding the term "addition" (*upasaṅkhyāna*):
the remainder is "the suffix *ṭhak* after [words ending in] *arha*. "Anger" (*kopana*) means increase (*vṛddhi*).
It should be stated: "and [the suffix applies] after *saṃnipāta*."

"And from the combination" (*saṃnipātāt*). The suffix *ṭhañ* (which becomes *ika*) is to be understood here in the sense of "its cause is a conjunction or an outbreak," according to the rule *tasya nimittam saṃyogotpātau*. Regarding *sāṃnipātika*: in medical science (*vaidyaka*), *saṃnipāta* is well known as the confluence of the humors (*doṣas*), namely wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*). That which has this as its cause is *sāṃnipātika*.

The onset of fever and other conditions, the consumption of unwholesome food and similar factors, as well as the blackness of the tongue and other signs indicating *saṃnipāta* (a complex disorder of the humors).

(1681) *godvyaco'saṅkhyāparimāṇāśvāderyat* | Pāṇini 5.1.39. [The suffix *yat* is applied after words meaning "cow" (*go*), words having two vowels (*dvyaca*), words that are not numerals (*asaṅkhyā*), words denoting measure (*parimāṇa*), and words beginning with "horse" (*aśva*), etc., when used in the sense of a collection.]

The term *godvyacaḥ* means that the suffix *yat* should be applied after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) consisting of two syllables (*dvyañc*), provided it signifies "the cause of that" (*tasya nimittam*)—that is, either a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or a portent (*utpāta*).
However, this does not apply to words denoting numbers, measures, horses, and so forth; rather, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak*. This is the meaning of *dvyañcaḥ*.

The phrase "is cited as an example" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding "dhanya" and so forth: the meaning is "for the sake of wealth, fame, and heaven. Regarding "vijayasya": the word "nimitta" (cause) is to be supplied. Regarding "vaijayika": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.63 (*ārhīya*). Regarding "pañcānām": the word "nimitta" is to be supplied. Regarding "pañcakam": [the suffix *kan* is applied].

The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "saṅkhyāyāḥ. Thus, *saptakam* means "the cause of seven. *Prāsthikam* means "the cause of a *prastha*. By the rule "ārhāt," when the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed, the suffix *ṭhañ* from the *prāgvatīya* group is used because of the exclusion of measures (*parimāṇa*). *Khārīkam* [is derived] from *khārī*.

The meaning is "on account of" (*nimittam*). [The suffix] *ṭharak* is added by virtue of the rule for the secondary suffix (*ārhīya*) [Pāṇini 5.1.63]. Regarding *āśmakam*: the meaning is "on account of the stone" (*aśmanaḥ*). [The suffix] *ṭhak* is added by virtue of the rule for the secondary suffix (*ārhīya*) [Pāṇini 5.1.63]. The elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the rule "ṭnastaddhite" [Pāṇini 6.4.143].
(1) There is an extension of the application [of this rule] to *brahmavarcasa*.
Regarding "from *brahmavarcasa*": the meaning is that it should be stated as "*brahmavarcasācca*" in the rule *godvyacaḥ*. "Brahmavarcasyam" means "that which has *brahmavarcasa* as its cause.
(1682) *putrāc cha ca* [Pāṇini 5.1.40].

And from the word *putra* [the suffix -ya is added] in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tasya nimittam*). How then is one to explain the statement: "The priests, with self-restrained souls, undertook the *putrīyā* sacrifice"? For the sacrifice itself is neither a conjunction nor a portent. It is replied: "That by which one is joined is a conjunction" (*saṃyujyate 'nena iti saṃyogaḥ*); for it is by means of the sacrifice that one is joined with the fruit, which is a son.
It is appropriate that he be the sacrificer.
(1683) *sarvabhūmipṛthivībhyāmaṇañau* |5|1|41|. From the words *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī*, [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *añ* [are applied].
*Sarvabhūmi*: [the rule] applies only when it means "the cause of that. From these two, *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī*—[the suffixes are added].
The suffixes *aṇ* and *nañ* occur according to their respective order. In the case of *sārvabhauma*, *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhañ*.
In the case of *pārthiva*, the meaning is "that which is caused by the earth," namely, a conjunction or a portent. [In the feminine form] *pārthivī*, [the suffix is *ṅīṣ*].
As for how there is vowel-vṛddhi in both members of the compound in the word *sārvabhauma*, [it is explained as follows]:...

He says: "It is read in the *anuśatikādi* group. Thus, the meaning is that by the rule "*anuśatikādīnāṃ ca*," there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) for both members of the compound. (1684) *tasyeśvaraḥ* | 5|1|42 |
"His lord is [the suffix *īśvara*].
(1685) And also [the suffix *vidita*] in that sense. This consists of two sūtras. "And also [the suffix *vidita*] in that sense. This is the second sūtra.

The phrase "from all [stems] denoting lands and earths" (sarvabhūmipṛthivībhyām) continues to apply. However, the rule "after that [stem], the suffixes -aṇ and -añ are applied due to connection with the word nimitta, provided it means 'falling'" is suspended, because the word "tasya" (of that) is stated again. Thus, in the sense of "lord of that" (tasyeśvara), the suffixes -aṇ and -añ are applied after a stem ending in the genitive case; whereas in the sense of "known therein" (tatra vidita), they are applied after a stem ending in the locative case.

This is the meaning. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding a corresponding numerical application (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), and for the purpose of ensuring that only the term *tatra vidita* is carried over into the subsequent sūtra. (1686) *lokasarvalokāṭ ṭhañ* | Pāṇini 5.1.44.

Regarding *lokasarva*: the meaning there is "known. The intention is that, by the force of the grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*), the term *tasyeśvaraḥ* does not carry over [to this rule]. Regarding *laukika*: the meaning is "known among people" (*lokeṣu*).
He states the specific rule regarding the compound *sarvaloka*—namely, that it is due to its belonging to the *anuśatikādi* group.

(1687) *tasya vāpaḥ* |5|1|45|. The meaning is that the suffixes *ṭañ* and others, as prescribed, are added to a word ending in the genitive case in the sense of "its sowing. For example, *prāsthikam*: the meaning is a field suitable for sowing seeds measuring one *prastha*.
In the rule for the suffix *ṭhak* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of "measure" (*parimāṇa*), the suffix *iṣṭhan* applies as before.
Thus, *drauṇikam*: here, *ṭhak* is applied because [the word *droṇa*] belongs to the *niṣka*-class. *Khārīkam*: here, *īkan* is applied after *khārī*.
The meaning is: "the sowing of a *droṇa* or a *khārī*."

From *pātra*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* [is applied]. [The governing rule] remains "the sowing of that" (*tasya vāpaḥ*). Thus, *pātrikam* means "the sowing of a vessel. He states that the suffix is marked with *ṣ* for the purpose of deriving the feminine form *ṅīṣ*: namely, *pātrikī*.

(1689) *tadasmin vṛddhyāyalābhaśulkopadā dīyate* || 5.1.47 || In this [sūtra], *tadasmin* [is used]; *vṛddhi*, *āya*, *lābha*, *śulka*, and *upadā*—this is the nominative plural from a dvandva compound. Now, one might ask: "If that is so, why is *dīyate* used in the singular? To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "Interest is given," and so forth, in sequence. Thus, the meaning is that when the senses [of the locative] are "interest is given on this," "income is given on this," "profit is given on this," or "toll is given on this," the suffixes *ṭhañ* and others should be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the first case (*prathamā*).

Regarding *pañcaka*: the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *saṅkhyāyāḥ*. Regarding *śatikaḥ* and *śatya*: the analysis is "in this, an interest, income, profit, toll, or bribe of one hundred is given. [The suffixes] *ṭhan* and *yat* are applied after *śata* by the rule *śatācca ṭhanyatau*. Regarding *sāhasra*: the analysis is "in this, one thousand is given," and so forth.
In the phrase "a hundred thousand," the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Regarding "wages for protection" (*rakṣānirveśa*): protection is the safeguarding of subjects;
wages for that purpose is "wages for protection. Regarding "bribe" (*utkoca*):
it is that which is taken after making an agreement such as, "If you give me something, I will be favorable toward you at the royal court," and so forth.

The meaning is that this is called "bribery" (*utkoca*). [Regarding the statement] "an addition for the sense of the dative": "for the sense of the dative" means that growth (*vṛddhi*) and so forth are given to him.
The meaning is that this should be added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Regarding the phrase "equal [offering] to a non-Brāhmaṇa" (*samam abrāhmaṇe*):
the point is that since the desired result is achieved by simply expressing the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) itself as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), this supplementary rule need not be respected.

(1690) *pūraṇārdhāṭ ṭhan* | Pāṇini 5.1.48. The rule *pūraṇārdhāṭ ṭhan* means that the suffix *ṭhan* is added after a word ending in a ordinal number (*pūraṇa-pratyaya*) and after the word *ardha*, provided they are in the nominative case, in the sense of "this [quantity] is given as an increase and so forth in this [place]."

Regarding "dvitīyika" and "tṛtīyika": by the rule *ṭha-arhāt*, the suffix *ṭhak* is set aside and replaced by *ṭhan*. Regarding "ardhika": the meaning is "that in which a half [of the interest] or the like is given. By the statement "*ṭhan* should be stated after *ardha*," the suffix *ṭiṭhan* is set aside and replaced by *ṭhan*; for if *ṭiṭhan* were applied, there would be the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

It might be so; however, the form *ardhikā* is intended only with the suffix *ṭāp*. The phrase "of a *rūpaka*" means "of a silver *kārṣāpaṇa*. Regarding the word "conventional" (*rūḍha*): the sense is that otherwise, because the word *ardha* would be dependent on the *rūpyaka*, there would be a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). This applies in the case of the expression "conventional in the sense of half of a *rūpyaka*."
The authority [for this] must be sought. However, they say that incapacity can be prevented because it depends eternally [on another factor].
(1691) *bhāgād yañ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.49).

The rule *bhāgādyacca* means that the suffix *yat* shall also be applied after the word *bhāga*, ending in the nominative case, in the sense of "that [interest, etc. is given in this [amount]. The phrase *cāṭṭhan* implies that *ṭhan* is drawn over from the preceding sūtra; thus, the word *bhāga* also [forms *bhāgya*] in the sense of "half of a *rūpaka*."
The word "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

(1692) *taddharati vahatyāvahati bhārādvaṃśādibhyaḥ* |5|1|50|. [The suffix *ṭhan* is added after words such as *vaṃśa*] meaning "he carries that," "he bears that," or "he brings that," provided they denote a load (*bhāra*) and follow words beginning with *vaṃśa*, whether used in the singular or plural.

Because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, there is a connection through different grammatical relations (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). And that [connection] is in reverse order, as established by the commentary. Thus he says: "after *vaṃśa* and so forth.
Following the words "ending in the second case," [the suffixes are applied] in the sense of "he carries away," "he bears," or "he brings," according to the prescribed rules.
The word "syāt" (should be) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the verb]. "Haraṇa" means bringing somehow to another place, or theft.

"Vahana" means conveying by means of a cart or similar vehicle. "Āvahana" means bringing near to oneself, or producing. Regarding the term "vāṃśabhārika": the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "ṭhārhāt. In this case—

Since there is no evidence for connecting the two words ending in the fifth case (pañcamyanta) either in reverse order or through grammatical non-co-ordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya), he says: "This is another explanation of [the rule] *bhārād vaṃśādibhyaḥ*.
This other explanation is intended to dispel the misconception that the meaning is "after the word *bhāra*, from [the group beginning with] *vaṃśa* and so forth."

He clarifies this with the words: "from bamboo and so forth which have become a burden. That the words "bamboo" and so forth possess the state of being a burden is to be understood from their function (*vṛtti*) as a burden consisting of bamboo and the like. In this interpretation, the singular form in *bhārāt* is a Vedic archaism (*ārṣa*). Alternatively, it may be intended to apply to each [item] individually. In reality, however—
This refers to those words such as *vaṃśa* ("bamboo") and others that denote a "burden" (*bhāra*); that is to say, [the suffixes are added] after words signifying such things.

(1693) *vasnadravyābhyāṃ ṭhankanau* |5|1|51|. [The sūtra states: "After *vasna* and *dravya*. The phrase "he carries it, he conveys it, or he transports it" (*taddharati-vahati-āyavahati*) is understood to follow from the previous rule.
With this intention, he says: "He takes the price," and so forth.
(1694) *saṃbhavatyavaharati pacati* |5|1|52|.
[The word] *saṃbhavati* and *avaharati* [are used]. The term *tam* (accusative case), ending in the second case, is understood to follow.

The meaning is that after a word ending in the second case (accusative), an affix shall be applied as prescribed when the senses of "originating from," and so forth, are intended. Regarding the example *prāsthika*: since the word *parimāṇa* (measure) is excluded in the rule *ṭhārhāt*, the affix *ṭhak* does not apply; instead, the affix *ṭhañ* belonging to the *prāgvatīya* group is used. Now, one might object: "Does not the word *saṃbhavati* mean 'is produced'?"
Since [the root *bhū*] has this meaning and is intransitive (*akarmaka*), one might ask how there can be an accusative case in the expression "a *prastha* is produced" (*prasthaṃ saṃbhavati*).

To this he says: "The meaning is 'he causes to enter' (*samāveśayati*). The intention is that this is due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*). Regarding the example "a Brāhmaṇī who possesses a *prastha*" (*prāsthikī brāhmaṇī*): the intention is that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because the word ends in the suffix *ṭhañ*. "He brings down" (*avaharati*) means "he carries away" (*apaharati*).

The meaning is "by the force of a prefix. Regarding the example *prāsthikī brāhmaṇī*: the meaning is that the suffix *ṅīp* is applied because the word ends in the suffix *ṭhañ*. He explains *avaharati* as "he brings together" (*upasaṃharati*). The sense is that he measures [the grain] in such a way that even if it is slightly less, it becomes a measure of one *prastha*. Regarding *tat pacati*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *droṇa*.
And so on. This is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* should also occur after the word *droṇa*, ending in the accusative case, in the sense of "he cooks.
The inclusion of the term *pacati* ("he cooks") is for the purpose of excluding *avaharati* ("he threshes"), which is also possible [as a meaning]. Regarding "and *ṭhañ*":

since the suffix *ṭhak* is prescribed by the rule *ṭhārhād* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), and because *ṭhak* is excluded here due to the exclusion of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) [from that rule], *ṭhak* does not apply.

The meaning is that the suffix *iṣṭhan* from the previous rule is drawn over [by the particle] *ca*. Regarding *drauṇī*: because it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding *drauṇikī*: because it ends in the suffix *ṭhañ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
(1695) After *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra*, the suffix *kha* is optionally [applied]. 5.1.53.

The meaning is that after the words *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra* ending in the accusative case, the suffix *kha* optionally occurs in the senses of "capable of containing," "carrying away," and "cooking. In the alternative case, the suffix *ṭhañ* applies.
The intention is that because of the exclusion of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) in the rule *ṭhārhātā* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply here.

(1696) *dvigoḥ ṣṭhṃaśca* | 5|1|54 | [The sūtra] *dvigoḥ ṣṭhṃaśca*. [The word] *ṣṭhankhau* [is used]. The intention is that by the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *kha* is drawn forward [from the previous rule]. [The phrase] "or (*vā*) it is *sta*" means that the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is understood [from the previous rule]. In the alternative case, there is the suffix *ṭhañ*.

The point is that because the term *parimāṇa* (measure) is excluded in the rule "from *sthālī* etc. (*ṭhārhāt*), the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply here. Because the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Regarding the form *dvyāḍhakikī*: in the sense of "that which contains two *āḍhakas*", "that which harvests two *āḍhakas*", or "that which cooks two *āḍhakas*", a *dvigu* compound is formed by the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*). Then the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied; because it is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, resulting in *dvyāḍhakikī*. [Two] *āḍhakas*.

In the sense of "producing," "harvesting," or "cooking" one *āḍhaka*, there is a *dvigu* compound by the rule *taddhitārtha-*; then the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied, which, being marked with *ṣ*, conveys the meaning of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. Here, the substitution *aij* (for *aṇ*) does not occur by the rule *na yvābhyām*, because that rule is taught as being conditioned by the prohibition of *vṛddhi*; since there is no suffix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*, *vṛddhi* is not applicable in the first place.
Regarding the form *dvyāḍhakī*: [in the compound] *khe rūpam* (the form in the neuter), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *dvigoḥ*. Thus we have *dvyāḍhakī*.
[In the case of] *ṭhañ*, by the rule *ṭhagadhvarthe* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. The meaning is that *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *dvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.21).
However, one should not apply *ṅīp* based on the suffix *ṭhañ* itself by resorting to the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of a grammatical operation conditioned by a suffix).

This has been stated in the rule *aparimāṇavistācita...* [Pāṇini 5.1.58]. In the case of *adhyardha*, there is elision (*luk*) of only the suffix *thañ*, and not of *ṭhan* and *kha* as well, because of the force of the specific injunction. Thus, we have the forms *dvyācitikī* and *dvyācitīnā*, which are the forms when *ṭhan* and *kha* are applied respectively. Now, when there is elision of *thañ* after the word *dvyācita* by the rule *dvigoḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.21]...

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *ṅīp* might apply, he says: "Because of the prohibition of *ṅīp* by the rule *aparimāṇa-*. In this way, through the suffixes *ṣṭhan*, *kha*, *ṭhañ*, and the elision (*luk*), forms such as *dvipātrikī* and so forth are derived.
(Pāṇini 5.1.55) *kulijāl luk-khau ca*. (Note: The rule *kulijāl luk-khau ca* is provided here as part of the commentary's context for the derivation of feminine forms from words denoting measures.)

"And *luk* and *khaū* after *kulija*. Intending to show that the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) carries over, he says: "or there may be *luk* and *khaū*. Since the suffix *ṭhak* is excluded by the rule "after a word denoting a measure" (*ārhāt*), when *ṭhak* is absent, the suffix *ṭhañ* (belonging to the *prāgvahatīya* group) would normally undergo compulsory *luk* by the rule "in the case of *adhyardha*" (*adhyardhe*); [the present sūtra] provides for the optionality of this *luk*.
The rule for the option: "and *ṣṭhṃa*. Thus, there is the elision (*luk*) of *ṭhan*, as well as *kha* and *ṣṭhṃa*.

In this way, a triad—namely, the elision of *ṭhan*, *kha*, and *ṣṭhṃa*—is presented as optional alternatives. Among these, in the absence of *ṣṭhan*, *kha*, and the elision of *ṭhan*, the result is the audible presence of the suffix *ṭhan*. This is what he says: "in the absence of elision..."

"The hearing of the suffix *ṭhañ*. Regarding "dvikulijī": this is the form when there is elision (*luk*) of *ṭhañ*. [The feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.21). Regarding "dvikulijīnā": this is the form in the locative case (*khe*). Regarding "dvikulijikī": this is the form in the suffix *ṣṭhan*.
Regarding "dvaukulijikī": this is the form when there is no elision of *ṭhañ*. [This applies] in the context of the rule "parimāṇāntasya" (Pāṇini 7.3.17).
Because of the rule "ṭhasaṃjñāśāṇakulijānām," there is no vṛddhi of the subsequent member [of the compound].
(Pāṇini 5.1.56) *so'syāṃśavasnabhṛtayaḥ*.

[The sūtra states: "That is its portion" (*so'syāṃśaḥ*). The word *saḥ* ("that") applies to each of the words beginning with *aṃśa*. [The examples are: "That is its portion" (*so'syāṃśaḥ*), "that belongs to it" (*tadasya*).

The meaning is that, in the senses of "price" (*vasna*) and "this is his wages" (*sā asya bhṛtiḥ*), suffixes shall be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the nominative case. Regarding the example *pañcakaḥ*: the suffix *kan* is added by the rule "after a numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*).
(Pāṇini 5.1.57: *tad asya parimāṇam* ("that is its measure").

This is its measure (*parimāṇa*). The meaning is that, in this sense, suffixes are applied to a word ending in the first case (*prathamā*) according to the rules prescribed. In the example *prāsthikaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* (which becomes *-ika*) is applied by virtue of the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ*, because the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) was excluded from the scope of the rule *ṭhārhāt*. In this context, even a number (*saṃkhyā*) is considered a measure (*parimāṇa*), even though...
Because of the separate mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) in the rule *ṭhagopuccchasaṃkhyāparimāṇād iti*, number is not [considered] measurement (*parimāṇa*);

nevertheless, in this context, number is also measurement because it serves as a delimiting factor, as indicated by the evidence that in the subsequent sūtra, number is qualified by measurement. Therefore, [the word] *ṣaṣṭiḥ* [is used].
The form *ṣāṣṭika* ("consisting of sixty") is thus established as its measure.
However, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that forms such as *dviṣaṣṭa* and others do not occur because they are not conventionally expressed (*anabhidhānāt*).
(1700) Pāṇini 5.1.58: *saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃjñā-saṅgha-sūtra-adhyayaneṣu*. [The suffix *kan* is added after a numeral when it denotes a name, a collection, a Sūtra, or a lesson.]

"Of a number" (saṅkhyāyāḥ). It is understood that [this] continues [from the previous rule]. Thus, the meaning is: in the sense of "this is its measure" (tadasya parimāṇam), suffixes shall be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the nominative case that denotes a measure consisting of a number.
A suffix should be stated to express the same meaning as the base when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding the statement "a suffix should be stated to express the same meaning as the base when it denotes a name": in the case of *pañcakāḥ śakunayaḥ* ("five-rupee birds"), the meaning "five is their measure" is not possible, because numbers up to ten denote the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).

The meaning is that since the word *pañcan* (five) functions as a number-denoting term (*saṃkhyeya-vṛtti*), a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "the measure is five" (*pañca parimāṇam*) would be untenable; therefore, it results that the suffix is applied to the numeral itself in its own primary sense (*svārtha*) when it serves as a name (*saṃjñā*). Or rather, [this applies] to the words *dvi* (two) and *eka* (one).

Even though it is a derivative formation (*samāsa-vṛtti*), in the case of the rule "dvyekayoḥ," it is accepted that the reference is to singularity and duality; otherwise, the dual ending in "dvyekayoḥ" would be untenable. Similarly, this applies even in the case of a secondary derivative formation (*taddhita-vṛtti*), as in "pañcakāḥ śakunayaḥ" (birds consisting of five).

The meaning is that, by accepting the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *pañcan*— which refers to the number five— in the sense that "its measure (*parimāṇa*) is five-ness," a suffix is justified after the word *pañcan*, which denotes five-ness, when applied to that which possesses five-ness as its measure. In this context, [the suffix] is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*) to form a name (*saṃjñā*).

He provides an illustration: "only five. He provides an illustration of the suffix applied to that which possesses a measure (*parimāṇin*): "five is the measure. This means "the state of being five" (*pañcatva*). Regarding the word "in a collection" (*saṅghe*): the meaning is that an example will be stated. "A group of five" (*pañcaka*): this means "the measure of a collection consisting of the state of being five."

The "fivefold nature" (*pañcatva*) of the *saṅgha* (the collection) is to be understood by way of its constituent parts. Regarding the word "sūtra": the phrase "is cited" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the expression "the *Aṣṭaka* of Pāṇini": the word "sūtra" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has eight chapters (*adhyāya*) as its measure. Here, the state of being eight is [determined] by way of the chapters.

It follows the *sūtra*. And the word *sūtra* refers here to a collection of *sūtras*, because it is impossible for the state of being eightfold to exist within a single *sūtra*. Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since the goal is already accomplished by mentioning the 'collection' (*saṅgha*) alone, the mention of 'sūtra' is redundant. To this he replies: "Of the word *saṅgha*... [and] "the study consists of five [parts]."

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has five as its measure (*parimāṇa*) is *pañcāvṛti*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed after a word denoting a number [when it means] 'this is its measure'": this refers to the application of the suffix *ḍa* when the sense is "this is its measure" (*tadasya parimāṇam*), provided the word expresses a number.
The word "should be added" (*upasaṃkhyātavya*) is the ellipsis. Kaiyaṭa holds that the word *stoma* is directly expressive (*śakta*) when referring to a collection of *sāman*-based mantras;
his intention is that when it refers to a collection of humans and the like, the word *stoma* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*). Thus he says: "fifteen mantras" and "the fifteenfold *stoma*."

When the suffix *ḍa* is added to the word *pañcadaśan*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final syllable) occurs by the rule *ṭeḥ*. This means a collection of fifteen mantras that serves as the substratum for the *sāman*. Now, one might object: even in the absence of the marker *ṅ*, the elision of the *ṭi* would be established simply by the rule *na-staddhite*; therefore, the presence of the marker *ṅ* is redundant. To this, he replies: *ekaviṃśa*.

Thus [it is said]. The analysis of the compound is: "that collection whose measure consists of twenty-one mantras. Regarding the suffix *ḍa*: by the rule *ṭi-viṃśater-ḍiti*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final syllable). However, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that [these are] things to be accomplished by means of chanted mantras denoted by words such as *pṛṣṭha* and *rathantara*, [and they are so designated] because of their possession of specific qualities (*guṇavatvena*).
Praise consisting of description is itself the *stoma*; that alone is the meaning of the suffix *-ḍa*.
The meaning is that a *stoma* is that which has the measure of fifteen chanted mantras.
The measure, consisting of the number fifteen, is to be understood as residing in the praise by means of the mantras. And thus:

They say that in such passages as "They praise with the fifteen-fold [stoma]," the coreferentiality of words such as "fifteen" with the act of praising—which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root—is logically established.
Relying on that view, he says: "In the Soma sacrifices," and so forth.
The words *paṅkti*, *viṃśati*, *triṃśat*, *catvāriṃśat*, *pañcāśat*, *ṣaṣṭi*, *saptati*, *aśīti*, *navati*, and *śata* [are used as feminine]. 5.1.59.

The words *paṅkti* and *viṃśati* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the suffix *śati*. The remainder [of the rule] is: "in the sense of 'this is its measure'. In the sense of "that which has five feet as its measure," the suffix *ti* is added to the word *pañcan*, there is elision of the final vowel of the base (*prakṛti*), and the letter *c* undergoes the change to *k* (*kutva*).

The *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* [substitutions apply]. The form is *paṅkti*. According to the science of prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*), "a *paṅkti* consists of five syllables and five feet. A group of ten is a *daśat*; it will be stated that "the words *pañca* and *daśat* [are used] optionally in the sense of a group. This collection has two *daśats* as its measure; thus, it is *viṃśati*.

The suffix *śati* is applied, the initial vowel of the base undergoes elision (*vinbhāva*), and an *anusvāra* is added. Here, the mention of "a collection" (*saṅgha*) continues [from the previous rule]. Thus, the form *gavāṃ viṃśatiḥ* ("twenty of cows") occurs.
However, when one intends to express the identity (*tādātmya*) between the collection and the members of the collection, the form *viṃśatir gāvaḥ* ("twenty cows") occurs.

The singular number and the feminine gender [are used] because of the unity of the inherent nature (*svabhāva*). The same applies to the numbers beginning with thirty. As Amarasimha states: "The numbers beginning with twenty are always used in the singular, [denoting] both the countable and the counting," and "Among those, up to ninety, they are feminine. Thus, that which has a measure of three times ten is "three hundred" (*triśat*).

The suffix *śat* is applied, and the original base (*prakṛti*) undergoes the substitution of *triṃśat*. That community has forty as its measure; [the suffix] *śat* is applied, and the original base undergoes the substitution of *catvāriṃśat*. That community has fifty as its measure; [the suffix] *śat* is applied, and the original base—

The substitution of *pañca* [for *pañcan*]: when sixty is the measure of this group, it is *ṣaṣṭiḥ*. The suffix *ti* is applied, and there is the substitution of *ṣaṣ* for the base, along with the absence of the *jaś*-substitution. When seventy is the measure of this group, it is *saptatiḥ*. The suffix *ti* is applied, and there is the substitution of *sapta* for the base.
