The phrase "*śadeḥ śitaḥ*" and "*mriyater luṅliṅośca*" constitute one sentence; [it applies] to that which is about to become *śit*.

The meaning is that the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] shall occur after the root *śad*, and the *ātmanepada* shall occur after the roots *mṛ* and *mṛṅ* when they serve as the bases for the *luṅ* (aorist) and *liṅ* (optative/mood) suffixes, and not otherwise. By this, forms such as *śīyate*, *mriyate*, and *mamāre* are established. Furthermore, there is another rule: "Not after *san*" (*sano na*). This applies to both *śad* and *mriyate*.
Furthermore, there is the rule that the ātmanepada is not used after a root ending in a *san* suffix; therefore, in forms such as *śiśatsati* and *mumūrṣati*, the ātmanepada does not occur.
(558) *propābhyāṃ yujerayajñapātreṣu* 1.3.64. [The ātmanepada is used after the root *yuj* when preceded by *pra* or *upa*, provided it does not refer to sacrificial vessels.]
Regarding "propābhyām," the word "ātmanepada" (the middle voice) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding "svarādyanta":

that which has vowels (*svara*) as its initial or final element is "svarādyanta. The meaning is that the *ātmanepada* suffix is applied to the root *yuj* only when it follows such a prefix (*upasarga*). Regarding "dvandvam": "dvandvam" means in pairs; [as in] *nyañci*.
The meaning is "not below" (*adhobhila*).
(559) *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ* |1|3|65|. [The word] *samaḥ* [is connected with] *kṣṇuvaḥ*. The remainder [of the sūtra] is "the ātmanepada [terminations]. [The word] *samo*...
In the rule *gamyṛccibhyām*, the author did not formulate the sutra as *samo gamyṛccchikṣ ṇuvaḥ*;
for if that were the case, because of the continued application of the condition "from an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāt*), the suffix would not apply after transitive verbs.
Indicating this, he provides the example: *saṃkṣṇute śastram* ("he sharpens the weapon").
The meaning is "he sharpens.
(560) *bhujo'navane* | 1.3.66 | Regarding *bhujo'navane*: *avana* means protection; [the rule applies] elsewhere than that.

The meaning is that the *bhuj* root takes the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) endings. Now, it is established in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) that *bhuja* means "to protect" (*pālana*) and "to eat" (*abhyavahāra*). In that case, in the expression "he enjoyed the earth" (*bubhuje pṛthivīm*), protection cannot be the intended meaning; for if it were, the *ātmanepada* would be improper due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not in the sense of protecting" (*anavane*).
Nor can there be consumption [by the earth], because that is impossible; for the consumption of the earth is not possible.

Likewise, the statement "an old person experiences hundreds of sufferings" is not tenable, because the sustaining and the consumption of hundreds of sufferings are both impossible. To this, he says: "In this case..."

The meaning of the root *bhuj* is "to enjoy. This is because verbal roots possess multiple meanings; such is the intended sense. In the phrase "he enjoys the earth" (*mahīm bhunakti*), the meaning is "he protects. Here, only the root belonging to the *raudhādika* class—namely, *bhuja* in the sense of "protection and eating"—is intended to be understood, and not the root *bhuja* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*).
The *Bhāṣya* states that this [rule] applies even to roots belonging to the *tudādi* class as well. In the example *bhujati vāsaḥ*, the meaning is "it becomes curved.
(561) *ṇer aṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartā'nādhyāne* | 1|3|67| *ṇer aṇau*: Here there are four subordinate sentences. The first sentence is *ṇeḥ*.
By the paribhāṣā rule regarding the inclusion of the suffix, "ṇeḥ" (of the causative suffix) is understood as referring to that which ends in it.

"Ātmanepadam" is the governing heading. Thus he says: "The ātmanepada [suffix] shall occur after a causative (ṇyanta) verb. The second sentence is: "That which was the object in the non-causative (aṇau) remains so in the causative (ṇau), provided it is not the agent. [This applies to the rule] "kartari karmavyatihāre" (when there is a reciprocal action, the suffix is used in the sense of the agent).
In this context, the word *karma* refers to the action (*kriyā*). Because of the constant syntactic connection between *yat* and *tat*, the word *tat* is understood.

Thus, the second sentence is obtained: "And so, if that which is the action in the *aṇ* [root] is [the same action] in the *ṇic*-ending [root]. This being the case, in examples such as *pacati* (he cooks) and *pācayati* (he causes to cook), [the action] is entirely in the *aṇ* [root].
Because [the action] must necessarily exist at the end of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), this second sentence would be redundant.

Therefore, the restrictive particle *eva* is understood as "if that very same action which exists in the non-causative (*aṇ*) is expressed by the causative (*ṇyant*). Consequently, he states the result of the second sentence: "If that very action which exists in the non-causative is expressed by the causative, then that [agent of the non-causative] is the agent [of the causative]. (*sa kartā*)
This is the third statement: "In this context, whatever kāraka is the object (*karman*) under the rule for *ṇic* (*ṭhaṇau*), that shall be the agent (*kartṛ*) under the rule for *ṇiC* (*iṇṇau*).

Here, the masculine gender of the pronoun *tat* should be understood in accordance with the word *kartṛ*, which is the term to be predicated (*vidheya*), just as in the expression: "That which is coolness is indeed the nature of water. Now, [the sūtra] says: "Except in the case of mental perception (*anādhyāne*)."

He explains the fourth statement—"but not in the case of *ādhyāna*"—as follows: *ādhyāna* is recollection preceded by longing. He considers this to be a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (an absolute negation), meaning that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not apply there.
However, in reality, if one adopts the interpretation that "the middle voice does not occur in *ādhyāna*," then it would follow [that it occurs elsewhere].

Because the negative particle (*nañ*) lacks syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*) when conjoined with [the term] *ādhyāna*, a compound with the word *ādhyāna* is impossible; therefore, this is indeed an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). The root text, "not in the sense of *ādhyāna*," is intended merely to state the resultant meaning. Thus, the rule means that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) shall occur after a causative (*ṇyanta*) root when it signifies a meaning other than *ādhyāna*.
Since the word *ādhyāne* (in the sense of "meditating upon") is construed only with the first sentence, it is logical that there are exactly three sentences;

indeed, the expression "three sentences" (*vākyatrayam*) is precisely what is seen in the Bhāṣya. Now, one might ask: since [the desired result] is already established by the rule *ṇicaśca*, for what purpose is this sūtra? To this he says: *ṇicaśce'ti*. [This is so] even when the fruit goes to another (*paragāmini*).

The meaning is "for the sake of the middle voice (ātmanepada). This might be so: the rule "vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne" will be stated [later]. Its meaning is that the middle voice which is prescribed when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent may optionally occur when the fact that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent is understood through an accompanying word (upapada).

The examples for [the rule] "ṭhsvaṃ yajñaṃ yajati yajate vā" and so forth are well known. However, regarding the rule "ṭhṇeraṇau," an example—"darśayate bhavaḥ"—will be stated immediately following this very point. In that context, in the sentence "darśayate bhavaḥ svayameva," when there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (kartṛgāmitva), [the ātmanepada affix is applied].

The *ātmanepada* ending is intended to be obligatory by the rule *ṇeraṇau*. In that case, however, the optionality provided by *vibhāṣopapadena* would apply because it is a subsequent rule (*paratvāt*). This is because *ṇeraṇau* finds its scope when there is no *upapada* (governing word) indicating that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*ātmagāmitva*). Furthermore—

It will be stated [in Pāṇini 1.3.87]: "After a root that is intransitive when not in the causative (*aṇyanta*) and whose agent is like one who possesses consciousness (*citavat*), the *parasmaipada* ending occurs after it in the causative (*ṇyanta*). The meaning of this is: after a root which is intransitive when not in the causative and whose agent is like one possessing consciousness, the *parasmaipada* ending shall occur when it is in the causative. For example: "Kṛṣṇa lies down" (*śete kṛṣṇaḥ*); "The cowherd girl makes him lie down" (*taṃ gopī śāyayati*).

However, the established rule is that the [causative] *ṇeraṇau* [Pāṇini 1.3.67] applies specifically to the example "bhavo darśayate" (Bhava causes himself to be seen). In that context, regarding the root *lū*, in the sentence "Devadatta cuts the field" (*lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*), because the agent possesses consciousness, the field becomes a "karmakartr̥" (an object-agent) in the passive construction "the field is cut" (*lūyate kedāraḥ*), where the object, the field, functions as the agent.

Because [the root] is intended to be transitive and is also intransitive, in the case of *lāvayate kedāraḥ* (he causes the field to be reaped), the ātmanepada prescribed by *ṇeraṇau* would be set aside by the subsequent rule *aṇāvakarmakāc cetanāvataḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.88),
and thus only the parasmaipada would apply; for the rule *ṇeraṇau* applies in cases such as *darśayate bhavaḥ*.
Because there is scope [for the application of the other rule], he says: "But when the agent's intention [is involved]" (*kartrabhiprāye tu*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of a prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*): the usage in the Bhāṣya, "the king shows himself" (*rājā darśayate*), is the authority for resorting to a prior prohibition; otherwise, in that case, the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt* would apply.

Because of the occurrence of the *parasmaipada* ending, in the sense that "he becomes an object of vision," the verb *dṛś* (to see) in the sentence *paśyati bhavaḥ* (Bhava sees) is both intransitive (*akarmaka*) and has an agent possessing consciousness (*cetana-vat-kartṛka*). Therefore, regarding the scope of the optional rule *vibhāṣopapadena* (Pāṇini 1.3.77), one must resort to the principle of *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of the former) to override the alternative; this, however, is merely a matter of interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).

[This is] the refuge. Others, however, maintain that the usage in the Bhāṣya, "darśayate rājā" (the king shows himself), will concern a case where the fruit of the action goes to another. And thus, when the fruit of the action goes to the agent, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the application of the rule "aṇau akarmakāt" (Pāṇini 1.3.88), because it is subsequent [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī].

They say that resorting to the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the rule of priority for the preceding) is questionable; however, that is questionable because, in the case of the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt*, its application would be unavoidable even when the fruit goes to another (*paragāmin*), since it is subsequent [to other rules]. For in the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt*, the term "kartrabhiprāya" (intended for the agent) does not apply.

Thus it exists; for [the application of] the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye* is [otherwise] very remote, as explained at length in the *Śabdaratna*. Now, one might object: in the case of *darśayate bhavaḥ*, meaning "Bhava becomes the object of seeing," when there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of Bhava—who is in reality the object of the act of seeing—then [the following applies]: his...

Since the status of being like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) would apply by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would thus be established by the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, the sūtra *ṇer aṇau* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "that which resides in the agent" (*kartṛstha*). Those for whom the state (*bhāva*) resides in the agent are called "those whose state resides in the agent" (*kartṛsthabhāvakāḥ*).

Those roots for whom the action resides in the agent are "agent-resident actions" (*kartṛsthakriyā*); such roots are the examples here in this sūtra. However, as for the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, its examples are those roots whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and those whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), according to the sūtra *karmavat karmaṇā* in the present context.

And this is clear from the Bhāṣya. Therefore, because the objects [of the two rules] differ, the sense is that the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87) does not render superfluous the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67). An action (*bhāva*) is a verbal root-meaning accomplished by means that do not involve physical motion, such as seeing, hearing, and so forth. [An action] accomplished by means involving physical motion...

The meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is action (*kriyā*), such as cooking (*pāka*) and so forth. Although in the act of seeing there is a movement consisting of the opening of the eyes and so on, there is no contradiction here because "movement" refers specifically to the gestures of the hands, feet, and other limbs, which are distinct from that [ocular movement]. In this regard, he provides an example of an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*): "They see Your Lordship."

Regarding the term "devotees" (*bhaktāḥ*): among transitive verbal roots (*sakarmaka-dhātu*), a root denotes both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). For example, in the case of the root *pac* ("to cook"), it denotes an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*). Therein, the softening is the result; the operation conducive to that is the act of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth. The agent (*kartṛ*) is the locus of the operation denoted by the root.

Devadatta and so forth [are the agent]. An object (*karman*) is that which serves as the substratum of the result conveyed by a verbal root whose operation has a different locus [from the agent]. For example, in the case of "he cooks rice" (*taṇḍulān pacati*), the established position is that the rice is the substratum of the softening (*viklitti*). And in the present context, if the root *dṛś* (to see) were to mean an operation conducive to visual cognition, its transitivity would be untenable, because the result...
Because visual cognition and the effort conducive to it share a common locus,

the meaning of the root *dṛś* (to see) is an operation conducive to the attainment of the status of being an object of visual cognition. In this context, the attainment of the status of being an object of cognition is the result (*phala*), and the effort and other such operations conducive to that [attainment] are the means.
[The action] resides in Devadatta.

And thus, it is logical that the pot and so forth are the object (*karman*), as they are the substratum of the result—namely, the state of being the object of visual cognition—which occurs at a time distinct from the operation such as effort. This is what [the author] expresses by saying: "the meaning is that they make [the pot] the object of visual cognition."

Regarding "impulsion" (*preraṇā*): when the meaning intended by the root *dṛś* (to see) is simply the attainment of the status of being an object of visual cognition, and not the effort conducive to that [attainment]—which is the element of instigation (*preṣaṇā*) understood from the root *kṛ* (to do)—then the sentence "Bhava sees" (*paśyati bhavaḥ*) has the meaning: "Bhava becomes an object of visual cognition."
It should be understood that, due to the desire to emphasize the excellence of ease (*saukaryātiśaya*), the aspect of the "conducive operation" (*anukūlavyāpāra*) is not intended to be expressed.

Thus, since the meaning of the root *dṛś* (to see) is simply the attainment of the status of being an object of visual cognition (*cākṣuṣajñānaviṣayatvāpatti*), the world (*bhava*)—which is the substratum of that [attainment]—is indeed the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore he says: "the meaning is 'it becomes an object,'" using [the term] figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*).

The meaning is that [the self] becomes the object of visual cognition; this is the sense. Nor should it be suspected here that, because the self is in reality the agent of the act of seeing, it would—by the rule "that which has an action equal to its object through its own object" (Pāṇini 3.1.87)—be treated like an object (karmavat), and thus suffixes such as *ya* would apply rather than *śap* and so on. This is not to be feared.
The rule *karmavat karmaṇā* applies to roots whose action resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and to those whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriya*).

Therefore, the meaning is that even in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), suffixes such as *śap* and so on are indeed employed. "From that" means setting aside the aspect of instigation (*preṣaṇāṃśa*) understood from the root *kṛ*.

The meaning of the causative suffix *ṇic* in the root *dṛś* (to see) is "the attainment of the status of being an object of visual cognition. In the expression "devotees cause You to be seen" (*darśayanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ*), the realized meaning of the causative form is "they bring about [Your] state of being an object of visual cognition. Thus he says: "the meaning is 'they see'"; that is, [they make You] an object of visual cognition.

The meaning is "they perform. Regarding the word *punar* (again): in the example cited—"darśayanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ" (the devotees show Lord Śiva)—where the sense is "they cause [him] to become the object of visual cognition," if the causative element (*ṇij-artha*), namely the aspect of "causing to attain," is not intended to be expressed, then by this very sūtra, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs, resulting in "darśayate."

The meaning is that "bhava" is the illustrative example. Here, there is an indication (lakṣaṇā) of the causative sense [of being] devoid of instigation (preraṇā). The presence of the causative suffix (ṇic) is like that of the feminine suffix ṭāp in the expression "gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ. Others hold that because the curādigaṇa is an open-ended class (ākṛtigaṇa), the ṇic is added in its own sense (svārthika). Regarding "iha": the state (avasthā)...
It is a specific arrangement of parts consisting of specific words.

The analysis of the compound *prathamatṛtīye* is "the first and the third" (*prathamā ca tṛtīyā ca prathamatṛtīye*); thus it refers to those two states. According to the rule *sarvanāmno vṛtimātre*, the word *prathamā* takes the masculine form [as *prathama*]. "Devotees behold the Lord"—this is the first state.
This refers to the arrangement of specific stages (*padaviśeṣasaṃdarbha*). In the root text, the term *kakṣyā* will be used as a synonym for "stage" (*avasthā*).

For *kakṣyā* denotes, in the context of a royal capital or similar setting, a residential area consisting of a gathering of specific classes of people that leads one to the immediately adjacent location. As it says in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "He did not [pass] beyond the fifth *kakṣyā*..."

"Someone prevented him," and so forth. This first sentence provides the justification for the second sentence, "He saw Bhava," by showing that there was a relinquishing of the element of instigation (*preraṇāṃśa*) regarding the object of sight, which is brought within the scope of visual cognition. Thus, there is a relinquishing of the element of instigation with respect to the visible object.
This is because it would be impossible in the absence of the first sentence, which contains the root *dṛś* (to see) qualified by the element of instigation (*preraṇā*).

When the element of instigation is abandoned, the second stage— *paśyati bhavaḥ* ("Bhava sees")— arises from the causative suffix *ṇic* added to the root *dṛś* in the sense of merely becoming the object of seeing, as in *darśayanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ* ("the devotees cause Bhava to be seen").

The third sentence, "devotees see Bhava," has the same meaning as the first sentence, which would entail [the same] entry [into the same grammatical category]. However, this third sentence— "they cause to see"—
is the object of perception for the fourth sentence, "Bhava causes himself to be seen," insofar as the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is not intended to be expressed.

It is quite clear that [the sentence] containing the causative suffix (*ṇic*) serves as a justification for the same meaning as the second statement, namely "bhavatīti. Thus, between the first and third stages—

the two cases of "devotees see Bhava" (*paśyanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ*) and "devotees cause Bhava to be seen" (*darśayanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ*), as well as "Bhava sees" (*paśyati bhavaḥ*) and "Bhava causes himself to be seen" (*darśayate bhavaḥ*)— [the relationship is established].

Thus, the meaning is that the sense is the same for the second and fourth stages (*kakṣyā*). Regarding this, considering that there is no possibility of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix in the first and second stages precisely because the root *dṛś* is not in its causative form (*ṇyanta*), he says: "In that regard, in the third stage, there is no *taṅ*. To the question "Why? [the answer follows].

He says: "Even when the action is the same. This refers to the fact that although the portion of the rule stating "the very action which exists in the *aṇ* [denominative] is expressed by the *ṇi*-ending" is valid for the third stage—"devotees show Bhava"—insofar as it has the same meaning as the first stage—"devotees see Bhava"—nevertheless, in the first stage, within the *aṇ*...

The meaning is that in the third stage (the *ṇic*-formation), because the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) of the *bhava*—which was the object (*karmakāraka*) in the original sense—is absent, [it cannot be called a *bhāva*]. Thus, it is stated that this third stage, which establishes the fourth stage, serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). The very same action that exists in the *aṇ* [denominative] base...

Regarding the portion [of the sūtra] stating "it is expressed by the suffix -ṇic," it will be explained that under the view of superimposed instigation (*adhyāropitapreraṇapakṣa*), the result is that the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings do not occur in the second stage. However, the fourth stage is the illustrative example for the present sūtra; thus he says: "But in the fourth [stage], there is *taṅ*. This refers to the rule *ṇeraṇau*.

The phrase "by the present sūtra" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. He establishes that very point by saying, "taking the second [case]": in the second stage, namely "Bhava sees," there is the action consisting in the attainment of being an object of visual cognition; it is precisely that same action which [is expressed] in "Bhava shows himself."

The meaning is that in the fourth example, it is because the root *dṛś* is used in its causative (*ṇic*) form. By this, the portion [of the rule] stating "if the action which is expressed by the root in the non-causative (*ṇau*) is expressed by the same root in the causative (*ṇyante*)" has been established. Now, he establishes the portion stating "if that which was the object (*karmakāraka*) in the non-causative (*ṇau*) becomes the agent (*kartā*) in the causative (*ṇau*)," beginning with the words "In the first [example], they see. They see...

The meaning is that in the first stage, Bhava is the object (*karman*) of the root *dṛś* in its non-causative (*aṇ*) form—as in "Bhava is seen"—and in the fourth stage, as in "Bhava causes himself to be seen" (*darśayate bhavaḥ*), he is the agent (*kartṛ*) of the causative (*ṇi*) form of *dṛś*.
Now, he provides an example of a verbal root whose action resides in the agent: "In the same way, the elephant causes itself to be mounted," and so forth. In that case...

He states the first level: "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant. Those who protect the elephant are *hastipās*; they themselves are the *hastipakas*. The suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*). The meaning of the root *ruh* is an activity conducive to ascending the upper part. In that regard—

In expressions such as "he ascends the palace," the action conducive to stepping upon the upper part consists of activities like climbing the stairs. Here, however, what is intended to be expressed as the action conducive to stepping upon the upper part is simply the act of making the tall elephant low; that is, the act of lowering it.

Thus it is said: "causing to bend downwards" (*nyagbhāvayanti*). Here, the operation (*vyāpāra*) consists of the striking of the goad and so forth, which is conducive to bending downwards in a manner favorable for ascending the upper part [of the body].
The result (*phala*) is the bending downwards that is favorable for ascending the upper part. Because he is the locus of that [result], the elephant is the object (*karman*).

Because they are the substrata of such an activity, the elephant-drivers are the agents. Therefore, he states the second stage with the words "then" (*tataḥ*). When the aspect of instigation (*preraṇā*) is set aside, [the verb] *ārohati* (he mounts) is used in the present tense (*laṭ*) to denote the act of bending down in a manner conducive to the mounting of the upper part; thus, "the elephant mounts."
The meaning is "it becomes subordinate. He states the result of the abandonment of the element of instigation (*preṣaṇāṃśa*) by saying: "the meaning is 'it becomes subordinate'.

Now he describes the third stage: "then the causative suffix *ṇic*. This means that when there is a desire to express instigation (*preṣaṇa*) from a root that has adopted the sense of "becoming subordinate" after abandoning the element of instigation, this is the causative suffix *ṇic* added for the sake of a motive (*hetu*).
The state [of the meaning]. Regarding "they cause to mount": the words "the elephant-keepers [cause] the elephant" are to be supplied as the remainder.
He states the realized meaning of the causative (*ṇijanta*) when the portion consisting of the command has ceased: "the meaning is 'they mount'.
That is to say, they bring the elephant down [to a level] for the purpose of mounting it. He states the fourth stage: from that...
Thus, when the element of instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, the form *ārohayate* arises from the causative (*ṇyanta*) root by means of the present sūtra;
this is the meaning. When the aspect of instigation is abandoned, he states the resulting meaning of the causative:
"the meaning is that it becomes bent down (*nyagbhavati*). In this very way, [the rule applies] to a root from which instigation has ceased, in its original sense (*prākṛte 'rthe*).
This was illustrated by relying on the view that "he causes to be purified" (*ṇijiṣyate*).

Now, relying on the view where the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, he says: "Or else," and "they see," as in "devotees see the Lord" (*paśyanti bhakta bhagavantam*) and "elephant-drivers mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ*).

The meaning is that the first stage (*kakṣyā*) is to be explained as before. He states the second stage with the words "then, from the object" (*tataḥ karmaṇaḥ*). The meaning is that because Bhava and the elephant—which were the objects (*karman*) in the first stage—are superposed with the status of being causes (*hetu*) consisting in their being instigating agents (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule for "causative [verbs]" (*hetumaṇṇic*). Thus: *darśayati bhavaḥ*.
Thus [it is said]. The word "devotees" (*bhaktān*) is to be supplied as the object. He states this: "The meaning is that he impels those who are ascending and those who are descending.

The meaning is that Bhava impels the devotees by bringing them within the range of visual perception, while he impels the elephant-drivers by making them subordinate, just as an elephant impels its drivers. In both cases, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used with a causal sense.

In this regard, the established position is that from the two roots *dṛś* and *ruh* in their primitive forms (*prakṛti*), there is one instigation each; however, by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), another distinct instigation directed toward those same objects is understood for each.
He states the fourth stage: "Then, by the two *ṇics*"—that is, by the two causative suffixes (*hetumaṇic*).

When the two causal suffixes (*ṇic*) derived from the roots *dṛś* (to see) and *ruh* (to ascend), which constitute the original bases, are dropped, the meaning results in "Bhava becomes an object of visual perception" and "the elephant submits," respectively. In that case, by the present sūtra, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied, as in *darśayate bhavaḥ* ("Bhava shows himself") and *ārohayate* ("he causes himself to be mounted").

The meaning is that it is established that [the self] is "an elephant. This is because, in the first stage—where [it is said] "devotees see the Lord" (*bhavaṃ paśyanti*) and "elephant-keepers mount the elephant" (*hastinaṃ ārohanti*)—the objects (*karman*) of the first stage, namely *bhava* and the *hastin*, become the agents (*kartṛ*) in the third stage; thus, the action which belongs to the causative suffix (*ṇi*) in the first stage [is the same as that of the agent in the third].

Thus, in this third stage, because *bhava* (the state of being) is the object (*karman*) and the elephant (*hastin*) is the agent (*kartṛ*), [the action] in the first stage— which consists of "making [the objects] the objects of visual cognition" or "subordinating them"— is the portion of the instigation (*preṣaṇāṃśa*) inherent in the verbal root (*prakṛti*) [of the causative], which [persists] in the third stage.

If it is argued that "only that action which [occurs] in the two stages of relinquishing and receiving would be expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*)," then how could there be any engagement [in the first stage]? This objection is invalid because, in the statement "only that [action] by the causative suffix," only an excess is excluded, not a deficiency as well. Now, [if one objects that] it is only in the second stage...
To the question "Why not?", he says: "In this view, [the rule applies] to the second [kakṣyā]. To the question "Why?", he says:

"Because of the absence of identical action (samānakriyatva). This means that in the second stage (kakṣyā), the condition that the very same action which belongs to the *aṇ* suffix must be expressed by the *ṇi*-derived suffix (*ṇyantena*) is absent.

He establishes that very point with the words "of the meaning of *ṇic*. Why [is there] the mention of *ṇeḥ*? [So that it does not apply] to cases such as "he sees" (*paśyati*) or "he climbs" (*ārohati*), where the causal impulsion (*preṣaṇā*) has ceased; for example, "the cuckoo remembers the forest thicket" (*smarati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ*). The meaning is: "it causes [the thicket] to become an object of memory. This [rule] applies in both views.
The first stage is also indicative of the second and third stages.

Among these, in the view where the causal operation (*preṣaṇa*) is withdrawn, the second stage is expressed as "the mango grove remembers" (*smarati vanagulmaḥ*), meaning it becomes the object of remembrance. [In the third stage,] one says, "the cuckoo causes the mango grove to remember" (*smarayati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ*).
The third stage: the meaning is that it causes [the object] to become the object of memory. The second stage:
under the view of instigation (*preṣaṇa*), however, the second stage is "the forest thicket makes the cuckoo remember" (*smarayati vanagulmaḥ kokilam*).
The meaning is that it impels one who is already remembering. Thus: "the forest thicket makes [him] remember."

This is a counter-example. It should be understood that this constitutes the fourth stage (*kakṣyā*) under the view that the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is withdrawn (*nivṛta*), whereas under the view that the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropita*), it constitutes the third stage. [In the form *smārayati*], because the root *smṛ* belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, it is marked with *mit*, and thus the vowel is shortened. The detailed discussion on this point is as follows.
This should be investigated in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, the *Śabdaratna*, and the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
(562) *gṛdhiñcyoḥ pralambhane* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.69]. Regarding *gṛdhi* and *vañci*: considering that "deception" (*pralambhana*) means "fraud" (*pratāraṇa*), he says: "in the sense of fraud."
Thus; "as before" means that the *ātmanepada* [endings] apply. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, these two [roots] function in the sense of "deceiving. (563) Pāṇini 1.3.71:
*mithyopapadātkṛño'bhyāse* ("After the root *kṛ*, when preceded by the word *mithyā*, [the *ātmanepada* endings are used] in the sense of repetition").

"From *mithyā* as an upapada": the meaning is that the *ātmanepada* ending is used after the root *kṛ*, when the word *mithyā* is employed as an upapada due to repetition (*abhyāsa*). From this point onward, the rule "after [roots] having *ṇi*" is no longer applicable. (564) *Apād vadaḥ* | 1.3.73 | [The *ātmanepada* ending is used after the root *vad* preceded by the preverb *apa*.]

*Apādvadaḥ*: This means that the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] suffix is applied after the root *vad* when preceded by the prefix *apa*. The phrase "he refutes the logical principle" (*nyāyamapavadate*) means he rejects it by means of a statement; this is according to the maxim: "What could a formal statement (*vacana*) not accomplish? There is no burden too heavy for a formal statement."

(565) *samudāṅbhyo yamo’granthe* |1|3|75|. The meaning is that the Ātmanepada is used after the root *yam*, preceded by the prefixes *sam*, *ut*, and *āṅ*, provided the sense does not concern a book (*agrantha*). Example: *vrīhīn saṃyacchate* ("he gathers the rice").
"Thus" means "he gathers. "He lifts a burden" means "he raises it up.
"He stretches out a cloth" means "he fastens it to a mat or similar object. "Only when [the action] is intended for the agent" is the rule;
thus, "he gathers rice" means "he gathers it for the sake of another. [The root] *āṅ-ya*...

Although the form would have been established by *yamahana* alone, the inclusion of *āṅ* is for the sake of [roots] that take an object (*sakarmaka*), since that [augment] applies only to [roots] that are intransitive (*akarmaka*). This is how it should be understood.
(566) *anupasargājjñaḥ* | 1.3.76 | [The suffix *ātmanepada* is used after the root *jñā* when it is not preceded by a prefix.]

"Anupasargājjñaḥ": the meaning is that the ātmanepada [ending] is used after the root *jñā* when it is not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). Since this would already be established by the rule "ṭhakarmakācca" (Pāṇini 1.3.46), which prescribes the ātmanepada for intransitive roots, this present rule is intended for the sake of transitive roots. Thus he says: "He recognizes the cow" (*gāṃ jānīte*). How so? Because the root preceded by *anu* has the sense of "consenting" (*anumati*).

The meaning is: since the verbal root *jñā* is preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), the present sūtra does not apply; and because it is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the rule "from an intransitive root" (*akarmakāt*) also does not apply—so how can there be the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the form *anujajñe*?
He provides the resolution: "the *liṭ* [affix] is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi liṭ*). And thus...

The intention is that the *ātmanepada* ending is used because of the rule "the [ending] of the agent and the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*). This results in the meaning: "the departure of the son was permitted. Now, one might ask: if this is so, how can the word "nṛpa" (king), which ends in the nominative case, be construed here? To this he replies: "there is a transformation [of case], [namely] 'by the king' (*nṛpeṇa*)."

In the phrase *avāluloce*, the word *nṛpaḥ* ending in the nominative case, which is connected [in the previous rule], is understood here as being modified by the third case; this is the meaning of "is supplied here.
(567) *vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne* | 1.3.77 | [The agent and the object are optionally not expressed when the meaning is already conveyed by a subordinate word.]

"With a qualifying word (*vibhāṣopapadena*). This refers to the group of five sūtras beginning with *svaritañitaḥ*, namely: *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*, *apādvadaḥ*, *ṇicaśca*, *samudāṅbhyo yamo'granthe*, and *anupasargājjñaḥ*. "Pronounced nearby" (*samīpoccāritam*)...
A "co-occurring word" (*upapada*) is defined by the technical convention: "therein, a co-occurring word is that which stands in the locative case";

this is because [otherwise] it would be impossible. Thus he says: "by a word uttered in proximity. Since the rule *pañcasūtrī* prescribes the Ātmanepada suffixes invariably when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, this present rule is an optional alternative (*vibhāṣā*). Therefore, [he says]: "not..."

This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *veti vibhāṣā*. Regarding the phrase *svaṃ yajñam* ("one's own sacrifice"), the meaning is "one's own. Here, since it is understood from the word *sva* itself that the fruit accrues to the self (*ātman*), this [sūtra] provides an option for the obligatory *ātmanepada* prescribed by the rule *svaritañitaḥ*. [Thus, one may say: *svaṃ yajñam*.

In the example *kārayati*, there is an option for the rule *ṇicaśca* by this [present rule]. In *svaṃ vrīhim*, there is an option for the rule *samudāṅbhyo yamaḥ* by this [present rule]. In *svāṃ gām*, there is an option for the rule *anupasargājjñaḥ* by this [present rule]. Thus ends the section on the formation of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
“Svarādi-nipātam-avyayam” (1.1.37). “Svarādi-nipātam-avyayam”: those which have *svara* as their first member are the *svarādayaḥ*;
these, together with the *nipātāḥ*, form a collective dvandva compound. He states the resulting meaning: "the *svarādayaḥ*."

He recites the *svarādi* group with the words "svar" and so forth. The separate recitation of the *svarādi* group and the *ca-ādi* group is for the purpose of distinguishing their accents, according to the rule: "The particles (*nipātāḥ*) beginning with *ca* are acute-accented (*ādyaudātāḥ*)"; furthermore, while only those [particles] among the *ca-ādi* that do not denote a substance (*asatvavācin*) are indeclinables (*avyaya*), this is not the case for the *svarādi*.

The purpose [of this section] is to establish the status of both those words denoting sentient beings (*satvavācin*) and those not denoting sentient beings (*asatvavācin*). *svar*—in heaven, in a specific kind of happiness pertaining to the next world, and in the other world. *antar*—in the middle. *prātar*—at dawn. *punar*—not for the first time, and in the sense of a distinction. *sanutar*—in concealment. These are the five beginning with *svar*.

Those ending in the letter *r* [are as follows]: in examples such as *rtena*, *svaryāti*, and *prātaratra*, there is no substitution of *u* by the rule *ṭh-śi ca*; for in that rule, the letter *u* is specified as an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) following *r* in the word *ror*. *Uccais* means "greatly"; *nīcais* means "slightly"; *śanais* means "in slowness of action"; *ṛdhak* means "truthfully."

Others say that [the word *viyogena*] is used in the senses of speediness of separation, proximity, and lightness. *Ṛte* means "except" or "without. *Yugapat* means "simultaneously" or "at one time. *Ārāt* means "far" or "near. *Pṛthak* means "separate" or "distinct.
*Hyas* means "on the past day. *Divā* means "during the day. *Rātrau* means "at night. *Sāyam* means "at the beginning of night."

*ciram* means for a long time; *manāk* and *īṣat*—these two denote "slightly. *Joṣam* means in happiness or in silence; *tūṣṇīm* means in silence. *Bahis* and *avastāt*—these two mean "outside. *Samayā* means near or in the middle. *Nikaṣā* means in the vicinity. *Svayam* has the sense of "by oneself."

*vṛthā*—in vain; *naktam*—at night; *nañ*—in the sense of negation. Others state: "Similarity, absence, difference from that, smallness, lack of excellence, and opposition are proclaimed as the six meanings of the negative particle (*nañ*). *hetau*—as a cause or motive; *iddhām*—I shall illuminate.

*Addhā* is used in the senses of "certainly" (*sphuṭa*) and "determination" (*avadhāraṇa*); others say it means "reality" (*tattva*) and "excellence" (*atiśaya*). *Sāmi* is used in the senses of "half" (*ardha*) and "despised" (*jugupsita*). By the word *vat*, the suffix *vati* is understood according to the rules: *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ*, *tatra tasyeva*, and *tadarham*. [The rule] *upasargācca chandasi*...

The root *vat* is not included in the phrase "in the sense of a verbal root" (*dhātvarthe*), because in the example "from the distant, from the downward, and from the upward slopes" (*parāvato nivata udvataśca*), it lacks the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). In fact, however, since the result is already established by the rule "a taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings [is an indeclinable]," the inclusion of *vati* here is indeed redundant. Examples: *brāhmaṇavat*, *kṣatriyavat*.

This is an example of a word ending in the suffix *vat*. There is no purpose for considering the suffix *kvasu* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), as there is no need for it to function as one. The triad *sanā*, *sanat*, and *sanāt* signifies "eternally" (*nitye*).
*Upadhā* means "distinction. *Tiras* is used in the sense of "disappearance," "sideways," and "defeat."

*Antarā* means "in the middle" (*madhye*) and "without" (*vinārthe*). *Antareṇa* means "excluding" (*varjane*). In reality, however, it should be understood as ending in *-e*. *Jyok* is used for the protraction of time, in questions, for the sense of "quickly," and for the sense of "just now. *Kam* is used for water, the head, censure, and happiness. *Śam* is used for happiness. *Sahasā*...

*Ākasmika* means "accidental" or "unexpected"; *avimarśa* means "lack of reflection. *Vinā* is used in the sense of "without" or "excluding. *Nānā* has the meanings of "various" and "without. *Svasti* is used for "auspiciousness" or "benediction. *Svadhā* is used when offering oblations to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). *Alam* is used in the senses of "ornament," "sufficiency," "capability," "prohibition," and "negation. *Vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* [are sacrificial interjections].
*Śrauṣaṭ*: these three [words] are used in the offering of oblations to the gods (*devahavirdāna*). *Anyat* is used in the sense of "another. *Asti* is used in the sense of existence (*sattā*).

Regarding the word *asti*, its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is established by the inclusion of words that resemble case-endings (*vibhaktipratirūpaka*) within the sub-grouping rule (*gaṇasūtra*) beginning with *ca*, namely: *upasargavibhaktisvarapratirūpakāśca*. Therefore, it is included here in the *svarādi* group.
It is established in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the *matup*-sūtra that its recitation is useless.
*Upāṃśu* means inaudible pronunciation and in secret. *Kṣamā* means patience.
*Vihāyasā* means the sky. *Doṣā* means at night. *Mṛṣā* and *mithyā*—these two mean falsehood.

*mudhā* means "in vain" or "uselessly. *purā* refers to that which is "uninterrupted," "long past," or "near at hand in the future. *mithas*—this pair [of forms] signifies "in secret" and "mutually. *prāyas* signifies "mostly" or "for the most part.
*muhus* signifies "again" or "repeatedly. *prabāhukam* signifies "at the same time" and "upwards."

*Pravāhikā* is an alternative reading. *Āryahalam* means "in the case of a loud cry. Śākaṭāyana, however, says that *ārya* means "obstruction" and *halam* means "prohibition" and "restatement. *Abhīkṣṇam* means "repetition. *Sākam*.
*sārdham*—this pair [of words] is used in the sense of "together with. *namas* is used in the sense of bowing. *hiruk* is used in the sense of exclusion.

*dhik* is used in the senses of censure and reproach. *am* is used in the senses of exhaustion and smallness. *ām* is used in the sense of assent. *pratām* is used in the sense of weariness. *praśām* is used in the sense of tranquility. *pratān* is used in the sense of expansion. In this context...

The reading "ṭh-pratān" is due to the force of its repeated recitation [in the list] ending in *n*. In the case of the two preceding forms, "pratām" and "praśām," there is no substitution of *n* for *m* by the rule "ṭh-mo no dhātoḥ. Furthermore, the reading "praśān" ending in *n* is not traditional; this is also the clear intention (*svarasa*) of the commentary on the sūtra "kṛnmejantaḥ."
This is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara*: "mā" and "māṅ"—these two [are used] in prohibition.

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); therefore, other words of this same type should be understood as belonging to the *svarādi* group. For example: *kāmam*—in the sense of "at will"; *prakāmam*—in the sense of "excessively."

*bhūyas*—in the sense of "again"; *sāmpratam*—in the sense of "properly" or "justly"; *param*—in the sense of "but" or "however"; *sākṣāt*—in the sense of "directly" or "perceptibly"; *sāci*—in the sense of "obliquely" or "sideways"; *satyam*—in the sense of "partial acceptance";
*maṅkṣu* and *āśu*—these two [denote] "speedily"; *saṃvat*—in the sense of "year"; *avaśyam*—in the sense of "certainly" or "necessarily."
*sapadi*—immediacy; *balavat*—intensity; *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ*—these two for manifestation; *aniśam*, *nityam*, *sadā*, *ajasram*, and *santatam*—this pentad for continuity;
*uṣā*—at night; *rodasī*—in the sense of heaven and earth; *om*—in the sense of acceptance.

And [the word] *brahmāṇi*. Here, in the collective dvandva compound *aśca uśca m ca*, the word *om* denotes Brahman as consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. However, the distinction is that when derived from the *uṇādi* suffix according to the rule "ṭh-vateṣṭilopaśca," it means "in the acceptance by Brahman."

The meaning of the rule *ṭhaviṣṭilopaśca* is as follows: after the root *avam*, there is the addition of the suffix *man* and the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi* (the first vowel) of that suffix. When *avam* is thus established, by the rule *jvaratvare* (Pāṇini 6.4.20), the semivowel *v* and the penultimate vowel *a* are replaced by *ūṭh*; subsequently, the two *ū* vowels undergo the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with them (*savarṇadīrgha*).

By the rule *sārvadhātuke*, there is *guṇa* substitution, resulting in the form *om*. Both [the word *om* and the particle *u*] belong to the class of *svarādi* (indeclinables beginning with *svaḥ*). It should not be argued that the status of the *uṇādi*-derived word is already established by the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*;
for in the *uṇādi* list, the term *cvyanta avyayam* is recited, which applies to those ending in the suffix *cvi*.

"Not otherwise" (*netara*). Consequently, since the status of *om* as an indeclinable (*avyaya*)—derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes—is not established [by other rules], its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar* is sufficient. *Bhūḥ*—on the earth. *Bhuvar*—in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
*Jhaṭiti*, *drāk*, *tarasā*—these three denote swiftness. *Suṣṭhu*—in the sense of praise.
*Duṣṭhu*—in the sense of base or vile; *su*—in the sense of worshipful; *āḥ*—in the sense of wonder; *ku*—in the sense of contemptible and slight;

*añjasā*—in the sense of reality and swiftness; *mithuṃ*—in the sense of two; *astam*—in the sense of destruction; *sthāne*—in the sense of what is fitting; *tājaka*—in the sense of swiftness; *cirāya*.

*cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*, *ciram*, *cireṇa*, *cirāt*—this group of six has the sense of "for a long time. *Varam* signifies slight excellence. *Ānuṣake* signifies succession. *Anuṣak* signifies inference. *Amenaḥ* signifies both speed and the present moment. *Sudi* signifies the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*).
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Vadi," and so forth. Thus end the particles beginning with *svara*.

Now he states the *cādi* (conjunction) group, beginning with "ca" and "vā": *Ca* is used in the senses of conjunction (*samuccaya*), disjunctive addition (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).

*Vā* is used in the senses of option (*vikalpa*) and so forth. As it is said: "The word *vā* may be used in the sense of option, comparison (*upamā*), the sense of 'as if' (*iva*), and also in conjunction."

*Ha*: in the sense of well-known (*prasiddhi*). *Aha*: in the sense of wonder (*adbhuta*) and distress (*kheda*). *Eva*: in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*). *Evam*: in the sense of referring back to what has been stated (*ukta-parāmarśa*). *Nūnam*: in the sense of certainty (*niścaya*) and conjecture (*tarka*). *Śaśvat*: in the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), eternality (*nitya*), and accompaniment (*sahārtha*). *Yugapat*: at one and the same time (*ekakāla*).

*bhūyas*—in the sense of "again" (*punar*) and "furthermore" (*ādhikye*). *kūpat*—in the sense of a question (*praśne*) and in praise (*praśaṃsāyām*). *kuvit*—in the sense of "much" (*bhūryarthe*) and in praise (*praśaṃsāyām*). *net*—in the sense of doubt (*śaṅkāyām*), negation (*pratiṣedha*), deliberation (*vicāra*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*). *cet*—in the sense of "if" (*yadyarthe*). *caṇ*—this [particle] is used in the sense of "if" (*cedarthe*).

The suffix *ṇit* is without an indicatory letter (*ananubandhaka*) in the sense of "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) and so forth; its result is a difference in accent (*svara*). *Kaccit* is used in an inquiry regarding what is desired (*iṣṭapraśna*). *Yatra* is used in the senses of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*), "endurance" (*avamarpa*), "censure" (*garhā*), and "wonder" (*āścarya*). [Examples: "I do not believe," "I do not endure," "I censure," or "It is a wonder that you [should act toward] a low-born man (*vṛṣala*)."

One should cause [him] to sacrifice at the commencement of a mountain. *Hanta* is used in the sense of joy, sorrow, compassion, and the commencement of a sentence. *Mākiḥ*, *mākim*, and *nakiḥ*—these three are used for exclusion (*varjana*).
*Māṅ* and *nañ* are mentioned among the *svarādi* (words beginning with *svara*) particles; it is more appropriate that they be read in both places rather than in only one.

The recitation [of this word] is indeed redundant. Nor should it be argued that its recitation here is for the sake of the accent of the particle (*nipāta*), because that is already established by the rule "the final syllable of a *phiṣ* is acute. Nor should it be argued that even if it denotes an existent entity (*satvavacana*), it is included in the list of *svarādi* words for the sake of its being an indeclinable (*avyaya*), for if that were the case, then the word denoting Lakṣmī would also [be an indeclinable].

Because the word *mā* would otherwise result in being classified as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), they say that *māṅ* and *nañ* are indeed included among the *cādi* group. *Yāvat* and *tāvat*—these two [are used] in the senses of totality, limit, measure, and restriction. *Tvai* is used for distinction and deliberation (*vitarka*). *Dvai* is used for deliberation.

*nuvai* is an alternative reading for *nvai*. *Rai* is used in the sense of giving and also in the sense of disregard. *Śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *svāhā*—these three are used in the offering of oblations to the gods. *Svadhā* is used in the offering to the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
Both readings are provided for the three polysyllabic words beginning with *śrauṣaṭ* in order to distinguish their respective accents.
*tum*—in the sense of *tuṅka*; likewise—*tathāhi*—in the sense of illustration;
*khalu*—in the senses of negation, embellishment of speech, and certainty; *kila*—in the senses of "as it were," report, and falsehood; *atha*—this.

[The particle] *atha* is used in the senses of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), immediate succession (*anantara*), commencement (*ārambha*), inquiry (*praśna*), entirety (*kārtsnya*), introduction of a topic (*adhikāra*), and collection (*samuccaya*).
It is also used at the beginning of a meter (*svarādi*). Therefore, although it denotes auspiciousness, it retains its indeclinable status when it signifies the welfare of beings (*sattvārthakatva*).
Thus says Śrī Harṣa: "Then, according to family custom, the group of matrons [prepared] the princess..."

"He caused her to bathe" (*snapayāmbabhūva*). Regarding the phrase "he caused her to bathe," the meaning is that he had her perform a ritual bath (*maṅgasnāna*). The particle *atha* is auspicious, like the sound of drums and other musical instruments. The repetition [of the word] is for the sake of a change in tone (*svarabheda*). *Sma* indicates the past tense.
And [it is used] for filling out a verse. *Ādaha* is used in the senses of beginning, injury, and reproach.

This is a rule concerning the *cādi* group. The meaning is that those which resemble prepositions (*upasarga*), those which resemble case-endings (*vibhakti*), and those which resemble vowels (*ac*) are included in the *cādi* group.

In this context, he provides an example of that which resembles a prefix (*upasarga*): *avadatam*. Here, *ava-* is a word-form resembling a prefix, but it is not actually a prefix. Consequently, the rule "after a prefix, [the suffix] *ṭhac*" does not apply, and thus the substitution of *t* for *a* does not occur. If there were indeed the substitution of *t*, the form would have been *avata*. [The example] *ahaṃyuḥ* is likewise explained.

In the word *ṭhahaṃ*, the particle *haṃ* is a substitute for a nominal ending (*subanta-pratirūpaka*). The suffix *yus* is applied according to the rule *ṭhahaṃśubhamoryuḥ* to express the sense of the abstract noun (*matvarthīya*). Here, *aham* is not the nominative singular form of the pronoun *asmad*;
for if it were so, the substitution of *mad* for the portion up to the final *m* (the *maparyanta*) would have occurred by the rule *ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca*.
[The examples] "madyauḥ" and "astikṣīrā" [are given]. Regarding "astikṣīrā": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has milk" (*asti kṣīraṃ yasyāḥ*).

Here, "asti" is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a verbal form (*tiṅanta-pratirūpaka*), but it is not actually a verbal form (*tiṅanta*). For if it were a verbal form, the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* would be impossible. This is because the rule for forming *bahuvrīhi*, "anekam anyapadārthe," [specifies that multiple words may be compounded when their meaning is something other than the individual members].

Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *sub* [from the previous rule]. And thus, in the formulation of the rule for *bahuvrīhi*, the Vārttika "an addition [*upasaṃkhyāna*] must be made for *ṭhak* in the case of *astikṣīra*" need not be composed;
this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *anekam anyapadārthe*.
He illustrates those [particles] that imitate accents with "a—" and so forth:

* *a*—in addressing (*sambodhana*). * *ā*—in speech and recollection (*vākya-smaraṇa*). * *i*—in addressing, disgust, and wonder (*sambodhana-jugupsā-vismaya*). * The group of seven—*i*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *āṬ*—is used in addressing (*sambodhana*) when followed by the suffix *itac*. * *paśu*—in the sense of "correctly" (*samyak*). * *śukam*—in the sense of "contempt" (*nindā*).

*yathākathāca* is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). *pāṭ*, *pyāṭ*, *aṅga*, *hai*, *he*, *bho*, and *aye*—these seven are used for addressing (*sambodhana*). *dya* is used in the senses of non-injury (*ahiṃsā*), opposition (*prātilomya*), and filling a verse-line (*pādapūraṇa*). *viṣu* has the meaning of "various" (*nānārtha*). *eka-pade* means "suddenly" (*akasmāt*) or "at this moment" (*idānīm*). *yut* is used in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*).

*Ātaḥ* is used in the sense of "from this. *Cādi* is also an *ākṛtigaṇa*. *Yat* and *tat* are used when there is a cause (*hetu*). *Āho-svit* is used in the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). *Sam* is used in the sense of totality (*sarvatobhāva*). *Kam* is used for filling a verse (*pādapūraṇe*). *Sukam* is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśaye*). *Anu* is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). *Śambat* (or *śbaṭ*) is used in the sense of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and in the sense of being face-to-face (*ābhimukhya*).

*va* is used for filling a metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*) and in the sense of *iva* (like). *Caṭua* and *cāṭua*—both mean pleasant speech. *Hum* is used in reproach (*bhartsana*). *Iva* means similarity (*sādṛśya*). *Adyatve* means "now" (*idānīm*), and so forth. Although here both the *svarādi* and *cādi* groups are open-ended classes (*ākṛtigaṇa*), those whose desired accentuation is that of a particle (*nipāta-svara*) are included among the *cādi* particles.
Others, however, [are included] among the *svarādi* group; those that possess two vowels (*svaradvayabhāj*) should be understood as belonging to both groups. Thus end the *cādayaḥ*.
(441) *Taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ* | 1.1.38 | Now he states the other indeclinables (*avyaya*), distinct from the *svarādi* and *cādi* groups: *taddhitaś cāsarva*...

*Asarvavibhakti* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In this context, a *vigraha* (analytic explanation) ending in the plural—namely, "that from which not all case-endings (*vibhakti*) arise"—is not possible, because it is accepted that all seven case-endings are produced from indeclinables (*avyaya*). For instance, in the present rule, *taddhitaśca*: *avyayād āpsupaḥ* // Pāṇini 2.4.82 // "Elision of the feminine suffix *āP* and of *suP* [case endings] occurs after an indeclinable. In this rule, the word *supaḥ* is used in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), and since it is a *sarvanāman* (distributive pronoun), it denotes all seven case endings. Therefore, it is established that all seven case endings are indeed produced after indeclinables. Consequently, a *vigraha* such as "that from which all case endings do not arise" is impossible. Thus, the term *asarvavibhakti* is understood here as a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that which does not possess all case endings. This refers to those words that, while having case endings, do not take all of them; specifically, it refers to the class of words beginning with *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsānta* suffixes, as well as indeclinables themselves. It is not intended to refer to indeclinables alone. If it were intended to refer only to indeclinables, the mention of *taddhita* in the rule would be redundant, as the elision of *sup* after indeclinables is already established by the aforementioned rule. Furthermore, if the term were restricted to indeclinables, one would have to explain how the elision of *sup* applies to words like *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya*, which are not indeclinables. Therefore, the term *asarvavibhakti* is taken to include all words that do not take every possible case ending. This is why the *Kāśikāvṛtti* explains: "The elision of *sup* occurs after words ending in *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and *samāsānta* suffixes, as well as after indeclinables. Thus, the elision of *sup* is taught for these four categories: *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes, *samāsānta*-suffixes, and indeclinables. However, even though the elision of *sup* is taught for these four categories, the elision of *āP* is not necessarily taught for all of them. This is because the elision of *āP* is taught only after indeclinables by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. Therefore, the elision of *āP* occurs only after indeclinables, whereas the elision of *sup* occurs after all four categories. Consequently, the elision of *sup* is taught for all four categories, while the elision of *āP* is taught only for one of them.
