In the Bhāṣya, however, having set aside the arrangement of the rules as "the dual and singular [are used] for two and one" and "the plural [is used] for many," he establishes the arrangement of the rules as "the singular," "the dual for two," and "the plural for many."

The singular number shall be applied as the general rule (*utsarga*), while the dual and plural numbers serve as exceptions (*bādhaka*) for the meanings of duality and plurality; such is the established position. Consequently, by the rule "the singular number," it follows that the singular number occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *ṭāp*.

By means of the general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*), it is obtained that the singular number (*ekavacana*) applies when there is an absence of duality and plurality. Thus, the result is that the singular number applies when there is oneness in the absence of duality and plurality, and when even that [oneness] is absent. In that context, since duality and plurality are already expressed by the dual and plural numbers respectively, the singular number applies elsewhere than those two.

Because [the singular number] is already established, the rule "ekavacanam" (singular number) serves to ensure its application even in the absence of [grammatical] objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth.

Thus, when the singular number is applied to indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack gender and number, it results in the singular of all case-endings (*sarvavibhakti*) due to the absence of any determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*). For this very reason:

In the rule *ṭhavyayādāpsupaḥ*, the mention of the pratyāhāra [āp] is meaningful. Therefore, the analysis is not "that from which all case-endings (*vibhakti*) [arise]," but rather, here the word *sarva* functions in the sense of completeness regarding parts, as in the expression "the entire cloth is burnt. And thus, *sarvā* consists of the three genders.

Intending to show that the result is that a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not produced [from it], but rather only singular endings are produced, and that such a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix should be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), he says: "yasmāt" (from which).
"Sarva" means consisting of the three numbers. "Not produced" means...
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "but only singular forms are produced.

This might be the case: when *tiṅ* is understood from the previous rule (*tiṅśca*), and the suffix *rūpa* is applied in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpam*), and the suffix *kalpap* is applied in the sense of partial completion (*īṣadasamāptau kalpap*), [the forms] *pacatirūpam* and so forth [are derived].
The form *pacatikalpam* means "he cooks well" or "he cooks slightly.

In this case too, there would be the status of an indeclinable (*avyayatva*), because it ends in a non-case-inflected (*asarva-vibhakti*) taddhita suffix. Furthermore, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the word *ubhaya*, since that too ends in a non-case-inflected taddhita suffix; therefore—
He says: "The enumeration. This is a *vārttika*. Regarding "beginning with *tasil*":
this means starting from *pañcamyāstasil* up to *dvitryośca dhamuñ*. Regarding "beginning with *śas*":
this means starting from *bahvalpārthāt* up to those ending in *ḍāc*, such as *avyaktānukaraṇāt*.

Regarding "am ām": by the rule *ṭhamu ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.4.12), the suffix *ām* is included; and by the rule *kimetiṅvyaye ṅamuṭ* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), the augment *ṅamuṭ* is also understood. Regarding "kṛtvo'rthāḥ" (those having the sense of "times"): this refers to the three suffixes—*kṛtvasuc*, *suc*, and *vibhāṣā bahoḥ*—which denote the counting of the repetition of an action (*saṅkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc*;
*dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*; *vibhāṣā bahoḥ*). Thus, the meaning is "three."

Regarding the term *tasivatī*: both the suffix *tasi*—prescribed by the rules "in the same direction as that" (*tenaikadik*) and "the suffix *tasi*" (*tasiśca*)—and the suffix *vati*—prescribed by the rule "that which is equal to that" (*tena tulyam*) and so forth—are included. As for the *tasi* prescribed by the rule "the suffix *tasi* after the ablative in the sense of a counterpart" (*pratiyoge pañcamyās tasi*), its inclusion is already established because it belongs to the group beginning with *śas*. And thus, [the form] *vat* is included among the *svarādi* (particle) group.

The purpose [of the rule] must be considered. Regarding the phrase "nānāñau": the suffixes *nā* and *añ* are prescribed by the rule "after the negative particle *nañ* and *ni*, the suffixes *nā* and *añ* occur when not used together. Thus, a restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) must be made—this is the syntactical connection.
The intention is that since the desired result is established by this very enumeration, the rule "and when it is a taddhita suffix" (*taddhitaśca*) need not be formulated.

(442) *kṛnmejantaḥ* | 1.1.39 | The analysis of *kṛnmejantaḥ* is as follows: *kṛt-mejanta*. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has *m* and *e* at its end. Thus it says: "a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *y* or *m*. This refers to that which ends in such [a suffix].

The intention is that because the simple [root] alone is unfit for application, the rule of "extension to that which ends with it" (tadantavidhi) applies even in the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhau*).

Regarding *smāraṃ smāram*: the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to the root *smṛ* by the rule *ṭhābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca*; then, by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), followed by the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel (*raparatvam*).

The doubling [of the word] occurs by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*. It is an indeclinable because it ends in a suffix marked with *m* (a kṛt-suffix). Regarding *jīvase*: the suffix *ase* is applied by the rule *tum-arthe se-senase-* etc. Regarding *pibadhyai*:
the suffix *śadhyaip* is applied by the rule *tum-arthe se-* etc. Due to its being marked with *ś*, it possesses the status of a sārvadhātuka suffix.

The meaning is that there is the substitution of *piba* [for *pā*] by the rule *ṭhpāghrādhmeṭ*. It is not [substituted] for the *śap* [affix], because that [substitution] is prescribed for a *sārvadhātuka* affix used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "indeclinable *kṛt* affixes denote the action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*). (443) *ktvātosunkasunaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.1.40.
Regarding *ktvā* and *tosun*: in the word *kṛtvā*, the suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule "when there are two actions having the same agent.
In the word *udetoḥ*, the suffix *tosun* is applied to the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ut-* by the rule beginning with "when [the action] characterizes another action" (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*).
In the word *visṛpaḥ*, the suffix *kasun* is applied to the roots *sṛp* and *tṛd*.

(444) *Avyayībhāvaśca* | 1.1.41. The remainder [of the rule] is: "An *avyayībhāva* compound shall be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). For example, *adhihari*. This is an *avyayībhāva* used in the sense of a case ending; it means "in Hari" (*harau*).

(445) *avyayādāpsupaḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.82. The term *āpsupaḥ* is a compound consisting of *āp* and *sup*, hence *āpsup*; the genitive case ending is used because it is a collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva compound. From the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe tyataḥ*, the word *lup* is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). This means that after an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *āp* and of all case-endings (*sup*).

Thus he says: "of that which is prescribed after an indeclinable. In the example "in the hall" (*śālāyām*), because *tatra* is an indeclinable, there is elision of the suffix *āp*. The form "*śālāyām*" is used to indicate its feminine gender.
Now, regarding "here" (*atha*): here there is elision of the case-ending (*sup*). Regarding "prescribed": this is stated without explicitly saying "following an indeclinable."
The intention is that this is because of the explanation [of the rule] as "prescribed after an indeclinable" (*avyayād vihita-*). Regarding the example *atyuccaisau*:

in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who has surpassed the high" (*uccair atikrāntaḥ*), there is a compound by the rule "atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe. Indeclinables, which primarily denote the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti-pradhāna*), become primarily denotative of the possessor of that power (*śaktimat-pradhāna*) in the scope of their *vṛtti*.
[These] occur; for example, "another day" (*anyamahar*) and "the night became day" (*divābhūtā rātriḥ*).

Therefore, because a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is impossible [in such cases], there is no contradiction in forming a compound with *atyādayaḥ* according to the rule for the second-case compound (*dvitīyā-samāsa*).
Here, although the *sup* suffix prescribed after the compound is elided, it remains as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) following the word *uccaiḥ*. From that [elided suffix],...

There is no elision (*luk*) because there is no absence of the suffix *vi* (i.e., it is not a case where *vi* has been dropped). However, the entire compound *atyuccais* does not possess the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because the word *uccais* alone is what is recited in the *svarādi* group; this is the intended meaning. Now, even though the word *uccais* alone is recited in the *svarādi* group, [the rule] "that which begins with *svara* and the particles (*nipāta*) are indeclinables" [applies].
The designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) indeed occurs [for *smṛt*], because of the statement: "The purpose is for the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronoun) and *avyaya*.
Thus he raises the objection: "In the case of the designation *avyaya*... He resolves it: "Even so...
[This refers to] the fact that in the context of the designation *sarvanāman*, the rule "not for a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)" is currently under discussion.

The meaning is that it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ" that the prohibition [of the term "indeclinable"] continues to apply in the rule prescribing the designation of indeclinables (*avyaya-saṃjñā*). Regarding the phrase "it would be useless": the words "in the rule 'avyayād āpsupaḥ'" are to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of gender": [this refers to] indeclinables.
The meaning is "due to the absence of gender.
And so says the Vārttika: "The statement regarding the elision (luk) of the suffix -āp after an indeclinable is purposeless, because of the absence of gender.
Likewise, in the rule "taddhitāś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ" [Pāṇini 1.1.38].

It is also stated in the Bhāṣya: "That which does not abandon these meanings—femininity, neuter-ness, masculinity, singularity, duality, and plurality—is indeclinable (avyaya). Now, if indeclinables lack gender, would this not contradict the Atharvaṇa Śruti which says, "It is similar in all three genders"?

Anticipating this objection, he provides the following resolution: "That which is similar. That which does not change—that is, does not undergo modification—across the three genders, all case-endings, and all numbers, but remains similar, being of one and the same form, is called *avyaya* (an indeclinable).

The application of the *Atharvaṇa-śruti*: here, the words *vibhakti* (case-ending) and *vacana* (number) refer to the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) and number (*saṅkhyā*), and not to the suffixes themselves, because otherwise the mention of "either one" (*anyatara*) would be redundant. Regarding the phrase *liṅgakāraka...*:
it means that for which the absence of gender, grammatical relation, and number is the supreme—that is, the intended object of its purport.

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: in the phrase "liṅgeṣu" and so forth, the locative case is prescribed by the rule "the seventh case [is used] for the locative and the sixth case in the sense of disregard. Thus, disregarding gender, grammatical relation (kāraka), and number, that which does not change—that is, does not undergo modification—but remains similar, being of one and the same kind, [is called *avyaya*].

This is the meaning of the scriptural citation "that is called indeclinable" (*tad avyayam*). In the commentary on the sūtra *taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, having introduced the point— "Those which do not lose these meanings— namely, the qualities of gender (masculine, feminine, and neuter) and the numbers (singularity, duality, and plurality)— are indeclinables"— it is cited there as authoritative evidence.

The intended meaning is that this has been cited from scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, this rule regarding the absence of gender, case-role (*kāraka*), and number applies only to particles (*nipāta*); however, for a few particles such as *svar* and others, there is indeed a connection with gender, case-role, and number.

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "svarādinipātamavyayam," it is stated that the designation [of indeclinable] applies only to particles such as *ca* when they express non-substance (*asattvavacana*), whereas for particles such as *svar*,
it applies whether they express substance (*sattvavacana*) or non-substance; thus, one says "he causes [the recitation of] *svasti*."

And because we observe the connection with the object-kāraka (*karmakāraka*) in such instances as "having pronounced *svasti*," "when merit is exhausted, one falls from heaven," and "he sacrifices in the morning. Now, in this context, he says: "He desires" (*vaṣṭi*). [This refers to] Bhāguri’s rule regarding the elision of the vowel *a* in the prefixes *ava* and *api*, and also regarding the feminine suffix *āp* after words ending in consonants.
The word *ācāryaḥ* means "he desires" (*vaṣṭi-icchati*). The particle *eva*, however, is for the purpose of completing the meter.
In the case of the prefix *ava*, there is elision of the initial vowel *ā* alone and not of the final one, due to its association with *api*.
Some read the word *bhāguri* as beginning with a dental labial (*dantyoṣṭhaḷadi*). However, in the *Tattvabodhinī*:
The fourth [letter] of the *pa* class (*pa-va-ga*) and so forth has been recited; this is likewise stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. As in the example "vācā.
Some maintain that this is an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*), while others hold it to be merely illustrative (*udāharaṇamātra*).
Although it will be stated later that the root *vaś* ("to move") has as its domain only Vedic meter (*chandas*), nevertheless, precisely because of this [present rule], [it is applied here].

They say that [gender] is also [determined] by indicative marks (*liṅga*) in common usage. However, in reality, the verse "vaṣṭi bhāgurirallopam" is not seen in the Bhāṣya; on the contrary, upon careful consideration of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, it is more appropriate to conclude that it does not exist there. In that regard:

Having stated, "The mention of *āp* (the feminine suffix) need not be made, for in cases such as *khaṭvā* and *mālā*, the formation is established by the fact that they are *prātipadikas* due to their being 'as if ending in [a vowel]'; and having raised the objection, "But the mention of *āp* is necessary for the sake of the nominative case endings (*svādi*) following words like *kruñcā*, *uṣṇihā*, and *devaviś*, which end in consonants and take the suffix *ṭāp*"; [he concludes], "One should sacrifice *kruñcās*..."

Regarding the rules "uṣṇihakakubhau devaviśaṃ ca" and "ṭāb-," it was established there that even in those cases, the mention of *āp* (the feminine suffix) is for the sake of forms such as *bahurājā*, *bahurāje*, and *bahurājāḥ*, [which would otherwise require] the rule "ṭhḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām. Therefore, [the suffix] is indeed *āp*.

Relying on the rule *halantānām*, it is incorrect to cite *vācā*, *niśā*, and *diśā*; for although the forms *niśā* and *diśā* are possible through the suffix *ṭāp* applied after the root *niś-* and *diś-*— which are characterized as having a penultimate *ig* vowel and ending in *k* (*igupadhāt kaḥ*)— the word *vācā* remains entirely ungrammatical, according to the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
[The section on] indeclinables in the *Bālamanoramā* is concluded.
In the Siddhāntakaumudī: The Section on Avyayībhāva Compounds.

(638) A rule concerning words applies when they are semantically connected (*samartha*). Now, among the types of compounds (*samāsa*), first is the *avyayībhāva*. Thus, having analyzed the meaning of the case-endings (*vibhakti*), [the author proceeds].

Intending to explain the compounds dependent on that [term *samartha*], he states as an introductory supplement: "A rule concerning words (*pada-vidhi*) applies when they are semantically connected (*samartha*).

The term *vidhi* means "that which is prescribed"—that is, a grammatical operation (*kārya*). The compound *padavidhi* is a genitive-tatpuruṣa (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) meaning "a rule pertaining to a word. Thus he says: "a rule that is related to a word. This depends upon semantic connection (*samartha*).

Thus, the meaning is that in the Sūtra, the word *samartha* (capable/related) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer to that which is based on *sāmarthya*. *Sāmarthya* is of two kinds: characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā-lakṣaṇa*) and characterized by the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva-lakṣaṇa*). Among these, [the latter arises] from words that terminate in their own respective meanings, by virtue of expectancy and so forth.

Mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) termed "expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*), based on the etymological derivation that expectancy which is specific is "expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*). It is also based on the etymological derivation that what has a connected meaning is "capable" (*samartha*). And this occurs only in sentences such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). In that case, whatever [meaning] belongs to each individual word...

Through that [connection], there occurs a relation with this or that [word] when it is proximate and suitable, as in "the king's man" and "the horse," "the man of King Devadatta," and "the man of the wealthy king. However, the semantic capacity characterized by the state of having a single unified meaning (ekārthībhāva) exists only during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*).

It consists in the capacity of words—which have been grasped individually as possessing their respective meanings—to convey a single qualified meaning through the power of their collective function (*samudāya-śakti*). This is based on the etymological derivation that "that which has a connected meaning is *samartha*," or "that which has a combined meaning is *samartha*. Here, "connection" (*saṅgati*) and "combination" (*saṃsarga*) refer to a state of unity (*ekībhāva*).

Thus, as in "clarified butter mixed with oil," it is understood that they have become one; or as in "fire [mixed] with [fuel]," it is understood that they have become one—so it is stated in the Bhāṣya. And this capacity exists only in a compound (vṛtti), such as *rājapuruṣa*. For this very reason, [the rule applies to] "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) when he is old.

Thus, in this manner, the qualification "prosperous" (*ṛddha*) does not apply to the king when he is qualified by "a particular man" (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*), because the qualified entity (the king as qualified by the man) constitutes a single referent (*ekapadārtha*), whereas the king is merely a part of that referent. However, in the case of "Devadatta’s teacher's family" (*devadatasya gurukulam*), the compound is formed because the subordinate member (*upasarjana*, i.e., the teacher) is necessarily dependent [on another word]. Or alternatively:
Even in the case of "Devadatta’s father," the relation (*pradāna*) relates specifically to the family (*kula*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

In that instance, the family is connected with the father by way of the relation of being produced (*utpādyatva*). However, Devadatta’s connection with the family—by virtue of being produced by that [man who is] his father—is mediated by the father (*gurugarbha*). And it has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "A word denoting a relative..."

"Everything that is dependent is always compounded; for that mutual expectancy (vyapekṣā) which exists in a sentence is not lost even in a compound. And: "Those whose connection is with the aggregate—as in the case of 'heavy syllables' (gurukalā) and so on—those parts, having been touched [by the relation], are joined with that which possesses them."
By this, the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra *ṭha-yaśśūla-* explains forms such as *ṭhśivabhāgavataḥ* in the sense of "a devotee of the Lord Śiva.
Furthermore, this state of semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) is postulated in the non-worldly analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*). For example:

Just as non-nominative coreferentiality (aprathamāsāmānādhikaraṇya) is attributed to the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes which have replaced the *l*-suffixes, it is likewise attributed to the *l*-suffix itself. For this very reason, since the *l*-suffix cannot be connected with a meaning that lacks coreferentiality with the non-nominative case, its replacement [by *śatṛ* and *śānac*] would otherwise be impossible; yet such [coreferentiality] exists in some instances.

Having raised the objection that [the substitution] is impossible due to the absence of application (*prayoga*), it is resolved in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* as follows: "Having observed the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the case of the substitute *ṭha*, one must infer through reasoning that this same [coreferentiality] belongs to the original base (*prakṛti*) as well. This is because the purpose of grammar is the descriptive explanation (*anvākhyāna*) of words already established in usage.
From the observation of usages such as "see Devadatta cooking" (*pacantaṃ devadattaṃ paśya*), it is indicated that even for the *sthānin* (the original element) *la*,

which is postulated for the sake of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), there must be assumed a capacity to convey meaning. Furthermore, regarding words heard in non-ordinary analytical sentences (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*), one cannot abandon their established expressive power (*klṛpta-śakti*).

Due to the absence of [separate] denotative power (*māna*), there arises the presentation of the qualified object through a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) assisted by the individual powers [of the constituents]. Consequently, this "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted as the *ajahatsvārthā* function (the function that does not abandon its own meaning). This is based on the premise that, within the domain of the complex formation (*vṛtti*), the individual words are devoid of meaning.

It is not proper to resort to the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) type of function (*vṛtti*), because in cases such as *mahābāhuḥ* and *supanthāḥ*, the substitution of *āt* and so forth would not occur; for in a compound, words like *mahat* and others become meaningless, and when it is possible to apply the rule regarding "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat*), a meaningless element cannot be taken.

Because [the meaning] cannot be grasped in such cases as "ṭhānmahataḥ" and so forth. As it has been said: "But the *jahatsvārthā* [type of metaphorical application occurs] only where the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is contradictory. The meaning of this is that it occurs only where the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*) is opposed to the meaning of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*), as in the case of "aśvakarṇa," "maṇḍapa," and so on.
The detailed discussion, however, should be sought in the *Śabdenduśekhara* and the *Mañjūṣā*. What is meant by "samartha" (semantically connected)? Consider:

*paśya kṛṣṇaṃ, śrito rāmaṃ mitram* ("See Kṛṣṇa; Rāma has resorted to his friend"). Here, because there is no mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) between "Kṛṣṇa" and "resorted to," they do not produce the cognition of a single integrated meaning, and thus there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*).

(639) *prākkaḍārātsamāsaḥ* |2|1|3|. Regarding *prākkaḍārāt*: since the word *prāk* would have been established by the very phrase *ākaḍārāt*, the explicit mention of *prāk* is for the purpose of indicating that even within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for a single technical designation (*ekasañjñā*), there is a cumulative application (*samuccaya*) of designations such as *avyayībhāva* and others.

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. The root *as* preceded by the prefix *sam* has the sense of "joining together," which consists of unification (*ekīkaraṇa*). A "compound" (*samāsa*) is that in which multiple words are joined together (*samasyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule *ṭhakartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*. For this very reason, it will be stated in the root text that "it is compounded" (*samasyate*).
And thus, this designation is etymologically meaningful.
(640) *saha supā* | 2|1|4|. [The word] *supā* [is used]. From [the rule] *subāmantrite*, the term *sup* is carried over (*anuvartate*). That which ends in a *sup* [suffix is the subject].

This results in the rule that what is uttered together with a word ending in a *sub*-suffix receives the designation of a compound (*samāsa*). This being the case, in examples such as *paryabhūṣayat*, there would be no compound of a *sub*-ending word with a *tiṅ*-ending word. To this, he says: "The connection [of the word] *saha* is split. Regarding the designation of a compound:

The intention is that since the term *saha* is already established by the mere mention of *sup*—because the word is etymologically meaningful (*anvartha*) and thus does not apply to anything else—the inclusion of the word *saha* itself is for the purpose of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*). In the rule *saha*, the term *sup* is understood from the preceding rule *subāmantrite*; and by the technical maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), this refers to the inclusion of words ending in those case-terminations.

From the rule "samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ" (a grammatical operation concerning words applies when they are semantically connected), the term *samartha* is carried over [by anuvṛtti] and is transformed into the instrumental case. This is what he expresses by saying "subanta... and so forth. "Is compounded" (*samasyate*) means that it is unified by speakers; that is to say, it receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "compound" (*samāsa*).
Some, however, hold that a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is compounded with a word capable of [denoting] the agent (*kartṛ*), in the sense of "becoming one.

The suffix *laṭ* occurs in the sense of the agent; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *upasargādasyatyūhyoḥ*. The word *samāsa* itself also ends in the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the agent due to the irregularity (*bāhulaka*), or else it ends in *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). This being the case:
They say that *samasyate* is a verb form (*tiṅanta*) in the active voice (*kartari*), intended to state the resulting meaning. Now, one might object:

if there were a compound in the expression "the pot becomes" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), then the usage *ghaṭabhavati* would also occur in common speech; to this he replies: "of the separation of the rule" (*yogavibhāgasya*). [The word] *katipaya* means "some. *Katipayāni*.

The analysis of the compound is "that whose subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. Regarding the example *paryabhūṣayat*, Kaiyaṭa states in the commentary on the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* that, according to the principle of "the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound" (*samāsāntodātatva*) and the "subsequent suppression of the accent" (*śeṣanighāta*), this is the case. However, in the instance *devo devān kratunā paryabhūṣat*, one should understand that there is a displacement of the accent (*svaravyatyaya*).

Regarding the phrase *anuvyacalat*: by the word *acalat*, there is first a compound with *vi* (the prefix *vi-*), and then a compound with that [resulting form] and *anu*. It is not, however, a simultaneous compound of both *anu* and *vi*, because the singular number (*sub*) is intended to be significant. For this very reason, in the example "the milk of the buffalo and the goat," [the term *kṣīram* is used in the singular].

Kaiyaṭa states that there is no compound between two words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*). From the rule *supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), the term *sub* is understood by way of anuvṛtti from the rule *subāmantrite* (Pāṇini 2.3.48). The term *samāsa* is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). Thus he says: *supsupā*.
The meaning is "a word ending in a case-suffix [is compounded] with another word ending in a case-suffix. Consequently, in the analysis (*vigraha*) *pūrvaṃ bhūtaḥ*, [the following applies].
The designation "compound" (*samāsa*) is established. Because it is a compound, it receives the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*);
the remainder [of the rule] is supplied as "by this [sūtra], *kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca*.
(641) *supo dhātu-prātipadikayoḥ* 2.4.71.
The term *sup* refers to the suffixes.
Regarding the statement "of these two," he explains that the genitive case in the rule *ṭhdhātuprātipadikayoḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, he says:

"there would be elision (*luk*) of the part belonging to these two. This refers to the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni luk*, which prescribes the elision of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) after words ending in *ṇya*, those denoting Kṣatriyas, those derived from Ṛṣis, and those ending in *añ*.

The meaning is that [the term *sup*] follows from that [previous rule]. Nor should it be argued: "Why could the term *sup* not be taken here as referring specifically to the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*)?

For, because the non-elision (*aluk*) is prescribed in the rule "after words beginning with *stoka*, the ablative [case-ending is retained]," it is understood that the term *sup* here refers to the entire pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation) of all case-endings.
Because it serves to make this known. And even so, in the case of the worldly analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "pūrvaṃ bhūtaḥ," when the two *sub*-ending words—

whose internal sandhi operations have been finalized— are compounded, one might assume that in the word "pūrvaṃ," the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the *ami pūrvaḥ* rule has the status of being "posterior" (*parādittva*), and thus the *ām* suffix would be elided (*luk*).

In the state of the compound (*samāsa*), the vowel *a* would not be heard after the letter *v*. However, if [the suffix] were treated as part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), then since the remaining *m* would no longer be a case-ending (*suptva*), one must explain how its elision (*luk*) occurs; for in the domain of elision by the rule *supo dhātu-prātipadikayoḥ*, the rule *antaraṅgān api vidhīn bahiraṅgo luk bādhate* (elision, though external, subverts even internal rules) applies.

It is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "pratyayottarapadayośca" that the formation of a compound occurs in the non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukikavigrahavākya*) even prior to the application of the rules for euphonic combination (*sandhi*), based on the principle that "the sheep does not harm [it]."

This has also been refined in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* under the rule "kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca," and we have explained it in detail in our commentary on the rule "bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvānām. Thus, since the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *am* occurs precisely at the stage of the ungrammatical analytical construction (*alaukikavigraha*)— namely, when [the words] are "pūrva am bhūta"— the aforementioned fault does not arise.

And thus, when the *sup* suffixes have been elided (*luk*), the form *bhūtapūrva* is established. Now, one might object: according to the rule for compound formation, "a word ending in a *sup* suffix is compounded with another word ending in a *sup* suffix," the word ending in a *sup* suffix is that which is designated in the nominative case (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*).
Since both [members of the compound] are equally words ending in *sup* suffixes, it follows that [the one designated in the nominative] is the one to be compounded.

Since the status of being an *upasarjana* (secondary member), which will be discussed below, applies equally to both, there would be no basis for determining (*vinigamanāviraha*) which one should be placed first according to the rule "the *upasarjana* comes first.
Therefore, he says: "In the sense of 'one who was previously [so-and-so],' the suffix *caraṭ* is applied. This means "one who was previously [a king]."
This is a laukika-vigraha (an informal, colloquial analysis). The word "pūrvam" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

The point is that because "bhūtapūrva" is a compound (*samāsa*), it functions as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); therefore, case-endings (*sub*) are produced again from the entire aggregate according to their respective rules.
(1) A compound with *iva*, and there is no elision of the case-ending.

Regarding "with *iva*": there is a compound of a word ending in a *sup*-suffix with the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *iva*. There is no elision [of the suffix] by the rule "the *sup* [suffixes] are elided after a verbal root" (*supo dhātu*). Furthermore, the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) prevails, and not the accent of the compound as a whole.

The meaning is that it should be stated thus. Although the compound is established by the rule *saha supā*, the specific prescription of a compound is for the purpose of preventing the word *iva* from being placed first; otherwise, since the word *iva* here is likewise a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it would [be subject to the general rules of compounding].
Because it is designated as the first [member] and is thus subordinate (*upasarjana*), it would have to be placed first [in the compound].

In the example *jīmūtasyeva*, the word *jīmūta* as the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is indeed oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of its *phiṭ-svara* accent, but the compound as a whole does not possess this oxytone quality. In this case—

However, this is not an *avyayībhāva* compound based on the sense of "according to the actual fact" (*yathārthatva*), because of the rule's specific mention of the form *tatra tasyeva*. Furthermore, this compound is only occasional; for this very reason, those who recite the *padapāṭha* of the Rigveda (Bahvṛcas) do not pause (*avagṛhṇanti*) between the words, whereas the followers of the Yajurveda (Yājuṣas) read them as two distinct words, as in: *udbāhur iva vāmanaḥ*.

Thus, such separate constructions as these are consistent. However, in the case of "O King, eat the myrobalan fruit, which is beneficial like a mother," one ought to say "mātaram iva" (like a mother).
This is because of the rules "the nominative case is used when coreferential with a finite verb" and "the nominative case is used when [the agent] has already been expressed."

Let us set aside for now the argument that the nominative case in "mātā" (mother) is ungrammatical in the sense of "one who resembles a mother," because the nominative occurs only when there is a connection with a verbal action, according to the natural sense of the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya which states that the nominative is a kāraka-case.

(642) *Avyayībhāvaḥ* |2|1|5|. *Avyayībhāvaḥ*: This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). Although this is within the section governing "single designations" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), it has been stated under the rule *prākkaḍārāt* that by this designation, the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*) is not superseded.

(643) An indeclinable [compound] is formed with words expressing case-meaning (*vibhakti*), proximity (*samīpa*), prosperity (*samṛddhi*), adversity (*vyṛddhi*), absence (*arthābhāva*), "with" (*saha*), "not yet" (*asamprati*), the manifestation of a word (*śabdaprādurbhāva*), "after" (*paścāt*), "according to order" (*yathānupūrvya*), simultaneity (*yogapadya*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), attainment (*sampatti*), entirety (*sākalya*), and limit (*antavacana*).
[Pāṇini 2.1.6] An indeclinable [is compounded] with a word denoting a case-meaning; even in the absence of the actual case-meaning, [compounds such as] *apadiśam* and so forth are formed.

To establish this, he says: "The word *avyayam* [is used], and the rule is divided. Here, from the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, the term *samartha* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and is transformed into the genitive case (*tṛtīyānta*). The terms *samāsaḥ* and *avyayībhāvaḥ* are also governing (*adhikṛta*) rules.
Thus he says: "An indeclinable with a capable word. "That is *avyayībhāva*.
The meaning is that this compound shall have the technical designation *avyayībhāva*.

And likewise, in the analysis of the phrase "the middle between two directions" (*diśayormadhyam*), where the words are not those of the compound itself (*asvapadavigrahe*), there is the indeclinable *apa*, which conveys the sense of "middle."

By the term *diśayoḥ*, the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*) is established, as well as the designation of "avyayībhāva" for that compound. Thus, because it is a compound, it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); when the case-ending (*sup*) is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, the form *diśā-apa* remains.
(644) That which is designated by the nominative case in a compound is called *upasarjana*. 1.2.43.

Intending to explain the grammatical operations pertaining to the *upasarjana*, the author states the definition: "that which is designated by the nominative. Now, one might object that if the definition is explained as "in a compound, that which is designated by the nominative is the *upasarjana*," it would be impossible, because in a compound...

This is because [in the rule] *sati ṭhsupo dhātu* (Pāṇini 1.4.13), the first case ending (*prathamā*) has been elided. However, if one were to explain [the rule] as "that which is designated by the first case when a compound is intended to be formed," then in the analysis (*vigraha*) of *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa) as *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ*,
the word *kṛṣṇa* would not be a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), since it is designated by the second case (*dvitīyā*).

Since the word *śrita* is indicated by the nominative case, it would become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Therefore, he explains: "by the rules for compound formation" (*samāsa-śāstraiḥ*). The sense is that the term "compound" (*samāsa*) refers to the rules that prescribe the formation of compounds. And thus, [the rule] "the second case [ending] when [the word] *śrita* follows" (*dvitīyā śrite*) [is applied].

In the rule prescribing the formation of compounds, the word *kṛṣṇa* ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) is designated as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) because it is indicated by the first case (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*) in the rule "the second case" (*dvitīyā*). Likewise, in the rule prescribing the compound "avyayībhāva," the word *apa* is established as a subordinate member because it is indicated by the first case in that rule.

(645) *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam* | 2|2|30|. The subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first. The heading "a compound (*samāsa*)" has been established [by the previous rule] starting from "before *kaḍāra*" (P. 2.2.38). By virtue of suitability, the word "in a compound" (*samāse*), which was in the nominative case, is transformed into the locative case. Thus he says: "In a compound... (*samāse*).

"The subordinate element (*upasarjana*) should be placed first"—the sense of this is that the word "before" (*pūrva*) means it should be employed before [the principal]. Thus, in the present case, the rule for employing *apa* first is established. Consequently, the form *apa-diśā* is settled.

(646) *Ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte* |1|2|44|. Here, he states that the word *diś* is also an *upasarjana*: [the sūtra] says *ekavibhakti*. From the rule *prathamānirdiṣṭaṃ samāsa upasarjanam*, the words *samāsa* and *upasarjana* are carried over (*anuvartate*).
By the term "compound" (*samāsa*), the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is indicated. That which possesses only one case-ending is *ekavibhakti*;

that is to say, it has a fixed case-ending. Thus, in an analytical sentence, that which has a fixed case-ending is an *upasarjana* when a grammatical operation other than prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) is to be performed.

The meaning is "it may be so. He states the conclusion: "that which is restricted in the analytical compound" (*vigrahe*). The word *niṣkauśāmbi* is the example. In that case, [the analysis is] "departed from Kauśāmbī. In the analyses *niṣkrāntaṃ*, *niṣkrāntena*, *niṣkrāntāya*, *niṣkrāntāt*, *niṣkrāntasya*, and *niṣkrānte*.
In the case of compounds formed according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.2.18),

such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *niṣkauśāmbim*, *niṣkauśāmbinā*, and so forth, the established position is that within the analytical statement (*vigraha*), the word "Kauśāmbī" itself possesses a fixed case-ending.

Its status as an *upasarjana* (secondary member) is established by this [rule]. In the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-śāstra*), the word "Kauśāmbī" is specified in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdiṣṭa*) and not in the nominative case (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*);
therefore, since its status as an *upasarjana* would not otherwise apply under the rule "that which is specified in the nominative" (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭam*), this statement is made. In that regard:

Even though the word *kauśāmbī* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) by virtue of this [sūtra], there is no mandatory prior placement [of the subordinate member]; rather, the compound is formed only with those words ending in specific case-terminations—this very sūtra is the authority for this point.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *tulyārthaiḥ*. The compound is formed only with a word ending in the nominative case.
This is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *itaḥ ṣṭhani kaḥ*. (Pāṇini 1.2.48) states: *go-striyor upasarjanasya*.

And in the present context, within the analytical sentences (*vigrahavākya*) such as "the middle between two directions" (*diśayor madhyaḥ*), "the middle" (*madhyam*), or "by the middle" (*madhyena*), [the feminine suffix is elided].

Because the word *diś* (direction) has a fixed case-ending, it acquires the status of an *upasarjana* by this rule [Pāṇini 1.2.43], even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the nominative case within the formulation of the compound rule. However, it remains established that it does not undergo *pūrvanipāta* (prior placement). [The rule] *go-striyoḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.48] [prescribes] the *hrasva* (short vowel).

From the rule *napuṃsake prātipadikasya*, the words *hrasva* and *prātipadikasya* are carried over [by anuvṛtti]. The term *upasarjanasya* is a qualifier of *goḥ*. The singular number is used with reference to each individual case. By the word *strī*, the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is understood.

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the inclusion of that which ends with a term, the rule of "ending-inclusion" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained; namely, that it applies to the word *go* when it is an *upasarjana* (secondary member) and when it ends in a feminine suffix. Both of these are qualifiers of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, there is an "ending-inclusion" [of those qualifiers]. This is what he states with the words beginning "the secondary member," and so forth. And here...

Only that which is technically a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is understood here, and not merely anything that is non-primary; for otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kumāry-brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin who desires or acts like a young girl). And because it is an *avyayībhāva*, it possesses the status of an indeclinable (*avyayatva*).

(648) *Nāvyayībhāvādato’m tvapañcamyāḥ* | Pāṇini 2.4.83. Thus, in response to the objection that the case endings (*sup*) produced from an *avyayībhāva* compound would undergo elision (*luk*) by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*, he says: "Not after an *avyayībhāva*; however, *am* [is used] except for the fifth case."

[The word] *chedaḥ* [is the heading]. The rule *ṭhnāvyayībhāvādataḥ* constitutes one sentence. From the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe’t*, the term *luk* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). And from the rule *avyayādāpsupaḥ*, the term *sup* is also carried over. Here, the *avyayībhāva* compound is qualified by the suffix *at*; therefore, the rule of "application to that which ends in this" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. This is what he states:

[The rule] "there is no elision (luk) of the case-ending (sup) after an indeclinable (avyayībhāva) ending in 'ad'" is one statement; however, there is another statement: "ṭham [is substituted] for [the case-endings] other than the fifth (pañcamī). This means that for case-endings other than the fifth, the substitute 'am' shall occur, whereas for the fifth case-ending, 'am' does not occur. Thus he says: "for that [compound], except for the fifth case."

Regarding the rule *am-ādeśaḥ*: here, because it is the immediately preceding one, this prohibition (*apañcamyāḥ*) applies only to *am*, and not to the prohibition of *luṅ* as well. Thus, for a *sup* following an avyayībhāva compound ending in *a*, there is no *luk* elision, but rather the substitution of *am*; however, for a *pañcamī* [ending], there is neither *luk* nor the substitution of *am*.
"It exists" is the meaning of *sthiti* (staying/abiding). In the Sūtra, the word *tu* is used precisely for the purpose of indicating this.

For if it were stated simply as "after an indeclinable compound ending in *a*, there is *am* except for the fifth case," then [the rule would apply] to the case endings (*sup*) other than the fifth case that follow an indeclinable compound ending in *a*.

It would only follow that the *luk* elision of *am* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the elision of] *am*. This being the case, since there is no *am* after the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*), the rule "after an indeclinable, the case endings beginning with *āp* and *sup* are elided" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*) would apply. Therefore, let it be granted for now that the *luṅ* elision is prohibited. As for *apadiśam*, this is an example of case endings other than the fifth.
For the fifth [case], however, *apadiśāt* should be cited as an example.

Although this could be established even by the shortening of the neuter gender— since neuter status will be stated [later] for the *avyayībhāva* compound by the rule *avyayībhāvaśca*— nevertheless, the rule *gostrīyoḥ* [is required for forms like] *citragu* and *atikhaṭva*.
Since such meanings are necessary, this [explanation] has been presented here as well because it is logical.
Thus, even though it is not seen in the Bhāṣya, he states— “the neuter indeclinable”— that the derivation of the form *apadiśam* by means of a word-split (*yogavibhāga*) is approved by the elders.

(649) *Tṛtīyāsaptamyor bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.4.84). Regarding the third case (*tṛtīyā*): from the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt* (2.4.83), the word *ataḥ* (from that which ends in *a*) is understood as being carried over; thus he says "from that which ends in *a*. However, in the absence of the substitution of *am*, there is no elision (*aluk*) by virtue of the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt*.

One might ask: "Since [the rule] is established by the word *vā* ('or'), what is the purpose of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ('diversely')? To this he replies: "Because of the inclusion of *bahulam*.

Having thus analyzed and explained the rule *tad avyayam*, he begins to explain the subsequent portion, stating: "This is the meaning of the passage beginning with *vibhakti*. By the word *vibhakti*...
The meaning of the case-ending (vibhaktyartha) is intended to be expressed. They are called "vacanāḥ" because they are spoken; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*).
[This refers to] that which is near to the case-ending (*vibhakti-samīpa*).

The compound consists of these sixteen items: *samṛddhi*, *vyṛddhi*, *artha*, *abhāva*, *atyaya*, *asaṃprati*, *śabdaprādurbhāva*, *paścāt*, *yathā*, *ānupūrvya*, *yaugapadya*, *sādṛśya*, *saṃpati*, *sākalya*, and *anta*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those [words] which are also indeclinables (*vacana*). The meaning is: "when the meanings of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) and so forth are to be expressed. The term *avyaya* (indeclinable) is understood from the previous rule. The governing headings *avyayībhāvaḥ* and *samāsaḥ* also apply. Thus he says: "when the meanings of case-endings and so forth [are to be expressed]. First, regarding the case-endings (*vibhakti*).

The meaning is that the first case is cited as an example for the sense of a case-ending (*vibhaktyarthe*). "In Hari" (*harau*) is the *laukika-vigraha* (popular analytical statement). The point is that whatever is understood from "in Hari" is expressed by the compound "over Hari" (*adhihari*) as well. The intention is as follows: when the word *adhi* is compounded with "in Hari" (*harau*) to form an *avyayībhāva*, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided; since the rule for forming compounds prescribes that an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is mentioned in the nominative case, *adhi* is placed first. Then, the case-ending produced after the compound is elided by the rule "after an indeclinable, the endings *āp* and *sup* are dropped."

Now, one might ask: why is the word *adhi* not included when forming the analytical (vigraha) sentence for this compound? To this he replies: "Because here [in this case], it is only the meaning of the locative case that is expressed. Thus, since the sense of location (*adhikaraṇatva*), which is indicated by *adhi*, has already been conveyed by the locative suffix itself, the word *adhi* is not mentioned separately; the point is that, as will be stated later, this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), and therefore an analytical sentence consisting of its own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*) is inappropriate.

One might object: "In the case of *harau*, once the sandhi operation has been finalized and the compound (*samāsa*) formed, the suffix *ṭā* (ṭāP) is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*; how then could the vowel *ī* following the *repha* (visarga) be heard in the compound? To this he says: *hari ṅi*. The point is that since the formation of the compound occurs precisely in the non-worldly analytical statement (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*) prior to the application of sandhi operations—this being the view accepted in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*—the form remains as such. This has been explained immediately following the discussion on *bhūtapūrva*.

[Objection: Since the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) has already been expressed by the particle *adhi*, how can there be a locative case (*saptamī*) in *harau*? To this, he says: "In this case, by the particle... [and] "by the statement... The sense is that, having carried forward the word *suptena* (with a nominal ending), the locative case must indeed occur here because of the force of the rule prescribing compounding with a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). In reality, however, in the Bhāṣya on the *Anabhihita-sūtra*, only the enumeration beginning with "by verbal endings (*tiṅ*), kṛt suffixes, taddhita suffixes, and compounds" is seen. Therefore, even though the status of being a locus is expressed by the particle *adhi*, the locative case remains unimpeded.

In the phrase "Even a poison-tree, having been nurtured, is not fit to be cut down by oneself," the word *iṣṭavya* ("is desired") must be supplied. Because [the tree] has already been designated as a "poison-tree" (*viṣavṛkṣa*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur after it. Nor should it be argued that the restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) [of cases where the second case is prohibited] in the rule *kṛtaddhitasamāsaiḥ* was rejected in the Bhāṣya; for it has been stated there that the purpose of that enumeration is established otherwise in examples such as *kaṭaṃ karoti bhīṣmam udāraṃ darśanīyam*. Let this matter rest for now. (650) *avyayībhāvaśca* | 2.4.18.
And the *avyayībhāva* [compound is neuter]. This [compound] is neuter. *Sa...* [The remainder of the commentary follows].
The intention is that this [term] follows from the word "napuṃsaka" [in the previous rule].

He states the result of its being neuter: "hrasvo napuṃsake" (A 1.2.47). Regarding "gopāyati": the meaning is "he protects. [The root] *gup* in the sense of "protection" takes the suffix *vic*; [the suffixes] *āya* etc. are optionally applied before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

This is the suffix *āya*. There is the elision of *y* by the rule "ṭhlopo vyoḥ. There is the elision of the letter *v* by the rule "verapṛktasya. Thus, the word *gopā* ends in the vowel *a*. The sense is that the word *gopā* is formed from the root *pā* (to protect) with the suffix *vic*, followed by a compound with the object (*upapada*) *go* (cow), resulting in the meaning "one who protects cows" (*gāḥ pāti*).

Regarding the term *adhigopam*: the intention is that when the case-ending (*sup*) is elided in an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending, and the word has become neuter and short, the form *am* is substituted by the rule "not after an *avyayībhāva*" (*nāvyayībhāvāt*), resulting in the single substitute of the preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*).
However, the rule "of *go* and feminine nouns" (*gostriyoḥ*) does not apply here, because there is no feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) at the end of the word.
Regarding the word *samīpe*: the meaning is that an example of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) having the sense of proximity (*samīpa*) will be stated in a compound.

"In the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya samīpam*): this is the ordinary analytical sentence (*laukika-vigraha-vākya*). Here, instead of the word *upa*, which is being compounded, the word *samīpam* is employed; however, one does not say "Kṛṣṇasya-upa."
The analysis (*vigraha*) is a *nitya-samāsa* (an obligatory compound), because it is appropriate for its analysis not to consist of its own constituent words (*asvapada-vigraha*).

Now, one might object: in cases such as *samayā grāmam*, *nikaṣā laṅkām*, and *ārād vanāt*, since the indeclinables (*avyaya*) beginning with *samayā* signify "nearness," they would form an *avyayībhāva* compound; and consequently, [the rule] "to the village" (*grāmam*)...
Otherwise, constructions such as *samayā grāmam*, *nikaṣā grāmam*, and *ārād vanāt* would not be possible;
for in an *avyayībhāva* compound, there is a fixed rule that the indeclinable (*avyaya*) must be placed first. To address this, he says: "In the case of *samayā*," etc. [He adds:
"By virtue of the force of the specific rule" (*vidhānasāmarthyāt*). This refers to instances such as *samayā grāmam*, *nikaṣā laṅkām*, and *ārād vanāt*.

Even though the genitive case ending remains as the "sixth" (genitive) in the remaining instances, when an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed, because it is a constituent part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is optionally a *luk*-elision of the genitive for the case endings of the subordinate word (*upapada*)— namely the second and fifth cases— and thus, when the meaning of the nominal stem and so forth is intended to be expressed from the compound, [the form applies] across all case endings.

When these [compounds] arise according to their respective possibilities and in their various permutations, there would indeed be the forms: *samayāgrāmam*, *nikaṣālaṅkam ārād vanam*, *samayā grāmeṇa*, *nikaṣā laṅkena*,
*ārād vanena*, *samayā grāme*, *nikaṣā laṅke*, and *ārād vane*.

Consequently, the prescription of the second and fifth case endings for the second and fifth [rules] would be redundant, as their purpose is already served by the sixth case ending. Nor should one suspect that the second and fifth case endings as *upapada*-case suffixes apply again after the formation of the compound, because once they have applied, it is impossible for them to apply again. In reality, however:

This [objection] is incorrect, because the prescription of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) when used in conjunction with words meaning "near" (*madhya*) or "time" (*samaya*), and the prescription of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) when used in conjunction with words meaning "far" (*dūra*), already serve their purpose. Furthermore, this being the case, one should not suspect that an *avyayībhāva* compound occurs in examples such as *samayā grāmam*, for [the rule] *abbhakṣa*...

This is because, as in such examples, only indeclinables (*avyaya*) that function solely in the sense of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) or proximity (*samīpa*) and so forth are intended to be included; whereas words such as *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *ārāt* primarily denote the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) and thus do not function merely in the sense of proximity. For their meaning is "in the vicinity of the village" (*grāmasya samīpe*).
The prefix *upa*, however, denotes "mere proximity. In the example "the devotee who is near Kṛṣṇa" (*upakṛṣṇaṃ bhaktaḥ*), the understanding arises that he possesses proximity to Kṛṣṇa.

Regarding "the prosperity of the Madras" (*madraṇāṃ samṛddhiḥ*): in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the word *samṛddhi* should be understood as a synonym for the indeclinable *sam*. This refers to the compound prescribed by this sūtra.
Because it is eternal (*nitya*), there is no dissolution of its own constituent members (*svapadavigraha*). This should be understood similarly in what follows as well. Regarding *saṃmadram*:

in all such cases, the elision of case-endings (*subluk*) and so forth should be understood as before. However, in examples such as *saṃṛddhā madrāḥ saṃmadrāḥ* ("the prosperous Madras"), it is not an *avyayībhāva* compound; for by the force of the mention of "number" (*vacana*), [the *avyayībhāva*] occurs only when the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is predominant.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya: "tatpravṛtteḥ" (from its occurrence). Regarding the Yavanas, there is "vyṛddhi," as in the example *duryavana*. In the analytical explanation (*vigraha*), the word *vyṛddhi* should be understood as having the meaning of the word *dur*. [The commentary says] "vigatā" (gone away);
the meaning is "that which has the absence as its counter-correlative. That is to say, *vyṛddhi* is the absence of prosperity (*ṛddhi*).

Nor should one be deluded by the thought that this [term] refers to the absence of the object itself, because what is intended there is precisely the absence of the meaning of the compound members; for here, the absence of the Yavana is not perceived, but rather the absence of the increase pertaining to the Yavana is perceived. Indicating this very point regarding the absence of the object...

He provides an example: "the absence of flies" is expressed as *nirmakṣikam*. The point is that in this analysis (*vigraha*), the word *abhāva* (absence) has the same meaning as the prefix *nir*. However, in the case of "the pot is not a cloth," there is no *avyayībhāva* compound; for, by the force of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) [in the rule], it is intended that only absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is meant here.

"The passing away of cold is 'atīhimam' (the end of cold). In this analysis (*vigraha*), the word *atyaya* should be understood as a synonym for the indeclinable *ati*. He dispels the charge of tautology with the phrase "absence of object" by stating, "passing away means destruction.
By the term "absence of object," absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) alone is intended. Therefore, [it does not apply] to a cloth...

The meaning is that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is "not being," which is to say it is not present. In the Sūtra, the term *asaṃprati* means "it is not appropriate at this time. According to Amara, "ṭhetarhi saṃpratīdānīm" [mean "now"].
Because there is a unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) through the inclusion of the action of "joining" (*yuj*), a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is formed. Thus he says: "sleep at this time..."

The phrase "it is not appropriate" (*na yujyate*) means "excessive sleep" (*atinidram*). One should understand that in place of the indeclinable *ati*, which here has the sense of "not now," the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is "it is not appropriate now. In the sūtra, by the term "manifestation of sound" (*śabdaprādurbhāva*), the intended meaning is the making known of the word.
Regarding this, he says: "The manifestation of the word *hari* is *itihari*. The indeclinable (*avyaya*) *iti* occurs in the sense of the manifestation of a word.
The meaning is that there is a compound of this [indeclinable] with the word *hari*, which refers to its own form and ends in the genitive case.
Similarly, "after Viṣṇu" is *anuviṣṇu*. The indeclinable *anu* occurs in the sense of "after."

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in the Bhāṣya": the meaning is that it is in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *acaḥ parasmin*. The intention is that if this were an avyayībhāva compound in the sense of "after that" (*tataḥ paścāt*), then the word *paścāt* would have to stand first [as per the rules for avyayībhāva].
It is precisely because of this usage in the Bhāṣya that, within this sūtra, [the word *para*] functions as a constituent of a term intended to convey that specific meaning.

It is understood that this compound does not occur with *avyaya* (an indeclinable) when it has such-and-such a meaning [namely, similarity]. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *yathā’sādṛśye*, it is stated: "The [compound] *sādṛśyasampatti* would result.
However, a compound does indeed occur with the word *yathā*, because of the commencement of the subsequent rule. In the sūtra...

The meaning of that [word] is indicated by the word *yathā*. Intending to convey that an indeclinable existing in the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe*) is compounded, he says: "fitness" (*yogyatā*). Regarding "in accordance with" (*anurūpam*): here the indeclinable *anu* is used in the sense of fitness;
therefore, the sense is that it functions in the sense of "according to" (*yathārthe*). [He repeats] "object after object" (*artham artham*).
*Pratīti* refers to a common worldly analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). Here, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

Because *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* when it signifies distributive repetition according to the rule "in the sense of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), state of being so (*itthaṃbhūta-ākhyāna*), or distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)," the second case (*dvitīyā*) is employed in connection with it. However, in a compound (*samāsa*), there is no reduplication.
"Because the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated by the compound itself"—so says Kaiyaṭa on the rule *hayavaraṭ*.

However, the truth is that it is expressed by the word *prati*; for it is the fact that it is expressed by *prati* that constitutes the reality. But one might object: the presentation of the common analytical expansion (*laukika-vigraha*) as "object after object" (*artham artham prati*) is not possible.
Because it would follow that the compound is obligatory, he says: "of the word *prati*. He says: "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*).

For if the *avyayībhāva* compound were obligatory, then even in the case of the genitive used as a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), since the case-ending (*sup*) is elided in the *avyayībhāva*, all case-endings would be replaced by the form *am*; and if there were an optionality regarding that [genitive], then for each respective meaning—

The sense is that since [the status of *prati*] as a term governing its own meaning (*pratyarthena*) and so forth is already established, the prescription of *karmapravacanīya* status for *prati* with the purpose of resulting in the second case (*dvitīyā*) would be redundant. However, in reality,
in examples such as *pratisthānam*, it serves the purpose of ensuring the absence of the cerebralization (*ṣatva*) prescribed by the rule "upasargāt sunoti."

The status of being a *karmapravacanīya* is indeed purposeful; for we see its usage in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *sarūpāṇām* in the phrase "for each object" (*artham artham prati* = *pratyartham*), and thus the truth is that here there is an optional compound (*vaikalpika-samāsa*). Regarding the expression "without transgressing power" (*śaktim anatikramya*), the suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule *parāvarayoge ca*.

And the status of being "higher and lower" belongs to the Buddha. Therefore, the sense is that the indeclinable *yathā* functions in the sense of not deviating from the meaning of a word. In *saharī*, there is similarity to Hari; the point here is that the indeclinable *saha* functions in the sense of similarity. [The phrase] "by what will be stated" means by the rule *avyayībhāve cākāle*.

"In the order of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasyānupūrvyeṇa*). The word "task" (*kāryam*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence], meaning "the task must be performed. This is stated with the intention of the alternative view that the analysis of the compound is according to each respective case-ending (*tat-tad-vibhaktyā vigrahaḥ*). *Anupūrva* means "in the sequence of what precedes" (*pūrvasya krameṇa*). From that, the suffix *yañ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). It was stated immediately below that there is no compound with an indeclinable (*avyaya*) included within this sūtra.

Nevertheless, there is a compound [formed] as *anujyeṣṭham* with *anu* included within the *sūtra*, because of the specific mention of *anupūrva*. In the *sūtra*, from the word *yugapat*, the term *yaugapadya* is derived by adding the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Indicating this, he says: "simultaneously with the wheel" (*cakreṇa yugapat*). This refers to the word *saha*, which is a synonym for *yugapat*.

The meaning is that the compound is formed with the word *cakreṇa*; however, there is no compound with the word *yugapat*, because [the former] is included in the rule (*sūtra*), such is the intention. (651) *avyayībhāve cā’kāle* 2.4.181.

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, the word "sa" (for *saha*) shall be substituted [by "sa"]. This is because the phrase "of *saha*, [the substitution of] 'sa' occurs when it is a name" (*sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām*) is understood to follow here. However, it is not [applied] when a word denoting time follows; that is to say, the substitution of "sa" for *saha* does not occur when a word expressing time follows. For example, *sacakram* ("together with the wheel"). [This is formed] with *cakreṇa*.
The meaning is "applied simultaneously. Regarding the example *saha pūrvāhṇam*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of proximity and so forth.
In the rule, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). Making this clear, he says: "similar to a friend" (*sasakhī*) means "with a friend" (*sakhyā saha*).
The point is that the indeclinable *saha* has the meaning of "similar to. Regarding the phrase "even though it is subordinate": [this refers to the fact that the companion is not the primary factor].

The point is that because the formation of a compound occurs only when the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is predominant—by virtue of the explicit mention of "vacana" (word)—the rule does not apply when similarity (*sādṛśya*) is subordinate; therefore, that [similarity] is included [in the definition]. For example, *sakṣatram* ("the prosperity of the *kṣatra*s") means an action appropriate to *kṣatriya*s. Here, the indeclinable *saha* is used in the sense of "prosperity."
The sense is that "it proceeds. He avoids the redundancy between the words *saṃpati* and *samṛddhi* by explaining [the latter] as "of prosperity" (*ṛddheḥ*). This means wealth, grain, and so forth.
Regarding the word "anurūpa": it means suitable (*yogya*); "ātmabhāva" means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). That is to say, an action appropriate to oneself.

Regarding the phrase "even a blade of grass" (*tṛṇam api*): the suffix *ktvā* is used here according to the rule *para'varayoge ca*. The relationship of priority and posteriority (*parā'varatva*) is purely conceptual (*bauddha*). The sense is that the word *saha* here functions in the sense of exclusion (*aparivarjana*), and not in the sense of coexistence with the grass. [Objection: If this is so, how can this serve as an example for the sense of totality (*sākalya*)? To this, [the author replies]: [The text continues: ...In this case, the word *api* expresses the sense of totality; it means "not even a single blade of grass was left behind. This is because the word *api*, when used with a negative particle, denotes the entirety of the set of things denoted by the noun it qualifies. For example, in the expression "he eats even all the rice," the word *api* indicates the totality of the rice. Similarly, in the expression "he does not eat even a blade of grass," the word *api* indicates the totality of the blades of grass. Therefore, since the word *api* here denotes the totality of the blades of grass, this is indeed an example of the sense of totality. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the word *api* is used to indicate the extreme limit of the object; it signifies that there is nothing else remaining beyond that which has been mentioned. For instance, in the expression "he eats even all the rice," the word *api* indicates that there is no other food remaining besides the rice. Likewise, in the expression "he does not eat even a blade of grass," the word *api* indicates that there is nothing remaining beyond the blades of grass. Consequently, the word *api* here denotes the totality of the blades of grass. Therefore, this is indeed an example of the sense of totality. Thus, there is no contradiction. Consequently, the word *api* here denotes the totality of the blades of grass. Therefore, this is indeed an example of the sense of totality. Thus, there is no contradiction. He says: "The meaning is 'in its entirety'. That is to say, he eats everything served in the vessel. But not "here" [in this case], because the eating of grass is not applicable; such is the sense. Regarding the word "ante" (at the end): the remainder of the sentence is "an example will be stated. By the word "anta" (end) in the sūtra, there is the accompaniment of the final constituent part.
Intending to express what is meant, he provides an example: "up to the end of the Agni-section," and so forth.

By the word *agni*, the text that expounds the *agnicayana* (fire-altar construction) is intended. The analysis of the compound is: "the text together with its final member (*anta-avayava*). Thus, it means "up to the end of the Agni-section."

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word "text" (*grantha*) is supplied as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), whereas "studied" (*adhīta*) is included within the compound itself. The meaning is: he studies that portion of the Veda, the *Kalpasūtras*, and so forth, which is accompanied by the section beginning with the *Agnigrantha*. In this case...

Because the entirety [of the Veda] is not to be studied, when one studies up to the end of the section on fire (*agnigrantha*), the totality of that [Veda] is not understood; therefore, it is mentioned separately from "completeness" (*sākalya*). (652) As in the rule: *yathā'sādṛśye* 2.1.7.

Regarding the rule *yathā’sādṛśye*: the analysis is *yathā-asādṛśye*. This is because of the [authoritative] commentary. Since the meaning is already established by the very fact that the indeclinable *yathā*—when occurring in the sense of non-similarity (*asādṛśya*), which consists of fitness (*yogyatā*), repetition (*vīpsā*), or not exceeding the scope of the word-meaning (*padārthānativṛtti*)—is compounded, [the rule is stated].

He says that this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction: "only in the sense of non-similarity. Now, one might ask: how can a word ending in the *thāl* suffix—prescribed by the rule *prakāravacane thāl*—function in the sense of similarity? To this he replies: "of Hari.
A *prakāra* (mode/variety) is a particularity that differentiates a general property; it is in reference to such a *prakāra* that the suffix *thāl* is prescribed.

The meaning of the rule "the suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a manner" (*ṭhprakāravacane thāl*) is as follows: consequently, when there arises the cognition that "Hari possesses that specific attribute which Hari possesses," the understanding of the non-difference between those two manners through the words *yad* and *tad* results in the perception of similarity (*upamānatva*).

The term *bhāvaḥ* [refers to the suffix]. The word *tena* is to be construed with the phrase *ṭhprāptam*. This means "by virtue of having the sense of similarity. Alternatively, [it refers to] the portion of the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti-* which states that an indeclinable (*avyaya*) expressing similarity is compounded; or [it refers to] an indeclinable existing in the sense of *yathā*.
The sense is that the operation of the *avyayībhāva* compound, which would otherwise apply by virtue of the word being a *samasyate* (compoundable) term, is prohibited.

However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the application [of the *avyayībhāva*] in connection with the word *yathā* used in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) is stated to be obtained solely through the rule for similarity (*sādṛśya*), and not through the application based on the meaning of "as it is" (*yathārtha*). This is because of the word *yathā*.

The intention [of the author] is that because [the word *yāvat*] is included in the list [of particles] beginning with *sūtra*, the rule *yatārtha* does not apply when it is used in conjunction [with another particle];
this is explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
(653) *yāvad avadhāraṇe* | 2.1.8 | "The word *yāvat* [is a karmapravacanīya] in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)."
The term *yāvat* is used in the sense of limitation (*avadhāraṇe*). When the sense of "limited to this extent" (*iyatāparicchede*) is to be understood, the indeclinable *yāvat* is compounded;
such a compound is an *avyayībhāva*. This is the meaning. Regarding the form *yāvantaḥ*:
in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*), "those whose measure is *yat*," the suffix *vatup* is applied according to the rule *yat-tadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatuP*.

The indeclinable *yāvat* alone is compounded; however, the analytical exposition (*vigraha*) must be made with a word ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), because it is a mandatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) and thus an analysis consisting of its own constituent members (*asvapadavigraha*) is appropriate. Why [is there] this restriction?
[Consider: *yāvad dattaṃ tāvad bhuktam*. The meaning is that he does not determine that "this much was eaten."

(654) *sup-pratinā mātrārthe* | 2|1|9 | The word *sup* is the division [of the compound]. *Mātrā* means a small portion (*leśa*). The meaning is that a word ending in a *sup*-suffix is compounded with *prati* when *prati* occurs in the sense of "a small portion. Since the term *sup* is understood from the previous rule, it continues to apply here.

The repetition of the word *su* is for the purpose of preventing the recurrence of the term *avyayam* (an indeclinable) from the immediately preceding rule; indicating this, he provides the example: *śākasya leśaḥ*. Here, the indeclinable *prati* has the sense of "a small measure" (*mātrārthaka*). Therefore, there is a compound of *śākasya*—which ends in a case-ending (*subanta*)—with that [indeclinable]. This occurs within the context of the rules prescribing compounds.

Because the word ending in a *subanta* (inflected noun) is designated as the first member (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*), it is treated as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) and therefore placed first in the compound; however, this does not apply to *prati*, because in the rule prescribing the compound, it is designated by the third case (*tṛtīyānirdiṣṭa*). In the example *vṛkṣaṃ prati*, there is no compound with *prati* because it lacks the sense of "measure" (*mātra*). Nor does the rule *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna-* [Pāṇini 2.3.21] apply here.

It should not be argued that, by the very force of the rule prescribing *karmapravacanīya* status, no compound will occur here; for if a compound were to occur, there would be no distinction between the elision (*luk*) of the second case (*dvitīyā*) or the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), since once [the suffix] has been applied, that case-ending is not produced from the compound. This is because in examples such as "he waters toward the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati*), [the case ending remains].

Since the status of being a *karmapravacanīya* has its purpose fulfilled by the removal of the *ṣatva* substitution [prescribed] by the rule "after a prefix, for the root *su*," the details are explained elsewhere.
(655) Pāṇini 2.1.10: Words denoting dice (*akṣa*), lotus-stalks (*śalākā*), and numbers (*saṃkhyā*) [are compounded with *pari* to form a *tatpuruṣa*].

"akṣa-śalākā"—the remainder [of the rule] is: "that which is compounded is *avyayībhāva*. Regarding the phrase "in the context of gambling" (*dyaūtavyavahāre*), this is a *vārttika*. This gambling is conducted with either five dice (*akṣa*) or five markers (*śalākā*).
If the dice or markers all fall face-up or face-down, then...

The thrower wins; otherwise, he loses—this is the established rule. In the phrase "akṣeṇa," the third case ending denotes the agent. In the expression "ṭhviparītaṃ vṛtam," the suffix *kta* expresses the state (*bhāva*) of the root *vṛt*. The word "viparītam" is an adverbial modifier of the action. It means that one should not act in a manner contrary to how one ought to turn [the dice] for victory.
The meaning is "surrounded. Regarding *śalākāpari*: the sense is that it is surrounded in a reverse manner by means of a tally-stick (*śalākā*).
Regarding *ekapari*: the meaning is that it is surrounded in a reverse manner by one [tally-stick]. In the same way, there are *dvipari*, *tripari*, and so forth.

(656) *vibhāṣā* | 2|1|11 | *vibhāṣā*. This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). Consequently, it is understood that this [term] continues to apply to the rules for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) that follow. Now, one might object: "But [the heading] 'before *kaḍāra*, there is a compound' [is the governing rule]."
To the question, "Why was the governing rule for optionality (*vibhāṣā-adhikāra*) not established earlier than this point, prior to the rule *saha supā*?

[the author] says: "By virtue of this [very fact]. It is precisely by virtue of the placement of the governing rule for optionality in the middle that the preceding rules are understood to prescribe obligatory compounds (*nitya-samāsa*).

The meaning is "it is understood.
