Although the eternality [of the compound] is established simply because there is no evidence for an option (*vikalpa*) regarding those [rules] preceding this one, nevertheless, its firmness is confirmed by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). This should be understood.
Now, if this were the case, even the rule *sup supā* would result in an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), and consequently, [the word] *pūrva*...

Otherwise, the worldly analytical statement (vigrahavākya) "bhūta" would be untenable; furthermore, it would contradict the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ā kaḍārāt," which, in the context of the rule "sup supā," clearly intends to demonstrate the analysis as "vispaṣṭam paṭuḥ" resulting in "vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ. Therefore, he says: "No."

Regarding the phrase "nityasamāsa" (an obligatory compound): from what [reason] is this known? To this he says: "because of the rule beginning with 'avyayam'. Since the formation would already be established by the rule "ā kaḍārāt," the inclusion of the word "prāk" (before) in the rule "prākkaḍārāt" is for the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence (samāveśa) of the technical designations (saṃjñā) such as *avyayībhāva* and others within the designation of *samāsa*. Otherwise, [this would not be the case].

It is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *thā-kaḍārāt* that because the governing principle is "a single designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), this would be a case of synonymy (*paryāya*). In that context, regarding the rules for *avyayībhāva* and other compounds—such as *avyayaṃ vibhakti* and so forth—the compound formed by *sup supā* is restated, and the designations of *avyayībhāva* and the like are not to be prescribed [as new]. This is because of the rule *upapadam atiṅ*.

In rules such as *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("An agent or instrument [expressed by a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix] is frequently compounded with another word ending in a *kṛt* suffix") and *ākhyātamākhyātena kriyāsātatye* ("A verb is compounded with another verb when there is continuity of action"), the compound of a *subanta* (a word ending in a case-suffix) with another *subanta* is not established as the subject [of the rule]; therefore, because the prescription of compounding in those cases is necessary and in accordance with the governing topic of meaning (*arthādhikāra*), [the principle applies] everywhere.
It must be accepted that the term *samāsa* (compound), which is carried over [from a previous rule], serves as the element to be predicated (*vidheya*).

In that regard, since the formation would already be established by the rule *sup supā* ("a case-ending word with another case-ending word"), the prescription of the technical name "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) in rules for avyayībhāva and other types—such as *avyayaṃ vibhaktau* ("an indeclinable with a case-ending word")—would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, this indicates that the preceding rule is optional (*vaikalpika*).

Furthermore, in the rules for *avyayībhāva* and other compounds, if there were no rule specifically prescribing the compound, then because words such as indeclinables (*avyaya*) would not be designated as the first member in the sūtra for compounds, they would lack the status of *upasarjana* (subordinate element), and consequently, the restriction regarding their mandatory prior placement would not apply.
It must be stated that the formulation of rules for compounds such as *avyayībhāva* is purposeful for that reason;

for in the rule "that which is indicated by the first case" (*prathamānirdiṣṭam*), the term "in a compound" (*samāse*) refers to the grammatical rules (*śāstra*) that prescribe *avyayībhāva* and other types of compounds, which are characterized by the property of being a compound.
Since it can be argued that the status of indeclinables (*avyaya*) and so forth as *upasarjana* (subordinate members) is established by the very acceptance of their meaning [as such],
it follows that the prescription of compounds in the rules for *avyayībhāva* and other types of compounds indicates that the general rule of compounding, *sup supā*,
is optional. This is the conclusion reached regarding the sūtra *ā kaḍārād ekā saṃjñā*.

The statement "ṭhsupsupe" (Pāṇini 2.1.4), along with the Bhāṣya passage there which aims to demonstrate the analysis (*vigraha*) as "vispaṣṭa-paṭu" and "avispaṣṭa-paṭu" within the domain of compounds, serves as the evidence here; enough of this prolixity. Thus, it is established that the rule "ivena samāsaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.4) and others are optional (*vaikalpika*). Even though [these rules] occur under the heading of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), [the optionality remains].
Regarding the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, Kaiyaṭa states that although the Vārttika *ivena* is recited there as well, it was already recited under *sup supā*, and is merely being reminded there too.
(657) *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* || 2.1.12 || [The particles *apa*, *pari*, *bahiḥ*, and *añcu* form a compound with a word ending in the fifth case.]

"Not outside" (*aparibahiḥ*). The remainder [of the rule] is: "those which are compounded form an *avyayībhāva*. In the example *apaviṣṇu*, the indeclinable *apa* here signifies exclusion (*varjana*). The meaning is: "transmigration excluding Viṣṇu.
*Apa viṣṇoḥ* is the colloquial analytical sentence (*laukika-vigraha-vākya*) for the compound.

Because it is optional, there is no fixed rule regarding the analysis (*vigraha*) of its own constituent words. Since *apa* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "exclusion" according to the rule *ṭhapaparī varjane*, it functions as a *karmapravacanīya*; in connection with it, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is employed by the rule *ṭhpañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ*. There is then an *avyayībhāva* compound of *ape* with that [fifth-case] ending. The elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) follows.

Because *apeta* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and is mentioned first [in the compound], it is placed first. From the compound, there is the derivation of the case-ending (*sub-utpatti*). Then, by the rule "after an indeclinable, the feminine suffix *āp* and case-endings (*sup*) are elided" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), there is elision (*luk*). This should be understood accordingly in what follows as well. Regarding *pariviṣṇu*: here too, *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

The fifth case (pañcamī) and so forth are as before: *bahirvanaṃ*, *bahirvanāt*. From this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the fifth case is used in connection with *bahis*. The rest is as before. Because [the stem] ends in the vowel *ā*, there is the substitution of *am* [for the case-ending]. *prāgvanaṃ*, *prāgvanāt*: when in connection with a word ending in a form of the root *añc*, the fifth case is used.

(658) *āṅmaryādābhividhyoḥ* |2|1|13|. Regarding the rule *āṅmaryādābhividhyoḥ*: [the word] *etayoḥ* means "when these two [meanings] are present," that is to say, when the meanings of *maryādā* (limit) and *abhividhi* (inclusion) are present.

He provides an example for the sense of "limit" (*maryādā*): *āmukti*. This means "prior to liberation. He provides an example for the sense of "inclusive limit" (*abhividhi*): *ābālam*. This means "starting from children. In both cases, because of the rule *ṭhāṅmaryādāvacane*, [the word *ā*] functions as a *karmapravacanīya*.
The ablative case is used here by the rule "ṭhpañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.10).

(659) "When *abhi* and *prati* denote direction toward a mark, [the second case is used]. (Pāṇini 2.1.14). Regarding the word "with a mark" (*lakṣaṇena*) in this sūtra, he explains it as "that which expresses a sign" (*cihnavācinā*).

"Prāgvat" (as before) means that "these [words] are compounded as an *avyayībhāva*. In the example *abhyagni*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *śalabhā agnim abhi*. Regarding the two prefixes *abhi* and *prati*, they are used with the sense of "towards" (*lakṣaṇetthambhūta*) and "for the sake of a portion" (*abhāga*), according to the rules "abhirabhāge" and "lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna-". *Śalabhāḥ* refers to a specific kind of small insect, namely large flies. *Agnim abhi* is the analytical statement.
The status of being a *karmapravacanīya* [is established]; the meaning is that the moth's falling is indicated by fire and is directed toward it.
(660) *Anuryatsamayā* | Pāṇini 2.1.15. *Anuryatsamayā*. The word "by a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇena*) is understood from the previous rule. The suffix *tyap* is used in connection with *samayā*.
The words *abhitaḥ* and *paritaḥ* govern the accusative case. They are neuter when used in a general sense;

thus he says: "the object" (*padārtham*). Regarding *anuvanam*: here the word *vana* (forest) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean a place near a forest. The fact that the vicinity of the forest serves as the basis for this figurative indication is indeed based on the actual state of things (*vastusat*).

Thus he says: "The meaning is that he has gone near the forest. In reality, this means that he has gone near the forest, which functions as the *lakṣya* (the object characterized). This rule is for the sake of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*), even though [the form] is already established by the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a case-ending," and so forth. Consequently, one obtains the form "vanasyānu" (near the forest).

A worldly sentence containing a *vigraha* (analytic compound) may be cited here. One should not suspect the application of the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* in this case, because what is intended as the cause (*nimitta*) here is the actual state of being a characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*), rather than the cognition of that state.
If, however, the cause were the cognition of the state of being a characteristic, then the sentence "vanamanu" (along the forest) would be the appropriate example to cite.

(661) *yasya cāyāmaḥ* | 2|1|16|. The phrase *lakṣaṇena* is understood [from the previous rule]. Having understood *anu*, it is repeated and transformed into the instrumental case. Therein, one instance is connected with *lakṣaṇena*.

The second [term], however, is *anunā*; this is connected immediately after the rule "and that whose length (*āyāma*)... with the word "is indicated" as the ellipsis. *Āyāma* means length. Thus he says: "of which the length. The meaning is: a length similar to that [original] length. It is compounded; thus: "that is an *avyayībhāva*."
This also should be understood. *Anugaṅgam* is a compound (*samāsa*).

He shows the common analytical statement (*laukikavigraha*) as "along the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyā anviti*). Here too, being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) is the actual cause (*nimitta*), not something merely indicated;
therefore, there is no status of being a *karmapravacanīya*. However, if [the relationship] were construed as being indicated (*dyotyatvena*), then...

It is appropriate [to say] *gaṅgām anu*. In the expression *anugaṅgam*, by the word *gaṅgā*, a length similar to the length of the Gaṅgā is indicated (*lakṣyate*). That alone is what is to be illuminated (*dyotya*). Thus he says: "the length of the Gaṅgā."

(662) *tiṣṭhadguprabhṛtīni ca* | 2|1|17 | "And the words beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*"—the meaning is that these are specific word-forms. "The cows stand" (*tiṣṭhanti gāvaḥ*) is an explanation of the resultant meaning. That time in which the cows stand... [is the meaning of the compound].

It should rather be stated as *tiṣṭhadgu*, because the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) is understood to apply here. "At the time of milking" (*dohanakāle*)—the meaning is that at that time, cows are neither lying down nor sitting.
"Āyatīgavam"—the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the time in which cows are coming. Here...

The meaning is "in the two examples. Regarding the term *śatrādeśa* (the substitution of *śatṛ*): the point is that since [the forms] *tiṣṭhantyo gāvaḥ* and *āyatyo gāvaḥ* stand in grammatical apposition with the nominative (*prathamā*), the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* does not apply; therefore, this is an instance of nipātana (irregular formation). Regarding the term *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior): [this refers to the application of the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*].

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the word *tiṣṭhatī*, the rule "the feminine [stem] is treated like the masculine" (*ṭhstriyāḥ puṃvat*) would otherwise apply to the word *āyatī*; therefore, its absence is prescribed by way of a nipātana (irregular formation). Regarding the phrase "and the compound-ending suffix": the compound-ending suffix *ṭac* is prescribed for the word *āyatīgo* by way of a nipātana, and this occurs only in a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
The intention is that the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.91] "vidhiḥ" (the suffix occurs after the word *go*).

It should be understood that by the word *ca* ("and") in the rule "samāsāntaśca" (Pāṇini 5.4.68), the *avyayībhāva* compound is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Consequently, the word *tiṣṭhadgu* takes the neuter short vowel [by Pāṇini 2.4.7]. Due to its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision of the case-ending (*sup*) by [Pāṇini 2.4.82].
From the words *āṬgati* and *āṬgava*, the substitution of *ām* [for the case-ending] follows by the rule "not after an indeclinable compound" (*na avyayībhāvāt*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": examples such as *khaleyavam* ("barley in the threshing floor") and *khalebusam* ("chaff in the threshing floor"), where there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending, are included under the word "and so forth."

(663) *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* |2|1|18|. Regarding *pāre madhye*: it is not the two words ending in the locative case that are being referred to, but rather the words *pāra* and *madhya* themselves; thus he says—“the words *pāra* and *madhya*. They are compounded.
It should also be understood that these two [words] bear the technical designation *avyayībhāva*. Now, one might ask:
"If the words *pāra* and *madhya* are taken as ending in the vowel *a*, how can there be a reference to them as ending in the vowel *e*?

To this he says: "And they end in *e*. One might further object: "Since the result is already established by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) 'optionally' (*vibhāṣā*), what is the purpose of explicitly stating 'optionally' (*vā*)?"

To the question "For what purpose?", he says: In the alternative view that this is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, if the mention of the word "or" (*vā*) were absent, this *avyayībhāva* compound—being prescribed as a specific rule—would subvert the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*.
The intention is that the mention of "or" is for the sake of not subverting that [the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*].

Regarding the form *pāregaṅgād ānaya*: when the analysis (*vigraha*) is *gaṅgāyāḥ pāram*, it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound. Upon the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*), the word *pāra* is placed first;

then, by specific rule (*nipātana*), the vowel *a* is changed to *e*, and the neuter shortening (*napuṃsakahrasvatva*) applies. From this resulting compound *pāregaṅgam*, [the suffix *tasil* is added] again.

The origin of the fifth case [ending]. There is no elision [of the case-ending] by the rule *avyayād āp* (Pāṇini 2.4.82), because of the prohibition *na avyayībhāvāt* (Pāṇini 2.4.83) which applies to forms ending in *ā*. Furthermore, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule *apañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.105), the substitution of *am* for *ā* does not occur; such is the intended meaning. [Thus we have] *gaṅgāpārāt*.

In the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it should be understood as *madyegaṅgāt*. The form *pāregaṅgāt* is like [the forms] *pāregaṅgāt* and so forth. As for *gaṅgāmadhyāt*, it should be understood as a genitive compound.
However, according to the explanation that "the words *pāre* and *madhye*, ending in the locative case, are compounded with a word in the genitive," [the analysis would differ].

In the analysis *gaṅgāyāḥ pāre madhye* (on the far bank and in the middle of the Gaṅgā), when the compound is formed, the elision of the two locative endings (*saptamī*) occurs by virtue of the mention of the word *bahulam* in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*. Following this, the neuter shortening (*napuṃsakahrasvatva*) takes place; then, from the resulting compound, a new locative case ending arises, which is changed to *am*, resulting in *pāremadhyam*.

If [the form] *pāregaṅgam* were already established [by the rule *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*], the mention of the vowel *e* would be redundant; therefore, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that the nipātana (irregular substitution) of the vowel *e* is for the sake of cases where the locative sense (*saptamy-artha*) is not possible.
It should be understood that the example ending in the ablative case is given precisely to indicate this. Now, if...

In this context, the inclusion of the word "vā" (or) would serve only to allow for the application of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*); if that were so, sentences such as *gaṅgāyāḥ pāraḥ* ("the far bank of the Gaṅgā") or *gaṅgāyā madhyam* ("the middle of the Gaṅgā") would not be possible. Therefore, he says:
"by means of the *mahāvibhāṣā*. The term "*mahāvibhāṣā*" is a technical designation for the rule "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) which is understood to apply to all [rules].
In the rules for compound formation (*samāsavidhi*), its importance should be understood from the fact that it generally recurs [in subsequent sūtras].

Now, although the *avyayībhāva* compound is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, since it is optional by virtue of the "great option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*), the general rule (*utsarga*) of the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* certainly proceeds in the alternative case where the former does not apply.

Since that genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) also falls under the scope of the rule *vibhāṣā*, it is optional; therefore, even in the absence of the compound, the analytical sentence (*vākya*) is indeed established. If it is argued that the inclusion of the word *vā* ("or") in this sūtra is thus redundant, it is replied: [This is not so], because where there is a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*),...

The mention of "vā" (or) here is for the purpose of making it known that once an option has been excluded by an exception (*apavāda*) in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply again. Consequently, in the previous case of "kāyasya," since the option was excluded by the *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound), the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) does not occur. [For example: "the offspring of Dakṣa."

In the case of *dākṣi*, since the suffix *iñ* is excluded by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by [Pāṇini 4.1.92] "tasyāpatyam" does not apply; rather, it is simply a syntactical compound (*vākya*), as is clear from the Bhāṣya. (664) Pāṇini 2.1.19: *saṃkhyā vaṃśyena*.

[The compound] with a word denoting lineage (*vaṃśya*) [is formed] with a numeral. Lineage (*vaṃśa*) is twofold. "Lineage" (*vaṃśa*) means continuity (*santati*). As Amarasimha states: "Santati, gotra, janana, kula, abhijana, anvaya, vaṃśa, anvavāya, and santāna [are synonyms]. Regarding "by learning and by birth": therein, lineage by birth refers to the succession of sons and so forth.

This is indeed well known. But by means of knowledge, the lineage is the succession of teachers; for "he from whom one gathers the dharmas is the Ācārya. One should never bear malice toward him, for he surpasses one through knowledge—that is his most excellent birth. It is the parents who produce the physical body.

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Āpastamba beginning with these words. Regarding the term *vaṃśya*, it means "one belonging to that lineage. The suffix *yat* is applied here because the word belongs to the *diṅnāman* group. It should also be understood that this may optionally be compounded as an *avyayībhāva*, according to the rule *so'vyayībhāvaḥ*. The phrase "two sages who are *vaṃśyas*" is the analytical explanation (*vigraha*). The word *muni* is used here to indicate that it refers to those belonging to a lineage of learning (*vidyā-vaṃśya*).

It was stated that these two belong to the same lineage (*vaṃśya*). Regarding the expression *dvimuni* in the rule *dvimuni vyākaraṇasya*: in the analytical compound (*vigraha*) "those two who are sages" (*dvau ca tau munī ca*), an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed, overriding the *karmadhāraya* compound [which would otherwise apply] by the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*.
Because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). This refers to the science (*vidyā*) of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).
The meaning is that there are two founding sages (*pravartaka*), namely Pāṇini and Kātyāyana. Regarding the term "three sages" (*trimuni*):

the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the three sages are Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali. Now, one might object: "In that case, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression 'the grammar of the three sages' (*trimuni vyākaraṇam*) would be untenable. To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "of the sciences and those who possess them. Although this is established even by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, they say that there is a difference in form when other case endings are used. Now, he gives an example of one belonging to a lineage by birth: "twenty-one Bharadvājas," meaning twenty-one [descendants] of Bharadvāja.

The *avyayībhāva* compound prevails by setting aside the *karmadhāraya*. In that regard, in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the suffix *añ* is applied after the word *bharadvāja* because it belongs to the *vida* group; this suffix is then elided by the rule *ṭhyañañośca*. However, in the compound, there is no elision by the rule *upakādibhyo 'nyatarasyām advandve*.

This is because, by observing the usage "ekaviṃśatibhāradvāja" in the rule *tṛtīyāsaptamyorbahulam*, one can infer that the word *bhāradvāja* is included among the *upakādi* group [of words that optionally form a tatpuruṣa compound with another word denoting a country].

"And by rivers (*nadībhiśca*). The phrase "as before" means that a numeral is compounded with rivers, and that [compound] is an *avyayībhāva*. Regarding the rule "and in the sense of a collective (*samāhāre ca*)," this is a *vārttika*. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*), because the reading in the *Bhāṣya* is without the word "and. The example is *saptagaṅgam*, meaning "of the seven Gaṅgās."

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "a collection" (*samāhāra*), the *avyayībhāva* compound prevails, overriding the *dvigu* compound [which would otherwise apply] by the rule "in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), in the case of a subsequent member, or in a collection. Thus, we have *dviyamunam*.
The analysis is "the collection of two Yamunās. Here, by the word "river" (*nadī*),...

It is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule defining *saṃkhyā* that there is the inclusion of both specific river names and words denoting rivers in general. By this, forms such as *pañcanadam* ("the land of five rivers") and *saptagodāvaraḥ* ("the region of seven Godāvarīs") are established.
(666) *anyapadārthe ca saṃjñāyām* 2.1.21. [A compound is formed with a numeral as the first member when it denotes another word-meaning, provided it is a proper name.]

And [in the case] of another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*). The term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is discontinued; "by feminine rivers" (*nadībhiḥ*) is understood to follow. Thus he says: "a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) with feminine rivers. "It is compounded"—it should also be understood that "it is an *avyayībhāva* compound. Regarding "because the designation is not understood": a *saṃjñā* (designation) is that which is fully known (*samyak jñāyate*).

The suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *sthā-ṇāp-upasarge* to form [the word] *unmattagaṅgam*. The meaning is that because the specific location is not understood through the analytical sentence (*vākya*) "that in which the Gaṅgā is mad," this is a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound). Consequently, there is no common usage analytical sentence (*laukikavigraha*); rather, it results in an analytical sentence consisting of non-co-referential words (*asvapadavigraha*). However, in reality...

Because this falls under the scope of the *vibhāṣā* (optional) rules, this compound is also indeed optional. For this very reason, in the rule *dvitīyatṛtīyau*, by the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*,
since the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) constitute a great-scope *vibhāṣā*, in the absence of the exception—
When the meaning "non-occurrence of the *utsarga* (general rule)" is indicated, *unmattagaṅgam* is cited as an example.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "When the *avyayībhāva* is excluded, the *bahuvrīhi* does not occur. If this compound were obligatory (*nitya*), that statement would be clearly inconsistent, because the exclusion of the *avyayībhāva* would be impossible at any time.

(667) *Samāsāntāḥ* | 5|4|68 | Regarding the heading "The suffixes added at the end of compounds" (*samāsāntāḥ*), the intention is that this applies until the end of the chapter (*āpādaparisamāpteḥ*). In this context:

The term "compound-word" (*samāsapada*) refers exclusively to the non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukikavigrahavākya*). For this very reason, there is no shortening of the vowel in the form *bahukumārīka*. This is clear from the Bhāṣya on both the sūtra *gostriyoḥ* and the sūtra *antaḥ*. Thus, in the non-ordinary analytical sentence, at the very moment the designation "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) applies, [the technical operations take effect].

It is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that [the suffixes] are "terminators of compounds" (*samāsānta*). The word *anta* denotes the final constituent member. For this very reason, in examples such as *upaśaradam*, the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by the rule *na avyayībhāvāt* applies. In that context, if the suffix *ṭac* were not a constituent part of the compound, then because the *avyayībhāva* compound would not possess the suffix *ṭac* as its final member, the feminine suffix *ām* would not occur. And so it is.
If the suffix *ṭac* were not an integral part [of the compound], the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables when followed by any *bha*-suffix" would apply.

However, since *ṭac* is an integral part, the entire form ending in it constitutes an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva-samāsa*); consequently, because *upaśarad* lacks the status of an indeclinable, there is no elision of the *ṭi*.

The suffixes that form compound endings (*samāsāntapratyaya*) occur only after the case-endings (*sup*) in the non-technical analytical statement (*alaukikavigrahavākya*). For this very reason, the example "bahucarmikā" cited in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *ṭhpratyayasthāt* is consistent. The detailed explanation, however, should be sought in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

(668) *avyayībhāve śaratprabhṛtibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.107. In the context of *avyayībhāva*, the suffix *ṭac* is understood from the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*. Therefore, it says: "after *śarat* and so forth. In an *avyayībhāva* compound, that which has *śarat* and so forth as its base constitutes the final member (*uttarapada*).

That which ends in a nominal suffix (subanta) shall have the suffix *ṭac* added after it; and this [suffix] is a constituent part at the end of an unformed analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*). For example, *upaśaradam*: by the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a word ending in a case-suffix" (*avyayaṃ vibhakti*), there is an *avyayībhāva* compound of the indeclinable *upa*, meaning "near," with the word *śaradaḥ* ending in the genitive case. Then the suffix *ṭac* is applied. [The form is thus derived from] *ṭac*.
Because the word ending in *tad* (i.e., *apaśarat*) is an *avyayībhāva* compound by virtue of being a member of a compound, the rule "not after an *avyayībhāva*" (*nāvyayībhāvāt*) applies.

Since *apaśarat* is not an *avyayībhāva* compound [in this specific context], it is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and thus the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables before any nominal suffix" (*avyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ*) does not apply. The word *vipāṭ* refers to a particular river.

Regarding *vipāśā*, Amara states: "But *vipāśā* and *vipāṭ* are feminine. The compound is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī*. He recites the *śarad*-group beginning with "śarad" and so forth; here, since the option [to add *ṅīp*] would apply by the rule *jhayaḥ* for words ending in *jhay*, this recitation is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*). Regarding *jarā*: [The text continues: ...of *jarā*... (Note: The provided source fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the grammatical analysis and commentary up to that point.)

The phrase "jaraśca" is a sūtra from the *śarad-ādi* group [of avyayas]. Its meaning is that the substitution of *jaras* for the word *jarā* should be stated when this group is applied. Regarding the example *upajarasam*: it means "in the vicinity of old age.
When the indeclinable *upa*, used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*), is compounded with *jarā* in the genitive case (*jarāyāḥ*) to form an *avyayībhāva* compound, the suffix *ṭac* is added.

The elision (*subluk*) occurs; by the rule of *upetya*, the former member is placed first. Since the suffix *-ṭac* is not a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the substitution of *jaras* for *jara* would not apply when it follows; therefore, this [rule] prescribes *jaras*.

The intention is that from a stem ending in *-ṭac*, the appropriate case-endings (*sup*) are applied, and then the substitution of *ām* for *su* occurs. The term *pratiparasam* is also [to be understood in this context].
This is the *guṇasūtra*. The meaning is that the word *akṣi* is included here in this list [of words] after these [others].
Regarding the rule *yasyeti ca*: since the suffix *ṭac* is a *taddhita*, the intention is that there is elision of the vowel *i* when this suffix follows.
As for *pratyakṣam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which faces the eyes" (*akṣiṇī prati*). The meaning is "directly facing the two eyes."

The second case ending [in *pratyakṣam*] occurs because of its status as a *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna...*. The compound is an *avyayībhāva* by the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied, followed by the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), and the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. The sense is that after the word *pratyakṣa*, the appropriate case endings arise, resulting in the substitution of *am* for the final vowel. Thus, it is called *param*.

The meaning is "separated" (vyavahita); that is to say, "not an object. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *akṣṇaḥ param*, the construction is that it is an *avyayībhāva*. Now, one might ask: since the word *para* is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), how can there be an *avyayībhāva* here? To this he replies: "By virtue of the rule prescribing the final member of the compound. [This refers to] *prati-paramam*.
It is understood from the inclusion of the word *para* in the *śarad-ādi* group that the suffix *ṭac* is intended for the word *akṣi* following *para*.

Since the suffix *ṭac* is prescribed in the rule "in an avyayībhāva compound, after words beginning with *śarat*," this implies by force of logic (*tatsāmarthyāt*) that even though the word *para* is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*), it forms an avyayībhāva compound.

Regarding the term *parokṣam*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "that which is beyond (*param*) the eye (*akṣṇaḥ*)," there is an *avyayībhāva* compound of the word *param* with the word *akṣi*. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied, followed by the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sub*). The word *para-* undergoes the substitution of the final vowel *o* for its final syllable. [By the rule of] *pararūpa*, the form becomes *parokṣa-*. Then, the appropriate case-endings (*sup*) are added according to the context. This is what is meant by "the change to *am*" (*ambhāva*).

The state [of being]. Regarding the suffix *ac*: in the sense of "this has something hidden" (*parokṣam asyāsti*), the suffix *ac*—prescribed by the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*—is added to the word *parokṣa*, which primarily denotes a property (*dharma-pradhāna*). Once the suffix *ac* has been applied, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, and after the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, the result is *parokṣā kriyā* ("hidden action").
The meaning is that such [examples] are to be understood. Here, the inclusion of the word *para-* in the *gaṇasūtra* is an interpolation;

for this is established by both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa on the rule *parokṣe liṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.115) through the very fact of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of the compound-final suffix as well. Regarding *samakṣam*: the meaning is "suitable for the eyes" (*akṣṇoḥ yogyam*).

The *avyayībhāva* compound is used in the sense of "according to the object" (*yathārthe*). The suffix *ṭac* is applied, and there is the elision of the vowel *i*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *anvakṣam*: it means "behind the eyes. The *avyayībhāva* compound is formed in the sense of "behind. The remainder is like *samakṣam*. (669) *anaśca* | Pāṇini 5.4.108. [Note: This rule provides for the substitution of *anaṅ* for the final syllable of the word *akṣi* when forming certain compounds.]

And [the word] *ana*. The term *avyayībhāve* is carried over [from the previous rule] and is transformed into the ablative case (*pañcamyā*). *Ana* is its qualifier. There is an application of the rule regarding the final element (*tadantavidhiḥ*). Thus he says: "from that which ends in *an*" (*annantāt*). (Pāṇini 6.4.144) *na-staddhite*. [The elision of the final *n* occurs before a taddhita suffix.]

In the context of *taddhita* suffixes, the word "ṭhan" is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). By this, the term "of a *bha*" (*bhasya*), which is under discussion as a governing rule (*adhikṛta*), is qualified;

thus, the rule applies to that which ends in "ṭhan. The sūtra "ṭeḥ" is understood to follow, as well as "lopaḥ" from the sūtra "ṭh-lopo 'naḥ. This is what he states: "of that which ends in -n," and so forth. The example is *uparājam* (near the king), [derived] from *rājñaḥ*.
The meaning is "nearby. The term *uparāja* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed with the prefix *upa-* in the sense of proximity. By the rule *ṭhanaśca*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied;

there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), and the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). From the word *uparāja*, the appropriate case endings (*sup*) are added, resulting in the feminine form *ambhāva*.
Since this is specifically an indeclinable compound ending in *ṭac*, when *ṭac* follows, the rule "for indeclinables, [the substitution occurs] upon any *bha*-suffix" applies.
The rule "ṭhnastaddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144) is introduced because the elision of the suffix *ṭi* does not apply here. Regarding the word *adhyātmam*:
it means "in the self" (*ātmani*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending. The remainder is as explained previously. (671) *napuṃsakādanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.109).

*napuṃsakād anyatarasyām*: The term *ṭhan*, which is carried over [from a previous rule], is a qualifier of *napuṃsaka*. This is a *tadantavidhi* (rule applying to what ends in that). Thus, "after a neuter word ending in *an*" is obtained. By this, the term *avyayībhāve*, which is also carried over, is modified into the ablative case (*pañcamī*) and becomes the qualified element; this is also a *tadantavidhi*.

Thus he says: "annantādityādi" (beginning with "after a word ending in -an"). "Upacarma, upacarma": the meaning is "in the vicinity of leather. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound of the indeclinable "upa" in the sense of proximity. When the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion; then the substitution of *ambh* occurs. In the absence of the suffix *ṭac*, the form is "upacarma."

(672) *nadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇībhyaḥ* |5|4|110|. [The word] *nadīpaurṇamāsī*. He explains the sūtra by supplying the remainder: "optionally *ṭac*" (*vā ṭac*). The meaning is that the words *anyatarasyām* and *ṭac* are understood from the previous rules. *Nadī*, *paurṇamāsī*.

This means that the suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *āgrahāyaṇī*. In this context, there is no inclusion of terms designated as *nadī* (feminine rivers), because the explicit mention of *paurṇamāsī* and *āgrahāyaṇī* serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For example, *upanadam*, which means "near the river" (*nadyāḥ samīpam*), [is used] in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*).

The term *upetya* is an avyayībhāva compound. [The suffix] *ṭac* is added; by the rule "ṭhyasyeti ca," there is the elision of the vowel *i*. From the word *upanada*, the case-ending *sup* is applied. The intention is that the substitution of *ambh* occurs. Thus, *upanadī* is the form when *ṭac* is absent, with the shortening of the neuter vowel and the elision of the case-ending *sup* by the rule "avyayād āpsupaḥ. The term *upapaurṇamāsam* is formed in the same manner.

The meaning is "in the vicinity of the full moon" (paurṇamāsī). The form [upanadam] is like [the word] upanadam [formed with the suffix] ṭac. *Upapaurṇamāsī* is the form when there is no *ṭac*. Similarly, it should be understood that *upāgrahāyaṇam* and *upāgrahāyaṇī* are formed in the same way. [The latter means] she whose *hāyana* (year) is near (*upa*) the beginning (*agra*).

The *āgrahāyaṇī* is the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. From this point onward, with the commencement of the sun’s northward course (*makarāyana*), the northern solstice (*udagayana*) begins; for it is well known that "the year consists of two courses of the sun, northward and southward," and thus the northern solstice itself is the beginning of the year.

(673) *jhayaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.111. Regarding *jhayaḥ*: the phrase *jhayā avyayībhāve*, which was carried over from the previous rule, is modified here by being changed into the ablative case (*jhayāḥ*). This is a rule involving reference to what ends with that (*tadantavidhiḥ*). The words *anyatarasyām* and *ṭac* are also carried over [from the preceding rules].
Thus he says: "after a word ending in a *jhay* sound.
(674) *gireś ca senakasya* | 5|4|112 | "And after *giri*, according to Senaka. Senaka was a teacher by name. [The mention of his name] is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtham*).

The sense is that the option is established simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*). Regarding *upagiram*: the meaning is "near the mountain. When the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there is the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. Then the substitution of *ambh* occurs. Here, because of the mention of Senaka, [the rule] *nadīpaurṇamāsī-* applies; [and] in the rule *jhayaḥ*, [the following applies].
Some maintain that the mention of *anyatarasyām* does not carry over [from the previous rule].
Thus ends the section on *avyayībhāva* compounds in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on *bahuvrīhi* compounds.

(818) *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ* | 2|2|23|. "The remainder is the *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding the word "of the triplet": this means "of the case-ending. Now, [one might object]: since there are rules such as "the second case in the sense of *śrita*," "the third case in the sense of *tatkṛta*," "the fourth case in the sense of *tadartha*," and "the fifth case... [and so forth].

By the rules "bhayena," "ṣaṣṭhī," and "saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ," the formation of compounds with the six case endings beginning with the accusative is prescribed; however, by the rule "viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa," etc., the formation of a compound even with the nominative case is also prescribed. Therefore:

Since the remaining case-endings would otherwise be difficult to obtain, he says: "by specifying" (*viśiṣya*). Although a possessive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) actually functions with the first case-ending, because there is no rule prescribing it by specifically pronouncing the first case-ending within the rules for compound formation, [the remaining endings are not obtained].

The meaning is that the nominative case (*prathamā-vibhakti*) is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) in relation to the six case-endings beginning with the accusative (*dvitīyā*) which have been specifically prescribed; this is what [the author] expresses by saying, "the sense is 'ending in the nominative'. And this is clear in the Bhāṣya.

(819) *anekam anyapadārthe* | 2|2|24|. "Aneka" [refers to] that which ends in the first case (*prathamānta*). This is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "śeṣa" (remainder). And thus, *sup-supā* does not apply here, as there is no purpose for it. "Aneka" [here means] "more than one" ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

The meaning is that even in the recitation [of the rule], it must end in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). Regarding the word *anyā* (other): the meaning is "other than the nominative-ending word that is present [in the context]. And thus, for the purpose of excluding a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *pañcabhukta*—meaning "one by whom food was eaten by five"—the term *bahuvrīhiḥ* [is employed].
Regarding the two Vārttikas established in the Bhāṣya— the one stating that "it should be stated [the rule applies] to those in grammatical apposition" (samānādhikaraṇānām),

and the other stating that "for the purpose of excluding [the application of] Bahuvrīhi in cases such as 'yo gataḥ sa vṛṣṭadevaḥ' when it means 'when the rain-god has rained,' a Bahuvrīhi should be prescribed for the sense of case endings other than the nominative"— neither of these is necessary.

He states what must be done: "The *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of a case other than the first. And it follows that [the compound] consists of words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). The word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is understood from the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣagrahaṇāt*). For the *Bhāṣya* says: "From the mention of 'remainder,' it is understood that [the first member] ends in the first case (*prathamānta*)."

Furthermore, in the case of "pañcabhir bhuktam asya" (five have been eaten by him), it follows that a *bahuvrīhi* compound cannot be formed because one of the two words being compounded does not end in the nominative case (*prathamā*). This is because the accepted meaning is that a word is compounded when it occurs in the sense of a word other than one ending in the nominative; therefore, in the phrase "dṛṣṭe deve gataḥ" (he went when the god was seen), a *bahuvrīhi* is likewise not formed.
The result is as follows: the meaning is that a word denoting something other than what is expressed by the final member [of a compound] is compounded;
since this is the accepted sense, it follows that there is no *bahuvrīhi* even in the case of "having gone when it had rained" (*vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ*).
This is the intended point.
Therein, he provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a second-case object as its referent: "prāptam" (attained).

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule "gatyarthākarmaka-". In this analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), water is the agent of the attainment whose object is the village; thus, the village functions as a qualifier.
However, there is the cognition of water as the qualificand in the case of [the verbal compound] *prāptodaka*. But in the case of a nominal compound (*samāsa*),

by virtue of the power of *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning), there is the cognition of the village as the qualificand— specifically, "the village which is the object of the attainment whose agent is water"— and the cognition of water as its qualifier.

In the same way, the reversal of the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) should be understood in subsequent cases as well. Now, he provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*): "the ox that has carried the chariot" (*ūḍharatho 'naḍvān*). The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "that by whom the chariot was carried. Now...

He provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the sense of the fourth case (*caturthyartha*): "a bull that has drawn a chariot" (*ūḍharatho 'naḍvān*). The analytical expansion (*vigraha*) is: "by whom a chariot was drawn. Next, he provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the sense of the fourth case: "Rudra to whom an animal has been offered" (*upahṛtapaśū rudraḥ*). The analytical expansion is: "to whom an animal was offered. Now...

He provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamyartha*): "a pot from which rice has been removed" (*uddhṛtaudanā sthālī*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that of which the rice has been removed. Next, he provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*): "Hari, who has yellow garments" (*pītāmbaro hariḥ*). [This means] "the yellow garment..."

The analysis (*vigraha*) is "of whom" (*yasya*). Now, he illustrates the *bahuvrīhi* with the sense of the locative case: *vīrapuruṣakaḥ grāmaḥ*. The analysis is "in which there are heroic men" (*vīrāḥ puruṣā yasmin*). The suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*.
Here, because the object (*karman*) and other factors are expressed by the compound itself, only the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs. However, regarding the meaning of the nominative...

"No," [he says]. The sense is that by the term "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*), only the meaning of a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth—distinct from that which ends in the first case (*prathamā*)—is intended. "Nor [of] words in different grammatical relations" (*vyadhikaraṇānām*); the sense is that this is because it has been stated that "more than one [word] ending in the first case" (*anekaṃ prathamāntam*) [is required].
The elision of the subsequent member [of a compound] after words beginning with *pra* and others should be stated as an option when it follows a word derived from a verbal root (*dhātujam*).

[The rule begins with: "After *pra* and others" (*prādibhyaḥ*). It should be stated that a Bahuvrīhi compound may be formed with another nominative case-ending word when there is a nominative case-ending word following *pra* and others that has a verbal root as its base (*dhātujaprakṛtika*). In that Bahuvrīhi, [the subsequent member] following *pra* and others...

The meaning is that the elision (*lopa*) of the final member, which is derived from a verbal root (*dhātuja*), is optionally to be stated. Here, the term "bahuvrīhi" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), while the elision itself is the actual rule (*vidhi*). Regarding the example *prapatitaparṇa*:
"fallen away excellently" is *prapatitam*; this is a compound formed according to the rule "prepositions [are compounded] with words meaning 'gone' and so forth. (*prādayo gatādyarthe*)

The analysis of the compound is: "that from which the leaf has fallen" (*prapatitaṃ parṇaṃ yasmāt*). Thus, it is *praparṇa*. This form arises when the derivative of the verbal root in the second member is elided after the first member *pra-patita*.

(This is according to the rule: "In the case of the negative particle *nañ* used with words having the sense of 'existence' (*astyartha*), the elision of the second member may optionally be expressed."

Regarding the rule *naño'styarthānām*: a bahuvrīhi compound should be prescribed for words ending in case-terminations (*subanta*) that follow the negative particle *nañ* and express the meaning of "to exist" (*astyartha*). Furthermore, it should be stated that there is optionally an elision (*lopa*) of those words expressing existence which serve as the final members (*uttarapada*) of the compound. For example, in *avidyamānaputraḥ*: first, there is the *nañ*-compound *na vidyamānaḥ*.

"Elision of *naÑ*. The analysis of the compound is: "one whose son is non-existent" (*avidyamāna-putraḥ*). The form *aputraḥ* arises from the elision of the word *vidyamāna*, which has the sense of "existing" (*asti-artha*). Here too, the term "bahuvrīhi" is understood by way of restatement (*anuvāda*). Regarding the rule "and [the suffix] after indeclinables," it is stated that "the bahuvrīhi is to be expressed."

The remainder [of the commentary] follows. Regarding the term *uccairmukha*: since the word *uccaiḥ* primarily denotes a locative sense (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), it ends in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and lacks the first case ending (*prathamā*). Consequently, as the condition for forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound is not met, this rule is stated.
[The rule is: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, when the preceding member is a locative or a word of comparison, there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapada-lopa*)."
"Regarding the rule *saptamyupamānapūrvapadasyottarapadalopaśca*:

that compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is accompanied by a locative case ending (*saptamyanta*) and a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is called *saptamyupamānapūrvapada*; [the meaning is] that from such a compound word, when combined with another word..."

The *bahuvrīhi* compound must be stated; the meaning is that when the preceding member consists of a compound word, the elision (*lopa*) of its final member must also be stated. In this regard, he provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* whose preceding member is a compound containing a word ending in the locative case—namely, *kaṇṭhestha*, and so forth. [The suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ*. [Thus: *kaṇṭhe*.

"Staying in the throat" (*kaṇṭhestha*) means "staying in the throat. This is an *upapada* compound. By the rule *ṭhamūrddhamastakāt*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending. Thus, *kaṇṭhestha* is a complete compound word. Its [subsequent] formation with the word *kāla* as a *bahuvrīhi* is what is being restated here. The case endings (*sup*) are elided. *Tara*.
In the compound *kaṇṭhestha*, the first member of the bahuvrīhi is accompanied by a word ending in the locative case;

the elision of the subsequent member *stha* therein is a specific rule (*vācanika*). Thus, *kaṇṭhekāla* is a bahuvrīhi containing within it a compound formed with a locative-ending word. [The elision applies] to that locative which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of that [bahuvrīhi].

The *luk* (elision) of the word *āditya* occurs when it follows *ṭha*, *mūrdhan*, or *mastaka*. Now, he provides an example of a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose prior member consists of a complete *upamāna* (standard of comparison): *uṣṭramukhaḥ*. In the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "the face of a camel" (*uṣṭrasya mukham iva*), there is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. The word *mukha* is used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean something resembling a face.

The word "iva" (as if) is used for the sake of indication. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one whose face is like that of a camel" (*uṣṭramukham iva mukhaṃ yasya*), it is stated that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In that case, "uṣṭramukha" is the prior member (*pūrvapada*) of the *bahuvrīhi*; the elision (*lopa*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), namely the word "mukha," is prescribed by rule.

[The rule] "saṅghātavikāra-ṣaṣṭhyāścottarapadalopaśca" [means]: when there is a compound of a word ending in the genitive case with another word [forming a *bahuvrīhi*], it should be stated that this applies to a word following a word ending in the genitive case that undergoes a change of its constituent parts (*saṅghātavikāra*), and furthermore, there is elision (*lopa*) of that subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For example: *keśacūḍa*.

The form *saṅghāta* arises from the elision of the word *śabda*. The form *suvarṇālaṅkāra* arises here from the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) of the word *vikāra*. And there are also forms such as *astikṣīrā*.

"‘Astikṣīrādayaśca’ (and ‘astikṣīra’ etc.)": the meaning is that words such as *astikṣīra* should be added to the list of *bahuvrīhi* compounds. In the example *astikṣīrā gāvaḥ*, this rule is provided because the *bahuvrīhi* would otherwise not apply; since the word *asti* is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), it lacks the status of being in the nominative case (*prathamāvibhaktyanta*).

In reality, however, he states that this statement need not have been commenced: "The word *asti* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a case-ending. Because it is a particle (*nipāta*) formed by resembling a case-ending, *asti* is an indeclinable according to the rule: "An indeclinable consists of particles beginning with vowels."

It possesses a meaning that exists [as a referent]. Therefore, since the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending occurs by the rule "soḥ ṭhavyayādāpsupaḥ," and because it is established as being in the nominative case by the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle, this specific statement need not be made; this is the intended sense.
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The mention of 'astikṣīrā' and so forth is unnecessary, or rather, it is not necessary because of its indeclinability (*avyayatva*)."

(820) A feminine word [ending in a *ṅī* suffix] becomes like the masculine form when it occurs in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with another feminine word, provided that the former does not end in *ūṅ* and is derived from a stem that has a corresponding masculine form, except in the case of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇī*) and words such as *priya*.
[The rule states: "A feminine [word] becomes like the masculine. The compound *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ* is a single word; [the term] *striyāḥ* [is understood].
Intending that this is an adjective in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), he explains it as "from that which has been spoken of as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*).

The explanation of *anūṅ* is "the absence of *ūṅ*; [this is formed] either as an avyayībhāva compound with the sense of non-existence, or as a negative (*nañ*) tatpuruṣa. In the term *bhāṣitapuṃskāt*, the ablative case is used in the sense of separation (*digyoge pañcamī*). "The subsequent... (*para*)...

Thus, the word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntam*) is to be supplied [in the analysis]. Consequently, it results that the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by analyzing it as "that which has a feminine suffix other than *ūṅ* following a stem that has been mentioned with a masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt parānūṅ yasya*). Now, one might object: "If a compound is formed, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *suk* for the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*). To this he says: "By virtue of an irregularity (*nipātanāt*). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that, due to this irregular formation (*nipātana*), the *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs even when the word is not in the nominative case, and there is also the elision of the word *para*. Alternatively, for this very reason of irregular formation, the ablative case is used even when the word *para* is not actually employed, provided its meaning is understood. [Objection: But even so, in the rule "striyāḥ," the word ending in the genitive case—

If "anūṅ" were a qualifier of "bhāṣitapuṃskāt," then one would have heard the genitive case ending in the form "bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ. Therefore, he says: "and there is elision of the genitive. The word "nipātanāt" (by irregularity) is to be supplied. That by which the masculine is expressed is "bhāṣitapumān."

"Tadbhāṣitapuṃskam" means that which has been expressed as masculine; "tadasyāsti" [forms the compound] with the suffix *ac* according to the rule beginning with *arśas*. That is to say, it possesses one and the same cause for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in both the masculine and feminine genders. This has been explained under the rule "tṛtīyādiṣu bhāṣitapuṃskam. He states this: "when equal..."

Regarding the phrase "in the cause of application" (*pravṛtinimite*): the expression "of the word denoting a female" (*strīvācakasya śabdasya*) means "of that which has the feminine gender" (*strīliṅgasya*). The intention is that the genitive ending in *striyāḥ* does not refer to a secondary suffix (*strīpratyaya*). The term *puṃvat* is a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*). The suffix *vati* is added to the genitive *puṃsaḥ*, meaning "like a male" (*puṃsa iva puṃvat*).

Thus he says: "The form is like that of a word denoting a male. The term *striyām* (in the feminine), though ending in the locative case, does not refer to a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), but rather to the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*). And this [gender] connects with the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) under the governing rule *aluguttarapade*. Thus he says: "when the subsequent member is of the feminine gender."

He explains the phrase "after a feminine ordinal (*pūraṇī*) and after *priya* etc. as follows: "but not when [the word] ending in a feminine ordinal suffix or when *priya* etc. follow. It should be understood that because of the mention of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*), a feminine ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is intended. This applies when the cause for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical.

Whom? *kuṭībhāryaḥ*. In this case, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) does not apply; for the word *kuṭī* is masculine when meaning "pot" (*ghaṭa*), but feminine when meaning "house" (*geha*). Thus, because the grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) differ, if it were stated that "the feminine suffix shall be like the masculine," it would result in the elision of the feminine suffix itself.

Furthermore, in the case of *paṭvībhārya*—meaning "one whose wife is clever"—if the *ṅīṣ* suffix were elided by depending on the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as the cause, then by the rule "that which precedes a substitute is as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *u* would occur. [This is why the rule specifies] "when a short vowel [follows]. For example, in the case of *citrāgavaḥ*, meaning "one who has brindled cows."

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided, the word "many" (*aneka*)— being specified as the first member in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), or because it possesses a fixed case-ending in the *vigraha*— is considered a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Consequently, in the word *citragu*, the vowel *o* [of *go*] is shortened to *u* by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*.

This is the meaning. Now, if one accepts the worldly compound *citrā gāvaḥ*, then after the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is formed— namely, the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) in *citras-as* and the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*) in *go-as*— and because that substitute is treated as the beginning of the subsequent element (*parādivadbhāva*), the vowel *a* would not remain in the word *citra* once the elision of *as* has occurred.

[Otherwise] the word *citraguḥ* would be heard [with a visarga], and the letter *u* would not be heard; however, if [the elision] were like that of the preceding part (*pūrvāntavat*), then because the remaining mere *s* would lack the status of being a case-ending (*suptva*), the elision (*luk*) would not occur. Therefore, he says: *citrā as*. [This refers to] the word *go*.
The feminine designation "citri" is used because it is a feminine noun and serves as an adjective [modifying a feminine term].
According to the view of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*,
by the maxim "the elision (*luk*), being external, subverts even internal rules," [the elision] occurs prior [to the application of other grammatical operations].
The intention is that there is elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*) due to the rule *pūrvasavarṇadīrghāt*. Regarding *citraguḥ*:
the intention is that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the feminine suffix is shortened, the word *citrā* undergoes masculine form (*puṃvat*). Regarding *rūpavadbhāryaḥ*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose wife is beautiful" (*rūpavatī bhāryā yasya*). Here, the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana-hrasva*) applies to the word *rūpavatī*.

The word *śabda* takes the masculine gender. Now, one might ask: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one whose cow is variegated and old" (*citrā jaratī gaur yasya*), how can there be a three-word *bahuvrīhi*, given that by the rule *sup supā* ("a case-ending [word] with another case-ending [word]") singularity is intended? To this he says: "because of the mention of 'many'" (*anekokteḥ*). From the inclusion of the term *śeṣa* (remainder), it is understood that [the compound consists of] words ending in the nominative case. Of one...

The meaning is that a compound of words ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) is not possible, because the technical name "compound" (*samāsa*) is understood to be etymological (*anvartha*); thus, since it is established by implication that there must be more than one word ending in the nominative, the mention of "more than one" (*aneka*) again serves to clarify—just as stated in the *Bhāṣya*—that a *bahuvrīhi* consists of two or many words ending in the nominative. This refers to the phrase "herein" (*atre*).
The meaning is: "in a three-word *bahuvrīhi*. For example: *citrājaratīguḥ* or *jaratīcitrāguḥ*.

The point is that since both the quality of being variegated (*citratva*) and the quality of being old (*jaratītva*) are equally qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the cow, either one may optionally be placed first according to the rule:
*saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau* ("in a *bahuvrīhi*, that which ends in the locative case [or] the qualifier [is placed first]").

"Thus, *dīrghā*": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose shanks (*jaṅghe*) are long (*dīrghe*) and slender (*tanvyau*). Regarding both cases, having raised the doubt that there might be *puṃvat*-substitution for the first and middle members [of the compound], he says: "in a three-membered [compound]. Regarding the phrase "of the final member": because it is the final constituent of the compound, the third member alone is here considered the "final member" (*uttarapada*).

This must be stated: the state of being followed by that [the third member] belongs only to the middle member, and not even to the first member, because the latter is separated from it by the middle member—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "In that case, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) of the middle member would be unavoidable, since the condition of being followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) exists. To this, he says: "The second [member] also is not [so]."

Regarding the term *puṃvat*: [the objection] "because of the absence of being a prior member (*pūrvapada*)" is raised. The status of being a prior member is obtained through implication by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). The intended meaning is that only the first constituent member of a compound is the *pūrvapada*, and not even a middle constituent member. Now, with respect to the middle member...

The first member possesses the status of being a prior member (*pūrvapada*), and the middle member possesses the status of being a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in relation to the first member; therefore, he says: "For the word *uttarapada*... [is] "conventional" (*rūḍha*), meaning established by the consensus of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasamayasiddha*). "Thus they say" means in this manner.

The grammatical connection is "some say. In that regard, it is logical that there is no *puṃvadbhāva* (substitution of the masculine form) for the first member in a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*, because it is not followed by a final member (*uttarapada*). However, for the middle member, even though it lacks the status of being a preceding member (*pūrvapada*), *puṃvadbhāva* certainly does occur; this is because in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*... [the condition applies].

Since the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) is not explicitly heard [in the rule] and there is no [contextual] recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), one must state that the meaning "the preceding word becomes like the masculine" is understood from the expression "in the subsequent word" (*uttarapade*). However, even that is not possible;
therefore, he says: "In this case, the preceding word is not implied. Here, [the term] *auṭ* refers to the feminine.

In the rule *puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34), by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *uttarapade* ("in the subsequent member"), the term *pūrvapada* ("the prior member") is neither implied nor understood by implication; this is the meaning. Why is this so? To this he says: "as in the case of *ānaṅ*.
The meaning of that [rule] is: *ānaṅ* shall be substituted for words ending in *ṛ* in a *dvandva* compound when there is a subsequent member. In that context, [it applies] to four...

In the rule *dvandve ṭhhotṛpotṛneṣṭodgātāraḥ*, the penultimate [vowel] of *neṣṭṛ* has been cited as an example in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*. In that context, if there were a restriction that the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) must be implied by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), then the penultimate [vowel] of the form *neṣṭṛ* [would not apply].

Because of the absence of the status of being a prior member (*pūrvapada*), the substitution *ānaṅ* would not be applicable. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no necessary restriction (*niyama*) that an operation prescribed for a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) must belong exclusively to the prior member. By the word "thereby" (*tena*), the meaning is "without implying a prior member. Regarding the phrase "of the penultimate" (*upāntyasya*), [it refers to] the final [letter].
"Nearby" (*samīpam*) means "the penultimate. This refers to the middle [element] situated near the final constituent part.
Regarding the phrase "just as in the masculine" (*puṃvadeva*), the word "form" (*rūpa*) is to be supplied.
He demonstrates this very point with the example: *citrājaradguru*. Here, the word *citrā* does not undergo the masculine form (*puṃvat*).
The sense is that [the rule does not apply] because of the intervention of a middle word, and because of the absence of being followed by a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*).
Regarding the phrase "and so forth": *jakatīcitraguḥ* (one whose brindled cows are small), *tanvīdīrghajaṅghaḥ* (one with long shanks that are slender).
Now, regarding the rule *ṭhānaRﬁĀtaḥ*, there is the example *hotṛpotṛneṣṭodgātāraḥ*.

Let there be no implication of a preceding word based on the examples in the Bhāṣya. To the question, "What is the proof that there is no such implication in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*? he says: "For this very reason. This means that even in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*, there is no implication of a preceding word.
Even though the word "dvandvagarbhe" occurs, the word "bahuvrīhau" is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding the statement "the Bhāṣya":
although the example *citrajaraṅguḥ* is not seen anywhere in the Bhāṣya during a thorough examination of the entire work, nevertheless, immediately after the phrase "*citrajaraṅgur iti*"...
The word "at Prayāga" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding the word "the Bhāṣya," the meaning is the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra, which reads "one whose wives are *paṭvī* and *mṛdu*.

The word "indicates" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [This is] in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra "striyāḥ puṃvat," concerning the example: "one whose wives (*bhārye*) are *paṭvyau* and *mṛdvyau*."

In the case of a *dvandva-garbha* bahuvrīhi, "paṭvīmṛdubhāryam" is cited as an example. Therein, the *dvandva* consisting of the words *paṭvī* and *mṛdu* constitutes the prior member (*pūrvapada*); since that [prior member] does not possess the quality of having been previously mentioned in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*), there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) for the *dvandva*.

Because of the rule regarding the gender of the final member [of a compound], in that *dvandva* compound, the word *paṭvī*, which is the first member, does not undergo the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*); this is because it is separated by the middle member and thus lacks the status of being immediately followed by the final member (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, because the middle member is not the final member and is not in grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), the substitution does not occur when it follows that [middle member].

The possibility of the masculine form (*puṃvatva*) arises as follows: since the word *mṛdvī* alone is both used in the masculine and feminine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) and is followed by another word (*uttarapada*), it undergoes the masculine transformation; this is the intended meaning. However, if one assumes that the term "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) is implied in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*, then [the application would concern] the word *mṛdu*.
Because the condition of being a prior member (*pūrvapadatva*) is absent, the application of the *puṃvat* (masculine) rule does not occur; thus, its [the opponent's] inconsistency is quite evident.

Consequently, the meaning is that the Bhāṣya statement "one whose wife is clever and gentle" (*paṭvīmṛdubhārya*) implies the usage "one whose cow is brindled and old" (*citrājaradgu*). Regarding the term "karmadhāraya": it refers to one who is both old and brindled (*jaratī cāsau citrā ca*).

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. By the rule "in a *karmadhāraya*, [the first member] is like the masculine" (*puṃvat-karmadhāraye*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* of the word *jaratī* is removed due to its being treated as masculine. Consequently, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose cow is old and variegated" (*jaraccitrā gauḥ yasya*), where the preceding member is a *karmadhāraya*, the rule "of the feminine, the masculine form" (*striyāḥ puṃvad*) applies to the preceding member, the word *jaraccitrā*.

The meaning is that because of the *puṃvat* (masculine-like) treatment, there is the removal of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding the phrase "after a *karmadhāraya*": in the *karmadhāraya* compound "she who is old and a cow" (*jaratī cāsau gauśca*), after the suffix *ṭac* has been applied by the rule *ṭhgorataddhitalukī* and the substitution of *ava* has occurred, the word *jaratī* undergoes *puṃvat* treatment by the rule *puṃvatkarmadhāraye*, resulting in the removal of the suffix *ṅīp*.

The word *jaradgavī* is formed by adding the feminine suffix *ṅīp* to *jaradgava*. Then, in the compound *citrā jaradgavī yasya*, which is a *bahuvrīhi* with a *karmadhāraya* as its final member, the suffix *kap* is added according to the rule *nadyutaśca*;
subsequently, the word *citrā* undergoes the *puṃvat* (masculine) transformation according to the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*, resulting in the form *citrajaradgavīka*. This is the meaning.
"What [is the form] for the feminine?"—this is a question regarding the word ending in the genitive case. Regarding "grāmaṇidṛṣṭi":

when the word *grāmaṇī* is in the neuter gender, by the rule "the short vowel is used in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*), the word *grāmaṇi* ends in *i*. The word *kula* is included for the purpose of indicating the neuter gender. By the word *dṛṣṭi*...
The intended meaning is that [the word *grāmaṇī*] takes the place of the eye (*netra*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is simply "one whose vision is the village-leader" (*grāmaṇi-dṛṣṭir asya*).

The point is that in the absence of the rule *ṭhstriyāḥ*, if the word *grāmaṇī* were to undergo masculine substitution (*puṃvat*), the short vowel of the neuter would be removed, resulting in the form *grāmaṇīkulam*. As for the example *gaṅgābhāryaḥ*, here...

The point is that because the word *gaṅgā* is eternally feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), it lacks the quality of having its masculine form optionally suppressed (*bāṣitapuṃsaka*); therefore, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Regarding the example *vāmorūbhārya*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose thighs (*ūrū*) are beautiful (*vāmau*). The suffix *ūṅ* is applied by the rule *saṃhita-śapha-lakṣaṇa-vāmādeśca*. [The suffix] belongs to that which ends in this [suffix].

The intention is that when the *puṃvat* (masculine-like) substitution applies and the suffix *ūṅ* is removed, the first member of the compound in the example "vāmorubhārya" would end in the vowel *ū*. The question "striyām kim? ("What [is the purpose] regarding the feminine? is a question concerning the locative case ending. In the example "kalyāṇīpradhāna," because the word *pradhāna* is invariably neuter.

The point is that even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *kalyāṇī*, because it is in the feminine gender, the masculine form (*puṃvatva*) does not apply when this [word] follows. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of a ordinal number" (*pūraṇyāṃ tu*), the remainder of the sentence is: "A specific distinction will be stated regarding the examples for the prohibition of the masculine form."

(821) *appūraṇī-pramāṇyoḥ* | 5|4|116|. The word *ap* is [the first member of] *ap-pūraṇī*. There is a split (*cheda*) at *avi*. From the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the suffix *ṅīp* is added after] *sakthi* and *akṣi*" (*bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇor ṅīp*), the term "*bahuvrīhau*" is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and qualifies both *pūraṇī* and *pramāṇī*; this is a rule concerning the final element of those words (*tadanta-vidhi*).

Because of the feminine designation, that which ends in a feminine ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is understood here as feminine. This is what he states with the words "by the preceding [sūtra], for the sake of the meaning," and so forth. "It should be *ap*"—it should also be understood that this is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) forming a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). "Fifth" means "that which completes five. [The rule] "in the sense of completing that, the suffix *ḍaṭ* [is applied]" [is the basis].

By the rule *ṭhnāntād asaṃkhyādeḥ*, the augment *maṭ* is added; because it ends in a *ṭ*-letter, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus we have *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ*. Here, once the *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, there is a prohibition against the masculine form (*puṃvat*) of the word *kalyāṇī* when it precedes the word *pañcamī*, which ends in an affix denoting a meaning [of number]. [The result is] *ap*.

This is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formed by the application of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). There is the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule "ṭāp ṭhyasyeti ca. Now, does the fifth night enter into the meaning of the other member of the compound, or not? It cannot be the first case, because as that [fifth night] constitutes the very object denoted by the member being compounded, it is impossible for it to be "other than" that. Nor can it be the second case, because of the [rule regarding] the fifth case...

If it is argued that, in the absence of the inclusion of "night" as a separate referent (*anyapadārtha*), the compound *kalyāṇīpañcamā* would result in the understanding of only four nights—excluding the fifth night—and thus the word *pañca* ("five") would be rendered inconsistent, [the response is: True; [it refers to] five...

The referent of the compound (anyapadārtha) is the collection itself, in which the distinctions between its constituent parts have emerged. In that case, even though the fifth night has entered [into the collection], it does not contradict the status of the collection as the referent of the compound, because the collection is distinct from its individual parts. The plural form "rātrayaḥ" [is used]...

This depends upon the multiplicity of its constituent parts (*avayava*), as has been explained in detail in the rule concerning the technical designation of pronouns (*sarvanāman*). Now, he provides an example for the application of the suffix *ap* after a word ending in *pramāṇa*: "strīpramāṇa" (one whose measure is a woman).

Here, the word *pramāṇa* ends in the *lyuṭ* suffix used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and is dependent on its substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*). Because it bears the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

When it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, with the suffix *ap* and the elision of the vowel *ī* by the rule "ṭhyasyeti ca," the form "strīpramāṇa" is obtained. However, because the first member of the compound is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*) and has not been previously used as a masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), there is no possibility of its being treated as a masculine (*puṃvad-bhāva*). This applies only when the ordinal number is the principal member (*pradhānapūraṇī*); this is stated in the rule "striyāḥ puṃvat."
The meaning is that in the rule for *ṭhappūraṇī*, the inclusion of the word "principal" (*pradhāna*) must be made. [Objection:

But in the example "the five nights ending with the auspicious one" (*kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ*), since the fifth night is the referent of the compound member (*samasyamānapadārtha*), how can it be considered "principal"?

Because a *bahuvrīhi* compound has as its primary referent a meaning external to its constituent members, he says: "In the example cited, 'the night is the completer and is the expressed meaning,' [the word] 'night' is primary. In the example cited, "the five nights having the auspicious one as the fifth," the night is that which completes the group of five.

The meaning is that even though it is the referent of the fifth case (pañcamī) being compounded, it is nevertheless expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound because it is included within the aggregate that constitutes the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*); thus, it becomes primary.

This is just as, for example, although the aggregate of nights (*rātrisamudāya*)—whose constituent parts are prominent—is primary, [the individual night] is [included] by virtue of being a constituent part thereof.

The first four nights are expressed as a compound; likewise, the fifth night is also expressed as a compound. The sense is that because the referent of the fifth night—which is being compounded—enters into the referent of the other word (anyapadārtha), it possesses predominance. "But elsewhere," however...

The meaning is that, in the expression "the fortnight having the auspicious fifth" (*kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*), because the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇī*) does not enter into the referent of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) and is therefore subordinate, the suffix *ap* does not occur; thus, a specific rule will be stated.

(822) *nady-ṛtaś-ca* |5|4|153|. From the compound *nady-ṛt*, a collective dvandva, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is derived. The term *bahuvrīhau* is carried over from the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇor-aḥ* and is transformed here into the fifth case.

The subsequent word (*uttarapada*) implied by that [rule] is qualified by *nadī* and *ūṅ*. This is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*).
