From the rule "after *uras* and so forth" (*uraḥprabhṛtibhyaḥ*), the word *kap* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "from a compound whose final member is a *nadī*. The meaning is: "from a compound whose final member ends in a *nadī*. It should be added that *kap* is both a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) and a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*).

It should be understood as follows: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "that fortnight (*pakṣa*) which has a blessed fifth day," when it forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because the final member is the word "fifth" (*pañcamī*), which ends in a feminine suffix (*nadī*), the entire *bahuvrīhi* ending in that member takes the suffix *kap* by virtue of being treated like a word possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). This is the intended meaning.

The rule "nadyantādbahuvrīheḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.153) has not been explained [in that way], because in the case of *bahudhīvarī*, since the *bahuvrīhi* ends in a feminine noun (*nadī*), the suffix *kap* would be required. However, if it were explained as "nadyantottarapada" (ending in a feminine noun as the final member), there would be no fault; for the word *dhīvan*, being the final member, ends in the letter *n* and thus lacks the status of a *nadī*.

The detailed explanation is in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the term "puṃvadbhāva" (masculine-like substitution): the sense is that because the ordinal *pūraṇī* [feminine] and *rātriḥ* [feminine] are not denoted by the compound, the prohibition [of masculine-like substitution] does not apply. (823) *ke'ṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.13.
"Ke’ṇaḥ": [the vowel] should be short. This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of that [rule] from "śṛdṛprām" [P.

6.4.125]. (824) "Na kapi" [P. 7.4.14]: "[The vowel] is not [shortened] before the suffix *kap*. This refers to the rule "aṇo hrasvaḥ" [P. 7.4.13], [which is drawn] from "ke’ṇaḥ" [P. 7.4.13] and from "śṛdṛprām" [P. 6.4.125].

The intended meaning is "because of its following after that. Now, one might object: in the expression "the fortnight characterized by the auspicious fifth day" (*kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*), since the fifth night is included within the fortnight—which consists of fifteen days and nights—as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), its predominance (*prādhānya*) is unavoidable. To this, he says: "In this case, [the word] is latent" (*tirohita*). [This refers to the night.]

The sense is that [the suffix] is not predominant because there is no occurrence of its application [in such cases]. In the Bhāṣya, this very example serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here. He provides an example of *kap* after a compound whose final member ends in *ṛ*: *bahukartṛkaḥ*.
The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "that which has many agents" (*bahavaḥ kartāro yasya*). Thus, in the rule *apūraṇī-priyādiṣu*, it is as follows.

Having elaborated upon the scope of *pūraṇī* (feminine ordinal numbers), he asks about the purpose of the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) when the subsequent member belongs to the class beginning with *priya*: "What [is the purpose] in the case of those beginning with *apriya*? He gives the example: *kalyāṇīpriyaḥ*.
The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is: "one for whom a beautiful woman (*kalyāṇī*) is dear (*priyā*). He recites the list of words in the *priyā*-class: *priyā*...
"Manojñā," and so forth. [The word] is neuter in its general sense.
Now, since the word *bhakti* is listed among the words beginning with *priya*, in the case of "one who has firm devotion is *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ*," [the following applies:]

To the question "How is there the masculine form?", he says: "The neuter is used in the sense of a general property" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*). The word "relying upon" (*āśritya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the word *dṛḍham*: according to the theory of word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra-pakṣa*), the word *dṛḍha* is derived in the neuter gender by relying on its status as a general property; subsequently, it is construed with the word *bhakti*.

The previously established neuter gender does not depart [from the word], because the specific gender is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*), just as in the case of "the Vedas are authoritative" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*). And regarding this point, in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Paspaśāhnika*, it is said: "And it is possible for him [to eat] even dog-meat and so forth..."

The usage "kṣutpratihantu" (to ward off hunger) is an indicative mark [of this]. Now, if this is so, one might object that the inclusion of the word *bhakti* among the "beloved ones" (*priyādi*) in the list is redundant; to this he says: "But when there is a desire to express femininity.

The sense is that, according to the view that grammatical refinement applies to the entire sentence (*vākya-saṃskāra-pakṣa*), the perception of femininity is necessarily determined by following the gender of the substantive.

(825) *tasil-ādiṣv-ākṛtvasucaḥ* | 6.3.35. In the case of suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with those other than *kṛtvasuc*, [the rule] "of the feminine, as the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*) continues to apply. *Ā...*
In the rule "kṛtvasuc," the prefix *āṅ* signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*), meaning "including that.
Thus he says: "in the suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *kṛtvasuc*. This refers to the section starting from "pañcamyāstasi" up to "saṅkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane."
The meaning is: "in those [suffixes] prescribed by the sūtras ending with *kṛtvasuc*.

Since the condition of being followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is absent, the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) does not apply; therefore, this present rule is stated. Now, one might object: since *til*, *thyan*, and *añ* are recited immediately after *kṛtvasuc* and are not included among *tasil* and the others, [how can they be governed by this rule?]

In the cases of *pareṣu ṭhvakṛtiḥ*, *ṭhajathyā*, and *bahuśaḥ*, there would be no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution), resulting in an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*). This is because *deśya* [in the rule] *īṣadasamāptau kalpabdeśyadeśīyaraḥ* and *rūpya* [in the rule] *ṣaṣṭhyā rūpya ca* are included within the group beginning with *tasil*.

Furthermore, since *pūrvavatva* (the application of the masculine form) would occur in the rules "parataḥ ṭhpaṭvīdeśye" and "śubhrārūpye," there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). To address this, he says: "It is a systematic enumeration (*parigaṇanam*). Regarding "under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*"):
non-application in the intended cases is under-extension; application in unintended cases is over-extension.
He states the method of enumeration with the words beginning "tratasau" and so forth. Regarding "bahvīṣu bahutra":

the meaning is that from the word *bahvī* in the sense of "in many," the suffix *tral* is applied by the rule "saptamyāstra"; when the masculine form is substituted and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed, the resulting form is *bahutra*. Regarding *bahutaḥ*: this is by the rule "pañcamyāstasi."
The suffix *atasil* is applied after the word *bahvī*; the intention is that because of the rule of *pūrvatva* (the substitution of the masculine form), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed.

Regarding the term *darśanīyatara*: in the sense that "of these two, this one is more beautiful to behold," the suffix *tarap* is added to the word *darśanīyā* by the rule *dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarab*.
The intention is that when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed. Regarding the example *darśanīyatama*:

in the sense of "she is most beautiful among these," the suffix *tamap* is added to the word *darśanīyā* according to the rule "the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used for denoting excellence. The intention is that when the masculine form is applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed.

Now, one might object: even in cases such as *paṭvītarā* and *paṭvītamā*, when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) applies and the suffix *ṅīṣ* is consequently removed, the forms would have to become *paṭutara* and *paṭutama*.
To this, he says: "by the rule *gharūpa-*. Thus, since the application of the masculine form is barred by the presence of a short vowel (*hrasva*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* [remains].
The meaning is that when its feminine suffix (*nivṛtti*) is absent due to the shortening [of the vowel], the form becomes *paṭvitara* and *paṭvitama*.

Regarding *paṭvacarī*: the intention is that from the word *paṭvī*, by the rule "in the sense of 'formerly so' (*bhūtapūrve*), the suffix *caraṭ* [is added]," there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*), resulting in the removal of the *ṅīṣ* suffix; thus, it means "one who was formerly clever" (*pūrvaṃ paṭvī*). Regarding *paṭvajātīyā*: [it means "of a kind similar to clever"].

The meaning is that from the word *paṭvī*, by the rule "the suffix *jātīya* expresses a manner," there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*), which results in the removal of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. Thus, it means "one who is similar to clever. Regarding the term *darśanīyakalpā*: by the rule "the suffix *kalpap* is used for 'slight incompleteness,'" the suffix *kalpap* is added to the word *darśanīyā*; when the masculine form is substituted, the *ṅīṣ* [is removed].
The sense is that there is a cessation [of the feminine suffix]. The meaning is generally "worth seeing. Regarding *darśanīyadeśīyā*:

by the rule *ṭhīṣadasamāptau*, the suffix *deśīyar* is added to the word *darśanīya*. The sense is that when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed. The meaning is that she is worthy of being seen because of her excellence.

Regarding *darśanīyapāśā*: the suffix *pāśap* is applied after the word *darśanīya* in the sense of "even slightly" (*īṣadadhike*). The intention is that when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided;
thus, the meaning is "unfit to be seen because of being contemptible. Regarding *bahuthā*:
the suffix *thāl* is applied after the word *bahvī* in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*). When the masculine form is applied, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is elided.

The meaning is "of many kinds. Regarding the term *vṛkatī*: while the word *praśaṃsāyām* (in the sense of praise) is understood as a governing rule, the suffix *atil* is applied to the word *vṛkī*—which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*)—by the rule *vṛkajyeṣṭhābhyāṃ tiltātilau ca chandasi*. When the masculine form is applied, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is withdrawn.
The meaning is as follows: regarding the word *ajathyā*, under the governing rule *tasmai hitam* ("beneficial for that"), the suffix *thyak* is applied by the rule *ajādivibhyāṃ thyak*.
Since the word *ajā* ends in this suffix, the feminine marker *ṭāp* is removed when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied; this is the intended sense.
In the expression *vṛkati-rajathyā*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) by the rule *jāteśca* does not apply.
Because of the capacity for enumeration:
[the rule] "before the suffix *śas*, the form of the word expressing 'many' or 'few' should be stated as being like the masculine" (*śasi bahvalpārthasya puṃvadbhāvo vaktavyaḥ*).
Regarding the term *śasi*: when *śas* follows, that which expresses a large number or a small number takes the masculine form.
The meaning is that it must be stated [as a special rule].
This statement is necessary because [the word *bahvībhyaḥ*] is not included among those enumerated in the rule beginning with *tratasau*. Regarding the form *bahvībhyaḥ*:
it is used in the sense of "give to many," according to the rule *bahvalpārthāc chas kārakād anyatarasyām*.

The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *bahvī*. The intention is that when the form becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed. The word "give" (*dehi*) is used to clarify the status of the recipient as the indirect object (*saṃpradāna*). Regarding "in small quantities" (*alpaśas*):
the meaning is "give from the few [women]. The intention is that when the form becomes like the masculine, the suffix *ṭāp* is removed.

Regarding the rule *tvatalorguṇavacanasya*: the meaning of "in the presence of the suffixes *tva* and *tal*" is that when these two suffixes follow, a word denoting a substance (*dravya*) where a quality (*guṇa*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*) must be treated as masculine (*puṃvat*). For example: *kartṛtvam*.

The sense is that because the word *kartṛ* (agent) is based on an action (*kriyā*), it does not possess the status of being a quality-word (*guṇavacana*). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ā kaḍārād ekā saṃjñā*, it is established that a meaningful verbal form—distinct from compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*), secondary derivatives (*taddhitānta*), indeclinables, pronouns, genus-words (*jāti*), numerals, and technical names (*saṃjñā*)—is designated as a "quality-word. And in the present context, it is precisely this [definition] that is intended by the term "quality-word. However, the definition of a quality found in the commentary on the sūtra *voto guṇavacanāt*—namely, "that which enters into a substance (*satva*), departs from it," and so forth—does not apply here.

For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhak-cha-raṇa-taddhiteṣu*—namely, that in the case of *ekatvam* (the state of being one) from *ekasyā bhāvaḥ*, since the word *eka* is not a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), the masculine form is prescribed here even though it was not otherwise applicable by the rule *tvatalorguṇavacanasya*—is consistent. However, forms such as *sakhītva* are indeed ungrammatical; this is explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Now, an objection is raised: in the case of *kṛtārthatā* (the state of having accomplished one's purpose), derived from *kṛtārthā* (she by whom the purpose is accomplished), how can there be masculine substitution? [The opponent argues that the feminine suffix should remain.]

Because the word *kṛtārtha* is a compound (*samāsa*), it lacks the status of being a "word expressing a quality" (*guṇavacana*) as previously stated; therefore, he says: "In the case of *śaradaḥ*. The intention is that one first derives the word *kṛtārtha* in its general sense—according to the method explained immediately following the term *dṛḍhabhakti*—as "that by which the purpose (*artha*) has been accomplished (*kṛta*)," and from that [base], one then derives the feminine suffix *tal* while disregarding the gender [of the original]. [Bhāṣya: "In the case of a *bha* stem, when a *taddhita* suffix other than one beginning with *ḍh* follows.

Regarding "in the case of a *bha* stem, when a *taddhita* suffix other than one beginning with *ḍh* follows": the meaning is that when a *taddhita* suffix other than those beginning with *ḍh* follows, the feminine form should be treated like the masculine (*puṃvat*).

The word *hāstika* is mentioned because it is not included among those already enumerated. Regarding the form *hāstikam*: under the governing rule *tasya samūhaḥ* ("a collection of that"), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *acittahasti-dhenor ṭhak*. By the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ*, the *ṭha* is replaced by *ika*. Since the word undergoes masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which would have been triggered by the final *n*—is removed. The intention is that the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) occurs by the rule *nastaddhite* ("the *n* is elided before a taddhita suffix").

Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of the masculine suffix *ṅīp*, the form *hāstika* is established through the elision of the long *ī* by the rule *yasyeti ca* and the subsequent elision of the *ṭi*-portion; for since the elision of the *ī* (by *yasyeti ca*) is considered *asiddha* due to its being an *abhīya* operation, and because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the condition of being followed by a *taddhita* suffix is not met.

There is no occurrence of the elision of the *ṭi* [portion]. Furthermore, the possibility of establishing the form through the rule "ṭhṭhakcchasośca" (Pāṇini 6.3.43) by treating it as a masculine is not to be suspected; for, due to the association (*sāhacarya*) with *cchas*, only the suffix *ṭhak* is understood there in the rule "bhavataṣṭhakcchasau" (Pāṇini 4.2.115). As for "rauhiṇeya," it is derived from the rule "varṇādanudāttāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.39).

From the word *rohita*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added and the letter *t* is replaced by *n*. In the sense of "the offspring of Rohiṇī," the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule *ṭhstrībhyo ḍhak*; this results in the substitution of *ey*. The intention is that, through the application of the rule *bhasya*, the word would undergo the masculine form (*puṃvat*), resulting in the removal of both the *ṅīp* and the *n*.
As for the phrase "it is accepted," the intention is that this is established through the authoritative commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

Regarding *agnāyī*: the wife of Agni is *agnāyī*. By the rule *vṛṣākapyagnī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; the vowel *i* of *agni* is replaced by the vowel *ai*, resulting in *agnāyī*. In the sense of "that which has Agnāyī as its deity," the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *agner ḍhak*;
for when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, it includes the stem qualified by gender as well. From that [suffix] *ḍhak*...

This is the substitution of *ey*. When the masculine form (*puṃvat*) applies, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the shortening of the vowel (*aitva*) are removed; thus, with *agni-eya* remaining, the elision of the *i* by the rule "of that which [ends in] *ya*" (*yasyeti ca*), followed by the initial vṛddhi, results in the form *āgneya*.
The point is that if the masculine form were prohibited, the result would instead be *āgnāyeya*. However, in reality...

It should be understood that because the basis for application (*pravṛtinimitta*) differs— being "the state of being fire" (*agnitva*) in the masculine, but "connection with fire" (*agnisaṃbandha*) in the feminine— the masculine form is not applied here.
The phrase "the word *sapatnī* is threefold" implies that this is due to the difference in its derivational analysis (*vyutpādana*).

"From a synonym for enemy (śatru-paryāyāt)"—the sense is that this is according to the lexicon (*kośa*) which states: "ṛpi, vairin, sapatna, ari, dviṣat, dveṣaṇa, and durhad are synonyms for enemy. This [term] is one whose masculine form has been previously mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). "Based on marriage" (*vivāha-nibandhana*) means caused by the specific consecration (*saṃskāra*) produced by marriage. [As it is said: "The status of husband (*patitva*) occurs in the seventh [generation]."
The intention is that this is based on the traditional rule (smaraṇa) beginning with "pade" and so forth. After the word "āśritya," the word "pravṛtta" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

[The term] *samānapati* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "one whose husband is the same. The substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the replacement of *n* for *t* occur by virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) prescribed in the rule "nityaṃ sapatnyādiṣu. Thus, it is always feminine in gender.

The sense is that the application of the term *pati*—which is based on the act of marriage—is prescribed with the substitution of *sabhāva* (the change of *p* to *b*) only when the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is feminine. This is because of the lexicon stating, "The term *pati* means husband" (*ghava*). Regarding the phrase "of the first two": the word *sapatna*, which is a synonym for enemy, is based on marriage.
The meaning is: "of the two words *sapatnī* which function by depending on the word *pati*. Regarding the form *sāpatna*:

when the sense is "the offspring of a *sapatnī*," the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by the rule *tasyāpatyam*) is superseded; and although the suffix *ḍhak* (prescribed by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*) would then apply, the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by the rule *śivādibhyo 'ṇ*) also applies [to the first instance of the word *sapatnī*].

Due to the application of the *puṃvat* rule because it is a word whose masculine form has been previously stated (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the *ṅīp* suffix is elided, resulting in the form *sāpatna*. However, there is no elision of the letter *n* either; for the word *sapatna*, as a synonym for "enemy" (*śatru*), is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpannaprātipadika*), and thus the *n* therein is not caused by the feminine gender.

However, in the case of the second [term] *sapatnī*, which is derived from the word *sapatna* by means of both the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*, once the *aṇ* suffix prescribed by the rule *śivādibhyaṣṭāp* is applied, there is no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) because the word lacks the quality of being "spoken as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). Rather, after the elision of *ṅīp* by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the form is *sāpatna*. If, however, *puṃvadbhāva* were to apply...
Upon the removal of the *ṅīp* and the *nakāra*, [the form] would be *sāpatī*. As for the phrase "in the third case":

the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that, based on the word *pati* as a synonym for "master" (*svāmin*), from the word *sapatnī*—which has been derived [from *sapatna*] with the suffix *ṅīp*—only the suffix *ṇya* applies by virtue of the rule concerning words ending in *pati* as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). [This refers to the feminine form] *sapatnī*.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the sense of "offspring" (*apatyam*), the suffix *ṇya*—as prescribed by the rule "after *diti*, *aditi*, *āditya*, and words ending in *pati*, the suffix *ṇya* [is applied]"—occurs, overriding the *aṇ* suffix prescribed by the rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*). Now, one might object:
the word *saptanī* does not have *pati* as its final member (*uttarapada*). To this, [the author replies:]...

He says: "By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding gender-distinction. He states what is excluded by the word *eva*: "but not after [a stem ending in] *aṇ*. Now, one might object that the suffix *ṇya* is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the *aṇ* prescribed after [stems beginning with] *śiva* and so on; to this he replies: "only those two which are conventional (*rūḍha*) in the list beginning with *śiva*. The word *sapatna*, when meaning "enemy," is purely conventional (*kevalarūḍha*). [The suffix applies] based on marriage.

However, that which functions by relying on the word *pati* as a *yogarūḍha* (conventional-derivative) [term] refers to the one who performs the marriage ceremony, because the etymological derivation (*yoga*)—as in "he protects" (*pāti rakṣati*)—is also present there. But that which functions by relying on the word *pati* as a synonym for "master" (*svāmin*) is purely derivative (*kevalayogika*). In the case of Śiva and others, only the two conventional (*rūḍhi*) senses are to be understood, and not the other.
The meaning is that the etymological (yaugika) sense is stronger than the conventional (rūḍhi) sense. To the question "What follows from this?", he says:

"having offspring" (*sāpatya*). Since the word *saptalī*—which contains the word *pati*, a synonym for *svāmin*—is a word whose masculine form has already been expressed (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), when the masculine form is applied, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and its nasalization (*natva*) are removed; thus, by the rule "of that which [ends in a vowel]... (*yasyeti ca*).
This means that there is the elision of the letter *e*, resulting in the form *sāpatya*. (1) Regarding the rule *ṭhak-chasoś-ca*:
this is a Vārttika. When these two suffixes follow, the feminine base takes the masculine form (*puṃvat*).

The word "must be stated" (*vaktavyam*) is the ellipsis. This is a statement [of a rule] because [the suffix] would not otherwise apply due to the absence of the condition *abh* [in the stem]. [The forms] *bhāvatkāḥ* and *bhavadīyāḥ* are derived as follows: under the governing heading *tasyedam* ("belonging to this"), the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha* are applied to the word *bhavat* by the rule *bhavataṣṭhakchasaú*.
Since the inclusion of the feminine form is also intended, the suffix *ṭhak* applies there as well. In that case, regarding the suffix *ṭhak*:

It should not be argued that since the form *ṭhbhāvatka* is established by applying the rule *ṭhisusuktāntā’d* [Pāṇini 7.3.51]— which prescribes the substitution of *kā*— to the state of the suffix *ṭha* itself, prior to the single-substitute (*ikādeśa*) operation and while it still has the form *ṭha*,
the mention of *ṭha* in the rule is redundant; for once the *ikādeśa* has been applied, the resulting form would be *mathadhitaṃ paṇyam asya*.
In this case, as in the example *māthitika*, because the substitution is not governed by a rule where *al* (a vowel) is the cause, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*;

or alternatively, due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*, the replacement by *kādeśa* would not occur. Therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* is necessary. However, when *śas* follows the word *bhavatī*, its status as a *bha*-stem is sublated by its becoming a *pada* according to the rule *siti ca*.

It might be argued that since the form *bhāvatka* is established by applying the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Pāṇini 1.4.18) to effect the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*), and then, because the element *ik* is the substituendum, the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.51) applies the substitution of *ka* for the suffix *taddhita*, rendering the mention of *thak* unnecessary. However, this is incorrect; for once the substitution of *ik* has been applied, [the derivation proceeds as follows]: *mathitam paṇyam asya*.

In this case, as in the example *māthitika*, because the substitution is not governed by a rule where an *al* (a vowel or consonant) is the cause of the operation, there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle;

or alternatively, due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*, the replacement by *kādeśa* would not occur. Therefore, the mention of *ṭhak* is necessary. However, when *śas* follows the word *bhavatī*, the status of being a *bha* is sublated by its becoming a *pada* according to the rule *siti ca*.

When the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) prescribed by the rule *bhasyāḍhea* is not otherwise applicable, the *puṃvadbhāva* is applied here by this [rule]. "This" refers to the Vārttika *ṭhak-chasośca*. Regarding *eka-taddhite ca*:
its meaning is that the short vowel (*hrasva*) occurs for the word *eka* when a *taddhita* suffix or a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows. For example: *ekasyā bhāvaḥ*.

Singular number (*ekatvam*), singularity (*ekatā*). "A single garment" (*ekaśāṭī*): [this refers to] a compound (*vṛtti*) consisting of a single word. The term "mere" (*mātra*) signifies totality. [The phenomenon of] *puṃvat* (masculine-like substitution) occurs even in the absence of the specific conditions mentioned in rules such as *ṭhstriyāḥ puṃvat*, according to the desire of the authors of the *Bhāṣya*.

The meaning is "by the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya. This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *dakṣiṇāttarābhyām*. The phrase "because its purpose has already been served" means that its purpose has been fulfilled; the sense is that this specific purpose is already accomplished by the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ* alone.
He provides an example for the rule *sarvanāmno vṛtimātre* in the context of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) formation: *sarvamayaḥ*.

The meaning is "come from everything" (*sarvasyā āgataḥ*). Under the governing rule *tata āgataḥ*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *mayaṭ ca*. By the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ*, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

The suffix *mayaṭ* may be used in its most literal sense, as in the word *cinmaya* ("consisting of consciousness"). Now, he provides an example from the commentary on verbal roots ending in *san* and others: *sarvakāmyati*. This means "he desires everything for himself. In this sense, the suffix *kāmyac* is applied to the word *sarva* according to the rule *kāmyacca*; furthermore, [the substitution of *ya* for the final vowel] applies by the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ*.

The rule for masculine behavior (*puṃvatvam*) applies. Because [the forms] ending in *san* and so forth are considered verbal roots by the rule *sanādyantāḥ*, they take suffixes such as *laṭ* and others. The intention is that since *mayaṭ* and *kāmyac* are not included among those specifically enumerated in the rule *tratasau* etc., the rule *asilādiṣu* would not apply here, and thus masculine behavior would not occur. He provides another example in the context of secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*): *sarvakabhāryaḥ*. This is indeed a compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*). Regarding *sarvapriyaḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose beloved (*priyā*) is all. This is a compound formation. The intention is that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words beginning with *priya* is useful in cases such as *rūpavatīpriyaḥ*.

In reality, however, when the suffix *akac* is added to the word *eka*, the substitution of *ī* for the vowel following the suffixal marker *ṭh* (by Pāṇini 7.3.44) results in *ekikā*. The state of being that [ekikā] is *ekikatva*. In this case, if the masculine form were applied, both the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and the substitution of *ī* would be removed, resulting in *ekakatvam*; thus, the vowel *i* would not be heard. This is because the suffix *ṭāp*, which was the cause for the substitution of *ī*, has been removed—just as in the case of *pācakajātīyā* derived from the word *pācikā* with the suffix *jātīyar*.

They say that since the suffix *ṭāp* remains by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* when [the compound] is short, there would be the hearing of the feminine suffix *ī*, as in *prāptajīvikā*; thus, because there is a difference in the result, the rule *ṭhak-chas-taddhite ca* is already covered [by this]. Now, one might object that in cases such as *taditarā* or *tadanyā*, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and therefore the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply; to this he says: "This [rule applies] only to the preceding. The meaning is that among the multiple parts that have entered into the compound, this prescription of the masculine form for the pronoun applies specifically to that which is preceding in relation to something else.

"By the indicative mark [found] in *bhastraiṣājājñādvā*. This means that by the rule *bhastraiṣā*, the substitution of *i* for the letter preceding *k* is prescribed even for the forms *eṣā* and *dvā* when they possess the suffix *kāc*. "By the indicative mark [found] in *bhastraiṣājājñādvā*"—the meaning is that by the rule *bhastraiṣā*, the substitution of *i* for the letter preceding *k* is prescribed even for *eṣā* and *dvā* when they have *kāc*; otherwise, [that rule] would be without scope. The intention is that in a secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*), those two [words] are necessarily subject to the masculine form (*puṃvat*) because they function as pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

He provides an example for the application of *akac* in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*): *sarvikā*. The sense is that from the word *sarvā*, when *sākac* is added and *ṭāp* follows, there would be the substitution of *i* by the rule *pratyayasthāt* and the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvat*), resulting in the disappearance of both *ṭāp* and the feminine suffix (*it*). He provides an example for the application of *ekaśeṣa*: *sarvāḥ*. [This refers to] "the eggs of *kukkuṭa* and others.
This is the nominative plural of a word ending in *ṭāp*; in the masculine transformation (*puṃvat*), the *ṭāp* is removed.

The intended meaning is "it may be so. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the eggs of a hen (*kukkuṭī*) and others," the remainder of the sentence is "the masculine form (*puṃvat*) must be stated. Indicating that this [rule] is for the sake of cases where there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), he provides an example of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*): *kukkuṭāṇḍam*. By virtue of the masculine form...
The meaning is that there is the cessation of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* due to the characteristic of genus (*jāti*). The same applies hereafter. Regarding "mṛgakṣīram" (deer-milk):

the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the milk of a female deer (*mṛgī*). Regarding "kākaśāva" (crow-cub): the analysis is "the cub of a female crow (*kākī*). Amara states: "potaḥ, pākaḥ, arbhakaḥ, ḍimbhaḥ, pṛthukaḥ, śāvakaḥ, and śiśuḥ [are synonyms for a child]."

(826) *kyaṅmāninośca* | 6|3|36| [The sūtra reads: *kyaṅmāninośca*. Regarding the phrase "of these two": it means when *kyaṅ* or *mānin* follows as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Regarding *enīveti*: *etā* means variegated in color. [The word] *citraṃ*...

According to Amara, "kirmīra, kalmāṣa, śabala, and etā" all mean variegated. The ritualists state that the word *eta* is a synonym for white. [In the formation of *enī*], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the nasal *ṇakāra* are applied by the rule "ṭhvarṇādanudāte. Furthermore, while the rule "upamānādācāre" (Pāṇini 3.1.10) is still in force, the suffix *ky-aṅ* is applied to the word *enī* by the rule "kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.11).

The intention is that when the masculine form [of the suffix] is applied, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *n* for *t* are removed; then, by the rule "ṭh-a-kṛt-sārvadhātukayoḥ," the vowel is lengthened, resulting in the form *ṭhetāyate*. Regarding the phrase "like a *śyenī*": the word *śyeta* is a synonym for white (*śveta*). As Amara states: "Śukla, śubhra, suci, śveta, viśada, śyeta, and pāṇḍura [are synonyms for white]."

The rest is as before. Now, one might object: since the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34) already establishes the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) when the word *māninī* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), what is the purpose of including the mention of *mānin*? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that the mention of *mānin* is for the sake of cases where there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) and for the sake of non-feminine genders (*astrīliṅga*).
Having intended this, he first provides an example with a non-co-referential (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) subsequent [term], namely: *svabhinnām* (one who considers herself different from him).

Regarding *darśanīyamāninī*: when the word *darśanīyā* ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) is an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇin* is applied by the rule *manaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.82), while the governing rule *supyajātau ṇiniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.78) continues to apply. Thus, the suffix *ṇin* is added after the root *man*.

This is an *upapada* compound, with the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). Even though the word *mānin* is not in apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), when it occurs as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) of a compound, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied by this rule; thus, upon the disappearance of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added according to the rule "after words ending in *ṛt* or *n*" (*ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*), resulting in the form *darśanīyamāninī*. This refers to one who considers herself alone to be beautiful.

In order to indicate that the status of being treated as masculine (*puṃvat*) for that beautiful woman is already established by the rule "of a feminine word [ending in a long vowel], like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskād anūṅ*), it is stated that she is "different from herself" (*svabhinnā*). This is because, although a single beautiful woman can simultaneously be both the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root *man* (to think), they are [distinguished here] by means of their actual non-identity.

The meaning is that this is because of the existence of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *māninī*. Now, he provides an example when the final member of the compound is not feminine: "darśanīyām. After the word "striyām" (in the feminine), the word "ātmānam" (himself) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Thus, one who considers himself a beautiful woman is called *darśanīyamānī*, such as Caitra.

This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). Here, although there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by taking the superimposed identity with [the woman]— even though the referent of the final member of the compound, *mānin*, is in reality a distinct beautiful woman— nevertheless, because the final member of the compound, the word *mānin*, is masculine, in that [case]...
The meaning is that by the statement "others do not attain the masculine form," the rule for that [masculine form] is thereby excluded.

(827) *na kopadhāyāḥ* | 6.3.37 | "Not [the feminine ending is replaced] when the word has *ka* as its penultimate letter. For example, *pācikābhāryaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose wife (*bhāryā*) is a female cook (*pācikā*)."

The suffix *ṇvul* [is applied] after the root *pac*. There is the substitution of *a*, the addition of *ṭāp*, and the addition of *it*. If there were "masculine-like" treatment (*puṃvat*), there would be the disappearance of both *ṭāp* and *it*. Thus: *rasikā*. [Derivation: "She who has *rasa*" is *rasikā*. [The suffix] *ṭhan* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *ṭha*, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* [are added]. [In *rasika*,] *ika* is substituted for *ṭha* by the rule "for *ṭha*, *ika*. Then *ṭāp* is added. [This prevents] the prohibition of "masculine-like" treatment. For if there were "masculine-like" treatment, [the feminine suffix] *ṭāp*...
There would be the substitution of the short vowel *i*. Regarding the form *madrikāyate*: *madrikā* refers to one born in a specific region called Madra.

[The suffix] *kan* is applied by the rule "madravṛjyoḥ kan," followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and the substitution of *it*. The meaning is: "she behaves like a Madrikā. Here, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) would have been applicable by the rule "kyahbhāninośca."

It is prohibited [to apply the masculine form]. In the case of *madrikāmāninī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *ṭhmanaśca* in the sense of "one who considers herself a Madrikā. This forms an *upapada* compound. Here too, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) which would otherwise be required by the rule *kyaṅmāninośca* is prohibited. In both cases, if the masculine form were applied, there would be the disappearance of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and the vowel *ī*.

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of *taddhita* and *vu*": this means that the rule *na taddhitavukopadhāyāḥ* should be recited. The result is that for a feminine stem, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) when the suffix *kakāra* is related either to a *taddhita* or to the suffix *vu*, provided it occurs as an *upadhā* (penultimate). Thus, we have *madrikāyate*.
In the prohibition regarding *kopadha* [words], there is the mention of *taddhita* [suffixes].
An example of a *taddhita* *kopadha* [word] is *pacikābhārya*. However, [the word] *pacikābhārya*...
The example is *vusabandhika-upadha*. He states the purpose of the inclusion of the suffix *-bu* in the word *taddhita*: "not here" (*neha*). Regarding *pāka*:
in the *Uṇādi-sūtras*, it is prescribed as a form ending in the suffix *ka*, with the rule "the words *arbhaka*, *pṛthuka*, and *pāka* denote age. This [is an example] of a *taddhita* [suffix].
The intention is that since there is no *k* in the suffix *vun*, there is no prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) here.
(828) *saṃjñāpūraṇyośca* | 6|3|38|.
Now, an objection: since the word *datā* is a name (*saṃjñā*), it applies to a single substance (*ekadravyaniveśitayā*).

Since there is an absence of the quality of having been previously used as a masculine (bhāṣitapuṃskatva), there is no possibility at all for the application of the rule "the feminine [stem] becomes like the masculine" (ṭhstriyāḥ puṃvat"); therefore, what is the point of prohibiting it? To this he replies: "caused by the act of giving" (dānakriyānimitta).
This word *data* is not like words such as *ḍittha* and the like; rather, it is applied only by taking the act of giving into account.

The meaning is that since [the word] is used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*) for both a woman and a man, it follows that because it refers to a male when spoken, the rule for "masculine-like" treatment (*puṃvat*) would apply; therefore, this is a prohibition. He provides an example of the prohibition of "masculine-like" treatment for a feminine ordinal number: *pañcamībhāryaḥ*. [This means] one whose wife is fifth.
The analysis of the compound is *yasya* (of whom). Here, the application of the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (a feminine word becomes like the masculine) is prohibited.

In the case of *pañcamī-pāśā* (a contemptible fifth), the meaning is "a censured fifth. Here, the application of the masculine form prescribed by the rule *tasil-ādiṣu* (in the case of suffixes beginning with *tasil*) is prohibited.

(829) And [the suffix] *taddhita* which has *vṛddhi* as its cause [is not elided], except when it denotes being colored (*rakta*) or a transformation (*vikāra*). "And [the suffix] having *vṛddhi* as its cause": the analysis of the compound is "that which is the cause (*nimita*) or reason (*hetu*) of *vṛddhi*. "Colored (*rakta*) and transformation (*vikāra*)" is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). From that, there is a negative determinative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*).

The meaning is: "existing in a sense that is distinct from a modification of *rakta*. By the word "vṛddhi," only that *vṛddhi* which is specifically prescribed [by rule] is intended here, as established by the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). He states this with the words beginning "by the word *vṛddhi*," etc.
"Ending in that" (*tadanta*) is obtained through the technical paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*). "Sraugghnī" [is derived from] *srugghna*.

*deśaḥ* (place). The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is elision of the vowel *a*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṇ*, there is vṛddhi of the first vowel (*ai* → *au*). By the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. The analysis of the compound is: "one whose wife is a *sraughnī*. Here, what would have been obtained by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* is prohibited. [Thus,] *māthurīyate*.

Regarding the term *māthurīmāninī*: that which exists in Mathurā is *māthurī*, formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, the vowel *a* is elided, and by *ādivṛddhiḥ*, the initial vowel is strengthened; then, by the rule *ṭiḍḍhea*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. To express the sense "one who acts like a woman from Mathurā," the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ*. [This is further treated] by the rule *sanādyantāḥ*.

Because it denotes a *dhātu*, the suffixes *laṭ* and so forth apply. *Māthurīyate*: she acts like a woman from Mathurā. *Māthuramāninī*: she considers herself a woman from Mathurā. By the rule "after *manas*," the suffix *ṇini* is applied. There is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. This is a compound with an *upapada*. The *sub*-case endings are elided (*subluk*). Because it ends in *n*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. In both these cases, the [prohibition of *puṃvat*] that would have been obtained by the rule "also in the case of *kyaṅ* and *mānin*" applies.

The masculine form is prohibited [in this case]. Regarding the example *madhyamabhārya*: *madhyamā* means "situated in the middle. The suffix *ma-* is applied by the rule *madhyānmaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose wife (*bhāryā*) is middle-aged (*madhyamā*). Here, the masculine form would apply by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvad bhāṣitapuṃskād anūṅ*, but it is prohibited because the suffix *ma-* is a *taddhita* suffix.

There is no prohibition of the *puṃvat* (masculine) treatment because there is an absence of the cause for *vṛddhi* (vowel lengthening). The example is *kāṇḍalābhārya*. [Derivation: From *kāṇḍaṃ lunāti* ("she cuts the stalks"), we derive *kāṇḍalāvī*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*; this is a *kṛt* suffix. By the rule *aco ñṇiti*, *vṛddhi* occurs, followed by the substitution of *āv*. Then, an *upapada* compound is formed, and finally the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* [is applied]. The analysis of the compound is: "one whose wife is a *kāṇḍalāvī*. Due to the rule of masculine equivalence (*puṃvat*), the suffix *ṅīp* is removed. Here, because the suffix *aṇ* has already been applied, there is no prohibition of masculine equivalence since it is not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Thus, we have *tāvad-bhāryaḥ*. [In the formation of] *tāvatī*: "that which has that much as its measure" (*tat-parimāṇam asyāḥ*). [This is derived from] *yat*, *etat*, etc., by [the addition of the suffix *ṭhaP*].

By the rule *parimāṇe vatup*, the suffix *vatup* is added to the word *tad* as a *taddhita*; by the rule *ṭhā sarvanāmnaḥ*, the vowel *ā* is substituted; and because it ends in an *ugit* vowel, the suffix *ṅīp* is added. The analysis of the compound is: "one whose wife (*bhāryā*) is *tāvatī*.
Due to the *puṃvat* (masculine-like) treatment, the suffix *ṅīp* is elided, and by the rule *ṭhā sarvanāmnaḥ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution of the vowel *ā* occurs.

Even though the suffix *vatup* is conditioned by the [presence of] the form *ākāra*, there is no prescription of *vṛddhi* for that form by means of the word *vṛddhi*; therefore, there is no prohibition of the masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a word ending in *vatup* conditioned by that. Regarding the phrase "but when [it refers to] being dyed" (*rakte tu*): the meaning is that there is no prohibition of masculine-like behavior for a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) existing in the sense of "dyed. For example: *kāṣāyī*.

*Kaṣāya* is a specific mineral substance, *gaurika*. That which is dyed with it is *kāṣāyī*. According to the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant of the first member], followed by *vṛddhi* of the initial vowel. By the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in *kāṣāyakaṇṭhī*. Upon the application of *puṃvat* (masculine-like) treatment, the *ṅīp* is removed. Here, the suffix is the *taddhita* *aṇ*.

Because [the word *raktā*] signifies "colored with," there is no prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Regarding the phrase "but in the sense of a modification" (*vikāre tu*): the meaning is that for a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) existing in the sense of a modification, there is no prohibition of the masculine form. As for *haimī*: the meaning is "that which has become a modification of gold. [The suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *ṭhanudātādeśca*; there is the elision of *ṭ*, and the initial vowel undergoes vṛddhi.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭhṭhiḍḍhea*. The form is *haimī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has a golden ring (*mudrikā*).

When the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied, the suffix *ṅīp* is removed. Here, because the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *añ* has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), there is no prohibition against the masculine form. This might be so; or [the word] may be feminine, as in "one who studies grammar" (*vyākaraṇamadī*).

The word *vaiyākaraṇī* is derived by adding the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *aṇ* according to the rule *tad adhīte tad veda*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*. Due to the *ṇit*-character of the suffix *aṇ*, the rule *na yvābhyām* prohibits the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise have occurred—by the principle of "operation like Parjanya" (*parjanyavat lakṣaṇapravṛtti*)—to the vowel *a* following the *y*.

There is also the augment *ai* before the letter *y*, and by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as "one whose wife is a female grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇī bhāryā yasya*), when the masculine form is applied (*puṃvadbhāva*) and the suffix *ṅīp* is removed, the resulting form is *vaiyākaraṇabhārya*. Similarly, [the word] *svasrīya* means the female offspring of one's sister. By the rule *ata*...
The suffix *iñ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *iña*; [the substitution of] *aṇ* occurs by the rule *śibādyaṇ*; and the elision [of the final vowel and consonant] occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
There is a prohibition against the initial *vṛddhi* of the vowel following the first *va* by the rule *na yvābhyām*.
Furthermore, there is the augment *au* before the first *va*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. Thus, [the word] is *sauvaśvī* as in "Sauvaśvī is the wife."

In the case of the bahuvrīhi compound *yasya*, when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is removed, the resulting form is *sauvaśvabhārya*; this is the established rule. Here, although the initial vṛddhi is prohibited in both instances by the rule *na yvābhyām*, the status of the *aṇ* [of *su-aśva-ṅīp*] as a cause for vṛddhi remains intact because it retains its inherent capacity (*svarūpayogya*) to trigger vṛddhi due to its being a *ṇit* affix.
Since the prohibition of *puṃvat* (masculine treatment) would otherwise be unavoidable, he says:

"Because there is an absence of being a contributing factor (*phalopadhāna*) with respect to the *vṛddhi*. After the word "pratīti" (perception/realization), the phrase "of the cause, namely the *taddhita* suffix" is to be supplied. By that which is the fruit of the *aṇ* [suffix] which is the cause of *vṛddhi*—namely, the *vṛddhi* itself—[the *puṃvat* treatment is prohibited].
The meaning is that there is an absence of "proximity" (*upadhāna*), which refers to immediate contiguity;

for even if it were stated simply as "of a *vṛddhi* [substitute] in a *taddhita* suffix," one could obtain the sense "of a *taddhita* suffix caused by *vṛddhi*" by resorting to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of a causal relationship (*nimittatva-sambandha*).
The point is that it is understood that by the mention of the "sign" (*nimitta*), what is intended is the status of being a sign as qualified by its result (*phalopahita*).
Although the *aṇ* suffix is indeed a sign qualified by its result with respect to the *vṛddhi* substitution established by the *aij-āgama* rule,
nevertheless, with respect to the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the word *vṛddhi* itself, [it is] qualified by its result.

There is no fault in [the view] that it is not at all the cause (*nimitta*). In the rule regarding the inclusion of *ig* when *vṛddhi* is prescribed by the word "vṛddhi," this very mention of "cause" (*nimittagrahaṇa*) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Otherwise, since even the status of being a cause qualified by the resulting fruit would exist here due to the introduction of the augment *ej*, the mention of that cause would be useless.
The detailed explanation, however, should be consulted in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
(830) *svāṅgāccetaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.3.40. [The word] *svāṅga* [is understood]; [the word] *itaḥ* is the division [of the sūtra]. Thus he says: "The letter *ī* which follows a *svāṅga* [member]."
Regarding the example *sukeśībhārya*: she whose hair (*keśāḥ*) is very beautiful (*su-śobhanāḥ*) is *sukeśī*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *svāṅgāccopasarjanāt*. There is a prohibition of the [substitution] that would otherwise be obtained by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*. Regarding *paṭubhārya*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he whose wife (*bhāryā*) is clever (*paṭvī*)."

Because *paṭu* is not a word denoting a body part (*asvāṅga*), there is no prohibition against its becoming masculine-like (*puṃvadbhāva*). Rather, the intention is that when it becomes masculine-like, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed by the rule "ṭh-voto guṇavacanāt. As for the example *akeśabhāryā*:
she whose hair (*keśa*) does not exist is *akeśā*, according to the rule "naño'styarthānām" (the negative particle *nañ* [is compounded] with words having the sense of "existing").

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the elision (*lopa*) of the word *vidyamāna*. Even though it refers to a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply, because of the prohibition stated in the rule *sahanavidyamānapūrva-t* (Pāṇini 4.1.57). Therefore, only the suffix *ṭāp* is applied. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "one whose wife is without hair" (*akeśā bhāryā yasya*). Even though it refers to a limb of one's own body, there is no prohibition against the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) because of the absence of the vowel *ī*.

However, the intention is that when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is eliminated. It should be stated [as an exception] that the word is "not ending in *mānin*" (*amāninī*). Regarding "not ending in *mānin*": the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 6.3.40] beginning with "and when a word for a body part (*svāṅga*)" does not apply when the word *mānin* follows.
The meaning is that it should be stated as "bhavatī" (she exists/is). Regarding the form *sukeśamāninī*: the sense is "one who considers herself to have beautiful hair.

In this sense, by the rule *ṭhmanaśca*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied; there is a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate syllable, a compound with an upapada, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending, and upon the application of the masculine form (*puṃvat*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed—this is the intended meaning.
(831) And [the feminine suffix] after a genus-word (*jāti*). Since the term *īta* does not follow because it is not marked with a svarita accent, he says:
"the feminine suffix which follows a genus-word. [The example is] *śūdrābhāryaḥ*. [This is governed by the rule] *śūdrā cāmahatpūrvā*.

The suffix *ṭāp* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* based on genus (*jāti*). Because the masculine form (*puṃvatva*) is prohibited, there is no disappearance of *ṭāp*; thus, we have *brāhmaṇī-bhārya*. Because the masculine form is prohibited, there is no disappearance of the suffix *ṅīn* belonging to the *śārṅgarava*-class; thus, [we have *brāhmaṇī-śatru*]. Now, one might object: in the case of *hāstikaṃ* (a collection of female elephants), where the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ṭhaci tahasti*, [how is it explained? [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on grammatical rules regarding the retention of feminine markers when forming compounds or derivatives, specifically concerning the prohibition of *puṃvat* (masculine-like) substitution.]
One might ask: "How can there be masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) for the word *hastinī* by the rule *bhasyāḍhea*, since it is prohibited by the rule *jāteśca*?
To this he says: "This prohibition applies only to that which is [prescribed] in the Sūtra.
The meaning is: "that which is ordained by a Sūtra. The intention is that the rule *bhasyāḍhea* is a Vārttika. And this...
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhan kopadhāyāḥ*.

(832) *saṅkhyayā 'vyayāsannādūrādhikasaṅkhyāḥ saṅkhyeye* || 2.2.25 || [The words] "by a numeral," "the remainder" (*śeṣa*), and "in the sense of another word" (*anekam anyapadārthe*) are no longer in force.

The term "bahuvrīhi" is understood from the previous context, as is the rule "sup-supā. The word "saṅkhyeye" (in the sense of that which is to be numbered) connects with "saṅkhyayā" (by means of a number). That which is delimited by a number is "saṅkhyeya.
Thus, the meaning obtained is "by a number existing in that [referent]. Furthermore, this word "saṅkhyā" (number) is not...

It does not refer to its own form (*svarūpa*), but rather to words beginning with "one" (*eka*) and ending with "hundred" (*śata*). Thus he says: "by means of a number [expressing] a numerable object.
This means by a word beginning with "one" that ends in a case-ending (*subanta*). Regarding the phrase "indeclinables and so forth":
this means indeclinables (*avyaya*), near-adjectives (*āsanna*), adjectives (*adūra*), and numbers (*saṅkhyā*)—these are what end in case-endings. Here too...

The word "number" (*saṅkhyā*) does not refer to its own form, but rather refers specifically to words such as "one" (*eka*) and so forth. Here, this should be noted: prior to twenty, words such as "one" denote the objects being numbered (*saṅkhyeya*) and take the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). From "ten" (*daśan*) onwards, they are invariably plural.

Words such as *viṃśati* (twenty) and so forth are always used in the singular number; they denote both the numeral and the thing numbered, and up to *navati* (ninety), they are invariably feminine. For example: *viṃśatir brāhmaṇāḥ* (twenty Brahmins) or *brāhmaṇānāṃ viṃśatiḥ* (a group of twenty Brahmins). When *viṃśati* and the others function as numerals, then...
The dual and plural numbers occur [with these words]. For example: *gavāṃ dve viṃśatī* ("two twenties of cows"), by which "forty" is understood;
*gavāṃ tisro viṃśatayaḥ* ("three twenties of cows"), by which "sixty" is understood.
Numbers beginning with *viṃśati* are always singular in form, whether they denote the number itself or the thing numbered, when used in the sense of a number.
"Two, many, and in them [the genders] except for the feminine," says Amara.

Here he gives an example of an indeclinable (*avyaya*): *upadaśāḥ*. It has been stated that the word *upa*, when meaning "nearby," forms an *avyayībhāva* compound; however, in this instance, the word *upa* functions in the sense of "that which is near."

The meaning is "those situated near ten. Consequently, since this [word] does not denote an external referent (*anyapadārtha*) and does not end in the nominative case, the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* does not apply; therefore, this specific statement is made. [It refers to] those situated near those ten trees and so forth.

He dispels the misconception regarding the meaning [of the compound] *gavādayaḥ* by stating that the meaning is "nine or eleven. Here, "proximity" (*sāmīpya*) is in relation to the "tenness" residing in the referent of the word *daśan*, due to the force of forming a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). Thus, the result is that the prefix *upa-* applies to those things possessing a number proximate to tenness. And therefore—
The final result of the understanding is that [the objects] possess a number proximate to ten. Regarding "ḍac":
the intention is that when the suffix *ḍac* is added to the word *upadaśan*, there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) by the rule *ṭhnastaddhite*.
(833) *ti viṃśaterḍiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.142).

When the word *āsanna* is compounded with the word *viṃśati* ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and the suffix *ḍac* is applied, the rule *ṭeḥ* would require the elision of the mere vowel *i*. To this, he says: *ti viṃśater ḍiti*.
Here, *ti* is a form where the sixth case ending has been dropped (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). The governing rule *bhasya* is understood. The phrase *allopo 'naḥ* is also carried over (*anuvartate*).

Regarding this, he says: "of *viṃśati* [the substitution of] *bhas*. It does not apply by the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52), because it has been stated that "the rule regarding the final *al* [does not apply] when [the substitute] is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lo'ntyavidhiḥ*). "Near-twenty" (*āsannaviṃśāḥ*) means those possessing a number close to the number twenty. When the suffix *ḍac* is applied...

When *āsannaviṃśati* remains, after the elision of *ti*, the rule *ṭhato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) applies a single substitute (*pararūpa*)—thereby overriding the rule for long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*)—and thus the word *āsannaviṃśa* ends in *a*. This is because, due to the absence of the condition of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), it is not a *pada* according to the rule: "And there is a prohibition regarding the status of not being a *pada* when a subsequent member [of a compound] is involved."
Now he gives an example for the word *adūra* (not far): *adūratriṃśāḥ*.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is "those not far from thirty. The meaning is: those possessing a number that is not far from the number thirty. When the suffix *ḍac* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion.
He gives an example for *adhika* (exceeding): *adhikacatvāriṃśāḥ*, meaning "those exceeding forty."
The compound is *vigraha*. It means "possessing a number greater than forty.

In the case of the suffix *ḍac*, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion. He provides an example of a compound formed by joining a word denoting a number with another word denoting a number: *dvitrāḥ* ("two or three"). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of "option" (*vārthe*). It means "either two or [more]."

This is the meaning. In the case of the suffix *ḍac*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). Now, if it is asked: "When it is said, 'Let two or three be brought,' and he sometimes brings only two, how then can the plural number be used?"—this is resolved by the statement in the Bhāṣya: "The plural should be employed when there is uncertainty. Likewise...
Regarding the statement that "when there is a connection with the effect, there is an option; however, from the word, there is the presentation of two alternatives by necessity;

after that presentation, the bringing of one or the other occurs according to desire; therefore, it is also resolved that from the word there is the necessary presentation of all five," [the author replies: this is not so, because of the primacy of the meaning.

It should not be argued that this is already established by the rule *anekam anyapadārthe* alone, because [the present rule] serves the purpose of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*) for the absence of the suffix *ka* according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. For it is clear from the Bhāṣya that the suffix *ka* applies only to a Bahuvrīhi compound formed under the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*. Now, regarding number (*saṅkhyā*):
He provides another example for a compound involving a numeral: *dvidaśāḥ* (twenty-two).

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that because the inherent nature of the word's expressive power (*śabdaśakti*) incorporates the meaning of the suffix *suc* within the prior member, and because the compound is based on the operation (*vṛtti*) of that prior member, the suffix *suc* is not heard [audibly] in the compound.
The meaning is that they possess the number ten with a dual count. He states the resulting conclusion: "the meaning is 'twenty'.

(834) *diṅnāmānyantarāle* | 2.2.26. [The sūtra begins: "Names of directions" (*diṅnāmāni*). After the word "names" (*nāmāni*), the remainder [of the rule] is "subanta [words] in mutual [combination]" (*subantāni parasparam*).

"As before" means that they are compounded, and that compound is a *bahuvrīhi*. Intending to show that the word "names" (*nāmāni*) implies plurality, he provides an example: "of the southern [direction]" and so on.
In "south-eastern," the feminine gender is due to common usage; or rather, here the term "intermediate direction" (*antarāla*) is understood as a cardinal direction itself.

The *Bhāṣya* states: "In all compound formations (*vṛti*), there is masculine treatment (*puṃvatva*) for a pronoun. Although it no longer possesses the status of a pronoun due to being an *upasarjana*, nevertheless, by recourse to its former state as a pronoun, masculine treatment occurs; this is precisely because of that *Bhāṣya*. Now, one might object:
Since the [result] would already be established by the phrase "in the interval between these," for what purpose is the mention of the name?
To this he says: "Because of the mention of the name. By the rule *diṅnāmāni*, words conventionally established in the sense of directions are intended. The word *aindrī*...
The word *kobairī* is derived etymologically (*yaugika*) from its connection with Indra and its connection with Kubera;
the sense is that it is not a conventional term (*rūḍha*).
(835) *Tatra tenedam iti sarūpe* | Pāṇini 2.2.27.

In this context, the terms "compound" (*samāsa*) and "bahuvrīhi" are understood as the governing topics. By the word "therein" (*tatra*), a word ending in the locative case is intended. The phrase "with respect to the domain of apprehension" (*grahaṇaviṣaye*), ending in the nominative dual, should be supplied as a qualifier for that [locative]. By the word "by that" (*tena*), however, a word ending in the instrumental case is intended.

In the intended sense, the phrase "in the domain of weapons" (*praharaṇaviṣaye*) is to be understood as a qualifier ending in the nominative dual; it should be supplied from below. The term "of the same form" (*sarūpe*) is a qualifier of the word (*pada*) ending in the nominative dual. As for the phrases "in the domain of taking up" (*grahaṇaviṣaye*) and "in the domain of weapons" (*praharaṇaviṣaye*), [they are to be understood accordingly].
The two words ending in the locative case and the two ending in the instrumental case follow in their respective order.
"Ṭhidam" (that which ends in ṭh or i) is the indication of the meaning. "A battle has commenced" is the substantive to be supplied as the qualifier.
"When the reciprocal action of an act is to be indicated" is also to be supplied. Thus he says: "in the locative case."
This is the dual number of the nominative case. Regarding the phrase "in the domain of grasping" (*grahaṇaviṣaye*):

that in which something is grasped is "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), such as a lock of hair and so forth; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). That which has this as its object—that is, that which has it as its expressed meaning—is "the domain of grasping. In other words, it means "expressing grasping. Regarding the phrase "in the domain of striking" (*praharaṇaviṣaye*).

That by which one strikes is a "weapon" (*praharaṇa*), such as a staff (*daṇḍa*) and so forth. Those two whose expressed object (*vācya*) is that [weapon] are "having a weapon as their object" (*praharaṇaviṣaye*); that is to say, when there is a word expressing a weapon. Here too, the condition *sarūpe* (when the words are identical in form) applies to the suffix *in*. This is in the sense of "this battle has commenced. [The example is] *idam*.

The mention of "general sense" (*sāmānyārtha*) is a general indication; the mention of "battle" (*yuddha*) is a specific indication. Therefore, there is no tautology in the expression "hand-to-hand battle" (*keśākeśi yuddham*). The mutual seizing and the mutual striking constitute the reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*). [Objection: But what is the purpose of supplying the words "in the domain of seizing" and "in the domain of striking"?
To provide the authoritative basis for this, he says: "from the word *iti*.

The word *iti* expresses a mode that is well-known in common usage. The meaning is that this *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs in whatever sense is well-established in common linguistic usage, such as in expressions like *keśākeśī*.
(836) *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* | 6|3|137| "It is also seen in others. This means it continues [from the previous rule]. The remainder is that this follows from the rule *ḍhralope*.
A long vowel is also observed in cases other than those mentioned in the preceding sūtra, *nahivṛtivṛṣi*, etc.

This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound involving reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), there is lengthening of the final vowel of the preceding member. The meaning is: "If it is a *bahuvrīhi*, then lengthening occurs only for the final vowel of the preceding member, and only when there is reciprocal action. By this rule, the long vowel [is applied] in forms such as *turāṣāṭ*.

It is unimpeded. This meaning is obtained from the inclusion of the term *dṛśi*. "It will be stated" refers to the rule *ṭhickarmavyatihāre* (Pāṇini 1.3.14); this is the ellipsis. Regarding "among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds," the commentary (*vṛtti*) itself is the authority here. As for its being an *avyayībhāva*, [it is because] in that context, the rule *avyayībhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.18) applies.

The meaning is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) [of the rule]. Regarding "the status of being an indeclinable" (*avyayatvam*), the ellipsis is "by means of the rule *avyayībhāvaśca*. The meaning is that the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* is the result thereof.
Regarding "having grasped," the ellipsis is "mutually" (*parasparam*). And as for the grasping of the hair...

One might ask: "Since the activity (*pravṛtti*) has a person as its agent and the battle has the combatants as its agents, there is an absence of a common agent; how then can the suffix *ktvā* be used here?
It should be stated that this is because, immediately after the word "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*), the words "of those who were standing" (*sthitayor*) and so forth are supplied. And thus, of this...

In the case of *keśeṣu keśeṣu*, because these two words are included within the compound by virtue of being its constituent parts, there is the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) when the compound is formed. There is lengthening of the vowel of the prior member (*pūrvapada*), the suffix *ic* as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*), and the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
The sense is that the case-ending is elided because [the resulting form] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Even though it functions as a word denoting a different referent (*anyapadārthavṛtti*), this *bahuvrīhi* compound is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of *ekaśeṣa*, and its meaning is not that of a word ending in the nominative case; for instance, [the analysis of] *daṇḍādaṇḍi* is "this is the staff of him" (*tasya daṇḍo 'yam*).
The meaning of the analytical statement (*vigraha*) is that this battle proceeded between those two who stood having struck one another, such that "this is the staff of him" and "this is his staff."

*Daṇḍādaṇḍi*: when *daṇḍam-daṇḍam* and *ari-ari* are combined into a compound through the inclusion of "striking with weapons" (*praharaṇa*), there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) upon compounding; the first member undergoes lengthening (*dīrgha*); the suffix *ic* is added;
and by the rule "*yasyeti ca*," the final vowel is elided. Due to its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the case-ending is elided. *Muṣṭīmuṣṭi*.

The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "This one [fights] with his fists against those [fists], and those [fists] against his; thus, while they stand striking each other, this battle has commenced. When *muṣṭau* and *muṣṭau* undergo composition, the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) and so forth occurs as before, resulting in *muṣṭāmuṣṭi*.
The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is indeed non-Pāṇinian.
(837) *orguṇaḥ* | 6.4.146. *orguṇaḥ*: *oḥ* is the genitive singular of the vowel *u*; by this, the governing term *bhasya* (of a *bha*-stem) is brought into effect.

It is qualified [by that]. The rule *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule concerning what ends with that) applies. The phrase *ṭhnastaddhite* ("ṇatva occurs for *n* before a taddhita suffix") is understood to follow.

Thus he says: "of that which ends in *u*. Regarding *bāhūbāhavi*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "this battle has commenced between two who stand having grasped each other arm-to-arm. This is a compound (*samāsa*).

There is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*); the first member of the compound takes its long vowel (*pūrvapadasya dīrghaḥ*), and the suffix *ic* is added. The rule *orguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146) applies, overriding the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), resulting in the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel *o*. This is then replaced by *ava* (*avādeśaḥ*). Due to its status as an indeclinable (*avyayatva*), the case-ending is elided (*supo luk*). Now, one might object that since the *guṇa* substitution occurs in place of the letter *u*, it must necessarily be the letter *o* due to their phonetic similarity; therefore, for the sake of brevity (*lāghavāt*), [the rule *orguṇaḥ* should not be stated].

Since the rule would be established simply by saying "ṭhor," the mention of the term "guṇa" (heavy syllable) as "ṭhguṇa" is redundant; therefore, he says "orod. Nor should it be argued that even so, the designation of a secondary derivative (taddhita-saṃjñā) remains unavoidable here; for [the principle applies] only where the word providing the thing to be enjoined (vidheya) is itself a technical name (saṃjñā).

This is because it is accepted that a grammatical operation is preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Nor should it be argued that [the letter *ṭ*] is for the purpose of the technical name "a sound with a following *ṭ* denotes its own duration" (P. 1.1.70), since the fact that it denotes its own duration is established simply by the fact that it is being prescribed; thus, the letter *ṭ* serves merely as a phonetic marker (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding *svāyambhuvam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the offspring of Svayambhū."

The term is *svāyaṃbhuvaḥ*. Since the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs when the quality (*guṇa*) is absent due to the fact that the rule is conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*), and because of the initial *vṛddhi*, this is the intended meaning. In the reading *svāyambhuva*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to him").
Regarding the phrase "with a club (*hala*) and a mace (*musala*)," the intention here is that the form *halāmusalī* does not occur because the two members are not of dissimilar form (*asarūpa*).

(838) *tena saha* [is used] in the sense of equal connection (*tulyayoga*) [Pāṇini 2.2.28]. Regarding *tena saha*: regarding *tulyayoge*; the meaning is "in connection with an action occurring at the same time. Regarding "with that which ends in the third case": the intention is that this is obtained by the word *tena*. "As before" [refers to the previous rule].

The meaning is that it is compounded as a *bahuvrīhi*. This [rule] is for the purpose of avoiding lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) and for the purpose of avoiding the suffix *kap*. (839) *vopasarjanasya* 6.3.82.

The term *vopasarjanasya* [is the heading]. The phrase *utarapade* (in a following word) is the governing rule (*adhikṛta*). From the rule *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām*, the portion *sahasya saḥ* is understood here as well.
That which possesses an *upasarjana* is called *upasarjana*; the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) according to the *arśa-ādi* group.
The compound whose final member is implied is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). This means "of a compound whose [final] member is subordinate (*upasarjana*).

Although every compound has some part that is indeed subordinate, nevertheless, by virtue of the contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is understood as "that which has all its parts subordinate. And thus:
By the rule *upasarjanasya*, it is understood that this refers to a *bahuvrīhi* compound. This is a genitive of a constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).
Thus he says: "of a constituent part of a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth. Why [specify] "of a *bahuvrīhi*"?
[Consider the example: *sahayudhvā*. Here, the suffix *kvanip* is applied by the rules *rājani yudhi kṛñaḥ* and *sahe ca*.

This is an *upapada* compound (*upapadasamāsa*). The substitution of *sat* for *saha* does not occur when it is not a member of a *bahuvrīhi* compound; thus, *suputraḥ* is the form resulting from the substitution of *sabha*. The meaning is "arrived together with the son. The term "generally" (*prāyika*) is understood from the word *iti*, as well as from the grammatical indications such as the rule *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya*.
The state [of being]. "Transitive" means having an existing object.
Here, even though there is no common connection (*tulyayoga*), the *sa* replaces *saha*. (840) *prakṛtyā''śiṣi* | 6.3.83 | [In the sense of a benediction, the word remains in its original form.]

In the rule *prakṛtyāśiṣi* ("in the sense of a benediction, [the word] remains in its original form"): the term *sahasya*, which was carried over from the previous rule *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām* ("*sa-* replaces *saha-* when a name is formed"), is modified here by being changed into the nominative case. Thus he says: "the word *saha*. Regarding *prakṛtyā*: the meaning is that it should remain in its own nature (*svabhāva*); that is to say, there is no substitution of the phoneme *sa*. As in the example *svasti*.
The word "may it be" (*bhūyāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding "together with his sons" (*saha-putrāya*):
when the compound *tena saha* is formed, the substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* does not occur because of its connection with the prefix *āṅ*. Likewise for "together with his ministers" (*sahāmātyāya*).
It should be stated that [the rule applies] except in the case of *go*, *vat*, and *hala*.

*agovatse* means that the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the word *sahasra* does not occur when it follows words such as *govatsa*. *Sagave* is an example for the rule "May it be well for the king" (*rājñe svasti*).

(841) *bahuvrīhau saṅkhyeye ḍajabahugaṇāt* |5|4|73|. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ḍac* is applied after a numeral denoting the thing counted (*saṅkhyeya*), provided it is not *bahu* or *gaṇa*.
Now, he states the uncommon suffixes for the *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, [the rule] "in a *bahuvrīhi*":

"that *bahuvrīhi* which [occurs] when a numeral is to be expressed. The remainder [of the rule] is "prescribed by [Pāṇini 2.2.25] *saṅkhyayāvyaya*" (by a numeral or an indeclinable). From that [suffix], [the word] "in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīhau*) [is used]; the sense is that the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. [The suffix] *ḍac* shall be applied.

It should be understood that this is a taddhita suffix forming a compound-final (samāsānta). Regarding the form *upadaśāḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "those which are near to ten. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed by the rule *saṅkhyayā 'vyayāsannādūrādhikasaṅkhyāḥ saṅkhyeye*. There is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). From the word *upadaśan*, when the suffix *ḍac* is added, there is the elision of the final vowel and what follows it (*ṭilopa*) by the rule *na-staddhite*. Thus we have *upabahavaḥ* and *upagaṇāḥ*.
Thus [it is said]. The analysis of the compound is "those who are near many" (*bahūnāṃ samīpe ye santi*) and "those who are near a group" (*gaṇasya samīpe ye santi*).

Because [the words] *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* are numerals according to the rule *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṅkhyā*, the compound is formed by the rule *saṅkhyayāvyaye*. Due to the prohibition [of the suffix] *ḍac* by the rule *abahugaṇāt*, the suffix *ḍac* is not applied.
