"It is remembered" (*smaryate*). The intention is that because it begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*), the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule "guṇe 'rtau" (Pāṇini 6.1.92).

Now, an objection might be raised: when the suffix *luṭ* is applied and we have *ṛ tā*, resulting in *smṛ*, the guṇa substitution would apply by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*) and its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), thereby preempting the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment, regardless of whether [the augment] has been applied or not.

Since the *iṭ* augment and the *guṇa* substitution would apply under the rule for *ciṇvadbhāva*, once the *guṇa* has been applied and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* has occurred, the root would no longer end in an *ac* vowel; consequently, there would be no *iṭ* under the *ciṇvadbhāva* rule.

Furthermore, because the root would then be considered non-*aniṭ*, the *iṭ* prescribed by the rule for roots beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) would also be absent, resulting in the form *asmartā* alone, rather than *āritā* or *smāritā*. Therefore, he says:

"Because it is subsequent," and so forth. The meaning is that even though the status of having a final vowel (*ajantatva*) is lost once *guṇa* has been applied and *ra-paratva* (the substitution of *r*) has occurred, the application of the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment remains unimpeded because of the rule stating "that which ends in a vowel which was [present] in the original formative instruction (*upadeśa*). Regarding *ārita*: although *guṇa* and *ra-paratva* have been applied, the *upadhā-vṛddhi* (penultimate vowel strengthening) occurs due to the *ciṇvad-iṭ*. Regarding *arta*: [this is the form when *guṇa* and *ra-paratva* have not been applied].
This is the form when the *iṭ* augment is absent in the *ciṇ* formation; likewise for *smāritā* and *smartā*. Now, one might object:

when the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the passive sense (*karmani*) from the root *kṛ* preceded by *sam*, with the *yak* affix, and after the substitution of *riṅ* for *ṛ* according to the rule *ṭhriṅ śayagliṅkṣu*—and provided that *suṭ* is applied according to the rules *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇe* and *samavāye ca*—[the form would be *saṃskriyate*].

It will be stated that [the root] is "refined" (*saṃskriyate*). In that context, one might think that by the rule *guṇo'rti* (Pāṇini 7.4.29), a *guṇa* substitution would occur because the root begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*);

therefore, he says: "because of the continued application of the mention of 'always' (*nitya*). This is because the word "always" (*nityam*) is carried over from the rule *nityaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.210) into the rule *guṇo'rti*, [implying that the *guṇa* applies] only to that which is always [beginning with a conjunct].

It is understood that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth are qualities (*guṇa*) characterized by that very [conjunction] itself. However, conjunction and so forth are not eternal, because in the absence of being preceded by *sam* and *pari*, they do not exist; this is the intended meaning.

Now, he states a specific rule regarding the suffix *yaK* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) from the root *sraṃs*: "there is elision of the *n* [of the root] according to the rule *aniditām*."

Thus [it is said]. Regarding "iditaḥ tu": from the root *ṭu-nad* (meaning "to prosper"), when the suffix *yaK* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-lakāra*), because it is marked with the *iD* indicatory letter (*idit*), there is no elision of the *na*; this is the meaning. Now, he states the specific rule for the root *yaj* when the suffix *yaK* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman-lakāra*)—namely, "vocalization" (*saṃprasāraṇa*). This is by means of the rule "vacisvapiyajādīnām."

The state [of the suffix]. Regarding the specific rule for the *yak* affix in the *bhāva-lakāra* (passive/impersonal voice) of the root *śīṅ*, he says: "In the absence of *ayaṅ*, [the vowel is long] before *kṅti*" (*ayaṅ yi kṅti*).

(583) *tanoteḥ yaki* | 6|4|44|. [The word] "before *yak*" [is understood]. From [the previous sūtra] "ṭhviḍvanor... [the word] "from the beginning" (*ād*) is supplied, and from "ye vibhāṣā" [the word] "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is supplied.
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) also carries over. Thus he says: "There may be the substitution of the final letter with the vowel *ā*.
This is a supplement to complete the sense. [Examples: *tāyate*, *tanyate*. Here, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*).

(584) *tapo 'nutāpe ca* ("In the case of *tap*, and also in the sense of repentance"). From the rule *cler sic* ("*sic* replaces *cli*"), the word *cleḥ* is understood; and from *ciṇ te* ("*ciṇ* is substituted for *cli* when followed by *te*").

From this [sūtra], *ciṇ* is understood; from the previous sūtra, *na rudhaḥ*, the word *na* is also understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). By the force of the word *ca*, the phrase *karmakartari* from the sūtra *acaḥ karmaṇi* is conjoined. Thus he says: "after *tap* and *cli*, etc.
Among these, he will provide examples for the *karmakartṛ* (passive-reflexive) in the section on *karmakartṛ* operations. Regarding *anutāpa* (remorse):

He provides an example for the *karmakartṛ* (passive-reflexive) construction: "anvatapta pāpena" (he was tormented by sin). Taking "pāpena" as the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), he says: "sin is the agent. If the root *tap* preceded by the prefix *anu* were taken to mean "remorse," there would be an inconsistency; for [remorse] does not belong to the sin.
The sun possesses the power to burn. Since [the root *tap*] would become intransitive if it were taken in the sense of "grief," he says:

"struck" (*abhyāhata*). The point is that the root *tap*, preceded by the prefix *anu* and influenced by the prefix *abhi*, has the meaning of "striking. And because that [root] is transitive, the use of the object-case (*karmalakāra*) is justified; thinking this, he says:

Regarding the rule "luṅ in the sense of the object" (Pāṇini 3.2.105): having relied on the sense of sorrow (*śoka*), one may explain it as *luṅ* in the sense of the state (*bhāva*), or alternatively, with the sinful person as the agent. The meaning is that, having acted rashly upon some improper deed without considering its consequences, he subsequently experienced suffering. Sorrow is the experience of suffering.
Because it is subsumed under the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), [the verb] is intransitive (*akarmaka*). The root *śuc* in the sense of "sorrow" is intransitive.
However, in the expression "he sorrows for his son" (*putram anuśocati*), the meaning is that he causes sorrow by remembering the son who has departed;
since the son is the object (*karman*) in the act of remembering, there is no contradiction in using the accusative case. Now, regarding the root *dā* and the verbal root...
Regarding the *yak* suffix in the *karmakartṛ* (passive-reflexive) construction, he states the specific rule: "there is *itva* by [Pāṇini 6.4.66] *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām...*".

Having raised the objection that the substitution of *eś* for the *t* of the *liṭ* [perfect] in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) from the root *glai* would be barred by the prohibition "not before a non-*śit*" (*aśiti*) regarding the substitution of *ā* by [Pāṇini 6.1.45] *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*, he says: "in the rule *ādeca...*". This is because [the term *aśiti*] consists of both *ś* and *it*.

By resorting to a *karmadhāraya* compound, the prohibition of *ātva* is obtained when a suffix beginning with the letter *ś*, which bears the technical designation *it*, follows. Even though *eś* has the property of being *śit*, because it lacks the status of having an *it* as its initial element (*ādibhūta-śakāretkatva*), there is no prohibition; thus, *ātva* occurs when that *eś* follows.
The meaning is "it indeed occurs. Regarding *jagle*: the intention is that once *ātva* has been applied, there is its elision by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64).
(585) *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33).
The term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is the governing factor (*adhikṛta*) and is qualified by *āt* (ending in ā). This is a rule of "designation of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*).

Regarding the rule *aco ñṇiti*, the phrase *ñṇiti* is a qualifier for *kṛ* alone, and not for *ciṇ*, because *ciṇ* never deviates from being marked by the *ṇi*t suffix. Thus he says: "of those ending in ā," and so forth.

Regarding *dāyita*: in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* (as in *ciṇvadiṭ*) is applied, the *yuk* augment is added. Regarding *adāyiṣātām*: having applied *ciṇvadiṭ* because it is subsequent, this overrides the rule *sthādhvor ic ca*; consequently, by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭi*, there is no substitution of *ī*, and because the root begins with a vowel (*ajādi*), there is no [application of the *guṇa* rule]. However, the rule *ṣṭhiv-ṣthā-dhvor ic ca* does not apply here, because [the root] begins with a vowel (*ac*) and is not preceded by a consonant (*jhal*). For in that context, the term *jhal* from the sūtra *iko jhal* is understood as a governing element (*anuvṛtta*). Thus, it is established that the *sic* suffix is *kit* only when it begins with a *jhal* sound; consequently, since the *sic* beginning with *iṭ* is not *kit*, they say that the substitution of *iṭ* for the initial [of the root] also does not take place due to its association with that *kit* status.

In reality, however, even if that [prohibition] were present here, there would be no harm at all; for even in the case of the root *sic* with the suffix *kit*, the form is established through the augment *vṛddhi* by way of indirect indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is the general direction. Now, he explains the passive voice (*karmalakāra*) of the root *han*: "it is killed" (*hanyate*). Regarding the rule *aciṇṇalōḥ*: in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), when the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment is applied...

In the case of *vṛddhi*, the substitution of *t* for the *n* of *han*—as prescribed by the rule *ṭhano'ciṇṇalor ar*—does not take place; the meaning is that this is because [the suffix] is treated like *ciṇ*. Regarding "the *kutva*" (the change of *h* to *gh*): the point is that although that [change] is prescribed by the rule *tasya ṇit*, it applies here because of the treatment as *ciṇvat*. As for the form *ghāniṣyate*: [this occurs] because [the rule] *ṛddhano'r* is superseded.

Because [the substitution] is permanent, the augment *iṭ* (as in *ciṇvadiṭ*) applies; however, once *ciṇvadiṭ* has been applied by the rule "ṛddhanoḥ" (*Pāṇ. 7.2.11*), [the substitution of *han* for *ghat*] does not occur, making it non-permanent. The point is that in that case, the term *vali* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Now, one might object: in the case of the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), where *ghāniṣīṣṭa* results from *han* + *sīṣṭa*, even though *ciṇvatva* should apply, it is superseded...

The substitution of *vadh* would apply because, since it is prescribed when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is intended to be expressed, the substitution of *vadh* is *antaraṅga* (internal); therefore, he says: "in the *āśīr-liṅ*," etc. [He asks:
how can the substitution of *vadh* apply in cases such as *ghānita*, given that the substitution of *vadh* has not yet become applicable?
Thinking that the substitution of *ciṇvadbhāva* might be an exception (*apavāda*), he says: "In an *ārddhadhātuka* [affix], before *sīyuṭ*.
In the rule *syasicsīyuṭ*, there are four cases for a stem ending in a short vowel:

before *sya*, before *sic*, before an *ārddhadhātuka* affix, and before *sīyuṭ*; and likewise for a stem ending in a short vowel before *tās*. Thus, there are four instances for a stem ending in a short vowel.
These are the sentences. Thus, for each of the roots *han*, *grah*, and *dṛś* as well, there are four sentences; this is the established position.

Among them, in the case of the root *han* before an ārdhadhātuka suffix, the rule prescribing *sīyuṭ* and the *iṭ* augment as if it were *ciṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *vadh* for *han*, because it is without scope (*niravakāśatva*), [applying] precisely where [the *vadh* substitute] would otherwise not have applied.

The substitution of *vadha* occurs from the point of the initial application [of the rule]. However, the substitution of *vadha* is not an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ciṇ-vat* augment; the sense is that in the case of *vadhyāt*, the *liṅ* (optative) has already served its purpose for the agent. Regarding "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*):

this refers to the alternative where there is no *ciṇ-vat* treatment. When the substitution of *vadha* is applied by the rule "the root *han* becomes *vadha* in the *liṅ*," and the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule regarding roots beginning with *val*.

Therefore, the form [is derived] by means of elision, because the substitute *vadh* ends in a long vowel (*ā*). Nor should it be argued that since the root *han* is anudātta and consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*) in its original teaching (*upadeśa*), the substitute *vadh* must likewise be so, and thus how could the augment *iṭ*—which is prescribed for roots beginning with a consonant (*valādi*)—apply here; for [the rule] "of a one-syllabled root in its original teaching... [applies].

In this context, since singularity is already established by the force of the word "ekasya" [in the rule *ṭhaca*], the explicit mention of "eka" (one) serves to ensure that the form is derived from the substitution of *vadha* for *han*, followed by the elision of the vowel *a* after the augment *iṭ*; this is because the substitute *vadha* ends in the vowel *a*. Nor can it be argued that because the root *han* is unaccented (*anudātta*) and consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*) in its original teaching (*upadeśa*), the same would apply to its substitute *vadha*.
Since that is the case here, one might ask how the augment *iṭ*—characterized by the letter *val*—could apply.

[The answer is: In the rule *ṭhekāca upadeśe*, although singularity is already established by the force of the singular number in the word *eka-aj*, the explicit mention of *aka-* (not *eka-aj*) by force of its inclusion implies that [the root] is one that has exactly one vowel in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), and never one with more than one vowel. By this, [the desired result is obtained].

By adopting the instruction that *vadhi* is a substitute for *han*, there is no prohibition [of the augment] even for a monosyllabic root; it was stated previously that this is because the root is polysyllabic at the time of the original instruction (*upadeśa*). However, in the *luṅ* [aorist], when the suffix *isic* follows, and after the substitution of *ciṇ*, the penultimate vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*, resulting in *gha* by the rule of *kutva*. By the rule "optionally in the *ātmanepada*," there is an absence of the substitute *vadha*.

*aghāniṣātām*: this is the form when the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is present and the substitution of *vadh* for *han* does not occur. *ahasātām*: this is the form when the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is absent; because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *hanaḥ sic*, the nasal is elided by the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikaḥ lopaḥ*. In the alternative case, it is *avadhi*.

The meaning is that this refers to the alternative view where *vadha* is the substitute [for *han*] by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām*. As for *avadhiṣātām*, the intention is as follows: since the substitute *vadha* is also optional by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām*, even when *vadha* does not apply, the introduction of the *ciṇvat* treatment is not an exception (*apavāda*). Now, regarding *ciṇi*:

Anticipating the objection that since the substitution of *vadh* is observed [in the sūtra], it might also apply to the forms beginning with *si* (the *liṅ* endings) because of the rule *ciṇvadbhāva*, he refutes this with the words "And not... (*na ca*), etc. The point is that the substitution of *vadh* applies only to the *aṅga* (the verbal base); however, the substitution of *vadh* is secondary (*dvaitīyīka*) and does not reside within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *aṅgas*. Now, regarding the root *grah* in the sense of "taking" (*upādāne*).

For this reason, he provides an example with a *l*-suffix denoting the object (*karmalakāra*)—namely, *gṛhyate*. Here, the semivowel is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16). Now, regarding the future suffix *luṭ*, when the suffix *tās* is added and the augment *ciṇvad-iṭ* is applied, one might suspect that the long vowel rule *graho 'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37) would apply; therefore, he says: "There is no lengthening due to the *ciṇvad-iṭ*. To the question "Why?", he replies:

Regarding the phrase *prakṛtasya* ("of that which is under discussion"): since the augment *iṭ* characterized by the rule *valādi* is what is under discussion, it is that very *iṭ* which is understood in the prescription of lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*) by the rule *graho 'liṭi*; it is not the *ciṇvad-iṭ*, as is clear from the Bhāṣya. Now, he provides an example for the root *dṛś* in the passive voice (*karmalakāra*): *dṛśyate*. In the perfect (*liṭ*), it is *dadṛśe*. In the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), [it is] with *tāsi*.
In the case where the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment is applied, [the forms] have been shown. In the absence of *ciṇvat*, there is *am* by the rule *sṛjidṛśor am*. Thus:

*draṣṭā*, *darśiṣyate*, *drakṣyate*, *darśiṣīṣṭa*. However, in the absence of the *ciṇvad-iṭ*, because the *s-* of *sic* is *kit* according to the rule *liṅsicāv ātmanepadeṣu*, there is no *am* by the rule *sṛjidṛśor am*.

Nor does the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) apply. [In the forms] *dṛkṣīṣṭa* and *adarśi*, there is the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel. [In the form] *adarśiṣātām*, it is the form with the *iṭ* augment as if it were *ciṇ*. Regarding the absence of the *ciṇvadbhāva* state, he says: "Because of the *kit* status of *sic*, there is no [guṇa]. This is because *sic* has the *kit* status by the rule "The *liṅ* and *sic* [are *kit*] in the *ātmanepada*."

The suffix *am* does not apply after the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś* because of the exclusion [in Pāṇini 6.4.71] by the condition "provided there is no *ak*" (*akitīti paryudāsāt*). Now, from the root *gṛ* (in the sense of swallowing) with the *lakāra* of the passive (*karmalakāra*), when the suffix *yak* is added, the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṝ* occurs, and by the rule "also before a consonant" (*hali ca*), the vowel is lengthened—thus, *gīryate*. In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the form is *jagare*. In the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), with the suffix *tās*, in the alternative where the treatment as *ciṇ* applies, the form is *gāritā*; in the absence of the *ciṇ*-treatment, [it is *garitā*].

When the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for the *valādi* [affixes], and after the substitution of *guṇa*, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*—the forms are *garitā* and *garītā*.

According to the rule *vṛto vā*, there is optionally a long vowel: *gāriṣyate*, *gariṣyate*, and *garīṣyate*. [The forms are] *gīryatām*, *agīryata*, *gīryeta*, and *gāriṣīṣṭa*. However, in the alternative where the *ciṇvat* treatment does not apply:

Regarding the root *gṛ* (to swallow), there is an option for the augment *iṭ* by the rule "ṭhliṅsicorātmanepadeṣu. In the absence of *iṭ*, the suffix is *kit* by the rule "uśca," which triggers the substitution of *it* (the short *i*), followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*. Then, the long vowel is applied by the rule "hali ca," and finally, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs, resulting in *gīrṣīṣṭa*. However, in the case where *iṭ* is present, it is *gāriṣīṣṭa*. In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, [the forms are] *agārīt* and *agāriṣātām*.

Taking *agīrṣātām* and *agariṣātām* as established forms, he says: "In the *luṅ* [aorist] with the suffix *dhvim*, there are one hundred and four. The word "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. He demonstrates this very point, saying: "For instance," and then gives the example *agāridhvam*. When *gṛ* + *s* + *dhvam* is situated, and the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is applied...

The intention is that in the first case, after the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (by the rule *vṛddhireci*), the form is derived by the elision of *s* according to the rule *dhi ceṭ*. In the second case, however, it is *iṭīti*.

This refers to the alternative view where the *iṭ* augment (as in *ciṇvadiṭ*) does not apply; instead, the *iṭ* is added to the *sic* suffix by the rule *valāditaḥ*, followed by the *guṇa* of the vowel *ṛ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, the elision of *s* by the rule *dhi ceṭ*, and finally the optional lengthening of the vowel by the rule *vato vā*.

The meaning is that there are two forms: *agaridhvam* and *agarīdhvam*. Regarding the word "of these" (*eṣām*): among these three, in each one, the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs by the rule "optionally before a suffix beginning with *ṭh*" (*ṭhaci vibhāṣā*).
Alternatively, the substitution of *ḍh* for *dh* occurs by the rule "optionally for *ṭ*" (*vibhāṣeṭaḥ*). Thus, this applies to *dh*, to the *ḍh* which is its substitute, to *v*, and to *m*.

The meaning is that there are five optional instances of doubling (*dvitva*): namely, two instances for *dha* and *ḍha*, one for *ma*, and two for *va*. The distinction is as follows: for *dha* and *ḍha*, the option of doubling arises by the rule "ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.111) combined with "aco rahābhyāṃ dve" (Pāṇini 8.4.46); for *va*, however, the option of doubling arises by relying on the fifth case in the rule "maya uño vo vā" (Pāṇini 8.3.33), which states "yaṇaḥ mayaḥ" (the *m* of *maya* is doubled). Although [the doubling] of *dha* and *ḍha* occurs by the rule "vasya masay... [etc.].

And while it would have been more appropriate to say "two twos and four" (*dvitva-catuṣṭayam*), nevertheless, because *ḍha* is the substitute for *dha*, the expression "three twos" (*dvitva-trayam*) is used with the intention that *dha* and *ḍha* are considered one. "In this way" (*ittham*) means as follows:
and thus, when there is an option regarding the substitution of *la* for these three, there are three forms containing *ra* and three containing *la*.

Six (6). Among these six, when there is an option for doubling the *dha*, there are six with one *dha* and six with two *dha*s, making twelve (12). Likewise, among the three containing *ra* and the three containing *la*, when there is an option for doubling the *ḍha*, there are six with one *ḍha* and six with two *ḍha*s, making twelve (12).

In the combination of both sets of twelve, there are twenty-four. Among these, when considering the option of doubling each, there are twenty-four single units and twenty-four double units, making forty-eight. Among these, when considering the option of doubling each pair...

The meaning is "ninety-six," namely forty-eight with one *mān* and forty-eight with two *mān*s. Regarding the phrase "by [the rule] *liṅsicor*"—this refers to the absence of the *iṭ* augment in the alternative case where the *ciṇvadiṭ* does not apply, because the *iṭ* characterized by the condition of being followed by a consonant (*valādi*) is optional by the rule *liṅsicor*. In the case of its absence...

The meaning is as follows: because the suffix *sic* is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *it*; by the rule *raparaḥ*, this is followed by the letter *r*; by the rule *hali ca*, the vowel is lengthened; and since the letter *ṛ* (repha) is followed by the suffix *iṇ*, the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam* applies, resulting in the obligatory replacement of *dh* with *ḍh*. Thus, the form *argīḍhvam* is produced. As for the form *ḍhavamānam*, [the *ḍh* is substituted] by the rule *aco rahābhyām*.

In the optional doubling of the *dvitva* [suffix], there are two forms: *ekaḍhṃa* and *dviḍhṃa*. When the doubling of these two occurs according to the rule "of *vas*, *ṭhyaṇ*, and *mayaḥ*," there are four forms: *ekave dve* and *dvive dve*. In these four, when the doubling of the *ma* occurs according to the rule "before *ṭha* and *anac*," there are four forms with one *m* (*ekamāni catvāri*) and four with two *m*s (*dvimāni*).

"Four" means eight forms. Regarding "ninety-six": the meaning is that it should be understood that when the previously mentioned ninety-six are added to the eight, the resulting number, one hundred and four (104), is what has been stated. He summarizes the aforementioned method in a verse: *iṭ-dīrgha*...
By these and other such rules: the *iṭ* augment is applied by the rule "valādi-lakṣaṇa-iṭ"; the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "vṛto vā";

the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment is applied by the rule "ajantalakṣaṇa-ciṇvat-iṭ"; the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs by the rule "aci vibhāṣā"; and the substitution of *ḍh* for *dh* occurs optionally by the rule "vibhāṣeṭaḥ".
Since there is an optionality regarding eight factors—the doubling of the three [consonants] *dha*, *ḍha*, and *m*—there are one hundred and four combinations.

The meaning is "forms" (rūpāṇi). He demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) for the phrase "mohaḥ śamyate mukundena" as follows: "from the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) [of the root *śam*]. From the root *śam*, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, the penultimate vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*; then, because it ends in *man*, it is designated as *mit*, which results in the shortening of the vowel. Thus, from the form *śamī*, the suffix *laḥ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), and not in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), because it is a causative formation (*hetumaṇṇyanta*).

The meaning is that it is because of the rule governing transitivity (*sakarmakatva-niyama*). Regarding *yag*: when the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes are applied, [the term] "ya" is supplied by the rule *sārvadhātuke yaK*. Regarding "elision of *ṇi*": the phrase "by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*" is to be supplied.

When the form *luṭ* [is applied], and after adding *tās*, *śam-i*, and *i*, the state is *i-tā*; then, because it ends in *am*, it is designated as *mit*, and consequently, the penultimate vowel is necessarily shortened.

When [the affixes] *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* are obtained—(Pāṇini 6.4.93): "In place of [the penultimate vowel of] *ciṇ* and *ṇamul*, a long vowel may optionally [be substituted]. From [sūtra 6.4.90], "after [the root] *duṣ* before *ṇi*", the word *ṇau* [is understood]; and from [sūtra 6.4.89], "for *guh*, when *u* is the penultimate [vowel]..."

Thus, from the rule *upadhāyāḥ*, and from the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*, the term *mitām* is understood to carry over. This is what he says with the words beginning "when followed by *ciṇ*" (*ciṇpare*). Now, one might object that the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) here is redundant, since the result would follow simply from the rule *ciṇṇamuloranyatarasyām* alone, even when [the rule] *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* is applied.

Since the option for the long vowel would be established by the option for the short vowel which is carried over from the preceding sūtra, he says "in the present context," etc. To the question "Why? he says: "after a causative [denominative] root ending in -ṇi, when followed by another -ṇi.
This refers to the case where, after the root *śam* with the causative suffix -ṇi, the preceding -ṇi is elided, and the suffix -luṭ (future) with -tās is applied.

Since the causative form (*ṇyanta*) ends in a vowel (*ajanta*), when the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment is applied, it is considered asiddha (non-existent) by virtue of being ābhīya; consequently, because the prohibition "when there is no iṭ" (*ṭhaniṭi*) does not apply, the *ṇilopa* occurs, and when the option for lengthening (*dīrghavikalpa*) takes effect, the two forms *śamitā* and *śāmitā* are desired. However, if the rule were a prescription for an optional short vowel (*hrasvavikalpa*), that optional shortening would not occur.

The meaning is that because of the first elision of the *ṇic*, the subsequent [element] is separated by the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*); therefore, it lacks the quality of being preceded by a *ciṇ* or a *ṇi*. However, there is no fault in the rule prescribing the optional lengthening;
thus he says: "In the case of the prescription of lengthening. For in the rule prescribing the optional lengthening of the first *ṇic*—

The elision (*lopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* because its status as *sthānivadbhūta* is prohibited in the prescription of a long vowel (*dīrghavidhi*); therefore, in this case, the optional application of the long vowel is established. However, in the prescription of a short vowel (*hrasvavidhi*), the status of the first elision of *ṇi* as *sthānivadbhūta* is unavoidable, because there is no prohibition of its being *sthānivadbhūta* therein—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in the Bhāṣya, however" (*bhāṣye tv iti*), [it means] not...

However, in the Bhāṣya on the *padānta* rule (*padasaṃjñāsūtra*), since [the desired result] is already established by the statement "when a preceding operation is not established, [the substitute] does not behave like the original" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*),

the doubling (*dvirvacana*), homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), nasalization (*anusvāra*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and *jaś*- and *car*-substitutions are rejected in the *padānta* rule. Thus, in the case of *sudhyupāsya*, the doubling [of the *dh*] by the rule "also when a non-vowel follows" (*anaci ca*) [is not required], and in the case of *śiṇḍhi*...
In *pratidīvn*, there is the substitution of anusvāra by the rule *ṭhnaśca*; in the same word, the substitution of the homogeneous nasal (*parasavarṇa*) by the rule *ṭhanusvārasya yayi*;
in *sagdhiḥ*, the substitution of the *jaś* sound by the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*;
and in *jakṣatuḥ*, the substitution of the *car* sound by the rule *ṭhkhari ca*.

The meaning is that [the operation] is not considered asiddha with respect to what precedes it. Now, one might object: when the lengthening prescribed by "ṭhciṇṇamuloḥ" is to be applied after a root ending in a causative suffix (ṇic), the substitution of the first ṇic-suffix must unavoidably be treated as sthānivadbhūta (as if it were still present), because the lengthening by "ṭhciṇṇamuloḥ" is not subject to the rule of being asiddha with respect to what precedes it. Consequently...

Because it is separated by the first *ṇic*, there is no occurrence of the long vowel (*dīrgha*). And since, in that case, the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is necessary to prevent the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule when the long vowel is to be applied, [the author asks] how the mention of "long" can be rejected; to this he says: "In the case of *ṇau*" etc. [referring to the rule] *ciṇṇamulor dīrgho 'nyatarasyām*.

In the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94), which states "there is lengthening when a *ciṇ* affix follows, as well as when a *ṇamul* affix follows, provided that a *ṇi*-affix follows," the mention of *ṇau* refers primarily to the class-property (*jāti*) of being a *ṇit*. Thus, it is understood that the lengthening occurs when the class-property of being a *ṇit* follows, whether that property belongs to a *ciṇ* affix or a *ṇamul* affix. Since this class-property of being a *ṇit* exists in both types of *ṇi*-affixes, the lengthening takes place even when the first *ṇi*-affix is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original).

"Unobstructed" (*nirbādha*) means that this is the intention of the *Bhāṣya* on the rejection of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule *na padānta*. Regarding *śāmitā* and *śamitā*: from the root *śam* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*) with the suffix *tās*, there is an optional long vowel due to the *ciṇ-vat* treatment. Regarding *śamiyitā*: in the absence of the *ciṇ-vat* treatment, the suffix *iṭ* is applied by the rule for roots beginning with a consonant (*valādi*).

Regarding the form *rūpam*: from the root *śam* with the suffix *yaṅ*, we have *śiṃśamy*. From this, by adding the causal suffix *ṇic*, the *yakāra* is elided according to the rule *yasya halaḥ*; then, after the elision of the *akāra*, from *śaṃśamī*, the *karmalakāra* (passive voice) is applied, and the *ṇic* is elided, resulting in the form *śaṃśamyate*. As for *śaṃśāmitā* and *śaṃśamitā*: [these are derived similarly].

The phrase "ṭhiṇmulo'ri" indicates an optional long vowel [substitution]. Regarding "śaṃśamayitā": this is the form when the *ciṇ* treatment does not apply, and the augment *iṭ* is added by virtue of the rule for roots beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). Regarding "in the opinion of the Bhāṣya," this means according to the view of the Bhāṣya which rejects the inclusion of the term "long vowel" (*dīrgha*) in the sūtra "na padānta...". "From a *yaṅ*-intensive base" (*yaṅntāt*).

The remainder of the rule is "after a root ending in ṭu or ṇi. When the suffix yaṅ has been added, followed by ṇic, and after the elision of *ya* and the elision of *a* have been performed, the form *śaṃśam* is derived.
From this, when the suffix *luṭ* (future) with *tāsi* is applied, and the augment *ciṇvad-iṭ* is added, because that [augment] is considered asiddha, the *ṇi* is elided.
In the resulting form *śaṃśamita*, due to the status of the elision of *a* (*allopa*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, the condition of being followed by *ṇic* is absent.

In the rule *ṭhaciṇṇamuloḥ*, the long vowel [substitution] does not occur; the meaning is that according to the view of the Bhāṣya, since there is no mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the sūtra *na padānta...*, there is no prohibition of the status of being *sthānivadbhūta*. Regarding the phrase *śamyate muninā*: the intention is that because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *la* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*).

(587) *nodātopadeśasya māntasyānācameḥ* || 7.3.34 || "Not for that which is taught with an udātta accent, nor for one ending in *m*, except for the root *ācam*. From the rule *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* [6.1.109], the word *vṛddhiḥ* is understood; from *ata upadhāyāḥ* [7.2.116], the word *upadhāyāḥ*; from *aco ñṇiti* [7.2.115], the word *ñṇiti*; and from *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* [7.3.33], the word *yuk*.

From this point on, the words *ciṇ* and *ṇakṛtoḥ* are understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Among these, the term *ṇiti* is a qualifier for *kṛt* alone, and not for *ciṇ*, because there is no deviation [in the case of *ciṇ*]. Thus he says: "of the penultimate vowel," and so forth.
Those [roots] taught with an anudātta accent have been collected; everything else besides them is [included in the remaining category].

The verbal root is taught with an udātta accent. *Ācamiḥ* means "excluding *ā-cami*," which is preceded by the prefix *ā*. Examples are *aśami* and *adamī*. In these cases, there is no vṛddhi substitution [of the penultimate vowel] because of the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), applied to the roots *śam* and *dam* in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *ic*. As for *agāmī*, the point is that the root *gam* is taught with an anudātta accent. *Avādī* [is explained similarly].
The meaning is that the verbal root *vad* does not end in the letter *m*. Regarding the form *ācāmi*:

because it is stated that "there is no prohibition of the penultimate vowel-vṛddhi for *ācam*" (*anācameḥ*), there is no prohibition of the penultimate vowel-vṛddhi here. The rule "of *ācam*, *kam*, *vi*, and *mī*" (*anācamikamivamīnām*) means "of those [roots] excluding *ācam*, *kam*, *vi*, and *mī*. And thus, there is no prohibition of the vṛddhi even for *kam* and *vi*.
This is the established conclusion. Now, one might object: since [the root] *kram* ends in the causative suffix *ṇiṅ*, there is no usage of it alone in forms such as the *ciṇ* [aorist];

to this he says: "In the *ciṇ* [aorist], *yaṅ*, etc. [The same applies to] *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic*. That is to say, whether from a form ending in *ṇiṅ* or from one ending in *ṇic*, when the *ciṇ* [aorist] suffix is applied and the *ṇi* is elided, the resulting form remains as previously described.
This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "The prohibition of the *vṛddhi* augment in the penultimate vowel by the rule *janivadhyośca* is redundant;

for since the substitute *vadha* ends in *a*, the absence of *vṛddhi* in forms such as *avadhīt* is already established simply by the fact that the elision (*alopa*) of the preceding *a* is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.
Anticipating this objection, [the author] maintains that *vadha* is indeed a different verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in a consonant (*halanta*).
Intending that [the term] *vadha* is understood in the rule *ṭhjanivadhyośca*, he says: "The root *vadha* ending in *hal* [is used] in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*).
(Pāṇini 6.4.33) *bhañjeśca ciṇi*.

And in the case of *bhañj* with the suffix *ciṇ*, [the penultimate vowel is not lengthened]; from the rule "ṭhśnānnalopaḥ" [it follows] that by the word "na" (not), we have *abhājī*. In the alternative where there is no elision of *n*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. (589) *vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ* 7.1.69.

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā ciṇṇamuloḥ*: considering that *labheḥ* is carried over from the rule *ṭhlabheśca* and *num* is carried over from the rule *idito num*, he completes the remainder [of the sūtra] by stating: "the augment *num* is optionally applied after the root *labh*. Now, [one might ask] regarding forms such as *prālambhi* and *upālambhi*...

Since there might otherwise be an option for the augment *num* even when the root *labh* is preceded by a prefix, he says: "it is restricted" (*vyavasthita*). This is because of the Vārttika: "The augment *num* is obligatory after a prefix preceding *labh*, but optional when it follows no prefix," and because in the Bhāṣya, the word "prefix" (*upasargāt*) [is understood to apply] from the rule "after a prefix, in the case of *khal* and *ghañ*" (*upasargāt khalghañoḥ*), and not [to the rule concerning *labh*].

Carrying forward the word *na* from the rule *sudurbhyām* (Pāṇini 7.1.68), it has been explained that the augment *ṇiṭ* is optionally applied after the root *labh* when preceded by a prefix, except in the cases of the *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* suffixes. By this, the interpretation that the root *labh* preceded by *pra* necessarily takes the *num* augment is refuted. [This is established] by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69).

Since [the suffixes] are not prescribed by the term *lakāra*, the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* suffixes will be stated [later] to occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*. Regarding those [suffixes], he states the restriction as to which of the two objects they occur in among roots that have two objects, with the words: "But in the case of roots having two objects... (*dvikarmakāṇāṃ tu*).

The phrase "the determination of the object-condition (karmapratyaya) will be explained" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. He demonstrates that determination with half a verse, beginning with "in the case of the secondary object" (gauṇe karmaṇi).
[The rule applies] to the roots duh, yāc, pac, daṇḍ, rudh, pracch, ci, brū, śās, ji, math, and muṣ, when the secondary object is intended.

The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is: "the *l*-class suffixes and so forth are considered [to denote] the primary object. It should be understood that according to the rule *akathitaṃ ca*, that which receives the designation of "object" (*karman*) is the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*). Regarding the phrase "in the primary [object]": the syntactic connection is: "the *l*-class suffixes and so forth are considered [to denote] the primary object in the case of the roots *nī* (to lead), *hṛ* (to carry), *kṛṣ* (to draw), and *vah* (to carry). According to the rule *akathitaṃ ca*, that which [receives the designation by] any other [rule]— [The sentence is incomplete.]

The term "action" (*karman*) here should be understood as primarily referring to the action [of the agent]. Now, regarding those verbs that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*) according to the rule *gatibuddhi* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), he states the established usage: "buddhi" etc. For verbs signifying cognition (*buddhyartha*), those signifying eating (*bhakṣārtha*), and those having sound as their object (*śabdakarmaka*), the suffixes such as *la* (tenses and moods) may, by the speaker's own choice, be applied to either the primary or the secondary object.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with the word "considered" (*matā*). Here, that which receives the designation of *karman* (object) by the rule *gatibuddhi-* is the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*);

the other, however, is the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*). Regarding the term "prayojya" (the one being prompted): this refers to others [than those mentioned] whose roots have the sense of motion and are intransitive, as well as the roots *hṛ* and *kṛ* included in the rule *hṛkroḥ*.

The syntactic connection is: "the *l*-affixes and others are considered [to apply] to the prompted object (*prayojyakarman*). It should be understood that this half-verse is a summary of the Vārttika and Bhāṣya located under the rule *akathitaṃ ca*. In the example "gaur duhyate payaḥ" (the cow is milked for milk), the word "by the cowherd" (*gopena*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Here, because the cow is the subordinate object (*apradhānakarman*), with respect to that object—

The suffix *lakāra*. Because the cow (*goḥ*) is expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*), it takes the nominative case. Because it is the primary object (*pradhānakarman*), "milk" (*payas*) ends in the accusative; this is because it is not expressed by a finite verb. "Bali is asked for the earth. "The ill-mannered man is asked for good manners. "Rice grains are cooked into porridge. "The Gargas [are fined] a hundred."

The staff is being held by him; the herd is being blocked by him; the boy is being asked about the path; the tree is being gathered for its fruits; the boy is being told or taught the Dharma; Devadatta is being caused to win a hundred [pieces of gold]; the ocean of milk is being churned for nectar; Devadatta is being robbed of a hundred [pieces of gold].

In these cases, the *l*-suffix denotes the secondary object (*gauṇakarma*). Now, regarding the primary object (*pradhānakarma*), he provides examples for the rule "in the case of *nī*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, and *vah*": *ajā grāmaṃ nīyate* ("The goat is led to the village"), and so forth.
In each action, the phrase "the goat [to] the village" (*ajā grāmam*) is construed [with the verb]. In the case of *uhyate* ("is carried"), [the same applies].

Due to the rule that *vahati* belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Here, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is used for the cow (*ajā*), which is the primary object (*pradhānakarman*);

the second case ending is applied to *grāma* because it has not been previously expressed by another grammatical element. He provides an example of a verb meaning "to understand": *bodhyate māṇavakaṃ dharmaḥ* (the boy is made to understand the Dharma), or *māṇavako dharmam* (the boy [understands] the Dharma). The word "by the teacher" (*guruṇā*) is to be supplied as the agent. In this case...

When the boy (*māṇavaka*) is the secondary object (*gauṇakarma*), or when *dharma* is the primary object (*pradhānakarma*), the suffix *lakāra* occurs after a root ending in the causative marker *ṇic*. However, for roots meaning "to eat" (*bhakṣ*), examples such as "the gods are made to eat nectar by Hari" (*aśyante devā amṛtaṃ hariṇā*) or "nectar is eaten by the gods" (*aśyate 'mṛtaṃ devaiḥ*) should be cited. For roots whose object is sound (*śabdakarman*), however, an example is "the Veda is caused to be studied by Hari for the sake of the gods" (*vedo 'dhyāpyate vidheṃ hariṇā*).
One may cite examples such as "the injunction is studied" (*vedo'dhyāpyate*) or "the injunction is known" (*vidhirvedyate*).

Regarding what was stated—that "for roots meaning 'motion,' for intransitive roots, and for *hṛ* and *kṛ*, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) occurs in the sense of the instigating object (*prayojyakarman*)"—he provides an example of a root meaning motion: "Devadatta is caused to go to the village" (*devadatto grāmaṃ gamyate*).

The word "by Yajñadatta" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Here, the suffix *la* (the present indicative) follows the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *gam* (to go), with Devadatta as the prompted object (*prayojyakarman*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Is the rule that for intransitive roots in their causative form (*ṇyanta*), the suffixes such as *la* apply only to the prompted object not redundant? For in those cases, there is no other object besides the prompted one. Anticipating this doubt:

By the Vārttika stating, "In connection with intransitive roots (*akarmakadhātu*), it should be stated that place (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and the path to be traversed (*gantavyo'dhvā*) are designated as the object (*karma*)," even intransitive roots,
when in their causative form (*ṇyanta*), become transitive (*dvikarmaka*) by virtue of having place, time, and so forth as their objects.

Intending that the rule "the *l*-affixes and so forth occur only with the prompted object (*prayojyakarman*) in those cases" is purposeful, he will provide the example "The boy is made to sit for a month" (*māsam āsyate māṇavakaḥ*) in the causative (*ṇyanta*); here, the *l*-affix occurs only with the prompted object, the boy (*māṇavaka*), and not with the object, the month (*māsa*). If this is so, then [what about] intransitive verbs in their non-causative (*aṇyanta*) state?

One might object that in the expression "māsa āsyate devadattena" (a month is sat by Devadatta), the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) would not occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*), because of the rule: "after transitive roots, the *lakāra* occurs in the sense of the object and the agent. One might further suspect that the *lakāra* would only occur in the sense of the object, as in "māsa āsyate devadattena. Anticipating this objection, he says: "of intransitive roots," and so forth. Those [roots] which...

Intransitive verbs— those devoid of the "object" (*karman*) established by the rules *ṭhkarturīpsitatamaṃ karma* and *ṭhtathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*, such as *āsa upaveśane* ("to sit") and *vṛtu vartane* ("to exist")— [take] the object [of the action] when joined with other intransitive roots, as established by the Vārttika rule *ṭhakarmakadhātubhiryoge*. This refers to the case of the object (*karmaṇi*).

And it is intended that the *l*-suffix occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). One should not be mistaken into thinking this is a *vārttika*, as it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*. Rather, it is based solely on reasoning (*nyāyamūlaka*), because the optionality of the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) for place, time, and so forth when in conjunction with intransitive roots is accepted in the *Bhāṣya* and other sources. For example:

We have already stated this during the explanation of the rule "ṭhakarmakadhātubhiryoge" (Pāṇini 3.4.72) in the section on agents (kāraka). Thus he says: "māso māsaṃ vā āsyate devadattena" (Devadatta sits for a month). Here, in the view that the month is the object (karman), the *lakāra* suffix is used in the sense of the object.

The first case ending (*prathamā*) is used because "month" (*māsa*) has been mentioned [as the subject]. However, in the alternative view where the month lacks the status of an object (*karmatva*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the abstract action (*bhāve*). The form *māse* is in the locative case; *māsam*, on the other hand, is a corrupt reading. Now, he returns to the subject at hand: "from the causative form (*ṇijanta*) of the root *ās*" (*āsadhātoḥ*).

The meaning is that because [the root] is devoid of an action established by its own nature (*prakṛti*), when the suffix *ṇic* is added, even though the month is the object (*karman*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) occurs only with respect to the prompted object (*prayojyakarman*). Thus: *māsam āsyate māṇavakaḥ*.

Here, after the causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the suffix *laḥ* occurs with respect to the prompted object, the boy (*māṇavaka*). Since the month is not already expressed [by another case ending], the second case (*dvitīyā*) is employed.

"Or rather, the servant is caused to be carried to the mat by Devadatta. This concludes the section on the formation of verbal roots (bhāva) and objects (karman). Now, [the suffixes] having the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) and the object (karman): [The following rules apply: Pāṇini 3.1.67: *bhāve* (in the sense of the abstract state). Pāṇini 3.1.68: *akarmakebhyo dhātubhyaḥ* (after verbal roots that are intransitive). Pāṇini 3.4.69: *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (the suffixes *la* [denoting tense and mood] occur after verbal roots in the sense of the object and the abstract state, and after intransitive roots in the sense of the abstract state). Pāṇini 3.4.70: *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* (the *kṛtya*, *kta*, *khal*, and suffixes having the sense of *artha* occur only in the sense of those two: the object and the abstract state). Pāṇini 3.4.71: *dhaḥ karmaṇi ca* (after the root *dhā*, [the suffix *kta* occurs] also in the sense of the object). Pāṇini 3.4.72: *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* (the suffix *kta* occurs in the neuter gender in the sense of the abstract state). Pāṇini 3.4.73: *lyuṭ ca* (and the suffix *lyuṭ* also occurs in the sense of the abstract state). Pāṇini 3.4.75: *puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ prāyeṇa* (the suffix *gha* generally occurs in the masculine gender when it denotes a name). Pāṇini 3.4.76: *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (the suffix *ka* occurs after roots ending in *i* or *u* as penultimate vowels, and after *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṛ*). Pāṇini 3.4.78: *ātaścopasarge* (the suffix *ka* occurs after a root ending in long *ā* when preceded by a prefix). Pāṇini 3.4.81: *paryāyārhaṇotpattipratipattisargādhyayaneṣu ṇaḥ* (the suffix *ṇa* occurs in the sense of turn, merit, birth, attainment, creation, and study). Pāṇini 3.4.82: *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (after the root *vad*, when a nominal stem follows, the suffix *kyap* also occurs). Pāṇini 3.4.83: *hano vā vadha ca* (after the root *han*, the suffix *kyap* occurs optionally, and *vadha* is the substitute for *han*). Pāṇini 3.4.84: *bhṛño 'saṃjñāyām* (after the root *bhṛ*, the suffix *kyap* occurs when it does not denote a name). Pāṇini 3.4.85: *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (there is *vṛddhi* [strengthening] in place of the vowel of the root *mṛj* when followed by the suffix *kyap*). Pāṇini 3.4.86: *kṛñaḥ śa ca* (after the root *kṛ*, the suffix *śa* also occurs). Pāṇini 3.4.87: *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (after the root *ghu* [meaning "to sound"] preceded by a prefix, the suffix *ki* occurs). Pāṇini 3.4.88: *ātaśca* (the suffix *ki* also occurs after a root ending in long *ā* when preceded by a prefix). Pāṇini 3.4.90: *iṇ niṣṭhāyām* (the substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the root *iṇ* occurs before the past passive participle suffix *niṣṭhā*). Pāṇini 3.4.91: *saṃyogāder āto dhātor yaṇ niṣṭhāyām* (for a root beginning with a consonant cluster and ending in long *ā*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs before the suffix *niṣṭhā*). Pāṇini 3.4.92: *oditaśca* (the substitution of *yaṇ* also occurs for roots marked with the indicatory letter *t* or *d* ending in *o*). Pāṇini 3.4.93: *lvādibhyaḥ* (the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for roots beginning with *lū* etc.). Pāṇini 3.4.94: *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe* (*kṣayya* and *jayya* are irregular forms used in the sense of "possible"). Pāṇini 3.4.95: *kṣayyajayyau śaktau* (the forms *kṣayya* and *jayya* are used in the sense of being capable). Pāṇini 3.4.96: *krayyastadarthe* (*krayya* is used in the sense of "meant for sale"). Pāṇini 3.4.97: *praṇāyyo 'sammatau* (*praṇāyya* is used in the sense of "disapproved"). Pāṇini 3.4.98: *nāyyaḥ pāpe* (*nāyya* is used in the sense of "evil"). Pāṇini 3.4.99: *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe* (reiteration for emphasis). Pāṇini 3.4.100: *kṛtyatṛcaśca* (the suffixes *kṛtya* and *tṛc* also occur in the sense of the agent). Pāṇini 3.4.101: *aco yat* (the suffix *yat* occurs after a root ending in a vowel). Pāṇini 3.4.102: *īdyati* (the vowel *ī* is substituted for the final vowel of the root before the suffix *yat*). Pāṇini 3.4.103: *pāyyasānnāyyanikāyyadhāyyamānahavirnivāsasāmidhenīṣu* (the forms *pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, *nikāyya*, *dhāyya*, *mānya*, *havir*, *nivāsa*, and *sāmidhenī* are irregular formations). Pāṇini 3.4.104: *ṛhalor ṇyat* (the suffix *ṇyat* occurs after a root ending in *ṛ* or *h* and after roots beginning with *l*). Pāṇini 3.4.105: *or āvaśyake* (the suffix *ṇyat* occurs after a root ending in *u* in the sense of necessity). Pāṇini 3.4.106: *āsu yuṭ* (the suffix *yuṭ* occurs after the root *āp* in the sense of necessity). Pāṇini 3.4.107: *ānāyyo 'nitye* (*ānāyya* is used in the sense

(1754) *tena tulyaṃ kriyā cedvatiḥ* | Pāṇini 5.1.115. Now, the meanings of the suffixes *vati* and *karmārtha* are being examined. [The rule states: "When there is equality with that (*tena tulyam*), if it refers to an action (*kriyā*), the suffix *vati* is used. The word "equality" (*tulyam*) is an adjective qualifying "action" (*kriyā*). It is neuter because it expresses a general concept.

The suffix *vati* shall occur after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) in the sense of "equal to" (*tulya*), provided that which is equal is an action (*kriyā*). In other words, *vati* occurs in the sense of "an equal action. For example: *brāhmaṇavad adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa"). Here, *brāhmaṇavat* is the illustration. [It is derived] from *brāhmaṇena*...

The analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is "he studies similarly. Here, by the word *brāhmaṇa*, the study performed by a Brāhmaṇa is indicated. The resulting cognition is: "the study performed by a Kṣatriya is similar to the study performed by a Brāhmaṇa. [The rule applies] when there is similarity of quality; it also applies when there is similarity of substance.
This is to be understood as follows: [the suffix] does not occur in cases such as "Devadatta is as wealthy as that Caitra.
In instances such as "this is not like that," the elders employ a verbal form (kriyāpada) to ensure the grammatical correctness of the suffix *vati*, saying, "[he] says."

(1755) *tatra tasyeva* |5|1|116|. The meaning is that the suffix *vati* occurs after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), in the sense of "in that place" (*tatreva*) and "belonging to that" (*tasyeva*).
This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Precisely because of this [rule]...

The *Bhāṣya* states that when words such as *nirdeśa* and others are joined [with another word], the locative case (*saptamī*) is used even in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Intending to show here that the term "if it is an action" (*kriyā cet*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], he provides the example: "In Snuhya, there is a rampart, just as in Mathurā" (*madhurāyām iva madhurāvatsnugne prākāraḥ*). Here, the phrase "just as in Mathurā" (*madhurāyām iva*)...

It is not the locative case used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇasaptamī*); for if that were the case, there would be a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*) due to the dependence on the verbal action expressed by the word "existing" (*vidyamāna*). For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya*—which states that the locative is used in the sense of the genitive when joined with words such as "like" (*iva*)—is consistent. [The example is: "The wall of Srughna is like the wall related to Mathurā."
"Prākāra" means an enclosure; "the state of being friendly" (*maitrasya bhāvaḥ*) means a circle (*vṛta*).

(1756) *tadarham* |5|1|117|. "Tadarham": that which it deserves is *arham*. [The suffix] *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). Here, "tat" is in the accusative case, ending in the second case, functioning as the object.

The meaning is that it becomes fit to be obtained. The absence of the sixth case (genitive), which would otherwise be required by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The term *vati* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning is that the suffix *vati* occurs after a word ending in the accusative case in the sense of "is fit for" (*arhati*).
Thus, *vidhim arhati* means "it is fit to obtain the injunction. [Therefore,] he is honored like the injunction (*vidhibat pūjyate*).
Thus [it is said]. The word "Hari" is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound]. The meaning is: worship of Hari which is worthy of being performed.
That is to say, it does not deviate from the prescribed method. Regarding the phrase "by frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakaplutyā*):
the intention is that [the term] does not carry over (*ananuvṛtti*) from the preceding rule.

(1757) *tasya bhāvastvatalau* | 5|1|119|. "The state (*bhāva*) of that": the meaning is that the suffixes *tv-* and *tal-* occur after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) in the sense of "the state of that. Since the word *bhāva* also functions in the sense of "intention" (*abhiprāya*) and so forth, he says: "State (*bhāva*) means mode (*prakāra*)."

When the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are produced from a word that serves as their base (*prakṛti*), and when the cognition of an individual (*vyakti*) arises from that base-word, whatever genus (*jāti*) and so forth appears as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is designated by the term "bhāva" (abstract property) as the qualifier of that individual.

The meaning is that it is what is intended to be expressed. For example, when the cognition of an individual arises from the word "cow" (*go*), the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) appears as its qualifier; this is because the word "cow" is understood to have a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect both to individuals possessing cowness and to cowness itself. Indeed, the word "cow" does not apply to individual cows while excluding cowness.

Regarding the apprehension of the word’s power (*śaktigraha*): it is not possible [to grasp it] because past, future, and present [individuals] are infinite, and thus cannot be presented simultaneously; furthermore, it would follow that from the word "cow" there would be a cognition of cow-individuals even in the form of being a living being, being an animal, and so forth. Therefore, [the word must denote] that which is common to all cow-individuals...

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) operates by taking as its primary determinant (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) a certain specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) that is excluded from other individual entities. Similarly, words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa-ādi-śabda*) also operate by taking as their primary determinant properties such as "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*). This very [property] is the ground for the application of a word (*śabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*).
"Bodhaḥ" [is masculine]. "That which ends in *tva* is neuter, and that which ends in *tal* is feminine"—this is established by the rules of the *Liṅgānuśāsana*.
(1758) "And [the suffixes] up to and including *tva*" (Pāṇini 5.1.120).

Regarding the [sūtra] *ā ca tvāt*: the words *tva* and *tal* are understood from the previous context. *ĀṬ* is used in the sense of a limit (inclusive). Thus he says: "The suffix *tva* occurs after *brahman* before this point. Now, one might object: since *tva* and *tal* are already established by their recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) in the subsequent rules from the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau*, this heading (*adhikāra*) is redundant.

Therefore, he says: "by exceptions" (*apavādaiḥ*). The meaning is that this is for the purpose of including the exceptions such as *imanij* prescribed by rules like "optionally after *pṛthu* and others, *imanij*" (*pṛthvādibhyaḥ imanij vā*).
For if this governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) did not exist, then in the subsequent rules prescribing *imanij* and so forth—

There would be no occurrence of the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, because the expectancy [of the base] is satisfied by the specific suffixes such as *imanij* and others which are explicitly mentioned in the rule. Otherwise, the sense is that the suffix *aṇ*, which is governed by the rule "before *dīvyati*, *aṇ*" (*prāgdīvyato ’ṇ*),
would also apply in rules such as "from *at*, *iñ*" (*ata iñ*).

He states another purpose [for the rule]: "from words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) and so forth. The intention is that otherwise, since *tva* and *tal* would have scope for application in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of these being superseded by *ṣyañ*, which is specifically prescribed for the sense of object (*karman*) after words expressing qualities and the like. One might object: "Even so, let it simply be 'ā tvāt' (up to the suffix *āt*)."

Since the recurrence of *tva* and *tal* from the preceding sūtra is established here simply by their being marked with the *svarita* accent, the particle *ca* (and) would be redundant for the purpose of drawing them forward; therefore, he says: "The particle *ca*... Otherwise, *tva* and *tal* would not apply after the words *strī* and *puṃs*, as they do elsewhere.

The meaning is that both [rules] are subject to exceptions (*sāvakāśatva*). Regarding *pāṃsunam*: when the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) is elided, the substitution of *r* occurs by the rule *pumaḥ khayyampare*. The nasalization (*anunāsika*) and the *anusvāra* are optional.
When the *visarga* is substituted, the substitution of *s* occurs. Similarly for *puṃstvam*; therein, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*.
It does not occur, because it is recited in the *savana* and other [sections].
(1759) Not [after a compound] preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, except for *acatura*, *saṅgata*, *lavaṇa*, *vaṭa*, *yudha*, *kata*, *rasa*, and *lasa*.

"Not after that which is preceded by *nañ*. This means "after this point," that is, subsequent to the rule for the suffixes *tva* and *tal*; for the *Bhāṣya* states that there is a prohibition of what follows [the previous rule] when preceded by *nañ*. This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).

"Excluding *catur* and the others" means excluding these: *catura*, *saṅgata*, *lavaṇa*, *vaṭa*, *yudha*, *kata*, *rasa*, and *lasa*. "The state of not being *apatya*" (non-descendant status): here, the suffix *yañ* does not occur [after these] because of the rule "after words ending in *ṭh* and after *purohita* etc. "The state of not being *apaṭu*" (non-aptitude).

In this case, the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed] by the rule "after a word ending in *ṭhik* and having a light penultimate vowel" does not apply. Thus, from *bṛhaspati*, one forms *bārhaspatyam* by applying the suffix *yañ* according to the rule "after words ending in *ṭhak* and after *purohita* etc.
From *apaṭu*, one forms *āpaṭavam* by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "after a word ending in *ṭhik* and having a light penultimate vowel. Regarding the word *apaṭu*:
The point is that because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and lacks the status of a *tatpuruṣa*, there is no prohibition of the suffix *aṇ*.
Regarding *ācāturya*: it is the state (*bhāva*) of one who is not clever (*acatura*); the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class.
Regarding *āsaṃgatya*: it is derived from the word *asaṅgata* with the suffix *ṣyañ*. Regarding *ālavaṇya*: [it is derived from *alavaṇa* with the suffix *ṣyañ*].

From the word *alavaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied. Regarding *āvaṭaḷ*: it is "not a *vaṭa*," hence *avaṭa*; from that, *ṣyañ* is applied. Regarding *āyudhyam*: from the word *āyudha*, *ṣyañ* is applied. Regarding *ākṛtyam*: from the word *akṛta*, *ṣyañ* is applied. Regarding *ārasyam*: from the word *arasa*, *ṣyañ* is applied. Regarding *ālasyam*: that which shines (*lasati*) is *lasa*; [it is] not [that].
*Lasa* means *alasa*. From that, the suffix *ṣyañ* [is applied].

(1760) *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā* | 5|1|122|. From the group beginning with *pṛthu*: the phrase "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*) is understood to follow. From words beginning with *pṛthu* ending in the genitive case...

The meaning is that the suffix *iman* (or *imanij*) may optionally (*vā*) occur after a noun stem (*bhāve*). Now, one might object that the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is redundant, since the formation of the periphrastic sentence is already established by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*) rule: "After a [stem] capable [of forming a derivative], [the suffixes are added] from the first [word]. Nor should it be said that the word "optionally" is for the purpose of including the suffixes *tva* and *tal* when *iman* is absent; for [the rule continues]: "And up to... (*ā ca...*) [and so forth].
To show that this is established through immersion (samāveśa) just as in the case of *tvāditya*, he says:

"The mention of *vapā* is for the purpose of [illustrating] immersion in *maṇa* and so forth. For in words such as *pṛthu* and *mṛdu*, there is the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *ṭhigantācca laghupūrvāt*; and in words such as *caṇḍa* and *khaṇḍa*, there is the suffix *ṣyañ* characterized as being used after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*).

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *añ*—which is characterized by age and speech—and the general suffix *āṬ* in words such as *bālavatsa*. Otherwise, according to the principle of the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), once a general rule has been superseded by an exception, the general rule does not apply again; as stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā."

The sense is that, since [the suffixes] *iman*, *ic*, *tva*, and *tal* have been established as the final conclusions, their application would not otherwise occur. (1761) *ra ṛto halāder laghoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.161.

*ra ṛto*: *ra* is the nominative singular form. "In the case of the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun*"—this completes the remainder [of the rule]. The intention is that this follows from the recurrence of the rule "*ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.3.111), which states that when *ṭh* is elided, the preceding vowel is lengthened. The governing term *aṅgasya* ("of the stem") is understood; thus, for a light *ṛ*-vowel belonging to a stem beginning with a consonant, *ra* [is substituted].
The meaning is that the *ādeśa* (substitute) consisting of the *rapara* (with *r* as a subsequent element) occurs when *iṣṭhan*, *iman*, or *īyas* follow.
(1762) *ṭeḥ* | 6|4|155|. The meaning is that the substitute consisting of the *rapara* [is applied] when *iṣṭhan*, *iman*, or *īyas* follow. (1762) *ṭeḥ* | 6|4|155|.

The word *ṭeḥ* [is used]. From the rule "ṭhiṣṭhemeyassu" it is understood that this applies; and from the rule "ṭhallopo'naḥ," the word *lopaḥ* is also understood. Thus he says: "There shall be elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi* [portion] before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *iṣṭha*, *iman*, and *īyas*. Regarding *prathimā*: the suffix *iman* is added to the word *pṛthu*. The letter *c* is for the sake of pronunciation (*it*). The vowel *a* after the *n* is for the sake of articulation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

For the vowel *ṛ*, there is *ra*; for the vowel *u*, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* takes precedence over the *guṇa* substitution. Thus, *pārthavam*: in the absence of the suffix *imanij*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *ṭha* or *ika* that has a light penultimate syllable. *Mradimā*: from the word *mṛdu*, when *imanij* is added, the *ṛ* becomes *ra*, and by the rule "elision of *ṭi*," the final *ṭi* is dropped.
Regarding "mārdavam": the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "ṭhigantācca" (Pāṇini 5.1.119).

(1763) Pāṇini 5.1.123: *varṇadṛḍhādibhyaḥ ṣyañ ca*. From words denoting color (*varṇa*) and from the group beginning with *dṛḍha*, when standing in the genitive case, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*).

The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* should also occur. Since the suffix *ṣyañ* is already established by virtue of [these words] being adjectives (*guṇavacana*), this statement is for the purpose of including the suffix *imanij* as well.
The substitution of *ra* occurs only for the words *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *bhṛśa*, *kṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha*.

He summarizes the meaning of the Vārttika—"One should remember these six in the rules for the suffix *ayi*: *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *bhṛśa*, *kṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha*"—in the words "pṛthu-mṛdu-bhṛśa," etc. By that [Vārttika]:
In forms such as *kṛtayati*, even though the treatment as if it were *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) applies, the substitution of *ra* for *ra* does not occur. Regarding *draḍhimā*:

from the word *dṛḍha*, when the suffix *iman* is added, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *ra*. Thus we have *bhraśimā*, *kraśimā*, *draḍhimā*, and *paribraḍhimā*. Now, since words ending in the suffix *ṣyañ*—such as *varṇa* and *dṛḍha*—are neuter according to common usage, [the rule] regarding *ṣyañ*...

To the question, "What is the purpose of [the marker] *ṣ*? he says: "*ṣo ṅīṣ-arthaḥ*" (The *ṣ* is for the sake of the suffix *ṅīṣ*). Regarding the word *aucitī*: from the word *ucita*, by virtue of its inclusion in the *brāhmaṇa*-group, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied; the feminine gender arises from common usage (*lokat*). Because of the *ṣ* being *śit*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, and by the rule *halas taddhitasya*, there is the elision of *y*. However, *ucita* is not part of the *dṛḍha*-group, as it is not found in that list.

Because [the suffix] is not seen [elsewhere], and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*inic-prasaṅga*). It should be understood that since this very *ṣyañ* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent sūtra, the purpose of its being marked with *ṣ* (*ṣitva*) is stated right here. Regarding *yāthākāmī*:

"according to desire" (*yathākāmam*) means not transgressing desire (*kāma*). From that, by adding *ṣyañ* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), because it belongs to the group beginning with *caturvarṇa*.
In the sense of "belonging to the world," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because of the presence of the marker *ṣ*.
(1764) Pāṇini 5.1.124: "After words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) and after the class beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of action (*karman*).
[The term] *guṇavacana* refers to those words which denote a substance (*dravya*) where the quality (*guṇa*) is subordinate. And [the rule applies] after the class beginning with *brāhmaṇa*.

The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied after words ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*). Regarding the rule *arhato num ca*: this is a *vārttika* [supplement] to the sūtra *arhaḥ praśaṃsāyām*.
Kaiyaṭa states that the word *arhat* in the sense of the present participle suffix *-śatṛ* denotes one who is worthy of honor (*pūjya*).

The meaning [of the rule] is that the suffix *ṣyañ* is added after the word *arhat*, and there is the augment *num* for the base. Because it has the marker *m* (indicating it is a *mit* suffix), the augment follows the final vowel.
There is then the substitution of *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*. According to worldly usage, there is both neuter and feminine gender.

Regarding that, he says: *ārhantyam*, *ārhantī*. From the word *ārhantya*, with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, there is the elision of *y* according to the rule *halastaddhitasya*. *Yathātatha* is a collection of indeclinables (*nipāta*). *Yathāpuram* is an avyayībhāva compound formed with the word *pura* in the sense of "not deviating from the state of things as they were" (*padārthānatikrame*). These two...
The two words beginning with the negative particle *nañ* refer to [the categories] starting with *brāhmaṇa*.

(1765) Regarding the rule *yathātathāyathāpurayoḥ paryāyeṇa* 7.3.31: he states a specific detail concerning the addition of the suffix *ṣyañ* and the resulting initial *vṛddhi* for those two—namely, for *yathātatha* and *yathāpura*.
This sūtra occurs within the section on initial *vṛddhi* (A 7.3.1–19), under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of the subsequent member and of the preceding member" (A 7.3.10–19).

From the rule "after *nañ*, [the first vowel of] *śuci*... (A 6.2.158), the word "*nañaḥ*" is understood by anuvṛtti. Thus he says: "of these two following *nañ*. This means: of the two words *yathātathā* and *yathāpura*.
"By way of alternation" means that sometimes it is the first member of the compound [that undergoes the change], and sometimes it is the second member.

Regarding "āyathātathyam": by virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the word *yathātatha*, when the suffix *ṣyañ* is added, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the initial syllable of the first member, resulting in *āyathātathyam*. Regarding *ayāthātathyam*: there is vowel strengthening of the initial syllable of the second member.

Regarding *āyathāpuryam*: from the word *yathāpura*, when the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of the initial of the first member (*pūrva-pada*), resulting in *āyathāpuryam*.

Regarding *ayāthāpuryam*: there is *vṛddhi* of the initial of the second member (*uttara-pada*). As for the rule "up to the end of the section" (*ā padāsamāpteḥ*), here the commentary itself is the only refuge.
There is an addition [to the rule] for *caturvarṇa* and so forth, in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*).

Regarding "of *caturvarṇa* and so forth": the meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* is added after *caturvarṇa* and the others in the sense of the base itself. As in *sarvaveda*: this is a compound formed according to the rule "pūrvakāla" (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

Regarding "lugiti": the remainder [of the rule] is "of the suffix denoting a student" (*adhyetṛ-pratyayasya*). "That very same [suffix] is *sārvavaidya*" means that the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after the word *sarvaveda*.
Regarding "caturvedasya": this is a *vārttika*; the remainder [of the rule] is "*ṣyañ*". [The resulting form is] *caturveda*.

The term *dvigu* is applied by the rule *taddhitārtha*. Thereafter, the suffix *aṇ*, which denotes a student (*adhyetṛ*), is elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*. Regarding the form *caturvidyasyeti*:
in the Vārttika *caturvedasyobhayapadavṛddhiśca*, the word *caturvedasya* occurs in place of [the intended form].

The meaning is that some read the word as *caturvidyasya*. In the sense of "one who studies four sciences" (*catasro vidyā adhīte*), a *dvigu* compound is formed according to the rule *taddhitārtha-*. Then, by the rule *vidyā-lakṣaṇa-kalpāntācca*, the suffix *ṭhak* is added; subsequently, by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, that suffix is elided. Finally, from the word *caturvidya*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
The intention is that when there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts [of the compound], the form *cāturvaidya* is produced.
(1766) *stenādyannalopaśca*. The analysis is *stena-āt-yan- lopaś-ca*. From the word *stena*, ending in the genitive case, [the suffix] *yañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

The meaning is that [the suffix] *yat* occurs when the sense is "action" (*karman*). "Not so; it is a reference to the combination" means that in the rule *nalopaśca*, the vowel *a* in the word *na* is not for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), but rather it is a reference to the combination of the letter *n* and the vowel *a*. "Theft" (*steyam*)—[is derived thus].

The intention is that when the suffix *yat* is added to the word *stena*, there is the elision of the *saṅghāta* [the entire syllable] according to the rule "na" (Pāṇini 6.4.143). Nor should it be argued that even if only the letter *n* were elided, the form *steyam* would still be established through the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.148); for the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "acaḥ parasmin" (Pāṇini 1.1.57) would act as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if the original element were present), thereby preventing the application of "yasyeti ca."

For, by relying on that [interpretation], there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ay* for the single vowel *e*. Nor should it be suspected that even if a "group" (*saṅghāta*) were intended to be grasped, the elision (*lopa*) would apply only to the final *a* according to the rule *ṭhalo’ntyasya*;
for since the elision of the vowel *a* is already established by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the prescription of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) here would be purposeless.
And because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] "when [a suffix] is meaningless, the rule regarding the final letter does not apply. Regarding the phrase "having divided the *yoga*":

*stenāt* is a separate sūtra. The term *ṣyañ* is understood to follow [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied after the word *stena* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*).

According to the perspective of the *Ākaḍāra-sūtra* commentary, a meaningful verbal form that is distinct from compounds (*samāsa*), primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*), secondary derivatives (*taddhitānta*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), pronouns (*sarvanāman*), genus-words (*jāti*), numerals (*saṅkhyā*), and technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) is designated as a "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*). Consequently, since the word *stena*, ending in the *pacādyac* suffix and thus being a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*), lacks the status of a quality-word, this rule would not otherwise apply; [therefore] this statement is made. Even if it were a quality-word by virtue of being an unanalyzed base noun (*pratipadika*), this statement is intended to ensure its optional coexistence with the suffix *yat*, which is an exception (*apavāda*).

Then there is another rule: *ṭhyannavalopaśca*. Since the word *stenāt* is understood from the previous context, the meaning has already been stated. Regarding the phrase "some say" (*kecit*): the sense is that this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) lacks authority, as it is not seen in the Bhāṣya.
(1767) *sakhyuryaḥ* | 5|1|126 | *sakhyuryaḥ*. From the word *sakhi*, ending in the genitive case, the suffix *ya* shall occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).

The meaning is that it must be stated [as a separate rule]. "It does not exist at all" means that since it is a *vārttika*, its inclusion in the *Bhāṣya* would have been necessary; however, because it is not found there, the sense is that this *vārttika* cited in the *Vṛtti* is simply unauthoritative.
If that is so, how [can one account for the forms] from *dūta* and *vaṇij* in the senses of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)?
