He says that it is not [the suffix] *yat*, but rather *ṣyañ* alone; however, because it belongs to the *brahmādigaṇa*, there is also *vāṇijya*. By the word "also" (*api*), the inclusion of *dautsya* is intended.
(1768) *kapi-jñātyoḥ ḍhak* 5.1.127.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *kapi* and *jñāti*. The genitive case is used here in the sense of the ablative;

thus, the meaning is that *ḍhak* is added after these two words when they end in the genitive, provided they denote the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). In this context, there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) between the words *kapi* and *jñāti* on the one hand and the action and object on the other, according to the traditional interpretation.

(1769) *patyantapurohitādibhyo yak* | 5|1|128|. The meaning is that the suffix *yak* occurs after words ending in *pati* and after the group beginning with *purohita*, when they are in the genitive case, to express the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*). [The example given is] *rājāse*.

This is a sūtra concerning the group beginning with *purohita*. The analysis (*cheda*) is *rājā-ase*. The term *sa* is the designation used by the Easterners (*prācām*) for a compound. Thus he says: "the word *rājan*" [becomes] *rājyam*.

[The suffix] *yak* is applied, and there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). However, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*)—by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*—does not apply here.

Because of the exclusion [paryudāsa] by the rule "ṭhabhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.150). Regarding the phrase "in a compound" (*samāse tu*): *adirājaḥ* means "a king who is not first. This is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound). Because of the exclusion by the rule "ase" (Pāṇini 6.2.151), there is no application of the suffix *ya*. Consequently, due to its inclusion in the *brāhmaṇādi* group, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied, resulting in the form *ādhirājyam*; this is the meaning. Regarding the accent (*svara*) of *yak* and *ṣyañ*:
The specific rule:

(1770) *prāṇabhṛjjātivayovacanodgātrādibhyo 'ñ* [Pāṇini 5.1.129]. Regarding *prāṇabhṛjjāti*: "possessors of breath" means living beings; [the suffix *añ* is applied] after words denoting the genus (*jāti*) of such beings.

The meaning is that the suffix *añ* is applied after words denoting specific stages of life (*vayoviśeṣa*) and after words such as *udgātṛ*, when they appear in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), to express the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*). The phrase "prāṇabhṛjjāti" indicates an example; likewise for "vayovacana."

(1771) *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo 'ṇ* |5|1|130|. The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after words ending in *hāyana* and after the group beginning with *yuvan*, when they are in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), to denote an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*). For example, *dvaihāyanam* means "the state of being two years old" (*dvihāyanasya bhāvaḥ*).
The analysis [of the compound] is *karma-vet*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ* prescribed for words denoting age or speech.

Likewise, there is also *traihāyana*. Regarding *yauvana*: because of the rule "there is no change to the original form" (*prakṛtibhāva*) when the suffix *ṭhañ* follows, there is no elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
(1) *Śrotriyasya yalopaśca* ("And for *śrotriya*, there is elision of *y*").

Regarding the word *śrotriyasya*: this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that after the word *śrotriya* ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or object (*karman*), and there is elision of the *y* of the base.

The term *saṅghāta* (composite) is used here [to indicate that the entire word is the base]. Regarding the word *śrotra*: in the sense of "one who has studied the Veda" (*cchando'dhīte*), the suffix *dhak* is applied to the word *cchandas*; when the substitution of *iy* for that suffix occurs, and the substitution of *śrotra* for the base *cchandas* takes place, the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*yasyeti ca*) results in the word *śrotriya*. This is used in the sense of "the state or activity of a *śrotriya*" (*śrotriyasya bhāvaḥ karma vā*).

From the word *śrotriya*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, there is the elision of the cluster consisting of the letter *y* and the vowel *a*; then, by the rule "ṭhyasyeti ca," there is the elision of the vowel following the *r*. Thus, the form *śrotra* is obtained. However, if one were to apply this [present] rule for the elision of the mere letter *y* after the elision of the vowel *a* following the *y* (by the rule "ṭhyasyeti ca"), then [the vowel following the *r* would remain].

[The suffix] *yaN* would [be applied]. Nor should one fear the elision of that [final vowel] by the rule *yasyeti ca*; for according to the maxim *lakṣye lakṣaṇasya sakṛdeva pravṛttiḥ* (a grammatical rule applies only once to its object), and because the status of being a *bha*-stem is absent for that which ends in *i*, due to the fact that the elision of the *a* is treated as having the status of the original locus (*sthānitva*). Some read the rule as *śrotriyasya ghalopaśca*.

(1772) *igantāccalaghupūrvāt* |5|1|131|. [The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a light (*laghu*) element as its preceding member. Furthermore, "preceding-ness" (*pūrvatva*) is understood specifically with respect to the *iK* vowel, based on the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). Thus, that which has a light [vowel] as its preceding member...

The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* shall be applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *iktadanta* (ending in *ikta*, *dan*, or *t*), provided it ends in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), when expressing the sense of an action (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to rules such as "after words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacana*). For example, in the word *kāvya* ("poetry"), since the word *kavi* has a light vowel (*laghu*) preceding its final consonant, the suffix *ṣyañ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule "after words denoting qualities"—is set aside, and *aṇ* is applied instead.

The objection—"How can it be called *kāvya* (poetry) given the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *aṇ*?"—is answered with the words "of the word *kavi*. Following the phrase "because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class [of nominal stems]," the ellipsis to be supplied is "having derived [the form] by means of the suffix *ṣyañ*. (Pāṇini 5.1.132): *yopadhādgurūpotamādvuñ*.

[The suffix] *vuñ* [is applied] after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the sixth case that has *y* as its penultimate letter (*yopadha*) and a heavy vowel in the final syllable (*gurūpottama*). The meaning is: *vuñ* is applied after a nominal stem ending in the sixth case to denote an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). For example: *rāmaṇīyakam*, from the word *ramaṇīya* with the suffix *vuñ*; and *ābhidhānīyakam*, from the word *abhidhānīya* with the suffix *vuñ*. Alternatively, it is applied after the word *sahāya*.

"Or from *sahāya*," etc.; the remainder [of the rule] is "with the suffix *ṭhañ*. In the alternative case, the suffix *ṣyañ* applies because [the word *sahāya*] belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class. This Vārttika, however, is to be sought in some places within the Bhāṣya.
(1774) Pāṇini 5.1.133: "Also after a Dvandva compound and after [words beginning with] *manojña*."

"And from *dvandva* compounds and from [the class beginning with] *manojña*. The meaning is that the suffix *vuñ* is applied after *dvandva* compounds and words such as *manojña* ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For example, *śaiṣyopādhyāyikā*: from the *dvandva* compound "pupil and teacher" (*śiṣyaśca upādhyāyaśca*), the suffix *vuñ* is added. Femininity is established by worldly usage (*lokāt*). Although this would be established even by the rule "*ṭhyopadhāt*" (Pāṇini 4.1.72), [the present rule is stated for the sake of clarity].
Nevertheless, the examples *gaupāla* and *paśupālikā* should be understood [as illustrations].
(1775) *Gotracaraṇāc chālāghātyākāratadaveteṣu* |5|1|134|.
From a *gotra* [name] and from a *caraṇa* [name]: that is, from a word ending in a *gotra* suffix and from a word denoting a follower of a Vedic school (*śākhādhyetṛ*).

The meaning is that the suffix *vuñ* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when expressing the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) or "object" (*karman*), provided the context concerns acts such as praising (*ślāghā*) and so forth. Regarding the statement "other than in the section on offspring (*apatya-ādhikāra*), what is well-known from the *Pravarādhyāya* is called *gotra*," the term "disparagement" (*atyākāra*) is explained as "insult" (*adhikṣepa*). From that, it is understood...

He explains this with the words "those [who know] the lineage" (*te gotre*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the action (*karman*) pertaining to lineage (*gotra*) and school (*caraṇa*) are intended.

The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *i* preceded by the prefix *ava*, meaning either "to reach" (*prāpti*) or "to know" (*jñāna*), in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, the analysis of the compound is: "those who have reached that" (*tad-aveta*), or "those who know that" (*tad-aveta*).
The compound [in *dvitīye*] is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). *Avagatavān* means "he has understood";

that is, he has known. Regarding *gārgikayā*: from the word *gārgya*, with the suffix *vuñ*, there is the elision of the *apatya* [suffix] by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti*; then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*; and finally, by worldly usage, the feminine gender is indicated by the suffix *ṭāp*.

The word *gārgikā* is formed by the substitution of *i* for the vowel following the suffix *ṭhak*, according to the rule *ṭhak-pratyayasthāditītvam*. One praises the *kāṭhikā* (the female follower of the Kāṭha school). This should be cited as an example from the category of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*). It should be understood here that words such as "praising" (*ślāghā*) are conveyed only by other words (*padāntara*) and are construed with the meaning of the suffix, rather than being directly expressed by the suffix itself.

(1776) *hotrābhyaś chaḥ* || 5.1.135 || The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). The intention is that this is based on established usage among ritualists (*yājñika*). The meaning is that the suffix *cha* occurs after words denoting specific types of priests ending in the genitive case, expressing the sense of the action or the object (*bhāva-karmaṇoḥ*).
Regarding the term *acchāvākīya*: it should be understood that the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are everywhere applicable even after words ending in *a*. (Pāṇini 5.1.136): *brāhmaṇastvaḥ*.

*brahmaṇas tvaḥ*. The term *hotrābhyaḥ*, which was understood from the previous rule, is modified here into the singular. Thus he says: "denoting a *hotṛ* priest. This means "denoting a sacrificial officiant (*ṛtvij*). Now, one might object: let it simply be *brahmaṇo na*; since the meaning "the *cha*-affix after *brahman*" is obtained, once the *cha*-affix is prohibited, [the rule] *ā ca*... [would apply].

Since the suffix *tva* would already be established for the meanings of "state" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*) by the rule *hotrābhyaśchaḥ* due to the governing context of *āditya*, he says: "Or (*vā*). One should not suspect that the rule for the suffix *tva* is prescribed merely to provide it for the "object" (*karman*) of *brahman*, because the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are [already] provided by the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau*. Thus, the suffix *tva* is not [merely] for the sake of [denoting] the object of *brahman*.

Nor should it be suspected that when "not a *brāhmaṇa*" (*na brāhmaṇaḥ*) is said, there would be a prohibition of the suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and *cha* prescribed by the preceding sūtra; for the prohibition applies only to the *cha* suffix which is explicitly mentioned in the word-form. He states the purpose of the continued application of the mention of *hotrā* here: "from a synonym of *brāhmaṇa*."
Thus ends the section on *nañ* and *snañ* in the Bālamanoramā.
The Siddhāntakaumudī:
its Uttarārdha. Now, the section on verbal roots beginning with *bhū* (tiṅanta-bhvādayaḥ).
May there be well-being for Pāṇini; may it likewise be so for the Sage [Kātyāyana] Vararuci;
and furthermore, may there be well-being for his brother Patañjali, as well as for my teacher Viśveśvara. (1)
This Siddhāntakaumudī has been explained by many eminent scholars;
Vāsudeva, however, desires this commentary, the Bālamanoramā, for it. ||2||

"Scriptures that begin with auspiciousness, have auspiciousness in their middle, and end with auspiciousness become renowned; they come to possess heroic persons and long-lived persons, and their students shall be endowed with auspiciousness"— this is the authoritative statement from the Bhāṣya regarding the inclusion of such [auspicious elements] within the body of the work.

Having performed the auspicious invocation for the purpose of warding off obstacles and so forth, he composes it at the beginning of the work for the instruction of his students, [beginning with] the word "śrotriya": a *śrotriya* is one who studies the Vedas,
according to the rule, "A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the *chandas*."

From the word *chandas*, which is a synonym for *veda*, the suffix *ghan* is applied in the sense of "one who has studied," with the substitution of *śrotra* for the base; thus, the state of being a *śrotriya* is *śrautra*. By the rule "for *śrotriya*, there is elision of *ya* when [the suffix] *aṇ* follows," there is elision of the *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) following that.

Upon the elision of the combination of the letters *ya* and *a*, there is the elision of the letter *i* according to the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. He is called an *arhat* because he is worthy (*arhati*)—that is, he becomes fit for those actions prescribed by the Vedas which are praised by the noble ones (*āryaiḥ*). The suffix *śatṛ* is applied according to the rule *arhaḥ praśaṃsāyām*. Of the *arhat*...

The word *bhāvaḥ* [here] means *ārhantī*. [It is derived as follows: from the root *arhat*, by the rule *ṭharhato num ca*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied; there is *vṛddhi* of the first vowel, and the augment *num* is added to the base. Because the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Then, by the rule *halastaddhitasya*, the *y* is elided, and by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the *a* is elided. Femininity is understood from common usage (*lokāt*). Thus, it is both *śrautraṃ* and *ārhantī*.
And "fitness for performing the rites prescribed by the Vedas" means, in short, by those who are well-known [for their excellence]. Regarding the term "by those possessed of qualities" (guṇibhiḥ):

it means by those endowed with such praiseworthy qualities as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, the perfection of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, and the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva).
In the rule *rūpād āhatapraśaṃsayor aṇ*, the suffix *yaP* is applied by the Vārttika *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*;
this is because the example *guṇyā brāhmaṇyā* is given in its commentary (*bhāṣya*).
Regarding the term *maharṣibhiḥ*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "those who are great" (*mahāntaḥ*) and "sages" (*ṛṣayaḥ*).
The substitution of *ā* [for *a*] occurs by the rule *ṭhānmahataḥ*. The meaning is "by those who are exceedingly ascetic" (*atitapasvibhiḥ*). Regarding *ahardivam*:

it is a *dvandva* compound formed with the elision of the case endings by the rule *ṭhacaturetyādi* used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), meaning "day and day" (*ahanyahani*). Regarding *toṣṭūyamāno'pi*: the root *ṣṭuañ* means "to praise" and is transitive (*sakarmaka*).

Praise (*stuti*) is the designation [of an object] by way of its qualities. Taking the status of being the object (*karman*) as determined by the act of designation, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) occurs in expressions such as "he praises the gods" (*devān stauti*). However, praise is not merely the designation of qualities;
for if it were so, since the quality would be subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the root would result in being intransitive (*akarmaka*).
By the rule *ṣṭhādyādēḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*, the *ṣ* is changed to *s*, whereby the *ṣṭu*-substitution is prevented;
then, by the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ*, the suffix *yaṅ* is added in the sense of intensity (*bhṛśa*); by the rule *ikṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, lengthening occurs;
by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*, reduplication takes place; and by the rule *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*, the *s* belonging to the reduplicated syllable [is dropped].
Upon elision [of the *yaṅ*], by the rule "ṭhguṇo yaṅlukoḥ," there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *u* of the reduplication;

then, by the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ," there is *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) for the following *s*; then, by the rule "ṣṭuan," the *t* is changed to *ṭ*; and finally, from this *yaṅ*-stem—which, by the rule "sanādyantāḥ," is designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*)—the suffix *laṭ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

When the suffix *śānac* (the present passive participle) replaces *laṭ*, the augment *muk* is added by the rule *muṭ* [Pāṇini 7.2.82]; then *yak* is added by the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* [Pāṇini 3.1.67]; finally, the *akāra* of the *yaṅ* is elided by the rule *ato lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.48], resulting in the form *stoṣyamāna*. The meaning is: "even though being intensely praised."

"Even though he is intensely celebrated as being endowed with infinite qualities such as the inconceivable arrangement of the world," and so forth—"he is without qualities (*aguṇa*)," meaning he is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "The witness, the conscious one, alone, and devoid of qualities. [The objection: How can that which is devoid of qualities be described as possessing qualities?

The word "api" (even/also) indicates the apparent contradiction that praise consisting of verbal description is contrary [to the nature of the Absolute]. However, there is no contradiction because, although qualities possess empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), they lack ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*); this is clear in the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā*. "Omnipresent" (*vibhu*) means all-pervading.

The meaning is "O Supreme Lord. Regarding the phrase *vijayatetarām*: the root *ji* means "to conquer" (*jaye*) and is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Conquest (*jaya*) is the act of existing in a state of excellence (*utkarṣeṇa vartanam*). The reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*. The suffix *tarap* is added by the rule *tiṅśca* to express intensity (*atiśāyane*). By the rule *kimettiṅavyayaghād ām*, the suffix *ām* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*) after that form ending in *tarap*.

The suffix *ām* [is added]. Since it is included among the *tasil*-type suffixes in the rule "that which ends in *taddhita* and does not take all case-endings is indeclinable" (*taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*), that which ends in *ām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Its meaning is "it exists with supreme excellence. Nor should it be asked how the suffix *tarap* can be added after this, given that the entire form "vijayate" is not a finite verb (*tiṅanta*).

For *ṭhvi* is indeed a separate word, since a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) as its final member is restricted solely to Vedic usage. Consequently, the suffix *-tarap* is added to *jayati* itself. Nor can it be argued that this applies to *jayate*, which has taken the ātmanepada by the rule *viparābhyāṃ je*.

One might suspect a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) due to the word *vi-* being dependent [on another]; however, since the prefix *vi-* functions as a dyotaka (an indicator) and thus lacks an independent meaning of its own, there is no obstacle to the nominal form *abhāva-*, which is the primary element, depending on the word *vi-*. This suffices for now. Having first explained the formation of the word:
He promises the description of those suffixes that are about to follow with the words "In the first half.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it is formed from the locative case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa-saptamī*). The meaning is: "among those suffixes occurring in the third chapter. Regarding the word "ten": there is a distinction of *lakāra*s due to the difference in their *anubandha*s (indicatory letters).

This is the intended meaning. Regarding "the fifth": it means the *leṭ* [mood]. Regarding "only in Vedic meter" (*cchandomātra*): the intention is that because the word "in Vedic meter" (*cchandasi*) is carried over from the preceding rule—"the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [moods] are used in Vedic meter"—to the rule "the *leṭ* is used in the sense of the *liṅ*," [the *leṭ* occurs here only in Vedic usage]. By this, [it is shown that] why would the *leṭ* not be applied here?
The doubt that [the suffixes] are not exhibited is dispelled.
(1) *vartamāne laṭ* | Pāṇini 3.2.123. *vartamāne laṭ*. The rule *dhātoḥ* [is understood]. From the sūtra...

The subject under discussion extends up to the end of the third chapter. The word "vartamāne" (in the present) connects with that [rule]. From this, it is understood that *laṭ* (the present tense suffix) occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when the meaning is "present. He states the result:
"of that which has the function of a present action. As for the "presentness" of the action, which is the meaning of the verbal root—

The state of existing in the present time. As for the presentness of time, it is the state of being a time distinct from the past and the future. The *Bhāṣya* states: "The present time is the antithesis of the past and the future. And this presentness is not...

The presentness [of time] is not a qualifier of the agent and so forth, who constitute the meaning of the suffix; for if it were, there would arise the undesirable consequence that one would say "he cooks" (*pacati*) even when the agent has already completed the action of cooking. Rather, presentness is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself, while the *laṭ* suffix merely indicates it. As for the statement "the augment *aṭ* and the suffix *it*," it is not the case that the letter *a*...

It should not be argued that [the letter *ṭ*] exists merely for the purpose of pronunciation; for it is necessary in order to distinguish [the suffixes] from those beginning with *liṭ*. And thus, since there would be no means of its removal without the designation *it*, the intention is that the *it*-designation must indeed be accepted.

(2) *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* |3|4|69|. "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object and [the agent]. This rule consists of two sentences. "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object and [the agent]" is the first sentence.
"The *l*" (*la*) is in the nominative plural. By the word "and" (*ca*), [the agent] is included.

From this point [the word] "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) is drawn over from the previous rule; the term "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). It is thus understood that the *lakāra*s shall occur after a root in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).
This applies exclusively to the domain of transitive roots (*sakarmaka-dhātu*); for intransitive roots (*akarmaka*), the term "object" (*karmaṇi*) [is not applicable].

Because [the agent] is sublated. Thus it is said: "The *lakāra*s [occur] after transitive roots. And so, the *lakāra*s denoting the impersonal state (*bhāva*) do not occur after transitive roots. However, if the *lakāra* denoting the impersonal state were to apply even after transitive roots—as in "a jar is being made by Devadatta" (*devadattena ghaṭaḥ kriyate*)—then by that impersonal *lakāra*, [the agent would be expressed].

The sense is that because the object (*karman*) has not been expressed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) would apply. The second sentence is "and [the sixth case is used] in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) after intransitive verbs. Here too, by the word "and" (*ca*), only the agent (*kartṛ*) is drawn forward, and not the object (*karman*), because it is impossible [for an intransitive verb to have an object]. Thus he says: "after intransitive verbs..."

Regarding the rule "in the sense of the action (bhāva) and the agent (kartṛ)": here, by the mention of "intransitive" (akarmaka), those verbs whose objects are not intended to be expressed (avivakṣitakarmaka) are also included. Therefore, in the example "it is eaten by Devadatta," even though an object in the form of rice exists, because it is not intended to be expressed, the *l*-suffix indeed occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāve*), as stated elsewhere.
The detailed explanation: (3) *lasya* |3|4|77|.
Regarding *lasya*: the term *dhātoḥ* (of the root) is understood as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*). The vowel *a* is not intended to be significant (*na vivakṣita*). Therefore...
This also includes the *liṅ* and other [moods]. Furthermore, there is no over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *cūḍāla*.
(4) *tiptasjhisipthasthamibvasmastātāṃjhathādhvamiḍvahimahiṅ* | Pāṇini 3.4.78.
*tip*, *tas*, *jhi*, *sip*, *thas*, *tha*, *mip*, *vas*, *mas*;
*ta*, *ātām*, *jha*; *thās*, *āthām*, *dhvam*; *iṭ*, *vahi*, *mahiṅ*.
This is the singular nominative case of a collective dvandva compound. The word *lasya* is understood as being in the genitive case denoting the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).

From this, it is understood that [the suffixes] are substitutes. He states the result: "these. The absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) in forms beginning with *tas* and so on is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage. However, the addition of the indicatory letter *p* to *ti* and the other suffixes is for the purpose of preventing the application of the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), as in the case of *dveṣṭi* and similar forms. Regarding the examples thereof:
This will become clear.

(5) *laḥ parasmaipadam* | 1.4.99. *laḥ para-*: the term *la* here is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). The word *ādeśa* ("substitute") is to be supplied [from the previous sūtra]. Thus he says:
Regarding "lādeśāḥ":

(6) *taṅ-anāv ātmanepadam* | 1.4.100. *Taṅ-anau*: this is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *taṅ* and *āna*. It is a *pratyāhāra* [abbreviation], beginning with *ṭha* from *ṭhakāreṇa saha ākārasya grahaṇam* and ending with *ātām* from *ātām-sic-īṭ*.
The remainder [of the rule] is "starting from the word *ta* up to *mahiṅ*, including the letter *ṅ*. Thus he says:

"the nine beginning with *ta*. Here, the word *la* is understood from the previous sūtra. Consequently, by the mention of *āna*, only the suffixes *śānac* and *kānac* are included, and not [the suffixes used in the sense of] habit, age, or ability (*tācchīlya-vayovacana-śaktiṣu*).

The suffix *cānaś* is also prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.2.128], as is *cānaś*; however, because that [latter] lacks the status of being a substitute for *la*, the suffix *cānaś* is established even after roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings—as in examples such as *nighnānāḥ*. Thus he says: "and *śānac* and *cānac*. This refers to those technical designations (*saṃjñā*).

The meaning is that they are designated as *ātmanepada*. "The previous designation" means that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *parasmaipada*. Thus, the designation *parasmaipada* is restricted to the nine suffixes beginning with *tiP*. Now, in response to the inquiry "From which verbal root (*dhātu*) is *parasmaipada* used, and from which is *ātmanepada*? he says:
*Anudātaṅtiḥ*: *Anudāta* and *ṅ* [form] *anudātaṅ*; that which has these two as its final elements (*it*) is *anudātaṅt*.

From that—[we derive] *anudātaṅtiḥ*. The word *ic* (i.e., *iti*), being heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, is connected with each member individually; thus, it is understood as "that which ends in an *anudāteta* vowel and that which ends in *ṅ*."

In the rule "anunāsika it upadeśe," the term "upadeśe" (in the original enunciation) is carried over by *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) and is connected with "ṅti," but not with "anudātet. This is because, outside of the context of the original enunciation, there is no possibility of an unaccented vowel being subject to the technical designation *it*, and thus there is no deviation [from this restriction]. [The rule] "bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ" (roots begin with bhū and so on).

Therefore, by the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkapluti) method, the term *dhātavaḥ* (roots), which is understood from the previous rule, is transformed into the ablative case (*dhātoḥ*) and qualifies *anudātet* (having an anudātta vowel). In that context, since there is no purpose for a *tadantavidhi* (specification of what ends in that) regarding the portion concerning the anudātta vowel, a *tadantavidhi* applies only to the portion concerning the *ṅit*. Thus he says:

By the rule beginning with *anudāteta* [Pāṇini 1.3.12], etc. "In the place of *la*"—this is obtained through the mention of *ātmanepada*, because there is a restrictive rule that *tiṅ* suffixes are substitutes for *l*. Why "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*)? Consider *cukuṭiṣati*.
Here, the *ṅ*-ness of the *san* suffix is merely derived by extension (*ātideśika*) from the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.2.1].

[The suffix] *ṇat* is not taught as an upadeśa [vowel-lengthening]. Why [is the word "dhātoḥ" mentioned]? Consider *adudruvat*. Here, by the rule *ṇiśri*, the ātmanepada ending does not occur after a stem ending in *caṅ*. If there were no provision for a rule to apply to that which ends in such [a suffix], then in forms like *bobhūyate*, the ātmanepada would not occur after a stem designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*) by the rule *sanādyantāḥ*, because it ends in *yaṅ*.

If one were to state only "ṭhṅti," then even though the affix *yaṅ* would have the marker *ṅ*, the ātmanepada would not occur because the verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in that affix would lack the marker *ṅ*.
(7) Pāṇini 1.3.72: A verb with a svarita accent or the marker *ñ* takes the ātmanepada when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.

*Svaritañitaḥ*: *Svarita* and *ñ* are *svaritañau*; the term is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that [root] which has these two as its *it*. The word *ic* (the vowel *i*) is connected with each [member]. Thus he says: "from that which has a *svarita* *it* and from that which has a *ñ* *it*. After the word *dhātoḥ* ("from the root"), the phrase "in place of *la*" (*lasya sthāne*) is to be supplied.

The term *kartrabhiprāyam* means "it goes toward the agent" (*kartr-abhi-praiti gacchati*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root denoting an object (*karmaṇi aṇ*). Thus it says: "residing in the agent. And so, in such cases as "the *hotṛ* priest performs the sacrifice with the *yājyā*," since the fruit of the sacrifice—namely, heaven—resides in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), [the action is considered to benefit the agent].

Because the result does not accrue to the agent (*hotṛ*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not used. Similarly, in the case of "Devadatta, hired by Yajñadatta for wages, cooks," the middle voice is not used because the fruit of the cooking—namely, eating—does not accrue to the cook. Furthermore, the acquisition of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth is not considered the [primary] fruit [of the action].

Because it is intended here that the term "result of action" (*kriyāphala*) refers precisely to that purpose for which activity proceeds, whether according to worldly convention or the Veda; thus, the meaning is:
"of a verbal root denoting an action whose result accrues to the agent. As for the *ātmanepada* [suffix], however...
It suffices to say that [the suffix] indicates that the fruit of the verbal root's meaning accrues to the agent.
(8) *śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam* | 1|3|78|.
From the remainder, when the agent is expressed, the *parasmaipada* suffixes are used. [This applies] by the rules *anudāttaṅtiḥ* and *svaritajitaḥ*.
The "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is that which is other than the domain of the previously mentioned *ātmanepada*.

Thus it is said: "from that which is devoid of the causes for *ātmanepada*. By this, the *parasmaipada* endings for the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) are established. Among the nine endings beginning with *tiP*, they apply either simultaneously or alternatively.
Having intended to state the rule of distribution—namely, "when *yuṣmad* is the co-referential upapada, even if it is not present [as a word], the middle [person] is used;

when *asmad* is [the upapada], the highest [person]; and in the remaining cases, the first person"—he first states the technical designations for the first person and so on: "The *tiṅ* [suffixes] are three by threes."
(9) *tiṅstrīṇi trīṇi prathamamadhyamottamāḥ* |1|4|101|.

There are six sets of three within the *tiṅ* [terminations], yet there are only three designations (*saṃjñā*). Since a one-to-one correspondence is thus impossible, and because each set of three would otherwise apply all three designations, [the author] says: "*tiṅ* [applies] to both types of words" [referring to the rule for *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada*].

From the rule "ṭhlaḥ parasmaipadam," the term *parasmaipada* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*), and from the rule "taṅānāvātmanepadam," the term *ātmanepada* is likewise carried over; these are then transformed into the genitive case. Consequently, there are three triplets for each of both the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* sets.

The sense is that the designations "first" (*prathama*) and so forth apply according to their respective order. It should be understood, however, that the designation "person" (*puruṣa*) regarding the first person and the others is established by the treatises of the ancient teachers.
(10) *Tāny ekavacana-dvivacana-bahuvacanāny ekaśaḥ* 1.4.102. [These are called] singular, dual, and plural respectively.]
Now, when among the first and subsequent persons— each person consisting of a triad of suffixes—
one suffix at a time is reached either simultaneously or successively,
[the rules] "for two or one, the dual and singular" and "in the plural, the plural" [apply].

He states the technical designations, such as "singular" and so forth, for the purpose of formal arrangement: "Those [are] each one. By the word *tat* (those), the three sets of three verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) called first, middle, and last, which were introduced in the preceding sūtra, are referred to. He says this: "having acquired the designations 'first' and so forth. Regarding the term *ekaśas*:
The commentary says: "Each one" (*pratyekam*). The intention is that the suffix *śas* is applied by the rule *saṅkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām*.

(11) When *yuṣmad* is the co-occurring word (*upapada*), being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the second person ending (*madhyama*) is used, even when [the pronoun] is not present (*sthānini*). 1.4.105.

*Upapada*: A word uttered in proximity to *yuṣmad*. The meaning is: when *yuṣmad* is uttered in proximity. The analysis of the compound is: that which has a common (*samāna*)—that is, one—substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) as its expressed meaning. And this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is intended with respect to the *lakāra* (tense/mood marker) which serves as the substitute for *yuṣmad* and the *tiṅ* (verbal suffix).

Because of the recurrence [of the word] from the rule "ṭhlaḥ parasmaipadam," he states the resulting conclusion: "in *yuṣmad* which denotes a case-role (*kāraka*) expressed by a *tiṅ*. A "substitute" (*sthānin*) is that which has a "position" (*sthāna*), meaning an occasion (*prasaṅga*); thus, it means "when there is an occasion. And this occasion is...
When that meaning is understood, there is simply no employment of the substitute form.

Thus, by the word "sthānini" (in the place of), the sense results in: "while [the original] conveys its own meaning without the employment of the *yuṣmad* used as an adjunct. He states this with the words "not being employed" (*aprayujyamāne*).
If the term "ṭhsthāninī" (occurring as a substitute) were not stated, the second person would apply only when *yuṣmad* is actually employed as an upapada;
consequently, there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "rāma pāhi" (O Rāma, protect). He states what is obtained by the word "api" (also):
"even when employed. If it were stated merely as "when *yuṣmad* occurs as an upapada, [provided it is] a substitute,"...

The intention [of the rule] is that because the second person would not occur in examples such as *rāma tvaṃ pāhi* ("O Rāma, protect yourself") when the word *yuṣmad* is used, the term "also" (*api*) is included. However, in the case of *atvaṃ tvaṃ saṃpadyate* ("he who was not you becomes you"), the second person is not used, because there the word *yuṣmad* is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*). This is also the case in examples such as *bhavān āgacchati* ("Your Honor is coming").

However, when used in conjunction with the word *bhavat*, the second person is not employed; for while the word *yuṣmad* has as its sole domain that which is being addressed, the word *bhavat* by its very nature is common to both those who are being addressed and those who are not— so much for this.

(12) *prahāse ca manyopapade manyateruttama ekavacca* 1.4.106. Regarding *prahāse ca*: this sūtra consists of two sentences. The first sentence is *prahāse ca manyopapade*. The term *madhyama* (the second person) is understood from the previous rule. The verbal root *man*, belonging to the *śyan*-class (*divādigaṇa*), is the *upapada* (governing word).

The term *yasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the force of hearing the word "another" (*anya*) as a separate member of the compound, the qualifier "in the case of a verbal root" (*dhātau*) is obtained.
Thus he says: "the verbal root meaning 'to think' (*manya-dhātu*), etc. Regarding the phrase "while that [root] is the base form" (*tasmin prakṛtibhūte sati*), the meaning is:
"in place of the *la*-suffixes of that verbal root. "The middle [person] should be used" refers to the rule: "when *asmat* is the co-occurring word (*upapada*)."

The remainder [of the rule applies]. This is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the subsequent sūtra, *asmadyuttamam*. And thus, this prescription for the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the highest person (*uttama-puruṣa*). The second sentence is: "In the case of the root *man*, the highest person is used and it is treated as singular. He explains that: "But in the case of *man*, the highest person should be used."
The phrase "when *yuṣmad* is an upapada" is the remainder [of the rule], because it is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding sūtra. Regarding "and that":
"that" refers to the middle and the highest persons; the meaning is that even when there is duality or plurality, the singular number is obtained.
This is for the purpose of reversing the order of the middle and highest persons. All of this will be illustrated immediately below in the examples.
It will become clear [later].

(13) *asmadyautamaḥ* | 1|4|107|. Regarding *asmadyautamaḥ*: "in such a state" means when that which is expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)—namely, the grammatical participant (*kāraka*)—is not being explicitly employed.
And the meaning is "while being employed.
(14) *śeṣe prathamaḥ* | 1.4.108. *Śeṣe*: that which is other than the domains of the middle and the first person already mentioned is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Thus he says: "It is not within the scope of the middle and the highest [persons]. However, in the case of "you and I cook" (*tvamahaṃ ca pacāvaḥ*), because of its higher status, only the highest person (*uttama-puruṣa*) is used, and not the middle person (*madhyama*). Furthermore, in "Devadatta and you two cook" (*devadattastvaṃ ca pacathaḥ*), the first person (*prathama-puruṣa*) is also not used; this is because the presence of *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun) precludes the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Enough of this.

The root *bhū* is used in the sense of "being. The word "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the meaning. This is the first root in the *bhvādi* class. In that class, the reading in the list is simply *bhū*; however, it will be explained that the specification of the meaning is a modern addition. Although "being" (*satā*) is a genus (*jāti*) and not an action (*kriyā*), nevertheless, it refers to self-maintenance (*ātmadhāraṇa*).
"It is called 'sat' (being)," which means "abiding in its own nature. Regarding the phrase "when there is a desire to express the agent":

from the root *bhū* (to be), which denotes the existence of the present, when used in the active voice (*kartari*) with the present tense suffix (*laṭ*), and because it lacks the conditions for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the parasmaipada endings—namely the nine beginning with *tiP*—are applied; even within that [set],...

The meaning is that because there is no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the second and first persons, we are in the three forms of the first person; even there, when the singular number of the agent is intended, the suffix *tip* occurs, and once *bhū-ti* has been established, the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) will be explained.

(15) *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam* || P. 3.4.113. Intending to explain the grammatical operations pertaining to the *sārvadhātuka* [suffixes], he states the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*: *tiṅśit*. The term *dhātoḥ* (after a verbal root) is understood [from the previous rule]. He explains this by saying: "those mentioned under the heading of 'verbal root' (*dhātu-adhikāra*). By this [rule],...
In the word *ṭhharīn*, the suffix *śas* does not possess the status of a *sārvadhātuka* affix; otherwise, by the rule *tiṅ-śit sārvadhātukam*, *śas* would be a *sārvadhātuka*,
and by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, it would be marked with *ṅ*, which would result in the *guṇa* substitution [of *i* for *e*] according to the rule *gher ṅti*.
It may be so.
(16) *kartari śap* | Pāṇini 3.1.68. Regarding *kartari śap*: from the rule *sārvadhātuke yaK*, the term *sārvadhātuke* is understood to carry over [by anuvṛtti].

From the rule *dhātor ekāco halādeḥ*, [the word] "from the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood. Thus he says: "for the sake of the agent," and so forth. The designation *vikaraṇa* (verbal suffix) for affixes such as *śap* and others, which are prescribed after roots ending in *tiṅ* (conjugational endings), is established by the ancient masters. [The phrase] *śapāvitau* refers to the phonemes *ś* and *p*.

The meaning is that [the terms] *ṭh* and *hal* are technical designations (*saṃjñaka*) according to the rules "ṭhlaśakvataddhite" and "halantya". Consequently, when the *ś* and *k* of *śap* are elided, only the letter *a* remains; this is the meaning. (17) *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.84.

When *bhū* + *ati* is established, by the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) "guṇa and vṛddhi [substitutes] take the place of [the final vowel of] a stem ending in an *ik* (short *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*) when followed by an *ārdhadhātuka* or *sārvadhātuka* suffix," the term *ika* is brought into play.

This qualifies the governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem). The rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. From the rule "guṇa [is substituted] for *mid*" (*miderguṇa*), the word *guṇa* is carried forward as an anuvṛtti.

He says this with the words "of these two," and so forth. Thus, the *guṇa* substitute for the vowel *ū* is *o*. Regarding the term "the substitution of *ava*," the remainder is that it applies to the vowel *o*. And so he states the fully established form:
"bhavati" (he is) and "bhavataḥ" (they two are). When there is a desire to express duality of the agent, the root *bhū* takes the suffix *laṭ*, and [subsequently] the replacement of *tas*.
In the *kṛt* [affixes]—*jho'ntaḥ*.
(18) *jho'ntaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.3. The analysis is *jhaḥ antaḥ*. The term *jha* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). The letter *a* in the substitute [is for the sake of] the following *takāra*.

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation. From the rule *ṭhāyaneyī*, the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) is carried over, but not the term "beginning with" (*ādi*) either, because it is unaccented (*asvarita*). And the carried-over term "affix" is understood to be in the genitive case denoting a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus he says: "of the constituent part of the affix."

"Of *jha*" means "of the phoneme *jh*. "There shall be an *anta*-substitute" means that this substitute *anta* shall apply. [The question is: Why specify "of a portion of an affix"? [Consider the example: *ujjhitā*. Here, the substitution does not apply to the *jh* which is a portion of the verbal root (*dhātu*). However, if the term *ādi* ("beginning") were continued [from the previous rule], then [the form] *śayāntaiḥ* would not be established.

It is established [that the substitution occurs] because, as is clear in the Bhāṣya, before the substitution of *ant* for the final letter (*anta-deśa*) takes place, the augment *āṭ* is applied to the *leṭ* by the rule *leṭo 'ḍāṭau*; consequently, the letter *jha* lacks the status of being the initial element of an affix (*pratyayādi*). Thus, in the case of *bhava-jhī*, when *ant* is substituted for *jha*, we arrive at the form *bhava-anti*; then, by the rule *ato guṇe*, [the substitution of *guṇa* applies].

The meaning is that when *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent vowel) has been applied as an exception to *savarṇadīrgha* (the long vowel substitute for two homogeneous vowels), the form is *bhavanti*. However, the pronunciation of the first vowel *a* in the rule for the final substitution (*anta-ādeśa*) is for the purpose of hearing the vowel *a* in forms such as *dviṣanti*, where the *vikaraṇa* suffix is elided (*luk*). As for *bhavasi*, this is in the second person singular.

The form *bhavatha* [is derived] from the second person dual *thas*, after the application of *śap*, the substitution of *guṇa*, and the substitution of *ava*; then, following the rules for *rutva* and *visarga*, the form is established. By the rule "na vibhaktau tusmāḥ," the *s* is not replaced by *it*. The form *bhavatha* [is derived] from the second person plural *thā* [suffix].
The form [is derived] by applying the *guṇa* substitution and the *ava* replacement in the case of the *śap* suffix.

(19) *ato dīrgho yañi* | Pāṇini 7.3.101. Even in the singular of the first person (*uttamapuruṣaikavacana*), when the *śap* suffix has been applied, the *guṇa* substitution made, and the *ava* replacement effected, the form *bhavami* stands; then, by [the rule] *ataḥ*... [the long vowel is substituted].

The term *dīrgha* (long vowel) qualifies what is governed by the rule *yañi ṭhaṅgasya*; this is a *tadantavidhi* (a rule concerning that which ends in such). From the rule *turustuśamyamaḥ*, the term *sārvadhātuke* (in a sārvadhātuka affix) is carried over and qualified by *yañ*;
this is a *tadādividhi* (a rule concerning that which begins with such). Thus he says: "of that which ends in *a*" and so forth. [In the form] *bhavāmi*, and not...
It must be stated that with respect to the *l*-substitute prescribed after the root *bhū*, the root *bhū* alone is the *aṅga* (base), and not *bhava* ending in the *vikaraṇa* suffix;

for by the inclusion of the term "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) in the rule "that which begins with [the element] from which the suffix is prescribed is the *aṅga* with respect to that suffix," the base is understood to include even that which is qualified by the *vikaraṇa*.

Because they are *aṅga*s (bases): *bhavāvaḥ* and *bhavāmaḥ*. [The forms are derived as follows: for the *laṭ* suffixes *vas* and *mas*, with the addition of the *śap* augment, the substitution of *guṇa*, the replacement of *o* by *av*, the lengthening of the vowel following *at*, and the application of *rutva* and *visarga*, the resulting forms are [bhavāvaḥ and bhavāmaḥ]. By the rule "not before a case-ending" (*na vibhaktau*), the *s* is not replaced by *it*. Now, having stated the arrangement of the first, middle, and last persons:
He says "sa bhavati" etc. in order to remind [the reader]. He provides an example for the rule *atha prahāse ca* ("and when used in jest"):

*ehi*. This sentence was uttered as a joke toward a son-in-law who had arrived to eat after everyone else had already finished eating: "O son-in-law! *ehi u*—come! (where *u* is an emphatic particle).
The meaning is that you think, "I shall eat the rice," but this is not logical. Why? To this he says:

"That has been eaten by the guests. This means that the rice was requested as alms by the guests. Here, although the first person would have been expected for the root *bhuj* (to eat), the second person is used; whereas for the root *man* (to think), the second person is indeed appropriate.

When the *uttama* (first person) is reached, [the forms are] *etam eta* and *ceti*. The meaning is: "O two sons-in-law! Come, let us two eat rice"—thus you two think; and "O sons-in-law! We shall eat rice"—thus you [plural] think. In both these cases, the *uttama* (first person) of the root *bhuj* (to eat) is employed.

When the middle [person] is applicable, the middle [suffix] is used; but when the middle is applicable, the highest [person] is used. He explains the use of the singular for both duality and plurality with the words "manyase" and so forth. The phrase "it continues" refers to the rule "prahāse ca" (Pāṇini 1.4.106); this is the remainder [of the explanation]. The example is "etu bhavān."
The sense is that it has just been stated that there is no synonymy between *yuṣmad* and *bhavat*.
Thus ends the section on the formation of the present tense (*laṭ*).
(20) "The *liṭ* [affixes] are used for the remote past. (Pāṇini 3.2.115).

The *liṭ* [affix] is used for the remote past (*parokṣa*). From the rule "the *laṅ* [is used] for what is not of today" (*anadyatane laṅ*), the term "not of today" (*anadyatana*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti. "In the past" (*bhūte*) is the governing heading. Remoteness (*parokṣatva*) is a qualification of the meaning of the verbal root; this is what he expresses with the words "past not of today," etc. [This refers to] the final watch of the past night.

In Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *luṅ* sūtra, it is established that "the present day" (*adyatana*) consists of the current day together with the first watch (*yāma*) of the coming night. Regarding "remoteness from the speaker's perception" (*parokṣatva*), some maintain it is the state of having occurred a hundred years ago;
others, that it is the state of having occurred a thousand years ago; and still others, that it is the state of having occurred two or three days ago.
Others say it is the state of being separated by three days; still others say it is being obstructed by a wall, a mat, or the like.

These positions are established in the Bhāṣya. Among them, however, it is universally agreed that "remoteness" (parokṣatva) consists simply in the fact that [the action] is beyond the range of the speaker's senses; so, enough of this. Regarding the rule *lasya tibādayaḥ*: the meaning is the group of nine beginning with *tiP*.
(21) *liṭ ca* | 3.4.115 | *liṭ ca*. Here, *liṭ* is a term with its sixth case ending elided (*lupta-sthāna-ṣaṣṭhyanta*).
From the rule *tiṅ-śit sārvadhātukam*, the word *tiṅ* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). [The term *ārdhadhātukam* is also understood.]
Regarding the word "śeṣa" (the remainder), [it refers to] that which is an *ārdhadhātuka*. Thus he says: "The substitutes for *liṅ* are *tiṅ*.
Since they fall outside the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for a single designation, there arises the possibility of their being included under the designation *sārvadhātuka* as well;
therefore he says: "They have the designation *ārdhadhātuka* alone. [This is established by the rule] "The *laṅ* [is used] only according to Śākaṭāyana."

The intention is that this follows from the restrictive particle *eva* in the sūtra itself. By the word "tena" (by that), the meaning is that because [the affixes] lack the status of being *sārvadhātuka*, the suffixes *śap*, *śyan*, and so forth, which are conditioned by that status, do not occur.
(22) *parasmaipadānāṃ ṇalatususthalathusaṇalvamāḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.82.
Intending that the word *liṭaḥ* (of the *liṭ* [perfect]) is carried over from the rule *liṭas tajhayoḥ*, he says:

"of the *ti* and other [suffixes] of the *liṭ*. Regarding "ṇal etc.": the meaning is that these nine—namely *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*; *thal*, *athus*, *a*; *ṇal*, *va*, *ma*—should be substituted respectively for the *parasmaipada* suffixes. Among those, for *tip*...

The substitute *ṇal* is a replacement for the whole [stem]. Nor should it be argued that because the letters *ṇ* and *l* possess the designation *it*—by virtue of the rules "ṭhcuṭū" and "halantya"—they are elided, and thus how can there be the status of being "multiliteral" (*anekāl*)?
This is because, prior to the application of the whole-stem substitute *ṇal*, the element lacks the status of an affix (*pratyaya*), and consequently the rule "ṭhcuṭū" does not apply.

In forms such as *juhāva*, the suffixal marker *ṇit* is for the purpose of [triggering] *vṛddhi*; the marker *lit* is for the purpose of the accent (*litsvara*). Now, one might object: since the vowel *a* is prescribed for the *tha* of the second person plural, by the rule "the substitute replaces the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*), it would apply to something else [than the whole ending]. However, the prescription of the vowel *a* for the [suffixal] *a* is...

If it is argued that [the rule] is for the purpose of establishing a numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyā*), that is true; however, it is clear in the *Bhāṣya* that because of the mention in the sūtra "after two *a*s, [there is] *ṭha*" in its full form (*parūpeṇa*), the substitute is a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) due to having more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). Nor [can it be argued that] because substitutes such as *atus* and so on lack the status of being case-endings (*vibhakti*) prior to their substitution, [the prohibition] "not... [does not apply].
It should not be argued that the substitution of *i* for the *s* is unavoidable because there is no prohibition against it being "divided" (*vibhakta*);

for, since the *s* at the end of the word following the initial *s* has been elided by the rule of *saṃyogāntalopa*, the [initial] *s* lacks the status of being the final letter (*antyatva*) in its original instruction (*upadeśa*). Thus, enough of this.

(23) *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.88. [The suffix] *vuk* is added after the root *bhū*. [The condition] "before a vowel" (*aci*) applies; the intention is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *aci śnu-dhātu-bhruvām yvoḥ iyaṅ-uvaṅau* from the preceding sūtra. Why does it say "before a vowel"? Consider the form *abhūt*. [Objection: But surely, in the case of the suffix *ṇal*, since it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it would override *vuk* and [apply the rule] *aco ñṇiti*...
[The rule] "ñṇiti" would require *vṛddhi*, whereas in the case of *babhūvitha*, [the rule] "sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ" would require *guṇa*; therefore, he says:
"because it is obligatory (*nityatvāt*). Even when [the suffixes] have already been applied...

The suffix *vuñ* applies by virtue of the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) even when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have not yet occurred; it applies even before they have taken place. Consequently, according to the maxim that "a rule which applies both when [the condition] has been performed and when it has not been performed is *nitya*," *vuñ*—being *nitya*—sublates *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. [In the suffix *vuñ*,] the letter *ka*...
The letter *u* [in *kit*] is for the purpose of pronunciation; due to its *kit* status, it is an internal constituent [of the suffix]. (24) *ekāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1).
When the form *bhū-v* is established, [the rule] *ekācaḥ* applies. This is under the governing authority (*adhikṛtya*) of *ajādeḥ*, as stated at the beginning of the sixth chapter.

The meaning is that these two [rules] are merely explanatory (*sūtraka*) and not prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*), because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); rather, they simply continue to apply from the rule "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *ṣṭhiv*, *kṣvi*, and *aṅ*" onwards.
(25) P. 6.1.8: "In the case of the *liṭ* [affix], [the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs] for a non-reduplicated verbal root."

In the context of the *liṭ* [affix], the rule "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood from the governing rule "the first [syllable] of that which has only one vowel is reduplicated" (*ekāco dve prathamasya*).

The term "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus he says: "of a constituent part of the root. Both "that which has only one vowel" (*ekācaḥ*) and "of the first" (*prathamasya*) are qualifiers of the constituent part of the root. [The compound] "that which has one vowel" (*eko'c yasya*)...

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of its members are understood as applying to the whole. Thus, the meaning is that when the *liṭ* suffix follows, there are two utterances of the first part of the verbal root consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*), provided it is distinct from the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). However, if one were to rely on a *karmadhāraya* interpretation for the term "single-vowel" (*ekāc*) in this rule, then forms such as *papāca* would not be accounted for.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya: "it should be established. The phrase "of the second [element] beginning with a vowel" (aj-ādeḥ dvitīyasya) is also governed [by this rule].
In that context, *ajādiḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both a vowel (*ac*) and the beginning (*ādi*)," and from this, the ablative case is used. Thus he says:
"of the second [element] following the initial vowel. The word "having a single vowel" (*ekāc*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the governing rule].

The meaning is that if reduplication occurs for a single-vowel (ekāc) element of a verbal root beginning with a vowel, then reduplication applies only to the second single vowel and not to the first. Here, by supplying the word "pronunciation" (*uccāraṇe*) after the word "two" (*dve*),
and by relying on a genitive case based on its connection to a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛdyogalakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of "of the first single vowel," there is a double usage.

It is explained in detail in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra that only this [substitution] is prescribed here, and not the view of substitution (ādeśapakṣa) based on a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* as well, only the view of double usage (*dviḥprayogapakṣa*) is stated. That has not been written here for fear of prolixity. [This applies to forms such as] *papāca*, *iyāya*, and so forth.

The status of being "first" (prathamatva) and having a single vowel (ekāctva) should be understood by means of the principle of "designation as if possessed" (vyapadeśivadbhāva). However, if one resorts to interpreting *ajādeḥ* as a bahuvrīhi compound, then in forms such as *indrīyati* (from *indram ātmana icchati*) and *indidrīyiṣati* (from *indrīyitum icchati*), the letter *d* [would not be elided] by the rule *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*.

And there would be a prohibition of doubling; for in that case, the phrase "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādeḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Why [is the word] *dhātoḥ* ("of a root") stated?

For in its absence, the meaning would be: "when *liṭ* follows, there is doubling of that which is the first monosyllable (*ekāc*). If this were so, doubling would occur only in cases such as *papāca*, but not in cases such as *jajāgāra*, as stated in the Bhāṣya.

This is clear. Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *papāca*, once reduplication has been applied by the rule *liṭi dhātor anabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), reduplication cannot apply again according to the maxim *lakṣye lakṣaṇasya sakṛtpravṛttiḥ* (a grammatical rule applies only once to its subject), and thus the mention of *anabhyāsa* (non-reduplicated) is redundant; for [reduplication] would indeed apply from a *yaṅ*-derived stem by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9).
Furthermore, because [the reduplication] is characterized by a reduplication caused by the suffix *san*, in order to prevent the reduplication caused by *san* from applying again,

and because when a *ṇic* is added to a stem ending in *san*— which has already undergone reduplication according to the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*— and the *luṅ* (aorist) affix is applied, the rule *caṅi* would otherwise cause reduplication once more; therefore, the mention of "non-reduplicated" (*anabhyāsa*) is necessary in the Bhāṣya.

But—as in the case of *kṛṣṇo nonāva vṛṣabho yadīdam* and so forth—after the root *nud* with the suffix *yaṅ*, which has undergone reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅeḥ*, and after the form *nonūya* derived from that [root] followed by *liṭ*, there is no application of *ām* because of the exclusion of mantras by the rule *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi*; subsequently, by the rule *yasya halaḥ*, there is the elision of the *yakāra*. From that...

In the case of *nonāvā* (from *naunāv*), where there is the substitution of *vṛddhi* and *ā*, [the form arises] from the addition of *san* to a *yaṅ*-intensive base, and then *ṇic* to that *san*-intensive; however, as stated clearly in the *Śabdenduśekhara*, such a usage does not exist at all in common worldly speech—this is the intended meaning. And in the present instance, regarding *bhūv-a*, there are four monophthongic (*ekāc*) vowels.
In this context, "bhū" is the first [element], "ū" is the second, "ū"—

by virtue of being treated as if it were designated (vyapadeśivadbhāva)— is the third monosyllable (ekāc), and the aggregate "bhūv" is the fourth. Since the entire aggregate is to be reduplicated, all its constituent parts are likewise reduplicated.
It is clear from the Bhāṣya that the reduplication applies to the entire cluster "bhū" itself. Thus he says:

"When it stands as *bhūv bhūv a*. Here, it should be understood that by virtue of being treated as a single unit (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the portion "bhū" possesses both the status of being a one-syllable element (*ekāc*) and the status of being a part of the verbal root (*dhātvaṅgatva*), as well as the status of being the first member.

(26) *pūrvo 'bhyāsaḥ* |6|1|4|. [The word] *pūrvaḥ* [is used here]. "In this context" means in the section on doubling (*dvitva*) belonging to the sixth book, namely *ṭhekāco dve prathamasya* (P. 6.1.1). By this, there is no inclusion of the doubling prescribed by rules such as *sarvasya dve* (P. 8.1.1). Of what is the *pūrva*?
In response to this inquiry, the word "dve" (two), which is carried over from the previous rule, is connected here by being transformed into the genitive case.
Thus he says: "of those two which have been prescribed. (27) *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.60.

*Halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*. Here, from the rule *lopo 'bhyāsasya*, the word *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplicated syllable) is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). That which remains is called *śeṣa*; it is derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The root *śiṣ* denotes remaining after the exclusion of others. Thus he says:

By the words "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*) and so forth; "there is elision of *v*" (*valopaḥ*). This means that in the form *bhūv-bhūv*, there is elision of the *v* of the reduplicated syllable.

When *bhū bhūv a* is established—[the rule] *hrasvaḥ* [applies]. From the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya*, the word *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplicated syllable) is carried over (*anuvartate*). Because of the hearing of the short vowel, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *acaḥ* (of a vowel) is supplied by the rule *acaśca*. Thus he says: "of the vowel of the reduplicated syllable. [The result is] *bhu bhūv a*.

Thus it is established. Although this is already accomplished by the rule for the insertion of *a* which will be stated later as "for the root *bhū*," nevertheless, this [present rule] is necessarily introduced right here because it is more appropriate for the sake of forms such as *lulāva*.

(29) *bhavateraḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.73. The analysis of *bhavateraḥ* is *bhavateḥ-a*. The mention of *bhavateḥ* refers to the verbal root *bhū*; this is because of the rule stating that "the suffixes *ik*, *śtip*, and others are used for the mention of a verbal root. Here...

From the rule *lopo'bhyāsasya*, the term *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplicated syllable) is understood as a governing reference (*anuvartate*). From the rule *vyatho liṭi*, the term *liṭi* (in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense) is understood. When the letter *a* occurs for the reduplicated syllable of the root *bhū*, it applies to the final letter *u* according to the rule *alo'ntyasya* (the substitution applies to the final letter). Thus he says: "of the *u* of the reduplicated syllable."

However, the rule "in the case of a meaningless [element], the operation applies to the final [sound]" does not apply here, because it is stated that "[this applies] except in the case of a modification of a reduplicated syllable. (30) *abhyāse carcā* 8.4.54.
When *bhabhūva* is established, the rule *abhyāse carcā* applies.

From the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the term *jhalām* is understood by anuvṛtti (carrying over). By the word *ca*, *jaś* is conjoined [with *carcā*]. Thus he says: "In the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), of the *jhal*s," and so forth. There are twenty-four *jhal* sounds; among them, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* are *śaraḥ*.

Regarding their substitution in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), it will be stated that "the *khay* sounds [are replaced] by those preceded by *śar*" (*śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*). However, for the letter *ha*, it will be stated in the reduplicated syllable that there is *cutva* (substitution by a *c-ṭ-u* sound) according to the rule "for *ku* and *hu*, [there is] *cu*" (*kuhoścuḥ*). Thus, among the *jhal* consonants, twenty *jhay* sounds are found here as substituends (*sthānin*) within the reduplicated syllable. Among these, which one is the substitute (*car*)?

In response to the doubt as to what constitutes *jaś*, he says: "The *jaś* [substitutes] for the *jhaś*. The third and fourth letters of the [five] classes (*varga*) are the *jhaś*. Their *jaś* substitutes are *ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da*; this is the meaning. It should also be understood that whatever class the original sounds (*sthānin*) belong to, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) belong to that same class. Regarding "the *car* for the *khay*"—[this refers to] the classes...

The first and second *kha*-series [consonants]; the meaning is that for these, the substitutes belong to the *ca-ṭa-ta-pa* series. Here too, it should be understood that whatever series the substituends (*sthānin*) belong to, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) belong to that same series. Regarding the phrase "there too": even among those series, by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*), they exist as *jaś* sounds by their own inherent character (*svabhāvena*).

The meaning is that those belonging to various classes (*varga*) which exist as *jaś* by their very nature (*svabhāva*) should be the substitutes; likewise, those belonging to various classes which exist as *car* by their very nature (*prakṛti*) or essence (*svabhāva*) should be the substitutes. The intention is that the application of grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa-pravṛtti*) is like a rain-cloud (*parjanya*). Why is this so?

To establish this, he says: "on account of internal similarity. There is a similarity in the effort (*prayatna*) of *ghoṣa*, *saṃvāra*, and *nāda* between the *jhaś* sounds and the *jaś* sounds; there is a similarity in the effort of *śvāsa*, *aghoṣa*, and *vivāra* between the *khay* sounds and the *car* sounds. Therefore, the substitutes (*ādeśa*) for each respective class of sounds are those belonging to that same class.
In this case, however, it should be understood that identity of position (*sthānasāmya*) is the restrictive factor. (31) *asiddham adatrā bhāt* | P. 6.4.22.
Thus, in the present instance, when the letter *b* is the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the form *babhūva* having been established, [the rule] applies before an *ac*.

He speaks to raise the doubt regarding the substitution of *uvaṅ* by the rule *anudhātu-*: "In this [section], it is as if unestablished. This sūtra is read in the fourth quarter of the sixth book (*pāda*) prior to the sūtra *śnānnalopaḥ*.

The particle *ā* in *ā bhāt* is used in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). The meaning is that it extends up to and including the governing heading (*adhikāra*) *bhasya*. And the heading *bhā*...

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [the rule applies] "until the end of the chapter" (*ā pādaparisamāpteḥ*). Thus, it is understood as "until the end of the chapter. The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) to be supplied is "an operation (*kārya*) prescribed [by this rule]. When there is an expectancy as to from where [it begins], because of its proximity, it is understood as "from this very sūtra onwards."

It is obtained. Consequently, from the rule "ṭhśnānnalopaḥ" (P. 6.4.23) up to the end of the *pāda*, whatever *ābhīya* operation is prescribed becomes as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*). The meaning is that even though it has taken effect, it remains as if it had not taken effect. This is an *adhikāra-sūtra* for what follows.

In rules such as *ṭhśnānnalopaḥ*, this [principle] applies to every individual sūtra. Thus, whatever is anuvṛtta (carried over) in a particular sūtra is understood to be *asiddha* (non-existent) when the specific operation (*ābhīya-kārya*) of that same sūtra is to be performed.
Consequently, an operation such as *ṭhśnānnalopaḥ* is *asiddha* with respect to another operation such as *ṭhśnānnalopaḥ*.

The meaning results in "when an operation is to be performed, it is as if it were not yet accomplished. By the word *atra*, which ends in the locative case denoting cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), one obtains the sense: "when an operation is to be performed that has as its cause that very thing which is the cause of the [other] operation becoming non-accomplished"; thus, it means "when an operation is to be performed upon a common locus."

All of this is established in the Bhāṣya. He states this with the words "from here onwards," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in that": the meaning is "when an operation dependent on that [subsequent rule] is to be performed. The examples are *edhi* and *śādhi*.

Here, in the case of *edhi*, there is the substitution of *e* for the root *as* by the rule *dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*; and in the case of *śādhi*, there is the substitution of *śā* for the root *śās* by the rule *śāhau*.

Because the absence of *ś* (the substitution of *ś* for *s*) is itself ābhīya and thus not established, the ābhīya rule "hu-jha-l-bhyaḥ her dhiḥ" applies to change *hi* into *dhi*. Similarly, forms such as *jaṅghahi* are also examples; this occurs when *sip* is replaced by *hi* after the root *han* in its yaṅluk form in the second person singular imperative.

Because the elision of *n* (nalopa), which is taught in the *Abhiya* section by the rule "anudāttopadeśa...", is considered *asiddha*, the *luṅ* substitution [of *hi* for *sip*] by the rule "ato heḥ" does not take place. Why is it said that they must have the same basis (*samānāśraya*)? Consider the form *papuṣaḥ*:

here, from the root *pā*, after the addition of *kvasu* following the *liṭ* suffix, there is reduplication by the rule "liṭi dhātoḥ," followed by the shortening of the vowel in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsahrasva*).
From a stem ending in *kvasu*, in the second case plural (*si*), there is the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *vasoḥ* according to the *ābhīya* rule.
When the elision of *ā* by the rule "elision of *āt* before *iṭ*" is to be applied, it is not considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purpose of the *ābhīya* operation.

This is because [the elision] has already been performed in the cases of *ciṇ* after *bhañj* and *ghan* after *rañj*, as per the rules "of *bhañj* in *ciṇ*" and "in *ghan* when denoting the action or the instrument."

Because the substitution of *nalopa* (the elision of the final *n*) is not considered *asiddha* when the *upadhā-vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening of the penultimate) is to be applied, which is not itself *ābhīya*. Why is the term *ābhāt* used with an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*)? If it were stated "prior to the section on *bhā*" (*bhādhikārāt prāk*), then in the case of *bhūyān*, the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu*—according to the rule "there is elision of *bahu* and *bhū* replaces *bahu*" (*bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ*)—would not be considered *asiddha*.

When the substitution of *orguṇa* is to be applied, there would be no status of being "asiddha" (not yet established), because it occurs after the rule *bhasya*. Enough of this. Thus, regarding the phrase "due to the asiddha-status of *vuk*":
since *vuk* is internal (*ābhīya*), when *uvaṅ*—governed by the rule *aci śnudhātu...*—is to be applied, [the former] is treated as asiddha.

The meaning is that when *uvaṅ* [substitution] for the vowel *ū* would have applied by virtue of the rule regarding the *guṇa* of a light penultimate syllable—as in *babhūva*—the present rule is intended.
The point is that the prescription of *vuk* serves its purpose as an exception (*bādhaka*) to both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the statement "the *vuk* and *yuṭ* [are substitutes] for *uvaṅ* and *yaṇ* respectively," there is a correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). As for *babhūva*, it is due to the suffix *ṇal*.

In forms such as *jagāda*, however, [the substitution of] *ṇit* is for the purpose of *vṛddhi*. In *babhūvatuḥ*, when *tas* is replaced by *atus*, the *vuk* augment and so forth are as before; the *s* undergoes *rutva* and then becomes a visarga.
In *babhūvuḥ*, when *ji* is replaced by *us*, the *vuk* augment and so forth are as before.
(32) *ārddhadhātukasyeḍÂvalādeḥ* 7.2.35: The augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant other than *y*.

When the form *sipasthali babhūtha* is established, the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeṭ* [Pāṇini 7.2.35] applies. Regarding this, it was rejected in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *neḍvaśi kṛti* [Pāṇini 7.2.8] that the mention of *iṭ* here is unnecessary, since the desired result is already achieved through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from that very rule. Why is the term *ārddhadhātukasya* used? [To exclude cases where the suffix is not ārdhadhātuka.]

He feels disgust (*jugupsati*). Here, because [the suffix] *san* is not prescribed under the governing rule "after roots beginning with *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*" (*guptijkidbhyaḥ*), it lacks the status of an *ārdhadhātuka*. Regarding *babhūvitha*: after the *sip* ending, there is the substitution of *thal*; with the augment *iṭ* applied to that, the *vuk* and other operations proceed as before. Regarding *babhūvathuḥ*: after the *thas* ending, there is the substitution of *athus*.

The *vuk* augment and so forth are as before. For the letter *s*, there is the substitution of *ru* and then *visarga*. Regarding *babhūva*: it has been stated in the rule *parasmaipadānāṃ ṇalatus* that the short vowel *a* is the substitute for the entire [stem] of the second person plural. The *vuk* augment and so forth are as before. Regarding *babhūva*: [this is derived from] *mip* in the presence of *ṇal*.

The *vuk* augment and so forth are as before. In *babhūviva*, when *vas* is replaced by *ādeśa*, the *iṭ* augment occurs because it begins with a consonant (*valāditvāt*); the *vuk* augment and so forth are as before. Nor should one suspect here a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment by the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogāder guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.5), because of the rule *kṛsṛbhṛvṛstudrusruśruvo liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.13).

Because the augment *iṭ* is established by the rule *krādiniyamāt*, [we have] *babhūvima*. When *mas* is replaced by *mā* and the augment *iṭ* is added, the *vuk* suffix and so forth are applied as before. Thus ends the procedure for the *liṭ* tense.
(33) *anadyatane luṭ* 3.3.15. [The suffix *luṭ* is used for the future not belonging to the current day.]

The suffix *luṭ* is used for the non-current future (*anadyatana*). The term "from the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood as a governing rule (*adhikṛta*). From the rule "in the sense of the future, [are used] *gami* and so forth," the word "future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is carried over (*anuvartate*). This "future" connects with the meaning of the verbal root as "non-current future. Thus he says: "in the sense of the non-current future. As for the word "non-current" (*anadyatana*), it appears in the rule "the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of the remote past" (*parokṣe liṅ*).
[The suffixes] have been explained. [The suffixes] *u* and *ṭ* are elided. The suffixes *tiP* and so forth apply after *luṭ*.
(34) *sya-tās-ī lṛ-luṭoḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.33. When *bhū-ti* is established, and *śap* is about to be applied by the rule *kartari śap*, [the following applies]: *sya-tās-ī lṛ-luṭoḥ*. And *sya-*...

*Tāsiśca* is the nominative dual from a *dvandva* compound. The vowel *i* in *tāsi* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). *Lṛluṭoḥ* is the locative dual from a *dvandva* of *lṛ* and *luṭ*. The mention [of *lṛ*] is because the form of *lṛ* is identical in both cases; this is the intended meaning. The term *dhātoḥ* (from a root) is supplied as a governing rule (*adhikṛta*).
Thus he says: "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*).
(35) *Ārdhadhātukaṃ śeṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.114. When *bhū-tās-ti* remains—[the rule] *ārdhadhātukaṃ śeṣaḥ* [applies].
The term *śeṣa* (remainder) refers to that which is other than the *tiṅ* and *śit* [pratyayas] mentioned in the preceding sūtra, "ṭh-i-ṅ-śi-t sārvadhātuka.

Thus he says: "other than *tiṅ* and *śit*. Regarding the word "vihita" (prescribed): the sense is that the governing rule "dhātoḥ" (after a root) is understood as qualifying "prescribed" (*vihita*). And thus, in cases such as *jugupsate*, etc., [the suffix is *sārvadhātuka*].

Since the suffixes such as *san* prescribed by rules beginning with "ṭhGuptijkidbhyaḥ" are not prescribed after the word "dhātoḥ" (the verbal root), they lack the status of being *ārddhadhātuka*; consequently, the augment *iṭ* does not occur.
[The phrase] "this should receive this designation" means that it should be designated as *ārddhadhātuka*. [The term] "*iṭ*" refers to the augment *iṭ*.
