The meaning is that, because the suffix *tā* is an *ārddhadhātuka* by virtue of the aforementioned sūtra, and because it is inherently preceded by a *val* sound, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule "an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a *val* sound takes the augment *iṭ*" (*ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*).
(36) Pāṇini 2.4.85: *luṭaḥ prathamasya ḍāraurasaḥ*.

When *bhū* + *itā* has been established, and after the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *u* with *av*, when *bhavitā* + *s* is established—[the rule] "of the first person of the *luṭ*" [is applied]. This is a compound (*dvandva*) consisting of *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*, in the nominative plural.
The term "*luṭaḥ*" is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is: "of the first-person substitute of the *luṭ*. [The application occurs] "in due order" (*kramāt*).

—[This is] obtained by "respective order" (*yathāsaṅkhya*). Now, one might object: "Since there are three first-person endings for the *parasmaipada* and three first-person endings for the *ātmanepada*, there are six substituends (*sthānin*), whereas the substitutes (*ādeśa*) are only three; how then can there be a correspondence by respective order? If this is asked, the answer is no, because [the substitutes] are formed as a *dvandva* compound of *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*.
This is because the *Bhāṣya* resolves the issue by resorting to the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) construction, namely "ḍā-raurasaś-ca ḍā-raurasaś-ca.

Furthermore, since the absence of *ḍā* (*ḍābhāva*) is a substitute (*ādeśa*), it lacks the status of an affix (*pratyaya*) prior to its application; consequently, the rule *cuṭū* does not apply, and thus [the elision] becomes a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). Once that [whole replacement] exists, it possesses the status of an affix, and thus the rule *cuṭū* applies.

It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the letter *ṭ* has the technical designation *it*. Thus, when the form *bhū-tās-ā* is established, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation—starting with the phrase "by virtue of the status of being *ḍit*. Even though the absence of *ḍā* (i.e., the suffix *tās*) is not included among the *svādi* group ending with the *kap* suffix, and therefore the designation *bha* would not apply when it follows, [the rule still operates] by the force of its *ḍit* nature.
The meaning is that, by the force of the designation *ḍit*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) according to Pāṇini 6.4.153 (*ṭeḥ*).
(37) [Pāṇini 7.3.86: *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*.
Thus, when *bhāv-i-t-ā* has been established, [the rule] *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* [applies]. [This follows] from the rule *midaco 'ntyātparaḥ* (1.1.47) and *mider guṇaḥ* (7.3.82).
The term *guṇa* is understood from the previous rule. The governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is taken here as a genitive denoting a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The phrase *pugantalaghūpadhasya* is its qualifier. That which has *pu* or *k* at its end is *puganta*; that which has a light (*laghu*) vowel as its penultimate (*upadhā*) is *laghūpadha*. Thus, [the compound means] "that which ends in *pu* or *k*, and that which has a light penultimate."

The genitive case [in *pugantalaghūpadhasya*] is derived from a collective dvandva compound. By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the *ṭhik* [element] [denotes] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*," the term "*ṭhik*" is understood as being in the locative case (indicating a position). Thus he says: "of that which ends in *pu*, etc.
[The phrase] "of the *iK* of the *aṅga*" means "of a constituent part of the *aṅga*. Examples include *dveṣṭi*, *dveṣṭa*, and so forth.
But surely, since the single consonant following that [vowel] which is a part of the *aṅga* intervenes, there is an absence of the condition "being followed by a sārvadhātuka suffix";

how then can *iko guṇaḥ* apply here? To this he says: *yena nāvyavadhānam*. By this, [it is meant] that by an intervening letter subsequent to the *sthānin*, there is no intervention for the cause that follows.

"Non-intervention" (nā'vyavadhānam) means that intervention is unavoidable; the meaning is that even when [the cause] is separated by such a phoneme, the grammatical operation conditioned by what follows still takes place. Why is this so? To this he says:
"On account of the authority of the statement. This refers to the application of the operation even when there is an intervention by such a phoneme.

The meaning is that the very commencement of the statement itself constitutes the authority. For the *guṇa* substitution is prescribed for an *ik* vowel that has a light penultimate (*laghūpadha*), and the status of being a penultimate belongs only to that which precedes the final consonant. Consequently, in the absence of a letter subsequent to the *ik*, there is an absence of the status of being a penultimate for that *ik*, and thus [the rule] applies to a base (*aṅga*) that has a light penultimate.
The sense is that the prescription of *guṇa* would otherwise be without scope; therefore, the intervention [of the augment] must be tolerated.

Now, one might object: if it is admitted that *guṇa* applies even to an *ik* that is intervened by [an augment], then in forms such as *bhinatti* and *chinatti*, *guṇa* would also apply to the vowel *i*. To this, he says: "by that" (*tena*).

The meaning is that this [rule] applies only when there is an unavoidable intervention. The intention is that since the status of being an *upadha* (penultimate) is possible by taking only the immediately following single phoneme, an intervention of multiple phonemes should not be taken into account.
"When *guṇa* is about to occur" refers to the stage where *bhavit* + *ā* has been established.

The meaning is: since the *ākāra* (the long *ā*) resulting from the substitution of *ḍā* is treated as *sthānivadbhāva*, it is considered a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; consequently, when this [suffix] follows, the rule for *guṇa* would apply to the vowel *i* which serves as the *upadhā* (penultimate) of the stem *bhavi*. However, [this does not happen] with respect to the *sārvadhātuka* suffix prescribed after the root *bhū*.
It must be stated that the root *bhū* alone is the *aṅga*, and not *bhavit* as qualified by the suffix (*vikaraṇa*);

for, according to the rule defining the technical term *aṅga*, the inclusion of the phrase "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) ensures that even that which is qualified by a suffix is considered an *aṅga*.
(38) *dīdhīvevīṭām* | Pāṇini 1.1.6. The terms *dīdhī*, *vevī*, and *iṭ*: *dīdhī* [is the root] ‘to shine’ and ‘to play’; *vevīṅ* [is the root] ‘to go’, having the same meaning as *veti*.
From the *dvandva* compound *dīdhīś ca vevīś ca iṭ ca*, the genitive case is used [by attraction]. [This is understood] from the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*.
Regarding the rule *guṇavṛddhī*, the word *na* is understood from the previous rule *na dhātulopa*.
(39) *tāsastyorlopaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.50. He says this: *tāsastyoḥ*. The word *si* is understood from the rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke*.

Because the suffix *pratyaya* implied by the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.62] is qualified by the word *sī*, the rule "in which there is an operation" (*yasminvidhiḥ*) applies as an *tadādividhi* (an operation that refers to what begins with that element).
This is what is meant by the statement "at the beginning of *sa*" (*sādau*). The same should be inferred for "at the beginning of *ra*" (*rādau*) and so forth.
(40) *ri ca* | 7.4.51 | [The suffix *si* is replaced by *ru* when it follows a verbal root ending in *r* or *ṛ*.]
"As before" means that there is elision (*lopa*) of the root *tās*. The root *as* is not connected here, because a suffix beginning with *ra* is impossible after it. (41) *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* 3.3.13.

*Lṛṭ śeṣe ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.13). Regarding the statement "the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are used] when one action is for the sake of another action" (*tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*), which was stated previously, he says "when it is otherwise" (*asatyām*) to indicate that "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to something other than that. He states the meaning of the word *ca* (and) as "truly" (*satyam*).
Haradatta, however, says: "Precisely because [the word *kriyārthāyām*] is not marked with a svarita accent, [it is understood to apply] only when one action is for the sake of another action."
[The opponent argues: "It does not follow [that the rule applies]. And thus, the phrase *śeṣe ca* (P. 3.3.16) would be easily dispensable. This is to be considered [with caution].

For in examples such as *śayiṣyata iti sthīyate*, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) being superseded by the *tumun* (infinitive suffix), because the rule regarding non-identity of forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply to *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and suffixes having the sense of *khal*. And here, the following is the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In the rule *ṭhpraiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca* ("The kṛtya suffixes are used in the senses of command, permission, and the arrival of the time [for an action]"), he will state later in the section on kṛt suffixes that "the prescription of kṛtyas is repeated so that they may not be superseded by the *loṭ* suffix. This too is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), though this is a separate point. As for what the ancients have illustrated with the example *bhaviṣyatīti vrajati* ("He goes because it will happen"):

That [objection] is merely superficial; for it is of no use in establishing that "the *lṛṭ* occurs even in the domain of the *tumun*, and the *lṛṭ* is not sublated by the *tumun*. Indeed, there is no possibility for the *tumun* to occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) in the case of the word "bhaviṣyati" (he will be), because that suffix occurs only in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Furthermore, it will be stated that [the rule governing the *tumun*] applies only when the agents are identical.
Even if the sūtra were formulated merely as "lṛṭ," the form "bhaviṣyati vrajati" would indeed be established; let that suffice for now. Regarding "sya iṭ":

when *tip* follows *lṛṭ*, the suffix *syat* is applied by the rule "syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ. Because this *syat* is an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*val*), the augment *iṭ* is added to it—this is the meaning.

The meaning is that the form *bhaviṣyati* arises as follows: after the suffix *syap*, with the augment *iṭ*, the *ū* undergoes *guṇa*, which is then replaced by *av*; since the *s* is part of the suffix, it becomes *ṣ*.
The forms *bhaviṣyataḥ* and so forth in the *tas*-beginning [case endings] should be understood in the same way. In *bhaviṣyāmi* and so forth, [the rule] "lengthening of *a*" (*ato dīrgho*) applies.
The substitution of *ya* is long [by Pāṇini 7.2.80]. Thus ends the section on the formation of the *lṛṭ* (future).

*loṭ ca*. [The suffix] *loṭ* [is used] in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), entreaty (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), and supplication (*prārthana*).

This [word "liṅ"] continues [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "in the sense of injunction and so forth. The words *vidhi* and so forth will be explained immediately below in the rule concerning the suffix *liṅ*.
(43) *Āśiṣi liṅ-loṭau* |3|3|173|. [In the sense of benediction, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used.]
*Āśiṣi liṅ*: the meaning is "also in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣyapi*). Benediction (*āśāsanam*) is the wish for the attainment of what is desired.
(44) *Eruḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.86. He states a specific rule regarding the *tip* suffix of the *loṭ* [imperative]: *eruḥ*. The analysis is *ṭheḥ-uḥ*. *Eḥ* is in the genitive case.
The term "of the vowel *i*" (*ivarṇasya*) is understood. From the rule "the *loṭ* [terminations] are like the *laṅ*" (*loṭo laṅvat*), the word "*loṭ*" is carried over (*anuvartate*).

Thus he says: "of the *loṭ*. Regarding the form *bhavatu*: after the suffix *tip*, with the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* substitution, and the replacement of *a* for *av*, the *i* of *tip* is changed to *u*.

(45) *tuhyaestātaṅṅaśiṣyanyatarasyām* || 7.1.35 || Now, he states a specific rule for the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*): *tuhyaestātaṅ*. The analysis of the compound is as follows: *tu* and *hi* form *tuhī*;
[the rule applies] to those two. *Tātaṅ* has the marker *ṅ* and the vowel *it*; the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.

The substitute *tāt* is taught [as the replacement for *tas*]. Now, one might ask: is this a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), or is it a replacement of the final phoneme (*antādeśa*) because it ends in *ṅ*? To this he says: "It is a total replacement because it consists of more than one phoneme. One might further object:

since the rule *ṅc ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the principle of total replacement, shouldn't it—just like *anaṅ* and other such substitutes—be considered a replacement of the final phoneme?

He raises the objection that even for *tātaṅ*, the status of being a substitute for the final letter (*antyādeśatva*) has been stated—this is expressed by "even though" (*yadyapi*). He refutes this with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The phrase "it is sublated by what follows" means that regarding the substitution of *tātaṅ*, this rule (*ṅcci*) is sublated by the subsequent rule (*anekāl śit sarvasya*).

Now, one might object: since it is a well-known principle that "among rules that are *ṭhpara*, *nitya*, *antaraṅga*, and *apavāda*, each subsequent one is stronger," the substitution of *tātaṅ* for *taṅ* is indeed more appropriate because an *apavāda* (exception) is stronger than what precedes it; therefore, he says: "it operates slowly. The remainder of the sentence is: "the rule 'ṅcci' [is meant]. Thus, the meaning is that the injunction "ṅcci" applies only after the other operations have taken effect. This is because the operation of the *apavāda* is delayed until the *antaraṅga* (inherently internal) operation has already occurred. Consequently, since the *antaraṅga* substitution of *śnā* for the root *manth* has already taken place, the *apavāda* rule "ṅcci" does not apply immediately to the form *math* before the *antaraṅga* rule has operated. Therefore, the *antaraṅga* substitution of *śnā* prevails, and the form becomes *māntha*. Following this, the *apavāda* rule "ṅcci" subsequently applies to the form *māntha*, resulting in the final form *mānthāt*. Thus, the sequence of operations is established.

The meaning is that because the rule *ṅcci* [Pāṇini 1.1.53] operates slowly with respect to the domain of *tātaṅ*, it is superseded by the subsequent rule for total replacement (*sarvādeśavidhi*). To the question "Why does it operate slowly?", he says: "Because it has no other purpose," and so forth; that is, there is no other purpose for *ṅt* than being a final substitute (*antādeśa*).

The property of having a *ṅ* (ṅtva) exists for no other purpose [than that]. For those [substitutes] such as *anaṅ* which possess such a property, the rule "and *ṅ*" (*ṅcca*) has fulfilled its function; that is to say, having achieved its objective, it proceeds only sluggishly.
However, he says that the *ṅ* in *tāt-aṅ* is not for no other purpose, because it depends upon being a substitute for the final letter (*antādeśa*).

Regarding the phrase "in a case where a purpose is possible": that for which purposes (prayojanāni) ending in 'a' are possible is "one in which a purpose is possible" (sambhavatprayojanaḥ); the meaning is "in such a tātaṅ [substitution] as has such a nature.
To the question, "How is it that there is the possibility of a purpose? [the answer follows].

He said: "For the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, and for the sake of *samprasāraṇa* and so forth. In examples such as *dviṣṭāt*, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution prescribed for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*). In examples such as *stutāt* and *yutāt*, there is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *uto vṛddhiluki hali*. In the case of *uṣṭāt* from the root *vaś* (meaning "to desire"), [there is a prohibition of *guṇa*].

By the rule *ṭhgrahijyāvayi*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *bruva īṭ* in the case of *brūtāt* is included. Now, one might object: even if the rule *ṅcci* operates slowly in the domain of *tātaṅ*, nevertheless...
By the maxim "Among rules that are subsequent, permanent, internal, and exceptions, each subsequent one is stronger," it would be appropriate for the rule *ṅcci* (P.
1.1.54), which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule prescribing universal substitution (*sarvādeśa*), to override even the latter;
therefore, he says: "In this case," meaning in the domain of *tātaṅ*, by the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (P. 1.1.55).

The meaning is that because the general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) and the specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*), namely "ṅcci," possess equal force, the general rule is not set aside by the specific rule. This is the underlying principle: that an exception (*apavādaśāstra*) possesses greater authority than rules that are subsequent, obligatory (*nitya*), or internal (*antaraṅga*).

The very lack of scope (*niravakāśatvam*) is the seed [of the argument]. And in the present case, the rule *ṅcci* is immediately [applied] because it has no other scope, as its sole purpose is to effect the substitution of *anaṅ*, *diṅti*, and *vam*,
in the absence of any other purpose.

Experiencing the state of having accomplished its purpose (*kṛtārthatā*) by being adopted [by the rule for *tām*], the suffix *ṅtvim* is disregarded because it finds scope through the existence of another purpose [namely, the substitution of *taṅ*]. As it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"Because *ṅtvim* has scope, by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *tāṅ* becomes a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Furthermore, [the following] is additional...

I desist here for fear of prolixity. Regarding the form *bhavatāt*: in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), from the root *bhū* with the suffix *loṭ*, after the addition of *tip* and *śap*, there is *guṇa* substitution and the replacement of *u* by *av*.

Then, by the rule *tasthasthamipāṃ tāntantāmaḥ*, the *tātaṅ* replaces the *ta* of *tip*; the letter *ṅ* serves as an *it* (indicating that the preceding portion is replaced), and the second *t* of *tātaṅ* has the vowel *a* solely for the purpose of pronunciation.

(46) *loṭo laṅvat* |3|4|85|. "Like the *laṅ*" means *laṅvat*. The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*. Thus it says: "like the *laṅ* of the *loṭ*. But [one might object]: "In that case, [the augment] *aṭ* would apply by the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ*..."

Thinking that the augment *aṭ* might also [apply], he says "by that" (*tena*). The meaning is: by resorting to the suffix *vati* after the genitive case ending of the word *laṅ*. The point is that the augment *aṭ* is not prescribed for *laṅ*, but rather for the *liṅga* (the marker) of *laṅ*. By what [are] *tām* and the others [prescribed], or by what...?

To this he says, "tathā hi" (for instance), meaning that *tām* and the others, as well as the elision of *s*, are stated clearly so that they may be understood. (47) *tasthasthamipāṃ tāṃtaṃtāmaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.101.
*tasthasthamipām*: This is the genitive plural from the *dvandva* compound of *tas*, *thas*, *tha*, and *mip*.

*tām tam ta ām*: This is the nominative plural from the *dvandva* compound of these [suffixes]. From the rule *nityaṃ ṅti*, the term *ṅti* is understood as a governing word (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "of the four, when ending in ṅ or t. [This applies to] those ending in ṅ.
The meaning is "of those [suffixes] which have become substitutes for the letter *l*. Regarding the word "in order" (*kramāt*):
this is obtained from the sūtra on "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
(48) *Nityaṃ ṅtiḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.99.

The suffix *ṅti* is always [used]. The purpose of this rule is specifically for the first person (uttama-puruṣa), though it has been introduced here incidentally. The rule "sa uttamasya" is understood to follow. In that context, "sa" is in the genitive case; by it, the first person is qualified. This is a case of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a rule to that which ends with the specified element). [Furthermore,] "the elision of *it*" (*itaś ca lopaḥ*) applies.
Therefore, the phrase "elision of *ṭh*" (*ṭh-lopa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of that which ends in *s* and has *ṅt* as its augment.
This means: of that substitute for *ṅt*, namely the letter *l*, which is the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*).
The word "always" (*nitya*) is included to ensure the cessation of the recurrence of the option (*vā-grahaṇa*) from the rule "optionally elsewhere" (*vaito'nyatra*).

By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, there is the elision of the final [letter]. In the form *bhavatām*: the suffix *tas* of the imperative (*loṭ*) is replaced by *tām*; the *śap* augment is added; then the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions take place. Nor is it the case that because the substitute *tām* replaces the whole of the suffix (*sarvādeśa*), it would not be considered a "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) prior to its application—thereby making the prohibition *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* inapplicable.

One might suspect that the letter *m* [in *bhavanti*] would receive the designation *it* because there is no prohibition; however, this is not the case because, due to the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) and the inclusion of the *m* at the end of the root, it lacks the status of being the final element in the original enunciation (*upadeśa*). Regarding the form *bhavantu*:

in the imperative (*loṭ*), after the substitution of *re* for the ending *hi*, the substitution of *guṇa* before the suffix *śap*, and the substitution of *ava* for *e*, the single substitute *pararūpa* applies to the two preceding *a*s.

The form *bhavantu* arises from the substitution of *u* for the *i* of *er* [in the case of *eru*]. Now, when the suffix *loṭ* takes the ending *sip*, and after the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions have occurred, resulting in *bhava si*—[at this point] the rule applies:
(49) *serhyapicca* | Pāṇini 3.4.87.
*serhyapicca*: the word *ṭhhi* here is a nominative singular with the case-ending elided. From the rule *ṭhloṭo laṅvat*, the term *ṭhloṭaḥ* (of the *loṭ* [imperative]) is understood. Thus he says:
"of the *loṭ* ending *si*. In forms such as *stuhi*, because the substitute *hi* for *sip* is marked with *p* (indicating it is not *pit*), the designation *sārvadhātukam apit* applies.

Since there is no *ṅ* [indicatory letter], when *guṇa* would otherwise apply, the explicit mention of *iṭ* is made. And thus, because of the *ṅ*, by the rule *kṅiti ca*, *guṇa* does not occur. However, it was not formulated as a rule that "after *si*, *hi* is substituted for *sip* after a root ending in *ṛ*" (*serharhiṅcca*), because if that were the case, since *sip* is *anudātta*, *hi* would also result in being *anudātta*. [Therefore, *bhava*...]
While [the rule] "hi sthite" remains—(50) *ato heḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.105.
In *ato heḥ*, "ataḥ" is the ablative case and "heḥ" is the genitive case. [This is derived] from the rule *ciṇo luk*.
The word "luṅ" (the aorist suffix) is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of what follows after this. Regarding "bhava":

the purpose of the rule for the suffix *hi* is for the sake of forms such as *stuhi*, etc.; this is the intended meaning. Regarding "bhavatāt": in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the suffix *loṭ* is applied;

when the suffix *sip* follows, it is replaced by *hi* according to the rule "serhyapicca"; then, after the addition of the *śap* augment, the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions occur, and finally, the elision (*luk*) takes place by the rule "ato he".

The meaning is that, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it sublates [the previous rule]; thus, according to the alternative view [of the Vārttika] "tuhyostātaṅ," *tātaṅ* is substituted. Regarding *bhavatam*:

when *thas* follows [the root *bhū*], after the addition of the *śap* suffix, the *guṇa* substitution, and the *av* replacement, we have *bhava-thas*. Since the *loṭ* [mood] is treated like the *laṅ* [mood] by the rule "loṭo laṅvat," the *thas* is replaced by *tam* by the rule "tasthasthamipām," resulting in the form [bhavatam]. Similarly for *bhavata*. [This applies to] *thas*.
The distinction is that it is *tādeśa* (the substitution of *ta*).

(51) *mer niḥ* |3|4|89|. When the *mip* of the *loṭ* [imperative] follows, after the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* [substitution], and the *avādeśa* [substitution of *ava* for *e*], there is the substitution of *am* for the *mip* by the rule *tasthasthamipām*.
When *me* is obtained—referring to the rule "the *me* of the *loṭ* [is like the *laṅ*]," which follows from the previous sūtra—it says:
"The *me* of the *loṭ*. (52) *āḍ uttamasya pi ca* 3.4.92.

When *bhava* is established as the final form—by the rule *āḍuttamasya*—the word *loṭaḥ* is understood from the previous rule *loṭo laṅvat*. Therefore, he says: "of the last person of the *loṭ*. In forms such as *stavāni* and *stavāva*, the mention of *pit* is for the purpose of preventing the application of *ṅt* by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*. Even though...

Since the substitute *naḥ* for the root *mip* is *pit*, the augment *at* added to it is also established as *pit*; nevertheless, the statement that it is *pit* is made so that the augment *āṭ* may not apply to *vas* and *mas*. Now, one might ask: why does the substitution of *u* by "ṭheruḥ" not occur in the example *stuhi bhavān*? To this, he says: "The substitution of *u* occurs only after *hi* and *ni*."
"No," [he says], "because of the force of the context. The sense is that otherwise he would have prescribed simply "hu-nu.

Regarding *bhavānī*: there is a long vowel by rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*) due to the augment *āṬ*. Nor should one suspect here that the elision [of the *n*] occurs by the rule "after an *it*, [the *n* of a suffix is dropped]"—as if it were a case of *laṅ*-like behavior—because of the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *i*. Otherwise, [he would have said] simply "mo na."

One should apply [the rule] in this way; the same should be understood for *he* as well. Although the substitution of a long vowel in forms such as *bhavāni* is already established by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*, making the prescription of the augment *āṭ* redundant, nevertheless, it is necessary for the sake of forms such as *stavāni*;
thus, because it is logically consistent, it has been introduced here as well. [The form] *bhavāva* [is derived accordingly].
In the *loṭ* [imperative] for the first person plural (*vas*), there is *guṇa*, the substitution [of *e*], the augment *āṭ*, and *savarṇadīrgha*.
Due to the treatment as *laṅ*, by the rule "nityaṃ ṅti," there is the elision of the *s* [of *mas*]. Thus, the form is *bhavāma* in *mas*. This concludes the procedure for *loṭ*.

(53) *laṅ* is used for what is not of today (*anadyatana*). Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.111. The governing terms *dhātoḥ* ("from a verbal root") and *bhūte* ("in the past") are understood [from the previous rules].
The term *bhūte* connects with the meaning of the verbal root. Thus it is said: "of that which functions with a past meaning that is not of today."
(54) *luṅ-laṅ-lṛṅ-kṣvaṅ udāttaḥ* |6|4|71|.

[The rule applies] in the case of *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*. The term "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is supplied from the governing context. That is to say: when these [suffixes] follow, [the augment *aṭ* is added] to the *aṅga*. Because it is *antaraṅga*, because it is *nitya*, and because it is subsequent (*para*), [the augment *aṭ* is applied] accordingly before the *tip* and *śap* suffixes.

When the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement by *av* have occurred, the augment *aṭ* is added to the stem (*aṅga*) as qualified by the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). However, another view established in the *Bhāṣya* is that the augment *aṭ* is added precisely while the suffix is still in the state of *l* (*lāvasthāyām*). (55) *itaśca* 3.4.100.

And for this reason as well: the word *lasya* is understood from the governing rule (*adhikṛta*). From the rule *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, the words *lopaḥ* and *parasmaipadeṣu* are carried over (*anuvartate*).
The term *parasmaipadeṣu* is transformed into the genitive case. Thus he says: *iṅtaḥ*.

By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, there is elision of the final [letter]. Thus he says: *abhavat*. Regarding *abhavatām*: the substitutes *tas* and *tām* are applied for the *laṅ* [suffix]; then *śap*, guṇa, and the ādeśa; then *aṭ*. Regarding *abhavan*: the substitute *jhi* is applied; then *śap*, guṇa, the ādeśa, and *aṭ*.

In *sthitaśca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. In *abhavaḥ*, there is the elision of the final consonant due to the rule of *saṃyogāntalopa* (elision of the final member of a conjunct). [The derivation is as follows: after the suffix *sip*, the addition of *śap*, the application of *guṇa*, the substitution of *av*, the addition of *aṭ*, the elision of the vowel *i*, and finally the application of *rutva* and *visarga*. In *abhavatam*, there is the substitution of *tam* for *thas*; then *śap*, *guṇa* and the subsequent substitution, and *aṭ*. In *abhavata*, there is the substitution of *ta* for *tha*.

In the case of *abhavam*: after the addition of the suffix *śap*, the substitution of *guṇa*, and the substitution of *av* for *u*, followed by the augment *aṭ*. In the case of *abhavāva*: after the substitution of *am* for *mip*, the addition of *śap*, the substitution of *guṇa* and *av*, and the formation of the single substitute (pūrvarūpa).

In the case of *abhavāma*: after the addition of *śap*, the substitutions of *guṇa* and *av*, the augment *aṭ*, the lengthening of the vowel by the rule "the long vowel replaces a short vowel before a suffix beginning with *yañ*," and the elision of the *s* by the rule "there is always elision of the *s* when a suffix beginning with *ṅ* follows."
Thus, "we were" is the form; this concludes the procedure for the *laṅ* tense.

(56) Pāṇini 3.3.161: "The *liṅ* [is used] in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), and entreaty (*prārthana*). [Commentary: Now, it may be objected that injunction and the others are not actually denotable by the *liṅ*, just as [the categories of] agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) are not denotable by the *l*-suffixes.
And because the rule *ca bhāve ca* teaches that the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the abstract state (*bhāva*) are denoted by the *lakāra* suffixes;
nor should it be argued that the grammatical rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* applies only to *lakāra* suffixes other than the optative (*liṅ*), for if that were the case—
Since [the suffixes] such as *yajeta* lack the capacity to denote the agent, there would be no application of the term *śa* and so forth; therefore, he says:

"in the case of those [suffixes] which are dyotaka (indicative). Although the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69) has a general scope, it is not set aside by the specific rule *vidhinimantraṇā...* (Pāṇini 3.3.161), because there is no contradiction between them. And thus:

Thinking that the result [of the rule] is that the suffix *liṅ* occurs when the agent and so forth are qualified by injunction (*vidhi*) and the like, he says: "or when they are the expressed meanings" (*vācyeṣu vā*).

Both of these two positions are established in the Bhāṣya. He summarizes the Bhāṣya statement "injunction (*vidhi*) is instigation (*preraṇā*)" according to its meaning: "injunction is instigation. Now, [an objection]:...
Since even invitations (*nimantraṇa*) and the like are included within instigation (*preraṇā*), [the author] explains [the distinction] to avoid redundancy:
"The instigation of a subordinate, such as a servant. For example, a master says to a servant:
"You should wash the garment. This is stated in order to show the difference from addressing (*āmantraṇa*).
He explains the word *nimantraṇa* (invitation): "An invitation is the act of enjoining (*niyoga*).

He dispels the misconception that the word *niyoga* is synonymous with the word *preraṇa* (instigation) by adding: "In the sense of what is necessary. This is because of such scriptural statements as: "Three things are pure at a *śrāddha*: a daughter's son, the *kutapa* [woolen blanket], and sesame seeds."
The sense is as follows: *bhāva* (existence/state) is, for example, [the expression] "May you eat at this funeral feast (*śrāddha*) for my daughter's son and others.

*Āmantraṇa* (invitation) means permission to act according to one's own desire; it signifies an authorization such as "Do as you wish. *Adhīṣṭa* (request/command) is an undertaking preceded by respect.

This is a sentence from the Bhāṣya. Its meaning is "acting with due respect. The root *iṣ* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, when ending in the suffix *kta* and denoting the abstract state (*bhāve*), takes on this specific meaning by virtue of the prefix.
For this very reason, based on its usage in the Bhāṣya, the word *adhīṣṭa* is masculine. It is simply "adhīṣṭa."
In some recensions, there is the following reading: "Māṇavakam bhavānadhyāpayet" (May you teach the boy) is the example.

Deliberation (*saṃpraśna*) is the determination after investigating whether "this should be done or not. For example: "O sir, do you study grammar? Entreaty (*prārthanā*) is a request. For example: "May you give me food."
"Easy to understand" means that the nature of *pravartanā* (the impulse to act) is woven through all four types of injunctions, such as the mandatory (*vidhi*) and others; this is the intended sense.

*Pravartanā* is an activity conducive to engagement. In this context, "engagement" (*pravṛtti*) resides in the student and so forth, while the "activity conducive to it" consists of the instigation (*preraṇā*).
[The suffix] is dependent on the instigator, the teacher, and so forth. The detailed exposition should be consulted in the *Mañjūṣā*.
Regarding the phrase "of the four": this means of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), entreaty (*āmantraṇa*), and request (*adhīṣṭa*).
(57) *yāsuṭ* is acute (*udātta*) in the *parasmaipada* when followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ*. Pāṇini 3.4.103.

Now, when the suffix *tiP* follows *liṅ*, after the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *itaśca*, and after the addition of *śap* and the substitution of *av* for *e* (guṇa), the form *bhava t* is established.

Here, from the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣu liṅaḥ sīyuṭ*, the term *liṅ* is carried over (*anuvartate*). The locative case is used in the sense of the genitive. This is what the author states: "of the *parasmaipada* substitutes of *liṅ*."

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *sīyuṭ*. In *yāsuṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of marking (*it*), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Due to its being marked with *ṭ* (*ṭit*), [the property of] *ṅt* resides in the initial portion of *ti* and the others. And because the property of *ṅt* resides in a part, by the maxim "when a property is purposeless in a part, it rests upon the whole along with its constituent members," it comes to rest in the entire complex beginning with *ti* as qualified by the augment. Thus, the augments...

Regarding the term *anudātā*: since the *yāsuṭ* augment would have been *anudātta* (unaccented) by default, this explicit statement [of its being *udātta*] is made. The *Bhāṣya* states that this very rule is the *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) for the principle that "augments (*āgama*) are *anudātta*. In forms such as *stuyāt* and *stuyātām*, the *ṅt* designation of *yāsuṭ* is prescribed to prohibit [the application of] *guṇa* and other such operations. Now, one might object: [why is this necessary?]
According to the principle *yadāgamāḥ*, the augment *yāsuṭ* is a part of the *liṅ* substitute parasmaipada endings;

therefore, since the status of being marked by *ṅ* (*ṅtvi*) is established for *yāsuṭ* simply by virtue of its being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule prescribing *ṅtvi* for *yāsuṭ* is redundant. Nor can it be argued that because the *ṅ* sound in the original *liṅ* (the *sthānin*) is not an *al*...

Since the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.56] *guṇaniṣedhavidhāv āśrayaṇāt* (because it is relied upon in a rule that prohibits *guṇa*) is based on its being a locus, one might suspect the prohibition *analvidhau* (not in a rule concerning an *al*). However, this is not so; for the *liṅga* (indicative mark) is the prohibition *na lyapi* (not before the suffix *lyap*), which negates the *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*) prescribed by the rule *ṭh-ghu-ā-sthā-gā-pā-jahāti-sām hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) when a *kṅit* suffix follows.
Thus, it is established that the principle *analvidhau* applies even to operations conditioned by *anubandhas*.
Because it would otherwise fail to indicate the absence of the prohibition, he says: "The mention of *ṅ*.

This means that even in certain operations involving *anubandhas*, the prohibition [of Pāṇini 1.1.56]—"not when a rule applies to what is not an *al*"—is applicable; thus, it is understood from the *ṅ*-ness of *yāsuṭ*. And so, it is precisely for the purpose of this indication that *yāsuṭ* is assigned *ṅ*-ness.
This is the intended meaning. The result of making this known is that there is no application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* in the case of the term *vakṣyamāṇā*;

otherwise, because the substitute *śānac* (the present middle participle suffix) would be treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element), it would possess the marker *ṭ*, and consequently the suffix *ṅīp* would have to be applied.

Now, one might object: "Is there not a prohibition [against treating a substitute] even in the case of operations concerning markers (*anubandha*), based on the rule *analvidhau*? To this, [the author replies] regarding the *yāsuṭ* [augment]:

The fact that [the augment] *yāsuṭ* has the marker *ṅ* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Even though there is no prohibition by the rule "not when a rule applies to what is not a letter" (*analvidhau*) regarding operations involving markers (*anubandha-kārya*), it is necessary for the purpose of [the *ṅ* marker] in *yāsuṭ* so that *tip*, *sip*, and *mip* may be substituted [for *ta*, *tha*, and *ja* respectively]. Otherwise, [the substitution would not occur].

Even though [the suffixes] are in the domain of *liṅ*, the property of having the marker *ṅ* for *tip*, *sip*, and *āmip* is obtainable through the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*; for this has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* with the statement, "When there is *ṅt*, it is not *pit*; when it is *pit*, it is not *ṅt*. Due to this underlying dissatisfaction, he says: "In this context, even the fact that *śnaḥ* (the substitute *śānac*) is marked with *ś* is a *liṅga* (indicative mark)."

The meaning here is that even in the case of an operation dependent on an *anubandha*, there is sometimes a prohibition according to the rule *analvidhau* ("not when an operation is prescribed with reference to an *al*");

in this sense, the fact that the substitute *śānac* for the *śna*-affix (which is ordained by the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau*) is marked with the *śit* designation serves as a *liṅga*—that is, an indicator. Otherwise, [the desired result] would follow merely through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

The sense is that since the existence of *śit* [as a marker] is not established for it, that statement would be useless. And whatever needs to be said on this point has been explained in detail under the heading "that which will be stated in the section on feminine suffixes" (*strīpratyayaprakaraṇe vakṣyamāṇa*). (58) *suṭ tithoḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.107.
And so, when *bhav-y-ās-ta* is established in the present context—the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* applies, with *liṅ* being supplied from the previous rule *liṅḥ sīyuṭ*.
From the compound *tiśca thaśca* (a *dvandva*), there is a genitive dual. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus he says: "the *ta*-portion of the *liṅ*."
In *suṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of pronunciation, and the letter *u* is for the sake of articulation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Thus, the form stands as *bhava-yās-s-t*.

Now, one might object: "But here, how is it that *yāsuṭ* is not superseded by the subsequent *suṭ*? Anticipating this objection, [the author] notes that in forms such as *bhaveyuḥ* and others, *yāsuṭ* has its purpose fulfilled in the case of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings.
He refutes [the objection] by stating: "The *yāsuṭ* is not superseded by the *suṭ*. Why is that? To this he says:

"In the case of the *liṅ*, there is *yāsuṭ*. The meaning is that because the domains differ—the *sīyuṭ* and the *yāsuṭ* augment belong to the *liṅ* itself, whereas the *suṭ* augment belongs to the *takāra*, which is a portion of the substitute for the *liṅ*—there is no conflict. And thus...

The sense is that because there is no impossibility of simultaneity and no contradiction, there is no sublation of the *yāsuṭ* augment by the *suṭ* augment even through the principle of *paratva* (subsequent application).
(59) *liṅḥ salopo 'ntyasya* 7.2.79. [In the case of the *liṅ* (optative), there is the elision of the final *s*.]

The word *liṅ* [in the rule] is a compound with the genitive case elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhī-pada*). From the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*, the term *sārvadhātuka* is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and is transformed into the genitive case.
Thus he says: "the *liṅ* [affix] which is a *sārvadhātuka*. The phrase "of both *sak*s" refers to this.

Since there is no distinction between the two *sakāra*s, the simultaneous elision (*yugallopa*) of both occurs; however, the principle that "a rule applies only once to its object" (*lakṣye lakṣaṇasya sakṛdeva pravṛttiḥ*) refers to the cessation of further application after an alternating occurrence (*paryāyeṇa*).
Although [the form] *bhavāst* could be established by the rule *skoḥ* alone, nevertheless...

The sūtra is for the purpose [of ensuring that forms] such as *bhaveyuḥ* [are produced]. Now, one might ask: "If there is elision (*lopa*) of *suṭ*, what is the purpose of the rule prescribing *suṭ*? To this he says: "But the hearing of *suṭ* occurs in the *āśīr-liṅ* (the benedictive mood)," as in *bhūyāstam* and so on. This is because, by the rule *liṅ-aśiṣi*, [the *liṅ*] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix in that context.

The sense is that there is no possibility of the elision of the letter *sakāra*. Based on the Bhāṣya statement—"There is no difference in pronunciation whether a single consonant or multiple consonants follow [a vowel]"—he says "more clearly" (*sphuṭataram*).
Even in that case, it is more clearly evident in the Ātmanepada forms such as *edhiṣīṣṭa*, where the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).

The meaning is "the hearing of two *sakāra*s. The point is that, in that case, due to the absence of *yāsuṭ* and the absence of the elision (*lopa*) of *s*, it is possible for the *sakāra* of *suṭ* itself to be heard distinctly and clearly. (60) *ato yeyaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.80.
And so, when *bhava-yā-t* is established, [the rule] *ato yeyaḥ* applies. The word *yā* is a term with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*).
*Ato* is in the ablative case. The word *parasya* (of the following) is to be supplied.
In *iya*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). [The suffix *śnā* is applied] by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*.

Thus, the term *avayava-ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive of part) is modified [to apply here]. He states this with the words "after this" (*ataḥ parasya*), and so forth. The form *bhave iy t* is established. Regarding "guṇa": the remainder of the rule is "by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.87). The form *bhavey t* is established. Regarding "elision of *y*" (*yalopa*): [the remainder of the rule is] "elision of... (*lopaḥ*).

The phrase "by this [rule]" refers to *vyor iti*. Regarding the word "bhavet" (it would be): one should not suspect the elision of the *hal* (consonant) by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* or the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) prior to the elision of *y*.

This is because the elision of *y* operates first due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal), and because the elision of the final consonant is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) as it belongs to the third section of Pāṇini’s rules (*traipādika*). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the question "What is meant by *sārvadhātuke*?"—the term *sārvadhātuka* is obtained through its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *ṛdādibhyaḥ*. The meaning of the question is: for what purpose is the phrase "of that which is a portion of a *sārvadhātuka*" [stated]?

[The answer is: in forms such as *bhūyāt*, because the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative) is an *ārddhadhātuka*, there is an absence of "that which follows an *a*" (*ataḥ paratva*), and therefore [the rule does not apply].
The intention is that since the absence of the substitution of *iy* is established [by other rules], the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *sārvadhātuka* is redundant.

Regarding *cikīrṣyāt*: from the root *kṛ*, with the desiderative suffix (*san*), in the āśīr-liṅ (optative) mood, we first arrive at *cikīrṣ-y-āt*; then, by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), the *a* is elided, resulting in the form *cikīrṣyāt*.

In that case, if the term *sārvadhātuka* were not carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *ato yeyaḥ*, then after the form *cikīrṣa-ya* is established, the substitution of *iy* by *ato yeyaḥ* would apply; following this, with *ād-guṇaḥ* and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), the result would be *cikīrṣet*. However, because the term *sārvadhātuka* is carried over, [the substitution does not apply].

The fault is that the *tiṅ* suffix of the *āśīr-liṅ* (the benedictive mood) will be classified as *ārddhadhātuka*, as will be stated later by the rule *liṅaśiṣi*. Now, one might object: when the form *icikīrṣyāt* is established for the benedictive, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *ato lopaḥ* due to its obligatory nature; once that has occurred, [what remains is] *ataḥ*...

Since the rule "āto yeya" does not apply precisely because of the absence of *paratva* (subsequent status), the continued reference (*anuvṛtti*) to the term "sārvadhātuka" there would be entirely redundant; therefore, he says: "By the maxim of the intermediate exception (*madhye'pavādanyāya*), only 'ato lopa' would be sublated. This refers to the rule "ato lopaḥ" in the fourth quarter of the sixth book [of Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī].

The established rule is that *ato yeyaḥ* is the sūtra in the second pāda of the seventh [chapter], whereas *ato dīrgho yañi* is the sūtra in the fourth pāda of the seventh [chapter]. In this regard, in the case of the āśīr-liṅ (benedictive) in an ārdhadhātuka suffix, as in *cikīrṣyāt*, there is the occurrence of elision (*allopa*), but in the vidhi-liṅ (optative), it is *bhivya*.

In the case of *yād*, because the substitution of *iy* is without scope (*niravakāśa*) due to the application of the rule for lengthening (*ato dīrgha*), one must rely on the "general consideration of what is to be sublated" (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*). Consequently, since it functions as an exception (*apavāda*), when either one of the two [rules] is to be sublated, the principle applies: "Exceptions sublate preceding rules, not subsequent ones."
Therefore, by logical principle, the elision (*lopa*) alone ought to take precedence over the substitution, and not the lengthening of the vowel after *ataḥ*; this is the meaning.

Thus, when *bhavyāt* is established in the domain of *ardhadhātuka*, the rule "lengthening of the vowel after *at* before a suffix beginning with *yañ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.101)—which prescribes lengthening when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with *yañ* follows—supersedes the substitution of *iy* on account of its higher status (*paratva*).

It would [be so]. Consequently, because there is an absence of *paratva* (subsequent application) from this point onward, the substitution of *iy* would not occur; thus, the meaning is that there would be an instance of under-extension (*avyāpti*). Nor should it be suspected that the substitution of *iy* subverts the long vowel (*dīrgha*) due to its lack of scope (*niravakāśatva*), for the substitution of *iy* applies in the domain of *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes such as in *cikīrṣyāt*, where the occurrence of the long vowel is impossible.

The intended meaning is "because there is scope [for the application of the rule]. Regarding the form *bhavetām*: after the substitution of *tām* for *tas*, the addition of the *śap* suffix, the *guṇa* substitution, the substitution of *ava* for *e*, the introduction of the *yāsuṭ* augment, the addition of *suṭ*, the elision of the two *s* sounds, the substitution of *iy* for *yā*, the *guṇa* substitution for the initial vowel (*ādguṇa*), and finally the elision of the *y*.

(61) *jherjus* | Pāṇini 3.4.108. Now, since the rule *liṅo jheḥ* [3.4.105]—which states that for the *liṅ* [optative], *jhi* is replaced by *jha* as its final element—would have applied, [the present rule] prescribes *jherjus*.
From the preceding rule *liṅaḥ sīyuṭ* [3.4.102], the word *liṅ* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Therefore, he says: "for the *jhi* of the *liṅ*."
Because it consists of more than one *al* (phoneme), it is a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). "ja id" means that, by virtue of being a substitute [for *jus*], it is a suffix;

and because it is a suffix, the letter *j* is designated as an *it* by the rule *cuṭū*. When *usi*, *śapi*, guṇa, the substitution of *av*, and *yāsuṭ* have occurred, and the *s* has been elided, the form *bhava yā us* remains; at this stage, [the rule for] the substitution of *iy* prevails, overriding [any other potential rule].

He speaks in order to raise the doubt regarding the application of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule: *usi apa*. The governing rule "ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ" is understood here. From the rule "ād guṇaḥ," the word *āt* is carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule "eṅi pararūpam," the word *pararūpam* is carried over. Therefore he says: "from that which is not at the end of a word" (*apadāntāt*). [The example is] *usi*.

The meaning is "when *u* or *ū* follows"; this is because the word *aci* is understood from the rule *iko yaṇ aci*. Although the form remains the same even when the entire *us* and the vowel *ā* undergo the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *us*, nevertheless, by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*...
It should be understood that the phrase "to the preceding" (*pūrvasya*), which occurs later in the rule, necessarily carries over here as well.

An example is *bhindyauḥ*. Regarding the statement "this being the case": in the sequence *bha-va-y-ā-u-si*, the single substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*)—the single *u*-vowel—occurs, overriding the *guṇa* substitution that would otherwise apply between the vowel *ā* and the vowel *u*.

The meaning is "when [the condition] has been met. He considers that if the *pararūpa* (single-substitute replacement) were to occur, the form *yā* would no longer exist, and thus the suffix *iñ* would not apply—on account of its being subsequent (*paratvāt*). Compared to *pararūpa*, the substitution *iy* is both subsequent and permanent (*nitya*), because it applies whether *pararūpa* has not yet occurred or has already occurred. When *pararūpa* has occurred...

The meaning is that the ancient grammarians believe that the form *bhaveyur* would result because the substitution of *iy* is unimpeded—either by the maxim of "substitution of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) or by treating the single substitute as being like the original prior element (*pūrvāntavat*). Thus, having set aside the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule, the substitution of *iy* occurs. Now, an objection: [nanu...]

The *pararūpa* (single-substitute form) is *antaraṅga* because it does not reside within the domain of a stem (*aṅga*) and thus does not depend upon a stem; however, the substitution of *iy* is *bahiraṅga* because, being a stem-property (*āṅgatva*), it depends upon both the base and the suffix.
Consequently, by virtue of its *antaraṅga* status, the *pararūpa* takes precedence over even the *nitya* substitution of *iy*.

One might raise the objection that, because it is stronger, the form of the subsequent element alone should occur here; thus he says, "Even though... He refutes this with, "...nevertheless. Therefore, the word division is *ataḥ-yāḥ-iy-yaḥ*. The word *yāḥ* is a term in which the genitive case ending is elided. Consequently, the meaning is: for this [word] *yāḥ* following *ataḥ*, *iy* shall be substituted.

The meaning is that [the rule] must be explained. Now, one might object: since the rule "there is elision of the *s* of the optative (*liṅ*) when followed by an affix beginning with *an*" applies invariably, it would supersede the substitution of *iy* for the *s*, and consequently, how could there be *iy* in place of *yās*? To this he says: "In this way," etc. [This refers to] the form ending in *s*, namely *yās*.

The meaning is that, by the very force of the rule prescribing the substitution of *iy*, this substitution of *iy* for the word ending in *s* occurs even before the elision of the *s*, thereby overriding the elision of the *s*. Thus,

the intention is that while the word is still in its state with the *s*, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) does not apply because the condition of being preceded by an *a*-vowel is absent.

Now, if the analysis were *ṭhyās-īyaḥ*, then after the *ru*-substitution for the *s* (by *sasajuṣo ruḥ*), the *ya*-substitution for *bho-bhago-* (by *bhobhago-agho-apūrvasya yo 'ś*), and the elision of that [ya] by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, one would obtain *ato-yā-īya*.

Since the elision of *ya* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the *guṇa* substitution required by *ādguṇaḥ* is to be applied, he says: "The euphonic combination (*sandhi*) is archaic (*ārṣa*)."

In the *ṭhāne mug iti* sūtra, however, the reading of the sūtra in the Bhāṣya appears to be *ṭhato yā—iya*. [The derivation of] *bhavet* is as follows: in the *sip* suffix, there is *guṇa* (vocalization) due to *śap*;

the substitution of *ava*; elision of the *ikāra* by the rule *itaśca*; the addition of the augment *yāsuṭ*; elision of the *sakāra*; the substitution of *iy*; and *ādguṇa* (the formation of a single *guṇa* vowel).

There is the elision of *y*. Then the substitution of *ru* and the visarga (*visarga*) [occur]. Similarly, when *thas* is replaced by *tam* and *tha* is replaced by *ta*, the forms are *bhavetam* and *bhaveta*. Regarding *bhaveyam*: in the case of *mi*, there is the replacement by *am*; then the *śap* suffix; then *guṇa*; then the replacement by *ava*; then *yāsuṭ*; then the elision of *s*; then the replacement by *iy*; then *ādguṇa*. Regarding *bhaveyuḥ*: [this is from] *vas*.

In the *śap* [suffix], by the rule "the *ṅt* [pratyāhāra] is always elided," there is the elision of the *s*. Then there is *yāsuṭ*, the elision of *s*, the substitution of *iy*, *ādguṇaḥ*, and the elision of *y*. In the same way, the form *bhavema* arises in the *mas* [ending].
Thus ends the procedure for the prescriptive optative (*vidhiliṅ*).
(62) *liṅaśiṣi* |3|4|11|. Now [the author] states a specific rule regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*): *liṅaśiṣi*. The word "liṅ" here has its genitive case ending elided.
From the previous rule *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam*, the term "tiṅ" is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "in the sense of benediction."

"Liṅ and tiṅ"—this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *sārvadhātuka*. Consequently, the grammatical operations associated with the *sārvadhātuka* designation, such as the suffix *śap*, do not apply. (63) *kidāśiṣi* 3.4.104.

Regarding *kid āśiṣi*: from the rule "liṅḥ sīyuṭ" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 3.4.102), the word *liṅ* is understood by anuvṛtti; and from the rule "yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣu" (3.4.103), the word *yāsuṭ* is also understood. Thus he says: "in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), [the suffix] *liṅ*.
The [augment] *yāsuṭ* in the rule "yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣu" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṅit*-ness [of the suffix]. Even though [the suffix] is indeed *ṅit*...

Although the negation of the *guṇa* [strengthening] is established, nevertheless, in forms such as *ṭhijyā* and *āditya*, the designation *kit* is necessary for the purpose of *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) according to the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kitī*; it is introduced here because it is the more logical [application].

Now, in the case of the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), when the suffix *tip* follows, since it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the substitution of *śap* does not occur; consequently, by the rule *itaśca*, the *ikāra* (the *i*) is elided.
When the augment *yāsuṭ* is applied, because there is no *ataḥ* (the suffix beginning with *a*) following it, and because there is no *sārvadhātuka* status, the substitution of *iy* does not occur.
Thus, when *suṭ* is added, the form stands as *bhūyās s t*. Regarding this stage of the derivation, he states:
"by the rule *skor*, there is elision. This refers to the rule *liṅsalopaḥ*.

Because it falls within the scope of *sārvadhātuka*, [the rule] "skor" applies; furthermore, because the *su* is at the beginning of a *saṃyoga* at the end of a word (*padānta*), there is elision (*lopa*).

Consequently, the *s* of *yāsuṭ* is also elided precisely because it is at the beginning of a *saṃyoga* at the end of a word; it is not, however, due to the *s* of *yāsuṭ* being at the beginning of a *saṃyoga* followed by a *jhal* consonant that the *s* of *suṭ* [is elided].

It would be correct [to argue] that there is elision because the word begins with a *saṃyoga* at the end of a word; however, if that were the case, since the elision of a *saṃyoga* beginning with a *jhal* followed by a *pa* would be considered *asiddha*, the elision of the final *saṃyoga* would result.
This is because the elision of a *saṃyoga* beginning with a *jhal* followed by a *pa* finds its scope of application in examples such as *bhraṣṭa*.

The detailed explanation in the *Śabdaratna* states that this is because [the rule for] the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) does not subvert [the present case]. Thus, when *bhūyās s t* is established, upon the removal of the two *s*-sounds, the form is *bhūyāt*. In that state, the question arises as to whether the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* should apply.

(64) *kṅiti ca* | Pāṇini 1.1.5. The term *kṅit* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of *k*, *ṅ*, and *it*. The letter *g* is included [in the compound] because of the substitution of *c* for the preceding *k* in the technical term *kit*. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has *k*, *ṅ*, or *it* as its final element. At the end of the copulative compound...

The meaning is "while being heard. By the mention of *ika*, it is understood that [the rule applies] when [the suffix] has been prescribed. From the rule *na dhātulopa ārddhadhātuke* ("not [before an ārdhadhātuka suffix] when there is elision of a verbal root"), the word *na* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "when caused by a *gi*, *ki*, or *ṅ*," and so forth. If *gi* were not mentioned, however, [the prohibition would apply] even in the case of the *gsnu* suffix in the rule *glājisthaśca gsnuḥ*.

In the case of *jiṣṇu*, there would be no prohibition of *guṇa*. Nor should it be argued that the suffix *snuc* should simply be made *kit*; for if that were so, the substitution of *ī* (as prescribed by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭi kiti*) would undesirably apply. However, if one maintains that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur when a *giṭ* or *ṅiṭ* suffix follows...

If it were explained in that way, then in the case of *cchinnaṃ* and *bhinnam*, where the suffix *kta* follows, there would be no prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), because the single substitute (*ik*) would be separated from its original locus (*sthānin*) by a consonant (*hal*). Nor should one invoke the maxim *yena nāvyavadhānam* (that which cannot be separated by anything else) here; for [the rule] *citaṃ*... [is intended to apply].

In examples such as *stuta*, the rule finds its application (*caritārtha*) in cases where there is no intervention. Furthermore, if the rule were explained simply as "guṇa and vṛddhi [substitute] for *ik*," and not as "guṇa and vṛddhi characterized by *ik*," then in the case of *laigavāyanaḥ*—
derived from *ligu* with the suffix *phak* because it belongs to the *naḍādi* group— the initial *vṛddhi* and the *guṇa* of the *o* would both be subject to the rule.
Since, in reality, [the root] has an *ik-sthānika* (a substitute for *ik*) vowel, the prohibition would apply; so enough of this. Regarding the word *bhūyāt*:
here, because it is an *ardhadhātuka*, the rule *liṅ-salopaḥ* does not apply; therefore, one must not forget that the *s* is elided by the rule *skoḥ*. Nor even so...
It should not be argued that because the elision of *saṃyoga* and so forth is considered *asiddha*, the elision of *hal* and *ṅy* etc. would still apply;

for when *suṭ* or *yāsuṭ* is present, that which is qualified by them alone constitutes the affix (*pratyaya*), and thus lacks the quality of being *apṛkta*. Enough of this. [The form] *bhūyāstām* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

When *liṅ* is replaced by *tām*, because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, *śap* is absent; when *yāsuṭ* is introduced, since there is no *at* (the short *a*) following it, the substitution of *iy* does not occur. With the addition of *suṭ*, because the *s* of *yāsuṭ* is part of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) beginning with a *jhal* letter, that *s* is elided, and there is also a prohibition against *guṇa*. Thus we have *bhūyāsuḥ*. [In the case of the third person plural], *jus* is substituted for *jhi*.

The form *bhūyāt* arises when the augment *yāsuṭ* is applied and the prohibition of *guṇa* occurs. In the case of the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative of benediction) with the ending *sip*, there is the elision of the *ik* vowel by the rule *itaśca*. There is the elision of the *s* of *yāsuṭ* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*, the prohibition of *guṇa*, and the application of *rutva* and *visarga*. Regarding *bhūyāstam*: when the ending *thas* is replaced by *tam* and *yāsuṭ* is added, there is the prohibition of *guṇa*.

Thus, even when *ta* is substituted for *tha*, the forms are *bhūyāstām* and *bhūyāsam*. In the case of *mip*, when *am* is substituted and *yāsuṭ* is applied, there is a prohibition of *guṇa*. [The form] *bhūyāsva* is derived from the *liṅ* suffix *vas*;
by the rule "nityaṃ ṅti," there is the elision of the *s*; then *yāsuṭ* is applied, followed by the prohibition of *guṇa*. The same applies to *mas*.
"May we be" (*bhūyāsma*) is the form. This is the procedure for the optative (*liṅ*) used as a benediction (*āśis*).

(67) *sme loṭ ca* |3|3|176|. After the word *sma*, there is also the *loṭ* [suffix]. By the word "also" (*ca*), the [suffixes] *māṅ* and *luṅ* are attracted [from the previous rule]. The analysis of the compound is: "that after which the indeclinable *sma* follows. Thus he says: "after *sma*, [the suffixes] *māṅ* [and so on]."
This is also an exception to all [other] verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).

(68) *cli* for the *luṅ* [suffix]. Pāṇini 3.1.43. *cli* for the *luṅ*. The term *cli* has its nominative case elided. After a verbal root (*dhātu*) followed by the *luṅ* suffix, the *cli* affix is applied.

The meaning is "it may be. Regarding the phrase "an exception to *śa* and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the conjugational suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) such as *śyan* is intended.

(69) *cleḥ sic* 3.1.44: "In place of *cli*, *sic* [is substituted]. Regarding "the *ic* augment": the purpose of the *cit* designation is the accentuation of the *cit*. As for the *idit* designation, however—

In the case of *amaṃsta*, the purpose [of the rule] is that the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*)— governed by the rule *ṭhaniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ*— does not take effect. (70) *gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.77).
*gāti-sthā-ghu*: This is the ablative plural of a dvandva compound formed from *gāti*, *sthā*, and *ghu*.

The word *parasya* (of the following) is understood as the remainder [of the construction]. *sicaḥ* is the genitive [referring to the suffix *siC*]. Because of the mention of *gāti* with the *śit* marker (*śtipā*), the root *gā* is included. By the term *ghu*, the roots *dā* and *dhā* are included according to the rule *dā-dhā-ghvadāp*.

There is the inclusion of both the root *dā* (designated by the technical term *ghu*) and the root *dhā*. From the rule "The elision (*luk*) of *ṇya* and *iñ* occurs after [patronymics] other than those of the Kṣatriya or Ārṣa classes when a younger descendant is denoted," the word *luk* is carried over even though it is separated [by intervening rules].
However, the mention of *ślu* from the rule "The *ślu* suffix occurs after roots such as *hu*" is not carried over, even though it is immediately preceding.

This is because of the explanation. He states this with the words "sicaḥ" and so forth from these [rules]. Regarding "gā-pā-vi-ha": here, by the rule *gāti-sthā-gā-pā-bhū-bhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), the term *gāti* in that sūtra and the inclusion of *pā* therein indicate both the substitution of *gā* for the root *iṇ* when followed by *luṅ* (the aorist suffix) which has the *luk*-vikaraṇa, as well as the root *pā*, which has the *śap*-vikaraṇa and is suitable for the substitution of *piba*.
The meaning is that these two [roots] are included. The intention is based on the Bhāṣya statement: "In the mention of *gā* and *pā*, there is the inclusion of *iṇ* and *pibati*.
Thus, when the *luṅ* suffix has been replaced by *ti*, the *ikāra* is elided by *itaśca*; when the *śap* affix is set aside and the *cli* affix is applied;
when *sic* is applied to that; when *sic* is elided; and when the augment *aṭ* is added, the form *abhūt* is established.
When *iṅ* is absent after the root *pā*, the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* would require *guṇa*;

however, [this is prevented by] *bhūsuvostiṅ* 7.3.88. From the rule *tiṅśit-sārvadhātukam* up to *midaco'ntyāt paraḥ*, the term *guṇaḥ* is understood from *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam* and *midaco'ntyāt paraḥ*. Furthermore, the term *na* is understood from *nābhyastasyāci*.

From the rule "pitī" (P. 7.3.78), the words "na" and "sārvadhātuke" are carried over. Thus he says: "of these two. This means "of these two," namely *bhū* and *sū*. Here, only the root *ṣūṅ* with the marker *luṅ* (indicating the vikaraṇa *śnā*) is to be understood as the referent, and not [the other root].
Even in the case of *suvati* and *sūyate*, which take the *śap* and *śyan* suffixes respectively— therein,
because of the intervention of the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) between the root and the *tiṅ* ending— one might suspect that the augment *iṭ* should be applied to the *t* in *abhūt*; therefore, he says:

(72) *asti-sico'pṛkte* [Pāṇini 7.3.96]. From the compound *asti-sicaḥ*, which is a collective dvandva, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is understood. The word *īṭ* is carried over from the rule *bruva īṭ*. By the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) *tasmād ity uttarasya*, [the augment *īṭ* is applied after the root *as* and the suffix *sic* when followed by an *apṛkta* suffix].

The word "ṭhastisicaḥ" is a fifth-case (ablative) term that brings about the interpretation of "apṛktasya" as a sixth-case (genitive). Consequently, the ancient commentators explain that the augment *īṭ* should apply to an unreduplicated (*apṛkta*) suffix following either the root *as* or the suffix *sic*. If that were the case, then in the formation of *abhūt* from the root *iṇ* in the *luṅ* tense—where *iṇ* undergoes the substitution of *bhū*—the form would not be possible, because [the substitute] would, by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, retain the status of being *as*.
In that case, because the augment *īṭ* would be unavoidable for an uncombined consonant (*apṛkta-hal*), and likewise in forms such as *agāt*, *asthāt*, and *apāt*— where,

even though the *s-* of *sic* is elided by the rule "gāti-sthā— " (Pāṇini 2.4.77), the augment *īṭ* would still occur due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if the elided element were present) since it follows *sic*— he explains [the rule] in another way: "and *sic*" (*sic-ca*).

[The author] explains this with the words beginning with *aśce* etc. Now, an objection might be raised: since the preceding portion of the word *sic-aś* is a *pada* due to the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhaktiḥ*), the rule *coḥ kuḥ* would entail the substitution of *k* for the *c*.

To this, he replies: "The status of being a *bha* [is established] by the Vedic aphorism (*sautram bhatvam*). Thus, because the status of being a *pada* is sublated by the status of being a *bha*, [the aforementioned fault does not arise].
The intended meaning is that there is the substitution of *k* for *t*. Now, one might ask:
since the root *as* is already obtained by the word *asi* within the term *sicaḥ*, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *asti*?
To this he replies: "It is a *karmadhāraya* compound with the indeclinable *asti*. The word *asti* is an indeclinable that functions as a substitute for a case-ending.

[The compound] has its case-endings (*sub-vibhakti*) elided and retains its meaning; thus, the meaning is that there is a *karmadhāraya* compound of the words *asti* and *sic*. Consequently, it is established that "astisica" is a single word. Regarding "the elision prescribed by Pāṇini": the remainder [of the explanation] is that this occurs by means of the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39). And so, [the form] is "astisica".

He states the meaning obtained from the word *padāt*: "from what exists," and so forth. Regarding "after a consonant" (*halīti*): the sense is that there is a transformation of the genitive case of the word *halī*, which has been carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the rule "vṛddhi is substituted for *u* when a consonant follows after elision" (*uto vṛddhir luki halī*). Regarding "thus there is no *iṇ*" (*itīṇneheti*): by this rule, the augment *īṭ* does not occur in the form *abhūt*; why? [Because the condition of being followed by a consonant is absent.]

Therefore, he says: "because of its elision. The sense is that by the qualification "being present," [the rule] does not apply to what follows an elided *sic*. And thus, in cases such as *agāt*, it has already been stated that there is no [substitution] for the *as* following an elided *sic*, nor for that which follows a *kṛt* [suffix] after the substitution of *bhū*. [The form] *aidhiṣi* [is derived as follows].

Regarding the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *edh*, the third person singular ending takes the augment *iṭ*. The point here is that although the vowel *i* follows the *sic* suffix, the augment *iṭ* is not applied because there is no *hal* (consonant) preceding it. As for *aidhiṣṭa*:
this is the third person singular *luṅ* of the root *edh*. Here, although *ta* follows the *sic* suffix...

The sense is that because there is an absence of being a single suffix (ekāl-pratyaya), there is an absence of being "uncombined" (apṛkta), and thus the augment *iṭ* does not apply. Regarding the form *abhūtām*: in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *tas*, there is the substitution of *tām* for it; then *cli*, then *sic*, then *aṭ*, and finally the prohibition of *guṇa*.

(73) *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 3.4.109. The rule *jherjus* is understood to follow here, as well as *ṅti* from the rule *nityaṃ ṅti*. Thus he says: "from the *sic*-affix, from the reduplicated (*abhyasta*), etc. This being the case... [iti prāpte].
The remainder [of the rule] is "ṭhliṅe jherjus" (Pāṇini 3.4.108).

(74) *Ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110): The word *ātaḥ* [is used]; the sūtra *jherjus* is understood to follow. [The phrase *ātaḥ* means] "after a root ending in /ā/ from which the suffix *sic* has been elided."

The Vārttika "vaktavyam" is recited in the Bhāṣya. Consequently, it is understood that *jus* replaces *jhi* when it follows a form ending in long *ā* after the elision of *sic*. Since this is already established by the preceding rule, "sijabhyastavidibhyaśca," the present rule is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Thus he says: "only from one ending in long *ā*. [The example] is *abhūvan*: *jhi*, *cli*, [elision of *sic*, substitution of *guṇa*, and application of the rule].
Thus: [the suffix] *luk*, *aṭ*, and *jho'ntaḥ*. By the rule *itaśca*, there is elision of the vowel *i*.

There is elision of the final consonant *t* due to the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*. By the rule *bhuvo vug luṅ-liṭoḥ*, the augment *vuk* is added. Because of the restriction that [the substitution of *jus*] applies only to what follows *āt* when *sij* has been elided, the *jus* substitution does not occur by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*; thus we have *abhūḥ*.

*sip*, *cli*, *sic*, *luk*, *aṭ*, and the elision of the vowel *i*. [Then] *rutva* and *visarga*. Thus: *abhūtam*. For *thas*, *tam*, *cli*, *sic*, *luk*, *aṭ*. There is a prohibition of *guṇa*. Similarly, with the substitution of *ta* for *tha*, the form is *abhūta*. For *abhūvam*: *mip*, *am*, *cli*, *sic*, *luk*, *aṭ*.

[The form] *abhūt* is derived as follows: from the root *bhū*, the suffix *cli* [is introduced], followed by *sic*, with the elision of *luk* and *aṭ*. By the rule *nityaṃ ṅti*, there is the elision of the *s* of *sic*. There is a prohibition of *guṇa*. In the same way, the form *abhūma* is obtained in the first person plural (*mas*). Now, he states the specific rule for the *luṅ* [aorist] after the prohibitive particle *māṅ*: "Not [is there the substitution of *aṭ*] when there is connection with *māṅ*. The sūtra is completed by supplying the remaining portion.

He explains: "They do not occur before [affixes] beginning with *a*. This is because the words from "In *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*, *aṭ* is udātta" (*luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāta*) and "The augment *āṭ* is added to those beginning with vowels" (*āḍajādīnām*) are understood to follow here. Thus: *mā bhavān abhūt*;
or *mā sma bhavat*, *mā sma bhūt*. Likewise in the plural: *mā sma bhavan*, *mā sma*.
And "bhūvan" should be understood as an example. Thus ends the section on the *luṅ* formation.

(75) *Liṅnimite lṛṅ kriyātipattau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.139). Regarding "on the occasion of the *liṅ*": this refers to the relationship between cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) and so forth; specifically, the rule *hetuhetumator liṅ*.

The conditions for the *liṅ* [optative] suffix, such as "in the sense of requesting (*ṭhicchārtheṣu*) one uses *liṅ* and *loṭ*," etc., will become clear in the section on the meaning of verbal suffixes (*lakārārthaprakriyā*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the future" (*bhaviṣyatyartha*), the intention is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "when expressing a limit in the future" (*bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane*). He explains the term *kriyātipatti*: "of the action..."

Regarding the term "aniṣpatau" (in the case of non-actualization): the example to be understood is, "If there had been good rain, then there would have been an abundance of food. As for the form "abhaviṣyat": this is the conditional (lṛṅ) tense; the suffix is *tip*;
the *it* portion is elided by the rule "itaśca"; and the suffix *śa*, which is an exception [to the general rule], is replaced by *syat* according to the rule "syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ."
The suffix *sya*, the augment *aṭ*, the augment *iṭ* prescribed for roots beginning with *val*, the substitution of *guṇa* and *avādeśa*, and the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus:

*abhaviṣyan*. [The process is as follows: the suffix *jhi*, the suffix *sya*, the augment *aṭ*, the augment *iṭ*, the substitution of *guṇa* and *avādeśa*, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "ṭhjho'nta" (the final substitute for *jh*), the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule "itaśca," the substitution of *ṣ*, and finally the substitutions of *ru* and *visarga*.

*abhaviṣyatam*: *thas* is replaced by *tam*; *sya*, *aṭ*, *iṭ*, guṇa, and the substitution of *ava*; the elision of the final *i* by the rule *itaśca*; the substitution of *ṣ*; and the substitutions of *r* and *visarga*. *abhaviṣyam*: *mip* is replaced by *am*; *sya*, *aṭ*, *iṭ*, guṇa, and *av*; the formation of the single preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*); the substitution of *ṣ*. *abhaviṣyāva*: [from] *vas*.

[The suffix] *sya* [is added]; *aṭ*; *iṭ*; by the rule "nityaṃ ṅti," there is the elision of the *s*; [then] lengthening of the vowel due to *ataḥ*; and the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus, the form *abhaviṣyāma* is obtained in the first person plural (*masi*). This concludes the procedure for the conditional (*lṛṅ*). Now, he states [the following] as an incidental remark: (76) *te prāgdhātoḥ* | Pāṇini 1.4.80.

"Those [are] before the verbal root. The explanation of "those" is: "the designations *gati* and *upasarga*. The sense is that this is because of the topical context of the rules "prepositions [are so called] when connected with an action" (*upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*) and "and a *gati* [is so called].
"Only before" means not after, nor separated [from the root]. Here, [they are placed] only before the verbal root.

The view that there is a restriction on technical designations (*saṃjñāniyamapakṣa*)— namely, that "those which are employed [as such] shall be termed prefixes (*upasarga*) and verbal roots (*gati*)"— is also established in the *Bhāṣya*.
(77) *āni loṭ* | Pāṇini 8.4.16.

The word *loṭ* [in the sūtra] refers to both *loṭ* and *āni*, with the genitive case ending elided. The rule *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* is understood to follow, as is the word *upasargāt* from the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi*.
Thus he says: "from a cause situated in a prefix. This means: from that which consists of the letters *repha* (r) and *ṣakāra* (ṣ).

The present undertaking is for the purpose of [establishing] the meaning of "non-identity of words" (*asamānapadatva*). The *Bhāṣya* states that the rule "even when there is intervention by *ṭh*, *ṭh*-consonants, *u*, *pa*, *āṅ*, *nuṭ*, or *m*" applies everywhere within the section on *ṇatva*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *dus* for the sake of *ṣatva*": the meaning is that when *ṣatva* and *ṇatva* are to be applied, there is a prohibition of the status of *dus* as a preposition (*upasarga*). For example, in the word *duḥsthitiḥ*.

In the case of *atropasargāt sunoti*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. In *durbhavāni*, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur due to the rule *āni loṭ*.
