Regarding the phrase "of the word *antar*": this means that when an *aṅ* suffix is prescribed, when a *ki* suffix is prescribed, and when the substitution of *ṇ* is to be applied, the word *antar* possesses the status of a prefix (*upasarga*). Since it lacks the status of being one of the [ten] prefixes beginning with *pra*, the [rule for *ṇatva*] would otherwise not apply.

The word *antardhi* [is derived as follows]: under the governing rule *striyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the root *dhā* takes the suffix *aṅ* by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (3.3.106). Then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in *antardhiḥ*. [The word] *antarbhavāṇī*: here the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *āni lo’ḍ* (8.4.17).

(78) *śeṣe vibhāṣā 'kakhādāvaṣānta upadeśe* || 8.4.18 || The rule is: "In the remaining cases, there is optionally [the substitution of *ṣ*], provided that the root does not begin with *ka* or *kha*, and ends in *a* or *ā* in its original form (*upadeśa*). The word *śeṣe* means "in the remaining cases. The analysis of the compound is *akakhādau*. The term "remaining" (*śeṣa*) refers to roots other than those mentioned in the preceding sūtra, *ṭhnergadanadapatapada...*.

Thus he says: "in another [word] than gadana, dā, etc. Now, the section on *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) occurs within the jurisdiction of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination). Consequently, if *saṃhitā* is not intended, there is no *ṇatva* because the condition of being preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) is absent; however, if *saṃhitā* is intended...
Since the substitution of *ṇ* is established by the alternative rule (*vikalpa*), one might ask: "What is the purpose of including the term *vibhāṣā* here? To this he replies:

"In this case, [the rule applies] to prefixes (*upasarga*). He says "it has been stated," with the word "in *hariṇa*" being the ellipsis. Here, by the phrase "in a single word" (*ekapade*), an indivisible word (*akhaṇḍa-pada*) is intended, as indicated by the mark "not in a compound" (*nityāsamāse*).

And "non-segmentation" (*akhaṇḍatva*) means the state of not being divided into further sub-units (*khaṇḍaka*). Otherwise, in forms such as *rājīyati*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) would not optionally occur due to the *śap* suffix. And regarding the "specification of meaning": this refers to the specification of meanings in the Dhātupāṭha, such as *bhū* [meaning] "existence" (*sattā*), and so forth.

"An illustration" (upalakṣaṇam) means it is merely an indication. Now, one might ask: why could this not be a restrictive definition (parisaṃkhyā) excluding other meanings? To this he says: "from sacrifice" (yāgāt). Nor should it be argued: "Why could there not be a secondary figurative sense (lakṣaṇā) regarding origination and so forth in such statements as 'heaven arises from sacrifice'?"

Because of the abundance of usage [in this sense]. For it is established in the commentary on the sūtra *ṭhcuṭū* that Pāṇini recites some roots in the Dhātupāṭha accompanied by their meanings and others without their meanings. Nor should an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) be feared, for roots indeed possess multiple meanings.

In the Bhāṣya, by the use of the word "api" (also), it is understood that [the assignment of meanings] follows actual usage. Furthermore, the assignment of meanings to all verbal roots is a modern innovation. Thus, because the term "gatau" (in the sense of going) is specifically mentioned in the rule "sedhateḥ gatau," the assignment of the meaning "gatyām" (in the sense of going) to the root *ṣidh* is certainly non-Pāṇinian.

[The author] indicates the direction. Now, if the root *bhū* alone has the meaning of "origination" and so forth, then prefixes such as [in] *udbhavī* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "But the prefixes...
Since the meaning of origination and so forth is understood from the root *bhū* even without a prefix, those [prefixes] employed in cases such as *udbhavati*...

The point is that even prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), not denoters (*vācaka*). To the question, "For what purpose should their status as indicators be accepted? he says: "It prevails," and so forth. "Prevailing" (*prabhava*) means manifestation, origination, or power. "Defeat" (*parābhava*) means being overcome.

*Sambhavaḥ*—possibility or expectation; *anubhavaḥ*—enjoyment; *abhibhavaḥ*—injury; *udbhavaḥ*—arising; *paribhavaḥ*—insult. And as for what was said: the word "to the deer" (*hariṇe*) is to be supplied [as the object]. *Prahāraḥ*—a blow from a whip or the like; *āhāraḥ*—eating; *saṃhāraḥ*—killing; *vihāraḥ*—... [leisure/play].

*Krīḍāparihāraḥ* means abandonment. Thus ends the section on the derivation of verbal roots (*bhūdhātuprakriyā*). Regarding the root *edh* in the sense of growth: "it is born, it exists, it transforms, it grows, it wanes, it perishes"—these are the six modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*). Among these, the fourth stage is growth (*vṛddhi*), which is accumulation (*upacaya*). [The suffixes] ending in *kattha*...
The meaning is that [the roots] ending with "ślāghāyām" (Pāṇini 1.4.34) are included. Regarding the term "anudāttet" (having an anudātta indicatory vowel):

the intention is that from these [roots], only the ātmanepada (middle voice) endings occur. In that context, from the root *edh* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), when the present tense (*laṭ*) is applied, and its ātmanepada first person singular ending (*ta*) is substituted, and the *śap* suffix is added, we arrive at the form *edhate*.

(79) *ṭita ātmanepadānāṃ ṭere* (Pāṇini 3.4.79). [Analysis: *ṭita ātma-* and *ṭeḥ*—the word *e* is the division [of the sūtra]. The term *laḥ* is supplied from the governing context (*adhikṛtam*). Thus he says: "of the *ṭit* [suffixes] belonging to *la*" (*ṭito laḥ*). The remainder [to be understood] is "of the substitutes" (*ādeśānām*). Here, by the word *ātmanepada*, only the *ta-re-āḥ* [suffixes] are grasped.
Even for *natvā* and so on; by that [reasoning], it is clear in the Bhāṣya that there is no substitution of *e* in forms such as *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*. Regarding *edhate*:

here, because the vowel *a* following the *t* is considered the final element by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which is designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it possesses the property of being *ṭit*, and thus the substitution of *e* occurs. Now, regarding the suffix *laṭ*...

In the dual of the first person, when *ātām* is substituted [for *tas*], by the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānām ṅit*, there is the substitution of *e* for *ām*. Thus, with the suffix *śap*, we arrive at the form *edh-āte*. Now, intending to state the operations pertaining to the marker *ṅ*, he says: *sārvadhātukam apit*. From the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyo ’ṅit*, the word *aṅit* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
Since it is not possible for a suffix beginning with *iṅ* to follow a verbal root ending in *ā*, it is understood that [the suffix] is *ṅt*.
Thus he says: "*ṅt*.
(80) "After a root ending in *ā*, the suffix *ṅti* [is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.1.81).

*Āto ṅtiḥ*. The term *ṅti* is a genitive of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). From the rule *ato yeya*, the word *ataḥ* (the ablative) and *iya* (the nominative) are understood to carry over. The letter *y* in *iya* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus he says: "after *at*" (*ataḥ parasya*). Immediately after [the mention of] *ṅtām*, [he says]...
The word "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the form *edhete*: once *edha-ātaḥ* has been established, the *iñ* substitute is applied for the vowel *ā*;

then, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs as the final replacement (*antādeśa*), followed by the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule; thus, the meaning is that the *etva* (change to *e*) is applied to the final *ā*. Now, when the first-person dual ending *thas* is substituted for the second-person singular of the present indicative (*laṭ*), [the suffix] *ṭit-*...
When the substitution of *e* for the *ātmanepada* endings is about to apply—(81) *thāsaḥ se* |3|4|80|.
*thāsaḥ se*: *se* is the nominative case with its case-ending elided. Regarding *edhasaḥ*: [it occurs] when *śap* follows *thās*.

The meaning is as follows: *edhethe*. This is derived from the present tense (*laṭ*) in the second person dual; with the substitution of *āthām* for the ending, the addition of the suffix *śap*, the change of *ām* to *e*, the substitution of *iy* for the vowel *ā*, the application of *guṇa*, and the elision of the semivowel (*yalopa*). *Edhadhve*: this is the form from the present tense (*laṭ*) in the second person plural; with the substitution of *dhvam* for the ending, the addition of the suffix *śap*, and the change of the final vowel *ṛ* to *e*. [End of] *laṭ*.

In the third person singular, after the substitution of *iṭ*, the substitution of *et* (for *a*), and the addition of *śap*, the form *edha e* is established; he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) with the rule *ato guṇe*. The meaning is that when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule *ato guṇe* is applied as an exception to *vṛddhi*, the form becomes *edhe*. [The form] *edhāvahe* is derived from *laṭ*.
In the first person plural, when *vah* is substituted [for the suffix], the *ṭi*-portion is replaced by *e*, and with the addition of the *śap* suffix, there is lengthening of the vowel *a*.

Thus: *edhāmahe*. In the first person plural of the present tense (*laṭ*), when *mahi* is substituted [for the suffix], the *ṭi*-portion is replaced by *e*, and with the addition of the *śap* suffix, there is lengthening of the vowel *a*. In the term *mahiṅ*, the letter *ṅ* serves to indicate that it is an *ātmanepada* (taṅ) suffix. This concludes the procedure for the present tense (*laṭ*).

(82) *ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ* |3|1|36|. The word *ijādeḥ* [is part of the sūtra]. The term *anṛcchaḥ* is the ablative case derived from *anṛccha*, which occurs in the compound *nañ-ṛccha*. The word *dhātoḥ* is understood from the previous rule *dhātor ekācaḥ*. [The word *am*] is understood from the rule *kāspratyayād ām...*.
The terms *ā* and *liṭ* carry over [from the previous rule]; thus he says "beginning with *ij*" and so forth.

Regarding *āskāsoḥ*: by the rules "after the root *kās* and after a suffix, *ām* is added in the *liṭ* tense, except in mantras" and "also after *day*, *āya*, and *ās*," the suffix *ām* is prescribed for the roots *kās* and *ās* in the *liṭ* tense. In that case, if the letter *m* were marked with the *it* designation...

By the rule *ṭhmidaco'ntyātparaḥ*, another long *ā* would follow the [final] *ā*; consequently, once the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied, the form would simply be *kās ās*, and thus the prescription of *ām* would be purposeless. Therefore, the meaning is that the *m* of *ām* is understood not to have the designation *it*. And so, *edh-*...

When *ām* is present—as in *ām la*—the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81) applies. From the rule *mantre ghasahvara-* [2.4.80], the word *leḥ* is understood; and from the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañita-* [2.4.58], [the word *lug* is understood].
And the word *liṅ* is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of the *liṭ* following *ām*.

Here, this must be noted: in the rule *kṛnmejanta*, if one explains it as "that which ends in a *mān* suffix belonging to a *kṛt* [verbal derivative] is an indeclinable," then forms such as *edhām* would not be indeclinables, because they belong to the *liṭ* [perfect tense], and that [the *liṭ*] is...
Because it lacks the property of ending in *m*. And thus, by the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), since it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*);

when the case-endings (*svādi*) are produced, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "ām. However, the word "liṅ" does not carry over [from the previous rule]. But in the interpretation that "that which ends in *m* and is a *kṛdanta* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)," by the definition of a suffix...

Because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, *edhām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in *m*. Consequently, when a case-ending (*sup*) arises after it, the elision (*luk*) is applied by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. However, since the elision of the case-ending *l* alone is established by the word *āmaḥ* through the principle of remainder (*pariśeṣa*), the term *leḥ* need not be supplied [from the previous rule]. Thus, the meaning is: "there is elision of the *l* that follows *āmaḥ*."

In the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*), however, the mention of *liṭ* is for the sake of clarity. Thus, there are two positions: whether *edhām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) or not; in either case, it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* that it is a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). (84) *kṛñ cānuprayujyate liṭi* | Pāṇini 3.1.40.

The word *ām* from the rule *kāspratyayādām am* is understood here and is changed to the fifth case (*pañcamī*). By the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), that which ends in the suffix is taken.

The syntactic connection is: "the root *kṛñ* which follows [a verbal base] when the *liṭ* suffix follows is employed as an auxiliary. He states the resulting meaning: "those ending in *ām*, followed by *liṭ*."

The meaning is "headed by the periphrastic perfect (liṭ). Regarding "kṛbhvastayaḥ," the intention is that the term *kṛ* includes the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. Regarding "are employed subsequently" (*anuprayujyante*), the meaning is that they are employed immediately after [the root] and following the prefixes *pra* and *anu*. This is for the purpose of excluding inversion and excluding intervention [by other elements].

This is established from both the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya. Consequently, such usages as "he first caused it to fall" (*taṃ pātayāṃ prathamam āsa papāta paścāt*) and "he who caused Nahuṣa to fall" (*prabhraṃśayāṃ yo nahuṣaṃ cakāra*) are merely erroneous. [The rule states:
"The affix *ām* shall be added after a verbal root, and the root *kṛ* is subsequently employed."

The particle *ca* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) as stated [in the rule]. Now, one might ask: since only the root *kṛ* is heard to be used in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), how can there be subsequent application of *bhū* and *as* as well? To this, he says: "like the *ām* affix," and so forth.
For, while in the rule "and *kṛ* is used in subsequent application" (*kṛñ cānuprayujyate*), only the single root *kṛ* is prescribed for subsequent application...

In the sūtra *ṭhāmpratyayavat*, the qualification "of the root *kṛ*" (*kṛñaḥ*) for the term "that which is employed subsequently" (*anuprayujyamānasya*) would be redundant, because the subsequent employment of any other verbal root is impossible [under those conditions]. Therefore, the meaning is that by the qualification "of the root *kṛ*," the subsequent employment of something else is also understood. But [one might object]:

One might ask: "How is it understood that *kṛñ* may be used as an auxiliary for others as well, and even for *bhū* and *as*? To this he says: "By that" (*tena*). This means: by the mention of *kṛñ*. [He adds: "Because of the recourse to the *pratyāhāra*. And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya*. Now, regarding those being used as auxiliaries...
To the question, "How is there a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, and those that serve as the bases for the *ām* affix?
he says, starting from "of these" up to "there is a connection by way of non-difference.
The sense is that a connection by way of non-difference is logical between a general property and its particulars, just as in the case of the root *kṛ*.

It should be understood that this is because both *bhū* and *as* denote general action (*kriyāsāmānya*), as verbal roots possess multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*). Now, one might object: between the two rules "in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*" (*kṛbhvastiyoge*) and "after *kṛ* when a second [accusative] follows" (*kṛño dvitīye*), the rule "also with *sam-pad* in the sense of limit-inclusive" (*abhividhau saṃpadā ca*) is recited. And thus...
To the question, "Why is *saṃpad* not also included in the *kṛn* pratyāhāra?", he says:

"But *saṃpad*... [The reason is] "because its meaning is not connected" (*ananvitārthatvāt*). The meaning of the root *saṃpad* is the transformation of an already established entity into another form. However, in the case of roots such as *edh*, which serve as the base for the suffix *ām*, [the meaning is different].

The meaning [of the suffix] is "increase" and so forth. The sense is that since both of these are specific forms, there can be no relation of general and particular between them, and thus a syntactic connection as identity (abhedānvaya) is impossible. This is why the *Bhāṣya* states, "therefore, the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are mentioned," which is consistent with this view. Now, one might object:

One might object that the sūtra prescribing the *ātmanepada* endings for the root *kṛ*, which is to be stated later as "like the *ām*-affix" (*āmpratyayavat*), would be redundant, since its purpose is already accomplished by the rule "the [roots] marked with a svarita accent or a ñ or ṇ" (*svaritañit*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "But of *kṛ*... (85) *āmpratyayavatkṛño 'nuprayogasya* | 1.3.63 |.
From the rule *āmpratyayavat kṛñ... anudātaṅti* (Pāṇini 1.3.66), the term *ātmanepada* is understood to carry over.

Since the affix *ām* itself does not possess the status of an *ātmanepada*, he says: "The *bahuvrīhi* compound here is one that does not include the qualities of those [members]. Of that other referent (*anyapadārtha*), the "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) are its specific attributes.
The forms of the constituent word-meanings possess a unified cognition (*saṃvijñāna*) through their connection with the action,
but this does not apply even to variegated cows. Likewise, in the present case, it is only the verbal root such as *edh*—
which is the base of the *ām*-affix and is itself divested of that *ām*-affix— that [is intended].
The intended meaning is that only a verbal root such as *edh* (to increase) and others is understood by the term "the suffix *ām*.

The suffix *vati* is applied to the word *āmpratyaya*, which ends in the third case (*āmpratyayena*). The term *anuprayoga* means "that which is employed subsequently"; it is derived from the root *yuja* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe ṣaṣṭhī*). This is what he expresses by the words beginning with "by the base of *ām*" (*āmprakṛtyā*). [The purpose is] for it to arise from the base of *ām*.

The meaning is that whatever *ātmanepada* ending is appropriate [for the root], it should also apply to the root *kṛ* when it is used as an auxiliary (*anuprayoga*). Regarding this, there is no reference to a *pratyāhāra* (a collective term for a set of suffixes); for the *Bhāṣya* states: "Since the rule would have been established by the words 'of the auxiliary' (*anuprayogasya*) alone, the explicit mention of *kṛ* here indicates that there is no reference to a *pratyāhāra*. This applies even when the action results in something external (*paragāmin*).

This introduction [of the rule] is for the purpose of the *ātmanepada* affix after the root *kṛ* when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. However, in cases such as *indam cakāra*, the *ātmanepada* does not occur by this rule when the fruit of the action goes to another, because there is no *ātmanepada* for the root *ṭhiv* (meaning "supreme sovereignty") which forms the base of the *ām* affix; that root is *parasmaipadi*.

It is for this very purpose that *āmpratyayavat* was included [in the rule]. Now, one might object: in cases such as *indāṃcakāra*, let there be no *ātmanepada* by this sūtra when the fruit of the action accrues to another;
however, when the fruit of the action accrues to oneself, the *ātmanepada* prescribed by the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* would be unavoidable.

This sūtra is capable only of prescribing the *ātmanepada*— which would otherwise not apply when the fruit of the action accrues to another— as in examples such as *edhāṃścakre*; it is not capable of excluding the *ātmanepada* that would already be applicable by the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent himself.
Because there is a lack of logical capacity [to establish this], he says "here" (*iha*). Here,
in the rule *āmpratyayavat kṛño 'nuprayogasya*, the word *pūrvavat* is carried over from the preceding rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ*.
One should form two distinct sentences: "ṭhāmpratyayavat kṛño 'nuprayogasya" (Pāṇini 1.3.63) as one sentence, and "ṭhpūrvavat kṛño 'nuprayogasya" (Pāṇini 1.3.62) as another.
In this context, the suffix *vati* is applied to the word *pūrva*, which ends in the third case (*pūrvavat*). [The term] *pūrveṇa* means "by what was previously employed."

The meaning is "equal to the roots beginning with *edh*. In that context, since two sentences would be redundant if they possessed the same meaning, the second sentence becomes a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).
It means: "the *ātmanepada* [suffix] occurs only as before, and not its opposite. And thus, by the first sentence, [the suffix is applied] in *edhāñcakre*.
In such cases as these, the rule for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed for the root *kṛ* even when the fruit of the action accrues to another;

however, by the second sentence, in cases such as *indāñcakāra*, where the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the application of the middle voice by the rule *svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* is precluded. Thus he says: "by that."

The meaning is "by the second sentence. "Not *taṅ*" means that the *ātmanepada* endings are not used. Thus, when the *liṭ* [perfect] of the root *kṛ* (to do) is subsequently applied, and the *taṅ* [ātmanepada] endings are present, in the first person singular, after the substitution of *ta*, the form stands as *edhām kṛ ta*.
(86) *liṭas tajhayor eś irec* [Pāṇini 3.4.81]. Regarding *liṭas tajhayo*: one might object that it should simply be *liṭas tajhayor iś iric*;

the vocalization of the letter *e* in the substitutes would be redundant, since the substitution of *i* for the *ātmanepada* endings ending in a *ṭit* suffix is already provided by [Pāṇini 3.4.79: *ṭita ātmanepadānām eñ*].
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of accomplishment," [the author] says "the utterance of the vowel *e*. He states the purpose of this indication:
"In that case, there is no *e*-substitution for *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*";

the meaning is that there is no substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* (the last vowel with its following consonant) of these substitutes for the *ātmanepada* endings—namely, *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. However, in reality...

It is stated clearly in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *luṭaḥ prathamasya* that once the substitution of *e* (for *ta*) has been applied by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the substitution of *ḍā* and so forth occurs; however, because of the maxim *lakṣye lakṣaṇasya* (the rule does not apply again to what it has already affected), the substitution of *e* does not take place again.
Thus, when the form *kṛ-e* remains, the single substitute *e* replaces the entire cluster consisting of the letter *t* and the vowel *a*.
The intention is that [the substitution] is a universal replacement (*sarvādeśa*) because it is *śit*.

(87) *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5): "The *liṭ* [affixes] following a root that does not end in a conjunct consonant are *kit*. *apiditi*: "[The affixes] beginning with *ap* are *sārvadhātuka*. *sārvadhātukam api*.

The intention is that [the rule] applies because it follows that [principle]. It should be understood, however, that the status of being marked with *ṅ* (ṅittva) by the rule "sārvadhātukam apit" does not apply here, because the substitutes for *liṭ* are treated as *ārdhadhātuka*. He states the result of the *kit* designation: "and when *k* or *ṅ* follow. [He says] "due to reduplication," meaning that when *liṭ* follows, [the rule] "dhātoḥ" [applies] after the root.

The results of [the suffix] *kit* should be understood from [the rules concerning] doubling (*dvitva*) and subsequentness (*paratva*), etc. He states the result of *kit*-ness: "and when *kṅit* follows.
Regarding "from doubling": the sense is that when *kṛ-e* is in this state, doubling would not occur by the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ*.

(88) *dvirvacane'ci* | 1.1.59 | Regarding *dvirvacane'ci*: that by which something is reduplicated due to a subsequent cause is called "reduplication" (*dvirvacana*); that is to say, it refers to the cause of doubling. This [word *dvirvacane*] is an adjective qualifying *aci*. [The word *aci* means] "in place of a vowel" (*acaḥ*).

From the rule *parasmin* [6.1.86], the word *acaḥ* is understood; from *sthānivadādeśaḥ* [1.1.56], the word *ādeśaḥ*; and from *na padānta-* [1.1.58], the word *na* is understood. The term *dvirvacane* is repeated. Thus, it is also understood that "when a doubling (*dvitva*) is to be performed."

Thus he says: "When the vowel is the cause of doubling," and so forth. By stating "when doubling is to be performed," [it follows that] in forms such as *cakre*, once doubling has been effected, the *yaṇ* substitution and other rules apply. Otherwise, they would not apply, because the vowel that is the cause of doubling would still exist. Why say "the cause of doubling"? Consider *dudyaūṣati*.
In the case of the root *div* with the suffix *san*, since the substitution of *ūṭh* occurs later than reduplication, the *yaṇ* substitution indeed takes place prior to reduplication.

Consequently, when there is reduplication of *dyaū*, the form *dudyaūṣati* is established. However, if the *yaṇ* were prohibited when reduplication is to be performed, then only the vowel *i* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable—namely, *didyaūṣati*—and not the vowel *u*.

If, however, the rule were stated as "dvitvanimite" (when there is a cause for doubling), then in a case like *uṭhi* followed by a vowel, the prohibition [of *yaṇ*] would not apply prior to the doubling, because the *ūṭh* substitution is not itself the cause of doubling. Why is the condition "before a vowel" (*aci*) specified? Consider *jeghrīyate*. Here, in the case of the root *ghrā*, before the doubling of the *yaṅ* suffix, the substitution of *ī* for the *ā* of *ghrā-dhmā-ḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.67) does not take place.

It is prohibited. Although the substitution of *ī* (ītva) is caused by reduplication (*dvitva*), it is not caused by that which is the cause of reduplication [namely, the suffix *yaṅ*]. Why "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider *asūṣupat*. Here, because of the reduplication of the root *svap* after the *caṅ* affix, the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *v* in *svap*—by the rule "after *caṅ*, there is substitution for the *v* of *svap*"—does not take place prior to the reduplication.

[The substitution] is prohibited because that [element] lacks the status of being a substitute for *aja* (a vowel). Consequently, once *saṃprasāraṇa* has been applied, when *sup* is doubled, the hearing of the letter *u* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is possible. However, if *saṃprasāraṇa* were prohibited, then when *svap* is doubled, the letter *u* would not be heard in the reduplicated syllable. And thus, in the present case...
Before the substitution of *yaṇ*, when the reduplication (*dvitva*) has been applied by the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ...* [Pāṇini 6.1.1] in the case of the suffix *liṭ*, the form *kṛ kṛ e* is established.
(89) *urat* | 7.4.66 | *urat*: The analysis is *uḥ* and *at*. The word *ṛt* is replaced by *ur*; this is the genitive singular of *ṛt*. Here...

From the rule *lopo'bhyāsasya*, the word *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplicated syllable) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. The term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). By virtue of that, it is understood as "when a suffix follows," because the designation *aṅga* is prescribed only when a suffix follows. This is what he states with the words beginning "of the vowel of the reduplicated syllable."

"Raparatvam" means that the vowel *a*, which is the substitute for the reduplicated syllable, takes the suffix *ra* as its subsequent element (*rapara*) by the rule "uraṇ rapara. Thus, when the form *kar kṛ e* is established, the rule "halādiḥ śeṣaḥ" [P. 7.4.60] applies;

the intention is that the *repha* (the letter *r*) is removed. [The question] "Why [is it said] 'when there is an affix'? [is asked] because [the substitution] occurs only through the *aṅga* (the stem).
The meaning is: since the condition (*pratyaya*) is already implied, for what purpose is it stated "when a suffix follows" (*pratyaye parataḥ*)? Regarding *vavraśca*:
from the root *vraścū* in the sense of "cutting," there is *ṇal* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), followed by reduplication.
By the rule *liṭaḷbhyāsasya*, the semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *ṛ* in the reduplicated syllable occurs, resulting in *ṛ*. Then, by *urat*, *ṛ* is replaced by *ra*.

[The root] *vṛ* and so forth; [the suffix] *śas*; the form is *vavraśca*. Here, regarding the vowel *a*—which results from the substitution of *u* for the semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) that replaced the *ṛ* of the reduplicated syllable—that *a* is treated as a semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) by virtue of the rule *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (P.

1.1.57). Consequently, by the rule *na samprasāraṇe* (P. 6.1.37), the semivowel *v* [of the reduplication] does not undergo semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) when that [substituted *a*] follows.

The established conclusion is that there is no *samprasāraṇa* because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] "samprasāraṇam. If, however, the phrase "when followed by an affix (*pratyaye parataḥ*)" were not stated in the rule *uraṅ*, then— since the vowel *a* which replaces the *ṛ* that has undergone *samprasāraṇa* would lack a subsequent cause— the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule would not even arise.

The sense is that because there is an absence of *samprasāraṇa*-ness, the prohibition— "there is no *samprasāraṇa* when a *samprasāraṇa* follows"— would not apply when that [suffix] follows. (90) *kuhoścu* 7.4.62.

And thus, when *kṛ-kṛ-e* has been established, [the rule] *kuhoścuḥ* applies. From the compound *ku-hoḥ*, there is a genitive dual. Here, the word *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplication") is understood from the previous rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya*. Therefore, he says: "of the reduplication."
Although there is no correspondence by number— since there are six *sthānins*, namely the gutturals (*kavargīya*) and the letter *ha*, while there are only five palatals (*cavargīya*)—

nor is there internal proximity based on place of articulation, because of the difference between the throat and the palate as their respective places; nevertheless, there is equality in terms of internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*).
The [place of articulation] for the *ka*-group and the *ca*-group is indistinct. However, for the *ha*-sound and the *ca*-group, that [place of articulation] does not exist at all;
therefore, in this case, the internal effort must be accepted as the determining factor based solely on the external effort.
Among those, for the first sound of the *ka*-group, the first sound of the *ca*-group alone occurs.

It is not the first [consonant], because of the similarity in its effort (*prayatna*) as being voiceless (*aghoṣa*), having a breathy release (*vivāra*), and having little aspiration (*alpapāṇa*); nor is it the second, because that has great aspiration (*mahāpāṇatva*). Nor are they the third and fifth, because those have the efforts of being voiced (*ghoṣa*), having a closed release (*saṃvāra*), and being resonant (*nāda*). Nor...

The fourth [consonant of each class] arises from the effort of being voiced, having a stoppage of sound, and possessing great breath; likewise, for the second consonant of the *ka*-class, the corresponding second of the *ca*-class occurs because it shares the effort of being unvoiced, having aspiration, and having a wide opening, but not the first, because that has little breath.

Nor are the third and fifth [of each class], because they possess the effort of being voiced, having a closed glottis, and having weak breath. Nor is the fourth [of each class], because it possesses the effort of being voiced, having a closed glottis, and [weak] breath. Likewise, for the third letter of the *ka*-class, the third letter of the *ca*-class is the substitute, because they share the effort of being voiced, having a closed glottis, and weak breath.

But it is not the first [type of sound], because its effort (*prayatna*) consists of being voiceless, having aspiration (*śvāsa*), and being spread (*vivāra*). For this very reason, it is also not the second, because its effort is that of a "great breath" (*mahāprāṇa*). Nor is it the fourth, because it is a "great breath. Nor is it the fifth, because although there is equality in terms of being voiced, having closure (*saṃvāra*), resonance (*nāda*), and "small breath" (*alprāṇa*), there is a distinction due to its nasality (*anunāsikatā*).

Likewise, for the fourth letter of the *ka*-group (*kha*), the corresponding letter of the *ca*-group (*cha*) occurs, because they share the same articulatory efforts of being voiced, having a closed glottis, possessing resonance, and being aspirated. It does not become the first letter (*ca*), because that possesses the efforts of being unvoiced, having an open glottis, and being unaspirated. Nor does it become the second letter (*cha*).

Because [the letter *ha*] possesses the effort-features (*prayatna*) of being voiceless (*aghoṣa*), open (*vivāra*), and accompanied by aspiration (*śvāsa*), it cannot be the third or fifth [consonants] of its class, since those are characterized by being "unaspired" (*alpaprāṇa*).

Furthermore, among the fifth consonants of the guttural class (*kavarga*), only the letter *ña* is applicable because it is nasal (*anunāsika*). However, since the letter *ha* possesses the features of being voiced (*ghoṣavat*), closed (*saṃvāravat*), sonorous (*nādamat*), and "aspirated" (*mahāprāṇavat*), it corresponds to the fourth letter of that same class, which is *jha*.

Analysis: In the present case, when *ka-kṛ-e* is established, the *k* of the reduplicated syllable becomes *c*, and the *ṛ* undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution to become *r*. Thus he says: *edhāṃcakra*. The meaning is: "an action consisting of growth, performed by a single agent, in the remote past (bhūta) not of today. *Edhāṃcakrāte*: [from] *kṛñ*.

In *liṭ* [the suffix] *ātām*, the substitution of *ē* for *ā* occurs. Since the rule "when there is reduplication, before a vowel" (*dvirvacane 'ci*) prohibits *yaṇ* [substitution], there is reduplication of the root *kṛ*; then *urat* [substitution] applies. Then *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* [remains]; then *ca*-substitution; then *yaṇ*. Now, even though *ātām* is the cause of reduplication, how is it that here—[given that] the vowel *ā* is not the cause of reduplication?

The point is that one must state that there is a prohibition of *yaṇ* by the rule "ṭhdvarvacane'cī" (Pāṇini 1.1.59), because the term "cause of doubling" (*dvitvanimitta*) is intended to refer specifically to that which is the cause of doubling, whether directly or as a constituent part of the whole. Thus, in the form *edhāṃcakrire*: [the suffix] *jhi* becomes *irec*, and [the root] *kṛ*...
The formation of the number two (*dvitva*) and so forth is as previously described.

(91) Pāṇini 7.2.10 states: *ekāca upadeśe 'nudātāt* ("A monosyllabic root that is unaccented in its original form [upadeśa]"). Now, when the *liṭ* suffix replaces *thās* with *se*, and after the reduplication (*dvitva*) of the root *kṛ*, we have *edhām ca kṛ se*.

When [the suffix] ṭhārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ applies, the augment iṭ would have to be inserted; however, [this is prevented by the rule] ekāca upadeśe. From the rule ṛta iddhātoḥ, the word *dhātu* (root) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). And from the rule neḍvaśi kṛti, the word *na* (not) also carries over. Thus he says: "a root which consists of a single vowel in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)."

The term *ekāc* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has one vowel. Regarding the phrase *ārddhadhātukasya*: although this is neither explicitly stated nor obtainable through *anuvṛtti*, it is nevertheless implied (*ārthika*), because the augment *iṭ* is applicable only to an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, the term *ārddhadhātukasya* is not mentioned. Now, [one might object]: "But what about a root that has only one vowel..."
In the rule *upadeśe 'nudāttāt*, if the term *upadeśe* were to connect with *ekācaḥ*, then there would be no prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of *kartum*;
for although the root *kṛñ* will be stated to be *anudātta* by the rule beginning with *ūdit-ṛdanta-* etc., [the condition of being *anudātta* in the original enunciation would not apply].

When the *tumun* suffix is applied, [the first syllable] becomes acute by virtue of the rule "that which begins with *ṭh*, *ñ*, or *ṇ* is always [acute]. However, if the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) is construed with "from that which is grave" (*anudātāt*), then although this fault does not arise— since even though it is acute once the *tumun* suffix has been applied, it was grave at the time of the root's original instruction (*upadeśa*)— [the following applies].

Since the prohibition of *iṭ* is thus unassailable, one might still object that in forms such as *edhāñcakṛṣe*, the prohibition of *iṭ* would not apply because the root is no longer *ac* (a single vowel) once reduplication has occurred; therefore, he says: "The term 'in the original enunciation' (*upadeśe*) applies to both. This word "original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) connects with both [the rule for] "a monosyllabic [root]" (*ekāc*) and with "unaccented" (*anudātta*).

The meaning is: "according to the principle of the middle [option]. Now, one might ask: since the roots enumerated by the rule *udṛdantaiḥ* etc.—namely those taught as having anudātta vowels—are invariably single-voweled (*ekāc*), the mention of *ekāc* need not be made; let there simply be the condition *upadeśe'nudātāt*, for by this much alone the prohibition of *iṭ* is established in forms such as *cakṛṣe*. Thus he asks: "Why [the word] *ekācaḥ*? [The answer is: "To exclude the *yaṅ*-lopa. That is to say, the mention of *ekāc* is for the purpose of excluding the prohibition of *iṭ* in cases like *carikṛteti* and others where the *yaṅ* suffix has been elided.

[Objection: But even if the mention of "a single vowel" (ekāj) is made, how is the exclusion of the *yaṅ* elision (*yaṅluk*) achieved? Examples for [the rule] beginning with "by means of *śtip*, *śap*, etc. will become clear in the discussion of *yaṅluk*. [Reply: Now, although the exclusion of the prohibition of *iṇ* in the case of *yaṅluk* follows from the mention of "a single vowel," the exclusion of those [roots] specified by *śtip* and so forth in the case of *yaṅluk*—though agreed upon by ancient teachers—is not accepted by Pāṇini. To this, he says: "And this... (*etacca*).

The meaning is this: although all of this is established by the *Śloka-siddha* (the metrical rule), it is indicated here in the Sūtra by the very mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*) through the principle of partial acceptance (*ekadeśānumati*). Now, one might object: [If that were so,] would not the singular number in rules such as *ṭhano vadha liṅ* and *ṭhluiṅ ce*—specifically in the phrase *aca ityekatva* and so forth, ending with *vyāvartyate*—be contradicted? For in the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudātāt*, even if the word *eka* were removed and only *aca* were stated, the sense "from a base consisting of a single vowel" (*ekāckāt*) would still be obtained; there is no authority for abandoning the singularity conveyed by the singular number.

It should not be argued that this being the case, one would obtain only "of what follows an *ac* qualified by oneness," and not "from that which consists of a single *ac*" as the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi*; for, by virtue of the inclusion of roots such as *śaklṛ*, *pac*, and *muc* in the enumeration of those taught with an *anudātta* vowel, it is possible to accept the inclusion of that which possesses a single *ac* by resorting to a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) for the term "*aj-vataḥ*."

Thus, since the rule would already be established by the word *ekācaḥ* alone, the fact that he employs the term *eka-* (in *ekācaḥ*) has the following force: by implication, it is understood that [the root] must be monosyllabic (*ekāc*) throughout its entire original enunciation (*upadeśa*), and not merely in some instances of its enunciation. By this reasoning, the possibility of excluding a root that is polysyllabic (*anekāc*) in its original enunciation is sometimes set aside. This is the meaning.

Since the meaning "only when [the root] is taught as having a single vowel" is obtained everywhere in the context of *upadeśa*, the phrase *hanty-upadeśe* means: "even though the substitute *vadhi* for the root *han* is [originally] a single-vowel [root] when taught as *han*," the prohibition of *iṭ* after it does not apply. Why? To this he says: *ādeśopadeśe*. The point is that in the case of *avadhīt*, the *Bhāṣya* states that the substitute *vadhi* for *han* must end in *a* (i.e., *vadh-a*) in order to prevent the application of the rule *ato halāder laghoḥ* (P. 7.2.7), which would otherwise cause *vṛddhi*.

Now, one might ask: "Which roots are *anudātta*? To this he says: "But the *anudātta* [roots] are immediately after. "Immediately after" (*anupadam*) means following the word; that is to say, when only a single word has passed. It means "right after. For example: *edhāṃcakṛṣe*. In the absence of *iṭ*, there is *ṣatva* because it is part of the affix. *Edhāṃcakrāthe*: here, *āthām* is the substitute for *liṭ*. The substitution of *etva* for *ṭi*, reduplication, and so forth, are as before. When *dhvam* is substituted for *liṭ*, and *etva* and reduplication have occurred, we have the form *edhācakṛ-dhve*. (92) *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dho'ṅgāt* | Pāṇini 8.3.78. [The substitute *dhi* takes the place of *dhvam* after an *aṅga* ending in *iṇ* (i, u, ṛ, ḷ) in the forms of *ṣīdhvam*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ*.]

The term *iṇaḥ* [is the ablative of] *iṇ*; *ṣīdhvam*, *ṣīdhvam*, and *luṅliṭ* form a *dvandva* compound; *dhaḥ* is the genitive singular. *Iṇ* is a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*). The rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. The governing rule *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* ("a retroflex substitute occurs for a non-final [consonant]") is in force. Thus he says: "from that which ends in *iṇ*" and so forth. For the letter *dh*, there is the substitution of *ḍh*.
It is a *mūrdhanya* [retroflex], due to the similarity in effort (*prayatna*) consisting of voicedness (*ghoṣa*), closure (*saṃvāra*), resonance (*nāda*), and great breath (*mahāprāṇa*).

Thus he says: "edhāṃcakṛṇḍhavaḥ. Regarding the first person singular, after the addition of *iṭ*, the substitution of *etva*, and having performed reduplication and so forth as before, he states the form: "edhāṃcakre. [And] "edhāṃcakṛvaha" [is the first person dual]. [This refers to] the *liṭ* [perfect tense].

When there is external substitution (*bahirbhāva*), the doubling (*dvitva*) and subsequent operations are as before. Likewise, in the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, when there is external substitution, the doubling and subsequent operations are as before. In all cases, because the suffixes of the *liṭ* [perfect] are marked with *k* when not preceded by a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyoga*), there is an absence of *guṇa* due to their being *kit*.
Now, he provides an example for the application of the root *bhū* at the end of a *liṅ* [periphrastic perfect]: *edhām babhūva*. [He also provides: *edhāṃ cakre*.

This has the same meaning as the preceding rule, because the root *bhū* when employed subsequently expresses the general sense of action (*kriyāsāmānya*). Now, one might object: since the substitute for *liṭ* (the perfect tense suffix) in the subsequent employment of the root *as* is an *ārdhadhātuka*, the rule *aster bhūḥ*—which prescribes *bhū* for *as* in an *ārdhadhātuka* context—would apply.
To the question, "Why would the substitution of *bhū* not occur [for the root *as*]? he says: "In the case of *anuprayoga*.

This means that because the rule for the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*—based on the inclusion of *as* within the pratyāhāra *kṛñ*—is established by the force of that very injunction, the substitution of *bhū* does not take place for the root *as*.

He establishes that very point with the words "otherwise": if one were to accept the transformation of the root *as* (to be) into *bhū* (to become) when it is not being perceived [as such], then the rule regarding subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)—namely, "the root *kṛ* is subsequently applied," or "either *kṛ* or *bhū* is subsequently applied"—would have stated either "the root *kṛ* is subsequently applied" or "either *kṛ* or *bhū* is subsequently applied. By that much alone, [the form] would have been *edhām babhūva*.

The meaning is "for the sake of establishing [the desired form]. Although there is brevity (*lāghava*) in stating *kṛ* (from the root *kṛñ*), the intention is that one should not undergo the trouble of using the pratyāhāra *kṛñ* merely to obtain the additional root *bhū* for a single instance. For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke*, regarding the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*):
The Bhāṣya statement, "there is no sublation [of the substitution] because of the state of being *bhū*," is thus consistent.

(93) *ata ādeḥ* 7.4.70. Consequently, when the root *as* is subsequently employed in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), the substitution of *bhū* is precluded; thus, in the case of the suffix *ṇal*, we have *edhām*.

When *as* is thus established, after doubling (*dvitva*) and the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, we have *a-as*. At this point, although *savarṇadīrghaḥ* would apply, it is superseded by *ato guṇaḥ*, which would result in the single substitute *pararūpa*. However, [the rule] *ata ādeḥ* applies; from the rule *atra lopaḥ*, the word *abhyāsasya* is understood to carry over, and from *dīrgha iṇaḥ*, the word *dīrghaḥ* is also carried over.

He says that regarding "of practice" (*abhyāsasya*): whatever needs to be said here will be explained on the occasion of commenting on the passage beginning with "he acts like *ṭha*" (*ṭha ivācarati*) in the section on the formation of nominal stems (*nāmadhātuprakriyā*). As for *edhāmāsa*:
one should not assume that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies here by analogy with the suffix *ām* [as in *edhām cakre*], based on the [unexpressed] roots *as* and *bhū*.
This is to be suspected, because it has been stated in the Bhāṣya that in that context, by the mention of *kṛñ*, there is no inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* (the group of suffixes).

Regarding "edhāmāsatuḥ" and so forth: *edhāmāsuḥ*, *edhāmāsitha*, *edhāmāsathuḥ*, *edhāmāsa*, *edhāmāsiva*, *edhāmāsima*. This is the procedure (*prakriyā*) for the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). Regarding *edhitā*: this is the substitution of the *tā* suffix for the *luṭ* [future] tense marker.

With *edh-ta* established, the suffix *śa* is set aside by *tas*. By the rule *luṭaḥ prathamasya*, *ḍā* is applied. There is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *ta*). Thus, the form is *edhita*. By the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel does not occur.
For *edhitārau*: the suffix *ātām* is applied to *luṭ*; *iṭ* is added after *tās*; and the substitution of *rau* occurs for *ātām*. *ri-* [is applied].

And there is the elision of *s* (*salopa*). Regarding *edhitāraḥ*: *jha* becomes *ra*, *tās*, *iṭ*, and by "if *ri*" there is the elision of *s*; then *ru*-ness and visarga. Regarding *edhitāsāḥ*: *thās* becomes *se*, *tās*, *iṭ*, and by "of *tās* and *asti*" there is the elision of *s*. Regarding *edhitāsāthe*: for *āthām*, there is the substitution of *e* (*etvam*), *tās*.

*iṭ* (94). And [the substitution of *e* occurs] before *dhi*. Now, when *dhvam* has undergone the substitution of *etva* (*e*) due to the augment *iṭ*, resulting in the form *edhitāsdhve*, the rule *dhi ca* applies. [The substitute *s* is applied. *saḥ*.

From the rule "syārdhadhātuke," the word "sa" (the suffix *s*) is carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule "tāsastyor luṅliṭoḥ," the word "lopaḥ" (elision) is carried over. The suffix, which is implied by the term "aṅga" (stem), is qualified by the word "dhī" (before the affix *dhi*). This is a rule for that specific occasion. Thus he says: "in the root. When the *s* of *tās* is elided, the forms are "edhitā" and "edhitādhve."

(95) *ha eti* | Pāṇini 7.4.52. Now, when the substitute *iṭ* for *luṭ* undergoes *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *ay*), and after *tāsi* followed by *iṭ*, we have *edhitās-e*. This being the state, [the rule] *ha eti* applies.
Here, *ha* is in the nominative case (*prathamāntam*). The vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The word *sa* [is understood] from the previous rule *saḥ syārdhadhātuke*.

Thus, the rule "there is elision of *tās* and *asti*" (*tāsastyorlopaḥ*) and the phrase "after [the suffixes] *tās* and *asti*" (*itastāsastyoḥ*) are understood to follow. Therefore, he says: "after *tās* and *asti*. Regarding the form *edhitāhe*: the *s* of *tās* becomes *h* before the [suffix] *he*. Regarding *edhitāsvahe*: there is the substitution of *vah* for *mas* (the first person dual ending) in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). There is the substitution of *e* for the final *ṭi* (the *a* of *svas*). Then comes *tās*, then *iṭ*. In the same way—

"edhitāsmahe"—in this case, the specific feature is the *mahinbhāva* (the substitution of the long vowel). This concludes the procedure for the *luṭ* suffix. Regarding "edhiṣyate": when the *ta* of the *lṛṭ* is substituted [by *te*], the *e* of *ṭe* is applied. By the rule *syatāsī*, *sya* is the substitute for *śab* (the marker of the future tense), and *iṭ* is added. Because it is a part of the affix (*pratyayāvayava*), the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) occurs. Regarding "edhiṣyete": [the suffix] *ātām* is used. The *e* of *ṭe* is applied, and then *sya*.

*it* [is added]. By the rule *ṭhāto ṅtiḥ*, the vowel *ā* is replaced by *iy*. By the rule *lopo vyor vali*, there is elision of *y*. By the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, *guṇa* substitution occurs. Then *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) is applied, resulting in *edhiṣyante*. Here, *etva* (the change to *e*) is applied to the *jha* suffix; that is, the substitute *anta* is applied to the letter *jh*. Then *sya* is added, followed by *iṭ*. There is *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form), and then *ṣatva*. This same process applies even when *thās* and other suffixes follow, as in the case of the *laṭ* tense.

Thinking that they are easy to construct, the forms have not been shown in detail. In this regard: for *thās*, there is *se*; then *sya*; then *iṭ*; then *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*); thus the form is *edhiṣyase*. Like *edhiṣyete*, in the case of *āthām*, the form is *edhiṣyethe*. For *dhvam*, there is *etva* (the substitution of *e*); then *sya*; then *iṭ*; then *ṣatva*; thus the form is *edhiṣyadhve*. [In the case of *idhve*], there is *etva* of *iṭ*.

The augment *iṭ* is applied; *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) occurs; by the rule *ato guṇe*, the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) applies, resulting in the form *edhiṣye*. For the first person dual and plural (*vahimahe*), the vowel *e* is substituted for *et*; *sya* is added; *iṭ* is applied; and by the rule *ato dīrghaḥ*, the long vowel is substituted, resulting in the forms *edhiṣyāvahe* and *edhiṣyāmahe*. Thus concludes the procedure for the *lṛṭ* (future tense).
(96) *āmetaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.90. The analysis is *ām-eta*. From the rule *loṭo laṅvat*, the word *loṭaḥ* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*).
Therefore, he says: "of the *e*-sound of the *loṭ* [imperative]. That is, of that which is a constituent part of a substitute for the *loṭ* suffix.

The meaning is "of the vowel *e*. Regarding *edhatām*: this is the form derived from the imperative (*loṭ*) after the substitution of *ta*, the replacement of *ṭi* by *e*, the substitution of *ām*, and the addition of the suffix *śap*.

Regarding *edhetām*: [this is formed] with *ātām*; there is the replacement of *ṭi* by *e*, the suffix *śap*, and because the suffix is marked with *ṅ* by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, the *ā* is replaced by *iy* according to the rule *āto ṅti*, followed by *guṇa*.

There is the elision of the letter *y*. In the case of *ṭhāmeta*, the vowel *e* is replaced by *ām*. Regarding *edhantām*: after the substitution of *ṭi* for *jhi* and the addition of the suffix *śap*, the letter *jh* is replaced by *anta*, and the vowel *e* is replaced by *ām*. Then, in the case of the imperative (*loṭ*), when *sthas* has been changed to *se* and the suffix *śap* is added, the form *edha-se* is established.

(97) *savābhyāṃ vāmau* | 3|4|91| The analysis of *savābhyām* is as follows: *sa* and *va* are *savau*; [the compound] *tābhyām* [is formed from them]. The two *a*-vowels are for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). *va* and *am* are *vām*; [the suffix] *ṭh* is [added] to the imperative (*loṭ*).

The words *laṅvad* (as if it were *laṅ*) from [Pāṇini 3.4.103] and *ṭhāmeta* (the substitute *eta* for *ṭhām*) from [Pāṇini 3.4.105] are understood here. Thus he says: "after the letter *s*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṭhāmeta*. Regarding *edhasva*: in the rule *edha-seṭaḥ*, there is a substitution of the cluster *va*—consisting of the vowel *u* and the consonant *v*—for the vowel *e*. Regarding *edhethām*: this is the form with *āthām*.

The state of being *ṭe* (the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the suffix). *Śap* (the present tense marker). By the rule *āto ṅit*, there is *iy* for the vowel *ā*. Guṇa substitution. Elision of *y*. *Ām* by the rule *āmeta*. Regarding *edhadhvam*: in the suffix *dhvam*, after *śap* has been applied and the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* has been made, *ām* is substituted for the *e* because it follows the letter *v* according to the rule *savābhyām*.

(98) *eta ai* | Pāṇini 3.4.93. When the suffix *iṭ* is applied to the third person singular (*uttamapuruṣaikavacana*), the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* occurs; then, with the addition of the suffix *śap*, the rule *thāmeta* would require the substitution of *ām* for the vowel *e*. To prevent this, the sūtra states *eta ai*. Here, *ai* is a genitive form whose nominative case ending has been elided (*luptaprathamākam*). [This applies] to the imperative (*loṭ*).

From the rule *laṅvadi* (Pāṇini 3.4.79), the term *loṭ* is understood; and from the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72), the term *ajādīnām* is understood as "of that which begins with a vowel," while from the rule *āḍutamasya piñca* (Pāṇini 3.4.92), the term *utamasya* ("of the penultimate") is carried over. Thus he says: "of the penultimate [vowel] of the *loṭ*. Regarding *edhai*: when *edha-e* is established, the substitution of *ai* for the vowel *e* occurs; then, by the rule *āḍutamasya*, the augment *āṭ* is added, and by the rule *āṭaśca*, vṛddhi is applied.

By the rule *vṛddhireci*, there is vṛddhi [substitution]. Thus: *edhāvahai*, *edhāmahai*. After the substitution of *et* for the suffixes *vah* and *mahy*, following the root *edh*, there is the application of *śap*; then, the substitution of *ait* for the vowel *e*, followed by the augment *āṭ*, results in the long vowel by the rule *savarṇadīrghaḥ*. This concludes the procedure (*prakriyā*) for the imperative (*loṭ*). (99) *āḍajādīnām* 6.4.72.

Now, regarding the root *edh*, when the augment *aṭ* is applied by the rule *aḍ udāttaḥ* in the *laṅ*, *luṅ*, *liṅ*, and *lṛṅ* tenses, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*)—by the rule *ato guṇaḥ*—would have been expected, thereby setting aside the *vṛddhi*.
However, [the rule] *āḍ ajādīnām* applies; the intention is that this occurs because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "in the *luṅ* etc. from the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣu*.
"An exception (apavāda) to *aṭ*": the meaning is that when *aṭ* is present, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply.

Immediately after "and after *āṭ*" (*āṭaśca*), the word "vṛddhi" is to be supplied as the remainder. Although this [form] is established by the rule "vṛddhir eci" (*Pāṇini 6.1.88*) when there is a vṛddhi [resulting from the combination of vowels], nevertheless, the sūtra is stated here as well for the sake of forms such as *aikṣata*.

It has been presented because it is logical. Regarding *aidhata*: in the substitution of the *laṅ* [for the root], with the addition of *śap* and the augment *āṭ*, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule *āṭaśca*. Because the substitutes of *laṅ* do not have the designation *ṭit*, the change to *etva* does not occur.
The rule *āḍajādīnām* has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. Regarding *aidhetām*: [this occurs] in the case of *ātām*.
The augment *āṭ* is applied, and by the rule "vṛddhir ādaic," there is *vṛddhi*. By the rule "āta ṅti," the *ā* of the root is replaced by *y*. Then, by the rule "ād guṇaḥ," there is *guṇa*.
The *vṛddhi* of *āṭ* results in *aidhāvahi* and *aidhamahi*. For the roots *vah* and *mah*, the suffix *śap*, the augment *āṭ*, and *vṛddhi* apply.
This is the procedure for the *laṅ* tense.

The suffix *sīyuṭ* is added after the *liṅ*. This is clear. Since the augment *yāsuṭ* is prescribed for the substitutes of *liṅ* that belong to the *parasmaipada*, this rule concerns the domain of the *ātmanepada*. In the suffix *sīyuṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is an *it*.
The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding "elision of *s*" (*salopa*), the remainder [of the rule] is "by the rule *liṅḥ salopaḥ*.

As for *edheta*: this is the substitution for the *liṅ* [optative] suffix; then *sīyuṭ* is added, followed by the elision of *s*, *ādguṇaḥ* (the guṇa substitute for the preceding and following vowels), and the elision of *y*.
As for *edheyātām*: here there is the suffix *ātām*, then *sīyuṭ*, *śap*, and the elision of *s*; then *ādguṇaḥ* and the substitution of *ran* for *jha*.

The term *liṅ* is understood from the rule *ṭhliṅḥ sīyuṭ*. Thus he says: "of the *jha* [suffix] of the *liṅ*. This means: of the *jha* that is a substitute for *liṅ*. Because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is a replacement for the whole. Regarding *edheran*: *ran* replaces the *jha*; the *śap* suffix; *sīyuṭ*; elision of *s*; *ādguṇaḥ*; elision of *y*. Regarding *edhethāḥ*: [the same process].

The suffixes *thās*, *sīyuṭ*, and *śap* [are applied]. There is elision of the *s* of *sīyuṭ*. [By the rule] *ād guṇaḥ*, [the *e* of the root and the *i* of *sīyuṭ* form] *e*. [Then] there is elision of the *y*. By the rules for *rutva* and *visarga*, the *s* of *thās* becomes *r* and then *ḥ*. Thus: *edhe-y-ā-thās* → *edhethās*. [For the second person plural: *āthām*. [The suffixes] *sīyuṭ* and *śap* [are applied]. There is elision of the *s*. [By the rule] *ād guṇaḥ*, [the *e* of the root and the *i* of *sīyuṭ* form] *e*. Thus: *edhe-āthām* → *edhethām*. [For the second person plural imperative: *edhedhvam*. [The suffixes] *dhvam*, *sīyuṭ*, and *śap* [are applied]. There is elision of the *s*.
*Ād guṇaḥ*. Elision of *y*.
The analysis of *iṭo't* is *iṭaḥ* and *at*. [The word] *liṅ* [is understood] from the rule *liṅḥ sīyuṭ*.

This [rule] continues [to apply]. Thus he says: "of that which has the place of the *liṅ*. Just as in the rule *acca gheḥ*, the letter *t* in the substitute is merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not designated as an *it*; this has been explained at length in the *Śabdenduśekhara* under the rule *diva auṭ*. Others, however, maintain that it is indeed designated as an *it*. [The prohibition applies] by the rule *na vibhaktau*.

But there is no prohibition [of the substitution], because it is an *ādeśa* (substitute) and thus lacks the status of being a "prior" (*prāk*) element relative to the case-ending. However, in the rule *jhasya raḥ*,
by resorting to the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*),
and by assuming the insertion of an additional *na* after the *n*, the *n* does not possess the status of being the final letter (*antyatva*) in its original form of instruction (*upadeśa*).

Enough with the term "net-saṃjñā" (the designation of *it*). [Now for the derivation of] *edheya*: the augment *iṭ*, its substitution by the vowel *a*, the suffix *sīyuṭ*, the suffix *śap*, the elision of *s* (*salopa*), and the *guṇa* substitution by the preceding *ā* (*ādguṇaḥ*). [Thus: *edhevahi*, *edhemahi*. For the suffixes *vah* and *mah*, there is *sīyuṭ*, the elision of *s* (*salopa*), the suffix *śap*, the *guṇa* substitution by the preceding *ā* (*ādguṇaḥ*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopaḥ*). This is the procedure (*prakriyā*) for the optative (*vidhiliṅ*).

"Because it is an *ārddhadhātuka* [affix]"—the meaning is that this is by the rule "liṅ-aśiṣi. "The elision of *s*"—the meaning is that the mention of "sārvadhātuka" is understood (anuvṛtti) in the rule "liṅḥ salopaḥ. "Of *sīyuṭ* and *suṭ*"—the meaning is that there is a renewed application [of the rules] because the objects of the grammatical operations (*lakṣya*) are different.

Others maintain that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs simultaneously for both [the initial *s* of *sīyuṭ* and the final *s* of *suṭ*]. Regarding *edhiṣīṣṭa*: this is the *liṅ* suffix in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). Because it is an *ārddhadhātuka*, there is no *śap* augment. There is the suffix *sīyuṭ*. The augment *suṭ* is added to the *t* of the suffix. The augment *iṭ* is inserted before the *s* of *sīyuṭ*. There is the elision of the *y*. [Finally, there is the elision] of the *s* of *sīyuṭ* and the *s* of *suṭ*.

The substitution of *ṣ* for [the dental *s*] occurs; for the *t* of *takāra*, there is the substitution of *ṭ* by virtue of the rule for *ṣṭutva*. Regarding *edhiṣīyāstām*: [the suffix] *ātām* is added, followed by *sīyuṭ*;

after the vowel *a*, *suṭ* is inserted before the *t*; *iṭ* is prefixed to *sīyuṭ*; then the substitution of *ṣ* for the subsequent *s* occurs. Regarding *edhiṣīran*: *jha* is replaced by *ran*, followed by *sīyuṭ* and the augment *iṭ*.

There is the elision of the letter *ya*. There is the substitution of *ṣ* (by *ṣatva*). Thus: *edhiṣīṣṭhāḥ*. [The suffix] *thās* takes *sīyuṭ*. *Suṭ* is added after the letter *tha*. *iṭ* is added before *sīyuṭ*. There is the substitution of *ṣ* for both *s*s. By the rule of *ṣṭutva*, the letter *tha* becomes *ṭha*. Then there are the substitutions of *ru* and the visarga (*visarga*). [Thus: *edhiṣīyāsthām*. [The suffix] *āthām* takes *sīyuṭ*.

The suffix *suṭ* is inserted before the letter *th* following the vowel *a*. The augment *iṭ* is inserted before *sīyuṭ*. Thereafter, the letter *s* undergoes the change to *ṣ*. Thus, [we derive] *edhiṣīdhvam*. [In this case], after *dhvam*, there is *sīyuṭ* and the elision of *y*. The augment *iṭ* is inserted before *sīyuṭ*, and then the change to *ṣ* occurs. Even though [the *iṭ*] follows an *iṇ*-vowel, it does not follow an *aṅga* (stem) that ends in an *iṇ*-vowel; rather, it follows the *iṭ* itself.
Because it is a portion of the suffix (*pratyaya-bhaktatvāt*). Consequently, the substitution of *ḍha* by the rule *ṭhiṇaḥ ṣīdhvam* does not occur.
[In the case of] *edhiṣīya*: the augment *iṭ*, the suffix *at*, the suffix *sīyuṭ*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *ṣ*.
[In the cases of] *edhiṣīvahi* and *edhiṣīmahi*: the suffix *sīyuṭ* for *vah* and *mah*, the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *ṣ*.

Thus ends the section on the optative (liṅ) with benediction. Regarding *aidhiṣṭa*: this is the third person singular perfect (luṅ). [The suffixes are: *cli*, *sic*, *iṭ*, *āṭ* after the root, *vṛddhi*, *ṣatva*, and *ṣṭutva*. Regarding *aidhiṣātām*: this is the third person dual perfect (*ātām*). [The suffixes are:
*cli*, *sic*, *iṭ*, *āṭ*, *vṛddhi*, and *ṣatva*.

(102) *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.5. Now, when the substitution of *jha* for the initial *jha* of *jhasya*—as prescribed by the rule *jho'ntaḥ*—is about to occur, [the sūtra states] *ātmanepadeṣu*.
From the rule *jho'ntaḥ*, the word *jha* is understood as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and is carried over (*anuvartate*). [The term] *ātmanepadeṣu* [specifies the context].
The locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe saptamī*). Thus, it is understood as "of the *jh* which is a part of the *ātmanepada*.

From the rule *ad abhyastāt*, the word *at* is carried over (*anuvartate*). *Na at* is *anat*; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "from that which is not *at*. He says this [in the commentary]: "from that which does not end in *a*" (*anakārāt*), etc. [The example is] *aidhiṣata*; [this refers to] the *jh* which is a constituent part of the *jha*.

The substitution of *āditya* [for *dhā*]. The suffix *cli*. The suffix *sic*. The augment *iṭ*. The augment *āṭ*. Vṛddhi [vowel strengthening]. The change to *ṣ* (*ṣatva*). Thus, *aidhiṣṭha*. Regarding *aidhiṣāthām*: [the root] *thās*. The suffix *cli*. The suffix *sic*. The augment *iṭ*. The augment *āṭ*. Vṛddhi. The change to *ṣ* (*ṣatva*). By the rule of *ṣṭuan*, the letter *th* becomes *ṭh*. The addition of *r* (*rutva*) and the visarga (*visarga*). Thus, *aidhiṣāthām*. [The suffix] *āthām*. The suffix *cli*.

Thus: *iṭ*, *āṭ*, *vṛddhi*, and *ṣatva*. Now, he causes one to remember the substitution of *ṭha* for the *dha* of *dhvam*: "after *iṇ*, [there is ṣ for *dhvam*]" (*iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*). [The form] *aidhiḍhvam* [is derived as follows]: *dhvam*, *cliḥ*, *sic*, *iṭ*, *āṭ*, *vṛddhi*. By the rule "when *dhi* follows" (*dhi ca*), there is elision of the *s*. By the rule "after *iṇ*, [there is ṣ for *dhvam*]" (*iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*), there is the substitution of *ḍha* for the *dha*.

The sense is that because the augment *iṭ* has been elided, the suffix *sij* is included within the stem (*aṅga*), and thus the stem ending in *iṭ* is considered to end in *iṇ*. "Only when different from *iṭ*" means that in the subsequent rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*,
because of the mention of *iṭ*, in the preceding rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*, only that *iṇ* which is different from *iṭ* is understood.

Thus some say. According to their view, however, because the *iṭ* augment follows [the root], there is no substitution of *ḍha* for the letter *ha*; thus the form is simply *aidhidhvam*. The word "tu" (however) is used to indicate that this is an alternative opinion not established in the Bhāṣya. As for the phrase "of *ḍha* and *dha*," this is stated by relying on a difference of opinion.

In the alternative where *ḍha* is substituted, there are two forms—*dvidham* and *ekadham*—due to the optional doubling of the letter *dha* by the rule *anaci ca*. Similarly, when *ḍha* is substituted, there are two forms—*dviḍham* and *ekaḍham*.
Even among these four forms, the term *mayaḥ* in the rule *ṭhyaṇo mayo dve vācye* [refers to all of them].

Based on the fifth [alternative], due to the optional doubling of the letter *va*, there arise four previously mentioned forms—those with one *va* and those with two *vas*. Thus, eight forms are produced. Due to the optional doubling of the letter *ma*, these eight forms become those with one *ma*.
The meaning is that sixteen forms are thus completed, including the two types [of first-person endings]. Regarding *aidhiṣī*: there is the *luṅ* suffix;
the substitution of *iṭ*; the *cli* suffix; the *sic* suffix; the addition of *iṭ*; the augment *āṭ*; and the *vṛddhi* strengthening.

For *vahimaḥ* and *asmaḥ*, when the *cli* suffix is replaced by *sic*, followed by the addition of *iṭ* and *āṭ*, and the application of *vṛddhi*, the resulting forms are *aidhiṣvahi* and *aidhiṣmahi*. Thus it is said.

The *luṅ* formation: *aidhiṣyata*. [This is derived as follows: the substitution of the *lṛṅ* suffix; the addition of *sya*; the addition of *iṭ*; the addition of *āṭ*; *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening); the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*; thus *aidhiṣyata*. *aidhiṣyetām*: [This is derived as follows: the suffix *ātām*; the addition of *sya*; the addition of *iṭ*; the change of the vowel *ā* to *iy*; the *guṇa* substitution (*e*); the elision of *y*; the addition of *āṭ*; *vṛddhi*; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*; thus *aidhiṣyetām*. *aidhiṣyanta*: [This is derived as follows: the suffix *jha*; the addition of *sya*; the addition of *iṭ*; the addition of *āṭ*; *vṛddhi*; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*; thus *aidhiṣyanta*.
In the case of *aidhiṣyata*, there is the substitution of *jha* for *jhāvaya*. Then comes *sya*, the augment *iṭ*, the augment *āṭ*, *vṛddhi*, and the change to *ṣatva*.

Thus: *aidhiṣyata*. In the case of *aidhiṣyethām*, there is *thās*. Then comes *sya*, the augment *iṭ*, the augment *āṭ*, *vṛddhi*, the *ru*-substitution and *visarga*. Thus: *aidhiṣyethām*. In the case of *aidhiṣyadhvam*, there is *āthām*.
Then comes *sya*, the augment *iṭ*, the change of the vowel *ā* to *iy*, *ādguṇa*, the elision of *y*, the augment *āṭ*, and *vṛddhi*. Thus: *aidhiṣyadhvam*.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. *aidhiṣyadhvam*: [the suffix] *dhvam*, [the augment] *sya*, [the augment] *iṭ*, [the augment] *āṭ*, [the resulting] *vṛddhi*, [the substitution of] *ai* for *e* [by *āṭ*], [the substitution of] *ṣ* [for *s*].

*aidhiṣya*: [the substitution of] *iṭ* for [the final letter of the root], *sya*, [the addition of] the augment *iṭ*, [the substitution of] *ṣ* [for *s*], [the formation of] *guṇa* by *ādguṇaḥ*. For *vah* and *mah*, let there be *sya*, *iṭ*, lengthening of the vowel (*ato dīrghaḥ*), *āṭ*, *vṛddhi*, [and the substitution of] *ṣ* [for *s*]: thus *aidhiṣyāvahi* and *aidhiṣyāmahi*.

Regarding the form *rūpe*: one might ask, "Since the root *edh* is marked with an anudātta (low-pitched) accent, why is the prohibition of *iṇ* not applied by the rule 'ekāca upadeśe 'nudātādiḥ'? To this, he says:
"Because it has an udātta (high-pitched) accent. Although the root *edh* is indeed anudātta, [the vowel *a*] which is anudātta...

The meaning is that when [the accent] has been elided, the remaining verbal root (dhātu) is not anudātta. Now, one might ask: "Since only a few roots were pronounced as anudātta by Pāṇini, how are they to be understood by people of the present day? To this, he says:
"By way of a consequence" (*prasaṅgāt*): a "consequence" (*prasaṅga*) is the state of being unfit for neglect once something has been brought to mind.

The sense is that it is possible for the present-day students to know those roots marked with a low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) by Pāṇini, just as they know [the rule regarding] nasality (*ānunāsikya*), through the contemporary tradition of pupils. "[With those ending in *ū*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ*]" (*ūdṛdantaiḥ*).
Among the verbal roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*),

with the exception of those ending in *ū* or *añ*, and excluding the roots *yu*, *ru*, *kṣṇu*, *śīṅ*, *snu*, *nu*, *kṣu*, *śvi*, *ṅīṅ*, and *śri*, as well as the two roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, all other single-vowel roots ending in vowels are designated as *nihita*.

They are recorded as *anudātta* (unaccented); this means they are known through the tradition of Pāṇini’s disciples. Now, he enumerates the *anudātta* roots among those ending in consonants: *śaklṛ*, *pac*, *muc*, etc.
[The list continues: *śaklṛ*, *pac*, *muc*, *ric*, *vac*, *vic*, *sic*, *praccchi*, *tyaj*, *nijir*.
The term *bhaj* refers to a *dvandva* compound of these [roots]. Among them, regarding those ending in *k*, there is one: *śaklṛ*. The letter *ḷ* is the *it*.
However, in the Bhāṣya, the reading is seen without the *anubandha*. Regarding those ending in *c*, there are six: *pac*, *muc*, *ric*, *vac*, *vic*, and *sic*. Here, only *ḍupacaṣ* is intended.

They say that because it is well-known, there is the inclusion [of the root *muc*] in the sense of "releasing," but not of *pac* in the sense of "manifesting. There is the inclusion of *muclṛ* in the sense of "liberation" (*mokṣaṇe*), but not of the root *muci* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* in the sense of "deceit" (*kalkane*). Others say that because there is no distinction, all [roots beginning with *muc*] are included. Among those ending in *ch*, *pracch* is the only one; it ends in the vowel *ī*.

This is for the purpose of pronunciation. In the case of *ṇijir*, it will be stated that *ira* is designated by the technical term *it*. From *bhuñja* and *bhuj* up to *sṛja*, it is one word. Among those ending in *j*: *tyaj*, *nij*, *bhaj*, *bhañj*, *bhuj*, *bhrasj*, *masj*, *yaj*, *yuj*, *ruj*, *rañj*, *sṛj*—these are fifteen. *Ad*... [text ends]
From *kṣud* up to *nuda*, ending with *nuda*, constitutes a single word. In that context, the vowel *i* in the root *tud* is for the sake of pronunciation.
*Padyabhid* is a single word; it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The mention of *padya* is by means of the suffix *śyan*.
The mention of *vidyati* is by means of the suffix *śyan*. The mention of *vinat* is by means of the suffix *śnam*.

The sequence beginning with *ṣad* and ending with *budhyati* constitutes a single compound (*pada*). It is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The forms *sad*, *skand*, *had*, and *kṣudh* are indicated by the vowel *i*. Regarding *bandhi*, there is the indication of the vowel *i*. *Yudhi* and *rudhi* are considered a single word; [the latter] ends in the vowel *i*.
The explanation: *rādhivyadhaśudhaḥ* is a single word. In *rādhi*, the vowel *i* is used for the purpose of grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*).
*Sādhisidhyatī* is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). In *sādhi*, the vowel *i* is used for the purpose of grammatical indication. Consequently, among the roots ending in *dh*:
*krudh*, *kṣudh* (taking the *śyan* suffix), *bandh*, *yudh*, *rudh*, *rādh*, *vyadh*, *śudh*.

*sādh* and *sidh*—these are eleven [roots] [taking the *śyan* suffix]. From *manya* up to *tip* is one word (*pada*). The mention of *manya* is by means of the *śyan* suffix. The mention of *chup* is by means of the vowel *i*.
The pair *tṛpyati* and *dṛpyati* is a *dvandva* compound; the mention is by means of the *śyan* suffix. From *lib* onwards is *yama*...

There are thirteen roots ending in *p*: *lup*, *vap*, *śap*, *khap*, *sṛp*, and so on. There are three ending in *bh*: *yabh*, *rabh*, *labh*. There are four ending in *m*: *gam*, *nam*, *yam*, *ram*.

The sense is that the reading [in the Dhātupāṭha] is due to the negligence of a scribe.
