The meaning is: "for the purpose of excluding other suffixes" (*vikaraṇa*). This will become clear later, in the detailed description of each *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. "These [are] likewise" means: for the purpose of excluding those [suffixes] that lack the aforementioned *anubandhas*. This too will become clear in the detailed description of each *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. These...
"So be it. This means the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) of those [roots] which lack the aforementioned adjuncts (*anubandha*).

This too will become clear in the description of each respective *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Regarding "vinditi": this is the root *vidlṛ* in the sense of "to obtain," belonging to the Taudādika class; it is accepted in grammars such as those of Cāndra and Daurga, and is also mentioned in the Bhāṣya.

"It is seen" means that the root *vid* (to find) is listed there among *vindati*, *vinatti*, and *vidyati*; this is the intended meaning. "This one" means *vindati*. "It is not read here" means that although it is not recited in this [Dhātupāṭha], its status as being without the augment *iṭ* (aniṭ) is established by the authority of the Bhāṣya. [The rule] "rañji-masjī" is one [sūtra].

The words *padam*, *nud*, and *kṣudh* are separated as distinct items. *ṭhśuṣipuṣī* constitutes a single word. Following *śiṣi*, the remainder of the rule is *ṭhityete*. Regarding the phrase *naveha*: the meaning is that nine verbal roots, though not mentioned in the Bhāṣya, are enumerated here among the anudātta (unaccented) roots. Why?

Therefore, he says: "because of the consensus of Vyāghrabhūti and others. The intention is that the enumeration of others in the Bhāṣya, besides these nine, is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an inclusive indication) of all nine of them as well.
[Examples include: *tena raktaṃ rāgāt*, *tadasminnannaṃ prāyeṇa*, and *kto'kṛtamitapratipannāḥ*.

The sūtra-usage such as *ṭhśuṣkadhṛṣṭau* (in the sense of "dry" and "bold") with a word ending in a *kta*-suffix qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*), and the Bhāṣya-usage such as *nunnaḥ*, *magnaḥ*, *puṣṭaḥ*, *maṅktā*, and *maṅktavyam*, serve as evidence for this.
[Thus end the *aniṭ*-karikās. Regarding *spardha* in the sense of "rivalry," the word *vartate* ("occurs") is to be supplied.

Regarding the term *parābhibhava*: the defeat (*abhibhava*) of another is *parājaya*; the meaning is "the desire directed toward that [defeat]. Now, one might object: since the defeat of another is the object (*karman*) of this desire, the root *spardh* (to compete) would be transitive (*sakarmaka*), and thus in examples such as *devadato yajñadattaṃ spardhayati* ("Devadatta competes with Yajñadatta"), [the verb would require an accusative].

Regarding the question of how the operation of an intransitive verb (*akarmaka-kārya*) applies under the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām*, he says: "Because [the object] is included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthenopasaṅgrahāt*). He holds that "transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in having an object external to the meaning of the verbal root. [This is illustrated by the example: *supa ātmanaḥ*...

The intended meaning is that this has been explained in detail in the *Kya’jiti-sūtrabhāṣya*. Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, there would be a contradiction with the root text regarding the formal arrangement of words in the rule *ṭhspardhāyāmāṅ*—specifically the statement: "‘Kṛṣṇa calls upon Aṇūra,’ which means ‘he competes [with him]’"; for in that context...

Enough with the discussion regarding the *vṛt* root preceded by *abhi* in the sense of challenging (*spardha*). As for *spardhate*: because it is stated that "the thirty-six roots ending in *kattha* are *anudātta*," the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] is employed. The intention is that the forms in the *laṭ* [present tense] are like those of the root *edh*. Since the root does not begin with a vowel (*ij-ādi*), the rule *ijādeśca* does not apply to the *liṭ* [perfect tense]; for this very reason, [the reduplication is not replaced].
Nor is there even an application [of the rule].

(103) *Śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.61). However, regarding the substitution of *ta* for *liṭ*, by the rule *liṭas tajhayor eś* (Pāṇini 3.4.81), *eś* is substituted for it; and by the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), [the reduplication occurs].

When there is reduplication (dvitva), by the rule "the first consonant is the remainder" (*ṭhhalādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), all consonants except the first one in the reduplicated syllable are eliminated. When this would result in [the form] *saspadhe*—[the author says] "śarpūrvāḥ" (those preceded by *śar*). The meaning is that the word "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) is understood here because it continues from the previous rule "there is elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*lopo'bhyāsasya*). In the rule "śarpūrvāḥ,"...

The compound *śarpūrvāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* that does not convey the quality (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). Consequently, the *śar* [consonants] are what remain (*śiṣyante*). The sense is that the word *śeṣaḥ*, which was inherited from the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, is understood here as ending in the suffix *ghañ* (denoting the object of the action) and is modified to the plural form. And thus:

In the present case of reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the letter *kh* is prescribed [in place of *cch*]. One should not suspect a prohibition of doubling for the *r*, as in the rule "the first members of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) consisting of *n*, *d*, or *r* are not doubled," because that prohibition applies only to a second single-consonant (*ekāj*) member. Thus he says: "he vied" (*paspardha*). Nor is it the case that in the word *vavraśca*, there is only the letter *c* in the reduplication.

It should be stated that [the word] "śiṣyeta" [is used]; for from the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, the word "ādiḥ" (the first) also carries over. The meaning is: those which constitute the beginning of the root with respect to letters other than the sibilants (*śar*).
[Examples: *pasparḍhāte*, *pasparḍhire*, *pasparḍhiṣe*, *pasparḍhāthe*, *pasparḍhidhve*.
The forms *pasparde*, *paspardivahe*, and *pasparcimahe* are easily understood as the forms in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense.

Regarding *spardhitā*: the sense is that the forms in the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) tense are easily understood, being similar to those of the root *edh*. Regarding *spardhiṣyate*: the sense is that the forms in the *lṛṭ* (simple future) tense are similar to those of the root *edh*. Regarding *spardhatām*: this is in the *loṭ* (imperative) tense.
The meaning is that the forms are like those of *edh* (to prosper). Regarding *aspardhata*: this is the *laṅ* [aorist]; the meaning is that the forms are like those of *edh*.

Because it begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), there is the augment *aṭ* and not *āṭ*; this is the distinction. Regarding *spardheta*: this is the optative (*vidhi-liṅ*); the forms are like those of *edh*. There is the augment *aṭ*, but not *āṭ*; this is the distinction. Regarding *aspardhiṣyata*: this is the conditional (*lṛṅ*).

The forms *edhivadrūpāṇi* (the forms like *edh*) are for the *luṅ* [aorist]; the addition of *aṭ* is the distinction, but not the addition of *āṭ*. The form *aspardhiṣṭa* is for the *luṅ*; the addition of *aṭ* is the distinction, but not the addition of *āṭ*. The form *aspardhiṣyata* is for the *lṛṅ* [conditional];
the addition of *aṭ* is the distinction, but not the addition of *āṭ*. The root *gādhṛ* meaning "to stand firm" ends in the fourth [consonant class]; it contains the vowel *ṛ*.

The phrase "ṭhnāglopiśāsvṛditām" is for the purpose of a prohibition. *Ajagādhat* means stability—remaining in a support. *Granthaḥ* means tying together, composition. Regarding *jagādhe*: in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, there is reduplication and so forth; the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); and the change to *c* (*cutvam*). *Bādhṛ* means striking back—afflicting.

*nāthṛ* and *nādhṛ*: these two roots end in the second and fourth [consonants of their respective classes]. *Upatāpaḥ*—affliction caused by fever. *Āśīḥ*—a prayer or benediction. He states the specific rule for the root *nāthṛ* ending in the second [consonant]:
*āśiṣi nātha*. Here, *nātha* is in the genitive case. [This is understood] from the rule *anudātaṅti*.

The term *ātmanepada* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Since the [formation of the middle voice] is already established by the fact that the root is marked with an *anudātta* vowel, this Vārttika is for the purpose of restriction; thus he says: "Only in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) [does the root *nāth* take the *ātmanepada*]. The *ātmanepada* occurs only when the root *nāth* functions in the sense of "blessing" (*āśāsana*). In its other senses, such as "begging" (*yācñā*), etc., the *parasmaipada* applies according to the rule "for the rest, in the sense of the agent" (*śeṣāt kartari*).

The meaning is "only for another. "Nāthate" means "he hopes for" (āśāste). "Anyatra" means "in cases where [the root] exists in the sense of begging and so forth. Now he gives an example of the root *nādh* ending in the fourth [conjugation class]: "nādhate. "Dadhe"—this also ends in the fourth [conjugation class].

(104) Now, regarding the rule *atha ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.120): having established the forms for the present tense (*laṭ*) as being like those of *edh*, when the *liṭ* suffix undergoes substitution by *ta* and that *ta* is replaced by *aiś*, and after reduplication, the form *dadh dadh e* is obtained. Then, by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye*: [the vowel *a* is elided] when it is situated between two single consonants, provided that the substitute (*ādeśa*) does not have [a vowel] as its initial element (*ādi*). "That which has a substitute as its initial" is the meaning of *anādeśādi*.

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is supplied as the referent for another word. The phrase "in *liṭ*" (*liṭi*) is a locative of occasion (*naimittika-saptamī*), which connects with the word "substitute" (*ādeśa*)—a part of the compound "not having a substitute as its initial" (*anādeśādi*). Thus, it is understood that the rule applies to such a stem whose initial is not a substitute when *liṭ* occurs as the occasioning condition.

The term *aṅgasya* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, it is understood as "of such a member of the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *at*. The word *eka* denotes "without a companion" (*asahāya*). As Amara states: "The words *eka*, *mukhya*, *anya*, and *kevala* [are synonyms]. The analysis of the compound is: *ekau* (two) *halau* (consonants) that are *asaṃyuktau* (unjoined) are *ekahalau*; [the substitute occurs] in the middle of those two, i.e., *tatra*. This refers specifically to the [substitute] *at*.

This is a qualifier. From the rule *dvasoreddhāvabhyāsasya*, the words *edit* and *abhyāsalopaḥ* are carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *gamahana...* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), the word *kiti* is carried over, but not *ṅti*;

for it is impossible for the substitutes of *liṅ* to have the marker *ṅ*. Furthermore, in the prescription of *etva* (the substitution of *e*) in the context of *liṭ*, there is a subsequent cause (*paranimitta*).
By way of ellipsis (*āvṛtti*), both meanings are obtained. He states this with the words beginning "liṇ-nimite" and so forth.

(105) *thali ca seṭi* | Pāṇini 6.4.121. Regarding "thali ca": it refers to what was previously stated—that which was previously mentioned under the rule *ekahalmadhye*—namely, the substitution of *etva* and so forth.
The meaning is that this [rule] should apply even when *thali* follows. Since *thali* is not *kit*, the rule does not apply by the preceding sūtra; hence, this statement is made.

Now, one might object: in forms such as *dedhe* and *petatuḥ*, since the rules "jaś for jaś" and "car for car" (Pāṇini 8.4.54) would apply—resulting in the substitution of *jaś* for *jaś* and *car* for *car* due to the cause of the *liṭ* affix—how can there be the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "And the term 'ādeśa' [is used here]. In this context, within the rule *ata ekahalmadhye*, by the word *ādeśa*, only a substitute (*ādeśa*) that is dissimilar (*virūpa*) to the original element (*sthānin*) is intended. And thus, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) do not occur for such a substitute alone.
The meaning is that substitutes (*ādeśa*) which are similar in form (*sarūpa*) to the original base (*sthānin*) are not excluded by this prohibition. Regarding the rule *śasidadyoḥ*:

the prohibition of the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) for the roots *śas* and *dad*—which are included in the group beginning with *śas*, *dad*, and *vada*—is stated [by the rule *na śasadadavādiguṇānām*].
If, in this context, there were an exclusion of substitutes and so forth in some arbitrary manner, then...

In the case of the reduplication of *śas* and *dad*, when the substitutes *ś* and *d* are applied to the *c* and *j* sounds of the *car-jaś* rule, the absence of *etva* (the substitution of *e*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable would be established simply by the fact that the substitute begins with those letters; therefore, the prohibition "not in *śas*, *sad*, or *ad*" (*na śasadadave*) would be rendered useless. Consequently...

The meaning is that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is understood to apply specifically to substitutes (*ādeśa*) and so forth that produce a change in form (*vairūpya*). "By that" means by the statement that there is no exclusion of a substitute that is similar in form (*sarūpa*) to the original element (*sthānin*). "Even though they exist" means even though substitutes such as *d* (as in *dedhe*, *petatuḥ*, etc. are present. "Dedhe" is an example.
When *dadh* followed by *dadha* is established, the form results from the substitution of *e* for the vowel following the *d*, along with the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*).
Here, one should understand that the *liṭ* affixes are marked as *kit* by the rule *ṭhasaṃyogālliṭ kit*. The forms are: *dedhira*;
*dedhiṣe*, *dedhāthe*, *dedhidhve*; and *dedhe*, *dedhivahe*, *dedhimahe*.

The meaning is that they "come into being" (saṃbhavanti). Regarding the form *didivatuḥ*: the meaning is that since there is no short *a* between the two consonants when the root *div* is reduplicated before the suffix *atus*, the substitution of *e* for *i* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur. Regarding the question "what is the purpose of *tatparaḥ*?": this means what is the purpose of making the *a* in the rule *ataḥ* long (*taparakaraṇa*)? [The example is] *rarāse* from the root *rāsṛ*.

In the word *śabda*, the root belongs to the *bhvādi* class and is *ātmanepada*. Here, the question is: what is the purpose of the condition "situated between consonants"? [The answer is: *tatsaratuḥ*. [This is derived from] the root *tsar* in the sense of "moving stealthily. In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffix *atus*, after reduplication, the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is not situated between unconnected consonants; this is the intended meaning. [Another example is] *cakaṇatuḥ*.

In the case of the root *ṭhkaṇ* in the sense of "sound," when the *liṭ* suffix *atus* follows, there is reduplication; by the rule *kuhoścuḥ*, the letter *k* is changed to *c*. Thus, because the substitute (the *c*) is different from the original (*k*), it is not considered "identical" (*ādi-tva*); consequently, by the rule [Pāṇini 7.4.59], the change to *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not take place.
Now, regarding the phrase *liṇnimittādeśādikam* [in the definition of *san-liṭ-ajādeśa*]: the term *liṇnimitta*...

He states the purpose [of the rule] with the words *liṭi* and *nemitha*. Regarding *ṇamu* [in the sense of] "bowing" and "sound": by the rule *ṇo naḥ*, there is the substitution of *na* for *ṇa*. Even though, when *iṭ* is added in the *thali* [suffix], there is reduplication and the substitution of *na* for the *n* resulting from the change of *ṇa* to *na*, the quality of being *natva* [remains].

The meaning is that because the cause for the substitution [of *liṭ*] is absent, and because the initiality [of the root] caused by *liṭ* is absent, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication are unimpeded. Regarding *sehe*: from the root *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance," the change of *ṣ* to *s* occurs by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*. Even though the initiality of the substitute *s*, which has resulted from this change of *s* (for *ṣ*), exists when *liṭ* follows and there is reduplication, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication remain unimpeded; the reason being that the cause for the substitution [of *liṭ*] is absent, and thus the initiality caused by *liṭ* is lacking. [Examples: *dadhitā*, *dadhiṣyate*, *dadhatām*, *adadhata*, *dadheta*, *dadhiṣīṣṭa*.
*adadhiṣṭa*; *adadhiṣyata*. *skudīti*: leaping up, moving by jumping.

(105) *idito num dhātoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.58. *iditaḥ*: "it" is a short vowel *i*; that which has such an "it" as its *itsaṃjñaka* (technical marker) is called *idit*; [the suffix *num* is added] to that.
The term *vigraha* means "the root characterized by that [nasal] indicator. Therefore, there is no fault in the case of roots such as *cakṣiṅ*.

In the augment *num*, the letter *m* is the *it* (indicatory), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Because it is marked with *m* (*mit*), it follows the final vowel. In the form *skundate*, the anusvāra is substituted according to the rule *naścāpadāntasya*, and it is then changed to the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). [In the reduplicated form] *cuskunda*...
Thus: when the *liṭ* suffix is applied and reduplication occurs, by the rule "śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ," the letter *k* remains in the reduplicated syllable;
then, by the rule "kuhoścuḥ," that *k* is replaced by *c*. [The form] *śvidī* means "making whiteness" (*śvaitya-karaṇam*). It is intransitive (*akarmaka*) because of whiteness (*śvaityasya*).

The intention is that [the action] is subsumed under the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). Consequently, in examples such as "Śvanda makes Devadatta swell" (*śvandayati devadattaṃ yajñadattaḥ*), the second case ending occurs by virtue of the rule "gati-buddhi-pratyavasāna... which prescribes the treatment of the object for intransitive verbs. Alternatively, *śvaityam* means "becoming white" (*śvetībhavanam*). Thus, [the form] is *śvindate*.
The meaning is "becoming white. Because it is marked with the *idit* (indicatory letter *i*), the augment *num* is applied; then the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa* [change] occur.
The activity that causes this—such as prostration and so forth—is "salutation" (*abhivādana*). Regarding *vandate*: because it is marked with *idit*, the augment *num* is applied.
Regarding *bhadī*: "blessing" means an auspicious action; "well-being" means the state of being happy. Regarding *bhandate*.
"Having known, he bound [the fetter]" (*iditvānnum babhanda*). In the reduplication, the letter *b* arises from the *jaś*-substitution of the letter *bh*.

"To rejoice" (*madī*); *modaḥ* means satisfaction; *madaḥ* means pride. "He rejoices" (*mandate*); because it is marked with the *it*-sign, the augment *num* is added. "He rejoiced" (*mamanda*); since the *num* is present, the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur, because the root stands between two conjunct consonants (*saṃyuktahal*).
The root *spad* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). [In the form] *spandate*, because it is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*it*), the augment *num* is added.
In *paspande*, by the rule "the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ*) preceded by a sibilant (*śar*)" (*śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*), the letter *p* remains in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). Regarding *klid*:
he explains the word *paridevana* (lamentation) as "sorrow" (*śoka*). Sorrow is the affliction (*kleśa*) resulting from recollection.

Thus he says: "sakarmaka" (transitive). Regarding "klindate caitram": the meaning is that having remembered Caitra from the past, one suffers. Because it is marked with the *idit* designation, there is the augment *num*. Regarding "ciklinda": the sense is that in the reduplication, the letter *k* becomes *c* by the rule of *cutva* (the substitution of *c* for *k*). Regarding "muda": it means joy—contentment. Regarding "modate": [he rejoices].

In *śap*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. In *mumude*, there is no *guṇa* because the suffix is *kit* by the rule "the *liṭ* [suffixes] following a root ending in a consonant cluster are *kit*.

In *dadāti*, giving (*dāna*) is the relinquishing of "mine" (*na mama*), and not merely the relinquishing of a substance; for if it were the latter, the verbal root's meaning would be subsumed within the action itself, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the verb being intransitive (*akarmaka*).

(106) *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* | Pāṇini 6.4.126. *na śasadada-*: This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *śasa*, *dada*, *vādi*, and *guṇa*. It is a genitive of relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). By the word *guṇa* here, only that which is specifically prescribed as a *guṇa* is intended; this [present case] is not such, because it lacks the status of being prescribed by the term *guṇa*.
This is a prohibition. However, *papratuḥ* is an example of *guṇa*;
it should be understood that because the vowel *a* is a constituent part of that which is prescribed by the term *guṇa*, [the prohibition does not apply].
Regarding *dadade*: after the root *dad*, when the *liṭ* suffix is replaced by *eś* and reduplication occurs, [the form is derived] by [the rule] *ata ekahalmadhye*.

In these cases, the elision of the suffix *va* does not occur. [The root] *ṣvad* means "to taste"—that is, experience—or it refers to a liking (*ruci*) consisting in becoming an object of pleasure. Thus he says: "this. The singular number is used with reference to each individual [instance].

(107) *Dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.64. [The word] *dhātvādeḥ* [is a compound]. *Ṣaḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). Thus he says: "In place of the *ṣ* at the beginning of a root, there shall be *s*. The meaning is: "In place of the letter *ṣ*, there shall be *s*. What is the purpose of mentioning "root" (*dhātu*)? [Consider the example: *ṣaṭ*. Here...

Because [the root] does not belong to the class beginning with *dhātu*, the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* does not occur. Why is the word "beginning" (*ādi*) included [in the rule]? [To exclude cases such as: *laṣati*. Nor should it be argued that even so, in forms like *ṣakārītyati*, the *s* would replace the *ṣ* even when it belongs to the beginning of a nominal stem (*subanta*) or a verbal root (*dhātu*), because the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*) is understood from the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śitī*. And thus:

In the case of [the rule] *ṣaḍ* etc., since the exclusion [of other sounds] is established simply by the continued application of the mention of the "uddeśa" (the subject), the mention of *dhātu* (root) in the Bhāṣya has been rejected. Now, one might object: "Let the letter *s* alone be taught in the Dhātupāṭha as in *svada*, *svarde*; and thus let even the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ* not exist. To this we say: do not say so.

This is because, in the form *asiṣvadat* derived from the causative (*ṇyanta*) root with the suffix *luṅ*, there must be the audible *ṣ* sound; for if the root were taught in the Dhātupāṭha with a *s* alone, then in *asiṣvadat*, since the *s* would not be an original substitute *s* (ādeśasakāra), the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) would be impossible. [Objection: But if this were the case, then in *anusvadate*...
To this, he says—"sātpadādyoḥ"—because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the substitution of *s* for the substitute *s*. Regarding *sasvade*:

the point is that since there is reduplication (*dvitva*) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) do not occur, as the root is situated between two conjunct consonants (*saṃyuktahalmadhyasthatvāt*).
Regarding *urdate*: some say that by the force of the word "ca" (and), it also includes the sense of tasting (*āsvādane*).

(108) *upadhāyāṃ ca* | 8|2|78| The word *upadhāyām* [is understood]. From the rule *sipi dhātoḥ*, from *rṭhvorupadhāyāḥ*, the word *rvorikaḥ* is carried over, and from *hali ca*, the word *halī* is carried over. The meaning is "in the case of a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)".
The term *upadhāyām* is an archaic Vedic usage. This is what [the author] states with the words "of the root," and so forth. Regarding the form *ūrdata*:

since the root here does not end in the letter *r*, the rules "of the penultimate [vowel] before *ṛt* and *thv*" (*ṛṭhvorupadhāyāḥ*) and "also before a consonant" (*hali ca*) do not apply; therefore, the rule "also when there is a penultimate [vowel]" (*upadhāyāṃ ca*) is introduced. If the word "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) were absent...

Because the word *pada* occurs within the governing context (*adhikāra*), the meaning would be "of those two [consonants] which constitute the penultimate (*upadhā*) of a *pada*. Consequently, this rule would apply only in cases such as *ūrṇu* with the suffix *kvip* (i.e., *ūrṇuvit*), but not in forms such as *ūrṇudate*.
What is the purpose of specifying "of the *repha* and *vakāra*"? Consider *puṣpyati*. What is the purpose of specifying "followed by a consonant (*hal*)"? Consider *ciriṇoti*.
What is the example? *nardati* (he roars) and *ūrdāṃcakre* (he has roared). Because it begins with *ij*, the suffix *ām* is applied;

then, by the rule "the root *kṛ* is also employed after [such roots]," there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of *kṛ*. Thus, *kurdate*. *Gud* is also a separate root. The mention of the meaning "only in the sense of play" is for the sake of specifying the scope; the particle *eva* (only), however, applies elsewhere than this.

This indicates that the mention of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). [Examples: *kūrdate*—the lengthening is by [Pāṇini 7.1.101] *upadhāyāṃ ca*. *cukūrda*—the substitution of *c* for *k* and *h* is by [Pāṇini 7.4.62] *kuhoś cuḥ*. *khūrdate*—the lengthening is by [Pāṇini 7.1.101] *upadhāyāṃ ca*. Similarly, *gūrdate*. *godate*—[this occurs] with the suffix *śap*.

The *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel [occurs]. Regarding *jugude*: because the suffix is *kit* by the rule "after a root ending in a consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*), there is no *guṇa*.

Regarding *sūdate*: it means "flowing"—that is, trickling. Regarding *sūdeta*: the meaning is "it flows. By the rule "of the root-initial" (*dhātvādeḥ*), the *ṣ* becomes *s*. Because the penultimate vowel is not light, there is no *guṇa*. Regarding *suṣūda*.

By the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvācamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75), the *ṣ* becomes *s*. In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, after reduplication and so forth, since the following *s* is that of a substitute (*ādeśa*), the *ṣ*-ness [of the preceding *ṣ*] occurs. If, however, the letter *s* were read directly in the Dhātupāṭha, then here—because it would not be a substitute *s*—the *ṣ*-ness would not occur. But in the case of a root taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), when the *ṣ* becomes *s*, [the *ṣ*-ness is maintained].

The intention is that, because the substitute *s* is preceded by an *ādeśa-sakāra*, the change to *ṣ* (ṣatva) is easily established. Now, one might object: "Which roots are recited in the Dhātupāṭha as beginning with *ṣ* (ṣādayaḥ), and which as beginning with *s* (sādayaḥ)?
For the reading of Pāṇini’s *ṣopadeśa* has now been lost. Anticipating this doubt:
He recites the *ṣopadeśas* established in the Pāṇinian tradition with the verse beginning "seṭ".

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "those monosyllabic roots whose final letters are a dental (*dantya*) or a vowel (*ac*), and which have *ṣ*, *s*, or *k* as their initial, shall be *ṣopadeśas*.
A "dental-vowel-final" (*dantyā'janta*) is that which has a dental (*dantya*) and a vowel (*ac*)—the two being "final" (*anta*), meaning immediately followed by them—as its final constituents.
"Of that kind" means those whose initial sound is *ṣ*; these are roots beginning with *ṣ*, ending in a dental (*dantya*), and having a final vowel (*ajanta*).

Those roots consisting of a single vowel (*ekāca*) which begin with *ṣ*—whether the *ṣ* is followed by a dental or a vowel—and which have now undergone the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* (*kṛtasatva*), even though they appear at present as beginning with *s*, [are to be understood as beginning with *ṣ*].

The meaning is that those [roots] taught by Pāṇini are to be understood as such. Even in the reading "ṣādayaḥ," it should be explained in exactly the same way. The *Bhāṣya* states: "Those beginning with *ṣ* followed by a vowel or a dental (*aj-dantya*) are roots taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*). Roots such as *ṣūd* (in the sense of "flowing") are examples of roots taught with an initial *ṣ* followed by a vowel. [The root] *ṣṭhā*...

However, *gatinivṛtā* and others are taught with a *kaṣ* (the letter *k*) followed by a dental (*dantya*). Why [is it specified] "followed by a dental vowel" (*dantyājanta*)? Consider *skudi*, meaning "to incline": *cuskunde*. Here, the *s* is neither followed by a dental nor by a vowel (*ac*). Why [is it specified] "of a monosyllabic root" (*ekācaḥ*)? Consider *sosūtryate*, from the root *sūtra* in the sense of "encircling."

The root beginning with *cur* and ending in *rj* is polysyllabic (*anekāc*). Although it is not seen as such in the Bhāṣya under the rule for monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*), nevertheless, the Bhāṣya statement that "it is indicated there by the prescription of the *yaṅ* affix" is the authority in this matter; this should be understood.
And thus, even though in [the Dhātupāṭha] such as "ṣādha saṃsiddhau" only the reading with the letter *s* is observed...

It is precisely because of the presence of an upadhā-vowel [before the suffix]. Now, these four—*ṣekṛ* (to go), *sṛplṛ* (to go), *sṛ* (to go), and *sṛj* (to emit)—have *s* as their initial consonant followed by a vowel (*ac*). *Stṛñ* (to cover) ends in *ṛ* and takes the *śnu* vikaraṇa;
*stṛñ* (to cover) ends in *ṛ* and takes the *śnu* vikaraṇa; *styai*...

Regarding the two groups of sounds [beginning with *ś* and *ṣ*]: these three—*śak*, *ṣañj*, and *ṣvañj*—have a dental (*dantya*) following them. Fearing the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) that these seven would also be designated as *ṣopadeśa* (roots taught with an initial *ṣ*), he provides the qualification "other than those" (*tadbhinnatva*) by stating:
"other than *sek*, *sṛp*, *sṛ*, *stṛ*, *sṛj*, *stṛ*, and *styai*. [The root *styai*...]

The mention of the verbal root with *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) is for the purpose of including it within the verse; for if there were a mention of the form ending in *ai*, namely *styai*, the fault of an extra syllable would arise in the phrase "ṭhstyāryanya". [Objection: Even so, there are the roots *ṣvaṣk* in the sense of moving, *ñiṣvidā* in the sense of perspiration of the limbs, and *ṣvada* in the sense of tasting.
Regarding the roots *ṣvañj* (in the sense of embracing), *ṣviṣvap* (in the sense of sleeping), and *ṣmiṅ* (in the sense of slight laughter)—

one might raise the objection that these would not be included among the *ṣopadeśa* (roots with initial *ṣ*) because their *ṣ* is neither followed by a dental nor followed by a vowel; having raised this concern regarding under-extension (*avyāpti*), [the author] includes them as well.

He groups them together: *ṣvak*, *svid*, *svad*, *svap*, *smiṅ*. The word "also" (*api*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Now, one might object that roots such as *ṣvṛ* (meaning "to sound" and "to afflict") would also be classified as *ṣopadeśa* (having an initial *ṣ*) because they have a dental *v* following [the *ṣ*]; therefore, he says: "dental."

"Only dental"? Why? To this he says: "Of *ṣvaṣka* and so on. The point is that otherwise, since [the rule] would already be established simply by the fact of being followed by a dental, the mention of *ṣvaṣka* and so on would be redundant. Although *ṣvaṣkati* is not seen here in the Bhāṣya, nevertheless, among the *sub*-dhātus, *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣki*...
The sense is that this [term] is obtained from the *Vārttika* stating "the prohibition of *sat*. Regarding *hlāda*: this contains the letter *r*.
It is an indistinct sound—meaning the speech of a non-human. Regarding *jahāda*: there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and the substitution of *c* for *j*.
Regarding *hlādī*: this contains the letter *l*. [This refers to the rule] *ṭh-svīdito...* [etc.]

The substitution of *ī* [for the radical vowel] is for the purpose of prohibiting *iṇ* [the augment]. In the case of *svād*, this is not a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*) because it lacks the quality of having only dentals following it. [Examples: *asisvadat*. Regarding *pad*:
it means "to move" (*gadarava*). Regarding *yat*: the designation *īdit* is for the purpose of prohibiting *iṇ*. [Example: *yete*. [Regarding *ṭhata*...]

In the case of *ekahalmadhye*, there is the substitution of *i* (itva) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). The roots *yutṛ* and *jutṛ* contain the vowel *ṛ*; this *ṛ*-designation (*ṛditva*) is for the sake of rules such as *nāglopiśāsvṛditām*. Thus, *yotate*: here, by the rule *śapi laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*, there is the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *u*]. *Yuyutaḥ*: here, because of the *kit* designation by the rule *asaṃyogāt*, there is no *guṇa*. The roots *vithṛ* and *vethṛ*...

These two [roots] end in the suffix -tṛ. Now, one might object: let it simply be *vithṛ*, since once the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel has occurred, the form *vethate* would be indistinguishable [from that of *vethṛ*]. To this he says: *vivite*, *vivethe*. The form *vivethe* belongs to the root *vethṛ*; however, for the root *vithṛ*, [the form is derived] by the rule *asaṃyogāl liṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5).
The commentator states that because of the *kit* designation, there is an absence of *guṇa*, resulting in the form *vivitha*.
Regarding *śrathī*: it ends in the accusative case; "looseness" means falling apart (*sraṃsana*). [The root] *śranth* takes the augment *num* due to its *idit* designation.
Regarding *grathī*: it ends in the accusative case; "crookedness" means becoming curved (*vakrībhavana*). [The root] *granth*... [takes the augment *num*].
Having understood this, he praises (*kattheti*). Praise (*ślāghā*) is the making known of qualities that do not exist.

Now, regarding "thirty-eight" (*aṣṭātriṃśat*): it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "eight and thirty," or "thirty with eight added. The substitution of *ā* [for *aṣṭan*] occurs by the rule "dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṅkhyāyām. However, in the reading "aṣṭatriṃśat," [the analysis is different].

"Aṣṭa" is a separate word. Regarding "parasmaipadinaḥ" (those that take the *parasmaipada* endings): the sense is that because they lack the properties of being *anudāteta*, *svaritet*, or having an indicatory letter *ñ*, they are exclusively *parasmaipadins* by virtue of the rule "śeṣātkartari. Regarding "ata": it means continuous movement—uninterrupted movement. In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, with the suffix *ṇal*...

When the state *a-a-t-a* arises after reduplication (*dvitva*) and the application of the rule *halādiśeṣa*, the formation of a single substitute by the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would be expected; therefore, he says: *ata ādeḥ*. The remainder [of the rule] is "there is lengthening" (*iti dīrghaḥ*). Thus, when the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is lengthened, the long vowel resulting from homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*) follows. This is what he expresses by saying: *āteti*. [This refers to] the vowel *a*.

Because there is no occurrence of a vowel situated between two consonants (*halmadhyasthatva*), the elision of *e* and the reduplicated syllable (*etvābhyāsalopa*) do not apply. Regarding the form *aluṅ*: after the root *at*, the suffix *luṅ* is introduced; then, by the rule *itaśca*, the *ikāra* is elided; then *sic* is substituted for *cli*; then the augment *iṭ* is added to that *sic*; then the augment *īṭ* is added by the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*; finally, the augment *āṭ* is added, resulting in *vṛddhi*, and the form stands as *ātis ī t*.
The meaning is "being present.
(109) *iṭa īṭi* | Pāṇini 8.2.28.
In *iṭa īṭi*, the word *iṭaḥ* is in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). From the rule *rātsasya*, the word *saḥ* [is understood].

The words "of that which ends in a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya*) and "elision" (*lopa*) are carried over [from previous rules]. Thus he says: "following *iṭ*. And so, when the state *āti s īt* has arisen, upon the elision of the *s*, the state *āti īt* results; then, by applying the rule for long vowels before homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*), he will state that the form is *ātīt*. In that regard:

Since the elision of *s* (*salopa*) is not established (*asiddhatva*), how can there be a long vowel by rule of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*)? To this he says: "The elision of *s* (*sijlopa*) must be stated as established (*siddha*) with respect to a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). [The example is] *ātiṣṭhām*. This is derived from *luṅ* with the suffix *tas*; for that, *tām* is substituted; then *sic* is substituted for *cli*; for that, *iṭ* is added;
then, after *āc*, there is *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *ṣ*. Because of the absence of being a single consonant (*apṛkta*), [the rule does not apply].

Due to the absence of the *īḍ* augment, there is no elision of the *s*. Thus: *ātiṣuḥ*. [Derivation: In the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *jhi*; *sic* replaces *cli*; *jus* replaces it; *iṭ* and *āṭ* augments;
*vṛddhi*; *ṣatva*; *rutva* and *visarga*. [The other forms are: *ātīḥ*, *ātiṣṭam*, *ātiṣṭa*;
*ātiṣam*, *ātiṣva*, *ātiṣma*.

(110) *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.3. Regarding this, he speaks in order to raise the doubt concerning *vṛddhi*: *vadavraja*. [The compound] *vadavraja* is a collective dvandva of *vada*, *vraja*, and *halanta*; from this, the genitive singular is applied. The term *aṅgasya* is supplied by context. [This refers to the rule] *sici vṛddhiḥ*.
The term *parasmaipadeṣu* (in the parasmaipada endings) is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says, starting with "of *vad*" and so forth.

Although [the desired form] is established simply because [the roots] end in a consonant (*hal*), the specific mention of the exclusion of *vad* is for the purpose of overriding the optional *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ* in cases such as *avādīt* and *avrājīt*.
(111) *neṭi* | Pāṇini 7.2.4. "Not when *iṭ* follows. This means that what was previously stated [by the rule *aco ñṇiti*] does not apply when *iṭ* follows.

Specifically, regarding the statement "*vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.3), this is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution that would otherwise be occasioned by the condition of having a consonant at the end (*halanta*). This is because [the rules for] *vad* and *vraj* have been specifically prescribed [as exceptions].

The *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by a final consonant, however, has its purpose fulfilled in forms such as *adhākṣīt*, where the suffix *sic* begins with a vowel other than *i*. One might object: "In forms like *āstīt*, whether or not the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *a* occurs, there is no difference in the resulting form once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with *āṭ* has taken place; so what is the point of prohibiting it? Anticipating this doubt, he says: *mā*...

*bhavānatīti*: The point is that the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is purposeful when the augment *āṭ* is absent due to the connection with the prohibitive particle *māṅ*. *citīti*: The status of being marked with *ī* (*īdit*) is for the sake of prohibiting the suffix *iṭ* by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*.

*cetatīti*: By the addition of the suffix *śap*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. *ciceteti*: Because the substitute *ṇal* for *tiP* is marked with *p* (*pit*), [the *guṇa* substitution does not apply].

Because there is no *asaṃyoga* (non-conjunct consonant), the status of being a *kit* does not apply, and thus there is no prohibition of *guṇa*. However, in forms such as *cicitatuḥ*, there is no *guṇa* due to the *kit* status. Regarding *acetīt*: by the rule *iṭa īṭi*, there is the elision of *s*. Regarding *acetiṣṭām*: because there is an absence of *apṛkta* (a single-consonant suffix), there is an absence of *īṭ*, and consequently, there is no elision of *sic*. This is according to the rule *neṭi*.

Due to the prohibition, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a suffix ending in *hal*. Regarding the term *cyuti*: here, since both the vowel *i* and the consonant *r* would each individually receive the designation *it*, and consequently the augment *num* would apply because of being *idit*, he says: "The sequence *ir* is designated as *it*. Thus, because the entire cluster *ir* is designated as *it*, it lacks the status of being *idit*, and therefore [the augment does not apply].

The sense is as follows: [in the form] *cyotati*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. In *cucyoteti*, because the *ṇal* suffix is marked with *p* (indicating it is not *kit*), there is no prohibition of *guṇa*; this is the sense.
However, in forms such as *cucyutuḥ*, there is no *guṇa* due to the *kit* designation. Now, regarding the *luṅ* [tense], when *sic* would otherwise apply after *cli*:

(112) *irito vā* | 3|1|57| The word *dhātoḥ* [“of a verbal root”] is supplied from *dhātor ekācaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.22]; the word *cleḥ* [“of the suffix cli”] is supplied from *cleḥ sic* [Pāṇini 3.1.44]; and the word *aṅ* [“the suffix aṅ”] is supplied from *asyativaktikhyātibhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.52].

The phrase "in the *parasmaipada* endings" is understood from the rule *ṭhpuṣādidyautādī* (Pāṇini 3.1.55). Thus he says: "from a root ending in *ir*," and so forth. Regarding *acyutat*: since the suffix *aṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. [The forms are: *acyutatām*, *acyutan*; *acyutaḥ*, *acyutatam*, *acyutata*; [and] *acyutam*.

*acyutāva*, *acyutāma*. Regarding the absence of the augment (*aṅ*), he says: *acyotīt*. By the rule *ṭhiṭa īṭi*, there is the elision of the *sic* suffix. *acyotiṣṭām*, and so forth. *Ścyutiḥ*: the forms are like those of *cyuti*. *cuścyoteti*: by the rule *śarpūrvāḥ*, the letter *c* remains.
"Even when devoid of the letter *y*"—the sense is that this is observed in such instances as "ṭhmadhuścutaṃ ghṛtamiva supūtam" and others. Regarding "mantha": it means churning or stirring.
"Manthati" and so forth are easy to understand. He states a specific rule regarding the *āśīr-liṅ* (the benedictive mood): "of *yāsuṭ*" and so on.

Regarding "kuth-": all four [forms] end in the accusative case. Because it is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*idit*), the augment *num* is added; thus, forms such as *kunthati* are easily understood. Regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) with the suffix *yāsuṭ*, although it is *kit*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not occur because of the exclusion rule "of those not having *it*" (*aniditām*); thus he says, "because it is *idit*. [The form] is *kunthyāt*.

One should say *punthyāt*, *lunthyāt*, and *manthyāt*. It is for this very reason that the root *manth* is taught separately as *math* [in the Dhātupāṭha]. Regarding the root *ṣidh* in the sense of "going": because it begins with the letter *ṣ* followed by a vowel (*ac*), it is a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*). Consequently, by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*, the *ṣ* is changed to *s*.

Regarding this, he says: *siṣedha* (he has warded off). Because the substitute [root] begins with the letter *s*, the change to *ṣ* occurs by rule (*ṣatva*). Since among the roots that do not take the augment *iṭ* (aniṭ), only the root *sidh* belonging to the *śyan*-conjugation is included, this [root] takes the augment *iṭ*. Thus, *asedhīt* (he warded off). By the rule "the elision of *iṭ* when *iṭ* follows" (*iṭa iṭi*), there is the elision of the *sic* suffix. Due to the prohibition "not when *iṭ* follows" (*neṭi*), the vowel lengthening conditioned by a final consonant (*hal-anta-lakṣaṇā vṛddhiḥ*) does not occur.

Regarding the passage beginning with *asedhiṣṭām*, etc.: one might raise the objection that since the rule *upasargāt sunoti* will later prescribe the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in cases such as *niṣedhati*, what is the purpose [of the present rule], since it would already be established by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: *sātpadādyoḥ*.

(113) *upasargāt sunoti-suvati-syati-stauti-stobhati-sthā-senaya-se-dha-sica-sañja-svañjām* | 8|3|65 | *upasargāt sunoti*. *upasargāt tad iti*. The word "prefix" (*upasarga*) is used here figuratively to mean "that which stands in the place of a prefix."

Such is the intended meaning (*itibhāvaḥ*). "From a cause" (*nimitāt*) means "from that which has the form of *iṇ*. Although the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "before *k*" (*ṭhiṇkoḥ*) is in effect, the word "k" (*kor*) is not connected here because it is impossible [for it to apply]. "Of *s*" (*sasya*): the meaning is that the genitive form "s" (*sa*), from the rule "the *s* of *sah*, when preceded by *sāṭ*, becomes *ṣ*" (*saheḥ sāḍaḥ sa*), is understood as continuing (*anuvartate*). "There shall be *ṣ*" (*ṣaḥ syāt*).

The intention is that this is because of the governing rule (adhikāra) "a cerebral [substitute] occurs for [a dental] at the end of a word. Regarding this, the ancients maintain that the mention of *sunoti* and so forth by means of the *śtip* affix is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-lopa; however, in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*, it is stated that it is for the sake of clarity. In the example *senayā*, the verbal root is a nominal derivative (*nāmadhātu*) ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*); whereas in *sedhati*, it is mentioned with the *śap* affix.
Because it is established by explicit statement (*nirdeśa*), there is no [need for] inclusion. "He presses" (*abhiṣuṇoti*) and so forth are the examples.
The citation of this rule here is for the purpose of excluding cases such as "he forbids" (*niṣedhati*) in the present context. (114) *sadir aprateḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.66.

He states [this] as a corollary: *sadiraprateḥ*. Regarding the term *upasargāt*: the meaning is "following an *iṇ* [consonant] situated in a prefix. Intending that *sadiḥ* is in the genitive sense expressed by the nominative, he says: *sadeḥ sasya* ("of the *s* of the root *sad*"). *Niṣīdati* ("he sits down") is the example.
(115) *stambheḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.67.

Regarding the mention of the word *stambheḥ*, he states the purpose of specifying it as having *na* as its penultimate letter: "by the rule of the Sūtra," meaning [the purpose is to exclude] that which is specified in the Sūtra *stanbhustunbhusumbhuskanbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 3.1.82) as having *na* as its penultimate letter. For that [latter form]...

This is stated as a specific rule (*pratipadokta*). However, the root *ṣṭambh* (from which *stambh* is derived) is not included [in the rule] because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical operation), owing to the presence of the *it* marker (*num*) after the vowel *i*. Consequently, there is no substitution of *ṣ* in forms such as *vistambhate*. In the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ*, however, both roots are included due to the inclusion of the term "having *m* as a penultimate letter" (*mopadha*).
Because the letter *m* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in both cases. Now, one might ask: why was the rule not formulated as a single sūtra, "ṭh-sadi-stambhyo 'prateḥ"?
To this he replies: "The division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows."

The meaning is that [the word *sadi*] is mentioned for the purpose of preventing its recurrence in the subsequent rule, "ṭhācca ālambanāvidūryayoḥ. Now, one might object: since *sadi* is not marked with the svarita accent and because it does not function in the sense of "support" (*ālambana*) or "proximity" (*avidūrya*), its non-recurrence is already established; therefore, to avoid this lack of elegance, he says: "Furthermore... and "it does not recur."
The intention [of the author] is that in the rule *stambheḥ*, the term *aprateḥ* should also be connected with *stanbhinā*.
He states— *bāhupratiṣṭambha*— that the non-connection of *aprateḥ* with *stanbha* follows the usage of the Vṛddhi grammarians.

(116) *avāccālambanāvidūryayoḥ* |8|3|68|. From the word *ava*, [the suffix *ṭi* is added] when it signifies either support (*ālambana*) or proximity (*āvidūrya*). This is a dual locative case derived from a *dvandva* compound consisting of *ālambana* and *āvidūrya*. Regarding the phrase *etoh*: [it refers to the suffix *ṭi*] which follows the prefix *ava* when it possesses the two meanings of support and proximity.
The connection [of the rule] is with the root *stambh*. This is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), because it would not otherwise apply due to the absence of a suffix following the root *iṇ*.
Regarding "support" (*ālambana*): for example, "he stands having supported himself on a staff. The meaning is "having resorted to" (*āśritya*).
Regarding "proximity" (*āvidūrya*): it means nearness. "The cow is held fast" (*avaṣṭabdhā gauḥ*) means that, being restrained, it remains in close proximity.
This is the meaning.
(117) *veśca svano bhojane* | Pāṇini 8.3.69. Regarding *veśca*: the word *ca* (and) is for the purpose of drawing in [the preceding rule regarding] *ava*. Thus he says: "by *vi* and *ava*."

*Viṣvaṇati* and *avaṣvaṇati* mean "he eats with sound. The change to *ṇ* [the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*] is by the rule *aṭkupvāṅ*. (118) *parinivibhyaḥ sevasitasayasivusahasuṭastusvañjām* | Pāṇini 8.3.70.

[The rule applies] after *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*. The letter *a* in *seva* is for the sake of pronunciation; it is the inclusion of the root *ṣevṛ* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*). [Examples: *pariṣevate*, *niṣevate*, *viṣevate*.
By the word *sita*, there is the inclusion of the form ending in *kta* from the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding. Or, [it refers to] the same root with the suffix *erac*.

Alternatively, the word *saya* ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *si*. [Examples: *viṣitaḥ*, *viṣayaḥ*. From the root *ṣivu* (to sew): *pariṣīvyati*. From the root *ṣaha* (to endure): *pariṣahate*. [In these cases] the augment *suṭ* is applied. Regarding *pariṣkaroti*:

although it would have been established by the rule "after *stu*, *svañj*, and [roots] not preceded by a prefix, [the augment *ṣat* is applied] before *sunoti*," the statement "*sivādīnāṃ ve*" [is made for the sake of other roots].
The repetition is for the sake of providing an alternative interpretation.
(119) *prāksitādaḍvyavāye’pi* [Pāṇini 8.3.66]. Regarding *prāksitāt*: the remainder of the sense is "those [roots] mentioned in the sūtra beginning with *upasargātsunoti*."

"Of them" means "of the fifteen. Regarding the word "he prohibited": since the vowel *i* is not followed by *ṇ* because it is separated by the letter *a*, the rule would otherwise not apply; therefore, this is a specific statement [to provide for such cases].
"He boiled thoroughly" (*abhyuṣuṇot*) should also be cited as an example.
(120) *sthādiṣvabhyāsena cābhyāsasya* |8|3|64|.

In the phrase *sthādiṣu*, the word *abhyāsena* ends in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). The term *prāksitāt* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Therefore, he says: "before *sit*" (*prāksitāt*). This refers to the rule *upasargātsunoti*.

The meaning is: "among those ten roots which are introduced prior to the word *sita* in the rule *ṭhparinivibhyaḥ sevasite* (Pāṇini 8.3.70), beginning with the root *sthā*. In forms such as *niṣiṣedha*, the rule [prohibiting *ṣatva*] does not apply because the *s* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is separated from the prefix (*upasarga*) by that reduplicated syllable; therefore, this statement is made to provide for it. Now, [one might object]:...

Regarding the rule *niṣiṣedha* and others, one might object that since the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* situated in the reduplicated syllable is already established by the rule *upasargād ṛti sunoti* (Pāṇini 8.3.65), the mention of *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplicated syllable") is redundant. Anticipating this objection, he states that it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), namely: "only for these [roots]. That is to say, if the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* situated in the reduplicated syllable is to occur, then...

The meaning is that this applies only to these ten roots. Thus, in the case of *ṣū* (in the sense of "impelling") as in *abhisusūṣate*, there is no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). However, for the *s* following the reduplication, there is no *ṣatva* because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that it occurs only in the case of the root *stu* and after the suffix *ṇi*.

(121) *sedhateḥ gatau* | 8|3|113| [The word] *sedhateḥ* [is used]; [the rule states] "there is no *ṣ*-ness. The intention is that this is because of the continuation of the word *na* from [the previous rule] *na rapara-* [8.3.110].
In the example *gaṅgāṃ visedhati*, the meaning is "he goes. Here, the *ṣ*-ness [of the prefix] would have occurred by [the rule] *upasargāt sunoti-* [8.3.65].

It does not apply. By the principle of "the immediate [preceding]," this prohibition applies only to the rule *upasargāt sunoti*, and not to the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* as well. Therefore, in forms such as *siṣedha*, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* certainly occurs. Regarding the root *ṣidhū*: but surely...

Since a treatise (*śāstra*), which consists of a specific collection of sentences, does not have the nature of an action (*akriyārūpatvāt*), how can it be the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvarthatva*)? To this, he says: "A treatise is instruction (*śāsana*). As for "auspiciousness" (*māṅgalya*), it refers to a virtuous act (*śubhakarma*); its forms are like those of the root *ṣidh* in the sense of "going."

(122) *svarati-sūrati-sūyati-dhūñ-ūdito vā* | Pāṇini 7.2.44. In this context, since *iṭ* would necessarily apply before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*), [the rule] states: *svarati*, *sūti*, *sūyati*. The phrase "*ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*" is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*). [The roots are: *svarati*, *sūti*, *sūyati*.

The word *dhūñ* and those ending in *ū*—this is the singular ablative of a collective dvandva compound. He states the result [of this analysis] with the words "of *svarati*, etc. The mention of *svṛ* as *svarati* is a reference to the root *svṛ* by means of the *śap* affix (*śap* = *a*).
The mention of *sū* as both *sūti* and *sūyati* is a reference to the root *sū* when it takes the *luṅ-vikaraṇa* (*śn*) and the *śyan-vikaraṇa* (*ya*), respectively. And thus...

The root *ṣū* meaning "to impel," belonging to the *tudādigaṇa*, is not included here. The root *dhūñ* meaning "to shake" belongs to both the *svādigaṇa* and the *kryādigaṇa*. Because of the specific mention of the indicatory letter *ñ*, the root *dhū* meaning "to shake off" (*vidhūnana*) is not included. The word *vā* (or) is mentioned here because the option (*vā*) following from the rule "iṭ sani vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.41) continues to apply.

The *Bhāṣya* states that this is for the purpose of removing the optionality (*vikalpa*) prescribed by the two rules, "thali ca seṭi" and "caṅyanyatarasyām. Thus, in the case where the augment *iṭ* is absent after the suffix *thal*, and after reduplication and other operations have occurred, the form stands as *sisedh-tha*.

(123) *Jhaṣas tathor dhaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.40. The rule *jhaṣas tathor dhaḥ* is as follows: *jhaṣaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). *Ta-thoḥ* is a *dvandva* compound; the vowel *a* after *ta-* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus, it is understood to mean "of *ta* and *tha*. *dhaḥ* is the nominative singular. Therefore, when a letter belonging to the *jhaṣ* class [the gutturals and the three retroflexes: *k, kh, g, gh, ṅ, ṭ, ṭh, ḍ, ḍh, ṇ*] precedes, the *ta* or *tha* [at the end of a word or before a suffix] is replaced by *dha*.

The letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; thus, *dha* is obtained. In the word *ṭhadha*, the suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) is understood, meaning "of that which is different from the root *dhā*. This is what he says: "of [the consonants] following *jhaṣ*. Regarding *jaśtva*:
when *sisedh dha* is established, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the first *dha* is changed to *da*.
The meaning is that *siṣeddha* is the form [of the second person singular]. *Siṣidiva*—*siṣidhva*; *siṣidhima*—*siṣidhma*.

However, the rule regarding the *krādi* group (Pāṇini 7.2.13) is a negator only of the absence [of *iṭ*] brought about by the preceding rule *neḍvaśi* (7.2.8), and not even of that which was optionally non-applicable due to the rule *vibhāṣā* (7.2.6), according to the maxim *anantarasya* (the operation applies to what is immediately preceding).

Regarding the alternative involving *iṭ*, he says: *siṣedhitha* (you have obstructed), *seddhā* (he will obstruct). [In the latter case: the suffix *lṛṭ*, the addition of *tās*, the absence of *iṭ*, the substitution of *ḍā*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion, *guṇa* strengthening, the change to *dha*, and then the change to the voiced unaspirated (*jaś*) sound. Thus we get *seddhāraḥ* and so forth. *Sedhitā* is the form when *iṭ* is present. *Setsyati* and *sedhiṣyati* [are formed] with *lṛṭ*; the suffix *sya* is added, and there is an optional presence of *iṭ*.

Regarding the form *asaitsīt*: it is derived from the root *as* with the suffix *luṅ*, *tip*, elision of the *ik* vowel, *cli*, *sic*, absence of *iṭ*, and the augment *īṭ* by the rule "after *asti* and *sic*. Then, there is *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule "for *vad* and *vraj*" (*vadavraja*), and the change of *dh* to *t* by the rule "of *ch*" (*coḥ kuḥ*). Finally, the elision of the *s* of *sic* occurs by the rule "after a consonant [ending in] *jhal*, before a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound" (*jhalo jhali*).

When *asaidh* is established [as the form], because it lacks the status of being *apṛkta* (not a single-syllable suffix), the augment *iṭ* does not apply; and since *iṭ* is absent, the elision of *sic* by the rule *iṭa īṭi* would not occur. [To remedy this, the following is stated: *jhalo jhali*. Here, *jhalaḥ* is in the ablative case. From the rule *saṃyogāntasya*, the word *lopaḥ* (elision) is understood, and from the rule *rātsasya*, the word *sasya* (of *s*) is understood.

And it follows [from that]. Thus he says: "of a letter other than *jhal*, etc. Regarding *aseddhām*: when *asaidh* + *tām* is situated, after the elision of *s*, the substitution of *dh* for *th*, and the substitution of the *jaś*-class letter (*d*), this form is obtained. Regarding "in the alternative": the meaning is "in the alternative involving the augment *iṭ*. Regarding *asedhīt*: there is elision of *s* by the rule *iṭa īṭi*; and by the rule *neṭ*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*.

The *laghūpadhaguṇa* (the guṇa substitution of a light penultimate vowel) applies. Regarding the form *khādṛ*, he states—intending that the presence of the marker *ṛt* is for the sake of rules such as *nāglopi*—"the letter *ṛ* is *it*" (*ṛkāra id*). [The form] *khadā* means steadiness—the act of becoming firm.

(125) *ata upadhāyāḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.116. Since [the root] does not end in a vowel (*ajanta*), the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) does not apply for the occurrence of *vṛddhi*. Therefore, [the present sūtra] states: *ata upadhāyāḥ*.
The meaning is that *vṛddhi* should take place, because the phrase "of *mṛj*" from the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) here.

He causes to eat (*cakhādeti*). However, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur here, because [the substitute] is *pit*, because it is not *kit*, because it begins with a substitute [consonant], and because the *vṛddhi* replacement takes precedence over that.
(126) *ṇal uttamo vā* | Pāṇini 7.1.91.

"ṇal is the last [suffix]. The intention is that it should be *ṇit*, because of the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "ṇit after a word ending in *go*. In *cakhāda* and *cakhada*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel due to the *ṇit* quality; in its absence, there is none. (127) *ato halāder laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7).

From this [sūtra], *halādeḥ* [is understood]. The phrase *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* is carried over (anuvartate). From *neṭi*, the word *iṭi* is carried over; and from *ūrṇoter vibhāṣā*, the word *vibhāṣā*. Thus he says: *halādeḥ*. The meaning is "of that which has a consonant as its initial [element] and is a member of the *aṅga*. The inclusion of the word *ādi* (initial) [is for the purpose of...]

This is for the sake of clarity, since the rule would have been established by [the general rule] *haloḥ parasya* alone. Examples: *akhādīt* and *akhadīt*. When there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) or its absence, the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule *iṭa īṭi*. Thus: *akhādiṣṭām*, *akhadiṣṭām*, and so forth.
The root *bad-* means "to become firm"—that is, the act of becoming stable. It begins with a labial (*pavargīya*).
The meaning is that it begins with the third letter of the *pa*-class (*pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*); the intention is not that it begins with a dental-labial (*da*, *dha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma*).

Regarding *babādeta*: the vowel *ā* is substituted by *vṛddhi* according to the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ. Regarding *bedatuḥ*: although there is the status of being "beginning with a substitute" (*ādeśāditva*) due to the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) for the reduplication, [the rule still applies].

The meaning is that because there is an absence of causing a change in form (*vairūpyāpādakatva*), the substitution of *e* for *i* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur. However, in the case of *babādhe*, because it is treated as having the *ṅit*-marker *p* (which prevents *ṅittva*), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not take place. In *beditha*, although it lacks the *ṅit*-marker, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication occur by the rule "and in *thal* when followed by *seṭ*. Now, for the first person singular (*uttama-puruṣa*) in the root *vid*.

Regarding the rule *ṭhṇal uttamo vā*, because of the optional status of the *ṇit* designation, there is an option regarding the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel; thus he says: *babāda*, *babadā*;
*bediva*, *bedima*; *abādīt*, *abadīt*. Here, the option for *vṛddhi* arises by the rule *ato halādeḥ*. *Gada* means distinct speech—the employment of sound produced by humans.

It says "jagāda": by the rules *cutva* and *jaśtva*, there is *upadhā-vṛddhi*. Because it begins with a substitute (*ādeśa*) that causes dissimilarity (*vairūpya*), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur. Thus we have *jagadatuḥ*, *jagaduḥ*, and so forth.

(128) *Nergadanadapatapadaghumāsyatihantiyātivātidrātipsātivapativahatiśāmyaticinotidegdhiṣu ca* | Pāṇini 8.4.17. In the case of the roots *gada*, *nada*, *pada*, *ghuma*, *as*, *ti*, *han*, *yā*, *vā*, *drā*, *psā*, *vap*, *vah*, *śam*, *ci*, and *digdh*, [the *n* of the prefix is replaced by *m*]. The rule *ṛṣābhyāṃ no maḥ* ("after *ṛ* and *ṣ*, *n* is replaced by *m*") is understood to carry over from this point. This is also understood from the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi* ("after a prefix, even when not in a compound...").

And regarding the rule *upasargād iti*: that [word *upasarga*] refers metonymically (*lākṣaṇika*) to what stands in an *upasarga*. Thus he says: "from what stands in an *upasarga*. The mention of the suffixes *śit* and *śap* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of *yaṅ*).

[The example is] *praṇigadati*. This is a statement [of a rule] because [the condition] would otherwise not apply due to the words being situated in different words (*bhinnapadasthatvāt*). [The example is] *radeti*, in the *ṇal* [suffix].

Intending to show the increase of the *upadhā* vowel, he says: *rarāda*, *redatuḥ*, and so forth; *arādīt*, *aradīt*. Regarding *ṇada*: it refers to indistinct sound—the utterance of sounds produced by non-humans, animals, birds, and the like. (129) *ṇo naḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.65.

*ṇo naḥ*: *ṭhṇa* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). Because [the word] "of the root-initial" (*dhātvādeḥ*) from the rule *ṣaḥ saḥ* is understood as a governing reference (*anuvartana*), he says: "of the beginning of the root. Therefore, there is no substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *aṇati*.
*naḥ syāt*: the meaning is that the letter *n* should occur. *nadati*.

The word "meghādi" (cloud, etc. is to be understood as the remainder [of the list]. Since the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* (by the rule *ṇo naḥ*) is not conditioned by anything else (*anaimitaka*), there is an absence of the condition for the substitution of *liṅ* (the augment *it*); therefore, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) indeed occur, as in *nedatuḥ* and so forth. Now...

He summarizes the Bhāṣya passage—"The roots *ṇṛt*, *nard*, *nand*, *nakk*, *nāṭ*, *nāth*, *ṛ*, and *nānṛ* are excluded from those taught with an initial *ṇ*"—in the following half-verse: "Those taught with an initial *ṇ*, however... [The roots are: *ṇarda* (to sound), *ṇaṭ* (to dance) belonging to the Curādi class, and *nāthṛ* / *nādhṛ* (to beg, etc.).

The second and fourth [roots] end in *ṇ*. From the eight roots— *ṭhṭua* (to prosper), *ṭhnaṭ* (to destroy), *ṭhnṛ* (to lead), and *ṭhnṛtī* (to move the limbs)— other roots beginning with *ṇ*, even though they appear now as beginning with *n*, are taught with the letter *ṇ* because their *n* has not yet acquired the status of *natva* (the change to the cerebral nasal).
The meaning is that they are to be understood [as such]. He states the purpose of the root *nāṭ* when it ends in *ṇi*—namely, "of *nāṭ*" (*nāṭeḥ*).

"Belonging to the *ghaṭādi* group" means that it is listed in the *ghaṭādi* group under the rule "naṭa nṛtau. Its result will be explained in the section on the *ghaṭādi* group. He states another opinion: "in the *tavarga*," etc.

The meaning is that, having accepted the absence of exclusion (paryudāsa) for the roots *nā*, *dadhāti*, and the two roots *nṛ* and *nand*— despite their ending in the fourth letter of the *tavarga* group— they assert that these too possess the status of being taught with an initial *ṇ*.
According to this view, the result is that those [roots] distinct from the five are the ones taught with an initial *ṇ*.
The contradiction with the Bhāṣya is the seed of dissatisfaction here.
(130) *upasargādasamāse 'pi ṇopadeśasya* Pāṇini 8.4.14. Now, having prescribed the letter *ṇ*, for what purpose is the letter *n* ordained in its place? [The answer is: the letter *n*.

Anticipating the question, "In that case, let it be taught thus," he states its purpose: [the rule] begins with *upasargāt*. The governing rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* is understood here. He says this by stating *upasargasthāt*. Since the word *samāse* (in a compound) is understood from the preceding rule *samāse 'ṅgule saṅgaḥ*, the substitution would not occur in a non-compound; therefore, the mention of *asamāse* (not in a compound) is made.
If that were the case, [the rule] would not apply in a compound such as *praṇāma*; therefore, the inclusion of the word *api* (also) is made.
Thus he says: "In a compound as well as in a non-compound. The analysis of the compound is: "that in which there is the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the letter *ṇa*.
In *praṇadati*, there is no application [of the rule] because it consists of separate words (*bhinnapadatvāt*). In *praṇinadati*, the substitution of *ṇa* occurs by the rule *ner dadeti*.

Nor should one suspect the substitution of *ṇ* for the nasal *n* of the root in this case by the rule "ṭhupasargādasamāse" (Pāṇini 8.4.14), because there is an intervention by an element other than those specified as *aṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, or *āṅ*. Regarding the form *ardati*: in the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 7.1.101), the term *ikaḥ* is understood to carry over; therefore, there is no lengthening of the vowel in forms such as *ardati*.

(131) *tasmān nuḍ dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.71). When the suffix *ṇal* follows the root *ard*, after reduplication (*dvitva*) and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the rule *ata āder* causes the lengthening of the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable; thus, we have *ā ard* + *ati*. At this stage, the rule *tasmān nuḍ dvihalaḥ* applies. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has two consonants (*hal*) [in its reduplicated form]."
By the word *tat*, that which has undergone lengthening according to the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75) is referred to.

Thus he says: "from that which has become long. The letter *ṭ* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is marked with *ṭ* (ṭit), it is the initial constituent. Thus he says: "in *nardati*" and "in *ārdīt*. In *ārdīt*, there is the elision of the *s*-augment (*sic*) by the rule *ṭhiṭa īṭi*. [The forms] *nardati* and so forth follow.

This is clear. Regarding *kardeati*: he says "kaukṣa" because by the word *kutsita* (contemptible), a specific type of contemptible thing is intended; the meaning is "born from the belly. Regarding *khareati*: *dandaśūkaḥ* is a snake whose nature is biting.
Amara states: "A *dandaśūka* is a hole-dweller [snake]. Now, as for the snake...

To the question, "Since there is an absence of the nature of action (*kriyātva*), how can there be the status of being a verbal root meaning (*dhātvarthatva*)?", he says: *daṃśana* etc.; *ati*, *adīti*. Because it is marked with the *it* (indicatory letter *i*), the augment *num* is added. Thus he says: *antatīti*. *Ānanteti*: the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ata ādeḥ*; the augment *nuṭ* is added by the rule *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*. Similarly: *andati*, *ānandeti* [with the addition of *nuṭ*].

*Āndīt*. *Idīti*: the supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*), that is, becoming the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*). *Indatīti*: because it is marked with the *idit* [indicatory letter], there is the augment *num*. *Indāñcakāra*: by the rule "after *ṭhi*, there is *ām* for roots beginning with a vowel. *Bidīti*: he says that because it is marked with *idit*, there is *num*; thus, *bindatīti*. [Objection: But since a part [of a word] cannot be of the nature of an action, how...

To explain the meaning of the verbal root, he says: "the meaning is 'he performs a part'. [Examples are] *abindīt*, *abindiṣṭām*, and so forth. "Ending in a *p*-class letter" means beginning with the fourth letter of the *pa*-class (*ḍa*).
Regarding *gaḍī*: "a part of the face"; the meaning is "in that action. [Examples are] *gaṇḍati*, *agaṇḍīt*.

Regarding "antatyādayaḥ": the meaning is that according to the opinion of Kāśyapa, these five verbal roots—*ati* (in the sense of binding), *adi* (in the sense of supreme sovereignty), *bidi* (in the sense of a part), and *gaḍi* (in the sense of a portion of the face)—are not bases for the *tiṅ* suffixes. Regarding "others": other sages besides Kāśyapa [hold that] even from these [roots], there are *tiṅ* suffixes.

The meaning is "they desire. Regarding *ṇidi*: because it is marked with the *it*-sign (*idit*), the augment *num* is added; because it is taught with an initial *ṇ* (*ṇopadeśa*), the *ṇ* becomes *n*.
Thus he says: "he censures" (*nindati*). In *praṇindati*, the *ṇ* occurs by the rule "even in a non-compound, after a prefix" (*upasargādasamāse’pi*).
Regarding *ṭua nadi*: "prosperity" refers to the abundance of progeny, cattle, and so forth.
