Regarding the word *grantha*: one might object, "Since a book (*grantha*) consists of a collection of sentences and is therefore not an action (*akriyā*), how can it be the meaning of a verbal root? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that here... *Grantha* means *granthana*, which is the state of being joined together (*saṅghībhāva*) or the act of joining together (*saṅghīkaraṇa*). Among these, the state of being joined together resides in the collection itself.

The act of forming a group (*saṅghīkaraṇa*), however, resides in the agent who forms the group. In this regard, when it has the sense of "becoming a group" (*saṅghībhavana*), it is intransitive (*akarmaka*); when it has the sense of "forming a group" (*saṅghīkaraṇa*), it is transitive (*sakarmaka*). This is the meaning. Regarding the word *ślokata*: it means "he becomes a group" (*saṅghībhavati*) or "he forms a group" (*saṅghīkaroti*). [The root] *drekṛ*.

*Dhrekṛ*: "The act of making sound is *śabda*. [Regarding the rule *eca igghrasvādeśe*: when the suffix *liṭ* takes the substitute *eś*, after reduplication and the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, we have the form *adredreke*. At this stage, while the short vowel is being applied to the *e* of the reduplicated syllable, by the rule *eca igghrasvādeśe*, it becomes *i*; such is the meaning. Thus, *didhreke*. [In the reduplicated syllable...]

The letter *dh* becomes *d* by the rule of *jaśtva*; the letter *e* becomes the short vowel *i*. Thus, *rekṛ*. "Doubt" (*śaṅkā*) means uncertainty or objection. Starting from *śīkṛ* (to sprinkle) up to this point, these roots are marked with the indicatory letter *ṛ* (*ṛditaḥ*). *Sekṛ*: the first two have the vowel *e* in the middle and are *ṛditaḥ*; the other three have *a* as their penultimate vowel (*adupadhāḥ*).

"Iditaḥ" means "of the three. This means that among the five [roots], the first three [are intended]. Regarding "because it is not an upadeśa with a *ṣ*": the sense is that because the root *sikṛ* is excluded [from the rule], there is no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). Having in mind the rule "ṭheca igghrasvādeśe," he says: "Because it lacks the status of being preceded by *sa*, it does not have the status of being an *upadeśa* with a *ṣ*. And therefore..."

The point is that there is no substitution of *ṣ* because the substitute *s* is not an original *sakāra*. With this in mind, he says "siseka" and so forth, based on the rule "ṭhaci igghrasvādeśe. In "sasraṅke" and similar forms, the augment *num* occurs because the root ends in *ad*. Regarding "śakī": he says "śaṅkate" and "śaśaṅka," noting that *num* is added because the root is marked with *id*. Regarding "akī": [the same applies].

*Lakṣaṇa* means "marking" (*cihnīkaraṇa*). Regarding *aṅka*: because it is marked with the *it*-marker, the augment *num* is applied. Regarding *ānaṅka*: the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "*tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*". The roots *vaki* (in the sense of crookedness) and so forth are clear. Regarding *kuka* and *vṛka*: the second [root] has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel. Having considered the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate short vowel (*laghu*) before the suffix *śap*, he says:
*Kokate* and *cukuke*: because of the *kit* designation by the rule *ṭhasaṃyogā'd*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).

In the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), there is the substitution of *cu* (i.e., *k* becomes *c*). Having considered that the *raparatva* (substitution of *r*) would apply after the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel, he says—*varkata*.

Regarding the *liṭ* [perfect tense], having considered that there is no *guṇa* due to the *kit* designation by the rule *ṭhasaṃyogā'd*, he says—*vavṛke*. There is the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratva*).

"Only the first [consonant] remains. Now, one might object that because the *kit* designation applies later, *guṇa* substitution should occur; however, [the root] *tṛp* is intransitive when meaning "to satisfy," but transitive when meaning "to strike.

Considering the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), he says: *ceka*. [And] *kakī*. These are fifteen roots. The first four are marked with the *idit* designation. The second begins with the letter *v*.

The third [root] begins with a palatal (*tālavya*). The fifth and sixth, as well as the first four beginning with the tenth, have *ṛ* as their *it*. The tenth and twelfth have *i* and *u* as their *upadha*. The fourth endings are *idit* and *laghu*. In forms such as *ṭhkaṅkate*, the augment *num* is applied because it is *idit*. In the case of *ḍuḍhāṬke*, however, *trau* and *ka* occur; in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the *ḍha* becomes *jaś* (i.e., *da*) by rule.

The letter *ḍa*; the short *u* for the vowel *o*. Now, regarding the root *ṣvaṣk*, since it is included in the list of roots taught with an initial *ṣ*, the rule *dhātvādeḥ* would require the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*; to this he says: *subdhātu-*.
Thus, *ṣaṣvaṣka*. Because it stands between two conjunct consonants (*hal*), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur.

Because of the subsequent conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and because the *liṭ* [affix] lacks the *kit* designation, [the rule does not apply]. Regarding "third": thus, the form is *svaṣkate*; since it lacks the property of having a *s* as the first member followed by a dental (*dantya*), it is not a *ṣopadeśa* root. Regarding *ṭekate*: there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Regarding *ṭīkata*: [there is the *vṛddhi* substitution].

Because of the long vowel in the upadhā, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Thus: *tekate*, *tīkata*; *raṅghate*, *laṅghate*. Because it is marked with the *idit* sign, the augment *num* is added. [The root] *laghi* also means "cessation from eating. "Cessation" (*nivṛti*) means turning away. [Thus one] *laṅghate*; the meaning is "he does not eat. [The root] *aghi*: all three [roots beginning with *taki*] are likewise.
Those ending in the fourth [consonant] class have the *it* augment. Regarding *ānaṅgha*: the *nuṭ* augment is applied by the rule "tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ.
Regarding *vaṅghate*: because it has the *it* augment, *num* is added. However, in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], the form is *vavaṅghe*;
this is because [the root] begins with a double consonant (*saṃyukta-hal*) and is situated between two consonants, and because the *liṭ* lacks *kit* status due to being followed by a *saṃyoga*.

In the rules "etvābhyāsalopau na" and "maghi kaitave ca," *kaitavam* means deception (*vañcanā*). Regarding *rāghṛ*, all three [roots] are *ṛdit*. *Sāmarthyam* means becoming capable of performing an action (*kāryakṣamībhavanam*). Regarding the statement "*dhrāghṛ* also," the meaning is that some recite even the fourth [root] and so forth. *Drāghṛ* means extension (*āyāmaḥ*).

*dīrghībhavanam* (becoming long). Regarding *ślāghṛ katthana* ("to boast"): boasting is praise. The forty-two roots beginning with *śīkṛ*, which take the ātmanepada endings, have been explained. *Phakka nīcaiḥ* and so forth are clear. In the form *pranikakhati*, there is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n* because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not when preceded by *a* and followed by *kha* etc. in the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā*.
The sense is "no. Regarding *okhṛ*: its meaning is "adornment" (*bhūṣaṇakriyā*), "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*), or "prohibition" (*vāraṇa*).

[Examples: *okhati*, *okhāṃcakāra*. Regarding *śākhṛ* and *ślākhṛ*: *ślāghṛ* ending in the fourth letter (the dental *gh*) belongs to the *ātmanepada* class. Regarding *ukha* and *ukhī*: there are fifteen [roots], ending with *ṭhīkhi*.

The remainder [of the rule] is "thirteen. The remainder [of the *gaṇapāṭha*] is "valgādayaḥ" (beginning with *valga*). In that list, because of the *idit* designation, there is the augment *num*, and in the *āśīr-liṅ* (precative), there is the absence of *lopa* (elision). Regarding "they read":

it should be understood that according to their view, there are nineteen roots ending in *kh*. Regarding "okhati": in the presence of the *śap* suffix, there is *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*).
(133) *abhyāsasyā'savarṇe* [Pāṇini 6.4.78]:

Since the *ṇal* suffix in the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is marked as *pit*, it lacks the *kit* designation; consequently, although the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would have applied, it is prohibited by the rule *dvirvacane'ci*. Thus, because the condition of having a heavy syllable (*gurumatva*) is absent, the *ām* augment does not occur, and [the reduplication] occurs first.

When reduplication has been performed and the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the initial consonant) applied, subsequently—by the paribhāṣā "an operation concerning a vowel (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)"—the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneous combination), though an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation, is superseded; then, when the *laghūpadhaguṇa* (guṇa substitution for a light penultimate vowel) is applied, we arrive at the stage *u okha a*. At this point, when the *yaṇ* (semivowel) substitution would apply to the *u*-vowel, [the rule] "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) applies before a vowel (*aci*).

From the rule *anudhātvi* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), the word *aci* is understood; from *yvoriyaṅuvaṅau* (Pāṇini 6.4.77), the phrase *yvoḥ* is also understood. The analysis of *yū* is *iśca uśca yū* ("the letters *i* and *u*"). This is an adjective qualifying the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), and it follows the principle of *tadantavidhi* (application to that which ends with such). Thus he says: "of that which has *i* or *u* as its final letter. Because of the marker *ṅ*, these are substitutes for the final letter (*anta-ādeśau*). [The example] *uvokha* is formed by [the application of] *aci*.

However, there is no application of the rule *śnudhātu* here, because that rule operates only when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), and furthermore, because the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not possess the status of being a stem (*aṅga*). Now, one might object: "Once reduplication has occurred, since the penultimate vowel is light (*laghu-upadha*), Guṇa will apply; and because the root then possesses a heavy syllable (*guru-mat*) due to the initial *ij-* [of the reduplication], the suffix *ām* should be added. To this, [the author replies:]...

He says: "In the case of *saṃnipāta*. The meaning is that the *guṇa* [substitution] does not apply to the *ām* suffix by relying on the status of being heavy (*guru*) due to the *am* ending—which possesses the *guṇa* prescribed when *ṇal* follows—because if *ām* were present, it would contradict the condition of the root being followed by *ṇal*. [The example is] *ūkhatur*.

The intention is as follows: because the suffix *kit* is present, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel; then, after doubling and applying the *halādi-śeṣa* rule, since a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) vowel follows, the *iyaṅ* substitution for the *abhyāsa-sakāra* does not occur by the rule "for a non-homogeneous [vowel]," and thus the form is established through the long-vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-dīrgha*). Now, one might object: in the case of *ūkhantu*, the *ū*-kāra has already been produced by the *savarṇa-dīrgha* rule.

He raises the objection—"In this case"—on the grounds that because [the substitute] is a single replacement (ekādeśa) and thus belongs to the preceding boundary (pūrvānta), it is connected with the reduplication; consequently, the short vowel prescribed for the reduplicated syllable by the rule "hrasva" would apply. He then refutes this, saying—"It does not occur. To the question "Why?", he replies—"Because it has already taken effect once (sakṛtpravṛttatvāt)."

He establishes that very point with the words "because it is subordinate" (*āṅgatvāt*). When *ukhatur* is established, by the application of the rule like Parjanya (*parjanyavat*), there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-hrasva*) and then a long vowel of the same class (*savarṇa-dīrgha*), resulting in the form *ūkhatur*. In that state, the shortening of the reduplicated syllable does not apply again to the letter *ū*, because a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies to its object (*lakṣya*) only once.
The meaning is that it follows the maxim *pravṛtti*. Now, one might object:
since the substitution of a long vowel with its homogeneous counterpart (*savarṇadīrgha*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends only on the phonemes (*varṇa*), it should occur first;
thus, the initial application of the short vowel rule is difficult to justify. To this, he says: *vārṇāt* (by the rule *vārṇād āṅgam*). And so, by this [maxim]...

The meaning is that, by virtue of the technical rule (paribhāṣā), the short vowel itself operates first, even though it is "external" (bahiraṅga). As for the phrase "and because of its posteriority" (paratvāt): one might object that this is untenable, since it is improper to speak of the short vowel as being "posterior" with respect to the homogeneous long vowel (savarṇadīrgha), which is "internal" (antaraṅga) according to the reasoning already stated. This is not so; for the term "because of its posteriority" refers to...

This is because [the subsequent rule] has already reached its time of application by implication. Since there is no mutual relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) among the modifications resulting from repetition, both *halādiśeṣa* and *hrasva* (shortening) are applied simultaneously.

Subsequently, when the *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of homogeneous vowels) is about to operate, each preceding rule is more "internal" (*antaraṅga*) than the one following it. Each subsequent rule is...
By the maxim "the external is as if non-existent," [the rule] does not apply because it is external; thus, enough [of this discussion]. Regarding *uṅkhati*:

due to the presence of the *idit* marker, the augment *num* is added. Regarding *vavākha*: from the root *vakṣ*, in the *ṇal* suffix, there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel. Regarding *vavakhatuḥ*:
because it begins with a *va*-sound, the substitution of *e* for *a* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur. Regarding *vaṅkhati*.

Because the root *makh* is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*idit*), the augment *num* is applied. Thus we have *vavaṅkha* and *meṅkhatur*. In these cases, the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) occur.

In *maṅkhati*, because the root *makh* is marked with the *it* indicatory letter, there is no elision of the reduplication; thus we have *mamaṅkha*. In this case, because the root consists of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyukta-hal*) situated between vowels, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur. As for *nakhati* and *naṅkhati*, [the rule applies] to the root *ṇakhi*.

The substitution of *na* for *naḥ* occurs [in the derivation of *rakhati*]. Regarding *rakhati*: in the case of the suffix *ṇal*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*), resulting in *rarākha*. In the case of *atus* and other suffixes, there is the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*), as in *rekhatur* and so forth. Regarding *raṅkhati*: because it is marked with the *idit* designation, the augment *num* is applied. *Raraṅkha*. Regarding *ekhati*: from the root *ikh*, when the suffix *śap* is added, there is guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).

*iyekha*, *īkhatuḥ*, *iṅkhati*. Because it is marked with the *it*-sign (*idit*), the augment *num* is added. *iṅkhāṃcakāra*, *īṅkhati*. Because the penultimate vowel is not short (*alaghūpadhatvāt*), there is no *guṇa* strengthening. *īṅkhāṃcakāra*. "He leaps" (*valgati*). In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), [the forms are] *vavalga*, *vavalgatuḥ*. "He moves gracefully" (*raṅgati*), "he lolls" (*laṅgati*). *raraṅgatuḥ*. "He moves" (*aṅgati*).

In the *liṭ* [perfect tense]: from *aṅgati*, *ānaṅga*; *ānaṅgatuḥ*. From *vaṅgati*, *vavaṅga*, *vavaṅgatuḥ*. From *maṅgati*, *mamaṅga*, *mamaṅgatuḥ*. From *taṅgati*, *tataṅga*, *tataṅgatuḥ*. From *tvaṅgati*, *tatvaṅga*.
*śraṅgate*; in the perfect tense (*liṭ*)—*śaśraṅge*, *śaśraṅgatuḥ*. *ślaṅgate*;
in the perfect tense—*śaślaṅge*, *śaślaṅgatuḥ*. *iṅgate*; in the perfect tense—*iṅgāṃcakāra*. *riṅgate*; in the perfect tense—*ririṅge*, *riraṅgatuḥ*. *liṅgate*.
Now, he provides examples of the four roots beginning with *rikh*, which are established according to other schools of thought—namely, *rekhati*.
With the suffix *śap*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel: *rirekha*, *ririkhatuḥ*. *Trakhati*.
In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense: *tatrākha*, *tatrakhatuḥ*. *Triṅkhati*. In the *liṭ* tense: *titriṅkha*, *tritraṅkhatuḥ*.

The root *śiṅkh* [is used] in the sense of "to sound. In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense: *śiśiṅkha*, *śiśiṅkhatuḥ*. The root *tvag* means "to tremble"; because of the word "and" (*ca*), it also means "to move. *tvaṅgati*, *tatvaṅga*. The roots *yug*, *bug*, and *jug*—all three are marked with the *idit* indicator. *yuṅgati*, *buṅgati*, *juṅgati*. The root *ghagh* means "to laugh. *ghaghati*. In the *ṇal* suffix...

There is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. *jaghāgha*, *jaghaghatuḥ*. Because the substitution caused by the *liṅ* suffix is preceded by [the root], there is no *etva* (change to *e*) or elision of the reduplication. Regarding *maghi* meaning "to adorn," because it is marked with *idit* (indicating the addition of *num*), he says—*maṅghati*. *mamaṅgha*, *mamaṅghatuḥ*. *Śighi* means "to smell."

Thus: *śiṅghati*, *śiśiṅgha*. The fifty roots beginning with *phakka* have been covered. Regarding *varca* in the sense of "shining": shining is illumination. Regarding *ṣaca* in the sense of "pouring": this is a root taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*) because it begins with a vowel followed by a consonant (*acpara*). Among those marked with a svarita accent, it will be stated that *ṣaca* means "to join together" (*samavāya*). [The form] *seca* [is derived from this].
Because the root *satt* lacks a nasalized marker (*liṅ*), even though it begins with a vowel, there is elision of the *et* (the *i*) and the reduplication (*abhyāsa-lopa*).

*Dambhaḥ* means deceit (*śāṭhya*). Deceit (*dambhaḥ*) is the practice of performing religious duties and so forth for the sake of gaining the confidence of others; it is synonymous with hypocrisy (*kāpaṭya*). As Amarasimha states: "Hypocrisy (*kapaṭaḥ*) is not feminine; it is a synonym for pretext (*vyāja*), deceit (*dambha*), and fraud (*upadhi*)."

*Śāṭhya* is crookedness (*kuṭilībhāva*). Amara states: "A *śaṭha* is one who is dishonest (*anṛju*) and deceitful. Regarding the root *paci*, it means "to manifest" (*vyaktīkaraṇa*); it will be stated in the *curādi* group that "the root *paci* [is used] in the sense of expansion (*vistāra*). Some say it is simply *pac*. Regarding *ṣṭua*, it means clarity (*prasāda*). The letter *ṣṭu* is the letter *ṭa* produced by the addition of the *ṣṭu*-augment; and thus, because it begins with a *sa* followed by a dental (*dantya*), [it is classified as such].

This is an instruction regarding the substitution of *ṣ*. In the case of *stuṣataḥ*, once the change of *ṣ* to *s* has occurred, the application of the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* is precluded; this is the intended meaning. In *tuṣṭuṣe*, by the rule *sarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*, the letter *t* remains as the remainder;
because it is a substitute *s*, it undergoes the change to *ṣ*. Regarding *ṛja gatau*: acquisition means bringing about or accomplishment.

*Upārjanam* means service or attendance. Others say it is from the root *ūrj*. Regarding *arjata*: there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel due to the suffix *śap*, followed by the replacement of *r* (raparatva). Regarding "in the rule for *nuṭ*" (*nuḍvidhau*): this is a *vārttika*. Regarding *ānṛja*:
because the suffix *liṭ* is *kit* according to the rule "after a non-conjunct [root]," there is an absence of *guṇa*; then, after reduplication, there is the substitution of *urat*.

The intention is that, after applying *raparatva* (the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*), the rule *halādiḥ śeṣe* applies, then the rule *ata ādeḥ* results in lengthening, and finally the augment *nuṭ* is added. Regarding the roots *ṛji* and *bhṛji*: both have *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). The first is marked with the *idit* designation; because the second is marked with the *īdit* designation, the augment *iṭ* is not applied by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*. Due to its *idit* status, the augment *num* is added, followed by the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* substitutions, resulting in *ṛñjāṃcakre*.

Thus: when the augment *num* is present, because the vowel *ṛ* is heavy (*guru*) by the rule "a conjunct consonant makes [the preceding vowel] heavy" (*saṃyoge guru*), there is the suffix *ām* by the rule "after a root beginning with a vowel and having *ijādi*" (*ijādeśca*). [The forms are: *ṛñjitā*, *ṛñjiṣyate*, *ṛñjatām*, *ārñjata*, *ṛñjeta*, *ṛñjiṣīṣṭa*. Now, he shows the form in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense:

*ārñjiṣyata*. [The form] *bharjate* [is derived as follows]: the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel occurs due to the suffix *śap*; then there is the change of *r* to *ṛ*. [The forms] *babhṛje*, *bharjitā*, and *bharjiṣyate* follow. *Bharjatām* and *abharjata* are likewise. *Bharjeta* is the optative (*liṅ*). Regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), he states the form: *bharjiṣīṣṭa*. For the aorist (*luṅ*), he states the form: *abharjiṣṭa*. [In this case], *ta* is the substitute for the first person singular ending; *cli* is replaced by *sic*; then *iṭ* is added; and finally, the *guṇa* substitution takes place.

The substitution of *ra* for *ra* (raparatvam); the augment *aṭ*; the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatvam); and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* (ṣṭuatvam). Regarding the *lṛṅ* (conditional mood): *ibharjiṣyata*. The roots *ejṛ*, *bhejṛ*, and *bhrājṛ*—the first two are marked with the indicatory letter *ṛ* (*ṛdit*) for the purpose of the rule "not when there is elision of a portion" (*nāglopi*). As for the third, however, although it has the vowel *a* as its *it* (indicatory letter), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established. There is no result whatsoever from its being marked with *ṛ*. No.

Furthermore, by the rule *caṅ-ṇau lopo* (Pāṇini 7.4.1), a shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) ought to occur when a *ṇi*-affix followed by *caṅ* is present; however, this is not the case here because, as will be stated later under the rule *bhrājabhās-* (Pāṇini 7.4.3), an optional shortening of the penultimate vowel is prescribed in those instances. Regarding the root *īja* in the sense of "to go": there is no *guṇa* substitution because the penultimate vowel is not light (*alaghūpadha*). Thus: *ījate*; *ījāṃcakre*.

The suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *ijādeśca*. The twenty-one roots beginning with *varc* have been listed. "Seventy-two"—this is the remainder [of the count], referring to those ending in the *ca*-class (the palatals). Regarding *śuca* (to grieve): grief (*śoka*) is the affliction resulting from recollection. As for *śocati*: the meaning is that one suffers by remembering a father or other relative who has passed away. *Kuca* means to sound.

Thus: *śabda* means "sound. [The roots] *cukoca* and *cukucatuḥ* [are derived from *kuñc*]. *Akocīt* [is from *kuc*]. *Kuñca* and *kruñca*—both have the fifth letter of the *ca*-class (*ṇ*) as their penultimate vowel. In the root list (*dhātupāṭha*), *kuñcatu* is indicated with a *ṇakāra* (ṇ), which is the result of the combination of an *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*.
This is because of the statement by the learned authorities: "In the Dhātupāṭha, after roots ending in *ṭh* or *n*, as well as *jū*, there is an *anusvāra* and the fifth letter [of the varga].

Thus he says: "of those not having *it*" (*aniditām*). Since the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa* are considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *n* remains; consequently, when the *n* is elided by the rule "of those not having *it* in the *āśīr-liṅ*," we have *kucyāt*.

The meaning is "having transcended form. However, in the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, as in *cukuñca* and *cukuñcatuḥ*, because the suffix is marked with *p* and because it follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is an absence of *kit*-status; consequently, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not occur. The root *kruñc*, moreover, has a naturally occurring *ñ* as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*), rather than a *ñ* produced through the application of the *anusvāra* or *parasavarṇa* rules.
Thus it is established in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule "ṭhpareśca ghāṅkayo'ri" (Pāṇini 6.4.123).

Therefore, in the case of that [root], there is elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule "ṭhiniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24) in the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*). This is what he says: "luñcyāt," etc. The same should be understood for the root *añcu* as well. Regarding the phrase "but in the sense of honor": "na añceḥ... [is the rule].

The sense is that [the formation] is prohibited by the rule *pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.90). Regarding the roots *vañcu*, *cañcu*, and *tañcu*: the first six have *n* as their penultimate letter (*nopadhā*). The mention of the letter *ñ* is due to the presence of the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*. Consequently, in the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative), there is elision of the *n* by the rule *ṭhiniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). Thus he says: "from *vacy-ādi*" (i.e., the group beginning with *vañc*). [This applies to] the *luṅ* (aorist).
*amluñcīt* and *amluñcīt* are forms where there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhayo rūpam*). There is elision of the *sic* suffix.
[Pāṇini 3.1.58 states: "After the roots *jṛ*, *stanbh*, *mṛc*, *mluc*, *gruc*, *gluc*, *gluñc*, and *śvi*, [the *aṅ* augment is applied].
From *jṛ*, *stanbh*, etc., [the rule] "after *cli*, *sic*" applies, as does "after *as*, *ati*, *vakti*, and *khyāti*."
Thus, from the rule "aṅ after [roots ending in] i" and from the rule "or aṅ after [roots ending in] ṭhi," the word "or" (vā) is understood to carry over.

Therefore, he says: "after these, clu takes either aṅ or [śnu]. [The roots are: *jṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vitality," *stambhu* which is a Vedic (sautra) root, *mrac* and *mluc* in the sense of "motion," *gruc*, *gluc* in the sense of "committing theft," and *gluñc*.

The meaning is "from these [roots] ending in -gati. Regarding *amrucat*: since the suffix *aṅ* is introduced by the rule *cleḥ aṅ*, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) does not occur because of its *ṅ*-marking. Regarding *amrocīt*: in the absence of *aṅ*, the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule *hiṭa īṭi*. Regarding *grucu* and *glucu*: he states that *aṅ* is optionally applied by the rule *jṛstanbhu*, etc., as in *agrucat* or *agrocīt*. This applies to the first [root].
Regarding *rūpe*: now he illustrates the alternative form for the second [root]—*aglucat*, *aglocīt*.

When *aṅ* follows, because it is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*). In the absence of *aṅ*, there is the elision of *sij*. Regarding *gluñcu* and *ṣasj*:
the first has *n* as its penultimate letter, while the second is taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśaḥ*), because it begins with *s* followed by a consonant other than a semivowel (*acpara*) or *k*.

Regarding the first [root], he states the specific rule for the *luṅ* [aorist]: "aṅ" [is applied]. The remainder [of the rule] is "by this [sūtra], *jṛ*, *stambh*, etc. The author of the *Vṛtti* maintains that because of the separate mention of *gluc* and *gluñc*, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Thus: *gluñcyāt*. Regarding "of *s*" (*sasya*): when the initial *ṣ* of a root becomes *s*, as in *sasj*.
The meaning is that when [the first *ś*] is present, the second *sakāra* becomes a *śakāra* by virtue of the rule for *ścutva*. Regarding "of that":
the meaning is that the *śakāra* becomes a *jakāra* by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*. Regarding *gujī*:
because it is marked with the *idit* indicator, there is no elision (*nilopa*) in the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative); thus he says the form is *laccchati*. *Lalacccha*.

[The root] *āñch* [is used]. In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), with the suffix *ṇal*, after doubling and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and after the shortening of the reduplicated syllable, the form *ā-āñcha-a* remains. At this point, one might suspect that the rule *ata ādeḥ* would apply to lengthen the initial vowel, and that the rule *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ* would apply the augment *nuṭ*. Anticipating this, he says: "from the initial [vowel] after *at*" (*ata ādeḥ*). For in that context, it is the long *ā* [that is affected].

Since there is no purpose for a long vowel in the rule prescribing lengthening, the long vowel *ā* is established even from the short vowel *a*; therefore, the use of the *tapara* marker (*at*) is for the sake of including only that short vowel *a* which possesses its own inherent nature. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "By that [marker]," in the context of the rule *ata ādeḥ*, which prescribes lengthening.

The meaning is that because only the inherent short *a*-form is grasped, there is no long vowel by the rule "ata ādeḥ," and thus the augment *nuṭ* does not occur. Regarding the form *āñcha*: the intention is that after doubling, the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and the lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha* [the form is established].
The phrase "for the sake of ease of pronunciation" means that even from a long *ā* that stands in the place of a short [vowel], [the same result follows].
The sense is that *nuṭ* necessarily occurs [after the root *yuc*]. The rule *hrīccha lajjāyām* and so forth is clear.

Regarding *yucch* meaning "to be negligent": this root begins with *y* and has *u* as its penultimate letter (*udupadha*). In the form *yucchati*, because the *tuk* augment (by the rule *che ca*) applies first due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), there is no *guṇa* substitution, as the condition of having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) is no longer met.

Regarding *uñchāṃcakāra*: once the augment *num* is applied, the vowel *u* becomes heavy according to the rule "a conjunct is heavy" (*saṃyoge guru*); consequently, by the rule "after a root beginning with *ij*," the suffix *ām* is added—this is the intended meaning. Regarding *dhṛja*: the first two have *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*), while the other four have *a* as their penultimate vowel (*adupadha*). The second, fourth, and sixth are marked with the indicatory letter *it*. [The form] *dharjati* is derived from the root *dhṛj* with the suffix *śap*.

The *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) occurs. The substitution of *ra* after *r* (*raparatvam*). [From the root *dhṛj*: *dadhārja*, *dadhṛjatuḥ*. [Optative: *dhṛjyāt*. [Aorist: *adharjīt*. [Root *dhṛñj*: *dadhṛñja*—because it is marked with the *idit* designation, the augment *num* is added; because it is marked with *idit*, there is no elision of the final *n*. [Optative: *dhṛñjyāt*. [Aorist: *adhṛñjīt*. [Root *dhraj*:
*dhrajati*. In the *ṇal* suffix: *dadhrāja*, *dadhrajatuḥ*. [Aorist: *adhrājīt*—or *adhrajīt*.
*Dhrañjati*: this root has *a* as its penultimate vowel. *Dadhrañja*. Because it is marked with the *it* marker, there is no elision of the *n*—thus, *dadhrañjatuḥ*.
*Dhvajati*: *dadhvāja*. *Dhvañjati*: *dadhvañja*. *Kūja* (to make an indistinct sound): this is clear.
In *sarjati*, because it belongs to the *ṣopadeśa* group, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. *Aja* (to go): in the present tense (*laṭ*), *ajati*, and so forth.

Taking it for granted [that the rule applies], he states the specific detail regarding the *liṭ* suffix: *ajervyaghañapoḥ*. The word *vī* ends in a long vowel (*dīrgha*) and has its nominative case ending elided. The governing rule *ārddhadhātuke* is supplied. This is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), not a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), according to the commentary. Thus he says: "in the domain of the *ārddhadhātuka*," and so forth.

The mention of "aj" (vowel) is by way of indicating the vowel *i*. The meaning is "of a verbal root (*dhātu*) beginning with a vowel. If one were to rely on a locative case (*parasaptamī*) in the rule "ārddhadhātuke," then the form *vevīyate* would not be possible;

for before the substitution of *vī* [for *vevī*], the root would begin with a vowel (*ajādi*), and thus the suffix *yaṅ* would be applicable. However, if one relies on a locative case of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), then [the suffix] *yaṅ* [is applied].

When the *vībhāva* (the substitution of *i* for *ya*) is intended, the suffix *yaṅ* is unimpeded because the root begins with a consonant (*hal*). Why say "except after *ghan* and *ap*" (*aghañapoḥ*)? Because after *ghan*, we have *samājaḥ*; and by the rule "after *sam* and *ud*, *ajaḥ* [takes *ghan*] when referring to animals," we also have *samajaḥ*. In this case, it need not be stated that "except after *ghan* and *ap*. The word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over from the rule "optionally before the *liṭ* [perfect]"; this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
The suffix *ghañ* does not apply at all; however, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the suffix *lyuṭ* and in *ārddhadhātuka* affixes beginning with *val*.
But in other *ārddhadhātuka* affixes, it is obligatory (*nityam*); this is the position established by the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Kaśikā. Thus he says:
"It is desired [to apply] optionally in *ārddhadhātuka* affixes beginning with *val*. This is an illustration of the aforementioned *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option).

Regarding *vivāya*: when the *ṇal* suffix is intended after the root *vī*, and the substitution of *vī* for *vi* has occurred, there is doubling in the presence of *ṇal*, followed by the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-hrasva*).
Then, by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before *ñ* and *ṇit* suffixes" (*aco ñṇiti*), the *vṛddhi* replacement results in the *āy* substitute; this is the underlying intention.
Regarding *vivyatuḥ*: when the substitution of *vī* for *vi* has occurred, there is doubling in the presence of the *atus* suffix, followed by the shortening of the reduplicated syllable.

Due to the *kit* status [of the suffix] by the rule *ṭhasaṃyogā’d*, there is an absence of *guṇa*; then, as an exception to *iyaṅ*, by the rule *ṭheranekācaḥ*, the form is derived through *yaṇ*. Similarly, the form *vivyur* is obtained in the case of *us*. Now, one might object that in *vivyatuḥ* and *vivyur*, because the second *v* is followed by a consonant (*hal*) consisting of *y*, the vowel *i* [of the reduplicated syllable] would be subject to the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca*.

Anticipating the objection that [the vowel] might become long, he provides the resolution: since the *yakāra* in place of the *īkāra* is treated as non-substituted (*asthānivadbhāva*) by the rule "when a suffix beginning with *ṭhak* follows," the second *vakāra* is not preceded by a consonant (*hal*); therefore, when this *vakāra* follows, the *īkāra* does not become long. This is expressed in the passage beginning with "atra vakārasya... and so forth.

This concludes the section ending with *acaparakatvam*. Now, one might raise the objection: "But since there is a prohibition by the rule *na padānte* regarding the application of the long-vowel rule (*dīrghavidhi*), how can the *yakāra* here be treated as *sthānivadbhūta*? Anticipating this, the author refutes it by stating:
"And there is no prohibition by the rule *na padānte*. The word "anticipating" (*śaṅkya*) is to be supplied. Why [is there no prohibition]? From this [it follows].

He says: "svaradīrgha" (regarding vowel-length), meaning "because of this statement. The words "by the author of the Vārttika" are to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding "thali ekāca" (in the case of *thali* after a monosyllabic root): even though the verbal root *aj* is not included among those taught with an anudātta accent, its substitute *vī* is anudātta; this applies to those roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*).
The meaning is that this is because it is accepted that the fourteen roots beginning with *ūdṛt* and ending with *ādi* are *anudātta*.
(135) *kṛsṛbhṛvṛstudrusruśruvo liṭi* | 7|2|13|. [The rule applies] to the eight roots: *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru*.

The ablative case [in *samāhāra-dvandvāt*] is used after a collective dvandva compound. The locative case [in *liṭi*] is used in the sense of the genitive. From the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti*, the words *na* and *iṭ* are understood [as governing this rule].

Thus he says: "from these. Now, one might ask: since [the prohibition of *iṭ*] is already established by the rules *ekāca upadeśe 'nudātāt* and *śyukaḥ kiti*, what is the purpose of this [present rule]?
Regarding the word "sūtram" (the sūtra), he says: "of *kṛ* and the others. This means of these [roots]: *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛ*.

He states the nature of the restriction: "based on the root," and so forth. For these three—*kṛ*, *sṛ*, and *bhṛ*—which are included among those taught with an anudātta accent, there is the designation of being "monosyllabic in their original teaching" (*ekāc upadeśe*).

The prohibition based on the root (*prakṛtyāśraya*)—which is the prohibition [of *guṇa*] for the root *vṛdh* by the rule "r̥t-ṣi-uk-aḥ kit-i"—and that which is the prohibition based on the suffix (*pratyayāśraya*), both of these apply only to the *liṭ* following the roots *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛ*, and not to the *liṭ* following any others; such is the meaning. Therefore, by this...

In forms such as *bibhidiva* and *bibhidima*, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule "ṭhekāca upadeśe" does not apply; likewise, in forms such as *babhūviva* and *babhūvima*, the prohibition by the rule "rṭhśyukaḥ kiti" does not apply. Now, he states the purpose of including the roots *stud*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru*—namely, "tataḥ" (from that) and "anyeṣām" (of others).

The remainder [of the sūtra] is "of four. The word "grahaṇam" (the taking/mentioning) is the remainder. Therefore, from among those—namely *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛ*—there is the mention of the others, *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru*, for the sake of [forming] *tuṣṭotha*, *dudrotha*, *susrotha*, and *śuśrotha* in the *thali* [suffix], according to what will be stated later by the rule "ṛto bhāradvājasya."

This is for the purpose of prohibiting the *iṭ* augment that would otherwise apply by the restrictive rule— "the *iṭ* is not added after [a root] ending in *ṛ*, but it must be added after any other"— as in the case of *tuṣṭotha*. Furthermore, in forms such as *tuṣṭuva* and *tuṣṭuma*, the prohibition of *iṭ* after the *liṭ* suffix applies only to roots beginning with *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛ* as stated in the rule "kṛ-sṛ-bhṛ-vṛ," whereas *iṭ* is added after [roots] other than these.
The meaning is that it is also for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *iṭ*, which would otherwise be required by the rule "syād eve" (Pāṇini 7.2.35).

Thus, it is established that when the root *aj* undergoes the substitution of *vī* before the suffix *thali*, the introduction of the augment *iṭ* is unimpeded because there is no prohibition by the rule "ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt" (Pāṇini 7.2.10).

(136) *acaḥ tāsvat thali aniṭo nityam* | Pāṇini 7.2.61. Since there is no *thal* suffix after a non-root (*adhātu*), he introduces two rules as a preliminary to stating that the augment *iṭ* after a root ending in a vowel followed by *tās* is optional in *thal* due to the rule of Bhāradvāja, saying: "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*) [and] "in *thal*" (*thali*). Because there is no *thal* after a non-root, [the word] "root" (*dhātoḥ*) [is understood].

The term "ṭhac" is a qualifier for that [root]; thus, there is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the suffix applies to that which ends with the specified element). It is established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ṛto bhāradvājasya* that the word "upadeśe" (in the original enunciation) is drawn over from the subsequent sūtra *upadeśe'tvataḥ*. The syntactic connection is: "[a root] ending in a vowel (*ajanta*) in its original enunciation. [The phrase] "not having an *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*) [is also understood].

The ablative case ending is used after a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The connection is with the words "always" (*nityam*) and "from that which lacks *iṭ*" (*iḍvihīnāt*). From the rule "tāsi ca klṛpaḥ," the word "tāsi" is understood here. The connection is thus: "always [after a root] which lacks *iṭ* in the *tās-* [future]. In the word "thali," the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive. From the rule "gameriṭ parasmaipadeṣu," the word "iṭ" is understood; [and from the rule] "na... [the negation is understood].

The word "na" (not) is understood from the rule "vṛdbhyaś-caturbhyaḥ. The term "tāsu" is a locative plural form. Thus he says: "that which ends in an *ac* vowel in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)," and so on, up to "it should not be *iṭ*.
The phrase "tāsu" is to be supplied [as the object of comparison]. Just as there is no *iṭ* after the suffix *tās*, so too there is none after *thal*.

The meaning is "not. Examples include *cicetha* and *juhotha*; here, the augment *iṭ*, which would have been required by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī* and others, does not occur. Why specify "from a root ending in a vowel"? Consider *bibheditha*. Why specify "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*)? Consider *ḍhṛñ*: *jahartha*. In this case, because the vowel-ending status is lost due to the substitution of *guṇa* and the subsequent replacement of *ṛ* by *ra*, the prohibition of *iṭ* does not apply.

The inclusion of the word *syāt* is for the purpose of providing instruction. What is the purpose of including the word *nitya*? [Consider] *sasvaritha* from the root *svṛ* (to go). Because the suffix *tās* in the rule *svarita-sūtī* is optionally characterized by the augment *iṭ*, there is no prohibition [of *iṭ*]. Why is *tās* mentioned? [Consider] *lūtvā* and *lulavitha*. Why is *thal* mentioned? [Consider] *papiva* and *pima*. In this case, the term *tāsī* is understood by simple reference (*anuvṛtti*).

Some say that the mention of *tāsvat* [in Pāṇini 6.4.122] is not very useful for the sake of the rule regarding *siddhi*. However, in reality, *tāsvat* is necessary for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* before the suffix *thala* when it follows that which exists as *tās* (the third person plural ending). By means of this, in the case of the substitution of *ghaslṛ* for *ad* by the rule *liṭi anyatarasyām*, [the prohibition of *iṭ* is secured].

In the case of *jaghasitha*, there is no prohibition [of the substitution of *sa* for *th*], because the root *ghas* lacks the suffix *tās*; this will be stated in the root-text itself under the verbal root *ad* (meaning "to eat"). As the *Bhāṣya* states: "That which has *tās* and is *aniṭ*. It should be understood that the same applies to the substitution of *vay* for *veñ*.

(137) *upadeśe'tvataḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.62. The analysis of the compound is *at-vataḥ*. Here, *at* refers to the short vowel *a*; that which possesses this is called *atvān*. Because of the rule *tasau matvarthe*, it is treated as a *bha*-stem, and thus the substitution of *jaś* [for *t*] does not apply. This is with the exception of the rule concerning vowels (*acaḥ*).
The previous sūtra also applies here; that which was carried over from it likewise continues. Thus he says:

"in the case of [a root] having the vowel 'a' in its original enunciation (upadeśa). Examples are *śaklṛ* (as in *śaśaktha*) and *pac* (as in *papaktha*). Here, the augment *iṭ*, which would otherwise be required by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*, does not occur. This is because [the root] has 'a' in its original enunciation.

What [is the meaning]? [The root] *kṛṣ* means "to scratch. [Example: *cakarṣitha*. Why [is the condition] "having *at*" (*atvataḥ*) specified? [Counter-example: *bibheditha*. Why [is it specified as] "followed by *t*" (*taparaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *rarādhitha*. Why [is it specified as] "in the *tās-*" (*tāsau*)? [Counter-example: *jagrahitha*. In the case of *jighṛkṣati*, [the root is] invariably *aniṭ* (lacking *iṭ*) due to the rule "and after *grah* and *guh* in the *san*" (*sani grahaguhośca*), but not in the *tās-*. This is because [the rule specifies it is] "invariably" (*nitya*).

What [is the point]? [The forms] *thañja* and *ānañjatha*. According to the Bhāṣya, because [the root] is marked with *ṭhū*, there is optionally no *iṭ* augment before *tās*. *Cakramitha* is also an example; for although it lacks the *iṭ* augment before *tās* in the middle voice due to the rule *snukramor aniṭi*, it possesses the *iṭ* augment in the active voice (*parasmaipada*).

(138) *ṛto bhāradvājasya* | 7|2|63| The rule *ṛto bhā-* [is explained as follows]: the words *tāsau nityamaniṭaḥ*, *thali*, *na*, and *iṭ* carry over from the previous rules. According to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the augment *iṭ* is not added after a root ending in *ṛ* when followed by the suffix *thal*.

[The form] *phalita* is established by the rule *ṭhacastāsvat*. Therefore, he says "only from that which ends in ṛ" (*ṛdantādeva*) to indicate that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). The meaning of the particle *eva* is that the augment *iṭ* must indeed occur after a suffix beginning with *thal* that does not end in ṛ. He states this as: "it would indeed occur for another."

The meaning is that *iṭ* must necessarily occur after a *thala* suffix following a root ending in *ṛ* (other than those already specified). Thus, according to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the result is that *iṭ* is not excluded for a *thala* following a root other than one ending in *ṛ*; this is the sense, and therefore [the rule] is not redundant. And so, for a *thala* following a root not ending in *ṛ*...

In the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the suffix *iṭ* is applied; however, in other schools of thought, because of the rules "acastāsvat" and "upadeśe'tvataḥ," the result is that the option of *iṭ* not being applied (*neṭ*) is established there. For example: *papitha* / *papātha*;
*pecitha* / *papaktha*. This [option] occurs here by the rule "kṛsṛbhṛvṛstudrusruśruvo liṭi."

The meaning is that the scope of the four rules—*ṭhacastāsvatthalyaniṭo nityam*, *upadeśe'tvataḥ*, and *ṛto bhāradvājasya*—will now be summarized. "Ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*) means: a verbal root which ends in a vowel other than *ṛ*, or which contains a short *a*.

*Tāsau nityā'niṭ* means that it is invariably *aniṭ* (without the *iṭ* augment) in the *tās* (the periphrastic future). The sense is that according to Pāṇini’s rule *ṭhacastāsvat*, and according to Bhāradvāja’s rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya*, it is invariably *aniṭ* in those forms. *Krādyanya* means that any verbal root other than the eight beginning with *kṛ* is invariably *seṭ* (with the *iṭ* augment) in the *liṭ* (perfect tense).
The meaning is that [the augment *iṭ*] is prohibited after these eight roots beginning with *kru* when followed by the *liṭ* suffix, because this is restricted by the rule *kṛsṛbhṛvṛ...*.

Now, one might object: by stating "other than those beginning with *kru*" (*krādyaṇya*) here, it is understood that these eight roots beginning with *kru* are invariably non-*iṭ* (never taking the augment *iṭ*) in the *liṭ*; however, that is untenable.

Because *stud*, *drus*, *srus*, and *śru* are included among those [roots] ending in short *u* (*mṛdant*) and are distinct [from the others], the prohibition "after these [roots], *thali*, there is no [augment] when preceded by *ac*" (Pāṇini 7.2.61) does not apply according to the opinion of Bhāradvāja; consequently, the optional insertion of the augment *iṭ* is unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, the mention of *stud*, *drus*, *srus*, and *śru* in the rule *kṛsṛbhṛvṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13) is redundant, for [the rule applies to forms such as] *tuṣṭuva*.

Having raised the objection that [the rule] is already fulfilled by the exclusion of *iṭ*—which would otherwise be required by the restriction for roots beginning with *kṛ* (krādinīyama) in cases such as *tuṣṭuvam* and so on—he refutes it, saying "and not" (*na ca*). To the question "Why?", he says:
"because of the rule *acaḥ tāsvat*. The prohibition of *iṭ* applies only to *thal* following a root ending in *ṛ*; it does not apply to *thal* following a root that does not end in *ṛ*.
However, the view of Bhāradvāja is that there is no prohibition of *iṭ* in this case;

and this prohibition of the prohibition of *iṭ* is a restorer of the prohibition of *iṭ* obtained by the two rules "āsvaḥ" and "upadeśe 'tvataḥ" in the alternative, but not a restorer of the *iṭ* obtained by the rule "krādi-niṣṭhāyām".

The meaning is "of the prohibition as well. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the immediately preceding [rule]. The sequence of the sūtras is: *acastāsvat*, *upadeśe'tvataḥ*, and *ṛto bhāradvājasya*;
however, the sūtra *kṛsṛbhṛvṛ* is separated from that by a great distance.

Furthermore, because the rule "ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.35), which prescribes the augment *iṭ*, is initiated after the section containing prohibitions such as "neḍvaśi kṛti," the prohibition of *iṭ* for the roots *stu*,
*dru*, *sru*, and *śru* before the suffix *iṇ* overrides the restriction of Bhāradvāja; thus, [the form is] "neḍvaśi."

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rules *kṛti* and *vasvekājādghasām*. Consequently, in the present case, when the suffix *thal* follows the root *aj*, the substitution of *vī* occurs; because the root then ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) and is invariably non-ṅit, there is an optional application of the augment *iṭ*. Thus it is established that the forms are *vivayitha* and *vivetha*. This refers to the substitute for *sip*.

In *thala*, because it is not a *saṃyoga* [beginning with a consonant cluster], there is an absence of *kit*-tva; consequently, there is *guṇa*. In the alternative where *iṭ* is present, there is the substitution of *ay*. Thus, *ājitha*. Regarding the form *ajitha*: since it is desired that [the substitution of] *vī* occurs optionally before *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with a *hal*, there is an absence of *vī*-bhāva. Consequently, because the root *aj* is excluded from those roots taught as *anudātta* (unaccented), *iṭ* is applied. Then follows reduplication (*dvitva*). The first syllable begins with a *hal*.

The remainder [of the derivation] follows. In *vivyathuḥ*, there is lengthening by the rule *ata ādeḥ*. Regarding *vivyathe*: when the suffix *athus* is applied, the substitution of *vī* occurs; then, after reduplication and the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsahrasva*), because the suffix is *kit* due to the rule *asaṃyogāt*, there is an absence of *guṇa*; subsequently, the *iyaṅ* substitute is set aside by the *yaṇ* substitute according to the rule *eranekācaḥ*, resulting in the form *vivyathe*. In *vivyaya*, the substitution of *vī* and so forth occurs when the suffix *tha* is replaced by *a*.

*vivāya* and *vivāyeti*: because of the optionality of the *ṇit*-designation by the rule "ṇalutamo vā," there is an optionality regarding the *vṛddhi* strengthening. *vivyiva* and *vivyima*: since it is other than a root beginning with *k*, there is necessarily *iṭ* in the *liṭ* [perfect] when it is *seṭ*. *vetā* and *ajitā*: in the *luṭ* [periphrastic future], there is an optionality regarding the substitution of *vī* for *vī*. *veṣyati*.

Regarding *ajiṣyati*: in the *lṛṭ* [future] with the suffix *sya*, there is an option for the substitution of *vī* [for *aj*]. Regarding *vīyāt*: because the substitute of the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative) is an *ārddhadhātuka* [suffix], the substitution of *vī* occurs.
(139) *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* 7.2.1: [In the presence of the *sic* suffix,] the *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs in the case of *parasmaipada* [endings].

Now, when the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix *sic* is present and its *vībhāva* (substitution of *ī*) has occurred, the rule "guṇa is substituted for an *ik* vowel before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes" would apply.

However, the rule "vṛddhi is substituted for an *ik* vowel ending in a stem before *sic*" applies instead. By the explicit mention of "vṛddhi," the term "an *ik* vowel" (*ikaḥ*) is brought into the context;

this qualifies the governing term "of a stem" (*aṅgasya*), and the sense is that the rule applies by means of the *tadantavidhi* (the principle that a grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the specified element).
And thus, in forms such as *akoṣīt*, there is no *vṛddhi* of the consonant. In *avaiṣīt*: the suffix *luṅ* with the ending *tip*;
elision of the vowel *i*; the substitution of *vī* for the root [vi-]; prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10); *vṛddhi*; the addition of the augment *aṭ*;
and the change to *ṣ*. In *ājīt*: elision of the *sic* suffix; and when *vṛddhi* conditioned by a consonantal ending applies by the rule "vadavraja" (Pāṇini 7.2.3), [the *iṭ* is added].

When [the augment] *āṭ* is prohibited by the rule "ṭhneṭī," the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by the rule "āṭaśca. In the conditional (*lṛṅ*) tense, [the forms] would be *aiṣyat* and *ajiṣyat*. [The roots] *teja* (to protect) and so forth are clear. Regarding *ejṛ* (to tremble): as for [the root] meaning "to shine," it was explained as being *ātmanepada*. Regarding *ṭua o sphūrja*: [the letter] *ṭu* is included because of the rule "ādirñiṭuaḍavaḥ."

In the *Upadeśa* (the original grammatical instruction), because of the presence of a nasal (*anunāsika*), the vowel *o* and the vowel *ā* are treated as *it*-markers. Furthermore, there is the rule *ṭhṭvito'thuc* [Pāṇini 3.3.89] which prescribes the suffix *athuc*, and the rule *ṭāditaśca* [Pāṇini 7.2.16] which prescribes the substitution of *n* for the final letter of the root in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). Additionally, by the rule *oditaśca* [Pāṇini 7.2.14], there is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* after the past passive participle. These are the results. Finally, there is the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.116].
The long vowel *ū* is recited here in order to indicate the length of the root;
therefore, they say that in forms such as *hurchati*, the vowel is not long. [Examples: *sphūrjati*; in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), *pusphūrja*, and in the aorist (*luṅ*), *asphūrjīt*.
Regarding *kṣi* meaning "destruction" (*kṣaya*): destruction means ruin. It has an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).

The meaning is "having the sense of destruction. Its placement among roots ending in vowels (*ajanta*) is appropriate. *Kṣayati* means "perishes" (*naśyati*) or "causes to perish" (*nāśayati*). In the presence of the *śap* suffix, there is *guṇa*, and then the substitution of *ay*. *Cikṣāya* [is formed] with the suffix *ṇal*; there is *vṛddhi*, and then the substitution of *āy*. *Cikṣiyatuḥ*: because of the prohibition "not after a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogāt*), the suffix is *kit*, and thus there is no *guṇa*.

*iyaṅ* [is substituted]. Regarding *cikṣayitha*—it is also *cikṣetha*. Because of the status of *pit* (being followed by a *p*-suffixed affix), there is an absence of *kitva* (the *k*-status), and thus *guṇa* [occurs]. Since it ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) and is invariably non-*iṭ*, the *thali* suffix optionally takes *iṭ* according to the rule of Bhāradvāja. In the case where *iṭ* is present, there is the substitution of *ay* [for *i*]. [Thus we have] *cikṣiyathuḥ*, *cikṣiya*, *cikṣāya*, and *cikṣaya*. But in the case of *vas* and *mas*, [the forms are as follows]:
By the rule *krādiniyamāt*, the augment *niṭ* is applied. Thus it says: *cikṣiyiva*, *cikṣiyima*.
[The forms are] *kṣetā*, *kṣeṣyati*, *kṣayatu*, *akṣayat*, *kṣayet*.
(140) *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.25. [This sūtra provides for the lengthening of the vowel in the penultimate position before certain suffixes.]

He states the specific [condition] for the benedictive (āśīr-liṅ): "akṛtsārva-aṅgasya" is the governing rule (adhikṛta). From the rule "ayaṅ yi kṅti," the word "yi" is understood as a locative ending; it qualifies the affix implied by the term "aṅga," and there is an application of the rule regarding the beginning of that [affix]. Due to the hearing of the word "dīrgha" (long vowel), the word "aca" (vowel) is brought forward as a qualifier of the "aṅga."

This is a rule concerning the final element of a compound (tadantavidhi). Thus he says: "of that which ends in *aj*," and so forth. Why [is the restriction] "before a non-*kṛt* suffix and before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix"? [Consider: *prakṛtya*. Here, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) does not occur because it is superseded by the *tuka*-augment due to its higher priority. [Consider: *cinuyāt*. Here, there is no long vowel because it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. [Consider: *kṣījeti*. This has *ī* as its penultimate letter (*upadha*). [Consider: *kūjinā*. [From the root] *kūj*.

The root *śabda* was listed immediately after [the previous entry] as "avyakte śabde" (in the sense of indistinct sound); it would have been more appropriate to list *ṭhkuja* and *kṣīja* in that very same place, because their meanings are identical—this is the intended sense. Regarding *laja* and *laji*: in some recensions, the reading is "bhartsane" (in the sense of reviling). Amara states: "Reviling (*bhartsanam*) is a song of reproach. The second [root] is marked with the *idit* designation.

The *āśīrliṅ* (benedictive): *lījyāt*, *lāja*, *lāji*. Regarding the reading "bharjana" in some places: [the rule] "ādupadhau" applies; the second [root] is marked with *idit*. *jaja*, *jajī*, etc., are clear. Regarding *vaja* and *vraj*: although the first [root] has an *a* following non-conjoined consonants (*asaṃyuktahalmadyasthā’kāravatva*), [the rule] "na... [does not apply].
Regarding the rule "śasadadavādiguṇānām," he states that the substitution of *e* (etva) and the elision of the reduplication (abhyāsalopa) do not apply here, as shown by the forms *vavajatuḥ*.

[The forms] *avājīt* and *avajīt* [are also examples]. However, for the second [root], because it contains the vowel *a* situated between two conjunct consonants (*saṃyuktahal*), there is no possibility of the application of either the substitution of *e* or the elision of the reduplication.
In the case of *ṭhavrājīt*, having raised the objection regarding the optional application of *vṛddhi* by the rule *ato halādeḥ*, he says:

"The *vṛddhi* [is applied] by the rule *vadavraja-*. The point is that since the form would be established simply because it ends in a consonant (*hal*), the inclusion of *vraj-* is for the purpose of setting aside the optionality prescribed by *ato halādeḥ*. The words beginning with *śuci-*..."

"Seventy-two are formed with *vṛt*. 'Ending in *śāḍ*'" means ending in the root *śāḍṛ* [DhP 1.270] "to lie down. There is a reading in some places as "ending in *śāḍṛ*. Regarding *aṭṭa*: this has the third letter of the *tavarga* (the letter *ṭ*) as its penultimate.
The mention of the penultimate *ṭ* is due to the rules of *cartva* and *ṣṭuatva*. Thus he says: "this has *ṭ* as its penultimate. And so it is.

When the suffix *san* with *iṭ* is added to the root *aṭṭ*, resulting in *aṭṭi-s*, the reduplication prescribed by the rule "the second [syllable] of a non-initial [root]" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*) applies; however, because the rules for *ṣṭu*-substitution and *cartya*-substitution are considered asiddha (unestablished), this reduplication occurs for the portion *ti-s*, excluding the letter *ḍ* according to the rule "not *n*, *d*, or *r* when they are the first members of a conjunct" (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*). Then...

By applying the *halādi-śeṣa* rule [to the result] after the substitution of *ṣṭu* and *cartya* for the letter *d*, the desired form *ṭhiṭṭiṣate* is established. If the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) were inherent in the penultimate letter, then because of the absence of the prohibition [stated in] *na ndrāḥ*, there would be reduplication of the entire sequence including both *ṭ*s; however, by the *halādi-śeṣa* rule, [only one remains].

The sense is that if the second *ṭ* were to be elided, the undesired form *aṭiṭṭiṣate* would result. "Another [teacher] says it has *t* as its penultimate" means that the designation as having *ṭ* as its penultimate is due to the application of the rule for the substitution of *ṣṭu* (Pāṇini 8.4.41).

In this view, although the substitution of *ṣṭu* is considered *asiddha* when doubling (*dvitva*) is to be performed in the suffix *san*, [the prohibition] "not *n*, *d*, or *r*" (Pāṇini 6.1.3) [applies].

The intention is that because there is no prohibition, when *tāṭis*—characterized by the letter *t*—is doubled, the letter *ṭ* is eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, resulting in the form *atiṭṭiṣate*. As for *ānaṭṭe*:
here, the prohibition "not *n*, *d*, or *r*" (*na ndrāḥ*) does not apply, because the phrase "of the second monosyllabic [part]" (*dvitīyasyaikācaḥ*) is understood to carry over from that rule.

Regarding *ghaṭṭa calane*: this [root] also belongs to the *curādi* class. Regarding *sphuṭa vikasane*: this [root] also belongs to the *kuṭādi* class. Regarding *aṭhi gatau*: having considered that in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], after the addition of *num*, doubling, and the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ*, there is lengthening by *ṭhata ādeḥ*, and then *nuṭ* by *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*, he says: *ānaṇṭha*.

Thus: "In *vaṭhi* [the sense of] solitary wandering" means in the state of wandering without a companion. And "in *maḍi*"—the term "dividing" (*vibhajana*) is supplied [from the previous rule]. *Maḍi* will be mentioned among the parasmaipada roots in the sense of "adornment" (*bhūṣā*).
"In *śāḍṛ* [the sense of] praise" (*ślāghā*); because of the identity of *ḍa* and *la*, Kāśyapa says "he praises" (*śālata*). Thus end the *aṭṭ*-class and so forth.
Thirty-six have been accounted for. Now, those ending in the *ṭa*-class consonants [are indicated by the phrase] "ending in *ga*, *ḍa*, and *la*.
This means they end with the root *gaḍi* (in the sense of "a part of the face"). Regarding *mleṭṭa* and *mreḍṭa*, these have *e* as their penultimate vowel (*edupadhau*).
The second [root] ends in *ḍ*. This means it ends in the third letter of the *ṭa*-class. But how can this [root] be included among those ending in *ṭ*?

Since it is more appropriate for this [root] to be read among those enumerated starting from *cuḍḍa* (DhP 1.259) and so forth, as its placement there is logical, he says: "in the midst of those ending in *ṭ*. This is like *nāth*.

Just as [the root] *nāthṛ* and *nādhṛ* are placed among those enumerated starting from *ṭhedha* (DhP 1.260) and so forth, which end with the fourth letter of the *tavarga* (the retroflex *ḍ*), so too is this.
The reading *yācñe* is also included because its meaning is identical to that of the word ending in the second letter of the *tavarga* (the dental *cha*), in the same manner as before.

Regarding *kaṭe*: it begins with a *kaṇṭhya* (velar) sound. Regarding *caṭe*: it begins with a *tālavya* (palatal) sound. He states that for the first root, there is *cutva* (substitution of *cha*) for the reduplication in the *liṭ* (perfect tense): *cakāṭa*; *cakaṭatuḥ*. For the second root: *ceṭatuḥ*.

Because it does not possess the status of being an *ādeśa* (substitute) or the like—which would cause a change in form (*vairūpya*)—there is neither the substitution of *e* nor the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*). Regarding the phrase "when [vṛddhi] has been obtained":

this means that when the optional *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *ato halādeḥ* is applicable, because the obligatory *vṛddhi* characterized by the condition of ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*) is prohibited by the rule *neṭi*.

(141) *hyantakṣamaśvasajāgṛṇiśvyeditām* |7|2|5| The compound *hyanta-kṣama-śvasa-jāgṛ-ṇi-śvi-edita* is a *dvandva* in the genitive case. Those which have *h*, *m*, or *y* at their end are called *hyanta*. Thus he says: "of that which ends in *h*, *m*, or *y*."
Regarding "kṣaṇādeḥ": by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the roots *śvas* and *jāgṛ* are included. Regarding "ṇyantasya" (of that which ends in the causative suffix):
the intention is that by the mention of *ṇi*, there is an inclusion of that which ends in it, according to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix.
Regarding "śvayateḥ": the meaning is "of the root *śvi*. Regarding "editaḥ": the analysis of the compound is "that whose *it* (the vowel *i*) is an *e*."

The meaning is that there would be no *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rules] "vṛddhi occurs before *sic*" and "not when *iṭ* follows. Regarding "before *sic* beginning with *iṭ*": the meaning is that "before *sic*" is carried over from "vṛddhi occurs before *sic*" and "*iṭ*" is carried over from "not when *iṭ* follows. As for *akaṭīt*: [it is derived from the root *kaṭ* with *aṅ*].

Since [the vowel] has been modified, there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution]. Regarding "aṭa paṭa," having considered that the lengthening occurs by the rule "ata ādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.2), he says "āṭa. Regarding "peṭatuḥ," there is the substitution of *etva* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). Regarding the root *vaṭ* in the sense of "encircling" (*veṣṭane*), [the form] is "vavaṭatuḥ"; here there is a prohibition by the rule "na śasadadavādiguṇānām" (Pāṇini 1.2.6). Regarding "vavaṭitha," here [the rule applies] because of the suffix *thal*.
Regarding *seṭ*: there is a prohibition by the rule "not after *śas*, *sad*, or *ad*" regarding what has been obtained [as a suffix]. As for *kiṭ* and *khiṭ* meaning "fear":

although the root *kiṭ* is listed later in the sense of "going" in the entry "iṭ, kiṭ, kaṭī gatau," it is nevertheless recited here again because of a difference in meaning. It would be more appropriate to list them as *khiṭ* in the sense of "fear" and *kiṭ* in the sense of "going."

*śiṭa* and *ṣiṭa*: the first has a palatal (*tālavya*) as its initial [consonant], while the second is a root taught with an initial *ṣ*. *jaṭa* and *jhaṭa*: for the first, because it begins with a substitute that prevents dissimilarity (*avairūpya*), there is the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication; but for the second, this is not the case. Thus: *jeṭatuḥ* and *jajhaṭatuḥ*. *ṇaṭa* (in the sense of "dancing") is a root taught with an initial *ṇ*; it belongs only to the *cur*-class (*curādi*).

This [root] *naṭ* is indeed taught with the upadhmanīya (*ṇ*) as its initial substitute; thus, one says *praṇaṭati*. Regarding the roots *iṭ*, *kiṭ*, and *kaṭī* meaning "to go," and *kaṭe* meaning "rain" and "covering": the root *kaṭ* was previously taught as having an *e*-vowel (*edit*), but here it is taught as having an *ī*-vowel (*īdit*). Because it lacks the quality of being an *e*-vowel (*edit*), the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *hy-antā-ṇ-ṇit-i* does not apply.

"Akaṭīt" and "akāṭīt. Now, one might ask: why is the root not simply read as "kaṭ"? To this he says: "The letter *ī*. Regarding the phrase "some, however": the meaning is that some, considering the reading to be "kaṭi" with a short vowel, apply the augment *num* because it is marked with the indicatory letter *id*, and then state that the form becomes "kaṇṭati" after the application of the *anusvāra* and its subsequent change to a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). Regarding *iyāya*: this is formed from the root *i* with the suffix *ṇal*; after reduplication and the *vṛddhi* strengthening, the *āy* replacement occurs.

By the rule *ṭhabhyāsasyā'savarṇe*, *iyaṅ* is applied, resulting in *iyuti*. Here, the vowel *i* is short.
