Regarding *iyaya*: because it is a *pit* suffix when there is reduplication, there is no *kit* status; thus, after the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement by *ay*, the *iyaṅ* is applied to the reduplicated syllable.

In the cases of *vasi* and *masi*, since the *iṭ* augment is obligatory by the rule of the *krādi* group, after reduplication and the *yaṇ* substitution for the *ṭhi* of the second member according to "anekācaḥ," the forms are *iyiva* and *iyima*. [The forms] *etā*, *eṣyati*, *ayatu*, *āyat*, and *ayet* follow.

In the āśīrliṅ (benedictive), there is lengthening by the rule *ṭhikṛtsārvadhātukayor dīrghaḥ*, resulting in *īyāt*. In the *sic* (aorist suffix), there is *vṛddhi* (strengthening), resulting in *aiṣīt*. [The form] *aiṣyat* is the conditional. Regarding the phrase "but of the long [vowel]," it means "of the root *ī* which is long.
Except for the *liṭ* (perfect), its forms in the *laṭ* (present) and other tenses follow the previous rules. He states the specific rule for the *liṭ*:

Regarding *ayāñcakāra*: after the root *ī*, when the suffix *ām* follows, there is the substitution of *aya* for the *guṇa* vowel, and there is also the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) [of the auxiliary verb]. Regarding *kuḍi vaikalye*: they say that "deficiency" (*vaikalya*) means lack of discrimination (*aviveka*), or else it refers to a state of incompleteness (*apūrṇabhāva*). Regarding *muḍa pruḍa mardane* and so forth: this is clear. Regarding the root *paṭh* in the *liṭ* tense, before *atus* and other *kit* suffixes:

There is *etva* (the substitution of *e*) and elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*). Thus he says: *peṭhatuḥ* and *peṭhitha*. Although [the root] is not *akit* because it has *ṭh*, there is *etva* and elision of the reduplication by the rule "and when *thal* follows, provided it is *seṭ*. [The forms] *apaṭhīt* and *apāṭhīt* show the optional *vṛddhi* by the rule "of a light vowel following a consonant beginning with *at*. [The root] *vaṭha* means "thickness" (*sthaulya*).
*Sthaulyam* means "becoming gross. Thinking that the rule *na śasadadavādiguṇānām* prohibits the substitution of *et* (e) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), he says:
*vavaṭhatuḥ*, *vavaṭhitha*. Regarding *dopadhā*, the term *ḍopadha* is used here because of the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṭu*.

The form *cud* [is derived as follows]: from the root *cuḍ*, by the elision of the suffix *kvip* and the subsequent elision of the *s* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, there is the elision of the second *ḍ* by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*.

Upon the removal of the *ṣṭu* quality, the form *cud* is established by the rule *ṭhāvasāne* (which allows for the substitution of *t* for *ḍ*). The form *ad* [is derived] from the root *aḍḍ*; the formation is as previously described.

*Kaditi*: This is the form of the root *kaḍ* with the suffix *kvip*. "And so forth" (*ityādi*): by the word "and so forth," forms such as *cud* (from *caḍ*) due to the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) are included. "Because of the traditional teaching of its being unitary" (*ekatvasmaraṇāt*): the remainder of the sentence is "in the *Śikṣā* and other texts. "In the sense of speaking, *gaḍaḍ*" (*gaḍaḍi vadane*): among those ending in the dental class (*tavarga*), *gaḍ* has already been dealt with; now follows *śauṭ*, which is parasmaipada.
The roots beginning with *garva* have been dealt with. Regarding *tipṛ*:

the first and third [roots] have a vowel as their penultimate (*idupadha*), while the second and fourth have the vowel *e* as their penultimate (*edupadha*). Furthermore, the third and fourth are *ṣopadeśa* (roots taught with an initial *ṣ*);
because the *ṣ* becomes *ṣṭu* (retroflex), the *ṭ* is specified [in the root list], and thus they are characterized by having a sibilant preceded by a dental. This refers to the first [root].
The meaning is "having three parts. The intention is that this [root] is listed among those taught with an anudātta vowel in the Bhāṣya and other sources.
Regarding *babhrāma*: the intention is that it contradicts the Bhāṣya. He provides an example of the first [case]: *tepate*;
here, there is guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel due to the presence of the *śap* suffix. Regarding *titipa*: [this is derived] by the rule *asaṃyogāl liṭ kit*.

But this is not a valid quality [of the root]. Now, regarding the form *titipiṣate*, having raised the objection that there should be a prohibition by the rule "ekāca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), he says: "because of the restriction for roots beginning with *kr*" (*krādiniyamāt*). Regarding *tepsyate*:

in the imperative (*loṭ*) and other moods, however, we have *tepatām*, *atepata*, and *tepet*. Now, in the optative of benediction (*āśīrliṅ*), with the suffixes *sīyuṭ* and *suṭ*, the form is *tipsīṣṭa*.
He will explain *rūpa* later. In that context, when the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) is about to apply—(142) *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu* 1.2.11.
The word *liṅ* [is understood], and the two sūtras *iko jhal* and *halantācca* also carry over.
[The rule] "after a conjunct beginning with ṭh" [is understood], as well as "kiṭ" from the previous context. The genitive case in *ikaḥ* denotes proximity; it follows *hali*. Thus he says:

"from that which is near an *ik*" and so forth. The state of being followed by an *ātmanepada* suffix is a qualification of *sic* alone, and not of the *liṅ*; for the *ātmanepada* which is a substitute for *liṅ* belongs to the *liṅ* itself.

Because [the condition of] being "para" (subsequent) is impossible. Why [specify] "ika" (an *ik* vowel)? [Consider the example: *vavakṣīṣṭa*. If the *k*-marker were present, there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacisvapi-*. Why [specify] "in the *ātmanepada* endings"? [Consider the example: *adrākṣīt*. If the *k*-marker were present here, the substitution of *am* by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakitī* would not occur. [The form] *āptiptā* [is also an example].

In the case of the substitute *luṅ*, the suffix *cli* is replaced by *sic*. There is elision [of the *s*] by the rule "ṭhjhalo jhalī" (Pāṇini 8.2.26). Because *sic* follows an *ātmanepada* ending, it is treated as *kit*, and thus there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Now, he states the purpose of the root *tepṛ* having a short *i* or *u* as its penultimate vowel—namely, that it is used in the form *titepe*. This is because of the presence of the short vowels *i* or *u* as the penultimate vowel (*idudupadhatva*).

The intention is that because of the *kit* designation, there would be no *guṇa* substitution. He indicates that this [root] is *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment) by providing the forms *tepitā* and *tepiṣīṣṭa*. [He also gives] *atepiṣṭa*. Regarding the root *ṣṭip*, however, since the *ṣ* at the beginning of the root is changed to *s* by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*, the *ṣṭu*-combination is removed; having thus established the form *stepate* in the present tense (*laṭ*), [he proceeds to derive it] in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

He states the form *tiṣṭipa*: by the rule "consonants preceded by *śar* [are retained]," the *t* is left remaining, because when the *ṣ* is removed, the substitution of *ṣṭu* is no longer applicable. Due to the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa*. The form *tiṣṭepa* is derived from the root *ṣṭepṛ*; and regarding the root *tepṛ*, it means "to tremble," while by the word "and" (*ca*), it also means "to flow. However, in reality...

Since the meaning of "flowing" (kṣaraṇa) is obtained through the letter *ca*, its reading in the previous [list] can be dispensed with. Some, however, read the beginning of the third class as *ḍepṛ*. [The root is] *vepṛ* in the sense of trembling and *gati* (motion); the letter *ca* has the sense of collecting what has not been mentioned—this is the intention. And this [is the case for] *tue vepṛ*, *kepṛ*, *gepṛ*...

Although the meaning "trembling" (*kampana*) would have been established [by the previous rule], it is obtained through this separate recitation because of a difference in meaning. The root *glepṛ* was previously listed as "in dejection" (*dainye*); here, however, it is recited again because of a difference in meaning. Otherwise, there would be the inconvenience of having to state:
"*glepṛ* in dejection, trembling, and going. This is the intended sense.
Regarding *trapuṣi*: the vowel *ū* and the letter *ṣ* are *it*-markers; it has a short vowel (*a*) as its penultimate. (143) *tṛphalabhajatrapaśca* | Pāṇini 6.4.122.

Since the rules for *etva* (change to *e*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) do not apply because the root is situated between two conjunct consonants (*saṃyukta-hal*), he says: *tṛphala*. [The rule begins with] *ata*.

From the rule *ekahalmadhye*, the words *ataḥ* and *liṭi* are carried over (*anuvartate*). From *dhvasoḥ*, the word *et* is carried over, as well as *abhyāsalopaśca*. From *gamahana*, the word *kiti* is carried over, as is the rule *thali ca seṭi*. He says this with the words "of these" (*eṣām*). By the word "guṇa,"...

This is a rule [prescribing *ṣṭun*] where it was not otherwise obtained, because [the roots] possess a cultivated (*bhāvita*) vowel, have *v*, *r*, *u*, *p*, *ā*, or *e* as their initial, and do not stand between two single consonants (*ekahalmadhya*). Regarding *ānba*: because it has two consonants (*dvihaltva*), the augment *nuṭ* is applied. Regarding *ṣṭabhi* and *skabhī*: the first is taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*). Because the letter *t* is indicated by *ṭ* through the rule of *ṣṭutva*, it is preceded by a *s*-sound that follows a dental (*dantya*). Then, when the *ṣ* becomes *s*, the *ṣṭutva* is removed. Thus he says: "he supports" (*stambhati*). Regarding "the *anusvāra* for *num*": because of the *idit* designation, *num* is added; then, by the rule "of a non-final *n*," its *anusvāra* occurs.

By the rule *anusvārasya yayi*, its [the anusvāra’s] replacement is the *parasavarṇa* letter *m*. However, if the reading were simply *ṣṭambhe*, then because it would be a *pratipadokta* (specifically mentioned) term, this very [form] would be understood in the rule *udaḥ sthe*; such is the intention. Regarding "pūrvasavarṇa" (the preceding homogeneous sound): the *th* replaces the *s*. By the rule *khari ca*, that [th] undergoes *cartva* (substitution by a voiceless unaspirated consonant), resulting in *t*; this is the meaning. Whatever needs to be said on this point has been explained at length under the section on *hal-sandhi* in the rule *udaḥ sthā-stambhoḥ*. [The form] is *viṣṭambhate*.

The intention is that the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) applies by the rule "ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41). Now, one might ask: even so, why would *ṣatva* not occur in the case of the root *stambh*? To this he says: "But there is no *ṣatva* in the case of *stambh*. Why not? To this he says: "In the rule for the insertion of *śnu*. The meaning is that in the rule for prescribing *ṣatva*, only that form of the root which is specifically mentioned (*pratipadokta*) in the sūtra "stanbhustunbuskanbhuskunbhuskuñbhyaḥ śnuśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.82) is taken.

If this were the case, then even in the rule prescribing the *pūrvasavarṇa* vowel (*ṭh-udoḥ sthā-stambhor ar* [Pāṇini 8.4.61]), only the Vedic (sautra) form would be included; therefore, he says: "But the reason for that... This means that the authority for including only the Vedic form in the rule prescribing *ṣatva*, while including both that and others in the rule prescribing *pūrvasavarṇa*, is as follows. Now, what is the authority for the fact that the word is read with a labial nasal (*m*) as the penultimate in the rule for *pūrvasavarṇa*, but with a dental nasal (*n*) as the penultimate in the rule for *ṣatva*? To this he says: "Thus says Mādhava."

The sense is that the very tradition of Pāṇini’s pupils is the authority in this matter. When the *ṣ* is removed by the rule "liṭi śapūrvāḥ khayaḥ," the *ṣṭu*-substitution is also removed, and thus the letter *t* remains [in *tastambhe*]. [The statement] "the *ṭ* is original" (*aupadeśika*) means that the *ṭ* is inherent, and not produced through the application of *ṣṭu*-substitution. Regarding the phrase "in his view": since, according to that view, the *ṣ* is also inherent, even if only *stanbhi* were mentioned in the rule prescribing *ṣ*-substitution (*ṣatvavidhi*), the presence of the *ṣ* would be unimpeded. [Thus we have the form] *ṭaṣṭambha*.

The meaning is that, according to the rule *ṭhśarpūrvāḥ*, only the letter *ṭ* remains. The roots *jabhī* and *jṛbhi* mean "bending of the limbs"; the bending of the limbs is their curvature. The first root has the marker *idit*; the second also has the marker *idit*. The fact that the first root has the marker *idit* is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *iṭ* by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*. (144) *radhijabhor aci* | Pāṇini 7.1.61. [The sūtra begins with] *radhijabhoḥ*.
Regarding the root *radh* in the sense of "injury," which belongs to the fourth class (*divādi*) and takes the suffix *śyan*, the vowel *i*...
This is the explanation. From the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the term *num* is understood by anuvṛtti.
Thus he says: "of these two. Because they do not have *it* as an *it* (i.e., they are *anit*), the application of *num* is prescribed. In *jambhate*, there is *num* before the suffix *śap*.
In forms such as *jambhita*, because there is an *ac* vowel preceding it, there is *num* before the augment *iṭ*. Why "before an *ac* vowel"? [Consider] *raddhā* and *jabdham*.
*Śrambhu*: with the vowel *a* in the middle (*akāramadhya*). Regarding *ṣṭuabhu* (the root *stambh*): by the rule *ṣṭuan*, the *t* becomes *ṭ*.
This is a root taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*). In *viṣṭobhate*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargāt sunoti*.
In *vyaṣṭobhiṣṭa*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *prāksitādaḍvyavāye 'pi*. [The root] *tipṛ*...

These roots beginning with *iti* and ending with *stobh*, being marked with an indicatory vowel *u* (*ūdita*), have been explained as having anudātta (low-pitched) vowels. Now, regarding *gupū rakṣaṇe*: this root has an indicatory vowel *ū*. (Pāṇini 3.1.28): "The suffix *āya* is added after the roots *gup*, *dhūp*, *vicch*, *paṇ*, *pan*."
Regarding the phrase "from these, *gup*, *dhūp*, etc.": this means from *gup*, *dhūp*, *vicch*, *paṇi*, and *pani*.

Since there is no explicit mention of the meaning [of the suffix], he says: "in its own sense" (*svārthe*). The suffix *āya* ends in the vowel *a*. The result of this is seen in the form *gopāya* in the verse: *gopāyataṃ naḥ sumanasyamānaḥ*.

Since the *dhātu* accent is an acute (*antodātta*), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the portion beginning with the syllable *śa* is also taken as acute; thus, by the rule "an acute followed by an unaccented [becomes] a circumflex" (*udātādanudātasya svaritaḥ*), the syllable *ta* in *tām*— which is unaccented because it follows an initial-vowel (*adupadeśa*) verbal root and is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix— is circumflex (*svarita*).
It should be understood that [the vowel] has the svarita accent.

Since the suffix *āya* is prescribed for a verbal root by the rule "dhātor ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.22), which includes the word "dhātoḥ" (of a verbal root) as an anuvṛtti, the suffix *āya* is classified as an *ardhadhātuka*; consequently, operations such as *guṇa* substitution take place.
Thus it says: "puganta-guṇa" (Pāṇini 7.3.86).
(146) *Sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32).
[Objection: But surely, since that which ends in the suffix *āya* is not recited among the roots beginning with *bhū*, it lacks the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*).
To the question, "How are the *laṭ* and other suffixes derived from this [root]? he says: *sanādyantāḥ*.

Having prescribed the *san* and other affixes by means of the sūtras beginning with *guptijkidbhyaḥ san* and ending with *kamerṇiṅ*, this sūtra is recited. Those whose beginning is *san* are called *sanādayaḥ*.
The analysis of the compound is: "those which have the suffix *san* and others as their beginning, and the suffix *ṇiṅ* as their end.
Thus he says: "the *san*-class and so forth.
[The verse continues: "The *san*, *kyac*, *kāmyac*, *kyaṅ*, *kyaṣ*; then the *kvip* of manner (*ācāra*), *ṇic*, *yaṅ*, and likewise *yak* and *āya*..."

"Īyaṅ and ṇiṅ—these twelve [suffixes] beginning with *san*," so says the *Saṃgraha*. In a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is a prohibition against including that which ends with it; therefore, in this case, inclusion of that which ends with it is intended.

"Because of its being a verbal root (*dhātu*)" means: because it ends in the suffix *āya*. "He protects" (*gopāyati*): [this occurs] when the suffix *śap* follows, [and] "of that which ends in *at*" (*ato*).
In the word *gaṇe*, there is a single substitute (*pararūpa*).

(147) *Āy-ādaya ārddhadhātuke vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.31). "Those beginning with *āya*" (*āyādayaḥ*): those for which *āya* is the first are "those beginning with *āya*. There are three: *āya*, *īyaṅ*, and *ṇiṅ*.

The [affixes] beginning with *āya* are considered [to apply when the suffixes beginning with *śnā* and *śnu* follow]. This is because of the reading in the sūtra: "the affix *āya* after the roots *gup*, *dhūpa*, *vicchi*, *paṇi*, and *pani*; the affix *īyaṅ* after the root *ṛt*; and the affix *ṇiṅ* after the root *kam*. Regarding the phrase "when there is a desire to express" (*vivakṣāyām*), the intention is that the locative case in "before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix" (*ārddhadhātuke*) is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). For if it were a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), however—

In the case of *gopāyita*, there would be no elision of the final vowel (*ato lopaḥ*), because at the time of the instruction of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, it does not end in /a/; this is the intended meaning. (148) *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi* | Pāṇini 3.1.35.
And thus, the optional application of the *āya* suffix is established for the *liṭ* [perfect] tense. Regarding that, he states [the rule] for the alternative involving the *āya* suffix:

*kāspratyayāt*. The analysis is *ām*—*amantra* (meaning "ām" except in the case of a mantra). It is intended that *ām* should also follow roots such as *cakāsṛ* ("to shine") and *jāgṛ* ("to wake"), even though they do not end in a suffix; this is obtained from the phrase "and after that which ends in a suffix."

And thus, in *ati* (meaning "he acts like 'a'"), the suffixes such as the present indicative (*laṭ*) are applied after a form ending in *kvip*. In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the desired forms such as *āṬ* and *atuḥ* would not be established, because the suffix *ām* would apply due to the word ending in a suffix.
However, if it were explained that [the rule applies] "after the root *kās*" and "after a polysyllabic word ending in a suffix," then—

Lest it be argued that [the suffix] *ām* would not apply to roots such as *cakās-* and *sṛj-*, he says: "having set aside the mention of *pratyaya*. Thus, the sense is that only this much is obtained—that *ām* follows the root *kāsa-* and roots with more than one vowel (*anekāc*)—and therefore the two aforementioned defects do not arise. In reality, however, [the form] *atīti* is derived from *a iva ācarati*.

That it does not exist at all will be explained in the analysis of the *sub*-suffixes. And thus, the form *gopāyā-ām* is established. (149) Therefore, [the rule] "there is elision" (*ato lopaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.4.48).

Therefore, there is elision (*lopa*). From the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti*, the term *upadeśa* (in the original state) is understood to carry over. The term *ārddhadhātuke* (before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). That [heading] is repeated here; one instance applies to "in the original state" (*upadeśe*), while the second serves as the cause for the elision (*lopa*). Thus he says: "in the original state of an *ārddhadhātuka*."

By the words *it* and so forth: what is the purpose of the phrase "in the instruction of an *ārddhadhātuka*"? Consider the roots *aya* and *paya*, meaning "to go. From these two, with the suffix *kvip*, there is elision by the rule *lopo vyor vali*; then, by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*, the augment *tuk* is added; and finally, after the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*), one desires the forms *at* and *pat*. In this case, if the *yalopa* (elision of *y*) were to occur, the elision of the *a* [by the rule *ato lopaḥ*] would not take place.
It occurs because the root ends in the letter *y* at the time of its instruction in the *ārdhadhātuka* section.

If the term *ārdhadhātuka* were omitted from the rule "in the instruction of the *ārdhadhātuka*," then in the word *cikīrṣita*, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) would not take place, because [the suffix] *san* is taught [as part of the root] at the time of its instruction.

Because it ends in the letter *n*. However, there is no fault if the term *ārddhadhātuka* is included [in the rule], since the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix *kta* arises precisely from the suffix *san* once its *anubandha* has been removed.
Why [is it said] "when an *ārddhadhātuka* follows"? Consider the example: *kathayati*. This root (*cur*) is one ending in *a* within the *cur-ādi* class. In this case—
The vṛddhi substitution does not take place because the elision (lopa) of the *ṭhak* suffix is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the subsequent element.

However, if the condition "when an ārdhadhātuka affix follows" were not stated, the elision would not be treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, since it would lack a subsequent cause (*paranimittakatva*). Thus, in the present case:

When "gopāya" followed by "ām" is present, the elision of the "a" (ato lopaḥ) results in the form "gopāyām. Although this could also be established by the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (savarṇadīrgha), the elision of the "a" is nevertheless presented because it is the more logical [or grammatically correct] option.
Regarding the alternative view where the āya-pratyaya suffix is absent, he says: "jugopa," because [the root] has the marker "p."

Because it is marked with *k* (kit), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*). Thus, *jugupatuḥ*. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa*; and because it is marked with *ū* (ūdita), there is optionally *iṭ*. This applies to the suffixes beginning with *th* and *la*, as understood from the context. *Jugupiva*—*jugupva*; *jugupma*.

However, the rule regarding the *krādi* class applies only to the absence of that which would otherwise be necessarily obtained by the prohibition (*nañ-prāptasya eva abhāvasya*), and not to that which is obtained through optional rules (*vibhāṣā*) and the like.

This was stated under the rule *ṣidhu śāstre* (DhP 1.3). Regarding the form *gopāyita*: in the case of the *luṭ* suffix with the *āya* affix, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory; in the case of the absence of the *āya* affix, *iṭ* is optional. This is because the quality of being marked with *ū* (*ūdittva*) has its purpose fulfilled only in the simple root. Thus he says: *gopitā*, *goptā*. [And] *gopāyiṣyati*.

*gopiṣyati*, *gopsyati*; *gopāyatu*; *agopāyat*; *gopāyet*. Regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) in the view that includes the suffix *āya*, he says: *agopāyīt*. In the view where the suffix *āya* is absent, he states the form with the augment *iṭ*: *agopīt*. By the rule "ṭhiṭa īṭī" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there is the elision of the *sij* suffix. By the rule "ṭhneṭ" (Pāṇini 7.2.4)...

There is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇa-vṛddhi*). However, in the absence of *iṭ*, since there is no suffix following *iṭ*, the rule *silopaḥ* does not apply;

thus he says: *agaupsīt*. [In this case] the *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule *vadavraja-*. [The forms] *agopāyiṣyat*, *agopiṣyat*, and *agopsyat* [are derived accordingly]. Regarding the root *dhūpa* meaning "to heat" (*saṃtāpa*), the suffix *āya* is applied by the rule *gūpū-dhūpa-*.

In the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, there is an option regarding that [substitution]. Regarding *ṣapa samavāye*: this is taught with the initial *ṣ*. Regarding *cupa mandāyām*: this begins with the first letter of the *ca*-class (*ca-varga*). However, that which begins with the second letter of the *ca*-class is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). Regarding *tupa* and *tumpa*: all eight have *u* as their penultimate vowel; the third and fourth, as well as the seventh and eighth, [belong to the *ta*-class].

That [the root] contains the letter *r* will become clear in the root-text (*mūla*). Regarding the form *tutumpatu*, having raised the doubt as to whether there might be elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*), he says: "because of a conjunct consonant" (*saṃyogāt*). He states the specific rule for the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*) as:
"the suffix *k* is applied in the benedictive" (*kidāśiṣi*). In the form *prātumpatāu*, this is a reference made by means of the *śtip* affix.
The meaning is that *suṭ* is inserted before the root *tup* when the prefixes *pra-* or *pari-* precede and when "cow" (*go*) is the agent. *Suṭ* is an initial constituent of the root *tup*.

Regarding this rule for the insertion of *suṭ*, he states the purpose of the technical designation *tumpati* by means of the suffix *śtip*—namely, that [the insertion of *suṭ*] does not occur in the case of *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*).

The intention is that this is because of the statement "by means of the *ṭh*, *ś*, or *p* as an *anubandha*. Regarding *ṣṛbhu* and *ṣṛmbhu*: these two are taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*) and have *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). Regarding *sṛbhyāt*: in the optative (*āśīrliṅ*), there is elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) because of the marker *n* (in *ṣṛbhū* being treated as *ṣṛbhū-n-ī*). Regarding *ṣibhu* and *ṣimbhu*—one [teacher] says so: the first has *i* as its penultimate vowel (*idupadha*), while the second has *m* as its penultimate vowel (*mopadha*). Regarding *śubha* and *śumbha*.

In the case of the second [root], there is no elision of *n* because of the rule *iniditām...*. Thus, the roots beginning with *gup* and ending with those having a labial (*pavargīya*) have been explained as being *parasmaipada*. "Ending with *kam*" means up to and including the root *kamu* (desire). Regarding *ghuṇa* and *ghūrṇa*, there is a reading of the second [root] with a long vowel.

The meaning is clear, for the long vowel is established by the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca* alone. Some, however, read *ghūrṇa* with a short vowel. The phrase "only in the sense of praise" means that the restriction does not apply to the sense of "transaction.
This is because of the separate mention; otherwise, [the root would have been listed] simply as *paṇa pana vyavahāre stutau ca*.

The intended meaning is that [the author] would have specified [them separately]. Although it could also be argued that the separate mention is for the purpose of avoiding a correspondence based on the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), nevertheless, this was stated in accordance with established tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
Regarding the phrase "due to association with the root *pan*": the verbal root *pan* occurs only in the sense of praising (*stuti*).

By association with that [stuti], in the rule *gupū-dhūpa-vichi-śata-paṇi* (Pāṇini 3.1.28), the root *paṇ* is understood only in the sense of "praising" (*stuti*), and not in the sense of "dealing" (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, the meaning is that the suffix *āya* is applied to the root *paṇ* only when it signifies praise, and not when it signifies dealing. [This applies] to the commodity to be purchased...

The legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) consists of questions and answers for the purpose of determining the price. Now, an objection is raised: the form *paṇāyati*, which will be mentioned in the context of praise, is untenable;
for since the root *paṇ* is *anudātta*, it would necessarily result in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Nor can it be argued that...

One might suspect that the *anudātta* (low-pitched) accent does not apply to the suffix *-āya* [in *paṇāya*], because the *anudātta* accent heard for the root *paṇ* would otherwise be rendered meaningless; however, by the principle of "that which is subordinate to it" (*tadaṅga-nyāya*), its application is justified as extending to the form ending in the suffix *-āya*. To this, he says: "In the sense of praising" (*stutau*). This refers to the *anubandha* (indicatory letter).

The meaning is that for a root ending in *i* which has anudātta as its inherent nature— since such a root has already fulfilled its purpose in the domain of ārdhadhātuka suffixes when occasionally deprived of the *āya* affix— the ātmanepada does not occur after a root ending in the *āya* affix. And thus:

It is indicated that because the same logic applies, the prohibition "for [roots] taught with a single vowel" does not apply here either. Regarding *kṣam* (to endure): the *ṣ* is for the sake of [forming] *aṅ* after roots beginning with *ṣad* etc. Considering the optionality of *iṭ* due to its being marked with *ū*, he says: *cakṣamiṣe*, *cakṣaṃse*. In the case of the absence of *iṭ*:

The lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *ṭh anunāsikasya kvijhalo 'ri* does not occur here, because in that rule, due to its association with *kvi*, only a root beginning with a *jhal* consonant that is distinct from a *tiṅ* affix is understood. Regarding the specific case when there is no insertion of *iṭ* after *vah* and *mā*, he says: *mvoś ca*. The phrase *mo no dhātoḥ* is understood to follow.
He says this: "of that which ends in *m*" (*māntasya*). Regarding "nasalization" (*ṇatvam*):
the meaning is that because of the suffix *ṣaṭ*, the *n* in *aṭ-kupv-āṅ-num-vyavāye'pi* undergoes nasalization (*ṇatva*). Regarding "the root *kamū* in the sense of desire" (*kamu kāntau*):

the designation *udita* is for the purpose of making the augment *iṭ* optional after the suffix *ktvā* by the rule *udito vā*. [This removes] the misconception that the word *kānti* refers to "splendor."

He explains: "kāntiraccheti" (desire for purity). The sense is that in such expressions as "svargakāmaḥ" (one desiring heaven), the root *kam* is frequently observed to be used in the sense of desire (*icchā*). Amara states: "Kāma, abhilāṣa, and tarṣa [are synonyms for desire].
(Pāṇini 3.1.30: *kamerṇiṅ*) [prescribes the addition of the affix *ṇiṅ* after the root *kam*].
Regarding the suffix *kaṅniṅ*: he explains the sūtra by completing the remainder with the words "in its own sense" (*svārthe*).
The intention is that no specific meaning has been specified. Regarding the suffixes *ṇa* and *ṇic*:

the addition of the indicatory letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of including both [suffixes] in the rule *ṇer aniṭi*. As for the phrase "because it is marked with *ṅ*, it is not treated as *tiṅ*": [this refers to the fact that the *tiṅ*-designation does not apply].
The meaning is that the property of being *anudātta* (unaccented) is purposefully applied in cases such as *ṭhakame*, which occurs when the suffix *ṇiṅ* is absent.

Regarding the form *kāmayate*: the suffix *ṇiṅ* is added, and by the rule *ita upadhāyāḥ*, the penultimate vowel undergoes *vṛddhi*, resulting in *kāmī* with the suffix *ṇiṅ*. The prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] by the rule *kṅiti ca* does not apply here, because the condition for that prohibition—namely, that the suffix be characterized by *it*—is not met, since *ṇiṅ* itself is not characterized by *it*. Thus, it is the form ending in *ṇiṅ*...

Because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*), the *laṭ* and other suffixes are applied. Among these, in the case of *laṭ*, after the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* substitution, and the replacement with *ay*, the form *kāmayate* is obtained. Forms such as *kāmayeta* and so forth are easy to understand. In the case of *liṭ*, by the rule *kāsyanekāca ām*, the suffix *ām* is added; then, by the rule *ām*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of *liṭ*. When the form *kāmi-ām* remains, [the rule] *sārvadhātuke* applies.

Setting aside the [suffix] *guṇa*, since the elision of *ṇi* would apply by the rule to be stated later, "the elision of *ṇi* occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel that lacks *iṭ*," [the following sūtra is introduced]:

(151) *ayāmantālvāyyetnviṣṇuṣu* 6.4.55. [The portion] *ayāmantā* is a split compound (*cheda*). From the previous rule, "the elision of *ṇi* occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel that lacks *iṭ*," the word *ṇeḥ* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).

Therefore he says: "There should be the substitution of *ṇerayādeśaḥ*. And thus, the form *kāmayāmi* remains ending in *am*. Then, considering that the suffix *liṭ* follows due to the rule "the root *kṛ* is also employed as an auxiliary," he says:
*kāmayāṃcakre*. Since the suffix *ṇiṅ* is included among the *āyādi* group, [the substitution of *ay* occurs] before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *liṭ*.
He causes [the student] to recall that which was stated regarding its alternative form: *āy-ādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.50). *cakame*: this [root] takes the augment *iṭ*.

*cakamiṣe*, *cakamidhve*, *cakamivahe*, *cakamimahe*. *kāmayiṣyate*: in the *luṭ* [future], in the alternative where there is *ṇiṅ*, after *tās* and the addition of *iṭ*, there is *vṛddhi*, then *guṇa*, and finally the substitution of *ay*—this is the resulting form. *kāmayatām*.

*akāmayat*, *kāmayeta*, *kāmayiṣīṣṭa*—or *kamiṣīṣṭa*. (152) *ṇi-śri-dru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ* [Pāṇini 3.1.48]. Now, from the root *kam*, which ends in the causative suffix *ṇic* (*kāmi*), when the *luṅ* tense is applied, the *tādeśa* (the substitution of *ta* for *ti*) occurs; then, although the *cleḥ sic* (the substitution of *sic* for *cli*) would normally apply—

The roots *ṇi*, *śri*, *dru*, and *sru* form a dvandva compound. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the mention of *ṇi* includes that which ends in it. From the rule "ṭhcli luṅi" (A 3.1.43), the word *luṅi* is understood; and from "ṭhcleḥ si"j" (A 3.1.44), the word *cleḥ* is also understood. Thus he says: "from a [root] ending in *ṇi*, etc."
*caṅ* has been mentioned.
(153) *ṇer aniṭi* | Pāṇini 6.4.51. Regarding *ṇer aniṭi*: the term *ārddhadhātuke* is supplied from the governing context. The word *lopa* is supplied from the rule *ato lopaḥ*.
This [word] "it" (it) continues [from the previous rule].

Because the term "ṭhaniṭi" is a qualifier of *ārddhadhātuka*, there is an application of the rule *tadādividhi* (the operation applies to that which begins with the specified element). Thus he says: "in a case beginning with one that lacks an *iṭ*. And so, when the *ṇi*-suffix has been elided and the form *kāma ata* remains, [he says] "because of its priority": this refers to the rule "heranekācaḥ" (*Pāṇini 6.4.82*).
The meaning is: since the rule for the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇeraniṭi*) is subsequent [to the rule for *yaṇ* substitution], it would supersede the *yaṇ* substitution if it were to apply;
however, once the *yaṇ* has been applied, the elision of *ṇi* becomes impossible because the *ṇi* no longer exists.
Even if the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*) were invoked, it is difficult for that which was superseded by the *yaṇ* to re-emerge. In fact, however...

In this case, the status of being "as if occupying the original place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is indeed difficult to establish; for the elision of *ṇi*, which operates by relying on the vowel *i*—the substitute for *yaṇ*—in its capacity as having a *ṇit* suffix, cannot be considered *sthānivadbhāva* because it is not a rule conditioned by that [original element]. This principle is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *bho-bhago-*.

Thus is the detailed explanation in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the rule *ṇyallopau*: the distinction is that the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) takes precedence over *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening (*dīrgha*), whereas the elision of the vowel (*allop*) takes precedence by way of prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over *vṛddhi* and lengthening. Consequently, due to this prior conflict, *yaṇ* [is applied] here.

It is established that the elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs by setting aside [other rules]. But surely, in the examples of the forthcoming Vārttika— namely *atatakṣat*, *āṭiṭat*, *kāraṇā*, *kārakaḥ*, and *kāryate*—
the elision of *ṇi* would necessarily be superseded by *iyaṅ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening (*dīrgha*) respectively.
Since this Vārttika would be redundant— because it is precisely due to the lack of scope (*niravakāśatva*) that *iyaṅ* and the others can be sublated,
as in *sudhiyau*, *pradhyau*, *kartā*, *cikāya*, and *sūyāt*, where *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *dīrgha* have their own scope— the author says: "of the elision of *ṇi*" (*ṇilopasya*).

Regarding "tviti": from the root *pac* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel, resulting in *pāci*. From this *ṇi*-stem, by the rule *striyāṃ ktin*, the suffix *ktin* is added. By the rule *tutratathasisusarakaseṣu ca*, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies.
Then, by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, the *ṇic* suffix is elided. Following the rules for *kutva*, the form *pāktiḥ* is established. Thus, it is called "ending in *ktin*."

In the reading [of the sūtra], however, *ktic* should be understood [as the suffix] by the rule *ṭhktic-ktau ca saṃjñāyām*. "Pākti" is the name (*saṃjñā*) of a certain thing. In this case, since the application of *iyaṅ* and so forth is impossible, the scope for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) is equally available. Therein, in forms such as *atatakṣat*, since *iyaṅ* and so forth would apply by virtue of being subsequent [rules], [the present rule] is intended to prevent that.
The sense is that this Vārttika must be commenced. He states that the Vārttika is indeed useless with the words "But in reality" (vastu tu). Regarding the phrase "merely an ārdhadhātuka":

the meaning is that the entire domain of ārdhadhātuka suffixes, beginning with those marked as aniṭ, is the scope for this elision of the *ṇi* affix. And thus, in forms such as *atatakṣat*, even [suffixes] that follow...

The substitution of *iyaṅ* and so forth subverts the elision of *ṇi* because it is an exception (*apavāda*), since an exception is stronger than that which it supersedes. For if one were to accept that the substitutions of *iyaṅ* and so forth subvert the elision of *ṇi* simply by virtue of being subsequent (*para*), then the restriction "provided there is no *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*) in the rule *ṇeraniṭi* would be redundant; [for in cases like] *kārayitā*, where an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *iṭ* follows, the elision of *ṇi* would already be blocked by the subsequent *iyaṅ* substitution.

Since the elision of *ṇi* is established by its very quality [of being a technical suffix], it is understood— by the force of the statement "in the case of a root that does not take *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*)— that the elision of *ṇi* occurs before every *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with one that does not take *iṭ*. And thus:

The point is this: in forms such as *atatakṣat*, although the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is otherwise eligible for the application of *iyaṅ* and so forth, the elision of the *ṇi* occurs everywhere because it is an exception (*apavāda*) that leaves no room for other rules; thus, since the elision of *ṇi* successfully blocks *iyaṅ* and the rest, this Vārttika is redundant. Therefore, [the author] states: "This is indeed an exception."

The meaning is "elision of *ṇi*. However, the elision of *at* (the *a* of the suffix) occurs by way of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), overriding both the *vṛddhi* [substitution] in the case of *cikīrṣakaḥ* and the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* in the case of *cikīrṣyā*. For the elision of *at* is not an exception (*apavāda*) to *vṛddhi* and lengthening.

In examples such as *gopāyita*, although neither *vṛddhi* nor *dīrgha* would otherwise apply, the rule for the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *at* is nevertheless initiated; enough of this digression. Regarding *iyaṅ*: this is merely an indication of an example.

As for *atatakṣid*: from the root *takṣ*, with the causative suffix *ṇi*, in the *luṅ* tense, third person singular (*tip*), after the elision of the *ik* (the *ṇic*), there is reduplication (*caṅ*) and doubling of the second syllable.

Because [the rule] "anekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.8) applies due to the requirement of being preceded by a conjunction of consonants (*saṃyoga*), the substitution *yaṇ* does not occur; rather, when *iy* or *īṅ* would have been expected, the form *atatakṣat* is derived through the following sequence:

first, by the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior counter-exception), there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*); then, by *halādiśeṣa*, the remaining consonant is established; and finally, with the addition of the augment *aṭ*.
The mention of "*yaṇ*" is an indication of the examples. The example is *āṭiṭat*.

From the root *aṭ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, after the augment *āṭ* [by P. 6.4.71], the suffix *luṅ* is applied; then, following the rule "after *i*", the *ik* vowel is elided. Then, by the rule "after *caṅ*", the reduplication occurs. Here, the *yaṇ* substitution (by P. 6.1.78) is set aside by the rule "for that which has more than one vowel" (*anekācaḥ*) due to the principle of "priority of application" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), resulting in the elision of the *ṇi* suffix.
Then, after the augment *āṭ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution takes place, yielding the form [āṭīt]. The term "guṇa" indicates an illustrative example. The term "kāraṇa" [indicates another].
In the section concerning feminine endings (*strī*), from the root *kṛ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the form *kārī* is derived by adding the suffix *ṇvul*.

Here, by means of the rule of "priority" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) prevails over the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the vowel. The word "long" (*dīrgha*) indicates an example. The phrase "it is caused to be done" (*kāryate*) [is the illustration].

From the verbal root *kṛ*, with the suffix *ṇvi* (forming *kārī*), when the present tense (*laṭ*) suffix *yaK* is applied to the object, the rule *ṭhakkṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25) would require lengthening; however, by a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), there is elision of the *ṇi*. Thus, in the case at hand, in the form *kāmi-a-ta*, [the elision applies].
In the case of *therane kā*, after the *ṇi* suffix has been elided by overriding the *yaṇ* substitution, the form remains as *kām ata*.

(154) *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.1. Regarding the rule *ṇau caṅ*: because the governing context (*adhikāra*) is that of *aṅga*, he says "that *aṅga*. Why [is there the mention of] "the penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāḥ*)?
He desired [the addition of the condition] "after a causative suffix" (*ṇau*). What [would happen] without it? Consider *kārayati*.

If it were stated simply as "there is shortening of the penultimate vowel before *caṅ*" (*caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*), then in the case of *adīdapat*—derived from the root *dā-* with a causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the *luṅ* tense, where the form after adding *caṅ* is *dā-i-i-t*—once the long *ā* is shortened, the substitution of *puṅ* would not occur. However, when "after a causative suffix" (*ṇau*) is specified, [the rule applies].

Because the vowel *ā* (of the root *kam*) is no longer in the position of an *upadhā* when the suffix *ṇi* follows, it does not undergo shortening. Furthermore, the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* need not be raised as a concern, because the cause of reduplication (*caṅ*) is separated from the *upadhā* by the intervening letter. Thus, in the present case, the form stands as *kam-a-t*. Then, by the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*, [the first syllable is doubled].

The rule *ṭhajāderdvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2) is also governing here. The sūtra *liṭi dhātoranabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), with the exception of the word *liṭi*, continues to apply. Thus he says: "caṅpi re," etc. Consequently, when there is reduplication of *kam*, and after the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the form stands as *ka kam a ta*.
(155) *sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'naglope* [Pāṇini 7.4.93]. The analysis is:
*sanvat* and *laghuni*, with the division *anaglope*. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
the sense is that it is analyzed as *caṅ paraḥ yasmāt* ("that after which *caṅ* follows"). Alternatively, by resorting to a *karmadhāraya*, it is analyzed as *caṅ pare*.

It is not [the case that] there is no purpose [for the mention of *para*], because the mention of *para* would otherwise be redundant. Now, even if one resorts to the *bahuvrīhi* interpretation, since the term *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplicated syllable) is understood from the rule "atra lopo 'bhyāsasya" (Pāṇini 7.4.58), the meaning obtained is: "when followed by *caṅ*, and when a light vowel follows, the reduplicated syllable is treated like *san*" (*sanvat*). This being so, [the rule would apply] to roots ending in *aṇ*.

In cases such as *aśiśriyat*, *adudruvat*, and *asusruvat*—derived from the roots *śri*, *dru*, and *sru* with the suffix *caṅ* where there is reduplication—the property of being "like the desiderative" (*sanvat*) would also apply. Consequently, by the rule "the long vowel for a light syllable" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*), the long vowel of the reduplicated syllable (which will be stated later) would occur in these instances of *sanvadbhāva*. To this, he says: "The *ṇi* [in the rule] refers to something other than the word-meaning [of the root]."

And thus, the condition "when followed by *caṅ* and *ṇi*" is obtained. The point is that in forms such as *aśiśriyat*, because of the absence of *ṇi*, there is no *sanvadbhāva*. Regarding the phrase "and that [belongs] to the *aṅga*": the *ṇi* is understood through a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
when the term "*aṅgasya*" is repeated, one instance connects with the phrase "when followed by *caṅ*. This refers to the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*).
The genitive [case ending] is used; and thus it is understood that [the rule applies] when a letter followed by *caṅ* is the cause for the designation of a verbal root (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, the letter followed by *caṅ* is, by implication, only the *i*-vowel of the suffix *ṇi*, and not the final letter of the roots *śri*, *dru*, or *sru*, because that [final letter] is not a suffix (*apratyayatvena*).

Because there is an absence of anything that could cause [the suffix] to be designated as an *aṅga*. For this very reason, it was accepted that the word "caṅpare" (when followed by *caṅ*) is construed with the genitive case ending of "aṅgasya" (of the *aṅga*), which has the *it* designation, as its cause (*nimitta*).
However, by the mere expression "caṅpare," the condition "in the presence of *ṇi*" (*ṇau*) is not obtained; [this is necessary] in the case of the roots *śri*, *dru*, and *sru*.

Because of the deviation [of the first interpretation]. As for the second [interpretation], the word "aṅgasya" (of the base) is connected with the term "abhyāsasya" (of the reduplicated syllable), which is supplied from the previous context. The suffix *vati* is used here in the sense of the locative case ending *-su*. Thus he says:
"the cause of the designation 'base' (*aṅga-saṃjñā-nimitta*)", and so forth. Alternatively—as in this other explanation—the phrase "when followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*)...

This [term *aṅgasya*] connects with the word *aṅgasya* here, but not with *laghuni*. Furthermore, the acquisition of the meaning "other than the suffix" (*anyapadārtha*) for *ṇi* follows precisely from the fact that the *aṅga* is caused by the suffix. However, *laghuni* connects only with the word *abhyāsasya*. Thus he says: "the *aṅga* which occurs when *ṇi* followed by *caṅ*," and so forth.

"Prāgvat" (as before) means that the operation [of *sanvadbhāva*] should occur as if *san* were present when *ṇi* is elided, even though it is absent. Here, only the first alternative is approved by the Bhāṣya, because of the statement in the Bhāṣya regarding "ṭhajajāgara": "In the case of a *caṅ*-following *ṇi*, that which is light is separated from the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the *ṇi*; therefore, there is no *sanvadbhāva*. And thus, in the first alternative—
In the case of a root ending in *ṇi* followed by *caṅ*, as in *undidi-a-t* (the reduplicated form of *und-ṇic*), there is no lengthening of the reduplicative syllable.

This is because, in the subsequent portion of the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsottarakhaṇḍa*) when followed by *caṅ* and *ṇi*, the condition of having a "light" vowel (*laghu*) is absent; consequently, the reduplicative syllable lacks the property of being followed by such a light vowel, and thus the *sanvadbhāva* rule does not apply.

In the second view, however, regarding the *aṅga* "tuṇḍi" when followed by a *ṇi* that is itself followed by *caṅ*: the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of that *aṅga* takes on the status of being followed by a light vowel (*laghupara*), either by taking the *caṅ* or by taking the elided *ṇi*. Consequently, due to the application of the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were the reduplication of a *san* affix), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable; such is the distinction. And thus, in the present case, in the form *ka-kam-a-ta*, [this applies].
In both commentaries, the status of being a *san* [augment] is established.
(156) *sanyataḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.79. [The analysis is: *sani ataḥ*. The division is *sani-ataḥ*. [The rule states: "In this case, there is elision."

Thus, "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*) is understood from the previous context. From the rule *bhṛñāmit*, the suffix *it* is applied. Therefore, he says: "of the reduplication. [The stem] stands as *ki-kam-a-t*. (157) *dīrgho laghoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.94.
"Long for the light [abhyāsa]. Here, "of the abhyāsa" is understood from the previous rule *lopo'bhyāsasya*.
Thus, it means "the long vowel for the light [consonant] that is a constituent part of the abhyāsa.
The rule *sanvallaghuni caṅpare* follows, with the exception of the word *sanvat*. And that...
This should be explained in two ways as previously stated. Thus, he states the resulting conclusion: "in the domain of *sanvadbhāva*.

It is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *dīrgho'kitaḥ* that the use of the phoneme *t* (as in *sanyataḥ*) in that rule is for the sake of clarity. Consequently, in the form *ki-kam-a-ta*, [the substitution applies] to the vowel *i* of the reduplicated syllable.

He states the fully established form *acīkamata* when there is long *ā*, the substitution of *kama* for *kram*, and the augment *aṭ*. Here, the fact that the light syllable is followed by a *ṇic* suffix is to be understood according to the maxim "that by which there is no intervention" (*yena nāvyavadhāna-nyāya*). As for the phrase "in the alternative where *ṇiṅ* is absent": this is because *ṇiṅ* is optional by the rule "the roots beginning with *āya* are optionally [treated as such] before an *ārddhadhātuka* affix."

The state [of the rule]. It is stated that *caṅ* should be prescribed after the root *kam* and after a root ending in *cli*. This is a specific injunction because [the substitution] would not otherwise apply, as the root lacks the suffix *ṇic*.

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of *ṇi*": in the alternative where *ṇiṅ* is absent, because the root *kam* is *anudāteta*, the augment *ai* does not occur in the third person singular of the present tense; in that case, by the rule *laghuni caṅpare 'naglope*...

And having applied this [rule], since it is stated that that [doubling] is prescribed only when a *ṇi* follows a *caṅ*, for this very reason, due to the absence of *sanvat*-treatment, the substitution of *i* for the *s* of the reduplicated syllable by the rule *sanyataḥ* does not occur. In the prescription of lengthening by the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ*, *sanvat*-treatment is not the cause; rather, it is the presence of a *laghu* [syllable].

Because the term *caṅpare* recurs there [in the rule], its application occurs in the domain of *sanvadbhāva*; therefore, the separate mention of "lengthening" (*dīrgha*) and "*sanvadbhāva*" is made. Thus, with five verses, he elucidates both the *sanvadbhāva* rule and the rule "the short vowel is lengthened" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*). Regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*):

By such statements [as these], one position in this treatise is that "technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) are [operative] at the time of the application of the grammatical operation.

The phrase "at the time of the application of the operation" means "at the location where the operation occurs. According to this position, the technical term rules and the interpretive rule rules [are to be understood] at those specific locations where the rules prescribing the operations occur.

And there is the presence of the Paribhāṣā-śāstra. There is another view: "Technical terms (saṃjñā) and Paribhāṣās [operate] according to their enunciation" (*yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*). "Enunciations" (*uddeśāḥ*) refers to the locations where the technical terms and Paribhāṣā rules are recited;
"according to their enunciation" (*yathoddeśam*) means not deviating from those locations. Thus, the Saṃjñā-śāstra and the Paribhāṣā-śāstra [operate] at their own respective locations.
The meaning is that it remains present and, depending on the specific rule (*vidhi*), presents its own respective meaning.

In this view, the established position is that in the context of operations (*kāryapradeśa*), it is only the meaning of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) or the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) that is presented, and not the technical name or the governing rule themselves. This is illustrated in the rule *sanvallaghuni*...
In the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.94), the terms "of the aṅga" and "of the reduplication" (abhyāsasya) are carried over by anuvṛtti.

Therein, according to the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that rules apply at the time the operation is to take effect), the rule "pūrvo 'bhyāsaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.4) is proximate. Consequently, of the two utterances of the aṅga, the first is designated as the "reduplication" (abhyāsa). That [first part]...

The result is that it "behaves like *san*. In this context, because of its connection with the word "utterance" (*uccāraṇa*) which ends in a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive case in the term *aṅgasya* denotes the object (*karman*), and not a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), since the genitive expressing a grammatical relation (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*) is more powerful. And the "stem" (*aṅga*) is [defined as such] when a suffix follows.

The entire form of the *aṅga* [base] is intended, and not merely a portion of it. Consequently, the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.94), which prescribes lengthening, and the rule "sanvallaghuni" (Pāṇini 7.4.93), which prescribes the treatment as *saN*, apply only where the entire *aṅga* is repeated twice and not merely a single part of it. And thus, regarding the *aṅga*...
Mādhava maintains that these two [rules] apply only when there is a single vowel (*ekāc*) [in the reduplicated syllable], because in that case the entire member (*aṅga*) is reduplicated;
however, they do not apply to members consisting of multiple vowels (*anekāc*), because in those cases only one single vowel,
which is a portion of the member, is reduplicated.

The meaning of the first verse: he clarifies what was stated as "not in many syllables" with the verse beginning "cakāsti. [The root] *cakāsṛ* means "to shine. In the sense of "he explains the meaning," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied;
then, by the rule "arthavedayoḥ," the augment *āpuk* is added to the base, resulting in the verbal root *arthāpi*. [The root] *ūrṇuñ*...

In the case of *ācchādane*, these three roots consist of more than one vowel (*anekāck*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such roots as *jāgṛ* (in the sense of "cessation of sleep"). From these and from those ending in *ṇi*, the entire stem (*aṅga*) is not reduplicated; rather, only some single-vowel portion (*ekāc-avayava*) of the stem is reduplicated. Because there is no double application (dvirukti) of the entire stem. Therefore, due to this lack of internal consistency, he adopts the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) view and says:
Regarding the word *vastutaḥ*: the genitive case in *aṅgasya* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, it is understood as "of the reduplicated portion which is a part of the stem.

Consequently, even though there is reduplication of the single element *nu* in *ūrṇuñ* when followed by *ṇic* and *caṅ*, in the form *aurṇunuvat*, the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes long according to the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ*.

The state of being a *saN* suffix (sanvatva), however, has been disregarded due to the absence of a purpose; for in the case of reduplication (*abhyāsa*), because of the absence of the vowel *a*, the rule "after a *saN*" (*sanyataḥ*) is impossible. In the sense of "he expresses the meaning" (*artham ācaṣṭe*), when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, the base takes the *āP* augment (*arthāp*), and after the *caṅ* [of the aorist], with the elision of *iṇ* and the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*), even though the syllable *thaP* is reduplicated...

Regarding the third verse, we understand that in the case of *tṛtīyapad* (from *tṛ-tīya-pada*), due to the application of the rule for treating a form as if it were a *saṇ* (sanvadbhāva), two things occur: the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable according to the rule *sanyataḥ*, and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsadīrgha*).
Furthermore, even under the view that [the term in Pāṇini’s sūtra] refers to "a part of a stem" (*aṅgasyāvayava*), he states the specific distinction regarding the root *cakās-*: "In *cakāsti*..."
"Tviti": this is the fourth verse. "Avasthā" means the state of affairs or the actual condition.

"Vyavasthayā" means by way of the two alternatives (pakṣadvayena). By the rule "caṅpare," the word "ṇau," which is obtained as the referent of another word (anyapadārthatayā), has the nearby term "laghuni" as its qualifier. Thus, [the meaning is] "when a *ṇi*-affix follows that is preceded by *caṅ*..."
The first explanation—that "light" (*laghu*) is the predicate—is thus established. Alternatively, the *aṅga* itself may be the qualifier of the *ṇi*;
in that case, the second explanation—that "the *aṅga* which occurs when followed by a *caṅ*-preceded *ṇi*"—is established.
Thus, by this systematic arrangement, both of these—*sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the *san* suffix) and lengthening (*dīrgha*)—apply according to the two alternative views.

In the case of the root *cakās* when it is causative (*ṇyanta*) and the *ṇi* suffix is elided, [the rule] would not apply to the form *acacakāsat* after reduplication; however, [if interpreted differently], it would apply—this is the connection [of the argument]. In that regard, if the explanation were "when a *caṅ* follows a *ṇi* which has a light vowel," then neither [of the two results] would occur, because the *ṇi* followed by *caṅ* is separated from the root by the element *kās*.

In cases such as *acīkamata*, however, a single intervening element must indeed be tolerated, according to the maxim *yena nāvyavadhānam* ("that by which there is no intervention"). But if one adopts the interpretation that "the *aṅga* [is that which ends] in a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ*," then in the case of *acīcakāsat*, both [conditions] would necessarily apply to the *aṅga*.

It should be understood that this is because the status of being "preceded by a ṇi" (ṇiparakatva) exists. Now, regarding the difference in interpretation—namely, whether it is "the light [syllable] which occurs when there is a ṇi followed by caṅ" or "the aṅga which occurs when there is a ṇi followed by caṅ"—what is the authority for this? To this he says:
"Because Kaiyaṭa himself has described the optionality of the interpretation. The word "to be respected" (ādartavyā) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

One might ask: "Since the application of the rule *ṇau* (Pāṇini 7.4.1) was accepted as being restricted [to cases where there is no elision], for what purpose is its connection maintained even when there is elision (*aglopa*)?

To this he says: "*ṇeraglope 'pi*" (even when there is elision of *a* after *ṇi*). "*Agitām*" means "of those [roots] beginning with *kamuka-antā-*" etc. "*Siddhayaḥ*" means "for the sake of establishing the long vowel and the *san-vat* treatment."

Otherwise, by taking the elision of the indicatory letters (anubandhas) such as *u* in roots beginning with *kam*, they would be considered *aglopi* (having lost a penultimate vowel); consequently, due to being *aglopi*, the rules for lengthening and the treatment as *sanvadbhāva* would not apply—this is the meaning. Thus, ten roots beginning with *ghiṇi* and ending with *kamu* have been covered. Regarding "ending with *kram*" (*kramyantāḥ*): the meaning is that they extend up to the root *ṭhkramu pādavikṣepe* ("to step").

The remainder [of the rule] is "ending in a nasal. Regarding *aṇa raṇa*: the fact that it has an indicatory letter *ṛ* (*ṛdit*) is for the purpose of prohibiting [the substitution of a long vowel] by the rule "not when there is elision of a portion" (*nāglopi*). Regarding *dhraṇa* meaning "sound": this has a short *u* as its penultimate (*adupadha*). Regarding "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*): in the original enunciation of the verbal root, this ends in the letter *n*. Upon the removal of the vowel *a*, which serves only for pronunciation...
The meaning is that it ends with the fifth letter of the *tavarga* (the dental class). If one asks, "In that case, how is the sound *ṇ* heard?", he says:

"The substitution of *ṇ* [occurs] by the rule *raṣābhyām*. Now, one might object: "Let it be that the *ṇ* is simply natural; why assume a description of the *n* as having undergone the substitution of *ṇ*? To this he replies: "Because of its being taught as a *ṇopadeśa* (a root beginning with *ṇ*)."

The meaning is that the result of the instruction [of the root] with *ṇ* in place of *n*—namely, the substitution of *ṃ* (anusvāra) by the rule "ṭhnaśca"—is to be understood as occurring in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ. Regarding the form *dandhranti*: from the root *dhraṇ*, after *yaṅ*-luṅ, doubling, and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the *ṇuṭ* augment is applied to the reduplicated portion (*abhyāsa*) by the rule "ṇugato 'nunāsikāntasya"; then, in the subsequent part (*uttarakhaṇḍa*)...

The meaning is that if [the substitution] were by *parasavarṇa*, then because that [substitution] is considered asiddha, there would be no change to *ṇatva*, and thus only the letter *ṇ* would be heard.

However, in the case of teaching the natural *ṇakāra*, the intention is that in the subsequent portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*), only the letter *ṇ* would be heard. As for the phrase "even *baṇa*," the meaning is that it begins with the third letter of the *pa*-group (i.e., *ba*). [The root is] *kan*.

Beginning with *dīp* and ending before the root *am* (meaning "to go," etc.), the roots end in the fifth letter of the *tavarga* (the nasal *ṇ*). Regarding *ṣṭan* and *van*: the first (*ṣṭan*) is a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*). Since it undergoes the substitution of *ṣṭutva*, the form contains the letter *ṣṭ*. Thus he says: *stanati*. Regarding *vana* and *ṣaṇ*: the second (*vana*) is a *ṣopadeśa*. Now, one might object: since the rule states *ṣṭana vana śabde* ("*ṣṭan* and *van* mean 'to sound'"), [is not *vana* already established? [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the grammatical analysis of the roots as presented.]

Since the repetition [of the root] would otherwise be useless, he says: "Because of the difference in meaning. For the root *van* is intended to have both the meanings of "sound" (*śabda*) and "to gather" (*saṃbhakti*), whereas for the root *ṣṭan*, only the meaning of "sound" is intended. The intention is that by stating "ṭhṣṭhana śabde" (DhP 3.2.179), whereas if one were to read "ṭhvana saṃbhaktau ca" (DhP 3.2.180), there would be prolixity. (158) *ye vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.43).

He states a specific exception regarding the optative (āśīr-liṅ): *ye vibhāṣā*. From the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ*, the portion *janasanakhanām* is understood by anuvṛtti. From the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām anunāsikalopo jhali kṅti*, the portion *kṅti* is understood. The word *ye* is a qualifier for that [suffix]. The letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). There is an extension (*vidhi*) based on the initial sound of that [suffix].

The term *āt* from the rule *ṭhviḍvanoranunāsikasyā't* (Pāṇini 6.4.41) is understood here. Thus he says: "of the roots *jan*, *san*, and *khan*," and so forth. Regarding the form *sāyāt*: when the *n* is changed to *ā*, there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). [The roots] *drama* and *hamma*: the first has a vowel as its penultimate. Regarding "no *vṛddhi*": this refers to the context of the rule *adramīt*.

When the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a final consonant is prohibited by the rule "ṭhneṭ" (Pāṇini 7.2.5), the meaning is that the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "hmyanta" (Pāṇini 7.2.5) does not apply because of the condition "ato halādeḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.7). Thus we have *jahammā*. Here, *ha* becomes *jha* by the rule for the change of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) to a cerebral (*cu*), and that *jha* becomes *ja* by the rule "abhyāse carcā" (Pāṇini 8.4.54). As for *mimīmā*, it is derived from the root *mīmṛ* with the suffix *ṇal*, following which the reduplication occurs.

"Abhyāsa-hrasvaḥ" (the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable); "ayaṃ śabde ca" (and *ay* is substituted for *i* when followed by a verbal suffix beginning with a consonant). The meaning is that it is derived from the root *mṛdh*.

(159) *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75): [The rule applies] to the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *klamu*, and *camu*. The term "it" (it) is understood here [from the previous rule]. By the hearing of the word "long" (dīrgha), the word "vowel" (ac) is supplied.

(162) *snukramoranātmanepadanimite* 7.2.36. [The long vowel is substituted for the final short vowel of the roots *snu* and *kram* before an affix marked with *ś*, provided it is not caused by the non-ātmanepada endings.]
The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative.
"Absence of a cause for the *ātmanepada*" means "that which is not a cause for the *ātmanepada*.

This statement is made because, although the augment *iṭ* would have been established for *snu* and *kram* by virtue of their being taught with an *anudātta* accent and not being included among those [roots] [that require specific conditions], this rule is provided [to ensure its application even in the absence of an *ātmanepada* cause].

He says it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), namely: "only here [in this context] does *iṭ* apply. And thus, in the case of *lakāras* denoting the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), *iṭ* does not occur. For example: *upastroṣyate jalena* (the water will be heated). This is the *bāvalakāra* (future passive participle). *Upakrasyate* (it will be undertaken); this is the *luṭ* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*). The *sya* suffix follows. However, in the word *prasruta*, there is no *iṭ* because of the prohibition by the rule *śryukaḥ kitī*.

This is because the section containing prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) is commenced prior to the rule prescribing *iṭ*— namely, *ṭhārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ*— by virtue of its own force. Furthermore, the rule was not formulated as *ṭhsnukramoranātmanepade*, for if that were the case, it would mean "when a non-ātmanepada (i.e., parasmaipada) follows."

The form *cikramiṣiṣyati* is not established because it is separated [from the condition] by the suffix *syen*. However, in the case of the Ātmanepada, where the prohibition of *iṭ* applies, the form *pracikraṃsiṣyata* would not be established; therefore, the mention of the "cause" (*nimitta*) is necessary—this is sufficient [for our purpose].
As for *akramīt*: there is no *vṛddhi* substitution because of the rule *hrm-ante* (Pāṇini 7.2.5). Thus end the roots ending in *kram* that take the Parasmaipada.
"Ending with *gā*. This means ending with the root *revṛ*, meaning "to leap or move. Starting from *aya* and *pay* up to before *śala* (meaning "to move"), the roots end in the letter *y*.

And *dāy-āy-ās*. This is the singular ablative case of a collective dvandva compound consisting of *day*, *aya*, and *ās*.
From the rule *kāspratyayādām amantre liṭi*, the phrase "ām... in the perfect tense" (*liṭi*) is understood. Thus he says: "ām shall be applied after these [roots] in the perfect tense."

(164) *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.79. The phrase "after *iṇ*" [from the previous rule] continues, as does "for the *dh* of *ṣīdhvam*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ*" [from 8.3.78], and from "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*) comes "the retroflex [substitute]" (*mūrdhanyaḥ*). "From *iṇ* etc. means "from a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *iṇ*. The meaning is that there is no substitution of *la* for *ya* because it is not followed by *aya*. The sense is that since that [root] lacks the *anudātta* designation, the application of the suffix *śatṛ* is unimpeded. [This is established] by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Since the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the root *cakṣiṅ* is itself *anudātta*, the *ātmanepada* ending is already established by that very quality of being *anudātta*; therefore, the inclusion of the marker *ṅ* indicates that the *ātmanepada* conditioned by the *anudātta* status is non-obligatory (*anitya*).
The sense is that if it were impermanent, the addition of the suffix *ṅti* for the sake of the meaning of the permanent *ātmanepada* would be purposeful;

however, this is not seen in the Bhāṣya. Regarding "because of being *vādi*," the meaning is that in the case of the root *vay* (to weave) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), when the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication do not occur due to its being *vādi*, the form is *vavaye*.
Thinking that the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* applies to the verbal root *ṇī*, he says "praṇayata" (they lead forth).

(166) *liṭ-yaṅoś-ca* |6|1|29|. The term *liṭ-yaṅoś-ca* is a locative case derived from a *dvandva* compound consisting of *liṭ* and *yaṅ*. The rule *pyāya-pī* is understood to follow here. Thus he says: "in *liṭ* and *yaṅ*. Now, [one might ask: does not reduplication (*dvitvam*) apply to the root *pyai* in *liṭ*?

Since the substitution of *pī* occurs later, it sublates [the reduplication]; once the reduplication has been sublated by the substitution of *pī*, the reduplication cannot occur again. This is because of the principle: "In the case of a conflict (vipratiṣedha), that which is sublated remains sublated. Thus, the form *pipye* is desired, where the reduplication is sublated by the subsequent substitution of *pī*, and then the semivowel *y* is replaced by *i* according to the rule *eranekācaḥ*. In that process, once the reduplication has been sublated by the subsequent substitution of *pī*, a further reduplication is not possible. This follows from the maxim: "In a conflict, that which is sublated remains sublated."

He states [the reason] starting from logic: "again, because of the recognition of recurrence" (*punaḥ prasaṅga-vijñānāt*). This is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "it is established because of the recognition of recurrence. Since it is accepted that even what has been superseded may apply again in the event of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), doubling (*dvitva*) and so forth are established even when the substitution of *pī* has already taken place.
That is its meaning.

(167) *dīpa-jana-budha-pūri-tāyi-pyāyibhyaḥ anyatarasyām* 3.1.61. [The rule begins with] *dīpa-jana*. From *cleḥ sic* [Pāṇini 1.2.15], the word *cleḥ* [is understood]; from *ciṇ te padaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.60], the word *ciṇ* [is understood].

Regarding the term "in the singular": the meaning is that because *dīp* and the others take the ātmanepada endings, there is a restriction that the word *ta* following them must be in the singular number.

The form *apyāyiṣṭa* [is derived from the root] *pyai*. Starting from *śala* (meaning "to move") up to before *tevṛ*, the roots end in *l*.

the intention is that *ṣatva* occurs because the substitute is a *sakāra*. "This is also a root taught with an initial *ṣ*" means:

Regarding the root *revṛ* in the sense of "moving by leaping," he says—"moving by leaping" means "moving by jumping"—thereby indicating that *plava* is not a separate root.

The roots beginning with *aya* and ending with *revi* have been covered. "Ending with *ava*" means up to and including the root *ava* in the sense of "to protect. Starting from *mavya* and extending prior to *ala* in the sense of "adornment," the roots end in the vowel *a*.
Starting from *ala* in the sense of "adornment" up to *khora* in the sense of "obstruction," [the roots end in *a*].
First, those ending in *l*.
(169) *ato larantasya* | 7|2|2|. The phrase "vṛddhi occurs after [a root] ending in *a*, in the case of *sic* and in the *parasmaipada*" is understood [from the previous rule].

From the collective dvandva compound *laśca raśca* ("l and r"), the singular genitive case ending is elided. Thus, it means "of that which has *l* or *r* as its final [element]."

The connection is by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The word "from this" (*ataḥ*) ends in the genitive case of a different referent (*vyadhikaraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*); it connects with the word "of the final" (*antasya*). Because *larsya* is a qualifier of the *aṅga*, the rule of "inclusion of that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. The word *ataḥ* is repeated and connects as the substituendum (*sthānin*) for the *vṛddhi*; this is what he expresses by saying "near an *at*" and so forth.

Vṛddhi has been prescribed after *a*; however, if "near *a*" (*ataḥ samīpāt*) were not stated, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *avabhrīt* and *aśvallīt*. The term *vṛddhi* is used because it serves to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when relying on the meaning [of the root]. Regarding *ñi phala*:

"falling apart" means becoming loose. The suffix *ñi* is applied by the rule *ādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ*. Its purpose is [to allow] the suffix *kta* by the rule *ñītaḥ ktaḥ*. Its status as being "initial" (*āditva*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the *iṇ* augment by the rule *āditaś ca*.

Since [the rule] does not apply because of the inclusion of *liṇ* in the list of substitutes for *ādi*, he says: *tṛphala*. *Mīla śmīla* means "to close"; *nimeṣaṇam* is the contraction of the eyes.
