It has been recited. Furthermore, there is a repetition of the reading due to the difference in the *anubandhas*: *kholṛ* and *khorṛ*. The second [root] ends in *r* and has an *ṛt* marker (*ṛdit*). From this point until before *ṣṭhiv*, [the roots] end in *r*. *Dhorṛ* means "extreme skillfulness"; the meaning is a specific gait of a horse. This [root] ends in *r* and is marked with *ṛt*. *Tsara*...

"Entering into deceit" means being in a state of guile. "The root *kṣmā* [is used] in the sense of bending," meaning becoming crooked. "The root *ṣṭhivu* [is used] in the sense of spitting"; it has an *i* as its penultimate letter (*idupadha*) and is marked with *u* (*udit*). From this point onward, until the end of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), the roots end in *v*. When the suffix *tip* follows, and the suffix *śap* is applied, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel would normally occur.

He says: "ṣṭhinv-klamvi-ti. However, in the case of the suffix *lyuṭ*, because there is no following *śit* suffix, the long vowel does not occur, and thus the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) applies. As for the form "ṣṭhīvanam," it should be explained by its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
Regarding the word "asya": it means that the second phoneme of the root *ṣṭhivu* is the letter *th*. This refers to the state after the change of *ṣ* to *ṣṭu* has been applied.

The meaning is "explanation" (*nirdeśa*). This is a root taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), because it begins with a *s* followed by a *th* that is purely dental. Even though it is taught with an initial *ṣ*, the substitution of *s* (*satva*) does not occur here, due to the prohibition in the rule *subdhātuṣṭhivuḥ*. However, in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, [the rule] *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* applies.
By the removal of the sounds *ṣ* and *v*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* (ṣṭutva) is also removed; thus he states the form as *tiṣṭheva*.
However, if the sound *ṭ* were inherent [to the root], the form would be *ṭiṣṭheva*. Regarding *ji* [in] *jaya*:
the root *ji* is one that lacks the augment *iṭ*. [The rule applies] by *saṃlliṭor jeḥ* and *abhyāsācca*.

The words "from the sūtra" and "from practice" (abhyāsāt) are understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. From the rule *ṭhcajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ*, the word *ku* is also understood. In the expression *saṃlliṭoḥ*, the locative case indicates the cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), which connects with "in the reduplication" (*abhyāse*). Thus he says: "the reduplication which is caused by *saṃ* and *liṭ*" and so forth. [And] in the case of *san* and *liṭ*, [the substitution occurs] after the reduplication.

If, however, the explanation were "the substitution of *ku* [for *j*]," then in the form *jejayiṣati* (derived from the root *ji* with the suffix *yaṅ*-luṅ and the desiderative suffix *san*), the substitution of *ku* would occur.
Therefore, Mādhava maintains that it should be explained as: "the reduplication which is caused by *saṃ* and *liṭ*.
As for *jigāya*: after doubling in the *ṇal* suffix, there is *vṛddhi*, and in the latter part, the substitution of *ga* for *ja* occurs by the rule of *kutva*.

Regarding *jigyatuḥ*: due to the *kit* suffix, there is an absence of *guṇa*. In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, although the prohibition of *iṇ* (the augment *iṭ*) by the rule "ṭhekāca" would apply, it is set aside; and since the rule for *krādiniyama* would require *iṭ*, the prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of *thal* by the rule "acastāsvat" is made optional by the *bhāradvājaniyama*. Thus he says: *jigayitha*, *jigetha*; [and] *jigyathuḥ*.
Having considered that *ṭh* and *ṇal* are the *uttama-puruṣa* (first person) endings, he says: *jigāya*, *jigaya*.
Having considered that *iṭ* applies by the rule for roots beginning with *krī* (*krādi-niyamāt*), he says: *jigyiva*, *jigyima*.
[The forms] *jetā*, *jeṣyati*, *jayatu*, and *ajayat* follow. In the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative), there is lengthening by the rule *ikṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*.

Having considered this, he says: *jīyāt* ("may he conquer") and *ajaiṣīt* ("he conquered"). The intention is that there is a vṛddhi [substitution] by the rule "sici vṛddhiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.1). [In the future tense] *ajeṣyate*. The root *ji* is a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*). Because the root contains the *it* marker *i*, the augment *num* is applied.

Thus he says: *invati* ("he impels") and *invāñcakāra* ("he has impelled repeatedly"). Because of the presence of *num* and because it begins with *ijādi* (a vowel other than *a*) and possesses a heavy syllable (*gurumat*), the suffix *ām* is applied.
The roots *piv*, *miv*, and so forth are marked with the indicatory letter *it*.
(170) *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* | Pāṇini 3.1.80. [The word] *dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ* [is used]; the term *ṭha* has its nominative case ending elided; [it refers to] the roots *dhinv* and *kṛṇv*.
The mention of *kṛ* and *anu* is for the purpose of specifying [the application of the suffix]. From the rule "tanādibhyaḥ uḥ," the word *uḥ* is drawn over by the letter *ca*;
from "kartari śa," the word *kartari*;

The vowel *a* replaces the letter *va*. Thus, we have *din a u ti*, which stands as it is. Regarding the rule *ato lopaḥ*:

although the suffix *u* and the vowel *a* are prescribed simultaneously by virtue of being taught as a combined operation (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*), their application proceeds according to the order in which they are heard. Consequently, at the time of the instruction of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, [the form] is *dhina*.
The meaning is that this [suffix] ends in the vowel *a*. Now, one might ask: "In this case, let only the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *va* be prescribed;

what is the need for a rule prescribing the letter *a*? To this he replies: "Of that" (*tasya*). The point is that if only the elision of the letter *va* were prescribed, it would not be a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*), and consequently, it would not possess the properties of its original locus (*sthānivadbhāva*). And thus, in *dhinoti*: [The text continues with the grammatical derivation.]

This being the case, he says: "of the suffix *u*. Regarding *dhinuta*: from the root *dhi*, with the suffix *anuṭ*, the suffix *u*, and the substitution of *a* for the letter *v*, there is the elision of the *a* (by the rule *ato lopaḥ*). Because the suffix *tas* is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *u*. Regarding *dhinvanti*: from the form *dhinv*, the suffix *jhi* is added; *jhi* is replaced by *anta*; then the suffix *u* is applied.
The letter *a* replaces the letter *va*. There is elision (*lopa*) of the *a* due to the rule *ato lopaḥ*. The intention is that the letter *u* undergoes the *yaṇ* substitution.

Here, although the letter *v* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* by virtue of being *sthānivadbhūta*, the augment *iṭ* does not apply. This is because the *ārdhadhātuka* status residing in the letter *u* is a property of the *al* (the phoneme), and thus it is excluded by the prohibition *na alvidhau*. This very point is stated in the rule *bho-bhago-*.
This is clear in the *Sūtrabhāṣya*. [The forms are: *dhinoṣi*, *dhinuthaḥ*, *dhinutha*; *dhinomi*.
(171) *lopaścāsyānyatarasyāṃ mvoḥ* |6|4|107|.
[The word] *lopaśca* [is used]; this refers to what was stated in the preceding rule: *utaśca pratyayādasaṃyogapūrvāt*.

The word "ukāraḥ" (the letter *u*) is referred to by the phrase "asya" (of this). The word "pratyaya" (suffix) refers to that which is connected with a suffix. Furthermore, the expression "asaṃyogapūrvāt pratyayāt" (from a suffix not preceded by a conjunct consonant) is construed with the letter *u*.

And that (*u*) is a qualifier of the "aṅga" (stem). This implies the rule of "tadantavidhi" (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends in such an element). Thus he says: "asaṃyoga... and so forth.

"Belonging to a suffix" (*pratyayokāra*) means the letter *u* that is connected with a suffix. If, however, one were to explain it as "the *u* of a suffix" (*pratyayasya ukāraḥ*), then [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *sanutnuḥ* and *sunumaḥ*, because in those instances only the *śnu* suffix is considered a suffix. Why say "belonging to a suffix"? [Consider: *yuvaḥ*, *yumaḥ*. [The rule applies only when the preceding element] is not preceded by a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogapūrvāt*).

What [is the result]? *śaknavaḥ*, *śaknumaḥ*; *dhinvaḥ*, *dhinuvaḥ*. Here, it should be understood that the upapratyaya has an *u*-vowel at its end by virtue of being treated as if it possessed its own designation (*vyapadeśivat*). Now, one might object: "In this way, in the case of *dhinomī*—where, after the suffix *mip* is applied, we have *dhinu mi*—there would be the elision of the *u*-vowel. To this, he says: "But in the case of *mip*... (referring to the rule that prevents such elision).
*didinv-a*, *dhinvitā*, *dhinviṣyati*, *dhinotu*.

(172) *utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt* [Pāṇini 6.4.106]. From the word *utaśca*: "There shall be elision (*luk*) of *hi*"—this is derived from both *ciṇo luk* [Pāṇini 6.4.104] and *ato heḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.105].
The meaning is: "because it follows that [rule]. When *loṭ* is replaced by *mip*, the suffix *up* is applied; the *v* becomes *a*, and the *a* is elided, resulting in *dhinu mi*.

At this stage, the substitution of *mi* for *mip* and the augment *āṭ* (by the rule *āḍuttamasya piñca*) are both superseded by the subsequent rule (*ukāralopaś cāsyānyatarasyām*), which effects the elision of the *u*.
Fearing such an objection, he says: "Because it is obligatory," and so forth. This is also an indication regarding the *nibhāva* (the elision of *ni*).

The point is that since the elision of *u* (as in *kṛta-ur-kāra-lopa*) is not applicable here, the augment *āṭ* is not treated as having the marker *ṅ*; consequently, because it lacks the marker *ṅ*, there is no substitution of *guṇa* for the *u* of *ukār-in*, and thus the form is *dhinavāni* after the replacement of *o* by *ava*. [The forms are: *adhinot*, *dhinuyāt*, *dhinvyāt*, *adhinvīt*, *adhinviṣyat*. [The phrase] "in *kṛṇoti* etc. refers to this.

The meaning is that they have the form of *dhīv* and *vṛ*. "And this [root] begins with *svā*" means it is *kṛvi*. "In *ava* [the sense of] protection" means the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Regarding "may you not say *avīt*": there is no *vṛddhi* substitution because of the rule *neṭ*. The roots beginning with *mavya* and ending with *av* have been explained as taking the *parasmaipada* (active voice). "In *dhāvu* [the sense of] motion."
"Udit" means "marked with the svarita accent. Consequently, the meaning is that the ātmanepada ending is used when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent;

otherwise, the parasmaipada ending is used. Now, regarding "those ending in a sibilant": therein, starting from *dhukṣe* up to before the root *kāsṛ*, the roots end in *ṣ*. Among them, the root *kleś* is the single one ending in *ś*.

Regarding *dīkṣamauṇḍalya*: the root *ṇeṣṛ* is taught with the initial *ṇ*. Starting from the root *kāsṛ*, up to the root *īh*, there are roots ending in *s*. Regarding *kāsaṃ cakre*: [the suffix] *ām* is applied by the rule *kāspratyayādām am ca*.
Both the root *ṇāsṛ* and the root *ṇas* are taught with the initial *ṇ*. Regarding *āṅ śasīti*: [the suffix] follows *āṅ*.

The root *śas* signifies "desire" (*icchā*). Starting from *īh* and excluding the root *kāś*, up to—but not including—*ghuṣi* in the sense of "splendor," these roots end in the letter *h*. However, the root *kāś* ends in the letter *ś*.
The root *plih* has a vowel as its penultimate letter (*adupadha*). Regarding *ūha* in the sense of "reflection" (*vitarka*), it means the determination of a meaning through reasoning (*yukti*).
Regarding the statement, "A wise person infers even what has not been said," it should be understood that the ātmanepada characterized by the anudātta accent is not mandatory.
Since the root *gāh* is marked with the udiṭ indicator, it optionally takes the augment *iṭ*. Thus he says: *jagāhiṣe* and *jaghākṣe*; in the absence of *iṭ*, [the forms are *jagāhe* and *jagāhe*].
When *jagāh-se* is established, by the rule *ṭh-ḍhaḥ*, and by the substitution of *bhaṣ* for *gha* according to *ṭh-ekācaḥ*, *ga* becomes *gha*.
Then, by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, *ḍha* becomes *ka*, and *s* becomes *ṣ*. Thus we have *jagāhiḍhave* and *jagāhidhve*.
In the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is present, there is an optional substitution of *ḍha* by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*. However, in the absence of *iṭ*, he says: *jaghāḍhave*.
Thus: when *jagādhve* is established, *h* becomes *ḍh*; *d* becomes *ḍh* by virtue of the rule for *ṣṭu*; and *g* becomes *gh* by the *bhaṣ*-rule.
The elision of the preceding *ḍh* occurs according to the rule to be stated later: "There is elision of *ḍh* before *ḍh*.
It would have been more appropriate to read the sūtra regarding the elision of *ḍh* at this very point. *Gāhitā* is the form in the alternative where *iṭ* is applied.

(173) *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.13. When the augment *iṭ* is absent, the form *gāh-tā* remains; then, by the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*, and by the rule *ṣṭuan* [which applies here as *ṭh-jhaṣas tathoḥ dho 'dhaḥ*], *ta* is replaced by *dha*. Subsequently, by the rule *ṣṭuan*, *dha* is replaced by *ḍha*. Thus, the form *gāḍhā* is established.

In the absence of *iṭ*, however, when *gāḍhā* is established [from *gāh-tā*], the rule *ḍho ḍhe* applies; here, *ṭh-ḍhaḥ* is in the genitive case. Thus he says: "of *ḍha*" (*ḍhasya*), meaning "of the letter *ḍha*. When the preceding *ḍha* is elided, the form *gāḍhā* results. However, the fact that the substitution of *ṣṭu* (the change of *t* to *ṭ*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) after the elision of *ḍha* does not apply here; for if it were so, [the desired form would not be achieved].

Because the rule for the elision of *ḍh* would otherwise be purposeless. Regarding "ghākṣyate": the meaning is that in the absence of *iṭ*, *h* becomes *ḍh*; *g* becomes *gh* (by the *bhaṣ*-rule) as *gh*; *ḍh* becomes *k*; and *s* becomes *ṣ*. Regarding "agāhiṣṭa": there is *iṭ* after the suffix *sic*, *s* becomes *ṣ*, and the *t* becomes *ṭ* by the rule of *ṣṭu* substitution. He states the form when *iṭ* is absent: "agāḍha". [The derivation is: *agāh* + *s* + *ta*.

This being the case, when there is an absence of *iṭ* after the suffix *sic*, there is elision [of the *s*] by the rule "ṭhjalo jhalī" (Pāṇini 8.2.26). Then follow the changes to *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭua*, and the elision of *ḍha*. However, the substitution of *bhaṣ* does not occur prior to the elision of *s*, because the substitution of *bhaṣ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of the elision of *s* by "ṭhjalo jhalī," which therefore operates first. Nor is it the case that...

One might suspect that even when the *s* has been elided, the substitution of *bhaṣ* (the voiced aspirate) would still be unavoidable because the suffix follows a *sakāra*, but the intention is that there is no application of the rule of "suffix-conditionality" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when the operation depends on a specific phoneme (*varṇāśraya*). Regarding *adhākṣātām*:
in the alternative where *iṭ* is absent, there is the sequence *ḍh-gh-k-ṣ*. Regarding *aghākṣata*: as before. Regarding *agāḍhāḥ*: [this is] the form with *thās*.
Thus: in the absence of *iṭ*, there is elision of *s*. Then [the rules for] *ḍhatva*, *dhatva*, *ṣṭutva*, and *ḍhalopa* apply, resulting in *aghāḍhvam*.

In the case of *dhvam* where *iṭ* is absent, there is elision of *s*; then *ḍhatva*, *dhatva*, *ṣṭutva*, and *ḍhalopa* apply. Prior to the *ḍhalopa*, which depends on *dhvam*, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs, resulting in *aghākṣīdhvam*. In the absence of *iṭ*, *h* becomes *ḍh*, then *bhaṣ* occurs, and then *ḍh* [becomes *kṣ*].
The intention is that there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. [Examples: *aghākṣvahi*, *aghākṣmahi*; [in the conditional: *aghāhiṣyata*, *aghākṣyata*.

The root *gṛhū* is marked with the *udit* indicator and has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). Thus, [in the present tense: *garhate*. When the suffix *tip* follows, after the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the light penultimate vowel, and *ra* is substituted for *ṛ*. [In the perfect tense: *jagṛhe*. This is because of the rule *ṭhasaṃyogā’di*.

There is an absence of *guṇa* due to the *kit* designation. Nor should one suspect that *guṇa* applies because it is subsequent to the *kit* designation; the intention is that, according to the Vārttika, "the *kit* designation for roots ending in *ṛ* is by way of a prior prohibition against *guṇa*. Considering the optional *iṭ* due to the *ūdit* designation, he says: *jagṛhiṣe*, *jaghṛkṣe*.

In the case of *abhyāsa* (reduplication), there is the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*), the augment *iṭ*, and the substitution of *ṣ*. However, in the absence of *iṭ*, there are the substitutions of *ḍha*, *bhaṣ*-bhāva, *ka* (for *ga*), and *ṣatva*. Having taken *jagṛhidhve* as established for the form *dhvam*, he states—assuming the absence of *iṭ*—*jaghṛḍhve*. Here, *ha* becomes *ḍha*; then *bhaṣ*-bhāva, *ṣṭutva*, and the elision of *ḍh* apply.
*garhate*: in the absence of *iṭ*, there is *guṇa*, replacement by *ra*, and then the substitution of *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, and elision (*lopa*). *gharṣyate*:
*guṇa*, replacement by *ra*, *ḍha* for *ha*, *bhaṣ*-bhāva, and *ka* for *ḍha* with *ṣatva*.
*agarhiṣṭa*: with *iṭ* after *sic*, there is *guṇa*, replacement by *ra*, and *ṣatva*; this is the form.

(174) *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.45. [The commentary explains: "śala igupadhā" means "those ending in *śal*" (*śalantaḥ*). Since the term "root" (*dhātu*) is understood from the preceding rule *dhātor ekācaḥ*, the sense is that this is a *tadantavidhi* (an application of a rule to that which ends with the specified element), qualifying the root.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *sic*. The substitute *ksa* ends in a vowel (*adanta*). The letter *k* is an *it*-marker. Regarding the form *aghṛkṣata*: *ksa* is substituted for *cli*;

because this [substitute] is marked with *k* (i.e., *kit*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ṛ*. The sense is as follows: *h* becomes *ḍh*, then *bhaṣ*-bhāva [of *ḍh* to *ḍ*], then *ḍ* becomes *k*, and finally the *ṣatva* [of *k* to *ṣ*].

(175) *ksasyā'ci* | Pāṇini 7.3.72. When *aghṛkṣa-ātām* is established, the substitution of *iy* [for *ā*] by the rule *āto ṅtiḥ* would apply; however, regarding *ksasya*: since the term *aci* is a qualifier of the suffix (*pratyaya*) implied by the word "stem" (*aṅga*), it follows the principle of *tadādividhi* (application to that which begins with the specified element). [Thus, the rule applies when the following suffix begins with a vowel. *Ghorlopaḥ*... [the elision of *ghu*].
From the rule "leṭo 'ḍāṭau," the word "lopa" (elision) is understood as a carry-over. Thus he says, "before an affix beginning with a vowel," and so forth.

Regarding "alo 'ntyasya" (of the final phoneme): the meaning is that there is elision of the final letter *a*. In reality, however, by carrying over the term "ātmanepade" from the subsequent sūtra "lug vā duhadiha," and treating it as an adjective to that [term *ac*], [the elision applies] before a vowel.
This is the rule for *ca* and so forth. Therefore, in forms such as *tādṛkṣāḥ*, where the suffix *kṣa* follows the root *dṛś*, this elision does not occur.

In some places, the reading is seen as "when *taṅ* begins with a vowel" (*ajādau taṅī*). Regarding the form *aghṛkṣātām*: when *aghṛkṣa-ātām* is established, since the letter *a* following *ks* has been elided, there is no subsequent *a*; therefore, [the rule] "of *āt*" (*ātaḥ*)... [does not apply].
The meaning of "not so" is that [the rule] does not apply here. Regarding *aghṛkṣanta*:

because *jh* is not followed by a vowel (an *ajādi*), when that [vowel] follows, there is no elision of the *akāra* of *ks*; consequently, since [the condition for the rule] is absent, the substitution of *at* by the rule "in the ātmanepada endings, [for the final consonant] other than *n*" (*ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*) does not occur. However, once the substitution of *jha* for *anta* has been effected...

There is elision of the vowel *a* of the root *kṣi*, or else the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Regarding *glaha*: the meaning is that the verbal root *glah* also functions in the sense of "seizing. This [root] has a short *u* as its penultimate vowel (*adupadha*). Regarding *ghuṣi* in the sense of "shining": this [root] has a long *ū* as its penultimate vowel (*udupadha*). Due to the presence of the *it*-marker *i*, the augment *num* is applied; then, by the rule *naśca*, the *anusvāra* is substituted. Because there is no following *ya* or *va* sound, the substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) does not occur.

He says this with the words "ghuṣata" (he proclaims). This [root] is *sekṭ* (belonging to the *tud*-class). However, in the alternative view where it is *adupadhā* (having a short vowel as its penultimate), it is *ghaṣate*. [The forms are: *jaghaṣe*. Those roots ending in sibilants (*ūṣman*) that take the *ātmanepada* endings have been covered. Now follow those ending in *arhat*, which take the *parasmaipada* endings. The phrase "those ending in sibilants" (*ūṣmāntāḥ*) is understood to carry over from the previous context. Among them, those ending in *ṣ* come before the root *tusa* (in the rule *hrasvaḥ*).

"Ghuṣi" [is the root]; "ir" [is its indicatory letter]. "Pratijñāna" means the acceptance [of a doctrine], such as the admission that "the Vedas are authoritative" (*pramāṇa*), and so forth. "In another than that" means: other than what is expressed (*viśabdana*)—that is, in non-expression (*aviśabdana*).
Regarding the phrase "optionally, because it has *ir* as an indicatory letter," the remainder of the sentence is "by this [rule] *irito vā*" (Pāṇini 3.1.57).

*aghuṣat*: because the suffix *aṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). *Aghoṣīt*: in the alternative where *aṅ* does not occur, after *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel, there is elision of *sij* by the rule "ṭhiṭa īṭi.
There is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* prescribed for stems ending in consonants (*halanta-lakṣaṇa-vṛddhi*) by the rule "neṭ. The root *ghuṣ* optionally takes *iṭ* because it is marked with *rud*.

(176) *akṣo 'nyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 3.1.75. The word *akṣaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). From the rule *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ*, the term *śnuḥ* is understood; from the rule *kartari śaḥ*, the term *kartari* is understood; and from the rule *sārvadhātuke yak*, the term *yak* is understood.

And the term *sārvadhātuka* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Therefore he says: "or *akṣu*. The fact that the suffix *śnu* has the marker *ś* (śitva) is for the purpose of making it *sārvadhātuka*. The result of this will be explained under the rule *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ*. In the form *akṣṇoti*, there is the suffix *śnu* after the root *akṣ*, and because that *tip* is marked with *p* (pitva), [the *śnu* becomes *sārvadhātuka*].

Due to the absence of *ṅ*-ness (*ṅtvābhāvāt*), there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "before an affix marked with *s* or *v*" (*sārvadhātuke*). Then there is *ṇatva*. Thus: *akṣṇute*. Because the suffix *tas* has *apitva*, it possesses *ṅ*-ness; therefore, there is no *guṇa* for the *śnu* augment. Thus: *akṣṇuvanti*. Due to *ṅ*-ness, in the absence of *guṇa*, there is *uṭ*. [The forms are: *akṣṇoṣi*, *akṣṇutha*; *akṣṇomi*, *akṣṇuvaḥ*.

*akṣṇumaḥ*, *akṣati*. In the alternative form with the suffix *śap*, the form is *ānakṣeti*. In the case of the suffix *ṇal*, because it consists of two consonants (*dvihal*), the augment *nuṭ* is applied:

*ānakṣatuḥ*, *ānakṣuḥ*. Regarding the alternative with the augment *iṭ* due to the root being marked with *ū*, he says: *ānakṣitha*. In the absence of *iṭ*, he says: *ānaṣṭha*. When *ānakṣ tha* is situated, there is the elision of *k* by the rule "ṭhskoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.29). [Then] of the *th*...

By the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), *ṭha* is substituted [for *tha*]. Thus, "aṣṭa. In the case of the absence of *iṭ* in the *luṭ* suffix *tāsi*, after the elision of *k* by *ṭhskoḥ* (8.2.29), *ṭha* is substituted for *ta* by *ṣṭuan*. When the form *akṣ sya ti* remains, he demonstrates the grammatical process: there is elision of *k* by *skor* (8.2.29), and *ka* is substituted for *ṣa* and *ḍha* by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (8.2.41). Furthermore, because it follows a *ka*, *ṣatva* is applied to the *sa*.

"Let him sharpen" (*akṣṇotu*). [Imperative forms: *akṣṇotu*, *akṣṇutāt* (2nd sg.), *akṣṇutām* (3rd du.), *akṣṇuvantu* (3rd pl.). "Sharpen thou" (*akṣṇuhi*). Because the root begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogapūrvatva*), there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi* by the rule *utaśca*. Since *hi* is not marked with *p* (*apit*), it is treated as having the marker *ṅ*;
thus, by the rule *śnornu-guṇaḥ*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the *nu* of the suffix. [Forms: *akṣṇutāt*, *akṣṇutam* (2nd du.), *akṣṇuta* (2nd pl.).

Regarding *ākṣṇavāni*: because the suffix *āṭ* is treated as having the marker *ṭ*, it lacks the marker *ṅ*; consequently, there is no prohibition of *guṇa*. [After applying] *guṇa*, the substitution of *ava* occurs. [The forms are] *ākṣṇuvan*, *ākṣṇoḥ*, *ākṣṇutam*, *ākṣṇuta*, and *ākṣṇavam*.
Regarding *ākṣṇava*: *am* is substituted for *mip*; *guṇa* is applied to the *śnu* affix; and the substitution of *ava* occurs. [The forms are] *ākṣṇuva* and *ākṣṇuma*.

*akṣṇuyāt*: This is the optative (vidhiliṅ) with *yāsuṭ*; because it is treated as having the marker *iṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the *ni* of *śnu*. *Akṣṇuyur*: Here, by the rule "the elision of *s* occurs in the optative," the *s* is dropped; the intention is that the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies according to the rule "for *u*, when not at the end of a word. [The forms are: *akṣṇuyāḥ*, *akṣṇuyātam*, *akṣṇuyāta*.

*akṣṇuyāt*, *akṣṇuyāva*, *akṣṇuyāma*; in the *śap*-pratyaya [present tense], *akṣet* and so forth; and *akṣyāt*. In the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative), because it is *ārddhadhātuka*, there is neither *śnu* nor *śap*. Regarding the specific rule for the *luṅ* (aorist) with *sic*, he says: "Because it is marked with *ū*, there is optionally *iṭ*. Therein, regarding the alternative where *iṭ* is present, he says: "Not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*).

The meaning is that the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by [a root] ending in a consonant does not apply. Nor should it be argued that, since the *vṛddhi* conditioned by a final consonant finds its scope in cases like *abhaitsīt* where there is an intervention by a single consonant, it would not apply here; for [the rule] must apply even when there is an intervention by multiple consonants in order to establish the *vṛddhi* in *araṅkṣīt* from the root *rañj*.

The intention is that the application of the *vṛddhi* substitution conditioned by a final consonant has been explained in detail in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. Regarding the example *mā bhavān akṣīt*: since there is no difference in form whether the augment *āṭ* is present—resulting in the *vṛddhi* conditioned by a final consonant—or it is absent, the form *mā bhavān* is employed. [The other forms are] *akṣiṣṭām* and *akṣiṣuḥ*.

Here too, the word "mā" is connected [to the preceding rule]. Regarding the phrase "but in the absence of iṭ": when *luṅ* with the suffix *tip* results in the form *akṣ s īt*, since the prohibition by the rule *neṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.4) does not apply due to the absence of *iṭ*, the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by the final consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇa*) takes place;

then, by the rule *skoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there is the elision of *k*; and by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41), there is the substitution of *k* for *ṣ*, resulting in *ṣatva*. This is the intended meaning here.

It should be understood that the form *mā bhavān* is also cited here precisely to clarify that, in the absence of the prohibition by *ṭhneṭ*, the vṛddhi substitution conditioned by a final consonant (*halanta*) is unimpeded.
Regarding *āṣṭām*: when *akṣ* + *stām* is situated, after the vṛddhi conditioned by a final consonant, [the rule] *jhalo...* [applies].

In the case of *ākṣuḥ*, when the suffix *s* is elided by the rule *jhalo jhali*, the *k* is elided by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*. Then, the *t* undergoes the substitution of *ṣṭu* (becoming *ṣ*). Thus, from the form *akṣ-s-us*, after the augment (*vṛddhi*) characterized by the final consonant has applied, the *k* is elided by *skoḥ*, the *ṣ* becomes *k* (by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*), and the *s* becomes *ṣ* (by *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*). The meaning is as follows: *ākṣīḥ*, *āṣṭam*, *āṣṭa*, *ākṣam*.

*ākṣva*, *ākṣma*; [the conditional] *ākṣiṣyat*—*ākṣyat*, *ākṣyatām*, *ākṣyan*; *ākṣyaḥ*, *ākṣyatam*, *ākṣyata*; *ākṣyam*, *ākṣyāva*, *ākṣyāma*. Regarding the roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū*: "thinning" (*tanūkaraṇa*) is the making thin of something large, such as wood, by removing some of its parts.

(177) *takṣa* [is used] in the sense of making thin; Pāṇini 3.1.76. Regarding "in the sense of making thin," he explains the sūtra by supplying the remaining words: "the suffix *śnu* may optionally occur in the domain of *śap*. From the rule *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.73], the word *śnuḥ* is understood; from the rule *kartari śap* [Pāṇini 3.1.68], the word *śap* is understood.
Regarding the term *kartari*: from the rule *sārvadhātuke yaK*, the word *sārvadhātuke* is carried over by anuvṛtti.

The resulting meaning is that the affix *śnu* occurs after the root *takṣ* when it signifies "making thin" (*tanūkaraṇa*), provided that a *sārvadhātuka* affix denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) follows. Nor is there any deviation [in this rule], because the root *takṣ* invariably possesses the sense of "making thin."

It should be stated that the inclusion of the term "tanūkaraṇa" (making thin) in the rule for the suffix *śnu* is redundant; for this very reason, it is understood that the mention of meaning (*artha*) in the Dhātupāṭha is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus, forms such as *takṣṇoti* and so forth [are derived]. The forms are like those of the root *akṣū*. In the *luṅ* [aorist], with the suffix *ic*, when *iṭ* is present, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "neṭi," resulting in *atakṣīt*; however, in the absence of *iṭ*:

And the form *atākṣīt* is like *akṣavat*. Likewise is the root *tvakṣ*. The root *ṇikṣ* is taught with the initial nasal (*ṇopadeśa*), as in *prakṣiṇati*; here the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "after a prefix, even when not in a compound" (*upasargādasamāse’pi*). Regarding *traṇ*, *ṣṭrakṣ*, and *gatau*: all three have the vowel *a* in the middle; the second is taught with the initial sibilant (*ṣopadeśa*).

Regarding this, he says: "srakṣati. The sense is that when *ṣ* becomes *s*, the application of the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41) is precluded. The root *ṇakṣ* is taught with an initial *ṇ*. In the *sic* suffix, by the rule "neṭ" (Pāṇini 7.2.8), the prohibition of the *vṛddhi* augment—which would otherwise be triggered by the rule concerning roots ending in consonants—is applied. *Vakṣa* means "anger"; it begins with a dental-labial (*dantoṣṭhya*) sound. The root *mrakṣ* has the vowel *a* in its middle.

The explanation of the word *tvacana* is "covering" (*saṃvaraṇa*). The verbal root *sūrkṣ* has the letter *r* in its middle. He states the reason for the incorrect reading [of *sūrkṣ*] as follows: "disrespect" (*avajñā*). If the root *sūrkṣ* had the meaning of "disregard," then the word *asūrkṣaṇa* would result in having the meaning of "respect," which contradicts the *Amarakośa*.

The sense is that there is a contradiction because [the term] is understood as a synonym for contempt (*avajñā*). Regarding "and in *ghoravāśita*": the word *ca* also implies "even in the case of desire" (*kāṅkṣā*). *Ghoravāśita* means a cruel sound. From *cūṣa* up to *ūṣa* (in the sense of "pain"), all have *u* as their penultimate vowel (*udupadhā*). *Īṣa* (in the sense of "gleaning") has *ī* as its penultimate vowel (*īdupadha*). From *kaṣa*... [and so on].

There are ten roots [ending in *ś*]. Among them, the third and the tenth have *i* as their penultimate letter (*idupadha*). The root *śiṣ* is devoid of the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*). By the rule governing the *krādi* group, the augment *iṭ* is obligatorily applied in the forms of *thal*, *vas*, and *mas*; however, because it lacks the vowel *a* at its end, there is no optionality (*veṭ*) regarding the application of *iṭ* in *thal*. Thus: *śiśeṣitha*, *śiśiṣiva*, *śiśiṣima*.

Regarding *aśikṣat*: the sense is that, by the rule *śala igupadhāḥ*, the root *śās* undergoes the substitution of *ksa* for *cli*; because this is marked as *kit*, the guna of the light penultimate vowel is prohibited; then, the *ṣ* of *śās* becomes *k*, and the *s* [of the suffix] becomes *ṣ*.
Regarding *vavaṣatuḥ*: due to the prohibition *na śasadadaḥ*, neither the elision of *et* nor the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) occurs.
The root *ruṣ* is *seṭ* (possessing an *iṭ* augment). It forms: *roṣati*. [Perfect: *ruroṣa*, *ruruṣatuḥ*, *ruruṣuḥ*;
*ruroṣitha*, *ruruṣathuḥ*, *ruruṣa*; *ruroṣiva*, *ruruṣima*. (178) Pāṇini 7.2.48: *tīṣasahalubharuṣariṣaḥ*.
The ablative singular of the dvandva compound *lubha-ruṣa-riṣa-eṣām* is used here.
He states this with the words "of *iṣ* and so forth. The form *icchati* is an indication (*nirdeśa*) by means of the *śtip* affix from the root *iṣ*;
the root *iṣ* is intended [here]. The root *iṣu* in the sense of "desire" belongs to the *tudādi* class and takes the *śap* suffix; [the other] is *iṣ* in the sense of "motion."

The root *div* belongs to the *divādi* class and takes the *śyan* suffix (*śyan-vikaraṇa*). The root *hiṣ* (meaning "to be angry") belongs to the *krayādi* class and takes the *śnā* suffix (*śnā-vikaraṇa*). Regarding that, according to the Vārttika rule—"there is a prohibition [of the substitution] for the *takāra* of *hiṣ* when the *śyan* suffix follows"—the root with the *śyan* suffix is not included [in this specific grammatical operation]. Thus we have *roṣitā* and *roṣṭā*; in the absence of the augment *iṭ*, the *takāra* becomes *ṭakāra* by virtue of the rule regarding the change of *s* to *ṣ*.

Considering that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the root *riṣ* from this point onward, he says: "reṣitā" and "reṣṭā. For the root *uṣ* meaning "to burn," this is *seṭ* (possessing the *iṭ* augment). Its forms are like those of the root *ukh*.
(179) *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo'nyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 3.1.38.

Regarding *uṣavid*: from the rule "kāspratyayāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.35), the phrase "ām liṭi" (the augment *ām* before the *liṭ* suffix) is understood. Thus he says: "after these [roots], when *liṭ* follows. Regarding the alternative where *ām* is absent, he says: *uvoṣa*. Here, the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule "abhyāsasyāsavarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.4.78). The roots *jiṣu*, *viṣu*, and *miṣu* mean "to sprinkle. The second [root, *viṣu*] begins with a dental-labial (*dantoṣṭhya*).

He states the distinction regarding *thali* and *vasi*: "The augment *iṭ* [is applied] by the rule for roots beginning with *kru* (*krādiniyama*). Thus, in *viveṣitha*, because it lacks the vowel *a* at the end (being *ajanta*), the restriction of Bhāradvāja does not apply; therefore, by the *krādiniyama*, *iṭ* is obligatory even in *thali*. In *veṣṭā*, due to the status of *ṣṭu* in *tāsi*, the *t* of *takāra* becomes *ṭ*.

"He will look" (*vekṣyati*): by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, the *ṣ* becomes *k*, and the *s* becomes *ṣ*. "He looked" (*avikṣat*): by the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*, the suffix *ksa* is applied; the *ṣ* becomes *k*, the *s* becomes *ṣ*, and because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Thinking that the root *puṣ* takes the augment *iṭ*, he says "it will nourish" (*poṣiṣyati*). "It nourished" (*apoṣīt*): [this is formed] by the rule *neṭ*.
Prohibition of *vṛddhi*: Now, one might ask, "Since *puṣ* is listed among the roots marked with *iṭ*, how can it be considered *seṭ* (having the augment *iṭ*)?

To this he says: "Among those [roots] that are *aniṭ*. Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): the meaning is that because it is *seṭ*, the suffix *kso* does not apply. Now, one might ask, "Why is the suffix *aṅ*, which is characterized by being prescribed for roots beginning with *puṣ*, not applied? To this he says: "In the rule prescribing *aṅ*."
This will become clear immediately following this, on the occasion of the commentary on the *puṣādi* group of roots.
"This one also" means that, like the root *puṣ*, the root *śliṣ* also belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and is *seṭ* (possessing the *iṭ* augment).
"Kaiyaṭa and others" refers to [their discussion] on the rule *śliṣa āliṅgane*.

The sense is that this has been elaborated upon by Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others. "The mention of both" means the mention of the roots belonging to the *bhū* class and the *div* class. "In his own statement" refers to the fact that in the rule *śliṣa āliṅgane*, the author of the Nyāsa [Jinendrabuddhi] stated that the *div*-class root *śliṣ* is included among the roots that lack an *iṭ* augment.

The sense is that this has been stated by Kaiyaṭa and others. The roots beginning with *pṛṣu* and *vṛṣu* and ending with *hṛṣu* have *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). *Alīkam* means either false existence or false speech. The roots beginning with *tusa* and *hrasa* and ending before *ṇaśa* (in the sense of "going") end in *s*. The root *ghaslṛ* is devoid of the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*).
"This" means that the root *ghaslṛ* is not to be employed in all instances. Why? To this he says: "In the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. If this were universal, it would be employed even in the *liṭ*;
consequently, the rule for the substitution of *ghaslṛ*—stated as "optionally in the *liṭ* after the root *ad* 'to eat'"—would be rendered useless.
The sense is: "it may be so. Since it is not universally applicable, he asks where its application lies and where it does not, and thus says:

"And therefore... The meaning is that its application occurs only where there is an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) or an explicit statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) regarding the use of the root *ghaslṛ*. First, he shows the indicative mark for that:

Regarding the phrase "atraiva" (right here): the meaning is that its recitation right here in this sequence within the *bhvādi* class is the indicator (*liṅga*) for its usage with the *śap* suffix and in the *parasmaipada*. Nor should one suspect that its recitation there is merely for the sake of establishing its designation as a verbal root (*dhātusaṃjñā*), because it is already established by its recitation before "dyauta dīptau" [and] after "anudātet" [in the Dhātupāṭha]. Here...

The sense is that [the rule] would otherwise be redundant in its sequence. Regarding the mention of *lṛdita* [in the sūtra], the word *aṅi* is understood; the meaning is that its inclusion in the list of roots ending in *lṛ* (anudātopadeśa) is a *liṅga* (indicative mark) for its application before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). Regarding the statement "in the *aniṭ*-kārikās," the meaning is that the reading of the root *ghaslṛ* among those roots taught as having anudātta vowels is a *liṅga* for its application before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant. Now...

In some instances of its usage, he shows a statement that is directly perceptible—namely, "kmarac. The specific mention of the root *ghas* in the rule "sṛghasyadaḥ kmaraḥ" is the authority for its usage with the suffix *kmarac*; this is the meaning. As for "ghasati": this is an illustration using the present tense (*laṭ*) with the ending *tas* and so forth; [it is also used] in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

Because there is no practical application [of this rule], he cites an example for the *luṭ* suffix: *ghastā* (he will eat). (180) *saḥ syārddhadhātuke* | Pāṇini 7.4.49. *sah syārddhadhātuke*. *sah si*. The word *saḥ* is the division [of the sūtra]. *sah* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). *sīti* [is the locative form of *si*].

The word ending in the seventh case (locative) is a qualifier of *ārdhadhātuka*. This is a rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*). From the previous rule, "ṭhaca upasargāt," the word *taḥ* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). The letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Thus he says: "there should be *ta* in place of *sa*"—meaning that in the substitute, because the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation, there should be the letter *t*.

(181) *puṣādidyautādyṛditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* | Pāṇini 3.1.55. When *isic* is about to be applied to the *cli* of the *luṅ* [aorist] tense—[the sūtra begins with] *puṣādi*. From the rule *cleḥ sic* [3.1.44], *cliḥ* is understood;
from the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyaḥ* [3.1.52], *aṅ* is also understood. [The groups are] *puṣādi* and *dyautādi*.

The term *lṛdit* is a compound in the sense of a collective copulative (*samāhāra-dvandva*), and it functions as the fifth case [denoting the cause]. Among these, the root *puṣ* exists in the *bhū*-class, the *ky*-class, the *cur*-class, and the *div*-class. In that context, if the *puṣ* beginning with *dyut* were taken from the *bhū*-class, then the mention of *dyut* and the others would be purposeless.
In this context, [the group] is specifically that following the *puṣ* group, because of its recitation within the *dyutādi* group; nor is it the sub-group beginning with *ṛk*.
For therein, only four roots are recited: *muṣ* (stealing), *khac* (manifestation of what has been), *heṭh* (injury), and *grah* (taking). If those alone were intended here as the *puṣādi* group...

In that case, for the sake of brevity, they should have been formed with the marker *lṛdit* alone. Furthermore, the *puṣādi* group from the *curādigaṇa* is not included here, because it is separated by the *ṇic* suffix and the *clī* (the *liṭ* substitute). Therefore, by process of elimination, only those [roots] beginning with *div* are taken. Thus he says: "belonging to the *śyan*-conjugation. [Examples are: *jarja*, *carca*, *jharjha*. Of these...

The reading is appropriate only at the end of the *ca*-class (palatal) consonants. [The examples are] *hasane* and *hasanaḥ*. [This is] the pair *edi*. "There is no *vṛddhi*"—the remainder [of the rule] is "by [Pāṇini 7.2.115] *ṭhmyanta-etc.*". [The root] *ṇiśa* means "to concentrate.
Because it is taught with an initial *ṇ*, there is *ṇatva* for the *n* by [Pāṇini 8.4.14] *upasargādasamāse'pi*. Thus he says:

Regarding *praṇeśati*: up to the root *śasu* (in the sense of "to injure"), the roots end in *ś*. However, *śavati* ends in *v*. *Śaṃsu* has *n* as its penultimate letter; the notation includes the *anusvāra* that has been added. From *caha* (in the sense of "imagining") up to *arhati*, the roots end in *h*. *Raha* is used in the sense of "abandoning."
This [root] is not *idit* because it is taught as *gatau* (in the sense of "going"). This one is *idit*, as in *dṛha* and *dṛhī*. These have *ṛt* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadhā*).

The second and fourth [roots] are not *idit*, as in *avṛhat* and *avarhīt*. The intention is that, because they are *irit*, there is an option regarding the suffix *aṅ*. [In the case of] *uvoha*, the reduplication occurs in the *liṭ* [perfect tense] of the root *ūh*.

In the case of *mā bhavān uhat*, after the substitution of the *halādiśeṣa* and the *guṇa* prescribed by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*, the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs by the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya*. In the form *auhīt*: because of the indicatory letter *ṛ* (in the root *uh*), the suffix is *aṅ*. In the alternative view where *aṅ* does not apply, the suffix *cli* is replaced by *sic*;
to this *sic* is added *iṭ*, and then by the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*, the augment *īṭ* is added to the *takāra* (the final consonant of the root). Finally, by the rule *iṭa īṭi*, the *sic* is elided.

In the case of elision (*lopa*), there is *vṛddhi* by the rule "āṭ-ṭha-āḍ-aj-ādīnām. But when joined with *māṅ*, as in *mā bhavān uhyāt* or *ānaṛhat*, there is the augment *nuṭ* after the lengthening of the initial vowel by the rule "ata ādeḥ. "Up to *kṛp*" means starting from "dyaut" and ending with *kṛp*.
(182) *dyauti-svāpyoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* | 7|4|67| [The rule] *dyauti-svāpyoḥ*: [the term] *abhyāsasya* [is understood here].
The sense is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *lopo 'bhyāsasya* from the preceding rule. [Thus we derive] *didyute*; [this occurs] after reduplication (*dvitve*).

When the elision of the letter *y* would have occurred by the rule "ṭhhalādiḥ śeṣaḥ," that is superseded as an exception by the rule "ṭhdyautisvāpyoḥ" which effects *saṃprasāraṇa*; subsequently, by the rule "ṭhsaṃprasāraṇācca," the letter *u* undergoes the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) process, resulting in the final form.

(183) *dyaudbhyo luṅ* | Pāṇini 1.3.91. From the plural form *dyaudbhyaḥ*, it is understood that the rule applies to the group beginning with *dyu*. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here in connection with *diś* (direction). By the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) *tasmād ity uttarasya*, the meaning "of what follows" is obtained.
From the rule "the rest [take *parasmaipada*] when denoting the agent" (*śeṣāt kartari*), the term *parasmaipada* is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "after *dyauta* and the others.

Regarding the statement "in *parasmaipada*, [the suffix] *aṅ*": the intention is that in the case of the *ātmanepada* alternative, there is only *sic*, not *aṅ*, because of the inclusion of the term *parasmaipada* in the rule concerning the *puṣ* group (*puṣādi-sūtra*). Thus he says: "after *dyauta* and the others."

In the case of the *parasmaipada*, [the suffix] is *aṅ* when it is not marked with *ṅ*. The intention is that in the *ātmanepada* alternative, only *sic* applies and not *aṅ*, because of the mention of "in the *parasmaipada*" in the rule concerning the *puṣādi* group. Thus he says: *adyotiṣṭa*. Regarding *śvitā varṇe* (to become white), this is the form in the *ātmanepada* alternative. In the same way, further on, the difference in forms for the *luṅ* [aorist] in the *dyutādi* group and others should be understood.
The root *mīd* means "to moisten. This refers to the meaning of the rule *ñit-ṣṇī-taḥ ktaḥ*.
(184) *mider guṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.82. In the form *mimide*, although the suffix *liṭ* is *kit* by virtue of the rule *asaṃyogāt*, there is nevertheless *guṇa* [substitution].

To address this doubt, he says: "There is guna for *mid*. In the rule *mideḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). By the mention of "guna," the technical term *ika* is supplied through the governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) *iko guṇavṛddhī*.
From the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvacamāṃ śiti*, the word *śiti* is carried over (*anuvartate*). This [term] consists of both *ś* and *it*.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. By this, the suffix (*pratyaya*)—which is implied by the governing rule (*adhikṛta*) and the word "root" (*aṅga*)—is qualified.
Thus, the rule applies to that which begins with such [a root]. It is understood that the suffix must begin with the letter *ś*, which bears the technical designation *it*.
This is what he states with the words beginning "of *mid*" (*mideḥ*). The root *mid* belonging to the *divādi* class takes the suffix *śyan*, resulting in *medyate*.

This is the first example. One might raise the objection: "Why not simply explain [the rule] as 'when a *śit* affix follows, there is *guṇa* for the *i* of *mid*'? Anticipating this, [the author] states that in order to prevent *guṇa* in forms such as *mimide*, [the rule must specify] "before an affix beginning with the letter *ś* which bears the technical designation *it*."

Intending to explain this, he says: "Because this [root] lacks the status of being an *ādiśit*. Regarding *ñiṣvideti*: this is a root taught with an initial *ṣ*. Since among the roots marked as *aniṭ* (those lacking an *iṭ* augment), only *svidya-* belonging to the *śyan*-class (*divādi*) is mentioned, this [root *ṣvid*] is *seṭ* (possessing an *iṭ* augment).
Regarding *ruca dīptāv abhiprītau ca*: "abhiprīti" means becoming an object of affection.

Give an example for the sense of "shining": *sūryo rocate* ("the sun shines"). The meaning is "it becomes manifest. Give an example for the sense of "pleasing": *bhaktir haraye rocate* ("devotion is pleasing to Hari"). The meaning is that devotion becomes an object of affection for Hari. The fourth case ending is used because of the rule *rucy-arthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.33), which prescribes the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) case. [The root] *kṣubh* means "to tremble" or "to be agitated."

Thus: *kṣobhate* and *kṣubhyati* belong to the *divādi* class; *kṣubhnāti* belongs to the *kyādigaṇa*. The root *ṇabh* is taught with the initial *ṇ* (ṇopadeśa) as *nabhate*; the first [meaning] is "non-existence," and by the word "and" (*ca*), it also includes "movement.
Therein, he shows the usage of the sense of non-existence: *nabhantām anyake same* ("May all others perish").

This is the mantra. Now, one might ask: why could the suffixes *ṇa*, *bha*, *iś*, *ha*, and *sā* not have their own specific meanings here? To this he says: "Let all others not be. The explanation of *nabhantām* is *mā bhūvan*. The meaning is "they do not exist" (*na bhavanti*). The explanation of *same* is *sarve*.
Regarding the term *nirukta*: *Nirukta* is a specific work composed by Yāska, consisting of an exposition of the Vedas.

In the rule *sraṃsu dhvaṃsu bhraṃsu*, the intended meaning is that these three roots have *na* (the letter *n*) as their penultimate vowel. As for *nāsrasat*, the reading *nāsraṃsat* is incorrect; nor is it the case that *nāsraṃsat* is the form of the imperfect (*laṅ*) tense.

It should be conjugated as *bhramitavyam*, because the *parasmaipada* endings are impossible there. The root *srambh* (to trust) has the vowel *a* in its middle. Regarding the root *vṛt* (to turn): it is marked with *u* (*udit*), has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter (*ṛdupadha*), and is *seṭ* (taking the augment *iṭ*). Thus, *vartate*: when the suffix *śap* is added, there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*. *Vavṛte*: due to the rule "after a root ending in a consonant other than *ṣa* and *ha*, [the suffix] is *kit*" (*ṭhasaṃyogā'dit*), there is an absence of *guṇa*.

In the dual number, after the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, and the application of *halādi-śeṣa*, the form is [vartitau]. In the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) tense—*vartitā*.

(185) *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* | 1.3.92 | Regarding *vṛdbhyaḥ*: because it is a plural form, it is understood to mean "from the roots beginning with *vṛt*. This is derived from the rule *śeṣāt kartari* [3.1.76].
The term *parasmaipada* is understood from the previous context, as is the word *vā* from the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ*. Thus he says:
"from *vṛt* and the others. (186) *na vṛdbhyaś caturthaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.59.

"Not after *vṛt* and the others. From the sūtra *se'sici*, the word *se* is understood, as is [the condition] from *ārddhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ*. "After these, when beginning with *s*" means: "in the absence of *taṅ* and *naṅ*.
From the sūtra *gamer iḍ*, the term *parasmaipadeṣu* (in the case of parasmaipada endings) is understood. And by that—
The absence of those two [suffixes] is indicated by the commentary; this is the intended meaning.

By this, the augment *iṭ* is established in *jigamiṣite*—derived from the root *gam* with the desiderative suffix (*san*) and the third-person singular suffix (*tṛc*)—and the prohibition of *iṇ* is established in *vivṛtsa*, where there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after the desiderative of the root *vṛt*. Thus: "he will act" (*vartsyati*).

In the *lṛṭ* [future tense], the suffix *sya* is applied. Regarding the option for the *parasmaipada* (active voice) by the rule "after roots beginning with *vṛ*, [the suffixes] *sya* and *san* [take the *parasmaipada*]," the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule "not after roots beginning with *vṛ*. [Thus,] there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatva*). In the absence of the *parasmaipada*, he says: "it will exist" (*vartiṣyate*). This is because of the statement "in the absence of *taṅ* and *ana*," and because of the rule "not after roots beginning with *vṛ*."
There is no prohibition of *iṭ*. The form *avartiṣṭa* is derived from the absence of both the *parasmaipada* suffix and *aṅ*.
As for *avartsyat*, it is formed with *lṛṅ* and *syi*; the sense is that there is also no prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "after roots beginning with *vṛt*, *syasana* [are not preceded by *iṭ*].
The two roots *vṛdh* and *śṛdh* have *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). In those cases as well, [the rule] "after roots ending in *u* or *ū*, *luṅ* [is used]" applies.

In the case of the *parasmaipada* (active voice), there is the suffix *aṅ* by virtue of the rule for roots beginning with *dyut*. Regarding the future (*lṛṭ*) and conditional (*lṛṅ*), in the *parasmaipada* alternative, there is the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "not after roots beginning with *vṛt*. Thus he says: "These two [roots] are *vṛt* and *tud*. [Examples: *vartsyati*—*vardhiṣyate*; *avṛdhat*—*avardhiṣṭa*.
*avartsyat*—*avardhiṣyata*. *śartsyati*—*śardhiṣyate*. *aśṛdhat*—*aśardhiṣṭa*.

*aśartsyat*—*aśardhiṣyata*. The root *syandū* is marked with *ū* (*ūdit*), has *n* as its penultimate letter, and is indicated with *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* following the *kṛt* suffix. [Examples include] *sasyan-di-se* and *sasyan-tse*, in the absence of *iṭ*.

Regarding *dasya cartvam taḥ*: [in the forms] *sasyandidhve* and *sasyanddhve*, when there is no insertion of *iṭ*, the letter *da* is substituted for the letter *dha*. Because the condition of being a *kharpara* (a consonant other than a nasal or semivowel) is absent, the substitution of *ca* (the rule of *cartva*) does not apply. [In the forms] *syānditā* and *syantsyanti*, when there is no insertion of *iṭ*, the substitution of *ca* applies to the letter *d*. Now, one might object: "But when the suffix *syat* of the *lṛṭ* [future tense] is present..."

In the case of the *parasmaipada* alternative under the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ*, since the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ* takes precedence over the optional *iṭ* conditioned by the marker *ūṭh*, the desired form is *syantsyati* alone, and not *syandiṣyate*.

This is incorrect; for it is more appropriate that the optional *iṭ* prescribed by the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.45]—which is characterized by the presence of the marker *ūṭ*—should apply due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the prohibition "not after *vṛt* and others" (*na vṛdbhyaḥ*) is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on specific factors such as the letter *s* and the absence of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes. Anticipating this objection:

He refutes [this] with the words "from *vṛt* etc. (*vṛdbhyaḥ*). The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when the Parasmaipada suffixes are applied by the rule "after *vṛt* etc., [the suffixes] *syasanaḥ*," the prohibition "not after *vṛt* etc. (*na vṛdbhyaḥ*) sets aside even the internal (*antaraṅga*) option. To the question "Why? he says: "Because of the lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*) of the mention of four [roots]. If...

In this case, there would only be an optional *iṭ* by virtue of the rule *ūdillakṣaṇa*, and not the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ*; therefore, the mention of "four" (*caturbhyaḥ*) would be redundant. Nor should it be suspected that the purpose of that [mention of "four"] is to exclude the root *kṛp*, because [the exclusion of *kṛp* is already established] by the particle *ca* in the rule *tāsi ca klṛpaḥ*.
Because it will be stated later that the prohibition of *iṇ* applies invariably even before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *s*,
the point is that the mention of "four" (*catur*) is for the purpose of prohibiting *iṇ* for all four [roots] everywhere. However, in the Bhāṣya,
by the maxim "prohibitions are more powerful," even that which is *antaraṅga* [is superseded].

Since the optional application of *iṭ* (augment) for roots marked with the indicator *ū* is successfully sublated by the prohibition "na vṛdbhyaḥ," the mention of the four [roots] (*caturgrahaṇam*) has been rejected. Thus, in the case of the future tense (*lṛṭ*) in the Parasmaipada alternative, the rule "na vṛdbhyaḥ" sublates the optional *iṭ* arising from the *ūdit* status.

It is established that, due to the permanent prohibition of *iṭ*, there is only one form, *syantsyati*. However, regarding the *ātmanepada* alternative, considering the optional application of *iṭ* because the root is marked with *ū*, he says:
*syandiṣyate* and *syantsyate*. In the absence of *iṭ*, there is *cartva* (the substitution of *s* for *d*). In the potential mood (*āsīrliṅ*), with the addition of *sīyuṭ*:
Considering that there is an option regarding the augment *iṭ* for roots beginning with *ū*, he says: "syandiṣīṣṭa" and "syantsīṣṭa.

The prohibition [by the rule] "na vṛdbhyaḥ" does not apply here; the point is that that [prohibition] takes effect only in the absence of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *parasmaipada* endings. He states the specific rule for the *luṅ* tense with the words "dyudbhyaḥ luṅi" etc., namely, "aṅ."

The phrase "characterized by *ṭh*, *dyaut*, etc. is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding "the elision of *n*," the phrase "by the rule *aniditām*" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. However, in the case of the *ātmanepada* alternative, since there is no *aṅ* suffix, considering the optional *iṭ* augment characterized by *ūdit*, he says:
*asyandiṣṭa*, *asyanta*. In that context, in the absence of *iṭ*, [the form is] *asyand s ta*.

When [the suffix] *si* is present, by the rule "ṭh-jhalaḥ jhal-i," the *s* is elided, and then there is the substitution of *c* for *d*. Nor should one fear the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule "ni-ditām" on the grounds that [the root] ends in a nasal (*ṅ*), because since the elision of *si* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the penultimate vowel is not followed by a nasal. This is the intended meaning.
*asyantsātām*, *asyantsata*; *asyanthāḥ*, *asyantsāthām*, *asyanddhvam*;
*asyanantsi*, *asyantsvahi*, *asyantsmahi*. [Conditional: *asyantsyat*, *asyantsyata*, *asyandiṣyata*.
(187) *anu-vipary-abhinibhyaḥ syandater aprāṇiṣu* (Pāṇini 8.3.72). [The commentary explains: "From *anu*, *vi*, *pari*, and *abhi*" means from these—namely *anu*, *vi*, *pari*, and *abhi*.
Regarding the mention of *sa*: because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the genitive form *saḥ* from the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (8.3.56).

The intention is that [the substitution] might be *ṣ*. This is because of the governing rule (adhikāra): "The cerebral [substitute occurs] for [a dental] not at the end of a word. Now, one might ask: how is there the substitution of *ṣ* in the example "fish and water flow together" (*matsyodake anuṣyandete*), given that the agency of a living being is also present? To this, he says: "among non-living things" (*aprāṇiṣu*).

Regarding the phrase "because it is an exclusion" (*paryudāsāt*): this is not a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) such as "not [the substitution] of that which has a living being as its agent," for if it were so, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur here because the action indeed has a living being as its agent. Rather, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is adopted, meaning "[the substitution applies to that] whose agent is other than a living being. And thus:

The point is that even for an action performed by both sentient and insentient agents, the status of being "performed by an insentient agent" is not lost; therefore, the substitution of *ṣ* here is unimpeded. Regarding the root *kṛpū* in the sense of "capacity":
capacity means becoming capable of performing an action. Because it is marked with *ū*, this root optionally takes *iṭ*; it has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel.

(188) *kṛpo ro laḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.18. When the first-person singular ending of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) has its *ṭi*-portion replaced by *e*, and after the addition of the *śap* suffix, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel and the replacement of *r* with *ra* have occurred, the form *kṛp-e-te* is established. Regarding the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*: the word "kṛpa" here is used without its case-ending (*luptavibhaktika*).

In the sixth case singular, *ud* is the form of that which has *ṛ* as its vowel; this is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). When *kṛp* + *ur* is situated, by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, it becomes *kṛpor*. The word *hraḥ* ends in the sixth case. When *kṛpor raḥ* is situated, by the rule *ro ri*, there is elision of the *repha* (visarga), and thus it becomes *kṛpo raḥ*. [The word] *la*...

Thus ends the first word (*prathamāntam*). The letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Therefore he says: "The division is *kṛpa-uḥ*, *raḥ*, *laṭ*" (i.e., *kṛpa-uḥ raḥ laṭ*). And this is established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ṛlṛk*. Now, one might ask: in the word *kṛpa*, which case-ending has been elided? To this he replies: "It is that in which the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is elided. The letter *a* follows the letter *pa*.

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation; it is understood that this refers to the verbal root *kṛp*. And "that is repeated" means that the three words *kṛpa*, *raḥ*, and *laḥ* are repeated. Thus, two sentences are formed:
"kṛpa raḥ laḥ" is one sentence. This is what he says: "The *l* should be substituted for the *r* which belongs to *kṛp*."

And thus, the statement "ṭhkalpate" occurs. The second sentence is "ṭhkṛpa uḥ raḥ laḥ". In that context, *kṛp* ending in the genitive case as a component (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) connects with *uḥ*; and *uḥ* ending in the genitive case as a component connects with *raḥ*. And so, that which is the *ṛ*-vowel which is a component of the root *kṛp*—its [substitution is...].

It is understood that the letter *la* should be the substitute for the letter *ra*. In that case, since it is impossible for the letter *ra* to be a constituent part (*avayava*) of the vowel *ṛ*, the word "repha" is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer to that portion of the vowel *ṛ* which resembles the letter *ra*.
Similarly, the word "la" is also used figuratively to refer to that portion of the vowel *lṛ* which resembles the letter *la*. Thus he says: "of the vowel *ṛ* of the root *kṛp*..."

Thus, with regard to the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, when the form *cakṛpe* is established as *cakṛp-e*, the absence of *guṇa* due to the *kit* designation results in the substitution of the *repha*-like portion of the *ṛ*-vowel for the *lakāra*-like [element]. Consequently, the form *caklṛpe* arises. This is based on accepting the analysis *kṛpaḥ raḥ laḥ*, whereby the *repha* of the root *kṛp* [is substituted].

If, however, one were to explain [the rule] as referring to the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix), then forms such as *caklṛpe* would not be established. With this in mind, intending to rely on a repetition [of the rule], he says: "it is fit" (*kalpate*) and "it was fit" (*caklṛpe*). Considering the optional application of the augment *iṭ* due to the root being marked with *ū*, he says: "you have been fit" (*caklṛpiṣe*) and "you have been fit" (*caklṛpse*).
Like *syandi*: *caklṛpāthe*, *caklṛpidhve*—or *caklṛbdhve*; *caklṛpe*, *caklṛpivahe*, *caklṛpimahe*—or *caklṛpmahe*. (189) *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.3.93.

In the rule *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ*, by the force of the word *ca* (and), the term *syasanoh* is drawn forward from the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ*; the term *parasmaipadam* is drawn from the rule *śeṣātkartari*; and the term *vā* is drawn from the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ*. Thus he says: "In the *luṭ* [affix], [the suffixes] *si* and *san*... and so forth.
(190) *tāsi ca* | Pāṇini 7.2.60.

The word *tāsi* [is the subject]. By the use of the particle *ca* ("and"), the ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with *s* is understood. From the rule *se'sici kṛtaḥ*, the word *se* is carried over; and from the rule *ārdhadhātukasya*, the phrase *ārdhadhātukasyeṭ* ("the augment *iṭ* for an ārdhadhātuka") is also carried over.

[The rule] "not" is taken from "not after vṛt and the others, [the ārdhadhātuka affix] fourth [in order]" (Pāṇini 1.2.7), and "parasmaipada" is taken from "iṭ after gami" (Pāṇini 1.2.13). Thus he says: "of the following of klṛp," and so forth. Regarding *kalptāsī*:

in the alternative view where there is *parasmaipada* by the rule "and in the case of luṭ, [after] klṛp" (Pāṇini 1.3.93), there is an optional *iṭ* characterized by the fact that [the root] ends in long *ū*.

Having set aside [the prohibition] by the rule "ṭhtāsi ca klṛpaḥ," there is a prohibition of *iṭ*; thus, with *guṇa*, *raparatva*, and *latva*, the form is [obtained]. However, in the alternative view where the Parasmaipada does not occur, considering the optional *iṭ* prescribed for roots ending in long *ū*, he says: *kalpitāse* and *kalptāse*. But in the case of the future tense (*lṛṭ*), [the rule applies] "luṭi ca klṛpaḥ."

In the case of the *parasmaipada* (active voice), having set aside the optional *iṭ* augment prescribed by the rule for roots ending in *ū*, and considering the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "tāsi ca klṛpaḥ," he says: *kalpsyati*. However, in the absence of the *parasmaipada*, considering the optional *iṭ* due to the root being *ūdita*, he says: *kalpiṣyate* or *kalpsyate*.

"May it be fit. *akalpa*. [In the potential mood: *kalpeta*. Regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), having considered the optional *iṭ* augment as characterized by the marker *ūdit*, he says: "may it be fit" (*kalpiṣīṣṭa*) and "may it be fit" (*klṛpsīṣṭa*). In the absence of *iṭ*, because the suffixes of the benedictive and the *sic*-aorist are *kit* in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), there is no *guṇa* substitution. [In the aorist: *aklṛpat*.

In the alternative where the *parasmaipada* (active voice) applies by the rule "ṭhyaudbhyo luṅi," the suffix *aṅ* occurs according to the rule for roots beginning with *dyaut*. Because *aṅ* bears the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. However, in the absence of *aṅ*, considering the optional *iṭ* augment conditioned by the marker *ū*, he says: *akalpiṣṭa* and *aklṛpta*. Regarding *akalpsyat*: this is the conditional (*lṛṅ*) with the suffix *sya*, according to the rule "lṛṭi ca klṛpaḥ."

The intention is that in the case of the *parasmaipada* (active voice), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "tāsi ca klṛpaḥ" overrides the optional application of *iṭ* conditioned by the presence of the vowel *ū*. However, in the case where the *parasmaipada* does not occur, he states "kalpiṣyate" and "akalpsyata," having in mind the optional application of *iṭ* conditioned by the vowel *ū*.

Regarding the word *vṛt*: the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *vṛt* in the sense of completion (*samāpti*) with the agent as the referent (*kartari*). Thus he says: "of *vṛta*. The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... (Pāṇini 3.4.72). The explanation of the word *vṛta* is "complete" (*sampūrṇa*).
The roots beginning with *dyut* and ending with *kṛp* have been listed as having anudātta indicatory vowels (*anudātet*). Now, those ending with *tvar* [are to be considered].

The meaning is that [the roots] end with "ṭhñi tvarā saṃbhrame. Regarding "and those marked with ṣ" (ṣitaḥ): this means those having the designation ṣit, or those which undergo the operations pertaining to ṣit. The intention is that after stating "ṭhñi tvarā saṃbhrame," it will be stated later that "the ghaṭādi roots are ṣit. As for the result of being ṣit, however, the result of being mit is as follows:

It will be stated that there is shortening before the causative suffix *ṇi* by the rule "ṭhmitāṃ hrasvaḥ," and lengthening by the rule "ṭhciṇṇamulordīrghaḥ. Furthermore, it has been said that "the indication of meaning in the Dhātupāṭha is merely illustrative" (*upalakṣaṇam*).
Consequently, even when the root *ghaṭ* functions with a different meaning, the grammatical operations specific to the *ghaṭādi* group certainly still apply.

Regarding this, he says: "it joins together" (*ghaṭayati*) and "it separates" (*vighaṭayati*). The meaning is "it causes to unite" (*saṃśleṣayati*) and "it causes to disunite" (*viśleṣayati*). This is an example of the short vowel before the causative suffix *ṇic*. Examples with the passive suffix *ciṇ* are *aghaṭi* and *aghāṭī*. Examples with the suffix *ṇamul* added to the causative form are *ghāṭaṃghāṭam* and *ghaṭaṃghaṭam*.

An example of the long-term conceptualization [of meaning] is the reduplication [of a word] by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*. Now, if the verbal root *ghaṭ* possesses the status of a *māṅ* (causative marker) even when it functions with a different meaning, then in cases such as *udghāṭanam* and *pravighāṭiyate*,
where the root *ghaṭ* has the sense of "opening" (*vikāsana*), [the same would apply] in the presence of the causative suffix *ṇic*.

He raises an objection, suggesting that because it is a *mit* [stem], it should be short: "How then? He says, "Listen," with the word "the solution" (*samādhānam*) understood as the ellipsis. Regarding "of the *caurādika* [root]": in the *curādi* class, the root *ghaṭa* is listed in the sense of "assembly. This [root] is indeed a different root from the *ghāṭādi* root *haṭ*. Of that [latter root], in the *ṇi*-affix...

The meaning is as follows: since there is no short vowel (*hrasva*) due to the absence of *mit* [designation], the forms "udghaṭanam" and "pravighāṭayiṭe" are indeed unobjectionable; for the mention of the meaning is merely illustrative, and thus the root belonging to the *curādi* class can apply even to the blossoming of something other than a cluster (saṅghāta). But [one might object]: [The objection: "But..."

The inclusion of roots that are recited elsewhere than in the *ghaṭādi* group—namely, in other groups—within this *ghaṭādi* group is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of their having the *mit* designation with respect to the very meanings specified for the *ghaṭādi* group;
it is not a different root (*dhātubheda*). Otherwise, one would have to take both the status of belonging to the *ghaṭādi* group and the status of residing in another group into account.

Because otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of an option (*vikalpa*) between the presence and absence of the *mit* designation. However, the established doctrine in works such as the *Dhātuvṛtti* is that for those verbal roots which are read only in the *ghaṭādi* group and not in any other group, the *mit* designation applies even when they function in a sense different from their primary meaning. As for the root *ghaṭ*, it is [listed] under "ghaṭa saṅghāte" (to assemble).

It is recited in the *curādi* group; therefore, it is understood that in this particular list, the mention of the root [in the form *mi*] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of its being treated as *mit* when it bears the meaning of "motion" (*ceṣṭā*). And thus, having raised the objection as to how there can be the status of *mit* for the causative form (*ṇyanta*) in cases such as *vighaṭayati* when it functions in a different sense, [the author proceeds].

He refutes this with the words "na ca" (nor). The meaning is that one should not say: "Since the root *ghaṭ* itself—specifically that belonging to the *cur*-class and so forth—is used in the sense of a particular action consisting of motion, the mention of its being *mit* would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Why? To this he says: "not others."

"mito 'hetau" (miT after a root ending in miT when not denoting an agent). This is a *gaṇasūtra* included within the *curādigaṇa*. For therein, having listed five roots—namely, "jñapa micca," "yama ca pariveṣaṇe," "caha pariveṣaṇe," "caha parikalkane," "raha tyāge," and "bala prāṇane"—as well as "ciñ cayane."

The reading "ṭhnānye mito'hetau" is given. In that context, some read "ṭhcape" instead of "ṭhcaha parikalkane. Thus, there is no contradiction regarding the number five. In all these five [rules], the term "mit" (having the augment *m*) is understood to follow. The word "ahetau" (not when denoting cause) is the division [of the compound]. From what are they different?

In response to this expectation, because of proximity, "from the five beginning with *jñā*" is obtained. By the word "cause" (*hetu*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) prescribed by the rule "also when there is a cause" (*hetumati ca*) is obtained. A *ṇic* other than that is a non-causative, being used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Thus he says: "in the non-causative, for its own meaning, the suffix *ṇic*. [The root] *jñap*.

The compound *ādiryeṣām* is a *bahuvrīhi* of the type where the qualities of the members are not understood as applying to the whole (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). The result is that among the roots beginning with *cur*, those other than the six—namely, the root *jñap* and the five following it—are not marked with the indicator *mi*. And thus, regarding the *cur*-class (*curādi*): [the rule applies].
Since there is no *mit* designation for roots other than the five beginning with *jñā*,

the mention of "ṭh ghaṭa ceṣṭāyām" (ṭh-ghaṭa in the sense of movement) is not properly understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to establish the *mit* status of the root "ghaṭa saṅghāte" belonging to the curādika class when it functions in the sense of movement; rather, [the *mit* status] applies here within this very *ghaṭādi* group, [to the root] "ghaṭa".
The root *ceṣṭ* is an unprecedented one; however, even when it functions in a different sense, its status as having the marker *m* (mit) remains intact.
Thus, the intention is that in forms such as *vighaṭayati*, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] is unimpeded because of the *mit* designation.

(191) *vyatho liṭi* | Pāṇini 7.4.68. The root *vyath* ends in a double consonant (*dvitīyānta*). Regarding *vyatho liṭi*: [the rule] "here there is elision" (*atra lopaḥ*) provides the word *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplicated syllable"), and [the rule] "for *dyauti*, *svāpi*, and *vyathi*" (*dyautisvāpyoḥ*) provides the word *saṃprasāraṇam* ("vocalization").

And it follows accordingly. Thus he says: "of *vyath* due to repetition," and so forth. "An exception to *halādiśeṣa*" means that when *vyath* and *vyath* stand [as *vyath-vyath-e*], the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) sets aside the elision of the letter *y* which would otherwise be obtained through *halādiśeṣa*.
And thus, when the *y* is replaced by *i*, there is the formation of the single substitute [the *pūrvarūpa*].

The form is *vivyathe*. However, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *va*, because of the prohibition: "When there is a *saṃprasāraṇa*, [the preceding] *saṃprasāraṇa* does not occur. Now, one might object that if the rule for the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*) were set aside by the *saṃprasāraṇa*, then the letter *tha* would also not be elided. To this, he says: "of the *tha*"—referring to the elision of the letter *ya*.

The point is that since the occurrence of *saṃprasāraṇa* is untenable without an annulment (*bādha*), even if that [annulment] were to occur, there is no evidence for the annulment of the elision of the letter *th*. Regarding the root *mṛd* in the sense of "crushing": this has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel. It forms *mardate*, *mamṛde*. The root *kṣañj* is marked with the *it* augment; it forms *kṣañjate*.

[Objection: Its inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group [of roots] is useless; for in the case of *kṣañjayati* (causative), once *num* has been applied, since the vowel *a* is no longer penultimate (*anupadhatvena*), the rule *upadhādīrghaḥ* does not apply.

Consequently, even though the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* would not have applied due to the lack of a penultimate vowel, there is no difference [in the result]. Therefore, [the inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group is redundant].

And because there is no possibility [of its application]. For this very reason, even in the case of *akṣañji*, *kṣañjam*, and *kṣañjim*, there is no possibility of the optional lengthening prescribed by the rule *ṭhciṇṇamulo’r* (Pāṇini 6.4.93); therefore, he says: "by the force of the designation *mit*. [The root] *dakṣa* means "to go. Now, one might object: "But *dakṣa* [is also used] in the sense of 'growth' and 'swiftness'."
Since this [term] is already established by its very inclusion among the *anudāteta* roots, for what purpose is it included here?
[The answer is: because the mention of the meanings serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is possible that it also possesses the meanings of "motion" (*gati*) and "injury" (*hiṃsā*).
To this, he says: "In the senses of increase (*vṛddhi*) and speed (*śaighrya*). By virtue of its status as a *mit* root, even though it lacks a penultimate vowel (*anupadhātva*), [the rule applies].

After a root ending in *ciṇ*, there is an optional lengthening of the vowel. Thus: *adakṣi* or *adākṣi*; *dakṣamdakṣam* or *dākṣamdākṣam*. Regarding the root *krap*: it means "to pity" and "to go. This root has a short *u* as its penultimate vowel; the meaning is "in pitying" and "in going. According to Nandin’s opinion, there are three roots: *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kladi*. And according to Kṣīrasvāmin’s opinion, there are exactly these three roots.

According to the opinion of Maitreya, it should be understood that there are four [roots]. In this regard, he avoids the redundancy of the three roots beginning with *id* by means of the passage starting with "of *kad*, *krad*, and *klad*" and so forth. Regarding the term *ñitvara*:

[the suffix] *ñi* is present; the suffix *kta* is applied according to the rule "after a root ending in *ñī*, the suffix *kta* is used. As for its being *ādi* (beginning with a vowel), it is due to the rule "and after those beginning with a vowel (*āditaḥ*)."
The inclusion of *ā* [in the rule] is for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle). In reality, however, the status of being *ādi* (beginning with *ā*) is redundant;

for even if it were short (*hrasva*), the *ātmanepada* would be established, and furthermore, the optional application of *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* is established by the rule "ruṣyamatvara-saṅghuṣā-svanām. The statement "the *ghaṭādi* roots are marked with *ṣ*" refers to the group ending with *tvarati*.

The remainder [is as follows]. The thirteen roots beginning with *ghaṭ* and ending in an unaccented vowel have been listed. It will be stated later that the *ghaṭādi* group concludes before the root *dyuta* in the sense of "shining. Now, regarding the phrase "ending with *phaṇa*": this means up to and including the root *phaṇa* in the sense of "moving. Regarding *jvara* in the sense of "disease": in the causative (*ṇic*), it becomes *jvarayati*; but in the passive (*ciṇ*)...
