It is for this very purpose that the root *vad* is mentioned separately in the rule "vada-vraja-halantasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.125).

The term *bhāvaḥ* [refers to the root] *ṭua o śvi*. If there is the vowel *u*, as in *śvayati*, then by the application of the *śap* suffix, *guṇa* and the substitution of *ay* occur. However, in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], when an affix beginning with *ṇal* that is not *kit* follows, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would necessarily apply by the rule *liṭaḷbhyāsasya*; whereas in the case of *kit* affixes such as *atus* and others, [the *saṃprasāraṇa* applies] prior to the doubling.
Since the rule *vacisvapi-* would have required the substitution of semivowels for vowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) invariably, he says:

(250) *vibhāṣā śveḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.30]. The word "substitution of semivowels" (*saṃprasāraṇam*) is understood here because it is carried over from the previous rule *ṣyaṅ saṃprasāraṇam*. This is the intended meaning.
The meaning is that [the rule] "liṭi yaṅ ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.19) applies because of the continued validity of the phrase "liṅyaṅoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.29). Regarding the form *śuśāva*:

in the case of the suffix *ṇal*, the substitution of semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the reduplication is set aside; rather, by virtue of its higher status, vocalization is performed by this [rule] even before reduplication.
Then, when reduplication occurs, the rules for *vṛddhi* and the replacement with *āv* take effect—this is the intended meaning.

Because [the root] has not undergone reduplication (*akittvāt*), the rule *vacisvapi-* does not apply here. Thus, in the singular *liṭ* forms where the suffixes are *kit*, this is an optional rule for *saṃprasāraṇa* which had not previously applied prior to reduplication.
However, in the dual and plural forms such as *śuśuvatuḥ*, the rule *vacisvapi-* applies prior to reduplication.
This is an optional rule (*vikalpa-vidhi*) regarding the *saṃprasāraṇa* that has already been established; thus, this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases.

However, in the case of the suffix *yaṅ*, this is an option for what was previously unestablished (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*): *śośūyate* and *śeśvīyate*. In that context, when the suffix *ṇal* follows, in the alternative where this *saṃprasāraṇa* does not occur, after the doubling of the element *śvī*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) takes place.
Since *śuśvāya* would [otherwise] result, he says: "There is a prohibition of the reduplication-mark [vowel change] for the root *śvi* in the *liṭ* [perfect].

This means that a prohibition must be stated regarding the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the reduplication in the *liṭ*. Thus, when *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs for the reduplication of *śvi*, and the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied, [the rule] "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" [applies].

The sense is that [the suffix] is long. He states a specific rule for the *luṅ* tense: *jṛstanbhu-*. Thus, when the form *aśvi-a-t* is established and *iy* or *aiṅ* would otherwise apply, [the following rule applies]:
(251) *śvayateraḥ* 7.4.18.
"Of *śvayati*, [the letter] *a*. The analysis is: *śvayateḥ*—*a*. The mention of *śvayateḥ* is by means of the suffix *śtip*;
the meaning is "of the root *śvi*. By the rule "of the last [letter] of the [root] ending in a consonant" (*alo'ntyasya*), it is understood that this refers to the final *i*-sound.
From the rule "after *ṛ* and *dṛś*, [the suffix] *aṅ*" (*ṛdṛśo'ṅe*), the word *aṅ* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "of the *i*-sound of *śvayati*."
When *aśva* is established, having anticipated the application of the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), he says: "the subsequent form" (*pararūpam*).

Because there is no final *a* in the original teaching of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) does not occur. Thus: *aśvan*. [The forms are] *aśvaḥ*, *aśvatam*, *aśvata*; *aśvam*, *aśvāva*, *aśvāma*. Regarding the alternative where the augment *aṅ* is absent, he says: "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). [In this case, the form is] *iyaṅ*.
It should also be understood that there is reduplication by the rule *ṭhcaṅi*. Thus he says: *aśiśviyat*.

However, in the absence of both *aṅ* and *caṅ*, when the form *aśvi īt* is established, and the vowel *i* undergoes *vṛddhi* before *sic*, followed by the substitution of *āy*, one would expect *aśvāyīt*; therefore he says: "By the rule *hmyanta...*, there is no *vṛddhi*."

The intention is that [the rule] is stated by including the word *aśvi*. Nor can it be argued that, in the case of *sici*, when the form *aśvi īt* is established by the rule *neṭi*, the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *i* would first occur—because it is both subsequent (*paratvāt*) and internal (*antaraṅgatvāt*) relative to the *vṛddhi* of *sici*—and once the single vowel *e* is produced, since the condition of being "ending in an *ik*" (*iganta*) no longer exists, the *vṛddhi* of *sici* would not apply; thus, after the *ayādeśa* has been applied...

Since the prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by a stem ending in a consonant (*halanta*) is already established by the fact that [the root] ends in a *y*, it might be argued that the mention of *śvi* in the rule *hmyanta* (Pāṇini 1.1.20) is redundant. However, this need not be explained further; for, being an exception (*apavāda*) due to its lack of other scope (*anavakāśatva*), it sublates the *guṇa* substitution, and thus the mention is intended to prohibit the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise apply after the suffix *sic*. This concludes the discussion on the term *vṛt*.

The explanation is: "yaj and others are included. Now, one might ask: why is it not explained as "bhū and others are included"? To this, he says: "But the *bhū*-class is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).
Regarding the word *culumpati*: the root *culump* has the meaning of "to swallow" (*lopa*), and it is also included in the *bhū*-class.

The intention is that [the status of] being a verbal suffix (śap-vikaraṇa) follows from the recitation [of the sūtra]. Regarding the phrase "thus end the bhv-ādi [roots]," one should not raise the objection: "If this is so, how can the status of being a root apply to those such as 'ada bhakṣaṇe' which are yet to be mentioned? This is because the meaning is that the bhv-ādi roots ending in the śap suffix have been concluded.
Thus ends the section on the *bhvādi* (first) class of roots in the *Bālamanoramā*. Now begins the section on suffixes having four meanings (*cāturarthika*).
(1259) *tadasminnastīti deśe tannāmni* | 4|2|67. Now he begins to explain the secondary suffixes (*cāturarthika*) [denoting four types of meanings]: *tadasminnasti*.
In the sense of "that exists in this," primary suffixes such as *aṇ* and others shall be applied to a word in the nominative case that is uttered first.

The meaning is that when a place named after its origin is to be understood, [the suffix] is added to a word ending in a *pratyaya*. The word "iti" is used for the purpose of indicating a well-known place. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *matup*.
(1260) Pāṇini 4.2.68: *tena nirvṛtam* ("produced by that").

"Formed by that" (*tena nirvṛtam*). The phrase "in a country named after that" (*deśe tannāmni*) follows [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that suffixes such as *aṇ* and others shall be applied after a word ending in the third case in the sense of "formed by that," provided it refers to a country bearing that name. (1261) "His dwelling" (*tasya nivāsaḥ*). Pāṇini 4.2.69.

"Its residence" means "in a country bearing that name. The meaning is that when the sense is "its residence," suffixes such as *aṇ* and others should be applied to a word ending in the genitive case, provided it refers to a country bearing that name. They say that while a "domain" (*viṣaya*) implies ownership, "residence" (*nivāsa*) is merely the act of dwelling, being common to both cases of ownership and non-ownership.

(1262) *adūrabhavaśca* |4|2|70|. Also [denoting] that which is situated nearby. The words *tasya* ("of that") and *tannāmni deśe* ("in a region bearing that name") are understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

The meaning is: when the sense is "situated nearby" (*adūrabhava*) of something, suffixes such as *aṇ* and others shall be applied after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), provided the resulting name refers to a region (*deśa*).

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the particle *ca* (and) used here? To this he says: "By the particle *ca*. The meaning is that immediately after the rule *adūrabhavaḥ*, the three previously mentioned meanings are presented once again.
Why is this done? To this he says: "By that [particle]. Otherwise, due to proximity, only the sense of *adūrabhavaḥ* (situated not far from) would be understood.
The sense is that [the suffix] should follow the subsequent rules. Regarding "cāturarthikatvam":

in the sense of "occurring in the four meanings" (*catur-arthī*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because it belongs to the *adhyātmādi* group; however, in a *dvigu* compound used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there would be elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision of the *dvigu* when not denoting a descendant. Some, however, [interpret] the four...
The meanings of the sūtras are fourfold; therefore, they say that those [sūtras] pertaining to them are *cāturarthika*. (1263) *orañ* | 4|2|71|.
*orañ*: [The suffix] *añ* is applied in these four senses, beginning with "that exists in this."

The suffix *añ* shall be applied after a word that is first uttered ending in a particular case-ending; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. The governing rule for *añ* extends as far as the sūtra "from *suvāstu* etc., [the suffix] *aṇ*" (*suvāstvādibhyo 'ṇ*). Regarding *kākṣatavam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that in which there is a *kakṣatru*," and so forth.
(1264) *matośca bahvajaṅgāt* | 4|2|72 | [The suffix *matup*] also [is applied after a word ending in *matup*]. Regarding *saidhrakāvatam*:
the four meanings—such as "that in which *sidhrakāvana* exists," and so forth—are to be understood according to the appropriate context.

Regarding "āhimatam": the meanings are such as "that in which there is *ahi* (a snake)" and so forth. The intention is that the suffix *añ* is applied because the word *ahi* consists of two syllables (*dvyacka*).
(1265) *Bahvacaḥ kūpeṣu* (Pāṇini 4.2.73).

The suffix *añ* is applied after polysyllabic nominal stems (*bahvac*) in four senses when forming names of wells (*kūpa*). This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. For example: a well completed with a long rope is called *dairghavaratra*. (Pāṇini 4.2.74) *Udak ca vipāśaḥ*: [The suffix *añ* is also applied] to the word *udaka* after the river Vipāś.
"Beyond the Vipāś, on its northern bank. The word *vipāś* ending in the letter *ś* denotes a particular river.
(Pāṇini 4.2.75): "And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *saṅkalā* and others."
"And from *saṅkala* and others. [The word] "nivṛtam" [is used]; the sense is that it is due to the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. [The example] "pauṣkalam": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has been prepared (*nirvṛtam*) by Puṣkala.
(1268) [Pāṇini 4.2.76: "In the case of women belonging to the Sauvīra, Sālva, and Prācya [tribes]."
Regarding "strīṣu sauvīra": the remainder [of the commentary] is "an example for *sauvīra* will be stated.

Regarding "dātāmitrī nagarī": the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. Regarding "sālve": the remainder is "it is illustrated. Regarding "vaidhūmāgnī": the meaning is "produced by Vidhūmāgni. [The suffix] *añ* [is applied].

The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied]. "Prācī" means it is cited as being in an eastern region (*prāci deśe*). "Mākandī" means that which is produced from a *mākanda* tree. (1269) Pāṇini 4.2.77: *suvāstvādibhyo’ṇ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* [is applied after the group beginning with] *suvāstu*.

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after *suvāstu* and others. Regarding the mention of *añ*: the meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṭha-ra-añ*. *Sauvāstavam* [is derived as follows]: when *aṇ* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution for the *o* [of *suvāstu*]. *Vārṇavam* means "that which has arisen not far from Varṇu. Now, one might object: since the desired form is already established by the rule *ṭha-ra-añ* alone...

Furthermore, since [the suffix] *aṇ* would already be established by the force of the rule itself even without the recurrence of that [word], the repeated mention of *aṇ* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "The mention of *aṇ*... (Pāṇini 4.2.78):
*roṇī*.

*roṇī*. This [example] has its fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) elided. Regarding the phrase *tadantāt* ("from that which ends in that"), the point is that even in the prescription of an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), there is the rule of "taking what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*), as established in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya*. *Rauṇaḥ* means a well produced from *roṇī*. *Ājakarauṇaḥ* [means a well produced] from *ajakaroṇī*.
The meaning is "completed" (*nirvṛta*). There is the elision of the vowel *ī* by the rule *aṇi ṭhyasya*.

(1271) *kopadhācca* | 4.2.79 | [The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word ending in *ka* as its penultimate letter. For example, *kārṇaccchidraka*. The meaning is: a well completed by means of *karṇaccchidraka*.

*Kārkavākavam*: the meaning is a well produced by *kṛkavāku*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied; there is *guṇa* substitution for the *o*, and with the initial *vṛddhi*, the substitution of *ra* occurs. *Traiśaṅkavam*: the meaning is a well produced by *triśaṅku*.

(1272) *vuñ*, *cchaṇ*, *ka*, *ṭhac*, *ila*, *sa*, *ini*, *ra*, *ḍhañ*, *ṇya*, *ya*, *phak*, *phiñ*, *iñ*, *ñya*, *kak*, *ṭhak* [are added] after *arīhaṇa*, *kṛśāśva*, *ṛśya*, *kumuda*, *kāśa*, *tṛṇa*, *prekṣā*, *aśman*, *sakhi*, *saṃkāśa*, *bala*, *pakṣa*, *karṇa*, *sutaṅgama*, *pragadin*, *varāha*, *kumuda*, etc. [to form patronymics]. 4.2.80.
*vuñ*, *cchaṇ*: *vuñ*, *cchaṇ*, *ka*, *ṭhac*, *ila*, *sa*, *ini*, *ra*, *ḍhañ*, *ṇya*, *ya*, *phak*.

*phiñ*, *iñ*, *ñya*, *kak*, and *ṭhak*: [this is] the nominative plural from the compound of these seventeen [suffixes]. *arīhaṇa*, *kṛśāśva*, *ṛśya*, *kumuda*, *kāśa*, *tṛṇa*, *prekṣa*, *aśman*, *sakhi*, *saṅkāśa*, *bala*, *pakṣa*, *karṇa*, *sutaṅgama*.

*Pragadin*, *varāha*, and *kumuda*: these form a *dvandva* compound of seventeen [items]. The ablative plural ending in the term "of which these are the first" (*yeṣām ādayaḥ*) arises from a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the two *kumuda* words has not been applied in order to ensure the understanding of their respective numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Furthermore, the absence of *nalopa* (elision of the final *n*) in the word *pragadin* is [due to a specific rule].

This is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that [the word *arīhaṇa*] ends in the vowel *i*. Since the word *ādi* (etcetera) is heard at the end of a *dvandva* compound, it is construed with each member individually in the list beginning with *arīhaṇa*. Thus, seventeen distinct rules are formed: *buñ* after *arīhaṇa* and the others, and *chaṇ* after *kuśāśva* and the others.

Thus he says: "from the seventeen. The meaning is that the suffixes *vuñ* and others occur in sequence after the seventeen groups beginning with *arīhaṇa*. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the four meanings" (*caturarthyām*): these are [the senses] expressed by the rules "that which exists in this place, being the name of the region," "produced by that," "his dwelling," and "located near that."

The result is that suffixes are applied as appropriate to words ending in various case-terminations when they are first uttered in four senses. Within these groups, there are both terms denoting sentient beings and terms denoting insentient things; in those cases, the application of the fourfold sense (*caturartha*) occurs as appropriate. Regarding the word *prekṣī*: one who looks is a *prekṣa*; by that...

The meaning is "extinguished" (*nirvṛta*). Or, it means "extinguished by observation" (*prekṣayā nirvṛtam*). The rule *pathaḥ pantha ca* is a sūtra from the *pakṣādi* group. Regarding *pānthāyana*, the meaning is "situated not far from a road.
(1273) *janapade lup* 4.2.81. [In this context, there is elision of the suffix when referring to a country.]

[The suffix] *lup* [is applied] in the sense of a country (*janapada*). This [condition], namely "of that which has the fourfold meaning" (*cāturarthika*), is obtained from the context. (1274) *Lupi yuktavad-vyaktivacane*. When *lup* [is applied], the gender and number are like those of the base (*yukta*). "Base" (*prakṛti*) refers to the word; "gender" (*liṅga*) refers to the specific form (*vyakti*).

The term *vacanam* refers to number; this is the convention of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). Thus he says: "When *lup* occurs, the gender and number are like those of the base (*prakṛti*). By *lup*, the non-appearance of an affix (*pratyayādarśana*) is meant. Prior to the application of *lup*, whatever gender and number belong to the base of the affix, those very same [gender and number] remain when *lup* is present.

The meaning is: [it is] yours, but not by following the specific object denoted by the suffix (*pratyayārtha-viśeṣya*). "Of the Pañcālas" means "of the kings named Pañcāla. Regarding "the Pañcālas": when the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *tasya nivāsaḥ* is elided by the rule *janapade lupa*, the plural number remains as in the base form (*prakṛtivat*).

The meaning is as follows: "Kuravaḥ" and so forth. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "the country (*janapada*) which is the residence of the Kurus, the Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, and the Kaliṅgas. However, when there is an extension of gender (*liṅgātideśa*), one should cite as an example: "the country not far from Kaṭubadarī is *Kaṭubadarī*."

(1275) *Tadaśiṣyaṃ saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt* | 1|2|53 | Pāṇini rejects this sūtra of the earlier teachers with the words: "That [distinction] need not be taught. Just as in the case of the word *dārāḥ* ("wife/wives"), there is the manifestation of a feminine object qualified by grammatical masculinity (*puṃstva*).

The point is that when *lup* occurs, the manifestation of its own meaning— specifically as qualified by the gender and number residing in the original base (*prakṛti*) according to the technical rules— is possible solely through common worldly usage (*sokavyavahāra*), and there is no requirement for the operation of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) regarding that portion. [This refers to] "of the names" (*saṃjñānām*).
The meaning is "of worldly conventions.
(1276) *Lup-yogā-prakhyānāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.54). And thus, he says that even the case-ending (*sup*) is not perceived: "because the connection with the elision (*lup*) is not observed."

The word "ṭhaśiṣyaḥ" (is not taught), which has been carried over [from the previous rule], is modified to the masculine gender and connected immediately after "ṭhlu". Thus he says: "even *lup* need not be performed. "Yoga" means the meaning of a constituent part; "of that"—the meaning is "because it is not manifest," i.e., because it is not perceived. Thus he says: "constituent part... For indeed...

The understanding that "the Pañcālas," "the Aṅgas," or "the Vaṅgas" arises from their connection with [the regions of] Pañcāla, Aṅga, Vaṅga, and so forth; therefore, the point is that in such cases, there is no suffix at all.
(1277) And when the application [of a term] is based on usage (*yogapramāṇa*), there would be non-observation in the absence of that [suffix]. 1.2.55.
He states the refutation regarding the acceptance of etymological derivation (*yoga*) as follows: "And in the case of the authority of *yoga*.

This means that when the etymological derivation—the meaning of the constituent parts—is the means of cognition for words such as *Pañcāla*, *Aṅga*, and *Vaṅga*, yet in the absence of that [derivation], namely, in the absence of a current connection with the Kṣatriyas of Pañcāla, Aṅga, and so forth...

The meaning is that since the word "Pañcāla" and others are not used for a country ruled by a Śūdra king and so forth, yet they are used [for certain countries], it is logical that words such as "Pañcāla" are merely conventional (*rūḍha*) with respect to specific countries. He states this: "For if [it were] due to etymology... and so on.

(1278) *Pradhānapratyayārthavacanam arthasyānyapramāṇatvāt* | 1|2|56 | Now, as an incidental digression, he refutes another rule formulated by the ancient teachers: *pradhānapratyayārtha*. Regarding the term *pratyayārtha*: with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

The meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the primary element (*pradhāna*), that is, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), whereas the meaning of the stem (*prakṛti*) is its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); such is the statement of the former teachers, and this is what is meant [by the present rule]. (1279) *Kālopasarjane ca tulyam* | 1.2.57 | "And [the same applies] to time and secondary elements."

And [the suffixes are applied] when there is a time-word (*kāla*) or a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). The locative case here indicates the scope of application, derived from the compound *kālaśca upasarjanaṃ ca* (a collective dvandva). The phrase "to be taught" (*aṣṭhaśiṣya*), which is supplied from the previous rule, is understood as having the sense of "being the primary subject. Thus, it refers to the domain of time-words and the domain of subordinate members.

The meaning is that even regarding the specific statements of the former teachers, the lack of being a student (*aśiṣyatva*) is the same. He explains that specific statement more clearly with the words "of the past," and so forth:
(1280) *viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ* |1|2|52|.

Regarding the rule *viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ*: when the expectation arises as to whose qualifiers [are meant], the word *lub* (from the previous rule) is supplied, transformed into the genitive case, and connected [to the present rule]. Thus, it is understood as "of that which has its suffix elided" (*luptapratyayārthasya*). This is what he says: "of the meaning of the *lup*" (*lubarthasya*). "In the same way" (*tadvat*) means "like the base" (*prakṛtivat*).

This sūtra, which is recited after the rule "ṭhLupi yuktavad-vyaktivacane," ought to be explained in that very context. [The example is] "pañcālā ramaṇīyāḥ" (The Pañcālas are pleasant). The meaning is: "the country which is the dwelling place of the Pañcālas. Here, even though it is a qualifier with respect to the country, which is the meaning of the suffix...

The plural number [of the word] *ramaṇīya* follows the base form [of the compound]. For example: *godau ramaṇīyau*. This means "the country inhabited by the two Godas. Here, the dual number is applied to the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*), namely the country, as well as to its qualifier, following the base form. For example: *pañcālā janapadaḥ*.

Because the word *janapada* denotes a genus (*jāti*), it does not take a plural number like its base; for example, "the two villages of Godau. Here, because the word *grāma* denotes a genus, it does not take a dual number like its base.
In the case of *harītakī* and similar words, the individual instance (*vyakti*) is expressed.

"In *harītakyādi* and so forth, there is [only] gender"—this is a *vārtika*. The remainder [of the rule] is: "In the case of *lup*, the gender is like that of the base (*prakṛti*), but not the number. For example: *harītakyaḥ*.
Here, by the rule "*harītakyādibhyaśca*," there is *lup* of the suffix denoting a derivative (*vikāra*). In this case, among the meanings of the suffixes...

The meaning is that in the case of fruits (*phala*), the feminine gender alone remains as in the base form (*prakṛti*), but the singular number does not; this is the intention. Regarding "the number [remains] in the case of *khalatika* and so forth": this is a *vārttika*. In these cases, when there is elision (*lup*), the number remains exactly as in the base form.
The meaning is that it becomes [neuter], but not [masculine] by virtue of its gender-mark (*liṅga*). Regarding the example *khalatikaṃ vanāni*:

by the rule *ṭhvaraṇādibhyaśca*, there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix. Here, the word *khalatika*, which ends in an elided suffix, does not retain its masculine gender like its base (*prakṛti*); rather, the intention is that it remains in the singular number alone.
"Prohibition regarding the elision of the suffix after 'manuṣya'": this is a Vārttika. [It states:

"There is a prohibition regarding the elision of the suffix after 'manuṣya'. That is to say, when the meaning of the suffix has been elided and refers to that which consists of a human being, those qualifiers [are not compounded].

The meaning is that there is a prohibition of gender and number [of the derivative] according to the gender and number of the base (*prakṛti*). For example: *cañcābhirūpaḥ* ("a handsome man who is a straw doll").

A *cañcā* is an image made of straw; a person resembling that is called a *cañcā*. Under the governing rule *pratikṛtau* ("in the sense of a likeness"), the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām*, and this is elided by the rule *lup manuṣye* ("there is elision when referring to a human being"). In this case...

The meaning is that when the word *cañcā*, which ends in a deleted suffix, denotes a human being, it takes the gender of its base (*prakṛti*), but this does not apply to its qualifier, the word *abhirūpa*. Thus ends the section on the treatment as a masculine (*yuktavadbhāva*).

(1281) *Varaṇādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 4.2.82]. Now he begins the subject at hand: *varaṇādibhyaśca*. This sūtra follows after *janapade lupa*. The meaning is that there shall be elision (*lup*) of the suffixes having fourfold significance (*cāturarthika*) when they follow words beginning with *varaṇa*.
Since this is already established by the previous [rule], for what purpose is this stated? To this he says: "for the sake of [designating] a non-village (ajanapada).
Regarding the term "of the Varaṇās": there is a river named Varaṇā well-known to the north of Kāśī.
The plural number is used either with reference to its constituent parts or for the sake of honor. [The compound means] that which is situated not far from the Varaṇās.
*Nagaraṃ varaṇāḥ*. Here, when the word *varaṇā*—which ends in a deleted suffix—is used to denote a city (*nagara*), it retains the feminine gender and the plural number of its base form (*prakṛti*).
(1282) *Śarkarāyā vā* |4|2|83|. [The suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied after the word *śarkarā* to denote a place.]

Or [the suffix] *śarkarāyaḥ*. The term *ṭhac* is understood from the preceding rule, and by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is understood to apply to the *cāturarthika* suffixes. Thus he says: "from this" (*asmāt*). (1283) *ṭhakchāṬ ca* | Pāṇini 4.2.84.

"And *ṭhak* and *chaṬ*. The word "of *śarkarā*" (*śarkarāyāḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "these two [suffixes] occur after *śarkarā*. Regarding "*ṭhac* and *kak*"—the distinction is that *ṭhac* is applied because [the word *śarkarā*] belongs to the *kumuda*-class, while *kak* is applied because it belongs to the *varāha*-class. Regarding the mention of the option (*vā*): otherwise, by the very force of its inclusion there [in the *gaṇa*], *ṭhac* and *kak* would [already] apply.

The sense is that [the rule] is redundant because the elision (*lop*) and the optional application (*vikalpa*) are already established. Regarding *śarkarā*: when the suffix *aṇ* is elided (*lup*), the form is *yuvata* (as if it were *yu*). Regarding *śārkaram*: this is the form with the suffix *aṇ*. Regarding *śārkarikam*: this is the form with the suffix *ṭhak*. Regarding *śarkarīyam*: this is the form with the suffix *cha*. Regarding *śarkarikam*: this is the form with the suffix *ṭhañ*.

*Rūpa* [is used]. *Śārkarakam* means "having gravel. What is the form? The meaning is "that in which there are gravel-stones" (*śarkarāḥ santi asmin*), or "produced from gravel-stones. (1284) [The suffix] *matup* is added after the word *nadī*. 4.2.85.

The suffix *matup* [is applied] after the word *nadī*. The phrase "cāturarthika" [in the rule] is a supplement to complete the sense. [The example is] *ikṣumatī*. In the case of *matup*, the letters *u* and *a* are elided. The meaning is: "in this place there are sugarcanes (*ikṣavaḥ*). (1285) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.86: "Also after *madhu* and others."
"And after *madhu* and so forth. He explains the sūtra by completing the ellipsis: "The suffix *matup* occurs with the fourfold meaning (*cāturarthika*).

Regarding *madhumān*: the meaning is "the abode of honey. Since this is already established by the preceding rule, he asks, "For what purpose is this [sūtra]? and answers: "It is for the sake of excluding that which is not near (*anadū-artham*)."

(1286) *kumudanaḍavetasebhyo ṅmatup* 4.2.87. The meaning is that the suffix *ṅmatup* is added after *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa*. The *ṅ* [indicates] that the augment *it* is added after the final vowel, and the *ṅ* itself is for the sake of the accent. Since this [suffix] is used only in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), [the rule] "not at the end of a word" (*na padānte*) applies.
This is established in the *Sūtra*, the *Bhāṣya*, and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. Regarding the form *kumudvān*:

the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is "that in which there are water-lilies" (*kumudāḥ asmin santi*). By the rule for the suffix *matup* being marked with *ṅ*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
Regarding *naḍvān*: the analytical derivation is "that in which there are reeds" (*naḍā asmin santi*). Amara states: "*kumudvān* refers to a place abounding in water-lilies."
Regarding "vetasvān": the analysis of the compound is "that in which reeds (vetasa) exist. Regarding the phrase "of the first two":
in the word *kumudvat* and the word *naḍvat*, the *m* of the suffix *matup* is changed to *v* by the rule *ṭhjhayaḥ*;
however, in the word *vetasvat*, the *m* is changed to *v* by the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ*. This is the meaning.

In reality, even in the case of the word *naḍvat*, because the rule *ṭhjhayaḥ* is considered asiddha (non-existent) [with respect to the present rule], the application of *mādupadhāyāḥ* alone is logical. This is because "within a single section (*prakaraṇa*), a preceding section is asiddha [to a subsequent one], but not within that very same section is a subsequent rule asiddha with respect to a preceding rule"— this is established by the rule *upasargādasamāse*.

Because this has been refuted in the Sūtrabhāṣya. However, in the case of *vetaḥsvān*, the substitution of *r* (rutva) does not occur, because of the status of the original locus (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the elision of the *al*. The prohibition "not at the end of a word" (*na padānte*) does not apply here; for, having analyzed the compound as "at the end of a word" (*pade anta*), it refers only to a substitute (*ādeśa*) of a vowel (*aj*) that occurs within a word when a final element of the word is to be applied.

Because the engagement in that prohibition is accepted in the Bhāṣya; furthermore, there is no prohibition [by the rule] "na sthānivat" regarding what is not established in the preceding context, because of the authority of the Bhāṣya which, having analyzed [the compound] as "pada-ante," establishes the exclusion of the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* in that case.

The *Śabdenduśekhara* explains in detail that only those rules belonging to the third section (*traipādika*) which are distinct from those prescribing operations for the final constituent parts of a word are to be understood here.
Furthermore, it should be stated that [the suffix] also occurs after the word *māhiṣa*.
Immediately after "māhiṣāt ca," the remainder [of the rule] is "ṭhḍbhatu'bi. Regarding *mahiṣmān*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that in which there are buffaloes" (*mahiṣā asmin santi*). Due to the *ṭit* designation, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion.

Because the elision of *a* is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no change to the voiced unaspirated sound (*jaśtva*). However, the rule "in the case of a *ṭha*-suffix, it is obligatory in the common language" (*bhāṣāyām*) does not apply here, because of that [specific condition].
This is because the rule applies when a homogeneous letter (*savarṇa*) follows; for there exists no nasalized (*anunāsika*) letter that is homogeneous with *ṣ*.

(1287) *naḍa-śādāḍ ḍvalac* [Pāṇini 4.2.88]. From *naḍa* and *śāda*, the suffix *ḍvalac* is added. Thus, *naḍvala*; because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). *Śādvala*.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which there is *śāda*. *Śāda* has a dental (*d*) as its penultimate letter; others say it has a retroflex (*ḍ*) as its penultimate.
Amara states: "In the sense of 'abounding in reeds,' there are the forms *naḍvān* and *naḍvala*," and also: "*śādvalaḥ* means green with *śāda* grass."

(1288) *śikhāyā valac* |4|2|89|. The suffix *valac* is added after *śikhā*. This sūtra is intended for the sense of "produced from" (*nirvṛta*) and so forth, and also to override the suffix *aṇ* when the name refers to a region (*deśa*). However, as will be stated in the fifth [book], *dantaśikhātsaṃjñāyām*, it applies even when not referring to a region.
*Śikhāvala* is an example of the suffix *cha* used for the sake of expressing form (*rūpa*).
(1289) Pāṇini 4.2.90: *utkarādibhyaś chaḥ*.
From *utkara* and other such words, the suffix *cha* is applied. The remainder [of the rule] is "pertaining to the four meanings" (*cāturarthika*). An example is *utkarīya*.

This is a specific locality (*deśaviśeṣa*). It means "produced by a heap" (*utkara*), or "his dwelling," or "situated not far from it. (1290) *Naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca* [Pāṇini 4.2.91]: For words beginning with *naḍa*, the suffix *kuk* is also applied [to form place names].

The *naḍādi* group [of suffixes] includes *kuk*. After stems beginning with *naḍa*, the suffix *cha* occurs in the four senses (*cāturarthika*), and there is the addition of *kuk* to the base. Furthermore, in the case of *kruñcā*, there is shortening [of the vowel]. This is a *gaṇasūtra* belonging to the *naḍādi* class. From the word *kruñcā*, the suffix *cha* is applied, *kuk* is added to the base, and the long *ā* is shortened. Thus, *kruñcakīya* means "belonging to the *kruñcās*."
The analysis of the compound is *asmin santi* ("they exist in this"), and so forth. There is also the elision of the *n* of *takṣan*. This is also a *gamaka-sūtra* (an explanatory rule).
From the word *takṣan*, the suffix *cha* is added, along with the augment *kuk* and the elision of the letter *n*.
(Pāṇini 6.4.153: "There is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha* after [words belonging to] the *vilvaka* group."
*Billvādibhyaḥ*. This is the sixth sūtra.
*Billvakādi* refers to the mention of the *billva*-group words from within the *naḍādi* class, with the augment *kuk* added.

The letter *k* [in *kakāra*] is for the sake of pronunciation; the vowel *a* [in *kakāra*] is for the sake of articulation. Regarding "in a secondary derivative" (*taddhite*): [this refers to the rule] "and of the patronymic suffix in a secondary derivative" (*ṭhāpatyasya ca taddhite*).
The meaning is that [the suffix] follows from that [base]. Regarding *bilvakīyā*: by the rule "for *naḍa* and others, there is *kuk* and *cha*," the suffix *cha* is applied;
in the present case, *kuk* is also added. Regarding *bailvakāḥ*: from the word *bilvakīya*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*);
the meaning is that when this [suffix *aṇ*] follows, there is elision (*luk*) of *cha*. Regarding *vetrakīyāḥ*: in this [place], there are *vaitrāṇi* (bamboo products).

The suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of "existing" (santi) because [the base] belongs to the *naḍādi* group; the point is that the augment *kuk* is added in the present context. Regarding "vaitrakāḥ": the meaning is "those who reside in Vetrakīyā. The point is that when the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *vetrakīyā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha*.
As for the question "Why [mention] *cha*?": this is a question based on the fact that only the suffix *cha* can possibly follow these [bases].

Regarding "saṃniyoga": the meaning is by the maxim, "Those taught as being in a state of conjunction (saṃniyoga) either operate together or cease together. Since the desired result is already established by carrying forward the word "lopa" from the rule "ḍhea lopo 'kaddvāḥ," he asks: for what purpose is the mention of "luk"? To this, he says: "the mention of luk..."

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of total elision" (*sarvalopārtham*): the intention is that since the very non-appearance of an affix is the meaning of the term *luk*, the elision of the entire suffix *īya* is obtained. However, this is not obtained when the rule is formulated as a simple *lopa* (elision);
thus he says: "For in the case of *lopa*... In the rule for *lopa*, [the word] *ya* is supplied from the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ*.

If this [rule] were not carried over (*anuvṛtti*), the meaning obtained would be that there is elision of the *yakāra* which serves as the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the *īya* that has undergone substitution for *cha* after words such as *bilva*; thus, there would be elision of the *yakāra* alone. However, if "ṭhyaḥ upadhāyāḥ" is not carried over, then by the rule "ādeḥ parasya," there would be elision of the *īkāra* itself.

The intention is as follows: there would be the elision of the letter *dy* alone. However, if the rule "ṭhya upadhāyāḥ" were not being followed, then by the rule "ādeḥ parasya," the elision would apply only to the letter *ī*. This is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the section on the fourfold suffixes (*cāturarthika*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.

The *tiṅ* and *kṛt* suffixes [have been discussed]; now the *cur*-class (*curādi*) roots, which take the *ṇic* affix in their own sense (*svārthika*), are being examined. Regarding the root *cura* (meaning "to steal"):
the letter *a* after the *repha* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not marked with the technical designation *it*, because there is no purpose for it.
And because the rule "ṭhṇicaśca" will be stated later regarding the establishment of the word-division, so it shall be hereafter as well.

(389) *satyāpapāśarūpavīṇātūlaślokasenālomatvacavamavaṇacūrṇacurādibhyo ṇicaḥ* 3.1.25. [The affix *ṇic* is applied after the words *satyāpa*, *pāśa*, *rūpa*, *vīṇā*, *tūla*, *śloka*, *senā*, *loman*, *tvaca*, *vama*, *vaṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and the group beginning with *cura*.]

From *satyāpa*, *asatyāpa*, *pāśa*, *rūpa*, *vīṇā*, *tūla*, *śloka*, *senā*, *loman*, *tvaca*, *varman*, *varṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and those beginning with *cur*—from these, [there is] the ablative case in a *dvandva* compound. Thus he says: "After these, there shall be the affix *ṇic*. When the question arises as to in what sense [this applies], he says: "After those ending in *cūrṇa*."

The meaning is that [the formation] from the twelve bases beginning with *satya* and ending with *cūrṇa*, as well as from verbal roots such as *karoti* and *ācaṣṭe*, is already established by the rule to be stated later: "The suffix *ṭha* is applied diversely (*bahulam*) after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the sense of a verbal root. One might object: since it is already established by that very rule, why is it mentioned here?
Regarding the sequence ending with *cūrṇa*, he says:

"Their inclusion here is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). Nor should it be argued that the rule for the causative suffix (*ṇic*) applies to them in their own primary sense (*svārtha*) alone; for [it is stated]: "But when *satya* is used with *kṛ*, the augment *puṅ* is not applied. [Thus one says] *satyaṃ karoti*.

The intention is that this would contradict the Bhāṣya statement beginning with "satyāpayati" and so forth. Examples of roots starting with *satyā* and ending with *cūrṇ* will become clear in the root text itself within the section on denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*). As for the phrase "from the *cur*-class [roots] in their own sense," the intention is that no other meaning has been specified. In this regard...

The term "dhātoḥ" (from a root) is understood from the rule "dhātor ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.120). Consequently, the result is that the suffix *ṇic* is applied after roots belonging to the *cur*-class and others. From this, the status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* (semi-verbal suffix) for *ṇic* is established.
Otherwise, because it would not be prescribed by the word "dhātoḥ," its status as an *ārdhadhātuka* would not obtain.
The object of understanding is stated as follows: "pugantalaghūpadhasya guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.86). Once the suffix *ṇic* has been applied, the form *cur-i* remains;

because *ṇic* is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, by virtue of the letter *c* [in the rule], there is *guṇa* substitution for the *u* of *cur* according to the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya. This is the meaning.

(390) *ṇicaśca* | Pāṇini 1.3.74. From the rule *anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam*, the term *ātmanepada* is understood; and from the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*, the phrase *kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale* is also understood. This is by virtue of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*).
It is understood that [the suffix] follows a causative (*ṇijanta*) form. Thus he says, beginning with "from the causative," and so forth.

*Corayati* (he steals), *corayiṣyati* (he will steal), *corayiṣyate* (he will steal [for himself]), *corayatu* (let him steal), *corayatām* (let them steal), *acorayat* (he stole), *acorayata* (he stole [for himself]), *corayeta* (he might steal). Regarding the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) in the active voice (*parasmaipada*), he says: *coryāt*.

The intention is that there is an elision of the *ṇi* suffix by the rule "ṭhṇeraniṭi. Regarding the ātmanepada form in the āśīrliṅ (precative), he says: *corayiṣīṣṭa*. Regarding the *luṅ* (aorist), he says: "ṇiśrītyādi" [and so forth]. [The lengthening of the vowel occurs] by the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ. The intention is that this falls under the scope of the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the *sa*-augment) by the rule "sanvallaghuni. [Now for the root] *citi* in the sense of remembering (*smṛti*).

Regarding the word *cintayati*: because it is marked with the *idit* designation, the augment *num* is applied; thus, the sense is that it is a verbal root ending in *ṇic* followed by a finite suffix (*tiṅ*), meaning "origination" (*utpatti*). Now, one might object:

let the *idit* designation not be used, for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), let it simply be stated as *cinta smṛtyām*. Nor can it be argued that the *idit* designation is necessary to prevent the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

It must be stated that in forms such as *cintayati* and *cintayāñcakāra*, there is no possibility of the elision of *n* precisely because the *ṇic* suffix lacks the *kṅit* designation. Nor can it be argued that the *it* marker is for the purpose of preventing the elision of *n* in the case of the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative) when the *ṇic* is absent— as in *icintyāt*— or in the passive (*karmalakāra*) with *yak*, as in *cintyate*.

An objection may be raised: since the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the *curādi* class is obligatory, a form such as *cintyate* from the simple root *cint*—without the *ṇic*—would be as impossible as a hare's horn; therefore, he says "cinta," etc. By the word "tena" (by that), he means "by way of being optional. And thus, at times...

The intention is that because the usage *cintyāt* (from the root *cint*) is observed as *cintyate*, the marker *it* has been added there in order to prevent the elision of the nasal (*n*). Now, one might object: even so, the optionality of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would apply only where the elision of the nasal is applicable—that is, in cases like *cintyāt* and *cintyate*—but not elsewhere.

Regarding the forms *cintati* and so on, one might raise the objection that since there is an intervention by the affix *śap*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) cannot apply there; anticipating this, the author provides an example—*cintiti* and *cintet*—with the intention that this indicator (*jñāpaka*) refers to the general class of the root *cint*. This indicator, however, refers to the general class of the *curādi* (the tenth class of roots).

He states another opinion with the words "And this... [etacceti]. Regarding the fact that the indicator depends on the general class of *cur*-beginning roots, he cites the consensus of the elders with the words "Therefore, one... [ata eketi]. If the indicator were restricted solely to the root *cit*, then the example *jagaṇatuḥ* from the *gaṇa* root belonging to the *cur*-class would clearly be untenable.

The term *bhāvaḥ* [refers to the state of being]. "Dependent on a specific [condition]" (*viśeṣāpekṣam*) means it has as its object the mere verbal root *cit*. He states that this very opinion is correct with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). Since there is an option regarding the suffix *ṇic* for all roots of the *curādi* class, [the rule] "optionally from *dhṛṣ* onwards" (*ā dhṛṣādvā*) applies to those few roots enumerated within the sub-group of *curādi*.

The sense is that [the rule] would be rendered useless for the causative (*ṇij*) and the non-causative (*vikalpita*). Regarding *yantra* in the sense of "confinement": in *yantrayati*, there is no *vṛddhi* because the vowel *a* lacks the status of being a *upadhā*. In *ayayantrad*, [there is no *vṛddhi*] because the vowel *a* is heavy (*guru*), and since it is not light (*alaghu*), the condition of being followed by a light vowel (*laghuparakatva*) is absent.

Due to the absence of the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment as if it were a *san*-affix), neither the *it* nor the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs. This should be understood similarly for other roots ending in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogānta*) that follow hereafter. Regarding the statement "it is possible to recite [the root with the *nakāra*]," the absence of the elision of the *nakāra* (*nalopa*) is not the result of its being marked with the *idit* designation; rather, the point is that the elision of the *nakāra* does not even arise because the *nakāra* cannot be an *upadhā* (penultimate vowel).

"That is to be considered" means that even if the roots *cint*, *kudrī* (meaning "speaking untruth"), *tatri* (meaning "supporting a family"), and *matri* (meaning "speaking secretly") were to end in *ṇic*, there would be no possibility of the elision of the *nakāra* because it is not preceded by a short vowel (*anupadhatvāt*). Therefore, the purpose for the substitution of *it* [for the penultimate vowel] would be absent; this is the intended meaning. Thus [it applies to] *kudrī*, *tatri*, and *matri*.
The meaning is that even among those roots to be read in the *curādi* (the tenth class) group, it is possible to abandon the status of being marked with an *it* (i.e., the *it*-augment).

*Laḍa* is used in the sense of "serving" (*upasevā*). From *lāḍayati*: in the *ṇic* formation, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*atupadhāvṛddhiḥ*). This should be understood similarly for what follows. *Alīlaḍat*. *Pīḍa* is used in the sense of "immersing" (*avagāhana*).

(391) *bhrājabhāsabhāṣadīpajīvamīlapīḍāmanyatarasyām* |7|4|3|. The rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ* ("and when there is *caṅ*, the penultimate vowel is shortened before a suffix marked with *ṇu*") is understood [to apply here]. Therefore, he says: "of these. Since the shortening of the penultimate vowel would have been obligatory, this is an optional rule (*vikalpa*). In the case where the short vowel is applied...
Intending to show that there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable because the following element is light (laghu) and because of the *sanvadbhāva* status, he says: *apīpiḍat*.

Here, in the latter part (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) there is a short vowel (*hrasva*), while in the former part (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*) there is a long vowel (*dīrgha*). However, considering that in the alternative case where the short vowel is absent, there is no lengthening of the reduplicated syllable due to the absence of a light following element and the consequent lack of *sanvadbhāva*, he says: [the other form].

Regarding *apīpīḍat*: here, there is a long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the latter part (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) and a short vowel (*hrasva*) in the former part (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*). [The root] *naṭ* is used in the sense of "trembling" (*avaspandane*). Trembling is acting (*nāṭya*). [Examples: *nāṭayati*, *anīnaṭat*. [The root] *śrath* is used in the sense of "exertion" (*prayatne*). [Examples: *śrāthayati*, *aśiśrathat*. In the rule prescribing the *sanvat* treatment, [the substitution occurs] even when there is an intervention by more than one consonant (*neka-hal-vyavadhāne’pi*).

The designation *laghuparata* (having a light vowel followed) is not contradicted, because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *atsmṛdṛtvarapraśām* which ordains *atva* as an exception to *ītva*. Otherwise, in forms such as *apaprathat*,
since *ītva* would not apply due to the absence of *laghuparata*— given the intervention of multiple consonants— what would be the purpose of that [exceptional *atva* rule]?

The root *pṛ* is used in the sense of "filling. Now, one might object: let this root be indicated with a short vowel (*pṛ*), for by that much alone forms such as *pārayati* and so on are established. Nor should it be argued that the long vowel is pronounced for the sake of the augment *iṭ* in the case where the causative suffix *ṇic* is absent—specifically in *paritā* and *pariṣyati*—because it is well known that roots ending in *ṛ* are *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). [This objection is not valid.]

Since the *ṇic* suffix added after roots such as *cur* is compulsory, the absence of that *ṇic* would be as impossible as a rabbit's horn; therefore, he says: "The pronunciation of the long vowel [in the root *pṛ*] is the indicator (*liṅga*) of the optional nature of the *ṇic*. The word "of the root *pṛ*" is to be understood as the remainder [of the statement]. If the *ṇic* were indeed optional...
The intention is that the long vowel in *parītā* and so forth is meaningful for the purpose of excluding forms such as *partā*.
Now, one might ask: even if the root ended in a short vowel, why would *iṭ* not occur in *paritā* and similar forms? To this he says:
"For that [long vowel] is for the sake of making it *seṭ*. Here, *hi* means "because," and *tat* refers to the long vowel.
The point is this: in the case of *parita* and so forth, the presence of the augment *iṭ* is for the sake of ensuring it is *seṭ*; however, if it ended in *ṛ*, it would not be *iṇ*.

This is because, among the *aniṭ*-rules (*aniṭ-kārikā*), by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots ending in *ṝ*, it is understood that roots ending in *ṛ* are *aniṭ*. [Objection: But what about the root *pṛ* with the suffix *ṇic*?
What is the purpose of indicating that [the suffix] is optional?

Since forms such as *paritaḥ* are established by the roots *pṛ* read with both the *śnā* and *vikaraṇa* affixes, he says "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*)— meaning, according to the stated method, from the root *pṛ* with the affix *ṇic*.
The meaning is: "when it has been made known that [the substitution] is optional. [Regarding *pārayati* and *parati*:

the substitution of *u* by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* does not occur, because it is superseded by the guna and vṛddhi substitutions; this is the intended sense. Regarding *ūrja balam*: the sūtra *sanvallaghuni* is interpreted in two ways.

This has been explained previously. In that context, because of the prohibition [stated] as "caṅ ṭhni ndrāḥ," and because of the doubling of the root *ji* when it is the causative form (*ṇijanta*), there is an absence of a light vowel in the subsequent segment (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) when followed by *caṅ* and *ṇi*; thus, in the first explanation, [the rule applies] to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Because it lacks such lightness of the suffix (*paraka*) and because it lacks the status of being a *san*-type suffix, there is no lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); thus, [the form] is *aurjijata*. However, according to the second interpretation, when a *ṇi* is followed by *caṅ*, the base (*aṅga*) is *ūrja*; then, either taking the reduplicated syllable of that base, or taking the *ṇic* which has been elided— [The rule applies.]

The long vowel [is substituted] for the practice of *laghūpadhatva* (light penultimate status), as in *āṬrjījat*. It should be understood in this very way regarding similar cases. Regarding the root *prath* in the sense of "making known," [the form] *prāthayati* is derived; the intention is that there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel due to the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Now, one might object: "Since this root belongs to the *ghu* class and so on, it possesses the marker *mit*, and therefore the penultimate vowel should be short. To this, he says: "Not others" (*nānye*).
The sense is that there is a prohibition of *mit* status for roots such as *cur*, which are distinct from the five beginning with *jñā*.
However, because a root such as *ghaṭ* (belonging to the *ghaṭādi* group) possesses *mit* status, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, the form is simply *prathayati*. Nor should it be argued:
"Why could the mention [of *ghaṭ*] in the *ghaṭādi* group not be merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*) for the sake of establishing *mit* status for the *caurādi* root? [This is not the case].
There is no need for further elaboration, as it is prohibited by the rule "ṭhānye mito'hetau" (Pāṇini 1.2.26).
(392) *at smṛ-dṛ-tvara-pratha-mrada-stṛ-spaśām* | Pāṇini 7.4.95.
Regarding *at smṛ*: [the word] "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) is understood here because of its recurrence from the previous rule "atra lopo'bhyāsasya" (Pāṇini 7.4.58).

The meaning is: "when followed by a *ṇic* that is itself followed by a *caṅ*. From the rule *sanvallaghuni*, the phrase "followed by a *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*) is understood to carry over. The term *caṅpara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that after which a *caṅ* follows.
The sense is that the referent of the other member of the compound is indeed the *ṇic* following the root *ṛ*. As for the word *itvā*, it refers to the rule *sanyataḥ*.

The meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning *itva*. Regarding the form *apaprathat*: because the substitution of *at* is prescribed here, it is understood that even when there is an intervention by multiple consonants (*anekahalvyavadhāna*), the condition of being followed by a light syllable (*laghuparakatva*) still applies. Otherwise, according to the maxim "that which cannot be separated" (*yena nāvyavadhāna-nyāya*), one would have to rely on an intervention by only a single consonant; therefore, [the rule] would not apply here.

Since the substitution of *it* does not apply simply because of the absence of *san*, what is the use of that [rule]? Because of the heaviness (*gurutva*) when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). In the case of the root *pṛth* with the suffix *kṣepa*: it has *ṛt* as its penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). Thus, "he causes to spread" (*parthayati*). In the *ṇic* formation, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), and the substitution of *ra* for the final element (*raparatva*).

(393) *urṛt* | Pāṇini 7.4.7. The term *urṛt* consists of the genitive form *ṝtaḥ*, meaning "of *ṝ*. The phrase *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* ("when *ṇic* follows, in the *caṅ* reduplication, of the penultimate vowel") is understood by context (*anuvartate*). The word *vā* ("or") is also understood from the rule *jighrater vā*. Thus, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*): one might object that a rule prescribing an *ṛ*-vowel for an *ṛ*-vowel is redundant; therefore, he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rules for] *i*, *ra*, *ā*, and *r*. In forms such as *acīkṛta* from the root *kṛt* (meaning 'to sound'), where the *itva* (change to *i*) and subsequent *raparatva* (substitution of *ra*) would apply by the rule *upadhāyāśca*, the form *ir* would result; however, in the case of *amīmṛjat*,...

The rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114) prescribes *ār*. However, in the case of the root *prath* under discussion, when *caṅ* is applied and the *iṇ* is elided, one might expect *ār* to occur by relying on the presence of the *ṇic* suffix through the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, which would trigger the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ar*.
The meaning is that [the present sūtra] is an exception (*apavāda*) to all of those. Thus, in *apīpṛthat*, the *guṇa* that was expected to occur by relying on the *ṇic* is [prevented].

The intention is that the form [is derived] by first applying the substitution of *ṛ* for *ar*, then doubling, then the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*urat*), then the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), then the *sanvadbhāva* substitution, then the lengthening (*dīrgha*). Regarding the form *apaparthat*: in the alternative view where the substitution of *ṛ* does not occur, doubling takes place before the *guṇa* substitution because of the prohibition "when there is reduplication, [the rule] does not apply to a vowel" (*dvirvacane'ci*), after which the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* and the retention of the initial consonant occur.

The sense is that by relying on the *ṇic* suffix for the root *ṛ*, when *guṇa* is applied and *ra* is substituted for *ṛ*, because there is no light vowel (*laghu*) following [the penultimate], the condition of being like *san* (*sanvadbhāva*) is absent; consequently, neither the *it* augment nor the lengthening occurs. Regarding *aṭṭa* and *ṣuṭṭa* in the sense of "disregard": the meaning is that this verbal root *aṭṭ* has a dental *da*. As for the letter *da*:
The intention is that the designation [of the root] is by means of the letters ṣṭu and cartva. He states the purpose of the status of being a *dopadha* (having *ṣ* as its penultimate):

"of the status of ṣṭu. Thus, having set aside the letter *da*, when there is doubling of the element *ṭi*, resulting in *ad-ṭiṭat*, and then the application of ṣṭutva and cartva to the *da*, the desired form *ṭhāṭṭiṭat* is obtained.

It is established. However, if the suffix were *ṭap* by its own nature (rather than being added as a technical marker), then because there would be no application of the prohibition "na ndrāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3), the reduplication of the causative form ending in *ṇya*—which includes two *ṭa*s—would result in the first *ṭa* not being removed during the process of "remainder of the initial consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*) in the reduplicated syllable; thus, the form would be *āṭiṭṭat*.

The sense is that the form would be undesirable. [Regarding the root] *ṣmiṅ* in the sense of "disregard": now, since the ātmanepada is established by the rule *ṇicaśca*, for what purpose is the addition of the suffix *ṅk*?
To this he says: "From the causative (*ṇijanta*), the suffix *taṅ*. This means the suffix *taReĀ* (i.e., the ātmanepada endings). [This applies] even when the result does not accrue to the agent.

The addition of the marker *ṅ* is for the purpose of [indicating] the *ātmanepada* ending after the causative (*ṇijanta*) form; that is to say, it serves as a mnemonic indicator (*ṅtkiraṇa*). Now, one might object: "Even if the marker *ṅ* is added, since the causative form itself does not possess the *ṅ* property, how can the stated purpose be achieved? To this, he says: "Because it would be useless with respect to a part. That is, the *ṅ* property is redundant with respect to the root *ṣmiṅ*, which is merely a constituent part of the causative form.

Because that [root] has no usage without the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the meaning is that the *ṅtv* (the property of having the marker *ṅ*) heard in the component [of the root] accomplishes its grammatical effect only when followed by the causative suffix. Regarding *smāyayate*: after the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) and the substitution of *āy* for *ai*; thus, from the causative form *smāyī*, with the suffix *laṭ* in the third person singular (*tip*), the *śap* augment is added, resulting in the *guṇa* strengthening and the substitution of *āy*—this is the intended sense.
He was astonished. [The root] *tul* is used in the sense of weighing. [Question: How so? [Answer: Because the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel would otherwise apply;

such is the intention. [Regarding the form] *tulanā*: the intention is that it is formed by the suffix *yu* according to the rule "after roots ending in *ṇi*, as well as *ās* and *śranth*, [the suffix *yu* is added].

He resolves [the objection] with the words "by [the rule] *atulopamābhyām*. [Regarding the term] "ending in *-ā*": it refers to the noun *tulā*, derived from the root *tul* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *ac*.

By virtue of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the word *tulā* ends in long *ā* when denoting the feminine gender due to the absence of *guṇa*. From that [root *tul*], by the rule "he does that" or "he describes that" (*tat karoti*, *tad ācaṣṭe*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied; because of the status of being like the *iṣṭhan* suffix, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*), resulting in *tulī*. Then, from the root ending in *ṇi*, by adding the suffix *ṇya* and subsequently the suffix *laṭ* with the termination *tip*, and further the suffix *yuc*, the forms *culayati* and *tulana* are produced. Regarding the elision of the vowel *a*, [the rule] *acaḥ*... [applies].

The intention is that because [the substitute] is treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva), there is no *guṇa* substitution in the form *parasmin*. Regarding *vraja-mārga*: one forms *vrājayati* and *mārgayati*. Alternatively, *mārga* is not a separate root;
rather, the meaning is that the root *vraj* signifies both the preparation of a path and going. Regarding *jñapa micca*: the root *jñap* takes the suffix *ṇic*.

The meaning is "possessing the notion of a friend" (mit-saṃjña), or "participating in the grammatical operations pertaining to a *mit*. He says "this one" because there is no indication of the meaning [of the root] in the Dhātupāṭha. In the rule *pracccha jñīpsāyām*, [the sense] is "desiring to know," whereas in the rule *ślāghaṅ-sthā-śapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ*, [the sense] is "informing."
The meaning is "because of the observation of its application.

(394) *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.92: "The short vowel for [the roots] marked with *mit*. [This rule follows] from the word *upadhāyāḥ* in the rule *ṭhūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*, and from the word *ṇau* in the rule *doṣo ṇau*.

Therefore, the word "ṇau" (in the presence of the causative suffix) is also understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of the penultimate vowel of the roots listed [in the *mit* list]," and so forth. Regarding "jñapayati": the sense is that when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel, and then [by this rule] shortening occurs. Regarding "yama ca pariveṣaṇe" (the root *yama* is also [included] in the sense of serving food): the word "ca" implies that "mid" is drawn in [from the previous rule]; the remainder [of the interpretation] is that the word "iti" is supplied. The root *yam* is used in the sense of serving food.
The meaning is that it always obtains [the designation], or rather, it becomes subject to the operations of *mit*. Alternatively, it means "that which bears the technical name *mit*.
Here, *pariveṣaṇa* refers to surrounding or encircling; the intention is based on the lexicon stating, "The enclosure (*pariveṣa*) is the perimeter (*paridhi*). It does not, however, mean eating.

From the verbal root *bhuj* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), under the governing rule "in the feminine" (*striyām*), the suffix *yuc* is applied according to *Pāṇini* 3.3.107 (*ṭhṇyāsaśrantho yuc*). Neuter gender is established by common usage (*lokāt*). In some readings, the word is simply *bhojane*. Here, the meaning is the preparation of food substances in the vessel of the eater, not the act of serving (*pariveṣaṇa*). [This occurs] in the context of eating (*bhojanāyām*).
The sense is that since *yami* ending in *ṇic* already possesses the designation *mit* simply by virtue of ending in *am*, [the rule applies].

The meaning "he surrounds" (*pariveṣṭate*) is intended; by this, it is indicated that here the word *pariveṣaṇa* is derived from *pariviṣ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the suffix *lyuṭ*. Nor is there any issue even regarding the sense of "encircling," because *yami* already possesses the designation *am*.
It should not be argued that the rule for *mit* is redundant once [the desired forms] are established;

for, by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "except when serving food" (*apariveṣaṇe*) in the *gaṇasūtra* "yamo 'pariveṣaṇe" included within the *ghaṭādi* group— which resides in the section on the prohibition of *mit* status by the rule "na kamyamicamām"— [the *mit* status applies] to instances other than eating.
Because, regarding the sense of "encircling" (*veṣṭana*), since the prohibition of *mit* status would otherwise apply, this [rule] serves to establish that *mit* status;

for in the rule "ṭhyamo'pariveṣaṇe," the word *pariveṣaṇa* is intended to mean specifically "serving food" (*bhojana*), and thus there would be the contingency of the prohibition of *mit* status for the root *yam* even in the sense of "encircling. Therefore...
The author of the root-text (Mūlakṛt) has explained that [the rule] "ṭhyami does not occur except after *bhojanā*" applies.

However, regarding the rule prohibiting *mit* status—namely, "ṭhyamo 'pariveṣaṇe"—since *bhojanā* is specifically excluded (*paryudāsa*) from it, there is no prohibition of *mit* status therein; thus, by the very fact of its being not [included] in that [list], [the rule applies].

Since *mit* status has not been established here, in the *curādi* class, by the word *veṣaṇa* (in the root *piṣ*), only "encircling" (*veṣṭana*) is intended, and not "eating" (*bhojana*); let that suffice for now. Regarding *caha* in the sense of "imagining" (*parikalpana*):

from this point until the root *ciñ* in the sense of "gathering" (*cayana*), the term *ca* continues to apply. Therefore, for those [roots], there is the shortening [of the vowel] before the causative suffix (*ṇic*) due to their *mit* status.

He says this: "it causes to move" (*cahayati*). Now, one might object that since this [meaning] is already established by this very [root], its inclusion in the *kathādi* sub-group within the *curādi* class at the beginning [of the list] is redundant; therefore, he says: "in the *kathādi* group.

It will be stated that "the *kathādi* roots end in short *a*. Therefore, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, after the elision (*al-lopa*) of the final vowel, as in *cahayati* and so forth, [the form is derived].

Because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original place) of the elision (*allopasya*), there is no difference [between the forms] whether the *vṛddhi* is prevented by the *mit* designation or the vowel is shortened. Nevertheless, when the elision of the penultimate vowel (*alopa*) occurs after a root ending in /a/ following the suffixes *caṅ* and *ṇi*, the absence of the *sanvat* rule and the long vowel due to its being an *aglopi* (having an elided penultimate) results in the form *acacchaḍ*; this is the intended meaning of the result. *Capa*.

"Thus say some": this means that some read "cape" in place of "caha parikalpane. "Raha tyāge ityeke" should also be explained in the same way. And thus, among the five roots beginning with *jñap*, the third is either the root *cah*, the root *cap*, or the root *rah*.

Having established that the *baladhātu* is the fourth and the *ciñdhātu* is the fifth, there is no contradiction in the status of the five beginning with *jñā*, since they constitute a group of five according to all three views. He states the result of including [the root] *ṭhraha* in the list beginning with *katha*—namely, that it belongs to the *ararahad* group—by saying: "But for those beginning with *katha*, [it is] *ararahad*."

The point is that because the root ends in a non-dental consonant, it lacks the *aglopi* (elision of a penultimate letter) condition, and therefore neither the lengthening (*dīrgha*) nor the treatment as *sanvat* applies. The root *bal* means "to breathe" or "to live.
Since the term *mit* is carried over by the continued application of the rule *ṭhce*, one considers it to have a short vowel and says: *balayati*.
(395) *cisphurorṇau* [Pāṇini 6.1.54].
Considering that "āt" is carried over from "ṭhādeca upadeśe" and "vibhāṣā" is carried over from "vibhāṣā līyateḥ," he completes the remainder [of the rule] by stating:
"there may optionally be ātva. When the root *ci* is in the *ṇic* form and *ātva* has been applied, the form stands as *cāi*.

(396) *arti-hrī-vlī-rī-knūyī-kṣmāyī-ātām-puṅ-ṇau* | Pāṇini 7.3.36. The compound *arti-hrī-vlī-rī-knūyī-kṣmāyī-ātām* is in the genitive case. The word *puk* is separated from *ṇau*. Thus he says: "For these [roots], *puk* is added when followed by *ṇi*. In *puk*, the letter *k* is an *it* (indicatory), and the letter *u* [is for the sake of pronunciation].

The purpose is for pronunciation. Because it has the *kit* designation, it is a suffix added to the end of the word. When the form *cāp* is established, by carrying forward the word *ca* and drawing in the *mit* designation, the *hrasva* (short vowel) occurs due to the *mit* status; thus, he states the final form before the *ati* and other suffixes as *capayati*. However, in the alternative case where the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) does not occur, he says *cayayati*.

The meaning is that there is *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitution of *āy* [for *ci*], and because of the designation *mit*, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*). Now, one might object:

the addition of the marker *ñ* to the root *ciñ* here is redundant, since the formation of both voices would already be established by the rule *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74) following a causative (*ṇi*-affix). This is because this root from the *curādika* group is invariably accompanied by the *ṇi*-affix, as in *cayati* and *cayate*.
Thus, because that which is solely the root-final (aṇyantam) is like the horn of a hare [i.e., non-existent], he says:

"By the force of the inclusion of the marker Ñ. And thus, in the absence of the causative suffix (ṇic), the inclusion of the marker Ñ here is purposeful for the sake of both word-meanings; such is the intention. [This applies] according to the rule: "In the remaining cases, optionally, provided it does not begin with k or kh."

Not considering [the root] *ṇatva* to be without alternative, he says: "praṇicayati" and "pranicayati. This refers to the rule of the *curādigaṇa*: "nānye mito'hetau. The analysis of the compound is "ahetau" (not when there is no cause).
When the expectation arises as to "in relation to what are they 'others'?", [the answer is] "prior to the *mit* roots."

It is understood [from the rule] "after roots such as *paṭh*, *jñap*, etc., ending in *ci*. Thus he says: "when *ṇic* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) and not for the sake of an external cause (*ahetau*)," and so forth. The explanation of the term "not for the sake of an external cause" is "when *ṇic* is used in its own sense. By this—meaning, by the prohibition of the *mit* designation for the *cur*-class roots other than those ending in *jñap*, *ādi*, and *ci*.

Regarding "of *śam* and so forth": this means of those roots such as *śam* (in the sense of "perceiving") and *am* (in the sense of "disease"), which will be listed later in the *curādi* group. Regarding "because of having *am* as an indicator": this means that [the rule] is caused by the fact of having *am* as an indicator, according to the rule *janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca*. *Kṛta*.
In the sense of "calling out" (*saṃśabdane*).
(398) *upadhāyāśca* | Pāṇini 7.1.101. [The word] *upadhāyāḥ* [is used]. The phrase *ṛta id dhātoḥ* is understood to carry over. Therefore, he says:

By the rule *dhātoḥ* etc., and by the rule *caṅi ṇer aṇau*, when the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is optionally *ṛ*, he says *acīkṛtat*. When the penultimate vowel is *ṛ*, after the doubling of *kṛt*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* occurs; then, because a light vowel follows, the *sanvadbhāva* applies, resulting in *it*-lengthening, and finally, by the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ*, the long vowel is substituted—this is the intended meaning. In the alternative case where the penultimate vowel is not *ṛ*:

He said: *acikīrtat*. The meaning is as follows: after [the substitution of] *i* for the final *an* and the substitution of *r* for the penultimate vowel (*raparatva*), the lengthening occurs by the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca"; then, after doubling the element *kīrt*, the *halādiśeṣa* rule applies, followed by the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsahrasva*) and the change of *t* to *c* (*cutva*).

Because there is no light vowel (*laghu*) following [the reduplicated syllable], the condition for the *sanvadbhāva* rule does not apply, and thus there is no lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.

Regarding the phrase "up to the ṭhak suffix" (*ṭhākusmāt*), he says "encompassing that" (*tamabhivyāpya*), considering that the particle *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Now, one might object:
since the reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established by the rule "after a root ending in ṇic" (*ṇicaśca*), its separate prescription here is redundant;

to this he replies: "not returning to the agent" (*akartṛgāmī*). Furthermore, one might ask: how can there be the form *daṃśati* in the sense of "biting" (*daṃśane*) when the causative suffix *ṇic* is absent?
Since the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings would be unavoidable even in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) due to the root belonging to the *ākusmīya* group, he says:
"the *ākusmīya* [group]. Anticipating the objection regarding the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule "ṭhdaṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapī," he says:

"in the case of the elision of *n*, [the form is] *sañjī*. Regarding the root *spaś* meaning "to perceive" (*grahaṇa*), [he gives the example] *apaspaśata*. [This is derived] by the rule "atsmṛdṛtvare."

The substitution of *a* for the penultimate vowel (*atva*) is an exception to the substitution of *i* (*itva*). The root *gūr* (in the sense of "lifting up") has a long vowel in its penultimate syllable;
thus, *gūrayate*. However, when it begins with *tad-* (as in *ta-gur*), the form is *gurī* (with a short vowel in the penultimate) in the sense of "lifting up.

Some maintain that in the *div-ādi* class, both *dhūrī* and *gūrī* have only a long vowel in the penultimate syllable in the senses of "injuring" and "going," while others hold they have a short vowel in the penultimate.

Thus say others. [The author] summarizes the distinction of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) according to the difference in meaning of the root *vid*: by the verse beginning with "it exists" (*vidyate*) in the sense of being (*sattā*), and so forth. Or, it may be the name of a noun (*nāman*). This is a *gaṇasūtra*. The word "kusme" is a separate word without a case ending. Thus he says: "the root 'kusma'."
The phrase "it occurs in the sense of contemptuous smiling" is a supplement to the text; the intention is that this is established through the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

Regarding *acukusmata*: because the vowel *u* is heavy (*guru*), the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) lacks the condition of being followed by a light vowel (*laghu-parakatva*), and thus the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were the suffix *san*) does not apply. [The word] "name" (*nāman*) is understood.

By virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*): thus, it follows that the suffix *ṇic* is applied either to the root *kusm-* or to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) *kusma-*. In that regard, intending the suffix *ṇic* to be *svārthika* (meaning-preserving) when applied to the root, he states the specific rule for its application to the nominal stem with the word "tat" (that). From that [nominal stem].

The meaning is "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the root-meaning" (*dhātvarthe*): this means in the sense of "he does" (*karoti*) or "he describes" (*ācaṣṭe*). Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṇic* is already established for a nominal stem by the rule "one who does that, one who describes that" (*tatkaroti tadācaṣṭe*), because [the present rule] is intended to restrict the occurrence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by the rule "from roots beginning with *ā-ku-smi* which are marked as taking the middle voice."

Thus end the rules concerning *ākusmīya*. Regarding the rule *śabda upasargāt*: the meaning is that the verbal root *śabda* occurs in the sense of "making manifest" when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). Regarding the rule *anupasargācca*:
the meaning is that the verbal root *śabda* also takes the causative suffix *ṇic* even when not preceded by a prefix.

The separate mention [of *āviṣkāre*] is for the purpose of ensuring the continued application of this very term. If it were stated merely as "in the sense of *āviṣkāra* (manifestation)," then [the suffix] would apply even to the act of speaking (*bhāṣaṇa*) when preceded by no prefix (*anupasarga*). Therefore, he says:
"only in the sense of *āviṣkāra*. Regarding the phrase "of *kāṇi* and so forth": this is a Vārttika.
This is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *bhrājabhāsabhāṣa-* etc.
The Bhāṣya says: "The six roots beginning with *kāṇi*—namely *kāṇi*, *rāṇi*, *śraṇi*, *bhaṇi*, *heṭhi*, and *lopi*—are the *ṣaṭkāṇyādayaḥ*.

Regarding the form *acīkaṇat*: the sense is that, according to the view that the root vowel is short, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) undergoes the *sanvat* treatment because it is followed by a light vowel (*laghuparakatvāt*).
Regarding "śaśapoḥ": this means in the case of the *śap* and *śa* verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). Regarding "hantyarthāśca":
this is a *gaṇasūtra*. For the root *han*, in the sense of "to kill" and "to go," the meanings are killing and movement.
All those roots having these meanings that are listed in the nine classes (*gaṇas*) beginning with *bhū* are [included].

The meaning is that they are to be understood as recited in the *cur*-class (the tenth class). Consequently, it follows that the causative suffix *ṇic* also optionally occurs after them in their own sense (*svārthe*). He states this with the words "navagaṇyām" and so forth. [The root] *div* [is used] in the sense of "crushing.
