Regarding "because it is marked with *u*": the addition of the marker *u* is for the purpose of [triggering the rule] "udito vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.56).

The suffix *ktvā* is mentioned for the purpose of allowing an optional *iṭ*. Examples: *dyūtvā*, *devitvā*. In the absence of *iṭ*, *ūṭh* is applied. However, when *iṭ* is present, the established rule is that there is *guṇa* substitution because the prohibition of *kitva* by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" does not apply here. Since this root is invariably *ṇi*-ant (ending in *ṇic*), the optional *iṭ* of *ktvā* is blocked by the intervention of *ṇic*.

The sense is that the mention of *udita* (the *udittva* designation) is purposeless since [the rule] does not apply; rather, it indicates that for this root *ghuṣ*, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the suffix *ṇic*. [The root] *ghuṣir* is used in the sense of "making known" (*viśabdane*).

"Making known" (*viśabdana*) means either the manifestation of one's own intention by means of sound, or a formal promise (*pratijñāna*). However, in the *Bhvādi* class, this [root is defined differently].

The verbal root *ghuṣ* is recited as having the meaning "not making sound. [In the rule] *ghoṣayati*, the meaning is that one makes manifest one's own intention by means of sound, or alternatively, that one promises. Regarding the phrase "on account of the indicative mark" (*liṅgāt*), it refers to the rule *ghuṣir aviśabdane* within the section concerning the prohibition of the suffix *iṇ*.

The meaning is that the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix *kta*) shall not take the augment *iṭ* after the root *ghuṣ*, when it does not mean "making a sound. For example: *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope is stretched out"); the meaning is "extended. Why specify "when not meaning making a sound"? Consider: *avaghuṣitaṃ vākyam* ("the statement was proclaimed"); the meaning is "asserted. In this case, because the root has the sense of "making a sound," there is no prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.

As for the word *sthiti*: in that context, since the root *ghuṣ* meaning "uttering" belongs to the *curādika* (tenth) class, it is necessarily *ṇij*-ant; because of this intervention by the *ṇic*, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) cannot follow it at all. Thus, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of "uttering" (*viśabdana*) within the prohibition of *iṇ* is rendered purposeless.
This [usage] indicates that for the root *ghuṣ*, which belongs to the *cur*-class and has the meaning of "making known" (*viśabdana*), the application of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is optional.

And thus, it is clear in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the expression "*avaghuṣitaṃ vākyam*" that there is no prohibition of the augment *iṭ* after the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) when the *ghuṣ* belonging to the *cur*-class has the meaning of "making known. Consequently, by virtue of its being marked with the indicatory letter *ṛ* (in *ghuṣir*), the suffix *aṅ* is optionally applied.

The phrase "in the case where the causative suffix (ṇic) is absent" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Now, one might object: since the optionality of the causative suffix (ṇic) is already established by the fact that the root is marked with the indicatory letter *i* (irit), the effort in the Bhāṣya to rely on the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not in the sense of sound" (*aviśabdane*) in the rule prohibiting *iṇ*—"ghuṣir aviśabdane"—as an indicator for the optionality of the causative suffix is redundant. This is not so; for it is precisely for this reason...

Because the *Bhāṣya* and other works state that there is no [application of] *itva*. Thus, in the rule "ghuṣir aviśabdane," one must rely on the fact that the form "ghuṣiḥ" is indicated with an *ik* vowel (i.e., as ending in *i*), and therefore its status as a nominative singular (*prathamānta*) alone must be accepted.
As for the root text stating "because of *itva*, there is *aṅ*," that should be disregarded due to its contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*; let this matter rest.

"tāvat| āṅḥ kranda sātatye" means that the prefix *āṅ* [when used] before the root *krand* receives the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of continuous calling. Alternatively, immediately after "āṅ," the word "ghuṣi" is understood [from a previous rule]; thus, [the meaning is] "in the sense of continuous calling."

Such is the indication of the meaning. He says this with the words "others, however. Regarding *lasa* in the sense of "application to craft," the meaning is "skill. Regarding *tasi* in the sense of "ornamentation," here *tasi* is generally preceded by *ava*. He says this with the words "it adorns (*avataṃsayati*). Regarding *jñā* in the sense of "employment," it is preceded by *āṅ*. He says this with the words—

Regarding "ājñāpayati": because the root ends in /ā/, the augment *puk* is applied. *Ajijñapat*. Regarding "yata nikāre": it begins with a palatal (*tālavya*) and a semi-vowel (*antaḥ-stha*). Effort or an order is "nikāra. *Yātayati*. *Ayīyatat*. Regarding "añca viśeṣaṇe": the meaning is "in distinguishing" (or turning away). Regarding "uditvam": [it refers to the fact that the root is marked with *u*].

The meaning is that [the root] *ṭhud* is cited in its non-causative (*aṇyant*) form for the purpose of allowing an option regarding the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā*. The intention is that, however, from the causative (*ṇyant*) form, there is no possibility of an optional *iṭ* because of the intervention of the causative suffix *ṇic*. Now, one might object that since this root is not invariably non-causative, its status as non-causative is unestablished; therefore, he says: "For this very reason," etc. [He cites] *cyu*.

Regarding *sahane*: [the root *cyu*] means "to cause to move. *Acucyavat*. Regarding *bhuvo'vakalkane*: the meaning is that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to the root *bhū* when it has the sense of "preparing" (*avakalkana*). Regarding *kṛpeśca*: the meaning is that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to the root *kṛp* when it has the sense of "preparing" (*avakalkana*). Regarding *kalpayati*: [this refers to the rule] *ṭhkṛpo ro...* [where the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* occurs].

The substitution of *la* for *ra* is indicated by the rule "laḥ. Regarding the phrase "from *ā-svad*, provided it is transitive," the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Thus he says: "including *svadi*. In that context, since the root *ṣvada* in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*) is intransitive, he specifies: "from those [roots] which can be transitive. From this point onward, the roots beginning with *ā-svad* are transitive.
One whose own skin is his object [of action]. "Paṭa-puṭa" (cloth-bag). There are thirty-one roots. The first three end in *ṣ*.

The first and second belong to the beginning of the *pa*-group (*pavarga*). Eleven begin with the fourth [consonant] and end in *i*. Some say that *tri*, *si*, and *pi* have *i* as their penultimate vowel; others say they have *a* as their penultimate vowel. The sixteenth and seventeenth are not well-known.
In the case of *alulokat* and *alulocat*, where the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) would otherwise apply—(399) *nāglopiśāsvṛditām* 7.4.2.
[The rule begins with] *nāglopi*. The phrase *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* is understood to carry over. The word *ṇau* is repeated.

The first [part of the rule], *aglopinah*, connects with the preceding [rule]; the second, however, serves as a prohibition regarding the cause that follows. Thus he says: "In the case of a *ṇic* suffix, when there is no elision of *a* (*aglopa*), etc. Regarding *alulokat*: because it contains an *ṛt* vowel (*ṛdit*), the prohibition "when there is no elision of *a*" (*an-aglopi*) applies;

consequently, since the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) does not become short, the condition of being followed by a light syllable (*laghu-parakatva*) is absent, and thus the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrgha*) does not occur.
This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "because it is marked with *u*": the root *vṛt* (in the form *vṛtu* / *vṛdhu*) is marked with *u*.

According to the rule *udito vā*, this marking serves to allow for the optional insertion of the augment *iṭ* after the non-causative (*aṇyantāt*) form when the suffix *ktvā* follows. However, in the case of the causative (*ṇyantāt*), because of the intervention of the *ṇic* suffix, there would be no occasion for the optional application of *iṭ*; therefore, it is understood that the optionality refers to the *ṇic* suffix itself.
[The root] *bhū* [is mentioned]. [The root] *pūrī* means "to fill. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the prohibition of *iṇ*":

the status of being marked with *īt* (īditva) is for the purpose of prohibiting *iṇ* after the suffix *ktvā* when the root is not followed by *ṇic*. Since there is no possibility [of the application of *iṇ*] after a root followed by *ṇic* due to the intervention of *ṇic*, the meaning is that the optionality of *ṇic* is thus understood. [This concerns] the root *svad*.
This is a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*). Thus it says: *asiṣvadat*. Because the substitute (*ādeśa*) has a *s*, [the original] becomes *ṣ*.

Due to the weight (*gurutva*) of the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), as it is followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsadīrghaḥ*). As for the phrase "but of the long [vowel]," the meaning is "but of that which has a long vowel in the middle. [The rule applies] because it is not a *ṣopadeśa*; [this refers specifically] to that which has a short vowel in the middle.
The point is that among the *ṣopadeśa* roots, [the root *svad*] is counted as belonging to the latter group. Thus end the [rules] belonging to [the author of the] *Ākhyāta*.

"Up to *dhṛṣ* optionally" (*ā dhṛṣād vā*) is a *gaṇasūtra*. "Those having optional *ṇic*" (*vibhāṣitaṇicaḥ*) means they are to be understood as having an optional *ṇic* suffix. Thinking that the prefix *āṅ* signifies pervasion (*abhivyāpti*), he says:

"Extending up to the root *dhṛṣ*. Regarding the alternative view that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent, he says: "He sacrificed" (*ayaukṣīt*). "The root *arc* means 'to worship'. According to Śākaṭāyana, this root is *anudāteta* (unaccented on the first syllable). Thus, one has *arcayate* and *arcate*.
Its inclusion in the *bhvādi* class is not authoritative (*anārṣa*), since its formation is established by this very [rule]; nor is it for the sake of the *parasmaipada* (active voice).

It should be stated that the root *arc* is listed in the *bhvādi* class; for Mādhava states that even in the *bhvādi* class, its status as an ātmanepada verb is according to the opinion of Śākaṭāyana.
Likewise, the roots belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group are listed here in the *bhvādi* class among the parasmaipada verbs.

They say that this is merely an error. [The root] *lī* means "to liquefy. Regarding the form *lāyayati*: the augment *nuṭ* does not apply here because, due to its association with *lā* (as in *lā-sā-hacaryāt*), it applies only to the causative (*hetu-maṇṇic*). Regarding *letā*: the substitution of *ā* (by the rule *vibhāṣā līyateḥ*) does not occur, because in that rule the reference is specifically to the roots ending in the *śnā* and *śyan* suffixes.

Thus, from the Bhāṣya: the root *vṛñ* means "to cover. The forms are *varitā* and *varītā*; the long vowel [in *varītā*] occurs by the rule *vṛto vā*. In the āśīr-liṅ (optative), the form is *vriyāt*. However, in the ātmanepada, there is optionally *iṭ* by the rule *liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu*. Thus, we have *vṛṣīṣṭa* or *variṣīṣṭa*. In the absence of *iṭ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *uśca*. Not...

In the case of the suffix *liṅ*, there is no lengthening of the *iṭ* augment. [The roots] *avṛt* and *ajri* are short-voweled. [The root] *ric* means "to separate"; it is *aniṭ*. Consequently, when the causative (*ṇic*) is absent, there is no *iṭ* augment. Thus he says: *rekte*. [The root] *śiṣ* means "not all"; this too is *aniṭ*. Thus he says: *śeṣṭa*. [The form] *aśikṣat*.

The suffix *ksa* is applied by the rule *igupadhāt kaḥ*. This [root] is preceded by the prefix *vi-* in the sense of "excess"; the word "occurs" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the expression "this is superior to that," the sense of "surpassing" (*adhika*) is understood. Regarding the root *tṛp* in the sense of "satisfaction": because it is indicated with the marker *śyan* among the roots that do not take the augment *iṭ*, this root is *seṭ* (possessing the augment). Thus he says: "tarpita. [The following is from the *chﬁadī* section.]

Regarding "saṃdīpane" (in the sense of setting on fire): the designation *īdit* is for the purpose of prohibiting the augment *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffix. Regarding "dhuvati" and "sphuṭitā": these are forms of the verbal root with the *śap* vikaraṇa. Because *ś* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign, there is no *guṇa* substitution, resulting in *uviṅ*. Regarding "prīñ" in the sense of satisfying: "prīṇayati" [is formed] because of the *vārttika* rule "dhūñ-prīñoḥ," which prescribes the augment *nuk*.

The meaning is as follows: by the phrase "Haradatta," it is indicated that this view is not supported by the Bhāṣya. Regarding the rule *upasargāt ca*: the meaning is that the root *tan* should be understood as being applicable after both prefixes (*upasarga*) and non-prefixes (*anupasarga*), provided it belongs to the *ā-dṛṣi* group. However, the intention is that in the case of *śraddha* and *upakrama*, the suffix applies only after a non-prefix. [End of] *vaca*.

Regarding *paribhāṣaṇe*: [the form] *avākṣīt* is used; the sense is that there is no *aṅ* substitute because of the indication [in the sūtra] by the elision (*luk*) in the rule *ṭhasyātivaktī*. There is *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule *vacisvapi-* [etc.], resulting in *ucyāt*. Thus end the roots belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group. Now, regarding "those ending in *a*": the word "will be explained" (*vakṣyante*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The letter *a* at the end is not designated by the technical term *it*.

The sense is that it is not for the purpose of pronunciation either. In that regard, from the root *kath* with the suffix *ṇic*, after the elision of the vowel *a* (by *ato lopaḥ*), from the form *kathi*, [the suffix] *tip* is added; then, with *śap*, there is *guṇa*, and by the substitution of *ay*, the form *kathayati* will be stated. Having raised the objection regarding the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) based on the presence of *ṇic*, he says: "of the elision of *a*" (*allopasya*).

"By virtue of the status of being a substitute" (sthānivadbhāvāt). The intention is that this is by means of the rule *acaḥ parasmin*. Here, this should be noted: it is precisely that grammatical operation which occurs when the original element (*sthānin*) is present that is extended to the substitute (*ādeśa*) by the rule *sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau*; however, that which [occurs] when the original element is present...
Because the destruction of the cause (nimitta-vyāghāta) occurs, that absence [of the substitute] is not sanctioned by the treatise (aśāstrīya), and therefore there is no extension (atideśa).
Otherwise, in the case of *nāyaka*, the substitution of *āy* for the *ai* that stands in place of the *ī* would not be possible;
for since the absence of *āy* is observed when *ī* is the original element (*sthānin*), it would likewise apply to *ai*.

Because of the context of extended application (*atideśa*). However, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭhacaḥ parasmin* that when there is a substituend (*sthānin*), there is an extended application (*atideśa*) not only of that grammatical operation (*śāstrīya-kārya*) which would otherwise apply, but also of its absence, even if that absence is not itself prescribed by a grammatical rule (*aśāstrīya*). Therefore, in this case, regarding the vowel *a* following the letter *th*:

It is established that even though the absence of vowel-lengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*) for what is applicable [by analogy] is not sanctioned by the grammatical treatise (*aśāstrīya*), there is nonetheless an extension (*atideśa*) of it. Regarding the rule *luṅ-ciṇ-ṭi-cakārāt* (Pāṇini 1.1.61), having raised the doubt as to whether the treatment of *san* (*sanvadbhāva*) might apply here, he says: "because of the absence of the elided penultimate vowel" (*aglopitvāt*). The lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) that occurs in the domain of *sanvadbhāva* [is blocked].

The separate mention [of the word *na*] is because it is not required [in other cases]. This should be understood to apply everywhere, starting with the root *var*. Regarding the root *gaṇ* (meaning "to count"):

since the substitution of *il* by *caṅ* would be treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, there would be an absence of both the long vowel (*dīrgha*) and the *sanvadbhāva* operations; thus, when one might expect only *ajagaṇat*, he says: [the rule applies].

(400) *ī ca gaṇaḥ* | 7|4|97| The rule *ī ca gaṇaḥ* follows from *sanvallaghuni* [6.1.31] by the term *caṅpare*, and from *atra lope* [6.1.56] by the term *abhyāsasya*. Thus he says: "of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of the root *gaṇ*."

The term *at* is drawn over from the preceding sūtra (*ṭhatsmṛdṛtvarē*) by means of the particle *ca*. Thus he says: "and *at*. Regarding *stanagadī devaśabde*: the meaning is "in the sense of the thundering of Parjanya.
*Stanagadī* is a *dvandva* compound. The form *gadī* is specified with the vowel *i*.

In the case of *gadi*, because the final vowel is elided (*alopa*), the form is cited as *gadī*; thus, its status as ending in a short *a* (as required by the context) is not contradicted. Regarding *pata gatau vā*: this means that in the sense of "going," the root *pat* optionally takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*). This is what he states: "optionally ending in *ṇic*."

Because there is no possibility of being overridden, this is an optional rule (*vikalpavidhi*). Alternatively, the word *vā* is construed only with the state of having a final *a* (*adantatva*). The causative suffix (*ṇic*), however, is indeed obligatory. Thus he says: "Some say that *vā* applies when [the root] ends in *a*. In the first alternative, however, there is only the state of ending in *a*. Thus he says: "In the first case, *patayati*. Due to the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, [the substitution does not apply].

Regarding *vṛddhi*: [the form] *patāñcakāra*. Even in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), because the root ends in /a/, the rule *kāsyanekāj* [Pāṇini 3.1.35] applies, which is the intended meaning. Regarding *caṅ*: [the form] *apapatat*. Because the root is *aglopi* (having its penultimate vowel elided), there is neither lengthening nor the *sanvadbhāva* treatment. Regarding the second [form], *pātayati*: since the vowel /a/ after the letter /t/ is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding *apīpatat*: the intention is that because there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*aglopi*), the rules for lengthening and the treatment as having *san* (i.e., *sanyataḥ*) apply. Regarding *kṛpayati*:

since this root ending in *-ad* is a distinct root [from *kṛp*], the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* does not apply. *Spṛh* means "desire" (*īpsā*); "desire" is the wish to obtain. Regarding *ababhāmat*: [this refers to] the elision of the *caṅ* suffix.

Because of the status as *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāhrasvaḥ*). [The root] *sūc* is used in the sense of "backbiting" (*paiśunye*). [The statement] "because it is not an *aṣopadeśa*" means that it is not a root taught with an initial *aṣ*; the intention is that it consists of more than one vowel (*anekāctvāt*). [The root] *kheṭ* is used in the sense of "eating" (*bhakṣaṇe*). [The phrase] "ending in the third [consonant]" means ending in the third consonant of the *ṭavarga*. [The root] *sām* is used in the sense of "employing conciliation" (*sāntvaprayoge*). "Employing conciliation" (*sāntvaprayogaḥ*) refers to...

"Speaking without harshness. Regarding *asasāma*, [the form] does not undergo the shortening of the penultimate vowel because the elision (*lopa*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). Now, one might object: "The inclusion of the root *sāma* in the *curādi* (X) class, prior to the *kathādi* (III) group—meaning 'to conciliate' (*sāntvana*)—is redundant, since the desired form is established by this very rule. To this, he replies: "But regarding the [root] *sāma* in the sense of 'conciliating' (*sāntvana*)... [which belongs to the *tudādi* class].

*asīṣamat*. In the root *sām* previously mentioned, because the vowel *a* following the letter *m* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārthatayā*), there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasva*) and the lengthening of the vowel before the suffix *san* (*dīrghasanvatve*).
Although this root was previously listed in the *curādi* class simply as "to conciliate" (*sāma sāntvaprayoge*), nevertheless, [the form] of conciliation...

The sense is that such a statement is made because [the form] is not different from the application of the *sāman* [suffix]. "Seeking" (*gaveṣa*) means searching or investigation. Due to the status of the elision (*ilopa*) as *sthānivadbhūta*, there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāhrasva*). Thus he says: "ajagaveṣat. [The root] *ni-vās* means to cover; [the form] is *aninivāsat*. [The root] *ūn* means to diminish.

*Parihāṇam* means "becoming diminished" (*nyūnībhāvaḥ*). It is derived from the root *ūnayati*; the sense is that the suffix *ṇic* is elided according to the rule *ṇer aṇau*. Now, one might object: when the form *luṅ-ciṅ-ūni-a-t* is established, after the elision of *ṇic*, by the rule *caṅi* [the reduplication applies] to the second syllable beginning with a vowel; thus, there is reduplication of the syllable *na*, followed by the elision of *at*. Consequently, because it is an *aglopi* (one where a vowel is elided), [the rule *sanvallaghuni caṅpare...* would not apply].

It will be stated that because *sanvat* does not apply, there is an absence of *it* and *dīrgha* in the case of reduplication; consequently, after the *vṛddhi* of *āṬ*, the form will be *āṬnanad*. However, this is untenable, because the *lopa* of *a* (by *ato lopaḥ*) would apply first due to its higher priority, and once the word *ni-* has been reduplicated, the result would be *āṬninad*, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of hearing the vowel *i* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Nor is it the case that...

When the doubling [of the penultimate consonant] is to be applied, one might suspect that the prohibition in the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* would block the elision (*lopa*) of the *y*. However, the inclusion of the letter *p* (in *pu*), the pratyāhāra *yaṇ*, and the letter *j*—when it could have been stated simply as *allopapavayor aparaḥ*—is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Where? [In the rule *aco ra ṛtaḥ*. The connection is as follows: if the intention were merely to state *allopapavayor aparaḥ*, then the mention of *pu* (to include the *p*-class), *yaṇ* (the pratyāhāra), and *j* would be redundant. Their inclusion serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that the prohibition of *dvirvacane 'ci* does not apply here. Where? In the context of the rule *aco ra ṛtaḥ*. [Note: The term *dvirvacane 'ci* prohibits doubling when a vowel follows. The argument is that since the elision of *y* occurs before a vowel (*aci*), this rule might prevent the subsequent doubling of the preceding consonant. The author argues that the specific wording of the sūtra *puṅavaḥ*—which includes *p*, *yaṇ*, and *j*—indicates that such a prohibition does not apply in this specific case.]

To provide the reason for this, he says: "In the case of *ṇic*, etc. The connection with the preceding statement is as follows: when a doubling (*dvitva*) is to be applied, there should be no substitution of a vowel (*ac*) caused by the presence of *ṇic*. This is the evidence (*liṅga*). To illustrate: there is the rule "ṭhoḥ puyaṇjyapare" (Pāṇini 7.4.80). [The commentary continues: "When *san* follows, that which is the base (*aṅga*..."
"The vowel *i* shall replace the vowel *a* belonging to that [root] when followed by the *pa*-group, *yaṇ*, or the letter *j*, provided these follow a vowel. Thus: from *ṭhap*, *pipāvayiṣati*;
from *ṭhbhū*, *bibhāvayiṣati*; from *ṭhyu*, *yiyāvayiṣati*; from *ṭhru*, *rirāvayiṣati*.

Examples are *lilāvayiṣati* (from the root *lū*) and *jijavayiṣati* (from the root *ju*). Here, regarding the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, since that prohibition does not apply to the causative (*ṇic*) which is the cause for the doubling, the rules for vṛddhi and āv-ādeśa take effect before the doubling due to their higher priority; consequently, there is an *ākāra* in the reduplicated syllables (*abhyāsa*).

Since the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] would already be established by the rule *sanyataḥ* when a suffix beginning with *san* follows, the inclusion of the letter *j*—which belongs to the pratyāhāra *yaṇ* consisting of the *pa*-class and *ya*—is redundant. However, the inclusion of *pa* and *ya* is not redundant; for although the shortening is established by *sanyataḥ* in cases such as *pipāvayiṣati* and *yiyāvayiṣati* according to the aforementioned method, it is not so established in *pipaviṣate*.

In the case of *yiyaviṣati*, [the rule] is necessary for the sake of *it* (the substitution of *i*) after the roots *pū* and *yū* when followed by *san* that is not preceded by a prefix (*aṇ-antāt*), because in that context— due to the *kit* status of *san* by the rule *iko jhal*, the prohibition of *iṭ* obtained by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* is set aside by the rule *smipūṅrañjvaśāṃ sani*.

When the augment *iṭ* is applied by the two rules "sanīvantarddhabhrasjadambhuśrisvṛyūrṇubharajñapisanām" and [the subsequent rule], since the *sana* beginning with *iṭ* is the cause for reduplication, the *iṭ* itself also becomes a cause for reduplication; consequently, by the rule "dvirvacane'ci," the prohibition of the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* applies.

When there is doubling of these two [roots] *ṭhpū* and *ṭhyu*, since the vowel *a* is absent in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the rule *sanyataḥ* does not apply; therefore, the mention of *payayaḥ* is necessary for the sake of that *it*-designation (*it-saṃjñā*).
The inclusion of the letter *ja* from the varga-pratyāhāra [is intended] so that, when doubling is to be performed, the substitute [of the root] remains in place of *ṇau*.

If this [rule] were not resorted to, it would be entirely useless. However, when it is resorted to, in cases such as *bibhāvayiṣati* and others, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is elided, and when the doubling (*dvitva*) is to be applied by the rule "caṅi," one must resort to the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇam*).

Consequently, when the prohibition of *guṇa* and *avādeśa* applies to the causative suffix, there is doubling of those ending in *u*, with the result that the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) ends in *u*.

Because the vowel *a* is absent, the rule *sanyataḥ* does not apply; therefore, the inclusion of the letter *ja* from the *vargapratyāhāra* (the *jha* group) is purposeful. Consequently, the meaning is that when the operation of doubling (*dvitva*) is to be performed, no substitution of *ṇa* for *ca* occurs. Now, [one might object] regarding the root *kṛt* in the sense of "making noise" (*saṃśabdana*), when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*:
The form *acikīrtat* is desired [by some] on the basis of the rule *ṭhūpadhāyāśca*, which prescribes lengthening; however, that is not tenable.

For when reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be performed, since the substitution of the penultimate vowel (*aca ādeśa*) is prohibited in the presence of the causative suffix *ṇic*, the reduplication of the root *kṛt* occurs first.

Then, after the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratvam*), the replacement of *r* by *a* (*raparatvam*), the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣaḥ*), and the substitution of *c* for *k* (*cutvam*), the following segment [is obtained].
Because [the forms] *ṛtīyate*, *raparatva*, and *upadhādīrgha* would result in the undesirable form *acakīrtat*, he says:

"In cases where there is reduplication," and so forth. This means that in a verbal root where, after reduplication has been applied in the *caṅ* (aorist) formation, the first vowel of the subsequent portion of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsottarakhaṇḍa*) is an *avarṇa* (a-vowel), only in such cases is the substitution of *ac* for the *ṇi* (causative suffix) prohibited when the process of reduplication is to be performed.

The construction is "there is a prohibition. Although, when reduplication is applied to a single-vowel (*ekāc*) constituent of a verbal root, the first vowel (*ādyo 'j*) [of the second part] is redundant because there is no second vowel in the portion following the reduplication, nevertheless, they say that it is stated for the sake of clarity. Now, an initial vowel (*aj-varṇa*) is indeed obtained in the portion following the reduplication.

In this regard, is the vowel *a* intended at the time of the application of reduplication, or is it intended in the final, established form? It cannot be the first, because in the case of *cukṣāvayiṣati*— derived from the root *kṣu* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the desiderative suffix (*san*)—
once reduplication has been applied to "kṣu," within the subsequent portion of the reduplicated syllable...

In the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), since the vowel *a* is absent, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *ā* would not apply; consequently, because the rule for doubling (*dvitva*) would operate first, and the rules for *vṛddhi* and *ā* substitution would follow due to their higher status, the form *kṣau* would undergo doubling, resulting in the undesired outcome *cikṣāvayiṣati*. Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because when the state *ūna i a t* has been reached...

If one were to apply the doubling (*dvitva*) of *ṭhna*, and after the elision of the *al* in the subsequent portion of the reduplicated stem, there were an absence of the vowel *a*, then because of that absence, the prohibition of the elision of *ṇa* would not apply; consequently, the elision of *at* would take effect first due to its higher priority, and then upon doubling *nī*, the form *āuṇanad* would result—therefore, he says: "In the process of derivation... (*prakriyāyām*).

The phrase "or in the completed form" (*pariniṣṭhite rūpe*) means that there is no insistence that it must occur only in that specific [intermediate] stage. The intention is that, in the case of *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *jaṃ* [substitutes], there is a rule requiring a vowel (*avarṇa*) to follow in the subsequent part (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) of the word when it is of the same class (*sajātīya*). As for the word "established" (*siddham*), it is because in the subsequent part—whether during the process of derivation (*prakriyā*) or in the final form (*pariniṣṭhite*)—there is no occurrence of the vowel *ṛ*.
The meaning is that there is no prohibition regarding the *it* (the augment). And thus, in the case of *cukṣāvayiṣati*,

although there is an absence of the vowel *a* in the posterior portion of the reduplicated syllable during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*) when "kṣu" is doubled, because that [vowel] exists in the final form (*pariniṣṭhita-rūpa*), the prohibition indeed applies when the doubling is to take effect after the substitution of *guṇa* and *avādeśa* have occurred following the suffix *ṇi*.

He states that even in the case of *āṬ nanat*, the prohibition of *al*-elision indeed applies after the substitution of *ṇi*—this is what he means by "but in the present case. [The phrase] "of the word *na*" means: if one resorts to the doubling of the word *na* even before the elision of *al*, then because the vowel *a* (avarṇa) is obtained in the subsequent portion during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), there is a prohibition of the *al*-elision.
The meaning is that there is doubling only of the word *na*, and not of the word *ni*. Regarding the word *tataḥ*:

the meaning is that after the doubling of the word *na*, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) occurs in the subsequent portion. In this context, the fact that the root *ūna* ends in *a* is established solely for the purpose of doubling the word *na*; there is no other result.

Indicating this, he says: "May you not [pronounce] *ūna*. The intention is that because the root is *aglopi* (one whose penultimate vowel is elided), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāhrasva*).
Regarding the "alternative reading" (*pāṭhāntara*), the meaning is that one should understand [the root] as beginning with "ṭhketa śrāvaṇe" and so forth.
From the word "ca" (and), the word "ket" is included; the ellipsis is "is added together" (*samuccīyate*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of contraction" (*saṅkocane*), [the following applies].

The word *iti* marks the end of an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). [Regarding] *stena*, it means "theft" (*caurya*). Thinking that this is not a *ṣopadeśa* root because it has multiple vowels (*anekāctvāt*), he says: "atistenat. [Regarding] *gṛha*, it means "seizing" (*grahaṇa*). This root has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). In the form *gṛhyate*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the *allopa* (elision of *a*) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.

The state [of the root]. *luṅ* [aorist]: *ijagṛhata*. Because of the elision of the penultimate vowel (*aglopitva*), there is no *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the reduplication of the *san* desiderative). *mṛg* in the sense of "searching": *mṛgayate*. Here too, because of the status of the elided vowel as *sthānivadbhūta*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. However, regarding the root *mārg* in the sense of "searching" belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group, both *mārgayati* and *mārgati* have already been explained. Meaning.

In the sense of "begging" (*upayācñā*), [the form] *arthayate* is derived as follows: when *artha-i* remains, the elision of the final vowel (*ato lopaḥ*) applies; however, the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by the rule *aco ñṇiti* does not apply, according to the maxim that "elision is stronger than *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, the suffix *āpuk* (as in *arthāpayati*) does not apply here, because that rule refers to nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [The term] *garva*...

In the sense of "pride" (māne), meaning "conceit" (abhimāne). Now, one might object that its inclusion in the list beginning with *kath* is useless, since there is no result from its being stem-final (*adanta*). Nor should it be suspected that its being stem-final is intended to prevent the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule and thereby ensure it is not *aglopi*; for that [application of *sanvadbhāva*] is impossible precisely because the following vowel is not light (*laghu*). Nor [is it for the sake of preventing] the elision of *a* (*allopa*).

One might suspect that the inclusion of the letter *a* at the end [of the root] is for the purpose of preventing the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel by means of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*; however, this is not to be feared, because such an application would not even arise since the vowel *a* following the letter *g* is not a penultimate vowel. Therefore, he says:
"By the force of its being *adanta*, there is an option regarding the suffix *ṇic*. But [one might ask]: in the case of *garvate*,...
Since the state of having a final *a* (adantatva) would be useless even in the case of the causative (*ṇij*) meaning, how could it serve as an indicator for the optionality [of the suffix]?

To this, he says: "The final vowel of the root is acute" (*dhātoranta udātaḥ*). By this, in the form *garvate*, the vowel following the *v* (the *a*) becomes acute; however, in the absence of the final *a*, the vowel following the *g* (the *a*) would be acute.

The sense is: "it might be. Regarding the rule *liṭaḷam ca*: in the example *agarvācakre*, the meaning is that the suffix *ām*—prescribed by the rule *kāsyanekācaḥ*—is also a result of the stem ending in the vowel *a*. Otherwise, because the stem would lack more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), the suffix *ām* would not occur; this is the intended sense. The same applies in the subsequent cases as well, such as *mūtra*.
The meaning is "in *prasravaṇa*," and so forth. Thus say the followers of Āgava. [The root] *sūtra* means "to wrap.
Because it has more than one vowel (*anekāc*) and because it is not taught with an initial *ṣ* (*aṣopadeśa*), its final vowel is short *a*; therefore, there is no optional *ṇic* suffix after it.
[The root] *katra* means "laxity. It is also *kartṛ*. By virtue of its having a short final *a*, this...

Thinking that this is without suffixal variation (*ṇij-vikalpa*), he says: "it causes to act" (*kartayati*) or "it acts" (*kartati*). This is a rule from the *curādi* class [of roots] regarding the formation of verbal bases (*dhātu*) from nominal stems (*prātipadika*). The suffix *-vat* is applied here in the sense of "like," following the example of the word *iṣṭhavat*, which ends in the locative case. Consequently, in the form *bhāvayati* (meaning "he describes existence"), the augment *yiṭ* does not occur, as per the rule "for *iṣṭha*, there is *yiṭ*."

He says this [in the verse]: "as in the case of *iṣṭha*. Here, by the phrase "in the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthe*), there is included [the suffixes] expressing instrumentality, narration, seeing, speaking, hearing, and so forth. Regarding the term "puṃvadbhāva" (masculine-like behavior): in the example *paṭiṣṭhā* ("most clever"), there is masculine-like behavior according to the rule *bhasyāḍhea*. In the example *draḍhiṣṭha*, [there is masculine-like behavior] according to the rule *ra ṛtaḥ*.
In *sādhiṣṭha* ("most excellent"), there is the substitution of *ra* for the vowel by the rule *halāderlaghoḥ*.

In *srajiṣṭha* ("most garlanded"), there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix by the rule *ṭerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ* (or as implied here, the elision of the *ṭi*). In *srajiṣṭha*, the suffix *vin* is elided by the rule *ṭhvinmatorluk*.
In *gaviṣṭha* ("most possessing cows"), there is the elision of the suffix *matup*. [The process continues] with "most... [possessing].

In forms such as *sthūlaḥ* and *sthaviṣṭhaḥ*, the elision of the semivowel (*yaṇādi-lopa*) and the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel for the preceding sound occur by the rule *ṭhsthūladūrayuvetyādinā*. In forms such as *preṣṭhaḥ* (from *atiśayena priyaḥ*), the substitution of *pra* and *stha* occurs by the rule *priyasthiretyādinā*. In the case of *srajiṣṭhaḥ* (from *atiśayena sragvī*), [the same applies].

Because [the word] ends in a vowel (bh), there is no substitution of *ku*. The meaning is that these [substitutions] occur even when followed by the suffix *ṇi*, just as they do when followed by the suffix *iṣṭhan*.

In the example *paṭayati*, the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "he speaks clearly" (*paṭum ācaṣṭe*), and so forth. The intention is that because of the status of being like *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) by the rule *ṭer lopaḥ*.

Now, one might object: "If the *ukāra* is elided as part of the *ṭi*, then because the stem becomes *aglopi* (one whose penultimate vowel has been elided), the condition for *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the suffix *san*) would not apply."
To address this, he says: "Since [the suffix] *para* (the subsequent element) takes precedence, when the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] has occurred, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi*.

When the *vṛddhi* of the vowel *u* has been applied by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* of the vowel *e*; however, when the *vṛddhi* has not occurred, there is the elision of the *ṭi* of the vowel *u*. Consequently, [this results in] a different word-form.

According to the maxim "a rule that applies when another rule is applicable is non-eternal" (*prāpnuvan-vidhir-anityaḥ*), the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is non-eternal. Furthermore, since the vowel increment (*vṛddhi*) does not occur once the elision of the *ṭi* has already taken place, that increment is also non-eternal. Thus, between the two—vowel increment and the elision of the *ṭi*—the increment of the letter *u* into the letter *au* occurs because it is subsequent in application.

The meaning is that, because it is subsequent and because a rule pertaining to a suffix (āṅga) is stronger than one pertaining to a phoneme (vārṇa), the *ṭi* portion of the vowel *au* is elided even before the substitution of *av*. Thus, considering that the root is not *anaglopi* (one whose penultimate vowel is not elided), the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the *san* suffix) applies;
with this in mind, he says "apīpaṭat. This point is found in both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *muṇḍamiśra*.

This is clear. Regarding the word "sthitam" (it remains): thus, since the *u* of the root *vṛdh* is elided prior to the *vṛddhi*, it is not treated as having an elided *a*-portion (*aglopitva*), and therefore there is no application of the *sanvat* rule; this is the meaning. It should be understood that because both views are seen in the Bhāṣya, both forms are correct. However, in the *Śabdenduśekhara*, it is stated: "In the case of *ṇi*, the elision is stronger than the *vṛddhi*."

The *sūtra-bhāṣya* on the rule "caṅi" is itself the authority. However, it has been explained in detail that the *sūtra-bhāṣya* on "muṇḍamiśra" represents the view of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*). Here, examples such as the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) are illustrated: from *enī* (a brindled cow), one says *etayati* (he describes her). Due to the masculine substitution, the *ṅīp* suffix and the *nakāra* are eliminated.

He expresses "firm" as *draḍhayati*. By the rule *ṛtaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100], there is the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. He expresses "one who possesses a garland" (*sragvin*) as *srajayati*. By the rule *vinmator luk* [Pāṇini 5.3.65], there is the elision of the suffix *vin*. He expresses "one who possesses cows" (*gomantam*) as *gavayati*. There is elision of the suffix *matup*; by the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening. He expresses "thick" (*sthūlam*) as...

In forms such as *sthāpayati*, there is the elision of the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) and so forth. In forms such as *priyam ācaṣṭe* → *prāpayati* and *sthiram ācaṣṭe* → *sthāpayati*, there are the substitutions of *pra*, *stha*, *sphā*, and so on. In these cases, the vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) certainly takes place, because of the mention of "two" (*dvayoḥ*) [in the rule], which precludes the application of the *aṅgavṛtta-paribhāṣā*.

Because it relies on impermanence (*anityatva*). One says "he causes [him] to wear a garland" (*srajayati*). When the suffix *vin* prescribed after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) undergoes elision (*luk*), the quality of being a *pada* (*padatva*)—which would otherwise trigger the change of *k* to *g* (*kutva*) due to the intervening case-suffix—is not realized because of its status as a *bha*. This rule, "that which he does, he describes," is also a sūtra from the *cur-ādi* (tenth) class of roots.

The term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that the suffix *ṇic* should be added after a nominal stem in the sense of "one does that" (*tat karoti*) or "one describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*). Like the *kvip* used for habitual behavior (*ācāra*), this also applies directly from the nominal stem. Now, one might object: since the desired result is already established by the rule *prātipadikād dhātvarthe* ("after a nominal stem, in the sense of a verbal root-meaning"), [is this not redundant?]

To the question "For what purpose is this?", he says: "It is an elaboration of the preceding [rule] itself. Now, one might object that because the present tense is indicated by the forms *karoti* and *ācaṣṭe*, they would not apply in the sense of past actions such as *akarot* and so forth; therefore, he says: "*karoti*, *ācaṣṭe*, etc. The phrase "in the sense of the *laṭ* (present tense)" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). By this, [the rule applies] to the past and the future as well.

The suffix indeed occurs even when there is duality or plurality. Therefore, one says *atikrāmati*. This is also a rule from the *Gaṇapāṭha*; it is an elaboration of the rule *prātipadikād dhātvarthe* [Pāṇini 3.1.25]. In the case of *vācā atikrāmati* → *vācayati*, the substitution of *k* for *c* (*kutva*) is not to be suspected, because the suffix is applied directly after a nominal stem (*asu-banta*) itself.

"Because the suffix arises from the nominal stem (prātipadika). 'And the form of a verbal root'—this too is a *gaṇasūtra*. Having supplied the words 'the base of the causative (*ṇic*)' and 'it undergoes [the state of]' (*pratipadyate*), he explains:

"The base of the causative undergoes the state of being the form of a verbal root. Now, [one might object]: if [the suffix arises] from the nominal stem for the sake of the meaning of a verbal root..."

The suffix *ṇic* occurs, and it is understood that the base of the *ṇic* assumes the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*). If one were to rely solely on this implied meaning, the form *bhuktayati* (he causes [him] to eat) would not be possible when expressing "he tells [that someone] has eaten," because the word *bhukta* would have to be a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the root *bhuj*. Therefore, he says: "the word *va* is for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned."
To address the question of what is being added that was not previously stated, he says: "And likewise the Vārttika.

Regarding the rule *ākhyānāt kṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.87), this Vārttika is established under the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26). *Ākhyānam* refers to a continuous composition of legendary tales (*vṛttakathā-prabandha*). [The suffix is applied] to a word denoting such a work.

When the suffix *ṇic* is applied to a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, such as *kaṃsavadha*, in the sense of "he causes that to be done," there is an elision (*luk*) of the *kṛt* suffix which constitutes a part of the original base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, there is a restoration (*pratyāpatti*) of that very verbal root (*dhātu*), such as *han*, which served as the base for that *kṛt* suffix.

The meaning is that [the root] remains in its own form by abandoning modifications such as substitution (*ādeśa*) and so forth. The portion [of the rule], "and the status of the *kāraka* is like that of the base" (*prakṛtivacca kārakatvam*), will be explained in the main commentary itself. An example is: *kaṃsam ācaṣṭe* (he tells the story of the killing of Kaṃsa) [which becomes] *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* (he causes Kaṃsa to be killed). Killing (*hanana*) is *vadha*. [This is based on the rule] *hanaśca*...

In the word *vadhaḥ*, the suffix *ap* is added to the root *han* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and the root undergoes the substitution *vadh*. Thus, "the killing of Kaṃsa" is *kaṃsavadhaḥ*. The intended meaning is a composition of sentences dedicated to the narration of that event. To express the sense "he narrates that," the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ap*, which is part of the *kṛt* suffix, while the original form [of the base] remains.
There is the cessation of both the verbal root *han* and its substitute *vadh*. He demonstrates the resulting form as follows:
"In this case, when *kaṃsaṃ han i* is situated... (Pāṇini 7.3.32): *hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ*.

*hanasta’ciṇṇaloḥ*. The term *hana* is in the genitive case. In the word *ta*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation; thus he says, "the *t* of *han*. The substitution of *ta* is established by the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*). Regarding the terms *ñiti* and *ṇiti*: this is because those [terms] are carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *aco ñṇiti*.

The meaning is as follows: thus, when the *n* of *han* is changed to *t*, by the rule "ho hanteḥ," the *h* becomes *gh*; consequently, the form *ghātī* is established with the suffix *ṇyat*. Thereafter, in the present tense (*laṭ*), the form *ghātatayī* is established. When the *kṛt* suffix is elided and the compound is dissolved, the case-ending elision (*subluk*) is also removed.

Regarding the form *kaṃsam* (as in *kaṃsaṃ hanti*), he introduces the doubt—beginning with "Now then" (*nanu*)—in order to address, as a response to that doubt, the portion of the Vārttika stating "the case-role (*kāraka*) is like the base (*prakṛtivat*)" which follows the rule "after a word ending in *ṭhak*.
He explains: "of what remains after *kaṃsa*" means "of the word *kaṃsavadha* itself. From that very [word].

The meaning is that this is because of the prescription of the suffix *ṇic*. Now, one might ask: "What is the harm if the word *kaṃsavadha* is treated as an *aṅga* (base)? To this he says: "Therefore...
Because the word *kaṃsavadha* would be an *aṅga*, there would be a fault regarding the application of the augment *aṭ* and reduplication.
The augment *aṭ* would occur before the word *kaṃsa*, and there would be reduplication of the element *kaṃs*.

However, what is intended is that both [the augment and the reduplication] apply to the root *han* itself, as in the form *kaṃsam ajīghatat*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and what": the meaning is that in the case of *kāsaṃ ghātayati*, the changes to *k* (*kutva*) and *t* (*tatva*) would not occur. Why? From this [it follows].

He says: "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*). This means that when there is a mention of a specific form, such as *dā* or *han*, the understanding of the grammatical operation applies to that affix which is prescribed after the root, according to the *paribhāṣā* rule: "When there is a mention of a root, the operation is understood to apply to an affix prescribed after that root. Therefore, in the case of *vārtraghnam*, [the substitution of *t* for the *n* of] *han* occurs by the rule *hanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ*.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), specifically regarding the rule *ṭhṇo hanteṣṭhano'ciṇṇalorṭaḥ*. Thus,
in the present case of *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*,

both the substitution of *gh* for *h* by the rule *ṭhṇo hanteṣṭhano* and the substitution of *t* for *n* by the rule *ṭhṇo hanteṣṭhano'ciṇṇalorṭaḥ* would not apply, because [the condition] *ṇic* [is absent].
The meaning is that because [the suffix] is prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is not prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Here, one should also understand the objection that, by the rule of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating a form as ending in an affix), it would be considered a *kṛdanta* (ending in a *kṛt* affix); consequently, since the meaning of the base of a *kṛt* affix functions as the object, the genitive case in *kaṃsasya* would result. Furthermore, the resolution of that objection is also to be understood.

Because this will be explained later, he dispels this doubt by partial acceptance, saying "True. The meaning is that while the status of the word *kaṃsavadha* as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) and so forth is accepted, the attribution of a fault is not accepted. [He refers to] the rule *prakṛtivat ca*.

In the *vārttika* "ṭha-khyānāt kṛtaḥ," the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "ṭhaprakṛtivat ca" is out of its proper order (*bhinnakrama*). The meaning is that the "ca" immediately following "prakṛtivat" should be placed after the word "kārakam. He demonstrates this very point by reciting it: "kārakaṃ ca" (and the case-role).

He states that this particle *ca* is for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned: "and the effect (*kārya*). The word "is also included" (*samuccīyate*) is to be supplied. Thus, the result is that both the agent (*kāraka*) and the effect are like the original base (*prakṛti*). Here, by the word *prakṛti*, the base of the causative suffix *ṇic* is intended, according to the commentary.
"As in the base" (*prakṛtāviva*) means "like the base" (*prakṛtivat*). The suffix *vati* is added after a word ending in the locative case. Thus he says:
"from the base, such as *han* etc., when followed by the causative marker *ṇic*. The words "being employed" (*prayujyamāne sati*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The explanation of the term "kāraka" is "ending in the accusative case."

The meaning is: that which ends in a case-ending such as the second (accusative), third (instrumental), and so forth. In examples such as *kaṃsaṃ hanti kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa kills Kaṃsa") and, in the sense of "he causes him to kill," *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he causes Kaṃsa to be killed") and *kaṃsam ajīghatat* ("he caused Kaṃsa to be killed"), whatever [element] ends in a case-ending such as the second and whatever grammatical operation occurs when a causative (*hetu-ṇic*) affix is employed—[that is what is referred to].

The result is that all such [grammatical operations] as the substitution of *ku* for *kavarga*, the addition of *ṭi*, and *advitva* (doubling) apply even in examples of the rule *ākhyānāt kṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.26),

such as *kaṃsam ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he narrates the slaying of Kaṃsa") and *kaṃsam ācaṣṭe kaṃsam ajīghatat* ("he narrates that he caused Kaṃsa to be slain"). In this context, by the term "kāraka" (participant in an action)...

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) after *kaṃsāt* is excluded; for in the cited instance of a causative (*ṇyant*) construction, since there is no connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, the accusative alone applies to the object. It should be understood, however, that by the word "kārya" (the effect), the dual number of *kaṃsa* is ruled out. Furthermore, the word "ākhyāna" (narration) [is used here].

In some cases, it is intended as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already occurred, and not as a narration of stories such as the slaying of Kaṃsa well-known from the *Mahābhārata* and other texts.

By this, expressions such as "he reports the arrival of the king" (*rājānam āgamayati*) are established. In the rule regarding the term "ending in the second case" (*dvitīyānta*), the mention of the second case is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore...
It is stated clearly in the Bhāṣya that [the form] *puṣyayoga* is derived from the sense "he joins with Puṣya," and thus it is established.

The rule *kartṛkaraṇāddhātvarthe* is also a *gaṇasūtra*; it is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the very rule *prātipadikāddhātvarthe*. The compound *kartṛkaraṇa* means "the agent and the instrument" (*kartuḥ karaṇam*), and not "the agent and the instrument" as two separate items.
The word *ca* (and) forms a *dvandva* compound, as established by the commentary. Thus he says: "for the sake of the agent’s operation.
This means for the sake of producing the desired result; that is to say, [it refers to] the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). Now, one might object:

if this is the case, since the rule would already be established by the phrase "from the instrument [used] in the sense of the verbal root," the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is redundant. To this, he replies:

But it is not merely the eye and so forth. They say that the mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) is made because, if one were to state only "from the instrument" (karaṇāt), the word "instrument" would be understood as referring to the sense organs such as the eye, since they are so well-known. In reality, however, the definition is "the most effective means is the instrument" (sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam).

They cited "devadattayati" as an example of the agent (*kartṛ*). [The rule] "kadāciddarśane" (when there is a rare or wonderful sight) follows from the word "citra. Thus he says: "this [word] 'citra' [is used]... The explanation of "kadāciddarśane" is "adbhutadarśane" (at the sight of something marvelous). [The word] "citra..."

It is more appropriately stated that [the roots] *citri* and *karaṇa* are seen [in the Dhatupatha] as having the suffix *kadācit*. Some say that *vaṭi* and *laji* belong to the *adanta* (ending in short *a*) group. Due to their inclusion in the *adanta* group, it is understood that these two—*baṇḍa* and *lajja*—sometimes possess the quality of being *adanta*. Furthermore, since there is no fruit [resulting] from their being *adanta*, [the suffix] *ataḥ*...

The meaning is that, having set aside *lopa* (elision), there is *vṛddhi* by the rule "ṭhaco ñṇiti," and then *puṅ* by the rule "ṛtithrī. He states the result: "vaṇṭāpayati. Regarding "Śākaṭāyanaḥ": this is a particular sage. [The word] *saṅgrāma* means "battle. This is a *gaṇa-sūtra*; the nominal stem *saṅgrāma* denotes battle.

The meaning is that [the word *saṅgrāma*] receives the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "to perform" (*karoti*). Now, one might ask: since this is already established by the rule "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*)," for what purpose is this [present rule] stated? To this he says: "provided it is anudāteta. The intention is that this is for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Now, regarding the nominal stem *saṅgrāma*:
To the question, "Since it ends in the vowel *a*, how can it have an udātta accent?", he says: "Because of the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*.
The meaning is that this is indicated by eliding the vowel *a* from the word *saṅgrāma*—which is [originally] anudātta and nasalized—and merging it into the following form.
[The example is] *asasaṅgrāmateti*; here, the suffix *ciṅ* follows the root *saṅgrām* in the *luṅ* tense, with the suffix *si*. The word *saṅgrāma* is derived from the causative (*ṇyanta*) stem.

The sense is that [the suffix] *aṇ* occurs before [the suffix] *aṅ*, because it is an *aṅga* (stem). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule for *bhṛśādi*. Because it lacks a penultimate vowel (*aglopin*), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel. [The word] *sukhaduḥkha* [is used] in the sense of "action toward that";
the meaning is: in an activity conducive to pleasure and an activity conducive to pain. [This is derived] from the nominal stems *sukha* and *duḥkha*.

The meaning is that the causative suffix *ṇic* should be applied in the sense of "he causes that to be done. Some say that the suffix *ṇic* is added by these two rules—namely, by the rule "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of verbal action" and by this very [present rule]. This is an illustrative example (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*). This is a *gaṇa*-sūtra; the meaning is that this is the enumeration (*pāṭha*) of these roots beginning with *katha*, which end in the vowel *a*. Thus he says:
Regarding "adanta" (ending in 'a'): he states the purpose of including the term *bahula* (in various cases) as "bāhulakāt" (by virtue of being manifold). Regarding "apaparṇat":

the intention is that because it is *aglopi* (having its penultimate vowel elided), the condition of being like the *san*-stem (*sanvadbhāva*) does not apply. The root *kṣip* means "to impel. [In the form] *kṣipayati*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because of the status of the elision as *sthānivadbhūta* (acting like the original element). The same applies in subsequent cases. The root *vas* means "to dwell. [In the form] *vasayati*.

Because it ends in a non-dental vowel (adanta), there is no vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). In forms such as *āndolayati*, because it ends in a non-dental vowel, it lacks the elision of the suffixal element (*aglopi*), and thus there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasva*). Having thus explained that the rule "this illustration is manifold" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*) pertains to cases where the root ends in a non-dental vowel, he states another opinion: "But others say," etc., regarding the *bhū* class.

The ten classes [of roots] are: *adādi*, *juhotyādi*, *divādi*, *svādi*, *tudādi*, *rudhādi*, *tanādi*, *kyādī*, and *curādi*; furthermore, there are those outside these [classes], such as the *sautra* roots beginning with *jup*, the worldly (*laukika*) roots beginning with *preṅkhola*, and the Vedic (*vaidika*) ones—

The meaning is that in such passages as "tadrakṣāṃsi rātribhirasubhnan," the *subh* and other roots are also included. He states another opinion: "But others [say]..."—the meaning is that because of the frequent application (*bahulagrahaṇa*) of the causative suffix *ṇic*, it is obtained even from those nine classes of roots cited as distinct from the *cur*-class.

He states another opinion: "only from the *cur*-class and so forth. In reality, however, Kaiyaṭa, having cited the portion of the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra—"by being recited [in that list], there is the designation *dhātu*"—states: "That recitation is not for the purpose of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); rather, it is for the purpose of establishing this much [of the meaning]. And thus...

It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that the *gaṇasūtra*, "this illustration is manifold" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*), is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*). The rule *ṇiṅ gān nirasanē* is a *gaṇasūtra*; it is clear.
Because of the marker *ṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is compulsory. *Śvetāśva-aśvatara-* is also a *gaṇasūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "of Śvetāśva and others": this means of Śvetāśva, Aśvatara, Gāloḍita, and Āhvaraka. Regarding the phrase "the [component] words beginning with 'aśva'": in the word *śvetāśva*, it is the word *aśva*; in the word *aśvatara*, it is the word *tara*; in the word *gāloḍita*, it is the word *ita*; and in the word *āhvaraka*, it is the word *ka*.

The meaning is that they are "subtracted" (lupyante). The phrase "and ṇiṅ" (ṇiṅ ca) is obtained by virtue of the particle "ca. Regarding the expression "in the sense of the root-meaning" (dhātvarthe), the meaning is that in the sūtra beginning with "śvetāśva," they carry forward only the affix ṇic and not ṇiṅ. He demonstrates the difference in result between ṇic and ṇiṅ with the words "according to that view" (tanmate).

"It is already established by the rule *dhātvarthe*"; this is said to be the statement of Bhīmasena, the author of the *Dhātupāṭha*. The meaning is that since [the suffix] *ṇic* is already established by the rule *prātipadikāddhātvarthe*, the rule *puccha-bhāṇḍa-cīvarāṇṇiṅ* need not have been formulated. But [an objection may be raised]: "But..."
Since the rule prescribing *ṇiṅ* in the words "puccha" and "bhāṇḍa" (Pāṇini 3.1.20) is necessary for the sake of the mandatory *ātmanepada*, he says:
"from the root ending in *ṇic* itself, because of the word 'bahula'";

that is to say, because of the inclusion of the term "bahula" in the statement "this is a general indication" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*). Now, [one might object] regarding the words beginning with "puccha":

Since the meaning is already established by the words *dhātvartha* and *ṇij*, the word *siddha* would appear redundant; therefore, he says: "the word *siddha*. The meaning is that the use of the word *siddha* at the conclusion of the work consisting of the Dhātupāṭha is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). For in the *Paspaśāhnika-bhāṣya*, it is said: "The relationship between word and meaning being established... (*siddhe śabdārthasambandhe*).

Thus, at the occasion of commenting on the first *vārttika* of the *Vārttikagrantha*, it was stated: "The employment of the word *siddha* is for the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), according to the principle that 'treatises which begin with an auspicious word,
contain an auspicious word in the middle, and end with an auspicious word, flourish.'"

The necessity of performing an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) at the conclusion of the work is established by the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra beginning with *bhū* (Pāṇini 1.3.1). The *cur*-class [roots] are now complete.
Thus ends the section on the *cur*-class roots in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the *divādi* [roots].
Next, the verbal roots with the *śyan* suffix are described—beginning with *dīvu* (to play). This root is marked with the letter *u*;

by virtue of this, there is an optionality regarding the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā*, and the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. [The group] ending with *jṛṣ* begins with *jṛṣ*.
The meaning is that [the roots] end with *jhṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vigor.

(333) *divādibhyaḥ śyan* |3|1|69|. From the group beginning with *div*: from the rule "after [roots] denoting the agent, *śa*" (*kartari śa*), the word "agent" (*kartari*) is understood, as well as "in a sārvadhātuka [affix]" (*sārvadhātuke*).
Intending to show that the words *yaḥ* and *sārvadhātuke* are carried over from the previous rule, he says:

"It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*. The letters *ś* and *n* are elided. When *div-yati* is established, he says: "The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *hali ca*. The point is that because *śyan* is treated as having the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
The forms *dīvyataḥ*, *dīvyanti*, and so forth, are easy to understand. Regarding *dideva*:

[the forms] *didevatuḥ*, *didevitha*, and *dideviva* indicate that it is *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment), as shown by the form *devitā*. The root *ṣivu* is also *seṭ* and is a *ṣopadeśa* (a root taught with an initial *ṣ*), just like the root *div*.
Regarding *rūpāṇi pariṣīvyati*: the meaning is that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *parinivibhyaḥ sevaḥ*.

Regarding *pariṣiṣeva*: the restriction (*niyama*) stated in *sthādiṣvevābhyāsasya* does not apply here; the reason is that in that context, the phrase *prāksitāt* is understood as being carried over (*anuvṛtti*). [This applies to] *sivādīnām*.

Thinking that [the rule] "vā'ḍvyavāye'pi" (also when there is separation by 'aḍ') applies here, he says: *nyaṣevīt* and *nyasevīt*. However, the root *sriv* contains a *repha* (r); it is *ṣṭhivu* in the sense of "spitting. In the form *ṣṭhīvān*, there is no substitution of *s* for *ṣ* according to the rule "subdātuṣvakkaṣṭhīvām. The forms *ṣṭhīvyati* and so forth are easy to understand.

In the case of ārdhadhātuka suffixes, however, the forms are like those of the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *budh*. The root *ṣṇasu* is also a *ṣopadeśa*. The root *nṛt* is for the purpose of [the rule] "gātravikṣepe" (*Pāṇ. 1.3.20*). It is marked with *ī* (īdit) for the sake of [the rule] "śvīdito niṣṭhāyām" (*Pāṇ. 1.2.19*) and so forth. This root is *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment).

(334) *se'sici kṛtacṛtachﬁadatṛdanṛtaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.57. [The augment *iṭ* is added after the roots *kṛ*, *cṛ*, *chṛ*, *tṛd*, *atṛd*, and *anṛd* when followed by a suffix beginning with *s* that is not *sic*.]

*se'sici*: the analysis is *se-asici*. The locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). From the compound *kṛ-cṛ-tṛ-chṛ-tṛd-nṛt* (formed by a collective dvandva), the ablative is employed. The word *vā* is understood from the rule *ṭhidito vā*, and *ārddhadhātukasyeṭ* also continues [from the previous sūtra]. Thus he says: "from these," and so forth. [This applies] when the augment *iṭ* is obligatory.
This statement is for the purpose of providing an option when [the augment] *iṭ* is applicable. Regarding "anartīt":
the sense is that *iṭ* is obligatory because of the rule "se'sici" (Pāṇini 7.2.57). Regarding the root *trasī* in the sense of agitation:
considering the optional substitution of *e* for *a* and the optional nature of the reduplication by the rule "vā jṛbhramutrasām" (Pāṇini 6.1.193), he says—*tresasuḥ*.

Regarding the root *satu*: the root *kuth* is used in the sense of "becoming putrid. This means "becoming purified" (*pavitrībhavana*) or "producing a foul odor. Amara states: "The word *pūtigandha* means a foul odor (*durgandha*). Regarding the roots *tima*, *ṣṭima*, and *ṣṭīma*:
the second and third are roots with *ṣ* as their upadhā (penultimate letter). The second has *i* as its upadhā; the third, however, [has *ṣ*].
The root has *i* as its penultimate letter (*īdupadha*). The roots *ṣaha* and *ṣuha* are taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*). Regarding the meaning "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*) for the root *cak*:

although it is stated that *cak* means both "satisfaction" and "obstruction," nevertheless, only satisfaction is intended here, according to the explanation (*vyākhyāna*). From the root *ṣuhi*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) in the neuter gender, according to the rule "the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter to denote the action itself."

The word *suhita*. Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra *pūraṇaguṇa*, states that *suhita* means "satiated. [Regarding the roots] *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ*: these two are *seṭ* (having an indicatory *i*). The meaning is that in the form *jīryati*, there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, and then lengthening by the rule *hali ca*. In the case of the suffixes *atus* and so forth, there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*.

The meaning is that, according to the rule *ṭhvā jṛbhramutrasām*, there is an option for both *etva* (the substitution of *e*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*). Thus we have *jajaritha*. Regarding the forms *jaritā* and *jarītā*, he says this in consideration of the rule *ṭhvṛto vā*. The root *ṣūṅ* means "procreation"—that is, production.
This is a root taught with an initial *ṣ*. As for the mention of "option," the phrase "even the subsequent [rule]" is to be understood as the remainder.

Regarding the phrase "when a prohibition has been established": the intention is that this follows from the force of commencing the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) earlier [in the grammar]. Regarding *dūṅ* "to cause affliction": the meaning is either "to torment" or "to become afflicted. In the first sense, it is transitive; in the second, it is intransitive. Regarding *dīṅ* "to perish": "perishing" means becoming small or destruction.
Or:
(335) *dīṅo yuḍ aci kṅiti* [Pāṇini 6.4.63]. Regarding *dīṅo yuḍ aci*: the governing rule *ārddhadhātuke* is qualified by the word *aci*.
This is a rule concerning that which begins with "tat" (the substitute). The word *dīṅ* is in the ablative case; the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive.

Thus he says: "of what follows after *dīṅ*," and so forth. When *didī e* is established, although the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *eranekācaḥ* would apply because it is subsequent, *yauṭ* is applied instead because it is obligatory (*nitya*). The letter *ṭ* is for the sake of marking the end of the suffix (*it*), and the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

The meaning is that *didīye* is the resulting form because the initial member [of the reduplication] ends in *ṭ*. Now, one might object: even if the suffix *yuṭ* is applied, since it is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the substitution of *yaṇ* would be unavoidable; consequently, the form would be *didyye*, where the vowel *i* would not be heard and two *y*s would be heard instead. To this, he says: "In the case of *vuk* and *yuṭ*... [referring to the rule *vugyuṭāvuvaṅyaṇoḥ paryāyeṇa*].

(336) *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca* | 6|1|50| The rule applies to the roots *mīnāti*, *minoti*, and *dīṅ*. From the previous rule, *ādeca upadeśe 'śitī* ("the *ec* vowels [of roots] are replaced by *ā* when taught, except before an affix marked with *ś*"), the word *āt* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*). Therefore, it says: "There shall be the substitution of *ā* for these [roots] even before the suffix *lyap*. By the force of the word *ca* ("and"), the term *ecaḥ* ("the *ec* vowels") and *aśitī* ("except before an affix marked with *ś*") are also understood here.
The word *nimite* (in the cause) is added [to the rule]. There, after *ṭhecaṭaḥ*, the remainder is *nimite*.
The resulting meaning is: "when an *ej*-based suffix (*ejnimite*) and when an *aśit* suffix follow.
Thus he says: "in an *aśit* suffix that is an *ejnimita*. The word *iti* (thus) is added; this is the remainder.
The *Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara* states: "adāsta. Here, although the substitution of *āt* has been applied and the condition for being a *ghu* root is met, the rule *sthādhvor ic ca* does not apply.

This is because of the *vārttika* cited in the *Bhāṣya* on the *ghu*-designation rule, which states: "there is a prohibition of the *ik* substitute for *dīṅ* when [the rule] *sthādhvor it* applies. Thus, *dīṅ* is used in the sense of "supporting" (*ādhāra*).
*Ādhāraḥ*—the act of supporting; that is to say, placing or establishing. The root *lī* is used in the sense of "clinging" (*śleṣaṇe*).

It is conjugated as follows: *līyate*, *lilye*, *lilyiṣe*. [Regarding the forms *lilyidhve* and *lilyidhveṭ*: (337) *vibhāṣā līyateḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.51. [Note: The forms *lilyidhve* and *lilyidhveṭ* refer to the Vedic or optional forms where the substitution of *iṭ* for *ya* occurs before the ending *dhve* due to this rule.]

Regarding the statement "vibhāṣā līyateḥ": one might object that because the term *līyateḥ* is specified with the suffix *śyan*, it would not include the root *līṅ* (meaning "to adhere") which takes the suffix *snā*. To this, he says: "the specification is by means of the letter *ya*. This means that the term *līyateḥ* is specified by the *yak* prescribed by the rule *sārvadhātuke yaK*; and that [specification]...

The meaning is that [the suffix] *yaK* is common to both *śyan* and *śnā*; this is because it is common to both. From the rule "mīnātiminoti" (Pāṇini 6.1.50), the word "lyapi" is understood; from "ādecaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the words "āt" and "ecaḥ" are carried over. He states this with the words beginning "lī-līṅoḥ," etc. [The suffixes] *svat* and so on are marked with the indicatory letter *od*.

This is a group-sūtra (gaṇasūtra) recited in the Dhātupāṭha. The meaning is that those beginning with *ṣūṅ* "to give birth to living beings" and ending with *vrīṅ* are subject to the grammatical operations pertaining to roots marked with the indicatory letter *o*. Regarding the phrase "the substitution of *ṇatva* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*)," the intention is that this occurs by means of the rule *oditaśca*. As for *prīṅ* "in delighting," delight (*prīti*) is satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*).

"Ṭhmutprītiḥ pramado harṣaḥ"—thus says Amara. In this case, it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). For example: *phalamūlādinā hariḥ prīyate* (Hari is pleased by fruits, roots, etc.). The meaning is "he rejoices. However, when *prītiḥ* means "satisfying," derived from the root *prīñ* in the sense of "satisfying" belonging to the *kryādi* class with the suffix *ktin*, then—
It is transitive. Thus he says: "transitive. Regarding "is pleased" (*prīyate*), the meaning is "satisfies.

Now, regarding "four [roots] ending in *parasmaipada*": the intention is that they end with the root *do* (meaning "to cut") in the sense of "cutting off. The root *śo* (meaning "to thin out") is *aniṭ*.

(338) *otaḥ śyani* | P. 7.3.71. With the understanding that the word "lopa" (elision) is carried over from the rule *ghorlopo leṭi vā*, he completes the remainder [of the sūtra] by stating: "there shall be elision. [The example is] *śaśau*. [This is derived from the root] *āṅ-śās* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*.
The sense is that in the present tense (*ātve*), there is the substitution of *āṬ* for *ṇal*. Regarding *śaśatuḥ*: [the forms are] *śaśitha* (or *śaśātha*), *śaśiva*.

Regarding *śāsyati*: [the forms are] *śyatu*, *aśyat*, *śyet*, *śāyāt*. He states the specific rule for the *luṅ* [aorist] when *sic* follows: "optionally after *ghu*" (*vibhāṣā ghuḥ*). Regarding the alternative where there is elision (*luk*) of *sic*, he says: *aśāt*. [This is because of the rule] "*ātaḥ raḥ*".

Thinking thus, he says *aśuḥ*. Thinking that there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic* and that *sag* and *iṭ* are present, he says *aśāsīt*. This root *chād* is like the root *śodh*. The meaning of *ṣo antakarmaṇi* is "in completion" or "in destruction. Its forms are like those of the root *śodh*. This is a root taught with an initial *ṣ*.

"syati"—here there is elision [of the *s*] by the rule "otaḥ śyani. "abhiṣyati"—here there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "upasargāt. "abhyaṣyat"—here there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "prāksitād. "abhisasau"—here there is no *ṣ* because of the restriction in the rule "sthādiṣu. [The root] *do* (in the sense of) cutting: "praṇidātā."
In *ṭhnergade*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. In *deyāt*, the *liṅ* (optative) is used;

by the rule *erliṅi*, *e* is substituted [for the root vowel]. In *adāt*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic* by the rule *gātisthāpābhūbhyo 'ṅ*. Now, regarding "those that are *ātmanepada*": this means those ending with *vāśṛ śabde*. In *janī prādurbhāve*, [the rule] *śvīdito...* [applies].
The *īt* designation [of the root] is for the sake of the meaning of "niṣṭhāyām" and so forth.
(339) *jñā-janor jā* | Pāṇini 7.3.79. Regarding *jñā-janor jā*: it is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that [term *śit*] from the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamām*.
The state [of being]. Regarding the word "is born" (*jāyate*):

since the verbal root *jñā* takes the *nu*-affix (*vikaraṇa*), "he knows" (*jānāti*) is the illustrative example. In both cases, when the substitute *ja-* ends in a short vowel, once the operations pertaining to the *aṅga* (stem) have been performed, the rule "there is no further operation pertaining to the *aṅga*" applies.

By the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "a long vowel is substituted for [the penultimate] *ṭh* before *yañ*" (*ṭhato dīrgho yañi*), the fact that the substitute ending in a long vowel (*jārdaśa*) was not applicable was disregarded, and the assumption was made that it ends in a long vowel. Thus, *jajñe*. In the case of *jajñe*, when the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule "for *gam* and *han*" (*gamahana*), the *n* is replaced by *ñ* through the rule for *ścutva*. [The forms] *jāyeta* and *janiṣīṣṭa* follow. When the *luṅ* [suffix] is applied, resulting in *ajan-ta*, he says:

It illuminates or it causes to be gathered; this is the remainder [of the rule] "ṭhcleḥ". When *ajan-i-ta* is established, and the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is about to occur—(340) *janivadhyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.35).
And in the case of *jan* and *vadhi*: from "ata upadhāyāḥ" [P. 7.2.116], the word *upadhāyāḥ*;
from "mṛjervṛddhiḥ" [P. 7.2.114], the word *vṛddhiḥ*; from "nodātopadeśasya" [P. 7.3.34], the word *na*;
from "āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ" [P. 7.3.33], the word *ciṇkṛtoḥ*; and from "aco ñṇiti" [P. 7.2.115], the word *ñṇiti*.

And it follows [the previous rule]. He says this with the words "of these two.
