The root *dīp* is marked with the indicatory letter *ī*; considering that there is an optional application of *ciṇ* by the rule "after *dīp*, *jan*, etc.," he says: *adīpi* or *adīpiṣṭa*. The root *pūr* is also marked with the indicatory letter *ī*; considering that there is an optional application of *ciṇ* by the rule "after *dīp*, *jan*, etc.," he says: *apūri*.

Regarding "apūriṣṭa": the roots beginning with *tūrī* and ending with *cūrī* (in the sense of burning) are indeed marked with the *īt* indicatory letter (*īdit*). Regarding *tapa* in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarye*), the remainder [of the rule] is "the *śyan* affix and the Ātmanepada" (*śyan ātmanepadaṃ ca*). Intending that both [the *śyan* affix and the Ātmanepada] are under discussion, he completes the statement: "the *śyan* affix and the *taR* affix. At other times...

"tviti" means "in the state of being employed for another's purpose due to [his] sovereignty. Regarding "kecit tu": it is established in the Dhātupāṭha that there are the roots "tapa aiśvarye" and "vāvṛtu varaṇe.
Therein, the meaning is that some desire the word "vā" to be the initial constituent of the root "vṛtu," such that it is "vā-vṛtu varaṇe. And thus...

The root remains simply as *tapa* in the sense of "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*). In this view, the intention is that the suffix *śyan* and the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are invariably applied to the root *tap*. Thus, *tapyate* means "he rules. In the first view, *tapatī* (he rules) also occurs in the sense of sovereignty. Regarding *pata iti*, it refers to the substitution of the letters *ta* and *pa* in the root *tap*.

The meaning is that there is an alternative reading: "ṭhpata aiśvarye vā" (ṭh-pat-aiśvarye vā), which involves a transposition of the syllables. Thus, he demonstrates the usage with such a transposed reading: "dyautadyāmā niyutaḥ.
This is a portion of the *ṛc* beginning with "pravāyumacchā bṛti. [In this context], the word "patyamāna" means "īśāna" (the lord).

This is the meaning. Here, the present tense suffix *laṭ* is replaced by the *śānac* ātmanepada suffix and the *śyan* affix. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative view": this means in the reading where the root is given as *vāvṛtu*. As for *vāvṛtyate*: the meaning is "he covers" (*vṛṇoti*), which is to say, "he requires" (*apekṣate*). He shows the usage of the root *vāvṛtu* as follows:

"Then, returning" means "looking back. "He wished to enter" (*nyavivikṣata*): the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule *nerviśaḥ*; the suffix *ksa* is applied by the rule *śala igupadhā*. Now, "the five beginning with *svarita*" means those ending with *śapa ākrośe*. "It becomes moist" (*śucyati*) means "it becomes wet."

Regarding *aśucat*: the sense is that *aṅ* is applied because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ṛ*. Regarding *ṇaha* in the sense of "binding": this is a root taught with the initial *ṇ*. It is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*).

Regarding *nanāha*: [the forms] *nehatuḥ*, etc., follow. Considering that by the rule of Bhāradvāja there is optionally *iṭ* in the *thal* suffix, he says: *nehitha* or *nanaddha*. In the case where *iṭ* is present, by the rule "and in *thal* when it has *iṭ*," there is the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel and the elision of the reduplication.

In the absence of *iḍ*, however, by the rule "ṭhnaho dhaḥ," there is *dha* for *ha*; this is the intended meaning. The root *rañj* means "to color" (*rāge*). It is *aniṭ*. [The form] *rajyati* is derived; the intended meaning is that the nasal (*n*) is elided by the rule "aniditām. [The forms] *rarañja*, *rarañjatuḥ* [are formed]. *Rarañjitha* becomes *raraṅktha*. *Rarañjiva*. [The forms] *raṅktā*, etc., follow. Now, regarding the eleventh [root]: *liśa*...
The meaning is that [the suffixes] end with *alpībhāve*. The root *pad* means "to go"; it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment).
[The rule] *ciṇ te padaḥ* [is understood as] *padaś cler iti*, following from the rule *cleḥ siñ* [3|1|44].

The sense is that the word *śliṣ* is understood [from the previous rule]. Regarding the phrase "in the word *ta*" (*taśabde*), the meaning is "in the first person singular of the ātmanepada. This is clear in the Bhāṣya.
As for the form *praṇyapāt*: when the suffix *ciṇ* follows *śliṣ*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel; then, by the rule *ciṇo luṅi*, the word *ta* [is substituted].

There is elision [of the nasal]. The intention is that there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by the rule "ṇer gade. The root *vid* is used in the sense of existence; thus, *veteti*. The intention is that it is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). In the *liṭ* [perfect], *iṭ* is added according to the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*. Similarly, *budhiṣṭa*; here, there is *kit* status by the rule "liṅsicau. Considering the optional application of *ciṇ* by the rule "dīpajana," he says:
"It is not understood as *abuddha*. [Question: "How does it take the form *yudhyati*? [Answer: "Because it is an *ātmanepada* verb"—this is the intended meaning.

He provides the resolution: "In the word *yudham*. The word *yudh* ends in the abstract suffix *kvip*. The meaning is that, in the sense of "one who desires battle" (*yudham icchati*), the *parasmaipada* ending occurs because of the *kyac* suffix prescribed by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ*.
The resolution that "the ātmanepada [ending] conditioned by the anudātta accent is not mandatory" is inappropriate,

because it is unauthoritative, being nowhere seen in the Bhāṣya. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "vyatyayo bahulam," regarding the example *pratīpam anya ūrmir yudhyati*, [it is explained that the ending occurs] by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

It is established that this is the *parasmaipada* [voice]. Regarding the rule *ano rudhaḥ*: the meaning is that the root *rudh*, when preceded by the prefix *anu*, functions in the sense of "desire. [The root] *yuj* means "concentration" (*samādhi*); it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) and intransitive (*akarmaka*).
The intention is that the state of being a mental activity (*cittavṛtti*) is already included within the meaning of the verbal root itself. However, in other meanings—

It can also be transitive, according to the Vārttika on the rule *karmavat* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), which states: "The roots *sṛj* and *yuj*, when transitive, behave like [the object]. This will be examined in the section on the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*).

Regarding the perfect tense (*liṭ*), we have *sasṛjiṣe*; the intention is that the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*. [The form] *sraṣṭā* [is derived as follows].

In *srakṣyate*, by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakitī*, the augment *am* is added; then, by the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogāderguṇaḥ*, the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *guṇa* (becoming *ar*), which is then replaced by *yaṇ* (*ra*). Then, by the rule *vraścabhrasjasṛjamṛjayajarājabhrājacchaśāṃ ṣaḥ*, the *j* is changed to *ṣ*. By the rule *ṣṭuan*, the *t* is changed to *ṭ*; this is the intended meaning. In *srakṣyate*, when the *j* of the preceding word [the root] is changed to *ṣ*, then by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, the *ṣ* is changed to *k*, and subsequently the *s* is changed to *ṣ*; this is the intended meaning. [This concludes the section on] the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*).

He says: *sṛkṣīṣṭa*. Here, having raised the objection regarding the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), he says: *liṅsicau*. Nor is there *am*; the meaning is that even the *am* prescribed by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti* does not occur here. The intention is that its prescription is restricted to cases where an *akit* follows. Regarding the *luṅ* [aorist], he says: *asṛṣṭa*. [This is] by the rule *jhalo jhali* [which causes the elision of the *sic*].

There is elision [of the suffix]. The sense is that because the *sic* suffix is *kit* by the rule "the *liṅ* and *sic* [are *kit*] in the *ātmanepada*," there is neither *guṇa* nor *am*. [The root] *liś* means "to become small. Regarding *likṣīṣṭa*: because the *liṅ* and *sic* are *kit* by the rule "the *liṅ* and *sic* [are *kit*]," there is no *guṇa*. Regarding *alikṣata*: the *ksa* suffix is applied by the rule "after a root ending in *śal* with a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* (igupadha)..."

"Until the end of the day" means up to the conclusion of the day's activities. Regarding "from the root *rādh* when intransitive, only in the sense of 'prosperity'," the word "after the suffix *śyan*" is the ellipsis.
The understood meaning is that the suffix *śyan* occurs after the root *rādh* when it is intransitive and only in the sense of prosperity. Thus...

The phrase "provided it is intransitive" (*sati akarmakāt*) would be redundant. Furthermore, the affix *śyan* would apply to the root *rādh* even in its other meanings; for indeed, in examples such as "he offends" (*aparādhyati*), *śyan* is desired even when the meaning is malice or the like. To this, he says: "The particle *eva* is out of its proper order. This means that the particle *eva*, which was read after the word "in increase" (*vṛddhau*) in the rule, [should rather be placed elsewhere].

The meaning is that "one whose order is different" refers to another sequence; that is to say, the letter *a* read immediately after the rule for *vṛddha* (Pāṇini 3.1.57) must be placed elsewhere. He demonstrates this very point by stating: "after *rādha* only when it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *śyan* [is applied]. And thus, the suffix *śyan* occurs even in other meanings.

It is established. Regarding the statement "he destroys the enemy" (*śatruṃ hinasti*), the intention is that in the sense of "he harms the enemy," because it has an object (*sakarmaka*), the suffix *śyan* does not apply. Then, one might ask: what is the purpose of [the condition] "in the case of a vowel increase" (*vṛddhau*)? Anticipating this doubt, it is stated that its purpose is to demonstrate that such [suffixes] apply only to intransitive actions (*akarmaka-kriyā*), and not otherwise.
He says "for the purpose of restriction" (parisaṅkhyānārtham) and gives an example, saying "in the case of vṛddhi.
Thus, the intention is that the mention of *vṛddhi* (increase) is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any intransitive action.
He cites other such meanings with the words beginning "yan mahyam," etc., under the rule *krudhadruhe*.

The state of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*). In the example "he divines for Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇāya rādhyati*), the state of being a recipient [is assigned] by the rule: "In the case of *rādhī* and *īkṣ*, that for whom there is an inquiry. Regarding "the deity": when asked what is now auspicious or inauspicious for Kṛṣṇa, the astrologer [observes] the positions of the sun and other planets which indicate his fortune or misfortune.

The meaning is that he examines [it] by means of the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Now, one might object: since fate (*daiva*) is the object (*karman*) in the act of deliberation, how can this verb be intransitive (*akarmaka*) here? To this, he says: "of fate" (*daivasya*). One might further object:
in the rule "the root *rādh* is used only with the sense of 'increase' (*vṛddhi*) when it is intransitive," the mention of "increase" is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Since *rādh* is taught by Pāṇini and others as having the meaning of "injury" (*hiṃsā*), one might object that in forms such as *rarādhatuḥ*, the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication—which are prescribed by the rule "for *rādh* in the sense of injury"—would apply. To this, he says: "In the case of *rādh*, [the rule] does not apply here. This means that in forms such as *rarādhatuḥ*, even though *rādh* has the sense of injury, [the aforementioned rule does not apply].

The meaning is that, because [the root] will be mentioned as "hiṃsāyām" (in the sense of injury), the doubling and the elision of the reduplicated syllable do not occur. To the question "Why?", he says: "of the root *rādh* in the sense of injury. This doubt does not even arise, because it is stated that only the intransitive (*akarmaka*) *rādh* belongs to the *devādika* class; and since *rādh* in the sense of injury is transitive (*sakarmaka*), [it does not undergo those changes].

The meaning is that because there is an absence of being caused by fate (daiva) and so forth, the aforementioned doubt does not arise. Now, one might ask: "How is it that [the root] *rādh* means 'he prospers' (*rādhnoti*) and 'he causes to prosper' (*rādhayati*)? To this he says: "This belongs to both the *svādi* and *curādi* groups. [Examples: *rarādhitha*.

By the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*, the augment *iṭ* is mandatory; and because it possesses a long vowel *ā*, [the prohibition of *iṭ*] by the rule "after a root ending in a short vowel in its original form (*upadeśe'tvataḥ*)" does not apply.

Because of the non-application of that [rule], and because in the rule *ajanta akāravān* (a word ending in a vowel and containing the letter *a*) only a short *a* is intended to be signified. *Rāddhā*, *arātsīt*. The root *vyadh* (meaning "to strike") ends in the fourth [consonant class] (*d*). It is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). From *vidhyati*: because the suffix *śyan* is marked with *ṅ*, [the rule] *gṛhijyā-* applies.
The meaning is that when there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *ya*, followed by the formation of the *pūrvarūpa*, the form *vidhyati* arises.
However, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *va*, because of the prohibition: "There is no *saṃprasāraṇa* in place of a *saṃprasāraṇa*.
Regarding *vivyādha*: once reduplication (*dvitva*) has occurred, [the rule] *liṭabhyāsasya* applies to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

The meaning is that there is *saṃprasāraṇa*. Regarding *vividhatuḥ*: the meaning is that because it is subsequent, *saṃprasāraṇa* is applied by the rule "grahijyā" etc., and then reduplication (*dvitva*) occurs. He says *vivyadhitha* and *vivyaddha* because, according to the *Bhāradvājaniyama*, there is an option for *iṭ* after *thal*. There is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule "liṭaḷbhyāsasya".

In the case where [the root] is *aniṭ*, the substitution of *dh* occurs by the rule *ṭhjhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*. Regarding *avyātsīt*: the *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule concerning roots ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*). Regarding *puṣa* (in the sense of nourishing): it is *aniṭ*. In *pupoṣitha*, because there is an absence of both a final vowel (*ajanta*) and the letter *a*, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory by the rule of the *krādiniyama*. Regarding *apuṣat*: [the same applies].

Because of the *aṅ* suffix after roots beginning with *puṣ*, there is no *guṇa*. The root *śuṣ* is *aniṭ*; thus [the form] is *aśuṣat*. This is because of the rule "after *puṣ* etc., *aṅ*" (*puṣādy-aṅ*). The same applies hereafter. *Tuṣ*, *duṣ*, and *śliṣ*—these are *aniṭ*.
Regarding the *luṅ* [aorist] of *śliṣ*: although the substitution of *sic* for *cli* would have been expected...

(342) *Śliṣaḥ* |3|1|46|. From the rule for *śliṣ*, the words *cleḥ* and *aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*—the latter being derived from the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*—are understood to carry over. Therefore, he says: "after this [root]," and so forth. Now, as for *śala*...
Since the suffix *kṣa* is already established by the rule "igupadhā'di," for what purpose is this [present rule] stated? To this he says:

"It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *aṅ* of the *puṣādi* group. The meaning is that, because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules], the *aṅ* of the *puṣādi* group would supersede the *kṣa* prescribed by the rule "śala igupadhādi"; therefore, the prescription of *kṣa* is repeated in order to prevent that. But [an objection may be raised]: nanu...
Just as the suffix *k* in the rule *ṭhśliṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.46) overrides even the subsequent *yaṅ* and other affixes beginning with *puṣ*,
so too does it override the subsequent *ciṇ* in the rule *ṭhciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.66). This being the case,
in the example *upāśleṣi kanyā devadattena*, the *luṅ* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*) is applied by the rule *ṭhciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

Lest it be thought that [the rule for] *ciṇ* would not apply, he says: "but not *ciṇ*. The meaning is that the prescription of *ksa* by the rule "after *śliṣ*" does not subvert the prescription of *ciṇ* by the rule "after [roots ending in a consonant], *ciṇ* is used in the sense of the action or the object. Why is this so? He says:
"because it precedes," namely the rules "after a root ending in *śal*, having a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, and being aniṭ, *ksa* is used" and "after *śliṣ*."
The intention is that this is the sequence of the sūtras: "ṭhpuṣādidyautādyalṛditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu" and "ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ. (343) [The suffix *liṭ* is used] in the sense of embracing. 3.1.46.

Regarding *āliṅgane* (in the sense of embracing): everything that was carried over from the preceding sūtra, namely *śliṣa*, is also carried over here. Thus, it is understood that *ksa* shall replace *cli* following the root *śliṣ* when it occurs in the sense of embracing. This is indicated by the term *śliṣaḥ*.
Since this is already established by the preceding sūtra alone, this [present rule] is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha). Thus it says:

"The suffix *k*sa occurs after the root *śliṣ* with the affix *cli* only in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*), and not elsewhere. Now, one might object: according to the maxim "that which is non-adjacent [is excluded]," this restriction would apply only to what is obtained from the sūtra "śliṣ" (Pāṇini 3.1.46), and not to [the form derived from] "śal."
To show that this [rule] applies even to the rule *igupadhā’dityasyāpi*, he says: "This restriction also applies to the rule *śala igupadhāt*.

Why? He says: "Because of the force of the division of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*). For if, in the case of the root *śliṣ*, the suffix *ksa* were restricted by the rule to occur only after roots ending in *i* or *u* (as *igupadha*) and only in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*), then the division of the sūtra would be purposeless.

It may be so; for even though *śliṣ* "to embrace" is treated as a single rule, the fact that the suffix *kso* does not apply when there is no embracing is already established. Therefore, the restriction is understood from the rule *śala igupadhā-* that the suffix *kso* applies to *śliṣ* only in the sense of embracing, and not even in the sense of non-embracing.

This is the meaning. "The girl embraced Devadatta" (aślikṣat kanyāṃ devadattaḥ) means "he embraced" (āliṅgat). Here, the suffix *ksa* is applied by this rule, overriding the *ām* suffix prescribed for roots beginning with *puṣ*. "The lac adhered to the wood" (samāśliṣaj jatu kāṣṭham): *jatu* is lac; its nature is such that it arises only when attached to wood. [The compound] *jatu ca kāṣṭhaṃ ca*...

This is a collective dvandva compound. The *Bhāṣya* states: "As in the case of *upāśliṣaj jatu kāṣṭham*. Here, because the root *śliṣ* does not have the meaning of "embracing," the suffix *ksa* is not applied; rather, the rule *puṣādidyutādyuditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.1.55) applies.
[Objection: But surely, since it lacks the initial vowel *a*, [the suffix *aṅ* would not apply]?
Since the augment *āṭ* is impossible [in this context], the form *samāśliṣat* would be incorrect; therefore, he says: "The prefix *āṅ*.

The meaning is that one should not mistakenly think that in the word *samāśliṣat*, the prefix *āṅ* occurs before the root *śliṣ*, rather than being the augment *āṭ*. Now, embracing is indeed *samāśleṣaṇa*; and thus...

Since the root *śliṣ* in the expression "let the lac adhere to the wood" (*samāśliṣajjatu kāṣṭham*) has the meaning of "embracing," the suffix *kso* would be unavoidable; therefore, he says: "In this context, however, [it refers to] proximity. Here, in the phrase "let the lac adhere to the wood," the root *śliṣ* denotes proximity—that is, contact—and not [embracing].

The meaning is: "in an embrace," which consists of a specific type of connection characterized by the joining of arms and so forth. Now, one might object: according to the rule that the substitution of *ksa* for the *cli* of the root *śliṣ* occurs only in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*) and not in the absence of embracing, the *ksa* substitution [prescribed] by the rule "śala igupadhā" would also not apply in the case of non-embracing.

It has been stated that [the application of] *bhavati* is incorrect; however, in the case of "let the lac adhere to the wood" (*samāśliṣajjatu kāṣṭham*), since there is no act of embracing, the suffix *aṅ* from the *puṣādi* group would apply by virtue of its higher status, overriding the rule for *ksa* (Pāṇini 3.1.45, *śala igupadhāt kit*), and thus *ksa* would not even be applicable. To this, he says: "when [the action] is directed toward an object" (*karmaṇi*). This is because the [action of] embracing does not occur when [the action] is directed toward an object.

From the root *śliṣ* in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), the suffix *cli* becomes *isic* in the *luṅ* tense, and not *aṅ* from the *puṣādi* group, because that [suffix *aṅ*] applies only to the active voice (*parasmaipada*), and because the *luṅ* in the passive is restricted to the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ. And for that [root], [the substitution of *īṭ*] occurs by the rule "śala igupadhāḥ."

The meaning is that it is logical that the *ksa* suffix, which is obtained by the aforementioned rule, is precluded even in the case of non-embracing (*anāliṅgane*). Regarding what was stated—namely, "In the case of embracing (*āliṅgane*), the *ksa* suffix for the root *śliṣ* is an exception (*apavāda*) only to the *aṅ* suffix of the *puṣādi* class, and not to the *ciṇ* suffix"—he states its purpose: "In the singular, [there is] *ciṇ*."

He demonstrates this very point by citing an example: "aśleṣī" (he embraced). The meaning is: "the girl was embraced by Devadatta. From the root *śliṣ*, which means "to embrace," the form is derived in the sense of the object (*karman*) using the *luṅ* suffix in the first person singular; when the suffix *ta* follows, [the rule] "ṭhciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" applies.

When *ciṇ* is applied, the *luk* elision of the *ta*-suffix occurs by the rule *ṭhiṇo luṅ*. Here, because the rule for *ksa* in the case of the root *śliṣ* is an exception (*apavāda*) only to *puṣādy-aṅ* and not an exception to *ciṇ*, *ciṇ* remains unobstructed;
this is the intended meaning. [This is illustrated] in the example: "The wood was embraced by lac" (*samāśleṣi jatunā kāṣṭham*).
Because the substitution of *ciṇ* for *cli* after the root *śliṣ* in the sense of "not embracing" (*anāliṅgana*) is unimpeded, the form *aśleṣīt* is indeed unobjectionable.

Thus, it is established that whether there is embracing (*āliṅgana*) or non-embracing (*anāliṅgana*), the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix in the passive voice of the root *śliṣ*, when followed by the singular ending *ta*, undergoes the *ciṇ* substitution. Now, regarding the root *śliṣ* in the sense of non-embracing:

The intention is that in the *luṅ* [aorist] of the passive (*karmaṇi*), in the form *ātām*, because there is no *ksa* for *cli*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, and then the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* [occurs], resulting in the desired form. Now, one might object: even if *ksa* were applied in *aślikṣātām*, the desired result would be established by the elision of the vowel *a* via the rule *ka-syāci*; therefore, the use of *luṅ* in the passive is not necessary. To address this dissatisfaction, [the author provides the following analysis].

He gives an example from the *Jhādiprakaraṇa*: *aślikṣata*, etc. When the form *aśliṣ s jha* is established, the substitution of *j* for the final letter is set aside by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.5), which prescribes the substitution of *at* for the root-final *s*. Then, the *s* of *sic* is changed to *k*, and the *s* of *sic* is changed to *ṣ*, resulting in the desired form *aślikṣata*. However, if the suffix *kṣa* were applied instead of *cli*, the form would be *aśliṣ s jha*.

This being the case, since the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ṭhksasyācī* would not apply, the substitution of *at* for *as* by the rule *ṭhātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* would not occur because [the former] is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. Thus, [the form] is *aśliṣṭhāḥ*. This is derived from the root *śliṣ* in the passive (*karmaṇi*) with the suffix *luṅ*, the replacement of *cli* by *sica*, and the elision of *sica* by the rule *ṭhjhalo jhalī*.

In the case of *ṣṭuatva*, the form *aṣṭhaśliṣṭhāḥ* is desired. However, in the case of *kse*, because [the condition for] *jhalo jhalī* is impossible, the intention is that it would be *aślikṣathāḥ*. As for *aśliḍḍhvam*: from the root *śliṣ* in the *luṅ* (aorist) passive, in the *dhvam* ending, after the *sic* suffix, by *jhalo jhalī* there is the elision of *s*, and by *jhaśtva*... [of *ṣ*].

In the case of the letter *ḍa*, by the rule of *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the *dha* becomes *ḍha*. The intention is that if *kṣa* were present, the form would be *aślikṣadhvam*. Regarding the statement "the root *śak* is optionally [treated as such]," the meaning is that in the sense of "endurance" (*marṣaṇa*), the root *śak* is not subject to optionality. Furthermore, this optionality pertains only to the domain of the present Parasmaipada (active voice) and does not pertain to its inclusion in the *divādi* class.
This is because of the [author's] explanation. He says this: "it takes both *padas*. Here, *marṣaṇa* means "capacity" (*sāmarthya*).

[The forms] *śaknoti* or *śakyate* mean "he becomes capable" (*samartho bhavati*). Regarding the statement "some say this root is *seṭ*," the intention is that in his own system it is indeed *aniṭ*. [Objection: But in the *aniṭ*-lists, [the root] *śaki* is listed as having the marker *ḷ*.

To the question, "How is it that [the root] is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) according to the recitation? he says: "According to their opinion. The meaning is that, relying on the opinion of those who state that *śaki* is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*), the root *śaki* is listed as having an indicatory *ṛ* (*ṛdit*) in the *aniṭ-kārikās*. Regarding the phrase "from the *kvip*-suffix of the *saṃpadādi* group": *kṣudh* is derived from the sense "he suffers hunger" (*kṣudhyati*), with the *kvip* suffix used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

The analysis of the compound is: *kṣudh* has arisen for him, thus he is "hungry" (*kṣudhita*). Regarding the rule *vasatikṣudhoḥ*: its meaning is that the augment *iṭ* should be applied after the roots *vas* and *kṣudh* before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. Regarding the phrase "it will be stated": the word "in the section on *kṛt*-suffixes" (*kṛtsu*) is to be understood as the remainder. Regarding *ṣidhu saṃrāddhau*: the meaning is "in the sense of completion. [The reading] "prāmādika" is an error.

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that this is the opinion of Mādhava and others. Regarding *radh* in the sense of "injury": it is *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment) and ends in the fourth [consonant, *dh*]. As for *rarandhatuḥ*: the intention is that, because the suffix is *akit*, the *num* augment—which is subsequent and applies after a conjunct consonant—prevents the elision of the *n* by overriding both the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication. Thus, there is no elision of the *n*.

(344) *radhādibhyaśca* | 7|2|45|. The phrase *ārddhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and *vā* is understood from *svaratisūtī*; with this in mind, he completes the remainder [of the sūtra]:—

Regarding the rule *valādy-ardhadhātukasya veṭ*: since the addition of *iṭ* to an *ardhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant would otherwise be compulsory by the preceding rule, this present rule provides an option. When *tāsi* follows the root *luṭ*, *iṭ* is added; however, when *num* is about to be applied to *radh* and *jabh* before a vowel by the rule *radhijabhor aci*, [the following applies]: (345) *neṭaliṭi radheḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.62: "The augment *iṭ* is not added to *radh* in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]."

Regarding *neṭaliṭi radheḥ*: from the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*, the word *num* is understood by anuvṛtti (carrying over). Thus it says: "before *iṭ*, excluding the *liṭ* [perfect] affix. Regarding *aṅtve*: the meaning is that when the *aṅ* substitute has been applied to the roots beginning with *puṣ* (i.e., the *puṣādi* group), the suffix *siC* is added. Regarding *aradhat*: [as in] "I have not failed (*aradham*) for the sake of the hater" (*mo ahaṃ dviṣate 'radham*). [The root] *ṇaś* means "disappearance" (*adarśane*).

This is an instruction regarding [the root] *naś* as being *seṭ*. By the rule "and after *radh* etc.," *vaṭ* is added. Regarding that, he says "neśitha" in the case where *iṭ* is present; the intention is that by the rule "and when *thal* is *seṭ*," there is *etva* (change to *e*) and elision of the reduplication.
In the case where *iṭ* is absent, having reached the stage *nanaś-tha*—

(346) *masjinaśor jhali* [Pāṇini 7.1.60]. The meaning is that the augment *num* shall be applied; this is because the phrase "for roots ending in *it*" (*idito num*) is understood to follow from the previous rule. Thus, one forms *nanaṃṣṭha*: here, *ṣatva* applies by the rule *vraśca-*, followed by *ṣṭutva*. Then, one forms *praṇaśyati*.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "ṭhupasargādasamāse" (Pāṇini 8.4.14).

(347) Regarding the rule "naśeḥ ṣāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.36): [the word] "naśeḥ" means "of the root *naś*"; "ṣāntasya" means "ending in *ṣ*. The word "ṇa" is supplied from the rule "raṣābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.4.1), and the word "na" is supplied from the rule "na bhābhūpū" (Pāṇini 8.4.34).
Intending to show that [the rule] continues to apply, he completes the sense by stating: "there would be no substitution of *ṇ*.

Why [is the condition] "ending in *ṣ*" stated? [Consider: *praṇaśyati*. [The term] "having previously been so" (*bhūtapūrva*) means that although it previously ended in *ṣ*, it now lacks the status of ending in *ṣ* due to the application of a substitute.

The meaning is that the mention of the word "anta" (end) is for the purpose of obtaining the prohibition of *ṇatva* [nasalization]. In the case of *pranaṅkṣyati*, even though *ṣatva* has been applied to the *ṣ*, there is no *ṇatva* because it is considered to have ended in *ṣ* by way of its prior state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). Regarding the root *tṛp* in the sense of "to satisfy": "satisfaction" and "the act of satisfying. In the first sense, it is intransitive; in the second, it is transitive.
Thinking that there is an optional insertion of *iṭ* because the root belongs to the *radh*-class and so forth, he says: *tatarpitha*, *tatarptha*, and *tatraptha*.
The intention is [the application of] Pāṇini 7.2.45: *anudātasya cardupadhāsyānyatarasyām*.
[The forms] *tatṛpiva* and *tatṛpva* are derived by the rule *sijveti*; the intention is that in one alternative, the *puṣādi* group applies.
There is an optional *iṭ* augment because the root belongs to the *radhādi* class. Regarding that, he says "ātarpīt" (*atarpīt*) in the case where *iṭ* is present;

he says "atārpsīt" (*atārpsīt*) in the case where *iṭ* is absent—the sense being that the *vṛddhi* substitution is conditioned by the rule for roots ending in *ra* or *hal*. He says "atrāpsīt" (*atrāpsīt*) in the alternative case governed by the rule "anudātasya ca". He says [the following] in the case of the *aṅ* suffix from the *puṣādi* class:

Regarding *atṛpat*: the sense is that there is no guṇa substitution because of the marker *ṅ*. [The root] *dṛp* means "to rejoice," and it is like the root *tṛp*. Now, one might object: since these two roots (*tṛp* and *dṛp*) are already included among those that optionally take *iṭ* due to belonging to the *radhādi* group, their mention in the list of roots that do not take *iṭ* (the *aniṭ-kārikā*) is redundant. To this, he says: "These two [are mentioned] because they belong to the *radhādi* group..."

Regarding the statement "veṭkāvam artham anudāttatā": in the case of the root *druh* (meaning "to wish harm"), although it lacks the quality of being anudātta (unaccented), the augment *iṭ* is optionally present because it belongs to the *radādi* group. In that context, he states the rule for the absence of *iṭ*: "vā druh-muh-... [Pāṇini 7.2.43]. Thus, in the form *dhrokṣyati*, when the substitution of *gh* is applied by the rule "vā druh-... [Pāṇini 8.2.33], the letter *d* becomes *bhaṣ*.

The form [is derived] by changing *gh* to *c* and *s* to *ṣ*. Even in the alternative where *ḍh* is substituted, this very same form results through the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* according to the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*.
Thus he says: "The form is the same whether *ḍh* or *gh* is substituted. Regarding *adruhat*:

the intention is that *aṅ* is the suffix because it belongs to the *puṣādi* class. Although there is an absence of the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent for the root *muh*, [the form remains as stated].

Regarding *radhādidveṭ* (the root *radh* etc., which optionally takes the augment *iṭ*): the form *mumohitha* is [used] in the case where *iṭ* is applied. In the case where *iṭ* is not applied, however, having considered that there is the substitution of *gh* by the rule *vā druhamuheḥ*, he says *mumogdha*. In the case of the substitution of *ḍh*, he says *mumoḍha*. As for *mokṣyati*, the form is the same whether there is the substitution of *gh* or *ḍh*. [The root] *ṣṇuha*.
[The roots] *ṣṇiha* and [the others] are taught with an initial *ṣ*. Thus he says: *suṣṇoha*, *siṣṇeha*.

In the case of the suffix *thal* and others, when there is the option of being *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment), there is an optional substitution of *gh* according to the rule "optionally for *druh*" (*vā druh*); in the alternative case, there is *ḍh*. These are the roots beginning with *ṛdh*. "Up to the end of the class" means up to the conclusion of the *divādi* class; these are the *puṣādi* roots.

This is the meaning. Regarding the term "siddhānta" (established conclusion): the sense is that Mādhava and others accept it as such. Regarding "upaśame": *upaśama* means destruction (*nāśa*) as well as restraint of the senses (*indriyanigraha*).
(348) *śamāṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* | Pāṇini 7.3.74. [In the presence of the suffix *śyan*, the long vowel is substituted for the finals of the eight roots beginning with *śam*.]

"Of the eight beginning with *śam*. This is clear. Because of the plural number, there is an inclusion of *śam* and the others. Thus he says: "of *śam* and the rest. [The traditional list is: "It is established that these eight—*śam*, *tam*, *dam*, *uram*, *urath*, *śram*, *bhram*, and also *kṣam*, *klam*, and *mad*—are the ones beginning with *śam*. Regarding the root *damu* in the sense of "to subdue": [one might object] "but *śam*..."

It would have been more appropriate to read "yam upaśame" [as the root]; therefore, he says: "upaśamaḥ" [is used] because it is the causative form (ṇyanta) [of the root]. The meaning is that when the suffix *ghañ* is added to the root *śam* in its causative form (*hetumaṇṇic*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening by virtue of the rule "nodātopadeśasya. He asks, "What follows from that? and replies: "By that," and so on. And thus...

The meaning of *dāmyati* is "he pacifies. Regarding the phrase "the rest is like *bhū*," this means that in the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes and in the alternative presence of *śap*, it is like the *bhū*-class (*bhvādi*). The root *kṣam* (to endure) is marked with *ū*; because it is *ūdita*, there is an option for *iṭ* before *thal* and in the *vam* group. Thus he says: *cakṣamita*, etc. [He now explains] the difference in result between its being marked with *ṣ* and not being marked with *ṣ*.

He summarizes [the meaning] with half a verse: "aṣitaḥ. The word *aṣitaḥ* is derived from the root *kṣam* (meaning "to endure"), which is listed under the *śyan*-conjugation (*kṣamate*). From this root *kṣam*, the form *kṣāntiḥ* is produced by adding the suffix *ktin*. Because it ends in *ṣ* (as *kṣam* is a ṣopadeśa root), the suffix *aṅ* prescribed by the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ* does not apply. However, the root *mūṣ* belongs to the *bhūvādika* class and is *ṣita*.
Since the lengthening is established even when *śyan* follows—just as it is when *śap* follows—the suffix *kṣap*—one might object:

"In the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śitī*, the mention of *klam* could simply be omitted. Anticipating this objection on the grounds that its inclusion is necessary for the sake of lengthening [the vowel] before *śap*, he refutes it with the words *śapīva*.

The passage beginning with *śyani api* and ending with *ghinuṇ-arthaḥ* means that the suffix *ghinuṇ* is prescribed after eight roots beginning with *śam*, according to the rule *śamityaṣṭābhyo ghinuṇ*. The phrase "the eight beginning with *śam*" refers to the eight roots enumerated starting from *śamu upaśame* (to pacify) and ending with *madī harṣe* (to rejoice). [The root] *asu* is used in the sense of throwing.
(349) *asyatesthuk* | Pāṇini 7.4.17. Regarding *asyatesthuk*, he completes the remainder [of the sūtra] with *aṅ pi re iti*.

The intention is that this is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] *ṛdṛśo’ṅī*. In the augment *thuk*, the letter *k* is an *it* (indicatory), while the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Due to its *kit* status, it is an internal constituent part of the root. Now, one might raise the objection: since the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* after the root *as* is already established by its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group, the explicit mention of *asyati* in the rule *ṭhasyativaktikhyātibhyo 'ṅ* is redundant. Anticipating this doubt:
He refutes this: "Because this [root] belongs to the *puṣādi* class, it takes *iṭ*;

therefore, [the mention of] *asyati* in the rule *paryāsyate* refers to the inclusion of *asyati* within the rule *ātmanepade'rṅthamasyativaktīḥ*, since the *aṅ* suffix following *puṣādi* roots is restricted solely to the *parasmaipada* and thus does not apply to the *ātmanepada*. Now, regarding *asyati*:
Since this root is exclusively parasmaipada, the ātmanepada suffix would be difficult to obtain; therefore, he says:

"But the taṅ [suffixes] will be taught after a prefix. The phrase "in the determination of verbal forms" (*padavyavasthāyām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. As for the root *yas* in the sense of "exertion" (*prayatna*), [the rule applies]:
*yaso'nupasargāt* 3.1.71.
*Yaso 'nupasargāt* (3.1.68).
*Saṃyasaś ca* (3.1.72). This consists of two sūtras. [The phrase] "the affix *śyan* may optionally occur" is to be supplied from the remainder [of the previous rule].

The meaning is that this follows from the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rules "śyan after *div* and so forth" and "optionally after *bhrāś* and so forth. The meaning of the first sūtra is that *śyan* may optionally occur after the root *yas* when it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). However, when it is preceded by a prefix (*sopasarga*), *śyan* occurs invariably, because the term "not preceded by a prefix" is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Since the suffix *śyan* is invariably obtained after the root *saṃ-pūrva-adya*, the second sūtra [is stated]. Regarding "ravi-uṣa-vibhāge":
the word "this" means that this root is recited in the Divādigaṇa itself, prior to the roots beginning with *puṣ*.
Anticipating the objection of tautology, he says: "But it is recited for the sake of a difference in meaning."

The purpose of reading this root again here, despite its meaning already being included in the sense of *puṣ* (to nourish) and others, is specifically for the sake of the meaning "division" (*vibhāga*).

Regarding *avyuṣat*: since *vyuṣ* was previously read as "to burn," it takes only the *sij* suffix [in the aorist], as in *avyoṣīt*. Regarding *oṣṭhyādi*: this root begins with a labial and ends with a labio-dental sibilant.
"Some think" means this is the sense [of the author's view]. Regarding "the letter *ya*":

others think that this very same [letter] which was previously stated as the giver (*dātṛ*)—beginning with the dentals and labials and ending with the dental sibilants—is here [the same] but devoid of the letter *ya*; such is the meaning.
In the reading "ṭhayakāram," it is an adverbial modifier. [The root] *pluṣ* means "to burn. Now, [an objection]:...
In some places, the reading of this [root] is observed in the *divādi* class among the *parasmaipada* roots, prior to the *puṣādi* group;
there, he dispels the suspicion of redundancy by stating: "The reading in the preceding [section] is for the sake of *sic*.
For if it were read only in the *puṣādi* group, only *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes would be heard, and not *sic*. [This applies to] the *puṣādi* group.

Even if it were read earlier, however, since the augment *aṅ* would be absent, the suffix *sic* would be heard [in its place]. Thus, the meaning of the earlier reading is that *sic* might sometimes be heard. The phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates the presence of a lack of conviction (an *asvarasa*). He shows the reason for this with the words "tadbhvādi" (beginning with those that become such).
The meaning is that it can be rightly said that its recitation in the *divādi* class prior to the *puṣādi* group is rendered purposeful solely by its inclusion in the *bhvādi* class.
And thus, from its recitation in the *bhvādi* class, the *śap* affix is established, as well as the hearing of the suffix *isic* in the *luṅ* tense; [this applies] in the *puṣādi* group.

However, according to the reading [of the Dhātupāṭha], the suffix *śyan* and the *aṅ* [augment] are established. Therefore, the intention is that its placement in the Divādigaṇa prior to the Puṣādi group is indeed redundant. With this very point in mind, the root *ṭhpluṣa dāhe* (to burn) was not recited in the Divādigaṇa before the Puṣādi group in the original text (*mūla*).

The root *mas* [is mentioned] in the sense of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). Its status as having an *it*-marker is for the sake of the rule "*śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*" [which prohibits the addition of *iṭ*].
[Examples: *masyati*. Some say there is also *samī*; [example: *samyati*. [The roots] *bhṛśu* and *bhraṃśu*:
[the author] states [the rule] regarding the second root with the words "*aniditām*" [Pāṇini 6.4.24]. [The roots] *yupa*, *rupa*, and *lupa*.

The reading "udit" has arisen from the scribal error of contradicting the *Dhātuvṛtti* and other authorities; the intended reading here, however, is as follows: the purpose of including *kṣubhi*, *nabhi*, and *tubhi* in this *divādigaṇa* is solely for the sake of the *śyan* suffix. In reality, these three should have been placed even before the *puṣādi* group.

The sense is that [the form] is correct. Regarding the root *ñi midā*: one says *amidadit*. But is it not the case that in the *bhvādi* sub-group, within the *dyutādi* section, the root *ñi midā snehane* is listed among the *ātmanepada* roots? Furthermore, in the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi*, an option for *parasmaipada* is stated regarding the *luṅ* tense. Moreover, the *aṅ* suffix after the *dyutādi* group occurs only with *parasmaipada*, and not otherwise.

If it is argued that, by the very recitation [of the root] in the *dyutādi* group, *aṅ* is obtained in the case of the *parasmaipada*, whereas in the case of *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada*), since *aṅ* is absent, *amediṣṭa* is established; and thus its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group is redundant because *śyan* is already established simply by its recitation in the *divādi* group—[to this we reply: [The response follows...]

By the phrase beginning with "simply because of its recitation in the *dyautadi* group" and ending with "since [the rule] is already established," he dispels this doubt: "lest there be a recitation here [in the *dyautadi* group] such as 'amedīt'.
The meaning is that its recitation among the *puṣadi* verbs is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] in cases like 'amedīt'. [It must be] precisely before the *puṣadi* group.
The intention is that if this [root] were read in the *divādi* class, then because *luṅ* would be possible from it, the form would have to be *amedit*.

Now, if this were the case, its reading in the *dyutādi* sub-group within the *bhvādi* class would be useless; it should rather be read among the *ātmanepadins* outside of the *dyutādi* group. And in that way, the form would be *amediṣṭa*.

Siddham. Here, having raised the objection that [the form] would be established by its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group under the rule *amantre*, he resolves it by accepting the desired outcome, stating "only externally" (*bahireva*). However, if the reading is *sūcitaḥ*, it should be explained as "all the more appropriate. [The roots] beginning with *ñi kṣvide* are clear. Thus end the *divādi* [roots].
Thus ends the section on the *divādi* (fourth class) verbs in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the copulative compound (dvandva).

(890) *cārthe dvandvaḥ* | Pāṇini 2.2.29. Now follows the definition of the *dvandva* compound. [The sūtra states: "A *dvandva* [is formed] in the sense of *ca* ('and'). From the previous rule *subāmantrite*, the term *sub* is carried over; and from the rule *anekamanyapadārthe*, the term *anekam* ("more than one") is also carried over. This refers to a *samāsa*.
Thus, the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is also governed here. He states this with the words beginning "anekam" (more than one). To the question "And what is the meaning [of 'ca']?", he says:
"samuccaya" (conjunction), etc. Amara states:

"The word *ca* [is used] in the senses of *anvācaya* (subordinate conjunction), *samāhāra* (aggregation), *itaretara-samuccaya* (mutual conjunction), and *samuccaya* (conjunction). Among these, [he explains] *samuccaya*.
He explains [the term] with the words "mutually" (*paraspara*) and "in one" (*ekasmin*).

The meaning is that when a single verb is repeated, *samuccaya* (conjunction) is the sense of the particle *ca* where there is first the connection of one word that is not being compounded, and immediately thereafter the connection of the other. For example: "Worship both the preceptor and the teacher. (*īśvaraṃ guruṃ ca bhajasva*)

For in that context, due to the connection with the word *ca* (and), the Guru’s dependence upon the Lord is implied, but not the Lord’s dependence upon the Guru, because the latter lacks a connection with the word *ca*. Therefore, only a single *ca* is employed here. Thus, there are two distinct sentences: "Worship the Lord" and "Worship the Guru."
It concludes [the discussion]. Now, he defines *anvācaya* (conjunction): "of either one" (*anyatarasya*).

Where there is a connection (*anvaya*) of one word with a single verbal action by way of being incidental—that is, as having activity for the sake of another—and of the other word with the other [verbal action], [that is *anvācaya*].

The meaning is that in a sentence of action (*kriyāpada*), there is a connection as the object to be enjoined (*uddeśyatvena anvaya*), and in that case, the sense of *ca* is "conjunction" (*anvācaya*). For example: "Go for alms and bring the cow. [The root] *aṭ* means "to go. The meaning is: "Obtain [alms] by going for alms. Go for alms; if at that time the cow is found, bring her as well, but not otherwise.

The intended meaning is that one must strive with focused intent toward the bringing of the cows. It defines *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) as follows: where there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of things joined together—which depend upon one another—within a single verbal action, that is *itaretarayoga*.

The meaning is that the sense to be understood is mutual association (*parasparasāharya*), as in the example: "the *dhava* and the *khadira* tree" (*dhavakhadirau*). Here, two uses of the particle *ca* are employed to indicate their mutual association.
Now, he defines the collective (*samāhāra*): "a collection is a collective."

The meaning is mutual association (*parasparasāhitya*). For example, the collection of technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) is called "the *saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*. In that case, within a copulative compound (*dvandva*) expressing mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the association is a qualifier of the substances (*dravyaviśeṣaṇa*). As in the example, "Cut the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," where they are understood as being joined together.
It is understood [that way]. However, in a *dvigu* compound denoting a collective (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the collective whole (*samūha*) is the predicate (*viśeṣya*).
For example, in the expression "the *saṃjñā*s and *paribhāṣā*s," it is understood as "the collection of those two.
In cases such as "they study the *saṃjñā*s and *paribhāṣā*s," the connection with the action belongs to the collective whole.
It is sufficient to understand that [these meanings] are to be understood through the door of *samūha* (aggregation). Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

the syntactical connection is that among those meanings, there is no *dvandva* compound in the case of *samuccaya* (conjunction) and *anvācaya* (sequential conjunction). For example, "Worship both the Lord and the Guru"—this is an illustration of *samuccaya*. "Go for alms and [then] look for a cow"—this is an illustration of *anvācaya*.
And the example "cānaye" has been explained immediately below. Regarding the phrase "due to lack of syntactic connection" (asāmarthyāt):

according to the method stated in the verse "īśvaraṃ guruṃ ca," when the words *īśvara* and *guru* are repeated independently of one another [in the sense of "to the Lord and to the Guru"], the word *bhajasva* [is connected with both].

Because there is a sequential connection and an absence of mutual connection, there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). In the case of "Go beg for alms and bring the cow," however, because the alms and the cow are connected respectively to begging and bringing while remaining mutually ignorant of one another's roles, there is an absence of mutual connection and thus a lack of semantic capacity.

This is quite clear. Consequently, since the meanings of *cā*—namely mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*)—possess a state of mutual association (*sāhitya*), they possess the required semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) for the formation of a *dvandva* compound. The detailed exposition should be consulted in the *Mañjūṣā*.
He illustrates *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) with the example "dhavakhadirau" (the dhava and the khadira).

This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the dhava and the khadira. Here, *dhava* is a specific type of tree and *khadira* is well-known; the understanding is that these two are taken together. He illustrates *samāhāra* (collective aggregation) with the example "saṃjñā" (technical name and rule): namely, both *saṃjñā* and *paribhāṣā*.
The analysis of the compound is "the combination of those two. Because the combination is a single entity, the singular number is used.

By the rule "that [compound] is neuter," its neuter gender is established. Now, one might object: in the rule "dvandva [is used] in the sense of 'and'," does not the phrase "sup with sup" already follow by anuvṛtti?

One might argue that since forms such as *dhavakhadirau* (the *dhava* and *khadira* trees) are established even without it, the recurrence of the term "multiple" (*aneka*) is redundant; therefore, he says:
"because of the mention of 'multiple'. Regarding *hotṛpotṛ*: the analysis is *hotā ca potā ca neṣṭā ca udgātā ca* ("the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Udgātṛ").
The point is that the mention of "multiple" is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound even when there are more than two members.

By the rule *ṭhānaRﬁĀto dvandve*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* applies only to the word *neṣṭṛ* because it is immediately followed by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), but it does not apply to the words *hotṛ* and *potṛ* either; for since the subsequent member is separated from them by the intermediate member, the words *hotṛ* and *potṛ* do not stand immediately before the subsequent member. [Objection: But then...

To the question "How [is this so]? regarding the phrase "Hotṛ, Potṛ, Neṣṭṛ, and Udgātṛ," he says: "Of the two. There is a *dvandva* compound of the two, Hotṛ and Potṛ; the word *hotṛ* undergoes the substitution *ānaṅ*.
Then there is a *dvandva* compound of the two, Neṣṭṛ and Udgātṛ; the word *neṣṭṛ* undergoes the substitution *ānaṅ*. From that...
The compound consists of two internal *dvandva*s: "the *hotṛ* and *potr̥*, and the *neṣṭr̥* and *udgātṛ*.
In this context, the purpose of the word *neṣṭodgātṛ* as the final member (*uttarapada*) is to trigger the substitution of *ānaṅ* for the word *hotāpotr̥*.
The form *ānaṅ* has the marker *ṅ*; because of this *ṅ*-marker, it is an initial substitute (*ādeśa*). The vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

By relying on the case-ending inherent within [the compound], the *n* is elided because of its status as a word (*padatva*). (891) In the group beginning with *rājadanta*, the subsequent member [is placed first]. In the word *neṣṭodgātṛ*, there is also the *guṇa* substitution for the initial vowels (*ādguṇaḥ*). In the group beginning with *rājadanta*, the subsequent member [is placed first].
The rule "the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first" is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "in these.

This means "in the *rājadantādi* group. The phrase "subordinate member" (*upasarjanam*) is to be supplied as a remainder before the words "fit for prior usage" (*pūrvaprayogārham*). As in the example *rājadantaḥ*, [it refers to] the word *danta*.

In the case of a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, although the word would normally be subordinated (*upasarjana*) because it is not the object of giving (*apradāna*), its placement at the end of the compound is prescribed. In this list (*gaṇa*), words such as *rājadanta*, *agra*, and *vaṇa* are *tatpuruṣa* compounds, while *viṣvaksena*, *arjuna*, and others are *dvandva* compounds; therefore, they are introduced here in the section on *dvandva* compounds.

In the compound *viśvaksenārjunau*, although the rule *ṭhajādyadantam* would require the word *arjuna* to be placed first, its placement at the end is maintained. Regarding the statement "there is no fixed order among words such as dharma," this is a *gaṇasūtra*; its meaning is that either of the two may be placed first. Thus, in the example *arthadharmau*, the word beginning with a vowel and ending in *a* [i.e., *artha*] is placed first.

The meaning is that, although a rule regarding the obligatory prior placement [of the word] would otherwise apply, this lack of such a rule must be stated. "It is treated as an irregularity" (nipātyate) means that the *rājadantādi* group is optional. Furthermore, even though the husband (*pati*) is more venerable, he is placed last. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form); however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), this entire group is [fully enumerated].
It has been recited: (892) *dvandve ghi* | Pāṇini 2.2.32.

In a *dvandva* compound, when a *ghi* [vowel] occurs, [the preceding member is the base]. The word "preceding" (*pūrva*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Therefore, he says: "it should be the preceding [member]."
Regarding "hariharādi": because the word *hari* possesses the *ghitva* designation, it takes the prior position [in the compound].
When multiple [options] are applicable, there is a restriction to one; in the remaining cases, there is no restriction.
But surely, in the case of "hariharaguravaḥ," since the word *guru* also possesses *ghitva*, it too would take the prior position?

To address this, he says: "aneka" (of many). The meaning is that when there is the possibility of a *dvandva* compound of several words bearing the technical designation *ghi*, there is a rule (*niyama*) regarding the prior placement of one such *ghi*-designated word; whereas in the remaining case—namely, regarding other *ghi*-designated words—the prior placement is optional (*vikalpa*). This...

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "alpāctaram. According to the view that [words denote] the universal (jāti), the various grammatical rules apply only once to all individuals by taking the form (ākṛti) as the primary basis, because they have been applied once; they do not, however, apply to each individual separately, for if that were the case...

Because it would follow that the rule applies to every individual instance. Consequently, when there is a co-occurrence (*samavāya*) of several items bearing the designation *ghisamjñaka*, and one such item is placed first, the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) does not apply again, because once the rule has applied once, its requirement is satisfied. As for the view of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*):

They say that no fixed rule is followed here, because it depends on the specific usage (*lakṣya*). Regarding the example *hariharaguravaḥ*, the intended meaning is that there is no restriction regarding the order of the words *hara* and *guru*. (893) *ajādyadantam* | 2.2.33 | [The dual and plural endings follow the word that begins with a vowel other than *a* and ends in short *a*.]
"A word beginning with a vowel other than 'a' and ending in 'a' [is placed first]. This means: provided it begins with a vowel other than 'a' (ajādī) and ends in 'a' (adantam).
Regarding the example "Īśa-Kṛṣṇau" (Lord and Kṛṣṇa): although Kṛṣṇa ends in 'a', because he does not begin with a vowel other than 'a', he is not placed first.
There is no restriction regarding multiple [words].
Regarding "there is no restriction regarding multiple [words]," the word "it should be stated" is to be supplied as the remainder.
A word beginning with a vowel other than *a* and ending in *ā* or *ī* takes precedence over one ending in *a*, by way of the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

One might object: "In the case of *indrāgnī*, why does the word *agni* not appear first due to its status as a *ghi*? To this, he says: "after a word ending in *gh*" (*dhyantāt*). By the term "ending in *gh*" (*dhyanta*), the rule *dvandve ghi* is intended. The ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*. [This refers to] the rule *dvandve* [governing the *vipratiṣedha*].
The meaning is that, setting aside the rule *ghī* (Pāṇini 1.4.7), the rule *ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 1.4.5) applies.
(894) *alpāctaram* | 2.2.34. *alpāctaram*: that which has fewer vowels (*ac*) is "few-voweled" (*alpāc*); that very thing is *alpāctaram*.

Precisely for this reason, by virtue of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the suffix *tarap* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) and there is an absence of *kutva*. The meaning is that in a *dvandva* compound, a word consisting of fewer syllables should be placed first. As in "Śiva and Keśava. The underlying intention is that any doctrine asserting the superiority of one over either Hari or Hara is a mere stone-thrower's argument (*pāṣaṇjavāda*). If...

The ancients held that if the suffix *tarap* were intended to express the sense of "the comparative" (*dvivacanavibhajya*) and so forth, then it would not apply to a plurality of items, as in the example "dhava-khadira-palāśāḥ. However, in the *Śabdenduśekhara*, it is established that this *tarap* indeed expresses excellence (*prakarṣa*).
Regarding "of seasons and lunar mansions having an equal number of syllables" (*ṛtunakṣatrāṇāṃ samākṣarāṇām*):

the meaning is that when seasons and lunar mansions— which possess an equal number of vowels (*ack*)— are combined in a *dvandva* compound, it must be stated that their prior placement occurs according to their respective order (*ānupūrvyeṇa*).

"Hemanta, śiśira, and vasanta"—this is the sequence of the three seasons as established by worldly convention. The same applies to the lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā. Regarding the expression "grīṣma-vasantau," because the syllables are unequal in number, *vasanta* does not take precedence; rather, *grīṣma* is placed first because it has fewer syllables.
The rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*):
that which has fewer syllables comes first.
That which has fewer syllables comes first; in a *dvandva* compound, that whose constituent members have fewer syllables should be placed first.
The meaning is that it should be stated [as follows]. Regarding "kuśakāśam": this is a collective dvandva compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
Regarding "abhyarhitam ca" (and the more venerable): the meaning is that it should be stated that "the more excellent should be placed first."

Regarding the phrase "the ascetic and the mountain": since a mountain possesses the nature of an immobile being (*sthāvara-janman*), it should be understood that the ascetic is more venerable than it. In the *Bhāṣya*, however, "mother and father" is cited as the example, based on such traditional law (*smṛti*) as: "By virtue of conceiving and nourishing [the child], the mother is weightier than the father."
That is the intended meaning:
"in the sequence of the phonemes.
Regarding the phrase "in the sequence of the phonemes," these are placed first according to their respective order.

Regarding the phrase "the castes are Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra," this is from Amarasimha. Their sequential order, however, is established by the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and other texts, beginning with: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I procreate'; he emitted the Trivṛt [stoma] from his mouth... and so forth.

Regarding "of the elder brother" (*bhrāturjyāyasaḥ*): the meaning is that the elder brother (*jyeṣṭhabhrātṛ*) is placed first [in the compound]. In this context, there are two rules: *dvandve ghi* ("in a dvandva, a word ending in *ghi* comes first") and *ajādyadantam* ("a word beginning with a vowel and ending in *a* comes first"). Furthermore, there are the rules *alpāctaram* ("that which has fewer syllables comes first") and *laghvakṣaraṃ pūrvam* ("that which has lighter syllables comes first").

This [rule] is superseded by the rules "the seasons and constellations," "that which is more venerable," and "an elder brother," because they possess greater force. However, in the Bhāṣya, an alternative view is established, stating that "that which is more venerable is placed first in every case."

(895) *dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām* |2|4|2|. "And a *dvandva* [compound] [is singular], as are [the members that are] limbs of living beings, musical instruments, and armies. This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) containing a *dvandva*: "limbs of living beings, musical instruments, and armies. The word *aṅga* ("limb"), which is heard at the end of the *dvandva*, is connected with each [of the preceding members].

Intending this, he says: "of these. This means: of the limbs of living beings, the limbs of musical instruments, and the limbs of an army. Regarding the term "dvandva": the meaning is that it is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (a collective copulative compound).
This is because, in the preceding sūtra—"*dvigurekavacanam*"—it was stated that "the mention of *samāhāra* (collection) must be made."
Because the *vārttika* also applies here. Regarding "as a single unit" (*ekavat*): the term "*ekavacanam*" (singular number) is understood from the previous context.
It is called "*ekavacanam*" because it expresses one (*ekaṃ vakti*); [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used. It is neuter by virtue of referring to a general category.
Regarding "hand-and-foot" (*pāṇipādam*): the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of the two hands and the two feet. Here...

In a collective compound (samāhāra), there is singularity, and by the rule "that [compound] is neuter," there is also neuter gender. This is an example of a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), since hands and feet are parts of a living being. Therefore, he gives an example for a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of musical instruments: *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (the drummers and the lute-players).

The words *mṛdaṅga* and *paṇava* refer to specific types of musical instruments; however, in this context, they also denote the playing of those instruments. In the sense of "one whose craft (*śilpa*) is the playing of the *mṛdaṅga*," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "ṭhak after *śilpa*.
Thus, the analysis of the compound is: "the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of the *mārdaṅgika* and the *pāṇavika*."

The singular number is used because it is a component of the army (*tūryāṅga*); its status as a component of the army is to be understood from the fact that it sounds [like one]. Its neuter gender follows from the rule *sa napuṃsakam*. He gives an example of a copulative compound of army components: *ratikāśvāroham*. Those who move by means of a chariot (*ratha*)...

*Rathikāḥ*. [The rule] *ṭh parpādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan* applies. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the collection (*samāhāra*) of charioteers (*rathika*) and horsemen (*aśvāroha*). Because it is a part of an army (*senāvayava*), there is singular number (*ekavadbhāva*). As before, there is neuter gender (*napuṃsakatva*). But surely, in a collective dvandva (*samāhāradvandva*), the analysis is "of the collection"? *Note: This is a commentary on the formation of the compound *rathikāśvārohāḥ* (charioteers and horsemen) as a neuter singular collective.*

Because it is a constituent part of an army, there is singularity (*ekatva*). As before, there is neuter gender (*napuṃsakatva*). Now, one might object: "In a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*), since the collection (*samāhāra*) is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and that [collection] is singular, this rule is redundant. To this he says: "Because the collection is singular. [The phrase] "only the collection" means... not [the individual members].
This refers to *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction). The meaning is that this sūtra serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) regarding their use in a *dvandva* compound.

Likewise, the subsequent sūtras also serve as restrictive rules for the case of *samāhāra* (collective) compounds alone. Otherwise, let this sūtra be intended to prescribe the singular number (*ekavattva*) for these [words] when used in an *itaretarayoga-dvandva*. Thus...
And it should be stated that the form *pāṇipādam* is masculine and singular;
for the vārtika from the previous sūtra, "the mention of 'collective' (*samāhāra*) must be made," is carried over here,
and in this entire section on the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*), the Bhāṣya consistently treats these as only collective dvandvas.

And because it has already been cited [as an example]. Nor should one fear the over-extension [of the rule] to cases such as *rathika-mārdaṅgikau* ("the charioteer and the drummer"), for there is a single-remaining compound (*ekavad-bhāva*) for mutual dvandvas of limbs of living beings, a single-remaining compound for mutual dvandvas of musical instruments,
and a single-remaining compound for mutual dvandvas of military units.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya: "Because it is accepted as being a singular entity.
(896) *anuvāde caraṇānām* | 2|4|3|. Regarding the restatement (*anuvāda*) of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), a *dvandva* compound of Vedic schools is singular.
The *cāraṇas* are those distinguished as students of specific Vedic branches (*śākhā*). There is a mutual *dvandva* compound of those terms.

The meaning is "as a single unit" (*ekavat*). He explains the phrase "in the restatement of what is already established" (*anuvāde*) as follows: "in the presentation of that which is already known," meaning in the communication of a matter already understood.
It should be stated: "after the roots *sthā* and *iṇ*, in the *luṅ* [tense].

Regarding "after *sthā* and *iṇ*": the singular number is used with the intention that it applies to each [root] individually in relation to "*luṅ*". Thus, when the root *sthā* ends in *luṅ*, and when the root *iṇ* ends in *luṅ*, [the suffix *ām* is applied] precisely when they are employed in a restatement (*anuvāda*) concerning the Vedic schools (*caraṇa*).

The meaning is that it should be stated that "a *dvandva* compound is singular. Regarding *udagāt*: the meaning is "it appeared"; this is the form of the root *iṇ* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. Regarding *kaṭhakālāpam*: those who study what was taught by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhas*;
[the suffix] *ṇini* is applied because he was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. For that [suffix], [the rule] "after *kaṭha* and *caraka*" applies.

*Luk*. Then, by the rule *ṭhproktālluṅ*, there is *luk* elision of the suffix denoting the student (*adhyetṛ-pratyaya*). [The derivation is as follows: "Those who study what was taught by Kalāpin" are the *Kālāpās*. In the sense of "taught by," the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *Kalāpin*.
By the rule *sabrahmacāripīṭhasarpi-tāpyānām ṭilopaḥ*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *i*) of *tāpin*. Then, the suffix *aṇ* [denoting] the student is applied.

The suffix *lu* is elided by the rule "after [a word] ending in the suffix *prokta*, *lu* is elided. The analysis of the compound is "the aggregate of the Kaṭhas and the Kālāpas. Regarding the form *pratyaṣṭhāt*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) form of the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *prati*. Regarding *kaṭhakauthumam*: those who study what was taught by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhas*; [those who study what was taught] by Kauthuma...

The Kauthumas are those who study what was proclaimed [by Kuthumin]. In the sense of "proclaimed," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tena proktam*. By the rule *sabrahmacārī*, there is the elision of the feminine suffix (*ṭilopa*). Then, there is the elision of the suffix *adhyetraṇ*. The analysis of the compound is: "the collective aggregate of the Kaṭhas and the Kauthumas. When the Kaṭhas and the Kalāpas are mentioned...

When the Kaṭhas and the Kauthumas were established, they made an agreement that "something must be said" at that time; these two sentences are [the result] of that agreement. Here, because there is a restatement of the previously established rising (*udaya*) and establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*), there is identity [of meaning]. Why [is it not so] in the case of the roots *sthā* and *iṇ*?
There were the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas. Why [is the word] *luṅ* used? [To show: "The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas stood.
(897) *adhvaryukratu-r-anapuṃsakam* | 2|4|4|.
[The compound] *adhvaryukratuḥ*. Here, the word *adhvaryu* refers to the Yajurveda which prescribes the duties of the Adhvaryu priest.

Thus he says: "The Yajurveda"; "the Arkāśvamedha. *Arka* is the Great Sacrifice (*mahākratu*). *Aśvamedha* is well-known [as a specific sacrifice]. Both are sacrifices prescribed by the Yajurveda. The analysis of the compound is: "the collection of both the Arka and the Aśvamedha. Regarding "the arrow and the thunderbolt": these two are specific types of sacrifices, not [ordinary weapons].
The intention is that these two are prescribed in the *Yajurveda*. If one asks, "In which Veda are they then prescribed?", he says: "In the *Sāma* [Veda]. Regarding the *Rājasūya* and *Vājapeya*:
although these two are prescribed in the *Yajurveda*, they do not take the singular form because they are neuter; this is the intention.
Since *rājasūya* and *vājapeya* are well-known as being masculine, he says "ardharcādi" (belonging to the *ardharca* group).

[The word] "adhyayanataḥ" [is explained as follows]: the analysis is "aviprakṛṣṭākhyānām" (of those whose names are not remote). In "adhyayanataḥ," the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the instrumental case.
(898) [The suffix *cha*] is applied after words denoting those who are not separated from their study [to form names of villages].
Thus it is said: "near by means of study. This means "in close proximity.
Regarding the terms *padaka* and *kramaka*: those who study the *padas* are called *padakas*; those who study the *kramas* are called *kramakas*.

The rule "from *krama* and so forth, the suffix *buṅ*" [applies]. The analysis of the compound is: "the collection (*samāhāra*) of *padaka*s and *kramaka*s. The sense is that the proximity existing in the study—namely, that the study of the *krama* follows immediately after the study of the *pada*—is superimposed upon the student. The term "*padakrama*" is not cited as an example [because it is a *dvandva*].

Since the rule "jātir aprāṇinām" [Pāṇini 2.4.6] would have already established this, the point is that when it refers to those who study [the Veda], it is not a *jāti* (genus). (899) *jātir aprāṇinām* |2|4|6|
"Jāti" [is used] for non-living things. The term "jāti" [is employed] by way of transposition (vyatyaya) in place of the genitive plural;
thus, it means "of those that denote a genus. Regarding "dhānā-śuṣkulī":
the analysis (vigraha) is "the collection (samāhāra) of dhānās and śuṣkulis. Because they denote a genus, there is singular number (ekavattva).

The intention is that [the vowel] is short because of its neuter gender. Regarding *viṭchūdrāḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the Vaiśyas and the Śūdras. Regarding the phrase "only for those belonging to the class of substances" (*dravyajātīyānām eva*): the intention is that this is obtained through the maxim of the connection with *nañ* and *iva*, since there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not for non-living beings" (*aprāṇinām*). Regarding *rūparasau*.

These two [words] express a genus (*jāti*) residing in a quality (*guṇa*). "Going" (*gamana*) and "contracting" (*ākuñcana*)—these two express specific genera residing in actions (*kriyā*). But surely, in the cases of *badarāṇi* (the fruits of the *badarī*) and *āmalakāni* (the fruits of the *āmalakī*), the suffix denoting a derivative (*vikāra*) is elided by the rule *ṭhphale luk*.

There is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix by the rule *ṭhak-chasor ady-antalukī*. These two [words] denote specific sub-species included within the genus "fruit. Consequently, how can there be two forms—*badarāmalakam* (neuter singular) and *badarāmalakāni* (neuter plural)—from the compound *badarāṇi cāmalakāni ca*?

Since the rule "jātir aprāṇinām" (Pāṇini 2.4.6) establishes that a genus is always expressed in the singular, he says: "when the genus is predominant. This means when there is an intention to express the genus as permeating all its individual instances, without regard for any specific individual.

For in expressions such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), by the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the meaning of words like "jar" is the universal (*jāti*) such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). And since a universal cannot exist without a substratum, [it requires an individual].

Because [the universal] cannot be present [in its entirety], when there is a requirement for an individual that serves as its substratum, the entire [class of individuals] is presented without distinction. In that regard, in usages such as "bring the jar," since it is impossible for the universal and all past, future, and present individuals to be connected with the action, the action finds its rest only by taking some particular individual. And this alone constitutes the primacy of the universal, consisting in its capacity to convey all those individuals that serve as the substrata of that particular universal.

In usages such as "white pots" (*ṭhghaṭāḥ śuklāḥ*), the universal (*jāti*) brings forth only specific individuals due to the influence of the co-occurrence with other words; thus, the universal is subordinate because it does not bring forth all the individuals that serve as its substrata. This is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *tasyāditaḥ*. Consequently, since there is no distinction between the universal of being a jujube fruit (*badaratva*) and the universal of being an *āmalaka* fruit (*āmalakatva*)—both of which are subsumed under the universal of being a fruit (*phalatva*)—all the individuals belonging to those substrata are brought forth, resulting in the singular collective form *badarāmalakam*.

Regarding the phrase *dravyaviśeṣa* (specific substances): in examples such as *āraṇyāni badarāmalakāni* ("wild jujubes and emblic myrobalans"), there is the presentation of only a few individuals qualified by *āraṇyatva* (wildness) and so on, through the universals (*jāti*) of *badaratva* (jujube-ness) and *āmalakatva* (myrobalan-ness), which are subsumed under the universal of "fruit-ness" (*phalatva*). Since domestic individuals are not presented, and since those two universals are not predominant, this is not a case for the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*). They say that the evidence for this is the usage in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra beginning with *kṣīrodake saṃpṛkte* ("when milk and water are mixed"). (900) *viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo 'grāmāḥ* | 2|4|7| [The names of] rivers and regions that possess distinct genders, provided they are not village names, [form a singular collective compound].
"Rivers and regions possessing specific genders, provided they are not villages. The word "agrāmāḥ" (not villages) is the correct division [of the compound].

The singular number is used for the plural by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*). The root *śiṣ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* signifies distinction, as seen in such rules as "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose gender (*liṅga*) is specified (*viśiṣṭa*)."

And thus, it is understood that a *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting rivers and words denoting regions—provided they are distinct from those denoting villages and possess different genders—shall be treated as a singular.
This is what [the author] states with the words "excepting villages" (*grāmavarja*). It means that in the case of a collective *dvandva*, the rule for singular treatment applies.

This is intended to convey the sense of the result (*phala*). For it has been stated immediately following this section on the formation of singular compounds (*ekavadbhāva*) that the restriction (*niyama*) for this context is that a *dvandva* compound denotes only a collective (*samāhāra*). Regarding "Uddhya": Uddhya is the name of a particular river. Irāvatī is the name of a certain river.

The singular number for those two [names] is due to their denoting specific rivers; this is because the word *nadī* (river) includes male rivers as well, otherwise [the application of the rule] would be impossible due to the difference in gender—this is the intended meaning. [The example] "jāmbavaśālūkiṇyau" is [governed] by the rule "grāmāḥ" (plural).

The exclusion of a *dvandva* compound whose constituent members are both parts of a village is intended here. The sense is that even this *dvandva*, which has both a city and a village as its constituents, is considered to have a village as one of its constituents; therefore, it is excluded.

(901) *kṣudrajantavaḥ* |2|4|8|. "Small creatures" (*kṣudrajantavaḥ*). The meaning is that the *dvandva* compound of these is singular.
