He states the result: "The *dvandva* of these occurs only in a collective sense (*samāhāra*). For example: *yūkālikṣam* ("lice and nits"). That is, *yūkāś ca likṣāś ca* ("both lice and nits").
The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: *yūkā* (lice) are specific types of sweat-born creatures found on the head, which is covered with much hair;

*likṣā* (nits) are also well-known. There is treatment as a singular (*ekavatva*) and the shortening of the neuter vowel. The phrase "up to the mongoose" (*ā nakulāt*) means that, according to the *Bhāṣya*, "creatures smaller than a mongoose are considered 'small animals' (*kṣudrajantu*). This is the intended sense.

(902) *yeṣāṃ ca virodhaḥ śāśvatikaḥ* || 2.4.9 || The sūtra is explained by completing the ellipsis with "of those which" (*yeṣām*), as follows: "of these, as before. This means that a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound) is treated as a singular. The indeclinable *śaśvat* occurs in the sense of "always" (*sadā*).

Then, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "becoming" (*bhava*). Due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) after indeclinables when followed by a mere *bha*-suffix; furthermore, the substitution of *ka* as prescribed by the rule "*ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ*" does not occur here. The meaning is "natural. Regarding the compound *ahinakulam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "snakes and mongooses. This [compound] refers to their natural [enmity].

The term *virodha* (opposition) is well-known here as enmity (*vaira*), and not as the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthiti*). Therefore, this does not apply in the case of "shadow and sunlight" (*chāyātapau*). However, in the case of "gods and demons" (*devāsurāḥ*), this singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur, because their opposition is merely occasional (*kādācitkatva*), being caused by factors such as the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).

For their opposition is indeed occasional, since there is no opposition between them at times such as during the churning of the nectar (*amṛta-mathana*). Now, it may be objected that in the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga-* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), an option regarding the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) for copulative compounds (*dvandva*) of animals and birds will be stated; of that—

In such cases as *gomahiṣu gomahiṣāḥ*, *haṃsacakravākaṃ*, and *haṃsacakravākāḥ*, there is scope for [the application of] Pāṇini 2.4.12 (*dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām*). For the rule *yeṣāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.9), there is scope in examples such as *ahinakulam*. In cases like *govyāghram* and *kākolūkam*, both rules would apply simultaneously. Regarding that:
Fearing that the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) about to be mentioned might apply because it follows [the previous rule], he says: "go-vyāghram.
Regarding the phrase "by the word *ca*," the meaning is: "by the word *ca* in the rule *yeṣāṃ ca*. This is clear in the Bhāṣya.

(903) [The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words denoting] Śūdras who are not excluded. ||2|4|10|| [The word] "of Śūdras" [is used]. He explains the term "aniravasita" as "those who are not excluded. Those by whom a vessel has been used is not purified even by the rite of washing with alkaline water.

"Excluded" (niravasitāḥ) refers to the Caṇḍālas and others; those by whom a vessel has been used [for eating] is purified through a rite of consecration (saṃskāra), they are "not excluded" (aniravasitāḥ)—this is clear from the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "of the Śūdras": by the word "Śūdra," those other than the three higher castes (trairvarṇika) are intended, as indicated by the mark (liṅga) in the term "of those not excluded."
"As before" means that it is a collective dvandva compound (samāhāradvandva) functioning as a singular. Regarding "takṣāyaskāram":

the analysis (vigraha) is "carpenters and blacksmiths. He states the purpose of the rule "ṭhaniravasitānām" with the words "pātrāt" etc. "Caṇḍālamṛtapā" refers to the vessel used by such [outcastes] for eating.
There is no purification even through ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*); this is to be understood from the very commentary (*bhāṣya*).
And this is well known in the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), as in the rule:
"Cows, horses, and so forth" (Pāṇini 2.4.11).

"And *gavāśva-vaprabhṛtīni* (cow-horse-buffalo, etc.). The meaning is that they are always [compounded] in exactly the same order as they are enumerated in the list (*gaṇa*). Regarding *gavāśvam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "cows and horses. Here, since it is a dual compound of animals (*paśu-dvandva*), the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣe* would have made the formation optional; however, this present rule makes it compulsory. In this regard, [the rule applies] everywhere.

In the case of *vibhāṣā*, because both the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) and the *pūrvarūpa* (substitution of the preceding vowel) apply, there is no restriction to a singular form such as *go-aśvam* or *go'śvam*; for it is stated that [the forms] are "as they are pronounced," and because in the *gaṇa* list only *gavāśvam* is indicated. Regarding compounds such as *gavāśva*, the *vārttika* states: "The *dvandva* compound functions exactly as it is pronounced."

Regarding *mānam* and *dāsīdāsam*: here there is a rule of singular number (*ekavattva-niyama*). However, the "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) rule—*pumān striyā*—does not apply here because of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). This is illustrated by examples such as *gavāvikam* (cows and sheep) and *gavaiḍakam* (cows and goats), which are clearly explained in the *Vṛtti*.

(905) *Vibhāṣā* [the compound may optionally be singular] for groups of trees, deer, grass, grain, condiments, cattle, birds, horses, mares, and for the pairs: prior-posterior and lower-upper. Pāṇini 2.4.12.

The term *vibhāṣā* applies to the word *vakṣa*. The term *dvandva* is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). Although there is only one genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it is divided according to the difference in its scope.
The connection [of the genitive] is as a constituent part for the seven beginning with *vṛkṣa*: "the dvandva of *vṛkṣa* and so forth."

It is understood that a *dvandva* compound consists of parts such as "trees" (*vṛkṣa*) and so forth. However, the three pairs beginning with "horse and mule" (*aśvabaḍaba*), "prior and posterior" (*pūrvāpara*), and "lower and upper" (*adharottara*) are construed non-differently (as a single unit), such that the *dvandva* is of the nature of "horse-and-mule," "prior-and-posterior," and "lower-and-upper."
In the case of "trees" (*vṛkṣa*) and so forth, there is the apprehension of the specific types themselves.
Thus he says: "of trees and so forth. "As before" means that they may optionally be treated as a singular unit.
Regarding "in the case of trees and so forth": this refers to words denoting specific types of trees, words denoting specific types of grass, and so on.

The meaning is: [it applies] to words denoting specific types of grain and words denoting specific types of animals; this is because it was stated as such in both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika on the sūtra *svaṃ rūpam*. Thus, the result is that this rule does not apply in cases such as *vṛkṣāśca dhavāśca* ("trees and dhava trees"), but rather—

By the rule "jātir aprāṇinām," there is always a singular number. Among the seven types of dvandvas (copulative compounds) consisting of parts such as trees, he gives *vṛkṣadvandva* as an example—namely, *plakṣa* etc.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "plakṣāś ca nyagrodhāś ca" (both *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees).
He illustrates the dual compounds for deer with "rurupṛṣatam": the analysis is *ruravaś ca pṛṣatāś ca* (male ruru deer and spotted deer).
He illustrates the dual compounds for grasses with "kuśakāśam": the analysis is *kuśāś ca kāśāś ca* (kuśa grass and kāśa grass).
He illustrates the dual compounds for grains with "vrīhiyavam": the analysis is *vrīhayaś ca yavāś ca* (rice and barley).
He provides an example of a copulative compound (*vyañjanadvandva*)—namely, *dadhi* (curds). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "curds and ghee.
He provides an example of an animal copulative compound (*pasudvandva*)—namely, *gomahiṣam* (cows and buffaloes). The analysis is: "cows and buffaloes.
He provides an example of a bird copulative compound (*śakunidvandva*)—namely, *śuka* (parrots). The analysis is: "parrots and cranes."
He provides an example of the dual compound for horse and mare: *aśvavaḍavam*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "horses (*aśvāḥ*) and mares (*vaḍavāḥ*).
According to the rule "the first member [retains its gender] in the case of *aśvavaḍava*," the masculine gender is applied here as it was in the first member of the compound *aśvavaḍavau*.

It should be stated that for the following—fruits, armies, trees, wild animals, birds, small creatures, grains, and grass—the *dvandva* compound, consisting of many elements, is optionally treated as a singular (*ekavad-bhāva*).
"Fruits and armies" (*phala-senā*): this is a *vārttika* forming a supplement to the section on *ekavad-bhāva*. And the *dvandva*...

The meaning of the rule beginning with *prāṇi* (Pāṇini 2.4.2) is that when a *dvandva* compound of words such as "fruit" (*phala*) or "army" (*senā*) becomes a singular entity, it occurs only when its constituent members end in the plural number, and not when they end in the singular or dual.
In this regard, he provides an example of a *dvandva* of fruits: *badarāṇi ca* ("and jujube fruits"). [This refers to] the fruits of the *badarī* tree.
The meaning is "and *āmalakī* fruits. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix [denoting] the fruit after a secondary derivative (*vikāra-taddhita*).

There is elision of the feminine suffix by the rule "when a *taddhita* suffix with the marker *k* has been elided, and when a *taddhita* suffix is elided" (*suk-taddhitaluki*). It is a genus (*jāti*), because it is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) whose constituent members end in the plural number.

The meaning is that there is "singleness" (ekavatva) by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*. He states the purpose of the phrase "only when it has many primitives" with the words *neha* ("not here"). Regarding *badarāmalake*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the jujube and the myrobalan. Because this is a *dvandva* compound whose members do not end in the plural number, [the rule does not apply].
By the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*, there is singular number [for a copulative compound of genus names]. As in *ratikāśvārohau* (the charioteer and the horseman);
here, although they constitute parts of an army (*senāṅga*), there is no singular number. As in *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha* trees);
here, although they form a copulative compound of tree names (*vṛkṣadvandva*), by the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣe*, singular number does not apply. "And so forth" refers to such cases.

*Rurupṛṣatau*: here, although it is a pair of animals (*mṛgadvandva*), there is no singular form. *Haṃsacakravākau*: here, although it is a pair of birds (*śakunidvandva*), there is no singular form. *Yūkālikṣe*: here, although it is a pair of small creatures (*kṣudrajantudvandva*), there is no singular form. *Vrīhiyavau*: here, although it is a pair of grains (*dhānyadvandva*)...

Not a singular form. *Kuśakāśau* (Kuśa and Kāśa grasses). Here, although it is a dual compound of two types of grass, there is no singular form. Now, one might object: since the option for a singular form is already established by the rule "A *dvandva* [compound] is used in the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*)," which includes both the *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection) and *samāhāra* (collective) types, why is the rule "optionally [singular] in the case of trees" (*vibhāṣā vṛkṣe*) stated?
Anticipating the objection that the Sūtra would be redundant, he says: "The term *vibhāṣā*," and so on, up to "for the sake of optionality.

In the case of dvandva compounds consisting of trees, wild animals, grasses, grains, and condiments—namely, *plakṣanyagrodham*, *rurupṛṣatam*, *kuśakāśam*, *vrīhiyavam*, and *dadhighṛtam*—the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* [Pāṇini 2.4.6] applies.

The meaning is that the mention of "non-living things such as trees" is for the purpose of establishing the non-occurrence of the rule of obligatory singular (*nityaikavattva*) [which otherwise would apply].

But even so, the mention of "animals" (*paśu*) is redundant; for in the example *gomahiṣam*, since the rule "the genus of non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*) does not apply, the restriction of obligatory singular would not occur anyway.

Because it is impossible for that [prohibition] to apply for the purpose of excluding them, he says: "The mention of 'animals' (*paśu*) is because [the prohibition] would otherwise apply invariably to elephants, horses, and so forth, by virtue of their being members of an army. The phrase "for the sake of an option" (*vikalpārtham*) is to be supplied.
But even so, the mention of "wild animals and birds" (*mṛga-śakuni*) is redundant; for in the examples thereof, [we have] the *ruru* and the *pṛṣata*.

In examples such as *śukabakam* ("parrots and cranes"), since neither the singular number prescribed by the rule *jātiprāṇinām* nor the singular number based on being a component of an army (*senāṅga*) applies, there is no need to exclude them; thus, the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ* [applies].

Since the option for singular number is established by both the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and *samāhāra* (collective compound) types of *dvandva*, he says: "Of deer, only with deer," and so forth, ending with "the mention of deer and birds.
[This means] that in both cases—whether in *itaretarayoga* or *samāhāra*—deer are [to be combined] only with deer.

The term "in the sense of 'and'" (cārthe) refers to a *dvandva* compound. For example: *śukabakam* (parrot-and-crow), or *śukabakau* (parrot and crow). In the case of animals [with others] and birds [with others], there occurs only an *itaretarayoga-dvandva* (copulative compound where each member is equally principal), not a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective compound). For example: *ruruśukāḥ* (stags and parrots). This is for the purpose of such a restrictive rule.

The meaning is "the catching of deer and birds. Now, one might object: is the mention of *pūrvāpara* (prior and posterior) and *adhara-uttara* (lower and upper) redundant, since the desired form would be established simply by [Pāṇini 2.4.2] *cārthe* ("in the sense of 'and'")?
For in that case, the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.6] *jātir aprāṇinām* ("a genus-term for non-living things," etc.), which prescribes obligatory singular number (*eka-vacana*), does not apply.

Because it is impossible for that [distinction] to be excluded, he says: "In this way, 'prior and posterior' and 'lower and higher' as well. Just as the capture of deer and birds is by means of deer themselves for deer, and by those very same [birds] for birds—in both cases a *dvandva* compound—so it is with the word "prior" (*pūrva*).

By the very mention of the word *apara*, and by the word *adhara* with the word *uttara*, a *dvandva* compound occurs in both cases—whether in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) or collective aggregation (*samāhāra*).
However, when combined with another word—as in the case of *pūrvottarau* and so forth—it occurs only in the sense of mutual conjunction.
The inclusion of the terms *pūrvāpara* and *adharottara* is for the purpose of establishing this restrictive rule.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object that the mention of "horse and mare" (*aśvavaḍava*) is redundant; for even though they constitute a part of an army, the optional singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*) would already be established simply because it is a *paśu-dvandva* (a copulative compound of animals). To this, he says: "horse and mare. The meaning is that it is for the sake of the optional neuter gender. But [one might further object] that since the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is inherently one...

It has been stated that this section on "treatment as a single unit" (*ekavatva*) is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), namely that a *dvandva* compound is exclusively a collective (*samāhāra*). Consequently, since there is an option regarding "treatment as a single unit" based on the nature of a *paśu-dvandva*, it results in a lack of restriction as to whether the *dvandva* is a collective or a copulative (*itaretarayoga*).

And thus, in the case where it is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), there is neuter gender by the rule *sa napuṃsakam*; however, in the case of a copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga*), this is not so. Since the optionality of the neuter gender is thereby established, the specific mention of "horse and mare" (*aśvavaḍava*) would be entirely redundant; therefore, he says: "Otherwise," etc. Here...
In the absence of a rule for neuter gender, even in the case of a collective dvandva compound,

the neuter gender prescribed by the rule *sa napuṃsakam* would be superseded by the subsequent rule *pūrvapadasya vaḍavau*, resulting in masculine gender here. However, when there is a rule for neuter gender, by virtue of its own expressive power (*sāmarthya*), it applies in the case of the collective dvandva.

The neuter gender indeed occurs here, overriding the rule "the words *aśva* and *vaḍabā* [form a compound] with a preceding word. The intention is that the rule "with a preceding word" (*pūrvapada*), which is obtained through the governing heading (*adhikāra*), finds its scope of application (*sāvakāśa*) in the case of a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*).

(906) *vipratiṣiddhaṃ cānadhikaraṇavāci* || 2.4.13 || And [the compound of] contradictory terms [is optionally a tatpuruṣa], provided they do not denote a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). The word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is understood from the previous rule. Contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) means opposition, characterized by the impossibility of coexistence. A substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is a substance (*dravya*). Thus, [the compound consists of] terms expressing contradictory meanings that do not denote a substance.
The meaning is that when there are multiple inflected words (*subanta*), the *dvandva* compound formed from them may optionally take the singular form.

He states the resulting conclusion: "of those with contradictory meanings. Examples include *gotvāśvatvam* / *gotvāśvatve*, and *sukhaduḥkham* / *sukhaduḥkhe*, and so forth. [Objection: But what about the rule "in the sense of *ca*" (*cārthe*)?

This [rule] is redundant because the optional application of the singular number (*ekavadbhāva*) is already established here through the two alternatives of *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection) and *samāhāra* (aggregation).

Nor should it be argued that this is for the purpose of providing an option where the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (P. 2.4.6) applies obligatorily; for that rule applies only to *dvandva* compounds consisting of words denoting substances whose basis for application is a genus (*jāti*). Therefore...
He says: "It is optional," and so forth, ending with "this is for the sake of restriction. By that [he means]:

by the aforementioned restriction. "Cold and heat exist in water"—the point here is that although these have contradictory meanings, because they denote substances (*dravya*), there is no *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound). "Nandaka and Pāñcajanya."

Viṣṇu’s sword is Nandaka, while his conch is Pāñcajanya; since these two reside together in the same person, Viṣṇu, they are considered contradictory—this is the established position. In this context, if the term *vipratiṣiddha* (contradictory) were not included [in the rule], then by the rule *cārthe*...

The restriction would be obtained that a collective dvandva (samāhāra-dvandva) occurs only for words that do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*). This being the case, the optional collective dvandva *nandaka-pāñcajanya* would not be possible;
for the rule "every collective dvandva occurs only for words that do not denote substances" would be established as a restrictive one.
This being the case, the compound *nandakapāñcajanya* would not be a *pākṣika-samāhāra-dvandva* (an optional collective copulative),
because every *samāhāra-dvandva* is restricted exclusively to those [words] that do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*). However,
when it is stated "of mutually contradictory things" (*vipratiṣiddha*), then a *samāhāra-dvandva* of things with contrary meanings is indeed possible.

The restriction "only for those denoting non-substances" (*adravyavācinām eva*) is thus obtained. However, because there is no contradiction in the case of *nandaka* and *pāñcajanya*, this restriction does not apply; consequently, even if they denote substances, a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) may occasionally occur by the rule *cārthe*.
Sometimes there is indeed a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of other types as well. Thus he says: "In this case, an aggregative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) certainly occurs.
(Pāṇini 2.4.14): *na dadhipayaādīni* ("The compounds beginning with *dadhi-payaḥ* [milk and curd] do not [form an aggregative compound]").

Not [the compounds] *dadhi-paya-ādi* (curd-milk and so forth). "They would not exist as a single unit" means that there is no collective dvandva compound for these. In the case of *dadhi-payasī*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *dadhi ca payaś ca* ("curd and milk"). This sets aside the obligatory singular number prescribed by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* ("a genus-term for non-living things [is always singular]").

Because there is a pair of consonants (*vyañjana-dvandva*), the rule for optional application (*vikalpa*) would have been obtained; however, that too does not occur. In the case of *idhmābarhiṣī*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Regarding the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the remainder of the rule is "of the word *idhma*. In the case of *ṛksāme*, the analysis is "the *ṛc* and the *sāman*."

In the phrase beginning with *ṭhacatureti*, the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). Regarding *vāṅmanase*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "speech and mind" (*vāk ca manaś ca*). The compound-final element is applied as before. In this list (*gaṇa*), "Brahmā and Prajāpati," and so forth, are recited.
Even though this is a section concerning the restrictive rule that "it is only in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*)," it does not [apply] by means of this very restriction.

This is a prohibition; for in cases such as "brahmaprajāpatī," a restrictive rule (niyama) does not apply, but rather only the singular number [of the compound] does. Thus, the result is the prohibition of the collective dvandva (samāhāra-dvandva) by the rule "cārthe."
(908) And [the suffix *tasi* is used] when the extent of the substratum is intended. 2.4.15. "And when the extent of the substratum": the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substance (*dravya*);
its "extent" (*etāvatva*) is the specific limit of its quantity. Thus it is said: "when there is the comprehension of the number of substances."

The meaning is that when the specific limit (*iyattā*) of the objects being compounded is understood through the juxtaposition (*samabhivyāhāra*) of other words. Regarding the phrase "there is no restriction": in cases such as *brahmaprajāpatī*, since the previously mentioned restrictive rule—that a *dvandva* compound must always be a collective (*samāhāra*)—does not apply, the prohibition of singular number (*ekavacana*) was resorted to in the preceding sūtra.

The sense here, however, is that since there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the prohibition is taken to apply specifically to the rule under discussion (*prakṛta-niyama*). Regarding the example *daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "teeth and lips" (*dantāśca oṣṭhāśca*).
This is an *itaretara-yoga* (copulative) *dvandva*, not a *samāhāra* (collective) *dvandva*.

In a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), there is no syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*) because the meanings of the words being compounded—which serve as qualifiers for the collective sense—depend on the number "ten" obtainable from another word. However, a copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga-dvandva*) certainly does occur, because in that case the meanings of the words being compounded themselves are the primary elements. [The rule] *upamitam*...

In the commentary on the sūtra "vyāghrādibhiḥ," since a compound is admitted even when the act of giving is dependent [on another factor], there is consequently no restrictive rule that it must be singular; thus,
because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), the status of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is precluded.

By process of elimination, it remains that there is only mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga). If, however, it were explained as "if it were not like a single unit," then the meaning would result in the negation of a collective compound (samāhāra-dvandva).
If that were the case, then the mutual conjunction compound "ten teeth and lips" (daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ) would not exist.

Furthermore, because of the prohibition [of the singular] by the rule "dvandvaśca prāṇitūrya" (Pāṇini 2.4.2), it would necessarily be a sentence (*vākya*) alone. Moreover, this prohibition of the collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*) is entirely redundant, since—as explained above—the compound would not even apply due to a lack of syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*) arising from mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*). Therefore, the restrictive rule "ekavad" (singular) does not apply.

One might explain it as "it should be so. And thus, when this prohibition negates the rule—which is based on the limbs of living beings—that "there should be only one [form]," a rule whose result is the exclusion of *itaretarayoga* dvandva, the persistence of *itaretarayoga* dvandva results; this is clear from the *Padamañjarī*.

(909) *vibhāṣā samīpe* | 2|4|16|. The phrase "in proximity" (*samīpe*) means when [the location] is delimited by proximity. It follows from the previous rule, *adhikaraṇaitāvatve*. He states the resulting meaning: "regarding the locus" (*adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the expression *upadaśaṃ dantoṣṭham*: it is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "near ten. Although there is a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) according to the aforementioned principle, a collective *dvandva* is formed by virtue of the explicit statement [of the rule]. The *Bhāṣya* states that because the *avyayībhāva* possesses the same gender and number, it alone is to be employed in the subsequent usage. Therefore...
Thus, the expression "teeth with the lip" (*dantoṣṭhena*) and so forth is established.
When there is an intention to express the non-difference between the proximate and the proximate object, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs;
for instance, [the expressions] "a collection of teeth and lips numbering nine" and "a collection of teeth and lips numbering eleven."
Or [it may mean] understanding. In the expression "nine or ten teeth and lips" (*upadaśā dantoṣṭhāḥ*), this is a *dvandva* compound of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those which are near to ten," that is, nine or eleven. Here, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) belongs specifically to the *bahuvrīhi*.

The *bhāṣya* states: "Because they have the same gender and number. (910) *ānaṅ ṛt-aḥ dvandve* [Pāṇini 6.3.25]. Regarding the rule *ānaṅ ṛt-aḥ dvandve*: [it applies] to those words denoting relationships based on learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*).

The meaning is: "of those expressing a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) and those expressing a relationship through birth (*yoni*). The intention is that this [suffix] follows from the rule "after [stems ending in] *ṛ*, [the suffix] *taddhita* *ṅa* is used to express relationships of learning and birth.
Regarding the phrase "of those ending in *ṛ*": although there is a plurality [of stems], the singular number in "after *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*) is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).

The meaning is: "of those [words] whose every constituent part ends in *ṛ*. The intention is that, although the term *ṛtaḥ* was already being carried over (*anuvartamāna*), the repetition of *ṛtaḥ* is for this specific purpose. Regarding the phrase "when a subsequent member of a compound follows" (*uttarapade pare*): the intention is that, although the term *ṛtaḥ* was already being carried over, the repetition of *ṛtaḥ* is for this specific purpose. When a subsequent member of a compound follows.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that this is because of the governing rule (adhikāra) "when there is no following word" (*alug-uttarapade*). Regarding *hotāpotārau*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the *hotṛ* and the *potr̥*. The relationship is based on their being priests at a single sacrifice through the medium of their learning.

[In the formation of the compound], *ānaṅ* is substituted; the *ṅ* is for the sake of the accent (*kāri*), the *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and by the rule "*ṅci*", the final portion (*anta*) is replaced.
The elision of *n* (nalopa) is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya; however, the *n* is retained for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ra* (raparatva).

In the example *hotṛpotṛ*, there is no *ānaṅ* substitution for the word *hotṛ* or the word *potṛ*, because of the intervention of the word *neṣṭṛ*, which results in the absence of being followed by a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*). And thus:

The substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs only for the word *neṣṭṛ*; however, the preceding member is not implied by the subsequent member, because the substitution of *ānaṅ* for the word *neṣṭṛ* is observed in the *Samartha-sūtra*. Now, he provides an example of the connection based on kinship: *mātāpitarau* ("mother and father").

The point is that in forms such as *pitṛpitāmahau*, the substitute *ānaṅ* does not occur because there is an absence of having all its constituent parts ending in ṛ. If so, how is it that *pitāputrau* is formed?
To this he says: "in the case of *putra*, optionally" (*putre 'nyatarasyām*). [This refers to the rule] *ṛto...* [Pāṇini 6.1.112].

Regarding the rule *vidyāyonisaṃbandhebhyaḥ* and the rule *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ*, he says "like a frog" (*maṇḍūaka*) because there is no connection between them in the intervening space. As for the phrase "due to the recurrence" (*anuvṛtteḥ*), one should not argue that the substitution would also apply in the case of *tātaputrau*; for the substitution *ānaṅ* occurs only when a stem ending in *ṛ* is followed by the word *putra*.
This is because it is explained through a division of the sentence as "it might be so.
(911) *Devatādvandve ca* |6|3|26|. And in a compound of two deities (*devatādvandva*), [the first member retains its original accent]. For example: *mitrāvaruṇau*. Here...
Since it does not end in the letter *ṛ*, this is a rule [prescribing a specific form] that was not otherwise obtained by the preceding rule.
There is a prohibition regarding the use of the word *vāyu*.
Regarding the phrase "the word *vāyu*": [it refers to its use] either as a prior member (*pūrvapada*) or as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

The meaning is that a prohibition regarding the truth of the *anaṅ* [substitution] must be stated. Now, one might object: since the mention of *dvandva* is already carried over from the preceding sūtra, its repetition here is redundant;
to this he replies with the word "again" (*punar*). [This applies] in cases such as the *nirvāpa* (offering).
The purpose is to include words that denote well-known deities associated with sacrificial offerings (*sāhitya*). Regarding the phrase "by that":

it means by the inclusion of well-known associations (*sāhacarya*). Regarding the word "this": it means that this pair consisting of Brahmā and Prajāpati is not well-known in the Veda as being entitled to a share of the oblation (*havirbhāgin*). Nor is it so in common worldly usage.

This is merely a bold assertion (prauḍhivāda), because we see in the Bhāṣya only the statement, "those which are prescribed in the Veda as being offered together," and because if one were to accept the co-occurrence (sāhacarya) well-known in common usage, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as "Pārvatī and Parameśvara."

(912) *īdagneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ* |6|3|27|. The phrase *īdagneḥ* means "only *īd*" [is substituted]. The meaning is that the governing rule *devatādvandve* continues to apply. When the words *soma* or *varuṇa* follow as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), *īt* is the substitute for *agni*.
The meaning is that [this rule] applies when there is a *devatā-dvandva* (a copulative compound of deities). It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ānaṅ*.

(913) *agneḥ stutstomasomāḥ* |8|3|82|. [The word] *agneḥ* [is in the genitive]; *stut*, *stoma*, and *soma* [are in the nominative]. From the *dvandva* compound consisting of *stut*, *stoma*, and *soma*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
From the rule "ṣaheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ," the word "sa" is understood as being in the genitive singular.
"Agneḥ" is in the ablative case. From the rule "samāse 'ṅguleḥ," the word "samāse" is understood.
Thus he says: "of those [sounds] following *agni*. "It should become *ṣ*" means: "for a non-final [consonant], there is a retroflex [substitute]."

The sense is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) [of the rule]. This is an exception to the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*. Regarding *agniṣṭud*: this is a specific sacrifice (*kratu*).
Regarding *agniṣṭoma*: this is the name of a specific hymn (*stotra*) and a specific ritual conclusion (*saṃsthā*).
Regarding *agnīṣomau*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "Agni and Soma. [The rules for] *ītva* and *ṣatva* apply.

Regarding *agnīvaruṇau*: the analysis is "Agni and Varuṇa. [The rule for] *ītva* applies. Why [is it specified] "in a dual compound of deities" (*devatādvandve*)? [Consider: "Agni" is the name of someone, and "Soma" is the name of someone else.

In *agnīsomau*, there is no substitution of long *ī* because it is not a *devatā-dvandva* (a copulative compound of deities). For this very reason, there is no application of the rule for *ṣatva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*), according to the Vārttika: "The [substitution of *ṣ*] is desired for *soma* following a long vowel in *agni*. In the rule for *id-vṛddhi*, the terms "*agneḥ*" and "*devatā-dvandve*" are carried over (*anuvartate*). By the word *vṛddhi*, that which possesses the *vṛddhi* increment is indicated.

In a *devatā-dvandva* (dual compound of deities), there is no possibility of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) consisting solely of a *vṛddhi*-strengthened vowel; therefore, he says "possessing *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddhimatī*). The letter *t* in *it* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Because it serves no further purpose, it does not receive the technical designation *it*. Nor is the *tapara* (the *t*) intended to restrict the scope [to long vowels], because the rule is already being enjoined [as a specific prescription].
Because it does not grasp [the object] while being armored (*savarmāgrāhakatvāt*). Regarding "Agni and Maruts" (*agnāmarutau*): the analysis (*vigraha*) is "Agni and Marut.

By the rule *devatādvandve ca*, the substitution *ānaṅ* is applied. Regarding "the rite for Agni and Maruts" (*āgnimārutaṃ karma*): the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sā'sya devatā*. Because it is a portion of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*).
Regarding *agnīvaruṇau*: [the form] *idagne* results from the substitution of *itvam*. Regarding *āgnivāruṇam*:

the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sā'sya devatā*. Now, one might object: since the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* prescribes vṛddhi for the initial vowel among the vowels of the stem, how can there be vṛddhi of the initial vowel of the second member (*uttarapada*)? [The answer follows:]...

He says: "In a compound of two deities (*devatā-dvandva*), there is vṛddhi of both members. Now, one might object that the rule for changing the *ik* vowel of *agni* into *ik* is redundant; therefore, he says: "having set aside *ānaṅ* and *ītvam*.
This refers to *ānaṅ* in the case of *āgnimāruta*, and *ītvam* in the case of *āgnivāruṇa*.

The meaning is that the vowel *i* is prescribed again for the *i* of the roots √bādh and √ni in order to prevent [the application of] the augment *ṇit*. Now, it will be stated under the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā* that the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs from a fully established form.
And thus, in the cases "he whose deities are Agni and Marut" (*agnāmarutau devate asya*) and "he whose deities are Agni and Varuṇa" (*agnīvaruṇau devate asya*), [the suffix would apply].

In the case of a compound (vigraha), from the word *agni* ending in *aruc* [the suffix *ruc*] and from the word *agnīvaruṇa*, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix *aṇ* is produced according to the rule "sā'sya devatā" (Pāṇini 4.2.24) from a dual deity compound that has been fully established through the application of *ānaṅ* and *ītvam*. Thereafter, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of both members caused by that suffix occurs; subsequently, the rule "idvṛddhau" (Pāṇini 6.3.28) takes effect.

[This is] the sequence. And therefore, since the substitution of *ānaṅ* and the designation *īt* have already taken effect prior to the production of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), how could there be a sublation [of those two] by the rule "when a *ṭhi* follows, there is vṛddhi"? For it is accepted that the relationship between the sublated and the sublater occurs only when they apply simultaneously. And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "To one who has already eaten, do not..."

If it is asked, "What would be achieved by saying 'having eaten' (bhuktvā)?"—to this he replies: "In the non-worldly [analytic] sentence (*alaukika-vigrahavākya*). This refers to the non-worldly analytic sentences for *taddhita* suffixes, such as "Agni and Marut are its deities" (*agni-marut-au devate asya*) and "Agni and Varuṇa are its deities" (*agni-varuṇau devate asya*), where the application of *ānaṅ* and *itva* is about to occur.

The meaning is that this rule (idvidhiḥ) operates by setting aside [the previous rule]. Although at that time the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) does not possess *vṛddhi* because of the absence of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), the intention here is that the subsequent member must indeed possess *vṛddhi* as a future state (*bhāvi*). This is the underlying sense.

(914) *id-vṛddhau* | Pāṇini 6.3.28. Regarding the example *āgneyendra*: *agni* and *indra* together form *agnendrau*. By the rule *devatā-dvandve ca*, the substitute *ānaṅ* is applied. Then, by *ād-guṇaḥ*, the guṇa substitution occurs. [The compound] *āgnendraḥ* is formed from the sense "that which has Agni and Indra as its deities" (*agnendrau devate asya*), by the rule *sā'sya devatā* with the suffix *aṇ*.
[The rule] "ādivṛddhiḥ" [does not apply here], because the subsequent member of the compound *indra* lacks *vṛddhi*.

The intention is that [the rule] "ṭhidvṛddhau" does not apply. Anticipating the objection that [the rule] "devatādvandve ca" might require *vṛddhi* for both members, he says: "not when *indra* [is the subsequent member]."
"Not in *viṣṇu*.
This means that when the word *viṣṇu* follows, it must be stated that the *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) of *agni* does not [change]. For example: *āgnāvaiṣṇavam*.
[In this case: *agniśca viṣṇuśca* = *agnāviṣṇū*. [This occurs] in a *dvandva* compound of deities.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sā'sya devatā*. In the sense of "Agni and Viṣṇu are its deities," the suffix *aṇ* is added [to form] *āgnāvaiṣṇavam havir* ("an oblation for Agni and Viṣṇu"). By the rule *devatādvandve ca*, there is vṛddhi (vowel strengthening) of both members of the compound.
Because the substitution of *it* does not occur, [the form remains] *āgnāvaiṣṇava*.

(915) *divo dyāvā* |6|3|29|. [The rule] "divo dyāvā" [is explained by] completing the remainder of the sūtra as "in a dvandva compound of deities. For example: *dyāvābhūmī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the heaven (*dyauḥ*) and the earth (*bhūmiḥ*). [Another example is] *dyāvākṣāmā rukmaḥ*.

This is recited in the *Ṛgveda* verse beginning with "antarvibhāti. The meaning is "between heaven and earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivyoḥ*). The analysis of the compound is *dyauśca kṣāmā ca* ("heaven and earth"). In the Veda, the word *kṣāmā* is a synonym for the earth. In that context, when forming a *dvandva* compound, there is the substitution of *dyāvā* for *divaḥ*. Furthermore, the genitive ending is replaced by *ḍā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
It is clear in the Vedabhāṣya that in a *devatā-dvandva* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of both the preceding and following members is retained;
this applies also to *divas* when combined with *pṛthivī*. (Pāṇini 6.3.30).

"And *divasa* [is substituted] for *div* on the word *pṛthivī*. It is precisely *diva*," means that the term *diva* indeed continues to apply; this is the sense, based on its being marked with the *svarita* accent. If one asks, "In that case, the particle *ca* is redundant," he says: "And by *ca*. Thus, when the word *pṛthivī* follows, there shall be both the substitution of *divasa* and the substitution of *dyāvā* for the word *div*.

The meaning is that [the rule applies] when a second member follows in a *devatā-dvandva* (dual compound of deities). Regarding the form *divaspṛthivyāḥ*, since the vowel *a* is not heard after the *s* in this case, the substitute *divas-* must necessarily end in *s*.
Therefore, one might ask: what is the purpose of pronouncing the vowel *a* after the *s* of the substitute? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "In the grammatical rule (ādeśa), there is the pronunciation of the vowel 'a'. The intention is that, by virtue of this [phonetic context], the substitution of *ru* according to the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ* does not take place. Now, one might ask: how is there a *dvandva* compound in the phrase *dyāvā cid asmai pṛthivī sannamete*, and how is it that *div* becomes *dyāvā*?
[Question: Why is this the case? Because the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is separated [from the preceding element] by the rule *ṭhcidasmai*.

To this, he says: "In the Veda, one follows what is observed. This is a statement from the Bhāṣya. The meaning is that in the Veda, one must follow what is actually seen [in usage]. Because the cessation of the *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) has already been stated. [Examples: *uṣāsoṣasaḥ*; *uṣāsāsūryam*.

Now, the procedure for reduplication:
8.1.1. *sarvasya dve* (The whole [word] is doubled).

Now begins the section on reduplication (*dvirukta*). With reference to the rule *sarvasya dve* ("of everything, two [are used]"), the remainder of the context is: "The rules for doubling shall now be enumerated. *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4): [A word is repeated] in the sense of continuity (*nitya*) and pervasiveness (*vīpsā*).

Regarding the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*: by the word *nitya*, "perpetuity" (*nityatva*) is intended. And that [perpetuity] is "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*), according to the Bhāṣya. "Repetition" (*vīpsā*) is the desire to pervade—that is, the desire to convey pervasion. And that [desire] is a property of the speaker; however, pervasion itself is the object of the verbal cognition.

This is the natural intention (*svarasa*) of the Bhāṣya. Accordingly, it would have been more appropriately stated as "by means of constant pervasion" (*nityavyāptyā*). And "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) here means a connection characterized by totality, due to the force of the prefix (*upa-*).
The term *padasya*, which was to be introduced later [in the sūtra], is drawn back (*apakṛṣyate*) to this point. The word *sarvasya* is a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The word "dve" (two) serves as the provider of the substitute (*ādeśa*). Its substantive (*viśeṣya*), namely "the two forms of the word," is understood by implication from the context of the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*). Furthermore, those two forms of the word are the most similar (*antaratama*) in their own nature; thus, it is obtained through the *paribhāṣā* rule "in place [of the original], that which is most similar."

Consequently, when repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) or totality (*kārtsnya*) is to be understood, it follows that there arise two words—each the closest equivalent in both meaning and sound—to the original word qualified by all its parts.
With this in mind, he says: "when frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) or distribution (*vīpsā*) is to be indicated" (*dyotye*). And "to be indicated" (*dyotya*) refers to that which is to be expressed.
And [the word *tasmin*] is that which is to be illuminated; the meaning is "in that.
[The form *tasmin*] results from the formation of a neuter singular remainder (*napuṃsakaikaśeṣa*) according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām*.
Both the singularity and the constant repetition (*nityavīpsā*) are understood from the base form (*prakṛti*), while the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is merely an indicator (*dyotaka*).
It should be understood that even though the base (*prakṛti*) is doubled, there is no addition to the base because the two utterances do not exceed the original base.

"There would be reduplication" means that there are two words as substitutes. In that case, the status of being a word (*padatva*) for the two constituent parts is established by itself; however, for the aggregate consisting of the two words—

Because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like that which occupies the place), there is the status of being a *subanta* (an inflected nominal stem). Consequently, in the case of *apacan apacan*, the augment *ṅmuṭ* is applied; in *vṛkṣān vṛkṣān*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* (nasalization) by the rule *padāntasya* applies; and in *agre agre*, the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute replacement) by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntāt* applies—such are the word-level operations (*padakārya*) belonging to the constituent parts.

They are established. By treating the entire aggregate [of the word] as *sthānivadbhāva*, it possesses the status of being a *subanta* (an inflected nominal); thus, by applying the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*) and the suffix *ṭhañ* in the sense of occurrence (*bhava*), the forms *paunaḥpunyam* and *paunaḥpunikaḥ* are established. However, if one assumes that "there are two utterances," then the entire word [is treated accordingly].

The resulting meaning would be "one should utter [the word] twice. Consequently, since *punaḥ*—being uttered twice—is not subject to the substitution of *punaḥpunaḥ*, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply; thus, lacking the status of being a *subanta* (an inflected nominal stem), the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would not occur.

Therefore, let it suffice to say that the position of substitution (*ādeśapakṣa*) alone is superior. Regarding the rule "frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) applies to verbal forms (*tiṅanta*)": frequency means repetition (*paunaḥpunya*).

And here, that [frequency] belongs only to the action which constitutes the primary element. Since primacy of action exists in verbal expressions (*ākhyāta*), as in the case of [the suffix *kan*] expressing praise...

This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the *rūpa* sūtra. Even among indeclinable kṛt suffixes, such as *ktvā*, *tumun*, and others, the action (*kriyā*) is predominant, because it is stated that "indeclinable kṛt suffixes denote the abstract state (*bhāva*).
Consequently, reduplication caused by repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) occurs both in verbal forms ending in *tiṅ* suffixes and in those ending in indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes.
The meaning is "not elsewhere. He illustrates this in the same way: *pacati pacati*, *bhuktvā bhuktva* ("he cooks again and again," "having eaten again and again").

Regarding the term "in the sense of repetition" (*vīpsāyām*), the words "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) are to be supplied. For example: *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam* ("tree after tree," i.e., every single tree). "Entirely" (*kṛtsnam*).

The meaning is "the tree. Here, the entirety of the trees located within that specific grove under discussion is understood, because it is impossible to water every single tree standing upon the surface of the earth. Although the word *sarva* denotes entirety (*kārtsnya*), it does not take the dual number; this was already explained immediately below in the section on *yathāsva*.

It will be stated [later]: in the expression *vṛkṣaṃ-vṛkṣam* (tree by tree), even though there is a comprehension of totality (*kārtsnya*), it is only the singularity residing in each individual that appears, not plurality; therefore, the plural number is not used. This is also because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *ekaikasya prācām*. In the absence of the word *sarvasya* ("of all"),...

In examples such as *vṛkṣābhyām*, if one were to rely on the status of being a "word" (*padatva*) established by the rule *ṭh-svādiṣu*, there would be reduplication of only the original base portion (*prakṛti-bhāga*). However, when the term *sarva* (entire) is included, the meaning obtained is that reduplication applies to the whole word—including all its constituent parts—provided it is not already subsumed under the definition of a word-part (*pada-avayava*). Thus, there is no fault. [The rule states: *padasya*.
What [is the purpose]? So that it does not apply to a sentence (*vākya*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.5) *parervarjane*: the meaning is that there are two forms of the word *pari* when it occurs in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). *Pari*.

"In *parivaṅgebhyo vṛṣṭaḥ*," the word *parjanya* (the rain-god) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sense]. Since *pari* is a *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule *apaparī varjane*, the ablative case is used by the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*.
However, in the example *pari hareḥ saṃsāraḥ*, it is stated that "it should be specified that [the ablative occurs] after *pari* when there is no compound (*asamāse*)."
The word *vārtika* means "twice" (*dvirvacana*).
[Pāṇini 8.1.7] *upary-adhy-adhasaḥ sāmīpye*: The words *upari*, *adhi*, and *adhas* are doubled when proximity is to be understood.
*Upary-adhy-adhasaḥ*: These words—*upari*, *adhi*, and *adhas*—become doubled when proximity is indicated.

This is the meaning. It should be understood that proximity (*sāmīpya*) occurs spatially in examples such as *uparyupari grāmam* ("above, above the village") and *adho'dho lokam* ("below, below the world"), whereas it occurs temporally in an example such as *adhyadhi sukham* ("again and again regarding happiness").

[The rule: *vākyāderāmantritasyāsūyāsaṃmatikopakutsanabhartsaneṣu* (Pāṇini 8.1.8): [A vocative] at the beginning of a sentence takes the pluti vowel when expressing envy, approval, anger, censure, or threatening.

[This refers to] the beginning of a sentence; the words "there are two" are to be supplied as the remainder. Although reviling arises from anger and censuring from envy, nevertheless, the separate mention [of these terms] in the Bhāṣya is clear because reviling and censuring can occur toward a pupil and others even without anger or envy. [The example is] "O beautiful one... and so forth.
This is the speech of one who cannot endure [her] beauty. "O King" means that your salutation is approved. "Ill-behaved" is the speech of one overcome by anger.

(Pāṇini 2.1.52) One [word] is treated like a *bahuvrīhi* compound. (Pāṇini 8.1.9)

"One [word] like a *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding "when reduplicated": the meaning is "when the occurrence of reduplication has been obtained. This is understood from the context and from the *Bhāṣya*, which states: "This applies solely to the domain of *vīpsā* (distributive repetition). By this—namely, by being like a *bahuvrīhi*—the elision of the case-ending (*sub-lopa*) and the masculine form (*puṃvad-bhāva*) are established. In that regard:
He illustrates the elision of the case-ending (*sublopam*) with the example "ekaikam" (one by one). Regarding the word "iha" (here):
in the case of "ekaikam," when the word "ekam" is doubled, resulting in the form "ekamekam," the case-ending (*sup*) is elided;
subsequently, the case-ending is added to the entire compound. Now, an objection is raised: "In a compound where the prior portion is a word (*padam*)," and so forth.

If it is argued that, because of the restrictive rule "only for a compound," the entire aggregate lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), how can there be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) here, or how can a case-ending be added to the aggregate?
To this, he says: "Precisely because of the treatment as if it were a *bahuvrīhi*."
"Because it is a nominal stem (prātipadika). This [reason] connects, by way of the "middle gem" (madhyamaṇi) maxim, with both the rule "supo luk" and the rule "samudāyāt sup.
Now, he provides an example even for the case of masculine-like behavior (puṃvatva): "ekaikayā āhutyā. [This occurs] when there is reduplication of the word "ekayā."
When *ekayā*— that is, *ekayā*— is established, because the entire compound (*samudāya*) is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of being treated like a *bahuvrīhi*,
there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*). Once the masculine form has been applied to the first member (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*),
when the third case-ending is produced again from the whole compound, the resulting form is *ekaikayā*.
However, in the absence of being treated as a *bahuvrīhi*,

there would be no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) because the entire compound lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the masculine form (*puṃvat*) of the first member would not occur because it is not followed by a "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*); for [the rule applies] only to the final constituent of a compound.

The intended meaning is that it is because [the word] is the latter member of a compound. In the case of *ekāikā*, even though there is the status of a *bahuvrīhi*, the masculine form (*puṃvat*) of the latter part—by the rule "in all compounds, the feminine of a pronoun becomes masculine"—is not applicable;
for it has been stated that this [masculine substitution] applies only to the former [member], based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the rule *bhastraiṣādve*. This is how it should be understood.

[Objection: But surely, when there is elision of the *sup* suffix, whether or not the preceding portion, the word *eka*, undergoes *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment), the form *ekaikayā* is established even after the application of *vṛddhi*. To this, he says: "In this case, in the prior part," and "in the *avagraha*. When a compound word is divided into two parts, the prior portion is the *avagraha*. Of that...

The *Prātiśākhya* states: "The preceding [member] is subject to elision (*avagraha*). Regarding the phrase "ekaikayā," it is intended that the first member [of the compound] retains its original form (*pūrvatva*). The implication is that, in the absence of the status of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the form would instead be "ekā-ekayā. However, the Taittirīyas...

Regarding *ṭhekaikayā*, they analyze it as *eka-ekayā*. Although [the desired form] would be established by the rule *ṭhekaṃ samāsava’d* (P. 1.2.48), the explicit mention of *bahuvrīhi* is for the sake of the accentuation governed by the rule *ṭhbahuvrīhau prakṛtyāpūrvapada’m* (P.
6.2.1). Now, one might object: if it were a *bahuvrīhi*-like compound, [the prohibition] *ṭhna bahivrīhau* (P. 6.2.173) would apply.

The meaning is: since the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is prohibited [in a *bahuvrīhi*], how can the grammatical operations pertaining to pronouns apply in cases such as *ekaikasmai dehī*? To this, he says: "In the rule *na bahuvrīhau*. For, although the desired result is already established by the continued application of the term *bahuvrīhi* from the preceding rule *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau*, [the author states it here for clarity].
In the rule *bahuvrīhau*, the repetition of the term *bahuvrīhi* is for the purpose of obtaining the primary *bahuvrīhi*.

Therefore, the meaning is that the prohibition of the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) does not apply to the extended (*atideśita*) *bahuvrīhi* by means of the analogy "as in a *bahuvrīhi*. He states this with the words "by that" (*tena*). Having thus stated the solution proposed by the ancients, [the author proceeds].

He states this according to the view of the Siddhāntin: "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). "This" refers to the rule *na bahuvrīhau*. Thus, since the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) is accepted by the Bhāṣya even for a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the sense is that the status of being a pronoun remains unimpeded even when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of a *bahuvrīhi*.

Regarding the phrase "even according to the Sūtra system": since the prohibition of the status of a pronominal (sarvanāmatva) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound is already established by the fact of its being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the rule "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" prohibits the status of a pronominal specifically within the non-grammatical analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*) intended for the *bahuvrīhi*, prior to the formation of the compound itself.

This has already been stated. Therefore, the meaning here is that there is no possibility at all of suspecting the absence of the grammatical operations pertaining to pronouns (sarvanāma-kārya) that would be triggered by the extended application (atideśa) of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
[For example,] in the case of "ekaikasmai dehi" (give to each one), although both *sup* suffixes have undergone elision (*luk*), [the operations still apply].

The intention is that because it ends in the single word *eka* which is listed first among all [the pronominals], it possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and thus undergoes the substitution of *sama*.
(Pāṇini 8.1.10) "And in the case of distress (*ābādha*). Distress means affliction. Thus he says: "in the case of affliction. An example is *gatagata*.
The phrase "without his beloved" (*priyā vinā*) is the ellipsis; the word "time" (*kāla*) is to be understood as the remainder. He speaks [the following] to demonstrate the affliction:
"from separation" (*virahāt*). This means "from separation from his wife. Regarding the expression "as if it were a *bahuvrīhi*":
when the word "gone" (*gata*) is doubled, because the entire compound functions like a *bahuvrīhi*, it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

The meaning is that the *sub* suffix arises from the entire compound (*samudāya*) after the elision of the initial *sub*. In the phrase "gone-gone" (*gatagatā*), the word "to the house" (*gṛhe*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

This too is the speech of one who is being tormented by separation from his wife. Because the single woman who is the agent of going is mentioned twice, the subsequent member of the compound is in the feminine gender and functions as a term of common grammatical core (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

The substitution of the masculine form [for the feminine] occurs by the rule *ṭhstriyāḥ puṃvad* (Pāṇini 6.3.34), because the condition of being the final member of a compound (*uttarapadatva*) is present due to the application of the *bahuvrīhi*-treatment. Thus he says: "In this case, there is the masculine substitution.
Regarding the subsequent [rules], it is like the *karmadhāraya* treatment. (Pāṇini 7.3.42)

"In the subsequent [rules], it is like a *karmadhāraya*. The word "the operation (*kāryam*) should take place" is the ellipsis. He states the result of being like a *karmadhāraya*: "the purpose (*prayojanam*). The singular number is used with the intention that [the operations], such as the elision of the case-ending (*sublopa*), apply individually. Regarding the phrase "having the final syllable as acute (*antodātatva*)," [it refers to] the rule "the unaccented (*anudātta*..."
The sense is that, although this [rule] is also under consideration, it is not connected here because of the authority of the Bhāṣya.

Intending to explain this, he says: "when similarity (*sādṛśya*) is to be indicated.
