Regarding the word "by that" (*tena*):

The meaning is "by virtue of being like a *karmadhāraya* compound. Regarding the term "masculine form" (*puṃvadbhāva*), the ellipsis is "by means of the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*" (Pāṇini 6.3.42). In the example *paṭupaṭvī*, when the word *paṭvī* is reduplicated, because it is treated as a *karmadhāraya*, the preceding portion [of the second member] becomes masculine by the rule *puvat karmadhāraye*.

The intention is that the form [is established] by virtue of the masculine treatment (*puṃvat*). Although this is already established by the rule "the feminine becomes like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*) even when the *bahuvrīhi* treatment applies, nevertheless,
the expression "as in a *karmadhāraya*" (*karmadhārayavat*) is stated for the sake of ensuring the masculine treatment even in cases such as *kārikā*, which have a penultimate *kā* vowel (*kopadha*).

The meaning is "the word. Regarding *paṭupaṭuḥ*: this is the form when there is reduplication in the masculine, in the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*. Regarding *paṭusadṛśaḥ*: the words "in this sense" (*ityartha*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. He states the resulting conclusion: "slightly clever" (*īṣatpaṭuḥ*). Here, the term "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*)...
He dispels the misconception that [the term] denotes a substance qualified by a quality (*guṇopasarjanadravyavācitva*)—namely, "qualified by a quality" (*guṇopasarjana*).

"White-white color" (*śuklaśuklaṃ rūpam*) means "similar to white"; that is to say, "slightly white. In the same way, it should be understood that "white-white cloth" (*śuklaśuklaḥ paṭaḥ*) has the same sense.
Two [terms] expressing sequence (*ānupūrvya*) are to be stated.
Regarding the term "sequence" (*ānupūrvye*), the phrase "as a *karmadhāraya*" from the *vārttika* does not apply here; this is because it is so stated in the *bhāṣya* regarding its illustration.
Intending that [the term] "sublopāt" means "due to non-perception," he provides an example: "mūle mūle.
This means that each preceding root-section is coarser than each succeeding root-section. Up to this point.
When an action proceeds with haste, the use of a word in various ways according to one's desire is established by logic.
Regarding the phrase "with haste": this is a *vārttika*. "Haste" (*saṃbhrama*) refers to the urgency caused by fear and the like;
when such haste is understood as being present, the word "in various ways" (*anekadhā*) may be used according to one's wish (*yatheṣṭam*).

The meaning is that it should be stated that [the word] ought to be employed. Because of the statement "in manifold ways" (*anekadhā*), the restriction to "two" is set aside. Because of the statement "as desired" (*yatheṣṭam*), there may be the employment of even a single [word] more than once. The meaning is that the employment of words culminates in the fruit consisting of comprehension (*bodha*). And this is stated in the Bhāṣya.

This is clear. Here too, because there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the status of being a *karmadhāraya*, there is no elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), as the *Bhāṣya* provides examples in exactly that manner.
(1) And [the suffix *loṭ* is used] in the sense of the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

"And in the case of *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition of an action). This is a *vārttika*. The words "two [forms] are used" are to be supplied as the remainder. *Kriyāsamabhihāra* consists of frequency (*paunaḥpunya*) and intensity (*bhṛśatva*). This rule applies exclusively to the domain of the imperative (*loṭ*). As stated in the rule: "In the case of *kriyāsamabhihāra*, the imperative suffix is used; for the imperative, *hi* and *sva* are substituted, and optionally so for *ta* and *dhvam*."

In the *Sūtrabhāṣya*, with reference to the reading "it should be stated that there is reduplication of the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of frequency (*kriyāsamabhihāra*)," he provides the example: "He cuts, saying 'cut! cut! (*lunīhi lunīhīty evāyaṃ lunāti*).
From the root *lūñ* (meaning "to cut"), the imperative (*loṭ*) is applied in the sense of frequency.
By the rule *loṭo hi-sv-au*, the imperative (*loṭ*) [is used]; for that, *hi* is the substitute [for the first person]. It takes the *śnā* conjugational suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

By this [rule], there is reduplication of the word *lunīhi*. By the rule *yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ pūrvasmin*, there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) [of the root]; from that, the present tense (*laṭ*) and so forth [are applied]. Or, it is repeated with excessive intensity.

The meaning of the double statement "lavanaṃ lunīhi" (cutting, cut! is [the repetition of the act]. The meaning of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) is the cutting performed by a single agent. As for the word *iti*, it conveys the intention (*tātparya*) toward a non-differentiated connection (*abhedānvaya*); this and other points will become clear in the section on the meaning of verbal suffixes (*lakārārthaprakriyā*) in the root text itself. Likewise...
And the resulting meaning is that the act of cutting is performed by a single agent with an exceeding degree of intensity. Regarding the word *nitya*:

although the doubling [of a word] is established by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* for the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), this Vārttika exists for the sake of doubling in the sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*). Now, one might object: "But this [word *nitya*] refers only to the sense of intensity..."
If the purpose were merely to effect reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the rule *bhṛśe ca* alone would suffice; thus, the inclusion of *kriyāsamabhihāre* would be redundant.

To this, he says: "even in the sense of repetition" (*paunaḥpunye*). This means that in examples such as *lunīhi-lunīhi*, the rule serves to combine both the *loṭ* suffix and the reduplication for the sake of expressing repetition (*paunaḥpunya*).

"Otherwise"—that is, even in the case of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). This means that in the example *lunīhi-lunīhi*, the reduplication serves to express both repetition and conjunction. Otherwise, since repetition would already be indicated by the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) itself, the rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) regarding "constant action" (*nitya*) and "intensity" (*vīpsā*) would not apply there.

The meaning is "it may be so. And thus, in forms such as *pāpacyate* derived from the root *pac* with the suffix *yaṅ* to express repetition (*paunaḥpunya*), there is no reduplication [of the root] by the rule "from a root having a single vowel" (*dhātor ekācaḥ*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.
(1) When expressing reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), two forms of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) are to be expressed.

Regarding the rule *karmavyatihāre*: "exchange of action" (*karmavyatihāra*) means a mutual interchange of actions; when this is to be understood, there is a doubling of the pronoun. And the meaning of those two doubled words is that they are, for the most part (*bahulam*), like a compound (*samāsavat*).
Here, the word "for the most part" (*bahulam*) connects specifically with "like a compound," whereas the doubling is indeed obligatory.

Regarding the phrase "of *anya* and *para*": the meaning is that the quality of being treated as a compound (*samāsavattva*) applies frequently only to the words *anya* and *para*, whereas for the word *itara*, it applies invariably. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya, an example is given for the word *anya* that lacks the treatment of a compound, while an example is given for the word *itara* that includes it.

It is observed that, likewise, from the usage of the Vārttika *parasparopapadācca*, it is understood that even the word *para* lacks the status of being a compound; this is the intended meaning. And thus, in the sense of frequent repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), there is obligatory reduplication (*nityadvirvacana*) of both the words *anya* and *para*. However, regarding the two [words] that have been reduplicated...
The occurrence of the compound form is frequent (*bahulam*). However, for the word *itará*, both [the singular and dual forms] are obligatory.
But for any pronominal term other than these three, this doubling does not occur; such is the established rule due to the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*).
When there is the treatment as if not being a compound (*asamāsavadbhāva*), it should be stated that the *su* [case-ending] of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) becomes *su*.

Regarding "when there is the treatment as if not being a compound": this applies only to the words *anya* and *para*, because for the word *itara*, its being treated as a compound has already been stated. Regarding "the *su* of the *sup*": *su* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term).

The meaning is that for all seven case endings when they occupy the position of the preceding member [in a compound], the substitution of *su*—the nominative singular—is to be stated. Some maintain that this prescription of dual and other numbers applies only to the nominative singular; however, this contradicts the Bhāṣya, as [stated] in the Bhāṣya.

Intending to provide examples for the second case (*dvitīyā*) and subsequent cases, he cites them, beginning with "the Brahmins bow to one another" (*anyonyaṃ viprā namanti*). Here, in the dual number, the *su* suffix replaces the *sup* suffixes of forms such as *anyaṃ* and *anyau*, as previously explained.
He states that this [rule] applies only to the nominative singular and not to the dual and so forth—

this being the consensus of poets— by saying "of one another," etc., up to "Māgha. Regarding the word *parasparam*, having raised the objection that the *upadhmānīya* might replace the *visarga* as an exception to the rule for *satva* (the substitution of *s*), he addresses it.

He says: "Because of the *kaskādi* group," and so forth. Regarding the term *itaretaram*: since *itarah*, *itarau*, and so on, function as compounds when in the dual, the case endings (*sup*) are elided; the point is that the case ending is then produced again from the entire aggregate.
The substitution of *ām* for the case-ending situated after the final member of a compound, when it denotes a feminine or neuter noun, should be stated as optional.
Regarding the phrase "of feminine and neuter [nouns]":
this applies to the words *anya*, *para*, and *itara* when they occur within a compound denoting reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) and denote feminine or neuter nouns.
The meaning is that when there is duality, the substitution of *ām* for the case-ending (*vibhakti*) standing in the second member of the compound should be stated as being frequent (*bahulam*).
Examples include *anyonyām* and so forth: *anyonyām*, or *anyonyaṃ*, *ime brāhmaṇyau kule vā bhojayataḥ* (these two Brahmin women, or these two families, feed one another);
likewise, *parasparām*, or *parasparaṃ*, *ime brāhmaṇyau kule vā bhojayataḥ*.
The grammatical construction (*anvaya*) is: "Feed these two Brahmin women, or [feed] them mutually, or feed [them] in their respective families.

In that context, because it will be stated later that "when there is doubling after *ṭhan* and *ya*, there is an absence of *ṭāp* in both parts," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided due to the masculine-like form (*puṃvat*). Consequently, since the compound status (*samāsatva*) does not apply, the case endings (*sup*) are dropped by *luk*.

When the case-ending (*vibhakti*) residing in the first member (*pūrvapada*) becomes *su*, and after the application of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), the substitution of *u* by "ṭhato ror aplutād aplute" and the *guṇa* substitution by "ād guṇaḥ" have occurred, the case-ending residing in the second member (*uttarapada*) undergoes the substitution of *ām* by this [rule], resulting in the form *anyonyām*. However, in the absence of the substitution of *ām*, due to the rule "puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed, and [the case-ending] residing in the first member [undergoes the same process].

In the case of the neuter gender, the form is exactly like that of the masculine: *anyonyam*. For example, "this Brāhmaṇī feeds another Brāhmaṇī, and the other [feeds] this one"—the meaning is that the two Brāhmaṇīs feed each other by way of exchange. Or, "this family, as the agent, feeds another family; another family, as the agent, [feeds] this one."

The meaning is: "feed [them] in the family" by means of this exchange, namely, that they are of the same family (*kulam*). Here, when the neuter word *anyat* is in the dual, the case-ending of the first member becomes *su* (the nominative-accusative dual ending), while the case-ending of the second member becomes *ām*; thus the form is *anyonyām*. However, in the absence of the change to *ām*, [the form is *anyonyam*].

It should be understood that because it will be stated later that "in the neuter, there is the absence of *ad* and *aṅ*, and [the suffix] *svam* is like the masculine," there is no substitution of *ad*; thus, in the case of the masculine, the form is simply *anyonyam*. Likewise, in the feminine, when the word *parām* is doubled, this applies to both halves of the compound.

Due to the *puṃvat* treatment, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided, the case endings residing in the preceding and following members undergo, respectively, the substitution of *su* and the substitution of *ām*; thus, the form is *parasparam*. However, in the absence of the substitution of *ām*, in the case of duality, due to the *puṃvat* treatment, when *ṭāp* is elided, the case ending residing in the preceding member undergoes the substitution of *su*.

The form is *parasparam*. However, in the neuter gender, when there is reduplication of *param*, because it is treated as masculine (*puṃvat*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed; then, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) belonging to the first member (*pūrvapada*) becomes *su*, while the case-ending belonging to the second member (*uttarapada*) becomes *ām*, resulting in the form *paraspam*. But in the absence of *ām*, when there is reduplication...

When the case-ending (*vibhakti*) of the first member remains as a *sub* (nominal suffix), the form is *parasparam*. When there is a dual number for *itarām*, the feminine suffix *āp* is removed due to the application of the *puṃvat* rule; then, when the case-ending of the second member becomes *ām* and the case-ending of the first member is elided because the compound is treated as a *samāsa*, the form is *itaretaram*.

In the absence of the *ām* suffix, however, the form is *itarētara*. But in the case of the neuter, when the word *itarat* is doubled, because of its *puṃvat* (masculine-like) treatment, there is an absence of the *adḍ* substitute;
consequently, after the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending of the first member, depending on whether the case-ending of the second member takes the *ām* suffix or not, [the forms differ].

There are two forms. Here, because examples ending in the second case (accusative) are cited in the Bhāṣya and other texts, the author states the opinion of the ancients—that the substitution of *ām* does not occur in other cases—by saying, "In this regard, some say that... and "By that [word], in cases other than the second. This refers to cases other than the accusative.

The meaning is "by the absence of the feminine suffix *ām*. Regarding the phrase "just like the masculine": when the feminine suffix *ām* is absent, because the term *bahuvrīhi* is included [in the rule], there is masculine-like treatment (*puṃvat*). Consequently, in the absence of the suffix *ṭāp*, the form in the first, third, and other case-endings is exactly like the masculine.
In the case of the neuter gender, however, in the first, third, and other case-endings—
The meaning is that because of the absence of the feminine suffix (*āp*), the form of the nominative singular is exactly like that of the masculine.

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "others, however" (*anye tu*). Regarding the phrase "because it is merely indicative" (*diṅmātratvāt*), the meaning is "because it is merely a demonstration of direction"; that is to say, because it is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The absence of the suffix *ṭāp* in the two duals, the absence of the suffix *adḍ* in the neuter [dual] *svamau*,
and the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending in compounds— these three are established by way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*).
Now, he cites an ancient verse intended to explain the purpose of the continued application of the term *bahulam* (optionally) in this context: "In the case of two parts," etc.
This refers to the feminine gender forms of the words *anya*, *para*, and *itara* when expressing reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) and when there is duality.

The meaning is that because the preceding and succeeding members [of the compound] are treated as masculine (*puṃvat*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided. Although in the case of "itaretara," the absence of *ṭāp* in the first member is already established by the rule "sarvanāmno vṛtimātre" (Pāṇini 1.1.29) due to its being a compound, nevertheless, regarding the subsequent member...
The intention is that the recourse to the rule of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*) is for the purpose of preventing the application of the suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding the term "in the neuter":

the meaning is that there is an absence of the substitution of *adḍ* in cases such as *anyonyam*. Regarding "of the *su*-case ending in a compound": the meaning is that it refers to that which resides in the prior member when a reduplicated form has been compounded with something else. "For instance" (*tathāhi*).
The meaning is that this is demonstrated by providing an example so that it becomes clear. Now, one might object:

since the rule "sarvanāmno vṛtimātre" (a pronoun takes the masculine form when in a compound) does not apply here, there is no occasion for the masculine form; why then is it mentioned? To this he says: "of the other and the subsequent," and "as in a compound."

The meaning is that it was stated previously that the status of being a compound (*samāsatva*) applies only to the word *itará* itself, and not to other words such as *anya* or *para*. Now, one might object: "Let us grant that there is no status of being a compound; nevertheless, by the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre*, there should be masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*)."

Anticipating the objection that [the rule] is difficult to maintain because reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is a form of derivation (*vṛtti*), he refutes it by stating: "And reduplication alone is not a derivation. The intention is that there is an exhaustive enumeration [of derivations] as follows: "The five types of derivations consist of *kṛt* [primary suffixes], *taddhita* [secondary suffixes], compounds (*samāsa*), *ekaśeṣa* [retention of one], and verbal roots ending in *san* and *ādi* [desiderative and intensive suffixes]. As for reduplication...

He states the objection regarding the inclusion [of the *dvirvacana*] within the *vṛtti*: "yāṃ yāṃ... etc. If the *dvirvacana* were included within the *vṛtti*, then in the verse—"yāṃ yāṃ priyaḥ praikṣata kātarākṣī sāsā hriyā namramukhī babhūva"—in the forms *yāṃ yām* and *sāsā*, [the rule] "sarvanāmno... [would apply].

The meaning is that there would be *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) for the first member (*pūrvakhaṇḍa*) when it ends in a mere suffix (*vṛtti-mātra*). He provides an example for the rule "and in the neuter, there is the absence of *adḍ*" with the word "anyonyam. Now, one might ask: how is it that [the rule] "in a compound, there is the elision (*luk*) of *sa-*" applies to the words *anya* and *para*?

Anticipating the objection that this is not a compound, [the author] intends to show that when a word formed with the suffix *dvit* (i.e., a reduplicated form) is compounded with another word, there is non-elision (*aluk*) of the *su* (nominal suffix) belonging to the preceding member; with this purpose in mind, he gives the example: "anyonyasaṃsaktam" (mutually joined). This means "joined with one another."

This is a *tṛtīyā*-compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). "Day and night" (*ahaś ca triyāmā ca*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The meaning is that day and night are joined with one another. Regarding "mutual dependence" (*anyonyāśraya*):
it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) meaning "the support of one another. Regarding "resemblance to each other's eyes" (*parasparākṣisādṛśya*): by means of the eye...
"Sādṛśyam akṣisādṛśyam" (similarity of the eyes); the analysis of the compound is "parasparasya akṣisādṛśyam" (the similarity of the eyes of one another).

Regarding the term "aparaspair": it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) meaning "not paraspara," i.e., "non-reciprocal"; in the analysis "tair" (by them), when these members of the compound have undergone reduplication (*dvitva*), the *s* of the case-ending (*su*) belonging to the preceding portion [of the compound] is elided (*luk*).

The meaning is "attained. The intention is that the rule for the application of the *subh* augment (*subhāvavidhāna*) finds its scope in non-compounds (*asamāsa*), such as in the example beginning with *anyonya*. Now, one might ask: what is the authority for the claim that this can be resolved by the mention of the term *bahulam* (in various cases)? To this, he says: "by the present Vārttika," namely, *strīnapuṃsakayoḥ*.

From the examples given in the *Prakṛtavārtika*—namely, "these two Brāhmaṇas [are] mutually" (*anyonyam ime brāhmaṇau*) and "these two families [are] reciprocally" (*itaretaram ime kule*)—it is understood that there is an absence of the suffix *ṭāp* when the word is in the neuter dual, and an absence of the suffix *adḍ* when it is in the neuter singular; thus, the form is *svam*. Furthermore, in the rule *striyām*, the term *anyonyasaṃśrayam* [is used].
The meaning is that, because of the usage of the word *aditi* (in the rule *aditi-vīpsā-yoḥ*), it is understood that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending in a compound.
**Pāṇini 8.1.13:** *akṛcchre priya-sukhayor anyatarasyām* (In the sense of "not difficult," [the case-ending is optionally retained] after *priya* and *sukha*).
*Akṛcchra*: *kṛcchra* means hardship or difficulty; *akṛcchra* means absence of effort or ease. [The suffix is optionally retained] for these two words when they signify that state.

There are two [possibilities] for the words *priya* and *sukha*: they may behave like a *karmadhāraya*. This is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the latter [compounds] are like a *karmadhāraya*. One should not suspect that the term "like a compound" (*samāsavat*) continues from the rule "and frequently like a compound" (*samāsavacca bahulam*), for that [rule]...

Because it is stated in the Vārttika, and thus, when there is doubling of both *priyeṇa* and *sukhena*, since they function as a *karmadhāraya*, the third-case singular suffixes are elided; consequently, it results that a third-case singular suffix is applied again from the entire compound.

*yathāsve yathāyatham* (Pāṇini 8.1.14). Regarding *yathāsve yathāyatham*: it is stated that *vīpsā* (distributive repetition) refers to a connection with totality (*kārtsnya*). When the totality pertaining to the meaning of the word *sva* (self/one's own) is to be indicated, the word *yathā* [is used].

The meaning is that [the compound] is an *avyayībhāva* by virtue of its own specific term (*svaśabda*). "Kṛtsna" (entire) and "sva" (one's own) form a non-elliptical analysis (*asvapadavigraha*), because it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). The word *sva*, however, denotes self, one's own, kinsman, and wealth; but here, it is understood only as denoting self and one's own, and not as denoting kinsman or wealth.

Intending to explain this, he states the resulting meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) as "two" (*dve*). The word "are" (*staḥ*) is to be supplied; the sense is that it is due to an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Nor should it be suspected that the doubling here is already established by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4) through the function of repetition (*vīpsā*), because [the rule applies] to a word that is the locus of the number two.

The meaning is that because the rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is prescribed specifically for distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) when the word functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote something qualified by totality;

otherwise, the word *sarva* in expressions such as "every jar" (*sarvo ghaṭaḥ*) would also incur reduplication. Regarding the neuter gender: the remainder of the sentence is "of the aggregate [of the words] *yathā-yathā*"; otherwise [the gender would not be neuter].

The sense is that because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), it would lack gender (*aliṅgatva*). And thus, when the doubling [of the suffix] has been applied, the shortening of the neuter vowel is also established as the result. Regarding the phrase *yathāyathaṃ jñātā*: here, *jñātā* ends in the suffix *tṛn*. Because of the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na loke* when used in conjunction with this [suffix], the second case (*dvitīyā*) is employed for the object.
But if it ends in *tṛc*, it is only when [the object] is known as "unfitting" (*yathāyatha*).
(Pāṇini 2.4.9) *dvandvam* is used in the senses of secrecy, limit, transgression, the employment of sacrificial vessels, and manifestation. (Pāṇini 6.1.15)

"Dvandva" means a secret. Regarding the phrase "of the first member": since there is a *dvigu* (numeral compound) in the sense of "two by two," the case-ending (*sup*) is elided due to its being a *karmadhāraya*;

then, when a case-ending is added again to the whole, the vowel *i* belonging to the first member is replaced by the suffix *ṭhañ*, which results in the substitution of the letter *m* for the final [vowel]. "The state of *at*" refers to the final member of the compound.

The meaning is that *akāra* is the substitute for the final sound. Nor should it be argued that the substitution of *at* for the final sound of the subsequent member (in *tyadādi*) is already established; for they say that this does not apply here because [the word] is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). And as for "neuter gender": the particle *ca* is used to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; namely, the neuter gender of that which has undergone reduplication (*dvitva*).
The meaning is that there is an absence of the dual number. Regarding the phrase *ācaturam hi*: the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*).
This forms an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *āṅmaryādāvacane*. Because it belongs to the *śarat-prabhṛti* group, the suffix *ṭac* is applied.
Thus, the resulting meaning is "up to the fourth. Animals [are counted] from themselves as the first up to the fourth.
The grammatical connection is: "they couple in pairs. By the word *mithuna*, sexual union (*maithuna*) is intended.

Sexual union is the action (*karman*) of a pair (*mithuna*). To express the sense of "desiring that," the suffix *kyac* is applied according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ*. He states the resulting meaning: "he goes to a pair"; the meaning is that he attains the state of being a pair.
The reading *mithunāyante* (they couple) with the suffix *ky-aṅ* is erroneous; rather, it means "having made [the limit] a boundary" (*maryādīkṛtya*).

The meaning is that it extends through the four starting from oneself. From the Bhāṣya, it is understood that "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) refers to worldly cognition arising from extreme constant association. Thus he says: the meaning is "by way of association" (*sahacaryeṇa*).

Thus [it is said]. Here, in the expression *dvandvaṃ nyañci*, one should understand that the doubling occurs due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), whereas elsewhere it occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). "Elsewhere too" means in cases such as *dvandvāni sahate*. Cold and heat constitute one pair (*dvandva*); pleasure and pain constitute another; and hunger and thirst constitute yet another.

In this case, it is a *dvandva* compound in its own sense (*svārthe*). The substitution of *ambh-* and so forth is as before. By the rule "a *dvandva* is formed in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*)," it is established that this applies even in other instances due to the fact that it is a *nipātana* (an irregularly prescribed form). Thus ends the section on reduplicated forms (*dvirukta-prakaraṇa*).

Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Ānandarāya Vidyāvācaspati, the preeminent scholar among all learned men, who was the chief minister to the illustrious Śāhajī Tukkojī Bhosale—the sovereign of the Cola land—and who presided over a grand and boundless series of great sacrifices, characterized by many virtues such as the continuous succession of the *śyena*, *kūrma*, and the sixteen-spoked wheel of a chariot; he was nourished by five generations of ancestors and [was himself] from his very childhood...

By him who had gratified the gods, headed by Indra, through sacrifices such as the Vājapeya, Sarvapṛṣṭha, and Aptoryāma—which were manifested by immeasurable fires kindled out of compassion; who, having crossed to the further shore of the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology, was a Brahmin who had performed the Vājapeya sacrifice for Viśveśvara and thereby attained clarity of knowledge; and who had demonstrated his sovereignty over all systems of thought through the composition of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti*.

The first half of the *Bālamanoramā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by the learned Vāsudeva Dīkṣita—son of Annapūrṇāmbā and born of the lineage of Mahādeva, who was a performer of the Vājapeya sacrifice and a master of the *Kalpasūtras* and their commentaries of Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Satyāṣāḍha, Bhāradvāja, Kātyāyana, Āśvalāyana, Drāhyāyaṇa, and others.
Now begins the section on *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member of a group).

Now, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is defined. Thus, having defined *dvandva*, he begins the section on *ekaśeṣa*, which is an exception (*apavāda*) to it, with the words "Now, *ekaśeṣa*. The word "is defined" (*nirūpyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Therein, wishing to explain the *sūtras* on *ekaśeṣa*, [the author] first [recalls] a *sūtra* that, although already explained, [requires further discussion].
For the sake of clarifying the context, he says: "of those that have the same form. He also recalls the illustration for that: "rāmau" and "rāmāḥ.
[This applies] even to those that have different forms, provided they have the same meaning.

Regarding the term *virūpāṇām*: by the rule *sarūpāṇām*, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) was stated for words that have the same form even when there is a difference in meaning; the meaning here is that a single remainder must also be stated for words that have different forms when they possess a single meaning.
In the example *vakradaṇḍaśca* ("and the one with a crooked staff"), although there is a difference in the verbal forms, because the meaning is identical, one of them is retained.
This is the intended meaning. (917) *vṛddho yūnā tallakṣaṇaśced eva viśeṣaḥ* | 1|2|65|.

[The rule] "an elder [is compounded] with a youth" (*vṛddho yūnā*). This is stated so that [the compound] may apply even when there is a difference in form and meaning. [The word] "with a youth" (*yūnā*)...
"But while a descendant lives" means [the case] ending in a *yuvan* suffix, which will be mentioned later.

"In the case of co-utterance" (*sahoktau*)—this is obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Regarding "lineage" (*gotram*): by the word *vṛddha*, the lineage defined in the sūtra "The offspring from the grandson onwards is the lineage" (*apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛti gotram*) is intended.
The meaning is that this is because it has been defined as such by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*) in the rule *apatyaṃ vṛddhaṃ*.

That is to say, it refers to [a term] ending in a *gotra* suffix. Nor should it be asked why the rule was not simply formulated as *gotraṃ yūne*; for outside the governing heading on *apatya* (*apatyādhikāra*), the term *gotra* is understood to mean the conventional [lineage].

The phrase "the *gotra* is intended" is for the purpose of making known the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Regarding the word "remnant" (*śeṣa*), the sense is that it follows [from the rule] as a form ending in the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the expression "characterized by that" (*tallakṣaṇa*), the analysis of the compound is: that which has as its characteristic (or cause) both the *gotra*-suffix and the *yuvan*-suffix.

*Viśeṣa* means distinction or dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*). Thus, the meaning is: if there is a distinction—that is, a difference in form—between two [words] ending in the *gotra* and *yuvan* suffixes, and if that [distinction] is characterized by those [suffixes], i.e., caused by the *gotra* and *yuvan* suffixes; [it does not apply] if it is caused by something else.

The meaning "if not" is thus established. He says this with the words *gotrayuva* (line 15). The word *kṛtsnam* (line 16) is to be understood from the force of the particle *eva*. [He gives the example] *gārgyaśca* (line 17): *gārgyaḥ* is the descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatyam*) of Garga;
[it is formed] by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*. [He gives the example] *gārgyāyaṇaḥ* (line 18): *gārgyaḥ* is the lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatyam*) of Garga.

His descendant who is a youth is Gārgyāyaṇa; [the suffix] *phak* is applied by the rule "ṭhyañiñośca. Regarding the form *gārgyau*, the point is that the dissimilarity between the word *gārgya* and the word *gārgyāyaṇa* is caused solely by the addition of the *gotra* and *yuvan* suffixes respectively; therefore, the word *gārgya*, which ends in the *gotra* suffix, remains as the survivor.

Regarding "gargagārgyāyaṇau": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "Garga and Gārgyāyaṇa. Here, although there is a difference between the word *garga* and the word *gārgyāyaṇa* caused solely by the addition of the secondary suffix denoting a descendant (*yuvan*), there is no application of the rule for "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) because they do not both end in a secondary suffix denoting a lineage (*gotra*). Thus, the meaning is that [the form] is *gargagārgyau*. In this case...

The point is that although the words *garga* and *gārgya* differ solely due to the addition of the *gotra* suffix, the word *gārgya*, ending in a *gotra* suffix, is not retained [in the compound] when used in conjunction with a term for a *yuvan* descendant, because there is no co-utterance (*sahokti*) with a *yuvan*. [Regarding the example] *bhāgavita-bhāgavitikau*: it means the *gotra* descendant of Bhagavita.

The term *bhāgaviti* is derived from the suffix *iñ*. *Bhāgaviteḥ* refers to the descendant of *bhāgaviti*, a Sauvīra; the young (yuvan) descendant who is contemptible is *bhāgavītikaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "ṭhak is added after a *vṛddha* [stem] for Sauvīras. In this case, there is no dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) in the word *bhāgaviti* caused merely by the addition of the *gotra* and *yuvan* suffixes.

The meaning is that because there exists even a deformity (*vairūpya*) produced by the *kutsā* (contempt) and *sauvīratva* (being a Sauvīra), the word *bhāgavi*, which ends in a *gotra*-suffix, is not taught [as a valid form].
As for "Gārgya and Vātsyāyana": Gārgya is the descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) of Garga; [Vātsyāyana is the descendant] of Vatsa.

*Vātsyaḥ* is the offspring of *Vatsa*; the suffix *yañ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *gargādi* group. *Vātsyāyanaḥ* is the youthful descendant (*yuvan*) of *Vatsa*; the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule "after *yañ* and *iñ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "Gārgya and Vātsyāyana.
In this case, there is [no elision] of the word *gārgya* or the word *vātsyāyana*.

The difference in form is caused solely by the *gotra* suffix and the *yuvan* suffix, because the natural difference in form is not caused merely by the *gotra* suffix and the *yuvan* suffix. Therefore, the meaning is that the word *gārgya*, which ends in the *gotra* suffix, is not retained [as the final form].

(918) *strī pumvat ca* | 1.2.66. "The feminine [word] is like the masculine. The word *vṛddhā* from [Pāṇini 1.2.65] is modified to the feminine gender. Thus he says: "When there is co-utterance with a youth (*yuvan*), the elder (*vṛddhā*) feminine [word] remains. This refers to a word denoting a female that ends in a *gotra* suffix.

The meaning is that it is taught [as an exception]. Because there exists an additional cause for deformity in the state of being female (*strītva*), this statement is made because the previous rule would not otherwise apply. "For its sake" means:
when the male is the referent of that which is about to be taught—the feminine *gotra* suffix—just as if it were a male.
The meaning is "it might be. Regarding *gargī*: it means the female descendant of Garga.
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *ṭhyaṇaśca*. Regarding *gārgyāyaṇau*:

the suffix *phak* is applied to form the word for a descendant from a stem ending in *yañ* (from the *garga*-class) according to the rule *yaūnyapatye ṭhyañiñośca*. Regarding *gargāḥ*: in this case...

Even when there is an excess of deformity caused by femininity, the word *gārgī*, which denotes a female and ends in a *gotra* suffix, remains; that [suffix] is treated like the masculine. To the question "When is the *yañ* and *kit* [suffix] not heard?", he says:
"Except in the feminine. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). [It refers to the rule: "In the case of a *tadrāja* [suffix], when many [descendants are meant]..."

The meaning is that while the words "except in the feminine" (*astriyām*), "by that very same [word]" (*tenaiva*), and "in the plural" (*bahuṣu*) are being carried over (*anuvartamāne*), the purpose of the rule *pūṃvat* has been stated by this. However, the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) as "Gārgī and Gārgyāyaṇa" has not been shown. Thus.

Because there is a plurality of [the suffix] *satr*, when the elision (*luk*) of *yañ* does not occur, the form is identical in both the masculine and feminine genders—namely, *gārgyau*. In that case, the masculine form would be redundant. He states another example: "and *dākṣī*. A female descendant in the lineage of Dakṣa is *dākṣī*.
From the word ending in *iñ*, namely *dākṣi*—formed by adding *iñ* according to the rule "ṭhitaḥ manuṣyajāteḥ"—the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Regarding the form *dākṣāyaṇa*:

the male descendant of Dakṣa is *dākṣi*; his young descendant (*yuvan*) is *dākṣāyaṇa*, formed by adding *phak* according to the rule "ṭhyañiñośca". In the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) of the compound "the female descendant of Dakṣa (*dākṣī*) and the male descendant *dākṣāyaṇa*," the word *dākṣī* [is used].
It remains [as the base]. For that [base], the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) would be meaningless.

He states another example: "and *dākṣī*. A female descendant in the lineage of Dakṣa is *dākṣī*. From the word ending in *iñ*—by the rule *ata iñ*—the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ito manuṣyajāteḥ*. And [the example] *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*.

In a compound (vigraha), the word *dākṣī* remains; when it undergoes masculine treatment (*puṃvat*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed, and from the word *dākṣi*, in the nominative dual, the form *dākṣī* arises. Here, the rule "provided there is a distinction characterized by that" also continues to apply. Consequently, [in the case of] *bhāgavittī* and *bhāgavittika*, and *gargī*...
And in the case of *vātsyāyanaśca*, [the elision] does not occur.

(919) *pumān striyā* | 1|2|67 | "The masculine [term] [is elided] when followed by the feminine. It is understood as "only when they share the same defining characteristic (*tallakṣaṇa*)," because that [condition] continues from the rule *vṛddho yūnā*.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the example *haṃsī ca* ("and the female swan"), here, because the dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is caused solely by masculinity and femininity, the masculine form *haṃsa* remains [as the single remainder]. Precisely because of this dissimilarity caused by femininity and masculinity, the rule *sarūpāṇām* ("of those that have the same form") does not apply. This is seen in the case of *mātṛ-mātarau* ("the mother and the father").

However, this single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) does not apply to the pair of words *jananī* and *mātṛ*, both signifying "mother," because the rule "of those with identical forms in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau sarūpāṇām*) is followed by the qualification:
"of those that lack dissimilarity caused by gender other than feminine and masculine. And in this case—

In the case of *mātarau*, there is also dissimilarity due to the presence and absence of the long vowel by the rule *ṛt-aḥ ṅi-ṣyaḥ* (*ṛt-aḥ ṅi-ṣyaḥ*); for this very reason, it is not [the case] even in *haṃsaś ca varaṭā ca*.
(920) *bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām* | 1.2.68 | [The dual endings of] *bhrātṛ* and *putra* [are used] with *svasṛ* and *duhitṛ*.

When "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) and "son" (*putra*) are mentioned together with "sister" (*svasṛ*) and "daughter" (*duhitṛ*) respectively, the forms *bhrātṛ* and *putra* remain. This rule is stated because, due to their dissimilarity (*vairūpya*), they would not otherwise apply even by their own nature. (921) *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām* | 1.2.69 | [A neuter noun remains when combined with a non-neuter noun, and optionally takes the singular number.]

It is neuter. The phrase "of either" (*anyatarasyām*) connects only with the rule for "as a single unit" (*ekavad*), due to immediate proximity, and not with the rule for "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*); thus he says, "And that. "Only when characterized by that" means: provided there is dissimilarity caused solely by the presence or absence of neuter gender. For example: *śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*.

"White cloth," "white garment"— in these cases, the word *śukla* (white) takes the masculine gender when co-occurring with the word *paṭa* (cloth), the feminine gender when co-occurring with the word *śāṭī* (dress),
and the neuter gender when co-occurring with the word *vastra* (garment); for words such as *śukla* denote a quality (*guṇa*).

The meaning is that, according to the statement in the *Amara-kośa*, "the words for qualities [take] the gender of the possessor of those qualities" (*puṃsi guṇiliṅgāstu tadvati*), the following applies:
*sa* (he), *sā* (she), and *tat* (it) = *tat*; *ayam* (this), *iyam* (this), and *idam* (this) = *idam*; *śuklaḥ* (white), *śuklā* (white), and *śuklam* (white) = *śuklam*.
In these cases, only the neuter forms remain, and they take the singular number.

"These are the white ones. When there is *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) in the neuter gender, the forms [of the plural] would not appear as singular. Furthermore, since the dual and plural endings are established when there is a desire to express mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), and the singular ending is established when there is a desire to express a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the term "as a single unit" (*ekavat*) would be redundant.

This must be stated, precisely because it is thereby indicated that the section on *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) does not apply to collective compounds (*samāhāra*). Consequently, from "rice and rice" (*odanaśca odanaṃ ca*), there is no formation of *odanam* in the sense of their collective compound.
For the word *odana* belongs to the *ardharca*-class [of *pūrvapadārthapradhāna* compounds]. Thus, "rice and rice."

Even in the case of a *dvandva* compound denoting mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the form "odanam" does not occur, because such usage is not sanctioned by linguistic convention (*anabhidhānāt*). And so, since one must necessarily resort to non-usage in certain instances, one may rely on the non-usage of the *dvandva* itself in cases where *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of a single term) applies, thereby attributing multiple meanings to a single word.
And relying on this, the section concerning *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member of a pair) was rejected in the Bhāṣya.
(922) *pitā mātrā* |1|2|80|. "The father [is retained] with the mother. This refers to the rule *pumān striyā*.

Because of the continued application of the rule "of those having the same form" (*sarūpāṇām*), this statement is provided where [the previous rule] would not otherwise apply, and it serves the purpose of providing an option.

In the case of *mātāpitarau* ("mother and father"), the prior placement of *mātṛ* is due to her being more venerable, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "The mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of reverence. The form [is derived] by applying the *ānaṅ* substitution [for the final syllable of *pitṛ*] according to the rule "ānaṅ ṛto dvandve" (Pāṇini 6.3.25).
(923) *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā* |1|2|71|. [The word] *śvaśuraḥ* [is placed first when compounded with] *śvaśrvā*. [The resulting compound is] *śvaśrūśvaśurau*.

Because it is stated that even the mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*) is equal to a mother, she possesses the status of being more venerable (*abhyarhitatva*). [As it is said: "The mother-in-law and the wife of an elder brother are equal to a mother."

This is because of the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "it is proclaimed. Here, the recurrence of the mention of that definition is for the sake of clarity, since the term "father-in-law" (*śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā*) is mentioned as a specific word-form.
(924) *Tyadādīni sarvair nityam* (1.2.72).

"Words beginning with *tyad* (pronouns). Regarding "with all": the meaning is "with the words beginning with *tyad* and with others. Regarding "those two": here the word *devadatta* is excluded, while the word *tat* remains; thus, one does not say *tad-devadattau*. Why "with all"? By virtue of proximity, the meaning is that it applies only when there is co-utterance (*sahokti*) with words beginning with *tyad* themselves.
This is for the purpose that [the former] should not [remain].

Regarding the rule "when pronouns beginning with *tyad-* are used in mutual co-utterance (*sahokti*), that which is subsequent remains": this is established in the Bhāṣya as "among those beginning with *tyad-*" and "that which is subsequent."

The meaning is that whichever [word] is recited later in the *tyadādi* group remains; this is the sense, based on the reliance upon the "conflict regarding word-order" (*śabdapara-vipratiṣedha*). Thus, *saśca yaśca = yau*, and *sā ca yā ca = ye*.
Because the word *yac* is recited after the word *tac* in the *tyadādi* group, by virtue of its posteriority, *sa* [remains].
The intended meaning is that [the word] alone remains; however, it may also remain as part of what precedes it.

"From *tyad* and so forth, when there is a remainder, the gender and number are those of the masculine or neuter.

When *tyad* and the others are intended to be expressed together, even if a feminine remains as the remainder, [the gender and number are determined] by whichever is masculine or whichever is neuter.
The meaning is that they serve to indicate gender (*liṅga*).
When there is an expectation as to which [words] these are, only those beginning with *arthāt* (meaning "from the sense") are connected. And that [is expressed as]:
"He and Devadatta, those two. Here, the word *tat* remains, as does the gender indicated by the co-occurring word *Devadatta*.

The meaning is "because of the comprehension of otherness.
It should be stated: "of non-dvandva [compounds] and tatpuruṣa compounds that are qualifiers.

For the rule *ṭhaparavalliṅgam* prescribes that the gender of a Dvandva or Tatpuruṣa compound is that of the final member.

Consequently, it is established in the works of Bhartṛhari and Kaiyaṭa that when there is an anvaya (subsequent application) of a qualifier for the Dvandva or a qualifier for the Tatpuruṣa, that very same gender must be used. And therefore—

In the example "ṭhkukkuṭamayūryāv ime," when analyzed as "this (ayam) and this (iyam)," although the masculine remains by the rule "pumān striyā" (when a masculine and a feminine are in apposition, the masculine alone remains), the word would take the feminine gender because it functions as an adjective according to the rule "paravalliṅgam. Consequently, by the rule "tyadāditaḥ" (words beginning with *tyad* etc. become masculine when followed by a masculine noun), the masculine form [of the pronoun] is applied.

There is no inconsistency in [the statement] that what was previously established is here negated. However, in some original manuscripts, the reading "imau mayūrīkukkuṭau" (these two, a peahen and a cock) is also seen; yet that is irrelevant to the present context, because the meaning of the dvandva compound "mayūrīkukkuṭau" is masculine, as in "this female and this male."

In the case of *imau*, even though it is used as a qualifier for that [referent], since the masculine form of the word *idam*— which remains according to the rule *pumān striyā*— cannot possibly be feminine,
the rule for masculine gender *tyadāditaḥ śeṣe* does not apply there.

Because the prohibition [stated in the rule] "of dvandvas, tatpuruṣas, and qualifiers" is not applicable here, he provides an example for the *tatpuruṣa*: "And that. Half of a *pippalī* is *ardhapippalī*.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound by the rule "the word *ardha*, when neuter [is compounded]. And *ardhapippalī* is also [equivalent to] *pippalyardha*.

"Half-pippalī" (*ardhapippalī*) and "pippalī" (*pippalī*): these two, [taken together], are *te*. In this context, the neuter gender in the word *ṭaḥ* (from *tad*) is intended with reference to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) "half of a pippalī" (*pippalyardha*). However, the feminine gender in *se* (from *sā*) is intended with reference to the qualified object "half-pippalī" (*ardhapippalī*). Here, [the rule] "pumān... [applies].

The application of the rule "striyām" (in the feminine) does not occur here at all; rather, by the rule "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavacca," the neuter form remains as the residue. In that case, the feminine gender is applied by the rule "paravalliṅgam. Since that [compound] is feminine, its qualifier also takes the feminine gender by the rule "paravalliṅgam."

The neuter gender that would otherwise apply to it by the rule *tyadāditaḥ śeṣe* is here prohibited. Thus, *te* is established as being exclusively feminine. Although there is no difference between the dual form *te* whether it denotes the feminine or the neuter, nevertheless, those [are] half-pippalīs.
Thus it should be cited. The analysis of the compound is: "that and that and she" (*tac ca tac ca sā ca*).
(925) Pāṇini 1.2.73: *strī* [is used] for non-youthful herds of domestic animals.
Regarding the term *grāmyapaśu*: "in these" refers to non-youthful domestic animals.

The meaning is "in the case of groups. Here, because the term *anapuṃsakena* (not neuter) is understood from the previous rule, he states that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] *pumān striyā* (a masculine [noun] is used with a feminine).
For example, in the case of the word *go* (cow) used in the masculine and feminine genders as "the cow and the cow and the cow" (*gauś ca gauś ca gauś ca*).

The meaning is that when [the words] are intended to be spoken together, the rule "pumān striyā" (a male [remains when joined with a female]) is set aside, and the female form alone remains. Now, one might object: "Whether there is the retention of the female or the retention of the male, there is no difference in form. To this he says: "imāḥ" (these). The point is that the difference in form results from the subsequent application of the suffix. [This applies to] "tyadāditaḥ" (from the group beginning with *tyad*).

They say that the rule *śeṣe* does not apply here, because of the usage in the Bhāṣya: *gāva imāḥ*. As for *rurava ime*: the *ruru* is a black deer (*mṛga*). Because it is a non-domestic animal (*agrāmyapaśu*), the feminine form is not retained as the remainder;
rather, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) according to the rule *pumān striyā*. Consequently, in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), the word *ime* is used.
The masculine gender alone remains, as in "these Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇā ime*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the Brāhmaṇī and the Brāhmaṇas.

Because it is not a compound of cattle (*apaśutvāt*), the feminine form is not retained; rather, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) according to the rule "the masculine remains for the feminine" (*pumān striyā*). Otherwise, it would have been "these Brāhmaṇīs" (*brāhmaṇya imā*). As for "these two cows" (*etau gāvau*), [it is] the feminine gender.

When two masculine [words] are stated together, the feminine is not retained because there is no plurality [of gender]. For the word "group" (*saṅgha*) applies to a collection of many; otherwise, since the function of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) inherently concerns multiple items, the inclusion of more than one would already be established—so what would be the purpose of that [term "group"]? This is the intended meaning.
However, in the case where only the feminine remains, the form would be "ete" in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), as in "vatsā ime.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is "these males and these males" (*vatsāśca vatsāśca*). Because of their youth, the female does not remain [as the residue]. Otherwise, the subsequent application would have been "vatsā imāḥ."
"It should be stated: 'in the case of animals with many hoofs'. This is a *vārttika*. Horses and the like have one hoof;

when they are mentioned together [with other animals], the suffix *ṭhak* [denoting a herd] does not apply by the rule "for domestic animals" (*grāmyapaśu*). For example: "these horses" (*ime aśvāḥ*). Because they have only one hoof, [the suffix does not apply].
The feminine form is retained; therefore, the intention is that the masculine gender applies in the subsequent application (anuprayoga). Now, one might object:

since the rule *sarūpāṇām* follows the mention of "dvandva" from the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvornakṣatradvandve*, and because the Bhāṣya states that the single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs within a dvandva compound, it follows that the *ekaśeṣa* takes place only after the dvandva has been formed.

To this, he says: "In this [context]. In all these examples cited here which fall under the scope of *ekaśeṣa*, the *dvandva* compound—which would otherwise apply everywhere—is set aside by *ekaśeṣa* because it has no scope [once *ekaśeṣa* applies]. The meaning is that once *ekaśeṣa* has been performed, the *dvandva* does not occur due to the absence of plurality (*anekatva*). [This is stated in the rule: "In a *dvandva* compound, there is *ekaśeṣa*."

The commentary, however, should be explained as follows: when a *dvandva* (copulative compound) is applicable, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member) occurs when there is a desire to express them together. Now, one might object: "Let *ekaśeṣa* occur after the *dvandva* has already been formed; what is the harm? To this he says: "By that" (*tena*). This means: by resorting to *ekaśeṣa* prior to the formation of the *dvandva*. [This is because] once the *dvandva* has been formed...

The meaning is that if one were to accept the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of only one member), then in the dual number, "śirasī" would become "śirāṃsi" in the plural; furthermore, by the rule "samāsasya," it would be oxytone (udātta on the final syllable), and because it consists of parts of living beings, there would also be the formation of a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*) by the rule "dvandvaśca prāṇī... and so forth. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), [the forms] "śirobhyām" and so on are included.
The phrase "with heads," etc., is a summary [of the examples]. Regarding the term "panthānau":

the point is that if one were to accept *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member) after forming a *dvandva* compound, then in forms such as *panthānau*, *panthānaḥ*, *pathibhyām*, and *pathibhiḥ*, the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* would have to be applied as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). And this is not the case here.

It should not be argued that the application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is easily avoided on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *ṭhito 't sarvanāmaḥ*, which prescribes the vowel *a* when a "strong case-ending" (*sarvanāmasthāna*) follows;
for even if one were to state *ṭhito 'di*, the form *panthāḥ* would still be established by carrying over the word *sau* [from the previous rule].

Because the rule *ṭhitho'di* (Pāṇini 5.4.153) finds its scope in examples such as *apanthānau*, where the suffix *ṭhaC* is absent due to the optionality of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) prescribed by the rule *ṭhpatho vibhāṣā*.
Thus ends the section on *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one member) in the *Bālamanoramā*.

*Ho ḍhaḥ* | 8|2|31|. Now follow those [roots] ending in *ha*. Therein, following the sequence of the traditional list of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*), he says first regarding that which ends in *ha*: *ho ḍhaḥ*. The word *ṭhha* is in the genitive case. [This is understood] from the rule *jhalo jhali*.

The term *jhal* is understood from the previous rule. The governing term *padasya* (of a word) is in force. From the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca*, the term *ante* (at the end) is also understood. Thus he says: "of *ha*" (*hasya*). Regarding *jhalīti*: the meaning is that [the substitution occurs] when a *jhal* sound follows the preceding *ha*, or when the *ha* is situated at the end of a word (*padānte*).

And it should not be asked why the letter *ḍ* was not prescribed instead; for that will be explained under the rule *ṭh-vā druheḥ*. "Because of being at the end of a word" (*padāntatvāt*): this should also be understood to mean that once the *su*-suffix has been elided, [the substitution applies] by relying on the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the technical status of an element as a suffix) and because of the presence of a *jhal* sound [the letter *ṣ*] following it. "In *liḍ*" refers to the root *lih*.

In *āsvādane*, there is no *kvip* suffix. By the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, there is elision of the *su* case-ending. The intention is that when *ha* is changed to *ḍha*, the substitution of *ca* (i.e., *ṭ*) for *ḍ* is optional by the rule *ṭhvāvasāne*. Regarding *liḍbhyām*:
because of the status of being a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*, the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte* applies.

The intended meaning is that there is *jaś*-substitution. Regarding "and so forth": *liḍbhiḥ*, *liḍbhyaḥ*, *lihe*, *lihaḥ*, *lihaḥ*, *lihām*, and *liṭtsu*. When *lih-su* is established, *h* is replaced by *ḍh*. By the rule of *jaś*-substitution, that [ḍh] becomes *ḍ*. Because the substitution of *car* (the replacement of a dental by a retroflex) in the rule *ṭhkhari ca* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this occurs prior to that.

By the rule *ṭh-ḍha-sī* [Pāṇini 8.2.40], the augment *dhuṭ* is added. Then, by the rule of *car*-substitution (*cartvam*), the *ḍ* becomes *ṭ*. Because the *t* produced by the *car*-substitution of the *dhuṭ* is considered *asiddha*, the rule *cayo dvitīyāḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.48] does not apply. Furthermore, by the rule *na padāntāt* [Pāṇini 8.4.42], the *ṣṭu*-substitution of the *t* does not take place. Thus, *liṭsu* is the form when there is an absence of *dhuṭ*.

The *ḍha* of *hasya* becomes *ḍa* by the rule *jaśtva*. That *ḍa* becomes *ṭa* by the rule *cartva*. Because that [substitution] is considered asiddha (not yet established), the rule "the second letters of the *cay* class" does not apply. The point is that, by the rule "not after a word-final [consonant]," there is no *ṣṭutva* for the *s*.

[The substitute] *ḍha* [is applied] for the initial *d* of a verbal root. (Pāṇini 8.2.32). When the elision of the suffix *su* occurs after the root *duh* ending in *kvip*, the rule for *ḍhatva* (the substitution of *ḍha* for *d*) would apply to the form *duh*. However, this rule for *ḍhatva* is here partially set aside by the rule "for a root beginning with *d*" (*dāder dhātoḥ*). The word "*ha*" is supplied from the preceding rule "ṭhho ḍhaḥ" (8.2.31).

The genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is carried over. The terms *jhalī*, *padasya*, and *ante* are carried over as before. The term *dhātoḥ* is also repeated; one instance of *dhātu-* is in the genitive case denoting a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and it connects with the letter *ha*: "of the *ha* which is a part of the root."
The term "dāder" (beginning with *da*) here connects in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "dhātoḥ" (of a verbal root).

The expression "daādir yasya" (that of which *da* is the beginning) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Furthermore, the second mention of "dhātoḥ" indicates the time of the verbal root's instruction (*upadeśakāla*). Consequently, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "in the instruction," and so forth.

The meaning is: "of the *has* (the letter *h*) which is a constituent part of that verbal root beginning with *d* at the time of its instruction (*upadeśa*). He asks for the purpose of including the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*), which was obtained by repeating the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*): "What [is the purpose] in 'instruction'? [He gives the example: *adhok*. [This is derived from] the root *duh* in the sense of "milking," in the imperfect (*laṅ*), with the augment *aṭ*, the suffix *tip*, and the suffix *śap* applied to it.

*luk* [is applied]; the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) occurs; by the rule *halṅyādi*, there is the elision (*lopaḥ*) of the suffix *tip*; by the rule *dādeḥ*, the *ha* is changed to *gha*. By the rule *ekāco vaśo bhaṣ*, through the *bhaṣ*-bhāva, the *da* is changed to *dha*. The intention is that, by the rule *vāvasāne*, the *jaś* and *cart* substitutions may optionally apply. Thus, it becomes *syāt*. The word *yathā* [is used] as follows.

Regarding "fitness for occurrence": the meaning here is that the substitution of *gh* is fit to occur only when the instruction (*upadeśa*) has been grasped; at the time the substitution of *gh* is about to take effect, the verbal root *duh* does not yet possess an initial *d*, because once the augment *aṭ* has been applied, it is held that "those augments are included by the mention of the element they augment."
Because [the root] begins with the letter *i*, the substitution of *gh* would not apply here; thus, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).
However, if the term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) is included, this fault does not arise.

The point is that although at the time the substitution of *gh* is to take effect the root *duh* does not begin with *d*, it did begin with *d* at the time of the original enunciation of the verbal root.

Having thus stated the result of avoiding under-extension (*avyāpti*), he states the result of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with the word "dāma" (rope). The word *dāma* is a synonym for the rope used for binding cattle such as cows around their necks. From the root *lih* (to lick) with the prefix *adāma*, we derive *dāmaliṭ* (one who licks the rope). In the sense of "one who desires that [rope-licker] for himself," the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*. Since the items ending in *san* and so forth are treated as verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffix *tip* is applied, and after the addition of the *śap* augment, the form becomes *dāmalihyati*. From that, the suffix *kvip* is applied.

The meaning is that from the word *dāmalih*—formed by adding the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*) to a root ending in *kyac*, with the elision of *a* and the elision of *y*, followed by the elision of the case-ending *su*—the substitution of *ḍha* for *ṭha* occurs by the rule "ṭh-ḍhaḥ," and then the optional substitution of *ca* for *ṭ* occurs at the end of a word by the rule "ṭ-vāvasāne," resulting in the forms *dāmaliṭ* or *dāmaliḍ*. In this context, [the author says] "let it not be" (*mā bhūt*). *Māṅ* is used here to indicate the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). The inclusion of the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśa*) is also for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution of *gh* does not occur here. When that [term] is included, the substitution of *gh* does not take place in this instance. The point is that in the original instruction (*dhātūpadeśa*), the form *dāmalih* is not recited as a nominal stem (*subanta*).

Thus, in the example under discussion, when *sau-dugh* remains [after the elision of *su*]: [The text continues: ...so too, in the present example, when *sau-dugh* is established— *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the grammatical analysis up to that point.*

*ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37). The analysis of the compound is as follows: *ekācaḥ* [refers to] a root having one vowel; *vaśaḥ* [refers to] the sounds *ba*, *ja*, *ga*, *da*, and *dha*; *bhaṣ* [is the substitute]; *jhaṣ-antasya* [refers to] a root ending in *jha*, *bha*, *ga*, *da*, or *dha*; *sdhvoḥ* [refers to] the suffixes *s* and *dhv*. Thus, *sdhvoḥ* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), while *ekācaḥ* is a genitive of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). The analysis of *ekācaḥ* is: "that which has one vowel (*ekaḥ ac*)".

The word *jhaṣantasya* (of that which ends in a *jhaṣ* sound) is the qualified term (*viśeṣya*) for the word *śabdasya* (of the word). The phrase *ekāckasya* (of that which consists of a single vowel) connects with the word *jhaṣanta*. The word *padasya* (of a word), which is supplied as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*) from the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, is followed by the word *ante* (at the end) which is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "a constituent part of a verbal root," and so forth. Now, [an objection]:

Since it is improper to resort to a construction involving different grammatical substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) when a construction with a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, the logical connection is that "of a root ending in *jhaṣ* which consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), [the substitute] *baś* [is applied] to its part"; therefore, he says: "of a single-vowel [root]."

"From the root," and so forth. Regarding *gardabhayati*: by the rule "he does that, he describes that" (*tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*), there is the suffix *ṇic*; because it ends in *san* and so on, it is a verbal root (*dhātu*) according to the rule "those ending in *san* and so on [are roots]. From that, *kvip* is applied;
the meaning is that *kvip* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) after the causative (*ṇyanta*) form *gardabhi*. The *k* and *p* are elided (*itau*). There is the elision of the *ṇi*.

Regarding "ṇilopa" (the elision of *ṇi*): the remainder [of the rule] is "by the [sūtra] *ṇeraniṭi*" (Pāṇini 6.4.51). Regarding "gardhab": from the root *gardabhi*, the suffix *su* is added; there is the elision of the final consonant and the following vowel (*halṅyādi-lopa*). By the rule "ekāco vaśo bhaṣ" (Pāṇini 8.2.37), the dental *d* becomes the retroflex *dh*.
By the rule "vāvasāne" (Pāṇini 8.4.56), the *dh* optionally becomes *t*. This occurs in connection with the rule "ekāco dhātor jhaṣantasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.39).

Because the verbal root *gardabhi* has more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the substitution of *bhaṣ* for the letter *d* would not occur [according to Pāṇini 8.2.37]. However, the intended connection is "of that which ends in a *jhaṣ* sound and is a part of a verbal root" (*dhātvavayavasya jhaṣantasya*). In this case, since *dabh*—which ends in a *jhaṣ* sound and has only one vowel—is a part of a verbal root, the substitution of *bhaṣ* for its constituent *d* is unimpeded; such is the meaning. In this regard:

Earlier commentators maintained that the term *jhal* is carried over [from the previous rule]. He says this is incorrect: "The term *jhal* has ceased [to apply]. The reason is "due to semantic necessity" (*sāmarthyāt*). The sense is that if *jhal* were carried over, it would be redundant. One might object: "Let there simply be the carry-over of *jhal*; let the term *sdhvoh* not be employed at all. To this he replies:

He says: "by that. The meaning is: by not continuing [the application of] the rule *jhalī* (Pāṇini 8.2.26). Regarding *dugdham*: it is formed from the root *duh* with the suffix *kta*. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no guṇa substitution for the penultimate vowel. By the rule *dāderdhātorghaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.32), the *h* is replaced by *dh*. By the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the *t* is replaced by *dh*. By the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the *dh* is replaced by *g*. Thus, the form *dugdham* is established.

Regarding the form *dogdhe*: [the suffix] *tṛc* is added to the root *duh*; the *guṇa* substitution occurs because the penultimate vowel is light (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*). By the rule "of *dādi*" (*dāder dhātoḥ*), the *h* is changed to *gh*.

By the rule "after *jhaṣ*, *t* and *th* become *dh*" (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*), the *t* is changed to *dh*. By the rule "for *ṛt*, *uśanas*, etc. (*ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasām ca*), *anaṅ* is substituted. By the rule "also in the *sarvanāmasthāna*" (*sarvanāmasthāne ca*), the vowel is lengthened. Then, the elision of the final consonant and the following *i* occurs by the rule "elision after *hal*, *ṅ*, and *ī*" (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*); finally, the elision of the *n* occurs by the rule "the *n* is not elided" (*na lopo naḥ*).

Thus, with the elision of the letter *n*, the form *dogdhā* is obtained. The intention is that, since the term *jhal* is understood [from the previous rule], once *ghatva* has been applied in both these instances, *bhaṣ-bhāva* would also occur. Now, one might object: from the root *duh* ending in *kvip*, when *s* is elided, and *ghatva* is applied by the rule *dādeḥ*, we have *dugh*.

[The rule applies to] a single-vowel [stem] ending in a *jhaṣ*. Since such a form is a verbal root (*dhātu*), it lacks the status of being a part of a verbal root; therefore, one might ask how the letter *d* could undergo the change to *bhaṣ* (becoming *dh*) here. To this, he says: "by virtue of having the designation of that which possesses [the property]. A specific designation (*vyapadeśa*) is a primary usage (*mukhya-vyavahāra*); that which has this [designation] is [so called].
"Vyapadeśin" means that which possesses a designation; "vyapadeśivat" means being like that.
The sense is that the conventional usage of a root as having parts (dhātvavayava) is merely figurative (*gauṇa*) within the root itself, just as in expressions such as "the head of Rāhu.
This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ādyantavadekasmin*. [The examples] are *dhuk* and *dug*.

The sense is that because the designation *dhātu* (verbal root), which had already occurred prior to the *kvip* suffix, has not been lost, the substitution of *gh* by the rule *dāder-dhas-tathoḥ* is applied;
then, due to the word ending in a *jhaṣ* consonant, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs, followed by the optional substitution of *c* (or *k*) by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*. Thus: *duhau*, *duhaḥ*;
*duham*, *duhau*, *duhaḥ*; [the form] *duhā*; and when *bhyām* and the following cases occur, the substitution of *gh* by the rule *dāder-dhas-tathoḥ* is applied.

In *svādiṣu*, because it is a word (*pada*), the substitution of *bhaṣ* (the voiced unaspirated stop) occurs due to its being at the end of a word. Then, by the rule *ṭhjhalāṃ jaśo’nte*, the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stop) occurs. Thus: *dhugbhiḥ*. [Similarly: *duhe*, *dhugbhyām*, *dhugbhyaḥ*;
*duhaḥ*, *duhoḥ*, *duhām*. When *duh* is followed by *su*, the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) proceeds as follows:

He demonstrates this with the word "ṣatve" (in the state of being *ṣ*): when *ghatva* has been applied, and *bhaṣbhāva* has occurred, the letter *g* arises by virtue of the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39). Since the substitution of *c* by the rule "khari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55) is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the rule "ādeśapratyayayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.59) applies to produce *ṣ*, and then by the rule for *cartva*, the form "dhukṣu" is obtained.

The meaning is as follows: from the roots *druh* (in the sense of wishing to harm), *muh* (in the sense of bewilderment), *ṣṇuh* (in the sense of vomiting), and *ṣṇih* (in the sense of affection)—all of which end in the *kvip* suffix—the *su* case ending is elided. Consequently, for *druh*, since it belongs to the *adādi* class, the rule for changing *dh* to *ḍh* would apply; however, that is superseded by the rule for the constant change to *gh*. For the other roots, since they do not belong to the *adādi* class, the change to *gh* does not otherwise apply.
This [sūtra] is now commenced:

*vā druhamuhaṣṇuhaṣṇihām* (Pāṇini 7.2.33). Regarding *druhaḥ*: from the rule *dāderghaḥ*, the word *gha* is understood to carry over. [The conditions *jhalī* and *padasya* apply to the end of the word.]

The phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) continues [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of these" (*eṣām*). This means: of the four beginning with *druh*. *Dhruk*—*dhrug*. The intention is that in the alternative where there is *ghatva*, there is *bhaṣbhāva*, and then an option regarding *cartva*. *Dhruṭ*—*dhruḍ*. In the alternative where there is no *ghatva*, there is *ḍhatva* by the rule "ṭh-ḍhaḥ".

Regarding the optional substitution of *jhaṣ* (the *jhal* consonants except *ha*) for *gh*, in this context, for the sake of the *bhaṣ* substitution itself, the rule "ṭh-ḍhaḥ" prescribes only *ḍha*, and not *ḍa*.

If it were *ḍa*, there would be no *bhaṣ* substitution because the condition of ending in a *jhaṣ* sound would not be met. Examples include *durham* and so forth in the case of vowel endings (*aci*) and locative plurals (*supi*). In the form *dhrugbhyām*, the *bhaṣ* substitution occurs under the alternative where *gha* is substituted.

Regarding *dhruḍbhyām*: in the alternative view where there is no substitution of *gh*, the form arises through the substitution of *ḍ* and then *jaś*. Similarly, there are two forms for *bhisi* and *bhyasi*. [The forms] *druhaḥ*, *druhaḥ*, *druhoḥ*, *druhām*, and *dhrukṣu*:

when *gh* is substituted, *bhaṣ* is substituted [for *k*], then by the rule "ṣṭunā ṣṭu" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), *ṣ* replaces *ṭh* [of the suffix], and finally by "ṭhkhari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), *c* replaces *ṣ*.

Regarding "dhruṭsu": in the alternative where *ghatva* does not occur, there is *ḍhatva*; then, by *bhaṣbhāva*, *ḍha* becomes *dha*. When *dhuṭ* follows, *jaśtva* applies; then, by *cartva*, *ḍa* becomes *ta*. Because *cartva* is considered asiddha (non-existent) for the purposes of the preceding rule, the substitution of *tha* for *ta* by the rule "cayo dvitīyāḥ" does not take place. Furthermore, by the rule "ṭh na padāntāt," the substitution of *ṣṭu* does not occur. Thus, [the form is] "dhruṭsu."
The form [is derived] in the absence of *dhuṭ*. *Ha* becomes *ḍha*; there is the substitution of *bhaṣ*; *ḍha* becomes *ḍa* by *jaś*-ness;
that [ḍa] becomes *ṭa* by *car*-ness. "In this way" means: the phrase "with the exception of the *bhaṣ*-substitution" is to be understood as the remainder.
In the sense of "it carries the universe," the suffix *ṇvi* is applied after the root *vah*, following the rule *vahaśca* which continues from the rule *bhajo ṇvi*.
The letter *ṇ* is elided. There is elision of *r*. By the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ," there is vṛddhi [of the penultimate vowel]. This forms a *upapada-samāsa*.

The resulting form is *viśvavāh*. Then, after the elision of the nominative suffix *su* by the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal," the substitution of *ḍh* for *h* occurs by the rule "ho ḍhaḥ. Finally, by the rule "vā'sāne," there is an optional substitution of *c* (or *ṭ*) for *ḍh* at the end of a word—resulting in *viśvavāṭ*, *viśvāḍ*, or *viśvāhau*.
*viśvavāhaḥ*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.45: *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*)—*viśvavāham*, *viśvavāhau*. These forms in the nominative case (*suḍ-vibhakti*) are omitted here as they are easy to understand.

Intending to state the operation of *saṃprasāraṇa* when a vowel follows [the semivowels] beginning with *śas*, he demonstrates the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*: "In place of *ig* (a vowel), *yaṇ* (a semivowel). The meaning of "in place of" (*sthāne*) is obtained through interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). However, the rule "the genitive [case ending] is used in connection with 'in place of'" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) does not apply here, because a *paribhāṣā* is not operative in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). When the genitive is heard [in the sūtra], [it functions as a signifier].

Because the attainment of the correct meaning is possible everywhere through explanation alone, and because the *Bhāṣya* has established as its final conclusion that the rule "the sixth case [denotes] connection with the substitute" (P. 1.1.49) is intended to mean "substitutes take the place of that which is being pointed out," [it follows that the term *saṃprasāraṇa* refers to the technical name]. Consequently, [the rule] "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *vas*" (P. 6.4.131) [applies].

In rules such as "ṭhvacisvapiyajādīnām," when *saṃprasāraṇa* is heard, it occurs in place of a *yaṇ*. Therein, by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratama*), it should be understood that for *ya* there is *i*, for *va* there is *u*, for *ra* there is *ṛ*, and for *la* there is *lṛ*.

*vāha ūṭh* |6|4|132|. Regarding *vāha ūṭh*: the governing rule *bhasya* is in force. From the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, the term *saṃprasāraṇam* is carried over (*anuvartate*). That [term] connects with this *ūṭh*.
He says this with the words "of *bha*, etc.
[Pāṇini 6.4.129]. [The sūtra] "And after a *saṃprasāraṇa*" (6.1.108).
Regarding the term "*saṃprasāraṇa*": by that, it is understood that for the *yaṇ* vowel *va* which occurs in the word *vāh*, there is the substitution of *ūṭ*.
If the term *saṃprasāraṇam* were not carried over [from the previous rule], then by the rule *ṭhalo'ntyasya*, [the substitution] would apply to the letter *h*.
However, because that term is carried over, since *ūṭh* is the substitute for a semivowel (*yaṇ*), the rule *nālo'ntyasya* applies.
When the state *viśva ū āh asi* has been reached—[by the rule] *saṃprasāraṇācca*—[the rule] *iko...* [applies].

From the rule *yaṇ aci*, the word *aci* is understood [by anuvṛtti]; from the rule *ṭhami pūrvaḥ*, the word *pūrvaḥ* is understood; and the governing rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* is in force. He states this with the words beginning "from the *saṃprasāraṇa*," etc.
When *viśva ūha asi* is situated, having raised the doubt regarding *ād guṇaḥ*, he says: "by *ety-edhaty-ūṭhasu*."
By this [rule], there is the substitution of *guṇa* for the elided [augment]; "vṛddhi" is the remainder [of the rule]. Examples include: *viśvauhaḥ*, *viśvauhā*, and so forth. [Namely:
