*viśvavāḍbhyām*, *viśvavāḍbhiḥ*, *viśvavāḍbhyaḥ*;
*viśvauhe*, *viśvauhaḥ*, *viśvauhaḥ*; *viśvauhoḥ*, *viśvauhām*; *viśvavāṭsu*.

In the word *viśvavāṭsu*. Now, regarding the rule for the suffix *ṇvi* [Pāṇini 3.2.64], some maintain that the phrase "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) from the preceding rule "after *sah*, in the Veda" (*ṭhcchandasi sahaḥ*) is carried over. According to that view, one might ask how the word *viśvāh* is used in common worldly speech; to this he replies: "If the position is that *ṇvi* occurs only in the Veda, then [the form] is derived from the causative stem (*ṇijanta*) with the suffix *kvip*."

In the sense of "it carries the universe" (*viśvaṃ vāhayati*), from the causative root *vah* (with the suffix *ṇic*), by applying the rule *ṭhanyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*, the suffix *vic* is elided; then, by the rule *neḍvaśi kṛti*, the augment *iṭ* is absent, followed by the elision of the *ṇic* suffix and the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*).
Upon forming the compound with the subordinate member (*upapadasamāsa*), the word *viśvāh* is ready for usage. However, the substitution *ūṭh* does not apply to it.

[The suffix] *bhavati* [is applied], because by the rule "when a subsequent suffix [follows]," there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) for the elision of *ṇi*; consequently, that [derivative form] lacks the status of a *bha*-stem. However, in the case of the word *viśvavāh* derived from *vāhayati* with the suffix *kvip*, the addition of *uṭh* is indeed unobstructed, because by the rule "what is elided before *kvip*," there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of *ṇi*. Thus, for that [form]...

Because it is not subject to elision (*apāya*). For this very reason, in the rule *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparahṇābhyām*, the usage *praṣṭhauhī* in the popular analytical sentence (*laukikavigrahavākya*)—namely, *praṣṭhauhī āgatam praṣṭhavāṅrūpyam*—is consistent. In some manuscripts, it is stated that "the suffix *ṇvi* occurs only in the Vedic language."

The reading "prāmāṇikāḥ" (those who follow authoritative sources) is cited. Its intention is that this [term] must necessarily be carried over to the subsequent sūtra, "kavyapurīṣa," and so forth. In the sense of "one who carries a cart" (*anaḥ-ūḍha*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *vah* after the word *anas*, and by the rule "anaso ḍaśca," the *s* is replaced by *ḍ*. [This applies to roots] such as *vac*, *svap*, *yaj*, and others.
In the word *kitī*, due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group, there is the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *v* into *u*.
By the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied, resulting in the form *anaḍuh*. From that, the case endings (*sup*) arise.
*Catvāraḥ* [is formed] by adding *ām*, which is udātta, after *catur* and *anaḍuh*.

When *anaḍuh* is followed by *s*, [the rule] applies. Regarding *caturanaḍuhoḥ*: the meaning is "of these two," namely *catur* and *anaḍuh*. Regarding *sarvanāmasthāne*: [this refers to the rule] *ṭita āt sarvanāmasthāne*.
Thus, with "s" established, [the rule] *sāvanaḍuhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.82) applies.
Regarding *sāvanaḍuhaḥ*: the word *asya* means "of the word *anaḍuh*. [The result is that] *num* shall be inserted.

The intention is that *num* is understood from the rule "ṣṭhiv-ūc-chī-nad-yo-nuṃ-m" (Pāṇini 7.1.59). In *num*, the letter *m* is the *it* (indicatory), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is marked with *m* (mit), it is placed after the final vowel. Thus, the form stands as *anaḍvān h s*.
Now, one might object: these two, *ām* and *num*, because they are marked with *m*, should both follow the final vowel, which is the letter *u*.

Regarding the attainment [of the case endings]: therein, the *ām* prescribed by the rule "caturanaḍuhoḥ" is a general rule occasioned by a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending. However, the *num* prescribed by the rule "sāvanaḍuhaḥ" is a specific rule, as it is enjoined specifically for the *sarvanāmasthāna* ending *su*. And that...

Because it leaves no room for application, it would sublate the general rule prescribing *āma*, since that [general rule] has its purpose fulfilled elsewhere. Consequently, one would have *anaḍuḥ* and not *anaḍvān*. Furthermore, in the vocative case, when *he anaḍuh* is established...

Regarding the rule *ṭhaṃ sambuddhau* (Pāṇini 7.3.106), the augment *ām* will be stated immediately below as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ām*. In that context, the augment *num*—by the rule *sāvanaḍuhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.82)—is also applicable; however, because it is prescribed both for the vocative (*sambuddhi*) and for non-vocative cases, it is a general (*sāmānya*) prescription. The rule *ṭhaṃ sambuddhau*, on the other hand, applies only to the vocative.

Because it is specifically prescribed, it is a special rule (*viśe�ṣavidhi*). And since it is without scope [otherwise], it would sublate the general *num* augment; for the prescription of *num* after the nominative singular suffix *su* has its purpose fulfilled except in the vocative. Consequently, the form *he anaḍvan* would not occur. Instead, by the rule "ḍha replaces ṭha," the form would be *he anaḍvaṭ*.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the governing context of *āditya*," and so forth, ending with "the *num* is not barred.

Regarding the prescription of *num* in the rule *sāvanaḍuhaḥ*, the word *āt* (from the rule *ācchīnadyoḥ*) is understood as a fifth-case form (*pañcamyanta*). Therefore, *num* follows after the vowel *a* of *anaḍuh*.

Even by a rule specifically prescribed for a particular case, such as the *num* augment in "sāvanaḍuhaḥ," the *ām* prescribed by the general rule "caturanaḍuhoḥ" is not superseded; this is because, with respect to the *num* which is enjoined after a vowel (*avarṇa*),
the *ām* is that upon which it depends (*upajīvya*).

Because there is no contradiction between the dependent (*upajīvya*) and the dependent-upon (*upajīvaka*), there is an absence of the relationship of the sublated (*bādhya*) and the sublater (*bādhaka*); on the contrary, since the application of *num* is impossible in the absence of *ām*. Likewise, because *ām* [is prescribed] by the rule "ṭāṅasiṅsām" in the vocative singular, there is an absence of the relationship of the sublated and the sublater due to their being specific rules; on the contrary, in the absence of *ām*...

The meaning is that there is no possibility of its application. Now, one might object: "Granted that *ād* continues to apply in the rule for the insertion of *num*—namely, *sāvanaḍuhaḥ*—nevertheless, *num* does not obtain the status of being dependent on *ām*, because even though the *n* and *a* of *num* follow [the final vowel] in *anaḍuh*, they do not follow *ām*."

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of "after *āt*," do not say so—for in the rule prescribing the augment *num* in the case of *anaḍuh*, the word *mit* being present, the phrase "after the final vowel" (*antyādacaḥ*) is supplied. And in that context, the continued application of "after *āt*" connects [with it]. Consequently, that which is the final form *a* in *anaḍuh*—
Therefore, *num* is obtained after what follows [the vowel], whereas the *ā* of *nakārāka* (the *ā* of *nā*) is not of such a nature;

thus, the dependence of *num* upon *ām* is entirely unassailable. In the same way, its dependence upon *am* in the vocative case (*saṃbuddhi*) should also be understood. In some manuscripts, it is stated that *num* does not occur after *ām*.

The reading "bādhyate" (is sublated) is found there; the interpretation is as follows: [An objection is raised]—"In the case of *bahvanaḍvāṃhi kulāni*, since the suffix *ām* is subsequent to the *num* prescribed by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the *ām* should occur first. However, once *ām* has been applied, *num* does not occur again; for that which is sublated by a *vipratiṣedha* (conflict of rules)..."
Because of the maxim "that which has been sublated is indeed [considered] sublated," he says: "And *ām* is not sublated by *num*.

According to the principle that "it is established through the recognition of recurrence," since there is a re-emergence of what was previously sublated by a prohibition in certain cases, even when *ām* is applied, *num*—by the rule "for neuter nouns ending in consonants or *ac*"—remains unsublated.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the rule "sorlopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.68), in the case of *anaḍvān* followed by *h*, the elision of the *s* occurs according to the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal" (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

Now, one might object: once the *s* is elided, the *h* would undergo elision as a final member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*), and since the *n* of the *num* augment would then be at the end of a word (*padānta*), the substitution of *d* for the *h* would apply according to the rule "vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.72).

To the question "Why should it not be so?", he says: "Because of the rule for *num*. For if, in this case, the *n* of *num* were to undergo the substitution of *d*, then even in the absence of *num* in the form *anaḍvāh*, the form *anaḍvād* would be established simply by the substitution of *d* for *h*;
consequently, the prescription of *num* would be purposeless. Therefore, the *n* of *num* does not undergo the substitution of *d*.
The meaning is that it is understood.
[Regarding the rule] *aṃ-saṃbuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.99):
Now, in the case of *anaḍvān* + *hi*, once the elision of the nominative suffix (*su*) and the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) have been performed...

Since the letter *n* is at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and also at the end of a word (*pada*), why would the elision of *n* not occur by the rule "there is no elision of a *n* that is at the end of a nominal stem" (*na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*)?

Nor should it be argued that the elision of *n* does not occur here due to the force of the rule prescribing the augment *num*, for [the same logic would apply] in cases where the elision of *n* is otherwise absent.

Since the rule for *nug* in the case of *anaḍvān* (in the form *anaḍvān*) has its purpose fulfilled by the prohibition of *nalopa* through the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*, [the author] says "samayogānta" [to address this];
for if the elision of *hakāra* were considered *asiddha*, then [the *nuk* would not apply].

The meaning is that there is no elision of *n* because it does not occur at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) nor at the end of a word (*pada*). Regarding *anaḍvān*: when *anuḍuh* stands with the suffix *si*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ*, the addition of *num*, the elision of the case-ending *s*, and the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Now, in the vocative singular, when *he anaḍuh* stands with the suffix *si*...

When the augment *ām* is about to be applied by the rule *caturanaḍuhoḥ*, [the condition] "except in the vocative" (*asaṃbuddhau*) applies. The phrase *caturanaḍuhoḥ* is understood [from the previous sūtra]. Thus he says: "of *catur* and *anaḍuh*. The *m* of *am* is *it*.
Because it is *mit*, it is placed after the final vowel. [Thus we have] *he anaḍvan*. [The derivation is: *am*, *yaṇ* [substitution], *num*.
There is elision of the *su* [suffix], and also elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Thus, *anaḍvāhau*.

Because it is a *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending], the augment *ām* is applied; however, the nasal augment *num* does not apply, because that is prescribed only after [the word] *sā* (the nominative singular). In *anaḍuhaḥ*, the meaning is that the word *anaḍuh* remains entirely unchanged before vowel-beginning case endings starting with the accusative plural (*śas*).

*Vasu*, *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *anaḍuh* take *r* [in place of the final *s*] before endings beginning with *bhyām* and so forth that start with a consonant (*hal*). The author states a specific rule regarding those beginning with *bhyām* and so forth: *vasusraṃsu*. *Vasu* is a suffix; by this, words ending in it are understood. *Sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* are verbal roots meaning "to fall down" (*avasraṃsane*). [This is derived] from the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*.
The word *saḥ* here has its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhī*), and it is understood (*anuvṛtta*) from the previous rule. By this, *vasu* is qualified.

This is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in [the specified element] (*tadanta-vidhi*). The state of ending in *s* (*sāntatva*) is not a qualifier for *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu*, because there is no deviation [from the rule's application to them]. Nor is it a qualifier for *anaḍuh*, because it is impossible [for *anaḍuh* to end in *s*]. The term *pada* (word), which is the governing topic (*adhikṛta*), is here to be understood in the plural.
It undergoes modification. By the rule *alo’ntyasya*, it applies to that which ends in [the letter specified].

He states the result with the words beginning with *sānta*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) and *ḍhatva* (the substitution of *ḍh*), as applicable. As for *anaḍudbhyām*, the intention is that it is a word (*pada*) because of the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*.

"Thus, etc. [The forms are: *anaḍudbhiḥ*, *anaḍudbhyaḥ* (dual), *anaḍuhe*, *anaḍuhaḥ*, *anaḍuhaḥ*, *anaḍuhoḥ*, *anaḍuhām*. After the substitution of *d* for *t* (*datva*), the change to *c* occurs by the rule "ṭhkhari ca" (*anaḍutsu*).
[Question: Why is it specified that [the word] must end in *s* (*sānta*)? [Answer: Because even the word *vasu* invariably ends in *s*, this question is raised.
Regarding the word *vidvān*: when *vidvas* is established, the vowel lengthening (*dīrgha*) occurs by the rule *ṭhaṭavasantasya*;
then, by the rule *ugidacām*, the *num* augment is added; after the elision of the case-ending *su* and the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the form is obtained.
The point here is that because the suffix *vasu* does not end in the letter *s* [in this stage], the substitution of *d* for *s* does not take place.

*srastam* and *dhvastam*: these end in the *kta* suffix. Here, because they do not occur at the end of a word (*padānta*), the substitution of *da* does not take place. Examples such as *vidvāṃsau* and *anaḍvāhau* should be cited as counter-examples for this rule.
Pāṇini 8.3.56: *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*. [The substitute *s* is applied in place of the initial *s* of the root *sah* when it follows a prefix ending in *ṣ*.]

From the word *turāsāh* followed by the nominative suffix *su*, after the elision of *hr-sv-ādi* (the case-ending), once the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha* has been made, he states a specific rule: *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*. According to the rule "The suffixes *ik* and *śtip* are used to indicate a verbal root," the suffix *ik* is added to the root *ṣaha* (meaning "to endure"), and by the rule "The initial *ṣ* of a root becomes *s*," the *ṣ* is changed to *s*.

The word *sahi* refers to the verbal root *ṣah*. It is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form *sāḍ*, which has undergone the changes of *ḍhatva*, *ḍatva*, and *vṛddhi*. Thus he says: "after *sāḍ*. Regarding the term "cerebral" (*mūrdhanya*): the meaning is that this falls under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "a cerebral [substitute] occurs for [a dental] not at the end of a word. In the head (*mūrdhan*).

*Bhava*—the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*). This means it has the *mūrdhan* (roof of the palate) as its place of articulation. Regarding *turāṣaṭ* and *turāṣāṭ*: when the suffix *su* is elided, the *ḍha* substitution occurs; then, by the rule for *jaś*-ness, the *ḍha* becomes *ḍa*, and the *s* is replaced by the retroflex *ṣ* because of the similarity in their open (*vivṛta*) effort. Even in the alternative case where the *ca*-substitution applies according to the rule "or [there is] *c* at the end of a word" (*ṭhvā vāsāne*), the retroflex [ṣ] occurs.
It indeed occurs; the point is that in the Sūtra, the mention of *ṣāḍa*—which represents the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*)—is intended as an indicator for word-final positions.

As in *turāsāhau*: the point is that because this is not at the end of a word, the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution does not take place. "And so forth" refers to forms such as *turāṣāḍbhiḥ* and *turāṣāḍbhyaḥ*.

*turāsāhe*, *turāsāhaḥ*, *turāsāhaḥ*, *turāsāhoḥ*, *turāṣāṭsu* (or *turāṣāṭtsu*). Now, he derives the word *turāṣāṭ*: in the sense of "one who endures (*sahate*) speed (*turaṃ*)" [the suffix] *kvin* is applied after the root *saha* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

The meaning of that [sūtra] is that the suffix *ṇvi* occurs after the root *sah* when a verbal noun (*karmopapada*) follows, in the Vedic language (*chandas*). The letter *ṇ* is indicatory (*it*), there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel, and the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛktalopa*). Now, since the suffix *ṇvi* pertains specifically to the Vedic domain, one might ask how the word *turāsāh* can be used in common worldly speech; to this he says: "But in the world... (*loke tu*).

The sense is that when the causative suffix *ṇic* is elided after the root *sah*, and the single-consonant suffix *kvip* is subsequently elided, the form is fit for usage in the world (*loka*). Now, one might object: since the rule "in the presence of *kvi*, after *nahi*, *vṛti*, *vṛṣi*, *vyadhi*, *srāvi*, *sāhi*, and *tani*" prescribes lengthening of the preceding vowel only when *kvi* follows *sāh*, how can this [lengthening] occur here?
To address this, he says: "of others as well. What is the purpose of including *saha*?

It refers to words such as *saḍa*, *umṛḍa*, and so forth, which are accompanied by the letter *ḍa*. One whose name contains such a word is also called *saḍa* by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). His offspring is [denoted by] *sāḍiḥ*. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied after a vowel [by Pāṇini 4.1.95]. Then, by the rule "when *yasya* follows," there is the elision of the final vowel [by Pāṇini 6.4.148].

The initial *vṛddhi* [is applied]. The form is *sāḍi*. It is established in the Bhāṣya that there is no retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) substitution here. Thus end the words ending in *h*. Now, those ending in *v*. The word *div* is feminine. As Amara states: "The two words *dyo* and *div* are feminine; [synonyms for sky are] *abhra*, *vyoman*, and *puṣkara*. [In the compound] *su-dyauḥ*, it means "one whose heaven is beautiful."
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *puṃs*, when the form *sudivaḥ* is established, [the rule] applies:
*diva āṬt* | Pāṇini 7.1.84. Regarding *diva āṬt*: from the rule *sāvanaḍuhaḥ*, the word *sau* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). The word *diva* [is the base].

The word ending in the sixth case [divaḥ] refers to the nominal stem (prātipadika) derived from the Uṇādi rule "diver ṅiviḥ" or as an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) stem; it does not refer to the verbal root "divu krīḍādau," according to the maxim: "When there is a mention of a base without an indicatory letter (anubandha), it does not include one with an indicatory letter. Thus he says: "of the nominal stem 'div'."

The letter *t* in *āṬt* is for the purpose of pronunciation; however, the letter *t* is not heard in the actual substitute (*āṬ*). Thus, there is no status as a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) based on having multiple letters (*anekāl*). Furthermore, the designation *itsaṃjñā* does not apply to the *t*, because there would be no result [of such a designation]. Nor is there any possibility here for the circumflex accent (*svarita*) prescribed for what ends in *ti*.

This is because of the Vārttika rule: *ṣṭhittipratyayagrahaṇam*. Now, one might object that in the case of *sudiv* (from *su-div*), when the *vakāra* (*v*) undergoes *autva* [becoming *au*] and the *ikāra* (*i*) undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution [becoming *u*], the *ākāra* (*ā*) would—by virtue of being *sthānivadbhūta*—be considered a consonant (*hal*), and thus the *su* would be elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. To this, he replies: "Because it is not an operation dependent on an *al*" (*alvidhitvena*).

The point is that the elision of *su* (sulopa), which operates by depending on the status of being followed by a consonant (*hal*) consisting of the letter *v*—which is the substituendum (*sthānin*) for the substitute *āṭ*—is not subject to the rule of *al-vidhi* (i.e., it does not depend on an *al* sound).

Thus, in the form *sudyauḥ*, because it is a stem (*aṅga*), the substitution of *au* occurs even for that which ends in it, followed by *yaṇ*. Then, the substitution of *ru* and the visarga (*visarga*) follow. In the case of *sudivau*, [the same process applies].
The meaning is that in the *ajādi* (feminine suffixes beginning with vowels) group, the word *sudiv* remains entirely unchanged.

Regarding the rule *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), which prescribes a specific modification before the *bhyām* and subsequent endings when a consonant follows, it states: "the final [letter] is replaced by *u*. This refers to an *antādeśa* (substitution of the final phoneme).

This is obtainable from the rule *alo'ntyasya*. The meaning is that the phrase *padāntāt*, which has been carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from a previous rule, is transformed into the locative case as *padānte*. As for the fact that the *u* is followed by *t* (*taparatva*), it is for the purpose of indicating that "an *u* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*)," as stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *titsvaritam*.

This is clear. Regarding the form *sudyaubhyām*: when the vowel *u* is substituted for *va*, the *i* undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution. In this case, the long vowel is not applied by the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), because it cannot be determined that the *u* in place of *va* is a *saṃprasāraṇa*; for the term *saṃprasāraṇa* refers only to that which is specifically prescribed by that technical name.

This is clear in the *Śabdenduśekhara* on the rule *igyaṇaḥ*, [which states]: "Because that which occupies the place of an *ik* vowel is a *saṃprasāraṇa*. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): *sudive*, *sudyobhyaḥ*, *sudivaḥ*, *sudivoḥ*, *sudivām*, *sudyauṣu*. These are the words ending in *-v*. Now, those ending in *-r*.

The word *catur* is derived in the *Uṇādi* list as being always plural; thus, *catvāraḥ* is the form in the *jas* case. By the rule *caturanaḍuhoḥ*, the suffix *ām* is added after the vowel *u*; the intention is that the *u* undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution [resulting in *o*]. Thus, *caturaḥ* is the form in the *śas* case and those following.

Because it lacks the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna*, it is not called a "name" (*nāman*). When the form *caturaḥ* stands [as a base], since it does not end in a short vowel, the augment *nuṭ* would not apply; therefore, [the rule] is stated:
*ṣaṭcaturbhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.55).

*ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca*. The term *ṣaṭcaturbhyaḥ* is in the ablative case. From the rule *ṭhāmi sarvanāmnaḥ*, the word *ām* is understood and is changed here to the genitive case. By *ṣaṭ*, that which bears the technical designation *ṣaṭ* is understood, and not the word *ṣaṭ* itself, according to the maxim *kṛtrimākṛtrimayoḥ kṛtrime kāryasaṃpratyayaḥ*. Thus he says:
By the rule beginning with *ṣaṭsaṃjñakebhyaḥ* and so forth: when the augment *nuṭ* is applied, the letter *ṭ* is the indicatory (*it*) letter; the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation.

Because it is marked with *ṭ*, it becomes the initial constituent [of the augment]. Regarding "the substitution of *ṇ*" (*ṇatvam*): the remainder of the rule is "by the sūtra *ṭhraṣābhyām*. Regarding "doubling" (*dvitvam*): the remainder of the rule is "of the letter *ṇ* by the sūtra *aco rahābhyām*."

Since the state of being double (dvitva) is not yet established, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs first, and subsequently the doubling of that *ṇ*. Nor should one fear the prohibition stated in the rule "pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane" (that which is considered asiddha [unestablished] regarding what precedes it does not apply when doubling is to be performed), for the meaning of that rule is that when doubling is to be performed, nothing else is considered asiddha; it does not mean that the state of being double itself is not asiddha.

The meaning of "for that purpose" (*tadarthe*) is that doubling occurs immediately after the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. When *catur-su* is established, the substitution of a visarga (*visarjanīya*) for the *r* would apply;
however, [this is prevented by the following rule]: *roḥ supi* (Pāṇini 8.3.16).
In the rule *roḥ supi*, because the term *khari* is understood from the previous context, *sup* here refers specifically to the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*).
Since the desired result is already established by the rule *khar-avasānayor visarjanīyaḥ*, this present rule is for the purpose of restriction;
thus he says: "only after *r*. However, a reverse restriction (that *r* occurs only before *sup*) is not intended, as [the rule] *halo 'nantarāḥ...* [would otherwise be contradicted].

This is because of the mention [in the sūtra] "saṃyoga. Regarding "ṣatvam" (the substitution of ṣ): the remainder [of the rule] is "by means of [Pāṇini 8.3.59] *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. The intention is that because the letter *r* is an *iṇ*-letter, [the following *s*] comes after it.
Regarding "the doubling of the *ṣ*": the remainder [of the rule] is "by means of [Pāṇini 8.4.46] *aco rahābhyām*."

*Śaro'ci* | (Pāṇini 8.4.49). From the rule *aco rahābhyām*, the word *dve* (twice) is carried over, and from the rule *nādinyākrośe*, the word *na* (not) is carried over. Thus he says: "when a vowel (*aci*) follows," and so forth. And so it is.

The form *caturṣu* consists of exactly one *ṣakāra*. One should not argue that this [doubling] is redundant because the desired form could be established simply through the elision (*lopa*) of the second *ṣakāra* by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe*, even though there is indeed a doubling;
for the intention is that such elision is optional. [The example] *priyāścatvāro yasya* means "one who has four beloveds."
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *priyacatur* is dependent on the gender of the object qualified (*viśeṣyanighna*) and takes the endings of the singular, dual, and plural.

He states its form in the nominative singular (*sau*): *priyacatvāḥ*. When the form *priyacatur s* remains, the suffix *ām* is added by the rule "after *catur* and *anaḍuh*" (*caturanaḍuhoḥ*). Since this [suffix] is part of the stem (*aṅga*), it applies even when [the stem] ends in that [suffix].

Because of the application [of the rule]. Therefore, there is *yaṇ* substitution for the vowel *u*; the intention is that the elision [of the final *r*] occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*.

"O *priyacatva*"—the intention is that this is due to the rule *ṭham saṃbuddhau*. "*Priyacatvārau*"—because the suffix *su* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, there is the augment *ām*. "*Priyacatvāraḥ*". "*Priyacatvāram*," [etc.]

The two forms *priyacatvār-au* [are derived as follows]. Before suffixes beginning with *śas* and so on, there is no substitution of *ām*. Thus: *priyacaturaḥ*, *priyacaturā*, *priyacaturbhyām*, *priyacaturbhiḥ*;

*priyacature*, *priyacaturaḥ* (dual), *priyacaturauḥ*. Fearing that the augment *ṭh-ṇuṭ* might apply by the rule "after words ending in six or four," he says: "when [the word] is secondary (*gauṇatve*)."

Regarding "tviti": the intention is that, because of the plural mention in the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca*, the augment *nuṭ* occurs only when the meaning of those [words] is predominant. Thus: *priyacaturi*, *priyacaturṣu*, and *paramacaturṇām*.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the intention is that because it is a stem (*aṅga*), the *nuṭ* is applied even after a form ending in that [word]. These are the words ending in *r*.
Now, those ending in the letter *l*. Regarding "kamalam": *kamala* means a lotus; *kamalā* means Lakṣmī.

In the sense of "he teaches *kamala*" (using the word *kamala*), or in the sense of "he teaches *kamalā*" (using the word *kamalā*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*, and then [the resulting verbal root] is treated as one ending in *san* etc., according to the rule *sanādyantāḥ*.

Because it is a *dhātu*, when the *sup* suffix is elided (*luk*), the prātipadika ending in *iṣṭhan* undergoes the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* (treatment like the superlative suffix); thus, after the elision of the *i* (*tilopa*), from the form *kamavi*, the *kvip* suffix is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), followed by the elision of the *ṇi* suffix according to the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, and finally the elision of the single-consonant suffix (*apṛktalopa*), resulting in the form *kamal*. From that [form]:

When the suffixes beginning with *ṣaṣ* (six) and *daśan* (ten) are elided, the form is *kamal*. Thus, *kamalau*. The sense is that in the case of *āṬ*, *jas*, and so forth, there is no modification whatsoever. [The forms are: *kamalam*, *kamalau*, *kamalaḥ*; *kamalā*, *kamalbhyām*, *kamalbhiḥ*;
[locative singular] *kamale*; [ablative plural] *kamalbhyah*; [genitive singular] *kamalaḥ*; [nominative dual] *kamaloḥ*.

Regarding the word *kamalām*, he states a specific rule for the locative case (*supi*): "there is *ṣatva* [the substitution of *ṣ*] in *kamalṣu*. The underlying intention is that the letter *l* possesses the property of being an *iṇ*-vowel. However, there are no words ending in *y* such as *toyi* (meaning "water") and so forth; for if one were to derive it with the suffix *kvip*, the elision of *y* by the rule "the elision of *y* and *v*" (*lopo vyoḥ*) would be unavoidable.
However, the status of *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply to the elision (*lopa*) of *ṇ*, because that is prohibited in the case of the elision of *y*.

In fact, Haradatta maintains that such cases are simply not expressed (*anabhidhāna*), based on the Bhāṣya on the *laṇ* sūtra which states: "There are no consonants at the end of a word that are *yaṇ*s."
Regarding the rule *ṭhbho-bhago-*, the *bhāṣya* statement *vṛkṣav karoti* is the assertion of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*);
such is its intention—enough of this. Thus end [the consonants] ending in *l*.
Pāṇini 8.2.64: *mo no dhātoḥ* (The *m* of a verbal root is replaced by *n*).

Now, those ending in *m*. Now, from the root *śam* preceded by *pra*, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the lengthening occurs by the rule "the long vowel replaces the nasal of a base before *k* or *jhal* suffixes beginning with *k* or *ṅ*" (*ṭhanunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti*), the word *praśām* is formed;

this expresses a specific [meaning]. [The rule] "a final *m* becomes *n* in a verbal root" (*mo no dhātoḥ*) applies: here, "of *m*" (*maḥ*) is in the genitive case, and it refers to the word "verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*).

This is a qualifier; therefore, by the rule of "at the end of that" (*tadanta-vidhi*), the term *pada* is understood as the governing heading (*adhikṛta*) from the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, and the word *ante* ("at the end") is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "of that which ends in m," and so forth. By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, the [substitution] applies to the final letter, which is the *m*. In that case—

When the elision of *ṣoḍaṅ* and so forth has occurred, one might suspect the elision of the *n* by the rule "there is no elision of a *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*), because it is both the final sound of a nominal stem (*prātipadikānta*) and the final sound of a word (*padānta*). Anticipating this, he says: "of the state of being *n*" (*natvasya*). [The form] is *praśān*. Even though it is listed among the words beginning with *svar* (in the *gaṇapāṭha*), its...

It does not have the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because it denotes a substance (*sattvavācitvāt*). The point is that if it were to denote a non-substance (*asattvavācitve*), it would indeed be an indeclinable due to its inclusion in the *svar-ādi* group. Regarding the form *praśānbhyām*:

the point is that the substitution of *n* for *t* occurs because the preceding element is a word (*pada*) by virtue of the rule *bhyām-ādiṣu hali* [Pāṇini 1.4.18], which states that the elements beginning with *bhyām* are words when they follow a stem ending in *su*, etc., provided they are not in the case of a nominal suffix (*asarvanāmasthāna*).
"and so forth" means: *praśānbhiḥ*, *praśāme*, *praśānbhyaḥ*, *praśāmaḥ*, *praśāmaḥ*, *praśāmoḥ*, *praśāmām*, *praśāmi*, *praśāntsu* / *praśānsu*.
Regarding the form *praśāntsu*, there is an optional substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule *naśca*. Now, [the word] is derived from the root *kāyati* with the suffix *ṅimic*.
Does the word *kim* function as an interrogative?
[The rule] *kimaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.103) applies.
He states its specific detail: *kimaḥ kaḥ*. [This applies] "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*). [This refers to the rule] *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.1.21).

The intention is that [the rule] follows from that very [context]. Now, one might object: let the sūtra simply be "imaḥ," since by the continued application (anuvṛtti) of "tyadādīnām," the meaning would be obtained as "the letter *a* shall replace the *i* of *tyad* and so on. However, the phrase "of those ending with *dvi*" is not connected [to this].

Since these [suffixes] are impossible in the case of *tyad* and other pronouns ending in *-dv*, and likewise, when the vowel *a* replaces *ṭhim* in the word *kim*, the form *ṭhka* is established as ending in *a*. Nor would the rule *ṭhalo'ntyasya* cause the vowel *a* to replace only the final *m* of *kim*; consequently—

It might be argued that when *yaṇ* follows *ik*, the form should be *kya*; however, since the rule "the substitution of the final letter does not apply when [the substitute] is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ*) prevents the operation of the *alontya-paribhāṣā*, the entire *imaḥ* would be replaced by *a*, thereby establishing the form *ka*. To this, he says: "of that which is accompanied by *akac*."

In the rule prescribing the substitution of *im* for the words beginning with *tyad*, namely *avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ*, when *akac* is applied to the word *kim*, resulting in *kakim*, and then *im* is substituted, the form would become *kaka*. However, if the rule *kimaḥ kaḥ* is stated, then even for the word *kim* accompanied by *akac*, [the substitution applies].

The meaning is that, by the maxim "that which falls in the middle of [a rule] is included by the mention of that [rule]," because it is the word *kim*, when the substitution of *ka* occurs, the form *ka* alone is established.

Here, having carried over the term *tyadādīnām* (of *tyad* and so forth) and modifying the number [to the singular], [the rule is interpreted as]: "for *kim* belonging to the *tyad*-class, there is *ka*."
This must be explained: because it is a grammatical operation belonging to the *sarvādi* group, the substitution of *kā* does not occur when [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

Thus, he states "kaḥ, kāu," etc., meaning that once the case endings have been produced and the substitution of *kā* has taken place, the forms are like those of the word *sarva*. "In the masculine, *kaḥ* refers to the wind, the creator (Brahmā), and the sun; *kam* refers to the head and water."
Thus says Amara. In that context, because the word *ka* lacks the form *kiṃ*, it does not possess the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

However, regarding the creator (Brahmā), the word *kiṃ* also exists; whether that [form] possesses the status of a pronoun or not is established as two alternative views in the Bhāṣya on the rule *kasyet*. [This is illustrated by the example: "What is this oblation? (*kāyaṃ haviḥ*), if [the word] is derived from *kim*.

Whether it be a substitution of a portion (*kādeśa*) or a different word (*śabdāntara*), in either case, the form should be "kasmā anubrūhi. For everything is designated as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and Prajāpati is everything;
and Prajāpati is "ka. Another says: in either case, it is simply "kāyānubrūhi"; this is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the term *tatrabhavataḥ*:
[the rule] *idamo maḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.108) applies.
Now, he states a specific rule for the word *idaṃ*: *idamo maḥ*. [The word] *sau* [is understood from the context]; [this refers to the rule] *tadoḥ saḥ sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.106).
The meaning is that [the substitute] follows from that [preceding rule]. By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, the final *m* is replaced by *m*.

Now, one might object that the prescription of *m* for *m* is redundant; therefore, he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *at* for *tyad*-class words. *ido'y puṃsi* (Pāṇini 7.2.111).

When [the rule] *ṭhidam s* is established—[it means] "of *id*, in the masculine. The term *ṭhidam* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). The word *ṭhidam* is carried over [from a previous rule]. This is a genitive of constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). From the rule *tyaḥ sau*, the word *sau* is carried over. Therefore, it says *idamaḥ*. The meaning is: of that *id* which is a constituent part of the word *idam*. [The result is] *ayam s*.
This being the case, [the rule] "there is elision of *s*" (*sorlopa*) applies; the remainder [of the rule] is "by *halṅyādi*. As for "this":

although one might expect an *anusvāra* for the *m* by resorting to the principle of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) once the *su* has been elided, it does not occur because of the specific injunction of the letter *m*. Otherwise, [the author] would have prescribed the *anusvāra* itself.

Furthermore, there is a prohibition based on the rule: "The characteristic of a suffix does not apply when [the suffix] depends on a letter of the *ṭh* class. Now, he states the specific rule regarding *āṬ*, *jas*, and so on—namely, "the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and the rest.

This means that when *idam* and *āṬ* are in the state [of being combined], the *m* of *tyadādi* is replaced by *a*. Regarding "the substitution of the subsequent form" (*pararūpatva*): [it occurs when] *ida* and *āṬ* [are combined].
This being the case, by the rule *ato guṇe*, the two *a* sounds become a single substitute form, namely the sound *a*.
Thus, we have *ida-aU*. At this point, the rule *daśca* [Pāṇini 7.2.109] applies.
"And *da*. The phrase "of *idam*, *ma*" (*idamo maḥ*) is understood to follow.

"*Da*" is in the genitive case; thus, it means "of the *da* of *idam*. Although the word "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) is very remote from the rule "ā is substituted for *aṣṭan* in a case-ending" (*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*), it is understood here by means of *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap). [The word "in a case-ending"] is also understood from the rule "for *tad* and *doḥ*, *sa* is substituted before *su*" (*tadoḥ saḥ sau*).

However, the word *sau* does not carry over [from the previous rule] even though it is proximate, because there is no *d*-substitution for *idam* when followed by *su*, and because of the explicit mention of *sau* in the subsequent rule, "ṭhyas sau. This is what he states with the words beginning "idamo dasya" and so on.
Thus, when *ima-au* is established, he says "imau" and so forth, noting that the forms are like those of *rāma*.

"There is no vocative case for words beginning with *tyad*," because the sense is that such usage is not commonly observed. An objection is raised: "If this were so, it would contradict the Bhāṣya statement 'he sa' in the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*"; to this he replies: "The term *utsarga* means 'general rule' (i.e., it is mostly applicable)."
*anāpyakaḥ* | 7|2|112 | He states a specific rule regarding vowels beginning with *ṭa*: *anāpyakaḥ*. The division [of the compound] is *an*, *āpi*, *aka*.
That which does not have *k* is *ak*; of that—*akaḥ*. The meaning is "of that which is devoid of the letter *k*. [This applies to the word] *idam*.
From the rule *maḥ*, the term *idam* is carried over; from the rule *ido 'py puṃsi*, the term *id* is carried over;
and from the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the term *vibhaktau* is carried over. Thus he says: "of that which does not have the letter *ka*" and so forth.
By the word *āpi*, he indicates that the inclusion of *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp* is not intended, as he says: "by *ā*" and so forth. [The suffix] *ṭā*.

The meaning is "beginning with this form. The intention is that because of the force of the word *vibhaktau* (in a case-ending) being carried over [from a previous rule], there is no inclusion of *ṭāp* and the other suffixes. Regarding the phrase *anenā*: when *idam* and *ā* are situated together, the substitution of *ya* for the *tyadādi* group occurs, followed by the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpatva*). Then, *id* is replaced by *ana*. When *ana* and *ā* are situated together, the substitution of *ina* occurs, and then the *guṇa* [substitution].
The meaning [of the sūtra] is as follows: *hali lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.68.

When the substitution of *t* for *tyad*-type stems has been applied and the subsequent monophthongization (*pararūpa*) has occurred, the rule *ṭhAnāpyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.94) would otherwise apply; however, it is superseded by the rule *hali*.
*Lopaḥ* (elision) is understood from the preceding rule *ṭhāpyaka*. From *ṭhidaṃmo maḥ*, the term *ṭhidaṃ* is carried over;

from *ṭhido'y puṃsī*, the term *ṭhida*; and from *ṭhaṣṭanaḥ*, the phrase *vibhaktau* (in a case-ending) is also carried over. The term *halī* (before a consonant) is a qualifier for the case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is a rule of initial application (*tadādividhiḥ*).

He says this with the words beginning "of that which does not have *ka* as its initial," etc. Fearing the elision of the *da* of *id-* by means of the maxim "the final [element] of an *al*," he says: "not when it is meaningless" (*nānarthake*). This maxim is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra defining the technical term *upadhā*. Since the portion *id-* within the word *idam-* is meaningless, the designation "ending in that" (*tadantya*) is not obtained for it.

Consequently, the intention is that there is the elision of the entire [root] *id*. If the phrase "not a modification of the reduplicated syllable" (*anabhyāsavikāra*) were not stated, then in forms such as *vibharti*, the substitution of *ṛ* (by the rules *mṛjāmit* and *artipipartyośca*) would apply to the entire reduplicated syllable; for once doubling has occurred, the meaningfulness belongs to the whole unit.

In the rule *ṭhhali lopa*, it would be more appropriate to formulate the sūtra simply as *ṭhhalya śi*, removing the mention of *lopa*. Because of the status of *śi* as a marker (*śit*), when the entire form *id* undergoes the substitution of a single substitute (*pararūpa*) with the vowel *a*,
the forms *ābhyām* and others are established by the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102], which prescribes the long vowel *Ā*.
"Like the beginning and the end, so in the middle. (Pāṇini 1.1.21).

Now, when *bhyām* follows [the pronoun *idam*], and after the substitution of the *tyad*-class forms, the application of the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*), and the elision of *id-* have been performed, the form *abhyām* remains.
Since the stem (*aṅga*) consists of the vowel *a*, it lacks the property of ending in *at*; how then can [the suffix] *sup* apply?
Regarding the rule "ce'ti dīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.73), he says: "as if at the beginning and the end" (*ādyantavat*).

Since being "at the beginning" (*āditva*) and being "at the end" (*antatva*) are always dependent on something else, the operations conditioned by those [states] do not apply to a single [phoneme]. This [sūtra] is commenced in order to achieve the application of those operations.

The word *eka* signifies "without a companion. As Amarasimha states: "In this sense, *mukhya*, *anya*, and *kevala* [are used]. The suffix *vati* is applied because the locative ending is present; this is seen from the fact that the locative case is used for the object of comparison in the rule "in the sense of 'there' (*tatra*) or 'belonging to that' (*tasya*)," which forms the *vati*. Furthermore, because the suffix *vati* is heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, it is connected with each member individually.

He says this with the words "in one [element]," and so forth. The meaning is that an operation performed upon the beginning and the end of something would apply even to that which is alone, as if it were at the beginning or at the end. Why say "in one"?
[To show that it does not apply] in cases such as *daridrāteḥ* with the suffix *ac*. The result of [the element] being like the beginning is seen in forms such as *aupagavaḥ*.

The suffix *aṇ* is udātta by virtue of its accentual rule. In forms such as *ābhyām*, the long vowel and other properties occur because [the single substitute] is treated as if it were the final element of the preceding member.

However, in the Bhāṣya, having removed the rule *ādyantavat*, the formulation of the sūtra is taught as *vyapadeśivadekasmin*. By this, in forms such as *iyāya*, the reduplication occurs according to the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*.

In the word *dhuk*, the substitution of *bhaṣ* (the voiced unaspirated stop) is established by virtue of its being designated as a part of the verbal root (*dhātu*) through the principle of "designation-like" (*vyapadeśivat*).

A "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) is a specific designation—that is, primary usage (*mukhya vyavahāra*). That which possesses this is "designation-like" (*vyapadeśī*), meaning it is primary. This applies even in the case of a single [element].
The result is that an operation conditioned by being "that as the beginning," "that as the end," or "that as a constituent part" would apply.

(In the rule) *idamo 'nvādeśe 'ś anudātastṛtīyādau* (Pāṇini 2.4.32), when *idam* is followed by *bhis*, after *tyadādyatva* and *pararūpa* have applied, [the *i* of] *id-* is elided by the rule *hali lopaḥ*.

When *lopa* (elision) has occurred and the form *abhis* remains, the rule *ṭāḍasi bhisa ais* would apply; however, this is precluded by the prohibition: *nedamadasorakoḥ*. From the rule *ṭāḍasi bhisa ais*, the portion *bhisa ais* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). The term *ṭakaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī*); it means "of those two [stems] in which the letter *k* does not exist" (*na vidyate kakāro yayos-tayoḥ*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. He states this with the words "of those [stems] not having the letter *k*" (*akakārayoḥ*), and so forth. Regarding "the substitution of *etva*," the remainder of the rule is "by means of the [sūtra] *bahuvacane jhalī*. Regarding the specific case of the suffix *ṅyi*, he states "the substitution of *atva*," and so forth; the syntactical connection is that "the substitution of *atva* occurs for the suffix *ReĀḥ* when it becomes *smai*. When the form *idam* itself remains as such, because the status of being *smai* is further removed, the substitution of *an* does not occur.

By the maxim "in a conflict of rules, that which is once sublated is indeed sublated," the *smai* replacement would not occur again; therefore, he says: "because it is obligatory" (*nityatvāt*). Since the *smai* replacement is obligatory—being applicable whether the substitution has occurred or not—it occurs prior to the substitution.
The intention is that, when [the suffix] *anādeśa* is applied, it is superseded by the elision (*lopa*) before a consonant (*hal*). Regarding "from these two" (*ābhyām*):

as before. Regarding "from these" (*ebhyaḥ*): the intention is that there is the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun *tyad*-class, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*), the elision before a consonant (*hal*), and the substitution of *et* [for the final vowel] when followed by a *jhala* sound in the plural (*bahuvacana*). Regarding "from this" (*asmāt*): there is the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun *tyad*-class.
The intention is that [the form] would be *sāt* due to the rules "pararūpatvaṃ hali lopaḥ" and "sa ṭhṅsiṅyoḥ. Regarding "asya":

the intention is that there is the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*), the replacement by *syādeśa*, and the elision (*lopa*) before a consonant (*hal*).
Regarding "anayoḥ": [there is] the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the substitution of the subsequent form, and [the application of] "ṭhanāpyakaḥ" and "osi."

The intention is that there is the substitution of *et* and the substitution of *ay*. Regarding "of these": the intention is that in the case of the suffix *ām*, there is the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), elision before a consonant (*hal-īti lopaḥ*), and the substitutions of *e* and *ṣatva*. Regarding "in this": the intention is that there is the substitution of *at*, the substitution of the subsequent form, the suffix *smin*, and elision before a consonant. Regarding "in *eṣu*": there is the substitution of *at*.

The intended meaning is that [the final *i*] takes the form of another letter (*pararūpatva*), there is elision of the consonant (*hal-lopa*) by the rule *hali lopaḥ*, and then the substitution of *e* and the change to *ṣatva*. Regarding the phrase "but when joined with *ka*" (*kakārayoge tu*): it means that when the word *idam* has the suffix *akac* added to it—by the rule *avyaya-sarvanāmna-akac-prāk-ṭeḥ*—and thus *akac* is present; [the result is] *ayakam*. This refers to the word *idakam* which is produced once *akac* has been applied.

The sense is that, by the principle of "falling in the middle" (*tanmadhyapatinyāya*), *mat* and the other suffixes are included by the mention of *idam* in rules such as *idamo maḥ*; however, the rules *anāpyakaḥ*, *hali lopaḥ*,
and *nedamadasorakoḥ* do not apply here because of the presence of the letter *k*.
With the intention of negating that [application], he says: *imakaina*, *imakābhyām*. "And so forth" (*ityādi*) refers to:
*imakaiḥ*; *imakasyai*; *imakabhyaḥ*; *imakasmāt*; *imakasya*, *imakayoḥ* (dual), *imakānām*;
*imakasmin*, *imakeṣu*.

*Idamaḥ anvādeśe aś anudāttaḥ tṛtīyādau* (Pāṇini 2.4.34). The analysis of *idamaḥ anvādeśe* is: *anvādeśe aś*. The clear meaning is: in the case of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the substitute *aś* shall take the place of *idam* when followed by the third case or any subsequent case-ending, and that [substitute] is unaccented (*anudātta*). [Example: *āśāste yam...* (He prays for whom...).

"This sacrificer" is the subject; having introduced [the passage] with "he desires long life," the example given is "may the gods grant that to him. The meaning is: "May the gods accomplish for this sacrificer (*asme*) that [long life] and so forth. Here, *asmai* is the example. When *ida-asmai* is in the state of standing [in the sandhi process], [it becomes *idamasmai*].

When the substitute for *śas* (*ādeśa*) is *prakṛti* (unchanged), being unaccented (*anudātta*), the vowel *e* in *smai* is unaccented by the rule "sup and pit [suffixes] are unaccented. Thus, *asmai* is entirely unaccented.
Similarly, examples such as *ābhyām* and others apply when the following element begins with a consonant (*hal*). In the case of vowels beginning with the second case (*dvitīyā*), etc.:

Because the specific substitution of *aś* is prescribed [by the rule *tyadādīnām aś*]. Now, one might object: "Let only the anudātta accent be prescribed here, and not the substitution of *aś* as well; for even in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), forms such as *asmai* and *ābhyām* would be established through the substitution of *at* for *tyadādi* elements and the elision of the following consonant. To this, he says: "The mention of *aś*..."

Regarding the phrase *sākackārtham*: in the case of the subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) "by these two, *ṭhi* and *imakā*, [something] was studied at night; by these two, it was also studied during the day," the form *imakābhyām* does not occur. Here, because the rule is formulated with the coalesced notation *a a*, it becomes a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) due to having more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). Therefore, the addition of the marker *ś* is not necessary.
That "it must be done" is clear from the Bhāṣya.

(Pāṇini 7.1.12) *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ*. [The rule] *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ*: the term *dvitīyāṭaus* refers to the second case (*dvitīyā*), the instrumental singular suffix *ṭā*, and the genitive plural suffix *aus*; [the rule applies] in these cases.

This is a *dvandva* compound. From the rule "ṭhidamo'nvādeśe," the terms "ṭhidamaḥ" and "anvādeśe" are understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). Also, from the rule "ṭhetadastratasoḥ," the term "etadaḥ" carries over.
Thus he says: "In the second case," and so forth. [He uses] the word "anvādeśa."

He explains with the words "something" (*kiñcit*). Regarding the phrase "to enjoin" (*vidhātum*), the meaning is "to cause the cognition of something previously unknown" (*apūrva*); that is, to bring about an understanding of what has not been established before. Having cited an instance of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), he demonstrates it with "as follows" (*yathā*). In the presentation of an example, the word *yathā* is used. [The rule: "The *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of this [pronoun] becomes *ām* when followed by *ṅti*, provided it denotes 'a little' (*īṣat*), is used in connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*), or signifies a limit (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*). [Pāṇini 5.4.50] *Ṭi* refers to the final vowel and following consonant of a nominal stem ending in *t*. *Ṅti* refers to a verbal suffix beginning with *ṅ*. *Ām* is a substitute for *ṭi*. The term *etad* refers to the pronoun *etad*. The word *ādi* indicates that other examples should be understood as well. For instance: *īṣad uṣṇam oṣṇam* ("slightly warm"), *uṣṇaṃ kṛtvā* ("having made warm"), *uṣṇaṃ kṛtam* ("made warm"). The particle *ca* implies that the same applies to the pronouns *idam* and *adas*. Thus: *idaṃ kṛtvā* ("having done this"), *idaṃ kṛtam* ("done this"), *amuṃ kṛtvā* ("having done that"), *amuṃ kṛtam* ("done that"). Furthermore, regarding the limit (*maryādā*): *ā pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained as far as Pāṭaliputra"); regarding inclusion (*abhividhi*): *ā saṃkāsye vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained including Saṃkāśya"). Similarly, *ā pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to Pāṭaliputra") and *ā saṃkāsye vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to Saṃkāśya") are examples where the limit is expressed by the ablative case (*pañcamī-vibhakti*). The particle *ca* implies that the same applies to the pronouns *idam* and *adas*. Thus: *ābhyām grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages"). Similarly, *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages") are examples where the limit is expressed by the locative case (*saptamī-vibhakti*). The particle *ca* implies that the same applies to the pronouns *idam* and *adas*. Thus: *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages"). Similarly, *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages") are examples where the limit is expressed by the locative case. The particle *ca* implies that the same applies to the pronouns *idam* and *adas*. Thus: *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages"). Similarly, *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages") are examples where the limit is expressed by the locative case. The particle *ca* implies that the same applies to the pronouns *idam* and *adas*. Thus: *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained from these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages"). Similarly, *ābhyāṃ grāmābhyāṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these two villages"), *ābhir grāmair vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), *ebhyo grāmebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained up to these villages"), and *eṣu grāmeṣu vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained in these villages") are examples where the limit is expressed by the locative case.
