In the rule *vidyā-vākya-smaraṇayor aṅit* (Pāṇini 1.4.29), however, there is no substitution of *enā*; this is because the first half of the verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to its connection with the word *yat*. Furthermore, in the phrase *kiñcit kāryaṃ vidhātum upātasya*, the inclusion of that [word] in the preceding sentence is intended in some way or another, and not—
This is clear from the Bhāṣya: "But this is a tenacity [of the view] that it must be exactly this. Thus end those ending in *m*. Now, those ending in *ṇ*:
[the word] *vijigāṇayiḥ* is derived from the root *gaṇ*. The root *gaṇa* (meaning "to count") belongs to the *curādi* group and ends in *a*.

From that, with the prefix *su-* and the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied. Due to the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel.

Therefore, by the rule *ṭhanyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*, there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix; then the elision of the *apṛkta* [suffix]; then the derivation of the case endings (*sub-utpatti*); and finally, by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, there is the elision of the *su*. Thus, the form is *sugaṇ*. *Sugaṇau*, *sugaṇaḥ*, and so forth, remain unchanged. In the locative plural (*sup*), by the rule *ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari*, [the augment *kuk* is applied].

There is an option regarding the *ṭuak* suffix. Intending that *ṭha* replaces *ṭa* according to the rule "the second letters [are substituted] for *ṭh-cay-ah*," he says: *sugaṇṭṣu*. He states the form when there is no *dvitīya* (i.e., no *ṭha*):
*sugaṇṭsu*. He states the form when there is no *ṭuak*: *sugaṇsu*.

Regarding *sugāṇ*: from the root *gaṇ*, there is the suffix *ṇic* (which ends in *a*), and the elision of the vowel *a* (*allopaḥ*). Because that [elided *a*] is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. From that [root *gaṇ* with *ṇic*], the suffix *kvip* is applied; the *ṇic* is elided, and the single-consonant suffix (*apṛkta*) is elided. By the rule "the long vowel for a nasal before *kvip* or a consonant beginning with *jhal*," the vowel becomes long. Thus, the form *sugāṇ* is established. [In the dual: *sugāṇau*.

Regarding "sugāṇ" and so forth: one should not suspect that the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the original element) applies to the elision of the *ṇi* suffix and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*allopa*) when a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is to be applied, because that [application of *sthānivadbhāva*] is prohibited in the case of a rule prescribing a long vowel, and because it is also prohibited with respect to a rule concerning a *kvip* suffix. Thus end those ending in /ā/. Now, those ending in /n/. He states the specific rule regarding the word *rājan*: "because it is subsequent" (*paratvāt*).

The meaning is that, because it is subsequent (paratvāt) to the elision of *hal* and *ṅī*-suffixes etc., the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne cā'saṃbuddhau" occurs first; only after that does the elision of *hal* and *ṅī*-suffixes etc.
take place. One might object: "But how can this be so, given the maxim 'in the case of a conflict (vipratiṣedha), that which is sublated remains sublated'?"
It should be stated that "there is elision of [suffixes] beginning with *hal* and *ṅ*," for [the rule] "it is established by the recognition of recurrence" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñānāt*) applies here.
The intention is that the principle "in case of conflict, that which is sublated [remains sublated]" is not universally valid. Regarding "elision of *n*" (*nalopa*):
the meaning is the elision of the letter *n* according to the rule "there is elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*).

*na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ* | 8|2|8 | When *he rājan s* is present, after the elision of *s* by *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (6.1.68), the elision of *n* would apply because it is at the end of a word (*padānta*) and at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadikānta*). [To prevent this, the rule] states: *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ*.

From the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, the phrase *nalopaḥ* (elision of *n*) is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). Therein, the word *ne* has its genitive case ending elided; this is indicated by the words "of *n*" (*nasya*), and so forth. In the example *he rājan*, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca* does not apply, because of the statement *asaṃbuddhau* (except in the vocative singular). Now, in this case...

The inclusion [of the word *chandasi*] would be redundant; for in the case of *rājan-i*, since it has the designation *bha*, it lacks the status of a *pada*, and thus the elision of the *n* (nalopa) does not even arise. To this, he says: "But in the Veda (*chandasi*) when followed by *ṅai*.
The meaning is: "only in the Veda" (*chandasyeva*). Now, one might object that even in the Veda, when followed by *ṅai*...

Since [the word *parama*] is a nominal stem (*bha*) and lacks the status of being a "word" (*pada*), how could there be the contingency of eliding the letter *n*, such that its prohibition would be meaningful? To this, he says: "of the case-endings" (*supām*).

But [one might object]: in examples such as *parame vyoman*, since the case-ending is elided by the rule for the elision of *ReĀr*, there is an absence of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); how then [could the rule apply] there?
He says "by the force of the prohibition" because the rule *na ṅsi-buddhyoḥ* would otherwise apply;

the sense is that even in Vedic usage, if *ṅluk* were to occur, the rule *na ṅsi-buddhyoḥ* would not apply due to the absence of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an elided suffix as present), and thus that [prohibition] would be rendered purposeless.

Now, if in Vedic usage— such as in *ṭhparame vyoman* and so forth— it is accepted that even when a suffix is elided by *ReĀrluk*, the operation of *na ṅsiṃbuddhyoḥ* applies by resorting to the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix), then [one might argue] that in cases such as *carmatilaḥ* (meaning "one who has sesame seeds on his skin") or *brahmaṇi*...

In the case of the compound *brahmaniṣṭhaḥ* (one who is established in Brahman), where the suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs, one might argue that by relying on the rule of "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) regarding the elision of the *ṅ* (the *ṭak*), the prohibition of the elision of the *n* in the rule *na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ* would apply.

To this, he says: *ṅavutarapade*. This means that when the *ṅ* occurs before a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*), [the rule does not apply]. When that *ṅ* is followed by a subsequent member, [the elision is not prohibited].

The meaning is that a prohibition must be stated against the prohibition [contained in the rule] "not after *ṅsi* or the vocative. And thus, in the case of *carmatilaḥ*, since there is no application of the prohibition "not after *ṅsi* or the vocative" when a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows, the elision of the letter *n* is unimpeded; this is the intended sense. However, in the Bhāṣya...

In the Vedic passage "ṭhparame vyoman," because the status of a *bha*-stem applies by the rule "ṭhayasmayādīni cchandasī," there is no possibility of the elision of the *n* due to the absence of *pada*-status; thus, the prohibition regarding the suffix *ṅe* need not be formulated, and the mention of *ṅi* is consequently rejected. Furthermore, [this does not apply] in the case of "rājanyati" in common usage (*loka*).

In the sense of "he behaves like a king" (*rājanīvācarati*), the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *adhikaraṇācca*. Then, because the group beginning with *san* (i.e., *san*, *kyac*, etc. is treated as verbal roots according to the rule *sanādyantāḥ*, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*.

From the form *rājanya-* [which results from *rājan* + *kyac*], when the nominative suffix *tip* is added, the case-ending that was previously present within the complex form (*antarvartin-vibhakti*) also causes the elision of the *kyac* suffix. Thus, one arrives at the form *rājanyati*.

It should not be argued that the *bhāṣya* which rejects [the necessity of] the mention of *ṅ* is untenable, because the mention of *ṅ* is indispensable for the purpose of prohibiting the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* when it occurs at the end of a word (*padatva*).
This is because of the authority of this very *bhāṣya*, and because of the rule "after the suffix *kvip*" (*adhikaraṇācca*), in the sense of "one who behaves like a king" (*rājanīvācarati*).

Enough of this, for it is accepted that [the form] is not denoted by the word *kyac*. In forms such as *rājānam*, there is lengthening by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*. Regarding the specific case of the *śas* [ending], he says: *allopo 'naḥ*.
By this sūtra, the meaning is that there is elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* following the letter *j*. Thus: *rājan-as*.
[The rule] "there is *ścutva*" [applies]. And thus, when the letter *n* becomes *ñ*, the form "rājñaḥ" is established.

Now, one might object: since the elision (*al-lopa*) is subject to the status of being "as if the original were present" (*sthānivadbhāva*) even with respect to an operation preceding it—by the rule "when a subsequent [element] follows an *ac*"—how can there be *ścutva* here? To this, he says: "and the elision of *a* is not *sthānivat*."

Why is this so? To this he says: "In the preceding case. The meaning is that, because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies when the substitution of *ścu* (the change of *t* to *c*) is to be performed according to the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*. Now, one might object: the elision of *al* (*allopa*) is *bahiraṅga*, as it depends upon the designation *bha* and depends upon the external suffixes beginning with *su* (*svādi*).

The substitution of *ścu* (the change of *s* to *ś*), however, is *antaraṅga* because it depends merely upon the presence of a *ścu*-sound. Consequently, by the paribhāṣā "that which is *bahiraṅga* is considered *asiddha* with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*," when the substitution of *ścu* is to be applied, the *bahiraṅga* elision (*allopa*) is treated as *asiddha*; thus, due to the intervention of the vowel *a*, how [can the rule apply] here?
To this, he says: "Nor even... [and so forth]. Regarding "according to the place of enunciation" (*yathoddeśa*):

there is one view that "technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and paribhāṣās [operate] according to the place of enunciation. "Enunciations" (*uddeśāḥ*) mean places of origin; "according to the place of enunciation" means not deviating from those places. Thus, technical terms and paribhāṣās remain in the very same place where their origin occurs.

The meaning is that [the two rules] operate in succession. This *paribhāṣā*, "what is external (*bahir-aṅga*) is not established (*asiddha*) when [an internal (*antar-aṅga*) operation is to take place]," is clearly indicated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the very rule *vāha ūṭh* (P.

6.4.132) in the sixth chapter. Consequently, this *paribhāṣā* belonging to the sixth chapter [is not applicable] to the *ścutva* [substitution] which belongs to the third section [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*].

Even when an internal (antaraṅga) operation is required, [the Paribhāṣā] does not apply; for with respect to that [substitution], the substitution of *ścu* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and since the *ścu* substitution itself is absent from its perspective, it is impossible for that Paribhāṣā to operate in its domain. And thus, regarding the *ścu* substitution:

The sense is that, since the elision of *a* (al-lopa) is not considered "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*) with respect to what is to be performed, the substitution of *ś* (ścutva) here is free from obstruction. There is also another view, namely: "Technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time of the operation.
According to this, technical names and rules of interpretation become active upon reaching each specific location where a rule is to be applied.

This is the meaning. In this view, although the *paribhāṣā* "that which is *asiddha* [unestablished] because it is *bahiraṅga* does not apply when [another rule] is *antaraṅga*" ought to apply here by prioritizing the *antaraṅga* substitution of *ścu*, nevertheless, for the sake of conforming to the observed forms (*lakṣya*), the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that rules take effect at the time the operation is to be performed) is not adopted here; enough of this. In the case of *jañ-yoge*:

The meaning is that such a sound is established both in common usage and in the Veda. However, this is not a separate phoneme (*varṇāntara*), because it is not observed in the *Śikṣā* and other such works. Therefore, they say that the substitution of *ścu* (the change of *n* to *ñ*) is established by the knowledge of this [sound].
For example, in *rājñaḥ* and *rājñi*: when a vowel beginning with *śas* follows, because the stem is treated as *bha*, the *l* is elided, and by the rule of *ścutva*, the *n* becomes *ñ*.

This is the sense. Now, an objection is raised: when *rājan-bhyām* is established, since it is a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*, the *na*-elision (*nalopa*) occurs; once that is done, the rule *supi ca* would require the lengthening of the vowel.
Similarly, when *rājan-bhis* is established, after the *na*-elision, the rule *ato bhisa ais* would require the substitution of *ais* for *bhis*.

Thus, when *rājabhyaḥ* is established, once the *n*-elision (*nalopa*) has occurred, the substitution of *e* (*etva*) would apply by the rule "in the case of a *jhāl* [suffix] in the plural" (*bahuvacane jhalyet*).

However, this is not so, because of the rule: "The elision of *n* does not take effect in rules concerning *sup*, accent, technical names (*saṃjñā*), or the application of *tuṅ* before a *kṛt* suffix" (*nalopaḥ supsvarasaṃjñātugvidhiṣu kṛti*).

Nor should it be argued that because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*), there should be neither the long vowel (*dīrgha*) nor the substitution of *ai* and *e* here;

for if the rule "what precedes is as if not having taken effect" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) were to apply to the domain of *nalopa*, then in cases such as *rājāśvaḥ* and *daṇḍāścaḥ*, the elision of *n* would likewise be as if not having taken effect, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) and the *yaṇ*-substitution would not occur. Therefore...

He says: *nalopaḥ sup*. "The elision of *n*" is *nalopaḥ*. The word *vidhi* is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*); "the act of prescribing" is *vidhi*. The compound *sup-svara-saṃjñā-tuk-vidhayaḥ* is a genitive compound of general relation (*sambandhasāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "the prescriptions for *sup*, accent (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), and *tuk*. However, in the case of the rule *kṛti*, it refers specifically to *tuk* alone.

It is connected [to the word *subvidhau*], because it cannot apply otherwise; thus he says, beginning with "in the rule for *sup*" (*subvidhau*). "The rule for *sup*" (*subvidhi*) means a rule concerning *sup*. A general relationship is intended. That is to say, it refers to a rule based on *sup*. "A rule for accent" (*svarasya vidhiḥ*). The genitive case is used to express the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*) of the object. Regarding accent...

The meaning is "to be prescribed. Similarly, in the expression *saṃjñāvidhau*, the genitive case is used because the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a residual factor (*śeṣatva*); that is to say, it means "when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be prescribed. *Kṛtitugvidhiḥ* refers to the prescription of the augment *tuk* which occurs after a *kṛt* suffix; here too, [the genitive] expresses the object (*karman*).
The genitive case is used here with the intention of expressing a remainder (*śeṣatva*). It means "when *kṛt* follows," that is to say, when that [suffix] is to be prescribed.

Since the rule would have been established by the principle "what precedes is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), he states "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*) to indicate that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) whose purpose is to exclude other [operations].
Having cited "anyatra" (elsewhere), he demonstrates this with the example "rājāśva" and so forth;

by the word "ādi" (and so forth), examples such as "daṇḍyaśva" are included. Here, since the rules for *savarṇadīrgha*, *yaṇ*-substitution, and others are not included within the rules governing *sup*-suffixes or those beginning with *ṭi*, when those [rules] are to be applied, there is no absence of the status of being "asiddha" (non-existent) regarding the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*).

The sense is that since the elision of the letter *n* is present, the formation of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) and so forth occurs without obstruction. He states—“because this is not established”—that in the present case, in forms such as *rājābhyām* and *rājabhyaḥ*, the substitution of a long vowel and so on does indeed not take place; for the rule prescribing the long vowel applies when a case-ending (*sup*) follows, whereas [the elision of *n*] applies to the ending *bhisaḥ*.

The meaning is as follows: since the rules for *ais* (in *bhyas*) and the rule for *etva* are rules based on *suptiṅa* suffixes, when these are to be applied, and in the absence of a prohibition of non-antecedent-status (*asiddhatva*) obtainable from a restrictive rule (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*), the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) would be considered non-existent according to the principle "what precedes is non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*); consequently, the long vowel of the *nadī* [designation] and other such operations would not take place.
In reality, however, the nature of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is precisely that of an injunction whose established subject has as its result the exclusion of other alternatives.

For this very reason, in the case of the statement "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," when there is a restriction regarding the eating of those five five-nailed creatures, the prohibition of eating five-nailed animals other than those is understood.
This has been explained in detail in the *Paspaśāhnika-bhāṣya*. Thus he says: "because of its being *asiddha*. Now, one might object:

in the case of *daṇḍiṣu*, once the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) has taken place, the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) applies because it follows after an *iṇ*-vowel; such is the established position. In that regard, since the rule for *ṣatva* is a rule dependent on a *sup* (case-ending), how can it be applied when the *nalopa* is *asiddha*?

If it is argued that [the rule for] *ṣatva* [is a *subvidhi*], let it not be so; for the rule prescribing *ṣatva* is not a *subvidhi*. Here, a *subvidhi* is intended as a rule that operates by taking as its basis either the property of being a *sup* (*suptva*) or a property subordinate to it (*tadvyāpyadharma*). And the rule for *ṣatva* is not of that nature. Therefore, in that case, there is no elision of the *n*.

Since the status of being established (*siddhatva*) indeed exists, the substitution of *ṣ* is beyond reproach. Or, even if the rule for *ṣ* were also a rule concerning *su*, nevertheless, when that [substitution] is to be performed, the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur at all.
For is that non-establishment brought about by the rule "what precedes is unestablished" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), or rather by the rule "the elision of *n*" (*nalopa*)?

Is it by this very rule, "sup-svare" (P. 8.2.2)? Not the first, because since the rule for the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) precedes the rule for *ṣatva*, it cannot be considered *asiddha* when *ṣatva* is to be applied.
Nor the second, for by the rule "sup-svare," [the elision of *n*] occurs in forms such as "rājabhyām."

The non-application (*asiddhatva*) of *nalopa* is not being enjoined as something new; rather, that which is already established by the rule "what precedes is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) is restated for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that rules such as the long vowel by class-similarity (*savarṇadīrgha*)— excluding the rules for case-endings (*sup*), accent (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), and the elision of *t* (*tuka*)— may be successfully applied in cases like *rājāśva*.

However, in the case of *daṇḍiṣu*, the non-application of the rule "what precedes is as if not having come into effect" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*)—which would otherwise cause the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) to be treated as non-existent—is not obtained; consequently, it is impossible for that [elision] to fall under the scope of the rule "the elision of *n* before a *sup*-affix or a vowel" (*nalopaḥ supsvare*).
Otherwise, by the rule "in the application of *sup*-affixes" (*subvidhau*), when the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) is to be applied in forms such as *daṇḍiṣu*...

Otherwise, the status of *nalopa* as being "not established" (*asiddha*) would have to be prescribed as something entirely new. However, in cases such as *rājabhyām*, where a long vowel (*dīrgha*) and so forth is to be applied, [the rule] is already established and is prescribed merely for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Thus, a discrepancy in the nature of the prescription (*vidhivairūpya*) would result.
Therefore, in cases such as *daṇḍiṣu*, when the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is to be applied...

Since there is no lack of *asiddhatva* regarding the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), the elision of *n* being present, the condition of being followed by an *iṇ*-vowel is not lost; thus, the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) is unimpeded. This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Let us return to the subject at hand. An example regarding the rules for accent (*svaravidhi*) is *pañcārmam*. Here—

Because the elision (*nalopa*) is considered *asiddha*, the word lacks the final vowel *a*; consequently, the rule "the first syllable of the prior member is udātta when the second member begins with a vowel and consists of two syllables" (*amecāvarṇaṃ dvyaññyaj*) does not apply. As an example regarding the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*): *daṇḍidattau* and *dattadaṇḍinau*. Here, the rule "in a *dvandva* compound, [the shorter member is placed first]" (*dvandve dhī*) establishes the restriction on the prior placement.
It does not occur because, in the rule prescribing the *ghisaṃjñā*, the elision of the *n* is considered as if unestablished (*asiddha*), and thus the quality of ending in *i* is absent.

As for the application of the *tuṅ* augment in the context of a *kṛt* suffix, consider the forms *vṛtrahabhyām* and *vṛtrahabhiḥ*. Here, although one might rely on the *kvip* suffix prescribed by the rule "kvip after *brahman*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra*," the *tuṅ* augment is nevertheless applied by the rule "the *tuṅ* augment follows a short vowel before a *pit* *kṛt* suffix."

[In the case of *vṛtra-han*], because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddhatva*), the short vowel is separated from the *n* [by that elision]. However, due to the qualification "before a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛti*), the elision of *n* is not treated as *asiddha* when the *tuk* augment is prescribed by the rule "before *cha*" (*che ca*). Consequently, in *vṛtrahaccchatram*, the *tuk* would indeed occur here by the rule "before *cha*" (*che ca*). But in the Bhāṣya...

In examples such as *vṛtrahabhyām*, although the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) occurs, the augment *tuk*—prescribed by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*—will not apply due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*. Therefore, the mention of the rule for *tuk* has been rejected [by the author of the *Kāśikā*].

This is because the condition for the application of the *tuk* is the status of being a *pada* (a word) established by the rule *svādiṣu*, which depends upon the *saṃnipāta* (immediate sequence) with the suffix *bhyām*.

The intention is that the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not cause the application of that which destroys it. Now, one might object: in the case of *vṛtrahadhanam*, the mention of the rule for *tuṅ* (*tugvidhi*) is necessary in order to exclude *tuṅ*; for there, having relied upon the status of being a word (*padatva*)—which itself arises by relying on the internal case-ending—the [elision of *n*] occurs.

If it is argued that this is not so because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) lacks the status of being caused by a *saṃnipāta* (a specific phonetic combination), we say no; for, on the authority of the Bhāṣya—which rejects the inclusion of the rule for *tuṅ*—one must assume that forms such as *vṛtrahañ-janaḥ*, where the elision of *n* is not caused by such a *saṃnipāta*, are included in the scope of the rule. Let this matter rest for now. In *rājñi* and *rājanī*: the meaning is that there is an optional elision of the *ī* vowel (*ilopa*) according to the rule *vibhāṣā ṅśyoḥ*. *Pratidivā*: [The root] *div* is used in the sense of "playing" and so forth. From that root, the suffix *kanin* is applied by the *Uṇādi* sūtra *kaninyuvṛṣitakṣī*. In *kan*, both *k* and *n* are indicatory (*it*). The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

From the word *pratidivan*, the case endings (*sup*) arise. By the rule "sarvanāmasthāne ca," there is lengthening [of the vowel]. Upon the elision of the case ending *su* by the rule "halṅyādi," the form is *pratidivā*. In the presence of the suffix *suṭ*, it is like *rājan*. Regarding the phrase "asya" (of this): it means when the vowel beginning with *śas* follows the word *pratidivan*, and the *an-lopa* (elision of the final *a*) has occurred by the rule "allopo'naḥ. [The sūtra] "hali ca" (8.2.77): "and before a consonant (*hal*). The phrase "lengthening of a short *ik* vowel that is a penultimate [vowel] before *r* and *v*" (*ṛv-ur-upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ*) is understood to carry over. [This applies] to the root [ending] in *sip*.
And [the word] "from this root" (*dhātoḥ*) is also [understood]. That [root] is qualified by the rule *rvoh* (Pāṇini 6.1.20). This is a *tadantavidhi* (a rule concerning that which ends in such).
Thus he says with the words "of that which ends in *r*" and so forth. An example of that which ends in *r* is *jīryati*.

Since [the condition of] not being at the end of a word (*apadāntatva*) applies, this is a rule [providing for] what was not otherwise obtained by the rule *ṛtvor upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19). And in the present case...

The meaning is that when *div* stands as *pratidivan*, the vowel *i* of the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the root *div* becomes long before a consonant (*hal*) following the *n* of the suffix *na*. Now, one might object: because of the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) for the elision (*lopa*) of the *ac* [the final *a*] by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*... [the elided *a* would still be present]. By the letter *a*...

Anticipating the objection—"How can there be a long vowel here, given the intervention [of the augment] and the absence of the condition 'being followed by a heavy syllable'?"—the author refutes it with "And not... He asks "Why? and answers: "Because of the prohibition of that [substitution] in the rule for lengthening.
The meaning is that, by the rule *na padānte*, the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element) is prohibited in the context of a prescription for lengthening.

But even so, since the elision of *a* (*allopa*) depends on the designation *bha*, it is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on an affix that is external; therefore, when the internal (*antaraṅga*) lengthening is to be applied, that elision is as if non-existent (*asiddha*).

Consequently, due to the intervention of the vowel *a*, there is no occurrence of a consonant (*hal*) immediately following [the *n*], and how then can there be lengthening here? To this, he says: "The external... (*bahiraṅga...*).

In the view that [the rule] is taught according to its specific mention (yathoddeśa), since the substitution of *ścu* is not established (*asiddhatva*) with respect to the sixth Paribhāṣā, the Paribhāṣā does not apply due to the absence of an *antaraṅga* [operation].
By the logic stated regarding the word *rājan*, the long vowel is not established; therefore, it is "not established" (*asiddham*) in its own domain.
The sense is that the *paribhāṣā* "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) does not apply" does not operate here. Regarding *pratidīvna*:
the prohibition by the rule "not after *bha*, *ku*, *ch*, or *u*" (*na bhakurchuarām*) does not apply because the *vānta* (the *au* resulting from *ava* + *ū*) is not a *bha*-stem.
"And so forth" refers to: *pratidivne*, *pratidīvnaḥ* (dual), *pratidīvnoḥ* (dual).

The meaning is that [the word *yajvan*] behaves like *rājan* when followed by the suffixes beginning with *bhyām* and when a consonant (*hal*) follows. He states that the word *yajvan* behaves like *rājan* when the suffix *suṭ* follows—namely, as *yajvā*.
(Pāṇini 6.4.137) "Not after a conjunct consonant ending in *v* or *m*."

When the elision (*alopa*) of *śas* would otherwise apply, [the rule] "not after a conjunct consonant ending in *v* or *m*" (*na saṃyogād vamantāt*) applies. The analysis of the compound is: *va* and *ma* are *vam*; that which has these as its final elements (*anta*) is [a word] ending in *vam*. The phrase "elision of *an*" (*allopo 'naḥ*) is understood to carry over.
Thus he says, beginning with "after *v*," etc. The inclusion of the term "final" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity, regarding *v* and *m*.
Because [the suffix] is obtained by virtue of being a qualifier of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the end of that [conjunction] is included. "And so forth" (*ityādi*) means:

*yajvane*, *yajvanaḥ* (dual), *yajvanoḥ* (dual). From the [case-endings] beginning with *bhyām*, when a consonant (*hal*) follows, it is like *rājan*. He gives an example of a *m*-final conjunction: *brahmaṇaḥ*. In the case of *śas* and other vowel endings, there is no elision (*allopa*) of the *n*.

The sense is that the remainder [of the description] is like that of a king. According to Amara: "Veda, *tatva*, austerity, and *brahman* [are synonyms]; *brahman* is a learned man (*vipra*) and the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*). Regarding the term *vṛtrahā*:

it is formed with the suffix *kvip* after the words *brahman*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra* in the sense of "one who has slain" them. The *k* and *p* are elided; there is the elision of the *apṛkta* [suffix]; and this is a compound with an upapada.

By the rule *supo dhātuḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending; thus, the word *vṛtrahan* is formed. From that, the case-ending arises. Regarding the specific rule for the nominative singular (*sau*), [Pāṇini] states: *inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau* (6.4.12). From the previous rule *ḍhralope*, the term *dīrghaḥ* (long vowel) is understood to carry over.

From the rule *ṭhnopadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* [is understood]. Thus he says: "of these. This means: of those ending in *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*. Since this is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem), there is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that).
Although [the lengthening] is already established by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, he says "only before a *ś* [ending]" for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

"Not elsewhere" means "in other cases. Regarding the phrase "when the prohibition has been reached": since there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that in the word *vṛtrahan*, the lengthening of the vowel for the element *han* occurs only before a *ś* (i.e., a *śit* suffix), the lengthening prescribed by the rule "before a *sarvanāmasthāna*" does not apply when the nominative singular suffix *su* follows; this is the meaning.
"And *sau* also" (6.4.13). The previous sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*). That which was carried over there is also [to be understood here].
Thus he says: "of those ending in *in*, etc. [The condition] "except in the vocative" (*asambuddhau*) applies; [the term *sarvanāmasthāna*] is supplied from the following rule.

The sense is that this is because [the previous rule] follows after it. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṭhinpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau*. In the form *he vṛtrahan*, there is no lengthening because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition *na saṃbuddhau*.

Since they are separate words, he says: "provided it consists of a single vowel (*ekāj*). Thus, *vṛtrahaṇau* and so forth. Due to the restriction (*niyama*) that [the elision of *n*] occurs only before *śa*, it does not [apply here].
The [suffix] *śas* and others beginning with a vowel: when *al*-lopa (elision of the penultimate *a*) has been performed, [the following applies].
Pāṇini 7.3.54: *ho hanteṛṇinneṣu*.
The word *haḥ* in *ho hanteḥ* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), while *hanteḥ* is a genitive of a constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). And *ñ*...

*ṇ* and *ñ* are [denoted by] *ñṇ*. Those two, when followed by *i*, are called *ñṇit*. The word *it* is connected with each [of them]. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: *ñṇitau* (those having *ñ* and *ṇ* followed by *it*), *naḥ* (the letter *n*), and *ñṇinnāḥ* (those ending in *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *n*); [the rule applies] "in those" (*teṣu*).

Because of the governing context of the *aṅga* (stem), the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*) is understood for *ñ* and *ṇ*. [The rule continues: "In place of *ṭh* and *ca*, *k* [is substituted]."

The term *ku* is understood from the rule *ghiṇyato'r*. This is what he states with the words beginning "before a suffix marked with Ñ" (*ñiti*). The mention of *han* is by means of the *śtip* affix; the meaning is "of the root *han*. In the present case, because the letter *ha* is followed by the letter *na*, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *gh* for *h*). In that regard, [the substitute] is voiced (*ghoṣavat*), sonant (*nādavat*), and aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*).

For the root *han* when its *kaṇṭhya* (velar) [consonant] is elided, such a fourth letter of the class, namely *gh*, [is substituted]. Thus, forms such as *vṛtraghnaḥ* and *vṛtraghnā* are established.
[Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.22: *hanteḥ*]

But surely, how is it that *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) does not occur here? For even though the words are distinct (*bhinnapadasthatva*), the application of *ṇatva* by the rule "ṭh-ekāj-uttarapade ṇaḥ" is unavoidable; because even when the elision of *aṅ* (*allopa*) has taken place, due to the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original) with respect to what precedes it, the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) remains a single syllable (*ekāc*). Even in the absence of *sthānivadbhāva*, [the fault remains].

Since the application of either *ṭhprātipadikāntatumvibhaktiṣu ca* or *ṭhkumati ca* would be unavoidable [in this case], the rule *ṭhhanteratpūrvasya* is explained by dividing it [into two parts] in order to prevent that. [The first part is: *hanteḥ*. The phrase *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* is understood to follow [as a governing rule].

From the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi*, the term *upasargāt* is understood to carry over [by anuvṛtti]. This is a designation based on location (*tātsthya-tācchabdyam*); thus, it is understood as "situated in a prefix. And that [designation] applies to each of the two [sounds], *ra* and *ṣa*. Therefore, he says: "from a cause situated in a prefix," and so forth.

By the word *nimita*, the letter *repha* (ṛ) and the letter *ṣakāra* (ṣ) are intended. Regarding the rule "one should strike" (*prahaṇyāt*): since the condition for the substitution of *ṇa* does not apply here because the words are separate (*bhinnapada*), this statement is made as a specific injunction.
[This applies] to that which is preceded by *at*.
He states what is relevant to the present topic: "of *han* preceded by *at*. The term "*han*" is understood from the previous rule, as is "*ṇaḥ* [replaces] *naḥ* after *ra* and *ṣa*.
However, "*upasargāt*" (after a prefix) is no longer in force. Thus, it is understood that the *ṇa* replaces the *na* of *han* when it is preceded by *at*.
Since this result is already established [by other rules], the present rule is commenced for a specific purpose.

He states that [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha), saying: "of *han* preceded by *at* only," and so forth. Regarding *praghnanti*: the suffix *laṭ* is applied to the root *han*, followed by *jhi*; *jhi* becomes *anta*; the *śap* augment is added; there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "gamahana-"; and by the rule "ho hanteḥ," the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *gh*) occurs. Thus, the form *praghnanti* is established. In this case...

Because the *repha* (r) follows the preposition (*upasarga*), the rule "of *han*" would have required the substitution of *ṇa*, but this does not occur due to the restriction "when preceded by *at*. In the case of *vṛtraghn*, the substitution of *ṇa* prescribed by the rule "at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and so forth" is set aside. Now, [one might object]: "But [the rule] 'and in the case of the end of a nominal stem, the augment *num*, and in inflectional endings (*vibhakti*)...'"?
The sequence of the sūtra readings is: "ṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 8.4.14], "kumati ca" [8.4.13], and "hanteratpūrvasya" [8.4.22].

Consequently, by the maxim "a rule applies to what is immediately preceding" (anantarasya vidhiḥ) and by the restrictive rule "of that which is preceded by 'at'" (atpūrvasya), in the case of "praghnanti," the substitution of ṇ for the h of "han" would be restricted solely to that instance where it is not separated [by other intervening elements].
To show that it is not otherwise, he says: "By *yoga*," etc. If, by the rule *atpūrvasya*, only the *ṇatva* (nasalization) of the root *han* were excluded, then there would be only a single sūtra:
*hanteratpūrvasya*. [This would mean: the *ṇatva* of the *n* of the root *han* when preceded by an *upasarga* and not preceded by *a*.

The meaning is as follows: since the prevention of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *praghnanti* is possible by the rule *ṇatvam* alone, it is understood—by virtue of the force of the division of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*)—that this restriction applies only to the substitution of *ṇ*. [This refers to the rule] *ekājuttare*. [It concerns] the rule *kumati ca* and the rule *prātipadikānte*.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that because of the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) even when a rule is prescribed based on what precedes it, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) remains monosyllabic (*ekāc*). Nor should it be argued that "the status of the substitute does not apply when a preceding operation is *asiddha*," for there is an exception to that rule stating, "there is a fault [in applying that principle]..."

This is because of the statement: "In the case of *sam-yoga*, elision (*lopa*), *la*-substitution, and *ṇa*-substitution [the preceding rule does not apply]. Now, one might ask: in the word *vṛtraghnaḥ*, how can there be *kutva* (the substitution of *gh*) by the rule "*ho hanteḥ*" (Pāṇini 7.3.54), given that the elision (*al-lopa*) of the preceding [augment] should be treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were still present) when the subsequent rule is being applied? To this, he says: "when followed by the letter *na*. This is the opinion of Mādhava.

He repeats [the opponent's view] in order to refute it: "yat tu" (as for what...). The particle *tu* indicates a difference from the previous case. "Vaikalpikam" means that which is prescribed by the rule "prātipadikānte" (Pāṇini 8.4.14). "Tadbhāṣye" refers to the statement in the Mahābhāṣya: "A prohibition must be stated regarding the substitution of *ha* when there is an intervening *ku*. What is the purpose? [To prevent the substitution in cases such as] *vṛtraghnaḥ* and *sugghaḥ*."

The *Bhāṣya* on the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* states: "In the rule *ṭhano’tpūrvasya*, the mention of *atpūrva* need not be made. Here, within the section on *ṇatva*, because it is understood that there is a prohibition when the substitute *ha* or the letter *k* intervenes, the *ṇatva* [substitution] also applies by the rule *prātipadikānte*.
It is understood that [the substitution] does not occur when there is intervention by an *ādeśa* (substitute) or a *ku*-sound;

the meaning is that Mādhava’s opinion should be disregarded because it contradicts this. "In this manner" means as in the case of the word *vṛtrahan*. This refers to the rules: *ṭhinhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau* and *sau ca*.
The example applies only to long vowels (*dīrgha*), and not to *kutva* and so forth, because such a change is impossible there.
In the sense of "he possesses a horn" (*śārṅgam asyāsti*), the possessive suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *ṭhata iniṭhanau*.
In the sense of "he possesses fame" (*yaśo 'syāsti*), the suffix *vin* is applied by the rule *asmāyāmedhāsrajaḥ*. [This is also governed by] *tasau matvarthe*.

Thus, because [the suffix] is a bh- sound, there is no substitution of *ru*. Now, one might raise the objection: "By the *arthavat-paribhāṣā*, in the rule *ṭhin-han* (Pāṇini 6.4.10), only an *in* that possesses meaning is to be understood; therefore, since the *in* in the suffix *vin* is meaningless, how can it be included?
Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the words beginning "yaśasvin" and so forth.

Regarding the expression *an-in-as-man-ni-ti*: this point is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya*. In the word *rājñaḥ*, the suffix *an* is meaningful (*arthavān*), whereas in *dāmnaḥ*, it is meaningless (*anarthaka*). In *śārṅgī*, the suffix *in* is meaningful, but in *yaśasvī*, it is meaningless. In *supayāḥ*, the suffix *as* is meaningful.

In the word *susrotāḥ*, however, [the suffix] is meaningless; the long vowel occurs because of its being a non-existent (*asan*) entity. In *suśarmā*, the suffix *man* is meaningful, whereas in *suprathimā*, it is meaningless. Regarding the form *manaḥ*, there is no application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. He states "aryamṇī" and so forth to show the specific difference regarding the elision of *al* in the words *aryaman* and *pūṣan*.

The elision of the *i* vowel is optional by the rule "vibhāṣā ṅśyoḥ. However, the meaning is that before vowel-beginning case endings starting with *śas*, the elision of *a* is generally established as obligatory. In the sense of "he is honored" (*māhyate*) or "he is revered," the suffix *kanip* is applied;
the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and the letter *k* is an *it*. Thus, the suffix *an* remains.

The suffix *av* is added to the root. Here, the letter *k* is for the sake of marking the suffix as *kit*, and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Because it is *kit*, it becomes an internal part of the word; furthermore, three things are prescribed by way of irregularity (*nipātana*) for the root *maha*: the substitution of *gha* for *h*.
[The form] *maghavān* occurs diversely.

[6.4.128] Regarding the word *maghavan*, which is derived from the *Uṇādi* sūtra "śvan-ukṣan-pūṣan-plīhan-kledan-asnehan-mūrdhan-majjan-aryaman-viśvapsan-parijman-mātariśvan-maghavan" (Uṇādi 1.159), he states a specific rule: *maghavā bahulam*. From the preceding rule "arvaṇas trāsau," the term *tṛ* is understood by anuvṛtti; this [term] has its nominative case ending elided. The form *maghave* is in the nominative case used with the sense of the genitive. Thus he says: "of the word *maghavan*" and so forth. [The suffix] *ṛt* is added. *id* [is the augment].

In the rule *ṭhupadeśe'janunāsika it*, the meaning is that the letter *ṛ* is designated as having the technical marker (*it*). The mention of *ṛ* without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*) does not cause any fault during the process of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, the *takāra* replaces the *nakāra*. It is not, however, a replacement of the entire word (*sarvādeśa*), because of the dictum: "The property of having more than one letter (*anekāltva*) is not caused by a technical marker (*anubandha*). When the form *maghavat-s* is established—[the following rule applies]: *Ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne'dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.70). *Ugidacām*: [This is a compound. *Adhātoḥ*: This is the division [of the rule]. Those which have *uk* [as a marker] are called *ugit*. *Ac*: [This refers to the suffix *ac*.]

And thus, there is the inclusion of the root *ṭhivu* (with its nasal elided) from the rule *ṭhivu gati-pūjanayoḥ*. The term "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) is a qualifier for *ugit*, but not for the root *añc*, because [the latter] is impossible [in that context].
From the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*, the word *num* is understood by anuvṛtti. This is what he says: "of a non-verbal root ending in an *ugit* [suffix]."

By [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā": in the augment *num*, the letter *m* is the meaningful element (*it*), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is designated as *mit*, it is placed after the final vowel (*antyādacaḥ*). Here, the term *aj* does not refer to the *ac*-pratyāhāra (the set of vowels), because of the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*) and because of the inclusion of *aj* in the rule "ṭhnapuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ". Otherwise, since the desired result would already be established by the rule "ugidacām" alone, there would be no need for this.

Because that [suffix] would be redundant; and because of the indicatory references (nirdeśa) such as "vṛddhir guṇaḥ" and so forth. As for the [restriction] "not after a verbal root" (adhātoḥ), this will be explained in the root text itself later on, at the occasion of defining the word *gomat*. Its purpose will also be stated in that very place. Regarding the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*): when the form *maghavant-s* is established...

The meaning is that when *su* is elided by the rule *halṅyādi* and the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogānta*) is elided, the lengthening occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*. Now, one might object: since the elision of the final consonant cluster is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*) when this lengthening is to be applied, the condition of ending in *n* (*nāntatva*) is absent; therefore, [the lengthening should not occur], as in the case of *pacan* and so forth.
Since [the suffix] *dīrgha* would not otherwise apply, he says: "when *dīrgha* is to be applied. Regarding the mention of the term *bahula* (diversity/optionality), it is said:
"Sometimes there is application, sometimes non-application; sometimes there is an option, and sometimes something else entirely.
This principle of *bahulagrahaṇa* is to be understood in the world by following the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*)."

The meaning is as follows: regarding the rule for *sthiti*, when a long vowel is to be applied here, the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). However, in cases such as *pacan* and the like, it is precisely because of the inclusion of the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the "diversely" rule) that this non-existence is obtained. Now, one might object: even in the view that the substitution of *trā* is applied, let it simply be *maghavan*; the meaning is that this is obtained through *bahulagrahaṇa*. But [is this not so]?

In the view that *tr* is substituted [for *tṛc*], let it simply be *maghavan*; for there is no evidence to assume that the rule regarding the non-application of the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) applies by virtue of the mention of "diversely" (*bahulagrahaṇa*).
As for the Veda, in cases such as *yajñena maghavān*, the long vowel will be due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). To this, he says: "Likewise..."

And thus: the meaning is that even while not admitting the non-invalidity (*asiddhatva*) of the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) in the alternative view where *tra* is the substitute.
"By way of irregular derivation" (*nipātanāt*) refers to these three: the suffix *kan*, the augment *avuk*, and the substitution of *gh*.
The meaning is that it is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Thus, the sense is that the word *maghavan* is established as ending in *n*.

Regarding the phrase "from the word *magha*": the meaning is from a synonym for wealth. The sense is that when the suffix *matup* is added in the sense of "one who possesses *magha*, i.e., wealth," the substitution of *v* for *m* according to the rule "after *mā* and after a penultimate vowel" results in the word *maghavan* being established as ending in *v*.

"In the spoken language as well" means in both the world (secular usage) and in Vedic meter (*chandas*). "Two words" refers to the two words *maghavan* and *maghavat*, which are the result of the rule "the word *maghavan* [is substituted] diversely. The meaning is: "having relied upon its establishment. "In the source" refers to the rule *keśād vaḥ*.

The meaning is that this is Kaiyaṭa’s commentary. For there it is stated thus: "The rule *maghavā bahulam* need not be formulated; because by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in *śvan-ukṣan-* etc., and by the suffix *matup*, the form *maghavān* is established even in the common language (*bhāṣā*). This refers to the alternative view regarding the substitution of *tra*.

The point is that because the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules), if one were to rely on the absence of the long vowel, the form would be *maghavan*; however, if the suffix *matup* were applied, the rule *ṭhatvasantasya ca* would require a long vowel, resulting in the form *maghavān*. Thus, since a difference in forms would arise, the [proposed] inconsistency is quite evident. In reality, however...

In the case of *kanya*, the final syllable is udātta by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). However, in the case of the suffix *matup*, although the rule "hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup" would normally assign an udātta accent to *matup*, this is prohibited by the rule "na gośvan. Consequently, because the suffix is treated as having an anudātta accent due to its being a *pit* suffix, the vowel following the letter *gha* (i.e., the vowel of *kanya*) becomes udātta by the *phiṭ-svara*.

The passage by Kaiyaṭa must indeed be considered questionable because of the difference in results. He states "havir" [as an example], meaning that the long vowel in *maghavān* is sanctioned by the learned. The meaning is: "In sacrifices (*makheṣu*), this Maghavan fearlessly devours (*jakṣiti*) the oblation (*haviḥ*). As for forms such as *maghavantau*, etc., [they occur] when the suffix *suṭ* is applied.

The intention is that there is both the substitution of *tr* and the augment *num*. In the case of the suffixes beginning with *śas*, there is the substitution of *tr*, but not *num*, because it is not a *na-lopa-sthāna* (a position where *n* is elided). With this in mind, he says: "of *maghavat*. [The forms] *maghavadbhyām*, etc., follow.

When the substitution of *tr* occurs, *jaś*-ness (*j* for *t*) applies because the word is a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*. When the substitution of *tr* occurs before a *sup* suffix, *jaś*-ness applies.

The form *maghavatsu* [is derived] by applying [the substitution] *tṛc* in the absence of *tṛn*. The intention is that when the nominative singular (*su*) follows a word ending in *n*, the form is like that of *rājan*. Now, regarding the rule *maghavā bahulam*, there is a statement in the Vārttika, the Bhāṣya, and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary: "The forms *arvan* with *tṛc* and *maghavan* need not be taught, for they are Vedic."

Since it is understood that the word *maghavan* has as its scope only the Vedic meters (*chandas*), one might ask how it is used in common worldly speech (*loka*). To this he says: "In the Veda, [the suffixes] *van* and *nip* [are added]," and so forth. This refers to the rule "In the domain of the suffix *matup*, [the suffix *va* is added after *keśa*, optionally]" (*keśād vo 'nyatarasyām*), and the subsequent rule "In the Veda, [the suffixes] *van* and *nip* [are also added]."

The *Vārttika* states: "In the Vedic language, the suffixes *-in* and *-van* should also be mentioned, as well as *-va* and *matup*. The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that passage provides examples such as: "Mudgalānī became a charioteer in the quest for cattle," "This bride is auspicious," and "We pray to the truthful Maghavan. In that context, regarding the word *maghavan*, which ends in the suffix *-van*:
By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the vowel *a* following the *v* is udātta. The word *magha*, by the *phiṭ-svara* rule, is antodātta (accented on the final syllable).

By the rule of the remaining accents (*śiṣṭasvara*)—"the word is anudātta except for one [syllable]"—the *a* following the *m* and the *a* following the *v* are both anudātta. [The subsequent *s* becomes] svarita according to the rule "after an udātta, an anudātta becomes svarita."

The vowel *a* following the letter *va* is circumflex (*svarita*). Thus, the form *maghavan* becomes accented on the middle syllable. This statement regarding the word *maghavan* refers to its Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). However, in the classical (*bhāṣya*) form of the word *maghavan*, the vowel *a* following the letter *va* is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix; the remaining vowels [are grave] by the rule of the rest (*śiṣṭasvara*).

The vowel *a* following the letter *m* and the vowel *a* following the letter *gh* are both unaccented (*anudātta*). Thus, the established rule is that the form *maghavan* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). Furthermore, such a word *maghavan* is common to both worldly (secular) and Vedic usage, as there is no evidence to restrict it to the Vedic domain alone. What [is the reason for this]?

And regarding the *sūtra* "ca ṭhvano ra ce" (Pāṇini 6.4.137), the *Bhāṣya* states: "The word *maghavan* is an un-derived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*). The point is that this word *maghavan* is also acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*) by the *phiṭ-svara* accentuation, common to both the world (*laukika*) and the Veda (*veda*), because there is no evidence for its being restricted to the Vedic domain alone.

In the *Śabdaratna*, however, there is no evidence for restricting the general application of the cited *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*— which state "it is not taught [by Pāṇini], for that is Vedic"— to the specific case of only those words with a middle-udātta accent.

Something exists. However, because numerous instances of error are observed among the usages of poets—such as in the case of the passage beginning "ṭha-tasthivāṃsaṃ nagaropakaṇṭhe"—even their usage does not serve to restrict the scope of the words of the Seers (ṛṣis). Therefore, [the rule applies] to every instance of the word *maghavan*.
It has been explained at length that [the form] is simply incorrect in common usage. Regarding the example *suṭi rājavat*:
the intention is that, in the alternative view where the suffix *tṛc* is absent, the long vowel occurs because the word ends in *n*.
(Pāṇini 6.4.133) *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite*.

When the rule "śasādāvaci maghavan as" (Pāṇini 6.4.133) and so forth is applicable, and the rule "allopo'naḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.134) would otherwise apply, [the following sūtra intervenes]: "śvayuvamaghonām. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan*. From the previous rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (Pāṇini 6.4.131), the term "saṃprasāraṇam" (vocalization) is understood to carry over.
The word "bhasya" (of a bha-stem) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). From the rule "allopo'naḥ," the term "anaḥ" (of *an*) is drawn back (*apakṛṣyate*).
That [term] qualifies each of the words *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* individually; thus, there is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that [stem] (*tadantavidhiḥ*).
He states the result: "of those ending in *an*" and so forth. By the rule "igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam," there is the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the letter *v*.

The *saṃprasāraṇa* is the vowel *u*. This means that because the substitution of *āT* does not occur for the word *aṣṭan* in the domain of the [nominative-accusative plural] endings *jas* and *śas* when it is used in a secondary (gauṇa) sense.

The phrase "only when [the word] is primary" means that in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, there is no evidence for adopting the view that the meaning of the word *aṣṭan* is the predominant factor, because it is indicated in the singular form as *aṣṭanaḥ*. The principle is: "Between the secondary and the primary, the grammatical operation applies to the primary."

It should be understood that even this [rule] does not apply here; for if it did, the plural number in *aṣṭābhya auṅ* would be rendered meaningless. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only when preceded by a consonant" (*halādau*), the exclusion of the *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) for the nominative and accusative dual endings (*jas-śas*) even in the alternative view is merely restated. However, in the case of *auṅ* and so forth...

Precisely because of the absence of the status of being *halādi* (beginning with a consonant), the application of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) does not occur. In the case of *priyāṣṭāḥ*, the intention is that when the nominative singular (*su*) follows, *ātva* is applied by the rule *ṭhaṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, and then *rutva* and *visarga* are applied. Furthermore, the rules *ṣaḍbhyo luk* and *ṣaṭcaturbhyaḥ* do not apply when [the word] is in its secondary (*gauṇa*) sense.

What was stated previously must not be forgotten. Thus, in all cases beginning with vowels (aj-ādi), the forms are exactly like those of *rājan*; in the case of suffixes beginning with consonants (hal-ādi), all forms [of *hāhā*] occur optionally. However, regarding suffixes beginning with consonants, there is another form as well, similar to that of *hāhā*, and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), also like *rājan*. Therefore, it is as follows here:
*Priyāṣṭan* (one who loves eight): *priyāṣṭāḥ*, *priyāṣṭānau*, *priyāṣṭānaḥ*;
*priyāṣṭānam*; *priyāṣṭānau*; *priyāṣṭnaḥ*; *priyāṣṭnaḥ*, *priyāṣṭābhyām*—*priyāṣṭabhyām*, *priyāṣṭābhiḥ*—*priyāṣṭabhyaḥ*.
*priyāṣṭnaḥ*, *priyāṣṭnoḥ*, *priyāṣṭnām*;

*priyāṣṭni*, *priyāṣṭani*, *priyāṣṭnoḥ*, *priyāṣṭāsu*—*priyāṣṭasu*. However, in reality, according to the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṣṇāntaṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 1.1.24), regarding the rule "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.2.84):

Having stated the exception (*apakarṣa*) regarding the rule *ṭhali*, a doubt was raised: "The forms *priyāṣṭau* and *priyāṣṭāḥ* are not established; rather, one would obtain only *priyaṣṭānau* and *priyaṣṭānaḥ*.

This was resolved by the principle: "According to the grammatical rule (*yathālakṣaṇam*), [the forms are correct] when they are not used [in actual speech]. Or rather: "The rule does not apply at all to what is not used."
"It proceeds [only] because it is the grammatical explanation of those very forms that have been applied," says Kaiyaṭa.
And thus, it is appropriate that these [forms] are not denoted at all. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the rule *aṣṭābhya auś*, it is stated:
"The substitution of *āT* for *aṣṭan* here is optional, since he makes a mention of that which has become *āT*—namely, *aṣṭābhya*."

Thus it has been stated: "Otherwise, he would have simply said 'aṣṭanaḥ'. However, if the word *priyāṣṭan* were actually in use in common worldly speech, then the mention of the plural number would be absolutely necessary to prevent the application of the substitute *auṭ* in its secondary (gauṇa) sense; therefore, [the absence of such a mention] is clearly inconsistent.

Therefore, the entire investigation into the usage of the word *priyāṣṭan* is merely a display of great ingenuity; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Thus end the words ending in *n*. Now, those ending in *dh*: from the root *budha* (in the sense of "understanding"), with the suffix *kvip* applied in the non-agentive sense (*akartari*), we have the word *budh*, which ends in the letter *dh*. From that...
Regarding the arising of the *sub* designation: he states the specific detail—namely, "the substitution of *bhaṣ*.

When the suffix *su* is elided by [Pāṇini 6.1.68] *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, then, either by resorting to the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that an operation dependent on a suffix applies even when the suffix is elided) because of the presence of the letter *s* following it, or because of its status as a word-final (*padānta*), the letter *b* is replaced by *bhaṣ*—that is, by the letter *bh*—in accordance with [Pāṇini 8.2.37] *ṭhékāco baśo bhaṣ*. This refers to the application of the *jhaś* and *cartva* rules.

The intention is that there is an option regarding the substitution of *c* (cartva) by the rule "ṭhvāvasāne. In the case of the suffixes beginning with *bhyām*, *padatva* is established by the rule "svādiṣu," which results in *bhaṣ*-substitution and then *jaś*-substitution.
Thus: *bhudbhyām*, *bhudbhiḥ*, *bhudbhyaḥ*, *bhutsu*. These are the forms ending in *dh*.
( ) *ṛtvig-dadhṛk-srag-diguṣṇigañcuyujikruñcāṃ ca* |3|2|59|. Now, those ending in *j*. Next, he states [the rule] to show the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *yuj*: *ṛtvig-dadhṛk*.
The governing term *dhātoḥ* (from a root) is understood. [This is derived] from the rule *spṛśo'nudake kvin*.

The term *kvin* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. Thus he says: "from these. This means: when the word *ṛtu* is the governing term (*upapada*), it applies to the verbal roots *yaj*, *dhṛṣ*, *sṛj*, *diś*, *ṣṇi*, *añc*, *yuj*, and *kruñc*. Now, one might object:
To the question, "Why do [phenomena] such as *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) and *dvitva* (reduplication) occur in words like *ṛtvij* and *dadhṛk*?

he says: "Even that which is not *lākṣaṇika*. That which is prescribed by the rules (*sūtra*) is *lākṣaṇika*. A grammatical operation (*kārya*) is [termed] *lākṣaṇika* even if it is not explicitly taught in the *sūtras*.

The meaning is that the established form is obtained through *nipātana* (irregular derivation) and the indication of the specific form. In this case, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *yaj* with *ṛtu* as the upapada.

Because the suffix is *kit*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "vacisvapiyajādīnām," and by the rule "vraśca," there is the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *j* to *g*), which is an exception to the application of *ṣatva*. For the root *dhṛṣ*, when *kvip* is applied, there is reduplication and the udātta accent on the final syllable.
And [the suffix *kvin* is applied] after the root *sṛj* in the sense of "stepping," with the augment *am*. After the root *diś*, *kvin* is applied in the sense of the object.

After the root *snih* preceded by the prefix *ud*, *kvin* is applied, with the elision of *ud* and *o*, and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. After the root *añc* when a *sup*-ending word is the upapada, *kvin* is applied. After the root *yuj* alone, *kvin* is applied. After the root *kruñc*, *kvin* is applied, with the absence of the elision of *n*.

It is elided. Although *añc* is mentioned in its isolated form, they say that due to its association with the word *uṣṇih*, only *añc* with a prefix is intended to be understood here. Regarding the phrase "from that which lacks a prefix": for the suffix *kvin*, the result of its application is precisely the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*) for the *n* of the *num* augment; and the *num* [is added] as well.

It will be explained only in the case of non-compounds (*asamāsa*). However, in compounds such as *suyuk*, since the result is already established by the substitution of a guttural (*kutva*) according to the rule *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ* for the *j* sound, there is no distinction between the suffixes *kvini* and *kvip*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "the suffix *kan* is elided": this is [derived] from the two rules *laśakvataddhite* and *halantyam*.

The remainder [is as follows]: the vowel *u* following the letter *v* is for the sake of pronunciation. Now, in order to state that a word ending in *kvip* possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of the rule "kṛt-taddhita" (Pāṇini 1.2.46), one must first establish that *kvip* has the technical designation of a *kṛt* suffix. This is stated in the sūtra: "kṛd atiṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.93).
Now, to declare that a word ending in *kvip* is a nominal stem according to the rule "kṛt-taddhita," [one establishes] the *kṛt* designation of *kvip*.

He demonstrates this with the example *kadatiṅ*. The governing rule (*adhikṛta*) is "after a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and "an affix" (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, "after a verbal root" is a qualifier of that which is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*).
By this, the meaning obtained is: "an affix prescribed after a verbal root. That is to say, it is an affix prescribed under the governing rule "after a verbal root."

He says this with the words "when [the suffix] is present. By this, the application of the causative marker *ṇic* and others is excluded. When the form *yuj-v* has been established, [the rule applies]:
"The *v* of an *apṛkta* [suffix] is elided" (Pāṇini 6.1.67).

The term *lopa* (elision) is understood from the rule *lopo vyoḥ*. The suffixes beginning with *kvip*, which have dropped their indicatory letters (*utsṛṣṭānubandhāḥ*), are included here by the word *veḥ*. The letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation, because of the mention of *apṛkta*; thus he says: "of the *apṛkta* [suffix] *va*."

Why does it say "of that which is not followed by a suffix" (*apṛktasya*)? [Consider the example: *jāgṛviḥ*. He states the purpose of the designation *kṛt* for the suffix *kvip*: [it is so that] the rule *kṛt-taddhita-...* applies.
[Also, the rule] *yujo 'samāse* (Pāṇini 7.1.71) [is applicable].
In the case of *yuj* when not in a compound: from the rule *ṭhugidacām*, the term *sarvanāmasthāne* is understood to follow;
and from the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*, the term *num* is also understood.
Thus he says, "there shall be *num*, etc. When *yunj* remains [after the application of rules], the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) proceeds as follows:

He demonstrates this by saying "there is elision of *su*. The intention is that because it is subsequent, *num* occurs first, and then there is the elision of the consonant and the following vowel (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*). Regarding "elision of the final member of a conjunct" (*saṃyogānta-lopa*), the word "of the letter *j*" is to be supplied as the remainder.
[Pāṇini 8.2.62: "The *k* substitute for a *kvip* suffix."

*kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ* (The *k* substitute occurs for a suffix ending in *kvip*). The phrase *ṭh-padasya* (of a word) is understood as the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). From the rule *ṭhjhalāñ-jaśo'nte* (jhaś letters are replaced by jaś letters at the end [of a word]), the word *ante* (at the end) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here. The term *kvin-pratyayaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which the suffix *kvip* has been elided. It does not mean "that which ends in *kvip*"; for if that were the case, [the rule would apply to] *kvinaḥ*...

One should simply say "kuḥ," because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) yields the meaning "that which ends in the *kvip* affix. This is what he states with the words beginning "the affix *kvip* from which...
As for the purpose of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, it will be explained in the root text itself during the analysis of the word *ghṛtaspṛś*.

In the word *kur*, the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) is understood because it is marked with the *u* indicatory letter (*udit*). In the rule regarding what is not desired to be elided (*aṇ-itsūtra*), the phrase "the suffix *ṭha*" is connected only with the term *aṇ*, and not with the *udit* letters, due to the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of the *u* indicatory letter. Therefore, even though *ku* is being prescribed [as a substitute], it includes its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrāhaka*). Now, as for the substitution of *k* for *n*...

The five sounds *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa* would all be subject to substitution [for one another] by turns, because there is no proximity (*āntarya*) among them in terms of place of articulation (*sthāna*), and because proximity in terms of the effort of contact (*spṛṣṭa-prayatna*) is common to all five; furthermore, [there would be proximity] between the letter *na*— which possesses voicing (*ghoṣa*), closure (*saṃvāra*), and nasality (*nādavat*), as well as being weakly articulated (*alpaprāṇavat*)— and the letter *ga*.

Because of its internal proximity (*āntarya*). Therefore, he says: "of that" (*tasya*). The sense is: because of the internal proximity [of the letter *ṇ*] to the location of the nose (*nāsikā-sthāna*).
Regarding the word *yuṅ*: the root *yujir* means "to join"; it belongs to the *rudhādi* class. It is called *yuṅ* because it joins (*yunakti*).
When the augment *num* is applied, the rule "the gutturals for the palatals" (*coḥ kuḥ*) does not apply to the *n* of that [augment].

The rule beginning with *ṭh-kvan-pratyayasya* is introduced. Now, he states the specific rule regarding the case endings *āṬ*, *jas*, and so on: *naśca*. Regarding *numaḥ*: the remainder [of the definition] is "prescribed by the rule *yujerasamāse*" (Pāṇini 7.1.71). Regarding *parasavarṇaḥ*: the *ñakāra* is the *parasavarṇa* [substitute] for the *anusvāra* according to the rule *anusvārasya yayi* (Pāṇini 8.4.58), as it is produced in the nose (*nāsikā*) and is nasalized (*tālavya*).
The intended meaning is "due to proximity. By this, forms such as *yuñjau* are established. Now, one might ask:
why does the substitution of *k* (known as *kutva*) not occur here for the letter *ñ*, according to the rule *ṭhcoḥ ku* [Pāṇini 8.2.30], when a *jhali* sound follows the letter *j*?
To this, he says: "of that" (*tasya*). This means "of the *parasavarṇa* [substitute]. As in *yugbhyām*. [This is governed by] *ṭhsvādiṣu* [Pāṇini 1.4.17].
The intention is that because *ja* is a *padādi* (initial in a word), it becomes *ga*.
[Pāṇini 8.2.30] states: *coḥ kuḥ* ("*cu* [consonants] become *ku* [gutturals]").
Intending to explain the word *suyuj*, which is an exception (*vyāvartya*) to the rule *ṭhasamāse*, he says therein: "In *yukṣu*."
He states the specific rule: *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30). From the previous rule *jhalo jhalī*, the term *jhalī* is understood by anuvṛtti.
The governing term *padasya* (of a word) is also in force. From the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, the term *ante* (at the end) is understood;
thus he says, "of the *ca*-class. Now, regarding the vowel *u* in the word *coḥ*:

If it is argued that there can be no inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) here because the vowel *u* lacks the status of being *udit* due to the absence of an explicit instruction (*upadeśa*), we say no; for by the very force of the mention of the form ending in *u* in the rule *cori*, the status of *u* as *udit* is permitted therein. Otherwise, [the author] would have simply said *ṭhcaḥ kuḥ*. This refers to the substitution of *ku*.

The meaning is that in the word *suyuj*, the substitution of *j* by *g* (known as *kutva*) occurs because of the commonality of being voiced (*ghoṣa*), having internal breath (*saṃvāra*), being sonant (*nāda*), and having slight aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*), as well as by virtue of the rule regarding their respective order. Now, one might ask:
why does the *kutva* substitution not occur here simply by the rule "of the suffix *kvip*"? Even though [the root] *yuja* is preceded by *su*.

By the rule *satsūdviṣa* etc., the word *suyuj* in this compound with an *upapada* is not itself *kvin*-ending; for it was stated immediately below that the suffix *kvin* is applied to the root *yuji* when it is without an *upapada*.
Nevertheless, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* analysis—namely, "that from which the suffix *kvin* [is derived]"—it is so now.

Even though it ends in the *kvip* suffix, the substitution of *k* (kutva) occurs by this very rule; therefore, he says: "because the substitution of *k* for the *kvip* suffix is not established (*asiddha*). Thus, the intended meaning is that in this case, the application of "the substitution of *k* for the two [sounds] *c* and *j*" (*coḥ ku*) alone is proper. *Suyuk-suyug*: here there is an option for the substitution of *c* (cartva) according to the rule "optionally at the end of a word" (*vā-avasāne*). Now, an objection:

How could the form *yug* also be desired [as a valid derivation], since the suffix *kvip* and the augment *num* are applied specifically to the root *yuñj*? Furthermore, in the sūtras *ṛtvig...* and *yujerasamāse*,
there is the mention of *yuj* specifically as characterized by the vowel *i* (i.e., *yuj-i*), which refers to the root *yuj* belonging to the *divādi* class meaning "to concentrate" (*samādhi*).

It should not be argued that because [the word] ending in *akāra* is not included, the form *yuk* is established by applying *kvip* according to the rule *ṭhkvip ca*, which results in the absence of *num* and the substitution of *ku*;
for since the suffix *ik* (as in *ik-śtipau dhātunirdeśe*) can apply to both cases,
*kvip* would be applied after both, resulting in *num*.
To the objection that [the suffix] *apit* is indeed attached [to the root], he says: "of *yuj*" (*yujeḥ*).

In the rule *yujerasamāse*, as well as in the rule *ṛtvigādi* where the form *yuj* occurs, and in the Dhātupāṭha where the root is read as *yujir yoge* (with the vowel *i*), it is precisely that [root] characterized by the vowel *i* which is understood here as having the letter *r* at its head; it is not the [root] ending in *ik*.

*Nirdeśaḥ* means "because of the explanation. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: *tena*. [The root] *khaj* (in the sense of "lameness in movement") takes the suffix *kvip*; because it is marked with *id*, the augment *num* is added. By the rule *naścāpadāntasya*, the anusvāra is substituted, and by the rule for *parasavarṇa*, it becomes the letter *ñ*. Thus, the word *khañj* is formed; he states its specific characteristic as *saṃyogānta* ("ending in a conjunct consonant").

By the rule *halṅyādi*, there is elision of the suffix *su*; then, by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, there is elision of the final consonant *j*. Consequently, due to the removal of the cause (*nimitta*), the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa* are also removed. The resulting form is *khann*. This is the meaning.
There is no elision of the nasal *n* by the rule *ṭhaniditām*, because [the root] is marked with the *idit* designation. [The root] *rājṛ* means "to shine."

Thus, from this [root], the word *rāj* is formed by means of the *kvip* suffix. He states its specific grammatical rule: "by *vraśca*. When the case-ending *su* is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.36). By the rule *jaś* (Pāṇini 8.4.53), the letter *ḍ* is substituted.
By the rule *vāvasāne* (Pāṇini 8.4.56), there is an optional substitution of *c*. In the forms beginning with *bhyām*, [the case-endings] are included under the category *svādiṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.17).

Because it is a pada, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, and the substitution of the *jaś* sounds. Thus, *rāḍbhyām* and so forth. Considering the optional application of *dhuṭ* by the rule *ṭhṅḥ si dhuṭ*, he says: *rāṭtsu*, *rāṭsv*. Similarly for *vibhrāḍ*.
The meaning is that the rules for the substitution of *ṣ* and so on apply just as they do for the word *rājan*. [The root] *ṭua bhrājṛ* (to shine) takes the suffix *kvip*. It is distinguished...

"Vibhrāt" means "one who shines. "Deveṭ" means "one who sacrifices to the gods. In the analysis of the compound *devān yajati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; because the root *yaj* belongs to the *yaja*-class, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *ava-ci-sva-pi*. Then, by the rule *ṭh-ad-guṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding "viśvasṛṭ": from the root *sṛj* (meaning "emission") with the suffix *kvip*, the change to *ṣ* and so forth occurs by the rule *vraśca*. Now, [an objection]:

One might ask: "Even when the word *devaj* ends in *kvip* and the word *viśvasṛj* also ends in *kvip*, why does the substitution of *k* for *j* (the *kutva* change) not occur here as well, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as 'that from which the suffix *kvin* [is elided]'—just as it does in the word *ṛtvij*?
To this, he says: "In this case," referring to the rule *sṛjidṛśo 'ri* and the rule concerning *kāmyac*.

The meaning is that, due to the usage in the Bhāṣya such as *viśvasṛgbhyām* and *upayakāmyati*, there is no *kutva* (the change of a semivowel to its corresponding stop) by the rule *kvinpratyayasya*. Regarding *parimṛḍ*: from the root *mṛj* in the sense of "cleansing," with the suffix *kvip*;
because of the prohibition [of vṛddhi] by the rule *kṅiti ca*, the rule *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* does not apply.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *ṭhvraśca*. That which wipes around (*parimārṣṭi*) is *parimṛṭ*. Now, regarding *vibhrāk*, this is a sūtra from the *ĀṬṇādi* group. From the preceding sūtra, *kvip* and *dīrgha* (long vowel) are carried over by the phrase "after *kvip*, *vac*, *pracch*, etc. The term *padānta* (end of a word) is connected only with the term *ṣ* [in the rule *ṣṭuanunāsike ca*].

But [the suffix] *kvip* does not apply even after [a root ending in] a long vowel, according to the explanation. Thus he says: "when *para* is the *upapada*, etc. And regarding *ṣatvam*: the intention is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "ṭhcoḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30).
In the sense of "he shines in the universe," when *kvip* is applied by the rule "satsūdviṣa... (Pāṇini 3.2.61) and there is a compound with the *upapada*, [the form is derived].
The words beginning with *viśvarāj*. (Pāṇini 6.3.128) [states]: "After *viśva*, [the final vowel of] *vasu* and *rāj* [is lengthened].
He states its specific detail: "after *viśva*, *vasu*. From the rule "ḍhralope" [it follows that] there is "lengthening" (*dīrgha*).
This [rule] continues to apply. Thus he says: "of the word *viśva*. Regarding *viśvavasu*:
the lexicon states, "The word *vasu* [is used] for a planet, fire, a yoktra, a horse, water, wealth, and a jewel.
The example "*viśvāvasu*" is incidental. [As in: "the Ādityas and the Viśvavasus."

In the usage of Amara, however, the vowel is not long, because the term "saṃjñā" (name) is understood to be carried over from the rule *nare saṃjñāyām*.
