Now, one might object that since the word *rāṭ* is cited here with the substitution of *ṭ* for *d*, the substitution of *j* for *d* would apply, and thus the vowel would not be long; to this he says: *rāḍ iti*.
"It is not intended to be expressed"—this is the sense, meaning it follows from the commentary. Regarding *viśvārāṭ* and *viśvārāḍ*:

the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ṭh-vraśca*. Then the substitutions of *jaś* and *car* apply. Since the mention of *car* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the end of a word (*padānta*), the long vowel [occurs] even in the alternative case of *jaś*-substitution; for although the rule *ṭh-vraśca* belongs to the final third of the grammar (*traipādika*).

Although the substitution of *k* (by the rule *ṣatvaṃ ṭhcoḥ kuḥ*) occurs after [the *ṣ*], nevertheless, in cases such as *vraśca* where the word ends in a *c*-class consonant (*cavarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* takes precedence because it is an exception (*apavāda*), and thus it is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). This is according to Viśvarāja’s statement: "An exception prevails by virtue of the authority of the specific rule. The intention is that there is no lengthening of the vowel because the word does not end in a suffix (*apadāntatvāt*). [The root] *bhrasj* [is used] in the sense of "cooking" (*pāke*) with the suffix *kvip*.

By the rule *grahijyā*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), whereby the letter *r* becomes *ṛ*. By the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the single substitute is the preceding form. Thus, the word *bhṛj* is formed. Then, the case endings (*sup*) arise.
[Then applies: *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29).
Regarding this, he states the specific rule: *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*. The term *padasya* (of a word) is understood from the governing context.

Because of the word *ca* (and), the term *jhalī* (when followed by a *jhal* consonant) is carried over from the rule *jhalo jhalī*. Thus, both *ante* (at the end of a word) and *jhalī* are connected with the word *saṃyoga* (conjunction). In the term *saṃyoge*, the genitive case ending is elided.
The term is analyzed as *pṛthak-padam* (separate words). The analysis of *skau* is *saśca kaśca skau*, "the two [sounds] *s* and *k*.

From the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* ("there is elision of a final conjunct"), the word *lopaḥ* ("elision") is understood to carry over. Thus he says, beginning with "at the end of a word," and so forth.
Here, in the example *kāṣṭhaśak sthātā*, since the *k* is at the beginning of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) followed by a *jhal* sound, there arises the contingency of its elision.
To prevent that [undesired application], the Vārttika is recited: "Instead of saying *jhalī*, it should be stated as *saṅī*.

This refers to a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term) beginning with the *s* of *san* and ending with the *ṅ* of *āmahiṅ*. This Vārttika has been rejected in the Bhāṣya with the remark: "Since even the woodpecker (*kāṣṭhaśak*) does not exist, how could there be two woodpeckers standing? (*kutaḥ kāṣṭhaśak sthāte*).

The intention is that there is no *kvip* suffix after roots ending in the letter *k*, because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage (*anabhidhānāt*). Nor should it be argued that the Vārttika "saṅī" is necessary to prevent the elision of the letter *k* in the form *pṛthak-sthātā*.

This is clear from the *Śabdenduśekhara*, which states that precisely because of the authority of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) rejecting those [rules], it is understood that examples suitable for the application of elision of *saṃyoga* and so forth of this kind are not used. Regarding *bhṛṭ-bhṛḍ*: when *bhṛsj* remains as *bhṛs j*, after the elision of the suffix by *halṅyādi* and the elision of the *s* by *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ kvoḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *j* by *vraścādi*, followed by *jaśtva* and *cartva*; such is the intended meaning.

Although *bhṛṣ* + *j* would result in *bhṛṭ* or *bhṛḍ*—since the *j* would be elided by the rule for the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the *s* would become *ṣ* by *ṭhvraśca*, and then the *ṣ* would undergo *jaś*-ness and *cartva*—nevertheless, because it is the more logical course, only the elision of the initial member of the conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) occurs here. Regarding the phrase "of the *s*" (*sasya*): in forms such as *bhṛsja* + *au*, there is no elision of the initial member of the conjunct because the *s* is not preceded by a *jhal* consonant at the end of a word. The intention is that, since the *jaś*-ness [of the *s*] is not established by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the *ścutva* (change to *ś*) applies to the *s*. Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*): it means "of the *ś*."

Because the letter *ś* has the palate (*tālu*) as its place of articulation, it is replaced by *j*. One should not suspect that the substitution of *ṣ* for *ś* (by the rule *vraśca-*) would apply here on the grounds that the substitution of *jaś* is considered *asiddha*; for the substitution of *ścu* is *asiddha* with respect to the substitution of *ṣ*. However, in forms such as *vyām*, there is the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*) because the word-status (*padatva*) applies by the rule *su-ādiṣu*. Then, the substitution of *ṣ* by *vraśca-* and the substitution of *jaś* take effect. [The forms] *bhṛḍbhyam* and so forth follow. Regarding the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā*: the root *ṛ* means "to go," and the suffix *tu* belongs to the *uṇādi* group. "Season" (*ṛtu*) refers to the act of going; what is intended here is the attainment of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā-dravya*).

In the sense of "they sacrifice" or "they perform sacrificial acts" (*yajanti-yajñiya-vyāpāram kurvanti*) upon the upapada *ṛtu*, the suffix *kvin* is applied to the root *yaj*. By the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *y* into *i*; this results in the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*), followed by the *yaṇ*-substitution. Thus, the form *ṛtvij* is established. Then, the case-ending *su* is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Having taken this much for granted, he says: "Because it ends in *kvin*, there is *kutva*. The remainder of the thought is that this is done by the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*. The implication is that the very prescription of the suffix *kvin* is for this specific purpose.

Nor should it be argued that this is already established by the substitution of *k* for *c* and *ū* [via the rule *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ*]; for the substitution of *k* by the rule *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ* would be sublated by the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ṭhvraśce*, since the latter is an exception (*apavāda*) to the former. However, the substitution of *k* by the rule *ṭhkvinpratyayasya* is not sublated precisely because of the specific force (*sāmarthya*) of the rule prescribing *kvin*. This is because the prescription of *ṣ* in forms such as *yaṣṭṛ* has its own scope of application. As for *ūrka* and *ūrk*: from the root *ūrj* (meaning "to strengthen" or "to give life") belonging to the *curādi* class, the suffix *kvip* is added after the causative marker (*ṇic*), resulting in the elision of *ṇi*; thus the form *ūrk* is obtained.

Then, by the rule *sor halṅyādi-lopaḥ*, there is the elision of the suffix *su*. By the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, the *j* (of *tyaj*) undergoes *kutva*, becoming *g*. By the rule *vā-avasāne*, there is an optional change to *c* (i.e., *k*). One should not suspect that the elision of the *ṇi* (in *tyā-j-i*) would act as a *sthānivadbhāva* when *kutva* is to be applied; for that is prohibited in the case of operations concerning the end of a word (*padānta-vidhi*), and because of the explicit statement: "In the case of what is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*. Thus end those ending in *j*. Now, those ending in *d* are examined. The word *tyad* is a synonym for the word *tad*. Regarding its specific modification, he says: "The substitution of *at* for *tyad*-class words [occurs], and there is the single-substitute form (*pararūpatva*)."

The meaning is that when any case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises everywhere, the final *d* is replaced by *a* according to the rule *tyadādīnām a*, and then the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied according to the rule *ato guṇe*. Thus, the sense is that the forms are like those ending in short *a* (*adanta*). When the form *tya s* remains: [the rule applies] *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.106), which means *tadoḥ saḥ sau*. [This is governed by] *tyadādīnām aḥ*.

The meaning is that [the substitute] follows from that [original]. Regarding "of the letters *ta* and *da*": the analysis of the rule is *taśca daśca* (both *ta* and *da*). The meaning is that the letter *a* after the *ta* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding "it would be *sa*":
even in the substitute, the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding "*tyau*": because it is stated as *sāu*, [the *au* is for the sake of pronunciation].

The meaning is "existence" (*satvam*). Regarding *tye*: because it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the rule for the substitution of *śī* for the nominative plural suffix *jas* applies; this is the intended meaning. This [mention of *tye*] is also an illustration for *smāy* and the other case endings. [The forms are: *tyam*, *tyau*, *tyān*; *tyena*, *tyābhyām*, *tyaiḥ*; *tyasmai*, *tyābhyām*, *tyebhyaḥ*; *tyasmāt*; *tyayoḥ*; *tyeṣām*.
In that [context], in these [words]. Thus, the word *tad*. Regarding "paramasa":
the intention is that because the substitution of *at* and so forth belongs to the *aṅga* (the stem), it applies even when [the suffix] ends in that [stem].
Now, since the word *yuṣmad* also belongs to the *tyadādi* group, in its first-person singular form *tvam*, [the rule] "of *tad* and *doḥ*" [would apply].
To the question, "Why should there not be *sa* for the form *sau*? he says: "up to two" (*dviparyanta*).

The meaning is that the Vārttika—"only those ending with the number two are desired"—which is read under the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ*, also applies here to the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*. What follows from this?

He says: "Not so. He states what is intended by the word *iha*: "you" (*tvam*). The point is that the word *yuṣmad* is recited in the *sarvādi* group immediately after the word *dvi*. [Objection: But surely, by the very force of the pronunciation of the letter *t* in the rule "ṭhvāhau sau," there is no substitution of *s* for *tvam* here; otherwise, [the rule would have been unnecessary].

One should simply say "ṭh svāhau sau". Anticipating the objection that the continued application (anuvṛtti) of the rule "of those ending in two [consonants]" would thus be redundant here, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
The syntactical connection is as follows: one should not say that the substitution of *s* (satva) does not occur here on the strength of the phonetic utterance of the letter *t*.

Regarding the word *atitvam*: if the phrase *dviparyantānām* ("of those ending in two [sounds]") were not understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then *satva* (the substitution of *s*) would also occur in the form *tvam*. Nor is the pronunciation of the letter *t* in the rule *tvāhau sau* redundant;
for in the case of the secondary (*gauṇa*) usage *atitvam*—meaning "one who has surpassed you"—where the word *yuṣmad* undergoes the substitution *tvad*, the rule *tvāhau* would otherwise apply.

The meaning is that the purpose for pronouncing the letter *t* has already been achieved. Nor should it be argued that, because the substitution of *s* would be unavoidable even in the case of *atitvam*, the pronouncing of the letter *t* in *tvāhau* is useless; for the substitution of *s* is a grammatical operation belonging to the sub-group (*gaṇa*) beginning with *sarva*, and thus [the rule] does not apply to the secondary sense (*gauṇa*).
Because it does not apply there. For this very reason, he says: "in the case of *saṃjñā*. Regarding *tyad*: this is the name of a certain person. Regarding *atityad*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has transcended *tyad*. Regarding *ya*:

when the word *yad* undergoes the substitution of *tyad*-class elements and the replacement by the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), its forms are like those of the word *sarva*. Due to the absence of the letter *t*, the substitution of *s* (*satva*) does not occur.

Regarding the word *eṣa*: when the word *etad* undergoes the substitution of the *tyad*-class elements (*tyadādyatva*) and the subsequent monophthongization (*pararūpatva*), its forms are exactly like those of *sarva*.

However, the specific distinction is that in the nominative singular (*sau*), there is the substitution of *s* for the letter *t*. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of subsequent reference" (*anvādeśe tu*):
the intention is that the rule *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* applies to the word *etad* as well.

*ReĀ prathamayoram* | Pāṇini 7.1.28. Now he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. In the rule *ReĀ prathamayoram*, the phrase "from *yuṣmadasmadbhyām*" is carried over from the preceding rule *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso'ś*.
The word *para* (subsequent) must be supplied [from the previous rule]. The form *ReĀ* is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided.
The *Bhāṣya* states that the expression *prathamayoḥ* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer to the first and second case endings (*vibhakti*).

This is what he expresses by saying "from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, etc. Once the substitution of *am* for the nominative singular suffix (*su*) has been made, [the prohibition] "not before a case ending" (*na vibhaktau*) applies.
Thus, there is no substitution of *m* for *as*. The forms *yuṣmad-am* and *asmad-am* remain.

Regarding the word "adhikṛtya" (with reference to), the ellipsis is "grammatical operations (*kāryāṇi*) will be stated. (Pāṇini 7.2.94: *tvāhau sau* (the substitutes *tvā* and *ah* occur in place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*).

*tvāhau sau*: *tva* and *aha* become *tvāhau* [before the nominative singular suffix *su*]. The rule *maparyantasya* ("of that which ends in *m*") is understood as the governing heading. From the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*, the term *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* ("of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*") is carried over. Thus he says: "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" and so forth. [The forms are] *tva ad am* and *aha ad am*.

It is established. Although the substitution of *tvad* for the word *yuṣmad* is already accomplished by the rule "ṭhtvamāvekavacane" (Pāṇini 7.2.97), nevertheless, the explicit prescription of *tva* for *yuṣmad* here is for the sake of the *tvad* substitution in the form *atitvam* ("one who has surpassed you"). For that [substitution] does not apply there [in the case of *atitvam*] by virtue of the rule "ṭhtvamāvekavacane."

Regarding the term "pravṛtti" (occurrence): here, the word *yuṣmad* occurs as qualified by plurality (*bahutva*). For the word "singular" (*ekavacana*) in that context denotes an occurrence qualified by singularity (*ekatva*), and not a suffix bearing the technical name "singular"; this will be explained immediately below.

*Śeṣe lopaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.1.63. "In the remaining cases, there is elision. From the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (7.2.84), the phrase "before a case-ending" (*ā vibhaktau*) is understood to carry over. The term "before a case-ending," which has been carried over, connects with the word "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*).

Since the substitution of *ā* (in *yuṣmad-ādeśa*) and *ya* (in *asmad-ādeśa*) have already been prescribed by the rules "ṭhyuṣmadasmadoranādeśe," "ṭhdvitīyāyāṃ ca," "ṭhprathamāyāśca dvivacane bhāṣāyām," and "ṭhyo'ci," the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) here refers to case-endings other than those specific instances.
The phrase "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtta*); thus he says: "of the *āt* and *yat* [substitutions].

Regarding the word "final" (*antyasya*), it is obtained through the paribhāṣā rule "the substitute takes the place of the final phoneme" (*alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*). Here, the inclusion of the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) as a qualifier for the case-ending is merely for the sake of clarity, because within its own scope, the *āt* and *yat* substitutions are specifically prescribed by other rules.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the present sūtra (*bādhasaṃbhavāt*) and on the sūtra *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso’ś*. Therefore, [the rule] *guṇe* [applies].
The meaning is that there is a substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the two preceding *a*-sounds. This occurs in the case of *tva am* and *aha am*.

Anticipating the objection regarding the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* rule, he says: "In the case of *ami*, the preceding [vowel]. Here he raises an objection with the word "nanu.
According to Amarasimha, "nanu" is used in the sense of expressing an objection (*virodhokti*); that is to say, in the sense of a doubt (*śaṅkā*).
He states "because it is internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*): because the feminine suffix *ṭāp* [prescribed] by the rule *ajādyataḥ* does not depend on any external cause.

It should be understood that [the substitution] is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the *pararūpa* [substitution]. He refutes [this objection] by accepting half [of its validity], saying: "True. It is accepted that [the substitution] is more internal than the *pararūpa*; however, the meaning is that its actual application (*pravṛtti*) is not accepted here. [This is because] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are without gender (*aliṅga*).

This is read in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *sāma ākam*. Because the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* here refer to the actual form of the words (*śabdasvarūpa*), they are neuter. Precisely because they refer to the word-form, the rule *tyadādīni sarvair nityam* does not apply to form a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*), as is also evident from the usage in the Bhāṣya itself. Therefore, [the form is] *tena*.

The meaning is "by way of not being a gender marker" (*aliṅgatvena*). Now, an objection is raised: in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *ṛṅeḥ prathamayoḥ*, it is argued that since the substitution of *n* in forms such as *yuṣmān* and *asmān* (in the masculine) is already established by the rule *tasmāc chaso na puṃsi*, the prescription of *n* in the rule *śaso na* would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, [the author] considers the feminine and neuter genders.

In the examples "yuṣmān brāhmaṇīḥ paśya," "asmān brāhmaṇīḥ paśya," "yuṣmān brāhmaṇakulāni paśya," and "asmān brāhmaṇakulāni paśya," it is established that the rule "śaso ne" prescribes the substitution of *n* for the sake of nasalization (*natva*). Furthermore, this occurs within the governing context of the rule "svamornapuṃsakāt."

In the sūtra *ṭhnetarāc chandasi*, as well as in the Vārttika and its Bhāṣya stating that "the substitutes for the case-endings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [take precedence] over the neuter substitutes by way of *vipratiṣedha*," it is established that the substitutes *tvā* and *āha* etc.
for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* take precedence over the neuter forms prescribed for the neuter gender, such as *śi*, *luka*, and *num*.
A contradiction has been raised; therefore, it is untenable that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* lack gender.

As for the statement in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *sāma ām*—"the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are without gender"—it means that they lack a specific gender (masculine, feminine, or neuter) when not used in proximity with other words possessing those specific genders.

It is stated clearly in that very Bhāṣya that [the rule] is intended only to mean "it is not understood from the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. And thus, because the feminine gender of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would make the suffix *ṭāp* unavoidable, he says "or rather" (*yadvā*) out of dissatisfaction with that view. [He explains: "by intending to express the sense of location (*adhikaraṇatva*). [This is so] because of the principle of "intention" (*vivakṣā*).

The intention is that this will be stated later, namely, "the case-factors (kārakas) [become the remainder]. For if "in the remainder" (*śeṣe*) were a qualifier of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it would be entirely redundant;
because the specific rules for *ātva* and *yatva* would suffice to sublate the elision (*lopa*) within their own scope. Therefore, [it qualifies] the remainder (*śeṣasya*).

The meaning "in place of" (sthāne) must be adopted. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "by that" (tena). This means by resorting to the sense of "in place of the remainder" (śeṣasya sthāne). Regarding the phrase "from the end of 'm'" (maparyantāt): the sense is that the word "of that which ends in m" (maparyantasya), having been drawn down [from a previous rule], is transformed into a form ending in the ablative case. And this [applies] to the rule "tyadādīnām aḥ."

"In the Sūtra, the elision of the *ṭi* [the final vowel and following consonant] must be performed for the sake of preventing the occurrence of the genitive suffix *ṣṭāp*; this is what was traditionally taught. Or else, "by means of the 'remainder-saptamī' (*śeṣasaptamī*), the elision is prescribed for the remainder.
This is clear from the Vārttika and its Bhāṣya. Nor, when the substitutes *tva* and *aha* have been applied to that which precedes the final *m*, is there anything remaining...

It should not be said that there is no "remnant" (*śeṣa*) beyond the limit of *m* in *adityasya*; for although at the time when the elision of *a* (*allopa`) is about to take effect— once the substitutes *tvā* and *āha* have been applied—
the word *ad-* is no longer a remnant of what precedes the limit of *m*, it was nonetheless a remnant of the word *ad-* prior to the application of the substitutes *tvā* and *āha*.

Even so, when *tva* + *ad-am* and *aha* + *ad-am* are established, since the elision (*lopa*) of *ad-* takes precedence over the formation of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), the suffix *ṭāp* would be unavoidable because the stem ends in *ad*. Therefore, he says:
"And that... The meaning is that there is elision according to the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*. [The phrase] "in the case of the internal" refers to the rule *ato guṇe*.
It should be understood that [the substitution] is *antaraṅga* (internal) in comparison to the elision (*lopa*) which depends on an external case-ending (*bahirbhūtavibhakti*).

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of being *adanta*" (ending in /a/): when *tva* + *ad* and *aha* + *ad* undergo the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), resulting in *tvad* and *ahad*, the elision of *ad* occurs; however, because *tv* and *ah* no longer end in /a/ (*adanta*), [the rule does not apply].

The meaning is *ṭāp*. Regarding "supremacy" (*paramatvam*): the intention is that because rules such as "ReĀ prathamayoḥ" apply to the entire complex, there is an extension of the rule to include what ends with that suffix (*tadantavidhi*). Regarding "atitvam":
the intention is that there is no evidence for these rules, such as "ReĀ prathamayoḥ," to fail to apply when the term is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).

*Yuvāvau dvivacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.92). When *yuṣmad-āṬ* and *asmad-āṬ* are present, and after *am* has been applied by the rule *reĀ prathamayor am*, resulting in *yuṣmad-am* and *asmad-am*, [the rule] *yuvāvau dvivacane* applies.
In the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*).
The term *maparyantasya* is supplied from a previous context. *Uktiḥ* means "utterance. *Dvivacanam* is an utterance consisting of two;
the meaning there is "of those two [words] that are semantically capable" (*samarthayoḥ*). This amounts to saying: "of those two which express a meaning qualified by duality."
The meaning is "when a suffix bearing the technical name *dvivacana* follows," because of the force of the mention of the word *vacana* (number).

Otherwise, he would have simply said "in the case of duality" (*dvitve*). Since the phrase "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) from the rule "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*), [the meaning is] when that case-ending which occurs in the state of duality follows.
This is because of the attainment of the intended meaning. Thus he says: "When two [words] are mentioned," and so forth.

The result of adopting [the reading] "when two are mentioned" will become clear later in the root text itself. Furthermore: "The first [case-ending] is used in the non-dual number in the common language. (Pāṇini 7.2.88)

When *yuva-* and *āva-* are established [as substitutes], the rule "there is elision of the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) would otherwise apply; however, this is superseded by the rule "and in the dual of the nominative" (*prathamāyāśca dvivacane*).
From the rule "of *aṣṭan* before a case-ending, *āt*" (*aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*), the mention of *āt* (*āgrahaṇam*) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).
And from the rule "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when not in the place of a substitute" (*yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*), the mention of *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* also carries over.
He says this with the word "iha" (here). The meaning is: when the first dual case-ending follows in the *bhāṣā* (vernacular).

As for the term "in the *bhāṣā*," its meaning is "in common worldly usage. [The forms] "yuvām" and "āvām" arise from the substitution of *ā* for the letter *d* in the forms "yuva-ad-am" and "āva-ad-am."

The sense is that when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule applies to the two preceding *a*s, and subsequently the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same class) rule applies, [the form is established] by the principle "in the case of *ṭha*, the preceding [vowel is substituted].

The point is that it would be more appropriately stated as "āṬṅī" alone, because the substitution of *ātva* is desired even in the dual of the second person. Thus, in the case of "yuvaṃ vastrāṇi," when *yuṣmad* is followed by *āṬ*, [the form *yuva* is derived] for that which ends in *map*.
The form [is derived] when the substitutes *yu* and *ava* have been applied and the remainder has been elided. [The question] "Why [specify] 'of that which ends in *map*'?

is asked because even if the substitutes *yu* and *ava* were applied to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* as whole words, the forms *yuvām* and *āvām* would still be established through the application of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) and the subsequent formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*). [The answer is: "[It must be stated] 'of that which possesses the augment *ka*' (*sākackasya*')."
By the rule *ṭhavyayasarvanāmnām iti*, *aK* is inserted before the final *ṭi*; thus, we have *yuṣmaka-d-āU* and *asmaka-d-āU*.

Then, by the rule *ṭhReĀ prathamayo'rityami*, *am* is substituted for *ReĀ*. By the rule *ṭhyuvāvau dvivacane*, the substitutions *yu* and *āva* apply to both [forms] together; and because they fall within that [complex form], the rule *ṭhtanmadhyapatitanyāyena* applies, resulting in the forms *yuvābhyām* and *āvābhyām* by the rule *ṭhprathamāyāśca*.

If the vowel *ā* were substituted for the letter *d* [in *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] before the case-ending *am*, and the preceding vowel were elided, the forms would simply be *yuvām* and *āvām*; the letter *k* would not be heard. This is the meaning of the rule "of that which ends in *m*, preceded by *ā*" (*Âto maparyantasya*). Now, one might object:
even if it is a substitution of the entire stem, [the rule] "the *ṭi* of a pronoun is elided before a case-ending beginning with *o*, *s*, or *bh*" (*sarvanāmnaṣṭeḥ*) [would apply].

In the case of *prāgakaci*, the forms *yuvakām* and *āvakām* are indeed established; however, because there is no possibility of the substitutes *yuva-* and *āva-* applying to those forms when they possess the augment *aK* (*sākackayoḥ*), he states "by you" (*tvayā*) and "by me" (*mayā*) out of this underlying dissatisfaction. For if the rule *maparyantasya* did not exist, then the substitutes *tva-* and *ma-* would apply by the rule *tvamāvekavacane*.

[The substitutes] would apply to both [yuṣmad and asmad] together. Consequently, when the third case singular ending is applied, resulting in *yuṣmad ā* and *asmad ā*, and the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* are applied in place of both [stems], resulting in *tva-ā* and *ma-ā*, the vowel *ā* would undergo the substitution of *ya* by the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), yielding *tvyā* and *myā*. Therefore...

The statement "up to the limit of *ṭha*" [is made]. When that exists, after the substitutes *tvam* and *mā* have been applied to the limit of *ṭha*, the forms *tva ad ā* and *ma ad ā* remain; then, by applying the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule to the two *a*-vowels and changing the *d* to *y*, the forms *tvayā* and *mayā* are established—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: instead of the rule "yo'ci" (Pāṇini 7.2.89)...

Let there be the rule *ṭe'*. Its meaning is that when a case-ending beginning with a vowel follows, the final letter of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* shall be replaced by *e*. Thus, even though *tvam* and *mayoḥ* are entire substitutes (*samastādeśa*), once the substitution of *e* for the final *a* and the subsequent substitution of *ay* have been applied, we obtain *tvayā* and *mayā*.
To show that [the desired form] is not established, he says: "By *yuvakābhyām* and *āvakābhyām*, it would not be established.
The remainder of the sense is: "if the statement ending in *map* were absent. By the rule beginning with "when *o* and *s* [follow]," etc., [the suffix] *bhyām* [is applied];
then, by the principle of "that which falls in the middle," in place of the two [bases] together with the *kac* augment, [the substitution occurs].

In the case of the substitutes *yuva-* and *āva-*, the forms would have been simply *yuṣmabhyām* and *asmabhyām*; the letter *k* would not have been heard. However, in the case of *yuṣmakad* and *asmakad*, since the substitutes *yuva-* and *āva-* apply only to that which ends in *map* (the portion preceding the case-ending), the substitution of *ā* by the rule "yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe" results in *yuṣvakābhyām* and *asmakābhyām*. Thus, [the forms become] *yuṣvakābhyām* and *asmakābhyām*.
The meaning is "without obstruction.
Regarding the rule *yūyavayau jasi* (Pāṇini 7.2.93), which states a specific exception when *jas* is replaced by *am* by the rule *reĀ prathamayoḥ* (7.1.28), [the author] says: *yūyavayau jasi*.

"Clearly" means that it is easy to understand that when *jas* follows, the substitutes *yūyam* and *vayam* replace the forms ending in *maparyanta* (the portion up to, but not including, the final phoneme) of the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. When the forms *yūya ad am* and *vaya ad am* are established,
after the application of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule, the *ado* following the *maparyanta* portion is elided by the rule "there is elision of the remainder."

He states the completed form as *yūyam* and *vayam*. [The form] *paramayūyam* [is derived] because the rule for *yūyam* and *vayam* is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), and thus there is an extension of the rule (*tadantavidhi*) to that which ends in it; this is the underlying intention. [The form] *atiyūyam* [is used] because there is no evidence to prevent its application even when [the stem] is secondary (*gauṇa*); this is the underlying intention. In this regard—

Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "iha" (here). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in this case, according to the view that "the elision [of the final phoneme] occurs when the suffix *śas* follows" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*), once the letter *d* has been elided, the substitution of *śī* for *jas* would apply because the pronoun ends in an *a*-vowel; however, this does not take place. To the question "Why?", he replies: "In the case of an operation on a stem (*aṅga-kārye*)."

The meaning is that once an operation prescribed under the heading of *aṅga* (stem) has been performed, an operation subsequently prescribed under the heading of *aṅga* does not take place again. Consequently, in the case of *tvam*, once the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form) has been applied, there is no inconsistency with the rule "the preceding [vowel] before *ṭhaM*" (*pūrvaḥ*). This is stated in the rule *jyādādīyasaḥ* and in the rule *jñājanorja*.
Furthermore, the *paribhāṣā* "there is no application of a rule when there is again an occurrence of a condition that has already been applied" (*ṭhaṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ*) is established;

and this has been included here for the sake of the meaning. Nor should it be argued that in the case of *dvābhyām*, once the substitution of *yatva* (the change to *a*) for the *tyadādi* group has occurred, the lengthening by the rule *supi ca* would not take place; for [this objection is refuted] by the very mention [in the sūtras] of forms such as *dvayor ekasya*.

This is because it makes known its impermanence (*anityatva*). And in the present case, since the elision of the *śeṣa* (the *lopa* of the final vowel) belonging to the *aṅga* has already taken effect, the substitution of *śī* does not occur for the *aṅga*; such is the intended meaning. Now, one might object that the *paribhāṣā* "in the case of an operation pertaining to an *aṅga*" (*aṅgakārye*) does not apply here, even though the substitution of *śī* is prescribed under the heading of *aṅga*.

Because there is an absence of having a member (*aṅga*) as its locus, and because that very understanding follows from the natural sense of the *paribhāṣā*—"there is no application [of a rule] when it has already applied to a member" (*aṅgavṛtte punarvṛtāvavidhiḥ*)—the substitution of *śī* is unavoidable here. Due to this lack of satisfaction, he says: "In place of *ReĀ*, [there is *am*] in the first two cases. In the rule "In place of *ReĀ*, [there is *am*] in the first two cases," *am* is the substitute.
Thus, the letter *m* is elided [from the end]. "Am" and "m" form a *dvandva* compound.

The final *m* is dropped by the rule of elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). And the elided *m* serves as a qualifier for "am"; by the rule of extension to that which ends in such a term (*tadantavidhi*), it is understood that "am" must end in *m*.

Because *am* ending in *m* is further prescribed to have *m* as its final letter, it is understood that it remains precisely one ending in *m* and does not undergo any modification; thus, the meaning is that there is no substitution of *śī*.
In reality, however, the insertion of an additional *m* should be disregarded, as it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*.

In this case, the substitution of *śī* does not occur precisely because of the principle of "annulment due to the destruction of the cause" (*saṃnipātaparibhāṣā*). For the elision of the remaining portion (*śeṣalopa*) of the *dakāra* proceeds by depending upon the conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) of the suffix *am*—which consists of the remaining case-ending other than those that are causes for the substitution of *āt* and *yat*—and of the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Consequently, if the substitution of *śī* were to take place, [the cause would be destroyed].

By the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, [the forms] *yūye* and *vaye* would result. In that case, if the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) were treated as belonging to the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), there would be a disruption of the phonetic combination with the suffix (*pratyayasannipātabhaṅga*) because it would have entered into the base (*prakṛti*). If, however, it were treated as belonging to the following element (*parāditva*), there would be a contradiction regarding the phonetic combination of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Enough of this.

*tvamāvekavacane* | Pāṇini 7.2.97. Now, when the singular case-ending *am* (the second-person singular) has been applied by [Pāṇini 7.1.28] *ṭāṅasiṅasām-inātsyāḥ* and [Pāṇini 7.1.28] *ReĀ prathamayor-ah*, resulting in the forms *yuṣmad-am* and *asmad-am*, [the rule] *tvamāvekavacane* applies. [This is further governed by] *yuṣmadasmador-anādeśe*.

Therefore, the phrase "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" (*yuṣmadasmadoḥ*) is understood to carry over. The term "ending in *map*" (*maparyantasya*) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). The word "singular" (*ekavacana*) is etymological (*yaugika*) alone, owing to the force of the inclusion of the word "number" (*vacana*).
He states this with the words beginning "of one," and so forth.

And [the substitution of] *tvad* and *mad* occurs in the second case. When [the forms] *tva ad am* and *ma ad am* have been established, the sūtra "and in the second case" (*dvitīyāyāṃ ca*) is explained by supplying the remainder [of the rule]: "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" (*yuṣmadasmadoḥ*). [This refers to the rule: "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when there is no substitute" (*yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*).

The meaning is that this is because of its recurrence from that [rule]. Regarding "ākāra" (the long vowel *ā*): the meaning is that this is because of its recurrence from the rule "ṭhaṣṭana ā vibhaktau. And thus, the result is that the long vowel *ā* replaces *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when followed by the second case ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*). By the rule "alo'ntyasya," [the replacement] occurs for the final letter, namely the *d*.

[The forms] *tva-a-ā-am* and *ma-a-ā-am* arise; then, after the application of the *pararūpa* (substitution by the subsequent form), the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel for homogeneous vowels), and the *ami pūrvarūpa* (the preceding form before the ending *am*), the final forms are stated as *tvām* and *mām*. [The forms] *yuvām* and *āvām* are likewise [derived] as before; the specific difference is that the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule "and in the second case" (*dvitīyāyāṃ ca*).
And because the rule *prathamāyāśca* does not apply here.
(Pāṇini 7.1.29) *śaso na*: Now he states a specific rule regarding the suffix *śas*—*śaso na*. [The rule] *ReĀ prathamayoḥ* [applies].

Therefore, *am* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], as is *yuṣmadasmadbhyām*. Thus, it is obtained that for the *śas* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, there shall be no *am*. Consequently, in the absence of *am*, when the substitution of *ā* by "and in the second case" (*dvitīyāyāṃ ca*) and the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) have occurred, and then the substitution of *na* by "after that, *śas* becomes *na* in the masculine" (*tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi*) has applied...
Regarding the form *yuṣmān*, although it is established as a masculine form, it would not be established for the feminine and neuter genders in such cases as "yuṣmān brāhmaṇīḥ paśya" (see you,

the Brahmin women), "asmān brāhmaṇīḥ paśya" (see us, the Brahmin women), "yuṣmān brāhmaṇakulāni paśya" (see you, the Brahmin families), or "asmān brāhmaṇakulāni paśya" (see us, the Brahmin families). Therefore, this is not the [intended] rule.
The [sūtra] "śaso na" is not intended to prohibit [the application of] "am," but rather intends that the letter *na* is substituted for the *śas* [ending].
Anticipating the objection—"In that case, why is the nominative form 'śaso naḥ' not heard?"—he says:
"The word 'na' is without a case-ending. This means that the nominative case-ending has been elided. And thus...

He states the result with the words "from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "an exception to *am*": since the rule "for the first two [cases], *ReĀ*" is applicable, this prescription for *na* is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) to that. When *yuṣmad-as* and *asmad-as* remain, the substitution of *ā* by the rule "also in the second case" occurs, and by this [present rule], the *n* replaces the *śas*.
And regarding that, he says "not of the final" (*nāntyasya*) by means of the rule "of the following" (*ādeḥ parasya*), [implying] "of the initial.
[He then states] "of the end of a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntasya*). The sense is that when the letter *n* is substituted for the letter *a*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *s*.
Even though the substitution of *am* for *śas* has been made, when the letter *n* is substituted for the letter *a*, [the elision applies to] the letter *m*.
Although forms such as *yuṣmān* and *asmān* are established through the elision of the final consonant in a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), nevertheless, according to the maxim "even when possible,

there is sublation" (*saty api saṃbhave bādhanaṃ bhavati*), the substitution of *na* is adopted as an exception (*apavāda*) to *am*. Furthermore, once *am* has been applied, in the rule *reĀ prathamayoḥ*, under the view that involves the insertion (*praśleṣa*) of another *m*, [the substitution of] the vowel *a*...

There is no need for further elaboration, as the elision of the final consonant (*makāra*) due to its being at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not apply when followed by the letter *nakāra*. Now, the third case:
when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are followed by *ā*, the situation is as follows—() *yo'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89).

The word *aci* [is understood]. The phrase *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* is supplied from the previous rule. From the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the word *vibhaktau* is also supplied. The term *aci* is a qualifier of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
He states the application of this rule [beginning with] "of these two" (*anayoḥ*), meaning: of the final letter of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
What is the purpose of the condition *aci*? [Consider: *yuvābhyām*. What is the purpose of the condition *anādeśe* (when there is no substitute)? [Consider: *tvat*, *mat*.

When the substitute *at* is applied by the rule *ṭh-pañcamyā at*, the substitution of *yatva* (the change of *d* to *y*) does not occur. However, in the case of *yuṣmad ā* and *asmad ā*, when the substitutes *tvam* and *mā* are applied for that which precedes the final *m* by the rule *ṭhvamāvekavacane*, the substitution of *yatva* occurs for the *d* [of *tvad* and *mad*].
And the sense is that "form" [is present] even in the form of another.
(Pāṇini 7.2.86) *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*. From the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, the word *ā* [is understood].

The word "vibhaktau" (in a case-ending) also carries over [from the previous rule]. From the rule "ṭhrāyo halī," the word "halī" (before a consonant) is carried over as a qualifier for the case-ending. This results in the application of the rule "tadādividhiḥ" (the operation applies to that which begins with it). Thus he says: "of these two. The meaning is:
"of the final [letter] of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. In reality, however, the word "halī" need not be carried over.
Because the substitution of *ya* is prescribed by the rule *ṭhyo'ci* for [stems ending in] vowels beginning with *a*, that [substitution] is established by elimination alone.

As for the forms *yuvābhyām* and *āvābhyām*: when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are followed by *bhyām*, the substitutes *yuvā-* and *āvā-* are applied; then, the *d* being replaced by *ā*, there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*). This is the intended meaning here.
While the term *hal* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), the mention of *ac* in the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ* need not be included.

This is because, as is clear in the *Bhāṣya*, the substitution of *ā* (in *yuṣmābhiḥ* and *asmābhiḥ*) is specifically prescribed for environments beginning with a consonant (*hal*), which alone ensures the prevention of the *yatva* (substitution of *ya*).
Thus we have *yuṣmābhiḥ* and *asmābhiḥ*, where the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*.
The intention is that there is a long vowel by the rule *savarṇadīrgha*. Now, for the dative case: when *yuṣmad* + *e* and *asmad* + *e* are established, the rule *tvamāv ekavacane* would apply;
however, [this is superseded] by *tubhyamahyau ṅayi* (Pāṇini 7.2.95).
The term *ṅyi* refers to the singular locative case ending *ṭhReĀ* [i.e., *ṅi*] in the forms *tubhyam* and *mahyam*.
From the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* is carried over (anuvartate).
The governing heading *maparyantasya* is also in force. Thus, he says: "of these two."

The meaning is "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Regarding "the substitute *am*," the remainder of the rule is "by [Pāṇini 7.1.28] *reĀ prathamayoḥ*. Regarding "elision in the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*), the meaning is that there is optionally the elision of the *d* of *adas*. Thinking [of the rule] "before *am*, the preceding [vowel and consonant form one syllable]," he says: "to you" (*tubhyam*) and "to me" (*mahyam*). "To the highest you" (*paramatubhyam*).
The sense is that because *tvad* and *mad* are subordinate (*aṅga*) to the suffixes *te* and *me*, their application occurs even at the end of a compound.
Regarding *atitubhyam*: the sense is that there is no evidence for their non-application when they are used in a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*).
Regarding *yuvābhyām* and *āvābhyām*: the sense is that it is like the dual of the third case.
*bhyaso 'bhyam* (Pāṇini 7.1.30). The analysis is either *bhyasaḥ abhyam* or *bhyam abhyam*. In that case, [the word] *bhyasaḥ* refers to [the suffix] *bhyas*.
The remainder [of the rule] is "after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" (*yuṣmadasmadbhyām parasya*), as in the rule "for *ṅsi* after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *aś* is substituted" (*yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso 'ś*).

Because of its subsequent recurrence [in other rules]. Now, one might object: "In the view that *byām* is the substitute, when *adaḥ* is elided by the rule 'śeṣe lopaḥ', the vowel *a* after the *m* in *yuṣmabhyam* and *asmabhyam* would not be heard. To this he says: "The first. In accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), the view of the elision of the final letter (*antyalopa*) must be adopted here.
One might object: "In the view that the final letter is elided, once the *d* is dropped, the substitution of *e* (by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*) would apply.

To this, he says: "In that case, by the principle *aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ*"—meaning, by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) stating that when an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅga*), there is no further application [of another rule]. That which has its occurrence (*vartana*) within the stem is what is meant by *aṅgavṛtta*.

"Enveloped by that subsidiary operation" means that when that [primary] operation has taken place, there is no injunction (*avidhi*) regarding the occurrence of another subsidiary operation within its scope; that is to say, it does not apply. And in the present case, when the subsidiary operation of elision (*śeṣalopa*) has taken place, this other subsidiary operation—namely, the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*)—does not occur.

"Bhāva" means "it exists. Regarding the phrase "but *abhyam*": the meaning is that the substitution of *abhyam* is favorable both in the case of the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) and in the case of the elision of the final [consonant]. In that regard, in the case of the elision of the final [consonant], because *abhyam* does not begin with a *jhal* sound, there is no *etva* (substitution of *e*) when it follows; rather, by the rule of *pararūpa* (the single substitute being the latter form), [the desired result is obtained].

The forms *yuṣmabhyam* and *asmabhyam* are established. However, in the alternative view where the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the substitution of *e* (etva) does not occur because the base (*aṅga*) no longer ends in *a*. Furthermore, [the rule] "and in the singular" (Pāṇini 7.1.32) applies.

Now, the fifth [rule]: *caikavacanasya*. From the rule *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso 'ś*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadbhyām* is understood by anuvṛtti, as is *pañcamyā at*; thus he says "from these two. This means "from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa).
By the rule "na vibhaktau," its *it*-marker is not applied. Thus, we have *tvat* and *mad*.

When *yuṣmad-as* and *asmad-as* are in this state, once the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* have been applied, and the substitution of *ad* for the case-ending *ṅsi* has occurred, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule applies; then, by the rule "śeṣe lopaḥ," there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). In the view that the elision is of the final letter (*antyalopa*), there is elision of the letter *d*.
The meaning is that when three *akāra*s [are present], it takes the form of the subsequent one. "It is easy to state" means because of parsimony (*lāghava*).
(Pāṇini 7.1.31: *pañcamyā at*.)

[The rule] *pañcamyā at* [is applied]. From the rule *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso'ṭ*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadbhyām* is carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *bhyaso'bhyam*, the word *bhyasaḥ* is carried over. Thus he says: "from these two" (*ābhyām*), meaning from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [The forms] *yuṣmat* and *asmad* [are derived].

When *yuṣmabhyas* and *asmabhyas* have been established, the substitution of *ad* for *bhyas* occurs, and there is the elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*). [The forms] *tava* and *mama* [are substituted] when the case-ending *ṅsi* follows. (Pāṇini 7.1.96)

Now the sixth [sūtra]: *tavamamau ṅsi*. From the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* is understood to carry over. The term *maparyantasya* is also governing. Thus he says: "of these two," meaning of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [The rule] *tvamāvekavacane* [follows].
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [rule].
(Pāṇini 7.1.27) *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅso'ś*:
"After *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the [suffix] *ṅsi* becomes *aś*. This is clear. [It applies] to that which follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
The meaning is that "ṅso'ś syāt" (the genitive case ending *ṅsi* becomes *aś*) is easy to understand. Because it is marked with the letter *s*, it replaces the entire form. Regarding "tava mama":

when *yuṣmad-as* and *asmad-as* are in the state [of being followed by the genitive suffix], after the substitutes *tavad* and *mavad* have been applied to the portions ending in *map*, and after the substitute *aś* has been applied, there is a single-substitute (*pararūpa*) of the two vowels preceding the *d* [with the *a* of *aś*]; then, by the rule *ado lopaḥ*, the [final] *a* is elided.
In the view that the final [vowel] is elided, there is the elision of the letter *d*, and the meaning is that the three *a*-vowels undergo the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

In the case of *yuvoḥ* and *āvoḥ*: when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are followed by the suffix *os*, after the substitutes *yuvā-* and *āvā-* have been applied to the portion ending in *m*, the *d* is changed to *y* by the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ*, and then the subsequent form is applied.
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied].
(Pāṇini 5.1.119) *sāma ākam* (Pāṇini 7.1.33).
*sāma ākam*. [This means] "from these two. [That is,] from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

The meaning is that [the word] *aś* follows from that [previous rule]. Regarding the term *sāma*: it means "of that which is accompanied by *sa-* (i.e., *su-*) and *ām*," that is to say, of *ām* together with *suṭ*. Now, one might object: when *yuṣmad* + *ām* and *asmad* + *ām* are situated thus, since there is no occurrence of an *avarṇa* (a vowel) preceding it, the application of *suṭ* would not be expected.

Nor should it be argued that once the elision [of the suffix] has been performed by the rule "the remainder is elided" (*ṭh-śeṣe lopaḥ*), the condition of being followed by a vowel (*añ-varṇa*) exists; for since the elision of the remainder is not applicable here prior to the substitution of *ākām* because the suffix has not yet been designated as *an*, the mention of the form with the *suṭ* augment would be both untenable and redundant. To this, he says: "of those about to be" (*bhāvinaḥ*).

The meaning is "will come to be. However, if it were stated simply as *āma ākam*, then once the substitute *ākam* is applied to *ām* and the remaining *d* is elided, the augment *suṭ* would have to be inserted because, by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitute *ākam* would possess the property of being *āmt* (ending in *ā*), and because it would follow an *avarṇa*. Therefore...
Since *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam* would result from the substitution of *etva* and *aṣatva*, the mention of the form with the augment *suṭ* (*yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*) is necessary.
Although the augment *suṭ* does not apply at the time the substitute *ākam* is introduced, nevertheless,
after the substitute *ākam* has been applied and the letter *d* has been elided, the *suṭ* reappears by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*.

It will come to pass that for him as well, cessation occurs because the sixth case-ending is accepted; the sense is that otherwise, the mention of *sasūṭ* (along with the augment *suṭ*) would be purposeless. However, if only the elision (*lopa*) of the remainder is resorted to, then even when the substitute *ākam* has been applied, [the form] *ado*...

Since the suffix *suṭ* cannot possibly apply because it does not follow a vowel (*avarṇa*) when [the final *m*] is elided, let there be no mention of *sasut* (i.e., the form with *suṭ*). For example, in *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*, once the replacement by *ākam* has occurred, the form results from the elision of *at*. However, if the *d* were elided instead, there would be a long vowel by rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). It is precisely for this purpose [that the rule is stated].
The long vowel is pronounced [in the sūtra] because otherwise there would be the occurrence of the single substitute form (pararūpa).

Nor should it be argued that the exclusion of the *pararūpa* is achieved solely by the power of pronouncing the long *ā*, for that [pronunciation] has its purpose fulfilled by preventing the *etva* substitution (of *ai*) in cases such as *ṭhak* → *ka*, where the plural ending *bahuvacana* would otherwise apply. Enough of this.

Regarding "tvayi" and "mayi": when "yuṣmad-i" and "asmad-i" are established, the forms arise through the substitution of "tvam" and "aham" for the entirety [of the stems], followed by the change of "d" to "y" by the rule "ṛtyakaḥ," and then the application of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule; such is the intended meaning.
Regarding "yuvayoḥ" and "āvayoḥ": it is as before. Regarding "yuṣmāsu" and "asmāsu": [the process is] the same.
The intention is that, by the rule "yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe," the letter *d* is changed to *ā*, resulting in a long vowel through *savarṇadīrgha*.

It is established that in the rules "tvamāvekavacane" and "yuvāvau dvivacane," the terms *ekavacana* (singular) and *dvivacana* (dual) are etymological (*yaugika*), and do not refer to [specific] suffixes.

He summarizes that result in four verses, beginning with "samasyamāne. In that context, the word "api" (also) should be supplied immediately after "ced" in the first verse. [The meaning is: if *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, while being compounded, denote duality or singularity, then...

The syntactical connection is as follows: even if the meaning of the compound has a different number, the forms *yuvā* and *āvā* (as well as *yuva* and *āva*) still occur. This applies when there is an analysis (*vigraha*) such as "one who has surpassed you or me" (*tvām mām vā atikrāntaḥ*), or "those who have surpassed [you or me]" (*atikrāntau*, *atikrāntāḥ*); and likewise when there is an analysis such as "one who has surpassed both of you or both of us" (*yuvām āvām vā atikrāntaḥ*), or "those who have surpassed [both of you or both of us]" (*atikrāntau*, *atikrāntāḥ*). Thus, in the sense of "surpassed" and so forth, the suffixes beginning with *ṭhaC* (i.e., *at*) are applied.

When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* receive a compound by [the rule] "dvitīyayā," provided they denote an object qualified by either duality or singularity, then the meaning of the compound, even if it possesses a number other than that of the primary qualificand, [is subject to the substitution of *tvam*, *aham*, etc. *Note:* This passage concerns the application of Pāṇini’s rules regarding the substitution of *tvam* and *aham* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when these pronouns occur within a compound (samāsa). Specifically, it addresses the conditions under which such substitution occurs even when the resulting compound has a different grammatical number (*saṅkhyā*) than the original pronoun. The phrase "dvitīyayā" refers to the rule Pāṇini 2.4.34 (*tvām-au-āv-am-au-yuṣmad-asmadbhyāṃ dvitīyāyāṃ ca*), which prescribes the formation of certain compounds with the second-case forms of these pronouns. The commentary explains that the substitution applies when the pronouns express an object characterized by either singular or dual number. Even if the final compound denotes a different number (such as plural), the prescribed substitutes still take effect.

With respect to the number inherent in the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, even if another number [is present], when there is duality in the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the forms *yuvā-* and *āv-* [are substituted]; and when there is singularity in their referents, the forms *tvam* and *aham* [are substituted],
even in the absence of suffixes that are dual or singular.

In the rule prescribing the substitutes *yuva-* and *āva-*, even if the number differs from the number inherent in the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the forms *yuvā-* and *āvā-* occur when there is duality of the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; likewise, the forms *tvam* and *aham* occur when there is singularity of those referents,
even in the absence of suffixes that are dual or singular.

This is because, in the rule prescribing the substitutes *tvam* and so forth, one must rely on the etymological (yaugika) sense of the words *dvivacana* and *ekavacana*. For if one were to rely on the meaning "when a suffix of the singular number follows" for *ekavacana*, and "when a suffix of the dual number follows" for *dvivacana*, then [the forms] *tvām* or *mām*...

In the analysis (vigraha) of *atikrāntau* and *atikrāntāḥ*, when the words *atiyuṣmad* and *atyasmad* are followed by dual or plural suffixes of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the forms *tvam* and *aham* do not occur.
Likewise, in the analysis of *atikrānto yuvām* or *atikrānto āvām*, *atikrāntau*, and *atikrāntāḥ*.

The meaning is that there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) of the rule, because *yuvau* and *āvau* would not occur when suffixes follow the dual or plural forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Now, one might ask: is it universally the case that *yuvau* and *āvau* apply when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* have a dual sense, while *tvam* and *aham* apply when they have a singular sense?

He says "no," [introducing the next section] with the words *sujasreṅsu*. In the second half of this second verse, the phrases beginning with *tvāhau* and so forth are citations (*pratīka*) of those respective sūtras. After the word *sthiti*, the word *ye* is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). [The sūtras are:
*tvāhau sau*, *yūyavayau jasi*, and *tubhyamahyam ṅyi*.

The meaning is that the substitutes *tvam* and *au* (for the singular), as well as *ṅsi*, which are prescribed by the rule "ṭhavamamau ṅsī," shall apply to the words *atiyuṣmad* and *atyasmad* even when they denote one, two, or many objects.
Now, one might ask: why are *yuvau* and *āvau* not applied there when there is a dual sense, and *tvam* and *au* when there is a singular sense?
"No," it is said in response; thus he says "eti" (they come). In the first half of the third verse, there is a single sentence:
"ete" refers to *etva*, *otva*, and so forth; these supersede *yu* and *au* in their own respective domains, such as the *su*-case ending and others.
Why? Because they are subsequent (*paratvāt*). The meaning is that these [rules] are subsequent in relation to *yu* and *au*.

[Objection: Let it be so that there is sublation (*bādha*) of the two [forms] *yuvām* and *āvām* by *tvām* and *mām* and so forth; however, since *tvam* and *au* are subsequent to those, how could they be sublated by them? To this, he says: "Even *tvam* and *au*. Regarding "prior": when there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), "prior" refers to a prior conflict. This is a compound formed according to the rule *sup supā*.

The suffix *tasi* follows a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). The intention is that, according to the rule on "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*), the word *para* signifies "desired"; thus, in certain conflicts, one may resort to the application of the preceding operation. However, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "ṭh-pratyaya-uttarapadayoś-ca," [it is stated] regarding "tvamāvekavacane":...
In the sūtra, having carried forward the term "ṭhśeṣe," it is explained as "in the case of suffixes other than su, jas, ReĀ, and ṅasi. Thus,
in the same manner, [the rule] applies here to the rules "tvamāvekavacane" and "yuvāvau dvivacane."

Having stated that the recourse to the etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) of the words "singular" (*eka*) and "dual" (*dvi*) serves to avoid the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), he states that it also serves to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the phrase "the number two" (*dvyaka-saṅkhyā*). In this fourth verse, the words "when" (*yadā*) and "then" (*tadā*) are to be supplied as ellipses (*adhyāhārya*).

When there is a compound formed from the analysis *yuṣmān* or *asmān* with *atikrāntau* or *atikrāntāḥ*, the meaning of the compound—characterized by duality or singularity—is the primary substantive (*mukhyaviśeṣya*) of the compound; whereas *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote plurality. In that case, the substitutions *yuvā-vau* and *tvam-au* do not occur, because those [substitutions] apply only when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote meanings qualified by duality or singularity. This is because the rules for *yuvā-vau* and *tvam-au* are understood to operate only when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* express meanings specifically characterized by duality or singularity.

The meaning is that if one were to rely on the sense—that [the suffixes] *dvivacana* and *ekavacana* occur when a suffix follows—then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in those cases. In this regard, during the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, while explaining the Vārttika stating that "in the case of the mention of *tri*, *catur*, *yuṣmad*, and *asmad*, the meaning is what is intended," the author proposes relying on the etymological (derivative) sense of the words *dvivacana* and *ekavacana* in the rules *yuvāvau dvivacane* and *tvamāvekavacane*. [This is illustrated by the examples: "one who has surpassed both you" (*yuvām*) or "both of us" (*āvām*), or "those two who have surpassed... (*atikrāntau*).

Having demonstrated the analyses as *atikrāntāḥ*, and having further demonstrated the analyses as *tvām mām vā atikrāntaḥ*, *atikrāntau*, and *atikrāntāḥ*, the substitutes *yuva-ādeśau* and *āva-ādeśau*, as well as the substitutes *tvam-ādeśau* and *mām-ādeśau*, have been illustrated and shown to apply everywhere—in all numbers (singular, dual, and plural) and in all case-endings—except for the suffixes *su*, *jas*, *ReĀṅ*, and *su* (the nominative singular), for the words *atiyuṣmad* and *atyasmad*. However, for the suffixes *su*, *jas*, *ReĀṅ*, and *su*, only these substitutes have been illustrated: *tvāhau*, *yūyavayau*, *tubhyamahyam*, and *tavamamau*.

This very point is summarized in four verses. Now, following the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which elaborates upon that, [the author] demonstrates it by citing the passage beginning with "tvā māṃ vā atikrāntaḥ" and so forth. This [example] is an illustration for the two analyses (*vigraha*), namely *atikrāntau* and *atikrāntāḥ*. After the word "in the analysis," the remainder of the sentence is "the forms will be stated. Except for the cases of *su*, *jas*, *ām*, and *ṅsi*, in all other case-endings (*vibhakti*) and in all numbers—singular, dual, and plural—the forms *tvam* and *mām* replace the portion ending in *map* (i.e., the stem).

The remaining grammatical operations should be understood as being exactly like those for the simple forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. However, in the cases of *su*, *jas*, *ām*, and *ṅe*, the substitutes *tvāhau*, *yūyavayau*, *tubhyamahyam*, and *tavamamau* occur by means of a prior prohibition (*pūrva-pratiṣedha*), thereby setting aside *tvam* and *mām*. Consequently, the conclusion is that in the cases of *su*, *jas*, *ām*, and *ṅe*, the forms are exactly like those of the simple *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Thus, [the forms] *atitvākam* and *atimākam* [are derived].

[Objection: But surely, because of the mention of *sāmaḥ* with the augment *suṭ* (*sasuṭ-kan*) in the rule *sāma ākam*, the substitution *ākam* should occur only where the possibility of *suṭ* exists for *ām*; however, here *suṭ* is not possible, since when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are used as secondary members (*upasarjana*), they lack the status of pronominals (*sarvanāman*), and *suṭ* is prescribed only after a pronominal followed by *ām*. [Reply: Not so; for the inclusion of *suṭ* (*sasuṭkatva*) is intended merely to indicate the possibility [of its occurrence]. Thus, the mention of *sāmaḥ* with *suṭ* is for the purpose of excluding *suṭ* in those cases where it would otherwise have been applicable.

However, where *suṭ* is not possible, there the *suṭ* is applied to the bare *ām*. In this regard, the example "atitvākam" and "atimākam" in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule "ṭhpratyayottarapadayośca" serves as the authority; let that suffice for now. Thus, having stated the examples for the case where the subordinate forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote a single referent (*ekārthavācitva*), he provides examples for their denoting two referents (*dvyarthavācitva*)—namely, "one who has surpassed you two" (*yuvām*) or "us two" (*āvām*). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the analyses "atikrāntau" (masculine dual) and "atikrāntāḥ" (masculine plural).

In this context, because *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote multiple referents, in all case-endings (*vibhakti*)—except for those ending in *su*, *jas*, *Re* (the dative singular suffix), and *ṅ*—the forms *yuvā* and *āvā* replace the entirety of the stems up to the final *m* in both singular and plural numbers. The remaining grammatical operations should be understood as being identical to those of the uncompounded *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. The conclusion is that in the cases of *su*, *jas*, *Re*, and *ṅ*, the forms are exactly like those of the uncompounded *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Now, he provides examples for when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* function as secondary members (*upasarjana*) denoting multiple referents: "yuṣmān asmān vā" (you or us).

The meaning is that these are examples for the analyses *atikrāntaḥ*, *atikrāntau*, and *atikrāntāḥ* [meaning "one who has surpassed you," "you two," or "you all," or "me," "us two," or "us"]. These are the illustrations for the fourth verse, which states: "The meaning of a compound consists of two, one, or many numbers. Here, because the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not denote a single or dual referent, the forms *tvam* and *au* never occur for the stem ending in *map* (i.e., *yuṣma-* and *asma-*) except after the case endings *su*, *jas*, and *ReĀ* (the nominative singular and dual); nor do the forms *yuvam* and *āvām* occur. However, rules such as *ReĀ prathamayoḥ* ("for the first two cases, ReĀ is substituted") certainly apply.

In the forms *su*, *jas*, *ām*, *ṅsi*, *ṅsu*, however, *tvāhau*, *yūyavayau*, *tubhyamahyau*, and *tavamamau* necessarily occur. This is because these [forms] lack a basis for distinguishing between singular and dual meanings. The phrase "as before" (*prāgvat*) means "just like the simple forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Regarding the phrase "having introduced this topic" (*ityadhikṛtya*), the ellipsis is "the rules (*vidhayaḥ*) will be stated. These sūtras are recited in the first quarter (pāda) of the eighth book (*aṣṭādhyāyī*). Among them, the term *padasya* is governed from the point of *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.55) onwards.

The rule *ṭhapādāt* is applied prior to *ṭhkṛtsane ca supyagotrādau*. However, the three rules beginning with *anudātaṃ sarvamapādādau* are governed [as exceptions] up until the end of the section on *padas*, as is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources. *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāsthayorvānāvau* (Pāṇini 7.1.27): For the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they stand in the sixth, fourth, or second case, the substitutes *va* and *na* [are applied]. This means that for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are specified by the sixth case, etc. [the substitutes apply].

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyā-sthau* means "those that stand together with the sixth, fourth, and second [cases]. This refers to those characterized by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth.
An analysis such as "those that stand when the sixth, fourth, and second cases follow" is not intended.

Because it would contradict the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of a word" (*padasya*). For the term *padasya*, which is understood from the previous context, is modified by the dual number [to become *padayoḥ*] and serves as a qualifier for the phrase "standing in the genitive, dative, or accusative" (*ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyā-sthayoḥ*). Indeed, the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*) does not occur when the genitive and other such case-endings follow; even though it does exist in forms beginning with *bhyām* and so on, [the rule would still be contradicted].

Because those [suffixes] do not exist in other instances, such as the second person and so forth. However, the purpose of including the word *sthā* (in place of) will be stated in the root [sūtra] itself.
(Pāṇini 7.1.20: *bahuvacanasya vas-nas-au* (The suffixes *vas* and *nas* replace the third-person plural endings).
The substitutes *vas* and *nas* take the place of the plural number. "Of the two forms mentioned" means:
of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when characterized by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. (Pāṇini 8.1.22) "The substitutes *te* and *me* take the place of the singular number. (Pāṇini 8.1.23)

"temayau" [means] "in the forms ending in the sixth and fourth case singular. Here, the mention of the second case does not carry over, because the substitutes *tvām* and *mām* will be taught for that [second case]. The intention is that in the rule "temayau," the analysis is *teśca meśca temayau* ("the two, *te* and *me*"). This also...
The exception to *vām-nau*.
(Pāṇini 7.2.94) *tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ* (7.2.94). The analysis of the compound is: *tvā* and *mā*. These two replace [the pronouns] in the second case.
The term *ekavacanasya* (of the singular) is understood [from the previous rule]. This is why he says "the second," and so forth.

Now, he provides examples according to the sequence of the case-endings—second, fourth, and sixth—and according to the sequence of the numbers—one, two, and many—beginning with "Śrīśa," etc. Therein: "May the Lord of Śrī protect you."

The first quarter is *māpīhe*. The Lord of Śrī—the Master, namely Viṣṇu—may he protect you; such is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). Here, for the two second-case singular forms *tvām* and *mām*, the substitutes *tvā* and *mā* are used respectively.
"May he also grant bliss to you and to me": that Lord of Śrī [grants] bliss (*śarma*) to you (*te*) and to me (*me*) as well.

The grammatical connection is: "May he grant happiness" (*sukhaṃ datāt*). From the root *dāñ* (to give) with the suffix *ṭhḍu*, in the benedictive (*āśiṣi*) *loṭ* mood, the form *datāt* is derived. In some places, the reading is *dadyāt*. Here, for the words *tubhyam* and *mahyam* ending in the fourth case singular, the substitutes *te* and *me* are applied respectively. He is the master (*svāmī*) both for you and for me.
Regarding the term *haririti*: here, in the expressions *tava* and *mama*, the substitutes *te* and *me* occur in the singular dative case.

In the phrase *pātu vām api nau vibhuḥ*, the grammatical connection is: "May the All-pervading Lord (*vibhuḥ*) protect both you two (*vām*) and us two (*nau*). Here, *vām* and *nau* are the substitutes for the dual accusative forms *yuvām* and *āvām*.

These are the substitutes. In the phrase "May the Lord grant happiness to *vām* or *nau*," the word *api* (also) is to be supplied after "*nau*. Thus, *vām* and *nau* are the forms of the dual dative ending (*caturthī-dvivacana*) for "to you two" and "to us two" respectively. In the phrase "Hari is the lord of *vām* or even *nau*," [the same applies]. Here...

In the forms *yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*, which are the genitive dual endings, the substitutes are *vām* and *nau*. In the phrase *so 'vyād vo naḥ*, the meaning is "May He protect you (*vaḥ*) and us (*naḥ*). Here, in the forms *yuṣmān* and *asmān*, which are the accusative plural endings, the substitutes are *vas* and *nas*. [Thus, the form is] *śivaṃ vo naḥ*.

"One should give" (*dadyāt*). "Auspicious" (*śivam*) means "well-being" (*śubham*). Immediately after "not" (*na*), the word "also" (*api*) is to be supplied. Here, *vas* and *nas* are the forms of the fourth-case plural for "you" (*yuṣmad*) and "us" (*asmad*). "He is to be served by you"—here, "he" refers to Hari.
"Vaḥ" means "to be served by you" or "to be worshipped by you"; the genitive case is used here according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*.
In this context, "yuṣmākam" and "asmākam" take the forms *vaḥ* and *naḥ*, which are the genitive plural endings for the second and first persons respectively.

As for the phrase "may he protect you" (*tvāṃ pātu*) and "may he protect me" (*māṃ pātu*), the genitive is not applied because the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not follow immediately after another word (*padāt*).

The meaning is that [the rule] "ṭh tvamau dvitīyāyāḥ" does not apply here. Although in this case the word *asmad* follows the word *pātu*, there is no fault because two sentences with different timings are intended here. [In the phrase] "saṃvedyo 'smān," the word *asmad* occurs at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*).

Because it is established [as such], there is no designation [of it as a foot]. Although this verse is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, the rule is that each foot therein consists of eight syllables. In that regard, in the absence of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), the phrase "asmān kṛṣṇaḥ sarvadāvatu" has nine syllables and therefore does not constitute a [valid] foot. However, when the *saṃdhi* is performed...

If the syllable *o* were initial, there would be a contradiction regarding the eight-syllable count; furthermore, since "saṃvedya" would not constitute a word (*pada*), the pronoun *asmad-* would not follow a word. However, if it were a final element (*pūrvānta*), then for the form *smān* situated at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), it would not have the nature of the word *asmac-chabda*; nevertheless, [the reading] is "saṃvedyaḥ."

Thus, because that which is distinguished by the single-substitute [okāra] possesses the status of a prior boundary (pūrvāntatva), it has the status of a word (pada). As for the form *asmāt*, however, by the maxim of "modification of a part" (ekadeśavikṛtanyāya), it has the nature of the word *asmad* ending in the second case. In reality, however, because the vowel *o* constitutes the prior boundary, the form *saṃvedyaḥ* possesses the status of a word.

Furthermore, there is the eight-syllable nature of *asmān* and so forth; and because it begins with the *para* (the subsequent element), it takes the form of the word *asmad*. Regarding the rule "when relying on both [an affix and a suffix], it is neither like the end nor like the beginning," we shall explain that this does not apply in the case of the root *iṇ* in the section on *iṇ-dhātu*. Some, however, ask: "What [is the result] when [the suffix] is at the beginning of a word? [Consider: 'May Govinda protect you (*yuṣmān*) and us (*asmān*).'"

They offer the counter-example: "kṛṣṇassarvadāvatu" (May Kṛṣṇa protect [you] always). That is incorrect, because the rule does not apply since the word "yuṣmān" lacks the status of being *para* (following) from another word. As for the word "asmān," although it is *para* from a word, it lacks the status of being *para* from a word situated within the same sentence (*samānavākya*). Now, regarding the rule "yuṣmadasmadoḥ... [Pāṇini 8.1.20]:

One might argue that the rule should simply be formulated as "of those ending in the sixth, fourth, and second [cases]," and what is the purpose of including the word *sthā* (standing)? Even with the inclusion of *sthā*, that same meaning could somehow be obtained. To this, he says: [the word] *hāsīḥ* is understood [from the root *sthā*]. Consequently, [the phrase] means "those which stand, i.e., do not abandon," the sixth, fourth, and second cases.

The intended meaning is "derivation" (*vyutpatti*). The sense is that this refers to those [words] which do not abandon their case-endings, such as the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth; the implication is that they are characterized by unelided genitive and other case-endings. Thus, in the example *yuṣmatputraḥ*, the word *iti* is used to ensure that [the compound] follows immediately after a word (*padāt*).
The analysis [of the compound] is: "the son of you two" (*yuvayoḥ*) or "of you all" (*yuṣmākam*), or "the son of us two" (*āvayoḥ*) or "of us all" (*asmākam*).

Here, because the case-ending is elided by *luk*, there is no occurrence of the substitute [form *yuṣmad-* or *asmad-*, which would require the suffix *-ad*], since the case-ending is not actually heard. [Thus, the form is simply] *tava putraḥ*.

The analysis "my son" (*mama putraḥ*) is not [the basis for this rule], because the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* will be prescribed there by the rule "ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca. "In the same sentence" (*samānavākye*) means that the cause (*nimitta*) and the element caused by it (*nimitin*) must reside within a single sentence.

The term *nighāta* denotes the *anudātta* (unaccented) tone. Regarding the rule *ekatiṅ*: by the word *tiṅ*, a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is intended. The analysis of the compound is "that which has one finite verb.

This is a definition of a sentence (*vākya*), and it is indeed useful for this grammatical system. Therefore, in examples such as "Look, the deer is running" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), [the definition applies].

That there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) is clear from the Bhāṣya on the *samartha* sūtra. Regarding "odanam": "odanaṃ paceti" is one sentence; "tava bhaviṣyatīti" is another sentence. Consequently, because the word "tava" follows a word situated in a different sentence from the word "yuṣmad," the substitute [tubhyaṃ/tava] does not apply.

The word *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Regarding the phrase *śālīnām*, it means "of rice" (*vrīhīṇām*). The genitive case is used here in the sense of the relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāve*).
And that these [words] such as *vāṃnāva* and so forth are included is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *sapūrvāyāḥ*.

Regarding the word *dhāteti*: this is a statement addressed to Mahādeva. He provides an example for the rule *ṭhanvādeśe tu nityam* [Pāṇini 8.1.26]—namely, *tasyai te namaḥ* (salutations to you for that).
