In this context, the preceding sentence, "The fire which is the carrier of oblations, the Indra whose arm wields the thunderbolt," and so forth, is to be understood.

And thus, since this is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*)—because that which was employed to enjoin one action is employed again to indicate another action—the sense is that the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indeed obligatory in that case.
(Pāṇini 8.1.24: *na cavāhā'haivayukte*).

Nor is there [the suffix] *vāh*. The word *ca* is an indeclinable used in conjunction (*samuccaya*); *vā* in the sense of option (*vikalpa*); *hā* in the sense of wonder (*adbhuta*); *aha* in the sense of distress (*kheda*); and *eva* in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). These form a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), as in "being joined" (*yukta*). Thus he says: "in connection with the five beginning with *ca*" (*cādipañcakayoge*). The meaning is: "in connection with any one of these five."

"These" means Vāṅnāva and so forth; the sense is that this follows from the application of those respective [rules] in sūtras such as "ṣaṣṭhī yuṣmadasmadoḥ. Regarding "and so on": "Kṛṣṇa, alas, is gracious to me"—the meaning is "this is wonderful. "Kṛṣṇa says to me... [and so on].

"He is pleased. The word *aha* expresses dejection. "Kṛṣṇa alone is to be served by me. Now, one might argue: let it simply be "na cavāhāhaivaiḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.24), and let there be no mention of the term *yukta*; for that [the sense of "alone"] would be obtained by the instrumental case itself, just as in the rule "vṛddho yūnā" (Pāṇini 1.2.65). To this, he replies: "Because of the mention of *yukta*. Here...

The meaning is that this prohibition applies only where the referents of *yusmad* and *asmad* have a direct syntactic connection (*sākṣād-anvaya*) with words such as *ca*, which signify conjunction and so forth. For example, in *haro hariśca* ("Hara and Hari"), the word *ca* has a direct connection with both "Hara" and "Hari. However, in the construction *svāmī samuccitayor hari-hariyoḥ* ("the master of the two, Hara and Hari, taken together"), the connection is not direct.

The word *svāmī* in the rule is connected with *me*. Consequently, since the particle *ca* has no direct syntactic connection (*sākṣād-anvaya*) with the word *asmad*, the prohibition of the substitution *me* does not apply; this is the intended meaning.
(Pāṇini 2.3.9) *paśyārthaiścā'nālocane*. 8.1.25.

And [the suffix *kvip* is used] after roots meaning "to see" (*paśya*) when there is no act of perceiving (*anālocane*). "Seeing" (*darśana*) is *paśyaḥ*. From the root *dṛśir* in the sense of "beholding," by this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *śa* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). By the rule *pāghrā*, the substitute *paśya* is applied.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: those whose object (*artha*) is seeing (*paśya*) are *paśyārthāḥ*; [the suffix is used] with those.
"Ālocana" is visual cognition; "anālocana" is that which is different from it. [The suffix -vat] refers to those things existing therein.

The meaning is "those whose purpose is seeing. By the root *dṛś* in the word "paśya," general cognition is intended, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of visual cognition in the term "anālocane. Thus he says: "not visual," and so forth.

Regarding the word *cetasā*: the word *deva* (O God) is to be supplied [as the subject]. The meaning is: "O God, [she] contemplates you with her mind. Regarding the word *paramparā* (succession): in the rule *na cavāhā*, it is appropriate to intend a direct connection (*sākṣāt-sambandha*) due to the force of the inclusion of the term *yukta*. However, in this case, if that were intended...

The meaning is that even in the case of a traditional succession (*paramparānvaya*), there would indeed be a negation due to the absence of a basis for cognition (*māna*). Regarding the phrase "your devotee" (*bhakta-stava*):

the word "O God" (*deva*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. The point is that here, the connection of the word "your" (*tava*) is through its form [as a possessive], and not directly with the verb "approaches" (*abhyāyati*). This refers to the rule *ṭhanālocane*.
He states the purpose [of the rule]: "But *ālocanā*," etc.

*Sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.1.26). [The commentary explains: For a first case-ending (*prathamā*) that is preceded by something else (*sapūrvā*), the substitutes *vām*, *nau*, and so forth, are optional (*pākṣika*) when there is no subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*); however, in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), they are obligatory.

It has been stated that [the suffixes] are compulsory (*nitya*). This rule is also intended to provide an option in certain cases of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*). Here, the word *saha* signifies "existing," as in the term *salomaka* and others. The analysis of the compound is: "that of which the preceding [element] exists. The compound is formed with *saha* according to the rule *tena saha tulyayoge*.

Since it will be stated that the mention of "tuṣyatu" (let him be satisfied) is merely conventional, the word "in the first" (*prathame*) is understood to include that which ends with it. This is what he expresses by saying "vidyamāna... and so forth.

After the words "of the two following" (*parayoḥ*), the phrase "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" (*yuṣmadasmadoḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the example "bhaktas tvam" (you are a devotee), the word "O Devadatta" (*devadatta*) and so forth must be supplied.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "O Devadatta, you too are a devotee, and I too am a devotee. Regarding the word "by him" (*tena*):
the meaning is "by virtue of being a devotee. Regarding the word "protects" (*trāyate*): the meaning is "he preserves.
Here, the referents of the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmad*) and the first-person pronoun (*asmad*), which were introduced in the preceding sentence, [are connected].
Furthermore, this is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) based on a prior mention. Here, the word *tena* exists previously; following that is *hari*, ending in the nominative case;
and even when the word *yuṣmad* is subsequently referred to, there is an option regarding the substitution of *tvad*. Likewise, [the form] *trāyate*.

This word *etat* exists previously; after that, there is *saḥ*, ending in the nominative case. Even when the pronoun *asmad* follows, there is the substitution of *mā* in its anvādeśa (subsequent reference). The word *trāyate* connects with both by way of the "middle jewel" maxim (*madhyamaṇinyāya*). Therefore, [the rule applies] between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*).
It should be understood that [the pronoun] *saḥ* must reside within the same sentence and must be preceded by something already mentioned.
(Pāṇini 2.3.48) *sāmantritam*: the first case ending (*prathamā*) prescribed in the sūtra for the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), [is called] *sāmantrita* by this term *sā*.

It is referred to [by the word *parāmṛśyate*]. From the rule *saṃbodhane ca*, the term *saṃbodhane* (in the sense of addressing) is carried over (*anuvartate*). Therefore, he says "in the sense of addressing," and so forth. The phrase "ending in that" (*tadanta*) is obtained through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā*). Because a "great designation" (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is employed, [the rule applies] even in the formulation of the technical name itself.
This refers to the inclusion of the final element (*tadanta-grahaṇa*). For this very reason, the designation [of *āmantrita*] is established for forms such as *he*, *hai*, and *bho*.
(Pāṇini 8.1.72) "A preceding vocative (*āmantrita*) is as if non-existent. This is clear because there is no other word to be supplied (*anuvartanīya*) [from a previous rule].

The state [of being treated as non-existent]. In the verse "O Agni, thine," [in the phrase] "O Agni, thine glory and vigor," the word "O Agni" is treated as non-existent. In the phrase "O God, us," the word "God" is treated as non-existent.
In the verse "O Agni, lead," the word "O Agni" is treated as non-existent. In the verse "O Agni, Indra, Varuṇa," [the word] "O Agni" [is treated as non-existent].

The sense is that [the words] are as if non-existent. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In this case" (*iha*). In the phrases "O Agni, thine" (*agne tava*) and "O gods, us" (*devā asmān*), the substitutions *te* and *naḥ* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur, because in the words *tava* and *āsmān*, there is no status of being after a word (*padāt paratvābhāvāt*), since they occur at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pādādau*).
And because of its status as a *pada*. In the example "agne naya," the word "naya" (which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix) does not receive the *anudātta* accent according to the rule "tiṅṅtiṅaḥ.
For the meaning of that rule is that a *tiṅ*-ending word is suppressed (*nihanyate*) when it follows a word that is not itself *tiṅ*-ending. And here, [the word] "agne" [is such a word].

Thus, because that which ends in a *tiṅ* affix is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), there is no absence of the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) due to its not being followed by a *tiṅ*-ending word. However, in the case of "agna indra varuṇa," the rule "āmantritasya ca" (Pāṇini 8.1.19) does not result in the entire word being unaccented; for the meaning of that rule is that a vocative (*āmantrita*) following another word is pronounced with a low pitch (*nihanyate*). And here [in the present case]...
Because the word *agni* is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), it lacks the status of being "after a word" (*padāt paratva*); therefore, the word *indra* does not have anudātta [accent].
Likewise, the word *varuṇa* also does not have anudātta, because the two preceding words, *agne* and *indra*, are treated as non-existent. Now, [one might object]: "Always protect..."
Regarding the question of how the substitution of *naḥ* occurs in the phrase "deva naḥ," since the word *deva* is treated as non-existent [in this context], he says:
"always. However, in instances such as "lakṣmīpate te 'ṅghriyugaṃ smarāmi" (O Lord of Lakṣmī, I remember Your pair of feet) and "pratāparudra!
te khyātiḥ" (O Pratāparudra! Your fame), the word "te" is an indeclinable that functions as a substitute for a case-ending (*vibhakti-pratirūpaka*). In those cases...
Because the vocative *yauṣmat* is treated as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), and because [the subsequent word] begins with *pādādi* (the beginning of a quarter-verse). "In this way" means:
in the mantra "idaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri stomam̐ paruṣṇi ā," there is a *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for all [the vocatives]; such is the connection. [This applies to] the vocative.

The meaning is that [the word] has an *anudātta* accent. He qualifies the word "all" (*sarva*) by saying "of those beginning with Yamunā. The analysis of the compound is: "those of which 'Yamunā' is the first. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the two names Sarasvatī and Śutudrī are included. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of the members are understood to apply to the whole.

The meaning is that among these words— *ṭhyamune*, *ṭhsarasvati*, and *ṭhśutudri*— there is a *nighāta* (elision of the accent) for all of them, namely *gaṅge*, *yamune*, and *sarasvati*, when they follow each one of those preceding [words]. However, there is no dispute that the word *śutudri* does not possess the quality of being *anudātta* (unaccented), because of its...

Because it occurs at the beginning of the second quarter (*pāda*). In the rule *āmantritasya ca*, the term *pada* is understood from the preceding rules *padāt* and *anudātaṃ sarvam apādādau*; thus, since the *ṛc* "imaṃ me" is composed in the *jagatī* meter, the first quarter ending with "sarasvatī," which consists of twelve syllables, is completed.

Now, an objection may be raised: it is appropriate that *gaṅge* be unaccented (anudātta), because it follows the word *me*; however, there can be no possibility of *yamune* and *sarasvati* being unaccented, since the preceding words *gaṅge* and *yamune* are treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*).

Because there is an absence of being subsequent to a word (*padāt*), he says: "Even though there is the status of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) for the vocative (*āmantrita*), [the rule applies] by relying on the word *me* alone. This should be construed as: "even though among the vocatives there is the status of being as if non-existent for these two, *gaṅge* and *yamune*. And thus, [the rule applies] "from *ṭi* and so forth."

Thus, the objection that the plural form "of all" (*sarveṣām*) is untenable has been refuted. In some manuscripts, the reading is seen as: "even when there is the status of being non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) for ancient vocatives such as 'O Yamunā' (*yamune*) and so forth."

In this context, by the first [word], "sarasvatī" is what is being referred to. It is quite clear that even when the vocatives "yamune" and "sarasvati"— which are both directed toward the east— behave as if they were non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), this *nighāta* (accentual suppression) is clearly heard at the time of the word-division (*padakāla*).

When there is a vocative in grammatical apposition, the word denoting the general class [is treated as if non-existent]. (Pāṇini 8.1.73). "In the vocative" (*āmantrite*): the phrase "a vocative is treated as if non-existent" (*āmantritam avidyamānavat*) is understood to carry over. By the term "the word denoting the general class" (*sāmānyavacanam*), a word that provides the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is intended.

Because the substantive (viśeṣya) possesses a general form in relation to its qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), it implies that qualifier. The term "samānādhikaraṇe" connects with that [implied qualifier]. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a common substratum (adhikaraṇa). The word *samāna* refers to oneness (*ekatva*).

With the intention that "the state of having a single referent" (ekārthavṛttitva) is intended by means of a word denoting the qualificand through the relation of non-difference (abheda-saṃsarga), he says "the qualificand," and so forth. In the example *hare dayālo* ("O compassionate Hari"),
the word *hari* [is used] when followed by the coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) qualifier *dayālaḥ*.

It is not as if [the word] were non-existent. Therefore, although the word "dayālo" is treated as if non-existent, the substitution of *na* for *s* does not occur because it follows the word "hare"; this is the intended meaning. In the example "agne tejasvin," here, while the qualifier "tejasvin" follows, [the rule applies to] the word "agne."

The intention is that because there is no absence of the status of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavattva*), the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies to the word *tejasvin* due to its following a word [ending in a case-suffix].
Regarding the rule *vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane* (Pāṇini 8.1.74):
in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *su-pādau yasya* ("one whose feet are beautiful"), by the application of the rule *saṃkhyā-supūrvasya*... [the elision of the middle member occurs].
When the final syllable ending in the word *pāda* is elided, the form *supāt* arises; its various forms with the suffix *su* are stated by [the author] beginning with "supād" etc.
[Pāṇini 6.4.130]: "In place of *pāda*, [the substitute] *pat* [is applied]."

He states the specific rule for the *śas* [nominative-accusative plural] case-ending: *pādaḥ pat*. The governing terms *bhasya* (of a *bha*-stem) and *aṅgasya* (of a stem) are also understood; the term *pādaḥ* serves as the qualifier for these. This is a rule involving the inclusion of that which ends in [the specified element]. Thus he says: "that which ends with the word *pād*."

Regarding the phrase "of the word *pād*": although the substitution of *pad* is prescribed for that which ends in the word *pād*, by the rule "substitutions apply to that which is explicitly mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*)," the substitution of *pad* occurs as a replacement for the entire word *pād* itself, and not merely for its final phoneme. This is the intended meaning. Examples include: *supade*, *supadaḥ*, *supadaḥ*.

*supadoḥ* (2). *supadi*. Thus end those ending in *d*. Now, those ending in *th*: *agnimaditi*. The root *manth* [is listed] in the *bhvādi* class with the meaning "to churn"; the root *manth* [is also listed] in the *kyādi* class with the meaning "to churn. From both of these, by the addition of the suffix *kvip*, and by the elision of the nasal (*n*) according to the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*, the form *agnimathi* is produced.

Then, *subutpatiḥ* (the arising of case endings). The intention is that [the *t* in *agni-t-su*] undergoes *jaśtva* and *cartva*. In the forms beginning with *bhyām*, the *th* is changed to *d* by *jaśtva*, resulting in *agnimadbhyām*, and so forth.
In the locative plural (*supi*), *cartva* applies by the rule *ṭhkhari ca*, yielding *agnimatsu*. This same form also belongs to the root *math* in the sense of "churning."

Regarding the rule "ṭhmathihiṃsāsaṃkleśanayoḥ," because it is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*idit*), there is no elision of the *n*; thus we have *agniman* and *agnimanthau*, and so forth. These are the words ending in *tha*. Now, those ending in *ca*: by the rule beginning with "ṛtvig... [we derive the forms]; in the sense of "he moves toward" (*pra-añcati*), from the root "añcu gati-pūjanayoḥ" [the suffix *kvip* is applied].

The meaning is that the suffix *kvip* is applied after a root denoting motion (*gati*) which has *n* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*). However, the case of a root meaning "to honor" (*pūjā*) will be explained later.
When *kvip* is added, the *n* becomes *it* (indicatory) by the rule *ṭh-ḍha-l-antya-*. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
The *k* is *it* by the rule *la-śa-k-vat-taddhite*. Then, by the rule *ver-apṛktasya*, the *v* is elided.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.24: *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*.

When *pra-añc* is established [as the base], the rule *aniditām* applies. The governing term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is modified by the plural number; *hal* is its qualifier. This is a case of *tadantavidhi* (the rule applies to that which ends in *hal*).

The term *aniditām* is also a qualifier of that [word *upadhāyāḥ*]. The analysis is as follows: *it* refers to the short vowel *i*; those which have *it* as their *itsaṃjñaka* (technical marker) are called *idinti*; those which are not *idinti* are *anidinti*, and the genitive plural of these is *aniditām*.
This [genitive] ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) referring to a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) connects with the word *upadhāyāḥ* [in the rule *aniditāṃ ca*]. [The word] *upadhāyāḥ*...

Thus, this too ends in a genitive case denoting a member of a compound (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). And that [genitive] connects with the elided sixth case-ending of the word *na* (from the rule *śnān na lopaḥ*), as *na* is understood there. The analysis of the compound is: *ka* and *ṅa* are *kṅ*; that which has these two as its *it* (indicatory letters) is *kṅit*.
This is what he states with the words "of those ending in consonants" (*halantānām*), etc. By the letter *ca* at the end of the rule, the *nakāra* (the letter *n*) preceding the *cakāra* is included.

There is elision (*lopa*). The form *prāc* is established from *pra-ac*. From that, the case-ending suffixes (*sup*) arise. Regarding the specific rule for when a suffix begins with *su*, he says: "the augment *num* [is added] by the rule *ugidacām*. From the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *prati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; there is *yaṇ*-sandhi; by the rule "ṭhaniditām," there is elision of the nasal (*n*); then the case endings arise. By the rule "ugidacām," the augment *num* is added; by the rule "halṅyādi," there is elision of the case ending *su*;
there is elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the letter *c*; and for the *n* of the *num* augment, the rule "kvinpratyayasya" applies.

The intention is that the sound *ṅ* occurs by virtue of being a *kutva* [substitution]. Regarding "pratyañcau": when *pratyac-au* is established, the *num* augment is applied by the rule *ugidacām*; then, the *anusvāra* is substituted for its *n*, and the *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous following sound) for that is *ñ*.
This is the intended meaning. Similarly: *pratyañcaḥ*; *pratyañcam*; *pratyañcau*.

Now, when *prati-añc* is established, since the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by virtue of being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), and subsequently the *n* is elided by *ṭh-aniditām*, the form becomes *pratyac*.

From this, when the case-ending *śas* follows, because it is not a sarvanāmasthāna, the *num* augment does not apply by the rule *ṭh-ug-id-acām*. Then, after the elision of the vowel *a* by *acaḥ*, the lengthening [of the preceding vowel] by *cau* does not take place.

Because the preceding *aṇ* (vowel) is absent, it would follow that [the form] should be *pratyaca*; therefore, he says: "by the elision of *ac*, etc. Due to the elision of *ac*, the vowel *a* which is the cause for the *yaṇ* substitution is on the verge of destruction; thus, the *yaṇ* substitution does not occur here. Consequently, the form remains as *prati ac as*.

When the *akāra* is elided by the rule *ṭhacaḥ*, and the *ikāra* is lengthened by the rule *ṭhcau*, the form *pratīcaḥ* is established without objection. It is precisely for this purpose that the rules *ṭhacaḥ* and *ṭhcau* were initiated.
In the case of *prācaḥ paśya*, even in the absence of elision and lengthening, the form is established simply through the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel coalescence).

Because the form is established [by other means]. In the Bhāṣya, however, it is resolved that there is no *yaṇ* substitution here precisely by the force of the introduction of the rule "ṭhcau. Nor should it be argued that this rule finds its scope of application in examples such as "prācaḥ paśye," because that is already accounted for by the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality) alone. This is according to the principle: "An internal operation (*āṅga*) is stronger than an external one (*vārṇa*)."

When the elision (*lopa*) of *ṭha* occurs by the rule "paribhāṣayā ṭhacaḥ," the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrgha*) is not established; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Thus, when we have *adas-añc*, and after the application of *kvip*, the formation of a compound with an upapada, and the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*), we arrive at the form *adas-añc*; then, by the rule "ṭhaniditām," there is the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*).
The meaning is: when *adas* followed by *ac* is present.
(Pāṇini 5.3.96) states: *viṣvag-devayoś-ca ṭer-adra-ḍ-acatau-apratyaye*.
[The word] *viṣvag-devayoś-ca* [is part of the rule]. *ṭeradri* has its first case ending elided. [The meaning is] "of these two."

The meaning is "of the words *viṣvak* and *deva*. Regarding the phrase "of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*), the intention is that this is drawn forward by the particle *ca* from the rule "ṭā sarvanāmnaḥ. Regarding the expression "not ending in an affix" (*apratyayānte*), in the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.38] *apratyaya*, since no affix is explicitly heard there, it means "that which has no affix."

The intention is that this is based on the understanding of the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that from which [the suffix] *kvip* and so forth [arise]. In the present context, having cited the substitution of *adraḷ* for *adas*, he demonstrates it by saying, "when *adadri-añc* is situated [there].
This substitution of *adraḷ* takes effect once the *na*-elision has been performed according to the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). As for the *na*-elision...
It should be understood that [the rule applies] because of its posteriority. Regarding "yaṇ": the remainder is "of the *repha* (r) and the vowel *i*.
From the word *adadraḷci*, the case-ending (*sub*) arises. The analysis of *adaso* is: *adasaḥ*, *aseḥ*, *dāt*, *u*, *daḥ*, *maḥ*.
The term *adasaḥ* ends in the genitive case expressing a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). The term *aseḥ* is its qualifier.
The analysis of the compound is: "that sword (asi) which has no 's' (siri) [before it]. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
In the rule "dāt" (Pāṇini 8.2.79), the ablative case is used in connection with direction (*digyoge*). The word "of the following" (*parasya*) is to be supplied.
[The sūtra: *adaso'serdādu do maḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80). [Translation: For the *ad-* of *adas*, when there is no *s*, after *dāt* (the letter *d*), the *d* is replaced by *m*.

Thus he says: "of *adas* when it does not end in *as*" (*adaso'sāntasya*). Why [specify] "not ending in *si*"? [Consider] *adasyati*. Why [specify] "ending in *t*"? [Consider] *amuyā*. Here, by the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*), the substitution does not apply to the letter *y*. Now, one might ask: how can it be said "when *u* and *ū* [follow]" (*udūtāviti*), since only *u* is heard? To this he says: "*u iti*. That is, *u* and *ū*; of these two...

In the analysis *samāhāra* (aggregation), when it is a *dvandva* compound, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided by *luka*. Then, by the rule *savarṇadīrgha*, a long vowel is substituted for the homogeneous vowels. Next, by the rule *sa napuṃsakam*, the neuter gender is applied; then, by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*, the final vowel of the nominal stem is shortened. Finally, because the aggregate is a single entity, the singular number applies, and by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, the nominative suffix *su* is replaced by *śi*.

The meaning is that the form [of the vowel] is *u* due to elision (*luki*). Regarding the phrase "due to internal similarity" (*āntaratamyāt*): for a consonant consisting of half a mora (*ardhamātra*), the short *u* (*mātrika*) is slightly similar;
however, for a short [vowel] consisting of one mora, the short *u* is similar by virtue of having the same duration of one mora (*mātrikatva-sādṛśya*), whereas for a long [vowel], it is...

The meaning is that the vowel *ū* is "two-mora" (*dvimātra*) because of its similarity to having two morae. Regarding the form *amumuyaṅ*: when *adadraṭ* + *ac* + *s* is established, the *num* augment is applied by the rule *ugidacām*; then, after the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes, the final *c* is elided as a member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*); and finally, the *n* of the *num* is changed to a guttural (*kutva*) by the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*.

The meaning is that when *adadraṅ* is established, after applying *mat* to the first *da*, *ut* to the following *a*, *mat* to the second *da*, and *ut* to the following *ra*, the form *amumuyaṅ* results. As for the sequence of the grammatical derivation (*prakriyākrama*): [it proceeds as follows].

This is easy for those who know the sequence of the Sūtras. *Amumuyaṃścau*—the form is like *prāñcau*. The substitution of *utva* and *matva* is as before. When *amumu i ac āṬ* is established, the specific rule is *yaṇ*. Thus we have *amumuīcaḥ*. [In the case of the neuter dual,] *amumu i ac as*.

The meaning is that, according to the stated principle—"when [the condition for] *ṭh* exists, even an *antaranga* operation such as *yaṇ* does not apply in the domain of the elision by *ṭhacaḥ*"—the *yaṇ* substitution has not yet occurred; thus, when the *akāra* is elided by *ṭhacaḥ*, the long vowel of the *ikāra* is substituted by *cau*. As for *amumuyagbhyām*, the distinction is that the substitution of *ku* occurs by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*.

Anticipating the objection that *yaṇ* might replace the vowel *u* following the consonant *m* when followed by the vowel *i*, he says: "Because the substitution of *m* for *n* (*mutva*) is considered asiddha. Thus: *amumuīce*, *amumuīcaḥ* (dual), *amumuīcauḥ* (dual), *amumuyakṣu*. He states another opinion: "When there is an obstruction to the final [element]."

The meaning is that, due to the non-application of the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (of the final [al]), when there is no operation on the final [element], the operation occurs on that which is adjacent to the final. And in the present case, the genitive in "adasaḥ" is not a partitive genitive (avayava-ṣaṣṭhī), but rather a genitive of position (sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī); consequently, the rule "alo'ntyasya" presents itself [as applicable].

The result is that for the final letter of *adas* when it is not preceded by *sa*, there is *utva* (the substitution of *u*) for the letter following *d*, and *m* is substituted for *d*. Furthermore, the final phoneme of *adas* is not a *s* followed by *d*; rather, once the *adr̥k* substitute has been applied, the final phoneme is *i*, and that too is not followed by *d*. Consequently:

The meaning is that, because the *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā* (the rule concerning the final letter) does not apply, there is an obstruction to the substitution [of the final letter]; consequently, the change to *u* occurs only for the letter following the *d*, and the *m* replaces the *d*, but the change to *u* does not occur for the *d* and the preceding vowel situated before it. Now, if this is the case...

If it is argued that the substitution of *na* for the initial *ṇ* of a verbal root, as prescribed by the rule "ṭhṇo naḥ," would apply only in the case of *netā* and not in *namati*, this is not so; for the *paribhāṣā* regarding the final letter does not apply here, and when both a letter in the final position and one not in the final position are simultaneously eligible, it is the letter in the final position alone that is affected.
The meaning of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is clearly explained at length in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "vocalization of the *ṣyaṅ*" (*ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇam*).

Although the technical rule "when there is no modification of the final [element], it applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final" (*anantyavikāre antyasadeśasya*) is cited both in the sūtra "vocalization of the *ṣyaṅ*" and in the present sūtra...

Nevertheless, that very [principle] is effectively included here. The term *antyavikāra* means a modification (i.e., a substitute) of the final [sound]. *Anantyavikāra* means the absence of such a modification of the final [sound].

According to the rule, "A negative (*nañ*) determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*) is optionally formed with an indeclinable (*avyayībhāva*) when there is an absence of meaning," [the term *anantyavikāra* is understood as an indeclinable compound].

Because it will be explained later, this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In the alternative view where it is an *avyayībhāva*, however, there is an absence of the substitution of *am* by the rule "optionally after the third and seventh case endings" (*tṛtīyāsaptamyorbahulam*). This means that, due to the non-application of the paribhāṣā "the substitute takes the place of the final letter" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*), there is no substitution for the final [phoneme]. Thus, [the form] is *adamuyaṅ*. Here...
The distinction is that there is no substitution of *m* for the preceding *d* and the following *a*.
He states another opinion: "for *aḥ*, [that is] for the *s* of *siḥ*. The explanation of *siḥ* is "for the *s*. This term *aseḥ* is not a negative *tatpuruṣa* compound; rather, it is *aḥ*...

The analysis of the compound *seryasya sa-asiḥ* is *tasya aseḥ*. Here, *seḥ* is a genitive in the sense of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and the meaning is "that which possesses an *a* in the place of the *s*. When the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of the initial of *adas* with *a*) has been applied to the word *adas*, it comes to possess an *a* in the place of the *s*. Therefore, it refers to that which possesses the *tyadādyatva* [substitution].

Thus, it is established that the *mutva* (the substitution of *m*) applies to the word *adas-* and not to any other. Therefore, when the substitute *adruḷ* occurs, because it lacks the vowel *a* which occupies the same position as the *s*, there is no *mutva*; this is the meaning.
He states that all three of these positions are approved by the Bhāṣya: "And it has been said."

When *adasaḥ* and *adreḥ* follow *vidhau*, in the case of *adadraḷci*, there is simultaneously *matva* (substitution of *m*) for both the first and second *d*s, as well as *utva* (substitution of *u*) for the subsequent *a*-vowel and *r*.
This is like the case of *latva*. Thus, in *calīklṛpyate*, once *carīkṛpyate* has been established—

Just as there is the substitution of *l* for *r* in the case of *repha* and *ṛkāra* according to the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*, so some desire this [substitution] here as well. For—since *mukha* (the substitution of *m*) is observed only for that *si* which possesses an *a* in the place of its *s*, the construction is to be understood through the *bahuvrīhi* compound *aḥ seḥ yasya*. Why [is it said] "of *viṣvak* and *deva*"?

The meaning of the question "What is the purpose of [the rule] *viṣvag-devayoś ca*? is as follows: regarding the example *aśvācī*, the intention is that because *viṣvak* and *deva* are absent here—and likewise the absence of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—the substitution of *adry-ala* does not occur. The meaning of the question "What is the purpose of [the rule] *viṣvag-devayoś ca*? is as follows: regarding the example *aśvācī*, [the same applies] here because of the absence of *viṣvak* and *deva*.

The sense is that because there is no [independent] word "sarvanāman," there is no substitution of *nādya*. Regarding *viṣvagañcanam*: the sense here is that since the suffix *ṭhan* (which is replaced by *lyuṭ*) is heard [in the derivation], the root *añc* does not end in a suffix (*apratyayānta*).

Now, one might object: since there is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the meaning would be "when *añc* is the subsequent member," and thus [the rule would apply] in the case of *viṣvagañcanam*.

Since the region of *ādraḍa* is not applicable [in this context], one might ask: "What is the purpose of including the term 'non-suffix' (*apratyaya*)? To this he says: "The inclusion of the term 'non-suffix'... By that [term]. Otherwise, in the rule *ataḥ kṛkami*, because the word *samāsa* (compound) is understood from the preceding rule *nityaṃ samāse*, and because that would imply a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), [the rule would apply] only when the subsequent member is the verbal root *kṛ*.
The meaning is that [the suffix] would apply only in *ayaskṛt* (iron-worker) for the sake of obtaining the object (*arthalābha*), but not in *ayaskāra* (iron-worker); such is the sense.
Regarding *udaṅ*: the intention is that in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "one who goes upward" (*ut añcati*), there is the application of *kvip* and so forth.
[Pāṇini 6.4.139: *uda īt*.

When the elision [of the *ṭhak* suffix] by the rule "after a word beginning with *śas*, etc., there is elision of *ṭhak*" is about to occur, [the rule] "uda īt" applies. The sūtra "ṭhacaḥ" is understood [from the previous rule], as well as "at" from the rule "allopaḥ". The governing term "bhasya" is also in force;
this is what he expresses by saying "from the word *udacchabda*, etc. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "that which goes together" (*sam añcati*), there is the addition of *kvip* and so forth.
*samaḥ sami* | 6|3|93|.

*samaḥ sami*: the word *samī* has its nominative case ending elided. The phrase *añcatāv apratyaye* (in the case of the suffix *añcu* when not followed by a *pratyaya*) is understood [from the previous rule]. With this in mind, he explains the sūtra by supplying the remaining words—namely, *apratyaye*.
Regarding the word *samīca*: after the elision [of the suffix] by the rule *ṭhacaḥ*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *ṭhcau*.
(Pāṇini 6.3.95) states: *sahasya sadhriḥ*.
That is, *sadhri* is the substitute for *saha* when followed by the suffix *añc* ending in a non-pratyaya (i.e., not beginning with a suffix). Thus, *sam-añc* becomes *samīc*.

The explanation has been omitted because it is easy to understand. Regarding *sadhryak*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) as "that which goes together" (*saḥ añcati*), the suffix *kvip* and so forth are applied as before. When *saha* is replaced by *sadhrī*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.
(Pāṇini 6.3.94) states: "In place of *tiras*, [the substitute] *tiri* occurs when [the suffix] *al* is elided."

Regarding the rule *tirasastiry-alo-pe*: the word *tiri* is in the nominative case with its case-ending elided. The phrase *ṭhañcatāv-apratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.3.79) is understood to carry over. The analysis of the compound *alopaḥ* is as follows: that [suffix] for which there is no *alopa*—meaning "the elision (*lopa*) of the *ac*" (Pāṇini 6.4.138)—does not exist; [the suffix is] *alopa*. This is what he states by saying "when [the suffix] is not elided," and so forth. Thus, *tiryaṅ*.

In the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "tiraḥ-añcati," [the suffix] *kvip* and so forth are applied. When *tiras* undergoes the substitution of *tiri*, the *yaṇ* [sandhi] occurs, resulting in *tiraścaḥ*.

Regarding the form *tiraścaḥ*: since the elision (*al-lopa*) of the *ṭhak* [suffix] applies before vowels beginning with the nominative plural marker *śas*, the substitution of *tiri* does not take place. The intention is that the *s* becomes *ś* by the rule of *ścutva*.

( ) *Nāñceḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.30). When the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *añc* in the sense of "worship," the elision of the nasal (*n*)—which would otherwise occur by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*—is prohibited by the rule *nāñceḥ*. [This is because the word *añc* is included in the list of exceptions to the application of *aniditām*. From the rule *aniditām*, [the phrase] *upadhāyāḥ* [is understood].

The term *ṭhkṅtī* is understood from the previous context. From the rule *ṭhśnānna lopaḥ*, the phrase *nalopa* is understood to carry over. The word *ne* has its genitive case ending elided. This is what he expresses by the words "of that which signifies honor" (*pūjārthasya*), etc.
The meaning is: "when honor is implied"; however, in this context, the verbal root *añc* itself does not possess the sense of honoring.

This is what is intended to be expressed. For this very reason, there is no elision of the *n* in the expression "he goes with composed limbs" (*añcitaṃ gacchati*). Here, the meaning of the root *añc* is "composure. It is understood that he goes having become composed. Composure, moreover, is the state of being undisturbed; thus, the meaning is that he goes undisturbed. And in going undisturbed, there is honor (*pūjā*).

It is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *ṭhañ caupādāne* that [the suffix] is applied, and not that this meaning belongs to the root *añc* alone. Regarding *prāṅ*: the suffix *kvip* is added to *añc* preceded by *pra*.
The meaning of *añc* here is "excellent" (*prakarṣeṇa pūjanam*). In the absence of the elision of *n*, the case-ending (*sub*) arises from the form *prāñcaḥ*.
The elision of the *hal* and *ad* suffixes occurs, followed by the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

Then, upon the removal of the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*, the *n* is replaced by *ṅ* according to the rule "the *k* substitution for the *kvip* suffix" (*kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*). This is the intended meaning. As for the form *prāñcau*: it refers to the natural *n*.

The intended meaning is that [the forms] *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* apply. Regarding the term *alupta*: since in the rule *ṭhugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70) only those stems ending in *añc* that do not undergo elision (*nalopin*) are understood, the augment *num* does not apply here. Consequently, the intention is that one need not fear hearing two *n*-sounds. Regarding "due to the absence of *nalopa*": this refers to the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138), which applies when a vowel beginning with *śas* follows.

The elision does not occur; the point is that only the root *añc* with the nasal *n* (*na-kāra*) is understood there [in the rule]. Regarding *prāñcaḥ*: when *pra* and *añc* stand together, the form is derived through the long vowel by class agreement (*savarṇadīrgha*).
Even if the rule "there is no *suṭ* for *añc* in the sense of honor" were not commenced, the form would still be established by the addition of *num* after *suṭ*.

In the case of *śas* and so forth followed by a vowel, the hearing of the letter *n* would not occur, because of the risk of its elision by the rule *ṭhaniditām*. Furthermore, since it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the addition of *num* by the rule *ṭhugidacām* is also not applicable; this is how it should be understood. As for *prāṅbhyām*: due to the status of being a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*, the *c* [is subject to modification].

The point is that when the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* is elided, and the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* have been removed, the *n* undergoes the substitution of *ṅ* by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya*, resulting in the form *praṅ*. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": [the forms are] *prāṅbhiḥ*; *prāñce*, *prāṅbhyām*, *prāṅbhyaḥ*; *prāñcaḥ*, *prāñcoḥ*, *prāñcām*.

*prāñci*, *prāñcoḥ*; *prāṅkṣu*. By the rule *ṭhṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk*, *kuk* is optionally applied; in the alternative view that "the second consonants of the *ṭh-cay* group" are substituted, *kha* is also to be understood. Thus: in the presence of the suffix *suṭ*, the forms are exactly as before. Before vowel-beginning suffixes such as *śas* and so on, [the suffix] *pratyayaḥ* applies: *pratyañcā*, *pratyaṅbhyām*.

*amumuyaṅcaḥ*, *amumuyaṅbhyām*; *udañcaḥ*, *udaṅbhyām*—and so forth should be understood. Regarding *kruñca* in the sense of "crookedness," it is said that there is also an absence of *na*-lopa (elision of the nasal). The absence of *na*-lopa occurs by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*; the meaning is that even when the suffix *kvip* is applied without an upapada, this form is a *nipātana* (irregular derivation). However, when [the suffix] *sat* is present...

If there were elision of the *n*, the letter *n* would not be heard; for the augment *num*—prescribed by the rule *ṭhugidacām*—would not apply even in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending]. In reality, however, since the verbal root is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with a naturally occurring penultimate *j*, there is no possibility of the elision of *n* here at all. For this very reason...

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhpareśca ghāṅkayoḥ*, regarding the word *kruñca*, a doubt is raised concerning the possibility of *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) by the rule *co kuḥ* when the letter *c* follows [the ṣatva]. It is then stated that because of the specific grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*) of the word *kruñc* in the sūtra *ṛtvig-ādi*, there is no *kutva*; this statement becomes consistent [only if one accepts the following]. However, if...

If the letter *ñ* were indicated by means of a nasal (*anusvāra*) or a corresponding homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*), then there would be no possibility at all for the substitution of *k* (the *kutva* change) according to the rule "ṭhco kuḥ," and thus that [rule] would be inconsistent; for when *kutva* is to be applied, the *parasavarṇa* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Let this matter rest for now.

Without assuming the status of being a *nopadha*, he says: *kruṅ*. When the suffixes beginning with *hal* and *ṅī* are elided, and the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogānta*) is elided, the *n* undergoes *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya*.
Thus, *kruṅbhyām*. Here, when the final consonant cluster is elided, the *n* undergoes *kutva*, becoming the sound *ṅ*. In this case...

In the nominative singular (*prathamaikavacana*), even when followed by *bhyām* and other suffixes, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) does not occur due to specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). The intention of the *bhāṣya* and *kaiyaṭa* on the rule *pareśca ghāṅkayoḥ* is that the fifth letter of the *ca*-class (*ca-varga-pañcama*), namely *ṅ*, occurs everywhere. Thus, [we have] *payomuk*. [The root] *muc* (in the sense of "releasing") takes the suffix *kvip*.

The word *suvṛśc* is derived from the root *vṛśc* (meaning "to cut") preceded by the prefix *su*, with the suffix *kvip* applied, followed by the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *ṭhgrāhijyā*. He states its specific feature: "the change to *ṣ*.
This means that once the suffix *su* has been elided by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, the letter *c* is changed to *ṣ*. [Then] there is the elision of *s*.

In the *dhātupāṭha*, the term *vraścū* is given; once the substitution of *ś* for *s* (the *ścutva*) has been applied, it is indicated as *ṭhvraścū*. Therein, because the *ścutva* is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the *s* is elided by the rule *ṭhskoḥ*.
By the rule *vāvasāne*, when the *cartva* (substitution of *c* or *ṭ*) applies, the *ṣ* becomes *ṭ*; in its absence, by the rule *jaśtva*, it becomes *ḍ*. This is the meaning.

Regarding *suvṛṭ-sviti*: since the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) is not yet established (*asiddha*), first the augment *dhuṭ* is applied by the rule *ṭh-ḍaḥ si*; thereafter, the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cartva*) occurs—this is the intended meaning. Thus end the words ending in *t*. Now, those ending in *t*. To state a specific rule regarding the word *mahat* when preceded by *accha*, he says: *vartamāne*. This is an *uṇādi* sūtra. [The forms] are "nipātita" (irregularly formed).

In this context, there is an absence of *guṇa* for the two roots *pṛṣu* (in the sense of "sprinkling") and *bṛha* (in the sense of "growth"); for the root *mahi*, the suffix *ati* is applied in the sense of the object; and for the root *gam*, there is the substitution of *jagā*. The phrase "like the *śatṛ*" means "as if ending in the *śatṛ* suffix. The phrase "because of being an *ugit*" refers to the state when *suṭ* is added due to that *śatṛ*-like behavior.
The meaning is that *num* is added because [the stem] ends in a vowel (*ugit*). Regarding "ending in *s*" (*sānta*): when *suṭ* is applied and the form *mahant-s-āṬ* etc.
is established, the meaning is that there is a lengthening of the vowel *a* preceding the *n*. Regarding "it is honored" (*mahyate*):

by means of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the rule "a *kṛt* suffix denotes the agent" (*kartari kṛt*) is set aside, and [the suffix is added] to the root *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*).
The intention is that the suffix *at* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman*). Regarding "mahān":

the intention is that after the application of the *num* augment, the lengthening of the vowel, and the elision of the case-ending *su*, there occurs the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Regarding "mahāntau":

the intention is that after the application of the *num* augment, the lengthening of the vowel, and the substitution of the *anusvāra* with its homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*), [the form is established]. Regarding "he mahann": [the same process applies].

The intention is that because the term *asaṃbuddhau* (in non-vocative cases) is understood [from the previous rule], there is no long vowel by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*. Regarding *mahataḥ*: because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* case ending, there is no long vowel before endings such as *śas*. In the sense of "one who possesses wisdom" (*dhīrasyāsti*), the suffix *matup* is added to the word *dhī*; the letter *p* is an *it*, and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix, [it is declined like a nominal stem].
Because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the case-ending (*sup*) arises.
[The rule] *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14) applies. When *dhīmat* is followed by *s*, [the rule] *atvasantasya* [applies]; here, *atu* is a term with its genitive case ending elided.
This is a separate word (*pṛthakpada*). Because it is an adjective qualifying a member (*aṅga*), the rule of "ending with that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.

The phrase *na-dhātoḥ* is an adjective qualifying *asan*. From the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* is understood by anuvṛtti. Thus, the meaning obtained is: "of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of that which ends in *at* and of that which ends in *as*, provided they are not verbal roots (*dhātu*)."
From the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsaṃbuddhau*, the term *asaṃbuddhau* is understood; from *sau ca*, the term *sau*; and from *ḍhralope*, the term *dīrghaḥ* is carried over.
Thus he says: "of that which ends in /a/, etc. Now, [one might ask: whether the long vowel has been applied or not, since [the condition for its application] is equally applicable...

One might ask: since the augment *num* has been applied because of [the word] being eternal (*nitya*) and superior (*para*), the letter *m* and the vowel *a* no longer exist; thus, in the absence of a final long *ā*, how can there be lengthening here? To this, he says: "Because it is superior" (*param*).
The meaning is that it is due to the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthyāt*); otherwise, the rule would become devoid of scope (*niravakāśatva*). Thereafter...

The meaning is that once *num* has been applied, [the long vowel] is produced as *num*. The principle that "in a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is once superseded is superseded forever" is not absolute, because it is stated that "a rule is established through the recognition of its reappearance (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). This is the intended sense.

Regarding "dhīmān": the intention is that the form arises through the addition of the *num* augment in the long vowel, followed by the elision of the consonant (*hal*) and the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogānta-lopa*). Regarding "he dhīman": the intention is that there is no lengthening because of the rule "in the vocative singular" (*ṭā-saṃbuddhyoḥ*). Regarding "like *mahat*": this is because, since it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, there is no *num* in the *śas* and other case endings.

This is the state of affairs. Although it would have been sufficient to say "ṭhātvasoḥ" (in place of ṭha and as), the inclusion of the term "anta" (end) is for the purpose of grasping only those [bases] that end in "at.

Otherwise, only those which end in "at" in their original enunciation (*upadeśa*) would be included, and not those ending in the *matup* suffix and so forth. For these do not end in "at" in their original enunciation. Now, one might object: does this [restriction] apply to the ending in "as" just as it does to the ending in "at"?

To the question "Why is there no qualification? he says: "Even of the verbal root (dhātuḥ). This means that although [the word] ends in *at*, it is treated as a verbal root for the sake of lengthening (*dīrgha*). The meaning is that the status of being a qualifier of *at-anta* was not adopted for the rule "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*). Now, one might object that a verbal root ending in *at* is not well-known in the Dhātupāṭha; to this he says: "gomantam."

Immediately after "he stands," the word "for the purpose of standing" (*ṭhityarthe*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In the sense of "desiring one who possesses cows" (*gomantamicchati*), by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the suffix *kyac* is applied; then, because the status of being a word (*padatva*) is absent due to the restriction *naḥ kye*, there is no application of the *jaś*-substitution. From the stem *gomatya*, by the rule *sanādyantāḥ...* [it is treated as a verbal root].

Because it is a *dhātu*, when the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), there is the elision of *y* by the rule "ṭhyasya halaḥ" and the elision of *a* by the rule "ato lopaḥ"; thus, after the word *gomat*, the case-ending (*sup*) arises. However, in the sense of "acting like one who possesses cows" (*gomān ivācarati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "it should be stated that *kvip* may optionally follow all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*"); then, [the word becomes part of a verbal base] by the rule "sanādyantāḥ... [which classifies such formations as roots].

Having raised the objection that since this [word *añcu*] is a verbal root (*dhātu*), how can there be the addition of the augment *num* by the rule "ṭhugidacām" (Pāṇini 7.1.70)—given that the rule for adding *num* applies only to non-roots (*adhātu*) ending in an *ugit* vowel—he says: "In the sūtra 'ugidacām'.
Let the sūtra simply be "ugitaḥ sarvanāmasthāne"; for [the form *añcu*] would be established by the fact that the root *añc* itself is *ugit*.
The meaning is that the inclusion of the term *añc* is redundant unless it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
He states the body of this restriction: "If [the operation] applies to a root (*dhātu*)...

This connects with the preceding statement as follows: "If an operation is to apply to a root ending in an *ugit* vowel, then it applies only to the root *añc*, and not to any other root"—this is the purpose of the restriction.
He states the fruit of the rule with the word "tena" (by that). The two verbal roots *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu*, meaning "to go," are marked as having the *ugit* designation.

From these two, by the addition of the suffix *kvip*, there is the elision of the nasal *n* according to the rule "aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ. Then, upon the formation of the nominal case-ending (*sup*), the elision of the case-ending *su* occurs by the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal. Finally, the substitution of *d* occurs by the rule "vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ," resulting in the form *srad*.

The form *dhvat* is intended [as the example]. However, if it were stated [in the rule] as "after a stem ending in a *ṭhukit* [suffix], before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending]," then *num* would occur here as well. But since the mention of *ac* (vowel) is made, the aforementioned restriction is obtained, and thus *num* does not occur here; this is the meaning. Now, if the desired result is established by this much alone, for what purpose is the term *adhātoḥ* ("not after a verbal root") included?

He says: "But [the word] *adhātoḥ*. That which was previously not a stem (*adhātu*) is called *adhātubhūtapūrva*. The meaning is that the term *adhātoḥ* is intended for the sake of applying the augment *num* even to that which was previously not a stem. Consequently, the rule *ṭhugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne* constitutes a single sentence; therein—

The meaning is that even in the absence of the condition "not being a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*), because of the inclusion of the term *aj* [in the rule], it is obtained that "for a verbal root ending in an *u*-vowel (*ugit*)"; thus, the augment *num* would apply to a verbal root ending in an *u*-vowel as well as to the root *añc* when its final nasal is dropped.
Furthermore, "not being a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) constitutes a separate sentence; the aforementioned augment *num* applies even to that which was previously not a verbal root.

The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs. And in the present context, although the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) arises after the derivation of *kyac*, *ācārakvib*, and so on, because the status of not being a verbal root existed prior to the derivation of *kyac* and the others, the addition of *num* is unimpeded; this is the meaning.
All of this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ugidacām*. Here, in the view that *kyac* is applied, there is lengthening (*dīrgha*).

Furthermore, when *num* is to be applied, the elision (*allopa*) is not treated as if it were still present (*na sthānivat*), because that [treatment] is prohibited in the case of a rule prescribing a long vowel (*dīrghavidhi*), and because it is stated:
"That which is elided before *kva* is not *sthānivat*. Now, he states the specific rule regarding the word *bhavat*: "from the root *bhā*, the suffix *ḍvatu*. This is an *uṇādi* sūtra.
The meaning is that the suffix *ḍvatu* should be added to the root *bhū*. The letter *ḍ* is an *it* (indicatory), and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

By virtue of being marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the final syllable even though it is not part of a *bha*-stem. Thus, the form is *bhavat*. [In the case of] *bhavān*: the suffix *su* is added to the word *bhavat*; by the rule *atvasantasya ca dhātoḥ*, there is lengthening of the vowel; and by the rule *ugidacām*, the augment *num* is added.

The intended meaning is that there is the elision [of the suffix] by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* and the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Regarding the form ending in *śatṛ*:

by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, the suffix *śatṛ* is substituted for the *laṭ* of the root *bhū*. The letter *ś* is an *it* (indicatory), the letter *ṛ* is an *it*, then there is *śap*, *guṇa*, the substitution of *av* for *u*, and the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), resulting in the form *bhavat*.

However, because that [suffix] lacks the quality of being "atyanta" (absolutely final), the lengthening prescribed by the rule *atvasantasya ca* does not occur; the meaning is that this is due to the inclusion of the indicatory letter *u* [in the technical term *asun*]. Regarding the form *bhavan*:

when the suffix *su* is present, after the application of *num* and the elision of the *hal* and *ṅit* endings, there occurs the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). As for *bhavantau* and so forth, however...
The meaning is "just as before. From the root *dāñ* (to give), with the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present tense marker (*laṭ*), there is the addition of *śap*.
By the rule "ṭhjuhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ" and "ṭhślau," there is reduplication; the shortening of the vowel in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-hrasva*);
and by the rule "ṭhśnābhyastayorātaḥ," there is the elision of the long *ā*. Thus, the form *dadat* arises. Thereafter, the case endings (*sub*) are produced.
Regarding the rule *ubhe abhyastam* (Pāṇini 6.1.5): when the augment *num* was about to apply by the rule *ugidacām*, its prohibition is established by the rule *na abhyastāt*.

About to state the technical designation *abhyasta*, he says: "Both [are] *abhyasta*. From the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya*, the word *dve* ("both") is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. The mention of *ubhe* ("both") is for the purpose of indicating the collective whole.
By the word *dve*, only that doubling (*dvitva*) prescribed in the sixth chapter is intended, because of the principle *anantarasya* ("of what is immediately preceding").
This is according to the maxim: "Whether it be an injunction or a prohibition. Thus he says, beginning with "of the sixth," and so forth.

What [would happen] if they were combined? In the case of *nenijati*, if the designation "abhyasta" (repeated) applied to each individual part, then by the rule "the first of abhyastas is acute," each part would individually become acute.
*nābhyastāc chatuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.78). From the rule *ṅidito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the word *num* is understood to carry over.
Thus he says [the commentary] with the words beginning "from the abhyasta," etc. *dadat* is formed from the word *dadat* with the suffix *su*.

There is elision of the *hal* (consonant) and those beginning with *i* [by Pāṇini 6.4.24]. Because of the prohibition "not for reduplicated bases" (*nābhyastāt*), the augment *num* does not apply by the rule "for *ugit* stems and for vowels" (*ugidacām*). Furthermore, because there is an absence of the suffix *at*, there is no lengthening; this is the intended meaning. [The roots are:
*jakṣ* in the sense of eating and laughing, *jāgṛ* in the sense of the cessation of sleep, *daridrā* in the sense of being in a miserable state, and *cakāsṛ*.

The seven verbal roots *dīp* ("to shine"), *śās* ("to instruct"), *dīdhīṅ* ("to shine" and "to play"), and *vevīṅ* ("equal to *veti*") are listed in the *adādi* (second) class; they take the *suk* suffix.

From these, when the present tense marker (*laṭ*) is replaced by the agentive suffix *śatṛ*, the *śap* suffix is elided, and after the formation of the nominal case endings, [the rule] "nābhyastāc chatuḥ" applies.
A prohibition is intended [for the following]:
"The six beginning with *jakṣ* [are designated as] *abhyasta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.6),
and also for the designation of *abhyasta*.
Since this [term] was not applicable here because it is based on duality, it is now commenced: *jakṣityādayaḥ*.

The term *abhyasta* (reduplicated), which is understood from the previous context, is modified to have a plural ending. In that regard, since *jakṣiti* is the first among those [verbs], when it is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound where the quality itself is included), [the group begins with] *jakṣ*.
If [the term] were begun from the root *dhātu*, there would be the inclusion of only six [roots], and *vevīṅ* would not be included.

However, if it were an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound, there would be the inclusion of six roots beginning with *jāgṛ*, but not *jakṣ*. Therefore, he explains: "six roots," and so forth. In this regard—

In the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*), there is the mention of *jakṣiti* by means of the *śtip* affix; this means the verbal root *jakṣ*. The form [is derived] with the addition of the augment *iṭ* according to the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*. In the sūtra, *jakṣiti* is a separate word. By the particle *iti*, the root *jakṣ* is referred to. Thus.

The term *ādi* (beginning with) forms an *adguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound. Consequently, by the phrase "the six beginning with *ṭhi*," the six verbal roots intended are those other than the root *jakṣ*, starting from *jāgṛ*.
The word *ca* (and) is to be supplied; thus, [the meaning is] the root *jakṣ* and the six [roots] beginning with the root *jāgṛ*.
The meaning is that it results in the seven *dhātu*s (roots) beginning with *cakṣiṅ* being designated as "repeated" (*abhyasta*).
This is clear in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the example *jakṣat*: the point is that because it is repeated, there is a prohibition of the augment *num*.
Now, one might object: since *dīdhī* and *vevī* have the marker *ṅ*, they are designated as "middle-voice" (*ātmanepada*) by the rule "*anudāttaṅti*".
Since the *śānac* replacement would apply to the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) rather than the *śatṛ* replacement, he says: "of *dīdhī* and *vevī*.

It will be stated in the section on verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) that *dīdhī* and *vevī* pertain exclusively to the Vedic language (*chandomātra*). Consequently, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) here is a Vedic anomaly according to the rule "there is much transposition" (*vyatyayo bahulam*). Therefore, because the *śānac* suffix is impossible [in this context], [the *śatṛ* suffix applies].
The meaning is that there is indeed the substitution of *śatṛ*. Regarding *dīdhyat* and *vevyat*:

when the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present suffix (*laṭ*) is applied to the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, and the *śap* affix is elided, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. The intention is that because they are *abhyasta* (repeated) stems, the augment *num* does not occur.
Thus end those ending in *t*. Now, those ending in *p*: regarding *gup*: from the root *gupū* "to protect," with the suffix *kvip*.
The intention is that the *āya* suffix is not applied because it is optional, according to the rule "ṭhāyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31).

Regarding "gubbhyām": the intention is that since the word is a *pada* by virtue of the rule "svādiṣu" (Pāṇini 1.4.17), there is *jaś*-substitution for the [dental] *b* in forms beginning with *bhyām*. Thus end the words ending in *p*.

( ) *tyadādiṣu dṛśo’nālocane kañ ca* ||3|2|60|| Now, the section on the *śānta* (consonants ending in *ś*). To derive the word *tādṛk*, he says: *tyadādiṣu*. By the force of the particle *ca*, the suffix *kvin* is drawn over from the rule *spṛśo’nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58).
In this context, "perception" (*ālocana*) is intended to mean cognition in general; thus he says: "in the case of *tad* and so forth," etc.

What [would be] in the absence of perception? [For example: "he sees him" (*taddarśaḥ*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after an object [of action]. However, if the suffix *kañ* were used, there would be no *guṇa* substitution because it is marked with *k*. When the word *tad* is the subordinate member (*upapada*), [the suffix] *kvip* is applied, and there is a compound with the subordinate member (*upapadasamāsa*).

When *sub*-elision has occurred and the form *tad-dṛś* remains, [the rule] applies: *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.91). The mention of *ā* here is without a case ending (*avibhaktika*). [This is governed by the rule] *dṛg-dṛśavatuṣu*.
The rule [Pāṇini 1.1.54] continues to apply. Thus he says: "of the pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*). "A final substitute" (*antādeśaḥ*):
this is obtained through the paribhāṣā [Pāṇini 1.1.52], *alo'ntyasya*. When the letter *d* is replaced by *ā*, there is a long vowel by rule [Pāṇini 6.1.101], *savarṇadīrghaḥ*.
The resulting form is *tādṛś*. Then, the case endings (*sup*) arise. Regarding "the substitution of *k*" (*kutvasya*): [this applies to] *tādṛś s*.

When the elision of *hal* and *ṅy* etc. has occurred, because the substitution of *k* for [the final consonant] of a *kvip* suffix is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya ku*, the rule *vraśca-* applies, resulting in the letter *ṣ*. The phrase "of that" means "of the letter *ṣ* produced by the rule *vraśca-*". The phrase "by the *k*-substitution of that" refers to the letter *ḍ*.
The meaning is that the letter *ga* is substituted by the rule "ṭh-kvin-pratyayasya ku" (Pāṇini 8.2.62). Regarding the phrase "by its *ca*-substitution":

this means that for the letter *ga*, there is an optional substitution of *ca* by the rule "vā-avasāne" (Pāṇini 8.4.56). As for the word "tādṛk": the analysis "it is seen like that" (*sa iva dṛśyate*) is not the correct one, because the suffix *kvin* is prescribed only in the sense of the agent according to the rule "kartari kṛt" (Pāṇini 3.4.67).

However, [the suffix] *kvin* occurs here in the sense of the agent being the object of the action (*karmakartari*). The meaning is: "this one sees like that," which is to say, "he becomes an object of cognition. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśeḥ*, where it is stated: "In this context, because the root *dṛś* functions solely in the sense of attaining the status of being an object of cognition, it does not have the meaning of 'knowing' (*jñāna*). [The word in question is] a conventional term (*rūḍhaśabda*).
"Others say it is exactly thus. Now, he refutes the opinion of Kaiyaṭa and others here: "Because it is an exception to the rule for *ṣatva*.

Although, even though *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) has not yet applied to the roots *dadhṛk*, *añcu*, *yuj*, and *kruñc*—since the rule "the *k* of the suffix *kvip*" (*kvan-pratyayasya kuḥ*) is initiated while *ṣatva* from the *vraśca*-group is still pending—even so, since the form is already established by *kvip* alone...

The prescription of the *kvin* suffix in the rules "ṭhspṛśo'nudake kvin" and "tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca"— which is formulated for the purpose of applying the *kutva* change via the rule "kvinpratyayasya kuḥ" to form words such as *ghṛtaspṛk*— would be entirely without scope (*niravakāśa*) if it were not applicable in cases such as *tādṛk*. Therefore, with respect to that domain:

The intention is that, by virtue of its result, this [substitution] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). It is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *spṛśo 'nudake* that the prescription of the *kvin* suffix is solely for the purpose of the *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *s*) according to the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*. And it is precisely because of its lack of occasion (*anavakāśatva*) that the *kutva* applies in the domain of the letter *ṣ*.

Nor is there the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*). Otherwise, rules such as *ṭhspṛśo'nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58) prescribing *kvin* after roots like *spṛś* would be rendered useless. And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*:
"An exception (*apavāda*) prevails by virtue of the authority of the specific statement. [The phrase] "it is the letter *kh*" means...

The intended meaning is that this is due to the similarity between the unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) and the aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*) [consonants]. Regarding "only *kha*": two forms, *atadṛk* and *tādṛk*, are desired. When the letter *śa* becomes *kha* by virtue of the rule for *kutva*, and when the rule *ṭvāvasāne* applies to change it to *ṭha* in the case of the alternative of *cartva* (the substitution of a sibilant), the form *tādṛk* is established; however, in the absence of *cartva*, the form remains *tādṛkh*.

The meaning is that, in such a case, the letter *ga* would not be heard. Now, one might object: "Let there be the substitution of *kha* for *śa*; nevertheless, even if the rule for *cartya* (the substitution of *ca*-class letters) does not apply, the substitution of *jaś* (the substitution of *ja*-class letters) will ensure that *ga* is established without obstruction.
To this, he says: "With respect to the application of *jaś*. This means that when *ga* is to be produced by the rule of *jaś*.

The meaning is that because the *kh* resulting from the substitution of *kutva* for the letter *ś* is considered *asiddha*, there is an absence of *jhal* [sounds], and consequently, the application of *jaśtva* is impossible. Now, in order to dispel the aforementioned objection according to the view of Kaiyaṭa and others, he says: "By the rule *digādibhyo yat*" (Pāṇini 4.3.54). [From the root] *viś* (meaning "to enter") with the suffix *kvip*, we have *viś*.

Regarding the form *rūpa*: he states its specific derivation—“*vraśca* etc., [there is] the substitution of *ṣ*. This means that when *viś* remains after the elision of the *haṅyādi* suffixes, the letter *ś* is replaced by *ṣ* according to the rule *vraśca*. Regarding “*jaśtva* and *cartva*”:
by the *jaśtva* substitution, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; then, by the rule *vāvasāne*, that *ḍ* optionally becomes *ṭ* through *cartva*.

This is the meaning. [The forms] *viḍbhyām* and *viṭsu* (from *viṭsu*). [The root] *naś* in the sense of "disappearance" takes the suffix *kvip*; thus the form is *naś*. Then, the case endings (*sup*) arise. When the elision of *s* occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* and the substitution of *ṣ* is invariably required by the rule *vraśca-*, etc., [the following applies]:
*naśervā* | 8|2|63|. From the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*, the word *kuḥ* is understood;
and from the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, the word *ante* is also understood. The term *padasya* and so forth are supplied from the governing context.

Thus he says: "of *naś*" and so forth. The substitution of the final letter (*anta-ādeśa*) is obtainable from the sūtra *alo'ntyasya*. In the alternative case, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by *vraśca* before a vowel (*aci*). Thus we have *nak* and *nag*. In the case of the *kutva* substitution, the two forms arise through *jaśtva* and *cartva*. [Similarly] *naṭ* and *naḍ* arise in the case of the *ṣatva* substitution through *jaśtva* and *cartva*. [The form] *nagbhyām*...

Regarding the rule *naḍhÂabhyām*: in the alternative where *kutva* applies, there is the letter *ga* by virtue of *jaśtva*; however, in the alternative where *ṣatva* applies, there is the letter *ḍa* by virtue of *jaśtva*. But the augment *num* [as prescribed] by the rule *ṭhmasjinaśorjhalī* does not apply here, because it will be stated later that its operation occurs only when a suffix is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*).

*Spṛśo’nudake kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58). Regarding *spṛśo’nudake*: the term *anudake* means "when [the word] *udaka* is not present," that is, when there is a *sup*-ending word other than the word *udaka*. The intention is that the term *supi* is understood here by anuvṛtti from the rule *supi sthaḥ*. For example: *ghṛtaspṛk* ("one who touches clarified butter").
In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who touches clarified butter" (*ghṛtaṃ spṛśati*), the suffix *kvin* is applied. This forms an *upapada* compound; the case endings (*sup*) are elided (*subluk*).
From the word *ghṛtaspṛś*, the case ending *su* arises. By the rule *sror halṅyādi lopaḥ*, the *su* is elided.

Since the substitution of *ṣ* for *k* (the *kutva* change) prescribed by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya* is considered *asiddha* (not yet established), the rule *vraśca-* applies first, changing the *ś* to *ṣ*. Of that...

The *ḍ* is replaced by *ja*; that [j] is replaced by *ga* by the rule for *kutva*; and that [g] optionally undergoes *cartva* (substitution by a voiceless unaspirated stop)—this is the intended meaning. Thus we have *ghṛtaspṛgbhyām* and *ghṛtaspṛkṣu*. Now, regarding the rule "the *k* of a *kvin* suffix" (*kvinaḥ kuḥ*), since the word "of a *kvin*" (*kvinaḥ*) alone would suffice to convey "of that which ends in *kvin*," the inclusion of the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) indicates that the *kvin* itself is the suffix.

Regarding the phrase "because," it was stated during the analysis of the word *yuk* that this is for the sake of obtaining a *bahuvrīhi* compound; he states its purpose as: "the quality of being *kit* occurs even when there is *kvip*. The ellipsis is "it occurs when [the suffix] exists. To begin with, the suffix *kvip* is prescribed after the root *spṛś* when a word other than *udaka* is present as an upapada. Therefore, [this applies] when there is no prefix (*nirupasarga*).

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *spṛś* as well. Even though it does not currently end in *kvip*, the substitution of *k* for *s* (*kutva*) still occurs; the point is that by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the mere potentiality of ending in *kvip*—even if only at some time—is sufficient to trigger the rule. The six *aṅga*-markers are as before.
The meaning is [that the change occurs] by means of the substitution of *ṣatva*, *jaśtva*, *kutva*, and *cartva*. Thus end the words ending in *ś*. Now, those ending in *ṣ*:

he shows the etymological derivation of the word *dadhṛṣ*—namely, from the root *ñi dhṛṣ*. The suffix *ñi* is applied according to the rule "the group beginning with *ñi* consists of *ñi*, *ṭu*, and *aṅ*. The vowel *ā* is an *it* (indicatory) according to the rule "in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is an *it*."

Regarding the phrase "by means of the *ṛtvij* and so forth": the three suffixes beginning with *kvin* are treated as irregular (*nipātana*). When *kvin* is elided, there is reduplication of the root *dhṛṣ*. By the rule *ṭhuraḥ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* occurs. By the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable are dropped. Because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel; thus, the form is *dadhṛṣ*.
The designation of the final syllable as udātta (antodātta) is for the purpose of preventing the udātta accent on the first syllable in forms such as *nityādi-nityam*.

Regarding the phrase "prior to *kutva*": because *kutva* is considered *asiddha* with respect to *jaśtva*, the meaning is that the substitution of *ḍa* for *ṣa* occurs first by means of *jaśtva*. [The form] *gaḥ kaḥ* [is derived] from *ḍa* being changed to *ka* by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya*.

The letter *ga*; the meaning is that it becomes *ka* by virtue of the rule for *ca*-class substitution (*cartva*). Regarding *ratnamuṭ*: [the root] *muṣ* (meaning "to steal") takes the suffix *kvip*, followed by a compound with an upapada; there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), elision according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (*halṅyādi-lopa*), and then the application of *jaśtva* and *cartva*—this is the intended sense. The word *ṣaṣ* always ends in the plural number. Of that...

He demonstrates the forms specifically in the plural: "ṣaḍbhyo luk" (there is elision after the six [numerals]). The remainder is: "by this [rule], there is elision of *jaś* and *śas*, and then *jaśtva* and *cartva*. Regarding "the rule applies to that which ends in [the specified stem]": the sense is that because the two rules "elision after the six" and "and after *ṣaṣ* and *catuḥ*" are *aṅga*-rules (rules concerning the base).

In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *priyaṣaṣ*, meaning "one to whom six are dear," there are singular, dual, and plural forms: *priyaṣaṭ*, *priyaṣaḍ*, *priyaṣaṣau*, *priyaṣaṣaḥ*, and so forth, just like the word *ratnamuṣ*. In this regard, [the rules] *ṭhṣaḍbhyo luk* and *ṭhṣaṭcaturbhyaśca* apply.

The meaning is that [the rules for] *luṅ* and *luṭ* apply. In the sense of "he desires to recite," from the root *paṭh* (in the sense of "distinct speech"), the suffix *san* is added by the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*. Then, by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*, reduplication occurs; by *halādiśeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant is elided; by *sanyataḥ*, the vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes *i*; then the augment *iṭ* is added to *san*, and the change to *ṣ* occurs.

By the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, [the form] possesses the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). From the form *pipaṭhiṣ*, [by adding] *kvip* and applying *ato lopaḥ*, we have *pipaṭhiṣ*, ending in the letter *ṣ*. Because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, it has the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), from which the nominative suffix *su* is added. Regarding this, he shows the specific detail: "with regard to *rutva*" (the substitution of *r*). [The rule] *kvau luptam na*...

The meaning is that because of the prohibition [of substitution] by the rule *sthānivat*, once the elision of the consonant (*hal*) and following vowels (*ṅy-ādi*) has occurred, the substitution of *ru* takes place by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*.
Nor should one fear the absence of the letter *s*, because with respect to the substitution of *ru*, the substitution of *ṣ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

*rvor upadhāyā dīrgha ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19). The analysis of *rvor upadhāyāḥ* is as follows: *ru* and *v* are *rvau*; [the rule applies] to those two. From the previous rule, *sipi dhāto rurvā*, the term *dhātoḥ* (of a verbal root) is understood by anuvṛtti. *Rvoḥ* is its qualifier.

Therefore, this is an *anta-vidhi* (an operation concerning the end). The phrase "of a word" (*padasya*) is supplied as a governing rule (*adhikṛta*). From the rule "of *sk* and *k*, when they are the first members of a conjunct" (*skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*), the word "at the end" (*ante*) is understood by *anuvṛtti*. Thus he says, beginning with "repha... and so on. Regarding *pipaṭhīḥ*: the meaning is that after the lengthening of the vowel following the letter *k*, the *repha* (visarga) is substituted for the *r*. [In the case of] *pipaṭhībhyām*.
