The intention is that because [the word] is a *pada* by virtue of the rule *ṭhsvādiṣu*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel before suffixes beginning with *bhyām* etc., as characterized by the rule *ṭhvorupadhāyāḥ*. He states the specific rule regarding the locative plural (*sup*)—namely, *vā śari*—as follows:
when *pipaṭhiṣ-su* is situated, since the status of *ṣ* is considered *asiddha*, *r* is substituted [for *s*], and then lengthening occurs.

Regarding the *visarjanīya*: by the rule "optionally, when followed by a sibilant (*śar*), the *visarjanīya* becomes *ṭh* or *t*," the *visarjanīya* is optionally replaced. In the alternative case where that [substitution] does not occur, the meaning is that the *visarjanīya* remains as itself (*satva*).
In that context, when the *visarjanīya* option is applied and the form *pipaṭhiḥ-su* has been established, [the rule] beginning with "after *iṇ* and the *ka*-group... [applies].
Since the quality of being "para" (subsequent) is absent, the rule *ṣatva* [Pāṇini 8.3.59], "in place of ṣ and before a suffix," does not apply.
[The sūtra] *numvisarjanīyaśarvyavāye 'pi* (8.3.58): *num*, *visarjanīya*, and *śar*—the words *ṭu* from *ṭunā ṣṭuḥ* and *mūrdhanyaḥ* are carried over [from previous rules].

He says this with the words "by each of these" (*etaiḥ pratyekam*), and so forth. Here, it is intended that there be an intervention by *num* and the others individually, and not an intervention as far as possible (as in the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*), as is clear from the Bhāṣya. Consequently, in the present case, under the alternative where there is a *visarjanīya*, by that [rule]:
The intention is that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs even when there is an intervention. Regarding the alternative where the *visarjanīya* becomes *s*, he says:

"by [the rule] *ṣṭuan*. When *pipaṭhīs-su* is established, since the first *s* provides an intervention by the *śar* sounds, the second *s* undergoes the substitution of *ṣ* because it follows an *i*-vowel (*ī*) which is an *iṇ* sound.

The *s* of the preceding [word] becomes *ṣ* by virtue of the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*; however, it does not become *ṣ* by the rule *ṣaḥ pratyayasya*, because the phrase "not being at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*) is understood to apply there—this is the intended meaning. And thus, since the desired result would already be established by the rule *numśarvyavāye’pi*, they say that the mention of *visarjanīya* [in the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ*] is redundant.

In this context, the inclusion of the *visarjanīya* among the *ayogavāha* sounds—even though they are listed in various recensions—is rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the form *niṃs-sva*: the root *ṇisi* in the sense of "kissing" takes the *lug*-vikaraṇa (*śap*).
By the rule "ṇo naḥ," the *ṇ* is replaced by *na*; because it ends in *it*, the *num* augment is added. Due to its being *anudātta*, the *ātmanepada* endings are employed.
The second person singular middle voice suffix is *thās*;
by the rule "ṭh-thāsaḥ se," it becomes *se*, and by "ṣa-vābhyāṃ vām-au," the vowel *e* is changed to *v*.
When *nin-issva* is established, the form *niṃssva* results through the insertion of an *anusvāra* by the rule "naś-cāpadāntasya. Here, as far as possible—

The point is that if one were to rely on a general intervention [by any intervening element], then the substitution of *ṣ* for the second *s* would occur even when it is separated from the preceding *n* by the *anusvāra* (which is the substitute for *num*) and the first *s*. Therefore, the intention is that the intervention must be considered individually [for each specific case].
Regarding *niṃsse*: this is the second person singular (*thās*) of the *loṭ* (imperative) mood from the aforementioned root; for that *thās*, [the rule *ṭhthāsaḥ* applies].

The substitution of *se* for *sa* occurs [in the rule *se 'ci*]. In the case of *niṃsse* as well, the change to *ṣ* does not occur for the second *s*, because the intention is that the intervention (*vyavadhāna*) is considered only with respect to each [individual letter] separately. [This refers to the root] *hiṃsi* in the sense of "injuring";
from this root preceded by the prefix *su-*, with the suffix *kvip* added, and *num* inserted due to its being marked with the *idit* designation, [the form is derived] in the seventh case plural.

When *suhin-su* is established, the first *s* is elided by the rule for the disappearance of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), resulting in the form *suhinsu*. Because of the rule *svādiṣu*, [the word] ends in a *pada*; therefore, the rule *naścāpadāntasya* does not apply, and there is no anusvāra. Furthermore, from the word *pum* in the seventh case plural, we have *puṃsu*.

When the first *s* remains after the elision of the final consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the form is *puṃsu*. In that regard, in the case of *suhinsu*, the substitution of *ṣ* would occur because of the intervention of the augment *num*. If the mention of *num* were intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the anusvāra, then *ṣ*-substitution would undesirably occur in *puṃsu* as well; therefore—

He says: "The mention of *num*. [This is] because of the explanation; that is to say, because it is explained in that manner in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the present sūtra and on the sūtra "hayavaraṭ. [Thus, there is] the mention of *num*.

He states that [the inclusion of] *num* is for the purpose of indicating the *anusvāra* that takes its place, as this follows the literal wording of the rule: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). The sense is that because the mention of *num* is intended to indicate the *anusvāra* that occupies its place, the mention of *num* would be redundant since the desired result is already established by the mention of *śar* alone, as the *anusvāra* is also included among the *śar* sounds. Regarding *cikīrṣ-*: from the root *kṛ*, with the suffix *san*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ṛ* because it is marked with *k* (by the rule *iko jhal*), and then there is the lengthening of the vowel by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*.

Then, from the root *kṛ*, there is the substitution of *i* by the rule "ṭhṛ iddhātoḥ," and lengthening by "ṭhhali ca. Next, there is reduplication by "ṭhsanyaṅeḥ. By "ṭhhalādiḥ śeṣaḥ" and "ṭhhrasvaḥ," [the form becomes *cikīrṣa*]. By "ṭhkuhoścuḥ," the *k* of the reduplicated syllable undergoes the change to *c*, and the *s* undergoes the change to *ṣ*. Thus, the form *cikīrṣa* is obtained. Because it is a verbal root by the rule "ṭhsanādyantāḥ," the suffix *kvip* is added. By "ṭhato lopaḥ," the *a* is elided. From this *cikīrṣa*, which ends in *ṣ*, when the case-ending *su* arises, after the elision of *su* by "ṭhhalṅyādilopaḥ," the form remains as *cikīrṣa*.

Having taken this much for granted, and having stated that by the rule *ṭh-rātsasya* there is no elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) because of the presence of the letter *ṣ*, he says: "by *rātsasya*. The intention is that this is because the substitution of *ṣ* (for *s*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). In the same way, forms such as *cikīrṣbhyām* are to be inferred. Anticipating the objection regarding the visarga, he says: "by *roḥ supi*. The intention is that in the present case, there is an absence of *ru*-hood (*rutva*) for the *r* that has been produced by the substitution of *ra* (for *repha*). Regarding *damer ḍos*, this is a sūtra from the *Uṇādi* [section].

The meaning is that the suffix *ḍoṣ* is applied to the root *ṭhdamu* (meaning "to pacify" or "to calm"). The letter *ḍ* is an *it* (indicatory letter). By virtue of being an *it*, [the rule] *yasyeti ca* applies. The meaning is that although the elision of *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is prescribed for a *bha*-stem by the rule *ṭeḥ*, it occurs here even though there is no *bha*-status, due to the force of the *ḍit* designation. Because the *s* is a constituent of the suffix, it undergoes *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*). Thus, the form *doṣ* ends in *ṣ*. Then, the suffix *su* is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Having taken this much as established, he says: "because *ṣatva* is considered asiddha. Because *ṣatva* is asiddha, when *rutva* (change to *r*) occurs, the *visarga* appears. Regarding the phrase *vā doṣan*: the remainder of the rule is *śasādau* (in the case of the nominative plural and other cases beginning with *śas*).

Regarding "doṣṇaḥ": the meaning is that when the substitute *doṣan* is applied for *śas*, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "allopaḥ anaḥ," and then the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "raṣābhyām. Thus, [the forms] are *doḥṣu* and *doṣṣu*. He derives the word *vivikṣu*: "from the root *viś*"—that is, from the desiderative (*sannanta*) form; the analysis being "one who desires to enter" (*veṣṭum icchati*).

From the root *viś*, the suffix *san* is added. Because *san* is *kit* by the rule "ṭhhalantācca," there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. By the rule "sanyaṅe," reduplication occurs. By "halādi śeṣaḥ," all consonants except the first are elided. Since the *ś* is followed by a *jhal* sound (the *s* of the suffix), it becomes *ṣ* by the rule "vraśce. Then, by "ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si," the *ṣ* becomes *k*. Because it is part of an affix, the *s* [of the reduplicated syllable] [becomes *ṣ*].

The change to *ṣ* [occurs]. Because [the root] ends in *san*, by the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots" (*sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*), it is a verbal root; thus, by the rule "elision of *a*" (*ato lopaḥ*), the form is *vivikṣ*, meaning it ends in *ṣ*. Regarding the change to *k*: after *vivikṣ*, when the case-ending *su* is elided by the rule "after *hal*, *ī*, etc. (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*), there is the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the *ṣ*.

The elision of the letter *k* by the rule "ṭh-ṣkoḥ" is not to be suspected; for when the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) is to be performed, the substitution of *t* for *ṣ* (by the rule "ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si") is considered asiddha (non-existent). Thus, by the rule "vraśca-", the [substitution of] *ṣ* occurs.
When the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) takes place, the cause—the letter *s*—is removed, and consequently, the substitution of *k* is also [removed].

In the case of *nivṛti*, since the condition of being followed by a *jhal* consonant (*jhal-paratva*) has ceased, the previously applied *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) also ceases; thus, because it is at the end of a word (*padānta*), the *ś* in *ṣṭhiv-raśca* is replaced by *ṣ*. Regarding "jaśtva and cartva": by *jaśtva*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; then, there is the optional application of *cartva* to that *ḍ*. Regarding "of *sakro*": [this refers to] *takṣū*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *tanūkaraṇa*. Then, after the elision of the case-ending *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, there is the elision of *k* by the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*.
By the rule of *jaśtva*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; the meaning is that there is an optional substitution of *ca* (cerebral *ṭ*) for this *ḍ*.
Thus we have *taḍṅyām* and *taṭtsu* (from *taṭ* + *su*). Regarding *goḍ*: [it is derived] from the root *rakṣa* in the sense of "protection."

When the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply with *karman* as the upapada, the form is derived like the word *takṣan* by means of the rule regarding optional dissimilar suffixes (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), following the addition of the *kvip* suffix and the subsequent formation of the case-ending (*sub*). Regarding the statement "from the roots *takṣi* and *rakṣi*": this is an indication made by the vowel *i*. From the two verbal roots *takṣ* and *rakṣ*, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added according to the rule *hetumati ca*; the letter *c* [in *ṇic*] is elided. Then, by the rule *cuṭū*, [the *ṇ* is also elided].

The letter *ṇ* is elided. Then, because [the stems] ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffix *kvip* is applied; subsequently, by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, the *ṇi* is elided. Once *kvip* has been elided, the forms *takṣ* and *rakṣ* end in the letter *ṣ*.
Then, when the case-ending *su* is elided, the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* serves as an exception to the elision of the final member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*).
Intending to show that the *jaśtva* and *cartva* substitutions apply to the letter *ka*, he says:

*tak-tag-gorak-gorag*. From the root *ḍu-pacaṣ* (to cook), with the suffix *san*, there is reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. By the rule *halādi-śeṣaḥ*, all consonants except the first are elided. By the rule *sanyataḥ*, the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable is changed to *i*.

By the rule *ṭhcoḥ kuḥ*, the letter *c* undergoes *kutva* (substitution by its corresponding velar). Because it is part of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*), the *s* is replaced by *ṣ*. Thus, the form is *pipakṣ*. Then, after the elision of the nominative suffix *su*, one might suspect that the *k* would be elided by the rule *ṭhskoḥ*. Anticipating this, he says: "Because *kutva* is asiddha" [with respect to the subsequent operation]. This refers to [the *k*] which stands in the place of the letter *c*.

The remainder [of the analysis] follows. When the *ṣ* is elided by the rule for the disappearance of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the status of being followed by a *jhal* consonant ceases; consequently, the previously applied *k* is also removed. Then, due to its being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*), the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*) applies, followed by the substitutions of *jaś* and *cart*. With this intention, he says: *pipak*, *pipag*. [The forms] *pipakṣau*, *pipakṣaḥ*, and so forth, are likewise formed. Thus...

*vivak*—this is derived from the root *vac* (meaning "to speak") in the sense of "one who wishes to speak" (*vaktum icchati*), following the pattern of the word *vivakṣa*. *didhak*—this is formed from the root *dah* (meaning "to burn") in the sense of "one who wishes to burn" (*dagdhum icchati*). After the suffix *san*, there is reduplication (*dvitva*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and the substitution of *abhyāsetva* (the change of the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable).

When *didahsa* is established, by the rule *dāder dhātor ghaḥ*, the *h* becomes *gh*, resulting in *didagh-sa*. Then, by the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ*, the *d* becomes *dh*, yielding *didhagh-sa*. Next, by the rule *khari ca*, the *gh* becomes *k*, giving *didhak-sa*. Since the *s* is part of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*), it becomes *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. Finally, with the *kvip* suffix and the elision of the *a* by *ato lopaḥ*, the form *didhakṣ* is obtained.

Therefore, when *su* is produced and *su* is elided, because the substitution of *ca* for *k* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the rule "ṭhskoḥ" does not apply; consequently, upon the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the letter *ṣ*, there is an absence of a following *khara* (sibilant), and thus the previously applied *k* is withdrawn.

The intention is that, because it occurs at the end of a word (*padāntatvāt*), *jaś*-ness and *cartva* apply. Thus we have *didhakṣau*, *didhakṣaḥ*, and so forth. These are the roots ending in *ṣ*. Now, those ending in *s*: *supīḥ*. The lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule *ṭhvorupadhāyāḥ*. Similarly, *sutūḥ*. *Vidvān*: from the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (belonging to the *adādi* class); in the present tense (*laṭ*), there is the substitution of *śatṛ* [for the suffix].

In the case of *vidvas* from the root *vid*, the suffix *śatṛ* is replaced by *vasu*. Because it is marked with *śit*, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and thus the augment *śap* is applied, which is then elided.

By the rule "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not *pit* is *ṅit*," the suffix is *ṅit*; consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Since it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, the word *vidvas* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). From this, the nominative singular suffix *su* is added, and because the stem ends in an *ugit* vowel, the augment *num* is inserted.

In the case of *vidvān*, the long vowel [ā] is applied by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*; there is elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*); then, by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, the *s* is elided. The point is that because this [elision of *s*] is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur. Since the word no longer ends in *s*, the substitution of *d* by the rule *vasusraṃsu* does not take place. Thus we have *vidvāṃsau*. When the suffix *suṭ* is added and *num* is applied, the rule *sāntamahataḥ* applies.

The intention is that [the vowel] is long, and by the rule "ṭhnaśca," an anusvāra is substituted. Regarding the vowels beginning with *śas*, he states a specific rule: "There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *vasu*. By the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), [it refers to the suffix *vasu*].
The term *vasoḥ* is taken as including its final element (*tadantagrahaṇam*), and the governing rule (*adhikṛtam*) is *bhasya*. Thus he says: "of that which ends in *vas*.

Regarding *pūrva*: when *śas* is applied, after the substitution of *u* for the *v* in *vidvas*, the form *viduas* results; then, by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the single substitute of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) applies, resulting in *vidus*.

The meaning is that the *ṣ*-sound [of *su*] occurs because it is a part of the suffix (*pratyaya*). One should not suspect that the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is non-existent (*asiddha*) by virtue of the rule "the operations of *ṣatva* and *tu* are asiddha," for that rule applies only to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of a word-final and a word-initial. In *vidvatsu*, after the substitution of *d* for *t* in the locative plural (*sup*), there is the substitution of *c* for *t*. Regarding *sedivān*: [it is derived from] the root *sad*.

In the sense of "falling apart," "going," or "weakening," from the root *vi-śṛ*, the *ṣ* at the beginning of the verbal root is changed to *s* by the rule *dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*. Then, by the rule *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavasaśruvaḥ*, the *kvasu* suffix is substituted for the *liṭ* (perfect) tense marker. The *u* and *k* are elided (*ukāvitau*). By the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ*, reduplication (*dvitva*) occurs. The remaining consonant is retained by *halādiśeṣaḥ*. Finally, by *ata ekahalmadhye*, the *e*-substitution (*etva*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) take place.
The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *ṭhvasvekājādhasām*. Thus, the word *sedivas* is formed. Then follows the suffix *su*; because it ends in an *u*-vowel (*ugit*), the augment *num* is added;

the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*; then there is the elision of *su*; the final *s* is elided by the rule for the elision of a consonant at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

Because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the *n* does not take place. Furthermore, because the word does not end in a *sānta* (ending in *s*) or *vasvant* (ending in *vas*), the substitution of *d* for *s* does not occur—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the form *sedivāṃsau*: the lengthening occurs by the rule *sāntamahataḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.10] when the suffix *num* is applied. Now, one might object: according to the method already stated, from the word *sedivas*, once it is established, when the suffix *śas* is added, the *v* in *vas* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) to *u*; then, after the formation of the single substitute *pūrvarūpa* and the application of *yaṇ* to the *i*, the form would have to be *sedyuṣaḥ*. Consequently, the form *seduṣaḥ* [would not be possible].

The form that is about to be mentioned would be incorrect. Nor should it be argued that, having considered the future result—the *saṃprasāraṇa*—the augment *iṭ* will not apply beforehand because the grammatical derivation is accepted as being delimited by the word (*pada*); for even so, [the fault remains].

Because the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution depends upon the designation (*saṃjñā*) of *bha*, which is caused by suffixes such as those beginning with *su* that are not *sarvanāmasthāna*, it is *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic) with respect to the base (*aṅga*);
since the augment *iṭ* is *antaraṅga* (intrinsic), it applies first, according to the principle that the *antaraṅga* rule takes precedence over the *bahiraṅga*.

To the objection that [the rule] is stronger, he says: "even though it is internal. Regarding the term *akṛta*: the sense is that the status of having a strong initial (*balāditva*) is on the verge of being destroyed by the future occurrence of the *saṃprasāraṇa*. In reality, however, let the derivation of the case-ending (*sub*) occur first from the word *sedivas* itself; nevertheless, as for the letter *va*—
When the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) has occurred and *u* has been substituted, even though the semi-vowel replacement (*yaṇ*) follows,

the form *seduṣaḥ* is established because the semivowel-vocalization is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being "external" (*bahiraṅga*), thereby allowing the elision of the *y* and *v* by the rule *lopo vyoḥ*. Nor does the principle apply here that "when there is immediate succession of vowels (*ajānantarya*), the status of being external is not reckoned."

An objection may be raised: [the prohibition] is to be suspected, because that [prohibition] is accepted to apply only when there is immediate sequence (*ajānantarya*) with respect to what occurs at a subsequent time; and here, since the elision of *v* occurs at a subsequent time, such [immediate sequence] is absent. Furthermore, even if *saṃprasāraṇa* were to take effect once *iṭ* has been applied...

When the augment *iṭ* is elided due to the removal of its cause—the form beginning with *valādi*—the form *seduṣaḥ* is established without objection, according to the maxim: "When the cause is removed, that which depends on the cause is also removed. Furthermore, even in the analysis where the word is the limit (*padāvadhika-anvākhyāna*), when the stage *sedvas-as* is reached, both the augment *iṭ* and the *saṃprasāraṇa* [apply].
They say that because [the substitution] is prescribed by a rule for a specific occasion (*pratipadavidhi*), it has immediate application; thus, the semi-vowel *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs first.

Consequently, since the suffix begins with a *val* letter [only after the change], there is no possibility of the augment *iṭ* at all, and so the form *seduṣaḥ* is established without objection. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": in *supi*, we have *sedivatsu*. [The root] *hisiṃ*...

In the case of *hiṃsā*, because it has the *it* marker, there is the addition of *num*. From the root preceded by *su*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; because of the *it* marker, there is no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). By the rule *naśca*, the *anusvāra* is substituted. After the word *suhuṃḍ*, the *su* suffix is elided;

the *sakāra* is then dropped due to the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), and because that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), there is no further elision of the *nakāra*. Nor does the rule for the *sarvanāmasthāna* apply.

The vowel is long [by Pāṇini 6.3.119]. Because the cause [for the nasalization] has been removed, the *anusvāra* is eliminated. He will state the form *suhin* in the nominative singular (*sau*). Anticipating the objection that the vowel should be long there by the rule "of that which ends in *s* or *m*, and of *mahat*" (Pāṇini 6.4.10), he says: "ending in *s* or *m*" (*sānta*). Regarding *suhinbhyām*: because it is a word-final (*padānta*) by the rule "in the presence of *svādi*" (Pāṇini 1.4.17), the *s* is dropped by the rule for the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).
The intention is that the *anusvāra* is removed because it is a marked (*nimita*) *apādya*. Regarding "subinsu":

when there is elision of a *saṃyoga*, the *anusvāra* is removed. However, an *anusvāra* does not reappear by depending on the *sakāra* of the *sup* suffix, because [the *sakāra*] is at the end of a word (*padāntatvāt*). Regarding "dhvaditi": [the root is] *dhvaṃsu* in the sense of falling away (*avasraṃsane*).

The mention of the *anusvāra* is made for a specific purpose. [In the case of *dhvaṃs*,] there is the elision of the *n* by the rule "aniditām" because the *kvip* suffix is present and the *anusvāra* is considered asiddha (non-existent) for the purposes of that rule. There is the elision of the *s* of the nominative suffix (*su*). Then, by the rule "vasusraṃsu," there is the substitution of *d* for *s*. The intention is that by the rule "vā'sāne," there is an optional substitution of *c* (or *t*) for *d*. Thus [is explained the form *dhvaṃs*]. Similarly, [the root] *sraṃsu* means "to fall down."

The sense is that *kvip* and so forth are applied as before. From the root *pūñ* (in the sense of "purifying"), the suffix *ḍumsun* is added by the *uṇādi* sūtra "pūño ḍumsun. The letters *ḍ*, *n*, and *u* are *it*.
By virtue of the *ḍ*-marker, there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭi*) even though it does not belong to a nominal stem (*abha*). From the word *puṃs*, the case endings (*sup*) arise.

Regarding the rule *puṃso'suṅ* (Pāṇini 7.1.89), the author states a specific detail concerning the suffix *suṭ*: "For the word *pum̐s*, [the augment] *asuṅ* [is applied] before a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending. Having in mind the continuation of the term "*sarvanāmasthāne*" from the preceding rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne*, the sūtra is completed by supplying the remaining words.

He explains: "in a sarvanāmasthāna [suffix]. The resulting meaning is: "asuṅ shall be substituted for *puṃs* in a sarvanāmasthāna. Now, one might object: in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *paramapumān*, when the suffix *su* is present, the rule "of a compound" (*samāsasya*) would cause the final syllable—the *u* after the letter *p*—to be udātta (accented) even before the substitution of *asuṅ*.

It might be argued that the accent of the compound would apply first because it is *antaraṅga* (internal) prior even to the arising of the *sarvanāmasthāna* case endings. However, this is not desired; rather, it is intended that when the suffix *su* has been applied, the accent should fall on the vowel following the *m*, as in *paramapumān*. Therefore, he says: "when [the application of the case ending] is intended."

In the rule *ṭhpuso'suṅ*, the term "sarvanāmasthāna" is not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*); rather, by supplying the word "when intended to be expressed," the meaning is understood to be that *asuṅ* occurs precisely before the *sarvanāmasthāna* is actually employed. And thus, [the substitution] takes place even prior to the arising of the *sarvanāmasthāna*.

The intention is that there is no fault because, when *asuṅ* is applied, the word *ṭhsimāsa* has an udātta accent on its final syllable; thus, in the case of *paramapumān*, the [udātta] occurs for the vowel *a* following the *m*, even though [the rule for *asuṅ*] is subsequent.

Furthermore, even under the view that the locative case [in the sūtra] refers to what follows (*parasaptamī*), before the emergence of the *sarvanāmasthāna* designation, [the substitution of *asuṅ*] is indeed *antaraṅga*.

It should not be argued that the accent of the compound does not apply to the vowel *u* following the letter *p* due to the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-application of grammatical operations when their result would be subsequently sublated),
because once the suffix *asuṅ* has been applied, the status of being a compound-final (*samāsānta*) for the vowel *u* following the letter *p* will be destroyed.
This is because the desired result is already established simply by resorting to the intended meaning (*vivikṣita*), rendering the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* unnecessary.

The sense is that [the vowel] cannot be accepted [as having an *it* designation]. Here, in order to refute the view of the ancients—that "the *ukāra* in *asuṅ* is for the sake of the operation of an *udit*"—he says: "for the sake of pronunciation. The sense is that it does not bear the technical name *it*, because there would be no purpose [for such a designation]. Now, one might object that the operation of an *udit* is indeed a purpose. To this [he replies]:...
He says: "Precisely by virtue of being *ugit*. Now, one might object that there is no decisive reason for this choice (*vinigamanā-viraha*); therefore, he says: "For the sake of [the suffix] *ṅīp*.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *bahavaḥ pumāṃso yasyām* (she in whom there are many men), when the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, the *asuṅ* substitution ceases because its cause has been removed; consequently, from the word *bahupuṃs*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by virtue of its being *ugit*."

The word *bahupuṃsī* [is an example]. Here, because the suffix *ṅīp* is not an *asarvanāmasthāna* (non-case-ending), when that [suffix] is intended, there is no possibility of the application of *asuṅ* at all. Since the suffix *ḍumsun* possesses the marker *u*, the suffix *ṅīp* must be stated [to apply] by virtue of that very *ugit* status.
For that purpose, the *ugit* status of *ḍumsun* is necessary; since the augment *num* is established by that alone, the vowel *u* in *asuṅ* [is superfluous].

The intended meaning is that it is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Although it will be stated in the *Uṇādi* [sūtras] that "from the root *pāti*, the suffix *ḍumsun* is added," nevertheless, this should be regarded as an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). However, in the *Sūtra*, the *Bhāṣya*, and the *Kaiyaṭa* commentary on the rule "in the feminine" (*striyām*), there is a *pa* substitute for the *sa* of the root *sū*, a short vowel for the *ū*, and the suffix *msun*.

Thus it has been stated: "pumān" (the word *pumān*). [The form] *ḍuṃsun* is given with an anusvāra in its grammatical description (*nirdeśa*). Consequently, when the nominative singular suffix *su* is intended after the word *puṃs*, the substitute *asuṅ* is applied. The letter *ṅ* is an *it* (indicating that the preceding vowel is nasalized), and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
By the rule "ṅci ce," there is an internal substitution (*antādeśa*). Upon the removal of the cause [the suffix *su*], the anusvāra is also removed.

From the word *pumān*, [the nominative singular suffix] *su* is added; because it ends in an *u*-class vowel (*ugit*), *num* is inserted; by the rule "of that which ends in *s* or *mahat*," there is lengthening; then there is the elision of *su*; and the *s* [of the base] undergoes elision due to being at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). The point is that because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the *n* does not take place. Thus we have *pumāṃsau*. When *asuṅ* is applied, the form stands as *pumis + au*; then *num* is inserted.

In the word *sānta*, the vowel is long. The intention is that, by the rule *naśca*, the *num* augment becomes an *anusvāra*. In the forms *puṃsaḥ* and *puṃse*, because they are not *asarvanāmasthāna* [cases] beginning with *śas* and so on, the *asuṅ* substitute does not occur; the intention is that there is no *parasavarṇa* substitution because of the absence of a following *y*. In *pumbhyām*, [the change occurs] of the *s*.

The sense is that when the *anusvāra* is removed due to the disappearance of its cause upon the elision of the final consonant of the conjunction (*saṃyogāntalopa*), one again relies on the letter *bha* (the preceding *m*) to produce the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*, resulting in the desired form. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": *puṃse*, *puṃsaḥ*, *puṃsoḥ*, *puṃsi*. Here, because there is no following *ya*-class consonant (*yay*), there is no *parasavarṇa*.

The intention is that since only the *anusvāra* having a nasal (*num*) as its original locus is indicated [by the rule], the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "ṭh-num-visarjanīya" does not apply here. From the root *vaś* (meaning "to move"), the suffix *kanas* is applied according to the rule "vaśeḥ kanasiḥ.
The letter *k* is an *it*, and the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation; because it has the marker *ṅ*, it undergoes replacement by the suffix *in*.

When *uśanas* stands [as the base], the long vowel of the penultimate syllable (*upadhādīrgha*) is applied; then, by the rule *halṅyādi*, there is elision of the case-ending *su*, followed by the elision of the final *n*. Thus, the form is *uśanā*; this is the opinion of Bhava. Although it will be stated in the section on the *luṅ-vikaraṇa* that the root *vaś* is Vedic (*cāndasa*), even so, that is merely the general rule, for [the grammarian] Vāguri says: "He desires (*vaṣṭi*)."

This is because of such indications [in the scriptures] and because of the lexicon which states, "Uśanas, Bhārgava, Kavi. Regarding the phrase "in its vocative form," this has been recorded in the Vṛtti. However, Mādhava, concerning the verbal root *vaś*, states:
"In the vocative, the word uśanas has three forms: ending in -s, ending in -n, and also ending in -a."

He says, "The Ślokavārttika. The authorities maintain that this is indeed unauthoritative because it is not seen in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the forms: *he uśanan*—this is the form when there is no elision of the *anaṅ* substitute; *he uśana*—this is the form when there is elision of the *anaṅ*; *he uśanaḥ*—this is the form in the absence of the *anaṅ* substitute.
Regarding *uśanobhyām*: when the *s* of *uśanas* undergoes *rutva* (conversion to *r*), the rule *ṭhhaśi ca* applies to change it to *u*, and then by *ṭhādguṇaḥ*, we get *uśanobhyām*.

For *uśanaḥsu* and *uśanassu*, [the same process applies]. Regarding *anehas*: by the rule *ṭhnañi hana eha ca*, the suffix *asun* is added to the root *han* with *nañ* as the upapada; *eha* is the substitute for the base, and there is a *nañ*-compound (*upapadasamāsa*). By the rule *nalopaḥ*, the *n* is elided.

From the negative particle *nañ* and [the root] *hana*, by the rule "tasmān nuḍ aci," the word *anehas* is formed. Then, after the addition of the nominative suffix *su*, there is the substitution of *anaṅ*, elision of *su*, lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*), and elision of *n*; such is the process. Thus: "O *anehas*! (he *anehas*). [The forms] *anehabhyām*, and so forth, follow.
Regarding *vedhāḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *dhā* with the prefix *vi-* and the suffix *kvip*, with the substitution of *vedha*.

From the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi*, the suffix *asun* is applied, and there is a substitution of *dh* for the initial *d*. In the suffix *asun*, the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Since it lacks the marker *u* (making it not an *ugit*), the augment *num* does not occur. Then follows the nominative suffix *su*; because the stem ends in *as*, the vowel is lengthened;

then the *su* is elided, followed by the application of *rutva* and *visarga*. This is the intended meaning. The root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*) belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class.

From this word preceded by *su*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, resulting in the form *suvas*. Then, after the addition of *su*, there is the elision of the final consonant and the following vowel according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), followed by the substitution of *ru* and its subsequent replacement by a visarga (*visarga*), yielding the form *suvaḥ*. Anticipating the objection that the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14) might require the lengthening of the vowel here, he says: "The long [vowel]. And this does not apply to the word *suvas*.

It should not be said that [the substitution] is long and difficult to prevent because [the vowel] is not a *saṃhitā* [vowel] and not part of a verbal root (*dhātu*); for one must rely on the principle that the long vowel applies to that which ends in *astan*, provided it is distinct from a portion of a verbal root.
[Examples such as] *suvobhyām* and so forth. However, this is not the form of the root *vas* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, meaning "to dwell."
Because that [root *yaj*] belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is the contingency of *saṃprasāraṇa*. The word *piṇḍagraś* is like the word *suvas*.
(Pāṇini 7.2.107) *adas* [takes the substitute] *auṭ*, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the case-ending *su*.

When the suffix *su* follows the word *adas*, the substitution of *yatva* (the replacement of the final vowel and consonant by *ya*) would apply; however, [Pāṇini] states: "For *adas*, there is *āṬ*. Here, *adasaḥ* is in the genitive case. *ĀṬ* is an indeclinable citation. From the rule "for *tad* and *doḥ*, *saḥ* in *su*," the term "*sā v*" is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "for *adas*. That this is a substitute for the final letter (*anta-ādeśa*) is obtained through the *al-antyaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning the final letter). [This applies] to the *sakāra*.

Once *āṬ* has been substituted, since there is no longer a consonant (*hal*) following it, the elision of the case-ending (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*) does not apply; therefore, this rule for the elision of *su* is established. Regarding "of *d* there is *s*" (*dasya saḥ*): the sense is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *m* (*mut*). Regarding "this" (*asau*):
when *adas* is present, after *āṬ* is substituted for *s*, *su* is elided, and *d* is changed to *s*, resulting in the form.
Therefore, regarding the form *adakaḥ* derived from *ada-* by the addition of *akac* after indeclinables and pronouns, he states a specific exception: "the prohibition of *auT*.

This is because, in the rule *adasa au sulopaśca*, the word *adas-* includes the form *adaka-* as well, according to the maxim of inclusion within the middle (*tanmadhyapatitanyāya*), which would otherwise result in the substitution of *au*.

When there is an option, that prohibition must be stated. The meaning is that when the letter *d* has been changed to *s* by the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sau," then for the vowel *a* following that *s*, the substitution of *u* should optionally be stated. Consequently, when the form *adakas* is established and the substitution of *au* (*āṬ*) does not occur, [the form remains] as *adas*.

When *satvam* (the substitution of *s*) occurs, and when the *a* following the *sakāra* is replaced by *u*, then after the application of *tyadādyatvam* (the substitution of *a* for the initial of *tyad*-class words), *pararūpam* (the single substitute of the subsequent form), *rutvam* (the substitution of *r*), and *visargaḥ* (the substitution of *visarga*), the form is *asukaḥ*. In the alternative case where the prohibition of *autvam* (the substitution of *au*) does not apply,
once *adakas* has been established, after *autvam* of the *sakāra*, the elision of *su*, and the substitution of *s* for *d*, the form is *asakau*.

He will state [the following]: In that regard, why would there not be an option for the substitution of *u* for the vowel *a* preceding the *s* after the substitution of *au* has been applied, in the case where the prohibition of the substitution of *au* is absent? To this he says: "by the prohibition," etc.
[This is based on the principle: "For those elements taught as being joined together (*sanniyoga-śiṣṭa*), there is either simultaneous application or simultaneous cessation."
The intended meaning is "by virtue of logic. Some say that forms such as *ṭhamukaḥ* or *ṭhamukaśarmā* are indeed incorrect.

Others, however, state that the word *amuka* is an unanalyzed (avyutpanna) synonym for the word *adas*. When *adas* and the suffix *au* are present, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*)—namely, the substitution of the *yatva* of the *tyadādi* group—and notes that the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule should also be understood to apply.

Regarding the phrase "matvotve": in the rule *adau*, the meaning is that the long vowel *ū* replaces the *āṬ* following the letter *d*, and the letter *d* undergoes the substitution of *m*. Having taken for granted the application of the *tyadādyatva* (substitution of *a* for the stem) and the *pararūpa* (single-substitute replacement) before the suffix *jas*, he says: *jasaḥ śī*. Following the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, the form *ade* is established.

In the rule *eta īdbahuvacane* (Pāṇini 7.3.103), when the substitution of *ūt* for the vowel *e* after the letter *d* would otherwise apply, *eta* is replaced by *īt*. From the preceding rule *ṭhadaso'serdādu do maḥ*, the portions *adaso dāḥ* and *do maḥ* are understood to carry over.

He says this with the words beginning "of *adas*," etc. Regarding the phrase "in the expression of a plural meaning": in the Sūtra, the word *bahuvacana* is used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*). For if the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense were taken, then although forms such as *amībhiḥ* would be established, the form *amī* would not be established; because in the rule *adeḥ*, the single vowel *e* is considered to be plural in number.

The intended meaning is that [the rule] does not have another element as its cause (*tatparakatvābhāvāt*). Now, one might object: in the case of *auṭ*, *jas*, and so on, after the substitution of *tyadādi* (i.e., *a*) and the subsequent formation of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), and once the substitutions of *utva* and *matva* have been applied, forms such as *amū-au* or *amū-aḥ* would result; since the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha*, the rule *ṭhyaṇ* would not apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the preceding [rule]."

"Vibhaktikāryam" means [operations such as] the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth. However, if— on the grounds that an operation must necessarily not take effect when "pūrvatrāsiddham" applies— one were to apply the *mutva* (substitution of *m*) belonging to the third chapter (*traipādika*) because it is subsequent, and thereby remove the vowel *a* which is the substitute for *u*, [then the following would occur].

Even if there were a superimposition (*āropa*) of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence upon the subsequent *m*, by the maxim "when the killer of Devadatta has been killed, Devadatta does not reappear," there would be no occurrence of *vṛddhi*, *guṇa*, and so forth, because the *a* that was the original element (*sthānin*)— the *a* following the *d*— would be absent. This is the case under the view that [the preceding rule] is non-existent (*asiddha*) for the sake of the subsequent rule.
However, if a subsequent treatise is intent on proceeding here,

then since the superimposition of non-existence is possible within that very treatise, when there arises the cognition of the destruction of the subsequent treatise— which acts as an obstacle to the preceding treatise— the rule "in case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" does not apply.
Thus it has been said: "In the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) because of the non-existence of the subsequent [rule].
Consequently, since there is no cessation of the original element (*sthānin*), namely the vowel *a*, the application of *vṛddhi*, *guṇa*, and so forth proceeds without obstruction.
And this [is explained] under the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* and under the rule *acaḥ parasmin*.

This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭhṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*. It has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara* and the *Śabdaratna*; let this suffice for now. Regarding the form *amum*: when *adas* + *am* is situated, the substitution of *yat* (the *tyadādyatva*) occurs; then the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule applies; then *ami pūrvaḥ* (the single substitute is the preceding vowel); finally, the substitutions of *utva* and *matva* take place.
The intended meaning is as follows: *amū* is the dual form of the second case (accusative), just like the dual form of the first case (nominative). Regarding *amūn*:

after the suffix *śas*, there is the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun stem *adas* (i.e., *ada*), the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the substitution of *n* for *m*, and finally the substitutions of *ut* and *at*.
In the singular of the third case (instrumental), when *adas* is followed by *ā*, there is the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun stem and the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

And having taken for granted that the substitution of *u* (for *au*) has already been established, he says: "not non-existence" (*nābhāva*). The meaning is that, since the designation *ghi* applies by the rule "the remainder is *ghi*, except for *sakhi*," the substitution of *nā* occurs by the rule "in place of the dative ending *āṅ*, *nā* [is substituted], except in the feminine. Now, one might object: according to the principle "what precedes is as if not to have existed" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), the operation of the case-ending should take effect first, and only afterwards the substitution of *u* for *au*.
It was stated previously; however, now, once *mutva* has been applied, it is said that *nābhāva* occurs when there is the designation *ghisaṃjñā*.
If it is argued that this is contradictory to what preceded and followed, that is true. Yet, only that case-ending operation for which *mutva* is not the cause occurs first, and not [the others].

It is intended that [the condition] be something else. And here, since mutva is not the cause with respect to the absence [of the rule], there is no contradiction in the initial application of mutva; this is because of the force of the introduction of the rule "na mu ne. Enough of this.

[Objection: Even if *mutva* (the substitution of *m*) were applied first, the absence of *nābhāva* (the substitution of *na*) would not be possible; for when that [substitution of *na*] is to be performed, because *mutva* is considered asiddha (non-existent), the condition of being followed by a *ghi*-stem would not be met. To this, he says: *na mu ne*.

The term *asiddham* (not established) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. *m* and *u* form a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*). In the expression *ṭhne*, *nā* is the locative singular. This is both a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) and a locative of condition (*satsaptamī*). Thus, it is understood that [the preceding rule applies] "when the substitution of *nā* is to be effected" and "when it has already been effected. This is what he expresses with the words beginning "in the case of the substitution of *nā*," and so forth.

And in the present case, since there is no lack of establishedness (*asiddhatva*) for the *mutva* [substitution] when the *nābhāva* is to be applied, the *nābhāva* follows because it occurs after the *he*-form, and thus remains unimpeded. However, if one were to maintain that the *mubhāva* is not *asiddha* when the *nābhāva* is to be applied, then once the *nābhāva* has been applied in the present case, [the rule] "supi ca" would apply.

A long vowel (*dīrgha*) would result [undesirably]. This is because when a long vowel is to be applied, the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the vowel *a* remains. Therefore, it is accepted that [the rule applies] "even when [the substitution] has been performed. Consequently, in the present case, even though the substitution of *na* (*nābhāva*) has occurred, since the substitution of *m* is not non-existent when the long vowel is to be applied, the vowel *a* is absent; thus, there is no long vowel. This is the underlying point.

Regarding *amūbhyām*: the meaning is that after the substitution of *tyadādi-ātva* (the replacement of the stem-final with *a*), the *pararūpa* (single substitute of the subsequent form) is applied, the lengthening (*dīrgha*) occurs by the rule *supi ca*, the *da* is replaced by *ma*, and the vowel *ā* is replaced by *ū*. Regarding *amībhiḥ*:
there is the substitution of *tyadādi-ātva*, the *pararūpa*, and the prohibition of *ais* by the rule *nedamadasorakoḥ*; [then] in the plural...

The intention is that *etva* (the substitution of *e*) applies by the rule *jhalyet*, while *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*) and *atva* (the substitution of *a*) apply by the rule *eta īd bahuvacane*.

Regarding *amuṣmai*: the intention is that *tyadādyatva* (the substitution of *a* for the final vowel of the pronoun), *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent form), *ReĀḥ smai*, *utva* (the substitution of *u*), *atva*, and finally *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*).
Regarding *amībhyaḥ*: [the steps are] *tyadādyatva*, *pararūpa*, and then *etva* by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*.

The sense is that there is *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*) and *atva* (the substitution of *a*). Regarding *amuṣmāt*: the sense is that there is the substitution of *a* for the *tyad*-class stems, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), the replacement of *ṅsi* by *smāt*, the substitutions of *utva* and *atva*, and the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding *amuṣya*: the sense is that there is the substitution of *a* for the *tyad*-class stems, the substitution of the subsequent form, the replacement of *ṅsi* by *syā*, the substitutions of *utva* and *atva*, and the substitution of *ṣ*. [Regarding] *amuyoḥ*...

The intended meaning is as follows: in *osi*, there is the substitution of *yat* for *tyadādi* (i.e., *t- > y-*), the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule, the substitution of *e* by "ṭhosi ca," the *ayādeśa* substitution, and the substitutions of *utva* and *atva*. Regarding *amīṣām*: in the case of *ām*, there is the substitution of *yat* for *tyadādi*, the single-substitute rule, the substitution of *smin* for *ReĀḥ*, the substitutions of *utva* and *atva*, and the substitution of *ṣatva*. Regarding *amīṣu*: this occurs in the case of the *sup* suffix.

The intended meaning is: the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), the substitution of *et*, the substitutions of *īt* and *at*, and the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus end those [stems] ending in *s*.
Thus end the masculine stems ending in consonants.
Now begins the section on feminine nouns ending in consonants (*halanta-strīliṅga-prakaraṇa*).

Now, those ending in *h*: from the root *ṇaha* (bandhane), "to bind," [the substitution of] *ṇa* for *ṇaḥ* [is applied]. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *upanahyate*, the suffix *kvip* is added after the prefix *upa-* because it belongs to the *saṃpadādi* group, [denoting] the object (*karman*). [The form is derived] by the rule *nahivṛtī* etc. [Pāṇini 6.3.117].

The first member of the compound takes the long vowel. The word *upānah* is feminine, denoting a sandal; as Amara states: "A sandal is called *pādu*, *uru*, or *upānat* (feminine). [In the rule] *naho dhaḥ*, the term *ha* is carried over from *ho ḍhaḥ*. The term *pada-* is supplied by context. From *skoḥ saṃyoge*, the word *ante* is supplied.

The term *anuvartate* (is carried over) [from the previous rule]. From the rule *ṭhjalo jhalī*, the term *jhalī* is carried over. Thus he says: "of *na*, of *ha*, etc. The rule *ho ḍhaḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ḍha*.
In the form *upānat*, there is the elision of the case-ending *su* by the rule *halṅyādi-lopaḥ*; then *ha* is replaced by *dha*, followed by the application of *jaśtva* and *cartva*.

The meaning [of the rule] is as follows: here, the substitution of *da* alone was not prescribed; for if that were the case, in the word *naddham*, the substitution of *na* would undesirably follow by the rule *radābhyām*. Enough of this. Regarding *upānadbhyām*: the intention is that after the substitution of *dha* for *ha*, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) occurs. Regarding *upānatsu*: after the substitution of *dha*, [the substitution of *ta* occurs] by the rule *khari ca*.
The intended meaning is "the state of being a *carti*. The word *uṣṇih* is feminine and denotes a specific type of meter.

To derive it, he says: "in the sense of affection" (*ṣṇiha prītau*), and so forth. Regarding "elision of the *da* and the substitution of *ṣ*" (*dalopaṣatve*): the meaning is that the elision of the *da* of *uda* and the substitution of *ṣ* for the *sa* are treated as irregularities (*nipātana*). Nor [does this conflict with] "of the root-initial... (*dhātvādeḥ*)...
One might ask: "Since the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in *ṣaḥ saḥ* is already established by the rule *ṣṭhādeśapratyayayoḥ*, what is the purpose of this nipātana (irregular citation)?
It must be stated that the nipātana of *ṣ* is necessary in order to override the prohibition [of *ṣ*] by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*. Nor is it the case that...

They say that because the word *uṣṇih* is a compound, before the case-ending (*sup*) is produced, *snihitī-* is not yet a word (*pada*). Therefore, it must be stated that the *s* is strictly at the beginning of a word; otherwise, under the alternative view of the rule "from a word" (*padāt*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of *ṣatva*. [The rule] "of *h*, *gh*" [is applied].

The intended meaning is that it is due to the similarity between the great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*) and the closure of the vocal organ (*ghoṣanādasaṃvāra*). Nor should it be argued that, because the substitution of *ḍha* for *gha* (by the rule *gho ḍhaḥ*) is more appropriate since the substitution of *k* (by the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*) is considered *asiddha*, [the latter should not apply];
for according to the view of Kaiyaṭa and others—that "the substitution of *k* is an exception to the substitution of *ṣ*"—the same logic applies to the substitution of *ṣ* as well.

Because even the substitution of *ḍha* is superseded by the substitution of *ku*. Regarding the rule for *jaś* and *car* substitutions: one should not suspect that when *jaś* is to be applied, the *ku*-substitution prescribed by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ* is *asiddha*, because the form *uṣṇig-añcu* (in Pāṇini’s sūtra) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that [the *ku*-substitution] is not *asiddha* when *jaś* is to be applied.

This is because it makes known the absence of the non-application (*asiddhatva*) of *kutva*. In reality, however, according to the view of the author of the root-text (*mūlakāra*), the rule "the substitution of *ku* for the *kvin* suffix" (*kvipratyayasya ku*) is not an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṣatva*;
by the same logic, it is also not an exception to *ḍhatva*. Consequently, according to that method, [the forms] are *ḍha-ḍga-kāḥ*.

"Bodhyam" (to be understood). Thus end those ending in *ha*. Now, those ending in *va*: "dyauḥ" (the sky). The word *div* is feminine. As Amara states: "The two forms *dyauḥ* and *divau* are [used] for the feminine. From that [base], the suffix *su* is applied; by the rule "diva āṬt," the *v* is replaced by *āṬ*.

The *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *i*, followed by the substitution of *r* and the visarga (*visarjanīya*). The point is that because the elision of the case-ending *su* depends upon the letter *v* which serves as the *sthānin* (the original element) for the substitution of *au*, it is not an operation based on an *al* (vowel); therefore, there is no absence of *sthānivadbhāva* (treatment as the original), and thus the elision of the feminine suffixes (*hal-ṅy-ādi*) does not apply. [This explains] *dyaubhyām*. In the presence of *bhyām* and other consonantal endings, [the rule] "diva u" [applies].

The sense is that the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule "udityutvam. Thus end the words ending in *v*. Now, those ending in *r*: regarding the word *gīḥ*. [The root] *gṛ* (in the sense of "swallowing") takes the suffix *kvip*; by the rule "Añta iddātoḥ," the substitution of *i* occurs, followed by the substitution of *r* for the vowel; from the word *gir*, there is the derivation of the case-ending *su*; *su* is elided; and by the rule "ror upadhāyāḥ," lengthening occurs for the *r*. As for the *r*...

The meaning is that there is a *visarga*. However, when the suffixes beginning with *bhyām* follow, there is lengthening by the rule "ṭhrvoḥ" [Pāṇini 6.1.111] in the case of a consonant (*hal*), as in *gīrbhyām*, and so forth. [In the locative plural], it is *gīrṣu*. In the same way, *pūḥ* is like *gīḥ*; this is the meaning.

[The root] *pṛ* [is used] in the sense of protecting and filling; with the *kvip* suffix, there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel by the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya" [Pāṇini 7.1.102], followed by the substitution of *r* for the semivowel.
The meaning is that after the word *pūr*, there is elision of the case-ending *su*, the long vowel [ā] occurs by the rule *rṭhvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.11), and the *repha* becomes a *visarga*.

Regarding the term "the substitute *catasṛ*": the meaning is that for the feminine word *catur* when followed by the case-endings *jaś* or *śas*, the substitution is made by the rule *tricaturoḥ striyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.99). Thus, [we have] *catasraḥ*.
Because it is subsequent, the substitution of *yaṇ* (for the *ṛ* of *catasṛ*) occurs, overriding the application of the suffix *ām* prescribed by the rule *caturanaḍuho 'm*.

Once the substitution of *catasṛ* has been effected, *ām* does not apply; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivat* sūtra according to the maxim: "In a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*), that which is overridden remains overridden."

Regarding "of the four": there is a prohibition of the long vowel by the rule *ṭhna tisṛcatasṛ*. Thus end the words ending in *r*. Now, those ending in *m*. Regarding *kima*: from the word *kim* in the feminine gender, when a case-ending follows, the base is replaced by *kā* according to the rule *kimaḥ kaḥ*; having thus become a stem ending in *ā*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied—this is the meaning. [The form] is like *sarvā*.

The meaning is "possessing all sounds. It is not the case that [the rule] "there is masculine substitution for a pronoun in all simple compounds" applies here; the point is that because this refers to the actual form of the word *sarva* as a secondary derivative (*gauṇatayā*), it never possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*).
[The sūtra: *yaḥ sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.110).

Now, he states the specific rule regarding the feminine gender of the word *idam*: "That which is *sau*" (referring to the rule *idamo maḥ*). From that [rule], *idamaḥ* is understood by anuvṛtti, and from *daśca*, *daḥ* is also understood in the genitive case. Thus he says: "of *idam*, of the *d*. However, this does not apply in the masculine.

Because of the specific injunction that "the neuter [suffix] remains as -ṭ" (*ṭhito 'puṃsīti*), it does not apply to the neuter either, since for the neuter the *su* suffix is elided by *luk*. Therefore, by process of elimination, this [suffix] must be *-ām* alone. Regarding the form *iyam*:
when *idam* is followed by *s*, the *d* is replaced by *y*, resulting in *iyam s*; then, the substitution of *a* for the final vowel of *tyad*-type stems (*tyadādyatvam*) applies.

The intention is that, by the rule *bādhitvā ṭhidamo maḥ*, the *m* of *idam* is replaced by *m*, and then the *su* suffix is elided by the rule *halṅyādi*. When the form *idam-āṬ* is established, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) as follows:

"the substitution of *tyadādi*," meaning that once the *tyadādi* substitution has occurred and the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule has applied, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added because it ends in the vowel *a*.

When *dakāra* is replaced by *mat* according to the rule *ṭhdaśca*, and the form *imā-āṬ* is established, the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule *āṬṅ āpaḥ*. Then, by the rule *ādguṇe*, the form *ime* is produced. Regarding *imāḥ*: in the case of *jas*, the substitution of *yat* for *tyadādi* occurs, followed by the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule, the addition of *ṭāp*, the replacement of *da* by *ma* according to *ṭhdaśca*, and finally the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). This is the intended meaning here.

It should be understood that when a case ending (*vibhakti*) follows, the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the pronoun], the formation of a single substitute (*pararūpa*), and the addition of the suffix *ṭāp* occur everywhere.
In the case of "imāḥ," once we have reached the stage *imā-as*, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) applies.
However, the rule *jasaḥ śī* does not apply here because, once *ṭāp* has been added, there is no longer an *adanta* (ending in short *a*) immediately preceding the suffix. Thus, we obtain *imām*.

The meaning is that when the substitution of *at* (for *idam*), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), the suffix *ṭāp*, and the feminine suffix *ām* have been applied, the rule "the preceding [vowel] is substituted" (*pūrvaḥ*) applies. Regarding *ime*: after the application of *āṬ* and *āṬvat*. Regarding *imāḥ*: when *at*, *pararūpa*, *ṭāp*, and *ām* have been applied, the long vowel of the homogeneous class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) is substituted; the meaning is that because it denotes femininity, there is no substitution of *n* (nasalization). Regarding *anayā*: when *idam-ā* is situated, *at* is applied.

The form *pararūpa* [is derived as follows]: by the rule "ṭāp, ṭhanāpyakaḥ," there is the substitution of *it* for *id*. When *an-ā* remains, by the rule "ṭhāṅ cāpiḥ," there is the substitution of *et*, resulting in the substitution of *ay*. It should be understood that this substitution of *an* occurs everywhere before suffixes beginning with vowels, starting from *ṭā*. Regarding the phrase "there is elision (*lopa*) before a consonant" (*hali lopa*), this refers to the consonants in *bhyām* and so forth.

The meaning is that there is elision (*lopa*) of the syllable *id*. Regarding the form *ābhyām*: when *idam-bhyām* is established, after the elision of *id*, the substitution of *at*, the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds (*pararūpa*), and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form [is obtained]; this is the intended sense. The form *ābhiḥ* is likewise. Regarding *asyai*: when *idam e* is established, after the substitutions of *at*, *pararūpa*, and *ṭāp*, and with the augment *syāṭ*...
Regarding *hrasvatve*, the intention is that there is elision (*lopa*) of the *id* [of *idam*] by the rule *ido lopaḥ*. The same applies to the rule *ṭhasyāḥ*. Regarding *anayoḥ*:

when *idam os* is situated, after the substitution of *id* for *idam*, and after the substitutions of *atva*, *pararūpa*, and *ṭāp*, the intention is that the substitution of *ay* occurs by the rule *ṭāhi cāpaḥ* due to the change to *e*. Regarding *āsām*: [this is derived from] *idam ām*.
The meaning is that when *su* follows, there is the elision of *id-* after [the stem] ending in *at*, *a*, *para-rūpa*, or *tāp*. Regarding "in this" (*asyām*):

when *idam* + *i* is present, there is the substitution of *at*, *para-rūpa*, *tāp*, the replacement by *ReĀrām*, the addition of the augment *syāṭ*, the shortening of the vowel, and the elision of *id-*. Regarding "in these" (*āsu*): when *idam* + *su* is present...

The intended meaning is that when *atva* (the substitution of *a*), *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the subsequent form), and *ṭāp* [the feminine suffix] apply, and when *Re*, *Ā*, *Rām*, and *syāṭ* are introduced, and *hrasvatva* (shortening) occurs, then by the rule *ido lopaḥ* (elision of *idam*), the form is established.

Regarding *āsu*: when *idam-su* is present, the intended meaning is that after *atva*, *pararūpa*, and *ṭāp* have applied, and then *hrasvatva* occurs, the *idam* is elided by *ido lopaḥ*. Regarding *anvādeśe tu* (but in the case of correlative reference): [the following applies].
The intention is that after the substitution of *en* by the rule "dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ," the forms are like those of *ramā* when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
Thus end the words ending in *m*. Now, those ending in *j*. He derives the word *sraj*: [the rule] "ṛtvig... [is applied].
From the root *sṛj* (meaning "to emit"), there is the suffix *kvip*; the augment *am* follows the vowel *ṛ*, and the letter *m* is the *it*.

The *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *ṛ* is the letter *r*. The word *sraj* is feminine; as Amarasimha states: "A garland (*mālya*), a wreath (*mālā*), and a string (*sraj*) [are placed] upon the head. Thus, we have *srak*, *srag*—the change to *k* (known as *kutva*) occurs by the rule "the *k* of a *kvip* suffix," and then the changes to *j* and *c* (known as *jaśtva* and *cartva*) occur; such is the meaning. These are the words ending in *j*. Now, those ending in *d*: the word *tyad*.

He demonstrates the grammatical derivation: "the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth. When the case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, after the substitution of *at*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form is "tyā. From that point on, all forms are derived like those of *sarvā*.
However, in the nominative singular (*sau*), there is this distinction: by the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sau," the *t* is replaced by *s*. "In this manner" refers to *tat*, *yat*, and *etad*.
From these [words], when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, all forms are derived through the substitution of *at*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and *ṭāp*. However, there is this distinction:

for the word *tad*, the *t* undergoes the substitution of *s*; whereas for the word *etad*, once the *t* has been changed to *s*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "ṣatva applies to the substitute *ṭha* and to suffixes. Thus end the words ending in *d*.
Now, those ending in *c*: *vāk*. From the root *vac*, by the rule "ṭhkvibvacī" etc., there is the suffix *kvip* and lengthening;

by the rule "vacisvapi" etc., there is the absence of *samprasāraṇa*. Thus the form is *vāc*. [In the nominative singular] there is elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*), *c* is changed to *k* (*coḥ kuḥ*), and then the *j*-series and *c*-series substitutions (*jaśtva* and *cartva*). These are the words ending in *c*. Now, those ending in *p*.

Regarding the word *ap*: according to the rule on gender instruction (*liṅgānuśāsana*) under the heading of feminine nouns, "The words *ap*, *manas*, *samāsika*, and *varṣā* always take the plural number [and are feminine]," its meaning is that it is invariably plural and feminine. Regarding "long" (*dīrgha*): the word *jasi* is to be understood as the remainder [of the context]. Regarding *apa*: this refers to the rule "aptṛn" (Pāṇini 6.4.11).

The intention is that there is no long vowel in the case of *śas*, because the phrase "and in a *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending], except for the vocative" (*sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*).

Regarding *apo bhi* (Pāṇini 7.4.48): the word *apaḥ* [is the base], and *bhi* [is the condition]. From the previous rule, "after a prefix ending in *a*" (*aca upasargāt*), the word *ataḥ* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*).

This [rule] pertains to the domain of *aṅga* (the stem). Consequently, when the suffix introduced by the term *aṅga* is specified by a word ending in the locative case, there is an application of the rule *tadādi-vidhiḥ* (the designation applies to that which begins with it). Thus he says: "when *p* becomes *t*" and so forth. Why [is the condition] "in a suffix" stated? [Consider the example: *abbhakṣaḥ*. [In this case, the substitution occurs] because of the word *adbhiḥ*; [specifically,] the substitution of *t* for *p*.

The meaning is that there is *jaś*-ness. Thus end those ending in *p*. Now, those ending in *ś*: regarding the word *dik* (direction). From the root *ḍiśa* in the sense of "bestowing," the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādi*; there is elision of the vowel (*sulopa*), *ṣ* is substituted for the *c* by the rule *vraśca-ādiṣu ca*, that *ṣ* becomes *ḍ* by *jaś*-ness, and that *ḍ* becomes *g* by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*. Of that [g]...

The meaning is that there is an option regarding the suffix *kvip*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "that by which objects are seen" (*dṛśyante arthā anayā*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *dṛś* because it belongs to the *saṃpadādi* group. Then, the elision of the case-ending (*sulopa*) occurs.
Anticipating the objection regarding the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ṭh-vraśca*, he says: "in the case of *tyadādi* [pronouns]. [He adds] "even elsewhere."

The meaning is: "even in the absence of an upapada such as *tyad* and so forth. The intention is that this is based on the understanding of the *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that from which the *kvin* suffix is prescribed. Regarding *dṛk*: the six *ṣaṭpratyayas* (the six grammatical operations) are as before. Thus end those ending in *ś*. Now, those ending in *p*. Regarding *tviṭ*: from the root *tviṣ* in the sense of "shining," the *kvip* suffix is applied; there is elision of the *su* (nominative case-ending).

The intention is that [the rule] *jaś-ṣṭvac-artve* applies. Regarding *sajūḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *juṣī* (meaning "to serve" or "to enjoy") with the suffix *kvip*; or, by the rule *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām*, or by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*.
Then, the *su* (nominative singular ending) is elided, and by the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, the *ṣ* is replaced by *r*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "ṛt-ṣṭhvor upadhāyāḥ. From the root *āṅ* with *śās* in the sense of "desire," there is the suffix *kvip*; the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule "aśāsaḥ kvāv upasaṅkhyānam," and the change of *s* to *ṣ* occurs by the rule "śās-vasi-ghasīnāṃ ca.
Having taken for granted that the word *āśis* is thus established, he says: "of the state of being *ṣ*."
Regarding "āśīḥ": the intention is that once the substitution of *ṣ* by *r* has been made, the lengthening occurs by the rule "ṛt-ṭhvor upadhāyāḥ.

Thus end the words ending in *ṣ*. Now, those ending in *s*. Regarding "asau": the meaning is that even for the word *adas* in the feminine, the form after the nominative singular (*su*) is exactly like that of the masculine. When *adas* and *āṬ* are in the state of being combined, [the following] is the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*).

He demonstrates this with the words "the substitution of *yat* for *tyad*" and so forth. When the sequence *ade* has been established—following the application of *atva*, *pararūpa*, *ṭāp*, the substitution of *āṬ* for *śī*, and *ādguṇa*—the meaning is that because the vowel *e* is long, there is the substitution of *ū* [for *e*], and the letter *d* becomes *m*. Once the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is present, *atva*, *pararūpa*, and *ṭāp* apply in every instance.

It should be understood as follows: *amūḥ*. In the case of the nominative plural (*jasi*), there is the substitution of *at* (by *ato guṇe*), followed by the single-substitute *pararūpa* (by *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*), then the substitution of *ū* (by *tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi*), and finally the substitution of *mat* (by *māduvaṅ*).

When the suffix *ṭāp* is present, because the word no longer ends in *ā*, the substitution of *śī* for *jas* does not occur; and because the vowel *e* is absent, the substitution of *it* (for the final *ā*) does not occur. *amūm*: this is like the masculine form; the only difference is the substitution of *ū*. *amū*: [this is the dual].

*āṬṭi āṬvat* | *amūriti* | The form is like that of the *śas* and *jas* [cases]. Due to its feminine gender, there is an absence of *natva* (the substitution of *n*). Regarding *amuyā*: when *adas* + *ā* is established, after the application of *atva*, *pararūpa*, and *ṭāp*, the *etva* [substitution] occurs by the rule "ṭhāṅ cāpiḥ," followed by the substitution of *ay* and then *utva* and *matva*; such is the sense. *Amūbhyām* [is formed similarly].

The meaning is that in the cases of *ātva*, *pararūpa*, and *ṭāp*, there is *ūtva* and *matva*. Thus [is derived] *amūbhiḥ*. As for *amuṣyai*: when *adas-e* is established, there is *ātva*, *pararūpa*, *ṭāp*, *syāṭ*, shortening (*hrasva*), *ūtva*, *matva*, and *ṣatva*; this is the intended meaning. *Amūbhyaḥ* is also like the *bhyām* case-ending. Regarding *ṭāp*:
Because the quality of having a final *d* is absent, the substitution of *e* does not occur. [In the case of] *amuṣyāḥ*: by the rule *ṅsiṅsorvevat*, there is the substitution of *e*;
however, the specific differences are the application of *r*-substitution (*rutva*) and the visarga (*visarga*). [In the case of] *amūyoḥ*:

the intention is that after the substitution of *atva*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and the addition of *ṭāp*, the substitution of *e* occurs by the rule *ṭāṅcāpiḥ*, followed by the replacement with *ay* and then the substitution of *m* (*mutva*). [In the case of] *amūṣām*.

The intended meaning is as follows: in *ām*, *at*, *para-rūpa*, *ṭāp*, and *su*, there is the substitution of *Re* (long *ī*), *Ār* (long *ā*), *ām*, *syāt*, *ḍhrasva* (shortening), and *mutva* (the addition of *m*).
Regarding *amūṣu*: in *sup*, there is the substitution of *at*, *para-rūpa*, *ṭāp*, *su*, *ūtva*, and *matva*, followed by *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*). Thus end those [stems] ending in *s*.
Thus ends the section on feminine gender.
Now begins the section on neuter gender.

Now, those ending in *an* [are considered]: in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *su-anaḍvāhaḥ*, meaning "the family whose oxen (*anaḍvāhaḥ*) are very beautiful," the suffix *su* arises from the neuter gender of the word *svanaḍuh*. But surely, when *su* follows there, [the following rules would apply]:

by *caturanaḍuhoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.98], the suffix *ām* [would be applied]; by *am saṃbuddhau* [Pāṇini 7.1.99], the suffix *am* [would be applied]; and by *sāvanaḍuhaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.82], [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel before the nominative singular suffix *su* would occur].

One might object that even after the elision of *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (*Pāṇini 6.1.68*), the suffix would still exist due to the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle; therefore, he says: "there is *luk* of *su* and *am*.
Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the *luk* prescribed by *svamornapuṃsakāt* (*Pāṇini 7.1.23*) overrides the elision by *halṅyābbhyo...*.

And thus, because the *luk* elision has occurred, there is an absence of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix); consequently, the augment *ām* and so forth do not occur—this is the intended meaning. Regarding "the substitution of *d*" (*datvam*), the remainder of the rule is "by [Pāṇini 8.2.72] *ṭhvasusraṃsu*. The intention is that since the prescription for the substitution of *d* occurs within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "pada," it applies even when [the suffix] is at the end of a word. Nor is it the case that even there...

One should not suspect the prohibition "ṭhna lumate" (Pāṇini 1.1.63), because the substitution of *d* for *t* is caused by the status of being a *pada*—defined here as having the form of a *subanta* (an inflected nominal)—and thus it is not an internal (*āṅga*) operation; so they say.
Regarding *svanaḍut*: after the substitution of *d*, there is an option regarding the substitution of *c* for *t*. However, the rule "ṭhuraḥprabhṛtibhyaḥ kaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.151) does not apply here.

This is to be suspected; for it will be stated in the *mūla* itself under the section on *bahuvrīhi* that in that *gaṇa*, only the singular form *anaḍvān* is recited. [The forms] *svanaḍuhī* and *svanaḍvāṃhī*:
in the former, the substitution of *śī* for *auṅ* occurs by the rule *ṭhnapuṃsakācca*; in the latter, [the substitution of *n* occurs] by the rule *ṭhjaśśaśoḥ*.

The meaning is as follows: from the root *śī* in the sense of lying down (*śayane*), because it is a base ending in a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, the augment *ām* is applied by the rule *caturanaḍuhorām*.

Then, by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the augment *num* is added, and by the rule *naśca*, the *anusvāra* is substituted [for the *m*]. Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the section on the masculine gender. Thus end the words ending in *ha*. Now, those ending in *va*.

The sky (*dyauḥ*) is the *ākāśa* of that day; thus, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound [vimaladiv], there is elision of the case-ending (*su*) after the word *vimaladiv*. Having taken this as already established, he says: "after *div*, [the vowel] *u*" (Pāṇini 6.1.131). Thus, [the form] is *ahar-vimaladyau*. The intention is that when *u* replaces *v*, the semivowel *y* is substituted for the vowel *i*. The mention of *ahar* [is made]...

[This is] for the purpose of indicating the neuter gender. Now, one might object: when *vimaladiv* + *au* is established, the form *vimaladivī* will be taught by applying the substitution of *śī* [for *au*] according to the rule *napuṃsakācca*; however, that is incorrect, because the substitution of *u* (by the rule *diva ut*) would then necessarily follow. Nor can it be argued that [the substitution applies] only to the entire aggregate *vimaladivī*.

It should not be argued that because it is a *pada* by virtue of having a case-ending (*subanta*), the letter *v* does not constitute the final element of the word-form *div*; for, by relying on the presence of the case-ending following the word *div*—which has been elided by the rule "supo dhātu" (Pāṇini 2.4.71)—through the principle of "treating as present what is elided" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the form *divi* retains its status as a *pada*. Nor can it be said that [the suffix] is absent because it has been elided by *luk*.
It should be stated that [the rule] has "having a suffix" (pratyayalaksana) as its characteristic;

for since the designation *pada* is a property of that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is not a property of the stem (*anga*), and thus the prohibition "not when there is elision by *lumat*" (*na lumatā*) does not apply therein. Otherwise, in examples such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* → *rājapuruṣaḥ*, [the designation *pada* would not apply].
Anticipating the objection that [the rule] such as *nalopa* (elision of *n*) might not apply to the prior member, he says: "that which stands within," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "and when it is the latter member": this refers to the designation of the second constituent (*uttara-khaṇḍa*) as a *pada* within a compound.

When a case ending (*vibhakti*) that is internal [to a word] is elided, a prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) must be stated, with the exception of rules concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*). This is a *vārttika*. For example: *vimaladivī*.
