The form *āṬ* is included here. Regarding *vimaladivī*: when the suffix *śas* follows, by the rule "for *jas* and *śas*, there is *śi*," it undergoes the substitution of *śi*.
The derivation of *rūpa* is as follows: because it does not end in a vowel (*ajhalanta*), the augment *num* does not apply. Regarding *dadhisecau*: [the root] *siñcati* takes the suffix *kvip*.

*Dadhisecau* means "the two sprinklers of curds" (*dadhnaḥ secau*). It is a settled rule that when there is elision (*luk*) of the case-endings (*sup*) belonging to the prior and posterior members in a compound, the case-ending (*sub*) is produced again from the compound as a whole. In that regard, one should apply the subsequent case-ending from the latter constituent part.

Relying on the elided suffix by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, the form *seciti* is treated as a word (*pada*); consequently, since its *s* is at the beginning of a word, the prohibition of *ṣatva* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* is desired. However, if only this much were stated—that "there is a prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*)"—then [the rule would apply] to the latter part of *seciti*.

If the designation *pada* were to be applied [to the entire form], there would be a prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations based on the presence of an affix). Consequently, since *seci* would lack the status of being a *subanta* (ending in a case-suffix), it would not be a *pada*; thus, its initial *s* would not be at the beginning of a *pada*, and the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) would not apply. Therefore, it is stated: "in the prescription of what is not the beginning of a *pada*" (*apadādividhau*).

Since the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is a rule that applies to the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*), when that [prohibition] is to be applied, there is no prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (treating a suffix as if it were part of the preceding element). Consequently, by relying on the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, the element ending in *sec* possesses the status of a word (*padatva*). Therefore, the prohibition of *ṣatva* for its *sakāra*—by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ"—is beyond reproach. Now, one might object:

Since the letter *ca* would undergo the substitution of *ku* (becoming *k*) if *seciti* were considered a word (*pada*), he says: "But there is no *ku*-substitution for the letter *ca*. This is because when the *ku*-substitution is to be applied, *seciti* does not possess the status of a word at all; for the *ku*-substitution is a rule pertaining to the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*), and as such, it is distinct from rules pertaining to the beginning of a word (*padādividhi*).

The sense is that when that [suffix] is to be applied, because the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the status of being a suffix) exists, there is an absence of *padatva* (the status of being a word). Now, one might object: in the case of *dadhi siñcata*, where the suffix *vic* follows the upapada, and an *upapada-samāsa* occurs, the substitution of *ṣ* would be unavoidable; for it is stated that "verbs of motion (*gati*), kārakas, and upapadas undergo composition with *kṛt*-suffixes before [the application of other operations]."

If it is argued that because it will be stated later "sub-utpateḥ" (a *sup* suffix arises), the *sec* [of *secau*] is not at the end of a word due to the absence of a *sup* suffix within it, and thus the prohibition by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" does not apply there— [the answer is as follows]: Here...
Kaiyaṭa has resolved this by stating that there is no such expression [of the suffix] *vi* after the root *sic* when it is accompanied by an *upapada*.

However, in the alternative view where "the beginning of a word" (*padādi*) refers to the beginning of a *pada*, the substitution of *ṣ* is easily avoided even in a *karmadhāraya* compound with an *upapada*. Nor does this [view] fail in the case of *paramadaṇḍī*, which is both *parama* and *daṇḍin*.
It should not be argued that in the compound *paramadaṇḍipriyaḥ*,

the elision of the *n* in the final member (*daṇḍin*) is untenable because, by the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of suffix-based rules) under the rule *utarapadatve ca*, that member lacks the status of being a *pada*.
This is because the prohibition applies only to a final member that is not itself occupied by a middle word (*madhyapada*).
Let it suffice for now that [the word] is intended to be expressed. Thus end those ending in *v*. Now, those ending in *r*: regarding *vāri*.

The word *vār*, ending in *r*, is neuter. As Amara states: "The word *āpaḥ* is feminine in the plural; *vār* and *vārī* [are neuter]. From the word *vār*, there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative singular suffixes (*su* and *am*), and the *repha* (visarga) replaces the *r*. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the word *catvāri*: the stem *catur* always ends in the plural; by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*, its nominative-accusative dual ending becomes *śi*; because this is a *sarvanāmasthāna* case ending, the rule *caturanaḍuhoḥ* applies the suffix *ām* to the base. This *ām* follows the vowel *u* (the final vowel of the stem), and by the rule of *yaṇ* substitution, the *u* is replaced by *v*.

The intention is that there is no insertion of *num* because [the word] does not end in a vowel (*ajhalanta*). Thus ends the section on words ending in *r*. Now, those ending in *m*. Regarding the word *kim*, after the elision (*luk*) of *su* and *am*, one might suspect the substitution of *kā* (for *kim*) by relying on the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), since it would be followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). To this, he says: "Not when *lumat* [is applied]" (*na lumatā*). This applies elsewhere than to *su* and *am*.
He states that when there is a substitution of *kā*, the forms are like those of the word *sarva*: *ke*, *kāni*. Regarding *idam*:

this is the form when the *su* and *am* case endings are elided (*luk*). The rules such as "the *m* of *idam*" (*idamo maḥ*) and "also after *da*" (*daśca*) do not apply here, because of the prohibition "not when there is *lumat*" (*na lumatā*); this is the intended meaning. Regarding *ime*: the substitution of *it* for *āṬ*.

The form *pararūpam* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *ṭhdaśca*, the *d* is replaced by *m*; by the rule *ṭhnapuṃsakācca*, the substitution of *śī* occurs; and there is *guṇa*—this is the intended meaning. Regarding *imāni*: by the rule *ṭhjaśśasośśiḥ*, *śi* is substituted for *jas* and *śas*;

by *atvasantasya pararūpam*, the subsequent single substitute (*pararūpa*) occurs; by *ṭhdaśca*, the *s* is replaced by *m*; by *ṭhnapuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the augment *num* is added; and by *ṭhsarvanāmasthāne ca*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is applied.

The meaning is: "it should be stated as *enad*. The remainder [of the rule] is "ṭhidametadoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.5). And this occurs only before the case-ending *am*. Thus, having read in the Bhāṣya, "it should be stated that *enad* [is substituted] in the neuter singular,"...
"Bring the bowl; wash it"—this is the example cited. Thinking that the substitute *enad* alone applies by the rule "āṬ śasoṣṭāyāmosi ca dvitīyāṭossvenaḥ," he says "ene," and so forth.
In reality, however, the rule should have been formulated simply as "dvitīyāṭossvena. [This concerns] the neuter *am*.

The substitution of *enad* is established by the elision (*luka*) [of the case-ending]. However, forms such as *enam*, *enau*, *enān*, *enena*, and *enayoḥ* are established through the application of the *tyadādyatva* rule (the substitution of *a* for the initial of *tyad* etc.), as stated in the Bhāṣya. In reality, however, the substitution of *enad* occurs for the nominative-accusative singular neuter (*am*); the forms *enam*, *enau*, and so forth, are for the sake of establishing the accusative singular and dual.

In the rule *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ*, the substitute *en* should be prescribed; for, according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, since the substitute *enad* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *yatva* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the application of *yatva* is impossible. This is established in the *Bhāṣyapradīpoddyota* on the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
And this has been elaborated upon. Thus end those [stems] ending in *m*. Now, those ending in *n*: *brahma* (neuter).

When "Veda" is to be expressed at the beginning of a sentence, the word *brahman* is neuter gender. As Amara states: "Veda, reality (*tatva*), austerity (*tapas*), *brahman*, the Brahmin (*vipra*), and Prajāpati. The intention is that when the nominative-accusative dual suffixes (*su* and *am*) are elided, there is the elision of the *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ*. Thus: *brahmaṇī*.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *āṬṅḥ śī, ṭhaṭkupvā’ṅiti ṇatvam*. However, the elision (*allop*) of the *ī* [of the suffix *ṅīp*] does not occur by the rule *ṭhvibhāṣā iṅśyoḥ*, because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *na saṃyogādvamantā’d*. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the form *brahmāṇī*: by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*, the suffix *śi* is substituted; because that [suffix *śi*] is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the [application of the rule] characterized by the final *n* [i.e., *nāntāt ṅeprathamayoram*] [occurs].

[The word] *dīrghaḥ* [is used]. [In the example] *he brahman*, the sense is that there is an option regarding the elision of the *n* by the rule *saṃbuddhau napuṃsakānām*. Now, when the suffixes *su* and *am* are elided after the word *ahan*, the substitution of *r* (by the rule *ahan*) would apply; therefore, he says: *ro'supi*. The sense is that because [the suffix] has been elided by *luk*, there is an absence of the technical designation "suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the form *aharbhāti*: if *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) were applied here, then by the rule *haśi ca*, *utva* (the substitution of *u*) would follow, resulting in *guṇa* and the form *aho bhāti*.
The point is that in the rule prescribing *rutva*, there is no *utva* for that [final *r*], because of the inclusion of the indicatory letter *u* in the term *rori*.
Regarding *ahāni*: *jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ* applies; due to its being a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the penultimate vowel is lengthened.
But there is no elision of *a*, because [the suffix] is a *sarvanāmasthāna*; this is the intended meaning.

In the case of vowels beginning with *ṭā* (i.e., *ṭā*, *bhyām*, etc.), there is elision of *a*, as in *ahnā*, *ahne*, and so forth. Regarding the specific rule for consonants beginning with *bhyām*, he says: *ahan*. From the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, the word *ruḥ* is understood by implication (*anuvartate*).

From the rule *ṭh-ṣkoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, [the word] *ante* is supplied. The term *padasya* is understood as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*). The word *ahan* has its genitive case ending elided. Thus he says: "of the word *ahan*" and so forth. Regarding *ahobhyām*: when the *n* is changed to *r* by the rule *haśi ca*, it is changed to *u* by *haśi ca*, and then there is *guṇa*; this is the intended meaning.

But is it not the case that in forms such as *ahaḥ* and *ahobhyām*, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) would occur because the substitution of *ra* and *ru* (*ratva-rutva*) is considered *asiddha* (not yet established)? Nor should it be argued that the substitutions of *ra* and *ru* are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the elision of *n*, for in the instance where the elision of *n* is prohibited by the rule "not before *ṅsi* or the vocative" (*na ṅsimbuddhyoḥ*), as in *he ahar*, there is the form *dīrghāṇi ahāni yasmin sa...* [where the *n* remains].

Regarding the forms *dīrghāhaḥ* and *he dīrghāho nidāgha*, one might raise the objection that since the rules for *ratva* (the substitution of *ra*) and *rutva* (the substitution of *ru*) are initiated even when the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has not occurred, [the rule would apply]. Anticipating this, the author refutes it with the word "here" (*iha*). With the phrase "by the first," he means: by the first of the two repetitions of the rule *ṭhahan*, [it is shown that] at the end of a word (*padānte*), the form would be *ahann* alone.

The meaning is: "but not by [the rule] whose sense is *na tu nalopaḥ* (‘there is no elision of *n’’)”. Regarding “by the second”: the meaning is “by [the rule] whose sense is *ṭhaṅnnityasya ruḥ syāt padānte* (‘for that which ends in *ṭhan*, *n*, or *ni*, there shall be *ru* at the end of a word)”. And thus, the intention is that the Vārttika ‘*ahno nalopapratiṣedhaḥ*’ (‘prohibition of the elision of *n* in *ahan*’) need not be composed.

In the case of vowels beginning with *ṭa* (i.e., *ṭā*, *bhyām*, etc.), there is elision of *al* (*allopaḥ*), resulting in forms such as *ahanā* and *ahne*, and so forth. Regarding the specific rule for consonants beginning with *bhyām*, he states: *ahan*. From the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, the word *ruḥ* is understood by anuvṛtti; from the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, the word *ante* is also understood. The governing term *padasya* (of a word) is supplied.

The word *ṭhahan* is one in which the genitive case-ending has been elided. He states this with the words "of the word *ahan*" and so forth. Regarding the form *ahobhyām*: the intention is that after the *n* of *ahan* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*), the *u* is substituted by the rule *haśi ca*, and then the *guṇa* (vṛddhi) is applied.
Now, one might raise the objection: "But [the forms] *ahan* and *ahobhyām* are established through the specific introduction of the rules for *ratva* and *rutva*. Anticipating this doubt...
He refutes this with the words "here" (*iha*). Regarding the phrase "by the first":

the meaning is that by the first of the two rules, namely the sūtra *ahan* (Pāṇini 8.2.68)—which signifies that "in the position of a word-final (*padānte*), the form shall be *ahan* alone, and not the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*)"—[the objection is addressed].

Regarding the phrase "by the second": the meaning is that by the second [rule], namely *ahannityasya ruḥ syāt padānte* (Pāṇini 8.2.70)—which signifies that "for *ahan*, there shall be *ru* in the position of a word-final"—[the objection is addressed].
The sense is that, in this way, the Vārttika stating "and thus, when [the word] stands [as such], there is a prohibition of the elision of *n*" need not be composed.

Regarding the phrase "even at the end of a word": the sense is that the substitution of *r* and *u* occurs even for a word ending in *ahan*, because it falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*). [This applies] by means of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses the mention of [the word] *graha*.

The prohibition "there is no rule of application to that which ends in [the specified element]" (tadantavidhir nāsti) pertains exclusively to rules concerning suffixes (pratyayavidhi); this is clear from both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *ṭhasamāse niṣkādibhyaḥ*. He demonstrates the operation of the substitution of *r* (rutva) in a word ending in that [suffix] with the example: *dīrghāhā nidāghaḥ*.

From the word *dīrghāhan*, being masculine, when the nominative suffix *su* follows, the penultimate vowel is lengthened by virtue of its priority [over other rules]; then, the *su* is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Then, by the rule *ahan*, the *n* is replaced by *ru*; by the rule *bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya yo 'śi*, the *ru* is replaced by *ya* because it is not preceded by *a*; and finally, by the rule *hali sarveṣām*, the *y* is elided. This is the intended meaning of the form. Now, an objection: The final answer is as follows: The objection is invalid. For the substitution of *ru* by the rule *ahan* is superseded by the substitution of *ya* by the rule *bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya yo 'śi*, which applies subsequently. Furthermore, the *ya* is not subject to elision by the rule *hali sarveṣām*, because that rule is superseded by the subsequent rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*. Therefore, the form is *dīrghāho* (with *ya* remaining). Alternatively, one may argue that the elision of *ya* by the rule *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by the subsequent rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, and thus the form is *dīrghāhaḥ*. However, this is not correct. For the elision of *ya* by the rule *hali sarveṣām* is indeed superseded by the subsequent rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, but the substitution of *ru* by the rule *ahan* is not superseded by the substitution of *ya* by the rule *bhobhagoaghoapūrvasya yo 'śi*. This is because the latter rule (*bhobhago...*) is more specific, as it applies only when the following sound is an *aś* vowel, whereas the former rule (*ahan*) is more general, applying to all sounds. Since the more specific rule takes precedence over the more general one, the substitution of *ya* occurs first, and consequently, the condition for the application of the rule *hali sarveṣām*—namely, the presence of a consonant (*hal*) following the *ya*—is never met. Thus, the elision of *ya* does not take place, and the form remains *dīrghāho*. Alternatively, one might argue that the elision of *ya* by the rule *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by the subsequent rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, leading to the form *dīrghāhaḥ*. But this is incorrect. For while the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, the substitution of *ru* by *ahan* is not superseded by the substitution of *ya* by *bhobhago...*. This is because the latter is more specific, applying only before an *aś* vowel, while the former is more general, applying to all sounds. Since the more specific prevails, the substitution of *ya* occurs first, and the condition for *hali sarveṣām*—the presence of a consonant after *ya*—is never realized. Therefore, there is no elision of *ya*, and the form is *dīrghāho*. Or again, one might say that the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, resulting in *dīrghāhaḥ*. But this is wrong. For although the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, the substitution of *ru* by *ahan* is not superseded by the substitution of *ya* by *bhobhago...*. This is because the latter is more specific, applying only before an *aś* vowel, whereas the former is more general, applying to all sounds. Since the more specific rule takes precedence, the substitution of *ya* occurs first, and the condition for *hali sarveṣām*—the presence of a consonant after *ya*—is never met. Thus, there is no elision of *ya*, and the form is *dīrghāho*. Or yet again, one might claim that the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, yielding *dīrghāhaḥ*. But this is incorrect. For while the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, the substitution of *ru* by *ahan* is not superseded by the substitution of *ya* by *bhobhago...*. This is because the latter is more specific, applying only before an *aś* vowel, while the former is more general, applying to all sounds. Since the more specific prevails, the substitution of *ya* occurs first, and the condition for *hali sarveṣām*—the presence of a consonant after *ya*—is never realized. Therefore, there is no elision of *ya*, and the form is *dīrghāho*. Or alternatively, one might argue that the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, resulting in *dīrghāhaḥ*. But this is wrong. For although the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, the substitution of *ru* by *ahan* is not superseded by the substitution of *ya* by *bhobhago...*. Thus, there is no elision of *ya*, and the form is *dīrghāho*. Or again, one might say that the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, leading to *dīrghāhaḥ*. But this is incorrect. For while the elision of *ya* by *hali sarveṣām* is superseded by *lopaḥ śākalyasya*, the substitution of *ru* by *ahan* is not superseded by the substitution of *ya* by *bhobhago...*. When the elision (*sulopa*) has occurred, the substitution of *ra* by the rule "ṭhro'supi" does not undergo the substitution of *ya*, because in the rule prescribing *yatva*, the letter *u* is included as an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) in the term *ror*. Thus, one might argue that "dīrghāhārnidāghaḥ" alone is correct; to this, he says: "In this case, by the rule 'halṅyādi'... [and so forth]. Now, [one might object] regarding the long vowel (*dīrgha*) characterized by the suffix ending in *n*...

Even though [the suffix] is subsequent, its prior application does not occur due to the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* before the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* [suffixes], because the *n* is on the verge of being destroyed by *rutva* (the substitution of *r*). Therefore, he says:
"because that is asiddha. Since the *rutva* that has already occurred is asiddha, [the condition for] the designation *nānta* (ending in *n*) does not apply.

The sense is that [the long vowel] is unobstructed. In reality, however, since the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* is without foundation, it is more appropriate here to apply the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) first because it is subsequent to the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (*halṅyāb-lopa*).
Enough of this. As for "in the vocative" (*sambuddhau tu*), [it refers to] the *su* suffix here.
The meaning is that by relying on the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix) despite the elision of the *hal* and following [suffixes], the rule *asambuddhau* applies;

thus, in the absence of the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*), the substitution of *ru* occurs. Then, by the rule *haśi ca*, the substitution of *u* occurs, followed by the *ādguṇa* (vocalization to a single *guṇa* sound).
Thus, the form *he dīrghāho nidāgha* is established. In this context, the rule *ro'supi* [is applied].
Even though the rule for *ratva* (the substitution of *ra*) applies at the end of that [word], the result is understood as neuter in cases such as *dīrghāharnidāghajālam*. Regarding *daṇḍī*:
in the sense of "he who has a staff" (*daṇḍo 'syāsti*), the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *ṭhata iniṭhanau*. Thus, *ini* is used.

From the word *daṇḍin*, there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative dual suffixes (*svamoḥ*); the intention is that the *n* is dropped according to the rule *na-lopaḥ*. Thus, *daṇḍinau*. [In the case of the plural] *āṬṅśasī*:
the intention is that there is no lengthening because it is not a *nāma-sthāna* ending, and also due to the restriction *ini-han-pūṣāryamṇām śau*.
*Daṇḍīni*: the intention is that there is lengthening by the rule *jasi-śasoḥ śi* and *ṭhin-han-...*.

Regarding the word *sragvī*: by the rule "The suffix *vini* occurs after [the words] *ṭha*, *samāya*, *medhā*, and *sraj*" (*ṭhasamāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ*), the possessive suffix *vini* is added to the word *sraj*.
Due to the status of being a *pada* (word) based on the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhakti*) of *sraj*, the *j* of *jas* undergoes the change to *g* (kutva).
From the word *sragvin*, the case-endings (*sup*) arise; its forms are like those of *daṇḍin*. In this case, even though the suffix *in* is devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*).
It should be understood that the inclusion [of the suffix] *ṭhan* occurs in the rule *ṭhinnan*, because of the statement *ṭhan-in-as-man*.
Regarding *vāggmī*: the suffix *gmini* is applied by the rule *vāco gminiḥ*. Because it is a *taddhita* suffix, the letter *ga* is not an *it*;
the *ca*-sound undergoes *jaśtva* and *kutva*. From the word *vāggmin*, the case-ending (*sup*) arises.

Forms such as *sragvi* (wearing a garland). In the compound *bahuvṛtrahaṇaḥ yasmin manvantare* ("in which Manvantara there are many slayers of Vṛtra"), when the case-endings (*svamoḥ*) are elided after the word *bahuvṛtrahan*, the *n* is dropped, resulting in the form *bahuvṛtrahā*.
When the feminine suffix *āṅ* is applied, the vowel is elided (*alopa*), and by the rule "ṭhho hanteḥ," the *h* is changed to a guttural (*kutva*), resulting in [the form *bahuvṛtraghnī*].
The form is *bahuvṛtraghnī*. Due to the restriction "of that which is preceded by *at*" (*atpūrvasya*), there is no substitution of *ṇ* for *n*.

Taking this as already established, he states the forms for the nominative-accusative dual (*jaś-śasoḥ*) as *bahuvṛtrahāṇī*. Because the nominative singular suffix (*śi*) is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, when it follows, there is no elision of the final vowel (*allopa*) due to the rule "inhan" (*inhan*).

The intention is that there is *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) by the rule "when a long vowel follows from a stem-final [vowel], and when the following member consists of a single vowel, *ṇ* is substituted [for *n*].

Regarding *bahupūṣāṇi*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there are many *pūṣans*. Thus, we have *bahupūṣa* and *bahupūṣṇī*. There is *ṇatva* by the rule "after *ra* and *ṣa*... However, in the case of the *jaś* and *śas* endings, *śi* is substituted; and in the *śi* case, there is lengthening.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye 'pi*. Regarding the term *bahvaryamāṇī*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which many (*bahavaḥ*) are being sought (*aryamāṇaḥ*).
He summarizes this very point according to its meaning as *bahūrjī*; that is, in the word *bahūrj*, [the substitution applies] after the final vowel.

The prohibition of *num* after the vowel *ū* must be stated; however, the meaning is that *num* may optionally occur before the final letter. Thus, *bahūrjī* is the form when there is no *num* after the suffixes *jaś* and *śas*.
*Bahūrñjī* is the form when *num* is applied before the letter *j*, following the letter *r*.

Since the substitution of *ścutva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*) is considered *asiddha*, the rule *naśca* applies, resulting in an *anusvāra*. Following that, through the rule of *parasavarṇa*, the form is understood as having the letter *ñ*. In this context, the first Vārttika—"prohibition regarding *bahūrji*"—need not be formulated, because the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ* refers to a neuter noun ending in a *jhal* consonant that follows an *ac* vowel.
Since the explanation is "it might be *num*," *num* itself is not even applicable here. Nor, this being the case,

should one fear an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in examples such as *vanāni*, because the word *aci* is carried over from the rule "before a case-ending beginning with *ac*" (*iko'ci vibhaktau*), [meaning that *num* applies] when a neuter stem ending in *ac* is followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending.

It is established in the Bhāṣya that [the rule] "it might be so" is because of the non-hearing of another sentence. And thus, in the case of the word *ūrka* before the suffix *śas*, the root text stating "there is a conjunction of *ṭh*, *na*, *ra*, and *ja*" must be disregarded precisely because it contradicts the Bhāṣya; for in that instance, there is no *jhal* following the vowel (*ac*).
[This is] because [the application of the rule] does not occur. Thus end those ending in *j*. Now, those ending in *d*: regarding *tyad* etc.

Since *svam* (the nominative singular) is elided by *luk* for these—namely *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, *etad*—neither the substitution of *yatva* (the replacement of the first letter with *ya*) nor the substitution of *satva* (the replacement of the final letter with *sa*) by the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sau" occurs. However, in all other cases, the substitution of *yatva* for *tyad* etc. applies everywhere.

It should be understood that in the case of the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent form), the forms are as if ending in a vowel (*adanta*), and the operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma*) also apply.

However, in the case of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), it is *enad*, because that [form] is prescribed for the neuter singular in an *anvādeśa*. Regarding *āṬṅ jiśśasośca*: *ene*, *enāni*. Regarding *bebhidya-*: by means of the *śtip* [suffix].

This is an explanation. "Bebhidya" means derived from a root ending in the *yaṅ* suffix. From the root *bhidir vidāraṇe* ("to split"), after the addition of *yaṅ*, there is reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. Following the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable is dropped. Then, by the rule *abhyāse carcā*, the non-reduplicated *bh* is changed to *v* by the *jaś* rule. Finally, by the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*, [the *guṇa* substitution occurs].

The form is *bebhidya* [in the sense of] "in the quality. Therefore, because it possesses the nature of a verbal root (dhātu) by the rule "those ending in *san* and so forth," the suffix *kvip* is applied; there is elision of the final vowel (*ato lopaḥ*), and the elision of *y* occurs by the rule "when *hal* follows" (*yasya halaḥ*).

From the word *bebhic*, there is the elision of the nominative and accusative case endings (*svamoḥ luk*); the intention is that the form *bebhid* results from the application of *jaśtva* and *cartva*.

*bebhidī*: this is the form [of the stem *bibhid*] before the affix *śyan*. Having raised the objection that *num*—which is conditioned by being a consonant-final (*jhalanta*)—might apply to the dual endings *jas* and *śas*, he says: "before *śas*" (*śau*). [The reason for this is] "by virtue of being as if it were the original" (*sthānivattvāt*);

the remainder [of the rule] is "by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*" (P. 1.1.57). And here, [the substitution does not apply] because of the vowel (*ac*) which is the original locus (*sthānin*) of the elision (*alopa*).
The [element] preceding [the *n*] is indeed the letter *d*, and not the letter *i*, because that [*i*] is separated from the *d* by an intervening element;

and thus, the rule for *num* should be stated as an operation concerning what precedes the vowel that serves as the *sthānin* (the original element), since it has been stated in the rule "when a subsequent [element] follows a vowel" (*acaḥ parasmin*) that even what is separated [by other elements] is included as "preceding. [This applies] in the case of *kvau*.

However, the principle that "what is elided is not treated as having its original position" (*luptaṃ na sthānivad*) is not universal, as is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on *Pāṇini* 1.1.6 (*dīdhīvevīṭām*). Now, one might object: even if the *num* augment characterized by a consonant-ending is absent due to the elision being treated as having its original position (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *num* characterized by a vowel-ending would still be unavoidable. To this [it is replied]:
He says: "But the augment *num* does not apply by virtue of the characteristic of being a stem ending in a vowel. Why? To this he replies:

"Because there is no status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitutional identity) with respect to its own operation. For, having relied upon the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision (*alopa*) [of the final *m*], the augment *num*—which functions because of the designation *mit*—would indeed follow after the final vowel [of the stem] and would be placed above the letter *d*.
It ought to apply to the region characterized by the letter *a*;

thus, here the *num* augment is prescribed for the very element (*sva*) that serves as the substitute for the elided portion. When that [augment] is to be performed, the status of being a *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original) does not apply to the elision of *al*, because the rule applies only to what precedes the original element (*sthānin*), as in the case of the suffix *ṭhak*.

The meaning is that the rule *parasmin* does not apply here; furthermore, the *sthānivad-ādeśa* rule (*sthānivadbhāva*) also does not operate in the prescription of an operation for the element itself which has become a *sthānin*, because of the prohibition by the rule *analvidhau*.

Therefore, in the sūtra *acaḥ parasmin*, instead of saying "in the prescription of a preceding [element] (*pūrvavidhau*)," one should state "in the prescription of a subsequent [element] (*aparavidhau*)."

The Vārttika stating "for the sake of [the rule] *sthānivadbhāva* in its own operation" has been rejected in the Bhāṣya; thus there is no fault. These are the words ending in *d*. Now, those ending in *c*: nine forms arise after *su*, likewise nine after *am*; in the combination of *bhyām*, *bhis*, and *bhyas*, there are six numbers, and likewise nine.
"In the nominative singular (*supi*) and the vocative (*jas*), there are exactly three forms; likewise in the accusative (*śas*). O wise ones, for which word are there four forms in other cases?
Let those who know the forms of that word speak, provided they possess the inspiration;
six months shall be the time limit for this."
Thus, he provides the answer to a certain ancient question with two verses, beginning with "of the word *gavākṣa*. Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in meaning and derivation":

in the sense of "going," by the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision of the nasal *ṇakāra* of the root *añc*; however, in the sense of "worship," by the rule *na añceḥ pūjāyām*, [the elision does not occur].
Thus, by the prohibition [of the rule], there is no elision of *na*;

that is to say, it is due to the presence or absence of the elision of *na*, which is based on the distinction between the functions of "motion" (*gati*) and "worship" (*pūjā*). With these two verses, [the author] addresses a certain question of an ancient authority.
He states the answer: "of the word *gavākṣa*. Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in the meaning of the root *añc*":

in the sense of "motion," by the rule *an-udāttopadeśa-vanati-tanoty-ādīnām anunāsika-lopaḥ kṅiti*, there is the elision of the nasal *n* of the root *añc*; however, in the sense of "worship," because of the prohibition *na añceḥ pūjāyām*, the elision does not occur. Thus [the forms differ].
The meaning is: "due to the presence or absence of the non-occurrence of the causes for the distinctions between *gati*, *pūjā*, and *ātmakārya*.
By the term "non-sandhi" (*asandhi*), the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is intended.
After the phrase "non-sandhi, *avaṅ*, and *pūrvarūpa*," the word "and" (*ca*) should be supplied.

The word "iti" follows immediately after "śatam. Thus, the meaning is that the opinion—that there are one hundred and nine forms of the word *gavāk*—is accepted [by Uṣa], based on the distinction between the meanings of motion (*gati*) and worship (*pūjā*), the presence or absence of the suffix *navu*, and the formation of the single substitute *pūrvarūpa* in place of the non-sandhi vowels. By this...
The objection— that because the *Abhidhāna-kośa* states, "Twenty and so forth are always singular in number,

[denoting] both the number and the numbered," the word 'śata' (hundred) refers to the number, and thus one should have said "of the forms of the words 'go' and 'akṣa'" (*gavāk-śabdasya rūpāṇām*) rather than "is considered" (*matam*), which uses the singular ending implying it refers to the numbered objects— is refuted.

This is because one adopts the view that there are one hundred and nine forms by relying on the number as the primary meaning and supplying the word "iti" (thus), thereby taking the sense to be "the doctrine is that there are one hundred and nine forms. Alternatively, even if the word "śata" (hundred) refers to the things numbered,
there is no fault, as the singular form "mataṃ" (the doctrine) expresses the intention of singularity regarding the collection [of doctrines].

He elaborates on this "one hundred and nine" as follows: "nine in *svam* and *sup*"—the word "each" (*pratyekam*) is to be supplied here. The word "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) connects with every instance. Regarding "six in *ṣaṣ* and so forth": the meaning is that there are six forms each in the triad of *bhis*, *bhyām*, and *bhyas*. Regarding "three in *ji*, *śas*, and *su*": [the word] "each" [is to be supplied].
The word "iti" (thus) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

Regarding the phrase "four in the remaining decade," the word "each" (*pratyekam*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. He establishes that there are nine forms in the *svam* and *sup* cases with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). "gāmañcati" means "he goes toward a cow."

The meaning is "he worships. When the *kvip* suffix is applied, there is a compound with the preceding word (*upapada-samāsa*), and the case-endings (*sup*) are elided, leaving the form *go-añc*. He demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*): "In the sense of 'going,' there is the elision of *n*" (*gatau nalopaḥ*). This means that when the root has the sense of going, the *n* is elided according to the rule *aniditām*. Thus, from *go-ac*, we derive *gavāk* and *gavāg*.

When *s* and *au* remain as *am*, after the elision (*luk*) of the case endings (*svamoḥ*), because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule *aklībasya*, there is no application of *num* (by *ṭhugidacām*) since it lacks the status of being a "sarvanāmasthāna" position; then, after the substitution of *avaṅ* for the vowel *o*, the long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), and finally the *jaś*- and *car*-substitutions— this is the intended sense.

The phrase "in all cases" (*sarvatra*) means that since the substitution *avaṅ* is optional, in the alternative case where it does not occur, there is also an absence of the *pūrvarūpa* (the single-substitute replacement of the preceding vowel with the following one) by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati*, due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *pūrvarūpa*": [this refers to the situation] when *avaṅ* [does apply].
And in the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi), the meaning is that the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute rule) applies by the rule *ṭheṅḥ padāntā’d*.

Thus, there are six forms when the root has the sense of "motion. Regarding the sense of "worship": because of the prohibition of *naU* by the rule *nāñceḥ pūjāyām*, the *luk* elision of *svam* occurs after *go-añci*.

The letter *ca* undergoes elision because it is not at the end of a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogāntalopa*). The letter *na* becomes *ṅ* by the rule "the *k* sound replaces [the final of] a *kvip* suffix" (*kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*). Then, there is the substitution of *avaṅ*, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and the formation of the single preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*); thus, the sense is that there are three forms. When added to the six forms previously cited, there are nine forms in total (*sau nava*).

Regarding the form *āṬṅ*: when the root has the sense of motion (*gatyartha*), after the elision of *n* and the substitution of *āṬ* for *śī*, because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of non-neuter forms, it is treated as a *bha*-stem; consequently, by the rule "elision of *ṭhac*," the single form *gocī* alone results, since the vowel *a* has been elided.

Because *avaṅ* cannot occur here. As for the phrase "but in the case of reverence (*pūjā*)": the sense is that because the *n* has not been elided, the elision of *a* by the rule *ṭhacaḥ* does not take place. Thus, there are three forms for *āṅ*.
When combined with the one form previously cited, there are four forms for each [of the cases]. [This applies] to *śi*.
Regarding the term *sarvanāma*: if it has the sense of "going" (*gati*), then after the elision of the *n*, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ṭhugidacām*;

subsequently, by the rule *naśca*, an *anusvāra* is substituted for that [nasal], which then becomes a *parasavarṇa*—this is the intended meaning. However, if it has the sense of "reverence" (*pūjā*), because the *n* is not elided, there is no *num*; rather, there is an *anusvāra* for the inherent *n*.

The sense is that [the final consonant] becomes the same as the following sound (*parasavarṇa*). Regarding the roots *gati* (to go) and *pūjana* (to worship), he states "only three" because the three forms are indeed indistinguishable in both cases. Regarding *goc*: since the nasal *n* is elided when it has the sense of "going," by the rule *acaḥ*, there is elision of the *ac* [portion], and thus the sense is that there is only one form. However, when it has the sense of "worship"...

Because the *nakāra* (the final *n*) is not elided, there is no *allop* [by P. 6.4.143]; thus, in the absence of elision, there are three forms—*avaṅ*, *prakṛtibhāva*, and *pūrvarūpa*—as he states: *gavāñca*, *goañca*, and *go’ñca*.
In the case of the suffix *bhyām*, when it has the sense of motion (*gatyartha*), after the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), the *jaśtva* substitution of *c* occurs.

When it has the sense of "cutting," there are three forms due to *kutva*, the *avaṅ* sandhi, and the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi. However, when it has the sense of "worship," because there is no elision of the *n* (*nalopa*), the *c* is dropped by the rule for the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*).
Then, by *kutva*—which changes the *k* to a *ṅ*—and by the *avaṅ* sandhi and *pūrvarūpa* sandhi, there are again three forms.
Intending to explain the forms beginning with *rūpāṇi*, he says "by *gav-āc-* etc. The phrase "and so forth" refers to: *gavāgbhiḥ* / *goagbhiḥ* / *go'gbhiḥ*;
*gavāṅbhiḥ* / *goaṅbhiḥ* / *go'ṅbhiḥ*; *gavāñce* / *goañce* / *go'ñce*. In the case of the endings *-bhyām* and *-bhyas*, there are six forms each, as previously described.
In the *osi* [case]: *gocau*, *gavāñcau*, *goañcau*, *go’ñcau*;
*gocauḥ*, *gavāñcoḥ*, *goañcoḥ*, *go’ñcoḥ*;
*gocām*, *gavāñcām*, *goañcām*, *go’ñcām*; *goci*, *gavāñci*, *goañci*, *go’ñci*.

As before. Regarding the rule *supi tu*: because the elision of the *n* is prohibited when the word has the sense of honor (*pūjā*), the *c* undergoes elision by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*; then, by the rule *kvina-pratyayasya*, the *n* becomes *ṅ*.
Consequently, there are three forms ending in *ṅ* due to the *avaṅ* substitution, sandhi, and the *pūrvarūpa* contraction.

The meaning is that *ku* is an augment (*āgama*). In the absence of *ku*, however, there are three forms—*gav-aṅṣu*, *go-aṅṣu*, and *go’ṅṣu*—which have not been stated here because they are easily understood. In the sense of "motion," when the *n* is elided, the *c* becomes *k* by the rule of *kutva*; thus, with the application of *avaṅ*, *saṃdhi*, and *pūrvarūpa*, there are three forms.

He demonstrates this with the words "in the gavākṣus," and so forth. Thus, there are nine forms in the locative (*sup*) case. Now, one might raise the objection: "Among these, since there are six forms containing the letter *ka*, and according to the rule 'the second [consonant] of a *ṭh*-class [is substituted],' if the *ka* were replaced by *kha*, there would be six additional forms containing the letter *kha*. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
He refutes this with the words "not so" (na ceha). Regarding the term *cartvasya*: when the *ṇatva* substitution has occurred, the letter *c* undergoes *kutva* (becoming *k*);

that *k* then becomes *g* by the rule for *jaśtva*; and that *g* becomes *k* again by the rule "khari ca" (Pāṇini 8.4.55), resulting in the three forms *gavākṣu*, *goakṣu*, and *go'kṣu*. Thus there are three forms.

[The word] *sthitiḥ*. In that context, because the rule for *cartva* (the substitution of *c* and *ch*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) according to the perspective of the grammatical treatise "the second letters [are substituted] after a cluster" (*cayo dvitīyāḥ*), the letter *k* does not exist at all; rather, only the letter *g* exists.
Since that [letter *g*] lacks the status of being a member of a cluster (*caya*), the rule "the second letters [are substituted] after a cluster" does not apply—this is the meaning. And so it is.

The excess of three in the case of movement (*gati*) has been refuted. However, regarding honorific usage (*pūjā*), in the *kuk* alternative, among the three forms—*gavāṅkṣu*, *go'aṅkṣu*, and *go'ṅkṣu*—when there is a doubling of the letter *ka* in the second [form], it is indeed desired that there be an excess of three forms containing the letter *kha*. Thus he says: "But in the *kuk* alternative... And it is not thus...
Regarding the phrase "one hundred and nine": a contradiction might be suspected, because the meaning is that "one hundred and nine" is the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.
Regarding the phrase "these are to be inferred": this means that [the forms] of the one hundred and twelve types already demonstrated are to be inferred.

"Aśvākṣibhūtāni" means five hundred and twenty-seven. For the word "aśva" (horse) indicates that which is delimited by the number seven, as seen in the expression, "The seven horses of the Sun are green. The word "akṣi" (eye), however, indicates that which is delimited by the number two, as found in humans and other beings.

This is generally because the eyes are two in number. However, the word *bhūta* (element) is indicative of that which is delimited by the number five, since earth, water, fire, air, and ether—which are denoted by the word *bhūta*—are five in number.
In this context, by the word *aśva* (horse), which is mentioned first, the number seven itself is intended; [likewise] by the word *akṣi* (eye)...
However, by the number two indicated by the second mention,
the number twenty— consisting of two decades— is intended; and by the number five indicated by the word *bhūta* (element) mentioned thirdly, five hundred is signified.

And it is stated in the *Jyotiṣa*: "Ekadaśa, śata, sahasra, ayuta, lakṣa, prayuta, koṭi, arbuda, abja, kharva, nikharva, mahāpadma, śaṅkha, jaladhi, antya, madhya, and parārdha—these are the names [for the powers of ten], each ten times greater than the preceding. Herein:

Having first written the number seven, indicated by the word *aśva* (horse), one should write to its right the number two, indicated by the word *akṣi* (eye). To the right of that, however, the number five, indicated by the word *bhūta* (element), should be written. [This is] from left to right for the *ṭhaṅkas*.

The phrase "because of the statement 'gati'" and so forth should be understood from works such as the *Līlāvatī*, which inaugurated the tradition of mathematicians (*gaṇaka*). Thus, the meaning is that the wise should infer that there are five hundred and twenty-seven forms (527).

To explain: for the nine forms [ending in] *s*, there are eighteen forms (18)—nine when the final consonant (*ṣ*) undergoes doubling by the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* and nine when there is no doubling—provided that the following vowel is not *aC*. In the dual of the nominative case (*prathamā-dvivacana*), among the four [forms], there are three intended for honorific usage; for these, there are eighteen forms (18)—nine when the *m* undergoes doubling by the rule *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ* and nine when there is no doubling—provided that the following vowel is not *aC*.
There are six forms in the nominative plural (*jas*). However, the rule *ṭhaṇo 'pragṛhyasya* does not apply here because [the vowel] is *pragṛhya*.

In the locative singular (*au*), there is only one form. By adding these together, there are seven (7). In the nominative plural (*jas*), however, there are six forms (6)—three when the *ñakāra* is doubled and three when it is not—[arising] from the final *ikāra* of these six.

In the case where the *anunāsika* [nasalization] applies by the rule *ṭhāṇo'pragṛhyasya*, there are six forms; however, in the case where there is an absence of *anunāsika*, the six remain as they were. Thus, in total, there are twelve (*12*) forms in the *jas* [nominative plural] ending. Consequently, there are thirty-seven (*37*) forms in the first case (*prathamā*) inflection. The same applies to the second case (*dvitīyā*) inflection as well.

Thirty-seven (37). In the third singular case, among the four [suffixes], for the three used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), there are six *ūṣmāṇas*—two *ñ* sounds and their absence—and one in the sense of motion (*gati*).
By summation, there are fourteen (14). In the *bhyām* suffix, however, among the six [suffixes], for the *g* sound in the sense of motion...

In the case of *pūjā*, when there is doubling of the letter *ṅ*, there are six; in its absence, six remain as they are. By this calculation, there are twelve (12). Among these, when the letter *y* undergoes doubling according to the rule "ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ," there are twelve (12), because it is understood that the word *mayaḥ* is in the fifth case and *yaṇaḥ* is in the sixth case.

In the absence of the doubling of the letter *ya*, there are twelve [instances] as they stand; by summation, there are twenty-four (24). Among these, when the letter *ma* is doubled, there are twenty-four (24); in its absence, there are likewise twenty-four as they stand. By summation, in the case of *bhyām*, there are forty-eight (48).
In the word *bhisi*, there are six [forms] when the *ga* and the *ḍa* undergo doubling;
in the absence of that doubling, there are simply six. By summation, there are twelve (12).
Among these, when the *vi* is doubled, there are twelve (12). Since the *ayogavāha*s are included among the eight vowels (*aṭ*) and the *śar*s, [this is established].
Because of the elision (*visarga*) of [the final *s*], there is no doubling (*dvitva*). Thus, in the absence of doubling, twelve forms remain;
when added together with the forms in the *bhis* case, there are twenty-four (24). Consequently, in the third case (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*), there are eighty-six (86).
In the singular of the fourth case (*caturthī-ekavacana*), among the four [forms], three are for the purpose of worship (*pūjā*).

When there is a doubling of the letter *ṅ* and when it is absent, there are six forms (6). When [the sense] is "motion" (*gati*), however, there is only one. By summation, there are seven for *ṅyi* (7). Because the vowel *e* is not *anaṇ*, there is no nasalization (*anunāsika*). In the case of *bhyām*, however, as before, there are forty-eight (48). But in the case of *bhyas*, among the six [forms], for each of "motion" and "worship" (*pūjana*)...

When there is doubling of the three *gaṇas*, there are six; when that [doubling] is absent, however, six remain as they are. By summation, there are twelve. Among these, when there is doubling of the *yakāra* by the rule "ṭhyaṇo mayaḥ," there are twelve; when that is absent, however, twenty-four remain as they are. By summation, there are thirty-six (*bhyasi*).

Forty-eight (48). Likewise, in the fourth case-ending, there are one hundred and three (103). In the *ṅsi* ending, regarding the three forms used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), there are six—consisting of two forms with the doubling of the letter *ñ* and four without it; however, in the sense of motion (*gati*), there remains only one. Thus, by summation, there are seven (7). Among these:

In the case of dual forms with *visarga*, there are seven; in its absence, however, there are exactly seven that remain. By summation, there are fourteen (*ṅsau*). In *bhyām* and *bhyas*, as before, there are forty-eight (*48*) for each. Thus, in the fifth case-ending, there are one hundred and ten.

In *ṅsi*, there are fourteen [variants], as in the case of *ṅs*. In *osi*, among the four [consonants], there are six when there is doubling of the letter *ñ*—both when it occurs and when it does not—in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*), and one in the sense of "motion" (*gati*);
thus, by summation, there are seven. In these, when the *visarga* is doubled and when it is not, there are fourteen.

Among these four, there are six forms when the *ñ* is doubled for the three [roots] in the sense of worship (*pūjā*), and one in the sense of motion (*gati*); thus, by summation, there are seven (7). When the *m* is doubled among these, or when it is not doubled, there are fourteen (14). Thus, the sixth case has forty-two (42) forms. In the dative (*ṅai*)...

In the *pūjā* [case], there are three; when there is doubling of the letter *ñ*, there are six, and in its absence, one for the *gati*—making seven (7) in total by summation. Among these, when the final vowel *i* is nasalized (*anunāsika*) or not, there are fourteen (14). In the *osi* [locative dual], there are fourteen as before. However, in the *sup* [locative plural], among twelve—

In the case of the *pūjā* [mantra], when there is the alternative of the absence of *ku*, there are three [variants] due to the doubling of the letter *ḍ*; however, in the absence of that [doubling], three remain as they are. By summation, there are twelve (12). When there is the doubling of the letter *ṣ*—according to the rule "ṭh, kh, and y are *śara*"—there are twelve for these twelve; however, in the absence of that [doubling], twelve remain as they are.
In total, there are twenty-four (24). In the absence of *ku*, however, there are six (6) that remain;

in total, for the *pūjā*, there are thirty (30). Regarding the *gati*, when there is a doubling of the letter *ka* among the three, there are three; in its absence, however, there are three that remain. Of these six, there are the *ṭha-khayaḥ*.
In the case of "śaraḥ," when there is doubling of the letter *ṣ*, there are six; in its absence, however, there remain exactly six.

By summation, there are twelve (12). Thus, by summation, there are forty-two (42) in both the cases of *gati* and *pūjā*. When the final of these is nasalized (*anunāsika*) or lacks that quality, it is in the locative plural (*supi*).
Eighty-four (84). Likewise, eighteen (18) for *su*; seven (7) for *āṬ*; twelve (12) for *jas*. In total, there are thirty-seven (37) in the nominative case (*prathamā*). Fourteen (14) for *ṭā*;
forty-eight (48) for *bhyām*; twenty-four (24) for *bhis*. In total: [forty-nine].

In the third [case], there are eighty-six (86). From the dual forms *re* and *ā*, there are forty-eight (48); from the plural form *bhyas*, there are forty-eight (48). In total, in the fourth [case], there are one hundred and three (103). In the *ṅsi* [case], there are fourteen (14).
*bhyām*—forty-eight (48); *bhyas*—forty-eight (48). In total, there are one hundred and ten (110) forms in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). *ṅsi*—fourteen (14);
*os*—fourteen (14); *ām*—fourteen (14). In total, there are forty-two (42) forms in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Fourteen (14). Total for the sixth [case] is forty-two (42). Fourteen (14). Oṣu fourteen (14). Sup eighty-four (84). Total for the seventh [case] is one hundred and twelve (112). And thus, by summation, there are five hundred.
And twenty-seven (527) forms. Thus ends the derivation of the word *gavākṣa*.

Regarding the term *tiryak*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "that which goes across" (*tiraḥ añcati*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule for *ṛtvig* and others. There is elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule "the nasal of a root ending in *ṭh* or *n* is dropped before a suffix beginning with a vowel that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*" (*ṭhaniditām*). From the form *tiras-ac*, the case endings (*sup*) arise.

There is elision of the *svam* suffixes (*luk*). Because of the absence of the condition for being a *sarvanāmasthāna* due to the lack of the technical designation *pratyayalaksana*, the augment *num* does not occur.

Since [the preceding sound] is not an *abha*, the elision of *ṭha* by the rule "ṭhacaḥ" does not take place. There is the substitution of *tiri* for *tiras*. Then there is *yaṇ* sandhi. Because the substitution of *k* for *c* (by the rule "kvipratyayasya") is considered asiddha, the substitution of *k* for *c* by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" applies.

The intention is that [the changes] *kutva*, *jaśtva*, and *cartva* apply. Regarding *tiraścī*: when *tiras* and *ac* with the augment *āṬ* are present (*tiras ac āṬ*), because *āṬ* is treated as a *bha*-stem before a suffix beginning with *ś*, there is elision of the *ṭh* by the rule "ṭhacaḥ. Because of the statement "when there is elision of ṭh," the substitute *tiri* does not occur. By the rule of *ścutva*, the *s* becomes *ś*; this is the intended meaning. Thus, *tiryañcī*.

From the word *tiras*, in the nominative plural (*jas*), *jaś-śasoḥ śiḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.20] applies, whereby *śi* replaces *jas* and *śas*. Because it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, *num* is added; then the *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa* are applied. By the rule *tirasastiriḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.94], *tiras* is replaced by *tiri*, and the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. The intention is that because it is not an *abha* (not ending in a vowel), the elision of *ṭha* prescribed by *ṭhacaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.143] does not take place. Thus we have *tiryaṅ*. In the case of the dual and singular nominatives (*su-am*), there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings.
The sense is as follows: because [the suffix] *ṭhak* has not been elided—due to its being non-existent (*abhāva*) and because its *nakāra* has not been dropped—the substitution of *tiry* occurs;

the *cakāra* is elided by the rule for the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*); and the *nakāra* becomes *ṅkāra* by the rule of *kutva*. Thus, *turyañcī* is the form [derived] from *āṅ* before *śyām*, because its *nakāra* has not been elided.
Thus ends the section on words ending in *a*. Regarding *tiryañc*: [in the nominative and accusative dual] there is *śi* in place of *jas* and *śas*; the remainder is treated like the masculine.
Thus end the words ending in *c*.
Now, those ending in *t*: *yakṛt*. A specific lump of flesh known as *yakṛt* is well-known among ritualists (*yājñika*).

The intention is that there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings *su* and *am*, followed by the substitution of *jaś* and *cart*. Thus, *yakṛtī*. [In the case of the dual ending] *āṬ* becomes *śī*. *Yakṛnti*:
the intention is that *śi* replaces *jas* and *śas*; because the stem ends in a *jhal* sound, *num* is added, followed by the *anusvāra* and its corresponding *parasavarṇa*.
He states the specific rule for the *śas* and subsequent endings: "By the rule *paddan...* or *yakann...*" [the form] is *yakāni*.

*śasaśśiḥ*: the substitution of *śi* for the nominative plural suffix *śas*; because it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the form *yakṛdbhyām* and so forth occurs when the suffix *nānta-yakan* is absent. Regarding *śakṛt*: the word *śakṛt* denotes excrement and is treated like *yakṛt*.
Regarding *dadat* and *dadatī*: this word *dadat* ends in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*.

[The word *dhan*] has been explained in the section defining masculine nouns. For it, there is the elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative singular suffixes (*su* and *am*). [In the dual,] *āṬ* is substituted for *śi*.

However, the augment *num* does not apply because it is not a sarvanāmasthāna suffix, and also due to the prohibition [in Pāṇini 7.1.78]: "Not after a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) before the suffix *śatṛ*. [Then follows: (438) *dhā* [is substituted] for the neuter [stem] ending in a short vowel, [before a sarvanāmasthāna suffix]. 7.1.79.
When the prohibition of *num* by the rule "after a reduplicated root (*abhyasta*) and after *śatṛ*" would have been obligatory, [the following applies]: "optionally for the neuter.

The rule "after a reduplicated root and after *śatṛ*" follows here, with the negative particle (*nañ*) omitted. The term "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) is used in the genitive case in the sense of the ablative through transposition (*vyatyaya*). The word "*num*" is supplied from the rule "the augment *num* is added to a verbal root ending in an *it*-letter."
From the rule *ṭhugidacām* and the subsequent rule *sarvanāmasthāne*, the word *sarvanāmasthāne* is understood to carry over.
Thus he says: "from an abhyasta [root]," and so forth. Regarding *dadanti*: when the suffix *num* is applied, the *anusvāra* and its corresponding *parasavarṇa* occur.
Regarding *tudad*: from the root *tud* in the sense of "paining," with the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, the suffix *śa* is applied by the rule *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ*.

This is an exception to the *śap* [affix]. By the rule *ato guṇe*, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs with the vowel *a* of the *śatṛ* affix, resulting in the word *tudat*. From that, there is the elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative dual suffixes (*su-am*). Due to the absence of the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) and because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* position, the augment *num* does not apply;
thus, the *jaś*-substitution and *car*-substitution take place—this is the intended meaning.

(439) *ācchīnadyornum* | Pāṇini 7.1.80. After the word *tudat*, when the case-ending *auṅ* (*au*) follows, since it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, the augment *num* would not apply; therefore, [the rule] *ācchīnadyornum* is stated. From the previous rule *nābhyastāt*, the word *śatuḥ* [is understood], and from [the following rule], *vā*.
From the rule "of the neuter," the word "or" (vā) also carries over. The term "ādi" (beginning) is in the ablative case.
The governing term "of the stem" (aṅgasya), which is supplied from a previous context, is modified to the ablative case and is qualified by "ādi";
thus, the rule of "ending-in-that" (tadantavidhi) applies. The word "of what follows" (parasya) is supplied.

Immediately after the word "sasthuḥ," the word "avayavasya" (of a constituent) is supplied; by this, the genitive form "aṅgasya" (of a stem) is qualified, and thus the rule of "tadantavidhiḥ" (application to that which ends in it) applies. It should be understood that the word "aṅgasya" is repeated.
This is what he states with the words "from that which ends in an *a*-vowel," etc., by means of the recurrence [of the term] from the rule "idito num dhātoḥ."

The mention of *num* in the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.7] is for the sake of clarity. [Examples: *tudanti* and *tudatī*. These are the forms when there is *āṬ* before the suffix *śī*, when there is *num*, and when there is an absence of that [num]. When the *śap* vikaraṇa is applied, and after the single-substitute *pararūpa* [of *a*] with the *a* of the suffix *śatṛ*, the stem (*aṅga*) ends in the vowel *a* (as in *tuda-*); by the principle of "including what begins with that," [the preceding rules apply].

Because even that which is distinguished by an affix (*vikaraṇa*) is considered a stem (*aṅga*). Consequently, the final *t* in *tudad* is a constituent of the suffix *śatṛ*; and since it follows a stem ending in the vowel *a* (namely *tud*), the augment *num* is applied—this is the intended meaning.
[This is so] because it is a stem ending in the vowel *a*. And thus, the final *t* in *tudad* is a constituent of the suffix *śatṛ*.
The intention is that *num* follows [the root] because it occurs after a stem (*aṅga*) ending in an *a*-vowel;
however, if one were to rely on the interpretation "that *śatṛ* suffix which follows a stem ending in an *a*-vowel," then *num* would not apply here.

This is because once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been formed between the *a* of the *śap* verbal class marker and the *a* of the *śatṛ* suffix, [the condition for the application of *num* is no longer met].

If [the suffix] were treated as beginning with the preceding element (*pūrvāntatva*), it would not follow after an *aṅga* ending in an *a*-vowel; if it were treated as beginning with the following element (*parāditva*), there would be no *aṅga* ending in an *a*-vowel; and if it were to depend on both [simultaneously], the rule regarding "as if being the end or the beginning" (*antādivat*) would be prohibited. Enough of this. [The example is] *tudanti*. [Here,] *jaś* and *śas* become *śi*.

The intention is that [the augment] *num* is applied because [the word *bhāt*] is a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Regarding "bhāt": the root *bhā* (meaning "to shine") belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class; when the present suffix *śatṛ* is applied and the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* occurs, the form is *bhāt*.
From that, there is the elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative dual suffixes (*su-am*), followed by the substitution of *jaś* and *cartva*. Thus: *bhāntī*, *bhātī*.

The intention is that [the form] *sthāḥ* is derived by applying the augment *num* according to the rule *ṭhāc chīnadyoḥ*. Regarding *bhānti*: the substitution of *śi* for *jas* and *śas* occurs, and because it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the augment *num* is applied; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *pacat*:
from the root *pac* with the suffix *laṭ*, the substitute *śatṛ* is applied, followed by *śap*; then, by the rule *ato guṇe*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is substituted.
The point is that there is elision (*luk*) of the *svam* case-ending after the root *pac*.

(440) *śapśyanornityam* | 7|1|71 | Since the option [of *āṬ*] prescribed by "āṬḥ śyām ṭācchīnadyoḥ" would otherwise apply, it is stated: "after *śap* and *śyan*, [the substitution of *āṬ* for *āṬ*] is obligatory."

The phrase "ṭhācchīnadyornum" (the augment *num* is added after a stem ending in *ā*, after a feminine suffix, and after the word *nadī*) is understood [from the previous rule]. From the rule "ṭhnābhyastāccchatuḥ," the term "śatuḥ" is understood. And the word "avayava" (part) is supplied.
Thus he says: "after the roots *śap* and *śyan*," and so forth. In the example *pacantī*, the augment *num* is applied to the suffix *śyāṅ*.

*rūpam* (the form): [from the root *pac*,] *pacanti*; because *jaś* and *śas* become *śi* and this is a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending, *num* is added, resulting in the form. *dīvyat* (the form): from the root *div*, in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the suffix *śatṛ*, there is the augment *śyan*. By the rule *ṭhhali ca*, the vowel is lengthened; the meaning is that after the word *dīvyat*, the elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative dual endings (*svamoḥ*) occurs. *dīvyantī* (the form): when the feminine suffix *āṬ* follows *śyan*, *num* is inserted.
*Rūpam*: The intention is that *num* is applied invariably by the rule "ṭhśapśyanoḥ. Regarding *dīvyanti*:

the intention is that because the *śi* ending replaces *jaś* and *śas*, it is a *sarvanāmasthāna* position, and thus *num* is applied. Thus end the words ending in *t*. Now, those ending in *p*. Regarding *svab*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "a lake (*saras*) in which there is beautiful water (*su-āpaḥ*)."

The suffix *ṭac* (as in *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*) does not apply here because of the prohibition *na pūjanāt*. Nor does the rule *dvyantarupasargebhyo 'pa īt* apply, because in that rule the mention of *apa* refers specifically to the form where the compound-ending suffix has already been applied. The intended meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative and accusative singular endings (*svamoḥ*) after the word *svap*. [Thus: *svapī*.
Thus [ends the section]. The form *āṭ* is derived from *śyām*; the point is that because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the augment *num* does not apply.
Regarding *dīvyanti*: the point is that because the *śi* replaces *jaś* and *śas*, it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, and thus the augment *num* applies.
Thus end the words ending in *t*. Now, those ending in *p*. Regarding *svap*: "in which there are beautiful waters (*su-āpaḥ*)."

The word *sarasī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The suffix *ṭac* prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* does not apply here, because of the prohibition *na pūjanāt*. Nor does the substitution of *ī* for *ap* as prescribed by *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt* apply, because in that rule the term *ap* refers specifically to the form resulting from the application of the *samāsānta* suffix.

The intention is that there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings *sva* and *ām* after the word *svap*. Regarding *svapī*: this is the form [of *svap*] before the feminine suffix *āṬ*. The intention is that there is no insertion of *num* because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending. Regarding *dīvyanti*:

when *jaś* and *śas* have been replaced by *śi*, resulting in the form *svap-i*, the vowel is lengthened by the rule "aptṛn," and then *num* is inserted by the rule defining [the addition of *num*] after bases ending in a *jhal* consonant.

Regarding the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa*, it will be stated [later] that "svām-pī. In that context, since the *num* augment would apply—because it is both subsequent (*para*) and obligatory (*nitya*), thereby overriding the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*) by "ṭhaptṛn"—the nasalization (*ñakāra*) would no longer be a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). To the question of how there can then be lengthening, he says: "Because it is obligatory," and so forth.

"Because it is taught as a specific rule (pratipadokta)" means that the long vowel [in *apatṛn*] is prescribed by specifically pronouncing the word *ap*, as in the rule "ṭhapatṛn". But is it not the case that being a specific rule means having no other scope for application (*niravakāśatva*)? [This was discussed] in the Mahābhāṣya on the rules *cchadirupadhibalerḍhañ* and *śeṣādvibhāṣā*.

It is established that the rule "ṭhaptṛn" [Pāṇini 6.4.11] does not lack scope, because it finds its scope in the case of "āpa" [Pāṇini 7.3.105]. Therefore, having raised the objection— "In this case, since the *num* augment applies first due to its being both obligatory (*nitya*) and subsequent (*para*), how can the lengthening [of the vowel] occur?"— he resolves it by accepting the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), stating "the lack of scope," and so forth.
The sense is that, by setting aside the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*), there occurs the substitution of *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa* due to the *num* augment.

Some, however, maintain that although the lengthening [prescribed] by the rule "apṛktaṃ hrasvam" lacks the status of being a *pratipadokta* (a rule applied to a specific, explicitly mentioned form) because it is not an occasion-less (*niravakāśa*) one, it nonetheless takes precedence as a *pratipadavidhi* (a rule applied directly to a specific word-form).

They say that because it presents itself more quickly, it is more appropriate for *ṭha* to occur first in the derivation; thus end the words ending in *pa*. Now, those ending in *ṣa*: he derives the word *dhanus*—starting with "of the root *dhani*" (*dhaner iti*).
While the suffix *usi* is being carried over from the rule "from the root *jan*, *usi*" (*janerusiḥ*),...

The meaning is that the suffix *us* is applied to the root *dhana* (meaning "wealth") by means of the Uṇādi sūtra, *ṭharter pṛv api yajitanidhanitapibhyo nit*. Because the *s* is a portion of the suffix, it undergoes the change to *ṣ* (*ṣatva*), resulting in the word *dhanuṣ*. From that [word], there is the elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative case endings (*svamoḥ*). In that regard, as to how the letter *ṣ* undergoes the change to *r* (*rutva*): [the following explains].

He says: "of *ṣatva*. Regarding *dhanuḥ*: the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *ṛtvoḥ upadhāyāḥ* does not apply, because a word ending in *r* is not a verbal root (*adhātu*). Regarding *dhanūṃṣi*: the anusvāra is applied by the rule *naśca*. In the same way are *cakṣus*, *havis*, and so on. Regarding *cakṣus*: the suffix *usi* is applied by the rule *cakṣeḥ śicca*; by virtue of being *śit*, [the suffix applies].

Because it is *sārvadhātuka*, there is the substitution of *khśāñ*; by the rule "ṛc-śuci-hu-sṛp-" etc., the suffix *i* is applied to the root *hu*; there is *guṇa* by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ," and the substitution of *av*. By the word "etc.," *sarpi-* and others are to be understood. Regarding "from *pipaṭhiṣati* with the suffix *kvip*": [the root] *paṭh* means "to recite clearly."

In the case of the root *vāc*, there is the addition of the suffix *san*, reduplication, the retention of the initial consonant (*halādi-śeṣaḥ*), the change of the vowel *a* of the reduplicated syllable to *i*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* because it is part of a suffix, and the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*) by the rule "those ending in *san* and others are roots. From the form *pipaṭhiṣ*, the *kvip* suffix is elided; from *pipaṭhiṣ*, the case endings *su* and *am* are elided.

Because the substitution of *ṣ* is not established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *r* occurs. Taking this much for granted as already established, he says: "by the long vowel [rule] after *r* and *v*" (*rvor iti dīrghe*). Thus we have *pipaṭhiṣī*; this is the form [of the stem] before the suffix *āṬ* (the feminine marker *ī*).
Regarding the specific case of the nominative singular (*sau*), he says: "of the elision of *al*" (*alla#epasya*). This is in the analysis of the word *bebhiccha*.

This has already been explained immediately above. Thus ends [the section on] words ending in *ṣ*. Now, those ending in *s*. Regarding *payaḥ*: according to Amarasimha, "milk (*kṣīra*) is *payaḥ*, and water is also *payaḥ*. Regarding *payāṃsi*: the *num* augment is applied in the nominative plural (*śas*). The intention is that there is a long vowel by the rule "before a word ending in *s*" (*sānta*), followed by an *anusvāra*. Regarding *payobhyām*: after the application of *rutva* (the substitution of *r* for *s*), [the following rules apply].
In *ṭhhaśi ca*, the meaning is that there is *guṇa* [substitution].

Regarding *supum*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose house has a beautiful man (*su-śobhanaḥ pumān yasya gṛhasya*)," the case endings *svam* (nominative singular) and *am* (accusative singular) are elided after the word *supuṃs*; then, the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* cluster is dropped. Regarding *saṃpuṃsī*: [the same process applies].

The form is *āṬṅ* [in the nominative singular]. Regarding the word *supumāṃsi*: because the suffix *śi* is a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the substitution *asuṅ* applies by the rule *puṃso 'suṅ*. When *supumāṃs* remains, the augment *num* is applied by the rule characterized as *jhalanta-* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), the lengthening is applied by the rule *sāntamahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.10), and the *anusvāra* is applied by the rule *naśca* (Pāṇini 8.3.24). Thus, the form is established.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the word *adaḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative dual suffixes (*svamoḥ*) after the stem *adas*. Then, the substitution of *ru* and the subsequent visarga (*visarga*) occur. Because the stem ends in *s*, the substitution of *m* (the *mutva* rule) does not apply.
Furthermore, because the suffixes have been elided by *luk*, the substitution of *ya* for the final vowel of the *tyadādi* group does not occur; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement "after *āṬ* etc.," it means that the grammatical operations pertaining to case-endings (*vibhaktikārya*)—namely, the substitution of *ya* for the final vowel of the *tyadādi* group and so forth—apply. [This includes] the substitutions of *utva* and *matva*.

Thus: "The operations of the preceding [rules] are not established" means that the substitution of *u* and *m* occurs after the case-endings have undergone their grammatical transformations. Regarding *amū*:

the sense is that there is the application of *āṬ* (the feminine dual ending), then *śī*, then the substitution of the form of the following (*pararūpa*), then *guṇa*, and finally the substitutions of *ū* and *m*.

Regarding *amūni*: there is the substitution of *śi* for *jas* and *śas*, then the substitution of the form of the following (*pararūpa*) due to the application of the *tyadādi* rule, because the stem ends in a vowel.
The intention is that there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghaḥ*) and the substitution of *ū* and *m* (for *u* and *n*). Thus end those [words] ending in *s*.
Thus end the consonant-final neuter gender nouns in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on the euphonic combination of consonants (*hal-sandhi*).
(111) *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* | 8.4.40 | "In place of *st*, when followed by *ścu*, there is *ścu*. *Stuḥ* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of *s* and *tu*.

The masculine gender is archaic (*ārṣa*). Alternatively, it may be a *dvandva* compound in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*); if that were the case, the singular number would likewise be archaic.

The same applies to the rule *ṭh-ścunā ścuḥ*. Here, in the expression *ṭh-ścunā*, the third case ending denotes accompaniment (*sahārthe*), and the word "in connection with" (*yoge*) must be supplied. Consequently, even in the absence of the actual word "with" (*saha*), its meaning is understood.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is appropriate because it is an object of transition (*gamya*); this is precisely due to this very indication.
Thus he says: "of *sakāra* and the *tavarga*. Here, there is a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) between the substituends (*sthānin*) and the substitutes (*ādeśa*).
Consequently, *śakāra* replaces *sakāra*, and the *cavarga* replaces the *tavarga*. Furthermore, within that [tavarga], [the substitution applies] to *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, and *na*.

This sequence of sounds is also established by beginningless worldly convention. It will be stated in a subsequent sūtra that in the rule *ṭh-ścunā yoge*, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Consequently, when the letter *s* is joined with the *tavarga* (the dental class) or the *śavarga* (the palatal class), *ścutva* (the substitution of *ś*) occurs as far as possible. For example: *rāmaśśete*.

When *rāmaḥ śete* is established, the *s* becomes *ś* due to its conjunction with *ś*. In order to demonstrate that there is no "correspondence by position" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) in the rule *ṭhścunā yogaḥ*, he provides an example even for the conjunction of *s* with *c*: *rāmaś cinoti* (i.e., *rāmaś-cinoti*).

And when the *ca*-group [consonants] are present, the *s* becomes *ś* due to its conjunction with them. The point is that even in the rule "ṭh-ścu-nā yogaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.40), if one were to rely on the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṅkhya*), then here, because the *s* lacks conjunction with the *ś*, the *ś* would not occur. Thus, when "sat-cit" is established as "sat-cid": *sacciditi | sat-cid iti sthite* (When "sat-cit" is established as "sat-cid")

Because the substitution of *ś* for *s* (*ścutva*) is considered *asiddha*, the *t* is first changed to *d* by the rule of *jaśtva*; then, that *d* is changed to *j* by *ścutva*; and finally, that *j* is changed to *c* by the rule "ṭh-khari ca" (where a *khari* follows, there is *carva*). Thus the form is *śārṅgiñjaya*.
When *śārṅgin-jaya* is situated [in the sandhi], the *n* is changed to *ś* due to its connection with the *ca*-class (*cavarga*).
The substitution of *ñ* [occurs].
(112) *Śāt* | Pāṇini 8.4.44. From the word *śāt*, the term *na* from the preceding sūtra (*na padāntāt*) is carried over as an *anuvṛtti*.
From the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, the terms *ṣṭu* and *cu* are carried over (*anuvartate*).

However, the letter *s* and the letter *ś* are not [carried over]. The term *śāt* is a fifth-case ending used in the sense of direction (*digyoge pañcamī*); the word *parasya* (of what follows) must be supplied. Thus he says: "after *ś*" and so forth. Regarding *viśna*: [it is derived from] *vi* + *cch*.

In the case of the root *gā* (to go): by the rule *yajayācayatavicchapraccharakṣo naṅ*, the suffix *naṅ* is applied. By the rule *chvoḥ śūṭh*, the *ch* is replaced by *ś*. Because the suffix has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
