Here, due to the connection with the letter *ś*, the *n* of the *tavarga* group would have been subject to replacement by *ñ* via the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*; however, this is prohibited. This is because the preceding rule states: "In conjunction with a *ścu* [sound]..."

In this case as well, if one were to rely on the principle of "respective correspondence" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), then since there would be no conjunction of the *nakāra* of *tavaka-* and *dīya-* with a *cavarga* sound here, the rule for *cutva* would not even apply; thus, its prohibition would be redundant.
And so, by virtue of this very prohibition, [it follows that] in the preceding sūtra, the phrase "in conjunction with a *cavarga*" (*ścunā yoge*) does not [apply].
It is understood that this refers to the sequential correspondence [of the letters]. Regarding the word *praśna*: from the root *pracch* in the sense of "desire to know" (*jñīpsā*).

It is derived with the suffix *naṅ* as prescribed for the *adādi* class. Here, the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) does not occur [as one might expect from the rule] *grāhijyā*, because of the specific grammatical indications such as [the rule] *praśne cāsannakāle*. In this context, although the fifth letters of the classes (*vargapañcama*) possess an additional nasal place of articulation (*nāsikāsthāna*), [they are still included].
We have already stated in the *tulyāsyaprayatna* sūtra that there is homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between those belonging to the same class (*varga*).
(113) *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ* | P. 8.4.41.
[The rule] *ṣṭuanā ṣṭuaḥ*: *ṣṭu* by means of *ṣṭu*. The phrase *ṣṭoḥ* from the previous rule is understood here. Thus he says: "of *ṣṭu*. In this case as well—

In the case of substituends (*sthānin*) and substitutes (*ādeśa*), there is a correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), but not in the rule *na ṣṭunā yoge*. For example, in *rāmaṣṣaṣṭhaḥ*:

when *rāmas-ṣaṣṭhaḥ* is established, because of its connection with the letter *ṣ*, the *s* becomes *ṣ* by virtue of the rule *ṣṭunā yoge*. Here too, this is shown as an illustration to demonstrate that in the rule *na ṣṭunā yoge*, the correspondence according to order does not apply.

He provides an example even for the combination of the letter *s* with the *ṭa*-class (*ṭavarga*): *rāmaṣṭīkate*. [The root] *ṭhṭīkṛ* means "to go. *Taṭṭīkā* is the analysis: "the commentary (*ṭīkā*) of that (*tasya*). When *tadṭīkā* is established, the *d* becomes *ḍ* by the rule of *u* (i.e., *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*), and then there is *cartyam* (change to *ṭ*). *Cakriṇḍhokase*: [the root] *ḍhāṬkṛ* means "to go."

In the case of *cakrin ḍhokase*, since the rule *ṭunā ṭuḥ* applies due to the presence of the *ṭa*-class [consonant], the *n* becomes *ṇ*. [The sūtra] *na padāntāt* [is stated]. The phrase *ṭhanām* is a qualifier for the [sūtra] *ṭho 'r*. Now, one might ask: "Since these [words] have different case endings (*vibhakti*), how can this be a qualifier for that? To this, he says: *anām*.

"Having the sixth case elided" means "of that which is distinct from a member of a name. The [sūtras] *stoḥ* and *ṣṭun* are understood to follow. (114) *na padāntāṭṭoranām* 8.4.42. [The substitution of ṣ for ṣṭu does not take place] after a final *ṭ* or *t* belonging to a word (*pada*), except when followed by a name (*nāman*).

He says this with the words beginning "from the end of a word" (*padāntāt*), etc. Regarding *īṭṭe*: the root *īḍ* meaning "to praise" is *ātmanepada*. When *īḍ-te* is established, *ḍ* undergoes *cartva* (substitution by a *c*-series letter) according to the rule *khari ca*;

consequently, the following *t* undergoes *ṭutva* (substitution by a *ṭ*-series letter). Even though that [substituted *ṭ*] follows a *ṭavarga* letter, it does not [undergo further change] because it does not follow from the end of a word (*padānta*).

The prohibition of *ṣṭutva* [is as follows]: in the case of *sarpiṣṭamam*, when *sarpiṣ-tamam* is established, because the word is a *pada*— either by virtue of the rule "in the presence of *su*-beginning suffixes that are not *sarvanāmasthāna*" (Pāṇini 1.4.17) taking into account the intervening case-ending, or because the *ṣ* is at the end of a *pada*— the *ṣṭutva* of the following *t* is not prohibited.

This occurs because there is no occurrence of a *ṭ*-class consonant following the end of the word (*padānta*). Nor should it be argued that since the *ṣ* would become *ḍ* by the rule "ṣṭuan" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), and because the *t* would then follow a *ṭ*-class consonant, the prohibition of *ṣṭu* would indeed apply; for [the prohibition applies] only when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *t* follows a short vowel, as stated in the rule "hrasvātādau taddhite."

Because the substitution of *ṣ* is not established (*asiddha*), there is an absence of the substitution of *j*. Here, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "for [the *s*] of a substitute and of an affix" (*ādeśapratyayayoḥ*) does not occur, because of the governing heading "a retroflex [substitute] for [the *s*] that is not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ*).
In the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣṭu*, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) applies only to the word *nāman*, and not otherwise.
The meaning is that an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) must also be stated for the letter *n* which is a constituent part of the word *navatinagarī*.

Regarding the form *ṣaṇṇām*: when *ṣaṣ-nām* is established, because it is a word-final (*padānta*) by the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*, the sibilant *ṣ* is changed to the voiced stop *ḍ* by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*; then, by the rule *pratyaye bhāṣāyāṃ nityam*, [the following nasalization applies].

For that [word], there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Here, due to its connection with the *ṭ*-class (*ṭavarga*), the *n* undergoes the *ṣṭuan* substitution (becoming *ṇ*). The prohibition by the rule *ṭhna padāntāṭṭoranām* does not apply here, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) contained in the rule *ṭhanām*. Thus, *ṣaṇ-ṇagaryaḥ* consists of two separate words;
it is not a *karmadhāraya* compound, because of the restriction in the rule *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām*. This also applies here.
In the word *nagarī*, the prohibition of the substitution of *ṭu* for the letter *n* [by Pāṇini 8.4.39] does not apply,
because the word *nagarī* is also excluded by the rule of *paryudāsa*.
(115) *toḥ ṣi* | 8.4.43 | [The substitution of *ṣ* occurs in place of *t* when followed by *ṣ*.]
The words "ṣṭu" and "na" (not) carry over from the previous rule. Thus he says: "of the *ta*-class.

Regarding the phrase "san-ṣaṣṭhaḥ" (the sixth [letter] with *s*): here, because the letter *n* is joined with *ṣ*, the application of *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) would have occurred, but it is prohibited.
From this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), in the rules "ṣṭunā" and "ṣṭuḥ," the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) applies to the phrase "in connection with *ṣṭu*."

It is not so understood; that [rule] was introduced incidentally during the discussion on vowel-sandhi (*ac-saṃdhi*) by means of the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39). Its reintroduction here, however, occurs in the context of consonant-sandhi (*hal-saṃdhi*).
(116) Pāṇini 8.4.45: "Before a nasalized semivowel (*yar*), a nasalized substitute may optionally take the place of a non-nasalized *yar*."
Regarding the rule *yaro'nunāsike*: from the previous rule *ṭunā ṭuḥ*, the term *padāntāt* is carried over (*anuvartate*) and is transformed into the genitive case;
thus he says: "of a *yar* [consonant] that is at the end of a word. In the example *etanmurāriḥ*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Since this [word] is established as *murāri*, the letter *n* becomes a nasal substitute for *d*,
due to the similarity of their dental place of articulation and the similarity of their contact effort (*spṛṣṭa-prayatna*).
But then, would not the letter *ṇ* also become a nasal substitute for the *r* in the word *caturmukha*?

Since there is a difference between the *repha* (the sound *r*) and the letter *s* regarding the distinction of their articulatory efforts (*prayatna*), even though they share the same place of articulation (*mūrdhan*), [the author] says "place" (*sthāna*)— referring to the fact that in examples such as "ṭhetan murāriḥ," the closest substitute is a *sparśa* (stop) by virtue of both place and effort.

The meaning is that this rule for the nasal [anusvāra], having already achieved its purpose—that is, having attained its objective—cannot apply again to the letter *r* by taking mere positional similarity (*sthāna*) as the basis for proximity (*āntarya*). The underlying idea is based on the maxim: "When a young woman has been obtained, how could an old woman take her pleasure? (i.e., once the desired goal is reached, there is no further need for the operation).
*Pratyayebhāṣāyām*: this is a *vārtika*. It refers to usage in the *Bhāṣya* and in common worldly speech (*laukikaprayoga*).

The meaning there is that when effort (*prayatna*) is present, the previously mentioned nasalization (*anunāsika*) occurs invariably (*nitya*) when a following nasalized sound (*anunāsika*) is present. Regarding *tanmātram*: that which has that as its measure is *tanmātra*; [this is formed with] the suffix *ṭha* in the sense of measure (*pramāṇe*).

The suffix *mātrac* is applied according to the rule "dvayasajdadhnañmātracaḥ. Regarding the term *cinmaya*: in the rule "nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ," the word "nityam" is treated as a separate *yogavibhāga*, whereby the suffix *mayaṭ* is added in the sense of identity (*tādrūpye*). [The opponent asks: "How then? [The answer is: If the nasalization were obligatory when a suffix follows, then...

The objection is: "How is Kālidāsa’s usage *ṭhmadodagrāḥ kakudmantaḥ* [possible]? The point is that since *matup* is an affix (*pratyaya*), when it follows, the letter *d* must necessarily become the nasal *n*. He resolves this by saying: "In the case of *yava* and so forth."

Because the letter *da* is specified in the word *kudmala* within the *yavādi* group, it does not possess a nasalization (*anunāsika*). The underlying sense is that if a nasal *na* were indeed intended there, then for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), he would have specified the letter *na* itself.

(117) *torli* | Pāṇini 8.4.60. Regarding *torli*: from the rule *ṭhānusvārasya yayi* [8.4.58], the phrase *ṭhparasavarṇaḥ* [8.4.59] is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "of the *ta*-class," and so forth. As for *tallaya*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *tasya layaḥ*.

When *tadālayaḥ* is established, the *para-savarṇa* (the homogeneous substitute) for the letter *d* occurs, which is the same class as the following cause, the letter *l*; and that is indeed the letter *l*, because no other [letter] possesses homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with it. Regarding the phrase "here, of the *n*"—in the case of *vidvān likhati*, when *vidvān likhati* is established...

The meaning is that when *l*— which is the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) of the nasal *n* that stands in its place— occurs, it becomes specifically the nasal *l* due to proximity (*āntarya*). (118) *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya* | Pāṇini 8.4.61.

In the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.61) and *ṭhanusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58), the term *savarṇa*—though mentioned as part of a compound—is extracted and connected here, because it is promised (*pratijñāna*) that the svarita accent applies to a single portion [of a compound]. The word *udaḥ* is in the ablative case; therefore, by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), it means "after that [element]."
By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "of that which follows *ṭh* or *ud*," [the word *para*] is obtained. Thus he says: "following *ud*.

Regarding the word "preceding" (*pūrva*): the meaning is that the substitute shall be a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound of the *d* of *ud*, which is the preceding cause. And this "homogeneous with the preceding" (*pūrvasavarṇa*) is, by the technical rule concerning the final letter (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*), [to be understood as replacing the final letter].

He states that the substitution of *na* for the final letter of the roots *sthā* and *stambh* does not occur, saying: "by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*" (Pāṇini 1.1.54). By this paribhāṣā, the meaning is that [the substitution] applies only to the initial *s* which is a constituent part of [the following element]. Thus, *utthānam*; from the root *ṣṭhā* in the sense of "cessation of motion" (*gatinivṛtau*), with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). And *utstambhanam*.

In the word *pratiṣṭambha*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) to the root *ṣṭabhi*, meaning "to obstruct. Alternatively, it may be a Vedic (sautra) root indicated in the rule prescribing the affix *śnu* in the form *stambhu*, meaning "to obstruct. This is because the mention of the vowel following a labial (*pavargīya*) in the rule *sthāstambhoḥ* applies to both roots. Now, as for the case of *ud-sthānam*:

In the rule prescribing a substitute homogeneous with the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇavidhi*) for the letter *s*, the preceding cause is the letter *d*; and those sounds homogeneous with it are only five: *t*, *th*, *d*, *dh*, and *n*. This is because they share the same place of articulation (the teeth) and the same mode of articulation (complete contact). However, the letter *ḷ* and the letter *s* are not included; for although they share the same place of articulation, they differ in their mode of articulation, as *ḷ* is produced with an open articulation (*vivṛta*). Nor is...

The *lakāra* is [not a substitute] because it is slightly contacted (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, all other phonemes (*varṇa*) besides these are not homogenous (*savarṇa*) with the *dakāra* because they have different points of articulation (*sthāna*). Consequently, all five phonemes—*ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, and *na*—which are homogenous with the *dakāra* that serves as the preceding condition, would be applicable in place of the *sakāra*.
Because the similarity based on place of articulation (*sthāna*) with the *s* that serves as the substitute is indistinguishable across all five [nasals],

and because there is no similarity based on internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) among any of these five; for the *s* that serves as the substitute possesses the effort of being open (*vivṛta*), whereas these five [nasals] possess the effort of being closed (*saṃvṛta*).

Because it possesses the effort of contact (*spṛṣṭa-prayatna*). Therefore, having taken internal effort from among the external efforts, he states the determination of one of the five [efforts] here: "of the unvoiced" (*atra 'ghoṣasya*).
By the term "unvoiced," it is effectively stated that it is also "possessing breath" (*śvāsavat*) and "possessing an open passage" (*vivara-vat*), because these properties are invariably concomitant.

First, the letter *sakāra*, having become the locus [of substitution] here, possesses a set of four efforts consisting of being voiceless (*aghoṣa*), aspirated (*śvāsa*), unobstructed (*vivāra*), and of great breath (*mahāprāṇa*). Among its counterparts—*ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, and *na*—the first, third, and fifth do not occur, because they possess only slight breath (*alpaprāṇa*). Nor does the fourth occur, because it possesses the efforts of being voiced (*ghoṣa*), nasalized (*nāda*), and obstructed (*saṃvāra*). However, the second, the letter *thakāra*, possesses the set of four efforts consisting of being voiceless, aspirated, unobstructed, and of great breath.

Therefore, the meaning is that this very *th* sound, being homogeneous with the preceding *d* sound which served as the cause for its substitution, replaces the *s* sound. Thus, when *ud-sthānam* is established, the *d* is replaced by *t* according to the rule *ṭhkhari ca*; then, the *s* is replaced by *th*, which is homogeneous with the preceding sound. Consequently, the form *utththānam*—containing one *t* and two *th*s—is established. This should be applied similarly to *utthatambhanam*, with the distinction that it contains two *t*s and one *th*. Regarding the word *tasya*:

The meaning is "of the letter *th* which has been substituted for *s*. And thus, the intention is that in the view where the first *th* is elided, the resulting form consists of one *t* and one *th*. Now, an objection might be raised: "In the view where there is no elision of the first *th*, it is untenable to claim the form consists of one *t* and two *ths*; for, since the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55) applies, the first *th* would undergo *cartya* [substitution by *t*], resulting in the undesired form of two *ts* and one *th*. To this, he says: "In the case of non-elision... [and] "...because it is *asiddha*."

The intention is that, with respect to the rule *ṭhkhari ca*, the form *udasthāḥ* takes precedence due to its posteriority [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī]. The reading *uttambhanam* with three *ta*-letters, however, is erroneous, because the aforementioned grammatical derivation applies equally to both forms. Some, however, having accepted a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) for *na mune* as "na" and "mune," somehow justify the form *uttambhanam* with three *ta*-letters by arguing that there is no lack of *asiddhatva* (non-validity) regarding the *cartva* (substitution of *tha*) for the preceding homogeneous *tha*-letter.

That [explanation] is not accepted as being based on the *mūla* (the root text), because the procedure is described in the *mūla* as being common to both. In reality, however, it follows the rule "dīrghād ācāryāṇām" (P. 8.4.52). Following the recitation of the six sūtras beginning with "anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ" (P. 8.4.58) up to "udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya" (P. 8.4.61), there follow these rules: "jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi" (P. 8.4.53), "abhyāse carca" (P. 8.4.54), "khari ca" (P. 8.4.55), "vāvasāne" (P. 8.4.56), and "aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ" (P. 8.4.57).

The reading known as *pañcasūtrī* refers to the sequence of sūtras accepted in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭh-ṣ-ṭha-lo yam-ām*. Thus, when the substitution of *c* for *khari* (*ṭh-khari ca*) is to be applied, because the *th*-sound—which would result from the rule *udaḥ sthā-stambhoḥ*—is not considered *asiddha*, the form *ut-th-tānam* contains two *t*s and one *th*, while the form *ut-t-ūstambhanam* contains three *t*s; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. (119) *jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām* 8.4.62.

"Jhayo haḥ. Here, "jhayaḥ" is in the ablative case (pañcamī). The word "ṭhparasya" is to be supplied [from a previous rule]. "ha" is in the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī). From the rule "udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ," the term "pūrvasya" is understood to follow; and from the rule "anusvārasya yayi," the term "savarṇa" is also understood to follow. Thus, he says: "of that which follows a jhay," and so forth.
The example is *vāgghariḥ*. The word *vāc* ends in the letter *c*; [by the rules of] *kutva* and *jaśtva*, it becomes *vāk*.

When *vāk-hariḥ* is established, for the application of the rule regarding the homogeneous substitute (*pūrvasavarṇavidhi*) for the letter *h*, the preceding letter *g* is the cause (*nimitta*). Of its five homogeneous letters—*k, kh, g, gh, ṅ*—the letter *ṅ* is the substitute (*sthānin*) by virtue of the letter *h*.

In terms of place of articulation (*sthāna*), the internal similarity (*āntarya*) is not distinguished [among the five]. However, there is no similarity in internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) between these five and their substitute, the letter *ha*, because of the difference between the efforts of contact (*spṛṣṭa*) and openness (*vivṛta*). Therefore, taking internal similarity based on external effort (*bāhya-prayatna*), he states the rule for determining any one of the five by means of "possessing voicing" (*ghoṣavat*).

By these and other such statements: the letter *ha*, having become the locus [of the rule], possesses the four efforts known as voiced (*ghoṣa*), sonant (*nāda*), nasalized (*saṃvāraṇa*), and aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*);
among the letters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa*, the first, third, and fifth do not occur [in its place], because they are unaspirated (*alpaprāṇa*).
The second letter, *kha*, also does not occur, because it possesses the effort-features of being voiceless (*aghoṣa*), unbreathed (*asvāsa*), and unobstructed (*avivāra*).

The fourth, however, is the letter *gha*, which possesses voicing (*ghoṣa*), resonance (*nāda*), obstruction (*saṃvāra*), and great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is that this very letter *gha* takes the place of *ha*; consequently, it becomes *vāgghari*.
But when there is the substitution of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*), the form is *vāg hariḥ*.
(120) *śaś chāe’ṭi* |8|4|63|. In *śaś chāe’ṭi*, the word ending in the fifth case, *ṭhjhayaḥ*, is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). *Śaḥ* refers to...

This is the sixth case singular. Thus he says: "of what follows after a *jhay*. When the form *tad-śiva* is established, the letter *da* is changed to *ja* by the rule for *cutva*, and then the letter *ja* is changed to *ca*; such is the sequence. (121) *khari ca* | Pāṇini 8.4.55.

To the question "By what [rule]? he says: *khari ca* ("and before a *khar* [voiceless consonant]"). From the rule *ṭhjhalāñjaśjhaśi* ("*jaś* and *jhaś* in place of *jhal* before *jhaś*"), the word *jhalām* is understood; and from the rule *ṭhabhyāse carc* ("*car* in place of [a letter] in reduplication"), the word *car* is understood. Thus he says: "before a following *khar*," and so forth. This refers to the substitution of *c* for the letter *j*; the intention is that this occurs because of their similarity in terms of place of articulation (*sthāna*). Consequently, there is the substitution of *ch*, and not [the others].

It should also be understood that [the substitution] occurs first. This is because, according to the rule *chatvam*, the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cut*) and the substitution of *t* for *t* (*tvat*) are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) in relation to one another.

However, in the sequence of rules as accepted in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *halo yamām yami lopaḥ*, once the substitution of *j* for *t* (*cut*) has been applied, the substitution of *ch* for *ś* (*chatvam*) occurs, followed by the substitution of *t* for *j* (*cartvam*). It does not occur that the substitution of *t* for *j* (*cartvam*) takes place prior to the substitution of *ch* for *ś*.
The substitution of *c* for *j* does not apply here because it is considered asiddha (non-existent). Thus, regarding "tacchiva":

the analysis is either "sa cāsau śivaśca" (he who is that Śiva) or "tasya śivaḥ" (the Śiva of him). However, the substitution of *k* for *c* (as prescribed by the rule *ṭhcoḥ ku*) does not take place, because the substitution of *ś* for *c* is asiddha.
The meaning is that one should state "amī" instead of "aṭi" in the rule *śaś chāe 'ṭi*; that is to say, the rule should be recited as *śaś chāe amī*. Regarding the phrase *tac chlokena*:
the analysis of the compound is either *sa cāsau ślokaś ca* (that which is both it and a verse) or *tasya ślokaḥ* (the verse of that).

Since the augment *aṭ* is external to the letter *l*, the substitution of *cch* (by the rule *śca-ndasi*) does not apply to the *ś* that follows it; therefore, this Vārttika is formulated. In the example *vākścyotati*, the substitution of *k* (*kutva*) certainly occurs, because the *c* is inherent (*svābhāvika*) and thus was not produced by the substitution of *ś* (*ścutva*).

Because there is no absence of *asiddhatva* [in this context]. Here, since the letter *ca* is not included within the *am* group, the ś-substitution does not apply to the letter *śa* that follows it. (122) *mo 'nusvāraḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.23. [The rule states: "In place of *m*, *anusvāra* is substituted [before a consonant]."

*ma* refers to the *anusvāra*. The term *padasya* (of a word) is understood as the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). The word *ma* is a genitive-case qualifier of *pada*; thus, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). From the rule "before a consonant (*hali*), for all [grammarians]" (*hali sarveṣām*), the word *hali* (before a consonant) is carried over (*anuvartate*). This is what he states with the words "of that which ends in *ma*" (*māntasya*), etc. The phrase *alontyasya* (the substitute takes the place of the final phoneme) is understood to apply here. The word *upatiṣṭhate* (is present/applicable) is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).

And therefore, the meaning is: "of that *m* which is the final [sound] of a word. This results in the sense: "of an *m* at the end of a word. For example: *hariṃ vanda* ("I salute Hari"). When *harim vanda* is situated [thus], the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*.
Regarding the form *gamyate*: the root *gamlṛ* means "to go"; it is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.13).
Thus, the suffix *yak* is applied in the *ātmanepada*. Here, because the *m* is not at the end of a word (*padānta*), the *anusvāra* does not occur.

(123) *naścāpadāntasya jhali* | Pāṇini 8.4.24. Regarding the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali*: by the particle *ca*, the [rule for] *m* is drawn forward from the previous sūtra, as is the term *anusvāra*. Thus, an *anusvāra* is substituted for a *n* that is not at the end of a word, when followed by a *jhal* consonant.

He says this with the words beginning "nasya" and so forth. Regarding "yaśāṃsi": from the word *yaśas*, the suffix *jas* is applied; by the rule *jas-śasoḥ śiḥ*, *śi* replaces *jas* and *śas*. By the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the augment *num* is added. By the rule *sāntamahataḥ*, the vowel is lengthened. When *yaśān-si* is established, the *n* undergoes *anusvāra*. Regarding "ākraṃsyate": [the form is derived from the root *kram* with the prefix *ā*].

The root *kram* means "to step. From the root preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *lṛṭ* (indicating the future) is applied in the active voice (*kartari*). By the rule *ṭhāṅ udgamane*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used;

then, by the rule *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ*, the suffix *sya* is added. Due to the restriction *snukramor anupasargayoḥ*, the augment *iṭ* is not inserted. When the form *ākram-sya-ta* is established, this rule is stated because the preceding [rule] does not apply since the letter *m* is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*).
Regarding the word *namyate*: the suffix *laṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and the augment *yak*.

Here, because the letter *m* is not followed by a *jhal* consonant, the anusvāra is not applied by this [rule]. Furthermore, because it is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the anusvāra is not applied by the preceding rule either.
(124) *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.58. [When an *anusvāra* is followed by a *yay* (semivowel or sibilant), it is replaced by a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*).]

"Of the *anusvāra*, [before] a *yay* [sound]" (*anusvārasya yayi*). "It is clear," because there is no other word to be carried over (*anuvartya*); this is the intended meaning. Regarding "marked" (*aṅkita*): in the *curādi* class, the root *anka*—meaning "to mark" or "to characterize"—is one whose penultimate letter is not *n*. Some maintain that this is a reference to the form where the *anusvāra* has been applied by the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali*. [The suffix] *-ta* is added after the causative (*ṇyantāt*) [root].

The suffix *kta* with the augment *iṭ*. By the rule "when a *niṣṭhā* [suffix] has *iṭ*," there is the elision of the *ṇi* [augment]. By this [rule], the *anusvāra* undergoes *parasavarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound). Here, the cause for the change is the letter *ka*; its *savarṇa* (homogeneous) class is the *ka*-group (*kavarga*). That which results from the *anusvāra*, being identical in its place of articulation—the nose—becomes the letter *ṅa*. Thus, [we have] *añcitaḥ*. [This is derived from] the root *añc*.

In the case of the roots *gam* and *pūj*, [the vowel] has no penultimate *u*. From that [root], the suffix *kta* is applied. In the sense of "worship," the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *añceḥ pūjāyām*.
Because of the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *nāñceḥ pūjāyām*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not occur by the rule *aniditām*.
Here, by the rule *naścāpadāntasya*, the *anusvāra* is replaced by the *parasavarṇa* letter, which is *ña*. Thus, [we have] *kuṇṭhitaḥ*.

The root *kuṭh* means "to strike. Because it is marked with the *iṭ* (indicatory letter *i*), the augment *num* is added. The suffix *kta* takes the augment *iṭ*. Here, by the rule *naśca*, the anusvāra is replaced by its homogeneous sound, the *ṇakāra*.

Regarding the word *śānta*: the root *śam* means "to pacify. The suffix *kta* is applied. By the rule beginning with *vā dānta-śānta-*, the augment *iṭ* is not applied. By the rule *anunāsikasya kvī*, the vowel is lengthened.

In *naśca*, the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*. By the rule of *parasavarṇa*, that [anusvāra] is replaced by the nasal *n*. Regarding the word *gumphita*: the root *guph* (meaning "to string together") ends in *ph*; it has *n* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*). The suffix *kta* takes the augment *iṭ*.
According to the rule *ṭhnopadhāt thaphāntādvā*, since the alternative view (*akittva-pakṣa*) applies here, there is no elision of the *n*. In this case...

In *naś-c-eti*, the anusvāra is replaced by the following homogeneous sound, which is the letter *m*. Now, [considering] the root *kṛ* with the suffix *laṭ*, then *jhi*, then *jho'ntaḥ*, then *tanādikṛñbhya uḥ*, then *guṇaḥ*, then *paratvam*, then by the rule *ṭhata utsarvadhātuke*, the *ukāra* undergoes *yaṇ*. [This is not applied] because of the prohibition *na bhakurchuarām*; however, by the rule *rvorupadhāyāḥ*...

It is not long. The form is *kurvanti*. Here, the substitution of *anusvāra* by the rule *naścāpadāntasya* is superseded by the substitution of *ṇa* by the rule *raṣābhyām*, because the latter is subsequent [in the order of the rules].
Nor is it the case that within the Tripādī, the rule *raṣābhyām* has greater force than *naścāpadāntasya*.

It might be argued that because the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (P. 8.2.1) renders [the operation of] *anusvāra* non-existent due to its posteriority, once *anusvāra* has occurred, there is the hearing of the *nakāra* itself due to the rule for *parasavarṇa*. Even so, it must be said that the application of *ṇatva* by the rule *raṣābhyām* (P. 8.4.1) to the *nakāra* obtained through the *parasavarṇa* rule would be unavoidable. Therefore:

He says: "They perform," and so forth. The point is that, although the rule *raṣābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.1] requires the substitution of a homogeneous letter (*parasavarṇa*), since this must occur after [the nasal], the *n* which is the *parasavarṇa* substitute for the *anusvāra* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the application of the rule for *ṇatva*; therefore, the change to *ṇ* does not take place.

(125) *vā padāntasya* |8|4|59|. The phrase "optionally (*vā*) for a final member of a word (*padāntasya*)" [is stated]. The rule "*anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*" (P. 8.4.58) is understood to follow here. Thus he says: "for a final member of a word," etc. Examples: *tvaṅkaroṣi* (from *tvam-karoṣi*).

When *sam* is present, the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*. By the rule of *parasavarṇa*, the *ṅ* [of *ṅyantā*] becomes the corresponding nasalized (*anunāsika*) *y*. In the alternative case where that [nasalization] does not occur, only the *anusvāra* is heard. Regarding the example *atra*: when *sam-yantā* is present, the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*.
That [anusvāra] becomes a nasalized *y* which is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the following *y* that serves as its cause.

Because of proximity (*āntaryāt*). Thus, the form *sayyaṅkānta* arises. When *saṃvatsara* is established, the anusvāra is replaced by its corresponding nasal (*parasavarṇa*), which is the nasalized *v* (*anunāsika v*); thus the form *saṃvatsara* is obtained.
When *yaṃ lokaṃ* is established, the anusvāra is replaced by its corresponding nasal, which is the nasalized *l* (*anunāsika l*).
The form is *yallāākam*. However, in the alternative view where the *parasavarṇa* substitution does not occur, there is simply an *anusvāra*; this is the meaning. (126) *mo rāji samaḥ kvau* | P.
8.3.25. [The rule] *mo rāji*: *maḥ* is in the nominative case. From the rule *mo'nusvāraḥ*, the word *maḥ* [is understood].
The term *sthāna* (place) ends in the locative case. The word *samaḥ* is a genitive of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).

By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), the mention of *kvi* results in the inclusion of that which ends in the *kvip* suffix. This is what he states with the words "ending in *kvip*" and so forth.
The phrase "that very [m]" means that it is the letter *m*, and not the *anusvāra*. Of the *m*...

The intention is that this rule establishes the *ma*-augment for the purpose of precluding the *anusvāra*. Regarding *samrāṭ*: from the root *rājṛ* (to shine), with the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām u ca*. By the rule *vraśca*, the letter *ṣ* is substituted;

by the rule *jaś*, it becomes *ḍ*; and by the rule *car*, it becomes *ṭ*. In this case, the *anusvāra* does not occur after the *m*. [This applies] when *ha* follows a *m* that is followed by another *m*.
Or [alternatively]: from the rule *ṭhmo'nusvāraḥ*, the term *ṭhma* is understood as being in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).

From the rule *ṭhmorājī*, the term *ṭhma* is understood as being in the nominative case (*prathamānta*). Furthermore, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that after which *m* follows. Thus he says: "when followed by *m*" (*mapare*). In the form *hmalayati*, the suffix *laṭ* is applied to the causative (*ṇic*) stem.
In the rule *ṭhvalahlasahmalanamāmanupasargādvā*, the substitution of a short vowel for the roots ending in *mit* occurs when the suffix *ṇic* follows; thus, there is a shortening of the vowel.

Regarding the expression *yavalapare*: the analysis of the compound is "that after which *ya*, *va*, or *la* follow. The meaning is that when followed by a *ha*-sound in which *ya*, *va*, or *la* follow (*yavalaparaka*), the *ma* [of the substitute] may optionally remain as *ma*.

(127) *Yathāsaṅkhyamanudeśaḥ samānām* 1.3.10. "In numerical order" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Here, "equality" (*sāmya*) is intended in terms of number. "Subsequent designation" (*anudeśaḥ*) means "prescription" (*vidhānam*). Regarding the term "of equals" (*samānām*): if this were a genitive case in the objective sense (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), then...

The application of the rule of correspondence (yathāsaṅkhya) should occur only where there is an equal number of substituends and substitutes, as in "aco 'yavāyāvaḥ" and similar rules; however, it would not apply in a case such as "samūlākṛtajīveṣu han-ṛñ-grahaḥ," because the substitute to be prescribed there, namely the suffix ṇamul, is singular.

Therefore, in the expression "samānām," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a general relationship. And thus, since the roots such as *han* and the items beginning with *samūla* are introduced in equal numbers, the prescription of a single suffix is itself a prescription involving a relationship between those of equal number; this applies there as well.
The application according to numerical order (*yathāsaṅkhyapravṛtti*) remains unimpeded. Thus he says: "having an equal relation" (*samasambandhī*).

Regarding "according to numerical order" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*): by the word "number" (*saṅkhyā*), properties constituted by number—such as being first, second, and so forth—are intended here; "according to numerical order" means not deviating from those. And therefore...
It follows that in rules such as *ṭhE-co-'y-av-ā-y-ā-v-āḥ*, the first substitute corresponds to the first original element (*sthānin*), the second to the second, and so forth;

thus, one must understand that the original elements, the substitutes, their causes, and so on—which are equal in number—are related to one another in their respective order. This is the result [of the principle] in the present case.

When followed by *ha* with *ya* (*ya*) or *va* (*va*) following, the *ma* becomes *ya*; when followed by *va* (*va*), it becomes *va*; and when followed by *la* (*la*), it becomes *la*. Thus, *kiy#Ä hya* is formed: this is the form resulting from the change of *ma* to *ya*. *Ṭhya* is an indeclinable meaning "on the previous day" (*pūrvedyur*). In the absence of the change to *ya*, *ma* becomes an *anusvāra*. *Kiv#Ä*... [is formed].
Regarding *hvalayati*: the substitution of *v* for *m*. The root *hvala* means "to move"; with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Regarding *hlādayati*: the substitution of *l* for *m*. The root *hlādī* means "to rejoice" (*sukhe*); with the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
(128) *na-paro naḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.27].
The terms *ṭhhe*, *ṭhve*, and *ṭhma* are understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. The analysis of the compound is: "that after which *naḥ* (the letter *n*) does not follow.

Thus he says: *napare*. Regarding the form *kiṃ hnute*: this is the form of the root *ḍhnuṅ* (meaning "to remove") when its *m* has been changed to *n*; in the absence of that change, there would be *anusvāra* for *m*.

(129) *ṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuak śari* [Pāṇini 8.3.28]. From the rule *ṅṇoḥ*, the word *vā* is understood as a carry-over from *ṭhhe mapare va*. *Kuk* and *ṭuak* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). These are augmentations (*āgama*), and this is obtained from the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau*.

And by the paribhāṣā *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence according to order), *kuṅ* is added after the letter *ṅ*, and *ṭuaṅ* after the letter *ṇ*. In both cases, the letter *k* is for the sake of the *it* designation, while the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation. When the forms *prāṅ ṣaṣṭhaḥ* and *sugaṇ ṣaṣṭhaḥ* have been established, *kuṅ* and *ṭuaṅ* are respectively added as preceding components to those two.
Fearing that *jaś*-substitution might apply because [the letter] is at the end of a word, he says: "In the case of *ku* and *ṭu-ka*.

Regarding the rule "the second of the *caya*s," he dispels the misconception that this refers to the word *pauṣkarasādi* itself—namely, that "the second of the *caya*s applies to the word *pauṣkarasādi*"—by stating: "The teacher Pauṣkarasādi. Thus, the intention is that an option (vikalpa) results.

When *ku* is applied [by P. 8.3.41], the form is *prāṅk ṣaṣṭhaḥ*. According to the alternative view that "the second consonant of a *caya* [group] is substituted" (P. 8.4.47), the form is *prāṅ kh ṣaṣṭhaḥ*. And in this case, there is no substitution of *ca* for *kh* by the rule *khari ca* (P.

8.4.55), because of the force of the specific rule prescribing the introduction of *kh*. [This is also seen in] the rule *nādinyākrośe* (P. 8.4.48) regarding the application of "the second of a *caya*"...

This is what is read in the Sūtra-bhāṣya. The form *prāṅ ṣaṣṭhaḥ* occurs when the suffix *ku* is absent. Similarly, in the case of *tu* as well, one has *sugaṇ-ṣaṣṭhaḥ*, and so forth. (130) *ṅsi dhuṭ* 8.3.29.

The rule *ṅḥ si dhuṭ* [Pāṇini 8.3.32] contains the ablative *ṭhḍaḥ*. Consequently, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "from that which follows," the locative *ṭhsī* becomes a genitive—meaning "of the *s* following a *ḍ*. From the preceding rule *he mapare ve* [Pāṇini 8.3.27], the word *vā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "following a *ḍ*," and so forth.

Regarding the rule "in that which is specified by the word *tasmin*," this does not apply here, because of the maxim: "When both [the locative and ablative] are specified, the ablative specification is stronger due to its posteriority. The term *dhuṭ* is a designation for the fourth letter, the phoneme *dh*. The *ṭ* is an *it*-marker (indicating that the preceding element is to be elided). The *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Thus, it is *thuṭ*.

In the second rule, by its own force, the substitution of *c* would not occur; otherwise, [the author] would have prescribed merely the letter *t*. However, the fourth rule lacks that force, because its purpose is fulfilled by the prevention of the application of the first rule, which would have resulted in the *c* being the second member of the *cay* group. Thus: *ṣaṭ santaḥ*.

In *ṣaṣiti*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ* by the rule of *jaś*-ness; thus, we have *ṣaḍ-santa*. Since the substitution of *c* for *ṣ* (*cartva*) is considered *asiddha* (unestablished), the augment *dhuṭ* is added as the initial member because it follows the *ḍ*. This *d* is then changed to *t* by *cartva*. The rule "the second of the *ṭh-c-ch-ṭ-t-k* series" does not apply here, because *cartva* is *asiddha*. Then...
Because of the distinction between the *lakṣya* (the subject of the rule) and the *lakṣaṇa* (the rule itself), the letter *ṭ* is replaced by *ḍ*.

(131) *naśca* | Pāṇini 8.3.30. [The word] *naḥ* [is used]. From the previous sūtra, the words *ṭsi*, *dhuṭ*, and *ve* are carried over (*anuvartate*). The term *naḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*).

Therefore, by the *paribhāṣā* "tasmād ity uttarasya" (of that which follows after this), the word "sī" becomes a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus he says: "after [a stem] ending in *n*, following [the suffix] *san*. In the form *sansa*, the *dh* of *dhuṭ* undergoes *cartva* (substitution of the first consonant of the varga). (132) *śi tuk* 8.3.31.

*Śituk*: From the previous sūtra, the word "na" ending in the ablative case is understood here as being in the genitive case, because the governing topic is "word" (*śabda*). The term "of a word" (*padasya*) is supplied by context.
It is understood as a partitive genitive. From the rule "he mapare va," the word "va" is understood to carry over.

Therefore he says: "of a word-final [element]. It would have been more appropriate to say "of a word ending in *n*. The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). When "san śambhuḥ" is established, the augment *tuk* is the final constituent part of the *n*. Now, an objection: the mention of *tuk* is redundant; one could simply carry forward *dhuṭ* from the rule "ḍaḥ si dhuṭ" (Pāṇini 8.3.29).

One might argue: "Let the substitution of *ś* for the *s* following the letter *n* be prescribed by the rule *khari ca*; thus, the form *san-ant-śambhuḥ* would be established. To this, he says: "The substitution of *ch* for *ś* is optional according to the rule *śaś chāe’ṭi*.
The word "of the letter *ś*" (*śakārasya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the statement]. However, if the rule were for the insertion of *dhuṭ*...

Because it begins with *para-* (the letter *p*) and because it lacks the status of being at the end of a word (*padānta*), the substitution of *ch* would not occur; for the rule prescribing *ch* has been established as the final position in the Bhāṣya that it applies only to a *ś* following a *jhaḷ* consonant that is at the end of a word and situated within the initial portion of a word. Otherwise, [the rule] would also apply to the *ś* in examples such as *visṛpaḥ* and *virapśin*.

Regarding "of the master of the umbrella" (*cchatvāpateḥ*): the word *pakṣa* means that sometimes, by the rule *jharo jhari*, there is the elision of the *t* of *tuk* after it has undergone the change to *ś*. Thus, in the form *sañcchambhuḥ*, when the *t* has changed to *ś* and is elided, the *n* undergoes the change to *ñ*, resulting in that form.

Regarding the form *sañcchambhuḥ*: when the letter *t* has undergone the substitution of *c* (by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*), if there is no elision (*lopa*) of that *t*, and the following *n* undergoes the substitution of *c* (becoming *ñ*), the resulting form is [sañcchambhuḥ]. However, the substitution of *j* for *t* (the *jaś*-substitution) does not apply here, because that [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *ścu*-substitution. For this very reason, the *jaś*-substitution does not take effect even after the *ścu*-substitution has occurred.
Regarding *sañśambhuḥ*: when the substitution of *ch* for *ś* does not occur, and the substitution of *c* and *t* for *n* and *k* respectively do occur, the form is *sañśambhuḥ*.
Regarding *sañśambhuḥ*: when the *tuṅ* augment (*tu*) is absent, and the substitution of *c* for *n* occurs, this is the form. This, then, is...
He summarizes the sequence of the four forms in a verse with "ñachāviti.

The syntactical connection is as follows: because of the optional elision of the *tuk*, the *ch*, the *tvac* (the *t*), and the *upā* (the *u*), there are four forms: ñachāṬ, ñacachā, ñacaśā, and ñaśā.

"ṅmo hrasvāt. The term "ṭhṅm" is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation). "Ṭhṅma" is in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*). Because it serves as a qualifier, the word "pada" (governing from the previous rule) is modified to the ablative case. Furthermore, "ṭhṅma" undergoes a connection with the qualifier "from a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*) and subsequently functions as a qualifier of the word "pada."
"bhajata-d-anta-param": here, the ablative case in *ṭhṅmaḥ* is used by force [of the rule] as a locative case in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*).

Thus he says: "following after a short vowel. Regarding the augment *ṅmuṭ*: the letter *ṭ* is the indicatory letter (*it*), and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). This [augment] is applied within a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*).

Because [the rule] would otherwise be purposeless, the quality of being *ṭit* (having ṭ as its indicatory letter) is connected with the named elements (*saṃjñin*) according to the maxim of "accessories belonging to the principal" (*tadaṅganyāya*). Consequently, the three augments—*Ruṭ*, *Ṇuṭ*, and *Nuṭ*—are established as the results. Due to their *ṭit* nature, they occur as initial components of the vowel, respectively, in accordance with the order of enumeration. This is in view of the rule: "*ṭh-He-mapare vā*" (Pāṇini 6.1.111).
The term *nitya* ("always") is included to eliminate the suspicion that the mention of *vā* ("optionally") might still be in force. Regarding *pratyaṅ-ātmā*:
when *pratyaṅ-ātmā* is established, the augment *Ruṭ* is inserted before the vowel *ā*. Regarding *sugaṇṇīśa*:
the root *gaṇ* (meaning "to count") belongs to the *curādi* class; after the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is the elision of *ṇi* when followed by the suffix *vic*, but not by *kvip*.

Because of the potential application of the rule "kvau ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.111), which prescribes lengthening for a nasalized vowel [before a suffix beginning with *k* or *v*]. However, when the augment *ṅmuṭ* is to be applied, the elision of *ṇi* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were still present), because it is stated: "That which is *asiddha* (non-existent) regarding what precedes it is not *sthānivadbhūta*.
Thus, in the form *sugaṇ-īśa*, the augment *ṇuṭ* is inserted immediately before the vowel *ī*. [The example] *sannacyuta* is likewise explained.

When *san-acyuta* is established, the augment *nuṭ* is inserted before the vowel *a*. Nor should it be argued that in the case of *paramadaṇḍin-au*, when it stands as *paramadaṇḍin-a-Ṭ*, the augment *nuṭ* would apply because the internal case-ending (*antarvatir vibhakti*) causes the status of a word (*padatva*) by means of the rule regarding the indication of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*); for there is the prohibition: "when [the first member] is the second member of a compound (*uttarapadatve*), the rules concerning what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādividhau*) do not apply."

This is because of the prohibition of the application of suffixal rules (*pratyayalakṣaṇapratiṣedha*). In reality, however, the rule "and when there is a subsequent member" (*utarapadatve ca*)—which prohibits the application of suffixal rules—operates only in cases where the subsequent member (*utarapada*) is the locus of the grammatical operation (*kāryitva*).
Otherwise, the prohibition "even when there is an intervention by a word" (*padavyavāye 'pi*) would not apply in the example *māṣakumbhavāpanena*.

It might be argued that, therefore, in order to prevent the application of *ṅmuṭ* in the case of *paramadaṇḍinau*, one must carry forward the word *pade* from the rule *tuñi ca vade* and explain [the sūtra] as "ṅmuṭ occurs after a word beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) when it is a *pada*"; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

(133) *samaḥ suṭi* | 8|3|5| The word *samaḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). From the rule *matuvaso ru sambuddhau*, the mention of *ru* is understood here. Therefore, he says: "There is *ru* for *sama*. In the term *ru*, the letter *u* is an *it*.

Regarding the rule *alo'ntyasya*: the phrase "it applies to the final [element]" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is to be understood as the remainder. From the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *tṛc*, the augment *suṭ* is inserted by the rule *samparibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇe*. Thus, when *saṃskartṛ* is established, the *m* undergoes *ru*-substitution (becoming *r*). When *sar-skartṛ* is established...
(134) *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* | Pāṇini 8.3.2. Regarding this [sūtra]:

*atrānunāsika*. This is recited immediately after the rule for the substitution of *ru* in *matuvasau ru saṃbuddhau*. Therefore, by the word *atra*, the meaning "in the section concerning *ru*" is understood. And "preceding" (*pūrvatvam*) refers to...
This is to be understood with reference to the word *ṭhru*, because it is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). Thus he says: "here" (*atre*).

Since the option is already established by the mere restatement of the alternative of the absence of the nasalization (*anunāsika*) in the subsequent rule, the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) is for the sake of clarity. [The meaning is: "the substitution of *r* is obligatory for the following [sound], whereas for the preceding [sound], there is an option regarding nasalization."
The word *tu* (but) is indeed for the purpose of highlighting that this irregularity (*vaiṣamya*) is already established; it is also for the sake of clarity.

With this very intention, the author of the *Mūla* himself stated in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* that the mention of the word *vā* (or) was omitted from the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*) in the root text. By means of this rule, [the substitution applies] in the case of *sar*.
The letter *a* following *sa* becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*). Thus, when we have *saṃskartā*, [the rule] applies:

(135) *anunāsikātparo'nusvāraḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.4. "From a nasal" (*anunāsikāt*): this is a fifth-case ending (*pañcamī*) used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*, meaning "after having left" (*vihāya*).
The word *gamyam* [is understood]. The term *pūrvasya*, which is carried over from the previous rule, is modified to have the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamyantatayā*).

"Antecedence" (*pūrvatvam*) is with respect to the *r* produced by the substitution of *ru*; "subsequentness" (*paratvam*) is with respect to that vowel which precedes the *r*. Thus he says: "leaving aside the nasalized [vowel]."

The meaning is: in the alternative where the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is absent. The status of being an augment (*āgama*) is obtained from the word *para*. Consequently, when the nasalization is absent, an anusvāra is the augment following the vowel *a* after the letter *s*;
[as in] *saṃskartā*. Now, he recalls the rule for the substitution of *visarga* for the letter *r*: "before a hard consonant (*khaR*) or at the end of a pause (*avasāna*)."
(136) *visarjanīyasya saḥ* | 8|3|34|.
[The rule] "of the *visarjanīya*, *sa*" [is stated]. From the rule "*kharavasānayoḥ*" [the word *saḥ* is supplied] by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method.

The term *khari* is understood here, because it has been declared that [the term] is *svarita* (accented) in part. Some, however, say that since the sound *visarga* is heard, *khari* is implied by the sense; but it has no connection with *avasāna* (pause), according to the explanation. Thus he says: *khari*. Since [the rule] *visarjanīyasya saḥ* is already established...
Since the re-statement "of *saṃ*, *pum*, and *kān*" would otherwise be redundant, he says: "by way of this exception.
The meaning is that the re-statement is for the purpose of setting aside the optional visarga prescribed by the rule "vā śari.
Regarding "saṃ-puṃ-kānām": for these—*saṃ*, *pum*, and *kān*—the visarga is replaced by *s*.
The meaning is that it must be stated [as such]. The remainder of the sense is: "By this *vārttika*, the substitution of *s* for the *visarga* occurs here invariably.
*saṃsskartā* is the form when the nasalized (*anunāsika*) alternative applies; *saṃsskartā* is the form when the *anusvāra* alternative applies.
*Rūpam*. In both cases, there is indeed a doubling of the letter *s*. Regarding the rule *samo vā*:

the meaning is that some teachers (*eke*) desire the elision of the *m* of *samaḥ* when followed by *suṭ*. The word *eka* is a synonym for "other"; as Amara states: "The words *eka*, *mukhya*, *anya*, and *akevala* [are synonyms]."

He states that even in the case of elision (*lopa*), there are two forms with a single *s* by means of the anusvāra and the nasalized (*anunāsika*) [variant], saying "of the elision as well. In the rule "here the nasalized [substitute occurs], but optionally for the preceding," the phrase "for the preceding" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the elision prescribed in the section on *ru* as well; otherwise, [the rule would not apply].
Because the meaning [of the rule] "in the section on *rūpa*" renders the term "*ṭhathve*" redundant;

likewise, in the rule "an unvoiced sound following an anusvāra," the phrase "from the preceding [element] of *ru*" would also be redundant. Consequently, since the elision of *ma* in *samaḥ* is also situated within the section on *rūpa*, [the rule would apply to] the vowel *a* that precedes that elision.
Sometimes there is the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*). In the absence of that, the augment *anusvāra* follows the letter *a*;

thus, the meaning is that there are two forms with one *s* each, due to the presence of either *anusvāra* or *anunāsika*. As for the form with two *s*s, it has already been explained—this applies to the case where *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) occurs; this is the remainder of the sense. Now, [one might ask] regarding the case of elision (*lopa*):

Since the form with two *s* sounds is already established by the doubling of the *s* of *suṭ* according to the rule *evā'naci ca*, the prescription of *ru*-hood (*rutva*) by the rule *samaḥ suṭi* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). This means:
in the case of the two forms containing two *s* sounds, when *ru*-hood has occurred, the *s* that stands in its place [is affected] by the rule *evā'naci ca*.

In the view that there are two *s* sounds, the meaning is that there are two forms, each containing three *s* sounds. The intention is that the rule for *ru*tva (the substitution of *r*) is prescribed precisely for this purpose. However, the elision (*lopa*) by the rule *skoḥ* does not apply here, because *ru*tva is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of that rule. Furthermore, even in the alternative where elision occurs, when the doubling of the *s* of *suṭ* takes place according to the rule *anaci ca*, the first *s* [would be subject to further doubling].

It should not be argued that, by that very same rule, two forms—each with three *s* sounds—are established when there is a doubling [of the consonant], and thus the prescription of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) is redundant; for this is due to the maxim: "A grammatical rule applies to its objective only once. Now, [one might ask] regarding the *anusvāra* in the traditional list of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*)...

Because of its absence from the recited text (*pāṭha*) and because it is not a phoneme (*anact*), one might ask: how can there be doubling of the following *s* in the alternative view where there is an *anusvāra*? To this he says: "In the case of *anusvāra* and *visarga*... This point is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *hayavaraṭ*. Regarding the phrase "above the letter *a*": if it were recited above the letter *i* and so forth, then in forms such as *payaḥsu*, [the doubling would apply] to *iṇ*.

The intention is that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, as prescribed by the rule "of the following [element] in the case of an ādeśa or a pratyaya," would otherwise apply. However, someone has erred in asserting that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "ṭhiṇaḥ ṣaḥ," for in that context, the prescription for the substitution of *ṣ* applies specifically to the *visarga*. Thus, in the case of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) alternative, there is one *sakāra*, and in the other, two *sakāras*.

"Trisakāram" means three forms. Thus, it is established that even in the case of the anusvāra, there are three forms. Regarding "of those possessing the nasal": in the case of the nasal (anunāsika), when there is doubling of the *k* in the forms with one, two, or three *s*s, there are three;
and in its absence, there are three—thus the meaning is six. Now, [one might object] that the *k* is not a vowel (*ac*).

To the question, "Since there is no *para* (subsequent) element here, how can there be doubling by the rule *anaci ca*?", he says: "By the rule *śaraḥ khayaḥ*. The meaning of this Vārttika is that when a *śar* follows, a following *khay* may optionally be doubled. Thus, in the case where the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form is adopted, there are three forms with two *k*s and three forms with one *k*, resulting in six forms in total.
But in the case where there is an *anusvāra*, he says "of those possessing an *anusvāra*" (*anusvāravatām*) to indicate that there are twelve forms.

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of the *anusvāra* also," the letter *ka* is included. In the case of the *anusvāra* alternative, among the forms containing one, two, or three *s*s, [the *anusvāra* occurs] before the sibilants (*śar*).
Since the reading is subject to doubt, when there is an option for doubling due to the presence of the *śar* sounds,

there are three with two *anusvāras* (3) and three with one *anusvāra* (3), making six (6). Then, when there is an option for doubling of the letter *ka* according to the rule "after *ṭha*, *śar*, and *khay*," there are six with two *kas* (6).

There are six forms beginning with the letter *ka*—meaning twelve (*12*) according to the view that includes the *anusvāra*. Thus, there are eighteen (*18*) forms in total: six (*6*) according to the nasalized (*anunāsika*) view and twelve (*12*) according to the *anusvāra* view.
Regarding "of these": of the eighteen forms mentioned, [the vowel] of the letter *ta*...
Regarding the phrase "by means of the two *ra*s," when there is an option for doubling, the first *takāra* undergoes doubling again according to the rule "ṭhyaṇo maya" (Pāṇini 6.1.79).
Thus, by calculating each as being single (*ekata*), double (*dvita*), or triple (*trita*),
there are eighteen instances of the single ones (18) and eighteen instances of the double ones (18).
The meaning is that by adding three and eighteen, a total of fifty-four forms (54) are produced.
Regarding the phrase "the nasality of *aṇ*": this refers to the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*.
When there is an option regarding the nasalization (*ānunāsikatva*) of the vowel *ā* following the letter *t*,
there are fifty-four forms if it is nasalized, and fifty-four if it is not; thus, by this summation,
one hundred and eight forms are produced— this is the meaning.

(137) *pumaḥ khayyampare* | Pāṇini 8.3.6. The word *pum-* [is the subject]. The mention of *ṣatva* (*ru*) is understood by anuvṛtti. The analysis of the compound is: "that after which *am* follows. Thus he says: "in *khay* followed by *am*. In the case of the *karmadhāraya* compound *pumān kokilaḥ*, [the elision of] the *sup* [case-ending occurs].

When the case-ending suffix (*sup*) is elided by the rule *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, and the letter *s* is dropped from the end of the conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, we arrive at the form *pum-kokila*. At this stage, the *m* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*), followed by the optional substitution of either an *anunāsika* or an *anusvāra*, and then a *visarga*. Finally, by the rule *saṃpuṃkānām*, the *visarga* is replaced by *s*. Now, [one might object]: The provided text consists of a grammatical derivation and a rhetorical objection. Here is the translation: When the case-ending suffix (*sup*) is elided by the rule *dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, and the letter *s* is dropped from the end of the conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, we arrive at the form *pum-kokila*. At this stage, the *m* undergoes *rutva* (becoming *r*), followed by the optional substitution of either an *anunāsika* or an *anusvāra*, and then a *visarga*. Finally, by the rule *saṃpuṃkānām*, the *visarga* is replaced by *s*. Now, [one might object]:
Since the rule "sa" [Pāṇini 8.3.34] would already suffice for the substitution of *s* for the visarga, the inclusion of the term "pu" in the rule "saṃpuṃkānām" (Pāṇini 8.3.6) is redundant;

therefore, he says: "In the case of derivation," and so forth. When both [the rules] "ika" and "ipayoḥ" apply, the sequence is "saṃpuṃkānām" followed by "sa". This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *s* prescribed by "visarjanīyasya sa" (Pāṇini 8.3.34).

It would have been more appropriate to state simply that the mention of *puṃs* (masculine) is for the purpose of overriding the rule "kupvo kaḥ pau ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.37); therefore, he says: "because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *ṣatva* [rule] by the phrase 'not being an affix' (*apratyayasya*).
The intention is that the visarga [in question] occupies the place of the letter *m* found in the *auṇādika* suffix *ḍumsun* attached to the root *pūñ*.

Now, one might object: since words such as *uṇādi* are unanalyzed nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), according to the perspective of the Bhāṣya on the rule *āyaneyīnīyiyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.2), there is no distinction between base and suffix in those forms ending in *uṇādi* suffixes; therefore, how can there be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the phrase "that which is not a suffix" (*apratyayasya*) in this context? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "In the view that words are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpattipakṣa*). Since there is no division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) in words formed by the *uṇādi* suffixes, how can there be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) here by the rule "not being a suffix" (*apratyayasya*)?
To this he replies: "In the view that words are derived through etymological analysis. Regarding words formed by the *uṇādi* suffixes...

Two positions regarding whether there is or is not an analysis into base and suffix are established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. Among these, according to the position that such an analysis exists, the word *puṃs* ends with the suffix *ḍumsun*. In that case...

Because the visarga in place of the letter *m* is excluded by the prohibition "not when it is not a suffix" (*apratyayasya*) in the rule *nedudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply there. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *puṃs-* in the rule *saṃpuṃkānām* is intended to override the rule *kupvoḥ*. [The term] *avyutpatti* means...

The meaning is that, in the case of words derived from the *āṬṇādika* list where there is no distinction between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), the exclusion rule "of what is not a suffix" (*apratyayasya*) does not apply here. Consequently, the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* (i.e., *idudupadhasya*) would otherwise apply; therefore, the mention of the word "male" (*puṃs*) in the rule *saṃpukānām* is intended to block that application of *ṣatva*. [Example: *puṃskokila*.
Thus is the form according to the *anunāsika* (nasalized) alternative. According to the *anusvāra* alternative, the form is *puṃskokila*.

[Note: The form *puṃskokila* is repeated in the source text. Now, one might object: from the root *cakṣiṅ*, meaning "to speak clearly," the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied; there is no substitution [of *khyā* for *cakṣ*]; rather, by the rule *cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ*, the form becomes *puṃsaḥ khyānam*.
Regarding the form *puṃkhyānam*, since the rule for the substitution of *ru* for the *m* of *pum̐s* would also apply here, he says:

"not when there is the substitute *khyāñ*. In the Bhāṣya, having read the rule as *cakṣiṅḥ khśāñ*, [the author] places it in the section on what is "not established" (*asiddha*)—specifically, after the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* by *raṣābhyām*—under the heading of what is not established in relation to what precedes it.

It will be stated that [the rule] "ṭhkhśāñaśśasya yo vā" has been recited. And thus, because the substitution of *y* (for *ś*) is not established, the *kh* is not followed by an *am*-vowel; therefore, by the rule "ṭhpunaḥ khayī," the substitution of *r* does not occur. In the case of *puṃkhyānam*, there is an optional substitution of the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) according to the rules "ṭhmo'nusvāraḥ" and "ṭhvā padāntasya."

Nor should it be argued that there is a prohibition of the *khśāñ* substitute in the case of exclusion (*vṛjane*), on the grounds that a prohibition applies when a non-prescribed form follows— as in the rule "and in the case of *asan*"— for how could the *khyāñ* substitute occur here?
This objection is untenable because the purpose of the *vārttika* concerning the *khśāñ* substitute is established by the usage of forms such as *puṃkhyānam*.

(138) *naś-chavi-apraśān* | Pāṇini 8.3.7. The word *naḥ* is a genitive singular (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) qualifying the governing term *padasya*. The rule *naś-chavi-apraśān* [means]: [A substitute] is applied in place of *na* before a *chav* sound, except for *praśān*. (Note: *naḥ* refers to the final *n* of a word.)

This is a rule concerning the final element of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*). The words *am-pare* and *ru* are understood from the previous context. Thus he says, "when followed by *am*" and so forth. In the expression *apraśān*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. Thus he says, "but not [in the case of]... The word "visarga" refers to the substitution of the visarga for the *n* in the forms *śārṅgi-c-chindhi* and *cakriṇ-t-rāyasva*, which stand as the bases for the application of this rule.

The substitution of *r* (rutvam) occurs. There is an option between the nasal (*anunāsika*) and the *anusvāra*. Then follows the *visarga*, which becomes *s* (satvam), and by the rule of *ścutva*, that *s* becomes *ś*; this is the meaning. Thus, *śārRiṃścchindhīti* is the form when the nasal alternative is applied. *ŚārRiṃścindhīti* is the form when the *anusvāra* alternative is applied.

In the case of the nasalized form (*anunāsika*), it is *cakrin strāyasva*; however, in the case of the anusvāra, it is *cakrin strāyasva*. The root *traiṅ* means "to protect"; because it has the marker *ṅ*, it is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The reading *trāhi* found in ancient texts is erroneous. [The word] *trāḥ* is derived from the sense "he protects" (*trāyate*); thus, one who acts like a protector (*trā*) is [called] *trā*.

The form *trātu* may somehow be justified as being the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) in the active voice (*parasmaipada*), derived from the root *trai* with the suffix *kvip* following the prefix *ā*.

Regarding *praśān*: it is formed from the root *śam* preceded by the prefix *pra*, with the suffix *kvip*. The lengthening of the vowel is according to the rule *anunāsikasya kvau*. The change of *m* to *n* is according to the rule *mo no dhātoḥ*. Because that [change of *m* to *n*] is considered *asiddha* (not yet established) for the purposes of the subsequent operation, the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) does not take place.

(139) *nṛn pe* |8|3|10|. The term *nṛn* refers to the form of the word ending in the accusative case; it is a genitive form (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) used as a technical designation (*svarūpapara*). The elision of the genitive case-ending (*luk*) is Vedic (*sautra*), and the absence of the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is likewise Vedic. [The rule applies] to the forms *mat* and *vas*.

From the word "ru," the term "ṭhru" is carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. From the phrase "ubhayatharkṣu," the term "ubhayathā" is carried over. The meaning is that the *ru* is to be understood as occurring "in both ways"—that is, sometimes it occurs and sometimes it does not; in other words, it is optional (*vikalpa*).

He says this with the words "of *nṛn* etc. and so forth. By the rule *alo'ntyasya*, when *nṛn pāhi* is established, there is the substitution of *ru* for the *n*. There is an option regarding the nasal (*anunāsika*) or the anusvāra.
(140) *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* || 8.3.37 || [The *ru* substitute becomes *k* or *p* when followed by a guttural (*ku*) or a labial (*pu*).]
When the rule "kharavasānayoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.15) mandates the obligatory substitution of *visarga* for the letter *r*, [the following applies]:

"kupvoḥ ka-pau ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.37). The analysis of the sūtra is "kupvoḥ". When the *s* of the case-ending *os* undergoes the substitution of *ru*, that *r* becomes a *khara* (voiceless consonant) due to being followed by a *para* (subsequent sound), and because the *jihvāmūlīya* is included among the *śar* sounds, it is a *khara*. And of that *visarga*...

The elision [of the *visarga*] occurs by the rule: "It should be stated that the *visarga* is elided before *khar* and *par*. Therefore, the *visarga* is not explicitly heard in the sūtra [as *kupvoḥ*]. From the rule "The *visarjanīya* becomes *s*," the term "*visarjanīyasya*" is carried over (anuvartate). Thus he says: "In the *ka*-group," and so forth. [The word] "in order" (*kramāt*).

This is obtainable from the *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence of order) sūtra. The meaning is that the word "visarjanīya" is carried over [from the previous rule] by the phrase "and [the word] 'visarga'" [in the rule] *cādvisargaḥ*, which itself draws upon the rule *ṭhśarpare visarjanīyaḥ*. The particle *ca* (and) serves, in effect, to include the *visarga* as an alternative option. Otherwise—
The sense is that there would be an absolute sublation of the *visarga* by both the *jihvāmūlīya* and the *upadhmānīya*.
And thus, in the present case, when followed by the letter *pa*, the substitution of *sa* (satva) for the *visarga* is sublated;
sometimes the *upadhmānīya* occurs and sometimes the *visarga*. There is a difference in their pronunciation.

In this context, the *k* and *p* in the substitutes [of *visarjanīya*] are for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and they do not enter into the category of what is to be prescribed (*vidheya*).

Now, one might object: just as the rule "before *k* or *p*" (*kupvoḥ*)—which prescribes the *jihvāmūlīya*, *upadhmānīya*, and *visarga*—sublates the substitution of *s* (*satva*) for *visarjanīya*, so too would the rule "before a *śarpara* [consonant], *visarjanīya*" [sublate it].

The rule for the exclusive occurrence of the visarga would also be sublated. Consequently, even in the case of *vāsaḥ kṣaumam*, both the jihvāmūlīya (the *k* sound) according to the rule *kupvoḥ* and the visarga might occasionally occur.
However, since only the visarga is desired in such cases, he says: *yena nāprāpte*. Regarding the phrase *yena nāprāpte*:
The maxim is: "Whatever rule is commenced [subsequently] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [preceding rule]. The word *prāpa* contains the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

In the word *yena*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* does not occur here, because of the prohibition in the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalathāṃ*. Two negative particles (*nañ*) indicate necessity (*āvaśyakatvam*). Of that...

The meaning is: "when there is the necessity of the application of a rule. By this logic, the rule *kupvoḥ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṭhvisarjanīyasya saḥ*, because the latter is applied precisely when the former would have otherwise obtained. However, the rule *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* is [an exception] to *kupvoḥ*.

It is not a negation (*apavāda*). The meaning is that in examples such as *kaḥ karoti*, although the rule *śarpare khar* would not otherwise apply, the rule *kupvoḥ* is nevertheless initiated. By this [statement], in cases such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumaṃ*, since there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the rule *śarpare* by the injunction *kupvoḥ*, the rule *śarpare khar* [remains applicable].

The meaning is that there is only a pure visarga (*visarga*). In the case of *nṛṃ pāhi* and *nṛṃ pāhi*, when the upadhmānīya is applied, there are two forms depending on whether the nasalization (*ānunāsikya*) or the anusvāra occurs:
*nṛṃḥ pāhi* and *nṛṃḥ pāhi*.

In the case of *visarga*, there are two forms due to the presence of the nasalized *anusvāra* and the *anusvāra* itself. When there is an absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), there is the form *nṛn pāhi*. Thus, there are five forms in total. In the rule (*sūtra*), the vowel *a* in the term *ṭhpe* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Consequently, there are likewise five forms in cases such as *nṛn yunāti*.

(141) *kānāmreḍite* | 8|3|12| The word *kān* refers to the form of a word ending in the accusative case; it is in the genitive case, though the genitive ending is elided by Vedic (sautra) usage. The absence of the *n*-elision (*nalopa*) is likewise due to Vedic usage.

By the paribhāṣā "alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52), it is understood that [the operation applies] to the final letter of the word ending in "kān. The term "ṭhru" is understood to carry over; thus he says, "of the letter 'na' of 'kān'," and so forth. Regarding the expression "saṃpuṃsānām":
when "kān" is doubled due to vīpsā, resulting in the form "kān-kān," [the rule applies] to the first 'na'.

When *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) occurs, there is an option regarding the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) or the *anusvāra*. Regarding the *repha* (the sound *r*), it becomes *visarga*. The meaning is that, although the rule "of that *visarjanīya*, [it becomes] *sa*" would normally apply to effect *satva* (the substitution of *s*), this is set aside by the rule "before *k* and *p* [there is *visarga*]," and thus *satva* is applied by the rule "in the case of *sam*, *pum*, and *kān*. In reality, however, the rule "in the case of *sam*, *pum*, and *kān*"...
In the *Vārttika*, he states that [the mention of] *kān* is fruitless, saying "or rather" (*yadvā*). (142) *kaskādiṣu ca* | 8|3|48|.
And in the *kaska*-group etc. The word *ṭhiṇaḥ* is understood here, and it is in the ablative case.
The word *visarjanīyasya* is carried over from the rule *ṭhvisarjanīyasya saḥ*.

The phrase *kaskādiṣu* is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). The meaning is that within the *kaska-* group, the substitution of *s* occurs for a *visarjanīya* following an *iṇ* vowel. From the rule *so'padādau*, the word *saḥ* is carried over as a nominative singular.

The meaning is that there shall be the substitution of *s* for the *visarga* following an *aniṇ* [i.e., a consonant other than *n*] when it occurs within the *kaska*-class words. Thus, two distinct rules are established. Since the members of the *kaska*-class are listed with their *ṣatva* and *satva* substitutions already applied, this constitutes a division of scope: [the present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules concerning *ika* and *ipaya*.

The mention of *ika* and *ipayoḥ* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes the *visarga* prescribed by the rule *kupvoḥ*. However, for any other [visarga], the rule *saḥ* applies. In the present case, because the *visarga* is not followed by an *iṇ* vowel, there is no change to *ṣ*; rather, the change to *s* occurs. Thus, *kāṃskān* is the form when the nasalized (*anunāsika*) alternative is adopted; *kāṃskān* is the other form.
This is the form according to the alternative view involving the *anusvāra*. Now, he recites the *kaskādi* group beginning with *kaska*:
in the case of reduplication for emphasis (*vīpsā*), there is the substitution of *s* for the *visarga* following the vowel *a* in the preceding member.
However, in the usage "ṭhkaḥ ko'tra bhoḥ" (Who is that there, O sir?), because there is no *saṃhitā* (continuous junction), the substitution of *s* does not occur.

They say that because the rule *kaskādiṣu ca* is situated within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *saṃhitā*—namely, *tayor yvāvaci saṃhitāyām*—[the substitution applies]. Regarding *kotaskutaḥ*: when there is reduplication for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), in the sense of "from where—from where has he come," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tata āgataḥ*. [This is] because of the rule *avyayānām...* [which prohibits *ṭi*-lopa].
In *bhāmātre*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) due to this very nipātana; therefore, the designation *avyaya* does not apply by the rule *avyayād āp-supaḥ*.

In *sarpiṣ-kuṇḍikā*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* because it follows *iṇ*. The same applies in *dhuniṣ-kapālam* and *catuṣ-kapālam*. Now, one might object that since the substitution of *s* is established for *kāṃskān* in the *kaskādi* group...
The sense is that in the rule *saṃpuṅkānām*, the mention of *kān* need not be made.
Regarding the phrase "having taken over [the heading] *saṃhitāyām*": the remainder of the sentence is "the rules beginning with *che ca* are prescribed."
Although this [rule] ought to have been stated right after *iko yaṇ aci*, it is nevertheless stated here in accordance with the sequence of the Sūtras.
(144) *che ca* | Pāṇini 6.1.74.
And furthermore: from the rule *hrasvasya pitī* (Pāṇini 6.1.71), the words *hrasvasya* and *tuK* are understood by anuvṛtti.
The term *saṃhitāyām* is also governing; thus he says—*hrasvasya*. The letter *k* in *tuK* is for the sake of indicating that it is an *it*;
the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Because it is *kit*, it is an internal constituent (*antāvayava*) of the short vowel. [The example is] *svasya-cchāyā*.

In the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), after the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) and the addition of the augment *tuk* to the vowel *a* following the letter *v*, the form *svacchāya* is established.
[The author] demonstrates the actual sequence of grammatical operations through the passage beginning with "of the substitution of *c*" (*cutvasya*).
Now, when *svac-chāya* has been established, regarding the short vowel that is a constituent part of the *tuk*:
