Anticipating the objection that the substitution of *k* for *c* (the *kutva* rule) might apply to the letter *c* in place of the *t* at the end of the word *padāt*, he says: "of the *cutva* [substitution]," [referring to] Pāṇini 6.1.74: *āṅbhāṅeśca*.

[The rule] "after *āṅ* and *bhāṅ*" follows from [the previous rule] "before *cha*, there is *tuṭ*. Thus he says: "of these two," meaning "after *āṅ* and *bhāṅ*. Now, since the result would already be established by the rule "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*), for what purpose is this stated? To this he replies: "it is an exception to the optional alternative" (*vikalpāpavāda*). Examples: *ācchādayati* and *mā cchidaditi*. [This occurs] when *tuṭ* is applied.
The procedure is as before. From the rule *dīrghāt* [P. 6.1.75], the phrase *che tug* is understood to carry over. (146) *dīrghāt* 6.1.75.
He states this with the words beginning with *dīrghāt*. When there is a mention of both [the ablative and the locative], the mention in the ablative [is preferred].

If the augment *tug* were an integral part of the letter *ch*, then from the root *chid* with *yaṅ* affixation, after doubling (*dvitva*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and the *cartva* (retroflexion) of the reduplication, the rule "guṇa for the reduplicated syllable in *yaṅluk*" would apply to produce the guṇa of the reduplication;
thus, with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix, we would have the form *ce-icchidyate*. However, this is not the case.

When the *tuk* augment is added to the final portion of the word *cch*, that *t* becomes *c* by the rule of *cutva*; then, the preceding *cch* becomes *c* by the rule of *cartva* (before a *khari* sound). Consequently, the form would be *ceccidyate*, containing only one *e* vowel followed by two *c*s, and the *cch* would not be heard; therefore—

He says: "This *tuṅ* (the substitution of *t*) applies to the long vowel. Consequently, when the *tuṅ* occurs after the long vowel preceding the letter *cch*, and after the application of *jaś*-ness, *cut*-ness, and *cartva*-ness, the form becomes *ceccchidyate*. Since the letter *cch* lacks the status of being a *khara-paraka* (followed by a sibilant), *cartva* does not occur; thus, there is the audible pronunciation of the letter *cch* following the letter *c*.
This is without objection. [The opponent asks: "But why is this *tuṅ* [substitution] for a long vowel? To this he says: "By the word *sena*.

Since the subsequent rule prescribes the optional application of *tuṅ* after a long vowel at the end of a word (*padānta*) before *cha*, he provides the example *ceccchidyate*, intending that this present rule concerns cases other than those at the end of a word. (147)
*padāntādvā* |6|1|76|. From a word-final [consonant], optionally. The [conditions] *tuk*, *che*, and *dīrghāt* are carried over.
Thus he says: "from a long vowel, from a word-final," and so forth. This *tuk* also applies only to a long vowel, and not otherwise.
Of the suffix *ccha*; because of the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Thus ends the section on Consonant Sandhi (*halsandhi*) in the *Bālamanoramā*. Now, the roots beginning with *hu* (*juhotyādayaḥ*). Next, the roots characterized by the *ślu* suffix are examined. [The root] *hu* is used in the sense of "giving" and "eating. In the sense of giving—
The meaning is "in eating. Regarding the phrase "the Bhāṣya": the word "iti" is to be understood as the remainder [of the citation] from the sūtra, *tṛtīyā ca hośchandasi*.

Now, one might object: if the well-known sense of "giving" (*dāna*) is intended here, then in the expression "he gives a cow to the Brāhmaṇa," the usage "he offers" (*juhoti*) would also be expected. To this [the author replies]:...

He says: "And here, 'giving' (dāna) means 'throwing in' (prakṣepa). But even so, one might ask: would the term *juhoti* ("he offers") not also apply to such cases as "he throws a jar into a well" or "he throws water into the Āhavanīya fire"?
To this he replies: "And that... That aforementioned throwing-in occurs upon a substratum prescribed by an injunction, such as the Āhavanīya fire and the like.
The syntactical connection is that [the offering] is understood as being "of the sacrificial oblation such as the *puroḍāśa*. To the question "Why?", he says:

"by its very nature" (*svabhāvāt*). This means: by the beginningless worldly convention established therein. And thus, when there is a locus prescribed by an injunction, [there occurs] the act of abandoning for the sake of a deity that is itself prescribed by an injunction.

The conclusion is that the verbal root *hu* (to offer) applies to the oblation (*havis*). This point was established previously in the third chapter of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, in the section titled "The Entirety of the Oblation is to be Offered, Because it is for That Purpose" (*sarvapradānam haviṣas tadarthatvāt*),
as explained in the *Adhvara-mīmāṃsā-kutūhala-vṛtti*.
This has been explained by us.
(318) *juhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ* |2|4|75|. After the roots beginning with *hu*, there is *ślu*. [The word] *śap* [is understood]. [The rule] *adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ*...
The meaning is that this [suffix] follows from that [previous rule]. When *hu* and *a* remain, and *śap* has been applied due to *ślau*, the form *hu ti* remains;

here *ślau* applies. The meaning is that this follows from the continuation of the phrase "after *ad* and so forth" from the rule *adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ*. When *hu* and *a* remain, and *śap* has been applied due to *ślau*, the form *hu ti* remains.

(319) *ślau* | 6.1.10. He completes the remainder [of the sūtra]: "the root is reduplicated" (*dhātor dve staḥ*). The intention is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of [the words] "for a monosyllabic [root]" (*ekāco dve*) and "in the *liṭ* [tense], for the root" (*liṭi dhātoḥ*). Once the doubling has been performed...
Intending to refer to the result of the practice, he says: "he offers" (*juhoti*). "The *yaṇ*"—the meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *uvaṅ*.

(320) *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-huvāṃ ślu-vacca* | Pāṇini 3.1.39. *bhī-hrī-*: From the *dvandva* compound *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. [This rule follows] from the sūtra *kāspratyayād...* (Pāṇini 3.1.35).
The phrase *ām liṭi* (the suffix *ām* occurs before the *liṭ* [perfect] affix) is understood to carry over. With this in mind, he says: "from these [roots].
Intending that the suffix *vat* is applied to the locative form *ślau*, he says: "as if in *ślu*, when there is an operation for *ām*.
The form *juhavāma* is explained by the thought that, as if in *ślu*, there is *guṇa* substitution upon reduplication. The form *juhāva* is likewise derived.
They two sacrificed (*juhuvatuḥ*). You sacrificed (*juhavitha*), you sacrifice (*juhotha*). Sacrifice! (*juhudhi*). [The form] *herdhi* is derived by the rule "ṭhhujhalbhyo herdhiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.101);

this is the intended meaning. In the case of *juhavāni*, since the augment *āṭ* is marked with *p* (indicating it is not *pit*), the rule "aṅgasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.1) would apply, resulting in guṇa; however, that being set aside, the rule "huśnuvoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.87) would result in *yaṇ*. But [this is not so].

He says: "Because it is subsequent. The meaning is that, in comparison with [the rule] *huśnuvoḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs because it is subsequent. Having taken for granted the forms *ajuhot* and *ajuhvatuḥ* in the *laṅ* tense, he speaks while anticipating the application of *yaṇ* by the rules *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* and *huśnuvoḥ*.
Because it is subsequent [to the preceding rule], the *guṇa* substitution applies by the rule *jusi ca*, resulting in *ajuhavuḥ*.
[The forms are: *ajuhoḥ*, *ajuhutam*, *ajuhuta*, *ajuhavam*, *ajuhuva*, *ajuhuma*. Regarding *ahauṣīt*: there is *vṛddhi* substitution before the suffix *sic*.

[The forms are] *ahauṣṭām*, and so forth. [In the conditional mood: *ahauṣyat*. Regarding the root *ñi-bhī* (in the sense of fear): it is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) and ends in long *ī*. [It takes] the suffix *śap*.
Considering that *slau* [the dual suffix] begins with a double consonant (*dvitva*), he says: "he fears" (*bibheti*).
[The rule] *bhiyo'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.115) applies. From the rule *iddaridrasya*, the word *id* is carried over; from the rule *gamahana...* [the word *jhaṣi* is carried over].

Intending that *kṅti* [from Pāṇini 1.2.4], *halī* [from 6.4.23], and *sārvadhātuke* [from 7.3.84] carry over, he completes the remainder of the rule with "the letter *i* would be [the augment]," and so forth. Regarding *bibhyati*: [this is derived] from *adabhyastāt* [Pāṇini 7.1.4]. Regarding *bibhayām*: [this is derived] from *adabhyastāt*.
The meaning is that because of the rule "ṭhbhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-v-ām śluvac ca," [the root *bhī*] undergoes reduplication and so forth as if it were in the *ślu* state.

Thus: *bibhāya*, *bibhyatuḥ*, *bibhayitha* (or *bibhetha*), *bibhyiva*, *bibhyima*. [In the present tense: *betati*. [In the future: *bheṣyati*. [Imperative: *bibhetu*, *bibhitāt* (or *bibhītāt*), *bibhitām*.

*bibhītām*—let them two fear; *bibhyatu*—let them fear. *Bibhihi*—fear thou; *bibhīhi*—fear thou; *bibhitāt*—mayest thou fear; *bibhītāt*—mayest thou fear; *bibhītam*—may you two fear; *bibhītam*—may you two fear; *bibhita*—may you all fear; *bibhīta*—may you all fear. *Bibhayāni*—may I fear; *bibhayāva*—may we two fear; *bibhayāma*—may we all fear. *Abibhet*—he feared; *abibhitām*—they two feared; *abibhītām*—they two feared; *abibhayuḥ*—they all feared. *Abibheḥ*—thou didst fear.
*Abibhitam*—*abibhītam*, *abibhita-abibhīta*; *abibhayam*, *abibhiva*—*abibhīva*, *abibhima*—*abibhīma*. *Bibhiyāt*—*bibhīyāt*, and so forth.
In the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*): *bhīyāt*, *bhīyāstām*. *Abhaiṣīt*. *Abheṣyat*. *Hrī*.

Regarding the root *hrī* (meaning "to be ashamed"): it is *aniṭ*. *Jihiyati*: [the suffix] *at* is applied by the rule *ad abhyastāt*; *iyaṅ* substitution occurs. *Jihriyāmi*: [likewise]. Future: *hraeṣyati*. Imperative: *jihraetu*—or *jihrītāt*; *jihrīhi*; *jihrayāṇi*.
Aorist: *ajihraet*. Optative: *jihrīyāt*; [also] *hrīyāt*. Periphrastic aorist: *ahraiṣīt*. Conditional: *ahraeṣyat*.

The root *pṛ* is *seṭ*. When *tip* of the *laṭ* [present tense] follows, after the substitution of *śap* by *ślau*, and after reduplication, we have the form *pṛ pṛ*. At this stage, [the rule] applies:
(322) *artipipartyośca* |7|4|77|. From the rule *atra lopaḥ* [6.4.111], the word *abhyāsasya* [of the reduplicated syllable] is understood here.

Intending that the word *it* follows from the rule "ṭhbhṛñāmi" and that the word *ślau* follows from the rule "nijāṃ trayāṇām," he completes the remainder of the statement with the words "of the reduplication," and so forth.
Thus, when there is *it*-substitution for the vowel *ṛ* in the reduplication, followed by the substitution of *r*, and the application of *halādiśeṣa*, [the result is] of the subsequent portion.

Regarding the substitution of *r* for the vowel *u* (*raparatva*), he will later state that the form is *piparti*. In that context, fearing that the substitution of *u* (*utva*) might apply to the *ṛ*-vowel in the latter part of the word, he says: (323) *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* | Pāṇini 7.1.102.

Regarding *udoṣṭhayapūrvasya*: the phrase *ṛta id dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100) and *ṛtaḥ* (from 7.1.102) are understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). The term *aṅgasya*, which is the governing heading (*adhikṛtam*), is repeated here.
One instance [of *aṅgasya*] ending in the genitive of a part-whole relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) qualifies *oṣṭhyapūrvasya*; the other, however, qualifies *ṛtaḥ*.

This is a rule concerning the final element (tadantavidhi). Thus he says: "The [substitution of] au for oṣṭha, etc., when it is a part of an aṅga," and so forth. Why say "when it is a part of an aṅga"? Consider the word *samīrṇaḥ*. The root *ṛ* meaning "to go" belongs to the *kryādi* (div) class. From this root, preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *kta*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ṛśyukaḥ kitī*; then, by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, *ṛ* is changed to *it*, which is then replaced by *ra* (raparatva); and finally, before a consonant (*hali*), [the rule applies].
In the case of *samīrṇa*, following the rule *ceṭi* for the long vowel and *ṭhradābhyām* for the substitution of *ṇ* for *t*, the form is established.

In that context, because the letter *m* is preceded by an *oṣṭhya* (labial) sound, the substitution of *u* would occur, overriding the substitution of *it*. However, if it were stated that [the preceding sound] must be a member of the *aṅga* (stem), then for the *m* and the *oṣṭhya*...

Because it lacks the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*), the substitution of *u* does not occur. Thus, even in the present case of *pṛṇāti*, the doubt arises that this substitution of *u* might apply; he removes that doubt with the words "guṇavṛddhī" (in the rule regarding Guṇa and Vṛddhi).
The word "imam" means "this [rule] prescribing the substitution of *u*. As for "piparti," because the substitution of *u* would have to follow [the application of] Guṇa, [Guṇa takes precedence].

The meaning is as follows: when *pipṛtas* is established, he says "the substitution of *u*" (*utvam*). Because there is an absence of *guṇa* due to the marker *ṅ*, the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*. The form *pipurati* is derived because, due to being an *abhyasta* (repeated) root, the substitute *ad* applies; and because of the marker *ṅ*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, resulting in the substitution of *u*. [The form] *piparṣi*...

*pipūrtha*, *piparmi*, *pipūrvaḥ*, *pipūrmaḥ*. Regarding the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffix *ṇal*, he says: *papāra*. The intention is that, because the substitution of *u* (by *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*) is subsequent [in the order of application], the *vṛddhi* (guṇa) takes precedence. The *it* augment is not applied to the reduplication by the rule "artipipartyośca," because there is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "when *ślau*" (*ślau*). As for the phrase "when it would otherwise apply": when the *guṇa* is invariably applicable.
This is the meaning.
(324) *śṛdṛprāṃ hrasvo vā* |7|4|12|. *śṛdṛprām*: a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of *śṛ*, *dṛ*, and *pṛ*. [The word] "in the perfect" (*liṭi*) [is understood]. [From the rule] *dayater digi*...
The intention is that [the rule] continues from there because of its recurrence.

Although the term *kiti* (before a *kit* suffix) is not seen anywhere in the preceding sūtras, nevertheless, since this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by "ṛcchatyṛtām," and since that *guṇa* is for the sake of a *kit* suffix, it is stated as "*kiti*."
Regarding *papruḥ* and *papṛtuḥ*: when *papṛ ātus* is established, the intention is that the vowel *ṛ* becomes short, and by the rule *ṛto yaṇ aci*, it undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution.
Regarding the alternative involving *guṇa*, he says: *paparatuḥ*. However, *guṇa* is not merely optional;
for in the absence of *guṇa*, the rule "that which pertains to the letter (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to the suffix (*āṅga*)" would override the *yaṇ*-substitution.
Because of the potential application of *ut* by the rule "ṭhudoṣṭhaḷe," [the forms] *paparitha*, *paprathuḥ*—*paparathuḥ*, *paprapa*, *papara*;

*papāra*, *papara*, *papruva*, *papariva* are formed. Considering the optional lengthening (*dīrgha*) by the rule "vṛto vā," he says: *paritā*, *pariteti*. [The future forms are] *pariṣyati*—*parīṣyati*.
*Pipartu*—*pipūrtāt*, *pipūrtām*, *pipuratu*; *pipūrhi*—*pipūrtāt*, *pipūrtam*, *pipūrta*; *piparāṇi*, *piparāva*, *piparāma*. Regarding the *laṅ* [aorist]:
it is said that it becomes *apipar*. When *api pṛ* is established, after applying *guṇa* and *rapara* substitution, [the form *apipar* is derived] by the rule *halṅyādi*.

Upon the elision of the letter *t*, the *repha* (the sound *r*) becomes a *visarga*. Thus, *apiparuḥ*. Because it is an *abhyasta* (reduplicated) form, the suffix *jus* is applied; once *jus* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule *jusi ca*, followed by the substitution of *ra* (*raparatvam*). [The forms are] *apipaḥ*, *apipūrtam*, *apipūrta*, *apiparam*, *apipūrva*, and *apipūrma*. Regarding the phrase "some say" (*kecid iti*), the meaning is "other teachers."
Regarding the view that [the root] ends in a short vowel, he says "pipṛta" with the thought that the substitution of *u* (by Pāṇini 6.4.19, *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ*) does not apply here.
Because the short-vowel-ending form is *aniṭ*, the forms in the *luṅ* and other tenses are *parta*, etc. [In the imperative,] *pipṛhi*. [In the *luṅ*: *apārṣīt*.
The point is that because the short-vowel-ending form is *aniṭ*, there is no elision of the *sic* suffix. Now, [one might object that] this is the consensus of other teachers...

To the question, "Why should we accept the short vowel ending? he says: "By Pāṇini. For if one were to rely solely on the long vowel ending as sanctioned by Pāṇini, then in examples such as *ṭhtaṃ rodasī pipṛtam*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*) would result in the non-occurrence of the hearing of the short *ṛ*-vowel in that context.
In such cases, one must resort solely to the Vedic character (*chāndasatva*) as a refuge; this is the sense. Regarding the root *ḍubhṛñ*:

it is without the augment *iṭ*. Because of the marker *ñ*, it is conjugated in both voices (*ubhayapadī*). When the *ślau* suffix is present, after reduplication and so forth, the forms *bibharti* and so on are established.

(325) *bhṛñām it* | Pāṇini 7.4.76. Regarding *bhṛñām*: because the plural number is used, it is understood that this refers to the roots beginning with *bhṛñ*. From the rule *atra lopaḥ*, the word *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplicated syllable") is supplied; and from the rule *nijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ ślau* ("there is guṇa substitution for the three [roots] beginning with *nij* when *ślau* follows").
Therefore, the phrase "for the three" (*trayāṇām*) and "before *śla*" (*ślau*) also recur here. Thus he says: "by means of *bhṛ*, *māṅ*, etc. [The forms are:
*bibhrati*—because it is an abhyasta (reduplicated) root, there is the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel when the *ad* replacement has occurred. [The forms are: *bibharṣi*, *bibhṛthaḥ*, *bibhṛtha*;
*bibharmi*, *bibhṛvaḥ*, *bibhṛmaḥ*. [In the middle voice: *bibhṛte*, *bibhrāte*, *bibhrate*; *bibhṛṣe*.

Having treated *bibhrāthe* as an established form, he says: *bibhṛdhve*. [The forms] *bibhre*, *bibhṛvahe*, and *bibhṛmahe* [are formed]. Regarding the phrase "due to the treatment as *ślu*": the intention is that this is by means of the rule *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-huvām*.
Regarding *bibharāmāsa*: the intention is that, by virtue of the force of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), there is no substitution of *bhū* for the root *as*.
Regarding *babhāra*: because of the continued application of the rule *ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10), the substitution of *ī* by *ām* (via 7.4.75, *bhṛñāmid*) does not occur.
One should also know that *babhratuḥ* and *babhruḥ* are formed in the same way. By the rule *kṛsṛbhṛvṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13), there is a prohibition of *iṭ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

In the case of the suffix *thal* as well, there is a mandatory prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *acastāsvat* (Pāṇini 7.2.61). Furthermore, because the root ends in *ṛ*, even according to the opinion of Bhāradvāja (as stated in Pāṇini 7.2.63), [the *iṭ* is prohibited].

Because of the prohibition [of *iṭ*]. He says this with the words "babhartha" and so on. Having treated "babhrathuḥ," "babhra," "babhāra," and "babhara" as established forms, he says "babhṛva. The point is that there is a prohibition of *iṭ* due to the root belonging to the *krād-i* group. [The forms are: babhre, babhrāte, babhrire; babhṛṣe, babhrāthe, babhṛḍhve; babhre, babhṛvahe, babhṛmahe.

*Bhartā* (he will support), *bhariṣyati* (he will support), *bhariṣyate* (he will support [for himself]), *bibhartu*—*bibhṛtāt*, *bibhṛtām*, *bibhratu*. Having thus treated these as established forms, he says: *bibhṛhi*. The intention is that because the imperative suffix *hi* is not marked with *p*, it is marked with *ṅ*, which prohibits *guṇa*. [The forms are] *bibhṛtāt*, *bibhṛtam*, *bibhṛta*.

Treating it as already established, he says: *bibharāṇi*. The intention is that because the augment *āṭ* is marked with *p*, it lacks the *ṅ*-mark; consequently, there is no prohibition of *guṇa*. [The forms] *bibharāva* and *bibharāma* follow. Regarding the *laṅ* [aorist], he says: *abibhar*.

When *abibhṛ t* is established, after *guṇa* and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*), and after the elision of the consonant by the rule *halṅyādi-lopaḥ*, [the form becomes *abibhar*]. As for the *repha* (the letter *r*):

The meaning is "visarga" (the final *s* sound). Regarding *abibharuḥ*: because it is an *abhyasta* (reduplicated) verb, *jhi* is replaced by *jus*; by the rule "*jusi ca*," there is *guṇa*. [The forms are: *abibhaḥ*, *abibhṛtam*, *abibhṛta*;
*abibharam*, *abibhṛva*, *abibhṛma*; *abibhṛta*, *abibhrātām*, *abibhrata*; *abibhṛthāḥ*, *abibhrāthām*.

*abibhṛdhvam*, *abibhri*, *abibhṛvahi*, *abibhṛmahi*. Regarding the āśīr-liṅ (precative), he says: *bhriyāt*. By the rule "ṛṅ śayagliṅkṣu," *riṅ* is substituted. Regarding the ātmanepada āśīr-liṅ, he says: *bhṛṣīṣṭa*. Because of the *kit* designation by the rule "uśca," there is no *guṇa* substitution. Regarding *abhārṣīt*: The translation of the grammatical commentary is as follows: In the *parasmaipada* āśīr-liṅ, the form is *bhriyāt*. According to the rule "ṛṅ śayagliṅkṣu," the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *riṅ*. In the *ātmanepada* āśīr-liṅ, the form is *bhṛṣīṣṭa*. Due to the suffix being designated as *kit* by the rule "uśca," the *guṇa* substitution does not take place. As for the aorist form *abhārṣīt*: [The text continues with the formation of the aorist. Final Answer: The final answer is the grammatical analysis of the forms *abibhṛdhvam*, *abibhri*, *abibhṛvahi*, *abibhṛmahi*, *bhriyāt*, *bhṛṣīṣṭa*, and *abhārṣīt*. I hope it is correct.

Because it is *aniṭ*, there is no elision of the *sic* suffix. There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] before *sic*, and the substitution of *ra* for the final vowel (*raparatvam*)—this is the intended meaning. Thus, *abhārṣṭām* and so forth. Regarding the *luṅ* [aorist] in the *ātmanepada*, he says: *abhṛta*.
By the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*, there is elision of the *sic* suffix. Thus, *abhṛṣātām* and so forth. [The root] *māṅ* means "to measure."

Thus [it is] *aniṭ*. Because of the marker *ṅ*, it is *ātmanepada*. When there is reduplication due to the *ślu* suffix, by the rule "bhṛñām iṭ" (*Pāṇini* 7.4.76), the *iṭ* augment is applied to the reduplicated syllable; thus, when *mi-mā-te* is established, [the following rule applies]:
(326) *ī halyaghoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.113.

The term "ī" here has its nominative case elided. The phrase "of the ā of śnā and the reduplicated [root]" (śnābyastayorātaḥ) is understood from the previous rule. From "gamahana... the word "before kṅit" (kṅti) is understood, and from "ata utsārvadhātuke" the word "before a sārvadhātuka affix" (sārvadhātuke) is understood. Thus he says:

[This is] by the rule beginning with *śnābhyastayoḥ*. Regarding *āllopaḥ*: the remainder [of the rule] is *ṭhajādau kṅiti sārvadhātuke*. *Mimate*—because it is abhyasta (repeated), there is the substitution of *ad*.
[The forms are: *mimīṣe*, *mimāthe*, *mimīdhve*; *mime*, *mimīvahe*, *mimīmahe*; [and the perfect forms: *mame*, *mamāte*, *mamire*.
mamiṣe, mamāthe, mamidve; mame, mamivahe, mamimahe. māyate; mimītām, mimātām, mimatām; mimīṣva, mimāthām, mimīdhvam;
mimai, mimāvahai, mimāmahai. amimīta, amimātām, amimata; amimīthāḥ.
Imperfect: amimāta, amimīdhvam; amimi, amimīvahi, amimīmahi. Optative: mimīta, mimīyātām, mimīran;
mimīthāḥ, mimīyāthām, mimīdhvam; mimīya, mimīvahi, mimīmahi. Benedictive: māsīṣṭa. Aorist: amāsta, amāsātām, amāsata; amāsthāḥ.

*amāsāthām*, *amādhvam*; *amāsi*, *amāsvahi*, *amāsmahi*. [In the potential mood: *amāsyata*. Regarding the rule "o hāṅ gātu-viti": it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). The vowel *o* and the consonant *k* are *it* (markers). Thus, [the form] *jahāti* arises.

When there is reduplication (*ślau*) due to the suffix *liṭ*, the meaning is that the *cutva* (change to *c*) applies to the reduplicated syllable. In the case of suffixes beginning with *t*, [the rule] "of the *ā* of *śnā* and the reduplicated root" (*śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*) applies.

When the state of being *nitya* (eternal/permanent) has been established—(327) *jahāteśca* | Pāṇini 6.4.116. [The rule] "and of the root *jahāti*" [is stated]; from the rule "the *it* augment for *daridra*" (*iddaridrasya*), and from the rule "for *bhī*, optionally" (*bhiyo'nyatarasyām*).

Intending "halī" (before a consonant), he completes the remainder with "itsyād vā" (the *it* augment may optionally occur). Regarding "jahāti": because it is reduplicated (*abhyasta*), the *ad*-substitute applies, and by the rule "śnābhyastayor ātaḥ," there is elision of the long *ā*. [The forms are: *jahau*, *jahatuḥ*, *jahuḥ*;
*jahitha*—*jahātha*, *jahathuḥ*, *dajaha*; *jahau*, *jahiva*, *jahima*. The future form is *hātā*.

*hāsyati* (he will abandon). *jahitāt* (let him abandon)—[the form] *jahitām*—*jahītām*, *jahatu*. (328) *ā ca hau* 6.4.117. The word *ā* here has its nominative case ending elided. [The rule applies] after the root *jahāti*.
The sense is that this [suffix] follows from the rule *jahāteśca*. Regarding "after *cādi* and *dīta*":
the sense is that those two are drawn back here by the particle *ca*, [the former] from the rule *iddaridrasya* and [the latter] from the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*. Thus, *jahitāt* means *jahītāt*.

*Jahita*—*jahīta*, *jahita*—*jahīta*; *jahāni*, *jahāva*, *jahāma*. In the *laṅ* [imperfect] it says: *ajahāt* (he abandoned); *ajahitām*—*ajahītām*, *ajahuḥ*; *ajahā* (I abandoned). *Ajahitam*—*ajahītam*, *ajahita*—*ajahīta*; *ajahām*, *ajahiva*—*ajahīva*.
*ajahima*—*ajahīma*.

(329) *lopo yi* | 6|4|118|. [The rule] "elision before *yi*" [is applied]. From the rule "and of *jahāti*" (*jahāteśca*), [the word] *jahāteḥ* [is understood]; and from the rule "of the long *ā* of the root *śnā* and of reduplicated stems" (*śnabhyastayorātaḥ*).

From this point, the word *ātaḥ* [from Pāṇini 6.4.64] and the word *sārvadhātuke* [from Pāṇini 6.4.106, "ata utsārvadhātuke"] are carried over (*anuvartate*). The term *yī* is in the locative case and qualifies *sārvadhātuka*. This results in the rule of "application to that which begins with it" (*tadādividhi*). He states this with the words beginning "of the root *jahāti*" etc.; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "and of *jahāti*."

Regarding the benedictive (āśīrliṅ), he says: "erliṅīti. [The example is] *ahāsīt*. By the rule "hyamarama," there is the insertion of *s* and *ṭ*. [In the future tense: *ahāsyat*. The root *du-dāñ* is both parasmaipada and ātmanepada, and is aniṭ. Regarding *praṇidadāti*: by the rule "nergade," there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Regarding *data*: when *dadā-tas* is in that state, by the rule "aghoḥ," [the substitution of *at* for *as* occurs].
Due to the exclusion [of the augment] by *paryudāsa*, there is no *it* (the feminine marker); thus, by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*, there is elision of the long *ā*. Hence: *dadati*.

Because it is an *abhyasta* (repeated) root, the substitution of *ad* occurs, and by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*, there is elision of the long *ā*; this is the intended meaning. [The forms are: *dadāsi*, *datthaḥ*, *dattha*; *dadāmi*, *dadvaḥ*, *dasmaḥ*. [In the middle voice: *date*; [the forms are: *dadāte*, *dadate*; *datse*.

*dadāthe*, *daddhve*; *dade*, *dadvahe*, *dadmahe*. He gave: *dadau* (as it is said); *dadatuḥ*, *daduḥ*. Thou gavest: *daditha*—*dadhātha*, *dadathuḥ*, *dada*. He gave: *dadau*, *dadiva*, *dadima*. She/he/it gave: *dade*, *dadāte*, *dadire*. Thou gavest: *dadiṣe*, *dadāthe*, *dadidhve*. We gave: *dade*, *dadivahe*, *dadimahe*. The giver (*dātā*).

He will give—*dāsyati*, *dāsyate*. Let him give—*dadātu*, *datāt*, *datām*, *dadatu*. Having thus established the forms as if they were already accomplished, [the author] says "ghvasoḥ" with regard to the form *dehi*:
let him give—*datāt*, *datam*, *data*; let me give—*dadāni*, *dadāva*, *dadāma*. Let them two give—*datām*, *dadātām*, *dadatām*; let you two give—*datsva*, *dadāthām*.

[The forms for the imperative are: *daddhvam*, *dadai*, *dadāvahai*, *dadāmahai*. Regarding the *laṅ* [aorist], he says: *adadāt*, *adaduḥ*, *adaduḥ*. Because it is an *abhyasta* (repeated) stem, there is the suffix *jus*. [The forms are: *adadāḥ*, *adataṃ*, *adata*, *adadām*, *adadva*, *adadma*. Regarding the optative (*vidhiliṅ*), he says: *dadyāt*.

(332) *janasana-khana-sam-jhalaḥ* | 6.4.42 | The rule *janasana-ṭviḍavana-ariti* is understood to follow from the preceding context. Thus it says: "the letter *ā* is the substitute for the final [phoneme] of these [roots], when followed by *san* or a *jhala* [consonant]. *san*, *jhala*.
Thus, from this *dvandva* compound, there is a locative dual. It is understood that [the rule applies] when a *san* suffix follows that begins with a *jhal* consonant.
From the rule "anudāttopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37), the phrase "when a *jhal* follows" (*jhalik*) and "before a *kit*" (*ṅtīti*) are carried over (*anuvartate*).

Therein, the word "when a *jhal* follows" (*jhalī*), being carried over, qualifies *san*. This is a rule of initial application (*tadādividhi*). Thus, it means "when *san* begins with a *jhal* consonant."

It is obtained. The term *kṅti*, which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the previous rule, is qualified by *jhal* within this sūtra; thus, there is an application of the "rule regarding the beginning of that" (*tadādividhi*). Consequently, it is understood as "when *san* begins with a *jhal* letter" and "when *kṅt* begins with a *jhal* letter. In this way, two conditions based on a subsequent cause (*paranimitta*) are obtained. Therefore, he says: "when *san* begins with a *jhal* letter."

Regarding the rule *jhalādau kṅiti ca*: why is *jhalādau* (beginning with a consonant) used as a qualifier for *san* (the desiderative suffix)? [Examples: *jijaniṣati*, *sisaniṣati*, *cikhaniṣati*. Now, he states the purpose of this [rule] as a qualifier for *kṅit* (affixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*) beginning with a *jhal* consonant: *jajñati*. This is derived from the form *janan ati*, where, although the suffix *ati* is not *kṅit*, [the substitution of *na* for *n* occurs].

The intention is that, because [the root] lacks the property of beginning with a *jhal* sound, there is no substitution of *ā*; then, by the rule "gamahana... (Pāṇini 6.4.98), the penultimate vowel is elided, and by the rule for the change of *n* to *ñ* (ścutva), the *n* becomes *ñ*. Alternatively, one may achieve the stated result by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) based on the rule "janasanakhanāṃ saṇ" (Pāṇini 6.4.42), and thus the inclusion of the term *jhal* in this sūtra is not necessary.

This has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. Regarding *jajaṃsi*: the anusvāra is applied by the rule *naśca*. [The forms are] *jajāthaḥ*, *jajātha*; *jajanmi*, *jajanvaḥ*, *jajanmaḥ*. Regarding *jajāna*: [the forms are] *jajñatuḥ*. This root is *seṭ* (having the augment *iṭ*). [The forms are] *jajanitha*, *jajñathuḥ*, *jajñiva*. [The future forms are] *janitā*, *janiṣyati*. [The imperative forms are] *jajantu* or *jajātāt*, *jajāhi*.

The forms *jajanāni*, *ajajam*, *ajajatām*, and *ajajñuḥ* [are derived from the root *jan*]. [In the imperfect], *ajajanam* and *ajajanva*. Regarding the potential (*vidhi-liṅ*), considering the rule "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the case of the suffix *ya*, he says: *jāyāt* or *jañjanyāt*. [In the aorist], *ajanīt* (or *ajānīt*). [In the conditional], *ajaniṣyat*. [The root] *gā* means "to praise. [Thus], "he praises the gods" (*devān jigāti*).
In the case of *bhṛñāmi*, the intention is that the shortening (*itvam*) of the reduplicated syllable occurs by virtue of the rule "often in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Regarding *jigīta*: the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule "ī for [the root vowel] before a consonant other than *y*" (*ī halyaghoḥ*). Regarding *jigati*:

because it is a reduplicated form, the *a*-substitution (*adādeśaḥ*) applies, and then the elision of the *ā* of the suffix *śnā* occurs by the rule "of *śnā* and reduplicated forms" (*śnābhyastayoḥ*). [The forms] *jigāsi* and *jigīthaḥ*.
He has conquered; he is about to conquer; he has conquered. He sang, they two sang, they sang; we two sang. He shall sing; he will sing.
Let him conquer—let him conquer, let them two conquer, let them conquer;
conquer thou; may I conquer. He conquered, they two conquered, they conquered; thou didst conquer; I conquered, we two conquered. May he be victorious.
In the benedictive (āśīrliṅ): geyāt; [in the imperfect: agāsīt; [in the conditional: agāsyat. Thus end the *juhoty-ādyaḥ* (the second class of verbs).
Thus ends the section on the *juhoty-ādyaḥ* in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, regarding the section on verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), the *kaṇḍvādi* group [is treated].

(502) Pāṇini 3.1.27: *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*. Now, the grammatical operations (*prakriyā*) of the *kaṇḍvādi* group are described. [The rule states: "The suffix *yak* is added after the roots beginning with *kaṇḍū*. [The word] "after roots" [is understood from the context].

The intention is that this [term] is understood from the previous rule, "dhātor ekācaḥ" (P. 6.1.1). Regarding the word "nityam" (always): the intention is that the mention of the option (*vā*) has been withdrawn; otherwise, forms such as *kaṇḍuvatī* would also occur. As for the phrase "for it is twofold": this is clear in the Bhāṣya. By this, the formation of unanalyzed forms such as *kaṇḍūri* is established.
Regarding *leṭita*: there is the elision of *y* by the rule *yasya halaḥ*. Regarding *medhā āśugrahaṇe*:
"quick apprehension" means understanding with speed. There is an alternative reading, *sugrahaṇe*. Regarding *sukhyati*:
there is the elision of the vowel *a* before the suffix *yak*. However, when *yak* is added to nominal stems (*prātipadika*), [the following applies].

It should be understood that because [the suffix] lacks the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka*, the elision (*al-lopa*) would not occur. However, for the two roots belonging to the *caurādika* class, it is stated that they form *sukhayati* and *duḥkhayati*. Regarding *arara*: "the action of an *ārā*. An *ārā* is a goad; the action performed by means of that is "the action of an *ārā*" (*ārākarma*). *Bhiṣaj* is used in the sense of medical treatment (*cikitsā*).
This [root] ends in *j*. It forms *bhiṣajyati* (he heals). Regarding *lekhā-skhalane ca*:

from *likh*, one forms *lekhāyati* (he scratches) and *lekhyati* (he scratches). When the suffix *yak* follows a root ending in *a*, there is elision of that *a*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form);
this means it belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* group. By this, roots such as *duvas* in the sense of "kindling" are included.
"ṭhsamidhāgnim duvasyate" (he honors Agni with fuel)— these belong to the *kaṇḍvādi* group. Now begins the section on grammatical relations (*kāraka*).
(524) *The first case ending occurs when there is mere expression of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), gender, measure, or number.* (Pāṇini 2.3.46).

Thus, having taken up the governing rule "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a nominal stem" (*ṅy-āp-prātipadikāt*), the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) have been explained in detail. Among those, [the following applies]:

He begins to demonstrate the specific determination of the meanings of the seven case-endings, starting with the nominative (*prathamā*) and ending with the locative (*saptamī*): [The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*)]. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the meaning of the nominal stem consists of a dyad—the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) and the individual (*vyakti*)? Or: "The meaning of the nominal stem consists of the ground for application, the individual, and gender (*liṅga*)..."

These are the positions: that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of a triad—namely, the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the individual (*vyakti*), gender (*liṅga*), and number (*saṃkhyā*);

or that it consists of a tetrad—namely, the basis for application, the individual, gender, number, and grammatical relation (*kāraka*); or that it consists of a pentad [adding case-role]. Such are these views.

In the sūtras such as *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau* and *striyām*, this point is established in the Bhāṣya and elaborated upon in the Mañjūṣā. In that regard, since gender (*liṅga*) is also part of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) under the views that [the stem denotes] a triplet [of number, gender, and case] and so forth, the separate mention [of gender] would be redundant; therefore, he says: "restricted" (*niyata*).

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose presence is necessarily [present]. The meaning is: when a nominal stem (prātipadika) is uttered, that object whose presence necessarily arises is its meaning. And thus, in the case of words with non-fixed genders, such as *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, there is no necessity for any [particular gender].

The point is that since gender (*liṅga*) is not present [in the technical term *prātipadika*], it is not included by the word *prātipadikārtha*; therefore, the separate mention of gender is necessary. He dispels the misconception that the word *mātra* might only be construed with the word *vacana*—by stating "of the word *mātra*. [The compound] is a *dvandva*: "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), gender (*liṅga*), measure (*parimāṇa*), and number (*vacana*). The analysis of the compound *prātipadikārthaliṅgaparimāṇavacanamātram* is not a *svapadavigraha* (analysis using its own constituent words), but rather: "only the meaning of the nominal stem, gender, measure, and number."

The word *mātra* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). As Amara states: "The word *mātra* [is used] in the senses of entirety (*kārtsnya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The compound is a mandatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) according to the rule "mayūravyaṃsakādayaśca. Since the word *mātra* is heard at the end of the *dvandva*, its meaning applies individually to each member—namely, to the nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*), gender (*liṅga*), measure (*parimāṇa*), and number (*vacana*). He will later state that "number" (*vacana*) means count (*saṅkhyā*).

One might object: "Is it not untenable that the first case ending (*prathamā*) occurs when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), merely gender (*liṅga*), merely measure (*parimāṇa*), or merely number (*saṅkhyā*), since gender and the others are never presented in isolation without the meaning of the nominal stem? Anticipating this objection, [the author] explains—intending to show that "precisely because of this counter-argument, what is intended is 'when gender alone is added' (i.e., as an excess)"—by stating: "when gender alone and so forth are added. This means: "when gender alone is added" and "when measure alone is added."

He provides examples for "the mere meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātra*)—namely, *uccaiḥ* and so forth. Now, one might object: since among indeclinables there is the appearance of neuter gender by the rule "the neuter is used in the sense of generality" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*), and since masculine gender appears in the word *kṛṣṇa*, feminine gender in the word *śrī*, and neuter gender in the word *jñāna*, how can these be examples of the "mere meaning of the nominal stem"? To this he replies: "they are without gender," and so forth.

According to the reasoning stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭhavyayādāpsupaḥ*—that "the mention of *āp* [in that rule] is redundant because indeclinables (*avyaya*) lack gender"—no gender whatsoever is presented in an indeclinable. Thus, an indeclinable serves as an example for the phrase "only the meaning of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātre*). In the word *kṛṣṇa*, there is the necessary manifestation of masculinity; in *śrī*, of femininity; and in *jñāna*, of neuter-ness. Because these possess fixed genders (*niyataliṅga*), gender is included within the meaning of the nominal stem itself. Therefore, the status of these words as examples for "only the meaning of the nominal stem" is beyond dispute. This is the intended sense.

Although the word *kṛṣṇa* is tri-gendered—as in "a black cloth" (*kṛṣṇaḥ paṭaḥ*), "a black garment" (*kṛṣṇā paṭī*), and "a black cloth" (*kṛṣṇaṃ vastram*)—the intention here is that the word *kṛṣṇa* is intended to refer specifically to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). Nor should it be argued: "What is the purpose of the nominative case when the meaning is already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? For its purpose is to convey the number, such as singularity and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that there is no purpose for the production of the first case ending (*prathamā*) from an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because the elision (*luk*) required by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* would necessarily apply; for the production of the case ending is necessary for the sake of establishing word-status (*padatva*). Nor should it be argued that there is no purpose for the production of the first case ending from an indeclinable, because the elision required by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* would necessarily apply; for the production of the case ending is necessary for the sake of establishing word-status (*padatva*).

By that [principle], in cases such as *uccaiḥ*, the substitution of *ru* and *visarga* occurs; and in cases such as *uccais te samyaguccāraṇam*, the application of *temayādi* (the suffixes *te* and *me*) is established. Regarding the term "indeterminate" (*aniyata*): words such as *taṭa* and others, which have indeterminate gender, serve as examples for the addition of mere gender. The meaning is that because genders appear without fixed necessity, they are not included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Examples include *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*; as Amara states: "*Taṭaṃ triṣu*" (the word *taṭa* is used in all three genders). Regarding "mere measure" (*parimāṇamātre*): the meaning is that an example will be stated later.

"Droṇa" means rice; "droṇa" is a specific measure of capacity. It is traditionally taught: "A *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust) is that which stands in a sunbeam through a lattice. Eight of those are a *likṣā* (nit); three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa* (black mustard seed). Three of those are a *gaura* (white mustard seed); six of those are a *yava* (barley grain); three of those are a *madhya* (middle-sized grain). Five of those are a *kṛṣṇala*; five of those are a *māṣa*; sixteen of those are a *suvarṇa*. Four or even five *suvarṇas* are proclaimed as a *bala*. Two *palas* are a *prasṛta*; double that is considered a *kuḍava*."

"Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*; four *prasthas* make an *āḍhaka*; and by those four *āḍhakas*, a *droṇa* is designated. Two *droṇas* are a *kumbha*; a *śūrpa* [is the same]; and sixteen *droṇas* are a *khārī*. This is because of such traditional authority (*smaraṇa*). Regarding the term "rice" (*vrīhi*): the singular number is used for the genus (*jāti*), according to the rule "In the case of a name denoting a genus, the plural may optionally be used even when referring to a single thing. It means, in effect, a heap of rice; for it is not possible for the measure of a single *droṇa* to belong to a single individual grain of rice.

[Objection: But how can there be a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) between a specific measure called a *droṇa* and an individual grain (*vrīhivyakti*), given that the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are distinct? To this, he says: "in the form of a *droṇa*" (*droṇarūpam*). The point is that since the relation of non-difference is indeed sublated, one must accept the relation between the measure of a *droṇa* and the individual grain by way of their being the delimiting factor (*paricchedaka*) and the delimited object (*paricchedya*); thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. [Objection: But since the word *droṇa*, which denotes a specific measure, is invariably masculine, the rule *prātipadikārthamātre* (Pāṇini 2.3.46) alone would suffice [to justify its use in the neuter]. However, if one were to follow the rule *astriyāmāḍhakadroṇau* (Pāṇini 3.3.93)...

If it is argued that [the rule] thus pertains to gender alone, and that it is established simply by the addition of gender, then what is the purpose of including the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*)?

To this he replies: "In the sense of the suffix, when it is measure. For [the suffix does not apply] to the word *droṇa*, which denotes a specific measure, in its own primary sense (*svārthe*) by way of the form "being a *droṇa*."
The nominative case is intended [here], so that there would be no redundancy with the rule stating "in the mere sense of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikārthamātre*). However,
when the specific measure of a *droṇa* is intended to be expressed by the word *droṇa*,
which denotes a measure as a *droṇa*-ness, in its general form as "measure-ness" (*parimāṇatva*), [the nominative is required].

The first case ending is prescribed. Consequently, within the general measure that constitutes the meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the base *bhakta* (rice-gruel)— which is a specific measure— relates to the meaning of the word *droṇa* through a relation of non-difference (*abheda-saṃsarga*) consisting of the identity of the general and the particular.

However, the referent of the cognition consisting of the generality of measure (parimāṇasāmānya) connects with the rice by way of the relation between the delimiting factor and the delimited factor (paricchedyaparicchedakabhāva). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The rice is delimited by that general measure which consists of the specific measure known as a *droṇa*. Otherwise, [the connection would not be established].
The cognition would be: "the rice is delimited by a specific measure called a *droṇa*.

However, the meaning of the suffix, which consists of the general category of measure, relates to the rice through the relationship of the delimiting and the delimited. And thus, [it refers to] that which consists of the specific measure named *droṇa*.
The understanding that results is: "rice delimited by whatever measure [is intended]. Otherwise, the understanding would be:

"rice delimited by a specific measure called a *droṇa*," and the general category of measure (*parimāṇasāmānya*) would not be perceived. Therefore, the purpose of including the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) here is for that reason.

The word "number" (*saṅkhyā*) [is used here] because the ancient teachers (pūrvācāryas) have designated it as such; this is the intended meaning. And thus, it is understood that the nominative case occurs when there is merely a number. Now, why is it not said "when there is merely a number" (*saṅkhyāmātrādhikye*), just as one says "when there is merely gender" (*liṅgamātrādhikye*) or "when there is merely measure" (*parimāṇamātrādhikye*)?

It must be said that [the term] has been explained; however, since there is no instance anywhere where singular number and measure appear alone, even if it were explained in that way, [the question remains] regarding the words *eka*, *dvi*, and *bahu* as to how singularity, duality, and plurality could exist in isolation.
Since the presence [of the meaning] is restricted, it is more appropriate to explain it as referring merely to "number" (*saṅkhyāmātra*).
For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the portion concerning the mention of "words," the examples "one," "two," and "many" are cited.
Now, one might object: in the case of "one," "two," and "many," because there is a restricted presentation of singularity, duality, and plurality...

Since the rule would have been established by the words "in the sense of the nominal stem" (*ṭhprātipadikārthe*) alone, the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*) is redundant; to this he replies: "In this case" (*iha*). The meaning is that because the numbers such as singularity and so forth are already expressed by the base stems themselves, the nominative case ending would not apply according to the maxim "that which has already been expressed need not be employed" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*); therefore, the inclusion of the term "number" is for the sake of that [application]. And thus:

The meaning is that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) used here is merely reiterative (*anuvādikā*) and should be employed for the sake of the grammatical correctness of the word, according to the principle established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1): "A base alone should not be used, nor should an affix alone. It is with this very intention that it has been stated:
In the Bhāṣya it is stated: "Even when singularity and so forth have been expressed, the first case ending [occurs].

Because of the inclusion of the word *mātra* ("only"), the first case ending does not occur when there is an addition of factors such as the kārakas. Regarding this, it has been elaborated upon in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* and other works that it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as *arthe prathamā* ("the first case occurs for the sake of the meaning").

(525) *sambodhane ca* | 2|3|47| "And in the sense of address. This means that the nominative case (*prathamā*) shall apply even when the sense of address is additionally intended. Address (*sambodhana*) is the act of making someone face [the speaker] for the purpose of informing them. For example: *he rāma*. [The word] *mām*...

The word "pāhi" (protect) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Here, the protection of Rāma is what is to be made known. Nor should it be argued that in the example "O King, become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth" (*he rājan sārvabhaumo bhava*), the nominative case would apply even after the word *sārvabhauma* because it is in the vocative; for the vocative is defined precisely as a complete act of addressing.

By the force of the prefix *sam*, it is understood that a certain meaning can only be communicated to a listener when that listener is specifically known [to the speaker] as being a king or the like, and not otherwise; therefore, it follows that this vocative case-ending pertains exclusively to that which is already established (*anuvādya*). It is not, however—

It has the predicated object as its referent. Thus, since the status of being a sovereign of the whole earth (*sārvabhaumatva*), which is the predicate, is not established at present and therefore cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvādya*), the vocative case is not applied to the word *sārvabhauma*;
this is explained in detail in the *Mañjūṣā*. (Thus ends the section on the nominative case.)

(526) "That which is most desired by the agent is the *karman*. [Pāṇini 1.4.49]. With reference to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the context of a *kāraka*," the remainder of the sense is: "the technical designations (*saṃjñās*) will be stated.
For the *bhāṣya* shows the etymological derivation: "A *kāraka* is that which produces an action; it performs (*karoti*), that is, it brings about an action."

In the expression "he sees the Brāhmaṇa’s son," the Brāhmaṇa is not a *kāraka* (participant in an action) because he is established by another means (*anyathāsiddha*). [The sūtra states: "That which is desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsita*). The term "in a *kāraka*" (*kārake*), which is carried over from the previous rule, is transformed here into the nominative case. "Desired" (*īpsita*) means that which is sought to be obtained (*āptum iṣyamāṇam*). [The root] *āplṛ* [is used] in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptau*).

From this [root] ending in the suffix *saṇ*, the suffix *kta* is applied while the rule "after roots meaning 'to think,' 'to know,' or 'to honor'" is in force; for *mati* means desire, since it is mentioned separately from *buddhi*. By the rule "and of that which ends in *kta* when expressing the present," the genitive case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*).
That which is most desired by excellence is the *īpsitatama*. The agent is the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root.

When there is an expectancy as to "by what [is it attained]," it is understood by implication that it is "by the activity which serves as a qualification of the agent. He states the result of this with the words "by the action of the agent," and so forth. However, the present tense conveyed by the suffix -kta (the past passive participle) is not intended to be significant here.
Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as "he makes a mat" (kaṭaṃ karoti) or "he has made [it]" (kṛtavān). *Āpti* means connection (*saṃbandha*).

Thus, the meaning is: that which is desired by the agent to be connected with the fruit produced by the operation residing in itself. For example, in the case of "he cooks the rice-grains" (*taṇḍulān pacati*).
The meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*).
Softening consists of a state of being soft and porous, characterized by the loosening of constituent parts produced by the sweating [of grains] due to heated water.
The operation conducive to that [result] consists of such forms as placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring water, adding fuel, removing [impurities], and kindling;

this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kārake* (Pāṇini 1.4.23). For this very reason, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that "the verbal root [denotes] both the result and the operation" (*phalavyāpārayordhātuḥ*). And thus:
The meaning is that one causes the rice grains to soften through operations such as placing them on the fire.

Because the rice grains are the substratum of the result—namely, softening—which is brought about by the operation of the agent consisting of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth, they possess the status of an object (*karman*). Now, [one might ask: what is the purpose of including the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*)?

It is redundant. Nor should it be said that [the mention of *kartṛ*] is for the sake of obtaining the term "operation" (*vyāpāra*), because when the expectation "by what [is the operation obtained]? arises, that [operation] is already obtained from the very heading on "factors of action" (*kāraka*).
Thus he asks: "What [is the purpose of mentioning] *kartṛ*? [The example is: "He binds a horse to the beans" (*māṣeṣvaśvaṃ badhnāti*). [This occurs] with respect to the beans (*māṣeṣu*).

The meaning is that one binds [the animal] elsewhere in order to turn it away from eating them, as it is about to proceed toward eating out of fear of abdominal pain. The point here is that the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the purpose of excluding the status of "object" (*karman*) from the *māṣas*.
He states—namely, "of the object"—that when the mention of the agent is made, the aforementioned fault does not occur.

The meaning is that here the beans (*māṣa*) are intended for the horse which has become the object of the act of binding, and not for the binder; this is because the act of guarding the horse alone requires them. [Question: What is the purpose of including the suffix *-tamap*? Since the term "object" (karman) is understood here by virtue of its recurrence from the previous rule, the explicit mention of "object" (karmagrahaṇa) would seem redundant; to this he says:

The meaning is that the mention of "object" is so that its recurrence might not also occur here. Now, [as in the example] *hariṃ...*.

Since that [suffix] will not recur in cases such as *bhajati* precisely because it is impossible there, he says "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth. The meaning of the particle *eva* is that [the suffix] would not occur in examples such as *hariṃ bhajati*.

"He worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*). The meaning of the root *bhaj* is an activity consisting of service that is conducive to [the deity's] satisfaction.
The sense is that one causes Hari to be satisfied through activities such as worship.
Hari is the object (*karman*) because he is the substratum of the result, which is the form of satisfaction, produced by the activity of worshiping and so forth residing in the agent.
The understanding is that there is a present activity residing in Devadatta, which is favorable to the satisfaction residing in Hari.
This is because of the statement of Yāska, the author of the Nirukta: "A verb (ākhyāta) has action as its primary meaning" (*bāvapradhānam ākhyātam*).
The meaning of that is that a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) has action as its primary element. And thus:

It has been explained in detail in works such as the *Mañjūṣā* that the cognition whose qualificand (viśeṣya) ends in the nominative case— namely, "Devadatta is the locus of the activity conducive to Hari’s satisfaction"— is not to be accepted as the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*).
Regarding the phrase "but when [the agent] is not expressed" (*abhihite tu*), the remainder of the sentence is "in cases such as ‘hariḥ sevyate’" (Hari is served).

"Only the first [case-ending]"—this is the sense, because there is no governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the term "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) in that specific injunction, and because of the *vārttika*: "when [the object] is not expressed, the first [case-ending is used]. Raising the objection that because the object (*karman*) has already been expressed by the second case ending (*dvitīyā*), the second case would not apply to *bhīṣma* and the others, it is enumerated [in the rule] as "non-expression by means of a finite verb (*tiṅ*), a primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), or a compound (*samāsa*). After the word "samāsa," the word "vivakṣita" (intended) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding "tiṅ":

this is an uninflected mention intended to indicate the term *tiṅ*. In the example "hariḥ sevyate" (Hari is served), the *lakāra* suffix occurs in the sense of the object according to the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (*Pāṇini 3.4.69*), and the *ātmanepada* ending occurs according to the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" (*Pāṇini 1.3.13*).

The point is that because the object (*karman*) "Hari" is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the second case ending does not occur. The meaning of the sentence "He worships Hari" (*hariṃ bhajati*) is as follows: according to the established doctrine of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasamaya*), the understanding of the sentence-meaning is identical whether the agent or the object is expressed by a verbal suffix (*lakāra*). [This applies to] the *kṛt* suffixes as well.

This [term] *tiṅ* etc., like *atiṅ*, is also an indeclinable designation intended to indicate its examples. Regarding the example "lakṣmyā sevitaḥ" (served by Lakṣmī): the word "Hari" is to be supplied as the remainder. In accordance with Yāska’s traditional rule that "names have substance as their primary referent," it is universally agreed that among nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the understanding has the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) presented in the nominative case as its primary object.

Here, because the object (*karman*) of Hari—who was served—is expressed by the *kṛt* suffix, the second case ending does not occur. [This is] what is meant by "by the secondary derivative suffix" (*taddhita*).

This [example] also is an indication without case-endings (*avibhaktika-nirdeśa*) for the purpose of pointing out its illustration. "Śatya" [is used]; the word "cloth and so forth" (*paṭādi*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) *yat* is applied by the rule "After *śata*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *yat* occur when [the meaning] is not one hundred.

This [term] *avibhaktika-nirdeśa* (an indication without case endings) is also intended to point toward its illustration: *prāptānandaḥ*.

The word "Devadatta and so forth" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the form *prāpta*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *gaty-arthākarmaka-* etc.
Because the object (*karman*), which is the meaning of the other member of the compound, is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the accusative ending does not apply].
The meaning is "the second [case]. The understanding is that [the tree] is the object of the attainment whose agent is Ānanda.

He shows the result of the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) with the words "in some cases" (*kvacid*). The phrase "even a poison-tree" (*viṣavṛkṣo 'pi*) connects with the word "it is not right" (*asāmpratam*). Regarding its connection with the words "having nurtured" (*saṃvardhya*) and "to cut down" (*chettum*), [the following applies].

This refers to the second case. Therein, by implication, "poisonous tree" (*viṣavṛkṣam*) is understood. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *na sāṃpratam*, it is a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound. Regarding the phrase "it is appropriate" (*yujyate*), this is the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in the sense of the object (*karman*) for the root *yuj* meaning "to join. It is not appropriate due to the context; that is to say, it does not conform to what is fitting (*aucitya*).

"According to Amara, *ṭhyukte* means 'two [accusatives] are used when [the object] is currently [connected to the action]'; here, because the object (*karman*)—the tree—is expressed by a verbal derivative (*nipāta*), the second accusative case does not apply—this is the intended meaning. In reality, however, the suffix *tumun* in the form *ṭhchetum*' is difficult to justify here, as it would be like the usage in *ṭhkṛṣṇaṃ draṣṭuṃ yātī'ti*" (he goes to see Kṛṣṇa).

Because there is no occurrence of a verb denoting action as a subordinate element (*upapada*), the rule *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* does not apply. Nor is the suffix *tumun* applicable by the rule *śaka-dhṛṣa-* etc., because there is no connection with verbs such as *śak* (to be able). Rather, [the suffix is applied] while the phrase *icchārtheṣu* ("in the sense of desire") is being carried over.

The suffix *tumun* is used here according to the rule "when there is a common agent, *tumun* [is employed]. This applies even when the accompanying word (*upapada*) does not denote an action, as in examples such as "he desires to eat" (*icchati bhoktum*). Thus, for the grammatical correctness of the *tumun* suffix, the word "it is desired" (*iṣyate*) must be supplied. Even a poison tree, having been nurtured...

The phrase "chetumiṣyate" means that which is improper or incorrect; thus, even here, the prevention of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) occurs precisely because [the object] is expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*), according to the *parigaṇana-vārttika* which states: "Expression [of the object] occurs through finite verbs (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*)."
It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that the addition of the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) is useless [in this context].

However, in the sentence "he eats cooked rice" (*pakvam odanaṃ bhuṅkte*), there are two capacities of objecthood (*karmatva-śakti*) as determined by the two actions of cooking and eating. Among these, [the capacity of objecthood] as determined by the subordinate action of cooking—

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that even though [the objecthood] is expressed by the *kta* suffix, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is unimpeded because it takes up the power of objecthood (*karmatva-śakti*) which is not expressed with respect to the primary action of eating. Now, one might object:

just as in examples such as "bahupaṭuḥ" (very clever), where [suffixes] like *kalpa* and so on do not occur because [the quality] has already been expressed by the *taddhita* suffix *bahuc*, [so too should it be here].

In the same way, in expressions such as "the mat is being made" (*kriyate kaṭaḥ*), the accusative case and others will not occur because the meaning has already been expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth, according to the maxim: "That which has its meaning already expressed is not employed. The second [case-ending] has scope in instances such as "the mat is made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*), where it simply does not occur because it is superseded by the first [case-ending], which has no other scope. Nor should it be argued that examples such as "the tree is a *plakṣa*" (*vṛkṣaḥ plakṣaḥ*) constitute the scope for the first case-ending;
for in those cases, since the subject functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the implied verb "is," the third case-ending would necessarily apply.

Or, even if there were scope for the first [rule] there, nevertheless, since both would have scope, the first alone would apply by virtue of its priority. And if it is argued that, in this case, the governing rule *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed") would be rendered useless—do not say so; for [the rules] such as *karmaṇi dvitīyā* ("the second case ending is used when the object is expressed") and *dvyekayordvivacanaikavacane* ("the dual and singular endings are used for two and one, respectively")...

And by the syntactic unity of the two rules, "in the plural [the plural suffix]" and "in the singular [the singular suffix]," it is obtained that when there is singularity, duality, or plurality in the object (*karman*), the singular, dual, and plural suffixes are applied respectively. In that context,
upon the introduction of the rule "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*), [it is understood that] when there is singularity in the object that has not been expressed...

The meaning would be "the second [case-ending]"; however, in the absence of the condition *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"), the rule would result merely in: "where there is singularity in the object (*karman*), the singular number of the second case is used. If that were the case, then in examples such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat was made"), although the mere object is expressed by the past passive participle (*kta*), its singularity would remain unexpressed.

The second singular case-ending would be unavoidable. Nor should it be suspected that the nominative case has no scope, because in cases such as "this is blue, not red," where the intention is to exclude other qualifiers, the verb "is" (asti) is not necessary. Therefore, in that instance—

Because the first [alternative] is subject to an exception; nor can it be argued that in those cases the first [case-ending] will apply by virtue of its priority, for in examples such as *kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ* ("the mat is to be made"), the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix would prevail even over that [first case], due to its higher status. And thus, number is the meaning of the case-ending.

If this is accepted, then since the *kāraka* (the factor of action) has already been expressed by the suffix *-kta* and others, there is no occasion for the application of case endings such as the second (*dvitīyā*). Furthermore, the cognition of numbers such as singularity (*ekatva*) is possible through the nominative (*prathamā*) alone, which functions with respect to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Therefore, [the rule] "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*)...
Thus, it is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, the Kaustubha, and other works that [the action] should not be commenced.

However, the extensive discussion should be sought in the Mañjūṣā. (529) Likewise: "And that which is not intended [by the agent], though connected [with the action], [is called karma]. (Pāṇini 1.4.50)

It is stated thus: since the word "tathā" (thus/in that manner), which denotes similarity, is dependent upon a correlative (*pratiyogi*), he says—*īpsitatamavat* ("like that which is most desired"). Because it was mentioned in proximity in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), the sense is that the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) alone is the correlative of the similarity. [The phrase] "by means of an action" (*kriyayā*).

The meaning is "connected with a fruit produced by an action. In the preceding sūtra, the status of being an object (*karman*) was stated for that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*). This statement is intended to include both that which is hated (*dveṣya*) and that which is disregarded (*upekṣya*).
In this regard, he gives an example of that which is disregarded: "While going to the village, he touches grass."

The meaning of the root *spṛś* (to touch) is an operation conducive to conjunction. In this regard, although the grass being touched lacks the status of being the most desired (*īpsitatama*), it is nevertheless treated as such, just as in examples like "he touches the Gaṅgā," where the Gaṅgā being touched is indeed the most desired object.
The meaning is that [the object] possesses the status of an *karman* because it is the substratum of the result, which consists of conjunction produced by the action.

He gives an example of the "object of aversion" (*dveṣya*): "He eats poison. This is the example when someone, being seized by a powerful enemy, eats poison; for [the action of] eating occurs in the mouth.
The meaning [of the action] is the operation of moving the jaw and so forth, which is conducive to the entry of the cast-in [poison] into the cavity of the throat.

Even though the poison lacks the status of being the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) because it is loathed, it is nevertheless related to the action just as the rice being eaten is related to the action in such expressions as "he eats rice."

The intended meaning is that [the object] possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) because it is the locus of the result consisting of entry into the cavity of the throat produced by the action. Nor should it be argued: "Let it simply be that 'an object is that which possesses the result presented by the verbal root'; what is the use of separately mentioning the 'desired' (*īpsita*) and the 'undesired' (*anīpsita*)?

For, in the case of the example "He wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), [if the definition were restricted to the desired result, the boy would not be considered an object].
By the rule "the desired object of roots meaning 'to ward off' [is the apādāna]," the status of the *apādāna* would apply to the boy (*māṇavaka*);

to prevent that, it must indeed be stated: "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*). And thus, for the sake of including both the hateful and the indifferent, the sūtra "and likewise that which is connected in such a manner" (*tathāyuktaṃ ca*) is necessary; let this suffice.
To that extent: (530) *akathitaṃ ca* | 1.4.50.
And that which is not specifically mentioned [as a kāraka]. He explains the word *akathita*: "by means of specific [kārakas] such as the ablative (*apādāna*) and so forth."

The seven factors of action (*kāraka*) are the ablative (*apādāna*), the dative (*saṃpradāna*), the locative (*adhikaraṇa*), the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the cause (*hetu*). The meaning is that when these are not intended to be expressed through their specific natures as "ablative" and so forth, but rather through the general nature of a relationship (*saṃbandha-sāmānya*), then they are designated as the "object" (*karman*). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: ...nanu... [the objection begins].

One might raise the objection that in the sentence *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("He hears from the actor"), the actor (*naṭa*) would also incur the status of an object (*karman*), because he is a *kāraka* by virtue of being connected with the action, and because, in reality, the source (*apādāna*) is intended to be expressed as having a relationship [with the agent]. Anticipating this, the author enumerates the specific cases: *duhyāj*.

This is a summary verse (*saṅgrahaśloka*) regarding the meaning of the *Vārttika*. Therefore, he explains it with the words "of *duh* and so forth. [The roots are: *duha* in the sense of "milking" (*prapūraṇe*); *ṭua* (or *yācṛ*) in the sense of "begging" (*yācñāyām*); *ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of "cooking" (*pāke*); and *daṇḍ* in the sense of "inflicting punishment" (*daṇḍanipātane*), belonging to the *curādi* class. Here, its meaning is "seizing" (*nigraha*). [The root] *rudhir*... [is used] in the sense of "seizing" (*grahaṇa*).

Regarding the root *ā-vṛ* in the sense of "obstructing," and *pra-chi* in the sense of "desire to know": in the verse [of Pāṇini's sūtra], the vowel *i* in *pracchī* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
If it were specified as *ik* (the short *i*), there would be the undesirable consequence of *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule *grāhijyā*. [The other roots mentioned are:

*ci* in the sense of "piling up" (*cayane*), *brū* in the sense of "distinct speech" (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*), *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭau*), and *ji* in the sense of "conquering" (*abhibhave*).
The meaning is "of twelve," namely from the roots *ṭhmantha* (to churn) and *ṭhmuṣa* (to steal).

"Of four" means from the four roots: *ṇīñ* (to lead), *ṭhhṛñ* (to take away), *ṭhkṛṣa* (to scratch), and *ṭhbaha* (to carry). Regarding the phrase "if it is impelled by an object": [this refers to the definition of the *karman* kāraka].

This is the explanation of the term *karmayu*. The sense is that when a verbal root has a *karaṇa* (instrument) as its *upapada*, and the *karman* (object) is to be expressed, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "satsūdviṣa... and so forth. Although it is stated: "In the case of the roots *duh*, *yāc*, *rudh*, *pracch*, *bhikṣ*, and *ciñ*, [the *kāraka*] which is the cause of the application (*upayoga*) is the object (*karman*) when a suffix not previously prescribed is to be applied."
"Whatever is associated with the qualities of the roots *bruvi* (to speak) and *śāsi* (to command) is [also] called *akīrtita* by the Poet [Pāṇini].

Thus, although *pac*, *math*, *muṣ*, and others are not explicitly listed in the *Ślokavārttika* on the sūtra in question, Kaiyaṭa maintains that they are nevertheless included by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule. For example: *gāṃ gogdhi*.
The meaning of the root *duh* (to milk) is an operation conducive to flowing, which is synonymous with "causing to flow.
Because it is the substratum of the result consisting of flowing, brought about by an operation consisting of causing to flow, the milk (*payas*) is the object (*karman*).
The cow (*go*), however, is the source (*apādāna*) with respect to that flowing. Disregarding its status as a source, [it is considered] by virtue of its being a related entity.

When there is an intention to express the cow [as the object], it becomes the *karman* (object) by this [rule]; consequently, once the *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive) of the *śeṣa* (remainder) is excluded, the *dvitīyā* (accusative) occurs. This very point has been stated in the *Prauḍhamanoramā*: "The meaning is 'the milking which has milk related to a cow as its object'. And thus, just as in the case of "one should not eat beans," [the genitive is replaced by the accusative].
This sūtra is intended to set aside the genitive case that would otherwise apply when there is a desire to express the sense of "remainder" (śeṣatva).
However, when the cow is intended to be expressed as the point of departure (apādāna), only the ablative case is used—as in *goḥ payo dogdhi* ("he milks milk from the cow").
The meaning is: "he causes the milk to flow out from the cow. But if the cow is instead a qualifier of the milk, then [the genitive applies].
It is simply the sixth [case]. The meaning is: "it causes the milk related to the cow to flow. The path followed by the ancients is that one should infer [the same] for what follows as well.
However, in reality, [the cow] is not intended to be expressed in its specific form as an *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth, but rather precisely as the *karman* (object).

The meaning is that what is intended to be expressed as "unspoken" (akathita)—that is, such [factors] as the *apādāna* and others—should bear the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "object" (*karman*), because the designations, which pervade the status of being a *kāraka*, convey that their respective objects possess the capacity for "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth;
and the cognition [of this] is likewise. And thus, in the sentence "he milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), [the cow] has the cow as its object (*gokarmaka*).
And the understanding is precisely that "milking has milk as its object.
For, in the case of the root *ava-dā*, "flowing" is indeed the separation of a liquid substance from its source;
and that [separation] is brought about by an operation residing in the cow. And thus...

Because the cow is the locus of a specific disjunction consisting of a flow brought about by the agent's operation, and because the milk [is likewise the locus of such a flow], both possess the status of *karman* (object) precisely by virtue of the two preceding sūtras. Therefore, it is logical that there is a cognition of both as the object (*ubhayakarmaka*), and not a cognition of the cow merely as a related entity (*saṃbandhitva*). For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra:

Having raised the objection that the two preceding rules are redundant because the desired result is already established by the rule *akathitam* alone, [the author] notes that if the designation *karman* were applied here by this very rule even to that which is merely intended (*īpsitamātra*), then the rule *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* would find no scope of application; consequently, in the example *agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the boy away from the fire"), [the boy would be designated as the object].

Since the designation "object" (karman) would also apply to the boy (*māṇavaka*), the rule "that which is most desired by the agent is the object" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*) must be formulated; and then, in order to include both the hated and the indifferent, the rule "likewise that which is connected [with the action] though not desired" (*tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*) must be formulated—thus it has been resolved: "By this, the entire designation of 'object'..."
"It is established by the rule concerning the 'unspoken' (akathita). In that case, what would be the purpose of designating the desired object as a *karman*?

That which was previously mentioned as being connected with the desired object is for the sake of its establishment; however, that which is indeed the desired object itself will be [covered] by the rule concerning the 'unspoken'. Thus, by these two verses.

This is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. As for the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "by this [it is shown that] the object," it is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s *Bhāṣyapradīpa* and in the *Uddyota*; let us leave it at that for now. Regarding the phrase "he begs Bali":
the word "Hari" is to be supplied as the remainder. Bali was a particular demon; the request is "give [it] to me."
