The meaning is that it has been stated in the textual passage beginning with "the genitive case [is used] in *sarpiṣaḥ*," etc., that there is a connection [expressed] by the particle *eva* alone, and not by *api*; thus,
being "connected with a *karmapravacanīya*" means precisely being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the relation manifested by a *karmapravacanīya*.

And in the present case, the meaning is that the very word *vindu* (drop) is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the aforementioned relationship which is being illuminated by *api*, and not the word *sarpiḥ* (ghee). Thus, having illustrated *api* as illuminating a word-meaning (*padārtha*), he now illustrates it as illuminating a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*)—namely, in the phrase "he might praise" (*api stuyāt*). [This refers to the rule: "In the sense of possibility, with *alam*..."

The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of "if it were established even without [actual] application. He explains the term "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*) with the words beginning "Possibility..."—one might praise even Viṣṇu, who is beyond the reach of speech and mind;
the meaning is that one would be capable of praising him. This is an exaggeration (*atyukti*).

Because Viṣṇu is beyond the reach of speech and mind, it is impossible for anyone to praise him. In that context, since [api] functions as a *karmapravacanīya*, its status as a prefix (*upasarga*) is sublated; consequently, the rule "after a prefix, [the s of] *su* becomes *ṣ*" does not apply.
He provides an example illustrating its use to indicate permission (*anvavasarga*) with the words "api stuhi" (even praise). Whether you praise him or not—
The meaning is "do as you wish. He explains the term *anvavasarga* (permission) as "authorization for acting according to one's desire.

[In the rule] *praiṣātisargayoḥ*, the suffix *loṭ* is used. He provides an example of the particle *api* indicating censure: *api stuyādvṛṣalam* ("one might even praise a low-born man"). Here, the suffix *laṭ* is applied, overriding [the application of] *loṭ* by the rule *garhāyāṃ laḍapijātvoḥ*.

The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used here because of the priority [of the action] and its being *antaraṅga* (internal), as well as the sense of possibility. Here, because the outcaste (*vṛṣala*) is censurable, the particle *api* highlights that his praise is itself understood to be censurable. "Fie on Devadatta! is a restatement of that. He provides an example of *api* as an indicator of conjunction (*samuccaya*): *api*.

"Siñca api stuhi" (Sprinkle as well, praise as well). Because the two particles *api* joined together indicate a conjunction (*samuccaya*), each retains its status as a *karmapravacanīya*; consequently, there is no substitution of *ṣa* for *sa* in either case. The meaning is: "Sprinkle, and praise."

(549) *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* [Pāṇini 2.3.5]. "Of time and distance" (*kālādhvanoḥ*). Here [the word] "here" (*iha*) is used; the meaning is "in the case of absolute connection between time and distance. Absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyogaḥ*) is uninterrupted connection. An "end" (*antaḥ*) is a separation (*vicchedaḥ*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has transcended" (*atikrānta*) is "extreme" (*atyanta*), and that is the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

By virtue of propriety, it is understood as [conjunction] with qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and substances (*dravya*). The meaning is that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall be used when an uninterrupted conjunction (*avicchinna-saṃyoga*) between time (*kāla*) and distance (*adhvan*) is to be expressed by means of qualities, actions, and substances. And that [second case ending]—

[The suffix *kṛtvasuc*] occurs only after words denoting time (*kāla*) and distance (*adhvan*), because it is so prescribed [by Pāṇini]. In that context, he provides an example for the "absolute connection with a quality" (*guṇātyantasaṃyoga*): *māsaṃ kalyāṇī*. The word "is" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. A month consists of thirty days. The meaning is: she possesses auspiciousness continuously throughout that month. [Next, regarding] the "absolute connection with an action" (*kriyātyantasaṃyoga*):

He provides an example: "He studies for a month" (*māsam adhīte*). The meaning is that he studies continuously at the appropriate time every day during the thirty-day period. He provides an example of absolute connection with a substance (*dravya-atyanta-saṃyoga*): "Jaggery-roasted grains for a month" (*māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ*). The meaning is that jaggery-roasted grains exist continuously every day throughout the month.

Having illustrated connection with an extreme limit of time (*kāla-atyanta-saṃyoga*), he illustrates connection with an extreme limit of space (*adhvan-atyanta-saṃyoga*) with the example "crooked for a *krośa*" and so forth. Regarding "twice in a month": since a month consists of thirty days, "twice" means once every day during those two days; thus, the meaning is that he has studied twice [in total] within the month.

In the rule *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*, the suffix *suc* is added to the word *dvi* in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*). In the phrase [“he studies] twice a day”], the genitive case is used according to the rule *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe*. Some maintain that this is the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). However, in the expression “one should stay awake on Śivarātri,” the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) [is intended].

They say that the locative case is used because it is intended [as a secondary factor]. Their intention is that the case endings of subordinate words (*upapada-vibhakti*) function only when there is a desire to express them as a residual relation (*śeṣa*). Thus ends the section on the accusative. (550) *svatantraḥ kartā* | 1.4.54 | "The independent agent is the *kartṛ*."

Now, the third [sūtra]: "The independent (svatantra) is the agent (kartṛ). Since this occurs within the governing rule (adhikāra) concerning *kārakas*, he states—"in an action" (*kriyāyām*)—to indicate that independence intended here is the capacity to bring about an action.
It is clear in the Bhāṣya that independence here means predominance (*prādhānyam*). But how [is this so] in cases such as "the pot cooks" (*sthālī pacati*)?

Since the agency (*kartṛtva*) of pots and the like is due to the absence of independence (*svātantrya*), he says: "the intended meaning. The sense is that this is based on the *Bhāṣya*: "Kārakas arise from intention (*vivakṣā*). Furthermore, independence is the state of being the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The meaning of the verbal root is an activity conducive to the result. In that regard—

In the expression *pacati* ("he cooks"), the term "activity" (*vyāpāra*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), which serve as the substratum for the result consisting of the softening of the grains. And it has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "An agent is always intended to be that factor (*kāraka*) whose action is expressed by the verbal root. This means [the agent] is one who possesses the activity denoted by the verbal root.

(551) *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam* | 1.4.42 | "The most effective means is the instrument (*karaṇa*). [The word] "in the accomplishment of an action" means "in the arising of an action. This is understood from the governing context of *kāraka*s. "That which provides the most excellent assistance" refers to that which, by the agent, [is employed] in the action...
That which serves as an auxiliary in that which is to be produced is called "beneficial" (*upakāraka*).

This is the explanation of the term *sādhakatama*. From the word *sādhaka*, the suffix *tamap* is applied in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*), according to the rule *atiśāyane tamap*. The meaning is: that which is the most excellent producer (*sādhaka*) is the "most effective producer" (*sādhakatama*).
That whose operation immediately precedes the accomplishment of the action is the *prakṛṣṭa* (the most excellent).

That is to say, when the accomplishment of the action occurs without interval following the operation of that [factor] which is itself dependent on the operation of the agent, that [factor] is the *karaṇa* (instrument) in respect to that action.
Why is the suffix *tamap* included? One might simply say "that which effects" (*sādhaka*).

Since this [designation] is already established by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *kārakas*, the question arises as to why the term *sādhaka* (the achiever) is mentioned again; it is understood from this very mention that the sense is "the most effective achiever. Regarding the example *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ* ("a hamlet on the Ganges"):
the intention is that the maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) does not apply elsewhere in the section on *kārakas* except for this specific rule.

The inclusion of the suffix *tam* is for the purpose of making this known. Otherwise, in the rule "the locus (*ādhāra*) is the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*)," since the status of being a locus would already be obtained through the force of the great technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) which is etymologically significant (*anvartha*), the mention of it again by its own name would— by virtue of that specific mention— indicate that the locus is one where there is a pervasion of all its constituent parts (*sarvāvayavavyāpti*).

Thus, the meaning would be "that which is the locus" (*adhikaraṇa*). And in that case, [the term] would apply only in instances such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) and "clarified butter in curd" (*dadhi sarpiḥ*), but it would not apply in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) or "Garga's family in the well" (*kūpe gargakulam*). Therefore, it is stated clearly in the *Bhāṣya* that the mention of the superlative suffix (*tamap*) is for this purpose.
What needs to be said regarding this will be explained under the rules "The locus is the *adhikaraṇa*" and "The locative case is used for the *adhikaraṇa* and [other meanings].
(552) The third case ending is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). Pāṇini 2.3.18.
"The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument. Because of the introductory rule "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*), he says "not already expressed.
Regarding *rāmeṇa*: the meaning is that Vālī is the object of the action of killing, which has Rāma as its agent and the arrow as its instrument.
(1) An addition [to the rule] regarding *prakṛti* and so forth:
"An addition regarding *prakṛti* and so forth. The word "of the third case" (*tṛtīyāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as a remainder.
This is a governing case (*upapada-vibhakti*). It is an exception to all case-endings as appropriate. For example: *prakṛtyā*.

Regarding the word "cāru" (beautiful): the meaning of the third case [in *prakṛtyā*] is relation (*saṃbandha*). *Prakṛti* means inherent nature (*svabhāva*); thus, the sense is "one who possesses beauty related to that [nature]. However, when it is intended to exclude other instruments by specifying that "this person is handsome by his very nature, and not through ornaments and the like," then the inherent nature functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The *Bhāṣya* states: "If that is intended to be expressed, then it is already established by the rule *kartṛkaraṇayoḥ*. The example *prāyeṇa yājñikaḥ* is given. The word *prāya* signifies "abundance" (*bahula*).
Thus, the meaning is "one who possesses the status of a ritualist (*yājñikatva*) in connection with frequent practice. And as for this connection:

This is the relationship between the signified (*jñāpya*) and the signifier (*jñāpaka*). In the sense of "one who possesses the status of a sacrificer (*yājñika*) by means of frequent practice (*bahulena ācāreṇa*)," the rule *itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe* [Pāṇini 2.3.21] alone suffices.
In the sense of "one who possesses the status of a sacrificer through being endowed with frequent practice," it follows simply from the fact that [practice] is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The *bhāṣya* states: "It is established. Regarding the example *gotreṇa gārgyaḥ* ("By lineage, he is a Gārgya"), the meaning is "His lineage is Gārgya.

In this case, the nominative case (*prathamā*) would have been expected; however, the *bhāṣya* states that it is established by the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.21), in the sense of "one who possesses the state of being a Gārgya made known by the cause of his lineage. Similarly, [the examples] *samena eti* ("He goes by level ground") and *viṣameṇa eti* ("He goes by uneven ground" are explained).

This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The meaning is that it performs a movement that is both even and uneven. Although the accusative case would have been expected [for *samam* and *viṣamam* as objects], the *Bhāṣya* states that when the sense is "he goes by a path that is even or uneven," it is established precisely because they function as instruments (*karaṇa*). Regarding *dvidroṇena*: [it means] of two *droṇas*.

The compound *dvidroṇam* is a collective (*samāhāra*). Because it belongs to the class beginning with *pātra*, it does not take the feminine gender; the meaning is "grain related to two *droṇas*. [In this sense] the genitive case would have been required. However, according to the *Bhāṣya*, when the meaning is "he buys for gold that has the value of grain measured by two *droṇas*"—that is, "he buys for two *droṇas" [of gold]—it is established precisely because [the measure] functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

"By means of happiness" (*sukhena*): the meaning is that he makes a vehicle that produces happiness; it is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The accusative case would have been expected [if it were a direct object]. Regarding "and so forth": in the example *nāmnā sutīkṣṇaḥ*, the meaning is "one who possesses extreme sharpness related to his name. Alternatively, the meaning is "one who possesses extreme sharpness made known by his name."

In the case of "dhānyena dhanavān," however, non-difference (*abheda*) is the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*). But in the sense of "one who possesses sharpness indicated by the name," the rule "itthambhūtalakṣaṇe" alone is sufficient.
However, in the case of "dhānyena dhanavān," [non-difference is the meaning].

The meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) here is non-difference (*abheda*). Thus, the sense is "one who possesses wealth that is non-different from grain. However, in the expression "I know fire by means of its fire-ness" (*vahnitvena vahnim jānāmi*), the meaning of the third case is being a qualifier (*prakāratva*).
The sense is "I am one who possesses a cognition of fire having fire-ness as its qualifier," and so on; this should be inferred accordingly.
(553) *divaḥ karma ca* | 1|4|43|. The word *karma* ("object") is also [included] after *divaḥ*. The term *sādhakatamam* ("the most effective instrument") is understood to follow as well.

Thus he says: "the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamam*) of *divaḥ*. This means that which is the most effective instrument with respect to the meaning of the verbal root *div*. By the particle *ca* ("and"), [the category of "instrument" is also applied here].
The meaning is that by the use of the word "ca" (and), the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa-saṃjñaka*) is also obtained.

(554) *Apavarge tṛtīyā* | 2|3|6|. [The rule states: "The third case ending is used when there is completion (*apavarga*). Completion (*apavarga*) means termination; as in the example: "When the ritual work is completed, the worldly fires [are extinguished]."

This is seen in such instances as these. However, in the present case, because an action generally extends until the attainment of its result, he says: "Apavarga is the attainment of the result. Regarding the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*:
by this, it is indicated that this [usage] is an exception to the application of the second case (*dvitīyā*) prescribed by the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*. The example is *ahnā*.
The meaning is that a section (*anuvāka*) has been mastered through study, whether during the day or at night, without interruption.
"It has not come" (*nāyāta*) means it has not been mastered.
(555) *Sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19). [This sūtra provides the basis for the usage of the instrumental case with words joined by *saha* when the sense is that which is subordinate.]

Regarding the rule *sahayukte*: although the inclusion of the word *saha* alone would have sufficed—as in the case of the rule *pṛthagvinānānābhiḥ*—the inclusion of the word *yukta* (joined) is for the purpose of including other words that carry the sense of "together," such as *sākam* and so forth; thus he says, "by means of a word having the sense of *saha*. For example: *putreṇa*.

In this case, the father’s connection to the action of coming is expressed by the word (*śābda*), whereas the son’s connection is understood through association with that [action] and is thus implied (*ārthika*); hence, the son is subordinate. Although the instrumental case for the son is established simply because he is the agent of the action of coming, nevertheless, his usage is seen only in such expressions as "stout with the son" (*putreṇa saha sthūlaḥ*).
It is clear in the Bhāṣya that this is the primary example. He states the purpose of including the word *artha* (meaning) as follows: "In the same way, [the word] *sākam*. Now, one might ask:

in the sentence "The father has come with the son" (*putreṇāgataḥ pitā*), since there is no word such as *saha* (with), how can the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) be applied? To this he says: "Even without," referring to the rule *vṛddho yūnā tallakṣaṇaśced*.

The meaning is that even in the absence of words such as *saha* ("with"), and even when their meaning is understood, the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is observed [in the rule]. (556) *yenāṅgavikāraḥ* | 2|3|20|.

"By which there is a modification of a limb (*yenāṅgavikāraḥ*). A "limb" (*aṅga*) is that which possesses limbs; it refers to the body (*śarīra*). [The suffix] *ac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *arśas*.

The analysis of the compound is: "a modification of that [body]. By the word "by which" (*yena*), the limb—which constitutes the meaning of the base noun—is referred to. For indeed, a modification of the possessor of the limb (*aṅgin*) cannot occur through a limb that has not itself been modified.

He states this with the words beginning "by which limb," and so forth. In the expression "blind in the eye" (*akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*), the word *kāṇa* refers to one who possesses blindness. The meaning of the instrumental case is relation (*saṃbandha*). This relates to blindness. He states this by saying "related to the eye. And the relation consists in being caused by a modification (*vikāra*).

This means one who possesses blindness caused by a deformity of the eye. Although it is said that "one eye being defective is called blind," nevertheless, the usage of a property belonging to a part [the eye] for the whole body—or rather, for the self delimited by that [body]—is well-established. The use of the word *akṣṇā* (in the singular) is like the expression *dvau viprau* ("two Brahmins").

*samarthyaḥ* | (557) *itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe* | 2|3|21 | Regarding the characteristic of one who has become such (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). "In this manner" is *ittham*; one who has reached (*bhūta*) that state is *itthaṃbhūta*. [The root] *bhū*...

In the word *prāptau*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* etc., either from the root *prāp* belonging to the *curādigaṇa* or from the root *āp* belonging to the *tudādigaṇa* (as per the rule *ṭhādhṛṣādvā*). *Lakṣaṇam* means an indicator (*jñāpakam*).
The meaning is: "an indicator of that which has attained a particular state. Thus he says: "a certain particular state" (*kaṃcitprakāram*).

"A *tāpasa* (ascetic) by means of matted locks (*jaṭābhiḥ*). One who possesses austerity (*tapas*) is a *tāpasa*. The possessive suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "after *tapas* and *sahasra*, [the suffixes] *vinī* and *aṇ* [are used]" (*Pāṇini 5.2.102*). It refers to one who possesses the state of being an ascetic. The meaning of the instrumental case here is the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). Thus he says: "indicated by the matted locks" (*jaṭājñāpya*). And not in the sense of cognition...

It should not be said that the third case ending is established here simply because of [the word's] being an instrument (*karaṇa*), for when the status of being an instrument is not intended to be expressed, but rather only the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) is intended, the third case is required by its meaning. (558) *saṃjño 'nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.22). [This rule provides an option for the third case when the word *saṃjña* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). When the word *saṃjña* is used in the sense of the object, the third case ending may optionally be employed. For example: *mātrā saṃjñitaḥ* or *mātrayā saṃjñitaḥ* ("recognized by his mother"). Alternatively, the second case may be used: *mātaraṃ saṃjñitaḥ*. The mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is for the purpose of introducing the subsequent rule (*vibhāṣā kṛñi*, 2.3.23), which applies specifically to the verb root *kṛñ*. Thus, in the case of *kṛñ*, the third case is not optional; it is mandatory. For example: *mātrā saṃjñākṛtaḥ* ("made known by his mother"). Here, since the action of making known (*saṃjñākaraṇa*) is performed by means of the mother, she is the instrument, and thus the third case is obligatory. However, in the case of *mātrā saṃjñitaḥ*, the action of being made known is performed by the mother, but the status of being an instrument is not intended to be expressed; rather, only the relationship between the indicator and the indicated is intended. Therefore, the third case is applied here by virtue of its specific meaning. Furthermore, this is not merely a case of the third case being used as a substitute for the second case, as in the examples *mātrā saṃjñitaḥ* and *mātrayā saṃjñitaḥ*; rather, it is the third case itself that is prescribed by the rule's own meaning. This is because the rule *saṃjño 'nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* prescribes the third case specifically for the word *saṃjña* when it denotes the object. If one were to argue that the third case is established here solely on the basis of the word's being an instrument, then the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) would be redundant, as the third case would already be mandatory by the previous rule (*karaṇe kṛtā bahulam*, 2.3.18). Therefore, the third case is indeed established here by the specific meaning of the rule, even when the status of being an instrument is not intended. Consequently, the third case is not merely a substitute for the second case in these instances. Moreover, the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) serves to introduce the subsequent rule regarding the verb *kṛñ*, ensuring that the third case remains mandatory in that context. Thus, the third case is established here by the specific meaning of the rule. As for the subsequent rule: *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (2.3.23). When the verb root *kṛñ* follows, the third case ending is optionally used with the word *saṃjña* in the sense of the object. For example: *mātrā saṃjñākṛtaḥ* or *mātrayā saṃjñākṛtaḥ*. Since the action of making known is performed by means of the mother, she is the instrument, and thus the third case is mandatory. However, in the case of *mātrā saṃjñākṛtaḥ*, the action of making known is performed by the mother, but the status of being an instrument is not intended to be expressed; rather, only the relationship between the indicator and the indicated is intended. Therefore, the third case is applied here by virtue of its specific meaning. Furthermore, this is not merely a case of the third case being used as a substitute for the second case, as in the examples *mātrā saṃjñākṛtaḥ* and *mātrayā saṃjñākṛtaḥ*; rather, it is the third case itself that is prescribed by the rule's own meaning. This is because the rule *vibhāṣā kṛñi* prescribes the third case specifically for the word *saṃjña* when it denotes the object. If one were to argue that the third case is established here solely on the basis of the word's being an instrument, then the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) would be redundant, as the third case would already be mandatory by the previous rule (*karaṇe kṛtā bahulam*, 2.3.18). Therefore, the third case is indeed established here by the specific meaning of the rule, even when the status of being an instrument is not intended. Consequently, the third case is not merely a substitute for the second case in these instances. Moreover, the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) serves to introduce the subsequent rule regarding the verb *kṛñ*, ensuring that the third case remains mandatory in that context. Thus, the third case is established here by the specific meaning of the rule. As for the subsequent rule: *paryāptivacaneṣv alamartheṣu* (2.3.16). When words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*) in the sense of "enough" (*alam*) follow, the third case ending is used with the word denoting the object. For example: *alaṃ śrameṇa* ("enough of exertion"), *alaṃ bhuktena* ("enough of eating"), *alaṃ pānena* ("enough of drinking"). Since the action of stopping is performed by means of exertion, etc., they are the instruments, and thus the third case is mandatory. However, in the case of *alaṃ śrameṇa*, the action of stopping is performed by exertion, but the status of being an instrument is not intended to be expressed; rather, only the relationship between the indicator and the indicated is intended. Therefore, the third case is applied here by virtue of its specific meaning. Furthermore, this is not merely a case of the third case being used as a substitute for the second case, as in the examples *alaṃ śrameṇa* and *alaṃ bhuktena*; rather, it is the third case itself that is prescribed by the rule's own meaning. This is because the rule *paryāptivacaneṣv alamartheṣu* prescribes the third case specifically for the word denoting the object when used with words expressing sufficiency. If one were to argue that the third case is established here solely on the basis of the word's being an instrument, then the mention of "words expressing sufficiency" (*paryāptivacaneṣu*) would be redundant, as the third case would already be mandatory by the previous rule (*karaṇe kṛtā bahulam*, 2.3.18). Therefore, the third case is indeed established here by the specific meaning of the rule, even when the status of being an instrument is not intended. Consequently, the third case is not merely a substitute for the second case in these instances. Moreover, the mention of "words expressing sufficiency" (*paryāptivacaneṣu*) serves to introduce the subsequent rule regarding the verb *kṛñ*, ensuring that the third case remains mandatory in that context. Thus, the third case is established here by the specific meaning of the rule. As for the subsequent rule: *kṛñi ca yasya viṣayasya darśanam iṣyate* (Vārttika). When the verb root *kṛñ* follows, the third case ending is used with the word denoting the object, provided that the perception of that object is intended. For example: *alam odanena kṛtam* ("Enough of rice has been made"). Since the action of making is performed by means of rice, it is the instrument, and thus the third case is mandatory. However, in the case of *alam odanena kṛtam*, the action of making is performed by rice, but the status of being an instrument is not intended

*Saṃjño ’nyatarasyām*. This is the genitive singular form *saṃjñaḥ*, derived from the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the verbal root *jñā* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Thus he says: "of the root *jñā* preceded by *sam*. This optional third case ending (*tṛtīyā-vikalpa*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case. The example is *saṃjānīte*; the meaning is "he knows thoroughly" (*samyak jānīte*).
The ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *saṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne*.
(559) *hetau* | 2|3|23|. Regarding "in the sense of cause": here, "cause" (*hetu*) is a synonym for "reason" (*kāraṇa*) and is purely worldly.

The intended [meaning] is this, and not the artificial [definition] "the cause that prompts that [agent] is also called *hetu*," because since that [prompter] also possesses the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) due to the word *ca*, its case would already be established by the third case ending (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) alone. Now, one might object: "But surely the third case ending is established for the *hetu* as well, precisely because it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Anticipating this doubt:

He states the distinction between being a cause (*hetutva*) and being an instrument (*karaṇatva*): "common to substance and so forth. By "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) are included. The meaning is that it exists in every instance of that which is productive with respect to a substance, a quality, or an action. And it is "common to both the accomplishment (*nirvṛtti*) and the activity (*vyāpāra*)."
The meaning is that [causality] exists both in that which possesses an intermediate operation (*dvārībhūtavyāpāra*) and in that which is devoid of it.

And thus, the result is that causality is defined by the three types of effects—substance, quality, and action—and resides in both that which is without operation and that which possesses operation. As for "instrumentality" (*karaṇatva*), however, it resides only in that which produces an action.
The meaning is that the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is precisely that which possesses activity (*vyāpāravat*).
And thus, since the state of being a cause (*hetutva*) and the state of being an instrument are distinct, one is not rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*) by the other; this is the intended sense.
In that regard, he provides an example of a cause with respect to a substance: "the jar [is produced] by means of a staff."

The meaning is that a jar has the staff as its cause (*daṇḍahetuka*). The point is that even though there is activity (*vyāpāra*) in the staff, it does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) because it lacks the quality of being a producer of the action (*kriyājanakatva*). He provides an example of a cause with respect to an action: "Hari was seen by means of merit" (*puṇyena dṛṣṭo hariḥ*). [This refers to] speech and so forth.

The *apūrva* (unseen potency), which serves as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) in the production of results such as heaven, is called "merit" (*puṇya*). The point is that although it brings about the vision of Hari, it does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) because it lacks an [external] operation. However, when it is the cause with respect to a quality (*guṇa*), [the suffix -tṛc is used], as in "by merit" (*puṇyena*).

The examples beginning with "brahmavarcasam" (Vedic luster) should be cited here. Now, one might ask: how can there be an instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the expression "he dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*), given that study lacks the status of being a cause (*hetu*) for residing at the teacher's house; on the contrary, study is rather something to be accomplished by means of that residence? To this, he says: "In this context, even the result is considered a cause. [This refers to] study.
Although the fruit of dwelling (*vāsa*) is [the result], it nevertheless also serves as a cause for the dwelling;

because the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is the cause of engagement, and the fruit of study produces dwelling by way of its own knowledge. However, when such causality regarding the fruit of study is not intended to be expressed...

If residence (*vāsa*) is intended solely for the purpose of study (*adhyayana*), then the fourth case (*caturthī*) alone occurs—as in *adhyayanāya vasati* ("he dwells for the sake of study"). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra under discussion.
Now, [one might object]: in the case of *alaṃ śrameṇa* ("enough with effort"), since there is no action...
Since it is not heard in any instance, and because [the requirements for] being an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*) are impossible, how can there be a third case ending?

To this he says: "Even when implied" (*gamyamānāpi*). The meaning is that it is not only an action (*kriyā*) that is explicitly heard which motivates a case ending, but rather even one that is merely implied.

Intending that this [instrumental case] is indeed the third [kāraka], he says: "Enough with this toil. This statement was addressed to one who is attempting to cultivate a saline field. Here, *alam* functions in the sense of negation, as in the meaning of "not. Amarasimha states: "The word *alam* denotes ornament, sufficiency, capability, and prohibition."

The word "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) is to be supplied by ellipsis. Thus he says: "There is nothing to be accomplished through exertion. Because it immediately produces weariness, the very engagement in the means of accomplishment is metaphorically designated as "exertion. Now, even so, since the fruit to be accomplished—such as rice and the like—is not of the nature of an action (*kriyā*), how can there be exertion directed toward it?

To [the objection] that [exertion] is merely an instrument (*karaṇatva*), he says: "In this context" (*iha*). Regarding the word "sādhya," the meaning is: with reference to that action of accomplishment (*sādhanakriyā*) consisting of origination (*utpatti*), which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) that serves as the base in that term. By this, the claim that exertion (*śrama*) and the action of accomplishment are identical is refuted; for by the word "exertion" (*śrama*),...

Because by the phrase "with respect to the action that is the means" (*sādhanakriyāṃ prati*), both the activity such as plowing conducive to the production of rice and the like, and the production of the rice itself, are intended to be expressed. Regarding the statement "even an implied action is the motivator for a case-ending," he provides another example: "by a hundred," etc., in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
The word is repeated. The understood meaning is that one causes the calves to drink [milk] by means of a hundred each.

In that context, since the number "hundred" residing in the calves lacks the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of drinking, it is understood as "having delimited" [the milk] by means of the number "hundred" for each individual calf. By means of the number "hundred" for each one...

The meaning is that she causes [them] to drink by separating the calves from those who possess more than [their share]. Thus, the sense is that the number "hundred" functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of separation.
(1) In the usage of unrefined people (*aśiṣṭa*), when the verb *dāṇ* (to give) is employed, the third case is used in the sense of the fourth case.

Regarding the term *aśiṣṭa* (unrefined): this will be explained in the section on the determination of words (*padavyavasthā*), where it is stated that this [usage] is made known by the rule "dāṇaśca sā ceccaturthyarthe" (Pāṇini 1.3.55). Those who follow the Vedic path are *śiṣṭas* (refined);
those who have departed from the Vedic path are *aśiṣṭas* (unrefined). Their *vyavahāra*—that is, their conduct—is the subject matter here.
The meaning is that when the root *dā* (to give) is employed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) in the sense of the fourth case (*caturthī*).

Regarding the example "dāsyā" (by/for the maidservant): the meaning is that the lover gives [something] to the maidservant. By the word "kāmuka" (lover), it is understood that this is for the sake of sexual pleasure (*raty-artham*). [This occurs] with respect to the maidservant.

The sense is that pleasure (*rati*) is not the practice of the cultured (*aśiṣṭa-vyavahāra*) because it is prohibited by the treatises on dharma (*dharma-śāstra*). He states the purpose of using the word *aśiṣṭa*: "But in the case of what is consistent with dharma" (*dharmye tu*). The meaning is "not deviating from dharma" (*dharmād-anapeta*). The phrase "not in the third [case]" (*na tṛtīye*) is to be supplied. This is according to the rule: "In the sense of 'not deviating from,' [the suffix yat is used] after the words *dharma*, *pathin*, *artha*, and *nyāya*. (*Pāṇini 4.4.92*)

*Ratnākara* [comments]: As for the reading *dharme tu*, it is indeed easy to understand. Thus ends the third [case]. (560) "That which one intends through an object is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). 1.4.32. Now, the fourth [case]: "that which one intends through an object. By means of an object designated as a "karma" (object), such as a substance like a cow, that which one intends—

The meaning is that one determines [the recipient] as being the "remainder" (śeṣin); "remainder-ness" (śeṣitva) means the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva). This is a designation based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): that to which something is given is the *saṃpradāna*. Consequently, when there is an expectancy as to which action's object it is, it is understood to be the object of the act of giving (*dāna*).

He says this with the words beginning "of giving" (*dānasya*), etc. The result is that the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is the intended object of the substance to be given. What is the purpose of saying "of giving"? [Consider: *payo nayati devadattasya* ("he brings milk for Devadatta"). Here, although Devadatta is the intended object of the bringing of the milk, he does not have the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), because [the milk] belongs to Devadatta.
Because it lacks the nature of the act of giving (*dānakarma*).
(561) *Caturthī saṃpradāne* |2|3|13|.
The fourth case ending is used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). As in *viprāya* ("to the Brahmin"). The meaning is: "he gives a cow with reference to the Brahmin."

"Only when not already expressed"—this is the meaning of "it continues to apply. In the example *dānīyo vipraḥ* ("the Brahmin to whom a gift is to be given"), the sense is "the intended recipient of a gift. Because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *anīyar* is used here in the sense of the *saṃpradāna* (recipient). Thus, by that [suffix], the status of being the recipient is expressed.

The intention is that because [the recipient] has been designated by the word *vipra*, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is not applied. Now, one might raise the objection: "If the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) belongs only to the intended object of the act of giving, then how can the husband in the expression 'she lies with her husband' (*patye śete*) be a recipient, since he is the intended object of the intransitive act of lying down? In response to this doubt:
The Vārttika "The mention of 'action' (kriyā) must also be made" has been introduced. [It states: "That person whom one intends through an action is also the recipient (saṃpradāna).
This very point is summarized according to its meaning as "that person whom [one intends] by means of an action. Thus, even that which is the objective of an action [is included].

"Saṃpradāna" means "giving. In the example "she lies for her husband" (*patye śete*), the meaning is that she lies with reference to the husband. Now, one might object: even so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the object] in "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) and similar cases also being designated as *saṃpradāna*. Nor should it be suspected that the rule prescribing the technical term "object" (*karman*) is redundant; for this very reason, in those cases...

If it is argued that this is not so because the optionality (*vikalpa*) between the status of object (*karmatva*) and recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) would be established, we say no; for the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna-saṃjñā*), which finds its scope in intransitive instances such as "she lies down for her husband" (*patye śete*), is superseded by the designation of object (*karman-saṃjñā*) in transitive instances. And thus, even that which is intended by an intransitive action [is designated as the object].
The meaning is that it bears fruit as "the recipient" (*saṃpradāna*).

[In this case,] there is the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) for the "object" (*karman*), and the designation of "object" for the "recipient. The statement beginning with "the designation of instrument for the object" is a *vārttika*. In a single sentence, regarding the object...
And the remainder [of the rule] is "when there is a conjunction with the recipient" (*saṃpradāna*).
Intending that this refers specifically to the domain of the verbal root *yaj* (to sacrifice), he provides an example: "He sacrifices to Rudra with an animal" (*paśunā rudraṃ yajate*).
Intending that here the verbal root *yaj* has the meaning of "giving," he says: "The meaning is 'he gives'" (*dadātītyarthaḥ*). This...
Kaiyaṭa states that the *vārttika* is indeed Vedic.

(562) *Rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ* | 1.4.33. Regarding "of those having the sense of *ruc*" (*rucyarthānām*): it refers to roots having the sense of *ruc*. [The root] *ruc* [is used] in the senses of "shining" (*dīpti*) and "pleasing" (*abhiprīti*).

In this context, "dīpti" (illumination) does not mean "desire," because that would contradict the term "prīyamāṇa" (being pleased). Thus, its meaning is "those things which have the purpose of generating pleasure. Regarding "prīyamāṇa": it means the substratum of pleasure by way of inherence (*samavāya*). In the expression "devotion is pleasing to Hari," devotion [produces] pleasure directed toward its own object, Hari.
The meaning is "he produces. Since Hari is the locus of the pleasure induced by the activity residing in devotion, he would attain the status of an object (*karman*);

this [sūtra] is an exception to that. Now, if this were so, then in the case of *harir bhaktim abhilaṣati* ("Hari desires devotion"), devotion would also have the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) because it is the object of the pleasure; to this he says: "when [the action] has another as its agent" (*anyakartṛke*).

The meaning of the verbal root *ruc* is a desire whose agent is something other than the locus of pleasure (*prīti*), with reference to that [locus] through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). A "desire" (*abhilāṣa*) is a specific kind of wish directed toward some object, having as its agent the locus of pleasure.
Consequently, because the verb *abhilaṣati* lacks the sense of *ruc*, there is no status of recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) when it is used in conjunction with it.

In the present context, Hari is the locus of love; devotion (*bhakti*) is that which is other than Him, and it is precisely by means of that [devotion] that love is produced—thus there is a connection with a root meaning "to please" (*ruci*). Now, one might ask: why is devotion not here treated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), since devotion too is the locus of love through the relation of being its object? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "Devotion (*bhakti*) is the agent of the pleasure residing in Hari. The point is that since Hari alone is the locus of pleasure through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), he is the one being pleased; and because devotion, as the agent, is not being pleased in the manner described above, it does not possess the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*). [Thus,] devotion [is directed toward] Hari.

However, in cases such as *prīṇāti* (he pleases) and *prīṇayati* (he causes to please), there is no possibility of *bhakti* being the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), because it is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and because it lacks the status of being the substratum of pleasure through inherence (*samavāya*). Nor can *hari* be the recipient,
since the suffix *sānac* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) in the word *prīyamāṇa* when joined with the root *prī*.

This is because the rule *rucyarthānām* (Pāṇini 1.4.33) is not applicable here, as it is understood [otherwise]; for otherwise, if the object of the root *prī* were designated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), it would be difficult to obtain the suffix *śānac* in the sense of the object. Regarding the example *modakaḥ pathi* ("the sweetmeat on the road"):
the point is that the road (*path*) cannot be the recipient because it lacks the quality of being pleased (*prīyamāṇatva*).

(563) *ślāgh-hnuṅ-sthā-śapām jñīpsyamānaḥ* | 1|4|34| The rule concerns the verbs *ślāgh*, *hnuṅ*, *sthā*, and *śap*. *Ślāghṛ* means "to praise" (*katthana*), *hnuṅ* means "to take away" (*apanayana*), *ṣṭhā* means "to stop moving" (*gati-nivṛtti*), and *śap* means "to reproach" (*upālambha*). These form a *dvandva* compound. After the word *śapām*, the word *prayoge* ("in the usage of") is to be understood.

This is to be supplied [in the text]. The meaning of *ślāgh* and the other [roots] is "making known" through praise and so forth, as indicated by the word *jñīpsyamānaḥ*. The suffix *śānac* is used in the passive sense (*karman*) derived from the desiderative form of the root *jñap*, which signifies "making known.
Thus he says: "In the usage of these," and so on. [The example is: "The cowherd woman [speaks] out of passion," etc.

The meaning is that, under the influence of the torment of love, Anopī makes Kṛṣṇa aware of her pain of separation through self-praise. However, some say that if Kṛṣṇa alone were the object of praise, the second person would be used.
Regarding "she conceals" (hnute): the meaning is that she makes Kṛṣṇa aware of her intention by removing her co-wife.

"Tiṣṭhate" means that even when told "you must go," she makes her intention known to Kṛṣṇa by remaining [there]. The ātmanepada ending is used according to the rule *ṭhprakāśanastheyākhyayośca*. "Śapate" means that she makes her intention known to Kṛṣṇa through reproach.
(564) *dhāreruttamarṇaḥ* | P. 1.4.35. Regarding *dhāreruttamarṇaḥ*: after *dhāreḥ*, the word *prayoge* ("in usage") is to be supplied.
The form *dhāreḥ* is the citation of the root *dhṛṅ* ("to stand, to persist") with the causative suffix *ṇic*.

He says this with the words beginning "of the root dhṛ" (to hold): a thing belonging to another owner that is taken for a fixed period with the intention of returning it is called a debt (*ṛṇa*). In that context, the one who takes the debt is the debtor (*adhamarṇa*), and the one who returns the debt—the owner of the wealth—is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that debt which has reached its maximum through an increase of eighty parts each month.

Regarding the word *bhaktāya*: it means that which sustains (*dhārayati*) liberation (*mokṣa*)—specifically, the particular, immeasurable, eternal bliss associated with the devotee (*bhakta*). Liberation is sustained [by Him].
The meaning is that He remains present. He impels, sustains, or—in other words—establishes that [devotee].
For a devotee, while worshipping, offers substances such as *tulasī* leaves; and Hari, receiving them with satisfaction, redeems those offered substances by granting liberation. Thus they say:
The Paurāṇikas say: "Whether it be water, a leaf, or whatever else is offered with devotion, the Lord considers that debt and regards liberation itself as the repayment.

Accordingly, in this context, because the devotee is the giver of the debt, he possesses the status of a creditor (*uttamarṇa*), and thus [the Lord] possesses the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
An exception to the genitive of relationship:

(565) *spṛherīpsitaḥ* | 1.4.36 | "The desired object of the root *spṛh*. The root *spṛh* meaning "desire" belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in a long vowel (*ā*). From that [root], in its own sense...

Because of the status as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if being the original) for the elision (*allopasya*) [of the penultimate vowel] in the causative (*ṇic*), there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitution [required by the rule] for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).
Therefore, the genitive singular is formed from the word *spṛhi*. The word "in usage" (*prayoge*) must be supplied.
Thus he says: "of the root *spṛh*" and so forth. But is it not simply "he desires flowers" (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*)?
It might be so, but [the form] *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* would not be [justified] either; yet both are desired. To this he says:

"merely that which is desired" (*īpsitamātre*). But when there is no intention to express even the state of being desired, but rather only the intention to express the mere state of being an object, then *puṣpāṇāṃ spṛhayati* is correct. [As in: *kumāryaḥ...*

This is because we see such statements as, "They tremble at their beloved and long for him. However, in the *Vākyapadīya*, it is established that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) and the genitive case of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) when used in conjunction with the verb *spṛhayati*. Helārāja also holds this view. According to his opinion, one says: *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers").
The forms such as *puṣpāṇāṃ spṛhayati* are indeed incorrect; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

(566) *krudhadruherṣyāsūyārthānāṃ yaṃ prati kopaḥ* | 1.4.37. [The rule] *krudhadruha-* [is explained as] *krudhādyarthānām iti*. [The roots] *krudh* [in the sense of] "anger" and *druh* [in the sense of] "malice."

The suffixes *śyan* and *vikaraṇa* [are applied]. *Īrṣya* in the sense of "envy" takes the *śap* suffix; *asūñ* in the sense of "affliction" belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose meanings are precisely the meanings of these [roots]. Regarding the example *haraye krudhyati*: the word *rāvaṇādi* (beginning with Rāvaṇa) is to be understood as the object of the remainder [of the sentence]. It means "he feels anger directed toward Hari."
The meaning is "he does. *Ghāti* (in *ghātayati*) refers to anger, which is a specific modification of the mind not necessarily concomitant with physical striking.

Since it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the genitive case would have been required [for the object]. Regarding *druhyati*: the meaning is that, out of anger, one performs an injury directed toward Hari. Since it is intransitive, the genitive case would have been required. Injury (*apakāra*) is that which produces suffering.

[The root] *kriyā* [is used here]. Because it includes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is transitive (*sakarmaka*). Regarding *īrṣyati*: *īrṣyā* is intolerance. The meaning is that he does not tolerate Hari due to anger. The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would thus be required for the object (*karman*). Or, regarding *asūyati*: *asūyā* is the attribution of faults to virtues. [This occurs] in the practice of actions as prescribed.
The meaning is that, having attributed hypocrisy and so forth [to Hari], he perceives Hari as possessing bad qualities out of anger in this instance.

Regarding the phrase "mainām": the meaning is that he attributes faults to the virtues of his wife for the purpose of ensuring that no one else sees her. Here, there is no anger directed toward the wife; rather—
It should be understood that what is intended to be expressed is simply that one cannot endure her being seen by another.

And thus, it is established in the Bhāṣya that this [usage] occurs only when anger, malice, envy, and jealousy are rooted in resentment (*kopa*). Consequently, forms such as *kupyati kasmai cit* (he is angry with someone) are indeed ungrammatical.
This is because [the root *man*] lacks the quality of being rooted in anger and lacks the meaning of "to be angry. For anger (*krodha*) is indeed fully developed wrath;
as stated in the Bhāṣya: "One who has not been provoked does not become angry" (*na hy akupitaḥ krudhyati*).
(Pāṇini 1.4.38): "When the roots *krudh* and *druh* are accompanied by a prefix, that which they govern is the object (*karman*)."

Regarding the rule *krudhadruhoḥ*: he explains the phrase *upasṛṣṭayoḥ* as "when accompanied by a prefix. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding sūtra. Since Hari is not the intended object of anger or malice, the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*)—defined by the rule *kriyayā yam abhipraiti*—"him whom one intends through the action"—does not apply here. Nor...

[This refers to] the dative case used in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*). Because *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice) are intransitive, Hari does not have the status of an object (*karman*). Therefore, when the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise apply, there is a specific rule establishing the status of the object.
(568) Pāṇini 1.4.39: *rādhīkṣyoryasya vipraśnaḥ*. [The person whose inquiry is made regarding someone else is the object of the roots *rādh* and *īkṣ*.]
Regarding *rādhīkṣyoḥ*: "yadīya" means "having that as its object. He explains the term "vipraśna" as "various questions. [The examples are: *kṛṣṇāya rādhyati* or *īkṣate*.
Regarding "pṛṣṭo gargaḥ": Garga was a specific sage (*ṛṣi*) who knew the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥ-śāstra*). He...
The grammatical construction is: "He divines or gazes for Kṛṣṇa. The roots are *rādha* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*) and *īkṣa* in the sense of "seeing" (*darśana*).

However, in this context, the meaning is the consideration of the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness regarding the subject of inquiry, as indicated by the rule "yasya vipraśne" (Pāṇini 1.4.39). Thus he says: "the meaning is that he considers the auspicious and the inauspicious. In this regard—

These two [roots] take as their objects the auspicious (*śubha*) and the inauspicious (*aśubha*), which are subsumed under the meaning of the verbal root; therefore, the suffix *śyan* in the form *rādhyati* is justified. Otherwise, by the rule "after the root *rādh*, when it is intransitive," the suffix *śyan* would not occur. And thus, when asked, "What is the auspicious or inauspicious for Kṛṣṇa?"...

The meaning is that Garga deliberates upon the auspicious and inauspicious concerning Kṛṣṇa. Kṛṣṇa’s status as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is established; this is an exception to the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
(569) *pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ pūrvasya kartā* (Pāṇini 1.4.40): [The agent of the preceding action is called the recipient when used with the roots *śru* preceded by *prati* or *ā*.]
[The rule applies] after *prati* and *āṅ*. In the expression *pratyāṅbhyām*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of direction (*digyoga*).

The word *parasya* (of another) is to be supplied as an ellipsis, serving as a qualifier for the root *śru*. [The root] *śru* [is listed] in the sense of "hearing" (*śravaṇe*), but here it functions in the sense of "accepting preceded by an instigation" (*preraṇāpūrvakābhyupagame*). The word *pūrva* [refers to] the operation consisting of instigation (*preraṇātmakavyāpāra*).

He reflects upon this and says, beginning with "by these two," and so forth. The explanation of the term "of the preceding" is "of that which consists of setting in motion"; the meaning is "of that which consists of impelling.
By the phrase "after *prati* and *āṅ*," it is not intended to mean "after [the verb] that follows both [prefixes taken together]."
However, both prefixes [pra- and prati-] are indeed required for this meaning; otherwise, he would have simply said "pratyāṅ śruvaḥ," as in the case of the rule "abhiniviśaśca.
With this intention, he provides the examples: "viprāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti" or "āśṛṇoti. Here, the root is preceded by both *prati* and *āṅ*.
The verbal root *śru* (to hear) denotes acceptance preceded by an instigation; consequently, it is understood that "one who has been instigated promises.

When there arises the expectancy as to "by whom was he instigated?", the Brahmin is construed as the agent (*kartṛ*). In that context, because the Brahmin is the agent of the instigation, he possesses the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Intending to state that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the instrumental case used for the agent, he says: "by the Brahmin" (*vipreṇa*).
The construction is as follows: having been asked by the Brahmin, "Give me desirable wealth such as cattle," Devadatta agrees, saying, "I give to you."

(570) *anupratiguṇaśca* |1|4|41|. The phrase *anupratiguṇaśca* [is the sūtra]. The word *pūrvasya kartuḥ* ("of the preceding agent") is understood here as well. Regarding the form *gṛṇaḥ*, it is the genitive case of the root *gṛ*—meaning "to sound"—which ends in *śnā* and is used here as a representative word (*anukaraṇaśabda*). In this context, the root is *gṛ*.

The root *śaṃs* functions in the sense of inciting someone toward the act of praising. In that context, the meaning is that the agent of the prior action of praising is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Thus he says: "by these two" (*ābhyām*), referring to *prati* and *āṅ* in the preceding rule.

By the force of the dual-number indication, it is determined that the connection with the verbal root applies to each [action] individually; intending that here too, by association with those [examples], the connection with the verbal root applies only individually, he cites:
"He responds to the Hotṛ, or he recites in response. Hotṛ...

Regarding the word "firstly": it means that he encourages the *hotṛ* priest, the reciter, toward the successive acts of recitation. The response formula (*pratigara-mantra*) is "o-tha mo-da vai. Here, "o" is used as a vocative; "modai" is the first person singular imperative; and "vai" [is a particle].

This is for the purpose of the particle *eva* (only/indeed). O Hotṛ! The meaning is: "Now, after your recitation (*śaṃsana*), I shall indeed be pleased. Since the Hotṛ would otherwise be understood as the object (*karman*) in the act of encouraging, his status as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is established because he is the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to the preceding activity, namely the recitation.

(571) *parikrayaṇe saṃpradānam anyatarasyām* | 1.4.44. Regarding "in the case of hiring": it means for a fixed period of time. [The construction is as follows: "This much wages are given to you; accepting that, you shall be my servant for this long a time. Thus.
The meaning of *parikrayaṇa* (purchase) is the acquisition [of a person] by means of a limited time as a servant.
The term *sādhakatamam* (the most effective instrument) is understood to follow here. Thus he says: "In that case, it is the most effective instrument.
In the absence of the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient), there is the designation *karaṇa* (instrument). As in the example: "by means of a hundred [pieces]."

The meaning is "by means of some hundred of substances such as gold. The dative case is to be stated in the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that). Regarding the rule "the dative is used in the sense of *tādarthya*," this is stated in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "the dative is used in the sense of the recipient" (*caturthī saṃpradāne*).

This has been recited. "Tadartha" means "for that purpose. There is an obligatory compound with the word *artha*. The state of being for that purpose is *tādarthya*. The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class of stems. And by this, the relationship of the beneficiary and the benefactor (*upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva*) is intended. In that context, the fourth case ending is used only after the beneficiary.

Intending to show that this is because it has been cited in the Bhāṣya as "wood for a sacrificial post" (yūpāya dāru) and "gold for an earring" (kuṇḍalāya hiraṇyam), he provides the example: "for liberation" (muktaye).
This means "for the sake of liberation. Furthermore, the state of being assisted is manifold, such as being produced and so forth. For example:

In the expression "He worships Hari for liberation" (*muktaye hariṃ bhajati*), it is understood that liberation is something produced (*janya*). Or, [it may be understood as] something to be attained (*prāpya*), as in "Curd for the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya dadhi*), where it is understood that the Brāhmaṇa is the recipient of benefit (*upakārya*), and so forth. Even if this were the case, since [the meaning] would already be established by this very [usage], the rule "The fourth case-affix is used in the sense of the *saṃpradāna*" (*caturthī saṃpradāne*) would be redundant if it were merely intended to prescribe the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *saṃpradāna*.

Nor should it be said that [the mention of the object] is redundant; for it is clear in the Bhāṣya that such [mention] is necessary in cases such as "devotion is pleasing to Hari" (*haraye rocate bhaktiḥ*), because of the rule "the one being pleased is the [object] of verbs meaning 'to please'" (*rūcyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*).
Also [the object is mentioned] in the case of the root *klṛp* when it signifies becoming (*saṃpadyamāne*).
Regarding the rule *klṛpi saṃpadyamāne ca*: *klṛpi* is the locative case.

*Saṃpattiḥ* means arising in the form of a transformation; that is to say, modification (*pariṇāma*). When the root *klṛp* is employed, the fourth case ending is used for a word expressing that which is being transformed.
The meaning is "is to be expressed. Regarding the word *bhakti*: the meaning is that it transforms into the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Intending to show that the root *klṛp* includes various meanings, he provides examples—such as *saṃpadyate* (is produced) and *jāyate* (is born).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), forms such as *pariṇamate* (transforms) are included.

This statement is intended to produce a cognition characterized by the mode of "being a transformation. Otherwise, they say it would already be established by the dative case itself when used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*).
[And it is also used] when something is indicated by a portent (*utpāta*).

"And when indicated by an *utpāta* (portent). An *utpāta* is a sudden, inauspicious transformation of natural elements; the meaning is that the fourth case (*caturthī*) should be expressed for the object indicated by such a portent. In the example "for the wind" (*vātāya*), the meaning is "indicative of a great wind."
And also in connection with *hita*.

Regarding "and also in connection with *hita*": the remainder [of the rule] is "the dative case (*caturthī*) when [the sense of] 'beneficial' (*vācye*) is to be expressed. In the example *brāhmaṇāya hitam*, the meaning is "beneficial to the Brāhmaṇa," that is, "that which produces happiness for the Brāhmaṇa. The remainder [of the context] is "such as officiating at sacrifices" (*yājanādi*).
(572) *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ* |2|3|14|. "Having an action as its purpose" (*kriyārtha*): that whose purpose or motive is an action is "having an action as its purpose.
The word "action" (*kriyā*) is to be supplied as the qualified term (*viśeṣya*). That is to say, it refers to a word denoting an action that has another action as its fruit.

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a verb as its *upapada* (governing word) for the sake of an action. This is an adjective qualifying the suffix *tumun*. An *upapada* is a word uttered in proximity [to another]. The term "*sthānin*" is also an adjective qualifying that [suffix]; the analysis is:
"that which has a *sthāna* (occasion of occurrence) is a *sthānin*. *Sthāna* means "occurrence" (*prasakti*). Thus is the analysis.

The phrase "of one who is not applying [the effort]" (aprayujyamānasya) is understood as the limit [of the application]. It follows that for such a word ending in *tumun*, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

By virtue of the rule prescribing *tumun*—"the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when another action is intended as the purpose of the action"—it is established that the subordinate word (*upapada*), which has an action as its fruit, must itself denote an action.

He says this: "An action [is used] for the sake of another action. The explanation of the term "of that which is not employed" (*sthāninaḥ*) is "of that which is not being used" (*aprayujyamānasya*). To the question, "In the example 'he goes for the sake of fruits' (*phalebhyo yāti*), what is the possibility of a suffix ending in *tumun*?
he replies: "in order to fetch the fruits" (*phalāny āhartum iti*). Here...

The act of going (*yāna-kriyā*) has as its purpose the act of fetching fruit (*phalāharaṇa-kriyā*). When that [act of going] is expressed as a subordinate element (*upapada*), the dative case is used for the fruits—which serve as the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of fetching (the meaning of which is obtained through the ellipsis of *āhartum* and is derived from the suffix *tumun*)—and thus it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accusative case. Nor is the meaning already conveyed by the dative case expressing "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya-caturthī*).
It is not to be doubted, for the act of going (*yāna*) is not for the sake of the fruit; rather, it is solely for the sake of the act of fetching which has the fruit as its object.

Therefore, there is no possibility of the dative case in the sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) applied to the fruits. And thus, the understanding is that the act of going is for the sake of the act of fetching which has the fruit as its object.
He states another example: "We pay homage" (*namaskurmaḥ*). He shows the ellipsis of the meaning of the suffix *-tumun* (infinitive) by saying:

"in order to propitiate Nṛsiṃha. Nor should it be argued that the dative case here is established by the rule *namaḥ-svasti-*, for "the case ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is stronger than a case ending based on a governing word (*upapada-vibhakti*)."
Thus ends the second case. This other example has been shown precisely for the purpose of indicating this.
(573) *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt* |2|3|15|. [The portion] *tumarthācca*: the rule is *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*.

When an action is the subordinate element (*upapada*) for actions whose purpose is another action, the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* occur in the future tense. For example: *bhoktuṃ vrajati* (he goes to eat) and *bhojako vrajati* (he goes as one who will eat).
Here, the verb *vrajati* (he goes) has as its purpose the future act of eating; this is the meaning of the suffix *tumun*.
The analysis of the compound is: "that from which the sense of *iva* [is derived]. *Bhāva* means action (*kriyā*). *Vacana* means that by which something is expressed;

thus, *bhāvavacana* means "expressing an action"—this is the analysis. It means, in other words, "expressing an action. The word "*pratyayāt*" (from a suffix) is to be supplied as the remainder. In this context, there is the rule: "*avyayakṛto bhāve*" (the *kṛt* suffixes added to indeclinables denote the action itself).

Since it is already established that a suffix expressing the sense of *tumun* (the infinitive suffix *-tum*) denotes "action" (*bhāva*) by virtue of being prescribed for that very purpose, the author states— "and those denoting action"— in order to include specific rules [of the *Pāṇinian* system].

The meaning is this: with the governing rule *bhāve* (in the sense of "being" or "state") in force, those suffixes such as *ghañ* that are prescribed [to denote a state] shall occur when there is a future action serving as an *upapada* (an accompanying word) for the sake of another action;
"he goes for the sake of sacrifice" (*yāgāya yāti*) and so forth are examples. And thus:
The qualification "after a word having the sense of *tumun*" (*tumarthāt*) is intended to secure the status of being a complement (*upapada*) for the sake of [denoting] the purpose of an action.

Since, in this case, the sense of "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) is already expressed by the suffix *ghañ* just as it is by *tumun*, the dative case expressing "being for that purpose" does not apply according to the maxim "that which has already been expressed need not be employed.
Consequently, when the nominative case would otherwise apply, this rule [prescribes the dative].

What is the purpose of the phrase "for the sake of that" (*tumarthāt*)? In examples such as *pākaḥ* ("cooking") or *tyāgaḥ* ("giving"), although the suffix *ghañ* occurs under the governing rule "in the sense of an action" (*bhāve*), the dative case does not apply; this is because, lacking a verb as a subordinate element whose object is the action, there is no sense of "for the sake of that. Why the phrase "from a word denoting a state of being" (*bhāvavacanāt*)? Consider *pācako vrajati* ("the cook goes").
The meaning is "he goes for the purpose of cooking. The suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *tumun-ṇvulau*.
Although this suffix has the sense of *tumun*, the dative case is not employed because there is no specific rule prescribing it under the governing heading *bhāve* (in the sense of an action).

Since the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is already expressed by the suffix *ṇvul* itself, the dative of purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*) does not apply; rather, the nominative case alone is used.

(574) *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alaṃ-vaṣaṭ-yogācca* || 2.3.16 || The word *yoga* means "that which is joined" (*yujyate*), derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, the meaning is: "when joined with [the words] *namas* and so forth. He states the resulting sense: "in connection with these. And not... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

It might be suspected that the meaning [of the sixth case] is already conveyed by the dative of purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*); however, this is not so, because the dative of purpose is intended to preclude the use of the sixth case when one wishes to express that the state of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*) constitutes a relationship of subordination (*śeṣatva*). For *tādarthya* is indeed the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor;
when this is manifested as a general relation, the sixth case is used, as in "this belongs to the teacher" (*guroridaṃ*) or "this is for the teacher" (*gurvartham*).

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. And thus, this sūtra is intended to establish that when words such as *namaḥ* (salutation), *svasti* (well-being), and others are used, the dative case alone must be employed even when there is a desire to express the "subordinate status" (*śeṣatva*) of the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*).
(1) The case ending denoting a kāraka is stronger than the case ending arising from a governing word (*upapada*).

One might object that the dative case should also apply here in the example "he pays homage to the gods" (*namaskaroti devān*). To this, he says: "of the case-ending of the subordinate word" (*upapadavibhakteḥ*).

A case-ending caused by connection with another word is a "case-ending of the subordinate word" (*upapadavibhakti*); the meaning is that the case-ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is stronger than that.

This statement is cited in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *antarāntareṇa*. And it is established by reasoning (*nyāyasiddha*). For the relationship between an action and its factor (*kāraka*) is indeed "internal" (*antaraṅga*). However, the relationship with the meaning of an upapada is based on some degree of the relation of action and factor; therefore, that [relationship] is [external].

Kaiyaṭa maintains that case endings (*vibhakti*) are extrinsic (*bahir-aṅga*). Others, however, hold that through the case ending of the *upapada* (governing word), a general relationship is understood, whereas the comprehension of the specific [relationship] is obtained by considering the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors; but by the case ending of the *kāraka* (grammatical participant)...

They say that because the specific relation, such as "being an object" (*karmatva*), is understood immediately, this [meaning] is stronger. For example, in the expression *namaskaroti devān* ("he pays homage to the gods"), the meaning is that he pleases them through the joining of hands to the head and so forth; for if it meant merely the joining of hands to the head and such, it would result in the verb being intransitive (*akarmaka*).
"May there be well-being for the subjects (*prajābhyaḥ svasti*). This means welfare pertaining to the subjects. "To Agni, *svāhā*" (*agnaye svāhā*);

this means the offering of a substance intended for Agni. "To the ancestors, *svadhā*" (*pitṛbhyaḥ svadhā*); this means the offering of a substance intended for the ancestors. According to the rule "the word's own form [is its name]," it refers to the word *ala* itself.

In the case of inclusion, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the example "ornaments for young girls" (*kumārīṇām alaṅkāraḥ*). Furthermore, [the rule] would apply only to "Hari is enough for the Daityas" (*daityebhyaḥ harir alam*), but not to "Hari is the master of the Daityas" (*daityebhyaḥ hariḥ prabhuḥ*);
therefore, he says: "by the word *alam*. This is a Vārttika. By this word *alam*...
The meaning is that there is the inclusion of words whose sense is "pervasion" (*paryāpti*). "By that" means by the inclusion of words whose sense is pervasion. "And so forth" (*ityādi*):
by the word "and so forth," the exclusion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "the ornament of young girls" (*kumārīṇām alaṅkāraḥ*) is included. Now, [an objection]:

Regarding the question of how the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in such examples as *prabhurbubhūṣurbhuvanatrayasya* ("desirous of becoming the lord of the three worlds"), he says: "The genitive is used in connection with *prabhu* and others. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the specific mention [in the rule] that 'this [word] is the leader (*grāmaṇī*) of these [words]'.
[Objection: If this were so, then in the case of *daityebhyaḥ prabhuḥ* ("the lord over the Daityas"), the dative case would not occur.

But since the word *alam* will simply mean "sufficiency" or something other than that, he says: "it is capable of that. Regarding *vaṣaḍ indrāya*: the meaning is the offering of oblation intended for Indra.
Now, in a benedictory sentence such as "May it be well with the cows," the dative case alone is desired; in that case—

Since the rule "ṭhcaturthī'cāśiṣyāyuṣye" (Pāṇini 2.3.73) and others would otherwise apply by virtue of their higher status (*paratva*), resulting in the possibility of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in certain instances, he says: "The particle *ca* is for the purpose of re-enjoining (*punarvidhāna*). By this—meaning, by the force of that re-enjoining.

(575) *manyakarmaṇyanādare vibhāṣā'prāṇiṣu* |2|3|17| The term is *manyakarmaṇi*; the word is divided as *aprāṇiṣu*. The root *man* meaning "to know" belongs to the *divādi* class and takes the *śyan* suffix (*man-yate*). Alternatively, the root *man* meaning "to perceive/understand" belongs to the *tanādi* class and takes the *ivikaraṇa* suffix (*man-u-te*). Here, the word *manyā* refers to [the former].

He states "of *manya*" because the root belonging to the *divādi* class is intended due to its specific mention (*nirdeśa*). Regarding "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*), this indicates that the dative case optionally applies in some instances, overriding the accusative case. Regarding "in the sense of contempt" (*tiraskāre*), this is an explanation of [the rule] *anādare*. Here, "contempt" (*anādara*) means disregard (*paribhava*).

According to Amara, *paribhāva* means "contempt" (*tiraskriyā*). The phrase "I do not consider you even a blade of grass" (*na tvāṃ tṛṇam iti*) means, O Devadatta, that I do not regard you even as a blade of grass. This meaning is obtained through the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Since the understanding arises that you are lower than even a blade of grass, an excellence of contempt is realized. [The text says: "tṛṇaṃ tvām... [meaning "you, a blade of grass..."].

If it were said, "I consider you as a blade of grass" (*tṛṇāya manye tvām*), one would perceive only equality with a blade of grass, and not even inferiority to it. With this very intention, the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed even in the Bhāṣya. Nor should it be suspected that the dative case should apply to the word *yuṣmad* as well, simply because there is no difference in its being the object of the verb *man* (to think).

This is because the intended meaning is "in an action that indicates disregard. For in this context, it is the *tṛṇa* (grass) itself that indicates disregard, not the referent of *yuṣmad* (you). Regarding the term *śyana*:

the sense is that after roots belonging to the *tanādi* class, when there is an object of the action, only the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used, and not optionally the fourth case (*caturthī*). Not so.

"I consider you a blade of grass" (*tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manve*). This is the first person singular of the present indicative (*laṭ*) with the *u*-vikaraṇa from the root *man*. [Objection: But then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as a fourth-case alternative would also apply in cases such as "I do not consider you a boat or food" (*na tvāṃ nāvam annaṃ manye*), and likewise in "I do not consider you a dog" (*na tvāṃ śune manye*), and so forth.
However, because [the object] possesses life, the fourth alternative would not apply, resulting in a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) on the grounds that "the object possesses life.
To this, he says: "having removed [the phrase] 'among those without life' (*aprāṇiṣu*). [The example is: "I do not consider you to be a boat.
This sentence refers to a dilapidated boat. [Another example is: "I do not consider you to be food."
This [example] should also be cited. This sentence refers to contemptible food.
The point is that although there is no life (aprāṇitva) in either case, there is no option for the fourth case (caturthī-vikalpa); rather, only the second case (dvitīyā) applies.
"I do not consider you to be a dog"—O Devadatta, I do not consider you even as a dog.

This is the meaning. One may also cite examples such as "I do not consider you a crow," "I do not consider you a parrot," and "I do not consider you a jackal. The point is that in these cases, despite the fact that the objects are living beings (*prāṇin*), there is no optionality regarding the fourth case (*caturthī-vikalpa*).

(576) *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturthyau ceṣṭāyāmanadhvani* | 2|3|12| [The rule] "gatyartha": bodily movement is *ceṣṭā*. Regarding the word *manasā*: since there is an absence of bodily movement here, the second and fourth case endings do not apply; rather, the intention is that only the second case ending is used.

He summarizes the meaning of the *vārttika*—"a prohibition must be stated regarding that which is already situated"—with the words "on that which is occupied by a mover.
