The meaning is that this prohibition applies specifically to a path already traversed by a mover, and not to a non-path; for example, as in the expression "he goes along the path" (*panthānaṃ gacchati*). [The path]...

The meaning is "he reaches. Here, because the path is the locus of reaching, it is presided over by the traveler; therefore, there is a prohibition [of the suffix *ktvā*]. He states the purpose of this Vārttika: "But when... From "utpathāt" means "from the wrong path," that is, from an improper route. The ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*. [He] set out to reach Ujjayinī.

The meaning is that when one has fallen from that path due to delusion and entered another path, and then desires to leave that [other path] and set out again upon the road to Ujjayinī, the fourth case ending indeed occurs because there is no prohibition regarding "an-adhvani" (not on the way). Such is the object to be characterized.

He demonstrates this by saying, "He goes on the path by way of a wrong path. After the word "by way of a wrong path," the phrase "unable to proceed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that, being unable to reach Ujjayinī by way of a wrong path, he abandons the wrong path and follows its [the city's] route in order to enter the road to Ujjayinī.
In this case, because the path to Ujjayinī is not occupied by a traveler (*gantr*), the prohibition [of the fourth case ending] as "not being on a path" (*anadhvan*) does not apply;
therefore, the fourth case ending occurs, and optionally the second case ending as well—this is the sense. Thus ends the section on the fourth case.
(577) *Dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24).

Now the fifth [rule]: *dhruvam apāye*. He explains the term *apāya*: "separation" (*viśleṣa*). The meaning is "disjunction. He explains the term *dhruva*: "that which has become a fixed point" (*avadhibhūta*). The established principle is that separation occurs when one of two conjoined things moves away from the other. In that regard—

The term *dhruva* refers to that which does not serve as the locus for such movement; the sense is that, in this context, it is intended by implication to be the fixed point of reference (*avadhi*). (578) The fifth case ending is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). A 2.3.28.

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used for the ablative (*apādāna*). It has not been explained here because it is clear. In the example *grāmād āyāti*, the meaning is "he comes from the village. Since the village is the object of the expectation "from what?", it is the *avadhi* (limit), and thus, by virtue of being the ablative, the fifth case is employed. This is also seen in examples such as *māthurāḥ pāṭalīputrakebhya āḍhyatarāḥ* ("the people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra").
It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the status of the *apādāna* (ablative point) is established by taking it as the limit (*avadhi*) for a distinction conceived through the intellect (*buddhikalpita*).

Now, one might object: "Let it be explained that the very thing which is not the locus of the movement conducive to separation is the *dhruva* (fixed point); what is the use of intending to express 'limit-ness' (*avadhitva*)? To this, he says: "He falls from a running horse."

The point is that although the horse is the locus of motion, its status as an *avadhi*—defined by being the object of the expectancy "from what [does it fall]? with respect to the action of falling—is not contradictory.
(1) An addition should be made for verbs meaning aversion (*jugupsā*), cessation (*virāma*), and negligence (*pramāda*).

The word *jugupset* [is used]. The meaning is that when there is a connection with verbal roots having the sense of "disgust" (*jugupsā*) and so forth, that which is the object of such disgust functions as the *apādāna* (ablative case). For example, in *pāpājjugupsate*, the meaning is that one does not take pleasure in the object of sin due to the cognition of its loathsomeness. [Similarly,] *viramati*.
The word "evil" (pāpa) is understood to be supplied [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that one does not engage in what pertains to evil.

Regarding the phrase "one neglects dharma" (dharmāt pramādyati), the meaning is that one becomes deluded with respect to dharma. This statement is made because there is no actual contact or separation [between the agent and the object]. However, when [the verb] "he feels disgust" (jugupsate) [is used],...
If the meaning of such passages is taken to be that [the agent] desists from [an action] due to disgust and so forth,
then the status of the *apādāna* (ablative) is established by taking the limit of separation as something mentally constructed; thus, this sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya.

(579) *Bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* || 1.4.25 || [The word expressing the cause of fear is the *apādāna*] in the case of roots meaning "to fear" (*bhī*) or "to protect" (*trai*). For example: *corādvibheti* ("he fears from the thief"). The meaning is: "by means of the thief as the cause. Since the instrumental case for the cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*) would have applied here, [the rule prescribes the ablative]. Similarly: *corātrāyate* ("he protects himself from the thief"), [meaning] "by means of the thief as the cause..."
The meaning is that he protects [the person] for the sake of preventing killing, imprisonment, and so forth caused by that [thief]. However,
when one fears a thief and desists out of fear, and it is understood that "he protects from the thief" means he causes himself to desist in order to protect himself, then—
The status of the *apādāna* (ablative) is established by taking it as the limit (*avadhi*) of a separation imagined by the intellect; thus, this rule was rejected in the Bhāṣya.
(580) *parājer asoḍhaḥ* | 1.4.26 | [The word denoting that which is not endured is the *apādāna* after the verb *parā-ji*].

*Parājita* means "not endured. When the suffix *kta* is added to the root *sah*, after the application of the rules for changing *dh* to *ḍh*, *ṣṭh* to *ṣṭ*, and the elision of *ḍh*, the form *soḍha* is obtained by the rule *sahivahor odavarṇasya*. In this context, the past time denoted by the suffix *kta* is not intended to be expressed. Thus he says: "in the sense of 'unbearable' (*asahye'rthe*)," meaning that which is impossible to endure.

This is the meaning. This [rule] is an exception to the instrumental case used for the cause (*hetu*). "The meaning is 'he becomes weary'"—the words "because of intolerance" (*asahanāt*) are to be supplied. However, when the meaning "he desists because of intolerance" is adopted, then [the status of] the *apādāna* (ablative) is established by the very rule *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.24); such is the intent of the Bhāṣya. "He overcomes."

The meaning is "he disregards. In this case, because the enemies are capable of being overcome, they lack the quality of being "unbearable" (*asahya*); therefore, they do not possess the status of an *apādāna*.
(581) *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ* || 1.4.27 || [The desired object of those [verbs] having the sense of warding off.]

"The desired object [is the *apādāna*] in the case of verbs meaning 'to ward off' (*vāraṇa*). Warding off means turning one away from engagement. In the example "from the barley" (*yavebhyaḥ*), the meaning is that he turns the cow—which was desirous of engaging with the barley—away from that engagement.
Since there is no separation preceded by conjunction here, this rule applies where the previous rule, "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) in the event of departure," does not apply.

Regarding the statement: in that context, the barley (*yava*) possesses the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) because it is desired as something to be protected by virtue of being one's own; however, this does not apply to the cow (*go*), because she is not desired as such since she belongs to another, and because her status as something to be warded off prevents her from being [simultaneously] desired.

And thus, according to the rule *tathāyuktaṃ ca*, the accusative case is used for the cow because it is the object (*karman*). However, when the barley belongs to another while the cow belongs to oneself, then the act of warding off (*vāraṇa*) is simply impossible. In reality, even if the barley belongs to another, demerit (*adharma*) would arise from its destruction; [for] the owner of the barley...

Having driven the cow away from the village, one should tie it up; and the owner of the fodder should fine the owner of the cow. Therefore, because the barley is intended to be protected and is the object desired [to be saved], it indeed possesses the status of an *apādāna* (ablative). As for the cow, although it belongs to oneself, because it is most intensely desired to be restrained for the sake of removing obstacles, it possesses the status of a *karman* (direct object). And not...

It should not be argued that even though there is "being most desired" (*īpsitatamatva*), since "being desired" (*īpsitatva*) is also present, why should it not be an *apādāna*? For when "being most desired" is present, the status of *apādāna*—which would otherwise apply by the rule "of those [verbs] having the sense of warding off" (*vāraṇārthānām*)—is set aside, and by the subsequent rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*), the status of *karman* (object) alone is obtained. Nor is it the case that...

One might suspect that the status of *apādāna* (ablative) prescribed by the rule "ṭhvāraṇārthānāmīpsitaḥ" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the status of *karman* (object) prescribed by "ṭhkarturīpsitatamaṃ karma". However, the status of *karman* according to "ṭhkarturīpsitatamaṃ karma" pertains exclusively to that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*), whereas the status of *apādāna* according to "ṭhvāraṇārthānām" [pertains to the object of the act of warding off].

It refers to the desired object. Since this [rule] finds its scope in the case of barley—which is the desired object for him (*tasya*) but belongs to another—it cannot serve as an exception to the status of "object" (*karman*) defined by the rule *karturīpsitatamam*. Therefore, by virtue of its superior force (*paratvāt*), it applies to one's own cow (*goḥ*) in relation to the barley belonging to another.

Because it is that which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*), it possesses the status of the object (*karman*) alone. Nor is the meaning [of the rule] "he turns the boy away from the fire," for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the boy being burned upon touching the fire.

Therefore, since the boy is the most desired object to be reached by the act of warding off—which consists in turning him away from activity toward that [fire]—the boy is the object (*karman*) because he is the most desired object of the warder-off. As for the fire, although it is the most desired object to be reached by the boy’s act of touching, it possesses the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) because it is the most desired object of the warder-off. This is established by the separate mention of these two.

This [objection] is refuted by the fact that it would encompass all observed instances (lakṣya), such as "he worships Hari for this very reason," "while going to the village he touches grass," and "he consumes poison. For if it were stated that "the object (karman) is the locus of the fruit produced by the agent's activity," then the rule *vāraṇārthānām* would be an exception (apavāda) to this [definition], because it is prescribed as a specific rule (viśeṣavidhi). And in that case, the boy (*māṇavaka*) would not be considered the object.

Nor should it be argued that the rule *agnau parikrīḍane* (Pāṇini 1.3.21) provides scope [for the application of the ātmanepada]; for here, the meaning of the root *vārayati* is the prevention of an activity whose result is contact. And that [prevention] consists in leading [the boy] away or similar actions. The result produced by such an operation is the absence of an activity on the part of the boy (*māṇavaka*) whose result is contact. In this regard, the aspect of "contact" resides both in the fire and in the boy, since contact, being of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), is inherent in two loci.

Furthermore, the absence of activity (*pravṛtiviraha*) resides in the fire by way of being its object (*viṣayatayā*), and in the boy (*māṇavaka*) by way of being its locus (*āśrayatayā*). Thus, since the status of being an object (*karmatva*)—defined as being the locus of the result brought about by the agent’s operation—is more general, it would apply to both cases. Consequently, the rule *apādānam* [P. 1.4.24], which prescribes the ablative case for things used with verbs meaning "to ward off" (*vāraṇārthānām*), would serve as an exception (*apavāda*) because it is otherwise without scope; this would result in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) being applied even after *māṇavaka*. To preclude that, the rule *kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma* [P. 1.4.49] must be commenced.

And thus, since the status of *apādāna* (ablative) which has scope for application when there is merely something desired is superseded by its higher priority over the *īpsitatama* (most desired), the sublation of that [apādāna] in the case of the boy (*māṇavaka*) who is the most desired is established. Furthermore, once the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*) has been initiated, the rule "likewise associated" (*tathāyuktam*) must also be initiated in order to include objects that are either undesirable (*dveṣya*) or indifferent (*udāsīna*). Let this suffice for now. In the *Bhāṣya*, however, this sūtra is rejected on the basis of the *apādāna* status being produced by a conjunction or disjunction imagined through the intellect (*buddhi-kalpita*).
(582) *antardhau yenādarśanam icchati* | 1.4.28. Regarding the word *antardhau*: he explains this term as "when there is an intervention" (*vyavadhāne sati*).

The meaning is "by means of an intervention. Regarding the phrase *yatkartṛkasya* ("of that which has someone as its agent"): the sense is that the word *yena* expresses the agent in the instrumental case (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*).

Regarding the phrase *ātmano darśanasya*: the genitive case in *ātmanaḥ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) due to its connection with the word *darśana*. The word *ātmanaḥ* is to be supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). For this very reason, the instrumental case in *yena* denotes the agent (*kartari tṛtīyā*).

It is connected [with the genitive]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the genitive case being applied by virtue of its connection with a *kṛt* suffix. However, when the word "ātmanaḥ" (of oneself) is supplied as an ellipsis, the genitive is not used due to the restrictive rule: "when both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] only for the object. By the word "ātman," the agent of the desire is intended. [This refers to] that which belongs to the agent of the act of seeing within its own domain through purification.
That is to say, he desires non-existence. Regarding the phrase "Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother":

the root *līṅ* means "to adhere," and it takes the *śyan* suffix (*liya-te*). However, here, by virtue of the prefix (*upa-sarga*), it functions to denote an activity conducive to the absence of being seen by another agent with respect to oneself, even when there is an intervention [of a wall or similar object]. And therefore—
The meaning is that Kṛṣṇa conceals himself with a wall or similar object in order to avoid being seen by his mother; here, based on this intervention,
the absence of the mother’s perception directed toward him is something desired by Kṛṣṇa.

The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used because the mother functions as the *apādāna* (point of departure). This [rule] is either an exception (*apavāda*) to the third case (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) or an exception to the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
However, in the Bhāṣya, this rule is also rejected by relying on a mentally constructed (*buddhi-kṛta*) status of being an *apādāna*.
(583) Pāṇini 1.4.29: *ākhyātopayoge* ("In the sense of instruction from an authoritative source").

Regarding the rule *ākhyātopayoge*: the division is *ākhyātā-upayoge*. The word *ākhyātā* is the nominative singular of a stem ending in the suffix *tṛc*. He explains the term *upayoga* as "preceded by a restriction" (*niyamapūrvaka*), because that is how it is stated in the Bhāṣya; this is the intended meaning. He explains the word *ākhyātā*, which ends in *tṛc*, as "the speaker" (*vaktṛ*).
The meaning is "one who causes to teach. Regarding the expression *upādhyāyād adhīte* ("he learns from the teacher"):

the meaning is that he repeats the utterance of the teacher preceded by specific rules of recitation. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive case. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that the Veda has emerged from the teacher...
This [objection] has been refuted by relying on the meaning "it grasps" (*gṛhṇāti*).
(584) *The source of that which is the agent of birth* (A 1.4.30). "Birth" (*jani*) means being born (*janana*), arising (*utpatti*). [The root] *janī-*...

In the sense of "manifestation," the root *jan* belongs to the *adaivādika* (curādigaṇa) class and is intransitive (*akarmaka*). The suffix *iṇ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *ṭhiṇjādibhyaḥ*.
There is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel because of the prohibition in the rule *janivadhyośca*. The analysis of the compound is *janeḥ kartā* ("the agent of *jan*");

this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*) formed with the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). The prohibition [of such a compound] by the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* applies only to the genitive used in the sense of a *kāraka* (participant in an action).
Thus it will be stated. Regarding the term "of that which is being born" (*jāyamānasya*): from the root *jan*, the suffix *laṭ* in the sense of the agent takes the form *śānac*;
then *śyan* is added, and by the rule *jñājanorjā*, *āne muk* is substituted. The meaning is "of that which has origination as its locus.
He explains the word *prakṛti* as "cause" (*hetu*). Regarding "of Brahman": the meaning is "of Hiraṇyagarbha."
The sense is that, like a potter with respect to jars and the like, [the Self] is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) in the production of progeny.

This view held by the author of the *Vṛtti* is incorrect; for since there exists conjunction and disjunction [of the body], the rule "that which remains constant when there is departure" (*dhruvam apāye*) already establishes this. Therefore, in this root text (*mūla*), the word "cause" (*hetu*) refers exclusively to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa, having cited the examples "scorpions are born from cow-dung" and "dūrvā grass is born from cow-hair and sheep-hair," [state that] even though there is a persistence of the constituent parts of the causal substance (*prakṛtidravya*) in transformations (*pariṇāma*), there is nevertheless a separation effected by the intellect (*buddhikṛtaviśleṣa*).

The rejection [of the rule] as being already established by the statement "dhruvam apāye" is thus consistent. And so, in the passage "from Brahman the creatures are born," it is precisely the consciousness of the Lord (Īśvara-caitanya) as conditioned by Māyā that is intended by the word "Brahman. For that...
"The adoption of all actions" is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Vedānta.

(585) *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* | 1|4|31|. "The source of the earth. In this previous sūtra, although the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) was mentioned as part of a compound, it is [to be understood] in its individual sense.
By the force of the declaration of the *svarita* accent, [the term from the previous rule] is carried over here. Thus he says: "of the agent of becoming" (*bhūkartuḥ*). "Becoming" is *bhū*;
[the suffix] *kvip* is applied because it belongs to the *saṃpadādi* group. The "agent of becoming" (*bhūkartā*) is the agent of that [becoming];
this is the meaning. Regarding "source" (*prabhava*): it is a "source" (*prabhava*) because one "originates" (*prabhavati*)—that is, first becomes manifest—in it.

The meaning is "the place of the first manifestation. If one were to take the word *prabhavati* in the sense of "is produced," there would be an inconsistency, because the Gaṅgā is not produced there. Thus he says: "the meaning is 'it manifests,'" which is to say that it manifests for the first time. For this very reason, [the objection] does not apply in the case of the expression "the Himavat also manifests."

[The suffix *lyap*] occurs. By this, the redundancy [of the present rule] with respect to the rules "the agent of the action of originating" (*ṭhjanikartuḥ*) and "that which is fixed when there is a departure" (*ṭhdhruvamapāye*) is refuted. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is established that it is already accomplished by the rule "that which is fixed when there is a departure" alone, by relying on the meaning "he departs."

"Regarding 'lyablope karmaṇyadhikaraṇe ca' [Pāṇini 2.3.28]: the phrase *lyablope* means that when there is an elision— that is, the non-appearance or non-employment— of a word ending in the suffix *lyap*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed optionally for the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to that implied meaning."
"He is ashamed" (*jihreti*)—the meaning is "he feels shame.

Now, one might ask: since there is no actual usage of the form ending in *lyap* (i.e., *hrītvā*) here, how can the status of [the object] as a *karman* (object) and so forth be understood with respect to that meaning?
To this, he says: "even when it is merely implied" (*gamyamānāpi*). This means "by means of context and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even when it is merely implied":

He states another purpose [for the question]: "From where? The intention is that the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative) depends upon the action of "coming" (*āgataḥ*), which is understood. The answer is "from the river.
The intention is that the status of being an *apādāna* depends upon the action of "coming," which is implied by the word "I have come" (*āgato'smi*).
"And from that which there is the measurement of distance or time, the fifth case [is used].

Regarding "yataḥ": the suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the third case (*yena*). One interpretation is that when the measurement—that is, the delimitation—of a path or of time is understood by means of a certain limit (*avadhi*), the fifth case should be prescribed after that word.
This is the statement. Even in the reading "tatra pañcamī," this is the very same meaning.
Thus, from that aforementioned path, the first and seventh [cases] are used.

Regarding the phrase *tadyauktāt*: the second sentence is "from that which is joined with it (*tadyauktāt*), when it is connected [with the word], and when it denotes a path (*adhvavācinaḥ*), the first and seventh case endings are used if [the distance] is to be expressed. There is another sentence: "The seventh case ending should also be stated after a word denoting time (*kālāt*. The term *tadyauktāt* is supplied (*anuṣajyate*) from the previous rule.

The meaning is that the seventh case suffix (*saptamī*) should be prescribed after a word denoting time when it is construed with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*). Regarding the example "from the forest" (*vanāt*): here, a distance of one *yojana* is delimited by the forest as the preceding limit, because the expectancy arises as to "from what [starting point] is this *yojana*? Thus, it is [measured] in the *yojana*.
In the expression "a yojana," the meaning of both the nominative and the locative cases is "existence in a location immediately following one's own [reference point].
The sense is that the village is in a location one yojana to the east, relative to a preceding limit consisting of a forest;
this remains so even when the existence of the limit is present.

The statement [of the rule] is made because there is no sense of separation (*viśleṣa*), and thus there is an absence of the status of an *apādāna* (ablative). Regarding "from Kārttikī" (*kārtikyāḥ*):

the construction is "in the month from Kārttikī, [until] Āgrahāyaṇī. Here, the measure of time consisting of a month is delimited by Kārttikī as its prior limit; starting from what [does the month begin]?
This is because such an expectation arises. As for the locative case in "māse," its meaning is "occurring in the time immediately following [the month] itself.
[Thus, it refers to] the time subsequent to the month, which has the full moon of Kārtika as its preceding limit.
The meaning is "the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.

(586) *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūtarapadājāhiyukte* | Pāṇini 2.3.29. Regarding *anyārāt*: he states that the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), thus [explaining] "in connection with these. [The words are: *anya*, *ārāt*,...

The meaning is: "when there is a connection with these eight [words]: *itara*, *ṛte*, words denoting directions (*dikśabda*), a word ending in *añc*, *āc*, and *āhi*. He states—"the inclusion of the sense 'other' (*anya*)"—in order to establish the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in connection with words such as *bhinna*; the intention is that this follows from the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

The result is that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used when joined with a word having the sense of "other" (*anya*). [Objection: Then the mention of *itara* is redundant, since the rule is already established by the fact that it has the sense of "other. To this he says: "The mention of *itara* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).
[He cites the root] *paci* in the sense of "expansion," [and notes] the word *anya*.
This means that the statement regarding the word "anyārthaka" being intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of stating its specific function.

"Anyo" means distinct (*bhinna*) or other (*itara*). This is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for such terms as "possessing difference" (*bhedavān*) or "dissimilar" (*vilakṣaṇa*). The meaning is: "possessing a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is Kṛṣṇa."

This is an exception to the sixth case (the ablative). Although there exists a restriction regarding a limit for words such as *anya* and others, the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative) does not apply here because there is no separation from a conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśleṣa*). The same applies in the subsequent examples as well.
Regarding *ārād vanāt*: the meaning is "far from the forest" or "near the forest."
"Nearness and vicinity," according to Amara. Regarding "except for Kṛṣṇa": *ṛte* is an indeclinable ending in the vowel *e*. "In the sense of exclusion," according to Amara.
The meaning is that there is no happiness except in the absence of Kṛṣṇa. As it is said: "Where does the destruction of karma bear fruit, except through the propitiation of the Supreme Person?"
The usage found in the *Stuti* within the *Śivarahasya*, however, follows the archaic (*ārṣa*) style;
alternatively, the accusative case is justified by the rule "It is also seen elsewhere," or by the Cāndra-sūtra: "The accusative is used with the word *ṛte*.
Now, he provides an example for the use with words denoting direction: *pūrvo grāmāt* ("to the east of the village").

The meaning is: "a village situated in the eastern direction relative to the limit of the village [itself]. Now, one might object: since in the expression "Phālguna is prior to Caitra," the word *pūrva* denotes time and lacks the sense of direction, how can the ablative case (*pañcamī*) be used in connection with it? To this, he says: "seen in the sense of direction. By conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), these words denote specific directions.
Only *pūrva* and the others are understood here, and not *aindrī*, *kakub*, and so forth. Regarding the word *saṃprati*:

the meaning is that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs when there is a connection with words denoting direction (*digvācaka*) as well as words denoting time (*kālavācaka*) such as *idānīm*. [Objection: If this were the case, it would also apply in an instance such as *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body"). To this [it is replied]:
He says: "denoting a part. Regarding the phrase "the latter of that": the word *tasya* (of that) refers back to the subject under discussion which has been mentioned twice;
its meaning is that the "latter" (*param*)—that is, the subsequent part—of what has been stated twice is the *āmreḍita*.
Regarding the phrase "the former of the body": the meaning is that it is the prior part of the trunk.

That which has *añcu* as its final member (*uttarapada*) is called *añcūttarapada*. This refers to words for the cardinal directions such as *prāk* and so forth, but not words like *sadhryaṅ* and the like, because of their association with words for the directions.

Therefore, in the phrase *sadhryaṅ devadattena*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) does not apply. [Objection: But surely, since this is already established simply by virtue of being a word for a direction...
To show that the mention of the word *añcu* as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would otherwise be redundant, he says: "of the word ending in *añcu* as the subsequent member.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because it is subsequent [to the previous rule], it would have obtained application after the rule 'in the sense of the sixth case' (*ṣaṣṭhyatasarthaiḥ*). "East or west of the village" means having the village as the limit. "Āj" refers to a construction with a suffix ending in the *ac* class.

This is an indication that an example will be stated. "dakṣiṇā grāmāt" means "in the southern direction having the village as its limit. "āhi" indicates an example in connection with the suffix *āh*. "dakṣiṇāhi grāmāt" [is such an example].

The meaning is "at a great distance" in the southern direction from Grāma. The suffix *āhi* is applied according to the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca*. Although words ending in the suffixes *āc* and *āhi* are directional terms (*dikśabda*), they are mentioned separately in order to override the application of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthaprayoge*. [Objection: Even so, [one might ask] regarding [the expression] *bhavāt prabhṛti* or *ārabhya*...
One might ask: how can the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occur in examples such as *sevyo hariḥ* ("Hari is to be served"), given the absence of connection with words like *anya* ("other")?

To this, he says: "in the sense of the *apādāna* (ablative)"; that is, "in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti* ('starting from,' etc.). For instance, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *apādāne pañcamī* ("the ablative is used for the *apādāna*").

Having cited the *Vārttika*—"And because there is measurement of space and time"—and having given the example "From the Kārttikī [full moon] to the Āgrahāyaṇī [full moon] is a month," he introduces the rejection of that *Vārttika* by stating, "This need not be stated. He then remarks:
"This [usage] ought to be employed here, yet it is not employed; [one should say] 'From the Kārttikī until the Āgrahāyaṇī is a month.'"

Thus it has been stated. The meaning is that even in the absence of the word *prabhṛti* (and its synonyms), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is established because the sense of that word is present. By stating this, the author of the Bhāṣya indicates the rule: "The ablative is used in connection with words having the sense of *prabhṛti*. Otherwise, since the Vārttika would be necessary to provide for the ablative case, the [Bhāṣya's] statement would be inconsistent.

This is indeed clear. Thus, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs even when joined with words that are synonyms of *prabhṛti*. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated, in the course of his commentary on the Bhāṣya regarding the phrase "from the Kārttikī full moon" (*kārtikyāḥ prabhṛti*), that it means "starting from that" (*tata ārabhya*). In that instance, the suffix *tasi* is applied to the ablative case form *tataḥ*.

Intending all of this, he provides the following illustration: "starting from birth" (*bhavāt prabhṛti*) or "beginning with birth" (*ārabhya*). *Bhava* means birth. The word *ārabhya* has the sense of "having taken as a limit. The indeclinable *prabhṛti* also has precisely this meaning.
Thus, the meaning is: "Hari is to be served, having taken birth as the limit."

The meaning is that Hari is to be served at all times, from this very moment until death—that is, throughout the entire subsequent period beginning with this instant. Here, because of the intention to express the object (*karman*) in relation to the action denoted by "starting from" (*ārabhya*), the accusative case alone is used;
for it is said: "A case ending expressing a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is stronger than a case ending based on a governing word (*upapada*). For example:

In such cases as "He recites [the mantra] starting from sunrise until sunset," the accusative case alone is used when there is an intention to express the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), because it has been stated that "a case ending denoting a kāraka (participant in an action) is stronger than a case ending based on a syntactical adjunct (*upapada*). This is as in the example:
"He recites [the mantra] starting from sunrise until sunset. However, when there is an intention to express the status of being a subordinate element...

The sixth case (genitive) is superseded by the fifth case (ablative) after the word *bhava*. However, when used in conjunction with the word *prabhṛti* in the sense of "starting from" (*ārabhya*), the second case is never employed; this is because the meaning of the word *prabhṛti*—namely, "having taken as a limit"—is constituted by a boundary and thus lacks the nature of an action (*kriyā*). [This is illustrated by the rule] *apaparī*...

The meaning is that, having taken for granted the use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in connection with the word *bahiḥ*, the ablative is understood to be employed when joined with *bahiḥ* because of the rule prescribing composition: *ṭhapaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.12).
This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhapaparī*. [An example is given: *karaṇasya karo bahiḥ* ("the hand is outside the instrument").
This is indeed incorrect; it must somehow be resolved by the principle that "what is established by a *jñāpaka* does not apply everywhere," or by some other means. (587) *apa-parī varjane* | 1.4.88.
*Apa* and *pari* [are *karmapravacanīya*s] when used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). They are *karmapravacanīya*s. "The *karmapravacanīya*s... [is the heading].
The meaning is that the word under discussion (*adhikṛta*) is modified into the dual number. Why [is the rule] stated as "in the sense of exclusion" (*varjane*)?
Consider *pariṣiñcati*. The meaning here is "he sprinkles all around. Because this is a prefix (*upasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*.
(588) *āṅ maryādāvacane* | 1.4.89.
Regarding *āṅ maryādāvacane*: "is designated as such" means it is designated by the technical term *karmapravacanīya*.
Now, one might object that since the rule would have been established simply by stating *āṅ maryādāyām*, the inclusion of the word *vacana* ("in the expression of") is redundant; therefore...

He said: "Because of the mention of 'words' (*vacana*). By that [word], *maryādā* (limit) is meant; by that [word], *abhividhi* (inclusive limit) is meant. Where the word *maryādā* is used, it refers to the rule:
"*ut* is applied in the sense of both *maryādā* and *abhividhi*. In that regard, which...

The meaning is that the prefix *āṅ*, when seen [in these senses], shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya*. Thus, the intended sense is that by this rule, *āṅ* becomes a *karmapravacanīya* when used with words such as *maryādā* and *abhividhi*. (589) *Pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ* | 2.3.10 | [The ablative case ending is used after a word joined with *apa*, *āṅ*, or *pari*].
"By *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*. This means by these [words], namely *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*.
"By karmapravacanīyas" is because that [term] is understood from the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.8). Examples:
*apa hareḥ pari hareḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("transmigration apart from Hari," "transmigration excluding Hari"). *Apa hareḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("transmigration apart from Hari").

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "you should avoid *saṃsāra*. The meaning is that, excluding Hari, one should avoid the wandering (*saṃsaraṇa*) consisting of the cycle of birth and death. Now, an objection may be raised: in examples such as "the lightning flashes toward the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate*) and "the devotee [is devoted] toward Hari" (*bhakto hariṃ prati*), the word is designated as a *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna... [Pāṇini 1.4.90].

Regarding the rule "the second case [is used] when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*," one might argue that the fifth case (*pañcamī*)—by the rule "the fifth case [is used] after *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*"—would apply instead, since it is both subsequent and an exception (*apavāda*) to the second case.
To this, he says: "after *pari*," because in the rule "the fifth case [is used] after *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*," the word *apa* has the sense of exclusion (*varjana*).

The meaning is that, due to association (*sāhacarya*), the prefix *pari-* is also understood here as having the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). "Until liberation" (*ā mukteḥ*) means "prior to liberation. "Up to the whole" (*ā sakalāt*) means that Brahman exists pervading the entire [universe].

(590) *pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ* | 1.4.92 | The word *prati* [is a karmapravacanīya] in the senses of "representative" (*pratinidhi*) and "giving back" (*pratidāna*). A representative is one who is similar; giving back that which was given is "restitution" (*pratidāna*). "Having the aforementioned designation" means having the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*.

(591) *pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ* | 1|4|92|. [The word] *prati-* [is used as a karmapravacanīya] in the sense of a representative (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*). "In this [context]" means within the scope specified by the rule. In the sūtra, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), precisely because of this very indication [in the rule]. As for the example "a representative of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya pratinidhiḥ*), [it is formed with the genitive].

This is to be resolved by the principle that "what is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) does not apply everywhere. Thus, the resulting meaning is: "the fifth case ending [is used] after a word joined with a *karmapravacanīya* which has as its correlate the substitution (*pratinidhi*) or the exchange (*pratidāna*) of something belonging to that [referent]. For example: *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati*. [This means] Pradyumna [is a substitute] for Kṛṣṇa in battle and so forth.

The meaning is: "possessing a similarity as defined by Kṛṣṇa. The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is similarity; *prati* is its indicator. Regarding "from the sesame seeds" (*tilebhyaḥ*): the meaning is that one returns the sesame seeds taken as a debt, either in their own form or by way of their value and so forth. Here, the ablative case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

(592) *Akartary ṛṇe pañcamī* |2|3|24|. "In the case of a non-agent, when [the cause] is a debt. The rule *hetau* ("when there is a cause") is understood to follow here. The meaning is: when the cause is a debt that is not the agent. He states the resulting sense: "excluding the agent."

The meaning is "devoid of the designation of an agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā-rahitam*). Regarding the example *śatād baddhaḥ*: the meaning is that when there is a failure to repay at the stipulated time, one is bound by reason of a debt of a hundred [gold pieces], such as gold and so forth; this is an exception to the instrumental case used for cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*). Regarding *śatena bandhitaḥ*, [the word] *adharmaṇaḥ* [is understood].

The word "by the creditor" (*utamarṇena*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *bandh* in its causative form (*ṇyant*) in the sense of the object. Thus, the meaning of the non-causative form is "the debtor is bound by the creditor. The meaning of the causative form is "the debtor is caused to be bound by the creditor," where the creditor is the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) and the debt of one hundred is the instrumental cause (*prayojaka*).

In this context, "a hundred" (*śatam*) is designated as both the *kartṛ* (agent) because it is the prompter, and as the *hetu* (cause), since the designation *kartṛ* is also prescribed by the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *tatprayojako hetuśca*. Consequently, from the word *śata*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) would apply by virtue of being an exception (*apavāda*), overriding the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) that would otherwise apply to the agent.

The intended meaning is that it is therefore stated [in the rule] "not when there is an agent" (*akartari*). The point is that even though "a hundred" (*śata*) functions as a cause (*hetu*), the fifth case ending does not apply because it possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*).
(593) *vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām* |2|3|25|.

The *Vibhāṣā* [states]: the word "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*) is understood to carry over. Thus it says: "when the cause is a quality (*guṇa*) not in the feminine gender. The word "existing" (*vidyamāna*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the form *jāḍya*: the state of being dull (*jaḍa*) is *jāḍya*.
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied by the rule "after words expressing qualities and after *brāhmaṇa* etc., in the sense of action (*karman*) and [cause]. Now, [one might object]:...

One might ask: how is the ablative case (*pañcamī*) justified in examples such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke" (*dhūmād agnimān*), given that smoke and the like are not qualities (*guṇa*)?
To this, he says: "by means of a split in the rule" (*yogavibhāgāt*). The rule *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is divided;
the term *hetau* ("in the sense of cause") is carried over [from a previous rule], as is *pañcamī*. The meaning is that the ablative case may optionally be used in the sense of a cause.
And from that, "he possesses fire because of smoke" (*dhūmād agnimān*) and so forth are established. Then, regarding the rule *guṇe 'striyām*:

there, the words *vibhāṣā* and *pañcamī* are understood to carry over. The meaning stated is that when a non-feminine quality (*guṇa*) serves as a reason (*hetu*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) may optionally be used. And from that, "bound because of dullness" (*jāḍyād baddhaḥ*) and so forth are established.

Now, one might object that since the rule is already established by the term *vibhāṣā* alone, the addition of *guṇe'striyām* (in the case of a quality, provided it is not feminine) is redundant; to this he replies: "In the case of a non-quality and sometimes in the feminine. The intention is that the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of achieving desired results. Here, he provides an example for "non-quality": *dhūmāt* (from smoke).

Immediately after "fire," the word "is known" (*jñāyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Since smoke is the cause for the cognition of fire, the sense is that here the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used because smoke functions as the cause, even though it is not a quality (*guṇa*).
He illustrates this with the example: "there is no jar. After the word "jar," [the word] "thus" (*iti*)...
The word "is known" (*jñāyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) as well: apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is cognition;

the absence of that is non-apprehension. This is a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compound. Nor should it be suspected that this is an *avyayībhāva* compound because of the absence of an object, since the optionality of those two [compounds] in the case of the absence of an object will be stated later.

(594) *pṛthag-vinā-nānābhis tṛtīyā 'nyatarasyām* || 2.3.32 || [The words] *pṛthak*, *vinā*, [and *nānā*]; [the rule] "the fifth and second cases" (*pañcamī-dvitīye ca*) applies here. The phrase "in the alternative when the third case is absent" (*tṛtīyā-abhāva-pakṣe*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sūtra].

[This refers to the rules: "the fifth case in the sense of the ablative" (*apādāne pañcamī*), "with a suffix having the sense of *tasi* etc., the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī atasarthapratyayena*), and "with *enap*, the second case" (*enapā dvitīyā*).
The sequence of rules in the Sūtra is "pṛthak-vinā. In that context, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not carry over because it is not marked with a *svarita* accent;

however, the ablative (*pañcamī*) and the accusative (*dvitīyā*) do carry over. Thus, the meaning is that in the absence of the third case (instrumental), there is the fifth and the second case. But [one might object]: in the absence of the third case, shouldn't there only be the second?

It might be argued that [the fifth case] could occur because of its proximity, but the fifth case is not [included], because there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of it in the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena*. Therefore, since the inclusion of the fifth case here is untenable, he says:
"The mention of *anyatarasyām*. This is sufficient by itself, namely, the phrase "and the third case."
The inclusion of the word "anyatarasyām" (in either case) involves a heavy grammatical effort because it establishes the conjunction with the proximate second case;
its purpose is to include the fifth case even when it is separated [from the first], since indeclinables possess multiple meanings—this is the underlying intention. Now, as for the fifth case...
Since it is impossible for [the word] not previously recurring in the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthaiḥ* to recur here, how can it be present here? To this he says: "The fifth and second cases also recur.
The remainder is: "by means of *maṇḍūkapluti*" (frog-leap). [The example is] *pṛthagrāmeṇa*.

The meaning is: "possessing a difference whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is Rāma. Similarly for *vinā* and *nānā*: [with] *vinā*, [the forms are] *rāmeṇa*, *rāmāt*, or *rāmam*; [with] *nānā*, [the forms are] *rāmeṇa*, *rāmāt*, or *rāmaṃ*.
Some maintain that all three—*pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*—have the sense of difference (*bheda*).

According to Amarasimha: "The words *pṛthak*, *vinā*, *antareṇa*, *ṛte*, *hiruk*, and *nānā* are used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). The meaning is that there is no happiness in the absence of Rāma.

(595) Pāṇini 2.3.33: "And [the ablative case is used] for the word expressing an instrument (*karaṇa*) when it is *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, or *katipaya*, provided they denote a non-substance (*asattvavacana*)."

And [the rule applies] when there is an instrument (*karaṇa*). "From these" means from the four: *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya*. He explains the term "non-substantive word" (*asattvapada*) with the words "not a substance" (*adravya*). The term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is understood to carry over, as is "the fifth case" (*pañcamī*). Consequently, it is obtained that the fifth case is optionally used for the instrument. In its absence, however...

The third case is already established. Thus he says: "the third and the fifth. "Released by a little" (*stokena stokāt*) means released with slight effort; the sense is that effort is not a substance (*dravya*). As for the phrase "but in the case of a substance": when there is a substance, as in "killed by a little poison" (*stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ*).
The meaning is that it is indeed the third [liberation]. One is liberated by a small means or from a small [obstacle], or liberated with difficulty or from a difficult [obstacle];
the meaning is "with hardship. Or one is liberated by a few [means] or from a few [obstacles]; the meaning is "by an incomplete means."

(596) *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca* |2|3|35|. Regarding the phrase *ebhyaḥ*: it means "from those having the sense of 'far' (*dūra*) and from those having the sense of 'near' (*antika*). The word *ca* ("and") is for the purpose of including the fifth (*pañcamī*) and third (*tṛtīyā*) case endings as well, even though they are separated [by other rules], and not [merely for the second case].

Regarding the rule *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyantarasām* (P. 2.3.34), it is understood from the commentary that this applies even to the proximate genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus he says: "and [the words] *pañcamī* (ablative) and *tṛtīyā* (instrumental) [are also included].
The intention is that this rule applies to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), as established by the commentary. And so it is.

The result is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the first [rule]. Because of the usage in the *Bhāṣya*, "dūrād āvasathān mūtram, dūrāt pādāvanejanam" (urine far from the dwelling, water for washing the feet far [from the dwelling]), this rule applies even to the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*), which has the sense of the seventh case.
Now, one might ask: why is the fifth case (*pañcamī*) not used in the expression "dūraḥ panthāḥ" (a distant path)? To this [it is replied]:...
He says: "of a word denoting a non-substance" (*asattvavacanasya*). In the example "the distant path" (*dūraḥ panthāḥ*), "path" (*panthā*) is a substance (*dravya*);
the intention is that the word "distant" (*dūra*) is its qualifier and thus denotes a substance (*sattvavacana*). Thus ends the section on the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
(597) *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* | 2.3.50 | [The sixth case ending is used for the remaining relations].

Now, the sixth [case]. "The sixth [case] occurs in the sense of the remainder" (Pāṇini 2.3.50). The "remainder" (śeṣa) is that which is other than what has been mentioned. For in the rules prescribing the second case and so forth—such as "the second case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2)—the grammatical relations (kārakas) of object, agent, instrument, recipient, point of departure, and locus have been enumerated.

In the rule for the first case-ending (*prathamā*), the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) has been enumerated. The meaning of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is that a relationship other than these—such as the relation between owner and owned—is the referent. In that context, when there is no subverting factor, the relationship appears both in its specific form and in its general form; for [a thing] does not exist without specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa*).

This is according to the maxim that "the general [is understood] when the specific is absent. However, when there is a subverting factor—as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) and so on—it appears merely as a relation (*saṃbandhatvena*). The established position is that if it were to appear even in its specific form as "object-ness" (*karmatva*) and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of requiring the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) and others. This is the case in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*).

The meaning of the genitive case is a relation characterized both by its specific nature as the state of being owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) and by its general nature as the state of being a relation (*saṃbandhatva*). The cognition is: "The person is the locus of a relation consisting of ownership (*svatva*), which is defined by the lordship (*svāmitva*) residing in the king. However, the status of being the locus (*āśrayatva*) and so forth appears through the force of the relational context (*saṃsargamaryādā*). In that regard, the person...

The primary element is the substantive (*viśeṣya*). The relation, however, is a qualifier of the person by way of being something contained within it (*ādheyatayā*). The king, on the other hand, is a qualifier of the relation by way of being its locus (*āśrayatayā*). Furthermore, the relation is the substantive with respect to the king by way of being contained within him, according to the rule stating that "the meaning of the suffix is the predominant factor."
Because the predominance [of the relation] is understood with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). For this very reason, the genitive case does not occur even after the word *puruṣa*;

for in the cognition "the person is the locus of the relation as defined by the king," it is untenable for the relation to appear both as a qualifier and as the qualificand with respect to the person, which is the meaning of the base.

However, when the cognition is that "the king is the locus of a relation characterized as ownership, which is defined by the ownership residing in the person," then the genitive case indeed occurs after the word "person" in the expression "the king of the person"; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
This is also the case in expressions such as "the path of the virtuous" (*satāṃ gatam*).
Anticipating the objection regarding the use of the third case (instrumental) for the agent and so forth, he says: "of the object and the rest as well.

The meaning is that when even the states of being an object, an agent, and so on, are intended to be expressed through their common nature as *saṃbandha* (relation), only the sixth case (genitive) is used, and not the case-endings of the *kārakas*. And thus [it is stated in Pāṇini’s grammar]: "And [the genitive is used] for that which has been designated by a *kṛt* suffix, when referring to the present time..."

Thus, the commentary on the Sūtra states: "The non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of [factors] such as being the object (*karmatva*) is the remainder (*śeṣa*). Regarding the phrase *satāṃ gatam*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

The meaning is "the going related to the virtuous" (*satsambandhi gamanam*). However, when there is an intention to express agency (*kartṛtva*), the instrumental case indeed occurs, as in *sadbhir gatam*. But the genitive case characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix does not apply here.

It occurs [as such], because of the prohibition "not in the world" (*ṭh na loke*). In the case of *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows by means of ghee"), when there is a desire to express the instrument (*karaṇa*), the meaning is that he proceeds by means of the ghee as an instrument (*upāya*).
However, when there is a desire to express the relation (*saṃbandha*) of the instrument, the genitive case is used; [the action] resides in the agent and is related to the ghee.

"Engagement" (*pravṛtti*) means cognition. In the expression "he remembers his mother," when the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is intended, the meaning is "he remembers the mother. However, when the status of being an object is intended as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the meaning is "the act of remembering, performed by Devadatta, which relates to the mother. In the expression "the fuel improves the water" (*edho dakasyopaskurute*).

The word *edhas* ends in the vowel *a* and is masculine, as evidenced by the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *kārake*: "the *edhas* will be explained. From the *dvandva* compound *edhāś ca udakāni ca*, the genitive case is applied.
By the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*, there is a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*). When the status of being the object (*karmatva*) is intended, it is expressed as *edhodakam*.

The meaning is that one embellishes [the fuel] by means of drying, the application of fragrant substances, and so forth. However, when the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the understanding is that "there is an embellishment related to the fuel and the water.
There is also a neuter form of the word *edhas* ending in *-s*. [Synonyms for fuel are: *kāṣṭham*, *dāru*, and *indhanaṃ*.

This is because of the lexicon [Amara-kośa] stating, "edha, idhma, medha, and samit denote firewood (striyām)," and also because of such scriptural observations as, "just as a kindled fire consumes fuel (edhāṃsi). If that were the case, the analysis of the compound would have to be *edha-dakasya*;
for if the word *udaka* were substituted, the form *edha udakasya* would result. Therefore, *udaka* is a synonym for [the term in question].

The word *daka* also exists, as evidenced by Halāyudha’s lexicon: "The world, nectar, life, and water shall be *daka*. Thus, the meaning is that "the fuel (*edhas*), acting as the agent, purifies the water (*udaka*).
However, when one intends to express the status of the object (*karman*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case is used.

The specific quality of water heated by a fire kindled with particular woods such as *nimba* and *karañja* is well-known in the medical treatises (*vaidyaśāstra*). Regarding the phrase "I worship the feet of Śambhu" (*bhaje śambhoścaraṇayoḥ*), here the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the feet because their status as the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). Thus, it refers to that which is related to the feet of Śambhu.

The meaning is "a vessel. Regarding the phrase "satisfied with fruits," here too, the sixth case is used because there is an intention to express the status of an accessory (*śeṣatva*) for the instrument. The understanding is that "satisfaction is related to the fruit" (*phala-sambandhinī tṛptiḥ*).
(598) *ṣaṣṭhī hetu-prayoge* | 2|3|26|. [When a word expressing a cause (*hetu*) is employed, the sixth case is used.]

[The rule applies] when there is the employment of a word expressing a cause (*hetu*). The term "in the sense of cause" (*hetau*) is understood from the previous context. Thus, he says: "when the cause is to be indicated. This means "when the state of being a cause is to be indicated. The result is that the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used after a word denoting the cause.

By this [rule], the sixth case supersedes the third case prescribed by the rule "in the sense of cause" (*hetau* [Pāṇini 2.3.23]). Why "when there is the employment of a word expressing a cause"? [Example: *annena vasati* ("He dwells because of food").
Why is it stated "when the cause is indicated"? [Consider: *annasya hetos tubhyaṃ namaḥ* ("Homage to you because of food"). Here, [the suffix] does not occur after the word *yuṣmad*.
(599) *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca* ("After a pronominal, the third case ending also [is used]").
"And the third case [is used] after a pronominal. The word "sarvanāmnaḥ" is in the genitive case. Thus he says:

"and after a pronominal and the word 'hetu' (cause). When the expectation arises as to "from what does it occur?", it is understood from the proximity that it occurs "after a pronominal and the word 'hetu'."

With this intention, he cites the example: "by what cause? (*kena hetunā*). It should be understood that if [the word] *sarvanāmnaḥ* were in the ablative case (*pañcamī*), then the genitive case would not occur after the word *hetu*. (1) Regarding "in the usage of synonyms for 'cause'": [this refers to] when synonyms for *nimitta* (cause) are employed.

The meaning is that the use of all case endings generally occurs after those [words] and after words in grammatical apposition with them. "What is the cause for dwelling?"—this should be understood as having both a nominative and an accusative ending. "And so forth" refers to: "from what cause," "of what cause," and "in what cause."
He states the purpose of employing the term *paryāya*—namely, "In this way, what is the reason? and so forth.

He states the purpose of employing the term *prāya*—namely, "Because of the employment of *prāya*. And thus, the two rules—"the sixth case [is used] when there is the employment of a cause" (*ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge*) and "the third case [is used] optionally after a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca*)—need not be formulated.

That which comes into being is a *bhāva*. (600) [Pāṇini 2.3.30] "With a word ending in the sixth case, and with a suffix having the sense of *tasa*. Regarding the phrase "in connection with this": [it refers to] "from words denoting direction" (*dikśabdebhyaḥ*).

Beginning with the rule "saptamī-pañcamī-prathamābhyo dig-deśa-kāleṣv astātiḥ" and ending with "ṭhāhi ca dūre" and "ṭhutarācca," suffixes are prescribed in their own sense (svārthe) after words denoting direction, place, or time. Among those, the suffix *atasuc* is prescribed by the rule "dakṣiṇottarābhyām atasuc."
The suffix *atas* has as its meaning that which consists of direction, location, and time;

a suffix whose meaning is that [same meaning] is an *atasartha* suffix, and the sense is "in connection with" such a suffix. Although among the *atasartha* suffixes *astāti* is indeed the first, the term *atasartha* is used for the sake of brevity rather than *astātyartha*.
Because of the weight [of the rule] due to its being composed of two combined syllables. Regarding the phrase "dikśabde" (in the case of words for directions):
the meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) prescribed by the rule *ṭhanyārādi*.
As for the example *dakṣiṇataḥ*: it is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) after words ending in the seventh, fifth, or first case endings.

From the word *dakṣiṇa*, which denotes direction, place, or time, the suffix *atasuc* is applied. The meaning is "in the southern direction," "from the southern direction," or "the southern [direction]. The same applies to place and time. Regarding *pura*:
from the word *pūrva*, in the sense of the suffix *astāti*, [the rule] "for *pūrva*, *adhara*, and *avara*, there is *asi*, and for these, *pura*, *adha*, and *ava*" [applies].

Thus, there is the *asi* suffix and the substitution of *pura* for the base (*prakṛti*). The meaning is "in the east," "from the east," or "toward the east. Regarding *purastāt*: when the suffix *astāti* is added to the word *pūrva*, the substitution of *pura* for the base occurs by the rule "ṭhāstāti ca.
This has the same meaning as the word *puras*. Regarding *upari*: [it is formed similarly].

By the rule *ṭhuparyupariṣṭādi*, the suffix *ril* is prescribed after the word *ūrdhva*; the suffix *atil* is taught as a substitute for *ril*, and the substitution of the base form [of the suffix] is also prescribed as a nipāta (irregular formation). Thus, the meaning is "in the upward direction," "from the upward direction," or "the upward direction. The same applies to place and time.

(601) *enapā dvitīyā* | 2|3|31|. Regarding the rule *enapā dvitīyā*: since the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena* would have rendered the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) mandatory [in such constructions], he says—by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the sūtra)—that the rule *enapā* is to be separated [from the rest]. Thus, the rule *enapā* is treated as an independent statement.

In the rule "ṣaṣṭhyatasarthaiḥ," the word "ṣaṣṭhī" (the genitive case) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. The meaning is that the genitive case should be used in connection with a word ending in the suffix *enap*. "Dvitīyā" is another rule; here, "*enap*" is carried over. The stated meaning is that the accusative case should be used in connection with a word ending in *enap*. For example: *dakṣiṇena*.

The suffix *enap* is applied [by the rule] "ṭhenab anyatarasyām adūre 'pañcamyāḥ. Thus, "uttareṇa" [is used]; the meaning is that "uttareṇa grāmam" or "grāmasya" is the example. It should also be understood that "pūrveṇa grāmam" or "grāmasya," and so forth, are examples as well, because the suffix *enap* is prescribed after words denoting directions (*dikśabda*). However, in the Bhāṣya...

It is stated in the *Pṛthagvinā* sūtra that the rule "ṭhenapā dvitīyā" (A 2.3.30) is read prior to the sūtra "ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena" (A 2.3.30). Therefore, even though there is a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) here,

since the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is impossible, it is logical that the genitive case is simply not valid when used in conjunction with the suffix *enap*.

(602) *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyanyatarasyām* || 2.3.34 || [The rule] *dūrāntikārthaiḥ*: by these [words]. That is to say, when used in conjunction with words having the sense of "far" (*dūra*) and words having the sense of "near" (*antika*).

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "and the fifth": the intention is that the fifth case (pañcamī) is carried over from the rule "the fifth case is used for the ablative (apādāna) when the sixth is absent. Although the second and third cases—by virtue of the rules "with *tena* and *pṛthak*" and "with *pṛthak*, *vinā*, and *nānā*, the third case is used"—are in close proximity, they [are not applied here].
They are both included, according to the commentary. (603) *jño'vidarthasya karaṇe* |2|3|51|.
[The sūtra reads: *jño'vidarthasya*. The division is *jñaḥ* and *avidarthasya*. [The word] *jñaḥ*...

The sixth case singular (*ṣaṣṭhyekavacana*) is used because it imitates the word *jña*. "That whose object (*artha*) is not knowledge" (*avidartha*) means that which does not have knowledge as its object; that is to say, something distinct from that which has knowledge as its object. Thus he says: "of the root *jñā* when it does not mean knowledge. "As a remainder" (*śeṣatvena*) means "as a relation" (*saṃbandhatvena*).

The intention is that [the word] "śeṣa" (remainder) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (continuation). In the example *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("knowledge of ghee"), the meaning is: an activity (*pravṛtti*) related to that ghee which is, in reality, the instrument (*karaṇa*). Precisely because of the indicator (*liṅga*) in the rule *avidarthasya*, the root *jñā* in the sense of "understanding" (*avabodhana*) is used here in the sense of "activity. [Thus, the genitive case is applied. The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*)...

Although [the rule] "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*) already establishes this, this statement is for the purpose of [prohibiting] the compound of a genitive case that is prescribed by its specific wording (*pratipadavidhānā*).
(604) *Adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.52): [The sixth case-affix is used] after verbs having the sense of *adhi-i* ("to remember"), *day*, and *īś*, when they denote the object.

"Adhīgartha... [refers to] "of these. The root *dhik* (√dhyai) preceded by *adhi-* is not invariably used in the sense of "remembering"; that which has a meaning similar to its meaning is "adhīgartha. That is to say, it means "having the sense of remembering. "The remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to the fact that the term continues from the rule "the genitive case is used for the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*). "The remembering of the mother" (*mātuḥ smaraṇam*).
The meaning is that, in reality, it is the remembrance related to the mother who has become the object (*karman*). "Giving of ghee" (*sarpiṣo dayanam*):

the meaning is that, in reality, it is the act of giving related to the ghee which has become the object. [The root] *day* is used in the senses of "giving," "going," "protecting," "injuring," and "giving. In the expression "he shows compassion to the miserable" (*dīnān dayate*), [the same applies].
The meaning is: "desiring to separate [them] from suffering. Compassion (*dayā*) is the desire to remove the suffering of others.

Regarding the phrase "or sovereignty" (*īśanam vā*), the word "of ghee" (*sarpiṣaḥ*) is to be supplied. In reality, the meaning is: the disposal as one pleases that pertains to the ghee which has become the object of the action. This also...
This is solely for the purpose of prohibiting compound formation. However, in the case of *lokānīṣṭe*, the meaning is "he commands according to his own will. (605) *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* [Pāṇini 2.3.53].

The word *prati* [is used] after the root *kṛ*. The words "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) and "the remainder" (*śeṣe*) are understood from the previous rules. "Exertion" (*pratiyatna*) means the imparting of a quality. Thus it says: "after the root *kṛ*, in the sense of the object. For example: *edhodakasyopaskaraṇam* ("the preparation of fuel and water").
The word *edhas* ends in *s* and is neuter; the word *daka* signifies water. And *edhas*...

The term *daka* forms a *dvandva* compound [with *edhas*]. Alternatively, the word *edha* ends in the vowel *a* and is masculine; thus, it has been stated immediately below that the *dvandva* consists of *edha* and *udaka*.
In reality, the meaning is "the preparation related to the fuel (*edhas*) and water (*udaka*), which have become the objects of the action."

(606) *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ* | 2|3|54| The analysis of *rujārthānām* is as follows: those whose meaning is "sickness," "affliction," or "disease. He explains the term *bhāvavacanānām* by saying "those having an abstract state (*bhāva*) as their agent" (*bhāvakartṛkāṇām*). [The word] *vakti* means "he speaks."

The suffix *lyuṭ* [denotes] the agent (*kartari*). The meanings of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) are not intended here. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose agent is the action (*bhāva*)," which is the meaning of the verbal root. This results in the sense "of those whose agent is the action," as is clear in the Bhāṣya. The words "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) and "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) are understood from the previous context. Thus he says: "in the object" (*karmaṇi*).

Regarding the word "śeṣa" (the remainder): this [rule] is also for the purpose of preventing the formation of a compound. In the example *caurasya rogasya rujā* ("the affliction of the thief's disease"), the term *rujā* refers to the suffering caused by a malady, such as fever or pain. The ultimate meaning is that the disease afflicts the thief with suffering and so forth; thus, it has the disease as its agent (*rogakartṛkā*).

In reality, the meaning is that there is suffering and so forth pertaining to the thief who has become the object [of the action]. Here, by the word *roga* (disease) ending in the abstract suffix *ghañ*, a specific bodily affliction such as emaciation is intended; and this [affliction] is the agent in the act of causing pain (*rujā*). When one intends to express the thief as the residual factor (*śeṣatva*) of that action, the genitive case is used: "of the thief" (*caurasya*). As for "of the disease" (*rogasya*), [it follows the same logic].
It should be understood that the compound *coraruja* does not occur.
It should be stated as *ajvari-saṃtāpyoḥ*.
Regarding *ajvari-saṃtāpyoḥ*: [this refers to] "of those verbs meaning 'to suffer' (*ruj-arthānām*) which express a state (*bhāva-vacanānām*)."
The meaning is that the rule *jvarisaṃtāpivarjitānām* should be stated [as a prohibition].

Regarding the example *caurajvara* (thief-fever) for "the fever of a thief": here, in the compound *caurajvara*, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) indeed occurs, because there is no further specific injunction regarding the remaining genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Likewise, [one may form] *rogasya caurasaṃtāpaḥ* (the thief’s affliction of disease).

This should also be understood here. Since the phrase "except for *ajvari* and *saṃtāpi*" is not stated here, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) such that the genitive case would apply to the word *caura* when used as the object of verbs meaning "to cause pain" (*rujārtha*) that express a state (*bhāvavacana*), even when the object is intended as a residual factor (*śeṣe*). To demonstrate this, he says: "having disease as its agent" (*rogakartṛka*). [The term] "having disease as its agent" means...

In reality, it refers to the fever or the heat associated with the thief who has become the object [of the action]. Thus, since *jvar* (to suffer from fever) and *saṃtap* (to be heated) signify illness and have as their agent an illness—which is a state (*bhāva*)—the sixth case ending is not applied by this rule when one intends to express the "residual relation" (*śeṣatva*) of the thief, who is the object; rather, it occurs through connection with a *kṛt* suffix.

The genitive case applies; by the rule "the genitive is used in the sense of the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*), the genitive is indeed employed. Therefore, the compound *caurajvaraḥ* ("the thief's fever") and *caurasantāpaḥ* ("the thief's affliction") certainly occurs—this is the intended meaning. (607) *nātha* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). Pāṇini 2.3.55.

The term *nātha* [is used] in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). The terms *śeṣe* (in the remaining senses) and *karmaṇi* (in the sense of object) also carry over. Thus he says: "of that which has the sense of benediction. This also is solely for the purpose of preventing the formation of a compound. "The praying for ghee" (*sarpiṣo nāthanam*)—this is the desire, "May this be mine," which is the act of blessing.
That alone is the meaning of the root *āśīṅ* (*nāthate*). In reality, the meaning is "the act of wishing for that which has become the object [of the wish], namely clarified butter.
(608) Pāṇini 1.4.56: *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ hiṃsāyām*. [In these cases, the agent is designated as the *karman* when the sense is that of injury.]

The phrase *jāsinipra* follows from the rule *karmaṇi śeṣe*. Thus he says: "of those [roots] meaning injury," and so forth. This also serves solely to prevent the formation of a compound. For example: *caurasyojjāsanam* ("the driving away of the thief"). [This is derived from] the roots *jasu* in the sense of "striking" (*tāḍane*) and *jasu* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsāyām*).

In the *curādi* [group], the meaning is "violence related to a thief who has become the object" (*karmībhūta*). However, the root *jasu* belonging to the *devādika* group is not included here, because it lacks the sense of violence and because of the specific grammatical indication *jāsī*. Regarding *niprau*: [it refers to] the root preceded by the prefixes *ni* and *pra*, as in *niprahaṇeti*.

This is the exposition of the verbal root *han*. In this context, the two elements *ni* and *pra* are taken together; they are also taken in reverse order as *prani*; and they are also taken separately as *pra* and *ni*. This is because of the [grammatical] explanation. He provides an example of them taken together: "the killing (*niprahaṇana*) of a thief."
In reality, the meaning is "the killing related to the thief who is the object [of the action]. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *hanter atpūrvasya*.

He gives an example with the order reversed: *praṇihanana*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *nergada-*, but there is no substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *han*, because of the rule *aṭkupvāṅ-*.
By rule (*niyamāt*), because the *ṇ* of *ṇi* is not included therein. He gives examples separately: "nihananam" or "prahaṇanam.
Due to the absence of the cause [for the substitution], in the word "nihananam," the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule "ṇatvam anter atpūrvasya" does not occur.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with *cur*": the root *naṭ* (in the sense of "dancing") is not included here, because its long vowel is explicitly pronounced as in *nāṭa*. The meaning is that the long vowel in *nāṭa* excludes it from this group. In the example *caurasyonāṭanam* ("the harming of a thief"), the meaning is that by the influence of the prefix (*ud-*), the root *naṭ* functions in the sense of "harming. In the example *caurasya krāthanam* ("the killing of a thief"):

The root *kṛth* is listed in the *ghaṭādi* group in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*). Although it is designated as *mit* by the rule *ghaṭādayo mitaḥ*, the shortening prescribed by *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* does not apply here, because a long vowel is specifically prescribed [for this root].
The phrase *vṛṣalasya peṣaṇam* means "the injuring of a low-born man. Regarding the roots *vyapa* and *hṛpaṇ*: [the sūtra] is completed by supplying the remainder [of the wording].

He explains the Sūtra: "The sixth case-ending (ṣaṣṭhī) shall occur for the object (karman) when it is intended as a 'remainder' (śeṣa). The analysis of the compound [samavyavahṛta] is: "those two whose meanings (arthau) are equal (samau), that is, identical. The single-substitute form (pararūpa) results from its inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group.
When the object of the root *hṛ* preceded by *vi-ava* and of the root *paṇ*, which possess a single meaning, is intended to be expressed as a remainder, [the sixth case is used].

The meaning is that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should occur. This [rule] is also solely for the purpose of preventing the formation of a compound (*samāsa*). Now, one might object: since the verbal root *paṇ*—in the sense of "to bargain" (*vyavahāre*) and "to praise" (*stutau*)—also functions in the sense of praising and not merely in bargaining, how can these two [meanings] have the same referent? To this, he says: "it is praised" (*dyate*).

The meaning is that *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ*, when used in the sense of playing with dice (*dyūta*) or in the context of bargaining over the price of buying and selling, have the same meaning. Thus, the implication is that they both result in the sense of such transactions. [An example is: "the dealing of a hundred."

"Or by wagering" (paṇanam) means that one takes [the stake] through the practice of gambling or through the practice of buying and selling. For if it were used solely in the sense of "transaction," it would result in the verb being intransitive. Thus, in reality, there is the taking [of the stake] by means of playing dice, which is connected to the hundred that has become the object.
The meaning is: "or the taking [of goods] through an agreement on the price regarding purchase and sale.

(609) *vyavahṛ-paṇoḥ samarthayoḥ* |2|3|57|. Regarding the phrase "when they are semantically connected" (*samarthayoḥ*), the question is: "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'when they have the sense of transacting' (*vyavahārārthayoḥ*)? This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the expression *śalākāvyavahāra*: he states that in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the verb *vyavahṛ* does not have the sense of "transaction" (*vyavahāra*), meaning it signifies "counting" (*gaṇanā*). In reality, this results in the meaning "counting related to the counting-sticks (*śalākā*) which have become the object [of the action]. Here, [the genitive case] of the sixth [case-ending applies].

The sense is that the compound indeed exists because there is no other rule [prohibiting it]. *Brāhmaṇapaṇanam* is a counter-example for the root *paṇ*. He states here that *paṇi* does not have the meaning of "trading" (*vyavahāra*), saying "the meaning is 'praise' (*stuti*).
In reality, the meaning is "praise related to the Brāhmaṇa who has become the object of the action. In this case as well—
The intention is that the compound indeed exists.
(610) *divastadarthasya* |2|3|58|.
In this sūtra, the word *tat* refers to *vyavahṛ* and *paṇa*, which were mentioned in the preceding rule, as being for that purpose (*tadartha*).
The two [roots] are examined. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "that whose object (*artha*) is the very object of those two, namely *vyava* and *hṛpaṇ*.
