He states this with the words: "of that which has gambling as its object" (*dyaūtārthasya*). The analysis of the word *diva* is: "that whose object (*artha*) is the grasping (*grahaṇa*) by means of playing with dice (*akṣakrīḍanena*), i.e., gambling (*dyaūta*). Regarding the word "purchase" (*kraya*): it refers to that whose object (*artha*) is the agreement on price (*mūlyasaṃvāda*) concerning purchase and sale (*krayavikraya*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Regarding the phrase "the genitive in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*), the intention is that the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not carry over here, according to the [author's] own explanation. Thus, since there is no desire to express the object as a "remainder," the rule "the genitive occurs in the sense of a remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*) would otherwise not apply; this statement is therefore made to provide for that case, and not specifically regarding the application of a *kṛt*-affix.
This is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the compound (*samāsa*). Indicating this, he provides an example: *śatasya dīvyati* ("He plays for a hundred").
The meaning is that he takes [something] by means of gambling with dice, or through an agreement on a price regarding purchase and sale.

Here, because the term *śeṣa* (remainder) does not recur, the cognition is characterized solely by the status of being an object (*karman*). For this very reason, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) [is applied].

In the subsequent sūtra, *brāhmaṇe*, the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa state that in the example *gāmasya tadahaḥ sabhāyāṃ dīvyeyuḥ* ("They should gamble for a cow on that day in the assembly"), a compulsory genitive (*nitya-ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise apply; therefore, the word *dvitīyārtham* ("for the sake of the accusative") is used [to justify the accusative]. This is explained in detail elsewhere.

(611) *vibhāṣopasarge* |2|3|59|. When there is an upasarga (preverb), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may optionally be used for the object of the root *div* when it has the sense of *vyavahṛ* (to deal in) or *paṇ* (to bet). This is the meaning.

(612) *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne* || 2.3.59 || Regarding *preṣyabruvoḥ*: "when there is a deity as the recipient" (*devatāsaṃpradāne*). This means: in that [verbal root] for which a deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Regarding *preṣyabruvoḥ*: the root *iṣ* meaning "to go" belongs to the *divādi* class and ends in the suffix *śyan*.

It functions in the sense of impelling due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*). The analysis of the compound is *preṣyaśca brūśca tayoḥ* ("the two, namely *preṣya* and *brū*"). Regarding the term "of the object" (*karmaṇaḥ*): the meaning is that the word "object" (*karman*), which was carried over from the rule "in the sense of *adhi* and *gṛ*" (*adhīgarthe*), is here transformed into the genitive case. Regarding "of the oblation" (*haviṣaḥ*): the word *havis* does not refer to its own form, but rather...

It refers to a word denoting the remainder of the oblation (*haviḥ-śeṣa*), according to the commentary. And thus, it refers to a word denoting the remainder of the oblation which has become the object of the two verbs *preṣya* and *brūhi*, both of which denote an action where the deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), according to the commentary. And so it is.

[The term *preṣya*] refers to that which denotes a specific oblation (*haviḥ*) which has become the object (*karman*) of the two verbs *preṣya* and *brū* when they denote an action directed toward a deity as the recipient (*sampradāna*). This is because of the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*). And thus, that which has become the object of the two verbs *preṣya* and *brū* when they denote an action directed toward a deity as the recipient—

The result is that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used after a word denoting a specific sacrificial offering (*havir-viśeṣa*). Here too, the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], according to the commentary. Thus, this is an exception to the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). For example: *agnaye chāgasya* ("of the goat for Agni"). This is an instruction (*sampraipa*) performed by the Adhvaryu priest directed toward the Maitrāvaruṇa: "O [Maitrāvaruṇa]..."
"O Hotṛ, announce the oblation consisting of the fat (medas) known as the omentum (vapā), which belongs to the goat and is to be offered to Mitra-Varuṇa and Agni.
[The meaning is: make it known by means of the *praiṣa* (directive) 'Let the Hotṛ worship Agni; may he enjoy the oblation of the goat's omentum-fat; O Hotṛ, sacrifice! In this regard, although...

In the Kalpasūtras, one sees only the injunction: "I summon for Agni the omentum and the fat of the goat," but not the phrase "of the oblation" (haviṣaḥ). Nevertheless, such an injunction is to be understood as existing in some Vedic recension based on examples cited in the Bhāṣya. By the word *medas* (fat), [something] like a piece of cloth is meant.

A specific type of meat is being discussed. [The instruction] "Recite" (anubrūhi) is given; however, in the *Kalpasūtras*, one sees only the formula: "O Hotṛ, give the command for the fat of the omentum of the goat-offering to Agni" (*agnaye chāgasya haviṣo vapāyā medasaḥ preṣya*), and not even the word "offering" (*haviṣaḥ*).
Nevertheless, such a formal command (*praiṣa*) is found in some recensional tradition (*śākhā*) as cited in the *Bhāṣya*.
It is to be understood as follows: by the word *medas* (fat), a specific part of the flesh resembling a fragment of cloth is denoted. Regarding the phrase "Recite [the invitatory verse] for...

(*anubrūhi*), one observes in the *Kalpasūtras* only the form "O [Hotṛ], give the command for the omentum and the fat of the goat's oblation to Agni" (*agnaye chāgasya haviṣo vapāyā medasaḥ preṣya*), and not even the word "oblation" (*haviṣaḥ*). Nevertheless, such a call (*praiṣa*)...

It should be understood that this occurs in a certain recensional branch (*śākhā*) based on the example given in the *Bhāṣya*. By the word "fat" (*medas*), a specific kind of flesh resembling a piece of cloth is denoted. Regarding the phrase "recite after" (*anubrūhi*): the example is "O Maitrāvaruṇa, recite after [the offering] for Agni, the omentum and fat of the goat's sacrificial oblation. O Maitrāvaruṇa!

The meaning is: "Make manifest by means of the *puro’nuvākyā* that sacrificial offering (*havis*) related to the goat, consisting of fat (*medas*) called the omentum (*vapā*), which is to be given with reference to Agni. [Question: What is the purpose of [specifying] *preṣya* and *bruvaḥ*? [Example:
"Offer the omentum, the fat, the offering of the goat to Agni. [Question: What is the purpose of [specifying] *haviṣaḥ*? [Example: "To Agni..."
"Send the cow-dung! Why [is it] "in the case of an offering to a deity"? [Example: "Send the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for the boy.
"A prohibition must be stated when the oblation (havis) is qualified by 'being set forth' (prasthita).
[Example: "Send the goat-oblation—the omentum and the fat—set forth for Indra and Agni. [The word used is] "set forth."
The meaning is "unmanifest.
(613) *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe* | [Pāṇini 2.3.64] Regarding *kṛtvo'rtha*: the phrase *kṛtvo'rthānām* means "those whose meaning is precisely the meaning of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*."

The meaning is that for those [words] whose meanings are "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*), their usage [is intended]. Regarding the phrase "the sixth case ending in the sense of the remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*): although the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) was interrupted in the preceding sūtra beginning with *divas tadarthasya*, it is carried over here by "leaping like a frog" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), according to the [traditional] commentary. [Example: *pañcakṛtvo 'hnaḥ*.

Regarding the term *bhojanam*: it means the meal belonging to that day which is actually the locus [of the action] five times. [This is according to the rule: "The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used after a numeral in the sense of counting the repetition of an action. Here, because the genitive case is prescribed again in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣe*), there is no compound. [Thus one says: "study twice on the day" (*dvirahanyadhyayanam*).

In the rule *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*, the suffix *suc* is used in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*). Here, because the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to be expressed, the locative case alone is used, and not the genitive.
(Pāṇini 2.3.65): *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* ("The [genitive] is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows").

"Kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti" means when a *kṛt* suffix is employed. He states the resulting meaning: "In connection with a *kṛt* [suffix]. Therein, he gives an example for the agent (*kartṛ*): "The creation of Kṛṣṇa. [This is formed] with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) in the feminine. The meaning is: "A creation having Kṛṣṇa as its agent."
He provides an illustration regarding the object (*karman*): "of the world" (*jagataḥ*).
The meaning is: one who possesses an activity conducive to the creation having the world as its object. Regarding "the secondary object" (*guṇakarmaṇi*):
the meaning is that when a root ending in a *kṛt* suffix takes two objects, the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is optionally desired for the non-principal object.

However, the genitive case is invariably used for the primary object (*pradhānakarman*). This point is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *akathitaṃ ca*. As in the example "netāśvasya" (the leader of the horse), under the rule *akathitaṃ ca*, it is explained in detail that in the illustrative example "grāmam ajāṃ nayati" (he leads the goat to the village), the goat is the primary object (*pradānakarman*), whereas the village is the secondary object (*guṇakarman*).
Previously [it was stated that] in this manner, it should be understood that here the horse (*aśva*) is the primary object (*pradhānakarma*), while *srughna* is the secondary object (*guṇakarma*).
It might be argued: "The word *kṛti* (referring to kṛt-affixes) is redundant. Nor should it be said that it is for the purpose of excluding *tiṅ*-affixes;
for in cases such as *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), where there is a connection with a substitute *lādeśa*, the rule *na loke* applies.
Since the absence of the genitive case is established by the very prohibition of the genitive, in examples such as "a horse bought for a hundred" (*śatena krītaḥ śatyo'śvaḥ*),
the genitive will not occur for the horse and so forth precisely because they are expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *ya*.
Nor [is there a problem] in cases such as "away from Devadatta" (*devadattaṃ hiruk*), where the action of exclusion and so forth is understood through the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *hiruk* and others.
One might suspect that the sixth case (genitive) ending would apply here because of the rule *pratipadika-kāraka-*, since it is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā-khal-artha-tṛṇām*.

However, when there is an intention to express the "remainder" (*śeṣatva*), the sixth case is indeed desired here. Thus, by process of elimination, this sixth case results only in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix; therefore, he asks—"In connection with a *kṛt*?"—to inquire what purpose the mention of *kṛt* serves.

"What is [the purpose]? He gives the answer: "In the case of a *taddhita* suffix. This means for the purpose of removing the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when there is a connection with a *taddhita*. The example is *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat").

The popular analysis (*laukikavigraha*) is: "A mat was previously made by him. In that context, "previously" (*pūrvam*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). [The formation follows] the rule *sup-supā*.

This is a compound (*samāsa*). When the word *anena* is understood from the preceding context, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *ini* is applied to the words *kaṭa-pūrva* and *sapūrva* by the rules *pūrvādiniḥ* and *sapūrvācca*. In that case, since the mat (*kaṭa*) is the object (*karman*) with respect to the action of making (*karoti*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would have been required; however, it does not occur because of the connection with the secondary suffix (*taddhita*). [Objection: But surely, the mat was made (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*)...

When the analysis (*vigraha*) is made as "pūrvaṃ anena" (previously by him), a compound of the word *kṛta* with the word *pūrva* is not possible, because the word *kṛta* lacks semantic independence (*sāmarthya*) due to its dependence on the word *kaṭa*. For this very reason, even the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) *-ini* is difficult to obtain. Furthermore, by means of the *kta* suffix in the word *kṛtam*, [the agent] of the mat (*kaṭa*)...

Since the object (*karman*) has already been expressed [by the suffix], there is no possibility at all for the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to arise from it; so what is the purpose of including the term *kṛt* [in the rule] to exclude that? If it is argued that because the object is already expressed by the suffix *kta*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) would also be difficult to obtain after the word *kaṭa*, do not say so, for [the sequence is] *kṛta-am* first, then *am*.

Thus, in the extraordinary (alaukika) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), because the mat (*kaṭa*) is not present and its connection as the object (*karman*) is impossible, the root *kṛ* is at that time intransitive; consequently, since the suffix *kta* cannot occur in the sense of an object (*karman*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule "the suffix *kta* occurs in the neuter in the sense of the abstract state."

Since the word *kṛta* (done) has no requirement for the word *kaṭa* (mat) once it has been formed, both the compound (*samāsa*) and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) are unimpeded. Consequently, in the case of *kṛtapūrvī*, which ends in a secondary derivative, the meaning resolves as "one who previously did [something]. When there arises a desire to know the object of what was done—namely, "what did he do?"—the word *kaṭam* (a mat) is construed with it.

For it is observed that even when an action is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), there is still a connection with the *kāraka*, as seen in examples such as *kaṭaṃ kṛtavān* ("he made a mat"). Furthermore, that status as an object (*karmatva*) is not expressed by the suffix *-kta*, because that suffix is prescribed to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*). Nor is it expressed by the suffix *-in*, because that suffix is prescribed to denote the agent (*kartṛ*). And thus:

In the absence of the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes], the genitive case would apply. It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the mention of *kṛt* is for the purpose of excluding that [genitive]. Nor should it be argued that the genitive will not occur here simply because of the prohibition regarding connection with a *niṣṭhā* suffix; for there is the supplementary rule:

"The genitive is prescribed after a word ending in the neuter *kta* when used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*)," and also the rule: "And [the genitive is used] after a word ending in *kta*..."

Since the prohibition of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in connection with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), as stated in the *vārttika* on the rule *vartamāne*, does not apply here, the genitive is absent;
and thus, because it has not been prescribed [as the genitive] according to the aforementioned method, the accusative (*dvitīyā*) is easily obtained. Nor even if...
It should be argued that when "kṛt" is mentioned [in a rule], the genitive case is unavoidable because there exists a connection with a *kṛt*-suffix in the form of the *kta* suffix;

however, this is not so, because by the force of the mention of "kṛt" and by the examples given in the Bhāṣya, what is intended is a connection with a *kṛt*-suffix that has not entered into the formation of a compound (*vṛtti*). And in the present context, the word "kṛtā" [refers to such a connection].

Because it is included within the operation (*vṛtti*) of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), its connection does not constitute a cause for the genitive case. Nor, if this were so, would there be a genitive in examples such as "the best cooker of rice" (*odanasya pācakatamaḥ*) or "the mention of the cooker of rice" (*odanasya pācakagrahaṇam*), because there would be an absence of connection with a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) that is not included within the *vṛtti*. And thus: "He is the best cooker of rice. (*odanaṃ pācakatamaḥ*)
It should not be argued that in the case of *odana-pācaka-grahaṇam*, there ought to be only the second [case-ending], for that is precisely what we accept (*iṣṭāpatti*).

For this very reason, under the section governing the suffix *matup*, the author of the root-text will provide the example *prājño vyākaraṇam* (an expert in grammar) under the rule *ṭhprajñā-śraddhā-arcābhyo ṇaḥ*. Nor does this imply that one would say *ghaṭaḥ kriyate* (the pot is being made).

In this case as well, one should not argue that since the intention to express the object (*karman*) is absent, when the abstract suffix (*bhāva-lakāra*) occurs, the word *ghaṭa* can subsequently be construed as the object; thus, because it is unexpressed (*anabhihita*), the accusative case would be unavoidable. This is incorrect, because there is a difference between the two cases. For in the expression *kṛtapūrvī*, during the stage of the non-orthodox analytical construction (*alaukika-vigraha*), [the analysis is as follows:]...

Since the word *kaṭa* is not present [in the compound], the intention to express the object (*karman*) is impossible; therefore, it is appropriate to rely on the view that the suffix *-kta* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). However, in the case of the word *kriyate*, such non-intention (*avivakṣā*) is simply not possible.

Because it is not included within the five types of *vṛtti*—namely, *kṛt*, *taddhita*, compound (*samāsa*), *ekaśeṣa*, and verbal roots with *san*-affixes and so forth—it is devoid of *vṛtti*; and thus, due to the absence of an analytical expansion (*vigraha*), this method of derivation applies only to the domain of *vṛtti*. This is the path following the opinion of the ancients. However, in the *Śabdenduśekhara*:
In such instances as *ṭhodanaṃ pācakatama* ("the best cooker of rice"), the accusative case is indeed incorrect;
rather, the genitive alone is correct, as has been explained in detail. For fear of prolixity, that is not written here.
Now, [one might object] regarding the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*: "By those who gave incomparable fragrance to those like me who were suffering... [and so forth].
There is a verse that reads: "Who would not be inflamed with passion when their body is as if cleansed by the winds?

This is the speech of Śrī Rāma, afflicted by the pain of separation. Here, the genitive case in *duḥkhasya* (of suffering) and *tanor* (of the body) is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). [The meaning is: "O you who give suffering to those like me," and so forth, regarding flowers and other objects.

The meaning is: who among conscious beings (*cetana*), by applying fragrance (*āmoda*) or perfume (*uparimala*) through unguents (*dhāya*) or ointments (*upoṣaka*), and by smearing their bodies (*tanoḥ uta tanum*) with them, would not be as if blazing (*jvala*), that is, shining brightly? In this context, the genitive case in "āmodasya" and "uttamasya" ought to be used in the sense of the object (*karma*).

If it is argued that this is because the word *dhāya* is a derivative formed with the *ṇa*-suffix from the root *dhā* (in the sense of nourishing) according to the rule *dadāti-dadhātyoḥ*, [we reply: no, for in such cases one must supply the word "having taken" (*gṛhītvā*) in connection with it, as in the expression "having taken the supreme fragrance of flowers and so forth" (*puṣpādīnām uttamam āmodam gṛhītvā*) or "the nourishers of suffering" (*duḥkhasya pauṣakair*).
[This is] the second [exception] to the rule of occurrence.

(615) *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* |2|3|66|. When both [agent and object] are possible, [the sixth case-affix is used] for the object (*karman*). From the preceding sūtra, the word *kṛti* is understood to carry over. "When both are possible" means...

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; its external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is a *kṛt*-suffix. Thus they say: "In that case where there is the possibility of [the genitive] for both. This means that when a *kṛt*-suffix occurs in relation to a single word, and the genitive would otherwise apply to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), the genitive shall apply to the object alone, and not to the agent.

Regarding the term *āścarya* (wonder): the meaning is that the milking which has no cowherd as its agent (*agopakartrka*) and for which the cows are the object (*gokarmaka*) is marvelous. If one were to resort to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) based on the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable" (*ubhayoḥ prāptau*), then in the case of "the cooking of rice and the appearance of Brahmins" (*odanasya pāko brāhmaṇānāṃ ca prādurbhāvaḥ*), the genitive would apply only to the object (*karman*), and not to the agent (*kartṛ*).

However, if a *bahuvrīhi* compound is resorted to, since only one [agent] is obtained as the cause [of the action], it results that this restriction does not apply when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise be required for the agent and object as defined by distinct actions.
This restriction does not apply to the feminine suffixes *a* and *ā*.

Regarding the phrase "of the two feminine suffixes," this is a *vārttika*. It refers to the application of the suffixes *a* and *ā* prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the suffix *ktin* is used in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ktin*).

The meaning is that the restriction stated in the rule "only for the object" (*karmaṇy eva*) does not apply. The result is that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs even when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Regarding *bhedikā*: the suffix *ṇvul* is used here to indicate the meaning of the verbal root; there is the substitution of *ak*, the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and the change to *ī* by the rule *pratyayasthāt*. Regarding *vibhitsā*: [this is derived] from the root *bhid* with the desiderative suffix *san*.

The suffix *ṭāp* is applied after the word *pratyaya* when it ends in the vowel *a*. The meaning is: "the act of piercing" or "the desire to pierce," where Rudra is the agent (*kartṛ*) and the world is the object (*karman*). [This is according to] the rule: "In the remaining cases, there is an option."

"Optionally in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*). This is also a *vārttika*. The meaning is that the restriction "when both [nouns] are applicable" (*ubhayaprāptau*) is made optional when there is a connection with a suffix other than the suffixes *ak* and *āk*. Regarding the statement "some say [it applies] when a feminine suffix follows," the aforementioned option is stated.

The meaning is that some maintain [the rule] applies only when there is a connection with a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Regarding "variegated" (*vicitrā*): the meaning is an action (*kṛti*) having Hari as the agent (*kartṛ*) and the world as the object (*karman*). Regarding "some [hold it applies] without distinction":
the meaning is when there is a feminine suffix other than *akā* and *ākāra*. Regarding "variegated": [it refers to] an action having Hari as the agent.

The meaning is that *kṛti* refers to action pertaining to the world (*jagat*). "Some [say] without distinction" means that when *kṛti* is employed with a feminine suffix distinct from *a* and *āk*, as well as with a non-feminine suffix, the aforementioned option applies. "Of words" refers to the work of the Teacher (Pāṇini).

The meaning is that it is an instruction (*anuśāsana*) regarding the sequence of words. Instruction (*anuśāsana*) is the discrimination [of correct forms] from the incorrect (*asādhu*). (616) *ktasya ca vartamāne* | 2.3.67.
Regarding *ktasya ca vartamāne*: [Objection] But surely [the desired result] is already established by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.

To the question "For what purpose is this?", he says: "Not by the world" (*na lokena*). "Esteemed by kings" (*rājñāṃ mataḥ*) means understood or honored. Regarding the suffix *kta*, it is applied to the roots *man* (to think), *budh* (to know), and *pūj* (to honor) according to the rule: *ṭhmatibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*. In that context, *mati* means desire.

Because of the separate mention of "intellect" (buddhi), the meaning is respectively: the object of a present desire whose agent is the King, the object of a present cognition whose agent is the King, and the locus of a present worship whose agent is the King. However, in cases such as "he who is worshipped by gods and demons" and "the jar is known by you," [the distinction does not apply].
The suffix *kta* should be understood as having the sense of the past tense (*bhūte*).

(617) *Adhikaraṇavācinaśca* | 2|3|68|. [The word] "and that which denotes the locus" (*adhikaraṇavācinaḥ*) [is supplied]. He explains the sūtra by completing the ellipsis: "in connection with [a word ending in] the suffix *kta*."

Regarding "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*): concerning "that which has been slept in" (*śayitam*). It is called *śayitam* because one sleeps in it (*śete 'smin*). The suffix *kta* is applied by the rule *śīṅ svapne* and *kto'dhikaraṇe ca dhrauvye*. In that context, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in *eṣām* (of these) denotes the agent (*kartari*), as the prohibition [of the genitive] in the sense of "in common usage" (*loke*) is set aside by this exception. However, for the root *bhuj*, [the rule does not apply].

Because it has the sense of "consumption," the suffix *kta* is applied in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*). However, in the example "this rice has been eaten by them" (*idameṣāṃ bhukta odanasya*), the genitive case is used for both the agent and the object. The restrictive rule "when both [agent and object] are eligible [for the sixth case]" does not apply here; this is because, according to the maxim of the intermediate exception (*madhye'pavādanyāya*), the rule "of the agent and the object" [takes precedence].
The word *kṛtī* [is used] precisely because that restriction is accepted for the genitive case alone.

(618) *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* | 2|3|69|. [The rule begins with] *na loka*. "Of these": *la*, *u*, *uka*, indeclinable (*avyaya*), past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), words having the sense of *khala*, and *tṛn*.

This is the meaning of "of these. In the case of *u* and *uka*, when the long vowel of homogeneous quality (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied, it becomes *ūka*. Then, in the case of *la* and *ūka*, when the *guṇa* substitution for *āt* is applied, it becomes *loka*. Regarding the term *lādeśa*: this is an indication without a case-ending (*avibhaktika-nirdeśa*), intended to point toward the examples of the *lādeśa* [substitution]. It refers to *la*.

The term *laḍādi* refers to the general class [of present tense suffixes]. Since these do not occur in direct usage (*sākṣāt-prayoga*), the intention is that their substitutes (*ādeśa*) are being referred to. In the examples *kurvan* or *kurvāṇaḥ*, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* replace *laṭ*. Here, because the prohibition of the genitive case applies to the object (*karman*), the accusative case is used. The particle *u* [indicates a pause or a specific nuance].
This is an illustration [of the rule]. By the word *u* (in the sūtra), because it is a specific designation (*viśeṣaṇa*), the rule of "that which ends with it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
In the example *hariṃ didṛkṣuḥ*, the suffix *u* is added to the root *dṛś* followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*) according to the rule *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ*.
Due to the principle of "acting like a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), this *kṛt*-suffix is considered to end in the vowel *u*.

The meaning is: "one who desires to see Hari as the object [of the action]. Or, "one who is habitually adorned" (*alaṅkariṣṇu*). The word *harim* is to be supplied [as the object]. By the rule *alaṃkṛñ-*, etc., the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied in the sense of habitual action and so forth. If, however, there were a restriction to the vowel *u* alone [in the rule], then this prohibition would not apply here. [Regarding] *uka*: this also...

This is for the purpose of indicating an example: "Hari is the slayer of the Daityas. This is formed under the governing rule *ṭhā kvestacchīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.134), by the specific rule *ṭhlaṣapatapadasthābhūvṛṣahanakamagamaśṛÃbhya ukañ* (Pāṇini 3.2.154), which prescribes the suffix *ukañ* in the sense of one who has that habit (*tacchīla*), that quality (*taddharma*), or who performs that well (*tatsādhukārin*).

The suffix *ukañ* is added to the root *han* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), resulting in vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel. By the rule "ṭhho hanteḥ," the *h* is changed to *gh*. By the rule "ṭhhanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ," the *n* is changed to *t*.
Thus, the meaning is one whose nature is to kill, whose characteristic is killing, or who is skillful at killing.
The prohibition of the chamber.

*kamer iti*: This is a *vārttika*. Its meaning is that there is no prohibition of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when used in connection with a word ending in *uka* derived from the root *kam*. For example: *lakṣmyāḥ kāmukaḥ* ("one who desires Lakṣmī"). [The suffix] *ukañ* is applied by the rule *laṣapatapada...* etc.
*avyayam iti*: This is an illustrative indicator (*udāharaṇasūcaka*). For example: *jagatsṛṣṭvā* ("having created the world").
The ellipsis is "Hari remains. The suffix *ktvā* is applied according to the rule "samānakartṛkayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.21).

Its status as an indeclinable is established by the rule "ktvātosunkasunaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.40). Regarding the phrase "to act with ease," the ellipsis is "Hari has power over the devotee. [The suffixes] *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when there is an action [toward another action].

The suffix *tumun* is used in the sense of "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārtha*). By the rule *ṭhkṛnmejantaḥ*, it possesses the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Some maintain that in this context, only a *kṛt*-derived indeclinable is intended; however, the truth is that there is no distinction, so even that which is not a *kṛt* derivative is included. [Example: *devadattaṃ hiruk*. The meaning is "exclusion having Devadatta as its object. Regarding the term *niṣṭhā*:

This is an illustration [of the rule]. [The sūtra states: "The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*. [Examples are: *viṣṇunā hatāḥ* ("slain by Viṣṇu"). Here, because the time is past (*bhūte*), the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense (*karmani*). Since the genitive case is prohibited for the agent (*kartari*), the third case is employed:
*daityān hatavān* ("having slain the Daityas"). Here, the suffix *ktavatu* is used in the active sense (*kartari*) for the past time. [In the passive sense: *daityā hatāḥ*.
Because the sixth case (genitive) is prohibited, the second case (accusative) is used. Regarding the phrase "khalarthāḥ": this is an indication of examples.
In the example *īṣatkaraḥ*, the suffix *khal* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal*.
Because of the inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning), the suffix *yuc*—which also has the meaning of *khal*—is understood from the rule *āto yuc*.

"Soma has been drunk only slightly by you. Now, if by the rule *tṛn* (Pāṇini 6.2.160) only the suffix *tṛn* were understood, then there would be no prohibition in cases such as "somaṃ pavamānaḥ" (the purifying Soma); therefore, he says: "The term *tṛn* is a pratyāhāra (a grammatical abbreviation). From where does it begin and which endings does it include? To this he says: "Starting from the word *tṛ*..."

Regarding the phrase "from *tṛn* up to the letter *n*": in the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, the word *tṛ* is a portion of the substitute *śatṛ*; the meaning is that [the operations apply] to those [suffixes] beginning from that *tṛ* up to and including the letter *n* found in the rule *tṛn*. *Laṭaḥ*...

The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are applied] when not coreferential with a word ending in a case-suffix other than the nominative; [also] in the vocative; [and] those two [suffixes] are called *sārvadhātuka*; the suffix *śānan* is applied after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj*; the suffix *cānaś* is applied [after a root] to express habit, age, or ability; the suffix *śatṛ* is applied after the roots *iṅ* and *dhāry* when there is no difficulty; [the suffix *śatṛ* is applied] after the root *dviṣ* in the sense of "enemy"; [and the suffix *śatṛ* is applied] after the root *suñ* when connected with a sacrifice.

The sequence of the sūtras is as follows: *ṭharhaḥ praśaṃsāyām*, *ṭhā kvestacchīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu*, and *ṭhtṛn*. Here, there is a reference to those suffixes ending in *śānan* and so forth, and those ending in *tṛn*; however, it is not a reference to the word *tṛ* in the rule *ṭhlaṭaḥ śatṛ*, which is merely a partial substitute (*ekadeśa*) for *śatṛ*, since that [word *tṛ*] never occurs independently anywhere.

Because it is unfit for application [to the suffix *śānac*]. Nor is it [the case] for *śānac*, since its establishment follows simply from its being a substitute for *l* (the *l-affixes*). Thus stands the settled rule. "Śānan" is mentioned here merely as an illustration. "Somaṃ pavamānaḥ" [is an example]; [this is derived by] the rule "pūyaṅkyoḥ śānan. "Ātmānaṃ maṇḍayamānaḥ" [is another example]; [this is derived by] the root "maḍi bhūṣāyām" (to adorn).
The suffix *cānaś* is applied by the rule *ṭhtācchīlyavayovacana*. "The suffix *śatṛ*"—this indicates an example.

"One who studies the Veda" (*vedam adhīyan*); here the suffix *śatṛ* is applied by the rule *iṅdhāryoḥ*. "The suffix *tṛn*"—this indicates an example. "One who creates the worlds" (*kartā lokān*); [this is formed] by the rule *tṛn*.

It should be understood that the suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of "having such a character" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; because words ending in *śānan*, *nā*, and *tṛn* do not undergo the substitution of *l* [for *śit*], the pratyāhāra [term *śit*] is resorted to.
(1) After the root *dviṣ*, the suffix *śatṛ* is optionally [used].

Regarding the rule *dviṣaḥ śatur vā*: the meaning is that when the root *dviṣ* is joined with a word ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, the prohibition of the genitive case should be stated as an option.
For example: *murasya* or *muraṃ dviṣan*. Here, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied by the rule *dviṣo 'mitre*.
Since this suffix is included within the *tṛn*-pratyāhāra (the group of suffixes beginning with *tṛn*), the prohibition [of the genitive] would apply obligatorily; however, it is here made optional.

This is an alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*). The sense is that [the rule applies] to everything according to the maxim *anantarasya* (of what is immediately preceding). As for the statement "the genitive is used in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), the sense is that the result is a difference in the mode of presentation (*prakāra*) within the verbal cognition (*śabdabodha*).
In the example *brāhmaṇasya kurvan*, the word *hariḥ* is to be supplied as the remainder; it is the present participle (*laṭ*) substituted by *śatṛ*. From the mouth...

The meaning is: "one who possesses an activity conducive to the creation related to a Brāhmaṇa. However, when the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is intended to be expressed, the accusative case alone is used. Regarding the phrase *naraka-sya jiṣṇuḥ*: by the rule *glājisthaśca gsnuḥ*, the suffix *gsnu* is applied in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. The meaning is: "one who possesses victory related to Naraka."
But when there is an intention to express the object (*karmatva*), only the second case suffix (*dvitīyā*) is used.

(619) *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* | Pāṇini 2.3.70. [The word] *bhaviṣya* [is understood here] from the rule *akenorbhaviṣyat*. The word *na* is carried over [from the previous rule]. The analysis of the compound is: "of *aka* and *in*" (*akaśca inaśca tayoḥ*).

"Bhaviṣyat" (future) and "ādhamarṇyam" (indebtedness)—these two form a *dvandva* compound. According to the Bhāṣya, a sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) is not intended here. The resulting meaning is that the genitive case is prohibited when used with an *akena* suffix in connection with a verb signifying the future or a state of indebtedness. In that context, the portion concerning indebtedness does not connect with the *akena* suffix.

This is because of the statement: "The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*avaśyaka*) and debt (*adhamarṇya*). Therefore, the future tense (*bhaviṣyat*) alone is construed with the element *aka*. However, the suffix *in* is construed with both the future and the sense of debt, as both are possible.
Thus he says: "In the future, [the suffix] *aka* [is used]; and [the suffix] *in* [is used] in the sense of the future and debt."

The meaning is "of that which has a future sense" and "of that which has the sense of debt (obligation). Regarding the phrase *sataḥ pālakaḥ* ("the protector of the virtuous"): the meaning is that Hari manifests himself intending to protect the good people (*sajjana*). [This suffix is] prescribed for the future tense by the rule *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*, and [it applies] in the future.

This is because of the rule "gamyādayaḥ. The meaning is "one who is about to go to the cow-pen" (goṣṭhaṃ gamiṣyan). Regarding "śataṃ dāyī," the meaning is "one who will repay a hundred [coins] taken as a debt.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied here in the sense of being a debtor, according to the rule "āvaśyakādharmaṇyayor ṇiniḥ. That [suffix] refers to the future.
Since there is no specific rule [to that effect], one should not suspect that the meaning has already been conveyed by the future sense [of the suffix].
(620) *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* | Pāṇini 2.3.71. Regarding *kṛtyānām*: he explains the sūtra by supplying the ellipsis—namely, "the genitive case may optionally be used."

The meaning is that, with reference to the heading "kṛtya," certain specific *kṛt* suffixes are prescribed; when used in conjunction with these, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) may optionally be employed for the agent (*kartṛ*). This is an optional rule, as the sixth case for both agent and object is already established as obligatory by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ. For example: *mayā mama vā sevyo hariḥ* ("Hari is to be served by me"). [This is derived from] the root *sevṛ*, meaning "to serve."

In the rule *ṭhṛhalorṇyaḥ*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Since the agent, which is the referent of the word *asmad* (we), has not been expressed [by that suffix], the genitive case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.65. Regarding the term *geya*: one might ask, "But here, since the status of the *sāman* as the object is already expressed by the suffix *yat* in *ṭhaco yaḥ*, how [can it be the object]?"

Because there is the possibility of the application of the genitive case [to both], he says: "the one to be brought" (*bhavya*). Now, in the example "The cows are to be led to the cow-pen by Kṛṣṇa," since the suffix *tavya* is designated as a *kṛtya*, the optional genitive for Kṛṣṇa would apply—bypassing the rule "when both [agent and object] are possible"—according to the rule *ubhayaprāptau*. However, from the word "cow-pen" (*vraja*), [the genitive applies] by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*.
Since it might be thought that [the word] *kṛti* always applies [to all kṛt suffixes], he says: "In this case, the connection is divided.

He shows the manner of division with the words: "of the kṛtyas. [The word] "is understood" [from the previous sūtra]. Thus, the result is that the genitive case, which would otherwise apply to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) when connected with a kṛtya suffix, is prohibited.

"‘The cows are to be led to the cow-pen’ (*netavyā vrajam*). Regarding this, the option [to use the locative case] for the object of a secondary action (*guṇakarma*)—as in "the leader of the horse to/from Srughna" (*netā aśvasya srughnasya srughne vā*)—does not apply here. This is because that rule, which finds its scope in cases where both [the primary and secondary objects] are eligible [for the locative] and excludes *kṛtya* suffixes (such as *-tavya*), is satisfied by examples such as "the cows are to be milked for milk by Kṛṣṇa" (*dogdhavyā gāḥ payaḥ kṛṣṇena*).

Because the secondary object (*guṇakarma*) has already been accounted for by this [rule], which finds its purpose in that context, it would sublate [the application of] the primary object (*pradhānakarma*) due to its posteriority. Therefore, regarding the phrase "or in the sense of the agent" (*kartari vā*): the meaning is that after the composition of the rule *kṛtyānām*, the rule *kartari vā* should be formulated separately. This is the stated meaning.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that, carrying forward the rule *kṛtyānām*, it should be explained that when used in conjunction with a *kṛtya* suffix, the genitive case may optionally be employed for the agent (*kartṛ*). This is the stated meaning;
that is, by carrying forward the rule *kṛtyānām*, it is understood that when used in conjunction with a *kṛtya* suffix, the genitive case may optionally be employed for the agent.

The meaning is that it must be explained. In cases where neither [the sixth nor the third case] is applicable, such as in "Hari is to be served by me" (*mayā mama vā sevyaḥ hariḥ*), this [third case rule] remains in force.

(621) *Tulyārthair atulopamābhyāṃ tṛtīyā 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.72). [This sūtra prescribes that] when used with words having the sense of "equal," except for *atula* and *upama*, the third case ending is optionally employed.

Now, the case endings used with secondary words (*upapada-vibhakti*). [The rule] "with words having the meaning of *tulya*" (*tulyārthaiḥ*): since the genitive of the residual category (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would necessarily apply here, this is an optional third case (*tṛtīyā*). Although the inclusion of synonyms is already established by the plural number in *tulyaiḥ*, the explicit mention of the word *artha* (meaning) is for the purpose of including those words that have the meaning of "equal" independently of any other word.

Therefore, they say that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as "gauriva gavayaḥ" (like a cow is a gavaya). Others maintain that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the words "atula-upamābhyām," this [rule] applies only in connection with indeclinables (*avyaya*).

(622) *Caturthī cāśiṣyāyuṣyamadrabhadrakuśalasukhārthahitaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.73): [The fourth case ending is used] also in benedictory expressions (*āśis*) when combined with *āyuṣya*, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita*.

"And the fourth [case]. Regarding "with words having these meanings": the meaning is "with words having the senses of *āyuṣya*, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita*. "In the alternative, the sixth case" means that by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the inclusion of that [sixth case] is understood; this is the sense. "A synonym for *āyuṣya* is *cirañjīvita* (long-lived)."
"Wholesome" (*kuśalam*) and "free from affliction" (*nirāmayam*) are synonyms for "auspicious" (*madrabhadra*). "Peace" (*śam*) is a synonym for "happiness" (*sukha*).

"Purpose" (*prayojanam*) is a synonym for "aim" (*artha*). "Beneficial" (*pathyam*) is a synonym for "welfare" (*hita*). Regarding the rule *hitayoge ca*, it should be understood that the constant use of the dative case does not apply when expressing a blessing (*āśis*). Now, as for the rule *svaṃ rūpam*...
Since it is appropriate to understand that by the technical definition (paribhāṣā) only words such as *āyuṣya* and others are to be grasped, he says:

"Because of the explanation" (*vyākhyānāt*). Now, one might object that because *madra* and *bhadra* are mentioned separately, this explanation—that [the rule applies] to words having these meanings—is incorrect; therefore, he says: "Of *madra* and *bhadra*. This is the genitive case.

(623) *Ādhāro’dhikaraṇam* | 1.4.45. "The locus (*ādhāra*) is the locus-case (*adhikaraṇa*). The governing term *kāraka* is modified to appear in the nominative case, and it serves as a qualifier for *ādhāra*; thus, [the meaning is] "the locus."
It is understood that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is a *kāraka*. A *kāraka* is that which is connected with an action (*kriyā*).
Thus, when there arises the expectancy "of what is it the substratum?", it is understood—by virtue of its being the most proximate—that it is the substratum of the action.
And the action intended here is that which resides in the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*). Furthermore, this status of being a substratum is not direct, but rather...
[The suffix *kta* occurs] precisely by way of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), as explained [in the commentary]. Thus he says: "by way of the agent and the object.
"Resting upon that" (*tanniṣṭhā*) means resting upon the agent and the object. (Pāṇini 2.3.36):
"The seventh case-affix is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and [the agent and object]."

"Also [the locative case] in the sense of locus (adhikaraṇe), and by the word 'ca' (and), also in the sense of distance. The meaning is that because of the word "ca," the phrase "dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ" (from words meaning distant or near) is drawn over from the preceding rule, "dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca" (after words meaning distant or near, the second case may also be used). Regarding the term "aupśleṣika" (contact-based):

*Upaśleṣa* means a connection such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*); the locus (*ādhāra*) produced by that is the first [type of locus]. *Vaiṣayika* means the locus established by the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*); this is the second [type of locus].
*Abhivyāpaka* means the locus established by the pervasion of all parts; this is the third [type of locus]. In that regard:
He provides an example of the immediate (āṬpaśleṣika) substratum (*ādhāra*) mediated by the agent, namely: "He sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*).

The word "Devadatta" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In that case, with respect to the action of sitting residing directly in the agent Devadatta, the mat is [the substratum] by virtue of its connection through conjunction (*saṃyoga*), mediated by Devadatta.

The status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) arises from being the substratum of that [action]. Now, he provides an example of a proximate locus (*upaśleṣika*) by way of the object (*karman*): "He cooks in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pacati*).

The word "rice" (*taṇḍulān*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, [the pot is the locus] because it is the substratum of the action of cooking, which resides directly in the rice, which constitutes the object.

The status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) arises from being a substratum through rice, by prioritizing the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandha*) with the cooking pot. In such cases as "there is 'color-ness' (*rūpatva*) in color" or "there is motion (*ceṣṭā*) in the body," it should be understood that the substratum-hood is "immediate contact" (*upaśleṣika*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*).
Now, he illustrates the objective substratum (*vaiṣayika-ādhāra*): "There is a desire for liberation" (*mokṣe icchāsti*).

Here, with respect to the action of existence (*satā*) residing in the desire which functions as the agent, liberation possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) because it serves as the substratum by way of desire, through the mediation of the relation of being an object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*).
Now, he provides an example of a pervasive substratum (*abhivyāpaka-ādhāra*): "The Self exists in everything.

Here, by prioritizing the total pervasion (*kṛtsnavyāpti*) regarding the action of existence (*satā-kriyā*) residing in the agent (*kartṛ*) which is the Self, everything possesses the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) because it is the substratum of existence by means of the Self. Now...

By the word "and" (ca), he provides examples from the meanings of "distant" and "near" which have been drawn forward: *vanasya dūre* or *antike* ("at a distance from the forest" or "near the forest").
The meaning is "far" or "near. This rule applies to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).
"By three case-endings" means by the second, fifth, and third case endings. In reality, however...

*Upa* means "nearby," and *śleṣa* means "connection" or "relation"; thus, by etymology, that which is produced by such [proximity] is *aupaśleṣika*. Therefore, proximity itself is the *aupaśleṣika* type of locus (*ādhāra*). For this very reason, it is said: "The locus is of three kinds: pervasive (*vyāpaka*), proximate (*aupaśleṣika*), and objective (*vaiṣayika*). However, in the case of a word [being related] to another word...

What other kind of connection (*abhisaṃbandha*) could there possibly be besides proximity (*upaśleṣa*)? Thus, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *saṃhitāyām*—specifically regarding *iko yaṇ aci*, which states "of that which is proximate to a vowel" (*acyupaśliṣṭasya*)—is consistent with this. Kaiyaṭa explains that "proximate to a vowel" (*acyupaśliṣṭasya*) means "pronounced in the vicinity of a vowel" (*acsamīpoccāritasya*). For this very reason...

In the case of the expression *māse 'tikrānte dīyate* ("it is given after a month has passed"), the month (*māsa*) is the locative substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) by way of immediate proximity (*upaśleṣika*). Consequently, this accords with the Bhāṣya on the rule *tatra ca dīyate kāryaṃ bhavavat*. For this very reason, in the rule *tadasminnadhikam iti daśāntāḍḍaḥ*, [the example] *ekādaśa bhāṣā adhike asmin* ("eleven coins are added to this") is appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "in a hundred kārṣāpaṇas," one might raise the objection: how can eleven [coins] which are additional [to the hundred] be the locus (adhikaraṇa) of the hundred?

In response, it is explained that since other types of loci—namely the pervasive (vyāpaka) and the objective (vaiṣayika)—are possible here, it is understood to be an immediate proximity locus (upaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa).

The Bhāṣya is consistent [with this]. And thus, the example of "he sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*) cited in the root text as an illustration of the *aupadeśika* (directly contiguous) locus is indeed untenable, because it contradicts the aforementioned Bhāṣya. And thus, in cases such as "he sits on a mat," by way of partial pervasion (*ekadeśavyāpti*)...

The status of being a pervading locus (*abhivyāpakādhāratva*) is secondary (*gauṇa*). The primary (*mukhya*) status of being a substratum (*ādhikaraṇatva*) consists solely in the occupation of all parts; for it is the opinion of the Bhāṣya that the objective (*vaiṣayika*) and the proximate (*aupaśleṣika*) are secondary. Precisely for this reason, in the rule *svaritenādhikāraḥ*...

And in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "The most effective [means] is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*), it is asked: "What does the Teacher consider to be the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)? It is where the entire nature of the substratum is pervaded. If that were so, then the locative case would apply only here: "oil in sesame seeds," "clarified butter in curds"; but not in cases such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" or "in a well."
However, one might object that in the case of *gargakulam*, the rule would not apply because grammatical operations are understood to pertain only to the primary sense (*mukhya*).

Anticipating this, it is resolved that there is no fault because of the statement "by means of the circumflex accent (*svarita*), an additional operation occurs" and because of the inclusion of the suffix *-tama*.
Thus, in examples such as *kaṭe āste* ("he sits on the mat") and *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ* ("the hamlet is on the Ganges"), [the secondary sense is accepted].

Even a secondary (*gauṇa*) locus has the sense of the locative case alone. However, if in examples such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the locative relationship based on proximity (*sāmīpika-adhikaraṇatva*) is not intended to be expressed, then it should be understood as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
A detailed discussion is to be found in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the rule *ktasyenviṣayasya*: and not... [text continues]

In the case of the expression *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*, the locative case (*saptamī*) might also be suspected [as the correct reading], because it is accepted that the meaning is "the object of that which ends in the suffix *in* when it follows a word ending in the suffix *kta*. [The alternative view is expressed as: "The suffix *in* [is applied] to the agent.
That is, when the suffix *ini* is applied to the word *adhīta*, which ends in the *kta* suffix used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).

The term *adhītī* results in the meaning "one who has studied. When there arises a desire to know the specific object of what was studied—namely, the question "What did he study?"—the word *vyākaraṇa* (grammar) connects as the object (*karman*) of the act of studying. And since that status of being the object of grammar has not been expressed by any other [inflectional] element, it is like the case of *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who previously made a mat").
The meaning is that when the second case is applicable, the seventh case is used by this [rule].
And regarding the usage of "sādhu" and "asādhu":
the phrase "and in the usage of sādhu and asādhu" implies the remainder, namely, "the seventh case should be stated. Regarding the word "sādhu":

The meaning is "one who does what is beneficial. Regarding "asādhu," the meaning is "one who does what is harmful. In both cases, this is an exception to the genitive case used for the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Since the rule *sādhunipuṇābhyām arcāyām* would have already established the usage, the inclusion of the word *sādhu* here is for the sake of excluding the sense of "reverence" (*arcā*). For example: *sādhuḥ mṛtyo rājñi* ("He is skilled toward the king [in killing]"). Here, it refers to the statement of a fact (*tatvakathana*).
The intended meaning is as follows: the purpose of including the term *sādhu* in the rule *sādhunipuṇābhyām* will be stated later.
[The next rule is: *nimitāt karmayoge*.

Regarding the phrase "from the cause" (*nimitāt*): the meaning is that the locative case should be expressed after a word denoting a cause when used in connection with an action. Now, one might object: "In the case of *'baddho jāḍyaḷena'* (bound by dullness), would there not also be a locative case? To this he says: "The cause here is the result. The meaning is "it is the result alone. This is because the cognition that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is what prompts activity.

It should be understood that the fruit (phala) also possesses the status of a cause. To exclude relations such as that between the produced and the producer, he says: "Yoga is conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between two things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*);
whereas for other [separably established] things, it is conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Regarding the phrase "in the skins": [he killed] the tiger for the sake of the skins.

The meaning is "he kills. Here, there is indeed inherence (*samavāya*) of the hide with the leopard as the object, because the part and the whole are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*). Regarding "of the tusks": the meaning is "for the sake of the tusks. Here, there is indeed inherence of the two tusks with the elephant as the object. Regarding "in the hair": [the meaning is "for the sake of the hair"].

The meaning is "for the sake of hair. *Camari* refers to a specific species of deer. Regarding the word *sīmni*: the meaning is "for the sake of a boundary. It should be understood that while the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is obtained by the rule for the cause (*hetu*), the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing purpose (*tādarthya*) is also applicable.
*Sīmā* means "ovarian capsule" (*aṇḍakośa*). As it is said: "The word *sīmā* is feminine when it denotes a boundary, a place of rest, a field, or an ovarian capsule."

Thus says the *Medinī*: "Puṣkalaka means a musk deer. Furthermore, the *Medinī* states: "The word *puṣkalaka* refers to a musk deer, a mendicant, and a boundary-pillar. Here too, there is indeed a connection (*samavāya*) of the boundary with the action performed by the *puṣkalaka*. Haradatta, however, [explains]: "A boundary (*sīmā*) is the limit of a village and so forth; for the purpose of knowing it..."

Puṣkalaka explains that "uśaṅku" means "struck" or "planted. Here, it should be understood that there is a contact between the boundary and the action performed by Puṣkalaka. Regarding the word "vetanena" (for wages): here, "vetana" refers to the substance of hire;
the meaning is "for the sake of that. In this context, the relationship of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) applies equally to the wages and to the grain being harvested.
The intended meaning is that it is a relationship (*saṃbandha*), but neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*).

(625) "And [the locative case is used] when the characterization of an action is by means of another action" (Pāṇini 2.3.37). Intending to explain that both words *bhāva* are synonyms for "action" (*kriyā*), he comments: "of which... (*yasya*).

Regarding the term "by means of an action" (*kriyayā*): an action has both an agent as its locus and an object as its locus. Among these, he provides an example of that which has an object as its locus—namely, *goṣu*. This is the answer to the question, "When did Devadatta go? Here, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of a defining relation (*lakṣakatva-sambandha*); it is an exception to the genitive case of the residual category (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The meaning is that he is one who has gone, as indicated by cows characterized by the act of milking currently taking place. Here, the act of milking is the direct indicator (*lakṣaka*), while the cows are so by virtue of being its substratum. Consequently, the final sense resolves to "he went at the time of the cow-milking. As for the expression "he went when [the cows] had been milked" (*dugdhāsu gataḥ*): [The remainder of the passage follows: ...in this case, the past passive participle (*kta*) denotes the completion of the action; however, because the action of milking is not yet completed, the word "gone" (*gata*) cannot denote the mere completion of the action. Therefore, the word "gone" indicates the state of having departed from the place where the milking was performed. Thus, the meaning is that he is one who has gone, as indicated by cows characterized by the act of milking already completed. Here, the act of milking is the indicator, while the cows are so by virtue of being its substratum. Consequently, the final sense resolves to "he went after the cow-milking was finished. In the case of "he went when [the cows] were being milked" (*duhyamānāsu gataḥ*), the same principle applies: the word "gone" indicates the state of having departed from the place where the milking was being performed.
