The meaning is: "one who possesses the act of going as indicated by cows distinguished by having already been milked.

The resulting sense is: "he went after the time of milking the cows. However, for an action residing in the agent, one should cite the example: "while the Brahmins were studying, he went out. In this regard, that which must necessarily [be repeated] again—

Furthermore, that which makes known the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*) is not necessarily a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); rather, it may also be something that makes [the object] known only once.

For example: "The student whom you saw with a water-pot in his hand is he. Although he was seen with the water-pot in his hand only once, nevertheless, the water-pot remains a defining characteristic of him.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sutra under discussion. However, in the case of "He offers the oblation when the sun has risen" (*udite āditye juhoti*), the meaning of the locative case is proximity as a locus (*sāmīpikam adhikaraṇatvam*). The sense is "the time proximate to the risen sun.
The resulting meaning is "the time immediately following the rising of the sun. [As for the example] "during an eclipse" (*uparāge*)...
In the case of "srāyāt" (he should eat), however, by the word *uparāga* (occurrence/affliction), the time which is the locus of that occurrence is indicated;
thus, it is indeed the locative case in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*). This is explained in detail elsewhere.
(626) *ṣaṣṭhī cā'nādare* (Pāṇini 2.3.38). [The sixth case ending is also used when disregard is expressed.]

"And the sixth [case-ending] in disregard (*anādare*). The term "and" (*ca*) here draws in the [mention of the] seventh case-ending from the preceding rule. "In disregard" (*anādare*) is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). The phrase "and of that which" (*yasya ca*) is carried over from the previous sūtra. The meaning is: when disregard is implied, and another action is indicated by means of a particular action, then the sixth and the seventh case-endings are used for that [agent].
He states the result: "when there is an excess of disregard" (*anādarādhikye*). The analysis of the compound is: that from which disregard is excessive.

Regarding the forms *rudati* and *rudataḥ*, this is the answer to the question, "When will you renounce? Here, the meaning of the genitive and locative cases is that of indication (*lakṣakatva*). The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the act of renouncing as qualified by disregard.

The sixth and seventh case endings serve to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Furthermore, "disregard" (*anādara*) has as its object the son or others who are the substrata of the action denoted by the indicator.
It is characterized by disregard, which is made known by the son or others as qualified by the present action of weeping.
The meaning is "going forth" (*pravrajanam*).
(627) *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyādasākṣipratibhūprasūtaiśca* | 2|3|39|.
He states the result [of the rule]: "while the son and others are weeping. [In the rule] *svāmīśvara*, the sixth and seventh cases [are used].

The intention is that by means of the letter *ca*, both of those [the genitive and locative] are drawn forward. Now, one might ask: since the genitive is already established as the "residual" (*śeṣa*) case, for what purpose is the genitive prescribed here? To this he says: "only the genitive. Examples are: *gavām* or *goṣu*—meaning "related to cows"; *gavām* or *goṣu īśvaraḥ*—"lord of cows. *Gavām* or *goṣu*.

The term *adhipati* means "lord" or "master. Regarding *dāyāda*: *dāya* refers to that portion of wealth acquired by a father or others which is fit to be taken by sons and other heirs. One who takes (*ādatte*) that is a *dāyāda*. Although the rule for the suffix *ka*—namely *ṭhāto 'nupasarge*—"the suffix *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix"—includes the condition "provided it is not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*), the suffix *ka* is nevertheless applied here precisely because of this specific irregularity (*nipātana*).

The meaning is "an heir related to the cows. Because the word *dāya* (inheritance/property) is inherently expectant [of a possessor], there is a compound (*vṛtti*). The resulting sense is "one who takes a portion consisting of cows.
However, in the commentary on the sūtra *yasmād adhikam*, the word *dāyāda* is stated to be a synonym for "owner" (*svāmin*).
It is established [as follows]: "born among cows" (gavām) or "among the cows" (goṣu). The meaning is "related to cows.
And this relationship consists in the form of being an enjoyer. Thus he says: "only cows" (gā eva).
By the word "only" (eva), there is the exclusion of buffaloes and the like.

(628) *āyuktakuśalābhyāṃ cāsevāyām* || 2|3|40 || The word *āsevā* is explained as "intense application" (*tātparya*), meaning "eagerness" (*autsukya*). As Amara states: "One who is intent upon that is *tatpara*, *prasita*, or *āsakta*; one who is devoted to a desired object is *udyukta* or *utsuka*. This refers to the term *āyukta*.
He explains: "employed" (vyāpārita) means "set in motion" (pravartita). Regarding the phrase "appointed or skilled" (āyuktaḥ kuśalo vā):

in the context of the worship of Hari, "appointed" (āyukta) means "set in motion. Here, since there was a requirement for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) due to the intended expression of a locative relation based on the object (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇatva*), this specific rule is stated.

*Āyukta* means "a cow" (*gaur*). The prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadarthe*). The root *yujir* means "to join" (*yoge*). Thus he says: the meaning is "slightly joined. (629) *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.41).

And because there is specification [of a part from a whole], as in "jāti-guṇa... etc.; the suffix *tasi* in both "yataḥ" and "tataḥ" has the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). This is because, from a certain aggregate (*samudāya*), a single part is specified by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*).

The meaning is that "separation" (*pṛthakkaraṇa*)—which consists in making known a specific property that distinguishes [an object] from others—is understood as what is expressed by words of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*); therefore, the genitive and locative cases are used. Here, the word "own" (*sva*) denotes a part (*ekadeśa*). In this regard, he provides an example of separation by means of a genus (*jāti*): *nṛṇām*...
Regarding the phrase "among men" (*nṛṣu*): the word *nṛ* refers to a collection of human beings.

The plural number is used because one intends to express the distinction between the individual members of that collection. The singular form "twice-born" (*dvija*), however, is intended to denote the genus (*jāti*). The genitive and locative cases here express the relationship between the part and the whole.

The meaning is "connection," specifically in the form of being the object of the aforementioned selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Consequently, the meaning is that a twice-born person (*dvija*), who constitutes a portion of the human collective, possesses the quality of excellence characterized by his distinction from others. He illustrates separation based on a quality (*guṇa*) with the example: "among cows, [the black one]" (*gavāṃ goṣu vā*).

The meaning is that a black cow, which constitutes a single part of the collection of cows, is the locus of the property consisting in having much milk as distinguished from others. He provides an example of separation by means of action: "among those going" or "while they are going."
The meaning is: one who belongs to a portion of a group (such as a crowd) and possesses the quality of speed, which is excluded from others [in that group], while running.
He illustrates the separation by means of a name with the words "of the students" (*chātrāṇām*).
One who belongs to a portion of the group of students, named Maitra, possesses the quality of proficiency, which is excluded from others [in that group].
This is the meaning.

(630) *pañcamī vibhakte* | Pāṇini 2.3.42. "The fifth [case-ending] is used when there is separation (*vibhakta*). Separation means being divided; this is because the suffix *kta* is understood here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

[This refers to] the state [of being]. The rule "yataśca nirdhāraṇam" (Pāṇini 2.3.41) continues to apply. In the case of the basis of selection (*nirdhāraṇāvadhi*)—such as humans—and those being selected (*nirdhāryamāṇa*)—such as the twice-born—there exists non-difference in their common nature and difference in their specific nature. And thus, in every instance of selection...
Since some degree of difference exists in every case, by the word "distinct" (*vibhakta*), the intended meaning is precisely that there is difference;
and therefore, this [term] applies only where there is indeed a difference between the basis of selection (*nirdhāraṇāvadhi*) and the thing being selected (*nirdhāryamāṇa*),
and not where there is non-difference through any superimposed form.

Intending to state the *pravṛtti* (the application of the rule), he says: "of that which is being delimited" (*nirdhāryamāṇasya*). The words "in the limit of delimitation" (*nirdhāraṇāvadheḥ*) are to be supplied, because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "and from that which [delimitation] proceeds" (*yataśca nirdhāraṇam*).
Here, there is only the communication of the possession of a property distinct from the limit; it is not, however, [the case that...].

Intending to show that the intended sense is "one part from the whole," he provides an example: *māthurāḥ* ("the people of Mathurā"). The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) here is the state of being a point of reference;
thus, the inhabitants of the region of Mathurā are "exceedingly wealthy" in comparison to those of the region of Pāṭaliputra.
This is the meaning.

Here, because there is a contradiction between being a resident of Mathurā and being a resident of Pāṭaliputra—just as there is a contradiction between "cowness" and "horseness"—there can be no identity in that form in any way whatsoever; thus, the intention is that the ablative case is used for the limit of selection (*nirdhāraṇāvadhau*).
(631) *sādhunipuṇābhyāmarcāyāṃ saptamyaprateḥ* | 2|3|43|.

[The suffix *kha* is applied] after the words *sādhu* and *nipuṇa*. This is an exception to the genitive case used for the remaining relations (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). "Skilled toward his mother" (*mātari sādhuh*) means one who performs what is beneficial; "or skilled [toward his mother]" (*nipuṇo vā*) means one who is proficient regarding his mother. The word "service" (*śuśrūṣāyām*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. "Skilled toward the king" (*nipuṇo rājñaḥ*); however, when the word *sādhu* is employed [in this context]:

The locative case (*saptamī*) occurs even without the sense of *arcā* (reverence), because it is stated [in the rule] that "it occurs in connection with both correct (*sādhu*) and incorrect (*asādhu*) words. However, the inclusion of the term *sādhu* here is for the purpose of precluding the locative case when used in connection with *prati* and other such particles in the sense of *arcā*.
It should be stated [as a restriction]: "not when used with *prati* and others."

Regarding the phrase "with *prati* and others": the meaning is that when there is a connection with these—*prati*, *pari*, and *anu*—the locative case is not used even when there is a connection with the words *sādhu* and *nipuṇa*.
(632) *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca lupi* |2|3|44|. When [the suffix] *lup* is elided after these two, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is also employed.

Regarding the words *prasita* and *utsuka*: according to Amara, "one who is intent on that is *prasita*, *āsakta*, or *iṣṭārtha-udyukta*; one who is eager is *utsuka*. This rule is stated because, although the locative case would have applied by default through its sense of being a locus (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*), this specific statement is made [to restrict its usage].

(633) *nakṣatre ca lupi* | 2|3|45|. Regarding the rule "and when [the suffix] is elided (*lupi*) in the sense of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatre*)," the phrase "when the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthe*) remains" is to be supplied immediately after "in the sense of a lunar mansion. By the word *lup*, the meaning of the suffix that has undergone the technical designation *lup* is intended. Thus he says: "in the sense of a lunar mansion."

Regarding "in the sense of the base" (*prakṛtyarthe*) and "in the sense of the locus" (*adhikaraṇe*): the intention is that this [term] is carried over by means of a *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) from the rule "the locative case is used in the sense of the locus" (*saptamy adhikaraṇe ca*). Regarding "by the root" (*mūlena*):
the meaning is "the time conjoined with the lunar mansion Mūla. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "time conjoined with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*).
The suffix *lup* is applied by the rule "ṭhlub aviśeṣe" [Pāṇini 4.2.41]. Why "in the sense of location" (*adhikaraṇe*)? [Consider: "He awaits the root" (*mūlaṃ pratīkṣate*).

Why "a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatre*)? [Consider: "He stays among the Pañcālas" (*pañcāleṣu tiṣṭhati*). Here, the *lup* is applied by the rule "ṭhjanapade" [Pāṇini 4.2.81]. (634) Pāṇini 2.3.7: "The locative and ablative case endings [are used] when between two factors of action (*kāraka*)."

The seventh and fifth [case endings]. The word *kāraka* refers to the capacities such as agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, and not to the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth themselves, according to the commentary.
Since a middle point depends upon two limits, the analysis of the compound is "the middle between two *kārakas*."

He says this: "between the two powers. He explains that the term *kālādhvanoḥ*, which is understood from the previous context, is modified to have an ablative ending (*pañcamyantatayā*), saying: "those two, time and space. Regarding the example *adya bhuktvā* ("having eaten today"):
since the locative case would normally apply here in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpikādhikaraṇatve*), this specific rule is stated. [The meaning is: having eaten today...

The meaning is that when two days have passed, one is to eat on the third day, which is near to that [time]. The suffix *luṭ* denotes the future tense. Regarding the phrase "of the agent and the capacity": this refers to the agency as determined by the act of eating occurring today, and the agency as determined by the act of eating occurring on the day after the two days have passed.

If the word *kāraka* were intended to refer specifically to the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, it would not apply here, because the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed when there is identity of the agent. However, the power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*) is indeed differentiated by the differences in the acts of eating.
He provides an example even between two [other] *kārakas*: "this person is standing here. Here too, it is by way of location.

Proximity (*sāmīpika*) is the meaning of the fifth and seventh case endings when they function as loci (*adhikaraṇa*). The sense here is: "Standing here, this archer shall pierce the target with an arrow in a location near the distance of one *krośa*. Regarding the phrase "between the two potencies of agent and object": this means between the two potencies consisting of agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*).

If the word *kāraka* were intended to mean "agent" (*kartṛ*) and so forth, this [rule] would apply only here; it would not apply in cases such as "having eaten today, he... This example was cited precisely to indicate that. Now, in expressions such as "Hari is superior to the world" or "superior to the worlds," there exists the relation of being a limit (*avadhitva*).

Anticipating the objection that the genitive case alone is appropriate for the remainder, he says: "by the word 'additional' (adhika). Regarding the phrases "in the world" (loke) or "from the world" (lokāt):
the meaning of the locative and ablative cases here is the relation of being a limit (avadhitva). The sense is that he is superior in comparison to the world.

(635) *adhir īśvare* | Pāṇini 1.4.97. Intending to state the grammatical operation (*kārya*) of the term *karmapravacanīya* for the prefix *adhi*, [the author] states its designation (*saṃjñā*): *adhir īśvare*. By the word *īśvara*, what is intended is "lordship" (*īśvaratva*), which consists of the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*).
The governing rule "karmapravacanīyāḥ" is modified to end in the singular number. Thus he says: "owner and owned.
(Pāṇini 2.3.9): "In the sense of that which is superior to something, and in the sense of that of which someone is the master, the seventh case ending is used there."

"From that which is exceeded" (*yasmād adhikam*). The phrase "when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*" (*karmapravacanīyayukte*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "here, [the word] *karmapravacanīya*. This is an exception to the genitive case used for the remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding "near a hundred thousand" (*upa parārdham*): the meaning of the locative case is the state of being a limit (*avadhitvam*). Thus he says: "the meaning is 'exceeded by a hundred thousand'. "From that which is exceeded" (*yasmād adhikam*).
There exists no other number beyond that *parārdha*; the meaning is "in relation to that. This is the result of the status of *upa* as a *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule *ṭhupo'dhike ca*.
Regarding the expression *yasyeśvaravacanam*, it means that from which [entity] the Lord (*īśvara*) is spoken of as being related.

The first meaning is that [the word] is in the seventh case (*saptamī*). Here, by the word "its" (*yat*), "its own" (*svam*) is expressed; thus, it is understood as "the seventh case [ending] after a word denoting its own. The word *īśvara* emphasizes the state (*bhāva*);
the second meaning is that the seventh case [ending] occurs after that from which its lordship (*īśvaratva*) is expressed.
The meaning is that the locative case is used because sovereignty (*īśvaratva*) is said to be "resting in" something;

specifically, the locative is understood to follow a word denoting a master (*svāmin*). Thus it is said: "In the sense of sovereignty, however, the locative is used alternately for both the self and the master."

Regarding "adhi bhuvi rāmaḥ": *adhi* is a synonym for *īśvara* (lord/owner). The meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*) is a relationship (*saṃbandha*). The sense is: "Rāma is the master of the earth. Here, the locative case follows a word denoting the possessor (*sva-vācaka*). Regarding "adhi rāme bhūḥ": here, *adhi* is a synonym for the word *sva* (self/belonging). The meaning of the locative case is a relationship. [The sense is: "the earth belonging to Rāma."
The meaning is *bhūḥ*. Here, the seventh case ending is used after a word denoting the possessor (*svāmin*).

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a compound," since the word *adhi* is listed in the *śauṇḍādi* group, when *adhi* is compounded with the seventh-case form *rāme*, the case ending is elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*.
From the word *rāmādhi*,

by applying the suffix *kha* according to the rule "ṭhaṣaḍakṣāśitaṅgvalaṅkarmālampuruṣādhyutarapadātkhaḥ," and then substituting *īna* for that suffix according to the rule "ṭhāyaneyīnīyiyaḥ," the form *rāmādhīnā bhūḥ* ("the earth is dependent on Rāma") is established.

The meaning is "having Rāma as its master. In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending, however, we have *adhirāmaṃ bhūḥ*, which means "the earth has Rāma as its locus" (*rāmādhikaraṇikā bhūḥ*). The suffix *-kh-* does not apply here, because the word *adhi* is not the final member of the compound.

(637) *vibhāṣā kṛñi* | 1.4.98 | *vibhāṣā kṛñi*. The term *adhiḥ īśvare* is understood [from the previous rule]. *karmapravacanīyāḥ* is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). Thus he says: "adhi [is optionally a *karmapravacanīya*] with the root *kṛ*. When the root *kṛñ* follows, *adhi* [is optionally a *karmapravacanīya*].

Or rather, it may be a *karmapravacanīya* (governing preposition) in the sense of lordship (*īśvaratva*), meaning "that which will authorize me in this matter. The phrase "in this matter" (*atra*) means "in this context," and the sense is that "that which will authorize me" is what is joined with effort. Here, because of its connection with a *karmapravacanīya*, the word "me" (*mām*) takes the second case (*dvitīyā*).

He explains the phrase "it will govern" (*adhikariṣyati*) as meaning "it will employ" (*viniyokṣyate*). If that is so, since the accusative case would be established by its status as an object (*karman*) alone, what is the purpose of designating it as a *karmapravacanīya*?
To this he replies: "because it is not a verb" (*agatitvāt*). [The rule] *tiṅ ca* means: when there is a *tiṅ*-ending word that possesses an acute accent (*udātta*).

The meaning is that the *gati* (preverb) is subject to elision (*nihanyate*). Here, the finite verb form *kariṣyati* is udātta because its elision (*nighāta*)—which would otherwise apply by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*—is prohibited by the rule *nipātair yadyadi...* and so forth. Consequently, since *adhi* functions as a *gati* here, its elision would be applicable; however, when it is treated as a *karmapravacanīya*, that [elision] does not occur.

Because [the word *bhavati*] exists, the status of being a finite verb (*gatitva*) is sublated by it. Therefore, it is established that this sūtra is intended to prevent the occurrence of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) for what follows [the particle].
Thus ends [the section] composed by the learned Śrīmad Vāsudevadīkṣita.
The Determination of the Meanings of Case-endings in the *Bālamanoramā*, a Commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī*.

Now begins the section on the agent and the object (*kartṛkarmaprakriyā*) within the chapter on verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*). Now, intending to describe the section on the agent that is also the object (*karmakartṛprakriyā*), he says "yadā" in order to establish the agency of the object. The established doctrine is that "the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes both the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*). For the root *pac* (to cook)— [The sentence continues: ...is indeed [used in this way]. When the rice, having become soft through its own operation, attains the state of being cooked, it is then called the "agent that is the object" (*karmakartṛ*). This is because the action of cooking, which consists of the softening of the rice, is accomplished by the rice itself; therefore, the rice is the agent. However, since it is also the substratum of the action of becoming cooked, it is the object as well. Thus, it is designated as the "agent that is the object. But when the rice is not yet soft, it is not an agent, because the action of cooking has not been accomplished by it. Therefore, it is said: "When the rice, having become soft... and so forth. Here, the word "rice" (*taṇḍula*) is used to denote the substance (*dravya*) that possesses the rice as its limiting attribute (*upādhi*). By the word "soft," the quality (*guṇa*) of softness is indicated. By the word "own," the exclusion of the operation belonging to another is intended. By the word "attained" (*prāpta*), the completion of the action is expressed. By the word "then" (*tadā*), the time of the action is indicated. By the word "called" (*ucyate*), the application of the technical term is shown. It denotes an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*). In this context, softening is the result (*phala*);

its substratum, the boiled rice (*odana*), is the object (*karman*); and the operation conducive to that is the effort of a person in the form of activities such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth.
Among these, "placing on the fire" (*adhiśrayaṇa*) consists of setting the pot containing rice upon the hearth (*cullī*).

Placement (*sthāpanam*). Placement is an activity conducive to persistence (*sthiti*). In this context, persistence is that which resides in the rice within the cooking pot; the activity conducive to it is a specific volitional effort (*ceṣṭā*) of the person. The person is the agent (*kartṛ*), because he is the substratum of the activity denoted by the verbal root and because he possesses independence (*svātantrya*). Independence is...

The commentary states that [the agent] possesses primacy. However, the established position is that the object, the instrument, and so forth do not attain the status of "agent" because they are dependent upon the effort of the person. In that context, when one wishes to emphasize the extreme ease [of the action], the activity—namely the effort—of the person who is the agent is not intended to be expressed; rather, what is intended is that which resides in the object and so forth.

The meaning is that when such an operation is intended to be expressed as being conducive to a result such as softening (*viklitti*), then even the *karma* (object) and other *kārakas* receive the designation of *kartṛ* (agent). Now, one might object:
since the operation residing in the object and other factors is dependent on human effort and is therefore not independent (*asvatantra*), how can the object [be called an agent]?

To explain why it is [the agent], he says: "Because of its independence in its own operation. This means because it is intended to be expressed as independent. As it was stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87):
"In the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), agency exists because independence is intended to be expressed. In this context...

The mention of "karma" (object) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other *kārakas* such as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the word "tena" (by that): although axes, hatchets, and the like possess the status of being instruments (*karaṇatva*) during the stage of usage such as "he cuts with an axe" (*asinā chinatti*), they are placed in the agent (*kartari*) case because they are intended to be expressed as the agent during the stage of usage such as "the axe cuts" (*asiś chinatti*).

The meaning is that the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) [is used here]. In the example "the sword cuts well" (*sādhvasiś chinatti*), there is an intention to express the instrument as the agent (*kartṛ*).

The word "well" (*sādhu*) is used to indicate an excellence of facility in the action. The meaning is that, due to extreme sharpness, the sword itself cuts by its own accord, even without a specific effort by a person or an excessive force of impact.

"Wood cooks"—here too, there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instruments (*karaṇa*). "The pot cooks"—here, there is an intention to express the agency of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
This is because, due to the extreme dryness of the wood, there is no need for fanning or blowing [by the agent], [the cooking being performed] by the pot.

Because of its extreme lightness, it should be understood as being easy to cook due to not requiring long boiling. Regarding the phrase "but of the object" (*karmaṇas tu*): in the case of roots such as *chid* (to cut) and *bhid* (to split), which have a single object, when there is a desire to express the agency of that object—as in "the tree cuts itself" (*vṛkṣaś chinatti*)—then although it was previously transitive, it is now [intransitive] with respect to the object.

The meaning is that these [verbs] are intransitive when there is an intention to express the agenthood [of one of the objects]. However, as for those [verbs] that have two objects (*dvikarmaka*), even when the agenthood of one object is intended to be expressed, they remain transitive because of the presence of the other object; hence the use of the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*). Consequently, in the case of those *dvikarmaka* verbs, [the rule applies] to the object (*karmani*).

The *lakāra* suffixes occur in both the passive (*karman*) and active (*kartṛ*) voices. Regarding these, an example of the *lakāra* in the passive voice is: "The nectar is being churned from the ocean of milk" (*sudhāṃ kṣīrasāgaro mathyate*). An example in the active voice is: "The ocean of milk churns the nectar" (*sudhāṃ kṣīrasāgaro mathnāti*). Now, as for what was stated—that when there is a single object, if one intends to express that object's status as the agent, the verb becomes intransitive (*akarmaka*)—

He states its purpose: "The *l*-suffixes [are used] after those [roots] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*)," but not in the sense of the object (*karman*), because that is impossible. Therefore, the intended meaning is that it has been stated: "After intransitive roots, the *l*-suffix is used in the sense of the abstract state and the agent. In that regard, when there is a desire to express the object as the agent after roots that have one object, [the suffix is used] in the sense of the abstract state.

He illustrates the suffix *lakāra*: "pacyate odanena" (it is cooked by means of rice). The meaning is: "the act of cooking has rice as its agent. Similarly, there is also "bhidyate kāṣṭhena" (it is split by means of wood). Although the root *pac* is transitive (having two objects), nevertheless, when the rice is not intended to be expressed, the status of having a single object is attributed to *pac*. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of the agent":

The meaning is that, among transitive verbs, when there is a desire to express the agency of the object, a specific rule regarding the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in the sense of the agent will be stated. (590) *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.87.
*karmavat karmaṇā*. From the rule *kartari śaḥ*, the word *kartari* is understood and is transformed into the nominative case. A "doer" (*kartā*) is one whose action is equal [to that of another].
By the term *karmaṇā*, the action residing in the object-factor (*karmakāraka*) is intended; [this refers to] the action of the [object].

Because the equality with the agent (*karmakāraka*) can only be established by taking into account the action residing therein, he says this with the words "residing in the object" (*karmasthaya*), and so forth. This means that when there is a desire to express the object as the agent (*kartṛtvena vivakṣāyām*), the agent is "like the object" (*karmavat*).
However, in the absence of the suffix *vat*, there might be the suspicion that the meaning is "that which is designated as the object" (*karmasaṃjñaka*). It is thus.

Since [the roots] are transitive, there would be no *lo* affix in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) in examples such as *odanena pacyate* ("the rice is cooked") or *kāṣṭhena bhidyate* ("the wood is split"). This is an extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*). Although there is no difference in result whether it is an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*) or an extension of the operation, nevertheless, even in the case of the extension of the rule—
The meaning is that, because the purpose is the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) and because that is primary, one must indeed resort to the extension of the operation.
The word "by that" (*tena*) connects with the word "syuḥ" (they should be). By the statement regarding "acting like the object" (*karmavat*), the operations belonging to the object are [extended]:
the *yak* suffix by the rule *sārvadhātuke yaK*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, and the *ciṇ* [substitution].

The meaning is that by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ," the *ciṇ* affix is applied, and by the rule "syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu," there is the *ciṇ*-like behavior (*ciṇvadbhāva*), as well as the augment *iṭ* prescribed in conjunction with that. The intention is that if one intends to express the agenthood of the object (*karmaṇaḥ kartṛtvavivakṣāyām*), the very rules ordained for the agent (*kartari*) would not apply. [This refers to] the word "of the agent" (*kartuḥ*).

The meaning is that when there is a desire to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the action, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) occurs in the sense of the agent; since the *tiṅ* suffixes, which are its substitutes, express the agent, [the agent is not further mentioned]. For example, in "the rice is cooked" (*pacyate odanaḥ*), [the rice] is the substratum of the softening (*viklitti*) without the specific excellence of human effort such as blowing upon it.

The meaning is "it becomes. In the example *bhidyate kāṣṭham* ("the wood splits"), the meaning is that it becomes split into two parts without the exertion of a person or the firm blow of an axe and so forth. Here, although the object functions as the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *yak* is applied because the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is extended [to the agent]. In the examples *apāci* and *abhedī*, the suffix *ciṇ* is applied because [the agent] behaves like the object (*karmavat*).

One might object: "If there is an intention to express the agency of the object (*karman*), then in the passive construction (*bhāvalakāra*) such as *odanena pacyate* (the rice is cooked) or *kāṣṭhena bhidyate* (the wood is split), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should apply because the *tiṅ*-suffix does not express the agent-object (*karmakartṛ*), since it follows the rule of 'acting like the object' (*karmavadbhāva*). To this, he replies: "No."
The meaning is that this objection does not arise. Why? To this he says: "Because it is expressed by the letter *l* itself.
And why is that? To this he says: "In the rule *liṅyāśiṣi*. In the reading where *liṅ* and *āśiṣi* are joined as *liṅyāśiṣi*, [the word] *lakārāt* appears before *liṅ*.

Another *l* (the *l* from *ṭhhalo yamām*) is elided and then reattached [to the previous *l*]. Consequently, from the sūtra *l l*, which contains two *l*s, the genitive form *l* is carried over (*anuvartate*) into the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*. Thus, it is obtained that "the agent (*kartā*) denoted by *la* is like the object (*karmavat*). This refers to being the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*).
This is the sense of the genitive case. Thus, the meaning results in the conclusion that "the agent expressed by the *l*-suffix is like the object.

One might ask: "Let this be so; what follows for the present topic? To this he replies: "Because, when there is an affix denoting a state (*bhāva*), the agent is not presented by the *l*-suffix," since in that case, the state alone is what is expressed by it.

The meaning is as follows: "For this very reason" means that because the rule of *karmavat-tva* (the treatment of the object-like agent) is prescribed only for that reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*) which is denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), the affixes—namely the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes—which are prescribed for the object, do not apply to the reflexive agent.
This is because, since that [reflexive agent] is not denoted by the verbal suffix, the rule of *karmavat-tva* does not operate there. And this...

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. Now, an objection is raised: "In the Vārttika on the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* suffix in the case of the root *si* (*sinoti*) when the object is the agent, how is it that the Bhāṣya cites 'sino grāsaḥ svayameva' (the morsel has bitten itself) as an example?
For the *kta* suffix does not occur in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). To this, it is replied: precisely because of that very Bhāṣya passage.

It is understood that the *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 3.2.102) in the sense of the object (*karman*) does not occur with a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). However, in the example *sino grāsaḥ svayam eva* ("the morsel has bitten itself"), the *kta* suffix prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule *gaty-arthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72) and others certainly occurs with a reflexive agent.
The detailed explanation is in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the example "one should fear the granary" (*bhetavyaṃ kusūlena*):

the meaning is that the action of splitting has the granary as its agent, independent of human effort. He raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely). "Now" (*idānīm*) means at the stage where there is a desire to express the agency of the object. But not...

Regarding the phrase "tatulyā" (equal to that): the sense is that equality is constituted by difference. He refutes [the objection] by accepting half [of it], saying "satyam" (true). The meaning is this: although it is correct that softening (*viklitti*) and becoming divided (*dvidhābhavana*) reside in the object (*karmastha*) at one time and in the agent (*kartṛstha*) at another, nevertheless, there is no absence of equality between those two.

Even regarding the state of being an object (*karmatva*): the states of being an object and being an agent (*kartṛtva*) are specific attributes (*dharma-viśeṣa*). The distinction between these two is itself the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that is, the cause;
by relying on such a difference in action—which has the same substratum as both objecthood and agency—the conventional usage of "identity" (*tulyatva*) is maintained.

This is the meaning. Although there is no real difference [between the agent and the object], because of the difference based on limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the agent of the action possesses an action equal to that of the object; this is the intended sense of "the object-agent" (karmakartṛ).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the instrument and the locus": as in the examples "he cuts with a sword" (asinā chinatti) and "he cooks in a pot" (sthālyāṃ pacati).

The meaning is that the very operation which belongs to the instrument (karaṇa) or the locus (adhikaraṇa)—as in "the axe cuts" (ṭhasiś chinatti) or "the pot cooks" (sthālī pacati)—is situated in the agent (kartṛstha); therefore, even in those cases, the status of being like the object (karmavadbhāva) would apply. To exclude that, the word "by the object" (karmaṇā) is used.

[Objection: But in the rule "like the object when [the agent is] by the object" (karmavat karmaṇā), [the word "object"] is understood from the previous rule "from a root having one vowel" (dhātor ekācaḥ).
The term "dhātoḥ" (of the root) is understood [from the previous rule]. The meaning is: that which has an action equal to the action expressed by the root.

Although the operation of the sword and the pot actually exists during their states as instruments and so forth, it is not included within the verbal root; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not arise. Anticipating this objection, he says—"Furthermore"—[in the example] "he goes to the village."

Thus, the meaning is that because the path is neither uneven nor thorny and is close at hand, it becomes a basis for attainment without exertion. "The elephant ascends" means that it lowers itself of its own accord, without the intervention of the mahout's activities such as striking with the goad.
The meaning is that he becomes the locus for ascending [to realization]. "He attains" refers to the first half-verse.
The second half-verse is: "Salutation forever to that Guru, by a mere fragment of whose compassion [this occurs].
By a mere fragment of the Guru’s compassion alone, one attains the meaning of the scriptures spontaneously, without effort.

The meaning is that it becomes the object of certainty, the object of memory, and the object of faith. In this case, because the village and so forth—which are the objects of the action—are characterized by an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*) and lack an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), they do not possess the status of an "object" (*karman*). Therefore, the grammatical operations pertaining to an object (*karmakārya*) do not apply.

[The author says: "But [the suffixes] *śap* and so forth denote the agent's action"—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: since the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), such as a village and the like, is the locus of the attainment and so forth, it indeed possesses an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*). To this he replies: "Where... That is, where a distinction—that is, a difference—produced by the action is seen, [or] perceived through direct observation.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: "In that case, the action existing in the object is called 'action residing in the object' (*karmasthakriyā*).
He demonstrates this by providing an example: "as in the case of cooked rice grains.
The ellipsis (*śeṣa*) to be supplied is: "a specific change produced by the softening (*viklitti*) is observed in relation to the state of the rice grains [prior to cooking]."

Elsewhere as well, he demonstrates the distinction produced by action by citing an example: "Or, for instance, in the case of wood that has been cut. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "A distinction is observed in comparison with what was not cut. He states "not so" in the case of "he goes to the village," etc., because it is not like that; [the example continues] "in the villages," etc.
This is an illustration. Just as a distinction produced by action is perceived among rice grains that are cooked and uncooked,
so too is such a distinction perceived between a village reached and one not reached,
an elephant mounted and one not mounted, a scriptural meaning understood and one not understood, a thing remembered and one not remembered, and a scriptural meaning trusted and one not trusted.

The meaning is that no difference [in the action] is observed due to the difference in the agent. The intention is that, in cases such as "he goes to the village," a difference such as fatigue is observed only in the agent. Now, an objection: since effort (*yatna*), like knowledge and desire, resides in the agent, the agent of the root *kṛ* (which denotes that effort) should not be treated like the object; and consequently—

Anticipating the objection that if [the agent] were expressed as "the jar is made by itself" (*kriyate ghaṭaḥ svayam eva*), the *yaṅ* suffix and other such markers would not be established, he states—refuting the view that the root *kṛ* has the meaning of "effort"—that "the root *kṛ* has the meaning of 'bringing into existence'.
This means it signifies an activity conducive to origination. And this is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*.

This is clear. However, if the root *kṛ* (to do/make) has the sense of "producing," he establishes that its action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) by means of the phrase "and production resides in the object. The intention is that a difference [between the states] is directly perceived whether the object has been produced or not yet produced. By the word "tena" (by that), [he refers to] the agent of the root *kṛ*.

The meaning is "by virtue of being an action residing in the object" (*karmasthakriyatva*). And thus, in the case of *ghaṭaḥ svayameva kriyate* ("the pot is made by itself"), the suffix *yak* [is applied].
However, regarding the suffix *tāsi*, if the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is present, the form is *kāritā*; if that is absent, it is *kartā*. Taking this as established, he says:
"in cases such as *kariṣyate ghaṭaḥ*" ("the pot will be made"). This refers to the *ciṇvadiṭ* alternative.

The form *kāriṣyate* occurs; however, in the absence of that [condition], by the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye*, there is the augment *iṭ*—thus *kariṣyate*. When the *sīyuṭ* suffix takes the augment *iṭ* as if it were *ciṇ*, the form is *kāriṣīṣṭa*; but in its absence, it is *kṛṣīṣṭa*. In the *luṅ* [past tense], it is *akāri* or *akṛta*. "Not this" means that the property of being like the object (*karmavatva*) does not apply.

The meaning is that [it] would be established. It should also be understood that, as in the case of the root *yat* (to strive), it would not be transitive at all. "By this" means by the demonstration that knowledge resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*). "In the object being ascertained" means in the object which itself attains the state of being the objective of a determination.
This is the meaning. "It has been explained" means it has been established. To the question "How has it been established?", he says:
"Because there is an absence of the *yaṅ* suffix due to the action residing in the agent. *Anuvyavasāya* is certainty; therein, the object is the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*).
That [object] does not have an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*), because there is an absence of any distinction produced by the *anuvyavasāya* in the object.

However, it is indeed an action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*), because joy and other such states are observed in Devadatta, who is the agent of the subsequent determination (*anuvyavasāya*). Consequently, since there is an absence of the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*), the suffix *yak* does not apply. But when *yaK* is used, due to its *kit* quality, the substitution of *ī* occurs according to the rule "ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāṃ," resulting in the form "anuvyavasīyamāna."
The meaning is "it might be so. Now, one might ask: "In the absence of the *ya*-affix (*yak*), how is the sound *ya* heard? To this he says: "In *śyan*.

From the root *ṣo* ("in the sense of finishing"), preceded by the prefixes *anu*, *vi*, and *ava*, the suffix *āna* is applied; because of the influence of the prefix, it acquires the sense of "certainty" (*niścaya*). When the *śyan* affix is added, the vowel *o* is elided by the rule "otaḥ śyani" (Pāṇini 7.3.71).

The meaning is that the grammatical form is established by the rule "anuvyavasyamāna. Now, one might object: "In the absence of the status of being an object (karmavatva), the ātmanepada suffix śānac cannot occur after the present tense marker (laṭ) here, because [the suffix] would not be applicable under the rule 'bhāvakarmaṇoḥ' (Pāṇini 1.3.13), since śānac is an ātmanepada suffix. To this, he replies: "In the sense of habitual action (tācchīlya) and so forth."

The meaning of *cānaś* is established by the rule *ṭhtācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś*. Since this suffix (*cānaś*) is not a substitute for *l* (as it is not a *lādeśa*), it does not possess the status of *ātmanepada*; consequently, although it lacks the property of being *karmavat*, its application to the *karmakartṛ* (the agent who is also the object) is unimpeded. This is what he says: "but it is not the *ātmanepada*. Now, [one might object]:...

In the case of "yajñadatta and devadatta touch each other," there would also have to be the *yaṅ* suffix and so forth due to [the presence of] the object (*karman*) status; for in that instance, the root *spṛś-* signifies an operation conducive to conjunction.
Both are agents (*kartṛ*) and both are objects (*karman*). Even though the act of touching is one, [the grammatical distinction remains].

Based on the difference of substrata, and depending upon that difference, Devadatta’s status as the object (*karman*) is with respect to the action of touching residing in Yajñadatta; likewise, Yajñadatta’s status as the object is with respect to the action of touching residing in Devadatta. In this way, agency (*kartṛtva*) should also be understood for both. And thus, for both...

If the very same action of touching (*spṛśi*) that exists in one agent or object were to exist in another agent or object characterized by agency or objecthood, then there would be the status of being "like the object" (*karmavat*); for it is possible for actions to be identical by relying on a distinction based solely on their substrata.

Because joy and its absence are observed to be produced by the mutual contact of the touched and the untouched, it is said: "There is a prohibition for [roots] that take an object. For roots such as *chid* (to cut) and *bhid* (to split), which have a single object, the status of the agent being like that of the object (*karmavat*) was stated when the object is intended to be expressed as the agent, thereby rendering them intransitive (*akarmaka*). As for those [roots]...

The meaning is that even when there is a desire to express the agency of the object (*karmaṇaḥ kartṛtva-vivakṣā*) in the case of roots that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), those roots remain transitive;

for such roots, a prohibition must be stated regarding the *karmakartṛ* (the agent who was the object) being treated like the object (*karmavat*). For example, in the case of *anyonyaṃ spṛśataḥ* ("they touch each other"), if it were treated like the object, then with the suffix *yak*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and the *ciṇ* augment would apply, resulting in the form *spṛśyete*.

[This is] the state [of the rule]. He states another example for the prohibition "there is a prohibition regarding transitive verbs" (*sakarmakāṇāṃ pratiṣedhaḥ*): *ajā grāmaṃ nayati* ("the goat leads to the village"). The meaning is that the goat reaches the village by itself. Here, even though there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the goat—which is the object (*karman*)—with respect to the act of leading, [the rule does not apply] because the verb remains transitive (*sakarmaka*) due to the presence of "the village."

The intention [of the author] is that it possesses the status of an action (*karmavatva*). However, in reality, because there is no distinction between the "gone" and the "not gone" village, the status of an action is not applicable here; therefore, this is not an illustration of this Vārttika. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states: "they embrace one another," "one another..."

It is clearly stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that "they touch" is cited as an example of being "mutually grasped. Regarding the rule *duhipacyoḥ*, the word "the state of being like the object" (*karmavatvam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sūtra].
Since these two roots are transitive (*dvikarmaka*), even when one of the two objects is intended to be expressed as the agent, [the action] is still connected with the other object.

Since this [root] is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the prohibition of its being treated like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) would have applied by the preceding Vārttika; therefore, this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*).
(591) *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* 3.1.89: For the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*, the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur.

The dual form *duha-duha* is not [the subject] here; rather, it is a *dvandva* compound. As for the phrase "in the case of the object acting as its own agent" (*karmakartari*), this cannot be obtained through *anuvṛtti* (carrying over from a previous rule), because it was not found in the preceding [sūtra]. Rather, it is obtainable only through the immediate proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the rule "that which has an action equal to that of the object by means of the object" (*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*). From the rule "after a vowel, in the case of the object acting as its own agent" (*acaḥ karmakartari*)...
Or, there may be its recurrence by means of a "frog-leap" (maṇḍūakapluti). Regarding the phrase "by this [sūtra] after *duh*":
the prohibition of *yak* alone for the root *duh* in the sense of the agent who is also the object is by the rule "not after *duh*, *snū*, or *nam*" (*na duhasnunamām*).
However, the *ciṇ* suffix will be stated as being optional by the sūtra to be mentioned later, "also after *duh*" (*duhaśca*). This is the meaning.

The meaning is that when the suffix *ta* follows [the root] in the sense of the agent being also the object (*karmakartṛ*), the substitution of *ciṇ* occurs for the root *duh*. There is a variant reading in some places: "the substitution of *ciṇ* is desired optionally. He demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) for the form *dugdhe*:

"there is elision of *śap*" (*śap-luk*). When the *yak* suffix is prohibited in the case of *duh* in the sense of the agent being also the object, the *śap* suffix applies; of that [suffix], there is elision.

The meaning is that there is elision [of the suffix] by the rule "ṭhadiprabhatibhyaḥ. In the example "gauḥ payo dugdhe," the meaning is that the cow itself emits the milk. The present tense suffix (laṭ) is used with the cow as both object and agent; even though the root is marked with the svarita accent, the middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs only by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ. Thus, because it is not "duha" [in this sense], the suffix yak is not applied.

The example *gāṃ payo dugdhe* (she milks the cow for milk) has not been cited here because it is stated: "The suffixes *la* and others are considered to apply to the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*) in the case of roots such as *duh*. Regarding the rule *acaḥ karmakartari*:
from the rule *cleḥ sic* [Pāṇini 1.4.52], the word *cleḥ* is understood; and from the rule *ciṇ te padaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.60], the word *ciṇ te* is understood.

The phrase "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is carried over from the rule "dīpajana... (Pāṇini 3.1.61). Since the term "dhātu" (root), which is carried over from the rule "dhātor ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.22), is qualified by the vowel "ac," the rule applies to that which ends in such a vowel.
This is what he expresses with the words "from that which ends in a vowel," etc. In the example "akāri," the ellipsis is "the mat by itself."

The *luṅ* [suffix] is used for the agent of the action (*karmakartṛ*). The *ciṇ* [substitute] replaces *cli*. There is *vṛddhi* [of the vowel], followed by the substitution of *ra* for the final element. By the rule *ṭiṇo luṅ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *ta*-portion.
Thus, we have *akṛta*. In the alternative case where *ciṇ* does not apply, there is elision of *sic* by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*.

(592) *duhaśca* |3|1|63|. The rule *duhaśca* [is as follows]: with the exception of the word *ṭhac*, everything from the preceding sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*) here. When the suffix *ta* follows, the root *duh* optionally takes the augment *ciṇ* in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*).

The meaning of "syāt" (it may be) is clear, so it has not been explained. The preceding sūtra was cited merely for the sake of ease of reference, even though it is not applicable to the root *duh* under discussion here. Regarding the form *adohī*:

this is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the sense of the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*) of the root *duh*. The ellipsis is "the cow [yielded] milk by herself. In the alternative where the *ciṇ* suffix is applied:

The *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*). Regarding the alternative view where the *ciṇ* affix is absent, he says: "In the alternative, *ksa*. The intention is that this is by means of the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*. [Regarding] "or elision" (*lugvā*): the meaning is that there is optional elision of the *ksa* affix by the rule *lugvā duhadihalihaguhām*. Now...
In the rule *ṭhduhapacyor arthe*, he gives an example for the root *pac* (to cook): "The *udumbara* fruit ripens" (*udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacyate*).

In the sentence "The *udumbara* tree cooks the fruit at a particular time," the root *pac* takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*). Here, however, the *udumbara* tree itself, without depending on a particular time, [becomes] the locus of the ripened fruit.

The meaning is "it performs. Here, when there is an intention to express the secondary object (*gauṇakarma*)—the *udumbara*—as the agent, the status of being "like the object" (*karmavatva*) would be prohibited by the rule "there is a prohibition for transitive verbs" (*sakarmakāṇāṃ pratiṣedhaḥ*), because [the verb] is transitive due to its primary object, which is the fruit (*phala*). However, [this prohibition is set aside] by the rule "for the roots *duh* and *pac*" (*duhipacyoḥ*), which establishes the status of being "like the object."

The sense is that [the rule] begins with *pratiprasava* (reversal of a prohibition) and so forth. In reality, however, since *pac* is not included among the two-object verbs (*dvikarmaka*) in the Bhāṣya, it does not possess two objects; this has been explained by us in detail under the section on *kāraka*. And thus, in the case of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*), as in "the fruit ripens" (*phalaṃ pacyate*), it is the fruit itself [that is the agent].

Although this counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) would be redundant— since when one intends to express that [the fruit] is the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being the object (*karman*), the root *pac* becomes intransitive and thus the prohibition "for transitive roots" (*sakarmakāṇām*) does not apply—
nevertheless, according to this view, in the case of "The *udumbara* tree ripens its fruit" (*udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacati*) where the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-lakāra*) is used:

Since the action of *pac* (to cook) resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*) and lacks an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriya*), the rule "the object behaves like an object" (*karmavat karmaṇā*) does not apply to the reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*) in the expression *udumbaraḥ phalaṃ pacyati*. Consequently, the status of behaving like an object (*karmavatva*) is not established here by that rule.
However, according to the rule *duhipacyoḥ*, the status of behaving like an object applies extensively; thus, in other instances, this is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) for *pac*.

The full detail [is as follows]: there is a Vārttika stating, "But [the suffix] *śyan* [is applied] after the roots *sṛj* and *yuj*. The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that states, "Of these two, when they are transitive," and so forth. Here, the *adādi* (second class) roots *sṛj* and *yuj* are not intended to be included, because their intransitivity has already been stated; rather, it refers to the root *sṛj* in the sense of "emission" (*visarga*).
There is the inclusion of both the *taudādika* root and the *raudhādika* root *yujir yoge*. In that context, *visarga* means production (*utpādana*), as in "he creates offspring" (*prajāḥ sṛjati*).
*Yoga* means conjunction (*saṃyojana*), as in "he yokes a horse" (*aśvaṃ yunakti*); it is understood as "he joins [the horse] with a chariot and so forth. [This applies to] the root *sṛj*.

Regarding the phrase "śraddhopapanne" (endowed with faith): the meaning is that the rule is stated specifically for the primary agent who possesses faith. In that context, since the status of being the object (*karmatva*) is absolutely unestablished for the primary agent, it is here frequently prescribed [as such].

This is because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "The rule stated for the root √*yaj* applies only to the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Consequently, in that case as well, [the rule] applies to the object (*karman*).

Since there is no distinction regarding the action performed (*kriyākṛta*), the status of being an object (*karmatva*)—which has not yet been established—is here prescribed extensively. When that status of being an object is present, the suffix *śyan* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *yak*. By means of this, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the initial syllable, as prescribed by the rule "the first syllable of a root ending in *ñ* or *ṇ* is always acute" (*ñṇiti nityam*), is established. However, if *yak* were applied...

By the rule *tāsyanudātenṅidadupadeśāl-lasārvadhātukamanudātam* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), since the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the *yak* suffix would be accented by the accent of the affix itself. In the example *sṛjyate srak bhaktaḥ*, the *lakāra* denotes the primary agent (*mukhyakartṛ*). Because it possesses the status of an object (*karmavat*), the *ātmanepada* ending is used. Here, *śyan* is the substitute for *yak*. [This occurs] through faith (*śraddhayā*).

The meaning is "he brings about. This is because verbal roots have multiple meanings; this is the intended sense here. In the case of the example "the devotee creates a garland" (*sṛjyate srajaṃ bhaktaḥ*), when the meaning is specifically "he brings about," and not "with faith," one simply says "he creates a garland" (*sṛjati srajam*). Now, he provides an example of the root *yuj*: "the religious student is joined" (*yujyate brahmacārī*).
Regarding the word *yogam*: here, the *Bhāṣya* states that the suffix *śyan* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *yag* [suffix] in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*).
Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, as it is well-known in the *Yogaśāstra*.
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the absence of sexual union with women; and this is also considered a limb (*aṅga*) of that [yoga].

It is well-known in the Yoga-śāstra. That yoga "yokes" (yunakti) the religious student (brahmacārin); that is, it joins him with the vision of the Self (ātmadarśana). Thus, in the active voice (kartṛlakāra), regarding the act of joining, yoga is the primary agent (mukhyakartā), while the religious student is the object (karman)—this is the established position. In that regard, concerning the object, the religious student...

When there is a desire to express agency (*kartṛtva*), as in the expression "the student applies himself to yoga" (*yujyate brahmacārī yogam*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) refers to the student as both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*); because he functions like the object, the suffix *śyan* (which is an exception to *yaṅ*) is applied. Thus, the student connects with yoga by himself, without the great exertion resulting from the practice of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the like.

This is the meaning. In that regard, the established principle is that when the student (*brahmacārin*) is the agent of the action, the connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) exists as the correlate (*anuyogitā*), whereas in the case of conjunction (*yoga*), it exists as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*). Now, although one would expect the third case (*tṛtīyā*) by the rule "sahayukte 'pradhāne" [Pāṇini 2.3.19] because of the conjunction with the counter-correlate, [the following applies].

Nevertheless, the meaning of the root *yuj* is a relation delimited by counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*). In that context, counter-positiveness is the result (*phala*) and the relation is the operation (*vyāpāra*). It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that the second case ending occurs because [the object] is the locus of the result in the form of counter-positiveness; this is based precisely on the usage in the *Bhāṣya*.

Others say that [the suffix *ya*] is second due to its connection (*yogāt*). The Vārttika states "bhūṣākarma" (adornment as the object). This is a *dvandva* compound of "bhūṣākarma," "kirādi" (verbs beginning with *kṛ*), and "san" (the desiderative suffix). Regarding "anyatra": the suffix *tral* is added in the sense of self (*svārthe*) after a word ending in the first case (*prathamāntāt*). Thus, it is understood that "other than the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)," there is the operation of the object (*karmakārya*). Those for whom adornment is the action (*kriyā*)...
Those verbal roots whose expressed meaning consists of the act of adorning are what is intended; that is to say, those expressing the action of decorating.
Thus he says: "of those expressing adornment," and so forth. "The maiden adorns herself" means that she herself possesses the act of decorating, without the exertion of another. In this [context]...

Because it has the sense of "adornment" (*bhūṣā*), the suffix *taR* (the *kṛ-ta* participle) occurs in the sense of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*), but not *yak*. Thus, one says *alamakṛta* ("he adorned himself"). Here, there is *taR*, but not *ciṇ*. However, in the future tense (*luṭ*), one says only *alaṅkartā* ("he will adorn himself"), and not with the *ciṇ-vat* augment *iṭ*. In the case of *avakirate hastī* ("the elephant scatters [flowers] over itself"), this refers to the primary agent (*mukhyakartṛ*) in the sense that "the elephant scatters flowers, etc., over itself."

The *lakāra* [is used]. In this context, the elephant is the object (*karman*). When there is the intention to express its agency (*kartṛtva*), the meaning is that it goes toward trees and so forth by itself, without human effort, and becomes strewn with flowers and the like. Here too, only the *ta-re* suffixes [are used], but not *ya*-class suffixes and so on. [Thus we have] *avākīrṣṭa*.

The suffix *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule "ṭhliṅsicorātmanepadeṣu. In the form *girate*, the ellipsis is "he swallows the food himself. The root *gṛ* (in the sense of swallowing) belongs to the *kirādi* group; when the *śap* affix is added, *riṅ* is substituted for *ṛ* by the rule "ṛṅ śayagliṅkṣu. In the expression *atithim ādriyate*, the agent is the primary one (*mukhyakartari*).
The form *ādriyate* is used in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). The meaning is that the object itself is the locus of the act of honoring.

Although there is no difference here between the suffix *śa* and *yak*, nevertheless *śa* alone is more appropriate because *yak* is prohibited [in this context]. Alternatively, there may be a difference in accent; however, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are established simply by virtue of the affix being marked with the indicator *ṅ*.

The distinction is that [the suffix] *prathama* is applied because it is designated as *atidhi*. Regarding *ādṛta*: when the prohibition of *ciṇ* is applied by this [rule], there is the elision of *sic* by the rule "hrasvādaṅgāt," and *kitva* is applied by the rule "uśca. Now he gives an example of a desiderative form: *cikīrṣate kaṭaḥ* ("the mat desires to be made"). [This occurs] by itself.

The meaning is: "the object of the desire to act. Now, one might object that since desire resides in the agent, who is the person, it does not reside in the object, which is the mat; furthermore, no difference is observed in the mat as the object whether the desire exists or does not exist.

Since the status of being "like the object" (*karmavatva*) does not apply here because there is an absence of action residing in the object, the prohibition of that status would be redundant; therefore, he says:
"Of desire" (*icchāyāḥ*).
(593) *Na rudhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.64).

[The root] *rudh* [is not included]. From this [sūtra], [the rule] "after this [root], when *ciṇ* follows" [is understood]. [In the example] "the cow was obstructed," the word "by itself" (*svayam eva*) is to be supplied as a supplement.

[The phrase] "only in the case of the reflexive object-agent" (*karmakartari eva*) is used because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] "after a vowel, in the case of the reflexive object-agent. [In the counter-example] "the cow was obstructed by the cowherd," since there is here an intention to express the cow—which is the object—as the agent...
The intention is that there is no prohibition of *ciṇ* because [the condition] is absent.

(594) *tapaḥ-tapaḥ-karmakasyaiva* (Pāṇini 3.1.88). [The word] *tapaḥ* in *tapaḥ-tapaḥ-karmakasyaiva* is the first *tapaḥ*, ending in the genitive case; it means "only for that which has *tapas* as its object."

The term "tapadhātoḥ" (of a root having *t* or *p* as its penultimate) is understood. From the rule "kartari śap," the word "kartari" (in the sense of the agent) is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and changed into the nominative case. Thinking that "karmavat" (like the object) is carried over from the rule "karmavat karmaṇā," he completes the remainder of the sūtra as "kartā karmavat" (the agent is like the object).

"This is for the purpose of an injunction. This will become clear immediately following this, at the occasion of explaining the example. Now, one might object: "If it is for the purpose of an injunction, then the particle *eva* (only/alone) is redundant.
To this he says: "But the particle *eva*... [The example is: "The ascetic performs penance" (*tapyate tapas tāpasaḥ*). Here, he states that the root *tap* has the sense of "acquiring" (*arjana*).

The meaning is "he acquires. This means he accomplishes austerity (*tapas*) consisting of *prājāpatya*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such *kṛcchra* penances. The suffix *la* [denotes] the primary agent (*mukhyakartṛ*). [This is so] because the act of accomplishment resides in the agent who is the ascetic, and because it does not reside in the object which is the form of the austerity itself.

By this sūtra, the status of being "like an object" (*karmavat*), which was not otherwise obtained by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, is prescribed. Consequently, the *yaṅ* affix, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and so forth [are applied]. However, when that [root] also refers to the state of torment (*saṃtāpa*) consisting of the production of suffering, then only the form *tāpasaṃ tapas tapati* occurs; the meaning is "he causes suffering. In this case...

*Tapas* (austerity) is the primary agent (*kartṛ*), whereas *tāpasa* (the ascetic) is the object (*karman*). Here too, because the operation (*vyāpāra*) of producing suffering resides in the agent in the form of austerity, it does not reside in the object in the form of the ascetic;
therefore, by the rule "karmavat karmaṇā," the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply to *tāpasa*. [The same applies to] *tapas*.

Because there is an absence of being an object (*karmakatva*), by this [rule] as well, there is no status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*). Therefore, the operations [pertaining to the object], such as *yaK* and so forth, do not apply.
Now, having raised the doubt that *ciṇ* might apply due to the status of being like the object in the case of the *luṅ* [suffix] following roots ending in *t* or *ap*, he says:
"Because of the prohibition of *ciṇ* by the rule *toṣu-anutāpe ca*, [the suffix] is *sij*. Upon its [the *sij*'s] elision by the rule *jhalo jhali*, [the form is established].

He states the established conclusion: "atapta" (not heated). As it is said, "the goldsmith heats the gold. In this case, because *tapaḥ* lacks an object (*karmaka*), it does not possess the status of being "like an object" (*karmavad-bhāva*). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that by the use of the particle *eva* (only), this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*); this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
By the phrase "those who follow the *vṛtti*," the contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* has been indicated; enough of this.

Previously, in connection with the rule for *duh* in the context of the prescription of *karmavat* behavior by the rule "duhipacyor bahulam," the sūtra "na duhasnunamām" was introduced. Now, [the discussion continues].

Following the maxim of the lion’s backward glance (*siṃhāvalokananyāya*), he introduces the rule concerning the root *snu*, which refers to the flowing of milk: "The suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are not used after the roots *duh*, *snu*, and *nam*" (*na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau*). Therein, he provides an example for the root *snu*: "it flows forth" (*prasnute*).
The root *snu* functions in the sense of the flowing of milk and in the sense of causing longing; [as in] "the calf [longs for] the cow."

In the expression "prasnauti" (it flows), when the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the primary agent (*mukhyakartari*), the meaning is that the calf causes the cow to long for the flow of milk. Here, the root *snudhātu* has an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartho*). In this context, the cow is the object (*karma*). However, the activity of longing resides in the calf, who is the agent (*kartṛ*). As for the longing itself—

The term *gorūpakarmaniṣṭhā* [refers to a case where] there is a desire to express the cow as the agent of the action. However, in the present context, it is the cow itself that is "eager" (*utkaṇṭhāvatī*) regarding the flowing of milk; this is the meaning. In that regard, the previous prohibition concerning the attainment of the object [of the action] is negated by this [rule]. [In the example] *prāsnāviṣṭa*, here...

Because it has an agent (*sakarmaka*), the *ciṇ* affix is not obtained; however, the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment occurs optionally in its place. But when the *ciṇvad-iṭ* is absent, the *iṇ* augment—conditioned by the rule "snukramoḥ" for roots beginning with *ni* and having a consonant other than a nasal or semivowel—is not applied. Thus he says: *prāsnoṣṭa*. He gives an example for the root *ṇam*: *namate daṇḍaḥ* (the staff bends); [and] *namati daṇḍam* (he bends the staff).

The meaning is "someone causes [the staff] to bend. However, when there is an intention to express the object as the agent, one says "the staff bends" (*namate daṇḍaḥ*). Here, although it possesses the status of an object, the *yak* suffix is not applied. Regarding *anaṃsta*: here, although it possesses the status of an object, the *ciṇ* suffix is not applied. Now, regarding the root *ṇam-*...

Since a root meaning "to bow" (*prahvībhāva*) is intransitive, the possibility of it having an object does not arise; therefore, the application of *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes is not possible. To this, he says: "In this context, the root *nam* has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) included within it. The intention is that roots possess multiple meanings. Regarding "*yakciṇoḥ*": [the rule] "na... [is applied].

The meaning is that in the prohibitive rule *duhasnunamām iti yakciṇoḥ*, one must state *duhasnunamām* as well as *hetumaṇṇiśribrūñām*. Regarding the example *kārayate*: the ellipsis is "Devadatta himself. Devadatta performs the action, and Yajñadatta prompts him.

The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) occurs in the sense of the primary agent (*mukhyakartṛ*) after a root ending in the causative marker *ṇi*. Here, when there is an intention to express the agency of Devadatta—the object of the causative—without depending on Yajñadatta’s instigation, the *lakāra* occurs in the sense of the "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*). The point is that even though it possesses the status of an object, the suffix is *taReĀva* (the *ta* suffixes), and not *yag* (the passive suffix). Thus: *acīkarata*. In this case...

Even though it is the object (*karman*), the *ciṇ* affix does not occur because of the rule "ṇi-śri-dru-stu-sru-ghasāṃ caṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.48). Thus, in the example *ucchrayate daṇḍaḥ*, the ellipsis is "by itself" (*svayam eva*).

The verbal suffix (*lakāra*) occurs in the sense of the primary agent (*mukhya-kartṛ*) [of the action of raising], where the stick (*daṇḍa*), as the object, is disregarded with respect to the activity of the agent.

When there is an intention to express the agent (kartṛtva) [in a passive construction], the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) occurs in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Even though the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) applies, the suffix *yak* does not occur; rather, there is *taReĀ*. Thus we have *udaśiśriyata*. Although the status of being like the object applies, because there is an absence of *ciṇ*, there is *caṅ* by the rule *ṇiśrī*. Now, one might ask: how is it that in *kāriṣyate* there are both *ciṇvad* and *iṭ*, given that the root ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) following a causative suffix (*ṇyanta*)?
To address the objection that [the augment] would not apply due to the absence of an original instruction (*upadeśa*), he says: "But the *iṭ* augment of the *ciṇvadiṭ* type must indeed occur.

For in the rule *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣuṭaḥ*, the meaning is not "of that which ends in a vowel in the original instruction," but rather "that which ends in a vowel which occurs in the original instruction. And thus...
The point is that even though there is no *upadeśa* (original instruction) for the causative (*ṇic*-ending), there is no fault because the *ṇi* itself exists as an *upadeśa*.
Regarding "ucchrāyiṣyate": since the root *śriñ* ends in a vowel (*ac*) at the time of its *upadeśa*, the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment applies.
Regarding "brūte kathām": the word "himself" (*svayam eva*) is to be supplied; someone tells a story.

When the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the primary agent, "story" (*kathā*) is the object; when the effort of the person is not intended to be expressed, the suffix occurs in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Because it possesses the status of an object, the *ātmanepada* affix *taṅ* is applied. Thus, in the absence of the expression "someone tells a story," where the suffix denotes the primary agent, "story" is the object; when the effort of the person is not intended to be expressed...

The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the agent as object (*karmakartṛ*). Because it behaves like an object (*karmavadbhāva*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes are applied; there is no *yak*. Thus, [the form] is *avocatā*.

Even though there is *karmavadbhāva*, there is no *ciṇ* substitution; rather, the intention is that by the rules "for the root *brū*, *vac* is substituted" (*brūvo vaciḥ*) and "after the roots *as*, *vac*, *khyā*, etc., the suffix *aṅ* is added" (*asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ*), and "for *vac*, *vaca*" (*vaca u*), [the form *avocat* is derived]. [This applies] to words through their utterance (*uccāraṇena*).
The status of the action as residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) should be understood from the observation of specific forms such as *prākāṭīt*. Regarding the rule *ṇi-śranthi-*:

the meaning is that according to the view of the Bhāradvājīyas, there is a prohibition of the affixes *yak* and *ciṇ* after the causative (*ṇyanta*) forms of the roots *śranth*, *granth*, and *brū*, as well as after intransitive (*akarmaka*) roots when the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed. Here, the term *ṇi* [refers to the causative suffix].

The inclusion of the general term "grahaṇa" (taking) is intended, and not merely the causative suffix *ṇic* with its cause (*hetu*). Consequently, thinking that the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not apply even to a form ending in *ṇiṅ*, he says: "The cow raises its tail; it is *utpucchayate*.

Here, the suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied by the rule "after *puccha*, when meaning 'raising' (*udasana*'). Now, one might object: "In this case, the tail (*puccha*) is the object (*karman*) of the act of raising."

The cow is the primary agent (*kartṛ*), not the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*); therefore, there is no possibility here for the application of *yak* or *ciṇ*. To this, he says: "when the causative sense is internalized" (*antarbhāvitaṇyarthatāyām*). This means that when one resorts to the internalized causative sense of the word "udasyati" as "udāsayati," [the rule applies] in such cases as "Devadatta causes the cow to toss its tail" (*utpuccchyate gāṃ Devadattaḥ*).

The cow is the object (*karman*); when there is an intention to express its agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to that action of raising its tail (*gaurūpa-karman*) without depending on the effort of a person who causes it to do so, the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is used in the sense of an "object-agent" (*karmakartṛ*), resulting in the form *utpuccchayate gauḥ*. The meaning is: "the cow raises its tail by itself."

*Bodhaḥ*. Regarding *udapupucchata*: here there is no *ciṇ* [affix]. Regarding *śy-acaṅoḥ*: in the example *utpuccchyate gauḥ*, because of the prohibition of *yak*, there is *śyan*; and in *udapupucchata*, because of the prohibition of *ciṇ*, there is *caṅ*—this is the meaning. Now, as for the roots *śrantha* in the sense of "releasing" and *grantha* in the sense of "tying."
