Regarding the roots *śranth* and *granth*, since they belong to the curādigaṇa (the tenth class), their forms would already be established by the inclusion of that class alone; therefore, the question arises as to why they are mentioned again.
To this, he says: "of *śranth* and *granth*. In the case of *granthati grantham*, the meaning is "he composes.
In *śranthati mekhalāṃ devadattaḥ*, the meaning is "he unties."

The term "Devadatta" applies to both [the book and the girdle]. Here, when there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the object—the book and the girdle—it becomes "the book knots itself" (*granthaḥ granthate*) and "the girdle knots itself" (*mekhalā śranthate*).

The meaning is that the book is itself the locus of the composition (*racanā*), and the girdle is the locus of the loosening (*sraṃsanā*). In that case, even though they possess the status of an object (*karmavatva*), [the rule does not apply].
The sense is "yag. Regarding *agranthiṣṭa* and *aśranthiṣṭa*, there is no *ciṇ*.

As for the phrase "but of the two [roots] belonging to the *kryādika* class": even though they possess the status of being like the object (*karmavat*), since *yak* is prohibited for them, the sense is that the *śnā* conjugational affix (*vikaraṇa*) occurs. He cites an example of that which is intransitive (*akarmaka*) when the rule for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied: *vikurvate*.

"Saindhavāḥ" means horses from the Sindhu region. Here, the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* signifies "leaping," due to the influence of the prefix. Thus he says: "they leap. The meaning is that they make a sound.

Because the action is subsumed within the meaning of the verbal root itself, this verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*). The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) denotes the primary agent (*mukhya-kartṛ*). [The rule] "after *vi*" refers to...

The meaning is that by the rule "ṭhakarmakācca," which is recited immediately after "ṭhveḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ," the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes are applied even when the fruit [of the action] goes to another. Now, one might object: since this verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the horses cannot be both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*), and thus there is no occasion for the application of *yak*. To this, he says:

Regarding the term *antarbhāvita*: when the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* functions in the sense of impelling one who is making a sound, then the form *vikurvate saindhavān* occurs. This means "he causes the horses (*saindhava*) to neigh. In that case, because there is no intention to express the impelling of the person (*puruṣa-preraṇā*) as an action toward the horses (*saindhava-karmaṇām*), [the horses themselves are treated as the agents].

When there is an intention to express agency (*kartṛtva*), the form *vikurvate saindhavāḥ* occurs; the meaning is "they gallop. Here, although the Saindhavas are both objects and agents (*karmakartṛ*), the suffix *yaK* does not apply. [In the example] *vyakāriṣṭa*, since the *ciṇ* affix is prohibited and there is an absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *caṅ* affix occurs.
The intention is that there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] when the *iṭ* augment follows the *ciṇvat* [treatment]. Regarding the alternative view where the *ciṇvat-iṭ* does not occur, he says:
"vyakṛta. Here, the elision of *sic* occurs by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*.
(595) *kuṣirañjoḥ prācāṃ śyanparasmaipadaṃ ca* | Pāṇini 3.1.90. || [In the opinion of the Eastern grammarians, the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj* take the affix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings.]

Regarding "of *kuṣ* and *rañj*": this means "of these two," namely of *kuṣa* (to extract) and *rañj* (to color). Regarding "in the case of the agent who is also the object" (*karmakartari*): the intention is that this term is supplied by jumping over [the intervening rule] from the rule "after a vowel, in the case of the agent who is also the object" (*acaḥ karmakartari*), as it continues [by *maṇḍūkapluti*]. [This is understood] from the rule "not after *duh*, *snuh*, or *nam*" (*na duhasnunamām*).

The words "not" (na) and "yag" continue [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "not yag. Rather, it is "śyan. The meaning is: "in the domain of yag. And thus, elsewhere than in the domain of yag, there is no application of śyan. If "not yag" were not stated, then even in the domain of yag, [the suffix] would apply to the ārdhadhātuka as well.

The intention is that the suffix *śyan* should occur. Because of the mention of "the Easterners" (*prācām*), there is an option. Thus he says: "the foot is injured (*kuṣyati*) or is injured (*kuṣyate*). The words "by itself" (*svayam eva*) are to be supplied as the remainder. When the primary agent is expressed by a verbal suffix, as in "Devadatta injures the foot (*kuṣṇāti pādam*)," the foot is the object; [in the passive construction], however, it is so without regard for human effort.

The meaning is that when there is a desire to express agency (*kartṛtva*), the form is *kuṣyati*, with the *śyan* affix and the *parasmaipada* ending; when both of those are absent, the form is *kuṣyate*, with the *yak* affix and the *ātmanepada* ending. There is a difference in accent between *yak* and *śyan*. In the case of *śyan*, as in the example *kuṣyantī vadhūḥ* ("the girl scratching herself"), [the accent falls on the first syllable].

By the rule *ṭhśapśyanornityam*, the augment *num* is obligatory; however, with the suffix *yak*, there would be an option by the rule *ṭhācchīnadyoḥ*. Thus, one says *rañjati* or *rañjate vastram*. When the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyarthatā*) is implied, because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* applies, and in the case of *rañjati vastram*, the meaning is "it causes the cloth to be colored" (*rañjayati*). In its primary sense...

The suffix *la* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). However, when there is a desire to express the agency of the object (*karmaṇaḥ kartṛtvavivakṣāyām*), it becomes "the cloth colors" (*rajyati*) or "the cloth colors itself" (*rajyate*); this is the meaning. As for the suffix *yak*, however, it does not exist at all; the intended meaning is that because of the rule "after [roots ending in] *śyan*" (*śyanniti śeṣaḥ*), the suffix *śyan* is prescribed in place of *yak* by the force of that specific injunction. Thus, having prohibited *yak*, the suffix *śyan* is ordained in its stead.
Regarding *koṣiṣīṣṭa*: because it is an ārdhadhātuka suffix, it does not fall under the scope of *yaṅ*;
consequently, since [the substitution of] *śyan* is taught as being conditioned by that (*yaṅ*), the parasmaipada endings do not occur when *śyan* is absent—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding *raṅkṣīṣṭa*: from the root *rañj*, with the addition of *sīyuṭ*, the *j* is changed to *g* by the rule for *kutva*. Of that...

[The suffix] *ka* [is applied] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). [This results in] the *anusvāra* and the *parasavarṇa*. In this section concerning the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), in all instances such as "the rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayam eva*) or "the wood splits by itself" (*bhidyate kāṣṭhaṃ svayam eva*), the word *svayam* means "by means of itself" (*ātmanā karaṇena*), and not "by itself as the agent" (*ātmanā kartrā*). For if that were the case...

It is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *ṇer aṇau* that *la* [affixes] should occur only when there is an object (*karman*). Thus ends the section on the agent as object (*karmakartṛprakriyā*).
Now begins the section on the kṛtya suffixes within the previous discussion of primary derivatives (*pūrvakṛdanta*).
Now, the formation of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛdanta-prakriyā*) is being described. Thus, having made the formal declaration:

"The *ṭha*-suffixes, which fall within the scope of the third chapter, are now being explained," among those *ṭha*-suffixes located in the third chapter, starting from the first pāda with the rules "the *ṭha*-suffix" (*ṭha-pratyayaḥ*) and "and it is subsequent" (*paraśca*), up to the rule "of *kuṣi* and *rañj*, according to the Easterners" (*kuṣirañjoḥ prācām*).
A few suffixes prescribed by the sūtras ending with *śyan* have been described.
Now, he begins to describe those prescribed by the subsequent sūtras—
"From the verbal root. "Up to the third [chapter]" means up to the completion of the third chapter;
this is clear in the Bhāṣya. Regarding that, the rule *upapadaṃ kṛd atiṅ* has been explained previously.
(650) *vā'sarūpo'striyām* 3.1.94.

"Or [the suffix] is optionally [used] when it is not similar in form, provided it does not denote the feminine. The analysis of the rule is *asarūpa* (not similar). This is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule), because if it were an *adhikāra* (a governing heading), there would be the cumbersome requirement of assuming the presence of the *svarita* accent; this is the intended meaning. The term *asarūpa* is a specification by gender (*liṅganirdeśa*). Wherever a suffix that is "not similar in form" is prescribed, the word *vā* ("optionally") applies there.

Before the word "ṭhve," the word "bādhaka" (sublative) is to be understood as a supplement. The meaning is that an asarūpa (dissimilar) suffix is optionally a sublative. When the expectation arises as to what it sublates, it is understood by implication to be the utsarga (general rule).
He states the resulting conclusion with the words "in this section on verbal roots," and so forth. The word *strī* is accented.

Thus he says: "except for what is stated in the section on feminine suffixes. This means: except for an exception (*apavāda*) situated within the upcoming section on feminine suffixes—namely, the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (A 3.3.94)—the sense is that a dissimilar suffix (*asarūpa-pratyaya*) situated in the section on feminine suffixes is always an exception (*bādhaka*) to the general rule (*utsarga*). [This refers to] the rule *ṇvultṛcau* (A 3.1.133).

This is the general rule (*utsarga*). The rule "after a root with *ṭh*, *ig*-upadhā, *jñā*, *prī*, or *kṛ*, the suffix *ka* is added" is an exception (*apavāda*). Even within the scope of that exception, the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* also occur. Examples: *vikṣipaḥ*, *vikṣepakaḥ*, *vikṣeptā*. Why specify "asārūpa" (when the suffixes are not identical in form)? Consider: the rule "the suffix *aṇ* after an object [in the accusative]" is the general rule; the rule "the suffix *ka* after a verbal root ending in *ā*, provided no upasarga precedes" is an exception. That...
However, because they possess the same form (*sarūpa*), it is always a sublater [of the general rule]. For example: *godah* (cow-giver), *kambaladah* (wool-giver).

According to the statement "lack of similarity is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*)," an indicatory letter does not obstruct similarity of form. Why say "not in the feminine"? Because "the suffix *ktin* occurs in the feminine" is the general rule (*utsarga*). *A-*...

The suffix *a* prescribed after a word ending in a *pratyaya* (such as *san*) is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) that sublates [the suffix *ktin*]. However, in cases such as *cikīrṣā* and *vyāvakrośī* (meaning "mutual reviling"), the suffix *ṇac*— prescribed by the rule *karma-vyatihāre ṇac striyām*— does indeed sublate *ktin*.

However, there is no prohibition by the rule "ṭhastriyām" (Pāṇini 3.3.124), because that [prohibition] is not stated within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "ṭhtasya ṭhṇacaḥ striyām" (Pāṇini 3.3.120).
(651) *Kṛtyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.95).
*Kṛtyāḥ* means those termed *kṛtya*. Consequently, [the term *kṛtya*] applies in rules such as *ṭhpraiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca*, *ṭharhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*, and *ṭhśaki liṅ ca*.
"Before *ṇvul*" means prior to the rule *ṭhṇvultṛcau*. And this is stated in the Bhāṣya.
This is clear.
(652) *kartari kṛt* | Pāṇini 3.4.67.
"A *kṛt* suffix [is used] when the agent is to be expressed. This is a statement of meaning (*arthanirdeśa*). Thus, when [the condition] is met...
The meaning is that since the suffixes such as *vakanīya*, *tavya*, and *ādya* are designated by the technical term *kṛt*, they would [otherwise] apply to the agent; however,
[the rule] "tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.70) restricts them to those two [meanings].

The kṛtya and khal-artha suffixes belong to those two [categories] alone. By restating the absence of the sense of the agent— which would otherwise be obtained because the "bhāva" and "karman" mentioned in the rule *ṭhlaḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca* are designated as *kṛt*— by means of the word *tat* (that), [the author] indicates them through their specific designation as *kṛtya*.
It indicates the non-contradiction of the notion of "entirety" (*kṛtsna*).
(654) *tavyat-tavya-anīyaraḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.96. *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar*: this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of these [suffixes]. They are suffixes (*pratyaya*).

"They may be"—it should also be understood that they are designated as *kṛt* and *kṛtya*. "For the sake of accent" means that [the markers] are for the purpose of specific accents, according to the rules "A *ti* [marker] has a circumflex accent (*svarita*)" and "In a *rit* suffix, the penultimate syllable has the acute accent (*udātta*). However, for the *tavya* suffix without an anubandha, [the accent is determined] by the general accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
It should be understood that the initial syllable alone is acute (udātta). He gives an example for the abstract action (bhāva): *edhitavyam*.

The meaning is "the act of increasing whose agent is you. Now, one might object: in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, only an abstract action (*bhāva*) that is not a substance (*asatvabhūta*) is intended to be included, because the *bhāvanā* expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is of the nature of a non-substance.

Because it has been so stated. Consequently, since that entity—which is of the nature of non-existence—is referred to here by the word "tat" in the rule *tayoreva kṛtya*, the connection with gender and number is untenable for the *tavyad* suffixes and others, as they denote non-existence; therefore, he says: "in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*)."

The meaning is that the intention is based on the established doctrine of the Bhāṣya, which accepts the wording of the sūtras as "the singular [is used] in the sense of one," and "the dual and plural [are used] in the sense of two and many," thus holding that the singular is employed when duality and plurality are absent. And as for its neuter gender: "monotony (ekaśruti) is the universal term (sarvanāman) for accent."
The point is that the term *napuṃsaka* (neuter) is a general pronoun (*sarvanāma*), according to the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *dāṇḍināyana*. He gives an example for the object (*karman*): *cetavya*.
This is based on the Vārttika: "The suffix *tavyat* occurs after the root *vas*, and there is the augment *ṇiC* when it denotes the agent. *Vāstavya* means "one who dwells" (*vastṛ*).

Because it has the marker *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* substitution for the penultimate vowel. Regarding the rule *kelimara*: it applies only to a verbal root (*dhātu*). This [suffix] occurs only in the sense of action (*bhāva*) or agent (*kartṛ*). In *kelimara*, the letters *ka* and *ra* are elided. In the case of *bhidelimāḥ*, because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel. *Saralāḥ* refers to a particular species of tree. Regarding the phrase *tadbhāṣye*: in the *Bhāṣya*.
The meaning is that by citing *bhidelimā* as an example, the sense is clarified by the explanation "it is to be broken" (*bhetavyā*).
(655) *kṛtyacaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.29. Regarding *kṛtyacaḥ*: the rule *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* is understood to follow. [And] *upasargādanotparaḥ*.
Therefore, regarding the rule *upasargād* as well, it is intended that [the prefix] must reside in an *upasarga*.

After the word *kṛti*, the word *vidyamānasya* (of that which exists) is to be supplied as a remainder. The term *acaḥ* is in the ablative case. Thus he says: "residing in an *upasarga*. This is a statement [of a rule] because [the application] would otherwise not occur due to the lack of being in the same word (*asamānapadatva*). [The rule begins with: *aṭkupvāṅnum...*.

The phrase "even in the case of sexual intercourse" (*vyavāye’pi*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "the *prayāṇīya*. Regarding the word "of one who is despondent" (*nirviṇṇasya*), the meaning is that there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the suffix *ṇa* after the root *nas*. [He says] "due to the absence of a vowel following [the *ṇ*]" because, when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *vid*, by the rule *radābhyām*, the *t* following the *d* and the preceding *d* [are both replaced by *ṣ*].

When the form *natve ṭhnirvin na* is established, since the letter *n* does not follow a vowel (*ac*), the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.29) does not apply; therefore, this statement regarding *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) is necessary. Furthermore, it should be understood that *ṇatva* is not applicable here because the *n* is separated [from the preceding vowel] by the letter *k*. Regarding the phrase "of the preceding": [this refers to the condition for] the *ṇatva* of the *n*.
The meaning is that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by virtue of being a *ṣṭu* sound; thus, the form contains two *ṇ*s.
(656) *ṇervibhāṣā* | Pāṇini 8.4.30. Regarding *ṇervibhāṣā*: the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* is understood [from the previous sūtra], as is *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ*.

In the rule "ṭhṇe," the term *vihita* (prescribed) is a qualifier for what has been formed. Thus he says: "from that which stands in an upasarga," and so forth. Regarding *prayāpaṇīyam*: from the root *yā*, after the addition of *ṇic* and *puK*, we have *yāp*;
from this *yāp* with the suffix *anīyar* and the elision of *ṇic*, there is an optional substitution of *ṇa* by this rule. Regarding *yakā*: [this refers to] *yāp*.

From the causative (*ṇic*) form of the root *īṣ* (to go), in the present tense (*laṭ*) with the suffix *śānac* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), after the application of the augment *muṭ* (by the rule *mug*), the addition of *yak*, and the elision of *ṇi*, in the word *prayāpyamāṇa*, the optional substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is desired. However, if one were to state that "the optional substitution of *ṇ* for *n* applies to a *t* situated after a *kṛt*-suffix," then [it would not apply here] because the *śānac* suffix is a *kṛt*.

Because of the intervention [of other elements], there would be no absence of posteriority (*paratva*) relative to the causative suffix (*ṇic*); consequently, the optional substitution of *ṇatva* for the *n* situated therein would not occur. Therefore, the meaning is that one must rely on the rule as having a "prescribed qualification" (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). In the Bhāṣya, however, even regarding the portion "a *kṛt* suffix following that which ends in *ṇi*," one should carry forward (anuvartayitavya) the rule *aṭ-ku-pv-āṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi* and so forth.

The optional application of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) even when there is an intervention by the letter *y* has been established. Regarding the form *duraḥ*, the intention is that it is by the rule "The status of being an *upasarga* must be denied to [words] in the case of *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*" (*ṣatva-ṇatvayor upasargatva-pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ*). Consequently, because *duraḥ* lacks the status of an *upasarga*, neither of the two rules applies to the *nakāra* situated after it in a *kṛt*-affix.
Intending to show that [the suffix] *lyuṭ* occurs [after a causative root], he provides the example: *duryānam*, *duryāpanam*.
From the root *yā* with the causative marker *ṇic*, when *lyuṭ* is added and the *ṇic* is elided, the form *duryāpanam* results.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini 8.4.31: *halaścejupadhāt*.

Regarding the rule *halacejupadhāt*: the meaning is not "from a root ending in a consonant," because a root having *ij* as its penultimate (*ijupadha*) never fails to end in a consonant. Rather, it is intended to mean "from a root beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*). Thus he says:
"from a root beginning with a consonant and having *ij* as its penultimate. The word "of the following [suffix]" (*parasya*) is to be supplied.
In the counter-examples such as *prohaṇīyam*, however, the substitution of *ṇ* is obligatory by the rule *kṛtyaca*.
(658) *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ* |8|4|32|. [The word] *ijādeḥ*: the phrase *ṇervibhāṣā* has ceased to apply. The phrase *kṛtyaca* is understood (*anuvartate*).
From the rule *halaścejupadhāt*, the word *hal* is also [understood].

Because it qualifies the base (*prakṛti*), there is an application of the "final element" rule (*tadantavidhi*). Thus, it is obtained that for a *kṛt*-suffix beginning with *n* following a base ending in a consonant (*hal*) that has *i* as its penultimate letter (*ijupadhāt*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs. And so, in cases such as *preṅkhaṇīyam*:

Since the rule would have been established by "ṭhkṛtyacaḥ" alone, he states that this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction: "if it has the augment *num*. After the words "only when situated in a *kṛt*-affix," the word "ṇatvam" (the substitution of *ṇ*) is to be understood as the remainder. Regarding "preṅkhaṇīyam": the root √ikṣ is accompanied by *num* because it is marked with an indicatory letter *it*; and from the root "ivi prīṇane" (ivi in the sense of pleasing), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied.

In the case of *tasyānādeśe prenvanam*, there would also be the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, because this [suffix] begins with *ij* and ends in a consonant (*hal*), even though it lacks the augment *num*. To address this, he says: "The mention of *num*, etc. Here, every *anusvāra* is included, not only that which takes the place of *num*, because there is no distinction made. Thus he says: "In this case..."

Regarding "tviti" and "prombhaṇam": the meaning here is that the root *umbh* possesses an inherent anusvāra, and not an anusvāra substituted for the *num* augment. (659) *Vā niṃsanikṣanindām* | Pāṇini 8.4.33.

The word *kṛti* is understood from the rule *niṃsa-ṣṭhāva-kṛtya-caḥ*, while *acaḥ* is no longer understood. Thus he says: "of these, [the substitution of] *na* [occurs] before *i*. (660) *na bhā-bhū-pū-kami-gami-pyāyi-vepām* 8.4.34.

"Not *bhābhū-prabhānīya*. The meaning is that here, the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva), which would otherwise apply by the rule "kṛtyacaḥ," does not take place. "In the section on *ṇatva*" refers to what is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "cakṣiṅḥ khyāñ.
"Prakhyānīya": here, because the substitution of *y* (yatva) is considered asiddha, there is an intervention by the letter *ś*.
The intention is that the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] does not apply by the rule "kṛtyacaḥ.

(661) *Kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* | Pāṇini 3.3.113: The kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes [are applied] diversely; they are applied even in senses other than those for which they have been prescribed from their respective roots.

The meaning is "they may be. In *snānīyam*, the suffix *anīyar* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). In *dānīya*, the suffix *anīyar* is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
However, in the Bhāṣya, after stating that "it should be said that *kṛt* [suffixes] are applied diversely," it gives the example:

*pādābhyāṃ hriyate pādahārakaḥ* ("he is carried by the feet, a foot-carrier"); here the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). [The example] *śvo'gnīnādhāsyamānena* ("by one who will establish the fires tomorrow") refers to a time other than the current day (*anadyatana*).
It has been stated that *lṛṭ* [the future suffix] will occur.
(662) *Aco yat* |3|1|97|. Regarding *aco yat*:
it could have been formulated as *ṛhalorṇyaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.124], which specifically prescribes *ṇya* after roots ending in *ṛ* or *hal*. Thus, [the rule *aco yat*] could have been dispensed with.

The meaning is that because [the suffix] is prescribed as *ṇyat*, the suffix *yat* does not apply after bases ending in consonants. Furthermore, the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply here because the two suffixes are similar in form (*sarūpatvāt*). The same applies to the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*); the meaning is that it is impossible to perform such an analysis. To the question "Why?", he says: "Only in the case of *tavyat* and so forth."
The meaning is that it is possible to read [the rule] as a single sūtra: *ṭhaktavyatavyānīyaraḥ*. (663) *idyati* | 6|4|65|.
Regarding *idyati*: the sense is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ātaḥ* from the previous rule, *āto lopa iṭi ca*.

Regarding "guṇa": the sense is that from the root *dā*, by [the application of] *yat* according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 (*dādhāghvadāp*), there is the substitution of *ī* for *ā* (by 7.1.84), and then there is *guṇa* by [the rule] *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*. Regarding "gleyam":

the sense is that from the root *glai* (meaning "in the destruction of joy"), by [the application of] *yat*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel (by 6.1.45), followed by the substitution of *ī* and then *guṇa*.
Regarding the forms *takiśasīti*: the verbal roots *taki*, *śasi*, *cati*, *yati*, and *janī* (in the sense of "manifestation") are cited here.

The distinction is that in all these cases, the suffix is added in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) when the roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), whereas when they are transitive (*sakarmaka*), it is also added in the sense of the object (*karman*). Now, one might object: according to the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*, the suffix *ṇyat* may also be applied to the root *jan* in the sense of "fitness" (*arha*), resulting in the form *janya*.

Since the inclusion of the root *jan* would be redundant for the purpose of establishing the form [of *janya*], he says: "for the sake of the accent" (*svarārtha*). This means it is for the sake of the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed by rules such as "after that which ends in *yat*, except in the case of *āvaḥ*" (*yato 'nāvaḥ*). Now, one might object that if the suffix *ṇyat* were used, there would be vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel;
therefore, anticipating this objection and refuting it, he states: "the rule for *yat* applies here so that there may be an absence of that [vṛddhi]."
"And there is no risk of over-extension" (vṛddhiprasaṅga). Why? To this he says: "In the case of *jan* and *vadhi*" (*janivadhyoḥ*). [Regarding] "or *hana*" (*hano vā*):

the meaning is that after the root *han*, either the suffix [is applied], or else the substitution of *vadha* for the base (*prakṛti*) occurs. "In the alternative" (*pakṣe*) means: in the alternative where [the suffix] is absent. "To be killed" (*ghātya*): when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, by the rule "of *han*, *ta* [is substituted] except before *aciṇṇal*" (*hanasto'ciṇṇaloḥ*), the *n* [is replaced].

[The suffix *kvip* is applied. There is the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *v* to *ū*). There is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel. However, the sense is that the substitution of *vadh* for *han* does not occur, because it is taught as being conditioned by the presence of the [suffix] *yat*. (664) *poradupadhāt* | Pāṇini 3.1.98.

[Objection: But in the case of *śapyam* and *labhyam*, since the rule *ṛ-halor ṇyat* applies, the suffix *ṇyat* might also occur; for the rule *vā'sarūpaḥ* operates when there is dissimilarity between *ṇya* and *ṇyat*. To this, he says:
"Dissimilarity is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). [This refers to] the rule *vā'sarūpaḥ*.

This is established in the Bhāṣya: the meaning is that dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) is intended only for those [suffixes] that are divested of their indicatory letters (*anubandha*). And in the present case, because the suffixes *ṇyat* and *kyap*, when devoid of their indicatory letters, are similar (*sārūpya*), the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply; thus, in examples such as *śapyam*, it is *kyap* alone that serves as the exception (*apavāda*) to *ṇyat*.
The state [of being].
(665) *Āṅe yi* | Pāṇini 7.1.65. From the rule *āṅe yi*, [the word] *num* is supplied from the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*, and from the rule *labheśca*.

The word "labheta" (one may obtain) also carries over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of that which follows the prefix *āṅ*. Regarding the term "when intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣite*), it is clear from the Bhāṣya that this is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). He states the purpose of the phrase "when intended to be expressed": "when *num* has been applied," because [the suffix] *yat* is intended to be expressed, and therefore its application occurs.

The meaning is that since the suffix *yat* would not apply once *num* has already been added—because the word would no longer have a vowel as its penultimate letter (*adupadha*)—only the suffix *ṇyat* applies. However, if the intention were for *num* to be added when *yat* follows, then because it would have a vowel as its penultimate letter, only *yat* would apply and not *ṇyat*. [Thus, the form is] *ālambhyaḥ*.

Regarding the word *gaura*: although there is no difference in form between the suffixes *ṇyat* and *yat*, nevertheless, when *ṇyat* is applied, by the rule *ṭitsvaritam*, the vowel becomes svarita; whereas when *yat* is applied, by the rule *yatonāvaḥ*, it becomes udātta at the beginning. Thus, the difference in accent (*svarabheda*) is the result.

(666) *upāt praśaṃsāyām* | 7|1|66| The meaning is: after the prefix *upa*, when a suffix beginning with *ya* is intended to follow, the augment *num* is added to the root *labh* if praise (*praśaṃsā*) is implied. For example: *upalambhyaḥ sādhuḥ* ("one who is easily obtained is excellent"). [In this case, *upa* means] "near."

The meaning is "having obtained. From the word *sādhu*, praise (*praśaṃsā*) is understood. Here too, once the augment *num* has been applied, because the vowel *a* is no longer penultimate (*adupadhatva*), only the suffix *ṇyat* is used. As before, there is a difference in accent (*svara*). (667) *śakisahośca* | Pāṇini 3.1.99.
And [the suffix] *śakisahaḥ*. The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative; the meaning is "from these two. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat*.
(668) *gadamadacarayamaścānupasarge* 3.1.100. *gadāmada-*: a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of the four roots *gada*, *mada*, *cara*, and *yam*. "Without a prefix" (*anupasarga*).

The seventh case [ending] is used in the sense of the fifth. The meaning is: "after these [roots], when no prefix (*anupasarga*) precedes, the suffix *yat* is applied. This is an exception to the rule for the suffix *ṇya*. When a prefix is present, *ṇya* alone is used, as in *pragādya* and so forth. "After the root *car*, when preceded by *āṅ*, [the suffix *yat* is applied] provided it does not mean 'a heavy load'"—this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is: even when *āṅ* is a prefix, *yat* shall be applied after *car*, provided it does not refer to a heavy burden (*aguru*).

"Ācārya" means "guru"; the meaning is that he is one who should be served. Now, one might object: since the form is already established by the rule *p-od-upadhāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.95), the inclusion of the root *yam* here is redundant. To this, he says: "For the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*) regarding *yam*.
The sense is that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to *yam* only when it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). He states the result of this:

[The author says: "Let it not be [the case] when preceded by a preposition (*upasarga*). But one might object: how can the suffix *yat* occur after the root *nam* when preceded by the prefix *ni-* in such instances as "ṭhaniyamyasya nā'yuktiḥ" and "ṭhvayā niyamyā nanu divyacakṣāḥ," given the prohibition that it occurs only after the root when it is *anupasarga* (without a preposition)? To this he replies: "It should indeed occur after [the root] preceded by *ni-*. [The suffix] *ya*..."

This is the remainder [of the commentary]. Why? To this he says: "Therefore, not there. He provides another solution: "Or, one who is proficient in restraint (*niyama*). The word *niyama* is derived from the root *yam* preceded by the prefix *ni*, with the suffix *ap* in the sense of an abstract state (bhāva), according to the rule *yamaḥ samupaniviṣu ca*. The meaning is "one who is proficient in restraint. In that regard...
The meaning is that the word *niyamya* is derived by adding the suffix *yat* according to the rule for words ending in *hit* (*prāg-dhita-ya-t*), as in "sādhuḥ.
(669) *Avadyapaṇyavaryā garhyapaṇitavyānirodheṣu* |3|1|101|.
[The words] *avadyapaṇya*: this is the nominative plural of a *dvandva* compound consisting of *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya*. *Garhya*...

*paṇitavya* and *anirodha*: this is the locative plural from a dvandva compound. The meaning is that the three roots beginning with *avad* are prescribed as irregular (*nipātana*) in the sense of the three objects beginning with "blameworthy" (*garhya*). Now, since the form would be established by the rule *vadaḥ supi* alone, the inclusion of *avadya* is redundant; to this he replies: "when *nañ* is the upapada."

The point is that there is a difference in accent between *yat* and *kyap*, as well as the presence or absence of *saṃprasāraṇa*. "Avadyam" means sin; the meaning is that it is "not to be spoken" (*avācyam*) because it is censurable. Regarding "anudyaṃ gurunāma" (the name of a teacher is not to be uttered): here, with the negative particle *nañ* as an upapada, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *vad* by the rule *vadaḥ supi*, and [the substitution of *u* for *o*] occurs by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kitī*.
The form [is derived] through *saṃprasāraṇa*. The meaning is "unfit for mention. The point here is that since reproach (*garhā*) is not perceived, the rule does not apply. Now, one might object:
"Since the name of a teacher (*guru-nāman*) is not inherently reproachable, how can it be unfit for mention? To this, he says: "For that [name] is not reproachable."
And [it is] "unfit for speech. Why? To this he says: "of the names of the self" (*ātmanām*). Regarding "a cow for sale" (*paṇyā gauḥ*):

the sense is that the suffix *yat* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) after the root *paṇ*, which has the meaning of "transaction" (*vyavahāra*). Although the root *paṇ*—in the sense of "transaction" and "praise"—has two meanings, nevertheless, regarding the word *paṇya*:

Because it must be employed by the force of usage (*prayoga*), and because it is conventional (*rūḍha*) in this context, it is taken here as having the sense of "to be used. Thus he says: "to be used" (*vyavahartavya*); the meaning is "to be purchased" (*kretavya*). Regarding "the price is something else" (*pāṇyam anyat*): the intention is that there is a vowel strengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*) due to the suffix *ṇyat*. The meaning is "other than what is to be used. Thus he says:

"Worthy of praise" (*stutyarham*). "Without obstruction" (*apratibandha*) means "without restriction" (*aniyama*). Regarding "the suffix *yat* after the root *vṛṅ*": here, only the root *vṛṅ* belonging to the *kryādi* class, meaning "to gather" (*saṃbhakti*), is intended to be taken; not the root *vṛñ* of the *svādi* class, meaning "to choose" (*varaṇa*). The point is that the sense of non-obstruction is consistent only when [the root] signifies gathering.

"Another [is] by means of a hundred [pieces]" (*śatena vārī anyā*): she is worthy of being taken by a hundred men; the meaning is that there is no restriction that she must be chosen by this [specific person] alone. "Another [is] by means of conduct" (*vṛttyā anyā*): she is to be chosen according to suitability. The suffix *kyac* is applied here by the rule *hetistuśāsvṛdṛjuṣaḥ kyac*. In this case, there is no fixed rule.
"Because it is not perceived [as such]. Here, because the word *vāryā* is taken in the feminine gender, there is the usage "the male *vāryās* are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
(670) *vahyam* [is used] for the instrument. 3.1.102.
*vahyam* is the instrument (*karaṇa*). The suffix *yat* is prescribed after the root *vah* when it denotes the instrument; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat*.
(671) *aryaḥ* [is formed] in the sense of "master" (*svāmin*) and "Vaishya.

Regarding *aryaḥ* [in the sense of] "master" and "Vaishya": the suffix *yat* is applied to this [root]. The word "is prescribed" (*nipātyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule]. This is an exception to *ṇyat*.

Thus, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat* which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *ṛhalo’r*. When the suffix *yat* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ṛ*, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*. This is what he states: "aryaḥ" means "master"; "āryaḥ" means "Brāhmaṇa. The sense is that when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, there is *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel *ṛ*, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra*.

(672) *upasaryā kālyā prajane* |3|1|104|. *Upasaryā*. *Prajana* means procreation; that is, the taking of conception (*garbhagrahaṇa*). The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). There is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *janivadhyośca*. *Kālya* means "one for whom the time has arrived"; [the suffix *yat* is applied] by the rule *tadasya...* [Pāṇini 5.1.95].
While the word "prāptam" (obtained) is understood from the previous rule, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "kālād yaḥ. The word "cet" (if) must be supplied.

Thus he says: "If [the time] for conception has arrived. The meaning is that if a female animal or woman intended for conception is meant to be expressed as having reached the proper time for impregnation, the form *upasaryā* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
The result is that the suffix *yat* is applied after the root *sṛ* preceded by the prefix *upa*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the suffix *ṇyat*.
(673) *ajaryaṃ saṅgatam* (Pāṇini 3.1.105).
[The word] *ajaryam* [is formed with] *yat* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). There is a Vārttika stating: "It should be stated that [the suffix is used] in the sense of the agent."
The intention [of the author] is that the sense "in the agent" is obtained through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Regarding the word *saṅgatam*: *saṅgatam* means meeting (*saṅgama*).

Regarding *ajaryam*: it does not decay; thus it is *ajaryam*. The word "friendship" (*mitratvam*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The meaning is that it does not become something that decays. In this regard, he cites the usage of Bhāravi with the words *tena*: "O Rāma! by him..."

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "O Noble One, quickly bring about a union—a meeting—that is ageless and imperishable. Now, one might ask: since the word *saṅgata* does not appear in the verse "mṛgaurajaryaṃ jarasā," how can [the term] *yat* [be applied]? To this he replies: "By the deer," and so forth. This is a poem by Kālidāsa. [Regarding the form] *ajarita*: [Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary commentary on a specific grammatical point regarding the formation of the word *ajarita* and its relation to the verse *mṛgaurajaryaṃ jarasā*. The core task is to translate the explanatory portion. The meaning is: "O Noble One, quickly effect a union—an association—that is free from decay and is eternal. Now, [an objection is raised]: "In the verse *mṛgaurajaryaṃ jarasā*, because the word *saṅgata* is absent, how can [the rule apply]? To this he says: "By the deer," etc. This is a work of Kālidāsa. [As for the form] *ajarita*: [it is derived from the root *jar* with the suffix *kta*].
The meaning is that [the suffix] *yat* does not apply because of the absence of the *tṛc* suffix.
(674) *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* |3|1|106|. Regarding *vadaḥ supi*: [the word] "in the sense of the abstract state" (*bhāve*) is supplied from the subsequent sūtra, *bhuvo bhāve*.

The meaning is that [the suffix] is elided. The intention is that, because the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the mention of "bhāve" (in the sense of an abstract action) in the subsequent sūtra would otherwise be redundant. Regarding the term "anupasarge" (without a prefix): the intention is based on the Bhāṣya statement, "The mention of 'anupasarga' applies even when a case-ending follows the root *vṛ*. Regarding the form *brahmodyam*: after the root *vad*, when the suffix *kyap* is applied, [the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* occurs] by the rule "vacisvapi... (*Pāṇini 6.1.15*).
Regarding *saṃprasāraṇa*: "In reality, however, the mention of *bhāva* (the abstract action) is not drawn down [from the previous rule] here;

rather, as stated in the Bhāṣya, 'The mention of *bhāva* there is for the sake of the subsequent rules'—following this view, he says: 'Some say that the suffixes occur in the sense of the object (*karman*)'. This means that the suffixes *kyac* and *kyaṅ* occur."
Regarding the rule *bhuvo bhāve*: [the term] *brahmabhūyam*—because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Its neuter gender is due to common usage (*lokāt*).
Regarding *bhavyam*: the meaning is "existence" (*bhāva*). Here, because there is no following *sub*-ending as an upapada, the suffix *yat* alone applies, and the *guṇa* substitution occurs.
In the word *vānta*, there is the substitution of *y* [for *v*]. In *prabhavyam*, the meaning is "power" (*prabhāva*).

(676) *hanasta ca* | Pāṇini 3.1.108. Regarding *hanaḥ ta*: the phrase "substitution of *t*" is understood from the context; the remainder is "in the present [rule]. Why [is the suffix] *ghañ* used in the sense of "state" (*bhāve*)? [Answer: As in *ghātya*.

*vṛṣalaḥ* (a low-born man). Why [is the condition] "in the absence of a prefix" (*anupasarge*) stated? [Consider: *praghātaḥ* (a slaughterhouse). However, the form *hatya* when used without a prefix is simply incorrect.
(677) *eti-stu-śāsu-vṛ-dṛ-juṣaḥ kyap* |3|1|109|. [The rule applies to] these six: *eti*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*.

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used after a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The rule *supi anupasarge bhāve* has ceased to apply here. Therefore, he says: "After these [roots], the suffix *kyap* shall occur. (Pāṇini 3.3.98). (Pāṇini 6.1.71):
*hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*—[the augment] *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a *pit* sound.

Regarding the short vowel: "spaṣṭam" (it is clear) is not explained [separately]. Regarding "itya": there is the *tuk* augment after the root *iṇ* when the suffix *kyap* follows. However, in the case of "upeyam," the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *īṅ* belonging to the *divādi* class. Regarding the mention of *vṛñ*: this is a *vārttika*. As for "not *vṛṅ*," [this refers to] the root *vṛṅ* meaning "to choose/to collect," which belongs to the *krayādi* class and is marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter.

The meaning is "not to be grasped. Regarding the word *vāryāḥ* [meaning] "the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," the sense is that they are necessarily to be honored. Here, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *vṛṅ* in the sense of "to honor" (*saṃbhakti*). It is not established by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) "in the case of *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya*," because here what is intended is the sense of restraint or restriction (*nirodha*).
But surely, since [the suffix] *kyap* is already established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "vadaḥ supi," its explicit mention here is redundant.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *kyap* is for the purpose of preventing the continued application of *yat*, which is drawn over by the particle *ca*; for the particle *ca* lacks the *svarita* accent, and thus [the rule] "bhuvo bhāve" [does not apply].
Because there is no recurrence [of this rule] in the subsequent sūtras beginning with "ityādi," he says: "parasyāpi" (also of the other).

This means [the suffix] prescribed by the rule "ṭhorāvaśyake. Regarding "veti kāśikā," [it means] "or kyap. In its absence, the suffix is ṇyat because [the root] ends in a consonant. The point is that this is not seen in the Bhāṣya. [The form] "śasyam" [is derived thus].

Regarding *śaṃsyam*: in the alternative involving the suffix *kyap*, there is elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*. Regarding *duhyam*: in the alternative involving *kyap*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is marked with *k*. Although the rule *śaṃsiduhiguhibhyo vā* (optionally [forming the gerundive] after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*) is not seen in the Bhāṣya, he states that the suffixes *ṇyat* and *kyap* after the root *śaṃs* are authoritative by saying *praśasyasya*. [This refers to the rule] *praśasyasya śraḥ*.

Thus, by the force of this grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*), the suffix *kyap* is established after the root *śaṃs*. Furthermore, in the rule prescribing the initial acute accent (*udātta*) for roots such as *īḍ*, *vand*, *vṛś*, *śaṃs*, and *duh*—specifically through the force of the reference to *śaṃs* as ending in *ṇyat*—the suffix *ṇyat* is established. Consequently, the two forms *śasyam* and *śaṃsyam* are established. As for the other two, however, namely *duh* and *guh*:

The meaning is that there is no root for the *kyap* suffix. Regarding the phrase "an addition" (*upasaṅkhyānam*), the word "*kyap*" is to be understood as the remainder. One should not argue that if it were preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, there would have to be an *avagraha* (separation) in the *padapāṭha* [as in *ājyam*]; for this is precisely what is desired. Furthermore, the absence of *avagraha* on the part of the authors of the *padapāṭha* is simply unauthoritative.

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that this is because the *padapāṭha* is a modern [reconstruction]. Consequently, the *avagraha* "asmadri-aga" for "asmadriyag" is entirely without authority. The *avagraha* "asmadri-ak" alone is appropriate, since the substitution of *adraḷ* for the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of the word "asmad" is prescribed; this and other such points should be inferred.

(679) Pāṇini 3.1.110: *ṛdupadhāccā’klṛpicṛteḥ*. The meaning is that the suffix *kyap* is applied after a root having *ṛ* as its penultimate letter (*ṛdupadha*), with the exception of the roots *klṛp* and *cṛt*. Now, one might ask: "Is the inclusion of *tapara* (the long *ṝ*) here redundant? To this he replies: "They are not invariably non-causative (*anitya-ṇyanta*). However, when they take the causative suffix *ṇic*, [the rule does not apply].
"Yadeva" means "by this [rule], namely *ṭhaco yaṅ*.
(680) *ī ca khanaḥ* |3|1|111|. "And *ī* after *khana*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), *kyap* is also included; thus, *kyap* is applied after the root *khan*.

The meaning is that the letter *ī* should be the substitute for the final portion of the root *bhṛ*. [An objector says: "A short vowel would be easier to recite"; the intention is that by applying the rule *ād guṇaḥ* to the short *i*, the form *kheya* is established. (681) *bhṛño'saṃjñāyām* | Pāṇini 3.1.112.
Regarding the rule *bhṛño’saṃjñāyām*: the word *kyaṅ* is understood as the remainder [of the sūtra]. The meaning is "servants" (*bhṛtyāḥ*), that is, those performing work.

The suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule *karmaṇi bhṛtau* (Pāṇini 3.2.22) to the root *kṛ*. The term "to be supported" (*bhartavyāḥ*) means they are to be dispatched to work for the sake of another through the payment of wages. Now, [one might ask] regarding the word *bhṛtya* in the sense of laborers...

Because it possesses the quality of *rūḍhi* (conventional usage), it is indeed a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*); therefore, he says: "it is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*). [The example given is] "a *bhāryā* is a Kṣatriya woman. The intention is that this is a conventional name applied specifically to certain Kṣatriyas.
Now, how can it be *bhāryā*? This is an objection based on the expectation that it ought to be formed with the suffix *kyap*. [The response is: But surely, in the case of a wife...

Since the word *bhāryā* is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), the restriction "not when it is a technical term" (*asaṃjñāyām*) in the rule *bhṛño'saṃjñāyām* is redundant; therefore, he says: "because it is excluded from being a technical term. He resolves this by saying: "True. In the root *ḍu bhṛñ* (meaning 'to support' and 'to nourish') belonging to the *juhotyādi* class, there is a short vowel, and it is marked with the indicatory letters *ḍ* and *ñ*.

The root *bhṛ*—meaning "to threaten" (*bhartsane*) and also "to support" (*bharaṇe*)—is long-voweled (*dīrghānta*) in the *kyādigaṇa*. From these two roots, by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*, only the suffix *ṇyat* is applied; however, the suffix *kyap* is applied only to the root *bharati*. The root *bhṛñ*—meaning "to support" (*bharaṇe*)—is short-voweled (*hrasvānta*) and marked with the *ñit* indicator in the *bhvādigaṇa*. It is precisely this [root] that [is used] in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*).

The intention is that in the rule *samajaniṣade'tra* and in the rule *bhṛño'saṃjñāyām*, there is the inclusion [of the root] by the mention of *bhṛñ*, but not of *ḍubhṛñ* belonging to the *jauhotyādi* class, nor of the long-voweled [root] *bhṛ* belonging to the *kraiyādi* class which lacks an anubandha. Why is this so? To this he says: "by that which has that as its anubandha" (*tadanubandhaka*).
The meaning is that this is according to the *paribhāṣā* rule: "When a term with a specific *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one without that *anubandha*.

This is the reason for the absence of the *kyap* suffix after the root *bhr̥*. It should be understood that the *kyap* suffix does not apply here because the root belonging to the *kr̥yādika* class ends in a long vowel (*dīrgha*).

(682) *mṛjervibhāṣā* |3|1|113|. Regarding the rule *mṛjervibhāṣā*, he gives an example for the alternative (*pakṣa*) involving the suffix *kyap*: *mṛjya*. Because the suffix is marked with *k* (*kit*), there is no *guṇa* substitution. (683) *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* |7|3|52|.

The rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* is stated without case-endings (*avibhaktika*). However, there is no application of the respective correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) between *cajoh* and *ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, because the substitution of *kutva* for *ja* is explicitly taught in the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* when the suffix *ghañ* follows.

(684) *rājasūya-sūrya-mṛṣodya-rucya-kupya-kṛṣṭapacya-avyathyāḥ* || 3.1.114 || *rājasūya*: [The word *rājasūya* is derived from *rājan* with the suffix *kyap*. "By a king" (*rājñā*) means by a Kṣatriya. "Pressing" (*abhiṣava*) refers to the crushing of Soma stalks with stones for the purpose of extracting the juice; it is through this process that [the sacrifice is performed].
The grammatical connection is that the specific sacrifice called *rājasūya* is to be performed. Or else:

the word "king" (*rājan*) is intended to refer to *soma*, which consists of a particular creeper, because it is well-known in such usages as "he buys the king" (*rājānaṃ krīṇāti*). That king is pressed—that is, extracted here.

The construction is "rājasūya" [derived] by the etymological analysis (vyutpatti) "a specific sacrifice" (yajñaviśeṣe). One might ask: since the governing rule is "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (kartari kṛt), how can there be an etymological derivation based on the locus (adhikaraṇa)? To this he says: "the suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of the locus. Why is that? He says: "because of an irregular formation" (nipātanāt). But [one might object]: if the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *ṣuñ*...

How is the vowel long? Since the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* applies to the formation of *kṛt* suffixes, he says: "The lengthening occurs by way of *nipātana* (irregularity). The term "*nipātanāt*" connects with both cases. Regarding "*utvam*" (the substitution of *u*), one should understand that when *rapara* (with *r* as the subsequent element) is applied, the lengthening also occurs by the rule *hali ca*. As for the word *mṛṣodyam*: [it is formed from *mṛṣā* + *vada* + *ya*, where the irregularity accounts for the form].

Regarding "kyapi ṭhvacisvapīti saṃprasāraṇam": the meaning is that from the root *ruc*, with the suffix *kyap*, the form "rocya" is produced according to the rule "vacisvapi... [Pāṇini 6.1.15]. Regarding "guper": the meaning is that from the root *gup*, the suffix *kyap* is applied, and the substitution of the letter *k* for the initial letter of the stem is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) when it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Wealth consisting of gold and silver is to be known as *kupya* (base metal/precious goods). And thus, after stating "gold and silver, whether wrought or unwrought," Amara says: "other than those two, that is *kupya*. Regarding the term *kṛṣṭa*: the meaning is that those which ripen or bear fruit spontaneously in a ploughed area are called *kṛṣṭapacya*.

Regarding "karmakartari": here the meaning is that the suffix *kyap* occurs when the object itself acts as the agent; this is the sense because of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding "śuddhe tu": in the case of the primary object (*mukhya-karman*), however, the form *kṛṣṭapākya* arises through the application of *ṇyat*, the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-vṛddhi*), and the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*. Regarding *avyathya*: here, due to a formal irregularity, it is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
The sense is "kyap.

(685) *bhidyo-dhyau nade* | 3|1|115|. Regarding *bhidya* and *udhya* in the sense of a river: [the rule] *kyap* [applies]. It is stated that [these forms] are irregularly derived (*nipātita*) in the sense of a specific type of river when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
The remainder [of the rule].

(686) *puṣya-siddhyau nakṣatre* |3|1|116|. [The words] *puṣya* and *siddhya* [are] irregularly formed (*nipātyete*); this is the remainder [of the rule]. The meaning is that they are used when a specific lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is to be understood.

(687) *vipūyavinīyajityā muñjakalkahaliṣu* || 3.1.117 || The forms *vipūya*, *vinīya*, and *jitya*—ending in the suffix *kyap*—are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when used respectively with *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali*. Thus it is said: "by the rule beginning with *pūṅ*" [Pāṇini 3.1.115].
The intention is that, due to its association with *ny* and other roots, only the root *pū* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class is understood here.
The explanation of the word *hali* is given as "ploughed" (*kṛṣṭa*). (688) *pratyapibhyāṃ grahe* 3.1.118.

"By [the rule] *pratyapibhyāṃ graheḥ* in the Veda"—this is a *vārttika*, but it has been inserted into the *sūtra* by the author of the *vṛtti*. To the question, "For what purpose is this Vedic usage presented here?", he says: "But in common usage (*loke*), however..."

(689) *padā'svairibāhyāpakṣyeṣu ca* |3|1|119|. The meaning is that the suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *grah* when the senses of "word" (*pada*), "not independent" (*asvairin*), "external" (*bāhya*), or "belonging to a faction" (*pakṣya*) are intended. For example: *avagṛhyaṃ padaṃ* or *pragṛhyaṃ padaṃ* ("a word to be separated" or "a word to be joined"), referring to a compound word.

In the *Prātiśākhya*, it is well known that "avagraha" is the pause between intermediate words, while "pragṛhya" refers to a word such as "pra" followed by "ava," which is marked with the particle "iti. Furthermore, the example from the rule "īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam" is also termed "pragṛhya."

(690) *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ* |3|1|120|. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*). Since the root *kṛ* ends in *ṛ*, the suffix *ṇyat* would apply to it invariably; and since the root *vṛṣ* has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*), the suffix *kyap* would apply to it invariably. This rule provides an option (*vibhāṣā*) for the application of *kyap*.
Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): the meaning is that a specific rule will be stated for the alternative case where the suffix *kyap* does not apply.
(691) *ṛhalorṇyat* | Pāṇini 3.1.124. The genitive case here has the sense of the ablative. Thus he says: "after a root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel."

(692) *yugyaṃ ca patre* |3|1|121|. The word *yugya*, ending in the suffix *kyap*, is an irregular formation (*nipātana*). It is an exception to [the application of] the suffix *ṇyat*. For example: *yugyo gauḥ* ("a yoke-ox"). The meaning is "one to be yoked by means of a cart, etc. The change of *g* to *k* (*kutva*) occurs due to this irregular formation (*nipātana*).

*Patram* means "a vehicle. In the sense of "that by which they fly" (*patanti*) or "go" (*gacchanti*), the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied according to the rule *dāmnīśas-* etc., to form the word *patra*. If the suffix *ṇyat* were used instead, the form would be *yogya*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.122) *Amāvāsyā* [is formed] optionally when the word *danta* follows.

"Amāvasyadaḥ" [is formed] by means of the locative case; this is obtained through the rule of irregular derivation (nipātana). "Saha" is the explanation of the word "ama. Although the rule "ṛhaloṇyaḥ" was already explained previously in its proper context, it is cited again here following the sequence of the sūtras. "Kutvam" refers to the substitution of the guttural *k* for the dental *t*.

The intention is that by the rule *pacerṇyati ṭhcajoḥ kahi*, there is the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *k*). Now, one might object: "The rule *pāṇau sṛjerṇyaḥ* is redundant, since [the desired form] is already established by *ṛhalorṇyat*"; to this he replies:
"of that which is characterized by having a vowel *ṛ* as its penultimate. This refers to the exception to *ṇyat* provided by the rule *ṛdupadāccākḷpicṛteḥ*.

*Kyapa* has the sense of "one who causes suffering" (*bādhanāthamatityarthaḥ*). Regarding *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ*: when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, there is the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* according to the rule *ṭhcajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ*. The phrase *samavapūrvācca* is a Vārttika; the remainder of the rule is *sṛjerṇyaḥ*.

(694) *na kvādeḥ* |7|3|59|. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has *ku-* as its initial. The rule *cajoḥ kuḥ* is understood [to apply here]. Thus he says: "of *kvādi*"—meaning "of that which begins with the *ka*-class (*kavarga*) of consonants. However, the author of the Vārttika [states] regarding *cajoḥ*: [the following applies].
In the sūtra *ku-ghṛṇṇyatoḥ*, it is supplemented by the phrase *niṣṭhāyām aniṭaḥ*. Thus, the resulting meaning is:

"When the suffix *ṇyat* follows, there shall be a *ku* (guttural) substitute for the *ca* and *ja* that are parts of a verbal root which is *aniṭ* (lacking an *iṭ* augment) in the *niṣṭhā* [past participles]. Similarly, the sūtra *na kvādeḥ* is supplemented by the phrase *ajivrajyośca*.

The meaning is that he rejected [the inclusion of] the mention of *yāca*, *ruca*, and *graha* in the rule *sūtraṃ ṭhyajayācarucapravacarcaśca*, stating that such a mention need not be made. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By that. According to the view of the Sūtra, there would be *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) for roots such as *arji* and *arji* when followed by the suffix *ṇya*, because of the prohibition "not for *kvādi* [roots]."

The meaning is that [the rule] does not apply there. Having thus stated the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) according to the view of the Sūtra, he states the under-extension (*avyāpti*): "of *gruc*, *gluc*, *gluñc*, and so forth.
Even though these belong to the *ka*-class (*kavarga*), in forms such as *grokyam* derived from the suffix *ṇyat*, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g* for *j*) would certainly be desired.

The point is that, according to the view of the Vārttika, the prohibition "not after *kvādi*" has been rejected; however, according to the view of the Sūtra, because of the prohibition "not after *kvādi*," the substitution of *ku*-tva (gutturalization) would undesirably apply in cases such as *gokya*, resulting in an instance of under-extension (*avyāpti*). Now, one might object that this Vārttika could even yield a contrary result.

He raises an objection, saying: "But because it is accepted [by all], it must indeed be adopted; for when there is a contradiction, one can simply state an option (*vikalpa*). This refers to the phrase "even though, according to the view of the Sūtra... He refutes this, saying: "nevertheless... and "according to the subsequent [view]..."; for this is the established convention of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇasamaya*).
(695) *ajivrajyośca* | 7|3|60| The rule beginning with *ajivrajayośca* is clear. (696) *vañcergatau* | 7|3|63| [The substitution of *aṭ* for *at* occurs after the root *vañc* when it means "motion"].

The root *vañc* means "to go. The phrase "there is no *kutva*" is a supplement to the rule. The intention is that this is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ku* from the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* and the term *na* from the rule *na kvādeḥ*.

(697) *ṇya* [is added] in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) [Pāṇini 3.3.170]. Regarding *ṇya* in the sense of necessity: "there is no *kutva*"—this is a supplement to the rule. The meaning is that when the suffix *ṇya* occurs in the sense of necessity, the substitution of *ku* for *c* and *j* (as prescribed by *ṭhcajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*) does not take place.

(698) *yajayācarucapravacarcaśca* | Pāṇini 7.3.66. [The rule states: "In the case of *yaj*, *yāc*, *ruc*, *pravac*, and *ṛc*, there is no *kutva* [change] before the suffix *ṇya*. This is a supplement to the sūtra. From the *dvandva* compound of *yaj*, *yā*, *ruc*, *pravac*, and *ṛc*, the genitive case is understood. For these roots, when followed by the suffix *ṇya*, [the rule regarding] *ca-ja* [changing to *ku*] does not apply.

The meaning is that there is no substitution of *k* for *gh* by the rule "ghiṇnyatoḥ. Now, one might ask: how is the suffix *ṇyat* applied in the word *arcyam*, given that the rule "ṛdupadhāccā'klṛpicṛteḥ" prescribes *ṇyat* as an exception (*apavāda*) to the condition of having *ṛ* as a penultimate vowel? To this, he says: "even though it has *ṛ* as a penultimate vowel. [This refers to the inclusion of] "tyaji-pūjyośca."
The remainder [of the rule] is: "there is no *kutva* in the case of the suffix *ṇya*.

(699) *vaco'śabdasaṃjñāyām* | 7|3|67|. Regarding *vaco'śabdasaṃjñāyām*: there is no *kutva* for the root *vac* when followed by the suffix *ṇya*, provided it does not denote a technical grammatical term (*śabdasaṃjñā*).

The meaning is "having excluded. Regarding the word "vācyam" (to be expressed), the word "vastu" (thing) is to be understood as the ellipsis. He states the purpose of the rule "aśabda-saṃjñāyām" (except when it is a technical grammatical term): "But in the case of what is called a 'word,' the sentence [is required]. The intention is that this [term] "vākya" is a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*), according to the definition "a sentence consists of one finite verb. However, in the case of the word "apravācyam,"...

Even though it is a specific designation for a particular text, this is not a prohibition of the prohibition of *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *g*), because in the rule *yajayāca...* the term *pravaca* is specifically mentioned; furthermore, the condition "not being a technical name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) finds its scope elsewhere than in the case of *pra-vac*. It is precisely with this intention that [the form] *pravācyam* [is cited].
It was stated previously that this refers to a "particular type of literary work" (*granthaviśeṣa*).
(700) *prayojya* and *niyojya* [are formed] in the sense of "capable" (*śakyārthe*). 7.3.68.
*prayojya-niyojyau*. In the sense of "capable," the suffix *ṇya* is applied, and the absence of *kvip* is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*). [The root is] *śak*.

Since the suffix *liṅ* (and by extension the *kṛtya* suffixes) is prescribed in the sense of "possibility" (*śakya*) as well as in the sense of "injunction" (*vidhi*), a word ending in the suffix *ṇyat* can also have the meaning of "possibility.
(Pāṇini 7.3.69) *bhojyaṃ bhakṣye*: [The word *bhojya* is formed with the suffix *ṇyat*] in the sense of "that which is fit to be eaten" (*bhakṣya*).

The word *bhojyam* is derived from the root *bhuja* with the suffix *ṇyat*. When the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of "that which is to be eaten" (*bhakṣye*), the absence of the *kutva* change (the substitution of *gh* for *bh*) is established as a *nipātana* (irregularity). This was incidental. Now, to the subject at hand: "and after the roots *lap* and *dambh*" (*lapidabhibhyāṃ ca*).
This is a *vārttika* belonging to the rule *ṛhalorṇyad*. It concerns that which was previously obtained by the rule *poradupadhāt*.
(702) *orāvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.135). Regarding the suffix *ṇyat*, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to that which follows from *yataḥ*.
In the case of *lāvyaṃ* and *pāvyaṃ*, [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied; then, by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] occurs, and [the form becomes] *vāntaḥ*.
The term *yī* refers to the substitute *yī*.
(703) *āsuyuvapirapiḷapaṭṭrapicamaśca* | [Pāṇini 3.1.26] This is a collective dvandva compound consisting of the roots *ā-su*, *yu*, *vapi*, *rapi*, *ṭrap*, and *cam*.
The word "ṭhṇya" is the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding "āsāvya," the intention is that it refers to the root *suñ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. (704) *anāyyo'nitye* |3|1|127|.
In the rule *anāyyo'nitye*, the division is *anitye*. It refers specifically to a particular *dakṣiṇāgni* fire.

This is a *vārttika*. Regarding the phrase "for he" (*sa hi*): the meaning is that the *dakṣiṇāgni* is indeed brought forth (*praṇīyate*) from the *gārhapatya* fire and others daily for the sake of the *agnihotra*.
By this, the meaning of the root *nī-* preceded by the prefix *ā-* has been stated. And [the phrase] "and it is non-eternal" (*anityaśca*).
The meaning is that, like the *gārhapatya* fire, there is an absence of constant maintenance (*nityadhāraṇā*). Thus he says: "constantly" (*satatam*).

The sense is: because of the absence of constant maintenance. Regarding the *dakṣiṇāgni*, it is stated in the *Kalpasūtras* that once its specific ritual function has been completed, it becomes a worldly fire: "When the rite has ceased, it is a worldly [fire]."

"It is accomplished here. Consequently, it should be understood that because of its repeated re-establishment (*praṇayana*), the Dakṣiṇāgni is non-eternal (*anitya*). Although the Āhavanīya fire is also re-established repeatedly, nevertheless, according to the Vārttika, the term refers specifically to the "Dakṣiṇā" fire; thus, the meaning is that the Āhavanīya is not included.

By the mention of a specific distinction, it is indicated that the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) is not included here under the category of fires to be maintained perpetually (*nityadhāraṇa*), because for those who have attained prosperity (*gataśrī*), even the *dakṣiṇāgni* must be maintained perpetually, according to the scriptural statement: "For one who has attained prosperity, the fires are to be maintained perpetually. Enough of this prolixity. [The fire] brought from the household of a Vaiśya...

Thus, with reference to the *dakṣiṇāgni*, it is heard in scripture: "One should fetch this [fire] every single day from the household of a Vaiśya. The point is that when such a *dakṣiṇāgni* is to be designated, the word *āneya* alone [is used].
(705) *praṇāyyo 'saṃmatī* |3|1|128|. Regarding *praṇāyyo 'saṃmatī*: when it refers to a woman who is not to be approached (*agamyā*), the form *praṇāyya* is established by nipātana.
In that context, he explains the word *saṃmati*, which is a portion of the compound *asaṃmati*.

"Being the object of affection. And since that is dependent upon action, he says: "the operation of action. Likewise, "attachment" means approval regarding enjoyments—that is, the experience of pleasure and pain. Since such approval does not exist, it is called "disapproval" (*asaṃmati*).
The result is *praṇāyyaś coraḥ* ("a thief who is not to be won over"). In the suffix *ṇyat*, there is *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel] and the substitution of *āy*.

(706) Pāṇini 3.1.129: *pāyyasāṃnāyyanikāyyadhāyyā mānahavirnivāsasāmidhenīṣu* ("The forms *pāyya*, *sāṃnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* are derived with the suffix *ṇyat* when they mean 'measure', 'oblation', 'dwelling', and 'verse for kindling the fire', respectively").

*pāyya*, *sāṃnāyya*, *nikāyya*, *dhāyya*—from these, the nominative plural follows from a *dvandva* compound. *Māna*, *havis*, *nivāsa*, *sāmidhenī*—from these, the locative follows from a *dvandva* compound. When the meanings of "measure" (*māna*) and so forth are to be understood, *pāyya* and the others are prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātana*) in their respective order.

The meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *mā* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and the substitution of *pa* for the initial *ma* of the root is prescribed by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).

Regarding the word "ātaḥ": when the suffix *ṇyat* is added to the root *mī*, the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the radical *ī*] according to the rule *mīnāti-ātvam*, and then the augment *yuk* is applied by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*. Regarding the word "ṇyat": it is prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātana*) in the sense of the object (*karman*) after the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *sam*.

This is the meaning. Regarding "āy-ādeśa" (the substitution of *āy*): the grammatical connection is that when [the suffix] *san* is applied, the substitution of *āy* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding "nivāsa" (dwelling): the meaning is that it belongs to the *kuśalādi* group. Regarding "adhikaraṇe" (in the sense of location): the grammatical connection is that the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed as an irregularity after the root *ci*. [The form] "āyi" [is derived accordingly].

The grammatical connection is as follows: because the substitution of *ā* (āy-ādeśa) is not otherwise applicable due to the absence of the suffix *acaḥ paraka*, it is prescribed here by way of a nipātana (irregular formation). "Dhāyyā" refers to a *ṛc* (verse); the meaning is that the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for the root *dhā* when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
The *sāmidhenīs* are specific verses used for the purpose of placing fuel on the fire (*samid-ādhāna*). In that context, [the verse] beginning with "samidhyamāno... [is cited].
The verse beginning with "pṛthupājā amartyaḥ" is well known as one to be inserted above the ṛc beginning with "adhvare.

(707) Regarding the rule *kratau kuṇḍapāyyasaṃcāyyau* 3.1.130: in the sense of a sacrifice (*kratu*), the forms *kuṇḍapāyya* and *saṃcāyya* are irregularly derived (*nipātita*). When a specific sacrifice is intended, these two are thus prescribed. [The derivation of] *kuṇḍapāyya* is by means of the word *kuṇḍena*.
The meaning is "with ladles provided with handles" (*atsarukaiścamasaiḥ*). The singular number is used in a general sense.

The Vedic scripture states: "That which they consume with ladles provided with handles is their *kuṇḍa*. Thus, *kuṇḍapāyya* refers to a specific sacrificial session (*satra*) consisting of a ritual (*ṛtu*). [This occurs] when the word ending in the third case, *kuṇḍena*, is used as an upapada.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). By the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*, the augment *yuk* is added after a stem ending in long *ā*.

Thus, the form *saṃcāyyaḥ* is derived; the meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *ciñ* preceded by the prefix *sam* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), and the substitution of *āy* for *i* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
A specific sacrifice named *saṃcāyya* is to be sought in certain Vedic recensions (*śākhā*).

(708) *agnau paricāyyopacāyyasamūhyāḥ* |3|1|131|. When "fire" (*agni*) is the object to be understood, the words *paricāyya*, *upacāyya*, and *samūhya* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). The word *agni* here refers to a specific altar (*sthaṇḍila*) constructed with bricks, [not one made] with clay.
"Since it is built with water and fire, why then is it called 'Agni'?

Because he builds it with the meters (chandas), and the meters are indeed fires, therefore it is called 'Agni'. Furthermore, this earth is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara; because he builds it with clay, therefore it is called 'Agni'."

And because of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). He says this: "by the holding of fire" (*agnidhāraṇā*). In that context, from the roots *ci* preceded by *pari* and *upa*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied with the *kṛt* affix *karṇi*, and the substitution of *āy* is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). But for *vah* preceded by *sam*, when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), vowel-contraction (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and lengthening are prescribed as irregularities. [As it is said: "One should pile the *samūhya*."

In the Taittirīya Śruti, it is stated: "One desiring cattle should pile the *paricāyya*; one desiring a village should pile the *samūhya*. Thus, *paricāyya* and *samūhya* are well-known [names for types of fire-altars]. However, the fire-altar called *upacāyya* must be sought in some other recensional branch (*śākhā*). Furthermore, the terms *citya* and *agnicityā* [are also included in this rule]. (709) Pāṇini 3.1.132.

Regarding *citya* and *agnicityā*: this is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *cityaḥ* and *agnicityā*. These two forms are irregularly derived (*nipātyete*) with reference to the root *ci*. In the case of *cityo 'gniḥ*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *ci* in the sense of the object (*karman*), and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*tuk*) is also irregularly prescribed.

In the case of *agneścayaḥ*, when the word *agni* ending in the genitive case is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *ci*, and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*tuk*) is likewise irregularly prescribed.
"Femininity" [is derived] from the world. Although it was already explained under the rule "ṭhpraiṣātisarge," it is recalled here.

Regarding "gamyam": this is the suffix *kyap*, which is an exception to the suffix *ṇyat* prescribed by the rule "poradupadhāt. Now, one might object: since the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed generally for both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), they would be established even in cases other than "commanding" (*praiṣa*) and so forth.

The rule for the *kṛtya* suffixes [denoting obligation] in the context of commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth would otherwise be redundant; for in the absence of such commands, the *kṛtya* suffixes have already fulfilled their purpose by applying to the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Therefore, the meaning is that the rule for *kṛtya* suffixes is stated again in order to prevent the sublation of those *kṛtya* suffixes by the *loṭ* suffix when they occur in commands and the like. But [an objection may be raised]: "However..."

Since the prohibition of the *kṛtya* suffixes by the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of commands and so forth would not occur by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpavidhi*) alone, he says: "after the section on feminine endings. This means "after the rule *striyāṃ ktin*" (Pāṇini 3.3.94). The *Mahābhāṣya* states: "The rule of non-identity of form applies prior to the section on feminine endings. Now, [an objection]: [The text provided ends here.]

Alternatively, since the rule for feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*) follows [the section on] *asarūpa* (non-identical suffixes), if that were not operative, the general rule "after roots ending in *ṣit* or *bhidādi*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the feminine" (*ṣidbhidādibhyo 'ṅ*) would permanently override the *ktin* suffix prescribed by the general rule "after a root ending in a consonant, *ktin* is applied in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ktin*). Consequently, forms such as *kṣamā* (patience) for *kṣānti*, and *bhidā* (cleaving) for *bhitir*, would not be possible.

It might be so; therefore, he says: "not in some cases. Since the word "in some cases" (*kvacit*) is not restricted, he says: "by that. "Established" (*siddham*): the meaning is that there is a restriction of the rule regarding non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) in these instances. In this matter, the commentary itself is the only refuge. [The rule] *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* has been explained previously.

It is reminded [of this] with the intention of specifying a particular case. It was stated previously that the particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣa*) the word *liṅ* from the rule *liṅyadi*. Now, one might object: since the *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* are already established by the general rule even in the sense of fitness (*arha*), the re-statement of them in this context is redundant; therefore, he says: "it sublates the *liṅ*."
If only "in the sense of *arha* (fitness)" were stated, then, because of the attraction by the particle *ca*, the rule for the optative (*liṅ*) alone would apply in the sense of *arha*;

consequently, there would be no rule for the gerundives (*kṛtya*) and the agentive suffix *tṛc* in the sense of *arha*, since the optative specifically prescribed for *arha* would sublate them, and the gerundives and *tṛc* would already have their purpose fulfilled in cases other than *arha*. However, as for the rule regarding alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), [it does not apply here].

It has already been stated that [the application of the suffixes] does not proceed beyond the section on feminine endings (*stryadhikāra*). Therefore, the meaning is that this rule for *kṛtya* and *tṛc* suffixes is intended so that there may be no sublation of the masculine gender marker (*liṅga*).
(710) *bhavyageyapravacanīyopasthānīyajanyāplāvyāpātyā vā* | Pāṇini 3.4.68.

Regarding the rule *bhavyageya-kartari vā*: the term *kartari*, which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the rule *kartari kṛt*, is connected with the word *vā*. Thus, it results that these [terms] are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), but not otherwise. Since "otherwise" (*anyatra*) has not been specifically defined there, he says: "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*). This also applies elsewhere.

Not everywhere; rather, by the rule "tayoḥ eva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ," it is meant that these *kṛtya* suffixes are to be understood as denoting the object (*karman*) when used with transitive verbs, and denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*) when used with intransitive verbs.
In the rule "tayoḥ eva kṛtya," [the word] "sakarmakebhyaḥ" (from transitive verbs) is supplied from the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca."

The sense is that [the rule] "after intransitive roots, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāva*)" continues [from the previous sūtra]. Regarding *bhavya*: when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *yat* is applied after a root ending in a vowel; alternatively, it means "that by which one is to be brought about.
