When denoting the action (*bhāva*), the suffix *yat* is applied. Regarding *geyaḥ sāmnām ayam*: the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *gā* (to sing) in the sense of the agent. By the rule "īdyati" (Pāṇini 6.4.65), the long *ī* of the stem is replaced by *ī*. Then the *guṇa* substitution occurs. [This applies] to the *sāman*s.

Because the objects (*karman*) are not expressed [by the suffix], the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix; because the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, the nominative (*prathamā*) is used. [In the example] "the *sāman* is to be sung by him" (*geyam sāma anena*), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) because the root is transitive, and not in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), since the agent is not expressed; thus, the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) is used. However, the genitive in connection with a *kṛt* suffix occurs when the agent is expressed in connection with a *kṛtya* suffix.

It is optional, because of the rule stating, "The *kṛtya* suffixes may optionally [denote] the agent. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": "The teacher is to be propounded (*pravacanīya*) of the Veda," meaning he is the expounder (*pravaktṛ*). Here, the suffix *anīyar* denotes the agent.
Alternatively, one may say, "The Veda is to be propounded by the teacher" (*pravacanīyo vedo guruṇā*). Or: "The disciple is to be attended upon (*upasthānīya*) by the teacher."

"He is to be attended upon" (*upasthānīya*) means he is a teacher (*guru*) [to the disciple]. Or: "He is one who is born" (*janya*); the meaning is that he is born (*jāyate*). Or: "He is one by whom [the lineage] is produced" (*janyamanena*). "He floats" (*āplavate*) means he is "one who is to be made to float" (*āplāvya*); the suffix *ṇyat* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *orāvaśyake*. Or: "He is one by whom [the disciple] is made to float" (*āplāvyamanena*). "He falls toward" (*āpatati*) means he is "one who is to be caused to fall" (*āpātya*).

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the agent by the rule *ṭhṛhalo’r*. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *āp* with the suffix *ktyap*. The rule *śaki liṅ ca* has also been explained previously; however, it is presented here according to the sequence of the sūtras due to the intention to state specific details.

Now, one might object that the prescription of the *kṛtya* suffixes, drawn over here by the particle *ca*, is redundant, since [the suffixes] apply both when there is ability (*śakti*) and when there is inability (*aśakti*).

Since it is already established that *kṛtya* affixes apply generally to both the agent (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), even when capacity (*śakti*) is present, [the author] says: "The *liṅ* would sublate. If only "in the sense of capacity (*śaki*), the *liṅ*" were stated, then in the case of capacity, the *liṅ*—being specifically prescribed—would sublate the *kṛtyas*; whereas in the case of incapacity, the *kṛtyas* [would apply].
The sense is that [the rule] has already achieved its purpose; moreover, it has already been stated that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*).

Regarding the term "for the sake of brevity" (*lāghavāt*): here, by the mere presence of the particle *ca*, it is possible to indicate that the *vāsarūpa* rule is non-mandatory (*anitya*) after the section on feminine suffixes; therefore, [the author uses] "in the case of command and permission" (*praiṣātisarge*).

The sense is that there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) if one were to rely on the indication [of this rule] by the inclusion of *kṛtya* in the *sūtra* "the *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc*" (*ṭharhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*), as well as by the inclusion of *kṛtya-tṛc* in the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc*. Thus ends the section on *kṛtya* formations.
Thus ends the section on *kṛtya* formations in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the *rkyādi* roots. Next, the verbal roots with the *śnā* vikaraṇa are described. Regarding the root *ḍu krīñ*:
(Pāṇini 3.1.81) "After the roots beginning with *krī*, the suffix *śnā* [is applied]."

*rkyādibhyaḥ śnā*: When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expressing the agent follows, the *śnā* affix occurs after roots beginning with *krī*, in the sense of their own meaning (*svārthe*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*. Thus, [from *krī* we derive] *krīṇāti*. The intention is that because the *śnā* affix is a *sārvadhātuka* ending in a non-pit letter (*apit*), it is marked as *ṅit*; consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ī*. *Ī*.

Regarding "halyaghoḥ": the sense is that there is the substitution of *ī* before a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*. When *krī* is followed by *nā* and *jhi*, one might suspect the application of *ī* according to the rule "halyaghoḥ"; therefore, he says: "prior to the substitution of *ī*. [He adds] "because it is obligatory" (*nityatvāt*), meaning that the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*) applies whether the substitution of *ī* has been performed or not.

The meaning is "due to the application [of the rule]. Similarly regarding *jhasya*: when *krī-ṇā-jha* is situated, the meaning is that the substitution of *at* (by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*) also occurs prior to the substitution of *ī*. Regarding *tataḥ*:

the meaning is after both the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*) and the substitution of *at*. [This applies] before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel that is marked with *k* or *ṅ*.
There is elision of the *ā* of the suffix *śnā*. Considering that, according to the rule of Bhāradvāja, there is an option for the augment *iṭ* in the case of *thal*, he says:
*cikrayitha* and *cikretha*. [He also says] *cikriyiva*; the intention is that the augment *iṭ* is applied here by the rule of the *krādi* group.
[Imperative: *krīṇātu*, *krīṇīhi*. [Aorist: *akrīṇāt*, *akrīṇīta*. [Optative: *krīṇīyāt*, *krīṇīta*.

(382) *stanbhu-satumbhu-skambhu-skunbhu-skuñ-bhyaḥ śnuś-ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.82]. These are from the Sūtras. It should also be understood that they have a penultimate *n*. Regarding "elision of *n*" (*nalopa*), the intention is that this occurs by the rule *aniditām* [6.4.24]. As for the form *viṣṭabhnoti*, [the suffix *śnu* is applied] by the rule *stanbheḥ* [8.3.67].
Regarding *avaṣṭabhnoti*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "also in the case of *ava*, *ālambana*, and *vidūra*.
Regarding *avataṣṭambha*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "in the case of roots beginning with *sthā*, when preceded by *ava*, before an abhyāsa (reduplication). Regarding *vyaṣṭabhat*:
the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "prior to *sit*" (Pāṇini 8.3.65).
(383) *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* |3|1|83|.
When the suffix *śna* is replaced by *śānac* before the suffix *jha*, [the final vowel] is elided by the rule *ato heḥ*.
(384) *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* |7|3|80|. [The penultimate vowel of roots] beginning with *pū* is shortened.

Intending that "the short vowel of *pū* and others" applies, and that the condition "when a *śit* affix follows" from the rule *ṭhṣṭhivuklamucamām* is understood to carry over, he completes the sense by stating: "when a *śit* [affix] follows. Regarding *pavitā*:
the intention is that because it ends in the vowel *ū*, it is *seṭ* (possessing an *iṭ* augment). The root *stṛñ* means "to cover"; it is *seṭ*.
Regarding *tastaratuḥ*: even though the suffix is marked with *k* (indicating the absence of *guṇa*), the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*.
Regarding *staritā* and *starītā*: the optional lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *vṛto vā*. In the benedictive (*āśis*) mood, *stīryāt*:

after the substitution of *it* by the rule *añjateiddhātoḥ*, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* by *ra* (*raparatva*), the lengthening occurs by the rule *hali ca*. [The form] *stṛṣīṣṭa* [is derived from the root] *stṛ*.

This being the case, he says: "Regarding *liṅ* and *sic*, [the suffix] *iṭ* may optionally be long. He recalls the rule for the optional prohibition of lengthening—namely, *vṛto vā*—by stating: "not in *liṅ*" (*na liṅi*). This means that the lengthening of *iṭ* after roots ending in *vṛt* (and its synonyms) does not occur. Anticipating the objection that there might be *guṇa* substitution in the alternative case where *iṭ* is absent—as in *stṛṣīṣṭa*—he says: "and after *u*" (*uśca*).

"What is this? [The author asks. Regarding the form *astariṣṭām* (third person dual, imperfect, parasmaipada, root √*stṝ*, with the suffix *sic*), when the option for lengthening the *iṭ* augment is applicable by the rule "vṛto vā" (*Pāṇini 7.2.38*), he says:
"and when *sic*" (*sici ca*). Thus we have *astarīṣṭa* and *astariṣṭa*;
here the lengthening is by the rule "vṛto vā. As for *astīrṣṭa*, this is in the alternative where the *iṭ* augment is absent, according to the rule "liṅsicorātmanepadeṣu" (*Pāṇini 7.2.42*).

The intention is that there is lengthening by the rule *ṛta id dhali ca*. The root *kṛ* is used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*). Regarding *cakare*: the guṇa substitution occurs by the rule *ṛcchatyatṛṇām*. Regarding the root *vṛ* in the sense of choosing (*varaṇe*): regarding the phrase "in the benedictive" (*āśiṣi*), the meaning is that when *vṛ* + *yāt* is established, the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *utva* (change to *u*) by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*. In that case...

The point is that there is the inclusion of even those preceded by dentals, labials, and *ḷ*. It should be understood that after the substitution of *u* for the final *n* and the subsequent substitution of *r*, the lengthening occurs by the rule "hali ca. Regarding *variṣīṣṭa* and *pūrṣīṣṭa*:
the augment *iṭ* is optional by the rule "liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu. In the absence of *iṭ*, because the suffix is marked with *k* by the rule "uśca," there is an absence of *guṇa*.

The intention is that when *ut* is substituted and *ra* follows, there is lengthening by the rule "ṭhali ca" (Pāṇini 7.2.35). Regarding *avāriṣṭām*: the intention is that there is no lengthening of the *iṭ* augment by the rule "sici ca" (Pāṇini 7.2.40). Regarding *avariṣṭa* and *avarīṣṭa*: the intention is that there is an optional lengthening of the *iṭ* augment of the *sic* suffix by the rule "vṛto vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.38). Regarding *dudhavitha*—*dudhītha*.
The intention is that [the suffix] *iṭ* is optional by the rule "svarati-sūti-sūyati-dhūñ-ūditaḥ. The root *śṛ* (meaning 'to injure') is *seṭ*.

In the *ṇal* [perfect ending], it becomes *śaśāra*. Regarding the form *śa atus*, although there is *kitva* (the status of being a *kit*), the rule "ṛcchatyṛtām" would necessitate obligatory *guṇa*; to this he says: "śṛdṛprām. This is a *pākṣika* (optional) exception to *guṇa*.

When the shortening occurs, the meaning is that the *ṛ* vowel undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution, resulting in the letter *r*. Thus, *śaśaritha*. The root *pṛ* is treated like the root *śṛ*. Regarding the form *pūryāt* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the intention is that the substitution of *u* (by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*) takes place. Regarding the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing," he states [the following], considering the optional shortening prescribed by the rule *śṛdṛprāṃ hrasvo vā*.

*dadaratuḥ* and *dadratuḥ*: [from] the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go. *arāñcakāra*: because it possesses a heavy vowel (*gurumattva*) by virtue of being treated as having a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix *ām* is applied. Regarding the *laṅ* [aorist], he says: *ārṇāt*. [From] the root *jyā*, meaning "loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*). It is *aniṭ*.
When *jyā* is followed by *na*, the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), and the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) follows.
When it is established that [the word] *jināti* [is formed by this rule], [we apply] Pāṇini 6.4.2: *halaḥ*.

This [rule] occurs in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) because of its connection with the word *diś-* (direction). It is understood as "of what follows after a consonant" (*halaḥ parasya*). [This refers to] the rule *saṃprasāraṇasya* [which states that the substitution of a semivowel for a vowel takes place before a following vowel].

The word *sūtra* (the rule) follows. The term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*), is repeated here and then split. One instance, ending in the genitive of a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), connects with the word *halaḥ*; thus, "from a consonant that is a part of the stem" is obtained.
The second instance, however, ends in the genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) and is qualified by *saṃprasāraṇa*. This is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that (*tadanta-vidhi*).
The term "long vowel" (*dīrgha*) is understood to carry over from the rule "ṭhḍhralope.

Thus he says: "from a constituent part of the *aṅga*," and so forth. The examples are: *vītaḥ*, *śūnaḥ*, *jīnaḥ*. Why [is it said] "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? [Consider: *utaḥ*, *utavān*. Why "from a constituent part of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgāvayavāt*)? [Consider: *niruktam*.
What is the purpose of the phrase "of that which ends in this"? [The example is] *vidhyati*. Regarding the phrase "of these": the meaning is "of *vṛ*, *bhṛ*, *kṣī*, and *mṛ*.
The intention is that, according to the view that only *lū* and the others are included [in the group], and not *pū* and the others. [The root] *jñā* is used in the sense of "knowing.
He causes one to remember the substitution of *jā* for *jñā* when followed by a *śit* affix, citing the rule *jñājanorjā*. [This applies] when there is the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*).
The sense is that even though [the root] begins with *p*, it is not short (hrasva) due to the power of the explicit utterance of the vowel *ā*. The root *bandh* means "to bind";
it is *aniṭ* and has *n* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*). Regarding the form *bandhāti*, the sense is that there is elision of the *n* by the rule *aniditām*.
Considering that, according to the rule of Bhāradvāja, there is optionally *iṭ* in the *thal* suffix, he says: *babandhitha* or *babaddha*.

In *akṛtvā*, there is no elision (*lopa*) of the *n*. However, in the case where [the root] does not take the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ-pakṣe*), the *th* is changed to *dh* by the rule *ṭhjhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*. Regarding *bandhet*: this is the form with the suffix *tāsi*. The *t* is changed to *dh* by the rule *ṭhjhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*. Regarding *bhantsyati*: by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt*, the *b* becomes *bh* (the *bhaṣ* substitute). The *dh* is changed to *t* by the rule of *cartva* (the substitution of *c* for *ṭ*). Regarding *badhāna*: by the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau*.

Thus [is explained] the suffix *śānac*. Regarding *abhāntsīt*: there is the vṛddhi substitution conditioned by the stem ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā vṛddhiḥ*), and the substitution of *bhaṣ* [for the dental *s*].
Regarding *abānddhām*, fearing that the substitution of *bhaṣ* might apply because of the presence of the letter *s* following it, he says: "as in the previous case," etc.

But surely, once the elision of the *sic* suffix has occurred, would not the substitution of *bhaṣ* apply due to the presence of the letter *s*, by resorting to the principle of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*)?
Because [the rule] is difficult to ward off, he says: "by the characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). Regarding *abānddhām*:
by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*, the *t* is replaced by *dh*. [The root] *śranth* means "to loosen. Regarding "by the rule beginning with *śranthigranthi*":
by the rule *śranthigranthidambhisvañjīnāṃ liṭaḥ kittvaṃ vā*.

The meaning is "by another grammatical treatise. Regarding the phrase "even in this view": according to the opinion of Sudhākara—that this [augment] is also *kit*—the form in the third person singular (*prathamapuruṣa*) with the suffix *ṇal* is *śaśrātha*;
however, Mādhava states that in the first person singular (*uttamapuruṣa*) with the suffix *ṇal*, the forms are *śaśrāya* and *śaśraya*. In that regard:

Regarding the word "mūlam": the meaning is that there is no basis (mūla) for the textual passage beginning with "etvābhyāsalopau" and ending with "mādhava" under the view that [the suffix] is *ṭh*. The intention is that such a Vārttika is not observed, precisely because [the root *kuṣ*] is situated between two consonants (*saṃyuktahalmadhyastha*). *Kuṣa*...
In the case of extraction (*niṣkarṣe*): (386) *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.46.

After the prefix *nir*, [the augment *iṭ* is added] to the root *kuṣ*. The phrase "for an ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant, *iṭ* is added" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
[The rule] "svaratisūti... includes the word "vā" (or). Thus he says: "after *nir-* and *par-*.
[In the example] *nirakukṣat*, the sense is that *ksa* is substituted by the rule "śala" when the *iṭ* augment is absent. [The root] *aś* means eating;
[in the form] *āśā*, the sense is that there is no *nuṭ* augment because it lacks two consonants (*dvihaltva*). [The root] *iṣ* is used in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*); [the suffix] *tāsi*.

Anticipating the doubt that there might be an optional application of the *iṭ* augment in the case of *tīṣasaha*, he says: "In the rule *tīṣasaha*. By the force of the mention of *saha* together with *śap*, it is the root *sah* belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa that is indicated here.
Due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with that, only the root *iṣ* belonging to the Tudādigaṇa is understood.

The intended meaning is: "because of the commonality of the suffixal class (*vikaraṇa*) *a*. Regarding the phrase "from the root *iṣ* when followed by the letter *t*, due to the suffix *śyan*": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which the suffix *śyan* [originates].
The sense is that the rule "after *tīṣ*, *sah*, etc. does not apply to the root *iṣ* when it is listed as having the suffix *śyan* and when the letter *t* follows.
The meaning is that the optional inclusion of *iṭ* for the root *iṣṇāti* has been established as a result [of this rule]. Regarding *prūṣa* and *pluṣa*:

the first has a long vowel in its penultimate syllable. *Puṣ* means "to nourish. Regarding *poṣitā*: since only the root *puṣ* with the *śyan* conjugational suffix (*śyan-vikaraṇa*) is included among the roots that lack *iṭ* (aniṭ), the meaning is that this [root] takes *iṭ*.
This is because [the rule] "*puṣādi-dyautādi*" [is intended to apply only to those specific groups].

Because only those [roots] beginning with *puṣ* that take the *śyan* suffix are understood here, there is no *aṅ* [suffix]. [The root] *khac* is used in the sense of "the non-manifestation of what has already come into being. "Exceeding the time of birth" means that for one who is fit to be born in the tenth month or so, the birth occurs in the eleventh month or so. Regarding *khacñāti*: by the rule of *ścutva*, the *n* becomes *ñ*.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "this has been vomited out" (*vānto'yam*): some read the root as *khava* ending in a dental and labial (*-ṣ*), in the sense of "the manifestation of a being. (387) *cchÂavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.19.
*Ch-ś-ūṭh anunāsike ca*. This is a dual genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-dvivacana*) from the *dvandva* compound *ch-ś-au*.
The letter *ca* is indicated by the substitution of *ścu* for the preceding *tuka*, while the letter *k* remains as it is. The word *śūṭh* is the division [of the sūtra].
*Ś* and *ūṭh* form a collective *dvandva* in the nominative. By the particle *ca*, [the rule] applies to *kvip* and *jhal*.
The term *kṅti* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of that which has the augment *tuk*, etc. For example: *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*.

When the suffix *naṅ* is applied to the roots *vicch-* and *pracch-* according to the *Āuṇādikasūtras*, the augment *tuk* is inserted because it is an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation by the rule *che ca*.
Once *tuk* has been applied, the letter *ś* is substituted for the *ch* that possesses the *tuk*, and [the rule applies] to the *v*.
He illustrates *ūṭh*: "khau-n-āti. When the form *khav-n-āti* is established, *ūṭh* is substituted for the letter *v*;

since the marker *ṭh* indicates that the preceding vowel is included, there is a *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule "*eṅi pararūpam*" and "*edhatyūṭhasu*. Thus we have *khaunītaḥ*, *khaunanti*, and so forth. When *khav-n-ahi* is established, [the rule] "halaḥ" [applies].

Having raised the doubt that *śānac* might be the substitute [for *laṭ*] by the rule *śnaśśānajjhau*, he says: "Because of the posteriority of *śānac*. Regarding *heṭha*: the meaning is that the root *heṭh* also occurs in the sense of "manifestation after being. Regarding *graha* in the sense of "taking": it has a vowel (*a*) as its penultimate letter; because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, it is used in both voices (*ubhayapadī*) before *kit* and *ṅit* suffixes.
It causes one to recall the rule for *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution): "grahijyā... [Pāṇini 6.1.16]. Thus, we have *gṛhṇāti* and *gṛhṇīte*.

The intention is that because the suffix *śnā* has the marker *ṅ*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *ṛ* sound, resulting in the single substitute of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). When *ṇal* follows, after reduplication has occurred, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable by the rule "liṭyabhyāsasya" [Pāṇini 6.1.17], followed by the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratva*) and the subsequent substitution of *r* for the vowel (*raparatva*).

In the case of *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*), there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*). Thus: *jagrāha*. In forms beginning with *atus*, etc., because the rule *grahijyā...* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) applies due to its subsequent position, *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) is performed, after which reduplication and other operations follow. Thus: *jagṛhatuḥ*, *jagṛhuḥ*; *jagrahitha*; *jagṛhathuḥ*, *jagṛha*; *jagrāha* (or *jagraha*), *jagṛhiva*.

jagṛhima, jagṛhe, jagṛhāte, jagṛhire; jagṛhiṣe, jagṛhāthe, jagṛhidhve; jagṛhe, jagṛhivahe, jagṛhimahe. (388) *graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ* || 7.2.37 || [In the periphrastic perfect, the long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of the root √grah.]
In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, there is lengthening for the root *grah*. In the rule "grahaṭaḥ," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with the word "diś" (direction/limit).
From the rule "ārddhadhātukasyeṭ," the term "iṭ" is understood and is transformed into the genitive case;
likewise, from the rule "ekāca upadeśe'nudātāḥ," the term "ekāc" is understood. Thus he says: "ekāca."

And so forth. Why [is the condition] "having a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*) specified? To prevent [the rule from applying] in the case of *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*); as in *jāgrahitā*. Why [is the condition] "of that which is prescribed" (*vihitasya*) specified? As in *gṛhitam*. When the *ṇi*-suffix is elided, although it follows the root *grah*, because it was not originally prescribed [as such], there is no long vowel for *iṭ*. Nor [can it be argued that the lengthening is blocked] by the status of the elision of *ṇi* as being "as if it were present" (*sthānivadbhāva*).
It should be stated that *iṭ* follows the verbal root *grah*; the intention is that there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because [the suffix] has a long vowel and the marker *k*.
He states the forms for the *liṅ* (optative) and *taṅ* (ātmanepada): *grahīṣīṣṭa*. There is lengthening by the rule "graho 'liṭi.

However, the prohibition of lengthening for *iṭ* by the rule "na liṅi" does not apply here, because the word "vṛtaḥ" is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) in that context. [The form] *agrahīṣṭām*.
In *agrahīṣuḥ*, there is lengthening by the rule "graho 'liṭi" (Pāṇini 7.2.37). *Agrahīḥ* and so forth [are formed similarly]. Regarding the *luṅ* in the *ātmanepada*, he says:
*agrahīṣṭa*. There is lengthening by the rule "graho 'liṭi". *Agrahīṣata*, *agrahīṣṭhāḥ*, and so forth are easy to understand. Thus end the roots beginning with *ṛ* (the *ṛkyādayaḥ*).
Thus ends the section on *rkyādi* (roots beginning with *ṛk*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on the meaning of the *lakāras* within the *tiṅ*-endings. Next, the formation of the meanings of the *lakāras* is described.
(596) Pāṇini 3.2.112: *abhijñāvacane lṛṭ* ("The *lṛṭ* [future tense] is used when there is a statement of recognition").

The suffix *lṛṭ* is used after a verb when there is a word expressing "recollection" (*abhijñā*). "Recollection" (*abhijñā*) means memory; the analysis of the compound is: that by which something is spoken of or made known. Thus he says: "when there is a word signifying recollection as a co-occurring term" (*smṛtibodhini-upapade*). This means when a word that causes the awakening of memory is employed in proximity. The governing rule "in the past" (*bhūte*) is understood. [The rule applies] in the case of the immediate past (*adyatane*).

The phrase "laṅ for the non-contemporary past" (anadyatane laṅ) continues [from the previous rule]. Therefore, he says: "in the non-contemporary past" (bhūtānadyatane). Regarding "laṅ": the meaning is that this is an exception (apavāda) to the rule "laṅ for the non-contemporary past" (anadyatane laṅ). Regarding "smaryase" (you remember): the meaning is, "O Kṛṣṇa!
do you remember that we dwelt in Gokula? Here, the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) is the object (karman). [The word] "kṛtam" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: up to the point where [the speaker says], "Do you remember dwelling in Gokula?"—that is, "Do you remember?"—even when there is a connection with words that indicate memory, such as *budhyase* ("you perceive/remember"), the suffix *lṛṭ* (the future tense marker) is used. Now, one might object:
since verbs such as *budhyati* do not have "memory" (*smṛti*) as their primary meaning in the form of recollection, how can this be so?

Regarding the rule *lṛṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.15), he says: "teṣām api" ("even for those"). Since they ultimately convey the sense of memory (*smṛti*), the suffix *lṛṭ* occurs even in connection with them. The intention is that the mention of the word *vacana* ("statement") is precisely for this purpose.

(597) *na yadi* |3|2|113|. Regarding *na yadi*: considering that *yadi* is in the locative case, he says "in connection with *yadi*. He states that [the rule] does not apply. The meaning is that the *lṛṅ* [conditional mood] does not occur when there is a statement of recognition (*abhijñāvacana*). As for *abhijānāsi*: in the forest...
"Abhuñjamahi" means "since you remember.
(598) *Vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe* |3|2|114|.
[The word] "vibhāṣā" [means] "in the aforementioned scope"; that is to say, when a word signifying recognition (*abhijñā*) is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*).

"By way of the relationship between the characterized and the characteristic" means by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier. In this matter, the commentary itself is the refuge. Regarding "do you remember": the meaning is, "O Kṛṣṇa! Do you remember that we formerly lived in the forest, and there in that forest we tended the cows? Here, although the word *yat* (that) is to be understood [from the context], its...

There is no connection [of the suffix] because of the absence of *prayoga* (usage). "Clothing is the characteristic" (*vāso lakṣaṇam*)—the word "of movement" (*cāraṇasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The meaning is that there is an option regarding the *lṛṭ* suffix in both cases, since the connection with a statement of recognition (*abhijñāvacana*) is not distinguished [between them].

Nor should it be argued that the option [of the *lṛṭ* suffix] should apply only when there is a connection with *yad*, by virtue of the rule "optionally when there is an expectancy" (*vibhāṣā sāṅkākṣe*).
One must understand that this is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whether it be "if" (*yadi*) or "whether" (*cāyadi*); thus he says:

"even when joined with the word *yat*. Although the rule "the optative (*liṅ*) is used for what is not witnessed" (*parokṣe liṅ*) was explained previously, it is recalled here because of a specific intention to state a distinction; for the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).
To the question, "Since there is an absence of being out of sight (*parokṣatva*), how can this be the third person (*uttama-puruṣa*) of the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*)," he says:
"In the third person, however" (*citā*). "I slept" (*suptaḥ*): because of having slept, the meaning is "I spoke while asleep.
Here, from sleep, there is a distraction of consciousness (*citta-vikṣepa*). "I spoke much" (*bahu jagade*): because of his state of madness, I spoke much before him.
The meaning is "having gone to the world. Here, "unmāda" (insanity) refers to the distraction of the mind; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), "vyāsaṅga" (preoccupation) is included.
Regarding the phrase "in cases of absolute denial": this is for the sake of making the matter perceptible. "You lived among the Kaliṅgas"—this is the question [implied]:
"Therefore, you are not fit to live with me. [The rule applies] in the case of Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga.

The meaning is that this is based on the statement: "One who has traveled to Saurāṣṭra and Magadha, unless it was for a pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā), deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) again. Thus, the reply is: "I did not go to Kaliṅga. Regarding the word *kaliṅga*—
Because it denotes a specific region (*janapada-viśeṣa*), the plural number is used. In this context,
regarding a question concerning the place of residence following his arrival in that country,
one should understand that there is an absolute denial (*atyantāpahnava*) due to the concealment of the very journey that served as the cause [for the inquiry].

Regarding the sentence "You lived in Kaliṅga," it has been established in the section on *kārakas* that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not apply, because the designation of "object" (*karman*)— as prescribed by the rule "place, time, and state [are called object] when used with intransitive roots"— is only optional in such instances.

(599) *haśaśvator laṅ ca* | 3|2|116 | After the particles *ha* and *śaśvat*, the *laṅ* [L-affix] is also used [in addition to the *liṭ*]. This is clear. (600) *praśne cāsannakāle* | 3|2|117 | Also in the case of a question concerning recent time, the *laṅ* is used.

Regarding the rule for the suffix *liṅ* (the precative) in the sense of "question" (*praśne*) when the time is not immediate (*āsannakāle*): by the word "in a question" (*praśne*), the object of the question is intended;
thus he says, "that which is to be asked is the 'question' (*praśna*). After the word "in the sense of" (*arthe*), the remainder is "from a verbal root denoting present action" (*vartamānāddhātoḥ*).
"Non-immediate time" (*anāsannakālatva*) means being beyond the range of the speaker's visual perception. However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*),...
It has been stated that a time more than five years past is called "not proximate" (*anāsannakāla*).

(601) *Laṭ sme* | 3.2.118 | *Laṭ sme*. The word *sme* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). The meaning is that when used in conjunction with *sme*, the present tense suffix *laṭ* shall be employed even in cases where the conditional tense (*liṅ*) would otherwise be required.
Regarding the phrase *yajati sma*: the word *sma* indicates past time.
(Pāṇini 3.2.119) *Aparokṣe ca*: "And when [the action] is not witnessed. Thus, *evam sma*: it means "the father spoke thus."

(603) *nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane* |3|2|120|. [The particle *nanu* is used] when there is a reply to what has been asked. The meaning is that this is established through grammatical exposition (*vyākhyāna*). "Did you do it? is the question; "Indeed, I am doing it" (*nanu karomi*) is the answer. The sense is "I have done it. Here, *nanu* is used for addressing or calling attention (*saṃbodhane*).

(604) *nanvor vibhāṣā* | 3|2|121|. There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) with regard to the two [particles] *na* and *nu*. This refers to a *dvandva* compound of these two. Thus he says: "in the word *na* and in the word *nu*.
Regarding the phrase "it may be in the present tense (*laṭ*)," the word "past" (*bhūte*) is to be supplied as a remainder. "Did you do it? is the question; [the answer is] "no."
In response to "Did you do it?", one says, "I did not do it," or "I am indeed doing it," or "I have indeed done it. According to Amara, this is *ṭharkya*.
(605) *Puri luṅ cā'sme* 3.2.122.

*Puri luṅ cāsme*: the analysis is *ṭhasme*. *Purī* is an indeclinable ending in long *ā*; *purī* is its locative singular. The elision of the final vowel (*āllopa*) occurs due to the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) beginning with *ātaḥ*.
Regarding the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*), here the commentary itself is the only refuge. From *cāllaḍ*, it is thus: And so: [the rule applies].

The result is that "luṅ" and "laṭ" are optionally [used] (*veti*). Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): this means in the case where there is an absence of the aforementioned two conditions. Regarding "as it occurs" (*yathāprāptam*): when [the action] refers to the remote past (*anadyatana-parokṣa-bhūta*), the *liṭ* [is used];
however, when the quality of being remote (*parokṣatva*) is not intended to be expressed, the meaning is that *laṅ* [is used]. This begins from the rule "abhijñāvacane... (Pāṇini 3.2.112).

These rules up to this point belong to the second section (dvitīyaka) of the third chapter (tṛtīya-adhyāya). Now, the rules belonging to the third section (tārtīyīka) of the third chapter will be stated. This is with reference to the word "bhaviṣyati" (in the future), as it is understood from the rule "bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ. This is the intended meaning.

(606) *yāvatpurānipātayor laṭ* | 3|3|4| [The suffix] *laṭ* occurs after [roots] when the particles *yāvat* and *purā* are employed. The meaning is that *laṭ* shall be used when these two words, *yāvat* and *purā*, are used. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] *luṅ* and other [tenses]. It indicates certainty. [The word] *yāvatāvac ca* [is mentioned in the commentary].

According to Amara: "The word *yāvat* is used in the senses of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Thus, [the phrase] means "as much as will be given, so much will be eaten. This means that whatever the extent of the transformation (of the food), that shall be the extent [of the eating]. The point is that because the suffix *-vat* is added by the rule "from *yat*, *etat*, etc., in the sense of measure, the suffix *-vat*" (*yatadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatu*), it is not a particle (*nipāta*); therefore, the substitution of *laṭ* (the present tense marker) does not apply.

Regarding the phrase "karaṇabhūtayā": "purā yāsyati" is another counter-example. The word *purā* here is the third-case form of the word *pura*. It is stated as "karaṇabhūtayā" (as an instrument) in order to clarify that.

(607) *vibhāṣā kadākarhyoḥ* | Pāṇini 3.3.5. Regarding *vibhāṣā kadākarhyoḥ*: the completion of the sūtra is "in the future tense, there shall be optionally the *laṭ*. In the alternative case where *laṭ* does not occur, the *luṭ* and *lṛṭ* suffixes apply as prescribed. Thus he says: *kadā*.

Or rather, [the question] is "When will he eat?", "He will eat," or "He is the eater. It should not be argued that when used with *karhi*, the *luṅ* (aorist) alone is appropriate under the alternative view where the *laṭ* (present) is absent, and not the *lṛṭ* (future), because of the contradiction with the rule *ṭhanadyatane rhil anyatarasyām* which prescribes the suffix *rhil* after *karhi*.
They say that the example for *lṛṭ* concerns only the connection with *kadā*, and so forth.
(608) *kiṃvṛte lipsāyām* |3|3|6|. Regarding *kiṃvṛte lipsāyām*: the term *kiṃvṛtam* is intended to mean "that which is formed or produced by the word *kim*" (*kiṃśabdena vṛtaṃ niṣpannaṃ*).

He said: "The term 'ending in a case-suffix' refers to the present tense (*laṭ*). However, in the absence of *laṭ*, the future tenses *luṭ* and *lṛṭ* apply as appropriate. It is logical that by the word 'kiṃvṛta' (that which is formed from *kim*), only those ending in the comparative suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* when followed by a case-suffix are intended; for example, *kaṃ*, *kataraṃ*, or *katamaṃ*. [As in the phrase] 'a hungry person desiring food'."

The remainder [is as follows]: (609) *lipsyamānasiddhau ca* |3|3|7|. Also when there is the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained. "Or the *laṭ* [present tense]"—in the alternative case, it is according to the rule as it applies. When there is the accomplishment of what is desired to be obtained.
Even though there is a desire [to know], he provides an example—thinking that this is for the sake of explaining what is not a "kiṃvṛtta" (interrogative)—with the words "yo 'nnam" and so on.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "He who gives food goes to heaven; he who will give food will go to heaven; he who is a giver of food has gone to heaven."

(610) And [the optative suffix] is used when the sense of the imperative is indicated. 3.3.8. "And when the sense of the imperative is indicated. The sense of the imperative consists of *praiṣa* (commanding) and so forth.

This is stated while the rule "in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), and entreaty (*prārthana*)" is being carried over; [thus, the suffix] *loṭ* [is applied].

The intention is that this is because the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix is prescribed [in such cases]. "If Kṛṣṇa" means: "At the time of Kṛṣṇa’s meal, you should tend the cows. Here, Kṛṣṇa’s eating is the *lakṣaṇa*—that is to say, the delimiting condition—of the injunction to tend the cows, which is the meaning of the *loṭ*. In the alternative case, the *luṭ* and *lṛṭ* [future] suffixes are used.

If Kṛṣṇa is the eater, or will be the eater, [then] you should tend the cows—this is the example to be cited. (611) *Liṅ* is also used when the time is after a muhūrta (*liṅ cordhvamauhūrtike*). In the rule *liṅ cordhvamauhūrtike*, the word *ūrdhvam* is an indeclinable that functions as a case-ending substitute (*vibhaktipratirūpaka*).

The analysis of the compound is *ūrdhvaṃ muhūrtād bhavaḥ* ("that which occurs after a moment"). Some, however, maintain that *ūrdhvam* ends in the accusative case, arguing that it functions as the object (*karman*) due to the rule "in connection with intransitive roots" (*akarmaka-dhātubhir yoge*). Thus, one forms *ūrdhvamauhūrtikaḥ*; this is derived from the word *ūrdhvamuhūrta* by adding the suffix *ṭhañ* in the sense of "occurring there" (*bhavārthe*), according to the rule *kālāṭ ṭhañ*.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Now, one might ask: since the words *dik-saṅkhye* (direction and number) are understood to follow from the rule *taddhitārtha-*, and because this falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "co-referential" (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*) compounds, how can there be a compound here? To this he says: "By virtue of irregular derivation" (*nipātanāt*). Having raised the doubt regarding the initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in the first member, he says: "And the *vṛddhi* in the second member."

The term "nipātanāt" (by irregular derivation) is understood as being supplied [from the previous rule]. Regarding "ūrdhvamauhūrtike": this means "occurring at a time subsequent to a muhūrta. And this [term] connects with the phrase "loḍarthalakṣaṇe" (when indicating the sense of the imperative).

Regarding "liṅlaṭau": the meaning is that by the word "ca" (and), the present tense suffix *laṭ* is also conjoined. Regarding "vā staḥ" (they may optionally occur): this refers to the alternative case.

The *luṭ* and *lṛṭ* [suffixes] occur as prescribed by the rules. "In the Veda" (*cchandaḥ*) means in the Veda (*veda*). Thus, in the third chapter, third section, the rules concerning verbal suffixes (*la-vidhi*) fall under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "that which will be. Now, within this very third section, he states several specific rules:

(612) *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* (Pāṇini 3.3.131). Regarding "in proximity to the present": the suffix *pyañ* is used in its own sense (*svarthe*). The intention is that this is either due to this very mention [in the sūtra] or because the group beginning with *caturvarṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Starting from this point...

In the second quarter of the third book, beginning from "vartamāne laṭ" (Pāṇini 3.2.123) up until the end of the chapter, and prior to the first sūtra of the third quarter, "uṇādayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.1), there is the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the present tense (*vartamāna*). Within that governing heading, by whatever qualifier [is applied] to whichever verbal roots (*prakṛti*) in the present tense...

All these suffixes are introduced by that very qualification; the meaning is that they occur after those verbal roots (*prakṛti*) in the past and future times that are proximate to the present. Here, "in the past" and "in the future" are implied, because proximity to the present exists only for those two. When?

"Have you come? is a question directed at one who has not yet arrived. "I am coming" is the reply; its meaning is that one has arrived at a time immediately preceding the present. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here for a past action occurring in a time proximate to the present. By the word "this" (*ayam*), there is an indication of the state at the time of arrival, such as being covered in perspiration, having one's belt tightened, and so forth.
Now, form (*rūpa*) is being specified in order to indicate the arrival; [the word used is] *āgamam*.

The suffix *luṅ* is employed for the past tense because there is an absence of the present state. When a question is asked prior to the departure, such as "When will you go?", the reply "I am going" (*eṣa gacchāmi*) is given; the meaning is that one will go immediately thereafter.
The word *teṣu*, however, should be explained like *ittham*. When the future is near the present time, the *laṭ* (present) suffix is used;

for example, *gamiṣyāmi vā* ("I shall go" or "I might go"). In the absence of the status of being like the present, the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix is used. (613) *Āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132): [When there is a sense of hope (*āśaṃsā*), the suffixes of the past tense (*liṭ*) are used as well as those of the future.]
"In the sense of hope (*āśaṃsā*), it is treated as if it were already past. It does not follow [the previous rule]. In this matter, the commentary itself is the refuge.

Hope is the desire for the attainment of something pleasant that has not yet been attained; and that [hope] pertains exclusively to the future, because there is an absence of desire regarding what is already past. Thus he says: "in the future time. "If the god... [The word] *deva* means...

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "If Parjanya has rained, we have sown the grain; if he rains, we sow; if he will rain, we shall sow. Because the past tense (*bhūta*) is used for the future (*bhaviṣyat*), the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is employed—thus one says "he has rained" (*avarṣīt*) and "we have sown" (*avāpsma*). This is the *luṅ* of the root *vap* in the third person plural.
The thought "we shall obtain" arises.
Since both rain and sowing are objects of expectation (*āśaṃsā*), the *luṅ* (aorist) is used in both cases.

However, if one adopts the view that [the action] is present (*vartamānavattva*), the *laṭ* (present) is used. But if neither of those two conditions applies, the *lṛṭ* (future) is used. Now, an objection:
To the question, "Why would *laṅ* and *liṭ* not also apply in the case of the general property of 'pastness' (*bhūtatva*)?", he says:

"In the case of a transfer of a general property" (*sāmānyātideśe*). The meaning is that because there is a transfer (*atideśa*) of what is prescribed for the general property of pastness, there is no transfer of *laṅ* and *liṭ*, which are prescribed for the specific [temporal] qualification of "immediate pastness" (*anadyatanabhūtatva*). And this is clear in the Bhāṣya.

(614) *kṣipravacane lṛṭ* |3|3|133|. The term "vacana" (expression) [in the sūtra] implies "in the sense of a synonym for 'quickly'. Thus he says: "in a synonym for 'quickly'. "In the previous scope" means "in the context of *āśaṃsā*" (expectation). [This refers to the rule] *āśaṃsāyām...* [etc.]

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *bhūtavacca*. Now, one might object: since the mere mention of "words signifying speed" (*kṣipravacanena*) would suffice—because by that alone it is obtained that when a synonym of "speed" is used as an attendant word (*upapada*) in the sense of benediction (*āśaṃsā*), the suffix will not function as in the past nor as in the present—the inclusion of the term *lṛṅ* (the conditional suffix) is useless. To this, he says: "It should have been stated as 'not' (*na*)."

When it is stated, "in the case of immediate speech (*kṣipravacana*)," according to the maxim "when there is an extension of a general rule, there is no extension of a specific [rule]," the prohibition would apply only to the *lṛṭ* (future tense) prescribed for the general future, but not to the *luṭ* (periphrastic future), because the latter is prescribed as a specific rule for the non-immediate future (*anadyatana-bhaviṣyat*). [Thus, one might say: "We shall eat quickly."

The word *śvas* is used to indicate that the action has not occurred within the current day; the intention here is that the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is not applied. (615) *āśaṃsā-vacane liṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.134):
"The *liṅ* (optative) is used when there is a statement of hope (*āśaṃsā*). This means that when there is a desire for the attainment of something in the past...
Thinking that [the action] will come to pass because it is possible, he says "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*).
This is an exception to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* ("in the sense of expectation, as if it were past"). Therefore he says: "but not as if past.
Regarding "if the teacher": the syntactical connection is "if the teacher should approach, I hope that I shall study quickly."

Even in the case of immediate action (*kṣiprayoga*), the *liṭ* suffix alone is used because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], and not the *lṛṭ*; this is the intended meaning. (616) Pāṇini 3.3.135: "Not so in the case of continuity of action or proximity; it is not like the *anadyatana* [past]. "Continuity of action" means uninterruptedness. Thus he says: "of action..."

Regarding the term *sātatye* ("in continuity"): by the phrase "as in the case of the non-recent past" (*anadyatanavad*), it is intended that the *laṅ* and *luṭ* suffixes prescribed for the non-recent past and the future are [here] excluded. Thus he says: "neither *laṅ* nor *luṭ*.
The meaning is that *laṅ* does not occur for the non-recent past, and *luṭ* does not occur for the non-recent future, when there is continuity of action (*kriyāsātatye*).

He illustrates the prohibition of the *luṅ* [aorist] tense with the example: "He ate food for as long as he lived" (*yāvajjīvam annam adāt*). Here, the *luk* elision of the *sic* suffix occurs by the rule *gāti-sthā-gāpā-bhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ*. Intending to illustrate proximity (*sāmīpya*), he says: "Proximity. Regarding the phrase "this which": it refers to the few days and nights in the dark fortnight following the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

Even when there is an intervention, proximity (sāmīpya) indeed exists, because there is no intervention by another full moon day (paurṇamāsī) of the same kind. Regarding the form *ādhitā*: from the root *dhā*, the suffix *luṅ* is applied;
by the rule *sthādhvor ic ca*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the root *dhā*, and the suffix *sic* is treated as *kit*; then, by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*, there is the elision of *sic*.
Regarding "he has sacrificed with Soma": the phrase "of this full moon that has passed" (*yeyam paurṇamāsy atikrāntā tasyām*) is to be supplied.

Now, he provides an example of the prohibition of the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) when there is continuity of action: "this new moon [that is coming]" (*yeyam amāvāsyā*), as in "he will sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyate*). [This refers to] "this new moon that is to come."
The word "of that" (*tasya*) is supplied here.

(617) *Bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane 'varasmin* (Pāṇini 3.3.135). [This sūtra means: "In the future, when there is a statement of a limit, provided it is posterior. The analysis of the compound is: *bhaviṣyati*, *maryādā*, and *avarasmin*. It is not like the case of the recent past (*anadyatana*).

The meaning is "having cut. The *Bhāṣya* states, "for the sake of the continuity of action," while Kaiyaṭa says, "and for the sake of proximity. Regarding the phrase "this which": it refers to that path which is to be traversed starting from Pāṭaliputra by one dwelling in a certain particular region; [it refers to] that portion situated in the middle of that path.
The construction is: "From Kauśāmbī, in that region which is further to the east, we shall drink barley-meal (saktu) starting from tomorrow.

Here, by the word *kauśāmbyāḥ*, the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) is understood; by the word *avaram*, the sense of being "further" (*avaratva*) is understood. The point here is that although the future tense refers to what is to happen today, the suffix *luṅ* (the aorist) is not used, but rather *lṛṭ* (the periphrastic future) alone.

Regarding the division of time: "the preceding rule" means the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.137], namely, *bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane 'varasmin*. Now, one might object that even in the case of a time-limit (*kālamaryādā*), the matter is already established by the preceding rule alone; therefore, he says: "day and night. And thus...

The meaning is that the rule previously stated—"when there is a statement of a limit (maryādā) regarding a division connected to a day-and-night"—does not apply here. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that 'bhaviṣyati maryādāvacane avarasmin kālavibhāge cānahorātrāṇām' is actually a single [sūtra]?"

Why is it not [taught] in the Sūtra? To this he says: "The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. This will become clear in the subsequent Sūtra. "This year which is to come" is an example of a temporal limit (*kālato maryādā*). "From Āgrahāyaṇī" means from the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.

This is the meaning. "Yuktāḥ" means "endowed with restraint. Regarding "adhyeṣyāmahe," the intention is that here there is not the *luṭ* suffix, but rather the *lṛṭ* suffix itself. "Pañcadaśarātrayuktāḥ" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that fortnight which has fifteen nights. This is because of the rule *ṭhac-praty-anv-ava-pūrvāt* [Pāṇini 5.2.35], where the term *aj* is understood.

The suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Alternatively, *pañcadaśarātraḥ* is the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of fifteen nights; here, the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule "after *ahan*, *sarva*, and parts [of a whole]," which prescribes the compound-ending *ac*. As for the statement "a *rātra* preceded by a numeral is neuter," it does not apply here because of the dictum: "gender is not to be prescribed, since gender depends on worldly usage."
It occurs.
(618) *parasmin vibhāṣā* (3.3.138).
Regarding *parasmin vibhāṣā*: it is understood that [the previous rule] continues. And thus, in the future tense—
When expressing a limit (*maryādā*) in the sense of "beyond" (*parasmin vibhāge*), it results that [the suffixes] *anadyatana* or *anadyatanavat* apply.

This was explained under the rule "In the case of a condition indicated by a verbal suffix (*liṅ-nimite*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used when there is non-occurrence of the action," during the discussion of the root *bhū*. Furthermore, [the conditional is used] in the past (*bhūte*). 3.3.140.

"And [the word] *bhūte* (in the past). This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). It follows [from the previous sūtra]. Thus, the result is that when the conditional mood (*liṅ*) is prescribed on account of a potentiality (*liṅ-nimitta*), the phrase "in the past" (*bhūte*) is governed as a condition for the use of the periphrastic future (*lṛṅ*) in cases of the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*). This is the intended meaning. (620) *votāpyoḥ* 3.3.141.

Regarding *votāpyoḥ*: this is also a governing rule (*adhikāra*). The analysis is *vā* (or) *ā* (the augment *ā*) [is applied] after *uta* and *api*. The terms *bhūte* ("in the past") and *liṅ-nimite lṛṅ* ("the conditional *lṛṅ* when there is a condition for the optative *liṅ*") do not carry over. Thus he says: "prior to *utāpyoḥ*. This means: prior to the rule *utāpyoḥ samarthayoḥ* (P. 3.4.17). But [one might object]: by this...

Since the scope of the governing rule "lṛṅ syāt" (Pāṇini 3.3.139), which applies when there is a past action as the cause for the conditional mood (*liṅ*), extends from the point where "utāpyoḥ" occurs, the preceding governing rule "bhūte ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.135) would otherwise be rendered purposeless; therefore, he says: "But the previous rule... [and continues] with "utāpyoḥ."

The meaning is that the governing rule (adhikāra-sūtra) "bhūte ca" (and [the suffixes] after verbs signifying a completed action), which precedes the rule "samarthayorliṅlyāribhya icchārthebhyo vibhāṣā," is operative. These two governing rules apply only where there is an injunction for *liṅ*, and not in the injunctions for *laṭ* and other such suffixes.
Because there is an absence of a cause for the indicative mood (*liṅ*).

(621) *P. 3.3.142*: "In the sense of censure (*garhā*), the present tense (*laṭ*) is used after the particles *api* and *jātu*. Here, *api* and *jātu* form a *dvandva* compound. In this context, by the rule *votāpyoḥ*, the tense refers to the past.

The governing rule "lṛṅ optionally [is used] when there is a condition for the optative (liṅ)" does not apply here. This is because the present tense (laṭ) is prescribed in that domain, and thus the conditions for the optative are absent. The phrase "in all three times" means in the present, the past, and the future; the specification "in the future" has ceased to apply. Therefore, this refers to time in general.
The sense is "laḍ" (the present tense). Regarding the phrase "because it is subsequent," one should also understand that "because it has no other scope" (*anavakāśatvāt*) is intended.
In the examples "api jāyām" and "jātu gaṇikām," the words *api* and *jātu* indicate censure. Thus he says: "This is contemptible."

(622) *vibhāṣā katham i liṅ ca* |3|3|143|. Regarding *vibhāṣā katham i*: the phrase "in the sense of reproach" (*garhāyām*) indeed continues [from the previous rule]. This is the meaning. The words "the optative (*liṅ*) for the three times" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sūtra]. The word "future" (*bhaviṣyati*) has ceased to apply. And because of the word "also" (*ca*), the present tense (*laṭ*) applies as well.

The word "is collected" (*samuccīyate*) is the ellipsis. Thus, when *katham* is employed, it results that the potential (*liṅ*) or the present (*laṭ*) occur in all three times to express censure (*garhā*). For example: *kathaṃ dharmaṃ tyajeḥ*. The meaning is: "you have abandoned," "you will abandon," or "you are abandoning"—in other words, "this is censurable."

How is this understood from the word *katham*? He provides an example in the present tense (*laṭ*)—namely, *tyajasi vā*. The meaning has already been stated. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): because of the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā*, in the alternative where the optative (*liṅ*) and the present tense (*laṭ*) are absent, the sense is that in all three times—the past, the present, and the future—the perfect (*liṭ*), the imperfect (*laṅ*), the aorist (*luṅ*), the present (*laṭ*), the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), and the simple future (*lṛṭ*) may be used. Regarding the word *atra*: here...

In the context already mentioned, since the action will not be accomplished in the future time, the *lṛṅ* (conditional) is used invariably by the rule "when the *liṅ* is the cause [of the conditional], *lṛṅ* is used for the non-occurrence of the action" (*liṅ-nimite lṛṅ kriyātipattau*). This is because the condition for the *liṅ*—namely, censure (*garhā*)—is present; the meaning is that it is so because it is prescribed as a specific rule.

The state [of the action]. Regarding "or in the past" (*bhūte vā*): since it is governed by the rule *votāpyoḥ*—"the conditional (*liṅ*) or the periphrastic future (*lṛṅ*) [are used] when there is a cause for the conditional in the past"—the meaning is that in the aforementioned context, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is optionally used in the past tense.
Regarding the rule "in the future, the periphrastic future (*lṛṅ*) is mandatory," he provides an example:
"How indeed... (*kathaṃ nāma*). The phrase "His Honor" (*tatra bhavān*) is a collective expression.

"Pūjya" means one who accepts the authority of the Vedas; that is to say, one who acknowledges the Veda as a valid source of knowledge. The sense is: how could such a person abandon dharma, since its abandonment is censurable?
(Pāṇini 3.3.144: "The suffixes *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* are used after interrogative pronouns.")

Regarding the phrase "kiṃvṛte liṅlṛṭau" (when [the word] formed from *kim* with a suffix of inquiry is used, the optative and periphrastic future suffixes occur): the sense is that [the previous condition] does not carry over, according to the explanation. It is stated that "formed from *kim*" (*kiṃvṛta*) refers to words ending in case-suffixes as well as those ending in the suffixes *-ḍatara* and *-ḍatama*. The meaning is that when such a word is employed, the optative (*liṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) occur in the sense of censure (*garhā*).

The commentary states that these are exceptions (*apavāda*) to all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). Regarding the phrase "the conditional (*lṛṅ*) as previously mentioned": the meaning is that one should also keep in mind here what was stated previously—that the conditional is obligatory in the future tense, while in the past tense it is optional.
The underlying intention is that the conditions for the optative (*liṅ*) exist, namely the presence of an interrogative particle (*kiṃvṛta*), censure (*garhā*), and so forth.

(624) *anavaklṛptyamarṣayorakiṃvṛte’pi* || 3.3.145 || [The suffixes *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* are used] after [roots expressing] impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*), even when [the particle] *kim* is not present. The intention is that this is based on the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
It is not intended that there be a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) between impossibility and intolerance with the two suffixes *liṅ* and *lṛṭ*.

The commentary states that this is because the word *amarṣa*, having fewer syllables, would otherwise have been placed first [according to the rule for two-member compounds]. "I do not believe" (*na saṃbhāvayāmi*) is an example when the particle *kim* is not present. The syntactical connection is: "That you, sir, should censure Hira—this I do not believe, or rather, I do not tolerate. He gives an example when *kim* is present: "Who..."

"What is the meaning of 'katara'? [The answer is: "As before, regarding the conditional (lṛṅ). The meaning is that one should also keep in mind here what was stated previously: that the conditional is used invariably for the future, or optionally for the past. (625) Pāṇini 3.3.146: When *kiṅkila* or words expressing existence (*astyartha*) are used, the present tense (lṛṭ) is employed.

*kiṅkilā* | *kiṃṅkila*—this is a *dvandva* compound of the word as a whole and words having the sense of "to exist" (*astyartha*). Regarding *yāvat*: it means "if [the particle] *ca* follows, provided it is used in the sense of censure (*garhā*). When *kiṅkila* and words having the sense of "to exist" are employed, the *lṛṭ* (future) suffix is used in the senses of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*).

The meaning is "it might be. Since both the conditional (*lṛṅ*) and the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) would apply by the preceding rule, this [sūtra] is intended to restrict it to the conditional alone; thus he says: "It is an exception to the optative (*liṅ*). "I do not believe" means "I do not consider possible. That which you say—"you will eat the food of a Śūdra"—I do not believe. I do not...
The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is: "Or will you endure it? The particle *kiṅkila* expresses anger.

Regarding the word *asti*: a Śūdra woman is a *śūdrī*; the connection is "it exists," "it happens," or "it is found" that you will go to her. Here, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is not used; for the future tense, *lṛṅ* is obligatory, whereas for the past [it is optional].
What was stated here [regarding the suffix *vā*] is not possible in this case, because in the absence of an injunction (*vidhi*) there is no occasion for the use of the optative (*liṅ*).
[Pāṇini 3.3.147 states: "The optative (*liṅ*) is used after the particles *jātu* and *yad*."

The rule *jātuyadorliṅ* means that the conditional suffix *liṅ* occurs after the words *jātu* and *yat* when they are used in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*). Here, *yat* is an indeclinable that functions as a substitute for a case-ending. This is based on the rule: *anavaklṛptyamarṣayorakiṃvṛte’pi*.
Since both *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* would otherwise apply [in these cases], this rule is intended to restrict the usage to *liṅ* alone. Thus it says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lṛṭ*.

Regarding the phrase "when *yadā* and *yadi* [are used]": the meaning is that even when *yadā* and *yadi* are employed, *liṅ* must be added to the aforementioned scope. Words such as *jātu* and others are provided as examples.

The suffixes expressing impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*) [are used with the conditional]. The syntactical connection is: "I do not consider it possible, nor do I tolerate, that one such as you should censure Hari.
The meaning of "I do not consider possible" (*nāvakalpayāmi*) is "I do not deem it probable. Regarding the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*), it is as explained previously.
The meaning is that what was stated regarding the future tense— namely, "the conditional (lṛṅ) shall always [be used] when [the action] has occurred"— should also be applied here;
the point is that the connection with words such as *jātu* and so forth serves as a cause for the conditional (*liṅ*) because they express impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*).

(627) *yaccayatrayoḥ* |3|3|148|. The meaning is that when the word *yacca* used as a compound (*samudāya*) and the word *yatra* are employed, the suffix *liṅ* shall be used in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) and impatience (*amarṣa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the future tense suffix *lṛṭ*.

The analysis of the rule (yogavibhāga), however, is for the purpose of carrying these two [terms] forward into the subsequent sūtra. In the examples, *yaccā* and *yatrā* indicate non-acceptance (*anavaklṛpti*) and intolerance (*amarṣa*). The syntactical connection is: "I do not believe that you should act in this way," or "I cannot tolerate it. Here too, [the suffix] *luṭ* (the future) is used invariably.

The rule "lṛṅ in the sense of the past, optionally" (3.3.139) should be understood as applicable here, because the condition for the use of the conditional (*liṅ*) is present. (628) *garhāyāṃ ca* (3.3.149).
[The word] "and in the sense of censure" (*garhāyām*) is included; the intention is that this is established by the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). [The phrase] "in the case of *yat* and *ca*"...
And the word *lihi* (the suffix *liṅ*) follows [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "in the connection of *yacca* and *yatra*" (*yaccayatrayoḥ*).

"Only *liṅ*" (*liReĀva*) means that it is not any other *lakāra* (verbal suffix). In the example, both *yacca* and *yatra* indicate reproach (*garhā*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "That you should cause a Śūdra to perform a sacrifice" (*tvaṃ śūdraṃ yājayeḥ*) is improper.
The *lṛṅ* [suffix] is as before.
(629) *citrīkaraṇe ca* |3|3|150|. Also when there is a sense of wonder (*citrīkaraṇa*), when *yat* and *yatra* are employed, the *liṅ* alone should occur to express astonishment, and not [the *lṛṅ*].
The meaning is "another *lakāra*. In the example, both *yaccā* and *yatra* indicate wonder (*āścarya*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "That you should cause a Śūdra to perform a sacrifice—that is a wonder.
(630) *Śeṣe lṛḍayadau* | 3.3.151.

"In the remaining cases, *lṛṭ* [is used], except after *yat* and *yatra*. This means that when there is a case other than those following *yat* and *yatra*, it is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). He says this: "in a case other than *yat* and *yatra*. The remainder is "when [the word] is different from *yat*. "*Lṛṭ* shall be used"—that is, another *lakāra* (tense/mood marker) is not used. "It is a marvel!"—[referring to] the blind man [seeing] Kṛṣṇa.
The construction is: "He will see—this is a marvel. The indeclinable *nāma* indicates a marvel. Regarding *mūka*:

the construction is "A mute person would study—this is a marvel. The word *yadi* indicates a marvel. (Pāṇini 3.3.152: *uta* and *api*, when used in the sense of "marvel," [govern] the potential mood (*liṅ*).
Regarding *utāpyoḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "those two whose meanings are equal.
Due to its inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group, there is a substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). The meaning is "of those two which have a single meaning.
To address how these two possess a single meaning by taking up the sense of "indeed" (*bāḍham*), he says: "Certainly. And thus:

The meaning is that when the words *uta* and *api*, which signify "certainly" (*bāḍha*), are employed, the potential mood (*liṅ*) shall be used and no other verbal suffix (*lakārāntara*). For example: *uta hanyādaghaṃ hariḥ* (Would Hari surely slay the evil?
and *api hanyādaghaṃ hariḥ* (Would Hari surely slay the evil?). Here, *uta* and *api* have the sense of "certainly. This is understood [from the rule].

In the phrase "the staff will fall," the word *uta* indicates a question. In the phrase "he will close the door," the particle *api* indicates that the root *dhā* has the sense of covering; this is the meaning. Regarding the expression "from here onwards":
in the rule "votāpyoḥ," the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). This [usage] begins from the rule "utāpyoḥ."

It is stated that in the rules concerning the past tense (*bhūta*), such as "when there is a cause for the conditional (*liṅ*) [but it is not used]," the *lṛṅ* is optionally employed; however, in the rules beginning with "after *uta* and *api*," it is specifically stated that "the *lṛṅ* occurs when there is a cause for the conditional in the past and there is a failure of the action (*kriyātipatti*). And thus, from the rule "after *uta* and *api*" onwards...

When there is a lapse of action (kriyātipatti) indicated by the conditional suffix (liṅ), the suffix lṛṅ is prescribed specifically for the past tense, and not the mention of the word "optionally" (vā). Therefore, in this context, lṛṅ is used invariably for both the past and the future when there is a lapse of action.

(632) *kāmapravedane 'kacciti* |3|3|153|. In the expression "kāmapravedane 'kacciti," the word "ca" (and) is understood [from the previous sūtra]. Therefore, it says: "but not when *kaccit* [is used]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). "Abhiprāyaḥ" means desire. "Kāma" means... you.

"bhuñjīta" means "it is my wish"; that is, it signifies a desire. Since the condition for the *liṅ* (optative) suffix is present here, the *liṅ* is used invariably even when the action is understood to have occurred in the past (*kriyātipatti*). The conclusion is that this is indeed a question indicating the disclosure of a wish. In this case, because the word "kaccit" does not itself possess the meaning of "wish," [the rule] "in the sense of wishing... (*icchārtheṣu*) [does not apply].
What is about to be stated does not apply here.
(633) *saṃbhāvane 'lamiti cetsiddhāprayoge* (Pāṇini 3.3.154).

In the sense of *saṃbhāvana* (possibility or presumption), the meaning of *alam* here is proficiency (*prauḍhi*), that is to say, sufficiency (*paryāpti*). It is transformed [into the instrumental case].

Thus: the word ending in the locative case, *saṃbhāvane*, is repeated and changed into the nominative as *saṃbhāvanam*; and the word ending in the nominative case, *alam*, is repeated and changed into the locative as *alām*. This is the meaning. [The form] is Vedic (*chāndasam*).

This is a supplement [to the rule] based on a transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*). Thus, "in the sense of possibility" (*saṃbhāvane*) is understood as ending in the locative case, while "possibility" (*saṃbhāvana*) is understood as ending in the nominative case. Similarly, "enough" (*alam*) is understood as ending in the nominative case, while "having obtained" (*alabhi*) is understood as ending in the locative case. Among these, regarding "in the sense of possibility":

The word ending in the seventh case (locative) is intended to indicate the meaning [of the suffix]; thus he says: "The suffix *liṅ* occurs in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvana*). Possibility is defined as a cognition in which one of two alternatives is predominant. However, the word "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanam*), being in the nominative case, is qualified by the word "sufficient" (*alam*), which is also in the nominative case. Thus.

He says that [in the verse]: "If that... The word *tat* refers to the possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). The word *alam* means "sufficient cause. Thus, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "if that [possibility] is sufficient. The word *siddha* is derived from the root *ṣidh*, which has the sense of "knowing," with the suffix *kta* applied in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*. When it is established (*siddhe*)...

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which has non-usage when the sense of 'enough' (alam) is already understood even though [the word] is present. Here, the word *alam* ending in the locative case (*alam-i*) is connected as the provider of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
This means: "even without the actual employment of the word *alaṃ*, when its meaning is understood. Thus he says:

"Success occurs when there is no [actual] application"—this is the remainder [of the sentence], meaning "it is sufficient. Regarding the phrase "even a mountain": this is an exaggeration (atyukti) made with reference to a powerful man; the sense is that he is generally capable of splitting a mountain with his head. This refers to the possibility of splitting a mountain.

The word "api" (also) indicates that [the action] has capability as its cause. Here, because there is the existence of a condition (*liṅ-nimitta*) and the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*) in the past, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used. It is well said: "In the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), when the action is established but not actually performed, the suffix *alam* is used."

(634) *vibhāṣā dhātoḥ saṃbhāvanavacane 'yadi* |3|3|155|. The analysis of the rule is *vibhāṣā dhātau*, with the word *ayadi* as a separate item. Thus he says: "but not when *yat* [is present]". In the absence of *liṅ*, there is *lṛṭ*, because of the subsequent application of the rule "in the remaining cases, *laṭ* [is used], except when *yadi* [is present]". [The example is] *saṃbhāvayāmi* ("I consider it likely"), which occurs generally.
The meaning is "capable of eating.
(635) *hetuhetumator liṅ* | 3|3|156|. Regarding the rule *hetuhetumator liṅ*, considering that the word *vibhāṣā* is carried over from the preceding sūtra, he says: *vā*.

"Syāt" means: in the alternative case, the *lṛṭ* (future) [is used]; that is to say, when a verbal root denotes a meaning that is either the cause or the result, the *liṅ* may optionally be used. "Only in the future" is the sense, because although *liṅ* was already being carried over [from a previous rule], the word *liṅ* is mentioned again. "Hanti" (he strikes).

*iti* here signifies "because" (*hetau*). The meaning is: "on account of the killing occurring in the present time. Since the condition for the *liṅ* (optative) is present here, the *lṛṅ* (conditional) occurs when there is a failure of the action in the future or in the past. (636) *icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau* |3|3|157| (The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [imperative] are used after verbs expressing desire).

"The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used] with roots having the sense of desire. When roots expressing desire are employed, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* suffixes occur. This is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). This rule concerns cases where the agents are not identical.
However, in cases where the agents are identical, it will be stated [later] that "the *liṅ* also [is used]. For example: "I desire that he eat" (*icchāmi bhuñjīta*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "you [should do it]," meaning "I desire [it]. Regarding the phrase "in the expression of one's own desire" (*kāmapravedane*): the meaning is that the rule "the optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*) are used after roots having the sense of 'desire' (*icchārtha')" applies when one reveals one's own intention to another. In the case of "he does while desiring," there is no such revelation of one's own intention to another; therefore, [the rule does not apply].

The [sūtra] "liṅ-loṭau" refers to the sense of intention (*bhāva*). However, it should be understood that the rule "kāmapravedane 'kaccit" (Pāṇini 3.3.154) applies to cases where the expression of desire is established through context and the like, and not when there is a governing word (*upapada*) expressing the meaning of "wish" (*icchā*). The subsequent sūtra from here is "samānakartṛkeṣu tumun" (Pāṇini 3.3.158).
However, this will be explained under the heading of *kṛt* suffixes.

(637) *liṅ ca* | 3.3.159 | *liṅ ca*. The phrases "when the agents are the same" (*samānakartṛkeṣu*) and "in the sense of desire" (*icchārtheṣu*) are carried over [from the previous rules]. Thus he says:

"Samāne" and so forth. "Bhuñjīya" means "he desires [that someone] should eat. Here, because the eater himself is the agent of the desire (*icchā*), there is identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). This sūtra is intended to prevent the application of the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix by the rule "samānakartṛkeṣu icchārtheṣu. However, in the case of the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*), it will necessarily apply.
The section beginning with *lṛṅ* and *bhūte ca* is complete. [Now begins the rule] *icchārthebhyaḥ*.

Only *liṅ* is carried over; however, *samānakartṛkeṣu* has ceased to apply. Indicating this, he gives the example: *icchet*, *icchati*. [This is contrasted with] the rule *vidhinimantraṇe* regarding the root *budh*.

The [use of the imperative] has been explained; because it is obtained through the rule for *sūtra*-operations, it is included here. "In the same way, *loṭ*" means that the *loṭ* (imperative), which is prescribed for injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth by the rule "*loṭ ca*" (P. 3.3.162), should also be illustrated in this manner.
(638) P. 3.3.163: *praiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu kṛtyāśca* (The *kṛtya* suffixes and the *loṭ* are also used in the sense of command, permission, and the arrival of the proper time).

Regarding the rule *praiṣātisargalauṭ ca*: the term *loṭ*, which was introduced in the preceding sūtra, is conjoined here by the particle *ca*. The meaning is that the affixes designated as *kṛtya* (which will be described later) and the affix *loṭ* occur in the senses of *praiṣa* (command) and so forth. He provides an example of a *kṛtya* affix used in the sense of *praiṣa* and *atisarga*:
"You must sacrifice" (*bhavatā yaṣṭavyam*): here the suffix *tavya* expresses the state (*bhāva*). He gives an example of the imperative (*loṭ*):
"May you sacrifice" (*bhavān yajatām*). Now, one might ask: why is there a re-introduction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the imperative by means of the word "ca"?

For since an injunction (*praiṣa*) has the nature of a prescription (*vidhi*), and a permission (*atisarga*) has the nature of an invitation (*āmantraṇa*), [the imperative] would be covered by the rule "and the imperative" (*loṭ ca*) alone.

To establish this, he says: "by the word *vakāreṇa*. Regarding the sense of "the time having arrived" (*prāptakāle*), as in: "The teacher should eat" (*guruṇā bhoktavyam*) or "The teacher shall eat" (*gururbhuñjīta*). The meaning is that the meal has reached its proper opportunity. However, if one were to state [the rule] simply as "kṛtya affixes are used when the time has arrived" (*prāptakāle ca kṛtyāśca*), then kṛtya affixes would also apply to invitations and other such contexts. Therefore...
The mention of *praiṣa* and so forth [is for the sake of including other types of commands].
(639) *liṅ cordhvamauhūrtike* |3|3|164|.
"The suffix *liṅ* is also used when the time is more than a *muhūrta* away. [This applies] where the sense of *loṭ* is indicated.

A sūtra of this kind, which prescribes the use of the *liṅ*, *laṅ*, *luṅ*, and *lṛṅ* [moods], was previously recited as "ceṭyuttaram. Therein, the word *ūrdhvamauhūrtika* was explained. Regarding the phrase "praiṣādayaḥ" (the commands and so forth), it is thus: "one should sacrifice after a muhūrta," "let them sacrifice," or "it is to be sacrificed. In this context...

In the case of *liṅ* used for what has not yet been attained when the time has arrived, it is an injunction (*vidhi*), because in the rule concerning the introduction of *liṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.161), there is no mention of "the time having arrived. However, in the cases of command (*praiṣa*) and permission (*atisarga*), *liṅ* is established by that very same introductory rule. But when *liṅ* itself is used here for an injunction, it supersedes the *loṭ* suffix and the kṛtya suffixes.
Therefore, it should be understood that by the word *ca* (and), the rule [of the optative] applies to them as well.
(640) *sme loṭ* | 3.3.165 | Regarding *sme loṭ*: this refers to the preceding sūtra. And thus, at a time subsequent to a *muhūrta*, [the optative is used].

The meaning is that in the senses of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*), only the *loṭ* suffix should be used, and not the *liṅ* or the *kṛtya* suffixes.
Thus he says: "This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *liṅ* and the *kṛtyas*. (641) And [it is used] in the sense of entreaty (*adhīṣṭa*). 3.3.166.
And [the suffix] *loṭ* occurs in the sense of entreaty (*adhīṣṭa*). This is an exception to the *liṅ* prescribed for entreaty.
It has been stated that entreaty is an activity preceded by respect. An example is the address to a teacher: "May you please teach me.
