Since the rule could have been established as a single sūtra—"In the sense of entreaty, *loṭ* occurs after a root ending in *sma*"—the division into separate rules is for the sake of brevity.

The term *ūrdhvamauhūrtika* is used for the purpose of excluding the subsequent application [of the rule]. As for the later sūtra, "In connection with *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*, the suffix *tumun* is used," that will be explained in the section on *kṛt* suffixes. (642) *liṅ yadi* 3.3.168.

The suffix *liṅ* occurs when words such as *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā* follow. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*), and it is also an exception to the suffix *tumun*. The syntactic connection is: "It is time, the occasion, or the hour for you to eat" (*bhuñjīta bhavān iti yatas tasya kālaḥ samayo velā vā*).

(643) *Arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* | Pāṇini 3.3.169. "In the sense of being worthy (*arhe*), the kṛtya suffixes, the suffix *tṛc*, and [the suffix *liṅ* are used]. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *liṅ* is also included. The meaning is that when a capable agent (*yogya-kartṛ*) is to be understood, the kṛtya suffixes, *tṛc*, and *liṅ* are employed. For example: *tvaṃ kanyāṃ vaher iti* ("You are fit to marry the girl"). This refers to one who is suitable for the marriage of a maiden.
This is the meaning.

(644) *śaki liṅ ca* | Pāṇini 3.3.172. Regarding *śaki liṅ ca*: the term *śak* is a form ending in the suffix *kvip*, used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). It means "in the case of capability."
The meaning is "while being gone over. Regarding "you should carry the burden," the meaning is that you are capable of carrying it.

Although [the rule] *māṅi luṅ* has already been explained, it is reminded again here because it follows in sequence and because there is a desire to state a specific detail. Now, it was stated that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*); if that is so, let it not be [an exception].
"How will it not be?"—thus the doubt is raised as to "how. He refutes this: "This [particle] is not *mā*.

Rather, the point is that the rule for the suffix *ṅ* applies even to the released (*mukta*) form, because it is listed among the indeclinables (*avyaya*). Nor is there any problem in the existence of usages such as *mā bhavatu*, by taking the word *mā*.

It should not be argued that the mention of *luṅ* [in Pāṇini 6.4.74] is redundant; for it is necessary in order to provide examples of the *luṅ* [aorist] ending devoid of *aṭ* and *āṭ* in all cases where [the augment] is prohibited by the rule "na māṅyoge" (Pāṇini 6.4.74).
(645) *dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.1): "Suffixes [are applied] when there is a connection with a verbal root."

"In connection with verbal roots" (*dhātusambandhe*). By the word "root" (*dhātu*), the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*) is indicated. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "connection between two roots," because a connection resides in two things. Thus, it is understood that suffixes (*pratyaya*) should occur when there is a connection between the meanings of two roots. When the expectation arises as to "in what sense [do they occur]?", [the answer is] "in time" (*kāle*).

It is understood that [the suffixes] are prescribed only for specific times, because starting from the rule "laṭ for the present" (*vartamāne laṭ*), we observe the prescription of suffixes precisely for those respective specific times. Since the suffixes are established by those various rules for those specific times, it is understood that [the present tense applies] at a time other than those. Thus he says:

By the words "of the root-meanings" (*dhātvarthānām*) and so forth, the meaning is "of two root-meanings. The plural number is intended to indicate a multiplicity of examples. In rules such as *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā*, whatever suffixes are prescribed for a particular time apply to those two root-meanings.

When a relationship is to be understood, [the suffixes] may occur even at a time other than that; such is the meaning. And thus, in the example "vasan dadarśa" (while living, he saw), it is established that the *śatṛ* affix, which is a substitute for *laṭ*, occurs in the past tense.
Now, one might object: why not simply have *laṭ* in the past tense in "vasan dadarśa," just as *liṭ* would occur in the present tense?

To address this, he says: "ending in a verbal suffix" (tiṅanta). In examples such as "vasan dadarśa" ("while dwelling, he saw"), the action expressed by the suffix ending in *taṅ*—such as the act of seeing—is primary;
however, the action of dwelling is subordinate because it exists for the sake of the action of seeing and so forth. Therefore...

The meaning is that here, in reference to other times, suffixes are prescribed after words expressing subordinate actions such as "dwelling" (vāsa), in accordance with the principal action such as "seeing" (darśana). Regarding the rule *bhūte laṭ* ("the present tense suffix *laṭ* is used for the past"): thus, the meaning is "having dwelt, he saw. He states this by saying "atīta" (past); [the compound] means "that whose agent (*kartṛ*) is the past dwelling."

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: based on the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) "in a *bahuvrīhi*, when a word in the locative case is a qualifier," a *bahuvrīhi* may have its members situated in different syntactical positions (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). He states another example: "one who has sacrificed with *soma*" (*somayājī*).

One who has performed a sacrifice (*iṣṭavat*) by means of *soma* is a *somayājī*. Here, the suffix *ṇini* is prescribed after the root *yaja-* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) and in the past tense (*bhūte*).

The form *bhavita* should be understood as referring to the future tense not belonging to the current day (*anadyatana-bhaviṣyat*), in accordance with the primary action denoted by the suffix *lṛṅ*. Thus he says: "one who intends to sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yakṣyamāṇaḥ*). Regarding the word *bhavanam*, it means "origination" (*utpatti*).
The example "the owner of cows was" (*gomān āsīt*) should also be cited here; in this case, [the sense is] "he possessed a cow," within the context of the action of existence (*asti-kriyā*).

In each instance where the [action] is present, the suffix *matup*— prescribed by the rule "that which belongs to this" (*tad asyāsti*)— occurs even when the action of existence (*asti-kriyā*) is past, as in "he was fair" (*gaura āsīt*), because there exists a connection between two meanings of the verbal roots. By this, the explanation that the connection between the two roots is mediated by their meanings is also accounted for.

This is refuted; for if that were the case, since one would obtain the meaning "suffixes [occur] upon the employment of two verbal roots expressing a mutually related meaning," the suffix *matup* would result in the form *gomān āsīt* (the cow-possessor existed), because there is no employment of two verbal roots here. However, if one accepts the meaning to be "in the relation between the meanings of the verbal roots," then...

In the case of *gomān āsīt*, although there is no employment of two verbal roots (*dhātu*), since the meanings of both roots are present, the suffix *matup* in the sense of "possessing" (*āsīt*) is not barred; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
(Pāṇini 3.4.2–4) *Kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ*, *loṭo hi-svau*, *vā ca tadhvamoḥ*.

3|4|2 *kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ*. Here there are four statements. Among them, the first statement is: "In the case of the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), the suffix *loṭ* [is used]. It has been stated that the intensification of an action consists of frequency (*paunaḥpunya*) and intensity (*bhṛśārtha*).

The phrase "in the sense of repetition of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre*) is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, it is understood that [the suffix] applies to a verbal root whose meaning is characterized by the repetition of an action. The imperative suffix (*loṭ*), however, is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). This is what he says: "when repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) and intensity (*bhṛśārtha*) are to be indicated."
This means that the *loṭ* [suffix] is applied to a verbal root (*dhātu*) whose function is characterized by the repetition of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*).

It is an exception (*apavāda*) to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). He explains the second sentence, "For the *loṭ*, there are *hi* and *sva*," with the words "of that" (*tasya*). The meaning is that for the *loṭ* prescribed by the preceding rule, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* occur.
"An exception to the *tiṅ* [suffixes]" means "two exceptions. The singular number is used with reference to each one individually.

Now, since both *hi* and *sva* are substitutes for *l*, would they not both be *parasmaipada*? If that were the case, the desired distinction—that *hi* is *parasmaipada* while the substitute *sva* is *ātmanepada*—would not hold.

It would not be established; because this substitute (*svādeśa*) is not included within the *taṅ* pratyāhāra, the rule "the [suffixes] *ta*, *āna*, etc., are termed *ātmanepada*" does not apply to it.
[The term *ātmanepada* applies] only to those such as *ta*, *ātām*, and so forth, which are mentioned in the sūtra beginning with "ti-pratas-jhi."

Because the designation *taṅ* applies [to them]. Furthermore, since these two, *hi* and *sva*, are not included within the rule "tiptasjhi," their status as *tiṅ* suffixes would be difficult to establish; therefore, he says: "And those two...
In the second statement, "the *hi* and *sva* of the *loṭ*," it is first stated that [these are used] in the sense of frequent repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāre*).

From the first sentence, the term *loṭ* (the imperative suffix) is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and, being transformed into a genitive case (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), becomes the third sentence. In that context, from the second sentence, the term *hi-svau* is carried over and is understood as referring to the grammatical properties (*dharma-param*). And thus:

It is understood that the substitutes for *loṭ* (the imperative) function like *hi* and *sva*. When the expectation arises as to "in what [context] do they occur?", it is understood from the preceding sentence that they occur where *hi* and *sva* occur. Consequently, those two forms of *hi* and *sva* mentioned here, which are included within the category of *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes), [are to be understood as such].
The third sentence results in the following: "The forms *bhavataḥ* are like the *hi* and *sva* contained within the *tiṅ* substitutes for *loṭ*.
In that regard, the *hi* and *sva* contained within the *tiṅ* endings possess, respectively, the status of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*.

And the status of being a *tiṅ* (verbal suffix) is well-established. Therefore, the meaning is that in the *prakṛti* (the verbal base), the forms *hi* and *sva* are designated as *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*, and they are also designated as *tiṅ*.
Because they possess the status of *tiṅ*, their status as a *pada* (word) is established. [Objection: But [it was stated] "or [the substitution of] *ta* and *dhvam*..."?

The optional substitution of *hi* and *sva* for *ta* and *dhvam* is untenable, because since *hi* and *sva* are substitutes for the *loṭ* [imperative], they are exceptions (*apavāda*) to *tiṅ*, and thus *ta* and *dhvam* cannot occur in place of the *loṭ*. To this, he says: "In the domain of *ta* and *dhvam*" (*tadhvamorviṣaye tu*). This is stated by resorting to a genitive of relation (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) referring to the *ta* and *dhvam* that are substitutes for the *loṭ*.

One should not be misled into thinking that the meaning is "his and svā occur in their respective places," for if that were so, the aforementioned fault would arise; rather, the meaning of the genitive case here is the relationship between object and subject (viṣaya-viṣayibhāva). Thus, the result is that *hi* and *sva* replace [the endings] in the domain (*viṣaya*) of *ta* and *dhvam*, while in the alternative (*pakṣe*), *ta* and *dhvam* themselves remain. This is the intended sense. In this regard:

The word *ta* is understood here as the second person plural (*madhyamapuruṣa-bahuvacana*) alone, because of the [traditional] explanation and because of its association with *dhvaṃs*. Now, one might object: since there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the status of being the singular of the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa-ekavacana*) to these two, *hi* and *sva*, they should only occur when there is coreferentiality with the second person (*yauṣmat-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and when singularity (*ekatva*) is present. If that were so, the statement in the Bhāṣya—"the suffixes *hi* and *sva* are desired for all persons and for all numbers"—would be untenable. To this, he says: "In the rule prescribing *hi* and *sva" (*hisvavidhāna*).

If *hi* and *sva* were to bear the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of the second person singular, then *hi* and *sva* would occur for the imperative (*loṭ*) only when there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *yuṣmad* and when singularity is present; otherwise, the substitutes *tiP* and so forth would apply according to the respective rules. That being the case, the prescription of *hi* and *sva* for the imperative would be purposeless; therefore, the meaning is that there is no extension (*atideśa*) of person and number. "By that" means: by the absence of the extension of person and number to *hi* and *sva*, and by their consequent acquisition of the designations *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* respectively. "Entirely" (*sakala*).

The suffix *hi* occurs in the domain of all verbal roots (*puruṣa-vacana*). And its occurrence is only after roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings, specifically in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and not after roots that take the *ātmanepada* endings in the senses of the impersonal action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), or the agent; this is because it is stated that "the *parasmaipada* endings follow the remaining [roots] in the sense of the agent. Regarding the phrase "after those that take the *ātmanepada* endings, *sva*": the meaning is that after verbal roots which are the objects of rules such as "the *ātmanepada* endings follow a root ending in an unaccented nasal consonant" (*anudāttaṅti ātmanepadam*) and "the *ātmanepada* endings follow [roots] in the sense of the impersonal action or the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), only the *sva* (middle voice) endings occur for the imperative (*loṭ*) in the senses of the impersonal action, the object, or the agent.

The point here is that, in the absence of rules defining the technical names *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* for these two [suffixes] in their respective order, both would—by virtue of being substitutes for *l*-suffixes—be considered *parasmaipada*. Consequently, the *parasmaipada* suffix would occur even after roots that are [otherwise] designated as *ātmanepadi*, provided they denote an agent (*kartṛ*). (647) *samuccaye'nyatarasyām* | 3|4|3|.
[This sūtra applies when there is] a conjunction (*samuccaya*). [The word] "repetition" (*samabhihāra*) is absent from the phrase "the action, the imperative, the imperatives" (*kriyā, loṭ, loṭau*).

The previous sūtra, "hisvau vā ca tahmau," is carried over [into this context]. The word *kriyā* (action), ending in the plural with its sixth case-suffix elided, connects with the word *samuccaya* (conjunction). Thus he says:
"when the conjunction of multiple actions is to be indicated. And so, by resorting to the conjunction of *kārakas* (grammatical factors) as well:

There is no application of this [rule]. It has been stated previously: "The *loṭ* suffix follows the verbal root; for that, *hi* and *sva* are substituted, which possess the well-known properties of *hi* and *sva*, or [the substitution occurs] in the domain of those two (*tadhmau*)"—this is the meaning.
"The subsequent employment [of the verb] is according to the original form" (*yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ*), as in the rule "in the case of the intensification of an action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre*).
The two rules prescribing the *loṭ* [imperative] mood—namely, "in the sense of accumulation" (*samuccaye*) and "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*)—have been stated.

Between those two, the preceding rule, "in the sense of repetition of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre*), is referred to by the word "first" (*ādye*). Thus he says: "in the first prescription of the *loṭ*," meaning without transgressing that injunction.

"According to the rule": it is understood that the verb from which the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix was prescribed must be employed subsequently. Thus he says: "only that which is the base (*prakṛti*) of the *loṭ*. Here, "subsequent employment" (*anuprayoga*) means employment after [the *loṭ* form]; however, immediate contiguity is not intended, as in [the example] *lunīhi*.
This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in the *Bhāṣya*: "He cuts [the grass] with the very thought, 'Cut!

(Pāṇini 3.4.3). (648) *Samuccaye sāmānyavacanasya* |3|4|5|. In a case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), [the verb retains its accent] when it expresses a general action. The word *vacana* means that by which something is expressed (*ucyate anena iti vacanaḥ*). It refers to that which denotes a general action.

This is the meaning. He states the conclusion: "of that which has a general sense. This means: of that which expresses the generality of the action being conjoined. "From the subsequent application" (anuprayogāt) means: from that which is subsequently applied. "Thence" (tataḥ).

The meaning is: [the expression of number and so forth occurs] by means of the verbal roots being employed, their prakṛtis (bases), the *la*-suffixes, and so on. However, by the *hi* and *sva* suffixes, there is no manifestation of number, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and the like. And thus says the Bhāṣya: "That which ends in *hi* or *sva* has its word-meaning unmanifest; therefore, the sense is incomplete," and so forth. [Furthermore, it is stated: "In the case of the intensification of action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*), two [words] are to be expressed."

The *vārttika* has been explained in the section on the formation of reduplicated words (*dviruktaprakriyā*). It is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that this rule concerns the domain of the imperative (*loṭ*) prescribed by the first sūtra. Regarding the example for the imperative used in the sense of frequent or intense action (*kriyāsamabhihāre*), the *Bhāṣya* provides: "He goes, [saying] 'Go! Go! (*yāhi-yāhīti yāti*). In the *Bhāṣya*.

The intended meaning is that this is because the word *sthiti* (staying) is observed [in the context]. Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in -hi": the meaning is "of *yāhi* and *yāhi*" (imperative forms). Regarding the phrase "an action having a single agent":

the meaning is that there is the cognition of both the agent of the act of going (*yāti*) and its oneness. Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-differentiation through syntactic connection" (*abhedānvaye*): and thus...

If the vehicle is that which is used repeatedly or with intensity, then the cognition is "the present vehicle belonging to that [agent] and having a single agent. This statement is made because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that in all cases involving verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), the cognition has the action as its primary qualificand (*kriyāviśeṣyaka*). Thus: "He went saying 'Go! Go! and "'Go! Go! [is said by him].
The meaning is that this should be illustrated by all such verbal forms of the word *yā* (to go) in the first person:

"He went" (*yāhi yāhi iti yayau*), "He has gone" (*yāhi yāhi iti yātā*), "He will go" (*yāhi yāhi iti yāsyati*), and "Let him go" (*yāhi yāhi iti yātu*). This applies to the substitutes for the imperative (*loṭ*) in the context of the second person plural.

The alternative of the presence of *hi* has been stated: "or [the substitution of] *tah* and *dhvam*. In that regard, having taken for granted the forms *yāhi*, *yāhi*, and *yūyaṃ yāta* under the alternative of the presence of *hi*, he states the forms under the alternative of its absence:
*yāta*, *yāta*, and *yūyaṃ yāta*. *yāhi yāhi* [was used] as *ayāt*. *yāhi yāhi* [would be used] as *yāyāt*.

The *luṅ* [conditional mood] states: "He went, saying 'Go, go! (*yāhi yāhīty ayāsīt*). It illustrates the *lṛṅ* [conditional mood]: "Or he would have gone" (*ayāsyad vā*). "He would have gone, saying 'Go, go!

(*yāhi yāhīty ayāsyat*) is the form of the *lṛṅ*. In the reading "or he will go" (*yāsyati vā*), it is an illustration of the *lṛṭ* [future tense]. However, the sequence is not intended to be significant. "In the alternative" (*pakṣe*) refers to the domain of *dhvam*.

The meaning is: in the case where there is no substitution of one's own form (*svādeśa*). "Yūyam adhīdhvam" (you all study) is the second person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*). However, in the case of the impersonal passive (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karman*), [the forms] are *bhūyasva bhūyasva* and *bhūyate*;
one should provide examples such as *pacyasva pacyasva* and *pacyate*. Now, regarding "in the case of accumulation" (*samuccaye*).
He provides an illustration of the term "sāmānyavacanasya" (of a word denoting a general category) with the words "samuccaye tu" (but in the case of conjunction).
Regarding "abhyavaharati" (he consumes): "pāna" is the drinking of liquid substances; "bhakṣaṇa" is eating without the crushing of teeth;
whereas "khādana" is the chewing of solid substances. Of these two...

"Eating" (*abhyavaharaṇa*) is the general form [of the action], because its essence consists in consuming in any manner whatsoever. "In the alternative, *hi* and *sva*" means that in the domain of *ta* and *dhvam*, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* optionally occur.
An example to be cited is: "He eats, saying 'Drink! Eat! Regarding this, "drink... [is the beginning of the citation].

The meaning is that in examples such as *khādeti abhyavaharati* ("He eats [and] swallows"), there is a non-difference relation (*abhedānvaya*) between the specific actions of drinking, eating, and so forth—which are being conjoined—and the general action consisting of swallowing expressed by the verb that follows (*anuprayujyamāna*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of *saktūn*" (barley meal): the sense is that in the alternative where there is no imperative suffix (*loṭ*) for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaye*), there is also no subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a verb expressing a general action. By this [it is meant].

The meaning is that by means of the two rules—"optionally in a copulative compound" (*samuccaye 'nyatarasyām*) and "in a copulative compound, of a word denoting a general category" (*samuccaye sāmānyavacanasya*)—and by demonstrating their respective examples, the verse from Māgha’s poem beginning with *purīm avaskanda* has been explained.

The powerful Rāvaṇa, having entered into hostilities—that is, conflict—with Indra, the enemy of Namuci, caused unrest day after day by means of such acts as the assault upon the city of Amarāvatī, the destruction of the Nandana grove, the plundering of jewels, and the abduction of the celestial damsels; this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). The word *ittham* is a synonym for *iti*; it conveys the non-difference between the specific actions such as the assault and so forth, and the general action of causing unrest.

He states the result [of the argument] with the words "from the forest of *avaskanda*," etc. By the word "etc.," plundering and seizing are included. He establishes that [the rule] is based on an error with the words "in the second sūtra. Regarding the phrase "due to non-continuation": the sense is that its continuation is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya. He states the objection to accepting its continuation with the words "of the *loṭ*-ending [verb]."

The meaning is that, since the rule *samuccaye 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.3) follows from the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre* (Pāṇini 3.4.2), there would result the doubling of imperative forms such as *avaskanda*, according to the principle that "in the case of the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), two [words] are to be expressed. The phrase "it is merely an error" means that it is an error regarding both the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) and the singular number (*ekavacana*). To the question "Why?", he says: "Because it has been stated here that the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of person (*puruṣa*) and number (*vacana*) do not apply [to these]."

In this commentary (bhāṣya), it is stated that since the forms ending in *hi* and *sva* do not manifest number and tense (*saṅkhyā-kālaka*), the application of an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*) is established by logic alone for their manifestation; therefore, let there be no specific rule (*vidhi*) for such an auxiliary. Consequently, in the Śruti passage—"These small beings that recur repeatedly exist; 'be born and die'—this is the third station"—the *loṭ* [imperative] endings *hi* and *sva* alone occur according to the rule "in a collective sense (*samuccaye'), optionally," and there is no auxiliary verb.

In that context, since only the actions of birth and death are intended to be expressed, the number and time are not intended; therefore, there is no purpose for a subsequent application (anuprayoga) of the verb. By this, the phrase "jāyasva mriyasva" in the work of Vācaspati—"Having observed oneself and the world of living beings revolving thus from Satyaloka down to Avīci, saying 'be born, die, be born, die,' one applies the constant reflection (prasaṅkhyāna) upon this cycle of existence as being eternal, impure, and consisting of suffering"—is also explained.

Furthermore, there is no fault here [in the argument that *asakṛt* conveys repetition], because it has already been stated that in the rule *samuccaye 'nyatarasyām*, the term *kriyāsamabhihāre* (intensive repetition of an action) does not recur; thus, how could repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) not be understood from the word *asakṛt*? However, in the *Kalpataru* commentary, it is stated that in the example *jāyasva mriyasva* ("be born and die"), the suffix *loṭ* is applied by the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre*; this, however, must be disregarded because it would result in reduplication (*dvitva*), as explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

Thus ends the section on the determination of the meanings of the verbal suffixes (*lakārārtha-prakriyā*) in the *Bālamanoramā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by Śrī Vāsudevadīkṣita.
Now begins the section on suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*).
(1821) *tadasminnadhikam iti daśāntāḍḍaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.44. "The suffix *ḍa* is added after a word ending in *daśan* to form a compound meaning 'this has more of that'."

Now, regarding the suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*): the meaning is that in the analysis (*vigraha*) "that is abundant in this" (*tad asmin adhikam*), or "that is abundant in this" (*tat adhikam asmin*), the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied after a compound ending in the word *daśan* which stands in the nominative case, in the sense of "in this.

The mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the purpose of excluding the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) in the context of suffix prescription; for this very reason [it is specified].

They say that the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative due to the specific rule (nirdeśāt). The *Bhāṣya* states: "The locative is used in the sense of immediate proximity (*upaśleṣika*) as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Kaiyaṭa explains: "Proximity is the locus. [The example is: "In this, there are eleven māṣas in excess. This means "from this," or alternatively, "adhering to this" (*asmin upaśliṣṭāḥ*).

Nor should it be suspected that [the suffix] would apply even from the word *daśan* alone when there is a designation [of a compound], because it is stated: "The status of being a designator does not apply to what is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*). (Pāṇini 1.1.73).
[Furthermore, the suffix applies] after words ending in *śat* and after *viṃśati*. (Pāṇini 5.2.46).

[The rule applies] to words ending in *śat* and to *viṃśati*. Because [the word *triṃśat*] does not end in *daśan*, it was not covered by the previous [rule]. Thus, we have *triṃśaṃ śatam*.

When [the suffix *ḍa*] is present, there is elision of the *ṭi*-portion by the rule "*ṭeḥ*". As for *viṃśam*: the analysis of the compound is "that in which twenty are added" (*viṃśatir asminn adhikā*).

In the rule *viṃśateḍiti*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the syllable *ti*. Because of the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*), the form *ekatriṃśaṃ śatam* ("one hundred thirty-one") is established. Otherwise, by the technical rule regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there would be a restriction to that which begins with it. Furthermore, by the Vārttika stating "the mention of 'end' applies even to *viṃśati*," forms such as *ekaviṃśaṃ śatam* ("one hundred twenty-one") are established.

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). Thus he says: "the price of a portion," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*), the meaning is "in the sense of 'of this'. The analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is: "two portions of barley are the measure (*nimāna*) for this portion of whey (*udaśvit*). From two [portions of barley]...

When one *prastha* of buttermilk (*udaśvit*) is produced from two *prasthas* of barley, the sentence "This buttermilk is made from two measures of barley" (*dvimayam idam udaśvid yavānām*) is employed as an example. Here, the genitive case in "of barley" (*yavānām*) expresses a general relationship; the meaning is that the buttermilk is to be purchased with two *prasthas* of barley.

Even though the word *dvi* (two), when functioning as a part [of a compound], is always dependent [on another element], the suffix [denoting measure] is still applied: *dvau vrīhiyavau nimānamasyodaśvitaḥ*.

The meaning is: "The two heaps of rice and barley, characterized by the number two, are the measure of this buttermilk (*udaśvit*). In this case, just as with the buttermilk, it is in relation to that [measure].

The state of being double (*dviguṇatva*) is not intended for the two heaps of rice and barley; rather, it is only the duality of the heaps (*rāśidvitva*) that is intended. Since the word *dvi* does not function as a part-whole (*bhāgavṛtti*) here, the suffix [for a *dvigu* compound] is not applied. (Pāṇini 2.1.51). [Now, regarding the formation of ordinal numbers: "The suffix *ḍaṭ* is used in the sense of 'completing that' (*tasya pūraṇe*). (Pāṇini 5.2.48).

Regarding its completion (*pūraṇe*): the term *saṅkhyāyāḥ* (of a numeral) is understood to carry over. The meaning is that the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied after a word denoting a number—which signifies a thing to be numbered—and ending in the genitive case, when the sense of "completing" (*pūraṇe*) the motivating factor (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) of that number is to be expressed. [The word] "is completed by this" (*pūryate anena*) [is the etymological derivation].

*Pūraṇa* means a completing part; that is the meaning of the suffix. Regarding "eleven" (*ekādaśa*): the meaning is a part that completes the number eleven. That which, when added, causes the number eleven not to be achieved, but which, when added, fulfills it—that is the part. It is a single portion (*ekadeśa*).
Up to this point: what is meant by "the cause of application" (*pravṛttinimitta*)? It is, for example, water and so forth that fills five jars.

"Maṭ is not [added] after *anta*, *asaṃkhyā*, etc. This means that the augment *maṭ* occurs after the suffix *ḍaṭ*. This is a completion of the rule by supplying the missing portion. (1826) *ṣaṭ-kati-katipaya-caturām thuk* | Pāṇini 5.2.51. [The suffix *thuk* is added after the words *ṣaṣ*, *kati*, *katipaya*, and *catur* when followed by a case-ending.]

Regarding *ṣaṭka*: here, the letter *k* is the affix; the vowel *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is a *kit* suffix, it follows the final vowel. Thus, [the form] is *ṣaṣṭha*. Because it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*), there is no *jaś*-substitution for the *ṣ*. Regarding *caturtha*:
because it is not at the end of a word, there is no *visarga* for the *r*.
"From *catur*, there is the suffixes *-cha* and *-tha*, and the elision of the initial syllable.

The phrase "and the elision of the initial syllable" means that the entire cluster beginning with *ca* is elided.

In *tamaṭ*, the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of indicating the accent (*it*), and the vowel *a* following the letter *m* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In this case...

Kaiyaṭa states that only those words beginning with "viṃśati" (twenty) that are enumerated in the rule *ṭhpaṅktiviṃśatī* are to be understood here, and not even the worldly terms such as "ekaviṃśati" (twenty-one) and so on, because of their remoteness [from the specific enumeration].

However, in the case of "ekaviṃśatitama," it will be explained later that the suffix *tamaṭ* is applied by means of the rule governing the addition of suffixes to a word ending in another suffix (*tadantavidhi*).

(1832) *nityaṃ śatādimāsārdhamāsasaṃvatsarācca* | 5|2|57 | "Always from *śata* etc. means that after [words] beginning with *śata*, as well as after *māsa*, *ardhamāsa*, and *saṃvatsara*, the augment *tamap* always occurs before the suffix *ḍaṭ*. Now, [an objection]:...

Since the word "śatatama" (the hundredth) would be established by the subsequent sūtra, "ṣaṣṭhaḷadeśca," he says "ekaśatatama" (the one-hundred-and-first). The point is that because of the exclusion [in the rule] "asaṅkhyādeḥ," the subsequent sūtra does not apply here.
Now, [one might ask] regarding the words "māsa," "ardhamāsa," and "saṃvatsara"...

Since these [words] do not denote numbers, the suffix *ḍaṭ* does not even apply to them; how then can there be the rule for *tadaṭ*? To this he says: "from *māsa*, etc. [The example is] *māsatamaḥ*, meaning "that which completes the month"—namely, a constituent part such as a half-month (*ardhamāsa*). [The example is] *ardhamāsatamaḥ*, meaning [that which completes] a half-month.
*Pūraṇa* refers to a part such as a lunar day (*tithi*) and so forth. *Saṃvatsaratama* refers to a part such as a month and so forth that completes a year.
(1833) *Ṣaṣṭhac-ādeś-cā-saṅkhyādeḥ* | 5|2|58 | [The suffix *tamaP* is applied after a word ending in the sixth case, provided it does not begin with a numeral.]

Regarding the rule "after a word ending in ṣaṣṭhī [ṣaṣṭha-] that does not begin with a numeral": the meaning is that the augment *tamaṭ* is invariably added to the suffix *ḍaṭ* following a word ending in ṣaṣṭhī when it has a numeral as its prior member (*pūrvapada*). This is an exception to the optional rule "after words beginning with *viṃśati*. Examples are *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ* and *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ*. Because it begins with a numeral, the suffix is necessarily applied.

In the absence of *tamaṭ*, there is an option for *tamaṭ* after words beginning with twenty by the rule "ṭhviṃśatyādibhyaḥ. In the absence of *tamaṭ*, when the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied, the form "ekaṣaṣṭa" arises through the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule "ṭhyasyeti ca. Now, one might object:
how can there be any possibility of the application of *tamaṭ* to a word like "ṣaṣṭi," which is prescribed as invariably taking *tamaṭ* when it is a simple ordinal number?

Although the rule for the augment *tamaḍ* is not a rule conditioned by a suffix (*apratyayavidhi*), it indicates that a *prātipadika* which contains the marker *ṭh* is subject to the extension of a rule to what ends with it (*tadantavidhi*). This is because of the marker *ṭh*;
thus, the preceding rule "from *viṃśati* and so on" applies even in cases such as *ekaviṃśatitamaḥ*, as is clear from the Bhāṣya.
And thus, it is also established that [the word] "ekānnaviṃśatitamaḥ" is valid. (1834) *matau cchaḥ sūktasāmnoḥ* | 5|2|59|.
Regarding *matau cchaḥ*: the word "matu" is used here as a metonym for the sense of possession (*matvartha*); hence he says "in the sense of possession. [The suffix] *acchā*...
Regarding the phrase *vākīyaṃ sūktam*: the analysis of the compound is either "that which has the word *acchāvāka* [as its subject]" (*asya asti*) or "that which exists in this" (*asmin asti*).

The meaning is "that which is joined with the word *acchāvāka*. From the word *acchāvāka*, which denotes the form of the word itself and ends in the nominative case, the suffix *cha* is applied. Regarding the phrase *vāravantīyaṃ sāma*: having added the suffix *ṭhañ*.
The meaning is that [the Sāman] is "superimposed" (*adhyūḍha*) upon this *ṛc* beginning with "vāravantīm. The same applies to the term "asyavāmīya":
it is derived from the word "asyavāma," which is an imitation of a portion [of the verse] starting with "asya vāmasya. From that, the suffix *cha* is applied;
the meaning is "that which is connected with the word 'asyavāma'."
Because the rule *ṭhprakṛtivadanukaraṇam* ("an imitation [word] is like its original") is not universally valid (*anitya*), there is no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*).

(1835) *adhyāyānuvākayorluk* | 5|2|60 | Regarding the elision of the case-ending when referring to chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*): [Objection] But if the chapter and section are the objects denoted, then for the suffix *ccha*...
How is the attainment [of the suffix] established? Since there is a restrictive rule stating "in the case of *sūkta* and *sāman*," he says: "for this very reason.

Regarding "the prescription" (*vidhāna*): Kaiyaṭa maintains that since this sūtra ought to have been formulated within the section on the possessive suffix *-matup*, the force of prescribing the elision (*luk*) of *ccha* here in this particular section [establishes it]. Others hold that it is established by the force of the prescription based on an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, the statement "the elision (luṅ) of the suffixes for chapter (adhyāya) or section (anuvāka) should be stated" has been introduced. Examples are *gardabhāṇḍaḥ* and *gardabhāṇḍīyaḥ*.
The meaning is that it refers to a chapter or a section associated with the word *gardabhāṇḍa*.
From the very examples cited in the Bhāṣya, one should search for a chapter or anuvāka bearing this name [i.e., *vimukta*] in some instances.
(1836) *vimuktādibhyo’ṇ* || 5.2.61 || From *vimukta* and others, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. For example: *vaimukta*.
The meaning is that a chapter (*adhyāya*) or a section (*anuvāka*) joined with the word *vimukta* [takes the suffix].
(1837) *goṣadādibhyo vun* | 5|2|62|.
From *goṣad* and others, the suffix *vun* is applied. For example: *goṣadaka*.
The meaning is: a chapter (adhyāya) or a section (anuvāka) associated with the word *goṣada*. Regarding the phrase *iṣetva*:
the meaning is "that which is joined with the word *iṣe tva*. In the case of *asyavāmīya*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) does not occur, according to the method explained therein.

(1838) *tatra kuśalaḥ pathaḥ* |5|2|63|. Regarding the rule *tatra kuśalaḥ pathaḥ*: the suffix *vuñ* is added. This means that the suffix *vuñ* is added after the word *pathin* ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) in the sense of "skilled in" (*kuśala*). Thus, *pathaka*. [In this formation], after the substitution of *āk*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion by the rule *ṭnastaddhite*.

(1839) *ākarṣādibhyaḥ kan* || 5.2.64 || [The suffix] *kan* is added after [the group of words] beginning with *ākarṣa*. For example: *ākarṣakaḥ*. Although this could have been formed by the suffix *vuñ* which is understood from the previous rule...
Nevertheless, the inclusion of *kaṅ* is for the sake of such meanings as "one who knows omens" (*śakunika*).

(1840) *Dhanahiraṇyātkāme* |5|2|65|. [The rule] "in that [context]" (*tatra*) is understood to follow. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *dhana* and *hiraṇya* when desire (*kāma*) is expressed.

The meaning is that the suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case when "desire" (*kāma*) is to be expressed. "Desire" means "longing" (*icchā*), and not "one who desires" (*kāmayitṛ*), according to the explanation; this is the intended sense. (1841) *svāṅgebhyaḥ prasite* (Pāṇini 5.2.66).

[The suffix *kan*] is applied after [words denoting] one’s own limbs (*svāṅga*) when they end in the locative case, provided the sense is "intent upon" (*prasita*). The word "therein" (*tatra*) is understood from the previous rule.
The meaning is that *kan* occurs after words ending in the locative case denoting one’s own limbs when the sense is "intent upon. "Intent upon" (*prasita*) means "eager" (*utsuka*).

Regarding the phrase "in its arrangement" (*tadracanāyām*), the meaning is "in the weaving together of braids and so forth" (*veṇyādigrathane*). Its grammatical correctness is established only in this specific sense, according to the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied].

(1842) *udarāṭ-ṭhag ādyūne* |5|2|67|. From the word *udara*, the suffix *ṭhag* is applied in the sense of "addicted to" (*prasita*), provided that the addiction is not for the purpose of eating (*ādyūna*). The phrase "addicted to" (*tatra prasitaḥ*) is understood to carry over from the previous rule.

Intending to convey that the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *udara* ending in the seventh case when the sense is "one who is hungry" (*ādya-ūna*), he explains the term *ādya-ūna*, saying: "not desiring to win" (*avijigīṣau*).
This is because [the rule] "after the root *div*, except in the sense of desiring to win" (*divo 'vijigīṣāyām*) restricts the application of the suffix to cases where there is no desire to win.

The meaning is that this is because [the text] prescribes [the action] as being for the sake of completion (*niṣṭhā*). Regarding "by hunger" (*bubhukṣayā*): it means that one who is actually afflicted by hunger is intent on rubbing his belly, and not, like a wrestler, out of a desire for victory in combat.
Regarding "Udaraka": the word "malla" (wrestler) is to be supplied; for he [is one who acts] out of a desire for victory in battle.

He becomes eager for such things as rubbing the belly; thus it says: "addicted to rubbing the belly," etc., with the word "for the sake of victory" (*vijigīṣayā*) understood. (1843) *sasyena parijātaḥ* | 5|2|68|.

"Born from grain" (*sasyena parijātaḥ*). The meaning is that the suffix *kan* is applied after the word *sasya*, which ends in the third case, in the sense of "born from. To the question, "Why does the suffix *ṭhak* itself not follow here? he replies: "The suffix *kan* is prescribed, but not *ṭhak*. However, if there were a commitment to the *svarita* accent [indicating its recurrence], [it would follow].

The tradition of Pāṇini alone is the authority. Regarding the term "guṇavācī" (denoting a quality), the commentary itself is the refuge here. Regarding "śasyena": from the root *śaṃsu* in the sense of "praise," the word *śasya*—formed with the suffix *yat* in the passive sense—is a synonym for "praiseworthy. The underlying idea is that what is praiseworthy is indeed a quality (*guṇa*). [The word] *parijāta*.
The explanation of this [sūtra] is "connected" (*saṃbaddha*).

(1844) *Aṃśaṃ hārī* |5|2|69|. Regarding *aṃśaṃ hārī*: the meaning is that the suffix *kan* is applied after the word *aṃśa* ending in the second case, in the sense of "one who takes" (*hārī*). Now, [an objection]:...
Since there would be the contingency of the genitive case being used due to its connection with a *kṛt* suffix [as in *aṃśasya*], how is it that the accusative (*aṃśam*) is used?
To this he says: "The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity. The remainder of the sense is: "by means of the rule *āvaśyakādhamarṇyayor ṇiniḥ*.
"There is no genitive" means that the prohibition of the genitive applies because of the rule *ṭhakānor arthāntarayoḥ*. This is the intended meaning.

(1845) *tantrādacirāpahṛte* |5|2|70|. The meaning is that the suffix *kan* is added after the word *tantra*, ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), when the sense is "recently removed. *Tantra* refers to the shuttle of a weaver. "Recently" means by a short period of time.
*Apahṛtaḥ* means "recently carried away. The compound is formed according to the rule *kālāḥ parimāṇinā*. *Pratyagra* means "fresh" or "new.
(1846) *brāhmaṇakoṣṇike saṃjñāyām* || 5.2.71 || [The suffix *kan* is applied after *brāhmaṇa* and *uṣṇa* when they form a proper name.]

Regarding *brāhmaṇakoṣṇika*: the meaning is that the suffix *kan* is applied after the word *brāhmaṇa*, when used in the sense of "in this [place]" (*asmin*) and ending in the nominative case, provided it refers to a region inhabited by those who live by arms (*āyudhajīvin*). Regarding the word *alpānna*: the suffix *kan* is added after the word *alpānna* ending in the nominative case in the sense of "in this," and the base form is replaced by *uṣṇa*.
The meaning is that [the suffix] is elided.

(1847) *śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi* | 5|2|72|. From the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa*, [the suffix *kha* is applied] in the sense of "one who acts. *Śītam iva śītam* means "slowly," as if it were cold. *Uṣṇam iva uṣṇam* [means "quickly," as if it were hot].

The meaning is "quickly. The sense is that the suffix *kan* occurs after these two adverbs ending in the accusative case. One who performs tasks that ought to be done quickly only after a long time is called *śītaka*;
however, one who performs tasks that ought not to be done quickly very quickly is called *uṣṇaka*.

In the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa states that this meaning is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *saṃjñāyām* ("when it is a name"). He says: "The word *śītakaḥ* means 'lazy,' and *uṣṇakaḥ* means 'one who acts quickly. (1848) *adhikaḥ* 5.2.73.

"Adhika" [is derived] from the word "adhyārūḍha"; this is merely an etymological derivation. It should be understood that this is strictly a conventional term (*rūḍha*). (1849) *Anuka*, *abhika*, and *abhīka* mean "one who desires. Pāṇini 5.2.74.
*anukābhikā*: a collective dvandva compound of *anuka*, *abhika*, and *abhīka*; the masculine gender is used according to the sūtra. (1850) *pārśvenānvicchati* (Pāṇini 5.2.75).

*Pārśvenānviccheti*: From the word *pārśva* ending in the third case, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "seeking" (*anvicchati*) when it denotes a name; this means "searching" (*anveṣaṇa*) or "investigation" (*umārgaṇa*). Like a side (*pārśvam*), a "side" (*pārśvam*) is a crooked means (*anṛjur upāyaḥ*). [It is not to be sought] by a straight means (*ṛjūpāyena*).
"The term *pārśvaka* refers to one who seeks objects that ought to be sought by means other than honest," so says the Bhāṣya. Thus he says: "dishonest" (*anṛju*), etc.
(1851) *ayaḥśūla-daṇḍājābhyāṃ ṭhak-ṭhañau* (Pāṇini 5.2.76).

*ayaḥśūla*. The meaning is that when *ayaḥśūla* and *jaṇḍājina*, ending in the third case, signify "one who seeks after," the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* are applied in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). *Ayaḥśūlam* means "like an iron spike"; it signifies a rash or reckless act (*sāhasa*). Whoever...

"Things that should be sought through gentle means, he seeks through harsh means; he is an 'āyaḥśūlika'," so says the Bhāṣya. Regarding this, he says: "by harsh means," and so forth. As for "deceit" (dambha):
the meaning is that because it serves the purpose of deception, the word *daṇḍājina* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote deceit.

(1852) *Tāvatitham grahaṇam iti lug vā* |5|2|77|. *Tāvatitham*: "The ordinal of so many" (*tāvatām pūraṇam tāvatitham*); this is a general designation for those [words] ending in ordinal suffixes. The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. The word *grahaṇam* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*, denoting the abstract action (*bhāve*).

And likewise, with the intention that the suffix *kan* occurs after a word ending in the third case and a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) in the sense of "taking [that much]," and that there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of that ordinal suffix, he says "kansyāt," etc. However, regarding that which ends in a ordinal suffix...

There is no elision (*luk*) of the base form, but rather only of the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*), as evidenced by the example in the *Bhāṣya*: "he takes with the sixth [part], [making] a group of six" (*ṣaṣṭhena gṛhṇāti ṣaṭkam*). By the phrase "by the second form," it is indicated that the third case alone is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*). By the word "iti," its conformity to common worldly usage is shown.
It is understood. And thus, in this context, the mention of *grahaṇi* results in [the application of the suffix] only with reference to the book (*grantha*).
Therefore, in examples such as "Devadatta takes hold of the staff" (*devadatena daṇḍasya*), it does not occur.
(1) The suffix *kan* should be stated [after the word] *tāvatitha* in the sense of "he takes hold of," and there is always elision (*luk*) [of the suffix].
Regarding the phrase "by that ordinal": since [the suffix] prescribed for the sense of "taking" (*grahaṇa*) would not apply to the "taker" (*grahītṛ*), this rule is commenced.

As for the example "Devadatta is sixfold" (*ṣaṭko devadattaḥ*), because it is cited in exactly this way in the Bhāṣya, it is understood that there is elision (*luk*) of only the ordinal suffix itself, and not of the entire word ending in that suffix.

(1853) *sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ* |5|2|78|. The meaning is: the suffix *kan* is added after a word ending in the nominative case that denotes a specific type of leader (*grāmaṇī*), in the sense of "he is the leader of these. For example: *devadatto mukhya eṣām* ("Devadatta is the chief among these"). By this [rule], the word *grāmaṇī*...

It is indicated that this is the primary derivative meaning (*mukhyaparyāya*). Amara states: "The word *grāmaṇī* refers to a barber in the masculine, to an excellent person, and to the lord of a village in the three genders. Regarding *tvatkāḥ* and *matkāḥ*, the analysis is: "You (*tvam*) or I (*aham*) am the chief (*mukhya*) among these. By the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, the forms *tvam* and *aham* become *tva* and *ma*; this is its chain of derivation (*śṛṅkhalam*).

Regarding the word *karabhe*: the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*). The term *bandhanam* is derived from the root with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*).

In the analysis (*vigraha*)—"the chain (*śṛṅkhalam*) is the bond (*bandhanam*) of this young elephant (*karabhasya*)"—since the word *śṛṅkhala* functions as an adjective qualifying the bond, it takes the nominative case; thus, from the word *śṛṅkhala* ending in the nominative, the sense "of this young elephant" is expressed.
The meaning is "from whom? Regarding *śrṛṅkhalaka*: it means one who is bound by a chain.
*Karabha* is a young camel. (1854) *Utka* means "eager" (*unmanāḥ*). 5|2|80.

*Utka* means *unmanāḥ* (one whose mind is distracted). It refers to one whose mental activity has arisen; the meaning is "one whose state of longing has arisen. (1855) *Kālaprayojanādroge* [Pāṇini 5.2.81]. Regarding *kālaprayojanāt*: this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*) consisting of *kāla* (time) and *prayojana* (purpose/motive).
Thus he says: "Because of the mention of time and because of the mention of purpose.

The phrase "ending in the appropriate case-ending" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, by the word *kāla* (time), only words such as *dvitīya* (second) and so forth—which denote time and end in a taddhita suffix of completion (*pūraṇapratyaya*)—are understood, and not others.

The word *māsa* (month) and so forth [is used] because of the [author’s] explanation. Thus he says: "on the second day. [In the term *prayojana*,] when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), it means the "means" (*sādhana*); but when *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), it means the "result" (*phala*). Thus he says: "the *prayojana* is either the cause of the disease or its result."

(1856) *tadasminn annaṃ prāye saṃjñāyām* |5|2|82|. The meaning is: after a word denoting food ending in the nominative case, the suffix *kan* shall be added in the sense of "this contains that," provided that abundance of food is implied and it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *ini* is prescribed after the word *vaṭaka*.

Thus, one says *vaṭakebhyaḥ*. However, by the rule *saṃjñāyām* [Pāṇini 4.3.147], the form *vaṭakinī* is also derived. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "In this full-moon day (*praurṇamāsī*), *vaṭakas* are generally the food."
(1857) *kulmāṣād-añ* | Pāṇini 5.2.83.

The suffix *añ* [is applied] after *kulmāṣa*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *kan*. Amarasimha states: "The *syādyāvaka*, *kulmāṣa*, *caṇaka*, and *harimantha* are synonyms for chickpeas."

(1858) *śrotriyaś chando’dhīte* | P. 5.2.84. The term *śrotriya* is formed when the sense is "one who has studied the Veda (*chandas*). The suffix *ghan* is applied after the word *chandas* ending in the second case, and the substitution of *śrotra* for the base is prescribed by nipātana. This is an exception to the suffix *itraṇ*.
Regarding the phrase "from *vettyavṛteḥ*": by means of a *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) [ellipsis], the word "in that many" (*tāvatitham*) is understood from the preceding sūtra.

Consequently, the sense is that when the suffix *ghan* does not occur, there is the suffix *adhyetraṇ*. It should be understood, however, that if the term *vā* ("optionally") were not carried over [by anuvṛtti], then *adhyetraṇ* would invariably supersede *ghan*.
(1859) *śrāddham anena bhuktam* (Pāṇini 5.2.85). The suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are applied after the word *śrāddha* ending in the nominative case, in the sense of "this has been eaten by him.
(The meaning is that these two suffixes occur in this sense). Here, the word *śrāddha* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer to the substances used for the *śrāddha* rite.
In the suffix *ini*, the vowel *i* following the letter *n* is for the sake of pronunciation.

(1860) *pūrvādiniḥ* | 5.2.86 | From "pūrva" comes *ini*. By this [sūtra], the word ending in the third case (*kartṛ-tṛtīyā*) meaning "by means of which" (*anena*) is understood as being carried over. Which action?

When there is an expectancy for an agent (*kartṛ*) in the form "by whom," some verbal action such as "eaten" (*bhukta*) or "drunk" (*pīta*) must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). Because it is what is most proximate, only the general action denoted by the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is understood. Consequently, in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*), it means "this was previously done by him."

The meaning is that the suffix *ini* should occur after the word *pūrva*— used as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) such as *kṛtam* ("done") and so forth— in the sense of "by this. (1861) *sapūrvācca* | Pāṇini 5.2.87.

*Sapūrvācca*: The meaning is that the suffix *ini* should also occur after the word *pūrva* when it is preceded by another [word], within the scope of the aforementioned rule. In other words, this applies when it is at the end of a compound (*pūrvāntāt*). Although there is a prohibition against treating a word as ending in a specific form (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is prescribed for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), this sūtra is provided because [the application] would otherwise not occur. Example: *kṛtapūrvī*.
Regarding the word *kaṭam*: whatever needs to be said here has already been stated under the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). (1862) *iṣṭādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.88):
from words such as *iṣṭa* and others, when they end in the third case, the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of "by means of this."
The meaning is "it may be so.
(1863) *Chandasi paripanthi-paripariṇau paryavasthātari* |5|2|89|.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the words *paripanthi*, *paripanthin*, and *pariparin* [are used] in the sense of one who stands as an obstacle.

These two [terms] are derived when the sense of "obstructor" (*paryavasthātṛ*) is to be expressed. When the suffix *ini* is added to the word *paryavasthātṛ*, the substitution of *pantha* for the word *avasthātṛ* results in the form *paripanthin*. When the suffix *ini* is added to the word *paryavasthātṛ*, the substitution of *para* for the word *avasthātṛ* [results in the form *parapathin*].

The word *paripari* [is used] as an example in the Śruti: "May those who lie in wait find you not; may those who waylay you find you not. This sūtra is more appropriately explained within the context of Vedic grammar itself.

(1864) *anupad* [is used] in the sense of "one who searches. 5|2|90. *anupad* means "one who searches. *Anupada* means "behind the foot" (*padasya paścāt*). It is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "behind. There is the substitution of *am* for the locative case ending. From the word *anupada*, the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of "one who searches."
It is elided.
(1865) *sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām* |5|2|91|. Regarding "the direct witness": *sākṣāt* is an indeclinable; here it refers to the form of the word itself.
The fifth case ending has been elided. The meaning is that the suffix *ini* occurs after the indeclinable *sākṣāt* in the sense of "one who sees.

Regarding the word *sākṣī*: one who does not personally engage in an action, but rather observes the action being performed, is called a *sākṣī*. The suffix *ini* is applied to the indeclinable *sākṣāt*.
There is elision of the *ṭi* portion by the rule "ṭhavyayānāṃ bhamātre" [Pāṇini 6.4.143].
(1866) *kṣetriyac* means "curable in another's field. [Pāṇini 5.2.92] *Kṣetriyac*. Another field (*param anyat kṣetram*) is the "other body" (*parakṣetram*).

"Cikitsya" means incurable; this is because it is stated that the root *kit* [is used] in the sense of "counteracting a disease. From the word *parakṣetra*, ending in the locative case, the suffix *ghac* is applied in the sense of "to be treated," and the elision of the word *para* is also prescribed by rule. "In another body" means: he is to be treated in a future body, but not [in the present one].
"Varmāne" means in the body; he states the resulting conclusion: "it is not remediable.
(1867) *Indriya* [is derived from] *indraliṅga*, *indradṛṣṭa*, *indrasṛṣṭa*, *indrajūṣṭa*, or *indradatta*. (Pāṇini 5.2.93).

*Indriya*: The word *indriya* occurs in such senses as "the mark of Indra" (*indra-liṅga*) and so forth. That is to say, from the word *indra*, ending in either the genitive or instrumental case, the suffix *ghac* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) according to the requirements of the sense, such as "mark" (*liṅga*) and so on. Thus, "Indra is the Self" (*indra ātmā*). [As it is said: "He [perceived] this very person as Brahman... (*sa etameva puruṣaṃ brahma...*);... [and so on].

The sense is that it is based on the Vedic scripture (Śruti): "He saw this [world] as extended; 'I have seen this,' he thought. Therefore his name is Idandra. Indeed, though he is Idandra by name, they call him Indra. Regarding the phrase "his mark" (tasya liṅgam), the meaning is that which serves as an inferential indicator (anumāpaka) of the Self.

He establishes its status as a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) with the words "by means of the instrument" (*karaṇena*). The meaning is that this follows from the inference: "The sense organs, such as the eye and so forth, must be presided over by an agent, because they are instruments, just like the staff and other tools used as instruments for making a pot. [This is known] through the sense organ being designated as "my eye" by the individual self (*indriya*).

The sense-faculty (*indriya*) is that which has been seen and known. Or, *indriya* is that which is favored, served, or gratified by Indra. This is a conventional term (*rūḍha-śabda*) that has been etymologically derived in some way. To establish that "the sense-faculty is difficult for Indra to conquer," he says: "the word 'iti'. The meaning is that it is the word "iti."

(1868) *tadasyāstyasminniti matup* | 5|2|94. Regarding the rule *tadasyāstyasminniti matup*: when there is an analysis (*vigraha*) such as "that belongs to him" (*tadasyāsti*) or "that exists in this" (*tadasminasti*), the suffix *matup* is applied after a word ending in the nominative case that is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the sense of "his" (*asya*) or "in this" (*asmin*).

The meaning is that the suffix *matup* should occur. [In the rule] "upādhviti," the word *iti* is for the purpose of specifying the particular scope [of the application]. He states this: "in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*) and in censure (*nindā*). This is a verse-commentary (*ślokavārtika*). "Abundance" means multiplicity; as in *gomān* (possessing cows) and *yavamān* (possessing barley). In the sense of censure—as in "a girl with a humpbacked deformity" (*kakudāvartinī kanyā*).

In the sense of praise: *rūpavān* (handsome). In the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*): *kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ* (trees that have [or are always] milky sap). In the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*): *udariṇī kanyā* (a girl with a prominent belly). In the sense of contact (*saṃsarga*): *daṇḍī* (staff-bearer) or *chatrī* (umbrella-bearer). A specific kind of contact that restricts the function is intended here; therefore, there is no such expression as *paruṣī daṇḍaḥ* (a harsh staff).

(1869) *rasādibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 5.2.95. [The sūtra states: "And from *rasa* and so forth, the suffix *ṭa* [is applied]. [The commentary adds: "The suffix *matup* [is also applied]. This is a supplement to the rule (*śeṣapūraṇa*). The phrase "in the scope already mentioned" (*uktaviṣaye*) is the remainder of the context. Since the desired form is already established by the preceding rule alone, one might ask: for what purpose is this [separate] rule stated? To this, he says: "To exclude other possessive suffixes" (*anyamatvarthīya*).
The meaning is that [the rule] is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] "ṭhata iniṭhanau" and so forth.

He recites "rasa" and the others—starting with "rasarūpa" and ending with "bhāva. Regarding "guṇāt": "ekācaḥ" is a *gaṇasūtra*. He provides an example: "svavān. Regarding the mention of "guṇa": [it serves as a qualifier].

The meaning is that the term "quality" (*guṇa*) is a qualifier for the six [categories] beginning with taste (*rasa*). Therefore, since only those words denoting qualities are included here, the intention is that words such as *rasa* when they denote water and so forth, as well as words such as *gandha* when they denote substances, are not included in this context. [As in the example: "one who relishes flavors" (*rasikaḥ*).

The actor [says]: "Because of the observation of usage such as *sparśikaṃ vāri* ('water that touches'), this sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. (1870) *tasau matvarthe* | 1.4.19 | [This sūtra, which prescribes the substitution of *t* for *ta* when followed by a suffix with the sense of possession (*matvartha*), is rejected. Because we see such usage as *sparśikaṃ vāri* ("water that possesses touch"), this rule has been set aside in the Bhāṣya. (1870) *tasau matvarthe* | 1.4.19 |

Now, one might object: since the word *vidvat* lacks the suffix *matup* followed by a root beginning with *yaj* or a suffix beginning with *sva*, it does not possess the status of a *bha*-stem; therefore, how can there be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "there is vocalization of the *vas* [ending]? To this, he says: "In the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), [the forms ending in] *t* and *as* [are treated as *bha*]."

Intending the rule *tadantavidhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element), because the base [of the word] is implied by the possessive suffix (*matvarthapratyaya*), he says: "those ending in *ta* and *sa*" (*tāntasāntau*). This means those ending in the letters *t* and *s*.

The statement "after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), the elision (*luk*) of the possessive suffix *matup* is desired" is a Vārttika. It refers to those words which are well-known as denoting either a quality (*guṇa*) or a possessor of a quality (*guṇavat*).

Only words such as *śukla* (white) and the like are understood here, and not words such as *rūpa* (form/color) as well; therefore, expressions such as *rūpaṃ vastram* (the cloth is form) do not occur. What must be said regarding this has been explained by us in detail in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* section of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākautūhala*.

(1871) *mādupadhāyāśca matvarthe 'yavādibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.121. *mādupadhāyāśca*: The analysis of the compound is *māt* and *upadhāyāḥ*. The term *māt* recurs [from the previous rule]. The form *mū ca aḥ* is a singular ablative case from a collective dvandva compound (*samāhāradvandva*) consisting of *m* and *a*. [The rule means: The suffix *matup* is applied after words ending in *m*, words ending in *a*, and words having *m* or *a* as their penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel, provided they are not among the group beginning with *yava*.
The suffix is used in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).

Because it serves as a qualifier for the nominal stem (prātipadika) implied by the suffix *matup*, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in [the specified letters]. One interpretation is: "The *m* of the suffix *mat* should become *v* when it follows a nominal stem ending in the letter *ṇ* or the letter *a*. In this context, the term "after *m*" (*māt*) is a qualifier of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), meaning "that which consists of the letter *m*."

And another meaning is that the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) which consists of the letter *a*, followed by this [suffix], causes the *m* of the suffix *mat* to become *v*. He states the resulting form with the words beginning "mavarṇa" etc.
He gives an example ending in *m*: *kiṃvān*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has 'what' (*kim*) in it" or "in this."

The same applies in the following cases as well. He provides an example from a word ending in *a*: *jñānavān* (possessing knowledge). Here, considering that the long vowel *ā* is also included because of the absence of the *tapara* marker (*ṛ*), he gives another example: *vidyāvān* (possessing learning). He provides an example from a word with *m* as its penultimate letter (*mopadha*): *lakṣmīvān* (possessing fortune).

He gives an example of a word with *a* as its penultimate letter (*adupadāt*): *yaśasvān*. Because of the rule "tasau matvarthe" (Pāṇini 1.4.19), it is treated as a *bha*-stem, and thus the substitution of *ru* does not take place. He gives an example of a word with *ā* as its penultimate letter (*ākāropadhāt*): *lakṣmīvān*.

He gives an example of a word with *a* as its penultimate letter (*adupadāt*): *yaśasvān*. Because of the rule "tasau matvarthe," it is treated as a *bha*-stem, and thus [the substitution of *ru* does not take place].
The substitution of *r* occurs. He gives an example from a word having *ā* as its penultimate (*upadhā*): *bhāsvān*.
(Pāṇini 8.2.10) *jhayaḥ*.
Now, regarding the form *vidyautvān*:

Since the conditions for the application of the rule *mādupadhāyāś ca* do not exist—namely, because there is neither the presence of the letter *m* at the end nor the presence of the letter *a* as a penultimate (*upadhā*)—the substitution of *v* does not apply;

therefore, he says: "after a *jhay*. The reason given is "because it is not at the end of a word" (*apadāntatvāt*). The underlying intention is that, by the rule *tasau matvarthe*, [the suffix] is treated as a *bha*-stem, which subverts its status as a *pada*.

(1873) *saṃjñāyām* |8|2|13|. Regarding the term *saṃjñāyām*: [the forms] *ahīvatī* and so forth are names (*saṃjñā*) of particular rivers or particular cities. "Because of being among the *śara*-group" means that there is lengthening of the vowel according to the rule *śarādīnāṃ ca*.

(1874) *āsandīvad-aṣṭhīvad-cakrīvad-kakṣīvad-rumaṇvad-carmaṇvat* (Pāṇini 8.2.12). Regarding *āsandīvat*: in a collective dvandva compound, there is shortening [of the final vowel]. It is stated that these are "irregularly formed" (*nipātyante*). Here, only the transformation into *āsandī* and so forth is irregularly formed; however, the suffix *-vat* is established by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (5.2.137).

Regarding the statement "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *kakṣyā*," the word "it is an irregular formation (*nipātita*)" is to be supplied as the remainder. However, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule "not when there is vocalization" (*na samprasāraṇe*), it is begun with the statement: "In the sense of the suffix *matup*, when it is a name (*saṃjñā*), vocalization of *kakṣyā* must be stated. Therefore, they say that the inclusion of the word *kakṣīvat* in this [present] sūtra is not the work of the Sage (*anārṣa*).

(1875) *udanvān* [is substituted for *udaka-vat*] in the word *udadhi* and when it is a proper name. That is, *udanvān* is used for *udadhi* when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). However, in reality...

It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as "udanvān ca," because by the continued application of the term "in a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām*), the word *udanvat* is already established for "ocean" as well.
(1876) *rājanvān* [is used] in the sense of good governance (*saurājye*). Pāṇini 5.2.14.
*Rājanvān* means "possessing good rule. A country whose king is very beautiful (*su-śobhana*) is a *surājā*;

the state of being such is *saurājyam*. In that sense, the suffix *matup* added to the word *rājan* results in the form *rājanvat*, where the substitution of *v* for *m* is established by the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ*. The absence of the elision (*lopa*) of the final *n* is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

(1877) *prāṇisthādāto lajanyatarasyām* |5|2|96|. The meaning is that after a word denoting something residing in a living being (*prāṇistha*), ending in the vowel *ā*, the suffix *lac* may optionally be added in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). For example: *śikhāvān dīpaḥ* ("a lamp with a flame"). Here, the word *śikhā* denotes the tip of the lamp.

The sense is that [the suffix] *lac* does not apply because there is an absence of the quality of denoting something residing in a living being (*prāṇistha*). The sense is that [the rule applies] "only from parts of a living being" (*prāṇyaṅgāt*), because such is stated in the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: if *lac* were applied, its formation would be useless, since the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) required by the rule "of a *cita*" (*citaḥ*) is already established by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*). To this, [the author replies:]...

He said: "By means of the accent of the suffix. [In the phrase] "cūḍālo'si," the word *asi* is elided by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. From *cūḍālaḥ*, after the substitution of *ru* and then *u*, because that [substitute] is a *suptva* (a case-ending), it is *anudātta* (unaccented). Then, for the resulting *guṇa* vowel *o*, by the rule *ekādeśa udāteneodāttaḥ*, it becomes *udātta* (accented). Of that...

The meaning is that when a single substitute (ekādeśa) replaces both the preceding and following elements, and that [substitute] is unaccented at the beginning of a word, the rule "svarito vānudāte" would apply because [the substitute] shares the same status as a single substitute with its predecessor; therefore, the marker *cit* is employed to prevent that application.

(1878) *Sidhmādibhyaś ca* | 5.2.97 | "And from *sidhma* and so forth. [The word] *lañ* may optionally [be applied]; this means it occurs in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), as is understood from the context. Regarding the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*): it is not the case that the word "optionally" is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the preceding rule.
The term *anyatarasyām* does not have the sense of an optional suffix *lac*, but rather has the sense of a collective [inclusion] of the suffix *matup*;

for *anyatarasyām* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and thus possesses multiple meanings. Consequently, it is understood that from the group beginning with *sidhma*, both the suffix *lac* and the suffix *matup* may occur. And this is not the case here for *anyatarasyām*.

Even though [the suffix] *lac* has the sense of expressing a conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*), it must be stated that when that [suffix] is absent, the suffix *matup* is established; for this purpose, a collective rule (*samuccaya-vidhāna*) is prescribed, meaning: "In the absence of *lac*, only *matup* occurs, and not *ini* or *ṭhan* after *at*. He says this with the words "by that" (*tena*). As for those [words] among the *sidhma*-group...
The meaning is that the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* do not apply after those words ending in the vowel *a*. All of this is clear in the Bhāṣya.

Words such as *sidhma*, *gaḍu*, *maṇi*, *vijaya*, *niṣpāva*, *pāṃsu*, *hanu*, and *pārṣṇi* are listed among the *sidhmādi* group. And thus, in the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇavākya*), it is said that there would be the suffix *lac*.

The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and). This mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) recurs in all subsequent sūtras concerning the prescription of suffixes with the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), but not in the case of conventional (*rūḍha*) words. Therefore, there is no compounding of *matup* with them; let this suffice for now. [The rule continues: "And *ūṅ* is substituted for the final vowel of *vāta*, *danta*, *bala*, and *lalāṭa*."

This is a sūtra from the *Sighmādi-gaṇa*. From these [roots], the suffix *lac* is applied, and *ūṅ* is the substitute for the original base (*prakṛti*). The letter *ṅ*, however, is for the purpose of indicating that it is not a suffix (*pratyaya*); otherwise, there might be a suspicion that it is a suffix. Examples: *vātūlaḥ*, likewise *dantūlaḥ*, *balūlaḥ*, *lalāṭūlaḥ*.

(1879) *vatsāsābhyāṃ kāmabale* |5|2|98|. From the words *vat* and *as*, the suffix *lac* is applied; this is to be understood as being for the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Intending that the words *kāma* and *bala* are used here figuratively to denote those who possess them, he says: "in one who has desire" and "in one who has strength."

(1880) *phenādibhyaś ca* |5|2|99|. [The word] *matvarthe* is to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule]. Because of the word *ca*, [the suffix] *lañ* is also included; the intention is that it is due to its proximity [to the previous rule].
Now, if this were the case, the suffix *matup* would not occur at all; therefore—
He said: "The mention of 'either one' (*anyatarasyām*). This has been explained in the sūtra on *sighra*, etc.

(Pāṇini 4.3.164). (1881) Pāṇini 5.2.100: *lomādipāmādipicchādibhyaḥ śanelacaḥ*. From the three groups beginning with *loman*, *pāman*, and *piccha*, the suffixes *śa*, *na*, and *ilac* are applied respectively.
"From *aṅga*, [the suffix] *na* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) when [the limb] is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*). This is a sūtra from the *pāmādi* group.
The meaning is that the suffix *na* is applied after the word *aṅga*—which is qualified by "auspicious," i.e., beautiful—in the sense of possession.
Regarding the form *aṅganā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose limbs (*aṅgāni*) are auspicious (*kalyāṇāni*)."

The *pāmādi-gaṇa* sūtra "lakṣmyācca" [Pāṇini 5.2.100] states that the suffix *na* occurs after the word *lakṣmī* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), and the final vowel of the base is replaced by the letter *a*. Thus, we have *lakṣmaṇa*. The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is: "he who possesses *lakṣmī*" (*lakṣmīr asya asti*). When the suffix *na* is applied, the final vowel of the base is replaced by *a*, and the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* takes place.
The word *viṣvak* [is formed] with the elision of the final member of the compound and without the application of sandhi.

Regarding *viṣvak*: some maintain that this is also a sūtra belonging to the *pāmādi* group. However, in the Bhāṣya, this is read as a Vārttika within the section on the suffix *na*. The indeclinable *viṣu* means "on all sides" (*sarvataḥ*).

*Viṣvaṅ* means "moving in various directions. Dhūrtasvāmin explains that the meaning is "one who goes everywhere. Bhavasvāmin states that the root *viṣu* has the sense of "obliquely. Bhaṭṭabhāskara says it means "turned away" (*parāṅmukha*). [Etymologically,] from the root *viṣu-añc*, the suffix *na* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) without the sandhi being applied.

It may be so; the meaning is that there is an elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*). Regarding the word *viṣuṇa*: the non-technical (secular) analysis is "one who possesses *viṣvañ*"; the non-technical analytical sentence is *viṣu-añc*.
When the suffix *na* is added to the word *viṣvak*—which has undergone sandhi—and the subsequent member is elided, [the rule] "elision of... [applies].
The intention is that by the elision of *y* according to the rule "vyoḥ," the form would become *viṣṇa*.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "samarthānām. (1882) Pāṇini 5.2.101: *prajñā-śraddhā-'rcābhyo ṇaḥ*.

*Prajñā-śraddhā-arcābhyaḥ ṣṇaḥ*: The meaning is that the suffix *ṣṇa* (which becomes *ina*) occurs after the words *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, and *arcā* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). For example, *prājñaṃ vyākaraṇam* ("grammar is possessed of wisdom"). Here, *prajñā* means "wisdom" (*prajñānam*).

Under the governing rule *striyām* ("in the feminine"), the suffix *ṭāp* is applied to the root *jñā* preceded by *pra* to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*), according to the rule *ṭāp caurupasarge*.

Aṅ: the analysis of the compound is "one who possesses wisdom" (*prajñā asyāsti*). Even though wisdom is here a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), it is not negated. What must be said regarding this has been explained in detail under the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*. Nor is one called "wise" (*prajña*) simply because he perceives (*prajānāti*); rather, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ṭhigupadh-*.

One might suspect that by adding the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense (*svārthe*) to the word *prajña*, the form *prājña* is established; however, if that were the case, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would follow. Thus he says: "prājña. Regarding "śrāddha," the analysis is: "one who has *śraddhā*. Regarding "ārca," the analysis is: "one who has *arcā*."
"And from *vṛti*.

This [phrase] "and from *vṛti*" is a Vārttika. The remainder [of the rule] is "the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Regarding *vārta*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who has *vṛti*."

(1883) *tapaḥ-sahasrābhyāṃ vinīnī* |5|2|102|. [The sūtra consists of] *tapaḥ-sahasrābhyām*, *vinīnī*. It is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the suffixes *vin* and *ini*. The phrase "in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*)" is understood as the remainder. The application follows the respective order. In the case of the suffix *vin* and the suffix *ini*, the letters *n* and *i* [are indicatory].
