[The two *n*s] are for the purpose of pronunciation. Now, one might ask: why is the *it*-designation not applied to the two *n*s? Nor is it the case that there is no purpose, since the accentuation of a *nit* (a suffix marked with *n*) would itself be the result. To this, he says: "for the sake of protecting the letter *n*. And thus, in the *upadeśa*...

The intention is that the designation *it* does not apply because [the word] lacks the status of being final (*antya*). Although the suffix *vin* is established after the word *tapas* simply by virtue of its having the *asan* suffix (via the rule *ṭhasmāyāmedha*), and the suffix *ini* is established after the word *sahasra* by the rule *ṭhata iniṭhanau*, nevertheless, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] specifically by the following rule.

Lest there be a sublation of the general rules regarding the suffixes *vin* and *ini* for words ending in vowels other than *a* and those ending in *a*, they are specifically prescribed here by the terms *tapaḥ* and *sahasra*. Furthermore, the prescription of *ini* here serves to prevent the application of the suffix *ṭhan*, which would otherwise apply to words ending in *a* due to the rule for *sahasra*. This is the resolution.
It is seen in some original manuscripts.
(1884) *aṇ* also [is applied].
5.2.103. *aṇ* also. The remainder is: "after *tapas* and *sahasra*, in the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*). Now, regarding *tapas* and *sahasra*:

Let there be only a single sūtra: *vinīnyaṇaḥ*. It should not be argued that the sūtras are formulated separately for the sake of establishing a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) between the two suffixes, *aṇ* and *vinīn*, and the two bases, *tapas* and *sahasra*; otherwise, all three suffixes would apply to both bases. This is because [the desired result] could be achieved by formulating the sūtra as *tapaḥsahasrābhyāmaṇvinīnī*.

Since the connection of *aṇ* with both [the preceding and following elements], as well as the respective correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) between *vin* and *ini*, is established simply by the utterance of different case endings, he says: "The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.
This means that it is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anuvṛtti*) *aṇ* alone in the subsequent sūtra.
There is an addition [to the rule] for words such as *jyotsnā* (moonlight):

*jyautsnaḥ*. The word "the bright fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the definition]. *Jyotsnā* means moonlight. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has this [moonlight]. *Tāmisraḥ*. The word "the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is to be understood as the remainder.

*Tamisrā* means nights joined with deep darkness (*tamas*). The analysis of the compound is: "those [nights] belong to him. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule for *jyotsnā* and others (Pāṇini 5.2.114). (1885) *Sikatā-śarkarābhyāṃ ca* (5.2.104): [The suffix *aṇ* is also applied after the words *sikatā* and *śarkarā* to form a Bahuvrīhi compound.]
And [the suffix] from *sikatā* and *śarkarā*. The remainder [of the rule] is that the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Thus, "a jar made of sand" (*saikato ghaṭaḥ*).

The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has sand" (*sikatā asya santi*). Since it will be stated later that there is elision (*lup*) when referring to a region, "jar" (*ghaṭa*) serves as the substantive. [This is according to the rule: "There is plurality for *ap*, *manas*, compounds, *sikatā*, and *varṣā*."
From the *Liṅgānuśāsana-sūtra*, the word *sikatā* is always plural.
(1886) *deśe lub-ilacau ca* | 5.2.105 | "In the case of a place-name, there is also *lup* and *ilac*. There is *lup* of the suffix *añ* prescribed by the preceding rule, and also *ilac*.

The meaning is "it may be so. [Regarding the phrase] "and not *aṇ*": the intention is that it is because of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). If that were the case, since the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply once it has been set aside by an exception (*apavāda*), the suffix *matup* would not occur at all; therefore, he says "and *matup*.
The intention is that this is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *anyatarasyām*, which signifies an option (*samuccaya*). [The example is] *sikatāḥ*.

The meaning is that after the word *sikatā*, which is invariably plural, when the suffix *aṇ* is elided (*lup*), the case-ending (*sup*) is also elided because it is part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, due to the rule of "behaving like that which is joined" (*yuktavadbhāva*), even though the location—the qualified object—is singular, the plural ending remains. This is stated in the rule *hayavaraṭ*: "And [the letter] *ekā*..."
The author of the *Liṅgānuśāsana* will state that the word *sikatā* also exists in the singular, based on its usage in the *Bhāṣya*: "Sands are incapable of yielding oil.
(1887) *danta-unnate urac* 5.2.106. [The suffix *urac* is applied after the word *danta* when it denotes something protruding.]
The meaning is that the suffix *urac* occurs after the word *danta*, which is qualified by *unnata*, in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*).
The term *unnata* is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). The word *danta* is in the locative case used in the sense of the ablative. (Pāṇini 5.2.107) *ūṣasuṣimuṣkamadho raḥ*.

*ūṣasuṣi*: This is the singular ablative case from a collective dvandva compound consisting of *ūṣa*, *suṣi*, *muṣka*, and *madhu*. The masculine gender here is due to the rule governing such compounds (*sūtra*). The meaning is that the suffix *ra* occurs after these words in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus, *ūṣara* means "possessing salt" (*ūṣaḥ*).

The analysis of the compound is: "that which possesses a particular kind of alkaline clay" (*kṣāramṛtikāviśeṣa*). Regarding the word *suṣira*: *suṣi* means a hole or cavity; the analysis is "that which possesses this. The word *madhu* refers both to the substance honey (*kṣaudra*) and to the specific quality of a particular taste characterized by sweetness (*mādhurya*). Among these, [the following applies] to that which denotes the specific taste.

He states that this is the inclusion here: "the sweetness of honey. The implication is that this is according to the Bhāṣya; otherwise, the word *madhura* (sweet) would have to be applied even to a jar containing the substance honey. *Khara* means a donkey or a fire-altar (*dhiṣṇya*). *Mukhara* means one who makes noise. *Kuñjara* means an elephant.
These are conventional words (*rūḍhaśabda*).
[The rule] "and from *naga*, *pāṃsu*, and *pāṇḍu*" is a *vārttika*. *Nagara* denotes a specific class [of things]. Therefore...
In the word *nagarī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Regarding *pāṃsura*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who has dust" (*pāṃsuram asyāsti*).

Regarding *pāṇḍura*: *pāṇḍu* is the white color; the analysis is "one who possesses that [white color]" (*sa asyāsti*). To the question "How is the word *pāṇḍara* [formed]?", he says: "But the word *pāṇḍara*... [as in] "the deer is *pāṇḍara*."
"Pāṇḍu" [is derived] according to Amara.
Regarding "kacchavā," there is also shortening.
"Kacchavā"—this is a Vārttika rule. The suffix *ap* is applied to the word *kacchū*, and there is shortening of the base form (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is that there is a substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*). *Kacchura* is a specific disease of dogs.
[Sūtra 5.2.108: "After *div* and *dru*, the suffix *ma*. Regarding the rule *diva u*: for the word *div*, which has undergone the substitution of *u* (becoming *dyu*), the form is *dyau*.
Explanation: The meaning is that the suffix *map* should be applied after the words *div* and *dru*. Thus, *dyaumaḥ* and *drumaḥ*; these two are conventional (*rūḍha*) words.
(1889) *keśād vo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.109). [The suffix *va* may optionally be applied after the word *keśa*.]
*Keśād anyatarasyām*: the remainder [of the rule] is "in the sense of the possessive suffix *mat*.

Now, one might object that the mention of *anyatarasyām* here is redundant, because the formation of the sentence would already be established by the option (*vā*) in the rule *samarthānām*. Nor can it be argued that [the sentence is not established] due to the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), which sets aside the exception.

It must be stated that the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* [in Pāṇini 4.3.59] is for the purpose of ensuring the application of the suffix *matup*, because the general rule would otherwise not apply—given that it was specifically stated in the rule *pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā* (P. 2.1.18) that the genitive is used here—and thus *matup* would fail to apply;
this is because the inclusion of *anyatarasyām* [in P. 4.3.45] follows from the rule *prāṇisthād iti*.
Since that [inclusion] would be established by the mere recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word meaning "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), he says: "by the subject under discussion" (*prakṛtena*).

Regarding the phrase "of *ini* and *ṭhan*": the meaning is "also of *ini* and *ṭhan*. Otherwise, as in the rule "and from *sidhma*, etc. (*sidhmādibhyaśca*), only *matup* would be conjoined, and not *ini* and *ṭhan*; this is the intention. And thus, when the suffix *vap* occurs:
He states that there are four forms for the suffixes *ini*, *ṭhan*, and *matup*—namely, "Keśava" and so forth.
Regarding the rule "it is also seen after others": this is a *vārttika*. It means that the suffix *va* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) after words other than "hair" (*keśa*).
The meaning is "is seen. Regarding the term *arṇasaḥ*: this is a Vārttika. Its meaning is that the suffix *vap* is applied to *arṇas*, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *s* of the base.
[This is stated as: "and the elision of the *s* of *arṇas*."

Regarding the term *arṇava*: *arṇaḥ* means water; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that in which this [water] is abundant. However, this *vārttika* is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*. (1890) *gāṇḍī-jagāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.110).
In the rule *gāṇḍījagātsaṃjñāyām*,

the mention of both *gāṇḍi* and *gāṇḍī*— that is, the forms of the word *gāṇḍi* and *gāṇḍī* after the suffix *yaṇ*— is made simultaneously, just as in the rule *khyatvātparasya* there is a simultaneous mention of the words *khiti* and *khītī*.

The meaning is "just as. Consequently, the suffix *vap* would occur after the words *gāṇḍi*, *gāṇji*, and *ajaga* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Because these are conventional (*rūḍha*) words, the suffix *matup* is not added here in conjunction with them. (1891) Kāṇḍa and aṇḍa take the suffixes *īran* and *īrac* respectively. 5.2.111.
*Kāṇḍāṇḍād īrannīracau*: The meaning is that the suffixes *īran* and *īrac* occur after the words *kāṇḍa* and *āṇḍa* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*).
(Pāṇini 5.2.112) *Rajaḥ-kṛṣi-āsuti-pariṣado valac*: [The suffix *valac* occurs after these words in the same sense].

The meaning is that the suffix *valac* is added after the words *rajas*, *kṛṣi*, *āsuti*, and *pariṣad* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Regarding the form *āsutīvala*: the root *ṣuñ* means "to press";
with the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ktin* is applied to form the feminine noun. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "before *vala*."
"Also seen after others.
Regarding "also after others": this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that the suffix *valac* is also seen after other roots besides those included in the rule beginning with "rajaḥ kṛṣi."

In *bhrātṛvalaḥ*, the long vowel [of the penultimate] does not occur by the rule *vale* because the word *aṇaḥ* is understood from the preceding rule *ṭhḍhralope*. Regarding forms such as *putravalaḥ*, one might suspect that the rule *vale* would apply the long vowel; therefore, he says: "in the case of *vale* here.
(1893) *dantaśikhātsaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.113).
Regarding the rule *dantaśikhātsaṃjñāyām*: the ablative case is used because it is a collective dvandva compound.
The meaning is that the suffix *valac* occurs after the words *danta* and *śikhā* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) when a name (*saṃjñāyām*) is being formed. (1894)

*jyotsnātamisrāśṛṅgiṇorjasvinnūrjasvalagominmalinamalīmasāḥ* || 5.2.114 || *jyotsnā*. [The word *jyotsnā* is derived] from *jyotis*. The particles of light are the *jyotīṃṣi*; that which possesses these is *jyotsnā*.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *santī*, the suffix *an* is added to the word *jyotis*, and the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *i* which constitutes the penultimate (*upadhā*) is prescribed by rule (*nipātyate*). When the vowel *i* is elided, since the condition of being followed by the root *iṇ* no longer exists, the substitution of *ṣ* (as in *ṣatva*) is precluded, resulting in the form *jyotsnā*. [Synonyms: *candrikā*, *kaumudī*.

"Jyotsnā" [is defined] by Amara. Regarding "tamasa": in the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) "that which has darkness (*tamas*)", the suffix *rak* is applied to the word *tamas*; furthermore, the meaning is that the vowel *a* following the letter *m*, which serves as the penultimate (*upadhā*), is irregularly changed to *i*.
"Tamisrā" is a night characterized by darkness (*tāmasī rātriḥ*), according to Amara. Now, one might object:
Regarding the word *tāmisram*, since it is in the feminine gender, one might ask how it can mean "a house completely enveloped in darkness";
to this he says: "the feminine gender is not essential. Regarding *śṛṅgiṇaḥ*: the remainder [of the rule] is "it is an irregular formation (*nipātyate*).
The analysis is: "one who has a horn" (*śṛṅgam asyāsti*). The suffix *in* is applied, and there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*.

"In the sense of 'conquering strength' (valajiti), [the suffix] *ṭh* is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*)," is the remainder [of the rule]. *Ūrjas* is a nominal stem ending in the suffix *asun*. Now, one might object: since the form *ūrjasvin* is already established by the rule "after *ūrj*, [the suffix] *lin* [is added] in the sense of 'possessing' (*asmāyāmedha-*)", the purpose of this irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *vin* is to ensure that the form *ūrjasvin* occurs. [The example is] *ūrjaḥ*.
The meaning is that the commentary stating "there is the augment *asuk* for the base after the word *ūrja* when *balac* follows" is untenable.

Why? To this he says: "as in the case of *ūrjasvatīḥ*. In the form *ūrjasvatīḥ*, because the suffix *matup* (expressing possession) is absent, the augment *asuk*—which is prescribed as being conditioned by that [suffix] (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*)—does not apply; therefore...

The nominal stem *ūrjas* must necessarily be accepted as ending in the suffix *asun*. This is because, by that very [stem], the forms *ūrjasvin* and *ūrjasvala* are established through the mere substitution of the suffixes *vin* and *valac*. As for the phrase "ending in *īma*," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is substituted after the word *mala*."

(1895) *ata ini-ṭhanau* | Pāṇini 5.2.115. The meaning is that after a stem ending in *a*, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* occur in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Because the term *anyatarasyām* (meaning "optionally") is understood from the previous rule as having a cumulative sense (*samuccaya*), the suffix *matup* also occurs.
The Bhāṣya states: "The [suffixes] *matup* and *vatup* are not prescribed after a monosyllabic word, after a *kṛt* [derivative], after a genus name (*jāti*), or in the locative case.
For example: *ekākṣarāt*—*subhagavān*; *kṛtaḥ*—*kārakavān*; *jāteḥ*—*vṛkṣakavān*;
*saptamyām*—*daṇḍā asyāṃ śālāyāṃ santi* → *daṇḍavatī*. This is a general rule (*prāyika*).
By this [rule], forms such as *kāryī* from *kārya*, *kāryika* from *kāryaka*, *taṇḍulī* from *taṇḍula*, and *taṇḍulika* from *taṇḍulika* are established; this is clear in the Bhāṣya.
(1896) *vrīhyādibhyaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.116).
"And from *vrīhi* and so forth. The remainder [of the rule] is "the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
(The suffix) *ini* is applied after *śikhā*, *mālā*, *saṃjñā*, and so forth.
*Śikhā*, *mālā*, etc.—this is a *vārttika*. [The words are: *śikhā*, *mālā*, *saṃjñā*, *vīṇā*.

The meaning is that after *baḍavā*, *balākā*, *patākā*, *varman*, and *śarman*, only the suffix *ini* is applied, and not *ṭhan*. Regarding *yavakhala*: after *yavakhala*, *nau*, and *kumārī*, only *ṭhan* is applied, and not *ini*. As for the remaining words listed in the *vrīhy-ādi* group:
"Both" is established by the sense [of the context]. This is clear in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
(1897) *tundādibhya ilacca* | 5|2|117|. From *tuṇḍa* and the others, there is also *ilac*; and *matup* as well.
The sense is that the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) continues to apply for the purpose of including both [the suffixes *lac* and *ini-ṭhan*].
The four words beginning with *udara-* are listed in the *tunda*-group of the Gaṇapāṭha. Regarding the rule "after a word denoting a limb of the body (*svāṅga*), when there is enlargement":
this is a *gaṇa*-sūtra. Because it pertains to the domain of enlargement (*vṛddhi*), the suffixes *lac*, *ini*, and *ṭhan* are applied after a word denoting a limb of the body.
The meaning is [the suffix] *matup*. Regarding "karṇila": the analysis is "one whose ears are large" (*vṛddhau karṇau yasya*).

(1898) *ekagopūrvāṭ ṭhañ nityam* |5|2|118|. From a word preceded by *eka* or *go*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied invariably. That is, it is invariably applied from a word preceded by *eka* and from a word preceded by *go*.
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* should occur. Although the application of *ini* and *ṭhan* is established even in the absence of the mention of "nitya" (invariably), nevertheless,
because the mention of *anyatarasyām* is intended to signify a collective option (*samuccaya*), it would follow that *matup* would also be added as an alternative.
The inclusion of the word *nitya* (always) is for the purpose of excluding that [specific case]. Regarding the term *aikaśatika*: it is a compound formed by the rule *pūrvakāla* (P.

2.1.49). However, there is no vṛddhi substitution in the final member according to the rule *saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsara-* (P. 7.3.15), because that rule applies specifically to compounds where the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning is expressed by a directly stated formation.

(1899) *śatasahasrāntāc ca niṣkāt* |5|2|119|. [The suffix *kan* is added] after a word ending in *śatasahasra* or *niṣka*. The meaning is that although there is a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) between these words and the following [word], a compound is nevertheless formed because it is a Vedic rule (*sautratvāt*).

(1900) *rūpād āhata-praśaṃsayor yap* || 5.2.120 || The suffix *yap* is added after the word *rūpa* when it is qualified by *āhata* or *praśaṃsā*, in the sense of possessing that quality (*matvarthe*).

*rūpād āhata*: [In the word] *āhata*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). [The rule applies] to the word *rūpa* when it is qualified by *āhata* or qualified by *praśaṃsā*. In the sense of "possessing" (*matvarthe*): [the form is *rūpya*].

The meaning is "that which will be struck. Regarding the phrase "the form produced by striking" (*āhataṃ rūpam*): the word *rūpa* refers to that whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is produced (*niṣpanna*) by being struck; this is the analysis of the compound. As for "a silver *kārṣāpaṇa*":
a *kārṣāpaṇa* is said to be a specific coin made of silver, gold, or the like, characterized by a particular weight and marked with a specific seal.

And its nature (*svarūpa*) should be understood as that which is produced by the act of killing performed by a goldsmith. "A silver bull" (*rūpyo gauḥ*): the meaning is one endowed with excellent form. "Snowy mountains" (*himyāḥ parvatāḥ*): the suffix *yaP* is used in the sense of abundance (*bhūmani*). The analysis of the compound is "those in whom there is abundant snow. "Virtuous Brahmins" (*guṇyā brāhmaṇāḥ*).
The suffix *yap* is used in the sense of praise; the meaning is "endowed with praiseworthy qualities.
[The rule] "it is also seen after others" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*)—this is a *vārttika*. The suffix *yap* is also seen after words other than *rūpa*.

This is the meaning. Regarding "himyāḥ parvatāḥ" (snowy mountains): the suffix *yaP* is used here in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*). The analysis of the compound is: "those in whom there is abundant snow.
Regarding "guṇyā brāhmaṇāḥ" (virtuous Brahmins): the suffix *yaP* is used here in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). The meaning is: "those endowed with praiseworthy qualities."

(1901) *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* || 5.2.121 || The rule *asmāyāmedhā* [refers to the suffix] *vin*. By the rule *ṭhasya*, it is intended that a word ending in *as* (*asanta*) is meant. The meaning is that the suffix *vini* shall be applied after words ending in *as*, as well as after *māyā*, *medhā*, and *sraj*. In this suffix, the vowel *i* follows the letter *n*.

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding "yaśasvī": the intention is that because [the word] is treated as a *bha* by the rule "tasau matvarthe," there is no application of *ru*-substitution. Regarding "yaśasvān": although the mention of "nitya" (invariably) in the sūtra "ekagopūrvāt" has removed [the optionality], the mention of "anyatarasyām" here is for the sake of inclusion (*samuccaya*), following the "frog-leap" method (*maṇḍūkapluti*).

The meaning is that [the suffix *vin*] follows [the rule], because the word *yaśasvān* is cited as an example in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "tasau matvarthe. Regarding the form *sragvī*, having raised the objection concerning the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "vraśca-," he says: "because it ends in the suffix *kvip*."
(1) There is the addition of *āmaya*, and [the lengthening of the vowel] in *āmaya*.
Regarding "of *āmaya*": the meaning is that from the word *āma*, the suffix *vini* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), and there is lengthening of the base (*prakṛti*).
(2) After *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*, the suffix *ārakan* [is applied].
Regarding "from *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*":
[the suffix] *inaC* is applied after *phala* and *barha*.
Regarding "from *phala* and *barha*": [the suffix *inaC* is applied].
"From *hṛdaya*, the suffix *cālu* is optionally [added].

This "from *hṛdaya*, the suffix *cālu*" refers to three *vārttikas*. "And the suffix *matup*"—the remainder is "it should be stated," because it is stated as such in the Bhāṣya. By the rule *cuṭū*, the letter *c* is designated by the technical term *itsaṃjñā*.

Because of the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), there is the absence of elision (*alopa*), and consequently the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are applied. Furthermore, because the term *anyatarasyām* is understood here as having a cumulative sense (*samuccaya-artha*), the suffix *matup* is also included. Thus, there are four suffixes in this case. This is what he states: "hṛdayāluḥ," and so forth.
Regarding the inability to endure cold, heat, and hunger/thirst:
the Vārttika, "śītoṣṇatṛprebhyastadasahane" (Pāṇini 3.2.35), which means "from the words śīta, uṣṇa, and tṛpra, when followed by 'na sahate' (does not endure)," summarizes the sense [of the rule].
Thus, from the words *śīta*, *uṣṇa*, and *tṛpra* ending in the accusative case, [the suffix *kha* is applied] in the sense of "not enduring."
The meaning is that it should be called "fourfold. The intention is that this is because it is stated as such in the Mantrabhāṣya: "The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is *tṛpra*.
(1) *Himocceluḥ*.

"himocceluḥ"—this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that after the word *hima* ending in the accusative case, the suffix *celuḥ* occurs in the sense of "not enduring. The letter *c* is *it* (indicatory).
[From this] *ūla* follows by force.

Regarding "balādūla": the remainder [of the rule] is that the suffix *ūla* should be stated in the sense of "not enduring" (*na sahate*). Regarding "vātātsamūhe ca": the meaning is that the suffix *ūla* should be prescribed after the word *vāta* ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) in the sense of a collection (*samūha*), and also after it ending in the accusative case (*dvitīyānta*) in the sense of "not enduring."
"From *parvan* and *marut*, *tap* [is added].
This is a Vārttika. The meaning is: "The suffix *tap* should be stated after *parvan* and *marut*.
Regarding this, the author of the Vṛtti and Haradatta state that "*tan* should be stated. [This is discussed] in the Prauḍhamanoramā.

However, the *nit* designation has been rejected [by some]. In the *Śabdenduśekhara*, on the other hand, the *nit* designation alone, as favored by Haradatta, has been established. Because the word is a conventional whole (*rūḍha*) and lacks a derivative meaning (*avayavārtha*), the suffix *matup* is not applied.
(1902) *Ūrṇāyā yus* (Pāṇini 5.2.123).

Regarding the suffix *yus* after *ūrṇā*: fearing that the elision [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca* might apply to the word *ūrṇāyu*, he says "because it is *sita*" (white). Regarding the phrase "they follow": the remainder of the sense is "from the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*."
(1903) *vāco gminiḥ* | 5|2|124 | The suffix *gmini* is added after the word *vāc*. The meaning is that the suffix *gmini* occurs after the word *vāc* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*).

The letter *n* and the vowel *i* [of *gmini*] are for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "not a *taddhita* suffix" (*ataddhite*), [the *ga* of *gmini* becomes *ka*].
The term *vāggmī* [is derived as follows]: from the word *vāc*, with the suffix *gmin* added, there is the substitution of *k* for *c* (*kutva*), and then the substitution of *j* for *g* (*jaśtva*).
The pronunciation of the letter *g* in the suffix, however, is for the purpose of preventing the nasalization [of the preceding vowel] that would otherwise occur by the rule *ṭhpratyaye bhāṣāyām*.

(1904) *ālajāṭacau bahubhāṣiṇi* | 5|2|125| The suffixes *ālac* and *āṭac* [are applied]. From the word *vāc*—namely *ālac* and *āṭac*—these two [suffixes] are used in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) when the meaning is "one who speaks much. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *gmin*. As for the phrase "he who [speaks] correctly," it is not [the case that] he does not speak much.
And regarding one who speaks what is not censurable, it must be asked: why should he not also be called "eloquent" (*vāggmī*)?
For, by the force of the *Bhāṣya*—which states, "He who speaks much correctly indeed becomes eloquent"—the previous sūtra applies only to one who speaks much correctly.
The meaning is: "because of the acceptance of active engagement" (*pravṛti*).
(1905) *svāmin* [is used] in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
[The rule] *svāminnaiśvarye* [states]: "in the sense of sovereignty. *Aiśvarye* means "in the sense of sovereignty."

Intending this as a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), he says: "from a word expressing sovereignty" (*aiśvaryavācakāt*). Regarding *āminaj*, the remainder [of the rule] is "it is an irregular formation" (*nipātyate*). Regarding *svāmī*: "one's own" (*svam*) means sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); thus, the meaning is "one who possesses that. In other words, it means "the controller" (*niyantṛ*). Because it is stated "in the sense of sovereignty," the form *svāmī* does not occur in the sense of "one who possesses wealth" (*dhanavān*).
(1906) *arśaādibhyo’c* | 5.2.127. The analysis of the compound is: "those for which *arśas* is the first. Thus, [the form] *arśasaḥ*.

*Arśas* is a specific disease of the rectum. (1907) *Pāṇini 5.2.128*: "The suffix *ini* occurs after a *dvandva* compound, after a word denoting affliction (*upatāpa*), and after a word denoting something censurable (*garhya*), when these refer to parts of a living being. [Explanation: After a *dvandva* compound, after a word expressing affliction, and after a word expressing something censurable—[the suffix *ini* is applied].

The meaning is that the suffix *ini* occurs after words denoting objects residing in living beings when the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is intended. The phrase "dvandva" serves as an indication of an example.

Regarding "kaṭakavalayinī": having postulated some distinction in form between a bracelet (*kaṭaka*) and a bangle (*valaya*), the term is formed as a *dvandva* compound. The word "upatāpa" is explained by the word "roga" (disease).

*Kilāsa* is a type of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). The explanation of *garhya* is "blameworthy" (*nindya*). Regarding *kakudāvartin*: *kakuda* is the part of the back below the neck; a whorl (*āvarta*) there is a *kakudāvarta*, and the analysis of the compound is "one who has that. Regarding *kākatālukinī*: [it means] like a crow's...
The analysis of the compound is: "those two [palates] are hers at the *kākatālukā*.

[This would normally require the suffix *ṭāp*, but it is not applied here. Regarding the rule "not after a member of the body of a living being" (*prāṇyaṅgāt na*), the commentary itself is the authority in this matter, for such is the nature of this kind of *vārttika*.

The sense is that [the suffix] *bh* is applied because [the word] is not seen [ending in *a*]; "from this very [rule]" means that, according to the manner of the commentary on the rule for compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), that [suffix *bh*] is understood here by means of a *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) [transposition]. Regarding the form *citrakalalāṭikāvatī*:
it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *citraka* and *lalāṭikā*. The sense is that because it does not end in short *a*, the suffix *ini* is not applied.

One might ask: since the rule is already established by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from "ṭhata iniṭhanau," what is the purpose of including *ini* again here? To this, he says: "the suffix being already established. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of *matup* is intended.

(1908) *vātātīsārābhyāṃ kuk ca* | Pāṇini 5.2.129. Regarding *vātātīsārābhyām*: the suffix *ini* [is added] after *vāta* and *atīsāra*, according to the rule *cādinir iti*. The meaning is that *ini* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*) after these two, and *kuk* is added to the base. In *kuk*, the letter *k* is the *it* (indicatory), and the letter *u* [is for euphonic purposes].
The purpose is for pronunciation. Due to the *kit* suffix, it becomes an internal constituent. "Vātakī" means one who has the disease of wind (*vāta*).
"Athīsārakī" means one who has the disease of dysentery (*atīsāra*). This [suffix] is desired after a word denoting a disease.
"And in the case of *roga*, this [suffix applies]"—the intention is that it is because of the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*). The meaning is "only in the sense of disease.
Regarding "a cave full of wind" (*vātavatī guhā*), the intention is that since "disease" is not perceived here, the suffixes *ini* and *kuk* do not apply.
And [the suffix does not apply] after *piśāca*.

"And after *piśāca*. This is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that the suffix *ini* is applied after the base *piśāca*, and the augment *kuk* is added [to the base]. (1909) Pūraṇa [suffixes] [are used] in the sense of age. 5.2.130.

[The suffix *ini* is applied] after words denoting age (*vayas*) because of their completion [of years]. Since *ini* is already established by the rule "after words ending in *ṭha*, there are *ini* and *ṭhan*" (*ṭhata iniṭhanau*), for what purpose is *im* prescribed? To this he says: "For the purpose of setting aside *ṭhan* and the others. (Pāṇini 5.2.131) "And after *sukha* and so forth. (*sukhādibhyaśca*)

"And after *sukha* and so forth. This means that the suffix *ini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), and not the suffix *ṭhan*. "After *mālā* when used in reproach (*kṣepe*). This is a sūtra belonging to the *sukhādi* group. (1911) "Also after words ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, and *varṇa*. 5.2.132.

*dharmaśīla*. Regarding the rule *dharmādyantāt*: the meaning is that the suffix *ini* is applied only after those ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, and *varṇa*. (1912) *hastājjātau* 5.2.133. [The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *hasta* when denoting a genus (*jāti*).]
[The suffix] *ini* is applied after the word *hasta* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), provided that the specific class (*jāti*) is understood from the whole [compound].
(1913) After a word denoting a caste (*varṇa*), [the suffix *ini* is applied] when referring to a religious student (*brahmacārin*). 5.2.134.

Regarding the word *varṇin* [as used] in the sense of a *brahmacārin*: the suffix *-in-* is applied after the word *varṇa* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), provided that the whole expression conveys the meaning of a *brahmacārin*. Thus, *varṇī* [is derived].
Here, *varṇa* refers to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) performed at the appropriate time—such as spring—for each respective caste, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
The analysis of the compound is "he who has this" (*so 'syāsti*).

(1914) *Puṣkarādibhyo deśe* (Pāṇini 5.2.135): after words beginning with *puṣkara*, when a location is to be understood, the suffix *ini* alone occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus, from the word *puṣkara*, only *ini* is applied when a place is implied.
"By virtue of the compound having 'bahu' or 'ūru' as its prior member. This is a *vārttika*. [The words] "bahu" and "ūru"—
The meaning is that the suffix *ini* alone is added after a word ending in *bala* when preceded by these [specific] initial words, in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*).
Regarding the phrase "and after *sarva* etc.": this is a *vārttika*; the remainder of the rule is "the suffix *ini* alone."

"And because of the object when it is not present. This is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that from the word "object" (*artha*), when its referent is absent, there is only non-existence (*anirdeśa*). Regarding the term "object" (*arthī*):
The analysis of the compound is "that for which the object (*artha*) is not present" (*asaṃnihita*). This means that the object does not exist.

Here, because of the contradiction, it cannot be connected with the word "exists" (*asti*). Kaiyaṭa states that the suffix *ini* is prescribed in the sense of "that for which the object is not present," even though [the object] has not yet been reached.
"And from that which ends in this.
Since the rule for the prescription of suffixes prohibits the extension of the rule to what ends in such a form, he says: "and from that which ends in this.
The meaning is that the suffix *ini* should also be prescribed after words ending in *artha*.

(1915) *balādibhyo matub anyatarasyām* | Pāṇini 5.2.136. Intending that the suffix *ini* is present when there is the option of not using the suffix *matup* after words such as *bala*, he provides the examples: *balavān* and *balī*.

(1916) *saṃjñāyāṃ man-mābhyām* | Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ man-mābhyām*: the word *prathamī* is formed by adding the suffix *iman* according to the rule *pṛthv-ādibhya iman-ic ca*. Here, even though the suffix *man* is devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), [the feminine suffix] *n* is applied by the rule *an-in-snañ*.

By the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to that which ends with it), the form ending in the suffix *imanij* is also included. From the word *prathama*, when the suffix *in* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant); then, by the rule for words ending in *n*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in the word *prathiminī*. As for *dāminī*:
the sense is that from the word *dāman*, when the suffix *in* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi*, and then the suffix *ṅīp* is added. As for *mā*.
This is an illustration of [words] ending in *mān*. The examples are *hominī* and *sominī*;
the intention is that the suffix *in* is added after the words *homa* and *soma*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. (Pāṇini 5.2.138) *kaṃśaṃbhyāṃ babhayustitutayasaḥ*.

"Kaṃśaṃbhyām": this is the nominative plural from the dvandva compound of the seven suffixes *va*, *bha*, *yus*, *ti*, *tu*, *ta*, and *yas*. It means that these seven suffixes [are applied] "in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*)," as is the understood remainder. "For the sake of *padatva*" (word-status): otherwise, if the suffix *ya* were applied to *kam* and the suffix *yap* were applied, [the form would not be correct].
The sense is that because [the letter *m*] lacks the status of being a "pada" (word) due to its being a suffix (*bha*), the anusvāra would not occur.
The compound *vakārayakāraparasya* is a bahuvrīhi; it means "of the anusvāra which is followed by *va* or followed by *ya*."

(1918) *tundi-vali-baṭer bhaḥ* | 5.2.139 | The meaning is that the suffix *bha* occurs after *tundi*, *vali*, and *baṭi* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). The word "pañcamī ekavacana" (ablative singular) is used because it is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The masculine gender is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). Thus, [the form] is *vaṭibha*.
The root *vaṭ* means "to surround" (*veṣṭane*). A surrounding is *vaṭi*. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has this [surrounding] belongs to it.
(1919) *Ahaṃśubhamoryus* | 5.2.140 | [The suffix] *yus* is added after *aham* and *śubham*. *Ahaṃyuḥ*: the masculine gender is archaic (*ārṣa*). Regarding *vaṭibha*: [the root] *vaṭa*...
[The suffix *i* is applied] in the sense of "encircling. *Vaṭanam* is *vaṭiḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has this [encircling].
(1920) *Ahaṃśubhamoryus*: the suffix *yus* is applied after the words *aham* and *śubham*. [This applies] in the case of *ahaṃyuḥ* and *śubhaṃyuḥ*.
Anticipating the objection that [the word *ahaṃ*] might be elided, he says: "beginning with *aham*" (*ahamityādi*). The inclusion of the word *siti* is for the sake of ensuring it is a *pada*.

By virtue of being a *pada*, the *anusvāra* is established, and through the rule of *parasavarṇa*, the correct phonetic correspondence is achieved. Thus ends the section on possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the derivation of denominative roots (*nāmadhātu*).

(481) *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* | Pāṇini 3.1.8. Now the derivations of denominative roots are examined. [Regarding the rule] *supa ātmanaḥ*: by the technical paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), [the word *sup* refers to nominal stems].
The term "ending in a case-suffix" (subanta) is understood [from the context]. Due to proximity, the status of being an object (karmatva) is intended specifically with respect to the desire (icchā).

The word *ātman* is a synonym for "self" (*sva*). When there is an intention to express the relationship of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) as a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the genitive case is used. From this, it is understood that [the object] is "one's own" (*svārtha*) object. And since "self" (*sva*) is brought into proximity by the desire, it refers precisely to that which is desired.

This is what is intended. And thus, the result is that when a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is desired for oneself, the suffix *kyac* may optionally occur after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) to express that desire. With this in mind, he says:
"of the object of the desire belonging to the desirer," and so forth. [It refers to] the object of the desire which has the desirer as its purpose.

This is the meaning. That which is desired for its own sake by the agent (eṣitr) is the object (karmakāraka); that is to say, from a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). "Because it is a part of the verbal root" (*dhātvavayavatvāt*): the intention is that when *kyac* is added after a nominal stem, the resulting form becomes a verbal root according to the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*.

(482) *kyaci ca* |7|4|33|. In the rule *kyaci ca*, the word *asya* is understood from the previous rule *ṭhasya cvau*; and considering that the mention of *ī* is also understood from the rule *ṭhī ghrādhmoḥ*, he completes the remainder [of the sūtra] by stating *asya*. This means "of the vowel *a*."

Regarding *putrīyati*: when the suffix *kyac* is applied, the form *putra-ya-* is established. In the case of *putrīyati* (meaning "he desires a son"), the suffix *kyac* is not added after the word *putra* [because it ends in a vowel]. Regarding *gavyati*: the meaning is "he desires a cow for himself. Regarding *nāvyati*: the meaning is "he desires a boat for himself. As for the phrase "because it is not at the end of a word": this refers to the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*.

The intention is that [the designation of] *pada* occurs only at the end of a word (*padānta*). Now, one might object that the status of being a *pada* certainly exists due to the intervening case-ending; therefore, he says "tathā hi" (for instance). The meaning is that it is explained how the status of being a *pada* does not actually occur.

(483) *naḥ kye* | 1.4.15 | In the rule *naḥ kye*, the letter *a* after *n* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). From the previous rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam*, the term *subantaṃ padam* ("a word ending in a case-suffix") is understood as the subject. The word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is qualified by the letter *n*. This is an application of the rule regarding the inclusion of that which ends in [the specified element] (*tadantavidhi*).

It is understood that a word ending in *su* (i.e., a nominal stem) ending in the letter *n* should receive the designation *pada*. Since the status of being a *pada* is already established by the fact of its ending in *su*, this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). By the mention of *kyac*, both *kyac* and *kyaṅ* are included, but not *kyaṣ*, because it will be stated later: "The suffix *kyaṣ* is prescribed after the words *lohita* and those ending in *ḍāj*."

Because there is no occurrence of *kyaṣ* after a word ending in a consonant (*halantāt*). This is what he states with the words "in *kyac* and *kyaṅ*" and so forth. Now, one might object that in the form *gavyāñcakāra*, it is impossible for the *v*—which has been substituted by the *ārdhadhātuka* affix *ām*—to serve as the cause for the elision of the *y*. This is the intended meaning. [The form] *gavyitā* is derived when the augment *iṭ* is applied.

Therefore, there is elision. Regarding the form *rājīyati*, he says: "there is elision of *n*. This means that when the sense is "one who desires a king" (*rājānam icchati*), and the suffix *kyac* is applied, resulting in the intermediate stage *rājan-ya-ti*, the *n* is elided because the preceding element is a *pada* by the rule *naḥ kye*. Having understood that once the elision of *n* has occurred, the vowel *a* becomes *ī* by the rule *kyaci ca*, he says: [the following].

Regarding the form *rājīyati*: one should not suspect that the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) is "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*) when the substitution of *ī* (*ītva*) is to be applied, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating "the elision of *n* [is asiddha] before case-endings (*sup*) and in accentuation (*svara*). This is sufficient. Now, in the cases of *tvām ātmānam icchati* and *mām ātmānam icchati*, since the suffixes *yuṣmad* and *asmad* undergo the *kyac* affix, the case-ending (*sup*)—being part of the verbal root (*dhātu*)—[is subject to the following].

Since there is an absence of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) when a suffix has been elided (*luk*), how could *tvam* and *au* occur according to the rule "tvamāvekavacane" (Pāṇini 7.2.97), given that those are prescribed only when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows? To this, he says: "and [in the case] of a suffix or a subsequent member" (*pratyayottarapadayośca*). Even though the *sup* suffix is elided by *luk*, [the operation applies] by taking into account the *kyac* suffix.

The intention is that "you" (tvam) and "I" (aham) apply to the limit of the entire [compound]. Now, one might object: in cases such as *yuṣmān ātmana icchati* ("he desires you for himself") and *asmān ātmana icchati* ("he desires us for himself"), the suffix *kyac* would also be included, and thus "you" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*) should likewise apply there;
to this he replies: "only when they have a single referent. This is because of the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* ("and in the case of a suffix or a subsequent member of a compound").
The sūtra "tvamāvekavacane" is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtta*). Furthermore, the word *ekavacana* is not used here in its conventional sense;

rather, as was explained at length previously in the section on the paradigms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, what is intended by the term *ekavacana* is the state of denoting an object qualified by singularity (*ekatva-viśiṣṭārtha-vṛttitva*). And thus:

The point is that *tvam* and *aham* do not occur [in place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] because [the bases *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] do not denote objects qualified by singularity (*ekatva*). Regarding the examples "he desires speech for himself" (*giram ātmana icchati*) and "he desires a city for himself" (*puram ātmana icchati*), he states the specific rule concerning the suffix *kyac* after the words *giri* and *puri*: "and before a consonant" (*hali ca*). The remainder of the rule is "lengthening of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhādīrghaḥ*). Now, an objection:
In the case of *divamicchati* and *divyati*, the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by the rule *hali ca* would also apply; therefore, he says:
"only after a verbal root (*dhātoḥ*). The intention is that in the sūtra *hali ca*, there is the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase *sipi dhātoḥ*. Thus: *divyati*.

The point is that the word *div* is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*). Regarding the phrase "here" (*iha*): the meaning is that Mādhava’s statement—that because the term *dhātoḥ* (of a verbal root) is understood in the rule *hali ca*, there is no lengthening in the form *puryati*—is questionable. Why? To this he says: "Because of the similarity between *pur* and *gir*."

The intention is that the words *gīḥ* and *ūḥ* are derived from the roots *gṛ* (meaning "to sound") and *pṛ* (meaning "to protect" or "to fill") respectively, by adding the suffix *kvip*, followed by the substitution of *it* for the root vowel according to the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the substitution of *u* for *ṝ* according to the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, and the subsequent replacement of *ṛ* by *ra*. Thus, they are established as *gir* and *ūr*. [The objection] that this is merely an error is [the view being refuted].

Since the word *div* is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), it does not possess the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Therefore, from the root *div* with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the feminine suffix *ūṅ*, the form is *dyaū*; and from this *dyaū* with the suffix *kyac*, the form *dyaūyati* alone is appropriate. However, in the case of the suffix *vic*, after the substitution of *guṇa* for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) and the elision of *vy* according to the rule "lopo vyoḥ," the suffix *kyac* would be added to the stem *de*.
The sense is that it is appropriate to say "he gives" (deyati). Regarding "adasyati": in the sense of "he desires that (adas) for himself," the suffix *kyac* is added to the word *adas*.

Since the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided by *luk*, there is no following case-suffix; therefore, the substitution of *yat* for the *t* of *tyad*-class words does not apply. Furthermore, because the stem ends in *s*, the substitution of *u* and *m* (for *a* and *d* respectively) does not occur. This is due to the restrictive rule "naḥ kye."

The sense is that because it is not at the end of a word (*padānta*), the *s* does not undergo the change to *r*. He states the specific rule regarding the suffix *kyac* after the word *kartṛ*: "after [a stem] ending in long *ī*. He states the specific rule regarding *kyac* after the word *gārgya*:
"and after [stems ending in] *kyac* and *yañ*. The sense is that there is elision of the *yakāra* of the patronymic suffix *yañ*. Once this has been performed...

Considering that the vowel *i* replaces the *a* of the suffix *kyac* by the rule "yalope ṭhkyaci ca," he says: *gārgīyati* (he acts like a Gārgya) and *vātsīyati* (he acts like a Vātsya). From the word *vātsya*, *kyac* is applied as before. Regarding the specific rule for the word *kavi* when *kyac* follows, he says:
"akṛtsārveti. Thus, *vācyati* (he speaks); from the word *vāc*, *kyac* is applied by the rule "naḥ kye."

Thus, by this rule, there is no substitution of *ku* (the replacement of *s* with *ū*) because the word lacks the status of being a *pada*. Furthermore, the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) prescribed by the rule *vacisvapi-* does not apply here, due to the restriction that "an operation stated for a verbal root applies only when a suffix is prescribed after that verbal root. [The form] *samidhyati* is derived from the word *samidh* with the addition of the *kyac* suffix, according to the rule *naḥ kye*.

Because there is no status as a *pada*, the substitution of *jaś* does not apply. When *luṭ* is replaced by *tās* with the augment *iṭ*, resulting in *samidhya + itā*, the rule "elision of *y* after a consonant" (*yasya halaḥ*) would invariably require the elision of *y*. However, this is overridden by: (484) *kyasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.50).

Regarding the option (*vibhāṣā*) for *kyac*: the word "hal" (consonant) from the rule "ṭhyasya halaḥ" is understood to follow here as a fifth-case (ablative) term. "Ārdhadhātuke" is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). Thus he says: "after a consonant, before the two suffixes *kyac* and *kyaṅ*. However, *kyaṣ* is not included here [in this specific context], because of [the rule] "lohita-ḍājbhyaḥ..."

Because [the suffix] will be stated as *kyap* later on, that [suffix] does not occur after a stem ending in a consonant (*hal*). Anticipating the objection regarding the elision of the final letter, he says: "of what follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*). Thus, when *sam-idh-a-it* is established, he says: "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*). And so, when *sam-idh-it* is established—

Anticipating the objection regarding the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), he says: "Because of its status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Regarding the rule for *kyac*, there is a *vārtika* stating: "There is a prohibition [of the application of *kyac*] after words ending in *m* and after indeclinables (*avyaya*).

If this were interpreted to mean that there is a prohibition after words ending in *m* and after indeclinables, then in the case of *putrīyati* (he desires a son for himself), the suffix would not apply.

[Otherwise], from [words] such as *putrīyati* itself, [the suffix *kyac*] would apply. If the meaning were "from those indeclinables ending in *m*" (*māntāni avyayāni māntāvyayāni tebhyah*), then there would be no prohibition of *kyac* in the case of *svarīyati*. Therefore, explaining that Vārttika, he says: "having *m* as its base" (*māntaprakṛtika*).

(485) *Aśanāyodanyadhanāyā bubhukṣāpipāsāgarddheṣu* | Pāṇini 7.4.34. *Aśanāyodanya-*: This is a dvandva compound consisting of *aśanāya*, *udanya*, and *dhanāya*. "They end in *kyac*" means that these three words are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the senses of hunger and so forth, respectively. This is the meaning.

The desire to eat is *bubhukṣā*; the desire to drink is *pipāsā*. *Garddha* means longing; it is derived from the sense "he desires to eat" (*aśanāyati*). That which is eaten is "food" (*aśana*, i.e., *anna*); the meaning is that he desires to eat that.
By the rule *kyaci ca*, the substitution of *ī* is prohibited, and by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs.

*Udanyati* means "he desires to drink water. Here, the substitution of *udann* for the word *udaka* is prescribed by rule, as is the non-elision (*abāva*) of the nasal *n*. *Dhanāyati* means "desiring more wealth" or "seeking excessive wealth even when one already possesses wealth for the sake of living. Here, the absence of the *ī*-vowel change (which would otherwise apply) is prescribed by the rule *kyaci ca*.

"Aśanīyati" means he desires food; that is, he wishes to collect provisions for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and other rites. "Udakīyati" means he desires water; that is, he wishes for water for the purpose of irrigating crops and so forth. "Dhanīyati" means being poor... [he desires wealth].
The meaning is: "one who desires wealth for the sake of living.
(486) *aśvakṣīravṛṣalavaṇānāmātmaprītau kyaci* | Pāṇini 7.1.51. Regarding *aśva-kṣīra-kyaci*: the phrase *asuṅ pare* is supplied as a completion of the rule.

The intention is that this [suffix] is included by the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṭhājjaserasuk*. In the suffix *asuk*, the letter *k* is the *it* (indicatory), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is *kit*, it is an ultimate constituent (*antyāvayava*). Regarding the phrase "of the horse and the bull" (*aśvavṛṣayoḥ*), this is a Vārttika.
*Aśvasyati vaḍavā* ("the mare desires the horse") means she desires the horse for the purpose of mating. *Vṛṣasyati gauḥ* ("the cow desires the bull").

The meaning is that she desires a bull for the sake of sexual intercourse. As for the lexicon stating "a *vṛṣasyantī* is a lustful woman," it is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote the mere desire for sexual intercourse, while setting aside the primary meanings of the roots *aśva-vṛṣa*. Regarding the phrase "of milk and salt"—this is a Vārttika; the word "in *asu*" (*asuṅ*) is to be understood as the remainder. *Lālasā*— The meaning is that she desires a bull for the purpose of sexual intercourse. As for the lexicon stating, "a *vṛṣasyantī* is a lustful woman," it is used figuratively to denote the mere desire for sexual intercourse, having abandoned the original meanings of the roots *aśva* (horse) and *vṛṣa* (bull). Regarding the phrase "of milk and salt"—this is a Vārttika. The word "in *asu*" (*asuṅ*) is to be understood as the remainder. *Lālasā*—

"Utkaṭecchā" (intense desire). "Of all nominal stems" (*sarva-prātipadikānām*). This is also a *vārttika*. The meaning is: the suffix *kyac* should be stated after all nominal stems when expressing intense longing (*lālasā*); furthermore, when that suffix follows, the augment *suk* and the replacement *su* for the final vowel of the base should be stated. [Objection: But is this not already established by this very *vārttika*?
One might suspect that the Vārttika "kṣīralavaṇayor lālasāyām" is redundant; however, this suspicion is unfounded,
for the Vārttika "kṣīralavaṇayoḥ" is indeed the work of Kātyāyana.

However, since the alternative view—that [the suffix applies] to all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadikānām*)—is held by others, there is no fault. This is also suggested in the *Bhāṣya* by the phrase "another says" (*apara āha*).
This sūtra follows after "supa ātmanaḥ kyac. Therefore, it says: "in the aforementioned scope.

Regarding *putrakāmyati*: the designation *it* is not applied to the *kāmyac* suffix because there is no result [of such a designation]. "Because it is meaningless" means that the letter *y*, which is a portion of the *kāmyac* suffix, lacks meaning. Now, one might object:
Since the *yakāra* in *bebhidita* would also be meaningless, its elision would not occur; therefore, he says:

"by the rule *yasyeti*. The meaning is that it was stated immediately after [the discussion of] the rule *yasya halaḥ* that by the word *yasya* there is the inclusion of the entire cluster consisting of the *yakāra* and the *akāra*. And thus...

In the case of *bebhidya-ita*, since the entire cluster [containing] the *yaṅ* suffix is meaningful, the elision of the letter *y* is unimpeded. However, in the present instance (*kāmya*), because the *y* which is a portion of the *kāmyac* suffix is meaningless, there is no elision; this is the intended meaning.
In *yaśaskāmyati*, the substitution of *s* occurs by the rule *so'padādau*. Now, what is for one's own sake?

How is it that one says *icchati* ("he desires") and *kiṃkāmyati* ("he desires what?"), as well as *svaḥkāmyati* ("he desires heaven")? [The answer is: because of the continued application of the rule "not after words ending in *m* or indeclinables" (*māntāvyayānāṃ na*).
Therefore, he says: "This [suffix *kyac*] occurs even after words ending in *m* and after indeclinables. (Pāṇini 3.1.10):
*upamānādācāre* ("after a word denoting a standard of comparison, when expressing an action similar to that").
Regarding the rule *upamānādācāre*: the word *supaḥ* is understood from the previous rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*;
the word *karmaṇaḥ* is understood from the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkāṭ*. Thus he says:
"from the object which is the standard of comparison," and so forth. [This refers to] that which is the factor of action (*kāraka*) serving as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

The meaning is "from that which ends in a case-ending. Regarding the example *putram iva* (like a son): by this, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *vā* ("or") from the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ* is indicated.
The meaning is: "he treats the student as a son. Regarding *viṣṇūyati*:
the meaning is "he treats the twice-born as Viṣṇu. And [the rule continues] with the words *adhikaraṇācca*.

The meaning is that it should be stated that *kyac* is added after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), even when that word functions as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) serving as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). For example: *prāsādīyati kuṭīṃ* ("he behaves toward the hut as if toward a palace"). The meaning is: "He remains joyful in the hut as if he were in a palace. And: *kuṭīyati prāsāde* ("he behaves toward the palace as if toward a hut"). The meaning is: "He remains distressed in the palace as if he were in a hut."
The meaning is "it exists.
(489) *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* |3|1|11|. *kartuḥ kyaṅ*: the word *kartuḥ* is repeated. The phrase *kartuḥ kyaṅ* forms one sentence; here—

The word *kartuḥ* ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). The [sūtra] *upamānād ācāre* (Pāṇini 3.1.10) is understood to carry over, as well as *vā* from *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.7). Thus he says: "from the standard of comparison" (*upamānāt*). The meaning is: from a nominal stem (*subanta*) derived from that which is the agent (*kartṛ*)—the factor of action (*kāraka*)—in the standard of comparison. [This is further specified by the rule: *kartuḥ salopaśca*.

This is the second statement. The word "ca" (and) is a synonym for "tu" (but), though its position is displaced. The word "saḥ" (that) is a separate item with the genitive case elided. It is an adjective qualifying the genitive form "kartuḥ".

This is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (the suffix applies to that which ends with the specified element). Thus he says: "But [of] that which ends in 's'. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative": this refers to the alternative in which the *kyaṅ* suffix does not occur.
This is the meaning. He dispels the misconception that there is a deletion of the *sakāra* in the alternative case where the *kyaṅ* suffix applies, by stating:

"but there is the deletion of [the suffix] ending in *s*. This is clear in the Mahābhāṣya. To the objection that the optional deletion of the *si* suffix would thus apply everywhere, he says: "and that is restricted. The meaning is that there is a deletion of the *s* of that which ends in *s*.
He demonstrates the very rule [of application]: "ojaḥ from apsarasaḥ. This is a *vārttika*.

Regarding the word *ojas*: this is a form ending in *kyaṅ*. Because it is a verbal root by virtue of the rule "sanādyantā dhātavaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.32), there is the addition of the suffix *vṛt* (i.e., the feminine suffix *ṅīp*). In that context, the meaning is that the word *ojas* refers to one who possesses vigor (*ojasvin*). Thus, [the form] is *ojāyate*.

From the word *apsaras*, [the suffix] *kyaṅ* is applied, with the elision of the final syllable and lengthening of the vowel. Because *kyaṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, the ātmanepada voice is used. He gives examples for the rule "for the others, it is optional" (*itareṣāṃ vibhāṣā*): *yaśāyate*, *yaśasyate*. The meaning is "he acts like one who possesses glory" (*yaśasvin*). *Vidvāyate*, *vidvasyate*. The meaning is "he acts like one who is learned" (*vidvan*).

The meaning is "he acts like one who knows. From the word *vidvat*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied, with the optional elision of the suffix *si*. [Examples: *tvadyate*, *madyate*. The meaning is "he acts like you" (*tvam-iva*) or "he acts like me" (*aham-iva*). From the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied;

by the rule "in the case of *kyaṅ* and in the presence of a suffix or a subsequent member," the forms *tvam* and *mam* replace the portions ending in *map* of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [Examples: *yuṣmadyate*, *asmadyate*.

The meaning is: "he acts like you" or "he acts like us. This is because, following the rule *tvamāvekavacane*, the term *ekavacane* is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*; thus, [the substitution of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] occurs only when they denote a meaning qualified by singularity.

The meaning is that *tvam* and *aham* are substituted for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Regarding the rule *kyaṅmāninośca*, he reminds us of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) after words such as *kumārī*: "he acts like a young girl" (*kumārāyate*). By virtue of the masculine treatment, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is removed, and the long vowel [of the penultimate] is applied. "She acts like a *hariṇī*" (*haritāyate*): this is from the word *hariṇī* with the suffix *kyaiṅ*.

By virtue of being treated as masculine (*puṃvat*), there is lengthening upon the removal of the *ṅīṣ* suffix and the substitution of *n* [for the final *t*] according to the rule *ṭhvarṇādanudātā’dit*.
Thus, from the word *gurvī*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied; upon the removal of *ṅīṣ*, there is lengthening, resulting in *gurūyate*.
From the word *sapatna*, which is a synonym for "enemy," [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] by virtue of its belonging to the *śārṅgaravādi* group.

The intention is that, by virtue of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment), the suffix *ṅīp* is removed and the long vowel [is substituted]. Regarding the form *sapatīyate*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose husband/owner (*pati*) is common (*samānaḥ*)," the word *sapati* undergoes the substitution of *n* [for *t*] and the suffix *ṅīp*; from the resulting word *sapatnī*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied, with *puṃvadbhāva*.

The meaning is that when the *ṅīp* and *natva* are removed, the long vowel [is applied]. Regarding *sapatnīyate*: from the word *yuvati*, the *ky-aṅ* suffix is added; when the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is applied, the *ti*-suffix is removed, the *n* is elided, and the long vowel is applied—this is the intended sense. For words denoting age (*vayaḥ*), the operation of a genus (*jāti*) is optional.

This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *jāter astrīviṣayād* (Pāṇini 4.1.63). By this, the argument that "masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) is difficult to obtain here because of the prohibition [by the rule] *jāteś ca*" is refuted; so it is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
Regarding the form *paṭvīmṛdūyate*: [it is derived] from the rule *avagalbhaklībahoḍebhya ācāre* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.1.11).

The *vārttika* is "kvibvacipracchiśridruśrupruṣaḥ. The word "upamānāt" (from the preceding rule) is understood here. Since the inclusion of the option (*vā*) could have been established by its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ... within this very section, the explicit mention of "vā" is redundant; therefore, he says: "Because of the mention of 'vā,' [the suffix] *kyaṅ* also [occurs]. Otherwise...

The intention is that because it is specifically prescribed, the *kvip* suffix would subvert the *kyaṅ* suffix. Thus, it follows that the word "optionally" (*vā*) here has the sense of an alternative. In this context, the term *sup* (nominal suffix) does not carry over [from the previous rule].
Some maintain that since the application of *kyaṅ* from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would otherwise not be obtained, the mention of "optionally" (*vā*) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Regarding "avagalbhāyata": it is established that from words such as *avagalbha*, the suffixes *kvip* and *kyaṅ* are applied in the sense of "he acts like one who is *galbha*" (bold), "he acts like one who is *klība*" (impotent), or "he acts like one who is *hoḍa*" (shameless).
He says "by the co-occurrence with *kvip*" (*kvipsaṃniyogena*) in order to obtain the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the form *avagalbhate*; [this refers to] the final [letter].

Here, it is stipulated (*pratijñāyate*) that the vowel *a* is unaccented (*anudātta*) and nasalized (*anunāsika*). Consequently, when it receives the designation *it* and is elided, the *ātmanepada* endings are obtained because of its unaccented nature. Thus he says:
"by that, *taṅ* [is applied]," as in *avagalbhate*. When the suffix *kvip* is added, the vowel *a* following the letter *bha* is elided.

The intention is that the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes occur after roots such as *halnata*, *laḍa*, and so on, according to the rule *śvi-iti*. Now, one might ask: how is it that the *ām* augment occurs in forms such as *avagalbhāñcakre*, *klībāñcakre*, and *hoḍāñcakre*, given that the final letters of these roots are removed by the designation of *it* and subsequent elision, leaving the roots with only a single vowel (*ekāc*)?

This is because the rule *anekācaḥ* does not apply here. Nor should it be argued that the root *avagalbh*, ending in *kvip*, possesses multiple vowels (*anekāctva*); for [it is stated]: "A preceding member whose form is identical to a preverb is separated from the root when a suffix that triggers the designation 'root' (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) is intended to be applied."
Since this will be stated immediately hereafter, he says: "even from what was previously so" (*bhūtapūrvāt api*).
The meaning is that one relies upon the state of having multiple vowels (*anekāctva*) which existed prior to the derivation of the *kvip* suffix, by way of considering what was previously so.
He states the authority for relying on what was previously so: "by this Vārttika."

Since forms such as *avagalbhate* and *avajagalbhe* are already established by the forthcoming Vārttika, "kvip is added after all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*)," the further prescription of *kvip* after these roots is for the purpose of formally asserting that the final phoneme becomes unaccented (*anudātta*) and nasalized (*anunāsika*), by means of the principle of "having previously existed" (*sadbhūtapūrvagatyā*) in conjunction with that [addition of *kvip*].

The meaning is that [the rule] indicates the recourse to multiple meanings [of roots]. Now, one might object: "Since the declaration of the anudātta and anunāsika accents is exhausted by the establishment of the ātmanepada endings, how can it serve as the aforementioned indicator? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words "And not... and so forth. Why? To this he says: "Of the simple ones. This is because there is the possibility of the occurrence of those very roots listed in the Dhātupāṭha as having anudātta accents—such as *galbh* and others—even when they are devoid of vowel-affixes (*ac-pratyaya*), in senses such as "he acts like one who is bold" (*avagalbhate*). And why is that? To this he says: "Because roots have multiple meanings."

And thus, it is established that the rule prescribing the *kvip* suffix in the forms *sthātṛ* and *avagalbha* indicates that the assumption of multiple vowels (*anekāctva*) is based on the consideration of what was previously true, for the purpose of attaching the *anubandha*.

Nor should it be argued that the addition of the indicatory letter (anubandha) [in the rule *avagalbha-kliba-hoḍebhyaḥ kyac*] is exhausted solely for the purpose of excluding forms such as *avagalbhate* when the suffix *kvip* is applied to the term *sarvapratāpidakebhyaḥ*, and therefore how could that [addition] serve as the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because, according to the Vārttika *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*, such usage with *kvip* would be accepted; furthermore, by the authority of the Bhāṣya which relies on the "former state" (*bhūtapūrvāśrayaṇa*), it is understood that the Vārttika *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ* does not apply to words like *avagalbha*. Let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the purpose of the prefix *ava-* in the rule *ācāre'vagalbhe* (Pāṇini 3.1.111), he says: "the prefix *ava-*, etc. [He explains: "from the simple [root]," meaning from the word *galbha-* when devoid of a prefix. "[From] another prefix," meaning from words such as *pragalbha-* or *anugalbha-*. "[With the suffix] *kyaN*" means that it is not with *kvip*. The mention of "Mādhava and others" is an expression of dissatisfaction [with their view]. He states the reason for this: "it is more appropriate to say 'taṅ [ātmanepada endings] do not occur.'"

From the word *galbha* alone, as well as from it qualified by other prefixes, and from words such as *pragalbha*, the suffix *kvip* is established without obstruction by this rule—even in the absence of [the specific rule for] *kvip*—by means of the Vārttika "from all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*). However, the meaning is that it is appropriate to state that the ātmanepada [suffixes] do not apply there because the addition of the anubandha occurs only when preceded by *ava*. Regarding the phrase "from all nominal stems," the word "in the sense of manner of behavior" (*ācāre*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule].

[Objection: Since this very Vārttika establishes [the desired result], the Vārttika "ṭhācāre 'vagalbha" is redundant; to this he says: "But the previous Vārttika... The meaning is that it is for the purpose of establishing the *itsaṃjñā* (technical designation) of the final phoneme. [Objection: In that case, the mention of *kvip* there is useless; to this he says: "There, *kvip* is restated. The meaning is that it is for the purpose of attaching the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) in conjunction with that [suffix]. "No word-operation (*padakārya*)" means that in forms such as "rājānatī," there is no elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and so forth.

The point is that otherwise, because [the word] would be a *pada* due to the presence of an internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), there would be elision of the *n* (via Pāṇini 6.4.24) and so forth. "The single substitute for the latter form" (*pararūpam*) means that after the root *kṛṣṇa-* ending in *kvip*, when *laṭ* and other suffixes are applied, the *śap* augment is added, and by the rule "guṇa for *ataḥ*," the single substitute of the latter form (*pararūpa*) occurs. Thus: *kṛṣṇāñcakāra*, *kṛṣṇitā*, *kṛṣṇiṣyati*, *kṛṣṇatu*, *akṛṣṇat*, *kṛṣṇet*, *kṛṣṇāyāt*. Because this [substitution] is subsequent to the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*), the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "dīrgha for non-ṅit suffixes in the general tenses" (*akṛtsārvadhātuke*). Others hold that the elision of *at* occurs first, on the basis of the established principle of "priority of application" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). "Like *a*" (*a iva*) means: *aḥ* is Viṣṇu; the sense is "like him" (*sa iva*).

*Ati* [is the result of] *śap* [being replaced by] *pararūpa*. *Asi*, *athaḥ*, *atha*; *āmi*, *āvaḥ*, *āmaḥ*. Having raised the objection that the suffix *ām* might apply in the case of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) because the root ends in the *kvip* suffix—by the rule "after roots ending in *kā* or a suffix" (*kāspratyayāt*)—he says: "the mention of 'suffix' (*pratyaya*) is removed. The forms *au*, *atuḥ*, and *ur* are shown as established forms. Therein he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*): "doubling" (*dvitvam*), meaning that in the case of the *ṇal* suffix, the elision [of the reduplicated vowel] is prohibited by the rule "when there is doubling, not before a vowel" (*dvirvacane'ci*). [The form is derived] by the rule "guṇa for *at*" (*ato guṇe*).

When the doubling has been performed and the state *a-a-a* is reached, the intention is that *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the latter form) applies, overriding *ato lopaḥ* (elision of the *a*) because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal). Regarding the rule *ata ādeḥ*: one should not argue that this rule (*ata ādeḥ*) must apply prior to *ato guṇe* because it is subsequent (*para*), obligatory (*nitya*), and an exception (*apavāda*). This is because *ata ādeḥ* is *bahiraṅga* (more external); furthermore, even though *ata ādeḥ* is an exception, it cannot act as an override in cases such as *ānardeti*, since it has already found its scope of application by virtue of being subsequent to *halādiśeṣaḥ*. Thus, it lacks the capacity to override.

Even an exception (*apavāda*) is set aside by an internal rule (*antaraṅga*) if it has already found its scope elsewhere; this is stated at length elsewhere. Although there is no specific difference in the result here due to the reversal of the order of operations, it is stated in this way because it is more logical. Regarding *ṇala āṬ*: when the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) and the long vowel (*dīrgha*) have been applied, resulting in *ā a*, the intention is that the substitution of *au* occurs by the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ*. Regarding "vṛddhi": when *ā āṬ* is established, the meaning is that the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by the rule *vṛddhireci*.

And thus the form *āṬ* is fully established. Regarding the forms beginning with *atus*: when *a-atus* and *a-us* are situated [after the root], there is doubling (*dvitva*), followed by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and then lengthening (*dīrgha*) according to the rule *ata ādeḥ*; the meaning is that the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) occurs. Only the suffixes *atuḥ* and *ur* remain. In the case of *thali*, when *iṭ* is added, there is doubling, lengthening, and the elision of *ā*. Thus: *itha*, *athuḥ*, *a*. *āṬ*, *iva*, *ima*. However, in reality, during the commentary on the Vārttika *kāsyanakājgrahaṇam*, it was stated in the Bhāṣya that the mention of "suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) should be removed.

The suffix *ām* is obtained after roots ending in *kāsa* and those ending in a suffix (*pratyaya*). For this very reason, in the Vārttika "after *avagalbha*, *klība*, and *hoḍa* in the sense of behavior" (*ṭhācāre'vagalbhaklībahoḍebhyaḥ*), the Bhāṣya states that in forms such as *avagalbhāṃcakre*, the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *kāspratyayāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.35), even though the root has only one vowel (*ekāctva*) because the final letter is an *anubandha*; this is explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. **Root *i* (to go):** Present: *eti*, *itaḥ*, *iyati* Imperative: *atu*—*atāt*, *atām*, *antu*; *a*—*atāt*, *atam*, *ata*; *āni*, *āva*, *āma* Optative: *āt*, *ātām*, *ān*; *āḥ*, *ātam*, *āta*; *ām*, *āva*, *āma* Potential (*vidhiliṅ*): *et*, *etām*, *eyuḥ*

*Eti*, *aitu*, *etām*, *eyuḥ*; *ema*, *eta*, *eyām*. In the *luṅ* [aorist]: according to some, after the elision of *s* by the rule "ṭhiṭi īṭi," the rule "āṭaśca" (Pāṇini 6.1.90) would block the *vṛddhi* [substitution] because it is subsequent; thus, after the elision of *a* by "ato lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.48), there is *vṛddhi* of *āṭ* together with *iṭ*, resulting in *ait*, *aiṣṭām*, *aiṣuḥ*, and so on. According to others, since the elision of *a* occurs at the very time of the instruction of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes—being subsequent—the *aṅga* no longer exists, and therefore *āṭ* does not apply; hence the forms are *īt*, *iṣṭām*, and so on. The conditional (*lṛṅ*) form is *aiṣyat*.

[Objection: But surely, since the word *mālā* ends in the suffix *ṭāp*, it lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); how then can there be the suffix *kvip* after it? To this he says: "liṅgaviśiṣṭa" (qualified by gender). In reality, however, there is no *kvip* in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*) after words ending in long *ā*; this was explained in detail during the analysis of the word *viśvapā*. [Regarding the phrase] "due to association with [the suffix] *ṅīp": the meaning is that because of their association with forms such as *agaurayat*—derived from the word *gaurī* ending in *ṅīp* and having the *kvip* of habitual action—the elision of those two (*ṭāp* and *ṅīp*) does not occur even after a word ending in long *ā*, since it is impossible for *tis* and *syas* to follow a word ending in long *ī*. [The example] "kavayati" [is given].

In *śap*, there are the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions; thus, *kavīyāt*. [In the case of] *luṅ*, when *ik-avi īt* is established, having raised the doubt regarding *vṛddhi* by *sicaḥ*, he says: "In the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ*... The point is that although the root (*dhātu*) is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) from *sic*, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, it is understood that "only that which is a root" is meant. As for Kaiyaṭa and others: the point is that this was stated similarly in the commentary on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, starting with *agavīt* after deriving *kvip* in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*) from the word *go*. As for Mādhava, however...

The intention [of the author] is that in the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.1), since there is no evidence for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "root" (*dhātu*) from the preceding rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (7.1.100), the meaning "that which is a root" cannot be obtained [for the word *sici*]. However, in reality, as stated in the *Bhāṣya* on rules such as *iko guṇavṛddhī* (1.1.3) and *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ* (7.2.3), it is said that there is no stem ending in *ej* (*e*, *o*, *ai*, *au*) before the suffix *sic*; therefore, the *ācārakviP* suffix does not occur after stems ending in *ej*. This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding *viriva*: *viḥ* means "a bird"; the sense is "like that [bird]."

"By way of being manifested": the sense is that this is according to the maxim, "Those whose word-meanings are manifested [are considered as such]. *bubhāva*: here there is no *vuk* augment, nor is there the substitution of *at* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). *abhāvīt*: here, by the rule *gāti-sthā-gati-pṛti-tyaji-añjām a-kṅiti*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. "Caṅ does not apply": the sense is that because the mention of *du* in the rule *ṇi-śri-dru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ* refers only to the root as it appears in the Dhātupāṭha.

(490) *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti* | P. 6.4.15. Regarding *anunāsikasya*: the term *aṅgasya* (of the stem), which is the governing topic (*adhikṛta*), is qualified by *anunāsikasya* (of that which has a nasal).

This is a rule concerning the final element of a compound (tadantavidhiḥ). From the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* is understood to carry over; from the rule *ḍhralope*, the word *dīrghaḥ* is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of that which ends in an anusvāra," and so forth.
