Regarding the form *idāmatī*: since there is no *kvip* suffix used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*) after bases ending in consonants, the rule *hrasvanadyāpaḥ* applies.
It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that this is clear in the *Sūtrabhāṣya*. Regarding the form *pathīnati*:

when the suffix *kvip* is added to the word *pathin*, the vowel *i* is lengthened by the rule *ṭhūlopo 'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143). However, this is in accordance with Mādhava; for even if *kvip* is admitted, the form *pathenati* would be more appropriate when the suffix *tip* follows.

They say that because of the restriction [imposed by the rule], a long vowel is not obtained; nor, because the restriction is antaranga, does the rule *anunāsikasya kvi jhaloḥ kṅiti* cause the lengthening of the penultimate vowel. Regarding *devatīti*:
from the word *div*, with the *kvip* suffix denoting habitual action (*ācāra*) and the *śap* suffix, there is the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel by the rule *naḥ kye*.
The point is that because [the word] necessarily does not end in a *pada*, the substitution of *u* by the rule "ṭhdiva uḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.131) does not apply. Regarding the mention of *ūṭh* here:
when the suffix *kvip* is added to the word *div*, the *v* is replaced by *ūṭh* according to the rule "ṭhcchÂavoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19).

This *ūṭh* supersedes the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel; subsequently, by the rule for *yaṇ* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the *i* is replaced by *yaṇ*. Then, from the stem *dyaū*, when the suffix *śap* is added, [the following occurs] regarding the *ū*-vowel.
The meaning is that the form *dyavati* is appropriate when there is no substitution of *av*. Regarding *cakau*:
from the root *ka*, with the suffix *kvip*, in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *ṇal*, after doubling and the change of *ca* to *cu*, we have *caka-a*.

At this stage, because the elision of the *a* following *k* (by *ato lopaḥ*) is superseded by the subsequent rule for vṛddhi, the vowel *ā* is substituted; then, by the rule "āta au ṇalaḥ," the final *ā* of *ṇal* is replaced by *au*. Thus, *cakau* is formed.
The meaning is that, by the rule *ety-edhaty-utsu*, there is a single substitute *vṛddhi* [for *e* and *a*]. Regarding "Mādhava, however":
when *caka-a* is established, because of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the *vṛddhi* is set aside;

then, after the *lopa* of the *a* following the *k* (by *ato lopaḥ*) has been performed, the form *caka-a* results from the combination of the *ṇal* with the vowel *a*. And this being so, [the form] behaves like *a*.

Even in the case of *ati*, *āṬ*, and *atuh* [in the forms *jagāta*, *jagāthuḥ*, etc.], one might argue that *ato lopaḥ* (P. 6.4.48) should apply, overriding the lengthening prescribed by *ṭhata āder iti* (P. 7.2.70). However, the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*), which is obtained through the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction) rule *ṇyallopāv* (P. 6.4.51), overrides only the immediately preceding lengthening rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (P. 7.4.25); it does not, however, override [the subsequent rule] *ata*.

They say that Mādhava’s intention is that [the substitution] is long even by the rule *ādeḥ* (P. 1.1.54), on the basis of the maxim *anantarasya* (P. 1.1.53). However, that is not based on the original source; the sense is that there is an absence of multiple vowels (*anekāctva*).
In reality, however, this is because the phrase "having removed the mention of the affix" (*pratyayagrahaṇam apanīya*) is not seen in the Bhāṣya.
It was stated immediately below that because it ends in a suffix, the augment *ām* certainly occurs, which is indeed correct.

(491) *bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacverlopaśca halaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.12. From *bhṛśa* and the others, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *bhū* (*bhava*), provided there is no *aci*; and there is the elision of the consonant [of the prefix]. He says this: "in the sense of 'becoming' (*bhavati-arthe*)."

The meaning is "in the state of becoming" (bhavane). "Kyaṅ should occur"—this is because of the continued application (anuvṛtti) of the rule "kyaṅ [is added] after the agent, and there is elision of that [agent]. Regarding the phrase "of these [roots] ending in consonants":
the meaning is that for those [roots] among the *bhṛśādi* group which end in consonants, there is elision [of the final consonant], as well as the addition of *kyaṅ*. Now, an objection:

From where is the phrase "in the sense of becoming what it was not" (abhūtatadbhāve) obtained? To this he says: "By the force of the exclusion (paryudāsa) of 'non-agitation' (acveḥ). The intention is that the Vārttika rule "the mention of 'becoming what it was not'" is intended merely to state the meaning already established [by the sūtra]. As for the expression "those who are very [active] at night": [this refers to those who are so by nature].
The meaning is that they possess an excellence of light. He cites an example ending in a *hal* (consonant) from the *bhṛśādi* group:

*sumanas*. Regarding *sumanāyate*, the meaning is "one who was not well-disposed (*asumanāḥ*) becomes well-disposed (*sumanāḥ*). Although under the governing rule for feminine nouns it is stated: "In the case of *ṭhac*, *apsu*, *manas*, *samāsi*, *katā*, *varṣā*, and [words denoting] plurality..."

In the *Liṅgānuśāsana-sūtra*, the word *sumanas* is prescribed as being invariably plural; nevertheless, that rule applies specifically to the conventional sense (*rūḍha*) of the word as a synonym for "flower" (*devādi*). The intended meaning is that when it is derived etymologically (*yaugika*) as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "one whose mind (*manas*) is good (*su*)"—it is *sumanāḥ* (singular). As for the form *sumanāyate*, it is derived from the suffix *kyaiṅ*.

In the case of *ṭhakṛtsārve*, there is a lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "a salopa ṭhakṛtsārve. Now, an objection is raised: it would be untenable for the form *svamanāyata*—which will be mentioned later—to occur with the augment *aṭ* preceding the word *sumanas* in the *laṅ* tense; for the augment *aṭ* is prescribed for the *aṅga* (the stem), and the entire compound *sumanas* alone constitutes the *aṅga* relative to the suffix *laṅ*.

Anticipating the objection that, by the rule "when a suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of that which begins with the element from which it is prescribed and ends with it," [the form would not apply], he says: "In the *curādi* [list], *saṃgrāma* is recited in the sense of 'battle'.

Consequently, due to the force of its being recited in some places with a prefix (*sopasarga*), [the suffix *kvip*] may be applied after another [root] that also has a prefix, in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*).

The meaning is that it is understood that a prefix does not enter into the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Now, one might object: in the *curādi* class, the word "saṅgrāme" is a complete verbal root; it is not the word "grāma" with a prefix attached.
And thus, since this [word "grāma"] lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), when *kvip* is applied after it along with its prefix, the prefix [would not be elided].

Regarding the phrase "the entry into the perception of the elements" (*dhātusaṃjñāpraveśa*), [the author] asks how this serves as an indicator and says: "In that context, *saṅgrāma* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

In the view that words are derived from roots, the word *grāma*—formed by the addition of the *man* suffix to the root *gras* according to the Uṇādi rule "after *gras*, [the suffix] *man* when *āc* follows"—possesses the status of a nominal stem by the rule "that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix is a nominal stem.
In the view that words are not derived from roots (*avyutpattipakṣa*), [it is a nominal stem] by its very nature.

The meaning is that [the word *cūta*] possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of the rule "that which has a meaning and is not a root is a nominal stem. Now, one might object: its inclusion in the *curādi* (the tenth class of roots) is for the sake of the *ṇic* suffix prescribed under the governing heading of "roots" (*dhātva-dhikāra*); and if this is so, its inclusion in the *curādi* list as a nominal stem would be redundant. To this, he says: "Therefore... (*tasmād iti*).

Therefore, although the causative suffix *ṇic* could have been derived from the nominal stem *saṅgrāma* by means of the *cur*-class suffix *ṇic*, the point is that *ṇic* is established here in the sense of "one performs that" (*tat karoti*). Now, one might ask: since the *ṇic* suffix is already established after the nominal stem *saṅgrāma* by the rule "one performs that" alone, what is the purpose of including it here in the *cur*-class?

To this he says: "by its conjunction with that" (*tatsaṃniyogena*). The meaning is: for the purpose of attaching the *it*-designation to the vowel *a*—which signifies the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*)—in conjunction with the suffix *ṇic*. Nor [is there any fault] in the *it*-designation of the vowel *a* following the *m*, regarding the elision of the *al*.

It should not be argued that because *saṅgrāma* lacks the suffix *ṇi*, the rule "ṇau caṅy upadhāyāḥ" would cause the shortening of the penultimate vowel in the form *asaṅgrāmat*. For this term *saṅgrāma* belongs to the *kathādi* group and ends in a long vowel (*ā*); therefore, the letter *a* is indeed distinct and is attached as an *anubandha*.

This is the meaning. And thus, when the *a* is elided after the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel because the root is *aglopi* (one whose initial part is elided). The intention is that this word is listed in the *curādi* group precisely to obtain the status of having a final *a*, which is characterized by its inclusion in the *kathādi* subgroup. Now, one might object:
since the word *saṅgrāma* in the *curādi* group [is used] with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) added according to the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*), [how can it be included in *kathādi*?]

Granted that there is attachment to the suffix *anubandha*, nevertheless, since an upasarga does not enter into the designation (*saṃjñā*) of a verbal root when the suffix *kvip* follows after the verb *ā-car*, how can this [sūtra] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? To this he says: "In the case of *yuddha*.
[He adds] "by virtue of the sense" (*sāmarthyāt*): for the word *saṅgrāma* is obtained simply by [the rule] "the root *gram* [takes *kvip*] in the sense of battle" (*grāma-yuddhe*).

The meaning is that the word *grāma* alone is never used in the sense of "battle. "A specific reading" means the inclusion of the word *saṃgrāma*. He states the implied meaning: "having the same form," referring to the element *sam* in the word *saṃgrāma*, which denotes battle.

It has been stated that [the element] is of the same form due to the absence of connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*). Regarding the phrase "in that which causes the designation *dhātu*": the remainder [of the context] is "in *kvip* and so forth. "It is separated" means that, consequently, it does not enter into the designation *dhātu*. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "by that"—referring to the word "sa."

The meaning is: "due to the absence of entry into the category of verbal roots (*dhātu*). And so, when the *kvip* suffix for denoting habitual action is intended after the word *sumanas*, since only the word *manas* is a verbal root, the *laṅ* suffix follows from that;
because *manas* alone is the base (*aṅga*), the augment *aṭ* occurs before it, and not before *sumanas*.

The meaning is "prior to the formation of the aggregate. By this, it should be understood that the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "only from *saṅgrāmayati* when preceded by a prefix, not from any other," located in the rule *bhṛśādibhyaḥ*, has been explained. Regarding *unmanāyate*: the suffix *kyaiṅ* is applied because [the stem] belongs to the *bhṛśādi* group.

[The suffix] *salopaḥ* [is applied]. And thus: by this aforementioned method, even in the rule prescribing *kvip* for the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāre*) as in *avagalbha*, because *ava* is separated [from the root], the meaning is that the augment *aṭ* occurs before the word *galbha*. Now, one might object: *ā-ūḍhaḥ* becomes *oḍhaḥ*; this is a compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*. From this [word *oḍha*], the suffix *kyaiṅ* [is added] because it belongs to the *bhṛśādi* group.
The form is *āṭ-ṭhoḍhāyate*, and so forth. Here too, the designation "root" (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) would not apply to *āṅ*.

In that case, although there is no difference in the resulting form whether the *āṭ* augment is applied before the suffix *laṅ* or before the word *ūḍhi* (or *āṅ*), the form *āṬḍhāyate* is established in either event. Nevertheless...
From the word *oḍhāya*, which ends in the *kyaṅ* suffix, when the *kvā* suffix is applied and the final vowel (*a*) is elided, the form *oḍhāyitvā* alone is desired.

Here, since the *kyaṅ* suffix is intended to be applied, according to the aforementioned method, the prefix *āṅ* is separated; and once separated, by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, it is compounded with the element ending in the *kvā* suffix, after which the final vowel (*a*) is elided.

It is intended that [the prefix] *oḍhā* itself [is used]. Here, when *kyaṅ* is desired to be applied, if one were to separate [the prefix] according to the aforementioned method, then for the separated *āṅ*, there would be a compound with the word ending in the suffix *ktvā* by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*.
Consequently, by the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap*, the suffix *lyap* would occur; therefore, he says:
And an indicator (*jñāpaka*) has as its scope only those items belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*). He establishes this very point with the words "by that" (*tena*).

In the *curādi* group, regarding the entry "saṅgrāma yuddhe," the separation of the prefix *sam-* [from the root] serves as an indicator; by relying on the principle that such an indicator applies only to members of the same class, wherever the nature of the prefix remains unaltered...

It is heard [in the tradition], but it has not been sublated by a single uniform rule; rather, the meaning is that it should be understood as the separation of the prefix (*upasarga*) in that very context.
The intention is that this is because the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), namely the *saṅgrahaṇa* in the rule for battle (*saṅgrāma*), is of such a nature.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And thus... and "having caused to be carried away" (*oḍhāyitvā*).
From the word *oḍha*, by virtue of its inclusion in the *bhṛśādi* group, the suffix *kyaiṅ* is applied;

from the form *oḍhāya*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied, followed by the suffix *kvap*. After the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel *a*, the form [is established]. Regarding the phrase "here" (*atra*): the connection is that "here [the suffix] *lyap* does not occur. This is because when *kyaṅ* is intended, the prefix *āṅ* is superseded by the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule.

The sense is that since there is no separation [of the prefix], there is no compound of that [prefix] with the word ending in the suffix *ktvā*; therefore, the substitution of *lyap* does not occur. "Unmanāyya" and "avagalbhyetivat" are negative examples (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).

From the word *unmanas*, because it belongs to the *bhṛśādi* group, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*); after the elision of the suffixal *s*, by the rule "*ṭhakṛtsārvadhātuka..."* [the final vowel is lengthened].
From the word *unmanāya* with the suffix *ktvā*, after the elision of *lyap* and the subsequent elision of the final vowel (*ataḥ*), the form *unmanāyya* is obtained.
From the word *avagalbha*, which ends in *kvip* in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāre*) as *avagalbha*, the form [is derived] after the elision of *kvip* and *lyap*.
Here, because the phonetic forms of the prefixes *ud-* and *ava-* are not elided, they remain before the *kyaṅ* and *ikvip* suffixes.

And when those two [roots] are intended to be treated as distinct, since there is a compound with a suffix ending in *ktvā*, the suffix *lyap* is appropriate. But here, in the case of *oḍhāyitvā*, that is not so;
thus, this is a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). He shows the evidence for the indicator (*jñāpaka*) being of the same class:
Regarding the word *jñāpakasya*, he shows the sixth [chapter] Vārtika: *usyomāṅkṣu*.
This is a *dvandva* compound of *usi*, *om*, and *āṅ*. This Vārtika is recited in the first quarter of the sixth chapter under the rule *omāṅośca*. He explains it as follows: *usyomāṅeśca*.

Regarding the phrase "of the two subsequent [sounds]": considering the continuation of the term *pararūpa* from the rule *ṭheṅi pararūpam*, he says—"*pararūpaṃ na*" (there is no single-substitute form). He first provides an example for *usi*: *āusrīyat*. This is derived from the root *usra-* with the suffix *kyac* according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyañca* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), meaning "he desired a cow for himself," followed by the optative (*liṅ*) suffix.

When the suffix *aṭ* is added before the word *usrīya*, the rule "the single substitute for [a vowel] at the end of a word" (*ṭhusyapadāntāt*) would have applied; this [present rule] prohibits that. However, the maxim regarding the mention of meaningful items (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) is not universal, as is evident from this very example in the Bhāṣya. Otherwise, in forms such as *bhindyauḥ*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would not occur.

When *laṅ* follows a root ending in *kyac*, after *āṭ* has been applied to the verbal base (*iṅga*), the substitution of the single substitute for the subsequent form (*pararūpa*)—as prescribed by the rule "ṭhemoṅeśca"—is prohibited by this [present sūtra]. To illustrate with *āṅ*: *āuḍhaīyat*. Here, *oḍhaḥ* is derived from *ā ūḍhaḥ*;
then, after *kyac* is added, when *laṅ* follows that *kyac*-ending form, *āṭ* is applied to the verbal base *oḍha*.

By this [rule], the substitution of a single substitute (*pararūpa*) that would otherwise have occurred in the case of *ṭhoma-aṅe* is prohibited. These three examples are established in the Bhāṣya. In that context, if there were a separation [of the components] even when the very form of the preposition (*upasarga*) is subsumed by a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), then, when *kyac* is intended to be applied, once the separation of *āṅ* has taken place—

Since the word *ūḍha* is derived from outside the *dhātu* (verbal root) class, when *āṅ* precedes it and *āṭ* follows, a single-substitute (*pararūpa*) would not even be applicable; thus, the prohibition of *pararūpa* by *āṅ* would be redundant.
However, if the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) applies to its own kind (*sajātīya*), then *āṅ* [is indeed applicable] here.

Because the substitution by a single substitute (ekādeśa) results in the absence of separate treatment, once the augment *āṬ* has been applied before the word *oḍha*, the substitution of a single long vowel (*pirarūpa*) would otherwise apply; therefore, the prohibition [of that substitution] becomes meaningful. Consequently, since the indicator (*jñāpaka*) applies to its own class (*sajātīya*), the mention of *āṅ* in the rule *ṭhusyomāṅkṣu* is for the sake of [excluding] *āṬ*, as in *āṬḍhaīyat*.

He demonstrates this with the words "of the substitution of *ḍha*, etc. The meaning is that because the substitutions for *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍha* are considered *asiddha*, the word *hata* undergoes reduplication according to the rule "the second member beginning with a consonant [is reduplicated]. As for the phrase "thus it has been stated," the remainder is "in the section on the derivation of roots with the *luṅ*-suffix, regarding the root *ūrṇuñ*. And thus, *ha*...

The meaning is that when the word *ti* is doubled and the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant) applies, the substitution of *c* for *h* occurs by the rule *ṭhkuhoścu*. Regarding the word *ḍhi*: the meaning is that although the principle *pūrvatrāsiddhīyamadvitve* ("that which is not established in what precedes does not apply in the case of doubling") is sometimes considered non-eternal, there is no evidence for its non-application here [in this specific context].

Regarding the form *ūḍhamākhyat*: from the root *vah* with the suffix *kta*, after the application of the rules for *ḍha*-ness, *dha*-ness, *ṣṭu*-ness, and the elision of *ḍh*, we have the word *ūḍha*.

From this, with the causative suffix *ṇic* and the aorist suffix *luṅ* along with *ciṅ*, because the rules for *ḍhi*-ness and so forth are considered asiddha (not yet applied), there is doubling of the substitute *ḍh* by the rule *ḍho ḍhe*, followed by the elision of the remaining consonant (*halādiśeṣa*) and the change of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) to a palatal (*cutva*). Thus the form is *āuḍaḍhat*.

In the case where there is no assumption of the non-application of the rule "that which is not established in the preceding [is treated as absent] except for reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyamadvitve*), the form results from the reduplication of the word *ḍha*. Now, one might object: since the elision of the vowel (*ṭilopa*) applies here by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), once that elision has occurred, whether the reduplication is applied to the entire element *hṛ* together with the *ṇic* suffix or to *ḍhai*, only the vowel *i* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and not the vowel *a*.
Therefore, he says: "oḥ puyaṇityādi" (Pāṇini 7.3.80). Fearing that the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel) might occur due to the suffix *ṇic* added to the word *sva*, he says:

"prakṛtyaikāj" (Pāṇini 6.4.163). Because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), there is no *ṭilopa*; thus, upon the *vṛddhi* of the letter *a*, the letter *ā* results, and the augment *puk* is applied. He states this as: "vṛddhipukau. This applies in cases such as *tvāpayati* and *māpayati*.

He demonstrates the grammatical derivation: "of that which ends in *map*" (*maparyantasya*). According to the rule "after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [the substitutes] *tvam* and *au* [are used] in the case of the suffix *ṇic* and in a following word," *tvam* and *au* replace the portions ending in *map*. Thus, we have the stages *tva-ad-i* and *ma-ad-i*. Regarding this, he says: "from the subsequent form" (*pararūpāt*). Whether the substitution of the subsequent form has been applied or not, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) [occurs].

The permanence of the grammatical operation (*pravṛtti*) should be understood. Regarding the statement *tva-i-ma-i*, he says: "There is *vṛddhi*. The vowel *ā* replaces the vowel *a*. One should not suspect that the elision of the *ṭi*-suffix (*ṭilopa*) possesses the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element), because it is not a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*). [The term] *puk* refers to the rule *artipivatyarti...* (Pāṇini 7.3.36); this is the intended meaning. Thus it is.
Having presented the view of the ancients, he states his own position with the words "tvādayati," etc.

He establishes that very point with the words "because it is internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*). When *tva* + *ad-i* and *ma* + *ad-i* are situated thus, the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) is applied—despite its being superseded by the obligatory elision of the suffixal *ṭi*—because it is an internal operation.

The intention is that, because the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of suffixal operations) applies by the rule "ṭh-prakṛtyaikāc," the elision of the *ṭi* portion (*ṭilopa*) does not take effect, and thus the *upadhā-vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening of the penultimate syllable) occurs. Now, to the question "What are the examples for the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *iman*, and *īyas*?", having shown the examples *preyān*, *premā*, and *preṣṭhaḥ*, [the author] states: "This is not a necessary purpose, as per the rule 'ṭh-prastha-sphē...'"

Having stated that because [the substitution of] *pra* and so forth is *ābhīya*, it is treated as *asiddha*, and therefore the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) does not apply there;

[the author then notes that] in the case of *śreyān* and *śreṣṭhaḥ*, since the substitute *śra-*—prescribed by the rule "for *praśasya*, [substitute] *śraḥ*" (Pāṇini 5.3.60)—is derived from the fifth book (*pāñcamika*), it lacks the status of being *ābhīya*. Consequently, as it is not *asiddha*, the elision of the *ṭi* would otherwise apply.

Having demonstrated another example for the rule regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) under the condition of *ṭhri*, and having stated that "in the case of the substitute *śra*, the elision of *ṭi* will not occur due to the force of the pronunciation of the vowel *a*," [the author] then addresses the need to prevent the elision of *ṭi* in cases such as *sragvitamaḥ* and *srajiṣṭhaḥ*, where the suffixes *vin* and *matup* have been elided by the rule *vinmatorluk*.

Having stated that this is a rule for establishing the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), [it was argued that] since the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) is already established, the *luk* elision—which is being introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to it—will necessarily subvert the *ṭilopa*.
Consequently, the rule "prakṛtyaikāc" (Pāṇini 6.4.163) was rejected in the Bhāṣya; thus, in forms such as *vādayati* and *mādayati*, [the elision does not occur].

Anticipating the objection that the presentation of the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) is not tenable, he refutes it with the words "And not... and so forth. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the Bhāṣya. For the intent of the cited Bhāṣya—such as in the cases of *preyān*, *preṣṭhaḥ*, and so on—is indeed to establish [the forms] even without the application of *prakṛtibhāva*, and not [to prescribe it].

The rejection of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) in such cases is intended; for it is necessary in examples such as *svam ācaṣṭe* and *svapāyati*. For this very reason, during the commentary on the Vārttika: "If [it is argued that] there is *prakṛtibhāva* in the case of a single-vowel (*ekāj*) base before the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *praśasya*, [we reply] no, because of the power of the explicit utterance [of the rule], and because it is not so stated, there is *prakṛtibhāva*."

It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) will occur even without the explicit statement. Otherwise, it would have been said, "only by means of the statement. Let that suffice for now. In the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, the term *ekavacane* (in the singular) is understood from the previous context. And that...
The etymological meaning is resorted to; thus, it is understood that [the rule applies] to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they denote a qualified singularity.

Thinking this, he says, "either you two" (*yuvām*) or "we two" (*āvām*). Nor should one suspect that the substitutes *yuvā-* and *āvā-* apply when two [persons] are expressed, because the case-ending has been elided by *luk*. And as for *luk*—
It should not be asked, "Why would the forms *yuvāvau* not occur even earlier?

The sense is that this is because of the rule: "An external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules. Regarding the form *śāvayati*, the meaning is "he describes a dog" (*śvānam ācaṣṭe*). When the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the word *śvan*, resulting in the form *śvani*, he says: *naḥ taddhite* ("the *n* [is elided] before a secondary suffix").
Thus, having raised the objection regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc*, he says: "But there is no preservation of the original form.

To the question "Why?", he replies: "By which... When the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* (the *ṭilopa*) by the rule *ṭeḥ* was about to take place, the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* was indeed commenced; [this applies] to forms such as *srajiṣṭha* by the rule *nastaddhite*.

The meaning is that the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) is initiated even when [the condition for its application] has not been met. Regarding the phrase "because of being a *bha*":

by virtue of being treated like the desiderative (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), it is a *bha*; thus, the meaning is that there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) according to the rule *śvayuvamaghonām ataddhite*. Consequently, when *śvan-i* remains and the *ṭi*-lopa (elision of the final vowel) occurs, because that [elision] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *ābhīya* (belonging to a subsequent rule), the word ends in *an*, and therefore... [the suffix *vas* applies].

In the case of *saṃprasāraṇa*, when the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied, there is the substitution of *āv* for the vowel *u* by means of *vṛddhi*. Regarding the phrase "others, however" (*anye tv iti*): the extension (*atideśa*) "like the *iṣṭhan*" applies only to that which is actually seen in the presence of the suffix *iṣṭhan*. The elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) is seen only in the presence of *iṣṭhan*, and not [by the rule] "*ṭhnastaddhite*" (Pāṇini 6.4.143).
Therefore, the meaning is that this [elision] is not extended [to other cases]. Now, [if one asks]: "By what is he a *brahman* in the highest degree?"

Since the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is observed in the word *brahmiṣṭha* by the rule *naṣtaddhite* ("there is no elision when a taddhita suffix follows"), he says: "in *brahmiṣṭha* and so forth. By the phrase "by that," the meaning is: by the non-application of the rule *naṣtaddhite*. Consequently, because the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is maintained, there is an absence of the elision [of the penultimate vowel] by the rule *ṭeḥ*; thus, after the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), one forms *śunayati*.
The meaning is "form" (rūpa). The phrase "they say" (āhuḥ) indicates a lack of conviction [in that view]. The seed of that [conviction] is as follows:

in the case of *brahma-vat*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied to words such as *śabda*, the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*)—which would otherwise be an exception—is indeed observed by the rule "the elision of *matup* after *ṭhan* and *vin*" (*ṭhvinmatorluk*), followed by the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) by the rule "of *naḥ* before a taddhita suffix" (*nastaddhite*). Consequently, in the case of *iṣṭhan*...

The statement "because that [suffix] has not been seen" is an overstatement. Furthermore, the claim that "in cases such as *brahmiṣṭha*, the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.155) applies because it is subsequent" is incorrect; for since the word *brahman* by itself denotes the Veda and the like, it lacks the quality of being a *guṇavacana* (an adjective expressing a quality), and thus the suffix *iṣṭhan* is difficult to obtain. [This is so] because [the rule] begins with *aj-*.

This is because it is stated [in the *Śabdakaustubha*] that [the suffix *iṣṭhan*] occurs only after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*). However, when *iṣṭhan* follows a word ending in *matup*, there is elision (*luk*) of *matup*; since this elision subverts the application of the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.155), that rule does not apply after the elision. Thus, the argument based on "priority" (*paratva*) is also untenable—this is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. [The form] *vidvayatī* is derived as follows: [...]

The suffix *ṇau* is added to the word *vidvas*, and there is the elision (*ṭilopa*) of the *ṭi*. Now, one might object that because it is treated like the desiderative (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), it would be a *bha*-stem, and thus by the rule "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *u* in *ṭh* and *vas*" [Pāṇini 6.4.131], a problem would arise; anticipating this, he says: "by the principle that 'when an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅgavṛtta*), there is no further application of a rule. This means by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) stating that once an operation affecting a stem has been performed, there is no further application of a rule. Once the stem-operation has been completed...

The meaning of that [statement] is that there is no need for the application of the *aṅga* designation. In reality, however, in the case of *vidhyati*, since the *as* is elided by the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143), the suffix does not end in *vas*;
consequently, because the condition for *saṃprasāraṇa* does not arise, the introduction of the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding operations on the *aṅga*) is [unnecessary].
The word "vṛthā" (in vain) indicates a lack of approval—this is what "some say" implies. Regarding the form *saṃprasāraṇe*:

others hold that when the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *vidvas*, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) occurs by virtue of its being treated like the *iṣṭhan* suffix; then, upon the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the *va*, the formation of the single preceding syllable (*pūrvarūpa*), the *vṛddhi* of the *u*, and the substitution of *ā* for *av*, the form *vidāvayati* is produced. This is the opinion of others.

This is the meaning. Here too, as before, there is a lack of conviction (*asvarasa*), because once the *ṭi*-elision has occurred, the word would no longer end in *vas*. Regarding the term "because it is obligatory" (*nityatvāt*): the *saṃprasāraṇa* is obligatory because it applies whether the *ṭi*-elision has been performed or not; however, the *ṭi*-elision applies only when the *saṃprasāraṇa* has already been performed.

The intention is this: since the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) rule has been applied, the form becomes *uso*; however, if it were not applied, it would be *asa*. Thus, [the rule for *usa*] is considered non-eternal (*anitya*) according to the maxim: "A grammatical operation that applies to a different word-form is non-eternal. Now, one might object:
even if the *saṃprasāraṇa* has been applied, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffixal *ṭi*) occurs as *asa* itself prior to the application of the *pararūpa* (subsequent single-substitute) rule.

To show that this [substitution] is not permanent, he says: "Because it is internal, the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for preceding and following vowels) takes precedence over the elision of the *ṭi*. By stating "others say," he indicates his own dissatisfaction with the view that once the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the *pūrvarūpa* have been applied, the *saṃprasāraṇa* would not occur again because the status of ending in *vasu* would be destroyed even when the *us* is elided. And thus...

The first position alone remains: that it means "he causes to know. In that case, it is established that the introduction of the technical term *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the operation within a base) is indeed useless. Regarding the form *udīcayati*: from the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *ut*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *ṛtvig-ādi* (*Pāṇini 3.2.59*);

then, by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (*Pāṇini 8.2.7*), the *n* is elided, resulting in the word *udac*. From that, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, [the form is derived] by virtue of its being like the *iṣṭhan* suffix.
The meaning is as follows: by the rule *bhatvādacaḥ*, the elision of the vowel *a* is set aside; then, by the rule *uda īt*, the substitution of *ī* occurs, resulting in *udīc-*.

From this causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the *laṅ* and other tenses are derived. Regarding *udaicit*: in the *luṅ* tense, because of the prohibition of the elision of the *ṇi* by the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, the syllable *ci* undergoes reduplication. [This applies when] the preceding member has the same form as a prefix (*upasarga*).

The meaning is that because of the statement, "When a suffix causing the notion of a root-element (*dhātu-saṃjñā*) is intended to be applied, [the preceding element] is separated," the *āṬ* is placed above *ud*. And thus, by the separation of *ud*, there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) due to the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) prescribed by the rule *prakṛtyaikāj*. Regarding the form *pratīcayati*: after the elision of *ac* by the rule *acaḥ*, [the form *pratic* arises] by the rule *cau*.

The long vowel of the preceding [element]. As in *pratyacicat*: here, after the elision of *ac* by the rule *acaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs for the *i* following the *ṭ* before the syllable *ci*; although the elision of the *a* by *acaḥ* is "belonging to the subsequent" (*ābhīya*), it does not have the status of being "as if non-existent" (*asiddhatva*) because they do not share the same basis (*asamānāśrayatva*), since the elision is caused by the *ṇi* suffix, whereas the *āṭ* augment...
Because it is not based on a scriptural rule (*luṅânimittatvāt*). Regarding the phrase "iko 'savarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.127), the prohibition "na samāse" (Pāṇini 6.1.131) does not apply here;

for by means of the separation [of the words], the application of the *samāsa* rule is excluded. In the form *samīcayati*, there is the substitution of *sami* for *sama* according to "samaḥ sami" (Pāṇini 6.3.93).
When the *lopa* of the vowel *a* occurs by "acaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.138), the lengthening of the vowel occurs by "cā" (Pāṇini 6.3.138). Thus we have *samyacicat*.

Because the substitute *sam* (for *saṃ*) is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), it retains its status as a prefix (*upasarga*); therefore, it is separated [from the root]. Due to this separation, even though the condition of being followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is absent, the substitution of *sam* for *saṃ*, having already occurred, is not revoked. Thus, we have *tirāyayati*. Here, *tiras* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). From that [prefix] preceding the root *añc*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied].

The meaning is as follows: when the *kvip* suffix is elided, after the word *tiras*, by the rule *ac-iti* [Pāṇini 6.4.139], the *ṇi* suffix is applied; then, by the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant), the verbal root is removed.

Subsequently, by the rule *tiraso 'tiryalope* [Pāṇini 6.3.94], *tiras* is replaced by *tiri*. Then, the vowel *i* undergoes *vṛddhi*, resulting in the substitution of *āy*; thus, from the form *tirāyī*, the *ṇyat* suffix is added, and from that, the *laṅ* and other verbal endings are derived. Nor is there [any issue] with *tiras*.

If there were a separation [of the prefix], one might ask how the elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs, given that the rule *prakṛtyaikāj* (Pāṇini 6.4.163) would cause the base form (*prakṛti-bhāva*) to remain; however, this is not the case because *tiras* is never an upasarga, and thus, lacking the status of having a form identical to an upasarga, there is no separation of it [from the verb]. But if this is so, [what follows?]

One might ask: "If there is an elision of the *iṭ* augment due to the root *añc*, then since the condition of being followed by *añc* is absent, how can there be the replacement of *tiras* with *tiri* here?
To this, he says: "by the elision of the *iṭ* of *añc*. [He explains:
"By virtue of being external (*bahiraṅgatvena*). The meaning is: because it is caused by a factor that is external (*bahirbhūta*). Nor... [is there any contradiction].

It might be argued that since there is a separation [of *tiras*], the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* (ṭilopa) would not occur due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "when a single vowel follows the root, it remains in its original form" (*dhātoḥ ṭhprakṛtyaikā’j*). However, this objection is invalid; for *tiras* is never an *upasarga*, and because it lacks the same phonetic form as an *upasarga*, there is no separation [of the prefix from the root]. But if this is so...

When there is an elision by the *iṭ* augment of the root *añc*, since the condition of being followed by *añc* is absent, how can there be the substitution of *tiras* for *tiras* here? To this he says: "by the elision of the *iṭ* of *añc*" and "on account of its being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)."
The sense is that [the substitution] is caused by a suffix external to the word-base (*bahirbhūta*). Now, one might object: let there be *tiri* for *tiras*;
in that case, would not the vowel *a* following the *r* be elided by the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143)? To this he says: "asiddhavadatrā—" (Pāṇini 6.4.22). The construction is:
"the first elision of *ṭi* is treated as if non-existent" (*asiddha*). This refers to the state when *tiras-ac-i* has been established and the first operation has already taken place.

The meaning is that the elision of the *ṭi* suffix in the form *aci* is considered "asiddha" (non-existent) when the elision of the *ṭi* in *tiraḥ* is to be performed, because it belongs to the *ābhīya* class [of rules].

Now, one might ask: how can the first elision of *ṭi* be considered asiddha when the elision of the *ṭi* in *tiraḥ* is to be performed, given that the rule for eliding *ṭi* is a single one? To this, he says: *ciṇo*...

Regarding the phrase "by the rule of *luṅ*": when the suffix *ta* of the third person singular (*prathamapuruṣaikavacana*) of the *taiṅ* [terminations] follows the root *pac* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), and when *luṅ* is applied, the substitution of *ciṇ* for *clī* occurs by the rule "ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ. Following this, with the occurrence of *vṛddhi* in the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) and the addition of the augment *aṭ*, we have *apāci*. From this form, the suffix *tarap* is added by the rule "tiṅśca."

When the suffix *ām* is added by the rule *ṭhkimetiṅvyayaghādāp* after that [form], resulting in *apācitatarām*, the elision (*luk*) of the first *ta*-suffix occurs by the rule *ciṇo luṅ*. However, there is no subsequent elision of the *tarap* suffix and the second *ta*-suffix, because the elision [of the first] was conditioned by a different locus (*sthānibheda*).
The established rule is that [the substitution] is not applied because it is separated by the fact that the first *luk* is treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the other.
The meaning is that it is the same here as well. "From this" means: because the first *ṭilopa* is treated as *asiddha*.
Or, by the *paribhāṣā* regarding what occurs within a stem (*aṅgavṛtta*), the phrase "not again when there is a *ṭilopa*" (*punarṭilope na*) is to be supplied. Nor is it...

It should not be argued that, due to the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding operations within the base), the rule "ṭeḥ" would prevent the elision [of the final 'i'], and consequently the *vṛddhi* substitution in *tirāyayati* would also not occur;
for the *aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā* is non-eternal (*anitya*), and thus it does not apply in the case of *vṛddhi*.
Regarding the phrase "because of being *aglopi*": when the rule *tiras-ac-i* has been applied, and the vowel of the root is elided by the rule *ṭe'r*, the form *tiri-* becomes *aglopi*.
The underlying assumption is that when a vowel of a root is elided, the letter *a* is also elided. Regarding the form *sadhrāyayati*: *saha-* becomes *sadhr-*.
The form is like that of *tirāyayati*. Because *saha* lacks the status of an *upasarga*, it is not separated [from the following element].

Thus he says: *asasadhrāyat*. Regarding *viṣvadraḷñcam*: when *viṣvak* and *ac* stand together, by the rule *viṣvagdevayośca*, the *ṭi* (the final vowel) of the word *viṣvak* is replaced by *adraḷ*, and by the rule *ṭeḥ*, the *ac* [is elided].

When the suffix *dhātu* is elided, the form *viṣvadri-i* being established, [the substitution of] *vṛddhi* and the replacement by *āya* result in *viṣvadrāyi*; from this causative stem (*ṇyantāt*), with the suffix *laṭ*, the form *viṣvadrāyayati* is obtained. Regarding *devadraḷñcam*:
having taken for granted that the word *deva* undergoes the replacement of its final vowel (*ṭi*) with *adraḷ*—resulting in *devadrāyayati*—he states the form in the *luṅ* tense: *devadraḷñcam*.
Regarding *adidevadrāyat*: the form is like *atitirāyat*. Regarding *ādadadrāyat*:

because the word *adas* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the substitute *adraḷ* occurs for its final vowel (*ṭi*). According to the view that "the substitution of *u* and *m* occurs only when the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and so on has taken place," [the form would be] *idam*; however, in the case of the word *adas*, the case ending is elided by *luk*.

Because the suffixes [of the case endings] do not follow immediately [after the base], the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of the initial of *adas* with *a*) does not apply. Relying on the view that "even when not subject to *tyadādyatva*, the substitutions of *utva* and *matva* do occur," he says: *amumuyañcam*. When *adas* + *ac* + *i* is established, the *adr̥l* substitute is applied to the final phoneme (*ṭi*), and upon the elision of the final phoneme of *ac*, the form *adadri i* remains.

According to the view that "the substitution of *m* for the *ṭha* [of *adas*] occurs separately from *adriḥ*," once the substitution of *m* for the *d* and *a*, and the substitution of *i* for the *r* and *e* have been applied, resulting in the form *amumu i*,
the first *i* undergoes *vṛddhi* by the rule *ṇici*, followed by the replacement with *āya*, yielding *amumu āyī*.

The sense is that the *laṅ* and other suffixes are applied after the causative (*ṇic*). Because the substitution of *m* (mutva) is considered *asiddha*, the *yaṇ* replacement does not occur. Regarding the form *adamūyayati*:

this is according to the view of "some" (*kecit*) who hold that [the rule applies] to the final portion of the word. Regarding *bhuvam*: the meaning is "he describes the earth"; the suffix *ṇic* is added to the word *bhū*. After the application of *vṛddhi* and the *āv* substitute, the suffixes *laṅ* and others are applied to the form *bhāvī*; such is the sense.
Regarding *abībhavat*: by the rule *oḥ puyaṇjī*, there is the substitution of *it* (the short vowel *i*). Regarding *abubhravat*:
because there is no following *pavarga* (labial consonant) preceded by an *avarṇa* (vowel), the rule *oḥ puyaṇjī* does not apply.
Regarding *svaśvam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a beautiful horse" (*su-śobhanaḥ aśvaḥ*). Regarding *svāśaśvat*.

Because the word *aśva* is separated from that which has the same form as a preposition (*upasarga*), there is reduplication according to the rule *ṭhajāderdvitīyasya* and the augment *āṭ*. Regarding *svariti*: from the word *svar*, after the application of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) by the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre*; this is because it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*bha*) due to its treatment as being like the original base (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*). However, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) does not apply here, because of the rule *prakṛtyaikāj*.

By the principle of "that which is not yet reached" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), this [rule] is indeed the sublater of *ṭhṭhe'ri* (Pāṇini 6.4.153). As in the example *asasvaditi*: when the doubling (*dvitva*) is to be applied, because the substitution of *ṇau* (the causative suffix) is prohibited, the doubling of the word *svar* takes place instead of subverting the *ṭilopa*;
since the elision of the *akāra* also occurs upon the elision of the *ṭha*.
The meaning is that [the substitution] is not an *ajādeśa* (a substitute beginning with a vowel). Regarding *asisvadat*:

according to the view that the elision of the *ar* (in *svarati*) is not an *ajādeśa*, when the operation of reduplication is to be applied, there is no prohibition of the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate syllable) after the causative suffix (*ṇic*);
thus, once the *ṭilopa* has been performed, the word *svi* undergoes reduplication along with the *ṇic*. Regarding *bahūn*: this refers to the word *bahu* followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "as in *iṣṭhan*," the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu* occurs according to the rule "there is elision of *bahu*,

and *bhū* takes the place of *bahu*. However, the augment *yiṭ* does not apply by the rule "the augment *yiṭ* is added to *iṣṭha*," because the intention is that the extended application applies only to those operations actually observed when *iṣṭhan* follows, as indicated by the locative case in the rule "as in *iṣṭhan*."
The sense is that because of the absence of the suffix *yiṭ*, there is also an absence of the substitution of *bhū* which is prescribed in conjunction with it.

Regarding *srajayati*: because of the status of being "like *iṣṭha*" (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup* according to the rule *vinmator luk*. Now, one might object that the suffix *iṣṭhan* is difficult to obtain from the word *sragvin* because of the restriction "only after words denoting qualities that begin with a vowel"; however, the status of being "like *iṣṭha*" applies here [to justify the elision].

One might ask how this is so; the intention is that by the rule *vinmatoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.122), which prescribes the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *vin*, the status of being treated as *iṣṭhan* is established for words such as *sragvin*. Anticipating an objection regarding the increase of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*), he says:
"There is no vowel increase because it is preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvakatvāt*). By this extension (*atideśa*) [stated] in *ṇāviṣṭhava*d... [the status of *vin* is established].
Kaiyaṭa states that there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the elision of *luk* applies to the whole word" (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*).

Regarding the form *śrīmatīm*: from the word *śrīmatī*, after the addition of the suffix *ṇic*, the masculine form is applied by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "as in the case of *iṣṭhan*" (*iṣṭhavad*), resulting in the rule "of the *bha*-stem, when followed by a non-feminine suffix" (*bhasyāḍhea*). Consequently, by the rule "the elision of *matup* and *vin*" (*vinmatoḥ*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup*, and [there follows the elision] of the vowel following the *repha*.
The meaning is that because of the rule "after [the augment] *ṭh*, *śrāyī*," the *laṅ* and other suffixes follow immediately after the root. Regarding *aśiśrayat*:

Mādhava holds that since there is no substitution for the *ā* in the causative (*ṇic*), the reduplication of the word *śri* occurs first—prior to the application of the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions—and only then do the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions take place in the second member, resulting in the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*).

Others hold that because the *akāra* is also elided when there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup*, the stem is treated as having its final vowel elided (*aglopin*), and thus the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) does not apply. Regarding the form *payasvinīm*: the intention is that when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, the suffix *matup* is elided by the rule *vin-mator luk* (Pāṇini 5.3.65), since the causative behaves like the primary derivative (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*). In the case of *payasayati*, one might suspect the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) due to *iṣṭhavadbhāva*; therefore, he says: "In this case..."

"The elision of *ṭi* does not [apply]. Why? To this he says: "Because of its exception" (*tadapavādasya*). Nor should it be argued: "Once the elision of *matup* has been applied, overriding the elision of *ṭi*, why would the elision of the *ṭi* of *payas-* not occur?
For, according to the maxim "an operation occurs even when there is a possibility of conflict," the elision of the *ṭi* of *payas-* [is indeed blocked].
This is because the elision (*luk*) of the *matup* suffix takes precedence. Regarding the form *sthavayati*:

from the word *sthūla*, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied, the *sthūla* portion undergoes elision of the *yaṇ*-class sounds (the *ū*) by the rule *sthūladūrayuvahrasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇām yaṇādilopaśca*; then, the *ū* vowel undergoes *guṇa*, which is replaced by *ava*.

Thus, from the stem *sthavi*, the present tense suffixes (*laḍ* etc. are applied—this is the intended meaning. [In this process], the *guṇa* of the *o* vowel [is not applied] because it is not an *ac* vowel.

One should not suspect that there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] by the rule *ñṇiti*; for once an operation on the *aṅga* has been performed, an operation on the *aṅga* does not apply again. Thus, in *davayati*, as before, there is the elision of the *yaṇ*-class vowels and so forth, as well as *guṇa*. [The questioner asks: "How then [is it formed]? [The answer is: By the rule *sthūladūrayuva...* regarding the elision of the *yaṇ*-class vowels and so forth.

The sense is that [the elision of *ṭi*] is an exception (*apavāda*). Regarding the form *dūramatī*: from the root *at* in the sense of "continuous motion" (*sātatyagamana*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*, resulting in the form *dūrāt*. From the root *aya* in the sense of "motion," *kvip* is applied; then, by the rule *lopo vyor vali*, there is the elision of *y*, and by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk*, [the augment *tuk* is added].
The form is simply *dūrāt*. From that, after the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the elision of the *ṭi* portion, we have *dūrī*.

From this causative stem, with the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), the verbal root vowel (*śap*), and the substitution of *ay* for the vowel *i*, the word *dūrayat* is formed; thus, *dūrayati* is the locative singular form—this is the intended meaning. Therefore, he says: "the meaning is 'making [something] distant'."

"Ṭhkurvatī" is a word ending in the locative case. Regarding "yavayati": from the word *yuvan*, with the suffix *ṇiC* [causative], there is the elision of the vowel following *yaṇ* (the *u*) according to the rule *sthūladūretyādinā yaṇādilopaḥ*. There is then the *guṇa* substitution for the preceding *u*, resulting in the *av* replacement. From the form *yavi*, the *laṭ* [present tense] and other suffixes are applied. "Kanayati" is the form when the substitution of *kan* for the word *yuvan* is adopted.

Thus he says: "yuvālpayoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.64). Regarding "nedayati": the word *antika* undergoes the substitution *neda* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, because it is stated that "for *antika* and *bāḍha*, there are the substitutes *neda* and *sādha*. Regarding "sādhayati": the word *bāḍha* undergoes the substitution *sādha* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*. Regarding "iha": in the expression "praśasyayati," [the substitute] *śra* occurs for *praśasya*.

The phrase "and *jya*" (*jya-ce*) means for the purpose of substitution. Why? To this he says: "of the prefix" (*upasargasya*). The intention is that when there is a separation [from the prefix], because the specific original form (*sthānin*) no longer exists, there can be no substitute. Thus, in the case of *vṛddham*—as in *jyāpayati*—when the word *vṛddha* undergoes the substitution of *jyā* by the rule "and of *vṛddha*" (*vṛddhasya ca*), [the result is *jyāpayati*].

The sense is "pug" (the augment *puk*). He provides examples according to the sequence of the rule *priyasthira* etc.: *priyam prāpayati* ("he causes the beloved to reach [it]"); when the word *priya* is replaced by *prā*, there is *vṛddhi* and the *puk* augment. *sthāpayati* ("he causes to stand"); when the word *sthira* is replaced by *sthā*, there are *vṛddhi* and *puk*. *varayati* or *vārayati* ("he chooses" or "he wards off"); [this is from] the word *uru*.

Mādhava states that because a rule preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably valid, there is an option regarding the *upadhā*-vṛddhi. Thus, from *baṃhayati*, the substitute *baṃha* is applied for *bahula*; from *garayati*, the substitute *gura* is applied for *guru*; and from *vṛddhaṃ varṣayati*, the substitute *varṣa* is applied for *vṛddha* by the rule "vṛddhasya ca" [Pāṇini 2.4.39], which prescribes the substitute *jyā*.
It is analyzed as follows: *trapayati* means "he causes to be ashamed. Here, *trap* is the substitute for *tṛpra*. It has a vowel *a* as its penultimate (*adupadha*).

Because the substitution is based on a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening, as in the case of *garayati* and others. In some places, the reading is *trāpayati*. *Drāghayati* means "he lengthens"; here, *drāgh* is the substitute for *dīrgha*. *Vṛndayati*... [is formed similarly].
The command of Bṛndāraka to Bṛndā. Thus ends the section on denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*). Now begins the section on causative formations (*ṇyantaprakriyā*).
(402) *tatprayojako hetuśca* | Pāṇini 1.4.55. "The instigator of that [action] is also called the *hetu* (agent/causal agent)."
Now, intending to state the rule for the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "causing" (*hetumat*), he states the technical designation "cause" (*hetu*):

"The prompter of that [agent] is also called the cause. The agent (*kartṛ*) introduced in the preceding sūtra by the rule "the independent one is the agent" is referred to here by the word "that" (*tat*). The prompter (*prayojaka*) of that agent—that is, the one who sets him into motion—is [the cause].

That which prompts that [agent] is the prompter (*prayojaka*). Thus he says: "The prompter of the agent is designated as the *hetu* (cause). The word "and" (*ca*) conjoins the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) introduced by the preceding rule.
Thus he says: "And it bears the designation of 'agent'. In the case of "Devadatta cooks; Yajñadatta impels him," [Yajñadatta is the *hetu-kartṛ*].

Since Devadatta alone possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*), consisting in being the locus of the meaning of the verbal root *pac* (to cook), which is an activity conducive to cooking, the prescriptive rule for the designation "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) applies to him; whereas the instigator lacks that [status]. Because the instigator is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) by means of the agent who is instigated, the designation "cause" (*hetu-saṃjñā*) does not apply to him; therefore, the prescriptive rule for the designation "cause" is provided.
(403) *Hetumati ca* | 3.1.26 | [The suffixes of the third conjugation class (*ṇic*) are applied] also when the sense is that of one who causes to act.

And [the suffix] *ṇic* is used when there is a motive (*hetumat*). From the rule "satyāpapāśa... (*Pāṇini 3.1.25*), the word *ṇic* is understood to carry over. A "motive" (*hetu*) is an instigator (*prayojaka*). That which possesses this [motive] by virtue of being its substratum is "having a motive" (*hetumān*), meaning the activity such as commanding that resides in the instigator. The meaning is that *ṇic* should be applied when that [activity] is to be expressed.
The term "dhātoḥ" (of a root) is understood from the rule *dhātor ekāco halādeḥ*. Thus he says:

"the operation of the instigator. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "commanding and so forth," there is the inclusion of requesting, assent, instruction, and the like. In that context, [it refers to] a servant or someone of inferior status.

*Pravartanā* (instigation) means sending forth; it means a command. *Adhyeṣaṇā* (entreaty) is the instigation of an equal or a superior, such as a friend or a teacher. *Anumati* (consent) is the approval of a king or similar authority. *Upadeśa* (instruction) is the instigation of one suffering from fever toward drinking a medicinal decoction by making him understand its benefit. [The instigation] out of fear of being killed...

Even the act of causing one who is fleeing to stop is the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the instigator (*prayojaka*). Thus, it is established that the suffix *ṇic* occurs when there is an instigation residing in the instigator. These specific details, however, are understood through context and other such means. But in the case of "the potter makes a jar" (*kulālo ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the suffix *ṇic* does not occur.

The engagement [of the suffix] occurs only when there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of both the one who causes to act (*prayojaka*) and the one who is caused to act (*prayojya*); this is explained in detail elsewhere. Regarding the word *bhavantam*: in such meanings as "Devadatta is a sacrificer" (*yajvā bhavati*) or "the officiating priest (*yājaka*) impels him," the primary agent (*mukhya-kartṛ*) of the action of becoming (*bhavana*), which is the meaning of the root *bhū*, is the sacrificer; and the one who impels that sacrificer toward the act of becoming a sacrificer is [the agent of the causative].

The priest and others are the instigators (*prayojaka*); the causative suffix *ṇic* is attached to the root *bhū* when it resides in them, resulting in the augment *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *ā*. Thus, *bhāvī* is the form ending in *ṇic*. From that, by adding the present indicative suffix *laṭ* to express an activity conducive to the process of becoming, the form *bhāvayati* is produced.

The realized meaning is that "he impels you. Regarding the form *bhāvayāṃbabhūve*: the intention is that even though the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the root *bhū* does not take the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and therefore the middle voice is not employed even for the auxiliary verb used in its wake.

(404) *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* | Pāṇini 6.1.91. *oḥ puyaṇ*: [The word] *ṭhu* [in the sūtra] is replaced by *ṭha* according to [the rule] *ṭhoḥ*. The analysis of *puyaṇji* is as follows: it is a locative case derived from a collective dvandva compound consisting of *pu*, *yaṇ*, and *j*. [The phrase] *aḥ paro yasmāt* means "that after which *a* follows. (Note: This is a commentary on the grammatical analysis of the sūtra *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*, which prescribes the substitution of *u* for *o* when followed by *pu*, a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*), or *j*, provided that these are not followed by *a*).
This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. From the rule "ṣanyaṭaḥ," the word "sani" is carried over (*anuvartate*).

The term "aṅgasya" is supplied as a governing heading (*adhikṛtam*). From the rule "atra lopaḥ," the word "abhyāsasya" is carried over, and from the rule "bhṛñāmid," the word "it" is carried over. Thus he says: when *san* follows.

By the rule beginning with "ityādinā," [we derive] *abībhavat*. When the form *bhū i at* is established and the process of reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be applied, because the substitution of a vowel in place of a vowel (*aca ādeśa*) is prohibited when reduplication is to occur, the word *bhū* is reduplicated first—prior to the application of the Vṛddhi and Avādeśa substitutions.
Subsequently, the Vṛddhi and Avādeśa substitutions are applied to the latter member (*uttara-khaṇḍa*).

The meaning is that when the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) has been shortened, there is no *akāra* in the reduplicated syllable; consequently, the rule *sanyataḥ* does not apply, and by virtue of the *sanvat* treatment, the substitution of *it* (short *i*) occurs, followed by lengthening. *Apīpavat* is the form derived from the root *pūṅ*. The meaning is that *amīmavat* is the form derived from the root *mūṅ*. *Ayīyavat* [is the form derived from the root *yu*].

*yudhāto rūpam* means "the form of the root *yudh*. *arīravaditi* [is] the form of the root *rudh*. *alīlavaditi* [is] the form of the root *lūñ*. *ajījavaditi* [is] the form of the root *ju*; this *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root mentioned in the rule *jucaṅkramya-*. Now, one might object: after reduplication (*dvitva*) in the case of *bhū-bhū*, there should be [the application of] *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *āv*.

If it is argued that once the *upadhā* lengthening and the shortening have been performed, because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no "light vowel followed by [the suffix]" (*laghuparatva*), and thus the condition for *sanvadbhāva* does not apply—how then can there be the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsavarṇa*) here?

This is not so; for precisely by virtue of the force of the rule's formulation (*ārambhasāmarthya*), the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply, and thus the substitution of *i* occurs.

(405) *sravati-śṛṇoti-dravati-pravṛti-plavati-cyavati-nām vā* || 7.4.81 || [The rule] *sravati-śṛṇoti* [is explained as follows]: the word *aparaḥ* (the other) is understood to carry over, but not the phrase *pu-yaṇ-jī*, because the occurrence of the *pa*-class consonants (*pavarga*) and the letter *j* is impossible here; furthermore, although there is a presence of *yaṇ* in *sravati* and the others, it is not subject to deviation [in this context].
Thus it says: "when followed by a verbal root syllable that has no vowel [other than *a*] before it. The word *akṣara* here refers to a phoneme (*varṇa*). For example: *asisravat*, *asusravat*.

The point is that because the rule for doubling a consonant cluster (*dvirvacana*) applies when there is a light vowel (*laghu*) following, since there is no light vowel following here, the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like the suffix *san*) does not occur.
Examples: *aśiśravat*, *aśuśravat*; *adidravat*, *adudravat*; *apipravat*.

*apupravat*, *apiplavat*, *apuplavat*; *acicyavat*, *acucyavat*. Now, regarding the example *sāsudhato raśaśāt*, he says: "not when there is elision of [the root-final] *n*" (*nāglopī*). *aḍuḍhāṭkaditi*: the meaning is that this is because the root *ḍhāṭkṛ*, meaning "to move," is marked with an *ṛt* (indicating it is *ṛdit*). *acīcakāsaditi*: the root *cakāsṛ* means "to shine."

Because it contains the sound *ṛ*, the penultimate vowel is shortened. The intention is that, according to the view [of some], there is "san-vat" behavior (i.e., the application of rules like Pāṇini 7.4.93) and lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) for that stem which is subject to reduplication when followed by *ṇi* and *caṅ*, provided that a light vowel follows. However, regarding the alternative opinion: according to the view that "the stem is reduplicated where it occurs," [the condition applies] when there is a light vowel following *ṇi* after *caṅ*.

The meaning is that this is according to the view that "the repetition of a root-stem (*aṅga*) is *tatpara*. Regarding the phrase "by [the rule] *āglopi*"—an example cited for the prohibition of the shortening of the *upadhā* vowel in the case of a stem losing its final letter (*aglopī*) is *mā bhavān ūnanat*.
The meaning is that another example, such as *atitirāyat*, will be stated later when the *sub*-derivatives are analyzed.

Now, from the root *cur* (in the sense of "stealing") with the suffix *ṇic* added in its own sense (*svārthe*), after the substitution of *guṇa* for the penultimate vowel, the form *cori* is obtained.
From that, when the causal suffix *ṇic* (*hetumaṇṇic*) is applied and the first *ṇic* is elided, the resulting form ending in the causal *ṇic* is indeed *coriṭ*.
Therefore, when *laṭ*, *tip*, and *śap* are applied, and after the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement by *ay*, [the form is *corayati*].

The form *corayati* alone is desired; however, that is not tenable because, when a causative suffix (*ṇic*) follows a causative suffix (*hetumaṇṇic*), the elision of the first *ṇic* would be superseded by the subsequent rule for *vṛddhi*, resulting in the substitution of *āy*.

From this form *corāyi*, the addition of the present tense marker (*laṭ*) would lead to the undesirable form *corāyayati*. Therefore, he says: "From a [root] ending in *ṇic*, another *ṇic* [is added]."

The syntactical connection is that the elision of the *ṇi* suffix (*ṇilopa*) sets aside the *vṛddhi* substitution [prescribed] for roots ending in *ṇi*. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhāt*). The intention is that this is according to the Vārttika: "The elision of *ṇi* and the elision of *y* and *l* take precedence by way of prior conflict over *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening. Or, "Because it is an exception" (*apavādatvāt*). [Regarding the root] *kam*:

The intention is that because the root *kānti* is explained in two ways; now, since it is followed by *ṇic*, and then by another *ṇic*, when the causal *ṇic* is elided, there is reduplication of *cur*. Because this falls under the scope of the rule for *sanvadbhāva*, [the author] says: "there is lengthening of the light vowel" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*). Thus, *acūcurat* is established. But [an objection]: nanu...
Both the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrgha*) are prescribed when a *ṇiC* follows a *caṅ*.

However, neither of these two can apply here by relying on the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the status of being followed by an affix) with reference to the first *ṇiC*, because that [first *ṇiC*] is separated from the *caṅ* by the second *ṇiC*, and thus lacks the quality of being "followed by a *caṅ*" (*caṅ-paraka*). Nor...

By taking the second *ṇic*, the occurrence of both [the first and second *ṇic*] is possible; the meaning is that the occurrence of the first [root] from the base of the second *ṇic* is not to be suspected. Why? To this he says: "because of the reference to the class (*ākṛti*) of *ṇi*.
In the rule "when *ṇa* is followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare ṇau*), regarding the term *ṇau*:
What is intended here is the state of being followed by one or more *ṇi*-suffixes that are themselves followed by *caṅ*.

Thus, even though the two *ṇi*-suffixes do not have *caṅ* immediately following them, the property of being a *ṇi*-suffix (*ṇitva*) does have *caṅ* following it; this is the sense in which the application of the shortening and lengthening rules occurs. In this regard—

It has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that it is incorrect to indicate [the root] by its class (*jāti*). From the root *śvi* (in the sense of "motion" and "growth") with the suffix *ṇic* added for causality, after the application of the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions, we have the form *śvāyī*;
from this, in the *laṭ* and other tenses, the form is *śvāyayati*. In the *luṅ* tense, with the *ciṇ* suffix, the form is *iśvi i a t*.
Regarding the specific rule for the [root] *sthā*, it says:
(406) *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ* |6|1|31|. The rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ* is understood to carry over. [The suffix] *ṣyaṅ*...

And he says this [to address the objection] regarding "saṃprasāraṇam" by means of the words "santaparaḥ" and so forth. Now, one might object: since the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) takes precedence, if the *vṛddhi* and *āy-ādeśa* were applied before the *saṃprasāraṇa*, and then the *saṃprasāraṇa* and the subsequent single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) were applied, the form would be *aśīśavat* and not *aśūśavat*.
To address this, he says: "The *saṃprasāraṇa* and that which depends upon it.

This statement is established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *liṭaḷbhyāsasya*. And thus, in the case of *aśvi i at*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *v*—which becomes the letter *u*—occurs prior even to the application of the *vṛddhi* and *ay-ādeśa* substitutions.

The result is established. Regarding the term "pūrvarūpa" (the single substitute for two similar vowels): consequently, when there is doubling of the syllable *śu*, the subsequent portion (*u*) takes recourse to the causative suffix (*ṇic*), whereby the substitution of *vṛddhi* and *āv* occurs; then, because the penultimate vowel is short, the condition for the *sanvat* rule applies, resulting in the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable. Thus, he states the final form: *aśūśavat*.
In the alternative view where *saṃprasāraṇa* does not occur, one might suspect the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsadīrgha*) in the form *aśiśvayat*; therefore, he says:
"because it is not heavy" (*alaghutvāt*). The intended meaning is that [the penultimate vowel] is not followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).
From the root *stambh* preceded by the prefix *ava*, in its causative form (*ṇyantāt*), we have *avaṣṭambhayati*, and so forth.

The substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule "ṣṭhivū-āmucamāṃ śiti" [Pāṇini 8.3.62]. Now, regarding the form *ātastambhat*—where the substitution of *ṣ* would otherwise apply—the following rule is stated:
(407) *stanbhusivusahāṃ caṅi* [Pāṇini 8.3.116]. [This rule prescribes the substitution of *ṣ* for the initial *s* of these roots when followed by the suffix *caṅ*.]

Regarding the *vārttika*: "A prohibition [of the cerebralization] applies when [the prefix] *stambhu* follows *si*. From the rule *na raparasṛpī*, the word *na* (not) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *sahe sāḍaḥ saḥ*, the genitive form *saḥ* is understood to carry over. The term *mūrdhanya* (cerebral) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "caused by a prefix" (*upasarga-nimitta*) and so forth: *stambh* is a root belonging to the *sūtra* (Vedic) roots. [The examples are] from the roots *ṣivu* (meaning "to sew") and *ṣaha* (meaning "to endure"): *paryasīṣivat* and *nyasīṣahat*. Here, the substitution of *ṣ* is not caused by the prefixes *pari*, *ni*, or *vi* according to the rule *parinivibhyaḥ seve*; rather, it is caused by the reduplication (*abhyāsa*).

The substitution of *ṣ* indeed occurs, as in *āṭiṭata* and *āśiśat*. When the forms *āṭ i a t* and *āś i a t* are established, one might suspect that doubling (*dvitvam*) would apply first—on the basis of the rule *caṅī* (Pāṇini 6.1.11)—before the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvaḥ*) by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.1). Anticipating this, he says: "Even though it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅgaḥ*)."

The shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon both the suffix *caṅ* and the subsequent [suffix]; however, reduplication (*dvitva*) is *antaraṅga* because it depends upon *caṅ* alone. Even so, the meaning is that the shortening of the penultimate vowel occurs even before reduplication. Why? To this he says: "of *oṇ*"—referring to the root *oṇṛ* in the sense of "removing."

The inclusion of the marker *ṛt* [in the root *oṇ*] is for the purpose of preventing the shortening of the penultimate vowel by the rule "not for a reduplicated stem ending in a elided element" (*noglopi*) in the case of forms such as *āuṇiṇat*. For if reduplication were to occur prior to the shortening of the penultimate vowel— on account of its being an *antaraṅga* operation— then in the intermediate stage *oṇ i a t*, [the rule would apply].

If, according to the rule *ṭhājāderdvitīyasya*, there were doubling of the element *ṇī* together with the suffix *ṇic*, then subsequently, because the vowel *o* would not possess the status of a penultimate (*upadhā*) when followed by *caṅ* and *ṇi*, a short vowel would not even be applicable; thus, the inclusion of the marker *ṛt* (in *oṇ*) would be redundant. However, if one accepts that "the shortening of the penultimate occurs prior to doubling," then [the form would be] *oṇ i a t*.
In this state, the employment of the term *ṛdit* (having an indicatory *ṛ*) is meaningful for the purpose of prohibiting the shortening (*hrasva*) that has been obtained;

therefore, the meaning is understood to be: "Even though the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) is 'external' (*bahiraṅga*), it must take place even before reduplication. Now, one might object: since forms such as *āṭiṭat* and *āśiśat* are established [by other rules] anyway, what is the use of this?
To explain this, he says: "mā bhavānididhat. When *edh i at* is established, if doubling were to occur first, then after *dhī* is doubled, the shortening of the vowel *e* would not take place.
However, if the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) occurs prior to doubling, then when *edh i at* becomes *idh i at*, the doubling of *dhī* can subsequently occur.

The meaning is that by the connection with the prohibitive particle *mā*, when the augment *āṭ* is absent, the desired form *ididhat* is established. Now, one might object: in the case of *mā bhavān predidhat*, once *pra ididhat* is established, even if the shortening (*hrasva*) has taken place, the root *edh* remains intact according to the principle of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*); consequently, by the rule *ṭhetyedhatyūṭhÂasu*, there should be a *vṛddhi* [substitution].
To address this, he says: "ejādāvedhatau" (Pāṇini 6.1.45).
The intention is that [the rule] has already been explained as "etyedhatyor avarṇāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.89), which applies when the root begins with 'e' or 'ai'.
Regarding "āṬndidad": once the form "und-i-a-t" is established, the intention is that there is reduplication of the syllable "dī".

Regarding *āḍḍiḍat*: the root *aḍḍ* has a dental *ḍ*. The letter *ḍ* is produced through the application of the rule for the substitution of a retroflex (*ṣṭu*). When the form *aḍḍi a t* is established, because the substitution of the retroflex (*ṣṭutva*) is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the doubling occurs of the sequence *ḍi* following the dental *d*; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *ārcicat*: when the form *arc i a t* is established, [the doubling occurs] after the letter *r*.

The intention is that there is doubling (dvitva) of the subsequent element, namely *cī*. Regarding the root *ubj* in the sense of "straightening": [an objection]—if there were doubling of *bjī* (the form *ubj*), then after the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the form would be *au-bibjad*;
however, the intention is that the doubling is of *au-bijad* itself. [Question: In that case, why is the letter *d* not heard?

Therefore, he says: "bhujanyubjau" (Pāṇini 6.1.142). Now, one might object: since the substitution of *ba* for *da* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it applies prior to [the application of] the dual number, how can the prohibition "na ndrāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3) apply here? To this he says: "sa ca" (and that...). Now, regarding the root *dru* in the sense of "to go," as in *drāvayati*, when *caṅ* is applied and there is reduplication of the root *dru*...

Regarding the form *adidravat*, which is desired when there is the substitution of the penultimate vowel by its short form (*upadhā-hrasva*) due to the *vṛddhi* of the root *utṛ* in the *ādeśa*, and the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) according to the rule "sravati-śṛṇoti-", that [form] would not be possible;
for by the rule "na ndrāḥ," the doubling of the letter *d* is prohibited. To this, he says: "only [the rule] 'of a root beginning with a vowel' (*ajādeḥ*) [is intended]."

In the rule *ṭhna ndrāḥ*, the phrase *ajādeḥ* (beginning with a vowel) indeed continues to apply; this was explained previously as "from the initial vowel. Consequently, the result is that *n*, *d*, and *r* do not undergo reduplication when they follow an initial vowel. As for *neha* (not here): in the present case, because [the *n*] does not follow an initial vowel, [the prohibition does not apply].
