The meaning is that there is a prohibition against the doubling of the letter *da*. In the reading *ṭhadidrapaṭ*, the form is derived from the root *drā* with the addition of *ṇic* and *puK*, resulting in *ṭhdrāpīṭ*. Now, one might object: "In the view where *aṭ* is added in the state of the *la* suffix, the condition of being followed by a vowel (*acaḥ*) certainly exists. This is not so; for in the rule *ṭhna ndrāḥ*, [it is understood] as *ṭhliṭi dhātoḥ*... [etc.].

They say that by carrying over the term *dhātoḥ* [from the previous rule], the interpretation is: "The *na*, *da*, or *ra* following the initial vowel of a root at the time it receives the designation *dhātu* is not doubled. (408) *rabher aśabliṭoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.63.
The word *rabheḥ* [is understood] from the rule *rabheraśabliṭoḥ*; *num* [is understood] from the rule *ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*;
and *aci* is carried over from the rule *radhijabhoracī*. Thus he says:
"the augment *num* after *rabhi*, etc."

(409) And after the root *labh*. 7.1.64. "And after the root *labh*. The rule *num* would also apply to *labh* before a vowel, but it is not explicitly stated because its meaning—that it does not apply before the suffixes *śap* and *liṭ*—is already clear. As for the form *ararambhat*: once the *num* augment has been applied, [the root becomes *alambh*, which is] followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).

The sense is that because the vowel *a* lacks lightness (*laghutva*), there is no application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule. Regarding the root *hi* in the sense of "going" and "increasing," he states that in the example *ijīhayat*, the substitution of *k* for the letter *h* (by the rule *heracaṅi*) does not apply; thus he says: "in *heracaṅi*. [He refers to] the rule *atsmṛdṛtvarapra...* [which applies] to the root *pratha* in the *curādi* class.

This has been explained under the verbal root *prakhyā* (DhP 1.642). Regarding the form *asasmarat*: here, although the substitution of *i* would have applied by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79), the substitution of *a* occurs instead. Precisely for this reason, it was stated previously that even when separated by multiple consonants, the condition of being followed by a light vowel (*laghuparatva*) still holds; [this is so] because [the preceding syllable] is followed by a *saṃyoga*.

Because there is no lightness (*laghutva*), there is no lengthening due to repetition (*abhyāsa*). The form *adadarat* is from the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*). Here too, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *sanyataḥ*. Anticipating the objection regarding lengthening, he says: "By virtue of the indicatory *t* (*taparatva*). [Examples: *atatvarat*, *apaprathat*, *amamradat*, *atastarat*.
He saw. (410) *vibhāṣā veṣṭiceṣṭyoḥ* | 7.4.96.
*vibhāṣā veṣṭiceṣṭyoḥ*. "In this case, there is elision."

From this [sūtra], "of the reduplication" (abhyāsasya) is understood from the previous context; "a" (at) is understood from "at smṛdṛtvarapra... (P. 7.4.95); and "when followed by caṅ" (caṅpare) is understood from "sanvallaghuni... (P. 7.4.93). The term *caṅpara* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that after which *caṅ* follows. The word *ṇau* (in the presence of the causative suffix *ṇic*) is to be supplied. Thus he says: "the substitution of *a* for the reduplication. For example: *abibhrajat*.

In the alternative where the penultimate vowel is short (*upadhāhrasva*), the *it* (the substitution of *i*) occurs for the reduplicated syllable because of the presence of a light vowel (*laghu*) following it and because of the condition of being like *san*. However, the rule "a long vowel replaces a light vowel" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*) does not apply here, because the vowel is not light due to being followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). Regarding the phrase "or in the case of *kāṇi*-type roots": the remainder of the rule is "there is a shortening of the penultimate vowel when there is *ṇi* and *caṅ*" (*ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ*). The forms *kaṇayati*, *raṇayati*, etc., are derived from the causative (*ṇic*) of roots such as *kaṇ*. *Kaṇa*... [text continues]

The meaning is that six verbal roots—*ṇimīla* (in the sense of closing the eyes), *aṭhraṇ* (in the sense of sound), *bhaṇ* (in the sense of sound), *śraṇ* (in the sense of giving), *lup* (in the sense of cutting), and *heṭha* (in the sense of harming)—are listed in the Bhāṣya as being causative (*ṇic*-formed) and belonging to the *kāṇi*-class. Regarding *hvāyi*: [it is derived from] *hveñ* (in the sense of rivalry and sound); when the vowel substitution (*ātva*) and the *yuk* augment have been applied...

And this is the explanation: the four roots *vaṇ* (in the sense of "sound"), which ends in a dental and has *u* as its penultimate; *luṭha* (in the sense of "striking"), which has the second letter of the *ṭ*-class as its penultimate; and *lapa* (in the sense of "distinct speech")—these four, which are not mentioned in the Bhāṣya, are read in the Nyāsa commentary as being formed with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). [The rule] *cāṇiloṭī* [is thus explained].
Thus: *caṇ* (in the sense of "giving") begins with a palatal (*tālavya*). *luṭ* (in the sense of "stealing") ends in the first letter of the *ṭa*-group and belongs to the *bhū-ādi* class;

it also occurs in the *cur-ādi* class in the sense of "speaking. The meaning is that these two roots, ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*, are recited in some other work, distinct from the *Bhāṣya* and *Nyāsa* texts. In this way...

"Twelve": by this distinction of opinion, the meaning is that there are twelve [roots], beginning with *kāṇ*. *Acīkaṇat*: in the view where the penultimate vowel is short, because it is followed by a light syllable (*laghu*), there is the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule and the lengthening of the vowel. *Acakāṇat*: this is the form in the view where the penultimate vowel is not short. *Ari-raṇat* / *ararāṇat*; *abī-bhaṇat*.
He caused to speak; he caused to sprinkle; he caused to cook. He caused to cut; he caused to cut off. He caused to vex; he caused to vex. He caused to call; he caused to call. He caused to weave;
he caused to weave. He caused to roll; he caused to roll about. He caused to talk; he caused to talk. He caused to chew.
*acacāṇat*. *alūluṭat* / *aluloṭat*.
(411) *svāpeścaṅi* 6.1.18. [The rule] "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) after *svap*" applies; [this is stated] because of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*.

The sense is that this [term] follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "saṃprasāraṇam. Regarding *asū ṣuṣupat*: because of the statement "vowel-substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*), that which depends on it, and the resulting operation are stronger," once the vowel-substitution has occurred, there is reduplication, the single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*), the long vowel as in the *san*-class, and the *ṣatva* change; such is the sense.

(412) *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.37). Regarding *śācchāsā*: the roots *śo* (in the sense of thinning), *chāe* (in the sense of cutting), *ṣo* (in the sense of finishing), *hvēñ* (in the sense of rivalry and sound), and *vyeñ* (in the sense of covering)—these are indicated here with their vowel-changes (*ātva*) already applied. [The root *vyeñ* is also included.]
The root *aṭhpā* (meaning "to weave") belongs to the *bhvādi* class. [The genitive plural] "of these" (*eṣām*) follows from a dvandva compound.

"When *ṇi* follows" is a supplementary statement (*śeṣa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *puṅ* augment characterized by a final vowel. In the case of *yuk*, the letter *k* is for the sake of the *it* designation; the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Due to its *kit* status, there is an augment at the end. Here...

Because of the rule stating that "when there is a choice between a root with a *luk*-elision suffix and one without a *luk*-elision suffix, the one without the *luk*-elision suffix is taken," the root *pā* in the sense of "to protect" (*pā rakṣaṇe*) is not included here. However, its form *pālayati* will be mentioned immediately below. [The forms] *śāyayati* and *iśīśayat* (luṅ) [are derived from *śī*]. [The forms] *chāyayati* and *aciccchayat* [are derived from *chā*].
From *sāyayati*, [the aorist] is *asīṣayat*. From *hvāyayati*, [the aorist is *ahvīṣayat*]. The specific form for the *luṅ* (aorist) will be stated later.
From *vyāyayati*, [the aorist] is *avivyayat*. From *vāyayati*, [the aorist is *avīvayat*]. From *pāyayati*, [the aorist is *apīpyat*]; however, the specific form for the *luṅ* will be stated later.

(413) *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* | Pāṇini 6.1.32. Regarding *hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*: the term *hva* is the genitive form of *hveñ* after its *atva* (vocalization) has been applied. Intending to show the continuation [of the rule] from "also in the case of *ṇi*, when followed by *san* or *caṅ*" (*ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ*), he says: "when followed by *san*" (*sanpara*), etc. [The example is] *ajūhavat*.

When *hvā-i-a* remains, because of the rule "vowel-substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the operation dependent upon it are stronger," vowel-substitution is performed first; then, after the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), there is doubling of the syllable *hu*.

Once the *vṛddhi* and *ā* substitution have been applied to the latter part, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*) and the lengthening due to the *sanvat* treatment occur—this is the intended meaning. Here...

When the *saṃprasāraṇa* has occurred and the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels) has been applied, the form *hvār* no longer exists; therefore, the substitution of *yuk* does not apply. From the root *pā*, with the addition of *ṇiC* and the augment *yuk*, we have *pāyi*. From this, when the *luṅ* suffix is applied along with *ciṅ*, and after the doubling of the consonant and other operations, the form stands as *apīpayat*.

(414) *lopaḥ pibater īccābhyāsasya* | Pāṇini 7.4.4. The rule *lopaḥ pibateḥ* [is understood] from the phrase *caṅpare ṇau*. The intention is that this is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyāḥ* [from 7.4.1]. Thus, we have *apīpyat*.

Because of the prohibition "there is no [application of] a rule concerning the final letter of a reduplicated syllable" (*anabhyāsa-vikāraḥ*) to the rule "in the case of a meaningless [element], a rule concerning the final letter applies" (*anarthake 'lo 'ntyavidhiḥ*), the substitution of *ī* occurs for the final letter of the reduplicated syllable. Here, once the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) has been elided, since the root is *aglopi* (having lost its penultimate) and the penultimate is not *laghu*, the conditions for the *sanvadbhāva* and the lengthening of the vowel do not apply; therefore, this rule for the substitution of *ī* is established.

The remainder [of the commentary] is: "Examples are given in order, beginning with *arti-hi*. Regarding *arpayati*: this is an example of the root *ṛ*. Because it is *nitya*, the suffix *puk* applies, overriding *vṛddhi*; then the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding *hrepayati*: this is the form of the root *hrī* in the sense of "shame. Regarding *vlepayati*: [this is the form of the root] *vlī*...
This is the form of the root *vi-śṛ* in the sense of "to dissolve. *Repayati* is an example of the root *hrī* in the sense of "to perish.
Intending to cite *knopayati* as an example of the root *knūyī* in the sense of "sound," he says: "there is the elision of *y*" (*yalopa*).
This means that when the suffix *ṇic* and the augment *puK* are added to the root *knūyī*, there is the elision of *y* according to the rule *lopo vyoḥ*. From that [point],...
When *knūp* is present, although the penultimate vowel is not heavy (*alaghūpadhatva*), there is *guṇa* substitution because it ends in *pu* (a labial) and a nasal (*pugantatvāt*).
Thus: *kṣmāpayati*. From the root *kṣmāyī* in the sense of "shaking," with the addition of *ṇic* and *puk*, there is the elision of *y*.
He gives an example of a root ending in long *ā*: *sthāpayati*. In the *luṅ* [aorist] with *ciṅ* [causative], it becomes *sthāp-a-t*.

Regarding the rule *sthite*—(415)—the word *it* [is understood] from *tiṣṭhaterit* |7|4|5|. The phrase *ṇau caṅyupadhāyāḥ* is also carried over [from the previous sūtra]. Therefore, he says: "of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*)..."
Thus:
(416) *jighrater vā* | Pāṇini 7.4.6. The meaning is that the penultimate vowel of the root *ghrā* optionally becomes *i* when followed by a *ṇic* suffix that is itself followed by *caṅ*.
When *ajighrapat* is established, there is an option regarding the penultimate vowel. Regarding *urṛd*:

it has been explained in the section on the *cur*-class that, when followed by a *caṅ* (the *aṅ* of the third person singular imperfect), the *ṛ* of the root's penultimate vowel may optionally become *ṛ*. Thus, *acīkṛtat*. When *kṛt-i-a-t* is established, in the case where *ṛ* is substituted, there is reduplication of the element *kṛt*.

In the case of *uradatve*, *halādiśeṣe*, *abhyāsacutve*, *sanvatvāditve*, and its subsequent lengthening (*dīrgha*), the form is *acikīrtat*. When *kṛ* + *i* + *a* + *t* remains, if the alternative view that the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) does not undergo *ṛtvātva* (the substitution of *ṛ*) is adopted, then by the rule *upadhāyāśca*, the penultimate vowel *ṛ* is changed to *i*, followed by *raparatva* (substitution of *r* for the semivowel), and then *kir* is doubled. Thus, the form is established.

In the case of *avīvṛtat*, the form is derived by applying the rule *ut-ṛk-ṛt-aṅ-ṇal-ut-tarapade ṭhūlope dīrghaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.94) for the lengthening of the vowel following *ṭh*. Regarding *avīvṛtat*: the root is *vṛtu* (in the sense of "turning").

After the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel is set aside by the rule *urṛt* (Pāṇini 7.1.102). Then, with the *caṅ* (the reduplication suffix of the third person singular imperfect), there is reduplication of the root *vṛt*; the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratva*) applies; and by the rule *sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'naglope* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), the *vṛddhi* (lengthening) occurs. Thus, the form is *avavartat*.

In the alternative where the root contains *ṛ*, when there is reduplication of *vṛdh*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (by *urat*) occurs; then, in the subsequent portion, the *guṇa* substitution takes place because the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is light (*laghu*). Due to the absence of a light vowel following [the reduplicated syllable], the *sanvadbhāva* and lengthening do not apply. *Amīmṛjat* is the form when the penultimate vowel is *ṛ*. *Amamārjit* is the form when the penultimate vowel is not *ṛ*, following the reduplication.

In the case of *uradatve* (the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*), in the northern region (*Uttara-khaṇḍa*), the form is derived by applying the rule "vṛddhir eci" (Pāṇini 1.1.1) to produce *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*).

Because there is no light vowel (*laghu*) following [the penultimate], the status of being like the suffix *san* (*san-vat-tva*) does not apply. Regarding "pātarṇau luk": this means that *luk* is an augment (*āgama*).

It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *puṅ*. That is to say, it is an exception to the *puṅ* augment characterized by [the condition of] ending in a long vowel (*ādanta*). Even though [the root] is *pāla*...
This is already established by the root *rakṣ* itself in the sense of "protection"; nevertheless, the result [of the rule] is the removal of the *puk* augment.
(417) *vo vidhūnane juk* | 7|3|38|. Regarding *vo vidhūnane*: from the root *ṭhu* in the sense of "drying" (*śoṣaṇe*), after the vowel has been changed to *a*, it becomes *ṭhva*.

The word ending in the sixth case [vāteḥ] follows from the rule *ṛt-ahrī-*. From that, the term *ṇau* is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of the root *vā*" and so forth. *JuK* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *puK*. Regarding the example *keśān vāpayati*: the meaning is "he makes them fragrant. In this case, there is only *puK* after the root *ve* (to weave), but here [after the root *vā*], it does not apply.

The inclusion [of *vā*] is due to its being a root that lacks a vocalic augment (*lug-avikaraṇa*). Some, however, say that here only *vā* is intended, and not *veñ*, nor even *vai*, because they are derivative forms (*lākṣaṇika*) and because they possess an indicatory marker (*sānubandhaka*).
He recalls the rule prescribing the substitution of *ā*: "Optionally for *lī*" (*vibhāṣā līyateḥ*). This refers to the substitution of *ā* for both *lī* and *līṅ*.

It was previously explained under the *śyan* conjugation that [the rule] applies when there is *ej*, *vi*, or *lyi*. In that context, the reference is made by means of the suffix *yak* (as in *līyate*), and not by means of *śyan*. Consequently, this includes both the root *lī* with the *śnā* conjugation (*lī śleṣaṇe*) and the root *līṅ* with the *śyan* conjugation (*līṅ śleṣaṇe*).
What was stated previously should not be forgotten. (418) *līlor nug lukāv anyatarasyāṃ snehavipātane* 7.3.39.
*līloḥ*: this is the genitive dual of the two roots *lī* and *lā*. Regarding *ṇau*: [this refers to the affix *ṇiC*].

The meaning is that [the suffix *ṇic*] follows from the word "artihrī" (Pāṇini 3.1.25); this is the intended sense. Regarding "sneha," which means oil (*taila*), "snehanipātana" refers to its liquefaction. Thus he says: "in the case of a liquid fat. Regarding the alternative view where the substitution of *ā* does not occur, he says: "it causes to melt. This form arises from the elision (*luk*) of the long *ī* in the roots *lī* and *līṅ*.

The meaning is "it causes to liquefy. Regarding the form *vilāyayati*—which is stated in the alternative view where the augment *nuK* and the substitution of *āT* for the root *lī* do not occur—it is the form [of the causative] when there is no insertion of the augment *luk*. Now, one might object: since the root *lī*, having undergone the substitution of *āT*, would still possess the property of being *lī* by the maxim of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*), the augment *nuK* should apply to it as well. To this he says: *lī ī*. [This indicates that the rule applies only to the root ending in *ī*. [Example: *loham*.

Regarding the term *vilāpayati*: because of the absence of *nuk* and *luk*, there is the substitution of *ā* (*ātvapakṣe*) along with the augment *puk*; however, in the case where *ātva* does not occur, there would be the application of *vṛddhi* and *ay-ādeśa*. Therefore, the meaning is that the substitution of *ā* must be stated as obligatory. (Pāṇini 1.3.70) *liyaḥ saṃmānanaśālīnīkaraṇayośca* ("And [the substitution of *ā* occurs] for the root *lī* in the senses of honoring and making humble").

Regarding *liyaḥ saṃmānane*: the term *liyaḥ* is a reference to the roots *lī* and *līṅ*. From the rule *anudātetaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is understood; and from the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67), the word *ṇeḥ* is carried over as an anuvṛtti. Although the desired result is already established by the rule *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74), this [present rule] is for the purpose of including cases where the benefit does not accrue to the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). "Honoring" (*saṃmānana*) means the attainment of respect.

*Śālinīkaraṇam*—[This is] a new [interpretation]. By the word "ca" (and), the inclusion of *pralambhana* (deceiving) from the preceding rule, *gṛdhivañcyoḥ*, is conjoined. Thus he says: "of *līṅ* and *lī*" and so forth.

(420) *bibheter hetubhaye* |6|1|56|. In the rule *bibheter hetubhaye*, the words *ecaḥ* and *āt* are carried over from the previous rule *ādeca upadeśe*. The word *vibhāṣā* is carried over from the rule *vibhāṣā līyate*.

From the rule *ṭhcisphuro'r* and from the rule *ṇau*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied]. "Fear caused by a cause" means fear arising from an instigator (*prayojaka*). He states this with the words beginning "of the root *bhī*" and so forth: (421) *bhīsmyorhetubhaye* 1.3.68.

In the rules *bhīsmyorhetubhaye* and *anudātetaḥ* [the suffix] *ātmanepada* is understood from the former, and *ṇeḥ* is understood from the rule *ṇeraṇau*. "Cause" (*hetu*) means the instigator (*prayojaka*). Thus he says: "from these two [roots] ending in *ṇi*, etc. This is for the purpose of expressing what is not intended for the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). Now, an objection:
If it is argued that the inclusion of both *bhaya* (fear) and *smaya* (wonder/amazement) is not appropriate because the word *smaya* is not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, he says:

"In the Sūtra, [the mention of] *bhaya*. The meaning is that the mention of *bhaya* in the Sūtra is also an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *smaya*, which is the meaning of the verbal root *smi*. In the example *muṇḍo bhāpayate* ("The shaven-headed one causes fear"), there is the substitution of *ā* and the augment *puk*.

And the *ātmanepada* endings [are used]. He states a specific rule for the case where the substitution of *ā* for *bhi* does not occur: (422) *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* | P. 7.3.40. *ṣuk* is added to *bhi* when fear is caused by a specific cause (*hetu*). Thus, *bhi* becomes *bhī*. By the rule of *savarṇa-dīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous sounds), from the word *bhī*—

The intended meaning is that it is the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī). This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivat* sūtra. He states "of that which ends in the vowel ī," which is obtained by the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel ī; by this, it follows as a result that there is no insertion of *ṣuk* in the alternative view where *āt* is substituted. Regarding "in the case of *ṇi*" (*ṇau*), the intention is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word from the rule "ṛt-ṛ-hrī... etc.

(423) *nityaṃ smayateḥ* | 6|1|57| The word *nityam* [is understood] from *smayateḥ*. From the rule *ādeca upadeśe*, the words *ecaḥ* and *āt* are carried over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *citphuroḥ*, the word *ṇau* is carried over; and from the rule *bibheterhetubhaye*.
Thus, [the rule] is "in the sense of fear" (*hetubhaye*). In that context, the mention of "fear" (*bhaya*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "pride" (*smaya*) as well;
however, here only "pride" is intended, because it is impossible for the root *smi* to have the meaning of "fear. This is why he says:
"after the root *smi*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied]," and so forth. [This is understood] from the rule "optionally after *lī*" (*vibhāṣā līyate*).

The inclusion of the word *nityam* (always) is for the purpose of excluding the application of the *vibhāṣā* (optionality). Now, he states the purpose of including the word *hetu* (cause) in the rule for the substitution of *āt* (*bibheteḥ hetubhaye*), in the rule for the prescription of *āt* (*nityaṃ smayate*), and in the rule for the prescription of the middle voice (*bhīsmiyor hetubhaye*).

Because it was stated that "fear and pride [occur] from a cause," it is not so here. Regarding the phrase "him with a key" (*kuñcikayainam*): a *kuñcikā* is a specific type of hair-braid; and since it functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it lacks the status of being the motivating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), and thus the substitution of *ātmanepada* endings and the suffix *ṣuk* do not apply—this is the intended meaning. He objects: The objection is raised: "If the *kuñcikā* is a specific kind of hair-braid, then how can it be the instrument? Furthermore, since the hair-braid is not sentient, it cannot be the motivating agent. Therefore, the rule for the *ātmanepada* ending and the suffix *ṣuk* should still apply. To this, he replies: "It is not so, because the word 'key' (*kuñcikā*) here refers to a small box containing a key, which is indeed a sentient object capable of acting as a motivator. Thus, the application of the *ātmanepada* and *ṣuk* is justified. The objection is refuted.

How so? In the *Raghuvamśa*, it is said in this verse: "The lion, his cow having been captured, spoke in human speech to that protector of the noble, the banner of Manu’s lineage, who was himself astonished at his own conduct; the lion, possessing the strength of a great bull, addressed him in order to cause him amazement. Thus ends the verse.

"Causing wonder" (*vismāpayan*) is an objection [asking] "how? The intention is that since there is an absence of a causal agent (*prayojaka*), the substitution of *āt* and the addition of the suffix *puk* are untenable. Now, one might object that human speech alone is the causal agent there; to this he says: "human..."—that is, "one who speaks like a human."

For in that case, the substitution of *āt* occurs precisely because the human voice, which is understood from the third case ending as the instrument (*karaṇa*), is the cause of the smile. Now, one might ask:
why is it not the case that the human voice, even as an instrument, is the motivator (*prayojikā*)? To this he says:
"Otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: having accepted that the human voice is the motivator of the smile, if one were to resort to the substitution of *āt*...

The meaning is that the ātmanepada ending would also occur by the rule *ṭhbhīsmyorhetubhaye*. It is indeed correct that "astonishment" (*smaya*) here is not based on a causal agent (*prayojaka*), but the objection regarding the introduction of the augment *puk* after the substitution of *ā* is not tenable;
he refutes this with partial acceptance, saying "True. Regarding the form *vismāyayan*: [it occurs] in the causative (*ṇau*).

In the case of the *āyādeśa* (the substitution of *āy* for *ai*), the great poet Kālidāsa employed the form *vismāyayan* itself—derived from the root *smāyī* with *laṭ*, *śatṛ*, *śap*, and the *guṇa* and *āyādeśa* substitutions for the *ṇi*-affix. The reading *vismāpayan* with the letter *pa* is, in his view, due to a scribal error. Alternatively: [The king...]

Dilīpa is amazed. The human speech uttered by the lion prompts him—“The human speech amazes the king. In this case, the human speech is the prompting agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), while the king is the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*); such is the established rule. Here, regarding the act of being amazed (*smaya*)—

Because it is rooted in the speech of a human being who is the causal agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), the augment *puK* is applied in the present tense (*ātve*). In the root [list], the reading "the causal agent" (*prayojya-kartrī*) is easily understood. The lion causes that human speech, which is the causal agent, to produce the effect of causing wonder in her; thus, he "causes her to be amazed" (*vismāpayati*). This is derived from the causative form of the root *smāp* (from *smi*), followed by another causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Considering that when the *ṇi* is elided, from the root *smi* with the suffix *catṛ*, the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* of *ṇi*, and the substitution of *ay* results in the form *vismāpayan*, he says "by her, [he was] like a lion. Here, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the causal agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs only after the causative (*ṇyant*) forms derived from the roots *bhī* and *smi*, and not otherwise.
The meaning is "from a causative base which itself is causative.
(424) *sphāyo vaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.41. Regarding *sphāyo vaḥ*: the word *ṇau* is to be supplied as a remainder (*śeṣapūraṇam*), because it continues from the rule *arti-hrī-* [7.3.36].
The state [of being].
(425) *śaderagatau taḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.42. Regarding *śaderagatau taḥ*, having understood that the word *ṇau* is carried over from the rule *artihrī-* (7.3.36), he says:

Regarding "śaderṇau": [the substitution of] *t* is the final substitute; the letter *t* is the meaning intended, while the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. (426) *ruhaḥ po 'nyatarasyām* | 7|3|43|.
"From *ruha*, *pa*"—the words "in the case of the causal suffix *ṇiC*" (*ṇau*) are to be supplied as a remainder.

(427) *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* | Pāṇini 6.1.48. The term *krīṅjīnām* is a *dvandva* compound consisting of the roots *krīñ* (in the sense of "exchanging goods"), *iṅ* (in the sense of "studying"), and *ji* (in the sense of "conquering"). The phrase "the substitution of *ā* for *ec*" refers to the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti*, which is understood here through its subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*). Thus, when these roots take the causative suffix *ṇic*, the vowel *ec* is replaced by *ā*.
The state [of the root] is as follows: *krāpayati* and *jāpayati*. When the substitution of *ā* occurs and the augment *puk* is added, the forms in the *luṅ* [aorist] are *acikrapat* and *ajījapat*.

Regarding *adhyāpayati*: this is the form when *iṅ* undergoes the substitution of *ā* and the addition of *puk*. When the sequence *adhi i i a t* is established, [the rule applies]: (428) *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.31. [The substitution of *ā* for *iṅ* occurs] before the causative suffix *ṇic*, as well as before *saṅ* and *caṅ*.

In the rule *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ*, it is clear from the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that this is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Thus, it is understood as "when the suffix *ṇiC* is intended [to follow]. From the rule *iṅśca*, the word *iṅ* is carried forward (*anuvartate*); from *gāṅ liṭi*, the word *gāṅ*;
and from *vibhāṣā luṅluṅoḥ*, the word *vibhāṣā*. He states this [as follows]:

"Sanpare caṅpare ca," etc. This means when a *ṇi*-affix follows that is itself followed by either a *san* (desiderative) or a *caṅ* (aorist). Regarding *adhyajīgapat*: when the *ṇi*-affix is applied, the root *iṅ* undergoes the substitution of *gāṅ*, the *puK* augment is added, and the penultimate vowel is shortened; thus, we have *adhi-gap-i-a-t*.

Then, after doubling the element *gap*, applying the rule for the retention of the first consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), and shortening the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsahrasva*), [the form is derived].

The form is derived by applying the rule for reduplication (*sanvac* etc.), lengthening the vowel, and changing the *abhyāsa* (reduplicated syllable) to *c*. Nor should one suspect that the substitution of *gāṅ* [for *iṅ*] is prohibited prior to reduplication by the rule "when a reduplication is to be applied, the substitution of *gāṅ* does not take place in the case of *ṇi*" (*dvitve kārye ṇāvajādeśo na*);
for it has been stated that this prohibition applies only when there is an *avarṇa* (a-vowel) in the subsequent portion following the *abhyāsa*. [This occurs] after reduplication.

The meaning is that when the substitution of *gāṅ* for the root *iṅ* (to study) is prohibited in the context of a grammatical operation (*kārye*), then by the rule "the second member beginning with *ṭh* or *j* is reduplicated," the reduplication occurs only of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Consequently, whether in the intermediate derivation (*prakriyā*) or in the final form (*pariniṣṭhite*), there is no *a*-vowel in the subsequent portion of the verbal root; thus, the resulting form is as stated. [The example is] *adhyāpipat*.

The intention is that when the vowel substitution (ātvam) has occurred by the rule "gāṅ-liṭi ca" and the augment *puK* has been added by the rule "ṭh-krīñ-jīnāṃ ṇau," resulting in the form *adhi ā p i a*, the word *pī* undergoes reduplication, and thus the form is established. [The term] *sidhyet* [is used] in the sense of "otherworldly" (*pāralaukika*); [the word] *ādecaḥ* is taken from the rule "ādeca upadeśe," and [the word] *ṇau* is taken from the rule "krīñ-jīnām."

And it follows accordingly. Thus he says: "In this world," and so forth. Regarding "food": the sense is that its production is for the sake of satisfaction, and therefore it pertains to this world (*aihalaiauika*). Regarding "reality" (*tatva*):
the meaning is the essential nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*). "The ascetic practices austerity" means [he cultivates] that reality.
The meaning is "it causes certainty. The intention is that the ascertainment of the reality of the Self has its fruit in the world beyond.
(429) *prajane vīyateḥ* | 6|1|55|. [The rule] *prajane vīyateḥ* [is derived] from the word *ādeca* in the rule *ādeca upadeśe...* [etc.].

Thus, from the rule *cisphuro 'rito ṇau* and the rule *vibhāṣā līyateḥ*, the word *vibhāṣā* is understood to carry over. Therefore he says: "of this very [root]," and so forth. The mention of *vīyate* is not by means of the suffix *syaN*; for some hold that [the root] is *vī* in the sense of "motion, procreation, standing, acquisition, and earning."

In reality, however, there is no inclusion of the root *vyai*, because it lacks the sense of "conceiving" (*prajana*), and because there is no difference in form between *vyāyayati* and [the other forms] due to the application of the augment *yuk* as an exception to *puṅ* by the rule *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*. This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. [The example is: *garbhaṃ grāhayati* ("she causes [her] to conceive a fetus").

It is well known that cows conceive during the time of the *purovāta* (the pre-storm wind). Now, [the author] recalls the rule for the substitution of *ū* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root *guh* (meaning "to conceal") when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel and having a *guṇa*-strengthening cause—namely, *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*. Thus, one forms *gūhayati*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa* substitution of a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).
The sense is that there is substitution of *ū*.
(430) *doṣo ṇau* | Pāṇini 6.4.90. Regarding *doṣo ṇau*: the phrase *ūdupadhāyāḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]. [The root] *duṣa* is used in the sense of "becoming corrupted."
The suffix *śyan* is the *vikaraṇa*. This is a reference to that [suffix] after its penultimate vowel has undergone the *guṇa* substitution.

Consequently, this rule concerns only the domain of *guṇa*. [The meaning is: "In place of the penultimate vowel of the root *duṣ*, there shall be *ū*, provided that *ṇā* follows. The word "provided that *ṇā* follows" (*ṇāv iti*) is the remainder [of the rule]. Thus, [the form] is *dūṣayati*. The substitution of *ū* is an exception to the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. [The rule] is simply stated as "in place of *duṣ*, when *ṇā* follows" (*duṣo ṇau*).
*su-vaca-m* (431). Regarding *vā citavirāge* |6|4|91*: the phrase *ūdupadhāyāḥ* and *doṣo ṇau* are carried over [from the preceding rules].

Regarding the rule *citavirāge duṣa upadhāyā ūdvā syāṇṇau*, the result is as follows: the word *virāga* is explained as "displeasure" (*aprītatā*), which means the absence of desire (*icchāviraha*). As for *cita*: "the mind becomes corrupted"; that is, it becomes indifferent toward daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) such as bathing and the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*).

The meaning is that desire (kāma) impels that [action]. Regarding the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92): although it was explained previously that there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of roots marked with *mit* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*, he recalls it here. Regarding "janījaṣ... (Pāṇini 6.4.42): this too, though already explained, is recalled. Regarding "jṛṇātestu": the point is that because the root *jṛ* belongs to the *śnā*-conjugation (*śnāvikaraṇa*), it does not possess the *mit* designation.

Regarding the rule *rañjerṇau*: since the suffix *ṇi* lacks the *kit* designation, the rule *niditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24) does not apply; therefore, this statement [of the Vārttika] is necessary. The explanation of the term *mṛgaramaṇa* is "hunting" (*ākheṭaka*). It means "the act of hunting" (*mṛgayā*).
[In the phrase] *rañjayati mṛgān* ("he delights the deer"), the root *rañj* is used with the *śap* verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), according to the rule *rañjeśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.85).

There is the elision of the letter *na*. "The deer run" means they become capturable; the meaning is that a king or similar person, addicted to hunting deer, makes those deer objects of such an activity. Here there is the elision of the letter *na*. [He says] "he causes the deer to rejoice by giving them grass," [referring to] the hunter of the deer.
The meaning is that by offering grass for protection, one causes [the animals] to go to the place of tethering.

Regarding the phrase "in the *cur*-class": the root *ci* exists within the group of five roots beginning with *jñap* in the *cur*-class. Therefore, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied in its own sense...

The meaning is as follows: in the *curādigaṇa*, according to the view that there is ātva (the substitution of ā for i) by the rule "ci-spṛśo 'ṇ," the form is *capayati* because the suffix *puK* is added and the penultimate vowel is shortened due to the status of being *mit*. However, in the absence of ātva, after the application of vṛddhi and the substitution of *āy*, the form *cāyayati* is stated because of the status of being *mit*. As for the phrase "but of *cinoti*": this refers to the verbal base taking the *śnu* vikaraṇa.

The meaning is that from the root *ci*, with the causal suffix *ṇic* (*hetumaṇṇi*), there is the substitution of *ā* by the rule "cisphuroḥ"; since there is no *puṅ* augment and no shortening due to the absence of *mit*-status, the form is *āyayati*. As for *sphārayati* and *sphorayati*: there is an option regarding the substitution of *ā* by the rule "cisphuroḥ". The form [of the root] *īrṣy* is derived from the causative (*ṇic*). It should be stated that "doubling" (*dvitva*) applies; this is the remainder of the sense. Or rather, the meaning is as follows:

this is clear in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *na ndrāḥ*. Regarding the phrase "in the first [case]": the meaning is "in the alternative view that doubling applies to the third consonant. Regarding the phrase "of the letter *ṣ*": otherwise, [the form would have been] *irṣy-i-a-t*.

If [the rule] "sthite ṭhna ndrāḥ" were applied, then—excluding the letter *r*—there would be doubling of the syllable *ṣyi* (which includes the letter *ṣ*). Consequently, after the elision of the *ṇi*-affix in the latter portion, the form would be *airṣiṣyat*, and the desired form *airṣyayat* would not be obtained. Therefore, it is stated that [doubling occurs] "of the third consonant. And thus:
The meaning is that when there is doubling of the *yakāra* and elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the desired form with a conjunct double *yakāra* is established. Regarding the phrase "in the second [case]":

this means in the explanation beginning with "the third one-moraic [root]" (*tṛtīyaikāc*). The phrase "it operates in the case of the desiderative" (*sannante pravartate*) has the word "the aforementioned Vārttika" as its ellipsis. When the augment *iṭ* is added to the root *īrṣy* in the desiderative, the state *īrṣy-isa-* is reached; [then] *īrṣy-*...

Thus, the first monosyllable is *prathamaikāc*, the second monosyllable is *ṣyiṣ*, and the third monosyllable is *sa*; this is the established state. In that context, because the third monosyllable is possible, its doubling is prescribed. Otherwise, [the rule] "of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*) would apply; such is the intention. [The example] *airṣyad* [shows] the doubling of the letter *y* alone.

In the case of reduplication (*dvitva*), with the elision of *ṇi*, the form is that which has two consonants joined together (*saṃyukta*) as its cause. Now, he states the form according to the second explanation: *airṣyiṣyat*. He explains this: "in the second explanation.
When the suffix *caṅ* follows the causative (*ṇyant*) root, the form stands as *īrṣy i i t*; then, due to the prohibition [of doubling] by the rule "na ndrāḥ," the *repha* (the letter *r*)...

Excluding [the application of] *ṭh-ja-ādeḥ dvitīyasya*, there is reduplication of *ṭh-ṣyi* and not of the letter *y* alone, because in the first explanation it was stated that "of the third consonant. In that case, even when the reduplication of *ṭh-ṣyi* has been performed, in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), it is the letter *ṣ* itself, with the vowel *i* as its head, that is the consonant (*hal*).
The meaning is that [the doubling] is heard, but the letter *y* is not. To the question "Why?", he says:

"Because of the rule *halādiśeṣa*" (Pāṇini 7.4.60). But as for the second explanation of the third [rule], one might ask how there can be doubling of the second monosyllable here; to this he says: "But the doubling is of the second alone."

The word "ṭhekāca" (the rule concerning a single-vowel root) is understood as the remainder [of the argument]. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the absence of a third [vowel]. In the form *īrṣyi-a-t*, *īrṣy* is the first monosyllabic element (*ekāc*), and *rṣyi* is the second monosyllabic element;
however, there is no third monosyllabic element in the *caṅ* reduplication. Therefore, the Vārttika "ṭhṛtīyaikācaḥ" does not apply here.
Therefore, the meaning is that reduplication applies only to the second *ekāc* (monosyllabic root).

And thus, the Vārttika "of the third *ekāc*" operates only in the case of a desiderative (*sannanta*), because, since the suffix *ām* follows the root *īrṣya*, there is no subsequent *liṭ* (perfect) suffix. But [one might object]: "They pray... (*prārthayanti*)...

In the *Māghakāvya*, the phrase "priyāḥ... śayanotthitaṃ" (the beloveds [prayed] to him as he rose from bed) does not contain the causative form derived from the *cur* class (*caurādika*) with an affixed *ṇic*, because that would necessitate the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) due to its being included in the *āgarvīya* group.
Nor is it the causative derived from the *hetu* sense (*hetumaṇṇic*), because that is impossible in the sense of "begging for what one desires. For indeed...

To show that its application occurs even in the absence of the activity of an instigator (*prayojaka*), he says: "from which the instigation has ceased" (*nivṛtapreṣaṇa*). This means that at present the instigation is not intended to be expressed. Therefore, having taken up the instigation by way of its prior existence, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to that root—
The meaning is that the same sense is understood from the root when it is pure, i.e., devoid of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

As it has been said: "The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to a root whose original impulsion has ceased, in the sense of its primary (prākṛta) meaning. This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṇeraṇau*.
Thus ends the section on the causative *ṇic* affix in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, regarding the suffix *cha* in the fifth chapter, the rule for its application is as follows:
(1639) *prāk krītāc chaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.1.1. [The suffix *cha* is applied after a nominal stem ending in *krīta* to form a word denoting the price at which something was purchased.]

Now begins the fifth chapter. [The rule] "cha after [words ending in] *krīta*": the word *krīta* here refers to the sūtra containing that term. Thus he says: "the suffix *cha* [is applied] in the sense of 'bought with that' (*tena krītam*). Prior to the sūtra "bought with that" (*tena krītam*), only meanings will be specified in the rules, and not the suffixes; in those cases, the suffix *cha* is understood to be present.

Up to this point: *ugavādibhyo yat*. [The analysis is: "u" and "gavādayaḥ"—this is the ablative case from a *dvandva* compound. [The meaning is] "from that which ends in the vowel *u*. Because it is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is an understanding of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*).
The point is that, according to the statement "except in the case of the suffix *ṭh*, a vowel, or *ugit*," there is an understanding of "ending in that" even when a suffix is being prescribed.
This rule also applies prior to the *kit* suffixes and remains in force for the subsequent rules where no specific suffix is mentioned:
"nābhi becomes *nabha*. This is a rule from the *gav-ādi* group.
The meaning is that the word *nābhi* undergoes the substitution of *nabha* and takes the suffix *yat*. As in the example: *nabhyo 'kṣaḥ* ("an axle fitted to the nave"). Where...
The axle-shaft is inserted; the hole situated in the middle of that wheel is called the *nābhi* (hub).

That which is beneficial for it is the *akṣadaṇḍa* (axle-shaft). Indeed, because of its suitability, it is beneficial for the hub. Regarding the phrase "anointing of the hub" (*nabhyamañjanam*): *añjana* means the pouring of oil. When the hub has been anointed, the wheel mounted upon it turns smoothly.

It is called *añjana* because it bestows the capacity for the functional activity consisting of the rotation of the nave (*nābhi*). Here, the word *nābhi*, which denotes a specific part of the body, is not intended; rather, it is the *nābhi* of a chariot that is understood, as the author intends by stating in the Bhāṣya: "This [suffix] occurs only after the word *rathanābhi*."

The meaning is that because the word *abhi* denotes a specific part of the body, the suffix *yat* alone—as prescribed by the rule "from a word denoting a body-part" (*śarīrāvayavād yaḥ*) which will be stated later—is applied, and not the substitution of *nabha*. "There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *śvan*" is a sūtra from the *gav-ādi* group; it means that the suffix *yat* occurs after the word *śvan*, with the base [undergoing the aforementioned changes].
"Vocalization" (saṃprasāraṇa); the meaning is that there is optional lengthening of that vocalized vowel.
"Śūnyam"—meaning "beneficial for a dog" (śune hitam). "And [the substitution of] anaṅ for ūdhas":
this is also a *gaṇasūtra*. The meaning is that after the word *ūdhas*, the suffix *yat* occurs, and the base undergoes the substitution of *anaṅ*.

In the substitute *ādeśa*, the letter *ṅ* is the *it* (indicatory letter); the vowel *a* following the *n* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because of its status as *ṅ*, it is replaced by *in*. (1640) *kambalācca saṃjñāyām* | 5|1|3|.

[The word] *kambalāt*: the meaning is that after the word *kambala*, the suffix *yat* shall occur in the senses previously mentioned (beginning with "purchased for"), provided it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
*Kambalyam ūrṇāpalaśam* means "suitable for a blanket" (*kambalāya hitam*).

(Pāṇini 5.1.4) *Vibhāṣā havir-apūpādibhyaḥ*: optionally [the suffix -yaṅ is applied] after words denoting specific types of sacrificial oblations (*havis*) and after the group beginning with *apūpa*. *Havir viśeṣa-vācibhyaḥ apūpādibhyaś ca*.
The meaning is that it may optionally apply to items purchased beforehand; in this alternative case, the suffix *cha* is used. Thus, *āmikṣyam dadhi* (curd for curds) means "beneficial for *āmikṣā*.
When curd is poured into heated milk, that which results as a solidified mass is called *āmikṣā*.

(1642) *tasmai hitam* |5|1|5| "Beneficial for that. In this sense, suffixes shall be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the dative case. For example, *vatsīyaḥ*. This form is derived by the addition of the suffix *cha*. It refers to one who, having milked cows, leaves some milk for the calves before milking them.

It is stated thus: *śaṅkavyam*. The meaning is "beneficial for a stake" (*śaṅku*). Because it ends in the vowel *u*, the suffix *yat* is applied. *Gavyam* means "grass and so forth beneficial for cows. This is the suffix *yat* according to the rule for words beginning with *go*. *Haviṣyam* means "beneficial for the oblation" (*havis*).

The word *havis* refers to [substances] such as cow’s milk and the like. However, in the rule *vibhāṣā haviḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.25), only those words denoting specific types of sacrificial offerings (*havir-viśeṣa*) are understood to be included, according to the traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
(1643) *Śarīrāvayavād yat* (Pāṇini 5.1.6): The suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting a limb of the body.

*Śarīrāvayavādyat*: This means that the suffix *yat* shall be applied after a word denoting a specific part of the body that ends in the dative case, in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hita*). It is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] *cha*.

From *nāsikā*, [the form] *nasyam* arises; the meaning is "beneficial for the nose. By the rule *paddan*, *nas* is substituted [for *nāsikā*], because the inclusion of *prabhṛti* in that rule is intended to indicate the class of words [to which it applies]. However, in the Bhāṣya, regarding *nāsikā*—

Because of that, it is read as *nās* in the sense of "small things. [The form] *nābhyam* means "beneficial for the navel" (*nābhaye hitam*). Here, *nābhi* refers to a part of the body; however, when referring to a part of a chariot, the substitution *nabha-* has been taught.
(1644) *ye ca taddhite* |6|1|61|.

Regarding *ye ca taddhite*: the meaning is that the substitution of *śīrṣan* [for *śiras*] occurs because of its continued application from the rule *śīrṣañ chandasi*. Thus, *śīrṣaṇya* means "beneficial for the head" (*śirase hitam*).

This is the meaning. Because it is a part of the body (*śarīrāvayava*), when *śiras* undergoes the substitution of *nā* by the rule *śīrṣan-nādeśe*, there is no elision of the suffixal *ṭi* due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*. [The form] *śirasyati* is derived as follows: from the sense "he desires a head for himself" (*śira ātmana icchati*), the suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ*, and then [the *y* of *kyac*] is replaced by *na* by the rule *naḥ kye*.
By rule, because it lacks the status of being a word (*pada*), there is no substitution of *ru*.
(*vā keśeṣu* | *vā keśeṣu* |) When the suffix beginning with *ya* that denotes "hair" (*keśa*) follows, [the preceding vowel becomes pluta].
The meaning is that "śiras" may optionally be replaced by "śīrṣan.
[The rule] should be stated as "śīrṣa [is substituted for 'śiras'] before a vowel. He states "before a vowel" (*aci*) because it arises in this context.

(1645) *khalayavamāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaśca* | 5|1|7 | The meaning is that the suffix *yat* is applied after words such as *khala*, etc., when they end in the dative case, in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hitam*).
Here, the word *vṛṣa* is understood as ending in the vowel *a* (i.e., *vṛṣa*), and not as ending in *na*. Therefore, [the form is] *vṛṣāya hitaḥ* = *vārṣaḥ*.
The phrase "beneficial to" (*hita*) is indeed a compound. The word *brahman* is understood here as referring specifically to a Brāhmaṇa, and not as referring to the Veda and so forth.

Therefore, it is clear in the Bhāṣya that this is indeed the phrase "beneficial to the Veda" (*brahmaṇe vedāya hita*). In the form *brahmaṇyam*, there is no *prakṛtibhāva* (absence of sandhi) due to the rule "and in the case of *ya*, when it does not denote an abstract quality or an action" (*ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*).

There is elision of the *ṭi* [suffix]. Regarding the phrase "and by the rule *cādrathyā*" (*cādrathyā*), the intention is that the particle *ca* serves to aggregate what has not been explicitly mentioned. (1646) *ajāvibhyāṃ thyan* | Pāṇini 5.1.8: "The suffix *thyan* after *aja* and *avi*. *Aja* and *avi* form a *dvandva* compound. Although the word *avi* undergoes the substitution of *dhi*, [the rule applies].

In the rule *ṭhājādyadantam*, the word *aja* is placed first [as the prior member of a compound]. Thus we have *ajathyā yūthī*. The meaning is "beneficial for goats (*aja*) or she-goats (*ajā*). By the paribhāṣā "a word qualified by gender [retains its gender]," the suffix *thyan* is added even after the feminine word *ajā*. By the rule *tasilādiṣu*, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Hence, *avithyā*.
The meaning is "beneficial for sheep. Femininity [of the word *avī*] is derived from common usage (*loka*).

(1647) Pāṇini 5.1.9: *ātman-viśvajana-bhogottarapadāt khaḥ*. From the words *ātman*, *viśvajana*, and those ending in *bhoga* as the final member of a compound—the suffix *kha* (forming *īya*) is applied in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hita*). Specifically, this applies to *ātmanjan*, *viśvajana*, and compounds where *bhoga* is the final member.
The meaning is that there should be the suffix *kha*. He will give "ātmānīna" as an example. Regarding rule 6.4.169, *ātmādhvānau khe*:
since the elision of the *ṭi* portion would otherwise apply there, it is stated: "In the case of the suffix *kha*, the words *ātman* and *adhvan* remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*)."

The meaning is that [the suffix] applies because of the recurrence of the rule "ekāj-prakṛtyā" (Pāṇini 6.2.49). "From the *karmadhāraya* compound alone"—this is said with the words "from the word *viśvajana*" as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). In this matter, the commentary itself is the only refuge.
Regarding *viśvajanīyam*: "the people of the whole world" (*viśvasya janaḥ*) is *viśvajanaḥ*, namely the common public, such as physicians and the like.
Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which all people (*viśva-jana*) are [possessors]. The analysis is: "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*).
There is an extension of the rule from the word *pañcajana*; thus, one forms *pañcajanīna*. The four castes (*varṇa*) are the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
And the *rathakāra* caste—these are the five classes of people (*pañcajana*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which is beneficial for them" (*tebhyaḥ hitam*).

[According to Pāṇini 5.1.9] "The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *khaś* are applied after *sarvajana*. This means that *ṭhañ* and *khaś* are added after *sarvajana*. The phrase "it should be stated that [the suffix is applied] after *sarvajana*" is the remainder [of the rule]. [This applies] "from a word in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇāt*).
The Vārttika "it should be stated" is established in the Bhāṣya.
[Regarding] "from *mahājana*, the suffix *ṭhañ*": the remainder of the statement is "it should be stated. This is mentioned in connection with *viśvajana*.

Two *vārttikas* have been presented. Now he provides an example for a compound where "bhoga" is the subsequent member: *mātṛbhogīṇa*. The meaning is "beneficial for the enjoyment of the mother. Regarding the word "ācāryāt": [it refers to] the substitution of *n* for the *n* of the word *bhogīna* when it follows the word *ācārya*.

The meaning is that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* must be stated [as an exception]. Nor should it be argued that this prohibition is redundant because the substitution of *m* for *n* does not even apply here due to the fact that the words are not situated in the same *pada*; for it serves the purpose of making known the substitution of *ṇ* in cases such as *mātṛbhogīṇa*.

(1649) *sarvapuruṣābhyāṃ ṇaḍhañau* |5|1|10|. [The rule] "from *sarva* and *puruṣa*": the meaning is that the suffixes *ṇa* and *ḍhañ* respectively follow the words *sarva* and *puruṣa* when they end in the dative case, in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hitam*).
One should state "sarvānna" or "veti.
Regarding the term *sarvānna*: because the word *sarva* here refers to its own form (*svarūpaparatva*), it does not undergo the grammatical operations associated with a pronominal (*sarvanāma*).
[This applies] in the case of derivatives formed from *puruṣa* when expressing killing, transformation, a collection, or that which is produced by it.

"From *puruṣa*, after [the word] *vadha* etc."—this is a Vārttika. The meaning is that the suffix *ḍhañ* should occur after the word *puruṣa* only in the sense of "killing" (*vadha*) and so forth, and not in the sense of "for the benefit of" (*hita*). Now, one might ask: since the entire expression *tena kṛtam* ("made by him") is not a nominal stem (*asubanta*), how can it be included within a compound? To this he says: "By the Bhāṣya. Since the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply...

Thus, the remainder [of the rule] is "ḍhañ by this. Regarding "prāṇi": the meaning is that when the suffix *añ* would otherwise apply by the rule "from *rajata* and so on" (*rajatādibhyaś cāñ*), *ḍhañ* is applied by this [rule]. Regarding "also when it denotes a collection" (*samūhe’pyaṇi prāpte*): the meaning is that when the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply by the rule "its collection" (*tasya samūhaḥ*) in the sense of "a collection of men," *ḍhañ* is applied by this [rule].

"Like those inhabited by men" means as if inhabited by a multitude of men; the sense is that [the reflection] is reflected all around in a mirror. Regarding the phrase "composed by him": when the suffix *aṇ* is applicable in the sense of "a book composed by a person" (*puruṣeṇa kṛto granthaḥ*), [it is not applied]; however, in the sense of "a palace built by a person" (*puruṣeṇa kṛtaḥ prāsādaḥ*), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied].
The meaning is that when no other suffix is applicable, this [suffix] *ḍhañ* is used. *Māṇava*.
The meaning is that the suffix *khañ* shall be applied after these two words ending in the dative case (*caturthyanta*) in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hitam*).
(Pāṇini 5.1.11): *māṇavacarakābhyāṃ khañ*.

Regarding the term *māṇavīna*: a *māṇava* is the contemptible offspring of Manu. According to the Vārttika on the section concerning offspring: "The suffix *aṇ* is traditionally prescribed for Manu in the sense of a contemptible, foolish offspring; and the substitution of a retroflex nasal (*mūrdhanya*) for the letter *n* results in the form *māṇava*. [Thus, *māṇava* means a contemptible descendant. [The word *māṇavīna*] means "beneficial for a *māṇava*."

Analysis: *cārakīṇam*—the word *cara* is derived from the root *car* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), meaning "one who moves. Then, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*), resulting in *caraka*.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is beneficial (*hitam*) for the *carakas*. (Pāṇini 5.1.12):

*tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau*—"The fourth case-ending is used after a word denoting a modification when it signifies that for the sake of which the modification exists, provided the word refers to the material cause (*prakṛti*)."

"For that purpose, [the rule applies] to the *prakṛti* from the *vikṛti*. The term "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) is neuter because it expresses a general sense. "For that purpose" means "this is for the sake of that. By the word "that" (*tat*), the *vikṛti* is referred to. The nominative case is used in the sense of the locative. Thus, the meaning obtained is "in the *prakṛti* which is for the sake of the *vikṛti*. And in this way, by the word "that" (*tat*):

The modification itself is indicated first by that which ends in the dative case; thus, it is understood as "from that which denotes a modification and ends in the dative. This is what he says with the words beginning "denoting a modification," etc., [meaning] "the suffix shall occur."

The phrase "as prescribed" (*yathāvihitam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "For the embers" (*aṅgārebhya etāni*) means "for the purpose of the embers. Because a compound with a word denoting purpose (*artha*) is prescribed as obligatory, this is an analysis where the constituent members do not stand as separate words (*asvapadavigraha*). In this context, the wood chips (*kāṇṭhāni*) are the raw materials (*prakṛtidravya*), while the embers (*aṅgārāḥ*) are the modified products (*vikṛti*).
From the word *aṅgāra*, which denotes that [object], with the suffix *cha* applied, the form *aṅgārīyāṇi* arises.

"The bricks are *prākārīyāḥ*" means: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "these [bricks] are for the walls" (*prākārebhya imāḥ*). The meaning is that they serve the purpose of the wall (*prākārārthāḥ*). Regarding *śaṅkavyam*: the analysis is "this is for the stake" (*śaṅkave idam*).
The meaning is "for the sake of a roof. [The suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule "after go and others" (*gavādibhyaḥ*).
(1652) *cchadir-upadhi-bal-er ḍhañ*. [The rule] *cchadir-upadhi-bal-er ḍhañ*: in the case of a collective dvandva compound of *cchadis*, *upadhi*, and *bali*.

The masculine gender is based on the Sūtra. The meaning is that the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after these words ending in the dative case in the sense of "for the purpose of" (*tādarthya*), when the original object (*prakṛti*) is to be expressed.

Regarding the form *chādiṣeyāṇi*: *cchadiḥ* means a layer of straw; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "these are for that. Thus, the meaning is "intended for a roof-covering. When the suffix *ḍhañ* is added and replaced by *ey*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs because it follows a *ṣ*.

"Bāleyāstaṇḍulāḥ" (rice grains for Bali). The analysis of the compound is "ime balaye" (these are for Bali). The meaning is "intended for the sacrificial offering. According to Amara, "bali" is masculine when referring to a tax or an oblation: "bhāgadheyaḥ karo baliḥ. Furthermore, it is stated: "bhāgadheyaḥ karo baliḥ."
The suffix *i* is desired after the word *upadhi* in its own sense (*svārthe*).

Regarding the phrase "after the word *upadhi*": this is a *vārttika*. [It is derived as follows: that which is placed upon (*upadhīyate*)—namely, that which is fixed or strung upon the tip of the axle—is called *upadhi*. This is derived from the root *dhā* by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*.
The suffix *kip* is applied. By the rule *ṭhātā lopa iṭi ca*, there is elision of the *ā*. "Upadhī" means a part of a chariot;
such is the sense, according to the Bhāṣya.
(1653) Pāṇini 5.1.14: *ṛṣabhopānahor ñyaḥ*.

*ṛṣabhopānahaḥ*. This is the ablative case from a collective *dvandva* compound of *ṛṣabha* and *upānah*. The meaning is that the suffix *ñya* occurs after the words *ṛṣabha* and *upānah* when they are in the dative case (*caturthī*) expressing "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), provided the original object (*prakṛti*) is to be expressed. Thus, *ārṣabhyaḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "this is for the bull" (*ṛṣabhāya ayam*).
The meaning is "for the sake of a bull. That calf which is nourished for the purpose of reaching the state of a bull is described in this way.
Regarding the example *āuṣānahye muñjaḥ*: the analysis of the compound is *ayam upānahi* ("this is for a sandal").
The meaning is "muñja grass for the purpose of sandals. In certain regions, sandals are made from muñja grass.

(1654) *carmaṇo’ñ* [Pāṇini 5.1.15]. Regarding the statement "even when it refers to leather": even when leather is to be expressed as the material cause (*prakṛti*), this suffix *ñya* alone is applied; this rule, by means of the principle of priority (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), sets aside even the subsequent rule *carmaṇo’ñ*.
This is the meaning. And this point is established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *gavādibhyaḥ*.

Regarding the form *aupānahyam*: it means leather intended for a sandal (*upānah*). [The suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *carmaṇo’ñ*. In the rule *carmaṇaḥ*, the word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is construed with the modified object (*vikṛti*). Thus he says: "that which [is made] from leather..."

"From that which denotes the modification"—the remainder [of the rule] is "from that which ends in the dative case used in the sense of 'for the sake of that' (tādarthya). "It should be added" (*añ syāt*)—the remainder is "when the original form (*prakṛti*) is to be expressed. "For Vadhryai" (*vadhraryai idam*) is an alternative reading.

[The word *vadhrya* is derived] from the root *vṛdh* with the suffix *ran*, and by the rule "ran after *vṛdh* and *vap*" (*vṛdhivapibhyāṃ ran*), there is the guṇa substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
In the case of *rapara* [substitution], the word *vardhra* denotes leather; therefore, with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of a derivative product, we have *vārdhrī rajjuḥ* ("a rope made of leather").
(1655) *tadasya tadasmin syāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.16):

"That [object] belongs to this, or that [object] is in this. This refers to the rule *tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau* ("for the sake of that, [the suffix is applied] to the raw material of a derivative product").

Kaiyaṭa says [the word] "nivṛtam" [is used]. The meaning is that, in the senses of "this belongs to it" (*tadasya syāt*) and "this is in it" (*tadasmin syāt*), an affix shall occur after a word ending in the nominative case, according to the rules prescribed.

In the word "syāt" here, the potential mood (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvane*), according to the rule "alamiti sambhāvane. [The example is: *prākāra āsām* ("a wall belongs to these").

When there is a desire to express the general relation of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), the genitive case is used. The resulting meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*)—“by these bricks, a wall can be made”—is as follows: *prākārīyāḥ* [bricks]. From the word *prākāra* ending in the nominative case, the suffix *cha* is applied; the bricks are the meaning of the suffix.
"Bricks suitable for a wall" means bricks that are sufficient for a wall. "Wood suitable for a palace":
the analysis of the compound is "that which would have a palace [built] from it"; it means wood sufficient for a palace.
"A region suitable for a wall": the meaning is that a wall is likely to be found in this region.

The meaning is that it is because the region abounds in stones, bricks, and other materials suitable for that purpose. By this, it is indicated that even if the phrase "in the modification for that purpose" (*tadarthaṃ vikṛtau*) were to follow here, [the suffix] would not apply. Now, one might object that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in a case such as "the palace belongs to Devadatta" (*prāsādo devadattasya*); therefore, he says: "the word *iti*..."
"Worldly intention" (*laukikī vivakṣā*) means the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭavyavahāra*).

(1656) *parikhāyā ḍhañ* | 5.1.17 | "The suffix *ḍhañ* [is applied] after *parikhā*. The phrase "in the scope of the preceding sūtra" is to be supplied as the remainder. [Thus, the derivative form is] *pārikheyī*.

Regarding the term *bhūmi*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "that which has a moat" (*parikhā asyā asti*) or "that which exists in a moat" (*asyām asti*). The meaning is "suitable for a moat. "The limit is complete up to the suffixes *cha* and *yat*" refers to the group of sūtras beginning with *prāgvateṣṭhañ* and ending with *dvitripūrvādaṇ ca*.

When specific suffixes have been enumerated [in the preceding rules], the rule "tena krītam" (Pāṇini 5.1.37) is recited. Consequently, one should not raise the objection: "Since it is stated 'before the suffix -krīta' (prāk-krītāt), why is there no continued application (anuvṛtti) of the suffixes -cha and -yaṭ in those subsequent rules as well? This is because, upon hearing specific suffixes [such as -krīta], the continued application of those two [suffixes] is impossible.
[The section on] *bhāva* [is concluded]. Thus ends the limit of the suffixes *ccha* and *yat* in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, those belonging to the fifth [chapter]: (1778) *khañ* is used after words for grains when denoting a field where they grow. 5.2.1.
Now, the suffixes belonging to the fifth chapter are defined. Regarding the rule for "the place where grains grow" (*dhānyānāṃ bhavane*):

the meaning is that the suffix *khañ* is applied after words denoting grains ending in the genitive case, when the sense is a field (*kṣetra*) where they grow. This is because the word *bhavana* is derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *lyuṭ* (denoting an action).
Because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "field" (*kṣetra*) would otherwise be untenable, he says: "it exists in this," and "existence.
The verbal root *bhū* signifies arising. Thus, "existence" (*bhavana*) is understood as a place of arising.
A field is a place where grain arises. Amara states: "A field is a *kedāra*."

In the absence of the word *kṣetra*, if one were to rely on the root *bhū* (to exist) as signifying mere existence, then by the etymological derivation "that which exists is a *bhavana*," one would obtain only a general locus such as a house, a granary, and so forth; therefore, the word *kṣetra* is used. However, in the absence of the word *bhavana*, by the word *kṣetra* alone—
Even a meritorious region such as Setubandha or Kāśī might be obtained; therefore, the term "bhavana" (abode) is used.
However, when both terms are employed together, what is obtained is specifically a region where grain grows; thus, there is no tautology.

(1779) *vrīhi-śālyor ḍhak* | 5.2.2 | The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *vrīhi* and *śāli* when they end in the genitive case, in the sense of "a field for growing" (*bhavana-kṣetra*). This means that the suffix *ḍhak* is added to the words *vrīhi* and *śāli* in the genitive case to denote a field where rice is grown. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *khañ*.

(1780) *yavayavakaṣaṣṭikādyat* || 5.2.3 || [The suffix] *yat* is applied after *yava*, *yavaka*, and *ṣaṣṭika* when they end in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), meaning "in the field where [these grains] grow. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *khañ*. Because the phrase "*dhānyānām*" ("of grains") is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) here as well...
The genitive case alone is the governing case [for the suffix *maya*].

(1781) *Vibhāṣā tila-māṣa-umā-bhaṅgā-aṇubhyaḥ* | 5|2|4|. The suffix *maya* is optional after the words *tila*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅga*, and *aṇu*. After these—*tila*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅga*, and *aṇu*—[the suffix *maya* is optionally used].
The meaning is that the suffix *yat* may optionally occur after words denoting specific types of grain when they end in the genitive case.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "Ṭhumā and bhaṅga are specific types of grain. Amara says: "Ṭhumā, atasī, and kṣumā [are synonyms].

Regarding *aṇavyam*: *aṇu* is a specific type of grain. When the suffix *yat* is applied, by the rule *orguṇaḥ* ("the guṇa substitute occurs for *o*"), and [by the rule] *vānto...* [the form is derived].
The substitution of *yī* for *tyap* is prescribed.

(1782) *sarvacarmaṇaḥ kṛtaḥ khakhañau* | 5.2.5. [The suffixes] *kha* and *khañ* are applied after the word *sarvacarman*, provided it ends in the third case, in the sense that "something has been made entirely out of leather. *Sarvacarmaṇaḥ*: from the word *sarvacarman* ending in the third case, meaning "made entirely by means of leather (*carmaṇā*)."

The meaning is that the suffixes *kha* and *khañ* occur. Due to the exigencies of the context (*aucitya*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*) here. Now, one might object: since the word *sarva* is connected with *kṛta*, it cannot be connected with *carman*; thus, due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), a compound with *carman* would be impossible, and how then could the suffix be applied from the word *sarvacarman*? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "Even in the case of incapacity. The analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is *sarvaścarmaṇā kṛtaḥ*. The meaning is: "made entirely with leather. [The form] *sarvacarmīṇaḥ* [is derived as follows]: there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) by the rule *ṭ-nastaddhite*. However, the suffixes *kha* and *khañ* do not apply when the meaning is "made with all the leather," because of the [traditional] explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

(1783) *yathāmukhasammukhasya darśanaḥ khaḥ* | 5|2|6| [The suffix] *kha* is applied after *yathāmukha* and *samukha*, when they are in the genitive case, in the sense of "that which shows" (*darśana*). The meaning is that the suffix *kha* occurs after these two words ending in the genitive, in the sense of "showing. That in which something is seen is called *darśanaḥ*, such as a mirror and the like. Now, [one might ask]: of the face...

One might ask: "How can *yathāmukham* be an *avyayībhāva* compound, given that the rule *yathā’sādṛśye* prohibits it when there is similarity (*sādṛśya*)? To this, he replies: "By way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In the word *sammukha*, the prefix *sam-*—which signifies direction toward (*ābhimukhya*)—is not involved; rather, it is the word *sama-* [that is used].

He says "of every alternative" (*sarvaparyāyasya*), [explaining]: "equal, all, face-to-face" (*samaṃ sarvaṃ mukhaṃ saṃmukham*). "All" (*sarvam*) is the gloss for "equal" (*samam*). The meaning is that the word *saṃmukha* is a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "equal" (*samam*) and "face" (*mukham*). It is stated as an irregular formation (*nipātyate*); this is clear in the Bhāṣya. And thus:
The intention is that this suffix is not desired when preceded by the prefix *sam* or other such prepositions.

(1784) *tatsarvādeḥ pathyaṅgakarmapatrapātraṃ vyāpnoti* | [The suffix *kha* is applied] after a word beginning with *sarva* when it denotes that which pervades a "path," a "limb," an "action," a "leaf," or a "vessel. [The words are: *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, *pātra*—of these...
The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamyarthe*) because it follows a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*).

Since it qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the rule of "extension to that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. However, the prohibition—"there is no extension to that which ends in [the specified element] when the nominal stem includes the suffix *ṭha*"—does not apply here, as these [suffixes] occur in their isolated forms.
Because it is impossible for [the word] to be the beginning of everything, the term *tad*— being in the accusative case—

connects with the word *vyāpnoti* (he pervades). Consequently, in the sense of "he pervades that," [the suffix *kan* is added] after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) preceded by the word *sarva* and ending in the accusative case.
The meaning results as follows: the suffix *kha* occurs after words ending in *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, and *pātra*.

He states this with the words "beginning with *sarva*" and so forth. Regarding the form *sarvapathān*: the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied by the rule *ṛkpū-*. [The example] *āprapadam*.

The meaning is that the suffix *kha* occurs after the indeclinable compound *āprapada*, when it ends in the second case and signifies "reaches. *Prapada* is the tip of the foot; as Amara states: "The tip of the foot is *prapada*.
[Pāṇini 5.2.8] *Āprapadaṃ prāpnoti*. (5.2.8) "He reaches as far as the tips of his feet."
Regarding "āprapadam": this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *ṭhāṅmaryādābhividhyoḥ*.

[The words] *anupada*, *sarvānna*, and *ayānaya* form a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva* compound, and thus take the second case ending. [The words] *baddhā*, *bhakṣayati*, and *neya* form a *dvandva* compound, and thus take the seventh case ending. The inclusion of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) within a *dvandva* compound is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage.
The meaning is that the suffix *kha* (which becomes *īna*) occurs after words such as *anu*, ending in the accusative case, in the successive senses of "bound" and so forth.

Regarding the rule *anurāyāme sādṛśye vā*: in the first case, when it means "extent," it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *yasya cāyāmaḥ*; in the second case, when it means "similarity," it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound.

(1786) *anupadasarvānnāyānayaṃ baddhābhakṣayatineyeṣu* | 5|2|9| Regarding *anupadaṃ baddhā*: because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the second case ending is used. *Anupadīnā upānad* means "a sandal that is in accordance with the foot. The meaning is that it is characterized by a length corresponding to the foot. [Alternatively,] it means "resembling the foot."
Or, it means "of equal measure. Regarding the term *āyānaya*: in the game of dice, the clockwise movement of the pieces is *āya* (gain), and the counter-clockwise movement is *anaya* (loss).
*Āyānaya* is *anaya* accompanied by *āya*. It refers to that initial position in which there is movement both clockwise and counter-clockwise.

The meaning is that the state of those pieces standing [on the board] not being attacked by the opponent’s pieces is indicated here figuratively by the term *ayānaya*. All of this is clear in the Bhāṣya: “The position of a piece accompanied by others is not attacked by the opponents; however, one who is without assistance is obstructed by an opponent’s piece.”

This is the established rule of the treatises on gambling (*dyaūta-śāstra*). The details, however, should be sought in Kaiyaṭa’s *Pradīpa*, the *Manoramā*, and other such works. Regarding the phrase "it should be led to him" (*taṃ neyaḥ*): the meaning is that he should be caused to reach that particular place called the *ayāna*.

The root *ṇī* (to lead) takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*). According to the rule, "the [kṛt] affix *yat* occurs with the primary object, while the secondary object takes the second case," [the word *tam* is used].
This will be explained in the section on the *lakāras* of the passive voice (*bhāvakarma*).

(1787) *parovaraparamparaputrapautram anubhavati* | 5|2|10|. From the words *parovara*, *parampara*, and *putrapautra*— [The suffix *cha* is applied after these words when they denote that which is experienced. *Parovara*, *parampara*, *putrapautra*—from these [words...]

The meaning is that the suffix *kha* occurs after words ending in the second case (accusative) in the sense of "experiencing. Regarding the form *parovarīṇa*: it means "one who experiences both the higher (*para*) and the lower (*avara*)," i.e., those who are superior and inferior. Regarding the statement "there is the substitution of *u* for *ava*": by the application of the suffix *kha*, the initial vowel *a* of the word *avara* is irregularly changed to *u*.
This is the meaning. And thus, in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), this substitution of *u* does not occur. Regarding the word "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*):

the meaning is that when the suffix *kha* follows a *dvandva* compound consisting of the words *para* and *paratara*, the state of being *parampara* is prescribed for the base by way of co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*) with that suffix. But if this is so—

Regarding the question, "In expressions such as *kalyāṇaparamparā*, how is the word *paramparā* [formed], given that the state of being a *parampara* (succession) is taught only in connection with the suffix *khap*?", he says: "But the word *paramparā*... [and so on]. "From that very [base]" means: from the unanalyzed nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) *paramparā* itself.

"How so? [This is] the objection: how can there be the form *pārovaryavat*? For, from the word *parāvara*, whether the suffix *ṣyañ* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or in its own sense (*svārtha*), there is the substitution of *u* for the initial *ava-* of *avara*, resulting in the word *pārovarya*.

From this, when the possessive suffix *matup* is added, one would expect *pārovaryavat*. The point is that the substitution of *u* is not prescribed as being co-occurrent with the suffix *khap*. [The answer is: the substitution of *u*...

He says that this is indeed difficult to establish: "it is simply incorrect. Now, one might ask: since there is the mention of *parovara* here, why should not the substitution of *u* for *o* occur elsewhere than after *kha*?
To this he replies: "only in conjunction with the suffix *kha*. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya.
