The intended meaning is that the analysis (*vigraha*) has been shown as "he experiences both those beyond and those below.
(1788) *avārapārātyantānukāmaṃ gāmī* | 5|2|11|. [The suffix] *kha* is applied after *avārapāra*, *atyanta*, and *anukāma* in the sense of "one who goes to" (*gāmī*).
*Avārapāra*; from *avārapāra*, *atyanta*, and *anukāma*, the suffix *kha* is used when the meaning is "one who goes to."
The meaning is "it may be. Regarding the word *gāmī*, its meaning is "one who will certainly go.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a root [ending in a vowel] when expressing necessity (*avaśyaka*) or debt (*adhamarṇya*). Its future tense is indicated by the rule "the words *gamyā* and so forth denote the future time. Alternatively, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "frequently" (*bahulam ābhīkṣṇye*). [This applies to the term] *avārapārīṇa*.

Thus: "one who goes from this shore to the other shore" (*avārapāra-gāmī*) is the analysis (*vigraha*). According to the commentary, the word *avārapāra* may also be analyzed in reverse order. As it says: "one who goes to this shore" (*avārīṇaḥ*) and "one who goes to the other shore" (*pārīṇaḥ*). Regarding the term *atyantīna*: here, the word *atyanta* [is used].
It is a word expressing intensity. Thus he says: "one who goes intensely. Regarding *anukāmam*: *kāma* means desire;

the meaning is "without transgressing that [desire]. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of not exceeding the meaning of the constituent words. (1789) *samāsamāṃ vijāyate* | Pāṇini 5.2.12.
"Year by year. The root *jan* preceded by the prefix *vi-* occurs in the sense of "releasing the fetus";
thus, "she gives birth" means "she releases the fetus. Because the meaning of the prefix is already included within the meaning of the verbal root, the verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
Consequently, there is no accusative case ending for the object. By means of the releasing of the fetus, the entire year [is completed].

Because there is no separation [of the action] from the object, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*)—which is characterized by absolute conjunction (*atyantasaṃyoga*)—does not occur; rather, only the seventh case (*saptamī*) applies.

In that context, when the word *samāyām*, which ends in the seventh case, undergoes reduplication (*dvirvacana*) according to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*, it should become *samāyām—samāyām*. In this instance, both words are [in the locative case].
The elision of the letter *ya* is indicated by the expression *samāṃ samām*.

This means "in every year" (*samāyāṃ samāyām*). Thus, in the sense of "she gives birth in every year," the meaning is derived from the combination of two locative endings; consequently, the suffix *kha* (which forms the word *sāṃvatsarika*) is established.

Now, an objection might be raised: if the suffix *kha* were produced from the aggregate of two words ending in the locative case (*saptamī*), then that aggregate ending in *kha* would be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Consequently, the two locative endings forming its parts would undergo elision (*luk*), and the form would have to be *samāsamīnaḥ*, whereas the desired form is *samāṃsamīnaḥ*. To this, it is replied: "There is the elision of *ya*" (*yalopaḥ*). This occurs because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is [retained] in the first member of the compound.

The meaning is that the elision (*lopa*) of the *yakāra* which is a constituent part of that [word], as well as the non-elision (*aluk*) of the remaining portion of the case-ending, are treated as a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). In the *Bhāṣya*, however, it is stated:
"Because of the formal irregularity consisting of the elision of *ya*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the remaining portion of the case-ending. Now, one might object:

Because of the specific mention "samām samām," it might be thought that the elision of the letter *y* would occur even when [the word] follows as a second member (*uttarapada*), and that there would be no elision (*aluk*) of the remaining portion of the case-ending; therefore, he says: "in the first member" (*pūrvapade*).
The intention is that this is based on the Vārttika: "The statement regarding the elision of *y* applies to the first member."
When the *kha* suffix does not arise, the elision (*lopa*) of *ya* should be stated.

Regarding the phrase "when the *kha* suffix does not arise," the remainder [of the rule] is "in both instances of the word *pada*. Here, by virtue of the optionality (*vibhāṣā*), when the *kha* suffix is sometimes absent, one says: "He gives birth every year" (*samāyāṃ samāyaṃ vijāyate*).
The meaning is that, in the state of a sentence (*vākyadaśā*), the elision of the letter *y* (*yalopa*) should be stated as optional for the two locative endings.

In that regard, the elision of *y* is established in both words by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*) alone, because they are pronounced in that manner in both instances within the sūtra. However, the optionality of the elision of *y* in the state of a sentence is based on a specific rule (*vācanika*).
Thus it should be understood; all of this is clear in the Bhāṣya.
(1790) *adyaśvīnāvaṣṭabdhe* |5|2|13|. [The sūtra reads:
*adyaśvīnāvaṣṭabdhe*. The form *adyaśvīna* is an indeclinable citation (*avibhakta-nirdeśaḥ*).

*avaṣṭabdha* means "near. This is because the rule *sthā-ācca ālambana-avidūryayoḥ* prescribes the substitution of *ṣa* for *sta* when the sense of proximity (*āvidūrya*) is intended. The meaning is that the suffix *kha* (which becomes *īna*) may be applied after the compound *adya-śvas* when the sense of "to be born today or tomorrow" is expressed, provided that proximity is understood; for example, *adyaśvīnā vaḍavā* ("a mare due to foal today or tomorrow"). Today... [text ends].

The compound is formed by the inclusion of *vā* in the sense of "or," as it is a nipāta (an irregularly formed word). When *kha* follows, there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix by the rule "of indeclinables, when a *bha*-suffix follows. If the sūtra had given the form *adyaśvīnā* with a feminine *ṭāp* ending—as in the example *adyaśvīnā go-samūhaḥ* or *adyaśvīnāṃ go-maṇḍalam*—then such forms would not be possible.

(1791) *Āgavīnaḥ* |5|2|14|. The term *āgavīnaḥ* [is formed]. Regarding the word *karmakare* ("a laborer"): this is obtainable from a Vārttika. A *karmakara* is one who performs work after having received wages; here, the cowherd (*gopāla*) is intended. For he [drives] the cow in the morning...
Having taken [the cow] and grazed it until evening, he leads it to his own house and returns it.

Thus it is said: "the returning of the cow. Regarding the term *āgavīna*: the word *go* is used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean the returning of the cow. In the compound *āṅ*, the prefix *āṅ* is an indeclinable (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) or inclusion (*abhividhi*).

In the case of *go-striyaḥ*, there is shortening by the rule *go-striyoḥ* [6.1.103]; in the case of *āgu-śabdāt-khe*, the substitution of *guṇa* occurs by the rule *orguṇaḥ* [6.4.146]. (1792) *anugvalaṅgāmī* [5.2.15]:
*anugvalaṅgāmī*. The term *anugu* is cited without a case ending; it means "behind the cow" (*goḥ paścāt*).

In the compound *anugu*, the indeclinable *anu* is used in the sense of "behind" (*paścāt*) within an *avyayībhāva* compound, and its vowel is shortened. The meaning is that the suffix *kha* (which becomes *īya*) occurs after this [term] in the sense of "one who goes along with" (*alaṅgāmī*). Regarding this, Haradatta maintains that because the word "along with" (*anugu*) functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the second case alone is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*).

Others say that this is the genitive case used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix. In the example "alaṅgāmī" (one who goes sufficiently), the word "alam" is explained as "paryāptam" (sufficient). It is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
(1793) Pāṇini 5.2.16: *adhvano yat-khau*. [This sūtra prescribes the suffixes] *yat* and *kha* after the word *adhvan* [in the sense of "fit for"].

The meaning is that the suffixes *yat* and *kha* occur after the word *adhvan* in the sense of "one who goes. Thus, [the forms] *adhvanyaḥ* and *adhvakhah* mean "one who goes the way. However, when the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who goes sufficiently" (*alaṃ gāmī*), the analysis for the word *adhvanaḥ* is simply *adhvano 'laṃgāmī*.

(1794) *abhyamitrāc cha ca* | 5|2|17 | [The suffix] *cha* also [is applied] after *abhyamitra*. *Amitra* means an enemy (*śatru*). The word *abhyamitra* is an avyayībhāva compound formed according to the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye*, meaning "having become facing toward him" (*tam abhimukho bhūtvā*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the suffix *cha* should be applied in the sense of "one who goes to.
(1795) *goṣṭhāt khañ bhūtapūrve* | 5.2.18 | From *goṣṭha*, the suffix *khañ* [is applied]; "having been previously" (*bhūtapūrva*) is a qualifier of the base word (*prakṛti*).
According to the author of the *Vṛtti*, the suffix *kha* occurs in its own sense after the word *goṣṭha* when it refers to something that existed in the past.

(1796) *aśvasyaikāhagamaḥ* | 5.2.19 | "The distance traveled by a horse in one day. [This means] the suffix *kha* occurs after the word *aśva* ending in the genitive case in the sense of "that which is traversed in one day."
The meaning is "he would go. He derives the word *ekāhagama*—namely, [the compound] *ekāhena*.

The intention is that by this very irregular formation (*nipātana*), the suffix *avi* is applied to the root *gam* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The compound is formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. The genitive case in *aśvasya* expresses the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, *āśvīna-adhvā* means "a path [traversed] by horse. By means of the horse...

The meaning is that it can be traveled by the agent in a single day. (1797) *Śālīna* and *kaupīna* [are used] in the senses of "timid" and "improper act," respectively. Regarding *śālīna*: [the derivation is] "one who deserves entry into a house (*śāla*) because he is timid."

The suffix *khañ* is applied after the words *śālā-praveśa* and *kūpāvataraṇa* in the sense of "that which ought not to be done," namely, "entering a house" and "descending into a well. When the final members of these compounds, *praveśa* and *avataraṇa*, are elided, the resulting forms are *śālīna* and *raupīṇa*.
"They are treated as nipātanas," so says the Bhāṣya. "Adhṛṣṭa" means one who is not bold.
That is to say, one who, due to a lack of boldness, is unable to go elsewhere and deserves only entry into a house (śālā) is called *śālīna*.
"Falling into a well" is an explanation of the term "descending into a well."

The word *kūpa* denotes hell; thus, *kaupīna* means "sin. The meaning is that sin is an improper act which is the means for falling into hell. These two meanings are conventional (*rūḍha*) for these two words.
[Objection: But then, the word *kaupīna* applied to the male organ would be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

"Because of its connection with that": the meaning is that the word *kaupīna* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for the male organ of a person, either because it is a means of committing sin, or because it must be covered like a sin. "Because of its connection with that":
[it refers] to the piece of cloth that covers the male organ, due to its connection with that male organ which is the referent (*lakṣya*) of the word *kaupīna*.
The meaning is that the word *kaupīna* is employed by means of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on a secondary characteristic).
(1798) *vrātena jīvati* |5|2|21|. The meaning is that the suffix *khañ* is applied after the word *vrāta* ending in the third case, in the sense of "one who lives by means of that."

A *vrāta* is a group (*saṅgha*) of people of various castes who subsist by performing arduous labor, such as carrying burdens, and who have not obtained the means for their livelihood. Regarding this, the commentary states that the term *vrāta* here refers to the arduous labor performed for the sake of their livelihood. From the word *vrāta*, which denotes such a group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to this").
His intention is that the word *vrāta* here is intended to refer to their specific activity;
thus he says: "by means of bodily exertion.
(1799) *Sāptapadīnaṃ sakhyam* | 5|2|22 | [Friendship is established by walking seven steps.]

*Sāptapadīnam*: The meaning is that from the word *saptapada*, ending in the third case, the suffix *khañ* is applied in the sense of "friendship obtained," resulting in the form *sāptapadīnam*. "By seven steps" means by seven strides.

(1800) *haiyaṅgavīnaṃ saṃjñāyām* |5|2|23|. *Haiyaṅgavīnam*. The indeclinable *hyas* means "on the previous day. The milking of cows (*godoha*) that occurs at that time is *hya-egodohaḥ*. From this word ending in the genitive case, the suffix *khañ* is applied in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*). [The resulting form is *haiyaṅgavīna*, meaning fresh butter].

When the substitution of *īn* occurs, followed by the substitution of *hyaṅgu* for the base, the *guṇa* of *o*, the substitution of *ava*, and the initial *vṛddhi*, the form *haiyaṅgavīna* arises; this is stated in the Bhāṣya regarding the technical name (*saṃjñā*).
He says this with the words "of the milk of a cow," etc. [The result is] *navanīta*. However, in the Bhāṣya...

The expression "haiyaṅgavīnaṃ ghṛtam" (freshly made butter) is seen. Regarding this, Amara states: "tattu haiyaṅgavīnaṃ syād hyaegodohodbhavaṃ ghṛtam" (that is called *haiyaṅgavīna*, which is butter produced from the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time yesterday).

[Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.24: "tasya pākamūle pīlvādikarṇādibhyaḥ kuṇabjāhacau" (the suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are applied after words such as *pīlu* and *karṇa* when they denote the cooking or the root of that thing).
In the phrase *tasya pākamūle*, the locative case is used from the compound *pākamūle*, which is a collective dvandva (samāhāra-dvandva).
*Pāka* means "ripening" or "transformation. The suffix *kuṇap* is applied after words such as *pīlu* when they end in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-anta*) in the sense of "ripening" (*pāke*).
However, after words such as *karṇa*, the suffix *jāhac* is applied in the sense of "root" (*mūle*). Because *kuṇapa* is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the letter *k* [is elided].
The designation *it* applies to the letter *n*. However, in the case of *jāhac*, the letter *j* lacks a purpose and therefore does not receive the designation *it*.
(Pāṇini 5.2.25) *pakṣātiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "only the mention of the root": in the preceding sūtra, [the term] *pākamūla* [is used].
The meaning is that even though it is taught as a compound, the *svarita* accent is prescribed for the first member (*ekadeśa*).

The word "of that" (*tasya*) also carries over [from the previous rule]. The sense is that the suffix *tip* occurs after the word *pakṣa* when it ends in the genitive case, in the sense of "rooted in" (*mūla*).

(1803) *tena vittaścuñcupcaṇapau* |5|2|26|. "By that, *vitta*: the meaning is that after a word ending in the third case, the suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* occur in the sense of 'famous by means of that' (*vitta*). "Famous" (*vitta*) means well-known. Regarding the letter *c*, there is no designation as *it*; the intention is that this is because [the *c*] is not at the beginning of an original instruction (*upadeśa*).

(1804) *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau na-saha* 5.2.27. From the prefixes *vi-* and *nañ*, the suffixes *nān* and *āñ* [respectively] are applied when used with the compound *na-saha*, which signifies "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*).

This is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). Thus he says: "in the sense of non-accompaniment" (*asahārthe*). Its explanation is: "in the sense of separation" (*pṛthagbhāve*). After the words "from those ending in *vartamāna*," the phrase "from *vi* and *nañ*" (*vinañbhyām*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the term "its own meaning" (*svārthe*): this is because no specific meaning for the suffix has been specified.

The state [of being]. Regarding "the two suffixes": the remainder is that they correspond respectively to *na* and *añ*. Regarding *vinā*: this is the form derived from the root *vi-* with the suffix *nā*. It means "separately. Regarding *nānā*: this is the form derived from *na-* with the suffix *añ*, with the initial vowel lengthened (*vṛddhi*). It means "separately. However, if the meaning of the suffix in the word *nasaha* were [to be taken as] the primary sense...
By the word "not" (na), it would be understood as "not together. This being the case, the meaning would be "it is not that they are not together,
but rather they are indeed together," according to the maxim "two negatives convey the original sense," as is clear in the Bhāṣya.
(1805) *veḥ* [the suffixes] *nānā* and *añ* [are added] after *vi-* and *nañ*, but not with *sa-* || 5.2.27 || *Veḥ śāla-chaṅkaṭac-au*. Regarding the phrase "kriyāviśiṣṭa":
the suffixes *śālac* and *chaṅkaṭac* are added in their own sense (*svārthe*) after a word denoting a kāraka qualified by an action.
...up to this point. And this is explained clearly in the Bhāṣya:
(1806) *saṃprodaścakaṭac* 5.2.29. [The suffix] *kaṭac* is added after *sam*, *pra*, and *ut*, when these denote an instrument qualified by an action.

The meaning is that the suffix *kaṭac* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). And [it applies] even after *cāvi*. *Saṃkaṭam*—the meaning is "congested" (*saṃhatam*), that is to say, "made dense. These are conventional words (*rūḍhaśabda*) that must be derived in some way or another.
(1) An addition (*upasaṅkhyānam*) should be made for the dust arising from *alābu*, *tila*, *umā*, and *bhaṅga*.

Regarding the phrase *alābūtileti*: the meaning is that from the words *alābū*, *tila*, *umā*, and *bhaṅgā*—which end in the sixth case (genitive) and denote substances belonging to the group beginning with *rajas*—the suffixes *goṣṭhaja* and so forth are to be stated in the senses of "place" (*sthāna*) and the rest. [The following explains] the suffixes *goṣṭhaja* and so forth, and the senses of "place" and so forth.
There are six *vārttikas*, beginning with "saṅghāte kaṭac" and ending with "śākaṭaśākinau," which are devoted to the elaboration of meanings. Among those four [rules],
the term "paśunāmabhyaḥ" (from animal names) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*).
The suffix *kaṭac* occurs after the word *saṅghāta* in the sense of a collection whose constituent parts are not spread out; *saṅghāta* means a mass.
The suffix *paṭac* occurs in the sense of expansion.

*Vistāra* (extension), however, consists of extended parts. Regarding the term *dvitve*: it means when there is duality residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). An example is *vṛṣagoyugam* (a pair of bulls).

The singular number is intended to denote a collection consisting of two members, just as in the case of words such as *dvaya* (a pair) or *yugma* (a couple). Some, however, say that the singular number occurs by its own nature (*svabhāvāt*) in the sense of "two bulls," as in the expression *vṛṣagoyuga*, just as in the case of "twenty" (*viṃśati*) and so forth. The same applies to *uṣṭragoyuga*.

*aśvaṣaṅgavam* | (1807) *avātkuṭārācca* | 5|2|30 | From *ava*, and from *kuṭāra*. The suffix *kuṭārac* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) after *ava* when it denotes a means (*sādhana*) qualified by an action (*kriyā*). *kuṭāra*.
The meaning is "it might be. Regarding the term *avācīna*: from the word *avāk* existing [as a base], the suffix *kuṭārac* is applied, resulting in the sense of *avakuṭāra*.
(1808) Pāṇini 5.2.31: "In the sense of 'bent,' when referring to the nose and as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the suffixes *ṭīṭan*, *ṭañ*, *nāṭac*, and *bhraṭac* are applied."

Regarding "nate nāsikāyāḥ" (when the nose is bent): "ava-ādi eva" means that after the word *ava*, in the sense of the nose being bent (*avanate'rthe*), the suffixes *ṭīṭac*, *nāṭac*, and *bhraṭac* may occur. Intending to show that the word *nata* is derived from the root *ṇamu* (meaning "to bend") with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an action (*bhāve*), he says: "nataṃ namanam" (bent means bending).

The meaning is "the state of being bent. Now, one might ask: if the bending of the nose is *avaṭīṭa*, then how can it be said that "the nose is *avaṭīṭa*"? To this he says: "due to connection with that" (*tadyogāt*).
The sense is that the term is used figuratively there because of its connection with the act of bending. Thus, even a person may be called *avaṭīṭa*.
The sense is: "due to being joined with such a nose.

(1809) *nerbiḍajvirīsacau* |5|2|32|. Regarding *nerbiḍajvirīsacau*: the phrase "in the sense of a name for a bent nose" (*nate nāsikāyāḥ saṃjñāyām*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
The meaning is that when the sense of "bent toward the nose" (*neḥ-nāsikāyā nate'rthe*) is intended, two suffixes, *biḍac* and *virīsac*, occur.

However, they say that the expression "dense trees" (*nibiḍā vṛkṣāḥ*) is due to its being a comparison (*upamānāt*). (1810) *inac-piṭac-cikac-i-ca* | 5.2.33 | [The suffixes] *inac*, *piṭac*, *cikac*, and *i* [occur after the word *ni* in the sense of bending toward the nose].

*inac-piṭac*: this is the nominative singular from the collective dvandva compound *inac-piṭac*. *ṭhcikaci*: this is also the nominative singular from the collective dvandva compound *ṭhicika-ci*. Regarding "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*): the meaning is "after *ni*. In that context, when *ina* or *ac* follows, *cika* is the substitute. In that case...
The letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. When *piṭac* follows, there is the substitution of *cī*. (|) It should also be stated that there is the suffix *ka* and the substitution of *cik*.
Regarding "the suffix *ka*": the meaning is that the suffix *ka* is applied after the aforementioned verbal root (*ni*), and the substitution of *cik* occurs for the base (*prakṛti*). This also...

The substitute is indeed that which ends in the letter *ka*. Regarding *cikinam*: when the suffix *in* is applied after a vowel, the form results from the substitution of *cik* for *ni*. Regarding *cipiṭam*: when the suffix *piṭac* is applied, the form results from the substitution of *ci* for *ni*. Regarding *cikkam*: when the suffix *kap* is applied, the form results from the substitution of *cik* for *ni*.
"His eyes are *cil-pil-la* when he is moistened;
his eyes are *cil-pil-la* when he is moistened. This is a *vārttika*.
[The form] *cil-pil-i* is the nominative singular from a collective *dvandva* compound. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "his eyes are moistened," [the form is derived as follows].

The suffix *la* is applied after the word *klinna* in the sense of "his eyes"; the meaning is that the base (*prakṛti*) undergoes the substitutions *cila* and *pila*. Thus, *klinne* means "possessing a flow of water caused by the application of collyrium to the eyes. *Cilla* and *pilla* [are derived in this manner].

The meaning is "one whose eyes are moist. Regarding *culca*: the meaning is that in the aforementioned context, the substitution of *cul* for *klinna* must be stated as occurring in conjunction with the suffix *lap*. Regarding *upādhibhyām*: from the two prefixes *upa* and *adhi*, which respectively signify "near" and "mounted upon," the suffix *tyakan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

The meaning is "it may be. "Near" (āsannam) means in the vicinity; "ascended" (ārūḍham) means high. Regarding the phrase "it follows" (anuvartate), the intention is that this is derived from the rule *nate nāsikāyāḥ*. When there is an expectancy as to whose vicinity or whose height [is meant], it is understood from the governing context (*saṃjñādhikāra*) that it refers to the mountain.

Intending this, he says: "of the mountain" (*parvatasya*). [The suffixes] *upatyakā* and *adhityakā* [are formed with the suffix *tyakan*]. Their feminine gender is established by common usage. Here, the substitution of *ī* [for *a*] by the rule *pratyayasthāt* does not apply, because of the specific statement *tyakanaśca*. (Pāṇini 5.2.35) *karmaṇi ghaṭo'ṭhac*: [The suffix *aṭhac* is applied after the root *ghaṭ* when an object is expressed.]

Regarding the suffix *aṭhac* after the word *karman*: the meaning is that the suffix *aṭhac* occurs after the word *karman* ending in the locative case (*saptamī*) when the sense is "that which accomplishes" (*ghaṭa*). He dispels the misconception that the word *ghaṭa* is synonymous with *kalaśa* (pot) by stating: "it accomplishes (*ghaṭate*) in the action. The meaning is "it is occupied with" (*vyāpriyate*). And thus, in this context—
The meaning is that the word *ghaṭa* is etymological (*yaugika*), as it occurs in the sense of "that which is being fashioned" (*ghaṭamāna*). Regarding *karmaṭha*:

when the suffix *aṭhac* is applied, there is elision of the final *ṭi* (the *a*) by the rule *ṭhnastaddhite*. The point is that because the *ṭha* of *aṭhac* does not follow the *aṅga* (the base), the substitution of *ik* (for the final vowel) does not occur.

(1812) *tadasya saṃjātaṃ tārakādibhya itac* | Pāṇini 5.2.36. The meaning of *tadasya* is as follows: the suffix *itac* occurs after words beginning with *tāraka* when they stand in the nominative case, in the sense that "this has arisen in him/her/it. For example, *tārakitaṃ nabhaḥ* ("the sky is starred"); the meaning is "the sky in which stars have appeared."

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words); by this, forms such as *puṣpito vṛkṣaḥ* ("a tree in flower") and *phalitaḥ* ("bearing fruit") are included. (1813) *pramāṇe dvayasaj-daghnañ-mātracaḥ* | Pāṇini 5.2.37. [The suffixes] *dvayasaC*, *daghnac*, and *mātrac* are added [to a word denoting a measure] when the sense is that of measurement.

Regarding the word *pramāṇe*: it is said that [the suffixes] "follow" (*anuvartate*). Consequently, in the sense of "this object of cognition (*prameya*) has that as its measure (*tat-pramāṇam*)," the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, and *mātraC* are applied after a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntāt*) which denotes a measure (*pramāṇe*). It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the meaning of the suffix here is "that which possesses this as its measure" (*pramāṇavān idamarthaḥ*). In that context:
"The first and the second are considered by me as measures of height," so it is stated in the Bhāṣya.

Here, *pramāṇa* means merely that which delimits; the suffix *mātraC* is used in that sense, as in examples such as *prasthamātra* (measuring a *prastha*) and *ūrumātra* (measuring the thigh), according to Kaiyaṭa. However, in reality, [the rule] is *yatadetebhyaḥ*.
Thus, according to the natural sense of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, the authority here is precisely that which delimits the extent [of the rule];
this is the detailed explanation in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
(1) *Laḥ* [is used] in the sense of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding "pramāṇe la": *luk* is a technical term established by the treatises of the ancient masters according to the rule "*ṭhloḥ*. The meaning is that the elision (*luk*) of suffixes such as *dvayasaC* and others, which are prescribed after a word denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*), should be stated. Examples are *śamaḥ*, *diṣṭiḥ*, and *vitastiḥ*. The analysis of these compounds is *rāmaḥ pramāṇam asya* ("Rāma is its measure"), and so forth.

The terms beginning with *śama* (such as *śama*, *sama*, and *viṣama*) are not specific types of height; therefore, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mātrac* occurs after them, because [the other two suffixes] are impossible in their case. Here, it is understood that "the suffix *ṭhañ* (which becomes *īya*) shall be the measure. And thus, in examples such as *ūrudvayasam*, there is no elision.
(1) *Dvigor nityam* ("Always after a *dvigu* [compound]").

This means that after a *dvigu* compound ending in a word denoting measure (*pramāṇa*), there is always elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *dvayasaC*, etc., that follow it. [This applies] to a *dvigu* compound ending in a word denoting measure.

Because it is a measure (*pramāṇa*), by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), the rule for elision of the final member (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies here. However, according to the preceding Vārttika, there is no application [of the elision] here, because a *dvigu* compound does not possess the status of being a measure. [The example is] *dviśamam*.
Here, the *dvigu* compound is formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Then, by this [rule], there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mātrac*.

Since the possibility of *vikalpa* (optionality) is already established by the fact that it was not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛtatvāt*), the inclusion of the word "nitya" (always) is for the purpose of causing the elision (*lup*) of the suffix *mātrac* in cases where doubt arises, as will be explained later. Otherwise, as in the case of *śamamātram*, the suffix *mātrac* would not be elided even after the word *dviśama*; this is clear from the Bhāṣya.
The suffix *mātraC* should be prescribed after words expressing measure (*pramāṇa*), weight (*parimāṇa*), and number (*saṃkhyā*) when there is uncertainty [regarding them].

"Measure" (*pramāṇa*) means that the suffix *mātraC* should be stated after words denoting measure, words denoting weight, and words denoting number when there is doubt. Here, "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is taken to mean length (*āyāma*) alone; as for length...
Because of the statement, "it would be a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaṃ syāt*). For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *parimāṇa* (measure/extent) is purposeful.
Regarding the phrase "mere tranquility" (*śamamātra*) and so forth: the analysis of the compound is "would there be tranquility, or not? and so on.
After a word ending in a *vat* suffix, the suffixes *dvayasaC* and *mātrac* are applied diversely (*bahulam*) in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

"From words ending in *vat*" (*vatvantāt*). This is a Vārttika. [The rule] "from *puruṣa* and *hastin*, also *aṇ*" (*puruṣahastibhyāmaṇ ca*)—the phrase "in the scope already mentioned" (*ukta-viṣaye*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Because of the word "also" (*ca*), the three suffixes beginning with *dvayasaC* are also included. (1814) *puruṣahastibhyāmaṇ ca* | 5.2.38.

The suffix *aṇ* is also applied after the words *puruṣa* and *hastin*; the phrase "in the aforementioned scope" is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Because of the word *ca* ("and"), the three suffixes beginning with *dvayasaC* are also included.
(1815) The suffix *vatup* is applied after the pronouns *yad*, *etad*, and *tad* when expressing measure (*parimāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase *yat-eta-ebhyaḥ*: the term *tad-asya* ("that of this") is understood to follow. The meaning is that the suffix *vatup* occurs after the words *kim*, *yad*, *tad*, and *etad*, provided they are in the nominative case and denote a measure (*parimāṇa*), in the sense of "that which has such a measure. Thus, for example, *yāvān* ("as much as"): from the word *yad*, the suffix *vatup* is added; *u* and *ā* are elided; and *ṭi* [is replaced by *ān*].
The substitution of *āt* [for the final vowel] occurs by the rule "sarvanāmnaḥ"; then *su* [is added]; *num* is inserted by "ṭhugidacām"; the lengthening occurs by "atvasantasya";

and the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*ṅy-ādi*) occurs by the rules for the elision of a *saṃyoga*. Thus: *tāvān*, *etāvān*. (1816) *kimidaṃbhyāṃ vo ghaḥ* |5|2|40|. [This sūtra prescribes that] after the words *kim* and *idam*, the suffix *vatup* is replaced by *gha*.
Regarding the rule *kim-idaṃbhyāṃ vo ghaḥ*: the words *tad asya* and *parimāṇe vatuḥ* are understood to carry over [from previous rules].

Thus he says: "From these two, *vatup* shall occur. This means that from these two [stems] ending in the nominative case, *vatup* shall occur in the sense of "that is its measure" (*tat-parimāṇam*). And regarding "gha for *va*": this refers to the substitution of *gha* for the letter *v*.

The meaning is "the letter *gha*. Regarding the question "how much" (*kiyān*): the analysis of the compound is "what is its measure? (*kiṃ parimāṇam asya*). From the word *kim*, the suffix *vatup* is added. The *u* and *p* are elided. The *va* is replaced by *gha*. The substitution of *iy* occurs.
When *kim* and *iyat* stand thus, by the rule "for *kim* and *idam*, there is *īś* and *kī*" (*ṭhidaṅkimorīśkī*), *kim* becomes *kī*. Then, by the rule "of that which... (*yasyeti*).
The meaning is as follows: after the elision of the vowel *ī* in *cet*, from the word *kiyac* followed by the nominative suffix *su*, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ṭhugidacām*;

then, by the rule *atvasantasya*, the vowel is lengthened; finally, the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the elision of the *saṃyogānta* (consonant cluster ending in a suffix) apply, resulting in [the form] *kiyat*.
Regarding *iyān*: from the word *idam* with the suffix *vatup*, the *v* is replaced by *gh*, and *idam* undergoes the substitution *iya*; thus, *idam* becomes *iyat*.

This being the case, by the rule *ṭhidaṅkimorīśkī*, because the suffix *śi* is marked with the letter *ś*, the word *idam* is replaced entirely by the vowel *ī*; then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the *ī* is elided, leaving only the suffix *iyat*.
Thereafter, the addition of *num* and so forth occurs as before when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*.

(1817) *kimaḥ saṅkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca* | 5|2|41 | The word *kimaḥ* [is the subject]; *saṅkhyā* [is the object]; *tadasya* is understood from the previous rule. *Saṅkhyāyāḥ parimāṇam* means the measurement or determination of a number. The word *kim* is used in the sense of a question. [The construction is: "What is its number? (*kā asya saṅkhyā*). Thus...

The meaning is that when there is a question concerning the object of delimitation by number, the suffix *ḍati* shall also be applied after the interrogative pronoun *kim* ending in the nominative case, in the sense of "of this" (*asya*).

Thus, one asks: "What is the number of this? (*katīti*)—that is, "What is the number of this? and "What is the number of these two? (*kā saṅkhyā anayoḥ*). It is not [the case that] such a question is not [permissible].

This is because singularity is known by the word "of this" (*asya*) and duality is known by the word "of these two" (*anayoḥ*), and a question is impossible regarding what is already known. However, the question "What is the number of these?
is possible; for although plurality is known by the word "of these" (*eṣām*) therein, [the specific number remains unknown].
This is because the numbers three, four, and so forth, which are pervaded by that [category], are not known [in this context]. And it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"There is no question regarding two or one. Consequently, this word *kati* is always plural; for, by the rule *ḍati ca*, it is designated as a *ṣaṭ* (a word ending in a ṣaṭ-pratyaya).

By the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *jaś* and *śas*. Thus, the analytical derivation (*prakriyā*) for *kiyantaḥ* is like that of *kiyān*. There is a distinction in the plural number. Because of the statement "when [the word] expresses a numerical measure" (*saṅkhyāparimāṇe*), the suffix *ḍati* does not occur when *kim* has the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). What is the number of these?

Regarding the phrase "of ten": this statement was made in reference to the gathering of those who merely claim to be Brahmins, as in the rule, "an assembly of at least ten. Here, the contempt for the number is understood through the objects being counted:
"Of those who are without vows, without sacred vessels, living by their birth alone, even if they have assembled by the thousands..."
For it is stated in the Smṛti: "The state of being an assembly does not exist.
(1818) *saṅkhyāyā avayave tayap* |5|2|42|. [The word] *saṅkhyāyāḥ* [is used]; *tad asya* is understood to follow. Parts numbering two, three, and so forth...

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *asyāvayavinaḥ*, the word *taya* has the meaning "of this whole" (*asyāvayavinaḥ*), derived from a first-case-ending term denoting a number that constitutes a part. Thus, *pañcatayam* means a collection consisting of five parts.

(1819) *dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyajvā* | 5|2|43|. The meaning is that after the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *tayap* shall optionally take the substitute *ayac*. Thus, from the word *dvi*, the suffix *tayap* takes *ayac*; then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. Hence, *dvaya*.
The meaning is "a collection consisting of two members. Likewise for the triad.
(1820) *ubhādudāto nityam* | 5|2|44|. Regarding *ubhādudāto nityam*: "and that [suffix] is udātta," meaning it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.

It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the status of having an udātta vowel within [the word] is established by the fact of its being a *cit* suffix. Here, only the *ṭhañ* suffix is prescribed, and not a substitute for *tayap*;
this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the *sthānivadbhāva* sūtra. As for the statement in the root-text (mūla) that it is "a substitute for *tayap*,"...
In accordance with the Vārttika. Thus ends the section on the fifth case (pañcamī) in the Bālamanoramā.
Now begins the section on the *parasmaipada* (active voice).
He proceeds to define the rules governing the *parasmaipada*: "From the remainder, [the *parasmaipada* suffixes are used] in the sense of the agent" (*śeṣāt kartari*).
(569) "After the roots *anu* and *parā*, [the *parasmaipada* suffixes are used] after the root *kṛ*. (Pāṇini 1.3.79)

[The rule] "after the prefixes *anu* and *parā*, [the suffixes] following the root *kṛ* [are used]. The remainder [of the sūtra], "the *parasmaipada*," is understood. Now, one might object: since the *ātmanepada* is prescribed by the rule "after a root marked with a svarita or a ñit" only when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, and since the *parasmaipada* is already established for cases where the fruit does not accrue to the agent by the rule "the remaining [roots take the *parasmaipada*] in the active voice" (*śeṣātkartari*), what is the purpose of this [present rule]? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "even when [the result] resides in the agent": "in the sense of threatening and so forth" means in the senses of threatening (*gandhana*), throwing down (*avakṣepaṇa*), serving (*sevana*), violence (*sāhasikya*), preparation (*pratiyatna*), describing (*prakathana*), and employment (*upayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "let it not be": this refers to the case where the *lakāra* suffix occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), even though [the result] resides in the agent.

The intention is that the term "kartari" (in the active voice) is carried over [from the previous rule] for the purpose of excluding the other [parasmaipada] endings in the case of the fruit [of the action]. Now, one might object:

even if "kartari" is carried over, in the example "śabdaḥ svayamevānukriyate" (the word is itself repeated), the parasmaipada would be unavoidable in the case of a reflexive object-agent (karmakartṛ); anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with "na ca" (and not).

The meaning is that even if "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) is thus understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*), one should not suspect the possibility of the *ātmanepada* ending occurring in the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Why? To this he says: "Because of the extension of the operation" (*kāryātideśa*).

In that regard, for a reflexive object-agent, the subsequent rule "that which has an action equal to [the action] of the object is like the object" (*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*) supersedes this [present rule].
The syntactical connection is that [the Parasmaipada] is set aside.

Now, that rule concerning the object which is extended to the reflexive object by the rule "karmavat karmaṇā," and thus, in this case of a reflexive object, the rule for Ātmanepada—"bhāvakarmaṇoḥ"—is applicable here. And of that...
Since there is an absence of *paratva* (remoteness), how could there be a sublation by the rule "ṭhanuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ"?

To this he says: "Because the position of the transfer of operation (*kāryātideśa*) is primary. Since the transfer of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*) exists for the sake of the transfer of the operation, the transfer of the operation is primary. Consequently, [the rule] "like the object" (*karmavat*).
By the rule *karmaṇi*, the ātmanepada prescribed for the object is ordained for the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).

The sense is that, because it is subsequent, this ātmanepada ought to supersede the parasmaipada *anuparābhyām tam* (Pāṇini 1.3.78) in the case of the object-agent. This is stated in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*.
Accepting the position that there is an extension of the rule from the *śāstra*, he says: "But in the case of the extension of the rule from the *śāstra*...

In the rule *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*, one instance of the term *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) is understood to carry over from the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*. Likewise, [the term *kartari*] from the rule *śeṣātkartari...* [is also understood].

The second mention of the term "kartṛ" (agent) from the rule *parasmaipadam* continues [into this sūtra]. Thus, it is understood that the *parasmaipada* endings are used after the root *kṛ* with the prefixes *anu* and *parā* only when the agent is one who is an agent by his very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), and not an agent by virtue of being intended as such (*vivakṣādhīnaḥ*)—that is, not a *karmakartṛ* (an object-agent). In this way...
And the meaning is that its application does not occur when [the agent] is both the object and the agent (*karmakartṛ*).
(570) *abhi-prati-ati-bhyaḥ kṣipaḥ* |1|3|80|.
[The words] *abhi*, *prati*, and *ati*—the remainder is "the *parasmaipada* [terminations]. Because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, therefore...

The sense is that although the *ātmanepada* would have been required when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, by this [rule], the *parasmaipada* is used even in that case. One should provide examples such as *abhikṣipati*, *pratikṣipati*, and *atikṣipati*. (571) *prād vahaḥ* | 1.3.81 | [This sūtra prescribes the *parasmaipada* after the root √vah preceded by the prefix *pra*.]
*Pradvahaḥ*: the meaning is that the *parasmaipada* ending is used after the root *vah* preceded by *pra*.
Since *vah* is marked with the *svarita* accent, the *ātmanepada* would have been expected when the action benefits the agent; however, by this rule, the *parasmaipada* is applied even in that case.

[The word] *paremṛṣaḥ* [is explained as follows]: the term *parasmaipada* is understood as the remainder [of the sūtra]. Since the root *mṛṣ* belonging to the *divādigaṇa*—as indicated by the rule *mṛṣa titikṣāyām*—is marked with the *svarita* accent, it would otherwise be applicable in both voices; therefore, this rule is stated.

Regarding this, he says: "he touches" (*parimṛṣati*). Even for the root belonging to the *cur*-class (*caurādika*), although it is marked with the *svarita* accent and thus lacks the causative suffix (*ṇic*) by the rule "from *ā-dhṛṣ* onwards," it takes only the parasmaipada ending—as in *parimarṣati*. But as for the root belonging to the *bhū*-class (*bhauvādika*), namely *mṛṣu* in the sense of "endurance" and "moistening": [it is different].

Because it is *parasmaipada*, the form *parimarṣati* alone is established; therefore, the intention is that it is not included in this rule (*amin*). Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): the rule *pareḥ* is divided [into a separate yoga]. The term *vahaḥ* is understood from the previous context. The meaning is: after the prefix *pari*, the verb *vah* takes the *parasmaipada*. Example: *parivahati*. Regarding the root *mṛṣ*.

Another rule (*yogāntara*). Here, the word *pareḥ* is understood to carry over; the meaning is that some say this is the sense expressed by the statement "after the root *mṛṣ*, the third person plural ending is used. However, this division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) is not seen in the Bhāṣya.
(573) *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.3.83.
After the prefixes *vi*, *āṅ*, and *pari*, the root *ram* [takes the *ātmanepada* endings]. The term "*parasmaipada*" is understood as the remainder [of the rule].
This is a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) because the root *ram* is *anudātta*. Examples include *viramati*, as well as *āramati* and *pariramati*, which should also be cited. (574) *Upācca* 1.3.84.

"And after *upa*": the meaning is that even after *upa* preceding it, the root *ram* takes the *parasmaipada* (active voice). In the subsequent sūtra, it was not stated as "after *vi*, *āṅ*, *pari*, and *upa*, [the root] *ram*" precisely so that only the word *upa* might be carried over (*anuvṛtti*).
Here, for the sense of "ceasing," *uparamati* is not cited as an example, because that [usage] is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

Because the subsequent sūtra prescribes an option for the *parasmaipada* (active voice), he provides an example with an object: "He causes Yajñadatta to cease" (*yajñadattam uparamati*). Now, one might ask: since the root has the sense of "ceasing," how can it be transitive?
To this he says: "The meaning is 'he causes [him] to cease' (*uparamayati*). One might further ask: how is this meaning obtained in the absence of the causative suffix *ṇic*?
Therefore, he says: "This [root] has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it. The intention is that roots possess multiple meanings. (575) *Vibhāṣā akarmakāt* 1.3.86.
The rule *vibhāṣā'karmakāt* [Pāṇini 1.3.85] applies; the words *upāt*, *ramaḥ*, and *parasmaipadam* are understood from the preceding context. Thus he says: "from *upa* and *ram*" (*upādramer*).
(576) *budhayudhanaśajaneṅprudrusrubhyo ṇeḥ* | Pāṇini 1.3.86.

The compound *budhayudha* consists of the roots *budh*, *yudh*, *naś*, *jan*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *dru*, *sru*, and *eṣ*. [Example: "He awakens the lotus"—the word "the sun" (*sūrya*) is to be supplied as the subject. The root *budh* has the meaning of "blooming.
Thus, the lotus blooms; the meaning is that the sun causes it to bloom.

However, the *parasmaipada* ending [in *yodhayati*] is not established by the rule "after a root that does not have an object (*akarmaka*) and whose agent is like one who perceives (*citavat-kartṛka*"), because in the case of the non-causative (*aṇau*), the wood (*kāṣṭha*) is the agent, and thus it lacks an agent like one who perceives. [The example is] "he causes the pieces of wood to fight" (*yodhayati kāṣṭhāni*). The meaning is: "the pieces of wood fight by themselves; he causes them to fight."
Because the agent [of the causative] does not possess the same nature as the agent [of the simplex], the rule *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāc citavatkartṛkāt* does not apply here.

For this very reason, *yodhayati devadattam* is not cited as an example, since the desired form is already established by the rule *ṭhaṇāvakarmakāc citavatkartṛkāt* alone. The same should be understood for subsequent cases as well.
"He destroys suffering" means that suffering perishes; the meaning is that Hari destroys it. "He produces happiness" means that happiness arises; the meaning is that Hari produces it.
"He causes [one] to study" means that the ritual injunction (*vidhi*) studies the Veda; the meaning is that he causes that [injunction] to study. [The root] *ṭhpru* [is used] in the sense of motion.
He provides an illustration of this with the word *prāvayati*. Considering that [the root] has the sense of "going," he says:

"the meaning is 'he causes to reach' (*prāpayati*). Regarding *drāvayati*, the meaning is "clarified butter (*ājya*) flows; he causes that to flow. Considering that the verbal root has the sense of "becoming liquid," he says: "the meaning is 'he causes to liquefy' (*syāndayati*). [Regarding the root *prī*: "joy... ]

The use of the ātmanepada ending in "janayate" (he causes to be born) regarding "bhaktajanasya" (of the devotee) is merely a scribal error. Alternatively, the form may be derived from the causative (ṇic):
the devotee produces love for Hari toward himself, and Hari causes that [love] to be produced;
thus, by intending to express the agent who prompts the action (prayojyakartṛ) as a subordinate factor (śeṣatva), the genitive "bhaktajanasya" is used.
They say [the genitive] is the sixth case.
(577) *Nigaraṇa-calanārthebhyaś-ca* |1|3|87|. *Nigaraṇa*: swallowing, i.e., eating. *Calana*: moving, i.e., shaking. [The rule applies] to roots having these meanings.

The meaning is that the *parasmaipada* suffix is used after [roots] ending in the causative marker *ṇic*. However, the inclusion of *pru*, *dru*, and *sru* in the preceding sūtra refers only to their senses of "flowing" or "moving. For this very reason, it was explained in the root text as "he causes to reach" (*prāpayati*), and so forth.
Even the drinking [of nectar] by the tongue of the *cakora* bird is somehow [possible] through this moonlight from the moon of her face—this...

In the verse by Śrīharṣa, "kimācāmayase na cakṣuṣī ciraṃ cakorasya bhavanmukhaspṛśī," the word *ācāmaya* is a separate term. [The analysis is as follows: *aḥ* is Viṣṇu; his wife is *ī*, namely Lakṣmī. Together with her (*tābhyāṃ sahitā*), it is *se*; this is the vocative of the word *se*, which ends in the vowel *e*.
It is established in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* that the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) occurs by the rule "ṭeḥ hrasvāt"; however, in reality,
since it is impossible for the eyes to perform the act of sipping (*ācamana*) consisting of drinking the moonlight of the face, the term *ācāmi* is used here in the sense of respect (*ādara*).

Regarding *lākṣmika*: because it lacks the sense of "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending does not apply. Nor should it be suspected that, this being the case, since it lacks the sense of "eating" (*pratyavasāna*), the status of the object (*karmatva*) for the roots *cakṣ* and *śruṣ* under the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasāna...* would not obtain; for here the root *ā-ci* does not function in the sense of mere "respect" (*ādara*), but rather—

The term *ādara* (respect) occurs when preceded by *darśana* (seeing); that is to say, it is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the sense of "respectful cognition. Consequently, because the root *ācam* signifies cognition (*buddhi*), the status of the eyes as the object (*karman*) is unassailable; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdakaustubha*. [This refers to the rule] "there is a prohibition regarding the root *ad*" (*adeḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*).

The meaning is that a prohibition of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) must be stated for the root *ad*, which would otherwise have obtained [the *parasmaipada*] because its meaning is "swallowing. In the example "he causes Devadatta to eat" (*ādayate devadattena*), since the *parasmaipada* would have obtained for the root *ad* because its meaning is "consuming," he says: "In the case of swallowing and moving... (*nigaraṇacalaneti*).

The meaning of the particle *eva* is that this prohibition applies only to what is obtained by the rule "śeṣāt kartari" (Pāṇini 3.1.76), and not to anything else; this is because of the maxim "anantarasya" (the rule of proximity). (578) Pāṇini 1.3.88: *aṇāvakarmakāccittavatkartṛkāt*.

"From that which is non-causative (aṇau) and intransitive (akarmakāt). The phrase "from that which ends in ṇi" (ṇyantāt) is supplied as a supplement, because the term "ṇeḥ" is understood from the preceding context; this is the intended meaning. That is to say: from a root ending in ṇi which is intransitive when not causative (aṇau) and has a conscious agent (citavat-kartṛka), the parasmaipada suffixes occur after the ṇic. Why specify "having a conscious agent"? [Example: *vāsayati vāsaḥ* ("he causes the garment to dwell"). Here, although the root is intransitive when not causative, it does not take parasmaipada because its agent is not conscious.

"The rice grains dry up; he causes them to dry. Why say "from an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāt*)? [Objection: He makes a mat; he causes it to be made (*kaṭaṃ kārayati*). (579) Pāda, dami, āṅ-yama, āṅ-ya, sa-pari-muha, ruci, nṛti, vada, and vas do not [apply]. 1.3.89.

One should not bend one’s foot. [The rule states: *pā-dami-āṅ-yam-āṅ-ya-sa-parimuha-ruci-nṛti-vada-vas*, where the ablative case is used after a collective dvandva compound of these roots. Since what has been established must be prohibited, he demonstrates that establishment by stating: "the root *pā* (to drink) has the sense of swallowing. And therefore—
The sense is that there is the application [of the rule] "from roots meaning swallowing and moving" (*ṭh-nigaraṇa-calana-arthebhyaḥ*). Regarding *nṛti*:
*nṛti* means "moving. The meaning is that [the action] has an agent who possesses consciousness (*cetana*) when not preceded by a causative suffix (*aṇau*), and it is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

"By two sūtras" refers to both "from intransitive roots when not preceded by a causative suffix" (*aṇāvakarmakāt*) and "and from those meaning swallowing and moving" (*nigaraṇa-calana-arthebhyaś-ca*).
The meaning is "by means of two sūtras. Regarding *pāyayate*: by the rule *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yuṅ*, the affix *yuṅ* (which is the apavāda of *puṅ*) is applied. Regarding *damayate*:
by the rule *janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca*, there is shortening due to its being marked with *mit*. Now, [one might object] regarding the *divādi* [class]:...

It has been stated that *dam* is transitive (*sakarmaka*); therefore, one might ask how the application of the rule "after roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*)" is possible here. [The answer is: because of the very prohibition of *dam* in the parasmaipada, *dam* is also intransitive.
Thus, there is no contradiction with the statement that *dam* is transitive. [The example is: *āyāmayate*.

In the case of *ṭhyamo'pariveṣaṇe*, there is no shortening because the prohibition of the *mit* designation applies. Regarding *vāsayate*: here, only the root *vasa* belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa (meaning "to dwell") is intended to be included, and not even the root *vasa* belonging to the Adādigaṇa (meaning "to clothe"), because the latter—being transitive by its very nature—is already excluded from the scope of this rule.

And because it is stated that "between a root with a *luk*-vowel-change and one with an *aluk*-vowel-change, only the one with the *aluk*-vowel-change is to be understood," there is the supplementary rule:

"the addition of *dheṭ* [is required]. This refers to the prohibition of the *parasmaipada* endings. The mantra is: *dhāpayete śiśum*. Now, [one might object]: in cases such as *vatsān pāyayati payaḥ* ("she causes the calves to drink milk") and *damayantī*...

How can there be the pride of desirability [in the sense] "alms cause one to dwell," given that the Parasmaipada is prohibited by the rule *na pādamyaṅyam*? To this he says: "when not intended for the agent" (*akartrabhiprāye*).
By the maxim *anantarasya*, [the prohibition applies to] the rules *nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca* and *aṇāvakarmakāccit*.
The meaning is that the prohibition "na pādami-āṅ-yama-aṅ-yamase" applies specifically to that which has attained [the status of] two sūtras.
Although "vā kyaṣaḥ" and so forth have already been explained, they are presented again here according to the sequence of the sūtras.
This concludes the determination of the parasmaipada endings.
Now begins the section on technical definitions (paribhāṣā).

(35) *iko guṇavṛddhī* |1|1|3| The term *ika* is a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), which, being used in its own form (*svarūpapara*), is neuter and ends in the nominative singular. [The case-ending] *su* is elided by *luk*.
Because [the vowel] has been elided, the rule *atvasantasya ca* does not apply, and thus there is no lengthening. The meaning is that the word *ṭhika* is [the subject].

The word "stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is to be supplied as the remainder. From the rules *vṛddhir ādaic* and *adeṅ guṇaḥ*, the terms "vṛddhi" and "guṇa" respectively continue to apply. The word "iti" (thus) is to be understood as an ellipsis. Where...

The word "therein" (*tatra*) must also be supplied as an ellipsis. The construction is as follows: having uttered the words "guṇa" and "vṛddhi," wherever guṇa or vṛddhi are prescribed, the word *ika* ending in the genitive case stands in apposition. Thus he says: "by the words 'guṇa' and 'vṛddhi,'" and so forth. "Stands in apposition" (*upatiṣṭhate*).
The meaning is that it becomes conjoined (*saṅgata*). The *ātmanepada* ending is used according to the rule *ṭhupād devapūjāsaṅgatikaraṇe*.
This position regarding the presence of the word-base (*pada*) has been established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāṣya* and other works.
Examples include [the rules] "before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes" and "there is *guṇa* for *mid*. [The term] *ika*...

The manner in which this [rule] applies will become clear in various places. By the statement "where two [operations] are enjoined," the term *ika* does not apply in an *anuvāda* (restatement) such as *vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ*;
for a paribhāṣā does not apply to an *anuvāda*. This is also the case in rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ*.
This [rule] does not apply there, because the words *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are not heard in that context.
(36) *acaśca* | 1.1.28 | "And of a vowel" (*acaḥ*). The word *acaḥ* is also a term ending in the genitive case; like *ikaḥ* in the preceding sūtra, it refers to its own form (*svarūpapara*).

From the rule *ūkālo’j* [Pāṇini 1.2.27], the terms *ṭha*, *hrasva*, *dīrgha*, and *pluta* are understood to carry over. The phrase "wherever *ṭh* is prescribed" is to be supplied as an ellipsis. He states the resulting conclusion with the words beginning with *hrasva*. However, this does not apply in rules such as *diva ut* [Pāṇini 6.1.131], because the words *hrasva* and so forth are not heard there. *Hrasva*...
The example for "of a nominal stem in the neuter" (*napuṃsake prātipadikasya*) and so forth is *śrīpam*. It is not the case here: *supāt brāhmaṇakulam*.
(37) P. 1.1.46: *ādyantau ṭakitau* ("Those marked with the markers *ṭ* and *k* are respectively the first and the last [elements of the item they are attached to]").

"Ṭ and k are [the markers] at the beginning and the end. *Ādyantau* means the beginning (*ādi*) and the end (*anta*). *Ṭakau* refers to *ṭ* and *k*. The vowel *a* in *ṭ* and *k* is for the sake of pronunciation. Those two whose *i* (indicatory letter) is *ṭ* or *k* are called *ṭit* and *kit*. The word *ic* at the end of the compound is connected with each member individually. Thus, those marked with *ṭ* and *k* are the constituent parts at the beginning and the end [of the element they are attached to].
When there is an expectation as to "whose [are they]?", the meaning is obtained by implication that they belong to those for whom they have been prescribed.
He states this with the words "ṭit, kit," and so forth. "Kramāt" (in order) is obtained from the sūtra according to numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
The meaning is that the *ṭit* has the initial part [as its marker], and the *kit* has the final part [as its marker]. And this being the case...

It should not be asked how there can be a *dvandva* compound here since there is no mutual connection (*anvaya*) between two things that have already been combined into one; for once the *dvandva* has come into operation by first taking up a mutual understanding of the two pairs as a collective form, the connection with each individual member is subsequently established through a consideration of the rule regarding "correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya*).

This same principle applies even in cases such as *ṭheco'yavāyāvaḥ*. It is clear from the Bhāṣya and other works that such usage is indeed ungrammatical (*asādhuh*) in common worldly usage. In this very context, it is appropriate to introduce the rule regarding the correspondence of elements (*yathāsaṅkhyasūtra*). [The rule] "ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ" [is also applicable here].

[The suffix] will be [added]. Regarding the rule *ṭhṅṇoḥ kuk ṭuk śari*, examples such as *prāṅ* and *ākṣaṣṭa* are given. According to the principle that "exceptions stated earlier subvert only the immediately following rules, not those further ahead," this is an exception specifically to the immediately preceding rule, *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*. By the rule *pratyayaḥ paraśca*, [the suffix is added] after [the base].
However, this [rule] is superseded by what follows it. Therefore, suffixes such as *iṣṭha* in *careṣṭaḥ* and *ṭak* in *gāpoṣṭak* occur only when they are subsequent [to the preceding rule].
(38) *midaco’ntyātparaḥ* | Pāṇini 1.1.47. [The augment *m* is placed after the final vowel of the stem.]

"Midac" means that which has the letter *m* (mit) following the final vowel (*antyādacaḥ paraḥ*). If this were the intended meaning, then [the rule] "śemucādīnām" would not apply, because in that case there is no final vowel; therefore, he says: "the word 'ac' is in the genitive case."
And because of the phrase "selection (*nirdhāraṇa*)," the word "from among" (*iti śeṣaḥ*) is understood. The singular number in the word *acaḥ* is not intended to be significant;

thus he says, "among the vowels," and so forth. Regarding the term "final constituent" (*antāvayava*), this is obtained through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "final" (*anta*) from the rule *ādy-antau*.

Because it is possible for the word *anta*, which is a single constituent part of the compound *ādyanta*, to be carried over by the force of the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) that it is *svarita* in its own right; however, if one were to carry over the word *ādi* and thereby accept [the suffix] as being *parādi* (beginning with the following element), then in the plural form *vārīṇi* when a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix] follows—

Furthermore, if [the suffix] were not a *bhakta* (an integral part of the word), then the lengthening prescribed for a stem ending in *n* in the rule "cāsaṃbuddhau ṭeḥ" would not be established. Moreover, in the case of *vahaṃlihaḥ*, where the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule "vahābhre lihaḥ" and the augment *muṃ* is added by the rule "arurdviṣadajantasya mum," the anusvāra prescribed for a word ending in *m* by the rule "mo'nusvāraḥ" would not occur.

It might be so; however, in reality, it should be explained that for whichever aggregate (*samudāya*) the *mit* augment is prescribed, it belongs to the final constituent part of that aggregate which stands among its vowels (*ac*). For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya, "the *mit* augment is shared by the aggregate," is consistent. This applies to rules dependent upon a compound (*samāsa*).
And Mūka will say: "Because *num* is prescribed for the *aṅga*, [the rule] 'for that which belongs to it (*tadbhakta*) indeed receives *num*' applies.

(39) "The genitive [case ending] denotes a relation of substitution (*sthāne-yoga*). 1.1.49. "The genitive [case ending] denotes a relation of substitution. He will state that "substitution" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). In that [context]...

That which has a connection (*yoga*) by way of being a designator (*vācakatayā*) is "connected by position" (*sthāneyogā*). Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "that which has a connection with a position. Due to irregular derivation, the vowel *e* is substituted [for *ai*]. The meaning is that in rules such as *ṭhiko yaṇ aci*, the genitive case signifies a relationship consisting of "position" (*sthāna*). This is so in common usage as well.

Thus, there are one hundred and sixty-six types of meanings: those based on purpose (*ārtha*), those based on kinship (*yauna*), and those based on speech (*maukha*); as well as those based on the sacrificial ladle (*srauva*).
Regarding words, there are only three types of relations with another word: contiguity (*ānantarya*), proximity (*sāmīpya*), and occasion (*prasaṅga*).
The *Bhāṣya* states that this *sūtra* is intended for the determination of one or another of these meanings. And thus, the *ṭhikā*...

In rules such as *yaṇ aci*, the genitive case in *ikaḥ* denotes the locus (*sthāna*). The meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) relates to that [locus] by way of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā*). Thus, the sense is: "when *aci* follows, in the event (*prasaṅga*) of *ika*, *yaṇ* should occur.
However, in this explanatory sentence (*vivaraṇavākya*), the genitive in *ikaḥ* does not denote the relation of being a determiner.
There is a suspicion of tautology— for instance, in the case of "the hand is a limb of Devadatta.
However, in the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*, the genitive in *goḥ* does not signify "location" (or "substitution-base"),
because its status as a partitive genitive is determined by its co-occurrence with the word *upadhā*.

Since technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) function precisely for the purpose of providing a restriction where there is no fixed rule, he states this with the words "anirdhārita... and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose specific relation is not determined. Thus, according to the manner of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) cited in the present context...

It is established that in rules such as *yaṇ aci*, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a specific relationship consisting of "position" (*sthāna*). However, in the Bhāṣya on the *matup* sūtra, it is established that terms such as *anantara* (immediate) and so forth are not meanings of the genitive. This being the case, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *yasyāḥ sthāne*, where the word *sthāne* is a locative-ending term, [the meaning is] "that [genitive] for which there is [the relation] 'in place'."

This is an imitation of a word ending in the locative case. When the genitive is heard, it results in the locative word "in place of" (*sthāne*) being supplied. This is based on the analysis of the compound as a third-case (instrumental) tatpuruṣa: "that which has a connection (*yoga*) with *sthāna*—meaning the referent of the word *sthāna*."
The meaning is that [the word *sthāna*] has as its referent a relation specified by a word whose locus (*sthāna*) has been supplied through ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*).

As for the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra—beginning with "There is a doubt regarding *asti*: does it mean 'in place' (*sthāne*), 'immediately after' (*anantare*), or 'near' (*samīpe*)?"—it refers to [the sense of] "immediately after" (*anantare*) in relation to *asti*.

The meaning is simply that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used when the relationship is determined by words such as "immediate" (*anantara*) which have been supplied [by implication]. However, it is established in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa* (the *Prakriyā-kaumudī*) under the rule *halantyam* that "immediate" and the others do not actually possess the status of being the referent of the genitive. This is also stated in the *Śabdaratna*, which is a commentary on that [work].
And this has been explained in many ways in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Why [is the word] "anirdhāritā" (unspecified) used?

[So that] in the rule "ūdupadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.7), the genitive case in "goḥ" (of *guh*) does not signify "place" (*sthāna*). For if even there the genitive signified "place," then [the substitution of] *ū* would apply to the final letter of *guh* as well as to its entire penultimate portion (*upadhā*).

It might be so. But surely the word *sthāna* is well-known in common usage as denoting a substratum (*ādhāra*), as in "Kailāsa is the *sthāna* of Śiva," "Vaikuṇṭha is the *sthāna* of Viṣṇu," and so forth. And thus, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, if the genitive case has the sense of *sthāna*, then the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) would stand in relation to it either as its determiner (*nirūpaka*) or through identity (*abheda*).

If there were only a sequence (anvaya), the meaning would be either "yaṇ should occur in the place of *ik*" or "yaṇ should have *ik* as its locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Consequently, there would be no disappearance (*nivṛtti*) of *ik*.
Therefore, he says: "And 'place' (*sthāna*) means 'occasion' (*prasaṅga*). [For example,] in certain *abhicāra* sacrifices, [it is said] "in the place of *darbha* grass..."
The point is that in the rule *śaraiḥ prastaritavyam*, the word *sthāna* (place/occasion) is seen to refer to the context of application (*prasaṅga*).

And thus, just as in that case the *darbha* grass is replaced by *śara* grass, so too in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, the *ig* vowels and others are replaced by the *yaṇ* sounds and others. And in that context, that which is applied and then replaced is—
That which is designated as the *sthānin* is that which is to be replaced; that which effects the replacement is the *ādeśa*. (40) *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ* | P. 1.1.50.
Regarding *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*: it has been stated that "place" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). Here, the word *antara*—

This refers to a similar substitute; "most internal" (*antaratama*) means more internal by way of excellence. Thus it says: "when there is the possibility," and so forth. The meaning is that when there is the possibility of multiple substitutes for a single original element (*sthānin*), that which is most similar to the original element—whether by place of articulation (*sthāna*), meaning (*artha*), quality (*guṇa*), or measure (*pramāṇa*)—that alone becomes the substitute.

In this context, by the word *sthāna* (place), the articulatory locations such as the palate (*tālu*) and so forth are intended; by the word *guṇa* (quality), the effort (*prayatna*) is meant; and by the word *pramāṇa* (measure), the duration consisting of one or two morae (*mātrā*) is meant. Among these, an example based on place (*sthānataḥ*) is: *dadhy atra*. Here, the letter *i*, whose place of articulation is the palate, is replaced by the letter *y*, which has the same palatal place of articulation. An example based on meaning (*arthataḥ*)...

For example: according to the rule *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*, when the word *kroṣṭṛ* ending in the vowel *u* undergoes the substitution of a form ending in the suffix *tṛc*, it is the word *kroṣṭṛ* itself that becomes the substitute ending in *tṛc* because of the identity of meaning (*arthasāmyāt*). An example based on quality (*guṇataḥ*) is *vāgghariḥ*. Here, the letter *ha* is the substituendum (*sthānī*).

Possessing the efforts of voicing (*ghoṣa*), nasalization (*nāda*), closure (*saṃvāra*), and great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*), the fourth [consonant] *gha*, being of the same phonetic class (*savarṇa*) as *ga*, becomes [the substitute] for it, because of the similarity of its efforts— voicing, nasalization, closure, and great breath-force— with the original element (*sthānin*) *ha*. However, it does not become *ka*, because of that [latter's different qualities].

Because [the first *ga*] possesses the effort (*prayatna*) of breath, unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), open (*vivāra*), and weak aspiration (*alpapāṇa*). Likewise, the second *kha* is also not [identical], because although it shares the effort of strong aspiration (*mahāpāṇa*), it differs in its efforts of breath, unvoiced, and open. Similarly, the third *ga* is also not [identical].

[It] occurs; for even though there is equality in the effort of voicing (*ghoṣa*), non-aspiration (*anunāda*), and closure (*saṃvāra*), because there is a difference in the efforts of breath (*śvāsa*), voicelessness (*aghoṣa*), and openness (*vivāra*) due to the substitute *ha*, yet there is equality in the effort of being "greatly aspirated" (*mahāprāṇa*), why might it not be the third *ga*? [This would be so] because of its similarity to the substitute *ha*.
Even though there is a difference in the effort of breath (*prāṇaprayatna*), there is an equality in the efforts of resonance (*ghoṣa*), sound (*nāda*), and the opening of the glottis (*saṃvāra*).
For this very reason, if it is asked, "Why then would not [the letter] *ṅ* [be included]?"—the answer is no;

for by the inclusion of the suffix *-tamap*, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is excluded. Indeed, that which is more internal (*antara*) is the "most internal" (*antaratama*). That which is most excelled is...

And there is an effort-based similarity between the letter *gha* and the letter *ha*, because both possess an excellence of similarity due to the equality of four efforts consisting of voicedness (*ghoṣa*), sonority (*nāda*), internal closure (*saṃvāra*), and great breath-force (*mahāprāṇa*). Even though the letter *kha* shares the effort of great breath-force, [it lacks the other three].

Because of the absence of the effort of voice-quality (*ghoṣa*), sound (*nāda*), and closure (*saṃvāra*). Although there is equality in the efforts of voice-quality, sound, and closure for the two [sounds *jha* and *ña*], [the latter] lacks the effort of being "greatly aspirated" (*mahāprāṇa*).

Regarding quantity (*pramāṇa*), as in: "For *adas*, [the *s* becomes *d*], and after *as*, [the *m* becomes *ṃ*]; and for *udaḥ*, [the *s* becomes *ṣ*]. [In this rule, the *u* of the short vowel is...]

The long vowel *ū* [is substituted] for [the short *u*]. Now, one might object: even so, in forms such as *cetā* and *stotā*, when the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* applies to the *i* and *u* vowels, why would not an *a*—which is similar to them in terms of its measure (*pramāṇa*)—be substituted instead? To this, he says: "where... By that [statement], [it is shown that] for the *i* vowel...

The *guṇa* substitute for the vowel *u* is *e*, and for the vowel *ū* it is *o*, because of the similarity of their places of articulation (*sthāna*), but not *a*, because of the difference in their places of articulation. It should not be argued: "How can there be a similarity of place between *i* and *e*, or between *u* and *o*, given that *e* and *o* possess an additional place of articulation in the throat (*kaṇṭha*)?"
Even though similarity of place (*sthānasāmya*) is a factor that brings about homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), in the examination of *āntaratamya* (closest proximity),
it is only similarity of place that serves as the determining factor in some way. In this sūtra,
the term *sthāne* is carried over from the preceding sūtra by virtue of the formal agreement (*svaritatva*) regarding its status as a recurring element (*anuvṛtti*) within a portion of the text.

And the word ending in the third case [“sthāne”] is modified. This term “sthāna,” which was understood from the preceding sūtra as referring to "occasion" (prasaṅga), here refers to the specific location such as the palate and so forth, because it relies on the governing context of "word" (śabda). The term “antaratama” is also connected with it. Consequently:

The phrase "by proximity of place, the most similar [is substituted]" becomes a separate rule. The meaning is that when it is possible, the most similar [substitute] occurs by virtue of the place of articulation (*tālvādi-sthāna*) alone.
Consequently, it is established that "where there is a multi-faceted proximity, proximity of place alone is more powerful."
[The rule] "bhavati" [occurs].

(41) *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* |1|1|66|. When [a term] is indicated by the word "in that" (*tasmin*), [the operation applies] to the preceding [element]. In the rule *iko yaṇaci*, [the word *aci* indicates the preceding element]; thus, in place of *ik*, there is *yaṇ* when followed by *ac*.

Thus it is understood. In that regard, since it is impossible for a vowel (*ac*) to serve as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for another phoneme, one must resort to a locative absolute construction (*satisaptamī*): "when a vowel exists (*aci sati*), *yaṇ* shall replace *ik*.

Consequently, the substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik* would apply both when there is an intervening element and when there is none. Therefore, in the case of *samidham*, [the rule would undesirably apply].

When the vowel *i* (the letter *i*) follows the letter *dhakāra* (the letter *dh*) and the letter *l*, the *yaṇ* substitute would apply to the vowel *i* following the letter *m*. Likewise, when a vowel (*ac*) follows, the *yaṇ* substitute would be obtained for either the preceding or the following *ik*.
Consequently, in the case of *dadhyudakam*, since the vowel *i* follows, the *yaṇ* substitute would apply even to the subsequent *u*, which is an *ik*.

In this context, [the operation] occurs only when the vowel (*ac*) is immediately adjacent (*avyavahita*), not when it is separated (*vyavahita*); and it occurs only for the preceding element (*pūrva*), not for the subsequent one (*para*). It is for this purpose that the present rule is commenced. In the expression *tasmin*, the word *tad* does not refer to its own form (*svarūpa*).
If it were so, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *tasminnaṇi ca yuṣmākāsmākau*, and not elsewhere.
In rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, however,
the word ending in the locative case, such as *aci* found in the sūtra *iko yaṇ aci*,
is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the term *tasmin*. After the word *iti*, the phrase "when [that meaning] is to be understood" (*gamye 'rthe*) is to be supplied as a remainder.

The prefix *ni-* signifies continuity (*nairantarya*), and the root *diś-* signifies utterance (*uccāraṇa*). Thus, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* and *rāyo halī*, when the sense is conveyed by a locative case ending— as in *ici* and *hali*— and provided that there is no vowel beginning with *a* (such as *at*), then in the state of usage such as *dadhy atra* and *sudhy upāsya*, [the substitution occurs].

The established meaning is this: when [a rule] is "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*), that is, uttered immediately without interruption, the operation applies to the preceding element; however, it does not apply when uttered with an interval, nor to a subsequent element. Furthermore, only an interruption caused by another phoneme (*varṇa*) is prohibited here, but not an interruption caused by time (*kāla*). [This is stated in the rule: *ṭhiko*...

In rules such as *yaṇ aci*, since the exclusion of temporal separation is obtained from the very heading (*adhikāra*) on *saṃhitā*, if temporal separation were also excluded by this very sūtra, it would result in the redundancy of the *saṃhitā* heading. And thus, those...

Those rules concerning the substitution of *ānaṅ* and other vowels— which fall outside the scope of the *saṃhitā* section, such as "in a *dvandva* [compound] ending in *ṭh* or *ṛt*" and "also in a *dvandva* of deities"— all apply even when there is an interval of time in the *avagraha*, provided the following member (*uttarapada*) follows, as in *aganāviṣṇū* and *agnāviṣṇū*.
Intending all of this, he states the final meaning with the words "by the mention in the locative case," and so forth.

This is the path that follows the literal wording of the sūtra. However, in the rule *atiśayane tamap*, this paribhāṣā does not apply, because the referent of the word *atiśayana* (excessiveness) ends in the locative case.
