Because it lacks the nature of being a word-form (*śabdarūpatva*), it is impossible for it to possess the status of being "designated" (*nirdiṣṭatva*) by virtue of being uttered immediately [prior].
Nor can it be argued that even so, this *paribhāṣā* would apply to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, resulting in both the genitive of the agent and the genitive of the object—
as in *kṛṣṇasya kṛtiḥ* (the act of Kṛṣṇa) and *jagataḥ kartā kṛṣṇaḥ* (Kṛṣṇa is the creator of the world).
It should not be argued that this [paribhāṣā] applies only here and not in cases such as *kṛtiḥ kṛṣṇasya* or *kartā jagataḥ*;

for it has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya on the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* that, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*), this paribhāṣā does not apply in certain instances of this kind.

In reality, however, according to the Bhāṣya, the mention of "nirdiṣṭa" (the specified) and the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) for *saṃhitā* in this present sūtra are indeed redundant; this will be explained under the rule *iko yaṇ aci*.
(42) *tasmād ity uttarasya* | 1.1.67 | [The word *tasmāt* (from that) refers to what follows. 1.1.67.

The word "tasmāt" (from that) refers to the subsequent [rule]. It is an imitation of the fifth-case form found in sūtras such as *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt*, *udasthāratambhoḥ pūrvasya*, and so forth. Following the word "iti," the phrase "when the sense of 'going' (*gamye'rthe*) is intended" is to be supplied as a remainder. The term "nirdiṣṭe" (when specified) is understood to carry over from the previous context.

The term *niri* signifies "without interval. The root *diś* means "to utter. In rules such as *dvyanta-* and others, when a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is indicated by terms like *dvyantara*, the substitution of *ī* occurs for what follows it only when that [fifth-case word] is uttered immediately (*avyavahita*), and not when it is uttered with an interval (*vyavahita*).
In the case of words such as *dvi* and so on, this [rule] is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that it does not apply to what precedes that [word].

Thus he says: "by the mention of the fifth [case]," and so forth. What about the subsequent [word]? The rule *tiṅṅtiṅ* (P. 8.1.28) applies the *nighāta* accent only to the subsequent [word]: *agnim īḷe*. It does not apply here in *īḷe agnim*. [This applies] when there is no intervention.
What [is the result]? In *ut-prasthānam*, the single substitute of the preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) does not occur by the rule *udaḥ sthā-stambhoḥ*.
(43) *alo'ntyasya* | 1.1.52 | "Of the final *al*. Here, *al* is a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) synonymous with "phoneme" (*varṇa*). Thus, "of the final phoneme."
[The word] "ṣaṣṭhyanta" [means] ending in the genitive case. From the rule "ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā" (P. 1.1.49), the phrase "ṣaṣṭhī sthāne" is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*).
That word "ṣaṣṭhī," which originally ends in the nominative, is transformed into the instrumental case.
The word "nirdiṣṭasya" (of that which is specified) is to be supplied [as the object]. After the word "sthāne," the word "vidhīyamāna" (being prescribed) is to be supplied.

The meaning is that a substitute being prescribed for a position (*sthāne*) shall apply to the final *al* (vowel or consonant) of that which is indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*). He states this with the words beginning "the genitive," etc. [Thus, in the rule] "for *tyad* and so on, *a*" [the result is] *saḥ*.
Why say "substitute" (*ādeśa*)? [Consider the counter-example: "the augment *iṭ* for the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix"—[here, the augment] should not be placed before the *ṛ*-vowel of the suffix *tṛc*.

It has occurred. Why [is it said] "ala"? [The answer is: so that the substitution of *d* prescribed by the rule *vasusraṃsu...*—which is formulated under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "of a word" (*padasya*)—should not apply to the final syllable of the entire word in the case of *paramānaḍudbhyām*. (44) *ṅcci* 1.1.53.
The suffix *ṅ* is that which has *ṅ* as its marker (*ṅt*). The rule "of the final [element]" (*antyasya*) continues to apply.
Thus he says: "this also. The meaning is "even this *ṅ*-marker. Examples of substitutes such as *avaṅ*, *tāvaṅ*, and *anaṅ* are given.
Since this [rule] would already be established by the preceding rule, *na-lo'ntyasya* ("not so for *l* and *u*; [an operation applies] to the final [element]"), for what purpose is this stated?

To this he says: *sarvasya*. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the forthcoming injunction that "that which has more than one letter or is marked with *ś* is a substitute for the whole" (*anekāl-śit sarvasya*). It is called an exception because by it something is set aside (*apodyate*) or superseded (*bādhyate*).

An exception (*apavāda*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) by way of frequent usage (*bāhulaka*). The definition of an exception is: "That rule which is formulated when another [rule] has not already taken effect is an exception to that. In the phrase "when not already taken effect" (*aprāpte*), the suffix *kta* denotes the state (*bhāve*). In the word "by which" (*yena*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the agent (*kartari*). Two negative particles (*nañ*) indicate necessity.

The meaning of this is that when a rule (*vidhi*) is commenced while something else is necessarily applicable (*avaśyaprāpti*), that commenced rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to, and thus a sublater (*bādhaka*) of, that which was necessarily applicable.
And this is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). For all substitutes such as *avaṅ* and others, when they have *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*it*), are indeed multiple-alphabetic (*anekāl*).

And among those various specific rules (*viśeṣa*), by the fact that [the suffixes] *ṅ*, *t*, and *ām* are prescribed as substitutes for the final phoneme (*antyādeśa*), the status of being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatva*)—which is necessarily applicable to its own domain by virtue of being prescribed as a general rule for multiple phonemes (*anekāl sāmānya*)—is sublated. This is because the former is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣa*) and because it is otherwise without scope (*niravakāśa*). For a specific rule...
It applies to specific cases immediately, because the specific cases are presented by their own words;

however, a general rule applies to specific cases only through the medium of the general category, and thus its application to them is slow. Therefore, the specific rule is more powerful. And it has been said in the Bhaṭṭavārtika:

"Indeed, the universal (sāmānya) necessarily moves toward the particular (viśeṣa); and as soon as it has reached it, it is firmly established in that particular. Furthermore, if the rule "ṅcci" were to apply to the *ṅt* suffixes across multiple particulars, then that rule would indeed be purposeless.

It may be so. However, even if the rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya* does not apply to those [substitutes] marked with *ṅ* or *t*, it is not purposeless; for it finds its scope of application in rules such as *tasthasthamipām tāntantāmaḥ* and *asterbhūḥ*, where the substitutes are both *anekāl* (having more than one letter) and marked with *ṅ* or *t*. Therefore...
"A specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) is more powerful. (45) "Of the subsequent [element], of the initial [element]. Pāṇini 1.1.54:

*ādeḥ parasya*. Regarding the word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*): it is used in such rules as *dvyantarupasargebhyo 'pa īt* ("after the words *dvi*, *antara*, and prepositions, the substitution of *ī* occurs for *ap-*").

Therefore, according to the *paribhāṣā* "tasmādityuttarasya" (P. 1.1.67), that operation which is restricted to what follows [the cause] occurs only for the initial [element] of that [following unit], and not for the final [element] by virtue of "alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52); this is the meaning of "tadantasya.
Thus he says: "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to 'alo'ntyasya'. In that context, the word "al" should also be understood as being carried over (*anuvartanīya*).

Therefore, in the word *dvīpa*, the substitution of *ī* does not apply to the entire group ending in *p*. (46) A substitute consisting of more than one letter (*anekāl*) or one marked with the *śit* designation replaces the whole [of the original]. *Aneka* means "not one" (*na ekaḥ*); that which has more than one letter (*al*) is *anekāl*.
*Śit* refers to that which has *ś* as its *it*. This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) meaning "that which is *ś* and that which consists of more than one letter (*anekāl*).
The word "clearly" (*spaṣṭam*) is used because there is no other word to be supplied from the context; this is the intended meaning.
An example is *asterbhūḥ* ("*bhū*" replaces the root *as*). Now, if it is stated that "*bhū*" occurs for the verbal root *as*, [one might object...]
Since the rule would have applied to the entire word, for what purpose is this sūtra commenced?

To this he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the sūtra *alo’ntyasya*. This is an imitation of a portion of the sūtra *ṭhalyontyāt*. Precisely because it is an imitation, it is not an incorrect form (*apaśabda*), according to the rule *adhirīśvare*.
This is because of the indication [provided] by the inclusion of "prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ" (P. 1.4.58) as part of the *sūtra* [in P. 1.4.57]. It might be argued as follows:

when the forms *aṣṭau* (nominative/accusative plural) and *aṣṭaḥ* (instrumental/dative/ablative plural) are derived from the word *aṣṭan*, the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel occurs by the rule "ṭaṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (P. 7.1.21), resulting in the form *aṣṭā-as*.
At this point, by the rule "aṣṭābhya auś" (P. 7.1.21), the substitution of *auś* would apply to the *aṣṭan* that has already undergone the change to *ā*.

When the substitution of *au* for the dual case endings *jas* and *śas* is prescribed, it would—by the rule *alo 'ntyasya*—be expected to replace only the final letter; however, by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, it is expected to replace the initial *a*. Furthermore, because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it is expected to be a replacement for the entire word. This is likewise the case in rules such as *ato bhisa ais*. Among these, which rule is to be sublated?
Regarding the question "Which one operates?"—what is the deciding factor here?
To this he says: "In the case of *aṣṭābhya āṬś* and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), rules such as *ṭhato bhisa ais* are included.
The syntactic connection is that even the rule *ādeḥ parasya* is superseded by this [present rule] because of its higher status (*paratva*).

The meaning is that just as in cases such as *aster bhūḥ*, the rule *alo 'ntyasya* ("of the final [element]") is superseded by the rule *ane kāl śit* ("that which has more than one phoneme or is marked with ŚIT"), so too in cases such as *aṣṭābhya auś*, the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("of the first [element] of what follows") is also superseded.
Now, one might object: in cases such as *aster bhūḥ*, since the rule *alo 'ntyasya* would apply...

The rule *anekāl-śit sarvasya* is not an exception (*apavāda*) [to *ādeḥ parasya*]. Even in cases such as *aster bhūḥ*, where *ādeḥ parasya* would otherwise not apply, that [rule, *anekāl-śit sarvasya*] nevertheless operates; therefore, he says: "because it is subsequent" (*paratvāt*).

This refers to the principle that "in a conflict between rules of equal strength, the subsequent one prevails" (*vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam*), which establishes the superiority of the subsequent rule when there is an opposition of equal force.

The meaning is that [this will] be stated later. The scope of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("of the substitute of what follows, [the replacement] is of the initial [sound]") is exemplified by *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt* ("after *dvi*, *antar*, and prepositions, *ap-* becomes *ī-*"), and so forth.

The scope of the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* ("that which has more than one letter or is marked with *ś* or *t* replaces the whole") is exemplified by *asterbhūḥ* ("*bhū*" replaces *as-*") and *idama iś* ("*iś*" replaces *idam-*"), and so forth.
Therefore, both possess equal force.

(47) *Svaritena adhikāraḥ* | 1.3.11 | "By means of the circumflex accent (*svarita*), there is governing authority (*adhikāra*). *Adhikāra* means active engagement or jurisdiction. Just as in common worldly usage, one who is "authorized" (*adhikṛta*)...

In the phrase "this [word] is in the village," it is understood that it is "active" (*vyāpṛta*). And the activity of a word consists precisely in its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) in subsequent sūtras. By means of a specific accent—the *svarita*—the governing rule (*adhikāra*), which is an operation in the form of recurrence in what follows, is to be understood. That word...

The meaning is that what has been uttered by the author of the treatise (*śāstrakṛt*) as distinguished by the specific accent called *svarita* is to be carried over (*anuvartanīya*) into the subsequent sūtras.
He states the resulting implication with the words "endowed with *svarita*-ness," and so forth.
The pronunciation of a vowel with *ānunāsikya* (nasalization) is also to be understood through the author's formal declaration (*pratijñā*).

Furthermore, the limit for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of a rule is to be understood solely from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Even if one were to argue that, just as cessation (*nivṛtti*) occurs through commentary, so too will continued application occur through commentary—rendering the *sūtra* unnecessary—[the answer is as follows].
Nevertheless, this purpose has been explained at length in the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the rule *paranitya* (P. 1.4.2): among the [conflicting] rules beginning with "later" (*para*), each subsequent rule is stronger than the preceding one; such is the meaning. In the expression *uttarottaram*, the word is doubled according to the rule for sequence (*ānupūrvye*).

The doubling [of the suffix] occurs because it is to be expressed (*vācye*). Due to the application of the rule "the subsequent [compounds] are like *karmadhāraya*," there is elision of the case-ending (*sup*) by virtue of the *karmadhāraya*-like status. From the word *balavat*, the suffix *īyasun* is applied according to the rule "when a dual number or a word signifying division is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are added."

By the rule *ṭhvinmatorluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup*. In this sequence—namely, that rules which are obligatory (*nitya*), internal (*antaraṅga*), and exceptional (*apavāda*) take precedence over those that are relative (*parāpekṣā*); that internal and exceptional rules take precedence over obligatory ones; and that exceptional rules take precedence over internal ones—the preceding [rule] takes precedence over each subsequent one.

The resultant meaning is that [a subsequent rule] possesses greater strength. However, it is stronger than a rule based on the *vipratiṣedha* (conflict) sūtra. An example of a subsequent rule (*para*) superseding a prior obligatory (*nitya*) rule is as follows: *tudati*. Here, the suffix *śa*, prescribed by the rule "śa after *tud* and others" (*tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ*), is set aside;
because of its posteriority, the *guṇa* substitution for the short penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) would have applied, but that [substitution] is superseded by the suffix *śa*.

When [the *śap* suffix] has already occurred, it is not eligible to occur again; however, the *śap* suffix is eligible to occur whether the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) has been performed or not, and thus it is obligatory (*nitya*). For its definition is: "A rule that applies regardless of whether [another rule] has been performed or not is obligatory. Therefore, the *śap* suffix is obligatory.

Having set aside the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), the [suffix] applies first. Then, because of the rule "sārvadhātukamapit" (Pāṇini 1.2.4), the suffix *śa* is treated as having the marker *ṅ*; consequently, by the prohibition "kiṅiti ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the *guṇa* does not occur.
This is because it is more appropriate to assume the non-application of an eternal rule (*nityaśāstra*) than to assume the non-existence of that which has already been established.

The assumption that this [application] belongs only to an *anitya* rule for which a specific purpose has been established is the seed for the superiority of a *nitya* rule. An example of "the internal (*antaraṅga*) prevails over the external (*para*)" is as follows: in the case of *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*, although the option prescribed by "prathamacarama...
is subsequent, it is set aside and the *nitya* application of "sarvādīni" takes effect.

The designation *sarvanāman* applies [to the word *tad*], because it is *antaraṅga* (internal) due to its independence from case-endings (*vibhakti*). For its definition is that "that which depends on fewer factors is *antaraṅga*. The meaning is that an external rule (*bahiraṅga-śāstra*) should be understood as non-existent. This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), however, is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *vāha ūṭh*. An example of a subsequent exception (*apavāda*) is *dadhnā*:

An example of an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) taking precedence over a constant (*nitya*) one is as follows: in the case of *grāmaṇini kule*, the substitution of *num* (as prescribed by P. 7.1.70, *iko 'ci*)—despite being constant—is set aside.

The short vowel is applied by the rule "ṭhhrasvo napuṃsake" (the neuter [stem] takes a short vowel). If *num* were applied first, the shortening would not occur because the stem would no longer end in a vowel (*anajanta*). An exception (*apavāda*) prevails over that which is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned), as in *daityāriḥ* and *śrīśaḥ*. Here, the *antaraṅga* rule for *guṇa* (by *ādguṇaḥ*) and *yaṇ* (by *vṛddhireci*) prevails, overriding even the subsequent rule for *savarṇadīrgha*.

When [the conditions for both rules] are met, the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) applies because it is an exception (*apavāda*). "The followers of Pāṇini do not perform *vyūha*": that by which the separation of base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) is made is *vyūha*; those who have not performed this are "those who do not perform *vyūha*" (*akṛtavyūhāḥ*).

"Pāṇinīyas" means "the disciples of Pāṇini"; this is the literal meaning of the words. If one were to object that, in that case, the entire treatise would be useless, the author explains by supplying the missing words, beginning with "nimitam" (the cause). An example is "seduṣaḥ" and so forth; and that occurs in the section on words (*śabdādhikāra*) at the point of defining the word "sedivas."
This will become clear at the very root [of the work]. It is stated clearly in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* that this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is both baseless and fruitless.
Thus ends [the section] in the commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by Śrī Vāsudevadīkṣita.

Thus: *etetau*.

In the word *rathaḥ*, this substitution of *ida* occurs for the base *idam*. However, when the suffix *thamu* follows the word *etad*, the substitution of *ida* occurs by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) as "this [substitution applies] after *etad*" (*etado 'daḥ*). (Pāṇini 5.3.25) *kimaśca*. (Note: The rule *etado 'daḥ* is understood as a split from the preceding rule *adaso 'ser dād u do maḥ* [5.3.22], which provides the basis for the substitution of *ida* for *etad* before certain suffixes.)
Furthermore: the remainder [of the rule] is "thamu after *kima* when it functions as a qualifier (*prakāra-vṛtti*)". How so? By the substitution of *ka* for *kima* according to the rule "kimaḥ kaḥ".
Thus ends [the section on] those beginning with *prāgdiśīya* which bear the technical designation of case-endings (*vibhakti*) in the Bālamanoramā.
The limit is full.
Now, the *prāgivīya* suffixes:
from words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*), the suffix *astāti* is added in the sense of direction, place, and time, after [stems ending in] the seventh, fifth, and first case endings.
|5|3|27| Now begins the section on words formed with *prāg-diśīya* suffixes—[starting with] "from words denoting direction" (*dik-chabdebhyaḥ*). [The phrase] "ending in the seventh case, etc.
(*saptamy-ādy-antebhyaḥ*) means ending in the seventh, fifth, and first cases (*saptamī-pañcamī-prathamāntebhyaḥ*). [The phrase] "from conventional (*rūḍha*) words" means...
This [term] is obtained through the inclusion of the word *śabda*. In the suffix *astāti*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

The suffix ends in the letter *t*. This rule extends as far as the sūtra "ṭhsaṅkhyāyā vidhārthe dheṭ," and within this range, the exclusion of *astāti* continues to apply. Here, there is no [application] of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) or of words such as *diś* and so forth.
According to their respective order, as explained [in the commentary]:

*pūrvādharāvarāṇām-asipura-dhavaś-ca-eṣām* (Pāṇini 5.3.39). [The analysis is: *pūrvādharāvarāṇām*; *ṭhasi* is a form with the first case ending elided; [it refers to] *pura*, *adha*, and *ava*. Of these...

The first case ending in the plural is used after a *dvandva* compound. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of *astāti*": this means [after words] denoting direction, place, or time. (Pāṇini 5.3.27) And [the suffix] *astāti*. (Pāṇini 5.3.40)

And [the suffix] *astāti*. The form *astāti* has its locative case ending elided (*luptasaptamīka*), or it is the singular locative of the word ending in *t*, namely *astāti*. The rule *pūrvādharāvarāṇām* and the term *puradhava* are understood to carry over. Thus he says: "in *astāti*. Although, according to the sequence of the sūtras...
The rule *pūrvādhare'ti* should be introduced along with the rule *astāti ca*.
Therein, the rule *pūrvādhare'ti* has also been introduced here for the purpose of demonstrating its continued application (*anuvṛtti*).
Regarding *pura*: from the word *pūrva*, the suffix *asip* is applied, and there is the substitution of *pur* for the base.
Regarding "purastāt": from the word *pūrva*, the suffix *astāti* is applied, and the base is replaced by the substitute *pur*.

Regarding "adhaḥ" and "adhastāt": from the word *adhara*, when the suffix *asi* or the suffix *astāti* is applied, the base is replaced by the substitute *adh*, resulting in those forms. Regarding "ava": from the word *avara*, when the suffix *asi* is applied, the base is replaced by *av*.
The form [is used] in the sense of an instruction (ādeśa).
(Pāṇini 5.3.41) *vibhāṣā 'varasya*. From the preceding sūtra, "astāti ca" is understood to carry over as "astāti".

He says this with the words "of the inferior" (*avarasya*). "In this way" (*evam*) means: a place or time that is prior to each preceding one—such as *puraḥ* (before) or *purastāt* (from the front), and so on. "In the prior teacher" (*pūrvasmingurau*) means:
in the one who performed the teaching at an earlier time. Now, [one might object] regarding the rule "from words denoting direction" (*dikcchabdebhyaḥ*).

Since the suffix *astāti*, which is prescribed as a general rule and finds scope in words such as *para*, would be sublated by the suffix *asi*—which is prescribed as a specific rule in relation to the words *pūrva*, *adhara*, and *avara*—the author says:
"And [the rule] 'if *astāti*... (*astāti ceti*), etc."

Pāṇini 5.3.28: *dakṣiṇottarābhyāmatasuc*. [The rule applies] after the words *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*. The remainder [of the sūtra] is: "when they denote direction, place, or time. Examples: *dakṣiṇatas*, *uttaras*. Now, one might ask: why not simply let the suffix *tasi* be the affix? [The answer is that] when denoting direction, [the form would be] *sarvanāmnaḥ*... [etc., as per the subsequent rules].

It should not be argued that forms such as *dakṣiṇataḥ* are established by the rule of masculine-like treatment (*puṃvat*) alone even when there is mere enclosure (*vṛti*), because [the explicit mention of the suffix] is for the sake of clarity. For this very reason, the vowel *a* was rejected in the Bhāṣya.
Some, however, maintain that the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is for the purpose of prescribing [the suffix] from other sources; by that, [the form] *purataḥ* [is explained].
Many scholars maintain that the reading "siddham" is like "samānakālīnam" and so forth, whereas the reading "purataḥ" is merely a scribal error.
(Pāṇini 5.3.29) *vibhāṣā parāvarābhyām*.

The *Vibhāṣā* [sūtra] states: "After [the word ending in] *ṭha*, *tasu*, and *añc*, the suffix *astāti* is optionally applied. (The remainder is supplied as *ṭhatasu'jiti śeṣaḥ*). In the alternative case, there is *astāti*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.30) "There is elision (*luk*) of *añc*. Regarding the example *prācyām*: by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning words qualified by gender), there is elision of *astāti*.
*Uparyupariṣṭāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.31).

Regarding *uparyupariṣṭāt*, the Bhāṣya states: "There is the substitution of *upa* for *ūrdhva*, with the suffix *ril* (*ri*), and the suffix *riṣṭāt* (*til*). This is what [the author] expresses by saying "in the domain of *astāti*" and so forth.
"He dwells," "he has come," and "it is delightful"— these are the examples corresponding respectively to the three case endings. (This follows below.)
"Subsequently: 'the substitution of *pañcan* for another [word], and the suffix *āti*', is this statement from the Bhāṣya.
In the suffix, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.
(Pāṇini 5.3.34): *uttarādharadakṣiṇādātiḥ*.
*Utarādhara*: In the suffix *āti*, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation; it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *astāti*.

*Enab-anyatarasyām-adūre-apañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.35): "The suffix *enap* may optionally [be used] when not far [from something], provided it is not the fifth case. Regarding the phrase "provided it is not the fifth case," the *Bhāṣya* states that this is because of the rule *prāg-aser-iti* (Pāṇini 5.3.1–40). This follows the sequence of the Sūtras.

Regarding "pūrvādhare," he will explain later that it means "prior to that. Regarding "uttarādibhyaḥ," the intention is that the rule *uttarādharadakṣiṇāt* is understood to follow. He explains *adūre* as "in the proximity between the limit and that which possesses the limit. [The phrase] "without the fifth case" [is used].

The meaning is that it does not occur after a word ending in the fifth case (pañcamyanta). Regarding *yathāsvam*: in the alternative when *enap* is absent, the suffixes *astāti*, *asi*, and *āti* are applied; this is the meaning. Regarding "only from words denoting direction" (*dikcchabdamātrāt*): this [suffix] does not apply after words ending in *añc*, because a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is resorted to. Therefore, forms such as *prācena grāmam* do not occur.
They say it occurs [as follows]:
*dakṣiṇād āc* (Pāṇini 5.3.36). Regarding *dakṣiṇād āc*: [this applies] in the scope of the suffix *astāti*. By this, it is indicated that *adūre* does not carry over [from the previous rule].

This has been indicated. And thus, there are three forms: [1] with the suffix *āc*, [2] with the suffix *āt* following *uttara*, *adhara*, and *dakṣiṇa*, and [3] with the suffix *atasuc* following *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*. (Pāṇini 5.3.36) [4] Also [the suffix *āhi* is applied] when [the word denotes] distance. (Pāṇini 5.3.37)

"And from 'āhi' and 'dūre'. The word "dakṣiṇā" is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. And by the word "ca" (and), it is meant that there are four forms, including the previously mentioned three along with "dūre.
[Pāṇini 5.3.38] "And from 'uttara'."
And from the subsequent [sūtra]: "After a word ending in *ṭhāc* and after *āhi*"—this is the remainder [of the rule]. Thus, there are four forms [ending] with *atasuc* and *āti*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.42): *dhā* is used in the sense of distribution (*vidhārtha*) after a numeral.

The suffix *dhā* is applied after a numeral in the sense of "division" (*vidhā*). The meaning of the word *vidhā* is "manner" (*prakāra*); thus, "in the sense of division" means *vidhārtha*. [As Amarasimha states: "The word *vidhā* is used in the sense of 'method' (*vidhi*) and 'manner' (*prakāra*). A "manner" (*prakāra*) is a specific attribute that differentiates a general category.
If it is understood that the nature of the verbal expression refers exclusively to the object of action (*kriyā*), then he says: "the manner of action" (*kriyāprakāra*).
[The words] "fourfold," "fivefold," and so on, require the supply of a verb such as "goes" (*gacchati*).
The understanding is that the action of going and so forth is of four kinds. This also applies in cases such as "substance is ninefold."
The verbal form "bhavati" (and so forth) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
[Pāṇini 5.3.43] *Adhikaraṇavicāle ca*: "adhikaraṇa" means substance (*dravya*); its "vicāla" means moving away from it.

It is the production of another number. Thus he says: "of the substance. And the production of another number consists in making a smaller number larger, and making a larger number smaller. Regarding the first case, he provides an example: "Make one heap fivefold."

In the second [case], however, "make the manifold one-fold" (*anekam ekadhā kuru*) should be cited as an example. Here, since only a manner (*prakāra*) pertaining to a collection (*rāśi*) is understood, and not a manner of action (*kriyāprakāra*), the rule is commenced.
(Pāṇini 5.3.44): *ekāddho dhyamuñ anyatarasyām* ("After the word *eka*, when followed by *dhā*, the suffix *dhyamuñ* is optionally used").

*Ekāddho*: the analysis is *ekāt-dha*. The word *dha* is the genitive singular form of the word *dhā*. The meaning is that for the suffix *dhā* following the word *eka*, there shall be the substitution of *dhyamuñ*. Thus, *aikadhyam*.
Nor [should it be argued] that the suffix *dhyamuñ* be prescribed independently from the word *eka* rather than [as a substitute].

It should be stated that [the suffix] *dha* is a substitute for [the suffix] *dhak*; for if that were the case, it would follow that it applies only to the "change of location" (*adhikaraṇavicāla*), because that is what is proximate [in the context].

(Pāṇini 5.3.45) *dvitryośca dhamuñ*. (Note: This is a commentary on the grammatical rule Pāṇini 5.3.45. The point being made is that if one were to simply state that *dha* replaces *dhak*, it would be restricted to the specific sense of "change of location" mentioned in the preceding rule, 5.3.44, rather than applying more generally to the senses of "born from" and "produced by" as well.)

The suffix *dhamuñ* is applied after the words *dvi* and *tri*. The genitive case here has the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*). The terms *dha* and *anyatarasyām* are understood from the previous rules. Thus he says: "after these two. The word "of the subsequent [element]" (*parasya*) is the ellipsis.
Furthermore, the suffix *ḍa* is seen after a word ending in *dhamuñ* in its own sense (*svārthe*).

Regarding the phrase *dhamuñantāt*: this is a *vārttika*. Because of the inclusion of the word *dṛśi* (in the rule), this [suffix] occurs only in certain instances. In the example *pati dvaidhāni*, the word *tṛṇāni* is to be understood as the remainder. The form [is derived] from the word *dvaidha* with the suffix *ḍa*;
the elision of the *ṭi* portion results in the form [dvaidha]. Nor is it the case that [the suffixes] beginning with *tasil* and ending before *pāśap* [apply here].

It might be argued that even a word ending in the suffix *ḍa* could be an indeclinable; however, this is impossible because, by its very nature, it denotes a substance (*sattvavacana*), and thus cannot be an indeclinable. This is also supported by the usage in the Bhāṣya: *dvaidhāni*.
[Pāṇini 5.3.46: *edhācca*] (And after *edhas*).

And *edhāc*: the meaning is that for the suffix *dhā* following the words *dvi* and *tri*, the substitute *edhāc* shall occur. The status of being an indeclinable (*avyaya*) belongs to those words ending in suffixes prescribed by the rules beginning with *pañcamyāstasi* and ending with *edhāc*.
*Yāpye pāśap* (Pāṇini 5.3.47).
Regarding *yāpye pāśap*: *yāpyaḥ* means "despised. As Amarasimha states: "The words *nikṛṣṭa*, *pratikṛṣṭa*, *arvā*, *repha*, *yāpya*, *avama*, and *adhama* [all mean 'low' or 'inferior']."
The meaning is that the suffix *pāp* occurs after a word denoting something contemptible (*kutsita*) when the sense is that of the thing itself (*svārthe*).

This [application] is for cases where the contempt pertains to the cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*). It is clear from the Bhāṣya that even when the contempt does not pertain to the cause of application, the form *kutsitaḥ*—which will be explained later—is also produced.

( ) *pūraṇādbhāge tīyādan* (Pāṇini 5.3.48). "After a word denoting a part [ending] in a *tīya* suffix used in the sense of a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), the suffix *an* occurs in the sense of its own meaning (*svārthe*). He states the purpose of the rule for adding *an*: "there is a distinction regarding the accent (*svara*)."
The meaning is that [the suffix] is *nitya* (obligatory) in accentuation by the rule *ṭhñnityādir nityam*.

(|) The suffix *īkak* may optionally be added after words ending in *tīya* in its own sense (*svārthe*). Regarding "after *tīya*, *īkak*": this is a *vārttika* established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *dṛṣṭaṃ sāme*.
"Not from *vidyā*.

Regarding "not from *vidyā*," this *vārttika* is also situated in that very same place [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*]. The meaning is that the suffix *īkaṅ* does not occur after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) derived from *vidyā*.

( ) *Prāgekādaśabhyo 'c chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.49). [The word] "prior to eleven" (*prāgekādaśabhyaḥ*) is used. He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "after a word ending in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇa-pratyaya*), the suffix *an* is added in the sense of a part (*bhāga*). From the words *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya*...

Since this [rule] is established by the preceding sūtra, the author intends it to have as its scope everything from the fourth up to the tenth word, and thus provides an example: "caturthe. One should not suspect that the preceding sūtra is redundant because this very rule establishes the point; for the purpose of that [preceding sūtra] is to ensure its application even in Vedic (chandas) usage. *ṣaṣṭhāṣṭamābhyāṃ ña ca* || 5.3.50 || [The suffix *ñya* is also applied after the words *ṣaṣṭha* and *aṣṭama*.]

"From the sixth and the eighth [stems], there is also *ñ*. The phrase "in the scope of the preceding sūtra" is to be supplied as the remainder. "*Ñe*" has its first case ending elided. There is vṛddhi of the initial vowel in *ñe*. By the word "also" (*ca*), the rule of corresponding order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) does not apply here, according to the explanation.

"Regarding *māna* and parts of cattle, there is elision (*luk*) or the suffix *kan*. [Pāṇini 5.3.51]" This means that for the word *aṣṭaka*, there is elision (*luk*) of both the suffix *ñ* prescribed by the preceding rule and the suffix *an*, by virtue of this [present] rule. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that [the suffixes] occur as they were previously obtained.

The meaning is that there is the suffix *ñ* and the suffix *an*. Now, one might object: since the option (*vā*) from the rule "samarthānām" [Pāṇini 4.1.82] continues here, even in the absence of the suffixes *ñ* and *an*, the form "the eighth part of a limb of cattle" would be established; therefore, the prescription of elision (*luk*) here is redundant. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by means of the Great Option" (*mahāvibhāṣayā*).
Regarding "pūrvatra" (in the preceding [rule]): this means in the sūtra "ṣaṣṭhā'ṣṭamābhyāṃ ña ca.
Thus, the meaning is that since the suffixes *ñ* and *an* are invariably obtained here from the words "ṣaṣṭha" and "aṣṭama," the rule for their occasional elision (*luk*) is purposeful.

*Ekādākiniccāsahāye* (Pāṇini 5.3.52). The meaning is that the suffix *ākinic* is applied in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*) after the word *eka*, when it denotes "one who is without a companion" (*asahāya*).
( ) *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* |5|3|53|. The meaning is: the suffix *caraṭ* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting something that existed in the past, in its own sense (*svārthe*).

*ṣaṣṭhaḷa rūpya ca* | 5|3|54 | "rūpya" has the first case ending elided. "bhūtapūrve" (in the sense of 'formerly been') is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus, [the suffixes] *tasil*, *kalpap*, *deśya*, *deśīya*, and *rūpya* are applied after a word ending in the sixth case in the sense of "having formerly been. In the sense of "having formerly been": The suffix *rūpya* is added after a word ending in the genitive case when the meaning is "that which formerly was [something else]. In the sense of "having formerly been": [Example: *pūrvasya kāśyasya bhūtapūrvaḥ* = *kāśī-rūpyaḥ* ("one who formerly belonged to Kāśī"). (Note: The commentary explains that the suffix *rūpya* is added after a genitive noun to denote a person or thing that previously possessed the status or nature denoted by the base noun.)

The syntactical connection is with "from that which ends in the sixth case [denoting] something existing. Since the phrase *bhūtapūrve* (in the sense of "having previously been") is understood by virtue of its being heard in the sūtra, it serves as a qualifier for the genitive. The resulting meaning is:

the suffix *rūpya* occurs in its own sense after a word ending in the genitive case when that genitive expresses a relationship of "having previously been. However, according to the literal wording [of the rule]:

There is a contradiction with the section on suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*). Regarding the example *kṛṣṇarūpya*: by way of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), it means a cow that was formerly connected with Kṛṣṇa. Having raised the objection that the word *śubhrārūpya* should undergo masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule *tasilādiṣu*, [the author] states: *tasilādayaḥ prākpāśapaḥ*.

Since *rūpya* is not included among those enumerated in the Vārttika beginning with "ityādi," he states that the masculine form (*puṃvat*) does not apply to it in that context, saying "and [the suffixes] beginning with *tasil*," etc. Regarding "a cow that was formerly white" (*śubhrāyā bhūtapūrvaḥ*), the word "*gauḥ*" (cow) is to be understood as the remainder. "A cow belonging to Śubhrā" (*śubhrārūpya*) means a cow connected with Śubhrā by way of having been so in the past.

*Atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* | Pāṇini 5.3.55. Regarding *atiśāyane*: the verbal root *śīṅ*, preceded by the prefix *ati*, denotes excellence (*utkarṣa*) due to the influence of the preposition (*upasarga*). This excellence is a state of being held in high esteem that results in superiority, rather than mere abundance; for if it were merely abundance, [the rule would not apply].

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence [of the verb] becoming intransitive (*akarmaka*). Nor is this an acceptable consequence, for if that were so, it would contradict the *Bhāṣya* which states, "The very dark one surpasses the white one" (*śuklam atiśete kṛṣṇataraḥ*), and so forth. The *Bhāṣya* explains that *atiśāyana* is derived from the root *śī* with the prefix *ati*, with the suffix *lyuṭ* added in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). For this very reason, the lengthening of the vowel occurs due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipāta*).

In the rule *atiśāyane*, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is qualified. The sense is that the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* should occur in their own sense (*svārthe*) after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) existing in the sense of "surpassing.
He states the resulting conclusion: "of that which functions with a meaning qualified by excellence" (*atiśayaviśiṣṭārthavṛtteḥ*). However, if [the word] *atiśāyana*...

In that case, since the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes a state (*bhāva*), the meaning of the affix would become predominant; consequently, from words such as *śuklatara*, the cognition would be "an excellence residing in the white," and not "the white that is excellent. Furthermore, [in that scenario], there would be no masculine gender in forms such as *śuklataraḥ* or *śuklataraḥ*.

Furthermore, femininity would not apply [in the case of *paṭvī*]. If the meaning were "existing in that which expresses excellence" (*atiśāyane vartamānāt*), then the suffix would arise only from words such as *atiśaya* and *prakarpa*, but not from words like *paṭu*.

If the meaning were "existing through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in that which is qualified by excellence," then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix arising even from the object being excelled (*atiśayyamāna*).

However, if one were to resort to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) for the agent of excellence (*atiśayanakartṛ*), then what was stated in the Bhāṣya alone would be correct; so let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the phrase "this one among these" (*ayameṣām*): the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun*, which will be explained later, are exceptions (*apavāda*) for the selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) of one out of two. Therefore, by process of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), this suffix *tamap* applies to the selection of one out of many.

The meaning is "occurrence. Regarding the phrase "intensely firm" (*atiśayenāḍhya*): excellence (*prakarṣa*) cannot be applied directly to a substance (*dravya*) or a genus (*jāti*), for otherwise such forms as *ghaṭatama* ("most pot") would result. Rather, substances and genera possess excellence only by means of their qualities (*guṇa*). And so, in the case of *āḍhatama*, [the excellence is understood through the quality].

The meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is "abundance" (*āḍhya*) qualified by excellence (*utkarṣa*); the suffix *tamap* denotes that [excellence]. Furthermore, when this [suffix] is present, there is elision of the nominal suffix (*sup*) by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. This is because it has been stated that the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises from a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) specifically by the application of the rule *ghakālataneṣu*. In this case...
A comparative suffix cannot be added after a word that already ends in a comparative suffix, because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage (*anabhidhānāt*).

This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The form *śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇe* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding the word *laghiṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *laghu*, the *guṇa* substitution would normally apply to the vowel *o*; however, this is prevented by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *iṣṭhemeyassu*.
By the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).

By the rule *tiṅ-śca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56), [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a *tiṅ* (verbal) form as well. Since this would not apply here because [the word *tamap*] is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), this statement is made to provide for it. Thus, [the form] *tamapsyāt* arises.

The intention is that, due to the restrictive rule "the suffixes beginning with *ṭha* are added only after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*)," the suffix *iṣṭhan* does not follow [in this context]. (Pāṇini 1.1.22) *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*. This is a sūtra from the first quarter of the first chapter.

At the end of the section on superlative suffixes (*ātiśāyanika*), although it could have been stated as "gha [is used] after *pitṛ*" or "gha [is used] after *tad* etc.," the fact that a separate heavy sūtra is composed in a different section indicates that even the *tarap* suffix— which is purely expressive of its own meaning (*atyantasvārthika*)— is intended to be included. This is for the purpose of including that *tarap*, which belongs to the extensive category of superlative suffixes.

They say that in another context, the composition of a rule (sūtra) is necessary; by this, [the rules] such as "that which has fewer vowels" (*alpāctaram*) and "elision is more powerful" (*lopaśca balavattaraḥ*) are established.
(kim etiṅ)

The analysis is *kim-etiṅ-avyaya-u*. The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). *Kim*, *ete*, *tiṅ*, and *avyaya*—this is a *dvandva* compound of these four. The term *kimetiṅvyayaprakṛtikaḥ ghaḥ* is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-elided) compound. He states the resulting meaning with the words "of *kim* ending in *e*" and so forth.

The meaning is "from among these. As for the word *katamām*, this suffix *-tamap* is used in its most literal sense (*atyantasvārthika*), and not in the sense of comparison (*atiśāyana*). This is because a grammatical analysis such as "that which is the most excellent (*atiśayena*) among these" is impossible—just as one cannot say "that which is the most firm (*atiśayena āḍhayaḥ*) among these"—since [the suffix] functions to distinguish a single part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*saṃjñā*).

For *nirdhāraṇa* (selection) is indeed separation (*pṛthakkaraṇa*). [In the example] "in the forenoon" (*prāhṇe tamām*), *prāhṇa* means the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). Amarasimha states: "The forenoon (*prāhṇa*), afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and midday (*madhyāhna*) are the three junctions (*trisandhya*). The meaning is "in the most excellent part of the forenoon. One should understand that the excellence of the day is understood from the excellence of its initial portion. In this context, [the word] *ahar*...

[The opponent argues: It is a substance (*dravya*), because the meaning of the word "day" (*ahan*) is precisely that period of time beginning from sunrise and ending with sunset; and since that [time] is constituted by actions such as rising and so forth, it does not possess substantiality (*dravyatva*). This is the intended sense. Regarding the example *pacatitamām*: the meaning is the excellence of the action of cooking (*pākakriyā*), among those words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*).

This is because it has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap* that the cognition has the action as its qualificand (*kriyāviśeṣyaka*). Therefore, the sense here is that the excellence (*prakarṣa*) belongs to the action alone, and not to the substance (*dravya*).
Regarding the example *uccaistamām*, the word *āśaṃsati* (he hopes for) is to be supplied; [it means] "to the highest degree."
The meaning is an action such as the act of aspiring for something high. Here too, it is the excellence of the action itself, and not of the substance.

In the example "the highest tree" (*uccaistamastaruḥ*), the meaning is "a tree that is exceedingly high. In this case, since the excellence of height is perceived in the tree, which is a substance, the [suffix] *āt* does not apply.

In examples such as *kim + tam*, the vowel *u* is pronounced in the form *ām* in order to prevent the application of the suffix *nuṭ*— which is conditioned by a stem ending in a short vowel— thereby overriding the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule *yasyeti ca* due to its superior status. However, if that [vowel *u*] were present, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating "when a term is cited without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), it does not include the same term with an indicatory letter" would apply.
The point that "it is not included in the rule for the substitution of *nuṭ*" and so forth has been explained in detail in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "*ṭhāmi sarvanāmnaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.57) [states: "The suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are used when a dual number or a word signifying 'dividing' (*vibhajya*) is the upapada."
"Dvivacana" (the dual number). "Vacana" means that by which something is expressed; thus, "dvivacana" is the expression of two meanings—that is to say, that which conveys two objects.

Here, the technical term *dvivacana* (the dual suffix) is not intended, because of the [author's] own explanation. It is to be analyzed as *vibhajyam* (to be divided). This is derived from the root *bhaj* with the suffix *ṇyat*, which supersedes the suffix *ac* prescribed by the rule *ṛhalo'ṇ*.
The suffix *yat* is applied here by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). "Dvivacana" and "vibhajya" form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
This, together with "upapada," forms a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*).
The resulting meaning is: "when there is an upapada that expresses two meanings and relates to something to be divided."
The terms *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") and *tiṅ* ("verbal suffix") are understood to carry over [from previous rules].

According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) arise from that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it follows that "ending in a case-suffix" is obtained as a qualification of the nominal stem. He states the resulting conclusion with the words "of one out of two," and so forth. Between the two...

The meaning is that the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* occur in their own sense after a word denoting its own referent as qualified by a degree of excellence in relation to one of two things, and after a word expressing a property (*dharma*) that serves as the basis for differentiation.
Although in this case there are two bases— namely, two forms ending in *su*-suffixes or *tiṅ*-suffixes— and two suffixes, [the rule applies].

Nevertheless, it is not according to the numerical order, because of the [authoritative] commentary. Now, he gives an example when a dual word is used as an *upapada*: "this [is] of these two. Here, the word uttered near [the other] is the *upapada*, and not a technical term (*kṛtrima*), because that is impossible in the rules for *taddhita* suffixes; [this applies] only within the governing heading on verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*).

Because its occurrence has already been stated; and that *upapada* (governing word) must necessarily be employed in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), but in the case of a *taddhita* derivative, it is not necessary because its meaning is already conveyed. Regarding the form *laghīyān*:

in the suffix *īyasun*, the letter *n* is an *it* (indicatory), the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation, *num* is added because it is an *ugit* stem, and the lengthening occurs by the rule "before *sānta*."
[The rules regarding] the elision of *hal* and the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) [apply].
Now, he gives examples with a separated (*vibhajya*) word as an upapada: "the Northerners from the Easterners" (*udīcyāḥ prācyebhyaḥ*).

Here, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used by the rule "the fifth case [is used] when there is a distinction" (*pañcamī vibhakte*). However, if the term were taken as referring to that which has the technical name "dual" (*dvivacana*), then [one would have] "the teeth are smoother" (*dantāḥ snigdhatarāḥ*).
Thus, it would not be established; for this is appropriate when there are many sons:

"This one is my eldest, this one is my middle, this one is my youngest," according to the usage found in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ādyantavat* (Pāṇini 1.1.21), and [according to the statement] "those from Nairdeśika are more eloquent."
Furthermore, because of the usage in the Sūtra-bhāṣya, "tasmin," they say that even when a word meaning "non-duality" (advaya) is the upapada, the suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are applied.
(Pāṇini 5.3.58): "The [suffixes] beginning with *aj* [i.e., *tama* and *īyasun*] are added only after a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*)."

"ajādī" (beginning with *ac*): four suffixes have been enumerated, namely *tarap*, *tamap*, *iṣṭhan*, and *īyasun*. Among these, the meaning is "those two which begin with *ac*, namely *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. Thus he says: "*iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. [Examples: *pācakataraḥ* (a better cooker), *pācakatamaḥ* (the best cooker).

The intention is that because these two [words] are action-words (*kriyāśabda*), the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īsun* do not apply. The word "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of excluding a contrary restriction, namely that [the suffixes] apply only after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) that begin with vowels. By this, forms such as *paṭuataraḥ* and *paṭuatamaḥ* are established.
*tuśchandasī* (Pāṇini 6.4.105). *tuśchandasī*: *tṛ* is the nominative singular of *tṛ*.

By the word *tṛ*, there is a general inclusion of both *tṛn* and *tṛc*. Because they are suffixes (*pratyaya*), the inclusion of those ending in them [is understood]. [This applies to] those beginning with vowels (*ajādī*).

The term "it" (iti) carries over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "from those ending in *tṛn* and *tṛc*. This rule is commenced for the purpose of obtaining [the suffix] even from words ending in *tṛ* that do not denote a quality (*aguṇavacana*). And thus, this is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for those two [suffixes] which were previously excluded by the restrictive rule (*niyama*), and not an entirely new injunction; this is what is indicated.
A Vedic usage is also presented here:
*turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154). Thus, even from a word that is not an adjective (*aguṇavacana*), such as *kartṛ*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied, [the form] *kartṛ-iṣṭha* results.
When the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *iman*, and *īyas* are prescribed, and the elision of the *ṭi* (the first vowel) would otherwise apply, [the following rule applies]:
*turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*. Here, *tuḥ* is the genitive singular of *tṛ*.
"In these" means in the case of *iṣṭhan*, *iman*, and *īyas*. This is the elision [of the *ṭi*].

By implication, this is a replacement for the whole (sarvādeśa), because [otherwise], since the rule *ṭeḥ* already establishes the replacement of the final *ṛ*-vowel, [the present rule would be redundant]. *Kariṣṭhaḥ*: the meaning is "this one is a doer to a greater degree than these two. *Dohīyasī dhenuḥ*:
the meaning is "this cow is a milker to a greater degree than these two. In the case of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, [the feminine form becomes masculine] by the rule *bhasyāḍhea*.

When the *ṅīp* suffix is removed and the *tṛc* affix is elided, the substitution of *gh* for *d* (by the rule *dāderghaḥ*) ceases because its cause (*paranimitta*) no longer exists; however, since the stem remains *ugit*, the *ṅīp* suffix is applied again, resulting in the form *dohīyasī*.

The *guṇa* substitution (by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*) does not cease, because even when the *tṛc* is elided, it still applies by virtue of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the principle that an operation dependent on an affix takes effect despite its elision).
Because of that [existence].

(A 5.3.60) *praśasyasya śraḥ* ("for *praśasya*, there is *śra*"). "In the case of *ajādi*" means "in the case of *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. "Beginning with *ṭha*" [refers to the suffixes beginning with *ṭha*].

The meaning is that the word *anuvṛtta* (carried over) is transformed into the locative case (*saptamī*). Although the word *praśasya* is not a synonym for "quality" (*guṇavacana*) because it is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*), nevertheless, by this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* are applied.

When the forms *pra-iṣṭha* and *pra-īyas* are established, the elision of the *ṭi* portion—which is prescribed after words ending in *pra* when the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun* follow—is about to occur.

*prakṛtyaikāc* | 6|4|163 | *prakṛtyaikāc*: "That which has one vowel (*ac*)" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [The word applies] "in the case of *iṣṭha* and so on," because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule "*turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*". [The rule] "*allopo'naḥ*" [is also understood].

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that this *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) applies to the rules beginning with "ṭhnastaddhite" (*Pāṇini 6.4.143*), "aṭyasyeti ca" (*Pāṇini 6.4.148*), and "ṭeḥ" (*Pāṇini 6.4.155*), within the scope of this section. Examples are *śreṣṭhaḥ* and *śreyān*.
The meaning is: "this one is more excellent than these two."

*Jya ca* |5|3|61|. *Jya* is a word whose nominative case ending has been elided. The words *praśasyasya* and *ajādī* are understood from the previous rules. Thus he says: "of *praśasya*. The form *jyeṣṭha* [is derived] by the rule *prakṛtyaikāj*.

Due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), there is no elision of the *ṭi* suffix. When the substitution of *nij* for *īyasun* is applied, and the form *jyeyān* is about to be obtained—[the rule applies]:
*jyādādīyasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.160). [The analysis of the sūtra is: *jyāt-āt-īyasaḥ*. [The meaning is: after *jyā*, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the following *īyas*.
The meaning is "it may be so. Since the substitution of the final letter (*anta-ādeśa*) would otherwise apply, he says: *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54).

Regarding the rule *vṛddhasya ca* (5.3.62), he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing words: "In place of *vṛddha*, there shall be the substitute *jya* when followed by a word beginning with *a* or *i*."
The meaning is [the application] of the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. Regarding *jyeṣṭha*: this means "this one is older than these two by a great degree.
(Pāṇini 5.3.63): *antikabāḍhayornedasādhau*.

Regarding the rule *antikabāḍhayor ajādyoḥ*: this is a supplement to the sūtra. The meaning is that when the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* follow the words *antika* and *bāḍha*, the substitutes *nedra* and *sādha* respectively take their place.
Thus, we have *nediṣṭhaḥ* and *nedīyān*. The meaning is: "this one is more proximate than those two."

"Sādhiṣṭhaḥ" means "sādhīyan. The meaning is that this one is more intensely "bāḍha" than the other. "Bāḍha" means "intense" (bhṛśa). Amara states: "Bāḍha is used for 'intense' and 'firm promise'"; and [the lexicon] also says: "'Ativelam', 'bhṛśam', 'atyartham', 'atimātram', 'udgāḍham', and 'nirbharam' [are synonyms for intensity]."

*sthūladūrayuvahrasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇādiparaṃ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ* || 6.4.156 || [The rule applies to] *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*. These are the words [referred to by] "of these. *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, *kṣudra*.
The meaning is "of these [elements]. Regarding the term *yaṇādi*: the analysis of the compound is "that of which *yaṇ* is the first.
The word *para* (subsequent) is an adjective qualifying *yaṇādi*; thus, the meaning is "a *yaṇ* and so forth occurring as a subsequent element.
Regarding the phrase *lupyate* (is elided): the word *lopa* (elision), which has been carried over from the rule *allopo'naḥ*, is used here in the sense of the object of the action.

The meaning is that a word ending in *ghañ* is resorted to; for if it were derived in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "param" would be impossible. Regarding the phrase "of the preceding": its status as "preceding" should be understood in relation to *yaṇ*. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *iṣṭha* etc.": this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "the *tṛ* [suffix] is elided before *iṣṭha*, *iman*, and *īyas*" (*turiṣṭhemeyassu*).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the word *sthaviṣṭha*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *sthūla*, the letter *l* is elided; the vowel *ū* undergoes *guṇa* substitution to become *o*.

Then, by the rule for the *av-ādeśa*, [the *o* becomes *ava*]. The meaning is this. However, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *orguṇaḥ* does not apply here, because the elision of the *yaṇ* and following sounds is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *ābhīya* (belonging to the intermediate stage). The same applies in the subsequent cases. Regarding *daviṣṭha*: [it is derived from *dūra* with the suffix *iṣṭhan*].
In *dūraśabdādiṣṭhani*, when the suffix *ra* is elided, there is the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *ū*, followed by the substitution of *ava*. Thus, *yaviṣṭha*:

from the word *yuvan* with the suffix *iṣṭhan*, when the suffix *ṭhvan* is elided, there is the substitution of *guṇa* and the substitution of *ava*. If the term "the following suffix" (*ṭhapara*) were not stated, there would be the elision of *yu* as well, starting from the *yaṇ*. Thus, *hrasiṣṭha*.

In the case of the suffix *iṣṭhan* applied to words such as *hrasva*, there is the elision of the syllable *ṭhva*. If it were not stated that "the [syllable] following *ṭh* is elided," then in this instance, the elision would apply to the entire portion beginning with *r*. Thus, in *kṣepiṣṭha*, when *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *kṣipra*, there is the elision of *ra*, and the vowel *u* undergoes *guṇa* substitution. Similarly, in the case of *īyasun*: *sthavīyān*, *davīyān*, *yavīyān*, *hrasīyān*.
*kṣepīyān*, *kṣodīyān*. He states the purpose for the continuation of the suffix *imanij*—namely, [the forms] *hrasvakṣipra* and so forth—in the rule:
"Of *priya*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *uru*, *bahula*, *guru*, *vṛddha*, *pradīrgha*, and *bṛndāraka*..."

*prasthasphavarbaṃhigarvarṣitrandrāghivṛndāḥ* || 6.4.157 || *priyasthira-*: [The suffix] *iC* is applied after the words beginning with *priya*. This means that for these ten—namely *priya*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *uru*, *bahula*, *guru*, *vṛddha*, *tṛpra*, *dīrgha*, and *vṛndāraka*—the suffix *iC* is added. *prādayaḥ*: *pra*, etc. [are called *upasargas*]. *Pra*, etc. means...

The meaning is that these ten—*stha*, *spha*, *var*, *baṃhi*, *gar*, *varṣi*, *trap*, *drāghi*, and *bṛnda*—are [the roots]. "In the case of *iṣṭha* etc. means in the case of *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun*. This is because of the recurrence of that [rule] from the rule "the *t* is elided before *iṣṭha*, *iman*, and *īyas*" (*ṭhuriṣṭhemeyaḥsu*). Regarding *preṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied to the word *priya*, [the substitution occurs] in place of the base.

The word *prādeśaḥ*. Because it is treated as *ābhīya* (belonging to the subsequent rule) and is thus considered *asiddha*, and by virtue of the power of the vocalization of the vowel *a*, there is no elision of the suffixal *ṭi*. Regarding *stheṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows the word *sthira*, the substitution of *sthā* for the base occurs;

due to the preservation of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*), there is no elision of the suffixal *ṭi*. Regarding *spheṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows the word *sphira*, the substitution of *sphā* for the base occurs.
Regarding "variṣṭha": when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows the word *uru*, *ṭhvar* is substituted [for *uru*]. Regarding "baṃhiṣṭha":

for the word *bahula*, *ṭhbahiṃ* is substituted. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation; otherwise, due to its being *ābhīya* (belonging to the intermediate stage) and thus considered *asiddha*, or by virtue of the power of its pronunciation, the elision of the vowel *i* would not occur.
Regarding *gariṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *guru*, there is the substitution of *ṭhgar*. Regarding *varṣiṣṭha*:

when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *vṛddha*, there is the substitution of *varṣi*; the long vowel *ī* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding *trapiṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *tṛpra*, there is the substitution of *ṭhtrap*, which has a short vowel as its penultimate (*adupadha*).

The word *tṛpra* is derived from the root *tṛp*, meaning "to satisfy," by adding the *uṇādi* suffix *rak*. Regarding *drādhiṣṭha*: in the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, the substitute *ṭhtrap* with a penultimate *a* (*adupadha*) is applied to the word *dīrgha*.
The word *tṛpra* is derived from the root *tṛp*, meaning "to satisfy," by adding the *uṇādi* suffix *rak*. Regarding *drādhiṣṭha*: [the same applies].
In the presence of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, the word *dīrgha* undergoes the substitution *drādh*. The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

Regarding *vṛndiṣṭha*: in the presence of *iṣṭhan*, the word *vṛndāraka* undergoes the substitution *vṛnda*; the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. Likewise regarding the suffix *īyasun*: [the forms] *preyān*, *stheyān*, *spheyān*.

*varīyān*, *baṃhīyān*, *garīyān*, *varṣīyān*, *trapīyān*, *drādhīyān*, *vṛndīyān*. Here, he states the purpose for the recurrence of the suffix *imanij*: "in the case of *priya*, *uru*, *bahula*, etc. By the phrase "and so forth," [he includes] *varimā*, *baṃhimā*, *garimā*, *drādhimā*.

*() Bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ* |6|4|158|. There is elision (*lopa*) of *bahu*; "bhū" is in the nominative case, though its case-ending has been dropped. The term "iṣṭheya-neyasu" is understood from the previous rule. Among these, [the substitution of] "bhū" occurs in place of *iṣṭhan* by the subsequent rule.
Because another operation is prescribed here, that [substitution] has no connection with this case. Thus he says: "of *bahu* and of those that follow.

By the rule "the first letter of what follows," there is the elision of the initial [letter] of the suffixes. Regarding the word *bhūma*: it means "abundance" (*bahutva*). From the word *bahu*, when the suffix *manic* is applied according to the *pṛthu*-class, there is the substitution of *bhū* for the base, and the elision of the *ik* vowel at the beginning of the suffix.

"And there is elision (lopa) of the greater [portion]"— this means that one of these two is exceedingly more. From the word *bahu*, which denotes abundance, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, the base undergoes the substitution of *bh* and there is elision of the vowel *i* at the beginning of the suffix.
Because the *bhū* stem is treated as non-initial (*abhīya*), it is not subject to the rule for the substitution of *guṇa*, and thus the *guṇa* does not occur.

(Pāṇini 7.4.159) "And *yiṭ* is substituted for *iṣṭha*. [The word] "there would be elision" (*lopaḥ syāt*) should be understood according to the rule "of that which follows, starting from the first letter" (*ṭhādeḥ parasya*).

The *yiṭ* [augment] has the letter *ṭ* as its indicator (*it*). When the initial [portion] of the suffix is elided (*lopa*), the augment *yiṭ* is applied. The letter *ṭ* is its indicator; because it is marked with *ṭ*, it becomes the first constituent part of the suffix. As for the change of *bahu* to *bhū*, it is already established by the preceding rule.
However, if the word "elision" (*lopa*) is removed [from the context], then according to the *Bhāṣya*, the letter *y* is the augment.

*Yuvālpayoḥ kan anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.64). Regarding *yuvālpayoḥ*: [the suffix] *kan* is used optionally in place of *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*. The sense is that this occurs because the term *ṭhajādau*, which is understood from the previous rule, is transformed into the locative case. Thus we have *kaniṣṭhaḥ* and *kanīyān*.
The meaning is that this one is the younger or smaller of the two by far. In the alternative case, it is *yaviṣṭha*.

From the word *yuvan*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added, by the rule *ṭhsthūladūretyādinā* there is elision of the *van* portion; then, after the *u* undergoes *guṇa* and is replaced by *av*, the form *yaviṣṭha* is obtained. As for *alpiṣṭha*: from the word *alpa*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
Regarding the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth): the two forms *yavīyān* and *alpīyān* are included by the word "ādi.

[The rule] *vinmatorluk* (Pāṇini 5.3.65) applies. Regarding [the rule] *iṣṭheyasor* (Pāṇini 6.4.158), the term *ṭhajādī* (beginning with ṭha and ja), which is understood from a previous context, is here [to be construed] in the locative case.

The meaning is "due to transformation" (*vipariṇāmāt*). Regarding *srajiṣṭha*: the meaning is that when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *sragvin*, the *vin* suffix is elided; because the status of being a *pada* (word) caused by that [suffix] is destroyed, the *kutva* substitution (of *k* for *s*) ceases. Similarly regarding *srajīyān*. Regarding *tvaciṣṭha*: when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added to the word *tvagvat*, the *matup* suffix is elided.
The intended meaning is that because the status of being a word (*pada*) caused by that [suffix] is lost, the substitution of *ku* (the *kutva* change) is precluded. Thus, we have *tvacīyān*.
For this very reason, by virtue of this indicator (*jñāpaka*), the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* follow the words *ābhi* and *abhya*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.66: *rūpap* is used in the sense of praise.

The suffix *rūpap* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). [The rule] "after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) or a verbal root (*tiṅanta*)" is stated; this is a supplement to the sūtra. The words *tiṅśca* (and after a verbal root) and *prātipadikāt* (after a nominal stem) are understood to carry over.
The intention is that, by means of the indicators (*liṅga*) such as *dhakāla*, it is understood that [the suffix applies] after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

The result is that [the suffix] *rūp* occurs after a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) or a nominal stem (*subanta*) when they denote their own meaning as distinguished by praise (*praśaṃsāviśiṣṭa*). For example, *pacatirūpam*. The meaning is "an excellent act of cooking. In this regard, the *Bhāṣya* establishes the principle that "a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, whereas a noun (*nāman*) has substance as its primary meaning."
Furthermore, in the cases of *pacatorūpam* and *pacantirūpam*, there is no dual or plural number,

because duality and plurality have already been expressed by the suffixes *tiP* and *śaP*. It is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya that the singular number will apply by default (*utsarga*), while the neuter gender is to be understood from common usage (*loka*).
[The suffix *kalpa* is used] in the sense of being slightly incomplete (*īṣadasamāpti*). When the meaning is qualified by slight incompleteness, as in *yaśaskalpam*:

the meaning is "incomplete fame. [The *s* in *yaśas* becomes *ṣ*] by the rule *so'padādau*. In *yajuṣkalpam*, the meaning is "incomplete *yajus*. [The *ṣ* in *yajuṣ* becomes *ṣ*] by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*. In *vidvaddeśyaḥ*...

The meaning is "one whose scholarship is incomplete. Thus, he is "one resembling a scholar" (*vidvad-deśīya*). In all these cases, it should be understood that the gender and number follow those of the base word (*prakṛti*), according to the rule: "Suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) do not deviate from the gender and number of the base. For example, *pacatikalpam* ("cooking incompletely"). It is incomplete.
The meaning is "the act of cooking. Just as in the case of *pacatirūpam*, the application of gender and number is maintained;
likewise, in examples such as *vṛṣabhakalpā iyam gauḥ* ("this cow is like a bull"), it should be understood that the gender of the base (*prakṛti*) is preserved.
As it is said: "In some cases, svārthika suffixes deviate from the gender and number of their base."
In expressions such as *guḍakalpā drākṣā* ("grapes that are like molasses"), there is a departure from the gender of the base (*prakṛtiliṅga*) due to the specific rule.
All of this is clearly explained in the Bhāṣya on this very point.
(Pāṇini 5.3.68): *vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāt tu* ("The suffix *bahuc* is optionally applied after a nominal ending, but it appears before [the stem]").

The *Vibhāṣā* [states]: "The phrase ‘in the sense of slight incompleteness’ (*īṣadasamāptau*) is understood [to follow]. Therefore, it says: “qualified by slight incompleteness. Regarding the word “precisely” (*prāgeva*): the meaning is that in the *sūtra*, the word *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). [The example is] *bahupaṭuḥ*.

When the suffix *bahuc* is added before the nominal ending (*sup*) of the word *paṭu*, the case-ending is elided because it is a constituent part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Subsequently, a new nominal ending arises from the entire complex form. This is not so, however, for the form qualified by the previously produced case-ending, because it lacks the status of being a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) and lacks the status of being a compound (*samāsa*).

It should not be asked how there can be elision (*luk*) here due to the absence of *prātipadika* status; for by the rule "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat*), it does possess *prātipadika* status. Even though the form *paṭuhari* ends in a *sup*-suffix produced previously, the entire aggregate *bahupaṭuḥ* [is considered a *prātipadika*].

Because there is an absence of being something ending in an affix (*pratyayāntatva*); for when an affix is mentioned [in a rule], only that which begins with the element from which that affix is prescribed is included. And it should not be argued that, this being the case, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) in the rule *kṛttaddhita-samāsāś ca* is redundant;
for [the point is that] if a collection (*saṅghāta*) consisting of words is to receive the technical designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then...

Because the rule [Pāṇini 1.2.46] "samāsasya eva" (only for a compound) serves as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*). And it should not be argued that, this being the case, how can the aggregate "bahupaṭuḥ"—which is qualified by the *su*-affix produced previously—possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since it is not a compound; for [the restriction applies only] where, in a complex, the preceding part...

It should not be forgotten that it was previously stated that if a portion of that [compound] is designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then by accepting the very formulation of the restrictive rule (*niyama*)— "only of a compound"— the [undesired application] is precluded. Nor is the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") redundant in the sūtra "samarthānām," since the desired result would already be established simply by the mention of *vā* ("or").
It must be stated [that the suffix *bahuc* is used] because, in the case where *bahuc* is absent, it serves the same purpose as *kalpap* and other suffixes prescribed by the preceding rule.

Otherwise, according to the established doctrine that "when an exception (*apavāda*) is set aside by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply," there would be only a sentence (*vākya*) in the absence of *bahuc*. Nor is there [a conflict], for *kalpap* and the others do not [supersede] *bahuc*.

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that the objection regarding the lack of scope [for the *luP* suffix] due to having the same object of application (*samānaviṣayakatva*) is to be raised on the grounds that those [suffixes] have scope when applied to verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*. With this intention in mind, he says: "as if it were *paṭu*" (*paṭukalpa*).

Now, an objection might be raised: since it is an established tenet (*siddhānta*) that secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) arise after a word ending in *luP*, the mention of *sub* here is redundant.

He asks: "What is the purpose of [mentioning] *sub*? The mention of *sub* is for the purpose of excluding the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "and *tiṅ*" (*tiṅśca*). Nor should it be argued that its continued application will not occur simply because it is not marked as *svarita*;
for [the continued application of *tiṅ* would still occur] in subsequent rules such as "of indeclinables and pronouns" (*avyayasarvanāmnaḥ*).

It is clear in the Bhāṣya that because the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "also" (*ca*) is necessary, its being marked with a svarita accent is likewise necessary. With this in mind, he says: "having the form of *yajati*. However, the mention of the *tuk* augment [is made] because it is said that "derivative suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base, though sometimes they do not."
This has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya for the purpose of making this known.

(Pāṇini 5.3.69) *prakāravacane jātīyar* ("The suffix *jātīyar* occurs when expressing a manner or kind"). Regarding "when expressing a manner or kind": [this rule] follows from the previous rule, *prakāravacane thāl*.
He states the distinction: "And this [suffix] occurs in that which possesses a manner" (*prakāravati*). The meaning is: "only in that which possesses a manner.

[The suffix] *thāl* occurs in the sense of mere manner (*prakāramātre*). In reality, however, it is logical that both [suffixes, *thā* and *thāl*] occur in that which possesses a manner, because there is no difference [between them]. Otherwise, in the case of *tathā*, the meaning would be merely "that manner" (*sa prakāraḥ*). And it is not [the case that...].

It should not be argued that the suffix *jātīyar* is barred by *thāl*, which is specifically prescribed after words such as *kim* (and others), resulting in the non-formation of forms like *tajjātīya*; for the form *tajjātīya* is established precisely by the suffix *cha* in the rule *jātyantāc cha bandhuni*. It is for this very reason [that the rule is stated].

The usage of the *bhāṣya* beginning with "of whatever kind" (*yathājātīyaka*) and so forth is thus consistent. Jayāditya, however, states here that "kind" (*prakāra*) means "distinction" (*bheda*), and that in the rule for the suffix *thāl*, a "kind" is a specific property that distinguishes a generality.
Vāmana, on the other hand, states that both similarity (*sādṛśya*) and distinction (*bheda*) constitute a "kind."
*prāgivāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.70). Considering that the word *iva* refers to the sūtra containing it, he says: "after *iva*.
*avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.71).
"Of indeclinables and pronouns. The phrase "it follows" (anuvartate) is supplied by means of the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkapluti) principle.

The meaning is that the suffix *akac* should be applied before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of indeclinables, pronouns, and verbal forms (*tiṅanta*). In *akac*, the vowel *a* following the letter *k* is for the sake of pronunciation; the letter *c* is an *it* (indicating that the preceding portion is the suffix); thus, the suffix ends in *k*.

This [sūtra] is also a governing rule (*adhikāra*), just like the preceding one. Regarding *kasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.72): although in the previous sūtra the compound *avyayasarvanāmnaḥ* was mentioned, [the word *sarvanāma*] is understood here as well.

By the force of the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) regarding the *svarita* accent for the single substitute (*ekādeśa*), the term "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) alone is understood to carry over here. In the word *kasya*, the vowel *a* following the letter *k* is for the sake of pronunciation; it is intended that [the rule applies to] the letter *k*.
Thus, because the indeclinable is the qualifier, the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. This is what he states: "of an indeclinable ending in *ka*."
The meaning is that [the letter *d*] is drawn forward by the word *ca* (and).

By this, it is stated that this letter *d* is indeed taught as being in grammatical conjunction (*saṃniyogaśiṣṭa*) with *akac*. This [rule] is also a governing heading (*adhikāra*) starting from *prāgiva*.
