(Regarding) *ajñāte* |5|3|73|.

When the meaning is unknown (*ajñāte*), the suffix *kap* occurs in its own sense after a *subanta* (inflected nominal) expressing that unknown meaning. Furthermore, *akac* is inserted before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of indeclinables, pronouns, and finite verbs (*tiṅanta*). In that case as well—

The meaning is that for indeclinables ending in the letter *ka*, the letter *da* shall be the substitute for the final phoneme. "Of what is this? means "it shall be. This is a dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) indicating ignorance. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "an unknown horse" (*ajñāto'śvaḥ*). Regarding *uccakaiḥ*: the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the indeclinable *uccais*. [Examples: *sarvake*, *viśvake*.
Now, since the word "sup" (inflected words) is understood in the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām*,

it follows that the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of all pronouns (*sarvanāman*) that end in a case-ending (*subanta*). This being the case, [the suffix would apply] to the final vowels of "yuvoḥ," "āvayoḥ," "yuṣmāsu," "asmāsu," "yuṣmābhiḥ," and "asmābhiḥ."
The result [of the rule] "prāgakac" is as follows: that being the case, in the instances *yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*,

*yuṣmāsu* and *asmāsu*, and *yuṣmābhiḥ* and *asmābhiḥ*, when *akac* is inserted before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the nominal stems ending in case-suffixes, we obtain *yuvakayoḥ*, *āvakayoḥ*, *yuṣmakāsu*, *asmakāsu*, and *yuṣmakābhiḥ*.

[Otherwise], forms such as *asmakābhiḥ* would not occur; rather, there would be *yuvayakoḥ*, *āvayakoḥ*, *yuṣmāsaku*, *asmāsaku*, *yuṣmābhakiḥ*, and *asmābhakiḥ*. However, if one does not carry forward the term *sup* [from the previous rule] and instead carries forward only *prātipadikāt*, then the *ṭi* of the pronouns (*sarvanāman*) would be replaced [by the suffixes] directly from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

The meaning would be that *akac* is inserted before [the case ending] (*prāk*); however, in that case, forms such as *tvayakā* and *mayakā* would not be possible. Since *akac* would have to be inserted before the final phoneme of the pronominal stem when a *sup* suffix beginning with *o*, *s*, or *bh* follows—resulting in forms like *tvakayā* and *makayā*—he says "beginning with *o*" (*okāra*). This is a *vārttika*.

The meaning is that the augment *akac* is inserted before the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when the locative case-ending (*sup*) begins with *o*, *s*, or *bh*; however, in other cases, *akac* is inserted before the *ṭi* of the pronoun only when it is already a declined nominal base (*subanta*).
This Vārttika, moreover, according to the Bhāṣya, concerns only the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

Because it has been cited in that very manner. However, for other pronouns (*sarvanāman*), the suffix *akac* is added to the *prātipadika* itself before the final vowel (*ṭi*), and not to the inflected word (*subanta*). By this, forms such as *sarvakena* are established. For this very reason, the substitution of *ka-* for *kim* prescribed when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows is intended to include the form with *akac*; thus, we have *kaḥ*, *kau*, and *ke*.

Thus the Bhāṣya is consistent. Regarding the forms *tvayakā* and *mayakā*: here, in the case of *tvayā* and *mayā*, the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the words ending in case-suffixes. However, if *akac* were added before the final vowel of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the forms would have been *tvakayā* and *makayā*; this is the intended meaning. As for the phrase "it should be stated as *kām*" (*kāṃ vaktavyaḥ*), it refers to the rule *kāmpratyaya*.

The derivation [of the term *pratyaya*] is to be considered, as the word *pratyaya* is not seen in the Bhāṣya; rather, this is simply an augment (*āgama*) due to its being marked with the indicator *m*. Thus he says: "due to its being marked with *m*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *akac*. Regarding the form *tūṣṇīkā*: it is formed by adding the vowel *ā* (as in *kā*) after the long *ī* of the indeclinable *tūṣṇīm*.

The traditional authority (*āgama*) states: "In *śīla*, [the suffix] *ka* and *malīpa*. Regarding the term "*śīle*": this is also a *vārttika*. From the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *tūṣṇīm*, the suffix *ka* is applied.

There may be the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *m* when "character" (*śīla*) is understood as the meaning; "character" (*śīla*) here means "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). Regarding the word *tūṣṇīka*, the meaning is "one whose intrinsic nature is silence. Since only the long vowel form is observed in usage in the *Bhāṣya*, the shortening prescribed by the rule *ṭh-ke'ṇaḥ* does not apply. This is because [the condition for that rule] is met by the rule *avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ*.

He states the purpose of the continued application of the term *tiṅ*—namely, "pacatakī. In the form "pacati," the suffix *akac* is added before the vowel *i*. The letters *k* and *c* serve merely for pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Otherwise, if *akac* were added before the vowel *i*, and the *guṇa* substitution of *ā* occurred by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, the result would be "pacatake"—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding *jalpataki*: the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the word *jalpati*. Regarding *dhakiditi*: it should be understood that the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel of the indeclinable *dhi*, and for an indeclinable ending in *kān*, the letter *d* is substituted as its final element. The rule *tiṅśca* also continues to apply here. Regarding *aśvaka*: [it is derived from] *dhāvati*.

The censure of the horse due to its lack of correctness (*asamyaktva*) is to be understood. All nouns, indeclinables, and verbal forms are to be illustrated as before. It is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that while the rule "ṭhyāpye 'pāśa" applies only when there is censure regarding the cause of activity (*pravṛttinimitta*), this present sūtra applies even when the censure does not concern the cause of activity.

The suffix *kan* is applied when [a word] is a name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 5.3.75) "When it is a name, *kan*. The term "when [the object] is contemptible" (*kutsite*) is understood from the previous rule. Thus he says: "when contemptible. Regarding "if by that which ends in it": this means that *kan* is applied in the domain of names where the cause of contempt is the basis.

Regarding the rule *anukampāyām* |5|3|76|: the meaning is that the suffix *ka* may be added in its own sense (*svārthe*) to a word expressing an object associated with compassion (*anukampā*). Example:
*anukampā-udarya*.
And [the suffix *ṭhak*] is applied after a word denoting a means of policy (*nīti*), provided that it is joined with that [policy].
(Pāṇini 5.3.77). Regarding "and [after a word] denoting a means of policy": this refers to *sāma*, *dāna*, and so forth; by "and so forth" (*ādi*), *bheda* and *daṇḍa* are included.
He explains the phrase "provided that it is joined with that" (*tadyauktāt*) as "joined with compassion" (*anukampāyuktāt*). [This applies to] indeclinables and pronouns...

The phrase "before *ṭi*" (*ṭeḥ prāk*) is understood [from the previous rule], as is "and for *ka*, *da*" (*kasya ca daḥ*). In the example *hanta te dhānakāḥ*, the word *dāsyante* ("they will be given") is to be supplied as the ellipsis. *Hanta* is an indeclinable expressing compassion and so forth; Amara states: "The word *hanta* is used in joy and compassion. *Hanta* ends in a short vowel (*at*). The word *putra* ("son") is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning is "grains" (dhānā) joined with compassion (anukampā). From the word *dhānā*, when the suffix *ka* is added, there is shortening according to the rule *ṭhke'ṇaḥ*; then, after [the stem] ending in *ka*, the feminine suffix *ṭhāp* is added.
Due to the optionality provided by the rule *abāṣitapuṃskācca*, there is an absence of the *it* augment in one alternative case, resulting in *ehakī*.
As for *ehī*: the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the verbal form *ehi*.
The intention is that in the rule *ṭhavyayasarvanāmnām*, the phrase *tiṅśca* is understood as a continuation. Regarding *addhakī*:
by the rule *ṭhaddhī*, *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the *tiṅ*-ending form *addhī*. Regarding "by the preceding [rule]":
the intention is that the scope of that [preceding rule] is compassion (*anukampā*). Regarding "even in the case of an indirect connection": [this refers to the application of the suffix].
The meaning is that the son is directly to be pitied, and by means of him, the grains are endowed with pity.

(Pāṇini 5.3.78) *bahvaco manuṣyanāmnaṣṭhaj vā*: "After a human name consisting of many syllables, the suffix *ṭhañ* [or *cha*] is optionally [added]. The analysis is *bahvacaḥ*, *manuṣya-nāmnaḥ*, *ṭhañ-vā*. This applies to the scope of the two preceding rules.

This is a supplement to the rule. Regarding the two sūtras "anukampāyām" and "nītau ca tadyuktāt," the meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* may optionally be applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consisting of more than two syllables that is a human name. In the alternative case, the suffix *ka* is applied.
*Ghanilacau ca* | 5.3.79.

*Ghanilacau ca*. "In that very same [context]"—this is a supplement to the rule (*śeṣapūraṇa*). The meaning is: "in the scope of the preceding sūtra, namely *bahvaca*. It also applies to the contexts of "*anukampāyām*" and "*nītau ca tadyuktāt*."
Regarding the scope of these two sūtras, the meaning is that for a human name consisting of many syllables, the suffixes *ghan* and *ilac* are applied.
(Pāṇini 5.3.83): *ṭhājādāvūrdhvaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ* ("When a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or a vowel follows, [the portion] after the second vowel [is the base]").

"Regarding *ṭhājādau* (in the case of suffixes beginning with *ṭha* or vowels): 'In this section' means in this section concerning 'compassion' (*anukampā*) and 'policy' (*nīti*). This [fact] is obtained through proximity. Regarding 'all':

this is obtained because of the mention of *ūrdhva*; otherwise, by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) 'of what follows that which begins with *ṭha*' (*ṭhādeḥ parasya*), [the desired result would not follow]."
The meaning is that [the substitution] should apply only to the first vowel of that which follows the second vowel.

Considering that the word "lopa" (elision) is carried over from the rule "ṭhājinau nityaṃ samāsārthottarapadalopaśca" and is understood here as a passive noun (karmasādhana), he says: "it is elided. Thus, [the form] is *devika*.

From the word *devadatta*, when the suffix *ṭhañ* is added, there is elision (*lopa*) of the portion following the second vowel, namely the syllable *data*, and the substitution of *ik*; thus the form is *deviya*. From the word *devadatta*, when the suffix *ghan* is added, there is elision of the syllable *data* and the substitution of *iy*; thus the form is *devila*. When the suffix *ilac* is added, there is elision of the syllable *data*; [thus the form is *devila*]. When the suffix *ka* is added, [the form is] *devadataka*.

When the suffix *kap* is present, because there is no initial vowel (*ajādya-bhāva*), there is no elision of the word *data*. Thus, in *vāyuka*, there is elision of the word *data* from the compound *vāyudata*; furthermore, because *uka* follows, the *ṭha* is replaced by *ka*.

Now, one might object: since the substitution of *i* for *ṭha* would already be established in a case such as *devika* simply because it begins with a vowel (*ajādi*), what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning the letter *ṭha*?

To show that [the rule] is not purposeless, he says: "The mention of *ṭha*. Only when the mention of *ṭha* has been made does the elision of the word *data* following the word *vāyu* occur, and then the substitution of *iy* takes place to form the word *devila*. In the case of *devila*, there is elision of the word *data* when the suffix *ilac* is present.
In the case of *devadattaka*, because the suffix *kap* is applied, there is no elision of the word *data* due to the absence of the conditions beginning with *ṭha* and *aj*.

Regarding "vāyaku": there is the elision of the word *data* from the compound *vāyudatta*. Because of the subsequent occurrence of *uka*, the *ṭha* is changed to *ka*. Now, one might object that since the substitution of *ik* would result in *devika* being established by the rule for initial vowels (*ajādi*) alone, the inclusion of the letter *ṭha* [in the rule] is redundant; to this, he says: "The mention of *ṭha*... [is for the purpose of... when [the suffix] has been applied.

Thus, by including the mention of *ṭha*, when the elision (*lopa*) of the word *data* following the word *vāyu* has been performed precisely while it is still in the state of *ṭha*— because that [elision] is obligatory— the substitution of *ka* for *ṭha* is established due to its being followed by *uka*. Otherwise, if the substitution of *ik* were performed first, the word *data* would undergo elision by prioritizing its status as beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*).

When *vāyu-ika* is established, since there is no *ṭha*, the substitution of *ka* would not occur. Nor can it be argued that the *ṭha*-ness of the *i* is obtained through *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), because in the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ*, the vowel *a* in both the original (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). This is according to the view [of the commentators].
This is clear from the Bhāṣya: "Because it is not prescribed by a rule [beginning with] *al*, and because it would contradict the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*.

Regarding the form *pitṛka*: from the word *pitṛ-datta*, when *ṭhañ* is added and the portion *datta* is elided, the *ṭha* is replaced by *ka* because it follows an *uk*. Now, regarding the rule: "After a word ending in the fourth case, before a suffix beginning with a non-consonant (*anaj-ādau*), there is optionally the elision of the final syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*)."
The elision of what follows the fourth vowel must be stated;

likewise, when a suffix beginning with a consonant (*apratyaya*) follows, this is desired, as well as the elision of *i* after a vowel (*uvarṇa*). Having thus broken apart the forthcoming verse-commentary (*ślokavārtika*), he explains the phrase "from the fourth vowel" (*caturthādaca*) as follows: "from the fourth vowel."

Regarding *bṛhaspatika*: from the word *bṛhaspatidatta*, when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied, the word *datta* is elided and the substitute *ik* is applied in place of *ṭha*. Since the condition of being "after a second [vowel]" (*dvitīyādūrdhvam*) does not apply here, this rule is stated as an exception where it would otherwise not have been applicable.
Furthermore, it should be stated that there is optionally an elision (*lopa*) of the suffix when it begins with a consonant other than a nasal (*anajādau*).

He explains the portion of the Vārttika beginning with "ve" (in the case of *ve*) as "anajādau ca" (and when [the suffix] begins with a consonant other than *a*). Although the reading "anajādau ca" is not explicitly present, it is obtained from the Bhāṣya by virtue of the term "vibhāṣā" (optionally); for there, in the example of the optional elision of *da* in the suffix *ka*—namely, *devatkaḥ* and *devakaḥ*—this is illustrated.
"Elision of the preceding member as well.

Regarding "elision of the preceding member," the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is understood from the previous rule. However, the condition "not beginning with *an*" (*an-aj-ādi*) does not apply here. Thus he says: "in *datika*, etc."
It should be stated that even without an affix, there may be the elision of either the preceding or the following word.

He explains the portion of the *Vārttika*—"In the case of *ṭha*, *aca*, *dhana*, *ilac*, and *ka*, the form [is as follows]; likewise it is desired in the case of the affix *ṭha*"—with the words "even without an affix. [Examples are: *dataḥ* and *devaḥ*.
Even in the absence of suffixes such as *ṭhañ* and others following the word *devadatta*, the form [is derived] by the successive elision of the preceding and following members;
[this applies] also when there is an *u*-vowel, and the *il* [suffix] is elided.

Regarding the phrase *uvarṇāt*: *ṭhla* is the technical term (saṃjñā) for elision (lopa) used by the ancient teachers. The meaning is that there is elision of the *ilac* [the suffix] following an *u*-vowel. By the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, there is elision of the letter *i*.
By means of the letter *ca*, the elision of everything after the second vowel in words beginning with vowels (*ājādi*), which is established by the sūtra, is restated.
"Also after the vowel *ṛ*.
This means that even after the vowel *ṛ*, there is elision of the initial *ilac*. For example:
*savitriyaḥ* and *savitṛlaḥ*; these are the forms when *dhan* and *ilac* follow. However, in reality...
The statement "also after a vowel containing ṛ" should be disregarded, as it is not seen in the Bhāṣya. [Vārttika:

"After a fourth [consonant], and when a non-vowel follows, there is elision of the preceding word; likewise, this is desired when there is no suffix (*apratyaya*); and after a vowel containing *u*, there is elision of *l*. (1)
Having thus explained [the previous portion], he recites the entire *Vārttika* beginning with "caturthāt" and so forth:
*prācām upāderaḍajvucau ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.80).
[The rule] "for the easterners, after [a word] beginning with *upa*, there are the suffixes *aṇ*, *ac*, and *vuñ*. Regarding the scope of the preceding [rules]: "after a polysyllabic [word]..."

The meaning is: "in the scope of the sūtra *manuṣyanāmnaḥ*. Regarding the phrase *cādyathāprāptam*, the meaning is that the suffixes *ṭac*, *dhan*, and *ilac* [are applied]. Since the rule would already be established by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *vā* from the preceding rule *ṭhajvā*, he states—referring to the mention of *prācām*—"the mention of *prācām*... [is for the sake of excluding others]. [The suffix] *upaḍ*.

Some maintain that when the suffix *aṅ* is added to the word *upendradatta*, the *e* at the beginning of the compound is elided by the rule to be stated later, "the second diphthong [is elided]. Others argue that, based on the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule *nendrasya parasya*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)— even though it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*)— takes precedence over an operation conditioned by both members of a compound.

Regarding the rule "there is elision of *i* and so forth before what has not previously occurred," this is stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. *Upaka*: This form arises from the suffix *vuñ*, with the substitution of *a* for *u* and the elision of *i* and so forth. *Upiya*: This is the form derived from the suffix *ghan*. *Upila*: This is the form derived from the suffix *ilac*. *Upika*: This is the form derived from the suffix *ṭhac*. *Upendradataka*: [This is the form derived from the suffix *ṭhak*.]

The form [is derived] with the suffix *ka*. Since it does not begin with *ā* or any other vowel, there is no elision (*lopa*). (Pāṇini 5.3.81) "The suffix *kan* follows a word denoting a genus (*jāti*). That is to say, [it follows] that which is a word for a genus—that which has a genus as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
The meaning is that he, being well-known, has become a human name. This is an exception to the two rules prescribed by the sūtras "anukampāyām" and "nītau.
(1) It should be stated that when this is a second diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), there is elision of its initial [vowel].

"If it is the second *sandhyakṣara*": this refers to the traditional teaching of the ancient masters that "the *ec*-vowels are the *sandhyakṣaras*. Regarding the example *kahoḍa*: this is the name of a particular seer (*ṛṣi*). Here, the second vowel is the *sandhyakṣara*; there is elision of that [vowel] at its beginning, and not only of what follows it.
The elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*) should be stated for those compounds whose prior member consists of a single syllable (*ekākṣara*).
"Single syllable" (*ekākṣara*) means a single vowel (*ac*) accompanied by a consonant; that is to say, it refers to a monosyllabic word (*ekāckam*).
Those words whose prior member is of such a nature are "those whose prior member consists of a single syllable" (*ekākṣarapūrvapadāni*).
The meaning is that among those [words], there should be the elision (*lopa*) of as many words as constitute the subsequent members (*uttarapada*).

Here, the word *uttarapada* is used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), and not as a technical term (*rūḍha*) for the final member of a compound, because of the [author's] own explanation. By the rule "after the second vowel" (*dvitīyādaca ūrdhvam*), it refers to that which is characterized by having a second vowel.
This statement is made because [the elision] would otherwise not apply. "One who utters blessings with speech" (*vāgāśīḥ*):

he whose blessing (*āśīḥ*) is in his speech, but not merely in his mind, is one who utters blessings with speech; thus is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *vāgāśīḥ*. Alternatively, *āśīḥ* means the act of wishing (*āśāsana*); thus, a blessing performed by speech is *vāgāśīḥ*. This is according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.

This is a compound. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "given by that blessing of speech" (*vāgāśiṣā dattaḥ*). The meaning is: "given by an instruction whose instrument is speech. Regarding the term *vācika*: when the suffix *ṭhak* is added to the word *vāgāśīrdatta*, there is elision (*lopa*) of both the word *vāk*—which consists of a single syllable—and the two words *āśīḥ* and *datta*.

Some maintain that the form *vācikaḥ* arises because, once the status of being a *pada* is established by virtue of the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhaktiḥ*), the application of *kutva* and *jaśtva* is blocked; since the status of being a *bha* (by virtue of the suffix *ṭhak*) sublates the status of being a *pada*, those two operations cease. However, in reality, this is so when [the suffix] is *ṭhak*.

They say that because the substitution of *ik* is considered *asiddha*, when the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*) is to be applied at the very stage of the *sthān* state, the rules for *kutva* and so forth do not apply beforehand. Even though, after the elision of the portion following the second vowel of the word *ṭhśīrdata*, the form *vāgā-ika* remains, [the rule] "of that which [ends in *i* or *u*]" (*yasyeti ca*)...

Even though the form *ṭhvācika* is established by the elision of the vowel *ā* according to the aforementioned method— resulting in the application of *kutva* and *jaśtva*— nevertheless, because the elision of *ā* is treated as *sthānivadbhūta*, the word is considered to end in *ā*. Consequently, by relying on this *ā*-ending as a *bha* base, [the subsequent rules apply].

Since there is no contradiction in the status of being a word ending in a consonant (*cakārānta*), the rules for *kutva* and *jaśtva* would apply, resulting in the form *ṭhvāgika*. However, when the final member of the compound is elided, because it is not an *ādeśa* (substitute) of a vowel or a consonant (*ajjhal-ādeśa*), the *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply; consequently, by the definition of *bha* which has the same scope [as that of *pada*], the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* applies.

The designation *pada* is sublated; the sense is that this occurs because of the superior force (*paratva*) of the governing rule concerning the single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*). [The questioner asks: "How so?

Here too, once the word *aṅgulidatta* has undergone elision (*lopa*), it lacks the status of a *pada* due to its being a *bha* element dependent on the suffix *ik*; therefore, the substitution of *jaś* is difficult to obtain—this is the question.

This is established by the mention of "ṣaṣṭha" and so forth. Regarding the word *ṣaṣa*: when the word *ṣaṣ* is the prior member [of a compound], the elision of everything after the second vowel is established by the rule *ṭhṭhājādau*; this, however, is not an elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*).

The meaning is that by this statement, the form *ṣaḍika* is established. And thus, in the case of *ṣaḍaṅgulidatta*, when the letter following the *ḍa*-vowel (*ḍa-kāra-akāra*) is elided, and subsequently the *ḍa*-vowel (*ḍa-kāra-akāra*) is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, then—by virtue of that [elision] being treated as *sthānivat*—the word becomes one ending in *a* (an *akārānta*). Relying on this *ik* (the *a*), the status of being a *bha* is attained.

The point is that since the status of being a *pada* for the word ending in *ṣ* is not obstructed by that [suffix] which ends in *a*, the substitution of *jaś* (the dental *d*) occurs without impediment. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭh-svādiṣu*.
(1) *Śevala-supari-viśāla-varuṇa-aryaman-ādīnāṃ tṛtīyāt* 5.3.84.

*Śevala*: "Of these" means [the words] *śevala*, *supari*, *viśāla*, *varuṇa*, and *aryaman* as their prior members (*pūrvapada*). "Of the preceding" means [the rule] beginning with "*ṭhaḥ ṭhājādau*" (Pāṇini 5.1.82). *Śevalika* is derived from the word *śevaladatta* by adding the suffix *ṭhak* and deleting [the portion] from the third vowel onwards.
There is elision of the word *data* (tooth) following another [word]. For example: *śevalila*. This is the form derived from *śevalidata* with the suffix *ilac*. *Suparika*.

This is the form derived from *suparidata* with the suffix *ṭhak*, involving the elision of the word *data*. *Viśālika*. This is the form derived from *viśāladata* with the suffix *ṭhak*. *Varuṇika*. [This is the form derived from *varuṇadata* with the suffix *ṭhak*.]

*Varuṇadatāt* means *varuṇikaḥ*. *Aryamikaḥ* means [derived] from *aryamadatāt*, thus *aryamikaḥ*. Regarding this, the Vārttika "of those whose sandhi has not been performed" (*ṭhakṛtasandhīnām eṣām*) is established in the Bhāṣya. By that, forms such as *suparyāśīrdataḥ* and *suparikaḥ* are established.
Pāṇini 5.3.82: *ajināntasyottarapadalopaśca* (and there is elision of the final member of a compound ending in *ajina*).

Regarding *ajināntasya*: [the example is] *vyāghraka*. *Vyāghrājina* is the name of a certain person. From that, when the suffix *kan* is added, there is elision of *ajina*. [The example is] *siṃhaka*; this is from the word *siṃhājina* with the suffix *kan*.
There is the elision of *ajina*. (Pāṇini 5.3.84) *Alpe* (5.3.85): When [the word] denotes something characterized by smallness (*alpatva*), the suffixes shall be applied as prescribed.
Regarding "tailakam": examples such as *sarvakam*, *uccakaiḥ*, and *pacatakī* should also be cited. [Pāṇini 5.3.56] *hrasve*:
The meaning is that suffixes are applied as prescribed when [the word-base] denotes something characterized by shortness (*hrasvatva*).

The distinction is that *alpatva* (smallness) is the opposite of *mahattva* (greatness), whereas *hrasvatva* (shortness) is the opposite of *dīrghatva* (length). [Pāṇini 5.3.87] "The suffix *kan* is used when it is a name (*saṃjñā*). For example, *vaṃśaka*: this is the name for a specific short variety of bamboo.

Pāṇini 5.3.88: *kuṭī-śamī-śuṇḍābhyaḥ raḥ*. [The suffix] *ra* is added after *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*. [Examples: *kuṭīraḥ* (a small hut). The rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasva*) still applies; thus, *kuṭīraḥ*. Since "suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*) sometimes deviate from the gender and number of the base," the word takes the masculine gender. Similarly, *śamīraḥ* and *śuṇḍāraḥ*.
Thus it is also said: *hrasvā śamī* means "a small *śamī* tree" or "the trunk.
[Pāṇini 5.3.89] states: *kutvā ḍupac*. From the word *kutū*, with the suffix *ḍupac*, the form *kutupa* is derived.

By the rule *ṅtyāṭṭilopaḥ*, there is elision of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Even in that case, as in the word *kuṭīra* and others, the feminine quality is set aside and only the masculine form remains. Regarding this, he cites the *Amarakośa* as authority: "The word *kutūḥ* means a small vessel (*kṛti*) or oil."
*kāsūgoṇībhyāṃ ṣṭarac* (Pāṇini 5.3.90).

From *kāsū* and *goṇī*, the suffix *ṣṭarac* [is applied]. The rule "a short vowel" (*hrasva*) still applies. Thus, *kāsūtarī*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṣ* (*ṣit*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added; this is the intended meaning. As for the statement: "The word *kāsū* refers to the intellect when it is to be expressed as 'bad speech,' but otherwise it means a weapon."
In the *Nānārtharatnamālā*: "In this way, the word *goṇī* is used in the sense of a boat. (Pāṇini 5.3.91):

"And after *vatsa*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*, and *ṛṣabha*, [the suffix *kan* is applied] in the sense of smallness. [The commentary notes: "The word *vatsa*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*, *ṛṣabha*; the rule for the short vowel (*hrasva*) has ceased to apply. *Vatsa*, *ukṣan*, *aśva*.

Ṛṣabha: The meaning is that the suffix *ṣṭarac* is applied after these words when they are qualified by "thinness" (*tanutva*). "Thinness" means deficiency. "Calf" (*vatsaḥ*) refers to the first stage of life. And the thinness of the first stage of life is to be understood as the attainment of the subsequent stage of life. Thus he says: "having reached the second stage of life."

Thus: "ukṣatara" means a young bull (*ukṣā*); the diminution of youthfulness is to be understood as the attainment of the third stage of life. "Aśvatara" means one produced from a mare by a donkey; "aśvatara-ness" is indeed inferior to "horse-ness."

Regarding the term *ṛṣabhatara*: an *ṛṣabha* is a bearer of a burden; its "thinness" (*tanutvam*) refers to a diminished capacity for carrying that burden, and the word means "one possessing that. Why is it not the case that a thin, emaciated calf is called a *vatsatara* (a young bull)? To this he says: "This [suffix -tara] applies only when there is thinness of the cause for activity (*pravṛtinimitta-tanutve*). And this is stated in the Bhāṣya.
This is clear. (Pāṇini 5.3.92):

*kiṃ-yad-adaḥ nirdhāraṇe dvayor ekasya ḍatarac*. [The rule means: after *kim*, *yat*, and *tat*, when there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) from among two, the suffix *ḍatarac* is applied. [In the commentary: "after *kim*, *yat*, and *tat*"—this is the ablative case derived from a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) of these three.

The meaning is that when the determination of one out of two is intended, the suffix *ḍatarac* shall be applied after words such as *kim* and others which denote the item being determined. For example: *anayoḥ kataro vaiṣṇavaḥ* ("Which of these two is a Vaiṣṇava?"). This means "Who is a Vaiṣṇava? Here, the referent of the word *ka-* (who) is determined by its Vaiṣṇava-ness (*vaiṣṇavatva-guṇa*) from among the two things denoted by the pronouns.

Therefore, when the suffix *ḍataraC* is added to the word *kim*, the *ṭi*-portion is elided because the suffix is marked with *ḍi*, resulting in *katara*. Similarly, from the words *yacch* and *tacch*, when *ḍataraC* is added, the *ṭi*-portion is elided, resulting in *yataraḥ* and *tataraḥ*. Why does the rule specify "from words denoting that which is being singled out"? [Consider: *kayor anyataro devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is one of the two").
In the rule "of two, one [is chosen]," why does [the suffix] not occur after words such as *kim*?

(Pāṇini 5.3.93): "Optionally, when there is an inquiry regarding the type among many, the suffix *ḍatamac* is used. [The words] "among many," "from *kim*, *yat*, and *tat*," "in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*"), and "of one" are carried over [from previous rules].

The genitive case in *bahūnām* is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Thus he says: "In the sense of selection among many, the suffix *ḍatama* (or *ḍat*) may be employed. After the word "among" (*madhye*), the word "of one" (*ekasya*) is to be understood as an ellipsis. It should also be understood that this applies when a question regarding a genus (*jāti*) is implied. This refers to both "genus" (*jāti*) and "question" (*paripraśna*).

This is a collective dvandva compound. The meaning is that [the rule applies] when a genus (*jāti*) or an inquiry (*paripraśna*) is implied. In this context, the phrase "when a genus is implied" qualifies all three words beginning with *kim* (i.e., *kiṃ*, *yad*, and *tad*). However, the mention of "inquiry" is a qualification of *kim* alone; furthermore, this is for the purpose of excluding the use of *kim* when it has the sense of censure (*kṣepa*).

That the inclusion of the term *paripraśna* (inquiry) is not a qualifier [of *kim* and so on] because it is impossible is clear from the Vṛtti. On this point, the Vārttika states: "Since suffixes are prescribed for *kim* and so on when they have a dual or plural sense, the inclusion of *paripraśna* is not a qualifier, because it is impossible"—thus says the Vṛtti.

This is clear. Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "Since suffixes are prescribed for the dual and plural senses of words such as *kim* and others, the mention of the condition (*upādhi*) is redundant. Kaiyaṭa explains: "The meaning is that the phrase 'in the case of two' (*dvayoḥ*) from the preceding rule and the phrase 'when asking about a genus' (*jātiparipraśne*) in this rule need not be stated."

Thus he says: "It has been rejected in the original source (*ākara*). His intention is that [the word *dvayoḥ*] is not included because its meaning, "rejection," is not denoted [by the suffix]. It should be understood that the word *dvayoḥ* is also present in the preceding rule. And so, in the example "Among these, who is the cook? Śūra, Devadatta?"—even though [the selection] is based on action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), or name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *ḍatama* occurs in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). In the example "Among these, which one is Devadatta? (*eṣāṃ katamo devadattaḥ*), the suffix *ḍatarac* occurs when selecting one from among many; this suffix is therefore [added] to the word *kata*. Thus, in the commentary on the Sūtra, it says: "When many are sitting, someone asks someone else: 'Which one... (*bahuṣv āsīneṣu kaścit kaṃcit pṛcchati kataraḥ*).

The usage "Devadatta" is thus justified. [In the question] "Which Kaṭha among you?", the status of Kaṭha as a genus (*jāti*) follows from the rule: "A lineage (*gotra*) is treated as a branch (*caraṇa*). The inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is for the sake of the *akac* suffix;
otherwise, by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), the base would be exempted by the exception.

The sense is that because it has been stated that the elision (*utsarga*) does not apply, the suffix *akac* would not occur. Nor should it be argued that the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is redundant— since the rule "of indeclinables and pronouns" (*avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ*) is a governing rule (*adhikāra*), and the desired result is established by its mere recurrence here— it is because the recurrence of that [governing rule] applies only to this very sūtra and not to the preceding one.
Because it serves the purpose of making something known (*jñāpanārthatvāt*). Therefore, *akac* does not occur in the domain of *ḍatarac*. [This is] by virtue of the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option).
For this very reason, the usage "What is the difference between these two meanings? found in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *ṭhavakṣepaṇe* is consistent.
The suffixes beginning with *tamap* are obligatory before the suffix *kan* used in the sense of disparagement (*avakṣepaṇa*).
The sense is that the statement "they are [mere] conditions" (*pratyayāḥ*) is merely general.
Regarding the phrase "in this case of *kim*": the meaning is that it applies even to the scope of the currently under discussion rule, *vā bahūnām*;
for the sense is that there is the usage found in the Bhāṣya, such as *bahuṣv āsīneṣu*.
*Ekācca prācām* (Pāṇini 5.3.94). Regarding *ekācca prācām*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "The suffixes *ḍatarac* and *ḍatamac* shall also [be applied].

The phrase "in the scope of the two preceding sūtras" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Since this is already established by the *mahāvibhāṣā* (the great option), [the present rule is stated for the sake of restriction].
The *Bhāṣya* states: "The mention of *prācām* (of the Easterners) need not be made. For this very reason, it is not for the sake of the suffix *akac*.

It is not merely "despised," but rather that which, though studied, becomes a cause for the disparagement of the student and brings about contempt; for is not contempt itself a form of disparagement? How then could grammar be considered contemptible, especially since this [term] is already covered by the word "despised"? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "by which the other... The intention is that the word *avakṣepaṇa* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

Now follow the suffixes beginning with *prāgdīvyatīya*.
(1492) "The modification thereof" [is expressed by the suffixes taught from here on]. Pāṇini 4.3.134.
Now, the suffixes expressing the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) are defined. [The rule] *tasya vikāraḥ* [is explained as follows]: "modification" (*vikāra*) means that which is modified;

it is derived from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karman*). The meaning is: having undergone a modification consisting of a different state of its original material cause (*prakṛti*). Regarding the sense of "modification," the suffixes *aṇ* and others are generally applicable after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).
The meaning is that the specific [suffixes] to be mentioned hereafter should be applied according to the rule.
Regarding the modification of *aśman*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix must be stated.
That is to say, when a suffix denoting a modification follows, there is the elision of the *ṭi* of the word *aśman*.

The meaning is that it should be stated [as an exception]. This is an exception to the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) prescribed by the rule "ṭhan. Regarding *āśma*: this form results from the elision of the *ṭi* portion when the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Similarly, a sheath (*kośa*) made from leather (*carman*) is called *cārmaḥ*. The elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs here due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating "after *carman*, when *kośa* follows. Regarding *bhāsmana*: this is a modification (*vikāra*) of ash (*bhasman*).
This is the meaning. Because of the rule *aṇi ṭhañi* (Pāṇini 6.4.164), there is no elision of the *ṭi* portion due to the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*). Regarding *mārtika*:

the meaning is "a product of clay" (*mṛttikāyā vikāraḥ*). This is an example distinct from the scope of the exceptions (*apavāda*) to be mentioned later, such as *ṭhak prāṇirajatādibhyaḥ añ*, *ṭhaño’ñ*, and *ṭhanudātādeśca*. In that regard:

The three words *aśman*, *bhasman*, and *carman* end in the suffix *manin* and are accented on the first syllable by the *nit-svara*. The word *mṛtikā* also ends in the suffix *tikann* according to the rule *mṛda-stikan*, and is accented on the first syllable by the *nit-svara*.

(1493) And when denoting a part, [the suffixes] *aṇ* and others— both those already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned— are applied after words ending in the genitive case that denote living beings (*prāṇin*), medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*), or trees (*vṛkṣa*). This applies both to a constituent part (*avayava*) and to a modification (*vikāra*).

The meaning is that [the suffix] would apply as prescribed, whereas for others there is merely a modification (*vikāra*). He gives an example for a living being (*prāṇin*): *māyūra*. Since the word *mayūra* has its middle syllable acute according to the rule "when the final syllable is light" (*laghāvante*), the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule "from living beings, *rajata*, etc. (*prāṇirajatādibhyaḥ*). He gives an example for a plant (*oṣadhi*): *maurvam*.

*Mūrvā* is a specific type of medicinal herb; the meaning is "a part" or "a product" of it. The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the general rule (*autsargika*). The suffix *añ*, which would be prescribed by the rule *ṭhanudātādeśca*, does not apply here because [the word *mūrvā*] has an acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule *tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyaṣām*.

He provides an example of a word for a tree: *paippalam*. This means "a part or a product of the *pippala*"; *pippala* here refers to the *aśvattha* (holy fig) tree. The word *pippala* has its middle syllable acute (*madhyodātta*) by the rule *laghāvante*.
In the absence of the suffix *añ*, which would otherwise be prescribed by the rule *anudātādeśca*, the general suffix *aṇ* is applied.

(1494) *bilvādibhyo’ṇ* | Pāṇini 4.3.136. The meaning is that after the words *bilva* and others, the suffix *aṇ* is applied: after those denoting living beings, herbs, and trees, it signifies a part (*avayava*) or a modification (*vikāra*); after the others, however, it signifies only a modification. For example, *bailvam* means "a part of a *bilva*."

The meaning is "or a derivative. *Bilva*, *vrīhi-kāṇḍa*, *mudga*, *masūra*, *godhūma*, *ikṣu*, *veṇu*, *gavedhuka*, *kārpāsī*, *pāṭalī*, *karkandhū*, and *kaṭī*—these are the *bilva*-group (*bilvādi*). Among these, since the suffix *aṇ* is already established for *gavedhuka* by the rule "after [a word] ending in *ṭh* or having *k* as its penultimate letter" (*ṭhkopadhācca*), [the mention here is for the sake of excluding other suffixes].

The recitation here is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *mayaṭ*; however, for the others, it is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *añ* [prescribed] by the rule "ṭhanudātādeśca" (Pāṇini 4.3.140)—this is the detailed explanation in the Kaustubha. (1495) Also after a word having *ka* as its penultimate letter: 4.3.137.

"And after a word ending in *ka*. The remainder [of the rule] is "the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *aṇ*. In that regard, after words denoting living beings, herbs, or trees, these suffixes are used for both a part (*avayava*) and a modification (*vikāra*); however, after other words, they are used only for a modification. For example: *tarku-*, *tārkavam*. *Tarku-* is the citation of the base form.
*Tarku* is the name of a particular tree; its part or modification [is expressed by the suffix].

The meaning is "he knows. The suffix *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṭhora'ñ*. The word *tiṅīka*, by the rule *laghāvante*, has its middle syllable udātta. The suffix *aṇ* is an exception to the rules *anudātādeśca* and *ekatyañ*.
(1496) *trapujatuno ṣuk* [Pāṇini 4.3.138]: [the suffix *aṇ* is added to *trapu* and *jatun* with the augment *ṣuk*].
The suffix *ṣak* is applied after the words *trapu* and *jatu*. Thus, *trāpuṣam* and *jātuṣam*; the meaning is "a modification (*vikāra*) of tin (*trapu*) and lac (*jatu*)" respectively.

(Pāṇini 4.3.139) *or añ*. The suffix *añ* is applied after a stem ending in *o*. (Pāṇini 4.3.139) *or añ*. The meaning is "a modification (*vikāra*) of that which ends in *o*. For example: *āśmaḥ* ("made of stone") and *aurṇaḥ* ("made of wool"). (1497) *or añ*. 4.3.139.

The meaning is that after a word ending in *u*, the suffix *aḍ* (which becomes *a*) is applied. This occurs after words denoting living beings, herbs, and trees, both when referring to a part (*avayava*) and a product (*vikāra*); however, after other words, it occurs only for a product. For example: *daivadāravam* and *bhādradāravam*.
The meaning is "a part or a product of the *devadāru* tree" and "a part or a product of the *bhadradāru* tree."

Since these two [words] are udātta by virtue of the rule "ṭh-pīta-dvārthānām" and so forth, they do not fall under the scope of the rule "anudātādeśca" (Pāṇini 4.3.140). (1498) Anudātādeśca |4|3|140|.

[The rule] *anudātādeśca* [is stated]. The remainder [of the context] is that [the suffix] *añ* occurs when there is a product (*vikāra*). The sūtra *avayave ca* is also connected here. *Dādhittham* means "a part or a product of the *dadhittha* tree. Similarly, *kāpittham*. Amara states: "For the *kapittha* tree, however, the names are *dadhittha*, *grāhimanmatha*, and others."
Because these two are not derived from a fully inflected nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), they are accented on the final syllable by the *phiṭ* accent rule.
(Pāṇini 4.3.141) "Optionally after *palāśa* and others. The suffix *ṭhañ* is understood here. [The rule] applies only when [the compound] denotes a part (*avayava*).
Since [the suffix] *anudāttādi* applies invariably to *palāśa*, *khadira*, *raśmi*, and *syandana*, and does not apply at all to the others, this is an optional rule (*vikalpa*).
(1500) *śamyāḥ ślañ* || 4.4.142 || [The suffix] *ślañ* is applied after the word *śamyā*. (Pāṇini 4.4.142)

*Śamyāḥ ṣlañ*: The word *śamī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (belonging to the *gaurādi* group). The meaning is that the suffix *ṣlañ* occurs after this word when it is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-anta*), denoting either a part (*avayava*) or a modification (*vikāra*). The letters *ṣ* and *l* are indicatory (*it*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule *ṭhanudātādeśca*. For example: *śāmīlaṃ bhasma* ("ash from the *śamī* tree"), which is a modification (*vikāra*) of *śamī*.

This is the meaning. Regarding "śāmīlī sruc" (a ladle made of *śamī* wood): the meaning is that it is a modification (*vikāra*) of *śamyā*. In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, ladles made of *śamī* wood are well-known. However, in this context, *śāmīlī* refers to a branch. (Pāṇini 4.3.143: "The suffix *mayaṭ* is used for these two [words] in the common language (*bhāṣā*), except when they denote food or clothing."

Regarding the rule *mayaḍvaitayoḥ*: since the application of *mayaṭ* for both "modification" (*vikāra*) and "part" (*avayava*) would already be established by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) itself, the explicit mention of "of these two" (*etayoḥ*) is stated in the Bhāṣya to ensure that *mayaṭ* optionally applies even in the scope of exceptions mentioned previously and those yet to be mentioned. Consequently, forms such as *vilvamayam* and *vailvam* are derived.

Intending to say that [it] is accomplished, he says: "from mere primordial matter" (*prakṛtimātrāt*). This means "from all primordial matter. Regarding "made of stone" (*aśmamayam*): by relying on the case-ending contained within the suffix *mayaṭ*, it attains the status of a word (*padatva*), and thus the elision of the *n* occurs. Regarding "of stone" (*āśmanam*): there was a certain king named Kalmāṣāṅghri.

From his wife, Vasiṣṭha begot one named Aśmaka. The suffix *ka* is added to the word *aśman* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*); in the absence of that suffix, the name would simply be *Aśma*. The meaning is that he is a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) of him. Because of the rule "ṭhan" [Pāṇini 4.3.138], there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Furthermore, if it were intended to mean "modification," [the suffix] *ṭhañ* would apply to *aśman*...

The elision of the *ṭi* suffix in the case of *vikāra* (a derivative meaning "modification" or "product") is not to be suspected here, because the intention is that only the word *aśman*, which is well-known as denoting a stone, is to be understood.
(Pāṇini 4.3.144): "The suffix *aṇ* is always applied after words denoting 'old age' (*vṛddha*) and after *śara* and so forth."
"Always [the suffix] *vṛddhi*. This refers to the rule "ṭhmayaḍ. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the aforementioned optional rule. (1) "Always for a monosyllabic [stem].
Regarding "always for a monosyllabic [stem]," this is obtained through the division of the *yoga* (sūtra-split) from the word "always."

Regarding the word *āṇṇantāt*: this [water] belongs to the waters (*apām*), hence it is *āpam*. From that, by the rule "this belongs to it" (*tasyedam*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Then, for the sake of expressing the same meaning (*svārthe*), the suffix *ṣyañ* is added because it begins with the group starting with *caturvarṇa*; thus the form is *āpyam*. (1503) *gośca purīṣe* (Pāṇini 4.3.145).
[The suffix *mayaṅ*] is also applied after the word *go* (cow) when followed by *purīṣa* (dung). The rule "always *mayaṅ*" (*nityaṃ mayaṭ*) continues to apply. Thus we have *gomayam* (cow-dung).
Although dung is neither a modification (*vikāra*) nor a constituent part (*avayava*) of the cow, this suffix is nevertheless used in the sense of "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).

(1504) *piṣṭācca* | 4.3.146. Regarding *piṣṭācca*: he explains the sūtra by supplying the remaining words—*mayaṭ* shall be used in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*). (1505) *saṃjñāyāṃ kan* | 4.3.147. In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *kan* is applied.
The suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of a specific modification (*vikāraviśeṣa*). The meaning is "apūpa.
Thus he says: "pūpa, apūpa, and piṣṭaka would be [synonyms]. This is from the *Amarakośa*.
However, the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) is not a *piṣṭaka*, because it is not an *apūpa*.
From the Vedic scripture: "He makes a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) shaped like a raised thumb, the size of a horse's hoof.
(1506) *vrīheḥ puroḍāśe* |4|3|148|.
[The suffix] *mayaṭ* is used after the word *vrīhi* when referring to a modification in the form of a *puroḍāśa*; it is used invariably in such a modification consisting of a *puroḍāśa*.
The meaning is "it might be. If so, for what purpose is there an entry in the *bilvādi* group? To this he says: "the other is *vraiha*. (Pāṇini 4.3.149):
*asaṃjñāyāṃ tilayavābhyām*. [This sūtra provides for the suffix *aṇ* after the words *tila* and *yava* when they do not form a technical name (*saṃjñā*).]

In the case of *asaṃjñā* (non-technical names), [the suffixes] *tila* and *yava* [are used]. The remainder is "the suffix *mayaṭ* is always [used]. Regarding *yāvaka*: from the word *yava*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a product (*vikāra*). Then, by the rule "from *yāva* and so on," the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*). (1508) *tālādibhyo’ṇ* | Pāṇini 4.3.152. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after words beginning with *tāla*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *tāla*. The rule "after *tāla*, when [the compound denotes] a bow" (*tālāddhanuṣi*) is a *gaṇasūtra*. Thus, *tālaṃ dhanuḥ* ("a bow made of palmyra wood").

This is an exception to the suffix *mayaṭ* prescribed by the rule "always in the sense of 'made of' when the first member is a word with a long vowel" (*nityaṃ vṛddhe*). In the case of *aindrāyudham* ("Indra's bow"), this is an exception to the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule "after a word beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudātādeśca*), because the compound has a final acute accent (*antodātta*) due to the accentual rule governing compounds.

(1509) *jātarūpebhyaḥ parimāṇe* |4|3|153|. [The word] *jātarūpebhyaḥ*. [The suffix] *aṇ*. This completes the remainder [of the sūtra]. The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* shall occur after words denoting *jātarūpa*—that is, gold—when a measure (*parimāṇa*) is understood as a modification (*vikāra*). Now, [an objection]:...
To the question, "Why is the word *jātarūpa* itself not taken [as the example]," he says: "Because of the plural number.

Regarding *hāṭaka*, etc.: the meaning is a modification (*vikāra*) of *hāṭaka*, *tapanīya*, or gold (*suvarṇa*), measured by a *niṣka*. Regarding *tāpanīya*: [it is derived] according to the rule "nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.144).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *mayaṭ*. In other cases, however, it is an exception to the suffix *añ* [prescribed] by the rule *ṭhanudātādeśca*. According to Amara: "Five *guñjās* make one *ādyamāṣaka*; sixteen of those make one *akṣa*. And also: "*suvarṇa* and *vīsta* refer to an *akṣa* of gold."

(1510) *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* |4|3|154|. From words denoting living beings and from the *rajatādi* group, the suffix *añ* is applied. For example, *śaukam* and *bākam*. This means "a part or a modification of a parrot (*śuka*) or a crane (*baka*). Because [the base words] are udātta-accented by the rule *prāṇinaḥ kupūrvam* and so forth.

The suffix *añ* does not apply by the rule "ṭhanudātādeśca" [Pāṇini 4.3.140]. Regarding the word *rājatam*: since the suffix *añ* would already be established by virtue of its being anudātādi (having an anudātta initial vowel), this specific injunction for *añ* is intended to preclude the suffix *mayaṭ*. (1511) Pāṇini 4.3.155: "And [the suffix *añ* is applied] after a word ending in *ñit*, provided that it is a secondary derivative (*tatpratyaya*)."

"And because of the suffix *ñi* from that [rule]. "That suffix" (*tatpratyaya*) refers to the suffix [denoted by] *ñi* applied to those two: the modification (*vikāra*) and the part (*avayava*). Thus he says: "in the case of *ñi*. "Of those very two" means "of the modification and the part alone.
Regarding "of *śāmīla*": *śāmīla* is a modification or a part of *śamī*. [This is derived by] the rule "from *śamī*, the suffix *ṣyañ*."

The meaning is that when the sense is "a modification or a part of *śāmīla*," the suffix *añ* is applied, resulting in the form *śāmīlam*. This is an exception to the rule for *mayaṭ* [which applies] "always after a word with a heavy vowel" (*nityaṃ vṛddhe*). Regarding *dādhittham*:
it means a modification or a part of *dadhittha*. Because it begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), the suffix *añ* is applied. [This refers to] *dādhitthasya*.

The modification (*vikāra*) of *dādhitya* is [denoted by] *mayaṭ*, which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *añ*. Thus, in the case of *bailvamaya*, [the derivation is as follows]: from the word *bilva*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "from *bilva* and others, *aṇ*" (*bilvādibhyo 'ṇ*), resulting in *bailvaḥ*. When the sense is "its modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*), only *mayaṭ* is applied, and not *añ*. The point is that *aṇ* lacks the *ñit* designation [which would have triggered *añ*]. However, in the Bhāṣya...

This sūtra has been rejected on the grounds that suffixes [denoting possession] do not apply again after a word ending in a suffix expressing a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*), because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage; thus, it is stated:
(1512) *krītavat parimāṇāt* |4|3|156|. "As in the case of *krīta*, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a word denoting a measure."
"krītavatpari" means "as if purchased. "By means of an attribute" (upādhinā) means by means of a qualifier such as the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

"Naiṣkika" [is derived] with the suffix *ṭhak* in the sense of "purchased," according to the rule "after *niṣka* etc., when not in a compound, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied]. "Śatyaḥ" and "śatikaḥ" [are derived] with the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭhañ* in the sense of "purchased," according to the rule "after *śata*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭhañ* [are applied]."
(1513) *uṣṭrādvuñ* |4|3|157|. From the word *uṣṭra*, the suffix *vuñ* [is applied]. Regarding the rule *prāṇyaña*: this means it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo’ñ*.

(1514) *umā-ūrṇayor vā* |4|3|158|. The suffix *ṭhan* (*anu*) is understood as the remainder. Regarding the example *aumakam*: *umā* is a specific type of plant. As Amara states: "Umā may be *atasī* or *kṣumā*. The meaning is: a derivative or a part of *umā*.

Regarding the word *āṬmam*: the word *umā* is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "and [the words] for grasses and grains. Consequently, since there is no application of the suffix *vuñ*, and because it does not begin with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), the general suffix *aṇ* applies. However, the word *ūrṇā* is acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*) by the Phiṭ-sūtras; therefore, since it does not begin with an unaccented vowel, there is no application of the suffix *añ* when *vuñ* is absent—this is the meaning.

"Ṭhūrṇā" occurs in the sense of "the wool of a ram and so forth," according to Amarasimha; "Ṭhsthūṇorṇe napuṃsake ca" is a sūtra from the *Liṅgānuśāsana*. (1515) [The suffix] *ḍhañ* [is applied] after "eṇī. Pāṇini 4.3.159.
The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the word *eṇī*. A part or a modification (*avayava* or *vikāra*) of an *eṇī* is called *aiṇeyam*. The substitution of *ey* for *ḍha* occurs;
then, by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *ī*. He states the purpose of specifying the feminine gender: "But [in the case] of *eṇa*... and so forth.

(1516) *gopayasoryat* | Pāṇini 4.3.160. Regarding the rule *gopayasoryat*: [the suffix] *yat* is applied after the words *go* and *payas*. For example, *gavyam* means "a modification or a part of a cow. [In this formation], the substitution of *ava* for *au* occurs by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*. *Payasyam* means "a modification of milk."

Since the rule "yaT" would already apply everywhere in cases where there is the possibility of suffixes such as *goraja* and others, the specific prescription "mayaḍ vaitayoḥ" is for the purpose of setting aside the optional *mayaṬ*. (1517) *droś ca* | Pāṇini 4.3.161.

And after [the word] *dro* [the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied]; this is the remainder [of the rule]. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to both [the rules] "after a monosyllabic [word], *mayaṭ* is obligatory" and "after *dhara*, *rañ*.
(1518) *māne vayaḥ* | 4.3.162 | [The suffix *vaya* is applied after a word denoting a measure.]

"Regarding measure (*māna*): [the suffix] *vayap* [is applied]. This means that when a derivative (*vikāra*) in the sense of "measure" is to be understood, the suffix *vayap* shall be applied after the word *dru*. (1519) "Elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] when it refers to the fruit (*phala*). 4.3.163.

*Phale luk* (the suffix is elided when the word means "fruit"). For example, *āmalakam*. When a tree has borne fruit, its fruit is both a part (*avayava*) and a product (*vikāra*). In that case, the suffix *mayaṭ* is elided; because of the rule *ṭhluktāddhitalukī* ("when an *addhita* suffix is elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is also elided"), the *ṅīṣ* is dropped. (1520) *Plakṣādibhyo’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.164): [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after words beginning with *plakṣa*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *plakṣa*. The remainder [of the rule] is "in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). In that context, since the words *śigru* and *karkandhū* end in a vowel of the *u*-class, the suffix *añ* would otherwise apply;
and since *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and so on, begin with an unaccented vowel, the suffix *añ* would also apply. Therefore, this rule ordains *aṇ*. Now, regarding its fruit:
To explain why there is no elision (*luk*) for the suffix *aṇ*, he says: "In the case of the rule for formation" (*vidhāne*). (Pāṇini 7.3.5) "And of *nyagrodha* alone.
[The commentary explains: "And of *nyagrodha*"—this is the subsequent rule [7.3.3] beginning with "not after *y* or *v*" (*na yvābhyām*). "Of this" means of the word *nyagrodha* when it stands alone.

The meaning is "of the *nyagrodha* tree. "Solely" (*kevalatvam*) means being devoid of any other word. Even though [the form] would be established by the rule *nayvābhyām* alone under the etymological analysis *nyak rohati iti nyagrodhaḥ*—since the letter *y* is at the end of a word (*padāntatvāt*)—nevertheless, the expression "of the sole [word]" is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*).

The Sūtra: [This rule applies] in the alternative view where there is no derivation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*); however, because the letter *y* is not at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*), it serves solely for the purpose of the grammatical injunction (*vidhy-artham*). What is the purpose of using the word "alone" (*kevalasya*)? [Answer: As in *nyāgrodhamūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice plants rooted at the base of a banyan tree"). (1522) *jambvā vā* | Pāṇini 4.3.165.

Or [the word] *jambū*. Regarding *jambū*: it means "the fruit of the *jambu* tree. Since the suffix *añ* is elided (*luk*), the form is neuter in accordance with the gender of the substantive; this is the intended meaning. (1523) *Lup ca* | Pāṇini 4.3.166.

"And there is elision (*lup*). Since the desired form is already established by simple elision (*luk*), he states the purpose of this rule regarding the formation of case-endings (*subvidhi*): "In the case of *lup*, it is like the original base" (*lupi yuktavat*), as in the example *jambūḥ*. The meaning is "the fruit of the *jambu* tree. When there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix denoting the fruit, because it is treated like the original base, the gender and number of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) are set aside, and instead the feminine gender and singular number [of the base] are applied. And so it is:
The fruits of the *jambū* tree are also [called] *jambū*.
[This is] an addition [to the rule] regarding those that wither at the ripening of their fruit (*phalapākaśuṣ*).
Regarding "at the ripening of their fruit" (*phalapāke*): those plants which wither through the ripening of their fruit are "those that wither at the ripening of their fruit" (*phalapākaśuṣaḥ*).

The meaning is that there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the elision (*lup*) of the suffix denoting the fruit (*phala-pratyaya*) after words expressing those [plants]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "there is elision when [the word] denotes the fruit" (*phale luk*). For example, *vrīhayaḥ* ("rice grains") means "the fruits of the plants known as *vrīhi*. Similarly, *mudgāḥ* ("mung beans"). In the case of *bilva* and others, there is elision of the *aṇ* suffix.
The masculine gender [of the compound] is due to its taking on the form of the [first] member (*yuktavadbhāva*), and not because it is dependent on the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*).

Regarding the rule "in the case of *puṣpa* and *mūla*, [the suffix is] frequently elided" (*puṣpamūleṣu bahulam*): this is a *vārttika*. It means that there is elision (*lup*) of the suffixes denoting a derivative or a part (*vikārāvayavapratyaya*).

The word "syāt" (it may be) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding the example "mallikā" as a flower: since the rule "atha dvitīyaṃ prāg īṣāt" is understood to follow, the word *mallikā* is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) by the *phiṭ-sūtra* "mādīnāṃ ca. Thereafter, the suffix *añ* is elided by the rule "anudātādeś ca."

The feminine gender [of *jāti*] is due to its being treated like that which it qualifies (*yuktavat*). Regarding the word *jāti*: by the rule "the final syllable is udātta when followed by a light vowel" (*laghāvante*), the word *jāti* is udātta on its final syllable. From that, by the rule "after a word beginning with an anudātta, there is *aṇ*" (*anudātādeśca*), the suffix *añ* is elided (*lup*) by this [present rule]. The feminine gender is due to its being treated like that which it qualifies. Thus, *jāti* is udātta on its final syllable by the rule "the final syllable is udātta when followed by a light vowel."

It is a generic term (*jātiśabda*). Therefore, by the rule "ṭhanudātādeśca," there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *añ*. Because it possesses the same properties as the base (*yuktavadbhāva*), it retains its feminine gender. Thus, *vidārī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, which is an affix belonging to the class of generic terms;
it is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the suffix. Since it begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), the suffix *añ* is elided.

The feminine gender [of *pāṭalā*] is due to its being treated as the base itself (*yuktavat*). Regarding *pāṭalāni*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the *bilva*-group. Similarly, *sālvāni*. Now, one might object: in cases such as "the flower of the *aśoka* is *aśoka*" and "the flower of the *karavīra* is *karavīra*," since the elision (*lup*) occurs by the rule "frequently in the case of flowers and roots" (*puṣpamūleṣu bahulam*), the word would be masculine due to being treated as the base (*yuktavat*), resulting in forms like *aśokaḥ puṣpam*.

Since it might be argued that [the word] *karavīra* would be [a neuter] *puṣpa*, he says: "because of the inclusion of the term *bahula*. Thus, since the application of the rule for agreement with the qualifier (*yuktavatva*) does not occur, there is indeed agreement with the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣyanighnatva*). This is the intended meaning. (1524) *Haritakyādibhyaś-ca* | Pāṇini 4.3.167.

"And from *harītakī* and others. This refers to the rule concerning *harītakī* and so forth; this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that for these [words], only the gender (*liṅga*) of the base (*prakṛti*) is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the meaning of the elided suffix, but not the number (*vacana*) of the base as well. For example: *harītakyaḥ*; here, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added because it denotes a genus (*jāti*).

The word *harītakī* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of its suffixal accent (*pratyayasvara*). Consequently, because it begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātādi*), when the suffix *añ* is applied, the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ* when it denotes the fruit" would apply; however, since the suffix is elided (*lup*), the feminine gender is maintained as if the suffix were present (*yuktavadbhāva*), and the plural number is used in accordance with the gender of the substantive.

(1525) *kaṃsīyaparaśabdayoryañañau luk ca* | 4|3|168 | Regarding the words *kaṃsīya* and *para*: here, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ*, because that would render the rule meaningless. Nor is there elision of the two bases, since *luk* is defined specifically as the non-appearance of a suffix. Therefore—
By process of elimination, it is understood that the suffixes *cha* and *yañ* are applied to a portion of the base (*prakṛti*).
Thus he says: "after *cha* and *yañ*. Regarding *kāṃsīyam*: *kaṃsa* is the name of a metal, a specific type of ore.

[The suffix] *cha* is applied in the sense of "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*). Regarding *kāṃsyam*: when the suffix *yañ* is applied to the word *kaṃsīya*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha*.

In the case of *ādivṛddhi*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. Regarding the word *paraśabdam*: under the governing rule *tasmai hitam*, the suffix *ya* is applied by the rule *ugavādibhyo ya*; then, the *guṇa* substitution for *u* occurs, and the vowel *a* is substituted for the final *v* by the rule *vānto yi*. Regarding *pāraśava*: from the word *paraśava*, the suffix *añ* is applied, and the *yat* portion is elided.

In the case of *orguṇa* (the substitution of *guṇa* for *o*), the form is *pāraśavaḥ*. However, [the elision of the suffix] does not apply by the rule *ṭhhalastaddhitasya*, because the word *īti* is understood as being carried over (*anuvṛtti*).
The intention is that since it is not a descendant (*apatya*), the elision [of the suffix] by the rule *āpatyasya ca* also does not occur.
Thus ends the section on *prāgdīvyatīya* suffixes in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on *prāgghitīya*.
(1605) *prāgghitādyat* | Pāṇini 4.4.75. [The suffix] *yat* is applied after [stems ending in] *prāgghita* [to form feminine nouns].

Now the section concerning *prāg-dhita* is examined: *prāg-dhitād yat*. The word *dhita* refers here to the sūtra containing that term; thus he says: "that which is beneficial for it" (*tasyai hitam*). (Pāṇini 4.4.76: *tad-vahati ratha-yuga-prāsaṅgam*. The suffix *yat* is applied after words beginning with *dhita* when they mean "beneficial for that," provided the word is used in the dative case. (Pāṇini 4.4.76: The suffix *yat* is applied to the words *ratha*, *yuga*, and *prāsaṅga* when they signify "that which carries or draws that."

The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ratha* (chariot) and others in the sense of "that which carries it. The meaning is that the suffix *yat* occurs after the three words *ratha*, *yuga*, and *prāsaṅga* when they are in the accusative case. Regarding the term *yugya*:
at the time of carrying a chariot or similar vehicle, that wooden pole which is slightly fixed or attached across the shoulders of horses and other animals is called *yauka*.

The meaning is "the obstruction of that. Regarding the phrase "at the time of training": having yoked two well-trained horses to pull the chariot and so forth, and having attached another yoke to their shoulders, untrained horses and the like are yoked to it for the purpose of training them in pulling; that is called *prāsaṅga*. [The definition: "*Prāsaṅga* is..."
"Yuga-ādyaugam" [is] Amarasimha’s lexicon.
(1607) *dhuro yaḍḍhakau* | Pāṇini 4.4.77. Regarding "dhuro yaḍḍhakau": from the word *dhur*, ending in the accusative case, the suffixes *yat* and *ḍhak* are applied in the sense of "carrying."

The meaning is "it might be. There is an alternative reading: *ṭhyaḍḍhakaño'viti*. Regarding the rule *hali ca*: [the root] *dhurvī* means "to injure"; by the rule *bhrājabhāsa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.177), the suffix *kvip* is applied; then by the rule *rāllopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.21), the *r* is elided.
A *dhuḥ* is the part of a yoke that is carried on the neck of horses and other animals. From the word *dhur*, when the suffix *yat* is added, [the form *dhurya* arises] by the rule *hali ca*.
The meaning is: "when length has been obtained.
(1608) *na bhakurchurām* | 8|2|79|.

[The rule] *na bhakurchurām* [is stated]. From the rule *ṛtvoḥ upadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* is carried over; thus, [the prohibition applies] to the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

And it follows [the previous rule]. Thus he says with the words "of *bha*, etc. Amara states: "Those who bear the yoke are called *dhurya*, *dhaureya*, and *dhurīṇa*. (1609) *khaḥ sarvadhurāt* | Pāṇini 4.4.78.
*khaḥ* [is substituted] for *sarvadhurāt*. *Sarvadhūr* is *sarvadhurā*. It is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *ṭhpūrvakāla-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

The suffix *ṛkpū-* (Pāṇini 5.4.74) applies as the final member of the compound. Because it is feminine by the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Pāṇini 2.4.26), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. However, in this instance, the neuter gender is used with reference to the phonetic form of the word itself.
The meaning is that the suffix *kha* occurs after the word *sarvadhura*, which ends in the second case (accusative), in the sense of "carrying. Thus, *sarvadhurīṇaḥ*;
the meaning is "one who carries all burdens. As Amara states: "But he is *sarvadhurīṇa* who is a carrier of all burdens (*sarvadhurāvahaḥ*)."
(1610) *ekadhurāl luk ca* | Pāṇini 4.4.79.

From the word *ekadhurā*, when it ends in the second case, the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of "bearing" (*vahati*). There is also the option of its elision (*luk*). Thus, we have *ekadhurīṇaḥ* ("one who bears a single yoke") and *ekadhuraḥ*. [This refers to] one who carries a single yoke (*ekadhurām*).
The meaning is "it carries.
(1611) *Śakaṭādaṇ* | Pāṇini 4.4.80. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *śakaṭa* ending in the second case, in the sense of "it carries"; this is the meaning.
Because of the subsequent exception:
(1612) *halasīrāṭṭhak* | P. 4.4.81.
The suffix *ṭhak* is added after the words *hala* and *sīra*, provided they are in the accusative case, in the sense of "that which carries [them]. This is the meaning.

(1613) *saṃjñāyāṃ janyāḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.82. Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ janyāḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *yat* is applied after the word *janī* ending in the accusative case, in the sense of "carrying," provided it forms a name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, *janī* means "bride" (*vadhū*), in the sense that "in her a fetus is produced" (*jāyate 'syāṃ garbhaḥ*).

The sense is that the word *janī* is derived from the root *jan* by adding the suffix *iṇ*, with the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "janivadhyośca," and then the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule "kṛdikārādaktinaḥ. Amara states: "A daughter-in-law (*snuṣā*), a wife (*janī*), and a mother-in-law (*vadhū*) are synonyms for *samāḥ*. [This applies] to the word *vahantī*.
The commentary [explains] "prāpyanti" (they reach). The word "varagṛham" (the bridegroom’s house) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding "janyāḥ" (kinsmen/friends):

the word "jāmātuḥ vayasyāḥ" (the friends of the bridegroom) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Amara states: "janyāḥ snigdhā varasya ye" (those who are the affectionate friends of the bridegroom are called janyas).
(Pāṇini 4.4.83) "vidhyatyadhanuṣā" (he pierces with something other than a bow).
"He pierces without a bow. The word *tat* (that) follows from the previous rule as the object in the accusative case.

In the expression *adhanuṣā*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the seventh case (*saptamī*). *Adhanuḥ* means "the absence of a bow"; the meaning is "when that [absence] exists. This is an instance where the negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) is optionally employed instead of the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) in the sense of the non-existence of an object.

Because it has been stated thus: [the suffix] *yat* occurs after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyāntāt*) in the sense of "pierces" (*vidhyati*), provided that there is an absence of the bow (*dhanus*) as the instrument (*karaṇa*). "If not in this case" (*na cetra*) means: if, in that piercing, the bow is not the instrument. "Padyā" (*padyā*): from the word *pāda*, with the suffix *yat* [added], the substitution of *pad* occurs by the rule *padyatyatadarthe*; [this is used] with the expression "without a bow" (*adhanuṣā*).
What [is the example]? "Devadatta pierces the thief with a bow. Here, the suffix *yan* does not occur after the word "thief" (*cora*).

Nor should it be argued that *yan* does not occur here simply because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*); for since the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) in "pierces" (*vidhyati*) is the primary element, its semantic competency remains intact even when it is dependent on another factor. Otherwise...

In examples such as *ṭhāṭpagavo devadatta upagunaptṛtvāt*, the suffix *aṇ* and others would not apply; furthermore, because a portion of the meaning of the suffix— namely, the act of piercing (*vyadhana*)— is invariably dependent upon a specific instrument, this is explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

(1615) *dhanagaṇaṃ labdhā* | Pāṇini 2.3.84. The meaning is that the suffix *yat* is applied after the words *dhana* and *gaṇa*, ending in the accusative case, in the sense of "having obtained. Now, one might object: since the word *labdhṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛc*, it is a *kṛdanta* (a derivative formed by a primary suffix), and therefore, when used in conjunction with [these nouns], [the rule regarding the sixth case would apply].

One might think that the genitive case should occur here [in the sense of the object], and therefore he says: "This [word] ends in *tṛn*. Thus, the intention is that the genitive does not apply because of the prohibition [contained in Pāṇini 2.3.69]: *na loke*.
(1616) *annāṇṇaḥ* | 4.4.85 | [The suffix] *ṇa* is applied after the root *ad* (to eat). (Pāṇini 4.4.85)
[The suffix] *anya* [is added]. The remainder [of the rule] is that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of "having obtained" (*labdha*).
(1617) *vaśaṃ gataḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.86. The meaning is that the suffix *yat* is added after the word *vaśa* ending in the second case in the sense of "gone to" (*gata*). [Thus: *vaśya*.

Thus [it is said]. The analysis of the compound is *vaśaṃ gataḥ* (gone under control). [The root] *vaś* [is used] in the sense of "desire" (*kānti*). Desire is longing (*icchā*). *Vaśa* is the act of desiring. According to the rule *vaśiraṇyor upasaṅkhyānam*, the suffix *ap* is applied. Thus, *vaśam* means desire; *gataḥ* means reached or attained. The meaning is "dependent on desire. It will be stated in the section on the elision of verbal suffixes (*lug-vikaraṇa*) that the root *vaś* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

The meaning is that this is the general rule (*tatprāyika*). Since everything follows its own will, he says "following the will of another" (*parecchānusārī*). (1618) *pada* [is used] in this sense [of "visible"] by Pāṇini 4.4.87.
The word *pada* is seen here [as the base]. This means that from the word *pada* ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntāt*), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "that which is seen.

Here, the word *tat*, which is understood from the previous rule and ends in the accusative (*dvitīyāntam*), is transformed into the nominative. (Pāṇini 4.4.88: *mūlam asyāvarhi*. "That whose root has been pulled out. [Note: The full sūtra is *mūlam asyāvarhi yat*. It prescribes the suffix *yat* after *mūla* when it is in the genitive case, provided that the root of the plant has been pulled out.]

"Ābarhi" means its root; "ābarhaṇa" means uprooting. Due to the influence of the prefix (upa-sarga), the verbal root *bṛh* (meaning "to lift up") functions here in the sense of uprooting. "Mūlyā mudgāḥ" means that they are to be uprooted from the root.
(1620) *saṃjñāyāṃ dhenuṣyā* |4|4|89|.

Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ dhenuṣyā*: [the suffix] *yap* is also applied. The intention is that if the suffix *yat* were used, it would be subject to the accentuation of the *tit* (the final vowel of the suffix). Thus, *dhenuṣyā*.
This refers to a cow which, for the purpose of milking, has been pledged by the debtor to the creditor.

This designation is applied to her; thus it says, "remaining as a pledge" (*bandhake sthitā*). This is the statement of Amara. The governing rule (*adhikāra*) beginning with "in a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) extends until the end of the chapter.
For by "name," conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is intended.
(1621) *ñya* [is added] after *gṛhapatinā* [in the sense of "connected with"].

4.4.90. Regarding the word *gṛhapatinā*: the meaning is that the suffix *ñya* occurs after the word *gṛhapati* ending in the third case when this sense [of being connected with] is intended. For example, *gārhapatyo 'gniḥ* ("the Gārhapatya fire"). This means a particular kind of fire. In that context...

In the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and the *agnihotra*, there is a connection with the householder (*gṛhapati*), because the oblation dedicated to the deity who is the householder is being performed. Even though, in the case of the *devasū* oblations, there is an offering of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eight potsherds to Agni Gṛhapati, as stated in the text: "He offers the sacrificial cake on eight potsherds to Agni Gṛhapati."
It is performed on the Āhavanīya fire; nevertheless, because of the governing role of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), its application is not [restricted] solely to the Āhavanīya.
Pāṇini 5.2.91: *nau-vayo-dharma-viṣa-mūla-sītā-tulābhyaḥ tārya-tulya-prāpya-vadhyā-ānāmya-sama-samita-saṃmiteṣu*.
