From the words *nau* (boat), *vayas* (age), *dharma* (duty), *viṣa* (poison), *mūla* (root), *sītā* (furrow), and *tulā* (scale), the suffix *yat* is applied respectively when the following meanings are expressed: that which is to be crossed (*tārya*), that which is equal (*tulya*), that which is to be reached (*prāpya*), that which is to be killed (*vadhyā*), that which is to be bent (*ānāmya*), that which is even (*sama*), and that which is measured (*saṃmita*). [Examples: *nāvā tāryam* = *nāvyam* (crossable by boat); *vayasā tulyaḥ* = *vayasīyaḥ* (equal in age); *dharmeṇa prāpyam* = *dharmyam* (attainable through duty); *viṣeṇa vadhyam* = *vaiṣyam* (to be killed by poison); *mūlenānāmyam* = *mūlyam* (to be bent/bought for the root-price); *sītayā samam* = *sītyam* (even with the furrow); *tulayā saṃmitam* = *tulyam* (measured by a scale/equal).

The meaning is "that which may exist" in the case of a sense that is both equal (*samita*) and comparable (*saṃmita*). It is understood from the context that this refers to words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāntebhyaḥ*), because such a [third-case] application is possible only when joined with words like *tārya* (to be crossed) in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the cause (*hetu*), and when joined with words like *tulya* (equal). In this regard:

The non-formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder compound) is for the sake of ensuring that the two base words (*mūlaśabdau*) apply according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Otherwise, there would be the misconception that a suffix is applied to each one of the seven bases (*prakṛti*) across all eight meanings.
The word *tāryam* means "capable of being crossed" (*tarītum śakyam*). [It is derived by] the rule *ṛ-halor ṇyat*. It is equal in age (*vayasā tulya*).
Thus [it is said]: this term *pratyaya* refers only to a friend (*mitra*) and not to an enemy, because it falls under the heading of "designation" (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the phrase "that which is bent down by the principal" (*mūlenānāmyam*): the "principal" (*mūla*) is the capital invested by merchants for the purpose of producing cloth and other goods.
That additional amount of wealth which is "bent down"—that is, paid as interest—along with that principal, belongs to the seller.

The meaning is that its price is obtained by means of agreement (*saṃmatīkaraṇa*). However, people in common usage treat all the wealth obtained by the seller as the "price" (*mūlya*); in that case, it should be understood as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which may be either current (*sāṃpratikī*) or conventional (*nirūḍhā*). Regarding the word *sītayā*: *sītā* is the track of a plough; by that [track].
*Samitam* means "joined together," that is to say, "plowed. *Tulā* means "a scale"; the meaning is "measured by it.
(1623) [Pāṇini 4.4.92: *Dharma*, *pathin*, *artha*, and *nyāya* [are used in the sense of] "not deviating from" [the preceding word].

The meaning is that the suffix *yat* is applied after the words *dharma*, *pathin*, *artha*, and *nyāya* in the sense of "not departed from" (*anapeta*). Because of the context, it is understood that these words must be in the ablative case. *Dharmāt anapetam* means "not fallen away from dharma. *Pathyam* means "not departed from the path. *Nyāyyam* means [not departed from justice].
The meaning is "not deviating from the rule.
(1624) *cchandaso nirmite* |4|4|93|.

[The suffix *yat* is applied] after the word *cchandas*, in the sense of "constructed," when [the word] ending in the third case is present. That is to say, the meaning is "that which is constructed from the *cchandas*."
Regarding the word *icchayā*: the sense is that the word *chandaḥ* denotes desire (*icchā*). Amara states: "The word *chandaḥ* [is used] in the sense of verse and in the sense of desire.
(Pāṇini 4.4.94): *uraso 'ṇ ca*.
"From *uras*, the suffix *añ* [is added]. The remainder [of the rule] is "in the sense of 'constructed from' when ending in the third case. Regarding *aurasya*:
the intention is that this is based on the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which says, "You are born from limb after limb; you are produced from the heart.
The term "son" (*putra*) is understood from the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning technical designations (*saṃjñā*).
(1626) *hṛdayasya priyaḥ* | 4|4|95 | The meaning is that the suffix *yat* is applied after the word *hṛdaya*, ending in the genitive case, in the sense of "dear to the heart.
(1627) *bandhane ca ṛṣau* | 4|4|96 | [The suffix *yat* is applied] also in the sense of "bond" when referring to a seer (*ṛṣi*).

In the case of *bandhana* and *carṣa*. (1628) *mata-jana-halāt karaṇa-jalpaka-rṣeṣu* |4|4|98|. [The word] "from *mata*, *jana*, and *hala*" [is understood]. [The suffix] *ya* is applied to these [words] in these senses respectively; this is the remainder [of the rule]. *Mataṃ*...
Regarding the word *jñāna*: the intention is that it is formed from the verbal root *man* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Regarding the word *karaṇa*:
the term *karaṇa* is derived from the verbal root *kṛ* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of either an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus, the meaning is that what is intended is either the act of producing (*jananakriyā*) or the means of production (*jananasādhana*). Regarding the word *satya*.
The meaning is: "the act of producing knowledge" or "the means for producing [knowledge].

(1629) *tatra sādhuḥ* |4|4|98|. The meaning of *tatra sādhuḥ* is: the suffix *yat* occurs after a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*) in the sense of "skilled in that" (*sādhu*). For example: *āgrayaḥ*.

The meaning is "excellent" (*sādhu*) at the beginning. Here, *sādhu* is understood as "expert" (*pravīṇa*), and not as "beneficial" (*hita*), because the latter sense will be addressed later by the rule *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5).
(1630) Pāṇini 4.4.99: *pratijanādibhyaḥ khañ*.

The suffix *khañ* is applied after words such as *pratijana*. The meaning is simply "suitable for that. The sense is that the suffix *khañ* occurs after these words ending in the locative case when the meaning is "suitable for that. For example, *prātijanīna*:
*pratijanam* is an indeclinable *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (distributive sense). The meaning is "suitable for each individual person. Similarly, *vaiśvajanīna*.

(1631) *bhaktāṇṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.100. From the word *bhakta*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied; the remainder of the sense is that it means "fit for" (*sādhu*) when [the base] ends in the locative case. (1632) *pariṣado ṇyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.101. [The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the word *pariṣad* in the same sense.]
The suffix *ṇya* [is applied] after *pariṣad*. The remainder [of the rule] is: "the meaning is 'one who is fit for' (*sādhu*), provided it ends in the locative case.

Regarding "the rule" (*yoga*): *pariṣadaḥ* is the first rule; its meaning is that the suffix *ṇa* should be applied after *pariṣad*. Following that, *ṇyaḥ* is the second rule; its meaning is that the suffix *ṇya* should be applied after *pariṣad*.
(1633) *kathādibhyaṣṭhak* | 4.4.102 | The rule *kathādibhyaṣṭhak* and so forth is clear. (1634) *guḍādibhyaṣṭhañ* | 4.4.103 |
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words such as *guḍa*. For example, *sāktuko yavaḥ* ("barley fit for groats"). The meaning is "that which is suitable for groats" (*saktuṣu sādhuh*).

Because it belongs to the *guḍādi* group, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; since the stem ends in a vowel (*u*), the *ṭha* of *ṭhañ* is replaced by *ka*. (1635) Pāṇini 4.4.104: The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the words *pathin*, *atithi*, *vasati*, and *svapati*.
*Pathya*, *atithi*, and so forth, are clear.

(1636) *samānatīrthe vāsī* |4|4|107|. [The suffix *cha* is added] after the word *samānatīrtha* ending in the locative case, in the sense of "one who dwells there. *Samānatīrthe vāsī*. [This means one who dwells at the same sacred ford. From the word *samānatīrtha* ending in the seventh case, [the suffix *cha* is applied] in the sense of "he dwells" (*vasati*).
The meaning is "that which exists. [The form] *vāsī* means "one who dwells"; the suffix *ṇini* is applied because the root *grah* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇas*.

The word *tīrtha* is explained by the term *gurau* (in the teacher). [The form] *satīrthya* is derived from the word *samānatīrtha* with the suffix *yat*, where, according to the rule *tīrthe ye*, the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs.

(1637) *samānodare śayita o codāttaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.4.108. The meaning is: after the word *samānodara* ending in the seventh case, the suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of "one who has lain down," and the vowel *o* [of the base] becomes udātta. The explanation of the term *śayita* is "one who has stayed" (*sthita*).
The sense is that such usage is observed in examples like *kuśeśayam* (lying in the grass) and *jaleśayam* (lying in the water). Regarding *samānodaryaḥ*:

it is a compound meaning "one who has the same womb" (*samānam udaram*). When the analysis (*vigraha*) is formed and the compound is established by the rule *pūrvāparaprathamā-* etc., the acute accent (*udātta*) on the vowel *o* replaces the *titsvara* (the accent prescribed for suffixes ending in *ti*). This is governed by the rule *vibhāṣodare*.
Thus, when the inherent state (*sabhāva*) is absent, there is the form [of the suffix].
Regarding *sodarād yaḥ*: the remainder [of the rule] is "after a word ending in the locative case, in the sense of 'lying upon'."

Because the suffix *ti* is absent, this word is acutely accented on the final syllable by the rule *pratyayasya ca*. The substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* occurs by the rule *vibhāṣodare*. However, in the passage "even a brother (*sodara*) abandons one who is traveling on the wrong path," the substitution of *sa-* for the word *sa-*—which is a synonym for *samāna*—occurs within the *bahuvrīhi* compound by the rule *vopasarjanasya*.
*Bodhyaḥ*. In this same manner, [the forms] *yatra bhrātā sahodaraḥ* and so forth are also established. Thus ends the section on *prāg-dhītīya* suffixes in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the section on the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

(89) *plutapragṛhyā aci nityam* | 6|1|125|. Now, regarding the term "prakṛtibhāva" (the state of original form): the word "is being examined" (*nirūpyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Pluta and pragṛhya": this means they will be explained by the rules beginning with *dūrāddhūte ca* and *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*.
Regarding the word *prakṛtyā*: the sense is that this [rule] follows from the previous rule, "by nature (*prakṛtyā*) within a quarter-verse" (*antaḥpādam*).
The meaning is that they should remain as they are by their very nature (*svabhāvena*). That is to say, euphonic combinations (*saṃdhi*) do not occur.
For example: *ehi kṛṣṇā3 atra*. Here, the vowel *a* [is substituted] for the nasal *ṇ* by the rule "also when calling from a distance" (*dūrāddhūte ca*).

The *pluta* vowel: for it, there is no long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrgha*) when followed by the vowel *a*. As in *harī etau*. According to the rule *ṛt-īdūded-dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, the vowel *ī* following *ṛ* is *pragṛhya*. For that [vowel], the substitution of *yaṇ* does not take place. Now, one might object: since the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) in the preceding sūtra is unaccented (*asvarita*), [the optionality] would apply everywhere.

He asks: "What is the purpose of including the word *nitya* (always) here, given that [the desired] non-application (*nivṛtti*) is already established? He provides the answer: "In the case of *harī etau*. Only when the word *nitya* is included does this very rule—"ṭhplutapragṛhyā acī" (A 6.1.125)—apply exclusively as the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in examples such as *harī etau*.

The meaning is "it might be. The word *yathā* is used in the sense of suitability (*yogyatā*). This very [substitution] is suitable to be obtained as the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form). And that would be obtained provided there is the mention of the term *nitya* (invariable);
such is the meaning. The same applies to similar cases hereafter. He shows what is excluded by the word *eva* (only/indeed): namely, the rule regarding *ik*.

The *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) accompanied by the short vowel—as prescribed by the rule to be stated later, "ṭhiko 'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca"—should not occur; that is, it must not take effect. [In this context,] *māṅ* is used with the *luṅ* suffix; it is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). If the mention of the word *nitya* were not made here, then because of its subsequent position in the sequence of rules, the *prakṛtibhāva* accompanied by the short vowel according to Śākalya’s view would apply.

[Otherwise] it would follow [that both apply]. However, when the word "nitya" (invariable) is included, by its very force, the subsequent Śākala rule—"ṭh-pluta-pragṛhyāḥ"—which prescribes a *prakṛti-bhāva* combined with shortening (*hrasva*), is superseded by the *prakṛti-bhāva* alone; such is the meaning.

(90) *iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca* | Pāṇini 6.1.127. Regarding *iko'savarṇe*: the term *ik* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). From the previous rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati*, the word *padāntāt* is understood (*anuvartate*) and is transformed into the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyantatayā*) to agree with *ik*.

The term *ṭhac* also carries over [from the previous rule]. Consequently, one sentence is: "An *ik* at the end of a word (*padānta*) shall become short (*hrasva*) when followed by an *ac* that is not homogeneous (*asavarṇa*). From the word *ca* (and), the term *prakṛtyā* (in its original form) is drawn over from the rule *antaḥpādaṃ prakṛtyā*. The term *hrasva* is also connected there. Thus, what was stated...

The sentence "it remains short by nature, that is, by its own essence" is thus formed. He states the resulting meaning with the words beginning "ikaḥ at the end of a word," and so forth. If the letter *ca* were not employed, then one would only obtain the rule: "a short vowel shall occur for an *ik* at the end of a word when followed by a non-homogeneous *ac*. Of that [rule]...

Otherwise, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical modification) would not be obtained for the short vowel. Consequently, when *cakrī-atra* is established and the short vowel *ī* undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution, the result would be only *cakryatra*;
the form *vakri-atra*, characterized by the *prakṛtibhāva* combined with the short vowel, would not occur. Yet, that form is indeed desired.
Therefore, the intention of the author of the Sūtras is that the particle *ca* is necessary for the purpose of drawing over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *prakṛtyā*.
(91) *hrasvaśca* | 6.1.127 | [The substitute *hrasva* also occurs].

He states the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya: "In this case, [the word] *hrasva* [is used]. Here, the particle *ca* (and) should not be employed, because its attraction (*anukarṣa*) from the preceding rule would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that its purpose is to prevent the substitution of *yaṇ* for the prescribed short vowel; for the prevention of *yaṇ* follows by the very force of the rule prescribing the short vowel.

The meaning is that it is established in the Bhāṣya that the particle *ca* need not be included for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *prakṛtyā*, because the desired result is accomplished otherwise; [otherwise], one would simply have prescribed the *yaṇ* substitution.

Thus, in the form *cakri-atra*, the short vowel occurs under the view where *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) does not apply; however, under the view where that [preservation] is absent, [the form is different].

The form here is *yaṇicakryatra*. Nor should one suspect the elision of the letter *k* by the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca*, because the *yaṇ* [substitution] is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original) by the rule *acaḥ parasmin*; since it is thus an *ac*, there is no *saṃyoga* (conjunction of consonants) at the end of the word. Nor does the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe* apply here.

The prohibition [of the application of Pāṇini 1.1.56] by the rule *na sthānivat* should not be suspected, because of the statement: "The fault of that [rule applies] only in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* for *r*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. "Not in a compound" (*na samāse*). This is a Vārttika. The meaning is that the aforementioned Śākala rule does not apply in a compound.
Regarding *vāpyaśva*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is *vāpyām aśvaḥ*.
Alternatively, because the group beginning with *śauṇḍa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, it is a compound by the rule *sup-supā*.
Regarding the rule *siti ca*: that which has *s* as its *it* is *sit*; when such a [suffix] follows, the *śākala* operation previously mentioned does not take place.
The meaning is "it exists. Regarding *pārśvam*: *parśu* refers to the rib-bone (*upārśvāsthi*). A collection of ribs is *pārśvam*.

[The suffix] *ṇas* is prescribed [after *parśu*] by the rule "ṭhparśvā ṇas vaktavyaḥ. There is initial *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitution of *yaṇ*. Here, when the form *pārśu-a* has been established, the rule of Śākalya mentioned [above] does not apply. Nor does the *guṇa* substitution of *oḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146) apply.

Because that [suffix] is prescribed for this very [word], and since the designation *pada*—by the rule "also when followed by *s*" (*siti ca*)—sublates the designation *bha*, the *vṛddhi* substitution [prescribed] by "after a vowel, before a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (*aco ñṇiti*) does not occur either, as it is sublated by the initial *vṛddhi*. And thus the author of the root-text will state: "The initial *vṛddhi* sublates the *vṛddhi* of the final and penultimate vowels. In this regard:

Regarding the *vārttika* "there is a prohibition of the Śākala [substitution] in the case of *sinnitya-samāsayoḥ*," that has been explained here by dividing it into two parts. Nor should it be argued: "If this is so, how is there a prohibition of the Śākala [substitution] in the case of *vopyaśva*, since the compound (*samāsa*) therein is optional? For [the answer is found] in the *Bhāṣya*.
Because the inclusion of the word *nitya* has been rejected.

(92) *ṛtyakaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.128. In the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*, the genitive case ending in *ṭhakaḥ* is used. The phrase *śākalyasya hrasvaśca* is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. [This applies] when there is no homogeneity (*asavarṇa*).

Thus ends the section on *nivṛtti*. From the rule "ṭheṅḥ padāntā'd" (Pāṇini 6.1.75), the term "padāntāt" (from the end of a word) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (carry-over). That [term] is then transformed into the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). Consequently, one sentence is formed: "For that which is at the end of a word (*padāntasya*), when followed by *ṛ*, there shall optionally be a short vowel. By the force of the particle *ca*, the term "prakṛtyā" (in its original form) is drawn over from the preceding rule. It has been stated: [the rest follows].
The second sentence becomes: "When *ṛ* follows, [the preceding vowel] remains short by its original nature (*prakṛtyā*). Thus he says:

"When *ṛ* follows, [the rule] is as before. In the case of *brahmā-ṛṣiḥ*, when *brahmā-ṛṣiḥ* stands, there is the shortening of the vowel *ā* and its state of original nature (*prakṛtibhāva*). Consequently, by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, the subsequent *a* does not occur.

In this case, since the letter *a* lacks the property of being an *ik*, the rule "an *ik* vowel followed by a non-homogeneous vowel" does not apply; therefore, this specific statement is made. In the example *brahmarṣiḥ*, when the alternative view is adopted that there is no *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) combined with the previously mentioned shortening, the rule "āṬt guṇaḥ" applies, resulting in the vowel *ā*. Then, the substitution of *r* follows. However, the rule was not formulated simply as "ṛti" [meaning "before *ṛ*"]; consider the example *hotṛ-ṛkāra*.

In this context, the mention of *ap* (the letter *a*) is necessary for the sake of preserving the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). "Only [those] at the end of a word" means that the mention of "end of a word" (*padānta*) must indeed be carried over here as well. Regarding *ārcchat*: from the root *ṛ* (to go), in the *laṅ* tense, with the suffixes *tip* and *śap*, there is the substitution of *ṛccha* by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdrśaḥ śaḥ*; then, by the rule *ṭhitaśca*, there is the elision of the *ik* vowel (*i*).

The augment *āṬ* is applied by the rule *ṭhāḍajādīnām*, and by the rule *āṭaśca*, there is *vṛddhi*. When the form *ā ṛcchati* is established, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) previously mentioned does not apply here because the vowel *ā* is not at the end of a word (*padānta*). He states "even in a compound" (*samāse 'pi*) to show that the prohibitory *vārttika* located in the preceding sūtra—namely, "not in a compound" (*na samāse*)—is not connected here.

Regarding "sapta-ṛṣīṇām": the compound is formed according to the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*. In the alternative where the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is maintained, the form is *sapta-ṛṣīṇām*; however, in the absence of that [original form], the vowel substitution (*guṇa*) applies by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, and with the replacement of the vowel *a* by *r* (*raparatva*), the form becomes *saptarṣīṇām*.

(93) *Vākyasya ṭeḥ pluta udāttaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.82. Now, between the *pluta* and *pragṛhya* vowels required by the rule *atha plutapragṛhyāḥ*, he begins the section on the *pluta* vowel, which occurs first: *vākyasya ṭeḥ*.

The term "of a word" (padasya) is understood [as the governing rule]. The meaning is that the final phoneme (ṭi) of a sentence, which is a constituent part of a word, becomes protracted (pluta), and that [protracted vowel] becomes acute (udātta).
Here, the recurrence of the term "of a word" (padasya) is for the sake of subsequent rules such as *naśchavyapraśān*, whereas in this present case, the recurrence [of that term] is discontinued.

Because it is impossible for [the term] to recur in what follows. If "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*) were absent and it were simply stated "of the final phoneme of a word" (*padasya ṭeḥ*), then a *pluta* would result for the final phoneme of as many words as there are in the sentence.
However, when "of the sentence" is stated, it is understood that the final phoneme of the sentence can only belong to the very last word; thus, [the undesired consequence does not arise].

There is a fault. In the absence of the mention of *ṭi*, when the rule "of a vowel" (*acaḥ*) is brought to mind by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "by the hearing of *pluta*," that [vowel] becomes a qualifier of the sentence; consequently, through the application of the rule "specification of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*), the meaning becomes "of a sentence ending in [a vowel]. Then, by the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*), it would follow that the *pluta* occurs for the final vowel of the sentence.
Otherwise, in sentences ending in consonants such as "vrajam gacchāgnicit" (go to the village, O Agnicit), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would not occur.

However, by including the marker *ṭ* [in the rule], its very force serves to qualify the vowel with the *ṭi* suffix; thus, the meaning obtained is that the protracted vowel belongs to the vowel which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the *ṭi*. Consequently, there is no fault.

This is clear in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "ity adhikṛtya" (having introduced this topic), the ellipsis is "the rules for *pluta* [protracted vowels] are commenced. (94) *pratyabhivāde 'śūdre* 8.2.83.

"In response to a greeting, except when addressed by a Śūdra. The governing rule "the final syllable of a sentence is protracted and acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.82) is understood here. The analysis of the compound is *a-śūdra* ("not a Śūdra"), meaning one of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). A "response to a greeting" (*pratyabhivāda*) refers to the formal benediction directed toward one who has greeted according to the prescribed rule.

The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). The meaning is that in this context of returning a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), the final syllable (*ṭi*) of the sentence should be protracted (*pluta*) and it should be acute-accented (*udātta*). Āpastamba states the rule for the salutation: "A Brāhmaṇa should salute, extending his right arm level with his ear; a Kṣatriya [should extend it] level with his chest."

A Vaiśya should bow with his head at the middle [of the body], and a Śūdra should bow low. "With palms joined" means: standing, until morning, one should perform the salutation, saying, "I am so-and-so, sir.
In the word "so-and-so," the mention of one's own name is intended; thus, one says, "I am Devadatta, sir."

*Abhivāda* refers to words of salutation and blessing. One should announce oneself as being fit for such a greeting. Consequently, the meaning is that one should extend the right arm according to one's caste and say, "I, Devadatta, salute you, sir. This is the manner of salutation.

The manner of returning a greeting has been shown by Manu: "In returning a greeting, a Brahmin should be addressed as 'May you be long-lived, O gentle one' (āyuṣmān bhava saumya). At the end of his name, the vowel 'a' should be pronounced with the preceding syllable protracted (pluta). Here, because of the expression "at the end of the name," [the term] "āyuṣmān" [is used].

Immediately after saying "Be gentle," it is established by another Smṛti that the name of one who does not offer a salutation should be used in the vocative case; this is what is being supported here. At the end of this name, the vowel *a* should be uttered—that is, applied. From that *a*, the preceding syllable—the vowel (*ac*) that precedes it—[is the one to be modified].

The meaning is that the *pluta* (protracted) vowel should be employed. Thus, the established rule is that the response to a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*) results in the sentence: "O gentle Devadatta, may you be long-lived! ā" [where the final syllable is protracted].
The phrase "I greet you, I am Devadatta" is shown as an example of the formula for greeting (*abhivāda*). O... [end of fragment]
This is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). "May you be long-lived, Devadatta!

is an illustration of the formula for returning a salutation (*pratyabhivāda*). The meaning of "I salute" (*abhivādaye*) is: "I inform [you] that a salutation and a benediction are to be spoken. Immediately after the word "be" (*bhava*), [the name is inserted].

The term *saumya* is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the vowel *a* following the word "Devadatta. Here, in the word "Devadatta," there is a protracted (*pluta*) vowel for the *a* after the letter *t*. Because longevity (*āyuṣmatva*) is that which is being predicated (*vidheya*), there is an absence of the vocative case ending. In this response-greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), the name ends in *śarman*.

The phrase "of a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth, does not apply [to the following rule], because in the *sūtra* *eco 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*, the *bhāṣya* provides examples of a name used alone, without words such as *śarman*; furthermore, this would contradict the stated *smṛtis* of Manu and others. Why [is it specified] "not for a Śūdra"? The *bhāṣya* says: "Are you well, O Tuṣajaka? And thus:
It is understood that in the case of a Śūdra, one should not employ the formula "May you live long" (*āyuṣmān bhava*).

Regarding this, there is a Vārttika which states: "It should be stated that [the prohibition] applies to women and to those who are envious. Thus, the prohibition of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not apply only to the case of a Śūdra, but also to the case of a woman and to the case of one who is envious.
The meaning is that it must be stated that there is a prohibition regarding the *pluta* (protracted) vowel.

In that regard, an example concerning a Śūdra has been cited. Now, he summarizes by way of meaning the Vārttika concerning women, dividing it: "Not in the case of a woman. This refers to what was stated in the formula for returning a greeting when a woman is the subject.

The meaning is that it is not a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). In the formula for salutation, "I salute you, O Gārgya," there is an option between using one's personal name (*nāman*) and one's lineage name (*gotra*). Thus he says: "either the name or the lineage. Here, by the word "name" (*nāma*), the rule "on the twelfth day the father shall give a name" is intended.

Only that which is specifically prescribed (*vihita*) is understood [by the term *nāman*]. For this very reason, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that there is no protracted vowel (*pluta*) in examples such as "O long-lived Daṇḍin! (*āyuṣmānbhava daṇḍin*). He states the purpose of the enumeration "whether a name (*nāman*) or a family name (*gotra*)" with the words "not here" (*nehā*). [In the example] "O long-lived one, prosper! (*āyuṣmānedhi*), the suffix *sip* is replaced by *hi* after the root *as*.

In *dhvasoḥ*, there is the substitution of *e* (by Pāṇini 6.4.119), and in *heḥ*, the substitution of *dhiḥ* (by Pāṇini 6.4.105). Regarding the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) does not apply here to the vowel following the letter *dh*, because it is neither part of a name (*anāman*) nor a *gotra* name.
[The rule] *bhorājanyaviśām* [applies to] the word *bhoḥ* and the final phonemes (*ṭi*) of names denoting Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

The meaning is that one must state that *pluta* (protracted) may also occur. This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the word *bhoḥ*, as it was not previously established [as subject to this rule], whereas for the other two [words], it is already established because they are proper names (*nāman*). In that regard, concerning the word *bhoḥ*, the Bhāṣya says: "O long-lived one, remain! O Devadatta! It is for this very reason [that the option applies].

At the end of a return greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), it is understood that there is an option regarding the use of either the word *bhoḥ* or the word *bhava* (or *edhi*) immediately after one's name. For example, for a Kṣatriya: *āyuṣmānedhi indravarman*, [or] *indravarman*. For a Vaiśya: *āyuṣmānedhi indrapālita*, [or] *indrapālita*.

The Bhāṣya states, "protected by Indra" (indrapālita). From this very Bhāṣya, it is understood that the following rules also apply in the formula of returning a greeting: the name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in *śarman*, that of a Kṣatriya in *varman*, and that of a Vaiśya in *pālita*.

Because of the contradiction with the aforementioned *smṛtis* of Manu and others, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Here, in this commentary (*bhāṣya*), by stating "another says," it is taught that in a response to a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), the word *bhoḥ* should be substituted for every name; having thus stated that the entire formula of a response to a greeting is simply "May you be long-lived, O [Name]!"—that is, ending with *bhoḥ*.

(95) *dūrāddhūte ca* | Pāṇini 8.2.84. Regarding *dūrāddhūte ca*: that region where one who is standing [there], even when being addressed, does not hear what is uttered with effort but requires greater effort, is "far" (*dūra*). *Hūta* means calling.

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). And that [suffix] is intended here as a vocative. The governing rule "the final syllable of a sentence is protracted (*pluta*) and acute (*udātta*)" is in force. Therefore, he says "in the case of calling from a distance," and so forth. However, if only the act of summoning were intended here, then [the form would be] *ehi*.

In cases such as *devadatta*, [the vocative marker] would occur only when there is a word expressing a call; however, intending to show that it occurs elsewhere even when not directed toward a person being addressed, he provides the example: *saktūn*.
(96) *haiheprayoge haihayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.85).

Regarding the rule *haiheprayoge*: when the two indeclinables *hai* and *he*, which indicate address, are employed, the *pluta* (protracted) vowel occurs for those two; such is the meaning. One might ask: since this is already established by the preceding rule (*guroranṛtaḥ*), for what purpose is this stated? Anticipating this doubt, it is said that this is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*).
He explains: "Only in the case of *hai* and *hai*" (*haihayoreva*). The meaning is that the phrase "only in the case of *hai* and *hai*" is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

In the example "pāhi hai3 rāma, pāhi he3 rāma," the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs only in the case of *hai* and *hai*, and not according to the rule "of a heavy syllable (*guru*) when not followed by *ṛ*" (*guroranṛtaḥ*), which would have allowed the final syllable to be protracted as well; this is precisely what is obtained by the expression "only in the case of *hai* and *hai*."

If the term "in actual usage" (*prayoga*) were not included, then because of the governing rule *vākyasya ṭeḥ* ("of the final [element] of a sentence"), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would apply only in cases such as *rāma hai3* and *rāma he3*;
therefore, the term "in actual usage" is included. Consequently, the protracted vowel occurs even for those two [vocative particles] when they are not at the end of a sentence.

(97) *guroranṛto'nantyasyāpyekaikasya prācām* | Pāṇini 8.2.86. *guroranṛtaḥ*: The phrase *dūrāddhūte ca* is understood [from the previous rule]. The governing heading is *vākyasya ṭeḥ pluta udāttaḥ*. In a sentence used for addressing someone from a distance, there...

The meaning is that when a word used in addressing someone is being called out, there shall be a protracted (*pluta*) vowel for a heavy syllable (*guru*) that is not the final one and is distinct from the letter *ṛ*; however, it shall also apply to the final heavy syllable as well as to a light syllable (*aguru*).
This is because the particle *api* conjoins [the final syllable] as well. He states this with the words beginning "from afar" (*dūrāt*), and so forth.
In all instances such as *devadatta*, the word *ehi* ("come") must be supplied;

otherwise, the status of these as sentences would be untenable according to the rule *ekatiṅ vākyam*. "For the sake of alternation" means that otherwise there would be a protracted (*pluta*) vowel for all the heavy syllables simultaneously—this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase *iha prācām*:

The rule *guroranṛto’nantyasyāpyekaikasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.86) constitutes one statement, while *prācām* (Pāṇini 8.2.87) is another. In this context, the word *pluta* continues to apply from the previous rule. The result is that, according to the opinion of the Easterners (*prācām*), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs, whereas it does not occur according to other opinions. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: *tena*. And thus, every protracted vowel [is subject to the following rule].

The sense is that the *vārttika*—"one who does not desire such rashness (*sāhasa*) should state it as an option" (*vibhāṣā vaktavyā*)—need not be composed. The meaning is: "one who does not desire such rashness," which consists in the abandonment of the rules concerning protracted vowels (*pluta*). That is to say, having set aside the stubborn adherence to the rules on protracted vowels. [The rule states: "as if not protracted" (*aplutavat*). What is this that is called "presented" (*upasthita*)?
The *Bhāṣya* states: "The particle *iti* that is non-ṛṣi-derived (*anārṣa*). This means a non-Vedic *iti*.
The word "protracted" (*pluta*) is to be supplied [to the sūtra]. The resulting sense is: when a non-Vedic *iti* follows, a protracted vowel shall behave as if it were not protracted.

(98) *aplutavad upasthite* |6|1|129|. He says this: "The *upasthita* [vowel] is as if not *ṛṣi*-derived. He states the purpose of its being treated as if not *ṛṣi*-derived: "The effect of a *pluta* [vowel], namely *prakṛtibhāva*. [This means] the non-*pluta* effects such as *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth.

"karoti" is an alternative reading. Regarding "suśloka3 iti": in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], the mantra is recited with a protracted final vowel as "suśloka3". At the time of the *padapāṭha*, the makers of the word-text recite the word "iti" after that [protracted syllable]. In that context, it is "suśloka3 iti".

Since the status of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) does not apply by virtue of the rule *sthite 'plutavat*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs, resulting in *suśloketi*. Here, the word *iti* is non-Vedic (*avaidika*), as it has been interpolated by the makers of the *pada-pāṭha*.
That very example, "suśloketi," remains established in the Bhāṣya; however, the makers of the *pada-pāṭha*...

Regarding the phrase "suśloka3 iti suśloka3 iti," they indeed pause [avagraha] in this manner. That too must be justified on the grounds that the *saṃhitā* (continuous flow) is not intended there; for it is precisely within the *saṃhitā* that rules such as *yaṇ*-sandhi are prescribed.
As for the question "Why 'vat'?"—the inquiry is: what is the purpose of including the term *vat* in the rule *aplutavat*?

He states the answer with the words "apluta" and so forth. By omitting the mention of *vad* (the substitute) and stating instead that "the non-protracted (*apluta*) is present," it is prescribed that the non-protracted itself takes the place of the protracted (*pluta*). Consequently, the protracted vowel alone would be set aside. Thus, in the case of *agnī3 iti*, where there is an imitation of the vocative dual ending, [it would be treated as] a *pragṛhya*.

The vowel *ī* with three morae (*trimātra*) is not heard [in the resulting form]. However, by employing the suffix *vat*, it is understood that only the *prakṛtibhāva* (the state of remaining in its original form), which is the grammatical operation of the protracted (*pluta*), is negated, and not the protracted vowel itself; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply—this is the meaning.

(99) *ī3cākravarmaṇasya* |6|1|130|. The term *ī3cākra-* is an indication (*nirdeśa*) of the protracted vowel *ī3*, with the first case ending elided. Because it is marked as *svarita* (circumflex), the previous rule [P. 6.1.129] regarding *upasthita* is excluded. The phrase *aplutavat* is understood from the preceding context. [The rule applies to] *ika-*...

The term *aci* is understood to carry over from the rule *yaṇ aci*. The meaning is that, according to the opinion of the sage Cākravarmaṇa, the protracted vowel (*īkāra*) becomes as if not protracted (*aplutavat*) when followed by a vowel (*aci*), but not according to any other opinion. Thus he says: "the protracted [vowel] before a vowel," and so forth.
*cinu hi3 idam* ("Gather this!"). This is the reply of one who has been asked, "What should I do? (*kiṃ mayā kartavyam*).

The form *cinviti* ends in the imperative suffix (*loṭ*). By the rule *utaśca pratyayād dher luki*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi*. The word *hi* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Its protracted form (*pluta*) occurs by the rule *vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ*.
Before *cinviti*, the word *devadatta* is to be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). As for the word *idam*:

It occurs within another sentence, and does not form a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the word *cinu*. Otherwise, because of the governing rule "of the final sound of a sentence" (*vākyasya ṭeḥ*), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) for the letter *i* in the word *hi* would not occur. Regarding the phrase "in both cases": [the prolation] is established as obligatory when followed by the word *iti*, whereas it is not established in other instances.

The meaning is that this option (*vibhāṣā*) applies in both cases from the point of its commencement. One should not say, however, that the word *vibhāṣā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because of the usage in the Bhāṣya: "or not—this is the option" (*na vā iti vibhāṣā*). It is called *vibhāṣā* because it is explained (*vibhāṣyate*) or optionally applied (*vikalpyate*). The suffix *ap* is added according to the rule "after a heavy vowel and a consonant" (*gurośca halaḥ*), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added.
(100) *īdūdeddvicanaṃ pragṛhyam* | Pāṇini 1.1.11. The term *īdūdeddvicanam* is a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva* compound consisting of *ī*, *ū*, and *ed*.

Since *īdūd-ed* functions as a qualifier for "the dual" (*dvivacanam*), the rule of "ending-inclusion" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. By the word "dual," [it is understood that the dual endings -ī, -ū, and -e are intended].

However, even though it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), that which ends with it is not included [in the application of the rule], because of the prohibition: "In a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with it. This is stated by the words beginning with "ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*," and so forth.
In the example *harī etau*, the dual number is established by resorting to the principle that the final element of a compound is like the initial element of the following word (*parādivadbhāva*).

Since [the vowels] are *pragṛhya*, there is no *yaṇ* substitution due to the rule "ṭhplutapragṛhyāḥ" which causes the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). The same applies in the case of *viṣṇū imau*. However, in the case of *gaṅge amū*, the substitution of *ay* does not occur.
He says "pacete" in order to demonstrate the purpose of the rule "īdūdeddvivacanam pragṛhyam," which is an *tadantavidhi* (a rule that applies to what ends with the specified elements).

Regarding the phrase *imau*: if the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) were not applied here, one would obtain the result that only a dual ending consisting of *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*. This being the case, in the example *pacete*, the dual ending *ite* would not possess the form *e*, and thus it would not be *pragṛhya*; this is the intended meaning. [The rule applies to] that which ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*.

If, however, the definition were explained as "that which ends in a dual suffix," there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kumāryor agāram* ("the house of two girls"), where the word *kumāryaḥ* ends in a dual suffix. But if it were explained as "that which has /ī/, /ū/, /e/, or /o/ at its end and is a dual suffix," there would be no over-extension, because the dual suffix *os* [of the genitive] does not end in those sounds.

This is because [the word *maṇī*] lacks the status of ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*. Now, one might object: in the verse from the *Mahābhārata*, "Two young colts (*vatsatarau*) dear to me are like two jewels (*maṇī iva*) of the camel," since the vowel *ī* in *maṇī iva* would be *pragṛhya*, it would undergo its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus the homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*) would not occur.
To this, he says: "In the case of *maṇī voṣṭrasya*... [referring to the fact that the rule does not apply here due to the specific context].

"According to the *Medinī*, [the word] *ṭhva* is used in the sense of 'knowing' (*pracetasi*) and as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) in the sense of 'or' (*vā*) or 'just so' (*yathā tathaiva*). According to the *Amara-kośa*: "The words *eva*, *yathā*, *tathā*, and *evam* are used in the sense of similarity (*sāmye*). (101) [The rule: "After *adas-* [the substitute *m* is applied] in place of the final vowel and the following consonant. (Pāṇini 1.1.12)

The word *adas-* [is used here]. The term *adasaḥ* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is: "from the letter *m* which is a constituent part of the word *adas-*. From the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, the words *īdūt* and *pragṛhyam* are understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). In the expression *māt*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of direction (*digyoge*). The word *para-* (meaning "following") is to be supplied (*adhyāhāryaḥ*).
He says this: "after *asmāt* and *parau*. The meaning is: after the letter *a*, which is a constituent part of the word *adaḥ*.
The term *e* does not carry over [from the previous rule], because it is impossible for an *e* to follow the letter *m* in the word *adaḥ*.
Furthermore, the term "dual number" (*dvivacanam*) also does not carry over, because there is no *ī* following the letter *m* in the word *adaḥ*.
Because of the plural number in "amī," and because the vowel *ū* following the letter *m* exists only in those [forms] ending in the dual, there is no [other] form to be excluded. "Amī īśāḥ":

from the word *adas* with the suffix *jas*, there is the substitution of *tyadādi* (the *a* of *adas*), followed by the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Then *jas* is replaced by *śī*. By the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, the *a* and *ī* coalesce into *e*. [The form becomes] *ade*.

This being the case, by the rule "ṭheta īt," the *ī*-quality (*ītva*) is applied to the vowel *e*, and the *m*-quality (*matva*) is applied to the consonant *d*. Thus, the form is *ṭhamīḥ*. Since the *ī* here is not a dual ending, the designation *pragṛhya* does not apply to it by the preceding rule; therefore, it is [designated as such] by this [present rule].
It is prescribed as follows: *rāmakṛṣṇāvamū* (Rāma and Kṛṣṇa).

From the masculine stem *adas*, in the nominative dual, the suffix *auṭ* is applied; then the substitution of *tyad*-class elements for the final vowel and following consonant (*tyadādyatva*) occurs, followed by the replacement of the preceding and following sounds with a single substitute (*pararūpatva*).
By the rule *vṛddhireci*, the form becomes *adau*. At this stage, by the rule *adaso'seḥ*, the *au* is replaced by *ū*, and the *d* [is replaced by *m*].

The form is *amū*. Although this vowel *ū* is a dual ending, nevertheless, when the status of being a *pragṛhya* is to be applied by the preceding rule (*aṇo 'pragṛhyasyādūrāddhūte pūrvasya plutavatkṛtasya*), since the substitution of *u* (*utva*) and *m* (*matva*) are considered *asiddha*, the vowel *au*—as seen from the perspective of the grammatical system—is present immediately after the letter *d*. Therefore, its status as a *pragṛhya* is established by that preceding rule.

By the phrase "not obtained" (na prāptam), [the substitution] is prescribed. However, with respect to the rule *ṭhadaso mā'd* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), the substitutions for *u* and *m* are not considered *asiddha*, because of the force of its specific formulation. But the preceding rule has no such force there, as it has already served its purpose in cases such as *harī etau* and *viṣṇū imau*. [The forms] *striyau*...

The word *adaḥ* in the feminine and neuter genders—as in "phale vā amū āsāte" (or those two fruits sit there)—is not an example here. For instance, from the feminine *adaḥ*, after applying *auṅ*, the substitution of *tyadādi* for *atva*, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), the addition of *ṭāp*, the substitution of *śī* for *au* by the rule "ṭāṅasiṅasām... āpaḥ," and the *guṇa* substitution by "ādguṇaḥ": [The process continues: ...and so forth. Thus, it is not an illustration of this [rule]. Similarly, in the neuter: *adaḥ* + *au* → *amū*. Here, after the application of *tyadādyatva*, the substitution of *pararūpa*, the addition of *ṭāp*, the substitution of *śī* for *au* by "ṭāṅasiṅasām... āpaḥ," and the *guṇa* substitution by "ādguṇaḥ," [the form is established]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-process; the full derivation would continue with the sandhi of *amū* + *āsāte*.)

The forms of *amū* for both the masculine and neuter genders are as follows: from the neuter base *adas*, after the substitution of *yatva* (the replacement of *t* with *ya*), the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) [for *a* and *au*], the substitution of *śī* by the rule "napuṃsakācca," and the Guṇa substitution [of *a* and *i*] according to "ādguṇaḥ," the forms become *amū* due to the substitutions of *utva* and *matva*. In this case, the status of being a *pragṛhya* is established by the preceding rule alone.

Even though the substitution of *utva* (for *adaḥ*) and *matva* (the addition of *m*) are not established [at this stage], because the singular *ekāra* (*e*) exists as a dual ending, the word *adaḥ* in the masculine gender alone serves as the example here; thus, "rāmakṛṣṇau" was stated to demonstrate this. [Question: Why is there the mention of "after *m*" (*māt*)? The rule could simply be "of *adas*" (*adasaḥ*); what is the purpose of including the mention of "*m*" (*māt*)?

The question is: "What is the purpose? [The answer is: In the form *amukatra*, [the process is as follows]: by the rule *avyaya-sarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.71), *akac* is added before the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of the indeclinable;

from the word *adakas* (the form of *tyad* with *akac*), when the nominative plural suffix *jas* is applied, there is the substitution of *yatva* for the initial of *tyad*-class words, followed by the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*); then *jas* is replaced by *śī*; the *guṇa* substitution of *ādguṇaḥ* occurs; and finally, the substitutions of *utva* and *matva* take place. Thus, the form *amuke* is obtained. Here, regarding the vowel *e*:

The mention of *māt* is for the purpose of preventing the status of being a *pragṛhya*. The intention is that once that [substitution] has been applied, the vowel *e* no longer stands before *mat*, and therefore it does not possess the status of a *pragṛhya*. Now, even so, the mention of *māt* would be useless; for here, without following the mention of *ed*, the rule could apply to *ī* and *ū* alone.

Since there is no possibility of the application of *pragṛhya* status in the case of "ṭhamuke" by virtue of accepting the rule for prescribing *pragṛhya* status [elsewhere], he says: "asati" (when it is absent). In the rule "adaso mā'd," among the *ī*, *ū*, and *e*t sounds contained within a single compound word (*ekasamāsapada*), both *ī* and *ū* are carried over (*anuvṛtti*).
Even in this case, since there would be the contingency of its recurrence [from the previous rule], the recurrence of *etaḥ* is blocked by the mention of *māt*.

However, in the absence of the mention of *māt*, there would be no sublater [of that recurrence], and thus the recurrence of *etaḥ* would also occur. Consequently, since there would be the contingency of the *pragṛhya* status for the vowel *e* even in the word *ṭhamuke*, the mention of *māt* is intended to prevent that.
But once that [pragṛhya status] has been established, because the non-occurrence of its recurrence is blocked, there is no pragṛhya status in the case of *amuke*.
Thus, the intention is that the mention of *māt* serves as a result for the non-recurrence of the vowel *e*.

*Śe*. This is a single-word sūtra. The term *pragṛhya* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Since *chandasi* (in Vedic) is also understood to carry over, the meaning is that the substitution *śe* ending in the vowel *e*—prescribed by the rule *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ*—should be *pragṛhya*. Thus he says: "this," namely *śe*.
The meaning is "in the place of [the suffix] ādeśa. Regarding *asme*: the meaning is "to us" (*asmabhyam*). The substitution of *śe* occurs for the [dative plural suffix] *bhyas*;

the letter *ś* is *it* by the rule "ṭhlaśakvataddhite. By the rule "śeṣe lopaḥ," the remainder is elided. Thus the form *asme* is established. This is stated because [the substitution] would not otherwise apply, as it is not a dual form. Although this is Vedic, [it is taught here].

Although [the analysis] should be restricted solely to the Vedic method, nevertheless, because the purpose of the *avagraha*— such as in the cases of *ṭhasme iti* and *ṭhtve iti*— also serves a worldly (secular) function, its application is established here; for the *padapāṭha* is a modern [artificial] construction.

(103) *nipāta ekājanāṅ* | 1|1|14|. A particle (*nipāta*) consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*) [is called *pragṛhya*]. The term "pragṛhya" is understood from the previous rule and is modified to agree in gender with the current subject. It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both a single one (*eka*) and a vowel (*ac*)."

He says this with the words beginning "Eko 'ji," etc. Regarding "i vismaye": the particle *i* belongs to the group beginning with *ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.57); its meaning is that it occurs in the sense of wonder (*āścarya*). *I* is Indra; *u* is Umā’s Lord (Śiva). The particles *i* and *u* are both monosyllabic and, being particles (*nipāta*), are *pragṛhya* by virtue of Pāṇini 1.1.14; therefore, there is no euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) between them when used in address.

He states the purpose of the *ṅ* suffix attached to *ṭh* in this context: "the mention of *an-āṅ*. [The example is] *ā evam iti*. This *ā*-vowel indicates that the meaning of the sentence previously introduced has changed.
The sense is: "Previously you thought thus, but now you think in this way. [The example is] *ā evam iti*.

This form *ā* indicates remembrance (*smaraṇa*). Here, in both cases, because the vowel *ā* lacks the marker *ṅ*, there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule *anāṅ*. Regarding the phrase "provided it has the marker *ṅ*": the vowel *ā* ending in *ā-kāriḥ* does not become *pragṛhya*, because of the exclusion by the rule *anāṅ*. As in *oṣṇam*: in the case of *ā-uṣṇam*, [the *ā* is not *pragṛhya*].

Since it lacks the status of being *ṅit* due to the absence of *prigṛhyatva*, the rule *ād guṇaḥ* applies. *uñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.17). This is a single-word sūtra. The terms *śākalyasya*, *itau*, and *pragṛhyam* are carried over from the preceding rules. The word *u* refers to the particle consisting of the phoneme *u* with the marker *ñ*. The meaning is that, according to the opinion of Śākalya, this [particle] shall receive the designation *pragṛhya* when followed by the word *iti*. Thus he says: *uña itau vā*.

The meaning is that the status of being a *pragṛhya* (non-sandhi vowel) is as previously stated. Regarding *u* and *viti*: since the rule "a single-vowel particle is always [a *pragṛhya*]" (*nipāta ekāj*) would apply invariably, this is an optional rule (*vikalpa*). In the case where it is a *pragṛhya*, the first form arises through the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). In the case where that is absent, the second form arises through the substitution of *yaṇ*.

(107) *uñ* |1|1|18|. This is also a single-word sūtra. The term *uñ* is an indication of the long nasalized vowel *ū*, with the first case ending elided. The word *uñaḥ* is understood from the previous rule, as is *itau śākalyasya*.

And [the rule] "pragṛhya" also applies. Thus he says: "uña itau. [The form] "īti" [is derived] when the substitution of *ī* for *u* is applied according to the aforementioned rule; due to its being a *pragṛhya*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). In the alternative case where this substitution does not occur, if it is a *pragṛhya* by the preceding rule, the form is "u iti. In the absence even of *pragṛhya* status...
When the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs, the form is *ṭhvit*; thus, three forms have been established as the result.

In this way, the single sūtra *uñaḥ ūṅ* has been explained by dividing it. However, if it were treated as a single sūtra, then when *it* follows *uñ*, the substitute would be the long, nasalized, and *pragṛhya* vowel *ūṅ*.

According to the view of Śākalya, this would be the case. However, under the alternative view that such [the status of being a single vowel] does not exist, one would obtain only the rule "a particle consisting of a single vowel is always *pragṛhya*. Consequently, there would only be the two forms *u āṣ* and *u iti*, and the form *v iti* would not be obtained. Therefore, it has been explained by dividing [the rule].
(108) *maya uño vo vā* | 8|3|33|. The term *mayaḥ* is in the ablative case, and *uñaḥ* is in the genitive case.
From the rule *ṅmo hrasvād aci*, the word *aci* is understood here; thus he says: "of that which follows *mayaḥ*."

Regarding the question "What was said? (*kimvuktam*): when *kimu uktaḥ* is established, since the *u* following the *m* is part of the particle *uñ*, it is invariably a *pragṛhya* by the rule *nipāta ekāc*. Consequently, because of its *prakṛtibhāva* (retention of its original form), the substitution of *yaṇ* would not occur; thus, this [rule] prescribes the change to *v*. Now, one might object: why is this stated immediately after the rule *iko yaṇ aci*? [The answer is: because of the particle *uñ*.

It should be read as "ve" for the sake of brevity, since there would be no need to mention "v". If it were read in the third *pāda*, there would be the disadvantage of having to include the mention of "v" as well, resulting in prolixity; therefore, he says: "of the quality of being 'v'. If the optional substitution of *yaṇ* for *uñ* from *mayaḥ* [in the rule] *iko yaṇaci* were indeed located in the first *pāda* of the sixth book...

If it were prescribed [in that context], then regarding the question "what is said?", by the rule *mo 'nusvāraḥ*, an anusvāra would occur for the letter *m* when followed by the letter *v*. However, in the prescription of *v*-substitution (*vatva*) within the Tripādī section, because that [prescription of *anusvāra*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), there is no *anusvāra*. This is because, in the Tripādī, the prescription of *v*-substitution takes precedence over the prescription of *anusvāra*.
The intention is that [this rule] is subsequent [to the previous one]. (109) *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe* (Pāṇini 1.1.19).
[The words] *īdūtau* and "and" (*ca*) [are used]. The term *pragṛhya* is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over). And that [term *pragṛhya*] is in the dual number.

It is modified. Since the nature of the sound (*śabda-svarūpa*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the rule *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a suffix to that which ends in it) applies. Although the desired result would have been established by the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyām* alone, because the word *artha* ("meaning") is included [in the sūtra], the case ending remains in the base itself to express the meaning of the locative, according to the maxim: "Where a case ending is elided by *luk*, that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided. Thus, the base itself conveys the sense of the locative.

The termination (*paryavasāna*) of the vowels *ī* and *ū*, ending in those sounds, is understood as being of such a nature. Thus, the literal meaning is: "Words ending in *ī* and *ū* which terminate in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī-artha*) are *pragṛhya*.
He states the resulting conclusion with the words beginning "in the sense of the locative case" (*saptamy-arthe*). For example: *somo gaurī*.

The meaning is "in Gaurī. By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending. Because it is a *pragṛhya* [by virtue of being a feminine noun ending in long ī], the original form is maintained (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus no *yaṇ* substitution occurs. However, forms such as *vātapramī* ending in the locative are not examples here; because the locative ending is not elided there, the base form does not apply in the sense of the locative. [Example: *māmakī*.

*tanū* means "in my own body. The locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (*Pāṇini 7.1.39*). This is because the use of the particle *iti* after *pragṛhya* vowels has been restricted by the authors of the *padapāṭha*; thus, in the *padapāṭha*, we find *māmakī iti* and *tanū iti*.
The fruit of being *pragṛhya* should be understood [as follows]. Now, one might object: let the rule simply be formulated as "ṭhīdūtau ca saptamyāḥ" (and *ī* and *ū* ending in the locative case).

Let the connection with the word "six" (*ṣaṭ*) be intended through the medium of its meaning; thus, the meaning "that which ends in *ī* or *ū* existing in the sense of the locative" would be obtained even without the explicit mention of the word "meaning" (*artha*).

He asks for what purpose the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is made: "What is the purpose of the inclusion of *artha*? This means: for what objective? The word *kim* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Regarding the phrase "in the *vṛtti*":
by the force of the inclusion of *artha*, the intended meaning is that it culminates in the mere sense of the elided locative case.

And therefore, when a compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*) occurs in which the locative case-ending is elided, and the [term *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*] applies to the meaning of the latter member (*uttarapada*) while bypassing the meaning of the locative in the former member (*pūrvapada*), the *pragṛhya* designation does not take effect.
[This is stated] lest it should occur. The rule *māṅi luṅ* is an exception to all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). For example: *vāpyaśvaḥ*.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "a horse in a pond" (*vāpyām aśvaḥ*), the form *vāpyaśva* arises through a compound (*samāsa*) according to the rule *sup-supā*; this is the meaning. Here, by the locative case in *vāpyām*, the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is understood, and that kāraka of locus requires an action. In that regard, [the sentence] means "a horse exists in the pond."

Whether there is the ellipsis of a verb (*kriyādhyāhāra*) or the action is understood as being in the present tense, the compound must be stated by taking into account the activity [of the horse] existing in the pond. And thus, in the compound,

even though the word *vāpī* has its locative case-ending elided, it transcends the meaning of the locative and [denotes] the horse as well, which is the substrate (*ādheya*) associated with that [locus].
The sense is that because the *pravṛtti* (the application of the rule) does not rest upon the mere meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*), there is no *pragṛhya* status.

(110) *Aṇo’pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57). [The sūtra reads: "Of an *aṇ* that is not *pragṛhya*. The phrase "optionally at the end of a word" (*vāṭhavasāne*) is understood to carry over. Therefore, he says: "of one that is not *pragṛhya*, etc."

In this context, the *aṇ* [pratyāhāra] includes only the *ṇakāra* from the preceding [sūtra], according to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*). Consequently, in the word *ṭhkartṛ*, there is no nasalization (*anunāsika*). Regarding the expressions *it-ac-sandhiḥ*, *alpāctaram*, *siddham anactvāt*, and *katham anactvam*, these are established solely on the basis of usage found in the Sūtras, Vārttikas, and Bhāṣya in similar instances.

The absence of *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) has been permitted for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; therefore, there is no fault here even in the absence of *kutva* and *cutva*. Thus ends the section on vowel-sandhi (*acsandhi*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now follows the section on chains of suffixes (*pratyayamālā*) ending in verbal terminations (*tiṅ*).

Now, intending to explain the series of suffixes (pratyayamālā), he says: "The desiderative suffix (san) [is applied] after the root *kaṇḍū*. The intention is that this is by means of the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of the first monosyllabic [root]," it should also be understood that this refers to the case where the doubling of the second monosyllabic [root]—by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya*—would otherwise have been required.
It should be understood that "of the third [syllable] of *kaṇḍvādi*" implies "the doubling of a monosyllabic [root]" (*ekāco dvitvam*).

Immediately after "*kaṇḍvādeḥ*," the phrase "ending in *ya*" (*yagantasya*) is to be supplied, because among the simple *kaṇḍvādi* roots, there is no third monosyllabic syllable. Thus, we have *kaṇḍūayi-yiṣati*.

In *kaṇḍūyayiṣati*, the suffix *san* is added after the root ending in *ya* (from *kaṇḍūy*), and there is the elision of the vowel *a*. By the rule *is*, there is reduplication of the third monosyllabic (*ekāc*) element. In *asūyiyiṣati*, the root *asu* (meaning "to feel pain") belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class;
here, there is reduplication of the third monosyllabic element following the initial vowel. This is an example of *san* being added after a root ending in *kyac*. Thus it is illustrated.

The remainder [is as follows]: "In the case of verbal roots derived from nominal stems (*nāmadhātu*), the substitution of *iṭ* is optional"—this is a Vārttika. The meaning is: "in the case of roots formed from nominal stems (*nāman*, i.e., *prātipadika*). As for the rule "for those beginning with *a*, however, after the first vowel, except for the others": the intention is that by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "beginning with *a*" (*ajādeḥ*), the sense obtained is that for monosyllabic roots other than those where the first vowel is followed by another vowel, the substitution of *iṭ* is optional.
Regarding the phrase "of the nasal sounds" (*nadaraṇām*): the meaning is that [the doubling] occurs only for a sound following the initial vowel among them.

Regarding "the desiderative (*sann*) of *indriyati*": the meaning is the desiderative suffix added to the root *indra* after it has undergone the *kyac* derivation. Regarding "of the two syllables *drī* and *yi*": because the letter *n* follows the initial vowel, there is no doubling.

The point is that because the letter *da* lacks a preceding vowel (*ac*), there is no prohibition against its doubling. Thus, in *cicandrīyiṣati*, there is doubling of the first simple vowel (*ekāc*) after the suffix *san*. In *candidrīyiṣati*, there is doubling of the second simple vowel. [Regarding] *priyam*:

In the sense of "desiring to tell what is dear" (*priyam ākhyātum icchati*), from the causative form [of *ā-khyā*] according to the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*, when the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added along with the augment *iṭ*, the word *priya* undergoes the substitution *prā* by the rule *priyasthirasphirorugurubahulatṛpradīrghavṛddhavṛndārakāṇām pra-sthi-sphā-vara-gara-baha-tra-padra-dra-ghā-vṛndāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.157). Following this, the augment *puK* is added, and after the loss of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions occur. Finally, the *ṣatva* change takes place, resulting in the desiderative form *prāpayiṣ*. Thus, the form ending in *san* is *prāpayiṣ*.

In the sense "he wishes to impel one who is announcing what is dear," from the root *prāp* (derived from the causative of *pra-āp*), when the suffix *san* is added with the augment *iṭ*, there is a second *ṇic*; then, by resorting to that second *ṇic*, the first *ṇic* is elided, and after the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions have occurred for the second *ṇic*, the form is indeed *prāpayiṣ*.

[This refers to] a form ending in a *saṇ* suffix. In that context, regarding the three roots beginning with *yatheṣṭaṃ nāmadhātuṣu*, when each of the single-vowel (*ekāc*) roots undergoes doubling, there are three forms such as *piprāpayiṣati*. [The word] "urum" [is used].

In the sense of "he desires to impel one who is explaining what is called *uru*," that is, in the sense of "he causes *uru* to be explained" (*uru-śabdam ācaṣṭe*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied. By the rule *priyasthirasphirorugurubahula...* (Pāṇini 6.4.157), the substitution of *vṛ* for *uru* occurs; with the subsequent vowel lengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*), we have *vār*. From this *ṇij*-stem, with the desiderative suffix *san*, the augment *iṭ*, and the subsequent *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions for the *ṇic*, followed by the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*], we obtain the desiderative form *vārayiṣa*.
In the opinion of Mādhava, because the addition of *vṛddhi* is accepted [by Pāṇini 7.2.116], from the causative form *vārī-* (of the root *vṛ*), when the suffix *san* is added with the augment *iṭ*,

followed by the elision of the first causative marker (*ṇic*) and the application of *ṣatva*, the resulting form is precisely *vārayiṣ-*. In that case, according to the rule "optionally among nominal stems" (*nāmadhātuṣu*), when there is reduplication of each single vowel (*ekāc*), [the desired result follows].
The meaning is that there are three forms, beginning with *vivārayiṣati*. Regarding *bāḍhamasisādhayiṣati*:
in the sense of "he wishes to urge one who is telling [something] emphatically (*bāḍham*)," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and so forth are applied as before.
By the rule *antikabāḍhayoḥ sāmīpye*, the substitution of *sādha-* occurs. In that case, because the *s* is not part of the substitute itself, it is not [subject to the following rule].

[The rule regarding] the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. He states this: "But the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. He demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) for *bobhūyiṣayiṣati* by saying "yaṅ": the remainder [of the context] is "from the root *bhū*. After reduplication, *bobhūya-* is established. Regarding "san" (the desiderative suffix): after the addition of *iṭ* and the elision of the *a* following it, and then the substitution of *ṣ*, *bobhūyiṣa-* is established.

The suffix *san* follows a root ending in *ṇic*. From *bobhūyiṣ*, with the addition of the causal *ṇic*, after the elision of the final vowel (*ato lopa*), the form *bobhūyiṣi* is established. From that, with the addition of *san* and the augment *iṭ*, and after the *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* substitutions for the *ṇic*, and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, the form *bobhūyiṣayiṣ* is established. Then, from that, with the addition of the *laṭ* suffix *tip* and the *śap* vikaraṇa, the subsequent form is [obtained] by the rule of *pararūpa*.

The form is *bobhūyiṣati*. Because of the rule "ṭhanabhyāsasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.8), there is no further reduplication. Now, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) for *bobhūyayiṣati*—starting with "yaṅ. The remainder [of the context] is "from the root *bhū*. After reduplication, it stands as *bobhūya*. Then comes the suffix *ṇic*.
From the root *bhū* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, following the rule "bobhūya," after the elision of the vowel *a*, the form *bobhūyi* is established.

Then, from this [form] *bobhūyi* with the desiderative suffix *san*—that is, when *san* follows a stem ending in *san*—with the augment *iṭ*, and after the guna and the substitution of *ay* for the *ṇic*, followed by *ṣṭu* (the *s* of *san*), the form *bobhūyayiṣ* is established. From that, with the causative suffix *ṇic* [added again], after the elision of the vowel *a*.
From the form *bobhūyayiṣ* [in the sense of "he desires to cause to become repeatedly"], when the suffix *tip* is applied and the *śap* affix follows,
the form *bobhūyayiṣayati* is established after the application of *guṇa* and the *ayādeśa* substitution.
The series of suffixes (*pratyayamālā*) is thus completed.
Now begins the section on primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*).
(711) *ṇvultṛcau* |3|1|133|. Now begins the section on primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*). The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* do not occur outside of the present tense (*vartamānakāla*).

The commentary says "prayoga" (usage). The sense is that it means "fit to carry," because of the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* ("the kṛtya suffixes and tṛc are used in the sense of being fit for"). Regarding "voḍhā": from the root *vah*, with the suffix *tṛc*, there is no augment *iṭ* due to its being unaccented; then, after the application of the rules for *ḍha*-ness, *dha*-ness, *ṣṭu*-ness, and the elision of *ḍha*, the substitution of *o* by the rule *sahivahoḥ* occurs. In the case of *kuṭitā*: [End of excerpt]

Anticipating the objection regarding the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), he says: "gāṅ. Then, fearing that *guṇa* would likewise not occur in *koṭakaḥ* (derived from the root *kuṭ* with the suffix *ṇvul*), he says: "because of the statement 'not after *añ* or *ṇit*. Anticipating the objection regarding the *guṇa* substitution in *vijitaḥ*, he says: "after *vij*, there is *iṭ*. The remainder [of the rule] is "when *ṭ* follows, there is *ṅtva*."

Regarding "vijita": because it ends in a ṅ-letter, there is no *guṇa* substitution; the reason for its being *aniṭ* is that it is taught with an *anudātta* vowel. Having raised the objection concerning the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel in the word "janaka," he recalls the prohibition of *vṛddhi*: [He says: "In the case of 'janaka,' having anticipated the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel, he reminds one of the prohibition of *vṛddhi*."

Regarding the rule *janivadhyośca*: the root *vadha* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) is a different verbal root belonging to the *bhū* class (Bhvādi), because the Bhvādi group is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). It is not, however, the substitute *vadh* for the root *han*. For if it were so, the mention of *vadh* in the sūtra prohibiting *vṛddhi*, namely *janivadhyośca*, would be redundant.

Since the substitute *vadha* ends in a short vowel (*a*), the absence of *vṛddhi* is established simply by the fact that the elision (*al-lopa*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Regarding the form *vadhaka*: the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule "janivadhyośca. In the cases of *randhakaḥ* and *jambhakaḥ*, since the suffix *num* does not apply because these roots do not have the marker *idit*, he reminds us of the rule for its application: "radhijabhoracī" (Pāṇini 7.1.61).

Regarding the form *radhitā*, having raised the doubt that the augment *num* should apply by the rule "ṛdhijabhorum" (Pāṇini 7.1.61), he says: "not in the iṭ or the liṭ" (*neṭaliṭi*). Thus we have *radhitā* and *raddhā*; the optional *iṭ* applies here by the rule "radhādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 7.2.45). When *masj-tṛ* remains, he says: "of *masji* and *naś*" (*masjinaśoḥ*). This is a rule for the insertion of *num*. Thus we have *maṅktā*; [the derivation from] *masj-tṛ*.

This being the case, according to the rule "it should be stated that *num* is inserted before the final letter of *mṛj*," *num* is placed before the *j* and after the *s*. With *mas-n-j-tṛ* established,
there is elision of the *s* by the rule "elision of *sk*," the *j* becomes *g* by the rule for *kutva*, that *g* becomes *k* by the rule for *cartva*, and then the *anusvāra* is applied.

The state [of the letter] is *ṅ* due to the rule of *para-savarṇa*. Regarding *naṃṣṭā* and *naśitā*: because it belongs to the *radhādi* group, there is optionally *iṭ*. In the alternative where *iṭ* is absent, after the insertion of *num* by the rule *masjinaśorjhali*, the form *nanś tṛ* is established;
then, by the rule *vraśca*, the *ś* becomes *ṣ*. The *n* becomes *anusvāra*, and then *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṭ* for *s*). By the rule *ramer aśabliṭoḥ*, [the *iṭ* is added].
Is this a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*)? Regarding *labdhā*: by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*, the *th* is replaced by *dh*;
then, by the rule for *jaś*-substitution, the *bh* is replaced by *b*. Regarding *tīṣasahe*: this is an optional augment (*iṭ*). Regarding *soḍhe*:

there is the substitution of *ḍh* for *th*, the substitution of *dh* for *ḍh*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭh*, and the elision (*lopa*) of *ḍh*. By the rule *sahivahoḥ*, there is the substitution of *o* for the vowel. Regarding *daridrāteḥ*: there is the elision (*ālopa*) of the long *ā*.
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is by the rule: "The elision of *ā* in *daridrāti* should be stated. Regarding "not in the case of *ṇvul*":

the meaning is that there is no elision of *ā* in *daridrāti* when *ṇvul* follows. The meaning is based on the *vārttika*: "There is no elision in *daridrāyaka*. Regarding *daridrāyaka*: the meaning is that the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "after [a root ending in] *at*, *yuc*."

Regarding the derivation of *pādahāraka* in the sense of "one who carries with the feet," he says— "by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*"— in order to establish the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the mere statement "*kṛtyalyuṭaḥ*," those *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes which have been prescribed in the various meanings [listed in Pāṇini 3.3.113] are also [applicable] in other meanings as well.

The inclusion of the word "bahulam" (in various cases) is for the purpose of obtaining this meaning and for the sake of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*): namely, that "kṛt suffixes which are prescribed for certain meanings may also occur in other instances. Thus, the suffix *ṇvul* is established even when [the action] is in the objective case (*karman*). As for the Vārttika "kṛto bahulam," however...

The intended meaning is that this is for the purpose of explaining the rule established by the division of *yogavibhāga*. Regarding the word "kramer": the meaning is that there is no *iṭ* augment for a *kṛt* suffix following the root *kram* when it belongs to the domain of the *ātmanepada*. This is a *vārttika* found within the rule *snukramor anupasarge kaḥ*. Regarding the form *prakrāntā*: [it is derived from] *propābhyām...* [etc.]...

This [rule] "samarthābhyām" concerns the domain of the ātmanepada. Now, one might ask: if this is so, how is it that there is *iṭ* in the form *kramitā*? To this he says: "The word 'domain' (viṣaya) refers to the state of being inseparable from anything else. The word "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
That is to say, it means "inseparable from the ātmanepada. [This applies to] "the root *kram*, which is ātmanepadi when used in the sense of the agent."
The intention is that since this is established by this much alone, the inclusion of the word "viṣaya" (object) yields this specific meaning.
Thus, it results in the conclusion that [the root] is always ātmanepada. Regarding the word "tena": in the case of *kramite* in the rule *anupasargād vā*, it refers to the root *kram*.

The meaning is that because the rule provides an option for the middle voice (ātmanepada), there is no prohibition of *iṭ* due to the absence of obligatory middle-voice application. He states another opinion: "only its fitness for that.
Fitness for the middle voice is precisely what constitutes being the domain of the middle voice; and therefore, in the case where the middle voice applies—

The meaning is that when there is a prohibition of *iṭ*, the form is *kṛntati*; however, in the alternative view where the *ātmanepada* endings do not occur, some say that with the addition of *iṭ*, the form is *kramitā*. In this view, the word "viṣaya" (scope/condition) serves no purpose; this is the underlying dissatisfaction [with that view]. Now, one might ask: how can there be *iṭ* after the suffix *san* in the case of *saṃjigamiṣita*?

Because *gama* is read among the roots ending in *niṭ*, and because the suffix *san* is not followed by a *parasmaipada* (active voice) affix, the rule "the augment *iṭ* is applied after *gam* in *parasmaipada* affixes" does not apply; therefore, he says: "in the rule *gamer iṭ*.
