The word "likewise" (*evam*) implies that in the rule "not after *vṛt* and the four [others]" (*na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ*), the term *parasmaipada* is also understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over).
The meaning is that it indicates the absence of those two [the suffixes *ta* and *na*]. Regarding "vivṛtsitā": this is the form of the root *vṛt* with the desiderative (*san*) affix;

there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is *kit* by the rule "halantācca. Regarding "yaṅntāt": the meaning is from the root *pac* with the intensive (*yaṅ*) affix, namely *pāpacya*, followed by the *ṇvul* affix. When the *akādeśa* (substitution of *a*) occurs for that [suffix], [the elision of the penultimate vowel] follows by the rule "yasya halaḥ."

When the *yakāra* is elided and the *akāra* following it is also elided, leaving the form *pāpac-aka*, one might suspect that the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of the penultimate (*upadhā*) would apply; therefore, he says: "There is no *vṛddhi* because [the elision] is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "from the *yaṅ*-luṅanta": since the elision (*luk*) of the entire *yaṅ* suffix is not a substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*), [the condition for *vṛddhi* does not arise].

Since the status of being "as if that which stood in its place" (sthānivadbhāva) is impossible here, the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (upadhāvṛddhi) remains unimpeded. Furthermore, the prohibition [by Pāṇini 1.1.4], "not when there is elision of a verbal root" (na dhātulope), does not apply;
for the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix is not occasioned by anything else, and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel is not characterized by the letter *i*.

(712) *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.134. The compound *nandigrahi* is a *dvandva* of *nandi*, *grahi*, and *paci*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: those for which *nandi*, *grahi*, and *paci* are the beginning members. The word "beginning" (*ādi*) results in being connected with each member individually. [The suffixes are] *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac*.

*ṇni*, *ac*, and *ā*—the nominative case is used for these following the *dvandva* compound; the connection is according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*). Thus he says: "of *nandi* etc. The term *nandi* includes the causative form (*ṇyant*) [of the root *nand*]. Thus he says: "he causes joy" (*nandayati*), and so forth.

There is no substitution of *an* for the *lyap* suffix, and by the rule "the *ṇi* is elided before a suffix beginning with a vowel that does not take *iṭ*," there is the elision of the *ṇi*. [The example is] "he destroys honey" (*madhuṃ sūdayati*).

A specific type of sweet wine (*madhurasura*); some [grammarians] derive this from the root *sūd*, which is not subject to the addition of the causal suffix (*ṇic*). In the rule, for the root *grah* meaning "to take," there is the mention of *grahī* with the vowel *i*. Because it is a Vedic (or *sautra*) usage, the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) prescribed by the rule *grahijyā* does not apply; thus we have *grāhī*. The suffix *ṇini* is added to the root *grah* because its penultimate vowel is short (*adupadha*), resulting in the form *grāhī*; the vowel *i* follows the letter *n*.

The purpose is for pronunciation. There is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel. Regarding the form *viṣayī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *śīṅ* (meaning "to sleep") preceded by the prefix *vi*; there are the *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* substitutions. Anticipating the application of *vṛddhi* by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, he says: "there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. Regarding the form *viṣayī*: [it is derived from] the root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind").

From this word *kṛta*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied. The *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions [of *ṛ* and *i* respectively] occur. Now, one might ask: why is there no *vṛddhi* here, and how is the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) justified, given that it occurs at the beginning of a word? To this, he says: "The *ṣatva* also.

The meaning is that by means of a *nipātana* (an irregularity or special rule), there is an absence of *vṛddhi* and the occurrence of *ṣatva*. This applies in cases such as *paribhāvī* and *paribhavī*.

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *ṇit* would necessitate a compulsory *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), he says: "occasional" (*pākṣika*). The roots beginning with *grah* are recited in the *vṛtti*. As for the statement that the *pacādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the meaning is that after listing a few roots such as *pac* and *vap*, the *gaṇapāṭha* explicitly states, "this is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. This is found in the *gaṇapāṭha*.

Even in the absence of a statement regarding its being an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class), he says: "Śiva-śam. The meaning is that this is because we observe the usage of the word *kara*, which is not listed in the *pacādi-gaṇa* but is formed from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ac*; and the usage of the word *ghaṭa*, which is formed from the root *ghaṭ* with the suffix *ac* according to the rule *karmaṇi ghaṭaḥ*. Thus, it is the suffix *ac*.

Furthermore, when the suffix *ac* follows a reduplicated form (*yaṅanta*), the elision of *yah* is prescribed by the rule "ṭhyaṅe'ci ca. Now, a reduplicated form is not explicitly listed in the *pacādi* group; therefore, this very fact indicates that the *pacādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). The meaning is that, since the *pacādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, [suffixes such as] *nadaṭ*, *coraḍ*, and so forth [are included].
In that case, the recitation [of those roots] would be useless; therefore, he says "of some.

The meaning is that it is for the purpose of making known the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) such as *ṭ*. But even so, what is the purpose of the recitation there of forms such as *vada* and *cala*, which are devoid of *anubandhas*? To this, he says:

For some, this is for the purpose of providing a counter-exception (*bādhaka*). Regarding the forms *jārabhara* and *śvapaca*, the *Bhāṣya* states that the words *bhara* and *paca* are listed [in the *gaṇapāṭha*] in order to block the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1, *karmaṇyaṇ*), which would otherwise override the suffix *ac* (prescribed by 3.1.134, *pacādyac*).
In cases such as *devaḥ* and *sevaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is specifically prescribed by the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135).

And for the purpose of subverting what has been prescribed, he establishes this with the words beginning "nadaḍ," etc. Now, one might ask: if the word *śvapaca* in the *pacādi* group is intended to subvert a sublater [of a previous rule], how then is the form *śvapāka* derived? To this he says: "Because it is read among the *nyaṅku*-class words, *śvapāka* is also valid."

The meaning is that sometimes there is the suffix *aṇ* and the substitution of *k* for *c*. He demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) in examples such as *cekrīyaḥ* and *marīmṛjaḥ* with the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca*: the meaning is that when a vowel-initial suffix follows, there is elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* affix after roots such as *krī*. When the state [of the form] such as *cekrī-a* has been reached following reduplication and other operations, he states [the rule]: *na dhātulopa-* (Pāṇini 1.1.4).

Thus: *cekriya*. Because there is an absence of a *guṇa* substitute, there is no *yaṇ* substitution due to the condition of being followed by a *saṃyoga*. *nenya*: here, *yaṇ* occurs by the rule "for a root having more than one vowel" (*eranekācaḥ*). *loluva*: here, *uvaṅ* occurs; but *yaṇ* does not, because of the specific mention of *u* in the rule "before a *sup* suffix" (*oḥ supi*). *marīmṛja*: here, [the *yaṇ* substitution] does not occur due to the prohibition "when there is elision of a verbal root element" (*na dhātulope*).

The rule *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* [means that there is vṛddhi for the root *mṛj*]. Regarding *caricalī-* etc.: the meaning is that when the suffix *ac* follows these roots, there is reduplication (*dvitva*) and the augment *āg* is added to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Now, one might object: in the case of *carācara*, would not the vowel *ā* following the *r* in the reduplicated syllable become short? Furthermore, by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, would not the *r* itself also be eliminated? To this, he says:

Regarding the term *āgāgamasya*: if the short vowel were present and the augment *ā* were added, the long pronunciation would be redundant, since it would have been possible simply to prescribe the augment *ā*. Likewise, if the *repha* (the letter *r*) were eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, then even with the short vowel, the form *ṭhcācara* would be established through the *savarṇadīrgha* rule; therefore, the long vowel is pronounced [for this specific purpose].
The meaning is that it indicates the absence of the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant). "In the case of the root *han*, [there is] *it*"—this is a *vārttika*.

Its meaning is that when the suffix *ac* follows the root *han*, there is both the substitution of *gh* for *h* and the doubling [of the following consonant]. Now, one might ask: since the substitution of *k* for *h* (*kutva*) is already established in the subsequent portion by the rule "*abhyāsācca*" (Pāṇini 7.3.55), what is the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *gh* here? To this, he says:
"Lengthening (*ghatva*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)," [this is] the meaning; the words "is prescribed here" are to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding "of *pāṭi*":

this is a Vārttika. From the root *pāṭi* (from *pāṭer ṇau*), after the suffix *ac*, there is elision of *ṇi* (*ṇer luk*), doubling of the root, and the augment *ū* for the reduplicated syllable. The meaning is that when the vowel of the reduplicated syllable is short, there is lengthening of that [vowel].

The rule for the elision (*luk*) of *ṇi* is for the purpose of preventing the increase [of the syllable count]. Because the long vowel is explicitly pronounced in the augment, there is no disappearance of the letter *ṭ* by the rule of "remainder of consonants beginning with a consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*).

However, in the case of *halādiśeṣa*, since the form *popaṭa* is established even with the augment *u* through the rule of "vṛddhi substitution for *āṭ*" (*ādguṇa*), [the elision of *ṇi* is necessary].

(713) *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.135. The term *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ* is a compound (*dvandva*) in the ablative case, consisting of *igupadha*, *jñā*, *prī*, and *kir*. Regarding *kir*: from the root *kṛ* "to scatter," after the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel and the subsequent replacement of that *i* by *ra* (*raparatva*), the form *kir* ending in *r* is obtained. The suffix *ka* is applied to these [roots] because they possess the property of being *kit*.

This is for the purpose of negating [the presence of] qualities. Regarding "jña": there is elision of the long *ā* (*āto lopaḥ*). Regarding "priya": from the root *prīñ*, with the suffix *ke*, the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs.
Regarding "kira": from the root *kṛ*, with the suffix *kapratyaya*, the substitution of *it* occurs, followed by the replacement of *a* with *ra* (*raparatvam*).
(714) *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136).

"And after the root *ā*, when a prefix (*upasarga*) [is present]"—the word "ka" should be supplied to complete the sense. This results in the meaning: "The suffix *ka* shall occur after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, when a prefix is present as an upapada. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇa*;
the intention is that *ṇa* is prescribed generally for roots ending in long *ā*, whether a prefix is present or not. Thus, *sugla*.
The intention is that when the substitution of *ā* for the root *glai* is made by the rule "ādeca upadeśe 'śiti," and the suffix *kap* is added, the *ā* is elided by the rule "āto lopaḥ.
Regarding the form *prajña*: the *ā* of the root *jñā* is elided.
(715) Pāṇini 3.1.137: *prāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*.

In the case of *prāghrā*, considering the rule "between a root with a *luk*-suffix and one without a *luk*-suffix, the one without the *luk*-suffix is taken," he says: "that which drinks is *piba*. When the suffix *śap* is added to the root *pā*, because it is marked with *ś* (indicating it is *sārvadhātuka*), the substitution of *piba* for *pā* occurs by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*. And that [substitute] ends in a short vowel (*adanta*).

Thus it has been stated. [The form] *jighra* is derived from the root *ghrā* with the suffix *śap*; by the rule *prāghrā*, there is the substitution of *jighra* for the root *ghrā*. [The form] *dhama* is derived from the root *dhmā* with the substitution of *dham* for *dhmā*. [The form] *dhaya* is derived from the root *dheṭ*: the suffix *śa*, the suffix *śap*, the substitution of *ay* for *e*, and then the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*);
this is the intended meaning. In the phrase *dhayā kanyā*, the root *dheṭ* is marked with the letter *ṭ*; it ends in *a*.

That which ends in *dha* and has the sound *ya* is not marked with the *ṭi*-designation; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply here by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. This is the opinion of Haradatta, beginning from the point "because *dheṭ* is *ṭit*. Regarding the form *stanandhayī*: it is derived from the root *dheṭ* with the word *stana* as an upapada.

In the case of *stanandhaya*, when the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *nāsikāstanayor vā*, the suffix *mum* is added by the rule *khyatyāt parasya*; thus the word *stanandhaya* is formed. In that context, just as the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to *stanandhayī* by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, based on the fact that the root *dhēṭ* has the marker *ṭi* when *khaś* is applied, so too would *ṅīp* be applicable here in the case of *dhayā kanyā*. That [is the point].

The meaning is that Haradatta states that the suffix *ṅīp* is not desired in cases other than *khaś*. However, in reality, this [view] is questionable because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, which maintains that in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, only the vowel *a* that is a constituent part of a *ṭit* element and so forth is intended to be included. Nor can it be argued that [the inclusion of the *a*] follows from the very force (*sāmarthya*) of the *ṭit* designation.

It should be stated that the suffix *ṅīp* applies after the word *stanandhayī*; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṅīp* even in the case of "a girl who drinks" (*dhayā kanyā*), since there is no evidence for the restriction that the suffix *khaś* is not desired elsewhere.
Therefore, the form *stanandhayī* is indeed unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*). If it were authoritative, [the word] would belong to the *gaura-ādi* group.

It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that [the suffix] *kalpya* is formed; for even with the addition of *ṅīp*, there is no difference in accent, since the *anudātta-nivṛtti-svara* (the acute accent replacing the final low tone) would apply. He gives an example of *dṛś*: *paśya*.

By the rule *pā-ghrā-dhmā-dheṭ-drśaḥ śaḥ*, there is the substitution of *paśya*. Regarding *ghraḥ saṃjñāyāṃ na*: this means that the suffix *śa* does not apply to the root *ghrā* when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*).
Why is this? To this he says: "by tigers and so forth. The intention is that otherwise he would have specified [the rule] as "by *vyājighra* and so forth.
(Pāṇini 3.1.138) *anupasargāllimpavindadhāripārivedyaudejicesātisāhibhyaśca*.

[3.1.138] *anupasargāt* [the suffix] *śa* shall occur. This is a supplement to the rule (*śeṣapūraṇam*). Examples: *limpaḥ*, *vindaḥ*. Since the roots *lip* (in the sense of "smearing") and *vidlṛ* (in the sense of "obtaining") belong to the *tudādi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied after them. [The suffix] *śa*...

The augment *num* is applied by the rule *mucādīnām*. In the sūtra, *limpa* and *vinda* are cited with the *num* already applied; therefore, only those two roots belonging to the Tudādi class are intended. Regarding *dhāraya*: from the roots *dhṛñ* (in the sense of "holding") and *dhṛṅ* (in the sense of "remaining"), with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the affix *śa* is added, followed by *śap*; then the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions take place.

"Pāraya": from the root *pṛ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *cha*, the *śap* affix, and the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions. "Vida": in the sense of "knowing," "naming," and so forth; from the root *vid* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *cha*, the *śap* affix, and the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions. "Udejaya": from the root *ej* preceded by the prefix *ud* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *cha*, the *śap* affix, and the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions. "Cetaya": [from the root *cit* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *cha*, the *śap* affix, and the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions].

The root *cit* (meaning "to perceive") takes the suffix *cha* after being converted to the causative (*ṇic*), followed by the *śap* affix; then the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions occur. The same applies to *sāti*. To establish the form *sāt*, he says: "By the principle of *vāsarūpa*, [the suffix] *kvip* [is applied]. Thus, *kvip* is added in the sense of "he causes happiness" (*sātayati*) or "he pleases.
There is the elision of the *ṇi* affix. Although *kvip* is prescribed as a general rule for the root *sāti*...
The suffix *śa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to that; nevertheless, by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*), the suffix *kvip* also occurs—this is the meaning.

"Sātparamātma" means that the Supreme Self is *sāt*, because the Vedic text "for He alone causes bliss" (*eṣa hy evānandayati*) makes it known that He is the one who bestows happiness—this is the intended sense. "Sātvanta" means *sāt* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The suffix *matup* is used in the sense of "one who is not to be worshipped by these. According to the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ*, the *m* is changed to *v*. Because of the rule *tasau matvarthe*, [the suffix] *vat* is applied; due to this, there is no status as a *pada*, and thus no change to the *jaś*-class (i.e., no change of *s* to *r*). Regarding *sāhaya*: from the root *sāh* (to endure), the suffix *śa* is added, followed by *śap*; then the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions occur. Regarding *pralipa*: the suffix *ka* is added according to the rule for roots ending in an *ik* vowel (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). [The word *nau* is provided as an example of a feminine noun.]

"Limpeḥ" (of the root *lip*): this is a Vārttika. The meaning is that when the prefix *ni-* is present as an upapada, the suffix *śa* should be stated [after the root *lip*]. Since it was previously stated "when there is no prefix" (*anupasargāt*), this rule is provided because the suffix would not have been applicable by the preceding rule.
"Gavādiṣu" (in the case of *go*, etc.): this is a Vārttika. The meaning is that when words such as *go* and others are present as upapadas, the suffix *śa* should be stated [after the root *vid*].

This is the meaning. This [rule] is for the purpose of restriction, namely "only when a name is being formed. Regarding *govinda*: the meaning is that he finds (*vindati*) the cows—that is, the words of the Upaniṣads—as authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding *aravinda*: the spokes (*arāḥ*) are the pieces of wood fixed between the hub and the rim of a wheel; the petals are similar to those.
The meaning is "he finds. This suffix *śa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed after verbal roots ending in a consonant.
(717) *dadātidadhātyor vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.1.139). Regarding *dadāti* and *dadhāti*: the suffix *śa* may optionally (*vibhāṣā*) be applied after the roots *dāñ* and *dhāñ*. [Thus] *dadaḥ*.
*Dadha* [is derived as follows]: the suffixes *śaḥ*, *śap*, and *ślu*. By the rule *ṭhślau*, there is reduplication (*dvitvam*). Then, by the rule *āto lopaḥ*, the *ā* is elided.
"To be mentioned later" means by the rule *syādvyade*. *Pradaḥ* and *pradha*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge*.

(718) *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.1.140. Regarding the phrase *jvaliti ādyarthaḥ*: thus, those roots which have *jval* as their initial (*ādi*) are called *jvalitayaḥ*; and since they are also *kasantāḥ*, the compound *jvalitikasantāḥ* is analyzed as "those [roots] beginning with *jval* and ending with *kas*. He states this as follows:

Regarding "from *jvala* and so forth": the meaning is from those beginning with *jvala* in the sense of "shining" up to those ending with *kasa* in the sense of "going. Regarding "there may optionally be *ṇa*": the intention is that the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is understood to carry over. In the alternative case, there is *ac*; one should also understand that *ka* applies by the rule "after a root with a penultimate *iṭ*, there is *ka*. Regarding "the addition [of a rule]": this refers to the rule "for *ṇa*."
The remainder [of the rule] does not apply; this is because the *Bhāṣya* provides "avatānaḥ" as the sole example. (719) Pāṇini 3.1.141:
*śyādvyadhāsrusaṃsvratīṇavasāvahṛlihaśliṣaśvasaśca*.

The term *śyādvyadhāsru* is a compound in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) formed from the collective dvandva of the eleven roots: *śyā*, *āp*, *vyadh*, *āsru*, *saṃsru*, *atīṇ*, *avasā*, *avahṛ*, *liha*, *śliṣ*, and *svas*.
The condition "without a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) is no longer applicable here, because that requirement is explicitly mentioned in the subsequent rule. And thus:
And the mention of *vibhāṣā* connected with that does not carry over [into this rule]. Thus he says: "nityam" (always). Regarding "śyaiṅ":
there is a mention in the sūtra of the root *śyaiṅ* preceded by *ava*, and of the root *ṣo*, both having undergone *ātva*.
Although these two would already be established simply because they end in long *ā*, their mention again is for the sake of [the application of] *ātaścopasarge*.

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of setting aside the *kap* suffix. *Avaśyāyaḥ*, *pratiśyāyaḥ*: after the substitution of *ā* in the root *śyaiṅ*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied; then *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yuk*. The mention of *āt* indicates an example of a word ending in long *ā*. *Dāyaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*: after the suffix *ṇa*, *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yuk*. *Vyādha*: from the root *iṇ* preceded by *ati*, with the suffix *ṇa*.

The two substitutes are *vṛddhi* and *āy*. Regarding *avasāya*: from the root *ṣo* meaning "to finish" (*antakarman*) preceded by the prefix *ava*, with the suffix *ṇa*, there is the substitution *yuk* for the vowel *ā*. Regarding *lehaḥ* and *śleṣaḥ*: with the suffix *ṇa*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate light vowel. Regarding *śvāsaḥ*:
with the suffix *ṇa*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel.

(720) *dunyor anupasarge* |3|1|142|. This means [the rule applies] to the roots *du* and *nī* when no prefix (*upasarga*) is present. To justify the form *dava*, he says: "on account of its association with *nī*" (*sāhacaryāt*). The root *nī* (P. I. 965) is accompanied by an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*).
The meaning is that, by virtue of its association with that [root], the suffix *ṇa* is applied specifically from the root *du* (meaning "to afflict") belonging to the *svādi-gaṇa*.

As for the phrase "from the root *du*," the meaning is that the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is applied to the root *du* (meaning "to go") belonging to the *bhūvādi-gaṇa*, which is devoid of an *anubandha*.

(721) *vibhāṣā grahaḥ* |3|1|143|. This is an optionally restricted rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), as is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *śācchāsāhvāvyāvepāṃ yuc*. By that [rule], when a water-dwelling creature such as a fish (*matsya*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇa* is applied.

The meaning is that when there is an increase in the substratum (*upadhāvṛddhi*), the form is *grāha* alone; however, when a celestial body such as the sun, moon, or stars is to be expressed with the suffix *ac*, the form is *graha* alone.
Regarding the phrase "and from the root *bhū*," the remainder of the rule is "optionally after the suffix *ṇa*" (*ṇo vā*).
In the alternative case, the suffix *ac* is applied. As for the example *kāśikā*, the point is that it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*. This [suffix] also...

This is indeed a settled *vibhāṣā* (optional rule). Thus he says: "bhavo devaḥ" (Bhava is God). The meaning is "Mahādeva. Here, the intention is that [the suffix] *ṇa* alone [is used]. "Bhāvāḥ padārthāḥ" (entities are things); here, the intention is that *ṇa* alone [is used]. Now, since the optional application of *ṇa* for the root *bhū* is not seen in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule "bhavateśca," how can this be according to the *Bhāṣya* view?

Regarding the word *bhāva*, he says: "But according to the view of the Bhāṣya... The meaning is that the word *bhāva* is derived from the root *bhṛ* (in the sense of "to reach" or "to attain") belonging to the curādigaṇa, which takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *ac*; thus, after the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*), the form *bhāvī* is obtained, and finally the word *bhāva*. The meaning is that [the word *bhāva*] signifies that which causes [an action] to reach or brings about its respective effect.

(722) *gehe kaḥ* |3|1|144|. The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *geha*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *vibhāṣā grahaḥ*. Thus we have *gṛham*. Here, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) according to the rule *grahijyā-vayi-vyadhi-vaśca-vaṣṭi-vicati-vaṭi-vṛścati-pṛcchatibhṛjjatīnām*. But how is it that [the word] *gṛhāḥ* means "wife," since it occurs in the sense of *geha*?
Since the suffix *ka* is prescribed only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is to be expressed, he says: "Because of its being located there" (*tātsthyāt*).

The meaning is that the word *gṛha* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for one who stays in the house. Regarding the phrase "the house is the wife," Amarasimha states: "The word *gṛha* is also used for wives."

(723) *śilpini ṣvun* |3|1|145|. Regarding the rule *śilpini ṣvun*: "Only after the roots *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj*"—this is a Vārttika. [The example is] *nartakī*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; this is the intended meaning. This is discussed under the rule *daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapī*.

The Vārttika states: "The addition of *rajaka-raja-nara-jaḥ* should be included. He summarizes its meaning as: "after the roots *asi*, *aka*, and *ana*. Regarding *rajaka*: from the root *rañj*, with the suffix *ṣvun* in the sense of an artisan (*śilpin*), there is the substitution of *a* for the suffix-initial, and the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Regarding *rajakī*: because the suffix is marked with *ṣit*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.

Because of the restriction [in Pāṇini’s rule] to *nṛti*, *khan*, and *rañj* alone, the form *vāya* is established from the root *veñ* (meaning "to weave") after its vowel has been changed to *ā* (by *ātaḥ kṛkami...*), followed by the suffix *ṇa* (by *śyādvyadha...*), and the addition of the *yuk* augment to the final *ā*. However, according to the opinion of the Bhāṣya, [the suffix applies] only after *nṛti* and *khan*. And this...

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhdaṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapīṭati*. Now, one might ask: according to the view of the Bhāṣya, how can there be the form *rajakī* with the suffix *kvun*? To this he says: "But in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), [the word] is *rajakī*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.146: *gasthakan*).

*gasthakan*. [The analysis is: *ṭhgaḥ*—the division is *thak-an*. From the root *gai*, after it has undergone *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*), we have *ṭhga*; this is in the ablative case. Thus he says: "from the root *gāyati*.
(725) *ṇyuṭ ca* | Pāṇini 3.1.147.

*ṇyuṭ* also [is applied]. The *ca* (and) serves to include what has been previously mentioned. From the root *gā* (to sing), *ṇyuṭ* and *thak* are applied in the sense of an agent who is an artisan (*śilpin*). Thus we have *gāyana*. [The form] *gāyana* arises through the substitution of *ā* (by *ātaḥ yuka ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*) and the addition of *yuk*. Because the substitution of *ā* (by *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*) is not dependent on a specific condition (*anaimitikatva*), it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the application of *vṛddhi*. Although [the rule] *gasthakan*... [is mentioned],...

The single rule "ṇyuṭ ca" alone would have been appropriate; nevertheless, the separation of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the purpose of carrying forward (anuvṛtti) only "ṇyuṭ" into the subsequent rule. (726) *haśca vrīhikālayoḥ* 3.1.148.

And *ha*: [the suffix] *ha* is the fifth case form (*pañcamyantam*) of the root *ṭhu* in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāge*) and of the root *ṭhu* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*). Thus he says: "of *hāka* and *hāṅ*.
(727) *prusṛlvaḥ samabhihāre vun* || 3.1.149 || [This sūtra prescribes the suffix] *vun* after the roots *pru*, *sṛ*, and *lū* when there is repetition of an action (*samabhihāra*).

"prusṛlvaḥ": it is observed [as such], and this is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya. [The form] is the ablative case from a collective dvandva compound of *pru*, *sṛ*, and *lū*. (728) *āśiṣi ca* | 3|1|150|.

And in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). "O Jīvaka" means one who is the substratum for the act of living that is being wished for. Likewise for *nandaka*. Regarding "benediction" (*āśis*): it is a wish, namely the prayer "May this person be thus," which has as its agent the speaker of the words; therefore, this is an utterance from the perspective of the one wishing the blessing, such as a father or other relative.

This is the employment of the word *nandaka*; the sense is that it is due to propriety (*aucityāt*). [Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter. Now begins the second quarter of the third chapter. (729) *karmaṇyaṇ* | 3.2.1 | [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root when [the object of the action] is the [agent of the desire expressed by the suffix]. 3.2.1.

Regarding *karmaṇyaṇ*: the phrase "when a word in the objective case (*karman*) is an *upapada*" is explained in the very same [sūtra] by the word *tatra* in the rule *tatrōpapadaṃ saptamīstham*, which states that this [term *upapada*] is understood there. However, the suffix (*pratyaya*) applies only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
The term "compound with an *upapada*" (*upapadasamāsa*) is used because of the rule *upapadamatinaṅ*. [The example is] *kumbhakāraḥ*.

"It makes" (*karoti*). This is a non-technical (laukika) analytical statement (*vigraha*) consisting of separate words. Alternatively, in the non-technical analytical sentence "kumbha-as-kāra," it has already been stated that the compound of the word *kumbha* ending in the genitive case with the word *kāra*—which ends in a *kṛt* suffix—occurs precisely before the application of case-endings (*sub*). Now, [regarding] *ādityam*...

One might think that [the suffix *aṇ*] would apply in cases such as "one who sees the sun" (*ādityadarśaḥ*), "one who hears the Himalayas" (*himavacchrāvaḥ*), or "one who goes to the village" (*grāmagāmaḥ*); therefore, he says: "[It is] not so, because there is no conventional usage (*anabhidhānāt*) in expressions such as 'one sees the sun'. This is clear in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the word *śālī*:
The meaning is that the suffix *ṇa* should be prescribed after the roots *śīl*, *kām*, *bhakṣ*, and *ācar*. Now, one might ask:
since the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1] "after a root ending in an object" would already suffice, for what purpose is this stated?
To this he replies: "for the sake of setting aside *aṇ*. For if the suffix were *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would occur; it is for the purpose of preventing that.

The sense is that this is the rule for the formation [of the word]. Thus he says: "māṃsaśīlā" (flesh-habituated). The root *śī* belongs to the *bhvādi* class in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhi*), but here it functions in the sense of "habitual practice by nature. The meaning is "one who habitually consumes meat by nature. Regarding "māṃsakāmā": she desires meat; thus, *māṃsakāmā*.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: *māṃsabhakṣā*—the analysis is "one who eats meat" (*māṃsaṃ bhakṣayate*). *Kalyāṇācārā*—the analysis is "one who practices what is auspicious" (*kalyāṇam ācarati*). In all these cases, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied. Regarding the rule "after the roots *īkṣi* and *kṣami*": this is a *vārttika*; the word "with the suffix *ṇa*" (*ṇa*) is understood as the remainder. [The question] "How? [is asked]; [the answer is: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman*), there is *gaṅgādhāra*.

The phrase "it would be so" (*syāt*) and so forth constitutes an objection. The point is that since the object (*karman*) is treated as a residual element (*śeṣatva*), the suffix *aṇ* does not apply due to the absence of the object as a governing word (*upapada*).

(730) *hvāvāmaśca* | Pāṇini 3.2.2. [Note: The rule *hvāvāmaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.2) prescribes the suffix *aṇ* after the roots *hve* (to call), *vye* (to weave), and *mā* (to measure), when the object is a residual element.]

And *hvāva*. [The forms] *ṭhhveñ* in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*) and *ṭhveñ* in the sense of weaving (*tantusantāna*)—these two are mentioned here with their vowel changed to *ā* (i.e., as *hvā*). *Māṅ* in the sense of measuring (*māna*). From this *dvandva* compound, the fifth case singular is used. "From these" means that when these roots have an object as a governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *aṇ* shall apply. But is it not already established by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*?

Since [the suffix] *ka* is already established [by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*], for what purpose is this stated? To this he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *kā*. The meaning is that it is for the purpose of subverting the forthcoming *aṇ*, which is an exception to [the rule] *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*. Here, the roots *māṅ* and *meṅ* are intended to be included, but not the root *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*), because that one is intransitive (*akarmaka*). As for the form *svargahvāya*: although...

It was stated that [the root *ji*] is intransitive because, in the case of the desire to overcome another (*parābhibhavecchā*) or in rivalry (*spardhā*), the act of overcoming (*paribhibhava*) is included within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Nevertheless, in this instance, the desire to overcome is the meaning of the root; the sense is "he desires to overcome heaven. Because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) applies.
When *kṛt* [suffixes] follow, *yuk* is added after a stem ending in long *ā*. The same applies hereafter. (731) *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* |3|2|3|.
[The rule] "After a stem ending in long *ā*, when no upasarga precedes, the suffix *ka* is added. For example, *pārṣṇitram*. Here, *pārṣṇiḥ* refers to the part at the base of the foot. That—

The word *vigraha* protects [from destruction]. [This is derived] from the root *traiṅ* in the sense of "protecting" (*pālane*); once the substitution of *ā* has been made, the suffix *ka* is applied. Regarding *gosandāya*: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, *yuk* is inserted after a vowel ending in *ā*. The statement "in all rules for the application of *ka*" is a *vārttika*. Its meaning is that, in every rule prescribing the suffix *ka*, a suffix *ḍa* should be stated as an exception (*apavāda*) to *ka* in cases where *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel-consonant contraction) would otherwise apply.

Regarding the term *brahmajya*: the root *jyā* (meaning "loss of vitality") takes the suffix *ḍa*. By virtue of the marker *ḍ*, there is elision of the final vowel even though it belongs to a non-*bha* stem. Here, if the suffix *ka* were applied, the rule *grahijyā* would require vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because *ka* is a *kit* suffix;
therefore, only *ḍa* is used, not *ka*. Regarding the phrase "in all cases": this also applies when a prefix is the *upapada*.

The construction is as follows: [the suffix] *ḍa* alone [is applied], and not *ka* by the rule "after *ā*, when preceded by a prefix" (*ātaścopasarge*), because of the inclusion of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).

Otherwise, according to the maxim "a rule applies to what is nearest," *ḍa* alone would apply, overriding *ka* by the rule "after *ā*, when no prefix is present" (*āto 'nupasarge*). Since that [suffix *ḍa*] is not *akit*, there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) conditioned by [the suffixes] beginning with *yac*. [The rule continues: "after the root *sthā*, when followed by a case-ending (*sup*)."

"The yoga is being analyzed"—this is clear in the Bhāṣya. Therein, he explains the portion "supi": "when a *sup*-ending word is the *upapada*. This [rule] is useless for mere prepositions (*upasarga*), since it is already established by the rule "ātaścopasarge" (Pāṇini 3.1.136); and it is likewise useless when a noun in the accusative case (*karman*) is the *upapada*.
Considering that [the rule] begins with "ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ," he provides the example: "dvābhyām.
Regarding the word "tataḥ": the meaning is that after providing another explanation for the portion "supi," the portion "stha" is now being explained.
But if [the desired form] is already established by the portion "supi" alone, for what purpose is this [rule]? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "due to the force of the initial statement": when the rule *supi* (Pāṇini 3.2.4) is established by the preceding rule, the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) does not recur [into it]. Since its meaning is not specifically prescribed, this suffix is *svārthika* (denoting its own base-meaning), like *sa* in *guptijkidbhyaḥ sa* (Pāṇini 3.1.5) and others; and it is clear in the Bhāṣya that its own base-meaning (*svārtha*) is indeed the abstract state (*bhāva*). It is not [the agent].

And this being the case, one should not say that the formation is established simply by the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of *ṭh* and *ghañ*," because [the rule] is intended for the sake of forming a compound with an obligatory subordinate word (*upapada*). For this very reason, showing a non-co-ordinate analysis (*asvapadavigraha*) with a form ending in *lyuṭ*, he says: "The rising of mice is *ākhūttha*."
(732) *praṣṭho 'gragāmini* | Pāṇini 8.3.92. Regarding *praṣṭho 'gragāmini*: from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *pra*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *ātaś copasarge*.
With the elision of the final *ā*, the word *prastha* is formed. When it denotes one who goes at the front (*agragāmin*), the substitution of *ṣa* for *sa* is applied.
It is elided. Since there is no [letter] following the root *iṇ* or the *ka*-group, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply.

In the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, the meaning is "he goes forward," due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*). In *praṣṭho gauḥ*, the meaning is "a bull that goes at the head. Similarly, *praṣṭho'śvaḥ* and so forth.

(733) *ambāmbago-bhūmi-savya-apa-dvi-tri-kuśa-e-ku-śaṅ-ku-aṅ-gu-mañji-puñja-parame-barhi-divi-agni-bhyaḥ sthaḥ* || 8|3|97 || [The suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied after the following words when followed by *stha*: *amba*, *āmba*, *go*, *bhūmi*, *savya*, *apa*, *dvi*, *tri*, *kuśa*, *e*, *ku*, *śaṅ*, *ku*, *aṅ*, *gu*, *mañji*, *puñja*, *parame*, *barhis*, *divi*, and *agni*. *amba*, *āmba*, *go*, *bhūmi*, *savya*, *apa*, *dvi*, *tri*, *kuśe*, *ku*.

*Śaṅku*, *aṅgu*, *mañji*, *puñji*, *parame*, *barhis*, *divi*, and *agni*—this is a dvandva compound of these eighteen [words]. *Ambaṣṭhaḥ*, *āmbaṣṭhaḥ*, *goṣṭhaḥ*, *bhūmiṣṭhaḥ*, and *savyeṣṭhaḥ*. [In these,] there is elision of the locative suffix due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), or according to the rule "after a word ending in a consonant, the locative suffix is elided. [The form] *apaṣṭhaḥ* occurs among these.
In some cases, the prohibition [of the suffix -tha] by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* applies. The same applies in the following instances as well. Regarding *dviṣṭha*:
the analysis is "that which stands by means of two" (*dvābhyāṃ tiṣṭhati*). Similarly: *triṣṭhaḥ*, *kuśeṣṭhaḥ*, *kuṣṭhaḥ*, *śaṅkuṣṭhaḥ*, *aṅguṣṭhaḥ*, *mañjiṣṭhaḥ*, *puñjiṣṭhaḥ*. Also *parameṣṭhaḥ*.

The absence of *luk* (elision) occurs either by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) or by the rule "after a word ending in *ṭh*, *hal*, or a vowel" (*ṭhhaladantāt*). Examples: *varṣiṣṭhaḥ*, *diviṣṭhaḥ*. As before, there is no elision: *agniṣṭhaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in the suffix *kap*": [examples include] *bhūmisthitam* and *ita ūrdhvam*; the latter means starting from the rule "after *tuṇḍa* and *śoka*" (*tuṇḍaśokayoh*). Regarding the phrase "after a *sup* [ending word]": but not...
The meaning is that [the suffix] cannot apply to the word *karman*.
(734) *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ* |3|2|5|. [The words] *tundaśokayoḥ*: *tundaśokayoh* is in the locative case. *parimṛja*, *apanuda*.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the ablative after this *dvandva* compound. Thus it says: "after these two as subordinate words (*upapada*).

Regarding *tundaparimṛja*: *tuṇḍa* means the belly. Here, the optional *vṛddhi* [strengthening] prescribed by the rule *mṛjer ajādau* does not occur; they say this is because of the reliance on a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). [The roots] *mūla*...

"Vibhujati" means "he crushes"; it belongs to the *tudādi* class in the sense of "crookedness. Here, by the power of the prefix (*upasarga*), its function is [extended] to crushing. Regarding "mahīdhra": the analysis of the compound is "one who bears the earth" (*mahīm dharati*). Because of the *kit* suffix, there is no *guṇa* substitution; the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *yaṇ*-sandhi to become *r*. If the suffix were *aṇ*, however, the form would be "mahīdhāra."

*Kudhra*: The analysis of the compound is "kuḥ" (the earth) and "dharati" (he supports); thus, he who supports the earth is *kudhra*. *Gila*: From the root *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing," the suffix *ka* is applied. Because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; instead, the vowel is changed to *i*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel (*raparatvam*).
According to the rule "aci vibhāṣā," the *r* may optionally be replaced by *l*, resulting in *gila*.

(735) *pre dājñaḥ* |3|2|6|. The word *pre* is a locative used in the sense of the ablative. *Dā* and *jñā*: from this *dvandva* compound, the fifth case singular is formed. [The meaning is] "preceded by *pra*" (*propasṛṣṭāt*).
The meaning is "preceded by a prefix. This undertaking is for the sake of [explaining] the meaning of [roots] with prefixes.
(736) *sami khyah* |3|2|7|. In *sami khyah*, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). Regarding *gosaṅkhya*: he enumerates the cows (*gāḥ saṃcaṣṭe*).
Such is the analysis of the compound. The form [saṃkhyā] is derived from the root *cakṣiṅ* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the substitution of *khyāñ*.

However, the root *khyā* (meaning "to tell") preceded by *sam* is not connected here, because it is never used in such a construction and because its application is restricted solely to the domain of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.

(737) *gāpoṣṭak* |3|2|8|. The suffix *ṭak* is applied after the roots *gai* ("to sing") and *pā* ("to drink") when a word denoting the object (*karman*) is used as an *upapada*. The form is derived by adding *yuK* to the vowel *ā*. Regarding "of *pibati*": this is a *vārttika*.
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭak* is applied to the root *pā-* when *surā* or *śīdhu* are the accompanying words (*upapada*). Regarding *kṣīrapā*:

in the sense of "one who drinks milk," since *surā* and *śīdhu* are not applicable here, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Regarding *pāyī*: it means "one who protects" (*rakṣati*), derived from the root *aj*.

*Udyamana* means *udgrahaṇa* (the act of lifting up). *Aṃśahara* means one who takes possession of a share (*aṃśasya svīkartā*). *Bhārahāra* means one who lifts up a burden (*bhāram udgṛhṇāti*). Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule]," the remainder is "of the suffix *ṭhac*. The root *grah* is used in the sense of "taking" (*upādāne*) and has a vowel as its penultimate letter (*adupadha*). If the reading is *gṛh*, it refers to the same root.

However, it should be understood that the mention of *ik* refers to the form after the semivowel has undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*. In *śaktigraha*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* because it is not an *akit* [suffix]. In *lāṅgalagraha*, and likewise in *aṅkuśagraha*, etc., the same principle should be applied as examples. Regarding the word "in the sūtra": this is a *vārttika*; [it applies] to the sūtra.
The meaning is that when a word expressing an object (*karman*) is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *iñ* is applied after the root *grah* in the sense of "holding.

(738) *vayasi ca* |3|2|10|. The meaning is that when a word expressing an object is used as a subordinate term and age (*vayas*) is implied, the suffix *añ* is applied after the root *hṛ*. Now, [an objection]:...

Since the rule is already established by [Pāṇini 6.1.145] *ṭh-tharater-anudyamane* ("the augment ṭh is applied after the root *tharati* except when meaning 'to lift up'"), for what purpose is this stated?
To this he says: "for the sake of [specifying] the sense of lifting up. (739) *āiṅ tācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.11).

The prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). When the root *hṛ* preceded by *āṅ* has an object as its *upapada*, the suffix *ac* shall be applied if habitual action is to be understood. Habitual action means being of that nature. For example, *puṣpāhara* ("one who gathers flowers"): the meaning is that his natural inclination toward gathering flowers is indeed independent of any expectation for fruit.

[The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *arha*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Although there is no difference between *aṇ* and *ac* when the form is *pūjārha* (worthy of honor), because the rule for *vṛddhi* does not apply due to the absence of a vowel *a* as the penultimate letter (*adupadhatva*), nevertheless, in the feminine, if it ends in *aṇ*— [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, specifically discussing the application of the suffix *cha* (which becomes *īya*) after the word *arha*, overriding the general suffix *aṇ*. The commentary notes that while phonologically there might be no distinction between *aṇ* and *ac* in this specific case, the grammatical outcome differs in the feminine gender.]
The suffix *ṅīp* would apply; to prevent that, the rule for the addition of *ac* is prescribed. Thus he says: "for the sake of honor," etc.
(741) *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ* |3|2|13|. Regarding *stamba* and *karṇa*: since the roots *ram* and *jap* are intransitive, the term "object" (*karmaṇi*) does not apply here.
It should be understood that the verbal root *jap*, which signifies the utterance of sounds, is intransitive because its object is included within the meaning of the root itself.

*Stamba* refers to a cluster of grass such as *darbha*. *Sūcaka* means a slanderer or informer. Why specify "of an elephant or a slanderer"? [Consider these examples: "A cow delights in a clump of grass" (*stambe rantā gauḥ*), or "A teacher whispers into the ear" (*karṇe japitā guruḥ*), or "A mosquito [buzzes] in the ear."

(742) *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām* |3|2|14|. [The word] *śami* is the locative case (*saptamyanta*) of *śam*. *Śam* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "happiness. When this is the *upapada*, the suffix *ac* shall be added to a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). Now, is not the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) redundant?

Nor should it be said that "that" (the suffix *ṇa*) does not recur for the sake of avoiding its application to the root *ram*; for its non-recurrence is established simply by the fact that it is not marked with the *svarita* accent. To this, he says: "The repetition of the word 'root' (*dhātu*). It will be stated that in the rule "after the root *kṛ*, [the suffix] *ṇa* [is added] in the sense of cause, habit, or compliance," the suffix *ṇa* subverts the suffix *ac*.
The meaning is: "for the purpose of refuting that.

(743) *Adhikaraṇe śeteḥ* |3|2|15|. [The rule] *adhikaraṇe*: when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ac* is added to the root *śīṅ*.
The meaning is "it may be so. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *pārśva* and others": here, the term "denoting the locus" (*adhikaraṇavācin*) is not connected [to the rule].

Indicating this, he provides an example: "by the two sides" (*pārśvābhyām*). Regarding the phrase "when *utāna* and others are the agents": this is a Vārttika; it means when words such as *utāna* are used as upapadas denoting the agent.
The meaning is "in the sense of lying down. Regarding the word *girau*: this is a Vārttika.

When *giri* is the upapada, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of even *śīṅ*, despite it being a root ending in a nasal. Although this should be explained only within the context of Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*), it is nevertheless presented here to demonstrate that in common usage (*loke*), the suffix *ḍa* does not apply, but rather only *ac*.
Intending to explain that, he provides an example of the *ac* suffix in common usage—namely, *giriśayaḥ*.
[The questioner asks: "How so? [The answer is: because the suffix *ḍa* is impossible in common usage; this is the intended meaning. He resolves this by stating:
"He possesses a mountain," and so forth.

(744) *careṣṭaḥ* | 3|2|16|. The word *careṣṭaḥ* [is analyzed as follows]: the division is *ca-re-ṭaḥ*. The remainder is "when the locative (*adhikaraṇe*) is the attendant word (*upapade*). This is because that [condition] is understood from the previous rule *ṭhadhikaraṇe śete*. Thus, *kurucaraḥ* means "one who moves among the Kurus. In the sense of "in the Kurus..."

The analysis [of the compound] is "he moves" (*caratīti*). Nor should one suspect that there is the status of an object (*karmatva*) [of the self] due to its connection with an intransitive root (*akarmaka-dhātu*), because it has already been explained in detail in that very [section] that such [objecthood] is optional. In this regard, the Bhāṣya on that [sūtra] is also authoritative.

(745) *bhikṣā-senā-dāyeṣu ca* | 3|2|17| The meaning is that the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *car* when followed by the upapadas *bhikṣā*, *senā*, and *ādāya*. Thus: *bhikṣāṃ carati* ("he begs for alms"). Here, the root *car* signifies acquisition preceded by wandering.

It occurs [as follows]: "he wanders for alms by means of his feet" (caraṇena bhikṣāṃ mārgayati) is the meaning; "army-goer" (senācara) means he causes the army to move. Regarding the form ending in *lyap* (i.e., *ācarya*), here the commentary itself is the refuge [for understanding]. "He wanders having taken" (ādāya carati) means he wanders having grasped the object obtained. As for "how" (*katham*), it is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*).

The intention is that the suffix *ṭa*, prescribed after the upapadas "bhikṣā" and "senā," cannot occur after the root *car* when preceded by *saha*. He provides the resolution: "In the *pacādi* group, etc.
Although the form is established by the *ac* suffix from the *pacādi* group in cases such as "bhikṣācara," nevertheless...
They say that this rule for the suffix *ac* is intended for the sake of forming a compound with a constant (*nitya*) upapada.
(746) Pāṇini 3.2.18: *puro'gratato'greṣu sarteḥ*.
When *puras*, *agratas*, or *agre* are used as upapadas, the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *sṛ*. Thus: *puraḥsaraḥ*, *agratas+saraḥ*, *agresaraḥ*.

The meaning is "it might be so. Regarding the term *agresara*: one might object that because it is a member of a compound, the case-ending (*sup*) would be elided by *luk*, resulting in the form *agrasara*;
therefore, he says: "In the Sūtra. He asks: "How?"—the meaning is: how can the word *agrasara* exist given that [the rule] prescribes the substitution of the vowel *e*? He provides the resolution:
"By way of frequent usage (*bāhulakāt*). In the preceding [sūtra], it refers to the agent (*kartṛ*). The word *kartṛ* here is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) to mean that which denotes the agent.
Thus he says: "denoting the agent.
(747) Pāṇini 3.2.20: *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu*.

Regarding *kṛño hetu-*: *hetu* means "cause" (*kāraṇa*). *Ānulomya* means "compliance," that is, acting in accordance with the wishes of one who is to be propitiated. The phrase "when these [meanings] are to be expressed" implies that the agent alone is what is denoted by the suffix. However, the meaning is not that [the suffix is used] when words such as *hetu* are present as *upapadas*.

[This is] because of the commentary. It should also be understood that [the rule applies] when a verbal root has an object as its upapada. Anticipating the possibility of a *jihvāmūlīya* [substitution] by the rule *kupvoḥ*, he says: *ataḥ kṛ-kami-* [Pāṇini 8.3.46]. He provides an example for the sense of "cause":
*vidyā yaśaskarī* ("knowledge is the cause of fame"). Knowledge is the cause of fame. [The example] *śrāddhakaraḥ* means one whose habit is the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.

This is the meaning. Regarding the term *vanakara*: it means one who follows the instructions of teachers and others. (748) *divāvibhāniśāprabhābhāskarāntānantādibahunāndīkiṃlipilibibalibhaktikartṛcitrakṣetrasaṅkhyājaṅghābāhvaharyataddhanuraruṣṣu* |3|2|21|.
divāvibhā— divā, vibhāṣā, niśā, prabhā, bhās, kāra, anta, ananta, ādi, bahu, nadī, kin, lipi, libi, bali, bhakti, kartṛ, citra, kṣetra, saṅkhyā, jaṅghā, bāhu, ahar, yad, tad, dhanus, arus.

The seventh case ending [saptamī] is used after these twenty-seven [words] due to their being in a copulative compound (dvandva). "In these" means: the remainder is that they are "in the presence of" (upapadeṣu) [these].
"Even in 'ahā' and so forth" means: even when [the meanings of] cause, habit, or conformity are not applicable.

The intention is that the mention of "cause" (hetu) and the others does not recur [from the previous rule]. By this, it is shown that this [rule] is for the sake of cases other than cause and the rest.

The sūtra has been stated. Here, the terms *karmaṇi* ("in the object") and *supi* ("in a case-ending") are understood as being carried over (*anuvṛtta*), and they apply according to their respective requirements. Regarding *divākara*: *divā* is an indeclinable ending in *-ā* meaning "day.

Although it primarily possesses the force of the locative case (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*), its status as the "object" (*karman*) within the scope of a compound formation (*vṛtti*) should be understood. [End of] *divā*.
Or, the analysis [of the compound] is: "one who makes living beings endowed with activity during the day" (u-ahani).

Regarding *vibhākara*: the analysis is "one who makes light" (*vibhām karoti*). Regarding *niśākara*: the analysis is "one who makes the night" (*niśām karoti*). Similarly, *prabhākara* [is formed]; in the analysis "one who makes radiance" (*bhāḥ karoti*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied.

In the word *kṛkami*, because the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.1) contains the marker *t* (indicating that the short vowel *a* is intended), the substitution of *s* (satva) does not apply; consequently, one might suspect the application of the *jihvāmūlīya* or the *visarga* by the rule *kupvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.37). To address this, he says: "Because it belongs to the *kaska-* group" (*kaskāditvāt*). Having taken *kārakaraḥ*, *antakaraḥ*, *anantakaraḥ*, and *ādikaraḥ* as established examples, he says: "*bahukaraḥ*."

Now, one might object that since the inclusion [of the term] is already established by the mention of "number" (saṅkhyā) alone, the mention of "much" (bahu) is redundant; to this he says: "Of the word *bahu*. It has been stated in the rule "The words *bahu*, *gana*, *vat*, and *uṭi* are numbers" (*pā. 1.1.23*) that this word, when signifying abundance (*vaipulya*), does not possess the nature of a number-word. For example: *nāndīkaraḥ* (one who performs a festive rite), *kiṅkaraḥ* (a servant).

Taking them for granted, he says: "the words *lipi* and *liś*. Likewise, taking as established everything up to *libikaraḥ* and *kṣetrakaraḥ*, he says: "*saṅkhyā*," with the word "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) understood as the ellipsis.
Having taken *jaṅghākaraḥ* and *bāhukaraḥ* for granted, [he speaks] regarding the word *ahaskaraḥ*.
Fearing that the *jihvāmūlīya* and *visarga* might apply according to the rule "kupvoḥ," he says:

"because it belongs to the *kaskādi* group. In the word *ahan*, which is derived from the root *jahāti* with the negative particle *nañ*, the word *han* serves as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*); therefore, because its *visarga* resides in the subsequent member, [the rule] "ataḥ" [applies].

The intention is that the rule *kṛkami-* does not apply here. Regarding the word *dhanuṣkara*, he says: "Always in a compound. The intention is that because it is a part of an affix (*pratyaya*), the rule *idudupadhasya ca* does not apply.
The statement "the prescription of *ac* after the root *kṛ*" is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [rule *kṛkami-*]. As for *kiṅkarā*, it is formed with the suffix *ap*.

The intention is that [the suffix] ṅīp would apply after [the word] *tuṣṭi*. The intention is that there is no basis for resorting to the rule of "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) in the case of [the suffixes] *hetu* and so forth. If one asks, "In that case, how is [the form] *kiṅkarī* derived?", he says:
"[The suffix] ṅīṣ is used in the sense of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). [The suffix] *karmaṇi* is used in the sense of wages (*bhṛti*).
While the term *karmaṇi* is understood from the previous context, the repetition of the word *karman* here is for the purpose of capturing the specific form of the word *karman*.
An example is *karmakaro bhṛtakaḥ* ("a laborer who performs work"). One who performs work for another after having received wages is called a *bhṛtaka*.

(749) *na śabdaślokakalahagāthāvairacāṭuasūtramantrapadeṣu* || 3.2.23 || *na śabdaśloka*: [The compound] *śabda*, *śloka*, *kalaha*, *gāthā*, *vaira*, *cāṭua*, *sūtra*, *mantra*, and *pada*—this is a *dvandva* compound of these nine. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *hetu* and so forth": [it refers to the rule for the suffix] *kṛñaḥ*.
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭa*, which would otherwise be obtained by the rule "in the senses of causality, habitual action, and conformity," is hereby prohibited.
(750) *stamba-śakṛtor-in* | 3|2|24|. [This sūtra prescribes the suffix *in* after the words *stamba* and *śakṛt* in the sense of "one who acts upon" (*karmaṇi*).]

*stamba-śakṛtoḥ-in*: When *stamba* (a clump of grass) or *śakṛt* (dung) is the object (*karman*) in composition, the suffix *in* is applied after the root *kṛ* (to make). The letter *n* is for the sake of [marking the accent]. "In the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and a calf (*vatṣa*)" means that when *vrīhi* or *vatṣa* is the agent (*kartṛ*).
There is a correspondence between *stamba* and *śakṛt* according to their respective order. Thus, *stambakari* (a rice plant) refers to rice; [it is that which] makes a clump.
The analysis of the compound is: "one who makes a heap of grass" (*tṛṇanicayaṃ karoti*).

(751) *harateḥ dṛtināthayoḥ paśau* |3|2|15|. [The rule states: "After the root *hṛ*, [the suffix *ṇini* is applied] when *dṛti* or *nātha* follow, provided the word refers to an animal. *Dṛti* means a leather bag. *Dṛtihariḥ* means a dog; such is the commentary (*vṛtti*).

The explanation of the word *nātha* is "the nose-rope" (*nāsārajjum*). This means the rope fastened to the nose. Regarding *nāthahari*: this term is conventionally used for a specific type of sacrificial animal that has a rope fastened to its nose.

(752) *phalegrahirātmambhariśca* |3|2|26|. *Phalegrhiḥ*: [This is derived] by the rule *graherinn* (Uṇādi 4.138). It is not, however, from the root *gṛhū* (meaning "to seize") by the rule *ṛdupadhāt...* (Uṇādi 4.120); such is the meaning. Regarding the augment *mum*: the meaning is that after the elision of the *n* in the word *ātman*, the augment *mum* is added after the vowel *a*.

Considering that the particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned, he says: "And [the term] *kukṣambhari*. In the Bhāṣya, however, it is established that one should state: "After the root *bhṛ*, when followed by *kukṣi* or *ātman*, there is the augment *mum*.
Amara, in his list of synonyms for trees, states: "It may be *avandhya* or *phalegrahi*. [The term] *ātmambhari* means "one who nourishes himself."
In the section on words whose gender follows that of the noun they qualify (*viśeṣyanighna*), it is stated: "The word *kukṣimbhari* means 'one who fills his own belly'.
To justify the form *udarambhari*, he says: "But according to the Cāndras...
[Pāṇini 3.2.28]: *ejeḥ khaś*.

The term *ejeh* refers to the root *ejṛ* when it ends in the suffix *ṇi*, and not a mere mention of the vowel *i*; this is the sense, based on the [authoritative] commentary. The letters *kha* and *śa* are elided. It should also be understood that this applies when a word denoting the object (*karman*) is present as a subordinate element (*upapada*).
(754) *arurdviṣadajantasya mum* 6.3.67.
*arurdviṣat*: This is a genitive case derived from a collective dvandva compound of *arus*, *dviṣat*, and *ajanta*.
Because of the governing rule *ṭhalugutarapade*, it is understood that this applies when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). [The preceding rule] *khityanavyayasya*...
From this point, *khit* is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtta*). Since *kit* is an affix (*pratyaya*), the rule of "that which ends in [the affix]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.

Thus he says: "when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ends in *khit*. Regarding *janamejaya*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who causes people to tremble" (*janān ejayati*). Because the affix *khaś* has the marker *ś*, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*; thus, the *śap* augment is applied, followed by *guṇa* and the *ay-ādeśa*.

The form *pararūpa* [is applied] when there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), and the augment *mum* [is added]. This is the Vārttika rule: *vāta-śunī-*. It is a locative dual compound of *vāta*, *śunī*, *tila*, and *śardha*. It is an ablative dual compound of *aja*, *dhṛṣṭe*, *tud*, and *dahāti*. The application follows the respective order. For example: *vātamajā* means "those who run after the wind."
The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: when there is *luk* elision of the case-ending (*sup*), the augment *mum* is applied. Now, regarding the analysis "it drinks a bitch" (*śunīṃ dhayati*):

when the word *śunī* is the subordinate term (*upapada*) for the root *dheṭ*, with the suffix *khaś*, the addition of *śap*, the substitution of *ay* for *e*, and the subsequent single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule, we arrive at the form *śunīdhaya*. At this point, he says:

(755) *khityanavyayasya* |6|3|66|. [The word] "of a non-indicative (*anavyaya*) [stem ending in a vowel] before a suffix marked with *khi*" [is understood]. [The meaning is: "there shall be a short vowel. The intention is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "for *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* [ending a stem], there is a short vowel before a suffix marked with *khi*, according to Gālava" (*iko hrasvo'ṅyo gālavasya*). Here, by the mention of "short" (*hrasva*), the term "vowel" (*ac*) is brought into the context.
It should be observed that the sequence is *mum* first; the meaning is that the short vowel is applied first, and then *mum*.

The point is that if *mum* were applied first, the shortening would not occur because the word would no longer end in a vowel (*ajanta*). Regarding the example *śardhañjahā māṣāḥ*, the reading in the Bhāṣya, however, is *mṛgāḥ*. *Śardhaḥ* refers to that which is situated at the anus.

Mādhava and others state that [the term] is "śabda. Regarding the phrase "antarbhāvitā" (with the meaning internalized), the resulting analysis (*vigraha*) is thus: "those who cause the abandonment of greed" (*gardham hāpayanti*). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the *vārttika* "vātaśunī" reads "gardheṣu" (in the sense of greed).

(756) *nāsikāstanayordhmādheṭoḥ* |3|2|29|. The word *nāsikā* [is formed] from *nasikā*; *stana* remains as it is. From this *dvandva* compound, the locative case is used. For *dhmā* and *dheṭ*, from this *dvandva* compound, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. The remainder is supplied by the rule *khaśi*. Since a correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhya*) would otherwise apply, [this sūtra is stated].

He says: "Regarding this, there is a Vārttika. [The phrase] "because *dheṭ* has the marker *ṭi*"—although it has been explained in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...* that a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṭi*, etc., which ends in a short vowel, [receives the suffix *ṅīp*], nevertheless, Haradatta maintains that the suffix *ṅīp* is applied because the status of being marked by *ṭi* (*ṭitva*) has no other function within its constituent parts. As for what must be said on this point:
This was stated in the rule *ṣṭhivū-prāghrā-dhmā-dheṭ-dṛśaḥ śaḥ*. Regarding the form *nāsikandhama*:
when the short vowel is applied, *mum* is added by the rule *nāsikāyā dhmaśca*; from the word *ca* ("and"), it is understood that this also applies after the root *dheṭ*.
He provides an example of it: *nāsikandhaya*.

(757) *nāḍīmuṣṭyoś ca* |3|2|20|. Regarding *nāḍīmuṣṭyoś ca*: it is not intended that there be a correspondence [of the order of words] here. This is clear in the Bhāṣya. *Ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and so forth, are clear.

(758) *udi kūle rujivahoḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.31. *Udi kūle*: The word *ud* [in this rule] is in the locative case (*saptamī*) with the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*) used in connection with a direction. *Rujivahoḥ*: The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). The root *ruj* (meaning "to break") belongs to the *tudādi* class. Here, [the suffix *khaś* is applied] after the root *ruj*.

Because the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), it is understood that [the suffix *kha*] occurs when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a governing word (*upapada*). Consequently, it is the bank (*kūla*) that is qualified, not the word *ut*, because the latter denotes an abstract state (*asattvavācin*). Thus he says: "from those preceded by *ut," and so forth.
Regarding the form *kūlamudrujaḥ*: the intention is that after the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), the augment *mum* is applied.
(759) *vahābhre lihaḥ* | 3|2|32|. The meaning of *vahābhre lihaḥ* is that the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *lih* when *vaha* or *abhra* are present as the object (*karman*) in composition.
The word *vaha* is explained as "shoulder" (*skandha*). Regarding the phrase "the elision of *śap*" (*śapo luk*), it is because *khaś* is marked with the *śit* designation.
The meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment because it belongs to the *sārvadhātuka* category.
(760) *parimāṇe pacaḥ* |3|2|33|.

Regarding *parimāṇe pacaḥ*: "measure" (*parimāṇa*) refers to a *prastha* and so forth. When such a measure is present as the object (*karman*) [of the action], [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the root *pac*.
The meaning is "one who cooks in a pan" (*khārīpaca*). There is shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *khityanavyayasya*, and then the suffix *mum* is added.

(761) *mitanakhe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.34). The meaning of *mitanakhe ca* is that the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *pac* when the words *mita* or *nakha* are used as the object (*karman*) in composition. [This applies to the word] *nakhānām*.
Because softening is impossible [in this context], he says: "paciratra" (here, the root *pac* occurs).

(762) *vidhvaruṣostudaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.35. Regarding *vidhvaruṣostudaḥ*: when the roots *tuda* [and others] have *vidhu* and *arus* as their objects (*karman*) serving as co-occurring words (*upapada*).
The meaning is "one who pierces. Regarding the term *vidhuntuda*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who pierces (*tudati*) the moon (*vidhu*)," which is the moon;

the meaning is Rāhu. Regarding the word *aruṣ*: when the suffix *muṭ* is added after the vowel *u*, there is elision of the final consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the letter *s*; thus, it becomes *aruntuda*. [The analysis is: "the vital spot (*aru*) is the *marman*; those who pierce that are called *aruntuda*."
The compound is *vigraha*.

(763) *asūryalalāṭayordṛśitapoḥ* |3|2|36|. In the rule *asūryalalāṭa*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in *dṛśitapoḥ* functions in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamy-artha*). [The compound applies] after *asūrya* and *lalāṭa*.

The meaning is that when a word denoting an object (*karman*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *dṛś* (to see) and *tap* (to heat). Regarding the phrase "asūryamiti":
in the example "asūryapaśyā," the term "asūryam" is an irregular compound (*asamarthasamāsa*) based on a Vedic rule (*sautra*).
To the question "Why is there a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*)? he replies with "dṛśineti. [This refers to] the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sense of "not seeing the sun."
The meaning is that there is no syntactic connection with the word "sūrya" because it is already connected with the root "dṛś" (to see).

Regarding the phrase "lalāṭantapaḥ sūryaḥ" (the forehead-burning sun): the analysis of the compound is "that which heats the forehead" (*lalāṭaṃ tapati*). The sense is that for one who looks at the sun, the forehead is necessarily heated.

(764) *ugraṃpaśye-raṃmade-pāṇindhamāś-ca* |3|2|37|. Regarding *ugraṃpaśya*: [the suffix] *khaś* is applied, followed by the substitution of *śap*, and the replacement of the root with *paśya*. The explanation of the word *irā* is "water" (*udaka*). Regarding *irammada*: there is shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *khityanavyayasya*.

Anticipating the objection that [the form] might be derived from the root *chā* with the suffix *śatṛ*, he says: "By virtue of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), it is *chāyan*.
