The meaning is that when *priya*, *vaśa*, or *karman* are used as upapadas, the suffix *khañ* is applied after the root *vad*. Since *khaś* is already established, the purpose of the rule for *khañ* in the subsequent sūtra will be explained later. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix] follows *gam* when *sup* is the upapada," the word "*khañ*" is to be supplied as the remainder. Now, one might object: if the term "in a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is understood to carry over from the previous rule, then by the rule "and after *gam*... [the desired form would follow].
Since this would already be established by the sūtra that is about to be stated, he asks: "For what purpose is this vārttika? To which he replies:
"This is for the sake of [forming] non-designations (asaṃjñā). Regarding *vihāyasaḥ*: the word *vihāyas* refers to the sky (*ākāśa*).
When this is the upapada, the suffix *khac* is applied to the root *gam*. This is according to the sūtra that is about to be stated: *gamaśca*.

The suffix *khac* is established by the preceding *vārttika* and is restated here by the rule *ṭhce*. The meaning is that, setting aside the base word *vihāyas*, the substitute *vihā* should be prescribed, and that [substitute] should be stated as having the marker *ḍi* when the suffix *khac* is applied. Thus, *vihaṅga*:

in the case where [the substitute] has the marker *ḍi*, by virtue of that very fact, there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) even though it is not part of a nominal stem (*abha*). *Vihaṅgama*: [derived] by means of the sky (*vihāyasā*).
The analysis [of the compound] is "he goes" (*gacchati*). Regarding *bhujaṅgama*: the analysis is "he goes by means of his arms" (*bhujaiḥ gacchati*).

[In the rule] "after *dviṣat* and *para*," the root *tap* meaning "to burn" belongs to the *curādi* class, while *tap* meaning "to heat" belongs to the *bhvādi* class; the mention of *tāpi* refers to both of these when they are followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). [The suffix] *khac* shall occur. [This applies after] *dviṣat*, *para*...
The meaning is that when the roots *dviṣ* and *tap* are used as upapadas, the suffix *khac* is applied after the root *tap*. When the form *dviṣattāpi-a* has been established, he says:
(766) *khaci hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.94). "Before the suffix *khac*, [the final vowel of the preceding element] becomes short."

The term *hrasvaḥ* ("short vowel") is understood from [Pāṇini 6.4.92]; *ṇau* ("in the presence of the suffix ṇic") is understood from [Pāṇini 7.3.36] (*ṭhdoṣo ṇau*); and *upadhāyāḥ* ("of the penultimate vowel") is understood from [Pāṇini 7.2.116] (*udupadhāyāḥ*). Thus he says: "when followed by a suffix containing *khac* and ending in *ṇic*. Since *khaś* is already established [by another rule], this prescription of *khac* here is for the sake of shortening the vowel and for the elision of the augment *aṇ*. However, in the case of *khaś*, both of these [effects] would not occur.

Since *khaś* is a *śit* suffix and thus a *sārvadhātuka*, the elision of *ṇi* is impossible. Nor should it be argued that *khaś* should be prescribed in this very rule and that *khaś* alone should be carried over from the preceding rule; for [the present rule] is intended to prescribe [the suffix] even from other roots. And thus, regarding the rule "after the root *gam*, when *sup* follows..."
They say that this Vārttika is intended solely to explain the meaning already obtained [from the rule].

(767) *dviṣat-parayos tāpeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.39). Regarding *dviṣantapa*: by the rule *arur-dviṣad-* etc., the augment *mum* is inserted before the letter *t*. Regarding *parantapa*: [the same applies to] *paraḥ*.

—The enemy. Now, one might object: by the rule regarding words qualified by gender (liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā), even when the word *dviṣatī* is the upapada, the suffix *khac* would apply to the root *tap*, resulting in *dviṣatītapa*; thus, the form ending in *aṇ*, namely *dviṣatītāpa*, would not be possible.
To this, he says: "ghaṭa-ghaṭī... [and so on].

Regarding the statement "there is an extension [of the rule] for *graheḥ* in the case of *śakti*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *yaṣṭi*, *tomara*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭī*, and *dhanus*," since the word *ghaṭī* would already be established by the mention of *ghaṭa* alone through the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the metarule concerning words qualified by gender), the explicit mention of *ghaṭī* again indicates that the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* does not apply here.

The meaning is that it is understood as "impermanent. It should also be observed that, according to the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, the paribhāṣā "the rule regarding gender-qualified forms does not apply in the prescription of an upapada" is not operative here. (768) *vāci yamo vrate* (Pāṇini 3.2.40).
"Restraining speech in a vow," and so forth, is clear.

(769) *vācaṃyamapurandarau ca* |6|3|69|. [The rule] "and *vācaṃyama* and *purandara*. [The forms] *vāk* and *pūḥ*: [he who restrains speech is *vācaṃyama*; he who takes the city is *purandara*. *vācaṃ* means that which is to be spoken; *puraṃ*...

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "it splits" (*dārayati*), the suffix *khac* is applied to the roots *yam* and *dār*. When the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, we have *vācyama* and *dāra*. At this stage, the meaning is that the final vowel lengthening (*āmanta*) is prescribed for *vāk* and *pūru*.
However, there is no possibility for the application of the *mum* augment by the rule "after *ṛt*, after a word ending in *dviṣat*, and before a suffix beginning with a consonant other than *y*."

(770) *pūḥ-sarvayordāri-sahoḥ* |3|2|41|. [The suffix *kha* is applied] after the roots *dṛ* (to tear) and *sah* (to endure), when preceded by the words *pur* and *sarva*, provided these function as objects. The genitive case in *dāri-sahoḥ* is used in the sense of the ablative. [That is to say, the suffix *kha* is applied] when the words *pur* and *sarva* are present as co-occurring objects (*upapada*) for the roots *dṛ* and *sah*.
The meaning is "one who breaks. The connection [of the suffixes] follows their respective order. In the case of *dārī*, the form ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is intended.

Regarding *purandara*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who breaks the city" (*puraṃ dārayati*), the suffix *khac* is applied after the root *dārī* (from *dṛ*), the *ṇi* is elided, the penultimate vowel is shortened by the rule "*khaci hrasvaḥ*," the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, and the suffix *khac* is replaced by *a* according to the rule "*vācaṃyamapurandarau ca*."

In the rule for the formation of denominative verbs (*vikalpavidhi*), since the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by] "P.3.2.1 *karmaṇyaṇ*" would already be established even in the absence of the word *khañja*, the explicit mention of *aṇ* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "for the sake of excluding technical names (*asaṃjñārtham*). Regarding "and in *bhaga*," etc., this is clear.
In "one who causes movement" (*ṛtihkara*), *ṛti* means going. [He uses] the word "one who causes fearlessness" (*abhayahkara*).
To establish this, he says: "By the word *bhaya*, the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* [applying to that which ends with it] is intended. This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*.
(771) Pāṇini 3.2.44: *kṣemapriyamadre’ṇ ca*.

Regarding *kṣemapriya*: indeed, since the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) is already established when the optional application of *khac* by the rule *kṣemapriyamadreṣu khac* (Pāṇini 3.2.44) does not take effect, the mention of *aṇ* [in that rule] would be redundant; therefore, he says: "when it should have been said *veti* (or). Regarding *hetvādiṣu*: this refers to what is prescribed by the rule *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20).

This is the meaning. [The opponent asks: "How then? The objection is that since the rule *kṛño hetu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20) is superseded by the suffix *aṇ*, the form should be *kṣemakāra*; however, if the suffix *khac* were applied, the augment *mum* would occur. He provides the resolution: "When the object is treated as a residual element (*śeṣatva*). Thus, the intention is that because there is no co-occurring object (*upapada*), the suffix *aṇ* does not apply, and consequently, the suffix *ac* is used.
Regarding *kṣemaṅkarī*, they say that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it belongs to the *gaura*-class [of feminine stems].

(772) Pāṇini 3.2.45: *āśite bhuvaḥ karaṇabhāvayoḥ*. Regarding *āśite*: he gives an example for the instrument (*karaṇa*): "that by which one is satiated" (*āśito bhavatyanena*). For the state (*bhāva*)...
He provides an example: "the dwelling of one who has eaten" (*āśitasya bhavanam*).

(773) *saṃjñāyāṃ bhṛtṛvṛjidhārisahitapidamaḥ* | 3|2|46|. [The suffix] *khañ* is applied after the roots *bhṛ*, *tṛ*, *vṛ*, *ji*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed. The word *khañ* is understood as the remainder. [The roots are: *bhṛ*, *tṛ*, *vṛ*, *ji*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam*.
*dami*—this is the ablative case derived from the collective dvandva compound *eṣām aṣṭānām*. *Viśvambhara* is a name for Viṣṇu.

*Viśvambharā* is a name for the Earth. *Rathantaram*—the suffix *khac* is added to the root *tṛ*. Since the capacity to cross by means of a chariot (*rathena taritṛtva*) is impossible in the case of a specific *sāman*, he says: [the following].

Regarding "iha": he gives examples from the root *vṛdh*—namely, *patiṃvara* and *śatruñjaya*. [The suffix] *khac* is applied after the root *ji*. Regarding the mention of the causative (*ṇic*) form in the rule "dhārī," he gives an example: *yugandhara*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which holds a yoke" (*yugaṃ dhārayati*). By the rule "the vowel becomes short before *khac*," there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*). There is also the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*). [The example for the root *sah* is] *śatruṃsaha*.

Thus: *śatrūn sahate* is the analysis (vigraha). *Hrasva-* and so forth are as before; likewise in what follows. *Śatruntapa*—the analysis is *śatrūn tapati*. *Ariṃdama*—the meaning is that he becomes tranquil (*śāmyati*) toward enemies (*ariṣu*) in the matter of subduing them. Regarding *damiḥ śamanāyām*, it is because the root is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as *ḍamu upaśame*.

In the word *upaśama*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *śam* with the causative marker (*ṇic*). Thus, according to the opinion of Mādhava and others, because the meaning of "to tame" (*dāmyati*) is taken as "to cause to become tranquil" (*upaśamayati*), this [root] is transitive; such is the sense. As for the phrase "but in another view": [it refers to the root] *ḍamu* in the sense of "tranquility" (*upaśame*).
The meaning is that Haradatta and others have stated that the root *dam* (to tame), when used in the sense of tranquility (*upaśama*), is intransitive (*akarmaka*). (774) *gamaśca* |3|2|47|.
[The word] *gama* [is also included]; the remainder of the rule is "the suffix *khan* is added when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed."

(775) *anta-atyanta-adhvan-dūra-pāra-sarva-ananteṣu ḍaḥ* |3|2|48|. The rule beginning with *anta-atyanta* is clear. Regarding *sarvatrapannayoḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *ḍa* is to be added to the root *gam* when the words *sarvatra* and *panna* are used as *upapadas*. Regarding *urasaḥ*: [the suffix is added] when *urasi* is the *upapada*.
The meaning is that it should be stated: "the suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *gam* when a word is in composition (*upapada*), and there is elision of the final letter of the word *uraḥ*.

Regarding "after *su* and *dur*": the meaning is that when *su* or *dur* are the words in composition, the suffix *ḍa* shall be applied to the root *gam* when the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is to be expressed. Regarding "it is also seen elsewhere": [this applies] even when other words are in composition.

The meaning is that the suffix *ḍa* is seen after other verbal roots as well. Since this [suffix] is already established by this very rule, the statement "in all cases, *panna-* [is used]" and so forth is merely for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). Likewise, in the rule "the suffix *ḍa* after the root *jan* in the locative case," the phrase "it is seen after others as well" is also merely for the sake of elaboration. [The mention of] "*ḍe ca*" [is likewise].

This statement [concerning the suffix *khac*] applies because the previously mentioned term *vihāyasa-vihe* has *kha* as its object; thus, the form is *vihaga*. However, when the suffix *khac* is applied with the augment *mum*, the form becomes *vihaṅgama*. (776) *Āśiṣi hanaḥ* |3|2|49|.

Regarding *āśiṣi hanaḥ*: when the object (*karman*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *han* provided that a benediction (*āśis*) is to be understood. For example, *śatrughāta*. Due to the absence of a benediction, when *ḍa* is absent, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; by the rule *ṭhhanasta*, the substitution of *t* for *n* occurs. Regarding *dārāvāhana*: this is a Vārttika. [The word] *dārau*...

The analysis is *āhanaḥ*, *aṇ*, and *antasya*. This is for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *ṭ* for the final letter in conjunction with the suffix *aṇ*. Regarding the rule *cārau vā*: this is a Vārttika. It means that when the word *cāru* is used as an upapada, the suffix *aṇ* is added after the root *han* preceded by *āṅ*, and the final letter may optionally be replaced by *ṭ*. [This applies] to the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
*sami ceti*—this is a *vārttika*. *uktaṃ vā*—"or it has been stated"; the meaning is that *aṇ* is added, and *ṭa* is substituted for the final [letter].
The mention of *karmaṇi* is for the purpose of suspending the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *cārāv*. (777) *ape kleśatamasoḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.50.

Regarding the rule *ape kleśatamasoḥ* and *ṭhāśiṣi hanaḥ*: since [the desired forms] would already be established by these rules, one might ask, "For what purpose is this [next rule] stated? To this, he says: "It is for the sake of excluding the sense of benediction (*anāśīrartham*). (778) *kumāraśīrṣayorṇiniḥ* | 3.2.51.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *han* when the words *kumāra* and *śīrṣa* are used as upapadas; this is the meaning. The letter *n* and the initial vowel *i* are for the sake of pronunciation. (779) Pāṇini 3.2.52: *lakṣaṇe jāyāpatyoṣṭak*. The suffix *ṭak* is applied after the root *han* when the words *jāyā* and *patnī* are used as upapadas in the sense of a "sign" (*lakṣaṇa*). The *ṭ* indicates that the feminine form ends in *ī*. The resulting forms are *jāyāghātī* and *patnīghātī*. The *ṭ* is also for the sake of pronunciation. The word *lakṣaṇa* here means "a sign of recognition. For example: *jāyāghātī jāyājñāne* ("one who kills his wife [is identified] by the knowledge of her [deeds]"). *Patnīghātī patnījñāne* ("one who kills his wife [is identified] by the knowledge of her [deeds]"). The word *jñāna* is understood from the context. The mention of *jāyā* and *patnī* is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*), so that the suffix does not apply in other senses. For example, *jāyāghāto dṛṣṭaḥ* ("the killing of the wife was seen")—here the suffix is not applied because it is not in the sense of a "sign. Regarding the term *lakṣaṇe*: the sense is that in the sūtra, the word *lakṣaṇa* ends in the suffix *ac* (added after the class beginning with *arśas*). "A *jāyāghna*" means a man possessing a mark indicative of the killing of his wife; the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *gamahana*. "A *patighnī* woman" [is one possessing a mark indicative of the killing of her husband].
The meaning is that it possesses the characteristic of indicating the act of striking. Because of the *ṭi*-affix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

(780) *Amanuṣyakartṛke ca* |3|2|53|. [In the case of] "non-human agent": when the sense of the verbal root refers to an action performed by a non-human agent, and when the object is used as an *upapada* for the root *han*, [the suffix *kyap* is applied].
The meaning is "suddenly" (*ṭagityarthaḥ*). "A mole that kills the wife" (*jāyāghnaḥ tilakālakaḥ*) means a black spot in the shape of a sesame seed (*tila*).
The intention is that the application of the preceding rule [Pāṇini 3.2.54] occurs when the agent possesses the characteristic [of being a non-human]. Now, as for the question "How [is this so]?":
this is an objection based on the fact that in cases such as *pralambaghna* ("the killer of Pralamba"), since the agent of the root *han* ("to kill") is a human being, the suffix *ṭak* is impossible.

He resolves [the objection]: "It is established by virtue of belonging to the *mūlavibhujādi* group"; the intention is that this is accomplished by means of the suffix *kap*. Now, one might ask: how is it that forms such as *coraghātaḥ hastī* (an elephant that kills thieves) are possible, given that the suffix *ṭak* after the root *han* would be unavoidable because the agent is not a human? To this he says: "In cases such as *coraghātaḥ*, etc."—it is by virtue of *bāhulaka* (generalization/irregularity) that the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
The meaning is that [the formation] should be justified by means of the suffix *aṇ* due to the inclusion of the term "in various ways" (*bahulam*) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
(781) *śaktau hastikavāṭayoḥ* |3|2|54|. Regarding the rule *śaktau hastikavāṭayoḥ*: "elephant-killer" (*hastighna*) means one who is capable of killing an elephant.
In this way, *kavāṭaghna* [is formed].
(782) *Pāṇigha-tāḍaghau śilpini* |3|2|55|. *Pāṇigha* and *tāḍagha*: one who strikes with the hand (*pāṇi*) is a *pāṇigha*. *Tāḍa* means striking; by that—

The word *tāḍagha* means one who strikes, such as a wrestler (*malla*) or the like. Regarding the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] for *rājagha*," the meaning is that there is an addition to the previously mentioned irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the word *rājagha*.

(783) After the root *kṛ*, when followed by the words *āḍhya*, *subhaga*, *sthūla*, *palita*, *nagna*, *andha*, and *priya*—which signify the sense of the suffix *cvi*—provided that *cvi* itself does not follow.

The suffix *khyun* is used after the root *kṛ* [meaning "to do"] when expressing the instrument (*karaṇe*). [The example is] *āḍhyaṃkaraṇam* ("the act of making wealthy"). The remainder [of the rule] is "following after *rājā* etc.
[from the previous sūtra]. From the root *kṛ*, the suffix *khyun* is applied; there is no substitution [of the root vowel], and by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*, the augment *mum* is added.
Examples such as *subhagaṃkaraṇam* ("the act of making fortunate") should also be cited. [The example] *āḍhyīkurvann etena* ("making one wealthy by means of this") is used here.
The intention is that because of the presence of the *cvī* suffix, there is no *khyun*. Now, one might ask:
"In the alternative where *khyun*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lyuṭ*—is absent, why is *lyuṭ*, which is the general rule (*utsarga*), not present?
To this he says: "In this case. If *lyuṭ*, the general rule, were to occur in the absence of *khyun*, the exception to *lyuṭ*, then...

In that case, the rule for *khyun* would be purposeless, because there is no difference in form between *khyun* and *lyuṭ* when an item ending in *cvī* is the upapada. Nor should it be argued that there is a distinction because the augment *mum* occurs in *khyun* while it is absent in *lyuṭ*;
for since an item ending in the *cvī* suffix is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), even if *khyun* were applied, [the augment would still not apply].
Because of the absence of the word *mum*, the term *avyayasya* (of an indeclinable) is understood to carry over into the rule *ṭharurdviṣadajantasya*;

and thus, by the force of the prohibition of *khyun* when a word ending in *cvī* is the *upapada*—as expressed in the phrase *acvoḥ*—it is understood that even *lyuṭ* does not apply in the absence of *khyun*. This is the meaning according to the *Kāśikā*. And so, [the rule] "in the case of *ac* and *vī*"...

It is established that when *cvī* is the upapada, there is a prohibition of *khyun*; this is for the purpose of preventing *lyuṭ* in the alternative case where *khyun* does not apply. However, according to the view of the Bhāṣya: "In the Bhāṣya it is stated: 'The prohibition of *cvī* [before] *khyun* is useless, because there is no difference between *lyuṭ* and *khyun*. If it is argued that it is for the sake of eliding the suffix (*mum*), [we reply] no, because [the word] is indeclinable (*avyaya*')."

In this and similar contexts, having rejected the inclusion of *ac* in the rule for the suffix *khyun*, it was stated that [the mention of *ac*] is for the sake of the rule *ṭhac ca*. According to that view, however, when a word ending in *cvī* is the *upapada*, *lyuṭ* would indeed apply once *khyun* has been set aside.

(784) *kartari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau* |3|2|57|. In the sense of the agent (*kartari*), after the root *bhū*, the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are applied. In *khiṣṇuc*, *khac* is elided; in *khukañ*, *khañ* is elided. For example: *āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "one who becomes wealthy (*āḍhya*) from not being wealthy (*anāḍhya*). [The form] *āḍhyaṃbhāvukaḥ* [is likewise formed].

Thus [is the rule]. Because of the *ñit* designation, there is *vṛddhi*. The mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the purpose of terminating the continued application of the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

As for the vowel *i* in *khiṣṇuc*, it is indeed redundant, since [the desired form] is established by the augment *iṭ*. What is the purpose of the condition "not being a vowel" (*acvau*)? [Consider: *āḍhyībhavitā*. The rule *spṛśo 'nudake kvin* has been explained in the section on stems ending in consonants (*halanta*).
Regarding the term *nivṛtim*: here, the commentary itself is the refuge [for clarification]. Regarding the rule *samānānyayośca*:

the meaning is that the suffixes *kvip* and *kan* are applied to the root *dṛś* when these two words (*samāna* and *anya*) are used as upapadas. In the examples *sadṛk* and *sadṛśa*, the analysis is not *samāno dṛśyate* (he is seen by one who is equal), because the suffix *kvip* is prescribed only for the agent (*kartṛ*). Rather, it refers to the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).

The suffixes *kvip* and *kañ* [are applied]. The analysis is "one who sees what is similar" (*samānaṃ paśyati*). It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the meaning is "it becomes an object of cognition by way of similarity. Regarding the form *sadṛk*, there is an option for the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* according to the rule *dṛgdṛśavatuṣu*. In this context, the option (*vibhāṣā*) is understood from the subsequent mention of *vibhāṣodare*.

The word *samānadṛk* means "one who sees similarly"; this is also supported by the usage in the *Bhāṣya*: *samānasadṛśaḥ sadṛśaḥ*. Regarding *anyādṛk*, the substitution of *ā* occurs according to the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "the suffix *kso* also": the meaning is that after words such as *tyad* (pronouns) and after the words *samāna* and *anya*, the suffix *ksa* is also to be prescribed for the root *dṛś*.

(785) *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasarge 'pi kvip* 3.2.61. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied after the roots *sad*, *sū*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *ji*, and *nī*, as well as *rāj*, even when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). *Sad*, *sū*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *ji*.

The word *nī* [is used here]; for these [words], the genitive case is employed in the sense of the ablative of a *dvandva* compound. Since the rule would have been established even by the removal of the restriction "only when there is no prefix" (*anupasarge*) from the rule *ṭh-anupasarge*, the explicit statement "also when there is a prefix" (*upasarge 'pi*) is for the purpose of indicating that elsewhere, when the term "sub" (nominal suffix) is mentioned, the mention of "upasarga" (prefix) does not apply.
Consequently, the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* ("after the root *vad*, when a nominal suffix follows, there is the suffix *kyap*") does not apply when a prefix is present.
This is clear in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the word *dyausad*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who sits in heaven" (*divi sīdati*).

There is no substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*. Nor does the substitution of *ṣ* apply by the rule *pūrvapadāt*, because that [rule] pertains to Vedic usage (*cchāndasa*). This is seen in the expression *āditeyā diviṣadaḥ*.
They say that [the substitution of] *u* occurs because [the word] belongs to the *suṣāmādi* group. Regarding *upaniṣad*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *sadiraprateḥ*.
Regarding "and so forth": *kāṣṭhabhid*, *rajjuccchid*, *śatrujit*; here, the augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *hrasvasya pitī*.
*Senānīḥ*, *virāṭ*, *aṃśabhāgī*; in these, due to the suffix being marked with *ṇ*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel.

(786) *ado'nanne* |3|2|68|. "After the root *ad*, [the suffix] *viṭ* occurs when the word *anna* is not present. This is a supplement to the rule. The resulting meaning is that when a *sup*-ending word other than the word *anna* is an *upapada*, the suffix *viṭ* occurs after the root *ad*. [The rule continues: *janasanakhanakramagamo...* [etc.]

From the *Chāndasa-sūtra*, the term *viḍ* is understood to follow from the rule for *vijiti*. From *sasyāt*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who knows the grain" (*sasyam vetti*). "One who eats food" (*annāda*): [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule for the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*). (787) *kravye ca* | 3.2.69.

"And with *kravya*. This [sūtra] is a supplement (*śeṣapūraṇa*) [to the previous rule]. The intention is that it serves to prevent the application of the suffix *aṇ*; for the sense obtained is that when *kravya* is the object, only the suffix *viṭ* applies after the root *ad*, and not *aṇ*. The objection is raised: "How then [is the form *kravyāt* derived]? Since there is a restrictive rule stating that "only *viṭ* applies when *kravya* is the object," the application of *aṇ* is impossible. He provides the resolution:

Regarding the term *pakvamāṃsaśad*, one might ask: "In that case, should it not be *pakvamāṃsāda*? To this he says: "The substitution of *kravyād* for *upapati*. Why is this so? He says: "Because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
(Pāṇini 3.2.70): *duhaḥ kabdhaśca*.
*Duhaḥ kubdhaśca*: When *duh* (to milk) has a word beginning with *su-* as its upapada, the suffix *kap* is applied, and the meaning is that *gha* is substituted for the final letter of the root.
Thus, *kāmadughā*; the word *dhenuḥ* (cow) is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound]. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she who milks what is desired" (*kāmaṃ u apekṣitaṃ dugdhe*).
(789) *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* | 3|2|75|. They are seen after others as well. Under the governing rules *vijupe chandasi* and *āto maninkvanivvanipaśca*, this [suffix] *it* [is added], the letter *i*.
The letter *k* in *vici* is for the purpose of pronunciation; the letter *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
(790) *neḍvaśi kṛti* [Pāṇini 7.2.8]. The locative case is used in the sense of the genitive. The word *vaś* qualifies the *kṛt* suffixes.

The rule *tadādividhiḥ* (the application of an operation to that which begins with the specified element) applies here; thus, [the term] "beginning with *vaś*" (*vaśādeḥ*). In *suśarma*, the suffix *manin* is added to the root *śṛ*. In *prātaritvā*, the suffix *kvanip* is added to the root *iṇ*.
(791) *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*: [In place of the nasal of a stem ending in a *viṭ* or *van* suffix, there is *ā* before an affix beginning with *y* or *v*.]

Regarding the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*: *viḍvanoḥ* is the locative case. *Anunāsikasya*—the analysis is *ād*. [The examples are: *vijāvā* and *avāvā*. [In *vijāvā*,] the suffix *vanip* is added to the root *jan*;
the *n* of *jan* becomes *ā*, and there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). [In *avāvā*,] the suffix *vanip* is added to the root *oṇ*.

The vowel *ā* replaces the *ṇ* of *ṇakāra*; there is the substitution of *ava*. [The word] *vijiti* is cited as an example; the phrase "is illustrated" is the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding *roṭ* and *reḍiti*: from the roots *ruṣa* and *riṣa* in the sense of "injury," the suffix *vic* is applied. By the rule *verapṛktasya*, there is the elision of the *v*.
Regarding *sugaṇṇiti*: from the root *gam*, the suffix *vic* is applied.

(792) *kvip ca* | 3|2|76|. "And *kvip*. This also [is taught]. The meaning is that *kvip* is seen after all verbal roots, both when accompanied by an upapada and when without an upapada, in the Vedic language (*chandas*) as well as in common usage (*loka*). Now, one might object: since this is already established by this very rule...
To the objection that the rule *satsūdviṣa-* would be redundant, he says:
"The rule *satsūdviṣa-* is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the rule *kvip ca*.
Regarding *ukhāsrad*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that from which the pot slips" (*ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate*). [The suffix] *kvip* is applied after the root *sraṃs*.
The elision of *n* occurs by the rule *ṭhaniditām*; the substitution of *d* for *t* occurs by the rule *vasusraṃsu*. Similarly, *parṇadhvat*:
the analysis is *parṇād dvaṃsate*. *Vāhabhraṭ*: the analysis is *vāhād bhraśyati*. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *vraścādi*.

(793) *antaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.4.20. The word *antaḥ* [is the subject]. The rules *ṭhānito't* and *raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* are understood to follow. The nominative case in *antaḥ* is used in the sense of the genitive; that which constitutes the end of a word (*pada*) is intended here.
From the rule "ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the word "upasargāt" (after a prefix) is carried over from the preceding rule "upasargādasamāse'pi". Thus he says:

"of a word-final [ṣ], etc. In the example "he prāṇ", after the root *an* preceded by *pra*, there is the suffix *kvip*; then, in the singular vocative case, the elision of the consonant and following vowel (*halṅyādi-lopa*) occurs, and the *n* is changed to *ṇ*.

But there is no substitution of *n* for *l*, because of the prohibition: "Not before the case-ending *ṅsi* (the genitive singular) or in the vocative. Regarding *mitraśī*: the analysis is *mitrāṇi śāsti* ("he instructs friends"). From the root *śās*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. By the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, the penultimate vowel is changed to *i*;
then, by the rule *ṛtvoḥ upadhāyāḥ*, the vowel is lengthened.

In examples such as *mitraśiṣau*, there is no lengthening because [the rule] applies only when not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Regarding *āśāsaḥ kvau*: the root *śās* with the prefix *āṅ* meaning "to desire" is *ātmanepada*. For that root, the substitution of *i* (by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*) does not occur, because in that [rule], only the *parasmaipada* form of *śās* is intended to be included. Otherwise, [one would have to say] *āśāste*.
Because [the rule] would otherwise lead to the substitution of *it* even in such cases as these, the injunction "āśāsaḥ kvau" (Pāṇini 6.4.34) is formulated. Regarding the phrase "it-utve":

from the root *gṛ*, after the elision of the *kvip* suffix, the substitution of *it* for *ṛ*, the substitution of *ap* (short *a*), the elision of the case-ending *su*, and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel by the rule "ṛtvor upadhāyāḥ," the form *gīḥ* is obtained. From the root *pṛ*, after the elision of the *kvip* suffix...

The meaning is that the form *pūri* arises through the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* by the rule *ṛt udhas-tha-l-pūrvasya*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*, the elision of the case-ending *su*, and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrgha*).
(794) *is-man-tra-ṇ-kviṣu ca* | Pāṇini 6.4.97.
*ismantraṇ*: *is*, *man*, *traṇ*, and *kvi*—this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of these four.

From the rule "ṭhchāderghedvyupasargasya" [Pāṇini 6.4.96], the word "chādeḥ" (of *chād*) is understood; and from the rule "khaci hrasvaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.4.94], the word "hrasvaḥ" (short vowel) is also understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Therefore, he says: "among these, [the shortening applies] to *chād*"—meaning, by implication, to the long vowel *ā*.

It is understood by relying on the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (*alontya-paribhāṣā*), because there is no purpose for the shortening of the vowel *i*. And thus, in the rule *ṭhūdupadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* need not be supplied as an *anuvṛtti*, since the root *chad-* (when followed by the suffix *ṇyat*) has *d* as its penultimate (*upadhā*) letter. Examples: *icchadiḥ*, *man-*.

The word *cchatram* [is derived from] *cchad* + *tra*. He gives examples for *kvip*: *tanucchad* and so forth; the analysis is "that which covers the body" (*tanum chādayati*). Now, he states the specific rule regarding *kvip* after the roots *tan* and *śam*: "of a nasal" (*anunāsikasya*). Regarding the form *akṣadyūḥ*, he says: "of *cch* and *v*" (*cchavoh*). When there is one [consonant] of *y*.

The form is *ūṭhijūri*. Likewise, from the root *tvare*, the form is *tūri*. From the root *sriv* with the suffix *kvip*, when *ūṭh* is applied to the *i* and *v*, the form is *srūri*. From the root *av* with the suffix *kvip*, when *ūṭh* is applied to the *a* and *v*, the form is *ūri*. Regarding "vṛddhi": it means "it protects people" (*janānavati*).

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *mūḥ*: from the root *mav* with the suffix *kvip*, after the substitution of *ūṭh* for the vowels *a* and *v*, the form *jana ū* remains. Here, setting aside the rule for *guṇa* (*ādguṇaḥ*), the rule "before *ṭh*, *eṅ*, *dhāt*, and *ūṭh*" applies, resulting in the substitution of the *vṛddhi* vowel *au*.
This is the meaning. Regarding *mūḥ*: from the root *mav* with the suffix *kvip*, after the substitution of *ūṭh* for the vowels *a* and *v*. *Sumbo sumba*.
Thus: the sense is that [the substitution] *yaṇ* occurs because there are multiple vowels (*anekāctvāt*) and because it precedes a verbal root (*gatipūrvatvāt*). Regarding *rāt*:

the sense is that from the root *mūrch*, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, the letter *c* is elided by the rule "ṭhrāllopaḥ"; then, after the elision of the case-ending *su*, the lengthening occurs by the rule "ṛvōḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.19); and finally, after the elision of the case-ending *su*, the form *dhūḥ* is established by the rule "ṛvōḥ". This is the intended meaning.
This is a supplement [to the sūtra] stating that there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*).
The intention is that this follows from the recurrence of the word "in the case of roots taught with an anudātta vowel" (*anudātopadeśa*) from the preceding rule.

This is a rule because [the condition] "anudātopadeśa" (from roots taught with an anudātta accent) does not apply here, as there is an absence of an affix beginning with a *jhal* sound following the root.

Regarding *aṅgagamat*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he goes to the region called Aṅga. After the *kvip* suffix, the *m* is elided and *tuk* is added. Similarly: *vaṅgagat*, *kaliṅgagat*, and so forth.

Regarding "of *gam* and so forth": the remainder [of the rule] is "there is elision of the nasal before *kva* and *an*. Regarding *purītat*: the analysis is "that which spreads over (*tanoti*) the *puri*"; *puri* refers to a specific portion of flesh called the heart, and it covers (*ācchādayati*) that.
It is a specific kind of fat that covers the lotus of the heart. For [it is said]: "by the *purītat*..."
"The heart is covered," so says the Śruti—this is the Karka-bhāṣya. [The formation of *saṃyat*: from the root *tan*, with the suffix *kvip*, there is elision of *n*;

then by the rule "tuk" (Pāṇini 6.1.71), *tuk* is added. By the rule "nahivṛtivṛṣi... (Pāṇini 6.3.116), there is lengthening of the first member. [The formation of *saṃyat*: from the root *yam*, with the suffix *kvip*. [Then] by the rule "malopa" (elision of *m*), *tuk* is added. [The formation of *sunat*: from the root *nam*, with the suffix *kvip*.

The meaning is that one should state: "In the case of *malop*, there is also [the substitution of] *ū*; and for the roots beginning with *gam*, there is the substitution of *ū* for the penultimate vowel. Regarding "and elision" (*lopaśca*): the sense is that by the word "and" (*ca*), the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is conjoined.
Regarding *agregūḥ*: the analysis is "one who goes before" (*agre gacchati*). There is the substitution of *ū* for the root *gam*.

And there is the elision of the suffix *ma*. In the case of *tatpuruṣa* compounds with *kṛt*-suffixes, the elision of *a* is not applied diversely (*bahulam*); thus we have *agrebhrūḥ*. Here, the vowel *a* of the root *bhram* is replaced by *ū*, and the suffix *ma* is elided. (796) *sthaśca ka* 3.2.77.

The [sūtra] is *sthaḥ ka ca*. The word *ṭhke* is without a case ending (*avibhaktika*). *Stha* is in the fifth case (*pañcamyantam*). And because of the word *ca* ("and"), it is established that the suffix *kap* occurs after the root *sthā* when preceded by an upasarga or even when not preceded by an upasarga, provided that *subandhu* is the upapada, as well as the suffix *kvip*. Thus, in *śaṃsthaḥ*, the indeclinable *śam* means "happiness."

From that same root *sthā* preceded by *śam*, with the suffix *kap*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* (according to Pāṇini 6.4.64). The form *śaṃsthā* is derived from the root with the suffix *kvip*. Its meaning is "that which establishes happiness"; here, the root *sthā* contains an implied causative sense (*ṇyartha*).
Because of the usage *śaṃsthāṭ* found in the Bhāṣya and because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the substitution of *ī* for *ā* (by Pāṇini 6.4.66, *ghumāsthā*) does not apply.
Some, however, say that because of the letter *ca* in the rule *ṭhka ca*, the word *dvi* is drawn forward [from a previous rule]. Now, one might ask:
since the suffix *kap* is established by the rule *supi sthaḥ* and the suffix *kvip* is established by the rule *kvip ca*, what is the purpose of this [present rule]?
To this he replies: "The vowel *a* [is added] after the root *śam*. Otherwise, by the force of the mention of the word "root" (*dhātu*), [the vowel would apply] to the root *kṛ*.

The intention is that, just as the suffix *ṭa* [is applied] after roots such as *hi*, the suffix *ac* would supersede both the suffix *ka* and the *kvip* suffix [which would otherwise apply] after the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *sam*.

(797) *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* | Pāṇini 3.2.78. Regarding *supyajātau*: since the term *supi* is already understood from the preceding rule *supi sthaḥ*, the repetition of *sub* here is for the purpose of including even prefixes (*upasarga*). Otherwise, [the suffix would not apply] by the rule *āto'nupasarge*.
Therefore, the phrase "in the absence of a prefix" (*anupasarge*) should be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule]. Indicating this, he provides the example: *uṣṇabhojī*.
The meaning is "one whose habit is eating hot food. The phrase "only when distinct from a prefix" implies that "in the absence of a prefix" continues to apply.
However, the inclusion of the term *su-* is for the purpose of terminating the carry-over of the phrase "even when there is a prefix" (*upasarge 'pi*) from the rule *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61).
This is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "only when distinct from a prefix" [is used because] the term *anupasarga* (not a prefix) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule].

However, the inclusion of the term *sub* (a nominal ending) is for the purpose of carrying over the phrase *upasarge 'pi* (even when there is a prefix) from the rule *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasaṃkhyānam*.
Regarding [the expression] "after *ud* and *prati*": this means when the suffix *āṅ* is employed after *ud* and *prati*.

The meaning of that [rule] is: "There is an addition [to the rule] for *sṛ* preceded by *tat* when followed by *ṇini*. The examples are *udāsāriṇī* and *pratyāsāriṇī*. [The phrase] "because of contradiction with the Bhāṣya" means that the mention of *sub* (a nominal ending) is for the purpose of removing the continued application of the mention of *upasarga* (a prefix), [applying] both when there is a prefix and when there is no prefix.

The point is that the *Bhāṣya* has cited only "the suffix *ṇini* [is added] when a word ending in *su* is an upapada" as the rule for the formation of the word *anugāmī*. Consequently, the statement "after *ut*, *prati*, and *āṅ*, the suffix *si* is added to the root *ṛ*" is not to be respected;
the intention is that its reading in the *Bhāṣya* is merely interpolated. For this very reason, it says "the suffix *ṭhak* is added after *anugādin*."

It should be understood that the application of the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.78] is thus consistent. They say that the view—that the suffix *ṇini* occurs only after a *sup*-ending word when it is not preceded by a prefix—is contrary to the usage of the learned;
for the suffix *ṇini* is well-established even after a prefix. This connects with the phrase "in cases such as... (*ityādau*).
Regarding the term *sādhukāriṇī*: the mention of the root *kṛ* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all verbal roots, as evidenced by the example *sādhukārī*. Regarding the phrase *brahmaṇi vada*:
the supplement is "the addition of the suffix *ṇini*. (The supplement "the addition of the suffix *ṇini*" is repeated.)
Now, one might ask: since the rule *supyajātau* alone would suffice, for what purpose is this Vārttika? To this he replies:

"It is for the sake of excluding the sense of habitual action (*atācchīlyārtham*). The example *sādhudāyī* ("one who gives well") is formed by the addition of *yuk* after a stem ending in long *ā*. The example *brahmavādī* ("a speaker of the Veda")—here, *brahman* means the Veda.

(798) *kartaryupamāne* |3|2|79|. Regarding *kartaryupamāne*: it means "the comparison of the agent. The word *ca* ("and") is to be supplied [from the previous rule]. Now, one might ask: since this is already established by the rule *supyajātau*, for what purpose is this stated? To this he replies: "It is for the sake of excluding the sense of habitual action (*atācchīlyārtham*)."

(799) *vrate* |3|2|80|. Regarding the rule *vrate*: it means that the suffix *ṇini* shall occur when a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) is the upapada and the sense of "vow" (*vrata*) is to be understood.
For example, *sthaṇḍileśāyī* ("one who sleeps on the bare ground"). Here, by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending.

(800) *bahulam ābhīkṣṇye* |3|2|81|. This rule is intended to ensure the application [of the suffix] even when a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) is the upapada. Indicating this, he provides the example: *kṣīrapāyiṇaḥ*.

(801) *manaḥ* |3|2|82|. [The word] *manaḥ*: Only the root *man* belonging to the *divādi* class is intended here, and not that belonging to the *tanādi* class, because the term *bahulam* ("variously") is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "of *manyati*" (*manyateḥ*). However, if it were the root *manu* that was intended...
The refutation will be stated in the subsequent sūtra.

(802) *ātmamāne khaś ca* | Pāṇini 3.2.83. [The suffix] *khaś* is also applied when there is self-pride (*ātmamāna*). "Self-pride" (*ātmamāna*) means pride (*māna*, i.e., thinking) regarding oneself (*ātmanaḥ*, i.e., one's own).

Thus he says: "in the sense of considering as one's own action" (*svakarmake manane*). Regarding *paṇḍitammanya*: because the suffix *khaś* is treated as having the marker *ś*, it is a *sārvadhātuka* affix, and thus [the root] takes the *yan* augment. Because of the marker *kh*, the *mum* augment is applied by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*. If, however, the root *man* belonging to the *tanādi* class were intended to be included here, the *u* vikaraṇa would occur. [The example is: *kālīm ātmānaṃ manyate*.

Regarding this meaning, when the suffix *khaś* is applied and the *śyan* affix is formed, he says: "by the rule *khityanavyayasya*" (Pāṇini 6.3.66). The meaning is that the shortening [of the vowel] occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], thereby overriding the *puṃvat* (masculine-like) treatment prescribed by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34). In the example *divāmanyate*, although the word *divā* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it functions as the object (*karman*) within the scope of the derivative formation (*vṛtti*).
The object of enlightenment.
(803) *ica ekāco'mpratyayavacca* |6|3|68|. [The word] *ica ekācaḥ*: the analysis is *ekāca am*. [The form] *am* is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of *am* and *am*. One...

The rule *ṭhica ekāco'm* constitutes the first sentence. Here, both *icaḥ* and *ekācaḥ* are ablative case endings (*pañcamī*). Since the governing heading *uttarapade* (in the following word) from the rule *ṭhaluk uttarapade* is implied, the term *pūrvapada* (the preceding member) is understood and serves as the qualifier for *icaḥ*. This results in a *tadantavidhi* (an operation applying to that which ends with the specified element).

Regarding this, he says: "Because it is known that [the augment] *am* does not follow after a monosyllabic [stem]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *mum*. The second part of the statement, "like the suffix *am*," is construed in grammatical apposition with the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*), which is a portion [of the compound *pratyayavat*].
Although there is no semantic connection [between the two parts], the suffix *-vat* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The second sentence is: "like the suffix *am*."

It is accomplished. Among the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings), that which is the second singular alone is intended here by the term *am*, according to the explanation. Thus he says: "And that [suffix] is like *su* etc., ending in *am*. All of this is clear in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "after a word ending in *khid*": the meaning is "when a word ending in *khid* follows as the subsequent member of a compound."
The intention is that the term *khit* continues to apply from the rule "ṭhkhityanavyayasya.
He states the purpose of the extension (*atideśa*) "as if it were the suffix *am*" with the words "āṬtomśasoḥ.

Regarding the example *gāmmanyaḥ*: in the sense of "he considers himself a cow," the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *man*, followed by the *śyan* augment and the elision of the case-ending (*sup*).

He states another purpose for the rule "luk, gośabdād am, ṭham-pratyayavat" by saying "vām-śasoḥ. Regarding "striyam-manyah": in the sense of "he considers himself a woman," the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *man*, followed by *śyan*. There is *luk* elision of the case ending (*sup*). From the word *strī*, [the form *striyam* is derived] by the rule "vām-śasoḥ."
This is an optional rule (*vikalpa*). Here, the prescription of *am* is for the sake of hearing the vowel *a* after the letter *y*.

However, in the case of the suffix *mum*, the vowel *a* would not be heard. For example, in *sātārīmanyaḥ*: in the alternative where *iyaṅ* occurs, [the form is derived] by the rule "the preceding [vowel is substituted] before *ṭhaM*" (Pāṇini 6.1.102).
He states another purpose for the rule "before the suffix *ṭhaM*" (Pāṇini 6.4.153): *nṛ-narammanyaḥ*.

The form *nṛ* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*), used here to indicate the inclusion of the word *nṛ* in the examples. In the sense of "one who considers himself a man" (*naram ātmānam manyate*), the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *man*, followed by the *śyan* affix; then the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, and the suffix *am* is added after the word *nṛ*. Due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "before the suffix *am*," the *guṇa* substitution occurs according to the rule *ṛtaḥ aṅi*.

In this case as well, the suffix *am* is prescribed so that the vowel *a* may be heard after the letter *r*; otherwise, due to the *mum* augment, the vowel *a* would not be audible. He states another purpose for the rule *ṭham pratyayavat*: namely, the example *bhuvammanyaḥ*. In the sense of "he considers himself to be the earth," the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *man*, followed by *śyan* and the elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sup*). Then, the suffix *am* is added to the word *bhū*.

By the extension (*atideśa*) "as if it were a *ṭha*-affix," the substitution *uvaṅ* applies according to the rule "in the case of an *ac* affix, for the roots *śu*, *nu*, etc. In the absence of this extension, however, *uvaṅ* would not occur, because that [substitution] is prescribed only before affixes beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). [The form] *śrimanyam* [is derived as follows]:
from the root *man*, the suffix *khaś* is added; then *śyan*. Here, the family (*kula*) is related to the action of thinking (*manana-kriyā*) by way of its form as the object (*karman*).

The established position is that [the clan] is the agent, and that very same clan is the object by virtue of its form as the superimposed Śrī. Thus, although the word *śrī* is eternally feminine, it takes the neuter gender when it functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote a clan. For where the metaphorical indication of the nominal stem itself is well-known, in that case—

There is a relinquishing of the original gender (*pūrvaliṅgatyāga*). For example, in the present context, the word *śrī*. However, where there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word, there is no relinquishing of the original gender, as in "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), according to the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* and the present rule.

The boundary is established in both the Bhāṣya and the Yaṭa commentary. Thus, in the expression "kālīmanyaṃ kulam" (a family considering itself Kālī), there is no abandonment of the feminine gender of the word *kālī*, because it is accepted that in that instance there is only a lakṣaṇā (indication) of the word-form [the stem], in accordance with usage. However, in the case of "śrīmanyaṃ kulam" (a family considering itself Śrī)...
According to the application [of the rule], since the term *śrī* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*),
it is understood as being in the neuter gender by abandoning its previous gender; consequently,
because the word *śrī* is here neuter, the shortening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *ṭhityanavyayasya* is considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).
Setting aside [the rule for the suffix], the short vowel alone is correct by the rule "a short vowel is substituted for the final of a neuter nominal stem" (*napuṃsake prātipadikasya*).

When the suffix *am* is applied by the rule "for a monosyllabic word ending in *ic*" (*ica ekācaḥ*) as an exception to the *mum*-augment, the elision of that [suffix] occurs by the rule "elision of *sva* and *am* after a neuter [stem]" (*svamornapuṃsakāt*). Thus, the form "śrimanyaṃ kulam" is established. And this is not the case even in examples such as "gāmmanyaḥ."

It should be stated that [the suffix] *sup* would undergo elision (*luk*) by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ"; however, because the *ām* [substitution] prescribed by "ica ekācaḥ" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of *sup* prescribed by "supo dhātu...", this [substitution] prevails.
Furthermore, the elision of *su* and *am* prescribed by "svamornapuṃsakāt" does not subvert this rule for the substitution of *ām*.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the present sūtra, according to the maxim that "an exception [applies] in the middle" (madhye'pavādanyāya).
He states this with the words "by the author of the Bhāṣya," etc.; the ellipsis to be supplied is "by the rule *hrasvo napuṃsake*.
And as for the absence of both *mum* and *am*: the *am* which is an exception to *mum* is prescribed by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*.
The meaning is that when there is elision (*luki*), the absence of the application of those two [suffixes] results.
(804) *bhūte* 3.2.84. *bhūte*: This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). The term *dhātoḥ* ("after a verbal root") is the governing rule (*adhikṛta*). And therefore—

The phrase "of a verbal root denoting an actual fact" (*bhūtārthavṛtter dhātoḥ*) is understood to carry over into the subsequent rules; this is the result. Regarding the word *vartamāne*: the meaning is "prior to [the rule] *laṭ for the present*" (*vartamāne laṭ*). In this matter, the commentary itself is the sole refuge. (805) *karaṇe yajaḥ* |3|2|85|.
In the case of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), as in "with soma" (*somena*), the meaning is that he performed a sacrifice with the juice of a specific creeper called *soma*.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that by means of a sacrifice having the substance of the *soma* creeper's juice, he produced the *apūrva* (the unseen potential merit). And this [is discussed] in the second chapter, second section.

This has been explained by us in detail in the *Adhvarāmīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti* under the section [Jaiminisūtra 4.4.1]: "The injunction regarding the animal and the Soma [is based] on the connection with substances. Regarding the term *agniṣṭomayājī*: it refers to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) resulting from the sacrifice named Agniṣṭoma.
The meaning is "he has cultivated.

(806) *karmaṇi hanaḥ* |3|2|86|. When *hana* [is used], [the suffix] *ṇini* occurs after [the root] *han* when it expresses a completed action (*bhūtārtha*), provided that an object (*karman*) is present as an upapada.
"Pitṛvyaghātī" means "one who has killed his paternal uncle. The suffix *ta* is applied by the rule *hanastaḥ*, and *gha* replaces *ha* by the rule *ho hanteḥ*.
(807) *brahmabhrūṇavṛtreṣu kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.87).

Because the word "action" (*karman*) is understood to carry over from the preceding sūtra regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or an embryo, he says: "in actions. Regarding "of the root *han* in the sense of a completed action" (*bhūte*), the meaning is "of the root *han* when it functions in the sense of a fact (*bhūtārtha*). Regarding "fourfold," the sense is that since the restrictive particle *eva* is obtained through the subsequent rule (*punarvidhāna*), and there is no reason for restriction (*vinigamanāviraha*), it applies to all four cases as well. In that regard:

Due to the restriction "the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *han* only when [the object] is *brahman* and so forth," the suffix *kvip* does not apply in the case of *puruṣaṃ hatavān* ("he killed a man").
Due to the restriction "the root *han* occurs only when [the object] is *brahman* and so forth," the suffix *kvip* does not apply in the case of *brahma adhītavān* ("he has studied the Veda").

Due to the restriction "the root *han* occurs only in the past tense when [the object] is *brahman* and so forth," [the suffix *kvip* does not apply] in the cases of *brahma hanti* ("he kills the Veda") and *brahma haniṣyati* ("he will kill the Veda").

In this case, the suffix *kvip* does not apply after the root *vid*. Due to the restrictive rule "kvibeve" (Pāṇini 3.2.17), the suffix *aṇ* does not occur after the expression "brahma hatavān," but rather *kvip* applies by the rule "brahmabhrūṇa-" (Pāṇini 3.2.87). However, the *niṣṭhā* suffix (*kta*) certainly does occur, because the restriction applies only to the exclusion of suffixes that follow a word with an upapada. [The term] "of two kinds" refers to [the *karmapravacanīya*] "ubhayataḥ."
The meaning is that this restriction—"only in the case of *brahmā* and so forth"—is stated in the Bhāṣya as "only after the roots *kvi* and *vī*.
And thus, the two restrictions—"only after the root *han*" and "only when it has become [a noun]"—are to be disregarded; this is the sense.
(808) Pāṇini 3.2.89: *sukarmapāpamantrapuṇyeṣu kṛñaḥ*. (The suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *kṛ* when followed by the words *su*, *karman*, *pāpa*, *mantra*, and *puṇya*).

The compound *sukarmasu-karma-pāpa-mantra-puṇya* consists of these five [words] in a dvandva. Regarding the term "threefold" (*trividha*): there are three views, namely, "after the words *sukarman* and so forth, when expressing the past tense, the suffix *kvip* is added only after the root *kṛ*"; "after the words *sukarman* and so forth, when expressing the past tense, the suffix *kvip* is added only after the root *kṛ*"; and "after the words *sukarman* and so forth, when expressing the past tense, the suffix *kvip* is added only after the root *kṛ*."

The meaning is that the suffix *kṛt* [in the form of *kvin*] occurs only after the root *kṛ* when preceded by "good action" (*sukarma*) and the other four [words], thus making three types [of examples]. The point is that the suffix *aṇ* does not occur;
however, the suffix *ktavatu* certainly does occur, because the restriction applies only to the suffixes that follow a word with an upapada (an accompanying word).
The phrase "only after those beginning with *su*" means "after the five beginning with *sukarma*."
(809) *samo muñaḥ* |3|2|90|. The meaning is that when *soma* is the object (*karman*) in composition, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *su* (to press) in the sense of the past tense.
"In four ways" is to be explained as before. "In this manner" refers to [the rule] *agnau*.
The meaning is that in the subsequent sūtra as well, there is a fourfold restriction.

(810) *agnau ceḥ* |3|2|91|. Regarding *agnau ceḥ*: when *agni* is the object (*karman*) in composition (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *ci* (*cinoti*) in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*).
The meaning is "it might be. Regarding the term *agnicit*: it means one who has piled up (*cita*) a specific sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) called "fire" (*agni*) by means of bricks.
[Pāṇini 3.2.92: *karmaṇyagnyākhyāyām* ("after a word denoting an object, when the word *agni* is used as a name").

Regarding the rule *karmaṇyagnyākhyāyām*: the term *karmaṇi* that is carried over from the previous rule serves to provide the *upapada* (governing word), whereas the *karmaṇi* found in this specific rule provides the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). Consequently, the term *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) is not connected here. Thus he says: "when *karma* is the *upapada*, etc. [and] "from the root *ci*," and so forth.
It should also be understood that [the suffix] *ini* is used in the sense of "being the actual object. Regarding the phrase "like a hawk" (*śyena iva*):
the meaning is that the word *śyena* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for something resembling a hawk; that is to say, it means "having the form of a hawk" (*śyenākṛtika*).
(812) *karmaṇīni vikriyaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.93. [The suffix *ini* is added after a verbal root] in the sense of the object, provided that the action results in a transformation (*vikriya*).

*karmaṇīni vikriyaḥ*: *ṭhin* is without a case ending; *vikriyaḥ* is the fifth-case form derived from the root *krī* preceded by the prefix *vi*. *Kutsite*: the meaning is that the aforementioned rule applies when a contemptible action (*kutsita-karman*) is the upapada. *Somavikrayī*: [referring to] the substance *soma*.
The meaning is that when something is being sold, it brings reproach upon the seller, because such a sale is prohibited.
(813) *dṛśeḥ kvanip* [Pāṇini 3.2.94].

The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the root *dṛś*. Although the suffix *kvanip* is already established by the rules "after [roots ending in] *ā*, the suffixes *manin*, *kvanip*, and *vanip* [are added]" and "they are seen after other [roots] as well," this [present rule] is intended to exclude *manin* and the others which co-occur with it, and to prevent the application of *aṇ* and other suffixes when there is a prefix (*sopapada*).
The completion [of the formation] indeed occurs, because here the suffix *kvip* with its accompanying prefix is specifically excluded by the repeated mention of *kvip*. [Examples:
*pāradṛśvā* ("one who has seen the further shore").
(814) *rājani yudhi kṛñaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.95. [This sūtra provides for the suffix *kvip* after the root *kṛ* when combined with the words *rājan* and *yudh*.]
"From *rājan* [as object], after *yudh* and *kṛñ*": [the word] "in battle" (*yudhi*) and "making" (*kṛñ*) form a collective dvandva compound, from which the ablative case is used.

The meaning is that the suffix *kvanip* occurs when *rājan* is the object (the upapada), following the roots *yudh* and *kṛñ*, provided they refer to the past or the present. Now, one might object: since *yudh* is intransitive, how can there be an object in its case? [The answer follows:]...

To the question "How is there positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?", he says: "The root *yudh* is included [within the scope of the rule]. Regarding the example *rājakṛtvā*, the meaning is "having made a king" (*rājānaṃ kṛtavān*).
(815) *Saha* also [is used with the gerund]. Pāṇini 3.2.96.
"And with *saha*. This means that when the word *saha* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *kvanip* is added after the roots *yudh* and *kṛ*.

(816) "After *jan*, the suffix *ḍa* is added when a locative [word] is the *upapada*. This means that when a word ending in the locative case is the *upapada*, the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *jan* in the sense of "become" (*bhūta*).

Regarding "sarasijam": by virtue of the indicatory letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the final syllable even though it is not a *bha* stem. Regarding "manduraja": according to Amara, "a stable for horses is called *mandura*. In this case, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) occurs either by the rule "haladantāt" or, alternatively, by the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam" (which allows for non-elision). However, here the elision applies. Thus, "born in a stable" (*manduraja*).

(817) *pañcamyām ajātau* |3|2|98|. Regarding *pañcamyām ajātau*: [the word] *janeḥ* [is understood]; the remainder [of the rule] is *bhūtārthāt*. *saṃskārajaṃ maṭ* means "the suffix *maṭ* is added after the word *saṃskāra* when it is used in the sense of 'born from' (*jātaḥ*)."

(818) *upasarge ca saṃjñāyām* |3|2|99|. "And when there is a prefix (*upasarga*),"—the rule *janer ḍaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.97] is understood as the remainder. "When it is a name (*saṃjñā*)" is an adjunct (*upādhi*) pertaining to the entire compound. (819) *anau karmaṇi* |3|2|100|. "With the prefix *anu*, in the sense of the object (*karman*)."

[The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs] after [the root] *anu* when there is an object. Now, since the root *jan* (to be born) is intransitive, how can the meaning of *ittham* (in that manner) be construed when an object is present as an *upapada*? To this he says: "having conformed to a man" (*pumāṃsamanurudhya*). The sense is that "conforming" (*anurudhya*) is the meaning of the verbal root. [In the form] *pumanujā*, there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct at the end of the preceding member, namely *puṃsi*.
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied].
(820) "It is also seen in other cases" (Pāṇini 3.2.101). It is also seen in other cases. *Aja* means "not born. *Dvija* means a Brāhmaṇa.

The meaning is "twice-born. The intention is that this is based on such Smṛti texts as: "They are born first from the mother, and secondly from the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass. Regarding the word *api*:
in the rules prescribing the suffix *ḍa*, such as "the suffix *ḍa* [is added] after the root *jan* when preceded by a locative case ending," those qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) which have been employed...

The meaning is that [the suffixes] have the specific forms of the *prakṛti* (base), and the phrase "when the agent is a *bhūta* (past action)" is a qualification of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), intended for the purpose of transcending that [general rule].
(821) *Kta* and *ktavatu* are *niṣṭhā*. 1.1.26.

*kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*. This is a *dvandva* compound of *kta* and *ktavatu*. The singular number in the term *niṣṭhā* is used with reference to each [member] individually. (822) *niṣṭhā* | 3.2.102.
The words "niṣṭhā" and "bhūte" are understood from the governing context of the sūtra. Thus he says: "bhūtārtha... and so forth.

[This refers to] the rule *kta* for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Consequently, the meaning is that in the domain of the *kta* suffix, the term "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) does not apply. [Furthermore,] the rule *ktavatu* applies to the agent; however, [the suffixes] *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khala* denote only the state of being (*bhāva*).

The sense is that it is because of the prescription of two actions (karmaṇoḥ). In the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*, from the preceding rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*, it is understood that after transitive verbs (*sakarmakebhyaḥ*), the suffixes are used for both the object (*karmani*) and the agent (*kartari*), whereas after intransitive verbs (*akarmakebhyaḥ*), they are used for the state (*bhāve*) and the agent (*kartari*). Consequently, after intransitive verbs, the suffix *kta* is employed in the sense of the state (*bhāve*).
Thinking that the rule "the [suffix] *kta* [is used] after transitive verbs in the sense of the object" (*sakarmakebhyaḥ karmaṇi*) is thus established, he provides examples:
"snātaṃ mayā" (I have bathed). Because it is intransitive, the *kta* suffix denotes the state (*bhāve*). "stutastvayā viṣṇuḥ" (Viṣṇu was praised by you).

Because it is transitive, the *kta* suffix denotes the object (*karmaṇi*). He provides an example for the *ktavatū* suffix denoting the agent (*kartari*): "viṣṇurviśvam" (Viṣṇu [has pervaded] the universe).

(823) *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe* |6|4|60|. Regarding the rule *niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe*: since the suffix *ṇyat* signifies the sense of "caused by" (*ṇyadartha*), which refers to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), and because the suffix *ṇyat*—being a *kṛtya* suffix according to the rule *ṛhalor ṇyat*—is applied only to the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) by the rule *tayor eva*, this is the intended meaning.
The phrase "elsewhere than that" means "in the case of the agent. This results in [the application of] the suffix *ktavatu*. The sense is that there should be lengthening of the vowel in *kṣi*:
the rule *kṣiyaḥ* from the preceding sūtra is understood here, and the word "lengthening" (*dīrgha*) is carried over from the rule *yupluvordīrghaśchandasi*. This is the intended meaning.
(824) *kṣiyo dīrghāt* | Pāṇini 8.2.46.

[The rule] "from *kṣi*, when it is long" (*kṣiyo dīrghāt*). The mention of "long" (*dīrghāt*) is a qualification of *kṣi*. Thus he says: "from *kṣi* when it is long. The meaning is: "when it ends in a long vowel. [The subsequent rule is: "the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] is not [replaced by *n*]. (*niṣṭhātasya naḥ*).

The intention is that [the suffix] *ktavatu* follows from the rule "ṭhradābhyām" (Pāṇini 8.2.42). Regarding the form *kṣīṇavān*: the suffix *ktavatu* is added to the root *kṣi* in the sense of the agent;

the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "niṣṭhāyāmaṇyadarthe" (Pāṇini 6.4.60); the substitution of *na* for *ta* occurs, and because of the presence of the letter *ṣ*, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* takes place. "My desire has been *kṣita*" means "it has been destroyed" (*kṣapita*). [This is from] the root *kṣi* in the sense of "decay" (*kṣaye*).

Thus, from this root *kṣi*, which has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the suffix *kta* is applied in the passive (*karman*). However, in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), one should cite the example *kṣitam kāmena*. Here, when the suffix *kta* is prescribed for the meanings of *bhāva* and *karman* belonging to the causative (*ṇyad-artha*), the lengthening of the vowel does not occur, because it is stated [in the rule] "when not having the meaning of the causative" (*aṇyadarthe*). Since there is an absence of a long final vowel, [the rule] "of *kṣi*" (*kṣiyaḥ*)...

The rule *dīrghādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.77) does not apply here because of the prohibition *na rśyukaḥ kitī*. This [sūtra] serves as a reminder of the prohibition of *iṭ* in cases such as *śrita*. Regarding *kṣuta*: the suffix *kta* is added to the root *ṭua kṣu* (meaning "to sound"). Now, one might ask:
how is *ūrṇuta* formed, given that because it consists of more than one syllable (*anekāckatvena*), the rule *na rśyukaḥ kitī* would apply?
Because the prohibition would not apply, he says: "as in *ūrṇunuvatuḥ*. This is a Vārttika.
(825) *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ pūrvasya ca daḥ* | 8|2|42|. Regarding *radābhyām*: the two *a*s in *radābhyām* are for the sake of pronunciation. Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "by means of the letters *r* and *d*": the analysis of *niṣṭhāt* is *niṣṭhāyās t-*, meaning "the *t* of the *niṣṭhā*. Thus he says: "*niṣṭhātasya*" (of the *niṣṭhā-t*). This means "of the letter *t* of the *niṣṭhā*. Regarding "*naḥ syāt*" (it should become *na*): this means "the letter *n* should [replace it]. In the sūtra, "*na*" is in the nominative case (*prathamāntam*). The vowel *a* [is for the sake of pronunciation].

The purpose is for pronunciation. In the rule "dakārasya ca," the word "nakāraḥ" is understood as an ellipsis (*anuṣajyate*). The intention is that in the sūtra, "da" is in the genitive case. However, in the words *caritam* and *uditam*, there is no substitution of *n* for *t*, because the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is separated from the preceding consonant by the augment *iṭ*, and thus it is not preceded by *r* or *d*.
He provides an example following the letter *r*: "śa".

This indicates the *kta* suffix from the root *śṛ*. Now, consider *kārtiḥ*, meaning "the descendant of Kṛti. Here, the suffix *iñ* is applied, there is initial *vṛddhi*, and the substitution of *r* for the semivowel (*raparatvam*). In this case, the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs because it follows the letter *r*.

To this he says: "by virtue of being external" (*bahir-aṅga-tvena*). He provides examples for [the substitution] following the letter *d*: *cchinnaḥ*, *bhinnaḥ*. The intention here is that there is the substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix and for the *d* at the end of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
(826) Pāṇini 8.2.43: *saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ*.
"From *saṃyoga* and so forth. "The suffix *kta* would be *niṣṭhā* for us [in this case]. This is a supplement to the rule. Regarding *drāṇa*:

from the root *ḍrā* (meaning "to revile" or "to go"), the suffix *kta* is applied; there is the substitution of *na* for *ta*, and the substitution of *ṇa*. Regarding *glāna*: from the root *glai* (meaning "loss of joy"), by the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*, the vowel *ā* is substituted, and *na* is substituted for *ta*. "From twenty-one roots beginning with *lū*" [is the meaning].
Among the twenty-two roots beginning with *pū* (the *pvādi* group), excluding the first, *pūñ*, the meaning is "from the twenty-one beginning with *lū*. *jyā-* indicates the verbal root (*dhātu*).
*grahijyā-* indicates the rule for *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution). *jīnaḥ*: when *jyā* is followed by the suffix *kta*, the form *jīnaḥ* arises by the application of the rule *saṃyogāder guṇaḥ*.

Because the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* (the *niṣṭhānatva*) is not established, the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the resulting single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) occur first; since the condition "after an *ā*" (*ātaḥ paratva*) is then absent, the rule "*saṃyogāderātaḥ*" does not apply, and thus the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by this [present rule]. The statement "*dugvā dīrghaśca*" is a Vārttika; it means that after the roots *duh* and *gu*, [the suffix *kta* takes the augment *iṭ*] and there is also lengthening.

The meaning is that there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the final *t* of the root, and the lengthening of the vowel of the base (*prakṛti*). Regarding the word *dutayā* in Māgha’s poem—used in the phrase *mṛdutayā dutayā*—he states [the derivation] as *ṭua du upatāpe* (DhP 1.970), etc., in order to justify the form *duta*. Regarding *gūna*, the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *guh*, with lengthening of the vowel. Regarding *pūño vināśe*, this is a Vārttika.
The meaning is that there is a substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following the root *puñj*, due to its sense of destruction (*vināśārtha*). Regarding "from *siñ*":

this is a *vārttika*. A "karmakartṛ" (agent as object) is one who is both the object and the agent; "grāsakarmakartṛka" means that whose object-agent is the act of swallowing (*grāsa*). Therefore, [the rule applies] to the *niṣṭhā* suffix following the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*).
The meaning is that there is substitution of *n* for [the *t*].

(827) *oditaśca* | Pāṇini 8.2.45. Regarding *oditaśca*: the meaning is that there is substitution of *n* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following a verbal root (*dhātu*) marked with the vowel *o*.
Regarding the word *bhugna*: because the substitution of *n* (*natva*) is considered *asiddha*, the change of *j* to *g* (*kutva*) occurs first, and only then does the substitution of *n* take place.
Regarding *ucchūna*: from the root *ośvi* preceded by the prefix *ud*, the suffix *kta* is applied;

due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), followed by the formation of the single substitute *pūrvarūpa*; the augment *iṭ* is not added because of the rule *śvīditaḥ*; [and then the suffix *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ* applies]. By the rule *halaḥ*,...

Thus [the vowel] is long, and there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* in the *niṣṭhā* suffix. In the word *prahīṇa*, [the root is] *hā* with the suffix *kta*; there is the substitution of *ī* by *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the substitution of *n* for *t*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by *kṛtyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.29). Regarding "beginning with *sū*" (*svādayaḥ*): this means that the nine roots beginning with *ṣūṅ prāṇiprasave* are stated in the *divādi* class as being marked with the indicator *o* (*odit*). In the word *sūna*, the suffix *kta* is applied to *ṣūṅ*.

Regarding *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *ṇ*): there is a prohibition of *ṇ* by the rule "kiti ca" [Pāṇini 1.1.5]. Regarding *dūna*: the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *dūṅ* (in the sense of "to afflict");

because it belongs to the *svadi* group, it is marked as *odit*, and thus *natva* applies. Now, one might ask: how is the form *uḍḍīna* derived from the root *ḍīṅ* (in the sense of "motion through the air"), given that it is *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment) and lacks the property of ending in an *u*-vowel?

Since the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 7.2.10], "there is no [substitution] when a kṛt-affix marked with K follows," does not apply here, he says: "Because of the force of its placement among the roots beginning with *odana*, there is no *iṭ*. The meaning is that if *iṭ* were present, then because the root *ḍīṅ* (to fly) would not follow a root ending in an *oṭ* vowel (*odit*), the substitution of *na* for the *niṣṭhā*-suffix *ta* would not even be applicable; thus, its placement among the *odit* roots would be useless.

(828) *dravamūrtisparśayoḥ śyaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.24. The term *dravamūrti* refers to the root *śyaiṅ* (meaning "to flow") after its vowel has been changed to *ā* (*ātva*), resulting in the form *śya*; this is the genitive case [of the verbal base]. The analysis of the compound is: *dravamūrtiśca sparśaśca* ("liquidity/form and touch"). The explanation of the word *mūrtau* is "in solidity" (*kāṭhinye*).

Thus, there would be *saṃprasāraṇa*. The intention is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "there is *saṃprasāraṇa* for *ṣyaṅ*" (*ṣyaṅḥ saṃprasāraṇam*). And so, when the suffix *kta* follows the root *śyaiṅ*, after the substitution of *ātva* and the *saṃprasāraṇa*, and the formation of the single substitute by the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), we arrive at the state *śita*.

(829) *śyo'sparśe* |8|2|47|. The analysis of *śyo'sparśe* is *śyaḥ* and *asparśe*. Regarding the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*), it is more appropriate to state that the lengthening occurs by the rule *halaḥ* [6.4.2] *before* the substitution of *natva* (the change of *n* to *ṇ*), because the *natva* substitution belongs to the third section of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* (the *traipādika* rules). Thus, we have *śīnaṃ ghṛtam* ("the melted ghee").

The meaning is "become solid" (*ghanībhūta*), because verbal roots have multiple meanings. Although a non-hot touch (*anuṣṇasparśa*) indeed exists even in clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the intention is that only a specific kind of touch called "cold" (*śīta*) is intended here. [The objection] "What [is the purpose of the suffix] *asparśe*? [refers to the rule]: the substitution of *na* for the *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) after the root *śyaiṅ*.
The word *syāt* means "let there be only this much. In the example *śītaṃ jalam*, the meaning is "possessing a cold touch.

Here, by the rule *dravamūrtī*, there is only vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and not the substitution of *ṇatva* for the final consonant; thus, this is an illustration for the word *sparśa* under the rule *dravamūrtisparśayoḥ*. [It is] not an illustration for the rule *śyo'sparśe*.

However, it should be understood that this is a counter-example. In the two sūtras, the word *sparśa* (touch) refers both to the primary [substance] and to the secondary [quality]. Among these, when it refers to the secondary [quality], it follows the gender and number of its substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*). For example: *śītā āpaḥ* (cold water), *śītaṃ jalam* (cool water), and so forth. But when the specific quality of touch is intended as the primary [referent],...
In that case, the neuter gender alone is intended; as Amara states: "śītam [is used] in the sense of a quality.
He asks regarding the rule for *saṃprasāraṇa*: "What about *drumūrtisparśayoḥ*? [The example is] *saṃśyānaḥ*.
Here, because the quality of touch (*sparśa*) is not perceived, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*; however, the substitution of *na* for *t* certainly does occur.
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied].
(830) *prateś ca* | 6|1|25|. [The rule] "and after *prati*" is stated so that the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) may occur even in cases other than those involving fluidity, form, or touch.
*Pratiśīnaḥ*: the meaning is "gone towards. Here, the substitution of *n* [for *y*] occurs by the rule *śyo'sparśe*.
(831) *Vibhāṣābhyavapūrvasya* |6|1|26|. *Vibhāṣā*: the root *śyaiṅ* is understood as the remainder. It means that there may optionally be *saṃprasāraṇa* [vocalization].

This is a supplement to complete the sense. Since the rule for *saṃprasāraṇa* would apply invariably to liquid form and touch, and would not apply elsewhere, this is an optional (*vibhāṣā*) rule. "Abhiśyānaṃ ghṛtam" (the clarified butter has congealed): here, there is an option regarding *saṃprasāraṇa* in the case of liquid form. "Avaśyānaḥ" or "avaśīnaḥ vṛścikaḥ" (the scorpion has become motionless): here...

Even in the absence of fluidity, form, and touch, there is an option regarding the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution. Having raised the doubt that there might also be an option for *saṃprasāraṇa* in the case of *samavaśyāna*, he says: "It is restricted" (*vyavasthita*). (Pāṇini 6.1.15) *añco'napādāne* (8.2.48).
