Thus [the vowel] is long. There is the substitution of *ṇ* for the final consonant of the *niṣṭhā* suffix. (895) *cchandasi liṭ* |3|2|105|.
In the Vedic language, the *liṭ* [perfect tense] [is used].
(896) After the suffix *liṭ*, the suffix *kānac* may optionally [be used]. (897) And the suffix *kvasu* [may also be used].

And *kvasu*. These are three sūtras. Here, with the intention of carrying forward the term *bhūte* from the first sūtra, he explains: "In Vedic usage, *liṭ* occurs in the sense of the general past (*bhūtasāmānya*).

The meaning is that in Vedic usage, the conditions of being non-recent (*anadyatana*) and being beyond the sight of the speaker (*parokṣatva*) are not intended to be expressed. [This is stated] in the rule: "After *liṭ*, there is optionally *kānac*."

The second sūtra: In this context, the words *cchandasi* (in Vedic) and *bhūte* (past) are understood to carry over. The meaning is that in Vedic, when referring to the past, there shall be the substitution of *kānac* for *liṭ*. The mention of *liṭ* is for the purpose of including *liṭ* in its entirety; by this, it also applies to that *liṭ* which is prescribed by the rule *parokṣe liṭ* ("*liṭ* is used for the remote past").

The purpose is for the sake of inclusion (*grahaṇārtha*). Otherwise, by the maxim "that which is not separated by anything else" (*anantarasya*), there would be the inclusion of only the *liṭ* under discussion; this is clear in the Vṛtti. However, the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is either for the sake of hearing the *liṭ* in its own form in certain cases, or for the purpose of indicating that the rule regarding the optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply to the substitutes of *l* (*lādeśeṣu*). As for the utility of that [indication]:

In the rule *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavaseḥ*, the purpose is for the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of *kvasu* alone. The meaning of these two—*kānac* and *kvasu*—is that they are substitutes for the *liṭ* [perfect] in the Vedic language (*chandas*) when referring to the past; and the *kvasu* is also a substitute for the *liṭ*. The separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), however, is for the sake of the continuation of *kvasu* alone in the subsequent rule. These two—*kānac* and *kvasu*—[are thus established].
"The two [forms] are Vedic" is stated clearly in this very context by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa.

He says this in the passage beginning with "tasya" and ending with "trimunimatam. However, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇe," it is said: "that which has come from one who has drunk is 'papivadrūpyam'."
It has been employed; by this, it is indicated that the *kvasu* suffix is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) in some instances even in common usage.
He says this with the words "But poets... and "tasthivāṃsam. [The form] *tasthivāṃsam* is derived from the root *sthā* with the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix *kvasu*.
In the second person singular, there is lengthening according to the rule *atvasantasya ca yatra*. Because it ends in an *ugit* vowel, the augment *num* is added. [Similarly for] *adhijagmuṣaḥ*.

Thus: from the root *gam* preceded by *adhi*, the suffix *kvasu* is applied in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By the rule *āṅe'yamahane*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule *śasi vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *v* in *vasu*. Then the *pūrva-rūpa* (the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels) and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occur.
(898) *vasvekājāddhasām* | Pāṇini 7.2.67. [The suffix *ām* is applied after a monosyllabic verbal base ending in *vas*, provided it is not followed by a *has* suffix.]

The term *vasu* is cited here without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). Thus, he will explain it as *vasoḥ*. One might ask: "Since reduplication (dvitva) is compulsory, once it has occurred, the stem no longer consists of a single vowel (*ekāctva*); how then could the augment *iṭ* apply? To this, he says:
"Of those that consist of a single vowel even after reduplication has been performed. This means that even when reduplication has taken place...

The meaning is: "of those which remain as single-consonant roots. He says, "not of others," because this is a restrictive rule (niyama) regarding the *iṭ* augment—which would otherwise apply everywhere by the rule of the *krādi* group—after overriding the prohibition [contained in] "neḍ vaśi kṛti. [The example] "ādivān" [is from the root] *ada* in the sense of eating.

When the doubling (*dvitva*), the *hal-ādi-śeṣa*, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-dīrgha*), and the lengthening of a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa-dīrgha*) have been performed, even though the root has undergone doubling, it remains a single-syllable (*ekāc*) root; thus, the augment *iṭ* is applied. For example, in *ārivān*:
having applied the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*, and having performed the aforementioned operations, this [root] is a single-syllable root.

Regarding the example *dādivān*: the root *ḍu dāñ* means "to give. Once reduplication has occurred, this [root] is no longer a single syllable (*ekāc*). Furthermore, the elision of the long *ā* (ā-lopa) is conditioned by the suffix *iṭ*; since that [suffix] is absent here, the elision does not take place. Thus, the mention of *āt* (the long vowel) is for the sake of cases where the root is not a single syllable after reduplication. Regarding *jakṣivān*: [this is derived from the root *ghas*, which becomes *jakṣ* through reduplication].

The substitution of *ghas* for [the root *ad*] occurs by the rule *ṭhliṭoranyatarasyām*; once reduplication has taken place, this [substitution] does not apply because [the reduplicated stem] is no longer a single vowel (*ekāc*), hence the mention of *ghas*. (899) *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavasaśruvaḥ* 3.2.108.

In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix *kvasu* is used] after the roots *sad*, *vas*, and *śru*. The dual number and masculine gender are archaic (*ārṣa*). And for that [perfect tense], *kvasu* is obligatory; this is clear from the *Bhāṣya*, where it is stated that the mention of "optionally" (*vā*) applies only to the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), whereas for that [perfect], *kvasu* is indeed obligatory. In the alternative case, there is the aorist (*luṅ*). For that...

Because it is prescribed for the general past tense (*bhūtasāmānya*). However, if the word "optionally" (*vā*) were not carried over [from the previous rule], this *liṭ* would be a constant exception (*nitya-apavāda*) to the *luṅ* in the general past tense, since they are of the same form (*sarūpa*). Furthermore, there is no *tiṅ* affix for this *liṭ* in the general past tense, because this *kvasu* is an exception to that [general *liṭ*]. As for the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*asarūpa-vidhi*), however—

The details regarding the prohibition of the *ṭhak* suffix in the case of roots ending in long vowels—specifically in the rule "ṭhali ca seṭi liṭaḥ kānac vā"—are explained at length in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
Regarding the form *niṣeduṣīm*: from the root *sad* preceded by the prefix *ni*, the *liṭ* suffix *kvasu* is applied; there is reduplication;

by the rule "ata ekahalmadhye," the *etva* (change to *e*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) occur; then the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *vasu* suffix takes place, followed by the formation of the single *pūrvarūpa* (the preceding vowel).

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. Regarding the form *adhyūṣuṣaḥ*: from the root *vas* preceded by *adhi*, the suffix *kvasu* is applied after the *liṭ* (perfect) tense marker; because the root begins with *yā* [i.e., *yaṅ*], there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *va*. This results in the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels (*pūrvarūpa*). Then there is reduplication of the syllable *us*, followed by the application of *halādiśeṣa* (retaining only the first consonant), and the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*. In the nominative plural (*śas*), there is vocalization of the *vas* ending, followed by the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels.

Regarding *śuśruvān*: this is formed from the root *śru* with the suffix *kvasu* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), followed by reduplication. (Pāṇini 3.2.109) states: "The forms *upeyivān*, *anāśvān*, and *anūcāna* [are valid]. Thus, *upeyivān* is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *upa*, with the suffix *kvasu* in the perfect tense, followed by the augment *iṭ*.

Because it is eternal (*nitya*), the doubling [of the *gh*] occurs. The augment *iṭ*, which would otherwise be prescribed by the rule for roots beginning with *val*, is prohibited by the rule "there is no *iṭ* after *vaś* and *kṛt*. That *iṭ*, however, arises again due to the restriction regarding roots beginning with *ka*. Furthermore, by the sūtra "after a root consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*) ending in *v* or *s*, and after *ghas*, [the augment *iṭ* is applied] to the following [suffix]," [the *iṭ* is applied] after a root that is monosyllabic and ends in *ā*, as well as after *ghas*.
It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the augment *iṭ*,

which was prohibited after the doubling [of the root] because it would then consist of more than one vowel— according to the rule meaning "the augment *iṭ* occurs after *vas*, but not after others"— is here restored by this specific nipātana (irregularity). Once *iṭ* has been applied, [the question arises regarding] the *ikāra* (the letter *i*) of the subsequent portion.

The long vowel of the reduplication is not prescribed as a substitute here. [An objector asks: "But surely, let the augment *iṭ* be prescribed as something not previously established (*apūrva*) in this case. To this he replies: "upeyuṣī. Because it possesses the *ugit* designation, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied; furthermore, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *vas*. However, the augment *iṭ*, which would otherwise be required by the rule for roots beginning with *val*, does not occur, because its cause...

Because the letter *v* is on the verge of destruction due to its vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). The sense here is that if the augment *iṭ* were introduced as something not previously established (*apūrva*), then *iṭ* would have to occur even in this case. The phrase "this is intended as a concession" (*upetyavivakṣitam*)—in this matter, the commentary itself is the only refuge. Regarding the root *aśnāti*: it is derived from the root *aś* (meaning "to eat") with the *śnā* conjugational suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

The suffix *kvip* and so forth; for the *liṭ* [perfect] there is *kvasu*; reduplication; lengthening by the rule "ṭhata ādeḥ"; a long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha*; and because it does not have two consonants (*dvahal*), there is no *nuṭ* augment. There is also no *nuṭ* by the rule "ṭhaśnoteśca," because in that context only [the root] having the *śnu* conjugational suffix is included. Then there is a negative compound (*nañ-upapada-samāsa*). [The rule] "nalopaḥ" [applies].

The meaning of *nañaḥ 'tasmānnuḍacī'* is that [the augment *nuṭ* is added] after the negative particle. "In the sense of the agent (*kartari*)" means it is not in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) or the object (*karmaṇi*). In the case of *kānac*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) because [the root *vac*] belongs to the *yajādi* group; then the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute for preceding and following vowels) and the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel for homogeneous vowels) follow. The rule beginning with "optionally in *gam* and *han*" (*vibhāṣā gamahane*) is clear.

(901) *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacāvaprathamāsamānādhikaraṇe* |3|2|124|. [The suffixes] *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are substituted] for *laṭ*. These two, *śatṛ* and *śānac*, belong specifically to that *laṭ* prescribed by the preceding rule, "In the sense of the present, *laṭ*," according to the maxim *anantarasya* ("of what is immediately preceding"). [This applies even] in the case of "proximity to the present" (*vartamānasāmīpye*).

This is clear from such commentaries (*bhāṣya*). In the *śatṛ* suffix, the letters *ś* and *ṛ* are elided. Thus, *pacantam* means "the substratum of the activity conducive to cooking," according to the established tenet that "a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, whereas nouns (*nāman*) have substance (*satva*) as their primary meaning. Because the *śatṛ* suffix is marked with *ś* (i.e., is *śit*), [it causes the substitution of the present stem for the root].
In the case of *sārvadhātuka* and *acch*, there is a single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule "guṇe. In the case of *śānac*, [the suffixes] *śa* and *ac* are elided.
(902) *āne muk*: the augment *muk* is added after *ān*. The governing term "of the base" (*aṅgasya*) is understood, as is the rule "after *at*, *yey*" (*ato yeyaḥ*).
The suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive), which has been carried over from the preceding sūtra, is modified to *atā* (the vowel *a*) and thus qualifies [the base].

This is a rule concerning that which ends in such [a vowel] (*tadantavidhi*). Therefore, he says: "of that which ends in *a*" (*adantasya*). In the case of *muk*, the letter *k* is an *it* (indicatory letter); the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation; because it is *kit*, it is an integral part of the end [of the base]. Regarding the phrase "while [the action] is continuing" (*anuvartamāne*), [this refers to the state of] "being present" (*vartamāne*).

The meaning is that when the sense already expressed is obtained through the substitution of the genitive case for the word *laṭ*—which has been carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the preceding sūtra—the term "additional" (*adhika*) refers to the attainment of a meaning not actually present in the syllables of the sūtra itself. Regarding the example *san brāhmaṇaḥ*: [it is derived] from the root *as* (meaning "to be") with the suffix *śatṛ*, and [the elision of] *śap*.

*Luk*, *śnasorallopaḥ*. Regarding *māṅi*: the meaning is that it should be stated that when *māṅ* is employed, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are used] for the present tense (*laṭ*) when reproach is implied. For example: *mā jīvan*—"He does not live";
the meaning is that he does not live because he is of no use, being as good as dead. *Mā pacamānaḥ* should also be cited as an example.

Since the rule "ṭhlaṭaḥ śatṛśānacau" already establishes this, for what purpose is the present [sūtra] stated? To this he replies: "māṅ luṅtīti" (and in the case of *māṅ* followed by *luṅ*). (903) "And in the vocative. 3.2.125.

And in the case of addressing [the vocative]. The phrase "with the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes" is understood as a supplement. This rule is commenced for the purpose of [applying to cases where the suffix] is in grammatical apposition with a word in the nominative case. Since this is already established by the fact that the re-mention of *laṭ* in the preceding sūtra is intended to prescribe a specific [non-present] tense, this present rule is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).

(904) *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* |3|2|126|. [The word *lakṣaṇa* means] that by which something is characterized (*lakṣyate*) or made known (*jñāpyate*); it is, therefore, an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus he says: "that which characterizes an action. When the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be indicated as either a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*), [the present rule applies].

Thus [it means]: the agent alone is the meaning of the suffix. For example: "The Yavanas eat while lying down. Here, the lying down at the time of eating indicates that the eater is a Yavana. He gives an example for the sense of cause (*hetu*):
"He dwells while acquiring. The meaning is: "He dwells for the sake of acquiring. He states another example for the sense of cause:

"Beholding Hari"—the meaning is that by the sight of Hari, one is liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra. Now, an objection is raised: since the acquisition of wealth and so forth is not accomplished by clothing, how can clothing be the cause of that [liberation]? To this he says:
"The cause, the fruit, and the instrument. This refers to the knowledge that [clothing] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) in relation to the activity of wearing it.

The sense is that even the acquisition, which is desired as a cause [for happiness], becomes a cause for dwelling [in misery]. Regarding the word *prapīyamāṇa*: since it occurs in separate words [from the preceding element], one might ask how the substitution of *ṇ* is possible; therefore, he says: "after a kṛt-affix ending in a vowel or after the letter *c*" (Pāṇini 8.4.29). (905) *īdāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.83).
*Īdāsaḥ*. *Āsaḥ* is the ablative case (*pañcamī*). [The word] *ānasya* [is used] because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of that [term] from the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (P.
1.1.50). (906) *videḥ śatur vasuḥ* (P. 7.1.36): [The substitute] *vasu* is applied for the [affix] *śatṛ* after the root *vid*.

Regarding the rule *videḥ śatur vasuḥ*: the term *veteḥ* refers specifically to the root *vid* "to know" (*vida jñāne*) which belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class, because the suffix *śatṛ* is a parasmaipada (active voice) marker; whereas *vidyati* and *vintē* are ātmanepada (middle voice).
Although *vindati* is ubhayapadī (both voices), it is not included here, because [the rule] applies only when a root without an *anubandha* is mentioned.
The intention is that this is because it was stated [in the rule] "of that which has a suffixal element" (*sānubandhakasya*). Regarding "or it may be" (*vā syāt*):
the intention is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "ending in *t*, *hy*, *e*, or *stāṅ*" (*tu-hya-e-stāṅ*). Regarding *viduṣī*:

[the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied because of the *ugit* designation; there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *van* and *as* [elements], the formation of the single preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*), and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
(907) *tau sat* | 3|2|127|. The word *tau* (those two) refers to the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes mentioned in the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*. Thus he says: "those two, *śatṛ* and *śānac*."
The meaning of *lṛṭaḥ sadvā* is that the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* optionally take the place of *lṛṭ*. [The word] *vyavasthita* [is used];
the intention is that this is due to the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*). [The word] *nityam* [is used]; by that, there is the exclusion of the verbal endings (*tiṅ*).

He provides examples for non-co-referentiality with a non-first case ending—namely, *kariṣyantam*. He provides an example when a suffix (*pratyaya*) follows—namely, *kāriṣyataḥ*. He provides examples for a following word (*uttarapada*)—namely, *kariṣyadbhaktiḥ* and *kariṣyantī bhaktiḥ*; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. He provides an example for the vocative case—namely, *he*.
Regarding "kariṣyan": the example for the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is to be cited as "the Yavanas will eat while [he] is about to lie down" (*śayiṣyamāṇā bhokṣyante yavanāḥ*).

He gives an example for the sense of cause (*hetu*): "he dwells because he intends to acquire wealth" (*arjayiṣyan vasati*). Regarding the phrase "even when there is coreferentiality with the nominative (*prathamā-sāmānādhikaraṇye*)":
the meaning is that it occurs even in some cases where there is an absence of coreferentiality with anything other than the nominative.

The word "kadācit" (sometimes) should also be understood [as included here]. Furthermore, it is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *anavaklṛptyamarṣe* that this [suffix] applies only to the *lṛṭ* prescribed under the heading of the future tense (*bhaviṣyat*) by the rule *lṛṭ śeṣe ca*.

(909) *pūṅyajoḥ śānan* | 3.2.128. The rule *pūṅyajoḥ śānan* [is explained as follows]: the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*). "In the present tense" (*vartamāne*)—this is a supplement to the sūtra.
The intention is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "in the present tense" from the previous rule, *vartamāne laṭ*.

However, the mention of *l* (the *l*-marker) has been withdrawn. Consequently, this [suffix] is independent, like *ṇvul* and others, and is not a substitute for *l* (as in *śatṛ*, etc.). Thus, it occurs only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and not in the senses of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Furthermore, even in the absence of being a substitute for *l*, there would not be a genitive case in the object (*karman*) in the example "somaṃ pavamānaḥ."
It must be stated that in the sūtra *na loka-*, the term *tṛn* is used as a pratyāhāra (a contraction), because it has been so explained.

(910) *Tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129). Regarding *tācchīlya*: in the suffix *cānaś*, the *ca* and *ā* are elided. Thus, *bhogaṃ bhuñjānaḥ* means "one whose nature is enjoyment" (*bhogaśīla*).

This is the meaning. "Wearing armor" (kavacaṃ bibhrāṇaḥ) implies being in the prime of youth. "Slaying the enemy" (śatruṃ nighnāḥ) means capable of slaying. Consequently, because there is no subsequent [suffix], the *muk* augment does not occur. Since the *cānaś* suffix is not a substitute for *l*, and since it is not designated as *ātmanepada*, its application occurs even after roots that are *parasmaipada*.
(911) *iṅ-dhāryoḥ śatr akṛcchriṇi* |3|2|130|. The analysis of the sūtra is: *iṅ-dhāryoḥ*, *śatr*, *akṛcchriṇi*. *Akṛcchra* means "absence of suffering";
one who possesses that is *akṛcchrin*. From the *dvandva* compound of these two roots, *iṅ* and *dhṛ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative.
"Adhīyan" means "may he study easily. "Dhārayan" means "may he retain [the text] easily.
(Pāṇini 3.2.131) "The suffix *śatṛ* is used after the root *dviṣ* when the sense is 'enemy' (*amitra*)."
*dviṣo'mitre* | The suffix *śatṛ* occurs after the root *dviṣ* when the agent is "not a friend" (*amitra*); this means it is used when the agent is an enemy.

(913) *suño yajñasaṃyoge* | 3.2.132 | After the root *sū* (in the sense of pressing) when connected with a sacrifice; the suffix *śatṛ* occurs after *sunoti* when it refers to a pressing connected with a sacrifice.

This is the meaning. The mention of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is for the purpose of including both the sacrificer and the owner; therefore, it does not apply to the officiating priests. In that context, the term *sunvan* (pressing [the Soma]), ending in the singular, refers to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and other such sacrifices, because they have a single performer.
However, the form ending in the plural number refers exclusively to the *sattra* sacrifice, because in that context even the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are considered sacrificers (*yajamāna*).
With this in mind, he says: "all [of them] are pressing the Soma" (*sarve sunvantaḥ*).
(Pāṇini 3.2.133) *Arhaḥ* is used in the sense of praise.

*Arhaḥ* is used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). *Arhaḥ* is the ablative case. The remainder [of the rule] is "the suffix *śatṛ*. Thus, *arhan* means "one who is worthy of receiving honor" (*pūjāṃ prāptuṃ yogyaḥ*). Here, because only that which is praiseworthy is worthy of honor, praise is understood.

(915) *ā kvestacchīlataddharmatatsādhukāriṣu* || 3.2.134 || [The word] *ā* [in the sūtra] is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Thus he says: "including the *kvip* suffix. This is based on the rule: *bhrājabhāsadhurvidyutorjipṛjugrāvastuvaḥ kvip*.

"Extending throughout the Sūtra" means as far as that point. In this regard, it is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhāḍhaḷsubhage* that suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*) generally do not occur after roots with prefixes (*sopasarga*). "Habitual" (*tacchīla*) means having that nature (*tatsvabhāva*).
That is to say, it refers to that which proceeds from its very nature without depending upon a result. He...

One who possesses a certain quality is "taddharmā" (possessed of that quality). One who proceeds [in life] thinking "this is my own duty" (*svadharma*) is the one who performs that duty well; he is the "tatsādhukārī" (one who does that well).
[The suffix] *tṛn* [is applied here according to Pāṇini 3.2.135].

The suffix *tṛn* is applied to the verbal root [to form a noun] when the agent possesses that habit and so forth. He gives an example for one who has that habit: *kartā kaṭam* ("one who makes a mat"). The meaning is "one whose habit is the act of making a mat. By the rule *na loke*, the use of the genitive case is prohibited; in the sūtra *na loke*, by the word *tṛn*, [the prohibition applies] to the present participle (*laṭ*).

This is because the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term) beginning with "śata" is employed here by means of the letter *ṇa* found in this very sūtra. An example of its application to that which possesses those properties (*taddharmiṇi*) is as follows: "The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas are *muṇḍayitāraḥ* (shavers) when they have taken a bride.
The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas are a specific class of people from a particular region; shaving the bride is their own established custom (*svadharma*).

The meaning is "those who perform [the action] accordingly. In the case of one who performs [an action] well (*sādhukārī*), the example is precisely "the agent of the mat" (*kartā kaṭam*). The meaning is "one who makes the mat well.

The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after the roots *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *dhū*, *sah*, and *car*. [Pāṇini 3.2.136] The suffix *dhañ* is applied after the root *alaṃkṛ*. [Roots: *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *dhū*, *sah*, *car*. [3.2.136] *alaṃkṛ-dhañ*. *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *dhū*, *sah*, *car*. *iṣṇuc*. [3.2.136] *alaṃkṛ-dhañ*. *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *dhū*, *sah*, *car*. *iṣṇuc*. [3.2.136] *alaṃkṛ-dhañ*. *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *dhū*, *sah*, *car*. *iṣṇuc*. [3.2.136] *alaṃk

From these twelve roots—*ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *sah*, and *car*—the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied when the agent possesses the qualities of habit (*tacchīla*), etc. Thus, for example: *nirākariṣṇuḥ*, *prajaniṣṇuḥ*, *utpaciṣṇuḥ*, *utpatiṣṇuḥ*, *unmadiṣṇuḥ*, *rociṣṇuḥ*.

*apatrapiṣṇuḥ*, *vartiṣṇuḥ*, *vardhiṣṇuḥ*, *sahiṣṇuḥ*, *cariṣṇuḥ*. (918) *ṇeśchandasī* | 3|2|137|. [The meaning of] *ṇeśchandasī* is that the suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after a verbal root ending in the causative marker *ṇi* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Example: *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*.

Thus, in the case of the root *pṛ* with the suffix *ṣṇuc* (as in *pārṣṇi*), the rule "the *ṇi* is elided" (*ṇer lopaḥ*) is superseded by the rule "the *ya* [is inserted] after a root ending in *a*, before *mant*, *ālu*, and *āyya*" (*yamantālvāyyet*). This sūtra is appropriately explained only within the context of Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*).

(919) *bhuvaśca* |3|2|138|. "And after the root *bhū*. It means that the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of "one who habitually does that" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, specifically in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). This rule is commenced for the sake of roots not ending in *aṇ*.

(920) *glājisthaśca* |3|2|139|. [The word] "nivṛttam" (excluded) [is understood]; this is the sense because of the [previous] explanation. By the word *ca* ("and"), the term *bhuvaḥ* (from √bhū) is drawn over from the previous rule. [The compound] *glājistha* is a *dvandva* (copulative compound), and the ablative case [ending] is used after it. [Thus, the roots are] *glā*, *ji*, *sthā*, and *bhū*.

The meaning is that the suffix *kṣnu* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of "having such a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. The letter *k* is for the sake of pronunciation (*itsaṃjñā*). Regarding the word *sthāsnu* in the rule *sthāsnu*, one might suspect that the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām iti* would apply because the suffix is *kit*; therefore, he says: "this [suffix] is *git*. The intention is that in the sūtra, the letter *k* is used as a representative marker (*cartva*) for *g*. Because it is *git*, there is no *guṇa* substitution, according to the rule *kkṅiti ca*.

The sense here is that in the word *cet*, the letter *ga* becomes *ca* by the rule of *cartva* (the substitution of *c* for *g*), and there is an insertion (*praśleṣa*) of another letter *ka*. Now, one might object:

in the word *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the augment *iṭ* would occur, because the prohibition of *iṭ* in the rule *r̥t-śyukaḥ kitī* applies only to a *kit* suffix, whereas this [suffix *nu*] is a *git* suffix. To this he says: "In the rule *r̥t-śyukaḥ*... [He adds: "...by way of insertion (*praśleṣāt*). [And he specifies: "...by way of *cartva*."

The suffix *knū* [is applied after the roots] *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip* [to form nouns denoting] a state (*bhāva*). (921) Pāṇini 3.2.140: *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ*. Regarding *trasigṛdh*: the phrase "when the agent possesses that habit, etc. (*tacchīlādiṣu kartṛṣu*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule]. Thus, *trasnuḥ* [is derived].
In *ṭhneḍvaśī*, there is no substitution of *iṭ*. In *gṛdhnuḥ* and *dhṛṣṇuḥ*, because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
(922) *śamiṣṭābhyo ghuṇ* |3|2|141|.
[The word] "eight" (*aṣṭā*) refers to the eight beginning with *śam*; the word "etc. (*ādi*) is a synonym for "beginning with. The roots *śam* and the others are situated in the *divādi* class.

The meaning is that the suffix *ghinuṇ* occurs after those eight [roots] in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. The designation *ghi* is for the purpose of the subsequent sūtra. The Bhāṣya states that *ghinuṇ* occurs only after roots that do not have an object (*akarmaka*). From the word *śamin*, in the feminine: *śaminitarā* or *śaminītarā*.

Regarding the suffix *ṅīp* ending in *nānta*, and *ṭāp* after *atarabanta*: there is an option for the short vowel. According to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, the short vowel occurs because of the presence of the *ugit* designation; however, according to the view of the *Kāśikā*, the short vowel does not occur due to the absence of the *ugit* designation. Nor should one suspect that in the absence of the short vowel, the rule "in the case of *tasil* and so forth" (*tasilādiṣu*) would cause the masculine form (*puṃvat*).

This is because of the prohibition [stated] in the rule *saṃjñāpūraṇyośca*. Now, one might raise the objection that if *ugitva* is accepted according to the method of the Bhāṣya, then in forms such as *śamī* and *śaminau*, the augment *num* would occur by the rule *ugidacām*; anticipating this, he refutes it with the words: "And even so, not [is there an error], for the mention of *jhal* is drawn back [into the previous rule]. This refers to the [rule] *napuṃsakasya...* [etc.].

The intention is that this follows from the subsequent rule, "jhalacaḥ. This is clear both in the commentary on the present rule and in the commentary on the rule "yuvoranākau. Anticipating the objection regarding the vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel when the suffix *ghinuṇ* is added after roots such as *śam*, he says: "not [after] an udātta [vowel]. [Examples include: *pramādī*. *Pramādī*.

Since it does not end in the suffix *mān*, there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi*. Now, one might ask: how can the suffix *ghinuṇ* be applied to form *unmādī* from the root *mad* preceded by the prefix *ut*, given that the rule *alaṅkṛñ-ādi-sūtra* specifically prescribes the suffix *iṣṇuc* for *mad* when preceded by *ut*?
To this, he says: "preceded by *ut*" and so forth. But how [is it] here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*)?

Since it might be argued that the application of the *vā'sarūpa* rule (the rule allowing alternative forms) does not apply to suffixes ending in *ghinuṇ*, because of the prohibition stating "there is no *vā'sarūpa* rule among those [suffixes] expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*"), he says: "among those expressing habitual action.
This *paribhāṣā* is indicated in the Bhāṣya by the forthcoming sūtra beginning with *nandigrahi...* and so forth.

This is clear. Regarding the term "generally" (*prāyikam*): this is evident from the inclusion of the root *dīp-* in the rule *sūdadīpadīkṣaśca*, as stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *jucaṅkramyadandramyasṛgṛdhijvalaśucalaṣapatapadām anupasarge*.

Pāṇini 3.2.142: *saṃpṛca-anurudha-āḍhya-māḍhya-parisṛ-saṃsṛja-paridevi-saṃjvara-parikṣipa-pariraṭa-parivada-paridaha-parimuha-duṣa-dviṣa-druha-duha-yuja-ākrīḍa-viviñci-tyaja-raja-bhaja-aticara-apacara-amuṣa-abhyāhana-śca*. [The suffix *khaś* is applied after the following verbal roots when used with the word *ātman* as an upapada: *saṃpṛc* (to touch), *anurudh* (to conform to), *āḍhya* (to become wealthy), *āḍyas* (to become wealthy), *parisṛ* (to move around), *saṃsṛj* (to join together), *paridevi* (to lament), *saṃjvara* (to burn with fever), *parikṣipa* (to throw around), *pariraṭ* (to cry out), *parivada* (to censure), *paridaha* (to burn), *parimuha* (to be bewildered), *duṣ* (to corrupt), *dviṣ* (to hate), *druh* (to injure), *duh* (to milk), *yuj* (to yoke), *ākrīḍ* (to play), *viviñci* (to separate), *tyaj* (to abandon), *raj* (to color), *bhaj* (to divide), *aticar* (to transgress), *apacar* (to go astray), *amuṣ* (to steal), and *abhyāhan* (to strike).

From this group of twenty-seven verbs—*duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *ākrīḍ*, *vivic*, *tyaj*, *rañj*, *bhaj*, *tīcar*, *apacar*, *āmṛś*, and *abhyāhan*—the ablative case is used after a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

Regarding the term *saṃparkī*: the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* (as per *ṭhcajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*) applies here. In forms such as *anurodhī*, there is the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel.

In the case of roots having *u* as their penultimate vowel (*upadha*), there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. [The example is] *paridevīti*. The root *divṛ* meaning "to play" belongs to the *bhvādi* class.

However, the form *dīvya-* is understood here as the causative (*ṇyanta*) root, because it is derived through a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇikatva*) and because of its association with non-causative roots.
[The example is] *abhyāghātī*. Here, the substitution of *t* for *h* occurs by the rule *hanasta'ciṇṇaloḥ*, and the change of *h* to *gh* occurs by the rule *ho hanteḥ*.
The substitution of *ku* [for *kva*].
(924) *vau kaṣalasakatthasrambhaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.143.
Regarding *vau kaṣalasa*: the ablative case ending is used here after the *dvandva* compound *kaṣa-lasa-kattha-srambhaḥ*. From these [roots]...
The suffix *ghinuṇ* occurs in the sense of habitual action (*syāt*) and so forth; this is the meaning. (925) *ape ca laṣaḥ*.

[Pāṇini 3.2.144] "And after the root *laṣ*, when *apa* is present. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that it also occurs when *vi* is present. Thus, the meaning is: even when *vi* is the governing prefix (*upapada*), as well as when *apa* or *vi* are the governing prefixes.
The meaning is "the suffix *ghinuṇ* after [roots] ending in *laṣ*. This applies only in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*) and so forth.
(926) *pre lapasṛdrumathavadavasaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.145.
Regarding *pre lapa*: *lap*, *sṛ*, *dru*, *matha*, *vada*, *vas*—of these six, the fifth case ending is used because they form a *dvandva* compound.
When these [roots] are preceded by a prefix (*upapada*), the suffix *ghinuṇ* shall be applied in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*) and so forth; that is the meaning.
(927) *nind*, *hiṃs*, *kliś*, *khād*, *vināś*, *parikṣip*, *pariraṭ*, *parivādi*, *vyābhāṣ*, *asūy*.

[The compound] *nindahiṃsa* is a *dvandva* of these ten: *ninda*, *hiṃsa*, *kliśa*, *khāda*, *vināśa*, *parikṣipa*, *pariraṭa*, *parivādi*, *vyābhāṣa*, and *asūya*. It is used in the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
"First": the intention is that the masculine gender and the singular number are used according to the Sūtra. "Vināśa-":

this is a reference to the causative form of the root *naś* preceded by the prefix *vi*, made by omitting the suffix *ṇic*. The vowel *a* after the letter *ś* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Some, however, read it as *vināśī*, retaining the causative suffix. "Parivādī-": [the same applies].
But [the suffix] is indeed applied to the causative (*ṇyanta*) form. Regarding "asūya"—it is a root belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* group ending in the *ya*-affix. Regarding "and so forth" (*ityādi*):

*kleśakaḥ*, *khādakaḥ*, *vināśakaḥ*, *parikṣepakaḥ*, *parirāṭakaḥ*, *parivādakaḥ*, *vyābhāṣakaḥ*, *asūyakaḥ*. Now, one might object: according to the rule *asūyo vuñ*, the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed specifically for the root *asūyati*.

Let *vuñ* be prescribed, and not even for [roots] such as *nind*, since those are already established by *ṇvul*. As for the accentuation of the *liṭ* suffix and the *niṭ* suffix, there is no difference, because in both cases the first syllable is udātta. However, in the case of *asūya* with *ṇvul*, by the rule "the *liṭ* suffix," the *u* preceding the affix is udātta; but with *vuñ*, however—
The specific distinction is that, by the rule *ṭhñnityādir nityam*, the vowel *a* of the verbal root is udātta.
Therefore, it is logical that the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed only after the root *asūyati*; to this, he says: "since [the form] is established by *ṇvul*. [He adds:
"there are no [suffixes] such as *tṛc*," because the rule of *vāsarūpa* applies to those [suffixes] denoting habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth.

Since the suffix *tṛn* would otherwise apply in that domain, the prescription of *vuñ* is meaningful; therefore, the rule regarding "non-identical forms" (*vāsarūpa*) does not operate in the case of those characterized by such habits and so forth—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, this [restriction] is generally applicable. Its result, however, is seen in the case of *madi* preceded by *ut*, where *iṣṇuc* is prescribed by the rule beginning with *alaṅkṛñ* etc., by means of the *vāsarūpa* rule.
The suffix *ghinuṇ* is also [applicable]; this was stated immediately after the root itself.
(928) *devi-kr̥śoś copasarge* (Pāṇini 3.2.147). [The forms] *devī* and *kr̥śī*: *devī* refers to the root ending in *ṇic* belonging to the *cur*-class, as well as to the root *div* meaning "to play."

The meaning is that when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied after the roots *devayati* and *kruś* to denote those who habitually perform such actions (*tacchīla*), and so forth.
(929) Pāṇini 3.2.148: After roots whose meanings involve movement or sound, provided they are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *yauc* is applied.
Regarding "calana-śabdana": the root *śabd* in the sense of "making sound" belongs to the *curādi* group.
"Making sound" (*śabdana*) means the utterance of a word. Because its own meaning is included within the verbal root itself, it is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
(930) [Pāṇini 3.2.149: "And [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] after a root beginning with a consonant that is marked with an *anudātta* accent."
Regarding the rule *anudātetaśca*: in the absence of the mention of "the beginning" (*ādi*), the meaning would be "from that which ends in a consonant" (*halanta*);

consequently, forms such as *jugupsanaḥ* would not be possible, because a root ending in a suffix (*sannanta*) does not end in a consonant. However, the quality of having an anudātta vowel does indeed belong to the root *gup* when it is alone.
Because there is no purpose [for the suffix], it has the meaning of a *saṇ*-derived form.
(931) *ju-caṅkramya-draṃsya-sṛ-gṛdhi-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ* | 3|2|150|.
*ju-caṅkramya*: *ju*, *caṅkramya*, *draṃsya*, *sṛ*, *gṛdhi*, *jvala*, *śuca*, *laṣa*.

The word *pata* [is used]; the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed here due to the *dvandva* compound of these ten [roots]. The meaning is that the suffix *yuc* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of "one who has that habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Since the root *juṅ* is not seen in the *dhātupāṭha*, he says "sautra" (belonging to the sūtras).
Regarding *caṅkramaṇa*: [it is formed] from the *yaṅ*-intensive of the root *kram* with the suffix *yuc*. By the rule "*yasya halaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.49), there is the elision of the *yakāra*; hence...

There is elision (*lopa*). In this manner, *dandramaṇaḥ*, *saraṇaḥ*, *garddhanaḥ*, *jvalanaḥ*, *śocanaḥ*, *laṣaṇaḥ*, *patanaḥ*, and *padanaḥ* are also to be cited as examples. "By the preceding [rule]" means by the rule *anudātetaśca halādeḥ*. "By that" [means] because this suffix *ukañ* falls under the governing heading of *tacchīla* (one who has that habit).

In that case, by the rule of *asarūpa* (non-identity of form) itself, there would be no sublation of the *yuc* suffix prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.148 (*ṭhanudātetaśca halādeḥ*) by the *ukañ* suffix; thus, the rule for *yuc* in 3.2.150 (*jucaṅkramya...*) would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, among those [suffixes] expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), they [mutually]—

The meaning is that it is understood that the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply here. In the sūtra *nindahiṃsa* (Pāṇini 3.2.146), it was indicated that suffixes such as *tṛc* do not apply by the rule of optional forms when [suffixes] expressing habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth are concerned. However, in this case, what is being indicated is that among those suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), there is no mutual application of the rule of optional forms; thus, there is no contradiction.
There is tautology [in the rule *tṛn*]. Regarding the word *tṛn*:

the suffix *iṣṇuc*, which is prescribed by rules such as *alaṃpūrvāt kṛñaḥ alaṃkṛñ* and which occurs within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for "one who is habitually so" (*tacchīla*), is superseded by *tṛn*, which is prescribed by a general rule (*sāmānyavihita*) and also occurs within the governing heading for "one who is habitually so."
This is the meaning.

(932) *krudhamaṇḍārthebhyaśca* | Pāṇini 3.2.151. [The suffix *khaś* is applied] after roots having the sense of *krudh* (to be angry) and *maṇḍ* (to adorn). [The root] *krudh* means "in anger," and *maḍi* means "in adorning"; [the suffix is applied] after roots having these senses.
The meaning is that the suffix *yuc* shall occur after verbal roots (*dhātu*) in the sense of "having such a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
(933) *na yaḥ* | 3|2|152|. [The word] *yaḥ* is a genitive singular form used as a qualifier for the root; it refers to that which ends in *ya*. Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "from those ending in the letter *ya*": [the forms] *knūyitā* and *kṣmāyitā*. [The roots] *ṭhknuyī* [meaning] "sound" and "moistening," and *ṭhkṣmāyī* [meaning] "shaking," have the suffix *yuc* prohibited by the rule *anudātetaśca halādeḥ*.
Thus, the suffix *tṛn* alone occurs.
(934) *sūdadīpakṣaśca* |3|2|153|. [The roots] *sūda*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ*: this is a compound in the ablative case. Regarding the word *yujña*:
this is a supplement to complete the sense. The suffix *yuc*, which would have been applicable by the rule *anudātetaśca*, is here prohibited.

But surely, the inclusion of *dīpa* here is redundant, because the suffix *ra*, being specifically prescribed by the rule "ṭhnamikampismyajasakamahiṃsadīporaḥ," necessarily sublates the suffix *yuc*. Nor should it be suspected that this sublation is prevented by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vā'sarūpa*), for the rule of non-identity of form is prohibited in the case of suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*). To this [the author replies]:

He says: "namikampīti. [The word] "reṇa" means by means of the suffix *ra*. [The word] "prāyikam" (common) implies that, since here it is possible for the suffix *yu* to be superseded even by the suffix *ra*—which expresses habitual action (*tācchīlika*)—according to the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the prohibition of *yu* after the root *dīp* is purposeful in this context. By that [is meant...]

The meaning is that even in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), there is sometimes the presence of the *vāsarūpa* rule [which allows for alternative forms]. "Kamnā" and "kamanā" mean "one whose nature is desire. Here too, the intention is that the suffix *yuc* is optionally barred by the suffix *ra* according to the rule *namikampi*.
He raises an objection with "yadi": if...

Regarding the rule "sūdadīpadīkṣaśca," the suffix *yuc* is prohibited after the root *sūd*; therefore, the connection [of the objection] is: "How then [can one explain] 'madhu-sūdana'? He provides the resolution: "It belongs to the *nandy-ādi* group. The word "sūdi" is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Thus, the intention is that the suffix *lyu* is applied according to the rule "nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ."

(935) Pā. 3.2.154: *laṣapatapadasthābhūvṛṣahanakamagamaśṛbhya ukañ*. After these ten roots—*laṣ*, *pat*, etc.—the suffix *ukañ* occurs in the senses of habitual disposition (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Regarding "and so forth": *pādukaḥ* (a shoe). [The suffix] *yuk* is applied after a root ending in long *ā*: *sthāyukaḥ* (one who stays), *bhāvukaḥ* (one who becomes), *varṣukaḥ* (one who rains), *ghātukaḥ* (one who kills).

In the case of *han*, there is the substitution of *t* [for *n*] by the rule *ṭhānastaḥ*. In the case of *han*, there is the substitution of *k* [for *n*] by the rule *ho hanteḥ*. Thus: *kāmukaḥ*, *gāmukaḥ*, *śārukaḥ*. (936) Pāṇini 3.2.155: *jalpabhikṣakuṭṭaluṇṭhavṛṅaḥ ṣākan*. The suffix *ṣākan* is applied after the verbal roots *jalp* (to chatter), *bhikṣ* (to beg), *kuṭṭ* (to crush), *luṇṭh* (to plunder), and *vṛ* (to choose). The marker *ṣ* indicates that the feminine form ends in *ī*, and the marker *k* causes the addition of the augment *ṭi*. Thus: *jalpākaḥ*, *bhikṣākaḥ*, *kuṭṭākaḥ*, *luṇṭhākaḥ*, *varākaḥ*. The suffix *ṣākan* is applied after these roots to denote an agent who habitually performs the action expressed by the root.

The suffix *ṣākan* occurs after these five [roots] beginning with *jalp*, in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Since *ṣ* and *n* are indicatory (*it*), the feminine form is made with *ṅīṣ* due to the presence of *ṣ*. Thus, we have *jalpākaḥ*, and so on.
(937) *prajoriniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.156).

*Prajoriṇaḥ*. *Ju* is a root belonging to the Sautra class. The meaning is that the suffix *ini* occurs after this root preceded by *pra* in the sense of "having such a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. The letter *n* and the vowel *i* are for the sake of pronunciation. (938) *Jidṛkṣiviśrīṇvamāvyathābhyamaparibhūprasūbhyaśca* | Pāṇini 3.2.157. [The suffix *ini* is added after the roots *ji*, *dṛkṣi*, *viśri*, *ṇu*, *mā*, *avyatha*, *abhi*, *paribhū*, and *prasū*.]

*jidṛkṣi*: a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of these ten roots: *ji*, *dṛ*, *kṣi*, *vi-śri*, *iṇ*, *vamu*, *avyatha*, *abhyama*, *pari-bhū*, and *pra-sū*. *ji* in the sense of victory; *ji* in the sense of overcoming; *dṛṅ* in the sense of respect; *kṣi* in the sense of destruction;
*kṣi* in the sense of dwelling and going; *śriñ* in the sense of service, preceded by the prefix *vi-*; *iṇ* in the sense of motion; *vamu*.

[The suffix *ini* is applied] after these: *ud-gir* (in the sense of vomiting); *vyath* (in the senses of fear and trembling)—preceded by the negative particle *nañ*; [here,] due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the *n* of *nañ* when it is compounded with a verbal root according to the rule "the *n* of *nañ* is elided"; *am* (in the senses of motion, etc.)—preceded by *abhi*; *bhū* (in the sense of existence)—preceded by *pari*; and *sū* (in the sense of impelling)—preceded by *pra*. After these, the suffix *ini* is applied.

The meaning is: [the suffix *cvi* is applied] after [roots denoting] that habit and so forth. However, because *sūti* and *sūyati* possess indicatory letters (*anubandha*), they are not included here.
(939) Pāṇini 3.2.158: *spṛhi-gṛhi-pati-dayi-nidrā-tandrā-śraddhābhya āluc*. [The suffix *āluc* is applied after these roots.]

From *spṛhi*, *gṛhi*, *pati*, *dayi*, *nidrā*, *tandrā*, and *śraddhā*, the suffix *āluc* occurs in the seventh case (locative), meaning "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Thus, *spṛhayāluḥ*: from the root *spṛh*, which ends in a short vowel, *āluc* is added. By the rule *ṭhayām ante*, the *ṇi* is replaced by *ay*; this is an exception to the elision of *ṇi*.

Due to the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elision (*allop*) of the *a*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Similarly, [we have] *gṛhayāluḥ*.
However, in *patayāluḥ*, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the *a*, there is no *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel.
Regarding *nidrāluḥ*: from the root *drā* in the sense of "censure" or "motion," preceded by the prefix *ni*, the suffix *āluc* is applied. That [suffix] is preceded by that [prefix].
Regarding "dreti": the meaning is that the root *drā* preceded by the word *tat* is understood here as *tandrā*.
Regarding "śraddhāluḥ": *śrat* is an indeclinable; the suffix *āluc* is added to the root preceded by that. Regarding "vācyaḥ śīṅaḥ": the remainder [of the rule] is "the suffix *āluc*."

(940) *dādheṭ-asi-śada-sado ruḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.159. The rule *dādheṭ* refers to the compound of the roots *dā*, *dheṭ*, *si*, *śad*, and *sad*; it is in the ablative case. The meaning is that the suffix *ru* is applied after these [roots] in the sense of "having such a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.

(941) *sṛghasyadaḥ kmarac* | 3.2.160. *sṛghasyadaḥ*: [This is] the ablative case from a *dvandva* compound of *sṛ*, *ghasi*, and *ad*. *Ghasi* is a distinct verbal root. (942) *bhañjabhāsamido ghurac* | 3.2.161.

*bhañjabhāsa*: This is the ablative case from the dvandva compound *bhañja*, *bhāsa*, *mid*. The meaning is that the suffix *ghurac* is added after these [roots] when expressing qualities such as habitual disposition (*tacchīla*). By the rule *ghacāvitau*, the *ghu* portion is elided. Thus, *bhaṅgura*. By the rule *ṭhcajo’r*, there is the substitution of *k* (resulting in *bhaṅgur*).

(943) *vidi-bhidi-chideḥ kuraC* | Pāṇini 3.2.162. Regarding *vidi*, *bhidi*, and *chidi*: [the suffix] *kuraC* is applied in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. They say that only the root *vid* meaning "to know" is taken here, and not the root *vid* meaning "to find," because of the [traditional] commentary. In forms such as *viduraḥ*, [the long vowel] does not occur because of the *kit* designation [of the suffix].
The *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel [occurs].

(944) *iṇ-naś-ji-sarti-bhyaḥ kvarap* | Pāṇini 3.2.163. From the roots *iṇ*, *naś*, *ji*, and *sṛ*, the suffix *kvarap* is applied; the meaning is that it is used in the sense of "one who habitually performs an action" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
The suffix *kit* does not cause *guṇa* substitution; however, its *pit* status is for the purpose of [accentuation]. (945) *gatvaraś ca* |3|2|164|.
Also *gatvara*. [The rule] "from the root *gam*" means: the suffix *kvarap* is added to the root *gam*, and the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
The meaning is as follows: because there is an absence of a suffix beginning with a *jhal* sound following it, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) does not apply.
[The suffix] *pit* is added by the rule *tuka*. In the word *gatvarī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. (946) *jāgurūkaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.2.165.

*Jāgurūkaḥ*. This is the fifth-case form of the root *jāgṛ*, namely *jāguri*. Thus he says: "of *jāgarti*. It applies only in the sense of "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. *Jāgarūkaḥ*: the *ṛ* vowel undergoes *guṇa*, and *ra* is substituted for the *ṛ*. However, the completed form was not explicitly stated [here] because the suffix *ūka* is taught in the subsequent rule.
Because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of non-application [of the rule].
(947) *yajajapadaśāṃ yaṅ* | Pāṇini 3.1.26. *yajajapadaśāṃ yaṅ*. This is a *dvandva* compound of these three: *yaja*, *japa*, and *daśa*. It is used in the sense of the ablative case.

The sixth [case ending]. He says this with the words "from these" (*ebhyaḥ*). It refers specifically to those characterized by that habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Now, one might ask: since the root *daṃś* has a nasal as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*), how can there be the form *daśām*? To this he replies: "by virtue of what is to come" (*bhāvinā*). This means that the reference here is to the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) which will occur once the suffix *ūka* has been applied.

In *yāyajūka*, there is the elision of *y* by the rule *yasya halaḥ*. Then, by the rules *ato lopaḥ* and *dīrgho’kitaḥ*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). In *jañjapūka*, there is the augment *nuk* added to the reduplicated syllable by the rule *japajabhadahadaśabhañjapaśāṃ ca*. Similarly, *dandaśūkaḥ*.

(948) *namikampismyajaskamahiṃsadīpo raḥ* | 3|2|167| The term *namikampismyajaskamahiṃsadīpaḥ* is a compound (dvandva) from which the ablative singular case ending is applied. From these seven roots, the suffix *ra* is added. [nami, kampi, smi, ajas, kam, hiṃs, dīp—after these, the suffix *ra* is applied.]
The meaning is "in the sense of having that as one's character" (*tacchīlādi*). Since the root *ajas* is not found in the Dhātupāṭha, he says:

"the root *jas* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. The meaning is that this root *jasu*, which [ordinarily] means "to release," functions—due to its inherent power (*śaktisvabhāvāt*)—when preceded by *nañ* in the sense of the continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*). Because of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), there is a compound of the negative particle with the verbal root.
There is elision of the *n* by the rule "ṭhnalopo nañaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.73). (949) "sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.168).
[The word] "sanāśaṃsa": this is the nominative singular of a *dvandva* compound consisting of the three words *san*, *āśaṃsa*, and *bhikṣ*.

The term *san* is taken here as that which ends in the suffix *san*. It does not include the roots *ṣaṇu* (to give) and *ṣaṇa* (to share), because there is evidence for this in the fact that the word *vijigīṣu* is not listed among the *gargādi* group. The meaning is that the suffix *u* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Regarding the form *āśaṃsuḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *śasu* with the prefix *āṅ*.
From the root *icch* [the suffix] *u* is added; (950) *vindur icchuḥ*. 3.2.169:
*vindur icchuḥ*. Regarding *veteḥ*: from the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (*vida jñāne*), the suffix *u* is added.

The augment *num* is added to the base. The meaning is that from the root *iṣ* (in the sense of "desiring"), when the suffix *u* is applied, the substitution of *ch* for the letter *ṣ* is prescribed by way of technical rule (*nipātana*).

"He desires" (*veti*) is an illustration of the verbal root. "One who has that as his nature" (*tacchīlaḥ*) means one whose nature is to know (*vedanaśīlaḥ*). "He desires" (*icchati*) is an illustration of the root *iṣ* (in the sense of "desiring").
The meaning is "one whose nature is seeking" (*eṣaṇaśīla*).

(951) *kyāc chandasi* |3|2|170|. Regarding *kyāc chandasi*: the meaning is that after a word ending in the suffix *kyap*, the suffix *u* may occur in the sense of "one who habitually does that" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, in Vedic literature (*chandasi*).

Regarding the word *sumnayu*: *sumnam* means happiness (*sukham*). In the sense of "one who desires that for oneself," the suffix *kyac* is added to the word *sumna*. Due to the prohibition in the rule *na ccchandasyaputrasya*, the substitution of *ī* by *kyaci ca* does not apply, nor does the lengthening [of the vowel] by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*. From the form *sumnaya*, which ends in *kyac*, the suffix *u* is added. Therefore...

Omission. (952) *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca* | Pāṇini 3.2.171. *ādṛgamahanajan-*: [This is] a compound (dvandva), followed by the ablative case, consisting of the roots *ā*, *ṛ*, *gam*, *han*, and *jan*. *Ki-kin*: [The suffixes] *ki* and *kin*.

This is a *dvandva* compound of these two. He explains [the rule] as "and *liṭ*"—that is, "those two are like *liṭ*. It applies only in the sense of "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. *Papiri*: from the root *pā*, there is the suffix *ki*; doubling and so forth, and the elision of *ā*. *Dadiḥ*: from the root *dā*, there is the suffix *ki*; doubling and so forth. *Babhriḥ vajram*: from the root *bhṛ*, there is the suffix *ki*.

*dvitvādi* (and so forth). *jaghniḥ*: [This is derived] from the root *han* with the suffix *ki*. *dvitvādi* (reduplication, etc.). By the rule *gamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule *ho hanteḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.54), there is the substitution of *k* for *h* (*kutva*). *jajñiḥ*: [This is derived] from the root *jan* with the suffix *ki*. *dvitvādi* (reduplication, etc.). It should be understood that the same applies when the suffix *kin* is used; however, there is a difference regarding the accent (*svara*). These two sūtras are also Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The phrase "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*) and so forth is introduced here for the purpose of explaining the subsequent *vārttika*.

Regarding "in the spoken language": this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that it should be stated that after these six roots—*dhāñ*, *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *gam*, *jan*, and *nam*—the suffixes *kikin* are applied, and that these two suffixes function like the *liṭ* (perfect tense) affixes.
Regarding "dadhi" and so forth: once the *kikin* suffixes have been applied, reduplication and other operations are to be understood as occurring according to their respective possibilities.
Regarding "nemi": from the root *nam*, the suffix *ki* is added; there is reduplication, and then the substitution of *e* for *a* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*).

Regarding "sāsahi": from the root *sah*, the *yaṅ* suffix is applied, followed by reduplication and so on; then, by the rule "the long vowel [is substituted] for a non-*kit* [root]," the vowel is lengthened, and finally the *kikin* suffixes are applied.

When the *yakāra* is elided by the rule "ṭhyasya halaḥ," the form "sāsahī" is established through the elision of the vowel *a*. Similarly, there are such indications for the forms derived from the roots *vah*, *cal*, and *pat* when they are in the *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅnta*) and the *kikin*-suffix (*kikinanta*). The meaning is that these must be added as specific grammatical exceptions (*nipātana*). Thus he says: "from the *yaṅ*-intensives of *sah* and so forth."
"Non-existence of *nīg*" means the absence of the augment *nīg* which would otherwise have been required by the rule "ṭhnīg vañcu-".

(953) *svapitṛṣornajiṅ* | 3|2|172|. [The suffix] *najiṅ* [is applied] after the roots *svap* and *tṛṣ*. The genitive case here has the sense of the ablative; [thus, the meaning is: *najiṅ* after *svap*.

The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs after the roots *chala* and others. The vowel *i* following *ja* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The letter *ṅ* indicates the *it* designation. Regarding *svapnaj*: the meaning is "one who has the habit of sleeping" (*svapanaśīla*). From *svapna-j*, we get *svapnajaḥ*. Similarly, *tṛṣṇak*:

the meaning is "one who has the habit of thirsting" (*tarṣaṇaśīla*). Regarding the rule "after the root *dhṛṣ*"—the remainder of the rule is "*nañi ṅit*" (after the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix is *ṅit*).
"In the *Kāśikā* and other [works]"—the sense is that this is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*. (954) *śṛvandyor āruḥ* | 3|2|173|.
*śṛvandyor āruḥ*: the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. [The roots] *śṛ* "to injure" and *vand*...

Regarding the rule for *abhivādana* and *stuti*: the suffix *āru* is applied after these two roots in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. (955) *bhiyaḥ kru-klukanau* | After the root *bhī*, the suffixes *kru* and *klukan* are applied in the sense of "having that as one's habit" and so forth. Because they are marked with *k* (kit), [the penultimate vowel is not lengthened].
The suffix *varaC* [is applied after the following roots]:

(956) *stheśabhāsapisakasaḥ* 3.2.175. [The roots] *sthā*, *īś*, *bhāsṛ*, *pisū*, and *pesṛ*: *sthā* (to stop, to stand), *īś* (to rule, to possess sovereignty), *bhāsṛ* (to shine), *pisū* and *pesṛ* (to go).

The suffix *varaC* is applied after the roots *gati*, *kasa*, and *gati* in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; however, the form *īśvarī* contains the suffix *ṅīṣ* because it denotes a female in connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). (Pāṇini 3.2.176) *ya* and *yaṅ*.

And as for *yaṅ*: the form *yā* is the imitation of the root *yā* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpaṇe*). The term *ṭhyaḥ* is the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) of *yā*. Thus he says: "of the root *yā*" (*yāteḥ*). [The suffix] *yaṅ* is added to the root *yā*; there is reduplication (*dvitva*), and so forth; by the rule "the long vowel for a non-*kit* [root]" (*dīrgho'kitaḥ*), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); thus [we have] *yāyāya*.

He states a specific exception regarding *yaṅ* and *ant*: "there is elision after *ataḥ*" (*ato lopaḥ*). Because there is no *hal* (consonant) following [the suffix], the elision of the *yakāra* does not occur by the rule "elision of that which follows a *hal*" (*yasya halaḥ*). When the form *yāyāy-vara-* is established, he says: "there is elision of the *yakāra* by the rule 'elision of *v* and *y*' (*lopo vyor*). Now, [one might object]: since the elision of *ataḥ* applies to an *ac* (vowel) [ending],...

One might ask: "Since the preceding [element] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original), there is an intervention by the root-form (*ākara*), and thus the condition of being followed by a light vowel (*valpara*) is absent; how then can there be the elision of *y* (*yalopa*)?

To this, he says: "Of that. The meaning is that when the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is to be performed, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is not subject to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānte*). And thus, [the elision applies] to the *akāra* of the *yaṅ*.

Regarding the elision of the letter *yakāra* in the word *yāyāvara*, having raised the objection that the elision of *ā* [as prescribed by] "ṭhāto lopa iṭi ca" might apply here, he refutes it with the words "allopasya.
This is done by relying on the status of *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of *yakāra* [of the *yaṅ* suffix] according to the rule "acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau."

The meaning is that since the long *ā* [of *ārdhadhātuka*] follows that which consists of the form *tad-ākāra*, the elision of *ā* by the rule "the elision of *ā* occurs before an *it*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*) would apply; therefore, the following solution is stated.
He states the solution itself: "that which is elided by *vṛddhi* is not like the original" (*vare luptaṃ na sthānivat*). Here, "elided" (*luptam*) is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

Regarding the suffix *kta*: by the phrase "in a *vara* [suffix]" within the rule *na padānte*, it is understood that what is prescribed when a *vara* follows is not *sthānivadbhūta*. This elision of *a* (*allopa*) is prescribed when a *vara* beginning with an *ārddhadhātuka* affix follows;

therefore, because it lacks the status of being *sthānivadbhūta*, the elision of the *ā* of the *yaṅ* [intensive] does not depend upon the *ā* [of the root], as in the case of the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*.

The meaning is that this [substitution] occurs when there is the occurrence (*pravṛtti*) of the word *cet*. Thus, it should be understood that for both the portion "in a vowel" (*vare*) and the portion "when there is elision of *y* or *l*" (*yalope*) in the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānte*), the example is *yāyāvara*.

(958) *bhrājabhāsaradhurvidyautorjipṛjugrāvastuvaḥ kvip* 3.2.177. From the eight roots *bhrāj*, *bhās*, *dhurv*, *dyut*, *ūrj*, *pṛ*, *ju*, and *grāvastu*, the suffix *kvip* is applied when the agent possesses the sense of habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Thus, *vibhrāṭ*.
In *bhās*, by the rule *ṭhvraśca*, the *s* becomes *ṣ*. Thus, from the root *bhās* with the suffix *kvip*, there is the substitution of *ru* for the final *s*, followed by the visarga.

In *dhūḥ*, from the root *dhurvī* with the suffix *kvip*, there is the elision of *v* by the rule *ṭhrāllopaḥ*. The form ends in *r* as *dhuḥ*. There is the elision of the case-ending *su*, and lengthening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *ṭhvorupadhāyāḥ*.

Regarding *pūri*: from the root *pṛ*, there is the suffix *kvip*. By the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, *u* is substituted [for the radical vowel], and *ra* is the substitute for that [vowel]. Thus, *pu* ends in *r*. Upon the elision of the case-ending *su*, the rule *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (or as interpreted here by *vo*) effects the lengthening. To establish the lengthening for the root *ju* with the suffix *kvip*, he says: "because the mention of *dṛśi* is also drawn down [from the previous rule]," meaning from the subsequent sūtra.

Regarding the sense [of the term]: here, the commentary itself is the refuge. Now, one might ask: how can there be a compound designation as "grāvastu," given that a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), namely *grāvan*, cannot form a compound with a verbal root (*dhātu*)?
To this he says: "of the word *grāvan*. Thus, *grāvastut*. [The suffix] *tṛc* is *pit*.

(959) *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* | 3|2|178|. "From others as well. [The word] *kvip* is supplied to complete the sense. This means "from others as well" in comparison with those [roots] mentioned in the rule beginning with *bhrājabhās-* and so forth.

The meaning is that the suffix *kvip* is seen after verbal roots when they function as agents in the sense of "having that habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in another rule" (*vidhyantareti*):
a "rule" (*vidhi*) is so called because it is prescribed (*vidhīyate*), that is, an operation (*kārya*). The meaning is that it is for the purpose of including other operations.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "sometimes long," and so on, by means of the rule beginning with *kakvibvacī*.

The meaning is that this is according to the *Uṇādi* sūtra: "In the case of the roots *sthā*, *kvip*, *vac*, *pracch*, *ay*, *yat*, *stu*, *kaṭapru*, *ju*, and *śrī*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] and no *saṃprasāraṇa*. This is so that it may not be superseded by the suffix *tṛn*.

The intention is that the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply to suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*). Regarding the word *vāk*: [it is derived] from the root *vac*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied; by virtue of the explicit statement [in the rule], there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), and by the rule "vacisvapi-", there is an absence of *saṃprasāraṇa*.

Similarly, in the word *kaṭaprūḥ*, there is lengthening. Regarding *prāṅ*: due to the explicit statement, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*. Regarding "it was stated in the case of *jūḥ*": the remainder of the phrase is "in the rule *bhrājabhās-*". Therefore, in this instance, that [rule] is not taken because it is not present.
The state [of being]. Regarding "śrī": there is lengthening when the suffix *kvip* follows the root *śri*. Regarding "dyauti":
the meaning is that it should be stated that for roots such as *dyaut*, *gam*, and *juhoti*, there is reduplication when *kvip* follows.
According to the rule "the preceding [portion] is the reduplicated syllable" (*pūrvo'bhyāsaḥ*), this applies only to the reduplication taught in the sixth book (*ṣāṣṭha-dvirvacana*).

Because the designation "abhyāsa" (reduplication) is stated for the preceding section, he says: "because of the inclusion of the term *dṛśi*. This means [the rule] "it is also seen after other [roots]" (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*). The sense is that, consequently, the operations pertaining to reduplication—such as the elision of the penultimate vowel (*hal-adi-śeṣa*) and so forth—apply here.

*Didyaud*: [This is derived from the root] *dyauti*; the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "of *dyauti*, *svāpi*, etc. (*dyautisvāpyoḥ*). *Jagat*: [This is derived] from the root *gam-* with the suffix *kvip*.

"ṭh-gamaḥ kvau": here, after the elision of *i*, there is the augment *tuk*. "juhoter-dīrghaś-ca": this is a Vārttika; and because of the word "ca," there is also *kvip* and reduplication. "hrasvaś-ca": this is a Vārttika; [and] when the short vowel is applied, there is *tuk*. "dhyāyate": this is a Vārttika; and because of the word "ca," there is *kvip*.

Regarding the word *dhī*: the sense is that from the root *dhyai*, with the suffix *kvanip*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution), followed by the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) sandhi, and then the lengthening [of the vowel] according to the rule *halaḥ*. On this point, some say that this Vārttika need not exist, because it is already taught in the *Uṇādi-sūtras* under the rule "from *dhyai*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa*. However, in reality, the *Uṇādi-sūtras* are not the work of Pāṇini.
However, since it will be stated that [these mantras] were composed by other sages (*ṛṣi*), there is no suspicion of them being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).

(960) *bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarayor* |3|2|179|. [The rule] "after the root *bhū*, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] when a name (*saṃjñā*) or another [meaning] is to be expressed. *ānañja*, *āñktām*, *āñjan*, *añjyāt*, *ajyāt*.

Regarding *añjeḥ sici*: from the rule *ṭhiḍatyartī* [6.1.58], the word *iṭ* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Because it is marked with the *ū*-diacritic (*ūdit*), it is already included by [the rule] *ūditavādeḥ* [1.2.2].

This [rule] is for the sake of establishing the permanence [of the form]. Thus he says, beginning with "añjeḥ" and so forth. The root *tañcū* means "contraction. It has a nasal (*n*) as its penultimate letter; the mention of the parasavarṇa [nasal] is made because it has already been applied. The forms of *añjū* are to be inferred accordingly. Regarding "o vijī": the vowel *o* is the *it* (indicatory letter). Among the roots that do not take the augment *iṭ*, those having *iṛ* as their *it*...
This [section] beginning with *grahaṇa* is marked with *seṭ*. [Now] the *rudh*-class verbs.
Thus ends the *rudh*-class verbs in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*).

(926) *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmā'nakṣe* | Pāṇini 5.4.74. [The suffix *aC* is applied after the words *ṛc*, *pura*, *abdhi*, *dhur*, and *pathin* when they form a compound, provided that the word *akṣa* does not follow.]
Now, the suffixes that do not form part of a compound (asamāsānta), which are common to all compounds, are being examined—beginning with *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*.

Regarding the word *cheda*, the sense is that in the sūtra the term *ṭ* is indicated in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), though its case-ending has been elided. The governing rule *samāsāntāḥ* ("compound-final suffixes") is in force. The compound is qualified by the words beginning with *ṛc*; thus, there is an application of the rule regarding what ends in those [stems] (*tadantavidhiḥ*).
Regarding this, he says: "ending in *ṛc*, etc. This means ending in *ṛk*, *pur*, *ap*, *dhur*, or *pathin*. "The suffix *a*" means a suffix consisting of the vowel *a*.
"The yoke (*dhur*) on the axle" means the yoke connected to the axle. [This is] in the Sūtra.

The locative case in *anakṣe* is used because the relatives (*saṃbandhin*) are intended to be the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The meaning is that the word *anakṣe* is connected only with the word *dhur*, as it is impossible for it to be connected with others. Regarding *ardharca*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "half of a verse" (*ṛco 'rdham*). The compound is formed according to the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*. [The final] vowel is *a*.

This is a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). By the rule *ṭhardharcāḥ puṃsi ca*, it takes the masculine gender. Regarding the terms *anṛca* and *bahvṛca*, they apply only when referring to the person who studies them. The analysis (*vigraha*) for *anṛca* is "one for whom Ṛg-verses do not exist.
For *bahvṛca*, the analysis is "one for whom there are many Ṛg-verses"—an example being a follower of the Ṛgveda branch (*ṛkchākhin*).
He states the purpose of the restrictive rule "only in the meditator" with the words "not here. Regarding "without *ṛc* and *sāman*":
the analysis of the compound is "that in which *ṛcs* do not exist. The *Hṛdaya-sāman* of Prajāpati is that which has no *ṛc* superimposed upon it.
Regarding "the *Sūkta* of the Bahvṛcas": the analysis of the compound is "that in which many *ṛcs* exist. Now...

He provides an example for a compound ending with the word *pur* (city): "of Viṣṇu... [Viṣṇupuram]. Now, one might object that since the word *pur* is feminine, it would be appropriate for the compound *viṣṇupura* to be feminine according to the rule *paravalliṅgam* (the gender of the last member prevails).
To this he replies: "The neuter gender [is established] from common usage (*lokāt*). Next, he provides an example for a compound ending with the word *ap* (water): *vimalāpam*.
Regarding "saras": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that in which the waters (*āpas*) are pure (*vimalā*). [Pāṇini 5.4.74] states: *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt*.
[The rule] *dvyantarupa...* refers to that which has received the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). This means it refers to that which ends in the suffix *a* [specifically *ap*]. From these...

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: "after these two, namely the prefixes. Regarding *apasya*: the meaning is "of the word *ap*, which ends in the suffix *a*. Regarding *ītsyāt*: by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which follows [an element] replaces its first letter," the meaning is "of the initial vowel *a*. Regarding *dvayorgatāḥ*: [the meaning is] "gone into two."

The analysis of *pārīpam* is "water (*āpaḥ*) which has gone (*gatāḥ*) to the opposite shore (*pāra-*)"; it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). [The suffix] *a* is applied, followed by the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel, and then the lengthening by homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). Thus, *antarīpam*. The analysis of *antarīpam* is "water (*āpaḥ*) which has entered within (*antargatāḥ*)"; [the suffix] *a* is applied, followed by the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel, and then the lengthening by homogeneous vowels. Thus, *antarīpam*. [The term] *pratīpam* means "water (*āpaḥ*) that is turned back (*pratikūlāḥ*)."
The analysis of the compound is *yasmin* ("in which"). Because it follows a prefix (*upasarga*), the vowel *i* is substituted [for *ya*]. Regarding *samīpam*:

the analysis is *saṅgatā āpo yasmin* ("that in which waters have come together"). This is another example following a prefix. An example is *samāpo devayajanam* ("the sacrificial ground where the waters are gathered").

This is a Vedic citation (*śruti*). The point here is that because it does not follow an *upasarga* (prefix), the substitution of *ī* does not occur. That in which the gods are worshipped is called *devayajana*, meaning a sacrificial ground. The masculine gender in the term *samāpaḥ* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). In the Bhāṣya, however, after stating that the substitution of *ī* does not occur for *samāpa*, it says "the place named *samāpa*."

It is declared as *devayajana*. In that context, the word *samāpa* is intended to denote a specific type of sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), because of the rule "in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*) and abundance (*samṛddhi*)" and because of the example given as "proximity" (*samīpa*) in the Bhāṣya. Regarding *sva*: the analysis of the compound is "that which has beautiful waters" (*śobhanā āpo yasya*). Not...

In *pūjanāt*, there is a prohibition against applying a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). Because the compound-final suffix has not been applied, the substitution of *ī* does not occur. [The form] *svapī* is the nominative dual. Regarding [the rule] "after a prefix ending in *a*, optionally": the meaning is that the substitution of *ī* for *āp* following a prefix ending in *a* should be stated as optional. *Prepam*.

"Prāpam": the analysis of the compound is *yasya prāgatā āpaḥ* ("that from which water has gone forth"). "Parepam" or "parāpam": the analysis of the compound is *yasya parāgatā āpaḥ* ("that from which water has departed").
(928) *ūdanordeśe* (Pāṇini 6.3.98).

Regarding the term *ūdano deśe*: this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ī*. It should be understood that [the substitution] of *ū* occurs according to the rule *sthādiḥ parasya*. The analysis of *anūpo deśaḥ* is "a region in which the waters are favorable" (*anukūlā āpo yasmin*).

The suffix *ap* is applied, followed by the substitution of *ū* and the long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrgha*). In the form *anūpa*, the word *ūpa* is used for the sake of ease in recitation (*avagrahaṇa*).

The *Bhāṣya* states that there is a long pronunciation [of the vowel]. However, the *Bahvṛcas* do not pause (*avagraha*) in the case of "gomān" in the word *gomān ṛk*. Thus, the word *ap* found in the rule *ṛkpūḥ* has been explained in detail. Now, he gives an example for a word ending in *dhū*: *rājadhurā*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the burden (*dhūḥ*) of the king (*rājñaḥ*)."

In this context, the word *dhūḥ* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean "kingdom. The suffix *-a* is applied; by the rule *ṭhparavalliṅgam*, it takes the feminine gender, and the suffix *ṭāp* is added. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of *akṣa*": the suffix *-a* is not applied after that which ends in *dhūḥ* when it is related to *akṣa*. Thus, one says *akṣadhūḥ*. *Akṣa* is the name [of a particular type of dice].
It is a specific part of the chariot’s pole (*daṇḍa*), the tip of that axle (*akṣa*) to which the two wheels are attached; this is the *dhūḥ*.

By this [rule], it is indicated that in the case of a compound meaning "axle" (*akṣe samāsārthe*), there would otherwise be no prohibition against the suffix *-a* being applied to *dhur* (as in *dhura*). Thus, we have *dṛḍhadhūr akṣaḥ*, meaning "an axle with a firm *dhūḥ*"—that is, one for whom the *dhūḥ* is firm.

[This is] the analysis of the compound. By this, it is indicated that in the previous explanation—where it was stated that the suffix *a* does not apply to the word *dhur* when it is the first member of a compound—the present prohibition would not have applied. Thus, the word *dhur* has been explained in detail under the rule *ṛkpūḥpathyapo't* [Pāṇini 5.4.74]. Now, he provides an example for the word *pathin*: "sakhipathau" (friend-path).
