It occurs as follows: since it will be stated later that a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises only from a fully established form by the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*, even when the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* has taken place, the word *samānatīrtha* exists either by the maxim of partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) or by recourse to its former state. Therefore, there is the condition of being followed by the suffix *yu*.

To explain how the word *samāna* functions, he says: "in the intended sense. Regarding the term *satīrthya*: it means one who dwells at the same *tīrtha*. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*). The word *samāna* is a synonym for "one" (*eka*).
The word *tīrtha* refers to a teacher; thus he says: "having the same teacher. This is the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
He shows the application of *taddhita* suffixes following compound formation—namely, "samāna-etc. [Pāṇini 4.1.114].
Amara states: "The word *tīrtha* refers to a drinking place (*nipāna*), a sacred bathing place (*āgama*), water resorted to by sages (*ṛṣijuṣṭajala*), and a teacher (*guru*).
(1000) *vibhāṣodare* [Pāṇini 6.3.88].

*Vibhāṣodare*: The meaning is that when the word *udara* follows, the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* may optionally take place. *Iti eva*: The meaning is that [the previous rule] indeed continues to apply. (1001) *Dṛg-dṛś-vatuṣu* 6.3.89.
In the case of *dṛk*, *dṛś*, and *vatu*: the rule "of *samāna*, [substitute] *sa*" is understood as a supplement. Thus, *sadṛk* and *sadṛśa*.
In the sense of "that which is seen as equal," the suffixes *kvip* and *kañ* are applied to the root *dṛś* by the rule "after *samāna* and others also.
It should be stated that this also applies to *dṛkṣa*.
Regarding the word *dṛkṣa*: the phrase "the substitution of *sat* for *samāna*" (*samānasya sattvam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding *sadṛkṣa*:

the suffix *ksa* is also applied after the root *dṛś*. Regarding the statement "the suffix *vatu* is for the sake of what follows": the intention is that since the suffix *vatup* occurs after the pronouns *yad*, *etad*, and so on when expressing measure, it cannot occur after the word *samāna*.
(1002) *idaṃkimorīśkī* | 6|3|90 | The words *īś* and *kī* are two separate items [in the sūtra]. [The forms] *īdṛk* and *īdṛśa* [are derived as follows]:

in the sense of "that which is seen as this" (*idam iva dṛśyate*), the suffixes *kvip* and *kañ* are applied to the root *dṛś* when preceded by the pronouns beginning with *tyad*. [In the case of *īś*,] the *ś* is for the sake of causing the substitution of *yaṇ* [for the preceding vowel].
"For the sake of [establishing] a universal injunction. "It will be stated" means that in the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the example *iyān* will be stated.
And [the rule applies] before *dṛkṣa*.
Regarding the phrase "dṛkṣe ca": the supplement [to the rule] is "īś and kī are to be stated after *idam* and *kim*. Regarding "ā sarvanāmnaḥ":

the word "ā" is in the nominative case, though its case-ending has been elided. In the forms *tādṛk* and *tādṛśa*, the suffixes *kvip* and *kañ* are applied by the rule "tyadādiṣu dṛśaḥ" in the sense of "that which is seen as such. Then, when the *da* of *tad* is changed to *ā*, there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowel lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*).
Regarding "tāvān": in the analysis of the compound *tat-parimāṇam asya* ("that much is its measure"), the suffix *vatup* is applied according to the rule *yatadetebhyaḥ*.

Regarding *tādṛkṣa*: the analysis is *tad iva dṛśyate* ("it is seen like that"). He shows the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) for *amūdṛg*—namely, that it involves a long vowel: once the substitution of *ātva* (the replacement of *adas* with *ā*) has been made, there is a *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality); from that, the substitutions of *ūtva* and *atva* [follow].

This is the meaning. Even in the explanation "ṭhaḥ se" (Pāṇini 6.1.79), since the letter *a* includes the letter *ā*, there is the substitution of *u* and *m*. (1003) *samāse 'ṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.80).
In a compound, there is the substitution of *saṅga* for *aṅguli*. (1004) [The word] *sthāna* follows *bhīru*. 8.3.81: *bhīroḥ sthānam*. [The word] *sthāna* follows *bhīru*.

(1005) *jyotirāyuṣaḥ stomaḥ* |8|3|83|. Regarding the rule *jyotirāyuṣaḥ stomaḥ*: within this set of three sūtras (*trisūtrī*), by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), [the suffix *ṭac*] is applied to those two [words, *jyotis* and *āyus*,] in the sense of "contact of a finger" (*aṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ*), "standing place of a coward" (*bhīroḥ sthānam*), "a hymn of light" (*jyotiṣaḥ stomaḥ*), "a hymn of life" (*āyuṣaḥ stomaḥ*), and so forth.
The meaning is that when there is a compound of two words (*padayoḥ*), the *s* belonging to the final member (*uttarapada*) becomes *ṣ*.

Making this clear, he provides a counter-example: "the contact of a finger" (*aṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ*), and so forth. Here, the rule *ṭiṇkoḥ* does not apply, according to the [authoritative] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

(1006) *suṣāmādiṣu ca* | 8|3|98| [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] also in the case of *suṣāmā* and others. This is clear. (1007) *eti saṃjñāyām agāt* | 8|3|99| [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] before the word *eti*, when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*), provided that the word *agāt* does not precede it.
This [rule] has proceeded from the section on *saṃjñā*. The meaning is that when the vowel *e* follows, *s* should become *ṣ*.
(1008) *nakṣatrādvā* | 8|3|100|. From *nakṣatra*, optionally. This is clear.

(1009) *aṣaṣṭhaḷtṛtīyāsthasyānyasya dugāśīrāśāsthāsthitotsukotikārakarāgaccheṣu* || 6|3|99 || [The word] "not standing in the sixth or third case" (*aṣaṣṭhaḷtṛtīyāsthasya*): it means that which stands when followed by [words] other than the sixth or third case endings.
"Not standing in the sixth or third case" means "of that which does not end in the sixth or third case.
Although the rule would have been established by using only the expression "not standing in the sixth or third case," the inclusion of two negative particles (*nañ*) is for the sake of clarity.
Regarding the phrase "in *āśis* and so forth": *āśis*, *āśā*, *āsthā*, *āsthita*, *utsuka*, *ūti*, *kāraka*.

The meaning is: in these cases, such as *rāga* and *ccha*. In the word *duk*, the letter *k* is for the sake of the *kit* designation; the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Because it is marked with *kit*, it is an internal constituent (*antāvayava*). Other examples such as *āśīḥ* are *karmadhāraya* compounds. "This is not a prohibition" means that the prohibition [stated] in the rule *ṭhaṣaṣṭhyatṛtīyāsthasya* does not apply to the suffixes *ka* and *cha* when they function as *kāraka*s (grammatical relations).
This is stated in the Bhāṣya: (1010) *arthe vibhāṣā* | 6|3|100|.
Regarding *arthe vibhāṣā*, the remainder [of the rule] is *anyasya dug*.

(1011) *koḥ kat tatpuruṣe 'ci* | 6|3|101|. The word *kaḥ* is replaced by *kat* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound when followed by a vowel-initial (*ac*) final member. The analysis of the rule is *kaḥ kat*. He explains the sūtra by supplying the remaining words: "when a vowel-initial (*aj-ādi*) final member follows. Examples are *kadaśvaḥ* ("bad horse") and *kadannam* ("bad food"). This is governed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* [Pāṇini 2.2.18].

The compound is *kūṣṭro rājā*. Because it is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one whose camel (*uṣṭra*) is contemptible (*kutsita*)," the substitution of *ka-* does not occur. [This applies] also in the case of the suffix *trau*.
"And before *tri*": the meaning is that the substitution of *kad* should be stated when the word *tri* follows.
This statement is necessary because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) does not begin with a vowel (*aj*).
(1012) *Rathavadyośca*: [The substitution of *kad* occurs] also before *ratha* and *vadya*.

And [the substitution of *ka* for *ku* occurs] before *ratha* and *vada*. The remainder [of the rule] is "ṭhkoḥ kat tatpuruṣe" (Pāṇini 7.3.52). Examples: *kadrathaḥ*, *kadvadaḥ*. The compound is formed by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18). [The word] *vadaḥ* means "one who speaks. A contemptible speaker is *kadvadaḥ*. (1013) And [the substitution of *ka* for *ku* occurs] before *tṛṇa* when it denotes a genus (*jāti*). 6.3.103.

And [the substitution occurs] in the word *tṛṇa* when it denotes a genus (*jāti*). When the word *tṛṇa* expresses a genus, the substitute *kat* is applied to the word *ku*. Thus, we have *katṛṇam*. This refers to a specific species of grass. As Amarasimha states: "Ṭhastrī, kuśa, kutha, darbha, pavitra, and also katṛṇa."

(1014) *kā pathyakṣayoḥ* | 6|3|104| The meaning is that when *pathin* and *akṣa* follow, the substitute *kā* occurs in place of *ku*. For example, *kāpatham*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "a contemptible path" (*kutsitaḥ panthā*).
The compound *kugati* is a [tatpuruṣa] compound. The suffix *ap* is applied by the rule *ṛkpū-*;
its neuter gender is established by the rule *pathaḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ*. However, in the reading *kāpatha*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
He demonstrates the formation of the compound with the word *akṣa*: "it is a *tatpuruṣa* with the word *akṣa*."
The meaning is that in the analysis (vigraha) "a contemptible sense-organ" (*kutsitam akṣam indriyam*), there is a compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

Regarding the word "eye" (*akṣi*): the meaning is that in the analysis "one whose eyes are contemptible" (*kutsite akṣiṇī yasya*), the suffix *ṣac* is applied according to the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ ṣac*.

(1015) *īṣadarthe* |6|3|105|. The meaning is that when *ku-* occurs in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), it undergoes the substitution *kā*. For example, *kājalam*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "slight water" (*īṣaj-jalam*), there is a compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

Because this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), the analysis using separate words (*asvapadavigraha*) is not shown. Regarding the form *kāmla* ("badly sour"), one might suspect that the substitution of *kat* for *ku*—by the rule *ṭhkoḥ kat-tatpuruṣe’ci*—would apply; therefore, he says: "even when [the following word] begins with a vowel. (Pāṇini 6.3.106) *vibhāṣā tatpuruṣe*.

The term *vibhāṣā* applies to the word *puruṣa*. The remainder [of the rule] is that there is the substitution of *kā* for *ṭhak*. One might object: "Is this not an optional rule where no [substitution] was previously established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*)? For when *ku-* has the sense of 'slight' (*īṣadartha*), the substitution of *kā* is obligatory by the rule *īṣadarthe*; how then is an option possible? To this he says: "For in the sense of 'slight' (*īṣadarthe*)," etc. This was stated in accordance with the *Vṛtti*.
Because a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) has not been stated in the Bhāṣya.

(1017) *kavaṃ coṣṇe* | 6|3|107|. "And *kavam*, and *kā*, [are used] in the sense of 'hot'. The intention is that this is because the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
In the absence of both [suffixes], the substitute *kad* occurs; thus there are three forms. As it has been said: *koṣṇam*, *kavoṣṇam*, and *kaduṣṇam*.
(1018) *Pṛṣodarādīni yathopadiṣṭam* (6.3.109).

Regarding the term *pṛṣodarādīni*: the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) here does not signify "starting with," because the reading of *pṛṣodarādi* as a formal list (*gaṇa*) is not observed in the grammatical tradition, and because the phrase "as taught" (*yathopadiṣṭa*) would otherwise be redundant. Rather, it signifies a "manner" or "type. Thus he says: "those of the type of *pṛṣodara*. "Type" (*prakāra*) means similarity; and that—

It should be understood as being free from omissions, additions, substitutions, and so forth as prescribed by the grammatical treatises; that is to say, those not sanctioned by the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). The root *diś* preceded by the prefix *upa* has the sense of "pronunciation. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, *upadiṣṭam* (the taught) is *upadeśaḥ*—namely, pronunciation.
"Not transgressing that" means according to what has been taught. An *avyayībhāva* compound occurs when there is no deviation from the meaning of the constituent words.
The word "by the learned" (*śiṣṭaiḥ*) is to be supplied [as the agent]. Thus, he states the resulting conclusion: "as they have been uttered by the learned. As for the learned:

"Yogins are those who have direct realization of the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*)," as is clear from both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa. Regarding "the elision of *t*" (*talopa*): the intention is that when there is a *ṣaṣṭhī*-compound, after the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) and the elision of *t*, the rule "ṭhād guṇaḥ" applies.
Regarding "of the prior member" (*pūrvapadasya*): in the word "vārivāhaka," it refers to the prior member, the word *vāri*.
The letter *ba* is a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). The meaning is that when the word *vāhaka* is the final member of a compound, the letter *va* at its beginning is replaced by the letter *la*.
(1) Through the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*), "haṃsa" becomes "siṃha"; through the transposition of a phoneme (*varṇaviparyaya*), "gūḍhotmā" [becomes "gūḍhātman"].

Due to the modification of a phoneme (*varṇavikṛti*) or the disappearance of a phoneme (*varṇanāśa*), there is the word *pṛṣodara*. Due to the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*), there is the word *haṃsa*. This means that from the root *has* with the suffix *ac* (as in the *pac-ādi* group), by the addition of an *anusvāra*, the form *ṭhhaṃsa* arises. [Similarly], from the root *han* with the suffix *ac*, by the addition of *sag*...

Others say that there is an *anusvāra* by the rule "ṭhnaścā'padāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.24). Regarding the word *siṃha*, it is said to arise from a reversal of phonemes (*varṇaviparyaya*). From the root *hiṃs* (meaning "to injure") with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), the augment *num* is added because it is marked with the *it*-letter; then, by the rule "ṭhnaśca," an *anusvāra* is added.
The substitution of *s* for *h* and *h* for *s* results in the form *siṃha*. This is the meaning. Although...

Although the derivation of words such as *haṃsa* and *siṃha* has already been stated in the *Uṇādi* [section], they say that there is no fault in providing the derivation here, because since the *Uṇādi-sūtras* were composed by Śākaṭāyana, they constitute a separate treatise. Regarding the phrase "the hidden self (*gūḍhātman*) due to the modification of phonemes": it means one whose self (*ātman*) is hidden (*gūḍha*).

The meaning is that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the initial vowel *ā* of the final member is changed to *u*, the form [is established] by the rule of *ād-guṇa*. Regarding *pṛṣodara*: it means that when the letter *t* is elided in the sequence *pṛṣat-udara*, the form *pṛṣodara* arises through the application of *ād-guṇa*.
From words denoting directions, the substitution of *tāra-* for *tīra-* may optionally occur.
This is a Vārttika stating: "from words denoting directions, [the substitution of] *tīra-*. Also:

after the prefix *dur-*, before the roots *dāś*, *nāś*, *dabh*, and *dhya*, there is the substitution of *u* for the final vowel, and the initial letter of the following word undergoes the change to a retroflex (*ṣṭutva*)."

"duro dāśeti" (Pāṇini 6.3.109). This is also a Vārttika. Its meaning is that when the words *dāś*, *nāś*, *dabha*, or *dhya* follow, the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the word *dur* and the retroflexion (*ṣṭutva*) of the initial letter of the following member must be stated. Thus, from "dur-dāśa," once the substitution of *u* for the *r* has occurred, [the form becomes] *dūḍāśa*.
There is a long vowel by the rule of *savarṇadīrgha*. In *dāśerdakārasya*, the letter *da* becomes *ḍa* by the rule of *ṣṭuan*. Thus, *dūṇāśa*.

When *dur-nāśa* is established, there is the substitution of *u* for the *repha* (the *r*), followed by *savarṇadīrgha*. The *na* of *nāśeḥ* becomes *ṇa* by the rule of *ṣṭuan*. Thus, *dūḍabha*. When *dur-dabha* is established, there is the substitution of *u* for the *repha*.
There is a long vowel by the rule of *savarṇadīrgha*. By the rule of *ṣṭuan*, the *d* of *dabh* becomes *ḍ*. Regarding the phrase "from the three roots beginning with *khal*" (*khaltribhyaḥ*):

the meaning is that the suffix *khal* is applied to the three verbal roots *dāśṛ* (in the sense of giving), *ṇaś* (in the sense of disappearance) in its causative form (*ṇyanta*), and *dabh* (in the sense of harming), according to the rule *īṣaddussuṣu*. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But surely..."
Since there is an absence of the *kṅit* suffixes, how can there be elision of the *n* here by the rule *aniditām*?

To this he says: "The elision of the *n* of the root *dambh* is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity). Thus we have *dūḍhya*. When *dur* and *dhya* are in combination, the *u*-vowel of the *repha* (*r*) occurs, followed by *guṇa* (which becomes a long vowel by the rule *savarṇadīrghaḥ*), and the *dh* changes to *ḍh* by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*. [This is further supported] by the rule *ātaśca*.

The meaning is as follows: from the root *dhyai* in the sense of "thinking" (*cintāyām*), with the suffix *kap* by the rule *ātaścopasarge*, the substitution of *ā* for the initial vowel by the rule *ādeca upadeśe*, and the elision of the final *ā* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, the word *dhya* is formed.

Regarding the term *sader*: from the root *sad*, in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), with the suffix *ḍaṭ*, [the form *sada* is derived]; and by virtue of the indicatory letter *ṅ*, this [suffix] also [applies].
The form *bruvant-sa* results from the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) in the compound with an upapada. When *bruvat-sa* is established, the substitution of *bṛ* for the word *bravat* occurs;

from the resulting word *bṛsa*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, yielding the form *bṛsī*. This is the intended meaning. The textual passage beginning with "from words denoting direction" (*dik-chabdebhyaḥ*) and ending here [is the relevant section].

This is an elaboration of the rule *pṛṣodarādīni*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words); that is to say, it belongs to the group beginning with *pṛṣodara*. By this, forms such as *kartukāmaḥ* and *kartumanāḥ* are included.
(1019) *saṃhitāyām* |6|3|114|. In a *saṃhitā*. This is easy to understand. (1020) *karṇe*...

[The vowel] of a mark (*lakṣaṇa*) consisting of eight, five, or one gem, or [a mark] pierced, cut, perforated, or having a *sruva*-shaped or *svastika* design, [becomes long] before *karṇa*. This is a rule for lengthening, because the word "ṭhḍhralope" is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) from that [preceding sūtra]. A mark in the shape of a sickle, a trident, a wheel, or the like, which serves to identify the specific owner of cattle.

That which is intended [to be expressed] is designated by the term "its characteristic" (*tallakṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *lambakarṇa* ("long-eared"). As for *dviguṇākarṇa*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose two ears have double lines.
Alternatively, in cases such as *aṣṭakarṇa*, it means "one whose ears bear the marks of the eight numerical figures."

(1021) *nahivṛtivṛṣivyadhirucisahitaniṣu kvau* | 6|3|116|. [The rule] *nahivṛti*: *upānat*. [Derivation: From the root *ṇaha* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*), by the rule *ṇo naḥ* [the ṇ is replaced by n]. Because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). That which is bound upon (*upanahyate*) is called *upānat*. [This applies] to the preceding member [of the compound].

The vowel is lengthened. By the rule *ṭhnaho dhaḥ*, [the *h* of *naha* becomes *dh*]. That which turns back (*nivartate*) is called *nīvṛt*. From the root *vṛtu* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*), with the suffix *kvip* in the active voice (*kartari*), the vowel is lengthened. That which rains down (*pravarṣati*) is called *prāvṛṭ*. From the root *vṛṣu* in the sense of "sprinkling" (*secane*), with the suffix *kvip*, the vowel is lengthened. By the rule *ṭhnaho dhaḥ*, that which turns back is *nīvṛt*. From the root *vṛtu* in the sense of "turning."

The suffix *kvip* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and there is lengthening (*dīrghaḥ*). That which rains is "the rainy season" (*prāvṛṭ*); [this is derived from] the root *vṛṣu* (in the sense of "to sprinkle") with *kvip*, and there is lengthening. That which pierces the vital spots is "one who pierces the vitals" (*marmāvit*); [this is derived from] *vidhyati* with *kvip*. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇam*) by the rule *grahijyā* etc. [Pāṇini 6.1.16].
Then follows a compound with an upapada (*upapadasamāsaḥ*), elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), elision of the nasal (*nalopaḥ*), and lengthening.

The word *nīruk* is derived from the root *ruc* (meaning "to shine") with the suffix *kvip*; there is lengthening of the vowel. The word *ṛtīṣaṭ* means "one who endures suffering"; it is derived from the root *ṛt* (in the sense of "enduring") with the suffix *kvip*. There is lengthening of the vowel, and by the rule *ṣaha* becomes *ḍha*.
Although the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would prohibit the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*], the substitution of *ṣ* occurs here by the rule *pūrvapadāt*.
Haradatta says: Others hold that [the form *parītat*] is due to its inclusion in the *suṣāmādi* group. [The word] *parītat* means "he extends" (*paritanoti*).

[The root] *tanu* in the sense of "extension," with the suffix *kvip*; the elision of the nasal is by the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "of *gam* and others" under the rule *gamaḥ kvau*. Then there is the *tuk* augment and the lengthening of the vowel. Now...
Anticipating the objection that a long vowel might occur in examples such as *paṭuaruk* and *tigmaruc*, he says "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*).
Thus, *paṭuaruk*: the analysis is *paṭua rocate*. In both cases, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Since the two preceding members (*pūrvapada*) lack the status of either a gati or a kāraka, the lengthening of the vowel does not take place.
When resorting to the established *Vibhāṣā* rules, the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*) alone is the refuge.
(1022) *vanagiryoḥ saṃjñāyāṃ koṭarakiṃśulakādīnām* || Pāṇini 6.3.117. Regarding *vanagiryoh*: this is a locative dual (*saptamī*). [The compound consists of] *koṭara* and *kiṃśuluka*.
The analysis of the compound is: "those for which *koṭarakiśulukau* are the first.
This results in [the meaning] "of the *koṭara*-type and the *kiṃśuluka*-type. The connection is according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
He states this with the words beginning "of the *koṭara*-type," etc. Examples include *puragāvaṇa*, and so forth.
They will be explained [later].

(1023) *vanaṃ puragāmiśrakāsidhrakāsārikākoṭarāgrebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.4). Therein, he demonstrates the rule for the substitution of *ṇ*: *vanaṃ puragā*. Regarding *vanam*, this is the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive.

Intending this, he says: "of the word *vana*. Regarding the phrase "from these": the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *vana*, which serves as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), occurs only after these—namely, *puragā*, *miśrakā*, *sidhrakā*, *sārikā*, *koṭara*, and *agre*. [This is derived] from the rule "after *ṛ* and *ṣ*" (*ṛṣābhyām*) by the rule "ṇ becomes *na*" (*ṇo naḥ*).
Because of this continued application (*anuvṛtti*). In the sūtra, *agre* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a word ending in the locative case. Now, one might object:

since these are separate words here, the rule *aṭ-ku-pvāṅ-num-vyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2) for the substitution of *ṇ* does not apply; therefore, because it is necessary that this be an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), how can it be said "only from these"?
Regarding the attainment of the restriction (*niyamalābha*), he says: "In this case, ending with *koṭara*.

The meaning is that in this rule prescribing the shortening of the vowel (*oṇatva-vidhi*), the five words *puragā*, *miśrakā*, *sidhrakā*, *sārikā*, and *koṭara* which are mentioned, are intended by the term *koṭara-ādi* (the group beginning with *koṭara*) in the rule prescribing the lengthening of the vowel (*dīrgha-vidhi*) for the words *vana* and *giri*.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of these. In the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, five words beginning with *pura* are indeed specified with long vowels. However, a long vowel for them is prescribed only when they function as proper names (*saṃjñā*) by the rule "*ṭhvanagiryor*" [Pāṇini 8.4.7]. And thus, in the case of these [words], when they do not function as proper names—

Because of the absence of lengthening (*dīrgha*), the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* in the word *vana* results in being restricted to cases where it occurs within a proper name (*saṃjñā*) by the rule "ṭh-van-ampura-gaḥ.

Consequently, since the *ṇ*-substitution of the letter *n* in the word *vana* is already established in those instances by the rule "pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ," there remains the case of the five-word group beginning with *puraga*, which has undergone lengthening.
The meaning is that in the rule prescribing *ṇatva*, the mention [of the word] serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Regarding the phrase "but of the word *agra*":
the mention of the word *agra* in the rule prescribing *ṇatva* is intended solely for the purpose of prescribing a *ṇatva* not previously established in the word *agrevaṇa*;

it is not for the sake of restriction. For in the case of the word *agrevaṇa*, when it is not a proper name (*asaṃjñā*), the *ṇatva* is already established by the rule "after a non-guttural vowel" (*ago’ṅgāt*).

Furthermore, the mention of the five items beginning with *puraga*—which have already been treated as having a long vowel—in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). As for the word *agra*, however:
the mention of the word *agra* in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* is solely for the purpose of prescribing a previously unestablished *ṇ* in the word *agrevaṇa*.

However, it is not for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because the word *agrevaṇa* is not a technical name (*asaṃjñātva*). This is the intended meaning. Nor should it be argued that, since the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* cannot apply here due to the intervention of the letter *g* in the word *puragāvaṇa*, the inclusion of *puragā* is intended solely as an original injunction (*apūrvaṇatva-vidhyartha*) for this case.

The word *ṭha* here refers to the fifth case (*pañcamī*). It is understood that there is no substitution of *ṇ* for a following letter when it follows a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) ending in the letter *g*. However, this word *puragā* ends in the vowel *ā*, not in the letter *g*; therefore, since the prohibition by the rule *agaḥ* does not apply there, the desired form is established simply by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*.

The inclusion of the term *puragā* is also for the sake of restriction; this is the intended meaning. *Puragāvaṇa* and others are names of specific hells. Regarding *asipatravana*: this is a specific hell.
Although it is a name (*saṃjñā*), the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* does not occur here, because [the rule applies] only to these [specific words].

The meaning is "because it is a rule" (*niyamāt*). Regarding the term *agrevaṇam*: the meaning is that there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) of the word *vana*, which ends in the genitive case, with the word *agra*. Now, one might object: "In that case, by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, the suffix *suk* would also apply to the seventh case ending. To this, he says: "in the group beginning with *rājadanta*. By this, [the elision of] the word *vana*...
The alternative grammatical placement (paranipāta) has also been indicated. Now, one might object that since the meaning of the locative case is predominant, the locative case ending should be used;
to this he says: "of the nominal stem" (prātipadika). The intended meaning is that the meaning of the locative case is already included within the nominal stem.
He provides an example of *kiṃśuluka* and others: "the mountain Kiṃśuluka."
The form *ṭhañjanāgiri* should also be cited as an example.
(1024) [Pāṇini 5.2.118] *vale*: after the word *vala*. For instance, *kṛṣīvala*. In the analytical explanation (*vigraha*), it means "one who possesses agriculture" (*kṛṣirasyāsti*).
The suffix *valac* is applied by the rule "ṭhrajaḥ-kṛṣi-āsuti... and so forth.

(1025) *Matau bahvaco 'najirādīnām* | 6|3|119 | When the possessive suffix *matup* follows, a long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of a polysyllabic word in a technical name (*saṃjñā*), provided it does not belong to the *anjira*-class. This [does not apply] when... [the following conditions are met].

The meaning is [the suffix *matup* is applied] after words such as *ajira*. Regarding *amarāvatī*: this is the name of Indra’s city. The analysis of the compound is "that in which immortals (*amara*) exist. The substitution of *va* for *ma* occurs either by the rule *mādupadhāyāśca* or by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. Regarding *ajiravatī*: this is the name of a particular river. Regarding *valayavatī*: [this is the name of a particular river].
The point is that even though [the word] does not belong to the *anajirādi* group, there is no lengthening because it is not a proper name (*asaṃjñātva*). (1026) *śarādīnāṃ ca* | 6|3|120|.
Regarding *śarādīnāṃ ca*: the remainder [of the rule] is "there is lengthening in the sense of the suffix *matau* when it is a proper name."
Because it does not consist of more than two syllables, the [suffix] is not obtained by the preceding rule. Regarding *śarāvatī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that in which there are reeds (*śara*).
It is the name of a particular river. (1027) *iko vahe 'pīloḥ* | Pāṇini 6.3.121.

In the case of *apīlu*, [the final vowel] becomes *i* (*ik*) even when it ends in *va*. The analysis is: *apīluḥ* [is derived from *a-pīlu*]. "Of that which ends in *ik*" (*igantasya*); the remainder [of the rule] is "of the preceding member" (*pūrvapadasya*).

(1028) *Upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.122): [The final vowel of] a prefix (*upasarga*) is diversely (*bahulam*) lengthened before a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*, provided it does not refer to a human being (*amanuṣya*).

Regarding *upasargasya*: *parīpāka*—the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *pac* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), resulting in vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel; then, by the rule *ṭhcajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, the substitution of *k* occurs. Regarding *niṣāda*:
a specific class of humans known as *pulinda*; it is called *niṣāda* because sin (*pāpa*) settles (*niṣīdati*) within them.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of locus according to the rule *hal-śca*. Regarding the word *pratīhāra* as denoting a doorkeeper (*dauvārika*), the lengthening of the vowel is without authoritative support. Alternatively, *pratīhāra* means "door" (*dvāra*); because he stands at that [door], its application to the person is figurative (*gauṇa*).

(1029) *ikaḥ kāśe* | 6|3|123|. [The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of a word ending in] an *ik* [vowel occurs] before the word *kāśa*. For example, *nīkāśa*. Since this is derived from the root *kāś* with the suffix *ac* (belonging to the *pacādi* group), the previous rule does not apply here. (1030) *aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām* | 6|3|125|. [The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *aṣṭan* occurs] when it forms part of a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

[The rule] "aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām" [is explained as follows]. He explains the sūtra by supplying the remaining words: "the long vowel occurs in the uttarapada. The example is *aṣṭāpadam*. Its status as a technical name (*saṃjñātva*) is to be investigated. (1031) "citeḥ kapi" [Pāṇini 6.3.127].
The suffix *kap* is added after *citi*; "long vowel" (*dīrgha*) is the understood remainder [of the rule]. Regarding *ekacitīka*:
"a particular altar (*sthaṇḍila*) designated as 'fire' (*agni')" is the understood remainder. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has one *citi*.
The suffix *kap* is a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*). Regarding *dvicitīka*: the analysis is "that which has two *citīs*."
(1032) *nare saṃjñāyām* | 6|3|129|.

Regarding *nare saṃjñāyām*: the phrase "lengthening of *viśva*" (*viśvasya dīrgha*) is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. From the preceding sūtra, "of *viśva* before *vasu* and *rāṭ*" (*viśvasya vasurāṭoḥ*), the term "*viśvasya*" is carried over (*anuvartate*).

(1033) *mitre carṣau* | Pāṇini 6.3.130. The meaning is that when the word *mitra* follows, the long vowel [substitutes for the final vowel] of *viśva* occurs, provided that a seer (*ṛṣi*) is to be expressed.
The long vowel [ā] should be stated for the words *danta*, *daṃṣṭrā*, *karṇa*, *kuṇḍa*, *varāha*, *puccha*, and *pada* [following the word *śvan*].

Regarding "the tooth of a dog" (*śuno danta*): the meaning is that the long vowel is substituted for the word *śvan* when followed by *danta* and the others. Thus, *śvādanta* is the analysis of the compound *śuno danta*. *Śvādaṃṣṭrā* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

Some maintain that the word *daṃṣṭra* is read with a long final vowel (*-ā*) in the Vārttika; others hold that it has a short final vowel (*-a*). Examples include *śvādaṃṣṭraḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [Other examples are] *śvākarṇaḥ*, *śvākundaḥ*, *śvāvarāhaḥ*, *śvāpuccham*, and *śvāpadaḥ*. The form *śvāpuccham avanāmitam* is simply incorrect.
(1034) *pra-nir-antar-śara-ikṣu-plakṣa-āmra-kārṣya-khadira-pīyūkṣābhyaḥ asaṃjñāyām api* || 8.4.5 || *pra-nir-antar*: "From these"— namely *pra*, *nir*, *antar*, *śara*, *ikṣu*, *plakṣa*, *āmra*.

The meaning is: from these words, *kārṣya*, *khadira*, and *pīyūkṣā*. Regarding the word *vanasya*: the intention is that this [suffix] follows from the rule "vanaṃ puragā-," as it is understood by recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). Regarding *pravaṇam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "an excellent forest" (*prakṛṣṭaṃ vanam*); it is a *prādi*-compound (prepositional compound). Regarding *iha*: in the word *kārṣyavaṇam*, because [the suffix] follows after the letter *ṣ*.
The meaning is that [the condition] is not met by taking the position of being after the *repha*, because there is an intervention by a *ṣakāra* other than those beginning with *aṭ*.
By this, it is indicated that the reading containing a palatal *śakāra* in the middle of "kārśya" is unauthoritative. If that were the case...

Because there is an absence of the cause [for doubling], doubling is impossible; for the letter *r* cannot be the cause [of doubling] since it is separated by a *ś* that is distinct from *aṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, and *āṅ*. Examples include: *nirvaṇam*, *antarvaṇam*, *śaravaṇam*, *ikṣuvaṇam*, *plakṣavaṇam*, *āmravaṇam*, *kārṣyavaṇam*, and *khadiravaṇam*.
*pīyūkṣāvaṇam* (a grove of date-palms).

(1035) *vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ* | 8|4|6|. [The rule] *vibhāṣauṣadhi* [states]: "The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs in the word *vana* when it follows a name of a medicinal herb (*oṣadhi*) or a large tree (*vanaspati*). That is to say, the *ṇ* replaces the *n* of *vana* when it follows a word denoting a medicinal herb or a large tree.

The meaning is that the *nakāra* (the letter *n*) of that [word] optionally becomes *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*). He gives an example from the category of *oṣadhi* (herbs): *dūrvāvaṇam* (a thicket of dūrvā grass). Amarasimha states: "Herbs (*oṣadhyaḥ*) are those that end with the ripening of their fruit.
Then he gives an example from the category of *vanaspati* (trees): *śirīṣavaṇam* (a thicket of śirīṣa trees). Although [a tree] is without flowers...

That very tree, such as the *udumbara* and others, bears fruit; for it is said that "the *vanaspati* [is] those that bear fruit without flowers, while the *vānaspatya* [is] those that bear both flowers and fruit. And although this *śirīṣa* tree possesses both flowers and fruit and is therefore not a *vanaspati*, it is nevertheless referred to here by the term *vanaspati*.

The commonality of being a tree (*vṛkṣasāmānyam*) is intended [to be expressed]. For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *supi yuktavadvyaktivacane*, it is stated that in the example *śirīṣavanam*, the status of being a great tree (*vanaspatitvam*) is attributed to the *śirīṣa*. This is the direction of the argument. Regarding the phrase "only from those ending in two or three syllables": this refers to the rule stating that "the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the following word *vana* must be prescribed."
The remainder: "devadāruvana" is a counter-example. A prohibition must be stated for words beginning with *irikā*.
"From *irikā* and so forth" means that there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *vana* when it follows these [words].

(1036) vāhanamāhitāt | 8|4|8| [The suffix ṭhak is applied after a word denoting a vehicle when it follows a word meaning "placed upon" (āhita). Regarding "vāhanamāhitāt": that which is placed upon a vehicle for the purpose of being carried, but is not itself capable of mounting [it], is called "āhita. This is what [the author] expresses by saying "having mounted" (āropya).

"From a *nimita*" means: from either the letter *repha* (ṛ) or the letter *ṣakāra*. "Of the *nakāra* of *vāhana*" means: of that *nakāra* which belongs to *vāhana*. By this, it is indicated in the sūtra that the word *vāhana* stands in the nominative case (*prathamā*) with the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding the example *ikṣuvāhaṇam*: for indeed, the sugarcane is for the purpose of carrying.

It should be understood that their state of being "mounted" (āhita) means they are made to carry [the load] by others, as they are not able to mount it themselves; that is to say, it refers to the vehicle, such as a cart, which is joined with the yoke that has been placed upon it. Regarding the term *indravāhana*: one might object that if the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *vah* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), [it would result in a different form].
How is there lengthening of the vowel in *upadhā* [in the case of *pāna*], given that it lacks the condition of being followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*?
To this, he says: "In the case of the root *vah*, when *lyuṭ* follows. (1037) *pānaṃ deśe* | 8|4|9|.
"Drinking" (*pāna*) [is used] in the sense of a location. Intending that the nominative case in the word "pānam" is used in the sense of the genitive, he says:
"of drinking" (*pānasya*). Regarding the term "Uśīnaras": this is a plural form denoting a specific region. Now, one might ask:

if the word *pāna* ends in the suffix *yuṭ* (forming an abstract noun), how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "milk is the drinking" (*kṣīraṃ pānam*)? To this [he replies]:
He says: "It is drunk" (*pīyate*).

(1038) *vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* | 8|4|10|. "Or [the suffix *ya* is used] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*)"—this very rule continues to apply; such is the meaning. [This applies] both in the sense of the abstract state and the instrument.

The meaning is that for the word *pāna*, the substitution of *ṇa* may optionally occur in the aforementioned scope. This statement is for the purpose of providing a formal substitute. Examples are *kṣīrapānam* and *kṣīrapāṇam*. The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is "the drinking of milk" (*kṣīrasya pānam*).
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of either the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, the meaning is either "the act of drinking" or "a drinking vessel."
Or [the rule applies] to words such as *girinadī*.

Regarding the phrase "of *girinadī* and so forth": the meaning is that there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) stating that the *ṇ* optionally replaces the *n* situated in the second member (*uttarapada*), provided it follows a cause (*nimitta*) situated in the preceding member (*pūrvapada*). The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is *gireḥ nadī* ("the river of the mountain").

Regarding the term *cakranitambā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose hips (*nitamba*) are like a wheel (*cakra*). (1039) [Pāṇini 8.4.11]: "In the case of the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the suffix *nuṭ*, and the case endings (*vibhakti*)," and "from what stands at the end of the preceding member."

The meaning is that this is because of the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "from a preceding word, when it is a technical name" (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*). "Situated in these" means existing in the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), in the *num* augment, and in a case-ending (*vibhakti*). "It may optionally [occur]" is because of the continuation of the rule "optionally, in the sense of an abstract state or an instrument" (*vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*). [This applies] at the end of a nominal stem.

Thus [it is said]. The remainder [of the sentence] is "an example will be stated. Regarding *māṣavāpiṇau*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "those two who sow beans" (*māṣān vapete*). By the rule "frequently" (*bahulam ākṣīkṣṇye*), the suffix *ṇini* occurs even when a genus (*jāti*) is the object and a nominal stem (*sup*) is the subordinate element (*upapada*).
This is a compound with an *upapada*. Because the word *vāpin* ends in a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*), [the following applies].

The intention is that because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) applies to that which ends in it. Regarding "in the case of *num*" (*numi*), the words "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) are to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding "rice-fields" (*vrīhivāpāṇi*), the words "families of farmers" (*kṛṣīvalakulāni*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is "those who sow rice" (*vrīhīn vapanti*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. From the neuter word *vrīhivāpa*, [the plural ending is added].

The meaning is that, after the application of *num* by the rules "ṭhjaśśasośśiḥ" and "napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ," there is lengthening by the rule "sarvanāmasthāne ca," and then the *ṇatva* (nasalization) of the *n* of *num*. Regarding the phrase "in a case-ending": the word "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder. In the example "māṣavāpeṇa," the *n* is situated within the third case ending.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*]. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*): the intention is that in the alternative where the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur, one should cite examples such as *māṣavāpinau*, *māṣavāpāni*, and *māṣavāpena*.
The substitution of *ṇ* applies only to the end of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the second member of the compound.

Now, one might ask: why does the optional substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* not occur in the word *gargabhaginī* (the sister of the Gargas), given that the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the nominal stem *bhagin*, which constitutes the final member of the compound? To this, he says: "That which is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)."
The substitution of *ṇ* occurs only for that which ends in it. By the preceding word, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is implied;

and that is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, not of what ends in it, nor of the *num* augment or the case-ending (*vibhakti*), because such [application] is impossible—this is the sense.
"No," [it is argued]. In the compound *gargāṇāṃ bhaginī* ("the sister of the Gargas"), the word *bhaginī* is the final member (*uttarapada*) of a genitive compound;

however, it is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because it ends in a suffix. By the rule concerning the inclusion of gender-distinct forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), when a nominal stem is mentioned, it includes that which is qualified by gender. Thus, the word *bhaginī*—[is included].

The meaning is that even when there is the suffix *ṅīp*, it is only the final vowel (*ī*) that is [the end of the word], and not the letter *n*; therefore, this optional substitution of *ṇ* does not apply to it. He states "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) to show that the author of the Sūtras intends the term *prātipadika* (nominal stem) to be qualified by the status of being the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). It is precisely because the nominal stem is thus qualified as the subsequent member...

The inclusion of the term *num* by the author of the Sūtras is purposeful; otherwise, it would be meaningless—this is the sense. Why? To this he says: "of the *aṅga*. In the rule prescribing *num*—"after a neuter [stem] ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or a vowel (*ac*)"—the word "*aṅgasya*" (of the stem) is understood. Thus, it refers to a stem (*aṅga*) that ends in a *jhal* or an *ac*.
The meaning obtained is that the augment *num* occurs for a neuter base (*klība*) when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix follows.
However, in the case of the word *māṣavāpāṇi*, the word *māṣavāpa* is the base (*aṅga*) with respect to the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.
The *num* augment prescribed for that base *māṣavāpa* becomes an integral part of that very base, and not [of the whole compound].

The word *vāpa* is indeed a constituent part (*avayava*) of that which serves as the final member (*uttarapada*). Thus, because it lacks the status of being the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that constitutes the final member, the optional substitution of *ṇ* (by the rule *prātipadikānte*) does not apply; for this reason, the mention of *num* [is necessary]. The status of being a final member belongs to the nominal stem.

The meaning is that, in the absence of a qualifier, since the *num* suffix—which is part of the word ending in *māṣavāpa*—is indeed a part of the base ending in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the rule would be established by the phrase "at the end of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikānte*) alone;
thus, the explicit mention of *num* would be redundant. Such is the case for the nominal stem.

It is established that the mention of *num* is an indicator (*liṅga*) for the qualification of being a final member of a compound. However, in reality, this is not an indicator; thus he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). The phrase "furthermore" is used to demonstrate a specific distinction.

[The root] *hivi* in the sense of "pleasing" belongs to the *bhvādi* class; because it is marked with *idit*, the augment *num* is applied, and the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is replaced by the suffix *śatṛ*.

In the case of *māṣavāpāṇi*, although the *n* of the *num* suffix is at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), in the word *prahiṇvan*, the *n* of the *num* suffix is not at the end of a nominal stem.

Consequently, the optional substitution of *ṇ* (the *ṇatva* option) by the rule "at the end of a nominal stem" (*prātipadikānte*) does not apply there; therefore, the explicit mention of *num* in the rule is necessary for that purpose. Hence...
If the status of being an *uttarapada* (subsequent member) were a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), how could the mention of *num* serve as an indicative mark (*liṅga*)?
Therefore, the intention is that the *Bhāṣya* itself is the sole refuge when [the status of being an *uttarapada*] is a qualifier of the *uttarapada*. Now, one might object:
in the case of *māṣavāpiṇau*, how can the nominal stem *vāpin* have the status of an *uttarapada*?

If it is argued that, according to the rule *gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛdbhiḥ saha samāsavacanam*, the formation of the compound occurs prior to the application of case-endings (*sub*)—that is, before the derivation of the nominal suffixes—it is not so; for the word *uttarapada* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to the final member of a compound. Enough of this. Now, [regarding] the root *ivi* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*).

After *id*, there is *num*. In the case of the suffix *lyuṭ*, there is no substitution [of *m* for *n*]. Since one might think that in a *prādi*-compound such as *prakṛṣṭaminvanam*, there would be an optional change of the *n* of *num* to *ṇ*, he says: *prenvanam*.
[This is because] it does not apply after words beginning with *yuvan*.

"yuvāder neti": the remainder [of the rule] is "the optional substitution of *ṭhuk*. This is a *vārttika*. "ramyayūna" [is formed as follows]: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who is both beautiful and young.
The application [of the rule] occurs because of the *nakāra* at the end of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). "paripakvāni": here, [the application] is of the *num* [augment].

The rule *kumati ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.13) would have necessitated the obligatory substitution of *ṇa* for *na* after the word *punar*, thereby overriding the optional application of *ṇa* prescribed by *ṭh-prātipadika-ante* (Pāṇini 8.4.12). However, that [obligatory substitution] is here prohibited because *punar* belongs to the *yuvan*-class. Furthermore, the rule *ekāj-uttara-pade ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.12), which applies when the subsequent member of a compound consists of a single vowel, has already been explained in the analysis of the feminine noun *punarbhū*.

It is remembered [as such] in accordance with the context; the meaning is that it was stated right there [in that very context]: "Because of the force of its introduction, this substitution of *ṇ* is obligatory (*nitya*).
Regarding *harimāṇī*: from the root *man*, after it has been converted by *ṇic*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca*.

The compound occurs before the application of case-endings (*sub*) according to the rule *gatikārakopapadānām*. Because it ends in *n*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Here, the base *mā* is the second member (*uttarapada*); since it ends in that, although the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would be optional by rule, the substitution of *ṇ* is mandatory. [This applies] when *num* follows.

The phrase "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Regarding *kṣīrapāṇī*: when the object (*karman*) is the upapada, the root *pā* takes the suffix *ka* by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*; then, by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, there is elision of the long *ā*.

From the word *kṣīrapa*, the substitution of *śi* occurs for the case-endings *jas* and *śas*. The augment *num* is applied because it ends in a vowel (*ajanta*), and then the vowel is lengthened. Of that [word].
The suffix *ṇa* is obligatory in the case of *am*. Regarding the rule "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*), it is said that "an example is given. This is the remainder [of the explanation].
In the example *kṣīrapeṇa*, the *ṇa* is not obligatory because it occurs within a case-ending (*vibhaktisthatvāt*).
He provides another example occurring in a case-ending: *ramyaviṇā*. Here, *viḥ* means a bird; it is both beautiful (*ramya*) and a bird (*viḥ*).
The analysis [of the compound] is *viś ca tena*. Nor should one suspect here the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.4.14]: "even when there is an intervention by a word (*padavyavāye*).

For is it intended that the status of being a word (*padatva*)—defined as "ending in a *sup* or a *tiṅ*"—is based on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*) when considering the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, or rather, is it [intended] when the third case-ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*) follows?

Is there "word-status" (*padatva*) by virtue of the rule *svādiṣu*? Not the first [alternative], because of the prohibition of the definition of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) by the rule *utarapadatve cāpadādividhau*. Nor the second, because by the rule *svādiṣu*, word-status is obtained for the word *ramyavi* alone, but not for the word *vi*, since it is the third case ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*).

Because the rule is prescribed for the whole complex [of sounds] itself. For this very reason, in the case of *punarbhūṇām*, the ancient grammarians maintain that since the word *bhū* alone does not possess the status of a *pada* when followed by *nām*, the prohibition in the rule *padavyavāye 'pi* does not apply, and thus the substitution of *ṇ* occurs. Regarding this, what must be said is as follows:
This will be explained immediately following the rule *ṭhpadatvayavāye’pi*.

(1040) *kumati ca* | 8.4.13 | "And when a word beginning with *ku-* follows. It is as stated before; that is, the *n* situated at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), in the augment *num*, or in a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is always [replaced by *ṇ*].
The meaning is that there would be the designation *matup*. This [example] has multiple vowels (*anekāc*) as the meaning of the subsequent member (*utarapada*). Regarding *harikāmiṇau*:

the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "ṇini is used diversely in the sense of repetition" (*bahulam ābhīkṣṇye*); the *ṇatva* (nasalization) occurs because it follows the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Regarding *harikāmāṇi*: the *ṇatva* is obligatory due to the presence of *num*, which is conditioned by the vowel-ending. Regarding *harikāmeṇa*: [the *ṇatva* applies].
An example of [a word] standing in a case-ending (*vibhaktistha*) is as follows:
(1041) *padavyavāye 'pi* | 8|4|38|. "Even when there is an intervention by a word (*pada*)," that is, "when there is a separation by a word. Immediately after the word "by a word" (*padena*),...

The phrase "of those who have a cause as their motive" (*nimitakāriṇaḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. [The word] "it would not occur" refers to the fact that the prohibition "not after *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, *kami*, or *gami*" (*na bhābhūpūkamigamī*) continues to apply; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the example *māṣakumbhavāpena*:
"a jar of beans" (*māṣakumbhaḥ*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "the sowing (*vāpa*) of that jar of beans. In this case...
There is no substitution of *ṇ* for the *ṇakāra* because of the intervention of the word *kumbha* between the cause (*nimitta*), the letter *ṣ*, and the effect (*kāryin*), the letter *ṇ*.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the fourfold army" (*caturaṅgayogena*): that which possesses four components—namely, chariots, elephants, cavalry, and infantry—is a "fourfold army" (*caturaṅgasainyam*); by that [army].
The analysis (*vigraha*) is "yoga. Here, because of the intervention of the word *aṅga* between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*kāryin*), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur.

In both cases, it should be understood that the status of being a word (*padatva*) for the words *kumbha* and *aṅga* is established by relying on the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhakti*) through the rule of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). [This applies] when the following member is a word ending in *ṭh*.

The prohibition "there is no prohibition regarding the application of *apadādi* [rules]" does not apply here, because that prohibition operates only when the subsequent portion (*uttara-khaṇḍa*) is subject to a grammatical operation (*kāryabhāk*). For this very reason, in the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, the example given for that paribhāṣā is precisely *paramavāc*.

An example has been stated in the Bhāṣya: for here, since the word *vāk* as the final member (*uttarapada*) possesses the status of being subject to the grammatical operation of *kutva*, it does not undergo *kutva* because it lacks the status of being a *pada* by virtue of depending on the internal case-ending (*antarvatiny vibhaktiḥ*). And for this very reason, in the rule *kumati ca*:

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated: "A jar of beans is *māṣakumbhaḥ*; the sowing of a jar of beans is *māṣakumbhavāpaḥ*. Therefore, in the expression *māṣakumbhavāpena*, the application of the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*)—namely, *prātipadikānte*—"is proposed so that the prohibition [stated in] *ṭhpadavyavāye 'pi* may take effect."

This is consistent. And this being so, in the case of *ramyaviṇā*, since the subsequent portion (*vi*) does not undergo the operation [of the suffix], the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule—namely, "when there is an *uttarapada*, the rule does not apply to that which is not at the beginning of a word"—does not take effect; thus, by resorting to the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), [the desired result follows].

The prohibition of *ṇatva* [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*] applies even when there is an intervention by a *ṭh*-class consonant (*ṭh-padavyavāye’pi*). By this, the *ṇatva* in the word *punarbhūṇām* is also unimpeded.
[However,] it should be stated that this does not apply when a *taddhita* suffix follows.

Regarding the phrase *ataddhite*: the meaning is that this prohibition applies when there is an intervention by a word that does not end in a *taddhita* suffix, but not when there is an intervention by a word followed by a *taddhita* suffix. In the example *ārdragomayeṇa*, *gomaya* means "cow-dung. The suffix *mayaṭ* is added after the word *go* ending in the genitive case, according to the rule *gośca purīṣe*.

This is a *taddhita* derivative; because it is a constituent part of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a *taddhita* suffix, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*). "Fresh cow-dung" (*ārdraṃ gomayam*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Although, by the rule regarding the presence of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the word *go-* is considered a "word" (*pada*) with respect to the internal case-ending, nevertheless, because it is followed by a *taddhita* suffix...

Therefore, even when there is an intervention, the substitution of *ṇ* for a letter following *r* certainly occurs, because in this section, the intervention of *aṭ*, *ku*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, *nu*, or *m* does not constitute an obstacle. The example "śuṣkagomayeṇa" illustrates [the rule] regarding what follows *ṣ*. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is stated that this applies to "that which is at the end of a word."

Intending the recurrence of the term *pada* from the preceding sūtra, or alternatively assuming that the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur when there is an intervention by a word (*padavyavāya*) before a word, this Vārttika has been rejected.
(1042) *kustumburūṇi jātiḥ* | 6|1|143 | [The word *kustumburu* is always plural when it denotes a genus.]

Now, with the word *suṭ* continuing from the rule "ṭhsuṭ kātpūrvaḥ," he begins to explain several sūtras: *kustumburūṇi*. Regarding this: the meaning is that when a particular species is to be expressed, the word *kustumburu* is prescribed as being accompanied by the augment *suṭ*.

*Kustumburu* is *dhānyāka*; it is well known as a specific type of shrub. The statement that "neuter gender is non-essential" means it is not intended to be significant. It should be understood that the [specific] word-form is also non-essential. Thus, in the form *kutumburūṇi*, because it lacks the status of being a denoter of the *dhānyāka* species, the suffix *suṭ* does not apply.
This is the meaning. Thus he says: "The sense is that the *tindukī* fruits are contemptible.
If the word *tumburu* is intended to denote the *tinduka* tree, a lexicon (*kośa*) must be sought [to support this].
(1043) *Aparasparāḥ kriyāsātatye* | 6|1|144|.

*Aparasparāḥ*: this is clear. *Goṣpadam*: since the word *goṣpada* cannot function [as a compound] when preceded by *nañ* (the negative particle) in the sense of "unfrequented," he provides the example with that prefix—namely, *agoṣpadāni*. The intention is that the suffix *suṭ* is applied even in cases where the movement of cattle is simply impossible.

(1044) *goṣpadaṃ sevitāsevitapramāṇeṣu* |6|1|145|. [The word] *goṣpada* [is used as a suffix] in the sense of measure when referring to what has been traversed and what has not been traversed. For example:

*goṣpadamātraṃ kṣetram* ("a field measuring a cow’s footprint"). By this, the smallness of the field's dimension is indicated. Therefore, there is no fault even if the field is larger than a cow’s footprint.

(1045) *āspadaṃ pratiṣṭhāyām* | 6|1|146| *āspadaṃ pratiṣṭhāyām*. "Ātma" means the maintenance of the self, that is, the preservation of the body; when that which is for the sake of this [preservation], namely a place (*sthāna*), is to be understood, the augment *suṭ* is added—this is the meaning. *Āpad-ād-āpadam* means from calamity to calamity. *Ā*... [text fragment]

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *padāt*, when it is an *avyayībhāva*, the meaning is "that which brings about misfortune" (*āpadam bhāvati*). However, in the reading *āpadāpadam*, the meaning of *āpadam* is "misfortune" (*āpat*).
(1046) *Āścaryam anitye* [Pāṇini 2.4.35].
Regarding *āścaryam* (wonder): when the sense is "marvelous" (*adbhuta*) and is to be understood, the suffix *suṭ* is added to the root *car* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.

This is based on the rule *ṭhcarerāṅ cā'gurau* (Pāṇini 6.1.143). Intending the Vārttika which states that the mention of "non-eternal" (*anitya*) should be removed and "marvelous" (*adbhuta*) should be stated instead, he says: "*suṭ* [is added] in the sense of 'marvelous'. By this, [the form] *āścarya* [is derived].

The phrase "the sky is blue" and "it is a marvel that the unbound stars do not fall from the atmosphere," and so forth, constitute this category [of the marvelous]. If it were stated that the marvelous is characterized by its occasional occurrence through the term "in the impermanent," this would not be established.

(1047) *avaskaraḥ* [is used] in the sense of *varcaska*. Regarding *avaskaraḥ* in the sense of *varcaska*: "Urine (*mūtra*), *prasrāva*, excrement (*uccāra*), *avaskara*, *śamala*, *śakṛt*, *gūtha*, *purīṣa*, *varcaska*, and *viṣṭhā*—these are not feminine; *viś* is feminine," according to Amarasimha.
(1048) *Apaskara* means a part of a chariot. 6|1|149. *Apaskara*: "The word *apaskara* denotes a part of a chariot," according to Amarasimha; and also, "the wheel is a part of a chariot."

"Ṭh-naga-uk-au-vāji-vikira-viṣkira-patat-trayaḥ"—thus says Amara. Regarding the phrase "by the mention of *vā* alone": in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the wording of the rule is "ṭh-vikiraḥ śakunau vā vi-kiraḥ.

Since the optional application of *suṭ* is already established there by the mention of *vā*, the inclusion of the term *vikira* [in the rule] indicates that *viṣkira* and *vikira* are both valid forms.

The phrase "only in the case of birds" (*śakunāveva*) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Therefore, the meaning obtained is that the application of both words does not occur elsewhere than in the case of a bird. For in the Bhāṣya, having cited the rule *viṣkiraḥ śakunau vā*, it is stated that by the mention of the word *vā* (or), there is an option regarding the suffix *suṭ*, but not—

It is established that the word *vikira* is not used for anything other than a bird, because it is observed elsewhere as well in the rule "ṭhvikiparaṃ vaiśvadevikam" (Pāṇini 4.3.129); this is the intended meaning. (1050) *pratiṣkaśaś ca kaśeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.152).

"And *pratiṣkaśa* [is derived] from *kaśi*. The word "from *kaśi*" (kaśeḥ) connects with the word "*kaśa*" (*kaśa iti*) in the rule. Thus, the meaning is that the augment *suṭ* is applied to the word *kaśa*, which is derived from the root *kaś*, when it follows the prefix *prati*.
"Only from *kaśi*" means that the word *kaśā* is derived solely from the root *kaś*.

Regarding the phrase *dhātvantareti*: in the example *pratikaśaḥ* (one who has gone toward the whip), the prefix *prati* is a preposition (*upasarga*) only with respect to the root *gam* (to go), and not with respect to *kaś* (whip), because of the rule: "Particles such as *pra* and others are [prepositions] when they are connected with the action [of a verbal root]. This is the meaning.

(1051) *praskaṇvahariścandrāvṛṣī* |6|1|153|. [The words] *praskaṇva* and *hariścandra* [are used as names of] sages (*ṛṣi*). [The word] "not for the purpose of a mantra" (*amantrārtham*) is included because, in the case of a mantra, the form is already established by the preceding rule: "*hrasvāccandrottarapade mantre*" (Pāṇini 6.2.192). This is the intended meaning.
That sūtra will be explained in the section on Vedic grammatical processes.

(1052) *maskara-maskariṇau veṇu-parivrājakayoḥ* | 6|1|154|. [The words] *maskara* and *maskarin*: the application is according to the respective order. Because of the inclusion of the term *maskarin*, it refers specifically to the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).
They say that the word is *maskari*, whereas elsewhere it is simply *makarī*.
(1053) *Kāstīrā* and *ajastunda* [denote] a city; the words *kāstīra* and *ajastunda* refer to a city.
The meaning is that [the two suffixes] are elided.

(1054) *kāraskaro vṛkṣaḥ* | P. 6.1.156: "The tree is called *kāraskara*. The analysis of the compound is: "one who performs (*karoti*) a deed (*kāram*). [This is formed by the rule] *kṛño hetutācchīlye*.
Thus ends the section on *ṭa*.

(1055) *Pāraskaraprabhṛtīni ca saṃjñāyām* | 6.1.157. Also, *pāraskara* and other such forms [are valid] when they are proper names (*saṃjñā*). Regarding *pāraskara*: the analysis of the compound is "he who makes the crossing" (*pāraṃ karoti*).
As before. Regarding *kiṣkindhā*: it is called *kiṣkindhā* because it "holds" (*dhatte*) some kind of monkey army (*vānarasainya*).

[The rule] *ṭhāto 'nupasarge kaḥ* applies; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is reduplication of *kim*, elision of *m*, the augment *suṭ*, and the change to *ṣ*. These are conventional words (*rūḍhaśabda*).
They are somehow explained; their etymological meaning need not be investigated.
Regarding the rule *tadbṛhatoḥ*: this is a sūtra from the *Pāraskara* group. Since the word *tat* lacks a final *t*, he says "before the *t*" (*tāt pūrvam*). [This refers to] the rule *talopaśca*.

The meaning is "before the letter *t*. The analysis of the compound is: "one who performs (*karoti*) that—namely, theft (*caurya*). The suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule "after the root *kṛ*, when denoting cause or habit" (*kṛño hetutācchīlye*). Regarding "Bṛhaspati":
the analysis is "the husband (*pati*) of Bṛhatī. The masculine form is applied according to the rule "for *kukkuṭī* and others, in the sense of *aṇḍa* and so forth" (*kukkuṭyādīnām aṇḍādiṣu*).

There is elision of the *tal* suffix. The *suṭ* augment is added. The *Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa* states: "Speech (*vāk*) is indeed the *bṛhatī* [meter]; he is its lord. Regarding the rule *prāyasya citi-citayoḥ*: this is a *gaṇa*-sūtra.
The analysis of the compound is *prāyasya citiḥ* or *citaṃ*. One should understand that *prāya* means sin and *cita* means a collection.
Its purification is "smṛti" (tradition). Regarding "vanaspati": the analysis of the compound is "the lord of the forest.
This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words); by this, forms such as *paraśśatāni* ("more than a hundred") and so forth are established.
Thus end the rules dependent on compounds in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the *Bālamanoramā* composed by Vāsudevadīkṣita:
(The Auspicious Invocation) Victorious is that Divine Lord of the Dance, who performs his dance in the assembly hall of the sky of consciousness (*cidambara*).
And by whose grace the sages, beginning with Pāṇini, attained their heart's desires. || 1 ||
Let there be salutation to Pāṇini; likewise, let it be so to the sage Vararuci.
And furthermore, let there be salutation to his brother Patañjali, to Viśveśvara, and to the Guru.
This Siddhāntakaumudī has been explained by many eminent scholars;
Vāsudeva, however, desires this [work], the Bālamanoramā, as its commentary. (3)

At the beginning of the work, [the author performs the auspicious rites], because it is established as a duty by traditional authorities (smṛti) such as the Bhāṣya on the *vṛddhi* sūtra, which states: "Treatises that have auspicious beginnings, auspicious middles, and auspicious ends become renowned; they come to possess heroic men and long-lived men, and their students shall likewise be endowed with prosperity."
Performing an auspicious invocation for the instruction of his disciples, he composes this at the beginning of the book;

and indicating that its subject matter is not already covered by ancient texts, while pointing out the subject (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), relationship (*sambandha*), and qualified student (*adhikārin*), he declares his intention to compose with the verse beginning "The Three Sages" (*munitrayam*). This [verse]: *This...*

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "The *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī* is being composed. By the word "this" (*iyam*), the intended meaning is the series of sentences constituting the work itself. Although the work is yet to come into being, it is referred to as "this" with a sense of direct perception (*pratyakṣavat*), because it is already grasped by the mind as an object of cognition. Those who study or know grammar [are called *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*].
Or rather, [it is] the *Kaumudī*—the moonlight—of those grammarians whose established doctrines have ascertained the meaning that "these words are correct.
This designation of identity is due to extreme similarity; for moonlight indeed dispels darkness.

Just as the sun illuminates objects and dispels the heat produced by contact with its rays, so too does this series of sentences in the form of a treatise dispel the darkness of ignorance and effortlessly illuminate the essential meanings of the works of the Three Sages.

Furthermore, it pacifies the mental anguish born from the intensive study of great works such as the extremely extensive and difficult *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa*; thus, due to extreme similarity, the identification [of this work] with the *Candrikā* is justified. It is "being composed" (*viracyate*), meaning it is being created (*kriyate*).

The designation "present" is used because of its proximity to the present time. To the question "Having done what?", he says: "having paid homage to the Three Sages. "Trayam" means that this collection has three parts; it is a collection consisting of three parts. The secondary suffix *tayap* is applied according to the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*. By the rule *dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyajvā*, the substitute *ayac* is applied for *tayap*. Thus, [the compound] is *munīnāṃ trayam* (the triad of sages).

This is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). It means, in effect, "the collection of three sages. Although the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would be impossible due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*)—since the word *muni* is dependent on the word *tri* for its non-differentiation (*abhedānvaya*)—nevertheless, there are three constituent parts.

First, it must be explained that "the triad of this collection" [is the meaning]; here, because the word *tri* (three) connects with the entire collection even without depending on the word *muni*, there is no lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). Consequently, in the phrase "the triad of sages" (*munīnāṃ trayaṃ*), the word *muni* connects with the collection, since it serves as the meaning of the suffix.

Because of its predominance. However, there is no syntactic relation of identity between the word *muni* and the word *tri*, which is a constituent part of the word *traya*, according to the maxim: "A word-meaning connects with a word-meaning, not with a constituent part thereof. Consequently, [this applies] to the words *muni* and *tri*.
When there is a syntactic connection with the aggregate according to the rules of word-meaning between two [words] that are unaware of each other's discourse,

then— since number has the nature of being a delimiter— upon the consideration of the object to be delimited, it is only the meanings of the other proximate words [that are so delimited], because they are presented by those other words.

They are connected by way of qualification—as "the collection of the three sages. This subsequent syntactic connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*) is easily understood by those who know the logic of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa* [PMS 3.1.12]; therefore, enough with further detail. In the term *munitrayam*, the accusative case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule "namas-svasti... [Pāṇini 2.3.16].

But the fourth case is not used here, because the greater strength of the kāraka-case (the accusative) will be explained later. "Having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*) means having gratified [the deity] by means of an action such as the joining of palms and the touching of the head.
[The root] *namas-kṛ* [implies] the joining of palms and the head...

If [the root] were to signify merely an operation consisting of conjunction and so forth, it would follow that it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), which would result in the impossibility of using the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). Now, one might object that since the established tenets of grammar are already fully satisfied by the very texts that summarize them, such as the *Prakriyākaumudī* and other works of the ancients; [therefore, a separate work is unnecessary].
To the question, "What is the purpose of this treatise? he says: "and having thoroughly reflected upon their statements. Their statements (*taduktayaḥ*) refer to the utterances of those three sages;
they consist of a series of sentences in the form of works comprising Sūtras, Vārttikas, and Bhāṣyas. Having thoroughly reflected upon these.
The meaning is "having correctly reflected. This form is derived from the root *bhū* with the self-referential suffix *ṇic*.

For the author of the *Mūla* himself will state that the root *bhū*, when ending in *ṇic* in the *Curādigaṇa* under the rule "bhuvo 'vakalkane," also possesses the sense of "reflecting" (*cintana*). Nor [does this contradict] the [rule regarding] "disrespect" (*anādara*).

One should not suspect a contradiction with the *Abhidhānakośa*, which states: "paribhavaḥ, parībhāvaḥ, tiraskriyā [are synonyms]," because that lexicon refers specifically to the root *bhū* when it is not followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). According to the rule "parau bhuvo 'vajñāne" (Pāṇini 3.3.54), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) to the root *bhū* preceded by *pari* when it functions in the sense of contempt (*tiraskāra*), provided it is not causative.

This is because the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *paribhāva* is understood [in this sense]. And thus, regarding the phrase "their statements" (*taduktīḥ*), since the pronoun *tat* refers to what is present in the mind, the explanation is that it means "having set aside the statements of the predecessors— the authors of the *Prakriyākaumudī*, the *Prasāda*, and so forth."

It was overlooked because it is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). By this, it is indicated that his own work follows the treatises of the Three Sages (*munitraya*), whereas ancient works such as the *Prakriyākaumudī* and others are contrary to them. And this has indeed been explained in detail by the author himself in the *Praudhamanoramā*.

By its etymologically significant name, *Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī*, the established doctrines of grammar (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntāḥ*) are the subject matter (*viṣaya*), as they are what is to be expounded. The purpose (*prayojana*) is the effortless comprehension of those doctrines. And the relationship (*saṃbandha*) between that treatise and [the purpose] is that of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*).
It is indicated that the qualified student is one who desires to know the established tenets of grammar (*vaiyākaraṇasiddhānta*).

Now, intending to set forth those established tenets of grammar, he recites the fourteen root-sūtras (*mūlasūtra*) of the science of grammar, beginning with *aiuṇ*. But [one may ask], what are these sūtras?
To the objection that [this system] is not authoritative because it stands outside the texts of the three sages (the Vedas), he says: "These are the Sūtras of Maheśvara.
They are called *māheśvarāṇi* because they have come from Maheśvara (*maheśvarād āgatāni*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "tata āgataḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.74).
That is to say, they were obtained from Maheśvara. As it has been said:

In the *Śikṣā* composed by the disciple of Pāṇini: "Salutation to that Pāṇini, who, having received the traditional collection of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*) from Maheśvara, proclaimed the entire grammar. This is stated in the commentary on these fourteen sūtras composed by Nandikeśvara.

It is also stated in the *Kāśikā*: "At the conclusion of the dance, the King of Kings of Dancers sounded his drum nine times with five strokes, desiring to uplift the Siddhas such as Sanaka and others through this web of Śiva-sūtras for their contemplation."
Here, the root *nad* in *nanāda* contains an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), meaning "he caused the drum (*ḍhakkā*) to resound.

*Nava-pañca-vāram* means fourteen times. This collection of phonemes (*varṇajāla*) has arisen from the drum of Śiva; the meaning is that I recognize it as the network of the *Śivasūtras* through contemplation (*vimarśa*). The *taṅ* suffix is used according to Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). And thus:

The claim that these [sūtras] are called "Māheśvara" because they were spoken by Maheśvara is refuted. By this, it is stated that there is no lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in these sūtras simply because they belong to Maheśvara.
Now, even so, one might object: what of these sūtras, which consist merely of a collection of meaningless syllables?
Since there would be no utility in introducing [the definitions of technical terms] here for the purpose of illuminating the established tenets of grammar, he says:
"They are for the sake of technical names such as *aṇ*. Those which have *aṇ* as their first are "those beginning with *aṇ*" (*aṇādayaḥ*).

These are both "those beginning with *aṇ*" and "technical names" (*saṃjñāḥ*), hence "technical names such as *aṇ*" (*aṇādisaṃjñāḥ*). These are the "purpose" (*arthaḥ*)—that is, the objective—of which [the rules].

These [terms]—such as *aṇ* and so forth—are technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for specific meanings. The sense is that although these sūtras consist of a collection of meaningless phonemes (*anarthaka-varṇarāśi*), they are not purposeless because they are employed in the technical designations such as *aṇ*, which are useful for the linguistic conventions found within the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*). How are these...?
To show that the *sūtras* have the status of being [technical] designations (*saṃjñā*) for their own final elements, he says: "The finals of these are *it*.

This means that among these aforementioned *sūtras*, the phonemes occurring at the end—such as the letter *ṇ* and others—are to be understood as having the designation *it*. In the *laṇ* *sūtra*, the word "and" (*ca*) implies that the vowel *a* is also included; the word "finals" (*itaḥ*) is supplied from the previous rule.
