And that [term] is modified into the singular number. The meaning is that in the *laṇ* sūtra, the letter *a* following the letter *l* is to be understood as having the technical designation *it*.
It is mentioned separately because it is not at the end [of the sūtra]. Now, one might object: if the letter *a* has the designation *it* in the *laṇ* sūtra itself...
Regarding the purpose of the repeated utterance of the vowel *a* in the passage beginning with *hayavara*, he says:

"The vowel *a* [is used] for the sake of pronunciation in the case of *ha* and the others. This means that the *a* is recited repeatedly for the sake of the easy pronunciation of *ha* and the other consonants. Otherwise...
The meaning is that otherwise, there would result the fault of a defiled (kliṣṭa) pronunciation, such as *hÂyÂva*.

Alternatively, since consonants (*hal*) cannot be pronounced without a vowel (*ac*), the repeated recitation of the letter *a* should be explained as being for the purpose of pronouncing the *ha*-sounds and so forth. For this very reason, [the sūtra] states: "That which is uttered loudly is udātta."

It is stated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya: "The pronunciation of a consonant does not occur without a vowel. In this regard, the repeated pronunciation of the letter *a* here serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus, when the suffix *kāra* is applied according to the rule *varṇāt kāraḥ*, forms such as *kakāra* arise.
Furthermore, [the rule applies] at the end of words such as *vāk*, and before conjunct consonants such as in *vṛkṣa*. At the end of a word, [the rule applies] after the consonants *c* and *j*.

This restriction does not hold, due to the force of rules such as "kuḥ" and others, as well as the authority of grammatical treatises such as "consonants that are not separated by vowels constitute a *saṃyoga*. Now, an objection may be raised: in the fourteen aphorisms, the designation *it* for the phonemes beginning with *ṇ* and ending with *m* has been promised by the statement, "the final letters of these are *it*."

That is untenable; for their *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it") must be stated by means of the rule *halantyam*. And that rule can only operate after the meaning of the word *hal* has been understood. Furthermore, the *halsaṃjñā* (the designation "hal") [depends on] the rule *hal*, provided that the *itsaṃjñā* of the letter *l* exists [therein], according to the rule *ādirantyena sahetā*.

This is to be stated by the rule [Pāṇini 1.3.3]. Furthermore, the designation *it* for the letter *l* in the rule *hal* (1.3.3) depends on the operation of the rule *halantyam* (1.3.3); and in the rule *halantyam*, the establishment of the technical term *hal* for the letter *l*—which itself has the designation *it*—depends on the rule *ādirantyena sahetā* (1.1.72). Thus, the two rules *halantyam* and *ādirantyena* are mutually dependent.

There is a lack of understanding due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). Thus, having raised the objection that it would be improper for Pāṇini to teach the *it*-designation for the letters in the *hal* group by means of the rule "the last letter of a *hal* [group] is an *it*" (*halantyam*)— without first relying on the designation *hal* itself and without having taught the *it*-designation for the letter *l* through some other rule in the *hal* sūtra— [the author proceeds as follows].

Without depending on the technical designation *hal*, he introduces the first rule—*halantyam*—by repeating the *hal* rule (*halantyam*) twice in order to prescribe the *it* designation for the letter *l*.
*Halantyam* | 1.3.3 | This is a single-word sūtra. The analysis of the compound is: that which is at the end (*antya*) of a *hal* [consonant] is "the final consonant" (*halantyam*).

Because the group beginning with *śauṇḍa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, there is either a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*, or a compound of two *sup*-inflected words (*sup-supā*). Here, the word *hal* refers to the technical term (*sūtra-param*). From the preceding rule, *upadeśe 'janunāsika it*, the word *it* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. Thus he says: "In the rule [beginning] with *hal*, etc. The phrase *itsyāt* means that it should be designated as having the technical name *it*.

This is stated because of the introduction of the term *saṃjñā* (technical name). Thus, by this sūtra, the designation *it* for the letter *l* in the *hal*-sūtra is established even without depending on the *hal*-designation; therefore, the sense is that there is no circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).
(2) *Ādir antyena sahetā* (P. 1.1.71): [A group of sounds] beginning with the first and ending with the final, together with the marker (*it*), constitutes a single technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Granted that the letter *l* has the designation *it* in the rule for *hal*. What follows from that? To this he says: "The first [element] together with the last *it*. That which exists at the end is "the last" (*antya*). The meaning is that the first element, when pronounced together with that *it*, such as *aṇ* or *ac*, is the technical name (*saṃjñā*). In this context, "the first" (*ādi*) refers to that before which nothing exists and after which something exists; "the last" (*anta*) refers to that after which nothing exists and before which something exists.
The commentary on the sūtra *ādyantavat* states: "That [is] the end. Thus, by the words "beginning" (*ādi*) and "end" (*anta*), those situated in the middle are implied;

consequently, it is understood that [the term *pratyāhāra*] is their designation (*saṃjñā*). From the preceding sūtra, the word *svam* ("its own form") is carried over (*anuvartate*); this is then transformed into the genitive case.

This is what he says with the words "by the last," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and of its own": here, by the word *sva* (its own), only the first [letter] included within the category of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is referred to, and not the last as well; for this is understood from the fact that the last is subordinate, as indicated by the instrumental case in the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* ("when joined with *saha*, that which is not the principal [is designated by the third case]").

Furthermore, since pronouns generally refer to the primary subject, one might object: "How can the pratyāhāras *ik*, *uk*, *ic*, *yay*, *may*, and so forth be formed, given that the sounds *i*, *u*, and others do not occupy the initial position [in the alphabet]? This objection should not be raised, for here "initial position" does not depend upon the order of the grammatical rules (*sūtra*).

However, it depends upon the collection [of sounds] implied by the terms "beginning" and "end. Consequently, having mentally conceived a collection of phonemes starting from the letter *i* in *aiuṇ* and ending with the letter *k* in *Añlṛk*, one may conceive of the letter *i* as being the beginning of that collection. The same applies to [the groups] beginning with *ij*. Likewise:
Even the final [letter] depends solely upon a collection imagined by the intellect (*buddhi-kalpita-samudāya*), and not upon the physical thread (*sūtra*).

Consequently, the *rapratyāhāra* (the pratyāhāra consisting of *ra*) is easily grasped; otherwise, because the letter *a* would lack the status of being "final" in the *laṇ*-sūtra, that [pratyāhāra] would not exist. In this regard, if either of the two words "beginning" (*ādi*) or "end" (*anta*) were absent...

The phrase "of those situated in the middle" would not be obtained. For, in the absence of the word "beginning" (ādi), a phoneme being pronounced together with the final *it* would be understood only as the name for those phonemes occurring prior to the final one. Consequently, even the vowels beginning with *a* would be included in the *hal* pratyāhāra.

Because there is no distinction in their being preceded by the final letter; for if the word "by the final" were absent, it would follow that the initial letter, when pronounced together with the designated [final], would be the name for the letters occurring after it. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of even the letter *ha* and others being included in the *ac* pratyāhāra.

Because there is no distinction in their being situated after the initial *a* [vowel], if both were mentioned, the term "those situated in the middle" would be understood; thus, there is no fault. That which has nothing before it when something else exists is the beginning (*ādi*); that which has nothing after it when something else exists is the end (*anta*).

In the Bhāṣya, by means of the etymological definition of the words "beginning" (ādi) and "end" (anta), the middle elements are implied through their inseparable connection with the beginning and the end. Although the terms "beginning" and "end" can apply to both [the first and the last],
since this does not contradict the stated etymology, nevertheless, in this context, the terms "beginning" and "end" do not refer to two things.

For if that were the case, the initial [phoneme] being pronounced together with the final *it* would be understood as the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for itself and its own predecessors; because, according to the method already stated, it is impossible for the word "self" (*sva*) to refer to the final [phoneme]. Consequently, in the case of the term *uṇ*, it would result in the letter *ū* being the technical name for the vowel *u*. In that situation, [there would be no name] for a single phoneme...

The formulation of technical names (*saṃjñā*) consisting of two phonemes would become useless due to the resulting prolixity (*gaurava*), since the purpose of *pratyāhāras* is to achieve brevity in usage. Therefore, in this context, the words "beginning" (*ādi*) and "end" (*anta*) refer only to the middle [phoneme] of the group; by means of these two, the inclusion of those situated in the middle is obtained. What is the purpose of the word "iti"? [It serves to exclude] the *pratyāhāra* *am*.

It should not be [assumed] that [the *suṭ* augment] is included by the letter *m* in the word *ñamaṅṇa*. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the *suṭ* pratyāhāra might instead be formed by the letter *ṭ* in the word *ṭā*, since that [letter *ṭ*] is final with respect to the entire group ending in *ṭ*;
for there is no reason to bypass the first [available] [letter], and thus the *suṭ* pratyāhāra [is correctly formed by *ṇ*].

Because it must be grasped by the very same *āṬ* and *ṭakāra*. And it has been stated by Jaimini: "Or rather, the first [element] should be restricted, because the cause [of the rule] cannot be overstepped. I desist here for fear of prolixity. Thus, regarding the technical name *hal*: in the *hal*-sūtra, the letter *la* [is included] by the first sūtra, *hal-antyam*, which was repeated.

The meaning is that when the designation *saṃjñā* exists, and the designation *hal* is established by the rule "the first [letter] by means of the last," then the status of being a *hal* for the final phonemes— beginning with the letter *ṇa*— is established within the fourteen sūtras.
(3) *Hal-antyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: *halantyam*. This is the second sūtra of the two recited [in the Mahābhāṣya].

The analysis is: *hal* (consonant) is *antyam* (final). The word *hal* exists even as a neuter noun, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the neuter *antyam*. [This refers to the rule: *upadeśe'janunāsika it*.
From the preceding sūtra, the terms "upadeśe" (in the original enunciation) and "it" (the final phoneme) are carried over by implication.
Thus he says: "The final [phoneme] in the upadeśa," and so forth.
This refers to the final phoneme of roots, nominal stems, particles, pratyāhāra-sūtras, suffixes, substitutes, and augments.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) asks: "Now, what is this so-called *upadeśa*? To this, he says: "*Upadeśa* is the first pronunciation. The prefix *upa-* has the sense of "first" (*ādi*). The root *diś-* refers to the act of pronouncing. The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), such is the intention. And this is explained in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *ādeca upadeśe*.

This is clear: the instruction of verbal roots, sūtras, word-groups (gaṇas), the *uṇādi* suffixes, syntactical rules, gender, and the teaching of augments, suffixes, and substitutes are proclaimed as "upadeśas" (original instructions).
This ancient *kārikā*, however, has been refuted in various ways in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa* (a commentary on the *Prakriyā-kaumudī*).

[The objection is: "In the rule *upadeśe 'j-dit-am-tha-m-uḥ*," when the suffix *thamu* is applied, the vowel *u*—which serves merely for pronunciation—is dropped; yet, even though the *m* remains as the final element of the suffix, it should not be subject to the designation *it*. Thus, in this manner...
By the repetition of the second sūtra (*halantyam*), it is established that the letters *ṇ*, *k*, and so forth, which are final in the fourteen-sūtra section, receive the technical designation *it*.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "From that, once the designations such as *aṇ* and *ac* are established. From that...
The meaning is that immediately after the designation *it* is established for the sounds beginning with *ṇa*, the designations such as *aṇ* are established by the rule *ādir antyena*.
(4) *upadeśe 'janunāsika it* 1.3.2.

In the *Laṇ* sūtra, it was asserted that the letter *a* [is also included]. Since that *a* is neither final (*anantya*) nor a consonant (*ahal*), the designation *it* (itsaṃjñā) does not apply to it by virtue of the rule *halantyam*. Therefore, he states the sūtra that provides for its application:
*upadeśe*. Because the topic under discussion is technical designations (*saṃjñā*), the word "designation" (*saṃjñā*) is understood [to be supplied].

Thus he says: "In the instruction [of the term], it is *anunāsika*, etc. In the sūtra, the absence of *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *g*) in the word *aj* is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage. In the commentary, which states "it shall have the designation *ajit*," the absence of *kutva* is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. Now, one might object: is not a phoneme pronounced through both the mouth and the nose called *anunāsika*?

This will be explained immediately below. Since these few phonemes were uttered by the author of the treatise in that specific manner, while others were merely uttered with the mouth, how is this to be understood by those of the present day? To this, he says: "The nasalized [phonemes] are indicated by a formal declaration (*pratijñā*)."
Regarding the term *pāṇinīyāḥ*: that which is promised (*pratijñāyate*) or accepted (*abhyupagamyate*) is a "promise" (*pratijñā*).

This word is permanently feminine. Under the governing rule *striyām* ("in the feminine"), the suffix *aṅ* is applied after the root *i* (from *iṇ*) preceded by the prefix *upa-* and the particle *āt*, according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. The state of having a nasal (*anunāsika*) is "nasality" (*ānunāsikyam*). [This refers to] the promise.

The meaning is that those for whom nasalization (*ānunāsikya*) is prescribed are the students of Pāṇini who have accepted nasalization; that is to say, through the lineage of students, such an articulation by the authors of the treatise is easily understood even by people of the present day. Thus, in the *laṇ* sūtra, regarding the vowel *a*:
The designation *it* is established because of its nasality (*anunāsikatva*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That which resides in the *laṇ*-sūtra.
That which resides in the *laṇ*-sūtra is "that which stands in the *laṇ*-sūtra" (*laṇsūtrastha*).
That [sound] is both the vowel *a* and [the sound] residing in the *laṇ*-sūtra; thus, the letter *ra* in the form "ra," when uttered together with that [vowel *a*], [is designated as *it*].

The meaning is that [the letters] *r* and *l* constitute a technical name (*saṃjñā*). In reality, however, it is clearly stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that there is no *rapratyāhāra* at all. Now, it is established by the rule *ādirantyena* (P.
1.1.71) that the letters situated between [the first and last] as well as the first letter itself constitute a technical name. And thus, in the case of *pratyāhāras* such as *ajādi*...

Even if there is no apprehension of the final letters among those that have entered into the category of technical names (*saṃjñākoṭi*), there would still be an apprehension of *ṇ* and the others as well, because they are not different from the intermediate ones. Consequently,
in the earlier text stating "the designation [applies] to *r* and *l*," the mention of *r* and *l* alone is insufficient, since the letter *ṭ* is also included among the intermediate ones.
To the objection that [the vowels] should be included because they possess the quality of being *grāhya* (to be grasped), he says: "In the *pratyāhāras*, there is no inclusion of these *it*s.
This means that within the *pratyāhāras*—namely, the technical names such as *uṇ*, *aṇ*, and so forth—even those *it*s situated in the middle are not included.

Why is this? To this he says: "Because of the mention [in the sūtras] beginning with ‘*anunāsika*’ (*Pāṇini 1.1.8*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of rules such as ‘*tṛṣimṛṣikṛṣeḥ kāśrapasya*’ (*Pāṇini 6.1.159*) is intended. How is this a mention?

He states "for not" (*na hi*) because [it serves as] the reason for the point already mentioned. The construction here is: "In this word *anunāsika*, when the letter *ka* follows, the grammatical operation applicable to the vowel *i*—namely, the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*—is not observed.
For if there were indeed an inclusion of the short *it* vowels within the pratyāhāras beginning with *ac*, then...
In the *ac* pratyāhāra, because the letter *k* is included in the rule *añ ṛk*, it possesses the status of being an *ac*.
When that [the *k*] follows, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the *ik* vowel occurs by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*.
Then, by the rule *lopo vyor vali*, there is elision [of the *y*]. Thus, the form would be *anunāska*; the vowel *i* is not heard.
And it is heard [in the tradition]: "Therefore, it is understood that there is no inclusion of these *it* vowels within the *pratyāhāra*s"—this is the intended meaning.

As for the case of *Añ-lṛk*, although the *k* is included in the *ac-pratyāhāra*, neither the *yaṇ* substitution nor elision occurs precisely due to the force of the rule prescribing *it*-ness, namely *pratyayasthāt* and so forth; otherwise, for the sake of brevity, one would have prescribed elision alone. Therefore, in the *pratyāhāra*s, the *it* vowels...
Regarding the statement "there is no inclusion [of the nasal]," some say that the mention of *anunāsika* and so forth is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

That is not correct; for in the rule prescribing elision—"the elision of the *a* preceding a *k* belonging to an affix occurs before an *āp*-ending that is not a *sup*"—there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the entire phoneme and so forth.
Because the meaning of the word *pratyāhāra* is not well-known, he says "the first [letter] with the last," etc.

The intention is that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is "those phonemes (*varṇa*) which are drawn back (*pratyāhriyante*) or condensed. Nor should one fear the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to technical names such as *aiu*, which are established by the rule *aṇudit sūtra*.

The sense is that such conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) arises from relying on both *yoga* (etymological derivation) and *rūḍhi* (conventional usage), as well as by virtue of what is established among grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).

In that regard, within the sūtras of the *varṇasamāmnāya*, there is one *pratyāhāra* with the preceding *ṇakāra*: *aṇ*; three with the *kakāra*: *ak*, *ik*, and *uk*; one with the *ṅkāra*: *eṅ*; and [one] with the *cakāra*.

There are four [pratyāhāras] beginning with *ac*: *ac*, *ic*, *ec*, and *aic*. With the letter *ṭ*, there is one: *aṭ*. With the following letter *ṇ*, there are three: *aṇ*, *iṇ*, and *yaṇ*. With the letter *m*, there are four: *am*, *yam*, *ñaṃ*, and *ṅm*. With the letter *ñ*, there is one: *yañ*. With the letter *ṣ*, there are two: *jhaṣ* and *bhaṣ*. With the letter *ś*, there are six: *aś*.

*Ha*, *va*, and *jhaś* [include] *jaś* and *baś*. With the letter *v*, there is one: *ec-chav*. With the letter *y*, there are five: *yay*, *may*, *jhay*, *khay*, and *cay*. With the letter *r*, there are five: *yar*, *jhar*, *khar*, *car*, and *śar*. With the letter *l*, there are six: *al*, *hal*, *val*, *ral*, *jhal*, and *śal*. With the letter *a*, there is one.

Regarding "rapratyāhāraḥ": there are forty-four *pratyāhāras* belonging to the traditional phonetic inventory (*vārṇasamāmnāya*), because only these are employed in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). However, *pratyāhāras* such as *iṅ*, *tyādi*, and so forth do not exist [in this context], because they serve no purpose and because they are not utilized within the treatise.
Regarding this, our summary verse (*saṅgrahakārikā*) states: "There may be one [substitute] with *ṅ*, *ñ*, *ṇ*, *va*, and *ṭ*; two with *ṣ*; three here with *k* and *ṇ*;
four with *c* and *m*; five with *y* and *r*; and six with *ś* and *l*.
(5) A vowel (*ac*) having the duration of *ū* is termed short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), or protracted (*pluta*). 1.2.27.
Thus, when the technical designations (saṃjñā) [of vowels] have been established, he prescribes the designations of "short" (hrasva) and so forth for the vowels (ac) with the rule:

*ūkālo’j*. The compound *hrasvadīrghapluta* is a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*), though its masculine gender is Vedic (*sautra*). Alternatively, it may be an associative dvandva (*itaretara-yoga-dvandva*). Likewise:

The singular number [in *satya*] is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). Regarding "u ū ū3": when these three—consisting of one mora (*mātrā*), two moras, and three moras—are formed into a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*), they are indicated as a conjunctive form (*praśliṣṭa-nirdeśa*) as "ū" by means of the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-dīrgha*). The duration (*kāla*) of those is "ū-kāla.
The word *kāla* is a synonym for *mātrā*, used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for that which resembles time. Thus, it is "ū-kāla."

The analysis of the compound is "that whose time is [such]. It is a two-member *bahuvrīhi* according to the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* may optionally be stated for a word preceded by a locative case or a word denoting a standard of comparison, with the elision of the subsequent member.
This is intended on the understanding that in the prior member of the word *ūkāla*, the subsequent constituent *kāla* is elided.

He states the established meaning with the words "vāṃ kāla iva," and so forth. The word *vaḥ* is the nominative plural of the pronoun *ū*. The word *vām* is the genitive plural. The phrase "vāṃ kāla iva kālo yasya" (that whose time is like the time of you two) expresses the resultant meaning. According to the method stated, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of only two members.
"Successively" (*kramāt*):
this is obtained from the *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence of order) sūtra. It would have been more appropriate to cite that sūtra right here.
Furthermore, how can the short, long, and protracted designations apply to the *u*-vowels *u*, *ū*, and *ū3*?

It should be stated that this is because they lack a time-period similar to that of the *ū* [vowel], since similarity is based on difference. In this context, the word *ū* is an imitation of the single-mora, two-mora, and three-mora crowing of a cock. As for "that" (*sa*): it refers to the short vowel.

The long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels (*ac*) each exist in three ways— meaning they occur in three modes— distinguished by specific properties (*dharmaviśeṣaṇa*) according to their being high-pitched (*udātta*), low-pitched (*anudātta*), or circumflex (*svarita*).

(6) *Uccair udātaḥ* | 1.2.29. He states the technical designation *udāta*: "The high-pitched [vowel] is *udāta*. Here, "highness" (*uccaiḥ*) is not intended to refer to a specific quality of the resonance (*nāda*), because that would result in non-application (*avyāpti*) to a vowel being pronounced in a whisper (*upāṃśu*).
However, the word *uccais* primarily denotes the locative capacity (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*) and functions in the sense of "in the upper part.

When there is a requirement for a whole (*avayavin*) for its upper part (*ūrdhvāvayava*), the meaning "of the places of articulation such as the palate, the throat, and so forth" is obtained by implication. [This refers to] the rule *ukālo'j*.
The term *aja* (unborn/unproduced) is understood to carry over from the preceding sūtra; this is what he expresses with the words beginning "in the palate and so forth.

The phrase "in the homogeneous parts" (*sabhāgeṣu*) is stated for the purpose of establishing that [the sound arises] in the "upper part," since if those [palates and so forth] were indivisible, the expression "in the upper part" would be untenable.

He illustrates the acute (*udātta*) accent with the example *ā ye* (from the Ṛgvedic verse *ā ye mitrāvaruṇā*). The meaning is that in this verse, the vowel *ā* and the vowel *e* are acute. (7) The grave (*anudātta*) is low-pitched. 1.2.30.

He states the definition of *anudātta*: "That which is produced low is *anudātta*. This is clear; the meaning is that, according to the method already described, a vowel (*ac*) produced in the lower part of the articulatory locations such as the palate (*tālu*) and so forth shall bear the designation *anudātta*. Thus, the purpose is to clarify this point. For example, in the Ṛgvedic verse "arvāṅ yajñassaṃkrāma," the initial vowel *a* is *anudātta*.
This is the meaning.
(8) *samāhāraḥ svaritaḥ* | 1.2.31 | Now he states the technical name *svarita*: "A combination (*samāhāra*) is *svarita*. From the two preceding rules, [the terms] *udātta*...

The term *anudāta* (unaccented) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. From the rule *ūkālo’j*, the term *ac* (vowel) is also understood to carry over. Consequently, the meaning understood would be that a vowel (*ac*) which is brought together as both udātta (acute) and anudātta (grave) is called *svarita* (circumflex).
This being the case, the designation *svarita* would apply to two phonemes (*varṇa*), not to one; therefore, this is not the intended meaning.

However, the two terms *udātta* and *anudātta*, which were previously understood as denoting the primary qualities (*dharma*), are here modified into the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). Thus, "samāhāra" refers to that in which there is a collection; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
Consequently, the vowel (*ac*) in which there is a conjunction of the two qualities—namely, the acute (*udātta*) and the grave (*anudātta*)—is [the one intended].
The meaning is that it is designated as *svarita*.

(9) Regarding [the rule] *tasyādita udātamardhahrasvam* (P. 1.2.32), he states the established conclusion with the words "the qualities of being *udātta* and *anudātta*" and so forth. Now, one might object:

Since there is a combination of both acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) tones within a single [svarita] sound, one might ask: in which part does the acute tone reside, and in which part does the grave tone reside? To this, he says: "Of that, from the beginning" (*tasyāditaḥ*).
This means that of that svarita, "from the beginning" (*āditaḥ*), i.e., in its prior portion, the first half-mora (*ardhahrasva*) is acute.

It is understood [from the context]. This being the case, this rule would not apply to long (*dīrgha*) and circumflex (*svarita*) vowels. Therefore, he says: "The mention of the short (*hrasva*) vowel is the governing factor" (*tantra*). *Tantra* means the primary element (*pradhāna*). As the lexicon states: "The word *tantra* is used for the primary element and for a settled doctrine. That which does not possess a primary element characterized by the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is *atantra*.
The meaning is that its sense is not intended to be expressed; that is to say, the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) need not be made.

The intention is that even in the case of long (*dīrgha*) and circumflex (*svarita*) vowels, the latter portion is observed to be unaccented (*anudātta*) in the Veda. Consequently, he states the resulting conclusion: "It should be understood that the first half of a *svarita* vowel is acute (*udātta*). Now, [an objection]:
To the question, "Why is the rule for the placement of the *anudātta* (unaccented) tone not stated? he says: "But the latter half [of the verse]," and so on.
Now, if this is the case, how is it that in the phrase *agnim īle*, when the vowel *ī* is *svarita* (circumflex), the latter half is not *anudātta*?
To this he says: "And of that," and so on. The word "and" (*ca*)...

This is for the purpose of poetic ornamentation (*vākyālaṅkāra*). Regarding that portion which is *anudātta* (unaccented): "having an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent following it" means that from which the *udātta* or *svarita* follows; the state of being such is "the condition of having an *udātta* or *svarita* following" (*udātasvaritaparatva*). This occurs when there is either the condition of having an *udātta* following or the condition of having a *svarita* following.

The meaning is that the hearing [of the sound] becomes clear. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": this means that when there is an absence of a following *udātta* or *svarita* accent, and instead there is a following *anudātta-pracaya*, the *Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya* prescribes an *udātta-śruti* for the portion of the *anudātta*; this is synonymous with being "more acutely accented" (*udātatara*). In that case—

It has been stated thus: "The remaining [portion] that follows is unaccented (anudātta), provided that it does not have the sound of an acute accent (udātta) nor is there any subsequent syllable pronounced as acute or circumflex (svarita). Thus, when the preceding part of a circumflex (svarita) is acute, the remaining following part is the latter portion.
It is to be understood as unaccented (*anudātta*). That which follows it is the remainder (*śeṣa*), yet in some cases it possesses the appearance of an acute accent (*udātta-śruti*).

Does this occur everywhere? No, he says—by the words beginning with "if not" (*na cet*). The construction is: "if no syllable, whether acute or circumflex (*svarita*), is uttered immediately after [it]. In that case, regarding the portion consisting of the unaccented [syllables]:

Having cited the clear hearing [of the svarita], he demonstrates it with the words beginning with "kva" and ending with "anudātta," stating: "In that context, *kva* is a short svarita; it is followed by the udātta vowel *o* in *vo*. *Ye'rā* is a long svarita; it..."

The meaning is that in such instances as these, the portion consisting of the *anudātta* (unaccented) is clearly heard: for example, in the word *ca*, the vowel *a* is followed by an acute (*udātta*) vowel; in the word *yaḥ* [of the phrase] *śatacakraṃ yaḥ*, the vowel *o* is a *kampa-svarita*; and that [svarita] is followed by the svarita vowel *a* in the word *hy a*. In other cases, however—

Having cited "tūdātaśrutiḥ," he demonstrates this by stating: "In *agnim īḷe* and so forth, there is the hearing of an acute accent (*udāttaśruti*). At the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, *agni-* is acutely accented on the final syllable; *īḷ* is grave (*anudātta*). Therein, according to the rule "after an acute, a grave becomes circumflex" (*udāttādanudātasya svaritaḥ*), the vowel *ī* becomes circumflex in the *saṃhitā*.

The *svarita* [accent]. By the rule "In *saṃhitā*, [the *pracaya* accent applies] to the *anudātta*s following a *svarita*," the letter *e* becomes *pracaya*. Consequently, since the letter *ī* is a *svarita* that does not have an *udātta* or *svarita* following it, the subsequent portion [of the vowel] possesses the quality of being more acutely accented (*udāttatara*), according to the aforementioned *Prātiśākhya* statement.

The meaning is that it becomes exclusively udātta (high-pitched). Thus, the short vowel is of three kinds: udātta-short, anudātta-short, and svarita-short. Likewise, the long vowel is also of three kinds, as is the protracted (pluta) vowel. Consequently, it is established that each individual vowel is ninefold. That...

"Even of nine kinds" means that, according to the method stated, even that [vowel *u*] exists in two ways—namely, by virtue of being nasal (*anunāsika*) and by virtue of not being nasal (*ananunāsika*). (10) A sound articulated through both the mouth and the nose is nasal (*anunāsika*). Pāṇini 1.1.8.
Thus, it is established that each vowel is of eighteen kinds, consisting of nine nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowels and nine non-nasalized (*ananunāsika*) vowels.
Now, he states the technical definition (*saṃjñā*) of the nasalized: "mouth-and-nose" (*mukhanāsikā*), meaning the nose together with the mouth.
"Mukhanāsikā" [is a compound] where the middle term "sahita" (accompanied by) is elided because it belongs to the class beginning with *śākapārthiva* (the king of vegetables).

It is called "vacanaḥ" (articulation) because it is spoken (*ucyate*) or uttered; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). The compound "mukhanāsikayā vacanaḥ" (articulation by means of the mouth and nose) is a third-case (*tṛtīyā*) tatpuruṣa compound, according to the rule "the agent or instrument is frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. This is what he expresses with the words "accompanied by the mouth," etc. However, it is not a *dvandva* (copulative) compound consisting of "mouth and nose."

That being the case, because of the rule "And a *dvandva* [compound] consisting of parts of living beings, musical instruments, or an army" which mandates a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva*, the neuter gender would apply by the rule "That [collective *dvandva*] is neuter. Consequently,
by the rule "The final vowel of a nominal stem is short in the neuter," the shortening of the vowel would occur, resulting in the undesirable form "mukhanāsikavacana."
Now, one might ask: "Are all eighteen varieties of vowels (ac) identical?

He says, "No"—namely, "That is thus" (*tad ittham*). The meaning is that this extensive elaboration of the varieties of vowels should be understood as being established "thus," in the manner that is about to be described.

"Eighteen varieties" means eighteen types. Regarding "due to the absence of the long [vowel]": thus there is the long *ḷ*-vowel with the acute (*udātta*) accent, the long *ḷ*-vowel with the grave (*anudātta*) accent, and the long *ḷ*-vowel with the circumflex (*svarita*) accent. And each of these is threefold—nasalized (*anunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*ananunāsika*).
The meaning is that since there is no absence of the six varieties [of short vowels], the expansion of the short and the expansion of the protracted (*pluta*) each consist of two types;
thus, the *ḷ*-vowel has exactly twelve varieties. This is because the long *ḷ* does not exist;
for instance, in the case of "hotṛ + ḷkāra," when the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) is applied, it becomes "hotṛkāra," which is indeed the same as the [long] *ṝ*-vowel.

In the *Akāravarṇa* Sūtra as well, the example cited in the Bhāṣya itself is the authority. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of short vowels": if the *ec* vowels were short, they would have been recited in the traditional list of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*) as *a, i, u*, and so forth, for the sake of brevity; they would not have been long, because that would involve prolixity. Therefore...

It is understood that there are no short *eco* vowels. Thus, because the sixfold division of the short *prapañca* vowels does not exist, the intended meaning is that these [diphthongs] possess only twelve varieties. (11) *Tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam* | 1.1.9 | [Vowels and consonants produced with the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*) are called homogeneous (*savarṇa*).]

Now, intending to state the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for *a*, *i*, *u*, and so forth—according to the rule "An *aṇ* and that which is marked with *u* [denote] their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), provided they are not suffixes" (Pāṇini 1.1.69)—he first states the definition of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*):
"Equal in the mouth" (*tulyāsya*). The word *āsya* means the mouth;

however, because the similarity of the mouth is indistinguishable across all phonemes and thus fails to serve as a differentiator, the word *āsya* here does not refer merely to the physical organ of the mouth.

However, *āsya* means that which exists in the mouth (*āsya*); it refers to the articulatory locations such as the palate and so forth. The suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" according to the rule *śarīrāvayavādyat*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel *a* of the base is elided. *Prayatna* is an effort that is pre-eminent (*prakṛṣṭa*). *Āsyaprayatnau* is the compound of *āsya* and *prayatna*. That collection of phonemes (*varṇajāla*) whose *āsya-prayatna* (articulatory location and effort) are identical [is what is meant].
The meaning is that those sounds which possess an identical articulatory effort (āsyaprayatna) shall be designated as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another.
He states this with the words "the place [of articulation] beginning with the palate," and so forth. The word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) means "with respect to one another.
When the expectation arises as to what the place of articulation is for which sound, the following are the determinants thereof:

He summarizes the statements of Pāṇini’s *Śikṣā* and others by their meaning, beginning with "akuha," etc. By "a," eighteen varieties are understood; by "ku," the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) consisting of the five letters starting with *ka* is meant. Nor is there any lack of application of the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya...* at this point.

How, in this case, can it be said that the eighteen varieties [of *a*] are included? This is because the rule proceeds by relying solely on worldly convention (*laukikaprasiddhi*). In the same way, a resolution should be understood for subsequent cases as well. The analysis of the compound is: *a* and *ku* and *ha* and the *visarjanīya*.
The word *visarjanīya* is also a synonym for *visarga*.

Regarding the rule *icuyaśa*: *i* refers to the eighteen varieties [of the vowel *i*]. *Cu* refers to the *cavarga* (the *c*-group). The analysis of the compound is: *i* and *cu* and *ya* and *śa*. *Tālu* means the palate (*kākuda*).

Regarding the term *ṛtuaraṣe*: *ṛ* refers to the eighteen varieties [of the vowel ṛ]. *Ṭua* refers to the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*). The analysis of the compound is: "ā," and "ṭua," and "ra," and "ṣa. The word *ṛ* takes the form *ā*, ending in the nominative singular, just as the word *dhātā* does.

Regarding *lṛtulaśa*: there are twelve varieties of *lṛ*. *Tu* refers to the dental class (*tavarga*). The analysis of the compound is: *ā*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa*. For the word *lṛ* as well, *ā* is the nominative singular ending. Thus: *ā*, *al*, *au*, *alaḥ*. By the word "tooth" (*danta*), the region of the root of the teeth is intended; otherwise, [the definition would be too narrow].
Because that pronunciation is impossible for one whose teeth are broken.
Regarding the rule *upūp* [Pāṇini 1.1.69]: *u* refers to the eighteen varieties [of the vowel *u*]; *pu* refers to the labial class (*pavarga*). The analysis of the compound is:
*u* and *pu*, together with the *upadhmānīya*. The word *upadhmānīya* itself [is defined] immediately below.

He will explain [the rule] as "ña-m-aṅ-ṇa-na. The analysis of the compound is: "ña and ma and ṅa and ṇa and na. By means of the word "ca" (and), there is a conjunction of each with its own corresponding place of articulation within its respective varga.

Regarding the term *edaitoḥ*: *e* and *ai* are *edaitau*. The addition of the marker *t* (the *tapara* suffix) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; it is not intended to restrict the application to only those sounds of that specific duration according to the rule *taparas tatkālasya*. Consequently, both protracted (*pluta*) vowels are also included. In the compound *kaṇṭhatālu*, since it consists of parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), which takes the singular number and neuter gender.

*odautoriti*: *od* and *aut* together form *odaut*. The inclusion of the *ta*-marker (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, as before. *Kaṇṭhaśca oṣṭhau ca* (the throat and the lips) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) because they are parts of a living being; it takes the singular number (*ekavadbhāva*) and the neuter gender.

Regarding the word "of *vakāra*": "teeth and lips" is a collective dvandva compound. The singular number and neuter gender [apply] to the term *jihvāmūlīya*. The word *jihvāmūlīya* will be explained later.
The same applies to the term *anusvāra*.
Regarding the phrase "thus the places": the meaning is that in this manner (*iti u*), the places for the manifestation of phonemes have been explained in detail.

Now, in this regard, does the *tulyāsyaprayatna* sūtra intend any similarity whatsoever of place of articulation, or rather a similarity of all places of articulation? It cannot be the first, for if that were so, since the phonemes *i* and *e* share the palate (*tālu*) as their place of articulation, they would become homogeneous (*savarṇa*); consequently, in the word *bhavaty eva*, when *e* follows *i*, [the rule for lengthening would apply].
Otherwise, the rule for long vowels of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) would not apply.

Nor should it be argued that the letter *e* lacks homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the letter *i* due to its inclusion in the phonetic inventory (*varṇasamāmnāya*), because the inclusion of *e* therein could serve the purpose of excluding it from the *pratyāhāras* such as *ak*, *ik*, and *uk*. Furthermore:

If the vowels *va* and *la* were to attain homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to the similarity of their dental place of articulation, then by the rule "after *t*, *l*" (*tor la*), the letter *l* would include *v* as well;

consequently, in the word *tadvān*, the letter *d* would undergo substitution by a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). Furthermore, the inclusion of *l* in the rule "when followed by *ya*, *va*, *la*, or *pa*, [the preceding semivowels] may optionally be *ya*, *va*, *la*, or *pa*" would be for the sake of establishing a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*).
It cannot be the second alternative, because even though *ka* and *ṅa* share the same place of articulation—the throat—[the rule would otherwise fail to apply to *ṅa*].

If it is argued that the equality of place (*sthānasāmya*) is difficult to establish— because if there were an excess of nasalization (*nāsikāsthāna*), the status of being a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) would not obtain, and consequently, the letter *ṅ* could not be included in the rules "acoḥ kuḥ" and "kvinpratyayasya," which would result in the letter *ṅ* not arising for the *n* of the *num* augment in words such as *prāṅ* by virtue of the rule "kvinpratyayasya"— then, regarding this:

We reply: the determining factor for homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) is precisely the identity of the place of articulation (*sthāna*). Thus, although the *i*-sound and the *e*-sound share the same palatal place of articulation, they do not possess homogeneity because the *e*-sound has the additional place of articulation of the throat (*kaṇṭha*). Furthermore, there is no homogeneity between the *v*-sounds and the *l*-sounds, because the *v*-sound...

This is because the lips constitute an additional point of articulation (*sthāna*). And thus, designations such as "tadvānāsām" (Pāṇini 1.1.69) and "yajuṣyekeṣām" (Pāṇini 1.2.34) are justified. Even though the letter *ṅ* has the nose as an additional point of articulation, it still possesses homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) with the letter *k*, since the requirement for homogeneity is merely the similarity of the oral cavity (*āsya*) as the place of articulation.
Because it serves as the basis for homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), and because the nose is not included within the mouth.

And it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "What, then, is the mouth? It is that which is worldly [i.e., physical], from the lips up to the *kākalaka*. Kaiyaṭa explains: "'Kākalaka' is the name for the elevated region on the neck below the chin.
Therefore, homogeneity is caused by the similarity of place (*sthāna*) as far as it exists within the mouth.

There is a detailed discussion in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Now, it has been established that in the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (P. 1.1.9), by the force of the prefix *pra-* in the word *prayatna*, internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) is intended. In that case, what is the purpose of the qualification "internal" (*ābhyantara*)?

Because there is no [other] thing to be excluded, he says: "Effort is twofold. That efforts are internal and external consists in their occurring respectively before and after the production of the phoneme; this is clear from the *Śikṣās* of Pāṇini and others.
Regarding the word "the first": the meaning is "internal effort. As to how there is a fourfold division, [he says]:
He says: "Touched" (*spṛṣṭa*).

In response to the inquiry as to which [articulation] belongs to which [effort], he recites the statements from the *Śikṣā* that establish this: "In that regard" (*tatra*), meaning among those [articulations]. "The act of effort" (*prayatanam*), meaning effort (*prayatna*).
He will explain the words *sparśa* and so forth later. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the short *a*-vowel is "closed" (*saṃvṛta*).

This much alone is the statement of the *Śikṣā*. [Objection: But if this were so, then in the case of *daṇḍa-āḍhakam*, because the two *a*-sounds would lack homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to the difference between the "open" (*vivṛta*) and "closed" (*saṃvṛta*) articulatory efforts (*prayatna*), the long vowel substitution for homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*) would not occur.

To this he says: "In usage" (*prayoga*). The meaning is that the state of being *saṃvṛta* (contracted) belongs to the short vowel *a* only when words such as *rāmaḥ* and *kṛṣṇaḥ*, which have been fully established through the grammatical processes (*prakriyā*) of the treatise, are actually employed in usage. Regarding "process" (*prakriyā*): at the time of the operation of the grammatical rules of the treatise, however...

The meaning is that even the short *a*-vowel is indeed *vivṛta* (open). Having set aside the natural *saṃvṛta* (closed) state of the short *a*-vowel— which is established by the statements of the *Śikṣā*— because it is taught as being *vivṛta* in the *Varṇasamāmnāya*, which is the root of the entire treatise, at the time of the application of all the grammatical processes (*prakriyā*) of the science...

It is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *aiuṇ* that even for the short *a*-vowel, because it is pronounced with a wide opening (*vivṛta*), operations such as the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) in forms like *daṇḍāṭatam* are unimpeded.
And thus, the statement in the Śikṣā that "the short *a*-vowel is contracted" (*saṃvṛta*) [is not contradicted].
The sense is that, by process of elimination, [the injunction] culminates precisely in the state of final perfection; therefore, it is not purposeless.

He states "And this" to show that this restriction of the words of the *Śikṣā* is also the view of the author of the Sūtras. To demonstrate that very point, he sets forth his proposition with "For thus."
The meaning is that this is clearly established in such a way as to be made known.
*a a*: This is the final sūtra of the grammatical treatise (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), consisting of two words. Therein, *a* is the first.

The first word has the vowel *a* followed by a *vivṛta* (open) sound, with the genitive case-ending elided; the second, however, has the vowel *a* followed by a *saṃvṛta* (contracted) sound, with the nominative case-ending elided. Consequently, having set aside the natural state of being *saṃvṛta* established by the rules of phonetics (*śikṣā*), [the text refers to] the vowel *a* which is taught as *vivṛta* in the traditional list of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*).

The meaning is that [the vowel] becomes closed (*saṃvṛta*) and lacks the quality of *avarṇa*. He says this with the words "having restated what was open" (*vivṛtamanūdya*). "Is prescribed" (*vidhīyate*) means "is reintroduced" (*pratiprasūyate*). Now, one might ask: why does this rule not apply even during the state of scattering (*prakriyā*)? To this he says: "And of this..."—that is, of this sūtra *oa* (P. 1.1.9), [referring] to its own preceding...

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the entire *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is *asiddha* (not yet established) [with respect to each other], it is non-existent; therefore, at the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), the state of being *vivṛta* (open) certainly exists. Now, one might ask: how can there be a departure from the natural state of closure (*saṃvṛtatva*) for a short *a*-vowel during the stage of derivation, or how can it possess the quality of being *vivṛta*? [This is so] because of that...

To the objection that [the reason] is "because it has the nature of being perceived," he says: "as seen in the treatise" (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*). Here, what is intended by "unestablishedness" (*asiddhatva*) is not actual, absolute non-existence;
rather, it consists precisely in the superimposition of non-existence. By this much, the intrinsic [nature] is not [negated].
The meaning is that there is no falling away from the state of being *saṃvṛta* (closed) for that [vowel], nor is its *vivṛtatva* (openness) real;

rather, *vivṛtatva* is superimposed for the sake of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Now, as to what proof there is for the fact that the rule "a a" (*a a*) is *asiddha* with respect to the entire *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, he says: "And thus..."

Regarding the term *sūtram*: the particle *ca* has the sense of "for" (*hi*). Thus, the meaning is that there exists a rule (*sūtram*) that makes [the matter] understood in that manner. (13) *pūrvatrāsiddham* 8.2.1.
He states such a rule: "That which is not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*). This refers to the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* composed by Pāṇini.

Among its parts, this is the first rule of the second quarter (*pāda*) of the eighth chapter (*adhyāya*). All the collection of rules preceding this is designated as the "seven chapters and a quarter" (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*). As for the subsequent [portion],...

It is an established principle that the entire collection of aphorisms (*sūtra-jāla*) is designated as the "Three-Footed" (*tripādī*). In this regard, if this aphorism were an independent injunction (*svatantra-vidhi*), then the meaning obtained would be that while the preceding section of the treatise is being applied, the subsequent section would remain unestablished. And consequently—

It would result in the conclusion that "the Tripādī is not established with respect to the Sapādasaptādhyāyī. This being the case, even within the Tripādī itself, the principle that "a subsequent rule is not established with respect to a preceding rule" could not be obtained.
If that were so, then in the example *kim u uktam* (*kimvuktam*), the rule *mo 'nusvāraḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.23]— [The remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

Regarding the rule *maya uño vo vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.32), which belongs to the third section (*traipādika*), he says "this is an *adhikāra*" so that this *traipādika* rule of substitution with *v* shall not be considered asiddha (non-existent) [with respect to other *traipādika* rules]. It is called an *adhikāra* because it is "governed" (*adhikriyate*)—that is, it is read as a supplement to the subsequent collection of sūtras. The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Its masculine gender follows from the rule *ghañajabantāḥ puṃsi*. The word "this" (*ayam*) refers back to it.

The mention of the masculine gender (*puṃliṅganirdeśaḥ*) is solely for the purpose of carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent rules; that is to say, it is not an independent injunction. In the rule *maya uño vo vā*, the phrase *pūrvatrāsiddham* (what is established in what precedes is as if non-existent) is carried over. Consequently, the substitution of *v* for the *u* following *mayat* is optional.
It may be so. This rule, "this treatise is not established with respect to what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), becomes a single syntactical unit with that [rule].

And in that context, by the word *pūrva* which is carried over [from the previous rule], the entire collection of sūtras situated in the three chapters (*tripādī*) as well as those situated in the seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*) prior to this is intended; thus, the rule "m becomes anusvāra" (*mo'nusvāraḥ*), which belongs to the three chapters...

Regarding the rule *maya uño vo vā*, he states that the non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of that rule is beyond dispute by saying "by that" (*tena*). This means "by virtue of being an *adikāra*. He says, "the subsequent rule is non-valid. And here, non-validity does not mean absolute non-existence; rather, it is as follows:

It was stated immediately above that [this] is "seen in previous treatises. By the phrase "the supreme treatise" (*paraṃ śāstram*), it is implied that the non-validity of the "non-completion of an operation" (*kāryāsiddhatva*) as taught in works such as the *Prakriyākaumudī* is unauthoritative.

This is because, after having raised the "non-completion of an operation" as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the status of "non-completion of a rule" (*śāstrāsiddhatva*) alone was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in this sūtra and in the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra "asiddhavad atrābhāt."
The difference in results between being established by a grammatical rule (*śāstrasiddha*) and being non-established due to its effect (*kāryāsiddhatva*) is clear in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

We shall elaborate upon this during our own commentary on the root text in the section on the sandhi of *svādi* (Pāṇini 1.4.17) regarding the word *manoratha*, as well as in the section on the derivation of the word *adaḥ* under the heading of words ending in consonants (*halanta*).

Thus, because the rule for *saṃvṛta* [vowels]—namely, "a a"—is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the entire preceding *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, it is established that during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), the short *a*-vowel is indeed *vivṛta*;
its *saṃvṛta* state occurs only in the final, perfected form (*pariniṣṭhita-daśā*). Even though...

In the state of final establishment (*pariniṣṭhita-daśā*), the rules of conventional usage (*saṃvṛta-vidhi*) are not applicable anywhere in this treatise; nevertheless, it must be understood that even when [the word] is in its established form, it is fit for usage only when there is knowledge of it as being conventionally established by the force of the rules of conventional usage.

Or rather, one should assume a difference in the articulation of the open (*vivṛta*) and the closed (*saṃvṛta*) vowels; enough of this prolixity. Now, he elaborates upon the external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*): "The external effort, however... Here, the prefix *pra-* is to be considered; for by the force of the prefix *pra-*, it is established in the *Tulyāsyasūtra* that only internal effort is denoted by the term *prayatna*.

Because it has already been stated, and because of the introductory statement "effort is twofold," the prefix *pra-* here does not intend its literal meaning. The words *udātta*, *anudātta*, and *svarita* refer to the properties [of sounds]. In response to the inquiry as to which [sounds] possess which external effort, he summarizes their systematic arrangement in two verses:
"By their exhaustion (*khayāt*). The word *yama* will be explained later.

Those whose secondary effort (*anupradāna*) is breath are "those with breath as their secondary effort," meaning they possess the external effort known as expiration (*uśvāsa*). "They open the throat":
the sense is that their effort is one of expansion (*vivāra*). "Closed" (*saṃvṛta*) means possessing the effort known as contraction (*saṃvāra*).
"Partakers of *nāda*" means those possessing the effort known as *nāda*. "The odd ones among the classes and the *yamas*" refers to the five classes:

the five beginning with *ka*, the five beginning with *ṭa*, the five beginning with *ta*, and the five beginning with *pa*. Among those situated in the classes and those situated among the *yamas*, the "odd ones" mean the first, third, and fifth letters.

"Having little *āsu* (vital breath)" means having few life-forces. Now, intending to explain the two verses, he first explains the word *yama* in a general sense with the words beginning "in the groups," etc. The phrase "of the first four" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

The sixth [case ending]. The word "from each one" (*ekaikasmāt*) must be supplied. By this, the objection that the genitive case is inappropriate for the first four [words] because the fifth case would apply due to the rule "with *anya*, *ārāt*, *itara*, *ṛte*, and *para*" (*anyārāditararte*) when joined with the word *para* is refuted. Regarding the phrase "the one named Yama": the word *nāma* is a synonym for *iti*.

This is the meaning: among the letters consisting of the five groups beginning with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*, when any one of the four initial letters of a group is followed by the fifth letter of that same group, the letter similar to the preceding one that occurs in between is known as a *yama* in the *Prātiśākhya*. Now...

Having introduced the term *yama*, he demonstrates them with the passage beginning with "the widow" (*palikknī*) and ending with "those very similar are the *yamas*. In this manner, the examples for the *yamas* of the other groups should also be understood as "begging" (*yācñā*), and so forth. Thus, having explained the word *yama* in a general sense, [he presents] two verses...
He explains this with the words beginning "therein" (*tatra*). Therein, the explanation of "the *kha-ya*s" is:

"the first and second [consonants] of the classes are the *kha-ya*s. The elaboration of "the *yam*s among the *kha-ya*s" is: "likewise, the *yam*s of those very [consonants]. [The explanation] of "the *ka-pau*s" is...

The commentary [states]: "the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya. Because it is well known, the word *visarga* is not explicitly mentioned [in the rule]. The commentary on the term *śara* is: "śa, ṣa, sa, and ha. He explains the statement, "These have aspiration as their secondary effort (*anupradāna*), are voiceless, and open the throat," by saying: "For these, there is openness (*vivāra*), aspiration, and voicelessness. "The others..."

He explains the statement "but the voiced [consonants] are those possessing sound (nāda) and voice (ghoṣa)" as follows: "for others, however, there is closure (saṃvāra), sound (nāda), and voice (ghoṣa). He explains the statement "the first, third, and fifth of the classes, along with the semi-vowels (yama)," as follows: "the first, third, and fifth of the classes..."

Regarding the phrase "the first and third [of each group] are *yamas*": the implication is that there is an absence of *yamas* among the fifth [vowels]. He explains the statement "the *yaṇs* are remembered as having little breath" by saying, "and *ya-ra-la-va* have little breath. Now, one might object: "In the two verses, it was not stated that these [other consonants] are *mahāprāṇas* (having great breath); therefore, there is an omission. Anticipating this doubt, he says that even this is effectively stated by implication through elimination: "the others are *mahāprāṇas*."

Thus [it is said]: "The second and fourth letters of the classes, as well as ś and ṣ, are mahāprāṇa (aspirated). Now, one might object that the detailed exposition of external effort (*bāhyayatna*) here is useless, because in the *Tulyāsyasūtra*, the word *prayatna* refers exclusively to internal effort; thus he raises this doubt with the words "And the external efforts. The phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*) indicates the nature of the doubt. He refutes it with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

Although there is no utility for the external efforts (*bāhyayatna*) in the context of the definition of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasaṃjñā*), they are not useless because they do have utility in the consideration of "nearest similarity" (*antaratama*) which will be stated in the rule *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*.
The detailed exposition of this point occurs here in the sūtra on the "equal oral cavity" (*tulyāsyasūtra*).
The sense is that this is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), because it is presented as the exclusion resulting from the qualification "being internal" (*ābhyantaratva*).

However, since it is well known that the triad beginning with *udātta* (high pitch) is a property of vowels (*aj-dharma*), their specific determination is not stated here. Now, regarding the section beginning with "the effort (*prayatana*) of the *sparśa* [consonants] is *spṛṣṭa* (contact)."

He explains the terms "touch" (*sparśa*) and so forth that were introduced by the verse beginning with *kādayo...*: "Those whose first letter is *ka* are the *kādayaḥ*; those whose last letter is *ma* are the *māvasānaḥ*. This is based on the reading as established in common worldly usage.
"Thus ends the distinction between place and effort (*sthāna-yatna-viveka*). This means that the analysis of places of articulation and efforts has been completed.
As for the reading *sthāna-prayatna* (with the prefix *pra*), it is to be considered doubtful, or the prefix *pra* may be intended as having no specific meaning here.

Since the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ* have different places of articulation—consisting of the palate and the teeth respectively—the technical designation of being "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) does not apply to them. Therefore, he recites the relevant Vārttika, which prescribes this status, summarizing its meaning: "There is mutual homogeneity between the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*. The expression *ā ca ā ca ralau* is explained as follows: *ṛ* and *ḷ* are denoted by the term *ra-lau*. Here, the word *ṛ* takes the nominative singular ending *ā*. Thus, *ā ca ā ca* refers to both *ṛ* and *ḷ*. These two are homogeneous with one another.

When *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *āṬ* stand [in the technical term *āṬ*], the *ḷ*-sound undergoes *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛto ṅ sirvanāmasthānayoḥ*, resulting in the vowel *a*. By the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, this becomes *la*-substitute (*laparatva*). Then, by the rule for *yaṇ* substitution, the *ñ* is replaced by *r*. Now, regarding the two phonemes *r* and *ḷ*: their mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*)—that is, their being of the same class (*savarṇatva*)—must be stated, because it is not obtained through the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (P. 1.1.9). Thus the author of the Sūtras is instructed (by the author of the Vārttikas). For a Vārttika consists of the consideration of what has been said, what has not been said, and what has been poorly said.

Regarding the statement "of *a* and *ha*": since both share the same place of articulation (the throat) and the same degree of opening (*vivṛta-prayatna*), they would attain the status of being homogeneous (*sāvarṇya*). However, there is no possibility of *a* being homogeneous with the *ka*-group (*kavarga*), because although they share the same place of articulation (the throat), they differ in their degrees of effort (*prayatna*), as *a* is produced with an open effort while the *ka*-group is produced with a contact effort (*spṛṣṭa-prayatna*). As for the visarga (*visarjanīya*), although it is included in the recitation [of the *śiva-sūtra*] after *a* and among the *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* sounds—thereby possessing an open effort—it does not receive the designation of being homogeneous with *a*, due to the absence of any purpose [for such a designation].

And thus, the implication is that homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) remains for the letter *a* with the letter *ha*. Regarding "of the letters *i* and *ś*": because they share the same place of articulation (the palate) and the same effort (openness), homogeneity is obtained for both. There is no possibility of homogeneity for the letter *i* with the *ca*-group or with the letter *ya*, because the letter *i* is open (*vivṛta*), the *ca*-group is closed (*spṛṣṭa*), and the letter *ya* is slightly closed (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the implication is that homogeneity remains for the letter *i* with the letter *ś*. Regarding "of the letters *ṛ* and *ṣ*": [the same logic applies].

Because of the similarity in their place of articulation (the head) and their open effort (*vivṛta-prayatna*), homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) would have resulted for both [ṛ and ṣ]. However, there is no possibility of homogeneity between the vowel *ṛ* and the *ṭ*-group or the letter *r*, because *ṛ* is produced with an open effort (*vivṛta*), the *ṭ*-group is produced with a contact effort (*spṛṣṭa*), and *r* is produced with a slight contact effort (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that homogeneity remains only between *ṛ* and *ṣ*. Regarding the pair *lṛ* and *s*: because of the similarity in their dental place of articulation and their open effort, homogeneity would have resulted for both.

There is no possibility of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between the sound *ḷ* and the dental class (*tavarga*) or with the letter *l*, because *ḷ* is produced with the mouth wide open (*vivṛta*), the dental class is produced with the organs fully touched (*spṛṣṭa*), and *l* is produced with the organs slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). Therefore, homogeneity for *ḷ* remains only with the letter *s*.
(14) *nājjhalau* | 1.1.10 | Having reached this conclusion, [the author] states a prohibition: *nājjhalau*. [The term] *ac* here includes both vowels (*a*) and consonants (*jha*).
The word *sahita* is elided because it belongs to the *śākapārthiva*-type compounds. From the rule *ā ca hrasvāt* [Pāṇini 1.1.73], the term *aj-jhalau* (vowels and consonants) is understood;

from the preceding sūtra *tulyāsya-prayatnaṃ savarṇam* [Pāṇini 1.1.9], the word *savarṇam* (homogeneous) is carried over as an anuvṛtti. That term is then transformed into the masculine gender and the dual number to agree with its context.
He says this with the words beginning "aj accompanied by a" (akārasahito'j), and so forth. Now, for what purpose is this prohibition?

To this he replies with the passage beginning "by that" (tena) and ending with "not yaṇ, etc. (yaṇādikaṃ na). By "that," he means by this prohibition. By "etc. (ādinā), the inclusion of the long vowel by position of homogeneous letters (savarṇadīrgha) is intended. [The examples are] *dadhī* [before *ha*, *ṣa*, or *sa*], where the *ikāra* [of *dadhi*] [is not replaced].

The meaning is that when followed by another vowel (aci), the substitution of *yaṇ* according to the rule "pare 'iko yaṇaci" does not occur, and in the case of *śītala*, where the letter *śa* follows, the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) also does not occur. Now, one might object: "Let there be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *a* and *ha*, *i* and *śa*, *ṛ* and *ṣa*, and *ḷ* and *sa*; nevertheless, in examples such as 'dadhi ṣaṣṭham', the application of *yaṇ* and so forth would not arise, because [the following sound] is not a vowel (*ac*). To this, he says "otherwise," etc. The connection is as follows: otherwise, if their homogeneity were admitted, then like the long vowels and so forth, the letters *ha* and the others would also possess the status of being vowels (*actva*).

Now, one might object: since letters such as *ha* do not occur between the letter *a* and the letter *ca* in the traditional sequence of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*), how can they possess the status of vowels (*actva*)? To this, he says: "By the force of the rule of inclusion" (*grahaṇakaśāstrabalāt*). That by which *a*, *i*, and so on, include their own homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) is "inclusion" (*grahaṇa*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), and the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*). The meaning is: "by virtue of the rule beginning with *aṇudit... (Pāṇini 1.1.69).

Although the term *ac* denotes only those phonemes included in the *vārṇasamāmnāya*, nevertheless, when *a*, *i*, and so forth are presented by the word *ac* in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, there occurs—by virtue of the rule *aṇudit savarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*—the presentation of their respective homogeneous phonemes (*savarṇa*), such as *ā* and so forth. Consequently, since *ā* and the others are denoted by what is denoted by the word *ac*, they would be grasped by the word *ac* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just like *h* and the other [consonants]. This is the meaning.

Nor can it be argued that in rules such as *iko yaṇaci*, since the meaning is possible by taking the primary sense (*śakyārtha*) alone, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is impossible; for in the rule *aṇudit sūtra*, [the primary sense] has its scope in instances like *asya cvau*. This must be stated because, by the force of indications such as *svādibhyaḥ*, metaphorical indication in the pratyāhāras is necessarily required to apply to what is denoted by their own expressed meanings. Thus, the phrase "it would have the nature of being a vowel" (*actvaṃ syāt*) means "it would be something denotable by the word *ac*. When the expectation arises—"What is that teaching which includes [the vowels]?"—he promises its demonstration with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
(15) *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* 1.1.69. [A vowel or the letter *u* followed by *it* denotes its homogeneous sounds, provided it is not itself an affix.]

Regarding the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya*: if the word *pratyaya* (suffix) were [taken as] "when followed by a suffix beginning with *aṇ* etc.," then there would be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*) for rules such as *atyadādīnām aḥ* and *idama iś*. Therefore, he explains [the term] as "that which is recognized" (*pratīyate*).

That which has *ut* as its [indicatory] letter (*it*) is called *udit*, such as *auk*, *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, *pu*, and so forth. By the word *ca* ("and"), the word *svam* (from the rule *svaṃ rūpam*) is understood to follow; and that [word *svam*] is transformed into the genitive case.

He says this with the words "not being prescribed," and so forth. Regarding the doubt as to whether the *aṇ* [pratyāhāra] is formed by the preceding or the following [ṇ], he determines it here: "in this very sūtra, *aṇ* is [formed] with the following ṇ; but elsewhere, in such rules as 'aṇo 'pragṛhyasya,' it is formed only with the preceding one. And here...
The commentary in the form of oral instruction through the lineage of teachers alone is the refuge. And thus,

by this sūtra *āṇ udit*, because the four vowels beginning with *a* include not only their own long and protracted counterparts but also consonants such as *ha* that are homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with them, when those [consonants] follow, the vowel *i*—
It is established that since there would otherwise be [the possibility of] *yaṇ*-substitution and so forth, the prohibition in the rule *nājjhalau* is necessary.
He states the result of the sūtra *aṇudit...*:
"In this way," meaning it bears fruit in the manner about to be described. Regarding "of thirty": [this refers to the fact that] the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ* do not substitute for one another.

The meaning is that, by virtue of being homogeneous (*savarṇa*), the letter *ṛ* includes its own eighteen varieties as well as the twelve varieties of the letter *ḷ*. The same applies to the letter *ḷ*.
The meaning is that the letter *ṛ* is also homogeneous with the letter *ḷ*. [Objection: But surely the entire range of *ai* is also included by the letter *e*?

By the letter *e*, the expansion (*prapañca*) of *ekāra* is included; likewise, by the letter *o*, the expansion of *aukāra* is grasped, and by *aukāra*, the expansion of *okāra*. Consequently, one might argue that the designation "eca" should apply to these four hundred [phonemes] rather than to twelve; therefore, he says: "of *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*."

To the question "Why is there no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*)? he says: *aiāṬj*. For if there were mutual homogeneity between *e* and *ai*, and between *o* and *au*, then by means of *e*, the entire range of *aikāra* [would be included], and by means of *o*, the entire range of *āukāra*, just as [the short and long vowels] *a* and so forth include their long and protracted forms.
Because their inclusion would otherwise be possible [by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*], the sūtra "aiāṬj" would not have been composed; yet it is indeed composed by the author of the sūtras.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no mutual *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between *e* and *ai*, nor between *o* and *au*. As for the pratyāhāras such as *ac*, *ic*, and *ec*, they are formed using the letter *ṅ* alone.
[The objection] is to be refuted. Nor should it be argued that the rule *aiāṬj* should exist for the sake of establishing the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) in the rule *eco'yavāyāvaḥ*;
for the sense is that the resolution of that [objection] will be stated by the rule *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ* itself. In reality, however, [the purpose of the rule *aiāṬj* is as follows]:...
In the absence of such a sūtra, in rules such as *vṛddhir ādaic*, *na tv ābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyām aic*,
and *plutāvaic idutau*, the mention of *eṅ* would entail the inclusion of both *e* and *o* as well; therefore, the pratyāhāra *aic* is necessary in order to exclude those.

Therefore, this very commencement of the *aiuṇ* sūtra is for that purpose. Consequently, since the commencement of the *aiuṇ* sūtra has achieved its intended goal, it is entirely untenable to state that it proves the absence of mutual *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between *e* and *ai*, and *o* and *au*. [Regarding] *e* and *ai*, and *o* and *au*:

The absence of mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) [between *ai* and *au*, and *e* and *o*] is easily established by the fact that in some instances, such as in the rule "vṛddhir ādaic," the term *aij* is used, while in others, such as "adeṅ guṇaḥ," the term *eṅ* is used. Otherwise, the author would have employed only *eṅ* everywhere or only *aij* everywhere, since that alone would suffice to include all four vowels. Therefore, [the terms are] *aic* and *eṅ*.

Due to the functional force of including two *pratyāhāra*s [in the rule *plutāvaica idutau*], there is no mutual homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *e* and *ai*, nor between *o* and *au*. Furthermore, because the inclusion of these two *pratyāhāra*s [in the rule *eco'pragṛhyasya*] would otherwise be redundant, this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
"By that" means: because there is an absence of mutual similarity between *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.

"It need not be raised as an objection" means: it need not be suspected. And thus, in the case of *sair*—meaning "that which exists together with *e*" (i.e., *ekāra*)—in the phrase *he sair*, there is no elision of the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhilopa*) by the rule *eṅ hrasvāt*.
In the case of *glāvam* and *glāvaḥ*, the substitution of *ā* [for *au*] by the rule *āṬtaḥ am-śasoḥ* does not occur. This might be argued:

there would be the designation of *savarṇa* (homogeneous) between the letter *ha* and the vowel *ā*, because their place of articulation (*sthāna*) and effort (*prayatna*) are identical, since the prohibition of *savarṇya* applies only to vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*), and only to those included in the phonetic inventory (*vārṇasamāmnāyika*).

This is because the term *ajjhal* denotes the letters (*varṇa*), and there is no evidence for the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*. Nor should it be argued that because the vowel *a* is an *ac*, the vowel *ā* is also included by the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*, and thus there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ā* and the consonant *ha*; for in the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*...

Only when it has already acquired its own nature (*labdhātmaka*) is it capable of undergoing application in rules such as *asya cvau*. Furthermore, at the stage when the rule *nājjhalau* is to be applied, the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule defining the technical term *grahaṇa*) has not yet acquired its own nature;
for that [rule] consists of the word *savarṇa*, and it acquires its own nature only after the meaning of the word *savarṇa* has been understood.
Furthermore, the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam*, which prescribes the designation of *savarṇa*, although it generally conveys its meaning,
becomes capable of performing its own function only after excluding the scope of the exception *nājjhalau* and thus reaching its final application within that very context.

As it has been said: "The general rule applies after the scope of the exception has been determined. And it is stated in the Bhāṣya: first there is the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇa*); after the instruction comes the designation *it*;
after the *it*-designation comes the formation of the abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*) by the rule "the first [phoneme] with the last"; and after the abbreviations...

The meaning is that by this combined statement—the definition of *savarṇa* (P. 1.1.9) and the subsequent sūtra *aṇuditsavarṇasya...*—there is the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) in other instances, such as in the rule *auṭhaścvau*. In this regard, the Bhāṣya states: "After the formation of the pratyāhāras..."

By the phrase "in the rule defining *savarṇa*," what is intended is the injunction regarding homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) together with the prohibition "not [between] vowels and *hal*-consonants" (*nājjhalau*). This is because a mere injunction of homogeneity, being independent of the technical abbreviations (*pratyāhāra*), cannot be subject to a restriction that it occurs subsequent to those abbreviations. Thus, regarding the sūtra *aṇ udit*...
Because the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (P. 1.1.9) operates only after the prohibition *nājjhalau* (P.

1.1.10), it has not yet acquired its functional status prior to that point; consequently, since the mention of *ac* in *nājjhalau* does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), there is no application of the rule for homogeneity, and thus the letters *a* and *ha* possess homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*).

He raises the doubt with the words "it might be so," [referring to] the rule *nāj-jhalau* and the discussion on homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), etc. The word "even though" (*yadyapi*) is used in the sense of possibility.
