The *akṣarasamāmnāya* is the fourteen sūtras. That which pertains to it is *ākṣarasamāmnāyika*. [The suffix] *-añ* is applied by the rule *bahvaco’ntodātāt*. Nor is there...

It should not be argued that, although the rule *aṇudit sūtra* does not apply during the stage of its actual operation (pravṛtidaśā) under the rule *nājjhalau*, the term *ac* in that context may nevertheless include long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since it was demonstrated immediately following this point that pratyāhāras possess secondary indication with respect to what is denoted by their own constituent sounds.
For secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) applies to the pratyāhāras with respect to their own denotata;

however, in this case, there is no status as a denotatum for the long and protracted vowels [by the term] *ac*, which denotes [only] *a* and so forth. The sense is that the rule *am udi t* does not apply here at present. He offers a rebuttal: "Even so... (*tathāpi*).

Even if one accepts that the prohibition "na-aj-jhalau" applies only to those vowels and consonants mentioned in the *vārṇasamāmnāya*, the meaning remains that the vowel *ā* is not a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) of the letter *h*. Why is this so? To this he says: "In that case also... (*tatrāpi*).
Here, the word "also" (*api*) is displaced [in the compound]. In that rule, "na-aj-jhalau," the vowel *ac* is accompanied by *ā*.
The meaning is that even the form *ā* is included by means of the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel resulting from the combination of homogeneous vowels).

Now, one might object: "Let there be homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the letter *ha* and the letter *ā*; what is the purpose of including the letter *ā* [in the rule] for the sake of prohibiting that?
To this he says: "By that"—meaning, by that [inclusion], [the homogeneity] of the letter *au* and the letter *ā*.

By means of the prohibition against homogeneity (*sāvarṇya-pratiṣedha*), since the vowel *ā* is not included by the letter *h*, the substitution of *ḍha* for *h*—as prescribed by the rule "ho ḍhaḥ" (*Pāṇini 8.2.31*)—does not apply to the *ā* following the *p* in the word *viśvapābhiḥ*. However, in the absence of the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the *ā*, because there would be homogeneity between that [long *ā*] and the *h*, the *ā* would be included by the *h*, and consequently, the substitution of *ḍha* would occur for it; such is the meaning. In this regard:

The modern grammarians maintain that since the substitution of *ḍha* is not established [as valid] at this stage, only the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) should be applied. In the rule "kāla-samaya-velāsu tumun," the mention of *velāsu*—specifically the vowel *ā* following the letter *l*—serves as evidence for the inclusion of the vowel *ā* in the rule *nājjhalau*. Otherwise, if *ḍha* were substituted or the final consonant elided there, the vowel *ā* would not be heard. This suffices for our purpose.

[Objection: "In the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*, let there be the mention of 'ac' alone; what is the use of the mention of 'aṇ', given that by the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya* [the term *aṇ* includes its homogeneous sounds], and since *hayavarala* have no homogeneous counterparts, the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* would be useless with respect to them? To this, he says: "anunāsika... etc. By "tena" (by that), he means by the aforementioned two-fold nature.
Because they are of the same class (*savarṇa*), those non-nasal *y*, *v*, and *l* are each the technical name for the pair [of nasals and non-nasals].

However, the nasal *y*, *v*, and *l* are not the names even for the non-nasals, because of the principle that "a quality is a differentiator," and because in the traditional list of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*), only the non-nasals are included among them.

And because of the reading [of the sūtra]. Thus, the intention is that in the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*, rather than including the mention of *aj* for the sake of including *ya*, *va*, and *la*, there is the mention of *aṇ*. (16) *taparaḥ tatkālasya* 1.1.70.

In the *Gṛhaṇaka-sūtra*, it was established that an *aṇ* vowel is the grasper (*grāhaka*) of its own homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*). This being so, since it would follow that *at*, *it*, *ut*, and other *aṇ*s ending in a *t* (tapara) would likewise grasp all their respective homogeneous vowels, this [new rule] is commenced: "A *tapara* [vowel] denotes only that which has its same duration. The term "*tapara*" is repeated.

First, regarding the word *tapara*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which *taḥ* [the letter *t*] follows. Second, however, it is a *pañcamī-samāsa* (ablative compound) meaning "after *taḥ*. From the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*, the term *aṇ* is understood to carry over.
This [term *tapara*] is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose duration is like the duration of the phoneme being uttered with the *taḥ* suffix."

The term *ūkālaḥ* is a compound, as in the case of *uṣṭramukha* and similar formations. Thus, the meaning is that the *aṇ*—consisting of *at*, *ṭhit*, and so forth—when pronounced with a *ta*-marker (*tapara*), becomes the designation for those sounds whose duration is similar to its own. Among these, *at*, *it*, *ut*, and *ṛt* are [examples of] such *tapara* forms.

The various durations of the short vowels *a* and so forth are their respective short elaborations (*prapañca*). However, for those [vowels] such as *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* which are followed by *t* (i.e., *et*, *ait*, *ot*, *āṬt*), the various durations are their respective long elaborations. Among these, regarding the short vowels *a* and so forth that are followed by *t*:

Since it is established in common worldly usage that short vowels such as *a* do not denote their respective long expansions (*prapañca*), while long vowels such as *ā* and others, when followed by *t* (e.g., *āt*), do denote their respective long expansions, this sūtra becomes a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) according to the maxim: "When something is already established, a new formulation serves to restrict it. Thus: *aṇ*.
If it is followed by *t*, it is a grasper (*grāhaka*) only of that which is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) and of the same duration (*tatkāla*), but not of that which is of a different duration.
