However, for the *pañcamī-samāsa* (the fifth-case compound), the example is the vowel *e* [as in *vṛddhir ādaij*]. But examples such as *āt*, *īt*, and *ūt* are not illustrations of the rule concerning *tapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.70). For, regarding the vowels beginning with *ā*, does the *tapara* rule serve to introduce a new prescription (*apūrva-vidhāna*), or is it for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*)? It cannot be the first case, because in the *tapara* rule...

Even in the absence of the continued application of the term *aṇ*, under the view that [the technical terms] denote a genus (*jāti*), the fact that long vowels such as *ākāra* express their own respective co-temporal manifestations is established by common worldly usage alone; therefore, the application of the rule *tapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) to those [long vowels] would be redundant. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because of the aforementioned reasoning regarding the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*.
Since that [term "tapara"] would have as its scope only those phonemes belonging to the Vārṇasamāmnāya, it could not apply to [sounds] such as the long *ā*; consequently,

it would be untenable for the rule *tapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) to serve the purpose of restricting [the application of a phoneme] by excluding those of a different duration (*atatkāla*) with respect to them, given that [the desired result] is already established.

Because it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) precisely for that which begins with a vowel (*satyārambhasya*). And thus, in cases such as *āt* and *īd*, the inclusion of the long vowels (*taparakaraṇam*) is solely for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; let this suffice for now. Therefore, the detailed exposition of the pratyāhāras and the detailed exposition of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* have been presented in this manner.
(17) *Vṛddhir ādaic* | 1.1.1 | Now, intending to prescribe other technical terms (*saṃjñā*), he first states the term *vṛddhi*: *vṛddhir ādaic*.
Although this is the very first sūtra in Pāṇini’s *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, nevertheless...

This [topic] was not introduced at the beginning, because this sūtra—containing the pratyāhāra *tapara*—is dependent for its application on the rules governing pratyāhāras and the sūtras that define them (the *grahaṇakaśāstra*), and thus it is appropriate to introduce it only after the detailed exposition of the system of pratyāhāras has been established. Nor should it be asked why the author of the sūtras did not adopt this very order of recitation; for the Great Sage, being independent, cannot be constrained. Furthermore, *ācca aicceti* is a collective dvandva compound.

The compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) prescribed by the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntāt* does not apply here; for this very reason, the rule for compound endings is understood to be non-universal (*anitya*), as indicated by that very grammatical reference. Furthermore, the substitution of *k* for *c* (*kutva*) prescribed by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* at the end of a word (*padānte*) also does not apply, because the status of being a *bha*-stem applies due to the rule *ayasmayādīni cchandasi*.

In the case of the *saṃhitā* reading "vṛddhir ādaij adeṅ," the substitution of the *jaś*-sound for the letter *ca* at the end of a word—as prescribed by the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte"—does indeed occur; this is because of the statement, "Even those [phonemes] possessing both designations are seen in the Vedic language (*chandas*)," and because the rules pertaining to the Vedic language apply to the *sūtras* as well, according to the principle that "the *sūtras* are like the Veda."

Nor should it be argued that even so, because it is a *pada*, there would be *kutva* [the substitution of *k* for *g*], and because it is a *bha*, there would be an absence of *jaśtva* [the substitution of *j* for *g*]; for this is precluded by the rule "in the Veda, one follows what is observed. Enough of this. Alternatively, *ācca aicca* may be a *dvandva* compound in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretara-yoga*). This being the case, the singular number in the sūtra is used according to Pāṇinian usage. Since this is an *adhikāra* (governing heading) concerning technical names (*saṃjñā*) established through the oral tradition of the teachers, the term "technical name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood. This is precisely what he states with the words "ādaicc... and so forth. (18) *adeṅ guṇaḥ* | 1.1.2 | *adeṅ guṇaḥ*. Because the context is the discussion of technical names, "technical name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood. It consists of *at* and *eṅ*.
This is a collective *dvandva* compound. He states this with the rule beginning "adeṅ ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.2).
(19) *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* | 1.3.1 | "The roots beginning with *bhū* and *vā* are verbal roots (*dhātu*). *Bhū* and *vā* are *bhūvau*. *Ādi* and *ādī* [are *ādyau*]. First...

The word *ādi* (beginning) signifies "starting with," while the second [instance of] *ādi* signifies "of the same kind. Those for whom *bhū* and *vā* are the beginning are called *bhūv-ādayaḥ*. The meaning is that those starting with *bhū*, as well as others similar to them, receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "verbal root" (*dhātu*). And the similarity to a verbal root consists in being expressive of action. Thus he says: "expressive of action" (*kriyāvācinaḥ*).

[The sūtra begins with] *tyādi-nā*. Why specify "expressing action" (*kriyāvācinaḥ*)? Because the word *yā* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha, one must ensure that in the phrase *yāḥ paśyanti*, the feminine form *yāḥ* (formed with the suffix *ṭāp*) does not incur the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*). For if it were a verbal root, the elision of *ā* prescribed by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* would apply. In reality, however, according to the *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning that which is defined by a rule versus that which is explicitly stated), there is no possibility of including the feminine form *yāḥ* here. The inclusion of the term "expressing action," however, is for the sake of [excluding] the particle *vā*, which signifies optionality (*vikalpa*).
This is for the purpose of excluding [the roots] from being *dhātus*, or because of their inclusion in the *dhātupāṭha* under the heading "vā.

Since the semantic specifications "vā in the sense of moving and scenting" and "yā in the sense of reaching" are modern [additions], there is no fault if one says "denoting an action" (*kriyāvācin*). This is because the meaning of "vā"—namely, optionality—lacks connection with past or future time, as in "it will be optionally" (*vā bhaviṣyati*) or "it was optionally" (*vā abhavat*).

"It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that [the term *kṛt*] does not apply because of the absence of the nature of an action (*kriyātvābhāvāt*). Why [specify] 'beginning with *bhi*' (*bhyādayaḥ*)?
So that the verbal root-status (*dhātutva*) of *hiruk*, which denotes the action of excluding, may not occur.
(20) "Prior to *rīśvara*, [the items listed are] particles (*nipātāḥ*). 1.4.56.

"Particles (*nipāta*) [begin] before *īśvara*. This sūtra, "And that which prompts [an action] is called the cause (*hetu*)," occurs at the end of the fourth quarter of the first book. The word "*īśvara*" is an imitation of a portion of the sūtra "With regard to sovereignty, [the term] *adhi* [is used]. Because it is an imitation, it is not an ungrammatical form (*apaśabda*). For this very reason, in the phrase from the *Cintāmaṇi*, "because it is dependent upon perception," [the word *pratyakṣa* is treated as such]. "Perception-knower" (*pratyakṣavit*).

The inclusion of the term *pratīka* is seen in its explanation: "From this point forward, up to the subsequent sūtra of this chapter, *adhir īśvare*, it should be understood that those [terms] preceding the word *īśvara* bear the designation of *nipāta* (indeclinables). This means that the word *nipāta* is to be carried over [as an anuvṛtti].

What is the purpose of including the letter *repha* (the *r*) in the mention? It is so that the rule "īśvare tosunkasunau" located in the third chapter (*Pāṇini 5.4.54*) does not serve as the limit (*avadhi*). However, if—due to the absence of a reason for skipping the first [rule]—the limit were taken to be "adhir īśvare" (*Pāṇini 1.4.97*) itself, then the inclusion of *repha* would be necessary.
The meaning is clear.

(21) *cādayo 'satve* 1.4.57. "The particles beginning with *ca* when not denoting a substance. Those whose first is *ca* are the *cādayaḥ*, established by their enumeration in the list (*gaṇapāṭha*). They are indeclinables (*nipātāḥ*).
This is the subject under discussion. By the word *sattva*, a substance (*dravya*) is meant; as Amarasimha states: "The word *sattva* [is used] for substance, life-force, and resolve.

A substance is that which is endowed with gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*). When meanings such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth, which are the referents of particles like *ca*, are conveyed by those particles, they are not then endowed with gender and the other [grammatical properties].

When they are understood through words such as *samuccaya* (conjunction) and so forth, they are then associated with gender and the like, due to the inherent nature of words. They are neither existent (*sat*), nor non-existent (*asat*), nor a substance (*adravya*). The meaning is that particles (*nipāta*) are those [words] such as *ca* and others which exist there as denoters; thus he says: "those whose referent is not a substance" (*adravyārthāḥ*).

Thus [it is asked]: "What [is the result] when there is no existence? [Answer: "The goat is the sacrificial animal (*paśu*). Although the word *paśu* is listed at the beginning [of the list of particles], it does not possess the status of a particle (*nipāta*) here because it denotes a substance (*dravya*). However, in this case, it would indeed [be a particle]: "He considers the well-fed one to be an animal" (*puṣṭaṃ paśu manyate*).
Here, *paśu* is used in the sense of "correctly."

(22) *prādayaḥ* | 1.4.58 | The term *prādayaḥ* [is the subject]. The [conditions] *asatve* and *nipātāḥ* are understood to carry over [from previous rules]. Thus he says: "not denoting a substance" (*adravya*).
"Likewise" (*tathā*) means that they are designated as *nipātas*.
(23) *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge* |1|4|59|. (24) *gatiśca* |1|4|60|.
"Prefixes" (*upasargāḥ*) and "motion-words" (*gatiśca*). These two sūtras have been presented together for the sake of ease of explanation.
The term *prādayaḥ* (the words beginning with *pra*) is understood [from the previous rule]. The singular number used for the plural "gati" is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
Thus he says, "the words beginning with *pra*" and so forth. "In connection with an action" (*kriyāyoge*) means when there is a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) with an action.
The term *nipāta* (particle) is also understood here, because its governing scope extends from the word *īśvare* onwards.
Consequently, the particles beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ), while being designated as *nipāta*s, also acquire the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*.

And [the rule] *ākaḍārāt* is thereby set aside. As for the co-occurrence of the designations *gati* and *upasarga*, their simultaneous application is established by the very word *ca* in the rule *gatiśca*. Thus it is accomplished. And therefore—

In examples such as *praṇeya*, the grammatical operations pertaining to prefixes (*upasarga*)—such as those established by the rule "even in a non-compound [following] a prefix" (*upasargādasamāse’pi*)—are accomplished, as are the operations concerning "verbs and their prefixes" (*gatikāraka*) and so forth, as well as those concerning "meaningless particles" (*nipātasyānarthakasya*).

Now, he recites the prefixes beginning with *pra* and *para*: *pra*, *para*, etc. The form *parā* ends in the vowel *ā*. In the case of roots beginning with *a*, the substitution of *l* for the *r* of *ni* and *dur* occurs before the root *aya* according to the rule "of a prefix before *aya*" (*upasargasyāyatau*), as in *nilayate* and *dulayate*.

In *niryāti* and *durayati*, there is no substitution of *l* for *r*, because the substitution of *r* (by the rule *su-duḥ-su-juṣo ruḥ*) is considered asiddha (unestablished) for the purposes of this rule. It is precisely for this reason that *nis* and *duḥ* are listed separately from *nir* and *dur*.

(25) *na vā* is *vibhāṣā*. 1.1.44. Regarding the statement "The ox used for sacrifice (*medhyaḥ paśuḥ*) is optionally [treated as] an animal (*anaḍvān*)," the word *vibhāṣā* is seen in the usage of ritualists (*yājñika*) to denote a simple option (*kevalavikalpa*). However, here—

This [sūtra] is commenced in order to make it known that the combined meaning of the word *vibhāṣā* in the treatise consists of both prohibition (*niṣedha*) and option (*vikalpa*). If the word *iti* were absent, then because of the rule "the form itself [is the name] of a word" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*), the meaning would be that the two words *na* and *vā* themselves, by virtue of referring to their own forms, would bear the technical designation *vibhāṣā*.
Consequently, in rules such as *vibhāṣā śveḥ*, there would arise the two substitutes *na* and *vā*.

However, this fault does not occur when the particle *iti* is used; for *iti* is connected with each [word] individually. Thus, the meaning understood by the word *na* is negation (*niṣedha*), and the meaning understood by the word *vā*...

The meaning that results is that the designation *vibhāṣā* applies to the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of those two combined. And thus, only the meanings of the words "optionally" (*navā*) are obtained as the designata (*saṃjñin*), not the literal forms of the words "optionally"; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Regarding this, he says: "Of the negation and the alternative," and so forth. This sūtra is for the purpose of [indicating] an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. To explain: there are three kinds of options—option when [an operation] has already been established (*prāptavibhāṣā*), option when it has not yet been established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*), and option in both cases (*ubhayatravibhāṣā*). An example of an option when [an operation] has already been established is: *vibhāṣā jasi* (Pāṇini 1.1.32). [An example is: *varṇāśrametare*.

In the case of *varṇāśrametarāḥ*, since the rule *dvandve ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.30) would have necessitated a permanent prohibition of the technical designation *sarvanāman* (pronominal), this [rule] provides an option (*vibhāṣā*). This is an "option for what was not otherwise obtained" (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*), as in the rule *tīyasya ṅitsu vā* (Pāṇini 1.1.25). For instance, in forms such as *dvitīyasmai* and *dvitīyāya*, the suffix *tīya* belongs to the *sarvādi* group.
Since the designation *sarvanāman* has not been previously established due to the absence of a rule prescribing it, this is an optional (*vibhāṣā*) rule.

It is an option in both cases, as in the rule "optionally for *śvi*" (*vibhāṣā śveḥ*). Regarding the root *śvi*, in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) and the intensive (*yaṅ*), this is an option for *saṃprasāraṇa*. Thus, in the perfect tense, one forms either *śuśāva* or *śiśvāya*.

Examples such as *śuśuvatuḥ* and *śiśviyatuḥ* [are given]; however, for the *yaṅ* [intensive], it is *śośūyite*. In this case, regarding the portion containing *yaṅ*, this is indeed an optional rule (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*). As for the *liṭ* [perfect], in the dual and plural endings that are *apit*, the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is invariably required by the rule "vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti";

however, in the singular endings that are *pit*, the *samprasāraṇa* is not applicable at all. [This is because of the rule] "asaṃyogālliṭ... [which restricts *samprasāraṇa* to roots ending in a single consonant].

Because the designation *kit* applies only where there is an *apit* (a suffix not having *p* as its marker), and because [the rule] is formulated whether the operation has already been established or is yet to be established, the consensus is that "vibhāṣā śveḥ" is an option for both cases (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*). In that regard, if the rule "na veti vibhāṣā" were not formulated, then, just as in the ritual usage "anaḍvān vibhāṣitaḥ," there would be a simple option (*kevala-vikalpa*) even in the case of "vibhāṣā śveḥ."

It would be understood as follows: first, the pair consisting of "existence" (bhāva) and "non-existence" (abhāva) is a conceptual alternative (vikalpa). Consequently, when the term *vibhāṣā* is heard, it is understood that both [the application] and "its own non-existence" (*tad-abhāva*) are to be enjoined.
In that context, if the alternative in the rule "vibhāṣā śveḥ" is expressed by way of affirmation—namely, "in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], of the root *śvi*"—[then...]

If it were the case that "samprasāraṇa occurs or does not occur," then the option would apply only to those suffixes marked with *p*. For in those cases, since the samprasāraṇa prescribed by the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) is not otherwise applicable, the first part—the occurrence—must be enjoined; and for the sake of making that optional, [the negation] *na* [is required].

The statement "it exists" (*bhavati*) must also be prescribed; however, in the case of *kit* suffixes, the application [of the rule] would not occur. For in those cases, since [the substitution] of *vac*, *svap*, *yaj*, and so forth is already established by the rule *kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), the portion concerning "becoming" (*bhavana*) cannot be the object of prescription at first. Rather, only the portion "it does not exist" (*na bhavati*) is to be prescribed. And thus...
Because the subordination of both parts [of the rule] cannot be achieved, this optional injunction would not apply there, and consequently,

the *samprasāraṇa* would occur invariably. However, if the option is expressed by way of prohibition— namely, "in the *liṭ* [perfect], the *samprasāraṇa* of the root *śvi* does not occur, [but] it does occur"— then [the option] applies only when there is a *kit* suffix.

[Otherwise] there would be the application [of the rule]. For in that case, since [the substitution of *i* for the root vowel] is already obtained by the rule *vacisvapi-* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), it would not occur; thus, its prescription [as a mandatory rule] must first be stated. Furthermore, to ensure that its non-occurrence is understood as being only optional, the form *bhavati* must also be prescribed. However, in the case of the suffixes marked with *p*, there would be no application; for in those cases, since the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) is not otherwise obtained, it would not [occur].

This is because the portion "bhavati" cannot initially admit of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Nor can it be argued that the rule operates in both ways— positively with respect to *pit* suffixes and negatively with respect to *kit* suffixes— because the word *vibhāṣā*, being heard only once,
cannot simultaneously convey a positive alternative in one instance [and a negative one in another].

Furthermore, it lacks the capacity to convey an alternative understanding through the perspective of negation (*niṣedhamukha*). If that were conveyed through repetition (*āvṛtti*), the same fault would persist. However, when the rule *na veti vibhāṣā* is introduced, because the understanding follows the sequence of the heard [words], the prohibition (*niṣedha*) first applies to the *kit* suffixes by means of the negative particle *na*.

Then, when everything that has the form of *kid* and *akid* has been rendered uniform by means of the absence of *saṃprasāraṇa* in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, an option (*vikalpa*) proceeds solely through the positive formulation (*vidhimukha*) in the uniform manner of "it occurs" or "it does not occur. Thus, this sūtra is for the purpose of an option that applies in both cases (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*).

However, there is no utility for this [option] in the case of an option regarding what is already established (*prāptavibhāṣā*), because in that case the aspect of occurrence (*bhavanāṃśa*) is already established and thus cannot be the object of an injunction. Nor is there utility for it in the case of an option regarding what is not yet established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*), because in that case the aspect of non-occurrence (*abhavanāṃśa*) is already established and thus cannot be the object of an injunction. And even so, [the rule] "uṇādayaḥ... [is not applicable].
It should not be argued that in rules such as *bahulam aṇ-ṛk-oh*, *chandasy ubhayathā*, and *anupasargād vā*,

where the word *vibhāṣā* is absent and only a simple option (*vikalpa*) is prescribed, the resulting lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) is unavoidable; for in this very sūtra [Pāṇini 1.1.44], the term *vibhāṣā*...

Because it is characterized by words that express conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, one should understand that the final meaning of the Sūtra is this: all those words in common usage which are synonyms for *vikalpa* serve as indicators of both negation and conceptual construction within this treatise. In the Bhāṣya, however, regarding words such as *vibhāṣā*...

Even if it were merely a matter of conceptual construction (vikalpa) following worldly usage, since the application of such construction— whether by way of affirmation or negation— is possible solely in accordance with the requirements of the subject to be defined (lakṣya), this sūtra has been rejected; enough of this prolixity.
(26) *Svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasyāśabdasaṃjñā* (Pāṇini 1.1.68). In rules such as *agner ḍhak*, *vāyvṛtupitruṣaso yat*, and *rājño yaḥ*,
the suffixes *ḍhak* and others denote the meanings of "fire," "wind," and so forth, which are presented through common worldly usage (*laukikavyutpatti*).

Because of the impossibility of [the word] preceding or following [the suffix], and because of the impossibility of its connection with the rule "from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), there would be the undesirable consequence of including synonyms for those respective meanings; therefore, this sūtra—"its own form" (*svarūpam*)—is commenced for the purpose of restricting that [application]. [This applies to cases such as] "the suffix *ḍhak* after *agni*" (*agner ḍhak*), where [it refers to] the word *agni* itself.

That very nature which is heard [in the word] is what must be understood by words such as *agni* and so forth, and not anything else, even if it be a synonym for it. The meaning is that this restriction does not apply to technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *vṛddhi*, *guṇa*, and so on, which are established by convention in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*). Thus he says: "the own-nature of the word."

"Saṃjñī" means "that which is to be designated. It should not be argued that the apprehension of those meanings will occur there simply by the force of the rules for technical designations (saṃjñā-vidhi), such as "vṛddhir ādaic" and "pugantalaghūpadhasya guṇaḥ," so what is the purpose of the phrase "aśabda-saṃjñā"? [For consider: in the rule "upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ," regarding the term "ghu"...

Since the designation "dādhā" (as in *dādhā ghu adāp*) is made for the sake of excluding the root *ghu* in the rule *śabde* (Pāṇini 6.1.159), and since that designation is necessary in rules such as *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāṃ hali* (Pāṇini 6.4.66), the functional force of the designation is exhausted there; thus, the matter is explained in detail elsewhere. This sūtra is discussed in the Bhāṣya.
It has been refuted.

(27) "That by which a rule is initiated applies to that [stem] and to what ends with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72): whatever grammatical operation is commenced by taking up the specific form of the word *yat*, that [operation] applies to that [word-form] and to what ends with it.

To explain how this comes to be, he says: "by which [there is] a prescription. A *vidhi* is that by which something is prescribed (*vidhīyate*). By the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*, the suffix *ki* is applied to the root *dhā* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). In the word *yena*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The agent is the one who prescribes the rules of the treatise (*śāstra*). Under the governing heading *dhātoḥ*, by the rule *erac*, the suffix *ac* is added after the vowel *i*.
Pāṇini prescribes the suffix *ac* for a verbal root by means of the instrument (*karaṇa*). And an instrument is that which possesses an operation (*vyāpāra*).

In the rule *erac*, the distinguishing factor—the vowel *i*—has as its operation, within the act of prescription performed by Pāṇini, precisely the exclusion of others. Consequently, in this context, it is the qualifier itself [that serves as the instrument].

The word "yena" (by which) is expressed with the instrumental case ending. From the rule "svaṃ rūpam" (its own form), the word "svam" (its own) is understood and is transformed into the genitive case. Thus, the result is that "the word which provides the qualifier denotes both its own form and that which ends with it."

Thus he says: "the qualifier," and so forth. This means that the word which conveys a qualifier should be understood as conveying both the word ending in that [qualifier] and the word that conveys the qualifier itself. Consequently, in the rule *er-ac*, the suffix *ac* would apply not only after a verbal root ending in the letter *i*, but also after a verbal root whose form is the letter *i*.

It bears fruit, as in the case of *caya* (accumulation) or *aya* (iron). Some, however, maintain that since an instrument (*karaṇa*) is dependent upon an agent (*kartṛ*), its dependence is indicated by the third case ending; and since this [dependence] constitutes the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for words, the word's orientation toward the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇaparatva*) is thereby obtained.
This has been refuted in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the term "samāse" (in a compound): this is a *vārttika*.
Its meaning is that a prohibition of *tadantavidhi* (the rule of extension to what ends with such a form) must be stated both in the prescription of compounds and in the prescription of suffixes.

Consequently, in the example "kṛṣṇaṃ paramaśritaḥ" (one who has resorted to the supreme Kṛṣṇa), the compound [by the rule] "dvitīyā śrite" (a word ending in the second case is compounded with *śrita*) does not take place.

*Sautranāḍiḥ* is the descendant of *Sūtranaḍa*. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*. The vowel lengthening of both members of the compound occurs by the rule *anuśatikādīnāṃ ca*. Here, the suffix *phak* does not apply by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak*. Now, if this were the case, then in the word *atipacantī*, meaning "one who has surpassed those who cook," [the suffix] *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ugitaśca*.

The suffix *ṅīp* would not be applied after a nominal stem ending in *ugit*, because the rule for the application of suffixes prohibits the extension of a rule to what ends with such a form (*tadantavidhi*). Likewise, in the case of *dākṣi*, the suffix *iñ* prescribed by the rule *ata iñ* would not apply.

To the objection that *iñ* should apply in the case of *asyāpatyam iri*, he says: "ugiditi. This is also a *vārttika*. The suffix *ṇamul* is used in the sense of "excluding" (*varjayati*) in the rule "dvitīyāyāṃ ca. It has been stated that the prohibition applies to the formulation of compound names and suffixes, with the exception of the mention of *ugit* and the mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*).
This is the meaning: [the suffix] *bhavati*. However, when there is a mention of an *ugit* [suffix] or a vowel (*varṇa*), the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (P.
1.1.72) indeed applies as a *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that). Consequently, in the case of *atipacantī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by [P.
4.1.6] *ugidacām... antāt* and [P. 4.1.6] *ugitaśca*; and in the case of *dākṣi*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied].

And the suffix *iñ* is established after words ending in vowels other than *a*. (28) *virāmo'vasānam* | 1.4.110 | "The pause is the term of finality (*avasāna*). *Virāmaḥ* means that in which one ceases [speaking].
The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*) with the meaning of proximity (*sāmīpika*). "Cessation" (*viramaṇam*) means the absence of activity;

and since this is discussed within the context of grammatical science (*śabdaśāstra*), it is understood as consisting in the absence of the utterance of phonemes (*varṇa*). Thus, the meaning is: "That final phoneme, upon whose utterance there follows immediately thereafter the absence of the utterance of other phonemes, is designated as *avasāna* (pause)."
It bears fruit. With this intention, he explains: "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*).

The explanation should be applied by supplying the words: "that final phoneme, upon whose utterance there is an absence of the utterance of other phonemes, is designated as *avasāna* (pause). Alternatively, [it may mean] the absence of the utterance of phonemes.

The term *virāma* (pause) is derived from the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, it is understood to occur precisely after the utterance of some phoneme, according to the traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*). On this view, the interpretation of the explanatory gloss (*vivaraṇa*) is as follows: "the absence of the utterance of other phonemes immediately following the utterance of some phoneme is *avasāna* (final pause). In that context:

In the first view, regarding the rule *khar-avasānayoḥ*, it should be understood that the substitution of *visarga* for the letter *r* occurs when followed by a *khari* (an unaspirated voiceless consonant), whereas in the case of *avasāne* (pause), the *r* remains as the original substitute (*sthānin*). Although there is only one locative case ending in *khar-avasānayoḥ*, it is differentiated due to the difference in the scope of application (*viṣaya-bheda*). In the second view, however, even for a non-existence (*abhāva*), there is a [distinction] produced by the intellect.
The state of being "other" (*paratva*) is to be understood.

(29) *Paraḥ saṃnikarṣaḥ saṃhitā* (Pāṇini 1.4.109). "The closest proximity" (*paraḥ saṃnikarṣaḥ*). "Other" (*paraḥ*) means "excessive" (*atiśayita*). [As stated: "The words *para*, *dūra*, *anātman*, and *uttama* [denote excellence]."
Thus says Amara. "Sannikarṣa" means proximity; it is the absence of an interval of time exceeding half a mātrā.
This is because an interval of half a mātrā is unavoidable.
With this in mind, he says: "exceeded," and so forth.

(30) *suptiṅantaṃ padam* | 1|4|14 | A word (*pada*) ends in a *sup* or a *tiṅ*. In the rule *svaujasamauṅ* [Pāṇini 4.1.2], the *pratyāhāra* "sup" begins from "su" up to the letter *p* in *sup*, and not [from the beginning of the list].
Only the locative plural is intended here, according to the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).

"Suptiṅanta" means that which has "sup" (nominal suffixes) and "tiṅ" (verbal suffixes) at its end. The phrase "a word-form" (*śabdarūpa*) is understood from the context of this treatise on grammar. Furthermore, the word "end" (*anta*) is connected with each [of the two categories] individually.
Thus he says: "ending in a *sub* [suffix].

(31) *Halo'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ* | 1.1.7 | Consonants (*hal*) that are without an interval (*anantarāḥ*) constitute a *saṃyoga* (conjunct). Here, the word *antara* refers to an interval (*vyavadhāna*). As Amarasimha states: "The word *antara* [denotes] space, limit, enclosure, disappearance, division, and purpose."

And "separation" (vyavadhāna) occurs only by means of a dissimilar element. The analysis of the compound is: "those for which there is no existing interval (antara), that is, no separation. The elision of the word *vidyamāna* occurs according to the rule *naño 'tyarthānām*.

This is what he expresses with the words beginning "by vowels" (*ajbhiḥ*). In that context, the term *halaḥ* is formed by the rule of *ekaśeṣa*: both "two consonants" (*halau*) and "consonants" (*halaḥ*), resulting in "consonants" (*halaḥ*).

By this, the designation *saṃyoga* (conjunction) is obtained for both [sounds]. Consequently, in the word *śikṣā*, the suffix *ap* is established by the rule *gurośca halaḥ*. In this context, the designation *saṃyoga* applies only to the aggregate, because of the formation of a "great" technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) and because of the explanatory tradition (*vyākhyāna*). It does not apply to each [sound] individually; for if that were the case, in the word *sudṛṣat-prāsāda*, the letter *t* would incur the status of being a *saṃyoga* due to its proximity to the letter *p*.

Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the final member of a *saṃyoga* (P. 8.2.23). Furthermore, even where many consonants are conjoined, the designation *saṃyoga* applies to each pair of two, and not to all of them collectively; this is clear from the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
(32) *hrasvaṃ laghu* |1|4|10|.
"A short [vowel] is light. Since the meaning—that a short vowel shall have the designation "light"—is self-evident, it has not been further explained.
Precisely because of this mode of expression, the word *hrasva* is also used in the neuter gender.

(33) A syllable containing a conjunct consonant is heavy (*guru*). 1.4.11. Regarding "a syllable containing a conjunct consonant is heavy": the term "short" (*hrasva*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].
Thus he says: "when followed by a conjunct," and so forth.
(34) And a long [vowel] is also [heavy]. 1.4.12.
"And a long [vowel]"—the term *saṃyoga* (conjunction) does not carry over. The meaning is that even a long vowel is designated as heavy (*guru*).
Thus ends the section on technical designations (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*).
The meaning is that the exposition of technical terms (*saṃjñā*) found in the first chapter, which are useful for the work on grammatical combination (*sandhi*), is completed.
Thus ends the section on technical terms (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*) in the *Bālamanoramā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by the learned Vāsudevadīkṣita.
It is finished.
[Repeated pattern of vertical bars]

Now begins the section on the *san* affix. Next, the rules for the formation of the *san* affix are described: (434) *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkād icchāyāṃ vā* ||3.1.7|| [The *san* affix is optionally applied after a verbal root whose object has the same agent as the subject of the desire].

Regarding the phrase "dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ" (from the root, when there is an object): the term *san* is understood to follow from the rule "guptijkidbhyaḥ. Since "desire" (*icchā*) is explicitly mentioned [in the sūtra], it is specifically with respect to that desire that the status of being an "object" (*karman*) is intended. Likewise, the requirement of having a "common agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) is also intended specifically as defined by that desire. Thus, the term "object" (*karman*) applies to the verbal root (*dhātu*) by way of its own designating word.

It connects by way of having the same substratum (mānādhikaraṇya). And thus, the result is that the suffix *san* may optionally occur after a verbal root that denotes an activity which is the object of a desire, provided that [the activity] has the same agent as the desire (*icchā*).
He states this with the words "of the object of *iṣ*" and so forth. *Iṣ* means desire; by means of *iṣ*.
The meaning is: "from a verbal root (*dhātu*) which expresses an action that has become the object (*karman*) of a single agent (*kartṛ*). Now, one might object:

by the very statement "having a common agent" (*samānakartṛka*), the word "verbal root" is already understood, since only the substratum (*āśraya*) of the action denoted by the verbal root can be the agent; therefore, he says: "of the verbal root."

The status of being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix belongs only to that suffix which is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and not to whatever follows a root. Otherwise, he states the result [of this restriction] regarding the *ārdhadhātuka* status in the case of *jugupsate*: namely, the rule for *iṭ*.
Regarding "doubling" (*dvitvam*): the intention is that this occurs by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. [He then mentions] the prescription of *it* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

He causes [the student] to remember: "he desires to recite. The suffix *tumun* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). This is because it is stated that "kṛt suffixes following an indeclinable denote the abstract state. The abstract state is said to be the very meaning of the verbal root.
Thus, the meaning of "paṭhitum" (to recite) is simply the act of reciting. Within that act of reciting, there is the state of desiring.

And the fact that the agent of the desire is the same as the agent of the action is understood from the suffix *san*. Thus, it is stated that the word *pipaṭhiṣati* occurs in the sense of "desiring to break [the letters] whose agent is oneself. Now, he causes one to remember the substitution of *ghaslṛ* for the root *ṭhā* (meaning "eating") when followed by *san*: [He says: "In the case of the root *ṭhada* (in the sense of eating), there is the substitution of *ghaslṛ* when *san* follows."

Regarding the rule *luṅsanorghaslṛ*: when *ghas* remains as *sa*, having raised the doubt concerning the augment *iṭ*, he says—“by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* [Pāṇini 7.2.10], there is no *iṭ*. When *ghas* remains as *sa*, he says—"there is the substitution of *t* for *s*" (the meaning being that this is done by the rule *saḥ syārddhadhātuke* [Pāṇini 7.4.49]). Thus we have *jighatsati*. Regarding the doubling [of the root]: [The text continues: ...in the state where *ghas* remains as *sa*, he says—"there is the substitution of *t* for *s*" (the intention being that this is effected by the rule *saḥ syārddhadhātuke*). Thus: *jighatsati*. In the case of reduplication...

The sense is that the changes to *ś* and *c* arise from repetition (*abhyāsa*). Regarding the rule "doubling of *ysan*" (Pāṇini 6.1.9), according to the view that "the third consonant [of the reduplicated syllable] is doubled," in the case of *īrṣy-isa*, when only the letter *y* is doubled, the form of the suffix *san* becomes one joined with two *y*s; this is the intended meaning. Thus he says: *īrṣyayiṣati*.
And likewise, in the *sannanta* (desiderative) forms, there are the letters *ī*, *r*, *ṣ*, *y*, *k*, *dvitva* (doubling), and *i*, *ṣ*.
Regarding the alternative view that "the third [consonant] of a one-syllable root is doubled," in the case of *īrṣya* + *iṣ* + *sa*, when *sa* is doubled,
he states the form after considering that both *s* sounds in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) become *ṣ* according to the rule for *ṣatva*.

Regarding *īrṣyiṣiṣati*: here, in the form ending in the desiderative suffix (*sa*), there are the sounds *ī*, *r*, *ṣ*, *y*, *ī*, *ṣ*, *ī*, *ṣ*, *a*. (435) Pāṇini 1.2.8: *rudavidamuṣagrahisvapipracchaḥ saṃśca* ("After the roots *rud*, *vid*, *muṣ*, *grah*, *svap*, and *pracch*, the suffix *san* [is also used]").
Because of the specific mention of the vowel *i* in *rudavidi*, the mention [of the root] is taken as having undergone *saṃprasāraṇa*.

However, the vowel *i* in *svapi* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not a mention of the vowel *i* [as a substitute], because if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *saṃprasāraṇa* applying to *supi*. By the force of the word "and" (*ca*), [the term *svapi*] includes the roots mentioned in the preceding rule, namely *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, and *guh*.
The word *ktvā* is understood [from the previous rule] as being conjoined here. Thus he says: "san and *ktvā*. Regarding the phrase "after a root ending in *k*":
the intention is that this is due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "after a non-conjunct [root], *liṭ* [is used].
Some hold that by association with *rud*, only the root *vit* is intended; others hold that because there is no distinction specified, it applies to all [roots].

Since the rule *ṭhhalantācca* already establishes [the prohibition of iṭ], the specific mention of *rud*, *vid*, and *muṣ* is for the purpose of setting aside the optional application of the rule *ralo vyupadhāt*. However, in the case of *grah*, it is for the purpose of setting aside the prohibition *na ktvā seṭ*. As for *svap* and *pracch*, however, even though they are *kit* in the *ktvā* suffix...

The mention of *san* is for the purpose of providing a rule that does not apply to the *sa*-suffix [used in the sense of the desiderative]. In forms such as *rurudiṣati*, because the *san* suffix is *kit*, there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel.
(436) *sani grahaguhośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.12).

In the case of *san* (the desiderative suffix) following roots ending in *grah* and *guh*, the word "uk" is drawn forward from the rule "ṛd-śryukaḥ kitī," but not the root *śri*, because its optionality will be stated later in the rule "sanīvantardha. From the rule "neḍ vaśi kṛti," the augment *iṭ* is prohibited; thus, when *sa* remains, [the following applies] regarding the *san*.

Because of the status as a *kit*, there is a *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *r* [of the root *grah*] into *ṛ*; this is the meaning of the rule "ṭh-grahī-jye. Now, one might object: when the form *gṛh-sa* is established, since the rule for *katva* (changing *h* to *k*) applies after the rule for *ḍhatva* (changing *h* to *ḍh*), and since the rule for *ṣatva* (changing *s* to *ṣ*) applies subsequently, the condition of being a *jhaṣanta* (ending in a *jhaṣ* letter) would no longer exist; how then can there be *bhaṣbhāva* (the change of *ḍh* to *dh*)? To this, he says: "Of the *ṣatva* of the suffix *san*... [meaning that the *ṣatva* of the suffix takes precedence].

It is sufficient to say that [the substitution of] *ka* is not established (*asiddhatva*). Regarding *jighṛkṣati*: when the form *gṛh-sa* is obtained, the substitution of *ṣa* (by P. 8.2.32) would apply to the letter following the *iṇ* sound *h*, since it is subsequent; however, because that [substitution of *ṣa*] is not established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *ḍha* occurs for *ha*, followed by the *bhaṣ*-substitution.
Then, the substitution of *ka* occurs, and subsequently the substitution of *ṣa* for what follows the *ka*. This is the sequence of operations—such is the intended meaning.

From the root *guh*, one should cite *jughuksati*. From a root ending in *u*—*bubhūṣati*. This is not established by the rule *r̥t-śyukaḥ kiti*, because that rule prohibits [the substitution] only when a *kit* affix follows. Furthermore, since the augment *iṭ* applies subsequently, the rule *iko jhal* does not apply here. And this is clear.

In the *Śabdenduśekhara*: "suṣupsati". Because the suffix *san* is *kit*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacisvapi-* and the absence of *guṇa* for the light penultimate vowel. (437) *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.2.75.
And [the suffix] *kira* follows five [roots]. *Kira* is the ablative case. What is intended is "after *kṛ* and the others.

In the *tud*-class, the roots *kṛ* (in the sense of scattering), *gṛ* (in the sense of swallowing), *dṛ* (in the sense of respect), *dhṛ* (in the sense of staying), and *pracch* (in the sense of desiring to know) are established. Thus he says: *kṛ*, *gṛ*.

By the words "ityādinā" (and so forth), the intention is that [the augment] *iṭ* follows from the rules "sanīṭ" (Pāṇini 7.2.49) and "iḍatyarti" (Pāṇini 7.2.76), due to their subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*). While for the roots *kṝ* and *gṝ* there is an optionality regarding *iṭ* before the suffix *san* by the rule "iṭ sani ve," for others there is a prohibition by the rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10).

This rule [for the substitution of *iṭ*] applies when [the suffix *san*] is present. However, in the *Śabdenduśekhara*, it is stated that this is a statement [of a rule] because the prohibition by the rules "when *san* follows" (*sani graheḥ*) and "a monosyllabic root" (*ekācaḥ*) would otherwise apply. Thus, we have *pipṛcchiṣati*. Because *san* is *kit*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "for *grah*, *jyā*, etc. (*grahijyā*). As for *cikariṣati*, [it is formed] by the rule "optionally when *ac* follows" (*aci vibhāṣā*).

The meaning is that there is an option regarding the *iṭ* augment. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "ṭhiṭ sani ve" (Pāṇini 7.2.49). Regarding the forms *cikariṣati* and *jigariṣati*, one might suspect the application of the long vowel by the rule "vṛto vā" (Pāṇini 7.2.38); therefore, he says:
"In this case, the lengthening of the *iṭ* is not desired. This Vārttika is established in the *Vṛtti*, but it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*.

The forms *didariṣate* and *didhariṣate* are derived from the roots *dṛṅ* (to see) and *dhṛṅ* (to hold), respectively, with the suffix *san* and the augment *iṭ*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ*. As for the question "how?", the connection is: "How [is] *uddidhīrṣuḥ*? The intention is that, because these roots belong to the *kirādi* group, there would otherwise be the undesirable application of the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding the phrase "of the two Bhauvādika [roots]": for these two Bhauvādika roots, namely *dhṛṅ* (in the sense of "remaining") and *dhṛñ* (in the sense of "holding"), when the suffix *san* is applied, because they do not belong to the *kirādi* group, the rule *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* applies to produce a long vowel; then, by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the *ṛ* is replaced by *it*; then, by *raparaḥ*, the *it* is followed by *r*; then, by *hali ca*, the vowel is lengthened; and finally, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs.

"Understand—that is, know—that the form *uddidhīrṣuḥ* is derived by adding the suffix *u* [via the rule] *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ* to the desiderative [root] *uddidhīrṣa*. This is the response to the objector. (438) *iko jhal* 1.2.9.

"iko jhal": [the meaning of] "igantāt" is that, because the suffix *san* is a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) implied by [the word] *san*, there is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that (i.e., *iganta*). "San kit":
this is [derived] from both "rudavidamuṣagrahi" and "asaṃyogālliṭ kit."

The meaning is "because of its following that. In *bubhūṣati*, there is no *guṇa* substitution due to the *kit* designation [of the suffix]. Because an *ik* vowel follows, there is no *iṭ* augment. In *didīṣate*, there is no *guṇa* because the *san* suffix is *kit*. Because the root *dīṅ* has the designation *iṅ*, the *ātmanepada* ending applies by the rule "pūrvavat sanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.62). [The phrase] "due to the absence of being the domain of *ej*" refers to the case of the *kit* designation.

The sense is that [the substitution of ā] is prohibited because of the presence of a *guṇa* vowel. "For this very reason" means: if the substitution of *ā* were to occur elsewhere even outside the scope of the *ej*-vowels, then the separate mention of *mīma-* would be purposeless, because of the rule stating, "In the case of the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction. This is the intended meaning.

(439) *halantācca* | 1.2.10. The phrase "from that which ends in a consonant" (*halantāt*) [is stated]. The previous sūtra, *iko jhal*, is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* the word *san* is understood; from the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit*, the word *kit* is understood. The term *hal* here has its fifth case ending elided (*luptapañcamīka*).
The word *anta* signifies proximity. Thus he says: "from that which is near an *ik*" and so forth.

In the form *jughukṣati*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix *san* is *kit*. Although the rule "in *san*, [the roots] *grah* and *guh* [are marked with *u*]" indicates that they are *udit*, the augment *iṭ* does not necessarily apply here. The intention is that after the change of *h* to *ḍh*, the substitution of *bhaṣ* occurs, followed by the changes to *k* and *ṣ*.

Regarding *bibhitsati*: because the suffix *san* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Regarding *yiyakṣate*: here, because the vowel following the *hal* (consonant) is not in immediate proximity to it, the *san* does not have the *k*-sign; for if it were *kit*, there would be *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the root *yaj*. Regarding *vivardhiṣate*: this is the form of the root *vṛdh* with the suffix *san*; here, the augment *iṭ* is added to *san*.

The sense is that [the root] does not have *jhal* as its initial. Now, one might object: the root *tṛṃhū* in the sense of "injury" belongs to the *tudādi* class and is not *nopadha* (having a nasal as its penultimate). This is an indication of the form after the addition of the *anusvāra*. From this root, when followed by *san*, the status of being *kit* is desired for the purpose of the elision of the nasal according to the rule *aniditām*. That, however, is not tenable; for it is not the case here...
The suffix *san* follows immediately after a vowel (*ic*), because it is separated [from that vowel] by the letter *ha*.

However, the *san* following *ha* does not follow immediately after a consonant (*hal*) that is proximate to a vowel, because it is separated from it by the *anusvāra*; therefore, he says: "The mention of *hal* refers to the class [of consonants]."

The meaning is: "referring to one or many individuals pervaded by the genus *haltu*. Regarding *tṛṃh*: this is an illustration from the verbal root *tṛṃh*. Regarding *titṛkṣati*: this is the form in the alternative case where the augment *iṭ* is absent because the root is marked with *ū*.

Due to the *kit* status of the suffix *san*, there is elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) and the absence of *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel. Then follow the changes to *ḍha*, *ka*, and *ṣa*.

Regarding the desired position, he says: *titṛṃhiṣati*. The point is that because it does not begin with a *jhal* sound, there is no *kit* status, and therefore the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) does not occur.
(Pāṇini 6.4.16): *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*.

*ajjhanagamāṃ sani*: This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *ac*, *han*, and *gam*. From the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*, the term *upadhāyāḥ* (of the penultimate vowel) is understood; it follows after *han* and *gam*, but not after that which ends in *ac*, because such a case is impossible.

The term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). Since *ac* is a qualifier of that [stem], there is an application of the rule by extension (*tadantavidhi*) to include what ends in *ac*. Here, the verbal root *gam* is intended.

It is clear from the commentary on the present sūtra that only the substitute *aj* (the vowel) is intended. From the rule "ṭhḍhralope pūrvasya," the word "dīrghaḥ" (long vowel) is understood as an anuvṛtti. This is what he states with the words "of those ending in *aj*" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "before a *san* beginning with a *jhal*": this refers to the discussion in the commentary on the sūtra "cchvoḥ śūḍ" concerning the rule "ajjhanagamāṃ sani."

The intention is that [the rule] "sanam jhalā viśeṣayiṣyāmi" (I shall qualify *san* by means of *jhal*) has been stated. Now, he recalls the rule for the substitution of *kutva* (the change to a guttural) after the reduplication of the root √*ji*: "sanliṭorjer" (after √*ji*, when followed by *san* or *liṭ*).
Thus: *jigīṣati*. In *jigīṣati*, there is *kutva* of the letter following the reduplication once the lengthening of √*ji* has occurred. Now...

It recalls the optional substitution of *k* for the following consonant after the reduplication of the root *ci*, by the rule *vibhāṣā ceḥ*. Thus we have *cikīṣati* and *cicīṣati*; the lengthening occurs because the root ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). In *jighāṃsati*, the lengthening of the vowel *a* occurs in the root *han* when followed by the suffix *san* according to the rule *ṭhajjhane* (Pāṇini 6.4.16), but it does not apply to the final *n*.

By the rule *dīrghaśrutyā ṭhacaṭaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhac* is introduced; thus, there is reduplication. By the rule *ṭhabhyāsācca*, there is the substitution of *k* (kutva). By the rule *naśca*, there is the insertion of an anusvāra. (441) *sani ca* 6.1.9. (Note: This is a commentary on the formation of the desiderative form *cikīrṣati* from the root *kṛ*.)
In the rule *sani ca*, the term *iṇaḥ* is carried over from *ṭhiṇo gā luṅī*, and the term *gamir abodhane* is carried over from *ṇau gamir abodhane*. Therefore, he says: "of *iṇ*, *gamir*, etc.
In the form *jigamiṣati*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *gameḥ*. Here, the long vowel is established by the rule *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani*.

The meaning is as follows: when the *san* suffix undergoes doubling by the rule "of that which begins with a *ṭh*-letter, the second [is doubled]," the *i* of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is applied; then, through the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) with *prati*, both *s* sounds become *ṣ*. Regarding the root *ik* in the sense of "remembering," he says: "the root *ik* is like *iṇ*. By this Vārttika, the meaning is that the root *ik* becomes like *iṇ*. Consequently, in the presence of *san*—

The intention is that *gam* is the substitute [for *iṇ*]. Regarding "the *taṅ* [suffixes] in the passive" (*karmaṇi taṅ*): this means that after the roots *iṇ* and *ig*, when followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), the *taṅ* suffixes are applied to the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive voice, according to the rule "in the sense of the action or the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*).
Regarding "in the parasmaipada [forms]": this is because of the statement "the augment *iṭ* [is added] to *gam* in the parasmaipada [forms]," which implies that the *taṅ* suffixes do not apply there.

The meaning is "not" (neṭ). Regarding "before a *jhal*-beginning [suffix]": the meaning is that the long vowel is prescribed by the rule "ajjhane" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.16) when there is a *san* suffix beginning with a *jhal*. *Jigāṃsyate*: the meaning is "it is desired to go"; this is a form of the root *iṇ*. *Adhijigāṃsyate*: the meaning is "it is desired to remember"; this is a form of the root *ik*. *Jigaṃsyate*.
Thus: from the root *gam* with the suffix *san*, in the passive voice, the form is *gamiṣyate*.

Because *gam* does not undergo the substitution of an initial vowel (*aj-ādeśa*), there is no lengthening of the vowel. (Pāṇini 1.2.442) *iṅśca* || 2.4.48 || The rule *iṅśca* (2.4.48) [is also applied]. This means that after the root *iṅ* (to study), the *ātmanepada* endings are used. For example: *adhyeṣyate*. Since *iṅ* is a substitute for *adhi-i*, it is treated as having an initial vowel (*aj-ādi*), and thus the rule applies. However, in the case of *gam*, because it is not a substitute for a root beginning with an *aj* vowel, the lengthening does not occur. Therefore, the form remains *gamiṣyate*. (Note: The commentary explains the formation of the future passive participle *gamiṣyamāṇa* and clarifies why the vowel is not lengthened despite the presence of the *san* suffix.)

And *iṅ* [is included]. The sense is that this follows from the recurrence of the rules "gamiḥ syāt sani" (Pāṇini 7.2.58) and "ṇau gamiḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.54), as well as "sani ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.9). Because *iṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, the suffix *taṅ* (i.e., *ātmanepada*) applies by the rule "pūrvavatsanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.62).
Since it was stated [in the previous rule] "parasmaipadeṣu," the augment *iṭ* does not apply. The sense is that the lengthening occurs by the rule "ajjhanagamāṃ sani" (Pāṇini 6.4.16).

(443) *ralo vyupadhāddhādeḥ saṃśca* [Pāṇini 1.2.26]. Regarding *ralo*: it means "after a root ending in a consonant (*ral*), having *v* or *y* as its penultimate letter (*vyupadhāt*), and beginning with *dh* (*dhādeḥ*). By the use of the particle *ca*, there is an attraction (*anukarṣa*) of the term *ktvā* from the rule *pūṅḥ ktvā ca* [1.2.22]; this is the intended meaning. Regarding *seṭau*: [this refers to the suffixes] *ktvā* and *san*. [The next rule is: *na ktvā*... [etc.]

The intention is that [the suffix] *seṭ* follows from that [preceding rule]. Regarding "optionally when followed by *kit*": the intention is that this follows from the rules "after a root with *n* as its penultimate letter, or after one ending in *th* or *ph*, [the suffix *iṭ* is optional]" and "after a non-conjunct [root], the *liṭ* [suffixes] are *kit*. As for *didyotiṣate*: the root *dyut* (meaning "to shine") is *anudātta*.

The intention is that when there is reduplication (dvitva) with the suffix *san*, because it is *kit*, the semivowel of the reduplicated syllable undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* according to the rule "dyauti-svāpyoḥ," and following the preceding form, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) due to the *kit* nature of *san*. He states "didyotaṣate" in the case where *san* lacks the *kit* designation; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "pūrvavat sanaḥ."

Regarding *eṣiṣiṣati*: this is the desiderative (*san*) suffix added to the root *iṣ*. The augment *iṭ* is applied. Since the root does not begin with a consonant (*hal*), it is not *kit*, and therefore *guṇa* substitution occurs. Thus, we have *eṣ iṣa ti*.

At this stage, by the rule "of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*), the portion *ṣis* undergoes reduplication. Following the elision of the remaining consonants (*halādiśeṣa*) and the application of the *ṣatva* (retroflex sibilant) to the *san* suffix, the form is established. Now, even though here...

However, since [the substitution of] *ṣi* is obligatory (*nitya*), it would override even the subsequent *guṇa* substitution; and once doubling has occurred by the rule for *ṣi*, the vowel *i*—being a part of the root—would no longer possess the status of being a *upadhā* (penultimate), and thus *guṇa* would not apply anyway. Therefore, the rule *halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) would be redundant. To this, he says: "In this case, even though doubling is obligatory, it is overridden by *guṇa*. Why?

Therefore, he says: "For the effect of the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is stronger because it is twofold. And why is that? To this he says: "Of *oṇ*" (*oṇer iti*). The connection is: "Because the fact that *oṇ* is marked with an *ṛt* (indicatory letter) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For instance:
from the root *oṇṛ*, with the causative suffix *ṇic*, in the *luṅ* tense, after the *ciṅ* (the *caṅ* substitute for *san*), [the rule] "ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ" [applies].

When the prohibition [of reduplication] applies by the rule *ṭhnāglopiśāsvṛditām*, and the form *oṇi-a-t* has been established, the reduplication of the syllable *ṇi* results in the form *mā bhavān oṇiṇat*. In this context, the designation *ṛdit* is applied to the root *oṇ* for the purpose of prohibiting the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasva*). For if the shortening of the penultimate vowel were applied, the form would be *uṇ i*.
When the form *oṇ-i-a-t* is established, if there were doubling of the element *ṇī*, the result would be *mā bhavān uṇiṇat*;

thus, the vowel *o* would not be heard—this is the established position. However, if, due to its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*) were to occur first, and doubling were to take place at this stage while the form was still *oṇ-i-a-t*, then [the vowel *o* would indeed be heard].

Since a short vowel would not even be applicable due to the very absence of a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the employment of the term *ṛdit* for the purpose of prohibiting that [shortening] would be useless. Therefore, the meaning is that it is understood that the penultimate operation consisting of a short vowel is stronger than reduplication.
Now, let it be granted that the shortening of the penultimate is stronger than reduplication; however, in the present case, it is the *guṇa* of the penultimate [that is at issue].

To the question, "How can it be stronger because of its duality? he says: "sāmānyāpekṣā" (with reference to the general). The meaning is that its strength is understood from its duality in the form of being an operation on the penultimate vowel (*upadhākārya*). In reality, however, that which was stated as a restriction in the rule *ṇau caṅyupadhāyā hrasvaḥ*—namely, that [the shortening] applies when the penultimate vowel is followed by a consonant (*mṛditam*)—[is not intended here].
It performs [the operation] and indicates that, because of the doubling (dvirvacana), shortness (*hrasvatva*) is more powerful; however,

since the mention of "shortness of the *upadhā*" (*upadhā-hrasva-grahaṇa*) is specific, the fact that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends on a general rule is to be considered as explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

(444) *sanīvantardhabhrasjadambhuśrisvṛyūrṇubharajñapisanām* | Pāṇini 7.2.49. The compound *sanīvantardha-* is analyzed as follows: *sani* (the suffix *san*), *ivanta* (those ending in *i* or *u*), *ṛdha*, *bhrasja*, *danbhu*, *śri*, *svṛ*, *yu*, *ūrṇu*, *bhara*, *jñapi*, and *san*. This is a *dvandva* compound. Those which have *i* or *u* at their end [are included in the category *ivanta*].

The suffix *ivant* [is formed]. From the rule "svarati" (Pāṇini 7.2.44), the word "vā" (optionally) is carried over; from the rule "iṇniṣṭhāyām" (Pāṇini 7.2.47), the word "iṭ" (the augment *iṭ*) is also carried over. Therefore, he says: "from those ending in *iv*" and so forth.
Intending to provide an example for the root *div* ending in *vant*, he says: "in the absence of *iṭ*" (*iḍabhāve*). Regarding the word "vasya": [it refers to the root *div*].

The meaning is "of the letter *va*. Regarding "yaṇ": the remainder is "of the vowel *i* following the letter *k*. Regarding "doubling" (*dvitvam*): the remainder is "of the word *dyau*. In the form *dudyaūṣati*, there is lengthening by the rule "ajjhane. Regarding the alternative involving the augment *iṭ*, he says: *dideviṣati*. Because it does not begin with a consonant (*ajhalāditvāt*), the suffix *san* is not treated as *kit*; therefore, the substitution of *u* for *o* does not occur.

However, the intended meaning is that there is the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Another example of a root ending in *-s* will be stated as *susyūṣati* from the root *siv*. In that case, having raised the doubt regarding the *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) of the second *s*, he says:
"by the rule *stautiṇyoḥ*" [Pāṇini 8.3.61]. Thus: *susyūṣati*. This occurs when the suffix *san* is added to the root *siv* in the absence of the augment *iṭ*.
The form is like *dudyoṣati*. Regarding the alternative involving the augment *iṭ*, he says: *siseviṣati*. Stating that the form of the root *ṛdh* with the suffix *san* will be *īrtsati*, he says:
(446) *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* [Pāṇini 7.4.55].

In the rule *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt*, [the word] *sani* is understood from the rule *sani mīmāghurabhalabhaśakapatapadām aca is* (*7.4.54*), and *acaḥ* is also carried over. From the rule *saḥ syārddhadhātuke* (*7.4.49*), the word *si* is carried over as a qualifier of *san*; the intention is that this is a *tadādividhi* (a rule concerning what begins with that).
(447) *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* |7|4|58|.
Here, there is elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). [This applies] by the rules *sani mīmā-* (P. 7.4.54), *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* (P. 7.4.55), *dambha icca* (P.
7.4.56), and *muco'karmakasya guṇo vā* (P. 7.4.57).
By the word "here" (*atra*), the operation prescribed by the preceding four sūtras is referred to. Thus he says:
"The [sūtra] beginning with *mīm* is commenced when there is *san*. This means: when the operations of the four sūtras have been performed. Regarding the form *īpsati*:
from the root *āp*, when *san* is added, the vowel *ā* becomes *i* (by *sani mīmāghurabhalabhaśakapatapadām aca isyaḥ*), and then, by the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya*, the portion *psa* is reduplicated.

The meaning is that there is elision of the reduplication when [the root] is doubled. "Raparatvam" (substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*) means that when the suffix *san* follows the root *ṛdh*, in the absence of the augment *iṭ*, the vowel *ṛ* is changed to *ī*, which is then followed by *ra*. "Cartvam" (substitution of *ca* for *ja*) means that when the form *īrdh-sa* is established, the substitution of *ca* for *dha* occurs;
then, excluding the *repha* (*r*) according to the rule "na ndrāḥ," the second syllable following the initial [consonant] is doubled according to the rule "ajāder dvitīyasya."

The intention is that when there is doubling of the element *ṭhtsa*, there is elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). It should be understood that the doubling occurs after the change to *c* has been applied, based on the rule: "That which is considered *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it does not [apply] when there is doubling. Regarding the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is present, he says: *ardidhiṣati*. This is from the suffix *san*.

The sense is that, because there is no *sāditva* (the state of having *sa* as the initial), there is no change to *ī*, and once *guṇa* and *raparatva* have applied, the form *ardhiṣa* is established; then, *dhiṣ* undergoes reduplication. Regarding the root *bhrasj* with the suffix *san* and the augment *iṭ*, he says "bibhrajjiṣati" in the absence of the augment *ra* (which would otherwise be applied by the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayoḥ*). This is due to the substitution of *ścu* for *s*.

The *ś* [is changed]; by the rule for *jaś*-substitution, the *ś* becomes *j*. Because it is not followed by a *kṅit* suffix, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) by the rule "grahi-jyā-". Thus, we have *bibharjiṣati*. When *iṭ* is added and the augment *ram* (*nuṭ*) is optionally applied, we have the form *bhrasj-iṣa*. At this stage, after the vowel *a*, before the *s* and prior to the *repha* (*r*), the *repha* and the *s* following the *bh* are dropped, resulting in *bharj-iṣa*.

This being the case, from the root *bhṛj*, after doubling, applying the *halādiśeṣa* rule, changing the abhyāsa vowel to *i*, and applying *jaś*-ness, as well as the *ṣatva* of the suffix *san*, the form is established. Thus, in the presence of the augment *iṭ*, there are two forms due to the presence and absence of the augment *ram*: *bibhrakṣati*. This is the form when *iṭ* is absent and *ram* is also absent. [The form] *jaḥ*... [is derived from] *jasya*.

The *kutva* (change to *k*) of this [root] becomes *ṣ*. Thus, *bibharṣati*: this is the form when there is the absence of *iṭ* and the addition of *ram*. Therefore, in the alternative case where *iṭ* is absent, there are two forms due to the presence or absence of the *ram* augment.
(448) *dambha icca* (Pāṇini 7.4.56).

In the rule *dambha icca sani mīmē* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), the words *sanī* and *aca* are understood from the preceding context. By the force of the word *ca*, *īd* is conjoined from the rule *āpjñapyṛdhām* (Pāṇini 6.1.15). The word *sī* is understood from the rule *saḥ sī* (Pāṇini 7.3.96) and serves as a qualifier for *san*; this results in a rule governing the initial portion of that [suffix]. Thus he says: "of *dambh*, the vowel (*ac*)."
And so forth. Regarding "the elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsalopa*), the remainder [of the rule] is supplied as "by this [rule], 'there is elision here' (*atra lopaḥ*).

When *dimbhas* remains, he explains how the application of the rule "after that which ends in a consonant" (*halantāt*) occurs, even though there is no immediate succession following the *anusvāra* from a vowel (*ik-samīpāt*): "in the case of 'and after that which ends in a consonant' (*halantācca*)," and so on.

The mention of *hal* (consonant) means that, as previously stated, a single or multiple individual instances pervaded by the universal *haltva* (the property of being a consonant) constitute an "unlimited" (*aparimita*) number. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "By that" (*tena*). Regarding *dhīpsati*:

this is the form derived when there is no augment *iṭ* due to the rule *sanīvanta-* and [the substitution of] *it*. Regarding *dhīpsati*: this occurs when there is no *iṭ* and [the substitution of] *it*.

*Rūpam* (the form). The sense is that in the case where *iṭ* is added (*didambhiṣati*), because the suffix *san* does not begin with a *jhal* consonant, it is not *kit*; consequently, there is no elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*). In *śiśrīṣati*, since *iṭ* is absent by the rule *sanīvante*, there is lengthening by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*. Because the suffix *san* is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.

Regarding the desired alternative, he says: *śiśrayiṣati*. Because it does not begin with a vowel (*ajhalāditvāt*), there is no *kit* status, nor is there lengthening by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*. He recalls the rule for the substitution of *u* for the *ṛ* of the root *svṛ* when followed by the suffix *san*:
*udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*. Thus, *susvūrṣati*. In the absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *sanīvante*, there is lengthening of the *ṛ* by the rule *ajjhane*.
The intention is that after the substitution of *u* and the subsequent substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*, the lengthening occurs by the rule "ṭhupadhāyāṃ ca.

Regarding *sisvariṣati*: the intention is that after the reduplication of the root *svṛ* and the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, the form becomes *itavam*. Regarding *yuyūṣati*: when the augment *iṭ* is absent by the rule "sanīvante," the lengthening occurs by the rule "ajjhane."

Regarding *yiyaviṣati*: in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is present, because of the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *dvirvacane'ci*, there is reduplication of *yu*; the intention is that the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *oḥ puyaṇjī*. Regarding *ūrṇunūṣati*:
in the alternative where *iṭ* is absent by the rule *sanīvante*, there is reduplication of *nu*, excluding the *repha* (the letter *r*) according to the rule *na ndrāḥ*.
When this [root] is doubled, there is lengthening by the rule *ṭhajjhane*. Because the suffix *san* is *kit* by the rule *ṭhiko jhali*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.

However, in the alternative case where *iṭ* is applied, considering that the *ṅtva* (the status of being treated as *ṅit*) of *san* is optional by the rule *vibhāṣorṇoḥ*, he says: *ūrṇunuviṣati* and *ūrṇunaviṣati*. This is in the case where *ṅtva* applies.

The meaning is as follows: in the case where there is no *ṅ* (the *ṅittva* designation), when the suffix *nu* is doubled, the *uvaṅ* substitution occurs in the second half [of the reduplicated stem]. In the alternative case where there is *ṅittva*, when "ṭhnu" is doubled, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions occur in the second half. In both instances, the vowel *u* is heard in the reduplicative syllable (*abhyāsa*). Now, one might object: in the case where there is no *ṅittva*, [the form would be] *ūrṇuṃ isa*.

One might raise the objection: since the rule for doubling (dvitva) applies before the subsequent rules for the substitution of *av* for *ava* and the substitution of *i* for the *a* of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*)—namely, Pāṇini 6.1.2 (*dvirvacane'ci*)—if the word *nav* were doubled first, and then the *av* substitution and the *i* substitution for the reduplication were applied, one would hear only the vowel *i* in the reduplication in the form *ūrṇinaviṣati*, and not the vowel *u*. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by stating: "dvirvacane'ci" [Pāṇini 1.1.59].

In this sūtra, by carrying forward the term "sthānivat" and relying on the transfer of form (rūpātideśa), one meaning is as follows: when a vowel (*ac*) that serves as the cause for reduplication follows, any substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) assumes the form of its original (the *sthānin*) when the reduplication is to be performed. By carrying forward the word "na" from the rule "na padānte," [the following is established].

The other meaning is that when reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be performed, an *aj*-substitute for a vowel that serves as the cause of reduplication (*dvitvanimitta*) shall not take effect. In that case, according to the first explanation, even though the *guṇa* substitution has already occurred,
because the original form of the *sthānin* (the vowel *u*) is still perceived, the letter *u* itself appears in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of the word *ṭhnu*.

It is heard [in the scriptures]. Even in the second explanation, since the *guṇa* substitution is prohibited prior to reduplication (*dvitva*), the sense is that when only the syllable *nu* is reduplicated as the *abhyāsa*, only the vowel *u* is heard. Now, one might object: since the root *ūrṇu* with the suffix *isa* (i.e., *ūrṇu-isa*) undergoes the operation of reduplication, the *isa* contained within it [should also be reduplicated].

Since this [substitution] is also an effect (*kārya*), it cannot be the cause (*nimitta*) for doubling, according to the statement: "For that which is an effect is not resorted to as a cause. And thus, when doubling is to be performed, how can the prohibition—which applies to a substitution following an *ac* vowel that is itself caused by doubling—apply here to the *guṇa*?

Anticipating the objection that [the suffix] *san* would be applicable, he refutes it with the words "nor [is it] ending in *san*. Regarding the phrase "experiencing the effect," here the commentary itself is the sole refuge. As for "nor is there *san* here," the meaning is: "What indeed is the word *nu*? [The example] "bubhūrṣati" [is formed as follows]: in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is absent by the rule "sanīvante," the root is *bhṛ*.
When [the suffix] *san* is present, by the rule "sthite ṭhaji," the long vowel is applied; then, by "ṭhudoṣṭhaḷpūrvasya," the *u*-substitution occurs, followed by the replacement of *u* with *ra*;
then, for the subsequent portion, by "ṭhhali ca," a long vowel is applied. The point is that because *san* is marked as *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
Regarding the alternative where *iṭ* is added, he says: *bibhariṣati*. When *bhṛ* and *isa* are present, after doubling and the *urat* substitution...

The sense is that after [the substitution of] *rapara* (the replacement of *ṇ* by *r*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, the substitution of *it* for the *at* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), and the *guṇa* of the subsequent portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*), there is again the substitution of *rapara*. Regarding the statement "the root *jñap* is designated as *bhī* when followed by *puG*," the remainder of the sentence is "it is included in the rule *sanīvante*" (Pāṇini 1.2.8). This refers to the rule "in the senses of killing, pleasing, and perceiving, [the root] *jñā* [is treated as *bhī*]" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.2.8).

In the case of *ghaṭa* and so forth: then, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *jñā*, because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* class, the penultimate vowel is shortened due to its being designated as *mit*; thus, the form *jñap* is understood to be included among those ending in *ṇi*. Furthermore, there is a root ending in *p* belonging to the *curādigaṇa*. That which is read in the *curādigaṇa* as "√*jñap* [is] *mit*" is inherently one that ends in *p*, and not one that has the augment *puk* added to it.

The meaning is that this [root] is also included in the rule *sanīvantardha...* (Pāṇini 7.2.49). Regarding the phrase "in the absence of *iṭ*": even when *iṭ* is absent, because the suffix *san* follows the causative (*ṇic*) of the root *jñap*, the rule *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9) causes the *san* to be treated as *kit*; consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the *ṇic*. The phrase "because of its priority" refers to the elision of the *ṇic*.

The intention is that because there is no *ac* vowel present, the long vowel does not occur. Thus, after doubling the root *jñīp* and applying the *halādi-śeṣa* rule, he states the final form—*jñīpsati*—after the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*atra lopaḥ*) according to the rule "atra lopaḥ". Regarding the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is applied, he says: *jijñapayiṣati*. He then states the form when the suffix *san* is added to the root *san*: [He says: *sisāsati*. Regarding the form *sisāsati*, the intention is as follows: the root *san* undergoes doubling, and by the rule "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.79), the short vowel *a* is substituted for the long vowel *ā*. Then, by the rule "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.9), the *yaṇ* substitute is applied to the *a* of the reduplicated syllable. Next, the rule "sanyataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.79) applies again to the *a* of the reduplicated syllable, and the *yaṇ* substitute is applied once more. Finally, the rule "hali ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.77) causes the doubling of the *s*. Thus, the form *sisāsati* is established.
