Regarding the phrase *janasana-khātyātva-*: the word "of the letter *n*" (*nakārasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding *siṣāsati*: once *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *as*) has been applied, there is reduplication of *sā*; then, after the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), the substitution of *it* (for the radical vowel), and the application of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*), the form is established. Nor should one suspect that the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvācamācaṃ yaṅi* (Pāṇini 8.3.64) applies here and thus *ṣatva* does not occur due to the restriction *ṣṭautiṇyoreva* (Pāṇini 8.3.61); for that restriction applies only when the *ṣatva* of the suffix *san* has already taken effect.

Because that [suffix] occurs [there]. Regarding the desired alternative, however, he says: *sisaniṣati*. Here, the substitution of *ā* in *jana-sana-* does not occur because the suffix *san* is not preceded by a *jhal* sound. The intention is that the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur due to the restriction "only after *stu* and *ṇi*. In *tanipati*, this is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*).
(449) *tanoter vibhāṣā* | 6|4|17|.

Regarding *tanoter vibhāṣā*: the rule "the penultimate vowel is lengthened" (*upadhāyā dīrghaḥ*) applies here because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rules "of a penultimate [vowel]" (*nopadhāyāḥ*) and "when there is elision of ḍh or r" (*ḍhralope*). [The suffix] begins with a *jhal* sound in the case of the desiderative (*san*).

The phrase "in the case of the *ṭh* affix" follows from that [previous rule]. The intention is that it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that this applies when a *jhal*-beginning affix follows. Regarding the term "in the sense of apprehension": the meaning is that the suffix *san* occurs in its own sense after a verbal root denoting an action that is the object of apprehension. As for "the dog desires to die" (*śvā mumūrṣati*): the meaning is that he becomes one whose death is apprehended. The bank...

"Pipatiṣati" means "it is about to fall," that is, it becomes one whose falling is apprehended. This form occurs in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "tanipatī. However, regarding the absence of *iṭ* after the root *pat* with the suffix *san*, he says:

(450) *sani mīmāghurabhralaśakapatapadāmaca is* [Pāṇini 7.4.54]. [This sūtra prescribes the substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the roots *mī*, *mā*, *ghu*, *rabh*, *lā*, *śak*, *pat*, and *pad* when followed by the suffix *san*.]
Regarding "sanimīmā-sādau sani": the intention is that the term *si* continues from the rule *saḥ si*, as it has not been withdrawn.

Regarding "elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsalopa*): the intention is that this occurs by the rule *atra lopaḥ*. When the form *piṣ-t-sa-* is established, he says: "by *skor*" (Pāṇini 8.2.29). Regarding the root *daridrā* with the suffix *san*: [the rule] *tanipatī...* [applies].

He illustrates the option regarding *iṭ* [the augment]: *didaridriṣati* and *didaridrāsati*. Regarding the roots *ḍu miñ*—namely, *ḍu miñ prakṣepaṇe*, which belongs to the *svādi* class, and *mīñ hiṃsāyām*, which belongs to the *rkyādi* class—the meaning is that the suffix *san* is applied after these two. This is because of the inclusion of the term *mī* in the rule *sani mīmā* [Pāṇini 7.2.76].

The intended meaning is that both of these are included. Now, one might ask: since the form *mī* is heard with a long vowel, how can there be an inclusion of the root *ḍu miñ*, which ends in a short vowel? To this he says: "of that which has had the long vowel applied.
This refers to the root *ḍu miñ* when the suffix *san* is added, by the rule *ṭhajjhane* (Pāṇini 6.1.7), whereby the long vowel is applied; likewise for *mīñ*.

The meaning is that because there is no distinction between the forms *mī* and *mīr*, both are included under the rule *hiṃsāyām iti*. Regarding the form *saḥ sī*: when both roots have become *mī sa*, the substitution of *is* by the rule *sani mīmā* occurs;
then, after reduplication, the elision of the abhyāsa (the reduplicated syllable) by the rule *atra lopaḥ* results in *saḥ*.

The term *sī* means that the letter *t* [is substituted for the final *m*]. Thus, from the roots *mitsati* and *mitsate*. Because the root [of the causative] is marked with *ñ*, it takes both voices (ubhayapaditva) according to the rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ*. Regarding the forms *māṅ* and *meṅ*:

when *meṅ* takes the suffix *san*, the vowel substitution (*ātva*) is applied by the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti*; since there is no distinction in the resulting form *mā*, it is included in the rule *sani mīmā-*.

The intention is that both [roots] are included. Regarding *dodoṇoḥ*: since the vowel *ā* is substituted for the root *do* (meaning "to cut") when the suffix *san* is added, both forms are included because they are indistinguishable in their *dā*-form; this is the intention. Regarding *ditsati*: [this is derived from the same root].

Because it ends in a consonant (*ṭh*), the *kit* suffix prevents the *guṇa* substitution of the penultimate vowel by the rule *ṭhhalantācca*. Regarding *deṅ*: since this root also undergoes *ātva* (the change to *ā*), it possesses the status of a *ghu* root; thus, its inclusion in the rule *sani mīmā...* is intended. *Ripsate* is a form derived from the root *rabh*. *Lipsate* is a form derived from the root *labh*. *Pitsati* [is a form derived from the root *pat*].

The form *patitsati* is from the root *patlṛ*. The form *pitsate* is from the root *pad*. Regarding the statement "the substitution of *i* should be prescribed for the suffix *san*," the remainder [of the rule] is "for the letter *ā*. In *ṣaritsati*, there is the substitution of *i* for the initial [of the suffix] *san*; here, by the rule "there is elision [of the reduplication]," the reduplication is elided.

(451) *muco’karmakasyo guṇo vā* || 7.4.57 || "Of the root *muc* when it is intransitive. This is a supplement [to the rule] regarding the suffix *san* beginning with *s*. The meaning is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *si* from the rule *saḥ si* and of *san* from the rule *sani mīmā*.

This statement is made because the prohibition of *guṇa* (vowel strengthening) would otherwise apply by the rule "ṭhhalantācca" [Pāṇini 1.2.10], since the suffix is *kit*. Regarding "the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*)," the remainder of the sense is that this occurs by the rule "atra lopaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.58]. As for "mokṣate," the elision of the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule "atra lopaḥ. Regarding "but the *taṅ* [ātmanepada endings]," this refers to the rule "ni vṛdbhyaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.3.91].

The sense is that this is because it has already been stated that the mention of the *parasmaipada* suffixes continues [from the previous rule]. In the form *ninṛtsati*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is *kit* by the rule "after a word ending in a consonant" (*halantācca*), provided that the *iṭ* augment is absent.
(452) *iṭ sani vā* | Pāṇini 7.2.41. [The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before the desiderative suffix *san*.]
Thinking that "vṛta" is understood from the rule "vato vā," he says "from vṛṅ and vṛñ," etc. This is an exception to the rule "sani grahaguhośca.
In cases such as *cikīrṣati*, once the lengthening has been applied by the rule "ajjhanagamāṃ sani," this [present rule] does not apply.

By carrying over the term "upadeśe" from the rule "ṭhēkāca upadēśē," and explaining it as "in the original instruction (upadēśa) [of a root] ending in ṛ," [the form] *titariṣati*—or *titarīṣati*—is derived.

When the suffix *san* follows the root *tṛ*, and the present tense (*laṭ*) is applied, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "vṛto vā. However, in the absence of the augment *iṭ*, he says:

Regarding *titīrṣati*: because the suffix *san* is marked with *k* by the rule *iko jhal*, there is an absence of *guṇa*; thus, the *ṛ* of the root *tṛ* undergoes *itva* (change to *i*), followed by *raparatva* (substitution of *ra*), and then, by the rule *hali ca*, the vowel is lengthened—this is the intended meaning.

He says: "Because that which is the subject of an operation (*kāryin*) cannot be the cause (*nimitta*). The sense is that, based on the prohibition—"for that which is the subject of an operation is not resorted to as a cause"—the augment *iṭ*, which is the subject of the operation of doubling for the suffix *san*, cannot be the cause of that doubling. [Objection: But surely the augment *iṭ* is a part of the suffix *san*; therefore, [the rule applies] to the sequence *is*.

Even though the aggregate (*samudāya*) consists of two parts, because the element *isa* itself lacks the status of being the object of doubling (*dvitva-kāryitva*), it is not subject to doubling; therefore, he says: "isiti.
Since the element *is*—which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the suffix *san*—is the locus of doubling, by means of its constituent part, the aggregate *isa* [is considered so].

The sense is that it functions as the object (*kāryitva*). Regarding *añjijiṣati*: after the root *añj*, when the suffix *san* is added with the augment *iṭ*, the doubling of the syllable *jis* occurs because of the prohibition of the *nakāra* by the rule "na ndrāḥ. Since the root is marked with *ū*, the optionality of *iṭ* would apply; however, here *iṭ* is compulsory. Regarding *aśiśiṣate*: [this is from] the root *aśū* in the sense of pervading (*vyāptau*).

When the option of *iṭ* (the augment *i*) has arisen because the root begins with a vowel (*ūdit*), *iṭ* is obligatory. However, the root *ṭhaś* in the sense of "eating" belongs to the *ky*-class and is always *seṭ* (possessing *iṭ*). Regarding *uccheḥ*: [the root] *ucchī* means "to dwell. Here, the meaning is that there is a *tuk* [augment] by the rule *che ca*. Regarding *ścutvam*: the remainder of the rule is *tuka*. Now, one might object: [in the form] *uccha-isa*,...

Since the substitution of *ś* for *c* (ścutva) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when [the reduplication] is present, the letter *t* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) along with the letter *t*. Therefore, he says "pūrvatra" and so forth. Regarding "halādiśeṣaḥ": when there is a doubling of *ccch*, by the rule of "remainder of the initial consonant" (*halādiśeṣa*), the letters *cch* and *s* are removed from the reduplicated syllable; thus, in the case of the augment *tuk*, the letter *c* and the vowel *i* remain.

The meaning is "it remains. Thus he says: *ucchichishati*. In the subsequent portion (*uttara-khaṇḍa*), when the letter *ch* follows the vowel *i*, the *t* of the augment *tuk* becomes *c* by the rule of *cutva*. Now, one might object: when *cchis* undergoes reduplication, due to the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, the *ch* and *s* in the preceding portion (*pūrva-khaṇḍa*) are eliminated; and since the cause [for the application of the rule] has ceased (*nimittāpāye*), [the resulting form would be incorrect].

By the maxim "even that which is occasioned [by a cause] ceases when the cause is gone," since the *tuk* suffix itself is withdrawn, how can its substitute, the *cakāra*, be heard in the reduplication? To this he says:
"When the occasion has ceased. How is it non-eternal? To this he says: "of *cha* and *ava*. Thus he is questioned.
In forms such as *pṛṣṭavān*, by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*, the *ch* of the root *pracch* is replaced by *ś*. Then, by the rule *vraśca-ādinā*, the *ś* is changed to *ṣ*.
Since this would result in the audible pronunciation of the *k* [of the suffix *ktavatu*], the inclusion of the *t* in the term *satuk* is for the purpose of preventing that.
In that case, when the *c* [of the suffix] is replaced by *ś*, the *tuK* augment also [does not apply] simply because its cause no longer exists.

The meaning is that the inclusion of the term *satuṅka* (with *tuṅka*) would otherwise be rendered useless for the sake of establishing the cessation [of the substitute], and thus it indicates the non-eternality (*anityatā*) of the rule "when the cause [of a grammatical operation] is removed" (*nimittāpāye*). Or, as stated by the phrase "due to the mention of the restoration of the original form" (*prakṛtipratyāpattivacanāt*):

from the rule "and *hana* becomes *vadha*" (*hanaśca vadhaḥ*), when the suffix *ap* is added to the root *han*, the word *vadha* is formed through the substitution of the original form (*prakṛti*) with *vadha*.

In examples such as *kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe* ("he narrates the killing of Kaṃsa") and *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* ("he causes Kaṃsa to be killed"), the suffix *ap* is elided by the rule *ākhyānāt kṛtas tad ācaṣṭe kṛl-luk-prakṛti-pratyāpattiḥ*. When the suffix *ap* is elided, the substitution of *vadha* for the root [han] is prescribed to be withdrawn. In that case, when the *kṛt* suffix is elided...

The meaning is this: since the cessation of the substitution *vadh* and so forth is already established by the very disappearance of the cause (*nimitta-apāya*), the statement regarding "return to the original form" (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*) would otherwise be rendered useless;
therefore, that statement indicates the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the rule "when the cause disappears.
Even though in this case the suffix *ap* and the substitute *vadh* are prescribed simultaneously for the word *vadha*, and not [subsequently] upon the suffix.

Others, however, maintain that although this is so, because the suffix is taught as being in grammatical conjunction (saṃniyogaśiṣṭa), its status as a cause (nimittatva) is understood to extend to the final result; for in reality, there is the rule "puṣyayoge jñī" which establishes the forms *puṣyayogaṃ jānāti* and *puṣyeṇa yojayati*.
The phrase "the restoration of the original form as stated in the Bhāṣya" serves here as an indicator [of the intended meaning].

For in that context, by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there is the substitution of *ku* (a guttural) when a *ghi*-affix follows. Otherwise, if the *luk*-elision of the *kṛt*-suffix were to occur, the removal of the *ku*-substitution would follow automatically by the *nimittāpāyaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the disappearance of the cause); so what [would be the purpose of the stated restoration]?

The detailed explanation regarding *prakṛti-pratyāpatti-anuvṛtti* is found in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Now, he states the specific rule concerning the *san* [desiderative] suffix after the two roots *adhi-iṅ* ("to study") and *o-śvi* ("to move" and "to grow") when they are followed by the causative (*ṇic*) suffix: "When *ṇic* follows... This refers to the second part of the sūtra: *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ*.

It occurs in the fourth *pāda* and in the first *pāda* of the sixth [chapter]. The meaning of the first [sūtra] is: "When followed by a *ṇi*-affix that is itself followed by *san* or *caṅ*, the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ* is optional. The meaning of the second [sūtra] is: "When followed by a *ṇi*-affix that is itself followed by *san* or *caṅ*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root *śvi* is optional. By the first sūtra, *gāṅ* is substituted for *iṅ*.

The meaning of the second sūtra is that both [the substitution of *gā* for *iṅ* and the substitution of *samprasāraṇa*] are optional by means of the word "or" (*vā*). Thus, *adhijigāpayiṣati*: when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is intended after the root *iṅ*, the substitute *gāṅ* applies;

then from the form *gāpi*, with the desiderative suffix (*san*), this form is derived. This is because the rule for the application of *gāṅ* states: "And when *ṇic* follows, as well as when *san* and *caṅ* follow."
It has already been stated that this is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*). Regarding the state of the root *gāṅ*, he says: *adhyāpipayiṣati*.

By the rule "ṭhkrīṅjīnāṃ ṇau," there is the substitution of *ā* [for the penultimate vowel], and then the augment *puK*. Regarding *śiśvāyatayiṣati*: from the root *śvi*, after the addition of *ṇiC*, the substitution of *vṛddhi* and the replacement by *āya* result in *śvāyi*; from this, with the suffix *san* following, the form is derived without the occurrence of *saṃprasāraṇa*.

Regarding the alternative involving *saṃprasāraṇa*, he says: "śuśāvayiṣati. When the suffix *san* is added to the causative (*ṇyanta*) root, resulting in the form *śvi i isa*, the rule "vowel-substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the operation dependent upon it are stronger" dictates that the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs first. This *saṃprasāraṇa* results in the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels (*pūrvarūpa*). Then, when the element 'śu' is doubled, [the result is] in the latter portion...
The meaning is that there are the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions for the vowel *u*, and the *guṇa* and *āya* substitutions for the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Now, one might object:

since the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions for the vowel *u* would apply first—due to their higher status (paratva)—before the reduplication (*dvitva*), then once the reduplication of "hau" has occurred, the substitution of *i* for the *at* of the reduplicated syllable would result in only the letter *i* being heard. To this [the author replies]:

He says: "Not because of the doubling [of the root]," as in *pusphārayiṣati*. In this case, from the causative (*ṇic*) of the root *sphur*, when the desiderative suffix (*san*) with the augment *iṭ* follows, the doubling of *sphur* occurs even before the application of the rule "ṭhcisphurorṇau" (Pāṇini 6.1.54).

This is because there is a prohibition against the substitution [of *ya*] for the element following the causative marker (*ṇau*) when an operation concerning doubling is to take place. Furthermore, the shortening of the vowel (*itva*) by the rule "o, puyaṇjī" (Pāṇini 7.3.80) does not apply here, because of the letter *ph*.
Because it is separated by the letter *sakāra*, there is no subsequent occurrence of a *pavarga* [consonant]. Thus, in the form *cukṣāvayiṣati*:

from the root *kṣu* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*) with the augment *iṭ*, there is reduplication of the syllable "kṣu. The point is that in the final established form, because an *avarṇa* follows, the substitution [of *av* for *o*] is prohibited by the rule *ṇau caṅy upadhāyā hrasvaḥ*. This refers to the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*.
Although this has already been explained in the section on the derivation of causative *ṇic* affixes, it is reiterated here:

*pipāvayiṣati*, and so forth. From the roots *pū*, *bhū*, *yū*, *ru*, *lū*, and *ju*, when the desiderative suffix (*san*) follows a causative (*ṇic*), the reduplication is applied after the augment *iṭ* has been added;
because the prohibition of the substitution of *av* applies to the entire root, the reduplication occurs only for those roots ending in the vowel *u*.

The intention is that there is the substitution of *it* for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root, as mentioned in the rule *ju-caṅkramya-*. Now, he recalls the rule *sravati-śṛṇoti*, which was explained in the section on the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) formation, stating: "there is the substitution of *it* [for the vowel] in *sravati*."
Regarding the form *śuśrūṣate*: the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *jñā-śru-smṛ-dṛśāṃ sanaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *stauti-ṇyoreva*: the mention of *san* here refers to that *san* which has undergone the change of *ṣ* to *s* (i.e., *ṣaṇ*). The governing rules *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ* and *iṇkoḥ* are in force. In this context, the mention of *ku* is set aside.

Because [the suffix] is impossible. By the mention of *ṇi*, that which ends in it is understood. From the rule "saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ," the genitive form *saḥ* is carried over (anuvartate). Thus he says: "by the *ṇi* in the reduplication," and so forth. "When it has become *ṣ*" means when the letter *ṣ* is about to occur, i.e., in the state of *san*. "Not elsewhere" means if [the *s*] follows the *ṇi* in the reduplication...
The meaning, then, is that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs only for the roots *stu* and *ṇyant* (causative) forms.

One should not suspect that the particle *eva* is redundant— arguing that since the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* already establishes the desired result, the restriction is obtained by the very force of the rule's formulation— because [the purpose is to ensure] that it occurs *only* for the *ṣuṇ* (the causative marker).

Because it is intended to exclude restriction (*niyama*). For if there were the restriction "only [in the case] of *stu*," then the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur in the form *tuṣṭau* (the locative singular of *tuṣṭu*). He gives an example of the root *stu*: *tuṣṭūṣati*. The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ajjhane*. Intending to give an example of the causative (*ṇyanta*) form, he says: *dyauti*. Regarding "the substitution of *u*" (*utvam*), it refers to the substitution of *u* for the letter *v*.

The meaning is that *saṃprasāraṇa* is the vowel *u*. Regarding the form *suṣvāpayiṣati*: from the root *svap*, after adding the causative suffix *ṇic* and applying the *vṛddhi* strengthening to the penultimate vowel, we have *svāpi*. From this, with the addition of the desiderative suffix *san* and the augment *iṭ*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *v* [of *svāpi*].
Then, *sup* is reduplicated, the *ṇic* undergoes *guṇa* and the substitution of *ay*, the *s* of *san* becomes *ṣ*, and [the rule applies] to the *ṇ* following the reduplicated syllable.

The intended meaning is that there is *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). Regarding *siṣādhayiṣati*: here too, because it ends in a causative suffix (*ṇic*), the intended meaning is that there is *ṣatva* for the *s* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Regarding *sisikṣati*: the meaning is "he desires to sprinkle. The desiderative suffix (*san*) is added to the root *sic*. Because the suffix is *kit* by the rule *halantācca*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). [And] if there is *ṣatva* for the *s* following the reduplicated syllable...
The point is that, in that case, because of the restriction "only for *stu* and *ṇi*," there is no change to *ṣ*. [Objection:

But how can there be the change to *ṣ* for the *s* following the reduplicated syllable in *pariṣiṣikṣati*, given the restriction "only for *stu* and *ṇi*" and the rule "in *sthā* and so forth, as well as with the reduplicated syllable"?
Since the substitution of *ṣ* would also be precluded by this very rule, he says: "after a prefix, [the *s* of] *at*" (*upasargādat*...).

The intention is that, by the restrictive rule "only after *stu* and *ṇi*" (*stautiṇyoreva*), the substitution of *ṣ* prescribed by "before a suffix beginning with *ṣ*" (*ādeśapratyayayoḥ*) is indeed barred by the principle of the exception (*apavāda*). He asks: "What is the purpose of [specifying] *ṣaṇi*? (i.e., why is it necessary to mention the condition *ṣaṇi*?).

The question is: for what purpose is the mention of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) made? [The example is] *tiṣṭhāsati*. When *ṣatva* is applied by the rule "dhātvādeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.64), there is the doubling of the syllable *sthā* (by Pāṇini 6.1.2), followed by the shortening of the vowel in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the substitution of *i* (by Pāṇini 7.4.60), and finally the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* (by Pāṇini 8.4.41).
This restriction [of doubling] applies only when *ṣatva* has already been effected; however, in this case, since there is no *ṣṭu*-substitution for the *san* suffix, [the rule would not apply].

The meaning is that, because the restriction (*niyama*) does not apply here, the substitution of *ṣ* is unimpeded. Regarding *suṣupsati*: from the root *svap*, when the suffix *san* is added, the semivowel is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "vacisvapi... (*Pāṇini 6.1.15*), followed by reduplication. Because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel. Here too, the rule "stautiṇyoreva" (*Pāṇini 8.3.61*) applies.

The meaning is that the restriction does not apply because there is an absence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) after the suffix *san*. Now, one might ask: "If *ṣatva* applies to an *s* following an *iṇ*-vowel before the suffix *ṣaṇ*, then let the rule simply state 'only in the case of [the roots] *stu* and *ṇi*;
what is the purpose of including the word 'abhyāsāt' (after a reduplication)? To this, he says: "Because of the mention of 'abhyāsāt', it is not so here."

Regarding the form *pratīṣiṣati*: when the suffix *san* is added to the root *iṇ*, by the rule "of that which begins with a non-j letter, the second [syllable] is reduplicated," the syllable *si* is reduplicated, and the first part becomes the abhyāsa (repeated portion). Here, since the *san* has become a *ṣ*, the *s* following the root *iṇ gatau* (*iṇ* meaning "to go") indeed undergoes *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*). This is because the application of the restrictive rule occurs only when the *abhyāsa* is followed by an *ṇ*.
The state [of the rule applies]. *adhīṣiṣati* is also treated in this same way. (454) *saḥ svidisvadisahīnāṃ ca* |8|3|62|.

The division is *saḥ svidi*. [This refers to] the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvācamācaṃ śāsvṛdṛśāṃ ti ca* (6.1.19), which states that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the root-initial *s* only when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṣ*, and for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of the roots *stu* and *ṇyanta* (roots ending in *ṇ*).
The word "excepting *stu*" (varjam) follows from the previous rule. From the rule "sahe sāḍaḥ saḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.56), the word "saḥ" is understood as being in the genitive case.
Thus he says: "by the repetition" (*abhyāsena*). He states that the prescription of the letter *s* is for the purpose of restriction:
"of *s*, only *s* [is substituted]. This applies to the desiderative (*san*) of the root *su* (to press/extract), by the rule "only after *stu* and roots ending in *ṇī*" (*stautiṇyoreva*).

Since, by rule, there is an absence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in the subsequent portion [of the reduplication], one might suspect that in *abhisusūṣati*, the reduplication would undergo *ṣatva* by the rule *upasargāt sunoti*. Anticipating this, he says: "only in the case of *sthā* and so forth.
[The phrase] "from a secondary derivative" (*śaiṣikāt*) is a *vārttika* found in the sūtra prescribing the suffix *san*. [It means: from a secondary derivative, a suffix of the same form...

A secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*) suffix is not [used] after another suffix that has the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*. The connection is: "a suffix having the same form as one that has the sense of *matup* is not [used] after another suffix that has the sense of *matup*. A *śaiṣika* suffix is one prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*). In the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *adhyātma*. That which occurs in the sense of *matup* is "having the sense of *matup*" (*matubarthīya*).

The suffix *cha* is applied because [the word *śālā*] belongs to the *gahādi* group. "Matubarthika" means that which has the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*). The suffix *ṭhan* is applied by the rule "ata iniṭhanau. Regarding the form *śālīya*: that which exists in a hall (*śālā*) is *śālīya*, according to the rule "vṛddhāc chaḥ. The meaning is that when the sense of "existing in what is *śālīya*" is intended, the suffix *cha* is not applied again from the word *śālīya*. Regarding the phrase "existing in Āhicchatra": [the suffix *cha* is applied].

The word *āhicchatra* ends in the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "originating from" (*bhavārtha*). Consequently, by the rule "after a word with a long vowel [ending in *a*, *i*, or *u*], the suffix *cha* [is applied] in the sense of 'originating from'," only *cha* occurs, and not again *aṇ*; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might ask: how is it that in forms such as *jugupsiṣate*, there is a further *san* after a stem already ending in *san*? To this he says: "the word *sarūpa* (having the same form) is supplied [from the previous rule]. [Thus, the rule applies only when the subsequent *san* is of the same form as the preceding one. It does not apply after a stem ending in *san*.
The meaning is that even in the case of "saniṣyate," the term "sarūpa" (having the same form) is understood by way of ellipsis. Now, one might ask:
even so, how can the suffix *san* apply in the case of "jugupsiṣate," since there is a difference in form? To this, he says:
"by way of meaning. Since a difference in form is impossible on the level of the word itself, similarity must be understood solely through the medium of meaning.

The meaning is that this is what is intended to be expressed. Regarding the word "tena" (by that): the sense is that from the desiderative suffix (*sann*) following another desiderative suffix, the form "icchāsann" is obtained.

Regarding "svārtha": the meaning is that the desiderative suffix *san* certainly occurs after a desiderative suffix used in its own primary sense (*svārtha*). Thus ends the section on the formation of desiderative stems (*sannantaprakriyā*).
Thus ends the section on the formation of denominative verbs (sannanta-prakriyā) in the Bālamanoramā.

Now begins the section on the remainder of all compound formations (sarvasamāsaśeṣaprakaraṇa). Next, as an incidental topic, the miscellaneous rules applicable to all compounds (sarvasamāsopayuktaprakīrṇaka) are presented.

He begins the section with the words *kṛttaddhita* etc. The meaning is that there are five types of *vṛtti*s: those ending in *kṛt* suffixes, those composed of *taddhita* suffixes, compounds (*samāsa*), *ekaśeṣa* formations, and verbal roots ending in suffixes such as *san*.
He states the general definition of *vṛtti*: "A *vṛtti* is the expression of another's meaning. [The word] *samarthaḥ*...

This point is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *padavidhiḥ*. The term *abhidhāna* is derived from the root with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). It is neuter because it denotes a general category. The meaning is that *vṛtti* (the derivative formation) is that which expresses a distinct, unified meaning different from the meanings of the individual words that constitute the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).

In the state of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), *vṛtti* refers to that which, through the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) of words initially analyzed as having individual meanings, conveys a single qualified meaning.

And this collective power is obtained through the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "An operation concerning words applies to those that are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*). In that regard:

The status of compounds (*samāsa*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) as *pada-vidhi* (rules dependent on words) is quite evident: for compounds are prescribed by carrying forward the rule *sup-supā*, and secondary suffixes arise from that which ends in a case-ending (*subanta*), as will be explained hereafter.
This also applies to certain primary suffixes (*kṛt*), such as in *karmaṇy-aṇ*, where the suffix is conditioned by a co-occurring subordinate word (*upapada*).

The status of being a rule dependent on a word (*padavidhitva*) certainly exists [in these cases]. Rules such as *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (P. 3.1.8) also possess the status of being rules dependent on a word. Furthermore, even in the rule for *ekaśeṣa*, because the term *dvandva* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*, that [formation of *ekaśeṣa*] is prescribed within the domain of *dvandva*;
thus, *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) certainly exists there. This is explained in detail in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works.

Regarding the phrase "it conveys the meaning through its function (*vṛtti*)," although it has been elaborated upon in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra* that it is precisely in a *vṛtti*— and not in a sentence— that there exists, by means of a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*), the capacity to convey a single qualified meaning, nevertheless...

It should be understood that a *vigrahavākya* (analytic sentence) is a collection of words ending in case-terminations suitable for forming a compound (*samāsa*), when those words are used separately. "Because it is fully established" (*pariniṣṭhitatvāt*) means because it has been refined by grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). "Unfit for usage" (*prayogānarha*) [refers to the compound].
The meaning is that there is an absence of the state of being uninflected (*avyākṛta*). The word "like" (*yathā*) is used to indicate an example.
"The king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*): the phrase "the colloquial analytical sentence" (*laukikavigrahavākya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"King-as-man" (*rājan-as-puruṣṛsu*): the phrase "the non-colloquial analytical sentence" (*alaukikavigrahavākya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

"A *nityasamāsa* (invariable compound) is one without analysis (*avigraha*). This means it is devoid of a popular analytical sentence (*laukikavigrahavākya*). The sense is that the compound is obligatory. "Not having its own members" (*asvapada*) refers to an obligatory compound whose analysis is performed using other words that have the same meaning as the words being compounded.

This is the meaning. However, in the case of a compound whose object is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), even if the name is not understood through the sentence, the employment of the explanatory sentence that conveys the meaning of the constituent members of the compound certainly occurs in order to inform one of the words forming the compound. In that regard, the claim that the compound is obligatory refers only to the sentence.

They say that [the term *samāsa*] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) because it lacks the same meaning as *vṛtti*. "Fourfold" means that it is of four types: *avyayībhāva*, *tatpuruṣa*, *bahuvrīhi*, and *dvandva*.
"A statement made for the most part" (*prāyovāda*): the indeclinable *prāyas* denotes abundance; thus, it refers to what is intended by way of majority.
The meaning is that there is a claim regarding its being of four kinds. To the question "Why?", he says: "In the case of *avyayībhāva*," etc.

Regarding the phrase "even of many compounds," the word "of compounds" (*samāsānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "Generally intended" (*prāyo'bhiprāya*) means having the sense of abundance. Regarding "sūpa-prati," etc., [this occurs] immediately after the rule "in the case of a *dvandva*," etc.
The word *śrutam* (is heard) connects with [the rules] immediately following *avyayībhāve*, immediately following *tatpuruṣe*,

and immediately following *bahuvrīhau*. In the case of the avyayībhāva compound *sūpapratīti*, because the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, [it is called] "the region of the mad Gaṅgā" (*unmatagaṅgam*) and "the region of the red Gaṅgā" (*lohitagaṅgam*).

The meaning is that in an *avyayībhāva* compound, because the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, there is an absence of predominance for the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārtha*). The meaning is that in a *tatpuruṣa* compound such as *atimāla*, because the meaning of the first member is predominant, there is an absence of predominance for the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*). [The example is] *dvitrāḥ*.

The meaning is that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because both members of the compound are primary, there is an absence of predominance by the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). In a *dvandva* compound such as "teeth-and-lips" (*dantoṣṭha*), however, it is the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) alone that is primary.

The meaning is that there is an absence of predominance for the meanings of both constituent words. "A *karmadhāraya* is a specific type of *tatpuruṣa*"—the intention is that this is because of the statement: "A *tatpuruṣa* whose members refer to the same substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is a *karmadhāraya*. "A *dvigu* is a specific type of that"—the meaning is that it is a specific type of *karmadhāraya*. [It is] "that which is preceded by a numeral..."

The intended meaning is that [the compound] begins with "dvigu" and so forth. "The state of having multiple words" means the state of consisting of two, three, four, or more words. The intention is that because the mention of "aneka" (multiple) occurring in the rule for the *bahuvrīhi*—namely, "anekam anyapadārthe"—is also carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule prescribing *dvandva* compounds.

"In some cases only" means, for instance, in examples such as *dvyahnajāta*. "It has been stated" implies that this was said in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works. The word *kiñca* is an indeclinable used here to indicate another specific point. Regarding the rule *supāṃ supā*: [it applies] between words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), with words ending in case-suffixes, or with verbal roots (*tiṅanta*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
And there is a compound with a *dhātu*. The word "atha" (now) serves to mark a break from the preceding statement. Regarding "tiṅām":

the meaning is that one should know that there are six types of compounds, namely, the compound of *tiṅ*-ending words with a *tiṅ*-ending word and with a *sup*-ending word. Regarding "supā": the meaning is that an illustration for the term "supā" will be stated.

Regarding "rājapuruṣa": this is a compound of the word "rājñaḥ" (in the genitive case) with the word "puruṣa," which ends in a *sup* suffix. Regarding "tiReĀti": the meaning is that an example for the [sūtra] "supāṃ tiReĀt" will be stated.
Regarding "paryabhūṣayat": because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) into "saha" and "supā" within the sūtra "saha supā," [the prefix] "pari" [is included].
A compound of that which ends in a *sup* [case-ending] with that which ends in a *tiṅ* [verbal suffix]. Regarding the word "nāmnā" (with a noun):
the meaning is that an example of a compound of *sup*-ending words with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) will be stated. As for "kumbhakāraḥ":
by the rule *upapadam atiṅ*, there is a compound of the genitive-ending word "kumbhasya" with the nominal stem "kāra".

The meaning is that this is because of the statement: "There is a rule for the compounding of words denoting direction (gati), case-roles (kāraka), and secondary words (upapada) with primary derivatives (kṛt) prior to the production of case-endings. Regarding the phrase "by a verbal root" (dhātunā):
the sense is that an example of the compounding of case-endings (sup) with a verbal root will be stated later. As for "kaṭaprūḥ": [this is the example].

By the Vārttika "kvibvacipracchāyāyatastukaṭaprujuśrīṇāṃ dīrgho'saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca," the compound is derived as a *nipātana* (irregular formation) from the root *pru* (meaning "to move") with the suffix *kvip*; one must not mistake this for a *tiṅ-anta-upapada-samāsa* (compound with a verbal form as a subordinate member), because here the rule for *kvip* is being applied.

Because there is no mention of the seventh case (saptamī), there is an absence of the status of being an *upapada*. Now, he provides another example of a verbal root (*dhātu*) with a case-ending (*sup*), namely *ajasram*.
This refers to the rule for the suffix *ra* in the sūtra: "The suffix *ra* [is applied] after the roots *nam*, *kamp*, *smi*, *aj*, *as*, *kam*, *hiṃs*, and *dīp*."

The negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is prescribed together with the verbal root *jas*. "Of verbal roots, [the suffix] *tiR* [is applied] after *ati*"—the meaning is that an example for this will be stated in the section on compounds. In "pibatakhādatā" (O, drink and eat!), there is a compound of a finite verb with another finite verb by virtue of its inclusion in the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-group. "A finite verb [is compounded] with a word ending in a case-suffix."

The meaning is that an example for a compound will be stated. Regarding *kṛnta-vicakṣaṇa*: O wise one (*vicakṣaṇa*), "cut" (*kṛnta*) means "cut off" (*ucchindhi*). To the question, "How can there be a compound here between a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*)?", he says:
"In the case of *ehi-ḍā* and so forth. Here, by the rule *supāṃ tiṅā*, [the case endings] of the verbal suffixes [are replaced].

Some say that because the term "subanta" (ending in a nominal suffix) is also included [in the definition], one should consider the compound (*samāsa*) to be of six types; however, it is more logical that there are only five types, since there is no distinction between the two cases in that both are composed of *sup* (nominal suffixes) and *tiṅ* (verbal suffixes). Others, however, [hold that] by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*,...
They say that by this [rule], there is the inclusion of a compound whose prior member ends in a *subanta* (inflected nominal) and whose subsequent member ends in a *tiṅnta* (inflected verbal);
whereas by the rule *tiṅāṃ subantena*, there is the inclusion of a compound whose prior member ends in a *tiṅnta* and whose subsequent member ends in a *subanta*.
Thus ends the section on the remaining general rules for all compound formations in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*). (1292) *Śeṣe* | Pāṇini 4.2.92. [The suffixes taught from here onwards are applied] in the sense of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Now the section on secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) is examined. Regarding the rule *śeṣe*: "the suffixes beginning with *aṇ*" means that these are the common suffixes starting from *ṭh* in the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* and so forth. Regarding *caturbhiḥ*:
the remainder [of the sense] is "by means of horses" (*aśvādibhiḥ*). Regarding *caturdaśyām*: [it refers to] the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśyām*).
"The Rākṣasas appear"—this is the traditional teaching (āgama). Regarding the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa):

the meaning is that [this sūtra] prescribes the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth for the purposes of "taking hold" (*grahaṇa*) and the rest, which have been demonstrated but not yet applied by the subsequent sūtras. The point is that if this were merely a governing heading (*adhikāra*), then because its recurrence would be obtained only within the subsequent sūtras themselves, this [specific rule] would not be established.
"And 'adhikāra' (heading/rule of application)"—the intention is that it serves as a governing rule for the subsequent sūtras because it is marked with the *svarita* accent.
He states the limit of this heading: "until [the sūtra] *tasya vikāraḥ*" (P. 4.3.134). Nor [is it limited] by the subsequent sūtras...

It should not be argued that the governing heading for the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is redundant because the distinctness from the meanings beginning with "offspring" (*apatya*) and ending with the four purposes (*caturarthī*) has already been established by the specific meanings previously taught;
for [the *śeṣa* heading] is necessary so that meanings beginning with "offspring" and ending with the four purposes are not included in rules such as "tasyeda" (Pāṇini 4.3.120).

Because that [the term *śeṣa*] is necessary. Nor should it be argued that since the suffixes *aṇ* and others are already established by the rule *tasyedam* for the purposes of "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) and so forth which have been demonstrated, the status of *śeṣa* as a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) need not be resorted to;
for even in cases such as *śaiṣikān matubarthīyāt*, there are instances where those very purposes of "grasping" and so forth are demonstrated.

This is because that [distinction] is necessary for the purpose of grasping [the meaning]. Even offspring and the like, though appearing as "this" (*idantvena*), are not *śeṣa* (remainder), according to the Bhāṣya: "For these—offspring, collection, modification, and dwelling—are indeed specific instances of 'this' (*idaṃviśeṣāḥ*). This has been explained in detail under the rule *tasyāpatyam*.
In the course of commenting on the *Ślokavārttika* passage beginning with "tasyedam ityapatye 'pi" (Pāṇini 4.3.120), [it is stated]:
"From *rāṣṭra* and *avārapāra*, the suffixes *dhak* and *kha* [are applied]" (Pāṇini 4.2.93). Regarding this, [the commentary says] "from these two."

The meaning is: from the word *rāṣṭra* and from the word *avārapāra*. Regarding *rāṣṭriya*: the meanings such as "born in the kingdom" (*rāṣṭre jātaḥ*) or "dwelling there" (*bhavaḥ*), and so forth, should be understood according to the respective context. [In this formation] *iya* replaces *dha*. Regarding *avārapārīṇa*:
*īna* is substituted for *kha*, and the *ṇa*-substitution [of the suffix] occurs.

It should also be stated: "even from *avārapāra* when it is not separated [by a suffix] and when it is reversed. This means that the suffix *kha* should also be stated even after the word *avāra* and the word *pāra* when they occur separately. "And when reversed" means...

The meaning is that [the suffix] is applied even from the words *pārā* and *avāra*. Now, one might object: starting from the rule *sārṣṭāvārapāre* and ending with *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām*, suffixes have been prescribed for the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*) after base-words such as *rāṣṭra* and others.
However, unlike in the case of "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) and so forth, specific meanings are not indicated; rather,

suffixes beginning with *gha* and ending with *ṭyaṇ*, *ṭyaL*, and *ṭyaLun* would apply after any specific bases such as *rāṣṭra* when followed by any case-ending, because the rule "after [words] whose capacity [is restricted], from the first [word]" (*samarthānāṃ prathamād vā*) is not present here.
Because there is no presentation of a specific case-ending uttered at the outset; furthermore, in subsequent sūtras such as *tatra jātaḥ*, only specific meanings are indicated.
In those cases, [the suffixes] are common to all words ending in those respective case-endings, beginning with the locative (*saptamī*) that is uttered first.
[The suffixes] would indeed be beginningless. To this, he says: "In this context, by means of the words 'prakṛti' and so forth.

[This refers to] the requirement for specific meanings and specific case-endings (*vibhakti*) when rules such as *rāṣṭrāvāra-* and others prescribe suffixes alone after specific bases (*prakṛti*). In that regard—

Furthermore, regarding the sūtras beginning with *jātaḥ*, which are solely intent on indicating specific meanings and whose respective bases (*prakṛti*) receive their particular case-endings by virtue of the sūtra *samarthānām*, when these [sūtras] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with one another due to the requirement for specific affixes to be prescribed, then in that context, *jāta*— [The remainder of the sentence would follow.]

The intended meaning is that suffixes beginning with *gha* and ending with *ṭhañ*, *yaṅ*, and *yuṅ* are applied to words such as *rāṣṭra* when they are uttered in the nominative case (*prathamā*) in senses such as "born there" (*jāta*).
However, from other bases such as *rāṣṭra*, common suffixes such as *aṇ* are applied in the same senses of being born there and so forth.
They indeed exist.

(1294) *grāmādyakhañau* |4|2|94|. Regarding *grāmādya-khañ-au*: [the word] *grāmya* is formed with the suffix *ya*; by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant of the base]. [The word] *grāmīṇa* [is formed with the suffix *khañ*].
Thus: there is the substitution of *īn* for *khañ*, and the change to *ṇ*. (1295) *katryādibhyo ḍhakañ* [Pāṇini 4.2.95]:
from *katrya* and so forth. Regarding *katrayaḥ*: there is a compound with the word *ku* according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*.
In the word *kātreya*, *ku-* is replaced by *kad-* according to the rule *ṭha-ṭhrau ca*. The suffix *ḍhakañ* is applied; the *ñ* of *ḍhakañ* is replaced by *ey*.

The *y* is elided by the rule *lopo vyoḥ*. The phrase "because of the recurrence" (*anuvṛtteḥ*) means that it is due to its being marked with a circumflex accent (*svaritatva*). Thus, the meaning is that the suffix *ḍhakañ* is also obtained after the word *grāma*.

(1296) *Kulakukṣigrīvābhyaḥ śvāsyalaṅkāreṣu* |4|2|96|. [The suffix] *ḍhakañ* is applied after *kula*, *kukṣi*, and *grīvā* when the meanings are "a dog," "the mouth," and "an ornament" respectively. [Kulakukṣi: After *kula*: *kauleyakaḥ* ("a dog born in a noble family"). After *kukṣi*: *kaukṣeyakaḥ* ("a sword," meaning "that which comes from the belly"). After *grīvā*: *graiveyakaḥ* ("an ornament for the neck"). Regarding the word *śva* ("dog"): the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one born in a family" (*kule jātaḥ*), etc.
*Kaukṣeyaka* means *asi* (sword). The meaning is: that which exists in the *kukṣi* (belly), namely a sword. *Graiveyaka*:
the analysis of the compound is "that which exists in the necks" (*grīvāsu bhavaḥ*).
[Pāṇini 4.2.97: *Nadyādibhyo ḍhak*. (4.2.97) [The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after words such as *nadī* to form derivatives denoting origin.]
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after words such as *nadī* [meaning river] and others. For example, *māheyam*: "mahī" means the earth; the meaning is "born in that [earth]" and so forth.
*Vārāṇaseyam*: the meaning is "born in Vārāṇasī" and so forth. (1298) The suffix *tyak* is applied after the words *dakṣiṇa*, *apaśca*, and *puras*. Pāṇini 4.2.98.

"Dakṣiṇāpaścāt. [The term] "ending in -ā" (ājanta) is an indeclinable; the meaning is that it is understood as ending in -ā due to its association with other indeclinables. The sense is that the suffix *tya* should be applied after these indeclinables—*dakṣiṇā*, *paścāt*, and *puras*—in the senses of "born there" (*jāta*) and so forth.

(1299) *kāpiśyāḥ ṣphak* | Pāṇini 4.2.99. The analysis of the rule is: *kāpiśyāḥ ṣphak*. The meaning is that the suffix *ṣphak* shall be applied after the word *kāpiśī*. *Kāpiśī* is the name of a particular region. [The derivative form is] *kāpiśāyanī*.

Regarding "drākṣā": because it has the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. (Pāṇini 4.2.100): *raṅkor amanuṣye 'ṇ ca*. After *raṅku*, when not referring to a human being, there is the suffix *aṇ* as well as *ṣphak*. Thus, *rāṅkavaḥ*.
"Gaura" refers to a specific region named Raṅku; the meaning is "born there," and so forth.

Regarding the term *rāṅkavaka* (a person from Raṅku): here, because it is a human being (*manuṣya*), the suffixes *ṣpha* and *aṇ* do not apply. Instead, the suffix *vuñ* applies according to the rule to be stated later: *manuṣyastatsthayor vuñ*. The substitution of *a* for the final vowel occurs, resulting in *rāṅkavaḥ*.
The reading "manuṣya" is a corruption.

(1301) *dyauprāgapāgudakpratīco yat* | Pāṇini 4.2.101. [The suffix] *yat* is added after *div*, *prāñc*, *apāñc*, *udañc*, and *pratyañc*. *dyauprāgapāk*: *div*, *prāñc*, *apāñc*, *udañc*, *pratyañc*. From these [words, the suffix *yat* is applied].

The meaning is "that which would be. In the sūtra, there is the designation *ut* by means of the substitution *ut* [of the final vowel] in the word *diva*. *Divyam* means "born in heaven" (*divi*), and so forth. *Prācyam* means "born in the eastern region" (*prāci*), and so forth.
When the taddhita suffix is produced and the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided (*luk*), the form *prāñc-ya* remains; then, by the rule *aniditām...* [the nasal is dropped].

When the *n* is elided by the rule "nalope ṭhacaḥ" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.143), the vowel *a* is elided; then, by the rule "ṭhcau" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.144), the preceding vowel is lengthened, resulting in the form *prācyam*.

As for *apācyam*, this is also formed in the same manner as above. As for *udīcyam*, the specific difference here is that the vowel *u* is changed to *ī* by the rule "uda īdi" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.145). As for *pratīcyam*, the formation is like that of *prācyam*.
(1302) *kanthāyāṣṭhak* |4|2|102|. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is added after *kanthā*. A *kanthā* is a collection of many pieces of cloth sewn together crosswise; others say it refers to a particular region.

(1303) *varṇau vuk* | 4.2.103 | Regarding *varṇau vuk*: [The suffix] *vuk* is added after the word *varṇu*. Thus, *varṇusamīpa* ("near Varṇu"). *Varṇu* is the name of a river, the Sindhu; in the sense of "located not far from that," the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the *suvāstu* group, and then the elision (*lup*) occurs by the rule "*janapade lub*" (Pāṇini 4.2.81). And so it is.
The word *varṇu* refers to the region near Varṇu; the suffix *vak* is applied to denote a *kanthā* (a fortified enclosure) located therein.
(1304) [Pāṇini 4.2.104: *avyayāt tyap* (the suffix *tyap* follows an indeclinable).
The suffix *tyap* follows indeclinables (*avyaya*). It occurs only after *am*, *iha*, *kva*, *tasi*, and *tra*.
That is to say, the suffix *tyap* is applied to these very indeclinables: *amā*, *iha*, *kva*, *tasi*, and *tra*.

This is a supplementary explanatory rule (*vārtika*) regarding enumeration. Regarding the term *amātya*: the meaning is "born near" or "born together. Regarding *aupariṣṭa*: since the indeclinable *upariṣṭāt* is not included among those enumerated [for the suffix *tyap*], the suffix *tyap* does not apply;
rather, the form *aupariṣṭa* is derived with the suffix *aṇ*. This is the meaning.

There is elision of the *ṭi* suffix for indeclinables (*avyaya*) when there is merely a *bha*-designation. To the question "How is there elision of the *ṭi* here?", he says: "of indeclinables. This is a *vārttika*. Regarding "merely a *bha*-designation": the word *mātra* signifies entirety. There is elision of the *ṭi* of the entire *bha*-portion of an indeclinable.

The meaning is that the condition (upādhi) beginning with "ṭh-nastaddhite" is not required. Now, one might object: if this were so, then from the indeclinable *ārāt*, when *cha* is substituted by *īya* and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the form would have to be *ārīya*;
to this he replies: "This [rule] is not universal (*anitya*)."

It should be stated that [the suffix] *tyap* follows *ni*. That is to say, *tyap* occurs after the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *ni* when "permanence" (*dhruva*) is to be understood. The *Bhāṣya* states: "That which exists invariably is 'eternal' (*nitya*)."

When *gata* follows, [the suffix] *nis* becomes *tya*. The meaning is that the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *nis* is designated as *tya* when *gata* is to be understood. Once *nis-tya* has been established, [the rule applies] to the letter *s*.
Since the condition of being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*) is absent and because it is not an integral part of an affix (*pratyaya*), the substitution of *ṣ* would not otherwise apply.

(1305) *Hrasvātādau taddhite* | Pāṇini 8.3.101. "Before a taddhita suffix beginning with a consonant other than *ṭ*, following a short vowel. The term *iṇ* is understood from the previous rule, *ṭhiṇkoḥ*. The term *sa* is understood from the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*.
Therefore, the word "sa" (of that) in the genitive case is carried over [from the previous rule], as is the rule "an uninitial [consonant] becomes a retroflex [if preceded by a retroflex or r].
Thus he says: "after a short vowel and the vowels iṇ. In the form *niṣṭya*, although *s* has become *ṣ* by the rule for *ṣatva*, the *t* becomes *ṭ* by the rule for *ṣṭutva*.

"From *araṇya* [comes] *āraṇya*, and *āraṇyāṇṇya*. The word "it should be stated" (*vaktavya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. An example is *āraṇyāḥ sumanasaḥ*. According to Amarasimha, "Sumanas refers to flowers" (*sthirayaḥ sumanasaḥ puṣpam*). In the sense of "those which exist in the forest" (*araṇye bhavāḥ*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied.
The form is *āraṇyā* when the suffix *ṭāp* is applied; however, the intention is that the suffix *ṅīp* would apply when the suffix *aṇ* is used. (*dūrādetyaḥ*).
Regarding *dūrādetya*, the word "it should be stated" (*vaktavya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. *Dūretya* means "one who has come from afar" (*dūrād āgataḥ*).

Alternatively, the meaning is "be far away. From the indeclinable *dūrāt*, with the suffix *atyap* added, there is elision of the *ṭi* by the rule "for indeclinables, when a *bha*-ending follows. [From *uttara*] the suffix *āhañ* is applied.

Regarding "autarāha," the word "vācya" (should be stated) is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. "Autarāha" means either "come from the north" (*uttarasmād āgataḥ*) or "belonging to the north" (*uttarasmin bhavaḥ*). However, "autara" is incorrect.
(Pāṇini 4.2.105) *aiṣamohyaḥśvaso 'nyatarasyām*.

"From *aiṣamaḥ*, *hyas*, and [the following]": this means from these words, namely *aiṣamaḥ*, *hyas*, and *śvas*. "The two to be mentioned later": the remainder of the sense is that [the suffixes] *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are applied by the rule "after the indeclinables *sāyam*, *ciram*, *prāhe*, and *prage*, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are added, along with the augment *tuṭ*". "*Aiṣamastyam*" [is derived as follows]: the indeclinable *aiṣamaḥ* refers to the present time.

It occurs within a year; the meaning is "that which exists therein. Regarding the forms *parut*, *parāri*, and *aiṣamaḥ*, Amara states: "The words *parut*, *parāri*, and *aiṣamaḥ* [denote] years, as do *pūrve*, *pūrvatare*, and *yati*. Regarding the form *aiṣamastanam*: the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are optionally applied. The letters *ṭ* and *ā* are indicatory (*it*), the *y* and *u* undergo substitution by *an*, and for that [suffix], the augment *tuṭ* is added. The letter *ṭ* is an *it*, and the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

The suffix *ṭya* is the first member [of the compound]. *Hyastya*, *hyastanam*: the indeclinable *hyas* means "on the day gone by" (*gate 'hani*). The meaning is "that which exists there. *Śvastya*, *śvastanam*: the indeclinable *śvas* means "on the day yet to come" (*anāgate 'hani*). The meaning is "that which exists there. Amara states: "In the past day, *hyas*; in the future day, *śvas*. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*):

The meaning is that by the rule *ṭhaśvasastuṭ ca*, when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied, there is the substitution of *ik* for it, the addition of the augment *tuṭ*, and by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca*, the addition of the augment *aij*; thus, the form *śauvastika* will also be explained as follows. (1307) *tīrarūpyottarapadādaññau* |4|2|106|.

*Tīrarūpa*: The meaning is that the suffix *añ* is applied respectively after a compound whose final member is *tīra* and after one whose final member is *rūpa*. *Kākatīram* means "that which exists on the bank of the Kāka. *Pālvalatīram* means "that which exists on the bank of a pond. *Śaivarūpyam* means "that which exists in the form of Śiva."

In some places, the reading is "rūpyottarapade. That being the case, when the suffix *ñya* is applied, the form contains two *y*s due to the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "yasyeti ca. Regarding the form *bāhurūpyam*: although the suffix *bahuc* is placed before the word according to the rule "vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastātu," even when it occurs at the end of the compound, [the same result follows].
The intention is that the suffix *ñya* does not apply because it lacks the status of having that [word] as its subsequent member (*uttarapada*).
(1308) *dikpūrvapadādasaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ* |4|2|107|. [The analysis is:
"from that which has a direction-word as its prior member" (*dikpūrvapadāt*). The locative case is used in the sense of the ablative.

The meaning is that the suffix *ñ* should occur after a compound whose first member is a cardinal direction (*dik*) and which has become a non-conceptual entity (*asaṃjñābhūta*). For example, *paurvaśāla*:
in the sense of "being in the eastern hall" (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*), the suffix *ñ* is applied after the compound formed by the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51).
(1309) After *madra*, the suffix *añ* [is applied]. (Pāṇini 4.2.108)
Regarding the rule *madrebhyo’ñ*: "only thus" means that the suffix *añ* is applied after the word *madra* when preceded by a direction-word (*dik*).

Regarding the phrase "due to exclusion" (*paryudāsāt*): this means that when there is an exclusion of the vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) of the second member of the compound, the initial vowel-increment (*ādivṛddhi*) applies.
Because of the plural number [in the sūtra], only those words denoting a country (*janapada*) are understood. Thus, *paurvamadra* [is formed] from "those in the east" (*pūrveṣu*).
The meaning is "originating from mothers.

(1310) *udīcyagrāmācca bahvaco 'ntodāttāt* |4|2|109|. [The suffix *cha* is applied] also after the name of a village of the Northern region that has more than two syllables and is oxytone. For example, *śaivapuram*. In the northern region, there is a place named Śivapura.

It refers to a specific village. The meaning is "that which exists there. By the rule *samāsasya*, the word *śivapura* is udātta on its final syllable. Why [is it specified] "having many vowels" (*bahvacaḥ*)? [Consider] *dhvāñjī*, a specific village in the northern region ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. That which exists there is *dhvāñjaḥ*. Why [is it specified] "from that which is udātta on the final syllable" (*antodātāt*)?

[The word] *śārkarīdhana* [is derived from *śarkarī-dhana*. By the rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member in a *kṛt*-derivation, the accent of the *lit*-suffix remains; thus, this [word] is *madhyodātta* (acute on the middle syllable).
(1311) Pāṇini 4.2.110: *prasthotarapadapaladyādikopadhādaṇ*.

The term *prasthotarapada* means that the suffix *aṇ* is applied after words ending in *prastha*, as well as after those beginning with *paladi* and others that contain the letter *k*. This is the analysis of the compound: "those for which *paladi* is the first" (*paladirādiryeṣām*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *aṇ* suffix characterized by being used for villages of the Northern region (*udīcya-grāma*). The example *māhikiprastha* means "one who resides in the village named Mahikiprastha. The word *pālada* [is likewise derived].
The meaning is: "one who resides in the village named Paladina. Regarding *nailīnaka*: the meaning is "one who resides in the village named Nilīnaka.
(1312) Pāṇini 4.2.111: *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* ("after *kaṇva* and others, in the sense of a lineage").

Regarding the rule "after Kaṇva and others, [the suffix denotes] a descendant in the lineage": *kāṇvyasya* means "the descendant in the lineage of Kaṇva," namely *kāṇvyaḥ*. [The suffix] *yañ* is applied according to the rule for the *garga*-class. For *kāṇvya*, the suffix *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *cha*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*; by the rule *āpatyasya ca*, there is the elision of the letter *ya*. Thus, the form is *kāṇvāḥ*.

(1313) *iñaśca* |4|2|112|. Also after *iñ*. For example, *dākṣāḥ*. [Analysis: *dakṣasya gotrāpatyam* (the lineage-descendant of Dakṣa) is *dākṣiḥ*. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*. [The compound analysis is: "the pupils (*chātrāḥ*) of Dākṣi. Regarding *saunaṅgameridam*: [it means] "this belongs to Sutaṅgama."
The residence is *sautaṅgami*. [This is derived] by the rule *sutaṅgamādibhya iñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.80).

In the sense of "belonging to Sautanigama," the suffix *cha* is applied after a *vṛddha* stem, and not *aṇ*, because the suffix *iñ* does not have the meaning of *gotra* here. In this context, *gotra* refers to the technical grammatical sense.

Although it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that, apart from the context of offspring (*apatya*), the lineage (*gotra*) is merely worldly (*laukika*), nevertheless, in these two rules, only the technical (*śāstrīya*) lineage is intended; this is because it has been stated as such in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *ṭhyūni luk*. [The word] *pāṇinīyam* [is derived from] Paṇina...

The offspring of Gotra is Pāṇinaḥ. His youthful descendant (tasyāpatyaṃ yuvā) is Pāṇiniḥ. "This belongs to him" (tasyedam) is Pāṇinīyam. [The suffix] *cha* is applied after a *vṛddha* [stem]; however, *aṇ* is not used, because the sense is that the word *pāṇini* already ends in a suffix denoting a youthful descendant (*yuvan*).

(1314) *na dvyacaḥ prācyabharateṣu* | Pāṇini 4.2.113. "Not from a base consisting of two syllables. The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* does not occur after a patronymic (*gotra*) ending in *iñ* that consists of two syllables, when followed by [descendants] belonging to the Easterners (*prācya*) or the Bharatas.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iña*; the meaning is that [the application of] *iña* is prohibited. Regarding *prāṣṭhīyāḥ*:
the meaning is "the pupils of Prāṣṭhi," where Prāṣṭhi is the descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) of Prāṣṭha. Regarding *kāśīyāḥ*:
the meaning is "the pupils of Kāśi," where Kāśi is the descendant in the lineage of Kāśa. Since the suffix *aṇ* is prohibited, the suffix *cha* is applied after a base ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel.

Regarding the word *siṅga*: by this [rule], in the case of "ĀṬddālaki is the father, ĀṬddālakāyana is the son," the elision (*luṅ*) of the suffix *ṭhiñ* does not occur according to the rule *bharatebhyaḥ luṅ na bhavati* (Pāṇini 4.1.178), because of the phrase *ṭhiñaḥ prācām*.
(1315) "That [stem] among whose vowels the first is a *vṛddhi* vowel is called *vṛddha*. (Pāṇini 1.1.73)
"Vṛddhi" refers to that [suffix] which possesses it. In the rule "of vowels" (*acām*), the plural number is an indication of multiplicity;

by this, the status of being a *vṛddha* (possessing a *vṛddhi*-vowel) is established even for the word *śālā*. By virtue of being treated as if it were a distinct designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the word *jña* is also considered a *vṛddha*.

(1316) *tyadādīni ca* | 1|1|74|. The sūtra *tyadādīni ca* explains the remainder by supplying the missing words: "they shall have the designation *vṛddha*. This rule is commenced because the initial vowel [of these pronouns] does not already possess the designation *vṛddhi*.

(1317) *vṛddhāc chaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.2.114. The suffix *cha* is applied after a word designated as *vṛddha* in the senses of "born there" and so forth. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. For example, *śālīyaḥ*, meaning "born in a hall" (*śālāyāṃ jātaḥ*), and so on. Similarly, *tadīyaḥ*.

(1318) *eṅ prācāṃ deśe* | 1.1.75. Regarding *eṅ prācām*: this is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), meaning that if it is the name of a specific region belonging to the easterners (*prāc*), then only a stem beginning with *eṅ* is designated as "vṛddha."
Alternatively, it should be stated that the designation "vṛddha" applies to a name (*nāmadheya*).

Regarding the phrase "or to a name": here, being a name consists in being a conventional term (*rūḍha-śabda*), and not merely being something recently designated by convention. By this, forms such as *ghaṭīyam* are established.

(1319) *bhavataṣṭhak-chasau* | 4|2|114 | [The suffixes] *ṭhak* and *chas* are applied after the word *bhavat*. [Thus we derive] *bhāvatkaḥ*. [In this case], by the rule *ṭhisusuktāntāt kaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is added. Now, one might object:
since the substitution of *īya* for *chas* occurs after the word *bhavat*, the status of being a *bha*-stem supersedes its status as a *pada*; how then [can the rule apply]?

To address the point that [the substitution of] *jaś* occurs, he says: "as for *jaś*. The intention is that because the status of being a *pada* (by the rule *siti ca*) subverts the status of being a *bha*, [the *jaś*-substitution applies]. Now, one might ask: how can there be the suffix *aṇ* in *bhāvataḥ*, since by the rule *tyadādīni ca*, the word *bhavat* is treated as *vṛddha*, and thus the suffix *cha* alone would be appropriate? To this [he replies]:

He says: because of the continued application of the word "from a vṛddha [stem]," [the suffix] is only *aṇ* after a stem ending in *śatṛ*. The intention is that among the *tyad*-type stems, only that which ends in *ḍavat*—as in the rule "after the root *bhā*, [the suffix] *ḍavat*"—is actually taught. (1320) Pāṇini 4.2.116: *kāśyādibhyaṣṭhaññiṭhau* ("After *kāśi* and others, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* [are applied]").
*ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* are the suffixes [added] after *kāśi* and other words. The suffixes are *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*.
In the case of the *ñiṭha* suffix, the entire cluster *ñi* is designated as an *it* by the rule "the initial letter of a suffix marked with *ṭ*, *ṇ*, *k*, or *n* is an *it*.
Since there is no purpose for the *ṇ* itself, the *ñ* alone is the *it*; its function is to determine the accent (*ñitsvara*). This applies only to *ṭhañ*.

In the case of the suffix *vidhi*, however, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply, and *ṭāp* would not. Now, if this were so, the substitution of *ik* for *ṭha* in the suffix *iṭha* would not occur, because the condition of being "following an *aṅga*" (*aṅgāt paratvam*) would be absent; therefore, he says:
"it is for the sake of pronunciation" (*uccāraṇārtha*). Thus, *kāśikī* means "born in Kāśī," and so forth.

The suffix *ṅīp* follows words ending in *ṭhañ*. For example, *kāśikā*: after the suffix *ñiṭha*, the substitution of *ik* occurs, followed by the addition of *ṭāp*. Similarly, *vaidikī* and *vaidikā*; here, *vedi* refers to a specific sacrificial ground. Regarding the rule "after a compound whose prior member is *āpad*, etc.": this is a *gaṇasūtra*. It simply means that the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* apply. The list beginning with *āpad* is as follows: *āpat*, etc.

The analysis of the compound is *ādiḥ yasya* ("that of which [the village] is the first"). Regarding *āpatkālikī* and *āpatkālikā*: [the former is derived] with the suffix *ṭhañ* followed by *ṅīp*, and [the latter] with the suffix *ñiṭh* followed by *ṭāp*. [The rule] *bāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* means: there are certain villages named Bāhīka;
the meaning is "from those that denote specific [subdivisions] thereof."
(1321) "And [the suffix] after words denoting Vāhīka villages" (Pāṇini 4.2.117). He says this: "after words expressing Vāhīka villages.
(1322) "Optionally [the suffix] among the Uśīnaras" (Pāṇini 4.2.118).

[The suffix] *vibhāṣā* applies after [words denoting] villages among the Uśīnaras. Although there was a collective mention in the previous sūtra, the term "from villages" (*grāmebhyaḥ*) is understood to carry over, because it is declared that [the preceding portion] has a svarita accent in its single part. Thus he says: "those which are villages among these. The meaning is: from words expressing specific [subdivisions] of those villages which are among the Uśīnaras. [Example: *saudarśanaḥ*.
*Nāma* is a certain village in the land of Uśīnara. Regarding *saudarśanīya*:

in the absence of the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, the suffix *cha* is applied after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable. (Pāṇini 4.2.114). [The rule] *ordeśe ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.119) applies.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied [after a word denoting a region] to form a name of a village. For example, *niṣādakarṣuḥ*—the remainder of the sense being "a certain village.

In the case of *naiṣādakarṣukaḥ*, the substitution of *kā* occurs because it follows a stem ending in a vowel other than *u*. (Pāṇini 4.2.120: *vṛddhāt prācām* ("After a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable, when denoting a region of the Easterners...").

"From *vṛddha* [names], [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] according to the Easterners (*prācām*). The [sūtra] "ṭhañ after *ṭha* when denoting a place" is understood here. The term "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is a qualifier of the region (*deśa*), and not for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), according to the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Since this is already established by the preceding rule, the present one is for the sake of restriction (*niyama*). Thus he says: "In the Eastern region," and so forth. The example is *āḍhakajambuka*.

There is a certain village named Āḍhakajaṃbū; the meaning is "one who resides there. Because it follows a word ending in the suffix *u*, the suffix *ṭha* is replaced by *ka*. By the rule "ṭhke’ṇaḥ," the vowel is shortened. Thus, [the derivative] is Śākajaṃbukaḥ. Regarding "Mallavāstu": the remainder of the sense is "a certain eastern village."

(1325) *dhanvayopadhādvuñ* | Pāṇini 4.2.121. [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after a word ending in *dhanvan* that has a vowel as its penultimate letter (*yopadha*). For example: *airāvataṃ dhanva*. This means "the desert named Airāvata. *Dhanvan* refers to a desert region; as Amarasimha states: "The words *marut* and *dhanvan* are synonyms. [The name] is called *Āṣṭaka*.

In *dhanve'ti*, the neuter gender is also [attested] according to the commentators (*bāṣya*). Regarding *airāvataka*: the meaning is "that which exists in the desert region named Airāvata. [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied, with the substitution of *a* for the final vowel. Regarding *sāṅkāśyakaḥ* and *kāmpilyakaḥ*: the meaning is "that which exists in Sāṅkāśya and Kāmpilya" respectively.

(1326) *prasthapuravahāntācca* |4|2|122|. [The suffix *ka* is added] after [a word] ending in *prastha*, *pura*, or *vaha*. "After that which ends in these" means: after a word ending in *prastha*, *pura*, or *vaha*. Now, is not the inclusion of *purānta* (ending in *pura*) redundant? [Because] in the case of *nāndīpuraka*, [the suffix *ka* is already applied by the previous rule].
Since this would already be established by the subsequent rule, "ṭhropadhetoḥ prācām" [Pāṇini 4.2.123], he says: "purānta... (1327) ṭhropadhetoḥ prācām 4.2.123.

"Of those whose [dhātu] has *r* as an upadhā, according to the Easterners. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "that which has *r* as an upadhā" (*ropadha*) and "that which ends in *ī*" (*ī*). The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. "Of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is an adjective qualifying the word *dheḥ*. Thus he says: "from that which has *r* as an upadhā," and so forth. Regarding "from *ī*": the words "is cited as an example" (*udāhriyate*) are to be supplied. Regarding "Kākandaka": [it refers to] the city named Kākandī.
*deśaḥ*: the meaning is "that which exists there.

(1328) *janapadatadavadhyośca* | 4.2.124 | [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a word denoting a country (*janapada*) or its boundary (*tadavadhi*). For example, *ādarśakaḥ*. *Ādarśa* is the name of a country; that which exists there [is called *ādarśaka*].

This is the meaning. *Trigarta* is the name for the boundary of a specific region (*janapada*). Although the word *trigarta* is already established as denoting a region, the inclusion here of its "boundary" (*avadhi*) is intended to override other rules where the word *garta* occurs as a final member of a compound. Thus he says: *traigartaka*.

(1329) [Pāṇini 4.2.125] "Even from a non-vṛddha [word], when it refers to a plural object. [The sūtra continues: "Even from a non-vṛddha [word] denoting a country (*janapada*). The word "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder. *Ājamīḍhakaḥ*: the meaning is "one who belongs to the Ajamīḍhas. Thus, *ājamīḍhakaḥ*.

The meaning is "one who belongs to the Ajamīḍhas. There is a country named Ajamīḍha which serves as the boundary for a certain region. [The rule] *vṛddhāj janapadāt* [is applied here]; the words "is cited as an example" (*udāhriyate*) are to be supplied. Regarding *dārvaka*: the term *dārvāḥ* is a plural form denoting a specific country.
It occurs [there]; the meaning is "one who exists there. Regarding *kālañjaraka*: the meaning is "one who exists in Kālañjara.
(1330) [A suffix is added] after a word ending in *kaccha*, *agni*, *vaktra*, or *varta* as the final member of a compound. Pāṇini 4.2.126.

*Kacchāgni*: the meaning is that [the suffix *kan*] is applied when *kaccha*, *agni*, *vaktra*, or *varta* follow as the final members of a compound. He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "when denoting a place (*deśavācinaḥ*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *cha* and *aṇ*. *Dārukacchaka* means "that which exists in Dārukaccha. *Kāṇḍāgnaka* [is explained similarly].
The meaning of *kāṇḍāgni-bhava* is "born in Kāṇḍāgni. In the case of the substitution of *a*, there is the elision of the vowel *i* according to the rule *yasyeti ca*.
*Saindhuvakraka* means "born in Sindhuvakra. *Bāhuvartaka* means "born in Bahuvarta."

(1331) *dhūmādibhyaśca* | 4.2.127. From *dhūma* and the others. The words "the suffix *vuñ* [is applied] when expressing a place" are to be supplied to complete the sense. (1332) *nagarātkutsanaprāvīṇyayoḥ* | 4.2.128. [The suffix *vuñ* is applied] after *nagara* in the senses of censure and proficiency.

The term *nāgarāḥ* means "those who revile the city" (*nagarāt kutsanā*). Regarding [the word] *kṣatriya* and others, the word *nagara* is understood here as a proper name (*saṃjñā*) due to its association with *Māhiṣmatī*. Therefore, the suffix *ḍhakañ* does not apply.
This is because it was stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭh prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām* that "[the inhabitants of] the city are called *nāgarāḥ*."
Thus, from the example [given]: (1333) *araṇyānmanuṣye* |4|2|129|. From *araṇya*, when referring to a human being: *āraṇyaka*. [Also] *panthā*, *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *vihāra*.
"A human being or an elephant. "Or on cow-dung"—this is a *vārttika*.

(1334) *Vibhāṣā kuruyugandharābhyām* | 4.2.130 | "Optionally after *kuru*. *Kuru* and *Yugandhara* are names of countries. [The suffix is applied] even after those two which do not have the *vṛddhi* vowel in their first syllable.
Since [the suffix] would have applied invariably by the rule "even after a word ending in ṭha-vṛddhi," this provides an option.
(1335) *madra-vṛjyos kan* | 4.2.131. [The suffix] *kan* is added after *madra* and *vṛji*. *Madra* and *vṛji* are specific names of territories (*janapada*).
The name of a country is an exception [to the rule regarding suffixes].

(1336) *kopadhādaṇ* | 4.2.132 | [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in the letter *ka*. For example, *māhiṣika*: there is a country named Mahiṣika; that which originates there [is called *māhiṣika*].

This is the meaning. Since [the suffix] would have been established by the rule *prasthotarapade* and others, this [sūtra] is intended to set aside the *vuñ* suffix prescribed after the class of words beginning with *janapada*. (1337) *kacchādibhyaśca* |4|2|133|.
"And from *kaccha* and so forth. Regarding *kāccha*: here, *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *vuñ*. Regarding *saindhava*:
this is an exception to *ṭhañ* [prescribed] after a country name (*janapada*).
(1338) Pāṇini 4.2.134: *manuṣya-tatsthayor vuñ*. "The suffix *vuñ* is applied [after a country name] to denote a person born there or something situated therein."
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [words ending in] *manuṣya* and those denoting its inhabitants. The phrase "after *kaccha*, etc. (*kacchādibhyaḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule].
Thus he says: "after *kaccha*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.133).
(1339) After *sālva*, when not denoting a person (*apadāti*), [the suffix *vuñ* is applied]. (Pāṇini 4.2.135).

[The suffix *cha* is applied] after *sālva* when it refers to something other than a foot-soldier (*apadāti*).
