Regarding the formation of *gārgam*: since it is stated that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after bases ending in *añ*, *añ*, or *iñ* when they denote a *saṃgha*, a *khaṇḍa*, or a *lakṣaṇa*, here too—when the suffix *aṇ* is intended in this sense—the elision (*luk*) of *añ* is prevented by the rule "there is no elision of *añ* in the case of a *gotra* [name] before a vowel. Thus, from the word *baida*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aka* prescribed by the rule "after a base consisting of two syllables ending in *ṛt*, the suffix *aka* is used for a *brāhmaṇa*. [The form] *gārgam* [is thus derived].

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a stem ending in *yañ*: thus, *dākṣam*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a stem ending in *iñ*: thus, *aupagavakam*. [The meaning is: "Aupagava" is one who is the offspring (*apatyam*) of Upagu; the sense is "that which has come from him. The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a *gotra* (patronymic) or a *caraṇa* (Vedic school).
Although this *vuñ* is prescribed in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*), [it is used here by extension].
Nevertheless, since that [suffix] is seen even after words ending in *añ*, *anya*, and *iñ* when used in the sense of "mark" (*aṅka*), there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of it here as well.
For the meaning is that the extended application here does not apply only to the *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣv añ*,
but rather to everything seen in the sense of "mark," according to the explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

(1438) *nañaḥ śucīśvarakṣetrajñakuśalanipuṇānām* | 7|3|10| After the negative particle *nañ*, [the augment *aṭ* is added] before *śuci*, *īśvara*, *kṣetrajña*, *kuśala*, and *nipuṇa*. This rule applies within the section concerning the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening, where it is understood that the augment may be added either to the second member (*uttarapada*) or to the first member (*pūrva*). Examples: *āśauca*—[meaning] impurity. *Āśauca*—[meaning] impurity.
The meaning is "come from the impure. According to the rule *tata āgataḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied;
here, the initial vowel strengthening (*ādivṛddhi*) of the first member of the compound is optional, whereas for the second member, the initial vowel strengthening is mandatory.

In the same way, in what follows, the meaning should be understood as "come from one who is not a knower of the field (*akṣetrajña*), from one who is unskilled (*akuśala*), and from one who is incompetent (*anipuṇa*)."

In the word *ānaiśvaryam*, however, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because the stem begins with *brāhmaṇa* and so forth. (Pāṇini 5.1.124) From causes and names of men, the suffix *rūpya* is optionally used [in the sense of "come from that"]. (Pāṇini 4.3.83) "From causes and names of men": this is exactly like the rule "come from that" (*tata āgata*). From causes...
He provides an example: "samādāgatam" and so forth. He provides an example of a word denoting a human being: "devadattarūpyam". (1440) *mayaṭ* also [is used after a word ending in *rūpya*]. 4.3.82.
"And *mayaṭ*. The remainder [of the rule] is "in the sense mentioned above" (*ukta-viṣaye*). (1441) *prabhavati* 4.3.83.

[The suffixes are applied] in the sense of "it originates from that" (*tataḥ prabhavati*), and not merely "it comes from that" (*tata āgataḥ*). The word "come" (*āgata*) has been removed; [the rule applies] in the sense of "it originates."
The meaning is that suffixes are applied as prescribed after a word ending in the fifth case (ablative). *Prabhava* means the first manifestation.

"It originates from the Himavat" (*himavataḥ prabhavati*) means it first appears in the Himavat. By the rule *bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ*, [the Himavat] functions as the *apādāna* (ablative point of departure).
(1442) *vidūrāñ ñyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.84. [The suffix] *ñya* is added after *vidūra*. It means "originating from that. The word *vidūra* has its *d* sound in the middle.
It is clear in the Bhāṣya that the word *vidūra* is a synonym for the region named Vālavāya.

(1443) *tad gacchati pathi-dūtayoḥ* | 4|3|85 | Regarding the rule *tad gacchati pathi-dūtayoḥ*: suffixes are applied after a word in the accusative case in the sense of "he goes," provided that the goer is either a path (*pathin*) or a messenger (*dūta*). This is the meaning.

(1444) *abhiniṣkrāmati dvāram* |4|3|83|. [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a city gate when it is the object of the action of "going out from. Example: *kānyeti*. This means "the gate of the region named Kānyakubja."

(1445) *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe* |4|3|87|. Regarding *adhikṛtya*: the meaning is that suffixes are applied after a word in the accusative case in the sense of "a treatise composed concerning [that]. For example, *śārīrakam*: this [treatise] pertains to the body (*śarīra*).

*Śārīraḥ* means the individual soul (*jīvātman*); this is the sense of "him. From the word *śārīra*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*), resulting in *śārīraka*. Because it contains a *vṛddhi* vowel, the suffix *cha* is applied [to form *śārīrakīya*].
This is according to Pāṇini 4.3.88: "The suffix *cha* is applied after *śiśukranda*, *yamasabha*, a copulative compound (*dvandva*), *indrajana*, and so forth."

The suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) occurs after the words *śiśukranda*, *yamasabha*, *dvandva*, *indrajana*, and so forth, in the sense of "a work composed concerning [that subject]. This is due to specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*). As for the rule "the word *sabhā* [is feminine] when preceded by a non-human [word]," the neuter gender does not apply here; for in that context, the term "non-human" is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*).
The intended meaning is that it is stated [in the sūtra] "rakṣaḥ-piśācādibhyaś chaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.136).
(1447) *so'sya nivāsaḥ* (4.3.89). The meaning is: in this sense, suffixes shall be applied after a word ending in the nominative case. Where...
"He dwells there; that is his residence," so says the Bhāṣya.
"And *abhijana*" [is added]. The word *saḥ* ("he") is understood from the previous rule. It should be explained as before. *Yatra...* [where...]

"He is one whose ancestors have dwelt there" is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. The sense is that this is the meaning of the aforementioned *Bhāṣya* regarding the word "where [he himself... (*yatra svayam*).
(Pāṇini 4.3.91): *āyudhajīvi-vibhyaś-caḥ parvate* ("The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting those who live by arms and after *vi*, when [the mountain] is a mountain").

[The suffix] is applied after words meaning "those who live by weapons" (*āyudhajīvin*). There is an alternative reading: *ṭhaparvata* (instead of *ṭhaṇ*). Regarding the phrase "from the word *abhijana*": the meaning is "from a word denoting one's native country. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "in order to denote those who live by weapons.
In the sūtra, the dative case is used according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya*. [The example is] *hṛdgola*.
This is a specific mountain. *Ṛkṣoda*—this also is a specific mountain.

(1450) *Śāṇḍikādibhyo ñyaḥ* | 4.3.92 | From *śāṇḍika* and others, the suffix *ñya* [is applied]. The remainder [of the rule] is: "when the sense is 'that is one's native place' (*so'bhijanaḥ*), [the suffix is added] after words ending in the nominative case."

(1451) The suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are applied after [words beginning with] *sindhu*, *takṣaśilā*, and others. [For example: *saindhava*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose native land (*abhijana*) is the specific region (*deśaviśeṣa*) called Sindhu."

(1452) *tūdīsalāturavarmatīkūcavārāḍḍhakcchaṇḍhañyakaḥ* |4|3|94|. From *tudī*, *salātura*, *varmatī*, and *kūcavāra*—when these appear in the nominative case—the suffixes *ḍhak*, *cchaṇ*, *ḍhañ*, and *yak* are respectively applied in the sense of "one's ancestral origin" (*asyābhijana*).
*tudīsalātura*: [The rule applies to] *tudī*, *salātura*, *varmatī*, and *kūcavāra*.
When these words stand in the nominative case, the suffixes *ḍhak*, *cchaṇ*, *ḍhañ*, and *yak* shall be added in the sense of "this is one's ancestral origin."

(1453) *bhaktiḥ* | 4|3|95|. The word *bhaktiḥ* [is understood] as being carried over [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that suffixes are applied after a word in the nominative case in the sense of "this is his devotion (*bhaktiḥ*)."

(1454) *acittād adeśakālāt ṭhak* || 4.3.96 || The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words denoting things other than those consisting of sentient beings (*aprāṇin*), provided they do not denote a place or time, in the sense already mentioned [above]. For example:
*apūpā bhaktiḥ* ("a meal of cakes"). The singular number in "a meal" (*bhaktiḥ*) is used with reference to the class in general; likewise, [the plural] "the Vedas" (*vedāḥ*).
As in the example *māṇava*. Regarding *pāyasika*: the analysis of the compound is "one whose devotion (*bhakti*) is to milk (*payas*).
(1455) *mahārājāṭ-ṭhañ* | P. 4.3.97. From *mahārāja*, the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied]. The remainder [of the rule] is: "in the sense of 'this is his devotion'. [The resulting form is] *māhārājika*.
Thus: the analysis of the compound is *mahārāja-bhaktir asya* ("he whose devotion is to the Great King").

(1456) *vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun* [Pāṇini 4.3.98]. From *vāsudeva* [the suffix *vun* is added]. The analysis remains simply *sa asya bhaktiḥ* ("he whose devotion is to him"). Thus, *vāsudevaka*. *Vāsudeva*...

The analysis of the compound is *bhaktir asya* ("he whose devotion is to him"). Similarly for *arjunakaḥ*. Now, one might object: since Vasudeva is the offspring (*apatyam*) of Vṛṣṇi, the suffix *aṇ* should apply by the rule *ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca*, and thus from the word *Vāsudeva*, the suffix *vuñ* alone should apply by the rule *gotra-kṣatriyākhyebhyo bahulaṃ vuñ*.
If it is argued that the mention of Vāsudeva is redundant because [the term] is already established [as referring to Brahman], we reply: true;

however, the word *vāsudeva* is not taken here in its conventional sense, but rather through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "He in whom everything dwells" (*vasati*), or "He who dwells in everything," and who is also *deva* (the radiant one). Thus, he is *vāsudeva*.
There is no fault here, for this word *vāsudeva* is both etymologically derived (*yoga*) and conventionally fixed (*rūḍha*) when applied to the Blessed One.
And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This is not a designation for a Kṣatriya; it is the name of that venerable one.
[Pāṇini 4.3.99 states: "The suffix *vuñ* is frequently applied after words denoting lineages (*gotra*) and names of Kṣatriyas."

*Gotrakṣatriyāḥ*: The meaning is that after words denoting *kṣatriyas* which end in a *gotra*-suffix, the suffix *vuñ* shall be applied diversely (*bahulam*) in the aforementioned scope. Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) is not used in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense. [The rule] "it sets aside *cha*" refers to the remainder [of the sūtra], namely in cases such as *aupagavaka*. *Glucukāyaniḥ*.
By the rule *ṭhak prācām avṛddhāt*, the word *glucukāyani* [is formed with] *phin*. *Nākulaka* is an example of a Kṣatriya name.
(1458) When words denoting a country (*janapada*) have the same form as the word denoting the people (*janapadin*) of that country, all [rules] apply as for the country in the plural.

*janapadinām*: When a plural ending follows, for those [names] denoting a country (*janapada*) which have an identical sound—that is, those whose phonetic form is identical to the word denoting the country itself—[the singular is used].
"Being of such a kind" means that for those [names] denoting the inhabitants of a country (*janapada*) or the ruler of a country,

everything should be as it is in the case of the country itself; that is to say, the suffixes prescribed in the section beginning with "janapadatadavadhyośca" (Pāṇini 4.2.125) apply, and the bases likewise remain the same.
However, the sense that "they exist" is obtained from the word *sarva*.
Thus he says: "of those denoting a country and its ruler," and so forth. "The Aṅgas are a country"—this is for the sake of illustration. The country inhabited by kings named Aṅga is "the Aṅgas."

By the rule "lup after [a suffix denoting] a country," there is the elision (lup) of the fourfold secondary suffix (*cāturarthika*). Just as in the case of *āṅgakaḥ*— where the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule "also after a country name and its limit" in the sense "this has that country as its devotion"— so too, in the sense "this has the Kṣatriyas who are lords of the country of Aṅga as its devotion," [the suffix is elided].

The meaning is that from the word *aṅga*, which denotes a Kṣatriya, when the suffix *vuñ* is applied, the form becomes *āṅgaka*. As for "the Brāhmaṇas of Pañcāla": here, the word *pañcāla* is applied to the Brāhmaṇas through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*).
In that case, because there is no transfer (*atideśa*) [of the Kṣatriya status], only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Regarding "Paurava": the word *paurava* is not...

The meaning is "the livelihood of a country. Why is the plural number used? [To show that] the extension (atideśa) applies even when there is a difference in the form of the word in the singular and dual numbers; for example, *āṅga* or *āṅgau* means "one whose devotion is to the Āṅgas," resulting in *āṅgaka*. Why is it said "and the base" (*prakṛtiśca*)? [To exclude cases such as: the king of the Madras is *mādraḥ*.

By the rule *ṭhañ magadhāt*, [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied. In the sense of "his devotion is toward the Madras," because of the extended application (*atideśa*), when *mādra* becomes *madra*, the form *mādraka* is established by the suffix *kan* according to the rule *madravṛjyoḥ*.
(1459) *tena proktam* | 4.3.101 | [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word denoting a person to form a word meaning "taught by him"].

By this it is stated: the meaning is that in this sense, suffixes are applied as prescribed after a word ending in the third case. In the example "pāṇinīyam," the word "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*) is to be understood as the remainder. [The suffix] *cha* is applied after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel [in its first syllable]. It means "proclaimed" (*prokta*), i.e., first made manifest. Here, however, it does not apply: "devadattenādyāpitam" (that which has been extended by Devadatta).

(1460) *titirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhāc chaṇ* || 4.3.102 || The suffix *chaṇ* is applied after *titiri*, *varatantu*, *khaṇḍika*, and *ukha* in the sense of "proclaimed by him" (*tena proktam*). This means that the suffix *chaṇ* shall be added to these words in the aforementioned context. From this point onward...

When the Veda is spoken of as ending with "tenaika-digiti," [the suffixes] occur because it is accepted that the mention of "Chandas" in the rule *śaunakādibhyaś chandasi* applies both by attraction (*apakarṣa*) from before that point and by continuation (*anuvṛtti*) after it. In this context, these words end in suffixes such as *chaṇ*.

The application [of the suffixes] is not for the Vedic texts alone, but rather only for those preceded by the notions of "one who studies" (*adhyetṛ*) and "one who knows" (*veditṛ*); thus he says: "the *chandas* and the *brāhmaṇas*.
"Having that as their object" means the rule regarding being preceded by the notions of "one who studies" and "one who knows."

Regarding the term *taittirīyāḥ*: when a Veda has been proclaimed [by someone], the suffix *cchaṇ* (which becomes *īya*) is applied. Thus, *taittirīya* refers to a specific branch (*śākhābheda*) [of the Veda];

in the sense of "those who study" or "those who know" that [branch], the suffix *aṇ* is applied. According to the rule *proktālluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]; this is the intended meaning. Examples include: *vāratantavīyāḥ*, *khāṇḍikīyāḥ*, and *aukhīyāḥ*. [The branch] was proclaimed by Tittiri.

But in the case of the word *śloka*, [the suffix -aC does not apply], because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "in Vedic meters" (*cchandasī*). And by the word *cchandas*, the Kalpa-sūtras are also included, because they consist of a compilation of injunctive statements found in all the recensions (*śākhā*). [Thus says] Kāśyapa: "By that..."
It is stated as "prokta" [meaning "declared"]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *cha*.

(1461) Pāṇini 4.3.103: *kāśyaparakauśikābhyāmṛṣibhyāṃ ṇiniḥ*. From the words *kāśyapa* and *kauśika*, when they denote sages (*ṛṣi*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied. Thus, *kāśyapinaḥ*. The suffix *ṇini* is added to the word *kāśyapa*; the letter *ṇ* is for the sake of the indicatory marker (*it*), and the letter *n* is for the sake of the augment *ikāra* [the substitution of *in* for *ni*].

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation. The intention is that from the word *kāśyapin*, by the rule "the suffix *lu* [is applied] after a word ending in *prokta*," there is the elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix denoting the student. The same applies to *kauśikinaḥ*. Why [specify] "from two sages" (*ṛṣibhyām*)? [Consider: *kāśyapīyam*, taught by a contemporary Kāśyapa.

(1462) *Kalāpivaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca* |4|3|104|. [The word] *kalāpi* [is mentioned]. The meaning is that the suffix *ṇini* shall be applied after words denoting pupils of Kalāpin and words denoting pupils of Vaiśampāyana, [under the condition] "by him" (*tena*), as already stated. [Examples: *kalāpyantevāsibhyaḥ*.

Thus [it is said]; the word "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding *hāridraviṇa*: Haridru was the name of a disciple of Kalāpin. From that [name], the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule [Pāṇini 4.3.101] *prokte ṇiniḥ*. Then, by the rule *orguṇaḥ*, there is *guṇa* substitution, and by *ādivṛddhiḥ*, there is initial *vṛddhi*.
The intention is that from the word *haridraviṇ* (the form derived from *haridraviṇ*), the suffix *adhyetraṇ* is added, and then it is elided by the rule *proktālluK*.

Haridru, Chhagali, Tumburu, and Ulapa—these four were the disciples of Kalāpin. Those who study what was proclaimed by Tumburu are called Taumburaviṇas. Regarding Chhagali, the suffix *ḍhinuk* will be taught [later].

[Those who study the work of] Ulapa are called Āulapinas. [The phrase] "from the pupils of Vaiśampāyana" [is used here], and the word "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding the term *ālambinaḥ*: Ālambi, Kaliṅga, Kamala, Ṛcābha, Āruṇi, Tāṇḍya, Śyāmāyana, Kaṭha, and Kalāpin—these are the nine disciples of Vaiśampāyana. Among them, from the word *ālambi*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "one who has studied" (*adhyetṛṇa*) after a word denoting what was taught; thus, from the word *ālambin*, [the form] *ālambinaḥ* is derived in the sense of one who has studied [it].

The suffix *lu* is elided by the rule "ṭhproktālluṅ. Thus: *ālambinaḥ*, *kāliṅginaḥ*, *kāmalinaḥ*, *ārcābhinaḥ*, *āruṇinaḥ*, *tāṇḍinaḥ*. Here, the *ya* is elided by the rule "āpatyasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.151). [The suffix] *śyāmāyaninaḥ* [is formed with *phak*]. Regarding *kaṭha*, elision will be stated [by a specific rule]. Regarding *kalāpin*, the suffix *aṇ* will be stated.

Kalāpin was a disciple of Vaiśampāyana. And since it would have been established that the disciples of Kalāpin were also disciples of Vaiśampāyana, the fact that they are mentioned separately makes it clear in the Bhāṣya that the disciples of those [disciples] are not included.

(1463) *purāṇaprokteṣu brāhmaṇakalpeṣu* |4|3|105|. The word *purāṇaprokteṣu* [is used]. The terms *tena proktam* ("proclaimed by him") and *ṇiniḥ* ("the suffix ṇini") are carried over [from the previous rules]. The *brāhmaṇas* are those portions of the Veda distinct from the *mantras*. The *kalpas* are the ritual manuals (*kalpasūtras*) such as those of Baudhāyana and others.

The meaning is that when the subject matter consists of ancient treatises (grantha) spoken by sages, the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a word ending in the third case. Thus he says: "after a word ending in the third case.
Regarding the phrase "that which was spoken," the singular number is used with reference to the category in general. This refers to the meaning expressed by the suffix.

The phrase "that which was proclaimed" means that which consists of the Brāhmaṇa-kalpas proclaimed by ancient sages. He explains the term "proclaimed in the Purāṇas" with the words "by the Purāṇa. He provides examples from the Brāhmaṇas: "Bhallu-Bhāllavinaḥ. Here, "Bhallu" is the citation of the base form (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that they study the portions of the Brāhmaṇa proclaimed by the ancient sage Bhallu; thus, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of "proclaimed. The intention is that when the suffix *adhyetraṇ* is elided after the word *bhāllavi*, the form *bhāllavinaḥ* results. He provides another example from the Brāhmaṇa: *śāṭhāyanaḥ*, *śāṭhāyaninaḥ*.

Thus: "Śāṭhāyanīya" is a designation of the original source (*prakṛtinirdeśa*). The meaning is that the form "Śāṭhāyaninaḥ" is derived from the word "Śāṭhāyanin"—which is formed by adding the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of "proclaimed" (*prokta*) to denote those who study the Brāhmaṇa portions proclaimed by the ancient sage Śāṭhāyana—after the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *adhyetraṇ*. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the word *kalpe*: the phrase "is illustrated" (*udāhriyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the example *piṅga-paiṅgī kalpaḥ*, *piṅga* is the indication of the base form (*prakṛtinirdeśa*). It is the form derived from the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of "proclaimed by Piṅga," an ancient sage.

(1464) *Śaunakādibhyaś chandasi* [Pāṇini 4.3.106]. Regarding the rule *Chandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi*, the restriction that [the names of] Vedic texts and Brāhmaṇas must end in suffixes denoting those who study them does not apply in all cases regarding the Kalpas; thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *Chandobrāhmaṇāni*.

This is clear. Regarding "Yājñavalkāni": the meaning is "proclaimed by Yājñavalkya. Regarding "Āśmaratha": the meaning is "proclaimed by Āśmarathya. Regarding "the elision of *y*": the words *yajñavalka* and *aśvaratha* belong to the *kaṇva* group; from these two, which end in *yañ*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, there is an elision of *y* according to the rule "of the descendant [suffix] as well" (*ṭhāpatyasya ca*).
There is a misconception that Yājñavalkya and Āśmarathya are modern figures; however, in the Bhāṣya, two statements were initiated:

first, that because they are contemporaries of Śāṭhāyanas and others, the suffix *ṇini* is prohibited after names such as Yājñavalkya; and second, that this prohibition does not apply in those specific instances. Let this matter rest for now.

(1465) *kaṭhacarakālluk* | 4|3|107|. [The suffix] after *kaṭha* and *caraka* is elided (*luk*). [The phrase] "of the suffix denoting 'proclaimed by' (*prokta*)" is understood from the context. Thus, *kaṭhāḥ*: the suffix *ṇini*, characterized by being a pupil of Vaiśampāyana, is elided; however, the suffix *adhyetraṇ*...

The suffix *lu* is elided by the rule "proktālluṅ. Thus, *carākāḥ* means "those who study what was proclaimed by Caraka"; that is the meaning. By this [rule], there is the elision of the suffix *aṇ* added after a word ending in *prokta*, and the suffix *adhyetraṇ* is also elided after a word ending in *prokta*. (1466) *kalāpino’ṇ* | 4.3.108 | [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *kalāpin*].

The suffix *aṇ* is applied [after *kalāpin*]. This is an exception to the suffix *ṇini*, which would have been applicable by the rule "proclaimed by him" (*tena proktam*), because [Kalāpin] was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. Thus, [the form] is *kālāpāḥ*. The meaning is that when the suffix *aṇ* is added to the word *kalāpin*, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) occurs;
then, from the word *kālāpa*, the suffix *cha*—which denotes a student—is elided.

Regarding the elision of the *ṭi* suffix (*ṭilopa*), there is an addition to the rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for words ending in *n* when they are among the following: *sabrahmacārin*, *pīṭhasarpi*, *kalāpin*, *kauthumin*, *taitilin*, *jājali*, *lāṅgali*, *śilālin*, *śikhaṇḍin*, *sūkara*, *sadman*, and *suparvan*.
Anticipating the objection that these forms would retain their original base (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "ṭhinaṇyanapatye" [Pāṇini 6.4.164], he says: "not for one ending in *n*" (*nāntasya*).

(1467) *cchagalino ḍhinuk* | 4.3.109 | The meaning is that the suffix *ḍhinuk* occurs after the word *cchagalin* in the sense of "taught by. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇini*, which would otherwise apply because [the author] is considered a "pupil of Kalāpin" (*kalāpyantevāsī*). Thus, the form is *chāgaleyinaḥ*.

The letter *ka* [is the suffix]; the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By the rule *ṭhḍhin*, [the suffix] *ṭhin* remains; for *ḍha*, there is *ey*; then there is the elision of the *ṭi*. Thus, the meaning is that there is the elision (*lug*) of the suffix denoting the student (*adhyetṛ-pratyaya*). "The suffix *ṇini* should occur in the sense of *pārāśarya*"—the phrase "in the aforementioned scope" (*ukta-viṣaye*) is to be supplied. [This occurs] by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūka-pluti*) [of the rule].

The meaning is that the suffix *ṇini* alone follows. That is to say, in the sense of "the Bhikṣu-sūtra proclaimed by Pārāśarya" and "the Naṭa-sūtra proclaimed by Śilālin," the suffix *ṇini* would occur after a word ending in the third case (instrumental) and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. The term *bhikṣavaḥ* refers to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*).
The *Bhikṣusūtra*, which has that as its subject matter, is well-known and was composed by Uvyāsu.
(1468) Pārāśaryaśilālibhyāṃ bhikṣunaṭasūtrayoḥ |4|3|110|.
Regarding "by Pārāśarya": from the word *parāśara*, [the suffix *yañ* is applied] in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*) because it belongs to the *gargādi* group.

*Yañi-ṭhpārāśaryaḥ* refers to Vyāsa. Here, however, the suffix *yañ* is applied because the status of a *gotra* (lineage) is superimposed upon the immediate descendant. From that [name], the suffix *ṇini* is added in the sense of "proclaimed by him" (*prokte*) to form *Pārāśarin*, referring to the *Bhikṣusūtra*. Then, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ccha* which denotes the student of that [text]. Thus, *pārāśariṇaḥ* is the form in the nominative plural (*jasi*). Similarly, *śailālinaḥ*.

The meaning is that when the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the word *śilālin* as prescribed in the *Naṭasūtra*, the *ṭi*-portion (*al*) is elided; then, when the suffix *aṇ* denoting the student is elided after the word *śailālin*, the form in the nominative plural (*jasi*) is *śailālinaḥ*.

(1469) *karmandakṛśāśvādibhya iniḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.111. This means that the suffix *ini* is applied to words such as *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva* when they appear in the third case, provided they signify "a Bhikṣu-sūtra taught by Karmanda" or "a Naṭa-sūtra taught by Kṛśāśva. In this suffix, the final [letter]... [is elided].

The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. The suffix *ini* is added after the word *karmanda*. Then there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *adhyetṛṇ*. In this same way, [one forms] *kṛśāśvinaḥ*.
(1470) [Pāṇini 4.3.112: *tenaikadik* ("in the same direction as that").
"Tenaikadik. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).

That which has a single direction as its locus is "ekadik. The meaning is that, in the sense of "existing in the same direction together with that," suffixes should be applied as prescribed after a word ending in the third case. Regarding the example *saudāmanī*: [this is formed] by the suffix *aṇ*.
Because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) by the rule *ṭhaṇi*, there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*. (1471) *tasiśca* | 4.3.113.
The meaning is that the suffix *tasi* also occurs after a word ending in the third case when the sense is "in the same direction as that. The vowel *i* [is for the sake of pronunciation].

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the phrase "because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *svara*": in the section [of Pāṇini's grammar] beginning with *svarādinipātamavyayam*, within the enumeration under *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ*, namely *tasilādayaḥ*, it means that it occurs after *tasi*.

(1472) *uraso yañ ca* | 4|3|114|. Regarding *uraso yañ ca*: the meaning is that [the suffixes] *yañ* and *cha* are applied after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāntāt*) when the sense is "in the same direction as" (*ekadik*) with the chest (*urasā*). (1473) *upajñāte* | 4|3|115|. [The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in the third case] when the sense is "discovered by" (*upajñāta*).

Regarding *upajñāte*: the meaning is that suffixes prescribed after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) should occur in the sense of "invented by him" (*tenopajñātam*). *Upajñātam* means "first known.
(1474) *kṛte granthe* [Pāṇini 4.3.116]: [suffixes are added] in the sense of "composed" when referring to a literary work (*grantha*).

Regarding the word *kṛte* [in the sūtra]: the meaning is that suffixes prescribed after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) should occur in the sense of "a book composed by him" (*tena kṛto granthaḥ*). (1475) *saṃjñāyām* 4.3.117. [This sūtra provides an exception when the word is a proper name.]

Regarding the term *saṃjñāyām*: "by that alone. This means that when the sense is "done by that," suffixes are applied as prescribed after a word ending in the third case, provided it is a name (*saṃjñā*). The word *granthe* (in the sense of a book) does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "for the purpose of [denoting] something other than a book."

(1476) *Kulālādibhyo vuñ* | Pāṇini 4.3.118. From *kulāla* and others, the suffix *vuñ* [is applied]. The phrase "in the sense of 'made by him' when it is a name" is to be supplied as the remainder of the rule.
*Vāruḍakam*: a *varuḍa* is a specific caste.

(1477) *kṣudrābhramaravaṭarapādapādañ* |4|3|119|. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the words *kṣudra*, *bhramara*, *vaṭara*, and *pādapa* [to form a compound denoting "made by that" when it is a name]. The phrase "in the sense of 'made by that' when it is a name" is supplied from the previous rule (*tena kṛte saṃjñāyām*). *Kṣudrāḥ* refers to small, lowly flies.

(1478) *tasyedam* |4|3|120|. Regarding *tasyedam*: in the sense of "this belongs to that," the general suffixes such as *aṇ* and others, as well as the specific suffixes such as *gha* prescribed by rules beginning with *rāṣṭrāvārapārād ghaḥ*, are applied after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), according to what has been ordained.
This is the meaning. Here, the term *śeṣe* (in the remainder) is understood from the previous rule.

Consequently, for meanings other than those beginning with *apatya* (offspring) and ending with the fourfold sense (*caturarthī*), all remaining specific meanings are obtained as the referents of the suffix in the form of general specifications; however, this does not apply to *apatya* and the others.
It was stated in the rule *tasyāpatyam* that this word-meaning (*idaṃśabdārthatva*) exists in some form or another.
Regarding the statement *vahesturaṇiṭ ca*: this is a Vārttika. The term *tuḥ* refers to the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*.

The inclusion is general. From the *tṛ* suffix prescribed after the root *vah*, there shall be the *aṇ* suffix, and there shall be the augment *iṭ* for the *tṛ* suffix. In that context, since *aṇ* is already established by previous rules, it is restated here for the purpose of prescribing the augment *iṭ*.
"The property of one who carries" (*saṃvoḍhuḥ svaṃ*) is an illustration of the analysis of the compound. [The word *saṃvoḍhṛ*] is derived from *vah* with either the *tṛc* or *tṛn* suffix.
Because the root *vah* is anudātta (unaccented), the augment *iṭ* does not apply by the rule "ekāca upadeśe.
Then, the substitution of *ḍha*, *dha*, *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍh* take place. Next, the substitution of *o* for the vowel *a* occurs by the rule "sahivahor odavarṇasya.

Thus, we have *sāṃvahitram*. Because the substitutions beginning with *ḍha* are considered asiddha (non-existent) [for the purposes of the subsequent operation], this occurs in the very pre-grammatical (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).
First, there is the suffix *iṭ*. Then, because the cause [for the application of the rule] is absent, the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth does not occur.

"In the sense of 'a shelter for the *agnīdh* priest,' the suffix *raṇ* is also applied. This is a *vārttika*; it means that when the word *śaraṇa* ("shelter") is the intended meaning, [the suffix *raṇ* is added].

The meaning is that from the word *agnīdh*, ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the suffix *raṇ* is added, and it should be stated that when this [suffix] follows, the status of being a *bha*-stem also applies.
*Śaraṇam* means "house. *Agnīdh* refers to a specific type of officiant (*ṛtvij*). It is derived from the root *indh* with the suffix *kvip*;
the nasal *n* is elided according to the rule *aniditām*. *Āgnīdhram* refers to the northern half of the great altar (*mahāvedi*) during the Soma sacrifice.

This word *pañcaratni* is to be understood as a specific designation for a particular square-shaped location. Because it is a Bahuvrīhi compound, the change to the *jaś*-class (the substitution of *d* for *t*) does not occur.

It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). However, in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], in passages such as "This indeed is the unconquered part of the sacrifice, namely the Āgnīdhra," this word has the acute accent on the first syllable.

It should be understood that the suffix *añ* is applied in its own sense (svārthika) according to the rule "the suffix *añ* should be stated after *āgnīdhra* as a common [denominator]. But if this is so, how can the word *āgnīdhra* refer to a specific officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in such passages as "the *āgnīdhra* should respond"? To this he says: "because of being located there" (*tātsthyāt*). This is because [the priest] is situated in the place called *āgnīdhra*.
The intention is that the word *āgnīdhra* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

[In the term] *samidhāmādhāna*, the suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* is applied. Regarding "of the *samidhs*": that by which something is placed is the "placing" (*ādhāna*), namely the mantra; thus, it means "the mantra of placing."

The meaning is that after the word *samidh* ending in the sixth case, the suffix *ṣyañ* is to be stated. He says "sāmidhenī" because the *ṣ*-quality [of the suffix] is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. From the word *sāmidhenī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied;
then, by the rule "halastaddhitasya," there is the elision of the *y*.

(1479) *rathādyat* | Pāṇini 4.3.121. The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ratha*. This occurs under the governing rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to that"). For example: *ratyam cakram* ("a wheel belonging to a chariot"). According to the specific rule *rathādrathāṅge* ("after *ratha*, [the suffix *yat* is applied] when referring to a part of a chariot"), the word *cakram* serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
(1480) *patrapūrvādañ* | Pāṇini 4.3.122. [The suffix] *añ* follows a word preceded by *patra*. It is understood that this applies after the word *ratha* as well. *Patra* means "vehicle.
As the lexicon (*kośa*) states: "The word *patra* denotes a vehicle and a wing."
(1481) *patrādhvaryupariṣadaś ca* |4|3|123|. [The suffix *añ*] is applied after *patra*, *adhvaryu*, and *pariṣad*. [The word] *añiti* [is used]; this is a supplement to the rule. [The meaning is:
after *patra*, when it means "external" (*bāhya*).

Regarding "from *patra*": the meaning is that it should be stated as "only outside of *patra*. Regarding "*āśvam*": the intention is that the term *patra* is used here to signify its meaning (the leaf). Regarding "*ādhvaryavam*" and "*pāriṣadam*":
the analysis of the compounds is "this belongs to the *adhvaryu*" and "this belongs to the assembly (*pariṣad*)."

(1482) *halasīrāṭ-ṭhak* || Pāṇini 4.3.124 || The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *hala* and *sīra* [to form a word meaning] "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*). For example: *hālikam*, *sairikam*.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "this belongs to the plough" (*halasya idam*) and "this belongs to the plow" (*sīrasya idam*).

(1483) *Dvandvād vun vairamaithunikayoḥ* |4|3|125|. From a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *vun* is applied when enmity (*vaira*) or sexual union (*maithunikā*) is intended to be expressed. The meaning is that after a *dvandva* compound ending in the genitive case, the suffix *vun* occurs when [the compound] is intended to be expressed as feminine. For example: *kākolūkikā*, [meaning] "the enmity between the crow and the owl. (*Kākolūkasya*...)

The meaning is "enmity. Femininity [in the suffix] *vun* is established by worldly usage. "Kutsakuśikikā" means the marriage between Kutsa and Kuśika; femininity [in the suffix] *vun* is established by worldly usage. "Mithuna" refers to a couple (husband and wife); its activity is "maithunikā. The suffix *vuñ* is applied because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group.

Femininity [is excluded] from the world; there is a prohibition regarding enmity, such as that between the gods and the asuras. "Regarding enmity, such as between the gods and the asuras"—this is a *vārttika*. [The example is] "the conflict between the gods and the asuras" (*daivāsura*).

The meaning is that there is enmity (*vaira*) between the gods and the asuras. In the absence of the suffix *vuñ*, the form is *aṇ* [yielding *devāsura*]. However, in the sense of sexual union (*maithunika*), the form is simply *devāsurī*. The reading "in a *dvandva* of gods and asuras" is a corruption; for in the Bhāṣya on this point, the Vārttika is read as "enmity" (*vaira*) alone. Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "in *śiśukranda* etc.," regarding the *dvandva*...

The rule "prohibition [of the suffix -aṇ] after words such as *devāsura*" has been recited, and *daivāsura* and *rākṣosura* have been cited as examples. The meaning is: an account (*ākhyāna*) composed concerning the gods, asuras, and so forth.

(1484) *gotracaraṇādvuñ*—from a word denoting a lineage (*gotra*) or a school (*caraṇa*), the suffix *vuñ* is added. The meaning is that the suffix *vuñ* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case that denotes a lineage-suffix (*gotrapratyaya*) or one expressing a follower of a Vedic branch (*śākhādhyetṛ*). Here, "lineage" refers to what is well-known from the *Pravarādhyāya*.
Intending [the word] "gotra," he provides the example: *āṬpagavakam*.
The meaning is "this belongs to ĀṬpagava. However, in reality, ĀṬpagava is not seen among the *pravarasūtras*.
In the commentaries (*vṛtti*) and other works, *glaucukāyanakam* is cited as the example.
It should be stated: "after *caraṇa*, [the suffix *vuñ* is applied] when *dharma* or *āmnāya* [is to be expressed].

Regarding "after *caraṇa*": the meaning is that the suffix *vuñ* which is prescribed after *caraṇa* occurs when *dharma* or *āmnāya* is to be expressed, and not otherwise. For example, "Kāṭhakam": those who study what was proclaimed by Kaṭha are the Kaṭhas.
The meaning is that their *dharma* is their *āmnāya*. *Āmnāya* refers to the study of the Vedas.

(1485) *Saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣvañyañiñāmaṇ* | Pāṇini 4.3.127: after words ending in *yañ*, *añ*, or *iñ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied when denoting a group (*saṅgha*), a mark (*aṅka*), or a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* is intended [to apply] when [the word] is expressed as "this" (*idantvena*). It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *cha*.
(1) The mention of *ghoṣa* must also be made.
Regarding *ghoṣa*: the meaning is that the rule *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇaghoṣeṣu* must be formulated.

And thus, there are three bases (*prakṛti*) and four meanings of the suffixes (*pratyayārtha*); therefore, there is no correspondence according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*). Regarding *gārgaḥ*: the remainder [of the rule] is "a corporation (*saṅgha*), a mark (*aṅka*), or a hamlet (*ghoṣa*). Regarding *gārgam*: the remainder is "a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Similarly, this applies to *dākṣaḥ* and *dākṣam* as well. Now, regarding the words "mark" (*aṅka*) and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*)...

Because they are synonyms, the separate mention [of the two] would be redundant; for this reason, he says: "in succession" (*paramparayā*). For example, a specific heated seal is a *liṅga* (mark) residing on a cow or the like; its connection to the owner is indeed mediated through the cow. "Directly" (*sākṣāt*) means that the specific knowledge resides directly in Devadatta.

The meaning is that it is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) because it exists directly [therein]. *Vaidī* means "knowledge of the Vedas. According to Amarasimha: "A *ṭhaghoṣa* is a cowherd settlement (*ābhīrapallī*). (1486) [The suffix *cha*] is optionally applied after *śākala*: Pāṇini 4.3.128.

Or [the forms] *śākalāt* or *śākalena* [are derived as follows]: from the word *śakala*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "taught by," there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting the student; then, from the word *śākala*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "from a gotra or a *caraṇa* [name]" (Pāṇini 4.3.126) as an exception to the suffix *vuñ* used for religious law (*dharma*) and sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). In the absence of that [exception], *vuñ* is applied.

(1487) *cchandogaukthikayājñikabahvṛcanṛtāñ ñyaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.3.129. [The suffix] *ñya* is applied after *cchandoga*, *aukthika*, *yājñika*, *bahvṛca*, and *naṭa*. The categories beginning with *saṅgha* are excluded here. Since *cchandoga* and the others denote Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), they are connected with the sense of "dharma" and "scriptural tradition" (*dharmāmnāya*). [The examples are: *cchandoga*, *aukthika*, *yājñika*, *bahvṛca*, [and *nāṭya*].

The meaning is that the suffix *ñya* should occur when *naṭa* is intended to be expressed as "this" (*idantvena*) in relation to both *dharma* and *āmnāya*. One might object: "Since a *naṭa* (actor) does not possess a *caraṇa* (Vedic school), how can there be a connection between him and *dharma* and *āmnāya*?

To this, he raises the doubt and replies: "It has been stated [in the rule] 'from *caraṇa*, [the suffix applies] to *dharma* and *āmnāya*. The words "even though" (*yadyapi*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
He refutes this by saying, "because of association with that. Even so,
due to association with the Chandogas and others, the meaning is that from the word *naṭa* as well, there arises a cognition of only the Dharma and the Āmnāya.

(1488) Not [is the suffix *cha* applied] after the word *daṇḍa* when followed by *māṇava* and *antevāsin*. 4|3|130. "Not *daṇḍa*": this is a *dvandva* compound meaning "those who are both *daṇḍamāṇavas* and *antevāsins*. Regarding the example *dākṣāḥ*:
*dakṣasyāpatyam* means "the offspring of Dakṣa," which is *dākṣiḥ*; the sense is "these are the *daṇḍamāṇavas* or students belonging to him (*tasyeme*)."
The suffix *vuñ*, which characterizes the meaning of "belonging to a lineage" (*gotra*), does not apply here; rather, only the general suffix *aṇ* applies. (1489) *Raivatikādibhyaś chaḥ* | 4.3.131.

[The rule] *raivatikādibhyaś chaḥ* [is stated]. The phrase "in the sense of 'this belongs to that'" (*tasyedam*) is supplied from the context as a completion of the remainder. [The previous rule regarding] *vuñ* [does not apply].
The meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule defining the *gotra* suffix *-ya*. Regarding *raivātikīyam*: the offspring of Revatī is Raivatika;
[the suffix] *-ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *ṭhraivatyādibhyaṣṭhak*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "this belongs to Raivatika.

Regarding *vaijavāpīyam*: the offspring of Vījavāpa is Vaijavāpi; [the suffix] *-cha* is applied according to the rule *itaś-chaḥ*, and the analytical explanation is "this belongs to him (Vaijavāpi)."
Analysis:

(1490) *Kaupīñjala-hāstipadād-aṇ vācyaḥ* [The suffix *aṇ* should be stated after *kaupīñjala* and *hāstipada*]. [The forms] *kaupīñjala* and *hāstipada* [are derived as follows]: immediately after [the rule] "the descendant of *kupīñjala*" (*kupīñjalasyāpatyam*), [the word] "in the sense of *iti*" (*ity-arthe*) [is supplied].

The remainder [of the commentary] follows. Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): in this *vārttika*, because of the mention of *kaupīñjala*, the meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* supersedes *iñ*. Regarding "from that which ends in it": the meaning is that from a base ending in *aṇ*, by this rule, *aṇ* is applied again in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*). Regarding "of *hastipāda*": [it means] one whose feet are like those of an elephant (*hastina iva pādau*).

The analysis (*vigraha*) of this [compound] is *hasti-pādasya* (of the elephant-foot); [the suffix] *ṭhak* does not apply because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] "not after *hastin* and so forth" (*ahastyādibhyaḥ*). [Thus,] the offspring of *hastipāda* is *hāstipadaḥ*. Here, by this very [rule], the suffix *iñ* is superseded and the suffix *aṇ* is applied due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*), as well as the change of *pāda* to *pad*. By means of this [suffix], it expresses the sense of "belonging to *hāstipada*."
The meaning is that it is derived from *aṇ*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *hotra-vuñ* and *ña*.
Kaiyaṭa says that this is a *sūtra*; others say it is a *vārttika*. [The rule states: "There shall be *aṇ*.
Thus, from the word *ātharvaṇika*, when the sense is "belonging to him" (*tasyedaṃ*), there shall be *aṇ*; and there shall be the elision (*lopa*) of the *ik* of the base (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is "and there is elision.
(1491) *Ātharvaṇikasyekalopaśca* |4|3|133|. Regarding the term *ātharvaṇika*: the Veda proclaimed by Atharvan is metaphorically designated as "Atharvan."
One who studies that [text] is called *ātharvaṇika*. By the rule *vasantādityāṭṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.

In the sense of "this belongs to an *ātharvaṇika*," by means of this [suffix], the suffix *aṇ* is applied; after the elision of the *ik* vowel, there is no elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) due to the rule *dāṇḍināyana*, resulting in the form *ātharvaṇa*. This refers to either the Dharma or the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).

The intended meaning is that this is because of the statement: "From [the name of] a *caraṇa*, [the suffixes] *dharmāmnāya* [are formed]. Now, one might object: since [the form] would already be established by the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that"), the prescription of the suffix *aṇ* is redundant; to this he replies: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* derived from a *caraṇa*.
The intended meaning is that the word *ātharvaṇika* denotes a student of the Atharva Veda.
Thus ends the section on secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.

(446) [The section] concerning the feminine: 4.1.3. Now, the feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). Thus, having taken as the governing heading (*adhikṛtya*) the rule "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṭā*, *ṅī*, or *āp*," and having explained in detail the sūtra "the suffixes *su*, *au*, *jas*, *am*, *auṭ*," etc.
To define the feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) that follow thereafter, he says: "In the feminine" (*striyām*).

This is an *adhikāra* (governing rule). The meaning is that this sūtra is for the purpose of being carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) in subsequent sūtras such as "ṭhājādyataṣṭāp," and is not an independent injunction (*svatantravidhi*). To what extent does this governing rule extend? [The answer follows:]...

He says: "samarthā" (capable). The word "yāvat" indicates a limit; the meaning is "prior to [the rule] 'of capable [words], the first [is compounded]'. Here, this should be noted: "One who possesses breasts and hair is a woman; one who is hairy is remembered as a man; that which is between the two, in its absence, is the neuter."

The worldly gender (*liṅga*) of women and men consists of specific configurations of limbs characterized by defining marks (*lakṣaṇa*). When that [gender] is absent—that is, when both of those are absent—what is intermediate between the two, meaning dissimilar to them, is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*); this is what constitutes worldly [gender].

Gender (liṅga) is not employed in this treatise, because it would be contradicted in the case of insentient objects such as beds and garlands, which would consequently fail to take feminine suffixes; furthermore, in forms such as *dārān*, the substitution of *na* by the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* would not occur. Rather, [gender refers to] the primordial qualities (*guṇa*) of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Increase is masculinity; decrease is femininity; mere persistence is neuter-ness.

For this very reason, even though there is increase and decrease, the common maxim "the neuter is used for the general" (sāmānye napuṃsakam) is established by taking only the state of mere persistence.

The meaning is that the neuter gender is used when there is an intention to express merely the state common to the three conditions— namely, increase, decrease, and equality. Such a triad of states is purely pervasive (kevalānvayi),
because the usage "this is a category" (padārtha), "this is an individual" (vyakti), and "this is an object" (vastu) is universal.
And this indicative mark (liṅga) is indeed grounded in the meaning itself. As it has been stated in the Bhāṣya:
"The difference in gender is observed because of the difference in words and because of the difference in constituent parts, even when the referent is one and the same.
This is because, with respect to a single referent, we observe a plurality of words such as *puṣyaḥ*, *tārakā*, and *nakṣatram*.

Kaiyaṭa states that because a difference in gender is observed when suffixes such as *ra* are added to words like *kuṭī* and *kuṭīra*, the meaning is that gender is indeed something distinct from [physical characteristics] such as breasts and hair. As for the conventional usage "the word is masculine" (*puliṅgaḥ śabdaḥ*) and so forth, it should be understood as being based on the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the denoted object and the denoting word.

Nor should it be argued that because the properties of accumulation (*upacaya*) and so forth are mutually contradictory, their coexistence in a single locus is impossible, and thus a single entity cannot possess two or three genders; for it is possible for all three properties to coexist within each individual object through the distinction of moments (*kṣaṇabheda*). And it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Someone indeed..."
A property such as existence (*sattva*) does not remain anywhere even for a moment;

rather, it must either increase or be joined with its opposite. And it should not be argued that this being the case, there would be the consequence of possessing two or three genders simultaneously, for such is not the case in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

The existence of objects co-temporal with [the speaker] would be the cause [of the word's application]; for if that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of linguistic usage regarding the past and the future. In that regard, some words are to be employed for an object qualified by only one gender, while some are used for two genders, and some...

The statement "it has three genders" is to be understood from the treatise on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*). Furthermore, the conventional designation (*saṃketa*) for these terms—masculine, feminine, and neuter—within this grammar must be known from that very treatise on gender, just as [the technical names] *vṛddhi* and so forth are known. And it is said in the Bhāṣya: "Necessarily..."
The meaning is that this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), according to which one must adhere to whatever conclusion has been reached.
Amara states: "The two *kṛtāntas* are Yama and established doctrines.

In that context, by the force of employing a "great designation" (*mahāsaṃjñā*) instead of creating a "light designation" (*laghusaṃjñā*)—just as in the case of technical terms such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha*—it follows that [the rule applies] when...
In this context, even the worldly characteristic (liṅga) such as "possessing breasts and hair" is relied upon; otherwise,

in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), since the quality of masculinity— which consists of existence and growth— is not absent even in a female individual, the rule *āṅenā'striyām* [would apply].

Since there would be no contradiction regarding non-existence, even a woman or a beast might be sacrificed; we have already discussed this in the commentary on the *Tantravārttika* under the section "Likewise the Gender" (*tathāliṅgam*) in the first quarter of the fourth book. This gender is indeed threefold.

It is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, just like genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). If it were the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it would result in its being the primary element; this would contradict the fact that in cases such as *ajā* ("she-goat") and *khaṭvā* ("bed"), our experience establishes a cognition of "goat" and so on as qualified by femininity through a relation of identity (*tādātmya*).

Furthermore, since words such as *mātṛ* (mother), *duhitṛ* (daughter), and *svasṛ* (sister) convey a meaning qualified by femininity even without suffixes like *ṭāp*, it is necessary to postulate that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) possesses expressive power (*śakti*) in that regard; thus,
to postulate expressive power for the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on as well would be redundant.
Furthermore, the rules of the *Liṅgānuśāsana* (Instruction on Gender), such as "the words ending in *ṛ*, namely *mātṛ*, *duhitṛ*, *svasṛ*, *yātṛ*, *nanāndṛ*;

and *prāvṛṭ*, *vipruṭ*, *ūti*, *viṣ*," are also seen to concern the base forms (*prakṛti*) themselves. For this very reason, in the rule "after a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix containing a long vowel other than *ktin*... [the gender is determined by the base].

In the case of the suffix *ktin*, [the addition of *ṅīp*] would be meaningless; otherwise, since femininity is already expressed by *ktin* itself, *ṅīp* would not apply, and its redundancy would be obvious. Nor should it be argued that even so, since femininity is expressed by the base (*prakṛti*) itself, how could *ṭāp* and the others apply?

Because, as in the case of [the rule] "two" (*dvau*) and so forth, that which is expressed by the base (*prakṛti*) does not exclude [other possibilities]. Otherwise, the prescription of the *ṭāp* suffix and others would be purposeless. Thus, in this context, femininity is the meaning expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, while the *ṭāp* suffixes and others are merely its indicators (*dyotaka*). And so, when the *ṭāp* suffixes and others are present, necessarily...

The rule is that there is the cognition of femininity (*strītvabodha*), but it is not a restriction that this occurs only when the suffixes *ṭāp* and others are present. (Pāṇini 4.1.4) *ajādyataṣṭāp*: "The suffix *ṭāp* [is applied] after [stems] beginning with *ajā-* and those ending in short *a*. Those whose first member is *aja-* are called *ajādayaḥ*, and these, together with those ending in *at* (*ac*), [form the scope of the rule].

This is a genitive case used after a collective dvandva compound. From the rule *ṭhṅyāpprātipadikāt*, the term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem) is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) and is modified into the genitive; it is then qualified by the words beginning with *aj* and by *at*.
This constitutes an application of the rule regarding suffixes following a specific element (*tadantavidhi*). In that context, regarding the domain of *at*, the rule *samāsapratyayavidhau* applies.

The prohibition stated in the rule "the prohibition must be stated regarding operations affecting the final element" does not apply here, because it has been specified that this applies "except in the case of the suffixes *ṭhuk*, vowel-roots, and the mention of phonemes. However, the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* does not carry over [from the previous rule], because those two are to be prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "in the feminine" (*striyām*). Nor [is there an application] by means of vowels and so forth.

It should be stated that even when it qualifies a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply, because of the prohibition "in the case of rules for compounds and suffixes" (*samāsapratyayavidhau*) and the prohibition "there is no extension to what ends with [a word] when that word is a nominal stem accompanied by a qualifying element" (*grahaṇavatā prātipadikena tadantavidhir nāsti*). However, this is not the case in the rule *śūdrā cāmahatpūrvā jātiḥ*.

By the statement "not preceded by *maha*t," it is indicated that the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply in other instances. Furthermore, the meaning is not "when a feminine individual (*strīvyakti*) is to be understood"; for if that were the case, then in examples such as *ajā* ("goat") and *khaṭvā* ("bed"), the suffixes *ṭāp* and others would have to occur because the feminine individual is actually understood through the form of the word *ajā*-ness and so forth.

Furthermore, if suffixes such as *ṭāp* were applied [directly], the manifestation of femininity would not be certain. Therefore, the expression "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; that is to say, it means "in the state of femininity.
This is what he states with the words "of those beginning with *aja*" and so forth; the meaning is "of those ending in *ajādi*. [The word] "when [femininity] is to be indicated" (*dyotye*).
The sense is that, according to the method stated, femininity is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*).

And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "From whatever nominal stem occurs in the feminine, *ṭāp* and the others arise in its own meaning (*svārthe*). Regarding the rule "ṭāp shall occur": the governing rules "it is an affix" (*pratyayaḥ*) and "and it follows [the stem]" (*paraśca*) are in force.

When the question arises as to why [the suffix] *para* occurs, it should be understood that it follows from proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) after words beginning with *aja* and those ending in *a*. Now, one might object: "The reading of forms ending in *a*, such as *ṭhaja* and *ṭhaśva*, in the *ajādigaṇa* is redundant, since the desired result is already established by their being *adanta* (ending in *a*). To this, he says: "The mention of *ajādi* [is for the sake of the rule] *vayasi prathame*."

The meaning is that the mention of "ajādi" (beginning with 'a-j') is for the purpose of setting aside both the *ṅīp* and the *ṅīṣ* suffixes— which will be discussed later under the rule *jāter astrīviṣayād*— and which serve as exceptions to the *ṭāp* suffix for words ending in short *a*. Thus,
it follows that while *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are exceptions to the *ṭāp* suffix for words ending in short *a*, they themselves are exceptions to the *ṭāp* suffix for words beginning with 'a-j'.
The word *aja* refers to the genus of goats. According to Amarasimha: "Aja is a male goat; *ajā*, *chāgī*, *tubha*, *chāga*, *basta*, and *chagalaka* [are synonyms] for a female goat.
From the word *aja*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied; by the rule *ṭāp-ṣpha-ṅīṣām ādiḥ*, the initial vowel is lengthened (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*).
Due to its status as a designated entity (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is considered to end in *aj*. Regarding the word "ataḥ" (from this): "An example will be stated later."

The remainder [of the commentary] begins with "khaṭvā" (bed). Regarding the word *khaṭvā*: from the root *khaṭ* in the sense of "desire," [the suffix] *kvan* is applied according to the rule *ṭhaśū-pruṣi-laṭi-kaṇi-khaṭi-viśi-bhyaḥ kvan*.

The word *khaṭvā* ends in a short *a*. From that, by adding the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, there is the lengthening of the vowel (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). A bed is called *śayana*, *mañca*, *paryaṅka*, or *palyaṅka*.

"Equal to a bedstead," according to Amara. Now, one might object: since the rule "paraśca" (and that which follows) is in force, and because [the word] is joined with a fifth case denoting direction (*digyoga*), the meaning would more appropriately be that the suffix *ṭāp* occurs after words beginning with vowels and after the word *ad*, when femininity is to be expressed; thus, resorting to the genitive in the rule "ajādyataḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.4) would be incorrect. To this [he replies]:

He says: "By means of *aja* and so forth. This means that by relying on the genitive case in the rule *ajādyataḥ*, the feminine gender (*strītva*) is qualified by *aja* and so forth—namely, by the suffix *ṭāp* applied when the feminine gender is to be expressed for words beginning with *aja* and those ending in short *a*.
Thus, in the compound *pañcājī*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the collection (*samāhāra*) of five goats (*aja*)," according to the rule *taddhitārtha-*.

By the rule "ityādinā" (and so forth), this is a *dvigu* compound. According to the rule "ṭhakārāntottarapado dviguḥ striyāmiṣṭaḥ" ("A *dvigu* whose final member ends in the vowel 'a' is desired to be feminine"), there is femininity. By the rule "dvigoḥ," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. By the rule "yasyeti ca," the vowel 'a' is elided. Now, one might object: since the word *aja* exists within this compound, the femininity must belong to that very word. To this, he says: "atra" (in this case).

The meaning is that because the word *upāñcaj* contains the term *aj*, the feminine gender residing in the collective sense (*samāhāra*) which constitutes the meaning of the compound belongs to the aggregate *pañcājī*, and not to the word *aj* itself; therefore, the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply here. Nor, according to the method mentioned, does the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) apply to [the word] ending in *aj*.
It must be stated that because the compound *pañcājī* is included [in the rule], femininity (*strītva*) is what is expressed by it;

for even though the rule applies to those ending in such suffixes (*tadantavidhi*), since the suffixes beginning with *añ* are directly mentioned (*śruta*), it is more logical that femininity is their qualifier. However, in the interpretation "the suffix *ṭāp* occurs after those beginning with *ṭhaÑ* when femininity is to be indicated,"...

The point is that since the feminine gender (*strītva*) cannot be expressed by words such as *aja* (goat), the suffix *ṭāp* would apply even by taking the feminine gender residing in the aggregate (*samāhāra*). Now, he illustrates the words beginning with *aja* with the verse starting with *aja* etc. Regarding *eḍakā*: "In the Amarakośa, it is said: 'eḍaka refers to meḍhra, urabhra, araṇa, ūrṇāyu, meṣa, vṛṣṇi, and eḍaka. As for its feminine state...
The feminine form *aśvā* is to be sought elsewhere in the lexicon; for Amara states: *aśvo vāmyaśvā vaḍavā*.

Regarding *caṭakā*: *caṭaka* is a specific species of bird. The feminine gender of this generic term is to be sought [in other sources]; however, Amara says: *caṭakaḥ kalaviṅkaḥ syāt, tasya strī caṭakā*. Regarding *mūṣikā*...

According to Amara: "The *ṭhcucundarī* is the musk-shrew (*gandhamūṣī*), while the *dīrghedehī* is the mouse (*mūṣikā*). Regarding the phrase "born in these": the meaning is that although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have applied to the five [words] beginning with *ajā* by the rule "for a genus, provided it is not feminine" (*jāter astrī*), that is set aside by the *ṭāp* of the *ajādi* group. Words such as *bālā* denote the first stage of life; among them, there are three beginning with *hoḍhā*.

Regarding the statement that [the word *prathama*] denotes the first stage of life (*prathamavayovācitva*), the lexicon (*kośa*) must be sought. As for the phrase "in these": among the five beginning with *bāla*, the suffix *ṅīp* would have been applicable by the rule *vayasi prathame*; however, the meaning is that this is superseded by the suffix *ṭāp* belonging to the *ajādi* group. Regarding *sambhasra*: this *vārttika* is cited in its sense within the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *pākakarṇe*.

It is included [in the rule]. The meaning is that even after the word *phala* when it follows these words—*sam*, *bhastra*, *ajina*, *śaṇa*, and *piṇḍa*—the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur by the rule "pākakarṇe," but rather only the suffix *ṭāp*. The analysis of *samphalā* is: "that which has abundant fruits" (*samṛddhāni phalāni yasyāḥ*).
Regarding the term *bhastrāphalā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has fruits like a bellows" (*bhastreva phalāni yasyāḥ*).

Amara states: "A *bhastrā* is a leather bellows. Now, since the word *bhastrā* is invariably feminine, it lacks the quality of having a corresponding masculine form; therefore, the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* [Pāṇini 6.3.34] does not apply.

Since the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is not applicable here, one might ask how the short vowel occurs; to this he says: *ṅyāpoḥ*. The meaning is that the shortening occurs by the rule: "The shortening of *ṅī* and *āp* is optional in names and in the Veda" (*ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam*). *Ajinaphalā*, *śaṇaphalā*, and *piṇḍaphalā* are names of specific medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*).

*sadackāṇḍa*. This is also a summary of the meaning of the *vārttika* read in the rule *pākakarṇe*. From the words *sat*, *ac*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, and *eka*, when the word *puṣpa* follows, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur by virtue of the rule *pākakarṇe*; rather, [the suffix *ṅīp* applies].
The meaning is "only there. Regarding *satpuṣpā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has good flowers" (*santi puṣpāṇi yasyāḥ*).
Intending that the verbal root *añc* (to bend/turn) is understood here with its nasal elided (*acaḥ*), he provides the example—*prākpuṣpā*.
The analysis is "that which has flowers turned forward" (*prāñci puṣpāṇi yasyāḥ*). [He gives another example: *pratyakpuṣpā*. [This refers to] those turned backward (*pratyañci*).
The analysis of the compound is "that which has flowers" (*puṣpāṇi yasyāḥ*). Examples include *kāṇḍapuṣpā*, *prāntapuṣpā*, *śatapuṣpā*, and *ekapuṣpā*.
The word *śūdrā* is also included. This is a *vārttika* cited under the rule currently under discussion: *ṭhājādyataḥ*.
If the word *śūdra* is to be designated as a genus (*jāti*), then when preceded by the negative particle *nañ* (a-), it takes the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

This is an exception to the *ṅīṣ* suffix prescribed for genus names. A woman born from a *śūdra* man to his own wife, who was wed according to the prescribed rite, is called a *śūdrā*. [This applies] to the term "genus" (*jāti*).

He states the purpose [of this rule] with the words "But in the case of connection with a male" (*puṃyoge tu*). Since the word *śūdra* is used here to denote a female specifically because of her connection with a male (*puṃyogāt*), it does not express a genus (*jāti*) and therefore the suffix *ṭāp* is not applied; rather, by the rule "after a word ending in *a*, when there is connection with a male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to denote a female," the suffix *ṅīṣ* alone is used. Thus, the form is *mahāśūdrī*. The analysis of the compound is: "she who is both great (*mahatī*) and a Śūdra (*śūdrā*)."

In the *karmadhāraya* compound, there is the masculine form (*puṃvat*) according to the rule "in a *karmadhāraya*, [the feminine] becomes like the masculine. Here, because it is preceded by *mahat*, the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply; rather, only the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies by virtue of it being a genus (*jāti*). Amara states: "The word *ābhīrī* is the same whether it denotes a genus or a connection with a male, as is *mahāśūdrī*. An *ugrā* is one born from a *śūdrā* woman by a Kṣatriya king; of her...

The *ābhīra* is born from a Brāhmaṇa; if [the female parent] is a woman, she is an *ābhīrī*. Regarding this, the investigation into the purpose of the mention of the word *jāti* (caste/class) and the mention of the phrase *amahatpūrva* (not preceded by the word *mahat*) is clear in the *Śabdenduśekhara* and the *Bhāṣyapradīpoddyota*. As for *kruñca*: the word *kruñca* ends in the letter *c*.
The word *ṛtvij*, ending in the *kvip* suffix according to the rule "ṛtvig... and so forth, denotes a specific species of bird;
as it says in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "That you killed one from a pair of *krauñca* birds while deluded by a crow.
The word *uṣṇih*, ending in the letter *h*, denotes a specific type of meter, formed with the *kvip* suffix according to the rule "ṛtvig... and so forth.
The word *devaviś* ends in *ś* and refers to the Maruts, who constitute a specific class of deities, according to the Vedic scripture: "The Maruts are indeed the *viś* (clans) of the gods.

Since these [Maruts] do not end in *ā*, the suffix *ṭāp* would not otherwise apply; therefore, they are listed among the *ajādi* (the group beginning with *ajā*) for the purpose of prescribing that suffix.

In the commentary on the sūtra *ṭhṅyāpprātipadikāt*, however, it is maintained that these three [suffixes] end in the vowel *a*; this has been explained immediately below, during the occasion of commenting on the verse *vaṣṭi bhāgurirallopaṃ*. [Regarding the form] *jyeṣṭhā*: when...

The words *jyeṣṭhā* and so forth denote "the first-born" and the like; in that case, the suffix *ṭāp* is established simply by virtue of their ending in the letter *a*. However, when there is the intention to express "the wife of the eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya strī*) and so on, even then, this entry [in the list] is for the purpose of providing the suffix *ṭāp*, overriding the suffix *ṅīṣ* which would otherwise apply due to connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). Thus is the meaning. [The example] is *kokilā*.

The meaning is that although *kokilā* belongs to the category of genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is the characteristic marker for genus—is set aside, and it is recited here for the sake of the suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding the phrase "after *mūla* when preceded by *nañ*": this is a Vārttika recited in the rule *pākakarṇa*.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after the word *mūla* when it follows *nañ*, according to the rule *pākakarṇa*.
But the meaning is "without roots" (*amūla*). Regarding the term *amūla*:

in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "that which has no root," the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed according to the rule "the negative particle *nañ* [is compounded] with words having the sense of 'existent' (*astyartha*), and there may be an elision of the final member.
Here, the rules "after *sambhas*, *trasa*, etc.," "after *sad*, *aca*, *kāṇḍa*, etc.," and "after *mūla* when preceded by *nañ*" apply.

Although the three *vārttikas* beginning with "aṭhpākakarṇe" are read in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the [Pāṇinian] sūtra, they have been explained in detail in the root-text (*mūla*) within the *ajādi* group because there is no difference in their result. One should not, however, fall into the error of thinking that these are *gaṇasūtras* included within the *ajādi* group; rather, *ajādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Therefore...
Thus, the usage "ṭāyām ādeśaḥ" found in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṭhana mu ne" is established.

For this very reason, in the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā, in the first quarter (pāda) of the second book, in the section concerning the Stotra and Śastra (Stutaśastrādhikaraṇa), it is stated: "But the Stotra and Śastra are purificatory acts (saṃskāra), because they denote the deity, just like the Yājyā."

Therefore, the sequential citation of the modification (*ūha*) "for the goat, for the omentum" (*chāgāya vapāyai*) during the commentary on the *guṇasūtra*— "Or it may be for the sake of a quality"— in both the *Śābarabhāṣya* and the *Bhaṭṭavārtika*, is consistent. For this very reason, in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*, in the fourth quarter of the first chapter...

In the section *acamasa-vad-aviśeṣāt*, both Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya and Vācaspati’s commentary justify the use of the feminine form *ajā* (ending in *ṭāp*) for the word "goat" (*chāgā*); otherwise, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been required by the rule defining feminine gender based on genus (*jāti*). Let this matter rest for now. [Regarding the rule] *ṛn-nebhyaḥ*...

The rule concerning neuter nouns ending in vowels (*sūtramajantastrīliṅga*) was explained incidentally in the section on feminine nouns; however, it is introduced here again in accordance with the sequence of the *sūtras*.
(448) *ugitaśca* | Pāṇini 4.1.6 | [Nouns] ending in an *ugit* vowel [take the feminine suffix *ṅīp*].

"And [after a stem] ending in an *ugit* [suffix]. *Uk* is a *pratyāhāra*. That which has *uk* as its *it* is called *ugit*. The term "ending in *ugit*" (*ugitaḥ*) is in the ablative case; it qualifies the word "from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*), and thus the rule of "ending-inclusion" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.

Because it is stated that "in the case of the mention of a phoneme in the rules for suffixes and compounds," the prohibition regarding "rules for compounds and suffixes" (*samāsapratyayavidhau*) does not apply here.
The term *ṅīp* is understood from the preceding sūtra. Thus he says: "from that which ends in an *ugit*.

An *ugit* is of two kinds: a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and an affix (*pratyaya*). Among these, he gives an example of a nominal stem: *bhavatī*. [This refers to] *bhavatu* in the list of words beginning with *sarva*.

Thus, this is taught as an unanalyzed nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Since it possesses the status of a designated entity (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied because it ends in the *ugit* class. The markers *ṅ* and *p* are elided.

The augment *num* does not apply by the rules "after a word ending in *āc*, *śī*, or *nadī*" or "after a word ending in *śap* or *śyan*," because it does not end in a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*).

Nor can it be argued that *ṭhugidacām* [is the cause], because it lacks the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Now, he illustrates the second type of *ugit*: *pacanti*. From the root *pac*, with the suffix *laṭ*, followed by *śatṛ* and *śas*, and after the application of the *pararūpa* rule, the word *pacat* arises. In this case, the suffix *śatṛ* is an *ugit*, and the word ending in it is *pacat*.

The sense is that [the word] is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); therefore, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, the augment *num* is applied by the rule "before *śap* and *śyan*" (*śap-śyanor-nuṃ*).

However, if the entry for *bhavat* in the *sarvādi* group is derived from the root *bhā-* by the rule "*bhāteḥ ḍavatuḥ*," then it should be understood as an example of a word ending in an *ugit* suffix. [This applies] to the root *bhū*.

In the case of the *śatṛ* suffix with *śap*, after the *guṇa* of the vowel *ū* and its replacement by *av*, the form *bhavat* is obtained; however, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, the form becomes *bhavantī* due to the *num* augment prescribed by the rule "the *num* augment is obligatory for *śap* and *śyan*.

Now, one might object: even though the word *bhavat* has been produced [as a base], how can it possess the quality of ending in an *ugit* vowel by virtue of being treated as if it were the same as its original form (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*)?
It should not be argued that this is because of the rule "the designation of a base as if it were itself applies [only] when not preceded by a nominal stem" (*ṭhvyapadeśivadbhāvo'prātipadikena*),

for that rule operates only when a nominal stem is grasped in its own specific form. The passage beginning with "in the sūtra *ugidacām*" has been explained in the section on bases ending in consonants (*halanta*) during the analysis of the word *gomat*.

"By that" means by obtaining the absence of the operation of the *ugit* suffix for verbal roots other than *añcu*. "A pot" (*ukhā*) refers to a cooking vessel (*kuṇḍī*). The analysis of the compound is: "it falls from the pot" (*ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate*) and "it falls from the leaf" (*parṇāt dhvaṃsate*).
Amarasimha states: "A *piṭhara*, a *sthālī*, an *ukhā*, and a *kuṇḍa* [are synonyms for a cooking vessel]. The roots *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* mean "to fall down" (*avasraṃsane*).

The meaning is as follows: with the word *sup* continuing from the previous rule, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "ṭhkvip ca"; there is a compound with the subordinate member (*upapadasamāsa*);

the case-ending (*sub*) is elided; there is no elision of the nasal by the rule "aniditām"; the case-ending *s* is elided by the rule "halṅyādi"; and the substitution of *d* occurs by the rule "vasusraṃsu". Regarding the phrase "syādeva" (it would indeed be so), the word "ṅīp" is to be understood as the remainder.
Regarding "prācī": from the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *pra*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā kvip*;

there is elision of the nasal (*n*) according to the rule *aniditām*. Because it ends in an *ugit* vowel, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added; then, with the elision of the letter *a* by the rule *acaḥ*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *cau*.

(449) *vana-ura-ca* |4|1|7|. The analysis of *vana-ura-ca* is as follows: *vanaḥ* and *ra*. The suffix *ra* has its nominative case ending elided; the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By the word *ca*, the suffix *ṅīp* is also included. *Vana* is in the ablative case (*pañcamyantam*).
By this [rule], that which ends in the suffix *van* and that which has it as its final member (*tadanta*) are intended to be expressed.
The governing rule *ṭh-prātipadikāt* is in force. This is what he states with the words "from that which ends in *van*" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "it is a substitute for the final letter" (*antādeśa*), the word "in the present context" (*prakṛte*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Since the suffix *ṅīp* is already applicable by virtue of the word ending in *n*, [the present rule serves to restrict it].

By virtue of that conjunction (*saṃniyoga*), only the letter *r* is to be prescribed here. Regarding the term "in general" (*sāmānya*): the meaning is that the mention of *ṭhvan*—when stripped of its indicatory letters (*anubandha*)—is common to all three [cases].
Now, one might ask: how is it that by the mention of *van*, both the suffix *van* itself and that which ends in it are obtained? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "In the case of the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*). This means that when a suffix is prescribed after a base (*prakṛti*), there is the inclusion of that entire collection [of sounds] which has that base as its beginning—that is, the base word is the beginning of which—and which has that suffix as its end—that is, the suffix is the end of which.
