The meaning is that there is the inclusion of both the aggregate of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya), as well as those elements situated between them.

In the rule *ṭhtiḍḍatiṅ* (Pāṇini 6.3.109), the mention of "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) is for the purpose of including the verbal suffixes such as *śap* and others within the term *tiṅ*. This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) in the rule *yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.13).

It is established in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*): the sense is that because the term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem) which is the governing heading is qualified by [the suffix] *vat*, the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) is not obtained once again. Nor should it be asked how, this being the case, the form ending in *vat* is obtained; for in the rule *ṭhy-an-vidhis-tadantasya* (P. 1.1.72), the word *svam*...

The intention is that, by carrying over the word "of itself" (*svasya*) from the rule *rūpam* and changing the case ending, one explains it as "and of its own [form]. This very point is indicated by the particle *api*. Some hold that [the term] ending in a suffix denoting a class (*van*-pratyaya) is treated like a single instance (*vyapadeśivat*), and thus [the compound] ends in a suffix denoting a class. [This applies] to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses such a suffix.

However, the rule regarding "tadanta" (ending in that) does not apply within this governing context of "striyām" (in the feminine), as indicated by the mark [liṅga] in the rule "śūdrā cāmahatpūrvā jātiḥ" (and *śūdrā* when not preceded by *amahat*, denoting a genus). Now, he gives an example ending in a suffix whose final element is *van*: "sutvānam. [The root is] "ṣuñ abhiṣave" (to press, to extract juice).
From the rule "su-jyoṅ-vanip" and "hrasvasya piti kṛti," the suffix *tuka* is added; thus, the word *sutvan* is formed.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "those who have surpassed the *sutvān*," the compound is formed by the rule "aty-ādayaḥ. Upon the elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and the *n* is changed to *r*, resulting in the form *atisutvarī*. Similarly, there is the form *atidhīvarī*.

From the root *ḍudhāñ* in the sense of "holding and nourishing," the suffix *kvanip* is applied even in the common language (*bhāṣā*) according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*. By the rule *ghumāsthā*, the vowel *ī* is substituted [for the penultimate *a*]. In the analysis of the compound as "those who have transcended the *dhīvān* (fisherman)," the compound is formed by the rule *atyādayaḥ*. Then, by the rule *ṅībrau ca*, the form *atidhīvarī* is produced. However, in the *Bhāṣya*:
It is established that [the form] *dhyāyan* is derived from the root *dhyai* with the suffix *kvanip*, where lengthening occurs by the rule *halaḥ*.
Regarding *śarvarī*: from the root *śṛ* (in the sense of "injuring"), the suffix *vanip* is applied—even in the common language—by the rules *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca* and *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*.

There is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ," and the suffixes *ṅīp* and *raṅ* by the rule "vano ra ca. This is an example of a word ending in the suffix *van*. However, if the reading is "atiśarvarī," then this too is an example of a word ending in *van* with the addition of the suffix *tṛc*. [The examples are] *sutvarī*, *dhīvarī*, and *śarvarī*.
Examples of [stems] ending in *van*: "vano na" (Pāṇini 6.1.25). As before, both that which ends in *van* and that which ends in a stem ending in *van* are included.

The word "ṭh-śaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.1) is in the ablative case; by means of this, the term "dhātoḥ" (from the root), which is supplied from the governing context, is qualified, and the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies.
The [sūtras] *ṅīp* and *raśca* are understood to follow [from the previous rule]. Thus he says, "ending in a consonant (*haśantāt*)", and so forth.

Demonstrating the purpose of qualifying the suffix that is prescribed, he says, "the root *oṇṛ*", etc., in order to show an example of a word ending in *van*. Regarding *vanip*: [it is taught that] "it is seen after other roots as well."

The word "thus" (*iti*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Regarding "āvau": from the root *oṇ*, with the suffix *vanip*, the rule *ṭhviḍvanoranunāsikasyā’d* applies, whereby the nasal *ṇ* is replaced by *ā*; then, the vowel *o* is replaced by *āv*, resulting in the form *āvān*. To indicate the feminine gender, the qualifier "Brāhmaṇī" is provided. Here, [the root] *oṇ*...

Thus, the suffix *van* is prescribed after a verbal root ending in *ha* or *ś*; because it ends in that [suffix], the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *ra* do not apply, but rather the form is like that of *rājan*. However, the intention [of the author] is that if one were to explain the rule as "the *van* which follows a verbal root ending in *ha* or *ś*," then once the substitution of *āt* has occurred, the *van* would no longer follow *ha* or *ś*, and consequently, the prohibition [of *ṅīp* and *ratva*] would not take effect.
He cites *rājayudhvā* as an example of a word ending in *-vant*. The meaning is "one who has fought with a king.
While the rule *kvip* for the past tense (*bhūte*) in the sense of an object (*karman*) is still in force, the suffix *kvanip* is applied by the rule *rājani yudhikṛñaḥ*.
The meaning of that [rule] is: when *yudh* (to fight) or *kṛ* (to do/make) have "king" (*rājan*) as an object-locus (*upapada*), the suffix *kvanip* is added.

In an *upapada* compound, following the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), there arises the word *rājayudhvan*. Here, the suffix *van* is prescribed after the root *yudh*; thus, the word *yudhvan* ends in that [suffix], and the word *rājayudhvan* likewise ends in it. Therefore, the meaning is that the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are not applied as substitutes.

"Or, in a *bahuvrīhi*. This is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that the rule "the substitution of *ra* for the final vowel of *van* [in a *bahuvrīhi*]" may optionally apply in a *bahuvrīhi*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition "not after *van* in a *bahuvrīhi*. For example: *bahudhīvarī*; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she who has many fishermen (*dhīvānaḥ*). Also: *bahudhīvā*.

In the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the augment *ratva*, the form is like that of *rājan*. Nor should it be argued that in the case of *bahuparvā* (she who has many joints), there too there would be an option between *ṅīp* and *ratva*; for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya that this Vārttika applies only in instances suitable for the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by the rule *allopo'naḥ*.

And in the case of the word *bahuparvan*, because the elision of the *ac* suffix is prohibited by the rule "ṭhna saṃyogādvanamantāt," [the form *bahuparvā* is not obtained]. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): this means that in the alternative where the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the accentuation (*ratva*) do not apply, the suffix *ḍāp* will be prescribed by the rule "ḍābubhābhyām. [In the derivation] *bahudhīvan-ā*, once the suffix is applied, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) occurs by the rule "ṭeḥ."
From the word *bahudhīvā*, after the elision of the nominative suffix *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the form is *bahudhīvaḥ*, which has the same shape as *ramā*.
In the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the *ṛt* [vṛddhi] substitution, as well as the suffix *ḍāp*, the form after *su* is simply *bahudhīvā*.
With the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṛt*, it becomes *bahudhīvarī*. However, in the case of the dual endings *au* and *jas*, etc., the forms are *bahudhīvaryau* and *bahudhīvaḥ*.
The intention is that there are three forms, beginning with *bahudhīvān*.

(450) *pādo 'nyatarasyām* |4|1|8|. [The word] *pādaḥ* [is used]; [it refers to] one for whom the compound-ending suffix has been applied. This means that when the compound-ending suffix, consisting of the elision of the final syllable, has been applied.
The meaning is that the word *pāc* (foot) which remains [after the elision] is understood here. Regarding "from that which ends in this":

the meaning is "from that which ends in the word *pāc*. The intention is that the term *prātipadika* (nominal stem), which is the governing rule (*adhikṛta*), is qualified by the ablative form *pādaḥ*. Thus, the suffix *ṅīp* may optionally occur.

The meaning is that this [suffix] continues from the rule "ṭhṛnnebhyaḥ. Regarding *dvipadī*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has two feet" (*dvau pādau yasyāḥ*). By the rule "saṅkhyāsupūrvasya," there is elision of the vowel *a* at the end of the word *pāda*. When the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, because the stem is then treated as a *bha*, the substitution of *pat* for *pāda* takes place.
The form is *dvipad* when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is absent; otherwise, it is *dvipād*. (Pāṇini 4.1.9) *ṭābṛci*:
[the word] "in the case of a verse" (*ṛci*) [is understood]. [The word] "ending in *pād*" [is understood]; the remainder [of the rule] is "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*).
The intention is that, because the word *pād* is carried over from the rule "pādo 'nyatarasyām," it qualifies the governing term *prātipadikāt*.
This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīp* prescribed by "pādo 'nyatarasyām. For example: *dvipadā ṛk* ("a verse of two feet"). Two...
The analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose feet [are such]. Regarding *ekapadā*: the analysis is "she who has one foot.

In both cases, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, and by the rule *pādaḥ pat*, the word *pāda* is replaced by *pad*. However, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, relying upon the word *pada* as being synonymous with the word *pāda*—

This has been refuted. Nor should it be said that this sūtra is intended to exclude the usage of *dvipadī* and *dvipād* when the referent is a Ṛc verse; for, according to the authority of the Bhāṣya on this very point, such usage is also accepted—this is incorrect. [The rule] "not six" (*na ṣaṭ*)...
This has been explained in the section on bases ending in vowels (*ajanta-adhikāra*) under the treatment of bases ending in *ṛ*. Regarding the word *pañca*:

here, although the suffix *ṅīp*—which is characterized by the presence of an *an* (short *a*) at the end of the base—is applicable due to its being an internal rule (*antaraṅga*), it is prohibited because the number is six (*ṣaṭ*). Consequently, by the rule "there is elision [of the case endings] after the six [numerals]" (*ṭh-ṣaḍbhyo luk*), there is elision of the nominative-accusative plural suffixes *jas* and *śas*. Once the *n* has been elided, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply because the base now ends in a short *a*. However, this is also prohibited.

The point is that the recurrence of the suffix *ṭāp* here for the purpose of prohibition is necessary. Nor should it be argued that because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*), there is no possibility of *ṭāp* occurring at all;
for since the rule for *ṭāp* is not included among the rules concerning case-endings (*sup*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), or the insertion of *t* (*tuṅvidhi*), when that [elision] is to be applied...

Because there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) for the *nalopa* (elision of *n*). Now, [one might object]: in the rule "not [the suffix] *ṭāp* after the six [numerals] and *svasṛ* etc.," the connection is with "not *ṭāp*. The remainder [of the meaning] is: "the *ṭāp* characterized by ending in *adanta* [is what is prohibited]. When the *ṅīp* characterized by ending in *n* has been prohibited, and the *luk* elision of the *jas* and *śas* case-endings has occurred, the *nalopa* is performed; then, because it ends in *adanta*, the *ṭāp* which would have applied is [prevented].

The point is that the recurrence of the suffix *ṭāp* here for the purpose of prohibition is necessary. Nor should it be argued that because the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*), there is no possibility of *ṭāp* occurring at all;
for since the rule for *ṭāp* is not included among the rules concerning case-endings (*sup*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), or the application of *tuk*, when that [elision] is to be performed...

Because there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*) for the *nalopa* (the elision of *n*). Now, one might object: even if the term *ṭāp* is understood to carry over into the rule "not [after] words ending in *ṣaṣ*, *svasṛ*, etc.," how can there be this prohibition based on the designation *ṣaṣ* in this instance?
For once the *nalopa* has been applied, the designation *ṣaṣ* is absent. Nor is it the case that when the prohibition of *ṭāp* is to be effected...

One might suspect that the *nalopa* (elision of the final *n*) is not established [by the rule], because the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is not included among the rules concerning case endings (*sup*), accents (*svara*), technical names (*saṃjñā*), or the application of *tuṅ*.
To this, he says: "Even when the *nalopa* has been performed," up to the end of the phrase "because it is not established. This rule prohibiting *ṭāp* also [applies to] the technical name *ṣaṣ*.

He establishes [this] by resorting to the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that grammatical operations take effect at the time they are required). Consequently, when that [operation] is to be performed, since the *navasup* rule is not yet established, the designation *ṣaṭ* remains unobstructed; thus, the prohibition of *ṣṭun* based on the designation *ṣaṭ* is here likewise unobstructed—this is the intended meaning. However, in reality...

They say that even though the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the prohibition of the suffix *ṭāp* is justified by relying on the previously established designation (*saṃjñā*) of "six" (*ṣaṭ*). For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *nalopaḥ supsvare* that there is no purpose for the non-existence of *nalopa* within the context of the designation "six."

(452) *manaḥ* |4|1|11|. The word *manaḥ* [is the subject]. From the rule *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ*, the word *na* is understood; from the rule *ṛnnebhyaḥ*, the word *ṅīp* is understood. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the term *mana* is taken as denoting that which ends in it.

He says this: "from a word ending in *man*" (*mannantāt*). Regarding *sīmā*: from the root *piñ* in the sense of "binding," the suffix *manin* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rules, with lengthening of the base vowel. When the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited after the word *sīman*, the form is like that of *rājan*.

The point is that if *ṅīp* were applied, there would be elision of the final nasal (*al-lopa*), resulting in the form *sīmnī*. [Objection: But what about the feminine suffix *ḍāp* which will be mentioned later?

One might ask: since the form *sīmā* is established by [the rule] *sau rūpasiddheḥ*, what is the purpose of the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp*? To this he says: *sīmānau*. The intention is that if the suffix *ḍāp* were applied, the form would simply be *sīme*. (453) *ano bahuvrīheḥ* | 4|1|12|.

The term "of a *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīheḥ*) is a qualifier for the rule "the suffix *ṭhan*"; thus, it is a *tadantavidhi* (a rule applying to that which ends in [the specified element]). The words "not" (*na*) and "the feminine suffix *ṅīp*" (*ṅīp*) are carried over from the preceding rule as before. Therefore, he says: "from that which ends in *anna*. For example: *bahuyajvā* ("one who has many performers of sacrifice"), meaning "she whose [husband] has many performers of sacrifice."
The compound is *vigraha*. Since the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *nāntalakṣaṇa* applies, the forms are like those of *rājan*.

Because of the prohibition [of *ṭhan*] by the rule *na saṃyogād*, this [word] does not undergo elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*); therefore, the optional application of the rule *ana upadhālopinaḥ* cannot take effect here.
(454) Ḍāb ubhābhyām anyatarasyām |4|1|13|. [The sūtra] states:
*ḍāb ubhābhyām*.
He explains the phrase "from both" (*ubhābhyām*) as "from those introduced by the two preceding sūtras. [The word] *manas*.
The meaning is "and from a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *mat* or *an*," as derived from the two rules beginning with "ṭhañ bahuvrīheḥ.
Now, one might object that the inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* here is redundant; for if it were absent, would not the suffix *ḍāp* be compulsory?

It might be argued that this need not be stated; for if the suffix *ḍāp* were compulsory (*nitya*), the suffix *ṅīp* would necessarily be superseded by it, rendering the prohibition of *ṅīp* redundant.

Furthermore, since the optionality of both the prohibition of *ṅīp* and *ḍāp* would be established through the very force of their explicit mention, the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") would be useless. To this we reply: it is for the sake of clarity.

Some [hold this view]. However, in the Bhāṣya, by relying on a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) of the sūtra *ṭhanyatarasyām*, the Vārttika *bahuvrīhau* is rejected. Regarding *sīmā*: from the word *sīman*, after the addition of the suffix *ḍāp* and the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*), the form *sīmā* is obtained; then, after the case-ending *su*, there is the elision of the consonant and the following vowel (*halṅyādilopa*).
Even in the alternative where the *ḍāp* suffix is absent, the prohibition of the *ṅīp* suffix by the rule *manaḥ* applies;
thus, in the nominative singular (*sau*), the form is simply *sīme*, identical to that of *rājan*. If one asks, "What then is the purpose of the prescription of *ḍāp*?
he says: *sīme, sīmānau*. He provides another example within the scope of stems ending in *man*: *dāma*.

The suffix *manin* is applied to the root *dā* according to the *Uṇādi* rules. He says "not masculine" because the word *dāma* is seen to be neuter in such instances as "the golden rope is the sacrificial fee" (*hiraṇmayaṃ dāma dakṣiṇā*). The meaning is that the word *dāman* is not masculine, but rather belongs to both the feminine and the neuter genders; for it is a rule that "when a gender is specifically prohibited, the remaining [genders] are intended."
Because it has been explained [in that way]. He provides an example of an *annanta-bahuvrīhi*: "bahuyaḍajvā" (one who has many performers of sacrifice).

The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "she whose [sons] are many performers of sacrifice. When the suffix *ḍāp* is applied and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, the case-ending *s-* is dropped after the word *bahuyajvā* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). Since the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited, this very form remains before the nominative *su*.

The form is like that of *rājan*. Regarding the suffix *ḍāp*, the author states the result: in the dual, *bahuyajvānau*; in the nominative plural (*śas*), *bahuyajvanaḥ*. Here, the elision of *at* (*allopa*) does not occur because of the prohibition:

"not after a conjunct consonant ending in *m* or *v*" (*na saṃyogādvamantāt*). For this very reason, [the rule] "after a word ending in *an* which has an elided penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*)...
This is not the scope [of the rule].
(455) *Aṅgasya upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.28).
Now, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one who has many kings," the suffix *ṭhan* is applied after the word *bahurājan*.

Since the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule *bahuvrīher añ*, and since the suffix *ḍāp* is introduced by the rule *ḍāb ubhābhyām*, both the state of ending in *n* and the state of ending in *ā* would result; however, the form ending in *ṅīp* is also desired.
To that end, this [rule] is commenced: *ana upadhā*. This sūtra is not recited within this particular section.
However, the rule "dāmahāyanāntācca" (Pāṇini 4.1.27) is recited later; it is presented here incidentally [in this context].
From the rule "bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ" (Pāṇini 4.1.25), the term "bahuvrīheḥ" (of a bahuvrīhi compound) is understood to carry over;
however, "dāmahāyanāntācca" is recited subsequently, and is thus introduced here by way of incidental discussion.
The term "bahuvrīheḥ" (of a bahuvrīhi compound) is understood from the rule "bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ," and "ṅīp" is understood from the rule "saṃkhyāvyayāder ṅīp.

The word "prātipadikāt" (from a nominal stem), which has been established by the previous rules, is qualified by the word "manaḥ" (ending in -man); thus, the rule of "tadantavidhiḥ" (application to that which ends in such a suffix) applies.
He says this with the words beginning "anantād" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the prohibition of *ḍāp* and *ṅīp* in the alternative":

the meaning is that sometimes there is a prohibition of *ṅīp*, and sometimes there is *ḍāp*. This is the purpose of including the term "anyatarasyām. If the inclusion of "anyatarasyām" were not made, then in a word such as *bahuyajvā*, [the suffix would apply].

In the case of the word *bahurājan*, there would be an obstruction (*bādha*) by the suffix *ṅīp*— which is without scope (*anavakāśa*) because it applies where there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*anupadhālopini*)— to both the prohibition of *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule "the suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited after a *ṭhan*-ending Bahuvrīhi" and the suffix *ḍāp* prescribed by the rule "the suffixes *ḍāp* and *ṅīṣ* [are applied] after both [types of Bahuvrīhis]. Thus, the *ḍāp* would be obstructed.

Regarding *bahurājñī*: the intention is that after the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, the *al* (the *a* of *rājan*) is elided, and then by the rule *sor hal-ṅy-ādi-lopaḥ*, the nominative case ending (*su*) is elided.

Regarding *bahurāja*: this is the form in the nominative (*su*) when the suffix *ḍāp* is applied and the *ṅīp* is prohibited. Regarding *bahurājnyau*: this is the form in the dual (*au*) in the alternative where *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *āṬ* (long *ā*) before a vowel-initial suffix beginning with *i*. Regarding *bahurāje*: this is the form in the dual (*au*) in the alternative where *ḍāp* is applied, resulting in *āṬ* before a vowel-initial suffix beginning with *e*.
In the case of *bahurājñī*, which is an example of the form ending in *āṬ* due to the prohibition of *ṣaṅīp*, [the following rule applies]:
(456) *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasyāt idāpyasupaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.44.
[The word] *pratyayasthāt* means "from the letter *k* situated in an affix. *K* refers to the phoneme *k*; that is to say, from the phoneme *k*. The vowel *a*...

The vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), according to the rule "after a consonant, [the suffix] *kāra*. Thus, it is indicated that in the sūtra *kāt*, the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation. "That which is *āp*" means that which is employed as the subsequent cause (*paranimitta*) in the rule prescribing the substitution of *it*. "Provided it is not followed by a case-ending" (*supaḥ paro na cet*).

In the sūtra "ṭhasupaḥ," the form ending in the fifth case (pañcamyanta) is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound). The intended meaning is that when a feminine suffix (*āp*) follows immediately after a *sup*-ending [base], the substitution of *it* does not take place; this is the underlying point. Regarding the word *sarvikā*:

from the word *sarva*, by adding the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and applying the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇa-dīrgha*), the form *sarvā* is obtained. Because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the end of the preceding element...

Because of its inclusion [in the category of *sarvanāman*], the operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma*) apply. Consequently, by the rule *avyayasarvanāmnām am*, the suffix *am* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*).

In this context, the letter *k* in the suffix is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), while the letter *c* is an *it*. Thus, the suffix *ak*—ending in *k*—is placed before the final vowel (*ṭi*). In the word *sarvaka*, the vowel *a* preceding the *k* undergoes the change to *ī* (by the rule *ata iti*).

The form is *sarvikā*. Now, one might object: "How can there be *itva* (the substitution of *i*) for the vowel *a* preceding the letter *k*, since it is separated by the letter *k* and thus lacks the condition of being immediately followed by an *āp*-affix?
This is not so; for, according to the maxim *yena nāvyavadhānam* ("that which does not cause a lack of immediate proximity"), such an intervention does not constitute an obstacle.

Regarding the word *kārikā*: [it is derived] from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*, the substitution of *a* for *ṛ*, the *vṛddhi* of the *ṛ*-vowel by the rule *ṭhaco ñṇiti*, the replacement of *ṛ* by *ra* (*raparatva*), the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* to the word *kāraka*, the long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*), and the change of the vowel *a* preceding the *r* to *i* by the rule *kātpūrvasya*. If, however, the term *kādi* were taken as referring to the entire cluster [of consonants], then the form *etikā* would not be possible.

It is established as follows: when *akac* is inserted before the *ṭi* (the final vowel) of the word *etad*, from the resulting stem *etakac*, the nominative plural suffix *jas* is applied. Then, the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems occurs, followed by the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule. Because the stem now ends in *ā*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Finally, by the rule "before *kā* [of the suffix *kāp*], the preceding [vowel] becomes *ī*," the form *etikā* is produced.

In this case, because the vowel *a* in *akac* serves merely as a phonetic marker (*uccāraṇārtha*), there is no occurrence of the word *ka* as part of an affix; therefore, the substitution of *ī* does not take place.
It might be argued that [the *it* of *kādeḥ*] refers to the letter ‘ka’ because the vowel ‘a’ following the letter ‘ka’ is not a constituent part of the *aK* suffix;

however, one should not suspect that the vowel ‘a’ in *aK* is merely for the purpose of pronunciation. For if that were the case, the form *nakiḥ* would not be possible from the indeclinable *nir*, as there is no *aK* suffix there. Therefore, by the rule *kād iti*, it must mean "from the letter ‘ka’."
This is what is intended [by the author]. This is also indicated by the fact that there is a prohibition against *itva* (the substitution of *i*) in the rule "na yāsayoḥ" regarding the form *sakā*;
otherwise, since the letter *k* belonging to the suffix would be absent there, *itva* would not apply anyway, so what would be the point of its prohibition? Enough of this.

Regarding *naukā*: the suffix *ka* is added to the word *nau* in its own sense (*svārthika*), followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. In this case, the rule *ataḥ* is stated to prevent the shortening of the vowel *au* (which becomes *ā*) that precedes the letter *k*. Regarding *śakā*: from the root *śaklṛ* meaning "to be able," the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is applied, followed by *ṭāp*. Here, because the letter *k* is not situated within a suffix (*pratyayastha*), the vowel preceding it is not shortened.

The substitution of *i* for *a*: as in *bahuparivrājikā*. [Derivation: From the root *vraj* preceded by *pari*, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. The compound *bahuvrīhi* is formed as "that in which there are many wandering mendicants" (*bahavaḥ parivrājakā yasyām*).

Upon the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added to the word *bahuparivrājaka*. Here, the substitution of *i* for the vowel *a* that precedes *ka* does not occur.
By the rule regarding the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the substitution of *āp* takes precedence because it is subsequent with respect to the case-ending *su*.

However, the prohibition "not when [a suffix] is elided by *lumat*" does not apply here; for that prohibition operates only upon an operation concerning a stem (*aṅga*) when a suffix has been elided by *lumat*.
Since the substitution of *it* (the shortening of the vowel) is not an operation concerning a stem when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is present, that prohibition does not apply in this case. But if...

If the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "after a *sup*" (*ṭhasupaḥ*) is resorted to, then in the case of *bahuparivrājaka*, since the entire complex (*samudāya*) is distinct from a *sub* suffix, the substitution of *it* would be unavoidable because it follows after that [complex]. This is the sense. Regarding *rākā*: [it is derived] by the rule "the suffix *ka* is added after roots ending in *kṛ*, as well as after *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kali*. (*kṛdādhārārcikalibhyaḥ kaḥ*).

The suffix *ka* is added to the root *rādh* according to the *Uṇādi* rules. Because of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule *ṭhūṇādayo bahulam*, the shortening prescribed by *ṭhke'ṇaḥ* does not apply, nor does the vowel *i* replace the *k*. The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Femininity is understood from common usage. As it is said: "When the moon is deficient in its digits she is called *Anumatī*; when full, she is *Rākā*."
Thus says Amara. Here, the intention is that because the vowel preceding the letter *ka* is long (*dīrgha*), the substitution of *it* does not occur.
(1) There is an extension of the rule to the words *māmaka* and *naraka*.
Regarding *māmaka*: the meaning is that for the words *māmaka* and *naraka*, the substitution of *it* for the vowel preceding *ka* must be stated.

Regarding the word *māmikā*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "this is mine" (*mama iyam*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca*; then, by the rule *tavakamamakāvekavacane*, the substitution *mamaka-* occurs; *vṛddhi* is applied to the first vowel, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added.
The suffix *ṅīp* is not applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...* etc., because of the prohibition in the rule *kevalamāmake...* etc.

Because the suffix *ṅīp* is restricted to the words *māmaka* only when they function as a noun (*saṃjñā*) or a verb (*chandas*), this rule is stated here since the condition "standing before a suffix" (*pratyayastha*) does not apply to the letter *k* in this context. Regarding the form *narān*: after the vowel substitution (*ātva*) of the root *nṛ* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe*, the suffix *ka* is added by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*.

Thus, with the suffix *ka*, there is the elision of *ā* by the rule "the elision of *ā* occurs before an *it*-augment" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*). This forms a compound with an upapada, followed by the elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*) and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Here too, because the letter *k* is not situated within a suffix (*pratyayastha*), the application of the rule "before a suffix containing *t*" (*pratyayasthāt*) would not otherwise obtain; therefore, this specific statement is made. [The rule] "and in the case of *tyak* and *tyap*" applies to that which ends in *tyak*.
The meaning is that when *tyap* follows, the vowel *a* preceding the *ka* situated in the suffix (*pratyaya*) should be changed to *i*.
This is an exception to the optional rule "udīcām ātaḥ sthāne" (Pāṇini 7.3.46). Regarding the form *dākṣiṇātyikā*:
in the analysis *dakṣiṇasyāṃ diśi adūre* ("not far from the southern direction"), the suffix *āc* is applied by the rule "dakṣiṇād āc".

Its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) follows from the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ*. From the word *dakṣiṇā*, the suffix *tyak* is applied in the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhava-ādi-artha*) by the rule *dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak*; the vowel substitution (*vṛddhi*) occurs by the rule *kiti ca*, resulting in *dākṣiṇātya*.
From the word *dākṣiṇātya*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Then, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*); by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, the final *ā* of *ṭāp* is elided.

The intention is that [the word] is short, and then there is the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, followed by *itvam*. As for the view that in the analysis "that which exists in the southern direction" (*dakṣiṇasyāṃ diśi bhavaḥ*), the suffix *tyakan* is applied directly to the word *dakṣiṇā* ending in *ṭāp*, this has been refuted in the *Prakriyākaumudī*. Regarding the form *ihatyikā*: the suffix *tyap* is applied according to the rule "after an indeclinable, *tyap*" (*avyayāttyap*).
[The suffix] *ṭāp*, then the *ka* suffix in its own sense (*svārthika*), the shortening [of the vowel] by the rule "ṭhke'ṇaḥ," and again *ṭāp*.
(457) *na yāsayoḥ* | 7|3|45|. [Regarding] *na yāsayoḥ*: here, there is no mention of the two words *yā* and *as* ending in the nominative case with the suffix *ṭāp* already applied. Because...

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that "dor" alone is intended [to be the condition]. From the rule *pratyayasthāt* [Pāṇini 7.3.44], the words *ataḥ* and *it* are understood as governing the present rule. Thus he says: *yata-doḥ*. [The examples are] *yakā* and *sakā*.

By the rule *avyaya-sarvanāmnaḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.71], the suffix *aK* is added before the *ṭi* of the words *yad* and *tad*; then, by the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ* [Pāṇini 7.2.102], the substitution of *a* occurs for the final vowel and following consonant of those words.

The external form is *ṭāp*; by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is elision of the case-ending *su*. In the word *tat*, the *t* is replaced by *s* according to *tadoḥ saḥ sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.106). In both instances, the substitution of *i* (ītvam) which would have been applicable by the rule *pratyayasthāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.44) is prohibited here by this [present] sūtra. Now, if *na yāsayoḥ* were an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a nominative singular form, what [would follow]?
To address this objection, he says: "The [suffixes] *yak* and *tak*.
There is also a prohibition of *tyakan*.
This means that there is also a prohibition of [words] ending in the suffix *tyakan*.
The meaning is that a prohibition of the substitution of *ī* for the vowel of the suffix *iti* must be stated when the suffix *ṭha* is present. [Examples: *upatyakā*, *adhityakā*. [Derivation:

By the rule "the suffix *tyakan* is added to *upa* and *adhi* in the sense of 'near' and 'ascended'," the suffix *tyakan* is applied; then *ṭāp* is added, and the elision of the case-ending *s* occurs by the rule "elision after *hal* and *ṅi*" (*halṅyādi-lopaḥ*). [The definition: "The ground near the foot of a mountain is *upatyakā*; the ground above it is *adhityakā*."
Thus says Amara. Now, one might object: "In the rule for the suffix *tyakan*, the vowel *i* does not occur simply by the power of the pronunciation of the letter *a*;
otherwise, the rule would have prescribed *tyikan* alone. Therefore, what is the purpose of this prohibition?
Do not say so—it is because [the *a*] is intended for the sake of hearing the vowel *a* in forms such as *pañcopatyako grāmaḥ*. Enough of this.

(1) *Āśiṣi vunaśca na* ("And not [the substitution of *ī*] after *vun* in the sense of benediction"). Regarding "in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi*): the meaning is that it must be stated that the substitution of *ī*—prescribed by the rule *ṭhpratyayasthāt*—does not apply to the vowel *a* which results from the *akādeśa* (substitution of *a*) for the *vun* suffix used in the sense of benediction. Examples: *jīvakā*, *bhavakā*.

The meaning is "may he live" (*jīvatāt*) and "may he become" (*bhavatāt*). From the roots *jīv* and *bhū*, the suffix *vuN* is applied by the rule *āśiṣi ca*; by the rule *yuvoranākau*, this [suffix] is replaced by *ak*;
and by the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, there is *guṇa* for the vowel *u* of the root *bhū*, followed by the replacement with *av*.
Regarding the term *uttarapada*: the meaning is that it must be stated that even when there is elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), the substitution of long *ī* does not occur.
As for *devakā*: this is formed by adding the feminine suffix *ṭāp* to the word *devadatta*. However, *devadatikā* is cited specifically to demonstrate the non-elision of the word *datta*.
"And [the rule] regarding *kṣipakā* and so forth.

Regarding "and regarding *kṣipakā* and so forth," the meaning is that it must be stated that the shortening (*itvam*) does not apply to words such as *kṣipakā*. He recites the *kṣipakā*-class: *kṣipakā*. [The root is] *kṣipa* in the sense of "propelling."

[The suffix] *ka* [is applied] after roots ending in *i* or *u*, or having *jñā*, *prī*, or *kṛ* as their penultimate (*upadha*). Because it is marked with *k* (kit), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. From the word *kṣipa*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of self-same (*svārthe*), and by the rule "ṭhke’ṇaḥ," the vowel is shortened; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Regarding *dhruvakā*: the root *dhru* meaning "stability" belongs to the *kuṭādi* group; its form is like that of *kṣipakā*. Alternatively, from the root *dhra* meaning "stability," the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* group.

In *dhruvā*, by the rule *ṭhGāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*, there is no *guṇa* due to the presence of the marker *ṅ*, and *uvaṅ* is applied. From the word *dhruva*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. Then, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*); by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened; then *ṭāp* is added again, resulting in *dhruvakā*. Regarding *kanyakā*: from the word *kanyā*, the suffix *ka* is added; by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened; then *ṭāp* is added again, resulting in *kanyakā*. Regarding *caṭakā*: [from *caṭa*... (Note: The provided fragment ends with "ṭhcaṭa", indicating the beginning of the derivation for *caṭakā*.)

By means of the suffix *pacādyac*, followed by *ṭāp*. Then the suffix *ka* is added for the sake of the base meaning itself (*svārthe*), which causes the shortening of the vowel according to the rule "ṭhke'ṇaḥ," after which *ṭāp* is added again.

The group beginning with *kṣipakā* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); therefore, words such as *alakā* and *iṣṭakā* are included. Regarding the phrase "tārakā [is used] for a luminary": this is a *vārttika*. When a luminary is to be expressed, the form *tārakā* occurs.

It does not exist in this manner; that is the extent of the meaning. [The word *tartī*] is derived from the root *tṛ* (meaning "to float" or "to cross over") with the suffix *ṇvul*, the substitution of *a* for the vowel, the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the *ṛ*-vowel, the replacement of *ṛ* by *ra* (*raparatva*), and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. By the term *jyotis*, both the constellation (*nakṣatra*) and the pupil of the eye (*akṣṇaḥ kanīnikā*) are intended. As it is said: "A constellation is called *ṛkṣa*, *bha*, *tārā*, or *tārakā*."
Thus [it is said]; and Amara states: "The pupil of the eye is called *tārakā*. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere":
the meaning is that when something other than light (*jyotis*) is to be expressed, the form is simply *tārikā*.
(1) *Varṇakā* refers to [a dye] on woven cloth (*tāntava*).

"Varṇaka means *tāntava*. This is also a Vārttika. When *tāntava* (woven cloth) is implied, the word *varṇaka* occurs; the meaning is that [the suffix] *it* does not apply. That which is a modification (*vikāra*) of threads (*tantu*) is *tāntava*, according to the rule *ṭhañ* [Pāṇini 4.3.138]. *Varṇaka* refers to a specific type of cloak (*prāvaraṇaviśeṣa*). [The root] *varṇ* is used in the senses of coloring, action, expansion, and qualities.

It belongs to the *cur*-class. From the causative form (*ṇyanta*), the suffix *ṇvul* is added; there is the substitution of *a* for the penultimate vowel, the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere":
the meaning is that the substitution of *i* (the *itva*) occurs as in *varṇikā*, which is other than *tāntavī*. *Varṇikā* means a female singer (*stotrī*).
Alternatively, *varṇikā* is the name of a specific type of literary work (*granthaviśeṣa*).
"Regarding *vartakā* as a bird in the East":
"Regarding *vartakā* as a bird in the East"—this is also a *vārttika*. A bird is a winged creature;
when that is to be understood, according to the opinion of the Easterners (*prācām*), the form *vartakā* occurs, meaning that the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) does not take place.

He states the purpose of including the term "prācām" (of the Easterners): "But according to the view of the Udīcas," etc. The meaning is that, in the opinion of the Udīcas, when a bird (*śakuna*) is to be understood, the form *vārtikā* occurs with the substitution of *it* [for the final vowel]. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *vṛt*, the suffix *ṇvul*, the substitution of *ak* for the penultimate, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the suffix *ka* in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. [The forms] *koyaṣṭika* and *ṭiṭṭibhaka* [are also derived similarly].
"Vartaka, vartikā, and so forth," according to Amara. However, in cases other than a bird, the vowel *i* is always substituted [for the final syllable].
"The Aṣṭakā [is] dedicated to the Pitṛs as its deity.
"The Aṣṭakā is dedicated to the Pitṛs as its deity"—this too is a Vārttika. And those Pitṛs...

The deities and the ancestral deities; for their sake, it is "pitṛdevatyam. [This is formed] by adding the suffix *yat* after a word ending in *devatā* in the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthye*). When an action intended for the ancestors is to be expressed, the form *aṣṭakā* arises. This is derived from the root *aś* (meaning "to eat") with the suffix *takan* according to the rule *iṣyaśibhyāṃ takan*.

The suffix *tak* is added; by the rule *vraścādi*, the *ś* is changed to *ṣ*; by the rule *ṣṭuan*, the *t* is changed to *ṭ*; and from the word *aṣṭaka*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied. Regarding the form *aṣṭikānyā*: that which has eight chapters as its measure is *aṣṭikā*, namely Pāṇini’s *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, according to the rule *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*.

The word "aṣṭau" is formed by adding the suffix *kan* to the nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because it will be established as a tenet that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are produced from words ending in case-suffixes. Consequently, since it ends in a secondary suffix, it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*);

thus, by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ," there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *jas*. Due to the removal of the cause [for the plural form], the word "aṣṭan" [undergoes its specific phonetic changes].
When the *āt* [of *aṣṭan*] has been elided, the *na*-elision occurs because of the status of being a *pada* by relying on the case-ending (*vibhakti*) contained within;

thus, after the word *aṣṭa*, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, the substitution of *ī* for *a* (by Pāṇini 7.3.44, *ṭhpratyayasthāt...*) certainly takes place. Nor should one suspect that the *ṭāp* suffix is not subsequent to the internal *sup* [case-ending], because of the intervention of the letter *k*. This is because of the rule *asupaḥ* [which excludes forms where the suffix follows immediately after a *sup*].

In the case of the word *bahuparivrājakā nagarī*, [the rule] is already satisfied by the application of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* after the *sup* (case-ending) that follows immediately; for this very reason, the prohibition "not for *kṣipakā* and others" is meaningful.
Otherwise, if the suffix *ka* were added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) to the word *kṣipā* ending in a *sup*, and the *sup* were elided...

Since the prohibition is established by the fact that the suffix *ṭāp*—relying on the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhakti*)—is subsequent to the *sup* endings, the [separate rule] stating "it is not [added] after a word ending in a *sup*" is redundant; what need is there for it? (However,) it should be stated that [the suffix *ṭāp* is added] after the words *sūtakā*, *putrikā*, and *vṛndarakā*.

He recites the Vārttika, "ṭhvā sūtakā-putrikā-bṛndārakāṇām," according to its meaning— namely, "sūtakā. Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states that the word *putrikā* here has the vowel *i* in the middle (i.e., it is *putrikā*), and not the vowel *a* in the middle (*putrakā*), because the word *putra*, when denoting a female, ends in the suffix *ṅīp* due to its inclusion in the *śārṅgarava* group.

Here, he prevents the confusion of [mis]interpretation: "or *vā* here" (*iha vā a iti*). The intention is that when the long vowel with its *varga*-mark (*savarmadīrgha*) is present, the designation is *vā*. In this context, *a* is a word whose nominative case ending has been elided (*luptaprathamāka*);
"after *k*" (*kātpūrvasya*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*), while "from *at*" (*ataḥ*) is discontinued (*nivṛtam*), as in the word *putrikā*.

Because of that absence. He says this: "of what precedes the *ka*. Now, one might ask: why is not simply an option for *itva* (the substitution of *i*) prescribed here? To this he replies: "by that," meaning by the prescription of *atva* (the substitution of *a*). Furthermore, from the word *putra*, because it belongs to the *āṅgirasādi* group, there is the suffix *ṅīn*; then, with the addition of the self-referential (*svārthika*) suffix *kapratyaya*, [the form becomes *putrikā*] according to the rule "ṭhke'ṇaḥ."

In the case of the suffix *hrasva* (short vowel), when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, there is the word *putrikā*. Here, regarding the rule for the optional substitution of the vowel *i*, [the forms] *putrikā* and *putrīkā* would result in a form with *in* in the middle (*putrin-kā*) and a form with *īn* in the middle (*putrīn-kā*), respectively. However, according to the rule for the substitution of the vowel *a* (*atva*), the forms *putrakā* and *putrikā* result, having *a* in the middle (*putra-a-kā*) and *i* in the middle (*putri-i-kā*). This is the intended meaning. Now, one might object:

Regarding the question of why the rule for changing the vowel *a* preceding the letter *k* is prescribed in the words *sūtakā* and *vṛndārakā*, he says: "In other cases. This means that since the substitution of *i* (by the rule *pratyayasthāt*) would have applied invariably to the words *sūtakā* and *vṛndārakā*, this rule is intended to provide an option for that.

The root *ṣūñ* is used in the sense of "the releasing of the embryo of a living being. Because its meaning is already included within the general sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is intransitive (*akarmaka*).

By the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... and so forth, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Then, the suffix *ka* is added as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) addition; by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ," the vowel is shortened, and again *ṭāp* is applied. In this case, regarding the alternative view where the long *ā* of the suffix does not undergo the change to *at*:

The substitution of *ī* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule "ṭh-pratyayasthādi-tītvam. In the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), as in "one who has a *vṛnda*," the suffix *ārakan* is applied according to the rule "śṛṅgavṛndābhyām ārakan. Furthermore, the word *vṛndāraka* denotes a deity, as stated by Amara in the passage beginning with "amarā nirjarā devāḥ" [the immortals, the ageless ones, the gods].
It has been enumerated among the masculine genders. The word *rūpin* denotes both form and excellence, and it is used in all three genders;
as Amarasimha states, beginning with "In the other three [genders]... and continuing, "The words *bṛndāraka* and *rūpa* denote 'excellent' (*mukhya*). In the feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
Here too, in the alternative view where the vowel *a* does not become *āt*, the substitution of *it* occurs.

(458) *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne yakaḥ pūrvāyāḥ* | Pāṇini 7.3.46. The phrase *udīcām ātaḥ* [is used]. The rule *pratyayasthāt* is understood to follow here. The analysis of the compound is: *yaś ca kaś ca yakau*, "those two which are *ya* and *ka*"; that which has these as its preceding elements is [the referent]. In the term *yak*, there is a reference to the phonemes (*varṇa*).
The letters *a* and *ā* serve the purpose of pronunciation. The phrase "preceded by *ya*, *ka*, or *p*" is a qualifier for the term "ending in *āt*.

Therefore, having superimposed the femininity residing in the meaning onto the vowel *ā*, the feminine designation "preceded by *ya*, *ka*, or *p*" is employed. By this means, the status of the vowel *ā* as a signifier of the feminine is obtained.

He says this with the words "of that which is preceded by *ya*" and so forth. It is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "na veti vibhāṣā" that the mention of "the Northerners" (*udīcām*) is solely for the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpa*), and not for the purpose of establishing a regional restriction. Furthermore, since the rule "the genitive [case] denotes the relation of substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) would already suffice, the explicit inclusion of the word "in place" (*sthāne*) here is not required.
It should not be said that [the mention of *sthāna*] is useless, because technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) do not apply to a restatement (*anuvāda*).

And in this regard, this very mention of *sthāna* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this very reason, in the rule "That whose first vowel among its vowels is a *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*," although it is a restatement in the form "that whose beginning is a *vṛddhi*," [the mention of *sthāna* is understood].

The paribhāṣā does not apply here. If it were to apply, however, the designation *vṛddha* would not be assigned to the word *śālā*, because the vowel *ā* following the letter *ś* is not the substitute for an *ik* vowel.
Consequently, in the form *śālīya*, the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* would not occur; [the suffix *cha*] would occur only in forms such as *aupagavīya*.
Let it be so; enough of this. Regarding the rule "ke'ṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.13], which prescribes a short vowel:

when the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*) to the word *āryā*, the vowel *a* of the syllable *ya* becomes short by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ. Then, with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form *āryakā* arises.
In that case, because the vowel *a* following the *ya* is in the place of the long *ā*, there is an option regarding its becoming short (*itva-vikalpa*).
This is an exception to the obligatory substitution of *i* (itva) prescribed by the rule "ṭh-pratyayasthāt" [Pāṇini 7.3.44].
Thus he says: *āryakā*, *āryikā*. This is an example for that which is preceded by the letter *y*.

Now he gives an example for that which is preceded by the letter *k*: *caṭakakā*, *caṭakikā*. [The forms are derived] from the word *caṭakā* with the addition of the suffix expressing its own meaning (*svārthe*).
The meaning is as follows: [from *ka*], by the rule "ṭhke'ṇaḥ," there is a short vowel; then again, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, and there is an option regarding the substitution of *it*.
Regarding the form *sāṅkāśyikā*: a city established by Saṅkāśa is *Sāṅkāśya*.

By the rule "ṭhvṛñcchaṇakaṭhañ... and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* is applied after words ending in *saṅkāśin*, resulting in initial vṛddhi; then, by the rule "yasyeti ca," [the final vowel and consonant are elided].

There is the elision of the letter *a* by the rule "yasyeti ca. From the word *sāṅkāśya*, in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule "dhanvayopadhād vuñ. There is the substitution of *a* (for the final syllable), the elision of the letter *a* by the rule "yasyeti ca," the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and the obligatory substitution of *i* for the vowel preceding the suffix by the rule "pratyayasthāt. Here, [the elision applies] to the letter *a* following the *y*.
The meaning is that because [the vowel *i*] does not occupy the position of the original form (*ākāra-sthānika*), the optional substitution of *it* does not occur. Now, one might object:

let it simply be that for a word denoting a feminine, there should be the optional substitution of *it* after *at*, and let the condition "after *āt*" (*ātaḥ*) not be required; for in the word *sāṅkāśyaka*, the vowel *a* following the letter *y* is part of the substitute *vuñ*.
If it is argued that [the suffix *kā*] does not indicate femininity, they say that the word *āt* is for the sake of clarity.
Regarding *aśvakā*: from the word *aśva*, the suffix *ka* is added; by the rule *ṭhke'ṇaḥ*, there is shortening of the vowel; then again, the suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in the form *aśvakā*.
Here, although the vowel *ā* is in the place of the vowel *a*, [the rule still applies].

The meaning is that there is no option regarding the absence of *it*-ness because it is preceded by *ya*; rather, by the rule "when a suffix follows" (*pratyayasthāt*), *it*-ness is obligatory. As for the question "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'a feminine suffix' (*strīpratyaya*)?", the question asks: what is the point of mentioning "of a feminine suffix," since that is already established by the mention of the feminine gender in the phrase "preceded by *ya*" (*yakapūrvāyāḥ*)?

Regarding the word *śubhaṃyikā*: *śubham* is an indeclinable ending in *m*. With this as an upapada (governing word), from the root *yā* in the sense of "reaching" (*prāpaṇe*), the suffix *vic* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*.

From the word *śubhaṃyā*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). By the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened, and with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form *śubhaṃyakā* is obtained.

The point here is that because the letter *a* following the *y* is not part of a verbal root (*dhātu*) and does not denote a feminine, the optional substitution of *i* does not apply; rather, by the rule "after [a suffix] ending in *ṭh*, [the preceding *a*] is always replaced by *ī*," the substitution of *ī* is mandatory. However, for the *y* at the end of a verbal root, the substitution is always mandatory.

He summarizes the meaning of the *vārttika*—"the prohibition [of *it*] applies to the final letter of a verbal root (*dhātu*) when preceded by *ṭhi* or *ka*"—as follows: "But for the *ya* at the end of a verbal root, it is always [so]. The analysis of the compound is *yaś ca kaś ca*.
This means that the vowel *a* following the *y* or *k* at the end of a verbal root is always subject to the change to *i*, and not otherwise.
The meaning is "but [it is] conceptual construction" (vikalpa). Regarding the word *sunayikā*: from the root *ṇīñ*, there is the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*.

By the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*, there is *guṇa*, and with the substitution of *ay* [for *e*], the word *naya* is formed. That which has a beautiful (*su*) method (*naya*) is *sunayā*. From that, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), according to the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*.

The word is *hrasvaḥ*. Again, with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, it becomes *sunayikā*. Here, because the letter *y* is at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*), there is no optionality regarding the substitution of *ī* for the subsequent vowel *a*; rather, by the rule "a vowel following a suffix ending in *ṭ* [is always replaced by *ī*]," the substitution of *ī* is compulsory.
This is the intended meaning.

(459) *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvā nañpūrvāṇām api* 7.3.47. Regarding *bhastraiṣā*: since the condition of being preceded by *ya* or *ka* is absent, this rule is stated because [the previous rule] *udīcām* would otherwise not apply. The word *svā* is the final member [of the compound]. *Bhastrā*, *eṣā*, *ajā*, *jñā*, *dvā*, and *svā*—this is a *dvandva* compound of these six words.

Then, there is the elision (*luk*) of the sixth case-ending by Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). The intention is that [the rule] *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvānām* is intended to be applied. Regarding the word *eṣām*: it means "of these," namely, of *bhastrā* and the others. Regarding *ata id vā*: [this is obtained] from the mention of *udīcām* from the preceding sūtra and the mention of *it* from the sūtra *pratyayasthāt*.

The intention is that [the rule] follows [from the previous]. Now, since it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), by the rule of "that which ends in... (*tadantavidhi*), it is understood as referring to words ending in *bhastrā* and so on; yet, by virtue of being treated like a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), it is also understood to apply to the simple forms themselves. And thus, for those preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*), those preceded by something other than that, and the simple forms—[all are included].
Since it would be redundant [to state] "even those preceded by *nañ* when [the suffix] is established," he says: "by the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* alone.

Now, if by the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* there is the application of [the suffix] to words such as *bhastrā* both when preceded by *nañ* and when not preceded by *nañ*, then the mention of "preceded by *nañ*" is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), meaning that it applies only to those preceded by *nañ*. Thus...

If it is argued that the word "also" (*api*) should be explained as being intended to exclude the application [of the suffix] to words such as *bhastrā* alone when they are present, we say no; for if that were the case, forms such as *nirbhastrika* would not be established.
Therefore, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that the phrase "of those preceded by the negative particle" (*nañpūrvāṇām*) is indeed for the sake of clarity. Now, [an objection]:

Since the word *bhastrā* is invariably feminine (*nityastrīliṅga*), the optional substitution of *it* (the long vowel *ī*) would already be established by the subsequent rule, "ṭhabhāṣitapuṃskācca" [Pāṇini 7.3.48]; therefore, the inclusion of *bhastrā* here is redundant. To this, he says: "The mention of *bhastrā* is for the sake of [words used as] secondary members (*upasarjana*)."

The meaning is that in the case of *nirbhastrikā*, because it is an *upasarjana* (secondary member), it possesses all three genders; consequently, since it is a word whose masculine form has been mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), the rule "after a word that does not have a corresponding masculine form" (*abhāṣitapuṃskāt*) does not apply there. As for the phrase "but of another," it refers to the word *bhastrā* when it is not an *upasarjana*, as in the examples *bhastrikā* and *paramabhastrakā*.

Since the optional substitution of *i* (mitvam) is already established by the subsequent rule, "ṭhabhāṣitapuṃskācca" [Pāṇini 7.3.48], because of its being eternally feminine, the inclusion of the word *bhastrā* in the rule "ṭhbhastraiṣā" [Pāṇini 7.3.47] is not intended for that purpose;
this is the meaning. But then, would it not also apply in cases such as *aneṣakā*, *paramaiṣakā*, *advake*, and *paramadvake*?

This optional shortening (*itvam*) might occur; therefore, he says: "this *dvā*. The meaning is that this optional shortening does not apply to these two when they are preceded by a preceding word. Why? To this he says: "the internal [vowel]," etc. The rule "even here, except for a case ending" (*ṭidāpy-asupaḥ*) continues to apply. However, in this instance, it is the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

The intended meaning is that [the suffix] follows a *sup* (case-ending). Now, one might object: "In this case, the *ṭāp* does not follow a *sup*, because—after the *ṭi*-portion of the word *etad* has been replaced by *akac* according to the rule 'avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ', and after the *s* has been substituted for the *t* of *etakat* by the rule 'tadoḥ saḥ sau'—[the *ṭāp* would not follow a *sup*]."

By the rule *ṭhādeśapratyayayoḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs; then, by the substitution of *at* for *tyad*-class stems, the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) is applied; because it ends in *ā* when feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is added; after the long vowel by class-similarity (*savarṇadīrgha*), the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes takes place, resulting in the form *eṣakā*. Then, in the analysis *na eṣakā*, when a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) is formed, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) occurs.

In the case of *nañ*, when the *n* of *nañ* is elided, the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule *tasmānnuḍaci*, resulting in the form *aneṣaka*. Similarly, in the compound *paramā eṣakā*, the form *paramaiṣakā* arises. Here, since the suffix *su* follows, one might ask: how can the feminine suffix *ṭāp* apply, given that it depends upon the final vowel being long *ā*, which is established here by the substitution of *at* for the stem beginning with *atad* (i.e., *eṣaka*)?
The suffix *su* would be subsequent. And it is not the case that, when the *su* of a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* has undergone elision (*luk*) in the compound,

and when the *satv*, the substitution of *tyadādi-ātva*, and the *ṭāp* have ceased, and then *su* is applied again after the compound, and once *satv*, *tyadādi-ātva*, and *ṭāp* have been performed, and the elision by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* has occurred— prior to the compound in the form *aneṣaka*.

It should be stated that the suffix *ṭāp* occurs only after a *sup* that has already undergone application (*pravṛtta*), because, in comparison with the elision (*luk*) of the compound-forming suffix,

the elision by *hal-ṅy-ādi-sūtra* is indeed more internal (*antaraṅga*) and thus applies first; consequently, even when the nominative case-ending (*su*) has been elided, the existence of the suffix is maintained by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the *nimitta* (the cause for application) has ceased, there is no cessation of the previously applied *satv*, *tyadādyatva*, and *ṭāp*.

If it is argued that this *ṭāp* is not followed by a *sup* [suffix], we reply here: by the paribhāṣā "an external (*bahiraṅga*) elision (*luk*) subverts even internal (*antaraṅga*) rules," [the *luk* of] the *sup*...

Regarding the rule "dhātuprātipadikayoḥ," even though the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (as prescribed by *halṅyābbhyaḥ*) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it does not take effect when there is the occasion for the elision of case-endings (*subluk*). Therefore, in examples such as *rājakumārī*, the compound formation (*samāsa*) proceeds while the case-ending (*sup*) is still actually present. And thus, [in the analysis] *gomān priyo yasya sa*...

Regarding the form *gomatpriya*, it is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhpratyayotarapadayośca* that because the suffix *su* has been elided after the word *gomat*, the rules for the augment *num* and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (as prescribed by *ugidacām*) do not apply. This point was further refined in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* on the sūtra *kṛttaddhite*.

Thus, when *nañ*, *su*, *eta*, and *tarap* stand [in sequence], once the *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compound has been formed, the substitution of *t* for the initial of *tyad*-type words occurs— by the maxim "even internal elements are superseded"— prior to the elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sāmāsika-luk*). Then, from the compound word *anetaka*, the nominative singular suffix (*su*) is applied again, and the change to *s* (*satva*) takes place.

When the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* occurs, followed by the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*), the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the long vowel by class (*savarṇadīrgha*), and the elision of the case-ending *su* by the rule *halṅyādi-lopa*,

the form *aneṣakā* results. Let it suffice to note here that, prior to the application of the *savarṇadīrgha* rule, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs after the *sup* ending that had already arisen before the compound was formed.

Regarding the form *advake*: when *na* and *dvakī* are present as *na + dvakī + auṭ*, by the maxim "even internal [rules] are superseded" (*antaraṅgān api*), the substitution of *tyadādi-ātva* (the replacement of the initial of the pronoun by *a*) occurs even before the compound is formed.

Once the *auṭ* of *dvakī* has been elided (*luk*) within the *nañ-tatpuruṣa* compound, the suffix *auṅ* is applied again after the compound *advaki*. Then, *tyadādi-ātva* applies, followed by the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

When *ṭāp* is applied, and *auṅ* is replaced by *śī*, and *ādguna* (the guṇa substitution of *ā* for *a* + *ā*) occurs, the form becomes *advake*. Here too, the intention is that *ṭāp* follows only after the *sup* case-ending *auṅ* that was produced prior to the compound. The same applies in the case of *paramadvake*.

It might be argued as follows: the word *sva* denotes one's self (*ātman*), one's own (*ātmīya*), a kinsman (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). Among these, when it refers to a kinsman or to the self, it is exclusively masculine; when it refers to "one's own," it takes the gender of the noun it qualifies; and when it refers to wealth, it is both masculine and neuter—as in the rule:
"The word *sva* [denotes] a kinsman and the self; *svam* [is used] in three genders for 'one's own'."

This is because of the lexicon [Amara-kośa] which states, "One's own (*sva*) is not feminine when it means wealth. However, when the word *sva* is a proper name for a specific female individual, it is then feminine.
In that case, since it is stated that "one's own (*sva*) is not called a kinsman or wealth," its status as a pronoun (*sarvanāmatva*) applies only when it does not denote a kinsman or wealth.

It does not exist. The status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) belongs only to those words expressing "self" (*ātman*) and "one's own" (*ātmīya*), and that [status] occurs only when they are not *upasarjana* (subordinate members of a compound), because of the established rule: "But those that have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or subordinate members (*upasarjana*) are not included among the 'all' (*sarva-*) group. In that context, when "one's own" (*ātmīyā*) is to be expressed, because it is a pronoun, the suffix *akac* is added; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; and then, by the rule "pratyayasthāt... [the *it* augment is added].

If [the *it* designation] were permanent, it would be desired that [the vowel] be *svika*. However, that is not tenable, because the optional application of *it* by the rule "bhastraiṣā-" and so forth is unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that this optional *it* does not apply here because the *akac* suffix *ka* is not in the place of an *āt* vowel; for [the rule] "eṣām ata id vā" [applies].
In the explanatory statement (*vivaraṇa*) "it would be so," because the phrase "in place of *āt*" is not understood to carry over [from the previous rule], he says:

"The mention of the word *sva* is for the sake of [distinguishing] technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*). Since the word *sva*, when functioning as a technical term, lacks the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there is no application of the suffix *akac*; consequently, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied and the nominative singular case ending (*su*) is added, [the form becomes *svā*].

When the suffix *ka* is added as an *svārthika*, then— according to the rule "an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules"— the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes is subverted; subsequently, by the elision of the nominative suffix *su* because it is a part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*.

Furthermore, from the word ending in the suffix *ka*, there is the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, resulting in the word *svakā*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "nirgatā svasyāḥ" (gone out from her own), the compound is formed by the rule "nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā" (words beginning with *nir* are compounded with a word in the ablative case when meaning 'gone out', etc.), followed by the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*). Then, by the rule "gostriyoḥ" (the final vowel of a word ending in *go* or a feminine stem is shortened), the vowel is shortened; then the suffix *ṭāp* is added, followed by the case-ending (*sup*), and then the self-referential (*svārthika*) suffix *ka*. Finally, by the rule "ke'ṇaḥ" (when *ka* follows, the final vowel of a stem ending in *aṇ* is shortened), the vowel is shortened.
Furthermore, there is also *niḥsvaka*. These two alone are the examples for the word *sva* under the rule *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvānām anaḥ*.

However, when the word *sva* means "one's own," it is neither a technical term (*saṃjñā*) nor a subordinate member (*upasarjana*); therefore, it is not an example [under that rule]. To the question "Why?", he says: "In this case..."

Regarding the word *hi*: in this rule, *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvānām* (Pāṇini 7.3.47), the phrase *ātsthāne* is carried over from the preceding rule *udīcām* (Pāṇini 7.3.46). That [phrase] qualifies the *at* of the word *sva* itself. Thus, it is understood that "for the *at* in place of the *ā* of the word *sva*, there may optionally be *it*. It is precisely with the intention of expressing this specific distinction [that the author says *hi*].

The meaning is that in the explanatory sentence *teṣām ata id vā syāt*, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ātaḥ sthāne* has not been explicitly shown. However, regarding *dvaiṣayoḥ*: the meaning is that in the case of *dvau* and *eṣāḥ*, the phrase *ātaḥ sthāne* is not connected [to the rule]. Why?

Therefore, he says: "because of impossibility. Since this [word] *dvi* belongs to the group beginning with *sarva*, it must necessarily be a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) due to the designation of its status as a pronoun based on its being the first member of that group; consequently, the suffix *akac* is applied. Regarding its initial vowel *a*:
The meaning is that there is no possibility of [the substitution] being in the place of the *āt* itself. Nor does it apply to others;
the meaning is that even for the words *bhastrā*, *ajā*, and *jñā*, the qualification "in the place of *āt*" does not apply. Why? To this he says:
"because of non-deviation. This refers to the words *bhastrā*, *ajā*, and *jñā*.

The meaning is as follows: because they lack the status of being pronominals (*sarvanāman*), they are not eligible for the *akac* suffix; and because they end in the *kap* suffix, the short vowel [of the preceding stem] is established by the rule "ṭhke’ṇaḥ. Consequently, since the rule "ata āt" (Pāṇini 7.1.1) restricts that short vowel to be the substitute for an *āt*, the qualification [of the word *sva*] would be redundant.
One might object: "Let the term 'of the *āt*' (*ātaḥ*), which is understood from the previous context, serve as a qualifier for the word *sva* itself; by that much [the purpose is achieved]."
To the question, "What follows from the doubt regarding the optional substitution of *it* in the case of *svikā*, which is derived from *ātmīyā*?

he says: "But the word *sva*... The word *sva*, when denoting *ātmīya* (one's own) and not being a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), is eligible for the suffix *akaC* because it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Therefore, since its vowel *a* is not in the position of *āt*, [the substitution of *it* does not apply].

There might be a suspicion of an optional *it* vowel based on the present sūtra; however, the meaning is that by the rule "ṭh-pratyayasthāt," the *it* vowel is indeed obligatory. Now, although the word *sva*—which denotes self (*ātman*), one's own (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*)—cannot serve as an example when it signifies "one's own" (*ātmīya*), it can do so when it signifies self, kinsmen, or wealth.

Since the possibility of [the word] being an example exists, it is untenable to claim that the inclusion of the term *sva* is for the sake of [excluding] technical names (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*). To this he says: "But in other meanings, *sva* is not feminine. In the senses of self, kinsman, and wealth, the word *sva* is not feminine; this is according to the system of the cited lexicons (*kośa*).

The meaning is that the word *sva* denoting "self" or "kinsman" is invariably masculine, whereas the word *sva* denoting "wealth" is both masculine and neuter. Consequently, since the condition "when followed by *ṭāp*" does not apply here, there is no possibility of it being an example [of that rule]. [This follows] from the rule *pratyayasthāt...* [Pāṇini 7.3.44].

The intention is that [the word] *āpi* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. This is also an illustration; one should also observe that when *ātman* is the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the word *sva*—being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—is subject to the addition of the suffix *akac*, and therefore the vowel *a* of that [suffix] cannot occupy the position of *āt*. Now, [one might object]:

How can the word *sva* itself serve as an example when it has become a technical term (*saṃjñā*) or a subordinate member of a compound (*upasarjana*), since even in that case, when *akac* is added, the vowel *a* does not occupy the position of the original stem-final (*sthānika*)?
To this he says: "But [the word] *sva* which has become a technical term or a subordinate member... [referring to] the word *sva* that has become a technical term or a subordinate member.

The meaning is as follows: because it is not a pronominal (asarvanāmatayā), it does not take the suffix *akaC*; therefore, when the suffix *ka* is added to the word *sva*—which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*)—as a *svārthika* suffix, and after the elision of that case-suffix (*sup-luk*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is subsequently applied, the resulting form becomes an example [of the rule] because the short vowel *a* (in *svakīyā*) arises from the substitution of *ā* for *at* by the rule "ṭhke’ṇaḥ. Nor should one suspect that the *ṭāp* here follows after an internal case-suffix (*antarvarti-sup*).

The sense is: "by what intervention? Thus, in the rule *bhastraiṣājājñādvāsvānañaḥ*, because the term *āt* (from the previous rule *ātaḥ sthāne*) which is being carried over (*anuvṛtta*) is understood to connect with the word *sva*, it is obtained that for the *at* in place of *āt* which is a constituent part of the word *sva*, there may optionally be *it*. He states the purpose of this: "And thus," according to the manner described.
Since the option for *itva* (the substitution of *i*) for the *a* in place of *āt* is obtained only by the word *sva*, and because the word *sva*— possessing its own form—
is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), when *akac* is added, the *a* of that [form] is not in place of *āt*; thus, since the option for *itva* does not apply, [the rule] "ṭhpratyayasthāt" [applies].

The meaning is that you are indeed eternal. Having thus stated the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), he states the actual examples (*udāharaṇa*) beginning with *nirbhastraka*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *niṣkrāntā bhastrāyāḥ* ("gone out from a bellows"), there is a compound according to the rule *nirādibhyaḥ krāntādyarthe*; then, by the rule *go-striyoḥ*, the feminine suffix is shortened.

Again, from *nirbhastra*, after adding the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, then the suffix *ka*, and applying the rule "ṭhak-e-’ṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.50) which shortens the vowel, one obtains the form *nirbhastraka*. From this, adding *ṭāp* again and applying the rule for the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), one arrives at the word *nirbhastrakā*. In that case, although the substitution of *it* (the change of *a* to *i*) would have been obligatory by the rule "pratyayasthāt" (Pāṇini 7.3.44), the present sūtra provides an option for this *it*-substitution, resulting in the form *nirbhastrikā*.

The two forms are *nirbhastraka* and *nirbhastrikā*. The sense is: "Why is it that the case-ending (*sup*) does not follow immediately [after the suffix] due to an intervention? Regarding *eṣakā* and *eṣikā*: from the word *etad* with the suffix *akac*, there is the case-ending *su*. Then, by the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*, there is the substitution of *s*; then *ṣatva*; then the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class words; then the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) [of the preceding and following vowels]; then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Finally, by the rule *pratyayasthāt*, [the *k* is changed to *ṅ*].
The intention is that this optional substitution of *i* (itva) would override the obligatory substitution of *i*. Now, one might object:

in forms such as *etike* and *etikāḥ*, derived from the word *etatkaccchabda* in the feminine through the case-endings *au* and *jas* etc., the obligatory substitution of *i* is desired; therefore, by this [rule], there would be an optional substitution of *i* overriding that [obligatory one].

He says: "when *ṣatva* has been applied. The meaning is that although one should have stated "after *bhastrā*, *eta*, and *jñā*," the fact that *eṣā* is cited with *ṣatva* already applied indicates that there is no optional substitution of *it* (the shortening of the vowel) in the case of *au*, *jas*, and so on, because *ṣatva* does not apply there.

[The forms] *ajakā* and *ajikā* are derived from the word *ajā*: the suffix *ka* is added, the vowel is shortened, then again *ṭāp* is added, and finally the long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*).

Thus, there is no conceptual construction (*avikalpa*). [The form] *jñikā* is derived from the verbal root *jñā* by applying the suffix *ka* according to the rule "ṭhigupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ," followed by the elision of the *ā* vowel according to the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca.

Since it ends in *ā* when feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied, resulting in a long vowel through the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). From the word *jñā*, which is now a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix, the suffix *ka* is added; the case-suffix is elided, and the vowel is shortened according to the rule "ke'ṇaḥ."

Again, there is *ṭāp*, *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel lengthening), the optional *itvavikalpa*, *āṬṅśśī*, and *ādguṇaḥ*. Thus we have *niḥsvakā* and *niḥsvikā*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "she who has gone out from her own" (*svasyāḥ niṣkrāntā*). The compound is formed by the rule *nirādayaḥ*.
There is shortening of the *upasarjana*, *ṭap*, *supi kaḥ*, and elision of the case-ending (*subluk*).
The meaning is that after a word ending in the suffix *kap*, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, there is a long vowel by *savarṇa-dīrgha* [sandhi], and the substitution of *it* is optional.

(460) *abhāṣitapuṃskācca* | 7|3|48|. From a word that does not have a corresponding masculine form (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. The phrase "in place of the *āt*" from the rule *udīcām ātaḥ sthāne* is understood here, as is the phrase *ata it*.

The analysis of the compound is: "the word whose masculine form has not been stated. The word *vihitasya* (of that which is prescribed) is to be supplied. He states this with the words "from this" (*etasmāt*). The meaning is "from a word whose masculine form has not been stated. This statement is for the sake of excluding those preceded by *aya*.
