[Examples: *gaṅgakā*, *gaṅgikā*. From the word *gaṅgā*, the suffix *ka* is added; then, by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, [the final vowel is shortened].
The short vowel [is used], with an option for the *it* augment. He states the result of qualifying the prescribed [element]—namely, "bahuvrīhi"—as follows:

in the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "she whose bed (*khaṭvā*) does not exist," once the bahuvrīhi compound has been formed according to the rule "the negative particle *nañ* [expresses] the meaning of words signifying existence, or there is optionally the elision of the final member of the compound," and after the elision of the word expressing existence, [there remains] the negative particle *nañ*.

When the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) occurs, in the alternative where the suffix *kap* is absent according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*, the word *akhaṭvā* undergoes shortening by the rule *gostriyoḥ*. Then, after the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, when the case-ending (*sup*) is added in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*), etc., the *luk* elision of the case-ending occurs.

Subsequently, the shortening occurs by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, and then again the suffix *ṭāp* is added in place of the long *ā* that was prescribed for a word not previously used in the masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*).

Therefore, because [the condition] is absent, there is no optionality regarding the substitution of *i*. Rather, the meaning is that by the rule "ṭhpratyayasthāt," the substitution of *i* is compulsory. However, if one were to explain [the rule] as "of that which follows a word not previously mentioned as masculine" (*abhāṣitapuṃskāt*), then since such a word *khaṭvā* would follow [the suffix], there would be an optionality regarding the substitution of *i* for the *ā* in place of *at*, because [the condition of being followed by a non-masculine-mentioning word] exists. This is the intended sense. [This applies] when the suffix *kap* is added as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*).

Regarding the word *tviti*: in the stage [of derivation] where *na* + *sakhi* + *as* exists, there is elision (*subluk*) of the case-ending by the rule for *kap*. Because both parts [of the compound] are *sub*-anta (ending in a case-suffix) by means of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the technical extension of grammatical operations to forms ending in suffixes), the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by the rule *naño 'styarthānām*. By the force of the etymological definition (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) of the term "compound-final" (*samāsānta*), it applies only to that which ends in *kap*.

[The word *akhaṭvā*] is a compound. Consequently, in the word *akhaṭvāka*, because the portion *akhaṭvā* lacks the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is a compound ending in a feminine suffix used as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the shortening [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *go-striyoḥ* does not occur. Nor does the shortening prescribed by *ke’ṇaḥ* apply, because of the prohibition *na kapi*.

Because of the prohibition. However, there is an optional shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *ṭhāpo 'nyatarasyām*. In that case, since the *ṭāp* preceding the *kap* prescribed after the word *khaṭvā* was prescribed after a stem not previously designated as masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), [the rule applies].
The meaning is that this optional substitution of *i* for the short *a* in its place indeed occurs.
However, in the alternative case where the short vowel is absent according to the rule *āpaḥ anyatarasyām*, one should understand that the form remains simply *akhaṭvākā*. (461) *ādācāryāṇām* 7.3.49.

This is according to the teachers. "In the scope of the previous sūtra" means: [the substitution] of *at* in place of the *at* that follows a stem not previously mentioned as having a masculine form (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). Regarding *śubhrikā*:
the word *śubhra* is *viśeṣyanighna* (adjectival) and is not restricted to a specific gender. From that, after adding the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the suffix *ka* is added to the word *śubhrā*.

By the rule *ṭhke'ṇaḥ*, there is a short vowel, followed again by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Here, because the *ṭāp* preceding the letter *k* is not prescribed after a word that is not inherently masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), the vowel *a* in its place does not undergo optional substitution with *ī*; rather, by the rule *pratyayasthāt*, the substitution with *ī* is obligatory—this is the meaning. He states the upper limit for the governing heading *anupasarjanāt*: "extending up to [the sūtra] *yūnastiḥ*. This means that this governing heading applies even in the case of *yūnastiḥ*, but not prior to it; in this matter, the commentary itself is the sole authority. Whatever needs to be said on this point will be stated under the sūtra *yūnastiḥ*.

One might object: in cases such as *bahukurucarā* (meaning "one who has many Kuru-dwellers") or *atinadā* (meaning "one who has transcended the river"), there is no possibility at all for the application of suffixes like *ṅīp*, which are prescribed by rules such as *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, from the subordinate members (*upasarjana*)—namely, the words *kurucara*, *nada*, and so on—because the prohibition of "extension to that which ends with [a specific element]" (*tadantavidhi-pratiṣedha*) applies to the prescription of compounds and suffixes. Therefore, the governing rule concerning "non-subordinate" (*anupasarjana*) would be redundant; to this, he replies: "This very [rule]... [The full response: This very [rule] is intended to prevent the application of suffixes to the subordinate member when it occurs within a compound ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). For example, in *paramakārīṣagandhyā* (meaning "one whose wife is supremely of the Kārīṣagandha lineage"), the word *kārīṣagandhyā* is a subordinate member within the compound *paramakārīṣagandhyā*. If the rule were not present, the suffix *ṅīṣ* (prescribed by *yañaśca*) would apply to *kārīṣagandhyā* alone, resulting in the undesirable form *paramakārīṣagandhyī*. To prevent this, the rule is stated: "A suffix is applied to a non-subordinate [feminine base]. Since *kārīṣagandhyā* is a subordinate member here, the suffix does not apply to it, and thus the desired form *paramakārīṣagandhyā* is obtained. Therefore, this rule is indeed necessary. Furthermore, it is intended to prevent the application of suffixes to the final element of a compound ending in a feminine suffix when that final element itself is subordinate. For instance, in *atikārīṣagandhyā* (meaning "one who has surpassed the Kārīṣagandhyā woman"), the word *kārīṣagandhyā* is subordinate within the compound *atikārīṣagandhyā*. Without the rule, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply to *kārīṣagandhyā* (the final member), leading to the undesirable form *atikārīṣagandhyī*. By means of the rule "A suffix is applied to a non-subordinate," since *kārīṣagandhyā* is subordinate, the suffix is blocked, and the correct form *atikārīṣagandhyā* is secured. Thus, the rule is both necessary and purposeful. It is not merely for the sake of excluding the application of suffixes to subordinate members within a compound ending in a feminine suffix; rather, it serves to exclude the application of suffixes to the final member of a compound ending in a feminine suffix when that final member is subordinate. Consequently, the rule is not redundant. As for the objection regarding *bahukurucarā* and *atinadā*, those objections are resolved by the fact that the rule is intended to apply to the final member of a compound ending in a feminine suffix, and in those examples, the final members (*kurucara*, *nada*) do not end in a feminine suffix. The meaning is that this very governing rule (*adhikāra*), "not when [the word] is a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanāt*), indicates that in the case of feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), there is an application of the rule regarding the inclusion of what ends with that suffix (*tadantavidhi*). This is clear in the *Bhāṣya*. As for its result, it should be understood that in the rule "*vano ra ca*" (Pāṇini 4.1.7), there is the attainment of the form ending in a word that itself ends in *van*, and so forth.

If it is objected: "Even if there is no application of the rule *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) regarding feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), since the governing rule *anupasarjana* (not being a subordinate member) is necessary to prevent the application of suffixes such as *ṅīp* in forms like *nadā*—meaning 'a woman who behaves like a river' (*nadīva ācarati*)—which are derived from a base formed by the *kvip* suffix used in the sense of 'behaving like' (*ācārakvibanta*) followed by another *kvip* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛkvibanta*), how can that rule [the *anupasarjana* rule] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the existence of *tadantavidhi* in rules prescribing feminine suffixes? The answer is: No. On the authority of the Bhāṣya, which states that the purpose of the *anupasarjana* rule in rules prescribing feminine suffixes is to indicate the existence of *tadantavidhi*, we infer that words formed by the *kvip* suffix in the sense of the agent, derived from a base formed by the *kvip* suffix in the sense of 'behaving like', are not actually employed (*anabhidhāna*) when denoting a female. Thus, this is sufficient.

(462) Pāṇini 4.1.15: *ṭiḍḍhāṇañdvayasajdaghnañmātractayapṭhakṭhañkañkvarapaḥ*. [The suffixes] *ṭit*, *ḍha*, *aṇ*, *añ*, *dvayasac*, *daghnac*, *mātrac*, *tayap*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhañ*, *kañ*, *kvarap* [are called feminine endings].
*ṭit*, *ḍha*, *aṇ*, *añ*, *dvayasac*, *daghnac*, *mātrac*.
*tayap*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhañ*, *kañ*, *kvarap*—this is the singular ablative case of a collective dvandva compound of these twelve [suffixes]. The eleven suffixes beginning with *ḍha* are [meant here].

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), there is the inclusion of that which ends in it. Because of the indicatory letter *ṭi*, the suffix as well as that which is not a suffix [is included].

The term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem), which is the governing rule (*adhikṛtam*), is qualified by *ṭidādibhiḥ* (by those beginning with *ṭit*); because it is a qualifier, the rule of "that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhiḥ*) applies. Consequently, it is understood that [the suffixes] are added from a nominal stem ending in a *ṭit* element, as well as from one ending in a suffix such as *ḍāc* or *āṇ*. From the rule *ṭhājādyataṣṭāp*, the word *ataḥ* (from [a stem] ending in short *a*) is carried over (*anuvṛttam*).
By that [term], the nominal stem (prātipadika) is qualified. This is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that (tadantavidhi).
The phrase "not being a secondary derivative" (anupasarjana) applies only to those items beginning with *ṭi* mentioned in the sūtra, and not to those ending in them.
The term "in the feminine" (striyām) is a governing heading (adhikṛta). Thus he says: "that *ṭi*-ending etc., which is not a secondary derivative," and so forth.
"Ending with that" (*tadantam*): this means ending with a *ṭit* suffix or a suffix beginning with *ḍha*. There are three types of *ṭit* [elements]:
a suffix (*pratyaya*), a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and a verbal root (*dhātu*). Among these, he provides an example of the first—*kurucarī*.

In the sense "she moves among the Kurus," the suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule "*careṣṭaḥ*" when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the subordinate word (*upapada*), signifying the agent (*kartṛ*). The letter *ṭ* [is the *ṭit* marker].

This is a *upapada-samāsa*. It should not be argued that because the suffix (*pratyaya*) itself possesses the *ṭi*-marker here, the paribhāṣā "when a suffix is mentioned, it denotes that which ends with it" applies such that only *car* is *ṭidanta*, and not the word *kurucara* due to the rule of "specification by the initial element" (*tadādiniyama*). [This is refuted] by the case of *nadaṭ*.
Even though *devaḍ* and similar forms are not suffixes (*apratyaya*), they possess the property of being *ṭit*;

since the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of suffixes (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply there, the condition of ending in a *ṭit* element exists for the word *kurucara* by the rule "whereby a rule is prescribed" (*yenavidhiḥ*). Now, he gives an example of a second *ṭit* form: *nadaḍ*.

This is a nominal stem (prātipadika) listed in the *pac-ādi* group. However, the third example, *stanandhayī*, will be cited under the section on primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*). He states the purpose of the qualification "not being accompanied by a prefix" as follows: *bahukurucara*. The analysis of the compound is: "that in which many Kurus dwell."

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant. Consequently, because the suffix *ṭāp* (which is marked with the indicator *ṭi*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*), the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. However, if "non-subordination" (*anupasarjanatva*) were a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then *ṅīp* would be unavoidable here. For this very reason, [the form] *āpiśalā* is derived as "one who studies what was taught by Āpiśali."

In the case of *brāhmaṇī* as well, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. For in that instance, when the meaning is "taught by Āpiśali," the word *āpiśala* is formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tena proktam*. Then, when the meaning is "one who studies the Āpiśala [text]," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tadadhīte tadveda*; subsequently, this suffix is elided according to the rule *proktālluk*. Thus, in the feminine, because the stem ends in a long vowel (*ā*), the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.

The form is *āpiśalī*. If the term *anupasarjanāt* were a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then because that which ends in the suffix *aṇ* (as in *prokta*) would not be a secondary member (*anupasarjana*) and would be present in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp*—which is conditioned by the presence of the suffix *aṇ*—would be unavoidable. And if that [suffix *ṅīp*] were connected with the explicitly mentioned *ti* and so forth...

It has been stated that there is no fault because [the suffix] *aṇ* is subordinate (*upasarjana*). However, the suffix *adhyetraṇ* is elided; since the rule "the vowel *a* of *aṇ*" is an interpretation based on the phoneme itself (*varṇāśrayatva*), the condition for the application of the rule regarding the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply. Nor does this concern the rule "in the feminine" (*striyām*).

It should not be argued that because [the suffix] *aṇ* is prescribed as a qualifier for *śruta*, *ṭid*, and so forth, there is no possibility of the application of *ṅīp* simply because it does not occur in the feminine; for once the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) is made known, it is more appropriate that the word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) serves as a qualifier for the base (*prakṛti*) of *ṅīp* due to its predominance, otherwise...

And because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding non-subordinate elements (*anupasarjana*) would otherwise be rendered useless. For this very reason, forms such as *atidhīvarī* (a woman who has surpassed a fisherman) are established; enough of this digression. It might be argued: from the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking," in the passive voice, with the future suffix *lṛṭ*, by the rule *lṛṭaḥ sadvā*, there is the substitution of *śānac* for it, and [the addition of] *syatāsī*.

In the case of *vakṣyamāṇā*, the form is derived as follows: from the roots *vac* and *khyā*, by the rule "lṛluṭoḥ," the suffix *sya* is applied; then there is the substitution of *ku* for *kh* (kutva) and *ṣ* for *ś* (ṣatva); the augment *muk* is added before the suffix *āna*; then *ṇatva* (the change of *n* to *ṇ*) occurs, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding this form, since the substitute of the *lṛṭ* [future] suffix is, by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva*, both *ṭit* and *ugit*, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rules "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... and "ugitaśca."

Nor should one suspect that the prohibition by the rule *analvidhau* applies here— on the grounds that the substitution of *ī* for the *ṛ* of the stem-forming suffix *lṛṭ* (which ends in *ṭ*) and for the *ṛ* [of the root] is dependent on an *al* (vowel), and thus the prescription of *ṅīp* would not be an *al-vidhi*—
because the *ītva* prescribed by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisāṃ halī* before *kṅit* suffixes is [not subject to that prohibition].

By the prohibition [contained in the rule] "lyapi," it is indicated that the restriction "analvidhau" (except in the case of a rule prescribing an operation dependent on a letter) does not apply to operations concerning *anubandhas* (indicatory letters). For if the restriction "analvidhau" were to apply even to operations concerning *anubandhas*, then since the substitute *lyap* for *ktvā* would not be subject to the designation *kit*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* following it [would not take the augment *iṭ*].
Since the application of *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*) is impossible in this case, its prohibition is clearly redundant.

Therefore, anticipating the objection that in the word *vakṣyamāṇā*, the suffix *ṅīp* would be unavoidable because the suffix *śānac* is treated as having the property of *ṭit* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva* and because of its *ugit* status, he refutes this with the words beginning "vakṣyamāṇā... regarding the term *vakṣyamāṇā*.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply because of the presence of the markers *ṭ* and *uk*. Why not? To this he says:
"Because of the indication (*jñāpana*) [contained] in the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣūdātto ṅcce*," and so forth, up to the end of the passage. [This rule states:
"In the case of parasmaipada endings, *yāsuṭ* is udātta and has the marker *ṅ*."

Regarding the substitutes for the *liṅ* [optative] suffixes—namely *ti*, *tas*, *jhi*, and so forth, which belong to the parasmaipada—the augment *yāsuṭ* is prescribed as having the marker *ṅ*. By the maxim "that which is an augment is part of that to which it is added," the augment *yāsuṭ* is a constituent part of the *liṅ* substitute.

Consequently, since the status of being marked by *ṅ* (*ṅtvam*) would already be established through the principle of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the prescription of *yāsuṭ* itself would be redundant; therefore...
It is understood that "the operation based on an *anubandha* does not apply to substitutes.

Consequently, in the case of *vakṣyamāṇā*, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which is an operation of a *ṭit* or *git* element—is to be applied to the *śānac* substitute for *lṛṭ*, the *ṅīp* does not occur because [the substitute] lacks the status of being a *sthānin*. Now, one might object:

Even if it were established that "an operation conditioned by *l* does not apply to substitutes," the augment *īṭ* prescribed for the *pit* [affix] by the rule *bruva īṭ* would still be unavoidable in the form *brūtāt*; for although that [augment] is conditioned by *ti*, it is not conditioned by *l*, and thus the *tātaṅ* substitute would have to apply when that [augment] is to be introduced.

Because the status of *pit* (the marker *p*) remains unimpeded by virtue of its being *sthānivadbhāva*, [the author], expressing a lack of satisfaction with that view, says: "The substitute *śānac* for *śna*.

From the word *śnā*, in the genitive singular (*ṣaṣṭhyekavacana*), after the elision of the *ā* (by *āllopa*), the form is *śna*. This applies even to forms other than verbal roots (*adhātu*), by resorting to a split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the sūtra *āto dhātoḥ*, where the portion *ātaḥ* is treated separately.

In some cases, because the elision of *ā* is accepted, the rule "ṭhhalaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau" prescribes the substitution of *śānac* for the suffix *śna*. In that context, since the desired result is already established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original), the fact that *śānac* is marked with the letter *ś* would be redundant. Nor should one fear the prohibition "na hyanalvidhau" (there is no [application of *sthānivadbhāva*] when a rule concerns something other than an *al*), as this is negated by the rule "na lyapi".

Since it was stated immediately following [the previous discussion] that there is no prohibition of the rule "analvidhau" (P. 1.1.56) regarding operations conditioned by an *anubandha* on account of its *liṅga*, it is understood that in certain cases, even for operations conditioned by an *anubandha*, the prohibition "analvidhau" does indeed apply. And so, in the case of the term *vakṣyamāṇā* (feminine),...

The meaning is that when the operations of *ṭit*, *dugit*, or *kit* apply, because the prohibition "not when a suffix is being prescribed" (*analvidhau*) takes effect, there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivattva*); consequently, since the properties of being *ṭit* or *ugit* are absent, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur.
In reality, however, this is based on the principle that "an operation dependent on an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) does not apply to substitutes," as seen in the case of the *ṅt* of *yāsuṭ*.

It is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because that [rule] is for the purpose of *tip*, *sip*, and *mi*. For even though they are substitutes for *liṅ*, the status of having the marker *ṅ* (*ṅtvam*) cannot be obtained for *tip*, *sip*, and *mi* by means of the principle of non-alteration of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*); this has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* as: "That which has *ṅ* is not *pit*; that which is *pit* is not *ṅit*. Likewise...

Furthermore, the fact that *śnaḥ* is marked with the *śit* designation is not an indicator [of the rule's application], because the *śit* status of that suffix has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. On the contrary, the Bhāṣya states that if the *śit* status were taken as an indicator, then the *apit*-ness of *hi* in the rule *serhyapicca* and the *ṅt*-ness of *tātaṅ* would both be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, because it is designated as a *dūṣaṇa* (a refutation), the suffix *ṅīp* alone is appropriate in the word *vakṣyamāṇā*; the suffix *ṭāp*, however, is simply incorrect. Alternatively, one might somehow justify it by claiming it is due to the word belonging to the *ajādi* group; but let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the term *sauparṇeyī*: it means "the female offspring of Suparṇī. In this sense, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule *ṭhstrībhyo ḍha-g*. Then, by the rule *āyane-y-i*, the element *ey* is substituted for *ḍhak*. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel *ī* is elided, and by the rule *kiti ca*, the initial vowel is subject to *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). From the word *sauparṇeya*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and again, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel *a* is elided.

The form is *sauparṇeyī*. One should not argue that, by the paribhāṣā "when a [suffix] with no *anubandha* is mentioned, one with an *anubandha* is not included," only the two rules "ḍhaḥ śilāyāḥ" and "ḍhaś chandasi" are to be understood here; for there is no other recourse, as those two do not apply to the feminine gender.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya, which states that there is a mention of the *ḍha* [suffix] along with its *anubandha*. Regarding the word *aindrī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "Indra is the deity (*devatā*) of this curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*). By the rule *sāsya devatā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel [of the first member] is elided; and the initial *vṛddhi* is applied. From the word *aindra*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and by the rule *yasyeti ca*, [the final *a* is elided].

There is the elision of the vowel *e* [in the compound]. Alternatively, the analysis is "this belongs to Indra" (*indrasyeyaṃ*), with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tasyedam*. Regarding *autsī*: Amara states that *utsaḥ* means "a spring" or "flowing water. Or, *utsaḥ* may refer to a particular sage. The analysis is "this belongs to Utsa" (*utsasyeyaṃ*). The suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule *utsādibhyo 'ñ*; then the *y* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.

The form *autsī*—meaning "the female offspring of Utsa"—is not an example [of this rule], because when the term *jātiḥ* (genus) is understood as a governing factor (*anuvṛtti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established by the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*. Furthermore, since the rule *gotraṃ ca caraṇaiḥ saha* states that a lineage (*gotra*) ending in an affix denoting offspring is a genus (*jāti*), [the application of *ṅīṣ* is secured]. Enough of this. [Examples of the suffixes *-dvayasaC* and *-daghnaC* are: *ūrudvayasī* and *ūrudaghnī*.

*Ūrumātrī*: the analysis of the compound is "that whose measure (*pramāṇa*) is the thighs (*ūrū*). [The suffix] *ṭha* [is applied] by the rule "the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, and *mātraC* are used in the sense of measure. [Then] *ṅīp* is added. *Pañcatayī*: the analysis of the compound is "that which has five parts (*avayava*). [The suffix] *tayap* is applied by the rule "the suffix *tayap* is used after a numeral in the sense of a part. [Then] *ṅīp* is added. *Ākṣikī*: [This is derived from *akṣa* with the suffix *ṭhak*].

The analysis of the compound is "one who plays with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*). According to the rule *tena dīvyati khanati jayati jitaṃ*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; there is initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), and by the rules *ṭhasyekaḥ* and *yasyeti ca*, the vowel *a* is elided.

From the word *ākṣika*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and again by *yasyeti ca*, the final *a* is elided. Regarding *lāvaṇikī*: it means "one for whom salt (*lavaṇa*) is the merchandise (*paṇya*)."

Such is the analysis (*vigraha*). From *lavaṇa* [with the suffix] *ṭhañ*, [by the rule] *ṭhasyekaḥ*, there is initial *vṛddhi*; then by *yasyeti ca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the word *lāvaṇika*. Although the formation would be established by the rule *yasyeti ca* alone, the separate mention of *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of excluding *ṭhan* and *ñiṭha*. [The example is: "she who has a staff" (*daṇḍa*).
*Daṇḍikā*: [The suffixes] *ini* and *ṭhan* [are applied after *daṇḍa*]. *Kāśikā*: that which exists in Kāśī;

[the suffix] *ñiṭha* [is applied] by the rule "after *kāśi* and others, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*. Regarding *yādṛśī*: [the suffix] *kañ* [is applied] after the root *dṛś* when words beginning with *tyad* are in apposition, according to the rule "after *dṛś* when preceded by *tyad* etc."; and the vowel *ā* replaces the word *yat* by the rule "the *ā* [replaces the final letter] of a pronominal."

[The suffix] *ṅīp* [is applied], and [the vowel] of that which ends in *ya* is elided. Regarding the word *itvarī*: from the root *iṇ* (to go), [the suffix] *kvarap* is added by the rule "after *iṇ*, *naś*, *ji*, and *sṛ*, [the suffix] *kvarap*. Then, by the rule "a *tuk* augment is added after a short vowel before a *pit* *kṛt* suffix," the *tuk* is added.

From the word *itvara*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. [The vowel] of that which ends in *ya* is elided. [The mention of *ṅīp* is] for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *varac* by the rule "after *sthā*, *īś*, and *bhās*... etc.

The inclusion of the *kakāra* (k) as an *anubandha* [is for the sake of excluding other suffixes]. As Bhāravi says: "The great medicinal herb of auspiciousness was placed upon the Lord" (*vinyastamaṅgalamahauṣadhir īśvarāyāḥ*). And in the Veda: "May the Lord not burn him" (*sainam īśvarāpradaha*). Even with the suffix *kvap*, since the exclusion of *varaC* is accomplished by either one of the *anubandhas*, the employment of both *anubandhas* [is for the purpose of distinguishing it from other suffixes].
The meaning is clear. As for *Īśvarī*, it is derived from the word *īśvara* by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *puṃyoge ṅīṣ* (Pāṇini 4.1.48), signifying "the wife of Īśvara.

Alternatively, it is formed from the root *ṭhu* (in the sense of "to move quickly") with the suffix *varaṭ* according to the rule *ṭhāśūsvasitruṣyatipūṣmīhībhyaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 269), resulting in *īśvara*; then, because it ends in *ṭh*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added.
Or else, it is formed according to the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74) and the subsequent rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.178).

The suffixes *kvun* and *vanip* [are applied] by the rule "vano ra ca" (*Pāṇini* 4.1.7), resulting in the feminine forms *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*. [This applies] also to the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of "having that as one's habitual disposition" (*tācchīlika*).

Regarding the phrase "also to the suffix *ṇa* in the sense of having that as one's habitual disposition": that which exists in the state of having that as one's habitual disposition is *tācchīlika*; thus, it means "having that as its purpose" (*tacchīlārthaka*).
Up to this point: the meaning is that when the suffix *ṇa* occurs, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* also occurs after a word ending in it.

This is established by an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). For instance, while the term "habitual character" (*śīla*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), once the suffix *ṇa* is prescribed by the rule "the suffix *ṇa* after *chatra* and others," the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to *aṇ* take place, as in the rule "the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] to form words denoting habitual character" (*kārmastācchīlye*).

This is because of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). In the analysis of the compound *karmaśīla* (one whose habit is work), when the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule for the *chatrādi* group, and the *ṭi*-portion is elided by the rule *ṭhnastaddhite*, the form *kārma* arises. It does not, however, undergo *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) by the rule *an*—which means that the suffix *aṇ* would remain as the base—such is the meaning. In this case...

Because the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical changes) prescribed for an *aṇ* suffix is prohibited when a *ṇa*-pratyaya follows, it is understood that the operations of an *aṇ* suffix apply to a *ṇa*-pratyaya used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). Therefore, the meaning is that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a word ending in a *ṇa*-pratyaya used in the sense of habitual action, which functions like an *aṇ*. For example, *caurī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose habit is stealing" (*curā śīlam asyāḥ*).

The suffix *ṇa* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *cchatrādi* group; there is vṛddhi of the first vowel; and [the final *a* is elided] by the rule *yasyeti ca*. From the word *caura*, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, [the final *a* is elided] by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
There is an inclusionary statement (*upasaṅkhyānam*) for the words *nañ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *khyaun*, *taruṇa*, and *taluna*.

The suffix *nañ* [is included]. The meaning is that the rule for the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* must also be stated for *nañ*, *snañ*, *īkak*, *khyun*, *taruṇa*, and *taluna*. These four, beginning with *nañ*, are suffixes; therefore, the rule of "application to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Examples are *straiṇī* and *pauṃsnī*, [formed] by the rule "from *strī* and *puṃs*" (*strīpuṃsābhyām*).

The suffixes *nañ* and *snañ*. In that context, from the word *strī* with *nañ*, there is initial *vṛddhi*, the substitution of *ṇa*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, and the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*ṭhyasyeti ca*). From the word *puṃs* with *snañ*, there is initial *vṛddhi*, *ṅīp*, and the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant. [The form] *śāktīkī* is derived as follows:
the analysis of the compound is "she whose weapon (*praharaṇa*) is a *śakti* (a specific type of missile)."

The suffix *yaṣṭhac* is added after the word *āḍhala*, followed by *īkak*. There is initial *vṛddhi*, the substitution of *ṇa*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, and the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*yasyeti ca*).

Thus, we have *āḍhaḷṅkaraṇī*. The analysis of the compound is: "that by which that which is not firm (*anāḍhalya*) is made firm (*āḍhalya*). The suffix *khyun* is applied according to the rule *āḍhalsubhagetyādinā*. By the rule *yuvor anākau*, there is the substitution of *ana* for the suffix. [The rule] *arurdviṣad...* [applies].

Thus, *mum*, the substitution of *ṇa*, the suffix *ṅīp*, and [the elision of] *ṭha* by the rule "of that which ends in *i*" (*yasyeti ca*). Regarding *taruṇī* and *talunī*: although the suffix *ṅīp* is established for these two by the rule "in the first stage of life" (*vayasi prathame*), nevertheless, because they are listed in the *gaura*-group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply; this statement [is made] to prevent that. Due to their inclusion in the *gaura*-group, if *ṅīṣ* were applied, there would be a difference in accent.
The meaning is "a distinction.
(463) *yañaśca* | 4.1.16 | [The word] *yañ* [is used]; because *yañ* is a suffix, there is the inclusion of that which ends in it. [This follows] from the rule *ṛnnebhyaḥ*.
The term *ṅīp* is understood from the previous context, and *striyām* (in the feminine) is the governing heading. Thus he says: "from that which ends in *yañ*.

Although it would have been more appropriate to include the mention of *yañ* in the preceding sūtra itself (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*), it is nevertheless stated separately here so that *yañ* alone may be carried forward into the subsequent sūtra, *ṣpha taddhitaḥ*.
The meaning is "the Sūtra. Regarding the phrase "when the letter *a* has been elided": he will give the example *gārgī*.

In the sense of "the female descendant of Garga," the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*; there is initial vṛddhi, and by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the vowel *a* following the letter *g* is elided. From the word *gārgya*, [the feminine suffix] *nīp* is applied.

The meaning is that after the elision of the letter *ya* by the rule "ṭhhalastaddhitasya" [Pāṇini 6.4.150], and subsequently the elision of the vowel *a* following the letter *ya* by the rule "yasyeti ca" [Pāṇini 6.4.148], the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) will be explained. (464) ṭhhalastaddhitasya |6|4|150|.

*Hala-staddhitasya*: The word *halaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of direction (*digyoge*). The word *parasya* (of what follows) is to be supplied. From the rule *yasyeti ca*, the word *īti* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), and from the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastya*, the genitive form *upadhāyāḥ* (of the penultimate vowel) is also carried over. From the rule *ḍhea lopo 'kadr̥vāḥ*, the word *lopaḥ* (elision) is carried over.

And so it is said: "of what follows after a consonant," and so forth. The elision of the letter *y* cannot occur prior to the elision of the letter *a*, because as long as the *a* exists, the *y* lacks the status of being followed by the vowel *ī*.
[Objection: But once the elision of the *a* has been performed, the *y* is indeed followed by the *ī*.

[Objection: "What is the status of being an *upadhā*? Furthermore, one should not suspect that the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) is subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, because that [rule] is prohibited in the context of the prescription for the elision of *y* (*yalopa*). [Response: This is not so; for when the elision of *y* is to be performed, since the elision of *a* is *asiddha* by virtue of being an *abhīya* [operation], it is possible for the *y* to have the status of an *upadhā*. If the term 'upadhā' were not repeated [in the subsequent rule],"

Since the elision of *tv* would be considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddha*), the *y* would not be followed by an *ī*, and thus the elision would not occur. However, if it is argued that—by the very force of the formulation of the rule—the elision of *y* is possible even when there is an intervention by an *a*, then the continued application of the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) need not be maintained. As in the case of *gārgī*.

In this context, although *gotra* (clan) is a genus (*jāti*) because it is said to be "together with conduct" (*caraṇaiḥ saha*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply despite its being a genus, because it is a word ending in a *yopadhā* (a penultimate *y* vowel), according to the rule *jāter astrīviṣayāt*. Regarding the phrase "under the heading of offspring" (*anapatyādhikāra*):
the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply after a word ending in *yañ* that is distinct from those prescribed under the heading of offspring (*apatya*) by the rule *tasyāpatyam*.

The meaning is that it must be stated. Regarding the term *dvaipī*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) of "that which exists on an island" (*dvīpe bhavā*), the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *dvīpādanusamudra yañ*. There is initial *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel]. Then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final *i* is elided. With the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, there is the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). The point is that because this *yañ* is not prescribed within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for "descendants" (*apatya*), the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. Now, one might object: [is it not] from a descendant?

Since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *dvaipyā* is already avoided by the mere mention of the suffix *ṅīp*, one might ask: for what purpose is the inclusion of the governing heading (*adhikāra*)? To this he says: "Because of the inclusion of the governing heading. The remainder [of the sentence] is "it is not [applied] here. In the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) "the offspring of Deva," the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule "from *deva*, *yañ* and *añ*"; there is then the initial *vṛddhi*.
Regarding the rule *yasyeti ca*: from the word *daivya*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, followed by the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution), resulting in the form *daivyā*.

However, if it were stated that "the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied after [a stem ending in] *yañ* when it does not denote a descendant (*anapatya*)," then because this *yañ* does denote a descendant, the prohibition of *ṅīp* would not apply.
But if the governing context (*adhikāra*) is taken into account, then the prohibition would indeed apply here as well, since this *yañ* denotes a descendant.
Because the rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) is outside the governing scope [of the subsequent rules].

He establishes this point with the words "from *deva*," etc. However, the rule "*yañ* and *añ* after *deva*" is recited within the governing scope of "before *prāgdīvyataḥ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.83), which precedes the governing scope of "his offspring."
And because that [suffix] is common to meanings ranging from "offspring" (apatya) up to "modification" (vikāra), it also occurs in the sense of offspring,

though not as one specifically read under the heading of "offspring" (apatyādhikāra). Although in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *ṭhyañaśca* it is seen stated that "the mention of 'offspring' (*apatya*) must be made," nevertheless, in that context...
It has been explained in detail in both the *Manoramā* and the *Śabdaratna* that the term *āpatya* refers specifically to those [suffixes] prescribed under the heading of *apatya* (offspring).
(465) *prācām ṣpha taddhitaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.17.

"Ṣpha is [the suffix] for the eastern grammarians when forming a taddhita. The word "ṭhyañaḥ" is understood [from the previous rule], and "in the feminine" is supplied from the context. In the expression "ṣphe," the nominative case ending is elided. Thus he says: "after a stem ending in yañ. (Pāṇini 1.3.6) "The letter ṣ is [the marker] of the affix. 1.3.6.

Regarding the suffix *ṣaṣ*: from the rule "ṭhādir ñiṭuaḍavaḥ," the word "ādiḥ" (the first) is understood to carry over; and from the rule "upadeśe 'janunāsika it," the word "it" (the marker *it*) is also understood. Thus he says: "the beginning of the suffix.
When the letter *ṣ* has been assigned the technical designation *itsaṃjñā*, it is elided.

(467) *āyan-ey-īn-īy-iy-aḥ pha-ḍha-kha-ccha-gh-ām pratyayādīnām* |7|1|2| *āyan-ey-īn-īy-iy-aḥ*: This is the nominative plural of a *dvandva* compound consisting of these five: *āyan*, *ey*, *īn*, *īy*, and *iya*. *pha-ḍha-kha-ccha-gh-ām*: Of these [five]: *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *ccha*, and *gha*.
This is a genitive plural in a *dvandva* compound. The vowel *a* in [the suffixes] beginning with *pha* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

The connection [of the elements] occurs in sequence according to the rule of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṅkhyaparibhāṣā*). Thus he says: "of those that have become the beginning of a suffix," and so forth. [In the case of *āyana*,] the *n* belongs to the *na*.
Even when there is the application of the substitution of *i* for *n*, the substitution of *it* does not occur, because the addition of *n* to the suffix *phin* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

By association with that, the *n* of *īn* also does not undergo the substitution of *it*. Furthermore, among the suffixes beginning with *ey*, those for which the substitution of *it* would apply do not admit the suffix *ṅīṣ*; therefore, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied after the word *kauravya*, while the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after *māṇḍūkāyana*—this is the intended meaning.
Although the reading *ṭh-ṭām-ṅīp-aḥ* is generally seen here, it is omitted for lack of necessity.

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of the designation *taddhita* for *ṣpha*? To this he says: "because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix. He states the purpose of [the word] being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when ending in *ṣpha*: "the *ṅīṣ* suffix to be mentioned [later]."
In the rule *ṭhṣidgaurādibhyaśca*, the term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem) is understood by way of anuvṛtti;
therefore, the point is that since a nominal stem ending in *ṣpha* lacks the status of a *prātipadika*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply. [Objection:
But surely, since femininity is already expressed by the suffix *ṣpha* itself, the principle applies that "that which has already been expressed need not be used again."

To the question, "How is the suffix *ṅīṣ* applied here according to the rule? he says: "By virtue of the presence of the marker *ṣ*. The meaning is that even though femininity is already indicated by the suffix *ṣpha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is employed due to the functional power (*sāmarthya*) of the marker *ṣ*. Regarding the form *gārgyāyaṇī*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the female descendant of Garga."

From the word *gārgya*, which ends in the *yañ* suffix belonging to the *garga*-class, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied. The letter *ṣ* is for the sake of marking the accent (*it*), and the letter *ph* undergoes the substitution of *āyan*. By the rule "of that which [ends in] *i* or *u*" (*yasyeti ca*), the vowel *a* following the letter *y* is elided.

However, the rule "of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a consonant" (*halastaddhitasya*) does not apply here, because the word *īti* (referring to the *it*-marker) is understood as a governing factor (*anuvṛtti*). [Then applies the rule] "of the descendant" (*apatyasya*).

Nor is it [the case that] "ce" [is applied], because of the prohibition by the term "anāt". [The suffix] ṅīṣ is applied because of the marker ṣit. This is the intended meaning regarding the substitution of ṇ for n.
(468) *Sarvatra lohitādikatantebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.18).

In all cases, "lohita" and so forth belong to the subgroup beginning with *garga*. The analysis of the compound is: "those for which *lohita* is the beginning" (*lohita-ādi*), and "those for which *kata* is the end" (*kata-anta*).

In the form *ṭhkatanta*, the substitution of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*) occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group. The term *yañ*, which is understood from the previous rule, is here treated as being in the plural.

It undergoes modification. The rule *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.17) continues [to apply] with the exception of the word *prācām*. "In all cases" means in all systems of thought; that is to say, invariably. This is what he states by the words beginning with *lohitādibhyaḥ*.

*Lauhityāyanī*: the analysis of the compound is "the female descendant of Lohita. From the word *lohita*, which belongs to the *gargādi* group and takes the suffix *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* is applied. The *ṣ* is for the sake of the feminine marker (*ṅīp*), the *ph* is replaced by *āyan*, and according to the rule "of that which [ends in] *ya*," there is the elision of the vowel *a* following the *y*. It is a *taddhita* derivative.
The intention is that because [the suffix] continues from this rule and is marked with *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Regarding *kātyāyanī*:
the derivation should be understood as before.
(469) *kauravyamāṇḍūkābhyāṃ ca* | Pāṇini 4.1.19.

"And by means of *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka*. Regarding "by means of these two": the meaning is "by means of *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka*. Regarding "in sequence": the meaning is that [the suffixes taught here] are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the feminine suffix *ṭāp* after the word *kauravya* and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* after the word *māṇḍūka*. This is because the word *kauravya* ends in the suffix *yañ*, while the word *māṇḍūka* ends in the suffix *aṇ*.

To dispel the misconception that "the suffix *ṅīp* is an exception [to the rule governing *ṅīṣ*]," he says, beginning with "from *kurū-* and so forth. Regarding the form *kauravyāyaṇī*: the analysis of the compound is "the female descendant of *kuru*.

By the rule "the suffix *ṇya* after *kurū-* and so forth," the suffix *ṇya* is applied. The letter *ṇ* is an *it*, "guṇa" is substituted for the *u* by the rule "guṇa for *u*" (*orguṇaḥ*), and "vṛddhi" is applied to the initial vowel.

Regarding the form *gotrā* (meaning lineage), although it denotes a genus (*jāti*) because it is used with the word *caraṇa*, the suffix *ṭāp* would normally apply by the rule *jāter astrīviṣayāt*. However, that is set aside by the application of the suffix *ṣpha*;
the *ṣ* is indicatory (*it*), which results in *āyan*; then, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel *a* is elided; and because the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
The meaning is "of whom" (yasya). Regarding *māṇḍūkāyanī*: the analysis is that Maṇḍūka was the name of a sage, and [the word refers to] his female descendant.
By the rule *ḍhak ca maṇḍūkāt*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; there is vṛddhi of the first vowel, and by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the final vowel is elided.
Since the rule states "a lineage (*gotra*) together with its branches (*caraṇas*) is a genus (*jāti*"), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applicable; however, [it is not applied here].

The sense is as follows: having set aside [the application of] *ṣpha*, [the suffix] *ṣa* becomes *it*; then *āyan*, and by the rule "ṭhi yasyeti ca," because it is marked with *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, and again by "ṭhi yasyeti ca. The reading "an exception to *ṭāp* and *ṅīp*" is erroneous.
The addition of *āsuri* [to the list of names] is required.

"The addition of *āsuri* [to the list]"—this is the remainder of the rule "after *ṣpha*. For example: *āsurāyaṇī*. The analysis of the compound is: "the female descendant of Asura. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied by the rule "ata iñ," followed by initial vṛddhi (*āsurī*). Then the suffix *ṣpha* is added; since *ṣ* is *it*, [the suffix] becomes *āyan*. By the rule "yasyeti ca," the final vowel and its following consonant are elided. Because [the suffix] has the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. Again, by "yasyeti ca," the final vowel and its following consonant are elided. Thus, there is *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*).
The state [of being]. (470) *vayasi prathame* |4|1|20|.
Regarding "in the first age": *vayas* is a particular stage of existence of living beings determined by time. And that...

It is threefold—childhood, youth, and old age—as seen in the statement: "In childhood the father protects, in youth the husband protects, and in the state of old age the son [protects]; a woman does not deserve independence. Others, however, say that there are four stages of life (*vaya*). In the first...

"Since it is seen [in the scriptures]: 'What will one do in the fourth stage of life, having failed to study in the first, failed to acquire wealth in the second, and failed to practice austerity in the third?'—after the words 'in the first stage of life,' the word 'being present' (*vidyamānā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is because of the continued application of the term 'from *at*' (*ataḥ*) from the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*."

The term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem), which is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*), is here specified. This is an application of the rule for suffixes following a compound ending in that [stem] (*tadantavidhiḥ*).
The term *striyām* (in the feminine), which is also the governing heading, is present. From the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*, the word *ṅīp* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*).
Thus he says: "of those denoting the first stage of life," and so forth. The example is *kumārī*.

The meaning is "one whose youth has not yet appeared. However, the term *vṛddhakumārī* ("an old maiden") should be understood as a case of superimposing the state of being a maiden upon one who is actually old.
(471) Or rather, it should be stated as *vayasyacarama* ("not the last of one's age").
Regarding the phrase "not the last" (*acarama*): "last" (*carama*) means the final stage of life; "not the last" (*acarama*) means different from that.

The meaning is that, having removed [the term] "in the first," one should say "not in the last. To the question "For what purpose? he says: "the young wife" (*vadhūṭī*) and "the mature woman" (*ciraṇṭī*). The point is that because these two denote the second stage of life, [the rule] would otherwise not apply.

Because these two [words] are not well-known in their second stage of life, he says: "expressive of youth" (*yauvanavācinau*). The intention is that this is based on the authority of the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the word *śiśu*:
although the word *śiśu* denotes the first stage of life, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply because it lacks the vowel *a* at its end. As for *kanyā*...
"No," [the author] says; the remainder [of the rule] is "ṅīp. Why? To this he says: "In the case of *kanyā*, [the form is] *kanīnā*.

Nor should one suspect that the suffix *ṅīp* applies even in cases such as *dvivarṣā strī* ("a two-year-old female"), because since words like *dvivarṣā* are also used for things such as a house (*śālā*), they do not denote a feminine primary referent (*prathamārtha*).
Because it is intended that only that which denotes age— without depending on the co-utterance of other words, context, and so forth— is [meant here]. (472) *dvigoḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.21.

The rule *dvigoḥ* [is governed by] the subsequent rules *ṭhstriyām*, *ṭhataḥ*, and *ṭhṅīp*. Thus he says: "from that which ends in /a/. Regarding *trilokī*: the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "the collection of the three worlds" (*trayāṇāṃ lokānāṃ samāhāraḥ*). The compound is a *dvigu* according to the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*.
Femininity [of the compound] is desired because of the rule: "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the letter *ṭh* is feminine.
From the word *triloka*, the suffix *ṅīp* applies as an exception to *ṭāp*; this is the intended meaning according to the rule *yasyeti ca*.
Now, one might object that *ṅīp* would also apply here in the cases of *triphalā* and *tryanīkā*; to this he says: *triphalā* [is formed] because it begins with the vowel *a*.

Regarding the term *tryanīkā*: the word *bhavati* (it becomes) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the analysis (*vigraha*) as "the collection of three fruits" (*trayāṇāṃ phalānāṃ samāhāraḥ*) or "the collection of three armies" (*trayāṇām anīkānām*), a *dvigu* compound is formed according to the rule *taddhitārtha-*. Femininity is established because the final member of the compound ends in the vowel *a*, and the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *dvigoḥ*.

The meaning is that, having set aside [the application of] *ṅīp*, [the suffix] *ṭāp* is applied because it begins with the letter *a*. The Mīmāṃsakas maintain in the section concerning the *tryanīkā* that the word *anīka* occurs in reference to the precedence of the Aindravāyava cup, the precedence of the Śukra cup, and the precedence of the Āgrayaṇa cup. The rule "after a *dvigu* compound ending in a non-measure word" (*aparimāṇa-ṭdvigoḥ*) also follows, as does [the mention of] *ṅīp*.

The governing rule *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") is qualified by the terms *aparimāṇa* ("measureless" and so forth). This is an application of the rule *tadantavidhi* ("the inclusion of that which ends with [the specified element]").
(Pāṇini 4.1.22): *aparimāṇabistācitakambalyebhyo na taddhitaluki*. He states this in the words beginning with *aparimāṇāntāt* ("ending in a word denoting a measureless quantity," etc.).

He provides an illustration of the "immeasurable" (aparimāṇa) limit with the word "by five" (pañcabhiḥ). He demonstrates the elision of the secondary suffix (taddhita-luk) by stating: "the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of 'worth' (*ārhīya*), and there is elision [of the suffix] after *adhyardha*" (*adhyardha*). In the analytical construction (vigraha) "bought for five horses," the term becomes a *dvigu* compound according to the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*).

In the section concerning the suffix *ṭhañ* (which becomes *-ika*) after words denoting a measure that does not signify a specific quantity (*aparimāṇa*), such as *agopucchasaṅkhyāparimāṇāt*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *tena krītam*.

This *ṭhak* is then elided by the rule *adhyardhapūrvādvigor lug asaṃjñāyām*. In this case, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not apply after the *dvigu* compound because it is a *dvigu* whose final member is not a word denoting a specific measure (*aparimāṇānta*).

But surely, even though the prohibition of *ṅīp* by the rule "dvigor" applies here, the *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... would still be unavoidable for the word *agnimitakā*. This is because in the case of *dviśatā*—meaning "bought for two hundred"—the suffix *kan* (by the rule "saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ") is elided by the rule "adhyardha-".
If it is argued that this is because the prohibition [in Pāṇini 1.1.28] "ṭha-aparimāṇe" has its purpose fulfilled [by excluding words like *pañca* which denote a measure], that is true;

however, in the rule "ṭi-ḍḍhā-ṇ-añ," by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), what is intended is that [the suffix] must end in the letter *ñ* which belongs to the group beginning with *ṭi*, *ḍ*, *ḍha*, *ā*, *ṇ*, and *añ*. And this word *pañcāśva* [ends in *añ*].

There is no fault, as [the word *vistā*] does not end in the vowel *ā* which is a constituent part of the suffix *ṭhak*. Nor should it be suspected that it ends in the vowel *ā* belonging to a suffix by virtue of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because there is no application of the characteristics of suffixes when the basis is a phoneme (*varṇa*). However, words such as *vistā* and others denote a specific measure (*parimāṇaviśeṣa*).
The separate mention [of the word *apramāṇe*] is because [the rule] would not otherwise apply by the [preceding rule] *ṭhaparimāṇe*. Regarding "two *bistas*":
Amara states, "A *suvarṇa* and a *bista* are [weights] of gold, [the latter being] an *akṣa*. And it is said: "Five *guñjās* constitute the first *māṣaka*;
sixteen of those [make] an *akṣa*. Thus, five *guñjās* are the measure of a *māṣa*, and sixteen *māṣas* [make an *akṣa*].

The measure of an *akṣa* consists of eighty *guñjās*; in that context of gold-measurement (*hemaviṣaya*), the words *suvarṇa* and *bista* denote that measure of an *akṣa*. In the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "he cooks two *bistas*," there is a *dvigu* compound according to the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*). Then, by the rule "when [the object] is possible, one carries away, or cooks" (*sambhavaty-avaharati-pacati*), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied.

In the word *tasyādhyardhe*, there is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix]. When the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule *dvigor iti*, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied, resulting in *dvibistā mūṣā*. The meaning is that it melts gold having the measure of two *bistās*. Here, the root *pac* should be understood in the sense of melting. Regarding *dvyācitā*: "ten *bhāras* are an *ācita*."
Thus says Amara: "A *tulā* is a hundred *palas* (feminine), and a *bhāra* is twenty [of those] (masculine).

Regarding the sense of "carrying two *ācitakas*," [the suffix] *kha* is applied optionally according to the rule "after *āḍhaka*, *aci*, *droṇa*, and *pātra*, *kha* is used optionally," and by the rule "in a *dvigu* compound, *ṭhañ* is also used."

In the absence of *khaṭhana*, the suffix *ṭhañ* applies as before; by the rule "in the case of *adhyardha*," there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. By this [rule], when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited by the rule "after a *dvigu*," the suffix *ṭāp* is applied, resulting in "a cart worth two *ācitās*" (*dvyācitā śakaṭī*).
Regarding *dvikambalyā*: the material which is the source of a *kambalya* is called *kambalya*; it is one hundred *palas* of wool.
In the sense of "for that purpose, from the modification [to the original]," the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *kambalācca saṃjñāyām*.

In the analysis *dvābhyāṃ kambalyābhyāṃ krītā* ("bought for two *kambalya*s"), the suffix *ṭhañ* prescribed by *tena krītam* is elided by *adhyardhapūrvād-dvigor-luk*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* prescribed by *dvigoḥ* is prohibited by this [present rule], resulting in *ṭāp*.

Now, one might argue: let there simply be the rule "na taddhitaluki" (P. 1.2.49). By that alone, forms such as *pañcāśvī* ("bought for five horses") would be established; thus, the rule "aparimāṇe" (P. 1.2.50) need not exist. Furthermore, since forms such as *dvibistā*, *dvyācitā*, and *dvikambalyā* would also be established in this way, the mention of *vistādi* (the group beginning with *visti*) in P. 1.2.51 need not exist either. To this [the author replies]:
He said: "Up to the limit of measurement. [The text continues: "Five *guñjās* shall be one *māṣa*;

sixteen [of those] shall be a *suvarṇa*. Four *suvarṇas*, or even five, are proclaimed as a *pala*. Two *palas* are a *prasṛta*; double that is considered a *kuḍava*. With four *kuḍavas* there is a *prastha*."

"Four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*," so says the *Smṛti*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound "one who cooks two *āḍhakas*," the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule "after *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra*, *kha* optionally [is added]," and since *kha* and *ṭhañ* are absent, the suffix *ṭhañ* from the *prāgvatīya* group is used. By the rule "in the case of *adhyardha*," there is elision (*luk*). By the rule "after a *dvigu*," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

The form is *dvyāḍhakī*. If it were stated only as "not [the application of] *ṅīp* when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix" (*ṭhan na taddhitalukī*), then the prohibition of *ṅīp* would apply here as well. Therefore, it must be stated: "after words not denoting a measure (*aparimāṇa*), [there is no *ṅīp*] when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. If that much were stated, then in cases such as *dvibisti*, because *bisti* is a measure, the prohibition of *ṅīp* would not apply.
Therefore, there is also the inclusion of *bista* and so forth.

(474) *Kāṇḍāntāt kṣetre* [Pāṇini 5.1.23]. After a *dvigu* compound ending in *kāṇḍa*, when it denotes a field (*kṣetra*), [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied]. The rules "after a *dvigu*" and "not when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix" (*na taddhitalukī*) are understood to carry over.

Thus he says: "In the field, that which... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "two *kāṇḍas*": the traditional rule (*smṛti*) states that a staff measuring sixteen *aratnis* in length is called a *kāṇḍa*. In the analysis of the compound as "that whose measure is two *kāṇḍas*" (*dve kāṇḍe pramāṇam asyāḥ*), the term *dvikāṇḍa* forms a *dvigu* compound according to the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*). When this [term] refers to a field...
The inclusion of the substantive "field-division" (*kṣetrabhakti*) is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that it might be neuter.

He says "when *dvayasa* follows a measure" (*pramāṇe dvayasac*) in order to demonstrate the elision of the secondary suffix (*taddhita-luk*). Nor is the mention of the word-final (*anta-grahaṇa*) redundant, on the grounds that the sense of "ending in that" is obtained because *kāṇḍāt* functions as a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-viśeṣaṇa*).

This is to be suspected; for if there were apprehension regarding the inclusion of the limit (*anta*), then "in the field" (*kṣetre*) would be a qualifier of the stem *kāṇḍa* itself, because that is what is heard [in the rule]. Thus, one would obtain the meaning "from that which ends with the word *kāṇḍa* when it occurs in the sense of 'field'," and consequently, in the case of "a two-sectioned field-division" (*dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ*), [the suffix] would apply only to the word *dvikāṇḍa*.

Since the word *kāṇḍa* here denotes a field (*kṣetra*) rather than a measure (*pramāṇa*), the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* would not apply. Consequently, in the case of *dvikāṇḍī*, meaning "purchased for two fields measured by a *kāṇḍa*," the prohibition of *ṅīp* would occur only in this specific instance. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *anta* (end/limit) [in the rule] is necessary; thus we have *dvikāṇḍī*.
Regarding the word *rajju*: as before, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mātrac*, and by the rule *dvigor ṅīp*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

The intention is that because it is not a measure of land (*kṣetra*), the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] does not apply. Now, in the preceding sūtra *aparimāṇe*, is the word *parimāṇa* intended to mean any kind of delimiting factor whatsoever, or...

According to the Vārttika—"Unmāna is indeed measurement by height; parimāṇa is measurement from all sides; whereas pramāṇa is length"—that by which something is measured on all sides, both in height and in circumference, is *parimāṇa*; thus, it refers specifically to measures such as the *āḍhaka* and *kuḍava*, being distinguished from length (*āyāma*).

What is intended? Not the first; for if that were the case, in the analysis *dvau hastau pramāṇam asyāḥ* ("two cubits are its measure"), resulting in *dvihastā bhittiḥ* ("a wall two cubits long"), there would be no prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* when the suffix *mātrac* is elided as before.
Nor the second; for likewise...

Since the word *kāṇḍa* in the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.24] refers to a measure of length rather than a general measure, it is possible that the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* in the case of "a field-division consisting of two *kāṇḍas*" (*dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ*) would already be established by the rule "after a word denoting a measure" (*aparimāṇe*). Therefore, the prohibition of *ṅīp* after words ending in *kāṇḍa* applies only when referring to a field, and not otherwise.
In examples such as *dvikāṇḍī rajjuḥ*, it is for the purpose of restriction; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
(475) *puruṣāt pramāṇe 'nyatarasyām* |4|1|24|. From *puruṣāt*: the words *dvigoḥ*, *taddhitaluki*, and *ṅīp* are understood to follow from the previous rules.

He says this with the words beginning "pramāṇe yaḥ" (in the sense of measurement, *ya*). "Pramāṇa" means length (*āyāma*), according to the statement: "But *āyāma* shall be *pramāṇa*. "Two *puruṣas*"—this is because of the *Śulvasūtra*: "A *puruṣa* is five cubits (*hasta*) in length. In the analysis of the compound as "that which has two *puruṣas* as its measurement," [the suffix is applied] by the rule "taddhitārtha... (Pāṇini 2.1.51).

Thus ends the section on *dvigu* compounds. Regarding the suffix *mātrac*, which is prescribed by the rule "the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnac*, and *mātrac* are added after a word denoting measure" (*pramāṇe dvayasaj-daghnañ-mātracaḥ*), the elision (*luk*) occurs according to the rules "in the case of measure, [the suffix] *la*" and "after a *dvigu* compound, it is obligatory. Here, following the aforementioned method, since the height (*āyāma*) of a person constitutes a measure, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is permanently prohibited by the rule "not after a word denoting measure" (*aparimāṇe*).

This statement is for the purpose of providing an option when [the suffix] *prāpta* is applied. Others, however, hold that it is due to the elision (*luk*) of either *ṭhak* or *ṭhañ* by the rule *adhyardhapūrva-dvigor lug* (Pāṇini 5.1.28), following the rule *tadasya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57).
For in that context, in accordance with the subsequent sūtra, the word *parimāṇa* is understood to mean any measure or delimiting factor whatsoever.
Let us leave it at that for now, as they have said: "the moat is *dvipuruṣī* or *dvipuruṣā*.

This means it extends across two *puruṣas* [in width]. A moat (*parikhā*) is a body of water surrounding a fort for the purpose of its protection. Now, regarding the term *ūdhas*: in the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it refers to one whose udder is like a bowl (*kuṇḍa*).
The word *kuṇḍodhas* [is an example]. (476) *Ūdhaso’naṅ* [Pāṇini 5.4.131].
Regarding this, he states the specific rule: *ūdhaso’naṅ*. [This is derived] from the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇor an* [Pāṇini 5.4.113].

The term *bahuvrīhau*, which is carried over [from the previous rule], is transformed into the genitive case; it is qualified by the word *ūdhasaḥ*, and the rule applies to that which ends in this [suffix]. Thus he says: "of that which has *ūdhas* as its final member.
Although it occurs in the section on compound suffixes (*samāsānta*), it should be understood as a substitute (*ādeśa*) for the feminine marker *ṅīp* and so forth. Thus, it is not *iṅ*.

Regarding the word *kṛte*: [the suffix] *anaṅ* is added with the marker *ṅ* and the vowel *i*; the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). By the rule *ṭhṅcce’t*, the final *s* is replaced by *an*. Thus, when the form *kuṇjodhan* has been established, this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase *ḍāb-ḍīb-niṣedheṣu*: [this refers to] the optional *ḍāp* by the rule *ḍābubhābhyām*, and the suffix *ṭāp*.

The meaning is: when the optional *ṅīp* [by rule 4.1.27] applies due to the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*), and when both of those [the optional *ṅīp* and the mandatory *ṅīp*] are absent, there arises the possibility of the *ṅīp* prescribed by "from words ending in *ṛt* and *n*" (4.1.5), which is then blocked by the prohibition "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the *ṅīp*] after *tan* [is not applied]" (4.1.11).
(477) *Bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ* (4.1.25).
[The rule] "from a *bahuvrīhi* [compound]"—the term "having *ūdhas*" (*ūdhas*) is a qualifier of the *bahuvrīhi*; it is a rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*).

The term "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is supplied as a governing heading (*adhikṛta*). Thus he says: "ending in *ūdhas*. In the example *kuṇḍodhnī*, once *anaṅ* has been applied, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added; the intended meaning is that [the form results] by the rule "elision of *an*" (*allopo 'naḥ*). As for *ūdhas*:

The Amarakośa states that *klība* means "swollen. However, the result of the specific rule for the suffix *ṅīṣ* lies in the difference of accent (*svara*). The question "What is meant by 'in the feminine'? asks for what purpose the term "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule for *ṅīṣ*.
[The example] *kuṇḍodho dhainukam* has the analytical explanation (*vigraha*): "that whose udder (*ūdhah*) is like a vessel (*kuṇḍam*)."

The word *dhainukam* is used as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) to indicate its neuter gender; it means "a collection of cows. [This is derived] by the rule *acitahastidhenoṣṭhak*. Then, by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is added, resulting in vṛddhi of the first vowel (*ādivṛddhiḥ*), and its neuter gender is established through common usage (*lokāt*).
The point here is that because there is an absence of femininity (*strītva*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. Now, one might object: let it be so.

[Objection: Why should not the suffix *ṅīṣ* apply, and why should there not be *anaṅ*? For in the rule prescribing *anaṅ* for the word *ūdhas-*—which occurs in the section on compound-endings (*samāsānta*)—the condition "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is absent. To this, he says: "In that rule. This means that because of the supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "in the feminine" (*striyām*) in the rule prescribing *anaṅ* for *ūdhas-*. [This applies] to the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

What [is the result]? In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who has reached the udder" (*ūdhaḥ prāptā*), the compound is formed by the rule *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* (Pāṇini 2.1.24), resulting in *prāptodhāḥ*.
(478) [The suffix] *ṅīp* is applied after a numeral or an indeclinable [ending in a consonant], according to Pāṇini 4.1.26.

*Saṅkhyāvyayāder ṅīp*: The meaning is that the suffix *ṅīp* occurs for feminine nouns ending in *ūdhas* when preceded by a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṅīṣ*; specifically, it is an exception to the rule *bahuvrīher ūdhaso ṅīṣ*. There is a distinction regarding the accent (*svara*).

He provides an example starting with *saṅkhyā* (numeral): *dvyūdhnī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "she who has two udders. [The rule] "only after a *bahuvrīhi*" means that the word *bahuvrīheḥ* continues [from the previous rule]. [The example] *ūdho'tikrāntā* (one who has passed beyond the udder) is a compound formed by the rule: "Words such as *ati* [form a compound] with a word in the second case when meaning 'having gone beyond' and so forth."
Because it is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. For this very reason, neither *anaṅ* nor *ṅīṣ* applies.

(Pāṇini 4.1.27) "And [the suffix *ṅīp* applies] after [compounds] ending in *dāman* and *hāyana*. From the sūtra "after [words] beginning with a numeral" and "the suffix *ṅī*," the word *ṅī* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*).

He says this with the words "of *saṅkhyā* etc. The inclusion of the term "avyaya" (indeclinable), however, does not carry over, because it is not marked as svarita; such is the intention. Since the rule is already established by the fact that [the word] qualifies a *bahuvrīhi*, the inclusion of the word "anta" (end) is for the sake of clarity. In the phrase "ending in *dāman*," it refers to the word *dvidāman* when it ends in *dāman*.

In the case of *dvihāyanī*, although the suffix *ḍāp* would apply by the rule *ṭhḍābubhābhyām*, and the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṭhana upadhālopinaḥ*, and the prohibition of *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṭhano bahuvrīheḥ*— nevertheless, since the word ends in *hāyana* and is not feminine (*adanta*), *ṭāp* would apply; however, this is precluded by the rule *dāmahāyanāntācca*.

The meaning is "speech. Regarding the term *dvidāmnī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has two ropes" (*dve dāmanī yasyāḥ*). The intention is that when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, the rule "elision of the *an* of *ana*" (*allopo'naḥ*) applies. Now, one might ask: what is the obstacle to the continued application of the mention of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*)? To this he says: "regarding the mention of the indeclinable. The example is *uddāmā*. [The analysis is: "that from which the rope has departed" (*utkrāntaṃ dāma yasyāḥ*).

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "Even the prohibition of *ḍāp*. By the word "even" (*api*), the suffix *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule "after a word ending in *ṭhan*, when there is a penultimate vowel" (*upadhā*) is included;

for when a term is mentioned, even that which is otherwise meaningless is understood. Now he gives an example of a word ending in *hāyana*: "a two-year-old girl" (*dvihāyanī bālā*). The analysis is: "she who has two years" (*dvau hāyanau yasyāḥ*).

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *hāyana* after the words *tri* and *catur* should be stated. The addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* are desired only when *hāyana* denotes age.
Now, regarding the form *trihāyaṇī*, since it consists of separate words (*bhinnapada*), the substitution of *ṇ* would not apply; therefore, he says: "after *tri* and *catur*" (*tricaturbhyām*).

[Objection: Even so, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply in the case of *dvihāyanā śālā*, and in the case of *trihāyanā śālā*, both *ṅīp* and *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would apply. To this, he says: "of that which denotes age.
[The word] "is desired" implies "by the author of the Bhāṣya."

(480) *kevalamāmakabhāgadheyapāpāparasamānāryakṛtasumaṅgalabheṣajācca* || 4.1.30 || The previous sūtra, "nityaṃ saṃjñāccchandasoḥ," is understood to carry over [into this rule]. [The suffix *cha* is applied after the words] *kevala*, *māmaka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *apara*, *samāna*, *āryakṛta*, *sumaṅgala*, and *bheṣaja*. [The result is that these words always take the feminine suffix *ī* when forming names or in Vedic usage.]
And thus, in this context, the mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) from the rule *upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām* is no longer operative.
From the rule *saṅkhyāvyayāder ṅīp*, the term *ṅīp* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). This is what he means by saying "from these":
*kevala*, *māmaka*, *bhāgadheya*, *pāpa*, *apara*, *samāna*, *āryakṛta*.
The meaning is "after these nine words beginning with *sumaṅgala* and *bheṣaja*. He cites examples from the Veda (*chandas*): *atha u ta indraḥ kevalīḥ* and *māmakī tanūḥ*.
The latter means "in my own [body]"; [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] by the rule *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca*.

In the expression *tavakamamakāvekavacane*, the substitution of *mamaka* occurs for the base [word *mad*]; then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending. [The mantra is: *mitrāvaruṇorbhāgadheyī stha*.
By the rule *bhāgarūpanāmabhyo dheyah*, the suffix *dheya* is added in its own sense (as a synonym). This refers to the word *bhāga*.

Even though [the base] is masculine, because "suffixes with an indicatory *ṭh* optionally differ from the gender and number of the original base (*prakṛti*) in certain instances," there is femininity, and thus the suffix *ṅīp*. [The form is] *tanvaḥ santu pāpīḥ*. In the sense of "she has sin" (*pāpa*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the word ending in the *arśa-ādi* *ac* suffix. [Then] *uta*...

"Maghavan has conquered [victory] over others. The word *apara* has its *pa* in the middle of the *pa*-class (*pavarga*). "Our intention is as one," and "the noble deed" (*āryakṛti*) should be sought in some Vedic text. Likewise with *sumaṅgalī*.
In the phrase "this bride is *sumaṅgalī*," the suffix *-in* (or *-vin*) is used in the sense of possession according to the rule "in the Veda, *-in* and *-vin* [are added]."

The suffix *ī* is applied. [In the phrase] "The auspicious one (*śivā*) is the remedy (*bheṣajā*) of Rudra," the word *bheṣaja* is well-known to denote a medicinal herb that removes disease; for this very reason, it also possesses femininity according to the rule. Alternatively, in the sense of "this belongs to the physician (*bhiṣaj*)," the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and by specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*), the vowel *i* is changed to *e*.

In the same way, the suffix *ṅīp* should be cited everywhere even for [words ending in] *saṃjñā*; for example, *sukevalā*, *māmikā*, and so forth—provided they are other than when used as proper names (*saṃjñā*) or in Vedic meters (*chandas*). Now, one might object that since the word ends in *aṇ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is already established by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, making the specific mention of *māmaka* redundant; to this he replies: "The mention of *māmaka*... [is for the sake of excluding the application of other suffixes].

The intention is that [the suffix] *ṅīp* is prohibited in the case of *asaṃjñā* (non-technical term) in common usage (*loke*). This should be understood similarly even though the word *bheṣaja* ends in the suffix *aṇ*. For this very reason, this has not been introduced in the section on Vedic grammar (*vaidikaprakriyā*).

(481) *antarvat-pativator nuk* | Pāṇini 4.1.32. Regarding *antarvat-pativator nuk*: it should be stated that *nuk* [is added]. The intention is that this is an augment (*āgama*), not a suffix (*pratyaya*), by virtue of the force of its being marked with *k* (*kit*). Because it is marked with *k*, it becomes an internal constituent part (*antāvayava*). Thus: *antarvat-n* and *pativat-n*.

This being the case, he says: "after vowels and *ṛt* [stems], *ṅīp*. Regarding "in the sense of *garbhiṇī*": the meaning is that for a woman who is pregnant and whose husband is alive, the two base-forms *antarvat* and *pativat* are prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātana*) by way of their connection with the suffix *nuṭ*. This is a Vārttika. In which [rule]?

To the question "What is being elided? he says: "Therein" (*tatra*). This means "between those two. The grammatical connection is as follows: in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound *antar-garbha* ("one who has a fetus within"), the suffix *matup*, which would otherwise not be applicable, is here prescribed by way of an irregular formation (*nipātana*). To the question "Why is the application of *matup* not otherwise applicable? he says: "Of the word *antaḥ*," and so forth, ending with "due to its absence."

In the sūtra *tadasyāstyasminniti matup*, the suffix *matup* is prescribed after a word ending in the nominative case that is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the verb "to be" (*asti*), and which primarily expresses the agent (*kartṛ*) as its grammatical factor (*kāraka*). For example, in cases such as *gaurasyāsti* ("he has a cow"), resulting in *gomān* ("cow-possessing"). In the present instance, [the word] ends in the nominative case.

The word *garbha* itself, having the agent (*kartṛ*) as its primary kāraka, is in grammatical apposition with the verb *asti*, and not the word *anta*; for since the latter has the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its primary kāraka, it is impossible for it to be in apposition with *asti*.

Therefore, the meaning is that the suffix *matup*, which would otherwise not apply here, is introduced by nipātana (irregular derivation). Consequently, [the rule] "after *mā* and after a vowel other than *u* in the penultimate position... [applies].

The meaning is that when the *m* of *matup* is changed to *v* by the rule "matorvaḥ," the resulting base form becomes *antarvat*.
