Regarding this change to *v*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "one who has an embryo" (*patirasyā asti*), because the *m* of *matup* is not preceded by a long vowel (*mā*) or a short vowel followed by a consonant (*adu-padhā*), the rule "mādupadhāyāḥ" does not apply.

The meaning is that the suffix *vat* is introduced as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) where it would otherwise not apply. Regarding the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*): since the suffix *matup* is introduced only in the sense of "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*), the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is simply "there is a jar in this house," and not "possessing a jar" (*ghaṭavat*) by means of *matup*. As for "the earth possessing a husband" (*patimatī pṛthivī*): [this applies] only in the case of one whose husband is living.
The meaning is that because of the elision of the *vat* suffix (*vatvanipātana*), there is an absence of *vat* here.
(482) *patyurno yajñasaṃyoge* | 4|1|33|. [The rule states:
"After *pati*, *na* [is substituted]. The word *pateḥ* is in the genitive case. In the term *naḥ*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

The term "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is understood as the governing rule (*adhikṛtam*). This is what he states with the words "of the word *pati*. Regarding the phrase "by means of sacrifice" (*yajñena*), this refers to a connection with sacrifice; that is, a connection by way of ownership together with the sacrifice. In other words, it means being the enjoyer of the fruit of the sacrifice.
This is what he states with the words "of that performed by him" (*tatkartṛkasya*). The meaning is "performed by Vasiṣṭha. Now, an objection:
It might be argued that since Vasiṣṭha alone is the performer of the sacrifice, it is appropriate for Vasiṣṭha alone to be the enjoyer of the fruit, and not even his wife;
for in injunctions such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*), the use of masculine terms indicates that only a man has the qualification (*adhikāra*).
To this, he says: "Because the husband and wife have joint qualification. And this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra.

For this very reason, in the Pūrvamīmāṃsā, in the first quarter (pāda) of the sixth chapter, in the section beginning with "Because of the mention of a specific gender, [the rite] is connected to males,

according to Aitiśāyana," and in the section beginning with "But for those who possess [their own] property, there would be a single performance because of the scriptural statement," [it is established that] the husband and wife [act together].
The joint application (*sahādhikāra*) has been established. This has been explained by us in detail in the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti*. (483) *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya* | Pāṇini 6.1.34.

The rule *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya* [Pāṇini 4.1.32] applies. The phrase *ṭhpatyunaḥ* is understood from the previous rule. The term *prātipadikāt*, which was understood from the preceding context, is modified here into the genitive case (*prātipadikasya*) and is qualified by the word *patyuḥ*; this results in the application of the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*).

The term *sapūrvasya* ("of that which has a preceding member") applies to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the word *pati*. The meaning is "together with its preceding constituent. This is what he expresses by saying "of that which ends in the word *pati*" and so forth. Even in the absence of a connection with a sacrifice (*yajña*), this is an optional rule (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*) for cases where [the feminine suffix] would otherwise not be applicable. Examples are *gṛhapatiḥ* (householder) and *gṛhapatnī* (housewife).

In the feminine gender, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṛn-nebhyo ṅīp*. Here, the meaning is that the word *gṛhapati* has the word *pati* as its final member and is accompanied by the preceding constituent *gṛha*. Nor should one fear the prohibition [of *ṅīp*] based on the rule "with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) containing [the letter] *ṛ*," because of the specific rule "and *śūdrā*, provided it is not preceded by *mahat*."

For it has been stated that the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.3] "striyām" (in the feminine) does not apply to that [suffix] when it is governed by the heading [of the sūtra]. Now, one might object: in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *dṛḍhaḥ patiḥ yasyāḥ*, the forms *dṛḍhapatiḥ* and *dṛḍhapatnī* are desired with an optional substitution of the suffix *ṅīp*, yet that is not possible because of the governing heading "anupasarjanāt" (when not a secondary member).

Because the word *pati* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) here. Nor should it be argued that the rule "from a non-subordinate" (*anupasarjanāt*) does not apply here; for its application is necessary here as well, so that it may carry over to the subsequent rules. Therefore, he says: "of a non-subordinate," etc. However—

Regarding the phrase *tadantasya* ("of that which ends in it"): since the rule *sapūrvāt* applies to a word ending in *pati*, it is logical that this [suffix] should serve as its qualifier; for only after the understanding of the intermediate sentence-meaning has occurred does the qualifier "not being a subordinate element" (*anupasarjana*) become operative, and at that time, because [the suffix] is heard as belonging to that which is preceded by something else (*sapūrva*), it is by that very [suffix] [that the qualification is established].

The sense is that once the relationship has been established, there is no further evidence for the application of the word *pati* (husband) subsequently. "By that" means by [the fact that] the quality of not being a subordinate term (*anupasarjanatva*) is a qualifier of the word ending in *pati*. Having carried forward the mention of the connection with a sacrifice (*yajñasaṃyoga*).

To the question, "Why would it not be a case of *prāptavibhāṣā* (an option regarding what is already established)? he says: "*vṛṣalapatnī*. [The analysis is as follows: a *pati* is one who protects (*pāti*) or guards (*rakṣati*); thus, the compound is analyzed as "the wife (*strī*) of a *vṛṣala* (outcaste). Since the eligibility of *Śūdras* for sacrifice was refuted in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, here, due to the absence of a connection with sacrifice, this [option] is simply not applicable.
The sense is that you have not explained [this]. He raises an objection with the word "atha" (now/then).
The word "atha" indicates the commencement of an objection, or it indicates a question.
As Amara states: "The words *atha* and *atho* are used in the senses of auspiciousness, immediately following, commencement, question, and totality. [He says] "when they are separate."

The meaning is "in a compound sentence. Consequently, because it is preceded by *sa* and lacks the augment *ṭi*, there is no optional substitution of *n* by the present sūtra. Furthermore, because there is no connection with a sacrifice (*yajña-saṃyoga*), there is no application of the preceding sūtra. Thus, the objection is raised that the phrase "the wife of an uninitiated *vṛṣala*" is untenable. To this, [the author] says: "If you object thus, it is not so. You raise this objection.
The meaning is that this is not logical. Regarding the phrase "like a wife" (*patnīvat*):

the word *patnī*, which is etymologically derived for a twice-born woman associated with a sacrifice, is applied here to a Śūdra woman—even though she is not associated with a sacrifice—by way of a secondary (metaphorical) usage based on the presence of dharma such as the taking of the hand in marriage. For example:
The use of the feminine form *gaṅgāyām* refers to the bank (*tīra*). And it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"It is established by way of comparison, as in 'the wife of Tuṣajaka'. As for the phrase "or else" (*yadvā*), this is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

Regarding the feminine gender, there are no *kvip*-derived words whose base is a word ending in *kvip* that functions as the stem for the suffix *ācārakviP*; this is because it has already been stated in the rule *ṭhañ anupasarjanāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.14] that [the suffix applies] to such bases. As for the question "Why [is the condition] *sapūrvaḥ* (preceded by another word) [stated]?", since the word *pati-* is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the status of being "ending in that" (*tadanta*) is obtained [for the whole compound].

The question is: since a word ending in *pati* is invariably preceded by something else, for what purpose is the phrase "preceded by something else" (*sapūrvasya*) stated? [The example is] *gavāṃ patiḥ strī*. The meaning is "mistress" or "protector.

The point is that because it is not a compound, the word *gavām* does not constitute the prior member (*pūrvāvayava*). Even though... [where] *ṭhi*... (Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available text.)

In the case of *saṅghāta*, if the preceding portion (*pūrva-bhāga*) is a word (*pada*), and if it is designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "only the compound" [is so designated], the entire aggregate *gavāṃ patiḥ* lacks the status of a nominal stem despite ending in the suffix *-pati*. Consequently, the optional substitution of *n* for *t* does not occur here. Nevertheless, *gavām*...

The intention is that in the word *patiḥ*, since the word *pati* itself possesses the status of being "designated as such" (*vyapadeśivat*), the rule [Pāṇini 6.4.143] would optionally apply the substitution of *n* for the final *t*; therefore, the statement *sapūrvasya* is provided to prevent that.
However, in reality, because of the prohibition—"the status of being designated as such does not apply to what is not a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*)—it does not apply here.

They say that because the word *kevalapati* lacks the suffix *-pati* at its end, the option regarding the substitution of *natva* is already established; therefore, the inclusion of the term *sapūrvasya* is for the sake of clarity. (484) *nityaṃ sapatnyādiṣu* 4.1.35.

"Always in the case of *sapatnī* and so forth. This is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). The meaning is that, for the sake of establishing that [form], there is always a substitution of *n* when the domain is *sapatnī* and so forth. "As an exception to the previous option" means that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the option provided by the rule "vibhāṣā sapūrvasya. Precisely because of the force of its formulation (*ārambha-sāmarthyāt*), [it sets aside the previous rule].

Since its permanence is already established, the inclusion of the word "nitya" (permanent) is for the sake of clarity. Now, one might object: if it is intended that "she who has the same husband is a *sapatnī*," then the substitution of *sa-* for the word *samāna-* would be untenable; therefore, the *bahuvrīhi* compound should be formed with the word *saha-* itself as a synonym for "similar. And thus:
Since the substitution of *sa-* for *sama-* is optional by the rule *ṭhvopasarjanasya*, he says: "of *samāna*.

In this list (*gaṇa*), *samāna*, *eka*, *vīra*, *bhrātṛ*, and *putra* are recited as beginning with *samāna*. Therefore, the word *samāna* here refers to that which is intended in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. And because of a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), its [substitution] is constant.

"Sabhāva" means "state" (bhāva). "Samāna-pati" [is the compound]: here, the word *samāna* is a synonym for *eka* (one), while the word *pati* is a synonym for the term *bhartṛ* (husband) based on marriage. Regarding "vīrapatnī": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose husband (*pati*) is a hero (*vīra*). The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule beginning with "sapatny-ādi."

(485) *pūtakrator ai ca* | 4|1|36 | Regarding *pūtakrator ai ca*: the word *ṭhai* is in the nominative case with its case-ending elided. The meaning is that after the word *pūtakratu*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* shall be applied, and the final phoneme of the base shall be replaced by *ai*.
This set of three sūtras is intended to apply only when there is a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).

"This set of three sūtras" refers to this Vārttika. The meaning is that the triad of sūtras beginning with *pūtakratoḥ* applies only when [the term] denotes a woman by virtue of her connection with a male. For example: *pūtakrāyī*. [The compound is analyzed as: one by whom the sacrifice (*kratu*) has been purified (*pūta*).

He is *pūtakratuḥ*; for the sense of "his wife," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, whereby the vowel *u* after the letter *t* becomes *ai*, and that [ai] undergoes the substitution of *āy*. This is the intended meaning. He states the purpose of the rule *puṃyoge* with the words "by whom.
[The rule applies to] *vṛṣākapi*, *agni*, and so on. The word *ca* (and) is understood from the previous rule; thus he says: "of these."

(486) *vṛṣākapy-ajhi-kusita-kusidānām udāttaḥ* |4|1|37|. In the case of *vṛṣākapāyī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; the final vowel of the base (*prakṛti*) is replaced by the acute-accented *aikāra* (*ai*), which undergoes the substitution *āy*.
Since this [substitute] takes the place of the *ekāra* (*e*), its *ākāra* (*ā*) is also acute-accented. The rest remains unaccented (*anudātta*).

By the rule "except for one syllable," the remaining *ac* vowels are *anudātta* (unaccented). Why [specify] "acute" (*udātta*)? Because according to the rule "when there is a light vowel at the end, or when there are two [light vowels], or when there are many heavy ones," the word *vṛṣākapi* has its acute accent on the middle syllable, as in:
"O Indrāṇī, I do not rejoice in the friendship of Vṛṣākapi. [This applies] when there is one [heavy syllable] at the end.

The meaning of that [rule] is that when there is a single *laghu* (light syllable), or when two *laghu* syllables exist, the preceding heavy (*guru*) vowel of a word with many syllables (*bahvac*) shall be acute (*udātta*). Consequently, once the vowel *ā* after the letter *ṣ* has become acute, the remaining vowels become grave (*anudātta*) according to the rule "a word is grave except for one [acute] vowel"; such is the established state of affairs. And thus:

Because the vowel *ā* following the letter *p* is unaccented (*anudātta*), the *e* that would replace it in its place should also be unaccented. Consequently, the *ā* that serves as its substitute (*ādeśa*) would likewise be unaccented. Therefore, in this case, there is a rule for prescribing the acute accent (*udātta*). As in the word *Āgnāyī*, and in such passages as "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*).

The word *agni* is udātta (accented) on its final syllable; from that, the suffix *ṅīp* is added, and the vowel *ai* is substituted for the final portion of the base. Since this substitution occurs, by the principle of proximity (*āntarya*), it is itself udātta. Consequently, because the udātta quality of the vowel *ā*—which results from the substitution of *āy* for that [final *i*]—is established, the term "udātta" cannot apply to the word *agni*.

Because there is no purpose [for such a derivation]. Regarding *kusitāyī* and *kusidāyī*: *kusita* and *kusida* are unanalyzed nominal stems (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) which are names of specific deities;

by the *phiṭ-svara* rule, they are oxytone (accented on the final syllable). From these, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and the final vowel *ai* is substituted for the end of the stem. And that...

It is established in the *Vṛtti* and other treatises that because the word *bhavat* is necessarily acute (*udātta*), the acute accent cannot apply to the words *kusita* and *kusida* either. For this very reason, he says: "but not with a long vowel in the middle.

For if there were a long vowel in the middle, then by the rule "when a light syllable stands at the end," the word would have an acute accent on the middle syllable according to the prescribed accentuation.

Since the vowel *a* following the letter *d* is unaccented (*anudātta*), the *ai* that replaces it would also be unaccented, and consequently, the *āy* that replaces it would likewise result in being unaccented; therefore, because the inclusion of the term "accented" (*udātta*) is necessary even there to prevent this outcome, the contradiction with the cited passages from the *Vṛtti* and other texts is evident.
Such is the intended meaning.
(487) *manor au vā* | P. 4.1.38. Regarding *manor au vā*: the words *ai ca*, *udāttaḥ*, and *ṅīp* are carried over [from previous rules].

He says this: "of the word *manu*"; and "or [the vowel] *e* may be acute. The meaning is that either the diphthong *au* or the acute vowel *e* may occur. By the compound designation "acute *e*," it is indicated that the word "acute" does not connect with the diphthong *au*; and this is stated in both the *Vṛtti* and the *Padamañjarī*.

This is clear. By the word "and" (ca), the suffix *ṅīp* is conjoined with the vowels *e* and *o*. Thus he says: "by those two. The meaning is that [the suffix] is prescribed only by way of conjunction with the vowels *e* and *o*. Consequently, it is understood that in the absence of both of those, the suffix *ṅīp* also does not occur.

The meaning is that this is due to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating: "Those taught in conjunction [with another element] either function together or cease together. This technical rule is established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *pūtakrator ai ca*. As for the form *manāyī*, it occurs in passages such as *yad vai kiṃ ca manur avadat*.

The word *manu* has its initial vowel (*ma*) as udātta by the rule "that which ends in *ṭha*, *ñ*, or *n* is always [udātta]. This is because, with the term *niṭ* continuing from the rule "in the sense of grain, [the suffix] *niṭ*," the suffix *upa* is prescribed after the root *man* by the rule "after *śṛ*, *svṛ*, *snih*, etc. Consequently, by the remaining accent (i.e., the *anudātta*), the vowel *u* following the *n* is *anudātta*. In place of that [vowel], the udātta vowel *ai* [is substituted].
The intention is that its substitute is *āy* and [the suffix] *ṅīp*. In the case of *manāvī*, the vowel *au* is indeed unaccented (*anudātta*).

Regarding *manuḥ*: it has already been stated that in the absence of both the *ai* and the *āu*, the *ṅīp*—which is taught as being conditioned by their presence (*saṃniyoga-śiṣṭa*)—also does not occur.

(488) *varṇādanudātātopadhāto naḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.39. The words *varṇāt*, *anu*, *veti*, and *ṅīp* are understood from the preceding rules. *Anudātāt* is a qualifier of *varṇāt*; it is a *tadanta-vidhi* (applying to that which ends in such a vowel), and *topadhāt* is likewise.

The word *varṇāt* is connected here; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has *takāra* as its *upadhā*" (penultimate letter). The vowel *a* after the *t* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the term *varṇāt*, it does not mean "from the word *varṇa*" according to the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya* (a word denotes its own form), because it is impossible for [the word *varṇa*] to have *t* as its *upadhā*. Rather, the meaning is "from a word denoting a phoneme."
This is intended [to be understood as follows]: the term *varṇāt* is a qualifier of the term *prātipadikāt*;
thus, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in [the former]. In the expression *ṭha*, the genitive case indicates "of the letter *t*.
In the word *na*, the vowel *a* after the *n* is for the sake of pronunciation; the meaning is simply "the letter *n*."

He says this with the words beginning "denoting a color" (*varṇavācī*), etc. Regarding the rule "after that [suffix], provided it is not a secondary member" (*tadantādanupasarjanāt*): the sense is that the term *anupasarjana* (not being a secondary member), which is understood from the previous context, connects with the word ending in a vowel (*varṇānte*), and not with the word "color" (*varṇāt*) itself. Examples are *enī* and *etā*, meaning "white. From the word *eta*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and the letter *t* [is elided].

And there is the letter *na*. In the absence of the suffix *ṅīp*, there is only *ṭāp*; however, the substitution of *na* does not occur, because it is taught as being conditioned by the presence of *ṅīp*. Scholars of ritual such as Dhūrtasvāmin, Bhavasvāmin, Rūdradatta, and others, who are commentators on the Kalpasūtras, state that the word *eta* is a synonym for "white."

Regarding "rohiṇī rohitā": the word *rohita* is a synonym for the color red. When the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied and the *ṇatva* (nasalization) occurs, it becomes *rohiṇī*; in the absence of that, the suffix *ṭāp* is used. He says "of colors" (*varṇānām*) in order to indicate that [the word] ends in an unaccented vowel. In the expression "ending in *ta*" (*tānta*), the letter *a* following the *ta* is for the sake of pronunciation.
The meaning is that for words ending in *ta*, *ṇa*, *ti*, *ni*, and *t*, the first syllable is udātta (acute-accented). Examples in order are: *etaḥ*, *śoṇaḥ*, *śitiḥ*, *pṛśniḥ*, and *pṛṣat*.
Since the vowel *e* in the word *eta* and the vowel *o* in the word *rohita* are udātta by this rule, [the subsequent vowels] are *anudātta* (grave-accented).

The meaning is that, according to the accentuation rule of the learned (*śiṣṭasvara*), because the remaining syllables are *anudātta* (unaccented) following the rule "except for one syllable" (*padamekavarjam*), the final syllable is *anudātta*. Now, an objection might be raised: since the term *anupasarjana* (not being a secondary member) is understood [from a previous sūtra], it is more appropriate for it to qualify the specific phonetic form (*varṇaviśeṣaṇa*) as it is heard, rather than [qualifying the base]. However...

Therefore, he says "tryeṇyā" [to show] that it is a qualifier of the final phoneme obtained through the rule of *tadanta-vidhi*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has these three white constituent parts," the word *tryeta* is formed;
however, because the word *eta*—which denotes a color—is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in that compound, the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *naṭ* would not apply.

The point is that if the term *anupasarjanāt* (not being a subordinate member) were a qualifier of the final phoneme (*varṇānta*), then there would be no fault because the word *tryeta* is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). Regarding the word *śalalyā*:
it is well known among ritualists (*yājñika*) that the quill-like hair growing on the body of a specific animal called the porcupine (*śalyaka*) is termed *śalalī*.

Regarding the term *gṛhya*: it refers to a specific class of *kalpasūtras* composed by Āpastamba, Āśvalāyana, and others, based on the etymology "that in which [rites] are grasped (*gṛhyante*) or collected (*saṃgṛhyante*)—namely, those rites to be accomplished with the *aupāsana* fire.
The *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in the word *tryeṇyā* is an archaic Vedic feature; however, in the Yajurveda, it appears as *tri-eṇyā śalalyā*.

The reading "nivartayete" is found [in the text]. There, the analysis (vigraha) is: "that which has these three white things. Bhaṭṭabhāskara states in his Vedabhāṣya that the absence of the *yaṇ* substitution and the presence of the *ṇa* sound are archaic (*ārṣa*).
Now, [one might object]: "Does not the rule 'ṭhvarṇānāṃ taṇati' [apply]?"

Because the word *śveta* has its first syllable acute (*udātta*), it must end with an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel according to the remaining accentual rule; therefore, he says: "of *ghṛta* and so forth. "From this alone" means that the word "from this" (*ataḥ*) continues from the rule "the suffix *ṭāp* follows [stems ending in] *aj* or *at*" (*ajādyataṣṭāp*). "The feminine *śiti*"—[in the lexicon] it is said: "the words *śiti* and *dhavala* mean white."
Thus says Amara. Regarding the word *piśaṅgī*:

although the word *piśaṅga* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) according to the rule "when the final syllable is light" (*laghāvante*), and thus, by the accentuation of the remaining syllables, ends with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*), the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply because it lacks a penultimate *t*.
Therefore, the addition of *ṅīp* is prescribed [by this rule]. This is according to the rule "from any other [than those ending in short *i*, etc.], *ṅīṣ*" (*anyato ṅīṣ*).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṅīṣ* suffix that will be mentioned later; there is a distinction regarding the accent (*svara*). [The rule] "not for *asita* and *palita*" is stated.
Regarding the word *asita*: this is a Vārttika. Since the word *asita* denotes the color black (*kṛṣṇa*), [the following applies].
Since the word *palita* denotes "white," the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṭhvarṇād anudātād*, and thus its feminine form would end in *-ā*;
however, here both the *ṅīp* and the substitution of *natva* (the change of *t* to *n*) are prohibited. Regarding the statement *chandasi knameke*, this is also a Vārttika.
Other teachers maintain that there is a substitution of *kn* for the *t* of *asita* and *palita* in conjunction with the suffix *ṅīp*.

The meaning is "so desiring. Regarding *asiknī*: from the word *asita*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied; when *takāra* is replaced by *knādeśa*, there is elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. Others maintain that the substitute *kn* is indeed ending in *nakāra*. Similarly for *paliknī*. Amara states: "Palita is the whiteness caused by old age."
Now, since the word *avadāta* denotes a color according to the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "white, bright, fair" (*sito gauraḥ*), and because it is oxytone by the rule *laghāvante* (Pāṇini 6.1.197),
it follows that it is anudātta-final; furthermore, since it has *t* as its penultimate letter (*topadha*), [the suffix *ṅīp* would apply] by the rule *varṇādanudātāttād anudāttāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.39).
Since it might be thought that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the substitution of *natva* (of *n*) would apply here, he says: "But the word *avadāta*...

The sense is that the word *avadāta* is derived from the root *daip* (meaning 'to purify') with the suffix *kta*, as established by the lexicon which states: "The word *avadāta* means white, yellow, or pure. And this...

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṭhpuṃyogādākhyāyām*. As for the lexicon stating "avadāta means white or fair," it should be understood as being based on the common property of purity (*śuddhatva*). (489) *anyato ṅīṣ* [Pāṇini 4.1.40].

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after [a word] other than [those previously mentioned]. The suffix *tasi* occurs after a word in the fifth case. From the words "after a color" (*varṇāt*), "after a word with an unaccented vowel" (*anudātāt*), and "after a word having *t* as its penultimate letter" (*topadhāt*), these are carried over [as governing conditions]. In that context, when there is an expectation for what "other than" (*anyataḥ*) refers to, it connects with "having *t* as its penultimate letter" (*topadhāt*) as its correlative—that is, "other than" [a word] having *t* as its penultimate letter.
He says this: "from [a word] ending in *t* and having a penultimate *u*, etc. Regarding *kalmāṣī*: it means "of variegated color. Amara states:
"The words *citra*, *kirmīra*, *kalmāṣa*, *śabala*, and *etā* denote the variegated (*karbura*). Regarding *sāraṅgī*:
Amara states, "the word *sāraṅga* is used in the masculine for the variegated. [In the rule *phiṣo'nta udāttaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.195),] the final vowel of a word ending in *phiṣ* is acute.

This dispels the suspicion that [the word] ends with an udātta accent—[as indicated by the rule] "laghau. This sūtra was explained during the commentary on the sūtra "vṛṣākapī. [The examples] "kṛṣṇā" and "kapilā":
the sense is that these two are antodātta (accented on the final syllable) according to the Phiṭ-svara rules.

(490) Pāṇini 4.1.41: *ṣidgaurādibhyaśca*. Those which have the marker *ṣ* are called *ṣit*; those beginning with *gaura* are called *gaurādi*. This is a *dvandva* compound meaning "those that are *ṣit* and those beginning with *gaura*. Regarding the example *nartakī*: [it is derived from] the root *nṛt*.

In the word *nartaka*, derived from the root *nṛt* with the suffix *ṣvun* (Pāṇini 3.1.145) for the sense of "one who performs bodily movements" (*gātravikṣepa*), the letter *ṣ* of the suffix is *it* by Pāṇini 1.3.6 (*ṣaḥ pratyayasya*), and the letter *n* is also *it* by Pāṇini 1.3.3 (*halantyam*).

By Pāṇini 7.1.1 (*yuvoranākau*), the substitution of *ak* occurs; then there is the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*) and the replacement of *a* by *r* (*raparatvam*). From the word *nartaka*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, which supersedes the suffix *ṭāp*.

The intention is that there is an elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "yasyeti ca. Regarding the word *gaurī*: the meaning is "white," because it has an udātta accent on the final syllable according to the *phiṭ*-sūtras; the intention is that this is a prescriptive rule here, as the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule "anyato ṅīṣ" would otherwise not have occurred. Alternatively, this is a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*). [As in: "Umā Kātyāyanī."
"Gaurī" is defined by Amara; the Smṛti states, "She who is ten years old shall be Gaurī.
[The suffix] *vā* is used after *anaḍuh* in the feminine:
*anaḍuhī*, *anaḍvāhī*. This means "the female of the ox" (*anaḍuhas strī*). [It is derived from] "she who carries the cart" (*ano vahati*).

Or it is etymological (*yaugika*). Because of the specific rule (*nipātana*) in the *gaura*-group, there is an optional application of the suffix *ṅīp*. Thus, the statement "it should be stated that for the word *anuḍuh* in the feminine, there is optionally *ām*" need not be made; this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "and *pippalyādi*": here [the group consists of] *gaura*, *matsya*, *manuṣya*, *śṛṅga*, *gavaya*, *haya*, [and so on].
Having recited *mukaya*, *gautama*, *anaḍvāhī*, *anaḍuhī*, *taruṇa*, *taluna*, and *śvan*,
and having stated "and *pippalyādayaḥ*," [the list] *pippalī*, *harītakī*, *kośātakī*, *pṛthivī*, *mātāmahī*, and so forth, is recited. Regarding the word *pippalī*:
Even though these words denote genus (*jāti*), they are included here because the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply due to their being restricted to the feminine gender.

As for the word *śvan*, since the suffix *ṅīp* would have applied by the rule "after *tṛn*, *kan*, and *neṣṭṛ* etc. (*tṛnnebhyaḥ*), it is included here for the sake of the suffix *ṅīṣ*; there is a difference in accent [between the two]. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); that is to say, it means "beginning with *gaura*."
The purpose of including [the group] beginning with *pippalī* as a sub-group (*avāntaragaṇa*) should be considered.
(491) *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* | P.
6.4.149. Regarding the word *matsya*, there is a specific rule (*viśeṣa*) due to the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group.
To demonstrate this, he says: *sūryatiṣṭhāgastya*. From the rule *ṭhḍhea lopo'kardvāḥ*, the word *lopa* (elision) is understood by way of anuvṛtti. The term *ya* is in the genitive case;

the governing term *aṅgasya* (of the base) is understood as a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and that [genitive] refers back to the preceding *upadhāyām* (in the penultimate position). [Thus, the meaning is: of the base... in its penultimate position.
It is understood that there should be elision of the *yakāra* which has become a substitute for the *upadhā*.

Furthermore, the rule "sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām" also connects with the *yakāra* as a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and not as a qualifier of the *aṅga*; this is what he expresses by saying "of the *aṅga*" and so forth.
(Regarding the rule) "matsyasya ṅyām":
[this means] "of *matsya* before the feminine suffix *ṅī*. Therefore, it does not apply here: *matsyasyedaṃ* = *mātsyam*.
(The rule) "sūryāgastyayośche ca ṅyāṃ ca" [means that the final vowel of *sūrya* and *agastya* is replaced by *u* before the suffix *cha* and before the feminine suffix *ṅī*].
And [the suffix] *cha* is applied after *sūrya* and *agastya*. [Examples: *saurīyaḥ*, *saurī*; *āgastīyaḥ*, *āgastī*.
But not here: *sauryam*, *āgastyam*.
It should be stated that when the suffix *aṇ* follows *tiṣya* and *puṣya* as names of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), there is the elision of *ya*.

The word *tiṣye* [is used]. The meaning is that when the suffix *aṇ*—prescribed by the rules "time joined with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*) and "the suffix *aṇ* after *saṃdhivelā*, etc., seasons, and lunar mansions" (*sandhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo 'ṇ*)—follows, there is the elision of *y* in *tiṣya* and *puṣya*.
Among these, the elision of *y* in *tiṣya* is restricted [by the present rule], whereas for *puṣya*, it is prescribed where it was previously unobtained.

*Taiṣa* refers to the full moon day conjoined with the asterism Tiṣya, or that which occurs during Tiṣya; likewise for *pauṣa*. It does not mean "belonging to Tiṣya" or "belonging to Puṣya" (as in *taiṣya* or *pauṣya*). Regarding the word *matsī*: from the word *matsya*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the *gaurādi* group, resulting in the elision of *y*, and then the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*.

Now, regarding the rule *ṭhpitṛvyamātulamātāmahapitāmahāḥ*, the words *mātāmaha* and *pitāmaha* are derived as irregular forms (*nipātita*) when the analysis is *mātuḥ pitā* (mother’s father) and *pituḥ pitā* (father’s father), with the suffix *ḍāmahac* added to *mātṛ* and *pitṛ* and the elision of the final vowel by *ṭilopa*. In that context, [one might ask] what the mother’s mother or the father’s mother is.
In the *Vigraha* [commentary], the status of being *ṣit* is prescribed for the suffixes *ḍām* and *hañ* by the rule "mātari ṣic ca.

Consequently, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is established precisely through this prescription of *ṣit*-ness, there is no need to include the word *mātāmahī* in the *Gaurādi* list. Nor should it be argued that the rule "mātari ṣic ca" should simply not be composed; for...
Regarding the word *pitāmahī*, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is required there, he says: "in the case of *mātṛ*" [and] "*daṃṣṭrā*.

In *daṃṣṭrā*, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied to the root *daṃś* by the rule *dābhyo niśāse*. The point here is that even though the suffix is marked with *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. [This concerns] the *yakāra* which has become the penultimate (*upadhā*) in the limbs of *sūrya* and so forth.

However, "lopa" (elision) has not been explained [in this context], for if that were the case, the form "saurī balākā" (the crane belonging to the sun) would not be established. In the sense of "being in the same direction as the sun," when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tena-ekadik*, the resulting stem ending in *aṇ*—and not the word "sūrya"—would be the base (*aṅga*) before the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; thus, that form would remain unestablished. This is the statement [of the objection].
However, [the rule] finds its application in the case of *sūrī* in the word *kuntī*; the details are explained elsewhere.

(492) Pāṇini 4.1.42: *jānapada-kuṇḍa-goṇa-sthala-bhājana-ānaka-kāla-nīla-kuśa-kāmuka-kabarād vṛtty-amatra-āvapana-akṛtrima-aśrāṇā-sthaulya-varṇa-anācchādana-yo-vikāra-maithunecchā-keśaveśeṣu*. [The suffix *cha* is applied after these words to form feminine nouns denoting: a profession (*vṛtti*), a vessel (*amatra*), a place for sowing (*āvapana*), something not artificial (*akṛtrima*), a warm meal (*aśrāṇā*), thickness (*sthaulya*), color (*varṇa*), an unlined garment (*anācchādana*), a modification of wool (*yo-vikāra*), a desire for sexual intercourse (*maithunecchā*), and a particular arrangement of hair (*keśaveśa*).
*Jānapada*: the word *jānapada* and so forth, ending with *kabarā*, constitutes a single compound.
The ablative case (*pañcamī*) arises from a collective dvandva compound. Regarding *jānapadī*: it means "one who exists in a country" (*janapade bhavā*).

Regarding *vṛttiśced*: it means "if she is understood as a livelihood" (*jīvikā gamyā cet*). Now, [one might object] that since [the suffix] *añ* applies because it is [a member of] the *utsādi* group...

Since the formation would be established by the suffix *ṅīp* alone, the prescription of *ṅīṣ* would be useless; therefore, he says: "Because of its being *utsādi*. The meaning is that if *ṅīp* were applied, the first syllable would be udātta according to the rule "anudātau suppitau," whereas if *ṅīṣ* were applied, the final syllable would be udātta due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Thus there is a difference. As for *kuṇḍī*, it means a cooking pot (*piṭhara*).

"Sthālī, ukhā, and kuṇḍa" [are synonyms for a cooking vessel], according to Amara. And since "pātra, amatra, and bhājana" [are also synonyms], the word *kuṇḍa* may also be feminine by virtue of the rule prescribing the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Viśva states: "In the case of a cooking pot (*piṭhara*), however, *kuṇḍa* is not masculine. Regarding the phrase "the *kuṇḍas*": the meaning is "those to be burned. That very thing...

He clarifies this with the words "in the burning of the hut" (*kuḍi-dāhe*). Regarding the phrase "of the guru": its meaning is that the suffix *ap* occurs after a verbal root ending in a consonant that possesses a *guru* (heavy syllable), in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*), when used in the feminine. Now, one might object:
"A son born from a paramour while the husband is alive is a *kuṇḍa*; one born while the husband is dead is a *golaka*."
One might ask: why could the word *kuṇḍa*, which denotes a specific human caste, not also serve as a counter-example?

To this he says: "But that which... [referring to the verse]. Regarding the phrase "characterized by a genus" (*jātilakṣaṇa*): the meaning is "having a genus as its cause," based on the rule *jāter astrīviṣayāt*.
Now, one might object: even in this case, the referent...

Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established by the rule for feminine gender based on genus (*jāti*) following the word *kuṇḍa*, that specific statement would be redundant. Nor should it be argued that the statement is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) to ensure that *ṅīṣ* occurs only when referring to a vessel (*amatra*); for if that were the case, *ṅīṣ* would not arise when the word denotes a particular class of humans. Therefore, he says: "For in the case of a vessel... (*amatre hi*).
By the rule *jāter astrīviṣayād ady-anta-upadhāt*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed for [words denoting] a genus (*jāti*) that are not invariably feminine.

However, the word *kuṇḍa* is invariably feminine when it refers to a vessel (*amatra*), because it is accepted that "invariable femininity" consists in the word's application to the feminine gender without depending on another word. [As an example: *kuṇḍī* [is used] in the sense of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).

And from the Medinīkośa: "The word *pumān* [is used] for a paramour, a husband, a wife, and a son. Thus, in the case of the word *kuṇḍa*, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is applicable by virtue of it being a genus name (*jāti*)—is simply enjoined, and not restricted.
Therefore, the point is that even though it denotes a human species, the application of *ṅīṣ* is unimpeded. As for the phrase "if it is a vessel" (*āvapanaṃ cet*).
The word *goṇī* is derived from the root *vap* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, in the sense of "that in which something is sown or deposited," with the suffix *lyuṭ*.

The phrase "other than [a cow]" (*goṇānyā*) refers to a certain specific name. Regarding the phrase "if it is not artificial" (*akṛtrimā cet*): land that has been recently prepared by human beings is "artificial"; the meaning here is "distinct from that."

"Sthalāni" means artificial [places]. As it says in the Yajurveda: "They collect water from dry land. Regarding "bhājī": it is derived from the root *bhaj* in the sense of being served or enjoyed, with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).
However, the rule "those ending in *ghañ* and *ac* are masculine" is merely general. Regarding "if it is boiled" (*śrāṇā cet*): [it refers to milk that has been boiled].

According to Amara, "ṭhyavāgūruṣṇikā śrāṇā" [means gruel]. Regarding the word "bhūjānī," it means "not cooked" (aśrāṇā). The root *śrā* is used in the sense of "cooking. By the rule "saṃyogāderāto dhātoryaṇvataḥ," there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), as well as the change of *t* to *ṇ*. Thus, it means "cooked. As for the word *nāga*, it refers to stoutness.

Because it is not well-known [in this sense] anywhere, he says: "denoting an elephant. "If it were a color" (varṇaścediti) means: if the color were the ground for the application of the term; that is to say, if it were qualified by color. Otherwise, since the word *kāla* [meaning black] is listed among "white and other words denoting qualities are masculine," it would follow that it must be masculine. [This applies] in the Sūtra.

The word division is *varṇā* (colors). [The feminine suffix] *ṭāp* is added to the form ending in the *yaj* suffix from the *arśas-* group. "Other than black" (*kālānyā*) means "endowed with cruelty," or it is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*). "If it is not a covering" (*anācchādanaṃ cet*) means "if it is something other than clothing, such as a cow and so forth. "Other than blue" (*nīlānyā*). Now, in this case, regarding the covering...

If it were the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), the feminine gender would be untenable. Even if *paṭī* (the cloth) were the qualified object, there would be no possibility of the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* in the sense of "a cloth possessing the color blue," because the restriction—"after [words ending in] *nīla* and others, when referring to a plant or a living being"—will be stated later. Therefore, he says: "colored by indigo" (*nīlyāraktā*). By [the word] *nīlyā*...

The meaning is that she has attained a particular state of passion (*rāga*) by means of a medicinal herb (*oṣadhī*). To the question, "How is this meaning obtained?", he says: "By *nīlī*," and so on. This refers to the Vārttika on the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt*.
When the suffix *an* is applied to the word *nīlī*, and the elision [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*, the form *nīla* is produced; of that...

The sense is that since the word *nīlī*, which denotes a blue color, possesses the quality of denoting a medicinal herb (*oṣadhi*) in its adjectival aspect, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply even though there is the restrictive rule "in the case of *nīla* when it means a medicinal herb or a living being. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "not denoting clothing" (*anācchādānām*) is for the purpose of precluding that [application of *ṅīṣ*]. Now, [one might object]: "But *nīlā*..."

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *ṅīṣ* might also apply here in the case of *kuṇḍī* because it is not a covering (*anācchādana*), he says: "even though it is not a covering. This is the Vārttika: *nīvādoṣadhau prāṇini ca*. Thus, the *ṅīṣ* occurring after *nīla-* even when it is not a covering, applies when it denotes a plant or a living being.

The meaning is that [the suffix] should occur only in this case and not elsewhere. And thus, the intention is that in examples such as *nīlakuṇḍī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. There is also the Vārttika rule: *saṃjñāyāṃ vā*.

The meaning is that in the aforementioned context of a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur even outside of those specific cases. [This applies when] it is a modification of iron (*ayovikāra*).

*Phālā* is well known [as a type of grass]. *Kuśānyā* is well known from the *Chandoga-sūtra*: "The *prastotṛ* should have [the sacrificer] hold *kuśa* blades; some say they should be made from a sacrificial tree such as the *khadira*; on long threads, they should be a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with the back of the *kuśa* facing outward, stripped of bark, and evenly trimmed. *Kāmukī* means "one who desires" (*kāmayitum*).
In the analysis of the compound *śīlam asyāḥ* ("this is her habit"), the suffix *ukañ* is applied according to the rule *ṭhaṣapate* etc., [forming *kāmukā*].

The meaning is "one who possesses a desire for sexual intercourse. The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added to the word ending in the *ac* suffix from the *arśa-ādi* group. *Kāmukānyā* means "one who possesses a desire for wealth and so forth."

(493) *śoṇāt prācām* | 4|1|43 | Regarding *śoṇāt prācām*: "Rohita, lohita, rakta, śoṇa, and kokanadacchavi" [are synonyms for red], according to Amarasimha. According to the rule "varṇānāṃ taṇatinitāntānām," the word *śoṇa* [is formed].
The first vowel is udātta and the final is anudātta. Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would necessarily apply by the rule *ṭhañ-yato-ṅīṣ*, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of providing an option.
(494) *voto guṇavacanāt* | Pāṇini 4.1.44.

The word *voto* [is understood] from *guṇavacanāt*. The term *prātipadikāt* is carried over [from the previous rule]. There is a division [of the sūtra] as *vā uta*. Because *uta* is a qualifier of the *guṇavacana* nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is an application of the rule to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says: "from one ending in *u*" (*udantāt*). Regarding "optionally *ṅīp*": *ṅīṣ* does not carry over here.

The intention is that [the suffix] *ṅīp* is applied after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) for the purpose of making the final vowel udātta, according to the Vārttika. Regarding the form *mṛdvī*: the suffix *ṅīp* is added to the word *mṛdu*, resulting in the *yaṇ* substitution. In this regard, the Bhāṣya states: "That which enters into a substance (*satva*), departs from it, is seen in various classes (*jāti*), is capable of being superimposed (*ādheya*), and is not produced by action (*akriyāja*)—that is a quality (*guṇa*) whose nature is non-substantial (*asatvaprakṛti*)."

The definition of a quality (*guṇa*) has been stated. *Satva* (existence) is substance (*dravya*), which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that a quality is that which resides in, or inheres in, that [substance] alone. That is to say, it is inherent in substance only. By the word "only" (*mātra*), the universal of existence (*sattājāti*) is excluded, because that [universal] resides in substances, qualities, and actions.
Now, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), he says: "it departs" (*apaiti*).
The meaning is that it departs from certain substances. The intention is that because substance-ness resides in all substances, there is no over-extension. Even so...
To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of action (*kriyā*), he says: "and that which is to be produced (*ādheya*) and that which is not born of action (*akriyaja*).
That which is placed (*ādhīyate*) or produced (*utpādyate*) is "to be produced" (*ādheya*); "not born of action" means not produced (*anutpādya*).
The meaning is that [the object] is of two kinds, by virtue of being either producible or non-producible.

Quality (*guṇa*) is of two kinds, distinguished as eternal (*nitya*) and non-eternal (*anitya*); for qualities residing in eternal substances are eternal, while those residing in non-eternal substances are non-eternal. The intention [of the definition] is that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to action (*kriyā*), because all action is produced. Nevertheless, even so, there is over-extension to substance (*dravya*).

Because it inheres in the substance that constitutes its parts, it disappears when the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)—namely, conjunction—is destroyed; because it exists in heterogeneous parts such as those of earth and so forth;
and because there exists a distinction between eternal and non-eternal [substances]. Therefore, he says: "Its nature is non-existence" (asattvaprakṛti). It is of a non-substantial (adravya) essence.
This is the meaning; that is to say, "distinct from substance. Here, by the word *mātra*, the exclusion of the universal *sattā* (existence) is intended;

by the phrase "it departs" (*apaiti*), the exclusion of *dravyatva* (substancehood); and by the phrase "it is seen among distinct universals," the exclusion of universals such as *gotva* (cowness). Thus, its distinctness [from these] is established.
By the statement "and that which is to be supported is non-originary from action," the exclusion of action is established, thereby resulting in the property of being distinct from action.
By the statement "those whose nature is not insentient," the exclusion of substance is established, thereby resulting in the property of being distinct from substance.
Thus, [the definition is]: being distinct from genus, while being distinct from action, while being distinct from substance.

The definition of a quality (*guṇa*) should be understood as its state of being inherent (*samavetatva*). By the absence of this state of inherence, non-existence (*abhāva*) is excluded. In this context, if one were to accept the category of "ultimate particularity" (*viśeṣa*) as favored by the logicians (*tārkika*), according to the view that "particularities residing in eternal substances are indeed infinite," [the following would apply].
The property of being distinct from that [the aforementioned categories] must also be included. However, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ākaḍārādekasaṃjñā*, it is stated:

"A meaningful verbal form, excluding compounds, words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*), words ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), indeclinables, pronouns, genus-words (*jāti*), numerals, and technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*), receives the designation 'quality-word' (*guṇavacana*). This [statement] should be understood as an elaboration of the definition provided in the commentary on the present sūtra. Nevertheless, in the commentary on the *ākaḍāra* sūtra, the exclusion of numeral-words (*saṃkhyāśabda*) is also mentioned; that too must be included in the stated definition.

Nor should it be argued that even so, words such as *mṛdu* (soft) and *paṭu* (clever) lack the status of being "expressive of qualities" (*guṇavacana*) because they denote substances qualified by qualities; for by the etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) "expressive of qualities," what is intended is precisely the denotation of a substance in which the quality is subordinate (*guṇopasarjana*). Thus, the word *rūpa* (form/color) does not possess the status of being "expressive of a quality," since it denotes form primarily and is never used in reference to that which possesses form (*rūpavat*).

If the word *rūpa* and others were also included under the term "quality-expressing words" (*guṇavacana*), then they would also be included in the rule "the suffix *matup* is optionally elided after quality-expressing words," which would result in the undesirable usage "a pot is *rūpa*" (*rūpo ghaṭaḥ*). This has been explained by us in the section on *ruṇā* in our *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti*. Regarding the word *śuci*: it means "white. As Amara states: "The words *śukla*, *śubhra*, *śuci*, *śveta*, *viśada*, *śyeta*, and *pāṇḍara* [are synonyms for white]."

Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṅīṣ* will not apply here simply because the word *śuci*, derived from the root *śuc* with the *iṇ* suffix by the *ki-dit* rule of the *Uṇādi* sūtras, is excluded from being a "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*) in the *Ākaḍāra* section of the *Mahābhāṣya*; for one must adopt the view that *Uṇādi* derivatives are underivable (*avyutpatti*). The word *ākhu* means "mouse" (*mūṣikā*). However, because *ākhu* denotes a substance qualified by a genus (*jāti*), it lacks the status of a quality-word mentioned above; therefore, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply. This is governed by the Vārttika: "Not after [stems ending in] *khara* or those having a conjunct as a penultimate (*saṃyogopadha*)."

The term *kharuśca saṃyogopadhaśca* is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The meaning is that the suffix *ṅīp*—which would otherwise apply by the rule *ṭvoto guṇavacanāt*—is not applied after the word *kharu* nor after words having a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as their penultimate (*upadhā*) syllable. He explains the word *kharu*, which is not well-known, as "a maiden choosing her husband" (*patiṃvarā kanyā*). This means she is one who possesses the longing (*autkaṇṭhya*) for obtaining a husband. Since it denotes a substance (*dravya*) where the quality (*guṇa*) characterized by longing is subordinate, it falls under the category of "denoting a quality," and thus the application [of the suffix] was initially expected. Regarding *pāṇḍu*: the meaning is "white. Because it has a conjunct consonant as its penultimate syllable, *ṅīp* does not apply. (495) *Bahvādibhyaśca* [Pāṇini 4.1.45].

Regarding the rule *bahvādibhyaśca*: the ancient grammarians (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that since [words like *bahu*] are already established as *guṇavacana* (quality-words), the explicit mention of *bahu* is indeed redundant. However, in reality, according to the perspective of the Bhāṣya on the *akaḍāra* rule cited immediately below, numeral words (*saṅkhyāśabda*) do not possess the status of *guṇavacana*; therefore, this [sūtra] serves to prescribe the suffix *ṅīṣ*, which would otherwise not apply.

They say that the word *bahu* is used here [in the sense of] "many. *Bahvī* and *bahur*—this word *bahu* denotes abundance (*vaipulya*). For if it were to denote a specific number not restricted to three or more, the use of the singular number would be untenable. Even if it denotes abundance, by the rule "the words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vat*, and *ḍati* are numbers" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.1.23), [it is classified as a numeral].
The point is that because it is a numeral word (*saṅkhyāśabda*), it does not denote a quality (*guṇavacana*), and thus there is no redundancy.

The rule *ṭhkṛdikārādaktinaḥ* is a sub-rule (*gaṇasūtra*) belonging to the group beginning with *bahvī*. It states that the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally be applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *i* which follows a *kṛt*-suffix, but not otherwise.

The meaning is "from that which ends in the suffix *ktin*. Examples are *rātriḥ* and *rātrī*. [The form] *rātri-* is derived from the root *rā* by the Uṇādi rule "from *rā* and *śad*, *trip*. Since it lacks the status of being a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) and lacks an *ū*-vowel at its end, this [rule] is stated because [the previous rule] would not otherwise apply. There is also the view: "Some say [it applies] after every [word] ending in *an*."

This is indeed a sūtra belonging to the *bahv-ādi* subgroup. The meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally occur after a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix containing the vowel *ik*, as well as after one not so ending; however, it does not occur after a word ending in a suffix having the sense of *ktin*. For example: *śakaṭiḥ* and *śakaṭī*.
Since the word *śakaṭi* is an underived nominal base (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*), it lacks the status of being a *kṛdanta*; therefore, [the rule] "sarvataḥ" [does not apply].
Such is the statement. In the view that [the suffixes] are not derived [from verbal roots], it should be understood that the word *rātri* is also an example.

Regarding *ajanani*: under the governing rule *striyāṃ ktin*, by the rule *ākrośe nañyaniḥ*, the suffix *ani* is applied to the root *jan* when *nañ* is the upapada. Since the term *ktin* is mentioned [in the governing rule], there is no prohibition in this case.

The sense is that the statement "after a word ending in *kṛt* other than a feminine suffix" is made for this reason. Now, one might object: from the root *han*, when the feminine suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the object, the *n* is elided by the rule "anudāttopadeśa... etc., resulting in the form *hati*;
since this ends in *ktin*, how can the suffix *ṅīṣ* be added to the word *paddhati*? To this he replies: "because it ends in *ktin*. [This refers to] the list (*gaṇa*).

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that it belongs to the *bahv-ādi* group. Now, one might object: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "striking with the feet" (*pādābhyāṃ hatiḥ*), because the word *pāda* is included in the rule "the agent and instrument [are compounded] with a *kṛt*-formed word diversely" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*), and because it lacks the designation *bha*, the rule "of *pāda* [there is substitution of *pada*] before *ājāti*, *gati*, and *upahata*" (*pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu*) would also not apply. To this [objection, the following is said]: its...

Because [the substitution] occurs only in the case of others such as *ājya*, he says: *himakāṣi*. The meaning of this is that the substitute *pada* should take the place of the word *pāda* when followed by *hima* and so forth. (496) *puṃyogādākhyāyām* | Pāṇini 4.1.48.

"Because of connection with a male" (*puṃyogāt*). In the term *puṃyogāt*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetau*). In the word *ākhyāyām*, the seventh case (*saptamī*) is a substitute for the fifth case, according to the statement: "It should be stated that substitutes for case-endings (*sup*) are themselves case-endings. By the word *ākhyā*, a denotative word (*vācakaḥ śabdaḥ*) is intended; [the question arises: of what?
When there is the expectation for a "designator" (*vācaka*), the word "of a man" (*puṃsaḥ*) is obtained because [the word] "due to connection with a man" (*puṃyogāt*) is present [in the mind].
Thus, by the term "in a name" (*ākhyāyām*), it is understood that [the suffix applies] to a word well-known as denoting a man.
The phrase "due to connection with a man" connects with the rule "for a woman" (*striyām*). And so, having recourse to the connection with a man...

It is understood [from the context] that [the suffix is applied] to a word denoting a woman by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Then, [this is explained] by the words "that which is called masculine," and so forth.

Regarding "ṅīṣ": the intention is that this is due to the recurrence (anuvṛtti) of the rule "ṭhanyato ṅīṣ" (A 4.1.40). However, in the preceding sūtra, "voto guṇavacanāt" (A 4.1.44), it is stated that "the addition of ṅīp and so forth after words expressing qualities (guṇavacana) is for the sake of making the initial syllable udātta."
Since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is obtained from the *vārttika*, there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of this [suffix] in that case. [The example is] "the wife of a *gopa*" (*gopasya strī*).

A *gopa* is one who protects cows (*gāḥ pāti*), according to the rule "after a verbal root ending in *ā*, when no prefix is present, the suffix *ka* is applied. However, although she lacks the act of protecting cows, she is designated as such because she is his wife. And therefore—

The intention is that because [the word *hari*] denotes a female by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its connection with a male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, and then the vowel *a* is elided according to the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. However, in cases such as "the wife of Hari" (*hareḥ strī*) or "the wife of Śambhu" (*śambhoḥ strī*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply, because the term *ataḥ* ("from [a stem ending in short *a*]") is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into the section prescribing feminine suffixes. As for she who herself [drives] the cows...

It means the wife of a cowherd (*gopa*), but not the female cowherd herself; she is called *gopā*. In this case, because the word *gopa* functions inherently in the feminine gender, it does not apply [to the wife] through connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). Nor should it be argued that the mother, mother-in-law, or maternal aunt of a cowherd would have to be called *gaupī*; for [the rule] applies to one who does not commit sin.

Based on the natural sense of the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which states that "just as one receives beatings, imprisonment, and so forth inflicted by a husband, so too does one receive his [the husband's] name," it is intended that the *puṃyoga* (connection with a male) refers specifically to the relationship consisting of wife and husband.
As for *kaikayī*, *devakī*, and others used for a daughter, they are listed in the *gaurādi* group [of feminine suffixes].

This is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. [Question: What is the purpose of including the term *ākhyā* ("name")? [Example: *prasūtā*. For this word denotes a woman who has given birth; and that birth is caused by union with a male (*puṃyoga*), and its application to a female is based on that cause. However, this word is not well-known (*prasiddha*) in the masculine, and therefore the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply here. In this regard—

The *vārttika* states: "There is a prohibition [of the suffix] for *gopālakā* and others. Here, by the word "others" (*ādi*), only those ending in *pālaka*, such as *aśvapālikā* and so forth, are included, because they alone are cited as examples in the *Bhāṣya*. Thus he says: "Not after those ending in *pālaka*. This refers to the [suffix] characterized by connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).

The word *ṅīṣ* is understood as the remainder [of the rule]. Regarding *gopālikā*: the meaning is "the female of a cowherd" (*gopālaka*). Now, one who protects is a *pālaka*; the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the agent, and by the rule *ṭhyuvoranākau*, there is the substitution of *ak*.
By the rule *ṇeraniṭi*, there is the elision of the *ṇi* affix. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "protector of cows," this forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

When the *sup* suffix is elided, the word *gopālaka* remains. In that case, is it the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of "the remainder" (*śeṣe*), or is it the genitive in the sense of the "object" (*karmaṇi*) according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*? It cannot be the first alternative, because by relying on the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* arises from the word *pālaka*—which is a member of the compound—and [the genitive] would then follow the *sup* suffix produced from that.

Because of the prohibition "not after a word ending in a case-suffix" (*asupaḥ*) regarding the status of being *para* (subsequent), the substitution of *it* [for *ṭh*] by the rule *ṭhpratyayasthāt* is untenable.

Nor can the second position—that the genitive case is used in the sense of the object—be maintained; for there is the rule: "The statement that prepositions (*gati*), case-words (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) form compounds with *kṛt*-derived words occurs before the application of case-suffixes."
It should not be argued that since the word *gavām* is compounded with the nominal stem *pālaka-* even before the formation of the derivative,
the *ṭāp* produced by the compound lacks the status of being followed by a case-ending (*sup*),
and thus the substitution of *it* (shortening) is unimpeded; for [the rule] "by *tṛc* and *aka*, when denoting the agent" (*tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*) [prohibits such shortening].

If it is argued that this is because the formation of a compound is prohibited by the rule regarding the genitive case used in the sense of a *kāraka* (agentive/active relation), it is not so: [the derivation is as follows]—one who protects cows is a "cow-protector" (*gopāla*). By the rule *karmaṇy-aṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; this is an *upapada* compound. "Cow-protector" itself becomes "cow-protector-ness" (*gopālaka*), with the suffix *ka* added in its own meaning (*svārthika*). Since it is a part of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is elision of the nominal ending (*subluk*). [The feminine form of] "cow-protector-ness" is...

This is because one relies on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "gopālikā" [meaning "one who protects cows"]. Indeed, in this case, the suffix *ṭāp* does not follow immediately after the nominal suffix (*sup*), because it is separated by [the element] *kena*. Or, even if one were to accept a compound with a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), even then *ṭāp* would not follow immediately after *sup*;
for even when there is an intention to express a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), in reality, since it functions as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), the nominal suffixes must arise prior to that.
Because the genitive case of the residual category (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) applies here, it is stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that for this very reason,

both in the present sūtra and in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "upapadamatik," the formation of the compound *kumbhakāra*— specifically the genitive-tatpuruṣa compound of *kumbhasya* with [the verbal root] *kṛ*— is presented as occurring prior to the derivation of the nominal suffix (*sub*), which is thus rendered consistent.
It has been explained.
Regarding the rule "after *sūrya*, when [the word] *devatā* follows":
this refers to the feminine form when it has become a deity (*devatā*).

The meaning is that the suffix *cap* should be prescribed after the word *sūrya* when it occurs in connection with a masculine [referent]. The mention of "connection with a masculine" (*puṃyogāt*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīṣ*. By the rule *capāvitau*, the *c* and *p* are elided. Thus, *sūryā*. When *cap* is applied, there is a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*). [The question] "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'in the sense of a deity'? refers to a woman who is [merely] named *Sūryā*.

The question arises because of the non-deviation from the status of being a deity. "Sūrī kuntī" [is formed as follows]: when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, there is the elision of the letter *y* by the rule *sūryatiṣye*; then there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
"This is a human woman" means that this Kuntī is a human being, not a deity. And this...

This is clear from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources. Nor should it be argued that one could simply say "after *sūrya*, when [the suffix] *ni* follows, provided it denotes a deity," because once *ṅīṣ* is prohibited, the form *sūryā* would be established by *ṭāp* alone; for if *ṭāp* were present, it would be unaccented due to its being a *pit* suffix, according to the rule "sup and *pit* suffixes are unaccented. However, this is not the case.
The distinction is that [the word] *citaḥ* has an udātta accent on the final syllable.
(497) For the words *indra*, *varuṇa*, *bhava*, *śarva*, *rudra*, *mṛḍa*, *himāraṇya*, *yava*, *yavana*, *mātula*, and *ācārya*, the suffix *ānuk* [is applied].

[4|1|49] Regarding *indravaruṇa* and the addition of the augment *ān*: the intention is that this is due to the indicatory letter *k* (kit), which serves as a marker for the application of the augment. Regarding *ṅīṣ*:
the intention is that this follows from the recurrence of the rule *ṭhanyato ṅīṣ*. [The context concerns] connection with a male (*puṃyoga*).

"It is desired [here]," because the term *puṃyogāt* ("due to connection with a male") is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), and the sense is that those [words] do not apply to the feminine state without such a connection with a male. Now, one might object: "If this is so, since the form is already established by *puṃyogāt* alone, the prescription of the suffix *ṅīṣ* is redundant. To this he says: "In that case," referring to *indrā* and others.

The meaning is that, since the suffix *ṅīṣ* is already established for the six [words] beginning with *mātula* and for *ācārya* by the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*, only the augment *ānuk* is prescribed as being co-occurrent (*saṃniyoga*) with that suffix. Regarding "of the others":
for *hāma*, *araṇya*, *yava*, and *yavana*, however, both the augment *ānuk* and the suffix *ṅīṣ* are prescribed; therein—

The meaning is that a connection with a male [consort] is impossible. Regarding *indrāṇī*: when the suffix *ānuk* is applied, the letter *k* is for the sake of marking the suffix as *kit*, while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation; because it is *kit*, it becomes an internal constituent [of the stem], resulting in a long vowel by the rule of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*), and finally the change to *ṇ* (*ṇatvam*).
Examples are *varuṇānī*, *bhavānī*, *śarvāṇī*, *rudrāṇī*, and *mṛḍānī*.

These have been set aside because they are easily understood. However, in the rule concerning the *nuk* augment (*anugvidhi*), if there were no long pronunciation [of the vowel], the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would result; for the explicit pronunciation of the letter *a* serves the purpose of preventing the elision of *al* (*allopa*).
But in the rule concerning the *nuk* augment, the elision of *al* (*allopa*) would otherwise occur; the details of this are explained elsewhere.

Regarding the greatness (*mahattva*) of snow (*hima*) and forest (*araṇya*): there is a Vārttika stating "in the case of the greatness of snow and forest. The meaning is that the suffixes *ānuk* and *īṣ* apply to the words *hima* and *araṇya* when they denote greatness. Thus, "great snow" is *himānī*.
Therefore, femininity is to be understood as occurring in connection with greatness, as in the case of *araṇyānī*; the meaning is "a great forest.
[The suffix] *doṣan* occurs after *yava* in the sense of a fault.

Regarding "yavād doṣe"—this is a *vārttika*. The remainder [of the rule] is "after ānuṅ and īṣ. From this very [rule], it should be understood that there is femininity when the word *yava* means a field of bad barley. After *yavana*, [the suffix applies] in the sense of a script.

"Also [the suffix] *ānuk* [is applied] after the word *yavana* when a script (*lipi*) is meant"—this is a Vārttika. *Vipra* means the arrangement of letters. In that regard, according to the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *lakṣa-mayā-vṛtau ānuṅ-ṅīṣau*, the meaning is "with *ānuk* and *ṅīṣ*.
(1) After the words *mātula* and *upādhyāya*, *ānuk* is optionally [applied].
"Ānugā after *mātula* and *upādhyāya*. This is also a Vārttika.

Here, the term "due to connection with a male" (*puṃyogāt*) is connected [to the rule], because—as in the case of *himā* and so on—there is no impossibility here [of such a connection]. In this instance, however, only *ānugā* is subject to option; even in the absence of *ānugā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* indeed occurs in one alternative.

When [the suffix *ṅīṣ*] is obligatory after *mātula*, it is optional (*vibhāṣā*) when it does not follow *upādhyāya*. Thus we have *mātulānī* and *mātulī*; the meaning is "the wife of a maternal uncle" (*mātulasya strī*). Similarly, *upādhyāyānī* and *upādhyāyī*;
the meaning is "the wife of a preceptor" (*upādhyāyasya strī*).
"Or rather, let the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* be prescribed there [after the word *adhyāpaka*] when it means 'one who teaches by herself.

As for the phrase 'when she herself,' this *vārttika* is read under the rule *ṭhihaśca* in the third *pāda* of the third *adhyāya*. It refers to one who teaches by herself and not as a subordinate teacher (*upādhyāya*)."
Regarding the word *strī*: the meaning is that even in the absence of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), the optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* must be stated.

This refers to women who were Vedic scholars (*brahmavādinī*) in other ages; for it is said: "In former ages, the binding of the girdle of muñja grass, the teaching of the Vedas, and the [recitation of] the Sāvitrī were desired for women."
The word is likewise [formed] because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*):
"From *ācārya*, there is the suffix *aṇ*. Furthermore, there is the Vārttika: "And from *ācārya*, there is the suffix *aṇ*. The particle *ca* (and) [includes] *ānuk* and *ṅīṣ*.
The sense is that of a collective group. Regarding the term *ācāryānī*: it means the wife of an *ācārya*.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] does not occur here, according to the rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*. "That twice-born man who, having initiated a disciple, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret portions (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*."

"The teacher [is so called] because he teaches a portion [of the Veda]," according to the Smṛti. "Only when there is a connection with a male" means that the mention of "connection with a male" (puṃyoga) indeed continues to apply here. He states its purpose: "the teacher" (ācārya), etc.
Here, he clarifies the absence of a connection with a male by saying, "she herself is the expounder."
The meaning is "one who instructs in the Dharma. The intention is based on the traditional legal text (*smṛti*): "He from whom one gathers the Dharmas is an Ācārya.
Alternatively, [the suffix] is applied to *arya* and *kṣatriya* in their own sense (*svārthe*).

The Vārttika states: "Or [the suffix] after *ārya* and *kṣatriya*. The remainder of the rule is "after [stems ending in] *ā*, *anuṅ*, and *īṣ*. The phrase "in its own sense" (*svārthe*) is obtained through the interpretation [of the rule], by which the application [of the suffix] when there is a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*) is excluded. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya says only "āryāṇī" and "aryā. However, if [the suffix] were to apply only when there is a connection with a male...

One should cite *upādhyāyī* and *āryī* as examples of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. He explains the word *ārya*: "The meaning is 'mistress' or 'a Vaiśya woman'. The intention is that this is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [stated in Pāṇini 5.1.124]: "The word *ārya* is used in the sense of a master or a Vaiśya. [He gives further examples: *kṣatriyāṇī* and *kṣatriyā*; [the latter] from a *kṣatriya* father and a *kṣatriyā* mother.

The meaning is "born of a wife. This is because, having begun with the statement, "From those of the same caste, sons of the same caste are born in women of the same caste," the Smṛti continues, "This rule is prescribed for married [women]. The word *vinnāsu* means "in married [women]" (*ūḍhāsu*). However, in the case of a relationship through a man (i.e., a concubine), they are called *aryī* and *kṣatriyī*; that is, the wife of an *arya* is an *aryī*.

The term *kṣatriyī* refers to the wife of a *kṣatriya*, meaning a *vaiśyā* or a *śūdrā*. The question "How? arises because the word *brahman* is not included in the rule beginning with *indravaruṇa*; therefore, one asks how the forms *brahmaṇī* and so forth—with the suffixes *ān* and *ṅīṣ*—are derived in the sense of "the wife of a *brahman*. He provides the answer: "brahmāṇam."

The explanation of "ānayati" (he brings) is "jīvyati" (he lives). [The root] √ṭhan means "to breathe. Breathing is life. From this root, with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel, the suffix *tip*, and the addition of *śap*, along with the substitution of guṇa and the change to *āy*, the form "ānayati" is produced. [This refers to] the sustaining of the husband's life.

Because it serves for the auspiciousness of the wife (*jāyāsaumaṅgalyārthatvāt*). Consequently, in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "he causes Brahmā to come" (*brahmāṇam ānayati*), there is first the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopa*) by the rule *ṇer aniṭi* from the rule *ṭhāni*. Then, by the rule *karmaṇy aṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added; subsequently, after the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*), the word *brahmāṇam* forms an *upapada-samāsa* with the word *āna*. Following this, there is the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*), and finally the long vowel by the rule *savarṇadīrgha*.

The intention is that from the word *brahmān*, by applying the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, and then deleting the vowel *a* according to *yasyeti ca*, the form *brahmaṇī* is obtained through the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* according to *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*.
However, the rule *ekājuttarapade* does not apply here, because when the suffix *aṇ* is present, it is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) [that undergoes the change].

Because [the word] consists of two syllables (*dvyackatvāt*), even though the *aṇ* suffix has been elided, the elision is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāvāt*). However, the rule "that which is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it is not subject to *sthānivadbhāva*" does not apply here, because it is stated that "this is an exception (*doṣaḥ*) to that [general rule]. (498) P. 4.1.50: *krītāt karaṇapūrvāt*.

[The rule applies] after a word ending in *krīta* that has as its initial member an instrument (*karaṇa*). The term *prātipadikāt* (after a nominal stem) is understood from the previous context, and by the term *krītāt* (after *krīta*) which is also understood, [the base] is qualified; thus, there is an application of the rule regarding the end of a compound (*tadantavidhiḥ*). This is what he states with the words "after one ending in *krīta*" and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose beginning (*ādi*) is an instrument (*karaṇa*)."
The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the qualificand; therefore, the masculine gender in the expression "of the instrument, etc. (*karaṇādeḥ*) is justified.

Regarding the example *vastrakrītī*: [one might object] that if the analysis is *vaстреṇa krītā* (purchased with cloth), where the word ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is used, then the resulting compound nominal stem—by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("with a *kṛt*-suffix denoting the agent or instrument, a compound is formed diversely")—would necessarily end in the vowel *ā*, and not...

If it is asked, "How can there be the suffix *ṅīṣ* here in the word *tvadanta*?", the answer is: true. First, the basis (*prakṛti*) for a compound is its non-ordinary analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigraha-vākya*). When the state "vastra-bhis krītaḥ" (bought with cloths) is established, the rule applies:
"The statement regarding the compounding of prefixes, verbal nouns (*kāraka*), and subordinate words (*upapada*) with *kṛt*-derived forms occurs prior to the production of case-endings (*sup*)."

The meaning is that, by this paribhāṣā, since the compound with the word *krīta* occurs even before the derivation of the case-ending (*sup*), the elision of the case-ending by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* results in the form *vastrakrītā*; thus, it is indisputable that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ends in the letter *a*. And this is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *puṃyogād ākhyāyām*.
This is clear. Since one might think that the suffix *ṅīṣ* would also apply here in the case of *dhanakrītā*, he says: "not in some cases.

By the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, it is understood that the rule *gatikārakopapadānām* does not apply in certain instances; therefore, in this case, [the compound is formed] with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

This refers to a compound (*samāsa*). In that case, since the feminine suffix *ṭāp* occurs even before the case-ending (*sup*) due to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, and because the case-ending is subsequently elided (*luka*) when there is a compound with a word ending in *sup* whose base is a stem ending in *ṭāp*, the word *dhanakrītī* does not end in the vowel *a*;
therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. And thus, [the rule] "after [a stem] ending in *a*, when *sup* follows... [is not applicable].
