The meaning is that when there is a compound with a *subanta* (inflected nominal) whose base ends in *-tā*, and the case-ending (*sup*) is elided (*luk*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply because the word *dhanakrītā* lacks a final short *a*. Thus, it is stated that this is the purpose of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "after [a word ending in] *ṭha*. And this [point] was made under the rule *upapadam atiṅ*.

This is clear in Kaiyaṭa. Why [is the condition] "preceded by an instrument" (*karaṇapūrva*) stated? [Consider] *sukrītā*. Even so, one should not argue that there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *ṅīṣ* in the sentence *vaстреṇa krītā* ("bought with a cloth"), because the nominal stem *krītā* is preceded by an instrument and ends in the vowel *a*. For [the rule states] "from that which is preceded by an instrument... (*karaṇapūrvāt*).

This is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *krīta*, and not of the word *krīta* itself. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the word *karaṇa* stands first. The meaning is: "from a nominal stem that is a compound ending in *krīta*, provided it has as its prior member the word *karaṇa*. The inclusion of the term "prior" (*pūrva*) is precisely for this purpose.

Otherwise, he would have simply said "after a word ending in *kta* that denotes an instrument" (*ṭh krītāt karaṇāt*). Enough [of this digression]. (499) Pāṇini 4.1.51: "After a word ending in *kta*, when it signifies something small. [The commentary explains: "After [a word] beginning with an instrument," because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "after [a word] preceded by an instrument" (*karaṇapūrvāt*).
The meaning is "abstract state" (*bhāva*). Regarding the phrase "from that which ends in *kta*":

the intended sense is "from that which ends in a suffix ending in *kta*," because the base noun (*prātipadika*) is qualified by the suffix ending in *kta* as obtained through the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "from that which ends in *at*": the intention is that this follows from the recurrence of the word "*ata*" [in the rule]. Regarding the phrase "when smallness is indicated": [this refers to the formation of feminine nouns expressing diminutiveness].

In the rule "ṭhalpākhyāyām," the term [alpa-] is an adjunct (*upādhi*) pertaining to the whole compound. *Alpatvam* (smallness) resides either in the instrument or in the action. For example, *abhraliptī dyauḥ* ("the sky is streaked with clouds") means "covered by few clouds" or "slightly covered by clouds."

(500) *Bahuvrīheś cāntodāttāt* |4|1|52|. From the word "bahuvrīheḥ" [the sūtra] continues the words "ktāt" and "ataḥ". Thus he says: "from a bahuvrīhi"; that is, "from one ending in a suffix marked with *k* (*ktānta*). The meaning is "from one ending in a suffix marked with *k*. By the phrase "by that," [it is meant] "from one preceded by a genus-word (*jāti-pūrva*)."

The meaning is that by means of this qualification, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after words preceded by *bahu* and others. In the rule "from *sukha* and so forth, when denoting the agent's feeling" (*sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām*), the group beginning with *sukha* is recited. [This is based on the rule: "The past participle suffix *kta*, except for those expressing clothing, follows nouns of genus (*jāti*), time, and *sukha* and so forth, when they do not mean 'done,' 'measured,' or 'attained'" (*jātikālasukhādibhyo'nācchādanāt kto'kṛtamitapratipannāḥ*).
The rules *ṭhnañsubhyām* and *ṭhbahornañvadutarapadabhūmnī* prescribe that a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a *kta*-suffix is oxytone; however,

because it is stated here [in the rule] that this applies when preceded by a genus-word (*jāti*), it follows by implication that even for a compound preceded by words such as *bahu*, the final syllable is acute.
The intended meaning is that it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion).
It should be stated as "preceded by a genus-word" (*jātipūrvāt*).
Regarding the example *ūrūbhinī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose thighs (*ūrū*) are split (*bhinnau*), i.e., separated (*asaṃyuktau*). This is because of the rule "*niṣṭhā*" [Pāṇini 2.2.36].

However, the word *bhinna* does not take the first position [in the compound], because of the Vārttika: "The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) should be stated as coming after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time, pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth. This [compound] is oxytone (accented on the final syllable) by the rule beginning with "jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ. As for the definition of genus (*jāti*):

This will be explained under the rule *jāter astrīviṣayād* (Pāṇini 4.1.63). Regarding the term *bahukṛtā*: the analysis of the compound is *yayā bahavaḥ kṛtāḥ*. Furthermore, the following are cited as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) in the Bhāṣya: *akṛtā*, *sukṛtā*, *māsayātā*, *sukhayātā*, and *duḥkhayātā*.

“Not after a word ending in *jāta*. This is a *vārttika*. The meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ*, which was prescribed by the rule “*bahuvrīheśca*,” does not apply here. For example, *dantajātā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is “she whose teeth have grown” (*dantā jātā yasyāḥ*). It is like [the formation of] *ūrubhinnī*.
This is a secondary formation (*paranipāta*).
[The term] *pāṇigṛhītī* is used in the sense of "wife";
thus, *pāṇigṛhītī bhāryāyām*. This also is a Vārttika. [She is] one who has been wedded according to the prescribed rule (*vidhivad-ūḍhā*).
The meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs precisely because the word *pāṇigṛhīta* applies to this [term] when it signifies a wife (*bhāryā*).

The analytical derivation (*vigraha*) is: "she whose hand has been formally taken according to the rules at the time of marriage. As for the word "another" (*anyā*), it means a female servant (*dāsī*) and so forth.

(501) *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā* |4|1|53|. After a Bahuvrīhi compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is not a word denoting a body part (*asvāṅga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally added after that which ends in a *kta*-suffix. The definition of a "body part" (*svāṅga*) will be stated in the subsequent rule. Thus, for a Bahuvrīhi where the prior member is not a body part, the suffix *ṅīṣ* follows that which ends in a *kta*-suffix.

The meaning of the sūtra is that it should be [interpreted] as such. Although it could also be explained as "from a bahuvrīhi compound ending in *kta* whose prior member is not a body part (*asvāṅga*)," nevertheless,
in the subsequent sūtra, the term "having a prior member that is not a body part" (*asvāṅgapūrvapada*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over).
In this case as well, an interpretation based on a *karmadhāraya* compound is appropriate. Now, one might object that in examples such as *bahukṛtā* and *akṛtā*,
there would also be an optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* because they are *bahuvrīhi*s ending in *tad* preceded by a non-body-part (*asvāṅga*) word.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "by the preceding [rule]. The meaning is that since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would necessarily apply here by the preceding sūtra, "And [the feminine suffix] after a Bahuvrīhi ending in an udātta vowel," its optional application is prescribed in this case.
And thus, the conditions "preceded by a genus-word" (*jātipūrvāt*) and "ending in an udātta vowel" (*antodāttāt*) apply here as well.

The intention is that there is no over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *bahukṛtā* because of the connection [with the specific condition]. In *surāpī*, [the form] is *surāpītā*; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that by whom wine (*surā*) has been drunk (*pītā*). The prior placement [of *surā*] follows the rule for *ūrubhinnī*. [The question] "Why [specify] 'from one with an udātta on the final syllable'? refers to what is heard in the rule *bahuvrīheśca*.

The question is: even though the term "antodātāt" (ending in an acute accent) is understood from the rule "ṭhasvāṅgapūrvapadādvā," for what purpose is it [repeated] here? Regarding the example *vastracchannā*:
the prior placement [of *vastra-*] follows the rule like that of *ūrubhinnī*. Now, concerning this *vastracchannā*...
Having raised the objection that [the word] would be oxytone by virtue of the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ*,

he refutes it with the words "because it is not clothing. Thus, because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies, and by the principle of the suppression of the remainder (*śeṣanighāta*), [the final syllable is unaccented].

The meaning is that this [word] ends in an *anudātta* vowel. "For this very reason" means that, by the rule *asvāṅgapūrvapadāt* and by the preceding rule *bahuvrīheśca*, the optional (*vaikalpika*) and obligatory (*nitya*) suffix *ṅīṣ* do not apply in the case of *vastracchannā*. [This is because of its] final acute accent (*antodātatva*).
The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs after both [types of words].
(502) *svāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt* |4|1|54|. [The word *svāṅgāt*], as well as *upasarjanāt* and *asaṃyogopadhāt*.

The term *svāṅgāt* ("from its own limb") connects with this [rule]. Furthermore, the term *svāṅgāt*, which is understood from the previous rule as well as the term *ataḥ* ("from that"), serves as a qualifier for the understood term *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem"); thus, there is an application of the rule regarding the end of a compound (*tadantavidhiḥ*).
This is what he states by saying "that which has a non-conjunct as its penultimate letter," and so forth. [He also says] "optionally *ṅīṣ*."

The intention is that this is because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule *ṭhasvāṅgapūrvapadādvā*, and of the word "*ṅīṣ*" from the rule *anyato ṅīṣ*. Having raised the objection—"While the term 'bahuvrīhi' is already being carried over [from the previous rule], what is the purpose of mentioning 'upasarjana'?"—he provides the answer with the example: "one who has surpassed her hair" (*keśānatikrāntā*).

The compound *sthādyaḥ krāntādyarthe* is a *tatpuruṣa*. Here, the intention is that the mention of the term *upasarjana* is for the purpose of securing [the application of the rule] even in the absence of *bahuvrīhi*-hood.
The word *keśa* attains the status of an *upasarjana* by the rule *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte*.
"Candramukhī, candramukhī": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose face is like the moon.

"Sugulphā": the analysis is "she whose ankles (*gulpha*) are beautiful. Regarding this, Amara states: "The words *pada*, *aṅghri*, and *caraṇa* are used for the foot (*caraṇa*), not in the feminine; the two knots at its [the foot's] base are called *ghuṭikā* and *gulpha*."

Regarding the question "Why [is it] from a subordinate member (*upasarjana*)?"—this question arises because the application [of the rule] would not otherwise occur for words such as *keśa* when they are not subordinate members, precisely because they lack feminine gender. As for the example *śikhā*: here...

It has been stated that the mention of the term *upasarjana* (secondary member) is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *ṅīṣ* from the word *śikhā* when it stands alone as a *svāṅga* (body-part). Otherwise, the intention is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* would optionally apply, overriding the suffix *ṭāp*. The reading found in some manuscripts, "ṭhśobhanā śikhā suśikhe," should be understood as an interpolation (*prakṣipta*), because in a compound ending in a form with the suffix *ṭāp*, there is no possibility [of the application of *ṅīṣ*] precisely because it does not end in the vowel *a*. Now, one might object: *svāṅga* is a body-part that belongs to oneself (*svasya*) as its constituent whole (*avayavībhūta*).

Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *sumukhā śālā* ("a house with a beautiful front"), because the meaning of the word *mukha* (front) is a constituent part of the house, which is the whole (*avayavin*). Moreover, there would be non-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of *sukeśī rathyā* ("a street with beautiful hair"), because hair is not a constituent part of a street. Therefore, he says: "One's own limb (*svāṅga*) is threefold. [The definition is: "A limb belonging to a living being, which is non-fluid, possesses form, and is not produced by modification."

The meaning is that here, the technical term *svāṅgam* (body-part) intended [by Pāṇini] is defined in three ways in the Bhāṣya: "that which does not reside in it, yet is seen in it; and if it is joined with it in that way. Regarding this, intending the first half-verse as the primary definition of *svāṅga*, he recites it separately: *adravam* ("not liquid"). That which has no liquidity is *adravam*.
A body-part (*svāṅga*) that is not liquid, possesses form (*mūrtimat*), resides in a living being, and is not produced by modification [is so called].
Form (*mūrti*) is the conjunction of parts; that which has this is *mūrtimat*.

The meaning is: a substance (*dravya*) is that which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the conjunction of parts; "located in a living being" (*prāṇistha*) means existing in a sentient creature; and "not produced by modification" (*avikāraja*) means not generated by pathological changes such as ulcers and the like—that is what constitutes a "primary limb" (*svāṅga*). [This applies to] the term "non-liquid" (*adrava*).

He states the purpose [of the rule] with the words "su-sveda" and so on. The analysis of the compound is: that which possesses a beautiful (*su*) sweat (*sveda*), meaning a flow of water born from heat (*ūṣmaja*). The beauty of the sweat, however, consists in the absence of foul odor.

Regarding the phrase "because of its being liquid" (*dravatvāt*), the ellipsis is "it does not have the status of a body-part" (*na svāṅgatvam*). Therefore, the sense is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied.

He states the purpose [of using] the word *mūrtimat* (embodied): "possessing excellent knowledge" (*sujñānā*). The analysis of the compound is: that which has very beautiful (*su-śobhana*) knowledge (*jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because of being formless" (*amūrtatvāt*), the ellipsis is to be supplied as "there is no status as a limb of the self" (*na svāṅgatvam*).
He states the purpose of the rule "located in a living being" (*prāṇistham*): "a creeper with a beautiful face" (*sumukhā śālā*). [The analysis is: very beautiful (*su-śobhana*)...

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose first part is the face. Regarding the phrase "because it does not reside in a non-living being," the remainder of the sense is: "it is not a *svāṅga* (a limb or part of the body). He states the purpose of the term "not produced by a modification" with the example *suśophā*: [it means] "she whose swelling (*śopha*)—that is, her inflammation—is excessive."

The analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "A swelling (*śopha*), however, is *śvayathu*," according to Amara. "Because it arises from a morbid transformation" means because it arises from a disease; the phrase "it does not belong to one's own limbs" is to be supplied. [This applies to] that which is not situated therein, yet is seen there.

"And that which is seen there, though not residing therein"—this is the second definition of a limb (*svāṅga*). By the word "that" (*tat*), a sentient being (*prāṇin*) is referred to. The meaning is: even that which does not reside in a sentient being (*atatstham*), but is seen (*dṛṣṭam*) in such a non-sentient thing (*tatra*), is also a limb. For example, "street-hair" (*rathyā-keśānām*); [this refers to] the hair found on a street.

The intention is that because it lacks the status of residing in a living being (*prāṇistha*), its status as a "limb" (*svāṅga*) is not established by the previous definition; therefore, a different definition is provided.

He applies the stated definition to the example with the words "even though not residing in a living being. The meaning is that even in the absence of residing in a living being, something may still be considered a limb because it has at some time resided in a living being.
"If it is thus endowed with that," "if it is thus by means of that"— this is the third characteristic of its own parts (*svāṅgalakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, [it is stated] in the Bhāṣya:

The word "limb" (*svāṅga*) has been supplied as a complement [to the rule] by the phrase "even if not belonging to a living being. The word *cet* means "if. Therefore, if that non-living substance—such as an image—is *yuta*, meaning "connected," with a specific part having the form of a limb such as a breast, which resides in a living being; then, like a non-living substance [possessing such a limb], [it is governed by the same rules].
The meaning is that even inanimate objects may possess the form of breasts and so forth, as in the expression "a beautiful-breasted image" (*sustanī* or *sustanā pratimā*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has two beautiful breasts, or parts having the form of breasts.
Regarding the two parts in the form of breasts belonging to the image, [at no time...]

Because it does not reside in a living being and because it is not observed in another similar thing, this is a different definition, as neither of the two previous definitions applies. Now, he applies the definition to the example—“like a living being” (*prāṇivat*). The suffix *vati* is added to a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*).
The meaning is that it is one's own limb (*svāṅga*) because it resides in an object such as a statue that resembles a living being.

Nor should it be argued that the suffix *ṅīṣ* would also apply in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one who has beautiful hands and feet" (*kalyāṇapāṇipāda*), because the phrase "optionally, when the preceding member is not a *svāṅga*" (*asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā*) is understood to carry over [into this rule]. For in this instance, the term "hands and feet" (*pāṇipāda*)...

The aggregate is not itself a limb (*svāṅga*), but rather it is the aggregate of limbs that constitutes a limb; for example, the word *pāda* is a limb, yet it does not follow immediately after a non-limb (*asvāṅga*) preceding member because it is separated by the word *pāṇi*. Thus, the limb *pāda* [is not preceded by a non-limb].
It is clear from the Bhāṣya that the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply here because there is no word following *kalyāṇa*.

(503) *nāsikodarauṣṭhajaṅghādantakarṇaśrṛṅgācca* | 4|1|55|. [The suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are applied after words ending in] *nāsikā*, *udara*, *oṣṭha*, *jaṅghā*, *danta*, *karṇa*, and *śrṛṅga*. From the rule *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā* [4.1.54], the word *vā* ("or") is understood, as well as [the suffixes] *ṭāp*, *ṅīp*, *ṅīṣ*, and *cha* from the subsequent rule.
The term *ṅīṣ* is understood from the previous rule and continues here. Thus he says: "from these.

This means "from those words ending in *nāsikā* and so forth that have become secondary members (*upasarjana*)," because the word *upasarjanāt* ("from a secondary member") is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Now, one might object: [is this not covered by] *svāṅgācca*?
Since this [rule] is already established by the preceding sūtra, he asks: "For what purpose is this? To which he replies: "Of the first two.
This means that regarding the words *nāsikā* and *udara*, the prohibition [of the suffix *ṅīṣ*] by the rule "not after *kroḍa* and polysyllabic [stems]" (*na kroḍādibahvacaḥ*) would otherwise apply;
that is set aside by this present rule, which prescribes the optional application of *ṅīṣ*. However, the prohibition based on the characteristic of being polysyllabic (*bahvac-lakṣaṇa*)...

The intention is that [the rule] has scope in cases such as *sujaghanā* and so forth. Now, one might object: even in cases such as *sahanāsikā*, *anāsikā*, *sahodarā*, and *anudārā*, let this [present rule] also override the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 4.1.58], namely *sahanañvidyamānapūrvāt*; for the term *sahanañ* [in that sūtra] applies in instances such as *sakeśā* and *akeśā*.

He says "before" because there is scope [for the rule]; the meaning is that it is according to the maxim: "Exceptions set aside the rules immediately preceding them, not those further away. Consequently, the prohibition by the rule *sahanaj* (Pāṇini 5.4.72) does not apply here, because it is separated by the rule *na kroḍādi* (Pāṇini 5.4.153).
The meaning is that [the rule] "ṭh-nāsikodara" does not cause an obstruction [to this]. He states the purpose of the group of five beginning with *oṣṭha*— namely, "of *oṣṭha* and so forth"—
with the intention that in cases such as *sugulpha*, the rule "asaṃyogāpadhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.130) has its scope of application.

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as *sahoṣṭhā* and *anoṣṭhā*, even the prohibition [stated] in the rule *sahanañi* should be set aside by this very [rule]. To this, he says: "An exception in the middle... The meaning is that this follows the maxim: "Exceptions in the middle set aside preceding rules, not subsequent ones. Now, [the objection continues]:...
The optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* in the rule "ṭhnāsikodara" (Pāṇini 4.1.55) finds its scope in cases such as *tuṅganāsikī*;
the prohibition by the rule "sahanañ" (Pāṇini 4.1.57) finds its scope in cases such as *sahakeśā*.
However, since both rules would apply simultaneously in cases such as *sahanāsikā*, the question arises: which one is sublated? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "But [the suffix] characterized by *ṅīṣ* [is applied] with the word *sahanam*. Regarding the word *asya*: the meaning is that it is because of the optional rule (*vikalpa-vidhi*) concerning *nāsikodara*. Thus, one forms *tuṅganāsikī* and *tuṅganāsikā*.

This is done by setting aside the prohibition of *ṅīṣ* characterized by the condition of having many vowels (*bahvac*), which is stated in the rule *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ*, by means of the rule *nāsikodara*.

Thus is the option [of the suffix]. Regarding "and so forth": *kumbhodarī* and *kumbhodarā*; here, setting aside the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule concerning bases with many vowels (*bahvack*), there is an option for *ṅīṣ*. *bimboṣṭhī* and *bimboṣṭhā*; *sujāṅghī* and *sujāṅghā*; *śubhradantī* and *śubhradantā*; *sukarṇī* and *sukarṇā*.

*suśṛṅgī* and *suśṛṅgā*. Even though [the stems] *oṣṭha* and others have a conjunct consonant as their penultimate (*upadhā*), there is an option regarding the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Regarding *sahanāsikā*: the word *saha* here has the sense of "possessing" (*vidyamāna*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose nose is possessed [along with it]" (*saha nāsikā yasyāḥ*). And the analysis is also "she whose nose is non-existent" (*avidyamānā nāsikā yasyāḥ*). In both cases here, [the same applies].

The meaning is that by the rule "sahanajvidyamāne," the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies, and not the optional application of *ṅīṣ* by the rule "nāsikodara. Regarding the statement "it should be stated": the remainder of the rule is "or *ṅī*";
this is a specific injunction because the word ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). In the example *svaṅgī*, the limbs (*aṅgāni*) are beautiful (*su-śobhanāni*).
The analysis of the compound is *yasyāḥ* (of whom). *Sugātrī* becomes *sugātrā*; *sukaṇṭhī* becomes *sukaṇṭhā*.
He shows the source of the rule by saying "this [is] also. Regarding the term *prāmāṇikāḥ*:
the sense is that *tanvaṅgī*, *sugātrī*, and *kalakaṇṭhī* are indeed corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśāḥ*).
And [the rule] "pṛcchācca" means that it should be stated that the suffix ṅīṣ is applied after words ending in "puccha," even though they end in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
"Always [after] *kavara-maṇi-viṣa-śara*.

Regarding "after *kabara* etc.": the meaning is that it should be stated that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is always applied after a word ending in the stem *puccha* when it follows *kabara* and so forth. This is an exception to the optional rule stated in [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.55] *pucchācca*.
The explanation of *kabara* is *tritra*. Regarding "and so forth": *maṇipucchī* is a scorpion;
*viṣapucchī* [is another]; *śarapucchī* is a specific species of bird. [This is derived] from the analogy of its wings and its tail.

"From *upamāna*": the meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied even after words ending in *pakṣa* and *puccha* when they follow a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). "The word *nityam*" [is understood]: the meaning is that the word *nityam* (always) continues to apply; this is an exception to the optional rule. Examples: *ulūkapakṣī śālā* ("a hall with owl-wings"). *Ulūka* is a specific type of bird.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has wings on its sides like the wings of an owl.

The formation of the compound follows the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* should be stated for a word preceded by a locative case or a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), with the elision of the final member (*uttarapada-lopa*).

This is a prescriptive rule because [the suffix] would not have applied due to the presence of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as the penultimate letter. Thus, one says: "an army with owl-tailed [flags]."

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose tail-end (*paścimānta*) is like the tail of an owl (*ulūka-puccha*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* in the first member. It is an exception to the optional rule [Pāṇini 4.1.55] beginning with *ṭhpucchāt ca*.
(504) Pāṇini 4.1.56: *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ*. [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is not applied after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *kroḍa* or a word with more than two syllables.]

"Not [the suffix] ṅīṣ after a word beginning with *kroḍa* or after a polysyllabic [word]. The analysis is as follows: "that which has *kroḍa* as its initial member" (*kroḍādi*) and "that which has many vowels" (*bahvac*).
The compound *kroḍādiśca bahvacca* is a collective dvandva. Regarding the term *kroḍādeḥ*:
the meaning is that the suffix ṅīṣ is not applied after a limb of the body (*svāṅga*) that ends in a word belonging to the *kroḍādi* group or is polysyllabic.

Regarding the term *kalyāṇakroḍā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose play (*kroḍā*) is auspicious (*kalyāṇī*). By the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*, the word *kalyāṇa* takes the masculine form. As for the phrase "of horses": according to the opinion of Haradatta and others, the word *kroḍā* is invariably feminine.

When the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) applies, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would otherwise be required by the rule *ṭhsvāṅgāccopasarjanād a-d-a-t-ah*—is prohibited because the word ends in *a*. However, Amara states that the word *kroḍa* (the chest) is both feminine and neuter in the verse *na nā kroḍaṃ bhujāntaram*; in some lexicons, its masculine form is also observed.

In the *kroḍādi* group, the nominal stem *kroḍa* is recited; thus, the examples are unobjectionable even in all three genders. "This is a class-name" (*ākṛtigaṇa*)—the remainder [of the rule] is "the *kroḍādi* group.
Regarding *sujaghanā*: this is an example of a polysyllabic word (*bahvac*), meaning "she whose hips (*jaghana*) are very beautiful (*suśobhana*)."
The compound is *vigraha*. (505) *sahanajvidyamānapūrvācca* [Pāṇini 4.1.57].
Regarding *sahanañ*: "from that which has *tri* as a prior member"—this is the remainder from the rule *svāṅgāt*. As in *sakeśā* ("having hair"). *Saha*...

The term *keśā yasyāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word *saha* here signifies "possessing" (*vidyamāna*). There is an optional substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* by the rule *ṭhvopasarjanasya*. This provides a prohibition of what would otherwise have been required by the rule *ṭhsvāṅgācca*. It has been stated that by this [rule], even the optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *nāsikodara* is superseded.
He provides an example to illustrate this, saying: "one who has a visible nose" (*vidyamānanāsika*).

This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose nose is visible. [Pāṇini 2.2.24] (506) [The suffix *ka* is applied after words ending in *nakha* and *mukha* when forming a name. [Pāṇini 5.4.115] 4.1.58.

Regarding "nakhamukhāt": this is a collective dvandva compound. He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing words: "the suffix ṅīṣ is not applied. This is a prohibition of what would otherwise be obtained by the rule "svāṅgācca" (Pāṇini 4.1.54). The example is "śūrpaṇakhā," which is the name of a particular rākṣasī; she is so called because her claws (kararuhāḥ) are like winnowing baskets (śūrpāṇi).

This is an *asvapadavigraha* (an analysis where the constituent words do not stand independently as separate words), because it is a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound) by virtue of being a proper name (*saṃjñā*). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs according to the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. However, if it were merely etymological (*yaugika*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would indeed occur, but the substitution of *ṇ* would not. *Gauramukhī*—this is the name of a certain woman; [it means] one who has a white face (*śvetaṃ mukham*).

The term *tāmramukhī* is an example where the analysis (*vigraha*) does not contain its own constituent words; this is a derivative (*yaugika*) term. Its analysis is: "she whose face (*mukha*) is copper-colored (*tāmra*).
[Pāṇini 4.1.60 states: "The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a word ending in *dik* (a cardinal direction) when it is the first member of a compound."

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied when the first member of the compound is a word denoting a direction (*dik*). The analysis of the compound is "that whose first member is a word denoting a direction. The term *svāṅgāt* ("from a body part") is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), as is the term *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem"). Furthermore, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which was introduced by the rule *ṭhanyato ṅīṣ*—is understood here and is modified to the genitive case. This is what the author expresses with the words beginning "dikpūrva... and so forth.

Regarding the term *prāṅmukhī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that whose face (*mukha*) is turned toward the east (*prāk*). He states the result of the rule for *ṅīṣ*—namely, that the word has an acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable—as follows: because *ṅīp* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*);
thus, by the general accentual rule for *bahuvrīhi* compounds, the acute accent falls on the first syllable. However, in the case of *ṅīṣ*, [the accentuation would be different].

The meaning is that the final syllable would be udātta by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Nor should it be argued that *ṅīp* alone should be prescribed independently; for if that were the case, even in examples such as *prāggulphā*, the suffix *ṅīp* would undesirably apply, overriding the prohibition stated in the rule *ṭhasaṃyogopadhāt*. [Regarding] *ṅīṣ*:
However, in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṅīp*, there is no fault, because the *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule "ṭhsvāṅgāccopasarjanādasaṃyogopadhāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.54).
If one accepts the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "asaṃyogopadhāt," there would be a lack of brevity (*pratipattigaurava*).
The word *bhāvaḥ* [is the heading].

(508) *vāhaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.61. Regarding *vāhaḥ*: the term *vāh* ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) is an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the word *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem"), which is understood from the previous rule.

This is a rule concerning the final element (tadanta-vidhi). Thus he says: "after [a stem] ending in vāh. The phrase "only ṅīṣ continues" means that the word "ṅīṣ" from the previous rule "anyato ṅīṣ" is understood here. As for "not ṅīp": although the mention of ṅīp was present in the preceding sūtra, "dikpūrvapadāt," its application does not continue here.

The meaning is "because it lacks the *svarita* accent. There is a distinction regarding the accent. Regarding the word *dityauhī*: first, each stage of life for cows consists of six months. The stages of life are enumerated in the section beginning with "my embryos and my calves. Among those, the third stage of life is expressed by the word *ditya*. Thus [it is explained].

This is clear in the *Yajurvedabhāṣya* and in the ritual commentaries (*kalpabhāṣya*) composed by Bhavasvāmin, Dhūrtasvāmin, and others. In the analysis of the compound as "that which carries Diti" (*dityaṃ vahati*), the suffix *ṇvi* is applied according to the rules *ṭhccchandasi sahaḥ* and *vahaśca*; there is vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel, and it forms an *upapadasamāsa*. From the word *dityavāh*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added [to form *dityauhī*]. [The rule regarding] *vāh*...
By applying the rule *ūṭh*—specifically "there is *vṛddhi* [substitution] for *ūṭh*, *eṭha*, and *edhatī*"—the form *dityauhī* is derived.

Since the suffix *ṇvi* is restricted solely to Vedic usage, a Vedic sentence has been cited as an example. In secular (non-Vedic) usage, however, from the root *vah* with the suffix *kvip*, and then adding the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* to the word *vāh*, the form *dityauhī* exists.
This sūtra, which ought to have been introduced within the Vedic procedure (*vaidikaprakriyā*), is presented here for this specific purpose:

(509) *sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām* | 4|1|62|. [The forms] *sakhī* and *aśiśvī*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) after the words *sakhi* and *aśiśu* when denoting a female in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). *Bhāṣā* refers to common usage. [Objection: In that case, it would not occur at all in the Veda.
To this he says: "the word *iti*. After the word "in the sense of manner" (*prakāre*), the word "occurs" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
"Manner" (*prakāra*) means similarity of kind (*sājātīyatā*). Regarding the phrase "in the spoken language," that word *iti*—

The meaning is that [the rule] is placed immediately after "in the spoken language" (bhāṣāyām). Consequently, the result is that [it applies] both in the spoken language and in the Veda. Now, one might object: if this is so, the mention of "in the spoken language" (bhāṣāyām) is redundant;
to this he says: "by that" (tena). By the inclusion of the term "spoken language," [the rule] applies everywhere in the spoken language, whereas in the Veda...

"Somewhere" (kvacid) means "is obtained. Regarding "sakhi": from the word *sakhi*, when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, there is the elision of the vowel *i* following the letter *kh* by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*. Why [is the condition] "in common usage" (*bhāṣāyām*) specified? [Consider: "O friend, become one who has taken the seven steps" (*sakhā saptapadā bhava*). Regarding "aśiśvī": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she for whom no child (*śiśu*) exists."

When the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to the word *aśiśu*, the *ukāra* undergoes *yaṇ* (substitution). According to Amara, "aśiśvī means 'without a child' (*śiśunā vinā*). He provides an example for the rule "even in the Veda, in some cases" (*chandasy api kvacid*): *ā dhenavo dhunayantām aśiśvīḥ*. This refers to the form *aśiśvīḥ* when the suffix *jas* follows the word *aśiśvī*, by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca*.
The absence of the prohibition against the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
(510) *Jāter astrīviṣayād ayopadhāt* | Pāṇini 4.1.63. [Regarding the term] *jāteḥ*: since an operation is impossible in the sense (*artha*), it is understood to apply to the word (*śabda*).
Thus he says: "denoting a genus" (*jātivācin*). And [the phrase] "not restricted to the feminine" (*na ca striyāṃ niyatam*):

the word *strīviṣaya* refers to that which has the feminine as its object (*viṣaya*) without restriction; this is understood through a *bahuvrīhi* compound as meaning "that which is not restricted to the feminine gender. And so, by the rule "not having the feminine as its object" (*astrīviṣayāt*), [it is excluded].
The intended meaning is "from an indefinite feminine gender"; the inclusion of the term *viṣaya* (object/domain) is precisely for the sake of obtaining definiteness.
Otherwise, he would have simply said *aṭhastriyāḥ*. [Objection:
But if the *jāti* (universal) is that which the logicians describe as "eternal, unitary, and inherent in many," then...

If the qualities such as whiteness (*śukla*) were held to be eternal and unitary, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *śuklā* (the white woman), and non-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *aupagavī* (the female descendant of Upagu) and *kaṭhī* (the female follower of the Kaṭha school). Furthermore, that which is acquired through birth—such as Brāhmaṇahood and so forth—is [defined] by such Smṛti texts as: "From those of the same class (*savarṇa*), upon women of the same class, are born those of the same lineage (*sajātayaḥ*)."

If "jāti" (genus) were intended [in Pāṇini’s rule], there would be non-application to the state of youth (*yauvatva*) and so forth; consequently, in the case of *yuvatitarā*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule *jāteśca* would not occur. If this is argued, it is not so, because "jāti" is that which is grasped through its form (*ākṛtigrahaṇā jātiḥ*), and it does not possess all genders (*liṅgānāṃ ca na sarvabhāk*).
"Jāti is that which grasps the form;
it is to be apprehended by a single manifestation, along with lineage and [the names of] Vedic schools"—
intending thus the threefold *jāti* mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*, he [states] the threefold nature as taught in the *Bhāṣya*.
He elaborates: "The genus (*jāti*) is that by which the configuration (*ākṛti*) is apprehended. The word "in the first [alternative]" is to be supplied as the remainder.

"Configuration" (*ākṛti*) refers to a specific arrangement of parts. "Apprehension" (*grahaṇa*) means that by which something is apprehended; it is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument, and the neuter gender is used for the general category. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose apprehension is the configuration."
Because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. He states the result [of this analysis] with the word "anugatā" (inherent).
This means that it is manifested by a single form—that specific configuration—within all individual instances such as jars and the like.

The term "grahaṇā" is derived from the root *grah* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the passive sense; however, it is not the case that it is a compound meaning "grahaṇa by means of ākṛti" (*ākṛtyā grahaṇā*).
This must be explained, because [if it were a word ending in *a*], the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. Regarding the word *taṭī*:
Amara states that *taṭaṃ triṣu* ("the bank is used in three genders"). A bank (*taṭa*) is a region near water characterized by a specific shape;
therefore, "bank-ness" (*taṭatva*) is a genus (*jāti*), as it is manifested by shape. Consequently, for the word *taṭa*...
The intention is that [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied because [the word *yuvati*] denotes a genus (*jāti*), because it has a fixed feminine gender, and because it has the letter *y* as its penultimate.

Furthermore, youthfulness and so forth are also indeed genera (*jāti*), since they are manifested by the configuration (*ākṛti*). By this first definition, the genus such as "bankness" (*taṭatva*) is stated, which is established through the cognition of a recurring form.
Furthermore, the [inferential] marks (*liṅga*) do not apply to all [individuals], as they are to be grasped through a single declaration.

[Objection: If this were the case, then [status such as] *vṛṣalatva* (the state of being a low-born) would not constitute a genus (*jāti*), because the physical configuration of its constituent parts is common to Brahmins and others; thus, for *vṛṣalatva* and the like—

Anticipating the objection that [this] is not because it is manifested by them (*tadvyaṅgyatvābhāvāt*), he says: "And [it is] not shared by all genders; it is to be grasped as expressed once. The words "another universal" (*anyā jātiḥ*) are to be supplied. In the word *liṅgānām*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is that it does not possess all genders. Regarding the word *nirgrāhyā*: *Note: This fragment appears to be from the commentary on Pāṇini 4.1.63, which deals with the gender of universals.*
The meaning is that [the universal] is easily understood even without instruction regarding another individual, due to the influence of the prefix *nir-* in the term *nirgrāhyā*.
After the word *nirgrāhyā*, the phrase "another universal" (*anyā jātiḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. He states the conclusion: "not-all... (*asarva...*).
Regarding the phrase "in one": because of the instruction "he is a *vṛṣala*" with respect to one individual, [it is understood] in another individual...

The meaning is that [the definition] is easy to understand even without that instruction. Regarding the phrase "another definition" (*lakṣaṇāntaram*): the sense is "a different genus" (*jātyantaram*). Otherwise, since the very genus such as "bankness" (*taṭatva*) has already been stated [as a genus], this would have to be considered a definition other than the one stated as "a genus is that which is grasped through its form" (*ākṛtigrahaṇā jātiḥ*); however, this is not tenable.
Because the bank possesses all genders. Regarding the term *vṛṣalī*:

for the state of being a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) does not possess all genders, because it lacks the neuter gender; when the state of being a *vṛṣala* has been taught with respect to one individual, that [state] exists in his offspring, siblings, and so forth even without such a teaching.

The sense is that [the caste] is easily grasped because it is apprehended upon being explained only once. As for Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇatva*), although it is not easily discernible in sons, grandsons, and so forth—since one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother lacks Brahminhood—it is nonetheless easily discernible in the father and others. The same applies to Kṣatriyahood (*kṣatriyatva*).

And the status of being a Vaiśya is easily established in his father and so forth. [The question] "What is the purpose of the phrase ending with 'satī'? means: what is the purpose of [the condition] "provided it does not possess all genders"? [The example] "śukla" [is given]; the word "in the case of *balākā*" is to be supplied. As it is said: "In the case of a quality (*guṇa*), words such as *śukla* are masculine; however, when they denote that which possesses the quality (*guṇin*), they take the gender of that [substratum]."

Because it conforms to the gender of the word it qualifies (*viśeṣyaliṅgatva*), it possesses all three genders; thus, due to the absence of non-universality (*asarvaliṅgatva*), "whiteness" (*śuklatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*).

Furthermore, because it is not manifested by the configuration of parts (*avayavasaṃsthānavyaṅgyatva*), it does not satisfy the previous definition either. [As for the example] "Devadatta": *devadatta iti* |

The sense is that, although [the category of] "name" (saṃjñā) is not of all genders because it lacks the neuter gender, it is nevertheless not graspable by a single mention. By this second definition,
there is an inclusion of universals such as Brahminhood, which are caused by birth.
[Objection: And [the definition includes] lineage (*gotra*) along with conduct (*caraṇa*).
[Response: Even so, there would still be no inclusion of cases such as "ĀṬpagavī" or "Kaṭhī," because *āṬpagavatva* and the like are not manifested by a recurring configuration (*saṃsthāna*).
And because it possesses all genders, he says: "and the lineage (gotra) together with the Vedic schools (caraṇas).

The word "jāti" (birth/class) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. By the word "gotra," offspring (apatya) is intended, and not the technical term [defined] as beginning with the grandson; this is because of the [author's own] explanation. Therefore...

Thus, the Bhāṣya on the rule *ṭhanupasarjanāt* is consistent with the view that in the case of *avantī*— which ends in the suffix *pratyaya* following *apatya*— the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by virtue of [the word] being a genus (*jāti*). However, in the *Śabdenduśekhara*, it is elaborated that here "lineage" (*gotra*) is intended in its technical sense alone.

The term *caraṇa*, however, is well-known as referring to one who studies a particular branch [of the Veda]. From this, it follows that lineage (*gotra*) and birth (*jāti*) are included along with the *caraṇas*. That is to say, lineage and the *caraṇas* constitute birth. Although birth is indeed of two kinds—namely, that which is cognized by a continuous uniform cognition and that which is conditioned by a specific parentage—[it is here subsumed under these categories].

In the world, *jāti* (genus) is well known; however, lineages (*gotra*) and religious sects (*caraṇa*) are not included therein. Nevertheless, with the intention that "in this context, the word for that [genus] refers to words denoting that [genus] for the sake of its grammatical operation," he explains by saying "ending in a patronymic suffix" and so forth. He illustrates a lineage with the example *aupagavī*.

In the sense of "the female offspring of Upagu," when the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyāpatyam*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by this [present rule] because it is subsequent, thereby superseding *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. There is a difference in accent. He gives the final example: *kaṭhī*. This means "one who studies what was proclaimed by Kaṭha. Similarly, *kalāpī*.

The suffix *ṇini* is based on the fact that [Vaiśampāyana] was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. By the rule *ṭhkaṭhacarakālluṅ*, there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. Then, by the rule *tadadhīte*, the *aṇ* suffix is applied; this is elided by *proktālluṅ*, after which the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added.
He states another example regarding the subject of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*): "bahvṛcī. This means that many *ṛc*s are to be studied.

He says: "In this case, [the word] *brāhmaṇī*. In the sense of "the offspring of Brahmā," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyāpatyam*;

then, by the rule *brāhmo'jātau*, there is no elision (*ṭilopa*) of the final vowel, and with the initial *vṛddhi* (guṇa), the word *brāhmaṇa* is formed. However, for the feminine, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would otherwise apply as a marker of a genus (*jāti*)—is set aside, and instead the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*.

The sense is that its inclusion in the *śārṅgaravādi* group would otherwise be without scope. Having thus stated the nature of *jāti*, he asks for the purpose of including it in the rule for the suffix *ṅīṣ*:
"What is the purpose of [specifying] *jāti*? He gives the example: "muṇḍā" (shaven-headed). For "shaven-headedness" (*muṇḍatva*) is...

The state of having all hair lost is not manifested by shape (*ākṛti*), because that shape remains even in the state where the hair has fallen out. Nor is it characterized by the definition "of genders" (*liṅgānāṃ ca*), because it possesses all genders. Nor is it included within a lineage (*gotra*) or a school (*caraṇa*); therefore, it is not a genus (*jāti*).

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Regarding the question "Why [specify] 'not having a feminine object' (*astrīviṣayāt*)?"—the meaning is: since the restriction is already obtainable through the inclusion of the term "object" (*viṣaya*), for what purpose is it stated "from that which is not invariably feminine" (*aniyatastrīliṅgāt*)? [The example] *balākā*: in the section on birds, Amara states, "a crane is *balākā* or *visakaṇṭhikā*. Since the state of being a crane (*balākātva*) is manifested by its form (*ākṛti*), [it is not invariably feminine].

The meaning is that even though it is a genus-term (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply because its gender is restricted to the feminine. Although there is a three-gendered nature when the word is derived etymologically as "one who nourishes strength" (*balām kāyati*), nevertheless, the sense is that [the term] is distinct from those words whose basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is uniform and which lack any gender other than the feminine.

This is established. Regarding the term "kṣatriyā": the point is that although the condition for the [suffix] *ṅīṣ*—namely, being a genus (*jāti*) characterized by the rule "and not all genders"—is present, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply because it ends in a short vowel followed by a consonant (*yopadhā*).
(In the prohibition regarding words ending in a short vowel followed by a consonant, there is no prohibition for the words *hayā*, *gavaya*, *mukaya*, *manuṣya*, and *matsya*.)

Regarding the rule *yopadhapratiṣedhe hayagavayaiḥ*: this is a Vārttika. Its meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* should be stated [as an exception] even when *hayā* and others have a *y* as their penultimate vowel (*yopadha*). Thus: *hayī* (a well-known female horse); *gavayī* (a specific four-legged species resembling a cow); *mukayī*.

This refers to a specific class of quadrupeds. Regarding the word *hal*: when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *manuṣya*, resulting in *manuṣya-ī*, the letter *y* is elided by the rule *halas taddhitasya*;
then, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Thus, the form *manuṣī* is established. This is according to the rule *halas taddhitasya*.

In order to demonstrate that the *yakāra* (the suffix *-ya*) undergoes elision (*lopa*) and is a constituent part of a *taddhita* derivative, he says: "in the sense of being born from Manu" (*manor jātāv iti*).
This rule belongs to the section on *apatya* (descendants) within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *taddhita* suffixes.

Regarding the word *matsya*: after the word *manu*, the suffixes *añ* and *yat* are applied to denote offspring, with the augment *ṣuk* added to the base, provided that the combination of base and suffix denotes a genus (*jāti*). This is the meaning.

Since the elision [of *y*] does not apply to the *y* in *mātsya-* because it is part of a *taddhita* suffix when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, he says: "In *matsya*, [the *y* is elided] before a *ṅī*. This is a *vārttika* on the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām ya upadhāyāḥ*.
It means that the elision of the *y* which is a constituent of *matsya* occurs only before a *ṅī* suffix.

This is for the sake of restriction. Regarding *matsī*: the sense is that when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied and the letter *y* is elided, there is the elision [of the final vowel] by the rule "when *ya* follows" (*yasyeti ca*). Why [is the word] *ṅyām* used? [Consider: *mātsya avatāraḥ* (the Fish incarnation).
(511) Pā. 4.1.64: *pākakarṇaparṇapuṣpaphalamūlavālotarapadācca*.

Pākakarṇa: Since this [formation] is already established by the preceding rule, "jāter astrīviṣayāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.63), for what purpose is this [sūtra] stated? To this he replies: "even from that which has the feminine as its scope.
This means: even from that which is restricted to the feminine gender.

The sense is that, because [the word] has a fixed feminine gender, the previous rule does not apply. To demonstrate that it denotes a genus (jāti), he says: "conventional as specific medicinal herbs"; the meaning is that they are devoid of etymological derivation from their constituent parts (avayava).

(512) *itaḥ manuṣyajāteḥ* |4|1|65|. He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing words: "*ṅīṣ syāt*" (the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied). The meaning is: the suffix *ṅīṣ* shall be applied in the feminine to words denoting a human genus (*manuṣyajāti*) that end in short *i*.

In the rules for the formation of feminine suffixes, because the term *ātaḥ* (from "ātaḥ" in Pāṇini 4.1.4) continues to apply, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not otherwise be applicable after a stem ending in short *i* when it denotes a genus (*jāti*) that does not apply to females. This rule provides for such cases. For example, *dākṣī*:

in the sense of "the female descendant of Dakṣa," the suffix *iñ* is added by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], followed by the elision of the final vowel (*allopaḥ*), the initial vṛddhi (*ādivṛddhiḥ*), and the suffix *ṅīṣ*; then, by [Pāṇini 6.4.148], the *y* of the suffix *iñ* is elided.
There is the elision of the suffix *ceti*. According to the rule "a *gotra* [name] is also [treated as] a class-name (*jāti*) when accompanied by a *caraṇa*," it denotes a genus.
*Dakṣa* is a specific type of Prajāpati. Regarding the phrase "even from one having *y* as an upadhā": the remainder is that this [suffix] is *ṅīṣ*.
The point is that by the repeated mention of the word "genus" (*jāti*), it is made known that the mention of "having *y* as an upadhā" does not continue [from the previous rule].

*Āudameyī*: There is a certain person named Udameya; his female descendant is formed by adding *ṭhak* (which becomes *iñ*), followed by the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*yasyeti ca*), the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening, and then the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* to the word *audameyi*, resulting in the elision of the short *i* (*yasyeti ca*). *Titirī*: A bird.
It is a specific class (*jāti-viśeṣa*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply in the feminine because it denotes a non-human species (*amanuṣya-jāti*); this is the intended meaning.

Nevertheless, according to the *Amarakośa*—which states, "The serpent has two, four, or six feet, and its offspring are both male and female"—this word can also be used for the feminine, as it possesses two feet.

(513) *ūḍutaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.66. The rule *ūḍutaḥ* follows from the previous rules *ṭhagopadhāt* and *manuṣyajāteḥ*. The term *utaḥ* is a qualifier for that [suffix], and the rule applies to what ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says: "from that which ends in the vowel *u*, etc."

*Kurūḥ* means "the female descendant of Kuru," who was the king of Kurukṣetra. Since the rule states, "A *gotra* [name] is treated as a genus (*jāti*) together with the names of Vedic schools (*caraṇas*"), the word *kuru* denotes a genus. From the word *kuru*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, resulting in the lengthening of the vowel by the rule of *guṇa* (vowel coalescence). The purpose of the explicit mention of the long vowel *ū* in the suffix *ṅīṣ* is clearly explained in the Bhāṣya.
Fearing that the suffix *aṇ* [as prescribed by] "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) might apply here, he says: "From *kuru*, *naḍa*, etc., the suffix *ṇya*.

This sūtra falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning offspring. The meaning is that by this sūtra, the suffix *ṇya* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*. If that were so, one might ask why it would not be heard [in the form]; therefore, he says: "of him" (*tasya*). [The example is] "adhvaryu."

The meaning is "one who studies the *Adhvaryu* branch [of the Veda]. Because it is a *caraṇa* (a Vedic school), it is a genus (*jāti*). As the *Smṛti* of Yama and others states: "In former ages, the binding of the girdle of muñja grass for women, as well as the teaching of the Vedas and the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*, were prescribed."
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding non-living things such as ropes (*rajjv-ādi*):
"and of non-living things. The remainder [of the sūtra], namely "of those that denote," is understood here.
Thus, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied even to words denoting non-living beings, provided they are distinct from ropes and the like.

The meaning is that this is an *upasaṅkhyāna* (an addition to the rule). Now, does the word *uta* connect here, or not? It cannot be the first case, because it would contradict the example given in the Bhāṣya, namely *alābūḥ*, since the word *alābū* ends in long *ū*.
Nor can it be the second case, because [the rule] *adantād api aprāṇijātivācina ūṅ apateḥ* [would apply].

He says: "By the exclusion of *rajjvādi* (the *rajjvādi* group). The word "here" (*uta*) is not connected [to that]. There is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to roots ending in *ad*, because—according to the maxim "that which is joined with *nañ* or *iva* refers to something else similar to it, for thus is the meaning understood"—only those ending in the vowel *u* that are similar to *rajjvādi* are included; this is the intended sense.

Regarding *alābvā*: from the word *alābu*, by the application of the suffix *ūṅ* and the lengthening of the vowel (*sivarṇadīrgha*), the word *alābū* ending in *ūṅ* undergoes the addition of case-endings (*sub*). When the feminine suffix *ṭā* is applied, it is replaced by *yaṇ*, resulting in the form *alābvā*. Similarly, from the word *karkandhū*, when *ūṅ* is added and *ṭā* is applied, the form *karkandhvā* is produced.

"Karkandhū is badarī," according to Amara; and "Tumbī and alābū are both the same. Now, one might object that since these two [words] end in *ū*, the rule for *ūṅ* is redundant; therefore, he says: "of these two.
*Kṛkavāku* refers to a specific species of bird. In this regard...
Because of the absence of the generic class *manuṣya-jāti*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply even by the preceding rule.
(514) *bāhvantāt saṃjñāyām* | 4|1|67|. From a stem ending in *bāhu*, when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). From the rule *ṭhūḍutaḥ*, the suffix *ūṅ* is understood as being carried over (*anuvartate*).

The governing rule "in the feminine" (*striyām*) and "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*) applies here. Thus it says: "In the feminine, *ūṅ* shall occur. Regarding *bhadrabāhūḥ*: this is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). As for the question "What is the purpose of [the condition] 'in a proper name' (*saṃjñāyām*)?": this is the inquiry as to what the purpose of the term "in a proper name" is. Regarding *vṛtabāhuḥ*: [it means] one whose arms are covered (*vṛtau bāhū*).

The analysis of the compound is *yasyāḥ*. Even in the case of a feminine [word], there is no *ṅīp* suffix. (515) *paṅgoś ca* |4|1|68|. Regarding *paṅgoś ca*: the remainder of the rule is *ṭhūṅ*. Lameness (*paṅgutva*) consists in having broken feet; it is not a genus (*jāti*).
Because it is difficult to grasp through its form while sitting or lying down— since even when lameness is taught of one individual by saying "this person is lame" (meaning he has deformed feet),
that lameness is difficult to perceive in other individuals who are in states such as sitting or lying down.

And because [the word *śvaśrū*] is not included within the *gotra-caraṇa* group, this rule is stated since the application of "ṭhūRutaḥ" would otherwise not occur. Furthermore, there is the elision of the phonemes /u/ and /a/ in the word *śvaśura*.
Regarding the mention of *śvaśura*: this has been recited in the *Vṛtti* and other works. By means of the particle *ca*, the suffix *ūṅ* is drawn over [from the previous rule].

In the sense of "the wife of a father-in-law" (śvaśurasya strī), when the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise apply by the rule for feminine derivation from a masculine base (*puṃyogalakṣaṇe*), the suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed as its exception; the meaning is that, in conjunction with that [suffix], there is the elision of the vowel *a* after the letter *r*, and the elision of the vowel *u* after the letter *ś*.

Furthermore, one should not suspect the elision of the vowel *a* after the letter *v*, because of the principle: "When the final [letter] is not subject to elision, [an operation applies to] that which is in the vicinity of the final."

Because of the explicit statement [of the rule]. However, the rule *yasyeti ca* does not apply here, because that [elision] is prescribed specifically for the vowel *ī* and for taddhita suffixes. [Objection: But how can the case endings (*svādayaḥ*) occur in the word *śvaśrūḥ*, given that their prescription is made under the governing heading *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, and this [word *śvaśrūḥ*]...

Because there is an absence of the suffix *ṅīp*, and because that which ends in *ūṅ* lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to being a derivative suffix, he says: "qualified by gender.
This is based on the principle: "When a nominal stem is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included."

The meaning is "by way of a technical designation. In reality, however, the statement "of the father-in-law" (*śvaśurasya*) is entirely baseless, because it is not seen in the Bhāṣya and because it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*. For in that [Bhāṣya] on the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*...

Having raised the objection that *ūha* must also be included as something to be grasped [by the rule], it is stated that *ūṅ* is prescribed after a word ending in *u*. In that case, once the single-substitute long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) has been applied, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is obtained by virtue of its being a "prior-final" (*pūrvānta*) element; thus, the desired form is established. For if the word *śvaśrū* is derived according to the method described above, then...
Since the letter *a* has been elided after the letter *r*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule does not apply; thus, the inconsistency [of the cited example] is quite evident.
Accordingly, it is clearly stated in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that *śvaśrūḥ* is an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

(516) *ūrūtarapadādaupamye* |4|1|69|. [The suffix *kan* is added after a nominal stem] ending in *ūru* as the final member of a compound, when used in comparison (*aupamye*). The analysis is: "that whose final member (*uttarapada*) is *ūru*"—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The term *prātipadikāt* ("after a nominal stem") is understood from the previous rule. By the mention of *uttarapada*, the *pūrvapada* ("prior member") is implied.
The word *aupamye* (in the sense of comparison) connects with that [term]. That by which something is compared is *upamā*; the act of comparing is *upamāna*.

"Comparison" (*aupamya*) is simply *upamā*, with the suffix *ṣyañ* added in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus he says: "expressing the object of comparison" (*upamānavācī*). Regarding the example *karabhorūḥ*:
the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose thighs (*ūrū*) are like the forearms (*karabha*). From the wrist (*maṇibandha*) to the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) is the hand.

According to Amara, *karabha* means "the forearm. This statement is made because the quality of having thighs like a *karabha* (*karabhoru*) is not a genus (*ajāti*) and thus would otherwise not be subject to the rule [of the feminine suffix].

This is because the form of the thighs—being common to both the thighs of a man resembling a *karabha* and those of a woman—is not something that can be grasped solely by its shape; therefore, the quality of having thighs like a *karabha* is not reducible to mere configuration.

And because of the absence of the state of not having all genders (*asarvaliṅgatva*) and so forth. Why [is it specified] "expressing a standard of comparison" (*upamānavacī*)? [Consider: *vṛtoruḥ* ("thighs like a tree-trunk").

In examples such as *karabhopamorūḥ* ("thighs like a young camel"), the augment *ṅ* does not occur, because the word *karabha* does not express a standard of comparison due to its not functioning (*avṛtti*) as a standard of comparison for the thighs.

(517) *saṃhita-śapha-lakṣaṇa-vāmādeś-ca* |4|1|70|. From words preceded by *saṃhita*, *śapha*, *lakṣaṇa*, or *vāma*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied when *ūrū* follows as the second member. For example, in the analysis *yasyā ūrū saṃhitau*, it is simply that [woman] whose thighs are joined together.
Regarding the term *śaphorū*: the meaning is that one whose thighs are joined together (*saṃhitorū*) is indeed what is called *śaphorū* by this [term].
He explains the word *śapha* as "the two hooves" (*khurau*). Although Amara states, "The word *śapha* is neuter;
*khura* is masculine," nevertheless, Hemacandra states, "*śapha* is the hoof of cows and other animals."

The sense is that masculinity [emerges] from the sheath of the moon. Now, one might object that the "hoof-like" nature (*śaphatva*) of the thighs contradicts direct perception; to this he says: "those two... Since they are like hoofs, therefore the thighs are designated by the word "hoof" (*śapha*). From what, then, does that similarity arise? To this [he replies]:

He says: "Because of being joined. If that is so, then it is already established simply because the preceding word expresses a comparison; therefore, he says: "By way of metaphorical designation" (*upacārāt*). The meaning is that, by relying on actual joining similar to that of a hoof, the state of being a hoof is superimposed [upon it]. And thus...
The point is that because the word *śapha* does not convey similarity [to the thighs], the aforementioned fault does not apply. Regarding the compound *lakṣaṇorū*:

the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose thighs (*ūrū*) are marked (*lakṣaṇau*). Now, one might ask: how can the word *lakṣaṇa*, which is a synonym for qualities such as softness, stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ūru*? To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "From the word *lakṣaṇa*. The meaning is that in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "those two for whom there is a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇam anayoḥ asti*), the suffix *-ac* is applied according to the rule *adarśādibhyo'c*. Thus, since the sense "possessing a characteristic" (*lakṣaṇayu*) is obtained, the aforementioned fault does not apply here; this is the intended meaning. [The example] is *vāmorūḥ*.

The analysis of the compound is: "she whose thighs are beautiful on the left" (*vāma*). Amara states: "The word *vāma* means 'beautiful' or 'opposite' (*pratīpa*)," and [the rule] should be stated as "with *sahita* and *saha*."

Regarding the word *sahitā*: the meaning is that it should be stated that the suffix *ūṅ* occurs even after the word *ūru* when it follows the words *sahita* or *saha*. Now, one might object: since this is already established by the principle of "modification of a part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*) through the very mention of *saṃhita*, the further mention of *sahita* is redundant. To this [the author replies]:...

He says: "By means of *hitena*. The meaning is that when there is an analysis (*vigraha*) as *hitena saha*, the word *sahita* arises through the substitution of *sa* for *sa-* in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *tena saha* by the rule *vopasarjanasya*. Now, an objection is raised: if the word *saha* signifies "existing together" (*vidyamāna*), then its employment in the phrase *sahorūḥ* ("having broad hips") would be redundant. To this [the author replies]:
He says: "They endure. The phrase "crushing during the time of pleasure" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
He states "or else" to show that even though the word *saha* signifies existence, it is not redundant;
the sense is that since what is intended is existence in an intensified degree, there is no redundancy.

(518) *saṃjñāyām* |4|1|72|. The word *saṃjñāyām* [is the governing rule]. The words *kadrukamaṇḍalvoḥ* and *ūṅ* are understood from the preceding rule, and *striyām* (in the feminine) is the governing heading. Therefore, he says: "In the case of *kadru* and *kamaṇḍalu*, etc."

Regarding "accchando'rtham": since the previous sūtra specified *cchandasī* (in Vedic), this present rule is commenced because [the desired forms] were not obtained in common usage (*loke*) when used as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*). *Kadrūḥ*: this is the name of the mother of the Nāgas; this is clear from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources. *Kamaṇḍalūḥ*: [this is the name] of a certain animal.

This refers to the word *saṃjñā*. For this very reason, under the rule *ṭhcatuṣpādbhyo ḍhañ*, the example *kāmaṃjaleya* will be cited. However, a synonym for *pātra* is not an example [under that rule], because it lacks the feminine gender.

(519) *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn* | 4|1|73|. The term *śārṅgaravādi* [in the sūtra] is a compound with its fifth case ending elided (*luptapañcamīkam*). The word *ṭhañaḥ* is in the genitive. The term *ṭhataḥ*, which is supplied by way of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over), follows as a fifth-case ending. [The meaning is: After the suffix *yañ* following the group beginning with *śārṅgarava*, the feminine suffix *ṅīn* is applied [in place of *ṭāp*]. The suffix *ṭhañ* is mentioned in the genitive because it is the item to be replaced; the term *ṭhataḥ* is understood from the preceding rule and connects here as a fifth-case ending.
The word *jāteḥ* (of a genus) is understood from the previous rule and serves as the qualifier. This is a rule concerning suffixes ending in that [genus].
Thus he says, "from *śārṅgarava*, etc. Regarding *śārṅgaravī*:
it means "the female descendant of Śṛṅgaru"; thus, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, followed by initial *vṛddhi*, substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*), and the *guṇa* substitution of *o*.
Regarding the form *vaidī*: since it is a genus (*jāti*) by virtue of the rule "the *gotra* [suffixes] along with the *caraṇa* [suffixes]," the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been required;
however, *ṅīn* is applied instead. There is a difference in the accent. The meaning is "a female descendant of Vida.

By the rule "after *vida* and others, the suffix *añ* is used when not a direct descendant of a seer (*anṛṣi*)," the suffix *añ* is applied. Since it is a genus by virtue of being a *gotra*, *ṅīṣ* would have been required; however, *ṅīn* is applied instead of *añ*.

Because of the qualification "ending in the vowel *a*," the word *iha-śūrasenī* does not apply here. [The suffix] *añ* is applied by the rule *janapada-śabdād apatye 'ñ* to form *śūrasena*. Then, by the rule *ataś ca*, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. In this case, only the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*—characterized by the class-name (*jāti*)—is applied, and not *ṅīn*;
for since *añ* has been elided, the vowel *a* following the *n* is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of the suffix *añ*.

"And the vṛddhi of *nṛ* and *nara*. By the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *ṅīn* is also included. Thus, *nārī*. This is an illustration for both the words *nṛ* and *nara*. In that regard, since the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise apply to the word *nṛ* by the rule *ṭhṛn-nebhyaḥ*, [the rule prescribes] *ṅīn*; there is vṛddhi of the vowel *ṛ*, and the substitution of *ra* (raparatva). As for the suffix *ṅīṣ* characterized as a generic class (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), however—

There is no application [of the suffix] from the word *nṛ*, because the term *ṭha* is understood to follow there [in the rule]. However, from the word *nara*, by adding the suffix *ṅīn*, there is a vṛddhi of the vowel *a* following the *n*. Now, one might object: even though the subsequent elision (*lopa*) by the rule *yasyeti ca* is set aside, the vṛddhi of the vowel *a* following the *r* occurs due to its being "internal" (*antaraṅga*) according to the maxim of the "final letter" (*alo'ntyaparibhāṣā*).

It might be argued: "Even when the *vṛddhi* substitution has taken place, one should not say that the elision of the vowel *a* would occur by the rule *yasyeti ca*; for the very force of the *vṛddhi* rule itself establishes the non-occurrence of that elision. To this it is replied: in the rule *nṛnarayoḥ*, the word *nar* [is used].

This is an imitation of the word ending in *repha* (the letter *r*) with its vowel *a* elided. The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: *naraḥ* and *ahaḥ* [become] *naraḥ*; *nā* means "woman" and *naraḥ* means "man," thus *nṛnarau*. One should not argue that even so there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the word *vānarī*, because only meaningful items (*arthavat*) are to be understood here. Nor does it follow that the suffix *ṅīp* would apply to the word *nṛ* after [the addition of] *vṛddhi*.

It should not be argued that the inclusion of the word *nara* (man) is redundant because the form *nārī* is already established; for it serves the purpose of excluding [the application of] the suffix *ṅīṣ*, which is prescribed for feminine gender after words denoting a genus (*jāti*) according to the rule for *nara*.
In reality, however, the *gaṇa*-sūtra "ṭhnṛnarayorvṛddhiśca" need not have been composed at all. [The intended meaning is: "That belongs to this..."

When the word *dharmya* is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*), by means of the rule *ṭhṛto 'ñ* and the Vārttika *narasya ceti vaktavyam*, the suffix *añ* is applied after the words *nṛ* and *nara* in the sense of "the duty of a man" (*nṛ-dharmyaḥ*, *nara-dharmyaḥ*). Subsequently, by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in the form *nārī*.

Since the initial syllable of the base is acute by the rule "ṭhñnityādirnityam," and since the suffix *ṅīp* is grave (*anudātta*) because it is marked with *p*, while even in the case of *ṅīn* the base remains acute due to the accent of the *nit* affix, there is no difference in accent. Furthermore, this being the case, the understanding would not be solely as a property of humans (*manuṣyadharmitva*).

It should not be said that [the cognition] does not arise as "human-ness," for by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*), that substratum is indeed cognized as qualified by the universal of human-ness (*naratva-jāti*). For this very reason, the form *vāstavya*— meaning "dwelling in a site" (*vāstu*)—
is established by the rule *digādibhyo yaḥ*, which prescribes the suffix *ya* in the sense of "being there" (*bhava*).

The *bhāṣya* statement that the rule "the suffix *tavyat* [is applied] after the root *sthā*, with *ṇic* in the sense of the agent" need not be formulated is thus consistent; furthermore, it is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that for conventional words (*rūḍha*), there is an etymological derivation (*anvākhyāna*) by whatever means possible, according to Kaiyaṭa.

The *yaṅ* and *āp*: the letter *p* is for the purpose of including [the suffix] in the rule *ṭh-ṅ-y-ābbhyaḥ*; the letter *c* is for the purpose of making it *cita*, which results in the final udātta accent. Regarding "in general": the form of *yaṅ* applies in both cases.
The meaning is "because it exists. He illustrates *ñyaṅ*: *āmbaṣṭhyā*.
This means "the female descendant of Āmbaṣṭha. By the rule *vṛddhetkosaleṣu ñyaṅ*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied;
from the word *āmbaṣṭhya*, the suffix *cāp* is added. He illustrates *ṣyaṅ*: *kārīṣagandhyā*.
*Karīṣa* is the dung of cattle and other animals; that which has the scent of this is *karīṣagandhi*.

By the rule *ṭhupamānāt ca*, the final vowel of *gandha* is replaced by *i*. To express "the female descendant of *karīṣagandhi*" in the sense of lineage (*gotrāpatya*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. By the rule *aṇiñoḥ anārṣayoḥ*, this *aṇ* is replaced by *ṣyaṅ*.

The suffix *āp* should be stated as an optional substitute for *yañ* following a word beginning with *ṣ*. The phrase "following *ṣ*" means that even after a *yañ* suffix which follows a *ṣ*, the suffix *āp* is applied.
For example, *śārkarākṣyā*: the meaning is "the female descendant of Śarkarākṣa. Similarly, *pautimāṣyā*.
The meaning is "the female descendant of Pūtimāṣa. In both cases, the suffix *yañ* is applied according to the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.105) *Āvaṭyaśca* (4.1.75).
[Objection: But how can the word *āvaya* have the form ending in *yañ* when it means "the descendant of Āvaya"? To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "The word *avaṭa*. [The form] is *āvaṭaḷā*. The meaning is "the female descendant of *avaṭa*. When the suffix *yañ* (from the *garga*-class) is applied, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, and after the initial vowel-vṛddhi, the feminine suffix *cāp* is added to the stem *āvaṭaḷ*.

(522) *taddhitāḥ* |4|1|76|. The meaning is that the suffixes (*pratyaya*) to be mentioned hereafter are to be understood as having the technical designation *taddhita*. This is an introductory rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*). It states the upper limit: "up to the fifth [chapter]."

(523) *yūnastiḥ* | Pāṇini 4.1.77. Regarding *yūnastiḥ*: the term *taddhitaḥ*, which was understood from a previous rule, is modified here to the singular number. Thus he says: "from the word *yuvan*" and so forth. The word *striyām* ("in the feminine") is to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule].

The sense is that the governing rule (adhikāra) for that [suffix] has been stated prior to the word "samarthanā. This is an exception to the *ṅīp* suffix characterized by the marker *n*. Now, one might object: "Is the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of 'taddhita' here not redundant? And it should not be argued that its continued application is for the sake of [the word's] being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by the rule 'kṛttaddhita-...'"

Even in the absence of *prātipadika* status, the derivation of case endings (*sup*) from a stem ending in the suffix *ti* is established by the *paribhāṣā* "a term qualified by gender [is treated as if it were not so qualified]. To this he says: "of that which is qualified by gender. Regarding *yuvati*: because it is a *pada* by the rule *svādiṣu*, there is the elision of the *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ*.

"Only from that which is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). This means it indeed continues to apply. In the case of *bahuyuvā*, because it is a subordinate member, the suffix *ṅīp*—which would otherwise apply by the rule "for a word ending in *n*" (*nāntalakṣaṇaṅīp*)—is prohibited by the rule "the suffix *ṅīp* is excluded after a *taddhita* suffix *ṭhan* in a *bahuvrīhi*. Consequently, the form is derived with the suffix *ḍāp* by the rule "ḍāp after both [the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*]. Now, [one might object]: "In the case of *yuvatībhiḥ*..."
Regarding the question of how the word *yuvatī* ends in the vowel *ī* in passages such as "surrounded by... and so forth, he says: "But *yuvatī* [is derived as follows].

The meaning is that the word *yuvatī* should be understood as a derivative formed from the root *yumiśraṇe* (to mix) with the suffix *laṭ*, followed by the suffix *śatṛ*, the elision (*luk*) of *śap*, and then the suffix *ṅīp* due to its being marked with the *uṅit* indicator. [She] [serves] her husband with ease.

A woman who mixes [with others] is called *yoṣit*. Others, however, say that the word *yuvatī* is derived from the root *yudh* with the suffix *kat* by virtue of the diversity (*bāhulaka*) of the *auṇādika* rules; due to the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution, resulting in *uvaṅ*, and because it is marked with *u*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to form the word *yuvatī*.
Thus ends the section on feminine suffixes in the *Bālamanoramā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by the illustrious Vāsudevadīkṣita.
Now, the rules for internal sandhi (*svādi-sandhi*).
(160) *sasajuṣo ruḥ* | Pāṇini 8.2.66. The analysis of the sūtra is *sa-sajuṣaḥ ruḥ*. By the rule *ro ri*, there is the elision of the *repha* (the *r* sound).

The analysis of the compound is: *saśca sajūśca* (the word *sa* and the word *sajūs*), [forming] *sasajuṣau*; [the meaning is] "of those two. In the rule prescribing the substitution of *ru*, the letter *u* is the *it*.

Its result, however, will be explained immediately below. By the word *sa*, the letter *s* is intended; the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The governing term *padasya* (of a word) is qualified by the letter *s* and by the word *sajūs*.
