To this he says: "when reproach is not intended"—that is, when there is a statement of the truth. [This applies] in the case of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) based on a different substratum.
"Resorting to various factions" means, that is to say, abandoning commonality with all and resorting to one side alone.
"Faction" (pakṣa) refers to the act of embracing [others] as one's own. "The gods were on Arjuna's side" means they were in the faction of Arjuna. And from disease; of disease...

*Pratīkāraḥ* means medical treatment (*cikitsā*). Regarding the phrase *pravāhikātaḥ*: it means the remedy for cholera (*viṣūcikā-pratīkāram*). [The suffix] *cv-* is applied after a word ending in the ablative case when used in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, provided that the agent of the action is the same as the subject of the resulting state (Pāṇini 5.4.50).

Regarding the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge*: "abhūta" means when a thing that previously did not exist in a certain form attains that very form. Thus, this suffix is applied only in cases where the original substance itself, undergoing a transformation, is intended to be expressed as non-different from that transformation.
Thus it is obtained. *Saṃpadyakartari* is a single compound word. *Saṃpadana* is *saṃpadya*.

From the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *sam*, by this very irregularity (*nipātana*), the suffix *śa* is designated as *kṛt*; because [the root] belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *yan* is applied. *Saṃpadyasya kartā* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
It should be stated as "the becoming of that which was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*).

This refers to [the suffix] occurring after a word in the present tense when it is undergoing such a transformation. When there arises the expectation as to "in what form" and "of what" there is this transformation, [the rule] "in the case of the becoming of that which was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāve*) [is applied].

From the Vārttika, it is understood that there is a transformation (*saṃpatti*) of the base (*prakṛti*) into the form of a modification (*vikāra*). In that context, the suffix is applied only after a word denoting the modification, provided it is in conjunction with the verbal root *as* (meaning "to be") or *bhū* (meaning "to become"). In the case of the suffix *cvi*, the letter *c* is an indicatory letter (*it*), and the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.
Regarding *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32):

[the word] *asya* [is used] in the sense of "there should be *ī*" [after it]. This is because the rule *ī dhrādhmoḥ* (6.4.113) is understood to apply here by implication (*tanuvṛtteḥ*). Regarding "the elision of *v*" (*velopaḥ*): this is a reference to the remainder [of the rule] *verapṛktasya* (6.1.67).

"Because it ends in *cv*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). This means that because it is a particle (*nipāta*) by the rule "the suffixes *cvi* and *ḍāc* [are particles] after *ūry-ādi*," it is an indeclinable according to the rule "particles beginning with *svara-*. Some maintain that it is an indeclinable because it is included among those enumerated in the rule "and a *taddhita* suffix not taking all case-endings," specifically within the list starting with *śas* and ending before the *samāsānta* suffixes. He gives an example in connection with the root *kṛ*: "Kṛṣṇa. The meaning is: being actually non-Kṛṣṇa, he attains the state of Kṛṣṇa through anointing and so forth. "He makes him so" means: he makes that which was non-Kṛṣṇa become Kṛṣṇa in form.

Regarding the form *kṛṣṇīkaroti*: here, in reality, the actor (*naṭa*) is the base entity (*prakṛti*), who is not black. As he undergoes the transformation (*vikāra*) of attaining the state of being black, because he is becoming that [state], he is the agent of the process of becoming (*sampadyakartṛ*). Relying on the superimposition of identity (*abhedāropa*) in that context, the word denoting the transformed black object is applied. From that [root], the suffix *cvi* is added. The letter *c* is for the sake of pronunciation, and the letter *u* is for the purpose of utterance. When that [suffix] follows, the vowel *a* becomes *ī*. By the rule *ṭhverapṛktasya*, the letter *v* is elided. Thus, *kṛṣṇī* ending in *ī* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Regarding the expression *brahmībhavati*: the meaning is that "that which is not Brahman (*abrahma*) becomes Brahman (*brahma*). The suffix *cvi* is applied after the word *brahman*. Because the case-ending (*vibhakti*) contained within the stem is taken into account, the final *n* is not elided due to the status of being a *pada*; this is the intended sense regarding the substitution of *ī*. According to the view of Nyaṅka, suffixes that are purely *atyanta-svārthika* (purely intensive/qualitative) arise only from nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and not from forms ending in case-endings (*subanta*). Therefore, it should be understood that the suffix *cvi* does not arise from a nominal stem, but rather only from a form ending in a case-ending.

For this very reason, the example from the Bhāṣya—"*agoḥ gauḥ samapadyata*, *go'bhavat*" (the non-cow became a cow)—is consistent with the rule for the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) taught in *Pāṇini 6.1.94*: "In place of *eṅ* [at the end of a word], when followed by *aṭ*. Enough of this. Regarding *gaṅgī syāt*: the meaning is that "that which is not the Gaṅgā (*agaṅgā*) should become the Gaṅgā. The change to *ī* occurs by the rule "*asva cvau*" (*Pāṇini 7.4.32*). Regarding *doṣābhūtam ahar*: the indeclinable *doṣā*, ending in long *ā*, signifies "night"; however, here it signifies "day" (i.e., night has turned into day).

"Adoṣābhūtam" means "it has become free from faults," [referring to] the darkness caused by the obstruction of thick clouds. Regarding "divābhūtārātriḥ" (the night became day): *divā* is an indeclinable ending in *-ā* meaning "day," but here it is used in the sense of "daytime. The meaning is that [the night] has become like day due to the excellence of the moonlight. Now, one might object: the Vārttika rule "there is no substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of an indeclinable in the case of *cvī*" is not seen in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "asya cvau. To this he says: "And this... [referring to the following]. *Kyacvyośca* (Pāṇini 6.4.152). Intending to say "Gārgībhavati," he states: *kyacvyośca*. From the sūtra *allopo'naḥ*, there is elision (*lopa*).

Thus, from the rule *ṭhhalastaddhitasya*, the word *halaḥ* is understood; from *ṭhsūryatiṣye*, the word *yaḥ* is understood; and from *ṭhāpatyasya ca*, the word *āpatyasya* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). Therefore, he says: "of that which follows a consonant. [The example is] *gārgībhavati*. An *āgārgya* becoming a *gārgya*...
The meaning is "it becomes. After a word ending in *yaÑ*, there is elision of the *yakāra* when the suffix *cvi* is applied. There is also elision of the *vikaraṇa* *l*.

However, elision of the *yakāra* by the rule "the elision of *āpatya* [suffixes] and *ya*" is not possible here, because it is separated by the vowel *ī*. Nor is elision possible by the rule "of a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a consonant," because that rule applies only before a suffix beginning with *ī*.
Because [the suffix] is prescribed only when it has meaning; therefore, the sense is that this is a specific statement (*vacana*). Regarding the rule *cvau ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.26):
now, intending to explain the form *śucībhavati*, he says—*cvau ca*. [The meaning is that] there should be lengthening [of the vowel] when the suffix *cv-* follows.
The sense is that this [rule] follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of an indeclinable" (*avyayasya*):

the meaning is that the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *cvau ca* does not apply to an indeclinable. Therefore, the sense is that in the example *svasti syāt*, there is no lengthening when the suffix *cv-* is applied. [The statement] "that is without foundation" means that it is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*.
[The author] states [the intention]: "The state [of the rule applies]. If that were so, the form *svasti syāt* would not be possible, because of the contingency of a long vowel;

therefore, he says: "But as for the form *svasti syāt*... Now, one might object: even if *svasti syāt* is established by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*) through the absence of the long vowel, the long vowel in *kadācit svastī syāt* would still be unavoidable.

Thus he raises an objection: "Even in the alternative where it is 'svasti' [without the visarga], it would follow [that there is a dual form]. He states that this is an accepted consequence: "Let it be so. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "there are two forms due to the presence and absence of the long vowel. The sense is that both should be respected because they are established by authoritative evidence. Now, an objection:
Since the learned do not accept [the suffix], how can there be respect for the long-vowel reading? To this he says: "yadi neṣyate" (if it is not desired), and so forth.
He states a specific rule regarding the *cvi*-suffix after the word *mātṛ*: "rīṅ ṛtaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.27). [Furthermore:
"The [final] syllable of *arus*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas* is elided [before the *cvi*-suffix]" (Pāṇini 5.4.51).

"Of *arus*, *manas*, *cakṣus*": this means of these—namely, *arus*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas*. Since the suffix is already established by the preceding rule, its final elision (*antyalopa*) is prescribed here in conjunction with that suffix. Thus, in the case of *arūkaroti*: "that which was not a wound (*anaruḥ*) becomes a wound (*aruḥ*)."
The meaning is "he makes that. When the final [letter] of the *prakṛti* is elided, there is lengthening of the vowel *u* by the rule *ṭhcvau ca*.
Thus, *unmanīkaroti* means "he makes one who is not *unmanas* into one who is *unmanas*"; the sense is that he causes someone to become *unmanas*.

In the case of the suffix *cvī*, there is elision of the final [letter] and the change to *ī*. Thus, *uccakṣūkaroti* means "he makes one whose eyes are not raised (*anuccakṣus*) into one whose eyes are raised (*uccakṣus*)."
The meaning is that he makes it become that. In the case of the suffix *cvī*, there is elision of the final letter and lengthening [of the vowel].
For example: *uccetīkaroti*. This means that one who was not a collector (*anuñcetā*) becomes a collector (*uccetā*), and he makes him so.
In this case, there is elision of the final letter and the substitution of *ī* for the vowel. For example: *virahīkaroti*. [This refers to] *rahaḥ*...

A secluded place (*vijanapradeśaḥ*) means a distinguished solitude or separation (*viraha*). The sense is that "it makes non-separation into separation" (*aviraho virahaḥ saṃpadyate tat karoti*). In the case of the suffix *cv-* [added after a verb], there is elision of the final phoneme and the substitution of *ī*. Thus, *virajīkaroti* means "it makes that which was not free from passion (*avirajā*) into something free from passion (*virajāḥ*). When the final phoneme is elided in this *cv-* suffix, [the rule applies].
And the substitution of *ī* [for *ai*].

(Pāṇini 6.1.44) Optionally *sāti* [is used] in the sense of totality. (Pāṇini 5.4.52) The word *sāti* has its nominative case ending elided. It occurs in the domain of the suffix *cv-* [which denotes becoming what one was not before].

The meaning is: when the suffix *kṛt* follows a root in the sense of "becoming that which it was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāve*) with the verb *sampadyate*, provided there is a connection with the verb *as*.

(Pāṇini 6.1.92) *Sātpadādyoḥ* | 8.3.111 | Regarding *sātpadādyoḥ*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "there is no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) for the *s* [of the suffix]."
The meaning is that there would not be the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root *sā-* (to flow) or for the *s* at the beginning of a word.

The intention is that the word "not" (*na*) is carried over from the rule "na raparasṛpī," and the word "retroflex" (*mūrdhanya*) is carried over from the rule "apadāntasya. He gives an example for the beginning of a word: *dadhi siñcati* ("he sprinkles curd").

In the case of the root *ṣic*, the *ṣ* is changed to *s* by the rule "the *ṣ* at the beginning of a root is *s*" (*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*). When the rule "before an affix or a substitute" (*ādeśapratyayayoḥ*) would have required the *ṣ*-substitution for that [s], this [present rule] prohibits it. Regarding the word *kṛtsnam*:
it means "endowed with all its parts. In the example *agnisāt*, [the *ṣ* is not substituted] because the *s* is a part of an affix.

Since the substitution of *ṣ* would otherwise apply, this [rule] provides a prohibition. In the case of *agnībhavati*, the long vowel is substituted by the rule *cvau ca*. "By the Great Option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*) means that the word *vā* (or) is understood from the rule *samarthānām*. Although the desired form is established by the Great Option, the explicit mention of *vibhāṣā* here [is for the sake of...]

But [this rule] is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the general rule (*utsargika*) with the exception (*apavāda*). (Pāṇini 5.4.63) "And [the suffix *ktvā* is used] with the word *saṃpad* in the sense of limit-inclusive (*abhividhi*). The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including the root *kṛ*.

Thus he says: "With *saṃpad*, with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. The gloss on the term *abhividhau* is "in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptau*). Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): in the alternative where the suffix *sāti* is absent, when there is a connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, the suffix *cvi* applies by the preceding rule; however, when there is a connection with *saṃpad*, in the absence of *sāti*, [the suffix *cvi* applies].
The meaning is that it is indeed a *vākya* (a syntactical construction), and not the suffix *cvi*, because that [suffix] is prescribed only in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*.

He gives an example in connection with the root *sampad*: "it becomes fire" (*agnisāt saṃpadyate*). He gives examples in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*: "the weapon becomes fire" (*agnisādbhavati śastram*) and "he makes it fire" (*agnisātkaroti*).
One should also cite "agnisāt syāt" as an example.

He states the distinction between the senses of "entirety" (kārtsnya) and "pervasion" (abhividhi) with the words beginning "of a single individual instance" (ekasyā vyakteḥ). [The sūtra: *tadadhīne vacane* 5.4.54. [This means: when there is a statement regarding that which is dependent on something else.
Regarding the state of being dependent on that: he explains the sūtra by completing the remainder with the words "sātiḥ syāt" and so forth.
The sense is that [the condition] "abhūtatadbhāve" (when there is the becoming of what was not previously so) is no longer applicable. (5.4.50) "And *trā* is used for what is to be given. (5.4.55)

*deye trā ca* | The phrase "a word denoting dependence on that" (*tadadhīnavacana*) continues [from the previous rule]. *kṛbhvādiyoge* means "in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, *as*, and *saṃpad*.

(Pāṇini 5.4.56) *devamanuṣyapuruṣapurumartyebhyo dvitīyāsaptamyor bahulam*: [The suffix *tra* is optionally applied] after the words *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puruṣa*, *puru*, and *martya*, when they are in the second or seventh case.

"Devamanuṣyapuruṣa": "from these" means from *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puruṣa*, *puru*, and *martya*. This suffix is purely taddhita (svārthika). The conditions "in connection with *sāti*" and "in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*" are also no longer applicable here. For example: *devatrā vande* or *rame*.
The meaning is: "I bow to the gods," or "I delight among the gods. *Manuṣyatrá*, *puruṣatrá*.
The word *puru* is a synonym for "many" (*bahula*). *Purutrā*. *Martyatrā*. Regarding the phrase "also elsewhere":
the meaning is "also other than [the cases beginning with] the gods. *Bahutrā jīvato manaḥ*—of the living person...
The mind of a living being (*jantu*) goes toward many objects; the meaning is that it pervades many.
(From the rule *avyaktānukaraṇād dvyajavarārdhādanitau ḍāc* [Pāṇini 5.4.57]:
"After an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*). This refers to a sound in which specific phonemes such as *a* and so forth are not manifested.
That is an indistinct sound (*avyakta-dhvani*). Its imitation is "imitation of an indistinct sound" (*avyaktānukaraṇa*).
He explains the word *dvyajavarārdha*: "having two syllables" (*dvyañ*); the analysis of the compound is "that which has two *ac* vowels.
He explains the word *avara*: "inferior" (*nyūna*). [The term refers to] that which has exactly two syllables.

The word *avaram* means "having a lower number"; its grammatical connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is with [the term *ardham*], meaning "not fewer than that. The sense is "consisting of a single vowel. He states the resulting conclusion: "as many as 'having more than one vowel' (*anekāj*). Regarding the phrase "such a thing": it refers to that which has more than one vowel as its half-portion (*ardha*).

"That"—meaning "consisting of at least two syllables. The sense is: "from that. Regarding the phrase "in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*," the intention is that this [rule] continues by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūakapluti*).
When the suffix *ḍāc* is intended to be expressed, [the word] is reduplicated diversely (*bahulam*).

And thus, it follows that the suffix *ḍāc* shall be applied after an indistinct imitation-sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) consisting of multiple syllables, when used in conjunction with a verb of action, a state of being, or existence (*kṛ-bhū-asti-yoge*). Now,
intending to provide an illustration of the suffix *ḍāṭ* after the indistinct imitation-sound *paṭat*, [the author] discusses the word *paṭat*.

He states the doubling [of the word]: "When *ḍāc* is intended, [the word] is doubled diversely (*bahulam*). Although in the section beginning with "doubling of everything" (*sarvasya dve*), the Vārttika is read in the Bhāṣya as "it should be stated that when *ḍāc* follows, there is doubling," the meaning there is not "when *ḍāc* follows"; for if that were the case, then once *ḍāc* has been added...

There would be a doubling of the word *paṭacc* [to form *paṭac-paṭac*], and if there were such doubling, since the resulting form would consist of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the suffix *ḍāc* would apply by rule Pāṇini 5.4.74; this would result in a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, it is accepted that the suffix *ḍāc* is intended [to apply] while the doubling has not yet occurred.
It should be stated that the suffix *ḍāc* is applied when there is constant repetition (*nityam-āmreḍite*).

Thus, when *ḍāc* is intended and the word *paṭat* has undergone reduplication, the form *paṭat-paṭat* possesses more than one syllable (*anekāck*) and contains a half-syllable (*ardha-bhāga*), making the application of *ḍāc* easily established. *Paṭat*, *paṭat*.
Since the form *ākaroti* is established, he demonstrates the grammatical derivation: "In the case of a constant reduplication (*āmreḍita*), [the substitution of] *ḍāc* [applies].

This Vārttika was recited in the commentary on the Sūtra *Nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* within the section on *pararūpa* (single-substitute for the latter) under the governing rule *Ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*. [The phrase] "preceded by *ḍāc*" means [the word] *ḍāc*.
The analysis of the compound is *paraṃ yasmāt* ("that from which there is another"). Regarding the letter *pa*:

the meaning is that when the form *paṭapaṭhat* (meaning "he does it repeatedly") is established, the suffix *ḍa* is applied; because it is marked with *ḍ*, the *ṭi*-portion (*at*) is elided, resulting in the form *paṭapaṭākaroti*.
[The question] "Why [specify] *avara*? means: let it simply be stated as *dvyajardāt* ("from a word consisting of two syllables ending in *ṛt* or *ṛd*").

Regarding the form *gharaṭagharaṭākaroti*: from the imitation of an indistinct sound *gharaṭat*, when the suffix *ḍāc* is applied, there is reduplication, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is substituted, and the *ṭi*-portion is elided; this is how the form is derived. However, if the rule were stated as *dvyajardhāt* (from a word consisting of two syllables or half a syllable), then because the portion *gharaṭat* consists of many vowels (*bahvacka*), the suffix *ḍāc* would not apply; such is the meaning. [The correct rule] is simply *anekācaḥ* (from a word with more than one vowel).
The meaning is that it would be more appropriate to formulate the rule simply as "avyaktānukaraṇād anekāco 'nitau ḍāc," having removed the phrase "dvyajavarārdhāt. For in this way—
as in the reading "anekāco 'nitau"— even before the reduplication of the word *paṭat*, [the desired form is obtained].

The intention is that since the suffix *ḍāc* can occur because [the base] consists of more than one syllable (*anekāctvāt*), it is possible to state: "there is reduplication when *ḍāc* follows. [The form] *paṭiti* [is derived as follows]: the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpam*) occurs by the rule *avyaktānukaraṇasya*. (Pāṇini 6.1.98). [The rule] *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījātkṛṣau* (5.4.58) [applies].

"Kṛño dvitīya" [means] "from *dvitīya* and so forth. This means from these: *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *śamba*, and *bīja*. "Only in connection with *kṛñ*"—the intention is that because of the mention of *kṛñ*, the rule for *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* does not follow here. [This is stated] in the rule: "After *madra*, in the sense of 'shaving' (*parivāpaṇa*)."
The phrase "up to *kṛñaḥ*" is understood [from the previous rule]. Regarding the expression "because of the mention of *bahulam*":

since the word *bahulam* appears in the rule "in the case of *ḍāc*, doubling occurs diversely (*bahulam*)," doubling applies only to an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) when followed by *ḍāc*, and not to anything else;
this is the meaning. As for the statement "the word *śamba* [is used] in the sense of 'contrary,'" the word "occurs" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

"He plows together with the seed. It is well known that after seeds such as *kulattha* have been sown in a field that has first been plowed, one plows again together with the seeds. According to the authority of the commentary on the rule "ṭhkarṣātvataḥ," the verbal root *kṛṣ* takes the *śap* suffix. Therefore...
One should not suspect that "he ploughs" (*kṛṣati*) alone is correct because it possesses a *śavikaraṇa* suffix.
[The rule] *saṅkhyāyāś ca guṇāntāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.59) [is relevant]. Regarding the phrase *saṅkhyāyāś ca*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "in connection with the root *kṛñ*."

( ) And after *samaya*, when there is a delay (*yāpanā*). 5.4.60. "And after *samaya*. The word *kṛṣau* (in the sense of plowing) is no longer applicable. The meaning is that the suffix *ḍāc* is applied after the word *samaya* when a delay is understood. For example: *samayākaroti*. Here, the root *kṛ* (to do/make) [is used].

Regarding the term *yāpanā*, he says: "it causes to pass" (*yāpayati*). The meaning is that it makes [the time] pass beyond [its limit]. That is to say, when it is said, "This must be done today," one brings about some obstacle and thus effects a delay in time. [The rule] *sapatraniṣpatrādativyathane* (Pāṇini 5.4.61) [is stated].

*Sapatra*: The meaning is that the suffix *ḍāc* is applied after the words *sapatra* and *niṣpatra* when there is "piercing through" (*ativyadhana*). The root *vyadha*, meaning "to strike," ends in the fourth case (the accusative). Piercing beyond [the target] is "piercing through" (*ativyadhanam*). A *patra* is that by which arrows fall upon the target; it refers to the feathers on the shaft (*puṅkha*) of arrows. Regarding the phrase "the surface of the earth" (*bhūtalama*): [it follows the previous rule].

The meaning is that by the entry of an arrow—either up to the end of its feathers or excluding the feathers—one makes the surface of the earth "with-feathered" (*sapatra*) or "featherless" (*niṣpatra*). In the case of *niṣkuṣaṇa* [the suffix] *ṇic* is applied after *niṣkula*. The remainder [of the rule] is "after [stems ending in] *ṭh* or *ḍ* there is *aC*.

*Niṣkoṣaṇam* means the bringing out of internal parts. For example: *niṣkulākaroti dāḍimam* ("he husks the pomegranate"). The compound *niṣkula* is a *bahuvrīhi*: that from which the *kula* (kernel/parts) has gone out. And the word *kula*...
It occurs in the sense of a collection of internal parts. Thus he says: "gone out," and so forth.

[Pāṇini 5.4.63: *sukhapriyādānulomye* (after *sukha* and *priya*, when compliance is to be understood). That is, after the word *sukha* and the word *priya*, when compliance (*ānulomya*) is to be understood.
The meaning is that the suffix *ḍāc* should be applied. *Ānulomya* (conformity) is the following of the thoughts of those to be propitiated, such as a teacher.

"He makes the teacher happy" (*sukhākaroti*) means "he makes him dear" (*priyākaroti*). By following the teacher's thoughts, he causes the teacher to be endowed with happiness and endowed with ease; this is the meaning. Thus it is said: "by being favorable" (*anukūla*).

( ) *duḥkhāt prātilomye* |5|4|64|. From the word *duḥkha*, [the suffix] *ṭhak* (which results in *-ika*) is added; this is the remainder [of the rule]. *Prātilomya* means acting contrary to one who is to be propitiated (*ārādhya*). The rest is as before.

( ) *Śūlāt pāke* |5|4|65|. After the word *śūla*, [the suffix] *ṇvul* (which results in *-aka*) is applied when the action refers to cooking. This is the remainder of the rule *ṭhḍāj*. An example is *śūlākaroti*. Here, the verb *karoti* signifies "cooking. Thus he says: the meaning is "he cooks with a spit."

*satyādaśapathe* |5|4|66|. After *satya*, [the suffix] *ḍāc* is applied when it does not mean "an oath. This is a supplement to the rule *ḍāc* (Pāṇini 5.4.57). Example: *satyākaroti bhāṇḍam*. The meaning is: he treats the collection of goods, such as jewels and the like, as real. Here, the word *satya* refers to "truth" (*tathya*). [The word] *satyam*...
The *Amara-kośa* states that *tathya*, *ṛta*, and *samyak* are synonyms. "Saying 'this is to be bought for this much'" means that one speaks of the matter exactly as it is, namely:
"This is worthy of purchase for this price alone, and not for a higher price. "A Brahmin makes [the word] true" (*satyaṃkaroti*) means that he makes an oath.

[The suffix] *ḍāc* [is applied] after *madrāt* in the sense of "shaving. The rule *ḍāci bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.4.14) is the remainder [of the governing context]. "For the sake of auspiciousness" means it is a synonym for "auspiciousness. "Shaving" (*parivāpaṇam*) means "shaving off the hair" (*keśān vapate*).

The sense is that such is observed in these and similar instances. "By means of a propitious tonsure" (māṅgalyamuṇḍanena) means by means of the *caula* ceremony. "He performs auspiciousness" (bhadraṃ karoti) means he brings about well-being (*kṣema*). The point here is that since the act of shaving (*parivāpaṇa*) is not perceived [as the primary meaning], the suffix *ḍāc* does not apply.
Thus ends the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita-prakriyā*) in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, among the secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), those expressing meanings such as "colored" (*rakta*) and so forth:
(1183) *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* |4|2|1|. [A word ending in the third case denotes that by which something is colored, provided it is a name for a dye.]

"Colored by that" means "due to passion" (*rāga*). Regarding the term *rajyate*: it means "it is colored," or "by this, another color is attained. When the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *rañj* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the *na* is elided by the rule *ca-ja-gha-jīnāṃ ku-ghiṇ-ṇy-at-su*; then, by the rule *ca-joḥ ku-ghiṇ-ṇy-at-su*, the *j* is changed to *g*, and with the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-vṛddhi*), the word *rāga* is formed.

This is the meaning. Thus, by the word *rāga*, the substance that serves as the means of coloring (*rañjana*) is expressed. The term "by that" (*tena*) is a general designation. Accordingly, in the sense of "colored by that"—meaning having attained another color—the suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word denoting a coloring substance (*rañjanadravya*) ending in the third case.
The meaning is "it may be so," because of the governing rule *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83). Regarding *kaṣāyeṇa*:

*kaṣāya* is a specific mineral substance, a dyeing material; that which is colored by it, having attained another hue, is called *kāṣāya*. Regarding *māñjiṣṭha*: *mañjiṣṭhā* is a specific type of dyeing substance.

(1184) *lākṣā-rocanā-ṭṭhak* | 4.2.2 | The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *lākṣā* and *rocanā*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *am*. For example, *lākṣikaḥ*; the word *paṭaḥ* ("cloth") is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound].
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "dyed with lac" (*lākṣayā raktaḥ*). Similarly, *raucanikaḥ*; the analysis is: "dyed with yellow pigment" (*rocanayā raktaḥ*).
There is an addition [to the rule] for *śakala* and *kardama*.
[The example is] *śākalikaḥ*. *Śakala* is a specific kind of dyeing substance. As for the word *vṛtti*, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
This has not been seen [in the sūtra].

[The rule] "nīlyā an" means "after *nīlī*, *an* [is substituted]. The word "it should be stated" (*vaktavya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. [Thus, the form is] *nīlī*.
A particular medicinal herb. [The suffix] *kan* is added after the word *pīta*.
[The rule] "after *pīta*, *kan*" is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. *Pīta* refers to substances such as yellow orpiment (*haritāla*).
The suffix *añ* is applied after the words *haridrā* and *mahārajana*.

The mention of *haridrā-mahā* [in the sūtra] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*; there is a distinction in the accent (*svara*). *Haridrā* is well-known. *Mahārajana* is a specific kind of dyeing substance. Thus ends the section on "dyed" (*rakta*).

(1185) *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* |4|2|3|. [The word] *nakṣatreṇa*: the meaning is that, in this sense, the *prāgdīvyatīya* suffixes are applied appropriately after a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) which is uttered in the nominative case.

The moon conjoined with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is intended by the word "lunar mansion" (*nakṣatra*). "Conjoined with Puṣya" means conjoined with the moon as it is joined with Puṣya. Regarding "the day of Pauṣa": from the word *puṣya*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, there is elision of *y* according to the rule "in the case of the suffix *aṇ* after the lunar mansions Tiṣya and Puṣya, there is elision of *y*. [Thus we get] *pauṣī rātriḥ* (the night of Pauṣa).

The meaning is "joined with the moon when it is conjoined with the asterism Puṣya. [In the formation of the feminine form] *puṣyā*, after the elision of the *yaṇ* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.
Why [is the word] "by an asterism" (*nakṣatreṇa*) used? [Consider: "the night joined with the moon" (*candreṇa yuktā rātriḥ*). Why [is the word] "time" (*kālaḥ*) used? [Consider:
"the moon joined with Puṣya" (*puṣyeṇa yuktaś candramāḥ*).

(1186) *Lub-aviśeṣe* |4|2|4|. [The suffix is elided] when there is no distinction. "Sixty daṇḍas": the established rule is that the moon is conjoined with each individual lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) during each period of time delimited by sixty *ghaṭikās*. Of that...

The meaning is: if it is not understood whether a specific sub-division of a period of sixty *daṇḍas* is a day or a night. Regarding the expression "today [is] Puṣya": the indeclinable *adya* denotes a day-and-night (*ahorātra*) and primarily expresses the locative case-power; however, in this context—
The time intended here is day-and-night (ahorātra) as divested of its functional capacity [to denote a specific action].

Thus, the meaning is: "this day-and-night is conjoined with the moon joined with the Puṣya constellation. Since no distinction is perceived as to whether it is day or night, there is elision (*lup*) of the *aṇ* suffix. How then [is this so]? [It is derived] from *paurṇamāsī*.

The objection is that since no internal distinction within the sixty *daṇḍas* (periods of twenty-four minutes) is perceived here, the elision (*lup*) [of the suffix] should occur. He provides the resolution: "By the rule *vibhāṣā*.
This refers to the words *phālgunī*, *kārtikī*, and *caitrī*, which—being formed with the suffix *aṇ* denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)—refer to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

One might ask: since the elision (*lup*) occurs on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) when it is conjoined with the asterism [Śravaṇā], how can there be the designation "Śravaṇā" (in the feminine)? To this he says: "The elision (*lup*) occurs precisely from the word *śravaṇa* itself. The meaning is that by the very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) stating "on Śravaṇā," the elision occurs for the full moon day. [Objection: But [the forms] *kṛttikā* and *śravaṇaḥ*...

Since the word *śravaṇa* is observed to be masculine in such passages as "That which is between Puṣya, Citrā, and Svātī," when the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form *śravaṇa*] and then elided by *lup*, the rule "In the case of *lup*, the gender and number are like those of the original base" necessitates that it must remain masculine; how then can it be [neuter] as in *śravaṇe*?

To address the objection that [the word *śrāvaṇī*] would have a feminine gender, he says: "and there is an absence of the treatment as if it were the base (*yuktavadbhāva*). The words "due to irregularity" (*nipātanāt*) are to be supplied. But if that is so, then *śrāvaṇī* would not be formed at all; to this he replies: "even those which are subverting [rules do not apply]. This paribhāṣā is established in the Vṛtti; however, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra concerning the *sarva* group of pronouns, it is stated that they are indeed subverting rules.
It has been stated that these are irregular formations (*nipātana*). (1187) *saṃjñāyāṃ śravaṇā'śvatthābhyām* |4|2|5|.
When it is a name (*saṃjñā*), there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) following the words *śravaṇā* and *aśvattha*.

The meaning is that [the suffix] occurs in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). Now, one might ask: since the result is already established by the rule *lub aviśeṣe*, for what purpose is this [new rule] begun? To this he says: "This commencement is for the sake of a specific case. An example is *śravaṇā rātriḥ* ("the night of Śravaṇā"). The meaning is: a night conjoined with the moon when it is in conjunction with the asterism Śravaṇā. [The rule continues: *vibhāṣā*.

In the sūtra *phālgunīśravaṇe ca*, it is understood that because the mention of *śravaṇā* refers to the general [asterism], the designation of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* (as in *śravaṇā*) does not apply even to the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).
Therefore, it is established that [the word] is *śravaṇā rātriḥ*; this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra.
"Aśvattha is a muhūrta. Aśvattha is the name of the asterism Aśvinī; that which is conjoined with it is "Aśvattha"—a specific muhūrta well known in astronomy.
[Pāṇini 4.2.6: *dvandvāc chaḥ*].

The suffix *cha* is applied after a copulative compound (*dvandva*). For example: *tiṣyapunarvasavīyam*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "Tiṣya and Punarvasū" is *tiṣyapunarvasū*; [the day] joined with those two is the compound. When the suffix *cha* is replaced by *īya*, the *guṇa* substitution of *o* occurs (Pāṇini 6.1.97). For example: *rādhānurādhīyam*. Here, *rādha* refers to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) Viśākhā.
*Rādhā* and *Anūrādhā* [form the compound] *rādhānūrādhāḥ*; the meaning is "the night characterized by those [asterisms].
(1189) *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma* | 4|2|7|. Regarding *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma*: the word *tena* (by that) indeed continues [from the previous rule]; this is the meaning. By that [seen], [it is called] *dṛṣṭaṃ*.
The meaning is that suffixes such as *aṇ* and others are applied after a word ending in the third case when it has the sense of "sāman.
Regarding this meaning, it should be stated that *aṇ* is optionally *ḍit*.
"Regarding this meaning" means that the *aṇ* which is applied in the sense of "a *sāman* seen [in this]" is optionally *ḍit*.
"Āuśana" is the form when there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix before the case-ending *am*.
(1190) *Kaler ḍhak* | 4.2.8 | "After *kali*, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied]. This is a *vārttika*.

(1191) *vāmadevāḍ ḍyaḍḍyaḷau* | Pāṇini 4.2.9. [The suffixes] *ḍya* and *ḍyaḷ* are added after *vāmadeva*. Thus, *vāmadevyam*. Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
The *t* in *ḍyaḷ* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). Now, since this could be established by the elision rule *yasyeti ca*, what is the purpose here?

If it is argued that the *ḍit* designation is for the sake of [preventing the application of] accentuation, this is true; however, if the rule were simply "of *ya* and *ya*" (*ṭhyayatoḥ*), then in the prescription of the final acute accent for what follows the negative particle *nañ*—namely, the rule "of that which ends in *ya* or *yat* when not having that meaning" (*ṭhyayatoścā'tadarthe*)—there would be a grasping of these two [suffixes].
To prevent that, the *ḍit* designation is made. But once the *ḍit* designation is applied, these two [suffixes] are not [included] in the prescription of accent.

The exclusion [of unintended forms] occurs by means of the two *paribhāṣās*: "When there is a mention of a [root or suffix] without an *anubandha*, there is no mention of that same [element] with an *anubandha*" and "When there is a mention of [a root or suffix] with a specific *anubandha*, there is no mention of that which has a different *anubandha*. These two *paribhāṣās* are, however, indicated right here [in this very rule].

And thus, this accent does not occur in the word *vāmadevyam*. He recites the verse from the Bhāṣya which summarizes this point: "In the case of what is already established by *yasya*," and so forth. Here, the first half of the verse is intended as an objection: since [the forms] *yayau* and *tattau* are already established by the elision rule (*yasya*), for what purpose [are these specific rules stated]?
The meaning is that [the letters] ḍ and t have been applied. Regarding the term "inclusion" (*grahaṇam*):

in the rule *nañ-svara-unañ-āśraya-svara-vidhau atad-arthe uṭ-hy-aya-toś-ca-atad-arthe*, there should not be an inclusion of these two, ḍ and ḍḍa, when the rule for the accent dependent on *nañ* applies to the word *vāmadevya*. This is because it does not pertain to that [specific case].
The purpose of making [the suffix] *ḍit* is so that [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* may not apply; this is the meaning.

(1192) *parivṛto rathaḥ* | Pāṇini 4.2.10. "A chariot surrounded by [something]. The word *tena* ("by that") is understood from the previous rule. Thus, it is for the sense of "a chariot surrounded by that."

The meaning is that suffixes such as *aṇ* and others occur after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Now, one might object that this would also apply in the case of "the chariot surrounded by students" (*chātraiḥ parivṛto rathaḥ*); therefore, he says "on all sides" (*samantāt*). The intention is that [the suffix applies] only from a word denoting that cloth or similar material which constitutes a part of the chariot for the purpose of covering it on all sides; this is because of the inclusion of the term "exclusive" (*ekānta*).
From the Vārttika: (1193) *pāṇḍukambalādiniḥ* |4|2|11|.
The suffix *ini* is added after *pāṇḍukambala*. The words "by that" (*tena*) and "a chariot covered by that" (*parivṛto rathaḥ*) are carried over from the previous rule.

In the suffix *ini*, the vowel *i* following the letter *n* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Now, one might object: since the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) is already established by the suffix *in* alone—as in the rule "after [a word ending in] *ṭhak*, there are *ini* and *ṭhan*"—what is the purpose of this [present rule]? To this he replies: "For the purpose of excluding *aṇ*."

(1194) *dvaipavaiyāghrādañ* | 4|2|12 | The suffix *añ* is applied after the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra*, when they end in the third case, in the sense of "a chariot covered with that. The phrases *tena* ("by that") and *parivṛto rathaḥ* ("a chariot covered [with]") are understood to carry over from the previous rule. Thus, from the third-case forms *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra*, the suffix *añ* is added in the sense of "a chariot covered [with that]."
The meaning is "it may be so. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. There is a distinction regarding the accent (*svara*).

Regarding the word *dvīpina*: *dvīpī* means a tiger; in the sense of "the hide which is a modification (*vikāra*) of that," the word *dvaipa* is formed by the suffix *añ* according to the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ*. Similarly, *vaiyāghra*: the hide of a tiger is *vaiyāghra*, [formed] by the suffix *añ*.
By the rule *ṭhna yvābhyām*, [the suffix] *aiC* is applied; thus, the sense is "covered by a tiger-skin" (*vaiyāghra*). (1195) *kaumāra-apūrvavacane*:
[The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after *kumāra*] when expressing that it was not previously so. The phrase "a chariot covered by that" is excluded [from this rule].

"Without a case-ending" (*avibhaktika*) means that the nominative case has been elided; this is the sense. He states that the word *apūrva* is used here with the abstract sense as its primary meaning: "this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) in the sense of *apūrvatva* (being previously unmarried).
In the sense of "a husband who has married a maiden who has no previous husband," she is called *apūrvapatī*, and he is her husband.

One meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kumārī* when it ends in the second case (*dvitīyāntāt*). Another meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kumārī* when it ends in the first case (*prathamāntāt*), in the sense of "having obtained a husband who was not previously married. He illustrates the first with the example "one who has obtained a husband not previously married" (*apūrvapatim*). Regarding the second...

He provides an illustration: "yad vā" and so forth. The distinction is that in the first case, the suffix denotes the one who causes the taking (*upayantṛ*), while in the second case, the suffix denotes the act of taking itself (*upayanā*) in its own sense (*svārtha*).
(1196) *tatroddhṛtam amatrebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.14).

Regarding the phrase *tatroddhṛtam* (taken out from there): the meaning is that a suffix occurs after a word denoting a vessel (*amatra*) ending in the locative case, in the sense of "taken out from there. A vessel (*amatra*) refers to a container such as a shallow dish (*śarāva*) and so forth. Now, one might ask: since the shallow dish functions as the ablative (*apādāna*) in the act of taking out—which is a process of separation—how can it take a locative case? To this, he says: "The verb *uddharati* here... [and so on].
The word "tatra" from the rule "sāsmin paurṇamāsī" (Pāṇini 4.2.21) is understood to follow here. (1197) *sthāṇḍilāc chayitari vrata* (Pāṇini 4.2.15).

[The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *sthāṇḍila*; that is, after the word *sthāṇḍila* ending in the seventh case, when the agent of lying down (*śayitṛ*) is motivated by a religious observance (*vrata*).
The meaning is that the suffix should occur when the object to be expressed is [the agent].

(1198) *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* | 4|2|16|. "Prepared food" (*saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*). They are eaten, thus they are "eatables" (*bhakṣāḥ*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object. The word "therein" (*tatra*) is understood as a carry-over.

He says this: "from that ending in the seventh case. The singular and plural numbers are intended generally, because of the rule stating, "the plural is used for a single thing when expressing a genus"; with this in mind, he says: "that which is prepared" (*yatsaṃskṛtam*). "Preparation" (*saṃskāra*) means the imparting of a specific quality through cooking and so forth. "Eight-pot-sherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*): this is a compound by the rule *taddhitārtha*. What is the purpose of the word "food" (*bhakṣāḥ*)? It means: what would [the suffix] be in the sense of "prepared in a flower-basket, [and it is] food"? "A pot" (*ukhā*) is a specific type of vessel; as Amara states: "A cooking-pot (*piṭhara*), a pan (*sthālī*), a pot (*ukhā*), and a bowl (*kuṇḍa*). (1199) *dadhnaṣṭhak* | 4.2.18 | [The suffix] *ṭhak* is added after the word *dadhi* [to denote that in which something is prepared].]

*dadhnaṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.18). The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after the word *dadhi* ending in the seventh case, in the sense of "prepared with" (*saṃskṛtam*) when referring to edible food (*bhakṣa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, *dādhikam*. When *ṭhak* is applied, the substitution of *ik* occurs, and by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*, the *ik* vowel is elided. Here, the preparation (*saṃskāra*) takes place in the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) of curd, by means of salt and other ingredients.

[The suffix *cha*] occurs [after a word ending in the third case]. However, in the rule *prāgvahateḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.77), it will be stated that the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word ending in the third case to form the sense of "prepared" (*saṃskṛtam*).
(1200) *udaśvito 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 4.2.19).

"From *udaśvit*, [the suffix] *ṭhak* should be applied. This is a supplement to the rule; it means that in the context already mentioned, the suffix *ṭhak* may optionally be applied after the word *udaśvit*.
(1201) Pāṇini 7.3.51: "After [stems ending in] *is*, *us*, *uk*, or *t*, [the suffix] *ka* [is applied]."

*Isusuktāntāt kaḥ*. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has *is*, *u*, *su*, or *kt* at its end. The vowel *a* after the letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation. [The rule means: "In place of *ṭha*, there shall be *ka*. In the suffix *ṭhak*, the letter *k* is an *it* (indicating that the suffix is treated as having an indicatory *k*). The vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation; thus, in place of the suffix *ṭhak*, the letter *ka* is the substitute. This is according to the rule "*ṭhasyekaḥ*" [Pāṇini 7.3.50].

Thus it has been stated there. The explanation of *śvayati* is "it increases" (*vardhate*). The point is that the root *śvi* (in *ṭua o śvi gativṛddhyoḥ*) is used here in the sense of increase. Regarding *udaśvit*: [the suffix] *kvip* is applied with *tuk*; by the rule "for *udaka*, *uda-* is substituted when a Name is formed," *uda-* is the substitute. [It means] *takra*.

"Hyaduśvinmathitaṃ pādāmbvardhāmbu nirjalam," thus says Amara. Regarding the phrase "of those mentioned as specific rules": this means that here, only those forms derived by the suffixes *it* and *us* that are specifically prescribed in the *Uṇādi* list are to be understood; for example, *sārpiṣkaḥ* and *dhānuṣkaḥ*.

Regarding the term *āśiṣika*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "one who moves" (*carati*). From the verbal root *śās*, with the *kvip* suffix, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule "the penultimate vowel of *āśās* becomes *i* when *kvip* follows. Thus, one who moves by means of *uṣas* (dawn) is called *āuṣika*. From the verbal root *vas*, with the *kvip* suffix and the occurrence of vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), the form *uṣ* is obtained; this is the third case ending [in the compound]. (Addendum on the suffix *doṣan*.
— [In the case of] *madya*, *dyūta*, *edha*, *matsya*, *dugdha*, and *kṣīra*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied [to form derivatives].
Regarding *soma*, [the suffix] *ya* is applied on the days of the sacrifice (*madyadya*), and *taddhita* [suffixes] are elided.

(Pāṇini 4.2.21): "In this [day], there is the *paurṇamāsī*. [The suffix *ya* is applied] to *soma* on the days of the sacrifice, and the *taddhita* suffixes are elided by the word "iti" in the rule *coddyataddve*. This is established in the Bhāṣya.
Regarding the term *pauṣī*: the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) conjoined with the lunar mansion Puṣya is *pauṣī*; the month in which that occurs is the Pauṣa month.

From the word *pauṣī*, by adding the suffix *aṇ* and applying the rule "when [the suffix] *aṇ* follows, there is elision of the *ī* of the *y* [in the feminine suffix]," the *ī* is dropped. Similarly, the full moon day conjoined with the Maghās is *māghī*; the month in which that occurs is the Māgha month. Likewise...

*Phālguna*, etc. Why [is the word] *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) used? [Consider: *pauṣī paurṇamāsī asmin pañcadaśarātre* ("the full moon day of Pauṣa occurs in this fifteen-night period"). (1204) *Āgrahāyaṇyaśvatthāṭ ṭhak* 4.2.22. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after *āgrahāyaṇī* and *aśvattha*.

*Āgrahāyaṇy-aśvatthāṭ-ṭhak*. The meaning is that in the scope of the previous sūtra, the suffix *ṭhak* shall apply after the words *āgrahāyaṇī* and *aśvattha*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. Regarding the word *hāyana*: it means "year" (*saṃvatsara*). [As it is said: "The year (*saṃvatsara*), the season (*vatsara*), and the year (*abda*)."
According to Amara, *hāyana* is not feminine. The meaning is that the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) on which the year begins is called *āgrahāyaṇī*.
[Objection: In that case, it should be *āgrahāyaṇā*. To this he replies: "from *prajñādi*.

The meaning is that by the rule *prajñādibhyaśca*, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), and then by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. [The word is] *aśvatthena*.

The meaning is "by means of the Aśvinī constellation. Regarding the word *aśvattha*, the intention is that the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.2.3] is elided by the rule "the elision (*lub*) occurs when no specific [lunar day] is intended" (Pāṇini 4.2.4). Now, one might object: does not the mention of the rule "optionally [the elision occurs] after *phālgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārtikī*, and *caitrī*" (Pāṇini 4.2.23) imply that the elision of the suffix [denoting the full moon day] applies specifically to the *paurṇamāsī*?
Since it has been stated that this [rule] does not apply, one might ask how *lup* occurs here; therefore, he says: "by virtue of an irregularity (*nipātana*).
Thus, the intention is that this indication—that there is *lup* in the case of *pauṇamāsī*—applies to instances other than those [already specified].

(1205) *vibhāṣā phālgunī-śravaṇā-kārttikī-caitrībhyaḥ* |4|2|23|. [The rule] *vibhāṣā phālgunī*: from these, the suffix *ṭhak* is optionally applied; the phrase "in the sense already stated as 'that occurs in this'" (*sāsmin*) is to be understood as the remainder. Thus: *phālgunikaḥ*—meaning either the month of Phālguna or [an event occurring] in Phālguna. *Phālgunī*.

The analysis of the compound is "that which has the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) in this [month]. In the same way, one forms *śrāvaṇika* and so forth. Thus end those [suffixes] having the sense of "connected with" and so on. (1206) *sā'sya devatā* (That is its deity). Pāṇini 4.2.24.

That [deity] is its *devatā*. The meaning is that in this sense, suffixes such as *aṇ* and others are applied to a word ending in the nominative case. For example, *aindraṃ haviḥ* ("an oblation for Indra") means "that which is related to the deity whose nature is Indra. Regarding *pāśupatam*, the analysis of the compound is: "Paśupati is its deity" (*paśupatir devatā asya*). Now, [one might ask] regarding the word *devatā*:

If [the suffix -ya] were to denote a specific class (jāti) well-known in the world, then expressions such as *pitrya*—meaning "that for which the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities"—would be untenable; therefore, he says: "with respect to the substance being abandoned.
This refers to cases such as "he gives the remainder of the oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*) to the officiating priests" or "he gives a cow to a Brahmin."

The specific mention [of "deity"] is for the purpose of excluding the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the Brahmin, and others from being considered deities. A deity is, in short, that which is the substratum of the benefit consisting of satisfaction and so forth—which is accomplished by the sacrificial offering being relinquished and which is imperceptible to people such as ourselves. And [it is known] through the praise of mantras; for example: "I praise Agni... (*agnim īḷe*).

The meaning is that even that [deity] which is presented in mantras such as "the domestic priest" (purohita) as being characterized by qualities such as being the priest of the sacrifice is also a deity. Here, this should be noted: one view is that in the word *kasya*, it is the genitive singular of the word *ka* ending in the vowel *a*. [The other view is that it is] of the interrogative pronoun *kim* as listed in the *sarvādi* group.

from the word *mātṛ*, the suffix *ḍāmahac* is added, and there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*). In the same way, *pitāmaha*.

Regarding the rule *mātari ṣic*: the meaning is that after the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ*, the suffix *ḍāmahaC* is applied when *mātṛ* is the referent, and this suffix is also *ṣit*. He states that the result of being *ṣit* is the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, as in the examples *mātāmahī* and *pitāmahī*.

Regarding "averdugdhe": the suffixes *soḍha*, *dūsa*, and *marīsac* are to be stated [after the word *avi*] in the sense of "milked by a goat" (*averdugdham*). That is to say, in the sense of "milked by a goat," these suffixes—*soḍha*, *dūsa*, and *marīsac*—are to be stated after the word *avi*. [This applies to] the *sakāra* of *soḍha*.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) because the word occurs in the *pratyāhāra* (*avayava*), he says: "It is not *ṣ*, due to the force of the non-reading of the letter *s*.
The sense is that otherwise, he would have taught it simply as *ṣoḍha*.
(1) From the word *tila* meaning "fruitless," the suffixes *piñja* and *peja* are applied.

Regarding the word *tila*: the term *tila* is primary (*mukhya*) when referring to a specific plant, but secondary (*gauṇa*) when referring to its fruit. In this context, when the word *tila* denotes the fruitless plant, the suffixes *peya* and *piñja* occur after it in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus end the [suffixes] having deities as their meaning.

(1224) *tasya samūhaḥ* |4|2|37|. The phrase *tasya samūhaḥ* continues [as a governing rule] up to the sūtra *initrakaṭhaḷcaśca*. In this sense, secondary suffixes (*prāgdīvyatīya*) such as *aṇ* and others are applied, as appropriate, to a word ending in the genitive case that is uttered first.

This is the meaning: having set aside the scope of exceptions such as "ṭhak, citahastidhenoṣṭhaṅ," etc., he provides examples—*kākam*, *vākam*. The neuter gender of words ending in collective suffixes is established by common usage (*lokāt*).

(1225) *bhikṣādibhyo 'ṇ* |4|2|38|. From *bhikṣā* and the rest, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied]. This applies in the sense of "a collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*). For example, *bhaikṣam* ("alms"). Here, *aṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak* which will be taught later in the rule *ṭhājādāv-astriyām* (Pāṇini 4.2.44). For example, *gārbhiṇam*.

When the possessive suffix *in* is added to the word *garbha*, according to the rule "the suffix is subsequent and has an acute accent on its first syllable," the vowel *i* becomes acute. Then, by the rule "the remainder of the word is unaccented," the rest of the word *garbhin* becomes unaccented;
thus, the word *garbhin* begins with an unaccented vowel. Subsequently, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied due to the word ending in *n*, that suffix is also unaccented.

Since *suppitau* [Pāṇini 6.1.200] prescribes anudātta for the suffix *pit*, the word *garbhiṇī* is also anudātta in its initial syllable. Consequently, when the suffix *añ* is applicable—by the rule to be stated later, *anudātāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44), which applies to the sense of a collection—the intention is that the suffix *aṇ* is used instead because [the word *garbhiṇī*] belongs to the *bhikṣādi* group. With the suffix *aṇ*, the word becomes udātta on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix; however, with *añ*, [it would remain anudātta].

There is a distinction in accent, such as the initial acute (udātta) resulting from the rule *ṭhñityādir nityam*. He shows that the absence of *ṭilopa* in the case of *aṇ* is also a purpose [of this rule], stating "here, when it is *bha*":
when *aṇ* follows the word *garbhiṇī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is removed by the application of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) according to the rule *bhasyāḍhea*.
The meaning is: when *garbhīṇī* is present, and the elision of the *ṭi* suffix [the long *ī*] is about to occur by the rule "ṭhnastaddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144), [this sūtra applies].
(1226) *inaṇyanapatye* |6|4|164|. The analysis of *inaṇyanapatye* is *in-aṇ-i-anapatye*. [The word] "prakṛtyā" [is understood from the previous sūtra].

The meaning is that this is because of the continued application (anuvṛtti) of the rule "ekāj-prakṛti" [Pāṇini 6.4.163]. The phrase "there is no elision of the *ṭi*" means that, whereas in the case of the suffix *añ* there would be elision of the *ṭi* due to the non-application of the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), here it does not occur. Regarding the word *yauvanam*: it ends in the *uṇādi* suffix *kanin* according to the rule "kaniny-ūṛṣi-takṣi," and it is acutely accented on the first syllable by the *nitsvara* (accentuation of a stem ending in *nit*).

Then, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṭhyūnastiḥ," and the suffix has received an acute accent (*udātta*) by the accent of the suffix itself, the word *yuvati* would—by the accent remaining after the elision of the suffix—be expected to take the *añ* suffix because it begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*).

However, since it belongs to the *bhikṣādi* class, the *aṇ* suffix is applied instead. Once the *aṇ* suffix is applied, the rule "bhasyāḍhea" causes the word to undergo masculine-like treatment (*puṃvat*), resulting in the elision of the suffix *ti*.

In the case of *nivṛti*, because of the rule "ṭhan" [Pāṇini 6.4.173], there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), and thus, in the absence of the elision of the suffix *ṭi*, the form is *yauvana*. However, the point is that if the suffix *añ* were applied, the preservation of the original form would not apply, and consequently, the elision of *ṭi* would occur.
In reality, however, regarding the rule "bhasyāḍhe taddhite" [Pāṇini 6.4.129], when a *taddhita* suffix other than one beginning with a vowel (*aḍha*) is intended to be expressed...

Therefore, the meaning is that it occurs even prior to [the application of] *puṃvat*. Consequently, since the word *yuvati* becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*) even before the production of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed, there remains the word *yuvan*, which ends in the suffix *kanin*.

Since the word *yuvati* has an acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable by virtue of the *nitsvara* rule, it lacks the quality of being "anudātta-initial" (having the first syllable unaccented). Consequently, the suffix *añ* does not apply. Instead, the suffix *aṇ* applies according to the rule *tasya samūhaḥ*. Due to the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of the original form), the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) does not occur, and thus the form *yauvanam* is established.
Therefore, the inclusion of the word *yuvati* in the *bhikṣādi* group [of words that take the suffix *aṇ*] is rejected in the works of Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa; so, enough of this.
Regarding the phrase "from the present participle" (*śatrantāt*): because it is oxytone by the accent of the suffix, this word *yuvan* has its first syllable unaccented (*anudātādi*).

Consequently, when the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which is marked with *u* (*ugit*)—is replaced by the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*), the suffix *añ* is applied to the word *yuvan* (which now begins with an unaccented vowel), resulting in the form *yauvatam*. This is the intended meaning.

*gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājarājanyarājaputravatsamanuṣyājādvuñ* | [The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after these: *gotra*, *ukṣan*, *uṣṭra*, *urabhra*, *rājan*, *rājanya*, *rājaputra*, *vatsa*, *manuṣya*, and *aja*. [From the commentary: "After these"—namely, *gotra*, *ukṣan*, *uṣṭra*, *urabhra*, *rājan*, etc.

The meaning is that [the suffixes apply] after these: *rājanya*, *rājaputra*, *vatsa*, *manuṣya*, and *aja*. Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the worldly sense, not the technical (Pāribhāṣika) sense. To the question "What is this worldly lineage? he says: "And that is merely offspring. This is what is enumerated in the *Pravarādhyāya*.

The meaning is "all offspring," such as sons, grandsons, and so forth. The intention is that this is because it was established as a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *strīpuṃsābhyām* and others, stating: "Since this occurs outside the governing context of 'offspring' (*apatya*), the term *gotra* is understood here in its worldly sense alone; the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition of *gotra* is not intended."
(1228) *yuvoranākau* | Pāṇini 7.1.1. *yu* and *vu* together form *yuvuḥ*. In this *samāhāra-dvandva* compound, the masculine gender is used according to Vedic usage (*sautra-puṃstvam*).
Thus he says: "of these two, *yu* and *vu*. It is desired [that the substitution occurs] when they are nasalized (*anunāsika*).
This is obtained from the *Vārttika*. [Question: What is the purpose of the mention of the two nasalized vowels (*anunāsika*)? [Answer: As in *ūrṇāyuḥ* and *glucukāyanīnām*.

From the word *glucuka*, the suffix *phin* is applied to form the patronymic according to the rule *ṭhprācām avṛddhāt*; then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *ṭhito manuṣyajāteḥ*, and the suffix *vuñ* is applied to form the collective (*samūha*). There is the substitution of *akāra* (the *vṛddhi* vowel).

There is initial vṛddhi. By the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. Thus, *aukṣakam*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of oxen" (*ukṣṇām samūhaḥ*). The suffix *vuñ* is applied; there is the substitution of *a* for the final syllable, the elision of the *ṭi* (the *u*), and initial vṛddhi. The analysis of *auṣṭrakam* is "a collection of camels" (*uṣṭrāṇām samūhaḥ*). *Urabhrāḥ* means rams; a collection of them [is *aurabhram*].

*aurabhra-kam*, *rājaka-rājanyaka-m*, *vātsaka-m*, *mānuṣyaka-m*, *ājaka-m*. Regarding the phrase "when the elision of *ya* is about to occur": this means that when the suffix *vuñ* is added to the word *rājanya*, the substitution of *a* for the final vowel occurs, and then, by the rule "the *ya* of a secondary derivative (*ṭhak-apatyasya*) is elided," the elision of the *ya* is about to take place.

"By their original form (*prakṛti*) when *ake* follows. This means it should be stated that when *ake* follows, the words *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* remain in their original form. The state of being young is *yauvanakam*.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *manojñādi* group; due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), there is no elision of the *ṭi* suffix.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] "also after a *vṛddha* [word].
Regarding "also after a *vṛddha*," it is the actual form of the word *vṛddha* itself that is understood, and not [any other word derived from it].

That which has [the vowel] "ā" as its initial among its vowels is designated as *vṛddha* by the rule "vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ," because the word *vṛddha* itself is cited as an example in the Bhāṣya. Thus he says: "vārddhakam. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of elders" (*vṛddhānāṃ samūhaḥ*).
(1229) *kedārād yañ ca* |4|2|40|.
From *kedāra*, the suffix *yañ* is also applied. Thus: *kaidāryam* or *kaidārakam*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "a collection of fields" (*kedārāṇāṃ samūhaḥ*).
In the case of *gaṇikā*, it should be stated that the suffix *yañ* is applied.
[The rule is: *gaṇikāyā yañ*. Because of the mention of *yañ*, the suffix *vuñ* is excluded. Thus, [the form] is *gāṇikyam*.
The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "a collection (*samūha*) of courtesans (*gaṇikā*)."

(1230) *ṭhañ* also after words ending in *kavacin*. [Pāṇini 4.2.41] The rule *ṭhañ* also after words ending in *kavacin*: the meaning is that the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied to form a collective (*samūha*) from both the word *kavacin* and the word *kedāra*. Thus, for *kāvacikam*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is added; following the substitution of *ik* for the final vowel, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion (*ṭilopa*).

(1231) *brāhmaṇa-māṇava-vāḍaba-ādibhyo yañ* 4.2.42. From *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, *vāḍaba*, and so forth, [the suffix] *yañ* [is applied]. Examples include *brāhmaṇyam* and others, meaning "the state or quality of Brāhmaṇas," "of Māṇavas," and "of Vāḍabas."

The analysis of the compound is *samūha* (a collection). A *māṇava* is the offspring (*apatya*) of *Manu*. By the suffix *aṇ*, the *n* becomes *ṇ*. According to the rule: "In the sense of a contemptible or dull-witted offspring, the suffix *aṇ* is traditionally prescribed after *Manu*; and by the substitution of a retroflex nasal for the letter *n*, the form *māṇava* is established," [and] according to the rule: "*añ* and *yat* are added to *Manu* in the sense of a class (*jāti*), with the augment *ṣuk*."
The commentary on the Sūtra states:
"An addition regarding 'from the *pṛṣṭha*':
[the word] 'from the *pṛṣṭha*'—the remainder [of the rule] is 'for the sake of' (*-artham*). Thus, 'the six-day period for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha*' (*pṛṣṭhārthaḥ ṣaḍahaḥ*')."

The collection of six days is a *ṣaḍaha*. In the sense of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), it is a *dvigu* compound. By the rule "after words ending in *rājan*, *ahan*, or *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ṭac* [is added]," the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) occurs.
There are six [sāmans] known as Rathantara, Bṛhat, Raurava, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants; by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the days connected with them are called *pṛṣṭhas*. The analysis of the compound is: "the collection of those.
(Pāṇini 2.4.2) [The suffix] *tal* is applied after [words ending in] *grāma*, *jana*, and *bandhu*. 4.2.43.

*Grāmatā* and so forth mean simply a "collection" (*samūha*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "a collection of villages, of people, and of kinsmen. The feminine gender of words ending in *tal* is established from common usage and from the grammatical rule on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana-sūtra*) stating, "words ending in *tal* are feminine."

It should be stated that [the suffix *tal*] is also applied after the words *gaja* and *sahāya*. That is to say, it should be stated that the suffix *tal* is applied after these two as well when forming a collective (*samūha*).
(1) After the word *ahan*, the suffix *kha* is applied when referring to a sacrifice (*kratu*).

"From *ahan* [comes] *kha* in the sense of a sacrifice (*kratu*). This is a Vārttika. Its meaning is that when the word *daha* occurs in the sense of a sacrifice, the suffix *kha* should be stated in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). Regarding the term *ahīna*: by the word *ahan*, the days of the Soma-pressing (*sautya*) are intended; "a collection of those" is the analytical explanation (*vigraha*).

From the word *ahan*, the suffix *kha* is applied, with the substitution of *īn*. The intention is that the elision (*lopa*) occurs by the rule "ṭhahnaṣṭakhoreva" (Pāṇini 6.4.145). He states the resulting form: "ahargaṇa" etc. Regarding "āhna": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of days" (*ahnāṃ samūhaḥ*). The intention here is that the suffix *kha* is not used because a sacrifice (*kratu*) is not being denoted. [This applies] according to the rule "acitahastidhenoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.47).
Anticipating this objection, he says "here" (iha). The meaning is that [the suffix] *aṭh* applies by the rule "and after *khaṇḍika* and so forth. Now, one might object:

"If that were the case, since the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of *ṭi*-elision) prescribed for *an* would be impossible here because it is prescribed for *aṇ*, there would be elision of the *ṭi* [of *ahna*].
To this he replies: "only after *ahna* when followed by *ṭha* or *kha*. Since there is no elision of the *ṭi*, [the form is established].
The intention is that after the elision of the letter *a* by the rule "ṭhallopo'naḥ," the form becomes "āhna.
(1) It should be stated that the suffix *ṇas* is applied after the word *parśu*.
Regarding "parśvā ṇas": this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. The word *parśu* ends in the vowel *u*, is feminine in gender, and [denotes] a rib.

It denotes the bone situated at the side. From that [base], when *ṇasi* follows, the *guṇa* substitution of *o* would have been required; however, by the rule *siti ca*, the designation *pada* applies.

From the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam*, the word *padam* is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). Thus he says: "When *sit* follows, the preceding [element] receives the technical name *pada*. That which has *it* (the letter *i*) as its *sakāra* is called *sit*.
Since the rule would have been established by "ṭh-svādiṣv-asarvanāmasthāne" alone, this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *bha*.
The phrase "because it is not *bha*" means that the status of being *bha* is sublated by this [designation of] *pada*. Regarding "pārśvam":
when "parśu-a" is in place, there arises a conflict between the shortening prescribed by "iko'savarṇe" and the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) taught by Śākalya.
The meaning is that if one were to negate that [suffix] by means of another rule found therein, namely "ṭhsiti ca," then the form would be *pārśvam* due to the substitution of *yaṇ*.
(1233) *anudātader añ* |4|2|44|.
The suffix *añ* is applied after words beginning with an unaccented vowel (anudātta), provided they denote a collection (*samūha*). Thus we have *kāpotam* and *māyūram*.

The point is that, according to the rule "in a word ending in a light syllable, or having two [light] syllables, or having many heavy syllables, the heavy syllable receives the acute accent," the words *kapota* and *mayūra* are oxytone (having the acute accent on the middle syllable).
Therefore, they do not begin with an unaccented vowel.

(1234) *khaṇḍikādibhyaśca* | Pāṇini 4.2.45. He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "the suffix *añ* shall be used. The word "in the sense of a collection" (*samūhe*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. This [sūtra] is for the purpose of making the initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*).
(1235) *caraṇebhyo dharmavat* |4|2|46|.

From [words denoting] *caraṇas*, [the suffixes] are like those used for *dharma*. *Caraṇas* are those who study specific branches [of the Veda]. Whatever suffixes will be taught after certain bases in the sense of *dharma*, those same suffixes are applied to those same bases in the sense of a collection (*samūha*).
The meaning is "they may be. Regarding *kāṭhakam*: the analysis of the compound is "the collection of the Kaṭhas.
The suffix *vuñ*, which will be prescribed for the subject of *dharma* by the rule *ṭhgotracaraṇādvuñ*, also occurs here in the sense of a "collection.
Regarding *chāndogyam*: the analysis is "the collection of the Chāndogas," who are the followers of the Sāma-veda branch.
The suffix *ñya*, which will be prescribed for *dharma* by the rule "ṭhcchandogaukthikayājñikabahvṛcanaṭāññyaḥ," also occurs in the sense of a collection (*samūha*).
(Pāṇini 4.2.47) *Acita-hasti-dhenoṣṭhak*: [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *ac*, as well as after *hastin* and *dhenu*.

*Acita-hasti*: The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* shall be applied after words denoting inanimate things (*acita*), as well as after the word *hasti* (elephant) and the word *dhenu* (cow), when forming a collective (*samūha*). Regarding *sāktukam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of barley-meal" (*saktūnāṃ samūhaḥ*).
Because the suffix *ka* [prescribed by] "after *ṭhi*, *su*, *uk*, and *tānt*, there is *ka*" follows the *u* of *ṭhak*, the *ṭhak* is replaced by *ka*, and there is vṛddhi of the first vowel.

Regarding *hāstikam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of elephants" (*hastinām samūhaḥ*). [The suffix] *ṭhak* is replaced by *ika*; there is elision of the final vowel with its following consonant (*ṭilopa*);

and there is vṛddhi of the initial vowel. Regarding *dhainukam*: the analysis is "a collection of cows" (*dhenūnām samūhaḥ*). Because it follows [the rule for] *uka*, the *ṭhak* is replaced by *ka*; and there is vṛddhi of the initial vowel.

(1237) *keśāśvābhyāṃ yañ-chāv anyatarasyām* |4|2|48|. From the words *keśa* and *aśva*, [the suffixes] *yañ* and *cha* are respectively applied optionally, provided that "a collection" (*samūha*) is meant. The meaning is: after *keśa*, *yañ* is optionally used; after *aśva*, *cha* is optionally used. Regarding the phrase "in the alternative cases": when *yañ* does not occur after *keśa*, *ṭhak* is applied by P. 4.2.51; when *cha* does not occur after *aśva*, *aṇ* is applied.

*Kaiśyam* and *kaiśikam*: when there is a collection of hair (*keśānām samūhaḥ*), these are the analytical compounds (*vigraha*). The suffixes *yañ* and *ṭhak* are applied respectively. *Aśvīyam* and *āśvam*: the suffixes *cha* and *aṇ* are applied respectively.
(1238) Pāśādibhyo yaḥ |4|2|49|. The suffix *ya* is added after [the group of words] beginning with *pāśa*.
The suffix *ya* is applied after words such as *pāśa*; the meaning remains simply "a collection. Examples include *pāśyā* and so forth.
The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "a collection of nooses," "of grasses," "of smokes," "of forests," and "of winds. Femininity is established by common usage (*lokāt*).

(1239) *khalagorathāt* |4|2|50|. From *khala*, *go*, and *ratha*. The term "collection" (*samūha*) is understood here as well. The meaning is that the suffix *ya* shall be applied after these: *khala*, *go*, and *ratha*. Thus, we have *khalyā*, *gavyā*, and *rathyā*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "a collection of threshing-floors," "a collection of cows," and "a collection of chariots."

Although it would have been more appropriate to list these [suffixes] only among the *pāśādya* group, they are listed separately here so that they may be carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent sūtra.
(1240) *initrakaṭaḷcaś-ca* | Pāṇini 4.2.51.

*Initra*: The meaning is that these suffixes—*ini*, *tra*, and *kaṭaḷc*—should occur. Regarding *khalinī*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a collection of threshing floors" (*khalānāṃ samūhaḥ*). In the suffix *ini*, the vowel *i* following the letter *n* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
Femininity is established from common usage (*lokāt*). Because it ends in *n*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding *gotrā*: [the analysis is] "a collection of cows" (*gavāṃ samūhaḥ*).
Analysis: *gośabdāntaḥ* (ending in the word *go*). Femininity is established from common usage (*lokāt*). The suffix *ṭāp* is applied. Regarding *rathakaṭaḷā*:

the analysis is *rathānāṃ samūhaḥ* (a collection of chariots). In the suffix *kaṭhaḷci*, the letter *k* does not become *it* (indicatory), because it is stated that this is not a *taddhita* suffix; due to its feminine nature, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied.
The suffix *ini* should be prescribed after words such as *khala*.

Regarding the phrase "after *khala* and so forth": instead of including the term *ini* in the rule *ṭhinitrakaṭaḷcaśca*, one should formulate the rule simply as *ṭhgorathātrakaṭaḷcau* and then [add] *khalādibhya ini*.
The meaning is that it must be separated.

(1241) *viṣayo deśe* |4|2|52|. [The word] *viṣaya* [is used] in the sense of "region. [The word] *samūha* ("collection") is excluded. *tasya* ("of that") is understood from the previous rule. Of that...

It is understood that suffixes are applied to a word ending in the genitive case when the sense is "object" (*viṣaya*). Thus he says: "from a word ending in the genitive. He explains the word *viṣaya* as:
"in an object that has been thoroughly mastered. [The example is: *devadattaviṣayo 'nuvākaḥ* ("the lesson whose object is Devadatta").
The sense is that this is because it is observed to be so in such cases. [Objection: In that case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there.
To this he says: "If that... This means: if that object which has been intensely cultivated (*atyantapariśīlita*) is the location (*deśa*).
And thus, the result is that there would be cognitions regarding a location that is not intensely cultivated when it is the object of cognition (*gamya*).

For this word *viṣaya* is used in some cases to denote a district consisting of a collection of villages; for example: "The territory (*viṣaya*) of the neighboring king has been seized by him. In other cases, it refers to that which is perceivable by the sense organs;
for example: "Form (*rūpa*) is the object (*viṣaya*) of the eye. In yet other instances, it is used in a different sense than enclosure (*āvṛti*).

Just as in the case of "water is the domain (*viṣaya*) of fish," it is understood that it does not exist elsewhere; however, in the present context, the meaning is "the section (*anuvāka*) is the domain of Devadatta. The point is that because the location is not perceived here, the suffix is not applied. Why [is the word] *viṣaya* used? [Consider: "Devadatta’s [path] to be traveled at some time."
[This refers to] the path. Nor should it be argued that in the expression "the house of Devadatta," there would be a [suffix] denoting a location because it is an extremely familiar place;
for what is intended here is specifically a region that consists of a collection of districts and is thoroughly traversed.

(1242) *rājanyādibhyo vuñ* | Pāṇini 4.2.53. The meaning is that the suffix *vuñ* is applied after words beginning with *rājanya*, provided they are in the genitive case, when the sense is "a region that is the domain of those [people]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*. For example: *rājanyaka*. In this instance...
The meaning is that for the *rājanya*s, the specific region [is the basis of the patronymic].

(1243) Pāṇini 4.2.54: *bhaurikyādyaiṣukāryādibhyo vidhalbhaktalau*. From the words beginning with *bhauriki* and those beginning with *aiṣukāri*, when they are in the genitive case, the suffixes *vidhal* and *bhaktal* are respectively applied. From the *bhaurikya*s and from the *aiṣukārya*s... [the suffixes are added].
In due order, these two suffixes, *vidhal* and *bhakta*, occur in the sense of "the region that is the domain" (*viṣayo deśa*).
