For example: *aiṣukāribhaktam*, meaning "the region that is the domain of the Aiṣukāris.
*Sārasāyanabhaktam*, meaning "the region that is the domain of the Sārasāyanas. Here...
The neuter gender [of *napuṃsaka*] is according to common usage.
(1244) *sa asyādiḥ* [is used] for Vedic *pragāthas*.
4.2.55. "That is its beginning. Two *ṛc*s are traditionally recited; by repeating the first half-verse (*pāda*), they become three *ṛc*s. And that...
The term *saṃpragātha* is well known in the *Chandogasūtra* and the *Bahvṛcasūtra*.

The use of the seventh case plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*) in place of the sixth case singular (*ṣaṣṭhy-ekavacana*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*). In the sense of "this is the beginning of this *pragātha*," suffixes such as *daṇ* and others are applied to a word denoting a specific type of *chandas* ending in the nominative case.
The meaning is "they may be. *Chandas* refers to a specific arrangement of syllables, such as the *gāyatrī* and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the *paṅkti* and so forth": the meaning is that a *pragātha* whose first verse is an *ṛc* in the *paṅkti* meter is called a *pāṅkta* *pragātha*.
(1) The addition [of the suffix] for the sake of the word's own meaning (*svārtha*).

Regarding "for the sake of the word's own meaning": the meaning is that there is an addition of suffixes such as *aṇ* for the sake of the word's own meaning after words expressing meters (*chandas*). For example: *traiṣṭubham*.

[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words denoting] the cause of battle and those who fight for a purpose, in the sense of "unmanliness" (*klībatvam*) toward the world. (1245) *saṃgrāme prayojanayoddhṛbhyaḥ* | 4|2|56|.
The word *saṃgrāme* follows [from the previous rule]. Thus, *saṃgrāme* is in the locative case, [while the word it qualifies is] in the genitive.

It connects with the word *vipariṇatam* (transformed) by means of this [suffix]. The meaning is that the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* should occur after words ending in the first case (*prathamā*) that denote either the purpose (*prayojana*) or the combatant (*yoddhṛ*) of this battle— for instance, in the sense of "this is the purpose of this battle" or "these are the combatants of this battle."

(1246) *tadasyāṃ praharaṇam iti krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ* | 4|2|57 | *tadasyām*. The meaning is: "that [instrument] is the weapon (*praharaṇa*) in this game. The sense is that the suffix *ṇa* shall be added after a word in the nominative case denoting a weapon, provided it refers to a game. [The derivation of *praharaṇa* is: "that by which one strikes" (*prahriyate anena*).
*Praharaṇam* means a weapon. Regarding *dāṇḍā*: the intention is that by the suffix *aṇ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would occur.

Regarding *mauṣṭā*: the analysis of the compound is "that game in which a fist (*muṣṭi*) is the weapon. (Pāṇini 4.2.58): "The suffix *ñ* [is applied] after *ghañ* [to form a feminine noun], meaning 'this is its activity' (*sā'syāṃ kriyā*)."

Regarding the rule *ghañaḥ sāsyām*: immediately after the word *asyām*, a feminine substantive such as *mṛgayāyām* (in hunting) and so forth must be supplied. The meaning is that the suffix *ñ* occurs after a first-case form derived from a stem ending in *ghañ* which denotes an action, in the sense of "that action [takes place] in this [action]," namely in an action such as hunting.

He states the result [of the rule] with the words beginning "from a word ending in ghañ," etc. Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of kṛt [suffixes]," its purpose will be explained immediately below. (1248) *śyenatilasya pāte ñe* |6|3|71|.

Regarding *śyenatilasya*: the sense is that the augment *mum* is applied because of its continued recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *ṭharurdviṣad...* (Pāṇini 6.3.67). Regarding "in the case of the suffix *ñ*": the meaning is that it applies when the word *pāta* occurs before the suffix *ñ*.
Regarding "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*): the sense is that this is due to the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the rule *aluguttarapade* (Pāṇini 6.3.1).
Regarding "śyenapāta": *pāta* means falling; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Regarding *śyenampātā*:

the suffix *ñ* is added to the word *śyenapāta*, which ends in *ghañ*. Although it is the word *pāta* alone that ends in *ghañ*, nevertheless, by virtue of the technical rule concerning the inclusion of *kṛt*-derived stems (*kṛdgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it should be understood that the entire compound *śyenapāta* is also included.

The compound *śyenasya pātaḥ* is a genitive-tatpuruṣa formed with a word ending in a kṛt-suffix. Consequently, there is vṛddhi of the first vowel in the word *śyenapāta*. In the expression *tailaṃpātā svadhā*, the word *svadhā* is feminine and denotes the ancestral rite (*pitryakriyā*), as seen in such instances as *namaḥ svadhāyai*.

By the word *svadhā* here, it is indicated that [the term] *krīḍāyām* ("in play") does not carry over; for although "in this" (*asyām*) was already present in the context of the previous rule, it is mentioned again here as "in this" (*asyām*). (1249) *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59): [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word denoting a treatise to form a noun meaning] "one who studies that" or "one who knows that."

The meaning is that the suffixes *aṇ* and others are applied after a word ending in the accusative case in the sense of "one who studies that" (*tad adhīte*) and in the sense of "one who knows that" (*tad vetti*). "Studying" (*adhyayana*) is the grasping of the sequence of syllables from the mouth of a teacher;
"knowing" (*vedana*) is the knowledge of the word and its meaning. By this, it is shown that the injunction for study extends up to the comprehension of the meaning.
The statement of certain Mīmāṃsakas is refuted, because the separate mention [of the suffix] would be redundant.
That this is so has been explained by us at length in the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti*.
Regarding the term *vaiyākaraṇa*: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, the augment *aij* (i.e., *ai*) is inserted according to the rule *ṭhañ-yvābhyām-aic*.

(1250) *kratūkthādisūtrāntāṭ ṭhak* [Pāṇini 4.2.60]. Regarding the meanings "one who studies that" and "one who knows that": the meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words beginning with *kratu*, *uktha*, and so forth, as well as those ending in *sūtra*.

"Only of those that denote specific sacrifices (*kratuviśeṣa*)," meaning not of the word *kratu* itself. The implication is that otherwise, the word *kratu* would have been included in the group beginning with *uktha*. Now, one might ask: how can there be the study of specific sacrifices, given that they do not consist of the grasping of syllables? To this, he says: "from them."
Words such as *agniṣṭoma* and others are primary (*mukhya*) with respect to specific sacrifices, but they are secondary (*gauṇa*) with respect to the texts that expound them. In this context,
from words such as *agniṣṭoma*, which have as their primary meaning the specific sacrifice, [the term is applied] to the knower of the Veda.

The suffixes [are as follows]: the meaning of *āgniṣṭomika* is "one who studies" those texts that explain the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and other such rituals, or "one who knows" the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice; that is, one who studies the texts that set forth it. This is because these suffixes occur by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the treatises that expound the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices.
The word *āgniṣṭomika* means either "one who performs the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice" or "one who studies the text that explains it."
The word *uktha* is primary when referring to the *sāmans*, but it is secondary (*gauṇa*) in the *Prātiśākhya*, which is a treatise on the characteristics of the *sāmans*.
In that context, he states that the suffix *ṭhak* is applied from the word *uktha* in its secondary sense, saying: "An *uktha* is a particular kind of *sāman*.
This is because the author of the *Vṛtti* has stated: "It is the *sāman* that is sung after the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*."
This is the state of affairs. In the Bhāṣya, however, it appears that the word *uktha* is used as a synonym for the word *sāman*.
From the word *uktha* in its primary sense, the suffixes *ṭha* and *gaṇa* are not desired.
Regarding the phrase "from its primary sense": the suffix *ṭhak* is not applied after the word *uktha* when it denotes the *sāman*. Since that [suffix] is prohibited...

The meaning is that the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.2.59] does not occur after this word. In the Bhāṣya, however, it appears that the suffix *ṭhak* is not applied after the word *uktha* when used in its primary sense.
He provides an example of the suffix *ṭhak* applied to words such as *nyāya*, which are listed in the *ukthādi* group: namely, *nyāyam*.

"Studies or knows"—the word "or" (vā) is to be supplied. Regarding *naiyāyika*: the augment *aij* is applied after the suffix *ṭhak*. Regarding *vṛttim*: "studies or knows"—the word "or" (vā) is to be supplied. Regarding *vārtika*:

after the suffix *ṭhak*, there is initial *vṛddhi*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the vowel. Regarding *sāṅgrahasūtrika*: [it refers to one who studies] that which is called the *Saṃgraha*.

The meaning of *adhīte* or *veda* is "he studies" or "he knows. Regarding the term *vidyā-lakṣaṇa*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in *vidyā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kalpa* in the aforementioned sense.
It should be stated that [the suffix] does not apply after words preceded by *aṅga*, *kṣatra*, *dharma*, or *tri*, even when they end in *vidyā*.

Regarding the word *aṅga*: the meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply after the compound ending in *vidyā*, preceded by these three—*aṅga*, *kṣatra*, and *dharma*. Consequently, only the suffix *aṇ* applies. As for the form *trividyā*:
the intention is that the word *vidyā* is elided because it belongs to the *śākapārthiva*-class (where the middle term is dropped). Thus, *tisro vidyāḥ* becomes *trividyā*.

Thus, there is no compound (vigraha), because of the restrictive rule: "In the case of direction and number, [only] when it is a proper name. Nor is it a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), as in "one who studies or knows three sciences" (*tisro vidyā adhīte veda vā*); for if that were the case, since the secondary derivative would be caused by the *dvigu*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule "there is elision of the secondary suffix after a *dvigu* when no patronymic is intended" would result. [This applies to the word] *tisṛṇām*.
The *dvigu* compound "vidyānāṃ samāharaḥ" is also entirely unobjectionable here.
Regarding the phrase "and from the *ākhyāna*, *ākhyāyikā*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*":
that is, from these—*ākhyāna*, *ākhyāyikā*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*—in the sense already stated.

The meaning is that the suffix *ṭhak* is to be prescribed. In this context, by the terms *ākhyāna* and *ākhyāyikā*, there is the inclusion of those words that denote specific types of narratives and specific types of tales respectively; however, for the words *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*, there is the inclusion of their own literal forms. "Narrative" (*ākhyāna*) is the name—

A continuous narrative (*kathā-prabandha*). According to Amarasimha: "An *ākhyāyikā* is one whose subject matter is derived from experience; a *purāṇa* has five characteristics; and an *itihāsa* is that which concerns past events. Furthermore: "Cosmogony (*sarga*), secondary creation (*pratisarga*), genealogy (*vaṃśa*), the periods of the Manvantaras (*manvantara*), and the history of the dynasties (*vaṃśānucarita*)—these are the five characteristics of a *purāṇa*. In that regard:

He provides an example from a narrative (ākhyāna): "Yavakrīta. He provides an example from a legend (ākhyāyikā): "Vāsavadattā. Regarding the statement "the elision (luk) should be stated," the remainder [of the rule] is "of the suffix already mentioned" (uktapratyayasya).
It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of both the initial *sarva-* and the initial *sa-*.
Thus, *sarvavedaḥ* [is formed]. When the *aṇ* suffix is elided, there is an absence of the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening. *Sarvatantraḥ*:
the meaning is "one who studies or knows all the systems (*tantra*s). *Savārtikaḥ*: together with the *vārtika*s.
[The form] *savārtika* [is derived as follows]: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule *tena saha*. The substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* occurs by the rule *vaupasarjanasya*.

The meaning is: "one who studies the Sūtra together with the Vārttika. Regarding the word *dvigoḥ*: in the sense of "one who has studied two Tantras" or "one who knows two," because the *aṇ* suffix is caused by a *dvigu* compound when it serves as the basis for a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix.
The meaning is that in the absence of initial *vṛddhi*, the form is "dvitantra.
Regarding the rule "from a word ending in *ikan* or having *pada* as its final member, after the words 'hundred' (*śata*) and 'sixty' (*ṣaṣṭi*), the suffix *ṣikan* is applied":
the term "having *pada* as its final member" (*padottarapada*) means that for which the word *pada* is the final member (*uttarapada*).

Therefore, the suffix *ikan* should be stated for the aforementioned meaning. [The rule] "after *śata* and *ṣaṣṭi*, *ṣikan* after *pathin*" means that the suffix *ṣikan* should be stated after the word *pathin* which follows the words *śata* or *ṣaṣṭi* in the sense mentioned. [The example] *pūrvapadika* means one who studies the *pūrvapada*.

The word *veti* means "or. Similarly, there is *autarapadikaḥ*. *Śatapathikaḥ* refers to one who studies or knows the *Śatapatha*, which is the name of a Brāhmaṇa text of the Vājasaneyins; the sense is "he studies it" or "he knows it. *Śatapathikī*: the intention is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because of the presence of the marker *ṣ*. Likewise, there are *ṣaṣṭhipathikaḥ* and *ṣaṣṭhipathikī*.

(1251) *kramādibhyo vun* | Pāṇini 4.2.61. The suffix *vun* is added after words such as *krama*, etc., with the sense "one who studies that" or "one who knows that"—this is the remainder [of the rule]. For example, *kramakaḥ* means "one who studies the *Krama*" or "one who knows the *Krama*. He recites the *kramādi* group beginning with *krama*, etc.
"Kramādi" means this group beginning with *krama*. Examples are "padakaḥ" and "mīmāṃsakaḥ.
(1252) *anubrāhmaṇādiniḥ* [Pāṇini 4.2.62]: The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *anubrāhmaṇa*.

[The suffix] *ini* after [words such as] *anubrāhmaṇa*. He explains the sūtra by completing the ellipsis: "in the sense of 'one who studies that' or 'one who knows that'. In the suffix *ini*, the vowel *i* following the letter *n* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Thus, because the letter *n* is not final in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), it does not receive the technical designation *it*. Now, one might object: "But there is the rule *ata iniṭhanau* [Pāṇini 5.2.115]..."
Since this [suffix] would be redundant because the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is already established by the suffix *ini* alone, he says: "For the purpose of supplanting *aṇ*.
However, in the Bhāṣya, this very rule has been rejected.
(1253) *vasantādibhyaṣṭhak* 4.2.63.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words such as *vasanta* [in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that"]. This follows the rule *tad adhīte tad veda*. For example: *vāsantikaḥ*.

Here, *vasanta* refers to a text devoted to the description of spring; the meaning is "one who studies that" or "one who knows that. Regarding *atharvāṇam*: it means the Veda proclaimed by Atharvan, who is called *Atharvan* because he is characterized by the power of *lakṣmī*; [the suffix denotes] one who studies or knows that.
In reality, however, there is elision (*luk*) of the aforementioned suffix by virtue of the rule "elision should be stated for [the suffix] after *ṛṣi*.

Regarding the form *ātharvaṇikaḥ*, he says "as in *dāṇḍināyana*" to preclude the fear that the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel) would apply according to the rule "of *na* before a *taddhita* suffix," because [the suffix here] is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) ending in a labial (*vānta*).
There is no elision [of the feminine suffix].
(1254) *proktālluk* | 4|2|64|. Now he begins to derive the word *pāṇini*: *proktālluk*.
By the word *prokta* (spoken/taught), the cognition of the meaning spoken is intended;
this is understood because the cognition of the student and the knower (*adhyetṛ-veditṛ-pratyaya*) is the subject under discussion.
Thus he says: "having the meaning of what was spoken. Regarding *paṇa*: it means "stuti" (praise). Now, [one might object] regarding the rule *halaśca*.
Since there would be vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, he says: "except for *ghañ*" (*ghañ-ṛte*). Regarding *paṇī*:
the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule *ata iniṭhanau*. Regarding *tasya*:
the form *pāṇina* arises by adding the suffix *aṇ*—according to the rule *tasyāpatyam*—to *paṇin* in the sense of a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*). This is the meaning here.

Since *aṇ* is not a secondary derivative (*apatya*), when it follows [the word *aṅga*], the rule "ṭi-ṇ-yaṇ-ya-na-patye" would apply, resulting in the absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) and thus necessitating the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). To prevent this, [the sūtra] states: (1255) *gāthividathikeśigaṇipaṇinaś-ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.165).
In the rule *gāthividathikeśigaṇipaṇinaśca*, the term *aṇ* is understood from the previous rule *ṭhinaṇyanapatye*;
and the term *prakṛtyā* is understood from the rule *prakṛtyaikāj*. Therefore, it says: "These [words] remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*) when the suffix *aṇ* follows.
These are: *gāthin*, *vidathin*, *keśin*, *gaṇin*, and *paṇin*.

This is the meaning. This [rule] is for the sake of preserving the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) even when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to denote a descendant. Then, regarding "a young descendant" (*yūnyapatye*):

*paṇi* is the root-primitive (*mūlaprakṛti*). With respect to that, when a fourth-generation descendant who is a youth is intended to be expressed, the form *pāṇiniḥ* arises from the word *pāṇinaḥ*—which ends in the *gotra* suffix *aṇ*—by the addition of the suffix *iñ*. This is the meaning.
If the word *pāṇini* were formed with a secondary suffix denoting an immediate descendant (*anantarāpatya*),

then the suffix *iñ* could not occur for the third generation— the lineage descendant (*gotrāpatya*)— relative to the original base (*mūlaprakṛti*), because of the restrictive rule "there is only one [suffix] in the lineage" (*eko gotre*). Nor could it occur for a fourth-generation descendant relative to the original base.
From the word *pāṇin* [denoting a descendant], the suffix *iñ* is possible when denoting a youth (*yuvan*), because of the rule:
"In the case of a youth, [the suffix] follows that which ends in a *gotra*-suffix, provided it is not feminine.
This is due to the restriction that for a youth descendant, the secondary suffix must follow only that which ends in a *gotra*-suffix. Therefore...

It should be understood that it has been stated that after the word *pāṇina*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ* derived from a *gotra* [patronymic] stem, the suffix *iñ* is applied to denote a descendant in the younger generation (*yuvan*).

(Pāṇini 2.4.58): "The elision of both *aṇ* and *iñ* occurs when denoting a descendant in the younger generation, except in the case of stems ending in *ṇya*, those belonging to the *kṣatriya* class, and those derived from *ṛṣi* names."
Regarding this, he states [the following] to address the apprehension that *iñ* might be elided: "The suffixes *ṇya*, etc., [are excluded] from *kṣatriya* and *ārṣa*.
All suffixes beginning with *ṇya* are understood here as exclusively *gotra* (lineage) suffixes, because of the statement "from a *gotra* [suffix], [the suffix] *yaūni* [is applied].
Thus he says: "from one ending in a *gotra* suffix," and so forth. He provides an example of the *ṇya* suffix: *kauravya*.
Thus: *kauravyaḥ* is the descendant of the *gotra* of Kuru. [The suffix] *ṇya-* is applied according to the rule "from *kurū-* and so forth, *ṇya-*.

In the sense of "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of *kauravya*," the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule "after that which ends in *at*, *iñ*. By this [present rule], there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].
He gives an example of a suffix denoting a *kṣatriya*: *śvāphalkaḥ*. [This is] the *gotra*-descendant of Śvaphalka.

*Śvāphalka*: [The form] *śvāphalkaḥ* is derived by applying *ṭhak* after *ṛṣyaṇdhraka*. In the sense of "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of Śvāphalka," the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*; its elision (*luk*) occurs by this [present rule]. He provides an example of a Vedic (*ārṣa*) suffix: *vāsiṣṭhaḥ*. The descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) of Vasiṣṭha is *vāsiṣṭhaḥ*, formed with *ṛṣyaṇ*. In the sense of "the young descendant of Vāsiṣṭha," the suffix *iñ* is applied.

By this [rule], there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]. He provides an example for one ending in *ñit*: "taikāyani. The offspring in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) of *Tika* is *Taikāyani*. By the rule *tikādibhyaḥ phiñ*, the suffix *phiñ* is applied. In the sense of "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of Taikāyani," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyāpatyam*. By this [present rule], there is elision of that [suffix *aṇ*]. [The example] "vāmarathyasya" is as follows.

Vāmarathya is the descendant of Vāmaratha. According to the rule *ṭhakurvādibhyo ṇyaḥ*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied; however, when the sense is "the pupils of Vāmarathya," the suffix *aṇ*—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*—is applied. The point is that by this [present rule], the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix *aṇ*] does not occur, because it lacks the sense of a youth (*yuvan*). Thus, there is elision of the *aṇ*.

"It does not occur. By the rule *ṭhṇyakṣatriye*, in the word *pāṇiniḥ*, there is no elision (*luṅ*) of the *ṭi* following the *aṇ* suffix. To the question "Why?", he says: "By the mention of *ārṣa* (Vedic).
This is because, in the word *pāṇini*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the base *paṇin* as a general rule (*autsargika*). In reality...

The point is that even though [the word *pāṇini*] denotes a seer (*ṛṣi*), since it is not mentioned by its specific form (*pratipadokta*) as a seer, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ* following it. Nor should it be argued: "Why could the suffix *aṇ*—by the rule 'ṛṣyaṇdhake'—not apply to the word *pāṇin* to denote a descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*)? For in cases where the general suffix *aṇ* is superseded by *iñ* and other such suffixes, [the former does not apply].

[This is] applicable, because an effort is made in that very context to refute it. In reality, however, according to the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *vānyasmin sapiṇḍe*, from the word *atri* [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*, resulting in *ātreya*;
and from the word *ātreya*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣe*.
Because it has been stated thus, this [view] should be disregarded. However, in the rule *ṇyakṣatriye*, only the word *rūṅ* denoting a seer (*ṛṣi*) is intended to be included.
The word *paṇin* and its derivative *pāṇina* (denoting his descendant) do not denote a seer. Therefore, the word *pāṇina* ends in the suffix *aṇ* by virtue of the general rule (*autsargika*).
This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding the term "by Pāṇini":

the meaning is that which was proclaimed by Pāṇini. In this sense, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *tena proktam* (Pāṇini 4.3.101) is superseded; instead, by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114), the suffix *cha* is applied, and upon the substitution of *īya*, the word *pāṇinīya* is formed. Now, [one might object]: when a taddhita suffix follows the word *pāṇini*...

Even though there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ* by the rule "elision of *yūni* [after] *iñ*" (*ṭhyūniluk*), one might still assume the status of ending in *iñ* by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix as if it were not elided), and thus expect the suffix *aṇ*—which is an exception to *cha*—to apply. Therefore, he says: "But the *aṇ* [prescribed] by the rule *iñaśca* does not apply. In the word *pāṇini*, the suffix *iñ* denotes a *yuvan* (younger descendant) alone, and not a *gotra* (lineage-descendant), because it belongs to the category of *yuvan*.

The meaning is that [the term] "gotra" is set aside because it would conflict with the designation [of *apatya*]. Although it has been stated elsewhere—outside the section on offspring (*apatya*)—that "gotra" is not technical (*pāribhāṣika*), nevertheless, in this context, only the technical "gotra" is understood;
this will be explained later under the rule *ṭhiñaśca*. From that [it follows].

The meaning is "from the word *pāṇinīya*. The intention is that when the suffix *aṇ* is added to the word *pāṇinīya* in the sense of "one who studies" (*adhyete*) or "one who knows" (*veda*), the elision of the suffix prescribed by the rule *ṭhproktālluK* occurs, resulting in the form *pāṇinīya*. Now, one might object: even if the suffix *aṇ* were not elided after the suffixes denoting "student" (*adhyetṛ*) or "knower" (*vettṛ*), the word *pāṇinīya* [would still be established].
It is indeed established; therefore, he says: "There is a distinction regarding the vowel and in the feminine.

In the absence of the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*—which denotes the student or knower—there would be an udātta accent on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix, and in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* would occur. However, when elision (*luk*) does take place, there is the long *ī* of the substitute *īya*.
The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Thus he says: "Pāṇinīyā, Pāṇinīyī.
(1257) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.65: "And [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after a neuter *sūtra* ending in *ka*."

And from the Sūtra: "After [a word] ending in *ka*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is added]. Immediately after "after [a word] having *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kakāropadhāt*)," the remainder is "of that which follows *ṭha*" (*ṭhaparasya*). Now, one might ask:
since the desired form is already established by the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix following *prokta*," for what purpose is this [present rule]?

To this he says: "The commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of [suffixes] other than *prokta*. The meaning is: it is for the sake of the elision (*luk*) of a suffix following even one that is not *prokta*. Thus, [we have] *aṣṭakam*.

Under the governing rule *tad asya parimāṇam* ("that is its measure"), in accordance with the rules *saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃjñā-saṅgha-sūtra-adhyayaneṣu* ("after a numeral, [the suffix *kan* is added] when meaning a name, a collection, a Sūtra, or a lesson") and *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* ("after a numeral ending in *ati* or *śat*, the suffix *kan* is added"),
the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "a treatise consisting of that many [sections]. Thus, from the word *aṣṭaka*, there arises the suffix for one who studies or knows [the work].
The meaning is that *luk* [elision] occurs by this [rule], because it is subsequent to the rule concerning words denoting a *sūtra* ending in the suffix *kap*.
It should be stated that [the word *sūtra*] has a numeral as its base (*saṅkhyāprakṛtika*). Regarding "having a numeral as its base": [it is taught] from the rule "and from *sūtra*" (*sūtrācca*).
The meaning is that the elision (*luk*) occurs only after a suffix whose base is a numeral, provided it ends in the suffix *kopadha* (having *ka* as its penultimate letter).

Regarding the term *māhāvārtika*: *mahāvārtika* is the name of a treatise (*sūtra*). One who studies that, or belongs to that, is called a *māhāvārtika*. In this case, there is no elision of the *aṇ* suffix.

(1258) *cchandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi* |4|2|66|. "Vedic meters (*chandas*) and Brāhmaṇas. Vedic meters are the mantras; Brāhmaṇas are the prescriptive statements. These form a copulative compound (*dvandva*). This refers to the Veda, for it is said: "The name 'Veda' applies to both mantra and Brāhmaṇa."
Because of the recollection [of the previous rule]. From the rule "proktāl luK" (Pāṇini 4.3.101), the word "proktāt" is carried over (anuvartate).
It is transformed into the nominative plural. Thus, it is understood that [the term refers to] those ending in suffixes called *prokta*.
He states this with the words beginning with "the Vedic hymns" (*chandāṃsi*). In the phrase "pertaining to that" (*tadviṣayāṇi*), by the word "that" (*tat*):

The terms "reciter" (*adhyetṛ*) and "knower" (*veditṛ*) are intended here as the cognizers (*pratyaya*). Those [scriptures] whose objects (*viṣaya*) are inseparably connected (*avinābhāva*) with them are "those having those as their objects. [The root] *ṣiñ* means "to bind. An object (*viṣaya*) is that which is specifically bound (*viśiṣya saṃyoga*).
That is to say, it is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). Thus, they are indeed conjoined with the cognitions of the reciter and the knower.
This is the meaning. He states the resulting conclusion: "without the suffix denoting the student or the knower.

*Pāṇinīyam* refers to the grammar taught by Pāṇini; *pāṇinīyāḥ* refers to those who study or know it. Thus, since usage would be established even without the suffix denoting the student, [the rule is necessary].

This is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Regarding the word "by Kaṭha" (*kaṭhena*): the intention is that the example is *kaṭhāḥ*, meaning "those who study what was proclaimed by Kaṭha. He explains this with the words "by Vaiśampāyana": in the sense of "proclaimed by Kaṭha," the suffix *aṇ* (which would otherwise apply) is set aside by the rule *vaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca* ("and [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the names of the pupils of Vaiśampāyana").

The meaning is that [the suffix] *ṇini* is used here. Regarding "of that": the meaning is that the elision (*luk*) of *ṇini* occurs by the rule "after *kaṭha* and *caraka*, there is elision" (*kaṭhacarakālluṅ*). Thus, it is established that the portion of the Veda taught by Kaṭha is called *Kaṭha*.
Then, regarding "from that, the suffix *aṇ*": from that word *Kaṭha*, in which the suffix indicating "taught by" has been elided, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "one who studies that."
The meaning is "of that. Regarding the phrase *tasya proktālluk* ("there is elision of that [suffix] when it denotes 'taught by'"):

the meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix *aṇ* which follows the word *prokta*. Thus, in the case of *kaṭhāḥ* (the Kaṭhas), who study what was taught by Kaṭha, the word *kaṭha*—which ends in the elided *prokta*-suffix—is eligible for usage only in conjunction with the suffix *adhyetraṇ*, and not by itself.
The sense is that this applies except in the case of a word ending in a suffix prescribed solely [for that purpose].
Thus ends the section on words having the sense of "colored" (*rakta*) and so forth in the *Bālamanoramā*.

Now, the *tan*-class and others. Next, the roots with the *u*-vikaraṇa are examined. The root *tan* is marked with *u*. The purpose [of this marker] is as stated in the rule "ṭhudito vā. [The suffix] *u* is added after the *tan*-class roots and the root *kṛñ*, when a *sārvadhātuka* affix expressing the agent follows.
The suffix *u* is applied after the root *kṛñ* in its own sense (without changing the meaning). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *śap* suffix. [Thus we derive] *tanoti*.

In the case of the suffix *u*, there is *guṇa* substitution by relying on the *tip* ending. However, in the case of the *tas* and other endings, there is no *guṇa* because they are marked with the *ṅ* indicatory letter (*ṅit*).

[Thus we have] *tanutaḥ*. When the substitute *jha* is applied as the final element, *yaṇ* is substituted for *i* by the rule "iko yaṇ aci. [Thus we have] *tanvanti*. [In the second person singular and dual: *tanoṣi*, *tanuthaḥ*.
Regarding the optional elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *ṭhlopaścāsyānyatarasyām*, he says: *tanvaḥ* and *tanuvaḥ*.
Regarding the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings, he says: *tanute*. [The forms] *tanvāte* and *tanvate*; [and] *tanuṣe*.
tanuthās, tanudhve; tanve, tanuvahe, tanvahe, tanumahe, tanhe.
tatāna, tenatuḥ, tenitha, tena, teniva; taṅyāha—tene. tenātha, tenire; teniṣe, tenāthe, tenidhve; tene, tenivahe.
He stretched; he will stretch; he will be stretched. Let him stretch—*tanotu*, *tanutāt*, *tanutām*, *tanvatu*.
Thinking that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi* by the rule "utaśca pratyayād," he says: *tanu*. [The forms] *tanutāt*, *tanutam*, *tanuta*;
*tanavāni*, *tanavāva*, *tanavāma*. He stretched (*atanot*).
*atanutām*, *atanvan*; *atanoḥ*, *atanam*, *atanva-*; *atanuva*. [In the potential: *tanuyāt*, *tanvīta*, *taniṣīṣṭa*. Considering the optional *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "ato halādeḥ," he says:
*atanīt*, *atānīt*. [In the aorist: *ataniṣṭām*, *ataniṣuḥ*; *atanīḥ*, *ataniṣṭam*.

*ataniṣṭa*, *ataniṣam*, *ataniṣva*, *ataniṣma*. In the alternative involving *vṛddhi*, [the forms] are *atāniṣṭām* and so forth. Regarding the conditional (*luṅ*), he states the specific rule for the third person singular and the second person singular:

(376) *tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ* | Pāṇini 1.2.4.79. The word *sicaḥ* is understood from the rule *gāti-sthā-gā-pā-bhū-bhyaḥ sicaḥ* (1.2.17); *luk* is understood from the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣa-jito yūni lugaṇiñoḥ* (2.4.58); and *vibhāṣā* is understood from the rule *vibhāṣā ghrādheṭśācchāsaḥ* (1.2.19). Thus he says:

By the phrase "tanādi" and so forth, it is meant that the term *ekavacana* (singular) is understood; however, the meaning is not that the substitutes for the *luṅ* [aorist], the *parasmaipada*, the middle voice (*madhyamapuruṣa*), and the plural number (*bahuvacana*) are also included. Regarding the form *yūyam*: when the *sica* suffix is applied in the *luṅ* middle voice plural, there is an optionality regarding the *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening].

The meaning is that in the forms *ataniṣṭa* and *atāniṣṭa*, this optional elision (*luk-vikalpa*) of the suffix *sic* does not apply. Having thus stated the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), he now demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) while stating the examples of the rule: "In the case of a root with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātetośca*), there is elision of the augment *ak* before the *taṅ* [suffixes]. Here, *taṅ* refers to the first person singular ending; in the word *taśabde*.
In the second person singular, when the suffix *ta* of the second person singular is present, and also when the suffix *thās* of the second person singular follows, there is elision (*luk*) of *sic*;
the meaning is that by the rule "anudāttopadeśa," the *n* is elided. Thus he says:
*atata*, *ataniṣṭa*; and likewise *atathāḥ*, *ataniṣṭhāḥ*. Forms such as *ataniṣātām* are easy to understand.

The root *ṣaṇ* means "to give. This is a root taught with an initial *ṣ*. Its forms are like those of *tanu*. *Asāt* is the form when there is elision (*luk*) of the *sic* suffix. *Asaniṣṭa* [is the form] when the *iṭ* augment is present; the point is that because it is not followed by a consonant beginning with a *jhal*, the substitution of *ā* does not occur. The root *kṣaṇ* has an *a* vowel in its penultimate position (*adupadha*). In the *Taittirīya [Saṃhitā]*, it is said: "In the case of a thunderbolt, the Adhvaryu priest *kṣaṇvīte*."

And [the root] *kṣiṇu*. It has *i* as its penultimate letter (*idupadha*). This also means "injury" (*hiṃsā*). A different recension (*śākhāntara*) cited in the Śābara-bhāṣya states: "The Adhvaryu priest injures with the thunderbolt" (*vajreṇādhvaryuḥ kṣiṇvīta*). Now, one might ask: why is there no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *i* in *kṣiṇoti*, given that the suffix *u* (*upratyaya*) is present and the condition of having a light penultimate syllable (*laghūpadha*) is met? To this, he says:

Regarding the term *upratyayanimita*: the root *ṛ* means "to go. Here too, depending on the difference of opinion regarding the elision (*kṣiṇuvat*), there is either the strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) or its absence. Thus he says: *ṛṇoti*, *armoti*. The same applies further on. In the form *arṇvanti*, the sense is that the *yaṇ* substitution occurs according to the rule *iko yaṇaci*.

The root *ḍukṛñ* is used in the sense of "doing. In the form *karoti*, the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution based on the suffix *upratyaya*, and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* applies (*raparatvam*). However, in the case of the *u* in *kurutaḥ*, there is no *guṇa* because it is based on the suffix *tip*. In the form *kurvanti*, since the suffix *tas* is marked with *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* for the *u*. When the form *kuru antī* is established, he says: "yaṇ" (the *yaṇ* substitute). [This refers to] *iko yaṇ aci*.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "by this [rule], *yaṇ aci*. When the substitution of *yaṇ* for the vowel *u* has been made, one might suspect a long vowel by the rule *hali ca*; therefore, he says: "not so" (*na-bhā*). Since the optional elision of the vowel *u* would apply by the rule *vasimasośca lopaścāsyānyatarasyām*, he states that it is "always" (*nityam*) [the case].
[The rule applies] to the root *kṛ*. The phrase "and after [a root ending in] *u*, when a suffix follows" (*utaśca pratyayād*) is understood from the previous context;

as well as "elision" (*lopaḥ*) from "and its elision optionally" (*lopaścāsyānyatarasyām*), and "before *m* and *v*" (*mvoh*). Thus he says: "of *kṛ*. Regarding *cakartha*: the point is that [the augment] *iṭ* does not apply here by the rule "after *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛ*," etc. (*kṛsṛbhṛvṛbhyo 'ṅ* / *na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ*).
Even though it ends in a vowel, according to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the augment *iṭ* is not applied because it ends in *ṛ*. Thus: *kariṣyati*. [Imperative:
*karotu*, *kurutāt*; *kuru*; *karavāṇi*; *kurutām*; *kurvātām*; *karavai*, *karavāvahai*, *karavāmahai*. [Aorist: *akarot*, *akurutām*; *akuruta*, *akurvātām*.
When the potential mood suffix *liṅ* is present in the form *kuryāt*, [the following applies]:

from the rule "ṭh-lopaś-cāsyānyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.4.105), the word "lopaḥ" (elision) and "asya" (of this) are carried over. By the word "asya" (of this), the "ut" (the phoneme *u*) mentioned in the preceding sūtra is referred to. [The elision of *u* is] obligatory...

From the rule "karoteḥ," the word "karoteḥ" is carried over (anuvartate). The suffix implied by the term "aṅga" is qualified by the letter *ya*; this is a rule concerning what precedes that [suffix] (tadādividhiḥ). Thus he says: "there is elision (*ulopa*) of the *ṛ* of *kṛñ*.
Regarding the form *kriyāt* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the point is that the substitution of *riṅ* occurs by the rule "ṛṅ śayagliṅkṣu."
Regarding *kṛṣīṣṭa*: the intention is that there is no *guṇa* substitution because the suffix is marked with *k* by the rule *ṭuśca*. Regarding *akārṣīt*:

the intention is that after the *vṛddhi* substitution [of the root vowel] in the *sic* augment, the *ra*-substitution (*raparatvam*) takes place. Now, one might object: when the form for the *luṅ* (aorist) active voice is established as *ikṛs ta*, the desired result is achieved even without the elision of *sic* by the rule *tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ*.
Since the *sakāra* would be heard [as the suffix] in the absence of the elision (*luk*) of *sic*, he says "tanādibhyaḥ" and so forth.
(377) *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇe* || 6.1.137 || [The rule begins with] *saṃparibhyām*.

(378) *samavāye ca* | 6|1|138|. Regarding *samavāye ca*: the augment *suṭ* is applied after the root *kṛ*. This is because the words "after *ka*" (*suṭ kātpūrvaḥ*) and "always for *kṛ*" (*nityaṃ karoteḥ*) are understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding rules; such is the intended meaning.

(379) *upāt pratiyatna-vaikṛta-vākya-adhyāhāreṣu ca* || 6.1.139 || [The word *prāguktau*] refers to the two [operations] previously mentioned; that is to say, *bhūṣaṇa* (ornamentation) and *samavāya* (inherence). Now, one might object: since the augment *suṭ* [in *saṃparyupebhyaḥ*] depends upon two words, it is *bahiraṅga* (external); however, reduplication (*dvitva*) [prescribed by] *liṭi dhātoḥ* is...

Because it depends only on the base and the suffix, it is *antaraṅga* (internal). Consequently, in the case of *saṃcaskāra*, even though *suṭ* is subsequent, once reduplication has occurred, *suṭ* would apply before the reduplication;
however, [this is prevented by the rule]: (380) *suṭkātpūrvaḥ* | P. 6.1.135. [This rule states that *suṭ* is placed before the root-initial *k*.]

*suṭ kātpūrvaḥ*. This sūtra belongs to the first quarter (pāda) of the sixth chapter. Its meaning is that it should be understood as governing [the rules] starting from *saṃparibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇe*, *samavāye ca*, and *upātpratiyatne*, up until *anudātaṃ padamekavarjam*. And thus:
The point is that because it is stated "before *kā*," the augment *suṭ* occurs before the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). Now, one might object:

how can *suṭ* apply here to the posterior member (*uttara-khaṇḍa*) when it is separated by the reduplication, since the rule for *suṭ* has already found its scope in cases like *saṃskaroti*, where there is no intervention? Furthermore, in *samaskarot*, [the augment] is [separated] by the *āṭ*.

[Objection: How can there be the augment *suṭ* when there is an intervention? For the augment *aṭ* does not belong to the root *kṛ*, since the status of being a stem (*aṅga*) belongs only to that which ends in a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). To this, he says:

"It has been stated that [the rule applies] even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or the reduplication. The word "Vārttika" is to be supplied as the remainder. [The intervention is] by *aṭ* or by the reduplication.
And even when there is an intervention, the meaning is that *suṭ* is inserted before the *k* following roots such as *sam*, *pari*, and so on.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": the meaning is that in the Bhāṣya this was rejected by suggesting that let only *suṭ* be the governing rule (*adhikṛta*), and let the rules "before the *k*" (*kātpūrvaḥ*) and "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* or the reduplication" (*aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi*) not exist.

He undertakes to demonstrate that very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). [The full statement is: "First the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with a prefix (*upasarga*); afterwards, with an inflectional suffix (*sādhana*). This is the remainder [of the sentence]. Consequently, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is caused by the relationship between the verbal root and the prefix which has occurred first.
That which is to occur later is *antaranga* (inner) with respect to an operation caused by the connection between a verbal root and its suffix, because it presents itself first.
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Having established that 'the root is joined with the prefix first,' the operation concerning the root and the prefix is *antaranga*. Thus he says:

Because *suṭ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), it is applied first; then, doubling (*dvitva*) occurs. Thus, when *suṭ* has been applied, after doubling the element *ṣkṛ*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uradattva*) takes place, followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *ra* (*raparatva*). Then, by the rule "the *khaya* sounds preceded by a *śar* sound are elided" (*śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*), the *repha* (r) and *sakāra* (s) are removed.
Finally, with the change of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsacutva*), the form *saṃcaskāra* is established.
The sense is that the rules "kātpūrvaḥ" and "aḍabhyāsavyavāye 'pi" need not be formulated. Likewise, in the case of *samaskarot*,
because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) with respect to the augment *aṭ* which is part of the suffix (*vikaraṇa*), [the substitution occurs] first.
It should be inferred that, considering that *suṭ* will indeed occur, the portion [of the rule] stating "even when there is an intervention by *ṭh* or *ḍ*" need not be formulated.
He states another result of adopting the principle "the root is first combined with the prefix" in the words "if this is so":
according to the stated method, since *suṭ* is applied because it is *antaraṅga*, after *saṃskṛ* has been formed, the suffix *atus* is added for the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
By the rule "the [vowel] of a root beginning with a conjunct consonant is strengthened (guṇa)," the forms *saṃcaskaruḥ* and *cakratuḥ* are established.
However, if one adopts the view that "the root is first joined with its grammatical operation (sādhana)," then [the form] *cakratuḥ* would be derived from the already completed base.

The sense is that because of the connection with the prefix *sam*, there is an absence of being "beginning with a conjunct consonant" (*saṃyogādi*), and thus the *guṇa* substitution is not established. Now, one might object that in forms such as *saṃcaskariva* and *saṃcaskaritha*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rules *kṛsṛvṛbhṛḥ* and *ṛto bhāradvājasya* would apply; to this, he says:

Regarding the rule *kṛsṛbhṛvṛsūtre* and so forth: [an objection is raised]—but why is there no substitution of *guṇa* in the case of the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) *siṃskriyāt*, given that the rule *guṇo’rtisaṃyogādyoḥ* prescribes *guṇa*? To this he says:
*guṇo’rtī* etc. [The answer is: But [in the form] *siṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, the suffix is *liṅ* (specifically *taṅ*), whereas in *siṃskṛta*...

Regarding the forms *samaskṛta* and *samaskṛṣātām* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, one might ask why the augment *iṭ* is not applied by the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*. To this, he says: "of *ṛt*" and so forth. Thus ends the section on the *tanādi* roots in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
(675) *Tatpuruṣaḥ* | 2.1.22 | [A compound] is called *tatpuruṣa*.
*Tatpuruṣa*. "Before" (*prāk*) means before the rule "the remainder is *bahuvrīhi*" (*śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ*). (676) *And the *dvigu* [is also *tatpuruṣa*]*.

"And the *dvigu*" means that the *dvigu* compound is also [a *tatpuruṣa*]. This refers to the rule: "In the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), for a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), and in the case of a collective (*samāhāra*)."
The designation *dvigu* will be prescribed for the compound about to be mentioned by the rule "a compound preceded by a numeral is *dvigu*.

This implies that such a *dvigu* compound is also designated as a *tatpuruṣa*. The point is that in the absence of this sūtra, because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) stating "there is only one designation," the *tatpuruṣa* designation would be sublated by the *dvigu* designation.
"This" refers to the rule "dviguśca. In that case, one might object that by the designation *dvigu*, the designation *tatpuruṣa* would be sublated; therefore, he says: "number," etc.
The rule prescribing the *dvigu* designation is "saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguḥ. In that [rule], there is the particle *ca*.

It should be read as such. Consequently, it is understood that a compound preceded by a numeral shall bear both the designation *dvigu* and the designation *tatpuruṣa*. And thus, since the designation *tatpuruṣa* is obtained through the concise particle *ca*, the cumbersome rule "and *dvigu*" is not required.

The meaning is that it must be performed. Now, one might object: "Let there be no status as a *tatpuruṣa* for the *dvigu*. To this he says: "The purpose [of the designation] is to provide a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). He demonstrates this by providing an example: "pañcarājam" (five kings). In the analytical statement (*vigraha*), "the collection of five kings," [the term is formed] according to the rule "taddhitārthe" (Pāṇini 2.1.51).

The *dvigu* compound; because it is a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac. By the rule "sa napuṃsakam," it takes the neuter gender. However, the rule "an akārānta-uttarapada dvigu is feminine" does not apply here, because the *samāsānta* suffix *ṭac* is an integral part of the entire compound.

Because it is not a constituent part of a subsequent member [of a compound]. Nor should it be argued that, given the reading "saṃkhyāpūrvodviguśca," the designations *dvigu* and *tatpuruṣa* would apply alternatively;
therefore, let there be a separate rule "dviguśca" for the purpose of conjunction. This is because [the word] "saṃkhyāpūrva" [is required].

And when the rule *dvigu* is divided into two separate rules— whereby the former prescribes the designation *tatpuruṣa* for a compound preceded by a numeral, and the latter, *dvigu*, prescribes the designation *dvigu*— then,
since the application [of both designations] is established as an option even without the particle *ca*, the purpose of the particle *ca* [is explained].
Because it is logical that [the word *samuccaya*] has the sense of "conjunction" (*samuccaya*).

(677) Pāṇini 2.1.24: "The second case [ending] is used with *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, *gata*, *atyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna*. That is, [the word] "the second case" refers to that which ends in the second case.

The rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) is obtainable through the *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*). [Objection: But surely, since *sup* is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*, it is transformed into the plural number; thus, by the *pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*, it refers to that which ends in a *sup*-affix.
The rule of *tadantavidhi* is indeed obtainable through the *pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*. [Objection: But surely *sup* is understood...
Transformed into the plural number, it refers to that which ends in a *sup* suffix by virtue of the *pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*.

Furthermore, by the *pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*, when a suffix is mentioned, the inclusion of the entire aggregate consisting of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix is obtained. Thus, [the meaning] of "by those ending in *sup*" is as follows:
The meaning culminates in [the phrase] "by the collection of *sup*-suffixes and their bases.

However, words such as *śrita* and so on end in the *kta* suffix and are not *sup*-ending (*subanta*), because they lack the nature of being a collection formed by a *sup* suffix; therefore, he says: "by those having *śrita* and so on as their bases."

Regarding the phrase "by those ending in case-terminations": the meaning is that words such as *śrita* (gone to) and others are used here figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for those bases that have *śrita* and so forth as their original forms. This, however, is not the scope of the rule stating that "gatis, kārakas, and upapadas are compounded with *kṛd*-derived words before the addition of case-terminations," because [the present case falls under] the rule "the agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a *kṛt*."

It is established in the *Prauḍhamanoramā* that [the suffix] *ṭhaC* is applied when [the word] *kṛta* follows, because no specific *kāraka* is mentioned. Nor can it be argued that since words such as *śrita* are qualifiers of the "capable" (*samartha*) [word], the rule of extension to what ends in them (*tadantavidhi*) results in the meaning "having as their base words ending in *śrita*" etc., and thus [the suffix would apply] even in the case of *kṛṣṇaṃ paramaśrita*.

It must be stated that a compound (*samāsa*) should occur; however, this is not possible because the rule for the formation of compounds and suffixes prohibits the extension of grammatical operations to what ends with such a form (*tadantavidhi-pratiṣedha*).

In the case of *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to Kṛṣṇa"), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72), since the root *śri* signifies a specific kind of motion. Furthermore, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*), because the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) resulting from connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is prohibited by the rule *na lokā-* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).

In the rule for forming compounds (*samāsavidhi*), because the word *kṛṣṇa* is indicated by the first case (*prathamānirdiṣṭatva*) in the rule "the second case" (*dvitīyā*), it takes the prior position (*pūrvanipāta*), resulting in *duḥkhātīta*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "one who has transcended suffering" (*duḥkham atītaḥ*). [The root] *iṇ* means "to go.
The suffix *kta* is applied after the prefix *ati-* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). "And so forth" (*ityādi*): one who has fallen into a pit is *gartapatitaḥ*.

The root *ṭhpallṛ* means "to go. The suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Since the suffix *san* optionally takes the augment *iṭ* after the roots *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā*, the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* would result in the prohibition of *iṭ* for the past participle; however, by this very nipātana (irregularity), *iṭ* is indeed applied here. One who has gone to the village is "village-gone" (*grāmagataḥ*).
*grāmamatyastaḥ* means one who has gone beyond the village (*atikrānta-grāma*). *Grāmaprāptaḥ* means one who has reached the village (*prāpta-grāma*).
*Saṃśayāpannaḥ* means one who has fallen into doubt (*āpanna-saṃśaya*).
[This is] due to the inclusion of *gamyā* and others in the list of examples.

Regarding the phrase "of *gamyādi* and so forth": this means that even when words derived from roots such as *gam* (to go) are *sub*-ending (*sup-prakṛtika*), they may be compounded with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*), and that compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. For example, *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village").
Here, the suffix *ini* is added by the Uṇādi rule *gameriniḥ*; furthermore, according to the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ*, these [words like *gamyā*] denote the future tense.

By virtue of the statement, it will occur at the [proper] time. Because of the prohibition of the genitive case in connection with a *kṛt* suffix by the rule "ṭhakau," the accusative case is used for the object. The meaning is "about to go to the village" (*grāmaṃ gamiṣyan*). Regarding "desiring to eat food" (*annaṃ bubhukṣuḥ*): from the root *bhuj*, there is the desiderative suffix *san*. By the rule "sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ," the suffix *u* is added. [The elision of *n* occurs] by the rule "na loke."

Because the genitive case is prohibited when joined with a *kṛt* suffix, the accusative is used for the object (*karman*). The point is that the word *bubhukṣu* is not listed among the words beginning with *gamy*. "With a *kta*-formed word" means that the indeclinable *svayam* is compounded with a noun ending in a *sub* suffix whose base ends in the *kta* suffix; such a compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. [The reason for this] is "due to unsuitability."

The intention is that since the indeclinable *svayam* has the meaning of *ātmanā* (by oneself) and primarily expresses the agentive capacity (*kartṛ-śakti*), the third case ending alone is appropriate. [An objection is raised: "What is the difference between the indeclinable *svayam* when it is in a compound and when it is not? For even in the non-compounded state, the elision (*luk*) applies by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. To this, [the author replies]: [The text continues: ...because even in the non-compounded state, the elision (*luk*) applies by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. Therefore... [the distinction remains].

He says: "The offspring of one who has made it himself" (*svayaṃkṛtasyāpatyam*). The point is that, in the sense of "the offspring of one who has made it himself," according to the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), the suffix *iñ* would be added to the word *svayaṃkṛta*; since it ends in the genitive case, when *iñ* is applied, the vowel *ṛ* undergoes vṛddhi at the beginning of the stem, and by the rule *rapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.51), the substitute *ra* takes its place, resulting in the form *svayaṃkārti*. However, in reality, this does not occur here because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*).
*Taddhita*. The purpose [of this rule] is for the *samāsa-svara* (compound accent) of the word *svayaṃkṛta*.

(678) *khaṭvā kṣepe* | 2.1.26. Regarding *khaṭvā kṣepe*: the word *ktena* is understood from the previous rule. Because it is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*), the rule of "mentioning the ending" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies. *Kṣepaḥ* means censure.

Regarding the term *nindā*: both [the words] *dvitīyā* and *sup* are understood by virtue of their recurrence (*anuvartate*). Both of these, by means of the technical rule concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), refer to that which ends in those [suffixes], and thus they refer to the entire aggregate consisting of the base and the suffix.
This is because it is impossible for the word *khaṭvā* or a word ending in *kta* to consist of an aggregate formed with a *sup*-ending [word]. In this case...

He states that the word *khaṭvā* and the word ending in the suffix *kta* are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) when their respective bases [are implied], saying "having the base *khaṭvā*" (*khaṭvāprakṛtika*). Regarding the example *khaṭvārūḍho jālmaḥ*:
according to Amara, *jālmaḥ* means "one who acts without reflection. [The analysis is: *khaṭvām ārūḍhaḥ*.

Thus is the *alaukika-vigraha* (ungrammatical analytical statement). He states that there is no *laukika-vigraha* (grammatical analytical statement) by saying, "This is a *nitya-samāsa* (an obligatory compound). To the question "Why is that?", he says, "For not by means of a sentence. A sentence that conveys the meaning of the *vṛtti* (the derived form) is the *laukika-vigraha*. In that regard:

The sentence "he has mounted the couch" (khaṭvām ārūḍhaḥ) does not, in itself, convey censure toward one in the householder stage of life. However, the compound "one who has mounted the couch" (khaṭvārūḍha) conveys censure by conventional usage (rūḍhi). Thus says the Bhāṣya: "Having studied and bathed, and being permitted by his teacher, one should mount the couch."

"One who acts otherwise is called 'this rogue has mounted the bedstead' (*khaṭvārūḍho 'yaṃ jālmaḥ*). Here, by the word *jālma*, it is indicated that this term is conventional (*rūḍha*) in its elevated sense, and one should not insist upon the etymological meaning of its constituent parts.

(679) *sāmi* | 2|1|27| The word *sāmi* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "half. The meaning [of the rule] is that it is compounded with a *subanta* (a declined noun) whose base is a word ending in the suffix *kta*. For example, *sāmikṛtam* ("half-done"). However, in the absence of such a compound, when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is to be formed...
The intention is that it should be "sāmikārti.
(680) *kālāḥ* | 2|1|28|. Regarding *kālāḥ*: the phrase "with a *kta*-suffix" (*ktena*) applies here as well; the meaning is that the term "*ktena*" continues to be understood from the previous rule.

The meaning is that words ending in the second case (dvitīyā) whose stems denote time are compounded with a word ending in a *su*-affix whose stem ends in the suffix *kta*. Now, one might ask: since this is already established by the subsequent rule, "In the sense of continuous connection (*atyanta-saṃyoga*), [the second case is compounded] with a word ending in *kta*," for what purpose is this [present rule]? To this he says: "not continuous" (*anatyanta*). For example: *māsapramitiḥ*, meaning "measured for a month. *Māsaṃ pramitaḥ*.

Such is the analysis (*vigraha*). The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *mā-* preceded by *pra-* in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), and since it is also used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), it denotes the agent here. Thus he says: "in order to measure the month. The point here is that there is no absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) between the first lunar day (*pratipat*) and the moon with respect to the month.

(681) *atyantasaṃyoge ca* |2|1|29|. And [a word] expressing time [is compounded with another word] when there is absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). It follows from this that words denoting time ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) are optionally compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) when there is absolute connection.

This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: since this is already established by the preceding rule "kālāḥ," for what purpose is this [new rule] stated? He says: "for the sake of [words ending in] the suffix -kta. The intention is that here the word "ktena" (by means of a *kta*-suffix) from the previous rule has ceased to apply.
For example: "muhūrtaṃ sukham" (happiness for a moment). Here, the accusative case is used to express continuous connection (*atyanta-saṃyoga*).
The meaning is "pleasure lasting for a moment.

(682) *Tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena* |2|1|30|. [The word ending in] the third case [is compounded] with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) that denotes what is produced by that [instrument]. Regarding the term *tatkṛta*, although the word *arthena* follows immediately after it, [the sūtra] sets aside that [proximity]...

In order to state the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) with the term "guṇavacanena" (by means of a word expressing a quality), he says: "tatkṛta" is a separate word with its instrumental case ending elided (*luptatṛtīyākam*).

Therein, by the word "tṛtīye," that which ends in the third case is intended. The word "tatkṛta" is a distinct word whose instrumental case ending has been dropped; by the pronoun "tat," there is a reference back to that which ends in the third case.
That meaning is indicated [by the word *artha*]. Furthermore, the phrase "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*) connects with the word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) by way of the quality itself.

Consequently, there are two distinct syntactical rules: "A word ending in the third case is compounded with a word expressing a quality produced by the meaning of that which ends in the third case," and "A word ending in the third case is compounded with the word *artha*."
This is established in the Bhāṣya by the statement "it becomes [accomplished]. Thus he says, beginning with "ending in the third case," and so forth.

Although the word *guṇe* requires dependence on that which is produced (*tatkṛtatva*), the compound is formed according to Pāṇinian rules (*sautra*). This sūtra operates only when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) mediated by the meaning of the word *kṛta*, and not otherwise.

This is clear from the Bhāṣya: "In the case of direct mutual connection. Nor should one fear an over-extension [of the rule] to the example *ghṛtena pāṭavam* ("cleverness by means of ghee"), because the word *vacana* (mention) is employed even though the term *guṇena* (by a quality) would have sufficed;
for the commentary explains that by this [mention], a word denoting a substance qualified by a quality (*guṇopasarjana-dravyavācin*) is understood.

Regarding "śaṅkulākhaṇḍa": the word "Devadatta" is to be understood as the remainder [of the phrase]. Indeed, the *Bhāṣya* cites exactly "śaṅkulākhaṇḍo Devadattaḥ. [The term] *khaṇḍa* is derived from the root *khaḍi* (meaning "to split") with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). Thus, *khaṇḍana* becomes *khaṇḍa*. The suffix *arśa-ādyac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) in *śaṅkulayā* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

The meaning is: "possessing the action of cutting with a wedge" (*śaṅkulākṛtakhaṇḍanakriyāvān*). As for what was stated in the commentary on the rule *ākaḍārāt*—namely, that "a meaningful form of a word, distinct from compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛdanta*), secondary derivatives (*taddhitānta*), indeclinables, pronouns (*sarvanāman*), genus-terms (*jāti*), numerals, and technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*), is designated as a 'quality-word' (*guṇavacana*)"—that does not apply here. This is because the commentary’s statement, "by a quality-word which has expressed a quality," makes it clear that the term is used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*). Therefore, in this context, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) intends to signify any property (*dharmamātra*) in general. Consequently, there is no fault even if the word *khaṇḍa* denotes an action (*kriyā*).

In the *Tattvabodhinī*, regarding the rule *guṇavacanād* (Pāṇini 5.1.124), it is stated that the term "quality" (*guṇa*) here refers to that which is defined by the characteristics such as "that which enters into a substance and departs from it. On the occasion of its commentary, it was also stated that action (*kriyā*) does not possess the status of a quality. However, in this [work], the status of being a "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*) is attributed even to the word *khaṇḍa*, despite its denoting an action. This must be disregarded, as it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* on the present sūtra and is inconsistent with what has been stated previously and subsequently. He gives an example of a compound with the word *artha*: *dhānyena*.

The word *artha* refers to wealth (*dhana*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). The meaning is "wealth caused by grain. Here, although wealth has grain as its cause, the separate mention is made because the status of being "produced by that" (*tatkaraṇakatva*) does not apply [to the wealth itself], and thus [the application of the rule] would otherwise not be attained. Some say: "In the example *dhānyena*, the third case ending is used because it belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*; the meaning is 'wealth non-different from grain. Now, one might ask: since the form *śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* ("a piece by means of a wedge") is already established by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (P. 2.1.32), the addition of *tatkṛta* is redundant; therefore, he asks: "What is the purpose of saying *tatkṛta*?"

Intending that the mention of "tatkṛta" (caused by that) is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that [the compound occurs] only when the word is a quality-denoting term (*guṇavacana*) caused by that—he provides a counter-example: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in the eye"). The sense is that blindness is not caused by the eye itself, but rather by disease and so forth. What is the purpose of the phrase "by a quality-denoting term"? Consider: *gobhir vapāvān* ("fatty because of cows"). Here, Devadatta’s state of being fatty is indeed caused by his consumption of milk and other products related to cows; thus, there is the quality of being caused by that. However, the word *go* (cow) is not a quality-denoting term. (683) *pūrvasadṛśasamonārthakalahanipuṇāmiśraślakṣṇaiḥ* | 2|1|31 | [The rule applies] with these: *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, etc. By these... [the compound is formed].
The meaning is "by means of these": *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, *sama*, *ūna*, *artha*, *kalaha*, *nipuṇa*, *miśra*, and *ślakṣṇa*.
Regarding the example *māsapūrva* ("one who is prior by a month"): the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is *māsena pūrvaḥ* ("prior by means of a month"). The meaning is "produced before a month.

Although, in the sense of a relationship of limit (*avadhi*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) would apply according to the rule *ṭanyārāditararte* when used with words denoting direction, [here it is not so].

[The word *diś*] is obtained [as the first member], because it is accepted that a word denoting direction is a "direction-word" (*dikśabda*). Nevertheless, from this very indicative source, the third case ending is applied according to the rule "the third case ending is used in the sense of cause" (*hetau tṛtīyā*).
Thus, in the analysis of *mātṛsadṛśaḥ*, the compound is resolved as *mātrā sadṛśaḥ*. Similarly, *pitṛsamaḥ* is [resolved as] *pitrā samaḥ*.
Such is the analysis [of the compound]. The third case ending is applied by the rule *tulyārthair atulopamābhyām*.

Regarding the term *tulyārthaiḥ*, some say that this is already established by a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with words having the sense of the genitive. The phrase *ūnārtha* is an illustrative example. The phrase *mātronam* is likewise.

The meaning is that the measurement is deficient by a specific measure known as a *mātrā*. For this very reason, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the ablative sense (*avadhitva*) or for the causal sense (*hetu*), based on this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, the mention of the word "meaning" (*artha*) connects only with "deficient" (*ūna*), and not with "prior" (*pūrva*) and the others, because "equal" (*sama*) and "similar" (*sadṛśa*) are mentioned separately.

He states the purpose of including the word *artha* (meaning): "deficient by a *māṣa*" (*māṣavikala*). The analysis of the compound is "deficient by means of a *māṣa*" (*māṣeṇa vikalam*). The meaning is "deprived of. The instrumental case is used as in the previous examples. "Verbal quarrel" (*vākkalaha*): the analysis is "quarrel by means of speech" (*vācā kalahaḥ*). "Skilled in conduct" (*ācāranipuṇa*): the analysis is "skilled by means of conduct" (*ācāreṇa nipuṇaḥ*).

The meaning is "one who possesses skill caused by proper conduct. Regarding the term *guḍamiśra*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "mixed with molasses" (*guḍena miśraḥ*). Regarding *ācāraślakṣṇa*: the analysis is "smooth through proper conduct" (*ācāreṇa ślakṣṇaḥ*).
The meaning is "one who possesses proficiency caused by proper conduct. Now, one might ask: how is it [formed] in the case of *guḍasaṃmiśrā*?

[Why is there no] compound? Because even though [the word *miśra*] functions as a qualifier of a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the rule prohibiting the extension of suffixal operations to the end of a complex form applies here. To this, he says: "In the inclusion of *miśra*, that which is accompanied by a prefix is also included.
Why so? He says: "And *miśra*... [The rule states: "In the absence of euphonic combination (*asandhi*), the final member (*uttarapada*) is *miśra* when it is devoid of a prefix."

The meaning of that [sūtra] is: "that which follows a word ending in the third case is udātta. Here, the meaning is that when the term *miśra* is used elsewhere [in the sūtra] without the prefix *an-*, it is understood to include [words] with prefixes (*sopasarga*).
(1) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) should be made for the word *avara*.
"By the month, inferior" (*māsenāvara*) means "by the month, prior. As for the sense of "inferior," it is already established by the very fact that the suffix *tun* has that meaning.
(Pāṇini 2.1.32: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("The agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, diversely").

*Kartṛkaraṇe*: This is the locative case derived from a collective *dvandva* compound consisting of "agent" (*kartṛ*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*). The term "third case" (*tṛtīyā*) is understood by ellipsis. By the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix, there is an inclusion of that which ends in it.
The same applies to the word *kṛta*. Thus, he says: "in [the sense of] agent and instrument. "As before" means as previously stated.

The meaning is that when [the words] are compounded, it is a *tatpuruṣa*. Here, according to the *Bhāṣya*, only the *kta* suffix is understood by the mention of "kṛt" (primary suffix), because of the inclusion of the term "bahulam" (variously). Therefore, he cites an example ending in *kta*: "trātaḥ hariṇā" (protected by Hari); the meaning is "pālitaḥ" (nourished). Now, even though a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix may qualify a related word (*samarthaviśeṣaṇa*),...
Since there is a prohibition against extending a rule (tadantavidhi) to that which ends in a compound or a suffix, [the rule] would not apply in the case of *nakhanirbhinna*; therefore, he says:
"In the case of the mention of a kṛt-suffix... This is a technical paribhāṣā established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *gatiranantaraḥ*. *Pacatitarām* means "he cooks with excellence."

With the words "ṭha" (in the sense of location), "śayane" (in the sense of lying down), and "ṭhiṅśca" (and after a verbal root ending in ṭhiṅ) being understood from the context, the suffix *tarap* is applied by the rule "dvivacanavibhajye".

Then, the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule "kimetiṅvyayaghādāmbadravyaprakarṣe". The intention here is that the mention of the word "kṛt" (a primary derivative suffix) is for the purpose of precluding the formation of a compound with a word ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

(685) *kṛtyair adhikārthavacane* | 2|1|33|. Regarding the rule *kṛtyair adhikārthavacane*: "statement of a figurative meaning" (*arthavādavacana*) means a statement that is not literally true. *Vātacchedyam*—the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is to be cut by the wind"; the meaning is "capable of being cut [by the wind]."

In the rule *ṭhṛhalorṇyaḥ*, the suffix *ṇya* is a *kṛtya* affix. [The word *kāmya*] may be a praise due to its softness, or a censure due to its weakness. Regarding *kākapeya*: by the rule *aco yaṭ*, the suffix *yat* is applied; by the rule *īdyati*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Here, it may be a praise because of the water being full, or a censure because of the water being meager.

(686) *anna* with *vyañjana*. 2|1|34. *Vyañjana* [is compounded] with *anna*. He explains the word *vyañjana*: "It is a *saṃskāra*. That by which something is refined—that is, made to possess a particular quality—is a *saṃskāra*; it is the means for sprinkling and so forth.
"If one were to say [it]," means "that which expresses it. Regarding "with the word for food": *anna* means boiled rice (*odana*).
The meaning is "by the word that denotes it. The lexicon states: "The feminine *bhissā*, as well as *bhakta*, *andhas*, and *anna*, mean food.
Regarding "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*): [an objection] "But here, by the word *dadhnā*..."
Since the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) depends upon the word "sprinkling" (*upasikta*), there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*); how, then, can there be a compound here?

To this, he says: "contained within" (*antarbhūta*). Because it is impossible for curd to serve as a refinement of the food without the act of sprinkling, the word "by curd" (*dadhnā*) [is understood] as "in the sprinkling which has curd as its instrument."

The meaning is that there is no lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) due to the exclusion [of the *vṛtti*]. This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "And semantic capacity exists because the intended meaning is understood.
(687) *Bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam* (Pāṇini 2.1.35): [The compound is formed] with an item denoting food when it signifies the act of mixing.

Regarding "with *bhakṣya*": *miśrīkaraṇa* means that by which an edible substance (*khādya*) is mixed, such as molasses (*guḍa*) and the like. The meaning is that a word in the third case expressing such a substance is compounded with a word expressing an edible. An edible is a solid substance; here, foodstuffs such as flattened rice (*pṛthuka*) are intended. Thus, for example, *guḍadhānāḥ*. [The word] *dhānā*...

"Women [are called] *bhṛṣṭayava*," according to Amara; the meaning is "parched grains mixed with molasses. Now, one might object that since the state of having molasses as the instrument (*karaṇa*) depends upon the word "mixed" (*miśra*), there is no semantic competency (*sāmarthya*). To this he says: "by means of the mixed" (*miśreṇa*). The sense is that the word "with molasses" (*guḍena*) does not lack semantic competency, because it functions in the sense of "mixing that has molasses as its instrument."
(688) "The fourth [case-ending] [is compounded] with *tadartha*, *artha*, *bali*, *hita*, *sukha*, and *rakṣita*.
[Pāṇini 2.1.36] "The fourth": by the paribhāṣā rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), the word "fourth" here refers to that which ends in the fourth case.
*Tadartha*, *artha*, *bali*, *hita*, *sukha*, and *rakṣita* form a *dvandva* compound. [The compound consists of] that which ends in the fourth case together with these.

It is compounded with six [words]; the result is that it is a *tatpuruṣa*. In the expression *tadartha*, the word *tat* is intended to signify the meaning of a word ending in the dative case. That which is for the sake of that dative meaning is *tadartha*.
This is a compound by virtue of the rule to be stated later: "A compound is obligatory with [a word] having the sense of *artha*."
That which has as its purpose that which is expressed by a word ending in the dative case results in the meaning "for the sake of that" (*tadartham*).
Thus he says: "for the sake of that which ends in the dative," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of being for the sake of that":

the statement that a compound occurs "for the sake of that" applies only when there is a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), and not otherwise; such is the meaning.

Why is this so? To this he says: "protected by Bali" (*balirakṣita*). If this compound were to apply merely to the sense of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*), then the restriction to the relationship between material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) would not have been stated; in that case, the mention of "protected by Bali" (*balirakṣita*) would be redundant. For [the same rule] would also apply in cases such as "an offering (*bali*) for the spirits" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) or "grass protected for the cows" (*gobhyaḥ tṛṇam*).

The point is that the compound is established as *tadartha* (for the sake of that) precisely because the grass is for the sake of the elephant (*balibhūta*) by virtue of its being the actual object, and because the grass is protected for the sake of the cow (*gavārtha*). Regarding the example *yūpāya*:

here, the wood is for the sake of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is denoted by the fourth case ending; therefore, there is a compound of the word *dāru* with *yūpāya*, [since] the sacrificial post...

And because it is a modification of wood; for the meaning of the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is precisely a tree that has been made eight-sided by a carpenter and others. Now, he states the purpose of grasping the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*)—namely, "not here" (*nehā*). "For cooking" (*randhanāya*) means for the sake of baking (*pākāya*). [The root] *radha*...

In the case of *hiṃsā*, "cooking" (*pāka*) is intended here. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), resulting in the substitution of *an*. By the rule *ṭhradhibhajoracī*, the augment *num* is applied. Even though the word ending in the dative case (*sthālyai*) expresses the purpose of cooking, no compound is formed because there is an absence of the relationship between material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*). [Objection: But is it not the case that *aśvaghāsaḥ* ("horse fodder") is a compound, as in *aśvebhyo ghāsaḥ*?
