Regarding the question of how there can be a compound in expressions such as *dharmāya niyamaḥ* (a restriction for the sake of Dharma)—forming *dharmaniyamaḥ*—given the absence of a relationship between a material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), the author says: "But [in the case of] *aśvaghāsa* and so forth...
Nor does it follow that, by this logic, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would also necessarily occur in the expression *randhanāyasthālī* (a pot for cooking).

It should not be argued that the rule regarding the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) is useless; for that rule is rendered effective by the distinction made in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) based on whether the relation is one of "being related as such" (*sambandhatva*) or "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthyatva*). Thus, when the relation is manifested as "being related as such," as in the case of *randhanasya sthālī* ("the pot for cooking"), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is indeed desired.

Furthermore, regarding the appearance [of the compound] as having that purpose (*tādarthyatvena*), one must resort to the restriction of the relationship between material cause and product (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) in order to prevent the formation of a *caturthī-samāsa*; let this matter rest for now.
Thus, the portion concerning "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*) has been explained in detail.
It should be stated that there is an obligatory compound with the word *artha*, and that it takes the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).
Now, he states the specific rule regarding the compound of a word ending in the dative case with the word *artha*: "with *arthena*.
It should be stated that there is an obligatory compound with the word *artha* when it follows a word ending in the dative case; otherwise, [the following would occur].

Due to the governing principle of *vibhāṣā* (optionality), there may be an alternative view: it should also be stated that "the gender of the qualified [word] is the same as the gender of the principal [word]. Otherwise, since the word *artha* is always masculine, the rule *paravalliṅgam* would result in the feminine form being used everywhere.
The meaning is "it might be. Here, the word *artha* refers to a thing (*vastu*).
As Amarasimha states: "The word *artha* [is used] in the senses of denotation, wealth, a thing, purpose, and cessation.
Intending here to refer to a thing that is beneficial, he provides an example: "for the sake of the twice-born" (*dvijārtha*). In that context:
"dvijāyārthaḥ" is an *asvapadavigraha* (a compound whose analysis does not use its own constituent words). In this case, the word "ayam" (this) is substituted for the word "artha" (meaning/purpose);

this is appropriate because it is a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound), for which an *asvapadavigraha* is fitting. The form "dvijāya" is in the dative case with the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*). The word "artha" at the end of that [compound] forms a compound with the word "sūpa" (soup), which is the substantive.
Because the compound is masculine, the entire compound takes the masculine gender. The meaning is "the soup is the agent for the twice-born" (*dvijasya*).

Regarding *dvijārthā*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "this [is] for the twice-born" (*dvijāya iyam*). Although the word *artha* is invariably masculine, it takes the feminine gender here according to the rule *paravalliṅgam*.

Having set aside [the neuter gender] by this [rule], the feminine gender follows the gender of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). For example, *dvijārthaṃ payaḥ* ("milk for a twice-born"). The analysis (*vigraha*) is *dvijāyedam* ("this is for a twice-born woman").
Here, due to following the gender of the qualified object, the neuter gender is applied. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is treated as the dative case itself.

Since the sense of "being for that purpose" (tādarthya) has already been expressed, the analysis (*vigraha*) with the word *artha* does not occur by the maxim "that which has already expressed its meaning is not employed"; thus, its status as a *nityasamāsa* (invariably compound) is established by logic itself. Furthermore, just as in examples such as *guroridaṃ gurvartham* ("this is for the teacher"), gender is also established from common usage; this is the intent of the present Vārttika.
It has been rejected. Regarding *bhūtabali*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "an offering (*bali*) for the spirits (*bhūta*).

It is a compound of the word *bali*, which ends in the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing purpose (*tādarthya*), with the word *bhūta*. Regarding *gohitam*: the analysis is "beneficial (*hitam*) to the cows (*go*).
The meaning is "favorable to cows. [This is governed by the rule] *hitayoge ca*.

The fourth case ending (*caturthī*) serves as an exception to the remaining sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). There is a compound (*samāsa*) of that which ends in the fourth case with the word *hita*. In the example *gorakṣitam*, the word "grass and so forth" (*tṛṇādika*) is to be understood as the remainder. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "protected for the cows" (*gobhyo rakṣitam*). There is a compound of the word *rakṣita* with [the word] ending in the fourth case in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*).

(689) *pañcamī bhayena* | 2|1|37| The meaning is that a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is compounded with the word *bhaya* when it is a *sub*-ending form. For example: *corabhayam* ("fear of a thief"). Here, the fifth case is used because of the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*, which prescribes the ablative (*apādāna*) for the cause of fear in the context of verbs meaning "to fear" or "to protect."

*bhayabhītabhīti*: Since the word *bhaya* alone is mentioned in the Sūtra, this statement is made because a compound with *bhūta* and so forth would otherwise not be obtained. For example: *vṛkabhīta*. One should also cite *vṛkabhītiḥ* and *vṛkabhīḥ*.
In this regard, the Bhāṣya states, "Another says [the following]," and then mentions the rule *bhayanirgatajugupsubhiḥ*.

Having said "it must be told," one who has gone out from the village due to fear of a wolf is cited as an example of "one who loathes unrighteousness" (*adharmajugupsu*). In cases such as "terrified by thieves" (*coratrasta*) or "ceased from enjoyment" (*bhogoparata*),
the compound is formed either by the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) or by inclusion in the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.

(690) *apetāpoḍhamuktapatitāpatrastairalpaśaḥ* | 2|1|38 | The term *alpaśaḥ* is formed by adding the suffix *śas* in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), precisely because of this specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). Thus it is said: "that which means 'little' (*alpa*) ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*). The suffix *śas* [prescribed] by the rule *bahvalpārthāc chas* does not apply here.
Because it will be stated later: "An auspicious expression [is compounded] with words meaning 'much' or 'little'.

(691) *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena* |2|1|39|. *stokāntika*: [The words] *stoka*, *antika*, *dūra*, those having these meanings, and *kṛcchra*—these [are compounded] with a word ending in the *kta* suffix.

The meaning is that words ending in the fifth case (pañcamī) are compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*. The inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*) is connected with the words *stoka*, *antika*, and *dūra*. "Released from a little" (*alpāt muktaḥ*) is an example of a synonym for *stoka*. "Come from nearby" (*abhyāśād āgataḥ*) is an example [of *antika*].

An example of a synonym for *antika* (near) is "come from nearby. A synonym for the word *dūra* (far) should also be cited. In the case of "stokena" (with a little), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used according to the rule *karaṇe ca stoke*.
However, in the expression "dūrād āgataḥ" (come from afar), the fifth case is used according to the rule *dūrāntikārthebhyaḥ*. Here, [the suffix] *sup-*...
Fearing that there might be an elision (*luk*) due to the term *dhātu*, he says: "There is no elision (*aluk*) by virtue of [Pāṇini 5.4.73] *stokādibhyaḥ pañcamyāḥ*.

(692) *ṣaṣṭhī* |2|2|8|. [The word] *ṣaṣṭhī* [is the heading]. The meaning is that a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is compounded with a word ending in a *sup*-suffix; that is a *tatpuruṣa*.

Regarding the example *rājapuruṣa*: in the ungrammatical analytical sentence (*alaukikavigrahavākya*) *rājan as puruṣa s*, when the compound is formed, the case-ending suffixes (*sup*) are elided. Then, by relying on the internal case-suffix through the rule of "treatment as a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the *n* is elided [by Pāṇini 8.2.7]. One should not argue that the treatment as a suffix does not apply because the suffix has been elided by *luk*; for [the condition of] being a word (*padatva*)...

The sense is that, because it is a property of a composite whole (*samudāya-dharma*) formed by being well-joined, it lacks the status of being the function of its constituent parts (*aṅga-kāryatva*). (693) [And] with words such as *yājaka* etc., [the genitive is used]. 2.2.9. And with words such as *yājaka* etc. Now, one might object: since this is already established by the preceding rule, "The sixth case [is used]... (*ṣaṣṭhī*), [what is the purpose of this new rule?]

To the question "For what purpose is this [sūtra]? he says: "By means of *tṛc* and *aka*" (*tṛjakābhyām*). Regarding the example *brāhmaṇayājakaḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the sacrificer of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇasya yājakaḥ*). From the root *yaj* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *ṇvul* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). There is the substitution of *ak*.
By the rule "The sixth case [is used] for the agent or the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows," the sixth case is employed for the object. Regarding *devapūjakaḥ*: [of] the gods...

The analysis [of the compound] is "one who worships" (*pūjaka*). The intention is that the word *pūjaka* belongs to the class beginning with *yājaka*. One should cite *bhūbhartṛ* as an example [of a similar formation], because the word *bhartṛ* belongs to the class beginning with *yājaka*.
[Furthermore,] it should be stated: "When [the suffix] *-tara* follows a quality-word (*guṇa*), there is the elision of *tar*."
Regarding the phrase *guṇāntareṇa*: this entire Vārttika is established in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *guṇe*.

The meaning is that a word ending in *tarap*—which is prescribed after a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*)—is optionally compounded with a genitive case-ending word, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of *tarap*. He states the resulting conclusion: "that which ends in *tarap*. Now, [one might object] regarding the word "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

If it is asked, "Since this is already established by the rule [Pāṇini 2.2.10] itself, for what purpose is this stated?", he says: "Not in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). However, in the Bhāṣya on the rule *sarvaṃ guṇe*, it is stated that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the prohibition] *pūraṇaguṇa-* etc.
Because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *sarva*, this [prohibition] applies only to the word *sarva*.

Intending this as a *vārttika*, he provides an example: "sarvaśveta" (all-white). The remainder of the rule is "the quality of cranes. The meaning is that, in comparison with the white color residing in other substances, the white quality of all these cranes is superior. [The suffix *tarap* is applied] when the word to be compared is present, according to the rule "dvivacana-vibhajya... (Pāṇini 5.3.57).

Regarding *tarap*: here, when the word *sarveṣām* (genitive plural) is compounded with the word *śvetatara*, the suffix *tarap* is elided, resulting in the form *sarvaśveta*. Regarding *sarvamahān*: the word *īśvara* is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound].
Here too, the suffix *tarap* applies; the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the greatest of all" (*sarveṣāṃ mahattaraḥ*).
The meaning is that the greatness of the Lord is superior even when compared with the greatness of other relatives.
(Regarding the rule) "the genitive case [ending] in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is to be stated as forming a compound":
the analysis of "in connection with a *kṛt*" (*kṛdyoga*) is "that whose connection (*yoga*) is with a *kṛt* suffix. [This refers to the rule] "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*).

Regarding the word *kṛtī*, the *Bhāṣya* states that it is prescribed [by the rule *kṛtiḥ*]. In the example *idhmapravraścanaḥ*, the word *kuṭhāraḥ* (axe) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sense]. It is called *pravraścanaḥ* because one cuts (*pravṛścyate*) with it; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). The analysis of the compound is *idhmānāṃ pravraścanaḥ* (the cutter of fuel-wood); here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*). This is according to the rule "when prescribed by a specific rule" (*pratipadavidhāne*).
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition that will be stated hereafter.
(694) *na nirdhāraṇe* | 2|2|10|.
[The rule] "not when there is selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*). For example: *nṛṇāṃ dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("Among men, the twice-born is the best"). Here, *nṛṇām* is in the genitive case.

A compound is not formed with the word *dvija*. However, in the case of *puruṣāṇām uttamaḥ* (the best among men), which becomes *puruṣottamaḥ*, there is only the genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), and not the genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). For that [genitive of selection] occurs only when this triad is present: that from which the selection is made, that which is selected, and the cause of the selection.

Kaiyaṭa says [the suffix] *pravṛtteḥ*. Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the *tarap* sūtra, states: "The prohibition by means of *guṇa* is non-eternal. Some, however, maintain that it is indeed a *karmadhāraya* compound, based on the statement in the *Gītā*: "But the Supreme Person is declared to be another, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)," because even though the word *uttama* is an adjective, [it functions as the first member].
They say that the reversal of word order occurs because [the compound] belongs to the *rājadantādi* group.
Alternatively, it should be stated that a genitive case ending prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not subject to compounding.
Regarding the term *pratipadavidhānā*: it is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed with the distributive sense (*vīpsā*), meaning "with respect to each individual word" (*padaṃ padaṃ prati*).

That which has its rule prescribed by a specific word (*pratipada*) is called *pratipadavidhānā*. According to the *Bhāṣya*, with the exception of the genitive case prescribed as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*, every genitive case is *pratipadavidhānā*.

In the example *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"), [the genitive is applied] by the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* ("of the root *jñā* when it does not mean 'to know,' [the genitive is used] for the instrument").

A compound is not formed with a word ending in the sixth case when it has already been prescribed [by another rule], as it is clear in the Bhāṣya that the prohibition "not in the sense of selection" (*na nirdhāraṇe*) should indeed be rejected; so, enough of this. (695) Pūraṇa-guṇa-suhitārtha-sat-avyaya-tavya-samānādhikaraṇena || 2.2.11 || [This sūtra states: A word ending in the sixth case is not compounded with a word expressing a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*), a word having the sense of *suhita*, the word *sat*, an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a word ending in the suffix *tavya*, or a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

*Pūraṇaguṇa*: those whose meanings are *pūraṇa* (ordinal numbers), *guṇa* (qualities), and *suhita* (satisfied) are called *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthāḥ*. These, along with a noun (*sat*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and the suffix *tavya*, when in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), form a compound; this is a collective dvandva in the instrumental case. Thus it says: "by means of words having the sense of ordinals, etc."—namely, *pūraṇe*.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "An example will be stated. Regarding the term *satāṃ ṣaṣṭhaḥ* ("the sixth of the good"): in the sense of "the completer of six," the rule *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* applies, and by the rule *ṣaṭ-kati-katipaya-caturāṃ thuk*, the suffix *thuk* is added.
Nor should it be argued that this prohibition would also apply to the word *kumbhapūraṇa* ("filling the jar"), because [the rule *so'ci lope* applies].
Because of the indication "if for the purpose of filling out a verse" (*cet-pādapūraṇam*), only a suffix having the sense of a numeral is understood.
However, in the phrase "the sandy banks marked by the sixth [verse] beginning with *uñch*," it should be explained as "the sixth consisting of *uñch*.
Regarding the word "guṇe" (in the case of a subordinate element), the meaning is: "an example will be stated later. Or else, [it may be taken] as the primary element.
Alternatively, the word *guṇa* denotes a quality by virtue of being subordinate (*upasarjana*), as established by the grammatical explanation.

Thus it is said: "the blackness of a crow" and "the whiteness of a Brāhmaṇa. From the word *kṛṣṇa*, the suffix *ṣṭañ* is applied in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ*. From the word *śukla*, however...

[The suffix] *matup* is elided after words expressing qualities by the rule "elision of *matup*. Now, one might object: since the word "teeth" (*dantāḥ*) must be supplied as a complement [to complete the sense], in the case of the meaning "the teeth of a Brāhmaṇa are white," the word *brāhmaṇa* would be construed only with the word *danta*, and not with the word *śukla*. Consequently, due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), how can [the compound] be formed here?
Regarding the application of compound formation, [the author] says: "When, by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth.

This means "by means of context" or "by means of the sense (*artha*). When, in the context of describing teeth—such as "teeth that are closely set bring good fortune, but not those that are spaced apart"—it is said, "The Brāhmaṇa has white [teeth]," then...

The meaning is "either from context (prakaraṇāt) or from the sense (arthāt). For example, when the description of teeth currently under discussion—such as "teeth that are closely set bring good fortune, but not those that are spaced apart"—is given, and one says "the Brāhmaṇa’s [teeth] are white," then by virtue of the context, the specific term "teeth" is brought to mind as the substantive (viśeṣya). Or, when [it is said] among all castes...

When it is stated that "for a Brāhmaṇa, [the teeth] are white" (*brāhmaṇasya śuklāḥ*) with reference to teeth, clothing, and ornaments (*danta-vastrabhūṣaṇeṣu*), then by implication the word "teeth" (*dantāḥ*) is understood as the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Since there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) in that case, a compound (*samāsa*) would otherwise be required;
however, the meaning is that this is prohibited. In this regard, the rule *ā kaḍārāt* applies.

There is no inclusion here of those qualities designated as *guṇavacana* (expressive of quality) that were explained in detail in the sūtra "the third case [is used] when [the action] is caused by that" (*tṛtīyā tatkṛte*), because the word *guṇavacana* does not occur in this [sūtra]. Rather, [it refers to those] ending in a *taddhita* suffix, as stated in the commentary on the sūtra "from a stem ending in *v*, there is the suffix *ṅīṣ* if it is expressive of quality" (*voto guṇavacanāt*).

The objection—asking how words such as *kārṣṇya* (blackness) can denote a quality since [the rule] excludes those that are "expressive of qualities" (*guṇavacana*)—is thereby refuted. Now, in order to justify the genitive compound in expressions such as *arthagauravam* (the weightiness of the meaning), he says: "This is non-eternal. [He gives the reason: "Because a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is the authority [for its formation]. Regarding the word *saṃjñāyāḥ*:

The analysis of the compound is: *pramāṇatvam* (the state of being a means of valid cognition), [and] *saṃjñāpramāṇatvam* (the state of having a name as its measure); therefore, [it is a tatpuruṣa]. In this regard, since *pramāṇatva* is a quality (*guṇa*), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would be prohibited; thus, the indication of a determinative compound (*niṣādhatsamāsa*) would be untenable.
Consequently, the meaning "there is a prohibition by reason of being a quality" is not seen in the Bhāṣya. Nor is it...
It should not be said that there is an impossibility of forming a compound in cases such as *kṛṣṇaikatvam* (the oneness of Kṛṣṇa),

because in the rule *paṅktiviṃśati-* it is stated that "words beginning with *viṃśati* denote an abstract state (*bhāva*"), [and thus] in the sense of "a group of twenty cows" or "a thousand cows," [the compound is justified].

This is because of usages such as *gorviṃśatiḥ* (twenty cows) and *gosahasram* (a thousand cows). Furthermore, in cases such as *arthagauravam* (weightiness of meaning), it should be understood that it is a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (compound with the middle term elided), meaning "the weightiness residing in the object" (*artha-gataṃ gauravam*). This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. [The word] *suhita*...

He explains: "The words *suhita* and *ārta* have the sense of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). The intended meaning is that the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter gender to denote an abstract state (*bhāve*).

In the phrase "one who is well-satisfied with fruits" (*phalānāṃ suhitaḥ*), since the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the fruits is not intended to be expressed, and the relationship (*saṃbandha*) is intended to be expressed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed.
Because of the inclusion of the word *artha*, there is no compound even in expressions such as *phalānāṃ tṛptiḥ* ("satiety from fruits").
To the question, "How then is the compound *phalasuhita* formed?", he says: "But [it is] a third-case compound.
When the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended, the third case is used; the compound is then formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.
This is the intended meaning. If that is so, then the prohibition of the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) in connection with words expressing satisfaction (*suhita*) would be useless;

therefore, he says: "There is a difference in accent" (*svare viśeṣaḥ*). In a third-case compound, by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. But in a sixth-case compound, however...

The point is that there is a difference in the result, namely that the compound would otherwise have an acute accent on its final syllable (*atyantodātta*) by the rule *samāsasya*. Regarding the word *sat*: the meaning is that the prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) when joined with *sat* is being illustrated. As for the phrase *tau sat*, the technical name *sat* will be assigned to the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*.

Now, one might object: in the example *dvijasya kurvan*, is the genitive not used in the sense of the object (*karman*)? [Note: This passage is an excerpt from a commentary (likely on the *Kāśikāvṛtti*) discussing Pāṇini 2.2.10, which prohibits certain compounds with *sat*. It addresses the distinction between the present participles *kurvat* and *kurvāṇa* and their interaction with the genitive case.]

This is because of the prohibition [stated] as "not in the world" (*na loke*). Nor can it be a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the jar and so forth—as in the example "making a jar for a twice-born man" (*dvijasya ghaṭaṃ kurvan*)—because, in that case, due to the lack of semantic independence (*asāmarthya*) resulting from having a further referent, the formation of a compound with the word *kurvan* would not occur. Therefore...
He says: "The meaning is 'a servant'. That is to say, the meaning is "serving a twice-born man.
It follows that the verbal root √kuñ is used here in the sense of "serving. Regarding the word "indivisible" (avyayam):
the remainder of the sentence is "an example will be stated. Regarding the phrase "preceding and following": [it refers to] by means of *sat* and *tavya*.

The meaning is "by two [words] ending in the suffix *kṛt*. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *anekam anyapadārthe*, the usage *sarvapaścāt* serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this point. Regarding *tavya*: the meaning is that an example will be stated. As in *brāhmaṇasya kartavyam*; [this is justified by the rule] *arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca*.

In the rule "ṭhṭhavyatavyānīyaraḥ," *tavya* is a *kṛtya* suffix. By the rule "kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā," the genitive case is employed [with it]. However, with *tavyat*, it indeed occurs; the remainder of the sense is that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Since only *tavya*—devoid of the indicatory letter *ṭh*—is mentioned in the sūtra, *tavyat* is not included.
The meaning is "one's own duty" (*svakartavyam*). The analysis of the compound is *svasya kartavyam* ("the duty of oneself").

Here, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*. The point is that because of the connection with the suffix *tavyat*, the prohibition of compounding does not apply here.
Now, one might object: since the formation of the compound *brāhmaṇakartavyam* is possible by relying on the suffix *tavyat*, why [is this explained differently]?

Regarding the phrase "by its prohibition when joined with *tavya*," he says: "there is a difference in accent. The point is that when *tavyat* is used, the accent of the base of the subsequent member (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*) applies, whereas it does not apply when *tavya* is used; thus, there is a difference in the resulting accent.
Regarding the term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*): a word ending in the genitive case is not compounded with a co-referential [word].

The meaning is that an example will be stated here. Regarding the phrase "of the serpent Takṣaka": the point is that once a compound has been formed, when a genitive case ending is subsequently produced from that compound, the form *takṣakasarpasya* does not occur. [Objection: Even if the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is prohibited, [the rule] "the qualifier... [still applies].

Since the *karmadhāraya* compound [of the form] "with the qualified" (*viśeṣyeṇa*) would be unavoidable, one might ask: "What is the point of prohibiting the genitive compound? To this he says: "But the compound with the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇasamāsas tu*).
Now, one might object that the *karmadhāraya* will simply not occur here by the very force of the prohibition of the genitive compound.

So why resort to the frequentative inclusion [of the term] as a last resort? Nor should it be said that the prohibition of the genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) is for the purpose of ensuring that the accentuation of a karmadhāraya occurs and not that of a genitive compound;
for in both cases, the fact that the final syllable of the compound is udātta remains the same by virtue of the rule "samāsasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.223).

If you say this, do not say so; for if it were a *karmadhāraya* compound, in examples such as *gamanasya śreyasaḥ*, the original accent of the first member would apply by the rule *śrajyāvamakanpāpavatsu bhāve*, whereas in a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*, the final syllable would be udātta. To prevent that [undesirable result], the inclusion of the term *bahula* was resorted to. And even so, it is not the case that...

It must be stated that if the analysis of the compound were *takṣakaḥ sarpaḥ* (with the nominative case ending), resulting in a *karmadhāraya*, then the form *takṣakasarpasya* would be unavoidable; however, precisely by the force of the prohibition [of such a form],
one resorts to a *karmadhāraya* where the first member ends in the nominative case.

This is because such constructions as "of the serpent Takṣaka" (takṣakasarpasya) are inferred to be non-existent [under these conditions]. Now, regarding the prohibition when there is grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇa), he states another example: "of a cow that is a milch-cow" (gordhenor iti).
In cases such as "of a cow that is a milch-cow," a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) would otherwise be applicable, but that too is precluded by this [rule].

This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of "yūnaḥ khalateḥ" and so forth is intended. Now, one might object: "A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) does not even apply here, because the subsequent genitive compound is superseded by the specific rule for the *karmadhāraya* [compound] in cases such as 'poṭāyuvati' and 'yuvā khalatī'."

Because it is sublated [by other rules], he says: *poṭāyuvatī* etc. Rules such as *poṭāyuvati* and *yuvā khalati* find their scope (*sāvakāśāḥ*) in instances like *gaurdenuḥ* and *yuvā khalati*, where the first case ending (*prathamāvibhakti*) is present. However, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) finds its scope in examples such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*.

In such cases as these, [the rule] has scope when there is no coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). In examples such as *gordhenoḥ* and *yūnaḥ khalateḥ*, both [rules] would apply. However, in compounds such as *poṭāyuvati* and *yuvā khalatī*, since [the application] belongs only to words like *go* and *yuvan*, there is a difference in the result.

Because [the meaning] is clear. Furthermore, this negation by means of a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is only occasional, since the term *anyapadārtha* is used to indicate the meaning of another word (*anyasya padasyārtha*). By that, expressions such as "the fragrance of the blue lotus" (*nīlotpalasya gandhaḥ*) are established.

(696) *ktena ca pūjāyām* |2|2|12|. [The word] *pūjāyām* in this rule is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*. Thus he says: "by means of the rule *matibuddhi...*". For example: *rājñā mato buddhaḥ pūjito vā* ("esteemed, known, or honored by the king").
The meaning is sequential: "being desired," "being known," and "being honored" by the king.

The suffix *kta* is applied according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*, which prescribes the use of *kta* in the sense of the present tense. The genitive case is employed by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. But if this is so, how is it that forms such as *rājapūjitaḥ*, *rājamataḥ*, and *rājabuddhaḥ* occur?
Regarding the compound, he says: "In cases such as *rājapūjita*," etc.
(697) *Adhikaraṇavācinā ca* | 2|2|13|. He explains the sūtra by supplying the remainder: "by means of a word ending in a *kta*-suffix. An example is: *idameṣām āsitam*.

"Whether he has lain down, gone, or eaten"— here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*) according to the rule "The suffix *kta* is used after roots meaning 'staying,' 'motion,' or 'eating' when the locus is expressed. Furthermore,
the genitive case is applied by the rule "And [the sixth case ending is used] after a word expressing the locus."

(698) *karmaṇi ca* |2|2|14|. Regarding the rule *karmaṇi ca*: the word *ktena* is no longer operative. The meaning is that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when it denotes the object (*karman*) is not compounded.

Since this prohibition is thus established even in cases such as *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters"), the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* ("with [words ending in] *tṛc* and *aka*, the genitive denoting the agent is not compounded") is stated.

It would be redundant; however, *ca* is a synonym for *iti*. The meaning is that when the locative singular *karmaṇi* is uttered, any genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) prescribed [by a rule] is not compounded.
He states the resulting conclusion with the words beginning "ubhaya... (both...). Regarding *āścaryam*: although here [the rule] "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*) applies...
The genitive case in "kṛtī" (in the word *kṛtin*) is used for the object (*karman*), and not by the rule "ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi";
for that rule is intended as a restrictive one (*niyamapara*), meaning that the genitive occurs only for the object and not for the agent (*kartṛ*).
Nevertheless, restrictive rules (*niyamasūtra*) function in two ways: both as positive injunctions (*vidhi*) and as prohibitions (*niṣedha*).

There is no fault because of acceptance [of the agent]. However, in the case of *śabdānuśāsanam*, although the Teacher is in fact the agent (*kartṛ*), since he is not explicitly mentioned (*anupādānāt*), the rule *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66) does not apply; therefore, this prohibition [of the genitive] does not take effect. This is because, by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *kṛtvo'rthaprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.64), both the agent and the object [are intended].
This is because its application occurs only when [the rule] is active; or else, by relying on the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā* (P.

2.3.50) as a general option (*aviśeṣeṇa vibhāṣā*), in the case where the prohibition does not apply—namely, under the condition *ubhayaprāptau* (P. 2.3.66)—the genitive case is already obtained by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (P. 2.3.65), so this prohibition does not apply. Enough of this.
(699) *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* | 2|2|15|.

Regarding the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*: the term "agent" (*kartari*) is a qualifier specifically for the suffixes *tṛc* and *aka*, because it is directly stated [in the sūtra], and not a qualifier for the genitive case. Thus he says: "by means of *tṛc* and *aka* which have the sense of the agent. *apām*...

"Creator of the thunderbolt, the bearer"—here, the suffix *tṛc* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *ṭhṇvultṛcau*. The genitive case is used for the object according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*. Similarly, in "cooker of rice," the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the agent after the root *pac*; the specific difference here is the substitution of *ak* [for the final consonant]. In the word *ikṣubhakṣikā*, [the suffix *ṇvul* is used] in the feminine...

In the section beginning with *ktin* and others, when there is the indication of a verbal root meaning (*dhātvartha*), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. There is a compound with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting the object (*karman*).

However, the prohibition [of compounding] by the rule *karmaṇi ca* does not apply here; for that [prohibition] operates only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. But would this prohibition not also apply in cases such as *bhūbhartṛ* ("the supporter of the earth") from *bhuvaḥ bhartā*? It is not so, because the word *bhartṛ*...

It should not be argued that a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) does indeed occur in cases such as *yājakādau* because the rule "with *yājaka* and others" (*yājakādibhiśca*) is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*); for if that were so, it would follow that a compound would also be possible in the case of *vajrasya bhartṛ*.
Therefore, he says: "in the sense of a husband" (*patyartheti*). [The restriction applies] only to the word *pati* when it has the sense of "husband" within the group beginning with *yājaka*.

The word *bhartṛ* (husband/master) is included [in the list] because of the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Consequently, the intention is that in the case of *vajrasya bhartṛ*, there is no compound by virtue of the rule *yajñakādibhiśca*. If so, how [is it formed]? *Tribhuvanam* is a collective term (*samāhāra*) of the three worlds (*bhuvana*). It is a *dvigu* compound according to the rule *taddhitārtha-*.

The rule "a *dvigu* compound ending in a word with the suffix *ṭhak* [or *ṭhañ*] becomes feminine" does not apply here, because it has been stated that this does not occur for words ending in *pātra* and so forth. As for the objection—"How can there be a compound with a genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*) when it is joined with the suffix *tṛc* in the phrase 'in the creation of the three worlds'?"—he resolves it by saying "by means of the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). This is due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
The meaning is that Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra *bahuṣu*, stated that this prohibition applies specifically to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used in the sense of a kāraka.

(700) *kartari ca* | 2.2.16 | "And [the genitive] when [denoting] the agent. This word *kartari* follows from the previous mention of *ṣaṣṭhī* and *anyasya*. Thus he says: "when [denoting] the agent."

Regarding "ṣaṣṭhyāḥ" (of the genitive): the sense is that this is because of the recurrence of the word "akena" from the rule "tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari" (Pāṇini 2.2.15). In the example "bhavataḥ śāyikā" (the lying down of you), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied under the governing rule "striyāṃ ktin" (Pāṇini 3.3.94) when there is a designation of the root's meaning; then the substitution of *akā* occurs, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. [The genitive case here is justified] by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ... (Pāṇini 2.3.65).

The genitive case here denotes the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*). Since *aka* here does not have the sense of an agent, the rule *tṛjakābhyām* (Pāṇini 2.2.15) does not apply. Now, one might object: "In the preceding sūtra, the compound term *tṛjakābhyām* was employed; how then can there be an elision (*anuvṛtti*) of *aka* alone here, and not of *tṛc* as well? To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "No. [Regarding] "in connection with that": since the suffix *tṛc* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), in examples such as *sraṣṭā kṛṣṇaḥ* ("the creator Kṛṣṇa"), the agent is already expressed by the *kṛt*-suffix; therefore, since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would not even apply there in the sense of the agent, the prohibition of its compounding is like "scratching with a rabbit's horn"—it is impossible.
The meaning is that [the formation of the feminine suffix] is refuted by the impossibility [of the action being performed], as if one were to say "it must be done.
(701) *Nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* | 2|2|17|. Regarding "always" (*nityam*) in the case of play (*krīḍā*): [the example is] *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*. *Uddālaka* is the *uśleṣmātaka* tree; of that...

"Puṣpāṇi" (flowers) and "teṣāṃ bhañjanam" (the breaking of them)—this is an *asvapadavigraha* (non-co-ordinate analysis). Regarding the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*): within the governing rule "ktin in the feminine," the word "in the sense of a name" indicates that the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Here, there is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*). However, in reality, [it should be understood] within the governing rule "ktin in the feminine."

Regarding the rule "ṇvul after a verbal root when its meaning is indicated," it is more appropriate that *ṇvul* denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*). However, as will be explained under the section on *kṛt* suffixes, the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This being the case, the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "that play in which *uddālakapuṣpa*s are broken."

Regarding the phrase "in [the sense of] livelihood" (*jīvikāyām*): the meaning is that an example will be stated. In the term *dantalekhaka*, the analysis of the compound is *asvapadavigraha* (an analysis not using its own constituent words), namely: "one who lives by the carving of ivory. The suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the root *likh* in the sense of the agent;
there is the substitution of *ak*. The "livelihood" is understood through the compound itself. [Objection: But surely, this could be accounted for by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* alone?
To the question, "Since the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is already established, for what purpose is this [rule] stated?", he says: "In that case" (*tatra*).

In those two examples cited, regarding the expression *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*, which denotes a game, the prohibition of the genitive compound would apply because it falls under the governing rule of the optional suffix *ṭhak*; however, in the case of that which denotes a livelihood (*jīvikā*), [the compound is formed].
In the case of the term *dantalekhaka*, since the prohibition of a genitive compound by the rule *tṛjakābhyām* would otherwise apply, this sūtra is commenced; such is the meaning.

(702) *pūrvāparādharauttaram ekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe* || 2.2.1 || [A word denoting a part—namely *pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, or *uttara*—is compounded with a word denoting the whole (*ekadeśin*) when they share the same grammatical locus.]

*Pūrvāpara*: This is the nominative singular from the collective *dvandva* compound *pūrvāparādharottaram*. The word *ekadeśa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a "part. That which possesses a part (*ekadeśa*) is the "possessor of parts" (*ekadeśin*), namely the whole (*avayavin*); thus, [the meaning] "by that" is obtained. *Adhikaraṇa* means a substance (*dravya*). A single substratum is "one-substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that when a substance qualified by oneness is present, the words *pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, and *uttara*, being themselves *sub*-ending, are compounded with a *sub*-ending word denoting the whole (*avayavin*); this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

He states the resulting conclusion with the words "together with the whole," and so forth. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that [the compound] is 'that which is both prior and a body' (*pūrvaścāsau kāyaśca*)?"

The forms such as *pūrvakāya* are established by a *karmadhāraya* compound alone; for, by figurative usage (*bhakti*), the word *kāya* can denote a part of the body, thereby making grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) possible. To this, he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound. This is because in the analysis (*vigraha*) *pūrvaṃ kāyasya*, the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* [Pāṇini 2.2.8] applies.

The meaning is that when there is a compound in a sūtra, because the word ending in the genitive case is prescribed as the first member in the rule for forming compounds (*samāsavidhi*), it would undergo *pūrvanipāta* (prior placement); this statement is intended to prevent that.
"Pūrvaṃ kāyasya" (the front of the body): here, "pūrvaṃ kāyasya" is the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*). [The term] "ardha" [is used].

It is "gamyam. The neuter gender is used because it refers to the object being qualified (*viśeṣya*). According to the rule *tasya param āmreḍitam*, since there is no ablative case when a word for direction functions as a part [of a whole], the genitive case is employed. In the example *pūrvakāyaḥ*, the word *pūrva* is placed first in the compound because it is specified in the nominative case in the rule prescribing the formation of the compound.

The intention is that [the word] takes the masculine gender according to the rule *ṭhparavalliṅgam*. Regarding this, it has been stated under the rule *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhaḷa vā*: "Where both a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) are made optional by the *mahāvibhāṣā*, once the [word] is released by the exception, the general rule does not apply again. Consequently, [this follows].

In the absence of an *ekadeśisamāsa*, a *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* does not occur. For example, in the case of *aparakāyaḥ*, the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is *aparaṃ kāyasya*. Thus, we have *aparakāyaḥ* and *utarakāyaḥ*. [Question: Why "with a word denoting a part" (*ekadeśinā*)? [Answer: Words such as *pūrva* and others are compounded with a word denoting a single substance (*ekadravyavācin*).

The meaning is "let it be exactly thus. Regarding the phrase "prior to the navel of the body": here, the word "nābheḥ" (of the navel) connects with the word "pūrva" (prior). The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in connection with a direction. The meaning is that the half which is prior in relation to the navel is a constituent part of the body. In this context, regarding the word "nābhi" (navel):
The connection is with the word *pūrva* (prior). Here, the navel (*nābhi*) is merely the limit of the prior portion, not the whole (*avayavin*).
Therefore, the meaning is that there can be no compound of the word *pūrva* with the word *nābhi*.
In the example "the first of the students" (*pūrvaś chātrāṇām*), the word *chātra* refers to the collection of students.
The plural number is used with reference to a collection whose constituent parts are manifest.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the relationship between part and whole. The meaning is "the first half of the collection of students.
Here, although the collection of students is a single entity, because its constituent parts are manifest—

The point is that because there is multiplicity, there is an absence of the qualification of the number "one," and thus no compound [is formed]. Now, one might ask: how can there be an *ekadeśi-samāsa* (part-whole compound) in the case of *madhyāhnaḥ* ("midday"), since the word *madhya* ("middle") is not included among the words beginning with *pūrva*? To this, he says: "Every part [is included]."

The meaning is that [the word *ahan*] is distinct from "east" (*pūrva*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to an indicator" (*jñāpakāt*): while the rules *tatpuruṣasya* and *ahassarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyāt* are in force, the rule *ahno'hna etebhyaḥ* prescribes the substitution of *ahn-* for the word *ahan* when it follows words denoting a part [of the day].

Then, in the analysis *ahnaḥ sāyaḥ* (the evening of the day), when the word *sāya*, which denotes a part, is compounded with the word *ahan*, which denotes the whole and ends in the genitive case, forming a *tatpuruṣa* compound,
the word *sāya* is placed first because it is the one designated by the nominative case.
When the word *ahna* follows the word *sāya*, which denotes a partial duration (*ekadeśavṛtti*), it is replaced by the substitute *ahan*;

and since the rule "rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi" prescribes the masculine gender, the form becomes *sāyāhnaḥ*. Therefore, when the locative singular case ending follows, by the rule "saṅkhyāvisāye," there is an optional substitution of *ahann* for the word *ahna* that is preceded by the word *sāya*.

It has been stated: *sāyāhni*, *sāyāhani*, *sāyāhne* are the examples. In that regard, if in the analysis (*vigraha*) "the evening of the day" (*ahnaḥ sāyaḥ*), the word *sāya* were not included among the words beginning with *pūrva* (in the sense of forming a compound), then there would be no compound with the word *ahan*. Consequently, by the rule "ṣaṣṭhī," the word *ahan* ending in the genitive case would [be compounded] with the word *sāya*.

Since, in the case of a compound, the word ending in the genitive case alone is prescribed for compounding by the rules on compounds (*samāsa-śāstra*), if it were to be placed first [in the compound], the rule prescribing the substitution of *ahan* for the word *ahar* following the word *sāya* would become purposeless; therefore, it is said that "every single part [of the day] is compounded with *ahar*."
The meaning is "it is known. Regarding *madhyāhna*: this is a compound formed from the analysis *ahno madhyam* ("the middle of the day").

By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied; by the rule *ahno'hna etebhyaḥ*, the substitute *ahna-* is substituted [for *ahan*]. Regarding *sāyāhna*: the analysis is *ahnaḥ sāyaḥ* ("the evening of the day"). It is like *madhyāhna*.

Now, one might object: "It is incorrect to say that 'every single part [of a word] is compounded with a temporal word,' because in the rule *saṃkhyā-viṣāya*, since only the word *ahna* is mentioned, it would be impossible to indicate that every other part of a word denoting time is to be compounded. To this, [the author replies]:

He says: "of the indicator" (*jñāpakasya*). Having taken for granted the formation of a *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compound) between the word *sāya* and the word *ahan*, [the author] employs the word *ahan* after the word *sāya*; therefore, by every word denoting time that expresses a whole, [the whole is understood].

The meaning is that a compound is indicated for [the word] *sarva* with respect to a single part (*ekadeśa*), because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) refers to the general case; it does not mean that a compound is indicated specifically between the word *sāya* and the word *ahan*, even though the latter is not included among the words beginning with *pūrva*. "Midnight" (*madhyarātra*) means the middle of the night. "The latter part of the night" (*paścimarātra*).
The analysis of the compound is "the latter part of the night. The suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *ahaḥ sarvaikadeśa-* to form the compound.
Regarding the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.2.2):
since the word *ardham* is specified in the neuter gender, it is understood to be neuter by that very designation.

Regarding the repetition of the term "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*), it is intended to include those words that are invariably neuter; with this in mind, he says: "The word *ardha*, when denoting an equal portion, is always neuter. The word "occurs" (*vartate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is because of the lexicon (kośa) which states: "In the masculine, *ardha* [is used] for a half, provided it refers to an equal share."
The meaning is as follows: the word *ardha*, when denoting a general part (*aṃśasāmānya*), occurs either in the masculine or in the neuter.

However, when it denotes an equal part (*sama-aṃśa*), the word *ardha* is exclusively neuter in gender. In the Bhāṣya, on the other hand, it is stated that the word *ardha* is neuter when referring to an equal division, whereas when it denotes a general part, [it takes both genders].
It was stated that [the word *ardha*] is masculine. "As before" means that this word *ardha*, which is eternally neuter, is compounded with a word denoting a whole (*avayavin*).
(1) The mention of "not ending in the genitive case" applies to the rule regarding words in the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktau*).

Since the word *ardha* is not included among the words beginning with *pūrva*, the [application of the] preceding rule does not apply. But will it not be stated that "half of a *pippalī* is *ardhapippalī*" as an example? In that case: *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* = *ardhapippalī*;
*ardhena pippalyāḥ* = *ardhapippalyā*; *ardhāya pippalyāḥ* = *ardhapippalyai*.

In the analyses (vigraha) such as *ardhātpippalyāḥ*, *ardhasya pippalyāḥ*, *ardhapippalyāḥ*, and *ardhe pippalyāḥ* (*ardhapippalyām*), because the word *pippalī* possesses a fixed case-ending (*niyatavibhaktika*),
it becomes a secondary member (*upasarjana*) by the rule *ṭhekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte*; consequently, [the feminine suffix] is elided by the rule *gostriyoḥ*.

To the objection that [the word *pippalī*] should be short [in its final vowel], he says: "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*). The meaning is that in the rule *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte*, it should be stated that "[this applies to] what does not end in the genitive" (*aṣaṣṭhyanta*). Consequently, since the word *pippalī* does not end in the genitive, it does not possess the status of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and thus there is no shortening of the vowel. But if this is so...
In analyses such as *pañcānāṃ khaṭvānāṃ samāhāraḥ* (the collection of five beds) or *samāhāraṃ samāhāreṇa*, although the word *khaṭvā* has a fixed case-ending,
because it ends in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*), the rule *gostriyoḥ* [applies].

If the short vowel [at the end of the first member] were absent, there would be no final *a*, and consequently, by the rule "dvigoḥ," the suffix *ṅīp* would not apply; thus, the form would be *pañcakhaṭvā* and not *pañcakhaṭvī*. To address this, he says: "in a *ekadeśisamāsa*. The example *pañcakhaṭvī* given in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule "apathaṃ napuṃsakam" is the authority (*liṅga*) for this point.
[This is] the state of being. Regarding the term *ardhapippalī*:
because the word *ardha* is designated as the first member [in the rule], it is an *upasarjana* (subordinate member), and thus it is placed first.
As for the word *pippalī*, although its case-ending is fixed in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), [the rule applies] by virtue of the phrase "when there is a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*).
The sense is that because [the word *ardha*] is negated and lacks the status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), there is no shortening of the vowel. Regarding the example *grāmārdha*:

the analysis (*vigraha*) is "half of the village" (*grāmasyārdhaḥ*). The meaning is "a portion of the village. Since the word *ardha* does not denote an equal division, it lacks the status of being invariably neuter; therefore, this is not [a case of] the aforementioned compound, but rather—

The rule "the sixth [case-ending] alone" implies that this is a compound; thus, there is the prior placement of the word ending in the genitive case. "Only when there is identity of substance" means that the requirement of "having a single substratum" (ekādhikaraṇa) continues to apply here. In the expression *ardhaṃ pippalīnām* ("half of the long peppers"), there is no compound because of the absence of identity of substance. If a compound were to occur, it would necessarily be *ardhapippalī*.

Because the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is one. This sūtra was rejected in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "the gender is like that of the subsequent word" (*paravalliṅgam*). (704) *dvitīyatṛtīyacaturthaturyāṇy anyatarasyām* 2.2.3. [The words] *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* [may optionally take the gender of the preceding word].

Regarding "dvitīyatṛtīya": "dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyāḥ" is an analytical compound (*vigraha*). The meaning is: "the second half of the alms. In the term *dvitīyabhikṣā*, the word *dvitīya* is placed first because it is mentioned in the nominative case [in the original rule]. Its feminine gender is established by the rule *ṭhparavalliṅgam*.

"Second [part] of the alms for the mendicant. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "the second portion of the alms for the mendicant. In the term *bhikṣāyāḥ*, the genitive case expresses a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and it connects with the word *dvitīyam*. Furthermore, the word *dvitīyam* connects with the word *bhikṣukasya*.
It connects as the object (*karma*). Because of the prohibition "not in *loka*" (*na loke*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply.

Here, the meaning is that the compound of *dvitīyam* with *bhikṣukasya* does not occur, because the beggar (*bhikṣuka*) is not a part-possessor (*ekadeśin*) in relation to the second [part]. [Objection: But surely, by virtue of the governing rule for optionality (*vibhāṣā-adhikāra*)...
Since the alternative (vikalpa) would already be established [by other rules], the mention of *anyatarasyām* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "in *anyatarasyām*.

The connection is that by the force of the mention of *anyatarasyām*, there is optionally (*pakṣe*) a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Otherwise, once the general rule (*utsarga*) has been superseded by this compound which serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive case, the general rule would not apply.
The meaning is that, according to the section on the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, when an exception (*apavāda*) has been set aside, the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply;

this is because it has been indicated by the inclusion of the option (*vā*) in the rule *pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*. Now, one might ask: since there is a prohibition by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa* (Pāṇini 2.2.11), how can a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) be formed here? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "By setting aside the prohibition [contained in] *pūraṇaguṇa*... The underlying intention is that otherwise, the mention of the term *aṅ* (in Pāṇini 2.1.32) would be redundant. [Thus ends the exposition on the *ekadeśisamāsa*.]
(705) *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā* |2|2|4|.

[The sūtra] *prāptāpanne ca*: the meaning is that these two words, *prāpta* and *āpanna*, are compounded with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*). The particle *ca* serves to include this as a compound with the second case. Thus he says: "in the alternative."

In fact, it is established in the Bhāṣya regarding the rule *dvitīyā śrite* that even the prescription of the second case (*dvitīyā*) for composition with the words *prāpta* and *āpanna* would be without scope [if the word *śrita* were not included]; therefore, since their inclusion is already established, the particle *ca* (and) does not serve the purpose of including them. In that regard:

By the present sūtra, in a compound, there is the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of *prāpta* and *āpanna*. However, in a compound formed by the rule "the second case [ending] with *śrita*," there is the prior placement of that which ends in the second case. Thus he says:
"one who has obtained a livelihood" (*prāptajīvika*), and so forth. Now, a woman who has obtained a livelihood is a woman who has reached a livelihood (*jīvikāmāpannā*).

Thus, when the compound is formed by the present sūtra from the analysis (*vigraha*) [of *prāptajīvika* and *āpannajīvika*], he says "in this sūtra" in order to establish that the final vowel of the two preceding members is replaced by the letter *a*. He says "the letter *a* also" because the sense obtained is: "the words *prāpta* and *āpanna* are compounded with a word in the second case, and for those two, the letter *a* is the substitute for the final sound."

The state [of being]. By that [word "tena"]—the meaning is: by the prescription of the vowel *a* in place of the final vowel of the words *prāpta* and *āpanna*. (706) *Kālāḥ parimāṇinā* | 2.2.5 | [Time-words are compounded with a word denoting the thing measured.]
"Times [are compounded] with that which possesses a measure. He explains the term "that which possesses a measure" as "denoting that which is to be delimited.

Because of the plural number in the word "kālāḥ," the meaning is "those denoting specific divisions of time. In the example *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month"), in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), the month is the primary element; however, in the compound, the one born is the primary element. Thus: *māsajātaḥ*.
In expressions such as *dṛśyatām jātaḥ*, there is the cognition of the one who is born (*jāta*) alone as the object of seeing and so forth;

however, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is established through the relation of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). With this very point in mind, it is read in some manuscripts of the root text as: "he for whom there is a month [elapsed] since birth" (*māso jātasya yasya saḥ*). In that case...
In the analysis (*vigraha*) "of one born" (*jātasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the relationship between the delimited (*paricchedya*) and the delimiter (*paricchedaka*).

The understanding from the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is that "the month is the delimiter of the birth. From the compound (*samāsa*), the understanding is that "the birth is delimited by the month. In that context, the month directly delimits the birth.
However, the term *jananāśraya* (the locus of birth) delimits Devadatta by means of the birth;
thus, from the compound, the understanding arises: "Devadatta is the locus of birth delimited by the month.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). For in a genitive compound, it would instead be *jātamāsa*.
Nor should it be argued that this is already established by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself as "one for whom a month has passed since birth" (*māsajāta*),

because the rule for *bahuvrīhi* compounds applies only to words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, it would result in the word *jāta* being placed first [by the rule *niṣṭhā*], according to which "the past participle suffix *niṣṭhā* follows words denoting genus, time, pleasure, and so forth."

Regarding the word *jāta*, its placement at the end of the compound (*paranipāta*) when it is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) does not occur; for there is no evidence to justify including it in the list [of words] beginning with *sukha*. Enough of this. As for the expression *dvyaho jātasya* ("born two days ago"):

it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhitārtha*), formed by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*; [and the form *dvyaha-* arises because] *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* [are included in the relevant rules].
The word "puṃsi" [indicates] the masculine gender.

For the sake of establishing *dvigu* compounds with a subsequent member denoting a measure (*parimāṇin*), there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of this rule to *tatpuruṣa* compounds consisting of many members.
Regarding the phrase "by the final member": this *vārttika* is cited in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *taddhitārtha*.

For by that rule, a *dvigu* compound is prescribed when a word denoting direction or number is compounded with a *sup*-ending word as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). And the word *uttara* is conventionally used to denote the final constituent of a compound.

Furthermore, in the analysis (*vigraha*) "two days old" (*dve ahanī jātasya*), when the three words are compounded and the word *jāta* has become the final member (*uttarapada*), it must be stated that the *dvigu* compound applies to the two preceding *sub*-ending words. And that compound [is formed] by the rule "time-measures [are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix]."

It is not possible for this to be governed by the preceding rule (*parimāṇini*), because in that rule (*sup supā*), singularity is intended to be expressed. Therefore, for the sake of establishing a *dvigu* compound, there must be many [words] by means of the subsequent member— a word denoting the object to be measured (*parimāṇin*) which serves as the external cause (*paranimitta*).
The meaning is that an additional rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be stated for the *tatpuruṣa* compound.

That is to say, in order to establish a *dvigu* compound where the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is conditioned by a further element, a three-membered *tatpuruṣa* must be asserted. This very point serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that, in the rule *sup supā*, singularity is intended to be expressed.

Regarding the two days: in the analysis (*vigraha*) "two days old" (*dve ahanī jātasya*), when the three words are compounded and the case-endings (*sup*) are elided, we have *dvyahanjāta*. Since the word *jāta* follows as the second member (*uttarapada*), the compound *dvi-ahan* forms a *dvigu* compound according to the rule *taddhitārtha-*; subsequently, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ*.

The meaning is that when the substitution of *ahna-* is applied by the rule "ṭhahno'hna etebhyaḥ," the form becomes *dvayahnaja*. The point here is that if the preceding two [compounds] were not *dvigu* or *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* and the substitution of *ahna-* would not occur.
Now, one might object: how was it previously stated that the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of two days is *dvyaha*?

Since there would still be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ahna* even in that case, he says: "But in the preceding [rule]," meaning "the prohibition," i.e., the prohibition of the substitution of *ahna*.
(707) *saptamī śauṇḍṬaḥ* | 2|1|40| [The word ending in the seventh case is compounded with words such as *śauṇḍa*, etc.]
The seventh case [is used] with *śauṇḍa* and others. Regarding the phrase "with *śauṇḍa* and others":

because of the use of the plural number and because of its inclusion in the list (*gaṇa-pāṭha*), the word *śauṇḍa* is [understood as] the first of that group. In the example *akṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ*, *śauṇḍaḥ* means one who is skilled in the activity [of gambling]. The seventh case is used here to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the dice.

The meaning is "skilled in games involving the senses. Regarding the word *atra*: it means "in the group beginning with *śauṇḍa*. Regarding *īśvarādhīna*: the word *prapañca* is to be supplied as the remainder. The analysis (*vigraha*) is *adhi īśvare*.
By the rule *adhir īśvare*, the term *adhi* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya*. [This is further explained by] the rule *yasmād adhikam*.

The seventh case [ending]. A compound is formed with *adhi* following that [seventh case form]. There is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sub*). By the rule *ṭhaṣaḍakṣeṇa*, since it is the final member of a bahuvrīhi, there is the suffix *kha*. The substitution of *īn* occurs. Thus, the form *īśvarādhīna* is obtained. (708) *siddha-śuṣka-pakva-bandhaiś-ca* [Pāṇini 2.1.41].

"Siddha-śuṣka": the word "saptamī" (locative case) is understood to follow here. Thus he says: "by these [words], that which ends in the locative case. For example, *sāṅkāśya-siddhaḥ*. *Sāṅkāśya* is the city established by Saṅkhāśa; one who is *siddha* there means one who has arisen or become known there. *Āta-śuṣka* means dried in the sun.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: "cooked in a pot" (*sthālīpakva*)—the analysis is "cooked in a pot" (*sthālyāṃ pakva*). "Wheel-binding" (*cakrabandha*)—the analysis is "binding in a wheel" (*cakre bandha*). These are mentioned separately because they are not included in the *śauṇḍa* group of words.

(709) *Dhvāṅkṣeṇa kṣepe* | 2|1|42|. Regarding the rule *dhvāṅkṣeṇa kṣepe*: the word *dhvāṅkṣa* is taken here as signifying "meaning" (*artha*), according to the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Thus he says: "by that which expresses the sense of a crow. He explains the word *kṣepa* as "in censure" (*nindāyām*).

Regarding the term *tīrkṣadhvāṅkṣa*: *dhvāṅkṣa* means a crow; the meaning is one who, like a crow, does not remain for long in the teacher’s household (*gurukula*). For in this way, there is a censure. He states the purpose of including the word *artha*—namely, [to form the compound] *tīrthakāka*.

(710) *kṛtyair ṛṇe* | Pāṇini 2.1.43. Regarding the rule *kṛtyair ṛṇe*: the word "seventh case" (*saptamī*) is understood by way of anuvṛtti. By the mention of the term *kṛtya*, according to the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a technical name (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there is the inclusion of words ending in suffixes that bear the designation *kṛtya*.
The *Bhāṣya* states: "The word *ṛṇapada* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of what is necessarily required. To this he says: "ending in the locative case," and so forth.

Regarding the word *māse*: the locative case is used here in the sense of a proximate locus (*sāmīpyādhikaraṇatva*). The meaning is that the debt is to be repaid at a time immediately following the month.
He states the purpose of the term *ṛṇa* being an obligatory indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) as follows: "It is to be sung in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇegeya*).

[In this compound] there is no elision (*aluk*) according to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*. The *Bhāṣya* states that only the suffix *yat* is intended here as a *kṛtya* (gerundive) suffix. Therefore, it does not apply in cases such as "alms are to be given in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇe dātavyā bhikṣā*).
(711) *saṃjñāyām* |2|1|44|. The word *saṃjñāyām* [is present]. The term *saptamī* (locative case) is understood from the previous rule. Thus he says: "ending in the locative," and so forth.
*Araṇyetilakāḥ* and *vane kaśerukāḥ* are both words used as proper names (*saṃjñā*).
The elision [of the case-ending] does not occur due to the rule *ṭhhaladantātsaptamyāḥ*.

The analysis of the compound is *ktenāho*: "parts of a day (ahan) and a night (rātra). The term *saptamī* is understood from the previous context. By the word *ktena*, there is a reference to that which ends in *kta*. Thus he says: "of *ahan* and *rātri*."
He gives an example of a part of the day: *pūrvāhṇakṛtam* ("done in the forenoon").
He gives an example of a part of the night: *apararātrakṛtam* ("done in the latter part of the night").
[Pāṇini 2.1.46: *tatra*].

In this context: "tatra" refers to the actual form of the word; "saptamī" and "ktena" are understood as being carried over from the previous rule. Thus he says: "this word 'tatra'... and so forth. Regarding "tatrabhuktam," the purpose is the accent of the compound. And [the example] "tātrabhuktam" is derived from "tatrabhuktasyedaṃ" (belonging to that which was eaten there).

In the sense of "censure" (*kṣepa*), the words "locative" (*saptamī*) and "by means of a word ending in *kta*" (*ktena*) are understood [from the previous rules]. Thus he says: "that which ends in the locative," and so forth.

In the example *avataptenakulasthitam ta etat* ("this [behavior] of yours is like a mongoose staying in a heated [hole]"), the word *sthitam* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). By the mongoose...

[The word *sthitam* is established. The compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned, it includes [a compound] preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*," the word *nakulasthita* is also understood as ending in a *kta* suffix; therefore, it is joined with *avatapte*.

When this [compound] is formed with a word ending in the seventh case, the elision of the case-ending is not applied by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "O Devadatta! this standing of yours—'a place where mongooses have stood in a heated spot'.
Just as mongooses do not remain for long in a heated region, so too [one should not remain] after having commenced tasks.
The meaning is that these [faults] do not cease despite your running here and there; thus, it should be understood as a censure: "you are unstable. (714) *pātresamitādayaśca* | Pāṇini 2.1.48.

"And *pātresamitā* and so forth. This means that these words are presented as being formed by the application of rules such as compound formation (*samāsa*). Regarding *pātresamitāḥ*: the root *iṇ* means "to go.

From the prefix *sam-* combined with this root, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-*. Due to a formal anomaly (*nipātana*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending.

The meaning is that they have gathered once the food has been placed in the bowls. He states the result: "at the meal," etc. Regarding "a hero in the house" (*geheśūra*): the meaning is one who displays valor only within the home, but not in battle. Regarding "one who roars in the house" (*gehenardī*): the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*) to the root *nard* (meaning "to sound"), since it is a verbal root ending in a consonant. This occurs when there is a compound.
The absence of elision (*aluk*) occurs by virtue of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The meaning is that [the word] roars only in the house, but does not engage in battle and the like.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of restriction" (*avadhāraṇārtha*): the meaning is that these [words] function exactly as they are recited in the list (*gaṇa*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "by that" (*tena*). And therefore, those which are *parama-*...
In examples such as *pātresamitāḥ*, a compound does not occur.

(715) *pūrvakāla-eka-sarva-jarat-purāṇa-nava-kevalāḥ samānādhikaraṇena* || 2.1.49 || [Words denoting prior time, *eka*, *sarva*, *jarat*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* form a compound with a word in apposition.]

"pūrvakālaika": the term *su* is understood from the previous rule and is changed to the plural; *sup* is also understood. That which has a prior time (*pūrvaḥ kālo yasya*) is "prior-time" (*pūrvakāla*).
The meaning is "that which exists at a prior time. Consequently, by this [term] "pūrvakāle,"...

The term "pūrvakāla" (referring to time) is understood here as a word expressing its own meaning [as a prior temporal relation]. However, words such as "eka" (one) and so forth refer solely to their own forms.

Thus, the meaning is that the seven [words] beginning with "pūrvakāla," when ending in case-terminations (*subanta*), are compounded with another word ending in a case-termination that is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); that is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. "Samāna" means "one."

The analysis of the compound is "that which has a substratum (adhikaraṇa) to be expressed. It follows that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) consists in the state of having a single referent. Regarding the rule on "prior placement" (pūrvanipāta):
[the word *snāta*] is intended to qualify [the word *anulipta*] by way of being "first bathed" or by way of being "first smeared with unguents."

It is possible; therefore, when the compound "viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa" (the qualifier with the qualified) applies, since either member might have been placed first, this rule is stated so that the word expressing the earlier time (*pūrvakālavṛtti*) alone is placed first.
The meaning is that this applies to *eka* and the others as well. Regarding the case of the word *eka*:

He states another purpose as well with the words "of the word *eka*. Since the rule "Directional terms and numerals are compounded when they form a name" (*diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*) is about to be stated, the compound *ekanātha* would otherwise be barred from being a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).
The inclusion of the term *eka* is therefore for the sake of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*) to that prohibition. This is the meaning.

Regarding the term *snātānulipta*: although the words "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*paścāt*) do not appear here, just as in the analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*), the sequence of bathing and anointing is understood from the compound itself. This is because when it is stated that "that which has a prior time [is compounded]," the meaning "by that which has a subsequent time" is understood by implication. Regarding *ekanātha*:
The analysis of the compound is "he who is both one and a protector" (*ekaś cāsau nāthaś ca*). Regarding "all ritualists" (*sarvayājñikāḥ*):

those who study or know the sacrifice (*yajña*) are ritualists (*yājñikāḥ*), according to the rule *ṛtūkthādisūtrāntāt ṭhak*. The analysis of the compound is "all those who are ritualists. Regarding "old Naiyāyikas": [those who] study Mīmāṃsā...
The Mīmāṃsakas [explain]: "The suffix *vun* is applied after *krama* and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "those who are both ancient (*purāṇa*) and Mīmāṃsakas.

Regarding "new reciters" (*navapāṭhakāḥ*), the analysis is: "those who are both new (*nava*) and reciters (*pāṭhakāḥ*). In this context, due to its association with "ancient," the word *nava* is understood only as signifying "recent," and not [in its other senses].

It denotes a specific number. "Kevalavaiyākaraṇāḥ" (mere grammarians): those who study or know grammar are *vaiyākaraṇāḥ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "tadadhīte tadveda" (he studies that or knows that). There is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "na yvābhyām" and the substitution *aij* occurs. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those who are both *kevalāḥ* (mere) and *vaiyākaraṇāḥ* (grammarians)."

(716) *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām* |2|1|50|. Regarding *dik-saṃkhye*: the meaning is that the term *samānādhikaraṇena*, which is found in the sūtra *pūrva-kāla-eka-* [Pāṇini 2.1.49], continues in force until the end of this *pāda*. Consequently, [the following rule applies].

The meaning is that direction and number are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) that stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and that [compound] is a *tatpuruṣa*. Now, one might object: if the compounding of direction and number were governed by the rule "the qualifier is compounded with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), then—since the body of the restrictive rule "only when there is a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām eva*) is accepted [for this specific case]—the preceding sūtra [would be unnecessary].

In cases such as "pūrvamāsaḥ" (the eastern month) and "pūrvasamudraḥ" (the eastern ocean), although they lack the status of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), a compound is indeed formed because they denote time and place. Now, one might ask: how is the usage of Kālidāsa in the phrase "trilokanāthaḥ pitṛsadmagocaraḥ" (the lord of the three worlds, whose domain is the abode of the ancestors) to be explained, given that the word *triloka*...?

Because it is not a designation (*asaṃjñā*). If one were to analyze the compound as "the collection of the three worlds" (*trayāṇāṃ lokānāṃ samāhāraḥ*), then by the rule *taddhitārtha* [Pāṇini 2.1.51], it would form a *dvigu* compound; however, this would entail the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *dvigoḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.21].
This is because a *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the letter *a* is desired to be feminine.

If it is argued that, by accepting that [the word *loka*] does not denote the feminine because it belongs to the *pātrādi* group, forms such as "yadi trilokī gaṇanāparā syāt" would be unjustifiable—this is true; however, the word *loka* here refers to a collection of worlds (*lokasamudāya*). It is a *madhyamapadalopī* (elliptical) compound meaning "a world consisting of three worlds" (*trayo lokā avayavā yasya sa trilokaḥ*).
This is a compound (*samāsa*). This point is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*.

As for the expression *ṣoḍaśapadārthānām*, it means "objects numbering sixteen"; thus, it is a *madhyamapadalopa* (middle-term-omitted) compound. Enough of this. Regarding *pūrveṣukāmaśamī*: [it is derived] from the word *pūrva*...
The compound is formed with the words *iṣu*, *kāma*, and *śamī*. This is the name of a particular region. "The Seven Sages" (*saptarṣayaḥ*):
this is the name of the seven sages beginning with Marīci and Atri. "Not here":
the meaning is that it is not a [proper] name [in this context].

(717) *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca* | Pāṇini 2.1.51. [The compound occurs] when there is the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), or when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), or in a collective (*samāhāra*). Although the locative case is used only once, it is differentiated according to the distinction of its objects. Among these, in the portion "in the sense of a secondary derivative," it functions as a locative of domain (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*); in the portion "in a subsequent member,"...

By taking proximity as the basis for the locus, the locative case ending results in a *parasaptamī* (a locative of reference). However, in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), the locative is used because the locus is directly expressed (*vācyatayā*). From the preceding rule, the phrase "direction and number" (*diksaṃkhye*) is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "in the domain of the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Regarding the meaning of a secondary derivative:
The meaning is: "when there exists an object of knowledge produced by a future secondary derivative (*taddhita*). This refers to the case where a *taddhita* suffix denotes the future.
