"As before" means: it is compounded with a word in grammatical apposition; that is a *tatpuruṣa*. He provides an example of a directional compound (*dik-samāsa*) denoting the sense of a *taddhita*: "in the eastern [direction]" (*pūrvasyām*). In the compound...

Regarding the word *kṛte*: the intention is that when the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which exists in the eastern hall" (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*), and after forming the compound by the rule "for the sake of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*), the suffix *ñ* is applied by the rule "having a directional term as the prior member" (*dikpūrvapadāt*), and after the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "and [the final vowel] of that which is designated by *yasya*" (*yasyeti ca*), there is the initial vṛddhi.
In all instances of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), there is the substitution of the masculine form for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

Regarding the term "of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*): the word "mere" (*mātra*) signifies entirety. Its meaning is that pronouns occurring within the context of a derivation—such as compounds (*samāsa*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and so forth—are treated as masculine. However, if...
If it is stated that "direction and number are compounded when a *taddhita* suffix follows," then the compound occurs once the *taddhita* suffix has been produced;
yet, once the compound is formed, the *taddhita* suffix is applied because the direction word is the first member (*pūrvapada*). This results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
However, it is not explained as "direction and number are compounded when the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix is to be expressed."

Since the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is expressed by that derivative itself, it cannot constitute the meaning of a compound; therefore, it is more appropriate to explain it as occurring in the context of a secondary derivative. Regarding *āparaśāla*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which exists in another hall" (*aparasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhava*). The formation of the compound and so forth is like that of *paurvaśāla*.

He provides an example of a compound of directions (*dik-samāsa*) when a subsequent member (*uttara-pada*) follows, beginning with "one for whom the eastern hall is dear" (*pūrvā śālā priyā yasya*). Now, one might ask: since the case-endings (*sup*) are elided once the *bahuvrīhi* compound has been formed, what is the purpose of this [further] compounding of the two preceding members when a subsequent member follows?

He says: "Therefore, in the word *śālā*, the vowel *ā* is udātta. This means that when there is an intermediate *tatpuruṣa* compound, the vowel *ā* after the letter *l* is udātta by virtue of the final member of the compound being accented. However, the sense is that if the intermediate *tatpuruṣa* were not present, the initial vowel would be udātta by the rule of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).
Now, one might object that the compound "samāhāraḥ pūrveṣāṃ puruṣāṇām" (the collection of former men) would also be a *samāsa* [and thus a *dvigu*]; to this he says:

"In the case of directions" (*dikṣu*). The meaning is that a *samāhāra* [compound] regarding directions does not fall within the scope of a *dvigu*. That is to say, there is no *samāsa* with a directional word as the first member when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*).

Regarding the rule *saṅkhyāyās taddhitārthe*: the meaning is that a compound is being illustrated. In that context, he provides an example for the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*): *ṣāṇmāturaḥ*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *mātur utsaṃkhyā-sambhadrapūrvāyāḥ*, and there is the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of the base, as well as the initial *vṛddhi* strengthening. Now, when followed by a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*)...
He provides an example: *pañcagava* ("five-cow"). Regarding the phrase "of the internal *tatpuruṣa*": the meaning is "that which is prescribed when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows.
Regarding the phrase "when an option (*vikalpa*) has arisen": the remainder [of the sentence] is "because of the governing rule of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Consequently, in the case where the word *pañcagava* does not constitute a *tatpuruṣa* compound...
The intention is that, in the absence of the *ṭac* suffix prescribed for *tatpuruṣa* compounds by the rule *ṭhgorataddhitalukī*, the form *pañcagodhana* would also be possible.
(1) Regarding *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, there is a statement concerning their obligatory composition when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

Regarding the phrase "dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ": the meaning is that the obligatory application (*nityatva*) must be stated for those *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds when they occur before a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). The mention of "compound" (*samāsa*), however, has crept in by way of association; it is not directly connected [to the rule], because there is no deviation from the technical designation "compound" (*samāsasaṃjñā*) when a subsequent member follows.
Because the word *uttarapada* is conventionally established as referring to the final member of a compound;
(718) *gorataddhitaluki* | Pāṇini 5.4.92:
[The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after the word *go*, when no *taddhita* suffix is elided.

The term *tatpuruṣasya* from the rule *ṭhpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* is understood [in this sūtra], and having been modified into the ablative case, it is qualified by the word *goḥ*. This is a rule concerning suffixes applied to the end of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*). From the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is understood. The governing heading *samāsānta* (suffixes at the end of a compound) is also in force.

He says this with the words beginning "at the end of *go*," etc. [The question is: Why does it say "provided there is no elision of a *taddhita* suffix"? Consider the example: *pañcaguḥ* ("bought for five cows"). Here, there is elision (*luk*) of the *taddhita* suffix by the rule "after *adhyardha*, etc. [Consider also] *pañcagavadhanaḥ*.
When a three-word *bahuvrīhi* has been formed, and the word *dhana* stands as the final member (*uttarapada*), [the rule applies].
The sense is that in the case of the two former [words] forming a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is the substitution of *ava* for *avā* when the suffix *ṭac* is applied.

Here, regarding the Vārttika "in *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds," it should be understood that the example for *dvandva* is: "one to whom speech (*vāk*) and skin (*tvak*) are dear" (*vāktvacapriya*). In this case, within the three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound...

Since the first two [members] form a compulsory *dvandva*, by the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in /c/, /ṣ/, or /h/, the suffix *ṭac* is applied in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*"), the suffix *ṭac* is likewise compulsory. Nor can it be argued that a three-word *bahuvrīhi* is impossible here because the words *vāk* and *tvak* lack mutual coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

It must be stated that this is possible by taking the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *priya* with both [members of the compound]. Furthermore, because a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound whose members have different referents) is possible—just as in examples such as *kaṇṭhekāla* ("one who has a black throat")—by virtue of the metarule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, when a locative case ending is used for a qualifier" (*saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau*). This is also supported by the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: *vāktvacapriyaḥ*.

The example itself here is sufficient as an indicator; enough with further elaboration. Now, in order to provide an illustration for the compound of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*), he shows the analytical resolution (*vigraha*): "the collection of five cows" (*pañcānāṃ gavāṃ samāhāraḥ*).
(719) A *dvigu* compound is that which is preceded by a numeral. Pāṇini 2.1.52.

In this case, since there is a compound, the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule "ṭhgorataddhitaluki," and after the substitution of *av* for *o*, one intends to prescribe the operation of a *dvigu* for the word *pañcagava*; thus, he states the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a *dvigu*: "A *dvigu* is that which is preceded by a numeral. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose prior constituent member is a numeral. [The remainder of the definition is: "for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)."
Thus, the compound prescribed by the preceding sūtra has as its external referent (*anyapadārtha*) [a meaning other than the members themselves], due to proximity.

This is what he states: "That which was mentioned in the rule *taddhitārtha-* is of three kinds. That is to say, it is of three types when preceded by a numeral: when a *taddhita* derivative is the sense, when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows, and when the collective sense (*samāhāra*) is to be expressed.

The compound has been explained; it is, in short, a *dvigu*. Thus, because the word *pañcagava* is a compound prescribed when a collective (*samāhāra*) is to be expressed, its designation as a *dvigu* is established. However, in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [in the case of] "a sacrificial cake prepared in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ puroḍāśaḥ*), it is called *pañcakapālaḥ*, according to the rule: "That which is prepared [is so called], as well as foodstuffs."

Thus, [the suffix] *aṇ* [is applied]. By the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of the *dvigu* when no descendant is meant," there is elision. As for an example where it occurs in a subsequent member (*uttarapada*): *pañcanāvapriyaḥ*. By the rule "the suffix *ṭac* is added at the end of a compound after *nau* in a *dvigu*," the suffix *ṭac* is applied. (720) A *dvigu* compound is singular. 2.4.1.

"A *dvigu* compound takes the singular number. From the *vārttika* stating "the term 'aggregate' (*samāhāra*) must be supplied here," it is understood that [the rule applies] to an aggregate. It is called "expression" (*vacana*) because it expresses; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent by virtue of its irregularity (*bāhulaka*). It is neuter in the general sense. A *dvigu* compound denoting an aggregate conveys a single meaning.

The word "syāt" (it may be) is understood. In that regard, if the word *samāhāra* is derived from the root √*hṛ* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), such that it primarily denotes that which is collected (*samāhṛta-pradhāna*), then an extension [of the rule] is established because duality and plurality residing in the collected items cannot logically exist as a single unit. Thus he says: "The meaning of a *dvigu* is a collection."
Regarding the term *ekavat* (as if one): when *samāhāra* means "collection" (*samūha*), then because that [collection] is inherently one, the desired result is already established;

thus, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that this rule need not have been commenced. Some, however, maintain that even though the collection is in reality one, it is treated as such by intending to emphasize the distinction between its constituent parts.

This is intended to exclude the dual and plural numbers. They say that as a result, one should not intend to express a distinction between manifest parts (*udbhūtāvayavabheda*) in this context. "That [compound] is neuter": a *dvigu* and a *dvandva* compound used in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*) shall be neuter.

The meaning of that will be explained in the root [sūtra]. [Thus ends the section on *dvigu* compounds. (721) "Words denoting things censured [are compounded] with words denoting the grounds of censure" (*kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ*, Pāṇini 2.1.53). "Things censured": the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the present tense, as established by the commentary. Therefore, he says: "those being censured."

In the word *kutsanaiḥ*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). "As before" means that it is compounded with a term in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and that compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. In the example *vaiyākaraṇakhasūciḥ*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "he who is both a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and a 'bad needle' (*khasūci*). This refers to one who, when asked about grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), [behaves like a bad needle].

He shows the sky, or looks at it, in order to cause one to forget the question; thus he is described. In this context, the grammarian is censurable for forgetting the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Pointing to the sky is the cause of the censure.
[The term] "a stubborn Mīmāṃsaka" (*mīmāṃsakadurdurūṭa*) is used: the root *ḍul* (meaning "to throw up") belongs to the curādigaṇa.
The suffix *kūṭa* is an *auṇādika* suffix added after the prefix *dur-* and others. The elision of the *ṇi* affix occurs by the rule "the *ṇi* is frequently elided elsewhere as well.

The substitution of *ra* for *la* follows from their non-distinction (*ralayor abheda*). One who, having studied Mīmāṃsā, understands it incorrectly and makes a false objection (*durākṣepa*) is described in this way. This sūtra is intended to ensure that the qualified noun (*viśeṣya*) is placed first.
In a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound), however, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) would normally be placed first.
(722) Pāpāṇakekutsitaiḥ | 2|1|54|. [The words] *pāpa* and *aṇaka* are compounded with words denoting contempt (*kutsita*). That [compound] is...

The meaning is "tatpuruṣa" (a determinative compound). Now, one might ask: since this is already established by means of a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (an adjective-noun compound), for what purpose is this [separate rule] stated? To this he says: "by the previous sūtra. [In the expression] "pāpam asyāsti," the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to the rule beginning with *arśa-*. Thus, the word *pāpa* refers to that which possesses sin. The word *aṇaka*...
It exists as *kurūpiṇī*. According to Amara: "The words *kurūpa*, *kutsita*, *avadya*, *kheṭa*, *garhya*, and *aṇaka* are synonyms.

Consequently, the words *pāpa* (sinful) and *aṇaka* (wretched) denote contempt, having as their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the sinful and deformed nature which serve as the causes for such censure.

Consequently, since these two would have appeared as the final member in a compound according to the previous rule, this present rule is intended to establish a restriction regarding their position as the prior member; such is the meaning. Regarding *pāpanāpita*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who is both wicked (*pāpa*) and a barber (*nāpita*). Regarding *aṇakakulāla*: he who is both low-born (*aṇaka*) and a potter (*kulāla*).
The analysis of the compound is "and the potter" (*kulālaśca*).
(723) *Upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.55). [Explanation:
*Upamānāni*. Those by means of which things are compared—that is, determined as being similar—are called *upamāna*s (standards of comparison).

The meaning is: "those which specify similarity. *Sāmānya* (the commonality) refers to the attribute shared by the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*). Words that express this are called *sāmānyavacana*. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule of *bāhulaka* (generalization). Having first stated the commonality...
That is to say, those words which terminate in a substance (dravya) following that [quality] are called "denotative of the universal" (sāmānyavacana). Thus,
words for comparison— synonymous with terms that define similarity—

are used in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with words denoting the common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma) belonging to both the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya).
The meaning is that those [words] are compounded; thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa*. Regarding the example "ghanaśyāma" (dark as a cloud):

one might object that here, in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "dark like a cloud," there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—defined as the two words "cloud" and "dark" functioning with a single referent—and how, therefore, can there be a compound in this case?

Because there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) due to the dependence on the word *iva*, he says: "In this case, the preceding word [is the upameya]. Thus, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word *ghana* (cloud) refers to Rāma who resembles a cloud, and the word *śyāma* (dark) also refers to Rāma;
therefore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For this very reason, [the phrase] "fickle like a doe" [is justified].

In the compound *mṛgacapalā*, the masculine form is established by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*. The word *ghana* must be understood as referring to the object of comparison (*upamāna*) by way of its previous state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*). Thus, the cognition is: "one who is dark like a cloud. Similarity (*sādṛśya*) consists in being different from that [object] while possessing the properties residing in it. And so, in this manner—

It is established that both the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the sub-correlate (*anuyogin*) of similarity must possess a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). And here, that common property is understood as being presented solely by the subsequent member of the compound, because of its proximity. Thus, the final cognition results in: "possessing a blackness similar to the blackness residing in a cloud. Now, one might object:
To the question, "Since this is already established by means of a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound), for what purpose is this rule?

he says: "Regarding the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). Otherwise, since both [words] would be adjectives (*guṇavacana*), there would be no fixed order due to the freedom of choice in the relationship between qualifier and qualified, resulting in an irregularity such as *khañjakubjaḥ* or *kubjakhañjaḥ*.
The intended meaning is "it may be so.

(724) *Upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyā'prayoge* [Pāṇini 2.1.56]. "That which is compared" (*upamitam*). "As before" (*prāgvat*). It is compounded with words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇaiḥ*), and that is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

This is the meaning. Here, because that which is compared always requires a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the sense that [the comparison is] "with tigers and so forth," which serve as the standards of comparison, is established by implication.
Now, one might ask: since this is already accomplished by a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) alone, for what purpose is this rule? To this [the author replies]:

He says: "of the qualificand" (*viśeṣyasya*). The meaning is this: since, in the co-occurrence of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the standard of comparison alone would normally be placed first as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), this [rule] is intended to ensure that the qualificand is placed first. For example, in *puruṣavyāghra* ("tiger among men"), [the compound consists of] *puruṣa* and *vyāghra*.

The analysis (vigraha) is as follows: "A man who is like a tiger in bravery. Here, the common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma) consisting of bravery, which serves to establish the similarity, is not explicitly mentioned; thus, a compound is formed. [The compound is] *puruṣo vyāghra iva śūraḥ* ("a man who is brave like a tiger").
This means that by virtue of his bravery, he is similar to a tiger. In this case—

The meaning is that because the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—namely, "bravery"—is explicitly employed as both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is no compound. As for Kaiyaṭa’s usage, "Where is the ocean of the Bhāṣya so exceedingly deep?", it must be explained either by treating it as belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group [of compounds] or as a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in which the Bhāṣya itself is the ocean. It is not [a case of a compound].

Furthermore, it should not be argued that because the word *puruṣa* is dependent on the word *śūra*, the compound cannot occur here due to a lack of semantic independence (*asāmarthya*), and therefore the rule "when there is no use of a general term" (*sāmānyāprayoge*) is redundant;
for it is only the subordinate member (*apradhāna*) among those being compounded whose dependence obstructs semantic independence, but not [the principal].

Regarding the primary member: likewise, in this case, although the person (*puruṣa*)—as the primary member—is dependent upon the hero (*śūra*), it still possesses the capacity [to form a compound], and thus the formation of the compound proceeds; therefore, the rule states "the non-employment of the general term" (*sāmānyāprayoga*) in order to prevent that [undesired] formation.
This very point shows that even when the primary member is dependent, [the compound is not barred].

This indicates that [the compound] obstructs the capacity [of the words]. Therefore, it is clear in the Bhāṣya that by this [rule], compounds such as *rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ* ("a beautiful king's man") are established.
(725) *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam* (2.1.57). "An attributive word [is compounded] with the substantive word diversely."

"A qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) [is compounded] with the qualified (viśeṣya). That by which something is distinguished is a qualifier; it is that which differentiates from others. The qualified, however, is that which is to be differentiated and is known as distinct. The term "with a coreferential [word]" is understood [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "that which distinguishes."

"As before" means that when [the words] are compounded, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), the word "blue" (*nīla*) first distinguishes the lotus from non-blue lotuses; thus, it provides the qualifier. Its compounding occurs with the word "lotus" (*utpala*), which provides the qualificand.

The point is that because it is mentioned first, the qualifier is placed at the beginning [of the compound]. Nor should it be argued that the word "lotus" (*utpala*) must also be considered a qualifier because it excludes blue from non-lotuses; for when a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*) is used in conjunction with a quality-word or an action-word, [it functions as the qualificand].

It is only that which conveys the substantive (viśeṣya), and not that which conveys the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), by its very nature. For example: "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*) and "cooking Brahmin" (*pācakabrāhmaṇa*). When two quality-words (*guṇaśabda*) are used in apposition, there is no fixed rule regarding the relationship of qualifier and qualified. For example: "lame and humpbacked" (*khañjakubjaḥ*) or "humpbacked and lame" (*kubjakhañjaḥ*).

There is also no fixed rule regarding the order of action-words (*kriyāśabda*). As stated clearly in the *Bhāṣya*: "For example, *khañjapācakaḥ* (the lame cook) and *pācakakhañjaḥ* (the cook who is lame). Similarly, in cases such as *kailāsādriḥ* (Mount Kailāsa), *mandarādriḥ* (Mount Mandara), and *ayodhyānagarī* (the city of Ayodhyā), even proper nouns (*saṃjñāśabda*) function solely as qualifiers.

By its very nature. However, when there is a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words denoting a general genus (*sāmānyajāti*) and a specific genus (*viśeṣajāti*), it is the specific genus alone that functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This should be understood from examples such as "the *śiṃśapā* tree. Now, since [the desired result] is established by the mention of the word "optionally" (*vā*), for what purpose is the mention of "diversely" (*bahula*)? To this he says: "Because of the mention of 'diversely' (*bahulagrahaṇāt*)."

(726) *pūrvāparaprathamacaramajaghanyasamānamadhyamadyamavīrāś ca* | 2|1|58 | *pūrvāpara* | The meaning is that *pūrva* and the others are compounded with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Since this [formation] is already established by means of a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound) alone, he asks: "For what purpose is this [rule]? To this he replies: "Regarding the rule for prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*). As for the example *aparādhyāpaka*: it is established in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra* that, due to the continued application of the term *bahulagrahaṇa* ("in various cases"), there is no compounding of words such as *pūrva* with action-words like *pācaka*. And therefore...
The example "ṭhaparādhyāpakaḥ" is to be disregarded; the example "ṭhaparamīmāṃsakaḥ" is appropriate. (1) The substitution of "pañca" for "apara" in the sense of "half" must be stated.
Regarding the phrase "in the latter half": this *vārttika* is established in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *paścāt*. [Examples:
*prathamavaiyākaraṇaḥ* (the first grammarian), *caramavaiyākaraṇaḥ* (the last grammarian); *madhyānmaḥ*: *madhyamavaiyākaraṇaḥ* (the middle grammarian);
*vīravaiyākaraṇaḥ* (the heroic grammarian). He raises an objection: how is it that there is the form *ekavīraḥ*? For [according to the rule],...
By this very sūtra under discussion, when the word *vīra* is compounded with the word *eka*, and given that *vīra* would take the prior position [in the compound], the form would be *vīraika*;
therefore, the connection [of the objection] is: "How then can it be *ekavīraḥ*? Now, one might argue that by the sūtra *pūrvakālaika-* [Pāṇini 2.1.49], the word *eka* [should indeed precede].

Since the compound *ṭhekavīraḥ* would be unobjectionable when [the rule] applies, he says: "Because it sets aside [the previous rule] by virtue of being subsequent, according to the rule *pūrvakālaika-*. He refutes this with: "By the phrase *bāhulatāt*.
Due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *bahula* (diversely), this rule does not apply, and thus the compound is formed simply by the rule *pūrvakāla-*.
The meaning is "it becomes.

(727) *Śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ* |2|1|59|. The group beginning with *śreṇi* is compounded with words beginning with *kṛta* when they are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). It is compounded with them.
The meaning is "tatpuruṣa. [The rule] regarding the suffix *cv* in the case of *śreṇi* and so forth must be stated.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of *śreṇi* and so forth": this refers to the statement concerning the suffix *cv* in the context of the composition rules for *śreṇi* and the like.

The meaning is that when the sense of the suffix *cvi*—namely, the transformation of something into something else (*abhūtatadbhāva*)—is to be understood, a compound of words such as *śreṇi* and others should be stated. Regarding the example *aśreṇayaḥ*: "guilds" (*śreṇayaḥ*) refers to groups of people who live by means of a craft or merchandise.
Those who were previously unable to live by means of a craft or merchandise, but now [live] by means of it...
The meaning is that when there is a compound in the sense of "made capable," the form *śreṇikṛtāḥ* arises.

The word *śreṇi* ends in a short vowel, as is illustrated in that very way in the Bhāṣya. However, when the *śreṇis* are already established and merely embellished, then no compound occurs, because the sense of the suffix *cvi* (indicating a change of state) is absent.

However, because it ends in the suffix *cvi*, there is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) by the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" [Pāṇini 2.2.18]. Following that, the lengthening of the vowel in the word *śreṇi* occurs by the rule "cvau ca" [Pāṇini 6.3.138]. (728) [A word] not consisting of a negative particle (*anañ*) is compounded with a past passive participle (*kta*) that is qualified by a negative particle (*nañ*). [Pāṇini 2.1.60]
"With a *kta*-ending word qualified by *nañ*, [there is] a *nañ*-less [word].
This means that a *kta*-ending word not containing *nañ* is compounded with a *kta*-ending word qualified by *nañ* that stands in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); it is a *tatpuruṣa*.
"And it is done" (*kṛtaṃ ca tat*): it is called "done" because one part has been performed.
Because one part of the whole is not performed, that very thing is considered "unperformed. This is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the prior placement [of words].

Furthermore, this compound does not apply in the case of *siddhaṃ ca tad abhuktaṃ ca* ("that which is prepared but not eaten"), for here the word *viśiṣṭa* signifies "surpassing" or "additional. For example, when it is said, "Yajñadatta is surpassed by Devadatta in Vedic study," [the former is distinguished by the excellence of the latter].

It is understood that [the word] is "additional" (*adhika*). It is qualified by the negative particle (*nañ*) itself; thus, it is obtained that [the word] must end in a *kta*-suffix with only the negative particle added. And in this way, it should be understood that the two words ending in *kta* have come to possess the same base form (*samānaprakṛtikatva*).
(1) An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made regarding the elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*) for the sake of establishing compounds such as *śākapārthiva*.

Regarding the phrase "of *śākapārthiva* and so forth": this Vārttika was recited in the Bhāṣya on the rule *varṇo varṇena* [Pāṇini 2.1.69]. As for *śākapārthiva*: one for whom vegetables (*śāka*) are dear is *śākapriya*. [The suffix *vā* indicates that the form is optional.]

In the expression *priyasya*, the word *priya* is placed at the end [of the compound]. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "one who is both fond of vegetables (*śākapriya*) and a king (*pārthiva*)," this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) containing a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). In that case, within the initial portion which is the *bahuvrīhi*, there is the elision of the final member, the word *priya*. As in the example *devabrāhmaṇa*: he for whom the gods are dear (*devāḥ priyā yasya sa*).

The analysis of the compound is: "devapriyaḥ" (one who is dear to the gods), and "saḥ" (he) plus "asau brāhmaṇaḥ" (that Brahmin). As in the previous case, there is elision of the final member of the compound.
Alternatively, the analysis is: "a Brahmin who worships the gods. (Pāṇini 2.1.61):
*san-mahat-parama-uttama-utkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ* (the words *sat*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* form a Tatpuruṣa compound with words denoting those being honored).

The rule *sanmahatparama*—with the remainder of the sūtra being *samānādhikaraṇaiḥ samasyante sa tatpuruṣaḥ* (words meaning "good," "great," or "supreme" are compounded with words in grammatical apposition, and that compound is a *tatpuruṣa*) applies here.
In the example *sadvaidya*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *san vaidyaḥ*.
"Goodness" (*satva*) consists in possessing knowledge that thoroughly penetrates the science of medicine (*cikitsā-śāstra*). By means of this, the physician is honored.
It is understood. This sūtra is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the prior placement [of a word]. Regarding the phrase "by what will be stated":

when there is a compound formed by this [sūtra] from the analysis *mahāṃścāsau vaiyākaraṇaśca* ("he who is both great and a grammarian"), the substitution of the final vowel *ā* for the word *mahat* occurs by the rule that will be stated, namely *ṭhānmahataḥ*, followed by the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*).
The meaning is that he is "a great grammarian" (*mahāvaiyākaraṇa*). Now, one might ask:

since in the expression "an excellent cow" (*utkṛṣṭo gauḥ*), the word *utkṛṣṭa* denotes excellence (*atiśaya*), and by that excellence the cow's honor is understood, why does a compound not occur here? To this, he says: "lifted out of the mud" (*paṅkāduddhṛta*).
The meaning is as follows: the intention is that the root *kṛṣ* preceded by the prefix *ut* here signifies "extraction" (*uddharaṇa*).

[Examples include] *paramavaidyaḥ*, *uttamavaidyaḥ*, and *utkṛṣṭavaidyaḥ*. This sūtra is intended to establish a rule for the mandatory prior placement of words such as *san* (good) and others when compounded with words denoting qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*).

(730) *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ pūjyamānam* || 2.1.62 || [The word *pūjyamānam*] is compounded with *vṛndāraka*, *nāga*, and *kuñjara*. The phrase "it is compounded with words in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇaiḥ samasyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule].

Since this would already be established by the *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound), this *sūtra* is intended to establish a restrictive rule regarding the prior placement of the word being qualified (*viśeṣya*).

Regarding the term *govṛndāraka*: the word *vṛndāraka* denotes a deity. As Amara states, beginning with "The immortals (*amarāḥ*), the ageless ones (*nirjarāḥ*), the gods (*devāḥ*)," he continues, "*vṛndārakāḥ* [are] deities. The analysis of the compound is: like a bull (*go*) that is a *vṛndāraka*. Similarly, like an elephant (*nāga*) that is a bull (*go*), one has *gonāga*; like an elephant (*kuñjara*) that is a bull (*go*), one has *gokuñjara*.

The words *nāga* and *kuñjara* denote an elephant (*gaja*). Here, because [the subject] is similar to *vṛndāraka* and others, excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) is understood; thus, there is the sense of being honored (*pūjyamānatā*). Now, one might ask: since [the class of words beginning with] *vyāghra* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, this [usage] is already established by the rule "that which is compared with *vyāghra* and so forth" (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*); for what purpose, then, is this [rule] stated?
He says: "of the tiger, etc. [This refers to] "sāmānya" (the general). The sense is that [it applies to cases such as] "The cow or the elephant is the best," and so forth.
(731) *Kataraka-tamau jātiparipraśne* (Pāṇini 2.1.63): [The suffixes] *katar* and *katama* are used when there is an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti*).

*Katara* and *katama*: when a question regarding a specific selection (*jāti-paripraśna*) is implied, *katara* and *katama* are compounded with a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For example, *katarakaṭhaḥ*. This means: "Which of these two is a Kaṭha? [The suffix] *ḍatarac* is applied after *kim* and *yad* when selecting one out of two. [One who] studies what was taught by Kaṭha...
*Kaṭha*: Because he was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *prokte* [Pāṇini 4.3.101].

Then, by the rule *ṭhkaṭhacarakālluṅ* [Pāṇini 4.3.107], there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Thereafter, by the rule *tadadhīte* [Pāṇini 4.2.59], the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and by the rule *proktālluṅ* [Pāṇini 4.2.64], there is elision of that as well. "Which Kalāpa? means: which among these is the Kalāpa?
One who studies what was taught by Kalāpin is called a *kalāpa*. [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *ṭhkalāpino’ṇ*.

[In the formation of *sabrahmacārī*,] there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) according to the rule *ṭhsabrahmacārī*. [And in the case of *katamaḥ kaṭhaḥ?*] the suffix *ḍatamac* is applied according to the rule *vā bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac*.

Now, one might object: "Being a student of the Kaṭha branch (*kaṭhaśākhādhyetṛtva*) and so forth is not a genus (*jāti*), just like potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like; for a genus is defined as that which is apprehended through form (*ākṛtigrahaṇā...*)."

Regarding the definition [of a universal] as "jāti" (genus), it does not apply to genders, because the definition—"comprehended by being denoted once"—does not apply there; therefore, he says "and gotra. In this context, the word "katama" (which of many) refers exclusively to an inquiry regarding genus.

The inclusion of the term *jāti-paripraśna* (inquiry regarding a genus) is solely for the purpose of providing a specific derivation (*vyutpādana*). Consequently, in the example "Of these two, which one is Devadatta?", no compound occurs. However, in the case of "Which among them is Devadatta? (*eṣāṃ katamo devadattaḥ*), [the rule] does not apply at all, because the suffix *-tamap* is prescribed only when there is an inquiry regarding a genus (*jāti-paripraśna*). In reality, however...

In the rule for the suffixes *ḍatarac* and *ḍatamac*, the mention of "between two" (*dvayoḥ*) and "among many" (*bahūnām*), as well as the phrase "in a question regarding a genus" (*jātiparipraśne*), was rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. Consequently, forms such as "Which among these is Devadatta? (*katama eṣāṃ devadattaḥ*) also exist.
Regarding this, the *Śabdenduśekhara* maintains that the inclusion of the phrase "in a question regarding a genus" is intended to prevent the formation of a compound (*samāsa*) in such cases.

(732) *kiṃ kṣepe* | 2|1|64 | *kiṃ kṣepe*. "Censure" (*kṣepa*) means reproach (*nindā*). When that [reproach] is implied, the indeclinable *kim* is compounded with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*);
the meaning is that this forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For example: *kutsito rājā* ("a contemptible king").

This is a compound whose analysis (*vigraha*) does not contain its own constituent members (*asvapadavigraha*). One should understand that the word *kutsita* (contemptible) stands in the place of the word *kim*.
This is because, since the censure is not understood through the sentence itself, a formal analytical statement (*laukikavigraha*) using the same words (*svapada*) is impossible.

Regarding the form *kiṃrāja*: the suffix *ṭac* [prescribed by the rule] *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac* does not apply here, because of the rule *kimaḥ kṣepe* ("the word *kim* takes [the elision of case-endings] when used in a sense of censure").
Because of the prohibition. Now, one might ask: "How can a king who possesses great wealth be considered contemptible?
To this he says: "He who does not protect. The grammatical connection is: "Who indeed is that king? (733)

*Poṭā-yuvati-stoka-katipaya-gṛṣṭi-dhenu-vaśā-vehat-baṣkayaṇī-pravaktṛ-śrotriya-adhyāpaka-dhūrta-aiḥ jātiḥ* || 2.1.65 || The meaning is: *poṭā-yuvati*. A word denoting a genus (*jāti*) is compounded with words such as *poṭā* and the rest when they stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); that [compound] is a *tatpuruṣa*.
(734) *Tatpuruṣa* with identical referents (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is called *karmadhāraya*.
Now, intending to state the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to the *karmadhāraya*, he declares its technical designation: "A *tatpuruṣa* [with] identical referents...
Two words whose expressed referent (*vācya*) is the same (*samāna*)—that is, one and the same (*eka*)—are "identical in referent" (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
The phrase *pade te asya staḥ* (the two feet are his) is a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) construction; the suffix *arśa-ādy-ac* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).

The meaning is that a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of multiple words in a co-referential relationship receives the designation *karmadhāraya*. This designation was not provided under the governing rule for *tatpuruṣas*, because [if it were], it would be so.
They say that because of the governing rule for the notion of "single-idea" (*eka-saṃjñā*), the designation of *tatpuruṣa* would be sublated by the designation of *karmadhāraya*.
(735) *puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu* | 6|3|42|.

*Puṃvat-karmadhāraye*: "The feminine [stem] becomes like the masculine" (*puṃvat*) applies when the compound is a *karmadhāraya*. The phrase "from a word that has a corresponding masculine form, provided it does not end in the suffix *ūṅ*" (*striyāḥ puṃvadbhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*) continues to apply here.
Although there is only one locative case (*saptamī*), it is divided according to the difference in its scope:

in the portion concerning the *karmadhāraya*, it is a locative of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*); regarding the scope of the suffixes *-jātīya-* and *-deśīya-*, it is a locative of reference (*para-saptamī*).

Thus he says: "In a *karmadhāraya*. After the word "tathābhūta," the phrase "denoting a female" (*strīvācaka*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. This will be clarified under the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* by the statement *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*. Now, one might object: is this not already established in a *karmadhāraya* by the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*?

Since the masculine form (*puṃvatva*) is established for the suffixes *jātīya* and *deśīya* by the rule "in the case of *tasil* and so forth, except for *kṛtvasuc*" (*tasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ*), he says: "it is not obtained in the case of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇī*) and *priyā* etc. The intention is that this is because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of non-ordinal numbers and *priyā* etc. [by the previous rule]. Thus, *mahānavamī* means "that which is both great (*mahatī*) and the ninth (*navamī*)."
Analysis of the compound: The compound is formed by the rule "sanmahat... and so forth. The word *navamī* means "that which completes nine";

it is derived from *nava* with the suffix *ḍaṭ* (i.e., *ima*) by the rule "tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ," and the augment *maṭ* is added because the stem ends in *n* and is not a numeral beginning with a letter other than *sa*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Here, since the word *navamī* ends in a suffix denoting ordinal completion (*pūraṇapratyayānta*), when it follows [the word *san*], the rule "striyāḥ puṃvat" applies.

By this [rule], the masculine form (*puṃvat*) which was not previously applicable is prescribed. The intention is that once the masculine form has been applied, the substitution of *ā* for *ṭhā* in *mahat* occurs by the rule "ṭhānmahataḥ. Regarding the term *kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*: it is that which completes fourteen, i.e., the fourteenth (*caturdaśī*). [The suffix] *ḍaṭ* is applied; there is elision of the *ṭi* portion by the rule "ṭ-nastaddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.143); and because it ends in a *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.

The analysis of the compound *kṛṣṇā-caturdaśī* is "that which is both Kṛṣṇā and the fourteenth day. Regarding *mahāpriyā*: the analysis is "that which is both great (*mahatī*) and dear (*priyā*"), forming a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The intended meaning here is that, because [the word] is excluded from the category beginning with *priyā*, this [rule] prescribes what was otherwise not obtained.

He states another purpose for the rule *ṭhpuṃvat karmadhāraye* with the words "likewise, [the prohibition] of that which has *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), etc. This refers to the group of five sūtras beginning with *na kopadhāyāḥ*, followed by *saṃjñīpūraṇyośca*, *vṛddhinimittasya ca taddhitasyāraktavikāre*, *svāṅgāccetaḥ*, and *jāteśca*.

The meaning is "it is prohibited. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *karmadhāraya* and so forth": the meaning is that [the prohibition applies] when a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed, and when the suffixes *jātīya* or *deśīya* follow. In the example *pācakastrī*:

this is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is both a female cook (*pācikā*) and a woman (*strī*). Here, by the rule "*na kopadhāyāḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.3.37), the status of being like the masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prohibited.

A prohibition is applicable [in the following cases]: *databhāryā* and *pañcamabhāryā*. In *databhāryā*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is given and is a wife," and in *pañcamabhāryā*, it is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "she who is fifth and is a wife. In these instances, the prohibition by the rule *saṃjñāpūraṇyośca* applies. [The example] *sraugghnabhāryā* follows.

In the compound *sraugghnī bhāryā*, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative). Here, the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by the rule *ṭhvṛddhinimitasya ca* is applicable. In *sukeśabhāryā*, it is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "one whose wife has beautiful hair" (*sukeśī bhāryā*). Here, the prohibition by the rule *ṭhsvāṅgācceta* is applicable.

Regarding the term *brāhmaṇabhāryā*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is both a Brāhmaṇī and a wife. Here, the prohibition [of the feminine suffix] by the rule *jāteśca* applies. Now, he provides examples for the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the suffixes *-jātīya* and *-deśīya*—thus, *pācakajātīyā*.

Regarding "pācakadeśīyā": the suffix *jātīyar* is applied by the rule *ṭhprakāravacane* ("in the sense of expressing a type"), and the suffix *deśīyar* is applied by the rule *ṭhīṣadasamāptau* ("in the sense of being slightly incomplete"). In both cases, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* ("not for a word ending in k as an upadhā") applies to the suffixes beginning with *tasil*. Thus, [the forms] such as *prāptajātīyā* and *dantajātīyā* [are derived].

*taddeśīyaḥ* (one belonging to that country); *pañcamajātīyaḥ*, *pañcamadeśīyaḥ* (one of the fifth caste, one belonging to the fifth country); *sraughnajātīyaḥ*, *sraughnadeśīyaḥ* (one of the Sraughna caste, one belonging to the Sraughna country); *sukeśajātīyaḥ*, *sukeśadeśīyaḥ* (one of the Sukeśa caste, one belonging to the Sukeśa country); *brāhmaṇajātīyaḥ*, *brāhmaṇadeśīyaḥ* (one of the Brāhmaṇa caste, one belonging to the Brāhmaṇa country). Thus, having examined the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*.
He provides examples for the rule *ṭhpoṭāyuvatī* in their respective order, beginning with *ibhapoṭā*.
It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "she who is both a *poṭā* and an *ibhī*. There is masculine substitution (*puṃvat*) for the word *ibhī*.
This rule is intended to ensure that the genus (*jāti*) is placed first [in the compound]. A *poṭā* is one who possesses the characteristics of both female and male.
This is a statement from the *Kośa*. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has the characteristics or marks (*lakṣaṇāni*) of both female and male.
Regarding the term *ibhayuvati*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she who is both a young woman (*yuvati*) and an elephant (*ibhī*).
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Regarding the example *agnistoka*: *stoka* means small; it is both that [small thing] and...

The analysis of the compound is *agniśca* (and fire). Regarding *udaśvitkatipayam*: according to Amarasimha, "curdled milk is *udaśvit*"; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "a small amount of that *udaśvit*. Regarding *gṛṣṭiḥ sakṛtprasūtā*:
this is a statement from a lexicon (*kośa*). Regarding *gogṛṣṭiḥ*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "a cow that is a *gṛṣṭi*," i.e., a cow that has calved once.

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. "A cow that has recently calved" (*dhenurnavaprasūtā*)—this is a statement from a lexicon (*kośa*). "A barren cow" (*govasā*)—the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "she is both a *vasā* (barren female) and a *go* (cow). "A cow that destroys its fetus" (*behadgarbhaghātinī*)—this is a statement from a lexicon. "A cow that miscarries" (*govehad*)—the analytical explanation is: "she is both a *vehat* (one that miscarries) and a *go* (cow)."
Regarding *baṣkayaṇī-taruṇa-vatsā*: according to Amara, "a cow that has recently calved is called *baṣkayaṇī*.
The reading *taruṇavatsā* is an error. Regarding *go-baṣkayaṇī*: the analysis of the compound is "she who is both a *baṣkayaṇī* and a cow.
Regarding *kaṭha-pravaktṛ*: a *pravaktṛ* is a teacher; the analysis of the compound is "he who is both a *Kaṭha* and a *pravaktṛ*."

Regarding "kaṭhādhyāpaka" (a teacher of the Kaṭhas): the analysis of the compound is "he is both a teacher and a Kaṭha. Regarding "kaṭhadhūrta" (a rogue Kaṭha): the analysis of the compound is "he is both a rogue and a Kaṭha. According to Amara, "dhūrta" means "one who gambles with dice";

others say it means "a libertine" (viṭa). Nor should one suspect that the formation is established by the rule "kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ" (words denoting contempt are compounded with words denoting the objects of that contempt), for [the following reason].
For that [suffix] occurs precisely when there is a censure of the cause of activity; indeed, being a *kaṭha* is not a censurable thing.
(736) *Praśaṃsāvacanaiś ca* | 2|1|66 | "And with words expressing praise. Regarding "with these": the meaning is, with those that by convention express praise.

Regarding the term *jāti*: the intention is that this follows from the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule beginning with *poṭāyuvatī*. "As before" means that it is compounded with words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and that [compound] is a *tatpuruṣa*.

This sūtra is for the purpose of establishing a fixed rule for the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of the genus-word (*jāti*). In the example *gomatallikā*, it is both *matallikā* and [the word *go*].

The analysis of the compound is *gauś ca* ("and a cow"). For *gomacarcikā*, the analysis is *macarcikā cāsau gauś ca* ("this is both a macarcikā and a cow"). For *goprakāṇḍam*, the analysis is *prakāṇḍam cāsau gauś ca* ("this is both a prakāṇḍa and a cow").
For *gavoddhaḥ*, the analysis is *uddhaś cāsau goś ca* ("this is both an uddha and a cow"). [In these cases], according to Sphoṭāyana, the suffix *ṭhavaṅ* is applied.
"By the rule *ṭhādguṇaḥ*, [the form] *gotallaja* is derived. The analysis of the compound is: 'that which is both excellent (*tallaja*) and a cow (*gauḥ*).
In all such cases, the gender of the final member prevails.
Because words such as *matallikā* are not well-known, he explains: 'the meaning is "an excellent cow. "
The feminine designation *praśastā* is used with the intention that the word *go* (cow) is feminine;
however, if the word *go* were masculine, the reading would be *praśastaḥ*. Now, one might object: if the word *go* is masculine, then for the words *matallikā*, *macarcikā*, and *prakāṇḍa* as well—

Because it would be subordinate to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), there would be the contingency of [the word] taking the masculine gender. Furthermore, if the word *go* were feminine, there would be the contingency of even words such as *prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, and *talla* becoming feminine;
therefore, he says: "such as *matallikā*," etc. [The verse continues: "*matallikā*, *macarcikā*, *prakāṇḍa*, *udgha*, *talla*."
"Amarasiṃha states that these [words] denote excellence. Regarding "kumārī-matallikā":
because the word *kumārī* denotes a specific age (*vayaḥ*) characterized by a particular stage of life, it does not denote a genus (*jāti*);
therefore, no compound is formed. For if a compound were formed, the rule "puṃvat-karmadhāraye" would require the word to take the masculine form.
The meaning is as follows: (737) *yuvā khalatipalitavalinajaratībhiḥ* |2|1|67|.

A word meaning "young" (*yuvan*) is compounded with words such as *khalati* ("bald") and so forth when they are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). [Thus: *yuvā khalati*. The word *yuvan* is compounded with *khalati* and the others when they share the same referent.

The meaning is that it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. To the question, "Since this is already established by means of an adjective compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), for what purpose is this [rule] stated?", he says:

"In the case of *pūrva*... Since the word *yuvan* and words such as *khalati* denote qualities (*guṇa*), they function as adjectives; consequently, because there is no fixed rule regarding their placement, an uncertainty arises as to which should be placed first.

The meaning is that this sūtra is intended to restrict that [application]. *Khalati* means one whose head is devoid of hair. Regarding *palita*, Amara states: "Palita is the whiteness caused by old age; *valina* and *valibha* are synonyms.

In the compound *yuvakhalati*, the elision of the *n* occurs because the word is a *pada* (an inflected word) by virtue of relying on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*). Now, as for the word *yuvā*...
Since the masculine gender is specified [in the rule], one might ask how the word *yuvati* (young woman) can enter into a compound;

to this he says: "qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*). Thus we have *yuvakhalatī* (a young bald woman). By the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* ("masculine form in a karmadhāraya compound"), the masculine form is applied. *Yuvajaratī* (a young old woman): *jaratī* means "old"; she is both a *yuvati* and a *jaratī*.

This is the analysis [of the compound]. The masculine form is applied by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*. Now, one might ask: "How can a young woman (*yuvati*) become an old woman (*jaratī*)? To this he says: "Only in the case of a young woman. [The rule:

*kṛtya-tulyākhyā ajātyā* || 2.1.68 || [A feminine word ending in a *kṛtya* suffix, or one denoting a comparison, when not expressing a genus, forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a word that does not denote a genus.]

The term *kṛtyatulyākhyā* means that words ending in *kṛtya* suffixes and words expressing similarity (*tulya*) are compounded with a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) that stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); such a compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. For example, *bhojyoṣṇam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is both edible (*bhojya*) and hot (*uṣṇa*)."

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṭhṛ-halorṇyat*. It is a *kṛtya* suffix used in the sense of fitness (*arhe*). Since the words *bhojya* (fit to be eaten) and *uṣṇa* (hot) are respectively action-words and quality-words, they may optionally be placed first when functioning as qualifiers; this [sūtra] is intended to provide a restriction. Regarding the example *tulyaśvetaḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which is both equal and white."

Although there is no fixed rule regarding which [of two] qualifiers should come first when both are adjectives expressing qualities, the word *tulya* alone is placed first. He states the purpose of including the term "name" (*ākhyā*)—namely, the example *sadṛśa-śveta* ("white-like")—with the underlying sense that the word *sadṛśa* is a synonym for *tulya*. [The example] *bhojya odanaḥ* ("edible rice") is given here.
The meaning is that because the word *odana* denotes a genus (*jāti*), this compound does not occur.

Now, one might object: even in the absence of this [specific] compound, a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) would still be unavoidable; to this he says: "because of the prohibition. Since the placement of the word *bhojya* at the beginning is indistinguishable in both cases...
The intention is that [the rule] "in the case of a common genus" (*ṭhājātyā*) would otherwise be rendered useless by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
(739) *Varṇo varṇena* |2|1|69|.
He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing words: "with a word in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇena*).

The meaning is that a word denoting a color is compounded with another word denoting a color that stands in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it; such a compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. For example, *kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ*. Here, *sāraṅga* means "possessing variegated colors. The word *kṛṣṇa* is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote something whose parts are black, thereby establishing the apposition. Thus, it is both "black" and [variegated].

The analysis [of the compound] is *sāraṅgaśca* (and it is variegated). Although this is established by a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), this [separate rule] is intended merely for the sake of elaboration.

As for the statement that "this is for the purpose of including only this [term], because it is explicitly mentioned in the rule for vowel accentuation: 'a color-word [is compounded] with another color-word, except in the case of *aneka*,'" [it follows that] by this [rule], *sāraṅgakṛṣṇaḥ* means "the black part of a variegated [animal]."
In this regard, the claim that the vowel [accent] does not apply by the rule "varṇo varṇeṣu" is to be considered;
for it is established simply by the reading of the rule "varṇo varṇeṣvanete" within the section on the accentuation of *karmadhāraya* compounds— this is the direction of the argument.

(740) *Kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye* | Pāṇini 2.2.38. The word *kaḍārāḥ* means "dark-brown" (*karma*). From the rule *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam*, the word *pūrvam* ("the former") is understood to carry over. Because the plural form *kaḍārāḥ* is used, it is understood as referring to the beginning of that group. Thus he says: *kaḍārādayaḥ*.
Thus. Since the rule "the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first" would apply invariably, this is an optional provision.
*Kaḍārajaiminiḥ*: the analysis of the compound is "he who is both Kaḍāra and Jaimini.
(741) *Kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.70): [The word *kumāra* is compounded with words such as *śramaṇa*, etc.]

The term *kumāra* [is compounded] with *śramaṇā* and so forth when they stand in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); the meaning is that this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In the example *kumāra-śramaṇā*, the masculine form is applied according to the rule *puṃvat-karmadhāraye*. A *śramaṇā* is one who has renounced all attachments.

[Objection: But since the word *kumāra* is read in the sūtra only in the masculine gender, how can there be an example here in the feminine? To this he says: "here" (*iha*). [Objection: But if only feminine forms are read in the list (*gaṇa*), how can the sūtra apply to them? And it is not...

One might argue that this should be stated by means of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding gender-distinctive forms), but since there is no evidence for its existence, he says: "Regarding gender," etc. "This very [point]" means "this also.
This is because the inclusion of the term *jaratī* in the rule *yuvā khalati* (Pāṇini 1.2.68) is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that [maxim]. For indeed...

The word *yuvan* has coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *jaratī*. (742) [Pāṇini 2.1.71: "A quadruped [denoted by a masculine noun] forms a compound with a feminine denoting a pregnant female. [Vārttika: "The mention of 'genus' (*jāti*) must be made [in this rule]."
Intending the Vārttika, he says: "jātirjāti" (a genus with a genus). "Gogarbhiṇī" (a pregnant cow):
the analysis of the compound is "she is both a pregnant woman and a cow. This sūtra is for the purpose of ensuring that the substantive (viśeṣya) is placed first.
Why [specify] "genus"? [Consider: "kālākṣīgarbhiṇī" (a pregnant Kālākṣī woman).

(743) *mayūravyaṃsakādayaśca* | 2|1|72 | [The compound] *mayūravyaṃsaka* and others [are formed]. These are stated as exceptions (*nipātana*). The meaning is that they are presented as having already undergone the grammatical operations required for compound formation. Regarding *mayūravyaṃsaka*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he who is both a deceiver (*vyaṃsaka*) and a peacock (*mayūra*)."
"Vyaṃsaka means a rogue. A lexicon (kośa) must be sought here [for this meaning].
Since the word *vyaṃsaka* is an adjective (*guṇavacana*), it would have been required to appear as the first member of the compound by rule; this statement [of the sūtra] serves to override that.
Regarding "uccāvacam": the word *udak* is replaced by *ucca*, and the word *avāk* is replaced by *avaca*.

"Uccāvacam means manifold," according to Amara. Regarding "niścapracam": it is a compound where the word *niścita* undergoes the substitution *niśca*, and the word *pracita* undergoes the substitution *praca*. Regarding "nāsti kiṃcana":
the indeclinable *cana* has the sense of "even" (*api*). It means "one for whom there is nothing whatsoever."

This is a three-member *tatpuruṣa* compound that serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *bahuvrīhi*. Furthermore, the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* in the negative particle *nañ* is prescribed by rule.

However, the rule "the *n* of *nañ* is elided" (*nalopo nañaḥ*) does not apply here, because the word *kim* lacks the status of being a final member (*uttarapada*) of the compound; for the term *uttarapada* is conventionally restricted (*rūḍha*) to refer only to the final constituent of a compound.
"From nowhere" (*nāsti kutaḥ*) means that there is no fear for him from any source whatsoever; this is the meaning of the analytical explanation (*vigraha*).

"Fearless from anywhere" (*akutobhaya*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound that serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *bahuvrīhi* rule. Regarding the term "another king" (*rājāntaram*), here the word *antara* is a synonym for "other" (*anya*); in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the word *anya* takes its place.

It should be understood as a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound), because it is appropriate for such compounds not to have a *vigraha* (analytic statement) using their own constituent words. That this is a *nityasamāsa* is to be known precisely from the explanation of the term *rājāntaram*. In this case, the word *antara* is placed at the end of the compound (*paranipāta*). Regarding the term *cinmātram*: according to Amarasimha, "the word *mātra* is used in the sense of totality (*kārtsnya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)."

The analysis using non-co-occurring words (*asvapadavigraha*) is intended to indicate that this is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). They say that the nasalization is permanent due to *nipātana* (irregular formation). Regarding the term "ākhyāta," this is a *gaṇasūtra*.

The meaning is that when continuity of action (*kriyāsātatya*) is implied, a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is compounded with another word ending in a verbal suffix; that is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Regarding *aśnīta-pibatā*: here, even though it lacks a case-ending (*asubanta*), it forms a compound.
Because the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—consisting of the action—is predominant, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied due to its feminine gender.
The same applies to examples such as *pacata-bhṛjjatā* and so forth. Regarding *ehī-jādayaḥ*: this is also a *gaṇasūtra*.
The meaning is that *ehi-īḍā* and other such forms are treated as *nipātas* (irregularly formed words) when they denote an external referent (*anyapadārtha*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is *ehi īḍe*.
In the form *īḍe*, this is the first person singular present indicative (*laṭ*). Due to the presence of the letter *ḍ*, the vowel *e* is replaced by the vowel *a*.
In the form *ehiyava*, there is a substitution of *yava* for *yaumī*. [And] for *utsṛje*...

The commentary says: "‘Dehi’ (give)"; "in this reading" means in the list beginning with *ehīḍa*. The *gaṇasūtra* ‘*jahikarmaṇā bahulam*’ is also [included]. "The agent is expressed" means that by the statement [of the rule], the agent is denoted.
In the example *jahijoḍa*, ‘*joḍa*’ is the name of a certain person; [the meaning is] "drive away Joḍa, drive him away."
*Jahijoḍaḥ* refers to one who repeatedly says "joḍa. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one who says 'jahi stambam, jahi stambam'. [Thus ends the section on Co-ordinative Compounds.
(744) *Īṣadakṛtā* | 2.2.7 | [A word beginning with *īṣat* forms a compound with a word ending in a kṛt suffix.]

"īṣadakṛtā" means that the word *īṣat* (slightly) is compounded with a *subanta* (inflected noun) whose stem (*prakṛti*) does not end in a *kṛt* suffix; such a compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. For example, *īṣatpiṅgalam* (slightly tawny).
The point is that the word *piṅgala* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is not derived through grammatical derivation (*avyutpanna*).

It should be stated as "by means of a word expressing a slight quality" (*īṣadguṇavacanena*), rather than "by means of a word expressing a slight quality" (*īṣadguṇavacana*). The phrase "excluding those ending in *ṭha*" (*ṭhakṛta*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule]. (745) *nañ* 2.2.6.

[The word] *nañ*. Intending that this [term] belongs to the section concerning co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), he says: "It is compounded with a case-inflected word" (*supā samasyate*). (746) *nalopo nañaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.3.73. [This rule states: "There is elision of the *n* of *nañ*."
There is no elision of the *nañ* [negation]. The word "na" (not) is a term with its genitive case ending elided. This is what he means by saying "of the *n* of *nañ*.

Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*), the intention is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "there is non-elision when there is a subsequent member" (*aluk uttarapade*).
Although the form would be established by the rule "the *n* of *nañ* before *aś*," the explicit mention of "elision" is for the sake of the form "akabrāhmaṇaḥ."

They say that [the negative particle] has the sense of "superimposition" (sākacamkāra). In the case of *abrāhmaṇa*, the meaning of the negative particle is superimposition (*āropitatva*). And this superimposition connects with the Brahmin by way of the property of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇatva*).
The resulting cognition is: "one who possesses superimposed Brahminhood. By implication, this results in the understanding that he is "distinct from a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇabhinnah*).

Some, however, say that the negative particle *nañ* expresses difference, meaning "different from a Brāhmaṇa. That is incorrect, because if the meaning were "different from a Brāhmaṇa," it would result in the predominance of the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*). And thus, it would contradict the statement in the Bhāṣya: "A *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the subsequent member as predominant."
Furthermore, in cases such as *ate*, *atasmai*, and *atasmāt*, the operations pertaining to pronouns—such as the substitution of *śī* and the addition of *smāy* and so forth—would not occur.
This is because, when the meaning of the word *tat* functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is subordinate (*apradhāna*).

This is according to the statement: "But those [words] that have become technical terms (*saṃjñā*) or secondary members (*upasarjana*) are not included among 'all' (the *sarvādi* group). The same applies in cases such as *asa*.

Otherwise, by the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ," the substitution of *sa* for *tad* and *doḥ*, which is a grammatical operation belonging to the *tyadādi* group, would not occur; furthermore, there would be the impossibility of the singular number in the word "anekam. This is because that which is distinct from "one" cannot possess oneness, and since duality and plurality are restricted [to those things], it would result in the application of the dual and plural numbers. Likewise...

Otherwise, the rule *sati ṭhanekamanyapadārthe* would not be applicable. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *anañ-samāsa* (non-negative compound) in the rule *etattadoḥ sulopaḥ* serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) for this point; for that [inclusion] is intended to prevent the elision of the *su*-case ending in examples such as *tasya śivaḥ* and *eṣaḥ śivaḥ*. However, in the sense of "different from him" (*tasmād bhinnaḥ*) or "different from this" (*etasmād bhinnaḥ*), [the form is established].

Since the meaning of the word *tat* and so forth would be subordinate (*upasarjana*), the substitution of *tyadādi* forms would not apply; consequently, the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*halṅyādilopa*) would be unavoidable, making the [proposed] rule clearly redundant. Therefore, following the primacy of the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*) as stated in the Bhāṣya, it is logical that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is simply "superimposition" (*āropitatva*).
