"The girl has no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*), "others are not cattle" (*apaśavo vā anye goaśvebhyaḥ*), and "it is unrighteousness" (*adharmaḥ*)—these they have cited as examples. In these cases, they say that similarity and so forth are to be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors. (747) *tasmān nuḍ aci* 6.3.74.

Therefore, *nuṭ* [is inserted] before a vowel (*aci*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the negative particle (*nañ*)—in which the nasal *n* has been elided—is referred to as understood from the preceding rule. The term "in the subsequent member" (*uttarapade*), which is carried over by implication, is qualified by the word "before a vowel" (*aci*).
This is a rule concerning the initial element of that [vowel]. When there is a mention of both [the fifth and seventh case endings], the mention of the fifth case is more powerful.
By the *paribhāṣā* "the seventh [case-ending] implies the sixth," the seventh case is understood as a sixth.

Thus he says: "from that in which the *n* has been elided. Regarding *anaśva*: when the compound is formed, the *n* of the negative particle (*nañ*) is elided, and the augment *nuṭ* is applied to the remaining *a*. The letter *ṭ* is for the sake of marking the accent; the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation.
The intention is that [the suffix] *ṭi* constitutes the first member [of the compound]. Why was *nuṭ* not applied? Because it would result in the undesirable application of *ṅmuṭ*.

Now, one might object: in cases such as "let there be no obstacle (*avighnam*) to the subsequent task," when a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa is formed in the sense of the absence of obstacles, the form would indeed be *avighnaḥ* because the gender of the latter member prevails. And this is not [unacceptable].

It should be stated that even in the absence of an object, the formation [of the compound] is achieved by means of an *avyayībhāva*; however, since the *avyayībhāva* finds its scope in cases such as *niramakṣikam*, the *tatpuruṣa* would apply instead due to its higher priority. To this, he says: "In the absence of an object. [This refers to] the word *rakṣā* in the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Bhāṣya*.

This is the statement: *rakṣā*, *ūha*, *āgama*, *laghu*, and *asaṃdeha* form a *dvandva* compound. According to the rule *ṭhparavalliṅgam*, the neuter gender is applied. Here, since the word *asaṃdeha* is used in the sense of "absence of doubt" (*saṃdehābhāva*), it is understood as a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Thus, the form *asaṃdehāḥ* is employed.
In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, there should be [the mention of] "protection, destruction, addition, brevity, and absence of doubt.

Regarding the phrase "not in rapid speech" (*adrutāyām asaṃhitam*), this is a *vārttika* recited under the sūtra "the closest proximity is *saṃhitā*" (*paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ saṃhitā*). The meaning is that in a non-rapid mode of pronunciation, there is an absence of *saṃhitā*. In this context, within the *avyayībhāva*:

From the usage *asati asaṃhitam*, it is understood that even in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the absence of meaning is conveyed by the negative particle *nañ*; otherwise, if it were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it would be *asaṃhitā* due to the rule of taking the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatvāt*). Consequently, when the absence is conveyed by *nañ*:

It is established that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *tatpuruṣa* and *avyayībhāva* compounds. By this [rule], the meaning is that in the case of "non-perception" (*anupalabdhiḥ*) and "absence of dispute" (*avivādaḥ*), the *tatpuruṣa* compound is established, while in the case of "unimpeded" (*avighnam*), the *avyayībhāva* compound is established. However, in the *Śabdenduśekhara*, this has been explained differently.

"Elision of the *n* of *nañ* occurs before a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the sense of censure. This is a Vārttika belonging to the rule "elision of the *n* of *nañ*" (*na lopo nañaḥ*). It means that the *n* of *nañ* is elided when followed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the sense of censure.

The meaning is that it should be stated [in the rule] as "in the sense of censure" (*nindāyām*). For example: *apacasi tvaṃ jālma* ("You cook poorly, you fool!"). The meaning here is "you cook in a contemptible manner. In this case, *a* is a separate word because there is no compound with the finite verb (*tiṅanta*).
This Vārttika has been introduced here incidentally. [It applies] to that which has the same meaning as *nañ*.

Thus, since this [form] is established even by the indeclinable [particle *eva*], the Vārttika is indeed redundant. Some, however, say that on account of this very Vārttika, the inclusion of the rule "ṭha" among the indeclinables is unauthentic. Now, one might object:
even in the case of *naikadhā*, when the *na*-negation compound is formed and the *n* is elided by the rule "the *n* of *nañ* is elided," [how is the form established?]

Therefore, since the augment *nuṭ* would apply by the rule "ṭh-tasmānnuḍaci," resulting in the form *anekadhe* alone, he says: "But in cases such as *naikadhe*. The intention is that for this very purpose, the marker *ñ* is included in the rule "na-ñ" and in the rule "na-lopo nañaḥ."

(748) *nabhrāṇnapānnavedā nāsatyā namucinakulanakhanapuṃsakanakṣatranakranākeṣu prakṛtyā* || Pāṇini 6.3.75. *nabhrāṇnapāt*: This is easy to understand. Regarding the word "anuvartamāna" (continuing): it refers to the rules governing compound formation (*samāsavidhayaḥ*).
The word "will be stated" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

(749) *kugatiprādayaḥ* | 2|2|18|. [The sūtra] *kugatiprādayaḥ* means that words beginning with *ku*, *gati*-words, and *prādi* compounds are compounded; it should also be understood that this forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound. An example is *kutsitaḥ*.

Regarding the term *puruṣa*: because it is a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound), it does not have a separate analysis (*vigraha*) using its own constituent words. Here, only the indeclinable *ṭhku*, which conveys the sense of "contemptible," is to be understood; it is not the synonym for the earth (*pṛthvī*), due to its association with other *gatis* (preverbs) such as *gatvā*.
It should be understood that the phrase "and the *gati*" is being carried over [from a previous rule], as is the phrase "when there is connection with an action."
(750) *ūryādicviṅacca* |1|4|61|. The suffixes *cvi* and *ḍāc* follow words beginning with *ūrī*. *Cvi* and *ḍāc* are two suffixes. For example: *ūrīkṛtya*.
Here, *ūrī* is an indeclinable meaning "acceptance" (*aṅgīkāra*); it forms a *gati*-compound with the word *kṛtvā* [via the suffix *ḍāc*].

In a compound that does not have *nañ* as its first member, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. For example: *śuklīkṛtya*. The meaning is "having made what was not white into white. The suffix *cvi* occurs here because of the rule "in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*," signifying the transformation of something into that which it was not previously. When the compound is a *gati*-compound, *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*; then, by the rule "of *v* and *e* when unaccompanied [by another consonant]," there is the elision of *v*. [The remainder of the rule is: "of this..."

In *cvau*, there is the substitution of *ī*. Regarding *paṭapaṭākṛtya*: the meaning is "having made the sound 'paṭapaṭā'. According to the rule *avyaktānukaraṇāddvyajavarārdhādanitau ḍāc*, after the word *paṭat*, when *ḍāc* is added, there is reduplication and the elision of the final *ṭi*. This is by the rule *nityamāmreḍite ḍāci*.
There is a single substitution of *pa* for both *ta* and *pa*. In a *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*.
There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the word *kārikā*.
Regarding the statement "there is an addition regarding the word *kārikā*," the remainder [of the rule] is "in the case of the designation *gati*."

He explains the word *kārikā*: "The word *kārikā* [is derived from] *kriyā*. Under the governing rule *striyāṃ ktin*, when there is a designation of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied. Thus, *kārikākṛtya* means "having performed the action" (*kriyāṃ kṛtvā*).

In the case of a compound with a *gati* where the second member ends in the accusative, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*, and there is elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). The word *kārikā* occurs here [in this sense].
It does not denote an agent, nor does it denote a verse, according to the commentary. (751) *Anukaraṇam cānitiparam* 1.4.62.
"And an imitation [is also so]. The meaning is that an imitation is designated as a *gati*, with the exception of when it is followed by the word *iti*.

Regarding the term *khāṭkṛtya*: it means "having made the sound *khāṭ*. In this *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Thus, it is "having made [the sound] *khāṭ*. Nor is it the case that the designation *gati* will fail to apply here simply because of the absence of connection with the verb due to being separated by the word *iti*; [for the rule applies despite such separation].
One might ask: "What is the purpose of including the term *aniti* (not denoting motion)? [The answer is: because there is a connection with action (*kriyā*) in some way or another.

The intention is that the rule *ṭhte prāgdhātoḥ* merely prescribes a restriction regarding usage, meaning: "These particles of motion (*gati*) and prefixes (*upasarga*) must be employed only before the verbal root (*dhātu*), and not after it."

(752) *ādarānādarayoḥ sadasatī* |1|4|63|. The meaning is that when the indeclinables *sat* and *asat* are present respectively in the senses of respect (*ādara*) and disrespect (*anādara*), they are designated as *gati*. For example, in *satkṛtya*, [the sense is] "having shown respect."

The meaning is "having done. Regarding "asatyakṛtya," the meaning is "having treated with disregard. In the *gatisamāsa*, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*. Regarding "khāḍiti kṛtvā": one might argue that because it is separated here by the word *iti*, there will be no designation as a *gati* precisely because of the absence of connection with the action (*kriyāyoga*).

In that case, one might ask why the mention of "another" (para) is necessary; [the answer is] because there exists a connection with action in some way or another. The intention is that the rule *te prāg dhātoḥ* is merely intended to regulate usage, meaning that particles (*nipāta*) and prefixes (*upasarga*) must be employed before the verbal root (*dhātu*) and not after it.

(753) *sadasatī ādarānādarayoḥ* | 1|4|63| The meaning is that the two indeclinables *sat* and *asat*, when used respectively in the senses of respect (*ādara*) and disrespect (*anādara*), are designated as *gati*s. For example: *satkṛtya* (having honored), which signifies respect.
The meaning is "having done. Regarding *asatkṛtya*: the meaning is "having shown disrespect. In a *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*.
(754) *alam* [is used] in the sense of ornamentation. Pāṇini 1.4.64.

Regarding "bhūṣaṇe'lam": the meaning is that the indeclinable *alam* when it signifies "ornamentation" (bhūṣaṇa) is designated as a *gati*. "Alaṃkṛtya" means having performed an embellishment by wearing bracelets and other such ornaments.
Thus, the indeclinable *alam*, when signifying ornamentation, is designated as a *gati*.
The meaning is "it might be so. Regarding the term *alaṃkṛtya*: the meaning is "having performed an adornment by wearing bracelets and other ornaments.

Regarding the phrase *kṛñ-viṣaye*: the meaning is that it occurs only in connection with the root *kṛ*. However, in reality, since there is no evidence for such a restriction, [the suffix] occurs even in connection with other verbal roots.
The application of the three sūtras is thus justified. For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti has provided the counter-example: "Having eaten the *ṭhala* vegetable, he went for the rice.
(755) antaraparigrahe | 1|4|65| [The locative case ending is used after a word denoting a direction when it signifies being enclosed within.]

*Antara-pari*: The meaning is that the indeclinable *antara*, when occurring in the sense of "without grasping" (*aparigraha*), shall be designated as a *gati*. "Having killed, he goes" (*hatam parigṛhyaiti*): killing and going constitutes "having killed," whether it occurs without grasping or with grasping. In this context, the first case is the example (*udāharaṇa*), and the second is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
"Non-possessiveness" (*aparigraha*) is merely a condition of application (*prayogopādhi*), and not something included within the range of the denotable meaning (*vācyakoṭi*).

(756) *Kaṇemanasī śraddhāpratīghāte* |1|4|66|. [The sūtra states: "In the case of *kaṇe* and *manas*, when there is an obstruction of faith. [The commentary explains: *kaṇe-manasī*. The word *kaṇe* and the word *manas* are designated as *gati*s when they denote the obstruction of faith.
Excessive longing is *uśraddhā*; its cessation is *pratīghāta*. Regarding the expression *kaṇehatya*:

in the compound with a verbal root (*gati-samāsa*), the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Regarding *manohatya*: the phrase "he drinks milk" (*payaḥ pibati*) is to be supplied. Now, one might ask: once the compound is formed, why does the locative case-ending of *kaṇe* not undergo elision (*luk*)?

He says: "the word *kaṇe*. Now, one might ask: how is the obstruction of faith understood here, given the absence of any word denoting faith? Or, if there is an injury to the mind, how can there be the drinking of milk? To this he says: "upon an excess of desire. The phrase "the word *kaṇe*" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].

The suffix *ktvā* is applied by the rule "ṭhparāvarayoge ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.20). The meaning is: "He drinks milk until his desire is satisfied. What is the purpose of the condition "when there is an obstruction to faith" (*śraddhāpratīghāte*)? [Consider: "He went away after striking at the grain" (*kaṇe hatvā gataḥ*).
A "grain" (*kaṇa*) is a minute particle of rice; the meaning is that he went away after striking at that [particle]. [Similarly: "Having struck at the mind" (*mano hatvā*).
"He has gone. This means he has gone after restraining the inclination of the mind toward drinking poison and so forth.
(757) *puro 'vyayam* | 1.4.67 | "The indeclinable *puraḥ*": the indeclinable *puraḥ* shall be designated as a *gati*. [Example: *puraskṛtya*.

In a compound denoting motion (*gatisamāsa*), the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Why [is it] "indeclinable" (*avyaya*)? [Consider: *puram*, *purau*, *puraḥ*—having placed [the city] before, he went. (758) *astaṃ ca* | 1.4.68 | [The word *astaṃ* is also included in this rule.]

And *astaṃ*. He says that the term "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) is understood from the preceding sūtra—hence [the rule states] "the indeclinable *mām*. Regarding *astaṅgatya*: the meaning is "having attained disappearance. Why [is it] indeclinable? [In the example] *kāṇḍamastaṃ kṛtvā*, the meaning is "having thrown away. *Acccha* has the sense of motion. Among roots meaning motion...
When the verbal root *vad* is employed, the indeclinable *acchā* shall be designated as a *gati*. (759) *Acccha* [is used] before roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) and the like.
1.4.69. Regarding *acchā-etya*: in a *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*. Regarding *acchā-odya*: from the root *vad*, the suffix *ktvā*.
In the context of *gati* compounds, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. The indeclinable *accham* signifies "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*).

For example: *barhiraccha yāti* ("he goes toward the sacrificial grass"). Thus it is said: "facing toward. In the phrase *jalamacchaṃ gacchati* ("he goes toward the water"), the word *accham* is not an indeclinable, nor does it have the designation of a *gati*, nor is it included among the particles (*nipāta*) prior to the rule *prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ*.

Thus ends the section on the technical designation of *nipāta* (particles). For when something is a *nipāta*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and consequently, there is elision of case-endings (*vibhakti-luk*);
this is the intended meaning. (Pāṇini 1.4.70) *ado’nupadeśe*.

*ada-anupadeśe*: The word *adas* shall be designated as a *gati* when it does not signify instruction (*anupadeśa*). For example: *adaḥ kṛtam*. In a *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. However, in the sense of "having done this sacrifice" (*amuṃ yajñaṃ kṛtvā*), there is also the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*). Thus we have *adaḥ kṛtam*. The result [of using the *gati* designation] is the accentuation according to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*.

When one reflects upon this oneself, then this is the illustration; [it refers to] "with regard to another," meaning in cases such as "having done this, do that. (761) *tiro* in the sense of disappearance (*antarddhi*). 1.4.71.

*Tiras* means "in concealment. *Antardhi* means "obstruction"; the meaning is that in this context, the indeclinable *tiras* shall be designated as a *gati*. In the example *tirobhūya*, the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā* in a *gati*-compound.
The meaning is "having become obstructed."

(762) *vibhāṣā kṛñi* | 1.4.72 | "Optionally before the root *kṛ*" means that when the root *kṛ* is employed, the indeclinable *tiras* may optionally be designated as a *gati*. Thus, one says either *tiraskṛtya* or *tiraḥ kṛtya*. In the case where it is designated as a *gati*:

In the compound *gatisamāsa*, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Regarding the form *tiraḥkṛtya*, there is an option for the substitution of *s* (satva) by the rule *tiraso 'nyatarasyām*. They say that in the alternative where it lacks the status of a *gati*, the substitution of *s* also does not occur, because the term *gati* is understood as a governing factor (*anuvṛtti*) in that specific rule. Some, however, hold that *tiraskāra* means "contempt" (*paribhava*).
Because it is observed in usage, when there is a prescription for a *sat* (present participle), they do not carry over the inclusion of the term "gati" (prepositional prefix).

(763) *upāje’nvāje* | 1.4.73 | *upāje’nvāje*. [The examples are] *upājekṛtya* and so forth. In the view that these have the designation *gati*, they form a *gati-samāsa* (compound with a preposition) after the suffix *ktvā*.
The *lyap* [substitute] applies. Similarly, in the case of *anvājekṛtya*, the two indeclinables *upāje* and *anvāje* signify "providing strength to the weak. Thus he says: "of the weak.
(764) *sākṣāt-prabhṛtīni ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.74).
"And *sākṣāt* and so forth. He explains the sūtra by supplying the remainder: "or after the root *kṛ*.
*Sākṣāt* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). It should be stated that it has the sense of the suffix *cvy*.
Regarding "the meaning of *cv-*": the intended meaning is that it should be stated, "when the transformation of something into what it was not is to be understood.

Regarding "having made manifest" (*sākṣātkṛtya*): the meaning is "having made that which was imperceptible perceptible. Since *ktvā* becomes *lyap* when [the preceding element] is a verbal root (*gati*), one might suspect the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) there; therefore, he says: "the state of ending in *-m*" (*māntatvam*). [Examples: *lavaṇam*, *uṣṇam*.
The meaning is that the status of ending in *m* is prescribed by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) for the five words beginning with *sākṣāt*—namely, *śītam*, *udakam*, and *āmi*.
(765) Pāṇini 1.4.75: *urasimanasī anatyādhāne*. In the sense of "not placing upon" (*anatyādhāna*), the locative case endings are elided after the words *uras* and *manas*.

Regarding *anatyādhāne*: the indeclinables *uras-i* and *manas-i*, which resemble case endings, are optionally designated as *gati*s when not meaning "placing upon" (*atyādhāna*). In the example *urasikṛtya*, if they are treated as *gati*s, the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā*. He explains that here "placing upon" is not understood, stating: "the meaning is 'having accepted'."

Regarding the term *manasikṛtya*: in the view that it functions as a verbal root (*dhātu*), the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. He states that even here, no "placing upon" (*atyādhāna*) is understood, meaning "having ascertained. Explaining the word *atyādhāna*, he states its purpose: "contact" (*upaśleṣaṇa*); the meaning is "conjunction. Regarding the phrase *urasi kṛtvā*:

The meaning is that he lies with his hand placed upon his chest. The point here is that because the contact of the hand is understood, the designation "gati" (preverb) does not apply. Regarding *madhyepade*: whether it has the status of a *gati* or lacks it, the final vowel *e* for these three words is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregular formation).

(766) *madhye pade nivacane ca* |1|4|76|. In the examples *madhyekṛtya* and *padekṛtya*, the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā* due to the formation of a *gati*-compound. The meaning is "having made [it] middle" (*madhyaṃ kṛtvā*) and "having made [it] a footstep" (*padaṃ kṛtvā*).

Regarding the phrase "having performed *nivacana*": the meaning is "having brought about the absence of speech. He states this by saying, "the meaning is 'having restrained speech. *Nivacana* is the non-existence (*abhāva*) of speech. The point is that an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed with an indeclinable when it denotes the absence of something.

(767) *nityaṃ haste pāṇāv upayamane* |1|4|77|. Regarding *nityaṃ haste*: he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing words—namely, *kṛñi*. The words *haste* and *pāṇau* are always designated as *gati* when used with the root *kṛ* in the sense of "marrying" (*upayamana*).

Up to: *hastekṛtya* and *pāṇaukṛtya*. This means having taken the hand in order to accept a maiden [in marriage]. The forms ending in *-e* and *-o* are irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) for these two. What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the context of marriage" (*upayamane*)? [Example: *haste kṛtvā suvarṇaṃ gataḥ* ("Having taken gold in his hand, he departed"). [This refers to taking it] with the thought that it belongs to another, in order to give it away.
The meaning is "turned away" (*parāvṛta*). (768) *prādhvam* [is used] in the sense of "binding. 1.4.78.
*prādhvam* [is used] in the sense of binding. *Prādhvam* does not [mean] "not."
He says that it ends in the accusative:

"The indeclinable *prādhvam*. The meaning is that when "binding" (*bandhana*) is understood, the indeclinable *prādhvam* is designated as a *gati*. In the form *prādhvaṃkṛtya*, there is the suffix *lyap* after the suffix *ktvā* in a *gati*-compound. Here, the indeclinable *prādhvam* ending in *m* [expresses] binding.

It occurs in the sense of conformity. He says this with the words "by means of bondage. He states the purpose of employing the term "bondage" with the words "by means of begging and so forth. (769) *Jīvikā* and *upaniṣad* [are used] in the sense of comparison. 1.4.79.

*Jīvikopani*: *Upama* itself is *aupamya*; in that sense, the words *jīvikā* and *upaniṣad*, when used in conjunction with the verb *kṛ*, receive the designation of *gati*. [The example is] *jīvikām iva*.
*Jīvikā* refers to the means of livelihood, such as food, drink, and so forth. The meaning is: "having necessarily made it like that."

Regarding "having made it a means of livelihood" (*jīvikākṛtya*): in this *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Regarding "having treated it like the *upaniṣad*" (*upaniṣadamiva kṛtvā*): the *upaniṣad* is the portion of the Vedas known as the Vedānta; the meaning is "having necessarily treated it as such. Regarding "having made it a means of livelihood" (*jīvikā kṛtya*): in this *gati*-compound, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. [The phrase] "having treated it like the *upaniṣad*" (*upaniṣadamiva kṛtvā*) [is explained as above].
The *upaniṣad* is the portion of the Vedas concerning the end (*anta*). The meaning is: "having treated it as something to be grasped in secret, as it were.
Regarding the form *upaniṣatkṛtya*: in the compound *gati-samāsa*, the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*. In both cases, there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sub*).
Thus, the compounds belonging to the category of *gati* in the rule *“kugatiprādayaḥ”* have been explained in detail. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues with the objection: "But..."
Since the formation would be established by the mention of *gati* alone, the inclusion of *pra* and other prefixes (*prādi*) is redundant; therefore, he says:

"The inclusion of *prādi* is for the sake of those that are not *gatis*. For example, in *supuruṣa*, although it is not a *gati* because there is no connection with a verb (*kriyāyoga*), a compound still occurs. This is even though *su-* has the sense of honor (*pūjā*).

Because there is an absence of connection with an action denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*), it does not possess the status of a *gati*. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, having removed the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* and stated in its place that "it should be said: *kvāṅsvatidurgatayaḥ samasyante* [the particles *kva*, *āṅ*, *su*, *ati*, and *dus* are compounded]," the examples *kubrāhmaṇaḥ*, *ākaḍāraḥ*, *subrāhmaṇaḥ*, and *atibrāhmaṇaḥ* are given.

The examples "durbrāhmaṇaḥ" (a bad Brahmin) and "ūrīkṛtya" (having accepted) have been cited. The statement from the Saunāga grammar—"*su* in the sense of praise, *dur* in the sense of censure, *āṅ* in the sense of 'somewhat,' and *ku* in the sense of evil"—is clear even in the Bhāṣya. Regarding this, there are the Vārttikas.

The meaning is as follows: having cited the *vārttika*—"it should be stated that *pra* and other [prepositions] form compounds when they signify 'gone' (*gata*) and so forth"—the five *vārttikas* established in the *Saunāga-vyākaraṇa*, which were recited in the *Bhāṣya* as the determinants therein, are now presented. Regarding the term "prādayaḥ" (pra and others): [they apply] when signifying "gone" and so forth.

The meaning is that the existing particles beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ) undergo composition (*samasyante*). In the example "the teacher has gone forth" (*pragata ācāryaḥ*), the word *gataḥ* is an analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of *pra*; however, "the teacher has gone" (*gata ācāryaḥ*) itself is not a *svapadavigraha* (analysis using its own constituent words), because it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). "Facing toward the face" (*abhimukhaḥ*) is one who has approached the face (*abhigato mukham*); "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) is one who has reached the sense-organ (*pratigato'kṣam*).
And so forth.
"Words such as *ati* [form a compound] with a word in the second case when they have the sense of 'having transcended' (*krānta*), etc.
Regarding the phrase "words such as *ati*": the meaning is that words beginning with *ati* are compounded when they convey the sense of having transcended, and so on. *Ati-krāntaḥ*...

Regarding the term *mālām*: the prefix *ati-* functions in the sense of "surpassing" (*krānta*). Thus, *krānto mālām* is an analysis where the constituent words do not appear as separate members of the compound (*asvapadavigraha*). In this context, the root *kram-* has the meaning of "transgressing" or "surpassing.
In the form *atimāla*, because the word *mālā* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) according to the rule *ekavibhakti ca*, it is subject to the rule *gostriyoḥ*.

Thus [the word] *hrasva* [is formed]. The words beginning with *ava* are compounded with a word in the third case when they have the sense of "repeatedly" (*kruṣṭa*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "words beginning with *ava*": the meaning is that words beginning with *ava* are compounded when they have the sense of "repeatedly" and so forth. For example: *avakokila*.
The meaning is "summoned by the cuckoo.
Regarding the rule "paryādayo glānādyarthe caturthyā" (Pāṇini 2.2.18):

the phrase "paryādayaḥ" means that words beginning with *pari* are compounded when they signify meanings such as *glāna* (weariness) and so forth, provided they are followed by a word in the dative case.
"Adhyayanāt" means for the sake of study; thus, the meaning is "exhausted by that. Here, the prefix *pari-* is used in the sense of "afflicted.
[This is according to the rule: "Words beginning with *nir-* [are compounded] with words ending in the fifth case when they have the sense of 'gone beyond' (*krānta*), etc."
Regarding the term *nirādayaḥ*: the meaning is that words beginning with *nir* form compounds when they convey senses such as "gone beyond" (*krānta*) and so forth.
In the example *niṣkoṣāmbiḥ*, the vowel is shortened according to the rule similar to that for *atimālava*. The indeclinable *nir* occurs here in the sense of "going out" (*nirgamana*).

(1) There is a prohibition regarding *karmapravacanīya*s. "There is a prohibition regarding *karmapravacanīya*s" is a *vārttika*. For example, in *vṛkṣaṃ prati*, because *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* by virtue of the rule *lakṣaṇetthambhūta...*, there is no *prādi*-compound. This is the *vārttika*.
This has been rejected in the Bhāṣya.

(770) *tatrōpapadaṃ saptamīstham* 3.1.92. Now, intending to explain the upapada compound (*upapadasamāsa*), [the author] states the technical designation of the upapada: "In that context, the upapada is that which stands in the locative case."
This [rule] is more extensive. By the term "saptamī," there is a reference to that which ends in the locative case.

That which stands in a word ending in the locative by way of the relationship of denoted and denoter is called *saptamīstha*. This means, in effect, that which is denoted by a word ending in the locative.
This is a subsequent sūtra following the governing rule (*adhikāra-sūtra*) "dhātoḥ.

Consequently, that which is uttered in the locative case within those sūtras included under that governing rule—such as *karmaṇy-aṇ* and others—is precisely what is intended here. And thus, in its illustration:

In the expression "the potter makes a jar" (*kumbhaṃ karoti kumbhakāraḥ*), that which is expressed by the word ending in the locative case—namely, "the jar" and so forth—is what remains as the final meaning. Since there is no purpose for the designation *upapada* (secondary word) to apply to the jar itself, the designation rests upon the words that denote it. And thus:
The resulting meaning is that one should understand it as being governed by the rule *karmaṇi* and so forth, which falls under the heading *dhātoḥ*;

that is, a word denoting something like "a jar" (*kumbha*), which is expressed by the locative form *karmaṇi* and so on, shall be designated as an *upapada*. Thus he says: "the word ending in the seventh case."

By such statements as these, there are three governing rules (*dhātvadhikāra*) concerning roots (*dhātu*), namely: "from a root denoting an action having the same agent" (*dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkāt*), "from a root consisting of a single vowel and beginning with a consonant" (*dhātor ekāco halādeḥ*), and simply "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*).
Among these, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), [the suffix] belongs specifically to that which ends in the locative case situated within the third governing rule concerning roots.

Because of the inclusion [of the word *dhātu*] in the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from a root having a single vowel" (*dhātor ekācaḥ*), the locative form in "clī luṅi" (*cli luṅi*) is not taken [as a condition].

Otherwise, as in the case of [the rule for] the object (*karmani*) and so forth, the meaning would be that the suffix *cli* is applied to the root when there is a locative ending such as "luṅ," as in the example *abhūt*. [Objection: But then the word *tatra* (in that case) is redundant.

Anticipating the objection that [the term *tasmin*] could be understood simply because the subject matter of the third chapter (*dhātu*) is currently under discussion, he says: "And only when that exists. The intention is this:
the word *tatra* constitutes a separate sentence and should be construed by transposing its position; it is that which stands in the locative case and is designated as an *upapada*.

It should be understood that "there" (*tatra*) and "this being present" (*asmin sati*) are supplied as governing conditions. Thus, when there is an *upapada* (an accompanying word), the suffix to be mentioned [later] occurs; this is the resulting meaning of "there. Consequently, this rule presents itself in the context of *karmaṇy aṇ* ("the suffix *aṇ* after an object [of the action]"). Regarding "in the object" (*karmaṇi*):

The word ending in the seventh case (*saptamyanta*) is transformed into one ending in the first case (*prathamānta*). The mention of the seventh case, however, is for the purpose of applying the technical designation *upapada* (governing word). [The rule] "the suffix *aṇ* shall occur after a verbal root in the sense of the agent;
but a word such as *kumbha*, expressing the object, is to be understood as having the designation *upapada*; when that *upapada* is present..."
The phrase "only when that [condition] exists" (tasmin saty eva) serves as a restriction;
for if it were absent, the suffix *aṇ* would apply even after a simple verbal root in the sense of the agent—as in *kāra*.
However, the mention of the locative case in "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) serves to designate [words like *kumbha*] as *upapada*s in examples such as *kumbhakāra*.

The rule *prātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1), by means of forming a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) with the word *ati* as an upapada according to *atiṅ*, has its purpose fulfilled by ensuring the grammatical correctness of forms such as *kumbha-ati* and *kāra-ati*. However, if it were stated that "only when that [word] is present as an upapada shall *aṇ* occur," then, upon the production of the suffix *am* from *kumbha-* and other such upapadas...

The suffix *aṇ* does not arise from the mere [presence of the word] because of the understanding that it is a cause (*nimitta*), since the designation of "co-occurring word" (*upapada-saṃjñā*) is understood to be taught as being in conjunction with the prescription of the suffix. In rules such as "the suffix *ṣṭran* after the root *dhā* in the sense of the object" and "after the root *bhū* in the sense of the abstract state" (*bhāve*), the locative-ending term is intended solely to indicate the meaning; this is established through the traditional commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
This is clear in the Bhāṣya, Kaiyaṭa, and other works. (771) *upapadam atiṅ* | P. 2.2.19.
"The *upapada* [is compounded] when not a finite verb (*atiṅ*). [It is] a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because that [term] is understood from the previous rule, *sub āmantrite*.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "by means of *samartha*," the sense is that the mention of *samartha*, which ends in the nominative case, is transformed into the instrumental case. Regarding the statement "and a compound (*samāsa*) is not [ending] in a *tiṅ*," the meaning is that in the rule, the term *tiṅ* is understood to include that which ends in *tiṅ*; thus, the meaning is that a compound does not consist of a word ending in a *tiṅ*.
Why is *atiṅ* [stated]? [Consider: *kārako vrajati*.

By the rule "the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used when a verb is employed for the sake of another action," the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the root *kṛ* with *vrajati* as the attendant word (*upapada*), and *ak* is substituted [for the *ṇvul*].
If it were stated merely that "an attendant word [is compounded] with a semantically related word" (*upapadaṃ samarthena*), then here too there would be a compound with the attendant word.

Therefore, the mention of *atiṅ* is necessary. Nor should it be argued that there is no purpose for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of *sup* [in this rule], because it serves the purpose of effecting the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) in the word *carmakāra*. However, if one were to explain [the rule] as "a non-*tiṅ* item (*atiṅ*) which is an *upapada* is compounded with a [verb] in its stem form (*samāna-tantra*)," then *sup* would not be carried over [from the previous rule]. And consequently—

The intention is that in the word *carmakāra*, there would be no elision (*lopa*) of the *n*. Regarding *kumbhikṛt*: the meaning is "one who makes a jar" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*). By the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* [Pāṇini 3.2.1], when the word denoting the object—the jar—is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of the agent. Then, by the rule *aco ñṇiti* [Pāṇini 7.2.115], *vṛddhi* occurs, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the vowel (by *rapara*).
The word "kāra" [is used]. Thus, the meaning is that when the word "kumbha" is compounded with it, the form "kumbhakāra" arises. Now, one might object:

how can "kumbhaṃ karoti" (he makes a pot) be shown as the analytical statement (*vigraha*), since it has been stated that "a compound consists of a nominal stem (*subanta*) and a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)"? To this, he says: "kumbha as kāra" is the non-worldly (*alaukika*) procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*).

The term *alaukikatva* (extraordinariness) refers to the state of being unfit for usage in the world (*loke prayogānarhatvam*). According to the perspective of the Bhāṣya on the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, the application of a compound occurs only in an extraordinary analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigrahavākya*). The meaning is that [sentences such as] *kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a jar") are merely for the purpose of demonstrating the meaning of that [compound]. [Thus, the analysis is] *kumbha am-kāra*.

This is a faulty reading (*apapāṭha*), because the genitive case is prescribed when used in conjunction with a *kṛt* suffix. [The example] "mā bhavān bhūt" (may you not be). Here, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* (not being a verbal form) is for the purpose of precluding compounding with *māṅ* when followed by a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), such as "bhūt.
The word "bhavān," however, is placed in the middle to indicate the absence of compounding. Now, one might object:

Since the status of being "prescribed in the seventh case" (saptamī-nirdiṣṭatva) is not observed for *māṅ* under the heading of the third verbal root (*dhātu*), a compound would undesirably result for one [who holds that view] because of its being an *upapada*. Therefore, he says: "*māṅ*" [in the rule]. Now, an objection: the mention of *atiṅ* (non-verbal suffix) is redundant; for in the example *mā bhavān bhūt*, the formation could be achieved simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *sup* (nominal suffix).

Because [the formation of] compounds would otherwise result in their cessation, he says: "The mention of *atiṅ*. And thus, it follows that a *upapada* is compounded with that which does not end in a case-suffix (*asu-banta*).
He further states—referring to the preceding rule—that a *gati*-compound is also [formed] with that which does not end in a case-suffix.

The recurrence of a term from a subsequent rule into a preceding rule is called *apakarṣa* (attraction). The two rules, "kuprādayaḥ" and "gatiḥ," are to be divided [into separate rules]. That is to say, it should be explained as follows: *kuprādayaḥ* are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), whereas a *gati* is compounded with a word that is semantically connected (*samartha*) [with it]; furthermore, the compound is one that does not end in a finite verb (*atiṅ*). This is the sense in which it should be interpreted.

To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And thus. The meaning is that the rule stated by the ancient grammarians—"A compound with words ending in *kṛt* suffixes should be stated to occur prior to the generation of the case-ending (*sub*) for the prepositional particle (*gati*), the agentive noun (*kāraka*), and the subordinate word (*upapada*)"—is thereby established. Although, according to the aforementioned method, only the prepositional particle (*gati*) and the subordinate word (*upapada*) are obtained [as objects of the rule], [the others are also included].

Nevertheless, this ancient grammatical maxim (paribhāṣā) is established by way of its partial acceptance. Now, in order to demonstrate the fruit of this maxim, he provides an example of a *gati-samāsa*: "vyāghrī.
[The word] *vyāghra* is derived from the root *ghrā* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-* according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*.

[The form] *kaḥ* [is derived as follows]: there is elision of the *ā* by the rule "elision of *ā* when followed by *iṭ*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*). However, the suffix *śa* prescribed by the rule "after the roots *pā*, *ghrā*, *dhmā*, etc., and *dṛś*, the suffix *śa* [is applied]" does not apply here, because of the prohibition: "it should be stated that after the root *ghrā*, there is no [suffix *śa*] in a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
There is a *gati*-compound of the prefix *āṅ* with the word *ghra*. There is a *gati*-compound of the prefix *ā* with the word *ghra*. In that case, if...

If the status of *ghrā* as ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) were required, then the production of a case-suffix would have to occur after the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) has been produced; for it is shown in the Bhāṣya on the rule *kutsite* that the operations prompted by meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) occur in a sequential order.

This has been explained by us in detail under the rule *ṭhṅyāpprātipadikāt*. Consequently, for the purpose of generating a case-ending (*sub*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and grammatical relation (*kāraka*) must be considered in sequence; thus, when there is a connection with gender first, the suffix *ṭāp* would apply because the stem ends in the letter *a*, and not the suffix *ṅīṣ* characterized by a genus (*jāti*).

The meaning is that since the word *ghrā* alone does not denote a genus (*jāti*), when it is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) as *vyāghra*, the word *vyāghra* would lack the final vowel *a*; consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed by the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*)—would not apply. Although this [form] is established even by treating it as an *upapada* (an accompanying word), nevertheless...

They say that this [is an example] merely because of the possibility of it being a *gati* compound. In reality, however, the word *āghra* is a *upapada* compound with the root *ghrā*, because of the mention of the locative case in the rule *ātaścopasarge*.
As for the root *vi*, it forms a *gati* compound with the word *āghra*; thus, they say that this portion serves as an illustration of a *gati* compound.

Now, he provides an example of a *kāraka-samāsa*: "aśvakrītī" (bought for a horse). In the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "aśvena krītā" (bought by means of a horse), there is a compound according to the rule "the agent or instrument [is compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. By the rule "after *krīta*, when preceded by an instrument," the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. However, if the compound were formed with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), then, following the aforementioned method, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would be applied first; consequently, because it would no longer end in the vowel 'a', the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply.
The intended meaning is "it might be so. He provides an example of an *upapada* compound: *kaccchapī*. "Kacccha" means a bank (*tīra*);

one who drinks (*pibati*) at that [bank] or from that [bank] is a *kaccchapa*. By the rule *supi sthaḥ*, through the separation of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*) as *supi*, the suffix *ka* is applied; this is an *upapada* compound. When there is a requirement for a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), it is according to the method stated above.
The intention is that there should be the suffix *ṭāp* alone, and not the suffix *ṅīṣ* characterized by [the presence of] a genus (*jāti*).
(772) *amaivāvyayena* | 2|2|20|. Regarding *amaivāvyayena*: immediately after *amaiva*, the phrase "having the same rule of application" (*tulyavidhānam*) is to be supplied.

In the rule *tulyārthair atulopamābhyām*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used. Regarding the phrase *amaiva tulya*: this means that whatever is prescribed as having the designation of an "upapada" (governing word) by a rule that prescribes only the suffix *am*—namely, together with that which ends in *am*—is compounded with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). [This is stated] because it would have been established by the preceding rule alone.

He says "this is for the purpose of restriction" with the words "that very [thing]. In the explanatory sentence (*vivaraṇavākya*), the second *evakāra* (the particle 'only') is obtained through restriction, but not the one situated in the sūtra; for that [sūtra's *eva*] has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārthatva*) regarding what is not otherwise established (*aprāpte*), since it serves as a rule of equal application (*tulyavidhānatve*). [The example is] "making it sweet" (*svāduṅkāram*).

The meaning is "having made [it] sweet. The ellipsis is "he eats the rice" (*odanaṃ bhuṅkte*). The suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *svādumi ṇamul*. The fact that the word *svādu* ends in the letter *m* is due to a *nipātana* (irregular grammatical formation).
Its status as an indeclinable follows from the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*. This is because of the restriction [contained in the rule] *tadeva*.
He states the purpose [of the rule] with "not so" (nehā). The remainder [of the rule] is "in the case of an upapada compound" (upapadasamāsa). Regarding "to eat" (bhoktum):

although time (*kāla*), occasion (*samaya*), and moment (*velā*) function as *upapadas* because of the mention of the locative case in the rule "at time, occasion, and moment" (*kālasamayavelāsu*), nevertheless...

The designation *upapada* for words such as *kāla* is governed by the same rule as *tumun*, and not by *am*. Therefore, the meaning is that even though *kāla* and others function as *upapadas*, there is no compound. Regarding the question "Why [specify] 'only with *am*'?", the query is: what is the purpose of the vowel *e* in the expression *amaiva*? [The answer is: "With *am* and with another," meaning with the suffix *am*.
The designation *upapada* is prescribed for the words *agra*, *prathama*, and *pūrva* together with the suffix *ktvā*;
therefore, because the status of being an *upapada* is not subject to the same rule (*tulyavidhāna*) as the accusative case (*am*), there is no *upapada-samāsa*. This is the intended meaning.

(773) *tṛtīyāprabhṛtīny anyatarasyām* | 2|2|21|. "The cases beginning with the third" (*tṛtīyāprabhṛtīni*). By the word "third" (*tṛtīyā*), there is a reference starting from the rule *upadaṃśas tṛtīyayā* up to *anvacīty anulomye*.

Thus, the subordinate words (*upapada*) included in the final sūtra are intended [to apply here]. The terms *ama* and *avyayena* are carried over (*anuvartate*). However, the particle *eva* (evakāra) is not carried over, because it is not marked with the *svarita* accent.
The word *ama* is a qualifier of the indeclinable (*avyaya*). This is what he states by saying: "When there is an object of comparison (*upadaṃśa*) in the third case," and so forth.

Regarding the expression *mūlakopadaṃśam*: the suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *tṛtīyāyām upadaṃśaḥ*. Since this is prescribed under the same conditions as the previous rule (*amaiva tulyavidhānatvāt*), this option prevails where the previous rule would have otherwise been mandatory. Now, one might object that because *mūlakena* is construed only with *bhuṅkte*, it cannot be construed with *upadaṃśa*.

If it is asked, "In this case, since there is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) and a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), how can there be a compound?"—do not say so; for the semantic status of the radish as the object (*karman*) with respect to the action of nibbling is established, thereby providing the required semantic capacity. As for the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), however...

It should be understood as an *upapadya* (a word that undergoes grammatical modification) because it conforms to the principal action and because it follows [the rule for] subsequent elements; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Regarding the form *uccaiḥkāram*: in the case of *uccaiḥkṛtvā*, however, [the rule] "after the root *kṛ*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* occur when an indeclinable expresses something unintended" applies. In that context, regarding the form *uccaiḥkāram*, the status of being an *upapada* [is established] only with the accusative (*am*).
Since there is an absence of equal application (*tulyavidhāna*), the rule *ṭhamaivāvyayena* does not apply; therefore, by this [present sūtra], an option is established.

In the case of a compound (*samāsa*), by the rule *ādir ṇamuly anyatarasyām*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—which is taught for kṛt-derivatives—is applied, resulting in the first syllable being udātta. However, in the case of a non-compound (*asamāsa*), it is simply *uccaiḥ*.
There is a difference in the result [of the two rules] regarding the acute accent on the final syllable according to the *phiṭ-sūtra*. Why [is it specified] "with an affix ending in *am*"?
Consider: *paryāpto bhoktum* ("sufficient to eat"). Here, the suffix *tumun* is used by the rule "in the sense of 'sufficiency' (*paryāpti-vacaneṣu*).
(774) And [a word ending in] *ktvā* [is also compounded with a gerundive]. 2.2.22.

And regarding *ktvā*: the preceding sūtra, "starting with the third case-ending," is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). In the word *ktvā*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. Others hold that the long vowel in place of the feminine suffix *ṭā* is due to the rule "supām sulukpūrvasavarṇa-," which prescribes the substitution of the preceding homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). Thus he says: "by the third [case-ending]. Now, an objection:
Since the rule prescribing *ktvā*—namely *samānakartṛkayoḥ*—is taught even before the rule *ṭhupadaṃśastṛtīyāyām*, how can *uccaiḥ kṛtvā* serve as an example?

To this he says: *avyaye 'yathā*. [The meaning is: "After the root *kṛ*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are employed when an indeclinable (*avyaya*) expresses something contrary to what was intended."
The meaning is "by means of this sūtra. Regarding the phrase *alam kṛtvā*: the rule *alam-khalvoḥ pratiṣedhayoḥ prācām ktvā* was recited even before the rule *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām*.

Therefore, because there is no compounding with the word ending in *m* (the object of the prohibition) with the *ktvā* suffix prescribed by that [former] rule, the substitution of *lyap* does not occur.
The suffix *bhāva* [is applied]. Thus end the compounds with subordinate words (*upapada-samāsa*). (775) *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.76.
Now, regarding the uncommon compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) in *tatpuruṣa* compounds:
He begins to explain: regarding the word *tad-aṅgul-asya*.
From the rule *ṭhac-pratyanvavapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.75), the term *ac* is understood by anuvṛtti; the governing heading *samāsānta* (5.4.68) is also in force.
By this, it is understood that [the suffix] is a final constituent part (*antāvayava*) of the compound. Furthermore, [by Pāṇini 3.1.2], it is a suffix (*pratyaya*) and follows [the base].

Thus, by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), although the suffix *ac* follows the *tatpuruṣa* compound, because that [suffix] is a constituent part (*avayava*) of it, the word "of the finger" (*aṅguleḥ*) is a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). The word "of the finger" is a qualifier of the *tatpuruṣa*; therefore, there is a rule applying to what ends in that [qualifier]. This is what is expressed by the phrase "after a numeral or an indeclinable, etc. (*saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*).
The analysis of the compound *saṅkhyāvyaye* is: "that which has a numeral (*saṅkhyā*) and an indeclinable (*avyaya*) as its first members.

Regarding the example *dvyaṅgulam*: it is a *dvigu* compound according to the rule *taddhitārtha*. [In this case,] by the rule *pramāṇe dvayasaj-daghnañ-mātracaḥ*, the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnac*, and *mātrac* are introduced after a word denoting a measure; however, by the rule *ṭha-pramāṇe-lo dvigornityam*, there is obligatory elision (*luk*) of these suffixes when they follow a *dvigu* compound.

From the word *dvyaṅguli*, by adding the suffix *ac*—since it is a *taddhita* suffix—there is the elision of the vowel *i* when this suffix follows, according to the rule *yasyeti ca*. Thus we have *niraṅgulam*. Here, the compound is formed according to the rule *nirādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*, and the suffix *ac* is added with the elision of the final vowel.

(776) *Ahaḥ-sarva-ekadeśa-saṃkhyāta-puṇyāc ca rātreḥ* |5|4|87|. [The rule begins with] *ahan*, *sarva*, *ekadeśa*, etc. The meaning is: after these—namely *ahan*, *sarva*, *ekadeśa*, *saṃkhyāta*, and *puṇya*—the word *rātri* [takes the suffix *ṭac*]. This refers to the word *rātri* when it follows a prior member such as *ahan* and so forth.
This refers to the *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in "rātryanta" (ending in "night").

The inclusion of the word "day" (*ahar*) is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound. Now, one might object: there is no such *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with "day" and ending in "night," such as "day-night" (*ahno rātriḥ*).
Or [one might argue] that it is "day and night" (*ahaśca rātriśca*); however, because that is impossible, he says:

"The mention of 'day' is for the sake of a *dvandva* compound. Nor should it be said that a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* is possible—meaning that the human night is a constituent part of that which is the day of Brahmā—for the mention of "day" [is intended otherwise].

Because of the authority of the Bhāṣya stating "dvandvārtham," it is inferred that there is no usage of a *tatpuruṣa* compound of this kind [where the first member is a numeral]. Regarding the form *ahorātra*: after the *dvandva* [compound], the suffix *ac* is applied, the *i* is elided, and by the rule "jātir aprāṇinām," it becomes a singular. This overrides the rule "sa napuṃsakam" [which would have made it neuter].
The word *sarvarātra* is masculine according to the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) "the entire night" (*sarvā rātriḥ*), it is a *karmadhāraya* compound by the rule *pūrvakālaika-*; the suffix *ac* is applied, there is elision of the vowel *i*, and the word is masculine by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ*. [This applies] because of the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre*.
Thus, there is the treatment as masculine (*puṃvat*).
Intending to show that the term "part" (*ekadeśa*) is taken here in its sense of "a portion," he provides an example: *pūrvam*.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *pūrvaṃ rātreḥ* ("the first part of the night"), there is a *ekadeśi-samāsa* (compound of a part and the whole) according to the rule *pūrvaparādharottaram*. [The suffix] *ac* [is applied].

*ilopaḥ* (elision of *i*); by the rule *rātrāhna*, there is masculinity. Regarding *saṅkhyātarātra*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) *saṅkhyātā rātriḥ*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound. By the rule *puṃvatkarmadhāraye*, there is the masculine form; *ac* [is added], followed by the elision of *i*. By the rule *rātrāhna*, there is masculinity. Thus, *dvirātram*.

The term *atirātra* is formed as follows: first, a *dvigu* compound is formed according to the rule *taddhitārthe*. Since it begins with a numeral, the suffix *ac* is applied, followed by the elision of the final vowel (*ilopa*). It is neuter in gender because of the rule *saṅkhyāpūrvaṃ rātraṃ klībaṃ*. Regarding the word *atirātra*: a compound is formed according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe*. The suffix *ac* is applied because it begins with an indeclinable (*avyaya*), followed by the elision of the final vowel (*ilopa*), and finally, the form is established by the rule *rātrāhne*.
Masculinity.

(777) *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* | 5.4.91. [The suffix] *ṭac* [is applied after the words] *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*. [This applies when these are] the final members of a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *aṅguli*.

Therefore, the term *tatpuruṣasya*, which continues from the previous rule, is modified into the ablative plural (*pañcamī-bahuvacana*) and is qualified by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*. This refers to the rule of "application to that which ends in [the specified stem]"; thus he says: "from that which ends in this. For example: *paramarājaḥ* (supreme king), meaning "one who is both supreme and a king."
The analysis is as follows: "kṛṣṇasakha" is a compound formed by the rule "ṭathādayaḥ. When the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there is the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
Thus, "kṛṣṇasakha" means "the friend of Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇasya sakhā*); here, the suffix *ṭac* is added at the end of the compound, and the vowel *i* is elided according to the rule "yasyeti ca."

(778) *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* | P. 6.4.145. Regarding *ahnaṣṭakhoh*: he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion—namely, "there shall be elision of *ṭi*" (*ṭilopaḥ syāt*). The word *ṭeḥ* is understood from the previous rule, and the sense is that this refers to the elision of *ṭi* as in the rule *ṭhallopo'naḥ*.
Since the rule would have been established by "ṭhnastaddhite" alone, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha), meaning: "only here [and not elsewhere].

The particle *eva* is used to exclude the reverse restriction, namely that "the suffixes *ṭa* and *kha* occur only after *ahan*. What is the purpose of saying "only after *ṭa* and *kha*"? Consider: *ahnā nivṛtam* (ended with a day) = *āhnikam*. [This is derived by] "kālāṭṭhañ".

Under this governing rule (*adhikāra*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "that which is prepared by that" (*tena nivṛtam*). Due to the absence of the elision of *ṭi*, there is the elision of *al*.

He provides an example with the suffix *ṭap*: "he says the best" (*uttamāha*). This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of "the best" (*uttama*) and "day" (*ahaḥ*). The suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule "after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ṭac*."

The suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule "ṭhāḍhaṇṭakhoreva. By the current sūtra, "ahnasṭakhoreva," there is elision (*ṭilopa*) of the final vowel; and by the rule "rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi," the word takes the masculine gender. He gives an example for the word *khe*: "dve ahanī bhṛtaḥ" (hired for two days). The accusative case is used here to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). The meaning of *bhṛtaḥ* is "purchased for hire" (*parikrīta*).

He demonstrates the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) for the term *dvyahīna*: "a *dvigu* compound when the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is intended. To the question "What is the secondary derivative here?", he says: "that which one is appointed to perform" (*tam adhīṣṭa*), and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that from the word *dvyahan*, by the substitution of *īn* for the suffix *kha*, and by the elision of the final *an* according to the rule "only after *ahan* before *kha* and *khara*," the form *dvyahīna* is produced.

Now, one might object: why should the substitution *ahn* not occur here by the rule "ṭhano’hn etebhyaḥ"? Nor should it be argued that the substitution *ahn* does not apply because of the force of the rule for the elision of the *ṭi*-portion in the case of *kha*, since that rule for the elision of *ṭi* in *kha* finds its application in the word *ahīna*. This is not so, because [the substitution] occurs when a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) follows.

Because the suffix *ṭac* is prescribed for [compounds ending in] *ahan* and so forth, whereas in the present case, due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule governing compound-final suffixes,

*ṭac* is not applied by the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ. Although the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) is already established by the rule "na-staddhite" in cases such as "uttamāhaḥ" and "dvyahīna," nevertheless...

In passages such as *āhnika*, the introduction of that [paribhāṣā] is justified because it is accepted that even a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) concerning what is necessary (*āvaśyaka*) operates by way of positive prescription (*vidhimukha*).

Now, one might object: in the case of *madrāṇāṃ rājñī* (the queen of the Madras), which becomes *madrarājñī*, would this not also apply by means of the paribhāṣā regarding forms qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*)?

Fearing that the suffix *ṭac* might apply by the rule "ṭhrājāhaḥsakhibhyaḥ," he says "liṅga" etc. [The reason] is "because it is not eternal. The sense is that, as stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṅyāpprātipadikāt," the paribhāṣā regarding words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) does not apply within the section dealing with compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*).

Regarding the term *madrarājñī*: one should not argue that even if the suffix *ṭac* is applied, the form *madrarājñī* is unobjectionable because the *ikāra* is elided by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*, and then the suffix *ṅīp* is added to the word *madrarājñ* due to its *ṭit* status;
for if *ṭac* were indeed applied, the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* would cause *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution), resulting in the elision of the *ṭi*.
The intention is that [the compound] would be "madrarājñī.
(779) *ahno 'hna etebhyaḥ* |5|4|88|. From these [words], *ahnaḥ* is replaced by *ahnaḥ*. In the previous sūtra, the words *ahaḥ*, *sarva*, *ekadeśa*, *saṃkhyāta*, and *puṇya* [were mentioned].

In that context, the word *cakāra* (the letter 'ca') draws in the categories of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) and "indeclinable" (*avyaya*). With the exception of the word *ahan* ("day"), all of those are referred to by this term [sarva-ādi], but not the word *ahar* itself; for it is intended that the word *ahan* cannot follow the word *ahar* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Bearing this in mind, he explains: "from *sarva* and the rest."

"Before a suffix added at the end of a compound (*samāsānte*)," this is understood from the context. (780) *Aho’dantāt* [Pāṇini 8.4.7]: "After *ahan*, when it ends in a short vowel. This is derived from the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*.

The term *pūrvapadāt* (from the preceding member), which is carried over [from a previous rule], connects with *adantāt* (from that which ends in /a/). The rule *ṭhraṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ* (after /ṭh/ or /r/ and /ṣ/, /n/ becomes /ṇ/) follows, with the exception of the letter /ṣ/.
By the phrase *pūrvapadāt*, it is intended to mean "situated in the preceding member. Thus he says:
*adantapūrva-* (preceded by that which ends in /a/). Since this is already established by the rule of *tadantavidhi* (the inclusion of that which ends in such), [the explicit mention is for clarity].

The inclusion of the word *anta* (end) is for the sake of clarity. It should also be understood that in the case of *lakṣāhṇa*—meaning "occurring on a hundred-thousand days"—the mention of *ṣāt* [in the rule] is intended to ensure the substitution of *ṇ*. Why is it said "when a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) follows"? Consider the example: *dvyahīnaḥ*, meaning "one who has been hired for two days. Here, because the application of the compound-final suffix is not mandatory (*anitya*), the suffix *ṭac* does not occur; consequently, the substitute *ahn* is not applied.

Regarding *sarvāhṇa*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) as "the whole day" (*sarvam ahar*), there is a compound by the rule *pūrvakālaika-*; then, by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied, followed by the substitution of *ah* for *ahan*. There is the change to *ṇ* (nasalization). By the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*, it takes the masculine gender. Regarding *pūrvāhṇa*: the formation of the compound and so forth is like that of *sarvāhṇa*. [The same applies to] *saṅkhyātāhna*.

Thus: *saṅkhyātamahaḥ* is the analysis [of the compound]. It is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), with the suffix *ṭac* and the substitution of *ahan* for *ahaḥ*. Due to the absence of a cause [for it], there is no substitution of *ṇa*. However, that which is preceded by *puṇya-* will be explained later.
He gives an example of that which is preceded by a numeral: *dvayor ahnoḥ*, etc. [The result is] *dvayahnaḥ*.

A *dvigu* compound is formed in the sense of a *taddhita* suffix. [The suffix] *ṭac* is added. Then, for the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; this is elided (*luk*), and the substitute *ahan* is substituted [for the final member]. He states [this] incidentally: "in the feminine" (*striyām*). Regarding *dvyahna*: the meaning is "that which occurs in two days. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied, and its elision (*luk*) is as before. By the rule "*ṭha*-parimāṇa-vistābhyām," the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur.
However, it has been stated in the rule *apari-māṇa-vista-* that the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur after a word ending in the suffix *ṭac*.

Even though *ṭac* is marked with the *ṭ*-indicator, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply because it is a neuter (*napuṃsaka*) stem according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ-*. In reality, however, there is no femininity (*strītva*) here at all, as it is stated that "the words *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine."
This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.

He provides another example for a compound preceded by a numeral: *dvyahnatriyaḥ*. The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "one for whom two days (*dve ahani*) are dear. Since this serves the purpose of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the *dvigu* compound is formed with the subsequent member; then the suffix *ṭac* is applied.
The intention is that there is the substitution of *ahn* for *aha*. He gives an example of a compound where an indeclinable (*avyaya*) precedes: *atyahnaḥ*.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has transcended the day" (*ahar atikrāntaḥ*). The compound is formed by the rule "atyādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18). The suffix *ṭac* is applied, and the intention is that there is the substitution of *ahn* for *aha*.

(781) And in the case of *kṣubh*-beginning words [Pāṇini 8.4.39]. In the rule "And in the case of *kṣubh*-beginning words," the word "ṇa" is carried over from "after *ṛ* and *ṣ*" (8.4.1), and the word "na" is carried over from "not after *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, or *kam*" (8.4.34). Thus he says: "in these."

"Dīrghāhnī prāvṛṭ" (the rainy season with long days). In the context of the rainy season (*varṣartu*), the word *prāvṛṭ* is feminine. As Amara states: "In the feminine, *prāvṛṭ*; in the plural feminine, *varṣāḥ*. The term *dīrghāhnī* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the days (*ahāni*) are long. The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ṅīp* is optionally [added] after a word ending in *an* when its penultimate vowel is elided."

There is elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule *ṭhallopo'naḥ*. As for the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule *ṭhahno'dantāt*, the intention is that it does not apply here because [the word] belongs to the *kṣubhnādi* group. Now, one might object: the inclusion of the form *dīrghāhnī* in the *kṣubhnādi* list is redundant; for in the rule *ṭhahno'dantāt*, the term *arhneḥ* is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to refer to what ends in *ahn-*.

First [interpretation]: The meaning is that the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *ahna-* occurs when it follows a cause situated in a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) ending in *a*. Now, in the case of *dīrghāhnī*, since the substitute *āhnā-* does not apply, the condition of ending in *a* is absent; therefore, since the substitution of *ṇ* would not even arise [under this interpretation], what [is the purpose of the rule]?
To show that [the inclusion of *udīrghāhnī*] is for the sake of following that [list], he says "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*), because it is recited among the *kṣubhna*-type words.

This being so—i.e., when the word *udīrghāhnī* is included in the *kṣubhna*-type list—for this purpose: namely, to prevent the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule "of *ahan* when preceded by a short vowel" (*ahno 'dantāt*), [the inclusion of *udīrghāhnī* serves] for the sake of the form *ahnā*.

The meaning is that one should not follow the rule for non-dental [nasals] (*adanta*) by following the nominative case in place of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe vyatyayena prathamā*), as that would bring about affliction (*kleśāvaha*). The intention is that the prevention of the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) is already established simply by the inclusion of [the word] in the *kṣubhna*-class. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of the absence of *ṇatva* in the word *dīrghāhnī*?

Since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether one should accept the inclusion of *kṣubhna* and others in the list, or rather that the word *ahan* ends in a short vowel (*adanta*), he says: "By the rule *prātipadikānta*...
Now, regarding the phrase *ahno 'dantāt*, if the term *adantāt* were a qualifier of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), then the purpose of the *t* in *tapara* [would be explained].

He states the purpose [of the rule]: "from that which ends in 'a'" (adantāt). Regarding "parāhna": the compound is formed according to the rule "prādayo gatādyarthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), followed by the suffix *ṭac*. Because it follows an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the substitution of *ahna* for *ahan* occurs.
The point is that since the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) "parā" does not end in the vowel 'a', the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not take place.

(782) *Na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre* [Pāṇini 5.4.89]. "Not after a numeral and so forth. The meaning is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ahno 'hnah* from the preceding sūtra. Now, one might object: since a *tatpuruṣa* compound other than one beginning with a numeral cannot exist as a collective (*samāhāra*), [the prohibition is redundant].
Since [the rule] "after *saṅkhyā* etc. would already establish this, it would be redundant; therefore, he says: "for the sake of clarity. Regarding *dvyaha*:
this is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). The suffix *ṭac* is applied, and by the rule *ṭhrātrāhne'ti*, the word takes the masculine gender.
This is a prohibition of the substitution of *ahna-* which would otherwise have been obtained due to the inclusion [of the word] among *saṅkhyā* etc. Regarding *tryaha*: [the same applies].

The analysis of the compound is "the collection of three days. The formation of the compound and so forth is like that of *dvyaha*.
