Since the substitution of *ahna* for the word *ahan* after the word *uttama* does not occur [in the case of the ordinal], the mention of *uttama* would be redundant; therefore, he says: "the word *uttama*. The word *uttama* refers to the final [member].
For example, in the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is understood as "the final day" in the expression: "the *udayanīya-atirātra* is the *uttama-ahaḥ* (final day)."

The meaning is that, among the terms mentioned in the rule *ṭhaḥ sarva-ekadeśa-saṅkhyāta-puṇya-ādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*, the final term *puṇya* is intended [to be included]. One might then ask: why was the rule not formulated simply as *puṇya-eka-bhyām*? Anticipating this objection:

Because the great sage [Pāṇini] has independent authority, he says: "only by means of *puṇya* and *eka*. Regarding *puṇyāha*: in the analysis (*vigraha*) as *puṇyam ahar*, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*); the suffix *ṭac* is applied, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
By the rule "also after *puṇya* and *sudinā*," the neuter gender is established. Regarding *ekāha*: [the same applies].

In the analysis (*vigraha*) of *ekamahar*, the compound is formed by the rule *pūrvakālaika-*. There is the suffix *ṭac* and the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi*-portion. Regarding the phrase "even of the penultimate," the word "by indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*) is to be supplied as the remainder. By not stating "in *paruṇi*" but rather using the mention of "*uttama*," that very mention is the basis for the indication. Furthermore, *uttama* and *eka* form a copulative compound (*dvandva*), which is [established] by the Vedic sūtra.
The intended meaning is that it is a dual form. Regarding the term *saṅkhyātāha*:

in the analysis (*vigraha*) as "the day numbered" (*saṅkhyātam ahar*), it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*); the suffix *ṭac* is applied, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion. By the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*, the word takes the masculine gender.
Because the word *saṅkhyāta* precedes the penultimate member, the substitution of *ahn* does not occur.

(784) *agra-ākhyāyām urasaḥ* | 5|4|93 | Regarding *agra-ākhyāyām*: he explains the sūtra by supplying the remainder—namely, that *ṭac* shall be the suffix. The locative case is used in the sense of the ablative. *Agra* means "foremost" or "principal"; [the word] which denotes that...
The meaning is that the suffix *ṭāc* (i.e., *ī*) occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *upa*. There is an alternative reading: *agnākhyāyām*.

[The word] *agraya* means "being at the front" (*agre bhavam*), that is to say, "principal. [The phrase] "like the breast of horses" means just as the breast is the principal part, so too [is it here]. Thus, the word *upa* functions in the sense of "principal."

This is the seed for the technical definition (*lakṣaṇā*). Regarding the example *aśvorasam*: the word *uraḥ* (chest) is used in its primary sense (*mukhyavācin*), forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The suffix *ṭac* is applied. By the rule "the gender [of the compound] follows that which ends in *ṭha*," it takes the neuter gender. Why is it said "when it is not called 'front' (*agrākhyā*)"? Consider: *devadatasyoraḥ* becomes *devadatoraḥ*.

(785) *anośmā'yas-sarasāṃ jāti-saṃjñayoḥ* || 5.4.94 || In the case of *anaḥ*, *aśman*, and *ayas*, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] when they denote a genus (*jāti*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*). *Upānasa*: This is a *prādi*-compound meaning "that which has approached" (*upagatamanas*). *Amṛtāśma*: The analysis (*vigraha*) is "immortal stone" (*amṛto'śmaḥ*). By the application of *ṭac*, there is the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*ṭilopa*).

Regarding *kālāyasam*: the analysis of the compound is *kālam ayaḥ*. The suffix *ṭac* is applied. By the rule *ṭhparavalliṅgam*, it takes the neuter gender. Regarding *maṇḍūakasarasam*: this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The suffix *ṭac* is applied. These are specific types [of iron]. [The others are] *mahānasam*, *piṇḍāśmaḥ*, and *lohitāyasam*.
*Jalasara-sam* and so forth are specific designations.
(786) *Grāmakauṭābhyāṃ ca takṣṇaḥ* |5|4|95|. [The rule continues: "And after *grāma* and *kauṭa*. From these two, the suffix *ṭac* is applied. After *grāma* and *kauṭa*, [the word *takṣan* follows].

The meaning is that the suffix *ṭac* occurs after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *takṣan*. In the example *grāmatakṣaḥ*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) due to the suffix *ṭac*. Regarding the term *sādhāraṇaḥ*: the meaning is that he is to be provided for by as many people as exist in the village. In the phrase *kuṭīṃ bhava*, [it means] having acquired a single hut through purchase or other means, reside there.

One who dwells [there], but not on land belonging to another, is a *kauṭa*; this is the meaning. He states the result: "independent" (*svatantra*). Regarding *kauṭatakṣa*: when the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). (Pāṇini 5.4.96) *ateḥ śunaḥ*. The meaning is that one who resides there, but not on a plot of land belonging to another, is a *kauṭa*. He states the conclusion: "independent. Regarding the term *kauṭatakṣa*: by the application of the suffix *ṭac*, there is elision of the *ṭi*. (Pāṇini 5.4.96) *ateḥ śunaḥ*.

*ateśśunaḥ*. The meaning is that the suffix *ṭac* is applied after a tatpuruṣa compound ending in the word *śvan*, provided that this word follows the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *ati*. For example, *atiśvaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "one who has surpassed a dog" (*śvānam atikrāntaḥ*). The compound is formed by the rule *atyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ*. When *ṭac* is applied, there is the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*ṭilopaḥ*).
The meaning is that a boar possesses greater speed than a dog. Regarding the term *atiśvī*:
it means "one who has surpassed a dog"; that is to say, she serves in a manner inferior to a dog. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
Because it is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and the vowel *a* is elided according to the rule *yasyeti ca*.

(788) *upamānādaprāṇiṣu* | 5|4|97 | [When a word] expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is used with non-living things, [the suffix *kan* is applied]. Example: *ākarṣaḥ śveva*. An *ākarṣa* is that by which grain located in a granary or similar place is drawn out—it is a specific type of wooden tool consisting of five fingers' breadth.

The compound *vyāghrādyupamitam* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. By [Pāṇini 5.4.91], the suffix *ṭac* is applied, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion, resulting in the form *ākarṣaśca*. Why "from a standard of comparison" (*upamānāt*)? Consider *niḥśvā*, meaning "one who has emerged from a dog.
(789) [Pāṇini 5.4.98: Also after *sakthi* when preceded by *uttara*, *mṛga*, or another word.

The meaning is that the suffix *ṭac* is applied after a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *sakthi*, provided that *sakthi* follows words such as *uttara*, *mṛga*, *ṭhutaḥ*, *ṭhmṛga*, or *pūrva*, or any other word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). For example, in the analysis *uttaraṃ sakthi* (the upper thigh), the form is *uttarasaktham*. In the analysis *pūrvaṃ sakthi* (the front thigh), [the suffix is applied] by the rule *pūrvakālaika-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49).

This is a compound. Regarding the example *phalakasaktham*: in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "the two thighs are like planks" (*phalakam iva sakthī*), the compound is formed because it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. In all such cases, the suffix *ṭac* is applied, and there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*).
(Pāṇini 5.4.99) *nāvo dvigoḥ*: [The suffix *ṭac* is applied] after the word *nau* when it is part of a *dvigu* compound.

The phrase "not when there is elision of a taddhita suffix" [is understood here] because of its continuation by means of a *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) from the rule "after *go*, except when there is elision of a taddhita suffix. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the form *dvināvarūpya*:

it is a compound in the sense of a taddhita suffix, followed by the suffix *ṭac*, the substitution of *āva*, and the suffix *rūpya* according to the rule "after words denoting cause or a person, *rūpya* optionally [is used]."

Fearing that the suffix might be elided by the rule "dvigor lug anapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.88), he says: "in this case [of the rule] 'dvigor lug anapatye'. Regarding the phrase "because of the extraction": the meaning is "from the subsequent sūtra, namely 'gotre 'lug acī' (Pāṇini 4.1.89).
The example is "pañcanāvapriyaḥ," which is derived from the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) "one for whom five ships are dear," with the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) [being present].

*Dvigu*, *ṭac* [suffix], and the substitution of *āv*. Thus, *dvināvam*. In the analysis (*vigraha*) "the aggregate of two boats," there is a *dvigu* compound; the suffix *ṭac*; the substitution of *āv*; and by the rule "it is neuter," it takes the neuter gender. Similarly, *trināvam* means "the aggregate of three boats."

The word *vigarahaḥ* [is explained as follows]: "like two ships" (*dvināvavat*), "like five ships" (*pañcanauriti*). This is a compound (*samāsa*) used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for items belonging to a price (*ārhīya*), and by the rule "after *adhyardha* and [words ending in] *ardha*, there is elision" (*adhyardhe'ti luk*), the suffix is dropped.
(Pāṇini 5.4.100) states: "Also after *ardha*."

"And after *ardha*. This means that when the word *nau* follows the word *ardha*, the *ṭac* suffix is added to that *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in it. Thus, *ardhanāvam*. The compound is formed by the rule "the neuter [word] *ardha* [is used in a bahuvrīhi]" (Pāṇini 2.2.2), followed by the addition of *ṭac* and the substitution of *āva* for *nau*. Here, one might suspect that the feminine gender would apply according to the rule "the gender of the final member [prevails]" (*paravalliṅgam*); therefore, he says: "Neuter gender [is established] from common usage" (*klībatvaṃ lokāt*).

(792) *khāryāḥ prācām* | 5|4|101| [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the word *khārī* according to the Eastern grammarians. This means that the suffix is applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in *khārī*, as well as after a *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with *ardha* and ending in *khārī*.

Regarding *dvikhāram*: when analyzed as "the collection of two *khārīs*," it forms a *dvigu* compound. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied; by the rule *ṭhyasyeti ca*, the final vowel is elided; and by the rule *sa napuṃsakam*, it takes the neuter gender. In the alternative case where *ṭac* is absent, it is neuter by the rule *sa napuṃsakam*, and thus the neuter short vowel [is applied]. Regarding *ardhakhāram*: [it is derived] from *khāryāḥ*.

The analysis of the compound is "half" (*ardham*). The compound is formed by the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*; the suffix *ṭac* is applied, and the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*yasyeti ca*) occurs. The neuter gender is established by common usage. In the case of *ardhakhārī*, the compound is formed as before. In the alternative view where the suffix *ṭac* is absent, the feminine gender applies according to the rule *paravalliṅgam*.

Because there is a single case-ending (ekavibhakti) and it is not in the genitive case (aṣaṣṭhyanta), and because it lacks the status of being a subordinate member (upasarjana), the short vowel [substitution] does not apply. There is a certain reading of the rule *ardhakhāryāḥ* with a short final vowel; in that case, its neuter gender is established by common usage (*lokāt*), and consequently, the short vowel for neuter nouns applies.

(793) *dvitribhyāmañjaleḥ* | Pāṇini 5.4.102. Regarding the rule *dvitribhyāmañjaleḥ*, he explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "the suffix *ṭac* may optionally occur. [This applies] when it is a *dvigu* compound; for example, *dvyañjalam*. This is derived from the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "the collection of two *añjali*s."

*Dvigu*, *ṭac* [is applied] by the rule "that which has [the suffix] *ṭi*", and "it is neuter. Regarding *dvyañjali*: it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). Since the suffix *ṭac* is absent, the neuter shortening occurs. The phrase "only when there is no elision of a *taddhita* suffix" continues to apply; this is the meaning. [The example] *añjalibhyāṃ krītaḥ* ("bought for two handfuls")...

The word *añjali* occurs in such cases as "grain measured by an *añjali*," because it is impossible for a mere *añjali* [as a physical gesture] to have a price. Since it denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; however, by the rule "*adhyardhapūrva-dvigor lug*" (Pāṇini 5.1.28), that suffix is elided.

(794) *brahmaṇo jānapadākhyāyām* |5|4|104|. Regarding the rule "after *brahman*, when expressing a name of a district": *jānapada* means "belonging to a district" (*janapade bhavaḥ*). This is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant.
When there arises the expectation "by what is that [state] expressed?", it is understood from the context of the present topic that it is by means of a compound.

It is obtained. Thus he says: "In brief," and so forth. After the word *jānapadatvam* (the state of being a native), the word *brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "A Brahmin in Surāṣṭra. Here the word *brahma* is masculine.
*Brahmā* means a *vipra* (twice-born). As Amara states: "The Veda, reality, austerity, a Brahmin, a *vipra*, and Prajāpati are all *brahma*. [This occurs] in the locative case (*saptamī*).

The compound is formed by the division of the *yogavibhāga*. [The suffix] *ṭac* is added, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*), and by the rule "the gender of the latter [member] prevails" (*ṭhparavalliṅgam*), the masculine gender is applied. Why [is the word] *jānapada* mentioned? [To exclude cases like] Devabrahmā Nārada. (795) *kumahadbhyāmanyatarasyām* 5.4.105.

In the case of *kumahadbhyām* [as an example], the form *kubrahma* arises when the suffix *ṭac* is absent; it is a compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*. In the form *kubrahma*, when the suffix *ṭac* is applied, there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*).
(Pāṇini 6.3.46): *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ*—[the substitution of] *ā* occurs for the word *mahat* when it is in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or followed by the suffix *jātīya*.
Now, intending to illustrate the optional substitution of *ṭac* for the word *mahat* when preceded by a great [word], he states a specific rule: *ānmahataḥ*.

This sūtra is situated within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the elision of *ṭa* when there is a subsequent member" (*ṭhalugutarapade*). The term "subsequent member" (*utarapade*), which is carried over from the previous context, connects with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and not with the suffix *jātīya*, because of that [restriction].

Because it is a condition (*pratyaya*). Thus he says: "The substitution of *āt* for *mahat*, etc. Regarding the term *mahābrahmā*: the analysis of the compound is "he who is both great (*mahān*) and Brahmā. The compound is formed by the rule *sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ*. There is the substitution of *āt*. [This results in] *mahābrahmā*; then, by the rule *savarṇadīrghaḥ*, there is the lengthening of the vowel. By the rule *kumahadbhyām ṭac ca*, the suffix *ṭac* is added. There is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi* (the final syllable).

By the rule *ṭha-paravalliṅgam*, the masculine gender is applied. Regarding *mahābrahma*: this is the form when the suffix *ṭac* is absent and the *ātvam* (substitution of *ā*) occurs. Now, intending to elaborate upon the rule for *ātvam* mentioned incidentally, he provides another example with a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*): *mahādeva*. He gives an example with a word ending in the suffix *jātīyar*: *mahājātīya*.

The meaning is "resembling a great one. [The suffix] *jātīyar* is used in the sense of expressing a kind or manner (*prakāra*). The substitution of *ā* (for the final vowel) is by way of *savarṇadīrgha*.

[Objection: Why specify "in a coordinate compound" (*samānādhikaraṇe*)? One could simply state: "In the case of *mahat*, there is the substitution of *ā* when *jātīya* follows," and since the particle *ca* would include the subsequent word, the substitution of *ā* for *mahat* would occur when *jātīya* is the subsequent member.

The question is: since the term "Mahādeva" and so forth is established simply by obtaining the meaning from the word *para* (the other), what is the purpose of the term *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential)? [The answer is: "It is for the sake of great service. Here, the intention is that the mention of *samānādhikaraṇa* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *āt* in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). But is it not a genitive compound?

The *lākṣaṇika* [compound] is so called because it is formed solely by a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), without specifically pronouncing the constituent words being compounded. However, this compound "san-mahat" is *pratipadokta*, because it is prescribed after specifically pronouncing the words "san," "mahat," and so forth, which are being compounded. And therefore...

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*), when the compound *sanmahat*— which is taught specifically in the rule *ṭhānmahato jātīye ca*— is understood as referring to the final member of a compound taught by that specific rule, it follows that the exclusion of the final member of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is already possible from that very source; therefore, [the inclusion of the word *mahat* in the rule] would indeed be redundant.
He raises an objection regarding the inclusion of the term "having a common substratum" (samānādhikaraṇa)—starting with the words "it would be figurative" (lākṣaṇika).
He refutes it with the words "Mahābāhu would not [be so called]. The analysis (vigraha) is: "one whose arms are great.
This compound is formed according to the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Pāṇini 2.2.24).

The meaning is that because [the rule] is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānyavihita*) and lacks a specific designation (*pratipadokta*), the substitution of *ātva* would not occur when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*);
therefore, the term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is included. Now, even if the term "co-referential" were included...

Since the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) would be unavoidable, the substitution of *āt* [for *a*] would certainly not occur in the word *mahābāhuḥ*; therefore, he says: "Therefore...
He explains the meaning of the word *tat* [in that sūtra]: "By virtue of the force of the mention of 'having a common substratum' (*samānādhikaraṇa*). And thus...

The intention is that the mention of "samānādhikaraṇa" (having a common substratum) is for the purpose of including even derivative forms (*lākṣaṇika*), thereby overriding the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that a term denotes only that which is explicitly stated by its own definition (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*). If so, one might ask: how is the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) justified in the example *sumahābāhuḥ* ("one whose arms are very great")? [The answer is: because the rule prescribing *āt*...

It should not be argued that there is no application of the rule *tadanta-vidhi* (the rule applying to what ends with a specified element) because the word is not situated under the heading of *pada-aṅga*;

for when the preceding member, which is implied by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), is qualified by the word *mahat*, the application of *tadanta-vidhi* is obtained. However, in the case of *paramamahatparimāṇavat*, [the analysis is] "the dimension of the great" (*mahataḥ parimāṇam*).

The term *mahatparimāṇam* (great measure) is a *karmadhāraya* compound containing within it a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, meaning "the measure that is great" or "the supreme great measure. This is because, in the rule *ānmahataḥ* ("the substitute *ā* [is applied] after *mahat*"), only *mahat* is mentioned;
whereas in the subsequent rule *dvyaṣṭanaḥ* ("after *dvi* and *aṣṭan*"), only *dvi* and *aṣṭan* are mentioned. Thus, in the case of *ekādaśa* ("eleven"), [the substitution does not apply].

To the question "How is there the substitution of *āt*? he says: "The substitution of *āt* [occurs] due to the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Since such a splitting of the rule is not observed in the *Bhāṣya*, he says: "Or rather, because of the specific mention (*nirdeśa*). Regarding "eleven" (*ekādaśa*):
it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "one and ten," or it means "ten with one added. In the rule "ānmahataḥ... [the same applies].

By the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a rule applies to a word qualified by its gender), when the suffix *jātīya* follows, the word *mahatī* would also become *mahatājātīya*; therefore, he says: "of the word *mahatī*. Nor should it be argued that, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the substitution of *ā* (by *ānmahataḥ*) would supersede the *puṃvat* transformation; for in the rule *ānmahataḥ*, [the condition is specified].

The intention is that the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender) does not apply, because this has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule for *ṅī* and *āp* suffixes (*ṅyāpsūtra*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of *mahat*": the meaning is that when followed by the words *ghāsa*, *kara*, or *viśiṣṭa*, the substitution of *ā* for *mahat* and its treatment as masculine (*puṃvat*) must be prescribed. [Objection: But [there is already the rule] *ānmahataḥ*...

Since the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) would already be established by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* when [the first member] ends in *ā*, for what purpose is this [present rule] stated? To this he says: "For the sake of non-co-referentiality" (*asāmānādhikaraṇyārtham*). *Mahākaraḥ* means a maker (*kara*) of something great, whether masculine or feminine. *Mahāviśiṣṭaḥ* means distinguished (*viśiṣṭaḥ*) by something great, whether masculine or feminine. *Adhikaḥ*.
This is the meaning.

Regarding the rule "aṣṭanaḥ kapāle haviṣi": when the word *kapāla* follows as the second member (*uttarapada*) and the sense to be expressed is an oblation (*havis*), the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* occurs.

The meaning is that it must be stated. Regarding the term *aṣṭākapāla*: in the sense of "a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on eight potsherds (*kapāla*)," there is a *dvigu* compound for the sake of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). [From this,] by the rule *saskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied.
By the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix. Then, the substitution of *ā* occurs, followed by the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*).

"And when *go* is joined [to a numeral]. This is a *vārttika*. To indicate that, he says: "the meaning is that it should be stated. An example is *aṣṭāgavaṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart yoked with eight oxen"). [The analysis is: *aṣṭau gāvo yasya*, a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [By this rule,] the substitution of *āt* [for the final vowel of *go*] occurs.
This is a case of *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening of a homogeneous vowel). The meaning is "yoked with eight cows. Now, one might ask:

since the rule *gorataddhitalukī* prescribes the suffix *ṭac* and applies only to *tatpuruṣa* compounds, how can the form *aṣṭāgavam* be justified? To this, he says: "In the case of the suffix *ac*, etc. (referring to the rule *ac-pratyayānto ’nv-eti*).

He states that in its status as a *tatpuruṣa*, the word *aṣṭagava* must indeed end in the suffix *ṭac*: "of eight," etc. Thus, because the *samāhāra-dvigu* (collective numeral compound) is a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *ṭac* is easily obtained by the rule "after *go*, when no *taddhita* suffix follows" (*gorataddhitalukī*).
[Objection: But if the meaning is "a collection of eight cows," how can there be a connection with the word "cart" (*śakaṭa*)?
Because there is an absence of functioning based on a literal meaning, he asks, "How then is the substitution of *ā* [for *i*] justified? and replies: "Because it is so joined.

The meaning is that the word *aṣṭagava*, which is derived from a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a neuter gender ending in *ṭac*, functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote that which is "joined by eight oxen," and thus the substitution of *ā* occurs.

(797) *dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṅkhyāyāmabahuvrīhyaśītyoḥ* | 6|3|47|. [The rule] *dvyaṣṭanaḥ*. He explains the sūtra by supplying the missing portion: "the substitution of *āt* shall occur. That is to say, when a word expressing a number (*saṅkhyā*) follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *āt* shall occur for the words *dvi* and *aṣṭan*, but not otherwise.

The meaning is "in the case of *bahuvrīhi* compounds and [numbers] up to eighty. He provides an example for the word *dvi*: "twelve" (*dvādaśa*). In cases such as *dvyekāḥ* (meaning "two and one") or *dvyeka* (meaning "one plus two"), [the rule] does not apply;
for according to the rule *cārthe*, "there are no *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa* compounds among the numbers from one to nine with one another."
It is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that this is because it is implied (*dhvanitatva*) in the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the form *dvāviṃśatiḥ*: it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of "two" and "twenty. It does not take the neuter gender according to the rule *sa napuṃsakam*, but rather takes the feminine gender by common usage (*lokāt*).

But there is no mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), because such a meaning is not expressed. Alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "twenty exceeded by eight. Now he provides an example for "eight": "eighteen" (*aṣṭādaśa*). This is either a *dvandva* compound meaning "eight and ten," or it means "ten exceeded by eight. [The example for] "twenty-eight" (*aṣṭāviṃśati*) is: "eight and..."
"Viṃśatiḥ" (twenty) is a collective dvandva compound; its feminine gender is due to common usage, or it may mean "twenty plus eight. Regarding "dvitrāḥ": the analysis is "two or three";
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed by the rule "saṅkhyāvyayāt" (Pāṇini 2.2.25). The suffix *ḍac* is applied by the rule "bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍaj" (Pāṇini 5.4.73).

Because this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the word *dvi* does not occur here; thus, it is *dvyaśītiḥ*. This is either a collective *dvandva* compound meaning "two and eighty," with femininity [of the ending] derived from common usage, or it means "eighty exceeded by two. In this case, because the word *dvi* is followed by *aśīti*, the substitution of *ā* does not take place.
It should have been stated as "before one hundred" (*prāk śatāt*).
Regarding the term *prākśatāt*, it means that the rule *dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṅkhyāyām* does not apply when followed by a numeral word beginning with "one hundred."

The meaning is that it should be stated. Regarding "dviśatam" (two-hundred): it is a collective *dvandva* compound consisting of "two" (*dvi*) and "hundred" (*śata*), or it means "a hundred increased by two. The same applies to "dvisahasram" (two-thousand).
(Pāṇini 6.3.48: *trestrayaḥ* ("for *tri*, [the substitute] *trayaḥ*").

Regarding *trestrayaḥ*: because the word *trayodaśī* is listed among the *sandhivelādi* group, he states that this substitute ends in *s*, saying "it should be *trayaḥ*. Regarding "in the previous case": the meaning is that when a numeral word precedes and another word follows as the *uttarapada*, [the substitution applies], but not in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound or when *aśīti* follows. Thus, *trayodaśa*.

The analysis of the compound is either "three and ten" (*trayaś ca daśa ca*) or "ten with three added to it" (*tryadhikā daśa*). When the case-ending (*sup*) is elided, the word *tri* becomes *trayaḥ*; then, by the rules for *rutva*, *utva*, and *ādguṇa*, [the form] is established. In the same way, *trayoviṃśatiḥ* is also formed.
As for *tridaśāḥ*, the meaning is "ten repeated three times. [This is explained by the rule: *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍac*.

Thus ends the section on *ḍac*. Now, one might object: since the word *trir* here ends in *suc*—by the rule *saṅkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc* and the rule *dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc*—there would result the audible presence of *suc* even in a compound. To this, he says: "A *bahuvrīhi* is used in the sense of *suc*. That is, in the sense of *suc*.

The meaning is that here, because the word *tri* exists through its figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote repetition of an action, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by the rule "a numeral with an indeclinable" (*saṅkhyā-avyaye*), and not with a form ending in the suffix *suC*. As for *tryaśīti*:
it is a collective *dvandva* compound consisting of "three" and "eighty. Its feminine gender is established by common usage (*lokāt*).

Or, it is "eighty-three" (*tryadhikāśīti*). Or, it is "three hundred" (*triśatam*). In the case of *triśatam*, it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*) consisting of "three" and "a hundred. Its feminine gender is according to common usage. Alternatively, it is "eighty-three," where "three" and "eighty" form a collective copulative compound; or it is "a hundred exceeded by three."
Or likewise, "three thousand" (*trisahasra*) and so forth.
(799) *Vibhāṣā catvāriṃśat-prabhṛtau sarveṣām* | 6|3|49|.
There is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the word "forty" (*catvāriṃśat*). This applies even when the rule *dvyaṣṭano'ṭ* [Pāṇini 6.3.47] is separated by other intervening rules.
"For the sake of connection"—meaning for all [the aforementioned words]. The meaning is: "after *dvi*, *aṣṭan*, and *tri*.
Thus he says: "after *dvi*, *aṣṭan*, and *tri*. (800) *ekādiścaikasya cādug* 6.3.76.
"And *eka* etc. [The word] *nañ* from the rule "ṭhnalopo nañaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.73) is understood as a genitive case ending; that is transformed into the nominative. From the rule "nabhrāṇnapāt...
(Pāṇini 6.3.75), the word *prakṛtyā* is understood. Thus he says: "the *nañ* is the base for *eka* etc."—*eka*.

The analysis of the compound is "that of which the first [member] is *ādi*. And [the rule] "there is the augment *ādu* for one" means that the division is either *ādu-uk* or *ṭhadu-uk*. Regarding the phrase "of *nañ* and *viṃśati*":
when there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) based on the analysis "not twenty," the word *navaṃśati* [is joined] with the word *eka*, which ends in the third case.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that "nine hundred" (*nava-śiti*) is a compound (*samāsa*) formed by the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.50] "by one" (*ekena*). Now, one might ask:
since the relation of being "made by that" (*tatkṛtatva*) and so forth is absent here, how can there be a compound with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*)?
To this he says: "due to the division of the yoga-rule" (*yogavibhāgāt*). Regarding the "option for the nasal" (*anunāsika-vikalpa*), this applies when there is a compound with the third case-ending.

When the *su*-suffix has been elided (*lup*), leaving the form *ekānaviṃśatiḥ*, the elision of the *n* that would otherwise have occurred by the rule "the *n* of *nañ* is elided" is prevented by the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form preservation). Consequently, the augment *āt* is added to the word *eka*.

Here, the letter *k* is an *it* (indicatory), and the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Because it is marked with *k* (*kit*), it is an internal constituent (*antāvayava*) [of the preceding element].

There is a long vowel by the rule *savarṇadīrghaḥ*. When *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ* is established, the meaning is that by the rule *ṭhyaro'nunāsike*, the letter *d* may optionally become a nasalized *n*. Even in the alternative case where the augment *aduk* is applied, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) does not occur because of the incapacity of the pronunciation of the vowel *a*. Thus: "not twenty by one."
This is the analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*). The meaning is that by one [unit] less, it does not become twenty;
thus, it is "one less than nineteen" (*ekānnaviṃśati*) or "one less than nineteen" (*ekādnaviṃśati*). There are two forms depending on whether the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) is present or absent.
The meaning is "nineteen" (*ekonaviṃśati*); the word "results" (*paryavasyati*) is to be supplied as the remainder. By one...
The analysis of the compound is "ūna" (deficient). The compound is formed by the rule "pūrvasadṛśe" (with a preceding similar word). That [word] is also "viṃśati" (twenty).

Regarding the rule "ṣaṣa utvam" (the substitution of *u* for *ṣaṣ*): when the words *datṛ* or *daśan* follow as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), or when the suffix *dhā* follows, the word *ṣaṣ* undergoes the substitution of *u*, and the subsequent portion—namely the word *datṛ* or the word *daśan*—[undergoes further changes].
The meaning is that it must be stated that for the *dhā* suffix, there is the substitution of *ṭu* for the initial *da* and for the *dhā* portion as well.

The analysis of the term is simply *ṭu-ātva*, and not *ṣṭu-ātva*, because there is no purpose [for the latter]. According to the *Bhāṣya*, by virtue of the plural number in the rule *dhāsu vā*, only the *dhā* suffix used in the sense of "restraining" (*vidhā*) is to be understood.

When the suffix *dhā* follows, the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of *ṣaṣ* may optionally occur. Kaiyaṭa maintains that the substitution of *ṭu* (ṭa) occurs invariably—following from the previous rule—both when the *utva* (substitution of *u*) takes place and when it does not. Haradatta, however, holds that the substitution of *ṭu* occurs invariably only when the *utva* takes place. Thus, we have *ṣoḍan*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *ṣaḍ-dantā yasya* ("one who has six teeth"), [the form *ṣoḍan* is derived] by the rule *ṭhvayasi*.

In *dantasyadatṛ*, the substitute *datṛ* is applied, and the vowel *ṛ* becomes *i*. The final *ṣ* becomes *u*. By the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs. The *d* becomes *ḍ* by the rule *ṭunā ṭuḥ*. With the suffix *su*, *num* is added because it is marked with the *u*-indicator (*ugit*). There is elision of the case-ending *s*. The final consonant cluster is elided. Because that [elision] is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*), the long vowel does not occur. Thus, the form is *ṣoḍan*.
*Rūpam* (the form). Regarding *ṣoḍaśa*: the analysis is either "six and ten" (*ṣaṭ ca daśa ca*) or "ten beginning with six" (*ṣaḍ-ādikā daśa*).

In the former case, there is the substitution of *u* for the final *ṣ*, the *guṇa* substitution by *ād guṇaḥ*, and the change of *d* to *ḍ* by the rule *ṭu-tāḍau*. Following the opinion of Haradatta, in the alternative where the substitution of *u* does not occur, it is *ṣaḍ-daśa*.

He provides an example for *ve*—namely, *ṣaḍdhā*. [The suffix] *dhā* is used after a numeral in the sense of distribution (*vidhārtha*). However, in the alternative where the change to *ū* (*utva*) does not occur for the final *ṣ*, the change to *u* (*atva*) also does not occur. The point is that, according to the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ* by the application of *jaśtva*. He provides an example for the alternative where *utva* does occur—namely, *ṣoḍhā*.

The suffix *dhā* is applied; the final *ṣ* becomes *u*, *ād-guṇaḥ* (the preceding vowel and *u* coalesce into a guṇa), and by the rule *ṭu-ta-ṣatva-dhatveṣu*, *dha* becomes *ḍha*—this is the intended meaning. However, in Kaiyaṭa’s opinion, even in the alternative where *utva* does not occur, the change to *ḍha* is obligatory. Thus, one has *ṣaḍḍhā*. Kaiyaṭa’s view alone is correct, for the Bhāṣya records only *ṣoḍhā* and *ṣaḍḍhā*.
This is established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* because it has been so cited.

(801) *Paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* | 2|4|26|. "The gender of the latter" (*paravalliṅgam*). The suffix *vati* is added to the word *para* ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyantāt*). Thus he says: "of these two."
Regarding the phrase "as if [the gender] of the subsequent member": here, the term *dvandva* refers specifically to the *itaretarayoga* (coordinative) type of compound.
This is because, in the case of a *samāhāra* (collective) compound, the rule *sa napuṃsakam* ("it is neuter") serves as an exception to that.

In the example "these are a cock and a peahen" (*kukkuṭamayūryāv ime*), since one might otherwise expect no fixed restriction regarding the gender of the individual members within this *dvandva*, [the rule is stated].

This is for the sake of restriction. In the case of *ardhapippalī*, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "the neuter [word] *ardha*" [forms a compound with another]. Since this *ekadeśi-samāsa* (part-whole compound) would—by virtue of being dominated by the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*)—be expected to take the gender of the first member, this rule is prescribed to ensure the gender of the second member (*uttarapada*). In this regard, the rule "in the case of *dvandva*s and *tatpuruṣa*s" [applies].

The word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) refers to the meaning [of the compound]; that is to say, it refers to the meanings of *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa*. And thus, even in the usage "these two are a cock and a peahen" (*kukkuṭamayūryāv ime*), the same gender applies.
A prohibition must be stated regarding *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *panna*, *alaṃpūrva*, and compounds with a *gati* as the first member.

Regarding the term *dviguprāpta*: the meaning is that a prohibition of the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅga*) must be stated in the case of these—*dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam-pūrva*, and *gati-samāsa*.
In the example *pañcasu*, since the final member is neuter, the entire compound would have attained neuter gender [by rule 2.4.26].
It does not take [the gender of] the latter member; rather, it takes the gender of the qualified noun (*viśeṣya*) itself, as in *prāptajīvikaḥ*.
In this case, whatever gender the word *jīvikā* (latter member) possesses, that gender does not belong to the compound.
He gives an example for a compound preceded by *alam*: *alaṃkumāriḥ*. Here...
The feminine suffix (*liṅga*) of the final member of a compound does not occur here. Now, one might object:

"Since there is no connection with the sense of *tad-artha* (for its sake) and so forth, this cannot be a fourth-case (*caturthī*) compound. Nor can it be [governed by] the rule *paryādayo glānādyarthe*, because that compound is compulsory (*nitya*), as stated in the Bhāṣya: "Enough for the maiden" (*alaṃ kumāryai*).

Because it is untenable to demonstrate a formal compound (vigraha), he says "for this very reason. Due to the status of the word *kumārī* as an upasarjana according to the rule "ekavibhakti ca," there is shortening [of the vowel].
He provides an example of a *gati* compound: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. In this case...

The gender of the word *kauśāmbī* does not apply to the compound. Although this is indeed a *nir-ādi* (prepositional) compound and not a *gati* compound— since it has been stated that the inclusion of the term *prādi* is intended to include those that are not *gatis*— nevertheless,
the intention is that the mention of the *gati* compound serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *prādi* compound.

(802) *pūrvapadaśvavaḍavau* |2|4|27|. Regarding *pūrvapadaśvavaḍavau*: in a *dvandva* compound consisting of "horse" (*aśva*) and "mare" (*vaḍabā*), this [sūtra] is intended to establish the gender of the preceding member, overriding the rule that the gender of a *dvandva* is that of the final member (*paravalliṅgam*). Thus, the *dvandva* is *aśvavaḍavau*.

Since the rule "the gender of the first member is obtained" would not apply in the case of the plural number or other case-endings, he says: "the dual number is non-essential. This is an illustration; the meaning is that both the dual number and the case-ending are not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Here, the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*)— [The text continues: ...is for the purpose of excluding the subsequent [member]. For example, in *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātryaḥ* ("five nights of which the fifth is auspicious"), although the word *pañcamī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rātri* (feminine) follows. However, in *pañcālāḥ* ("the people of Pañcāla"), the plural ending is used because the word *janapada* (masculine), which is the first member, is understood. Similarly, in *sarvāsāṃ khalvāsāṃ vīṇānāṃ madhye eṣā sarvasvarā*, although the word *vīṇā* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *madhya* (neuter) follows. Furthermore, in *sarvāsāṃ khalvāsāṃ vīṇānāṃ madhye eṣā sarvasvarā vīṇā*, although the word *vīṇā* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *madhya* (neuter) follows. Thus, the mention of "preceding" is for the purpose of excluding the subsequent [member]. The mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) is for the purpose of excluding number (*saṃkhyā*). For example, in *paṭurūpā strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "number" (*vacana*) is for the purpose of excluding case-endings (*vibhakti*). For example, in *paṭurūpau strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) is for the purpose of excluding the dual number. For example, in *paṭurūpe striyau*, although the word *striyau* (dual feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "both" (*ubhaya*) is for the purpose of excluding the singular number. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "neither" (*na vā*) is for the purpose of excluding the dual number. For example, in *paṭurūpe striyau*, although the word *striyau* (dual feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of excluding the plural number. For example, in *paṭurūpāḥ striyaḥ*, although the word *striyaḥ* (plural feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the neuter" (*napuṃsake*) is for the purpose of excluding the masculine gender. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is for the purpose of excluding the masculine gender. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*) is for the purpose of excluding the neuter gender. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in all cases" (*sarvatra*) is for the purpose of excluding specific instances. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the same" (*samāne*) is for the purpose of excluding different genders. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "of the first member" (*pūrvapadasya*) is for the purpose of excluding the subsequent member. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) is for the purpose of excluding number. For example, in *paṭurūpā strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "number" (*vacana*) is for the purpose of excluding case-endings. For example, in *paṭurūpā strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) is for the purpose of excluding the dual number. For example, in *paṭurūpe striyau*, although the word *striyau* (dual feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "both" (*ubhaya*) is for the purpose of excluding the singular number. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "neither" (*na vā*) is for the purpose of excluding the dual number. For example, in *paṭurūpe striyau*, although the word *striyau* (dual feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of excluding the plural number. For example, in *paṭurūpāḥ striyaḥ*, although the word *striyaḥ* (plural feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the neuter" (*napuṃsake*) is for the purpose of excluding the masculine gender. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is for the purpose of excluding the masculine gender. For example, in *paṭurūpaḥ strī*, although the word *strī* (feminine) is used, it does not take the gender of the first member because the word *rūpa* (neuter) follows. The mention of "in the masculine" (*pu
The meaning is: since the gender would be established by the very act of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), what is the purpose of that [rule]?
(803) *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi* | 2.4.29.

[The words] *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* [are masculine]. The phrase "in compounds consisting of dvandva or tatpuruṣa" (*dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule], [and it is now] put in the nominative plural.

That which has undergone transformation (*vipariṇata*) is distinguished by [the words] *rātri* and so forth; this is the rule for what ends in that [suffix]. The meaning is: "Compounds ending in *rātra*, *ahna*, or *aha*, as well as *dvandva*s and *tatpuruṣa*s, are masculine.
He states the result: "Those ending in these [words]," which is an exception to the rule of taking the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*). Now, regarding *ahorātra*:
Thus, in the case of a collective dvandva compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of neuter gender according to the rule "sa napuṃsakam" (Pāṇini 2.4.17).

Nor should it be argued that this rule for masculine gender is an exception (*apavāda*) to the neuter gender; for, as the principle states: "Exceptions set aside [rules] immediately preceding them, not those further away."
Because, according to the logical principle (*nyāya*), this rule prescribing the masculine gender is merely an exception to the rule regarding the gender of a compound being that of the final member;
therefore, it would have been more appropriate to cite *ahorātrau* as an example of a reciprocal copulative compound (*itaretaradvandva*).
To this, he says: "Because of its proximity" (*anantaratvāt*). The word "this" (*ayam*) refers to the "rule prescribing the masculine gender"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Regarding "ahorātra": it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "day and night" (*ahaśca rātriśca*). Because it is a *dvandva*, the neuter gender applies by virtue of the subsequent rule; however, this [present rule] establishes the masculine gender by overriding both that neuter gender and the rule *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*. [The suffix] *ac* is applied by the rule *ahaḥsarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyācca*. For example: *pūrvāhṇaḥ*. Thus, [the form] *ahnaḥ* [is derived].

The term *pūrva* forms a *ekadeśisamāsa* (compound denoting a part of a whole). By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied; by the rule *ahno'haḥ*, the substitute *ahan* is replaced by *ahaḥ*. Having set aside the neuter gender and the rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgam*), the masculine gender is maintained.
In the analysis *dvayor ahnoḥ samāhāraḥ* ("the collection of two days"), it is a *dvigu* compound; *ṭac* is applied, and [by the rule] *na...* [the neuter ending is prohibited].

By the rule "saṅkhyādeḥ samāhāre," the substitution of the form *ahan* is prohibited. Having set aside the general rule that "the gender of a compound follows the final member" (*paravalliṅgam*), the masculine gender is applied. Because the final member, the word *ahan*, does not end in the vowel *a*, the feminine gender does not apply; for the final member of the compound is a constituent part of the whole compound.

This is a sūtra for the instruction on gender (liṅgānuśāsana) preceded by a numeral; it is not a sūtra belonging to the Aṣṭādhyāyī, nor is it a vārtika, because it is not seen in the Bhāṣya. It is an exception to [the rule] "rātra-ahna-ahaḥ are masculine. For example, *dvirātram* (a two-night period); this is a collective dvigu compound (*samāhāra-dvigu*).
In the rule *ṭhahaḥsarvaikadeśe’tyac*, the word *gaṇarātram* is used. The word *gaṇa* is a synonym for "many" (*bahu*);
by the rule *bahugaṇavati saṅkhyāvat*, it possesses the status of a numeral (*saṅkhyā*). The compound *gaṇarātra* is a *dvigu* meaning "a collection of many nights. The suffix *ac* is applied.

(804) *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* | 2|4|30|. The word *apatha* is neuter. In the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) "not a path" (*na panthāḥ*), when the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is formed and the *n* of *nañ* is elided, the suffix *ap* is applied by the rule "ṛkpūḥ," followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion; thus the word *apatha* is formed, and its meaning is that it is neuter.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*). The phrase "only when it is a *tatpuruṣa*" is used because that [rule] continues to apply from the preceding sūtra, "the gender is that of the final member" (*paravalliṅgam*); however, the mention of *dvandva* does not continue, as it is inapplicable here. The phrase "but elsewhere," however, means "in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*."

Regarding the word *apantha*: the optional application of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is governed by the rule *patho vibhāṣā*. This sūtra is already covered by the forthcoming vārttika, *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*. (805) *ardharcāḥ puṃsi ca* (2.4.31).
Regarding the term *ardharca*: because it is a plural form, he states that it includes those words beginning with it—namely, "the *ardharca* group.

As for the example *ardharcam*: in the analytical compound (*vigraha*) "half of a verse" (*ṛco 'rdham*), the compound is formed by the rule "the word *ardha* is neuter [when compounded with another word].
By the rule "ṛk-pūḥ," the suffix *ac* is applied. This neuter gender overrides the feminine gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅgam*).
The alternative [view] regarding the neuter gender of masculine nouns:

(806) *jātyākhyāyāmekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.58). Regarding the expression of a genus (*jāti*): according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) [denote the universal].
The present rule is commenced because, since [words] denote a genus (*jāti*) and a genus is a single entity, only the singular number would otherwise apply.

The literal meaning of the words is that in the case of a genus-word, even when there is singularity, the plural number might occur. Anticipating the objection that if this were so, forms such as *brāhmaṇā bhojyāḥ* ("Brāhmaṇas should be fed") would not be possible due to the presence of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), [the author states: "in the case of a single referent..."

Intending to show that a word existing [in the plural] expresses many meanings, and thus it is understood that "that which has a single meaning becomes plural," he says: *eko 'py arthaḥ* ("even a single meaning"). The meaning is that it receives an operation (*kārya*) conditioned by plurality.
(807) *asmado dvayoś ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.59).
[The rule] *asmado dvayośca* [is stated]. There is a prohibition regarding that which has a qualifier (*saviśeṣaṇasya*).
Regarding "that which has a qualifier": "You are the king."

In the phrase "we too, elevated by the pride of wisdom derived from having served our gurus," however, the plural number is intended to express the plurality residing in the individual parts [of the group].
(808) Pāṇini 1.2.60: "And [the dual is used] for the asterisms Phalgunī and Proṣṭhapada."

*Phalgunī*: [This is] the nominative dual. The meaning is: "if it denotes two *nakṣatra*s. By the word *ca* ("and"), there is an attraction (*anukarṣa*) of the term "two" (*dvayoḥ*). Thus he says: "in the case of duality. Regarding "the two *pūrva-proṣṭhapada*s": because they are feminine, the substitution of *auṅ* for the dual ending occurs. [The forms are] *proṣṭhapade* and *bhādrapade*.

According to Amara, [the word] *strī* means "woman. Regarding the phrase *phalgunyau māṇavike*: this means they were born at a time conjoined with the *Phalgunī* lunar mansion. The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ*; then, by the rule *lubaviśeṣe*, there is elision (*lup*) of that suffix.
Thereafter, for the sense of "born under" (*jātārthe*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule *phalgunyaṣāḍhābhyāṃ ṭānau*. Because it has the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
(809) In a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of the two asterisms *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*, the dual number is obligatory in place of the plural. 1.2.63. [Examples:
*tiṣyapunarvasū*; *viśākhānurādhāḥ*. [Analysis: *viśākhe ca anurādhāśca* ("Viśākhā and Anurādhā").
The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ* means "Tiṣya and Punarvasū.

From the word *tiṣya* and from the word *punarvasu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "connected with a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ*). This suffix is then elided by the rule "elision when no distinction is intended" (*lub aviśeṣe*). Thereafter, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "born under" (*jātārthe*) by the rule beginning with "sandhivelā-".

The elision [of the dual suffix] occurs by the rule *ṭhśraviṣṭhāphalgunī* etc. The applicability of the four sūtras beginning with *jātyākhyāyām* in this context is to be considered. (810) *sa napuṃsakam* || 2.4.17 || [That [dual] is neuter.]

That [compound] is neuter. By the rule "the *dvigu* is singular," the *dvigu* is mentioned; and by the rule "the *dvandva* [is singular] when it refers to living beings," the *dvandva* is also referred to by the word "that" (*tat*). Both of these are intended to signify a collective (*samāhāra*) meaning, as established by the commentary. Thus he says: "in the sense of a collective. For example: *pañcagavam*.

The term *pañcagavam* is a *dvigu* compound meaning "a collection of five cows. Regarding *dantoṣṭham*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the teeth and the two lips. This is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound) according to the rule "and a *dvandva* [of non-animate things] when preceded by a word denoting a living being. A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in the vowel *a* is desired in the feminine gender.
Regarding "ending in *akāra*": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that whose final member (*uttarapada*) ends in *akāra*.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "it is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*). In the case of *pañcamūlī*, it is a collective *dvigu* compound; its feminine gender is established by the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule "after a *dvigu* [ending in *a*]."

"Or ending in -ā. This means that it should be stated: "or [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is optionally applied after a word ending in -ā. Regarding *pañcakhaṭvam*: this is a collective *dvigu* compound; because it is neuter, the vowel is shortened. Regarding *pañcakhaṭvī*: here, the shortening of the *upasarjana* applies.
Because [the stem] ends in a non-dental consonant, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "dvigoḥ.
Regarding the statement "ano nalopaśca vā dviguḥ striyām":
the term *an* is repeated. One instance is transformed into the nominative case.

The term *dvigu* is connected here [with the word *annanta*]. This is a rule concerning that which ends in such a suffix (*tadantavidhi*). The meaning is: a *dvigu* compound ending in *an* may optionally be feminine; furthermore, there should be the elision (*lopa*) of the *n* of *an*. The mention of the option (*vāgrahaṇam*) is connected only with the word "feminine" (*striyām*), and not even with the elision of the *n*; therefore, even in the absence of femininity, the elision of the *n* still occurs.

Regarding *pañcatakṣī*: the sense is that it is a *dvigu* compound meaning "the collection of five carpenters" (*pañcānāṃ takṣṇāṃ samāhāraḥ*). Femininity is applied, the *n* is elided, and by the rule *dvigoḥ*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added. Regarding *pañcatakṣam*: this is a *samāhāra-dvigu*.
In the alternative view where femininity is absent, there is neuter gender by the rule *sa napuṃsakam*, and the *n* is elided.

Nor should it be argued that, by relying on the internal case-ending, the word *takṣan* becomes a *pada* as a form ending in a *su*-affix, and thus the elision of the *n* will occur by the rule "the *n* is elided in a nominal stem" (*na lopaḥ prātipadika*);
for this is precluded by the prohibition of the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) in the rule "and when it is the second member of a compound" (*uttarapadatve ca*).

"Not for that which ends in *pātra* and so forth. This means it must be stated that for a *samāhāra-dvigu* compound ending in a word belonging to the *pātra*-class group, feminine gender does not apply. Examples are: *pañcapātram*, *tribhuvanam*, and *caturyugam*.
The intention is that in the absence of femininity, there is neuter gender according to the rule *sa napuṃsakam*.
Regarding the phrase "puṇya-sudinābhyām ahnaḥ": it is desired that the neuter gender applies to a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending with the word *ahan* when it follows the words *puṇya* or *sudina*.
As for *puṇya*: [this refers to] a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *ahan* which occurs after the words *puṇya* or *sudina*.

The meaning is that the neuter gender must be stated; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *rātrāhna*. In the case of *puṇyāham*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "an auspicious day. By the rule *rājāhaḥ*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied, resulting in the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). By the rule *utamaikābhyāṃ ca*, the substitution of *atyahna* is prohibited. In the case of *sudināham*:

*Sudinam ahaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; [by adding] the suffix *ṭac*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion. Since the word *sudina* is a synonym for "excellent," there is no tautology. [This applies to compounds] beginning with a numeral or an indeclinable, such as *patha*.

Regarding the rule *pathaḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ*: the remainder [of the sūtra] is "neuter gender must be stated. *Saṅkhyāvyaya* is a collective dvandva compound. *Saṅkhyāvyayam ādiḥ* is a karmadhāraya compound; the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of a directional relation (*digyoga*). The word "para" (following) is the ellipsis. [The base is] *patha*.

The nominative case is applied to a word ending in *a* that has taken a *samāsānta* suffix. Thus it says: "after a numeral or an indeclinable, etc. This is an exception to the rule regarding the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅgatā*). Regarding *tripatha*: the suffix *ap* is added by the rule *ṛkpūḥ*, and there is elision of the *ṭi* portion. Similarly, *vipatha* is also formed. The compound is formed by the rule *prādayo gatādyarthe*.

Regarding the examples *supanthāḥ* and *atipanthāḥ*: the compound is formed by the rule *ṭh-svatī pūjāyām*. By the rule *na pūjanāt*, the addition of a *samāsānta* suffix is prohibited. Since this [prohibition] is already established by necessity, the rule *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* need not be formulated.
"Neuter in the sense of a generic quality (*sāmānya*). This rule that "it is neuter in the sense of a generic quality" is established by logical necessity (*nyāyasiddha*),
since when both the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) are in proximity, neither femininity nor masculinity is manifested.

Because it is only the neuter gender— defined by the characteristic "that which is the interval between the two [masculine and feminine] is the neuter in their absence"— that is logically correct; for this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *dāṇḍināyana* that "the single-enunciation (*ekaśruti*) is a universal term for accent (*svarasarvanāma*), and the neuter is..."

It has been stated that [the term] *liṅga-sarvanāma* [is used]. In the example "mṛdu pacati" (he cooks softly), this is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) ending in the accusative case. For the meaning of the root *pac* is an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*). In that context, the quality of softness (*mṛdutva*) relates to the aspect of softening, and the softening relates to the operation.

It connects as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus, because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the aspect of softening (*viklitti*), which serves as the object (*karman*) relative to the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root, the word *mṛd* takes the accusative case. However, in cases where the meaning of the verbal root connects as the instrument (*karaṇa*), such as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), there [the connection is] heaven by means of the sacrifice.

The meaning is that one should perform [it]. In this context, the instrumental case ending for an adverbial modifier occurs, as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase *prātaḥ kamanīyam*, the meaning is "delightful. Here too, [the usage] of the indeclinable *prātaḥ* [is to be understood].

The sense is that because the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) lacks gender, its qualifier—the word *kamanīya*, which is not an indeclinable—lacks the capacity to convey a specific gender; therefore, it must necessarily be neuter. Furthermore, this applies specifically to cases where the gender is not fixed. Consequently, in examples such as *ādiṃ pacati* or *prātarādiḥ*, [the rule] does not apply.
It occurs [in the neuter], because the word *ādi* has a fixed gender.

(811) *tatpuruṣo’nañ-karmadhārayaḥ* | 2|4|19|. A *tatpuruṣa* compound that is not a negative (*nañ*) compound and is distinct from a *karmadhāraya* compound. A *tatpuruṣa* other than a negative compound and a *karmadhāraya*.

The meaning is that it participates in the grammatical operation to be stated hereafter. He says this: "This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*)," with the understood phrase being "prior to [the rule] *paravalliṅgam*" (Pāṇini 2.4.26).
(812) *saṃjñāyāṃ kanthośīnareṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.20): [The suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *kantha* when it denotes a name, provided it refers to the people of the Uśīnara region.]

Regarding *saṃjñāyāṃ kantho*: this is very easy to understand. Regarding *upajñā*: it is called *upajñā* because it is first known (*upajñāyate = prathamam jñāyate*). In the section governing feminine nouns ending in *ktin*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge* to form the object [of the action].
Regarding *upakrama*: it is called *upakrama* because it is undertaken or begun (*upakramyate = ārabhyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied to denote the object [of the action].

There is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "ṭhnodātopadeśasya". The compound *upajñā-upakrama* is a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva*. This is a specific application of the term "tatpuruṣa". There is an extension of the rule to that which ends in [the aforementioned words] (*tadantavidhi*).
From the rule "sa napuṃsakam", the word "napuṃsakam" (neuter) is carried over as an *anuvṛtti*.

(813) *upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām* | 2|4|21|. He says this: "ending with *upajñā* and ending with *upakrama*. By the word *tat* (that), *upajñā* and *upakrama* are intended. The word *ādi* (beginning) has the sense of priority (*prāthamya*) and emphasizes the state of being first.
The "beginning" (*ādi*) of those two refers to their priority—that is, the beginning of them. The "desire to explain" (*ācikhyāsā*) is the wish to declare that;
it amounts to the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). Thus he says: "the beginning of those two," and so forth.
In the expression "Pāṇini’s *upajñā*," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*). [The compound] "the treatise whose *upajñā* is Pāṇini's" means...

The meaning is "first known by Pāṇini. This section is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules regarding the gender of the compound being that of the final member (*paravalliṅgatva*) and the gender following the substantive (*viśeṣyanighnatva*). In the example *nandopakramaṃ droṇaḥ*, the meaning is "commenced by Nanda. This is a compound with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

(814) *chāyā bāhulye* | 2|4|22|. Regarding the rule *chāyā bāhulye*: since the word *chāyā* functions as a qualifier of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, he states "ending in *chāyā*" with the intention of applying the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) to compounds ending in that term. [He further explains] "the meaning of the prior member" (*pūrvapadārtha*).

When the question arises as to "in whose abundance [is the shadow abundant]?", since the shadow is caused by the substance that serves as its substratum (āpādaka-dravya), it is understood that [the abundance occurs] in the abundance of that [substratum]. And the sense is that, by implication, that substratum constitutes the prior member of the compound (pūrvapadārtha).
What is the purpose of the mention of "abundance" (*bāhulye*)? [Example: *kuḍaḷsya chāyā* = *kuḍaḷcchāyā* ("the shadow of a water-jar").
(815) *sabhārājā'manuṣyapūrvā* |2|4|23|. [The word] *sabhā*; and *rājan* and *amanuṣya* together form *rājā'manuṣyau*; that which has these two as its prior members [is called *rājā'manuṣyapūrvā*].
The analysis of the compound is *sā rājā amanuṣyapūrvā* ("she whose preceding word is 'king' and who is preceded by a non-human").

Because it is a qualifier of a *tatpuruṣa*, the suffix *vidhi* applies to that which ends in [the word "king"]. By the word "king" (*rāja*), only a synonym for "king" is intended, not the specific word *rājan*. Thus he says: "preceded by a synonym for king."
"Ina-sabhā" means "īśvara-sabhā. The analysis of the compound is "the assembly (sabhā) of Ina or of Īśvara.
The point is that the words *ina* and *īśvara* are synonyms for "king" (*rājan*).
It is held that [the rule applies] only to a synonym.
He shows the authority for taking only the synonym by stating: "it is desired only for the synonym.

The word "by the author of the Bhāṣya" is to be supplied as the remainder. The sense is that in the rule *svaṃ rūpam*, the Vārttika—"only for a synonym denoting a king (*rājan*) and so forth when [the suffix] *jit* follows"—is recited in the Bhāṣya. The example is *rājasabhā*.
The sense is that although [the compound] is preceded by the word *rājan*, it is not preceded here by a synonym (*paryāya*) of "king.

As for the example *candraguptasabhā*: the sense is that "Candragupta" is the name of a specific king, and not a synonym for it. [Objection: But surely, because it is preceded by a non-human (*amanuṣya*), [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *devasabhā*?
To this he says: "The word *amanuṣya* is conventional (*rūḍha*). The intention is that the word *asura* refers to Daityas and the like. (816) *aśālā ca* | 2|4|24|.
And "non-hall" (aśālā). This means it has the sense of something other than a hall. The word *sabhā* occurs in the sense of a "hall" (*śālā*) and in the sense of a "gathering" (*saṅghāta*).

Among these, in the preceding rule, the neuter gender was stated for the word *sabhā* when it denotes a hall preceded by a non-human [word] as its first member; now, however, [it is stated] for the word *sabhā* denoting a gathering.
He says that "neuter-ness" is being stated: "the word *sabhā* which has the sense of a collection. This means the word *sabhā*. (817) *Vibhāṣā senā-surā-cchāyā-śālā-niśānām* | 2|4|25|.
[The rule] "optionally (*vibhāṣā*) for *senā*" [is explained as follows]: the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative. The term "*tatpuruṣa*" is understood [from the previous rule].

It is qualified by *senā* and so forth; this is an application of the rule regarding what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*). Thus he says: "ending in this. The singular number is used with reference to each individual member. Regarding *śvaniśam*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is *śuno niśā* (the night of the dog). They say it refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*), as in: "We see the dog fasting on the fourteenth day."

This is established in the *Śābarabhāṣya* under the section concerning animals (*tiryagadhikaraṇa*). Regarding the example "Dṛḍhasena": it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose army (*senā*) is firm (*dṛḍhā*). Because it lacks the status of a *tatpuruṣa*, there is no option for the neuter gender.
Regarding "Asena": even though it is a *tatpuruṣa*, because it is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), there is no option for the neuter gender.
Regarding the term *paramasenā*: because it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, it does not take the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
Kaiyaṭa has explained in detail that the purpose of the introductory rule "a *tatpuruṣa* that is not a negative (*nañ*) *karmadhāraya*" applies precisely here.
Thus concludes the section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
