It is understood that a *repha* should not be applied after the letter *bha*, nor should a *sakāra* (the sound *s*) be applied before the letter *ja*. Thus, the result is the exclusion of those two [sounds]. Consequently, when the form *bharj* is established:

He states the form for the dual and subsequent endings with the word *babharja*. Even in the case of *atus* and other endings, because they follow a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is an absence of *kit*-status; therefore, by the rule *grahijyā*, no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs.
Since the optionality of the augment *iṭ* in the *thali* ending is governed by the Bhāradvāja restriction, he says: *babharjitha* or *babharṣṭha*.
In the alternative view where *iṭ* is absent, the form *bhrasj tha* being established, the rule *vraśca* changes the *j* to *ṣ*. By the rule *ṣṭuan*, the *th* becomes *ṭh*;

this is the intended meaning. [The forms] *babharjiva* and so on follow. Regarding the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings of the perfect tense (*liṭ*), he says: *babharje*. *Babharjāte* and so forth are easy to understand. In the absence of *ram*, he says: *babhrajja*. In the case of the suffix *ṇal*, [the stem is] *bhrasj a*.

When the state *babhrasj-a* is reached—following the establishment of reduplication (*dvitva*), the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) for the initial of the reduplicated syllable—the letter *s* is replaced by *ś* according to the rule of *ścutva*, and the letter *ś* is replaced by *j* according to the rule of *jaśtva*; this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) applying to the reduplicated syllable by the rule *liṭ-abhyāsasya*, because the *halādiśeṣa* has already taken effect on the reduplication.

Because of the absence of the letter *r*. Regarding *babhrajjatuḥ*: the intention is that there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) by the rule *grahijyā-*, because [the root] follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), is not followed by an affix beginning with *k* (*akitvāt*), and so forth. Regarding *babhrajjitha*: since the augment *iṭ* is optional according to the Bhāradvāja-rule (*bhāradvājaniyama*) in the case of the *thal* suffix, he states *babhrajjā* for the alternative where *iṭ* is absent and the *ram* augment is also absent.

*babhrāja* (he shone), *babhrajiṣe* (you have shone)—these and others are easy to understand. Regarding *bhraṣṭā*: this is the form when the substitution of *ra* (*rambhāva*) takes place. Regarding *bharṣṭā*: when *ram* is inserted, we have *bharj-tā*; then, by the rule *vraśca* etc., the *ja* is changed to *ṣ*, and by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, the *ta* is changed to *ṭ*—this is the intended meaning. Similarly: *bhrakṣyati* and *bharkṣyati*.

The specific rule here is that when *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* applies [to change the *ṣ* to *k*], there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. Thus: *bhṛjjatu*, *abhṛjjat*, *bhṛjjēt*. Now, one might object: in the case of the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) where the form *bhrasj-yāt* is established, since the augment *yāsuṭ* is *kit*, there would be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyāvayi-vyadhivaṣṭivicati-vaṭi-cchadī-nāṃ ca*, followed by the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds (*pūrvarūpa*). Then, by the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*, the *s* would become *ś*, and for the *ś*...

He will state that the form *bhṛjjyāt* occurs when [the substitution] *jaś* applies as *jakāra*. That is incorrect; for, since the augment *ram* would apply later and thus override *saṃprasāraṇa*, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be *bharjyāt*. Therefore, he says: "The augment *ram* [is applied] before *kṅit*. This refers to the *āśīr-liṅ* (optative) in the *ātmanepada*, with the suffix *sīyuṭ*.

Regarding the alternative where the augment *ram* is applied, he says: *bharakṣīṣṭa*. But in the absence of *ram*, since the root is not *akit*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*; thus he says: *bhrakṣīṣṭa*. Regarding the *luṅ* [aorist] in the parasmaipada, considering the optionality of the *ram* augment, he says: *abhārkṣīt* and *abhrākṣīt*. In the ātmanepada, [the form is derived] with *sic*.

Having considered the alternative view regarding the arrival of *ram*, he says: "abharṣṭa," "abharṣṭa. There is the elision of the *sic* suffix by the rule *jhalo jhali*. Regarding the root *kṣip* in the sense of "impelling," it is *aniṭ*.
Because it lacks the vowel *a* at its end (*ajanta*), the *iṭ* augment is obligatory in the *thal* suffix by the rule *krādiniyama*; thus: *cikṣepitha*. Likewise...

The root *kṛṣ* also [is treated similarly]. In the periphrastic future (*luṭ*), after the suffix *tās*, there is an optional insertion of the augment *am* by the rule "anudātasya cardupadhasya. In the absence of the augment *am*, there is *guṇa* substitution, followed by the replacement of the vowel with *ra* (raparatva).
Thus he says: *kraṣṭā* or *karṣṭā*. Regarding the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*) in the parasmaipada, he says: *kṛṣyāt*.

The sense is that because [the root] ends in *k* and lacks the *aj-jhal-āditva* (beginning with a vowel or *jhal* consonant), there is neither the augment *am* nor *guṇa*. Regarding the *āśīr-liṅ* (precative) in *ātmanepada*, he says: *spṛkṣīṣṭa*. The sense is that because of the *kit* designation by the rule *liṅ-sicau*, there is neither the augment *am* nor *guṇa*. Regarding the *luṅ* (aorist) in *parasmaipada*, he says: *spṛśamṛśeti sijvā*.

Regarding the phrase "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): the meaning is that in the alternative where the *sic* suffix is absent, the *ksa* suffix applies by the rule "after *śal*" (*śalaḥ*). Regarding "in the case of *sic*, there is optionally *am*": the meaning is that in the case of *sic*, the augment *am* is optional by the rule "and after an unaccented [root]" (*anudātasya ca*). The point is that in the case of *ksa*, however, because it is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), the augment *am* does not occur. As for *akrākṣīt*: this is the form when *am* is added in the case of *sic*.
Regarding *akārṣīt*: the intention is that when the substitution of *s* for *sic* does not occur, there is *vṛddhi* by virtue of the rule concerning stems ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*).

Regarding the alternative where the substitution of *ks* occurs, he says: *akṛkṣat*. One should understand that because of the *kit* designation, there is no augment and no *guṇa*. Regarding *akṛṣṭa*: the intention is that the *sic* is elided by the rule "when a *jhal* [consonant] follows a *jhal* [consonant]" (*jhalo jhalī*). Regarding *akṛkṣat*.

The meaning is that there is no *kit* affixation nor *guṇa* substitution. Regarding "in the case of *taṅ*": when *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* ending) is applied in the alternative involving *sic*, we have the form *akṛṣ + s + ta*; the meaning is that there is no *kit* affixation by the rule "liṅsicau". It should be understood that *guṇa* also does not occur. Regarding "akṛṣṭa": the meaning is that the *sij* suffix is elided by the rule "jhalo jhalīṭ". Regarding "akṛkṣata": [the same applies].

In the view that there is the substitution of *ad*, the sense is that because it follows after a non-*an* vowel, the substitution of *ad* occurs by virtue of its being subsequent [in the rule]. Regarding the view that there is the substitution of *ks*, he says: *akṛkṣata*.

The sense is that because of the *kit* designation, there is no lengthening (*am*). As for *akṛkṣanta*: in the view that there is the substitution of *ks*, when the form *akṛkṣa-jha* is established, because there is no *ac* vowel following immediately after, the elision of the *a* of *ks* (by the rule *ksasyāci*) does not occur; therefore...

The intention is that, due to its being subsequent, there is no substitution for the initial [augment], but rather a substitution for the final [element]. Regarding the root *ṛṣ* (in the sense of "to go"):

it is *seṭ*. [Examples: *ānarṣitha*, *ānarṣiva*; [future] *arṣitā*; [aorist] *ārṣīt*. Regarding the root *vij* (in the sense of "fear"): it is *seṭ*. In cases such as *udvijita*, when the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would otherwise apply—

(365) *vija iṭ* |1|2|2|. From the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyo ṅit*, the term *ṅit* is understood to carry over. Thus he says: "after the root *vij*" and so forth. [Examples: *udvijitā*, *udvijiṣīṣṭa*, *udavijiṣṭa*.

Because the root *vraśc* is marked with the *udit* designation, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied. When the rule *grahijyā* applies and the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) follows, the form is *vraśc ati*.

Since the suffix *śa* is treated as having the marker *apit*, it is considered *ṅit*; consequently, by the rule *grahijyā*, the semivowel *r* undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) to become *ṛ*, followed by the formation of the single substitute (pūrvarūpa). This is the intended meaning. Thus he says: "he cuts" (*vṛścati*), "they two cut" (*vṛścataḥ*), "they cut" (*vṛścanti*), and so forth.
*vavraśca*—this is the form in the *ṇal* suffix. The procedure for the *thal* suffix will be explained immediately below.

In the case of *atus* and so on, because they follow a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is no *kit* status; therefore, by the rule *grahijyā*, there is no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). Thus he says: *vavraścatuḥ*. Because it has the marker *ū* (ūdit), there is optionally the augment *iṭ* in the *thal* suffix. Thus he says:

Regarding the form *vavraścitha* from the root *vraśc*: in the Dhātupāṭha, under the entry *vraścū*, the root is presented as *vras-c* with the letter *ś* (śakāra) used in place of *s* due to the rule of *ścutva*. Thus, when we have *vavraśc-tha*, because *ścutva* is considered *asiddha* (not yet applied), the *s* is elided by the rule *skoḥ*, and then [the following applies] to the *c*.
By the rule *ṭh-v-raś-c-eti*, the letter *ṣ* is substituted; then, by the rule *ṣṭuan*, the letter *th* is changed to *ṭh*, resulting in the form *vavraṣṭha*. Similarly, *vavraściva*.

Now, one might object: when reduplication (*dvitva*) has occurred for both the *ṇal* and *thal* suffixes—which are not *kit*—then, according to the rule *liṭ-abhyāsasya*, should not both the *v* and *r* belonging to the reduplicated portion [be subject to change]?

There would be *saṃprasāraṇa*. Nor should one fear the prohibition of *saṃprasāraṇa* for the letter *v* by the rule "there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* when there is [already] *saṃprasāraṇa*" (*na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam*), because the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *v* is possible first; therefore, he says:
"in the case of the reduplication of the *liṭ*. Precisely because of the prohibition "there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*... [the rule applies].
The meaning is that, by way of indication (*jñāpaka*), the *ṛ*-vowel is first the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitute for the *r*-phoneme.
He causes one to remember the rule for the substitution of the vowel *a* for that *ṛ*-vowel which has been produced as a *saṃprasāraṇa*, namely: "ur aṇ raparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.50).
[Objection: But once the *ṛ*-vowel has been changed to *a*, would there not then be a *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution for the *v*-phoneme?

Since the prohibition "na saṃprasāraṇe" (Pāṇini 1.1.45) does not apply here—because there is an absence of a subsequent *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel—he says: "And of that," meaning "of the vowel *a*. Nor should it be argued:

"How can there be the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* [substitute] for the *u*, given that the cause (*nimitta*) for the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* is not heard [as being present in the subsequent element]?"

Having accepted that "the section on *aṅga* extends until the end of the *pāda*," one accepts that [the rule] is caused by the suffix (*pratyaya*) which brings about the designation of *aṅga*. However, the maxim that "a rule applies only once to its object" does not apply here, precisely because of the prohibition in the rule "not when there is *saṃprasāraṇa*."

It is understood that [the rule] operates when there is a difference in the locus (*sthānin*). For this very reason, in cases such as *śuddhyupāsya*, once the doubling of the letter *dh* has occurred, the preceding *dh* becomes *d* by the application of the *jaś*-rule, and then that *d* undergoes doubling; let this matter rest for now. In the benedictive mood (*āśīr-liṅ*), [the example is] *vṛścyāt*.

The sense is that there is *saṃprasāraṇa* because [the root] ends in a *kit* suffix. Regarding *avrākṣīt*: when the form *avraśc sīt* has been established, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by virtue of the rule for roots ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā-vṛddhi*). Because the change of *ś* to *ṣ* (*ścutva*) is considered *asiddha*, the *s* is elided by the rule *ṭhskoḥ*.
Then, by the rule *vraśca*, the *c* becomes *ṣ*; by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kassi*, that *ṣ* becomes *k*; and the *s* of the suffix becomes *ṣ*. This is the intended meaning.

They say: "In verbal roots beginning with *jhal*, the fifth letter of the *anusvāra* group [nasals] arises from *ṭha*; the letter *śa* arises from *sa*; *śca* [the palatals] arise from *ṣa*; and the *ṭa*-group arises from the *ta*-group. Regarding the root *vyac*, which is *seṭ* (having an indicatory *i*), having considered that there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "*grahi-jyā-vayi-vyadhi-vaś-ciy-aḥ*", he says: *vicati*. [The perfect form is] *vivyāca*.

By the rule *ṭhliṭaḷbhyāsasya*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *y* of the reduplicated stem; by the rule *ṭhna saṃprasāraṇe*, there is no vocalization of the *v*. Thus, one has *vivicatur*. The intention is that because it is marked with *k* (kit), vocalization occurs according to the rule *ṭhgrahijye*, after which reduplication takes place. [The forms are] *vivyacitha*, *viviciva*, and *vicyāt*.

In the benedictive (āśīrliṅ), because the suffix begins with *ik*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *y*. Considering the optional *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "ato halādeḥ," he says: *avyācīt* or *avyacīt*. Now, one might object that since it is stated that "the root *vyac* belongs to the *kuṭādi* group except when followed by the suffix *anas*," [the form] would be *vyacitā*.
In forms such as *vyaciṣyati* and others, since the root begins with a guttural (*kuṭādi*), the substitution of *iṭ* for *sa* (the *siṃprasāraṇa*) would occur by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*;
therefore, he says: "of *vyaci*. [The phrase] *kṛnmātra* contains the word *mātra* used in the sense of restriction.
The roots *ucchi* (meaning "to glean") and *uchī* (meaning "to shine") are listed in the Bhvādi class; however, their inclusion here [in this specific context] is...

The suffix *ś* serves the purpose of forming a feminine derivative (*śavikaraṇa*). By means of that, in the forms *uñcchatī* and *uñchantī*, as well as *uccchatī* and *uccchantī*, the optional insertion of *num*—governed by the rule *ṭhācchīnadyo'r*—is established. As for its inclusion in the *bhvādi* class, it is for the sake of the accentuation of the *pit* suffix; this is explained in detail elsewhere. Regarding the root *ṛccha* meaning "to go," when the augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *che ca*, that [augment] becomes *ś* by virtue of the rule *śacutvena*.

This is an irregular (cakāni) designation. Regarding the root *ṛcchati*: since the condition for *guṇa* substitution does not apply because the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is not light (*laghu*) in the *ṇal* suffix, he says [the rule] "ṛcchatyṛtām.

After doubling, the substitution of *ur*, the application of *halādiśeṣa*, and the lengthening by "ata ādeḥ," we arrive at the form *ārccha*. Since there are many consonants (*bahuhaltva*), the condition for *nuk* does not apply because it requires two consonants (*vihaltva*); regarding this, he says [the following].

Regarding the mention of "dvihal" (having two vowels): in *ānarccha*, there is no *ām* because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of roots ending in *ṛcch* in the rule *ijāder ṇaḥ*. In *ṛcchata*, the point is that there is no *guṇa* substitution because the word "liṭi" (in the perfect tense) is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*) in the rule *ṛcchatyṛtām*. The root *lubh* is *seṭ* (possessing an indicatory *i*); considering that it takes *iṭ* optionally by the rule *tīṣasaharuceṛkṣiyakṣmāyyātāṃ puṅ ṇau*, he says:

"Lobhitā" means "greedy. "Śiśum na" [is used]; here the particle *na* has the sense of *iva*. "The sages lick the child with their intellects"—the meaning is that they do not harm him. The root *tṛp* takes only the *śyan* suffix and is *aniṭ*;
this is because it is an exception (*apavāda*) [to the general rule], and the intention is that an exception must occupy the same position as its general rule (*utsarga*). *Cṛtī*...

Regarding the statement "hiṃsā-śranthanayoḥ": *śranthana* means loosening (*visraṃsana*). The forms *cṛtati* and so forth are easy to understand. As for Āśvalāyana’s rule, "then he loosens its thong" (*athāsya yoktraṃ vicṛte*), the meaning is that he should cause it to loosen (*visraṃsayet*), due to the influence of the prefix. However, in the Āpastamba Sūtra, "the sacrificer loosens his girdle" (*yajamāno mekhalāṃ vicṛtate*), [the sense is different].

That is an archaic form. The root *ṣu* is taught with an initial *ṣ*. Regarding *kura* in the sense of "sound," the fact that it is derived from *kṛ* alone is the only authority here; this is simply a matter of traditional explanation. The root *vṛh* has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel. Because it is marked with an indicatory *ū* (*ūdit*), it optionally takes the augment *iṭ*. "Beginning with the labial class" (*pavargādi*) means beginning with the third letter of the labial class. [The roots] are *tṛh*, *stṛh*, and *tṛṃh*.
All three [roots] contain the letter *ṛ*. The third [root] contains an *anusvāra*. Because it has an *udātta* accent, the augment *iṭ* is optional.

Thus: *tarḍhati*. From the root *tṛh*, after the suffix *tāsi*, there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *tha*, the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu*, and the elision of *ḍha*. Similarly: *starḍhā*, *tṛṇḍhā*. [In the aorist: *atarhīt* or *atārkṣīt*; *astarhīt* or *astārkṣīt*.

He states [the forms] as if they were already established: *atṛṃhīt* and *atārṅkṣīt*. In the alternative where there is no *iṭ* augment after the root *tṛṃh*, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule for roots ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇa-vṛddhi*), followed by *raparatva*.
Then *h* becomes *ḍh*, *ḍh* becomes *k*, and *ṣatva* is applied. The intention is that the *anusvāra* becomes a *ṅ* sound through *parasavarṇa*. As for *atārḍhām*:
The intention is that the *anusvāra* becomes a *ṅ* sound through *parasavarṇa*. As for *atārḍhām*: [the formation follows the same process].

The meaning is as follows: from *tṛh* (to injure), in the third person plural (*tas*), after the elision of *si* in the absence of the augment *iṭ*, there is the lengthening (*vṛddhi*) conditioned by a consonant at the end of the root; then follow the changes of *ḍhatva*, *dhatva*, *ṣṭutva*, and the elision of *ḍha* and *ñ*. Thus: [from *stṛh*]—*astārḍham*;
[from *tṛṃh*]—*atārṇḍham*. The root *sphur* means "to quiver."

(366) *sphurati-sphulatyornirnivibhyaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.76. [This rule applies to] the roots *sphurati* and *sphulati*. The term "retroflex" (*mūrdhanya*) is understood from the governing context. From the rule *sivādīnāṃ vā*, the word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over. Therefore, he says: "there may optionally be the substitution of the sibilant *ṣ*. [The root] *ṇū* means "to praise."

This is an instruction (*upadeśa*). Regarding the word *pariṇūta*: by the rule "there is no *iṭ* after a root ending in *śri*, *yu*, or *ku* followed by a *kit* suffix," there is no *iṭ*. The root *kuṅ* means "to sound"; it ends in a long vowel, and therefore it is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*). The root *pṛṅ* means "exertion"; it ends in a short vowel and is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). Thinking that [the root] would take *iṭ* by the rule "there is *iṭ* before *sya* after roots ending in *ṛt* or *han*," he says: *vyāpariṣyate*.
Thus: the root *mṛ* is *aniṭ*.
(Pāṇini 1.3.61) *mriyate-luṅ-liṅoś-ca*. From the rule "anudātta-hitaḥ," the term "ātmanepada" is understood to carry over. By the word "ca" (and), [the suffixes of the luṅ and liṅ are also included].

From the rule "ṭhśadeḥ śitaḥ," the term "śitaḥ" is drawn over [by anuvṛtti]. The word "prakṛtibhūtāt" (from the original base) is to be supplied. Thus he says: "luṅ-liṅoḥ. "Taṅ syāt" means that the ātmanepada suffixes would occur; this is also the case for the nasal [augment] in "mriyamāṇa."

Because it is desired. Now, one might object: "Since this is already established by the very fact of being *hit*, for what purpose is this [rule] stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*) to indicate that it is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*). Then, one might ask: "In that case, the *ṅt* suffix is redundant. To this he replies: "The *ṅt* suffix is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtham*)."

The meaning is that [the rule] "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following a root taught with an *anudātta* vowel or marked by *ṅ* or *it* are *anudātta*" applies here. Thus, in the case of *mriyate*, once the *śe* affix is applied, the sense is that the *riṅ* substitution occurs by the rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*. He says "even in the opinion of Bhāradvāja" because, due to the root ending in *ṛ*, the augment *iṭ* does not apply; hence he says "mamartha. In *mamṛv-e*, the *iṭ* is added by the rule *krādiniyamāt*. In *martā*, having considered the *iṭ* by the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye*, he says "mariṣyati. As for *ri pi gatau*, these two roots are both *aniṭ*.

[Objection: But once *śe* has been applied, since the *ik* vowel [of the root] follows [the suffix], wouldn't the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) take effect because it is subsequent? To this he says: "Because it is internal (*antarangatvāt*), *iyaṅ* [applies]. Regarding *kṝ* in the sense of "scattering": this [root] has a long vowel and is not nasalized (*anata*); it takes the augment *iṭ*. Thus, *kirati*. The substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (P. 7.1.100), and then there is the substitution of *ra* [for *ṛ*]. Regarding *cakra-tuḥ*: the intention is that even though the suffix is *kit*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "ṛcchatyṛtām" (P. 7.4.11). Thinking of the rule "vṛto vā" (P. 7.2.38), he says: *karitā* or *karītā*. (368) P. 6.1.140: "In the case of *kṝ* when meaning 'cutting' (*lavane*). Regarding "after *upa*": this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "after *upa* in the sense of 'effort toward something' (*pratiyatne')" from the previous sūtra.
The meaning is that *suṭ* is an augment (*āgama*). The intention is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "suṭ is placed before the root-initial *k*.

The Vārttika states, "even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). This is obtained through the continued application of the rule "suṭ is placed before the root-initial *k*."

(369) *hiṃsāyāṃ prateśca* |6|1|141|. Regarding the rule "in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*) and after *prati*": by the word *ca* ("and"), *upa* is also included. Thus he says: "*upa*" [is understood]. The root *gṛ* means "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*). Swallowing is eating. It takes the augment *iṭ*.

(370) *aci vibhāṣā* | Pāṇini 8.2.21. The term *aci* means "before a vowel. From the rule *gro yaṅi*, the word *gra* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*). From the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*, the phrase *ro laḥ* is understood. Thus he says: "of the root *gṛ*" (*girateḥ*). "Before a vowel-initial [suffix]" (*ajādau*) [is understood] from the rule *dhātoḥ*.

When an operation (*kārya*) is being stated, it occurs in relation to that which is a suffix (*pratyaya*); thus, by qualifying the suffix—obtained through a *paribhāṣā*—with the vowel (*ac*), the rule of "specification of the beginning" (*tadādividhi*) applies. Consequently, in forms such as *girau*, [the substitution does not occur], as is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" (*mṛjervṛddhiḥ*). The root *dṛṅ* means "to respect."

This [root] ends in a short vowel. Because it is marked with *k* by the rule "ṭhuśca," there is no *guṇa* substitution. Regarding *ādṛta*: the elision of *s* occurs by the rule "hrasvādaṅgāt. Regarding "pracccha jñīpsāyām": the desire to know is *jñīpsā*.
This root is without the augment *iṭ*. In *pṛcchati*, because *ś* is marked with *ṅ*, the *r* is replaced by *ṣ* according to the rule "gṛhijyā-."

The meaning is that there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization), which becomes the short *ṛ*-vowel, followed by the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute for the preceding vowel and the *ṛ*). Regarding the form *papracchatuḥ*:
because it follows a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant), the suffix lacks *kit*-status, and thus there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*; this is the intended sense.
According to the rule of Bhāradvāja, the suffix *thal* may optionally take *iṭ*; hence he says: *papracchitha* or *papraṣṭha*.

In the alternative where *iḍ* is absent, the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch* occurs by the rule *vraśca-ādi-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), and the substitution of *ṭh* for *th* occurs by the rule *ṣṭuan* (Pāṇini 8.4.41);

this is the intended meaning [of the forms] *papracchi-va* and *praṣṭṛ*. Regarding the substitution of *ṣ* for *ch*, it is because the rule *vraśca-* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) includes the *ch* with its inherent *t* (i.e., *cch*).

As for the statement "the roots beginning with *kṝ* are listed as *vṛt*" (Pāṇini 7.2.58), it is not the case that, such being the situation, [the rule] *kiraśca pañcabhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.75) [would apply].

It should not be argued that the mention of "five" (pañca) is redundant because the roots beginning with *kṛ* are five; for this is intended for the sake of the subsequent rule, *ṭhrudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*. [The root] *sṛj* (to emit/cre-ate) is *aniṭ*. [Examples:

*sṛjati*, *sasṛja*, *sasṛjatuḥ*. Even though there is an absence of being both vowel-ending (*ajanta*) and having the vowel *a* (*akāravat*), [the rule applies] by virtue of the optionality [stated in] *vibhāṣā*.
Thinking that by the rule *sṛjidṛśor ar* [Pāṇini 7.2.59], there is optionally *iṭ* before the suffix *thal*, he says: *sasarjitha* and *sasraṣṭha*.

In the absence of *iṭ*, by the rule *vraśca-* [Pāṇini 8.2.36], the *ṣ* replaces the *j*; by the rule *ṣṭuan* [Pāṇini 8.4.41], the *th* becomes *ṭh*; and because it is *pit* (having *p* as its marker), it is not *kit*, so by the rule *sṛjidṛśor ar* [Pāṇini 7.2.59], the augment *am* is applied—this is the intended meaning.
[The form] *sasṛjiva* [is formed]. Now, the root *masj* (to immerse).

Regarding *majjati*: the substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs by the rule of *ścutva*, and the substitution of *j* for that *ś* occurs by the rule of *jaśtva*; this is the underlying idea. Regarding *mamaṅktha*: after the reduplication of the root *masj*, the rule of *halādiśeṣa* applies, resulting in *mamasj tha*.
Then, by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*, the *s* is elided, leaving *mamaj tha*. Finally, the substitution of *g* for *j* occurs by the rule of *kutva*.

It should be understood that when the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ṭhmasjinaśor ar*, the *anusvāra* replaces it, which is then changed to *ṅ* by the rule of *parasavarṇa*, and the *g* is changed to *k* by the rule of *cartya*. Although this result is achieved even if *num* were placed after the vowel *a*, nevertheless, in forms such as *magna*, the rule *ṭhantyātpūrvo num* [is required].

The elision of *n* is the result; otherwise, due to the absence of the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the elision of *n* would not occur—this is the intended meaning. Similarly, [one forms] *maṅktā*. However, in *maṅkṣyati*, the specific difference is the change of *s* to *ṣ*. Starting from the root *ruj* (in the sense of "breaking") up to before *viccha* (in the sense of "going"), these roots are *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). Regarding the rule *anudātasya*...
Considering that there is an option for the augment *it* when a root has a consonant as its penultimate letter (*cardupadhasya*), he says: "spraṣṭā, spaṣṭā. The root *ṇud* means "to impel";

this is a root taught with an initial *ṇ*. From the root *viś* ("to enter") up to *sadlṛ* ("to perish"), all are *aniṭ* (not taking the augment *iṭ*). Among them, for a root with a short vowel as its penultimate letter (*adupadhasya*), the augment *iṭ* is optional after the suffix *thali*; however, for any other [root], the *iṭ* is compulsory. This applies to the root *mṛś*.
There is an optional alternative due to the rule *anudātasya ca*. Thus he says: *amrākṣīt* and *amarkṣīt*.

The intention is that by the rule *spṛśamṛśakṛṣatṛpāṃ sij vā*, the *sij* affix is optionally applied. When *sij* is absent, considering the rule *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*, he says: *amṛkṣat*. The root *nud* is taught with a *ṇ* (i.e., it is a *ṇopadeśa*). [Objection: But [it belongs to] the *tanādi* class...
One might ask: since this root has already been read among the *svarita*-marked roots, for what purpose is it read here? To this he says:

"even when the action benefits the agent" (*kartrabhiprāye’pi*). One might further object that since forms such as *sīdati* are established from the very root *ṣadlṛ* read in the *bhvādi* class, its reading here is redundant; to this he says: "the reading here [is for the following reason]."

Regarding the word *sīdanti*: the inclusion here is for the purpose of making the *num* augment optional by means of the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle), followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, and then applying the rule *ṭācchīnadyor nuṃ*. The intention is that if it were included only in the *bhvādi* class, the *num* would be compulsory by the rule *śapśyanornityam*. If that were so—
Since its inclusion in the *jvalādi* sub-group within the *bhvādi* class would otherwise be redundant, he says: "In the *jvalādi* group.

The intention is that it is for the sake of the *ṇa*-suffix in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *ṭhjvalitikasantebhyaḥ*. He demonstrates this by providing an example: "sādaḥ" (sinking). He states another result of its being listed in both groups: "and for the sake of the accent" (*svarārthaśca*).

He clarifies that very point: "śa-anudātta" (the root *śa* is unaccented). The intention is that this is due to the accent of a *pit* suffix, according to the rule "anudātau suppitau. As for "śas-tūdāttaḥ" (the suffix *śas* is accented), the intention is that this is by the rule "pratyayaḥ" and "ādyudāttaśca. [An objection: But surely [the root] "śadlṛ śātane" (to fall off) occurs in the *bhvādi* class?
Since [the form] would be established by the mere recitation [of the root], the inclusion here is redundant; therefore, he says: "only for its own sake.
This means it is solely for the purpose of the difference in accentuation caused by the previously mentioned *pit* and *apit* status. √*muc*ḷ, in the sense of releasing.
(371) *śe mucādīnām* 7.1.59.

"Of *muc* and the others: there shall be *num*. This is a supplement to the rule (*śeṣapūraṇam*). The intention is that this follows from the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "a root marked with *ṭh* or *id* takes *num*" (*ṭhidito num*). Regarding *mukṣīṣṭa*: the intention is that there is no *guṇa* substitution because [the suffix] is *kit* by the rule "the *liṅ* and *sic* [are *kit*]" (*liṅsicau*). Regarding *amucat*: the intention is that *aṅ* is substituted because it is marked with *ḷ*. [This concerns] *luṅ*.

Regarding the form *taṅāhi*: it means "not released. [The rule] *ṭhjalo jhalī* applies for the elision of the *sic* suffix. [The root] *lip* means "to smear. Regarding *taṅ tu vai*: the remainder [of the explanation] is that this is by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām*. [The root] *ṣic* means "to flow. Regarding *abhiṣiñcati*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*.

Regarding *abhyaṣiñcat*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *prāksitāḍvyavāye 'pi*. Regarding *abhiṣiṣeca*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena*. Regarding *kṛtī chedane*: the presence of the marker *ī* is for the sake of the rule *śvīdita*. Thinking that there is an option for the augment *iṭ* by the rule *seca sicī*, he says: *kārtiṣyati*.

"He will cut" (*kartsyati*). [The root] *piś* means "to divide" (*avayava*); the meaning is "in the act of dividing. "May he manifest forms" (*rūpāṇi piṃśatu*); the meaning is "may he reveal. Thus end the *tud*-class roots.
Thus ends the section on the *tud*-class roots in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now begins the section on the *uṇādi* suffixes.
Now begins the first quarter (*pāda*).
Now follow the *uṇādi* sūtras beginning with *kṛ-vā-pā-jī*, both in the root-text and in the *Prakriyā-prakāśa* (the *Prakriyākaumudī*), as well as in the *Prakriyā-kaumudī-manoramā*.

These have been clearly explained; nevertheless, they are now being explained by us as well, without excessive prolixity. Furthermore, these sūtras were composed by the sage Śākaṭāyana and not by Pāṇini, as stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṭuṇādayo bahulam" under the heading "nāma ca."

It is stated in the *Nirukta* that [the word] is "born from the elements" (*dhātujam*), and it was mentioned during the commentary on the *Vārttika* regarding the word *śakaṭasya tokam*. Kaiyaṭa maintains that the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) is for the purpose of authorizing the correctness of the *uṇādi* suffixes which are recited in other treatises; for these [suffixes] do not...

The term "other treatises" (*śāstrāntara*) is applicable to the Pāṇinian system. Words ending in *uṇādi* suffixes are indeed unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) according to the doctrine of Pāṇini. For this very reason, in the rule *ṭhāyaneyī*, it is established that for the venerable Pāṇini, [the status of] *uṇādi* suffixes is due to their being recognized as nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
It is stated in the Bhāṣya that "the *uṇādi* suffixes are unanalyzed nominal stems (*avyutpannāni prātipadikāni*). For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, it is said:
"The *uṇādi* suffixes are indeed unanalyzed nominal stems"; [and] subsequently, regarding forms such as *sarpiṣā* and *yajuṣā*:

Having raised the objection that there would be an absence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) due to the suffix not being a *pratyaya*, [the author] established *ṣatva* by relying on the designation of *pratyaya* based on the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*), and thereby rejected the view that [the Uṇādi suffixes] are derivational (*vyutpattipakṣa*). For this reason also, the Uṇādi-sūtras are not the work of Pāṇini. Precisely for this reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṭhajervyaghañapoḥ," it is stated:

The word *vāyu* is derived from the verbal root *aj* with the suffix *yu*, where the suffix denotes the action itself (*bhāva*). For if the *uṇādi* sūtras were indeed composed by Pāṇini, it would have been derived by relying on the suffix *u* according to the *uṇādi* rule "kṛ-vā-pā-ji... (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.1). And thus...

In some commentaries, the reliance on the derivation of *uṇādi* words is based solely on other grammatical treatises; this has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Consequently, there is no suspicion of redundancy between the *uṇādi* rules such as *kvibvacipracchiśridruśrupruṣaḥ saṃjñāyām* and similar *vārttikas*. Now, the *uṇādi* suffixes.

(1) The suffix *uṇ* is added after the roots *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*, *ji*, *mi*, *svad*, *sādh*, and *aś*. [Pāṇini 3.1.140] *kṛ-vā-pā-ji-mi-svad-i-sādh-aśū*: *ḍu kṛñ* (to do/make), *vā* (to go/to smell), *pā* (to drink), *ji* (to conquer), *ḍu miñ* (to throw), *svada* (to taste), *sādh* (to accomplish), *aśū* (to reach).

Regarding the term *vyāptau*: this is the ablative case (*pañcamī*) derived from a *dvandva* compound. The meaning is that the suffix *uṇ* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
As for the form *kārūḥ*: when *uṇ* is added in the sense of the agent, the form is produced by the application of *vṛddhi* according to the rule *aco ñṇiti*.
The *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *kāruḥ* is masculine in the sense of Viśvakarman; it is used in the three genders in the senses of 'agent' (*kāraka*) and 'artisan' (*śilpin*)."

He causes one to recall the rule for the suffix *uṇ* after the root *vā*: "āto yuṅ" (Pāṇini 3.2.178). "Pāyu" means the anus; the sense is that the suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule "āto yuṅ. Amara states: "The anus is called *apāna*, and its name is *pāyu*. However, when [the suffix] *uṇ* is applied to the root *pā* (in the sense of "protection"), [it forms *pāyu*].

It is also called *rakṣaka* (protector). It is called *jāyu*: from the root *ūṇ* (to grow), with the suffix *uṇ*, there is the substitution of *vṛddhi* and the replacement by *āya*; thus the form is established. The *Amarakośa* states: "A medicine that is a protector (*jāyu*) is called *agada*. From the root *ḍu miñ* (to cast/throw), the suffix *uṇ* applies;
setting aside the *vṛddhi* [which would normally occur], the rule "after *mīnāti*, *minoti*, etc. causes the substitution of *ā*, and then [the addition of] *ātaḥ*.

The form [is derived] by the addition of the *yuk* suffix according to the rule *yukciṇkṛtoḥ*. According to Amara, "māyuḥ pittaṃ kaphaḥ śleṣmā" (bile, phlegm, and *śleṣman*). Regarding "svādu": that which tastes well or is pleasing is *svādu*, as in "svāduḥ paṭaḥ" (a sweet cloth).
This word is *viśeṣyanighna* (its gender depends on the noun it qualifies); thus one should understand examples such as "svādu phalam" (a sweet fruit) and so forth. It accomplishes (*sādhnoti*).
In the sense of "one who performs another's work," the suffix *uṇ* is applied to the agent. Regarding the word *āśu*, it means "quickly.

It is neuter when its meaning is restricted to the mere absence of delay; however, it should be understood as having all three genders (*triliṅga*) when it refers to a substance qualified by that [quality]. This is because of the rule: "The *uṇ*-suffixes and others are applied diversely (*bahulam*)."

The rule is established according to usage due to the presence of the term "generally" (*bahula*). From the root *rah* (to abandon), with the suffix *uṇ* and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-vṛddhi*), the form *rahuḥ* arises. Similarly, from the root *vas* (to dwell), with the suffix *uṇ*:
that in which everything dwells is *vāsuḥ*. He who is both *vāsuḥ* and *devaḥ* is Vāsudeva. Even though...

Although the form *Vāsudeva* is established by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "after *ṛṣi*, *Andhaka*, *Vṛṣṇi*, and *Kuru*" in the sense of "the offspring of Vasudeva," the intention is that this is a different derivation for that word.
(2) *Chandaśīṇaḥ* ||2||
The suffix *uṇ* follows. The meaning is that the suffix *uṇ* occurs after the verbal root √i (*igati*) in the Vedic language (*cchandas*).
[Thus,] "it goes" (*eti*) or "it moves" (*gacchati*) is *āyuḥ*. This word is masculine.
(3) After the roots √dṛś, √san, √jan, √car, and √caṭ, the suffix *ñuṇ* [occurs].

*dṛṣanijani*: from the roots *dṛ* (to split), *ṣaṇ* (to give), *jan* (to be born), *car* (to move), and *caṭ* (to break); the ablative case [is used] after this compound. Regarding *dāru*: "wood (*kāṣṭham*), *dāru*, fuel (*indhanam*), and *edhas*"—thus says Amara. There is vṛddhi [substitution] for the vowel *a* before suffixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*. *Sānuḥ* means a plateau (*prasthaḥ*). For this meaning, consult a lexicon.

Regarding *prayāṇayati*: the term *snu* refers to a ridge or plateau, as in the rule "the words *snu*, *prastha*, and *sānu* are not feminine. Regarding the form *jānu*, he states that it is derived from the root *jan* with the suffix *ñuṇ*. The intention is that the vowel substitution (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate letter occurs by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116).
Now, an objection might be raised: "If the form *jānu* results from the *vṛddhi* substitution of the penultimate vowel [as you have stated]..."

That is incorrect; for one might object that by the rule *ṭhjanivadhyośca*, there would be no vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel in these two roots due to the prohibition of vṛddhi [applicable] after a *ciṇ* suffix, a *ñ-ṇit* suffix, or a *kṛt* suffix.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "by the force of the two indicatory letters (*anubandha*)."

It should be understood that although the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*] is established here by means of a single *anubandha*, the employment of two *anubandhas* is for the purpose of indicating that *vṛddhi* must also occur in this case. From the root *car* with the suffix *ñuṇ*, the form *cāru* is derived through the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

This word is neuter. Regarding the form *cāṭua*: one might object that since the vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel is obligatory, it should necessarily be *cāṭua* and not *caṭua*; yet poets do employ the latter—anticipating this doubt, he says: "because it belongs to the *mṛgayv-ādi* group."

(4) *kiṃjarayoḥ śriṇaḥ* |4| [The suffix] *ñuṇ* is applied after the roots *śrī* and *iṇ* when preceded by *kim* and *jara*, respectively. The application follows the respective order. He provides an example for the root *śrī* with *kim*: *kiṃśāruḥ* ("awn").
Regarding "sasyaśūka": the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *kiṃsāru* refers to the awn of grain (*sasyaśūka*), an arrowhead, and the *kaṅka* bird.
(5) [In the rule] *tro raśca laḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.47], the *ra* is also replaced by *la*.

*tro raśca laḥ*. The analysis of the compound is *traḥ* and *raḥ*. The meaning is that the suffix *ñyuṇ* is applied after the root *tṛ* (in the sense of "floating" and "crossing"), and the letter *r* is replaced by the letter *l*. Thus, *tālu-* [is derived] from the sense "that by which they cross"; the meaning is that there is a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) and the replacement of *r* by *l*.

(6) *kṛke vacaḥ kaśca* | 6 | *kṛke vacaḥ kaśca*. When *kṛka* is the upapada, the suffix *ñuṇ* is applied to the root *vac*, and the letter *c* [of the suffix] is replaced by *k*; this is the meaning. This is stated because [the substitution of *k* for *c*] would not otherwise apply by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*.

This is the rule for derivation: *kṛkavākuḥ*. From the root *vac*, with the suffix *ñuṇ* and the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the penultimate vowel, the form *kṛkavākuḥ* is obtained through the change of *c* to *k*. Explaining the meaning of the word *kṛkavākuḥ*, he cites a lexicon:
"The word *kṛkavākuḥ* [denotes] a peacock," and so forth.
(7) After the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śī*, *tṛ*, *car*, *tsar*, *tan*, *dhan*, *ni*, *mi*, *mas*, and *aj*, the suffix *u* is applied.
[The roots] *bhṛmṛśītṛ*: *bhṛñ* in the sense of supporting; *mṛṅ* in the sense of giving up life; *śīṅ* in the sense of sleeping;
*tṛ* in the senses of swimming and crossing over; *car* in the sense of moving; *tsar* in the sense of moving stealthily; *tanu* in the sense of expansion; *dhana*... [the root *dhan*].
From the roots *dhāny* (in the sense of "to throw"), *ḍumiñ* (in the sense of "to cast"), and *ṭua masj* (in the sense of "to purify")—the fifth case ending [is used] after this *dvandva* compound.
The suffix *u* shall be applied after these. Since *uṇ* was already prescribed, the specific rule for *u* is for the purpose of preventing *vṛddhi*.
He gives an example of the root *bhṛñ* with the suffix *u*: *bharuḥ*. [The commentators] say: "Bharu means Śiva. [Thus ends the section on] *bharu*.

The sense is that [the word *hari*] means gold, as per the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "in the masculine, *hari* means gold. Regarding *śayu*: he says "the python is *śayu*" based on Amara’s statement "the python is *śayu*. (8) And [the suffix] *aṇ*. 8.1.2. The sense is that [the word *hari*] means gold, as per the lexicon (*kośa*) stating "in the masculine, *hari* means gold.
Regarding *śayu*: he says "the python is *śayu*" based on Amara’s statement "the python is *śayu*.
(8) And [the suffix] *aṇ*. 8.1.2.

And *aṇ*. From the root *ṭhaṇ* (meaning "to sound"), the suffix *u* should be applied; thus, *aṇuḥ*. He states the purpose of the word "and" (*ca*)—namely, "by *ca*" (*cāt*). The meaning is that the suffix *u* also occurs after the roots *kaṭe* (in the sense of "raining" etc. and *vaṭe* (in the sense of "encircling"); hence *vaṭuaḥ*. As it is said: "The son of a twice-born man is known as *vaṭua*."
*Medinī*. (9) *Dhānye ṇit* |9|.
Regarding *dhānye ṇit*: the term *aṇ* is understood from the previous rule, as is *uḥ*. [The suffix] *ṇit* is applied after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when the meaning is a type of grain (*dhānya*).

The suffix *upratyaya* is added, and its purpose is that [the resulting form] becomes a *nit* (having *n* as an *it*-marker). He states the purpose of being a *nit*: "acute-accented on the first syllable" (*ādyaudāta*). Regarding "pervading" (*abhivyāpya*): the meaning is that [the property of being *nit*] continues to apply even in that subsequent rule.

(10) *śṛ-sva-snihi-trapi-asi-vasi-hani-kli-di-bandhi-manibhyaś-ca*. 10.127. [The suffix *upratyaya* is added after the verbal roots] *śṛ*, *svap*, *snihi*, *trap*, *as*, *vas*, *han*, *klid*, *bandh*, and *man*. 10.127.

The roots *śṛ*, *svṛ*, *snih*, *trap*, *as*, *vas*, *han*, *klid*, *bandh*, and *man*—the ablative case ending [is used] after these in a copulative compound (*dvandva*). *Śṛ* means "to injure"; *svṛ* means "sound" and "affliction"; *snih* means "affliction"; *trap* means "shame"; *as* means "throwing"; *vas* means "dwelling"; *han* means "injury" and "going";
*klid* means "becoming moist"; *bandh* means "binding"; and *man* means "knowing. [The ablative is used after these] because they form a copulative compound.
The word "ur" is understood [from the previous rule]. *Trapu* means lead; for it, upon seeing fire, seems to feel shame (*trapate*), as it were.
(11) In the case of the root *syand*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of *dh*. 11.

In the word *syanda*, the suffix *u* is applied to the root *syandū* in the sense of "flowing" (*prasravaṇa*). There occurs vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *y*, and the letter *d* becomes *dh*. (12) [Pāṇini 6.4.12] *undericcādeḥ*. 12. [The substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel occurs when the suffix *u* follows, provided the root begins with a vowel.]

[The suffix *u* is added] after the root *und*, as in *induh*. The suffix *u* occurs, and the initial vowel *u* becomes *i*. (13) After the root *īṣ*, [the suffix *u* is added] and it is also *kṛt*. 13.
The suffix *u* is added to the root *īṣ*, and it is *kit*; furthermore, the initial vowel *ī* is replaced by *i*. Thus, *iṣuḥ*. (14) After the root *skand*, there is also the elision of *s*. 14.

There is the elision of the *s* in *skandi*. From the root *skandi*, meaning "to move" or "to leap," the suffix *u* is applied, and there is the elision of the letter *s*. Thus, *kandu*. It is called *kandu* because people suffer (*skandati*) therein.

(15) *sṛjer asum ca* | 15 | Regarding *sṛjeḥ asum ca*: from the root *sṛj* (meaning "to emit" or "to create"), the suffix *u* shall be applied; by virtue of its connection with that [suffix], the augment *asum* is added, and there is the elision of the initial *s*. Thus, [the form] *asumaḥ* [is derived].
The augment *mit* occurs after the final vowel. When *sṛ-asj* is established, the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *yaṇ*-substitution;
the *s* becomes *ś* by the rule of *ścutva*; the *ś* becomes *j* by the rule of *jaśtva*; and the initial *s* is elided. With the addition of the suffix *upratyaya*, the form *rajjur* is obtained.

(16) And there is a transposition of the beginning and end of the suffix *kṛti*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *kṛti* [is used] in the sense of cutting" (*kṛterādyantaviparyayaśca*): from the root *kṛt* (meaning "to cut"), the suffix *up* occurs; the initial *ka* is placed at the end, and the final *ta* is placed at the beginning. Thus, with the suffix *up*, [it becomes *kartṛ*].
The suffix *guṇa* follows. The form is *tarku*. And that is a particular kind of tool.
(17) Not after *añc*. 17. Not after *añc*. From the root *añcu* in the sense of "going," the suffix *up* is applied when the prefix *na* is present.
It may be so. He recalls a rule: "Because it belongs to the *nyaṅku*-class. For example, *nyaṅkuḥ* means "deer.
As the *Medinī* lexicon states: "*Nyaṅkuḥ* is used for a sage and a male deer.
(18) *Phali-pāṭi-nami-manij-ajāṃ guk-paṭi-nāki-dhataś-ca* || 18 ||

Regarding *phalipāṭinamimanijanām*: *phala* means "to bear fruit"; *paṭ* means "to go," and here the form *pāṭī* is understood as the causative (*ṇyanta*); *ṇam* means "to bow" or "sound"; *man* means "to know"; *janī* means "to appear.
The genitive case is used because these are in a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The suffix *u* is applied after these. The genitive in *janām* is for the sake of what follows later.

The augment *guṇ* occurs in view of the *guṇa* being enjoined, due to the indicatory letter *k*. The others are substitutes (*ādeśas*). Here, although there is only one genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it is differentiated by the difference in its scope;

thus, it should be understood that with respect to *guṇa*, it is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), whereas with respect to the other substitutes, it is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). In reality, however...

Since the view that "substitutes are accompanied by their original bases" (*sāgamaka*) is also observed in works such as the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*, the genitive case expressing the *sthāna* (original base) is entirely correct. When the suffix *u* is added to the root *phala* and the augment *guṇa* is applied to the final constituent part, the form *phalgu* is produced. [Likewise] when the suffix *u* is added to *pāṭi*...

In the *prakṛtibhūta* (original) reading, *paṭi* is the substitute for *paṭu*. The letter *i* is to be understood according to the rule stated as "*ṭhik-śtipau dhātunirdeśe*" (the suffixes *ṭhik* and *śtip* are used when indicating a verbal root). Thus, the form is *paṭuḥ*. Regarding *nāku-valmīkam*:
*nāki* is the substitute for the verbal root *nam*. According to the rule "*vāmalūrūśca nākuśca valmīkam*" (both *vāmalūra* and *nāku* denote an anthill).
"Masculine and neuter," according to Amara.
(19) *valerguk ca*.
19. *valerguk ca*. From the root *val* (to cover), the suffix *u* is applied, and there is also the substitution of *guk*. [Thus, the form *valgū* is derived from the root *val* meaning "to cover."]

By its conjunction with that [suffix], there is the addition of a *guṇa* vowel to the base; thus, the form is *balgu*. On this point, some read *balgu*, but that should be disregarded because it contradicts attested usage (*lakṣya*), such as in the verse beginning, "simultaneously with that beautiful (*tadvalgunā*) opening... and so forth.
(20) *śaḥ kitsanvacca* | [Pāṇini 6.1.34] The suffix *up* is applied after the root *śo* (meaning "to sharpen" or "to make thin"), and that suffix is both *kit* and behaves like *san*.
Thus, from the root *śo*, with the suffix *up*, because of its *kit* status, [the rule] *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* applies. This results in the form *śiśuḥ*.

Thus, after the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel and the doubling of the consonant, the substitution of *i* for the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) occurs by the rule "sanyataḥ. Then, the elision of the *ā* occurs by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca," because that [substitution of *i*] is prescribed before an ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with a vowel that has the marker *k* or *ṅ*. Consequently, the form is *śiśuḥ*.

(21) *yo dve ca* | 21 | Regarding *yo dve ca*: in the rule *yā prāpaṇe*, the word *yaḥ* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). The meaning is that the suffix *up* is added after the root *yā* in the sense of "attaining," and the reduplication (*dvitva*) of the base occurs. However, regarding the status of being like the *san* suffix (*sanvadbhāva*), [the following applies].

The substitution of *it* would have occurred [by the rule] "san-yataḥ"; therefore, that is not prescribed here. He states this very point with the words beginning "as in the case of *san*" (*san-vat-iti*), etc.
(22) *kurbhraś-ca* | 22 | [In the formation of the desiderative stem], the substitution of *u* for the root *kṛ*, and the suffix *bhraś*, also [take place]. 22.

*Kurbhraśca*: The word *ca* (and) carries forward the sense of "two" (*dve*). The meaning is that from the root *bhṛñ* (to support), the suffix *kup* occurs, and there is reduplication of the base (*prakṛti*). Thus, "he supports" (*bharati*) becomes *babhruḥ*. He states the lexicon: "*Babhruḥ* [is used] for a particular sage. This is the *Dharaṇi-kośa*. Now, as for *cakruḥ* and so forth...

In response to the question "How so?", he says: "And also from others. The meaning is that the suffix *kup* occurs after other verbal roots as well, and there is reduplication of the base (*prakṛti*). Regarding the form *jaghnuḥ*:
by the rule *gamahana*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).

(23) From the roots *pṛ*, *bhid*, *vyadh*, *gṛdh*, and *dhṛṣ*. [Pāṇini 3.3.104] *pṛ-bhid-vyadha-gṛdhi-dhṛṣibhyaḥ*: *pṛ* in the sense of protecting and filling; *bhid* in the sense of splitting; *vyadh* in the sense of striking;
*gṛdh* in the sense of longing for; *ñi dhṛṣā* in the sense of being bold. The ablative case is used here because these are in a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

The suffix *ku* is applied after these [words]. As in *puruḥ*: when the suffix *ku* follows, the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, and *r* is substituted for *v*. Regarding the derivation of *vidhuḥ*, he states: "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā*. Because the root *vyadh* has the meaning of "striking," he says: "the one separated from his beloved (*virahiṇam*)."
He cites the *Kośa* as authority with the words "vidhaḥ śaśāṅka" and so forth. This is the *Viśvakośa*.
(24) *kṛ-gror ucca* | 24 | *kṛ-gror ucca*. From the roots *ḍu kṛñ* (to do/make) and *gṛ* (to swallow), the suffix *ku* is applied, and the vowel *u* is substituted for the radical vowel.
The letter *u* is the final substitute, followed by *r*. Thus, the forms *kuruḥ* and *gurur* are produced.
(25) *apaduḥsuṣu sthaḥ* | 25 | When *apa*, *dus*, and *su* are used as upapadas, the suffix *ku* is added to the root *sthā*.
It may be so. When there is elision of the vowel *ā*, forms such as *apaṣṭhu*, *duḥṣṭhu*, and *suṣṭhu* arise.

(26) *raper ic copadhāyāḥ*. From the root *rap*, the suffix *ku* is applied, and the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel [is replaced by *i*]. From the root *rap*, the suffix *ku* shall be applied, and the penultimate [vowel]...
And there is the substitution of the vowel *i*.
(27) *arji*, *dṛśi*, *kami*, *ami*, *paśi*, *bādha*, *amṛji*, *paśi*, *tuka*, *dhuka*, and long *h* are also [the bases].
(27) *arji*, *dṛśi*: *arja* in the sense of acquisition; *dṛśi* in the sense of seeing; *kamu* in the sense of desire; *ama* in the sense of motion and so forth.

The root *paś* is used in the sense of "destruction"; this is a Vedic (sautra) root. *Bādhṛ* is used in the sense of "shaking. From these six [roots], following a *dvandva* compound, the genitive case is employed.

After these, the suffix *kupratyaya* occurs; by virtue of its co-occurrence (*tatsaṃniyogena*), among the six original bases beginning with *arji*, the two roots *ṛji* and *aṛś* undergo total substitution (*sarvādeśa*) by *ṛja* and *paśa* respectively.

The augment *tuk* is added after the root *kam*. The augment *dhuk* is added after the root *am*. The root *paś* is marked with the *it* designation; because of this *it* designation, the nasal augment *num* is applied.

By this [rule], a long vowel is prescribed. For the root *bādh*, the final letter is replaced by *h*. It has been stated that even a single genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is differentiated according to the difference in its scope; thus, the genitive is connected both to the substitute (*ādeśa*) and to the augment (*āgama*).
*Kantu* is *madana*.
(28) There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the elision of *s* for the roots *prath*, *mradi*, and *bhrasj*.
(28) [The rule applies] to *prath*, *mradi*, and *bhrasj*: *prath* in the sense of "becoming famous," *mrada* in the sense of "crushing," and *bhrasja* in the sense of "cooking. From these...

The meaning is that there is the suffix *ku*, as well as vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), and the elision of the *s* belonging to the root *bhrasj*. Because the elision of *s* is impossible elsewhere, the word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) refers specifically to the root *bhrasj*. From the root *prath* with the suffix *ku* and vocalization, the form *pṛthu* is derived. Regarding the word *bhṛgu*: * *bhrasj* + *ku* → *bhrasj* + *u* (the suffix *ku* becomes *u* after the vocalization of *r*) * *bhrasj* + *u* → *bhṛsj* + *u* (vocalization of *r*) * *bhṛsj* + *u* → *bhṛj* + *u* (elision of *s*) * *bhṛj* + *u* → *bhṛgu* (substitution of *g* for *j*) Thus, the form *bhṛgu* is established.
He justifies the form *kutva* [the substitution of *k* for *g*] by stating: "because it belongs to the *nyaṅkv-ādi* group.

(Pāṇini 7.3.53) (29) *laṅghibaṃhyaernalopaśca* | 29 | [The suffix *ku* is applied after the roots *laṅghi* and *baṃhi*, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the nasal. [Roots: *laghi* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), and *baṃhi* in the sense of "growth" (*vṛddhau*). From these two, the suffix *ku* is applied.

There may be the elision of the letter *na*, resulting in the form *laghubahu*. Regarding the specific rule for the word *laghu*, he says: "vālamūla... [and so on]. The term *la* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). The meaning is that the letter *l*, which is a constituent part of this word, optionally undergoes the change to *r*. In this way, the form *raghu* is produced.
(30) *ūrṇoter nulopaś ca* | [A *ku* suffix is applied after the root *ūrṇu*, and by its very application, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n*. The form *ūru* is thus produced.]

(31) "Mahati" and "hrasvaḥ" [are used]. 31. In the case of the qualifier *mahat* ("great"), the form *hrasvaḥ* ("short") is also employed. Thus, the form *uru* ("wide") is used. (32) And after the root *śliṣ*, the suffix *ka* is applied. 32.

Regarding *śliṣeḥ kaśca*: from the root *śliṣ* (meaning "to embrace"), there is the suffix *ku*, and *ka* is the substitute for the final letter. Thus, *ślikuḥ* means "a servant"; this form arises through the substitution of *k* for *ṣ*. He states another meaning for *śliku*:
"one who has raised up light."

(33) *āṅ-parayoḥ khani-śṛbhyāṃ ḍicca* |33| [The suffix] *ku* is added after the roots *khanu* (in the sense of digging) and *śṛ* (in the sense of injuring), when preceded by *āṅ* and *pari* respectively; and this [suffix] is also *ḍit*. Because it is *ḍit*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). Thus, *ākhur iti* ("a mouse").

"It digs" (*ākhanati*); the word "earth" (*bhūmi*) is to be supplied as the object. "It pierces the enemy" (*paraṃ śṛṇāti*); the meaning is that it strikes the foe. Regarding the etymology of *parśu*, he says: "Because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
(34) "The wood of *hari* and *mita* [is used for making] arrows" (34).

The suffix *ku* is applied after the verbal root *dru* (meaning "to run") when *hari* or *mita* are used as upapadas; this suffix is marked with the *ḍi*-diacritic. Thus, *haridruḥ* is formed. The suffix is *ku*;
because it is *ḍit*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*). The form *mitadruḥ* is likewise derived in exactly the same manner.

(35) And when *śata* follows: 35. When the word *śata* is used as an upapada, the suffix *ku* is applied to the root *dru* in the sense of "going. Furthermore, according to the rule that this suffix is marked with *ṭi*, there is elision of the *ṭi*. [Question: How is it in the case of *dru*?

Since the suffix *ku* is not observed anywhere as being prescribed independently, he says "by virtue of *bāhulaka* (irregularity). Regarding "possessing that" (*tadvān*): the possessive suffix *ma* is applied according to the rule "after *dyu* and *dru*, *ma*" (*dyaudrubhyāṃ ma*).
(36) [The suffix *ka* is added after] *khara*, *ūśaṅku*, *pīyu*, *nīla*, and *aṅguli*. (36)

From these five verbal roots—*kharu* (from *khan*, meaning "to dig" or "to split"), *śaṅku* (from *śak*, meaning "to fear"), *pā* (meaning "to drink"), *lagi* preceded by the prefix *ni* (meaning "to go"), and *lage* (meaning "to cling")—the suffix *kup* is applied, and these forms are thus derived as irregularities (*nipāta*). He states the specific irregularity (*nipātana*) itself: "In the case of *khan*, there is the substitution of *repha* (the letter *r*) for the final [nasal] *n*. [This refers to the replacement of the nasal *n* with *r*.]

With the substitution of *ra*, the form becomes *kharuḥ*. He explains the meaning of *kharu* with the words beginning with "kāma" (desire). It should also be understood that "a maiden who chooses her own husband" (*pativarā kanyā*) is also [denoted by] *kharuḥ*. He explains the word *śaṅku* by means of a lexicon (*kośa*), stating "pīyuḥ," etc.; here, there is the substitution of *ī* and the addition of the augment *yuk*.
It is elided. Thus, *nīlaṅguḥ*. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *nīlaṅgu* is masculine when it means a worm, but feminine when it means a female bee.
(37) And [the words] *mṛgayu*, etc., [are formed with this suffix]. 37.

And *mṛgayu* and so forth: words such as *mṛgayu* and others are derived by the application of the suffix *ku*, with irregular forms (*nipātana*) applied. Examples include *bhṛgayuḥ*, *devayuḥ*, and so on. It is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); by this, the derivation of *pīlu*, *pāṇḍu*, and others is established.

(38) *urac* is added after the roots *mandi*, *vāśi*, *mathi*, *cati*, *caṅki*, and *aki*. The roots *mandi* (in the sense of praising, etc.), *vāśṛ* (in the sense of sounding), *mantha* (in the sense of churning), *cati* (in the sense of begging), *caṅki* (a root belonging to the *sūtra*-language), and *aki* (in the sense of marking)— after these, the suffix *urac* occurs.
Regarding *mandurā*: "But *mandurā* is a stable for horses," according to Amara. Regarding *vāśurā*:
"The word *vāśurā* [is used] for a female horse and for night," according to Medinī. Regarding *caṅkura*:
"The word *caṅkura* [is used] for a chariot and for a tree," according to Medinī. Now, one might ask: how is it that [the form] is *aṅkūra*?
In response to the doubt that the word *aṅkura* alone is correct when the suffix *-an* (*uran*) is applied, he says:
"because it belongs to the *kharjūrādi* group. The implication is that by virtue of this, the word *aṅkūra* is also indeed correct when the suffix *-ūra* (*ūran*) is applied.

(39) *vyatheḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ kicca* | 39. From the root *vyath*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* and it is *kit*. The meaning is that from the root *vyath* (in the sense of "fear" and "trembling"), the suffix *urac* shall be applied; and that [suffix] is *kit*, and there is *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root.

The example is *vithura*. It should not be argued that since the samprasāraṇa of the root [in *vithura*] is already established by the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16) through the very prescription of the *kit* suffix for *urac*, the separate prescription of samprasāraṇa here is redundant; for [the rule *grahijyā*... applies...

Because the verbal root *vyadh* is specified as ending in the fourth letter of the *tavarga* [the letter *dh*], and since this [root *vyadh*] ends in the second letter of the *tavarga* [the letter *t*], the [application of the rule] does not occur [for it]. (40) *makura-dardurau* || 40 ||

*Makura* and *dardura*: the meaning is that from the roots *maki* (to adorn) and *dṛ* (to tear), the forms *mukura* and *dardura* are irregularly derived (*nipātita*). In the first case, the suffix *urac* is applied, and the vowel *u* is irregularly substituted for the penultimate vowel of the root. But how is it that [the form] *makura* occurs, given this rule for *mukura* and *dardura*?

The meaning is that [the suffix] is elided. In the first case, the suffix *urac* is applied, and the vowel *u* is also elided from the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the root. Now, one might ask: "How then is the form *makura* derived, given that the substitution of *u* for the penultimate vowel prescribed by this rule would be obligatory? To this he replies: "By virtue of *bāhulaka* (diversity/irregularity). By virtue of *bāhulaka*, the penultimate...
The meaning is that there is no option regarding the elision (*ut*).
He states the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *dṛḍha* with the words "doubling of the root," and so forth.

When there is doubling of the root *dṛh*, the guṇa substitution occurs; then, by the rule for changing the semivowel of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) to *u*, the *hal-ādi-śeṣa* (retention of the first consonant) applies, and finally, the augment *ru* is added to the reduplication.
The intention is that by the elision of the *ṛ* sound (*ṛtilopa*), the form *dardura* arises through the addition of the suffix *urac*.

Explaining the meaning of the word *dardura*, he cites a lexicon (*kośa*) with the verse beginning "darduraḥ toyade bheke" (Dardura means a cloud or a frog). Some, however, hold that from the root *dṛ*, there is the substitution of *guṇa*, the augment *duk*, and the suffix *urac*.
They say that [the word *madgura*] is derived through a specific grammatical combination (*saṃniyoga*).

(41) *Madgura* and others. (41) *Madgura* and others. [The roots] *madī* (to rejoice), *bandh* (to bind), *kabṛ* (to color), and so forth, ending in the suffix *urac*, [form the words *madgura*, etc.]

The meaning is that they are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). From the root *madī* in the sense of "joy," the suffix *urac* is applied according to the rule; by virtue of its association with that suffix, the substitution of *guṇa* is also irregularly prescribed. From the root *kabṛ* in the sense of "color," the suffix *urac* is applied, and by virtue of its association with that suffix, the augment *ruk* is ordained. Because of the marker *m*, it occurs after the final vowel. Thus, the form *bandhura* is derived.
To the question, "How is it that [the word] *bandhūra* [is derived]? he says: "from *kharjūra*, etc. Alternatively, from the root *kokat*, there is the suffix *ku*.
There are two forms, *kukkura* and *kukkura*, because of the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), which indicates that the suffix *kuk* is optional. (42) From the root *as*, the suffix *un*. 42.

*Aseruṇ* and *āsura*: because *uran* is prescribed for the base form *urac*, there is a difference in accent. Regarding the derivation of *āsura*, he says: "by *prajñādyaṇ*" (*Pāṇini 5.4.38*).
