And from the root *masi*: [the suffix] *ūr* is added after *masi* in the sense of transformation (*pariṇāma*). The remainder is that [the suffix] *uran* is added; thus the form *masurāḥ* is produced. He establishes the word *masūrāḥ* by stating that he will say [later], "after *masi*, [the suffix] *ūr*. (44) After the root *śavaś* in the sense of obtaining (*āpti*). 44.

Regarding *śvaśur* in the sense of "attainment" (*āpti*): the word *āśu* is formed by the elision of the vowel *a* [from *āśu*]. With that as an upapada, the suffix *uran* is applied to the root *aśū* (meaning "to pervade"), provided that "attainment" is understood. Thus, the form *śvaśura* is derived. He states its definition: "of the husband and wife."

(45) *avi-mahi-eṣ-ṭiṣac* ||45|| [The suffix] *ṭiṣac* is applied after the roots *ava* and *maha*. [The root] *ava* means "to protect," and *maha* means "to honor. The suffix *ṭiṣac* occurs after these two. By the rule of *ṭac*, the initial and final phonemes are elided. The presence of the marker *ṭ* is for the purpose of applying the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Thus: *aviṣaḥ* (masculine), *aviṣī* (feminine); *mahiṣaḥ* (masculine), *mahiṣī* (feminine).
(46) *amer dīrghaś ca* | [The suffix] *ṭaṣac* is applied after the root *am*, and there is lengthening of the vowel *a* of the base. Thus,
the form *āmiṣam* is derived.
(47) And there is vṛddhi for the root *ruh*. 47.
And there is vṛddhi for the root *ruh*. From the root *ruh* in the sense of "growing from a seed," the suffix *ṭiṣac* occurs, and there is vṛddhi of the stem; thus the form is *rauhiṣa*.
(48) *taveṇidvā* | 48 | Regarding *taveṇidvā*: *tavi* is a root found in the *sūtra* tradition; from this, the suffix *tiṣac* is added, and it is optionally *ṇit*.
The meaning is that in the alternative where it is *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). In the absence of that [the *ṇit* designation], there is no *vṛddhi*.

(49) *nañi vyatheḥ* |49| When *nañ* is the upapada, the suffix *ṭiṣac* is applied after the root *vyath*. [Example: *avyathiṣaḥ*. Because it is marked with *ṭ*, the feminine form is *avyathiṣī* by means of the suffix *ṅīp*.
(50) *kila* and *buk*. [Vārttika 50: After the root *kila*, the suffix *ṭiṣac* is applied, and there is also the augment *buk* to the base root. Thus, the form *kilbiṣam* is derived.
(51) After the verbal roots *iṣ*, *mad*, *mud*, *khid*, *chid*, *bhid*, *mand*, *candi*, *tim*, *mi*, *hi*, *muh*, *muc*, *ruc*, *rudh*, *bandh*, and *śuṣ*, the suffix *kirac* is applied.
[The roots are: *iṣu* in the sense of "desire," *madī* in the sense of "joy," *muda* in the sense of "joy," *khida* in the sense of "dejection," *chidir*...
Of these: *dvaidhīkaraṇe* (in the sense of making two), *bhidir* (in tearing apart), *madi* (in praising, etc.), *cadi* (in delighting),
*timi* (in becoming moist), *miha* (in sprinkling), *muha* (in bewilderment),
*muclṛ* (in releasing), *ruca* (in shining), *rudhir* (in obstructing), *bandha* (in binding), and *śuṣa* (in drying).

The fifth case ending is used after these [compounds]. The suffix *kirac* shall occur after these; thus, *iṣira*. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Thus, *iṣira*. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. (52) After the root *aś*, [the suffix *kirac* occurs] when it is marked with *ṇ*. 52.

*āśirṇit*: From the root *aś* meaning "to eat," the suffix *kirac* is applied, and it becomes *ṇit*. Due to its being *ṇit*, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel; thus the form *āśiraḥ* is obtained. (53) *ajira-śiśira-śithila-asthira-sphira-sthavira-khadirāḥ* || 53 ||

The word *ajira* is derived from the following roots: *aja* (in the sense of moving and throwing), *śaśa* (in the sense of leaping), *śratha* (in the sense of loosening), *ṣṭhā* (in the sense of stopping), *sphāyī* (in the sense of increasing), and *khada* (in the sense of harming). This is a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) applied when the suffix *kirac* is added; first, [the root] *aja*.

From the root *kṛ* (meaning "to go" or "to throw"), the suffix *kirac* is applied; however, the substitution of *vī* for the original base is not prescribed here by rule, but rather established as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

Regarding the word *śiśira*, he says: "of the root *śas*, [there is substitution] of the penultimate vowel. From the root *śas* (meaning "to leap" or "to move swiftly"), when the suffix *kirac* is applied, the vowel *i* is substituted in place of the penultimate vowel *a*; thus, the form *śiśira* is produced.

Regarding the word *śithila*, he says with the words beginning "śratha": there is the substitution of *la* for the *repha* (the letter *r*) when it occurs in an affix; thus the form is *śithilam*. Regarding the words *sthira* and *sphira*, he says "of *ṣṭhā* and *sphāyi*. Regarding the word *sthavira*, he says "of *tiṣṭhati*": from the root *tiṣṭhati*, by means of the suffix *kirac*, in conjunction with that [suffix].

The meaning is that *vu* is substituted for the verbal root, and the short vowel is substituted for the letter *ā*. *Khadira* is a specific type of tree. He derives the word *śibira*: from the root *śīṅ*, meaning "to sleep," with the suffix *kirac*; the augment *yuk* is added to the base, and the shortening of the letter *ī* is also prescribed by rule. Thus, *śibiram*.

*rūpam* | (54) *salikalyanimahibhaḍibhaṇḍiśaṇḍipiṇḍituṇḍikukibhūbhya ilac* | 54 | *salikalyanimahi*: *ṣala* in the sense of going; *kali* in the sense of counting; *ana* in the sense of reaching; *maha*... [in the sense of greatness].

In the sense of worship (*pūjā*), [the root] *bhaḍi* is used in the sense of reviling (*paribhāṣaṇa*), *bhaḍi* in the sense of auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*), *śaḍi* in the sense of affliction (*rujā*), *piḍi* in the sense of compression (*saṅghāta*), *tuḍi* in the sense of breaking (*toḍana*), *kuka* in the sense of taking (*ādāna*), and *bhū* in the sense of existence (*sattā*). Regarding "salila":
it is called *salila* because it flows (*salati*); the remainder [of the meaning] is "low-lying ground" (*nimnapradeśa*). Of the base (*tala*)...
The intended meaning is "because of its tendency to flow downwards. Regarding *salila*, Amara states: "Salila, kamala, and jala [mean water]. Regarding *kalila*, Amara states:
"Kalila and gahana are synonyms [meaning dense or impenetrable]. *Anila* means wind. Regarding *mahilā*, the meaning is "one who is venerable" (*pūjyā*).
Now, one might ask: why is it not *mahele*? For the suffix *ilac* is prescribed [to form such a word]. To this, he says:

"Because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group"—this is the sense that there is a *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *i*. And so Śrīharṣa employed [the term] in the verse: "Though devoted to another's wife (*paramahelārata*), he was not an adulterer (*apāradārika*). This is an ornament of apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa-alaṅkāra*), for although he is devoted to another's wife—another man's woman—he is not an adulterer. *Paramā-*... [text fragment].

The resolution of the apparent contradiction is that he is "delighted" (*rata*) in "excellent sport" (*helā*), which is play. He says "by way of *bāhulaka*" because the root *kuṭ* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) has not been mentioned [in the rule]. (55) *kameḥ pañca*. 55.

After the root *kam*, [the suffix] *ilac* occurs; by virtue of its association with that suffix, the letter *p* becomes the final substitute for the verbal root. Thus, the form *kapila* is derived. As it is said:
"The word *kapilā* refers to the plant *reṇukā*, the *śiṃśapā* tree, a particular type of cow, and a female elephant marked with white spots."

The word *triliṅga* occurs in the sense of a distinction of color; according to the *Medinī*, it also means fire (*anala*), Vāsudeva, a particular sage, and a dog. (56) [The suffix *ac*] is added after roots such as *gup* and others, with the marker *k*. 56.

The suffix *ilac* is added after the roots *gup*, etc., and it is *kit*. [The roots are: *gup* (to protect), *tij* (to sharpen), and *guh* (to conceal). From these, *ilac* is applied, and it is *kit*. Because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Thus: *gupilaḥ*, *tijilaḥ*, *guhilaḥ*. (57) And *mithilā* and others [are formed in this manner]. 57.

And *mithilā* and others: words such as *mithilā* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) by means of the suffix *ilac*. In the case of *mithilā*, from the root *manth* (meaning "to churn" or "to agitate"), the suffix *ilac* is applied; due to its *kit* status, there is elision of the nasal, and the vowel *a* is irregularly changed to *i*. [The same applies to] *pathā*.
From the root *gata* [in the sense of "gone"], the form *pathila* is derived.
(58) *Pati-kaṭhi-kuṭhi-gaḍi-guḍi-daṃśibhya erak*: 58. *pati*, *kaṭhi*, *kuṭhi*: [The roots] *patlṛ* (to go), *kaṭha* (to live in hardship), and *kuṭhi* (to live in hardship).

The roots *gaḍ* (in the sense of sprinkling), *guj* (in the sense of protecting), and *daṃś* (in the sense of biting)—from these, by virtue of being in a dvandva compound, the fifth case ending [is used]. The suffix *erak* shall be applied after them. Thus: *pateraḥ*, *kuṭheraḥ*, *kuṭheraḥ*. Now, one might object that since the root *kuṭh* is marked with *i* (an *idit*), the augment *num* would apply according to the rule "the augment *num* is added to a root marked with *ṭ* or *i*" (*ṭhidito num dhātoḥ*). To this, he says:
"By way of frequentative usage" (bāhulakāt).

(59) *kumbernalopaśca* | 59. [The suffix] *erak* is added to the root *kub*, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the nasal (*n*). From the root *kubi* in the sense of "covering," [the suffix] *erak* is applied, resulting in *kubera*.
*rūpam* | (60) *śadeṣṭaca* | 60. From the root *śadlṛ*, meaning "to fall away" or "to perish," the suffix *erak* is applied, and the letter *t* is substituted for the final [radical] sound.
The form is *śatera*.
(61) *Mūlerādayaḥ* | 61 | *mūlerādayaḥ*. Words beginning with *mūlera* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) by adding the suffix *erak*. For example: *mūlera*.
From the root *mūla* with the suffix *pratiṣṭhā*, [the form] *mūlaka* is derived by adding *era*. From *gudha*—that is, *gudha* in the sense of "enveloping"—[the form] *gudhera* is derived.
From *guh*—that is, *guhū* in the sense of "concealing"—[the form] *guhera* is derived. From *muha*—that is, *muha* in the sense of "bewilderment"—[the form] *muhera* is derived.
(62) After the root *kabṛ*, the suffix *ota* is added, and *paśu* is substituted. 62.

*kaberotac* and *paśca*. The analysis is *kaberotac* and *paśca*. From the root *kabṛ*, meaning "to color," the suffix *otac* is applied, and the letter *p* is substituted for the final [radical] sound. Thus, *kapotaḥ* means a specific kind of bird.
As Medinī states: "The word *kapota* may refer to a peacock (*citrakaṇṭha*), a pigeon (*pārāvata*), or a bird (*vihaṅga*)."
(63) *bhāter ḍavatuh* | 63 | [The suffix] *ḍavatuh* is added after the root *bhā*. In the rule *bhāteḥ*, the mention of *bhā*—meaning "to shine"—is made by means of the *śtip* designation (*bhāti*).
Thus, *bhavān*. This is a word belonging to the class of pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

(64) *kaṭhi-cakibhyām oran* | 64 | From the roots *kaṭh* and *cak*, the suffix *oran* is applied. *Kaṭh* means "to live in hardship," and *cak* means "to be satisfied. From these two, the suffix *oran* occurs; thus the forms *kaṭhoraḥ* and *cakoraḥ* are produced.
(65) *Kiśorādayaś ca* | 65 | *Kiśorādayaś ca*. These words ending in the suffix *oran* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*). Regarding the rule "of that which is preceded by *kim*":
the suffix *oran* is applied to the root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure") when it is preceded by *kim*. When that suffix follows, [the substitution of *ṝ* for *śṛṇāti* occurs].

The meaning is that the elision of the letter *ṭi* and the elision of the *m* at the end of the word *kiṃ* are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). Regarding *sahora*: this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) from the root *ṣaha* (meaning "to endure").
(66) From the roots *kapi*, *gaḍi*, *gaṇḍi*, *kaṭi*, and *paṭi*, the suffix *olac* is added. (66)

*Kapigaḍi*: from *kapi* (to move), *gaḍa* (to sprinkle), *gaḍi* (a part of the face), *kaṭe* (to rain or cover), and *paṭa* (to go)—the fifth case ending is used here after this compound. The suffix *kolac* is applied to these [roots]. Thus:
*kapolaḥ*, *gaḍolaḥ*, *gaṇḍolaḥ*, *kaṭolaḥ*, *paṭolaḥ*. Now, as for *kapi* (to move)...

To the objection that "because this [root] is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*idit*), the augment *num* should occur," he says: "Because of the mention as *kampī*. The sense is that although the mention should have been made as *kamp*, the mention preceded by the prefix *upa* (i.e., *upakamp*) is intended to indicate the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

(67) *mīnāteḥ ūran* | 67. After the root *mīnāti*, the suffix *ūran* is applied. With the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement by *ay*, the form *mayūra* is obtained. (68) *syandeḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca* | 68. After the root *syandi*, the suffix *ūran* is applied, and there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

There is *saṃprasāraṇa* [vowel substitution] for the root *syandi*. From the root *syandū*, meaning "to flow," the suffix *ūran* is applied, and there is also *saṃprasāraṇa* of the base *syandū*. Thus, the form *sindūra* is produced. As it is said: "The word *sindu* refers to a particular type of tree; *sindūra* refers to red powder."
medinī| (69) *sitanigamimasisacyavidhāñkruśibhyas tun* | 69 | *sitanigami* | [The roots are] *ṣiñ* (to bind), *tanu* (to expand), *gamlṛ* (to go), *masī*...

The meaning is that the suffix *tu* occurs after these roots: *pṛ* (in the sense of transformation), *sṛ* (in the sense of flowing together), *ava* (in the sense of protection), *ḍudhāñ* (in the senses of holding and nourishing), and *kruś* (in the sense of crying out). The ablative case is used here because they form a *dvandva* compound. Examples include *setuḥ*. Now, one might object that the augment *iṭ* should be inserted; to this he says: "by the rule *titutra...*, there is no *iṭ*. [This applies to] *ava* in the sense of protection.

Therefore, he says: "by [Pāṇini 6.4.20] *jvaratvaretyūṭh*. When *av tu* remains, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *va*, resulting in the letter *u*; with *guṇa* applied, the form *otur* is obtained. Regarding another opinion, he says:
"due to *bāhulaka* (irregularity). From the word *kroṣṭṛ*, when the suffix *sup* is added, by the rule *tṛjvatkroṣṭuḥ*...
Regarding the derivation [of *kroṣṭu*], he says: "By *kroṣṭu*" (sūtra 70).
"The suffix *pa* is *kit*.
(70) "The suffix *pa* is *kit*. Regarding *pitṛ*: because the suffix is *kit*, there is the substitution of *i* for *u*.

(71) *arteśca tuḥ* |71| After the root *ṛ* "to go," the suffix *tu* [is applied]. Since *tu* was already established [by the previous rule], its specific prescription here is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). (72) *kamimanijanigābhāyāhibhyaśca* |72| [The suffix *tu* is also applied] after the roots *kam*, *man*, *jan*, *gā*, *bhā*, *yā*, and *hi*.

*Kamimanijani*: from *kam* (desire), *man* (to know), *janī* (to be born/manifest), *gai* (to sing/sound), *bhā* (to shine), *yā* (to go/attain), and *hi* (to go)—the fifth case ending is used here because these form a *dvandva* compound. The suffix *tu* occurs after these [roots]. Examples are: *tatantuḥ*, *mantuḥ*, *jantuḥ*, *pātuḥ*, *bhātuḥ*, *yātuḥ*, and *hetuḥ*.

The word *kantu* is established by the previous rule, *ṛjidṛśi*, etc., through the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the suffix *ku*; its repetition here is for the sake of demonstrating the variety of etymological derivations. (73) From the root *cāy*, the suffix *ki*. 73.

The word *cāyaḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the root *cāyṛ*, meaning "to worship" or "to observe," the suffix *tu* is applied, and the root undergoes the substitution of *ki*. After the application of *guṇa*, the form *ketuḥ* is obtained. (74) [In the case of] *āpnoti*, there is also shortening. 74.

"From the root *āp*, there is the suffix *tu* and [the vowel] becomes short. From the root *āplṛ* in the sense of "pervasion," the suffix *tu* is applied, and the base vowel becomes short. Thus, *aptuḥ* means "body. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "it pervades" (*āpnoti*).
(75) "From the root *vas*, the suffix *tu*. 75.
*vastu* [is derived as follows]: from the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling," the suffix *tun* is applied, resulting in *vastu*. (76) *agāre ṇicca*:
when the word *agāra* ("house") is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇic* is applied after the root *vas*, and the suffix *tun* is applied after that. Thus, *agāra-vastu*.
The meaning is that it becomes *ṇit*. Because it is *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel. (77) *kṛñaḥ katuḥ* | 77 | From the root *kṛ*, the suffix *katu* occurs.
From the root *ḍukṛñ karaṇe* ("to do/make"), the suffix *katu* is applied. Of that...
Due to the absence of *guṇa* because of the *kit* designation, and with the substitution of *yaṇ*, the form is *ṛtuḥ*.
(78) *edhivahyaeścatuḥ*.
After the roots *edh* (to grow) and *vah* (to carry), the suffix *catuḥ* is applied. From these two, [the forms] *edhatuḥ* and *vahatuḥ* are derived.
*vahatuḥ* | (79) *jīverātuḥ* | 79. From the root *jīv* [meaning] "to live," the suffix *ātu* is applied; thus, *jīvātuḥ*.

(80) *ātṛn* and *vṛddhi*. The term *jīva* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. From the root *jīv* (to live), the suffix *ātṛn* occurs, and there is *vṛddhi* of the *ik* vowel of the base.
The form is *jaivātṛka*. [Pāṇini 3.2.184] states:
"After the roots *kṛṣi*, *cam*, *tan*, *dhana*, *nisṛj*, and *kharj*, the suffix *ū* is applied.
[The roots are: *kṛṣ* (to plow), *cam* (to eat), *tan* (to expand), *dhana*...

The root *sṛj* in the sense of "emission" (*visarga*) is not included here; for even if it were indicated by the form *sṛji*, since the suffix *ik* is marked with *k*, there would be no *guṇa* substitution, and thus it should have been indicated simply as *sṛji*. "Syāt" is defined in the *Medinī* [lexicon]. Regarding "mārjālīya," the *Medinī* states: "The word *mārjālīya* is recorded as referring to a Śūdra, a cat, and the purification of the body.
(114) [The suffix] *ālañ* is applied after the roots *pati* and *caṇḍi*. 114.

The suffix *ālañ* is applied after the roots *pat* and *caṇḍ*. The root *pat* means "to go," and *caṇḍ* means "to be angry"; the suffix *ālañ* occurs after these two. Because *ālañ* contains the marker *ñ*, there is vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel. Thus, *pātālaḥ*. It is called *pātāla* because beings fall (*patanti*) into it. *Caṇḍālaḥ*. Because the root *caṇḍ* is marked with the indicator *id*, the augment *num* is inserted; since it is no longer a vowel-penultimate (*adupadha*), there is no strengthening. Thus, *cāṇḍāla*.

However, Ujjvaladatta and others state that [the form] *abodhya* is derived from the group beginning with *prajña*. To this he says: "one" (*eka*). The seed of dissatisfaction here is precisely the contradiction with the Vārttika and its Bhāṣya, which states: "The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *kulāla*, *varuḍa*, *nikhāda*, *caṇḍāla*, and *amitra* in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*). For in that context, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after these very words in their own primary sense.

(115) *tami-viśi-biḍi-mṛṇi-kulipi-palipi-pañci-bhyaḥ kālan* || 115 || *tami*, *viśi*, *biḍi*, *mṛṇi*, *kuli*, *pi*, *palipi*, *pañci*. *tamu* in the sense of longing; *viśa* in the sense of entering; *biḍa* in the sense of reviling; *mṛṇa* in the sense of injury; *kula* in the sense of gathering; *kapi* in the sense of moving; *pala* in the sense of going; *pac* in the sense of expansion.

The ablative plural ending is used here after a *dvandva* compound. Regarding *tamāla*: according to the *Medinī*, "the word *tamāla* refers to a *tilaka* tree, a sword, the *tāpiccha* tree, and the *varuṇa* tree. *Viśāla*. *Biḍāla*. According to the *Amara-kośa*, "the words *ṭhākhu*, *biḍāla*, and *mārjāra* [all mean] a cat. *Mṛṇāla*. *Kulāla*. According to the *Amara-kośa*, "the word *kulāla* refers to the *kakubha* tree and a potter."
Thus [ends] the *Medinī*.
(116) *Pateraṅga* means a bird.
(116) Regarding *pateraṅga* meaning a bird: from the root *patlṛ* in the sense of "to go," the suffix *aṅgac* is applied, [denoting] a bird.
The meaning is "to be expressed. Regarding *pataṅga*: the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *pataṅga* [denotes] a locust, a variety of rice, a bird, and the sun.
(117) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after roots such as *tṛ* ("to cross") and others. 4.3.117.

"From *tarati* and so forth. The term *aṅgac* continues [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that the suffix *aṅgac* occurs after verbal roots such as *tarati*. Regarding *tarati*: this is a reference by means of the *śtip* marker to the root *tṛ* (meaning "to swim" and "to cross"). Regarding *lavaṅgam*: [this is derived from] the root *lūñ* (meaning "to cut").
Thus, from this [root] *aṅg*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
(118) *biḍādibhyaḥ kit* (Pāṇini 3.1.140): after roots such as *biḍa* in the sense of "abuse," etc., [the suffix *kvip* is added] with the *kit* marker. From roots beginning with *biḍa*...

The meaning is that the suffix *aṅ* becomes *kit* when [the root] *jan* is being applied. In *biḍaṅga*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because of the *kit* designation. Medinīkāra states: "The word *biḍaṅga* occurs in the three genders (*triṣu*) in the sense of 'one who knows,' and as masculine and neuter (*puṃnapuṃsakam*) in the sense of 'a destroyer of worms' (*kṛmighna*).
In *mṛdaṅga*, the suffix is applied to the root *mṛd* in the sense of 'crushing' (*kṣoda*). Of that...

However, this is not a merit [of the rule]. Regarding the word *kuraṅga*, it establishes the substitution of *u* (*utvam*) when a suffix follows by means of the principle of "diversity" (*bāhulakāt*). But if one derives it from the root *kura* (meaning "to sound") with the suffix *aṅgac*, there is great parsimony.

(119) *sṛvṛñor vṛddhiś ca* | [The meaning is: after the roots *sṛ* (to go) and *vṛñ* (to choose), there is the suffix *aṅ*, and there is also vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the verbal base. Thus, *sāraṅga*.
According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *sāraṅga* denotes a male deer and a *cātaka* bird in the masculine; it is used in the three genders when meaning variegated.
(120) The suffix *gan* is applied after the roots *gam* and *ad*.
(120) Regarding *gam gamyadyoḥ*: the root *gamlṛ* means "to go," and *ada* means "to eat"; the suffix *gan* is added after these two.
*Gaṅgā*, *adgaḥ*; by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), *aṅga* and others are also included. From the root *am*, the suffix *an* is applied. (121) *chā-pū-khaḍi-bhyaḥ kit*.

[The suffix *an* is applied] after *chā*, *pū*, and *khaḍi*, and it is *kit*. *Chā* in the sense of cutting, *pūṅ* in the sense of purifying, and *kaḍa* in the sense of piercing; having taken these together—

The suffix *gan* occurs after three roots; it is also *kit*. Thus: *chāgaḥ*, *pūgaḥ*. Because it is *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. That which is cut (*chāyate*) for the sake of sacrifice is a *chāga* (goat). That by which the mouth is purified (*pūyate*) is a *pūga* (betel nut, etc.). [The root is] *pūg*.

Regarding *kramuka* and *vṛnda*, Amarasimha states: "The word *vṛnda* [is used] for a betel nut tree and a multitude. Regarding *khaḍga*, the Medinī lexicon states: "The word *khaḍga* [is used] for the horn of a rhinoceros, a sword, and a type of Buddha; [it is also used] for a rhinoceros.
(122) [The suffix] *ki* with the augment *nuṭ* follows the root *bhṛñ*. 122.

*ṛtanyañjibhrasjibhyaśca*: After the roots *ṛ*, *tan*, *añj*, and *bhrasj*, [the suffix] *gan* is applied, and it is *kit*. The meaning is that after the root *bhṛṅ* (in the sense of "supporting"), the suffix *gan* is produced, and it becomes *kit*, and there is also the augment *nuṭ*.
Since the word *kit* was already carried over from the previous rule "after *chā*, *pū*, *khā*, and *ḍi*, [the suffix is] *kit*", its mention again here [is for the purpose of...]
For the sake of clarity: the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *bhṛṅga* [is used] for the *dhūmyāṭa* and the *ṣiṅga*.
(123) "From the root *śṛṇāti*, there is also the short vowel.
(123) "From the root *śṛṇāti*, there is also the short vowel. From this root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure"), the suffix *gnap* occurs, and the vowel is shortened.
The meaning is that there is shortening of the root-vowel (*dhātu*), as well as the *kit* status of the suffix and the augment *nuṭ*.

Thus, the form is *śṛṅgam*. [As for the word *śṛṅga*,] it is used in the senses of sovereignty, a peak, a mark, a water-fountain for play, a horn, and excellence; furthermore, *śṛṅgaḥ* [is used in the masculine].

The word *syāt* [is used] in the sense of a tufted head (*kūrcaśīrṣaka*), a female fish (*viṣā*), a type of goldfish (*svarṇamīna*), and the medicinal herb *ṛṣabha*; thus says the *Medinī*. (124) *Gaṇ* [is used] in the sense of a bird (*śakuna*). 124.

Regarding *gaṇ* and *śakuni*: the word *śṛṇāti* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. When *śakuni* (bird) is to be expressed, the suffix *gan* is applied to the root *śṛ*, along with the augment *nuṭ*. Thus, *śārṅga*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule "ṭhaco ñṇiti," and the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* substitutions occur for the *nuṭ* augment. *Śārṅga* refers to a bird.
The word *śārṅga* as a name for a bow (*dhanuḥ*) should be understood in the sense of "a modification of horn" (*śṛṅgasya vikāraḥ*).
(125) [The suffixes] *ga* and *ga* follow *mudi* and *gṛ*.
(125) *mudi* means joy; *gṛ* means swallowing. From these two, respectively—

The two suffixes *gak* and *ga* exist [as follows]: *mudga* is a specific type of grain, well-known in the Dravidian language as *ṭhpayaru*. Because the suffix *gak* has the *k*-marker (*kit*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel. Thus, *garga* [is formed]; he is a specific sage (*muniviśeṣa*). When the suffix *ap* is applied, *guṇa* occurs. It is precisely for this purpose that *gak* and *ga* are mentioned.
These two are prescribed separately.
(126) *aṇḍan* [is added] after *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛñ*. [The roots are: *ḍukṛñ* in the sense of making, *sṛ* in the sense of moving, and *bhṛñ* in the sense of supporting.
The root *vṛñ* means "to choose. From these [roots], by virtue of a collective dvandva compound, the fifth case ending is used; thus, the suffix *aṇḍan* shall be applied after them.

In the form *karaṇḍa*, there is *guṇa* substitution when the suffix follows. (127) *śṛ-dṛ-bhr-aḍiḥ*. 4.1.35. (Note: The rule *śṛ-dṛ-bhr-aḍiḥ* is provided as a reference for the grammatical operation mentioned in the commentary.)

*Śṛ-ḍṛ-bhaso 'diḥ*: after the roots *śṛ* (injury), *ḍṛ* (tearing), and *bhas* (threatening and shining), the suffix *adi* is applied. The letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus, *śarad*. When the suffix follows, there is *guṇa* substitution. "The word *śarat* [denotes] a year and also the season. [Similarly,] *darat* denotes a woman.

And [the word *prapāta*] means a precipice; [it is used] for both fear and a mountain. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The feminine form *bhās* occurs in the sense of a woman, existence, sound, and the female organ.
(128) [The suffix] *ṣug* and a short vowel [are applied] after the root *dṛ*. 128.

The meaning of the sūtra is: from the root *dṛ* (in the sense of "tearing apart"), there is the suffix *adip*, as well as the augment *ṣuk* and the shortening of the vowel. Thus, the form *dṛṣid* is produced. (129) From the roots *tyaj*, *tan*, and *yaj*, the suffix *ḍit* [is applied]. 129.

The suffix *adi* is *ḍit* after the roots *tyaj*, *tan*, and *yaj*. The suffix *adi* arising after these roots—namely, *tyaj* in the sense of "abandoning," *tan* in the sense of "expansion," and *yaj* in the sense of "worship of the gods" and so forth—is *ḍit*. Thus, *tyad*.
Because the suffix *adi* is *ḍit*, there is elision (*ṭilopa*) of the final vowel and what follows it.
(130) *etu-stuṭ ca* | 130. *etu-stuṭ ca*. The meaning is that from the root *iṇ* ("to go"), the suffix *ip* is applied, and the augment *tuṭ* is added to it; thus, the form *etad* is produced.

(131) *sarter aṭiḥ* | 131. From the root *sṛ*, meaning "to go," the suffix *aṭi* is applied. Explaining the meaning of the word *saraṭ*, he cites a lexicon: "The word *saraṭ* may denote wind or cloud."

(132) *laṅghernalopaśca* | [Sūtra 132: After the root *laṅgh*, there is also the elision of *n*. [Explanation: The root *lagh* means "to dry up"; from this, the suffix *aṭi* is applied, and there is the elision of the letter *n*.
(133) *pārayateḥ ajir* | 133.

From the root *pārayati*, the suffix *aj* [is applied]. The root *pār* belongs to the *curādi* group and ends in the causative marker *ṇic*. The meaning is that the suffix *aj* should be added to this [root]. Thus, we have *pāraga*. When the suffix *aj* is applied, the *ṇi* is elided by the rule "the *ṇi* is elided before a suffix beginning with a vowel that does not take *iṭ*" (*ṇer aniṭi*).
By the characteristic of that [suffix] being a *pratyaya*, there is indeed the *upadhā-vṛddhi*. Regarding the form [with] *kutva*:
(134) *pratheḥ kitsaṃprasāraṇaṃ ca* | 134. From the root *prath* [in the sense of] "becoming manifest," there is the suffix *ac*, and it is also *kit*.

The root becomes *kid* and there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel. [The word] "separately" (*pṛthak*) means that it is recited in the list beginning with *svar-ādi* for the purpose of a separate rule; such is the intention.
(135) *bhiyaḥ ṣuk hrasvaśca* | 6.1.57. [The suffix *kvip* is added after the root *bhī*, and the augment *ṣuk* is inserted, and the vowel is shortened. 135.

*bhiyaḥ ṣuk hrasvaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 135): From the root *bhī* in the sense of "fear" (*bhaye*), the suffix *ac* is applied, and there is the augment *ṣuk* as well as the shortening of the vowel; such is the meaning. The resulting form is *bhiṣaj*. (136) *yuṣyasibhyāṃ madik* (Uṇādi Sūtra 136).

Regarding the rule *yuṣyasibhyāṃ madik*: since the root *yuṣ* is not found in the Dhātupāṭha, he says—“*yuṣ* is a root belonging to the sūtra (i.e., a conventional root). *asu* in the sense of “throwing” belongs to the Divādi class. From these two, the suffix *madik* is added. Thus the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are produced. [From these,] *tvam* and *aham* [are derived]. [This is according to the rule: “*tvāhau sau*” (Pāṇini 7.2.94).
The sense is that he has thus stated [the rule] as "ādeśāu" (two substitutes).

(137) *artistusuhusṛdhṛkṣikṣubhāyāvāpadiyakṣinībhyo man* || 137 || [The suffix] *man* [is applied] after the roots *ṛ*, *stu*, *su*, *hu*, *sṛ*, *dhṛ*, *kṣi*, *kṣubh*, *ā-yā*, *ā-pat*, *i*, *akṣi*, and *nī*.
*ṛ* (to go), *ṣṭuañ* (to praise), *ṣuñ* (to press), *hu*... [and so forth].

The fifth case ending is used after the following group of roots in a copulative compound: *dā* (to give), *ad* (to eat), *sṛ* (to go), *dhṛ* (to hold), *kṣi* (to destroy), *ṭua kṣu* (to sound), *bhā* (to shine), *yā* (to reach), *vā* (to go or to smell), *pad* (to go), *yakṣa* (to worship, belonging to the *curādi* class), and *ṇī* (to lead). From these, the suffix *man* is applied.

"Arma": this form results from the suffix *man* and the application of *guṇa*. "Stoma": the meaning is a collection or assembly. "Soma": as in the definition, "soma [is used] for the cool-rayed moon. To justify the word *kṣauma*, he says: "by the suffix *aṇ* after *prajñā* and so forth."

(138) *jahāteḥ sanvad ālopaśca* | [The meaning is: after the root *jahāti*, there is the suffix *man* as if it were *san*, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the *ā*. [That is to say: from the root *ava* in the sense of "protection" and so forth, the suffix *man* is applied, and there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the suffix *man*. Now, one might object: regarding the phrase "and the elision of the *ṭi*" in this very rule—
The suffix *man* being subject to application, it becomes like *san*, and there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Thus, the form *jihma* arises.
(139) From the root *av*, there is also the elision of *ṭi*. 139.

"Avateṣṭilopaśca": [The meaning is] that from the root *ava* in the sense of "protection" and so forth, there is the suffix *man*, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṭi* portion of that *man* suffix. Now, one might object: in this very rule, "ṭilopaśca," since the *man* suffix is a subordinate element (*vidheya-bhūta*) within this same rule, it would not be the subject of reference (*uddeśyatva*). Therefore, [the rule] "ṭilopa" [is stated].

[The opponent argues: "In that case, the *prakṛti* (the base form) itself would have to be the object of the designation. To this he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: if one were to accept the elision of the suffix (*ṭilopa*) for the *prakṛti*. [He explains: "By *ḍit* alone"—this means because the elision of the suffix (*ṭilopa*) is possible by the rule *ṭer iti*. [He further explains: "By *ūṭh* in the rule *jvaratvara-*"—this refers to the substitution of *ūṭh* for both the letter *v* and the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).

The meaning is "in the proper place. Regarding the phrase "of those two": the meaning is "of the two *ūṭh* vowels that take the place of [the *akāra* and *vakāra*]. This is stated with the intention of the view that there is a separate *ūṭh* for each. However, according to the opinion that there is only one *ūṭh* in the place of both the *upadhā* vowel and the *vakāra*, there is no disagreement whatsoever. He states the proof for its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
"Because it is recited in the *cādi* group. "That is not so. He refutes that view, stating: "Because they are non-existent.
(140) *graserā ca* | 140. *graserā ca*. [The root] *grasu* means "to devour"; from this, the suffix *man* is applied.
The vowel *ā* is substituted for the final letter of the root; thus, the form is *grāma*. (141) From the roots *avi*, *siv*, *si*, and *śuṣ*, [the suffix *man* is added] with the *k*-marker.
(141) *avisivi*: *ava* in the sense of protection and so forth, *ṣivu* in the sense of weaving, *ṣiñ* in the sense of binding, and *śuṣ* [in the sense of drying].
Regarding the root *śuṣ* (to dry): from these [roots], the suffix *man* is applied, and it is *kit*. The substitution of *ūṭh* and so forth is as before. Thus, *ūma*:

when the suffix *man* is added to the root *av*, the form is derived by applying *ūṭh* according to the rule *jvaratvaretyūṭh* and then performing the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). Regarding *syūma*:
when the suffix *man* is added to the root *ṣivu*, the form should be understood as resulting from the substitution of *ūṭh* for *va* according to the rule *cchÂavoriti* followed by the *yaṇ* sandhi.
Regarding the word *sīmā*: it is a form derived from the root *ṣiñ*. This root is listed in the *sarvādi* group [of indeclinables].
(142) *iṣiyudhondhidasiśyādhūsūbhyomak* || 142 || [The suffix] *mak* is applied after the roots *iṣ*, *yudh*, *indh*, *das*, *śyā*, *dhū*, and *sū*.
*iṣiyudhīndhi*: *iṣa* (in the senses of moving, injuring, and giving), *yudha* (in the sense of combat), and *ñi indhī* (in the sense of kindling).

From the fifth case [ending] after this dvandva compound: *dīp* (to shine), *das* (to perish), *śyaiṅ* (to go), *dhūñ* (to shake), and *ṣūñ* (the emission of the embryo by a living being). Regarding *yudhma*:
the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *yudhma* occurs in the sense of a bow or a battle. Regarding *dasma*: the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *dasma* may refer to a sacrificer (*yajamāna*)."

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "In the sense of a thief and fire. Regarding the word *śyāma*: according to the *Amara-kośa*, "The word *śyāma* [is used] in three genders for green and black; *śyāmā* refers to the *śārivā* plant and the night.
(143) [Pāṇini 3.2.150]: *yujirucitijāṃ kuśca*. 143.

Regarding the roots *yuj*, *ruc*, and *tij*: from the compound of these—*yuj* in the sense of "joining," *ruc* in the sense of "shining," and *tij* in the sense of "sharpening"—the suffix *mak* shall be applied, and there shall be the substitution of *k* for the final letter.
(144) *hanter hi ca*: [The suffix *mak* is applied after the root *han*, and *hi* is substituted for its final. 144.
And *hantri*: from the root *han* in the sense of "killing" or "going," there is the suffix *mak*, and the substitution of *hi* for the root.
(145) *bhiyaḥ ṣug vā*: 1.4.25. From the root *bhī* in the sense of "fear," the suffix *mak* is applied; and there is the augment *ṣuk* added to the root.
Or [it] may be *bhīma*; this is the form when there is no substitution of *ṣuk*. *Bhīṣma* is the form when *ṣuk* is applied.
(146) *Gharmaḥ* | 146 | *Gharmaḥ*: the meaning is that *gharma* is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) with the suffix *mak*. This is by way of distinguishing between the base and the suffix.

He demonstrates this with the suffix *mag* after the root *ghṛ*: the intention is that it is derived from *ghṛ* in the sense of "flowing" or "shining. He says "and there is *guṇa*" because the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *kṅiti ca* applies since *mak* is marked with *k*. (147) *grīṣmaḥ*. 147.

*Grīṣmaḥ*. [Derived from] the root *grasu* in the sense of "devouring" (*adane*). From this [root], the suffix *maki* is introduced; the meaning is that the substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel is a grammatical anomaly (*nipātyate*). (148) *Pratheḥ ṣivan saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca* | 148. [The suffix] *ṣivan* is added after the root *prath*, and there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) [of the semivowel]. 148.

Regarding the rule *pratheḥ ṣivan saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*: the meaning is that from the root *prath* (in the sense of "becoming famous"), there is the suffix *ṣivan*, and the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root [occurs]. Because the suffix *ṣivan* contains the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Some say it is *ṣavan*; this means that the suffix *ṣavan* is added to the root *prath*. If it were so, the form would be *pṛthavī*.
"pṛthivī, pṛthavī, pṛthvī"—thus says Amara.

(149) "From the roots aśū, pruṣ, laṭi, kaṇ, khaṭi, and viśi, the suffix *kvan* is applied. (150) [The roots are: aśū in the sense of pervading (vyāptau), pruṣ in the sense of moistening and so forth (snehanādau), laṭi in the sense of childhood (bālye), kaṇ... [and so on].

The word *nimīlana* means "closing," *khaṭi* means "desire," and *viśa* means "entering"; from these, the fifth case ending [is used] after a copulative compound (*dvandva*). From these [roots], the suffix *kvansu* occurs. Regarding *aśva*: according to Amarasimha, "ghoṭaka, vīti, turaga, tuṅga, aśva, and turaṅgama" [are synonyms for horse]. Regarding *pruṣva*: [it is derived from] the root *pruṣ*.

*Rūpam* (the form). *Laṭvā*: according to Amara, "The *jhallarī*, *carcarī*, *pārī*, *horā*, *laṭvā*, and *sidhmalā* [are synonyms]. According to Viśva, "The word *laṭvā* may refer to a species of *karañja* tree, a fruit, a musical instrument, or a particular bird. Regarding *kaṇvam*: according to Medinī, "The word *kaṇva* denotes sin; as a masculine noun, it refers to a sage (*muni*)."
Regarding *khaṭvā*: "A bed (*śayana*)—namely *mañca*, *paryaṅka*, and *palyaṅka*—is synonymous with *khaṭvā*," according to Amara.

Regarding *viśva*: "The *ādityas*, *viśvedevas*, and *vasus* [are denoted by *viśve*]," according to Amara; and "In the *Medinī* lexicon: *viśvā* is feminine when referring to *ativiṣā* (a medicinal plant), and neuter when referring to the world (*jagat*)."
(150) *iṇ-śībhyāṃ van* | 150. From the roots *iṇ* and *śī*, the suffix *van* [is applied]. *iṇ* means "to go," and *śīṅ* means "to sleep"; from these two, the suffix *van* occurs.
*Eva* is a form of the root *iṇ*. *Seva* is a form of the root *śīṅ*.

(Pāṇini 8.3.110). "Not [the substitution of ṣ for s] after *ra* followed by *ra*, nor in *sṛp*, *sṛj*": the term *rapara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [This refers to the rule] "A retroflex [substitute occurs] for [a dental] not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ*).

This is the subject under discussion. The roots *sṛplṛ* (in the sense of moving), *sṛj* (in the sense of emission), *spṛś* (in the sense of touching), *spṛh* (in the sense of desiring, belonging to the *curādi* class), and *sav-* (beginning with *su*)—the genitive case [ending] follows from this *dvandva* compound.
The meaning of the genitive here is the relation between a part and a whole. Thus, the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply to the *s* that is a part of these [roots].

The meaning is "it may be. Regarding *usra*: the form is derived from the root *vas* with the suffix *rak*; due to the suffix being marked with *k*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), and by this [rule], the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) occurs. Now, one might object that the statement here regarding the absence of *ṣatva* is inconsistent, because this rule [would apply] to the *ṣatva* already established by the rule "after a preceding member, in a compound name, the *g* sound [is replaced by *gh*]" (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ*).

Since the status of being a prohibitor has been stated regarding *vṛtti* and so forth, one might raise the objection that in this case (*atra*) there is no attainment of *ṣatva* by that [rule], but rather only by the rule "śāsivasī-". Anticipating this doubt, he says: "with the intention of [stating] more. Therefore, the meaning is that the text of the *Vṛtti* is indeed an indicator of this prohibitory status as well. *Usraḥ*.

Regarding *raśmi*: the sense is that it means "ray," as per Amara’s lexicon, which states, "kiraṇa, aśra, mayūkha, and aṃśu [are synonyms]. Medinī also states, "ṭhusra [is used] for a bull and a ray. Regarding *usra*: Amara states, "māheyī, saurabheyī, gauḥ, usrā, mātā, and śṛṅgiṇī [are synonyms for a cow]. Regarding *vāśra*: this is a form derived from the verbal root *vāśṛ*. Regarding *musra*.
The form [musa] is derived from the root *mus* in the sense of "crushing.

(171) *caki-ramyo-ruc-copadhāyāḥ* | 171 | Regarding *caki-ramyo-ruc-copadhāyāḥ*: from the roots *cak* in the sense of "satiety" and *ram* in the sense of "sporting," the suffix *rak* is applied, and the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is replaced by *u*.
The meaning is that the letter *u* is substituted for the penultimate vowel. Regarding "cukra": Amarasimha states, "Cukra is the thousand-piercing [plant], the sour cane (*amlavetasa*).
(172) *vau kaseḥ* | 172 | [The suffix *kan* is applied after the root *kas* when the word *vi* precedes. 172.

From the root *kas* [meaning] "to go," the suffix *rak* is applied after the prefix *vi-*, and there is vocalization (*utva*) of the penultimate vowel; thus the form *vikusra* is obtained. (173) *amitamyordīrghaśca*: [The suffix *rak* is applied] after the roots *am* and *tam*, and there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel. 173.

The [root] *am* is long and the [suffix] *rak*. The meaning is that from the roots *am*, in the sense of "going" and so forth, and *tam*, in the sense of "desire," the suffix *rak* is applied, and there is lengthening of the vowel of the base (*prakṛti*). Regarding *āmra*:
Amarasimha states, "This *āmra* is the *cūta* and the *rasāla*. Regarding *tāmra*: this is a form derived from the root *tam*.

(174) *nindernalopaśca* | 174. *nindernalopaśca*. From the root *ṇidi*, meaning "to reproach," the suffix *rak* is applied; the meaning is that by virtue of this [suffix], there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* of the root. Thus, [the word] *nidra*.
The meaning is that after [the suffix] *it*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of *num*. Amara states: "Nidrā, śayana, and svāpa mean sleep.
(175) *Ardeḥ dīrghaśca* | 175 | *Ardeḥ dīrghaśca*. From the root *ard* in the sense of "going" or "begging," the suffix *rak* is applied, and there is lengthening [of the vowel].
The meaning is that there is lengthening of the root vowel. The form is *ārdram*. According to Amara: "Ārdra, sārdra, klinna, and timita" all mean moist. (176) [Pāṇini 3.2.150] *śucer daś ca*. 176.

And [the word] *śūdra*: from the root *śuc* (to grieve), with the suffix *rak*, there is the substitution of the letter *d* for the final [consonant] of the root, and lengthening of the penultimate vowel—this is the meaning. Amara states: "The *śūdras*, those of the lowest caste (*avaravarṇa*), the *vṛṣalas*, and those born of the lowest rank (*jaghanyaja*)."

(177) *durīṇo lopaśca* | 177. The meaning is that after the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") with the prefix *dus*, there is the suffix *rak*, and there is also elision (*lopa*) of the verbal root. When the suffix *rak* is applied, the *r* of the root is elided by the rule *rori*, and then [the preceding vowel is lengthened] by the rule *ḍhralope*.
The meaning is "long.

(178) *kṛteś chaḥ krū ca* | 178. After the root *kṛt*, [the suffix] *cha* is applied, and there is also the substitution of *krū*. From the root *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting," after this base, [the suffix *cha* is applied], and for the final letter of the base...

The meaning is that there would be a substitution of the letter *ch* for the letter *t*, and because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would be a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) according to the rule *ṭhkr̥*. It is said: "Kaṣṭa, kṛcchra, and ābīla—these three are adjectives when they qualify something else; likewise, devabhūya and so forth, as well as kṛcchra such as sāntapana and so forth. And: "Nṛṃśasa means a killer."
"Krūraḥ" generally means a rogue or a deceiver; thus says Amara.
(179) *Roder ṇiluk ca* | 179.
Regarding "roder ṇiluk ca": from the root *rudir*, meaning "to shed tears," with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *rak* is applied, and there is the elision (*luk*) of the *ṇi*.

There shall also be *ṇiluk* (elision of the *ṇi* suffix). Although the elision of *ṇi* is already established by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, the explicit mention of *luk* is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* substitution by means of the technical designation (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) of the suffix. Thus, *rudra* is the form [derived] with the suffix *rak*. (180) *Bahulam anyatrāpi saṃjñācchandasoḥ* | 180 || [The suffix *rak* is applied] diversely elsewhere as well, in names and in Vedic meters.

"Abundantly elsewhere as well. This means that, apart from technical names (*saṃjñā*) and Vedic usage (*chandas*), the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṇi* should be stated abundantly even when derived from other verbal roots (*dhātu*) or when followed by other suffixes. An example in the sense of a technical name is: "He nourishes (*bṛṃhayati*) or increases (*vardhayati*) the subjects," hence he is called *brahmā*. Here, there is the elision of *ṇi*. In Vedic usage, however, [we find]: "May they increase thee (*vardhantu tvā*)."

The meaning is that "the well-being-promoters" (suṣṭutayaḥ) should cause [them] to increase. He states—by way of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), which allows for the occurrence [of a grammatical form] even in the absence of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) or Vedic meter (*chandas*)—that "the winds blow, drying the leaves" (*vānti parṇaśuṣaḥ*). First, the winds blow that dry the leaves; the meaning is that they wither the foliage. After the withering of the leaves, [come] the leaf-shedders (*parṇamuc*).

The winds blow; they cause the leaves to fall, thus they are "leaf-shakers" (*parṇamuc*). After the shaking of the leaves, the "leaf-growers" (*parṇaruha*) winds blow; they cause the leaves to grow, thus they are "leaf-growers. The meaning is that thereafter the god sends rain. Here, even though it is neither a technical name (*saṃjñā*) nor a Vedic verse (*chandas*), there is elision of the suffix *ṇi*.
(181) *jorī ca* | 181 | *jorī ca*. The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root. From this, the suffix *rak* is applied;
the meaning is that the vowel *ī* is substituted for the final letter. Thus, *jīra*. As it is said: "But *jīra* [is used] in the sense of 'aging' and 'sword'."

Regarding the statement "medinī and jya are one": the root *jyā* means "to lose vitality" (*vayohānau*). From this root, with the suffix *rak*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyā-*, followed by the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), and finally, by the rule *hal*, the long vowel is applied, resulting in the form *jīra*.
This alone is correct; for this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra concerning the elision of a root-vowel (*na dhātulopa-*), it says: *jīveradānuḥ*.
Thus, for the purpose of rejecting the Vārttika, it was stated: "This is not a form derived from the root *jīv*, but rather from the root *jyā* with the suffix *rak*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.150) *su-sū-dhā-gṛdhibhyaḥ kran*. 3.2.150.

The suffix *kran* is added after the roots *su*, *sūdhā*, *gṛdh*, and so on. [The roots are: *ṣuñ* (to press), *ṣūṅ* (to release the breath or fetus), *ḍudhāñ* (to hold and nourish), and *gṛdhu* (to desire). The ablative case here follows from their being in a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The meaning is that the suffix *kran* is applied after these. In the word *sura*, because the suffix is marked with *k* (*kit*), there is no *guṇa* substitution. The letter *r*...

The rule regarding *kr* [the substitution of *kṛ*] when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows is for the sake of the *nit*-accent. Regarding *surā*: Amara states, "surā, halipriyā, hālā. Regarding *sūra*:
Amara states, "sūra, sūrya, aryaman, āditya, dvādaśātman, divākara. Regarding *dhīra*:
by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām*, there is the substitution of *ī*; Amara states, "dhīra, manīṣī, jña, prājña."

(183) *śusicimīnāṃ dīrghaśca* | The suffix *kran* is applied after the roots *śu* (to go), *si* (to bind), *ci* (to accumulate), and *ḍu mi* (to throw); furthermore, there is lengthening of the vowel of these roots which serve as the bases.
And [the word] *dīrgha*. Since the root *śu* is not seen in the *Dhātupāṭha* in the sense of "going," he says: "*śuḥ sautraḥ*" (the root *śu* is from the *Sūtra*).
Regarding "*cīram*": Amara states, "The ruby, the commentary, vermilion, *cīra*, *cīvara*, and *piñjara*. Regarding "*mīra*": it is a form derived from the root *miñ*.
(184) *vā vindheḥ* | 184. *vā vindheḥ*. This means that the suffix *kransya* is optionally applied after the root *indhī* (meaning "to shine") when *vi* is the upapada.
Thus we have *vīdhram*. [In this form] there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditām*. It is said: "But *vīdhram* is of a pure nature."
Thus says Amara.

(185) *vṛdhivapibhyāṃ ran* | [Pāṇini 3.2.163] From the roots *vṛdh* (to increase) and *vap* (to sow/secrete), the suffix *ran* is applied. *Vṛdh* means "growth," and *ḍu vap* means "the sowing of seeds. From these two—

The suffix *rani* would apply [here]. In the word *vardhra*, there is the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel. Amara states: "A leather thong (*varatrā*) is called *nadhrī* or *vardhrī*. In the word *vapra*, Amara states: "*Vapra* is masculine when meaning a rampart, and feminine or neuter when meaning a bamboo thicket, a heap of earth, or a riverbank."

(186) *ṛjra*, *indra*, *agra*, *vajra*, *vipra*, *kubra*, *cubra*, *kṣura*, *khura*, *bhadra*, *ugra*, *bhela*, *śaśukra*, *śukla*, *gorava*, *nerā*, *mālā*. *ṛjra-indrāgra*: *ṛji* (to go, to stand, etc.); *idi* (supreme sovereignty); *agi* (motion); *vaja* (motion); *ḍu vap* (to sow, the continuity of seeds); *kubi* (to cover); *cubi* (contact with the mouth).

The roots *kṣur* (to shave), *khur* (to cut), *bhad* (auspiciousness), *uc* (collection), *ñibhī* (fear), *śuc* (sorrow), *guṅ* (indistinct sound), *van* (to gather), *iṇ* (to go), and *mā* (measure)— these are prescribed as ending in the suffix *ran*. Regarding the form *ṛjra*, he speaks while anticipating the objection that the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel would apply.
Regarding the term *nipātanāt* (due to irregular derivation): because the root *agi* has the marker *i*, he says—“there is elision of the *n* of the *aṅga*. The remainder is clear.
(187) *sami kasa ukan*. 187.
The suffix *ukana* is applied after the root *kas* when *sam* is the preceding prefix; this means that the suffix *ukana* follows *kas* with *sam* as its upapada.
The resulting form is *saṅkasuka*.
(188) The suffix *ṇukan* is applied after the roots *pac* and *naś*, and there is also the substitution of *kanum*. 188.

Regarding *paci-śor-ṇuk-anum* and *ca*: the suffix *ṇukan* is applied after the roots *ḍupacaṣ* (to cook) and *ṇaś* (to disappear). The meaning is that for these two roots, respectively, the substitution of *kā* and the augment *num* occur. Due to the *ṇit*-nature of *ṇukan*, there is vṛddhi [of the root vowel]. Thus, the forms are *pākukaḥ* and *naṃśukaḥ*.

(189) *bhiyaḥ krukan* | 189 | The suffix *krukan* is added after the root *bhī*. The meaning is that the suffix *krukan* is applied to the root *ñi-bhī* (to fear). The resulting form is *bhīruka*. Amara states: "A coward is called *bhīruka*, *kāruka*, *srasta*, *bhīru*, *bhīruka*, and *bhīluka*."
(190) *kvun* [is added] after [roots ending in vowels], even when not preceded by anything else, when a craftsman (*śilpin*) is to be expressed or when a name (*saṃjñā*) is understood.
*Kvun* occurs when a craftsman is to be denoted or when a name is implied.
"Even when not preceded by anything else" means when there is no prefix (*upapada*). The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative.

By virtue of the word *api* ("also"), [the suffix applies] even when accompanied by a prefix (*upapada*). He gives an example for an artisan (*śilpin*): *rajakaḥ*. From the root *rañj* (in the sense of "coloring"), with the suffix *kvun*, there is the elision of *n* and the substitution of *a* [for the penultimate vowel], resulting in this form. Amarasimha states: "A *nirṇejaka* is a *rajaka*; a *śoṇḍikika* is a *maṇḍahāraka*. He gives an example for when it is accompanied by a prefix:
Regarding *ikṣukuṭṭaka*: the root *kuṭṭ* means "to cut"; one who cuts sugarcane (*ikṣu*) is an *ikṣukuṭṭaka*.

He gives an example of a technical name (*saṃjñā*): *caraka*. Amara states: "In [the sense of] a 'sinner,' 'exertion,' 'wanderer' (*caraka*), 'tamāla,' and 'lac,' the suffix *naḍ* is applied. Regarding *caṣaka*: a *caṣaka* is a drinking vessel (not feminine).
"Also, *sāraka* means 'one who thirsts excessively,'" according to Amara. Regarding *śunaka*:

this is a form derived from the root *śun* (meaning "to move") with the suffix *kvun*. Regarding *bhaṣaka*: this is a form derived from the root *bhaṣ* (meaning "to bark"). [The verse states: "A *śunaka*, a *bhaṣaka*, and a *śvā* are synonyms; however, that which is devoid of barking is called an *alarka*."
Thus says Amara.

(191) *rame raś ca lo vā* | 191. *rame raś ca lo vā*. From the root *ramu* in the sense of "playing," the suffix *kvun* is applied, and the letter *ra* of the root is optionally replaced by *la*. From the root... [text truncated]
The meaning is that the letter *l* may optionally replace the letter *r*. Thus, the forms *ramakaḥ* and *lamakaḥ* are derived.

(192) *Jahāteḥ dve ca* [Kāśikā 3.2.167]: after the root *hā* (in the sense of "abandoning"), the suffix *kvun* is applied, and there is reduplication of the root. The root *hā* (meaning "to abandon") takes the suffix *kvun*, and the root undergoes reduplication.
The meaning is "it may be. The form is *jahaka*.
(193) *dhma* becomes *dham*. 193. *dhma* becomes *dham*. The root *dhmā* means "sound" and "contact with fire"; from this [root], the suffix *kvun* is applied.
The meaning is that the suffix *ka* is added after a verbal root (*dhātu*) beginning with *dha*. Thus, the form is *dhamaka*.

(194) *hano vadha ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.108]: "After the root *han*, there is the substitution of *vadha* [before the suffix *ka*]. Thus, *vadhaka*. The root *han* means "to kill" and "to go"; when the suffix *kvan* is applied, the root undergoes the substitution of *vadha*.
And *rūpa*.
(195) *Bahulam anyatrāpi* | 195 | [The suffix] *kvun* occurs abundantly even after other roots as well. After the root *kuh*, there is *kvun*.
The form is *kuhaka*, meaning "one who acts artificially" (*kṛtakam*). [The root] *kṛtī* means "to cut.

(196) *kṛṣervṛddhiścodīcām* | 196. Regarding the rule *kṛṣervṛddhiścodīcām*: from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" or "scratching," the suffix *kun* is applied according to the opinion of the Northern grammarians.
The meaning is "and there is vṛddhi. Because of the mention of "the northerners" (udīcām), this rule for vṛddhi is optional. Thus, the forms are *kārṣakaḥ* and *kṛṣakaḥ*.
(197) And [the word] *udaka*. 197.

And *udaka*. From the root *undī* in the sense of "moistening," the suffix *kvip* is applied. One might object: "Is this not already established by the rule *kvun śilpisaṃjñayoḥ* etc., since it is a technical term (*saṃjñā*)? To this he replies:
"For the sake of elaboration (*prapañcārtham*)."
(198) *vṛddhikṛṣyoḥ kikan* | 198. After the roots *vṛśc* and *kṛṣ*, the suffix *kikan* is applied. From *vraścū* (to cut) and *kṛṣ* (to plough), *kikan* occurs.
The form *vṛścikaḥ* results. [The word] *kiṣkuḥ* [is used] for a cubit and a span.

Regarding *śūkakīṭa*, Amara states: "The word *śūka* refers to a scorpion. Regarding *kṛṣika*, Amara states: "One who lives by the field is called a *karṣaka*, a *kṛṣika*, and a *kṛṣīvala*. (199) [The rule] *prāṅ piṇikaṣaḥ* || 199 || [is explained].

*Prāṅpiṇikaṣaḥ*. The meaning is that the suffix *kikan* is applied after the roots *paṇ* (in the sense of trade and praise) and *kaṣ* (in the sense of harming), preceded by the prefix *pra-āṅ*. *Prāpaṇikaḥ* is a form derived from the root *paṇ* with the prefixes *pra-* and *āṅ*. *Prākaṣikaḥ* is a form derived from the root *kaṣ*.

(200) *muṣer dīrghaś ca*: The meaning is that from the root *muṣ* (in the sense of "stealing"), the suffix *kikan* is applied, and there is lengthening of the vowel of the root. The resulting form is *mūṣika*.
As Amarasimha states: "The *ṭhundu*, the *mūṣika*, and the *ākhu* [are synonyms for a mouse]."

(201) *syameḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca* | [Pāṇini 4.3.147] The meaning is: from the root *syam*, which means "to sound," the suffix *kikan* is applied, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root vowel, and it becomes long; thus the form is *sīmika*.

(202) *kriya ikan* | 202 | *kriya ikan*. The meaning is that the suffix *ikan* is applied after the root *krīñ* (meaning "to buy" or "exchange of goods"). Thus, the form *krayika* arises through the substitution of *ay* for the vowel [of the root].

(203) *āṅ piṇi-pani-pati-khani-bhyaḥ* |203| The rule concerns the roots *piṇa*, *pana*, *pati*, and *khanu*. From the compound of these—*piṇa* and *pana* meaning "transaction" and "praise," *patlṛ* meaning "to go," and *khanu* meaning "to dig"—the fifth case ending is used. When *āṅ* is the prefix, the suffix *ikan* is added to these roots.

Since the form is established by the suffix *ikan* after the prefix *upa*, the mention of *paṇi* in the rule "ṭhprāṅ piṇikaṣa" is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). Alternatively, it is for the purpose of excluding other prefixes.
(204) After the roots *śyai*, *styai*, *hṛ*, and *ava*, the suffix *inac* [is applied]. 2.4.52.

The suffix *inac* occurs after the roots *śyai*, *styai*, *hṛ*, and *ava*. [The root] *śyaiṅ* means "to go"; *ṣṭyai* (here *ṣṭya*) means "sound" and "collection"; *hṛñ* means "to take away"; and *ava* means "protection" and so forth; from these, *inac* is applied. Thus, *śyena* ("hawk"). Amara states: "A hawk (*śyena*) is a bird of prey; an owl (*ulūka*), however, is a crow (*vāyasa*), an enemy (*arāti*), and a night-prowler (*pecaka*). *Styena* means a thief. *Hariṇa* means... [deer].
"Ṭhmṛge kuraṅgavātāyuhariṇā'jinayonayaḥ" (deer, antelope, vātāyu, hariṇa, and those born from skins)—thus says Amara.
(205) "vṛjeḥ kicca" | 205. From the root *vṛj*, the suffix *inac* is applied, and it is also *kit*. The root *vṛjī* means "to avoid" or "to exclude"; from this, *inac* shall occur, and it is...
The meaning is "becomes a child. Regarding the word *vṛjinam*:

Amara states, "Kaluṣa, vṛjina, enas, agha, aṃhas, durita, and duṣkṛta [are synonyms for sin]. Medinī states, "Vṛjina is used in the neuter gender to mean impurity (*kalmaṣa*). (206) *Ajer aja ca* | 206 | [This is the sūtra: "After the root √aj, the suffix *ac* is added, and *aja* is the substitute [for the root]. (206)
And [the word] *ajeraja*. The root *aja* means "to go" and "to throw"; from this [root], by the rule *ajerajaḥ*, the substitute *aja* is applied—this is the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the prescription of the substitute *aja* for *aji* is redundant, because it is necessary for the purpose of subverting the substitution of *vī* (as per *ajervī*). Amara states: "A leather garment is called *ajinam*; it is a feminine derivative (*kṛtiḥ*)."

(207) *Bahulam anyatrāpi* | [Pāṇini 3.3.120] "Abundantly even elsewhere. This means that the suffix *-inac* should also be stated after other verbal roots. For example, *kaṭhinam* ("hard"). This form is derived from the root *kaṭh*, meaning "to live in hardship. For example, *nalinam* ("lotus"). [This is derived from the root] *ṇal*.
*gahana* is a form derived from the root *gah*. *Malina* is a form derived from the root *mal*, meaning "to hold.
*Kuṇḍina* is a form derived from the root *kuḍi*, meaning "to burn. (208) [The word] *dyateḥ* [is used]. 208.
Regarding "from *dyati*": the meaning is that the suffix *inan* would occur after the root *do*, meaning "to cut" (*avakhaṇḍane*). The resulting form is *dina*.
(209) [The suffix] *inan* occurs after the roots *dru* and *dakṣi*. 209.

*Drudakṣibhyāminan*: from the roots *dru* (to move) and *dakṣ* (to increase), the suffix *inan* is added; this is the meaning. Regarding *draviṇam*, Amarasimha states: "Gold is *hiraṇya*, *draviṇa*, and *dyumna*. Regarding *dakṣiṇa*, Amarasimha states: "*Dakṣiṇa* refers to one who is straightforward and generous, as well as to one who is skillful, a giver, or an enjoyer."

(210) *arteḥ kidicca* | [Pāṇini 3.3.97] From the root *ṛ* (to go), the suffix *inan* is applied; it is marked with *k* and *it*.
