And *syamer īṭ*. From the root *syam* in the sense of "sound," the suffix *kan* is applied, and there is the augment *īṭ*; thus the form *syamīka* is obtained.
(328) *Aji-yu-dhū-nībhyo dīrghaś ca*: [The suffix *kan* is applied after the roots *aj*, *yu*, *dhū*, and *nī*, and there is lengthening of the vowel. 328.

Regarding *ajiyudhūnībhyo*: from the roots *aja* (in the senses of motion and throwing), *yu* (in the senses of mixing and not mixing), *dhūñ* (in the sense of shaking), and *ṇīñ* (in the sense of leading)—the suffix *kan* is applied, and there is lengthening of these [roots]. As for *vīka*:
when the suffix *kan* is added to the root *aja*, the base undergoes the substitution *vī*, and that [vowel] is lengthened.

Due to the force of the long-vowel prescription, there is an absence of guṇa. Regarding the word *yūka*: the root vowel is lengthened by the suffix *kan*. (329) *hriyo raśca lo vā* | 329. From the root *hrī* (in the sense of "shame"), *kan* is added; the root vowel is lengthened, and the *ra* of *hrī* optionally becomes *la*. Thus, *hrī* (to feel shame). From this [root], *kan* is added; the root vowel is lengthened.
The meaning is that there is either the letter *ra* or the letter *la*. Regarding *hrīkā*:
due to the force of the rule prescribing the long vowel, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Regarding *hlīkā*: this is the form resulting from the substitution of *la* for *ra*.

(330) *śaker unontauntiṇayaḥ* | 330 | From the root *śaklṛ*, meaning "to be able," the four suffixes *una*, *unta*, *unti*, and *uni* are applied. [The resulting words are] *śakunta* (bird), *pakṣin*, *śakuni*, *śakunta*, *śakuna*, and *dvija*.
Thus says Amara.
(331) *bhuvo jhic* | 331. *bhuvo jhic*: From the root *bhū*, meaning "to exist," the suffix *jhic* shall be applied. [By the rule] *ṭhjo'ntaḥ*, the letter *ṭh* becomes the final element.

This is the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*). Regarding the form *bhavanti*: this form arises through the substitution of the final letter, followed by *guṇa* and the substitution of *ava*. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya, "The root *as-* exists even when not employed, provided that *bhavanti* follows," he says "by way of *bāhulaka*" (due to irregularity) in order to establish forms such as *avantih*.

(332) *kanyuc* after *kṣip* and [the root *bhū*]. 332. *kanyuc* after *kṣip* and [the root *bhū*]. The meaning is that the suffix *kanyuc* is applied to *kṣip* (in the sense of "impelling") and, because of the word "and" (*ca*), also to *bhū*. Thus, *kṣipaṇyuḥ*; here, the substitution of *ṇatva* occurs by the rule *aṭkuvāṅ*. *Bhuvanyuḥ*.
The form [of *kṣip*] arises from the absence of *guṇa* due to the *kit* designation and the substitution of *uvaṅ*.
(333) *anuṅ* is substituted for *nad* and for *kṣip*.
(333) *anuṅ* is substituted for *nad* and for *kṣip*. *Nad* means "inarticulate sound. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), *anuṅ* shall also be substituted for *kṣip*.
Regarding the word *kṣipaṇu*: because the suffix has an indicatory letter *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. (334) *Kṛ-vṛ-dāribhya unan*.
[The suffix] *unan* is added after the roots *kṛ* (to scatter), *vṛ* (to choose), and *dṛ* (to tear). *Kṛ* means "to scatter," *vṛñ* means "to choose," and *dṛ* means "to tear."
The suffix *unan* is added after these [roots] ending in *ṇi*; this is the meaning. (335) *tro raśca lo vā*.
After the root *tṛ* (meaning "to tremble" and "to cross over"), the suffix *unan* is applied, and the *ra* of *tṛ* is optionally replaced by *la*. Thus, from *tṛ*, the form *taruṇa* is derived.
The meaning is that *la* replaces *ra*. Regarding "taruṇa": by the suffix *un*, there is guṇa of the root. Amara says: "One who is in the prime of youth is *taruṇa*, a young man.
(336) [The suffix *un* is added] after the roots *kṣudhi*, *piśi*, and *mithi*, and it is *kit*. (336)

The suffix *unan* is added after the roots *kṣudh*, *piś*, and *mith*, and it is *kit*. The meaning is that *unan* follows these roots—namely *kṣudh* in the sense of hunger (*bubhukṣā*), *piś* in the sense of dividing (*avayava*), and *mith* which is a Vedic root (*sautra*)—and it is *kit*. Thus, we have *kṣudhuna*. Because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. (337) *phaleḥ guk ca*: [The suffix *unan* is added] after the root *phal*, and there is the substitution of *guk* [for the final consonant]. 337.

And *phalerguk*: the meaning is that when the suffix *unan* follows the root *phal* (in the sense of "producing fruit"), there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel. Thus, *phalguna* means Arjuna. Now, one might ask: how is it *phālguna*? To this he says: "by the *aṇ* suffix [added] after *prajñā* and so forth."
(338) *aśerlaśaśca* | 338. *aśerlaśaśca*. The meaning is that from the root *aś*, signifying "eating," there is the substitution of *laś* for the suffix *un*.
Regarding *laśuna*: Amara states, "The garlic plant is called *laśuna*, *guñjana*, *ariṣṭa*, *mahākanda*, and *rasonaka*."

*Arjerṇiluk ca*: The root *ṛj*, meaning "to go," "to stand," or "to acquire/earn," takes the suffix *un* (forming *arjun*), and by virtue of that suffix, there is the elision (*luk*) of the causative marker *ṇi*. Thus, the form is *arjuna*. Because of the intervention of the letter *ja*, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not occur. Amara states: "*Ṭhvalakṣo dhavalo'rjunaḥ*" ("*Ṭhvalakṣa*, *dhavala*, and *arjuna* mean white"). In this case, [the rule] is established by the rule *ṇer aniṭi* alone.

Since the disappearance of the *ṇi* affix is already established by the rule for its elision (*ṇerlope*), the prescription of its elision as *ṇiluk* has a purpose that must be considered. Nor is the prescription of elision necessary merely to prevent the *guṇa* substitution of a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) which would otherwise apply by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); for when there is elision (*luk*), that substitution is prohibited by the rule "not when a suffix marked with *lu* follows" (*na lumatāṅgasya*).

It must be stated that [the suffix] *prāpti* [is intended]; for even if the elision (*luk*) is prescribed, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) remains unavoidable on account of the presence of *un*. Now, if there is an insistence on justifying this text by any means whatsoever, then it should be explained as follows: in this sūtra, the term *kit* should be understood as being carried over (*anuvarteta*), and consequently, from *un*.
Since there would be no *guṇa* substitution when [the suffix] has the marker *k*, whereas there would indeed be *guṇa* when it is elided (*lopa*), the result would be the opposite;

in that case, even the form *arjunaḥ* would not be established. Therefore, *kit* should certainly not be carried over [from the previous rule], and the prescription of elision (*luk*) would be redundant.

( ) *Ajer ṇiluk ca* | 338 | Regarding *ajer ṇiluk ca*: the root *ṛji* is used in the senses of going, standing, earning, and acquiring. From this root, the suffix *un* is applied, and by virtue of its presence, there is the elision (*luk*) of the causative marker (*ṇi*). Thus, the form is *arjuna*. Because of the intervention of the letter *j*, [the rule does not apply].

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs. According to Amarasimha, "ṭhvalakṣa," "dhavala," and "arjuna" are synonyms for white. Here, since the elision of the suffix *ṇi* is already established by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*, the prescription of its elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṇiluk* serves no apparent purpose.

Nor can it be said that this is intended to prevent the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) which would otherwise apply by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the suffix retaining its influence).

It must be stated that the prescription of *luk* elision is necessary; for it might be argued that when *luk* occurs, there is no application [of the rule] due to the prohibition "na lumatāṅgasya. However, even if *luk* were prescribed, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) would still be unavoidable by resorting to the suffix *an*. Now, if there is a persistent insistence on justifying this text in some way or another, then...

It should be stated thus: "In this sūtra, 'kit' should be understood as carrying over; consequently, because of the *kit* status, there is no *guṇa* [vowel strengthening] for the *un* suffix, whereas if it were elided, the *guṇa* would certainly occur. If this were the case, the form *arjuna* itself would not be established.
Therefore, *kid* should certainly not be carried over [from the previous rule], and the prescription of *luk* (elision) would be redundant.
(*tṛṇākhyāyāṃ cit*) "In the case of a name for grass": *tṛṇākhyā* means "a name for grass" (*tṛṇasyākhyā*); when that [name] exists, [the suffix *kvip*] is applied after the root *ṛj*.
The meaning is that it would be *cit*. He states the result of being *cit*: "Because it is *cit*, it is udātta at the end.
(Pāṇini 6.1.163) And from the root *ṛ* [3.40]: "And from *ṛ*. The root *ṛ* means "to go"; the suffix *unans* is added to this, and it is *cit*—this is the meaning. Thus, *aruṇa*.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *raṣābhyām*. Amara states: "The word *aruṇa* may refer to the sun, and also to a variety of color; it is used in three genders.
(Pāṇini 3.2.171) *aji-yami-śīṅ-bhyaś-ca*. 341.

"And after the roots *aja*, *yamu*, and *śīṅ*. [The meaning is: after the roots *aja* (to move/to throw), *yamu* (to cease), and *śīṅ* (to sleep), the suffix *unan* occurs, and that [suffix] is *cit*. Regarding *vayunam*: there is the substitution of *vī* for *aj*, *guṇa* [vṛddhi], and the replacement by *ay*. Regarding *yamunā*: "Yamunā is the sister of Śamana," according to Amara.

( ) *vṛtṛvadihanikamikaśibhyaḥ saḥ* || 342 || From the roots *vṛ*, *tṛ*, *vad*, *han*, *kam*, and *kaś*, the suffix *sa* is applied. *Vṛ* (in the sense of choosing), *tṛ* (in the sense of floating or crossing), *vad* (in the sense of distinct speech), *han* (in the sense of killing or going), *kam* (in the sense of desire), and *kaś* (in the sense of harming)— from these, the suffix *sa* is added.

This is the meaning. Regarding *varṣam*: the change to *ṣ* occurs because it is a part of a suffix (*pratyaya*). Regarding *tarṣam*: Amara states, "Thirst (*tarṣa*), eating (*jagdhi*), and feeding (*bhojana*). Here too, the change to *ṣ* occurs after the internal vowel strengthening (*guṇa*) has been applied. Regarding *kakṣam*: the change to *k* occurs according to the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*.
In the root *pluṣ*, the penultimate vowel is replaced by *ū*.

The suffix *sa* is applied after the root *pluṣ* (meaning "to burn"), and the vowel of the penultimate (*upadhā*) is replaced by *a*. Thus, the meaning is that *sa* follows *pluṣ*, with the penultimate vowel becoming *a*. Amara states: "Plakṣa, catintiḍī, and ciñcā [are synonyms for the tamarind tree].
Furthermore, the suffix *sa* is applied after the root *man*, and the vowel is lengthened.
And [the vowel of] *man* is long. The meaning is that from the root *man* (in the sense of "knowing"), the suffix *sa* is added, and the vowel of the root becomes long.
Regarding the word *māṃsam*: the anusvāra is applied by the rule "naścāpadāntasya.
[The root] *aś* [is used] in the sense of eating.

*aśerdeavane*: from the root *aś* in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the suffix *sap* is added; the meaning is that it is used when "gambling" (*devana*) is to be expressed. Regarding *akṣa*: the intention is that by the rule *vraśca* etc., there is the substitution of *ṣṭu*, the change to *k*, and the change to *ṣ*. [Uṇādi Sūtra 3.64: *snuvraścikṛtyṛṣibhyaḥ kit*.

The meaning is that the suffix *sap* should be added after the roots *snu* (in the sense of flowing), *vraścū* (in the sense of cutting), *kṛtī* (in the sense of cutting), and *ṛṣī* (in the sense of going), and that suffix should be *kit*. Regarding *snuṣā*: because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Regarding *vṛkṣa*: because the suffix following the root *vraśc* is *kit*, [the rule] *grahijyā...* [applies].

The form [is derived] by means of *saṃprasāraṇa*, the elision of *s* according to the rule *skori*, the substitution of *k* for *c* according to the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
(Pāṇini 6.4.151) [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] after the word *ṛṣi* when denoting a genus (*jāti*).

Regarding the rule *ṛṣerjātau*: the meaning is that from the root *ṛṣ* (meaning "to go"), the suffix *sa* should be applied when [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*), and that suffix is *kit*. Since this was already established by the preceding rule, this present rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*): namely, that the suffix *sa* is applied after *ṛṣ* only when denoting a genus. Consequently, it does not apply in the case of a derivative based on etymology (*yaugika*). However, from other [roots],...
It occurs in both cases as well:
[the suffix *ka* is added] after the roots *undi*, *guh*, and *kuṣ*.

The meaning is that the suffix *sa* is kit after the roots *undī* (to moisten), *gudh* (to be angry), and *kuṣ* (to extract). Regarding *utsa*: there is elision of the nasal by the rule *aniditām*. Amara states: "A spring (*utsa*) is a flow of water. Regarding *gutsa*: the change to *c* occurs by the rule *khari ca*. Regarding *kukṣa*: [the same applies].
After the roots *ṣaḍh* and *gṛdh*, [the suffix] *ka* is applied;
and after *paṇ*, *dak* is also applied.

And *gṛdh* and *paṇ* take the suffix *u*, and there are also the substitutions of *da* and *ka* for the final letters of the roots respectively. The meaning is that from the roots *gṛdh* (in the sense of longing) and *paṇ* (in the senses of trading and praising), the suffix *u* is added, and the final letters of the roots are replaced by *da* and *ka* respectively. Thus, *gṛtsa*. Because the word "kiṭ" (having the augment *k*) is understood to follow, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. [The substitution of] *da* for the letter *dh*.

The substitution of *da* is for the purpose of preventing the elision of the *it*. Now, one might object: "Since the form *gṛtsa* can be established by changing the *dha* to *ta* through the rule *khari ca*, what is the point of such an effort to prescribe *da*?

To this they reply: Because the substitution of *ca* (the change to *ta*) under the rule *khari ca* is considered *asiddha* (not yet applied), [the condition for] the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣi* does not apply.

Otherwise, the substitution of *bha* would result; to prevent that, the rule for *da* was prescribed. However, for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), *ta* alone was not prescribed, because under the alternative view that "the second consonants [of a *cay* group] are substituted," the substitution of *tha* would have occurred. But when *da* is prescribed, the substitution of *ca* (for *ta*) does not take place because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). This is the case.
Thus [it is said]. This is a form derived from the verbal root *paṇ*. Because it follows the letter *k*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs.
(In the case of *aśe*, there is the suffix *sara*).

*aśe saraḥ*: the suffix *sara* is added after the root *aśū*, meaning "to pervade"; this is the meaning. Regarding *vatsara*: by the rule *saḥ syārddhadhātuke*, the substitution of *t* for *s* occurs.
[The word *vatsara*] is formed with the prefix *sam* and the suffix *cit*.

The meaning is that the suffix *sar* produced from the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *sam* is marked with the indicator *cit*. The purpose of the *cit* indicator is to ensure that the word has an acute accent (*udātta*) on its final syllable. In this context, the natural reading is "sapūrvāccit" (from what is preceded by *sa-* and marked with *cit*), even when it is preceded by something other than *sam*.

Because of the observation of suffixes along with their respective conditions (*sarapratyayadarśanāt*), as in the examples "thou art *saṃvatsaraḥ*," "thou art *parivatsaraḥ*," "thou art *ilāvatsaraḥ*," and "thou art *idvatsaraḥ*," and so forth;
[this applies] by the rule "after the roots *kṛ*, *dhū*, etc., [the suffix *san* is added] with the *kit* designation."

The meaning is that after the roots *kṛ* (in the sense of making), *dhū* (in the sense of shaking), and *mad* (in the sense of rejoicing), the suffix *sar* is added, and that suffix shall be marked with the *kit* designation. One might ask: why is the *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) not applied in the word *kṛsara*, given that the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.59] for *ṣṭutva* applies because the suffix follows *i* and is a part of the word? To this, he says: "by virtue of *bāhulaka* (irregularity)."

Explaining the meaning of the word *kṛsara*, [the author] cites the *Amarakośa*: "It should be *kṛsara*. Regarding *dhūsara*: because of the suffix *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; thus, "that which is slightly pale is *dhūsara*. Regarding *matsara*: the *Amarakośa* states, "In the sense of hating the good fortune of others, *matsara* is used; likewise, it is used for a miser in three genders."
In the *pāda*, *ra* and *la* [are also valid].
*Pate-raś-ca-laḥ*: from the root *patlṛ* (to go), the suffix *sara* is applied, and the meaning is that the letter *ra* is replaced by *la*. Thus, the form *patsala* is obtained.
(*Tany-ṛṣibhyām ksa-ran*).

*tan* and *ṛṣi* take the suffix *ksaran*. The meaning is that the suffix *ksaran* is applied after the roots *tan*, meaning "to expand," and *ṛṣi*, meaning "to go. Regarding the form *tasara*: because the suffix is marked with *k* (indicating it is *kit*), the nasal is elided by the rule beginning with "anudātopadeśa... [Pāṇini 6.4.37]. From the root *ṛṣ*, [the form] is *ṛkṣara*.
Thus is the form. Because of the *kit* suffix, there is no *guṇa*. There is *katva* (change to *k*) and *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*).
[From the roots] *prī*, *yuj*, and *kvani*, the suffix *kālan* is applied; there is shortening of the vowel and *saṃprasāraṇa*.
[The suffix] *kālan* is applied after the roots *prī* and *kvaṇ*. Since the root *prī* is not found in the Dhātupāṭha, he says "sautra" (belonging to the Sūtras).

[The meaning is: the suffix *kālan* is added after these two; respectively, there is shortening of the vowel for the root *prī*, and vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *kvaṇ*. Thus, *priyāla* is the form with the short vowel. *Kuṇāla*.
Thus [the form is derived]: by means of *samprasāraṇa*, the letter *va* becomes *u*, and with the application of the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi, the form is established.
Amara states in the section on trees and medicinal herbs (*vanauṣadhivarga*) that "the *priyāla* tree is called *rājāna*, *sannaka*, *drudhu*, and *paṭa*.
From the roots *kaṭi* and *kuṣi*, the word *kākuḥ* is formed.

The suffix *kāk* is applied after the roots *kaṭ* and *kuṣ*. From *kaṭ*, meaning "to rain" or "to cover," and *kuṣ*, meaning "to extract," the suffix *kāk* is added; the resulting forms are *kaṭākuḥ* and *kuṣākuḥ*. [Also,] after the root *sṛ*, the suffix *du* is applied, and the penultimate vowel is replaced by *u*.

The suffix *duk* also [is applied] after the root *sṛ*. The meaning is that the suffix *kāku* occurs after the root *sṛ* (meaning "to go"), and the augment *duk* is added to the root. Thus, the form *sṛdākuḥ* is derived; because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
[Furthermore,] after the root *vṛt*, there is also *vṛddhi*.

"And there is the vṛddhi of the root *vṛt*. The meaning is that from the root *vṛt* (in the sense of "turning" or "existing"), the suffix *kāku* is applied, and there is vṛddhi of the verbal root. Thus, one derives the word *vārtāku*. He establishes the word *vārtāka* by means of the rule of "diversity" (*bāhulaka*).
There is vocalization of the semivowel *par* and the elision of the syllable *al*.

The rule *pardearnitsaṃprasāraṇamallopaśca* means that from the root *pard*, signifying "censured sound," the suffix *kāku* is applied; this suffix is marked with *n* (indicating it is *nit*), whereby the *ṛ*-vowel is the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitute for the *r* of the root, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* following the *p*. Thus, [the word] *sarpaḥ*, *pṛdākuḥ*, and *bhujagaḥ* [are formed].
According to Amarasimha, "bhujaṅga," "ahi," and "bhujaṅgama" all mean "serpent.
[The suffixes] anyuc, āgūc, and knuc are added after the roots sṛ, yu, vac, and ci respectively.
From the roots *sṛ* (to go), *yu* (to mix), and *vac* (to speak), the suffixes *anyuc*, *āgūc*, and *āknuc* respectively shall be applied.
Thus, *saraṇyuḥ* is formed; when *anyuc* is added, the root undergoes guṇa substitution and the change of *ṇ* [in the suffix], resulting in this form.

The form *yavāgūḥ* [is derived] by applying the *guṇa* substitution and the *ava* substitute [for the vowel]. Amara states: "Yavāgū, uṣṇikā, and śrāṇā [mean 'gruel']. Medinīkośa states: "Vacaku is masculine, meaning 'Brahmin'.
(From the root *śīṅ* with the suffix *nak*.)
The suffix *ānaka* is applied after the roots *śīṅ* and *bhī*. *Śīṅ* means "to sleep" and *ñi bhī* means "to fear"; the meaning is that *ānaka* is added after these two.
Thus, we have *śayānaka* ("one who sleeps") and *bhayānaka* ("terrifying"). These forms arise through the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel and the replacement by *ay*.
(The suffix) *āṇaka* is applied after the roots *lū*, *dhū*, *śiṅgh*, and *dhāñ*.

The meaning is that the suffix *āṇaka* is applied after these roots: *lūñ* in the sense of cutting, *dhūñ* in the sense of shaking, *śighi* in the sense of smelling, and *ḍudhāñ* in the senses of holding and nourishing. Regarding the form *śiṅghāṇakam*, the augment *num* is added because the root is marked with the indicatory letter *id*.
Those who perform the *darvihoma* using a firebrand (*ulmuka*).

The meaning is that three words—*ulmuka*, *darvi*, and *homī*—are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). He states the very derivation: "and the suffix *mu*. The word "is irregularly formed" (*nipātyate*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. According to Amara: "A firebrand, a brand, and a torch are *ulmuka*. Regarding the word *darvi*, he says: "from the root *dṛ*" (*dṛṇāteḥ*).

"Clarified butter, a ladle, and a stirring-stick"—thus says Amara. Regarding the word *homī*, he says: "from the root *hu* [comes *homī*]. [The rule is: "After the roots *hṛ* and *hi*, the suffix *kuk* is added, and there is elision of the final letter."

*Hrī-ku-k-raś ca lo vā*: From the root *hrī*, meaning "shame," the suffix *kuk* shall be applied, and there shall be either the letter *ra* or the letter *la* [in place of the *repha* connected to the verbal root]. Thus, *hlīkur*.
Due to the *kit* status [of the suffix], there is a prohibition of *guṇa*.
The laughing deer-like ones have indeed carried this [soma] away from the fearsome ones.

The suffix *tan* is applied after these verbal roots: *has* (to laugh), *mṛ* (to die), *gṛ* (to swallow), *iṇ* (to go), *vā* (to go or to scent), *am* (to move, etc.), *dam* (to subdue), *lūñ* (to cut), *pūñ* (to purify), and *dhurvī* (to injure). [From these, the word] *hasta* [is derived].

Having raised the objection regarding the augment *iṭ* conditioned by the suffixes beginning with *val* in such cases, he says: "By the rule *titutreṣvagrahādīnām*, there is no *iṭ*. Because the root *tan* lacks the *kit* designation, there is no lengthening [of the vowel] in forms such as *danta* by the rule "*anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*" [Pāṇini 6.4.15].
*Marta* means the world of mortals (*bhu-loka*). That which exists therein is *martya*. The suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. *Dhūrta*.
Thus, when the suffix *kṛt* is applied, there is elision of *v* and *y* by the rule "ṭhlopo vyor vali," and lengthening occurs by the rule "hali ca.
[The suffix] *nañ*, *āp*, and *iṭ* [are also applied].

The meaning is that when *nañ* is the upapada, the suffix *tan* is applied to the root *āplṛ* (in the sense of pervasion), and the augment *iṭ* is added. Thus, *nāpitaḥ*. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is no elision of the *n* of *nañ*. Amara states: "A barber (*kṣurī*, *muṇḍī*, *divākīrti*, *nāpita*) is an outcaste (*antāvasāyin*)."
The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *tan* and *mṛj*.

The suffix *ki* is added after the roots *tanu* (in the sense of expansion) and *mṛṅ* (in the sense of giving up life). The meaning is that the suffix *ki* is applied after these two, and it is marked with the *k*-sign. Thus, we have *tatam*. Because of the *k*-sign, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*).
As Amara states: "A musical instrument such as the lute is called *tataṃ*."
The suffix *kta* is applied after the roots *añj*, *ghṛ*, and *si*.

The suffix *kta* occurs after the roots *añj*, *ghṛ*, and *ṣi*. After *añjū* (in the senses of manifesting, smearing, shining, and moving), *ghṛ* (in the senses of flowing and shining), and *ṣiñ* (in the sense of binding), the suffix *kta* is applied; thus we have *akta*. The form [is derived] by the elision of *n* and the change to a *ku*-sound (*k*).
After the roots *du* and *tan*, there is also lengthening [of the vowel].

After the roots *du* (to go) and *tanu* (to expand), the suffix *kta* occurs, and there is lengthening of the root vowel. Thus, *tāta*. Because the suffix *kta* is marked with *k*, there is elision of the *n* and lengthening of the vowel, resulting in the form [tāta].
Furthermore, after the root *ji* (to conquer), the augment *mūṭ* occurs, and it is udātta-accented.

*jermūta* is udātta. From the root *ji* (in the sense of "conquering"), the suffix *kta* is applied; for this, there is the augment *mūṭ*, which is udātta, and the vowel of the root becomes long. Thus, the form *jīmūta* is obtained. *Loṣṭa* and *palita*—these two are treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*). He states the manner of their derivation: "from *lūñ*" (*lunāteḥ*). [The root is] *lūñ*.

The meaning is that from the root *chid* (to cut), the suffix *kta* is applied, the augment *sūṭ* is added, and the guṇa of the root is irregularly prescribed (*nipātana*). According to Amarasimha: "Clods (*leṣṭu*) are masculine," and "Grayness due to old age is *palita*."
Measured by the two visible [eyes].

The meaning is that the suffix *itan* is applied after the roots *hṛñ* (in the sense of taking) and *śyaiṅ* (in the sense of going). Regarding *śyeta*: by the application of *itan*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the preceding vowel (*ādguṇaḥ*). Regarding "the two distinct colors": Amara states, "pālāśa, harita, and harit mean green," and "śukla, śubhra, śuci, and śveta mean white."
In the case of the root *ruh*, the letter *r* may optionally be replaced by *l*.

*rūhe raśca lo vā*: from the root *ruh* (meaning "to grow" or "to be born from a seed"), the suffix *it* [i.e., *kan*] is applied; the meaning is that there is optionally a substitution of *l* for the *r* belonging to the verbal root. Thus, *rohita*. As in: "the *camara* deer is *rohita*," "the *madgura* fish is *rohita*," "the *śāla* tree is *lohita*."
And Amara [says] "raktaḥ";
[the suffix] *ka* is applied after the root *piś* and it is *kit*.

The suffix *it* is applied after the root *piś*, and it is also *kit*. The meaning is that the suffix *itan* is added to the root *piś* (meaning "to divide" or "to cut"), and that suffix is *kit*. Thus, the form *piśita* is derived; because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
After the roots *śru*, *dakṣi*, *spṛhi*, and *gṛhi*, the suffix *āyya* is applied.

The suffix *āyya* is added after the roots *śru*, *dakṣ*, *spṛh*, and *gṛh*. [That is,] after *śru* (to hear), *dakṣ* (to increase), *spṛh* (to desire/harm), and *gṛh* (to seize), the suffix *āyya* occurs. Here, *spṛhi* and *gṛhi* are forms ending in the causative marker (*ṇi*). When the suffix *āyya* is added to those two, the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi* takes place by the rule "when *āya* follows."
With this intention, he provides the following examples: *spṛhayāyya*, *didhiṣāyya*.
The meaning is that *didhiṣāyya* is derived through this specific grammatical substitution (*nipātana*). He explains the manner of this substitution by saying "of the root *dadhāti*.

From the root *ḍu dhāñ*, meaning "to hold" or "to nourish," the suffix *āyya* is added; the meaning is that reduplication, the change of the vowel *ā* to *i*, and the addition of the augment *ṣuk* are all substituted [by rule]. Thus, the form *didhiṣāyya* is established.
He states the locus of the application: "like a friend.
[This is] from the root *vṛñ* with the suffix *eṇya*.
The suffix *eṇya* is applied after the root *vṛñ*. Since *vṛñ* means "to choose," the suffix *eṇya* is added to it. After the application of *guṇa*, the form *vareṇya* is obtained.

As stated in the Amarakośa: "The words *mukhya*, *varya*, and *vareṇya* [mean 'chief' or 'excellent']. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *kṣeyya* is applied after the root *stu* (to praise).

*Stuvaḥ kseyyaś chandasi*: regarding the rule *stuñ* in the sense of praise, the meaning is that the suffix *kseyya* is applied to this root in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Thus, *stuṣeyyam*. Because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; and because it is part of the suffix, the *ṣ* is substituted for the dental *s*. *Rājer anyaḥ*: [the suffix] *anya* is applied after the root *rāj*.

*Rājanya* [is derived as follows]: from the root *rājṛ* meaning "to shine," the suffix *anyat* is applied. Thus, *rājanya* means "fire. However, when it denotes a Kṣatriya—as in the expression "the consecrated king is the *rājanya*"—it should be understood that the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *rāja-śvaśurād yat*.
And [the suffix *yat* is applied] after the words *śṛ* and *ramya*.
And after the roots *śṛ* and *ram*, [the suffix *anya* is applied]. In the sense of "to injure" (*śṛ hiṃsāyām*) and "to sport" (*ramu krīḍāyām*), the suffix *anya* occurs after these two. Thus:

*śaraṇyam* and *ramaṇyam*. The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* is by the rule "after *ra* and *ṣa*" (*raṣābhyām*). [The suffix *anya*] is also applied after the root *ṛ*, and it is *niṭ* (i.e., causes the elision of the penultimate vowel).
The root *ṛ* means "to go. From this root, the suffix *anya* is applied; the *n* in *nitya* indicates that it is a *nit* suffix.

The status of being a *nit* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). Thus, we have *araṇyam*. The point is that there is *guṇa* substitution when the suffix *anya* follows. Amara states: "A forest (*aṭavī*), a wilderness (*araṇya*), and a thicket (*vipina*)."
Parjanya.
*Parjanya*: the meaning is that it is thus irregularly formed (*nipātyate*). He states the very formation itself: *pṛṣu secane*.
From this root, the suffix *anya* is applied; the letter *ṣ* becomes *j*, and there is the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel—this is the sense.
Because of the intervention of the letter *j*, the change to *ṇ* does not occur.
Another [example] of the father.

*Vadānyaḥ*: [The suffix] *ānya* is added after the root *vad*, meaning "to speak clearly. Thus, the word *vadānyaḥ* is formed. According to Amara: "The words *vadānya*, *sthūlalakṣya*, and *dānaśauṇḍa* denote one who gives much.
[The suffix] *atraṇ* is added after the roots *ami*, *nakṣi*, *yaj*, *vadh*, and *pati*.

The meaning is that the suffix *atran* is applied after the roots *ama* (in the sense of moving, etc.), *nakṣa* (in the sense of moving), *yaja* (in the sense of worshipping the gods, etc.), *vadha* (in the sense of killing), and *patlṛ* (in the sense of moving). Although [the word] *nakṣatra* is [already established] by the rule *ṭnabhrāṇnapāt* within the section on *tatpuruṣa* compounds...
Nevertheless, it should be understood that this is a different derivation [of the word].
(Pāṇini 3.1.27) *gaḍer ādeś ca kaḥ*.

"Kaḥ [is substituted] for the initial [consonant] of *gaḍi*. This means that after the root *gaḍa* (in the sense of "to sprinkle"), the suffix *atraṇ* occurs, and the letter *ka* is substituted for the initial *ga*. Thus, *kaḍatra* is formed; this is the form resulting from the substitution of *ka* for *ga*. Now, raising the doubt as to how the word *kalatra* is used, he says: "In the case of *ḍa* and *la*... [Thus] *kalatraṃ*.
[The suffix *niṣ* is applied] after the roots *śri*, *vṛ*, and *bhṛ*;
[the suffix *niṣ*] is also applied after the root *vṛñ* when it is marked with the indicatory letter *c*.

*Vṛñaścit*: from the root *vṛñ* (to choose), the suffix *atran* is added with the augment *cit*; this means that *atran* follows *vṛñ*. The *cit* designation is for the purpose of accentuation (*svarārtha*). Thus, *varatrā*. Here, by the suffix *atran*, the root undergoes *guṇa* substitution. As Amara states: "nadhrī, vadhrī, and varatrā [mean 'leather thong']."
The agent of perfect knowledge.

The suffix *katran* occurs after the root *jñā* (to know) when preceded by the upapada *su*. Thus, the meaning is that *katran* is added [after *su-jñā*]. In the form *suvidatram*, because the suffix is marked with *k* (kit), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. [Also,] there is the augment *num* for the root *kṛt*.

And [the suffix] *katra* is added after the root *kṛtī*. The root *kṛtī* means "to cut"; from this, the suffix *katra* occurs, and there is the augment *num* for the verbal root. Thus, *kṛntatram*; this is the form with the *num* augment.
(From the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śī*, *yaj*, *parv*, *pac*, *yam*, *tan*, *nam*, *hi*, and *hṛ*, the suffix) *atac* occurs.

The suffix *atac* is applied after the following roots: *bhṛ* (to support), *mṛ* (to die), *dṛś* (to see), *yaj* (to sacrifice, worship the gods, etc.), *pṛ* (to fill), *ḍupacaṣ* (to cook), *am* (to go, etc.), *tam* (to desire), *ṇam* (to bow, to sound), and *harya* (to move, to desire). *bhṛ* in the sense of supporting; *mṛṅ* in the sense of giving up life; *dṛś* in the sense of seeing; *yaj* in the sense of worshiping the gods and so forth; *pṛ* in the sense of filling; *ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of cooking; *am* in the sense of going and so forth; *tam* in the sense of longing; *ṇam* in the sense of bowing and sound; *harya* in the sense of moving and desiring—from these [roots], *atac* [is added].
The meaning is "condition" (*pratyaya*).
[The suffix *ka* is added] after the roots *pṛṣi* and *rañji*, with the augment *kit*.

The suffix *at* is added after the roots *pṛṣ* and *rañj*, and it is marked with the *k*-sign. *Pṛṣu* means "to sprinkle" and *rañj* means "to color. From these two, the suffix *at* is applied as *kit*. According to Amara: "The words *pṛṣanti*, *bindu*, and *pṛṣat* mean 'drops'.
[Also derived from this rule is] *khalatiḥ*.

*Khalatiḥ*—the meaning is that it is thus derived as an irregular form (*nipātana*). He explains the method of this derivation by saying "from *skhala*": the sense is that it is from the root *skhala* meaning "to stumble" or "to move unsteadily.
[The suffix] *atha* is applied after the roots *śīṅ*, *śapi*, *ru*, *gami*, *vañci*, *jīvi*, and *prāṇi*.
The meaning is that the suffix *ap* occurs after the roots *śīṅ*, *śap*, *ru*, *gam*, *vañc*, *jīv*, and *an* preceded by *pra*.
Regarding *śayatha*: there is the substitution of *ay* for the *guṇa* vowel. Regarding *prāṇatha*: [this is due to the rule] "before *an*, [the root-final *n* is replaced by *ṇ*]."
The substitution of *ṇ* occurs [for the *n* of the root *bhṛñ*] when it is followed by the affix *cit*.
From the root *bhṛñ* (meaning "to carry" and "to nourish"), the suffix *ath* is applied, and it is marked with the *cit* designation. The *cit* designation is for the purpose of a specific accent.
From the roots *rud* and *vid*, the suffix *iṅat* is applied.
The suffix *ṅt* is added after the roots *rud* and *vid*. *Rud* means "to shed tears" and *vid* means "to know";

from these two, the suffix *ath* occurs with the marker *ṅt*. Thus, *ruditha*. Because it is marked as *kit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. After the root *vas* preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), [the suffix *ath* occurs]. From the root *vas* meaning "to dwell," when a prefix is present, the suffix *ath* occurs. Thus, *āvasatha*.

The suffix *āṅ* is added after the root *vas* when preceded by the word *upari*. [And] the suffix *asac* is added after the roots *at*, *av*, *cam*, *tam*, *nam*, *rabh*, *labh*, *nabh*, *tapi*, *pati*, *pani*, *paṇi*, and *mahi*.
*Ati*, *avi*, *cam*, *tam*: [roots] *at* in the sense of continuous motion; *ava* in the sense of protection and so forth; *cam* in the sense of eating; *tam* in the sense of longing;

*ṇam* in the sense of bowing and sound; *rabh* in the sense of impetuosity; *ḍulabhṣ* in the sense of obtaining; *ṇabha* in the sense of injury; *tap* in the sense of heating; *patlṛ* in the sense of going; *pana* in the sense of transaction and praise.

The meaning is that the *asac* suffix is added after the roots *paṇ*, *maha* (in the sense of worship), and so forth. Regarding *atasī*: according to Amara, "ṭhatasī syādumā kṣumā"; the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group. The rest is clear.
(*Veñ* [to weave], however, has the augment *tuṭ*.)

"Veñ-tuṭ ca": from the root *veñ* (meaning "to weave"), the suffix *atasac* occurs, and there is the augment *tuṭ* added to the suffix; this is the meaning. Now, one might object that the form *vetasa*, which is about to be mentioned, is inconsistent because the substitution of *ā* for the initial vowel by the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti* would be unavoidable; to this he replies: "By virtue of *bāhulaka* (irregularity)."
The suffix *ṇiC* is applied after the roots *vah* and *yū*.

The suffix *asac* is added after the roots *vah* (to carry) and *yu* (to mix), and it is marked with the *ṇit* designation. Thus, from these two roots, the suffix *asac* is applied; because it is *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of the penultimate vowel. The form is *vāhasa*.
According to Amarasimha, "Both *śayu* and *vāhasa* [denote a horse]. As for *yāvasa*, because the suffix is *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi*.
And [the word] *vayaḥ*.
And *vaya*: from the root *vaya* in the sense of "going," the suffix *asac* is applied, and that [suffix] is marked with the indicator *ṇit*. Thus, *vāyasa*.
Amara states: "The crow is also called *balibhuj*.
[From the root] *div*, the suffix *kit* is applied.

From the root *div* (in the sense of playing, etc.), the suffix *asac* with the marker *kit* is applied. Regarding *divasa*: because of the *kit* marker, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Amara states: "The words *divasa* and *vasara* are neuter.
From the roots *kṛ*, *śṛ*, *śal*, *kali*, and *gard*, the suffix *abhac* is applied.

The meaning is that the suffix *abhac* is applied after the roots *kṛ* (to scatter), *śṛ* (to injure), *śal* (to go), *kal* (to sound), and *gard* (to sound). According to Amara, "the outer part of the hand from the wrist to the little finger is called *karabha*."
The suffix *ki* is applied after the words *ṛṣi* and *vṛṣi*.

The suffix *a* is added after the roots *ṛṣi* and *vṛṣi*, and it is *kit*. The root *ṛṣi* means "to go," and *vṛṣu* means "to sprinkle. From these two, the suffix *a* occurs, and it is *kit*. Thus, the form is *ṛṣabha*. Because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. (From the root *ruṣ*, the suffix *ni* is added, and *luṣ* is substituted [for *ruṣ*]).

From the root *ruṣ* (meaning "to injure"), the suffix *abha* is added, with the augment *niṭ*, and the root undergoes the substitution of *luṣ*. Also [the suffix *abha* is added] after the roots *rās* and *vall*.
And from the roots *rās* and *vall*. The meaning is that the suffix *abhac* is added to *rāsṛ*, which means "to sound," and to *valla*, which means "to cover"; furthermore, that suffix is *nit*.
(From the roots) *jṛ* and *viś*, the suffix *jhac* [is applied].

The suffix *jhac* is applied after the roots *jṛṣ* and *viś*. The meaning is that the suffix *jhac* is added to *jṛṣ* (in the sense of "wasting away" or "aging") and *viś* (in the sense of "entering"). Thus, from *jarantaḥ*: by the rule *jho'nta*, the letter *jh* is replaced by *ant*; the intention is that there is *guṇa* substitution. Similarly, *veśantaḥ* is also formed. [A *veśanta*] is a small pond, a pool, or a small lake; whereas a *vāpī*...
"Long-lived" (dīrghāyus) [is defined] thus by Amarasimha.
[The suffix] *ṣyan* is applied after the roots *ruh*, *nandi*, *jīv*, and *prāṇi* when expressing a benediction (*āśis*).

*Ruhinandijīvi*: [The suffix] *jhac* is applied after the roots *ruh* (to grow/germinate), *ṇad* (to increase/prosper), and *jīv* (to sustain life), preceded by *pra*, in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), and that [suffix] is marked with the indicatory letter *ṣ*.

Regarding *rohantaḥ*: this form arises from the substitution of the final letter of the suffix *jhas* [with *at*] and the *guṇa* strengthening of the penultimate vowel. He demonstrates the purpose of the *ṣit* designation as follows:
He provides an example for the suffix *ṅīṣ* [applied] by the rule "after *ṭhṣit*, *gaura*, and others," saying: "they grow" (*rohanti*).
[The suffixes are applied] after the roots *tṛ*, *bhū*, *vah*, *vas*, *bhās*, *sādh*, *gaḍ*, *maṇḍ*, and *nand*.
From the roots *tṛ* (to cross or to save),

*bhū* (to exist), *vah* (to carry), *vas* (to dwell), *bhāsṛ* (to shine), *sādh* (to accomplish), *gaḍ* (to sprinkle), *maḍi* (to adorn), *ji* (to conquer), and *ṭu nadi* (to increase)— the suffix *jhac* is applied; and the meaning is that this suffix is also marked with the letter *ṣ*.

Regarding *taranta*: there is the substitution of *jha* for the final [consonant]. He says "the boat crossing" (*tarantī nauka*) in order to demonstrate the purpose of the *ṣit* designation. Regarding *gaṇḍayanta*: the root *gaḍi* means "to sprinkle"; the suffix is applied after this root in its causative (*ṇic*) form. Now, one might ask: why is the vowel lengthening of the penultimate (*upadhā-vṛddhi*) not heard in the causative? To this he replies: "ghaṭādayaḥ" (the roots beginning with *ghaṭ*).

To the question, "What follows from [the root] *mit* being short? he says: "By the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*" and so forth. Now, one might object that there would be a loss of the suffix *ṇi* by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*; therefore, he says:
"This [root] ends in a long vowel (*ānta*). The same applies to the form *maṇḍayantaḥ*.
And [the suffix] muṭ is indeed applied after the root han.

*hanter muṭ ca*: From the root *han*, meaning "to kill" or "to go," the suffix *jhaC* is applied, and there is the augment *muṬ*. There is also the substitution of the sound *hi* for the root. Thus, *hemanta* (winter). When *hi* is substituted for the root, there is *guṇa* (vowel strengthening).
And there is the elision of the final phoneme of *bhandena*.

*bhandernalopaśca*: From the root *bhad* (meaning "to be auspicious"), the suffix *jha* occurs; furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *na* obtained because the root is marked with the *it* indicatory letter *i*. Thus, the form *bhadanta* arises from the elision of *na* and the substitution of *anta* for *jha*.
The suffix *ara* is applied after the root *ṛcch*.

"From the root *ṛcch*, the suffix *ara*. This means that from the root *ṛcch* (meaning "to go"), the suffix *ara* is applied. He says "by virtue of diversity (*bāhulaka*)" because words such as *jarjara* and *jharjhara* are also observed in common usage.
The suffix *cit* is applied after the verbal roots *arti*, *kami*, *bhrami*, *cam*, and *divāsi*.

The suffix *ara* is applied after the roots *ṛ* (to go), *kam* (to desire), *bhram* (to wander/instability), *cam* (to eat), *div* (to play, etc.), and *vas* (to dwell). This suffix is *cit*; its *cit*-status is for the purpose of accentuation. Thus, the form *araram* results from the root *ṛ* with the substitution of *guṇa*.

The suffix *ṭha* [forming *maru*] is applied to the words *kapāṭa* and *marara* as synonyms; furthermore, under the continued application of the rule "brothers" (*bhrātaraḥ*), the *Mādhavīyā-dhātuvṛtti* states that *devṛ* and *devara* mean "husband's brother.
From the root *kuva*, the suffix *kraran* is applied.

*Kuvaḥ karan*: from the root *ku* (meaning "to sound"), the suffix *karan* is applied. The letters *ka* and *na* are elided. Thus, *kukara*. Because the suffix is marked with *k* (kit), there is no *guṇa* substitution. According to Amara, "the *ṭhukka*, the *utkrośa*, and the *kurara* [are synonyms for the osprey]. (*Aṅgimadimandibhya āran*).

Aṅgimaṭi. The root *agi*, listed in the Daṇḍaka group with the meaning "to go," is *agi*; *madi* means "praise" and "joy," as in *madī* (to rejoice). From these, the suffix *āran* is applied. Thus, *aṅgāra* and so forth. [From] *gaḍi*, there is also the substitution of *kaḍ*.

*gaḍeḥ kaḍa ca*: From the root *gaḍ* (to sprinkle), the suffix *āran* occurs and *kaḍ* is the substitute [for the root]; this is the meaning. Amara states: "Kaḍāra means tawny; *kapila*, *piṅga*, *piśaṅga*, *kadrū*, and *piṅgala* [are synonyms]."
The Śṛṅgāra and Bhṛṅgāra [vessels].

The words *śṛṅgāra* and *bhṛṅgāra* are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*). He explains the manner of this formation as follows: "from the roots *śṛ* and *bhṛ*. From the root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure") and the root *ḍu bhṛñ* (meaning "to support" and "to nourish"), the suffix *āran* is applied; the augment *num* is added to the roots, the vowel is shortened, and the substitution of *guṇa* is also irregularly prescribed.
This is the meaning. Regarding "the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*)," Amarasimha states: "The *śṛṅgāra* is pure and brilliant," and also: "The *bhṛṅgāra* is a golden water-pot.
[The suffix] *cit* is applied after the roots *kañji* and *mṛji*.

The suffix *cit* is added after the roots *kañji* and *mṛji*. Since the root *kañj* is not found in the standard list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), he says "it is mentioned in the sūtras" (*sautra*).

*Mṛjū* means "to clean. From these two roots, the suffix *āran* is added, and that [suffix] is *cit*. Thus, *mārjāra* is formed; there is a vowel-lengthening (*vṛddhi*) for the root *mṛj*. Amarasimha states: "A cat is called *otur*, *biḍāla*, or *mārjāra*."
The root *kam* takes the augment *k* [after the suffix *san*], and its penultimate vowel is replaced by *u*.

*kameḥ kiduccopadhāyāḥ*: from the root *kamu* (meaning "to desire"), the suffix *āran* is applied; it is *kit*, and the vowel *u* replaces the penultimate (*upadhā*) *a*. Thus, *kumāraḥ*. Because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
Also, *tuṣāra* and others [are formed in this manner].

*tuṣāra* and others are also derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*). Regarding *tuṣāra*: from the root *tuṣ* (to be satisfied), the suffix *āran* is applied; because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel. Regarding *kāsāra*: from the root *kāsṛ* (to utter contemptible sounds), belonging to the *bhvādi* class; the form is derived by adding the suffix *āran*. Regarding *sahāra*: from the root *ṣaha*...
In the sense of enduring (*marṣaṇe*). According to Amarasimha: "A lake is called *kāsāra*, *sarasī*, or *saraḥ*. [The suffix] *nuṭ* is added after the root *dīṅ*.

*dīṅe nuṭ ca*: after the root *dīṅ* (to decay), the suffix *āran* is applied, and there is also the augment *nuṭ*. The term *kit* continues to apply [from the previous rule]. Therefore, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Thus, the word is *dīnāra*. As Amara states: "The *niṣka* is also called *dīnāra*, and it is not feminine."
The suffixes *sar*, *tṛc*, and *arap* take the augment *ṣuk*.

*sarṭearapaḥ ṣuk ca*: from the root *sṛ* (to move), there is the suffix *ap* and the augment *ṣuk* added to the root. Thus, *sarṣapa*. When the suffix *ap* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel. Amara states: "The words *vanamudga* and *sarṣapa* [are synonyms]."
The suffix *kapan* is applied after the roots *uṣi*, *kuṭi*, *dalika*, and *cikhaji*.

The suffix *kapan* occurs after the roots *uṣ* (to burn), *kuṭ* (to bend), *dal* (to split), *kac* (to bind), and *khaj* (to churn). The letters *ka* and *n* are elided by the rule *kanāvitau*. The form *uṣapa* [is derived as follows]: because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. The *niṭ* designation is for the sake of accentuation. The remainder is clear.
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *kvaṇ*.

"Kvaṇeḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca" (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.89). The meaning is: from the root *kvaṇ* (to sound), the suffix *kapan* is applied, and there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel *va* of the root. Thus, "kuṇapam. When the *va* is vocalized to *u*, and by the rule "saṃprasāraṇācca" (Pāṇini 6.1.108) there is the single substitution of the preceding form for the *u* and *a*, the form is established. [Thus] "kuṇapaḥ" (a corpse).
"Śava" is used in the masculine and neuter genders, according to Amara;
and "kapa" belongs to the school of Ākravarmaṇa.

Regarding *kapa* [as an affix] for Cākravarmaṇa: the phrase "vowel-contraction (*saṃprasāraṇa*) after the root *kvaṇ*" is understood to follow here. The meaning is that, according to the opinion of Cākravarmaṇa, the affix *kap* is added to the root *kvaṇ*, and there is vowel-contraction.
In this case as well, the resulting form is simply *kuṇapa*. Now, one might object: [is this not so?]
Since there is no difference in form (*rūpa*), for what purpose is this [rule] stated? To this he says: "There is a difference in accent" (*svarabheda*).
The meaning is that while in the former case there is the *nitsvara* (the accent on the *ni*), here it is not so; thus there is a difference.
[The suffixes *viṭap*, *piṣṭap*, *viśipa*, and *ulapa* are formed with *aṇ*.]

The meaning is that these two words, *viṭapa* and *piṣṭapa*, are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). He explains the manner of this irregular formation: regarding the word *viṭa*, the remainder [of the rule] is "the suffix *kapan* is added after this. Due to its being marked with *k* (kit), there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Regarding *piṣṭapa*, he says: "from *viśati*" (*viśa*); the suffix *kapan* is added after the root *viśa* (meaning "to enter"). Due to its being marked with *k* (kit) [there is no *guṇa*].

The meaning is that the letter *p* is substituted for the initial *v* of the root, and the augment *tuṭ* is added to the suffix; thus, through the application of the rule *vraśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.36) for the substitution of *ṣ*, and subsequently the rule for *ṣṭu* (8.4.41), the form is established. Regarding the word *viśipa*, he says "of the root *viś*" (*viśateḥ*). Regarding "of the root *val*" (*valateḥ*), the meaning is "from the root *val* in the sense of covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*).

Regarding "vocalization" (*saṃprasāraṇa*): this refers to the substitution of *v* for the initial *ṭh* and so forth. In Amara’s lexicon, the word *viṣṭapa*—as in the definition "the world is *viṣṭapa*, *bhuvana*, or *jagat*"—is read with an initial *v*;
however, the rule (*sūtra*) follows another school of thought. Furthermore, Amara states: "*gulminī* and *ulapa* [are synonyms for grass]."
The covering of the body.
The suffix *itkan* [is applied after the root *vṛt*]. That is to say, from the root *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*), the suffix *itkan* is added. Regarding *vartikā*:
there is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Regarding *vartikā*: by the rule *ṭhhalo yamām*, there is an optional elision of the semivowel (*ya*) which is the marker (*m*).
The suffix *kit* is applied after the roots *kṛt*, *bhid*, and *lati*.

From the roots *kṛtī*, *bhidṛ*, and *lati*: the suffix *ktin* is applied after these—namely, *kṛtī* in the sense of cutting, *bhidṛ* in the sense of splitting, and *lati*, which is a root mentioned in the *sūtra*—and it is *kit*. [The example] is *kṛtikā*; because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
The suffix *takan* is added after the roots *iṣ* and *śas*.

The suffix *takan* is added after the roots *iṣ* (in the sense of "desiring") and *aś* (in the sense of "pervading"). The meaning is that this suffix is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*). Thus, we have *iṣṭakā*. Because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Furthermore, the substitution of *i* for *a* (by the rule *pratyayasthāt...*) does not occur here, because of the specific mention in the rule: *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃ citatūlabhāriṣu*.

Regarding *aṣṭakā*: by the rule beginning with *vraśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), there is the substitution of *ṣ*, and subsequently *ṣṭu* (8.4.41). It does not take the feminine suffix *ṅīp* because it is stated that "the word *aṣṭakā* [denotes] a rite for the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*).
[Next: from the root *iṇ* (to go), the suffixes *tasan* and *tasun* are applied.
Regarding *etaśan* and *etaśasun*: from the root *i*, meaning "to go," the suffixes *taśan* and *taśasun* occur;

this is the meaning. In *etaśa*, there is *guṇa* [substitution]. In *etaśā*, because the *u* and *n* of the suffix *taśasun* have the designation *it*, this word ends in *s*. [This is governed by] the rule *atvasantasya...* [Pāṇini 6.4.14].
The suffix *dīrgha* [is formed]; in the case of *taśasun*, the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), and the letter *n* is for the purpose of the *nit-svara* accent.
[The suffix] *tanan* is added after the roots *vī* and *pati*.

The suffix *tanan* is applied after the roots *vī* and *pat*. The meaning is that the suffix *tanan* follows these two roots: *vī* in the senses of motion, pervasion, procreation, shining, throwing, and eating;

and *patlṛ* in the sense of motion. Regarding the word *vetanam*: it is formed with the *guṇa* vowel substitution. According to Amara, "wages" (*vetanam*) is synonymous with "maintenance" (*bhṛti*), "support" (*bharmam*), and "salary" (*bhṛtiḥ*); and "falling" (*patanam*) is synonymous with "marketplace" (*puṭabhedanam*).
The suffix *bha* is applied after the roots *dṛ* and *ḍṛl*.

The suffix *bha* is added after the roots *dṛ* and *dal*. The meaning is that the suffix *bha* is applied to these two roots: *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing" (*vidāraṇe*) and *dal* in the sense of "opening" or "expanding" (*vikasane*).

Regarding the word *darbha*: it is called *darbha* because it tears (*dṛṇāti*) the eye of the demon Kāka; here the suffix *bha* is used in the active sense (*kartari*), and the vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution.
[The suffix *bhan* is also applied] after the roots *atṛ* and *gṛ*.

The suffix *bhann* is added after the roots *ṛ* and *gṛ*. *Ṛ* (meaning "to go") belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, and *gṛ* means "swallowing"; the meaning is that *bhann* is added after these two. Thus, *arbha* [is formed], with *guṇa* substitution. However, it should be understood that *arbhaka* is derived by adding the suffix *kan* when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
[Next: *iṇaḥ kit* ("after *iṇ*, [the suffix] is *kit*").
*Inaḥ kit*: From the root *iṇ* (to go), the suffix *kit* is applied. Thus, *ibha*. Because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
Amara states: "An elephant is called *ibha*, *stamberama*, or *padmī*.
(*Asisañjibhyāṃ kthin*).
The suffix *kthin* is applied after the roots *as* (to throw) and *sañj* (to cling).
[The suffix] *ksi* is applied after the roots *pluṣ*, *kuṣ*, and *śuṣ*.

The suffix *kṣi* is applied after the roots *pluṣ*, *kuṣ*, and *śuṣ*. [That is,] after *pluṣ* (to burn), *kuṣ* (to extract), and *śuṣ* (to dry), the suffix *kṣi* occurs. In words such as *plukṣaḥ* and others, because the suffix is marked with *k* (kit), there is no *guṇa* strengthening; then, by the rule "ṭhṣaḍhoḥ," the *ṣ* is changed to *k*.
They have come to rest.

From the root *aś*, meaning "to pervade," the suffix *ksin* is applied with the augment *nit*. Thus, *akṣi*. By the rule *vraśca* etc., there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. (The suffix) *ksu* is applied after the root *iṣ*.
The suffix *ksu* is applied after the root *iṣ* [meaning] "to desire"; the meaning is that *ksu* occurs after this root.
The suffix *ī* is applied after the roots *av*, *stṛ*, and *tṛ*.

The suffix *ī* is applied after the roots *ava*, *tṛ*, and *stṛ*. The meaning is that the suffix *ī* is added to these: *ava* in the sense of protecting and so forth, *tṛ* in the sense of floating and crossing over, *stṛ*ñ in the sense of covering, and *tatri* in the sense of supporting a family. The form *avī* means "a woman in her menses."
And [the rule] regarding *yāp* and *kiddva*.

The suffix *ī* is added after the roots *yā* (in the sense of going) and *pā* (in the sense of drinking). There is reduplication of the root, and the suffix is *kit*. Regarding the form *yayī*: because the suffix is *kit*, there is elision of the *ā* by the rule "elision of *ā* when *iṭ* follows."
The suffix *muṭ* is also applied after the root *lakṣ*.

*Lakṣer muṭ ca*: From the root *lakṣ* (meaning "to see" and "to mark"), the suffix *ī* shall be applied; this suffix is *kit*, and there is the augment *muṭ*. This [root] belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in *ṇic*; when the suffix *ī* is applied, there is the elision of *ṇi*. "Lakṣmī, Padmālayā, Padmā"—thus says Amara. Thus ends the third quarter.
Now begins the fourth quarter:
(1) Vātapramīḥ.

The word *vātapramīḥ* is derived through this specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). To explain the irregularity itself, he says: "when the word *vāta* is the subordinate term (*upapada*). Regarding the root *mā*: the meaning is that it is from the root *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*). And it is marked with the *k* indicator (*kit*); because of its *kit* status, there is the elision of the long *ā* according to the rule *āto lopaḥ*. Thus, *vātapramīḥ* means "a wind-animal" (a deer).
Thus says Amara. "This" means the word *vātapramī*.

[The rule is: From the roots *ṛ*, *tan*, *añji*, *vanj*, *arpi*, *mad*, *tyaṅg*, *ku*, *yu*, *kṛś*, there are the suffixes *kan*, *nij*, *tu*, *jal*, *iṣ*, *thu*, *ajiṣṭha*, *ansyan*, *ithin*, *ul*, *yas*, *ās*, *ānuk* respectively.

*ṛtanyañjivanyañji*: *ṛ* (to go), *tanu* (to expand), *añjū* (in the sense of manifestation and so forth), *vanu* (to request), *añjū* (in the sense of manifestation and so forth), *ṛ* (to go) with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*), *madī* (joy), *ata* (continuous motion)— this is recited in the *daṇḍaka* list as *aghi-vami-gī*, where *agi* has the meaning of going— and *ku* (sound).
The roots *yu* (in the sense of mixing) and *kṛś* (in the sense of making thin); [the case ending] *pañcamī* (ablative) from the compound of these;

and *katnic*, *yatuc*, *alic*, *iṣṭhuac*, *iṣṭhac*, *isan*, *syan*, *ithin*, *uli*, *asa*, *āsa*, *ānuk*—the nominative plural from the compound of these. [These suffixes follow] after the twelve previously mentioned [roots].

From these roots, these twelve suffixes occur in sequence. From the root *ṛ* with the suffix *ktnic*: the letters *ka* and *ca* are elided. Due to the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution; rather, through the *yaṇ* replacement, the form *ratniḥ* is obtained. He states the meaning of the word *ratni*: "A hand with a closed fist is called a *ratni*. [The word] *hastaḥ*.
"Having bound [it] with a fist, that is a *ratni*; however, an *aratni* is [as follows]," says Amara. Regarding the term *aratni*:
it is formed as a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) meaning "not a *ratni*" (*na ratniḥ aratniḥ*). The rest is clear. (The remainder is easy. Śrīkara.

The suffix *kan* is applied to the root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure") in the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*). Thus, we have *śarkarā*; this form arises from the application of *guṇa* to *karana*. But is this not incorrect? For the letter *k* of *karana* would unavoidably be subject to the designation *it* by the rule *ṭh-lopa-ś-kat-taddhite*. Nor can one argue that the elision of the *k* is prevented by the force of its pronunciation, as is the case with suffixes such as *kāmyac* and others.

It might be argued that since there would be no result in the absence of elision (*lopa*), the designation *it* should also not apply; however, this is not so, because the prohibition "and when *k*, *ṅ*, or *t* follow" exists, and thus it can achieve its purpose by effecting the prohibition of *guṇa*. Therefore, he says "in the subsequent rule," meaning that in the subsequent rule "after *puṣ*, [the suffix] *ki*... the designation *it* is indeed unavoidable.
This is what is read there; in that context, the word *karaṇa* continues [from the previous rule]. It is the *kit* status of *karaṇa* that is being prescribed.

If this letter *ka* were to have the designation *it*, then since *kit* status would be established by itself, what would be the purpose of this prescription of *kit* status? Thus, the meaning is that the designation *it* does not apply here.
The suffix *puṣ* is marked with the *k*-indicator.
The suffix *kit* is applied after the root *puṣ*. Thus, *puṣkara*. Because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
And [the suffix] *kalañ* [is also applied].
And *kalaṅ*. The term *kit* is understood to follow. The suffix *kalan* shall be *kit*. (From the root *gam*, the suffix *ini* [is applied]).

The word *gamiṇī* [is derived] from the root *gamlṛ* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *ini*. To address the inquiry as to what meaning this conveys, he says: "she will go. The author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*) will explain the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* under the section on subsequent kṛt-suffixes; we, however, have already discussed it prior to the analysis of the *uṇādi* suffixes.
It has been explained. Because of the restriction by that rule that [the suffix] will occur [only] there, it is understood that it will occur here.
(The augment) āṅ is added before the root iṇ.

The suffix *ini* follows the root *gam* when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. This means that when *gam* occurs with *āṅ* as its upapada, the suffix *ini* will apply in the sense of "one who is about to go. Because it is marked with the *ṇi*t indicator, there is vṛddhi substitution for the penultimate vowel.
(And [the suffix *ini* also applies] after the root *bhū*).
And *bhuvaḥ*: [the root] *bhū* in the sense of "being" (*satāyām*); from this, the suffix *ini* is applied, and the meaning is that it (*ini*) should be *ṇit*.

Thus, *bhāvī*. Because it is *ṇit*, by the rule *aco ñṇiti*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). This one also has only the future sense, because it was stated [in the previous rule] that "it applies to *gam* and so forth."
You two stand before me.

*Prasthaḥ*: From the root *sthā* (meaning "to stop" or "cease moving") preceded by the prefix *pra*, the suffix *ini* is applied; furthermore, this suffix is *ṇit*. Thus we have *prasthāyī*. Because the suffix *ini* is *ṇit*, the rule *ṭhāto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* applies, resulting in the augment *yuk*.
Although *yuk* is prescribed for roots ending in a *kit* suffix, there is no elision of the vowel *ā* because the preceding syllable does not begin with a vowel (*ajādi*).
In the supreme state.
Regarding *parame kit*: when the word *parama* is used as an upapada (governing word), the suffix *ini* is added to the root *sthā*, and that suffix is *kit*.

Thus we have *parameṣṭhī*. Because the suffix *ini* is *kit*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ā*) of the root; furthermore, because the suffix is *kit*, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) in *parame* does not undergo elision (*aluk*), according to the rule "after a word ending in a consonant or *ṛ*, the seventh case ending is not elided."
The churning.

*Manthaḥ*. [The root] *manth* means "to stir" (*viloḍane*); from this [root], the suffix *ini* is added with the sense that it is *kit*. Because of its *kit*-status, there is elision of the *n* of the verbal root. Thus, the word *mathin*. [In the form] *manthāḥ*, by the rule *pathimathy-*, there is *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel). By the rule *ito't sarvanāmasthāne*, there is the substitution of *at* for the *ikāra* (the short *i*). [Then,] *tho*...
The substitute *ny* is applied [to the root *pat*];
furthermore, *stha* is substituted for *pati*.

And *patastha*. The meaning is that from the root *patlṛ* (to go), there is the suffix *ani*, and the letter *tha* is substituted for the final [radical] sound. Thus, *panthāḥ* [is formed]; this is the word *pathin*. The grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) is as before.
(*Khajer ākaḥ*).
*Khajerākaḥ*. This means that the suffix *āka* is added to the root *khaja*, which signifies "to churn. Amara states: "A ladle is called *darviḥ*, *kambiḥ*, and *khajākā*.
[The words] beginning with *balākā* are also included.

And *balākā* and others: these are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the suffix *āka*. Since this [form] is already established by that very rule, the previous sūtra "from *khaja*, the suffix *āka*" is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). Regarding *balākā*: the root is *bala* in the sense of "attaining.
Regarding *śalākā*: the root is *śama* in the sense of "motion."
And [the weapons] such as the Pināka and others.

And [the words] *pināka* and so forth; the meaning is that these are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) with the suffix *āka*. He states the method of their formation: "of the root *pāti*" etc. The meaning is that from the root *pā* (in the sense of protecting), the suffix *āka* is applied, and the substitution of *i* for the final letter of the root, as well as the augment *num*, are irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*). He cites the *Amarakośa*:
The word *pināka* may denote both a eunuch and a man;
[the suffix] *īkan* is added after the roots *kaṣi* and *dūṣi*.

The suffix *īkan* is applied after the roots *kaṣ* and *duṣ*. *Kaṣ* means "to injure," and *duṣ* means "to become discolored"; from these two, the suffix *īkan* is added. Regarding the form *dūṣīkā*, the suffix is added to the causative (*ṇyanta*) form. By the rule "doṣo ṇau," the vowel *ū* is substituted for the penultimate vowel. He states what is found in the *Amarakośa*: "dūṣikā. [The suffix] *āḥ*...
"What kind of thing is the eye-salve for the three eyes of the Sage?"—thus [asks] Murāri.
[The suffix] *ki* is applied after the roots *naś* and *hṛṣ*.

The rule *anahṛṣibhyāṃ kicca* means that the suffix *īkan* is added after the roots *ana* (to breathe) and *hṛṣ* (to be pleased), and it is also *kit*. Thus, *hṛṣīkaṃ* is formed; because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Amara states: "A sense-organ is called *hṛṣīka*, as it has the objects [of the senses] as its domain."
Caṅkaṇa and Kaṅkaṇa.

*Caṅkaṇaḥ* and *caṅkaṇaśca*. The word *caṅkaṇa* is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). From the root *kaṇ* (meaning "to close the eyes"), when the suffix *yaṅ* is elided, one resorts to the rule of "indicatory presence" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) [to treat it as if the suffix were still present]. Then, by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*, reduplication occurs; subsequently, by the rule *kuhoścuḥ*, the consonant *k* of the reduplicated syllable is changed to *c*; and finally, by the rule *nugato'nunāsikāntasya*, the augment *nuK* is added.

The meaning is that from the verbal root *caṅkram*— which undergoes the substitution of *anusvāra* and the subsequent assimilation (*parasavarṇa*)— the suffix *īkan* is added, and the root is replaced by *kaṅkaṇa*; thus, the form is *kaṅkaṇīka*.
For the roots *śṛ*, *pṛ*, and *vṛ*, there is reduplication and the augment *ruk* is added to the reduplicated syllable.
The suffix *īkan* is applied after the roots *śṛ*, *pṛ*, and *vṛ*; there is reduplication of these roots, and the augment *ruk* is added to their reduplicated base.

Regarding the form *śarśarīka*: when *śṛ* is reduplicated, the substitution of *u* for the root vowel occurs (*uratva*), followed by the substitution of *ra* for that *u* (*raparatva*), and then the remaining consonant is retained (*halādiśeṣa*).
In the case of *repha-nivṛtti*, by this [rule] the form is *ruki*; likewise, *parparīka* and so forth, as well as *pharpharīka* and others.

And [the words] *pharpharīka* and so forth. He states the very rule for their formation: "the root *sphur* means 'throbbing'. From this, the suffix *īkan* is added as a constant [by rule]. Regarding *dardarīka*:

from the root *dṛ* (meaning 'to tear'), the suffix *īkan* is added, and the substitution of *dardara* for the root is prescribed. Alternatively, doubling of the root occurs, and the augment *ruk* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable; both are prescribed by rule (*nipātyate*).
Regarding *jharjharīka*: the root *jhṛṣ* means "to lose one's youth" (*vayohānau*). From this root, the suffix *īkan* is applied, and the substitution of *jharjhara* for the root occurs.
Alternatively, it may be explained here as well that the doubling of the root and the addition of *ruk* to the reduplicated syllable are treated as irregularities (*nipātyate*).
Regarding *titihīka*: from the root *tim*, with the suffix *īkan* and the substitution of *ḍa* for the final letter of the root, followed by doubling.

And after the root *sṛ*, [the suffix] *īkan* occurs; from the root *sṛ* (meaning "to go"), *īkan* shall be added as a *kit* suffix, and there is also the augment *num* for the root.
Thus, *sṛṇīka*. Because of the *num* augment, there is the change to *ṇ*; because it is a *kit* suffix, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
After the root *mṛḍ*, the suffixes *kīkaca* and *kaṅkaṇa* occur.

*mṛṅ* [takes] *kīkaca* and *kaṅkaṇa*. The meaning is that from the root *mṛh* in the sense of "moistening" (*secane*), the suffix *īkan* is added, and the substitutions *kīkaca* and *kaṅkaṇa* for the root occur alternatively. Some say that the forms *kīkīna* and *kaṅkaṇīna* also arise from *mṛḍi*; however, that is entirely inconsistent. Why?
Moreover, both of these suffixes [are applied] to form the words *mṛḍīkaḥ* and *mṛḍaṅkaṇaḥ*;
and there are also [words] such as *alīka*.

And *alīka* and so forth: the meaning is that these are derived as *kīkan*-ending nipātanas (irregularly formed words). Regarding *valīkam*: the suffix is applied to the root *vala* (meaning "to cover"). [The suffix] *īṣan* is applied after the roots *kṛ* and *tṛ*.

The suffix *īṣan* is added after the roots *kṛ* and *tṛ*. *Kṛ* means "to scatter," while *tṛ* means "to swim" or "to cross"; the meaning is that the suffix *īṣan* is applied to these two. Regarding the word *karīṣa*: Amara states, "Dry dung is called *karīṣa*, and it is not feminine."
The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *śrī* and *pṛ*.

Regarding *śṛpṛbhyāṃ kicca*: the roots *śṛ* (in the sense of harming) and *pṛ* (in the senses of protecting and filling) take the suffix *k*, and that [suffix] is marked with *k* (indicating it is *kit*). Thus, *śirīṣam* is formed; by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *i*. *Purīṣam* is formed;
by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *u*.
And [the suffix] *arj* and *ṛj*.
And [the suffix] *iṣan* is added after the root *arj*. From the root *arj*, meaning "to acquire," the suffix *iṣan* is applied, and it is *kit*;

furthermore, there is the substitution of *ṛj* for the root. Thus, *ṛjīṣam*. As Amarasimha states: "Ṛjīṣa is a vessel for baking flour; *kaṃsa* is a drinking vessel, not feminine. [The word] *ambarīṣaḥ*. He explains the method of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*) itself: from the root *ab*, meaning "to sound."

Thus [it is said]. Because of the marker *it*, the augment *num* is applied; the meaning is that the augment *aruḍ* is introduced by way of a nipātana (irregular formation) after this [root] with the suffix *īṣan*.
He states the *Amarakośa*: "In the neuter, *ambarīṣam*. [The rule is:
*kṛśṛpṛkaṭipaṭiśauṭibhya īran*.

The roots *kṛ* (to scatter), *śṛ* (to injure), *pṛ* (to protect and to fill), *kaṭe* (in the sense of raining and covering), *paṭa* (in the sense of speaking), and *śauṭṛ* (in the sense of pride)—from these [roots], following the rule of the fifth case after a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the suffix *īran* is applied. Thus, *karīra*. [As it is said: "In the sense of a bamboo sprout, *karīra* is not feminine; it refers to a particular type of tree."
"And *ghaṭa* means 'not'—thus says Amara. Regarding *paṭīra*: [with the suffix *aṇ* added according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*, there is also *pāṭīra*.
From the root *vaś*, [the suffix *īran* is added] with the *kittva* designation.]

[The suffix] *i* is added after the root *vaś*, provided it is marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*). The root *vaś* means "to desire"; when followed by this suffix, the vowel becomes *ī*. Thus, *uśīra*.
Because the suffix is *kit*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the semivowel. [Furthermore,] after the root *kaś*, the augment *muṭ* is added.
*kaśermuṭ ca*: The root *kaś* is a Vedic (sautra) root; from it, the suffix *īran* occurs, and there is the augment *muṭ* for it. *kṛña ucca*.

The rule *kṛña ucca* [Pāṇini 4.1.45] means that after the root *du-kṛñ* in the sense of "making," the suffix *īran* is added, and the final vowel *u* of the root is replaced by *u*, which is followed by *r*. Thus, *kurīram* is formed; here, the substitution of *u* (utva) and its being followed by *r* (raparatva) apply. [The rule] *ghaseḥ kicca* [Pāṇini 4.1.46] follows.

The suffix *īran* is applied after the root *ghas* (to eat), and it is *kit*. From the root *ghaslṛ* (to eat), [the form] *kṣīra* is derived: the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule *gamahana-*, the *s* is changed to *ṣ* by the rule *kharicaṭ*, and then [the *ṣ*] becomes *kṣ*. The words *gabhīra* and *gambhīra* mean "deep."
The two forms *gabhīra* and *gambhīra* are derived as irregular formations (*nipātana*). He states the rule for their formation: "from the root *gam*" (*gamer iti*).

The meaning is that from the root *gamlṛ* (meaning "to go"), the suffix *īran* is applied, the letter *bh* is substituted for the final [radical], and the augment *num* is optionally added. Amara states: "It is called *bhinna*, *gabhīra*, and *gambhīra*."
The dwelling of the poison.

The words *viṣā* and *vihā* are substituted [for *viśva* and *viha*]. He states this very point: "of the root *syati*" (*syateḥ*). This means from the two roots *ṣo* (in the sense of "ending" or "concluding") and *o hāk* (in the sense of "abandoning"). *Viṣā* also refers to a species of tree; as Amarasimha says: "*viśvā*, *viṣā*, and *prativiṣā*."

*paca elimaṭ*: from the root *paca* (meaning "to cook"), the suffix *elimaṭ* is applied; this is the meaning. However, in the section on the formation of kṛtya suffixes, it is stated that there is an "addition" (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *kelimara*.
[The suffixes] *dhuk*, *lavalan*, and *vālana* are applied after the root *śīṅ*.

Because the suffix *dhuk* is marked with *k* (indicating it is *kit*), there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Amara states: "Maireya, āsava, and śīdhu are synonyms for liquor. *Śīla*. Because the suffix *lak* is *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. *Śaivala*.

Amara states: "Jalanīlī is śevāla; śaivala is [another name for] kumudvatī.
From the roots *mṛk* and *kaṇi*, the suffixes *ūka* and *okaṇ* [are applied].

From the roots *mṛk* and *kaṇ*, the suffixes *ūka* and *ūkaṇ* respectively occur. The meaning is that from *mṛṅ* (in the sense of "giving up life") and *kaṇ* (in the sense of "closing the eyes"), the suffixes *ūka* and *ūkaṇ* are applied in order. In *maruka*, there is *guṇa* [substitution] due to the suffix *ūka*. In *kāṇūka*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel because the suffix *ūkaṇ* has the marker *ṇ*.
Valerūka.
*Valerūkaḥ*: [The suffix] *ūka* is added to the root *val*, meaning "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*); this is the meaning. (And *ulūka* and others are also formed in this manner.)

"Ulūka" and others are also [formed]; the meaning is that they are irregularly formed (nipātyante). He states the very irregular formation: "of the root *vali*. "An eloquent speaker is called *vāvadūka*," according to Amara. Regarding *bhallūka*:
it is a form derived from the root *bhall*, which is listed as meaning "to speak, to pierce, or to give without injury.
"The *ṛkṣa*, *cchaballa*, and *bhallūka* [are synonyms]," according to Amara.
And [the suffix] -śam- and -buk [are applied].

From the root *śam* (in the sense of "to pacify" or "to cease"), the suffix *ūka* is applied, and there is the augment *buk*. According to Amara, "śambūkāḥ" refers to "aquatic snails. [The suffix] *ūkaṇ* is applied after the roots *śali* and *maṇḍi*.

The suffix *ūkaṇ* is applied after the roots *śal* (in the sense of "going") and *maḍi* (in the sense of "adornment"). This means that the suffix *ūkaṇ* follows these two roots. Regarding the form *śālūka*: because the suffix *ūkaṇ* has the marker *ṇ*, there is vṛddhi (vowel strengthening) of the penultimate vowel. As Amarasimha states: "The bulbous root of these [plants] is called *śālūka*. Regarding *maṇḍūka*: even though the suffix is marked with *ṇ*.
Because the letter *ā* is not part of the *upadhā* (penultimate syllable), there is no *vṛddhi* substitution.
[The suffix] *ni* is *miṭ*.

*Nemiḥ*: [The root] *ṇīñ* means "to lead" (*prāpaṇe*); *niya* is its fifth-case form (*pañcamyantam*). The meaning is that the suffix *mip* is added to this. Regarding *nemiḥ*: Amara states, "The wheel (*cakra*) is a part of a chariot; at its edge (*anta*) is the *nemi*, which is feminine, while the *prathi* is masculine."
The high [notes] are for the *ṛc* verses.

The word "arter" (from the root *ṛ*) follows [as a governing term]. From the root *ṛ* in the sense of "to go," the suffix *mi* is applied; the meaning is that it is marked with the *k* indicator (*kit*). Regarding the form *ūrmi*: there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the root, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. [Then] from the root *bhū*, the suffix *kit* [is applied].

*bhuvaḥ kit* (Pāṇini 3.2.178). This means that from the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*satāyām*), the suffix *mip* is added, and it is marked with the *kittva* designation. Thus, *bhūmiḥ*. Because of the *kittva*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. In this context, one could have formulated the rule simply as *ṛtibhuvor ūcca* (Pāṇini 3.2.176), and instead of saying *bhuvaḥ kit*, one could have said *bhūmer ūcca*. However, in the case of *bhūmiḥ*, [the *kittva* is necessary to prevent *guṇa*].
There would be the undesirable consequence of *guṇa* substitution; however, by the force of the rule prescribing *ū* for the vowel *u*, the absence of *guṇa* is established.
[Vārttika: "And [the substitute] *raś* [is applied] after the root *aś*."
From the root *aś* (meaning "to pervade"), the suffix *mi* is applied, and the root undergoes the substitution of *raś*. Thus, *raśmiḥ* is formed.
Amara states: "The two words *raśmi* [denote] an instrument and a rein.
[Also derived from this root is] *dalmiḥ*.
The word *dalmi* is thus derived as a nipātana (irregular formation). He shows the root: *dala* in the sense of "splitting apart.
[The suffix] *ni* is applied after the roots *vī*, *jyā*, *val*, and *ari*.

The suffix *ni* is added after the roots *vī*, *jyā*, and *jvar*. This means that the suffix *ni* is applied to these roots: *vī* in the sense of movement, pervasion, and so forth; *jyā* in the sense of the loss of youth (aging);
