and *jvar* in the sense of disease. Now, one might ask: how is there the change of *ṇ* in the word *veṇi*, given that it is not preceded by *ra* or *ṣa*? To this, he says: "by virtue of irregularity (*bāhulaka*). He cites the *Amarakośa*:
*Veṇiḥ* means "loss" (*jyāniḥ*), that is to say, "deprivation" (*hāniḥ*). *Jūrṇiḥ*:
from the root *jvara*, with the suffix *nip*, there is the substitution *ūṭh* by the rule *jvaratvara-*.
[The suffix *ni* is added] after the roots *sṛ* and *vṛṣ*, being *kit*.

[The suffix] *ni* is added after the roots *sṛ* and *vṛṣ*, and it is *kit*. *Sṛ* means "to go," and *vṛṣu* means "to sprinkle"; from these two, *ni* is added as a *kit* suffix. Thus, *sṛṇiḥ*. Because it follows the vowel *ṛ*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*]. Due to its being *kit*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Amara states: "A goad (*aṅkuśa*) is called *sṛṇi*; it is not feminine, though it is used in the feminine. Regarding *vṛṣṇiḥ*: because it follows the consonants *ra* and *ṣa*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*].
And there is the elision of the final phoneme of the [preceding] member.

*An-lopaś-ca*: [The suffix] *niḥ* occurs after the root *agi*, which means "to go"; furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* acquired because the root is marked with the *it*-sign *i*. Although the rule for the *kit* designation of *niḥ* is established by carrying forward the term *kit* from the previous sūtra, the elision [of the final vowel] does not occur here because the rule "there is elision of the final vowel of a root ending in an *it*-sign" (*an-iditām*) applies.
The rule for the elision of the letter *n* has been established as "syāt. [Furthermore:
"After the roots *bahi*, *śri*, *śru*, *yud*, *dru*, *glā*, *hā*, *āt*, and *vṛ*, the suffix *ni* is applied."

The suffix *nip* occurs after the following roots: *vaha* (in the sense of carrying), *śri* (in the sense of service), *śru* (in the sense of hearing), *dru* (in the sense of going), *glai* (in the sense of loss of joy), *hā* preceded by *o-* (in the sense of abandoning), and *tvar* (in the sense of haste/agitation). This suffix is *nit*. Its being *nit* is for the sake of accentuation. Thus, from the root *tvar*, we have *tūrṇiḥ*.
In the suffix *pratyaya*, by the rule *jvaratvaretyūṭh* [Pāṇini 6.4.20], the vowel *ū* is substituted; then, by the rule *raṣābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.1], *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) occurs.
[The forms] *ghṛṇi*, *pṛśni*, *pārṣṇi*, and *bhūrṇi* [are derived in this manner].

The words *ghṛṇi* and *pṛśni* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). Regarding *ghṛṇi*: from the root *ghṛ* (in the sense of "flowing" and "shining"), with the suffix *ni*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs; the absence of *guṇa* is due to irregular formation (*nipātana*). Regarding *pṛśni*: from the root *spṛś* (in the sense of "touching"), with the suffix [ni], there is the elision of the letter *s*.

And the absence of the *guṇa* vowel is also prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*). Regarding *pārṣṇi*: from the root *pṛṣu* (in the sense of "to sprinkle"), the suffix *nip* is applied, and the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root is prescribed as an anomaly. The *ṛ* vowel undergoes *vṛddhi* to become *ār*, and by the rule *raṣābhyām*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs. Regarding *cūrṇi*: from the root *car* (in the sense of "to move"), the suffix *nip* is applied, and by the rule *raṣābhyām*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs.

The meaning is that the substitution of *ū* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*). Regarding the form *bhūrṇi*: from the root *ḍu bhṛñ* (in the sense of supporting and nourishing), with the suffix *nip*, there is the anomalous substitution of *ū* for the final vowel of the root;
then the substitution of *r* for the semivowel (*raparatva*), and finally the change of *n* to *ṇ* by the rule *raṣābhyām*.
The suffix *vin* is applied after the roots *vṛ* and *dṛ*.

The suffix *vin* is applied after the roots *vṛ* and *dṛ*. That is to say, *vin* is added after *vṛñ* (in the sense of "choosing") and *dṛṅ* (in the sense of "respecting"). [The form] *varvīr* results from the *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel.
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *jṛ*, *śṛ*, *stṛ*, *jā*, and *gṛ*.

Regarding the roots *jṛ*, *śṛ*, *stṛ*, and *jāgṛ*: from these roots (*jṛ* "to decay," *śṛ* "to injure," *stṛñ* "to cover," and *jāgṛ* "to wake"), the suffix *kvin* is applied; by the rule *kanāvitau*, the letters *ka* and *na* are elided. Thus, we have *jīrvir iti*. Because the suffix is marked with *k* (indicating it is *kit*), there is no *guṇa* substitution; then, by the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the *ṛ* is changed to *it*; and finally, by the rule *hali ca*, the vowel is lengthened.

The form is *rūpam*. The elision [of the *y*] by the rule "ṭhve'pṛktasya" does not occur, because of the mention of the term "apṛktasya" (of that which consists of a single phoneme). [In the case of the root] *div*, there is reduplication and the long vowel for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

From the root *div* (in the sense of playing, desiring victory, etc.), the suffix *kvip* is applied; there is reduplication of the root. Since there is no purpose in prescribing a short vowel for the *ikāra* (the *i*) following a long vowel of the reduplicated syllable, the shortening does not take effect; thus, it follows the principle that "a grammatical rule does not apply to that which has already been affected by another rule" (*na lakṣye lakṣaṇam*).

It should not be said that this contradicts logic, because even in the absence of a result, the application of the rule for the short vowel before the long one is unavoidable due to the operation of the scripture being like a rain-cloud (parjanya). [As Amara says: "Odana is not feminine; it is dīdivi."
Kṛvī, ghr̥ṣvi, chavi, sthavi, kikīdivi.

The meaning is that *kṛvighṛṣvicchavi*—namely, the roots *ḍukṛñ* (to make), *ghṛṣu* (to sprinkle), *chāe* (to cut), *ṣṭhā* (to stand, to cease from motion), and *divu* (to play, etc.)—preceded by the suffix *ki*, are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) with the suffix *kvip*. Among these, in the case of *kṛviḥ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution because of the *kit* designation. Likewise...

In the case of *ghṛṣvi* as well, [the same applies]. Regarding *cchavi*: from the root *chā* in the sense of "cutting," after the addition of the suffix *kvip*, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti* [Pāṇini 6.1.45] occurs, and its shortening is prescribed here by this [rule]. Similarly, *sthavi* is also formed. Regarding *kikidivi*:
from the root *div*, preceded by *kiki*, with the suffix *kvip*; because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is an absence of *guṇa* for the light penultimate vowel.

By the rule "ṭhlopo vyorvali," the *v* of the verbal root is elided; then, the long vowel is prescribed by *nipātana* for the final *i* of the word *kikī*. Amara states: "Now, the blue jay is *cāṣa*, *kikī*, or *divi*. In the form *vinimaya*, the *i* of the word *div* is lengthened.

The short vowel for the component of the word *kikī* is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). The intention is that both forms are seen in common usage. He states this very point: "by a *cāṣa* [bird], by a *kikidīvi*.
[The suffix] *ḍati* is applied after the root *pat*.
*pāter ḍatiḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *ḍati* is applied to the root *pā* (in the sense of "protection"). Thus, *patiḥ*.
Because of the *ḍit* designation, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the suffix]. *śaker ṛtin*.
*Śakṛt*: from the root *śaklṛ*, meaning "to be able"; the suffix *ṛtan* is added to this [root], such that the meaning is "that which is capable. Amara states: "Excrement is *śakṛt*.
*Amiti*: from the root *am*.
*Amateriḥ*. The meaning is that the suffix *ati* is applied to the root *am*, which belongs to the class beginning with "to go" (*gaty-ādi*).
[The rule] *vahivasyartibhyaścit* [is also applicable].
[The suffix] *ati* is added after the roots *vah*, *vas*, and *ṛ*; and it is *cit*. [Thus we have] *vasatiḥ*. As Amarasimha says: "The word *vasati* denotes both night and a dwelling."
Or, after the root *añc*, [the suffix] *ka* is applied.
The root *añc* means "to go"; the suffix *ati* is applied after it, and the letter *k* optionally serves as a substitute for the final portion [of the root].
After the root *han*, the suffix *ati* is applied and *ah* is substituted [for the root].

And [the word] *hanati*. The root *han*, meaning "to kill" or "to go," takes the suffix *ati*; the meaning is that there is a substitution of *ah* for the root [initial]. Explaining the meaning of this term *ahan* (non-killing), he quotes what Amara said: "It is *prādeśana* and *nirvapaṇa*."
Constantly delighting in joy.
*ramernit*: From the root *ram*, meaning "to play" and so forth, the suffix *ati* is added; furthermore, it is *nit*. Its status as *nit* is for the sake of accentuation.
(From *sūḍ*, the suffix *kri*.)

The suffix *kri* is applied after the root *sūṅ*. The meaning is that the suffix *kri* is added to the root *sūṅ*, which means "the birth of living beings. Regarding the form *sūri*: due to its *kit* status (indicating that the suffix is marked with *k*), there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution. As Amarasimha states: "A wise man is called *dhīmān*, *sūri*, *kṛtī*, or *kṛṣṭi*."
The suffix *krin* is applied after the roots *adi*, *śadi*, *bhū*, and *śubh*.

The suffix *krin* is added after the roots *ada* (to eat), *śadlṛ* (to destroy), *bhū* (to exist), and *śubha* (to shine); this is the meaning. The letters *k* and *n* are elided; the *n* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta-accented.
*Varṅkī* and others are also formed in this manner.
And *vaṅkri* and others: these are irregularly formed (*nipātita*). He states the suffix: "ending in *kin*. Regarding *vaṅkri*:

from the root *vaki* (meaning "crookedness"), the suffix *kin* is applied; because the root is marked with *i*, there is the augment *num*, followed by the substitution of the nasal (*anusvāra*) and its homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*). Regarding *vapri*: this form is derived from the root *ḍu vap* (meaning "to sow seeds").
Although the suffix *kit* is present, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The root *ahi* is for the purpose of denoting speech;

furthermore, *athi* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as meaning "to move" or "to throw. From these two roots, with the suffix *krin*, the forms *aṃhri* and *aṅghri* are produced. In both cases, because the root is marked with *it*, there is no elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*).
The suffix *trip* is applied after the roots *rāś* and others.
The suffix *trip* occurs after the roots *rā* (in the sense of giving) and *śadlṛ* (in the sense of falling away). Furthermore, the suffix *trin* also occurs after the root *ad*.
*Adestriniśca*. From the root *ad*, meaning "to eat," the suffix *trini* is applied; by the word *ca* ("and"), *trip* also occurs.
Regarding *trini*: *atrī* and *atriṇau* are cited to demonstrate that it ends in the letter *n*. *Atrir iti* is the form when *trip* is applied.
May he protect us from the devourer.
*Patera* means "one who flies. The meaning is that the suffix *atrin* is applied to the root *patlṛ*, which signifies "going. Thus we have *patatrī*.

Because of the indicatory letter *ṇ* (in *atrin*), the first syllable is udātta by virtue of the rule on initial accentuation (*nit*). Amara states: "Patatrī, patri, pataga, patat, patraratha, and aṇḍaja are synonyms for 'bird' (*pakṣin*).
[From the roots] *mṛk* and *kaṇi*, the suffix *īci* is applied.
The suffix *īci* follows the roots *mṛh* and *kaṇ*. The meaning is that the suffix *īci* is applied after these two: *mṛh*, in the sense of "giving up life," and *kaṇ*, in the sense of "sound.
[And] the root *śvi* is *cit*.
After the root *śvi* (meaning "to swell" or "to grow"), the suffix *īc* is applied; it is designated as *cit*.
The *cit* designation is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta-accented. After the root *veñ*, the suffix *īc* is applied, and it is also *ḍit*.
From the root *veñ* (meaning "to weave"), the suffix *īci* is applied with the marker *ḍ*. Thus, from *veñ*, *īci* is added;

because it is marked with *ḍ*, there is the elision of the suffix *ṭi*. Otherwise, if the substitution of *ay* were to apply, the form would be *vayīciḥ*, as in the case of *śvayīciḥ*. [The suffix] *ūṣan* is applied after the roots *ṛ* and *han*.

The suffix *ūṣan* is added after the roots *ṛ* and *han*. The root *ṛ* means "to go," and *han* means "to kill" or "to go"; from these two, the suffix *ūṣan* occurs. Thus, *arūṣa*. In the case of *ūṣan*, there is *guṇa* (vocalization).
After the root *pṛ*, the suffix *kuṣan* is added.

From the root *pura* (meaning "to go before"), the suffix *kuṣan* occurs. Thus, we have the word *puruṣa*. Because the suffix *kuṣan* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), there is an absence of *guṇa* [vowel strengthening]. Now, one might ask: how then is the form *pūruṣa* derived? To this, they say:
by the rule *anyeṣām api* ("also for others").
The suffix *uṣac* is applied after the roots *pṛ*, *ṇah*, and *kḷp*.

The suffix *uṣac* is applied after the roots *pṛ*, *ṇah*, and *kal*. [The root] *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling; *ṇah* in the sense of binding; and *kal* in the senses of sound and counting. After these, *uṣac* occurs. (*Pīyerūṣan*) [is another rule].
Regarding *pīyeruṣan*: since the root *pīy* is not seen in the Dhātupāṭha, he says "sautra" (belonging to the Sūtras).
[The rule] *masjernum ca* [is stated].

And [the suffix] *num* [is added] after *mañj*. The meaning is that after the root *majj* in the sense of purification (*śuddhi*), the augment *num* should be stated as an option. Regarding the form *mañjūṣā*: one might object that because *num* is marked with *u* (indicating it is *it*), the rule *midaco 'ntyādi* would cause the *num* to be placed after the vowel following the *m*, namely the *ā* after the *k*, and thus the *s* of the suffix should be heard. To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "prior to the elision" (*masjerantyāt pūrva*): the intention is that when *num* follows the letter *s*, and the *s* is subsequently elided by the rule *ṭhskoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*, this form [is produced]. (From *gaḍeśca*).
And from the root *gaḍ* [the suffix *uṣan* is applied]. From *gaḍi*, meaning "a part of the face," the suffix *uṣan* occurs. Thus, *gaṇḍūṣa*.
Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the augment *num* is added, followed by the anusvāra and the corresponding homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*).
From the root *ṛ* (to go), *aruḥ* [is formed].

*Araruḥ*. The root *ṛ* means "to go"; the suffix *aru* is added to this root—this is the meaning. Regarding the form *araru*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel. He says "*ararū*" in order to prevent the misconception that the suffix ends in *s*. (From the root *kuṭ* with the suffix *kvi*, which is also *kit*).

*kuṭaḥ kicca*: From the root *kuṭa* (meaning "to be crooked"), the suffix *aru* is added, and it is *kit*. Thus we have *kuṭaru*. Because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Now, one might object that the *kit* designation here is redundant, since the absence of *guṇa* is already established by the fact that the suffix [added after] roots beginning with *gāh* and *kuṭ* is marked with *ṅ*. To this, he says:
The suffix *aṭan* is applied after [the word] *śaka* and others in the sense of "you are here."

The suffix *aṭan* is applied after [roots] such as *śak*. The nasal *ṇ* in *aṭani* is for the purpose of making the first syllable udātta (accented). Thus, *śakaṭa*; this form is derived from the root *śaklṛ*, meaning "to be able. Regarding *kakir gatyarthaḥ* ("the root *kaki* has the sense of motion"), the remainder [of the rule] is that *aṭan* is applied after it. According to Amara: "Armor (*kaṅkaṭaka*) is called *ṭhuraśchadaḥ*. Regarding *devaṭa*: [this is derived from] *divu*...
In words such as *krīḍā* (play) and *vijīgīṣā* (desire to conquer), there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule "ṭhpugante" after the suffix *aṭan*.
[The suffix] *ambac* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *kaḍ*, and *kaṭi*.

The meaning is that the suffix *amvac* is applied after the roots *kṛñ* (in the sense of "making"), the two sūtra-derived roots *kaḍi* and *kaḍī*, and *kaṭe* (in the sense of "raining" and so forth). Regarding the form *karamba*: there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel. Amara states: "The words *kalamba*, *vesavāra*, and *upaskara* [are synonyms]."
[The suffix] *kadr̥c* is applied to denote a bird.

Regarding *kaderṇitpakṣiṇi*: the meaning is that the suffix *amvac* arising from the root *kad* prescribed in the Sūtra is *ṇit* when a female bird (*pakṣiṇī*) is to be expressed. Thus, *kādamba*. Because of the *ṇit* designation, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel.
(From the roots *kal* and *kard*, the suffix *ama* [is applied]).
The suffix *ama* occurs after the roots *kala* and *karda*. *Kala* means "to count" (*saṅkhyāna*) and *karda* means "a contemptible sound" (*kutsite śabde*); from these two, *ama* is applied.
Thus, *kalamā* [is formed]. Amara states: "The *sāli* rice, the *kalamā* rice, and so forth.
After the roots *kuṇi* and *puli*, the suffix *kindac* is applied.

The suffix *kindac* is applied after the roots *kuṇ* (meaning "sound" and "instrument") and *pul* (meaning "greatness"). The *kac* and *ac* [of the suffix] are elided. Thus, *pulinda*. Because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Amara states: "Kirātas, Śabaras, and Pulindas are tribes of Mlecchas."
Or, after the word *kupu*, there is optionally the substitution of *va* for *cha*.

The suffix *kindac* is applied after the root *kup*, and there is optionally the substitution of *va* for the final letter [of the root]. The meaning is that the suffix *kindac* is added to the root *kup* (meaning "to be angry"), and the letter *v* optionally replaces the final letter of the root.
Thus, *kuvinda*. Amarasimha states: "A weaver of threads is called a *kuvinda*.
The suffix *ghathin* is applied after the root *ṣañj* when preceded by the prefix *ni*.
The suffix *ghathin* is added after the root *sañj* (to adhere). The meaning is that *ghathin* occurs after the root *sañj* when no other word (*anupapada*) follows. Thus, we have *niṣaṅgathi*.
Regarding *niṣaṅgathi*: the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *upasargātsunotisuvatisyatistautistobhatisthāsenayasedhasicasañjasvañjām*.
Because *ghathin* has the marker *gh*, the substitution of *k* for the *c* and *j* sounds occurs by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*.
The mind is stirred up.

*Udyartiścit*: When *ud* is the upapada (preverb), the suffix *ghathin* is added to the root *ṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), and that [suffix] is *cit*. Thus, *udarathiḥ*. Once *ghathin* has been applied, there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel.
(From the root *sṛ*, the suffix *ṇic* is added.)

*sarterṇicca*: From the root *sṛ* (to go), the suffix *ṇic* is applied; this means that the suffix is marked with the indicator *ṇ*. Thus, *sārathiḥ* [is formed]. Because of the *ṇit* indicator, there is vṛddhi [of the vowel]. Amara states: "The charioteer (*niyantā*, *prājitā*, *yantā*, *sūtaḥ*, *kṣattā*, and *sārathiḥ*)."
From *kharjū*, *piñjū*, and others, the suffixes *ūru* and *lac* [are applied].

From roots such as *kharj* and *piñj*, the suffixes *ūra* and *ūlac* are applied respectively—specifically from *kharj* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjanam*) and *piñj* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*). The meaning is that *ūra* is added after *kharj* and its class, while *ūlac* is added after *piñj* and its class. The form *karpūra* is derived from the root *kṛpū* in the sense of "capability" (*sāmarthyam*).

In the case of *vallūra*, by virtue of the rule *bāhulakāt kṛpo ro laḥ* (the substitution of *l* for *r* in the root *kṛp* occurs diversely), there is an absence of that substitution. The form [of *vallūra*] is derived from the root *vala* or *valla* listed in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*). Regarding *aṅgūra*: from the root *lagi*—which is read in the *daṇḍaka* list as *agi*, *vagi*, *magi*, etc., and which has the meaning of "motion" (*gati*)—the suffix *ūla* is applied according to the rule *piñjāder ūlaḥ*. Vṛddhi is also applied [to the initial vowel].
The meaning is "it exists. Regarding *kusūla*: the suffix *ūlac* is applied because it belongs to the *piñja*-class and so forth. The root is *kusa* (to adhere).

Regarding *tāmbūla*: from the root *tamu* (to be weary), by the application of the suffix *ūlac*, there is the augment *vuk* and the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root; thus, from *tamu* (to be weary), with the addition of *vuk* in connection with the suffix *ūlac* and the *vṛddhi* of the root, we have *tāmbūla*.

"From the root *śṛ* [there is the suffix] *ūlac* and there is also *dug* and *vṛddhi*. The meaning is that from the root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure"), by the application of the suffix *ūlac*, there shall be the augment *dug* and *vṛddhi*. "And *kuk* after *du* and *ku*. The meaning is that after the roots *du* (meaning "to go") and *ku* (meaning "to sound"), by the application of the suffix *ūlac*, the augment *kuk* is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
And [the suffix] caṭ is long when preceded by ku.

The meaning is: "And *caṭ* [is added] after *ku*, and there is lengthening. From the root *ku* (meaning "to sound"), the suffix *caṭ* is applied, and there is lengthening of the root vowel. *Kūca* is a synonym for *kuc*. This is according to the lexicon which states: "Both *kuc* and *kūca* are considered to mean 'breasts'. He states the result of the suffix being marked with *ṭ* as follows: "*kūcī*."
The roots ending in *sam* take the suffix *iṇ*.

*samīṇaḥ*: When *sam* is the prefix, the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") takes the suffix *caṭ*, and there is lengthening of the vowel of the root. Thus, *samīcaḥ*. This is the form resulting from the lengthening of the root vowel. Demonstrating the purpose of the *ṭ*-marker, he gives the example: *samīcī*.
And the augment *ū* is added after the root *iṣ*, when followed by the suffix *kta*.

And after the root *ṣiv*, the suffix *u* is applied; the meaning is that the suffix *u* occurs after the root *ṣivu* (meaning "to weave" or "to continue a thread"), and there is the substitution of *ū* for the *ṭi* (the final vowel) of the root.
After the root *śam*, the suffix *van* is applied.
From the root *śam*, meaning "to pacify," the suffix *van* occurs; the form is *śamva*.
And [the words] beginning with *ulva* [are also formed in this manner].

"And *ulva* etc."—the meaning is that these are derived with the suffix *van* as irregular forms (*nipātana*). He shows the verbal root: "√*uc*, to gather. From this [root], the substitution of *l* for *c*, the absence of *guṇa* in the root, and the addition of the suffix *van* are established as irregularities; the meaning is thus. "The womb is *jarāyu*; but *ulva*... [is another term].
Regarding *kalala*, Amara states: "The word *kalala* is not feminine. Regarding *śulva*: from the root *śuc* (to grieve), the suffix *vani* is applied;

the letter *c* is changed to *l*, and the absence of *guṇa* is also prescribed by nipātana. Amara states: "*Śulba* and *varāṭaka* [are synonyms], while [the word] *strī* [is feminine]. Regarding *bilva*: from the root *bil* (to split), the suffix *van* is applied.
Because there is no difference between the *vaba* [suffixes] and the *vilva*, it is also called *vilvam*.
The two suffixes *staḥ* and *sto* [are used for] the lotus (*ambuja*) and the crane (*baka*).

The suffixes *ambac* and *abaka* are applied after the root *sthā*, meaning "to stop" or "to cease moving. Along with these suffixes, there is also the substitution of *stā* for the root *sthā*. Because this substitute *stā* consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the entire original form. Thus we have *stamba*. Regarding this, the *Amarakośa* states:
A "stamba" (thicket) is a cluster of grass and so forth;
[the suffix] *danaC* is applied after the roots *śas* and *pi*.
The suffixes *da* and *dan* are applied after the roots *śo* (in the sense of thinning) and *śapa* (in the sense of reviling), respectively. Regarding the *Amarakośa*, it says:
"In the case of *jambāla* and *śaṣpa*. As for the word [ending in] *-śabda*, there is the substitution of a *jaś*-sound [for the *śa*] by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*.
And [the suffixes] *abdā* and so forth [are used].

*Abda* and others: these are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the suffix *dan*. In the word *abda*, meaning "that which falls" (*avatīti*), the substitution of *ba* for *va* is irregularly applied. Regarding *kunda*: from the root *kuṣ* (meaning "to sound"), the suffix *dan* is added along with the augment *num*; this is the meaning. Thus, *kunda* [is derived]; it is said that "the *kunda* is white, while the *raktaka* is red."
In the section on forest herbs, the *Amarakośa* states:
"The suffix *kyaN* is applied after the roots *vali*, *mali*, and *tani*."

The suffix *kayan* occurs after the roots *val*, *mal*, and *tan*. *Val* means "to cover," *mal* means "to hold," and *tan* means "to expand. The marker *k* in *kayan* is for the sake of subsequent rules. Thus, *valayan*.
[In the case of *vṛh* and *vṛdh*, there is the substitution of *ṣuk* and *duk* respectively.]

*vṛhroḥ ṣugdukau ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.120). From the roots *vṛñ* (to choose) and *hṛñ* (to take), the suffix *kayan* is applied; according to their respective order, the augments *ṣuk* and *duk* are added. Thus, *vṛṣayaḥ*. Because the suffix *kayan* is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution here. *Hṛdayam*: it is called *hṛdayam* because it is "carried away" (*hriyate*) by the objects of the senses (*viṣayaiḥ*).
The suffix *ru* is applied after the locative case endings *mip* and *bhyām*.

The suffix *ru* is applied after the roots *mī* and *pī*. The root *mī* (ḍu-miñ) means "to cast" (*prakṣepaṇe*), while the root *pī* is listed under the heading "ri-pī gatau" (ri-pī, meaning "to go"); this root *pī* has the sense of motion (*gatyarthaka*). From these two, the suffix *ru* occurs. Thus, *meruḥ*. When the suffix *ru* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution. Amarasimha states: "Meru, Sumeru, and Hemādri [are synonyms]."
And [the suffixes] beginning with *jañ* [are applied after verbal roots].

These are derived with the suffix *ru* and are treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*). Regarding *jatru*: from the root *janī* (to appear), the letter *n* is irregularly changed to *t* before the suffix *ru*. Regarding *aśru*: from the root *aśū* (to pervade), the suffix *ru* is applied. [The suffix] *kru* is applied after the roots *ru* and *śāti*.

From the roots *ru* (to go) and *śad* (to fall), with the suffix *krun*. *Ru* means "to go" and *śadlṛ* means "to fall," which takes the causative (*ṇyanta*) suffix. Regarding the form *śātī*, the rule "the root *śad* becomes *ta* when not meaning 'to go'" prescribes the substitution of *t* for *d*;

thus, the citation is given as *śāti*. As for *ruru*, Amarasimha states: "The black antelope, the *ruru*, the *nyaku*... Now, one might raise the objection: how is there shortening of the vowel in the word *śatru*? In response to this doubt, he says:
Regarding the rule *prajñādibhyaś ca*:
after the roots *jan*, *dā*, *cyu*, *sṛ*, *vṛ*, *mad*, *iṣ*, *mi*, and *bhṛ*, the suffixes *itvan*, *tvan*, *tanaṇ*, *knin*, *śak*, *syaṅ*, *ḍhaṭ*, and *aṭac* are applied.
The suffix *itvan* is applied after the following roots: *janī* (to appear), *ḍudāñ* (to give),
*cyuṅ* (to move), *sṛ* (to go), *vṛñ* (to choose), *madī* (to rejoice), *ṣama* (to be unimpaired), *ṇamu* (to bow and to sound),
and *ḍubhṛñ* (to support and nourish).

The suffixes *tvan*, *tanaṇ*, *knin*, *śak*, *say*, *ḍha*, *ḍaṭa*, and *aṭac* shall occur [after the root *kṛ*]. In *cyautna*: due to the *ṇit* nature of *tanaṇ*, there is *vṛddhi*. In *sṛṇi*: due to the *kit* nature of *knin*, there is no *guṇa*. In *vṛśa*: due to the *kit* nature, there is no *guṇa*. In *matsya*: by the rule *khari ca*, there is the substitution of *c* for *s*. *Ṣaṇḍha*.

Thus [it is said]. Because of the predominance [of this rule], the *s* [augment] does not apply by the rule "after a verbal root beginning with a consonant. Regarding *naṭa*: because it has the marker *ḍ*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the *a* of the suffix). Because it has the marker *ṭ*, [the feminine form] is *naṭī*.
[The suffixes] are seen after other [roots] as well.

The phrase "also from others" means that suffixes such as *itvan* and others also occur after other verbal roots (*dhātu*). Regarding *petvam*: from the root *pā* (to drink), with the suffix *itvan*, there is *ād-guṇa*. Regarding *bhṛśam*: from the root *bhṛñ*, the suffix *śak*; because it is *kit*, there is no *guṇa*.
These [are] the sources of doubt.

*Kusumbha* is derived from *kus*. From the root *kus*, meaning "to adhere," the suffixes *umbha*, *uma*, *īda*, and *ita* occur. Thus, *kusumbham*. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. As Amara states: "The word *mahārajana* is neuter; *kusumbha* is [also] neuter, while in the sense of a water-jar it is masculine."
Sānasi, varṇasi, parṇasi, taṇḍula, aṅkuśa, caṣāla, ilvala, palvala, dhiṣṇya, and śalya.
The meaning is that [the suffix] *it* is irregularly applied (*nipātyante*) after roots such as *ṣaṇu* (to eat) and others, as in *sānasi* and *varṇasi*.

Regarding *sānasi*, they say: [it is derived] from the root *sanoti* (to gain). "And there is vocalization of the penultimate vowel" (*upadhāvṛddhiśca*) means that there is the substitution of the vowel *ā* for the *a* of the root. "And [the suffix] *nuk* after *vṛñ*" means that the suffix *asi* is added to the root *vṛñ* (to choose).

The meaning is that the augment *nuk* is added to the root. After the *guṇa* substitution of the root and the application of *ṇatva* by the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām*, the form *varṇasiḥ* is obtained. Regarding *parṇasiḥ*: from the root *pṛ* (in the sense of protecting and filling), the suffix *asi* is applied and *nuk* is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*). After the *guṇa* substitution of the root and [the application of *ṇatva*] by the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām*...
The form is *taṇḍula*. Regarding the word *taṇḍulāḥ*, he says: "the root *taḍ* [means] 'striking'.

From this root, the suffix *ukac* is applied, and *num* is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Alternatively, *num* is established by virtue of the root being marked with the *idit* designation.
The *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* substitutions then follow. Regarding the word *aṅkuśa*, he says: "the root *aki* [means] 'marking'."
Having understood [the rule regarding] *it*, *num*, *anusvāra*, and *parasavarṇa*, he says "caṣāla" here—[explaining] "from the root *caṣ*" (*caṣeḥ*).

This means from the root *caṣ* in the sense of "eating. Amara states: "The *caṣāla* is the ring of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Regarding "ilvala": the root *il* is a Vedic (Sautra) root; from it, the suffix *valac* is applied, and the absence of *guṇa* is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding "palvala": [the root is] *pā*...
From the root *pā* ("to drink"), the suffix *valac* is applied; the augment *lag* is inserted by way of a nipātana (irregular formation), and there is shortening of the vowel.

The suffix is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning "that in which one drinks. Regarding *dhiṣṇya*: from the root *dhṛṣ* (ÑI *dhṛṣā*) in the sense of daring or boldness, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. The *ṛ* of the penultimate vowel of the root is changed to *i*, and there is an absence of the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*.

And the absence of the suffix *guṇa* is prescribed by nipātana. Amara states: "Dhiṣṇya means a place, a house, a star, or fire; bhāgya means good or bad fortune (karma). Regarding the word *śalya*, he says: "From *śal*"—that is to say, from the root *śala* meaning "to go. [The suffix] *kla* is applied after the roots *mū*, *śak*, and *vī*. [The roots are] *mūṅ* (in the sense of binding) and *śaklṛ* (in the sense of being able).

The meaning is that the suffix *klap* is applied after the roots *śak* (to be able), *abi* (to go), and *śabda* (to sound). Regarding "mūlam": because of the *k*-marker, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
Regarding "śakla": according to Amara, "durmukha" means one who is talkative or has an unrestrained mouth, while "śakla" means one who speaks kindly.

[The suffix] *ya* is applied after the roots *mā* (to measure), *chā* (to cut), and *sas* (to sleep). After these—*mā* in the sense of measuring, *chā* in the sense of cutting, and *sas* in the sense of sleeping—[the suffix *ya* is added].
The meaning is that the suffix *ya* is applied. This is clear.
(From the root) *jan*, the suffix *yak* [is applied].

The suffix *ya* [is applied after the root] *jan* in the sense of "begetting"; that is, from this [root], the suffix *ya* occurs. The fact that *ya* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*) is for the sake of what follows. He causes one to remember the substitution of *ā*: "after *ye*, it is optional" (*ye vibhāṣā*).
And [the words] beginning with *adhnyā* are also [formed in this way].

Regarding *adhnyā*: the suffix *ṭāp* is applied in the feminine. According to the *Amarakośa*, "The words *arjunī*, *adhnyā*, and *rohiṇī* mean a reddish-brown cow. Regarding *kanyā*: this is a form derived from the root *kan*. As for *bandhyā*: since the root *bandh* means "to bind," if the suffix *yak* were applied to it, the form would have to be *bandhyā* and not *vandhyā*;
therefore, he says: "because of the substitution of *va* for *ba*."
The suffix *vanip* occurs after the roots √snā, √dīp, √rī, and √pṛśak.

From the roots *snā* (to bathe), *mad* (to rejoice), *pad* (to go), *ṛ* (to go), *pṛ* (to protect and to fill), and *śaklṛ* (to be able), the suffix *vanip* is applied. Thus, *snāva* is formed; [here] there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel and elision of *n*. *Arva* is formed from the root *ṛ* with the suffix *vanip*, where *guṇa* substitution occurs.

"Ṭhbājivāhā'rvagandharvahayasaindhavasaptayaḥ'"—thus says Amara. Regarding "ṅībrāviti": [it refers to] "vanora ca" and so forth. (The suffix) *kvanip* is applied after the roots *śīṅ*, *kruśi*, *ruh*, *ji*, *kṣi*, *sṛ*, and *dhṛ*.
From the roots *śīṅ*, *kruś*, *ruh*, *ji*, *kṣi*, *sṛ*, and *dhṛ*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied.

Regarding *jitvā*: because *kvanip* is marked with *p* (indicating it is a *pit*), the augment *tuk* is inserted by the rule "a short vowel takes *tuk* before a *pit* affix that begins with a consonant. Thus...
After the roots *kṣi* and *sṛ*, and so forth;
and there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the roots *dhyai* and *pyai*.

"Samprasāraṇa also occurs for the roots *dhyai* and *pyai*. The meaning is that the suffix *kvanip* is added after *dhyai* (in the sense of 'thinking') and *pyaiṅ* (in the sense of 'growth'), and there is samprasāraṇa. [The form] *dhīvā* arises because, upon samprasāraṇa of the vowel *i*, the rule *'hala'* prescribes the lengthening of the vowel."
And half [a day].
And *adar-dha*. The meaning is that from the root *ad*, signifying "eating," the suffix *kvanip* is applied, and the letter *dh* is substituted for the final [letter].
(*pra īra-śado-stuṭ ca*).

The suffix *kvanip* occurs after the roots *īr* (to move) and *śadlṛ* (to perish) when preceded by the prefix *pra*, and there is the augment *tuṭ*. Thus, from *pra-īr-van* and *pra-śad-van*, we have *prertvā* and *praśattvā*. When *pra īr vā* is established, by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, we get *prertvarī*.
By the rule *ṭhvano ra ca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and *ra* is substituted for the final vowel. In the same way...
The suffix *in* is applied after all verbal roots to form the word *praśatvarī*.

"From all roots" (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ*) means that the suffix *in* is applied after all verbal roots. Regarding the form *pacih*: from the root *ḍupacaṣ* (meaning "to cook"), the suffix *in* is added. Now, one might ask: in the word *koṭi*, since the suffix *in* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign by the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ*, how can there be *guṇa* (vocalization) here? To this he replies: "by virtue of *bāhulaka*" (due to irregularity).
[The suffix *kan* is applied] after the verbal roots *hṛ*, *piṣ*, *ruh*, *vṛt*, *vidi*, *cid*, and *kīrti*.

The meaning is that the suffix *in* is applied after the roots *hṛ* (to take away), *piṣ* (to crush), *ruh* (to sprout from a seed), *vṛt* (to turn/occur), *vid* (to know), *chid* (to split into two), and *kṛ* (to sound). Although this is already established by the preceding rule, this statement is made to indicate that [the suffix *in*] is also applied after a root ending in a vowel, as in the case of *ṭhacaḥ iḥ*.

In *ṭhigupadha*, the suffix *ka* is applied; this is for the purpose of preventing both [the application of the suffixes *in* and *ac*]. In *hariḥ*, there is the substitution of *guṇa*. Regarding this, Amara states: "The word *hari* [is used] in the sense of Viṣṇu, lion, sun, horse, Venus, fire, monkey, and frog; it means 'tawny' in the three genders. Here, the suffix *i* (from the rule *aca iḥ*) would have been applicable. In *peṣiḥ*: [End of excerpt]
The suffix *ka* is obtained after a root with *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter; [this suffix] is also *kit* after such a root.

"From a root having *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter (*igupadhāt*), [the suffix] *kit*. The term *in* is understood to carry over from the previous rule. The meaning is that the suffix *in* may also be applied after other roots having *i* or *u* as their penultimate letters, and it shall be *kit*. In the preceding sūtra, the mention of *piṣ* and others was for the purpose of excluding the *kit* designation. For this very reason, in the form *peṣiḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution is established. [Similarly,] *kṛṣiḥ*.
But this is not a suffix (*guṇa*). The root *kṛṣ* means "to scratch" or "to furrow.
[The suffix] *man* is added after the root *bhram*, and there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel.

"And there is the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *bhramiḥ*. The meaning is that from the root *bhramu* (in the sense of "unsteadiness"), the suffix *in* should be applied, and it is *kit*, as well as undergoing *saṃprasāraṇa*. Thus, *bhṛmiḥ*. Because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Now, one might ask: how is it that [the word] is *bhramiḥ*? To this he says: "by virtue of *bāhulaka* (diversity of application)."
And hereafter, the sequence of the hundred-fold obstacles shall be explained.

*kramitami*: from the roots *kramu* (to step), *tamu* (desire), and *śati* (stiffness)—which is a Vedic root—the suffix *ini* is added, and it is *kit*; furthermore, the vowel *a* of these [roots] is replaced by *i*. Thus, *krimiḥ*. The form arises through the substitution of *i* for the [root-final] *a*. He states that the meaning is "a worm" (*kṛmi*).
This is because of the continued application (anuvṛtti) of the term "vocalization" (saṃprasāraṇa). Vocalization and the substitution of *i* occur alternatively;

for when vocalization takes place, there is no result for the substitution of *i*, and when the substitution of *i* occurs, there is no difference in the resulting form due to the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) rule following from "after a vocalized vowel" (saṃprasāraṇācca).
Having understood this, one should reflect upon it.

*Maneru* [is derived from] *man*, meaning "to know"; the suffix *ḍin* is applied, and the vowel *a* is changed to *u*. Thus, the meaning is "one who knows. Regarding *muni*: because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution. Amara states: "A *muni* is one who restrains his speech (*vācaṃyama*). [The rule] *varṇeṣvaliśca ahiraṇye* [applies].

Regarding the form *varṇeli* [meaning a non-metallic substance]: since the verbal root *varṇ* is not seen in the standard list of roots (*dhātupāṭha*), he says—"*varṇi* is from the sūtra"—meaning that the suffix *in* occurs after this root when a non-metallic substance is to be expressed, and there is the substitution of *bali*. (From the roots *vas*, *vap*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *vraj*, *sad*, *han*, *vāś*, *vā*, and *vṛ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied.)

*vasi-vapi-yaji-rāji-vraja-ṣad-lṛ-hana-vāśṛ-vada-vṛñ*: *vas* (to dwell), *ḍu vap* (to sow/germinate), *yaja* (to sacrifice/worship the gods), *rājṛ* (to shine), *vraj* (to go), *ṣadlṛ* (to perish, etc.),
*han* (to kill/to go), *vāśṛ* (to sound), *vad* (to speak clearly— causative), *vṛñ* (to choose).

The suffix *iñ* is applied after these [roots] ending in *ṇya*; this is the meaning. Regarding *vāśiri*: because the suffix *iñ* has the marker *ñ*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of the penultimate vowel. The rest is clear.
(*naho bhaśca*) [Pāṇini 3.2.172].

*nah* and *bha*. From the root *nah* (in the sense of "binding"), the suffix *iñ* occurs, and the letter *h* is replaced by *bh*. Thus, the form *nābhi* is derived. Furthermore, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is a vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) for the root *kṛṣ*.

"In the Vedic language (chandas), there is vṛddhi for [the root] kṛṣ. This means that from the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" (*vilekhana*), the suffix *iñ* is applied, and there is *vṛddhi*. Thus, *kārṣiḥ*; here, the *ṛ*-vowel undergoes *vṛddhi* to become *ār*. However, in common usage (*loka*), by the rule *igupadhātkit* [Pāṇini 3.1.135], the suffix *ini* is applied, and the form is simply *kṛṣiḥ*.
() Śraḥ, the two birds.

*Śraḥ śakunau*: after the root *śṛ* (meaning "to injure"), the suffix *iñ* is applied when a bird is to be expressed; thus, *śāri*. Because the suffix *iñ* has the marker *ñ*, there is *vṛddhi* [of the first vowel].
(*Kṛña udīcāṃ kāruṣu*: [the suffix *iñ* is applied] after the root *kṛ* when Northerners are the artisans).

After the root *kṛ* (in the sense of "making"), the suffix *iñ* is applied when artisans (*kāru*) are to be expressed, according to the Eastern grammarians. From the root *ḍukṛñ* (in the sense of "making"), *iñ* is applied when artisans—that is, craftsmen—are to be expressed. Example: *kāriḥ*. [The suffix] *iṇ* is applied after the roots *jan* and *ghas*.

The suffix *iṇ* is applied after the roots *jan* and *ghas*. *Jan* means "to appear," and *ghaslṛ* means "to eat"; the suffix *iṇ* occurs after these two. Regarding the form *janir*: there is a prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule "and in the case of *jan* and *vadh*" (*janivadhyośca*).
And [the suffix *iṇ* is applied] after *aj* and *ati* as well.
And from the roots *aj* and *at*. From *aj*, meaning "to go" or "to throw," and *at*, meaning "continuous motion," the suffix *iṇ* is applied.
Thus, *ājiri*. In the case of the suffix *iṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel; however, the substitution of *vī* (for *ai*) does not occur due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
Amara states: "The word *ājir* is used for a level ground, the earth, and a battle."
And [the elision of *a*] occurs before the word *pāda*.

And with *pāda*: when the word *pāda* is an upapada, the suffix *iṇ* is added after the roots *aj* and *at*; this is the meaning. Thus, *padāji*. In the case of *padāji*, the substitution of *pada* for *pāda* occurs by the rule:

"The substitute *pada* is used for *pāda* before *aji*, *āti*, *ga*, and *upahata*. (Pāṇini 6.3.52). [The rule continues: "After the roots *aś* and *paṇāy*, the suffix *ruṭ* is added and there is elision (*luk*) of the [augment] *ya*. (Pāṇini 3.1.28).

Regarding *aśipaṇāyyoḥ*: the analysis of the compound is "of *aśi* and *paṇāyi*. *Aśū* means "to pervade," and *paṇa* means "in trade"; the latter ends in the suffix *āya*. From these two, the suffix *iṇ* shall be applied.
For these two, respectively, there shall be the augment *ru* and the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *āya*.

*rāśiḥ*: with the augment *ruṭ* and the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel, this form is obtained. *pāṇiḥ*: with the suffix *iṇ*, upon the elision (*luk*) of the *āya*-pratyaya and the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate *a*, this form is obtained.
(From the root *vā* [to blow], the suffix *ḍi* is applied).
From the root *vā*, meaning "to go" or "to smell," the suffix *iṇ* occurs; and that [suffix] is marked with the indicator *ḍ*.

Because it is marked with *ḍ*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion. Thus he says: *viri*. According to Amarasimha: "The words *naga*, *oka*, *vājin*, *vika*, *ravi*, *viṣkira*, and *patatrin* [denote birds]. [This applies] in the feminine gender.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule "kṛdikārād aktinaḥ";
[the form] *praharī* is derived from the root *hṛ* with the prefix *pra*, denoting a well (*kūpa*).
The suffix *iṇ* is applied after the root *hṛ* (meaning "to carry") when preceded by *pra*; furthermore, this suffix is marked as *ḍit*. Thus he says: *prahiḥ*.
Because it is *ḍit*, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the prefix]. Amara states: "In the masculine, *andhuḥ*, *prahiḥ*, and *kūpaḥ* all mean 'well'."
When *vyo* follows, there is the elision of *y*, and the preceding vowel is lengthened.

"Nau-vy-ya-lopaḥ": when *nau* is the upapada, the suffix *iṇ* is added after the root *vy-eñ* (meaning "to cover"), and that suffix is marked with *ḍ*; furthermore, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *y* of the root, and the lengthening of the vowel *i* of the prefix (*upasarga*). Thus, the form *nīviḥ* is derived from the root *vy-eñ* by adding *iṇ*, and due to the *ḍit* designation, there is *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel), followed by the elision of the root's *y*.

The form [nīvī] occurs both when there is elision (*lopa*) and when there is lengthening (*dīrgha*). Amarasimha states: "The word *nīvī* refers to the knot of a woman’s garment (*strīkaṭīvasrabandha*) and also to a stake (*paripaṇa*). Here, *paripaṇa* means capital or principal wealth (*mūladhana*). Thus he says: "In the sense of a cloth-knot and in the sense of capital wealth."
When the *khy* is identical, that [preceding vowel] is also udātta.

*Samāne khyah*: When the word *samāna* is the *upapada*, the suffix *iṇ* shall be applied after the root *khyā* (meaning "to tell"). The analysis of the rule is: "and that [suffix] is udātta. Thus, the meaning is: that [suffix] *iṇ* shall be *ḍit*, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ā*; furthermore, for the word *samāna*, there is the substitution of *sā* which is udātta. Consequently, with the substitution of *sā* for the word *samāna*, the form is *sakhi*.
The suffix *ap* is added after the roots *rūp*,
*āṅ-pūrvaka-śri*, and *han*, and the vowel is shortened.

Regarding the roots *āṅ* with *śri*, *āṅ* with *śriñ* (in the sense of service), and *āṅ* with *hana* (in the senses of injury and motion): the suffix *iṇ* is applied after these, and it is also *ḍit*; furthermore, there is shortening of the vowel of *āṅ*. Thus, the forms are *aśriḥ* and *ahiḥ*.
Here, he cites the statement of Amara [Kośa] beginning with "striyaḥ" etc.
In this case, the suffix *i* is applied.

Here, the suffix *i* [is applied]. Because of its qualification by the word "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*), there is the understanding that it applies to that which ends in such a root. The meaning is: the suffix *i* is applied after a root ending in a vowel (*ajanta*). Regarding *ravi*: from the root *ru* (to sound), the suffix *i* is applied. Since the marker *ḍit* is not being carried over (*ananuvartanāt*), there is no elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). Regarding *pavi*: from the root *pūñ* (to purify).
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after the words *khaṇḍika*, *uṣyaka*, *viśva*, *sivi*, *nisa*, *dhvaja*, *granthi*, and *cali*.

The suffix *i* occurs after the following roots: *khanu* (to dig), *kaṣa* (to injure), *aja* (to move or throw), *asu* (to throw), *vasa* (to cover), *vana* (to desire or collect), *ṣaṇa* (to collect), *dhvana* (to sound), *grantha* (to bind), and *cala* (to tremble). According to Amara, "a mine" (*khani*) is a feminine term for a source of minerals.
*Ajiri*: due to the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*), there is an absence of *vībhāva*. [The suffix *ini* is applied] after the root *vṛt* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

*vṛteś chandasi*: after the root *vṛt* (meaning "to turn"), the suffix *i* occurs in the Vedic language. Thus, *varti*. [The guṇa substitution occurs] because of the light penultimate vowel. *bhujeḥ kiñ ca*: [the suffix *i*] also occurs after the root *bhuj*, and it is marked with the *k*-sign.

*bhujeḥ kicca* (A 3.2.178): After the root *bhuji* (meaning "to protect" and "to eat"), the suffix *i* is applied as *kit* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). It is also used occasionally in common worldly usage (*loka*). *kṛgṛśṛpṛkuṭibhidicchidibhyaśca* (A 3.2.179): The suffix *i* is also applied as *kit* after the roots *kṛ*, *gṛ*, *śṛ*, *pṛ*, *kuṭi*, *bhidi*, and *chidi*.

Regarding the roots *kṝ*, *gṝ*, and *śṝ*: *kṝ* means "to scatter," *gṝ* means "to swallow," *śṝ* means "to injure," *pṝ* means "to protect" and "to fill," *kuṭ* means "to be crooked," *bhid* means "to split," and *chid* means "to divide. From these, the suffix *ip* is applied, and it is understood that this suffix is *kit*. Thus, [the form] *kir-i-ṛ* results from the root *kṝ*.
The substitution of *it* occurs here, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *r*. According to Amarasimha: "Varāha, sūkara, gṛṣṭi, kola, potrī, kiri, and kiṭi" are synonyms for boar.
Regarding *giri-kiri*: "Adri, gotra, giri, and grāvan" are synonyms for mountain, according to Amarasimha. Regarding *puri*: the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya."
In the case of *kuṭī* and *kaṃpī*, there is also the elision of the nasal (*n*).

The meaning is that the suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *kuḍi* (to burn) and *kapi* (to move), and there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) of the root. Although the suffix is marked with *k*, the elision of the nasal would not apply because the root is marked with *it*; therefore, that [elision] is specifically prescribed. Thus, the form is *kuḍi*. Because the suffix is *kit*, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel does not occur.
"Kapi" means monkey; according to Amarasimha, "kapi, plavaṅga, plavaga, śākhāmṛga, and valīmukha" are synonyms.
[The suffix] *manin* is applied after all verbal roots.
The suffix *manin* is applied after all verbal roots. That is to say, *manin* may be added even after all roots. Regarding *karman*:

from the root *ḍukṛñ* in the sense of "making," *manin* is applied, and there is *guṇa* substitution. Regarding *carman*: from the root *cara* in the sense of "moving. Regarding *sutrāman*: from the root *traiṅ* in the sense of "protecting"; one who protects well (*suṣṭhu*) is a *sutrāman*.
Nor should one increase [the syllables].

Regarding *bṛṃher-na-uc*: there is no elision (*lopa*) of the *na* from the root *bṛṃh*. The meaning is that from the root *bṛh* (meaning "to grow"), the suffix *manin* is applied, and the vowel *a* is substituted for the *na* resulting from the addition of the *num* augment. Thus, one says *brahma*.
When the *na* is replaced by *a*, the semivowel substitution (*yaṇādeśa*) of the *ṛ* vowel occurs. As stated in the *Amarakośa*: "Brahma is the Absolute Reality (*tattva*)."
In the Vedic language, [the suffix *kan*] is applied after the roots *aś* and *śak*.

Regarding the rule *aśiśakibhyāṃ chandasi*: the meaning is that the suffix *mnin* is added after the roots *asū* (in the sense of pervasion) and *śaklṛ* (in the sense of being able). "Aśma" [is derived thus]. According to Amarasimha: "pāṣāṇa, prastara, grāvan, upala, aśman, śilā, and dṛṣad" are synonyms for stone.
The suffix *iman* is applied after the verbal roots *hṛ*, *bhṛ*, *dhṛ*, *sṛ*, *stṛ*, and *śa*.

The meaning is that the suffix *iman* is added to the roots *hṛ*, *bhṛ*, *dhṛ*, *sṛ*, *stṛ*, and *śṛ*. Specifically: *hṛñ* in the sense of taking away (*harane*), *ḍubhṛñ* in the sense of supporting and nourishing (*dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ*), *dhṛ* in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇe*), *sṛ* in the sense of moving (*gatau*), *stṛñ* in the sense of covering (*ācchādane*), and *śṛ* in the sense of harming (*hiṃsāyām*). Regarding the form *harimā*: when the suffix *iman* is applied, the *i* and *m* are elided, and the root undergoes *guṇa* substitution.
The suffix *imanin* is applied after the words *jani* and *mṛd*.
The suffix *imanin* is added after the roots *jan* (to be born) and *mṛ* (to die). The specific distinction here is the *nit-svara* (the acute accent on the first syllable).
[The suffix *imanin*] is also applied everywhere after the root *veñ* (to weave).

*Veñ* occurs everywhere. The meaning is that from the root *veñ*, "to weave" (*tantu-santāne*), the suffix *imanin* is applied in both Vedic and worldly usage. Regarding *vema*: Amara states, "In the masculine, *vema* is a weaving shuttle" (*puṃsi vemā vāyadaṇḍaḥ*). [The following are derived with the suffix *man*: ] *nāman*, *sīman*, *vyoman*, *roman*, *loman*, *pāpman*, *dhyāman*.

Regarding the words *nāman*, *āsīman*, and *vyoman*: they are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). The phrase "ending in the suffix *manin*" is the remainder [of the rule]. He explains the manner of their formation: "it is remembered" (*mnāyate*). From the root *mnā* (meaning "to study" or "to repeat"), with the suffix *manin*, the lengthening of the vowel of the root is treated as an irregularity (*nipātyate*). In another view, the feminine suffix *ḍāp* is applied.

By the rule *ṭhḍābubhābhyām anyatarasyām*, [the suffix ṅīp is optionally applied]. Regarding *vyeña*: from the root *vyeñ* (to cover), the suffix *manin* is added; the change of the vowel *e* to *o* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Amara states: "The sky is called *vyoman*, *puṣkara*, and *ambara*. Regarding *rauteḥ*: from the root *ru* (to sound). Regarding *lometi*: from the root *lūñ*.
In the word *chedane*, [the suffix] *mani* is applied; in *pāpmā*, from the root *pā* (to drink), the suffix *mani* is applied with the augment *pu* as a nipātana (irregular formation).
In the sense of "pairing" (*mithuna*), the suffix *mani* is applied.

The suffix *man* [is applied] after *mithun*. He explains the meaning of the word *mithuna*: "by means of a prefix," etc. The sense is that this [specific form] alone is intended here. And thus, the meaning is that the suffix *man* is applied to a verbal root when it is accompanied by a prefix. Now, since the formation is already established by *manin* itself in the rule "after all verbal roots, *manin* [is applied]," for what purpose [is this stated]?

Because there would be the fault of applying the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*), he says: "for the sake of the accent" (*svarārtham*). The intention is that, by the rule for *nit* suffixes, the word would otherwise have the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*).
[The rule: *sāti-bhyāṃ manin-maniṇau*.

The suffixes *manin* and *maniṇ* follow the roots *sāti* and *at*. The meaning is that these two suffixes, *manin* and *maniṇ*, respectively follow the root *ṣo* (meaning "to finish") and the root *at* (meaning "to go continuously"). Regarding *sam*: when *manin* follows, there is the substitution of *ā* for the initial vowel according to the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*. Regarding *ātman*: when *maniṇ* follows, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel because the suffix is marked with *ṇ*.
The suffix *śikan* is applied after the roots *han* and *maś*.

The suffix *sikan* is added after the roots *han* and *maś*. The meaning is that *sikan* follows these two: *han*, in the sense of "killing" or "going," and *maś*, in the sense of "sound. Thus, from *han* we derive *haṃsikā* ("female bee"), and from *maś* we derive *makṣikā* ("fly"). Regarding the change of *ś* to *ṣ* by the rule *śasya vraśca*, and then the change of *ṣ* to *k* by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, there is also the restoration of the *ṣ*-sound.
The Kauravas.
*Koraran*: the meaning is that the suffix *aran* is applied to the root *ku* (to sound). *Kavara*: there is *guṇa*, and the substitution of *ava*. (*Gira-uḍac*).
The suffix *uḍac* is applied after the root *gṛ* (in the sense of swallowing). Thus, *garutmān*, *garuḍaḥ*, and *tārkṣyaḥ* [are formed]; so says Amarasimha.
The suffix *kami* is applied after the root *ind*, with the elision of the nasal (*n*).

*Indeḥ kamiḥ nalopaśca*: from the root *idi*, meaning "supreme sovereignty," the suffix *kami* occurs and there is the elision of the letter *n*; this is the meaning. *Idam*—this is a pronominal term. *Kāyateḥ ḍimiḥ*.
The suffix *ḍimi* is applied after the root *kai*. The meaning is that the suffix *ḍimi* is added to the root *kai* (in the sense of "sound").
Because it is marked with the indicator *ḍ*, there is elision of the *ā* vowel (*ṭilopa*). This [root] is also indeed among those beginning with *sarva*.
[The suffix] *ṣṭran* is applied after all roots.

The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after all verbal roots (*dhātu*). This means that the suffix *ṣṭran* is added to every root. Regarding the word *vastram*: from the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*), meaning "because of covering. The root *chad*, meaning "to conceal" (*apavāraṇe*), takes the causative marker (*ṇic*). [According to the rule: "In the case of *bhrasj*, *gam*, *nam*, *han*, *ni-viś*, and *yaś*, there is also *vṛddhi* [of the vowel]."

The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after the roots *bhrasj*, *gam*, *ṇam*, *han*, *viś*, and *as*, and there is vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) for these roots. From *bhrasj* (to fry), *gamḷ* (to go), *ṇam* (in the sense of bowing and sound), *han* (in the sense of killing and going), *viś* (to enter), and *asū* (to pervade), the suffix *ṣṭran* occurs, and their [roots] undergo strengthening. Thus, *bhrāṣṭra*. [The *ṣ* is applied] by the rule *vraśca* etc., and there is strengthening. In the neuter gender, it is *ambarīṣa*.
The *Amara-kośa* states: "Bhrāṣṭra means fire.
(From the root) *div*, [the word] *div* means heaven.

From the root *div*, meaning "to play" and so forth, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied; there is the substitution of *dyau* for the root and the application of *vṛddhi*. The resulting form is *dyautra*. (The suffix *ṣṭran* is also applied after the roots *uṣi* and *khan*, with the *ṣ* being *kit*.)

The suffix *ṣṭran* is added after the roots *uṣ* and *khan*, and it is marked with the *k*-sign. *Uṣ* means "to burn," and *khan* means "to dig. From these two, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied as a *kit*. Thus we have *uṣṭra*. According to Amarasimha: "For the camel (*uṣṭra*), the terms *kramelaka*, *mayūra*, and *mahāṅga* are used. Regarding *khātra*: by the rule "the substitution of *ā* occurs for the vowels of *jan*, *khan*, and *san* before the suffixes *saN* and *jhal*" (*janakhanasanām sañjhaloḥ*), the vowel *a* is substituted for the radical vowel.
(0) The [suffix] uṣṭra is also applied after śivi and mucya.

The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after the roots *ṣivu* (in the sense of weaving) and *muc* (in the sense of releasing). Regarding the word *sūtram*: from the root *ṣiv*, with the suffix *ṣṭran*, the substitution of *ūṭh* occurs for *va* by the rule *chvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*;
then, the penultimate vowel becomes *ū*, and through the combination of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), the form is established. In the term *ṣṭran*, the *ṣ* has been replaced by *ṣṭu*.
The explanation: when *ṣa* undergoes *it*-vṛddhi (change to *ī*), *tran* is prescribed [as the suffix]. *Mūtram* is the form resulting from the change of the final vowel (*ṭi*) to *u*.
[The suffix] *ktra* is added after the roots *ami*, *cimi*, *midi*, and *śasi*.

The meaning is that the suffix *ktra* is applied after the roots *ama* (in the sense of moving, etc.), *ciñ* (in the sense of piling up), *ñi midā* (in the sense of moistening), and *śasu* (in the sense of harming). Regarding the word *āntram*: the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "the vowel of a nasalized [stem] is lengthened before *kvip*. The rest is clear.
The *pu* [consonant] and the short vowel [are called *laghu*].

The suffix *ktra* is applied after the root *pū* (meaning "to purify"), and there is shortening of the vowel of the root; thus, *putra*. Because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
[The suffix] *ḍraṭ* is applied after the root *styai*.

The suffix *ḍraṭ* is applied after the root *styai*. From the root *styai* (ṣṭaḷṬ), meaning "to sound" or "to collect," the suffix *ḍraṭ* occurs. Thus, *strī*. Because it is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the *i* vowel (*ṭilopa*). By the rule "ṭhlopo vyoḥ," there is elision of the *y*. According to Amara: "A woman is called *strī*, *yoṣit*, *abalā*, *yoṣā*, *nārī*, *sīmantinī*, or *vadhū*."
The suffix *tra* is applied after the roots *guh*, *ṛ*, *paci*, *vac*, *yam*, *si*, *sad*, and *kṣadi*.

The meaning is that the suffix *trap* is applied after these roots: *guṅ* (in the sense of indistinct sound), *dhṛñ* (in the sense of holding), *vī* (in the sense of motion, procreation, etc.), *ḍupacaṣ* (in the sense of cooking), *vac* (in the sense of speaking), *yam* (in the sense of stopping), *ṣadlṛ* (in the sense of falling apart, etc.), and *kṣadiḥ*, which is a root from the *sūtra*. Regarding the word *gotram*: there is *guṇa* substitution for *tre*.
Regarding *gotra*: Amara states, "A mountain peak, a mountain, and a stone are *gotra*; lineage and progeny are also *gotra*. Regarding *satra*:
Amara states, "*Satra* means a covering, a sacrifice, a constant gift, and also a forest.
[The suffix] *tran* is applied after the roots *hu*, *yā*, *mā*, *aśu*, and *bhas*.

The meaning is that the suffix *traṇ* is applied after the roots *huyāmā*—namely *hu* (to give or sacrifice) and *dān* (to give), *yā* (to go), *mā* (to measure), *śru* (to hear), and *bhas* (to revile or shine). Amara states: "A *bhastrā* is a leather bellows."
And [the rule] regarding the *gamer* vowel.
And [the suffix] *gamerā*. From the root *gamlṛ* in the sense of "going," after this [root], there is the substitution of *ā* for the final *m* of the verbal root; thus, *gātram*.
[This is taught by the rule: *dādibhyaśchandasī*.

*dādibhyaśchandasī*: In the Vedic language, the suffix *tra* is applied after roots such as *dāp* (to cut) and others. Thus, *dātram*. Amara states: "A sickle (*dātra*), a reaper (*lavitra*), and a binding (*ābandha*). And *pātram*: Amara states: "'Pātra' refers to both what is suitable and a vessel."
The suffix *ṇitran* is applied after the verbal roots beginning with *bhū* and ending with *gṛ*.

From the roots *bhū* and others, as well as from *gṛ*, the suffix *ṇitran* occurs. From *bhū* in the sense of "existence," *vad* (with the causative marker *ṇic*) in the sense of "articulate speech," and *gṛ* in the sense of "swallowing," the suffix *ṇitran* is applied. Thus, *bhāvitram*. Because of the *ṇit* designation, there is vṛddhi [vowel strengthening].
*Vāditram*: Amara states, "This fourfold musical instrument is called *vādya*, *vāditra*, and *ātodya*."
Except for the case of *car* (to move).

The suffix *ṇitran* is applied after the root *car* (meaning "to go") when the sense of "conduct" (*vṛta*) is to be expressed; thus, *cāritra*. Because the suffix is marked with *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel.
[From this point, the rule] *aśitrādibhya itrotrau* applies.

*Itrotrau* [are added] after *aśitra* and others. The analysis of the compound is: *aśiśca traśca* = *aśitrau*; those which have these two (*aśi* and *tri*) as their initial elements are "those beginning with *aśitra*. The word *ādi* (beginning), heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, is connected with each member individually. After those beginning with *aśi* and those beginning with *tri*, the suffixes *itra* and *otra* respectively are applied. Thus, *aśitram*. [The root is] *aśū*.

In the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), [the suffix] *itra* is applied after this [root]. *Vahitram*: from the root *vah*, meaning "to carry. *Dharitrī*: from the root *dhṛ*, meaning "to hold"; the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group. *Trātram*: from the root *traiṅ*, meaning "to protect"; with the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) and the application of *ādguṇaḥ*.
He hates even his own kinsmen.

The suffix *itra* is applied after the root *am* (in the sense of "to go," etc.), and it is *cit* when the meaning to be expressed is an enemy (*śatru*). According to Amara: "Dviṭ, vipakṣa, ahita, amitra, dasyu, śātrava, and śatru [are synonyms for enemy].
[The suffix] *āḥ* is applied after the roots *sami* and *nikṣi*.
Āḥ: From the root *iṇ* (to go) preceded by *sam*, and from the root *kaṣ* (to injure) preceded by *ni*, the suffix *āḥ* is applied.
Thus, *samayā*. This form arises through the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement with *ay*.
Amara states: "The word *samayā* is used in the senses of 'near' (*anta*) and 'middle' (*madhya*)."
What is the essence of the earth, and what is it?

The word *cikkaṇa* is derived from the root *cit* (meaning "to perceive" or "to know") with the suffix *kaṇ*; the meaning is that the suffix *kaṇ* is added to this root, and the final letter of the root is replaced by the letter *k*. He states the *Amarakośa*: "cikkaṇam.
[The word *sūkṣma* is derived] from the root *sūc* with the suffix *man*.

From the root *sūc*, with the suffix *man*. *Sūc* meaning "malicious speech" belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in *ṇi*; from this, with the suffix *man*, there is elision of *ṇi*, followed by the change to *k* (kutva) and the change to *ṣṭ* (ṣṭutva), resulting in the form *sūkṣma*.
From the root *pat*, with the suffix *ḍumsun*.
The suffix *ḍumsun* is applied to the root *pā*, meaning "to protect. Thus, we have *pumān*.
Because the suffix *ḍumsun* has the marker *ḍi*, there is elision (*ṭilopa*) of the final portion [of the suffix]. Some maintain that the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation;
however, even for them, since elision is impossible without the designation of *it*, the grammatical operation based on being *ugit* is established.

For it is accepted that even for letters whose purpose is pronunciation, their cessation occurs precisely through the designation *it* and its subsequent elision; this is clear in the *Śekhara* on the rule *diva aut*. The result of this is that in forms such as *supuṃsī*, the suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ṭhugitaśca*. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, [the form] from the root *sū* is *sa-*.

The word *pumān* is derived as "one who procreates" (*prasave*). The derivation is as follows: from the root *ṣūṅ*, meaning "the release of the embryo of living beings," the suffix *sun* is applied; the *s* of the root is changed to *p*, and the *ū* is shortened—this is the sense. This is explained in the *Śekhara* under the section on masculine words ending in consonants.
This is clear on the occasion of explaining the sūtra "ṭhpuṃso'ṅi" (Pāṇini 7.1.89).
[Now,] from the roots *ruc* and *bhuj*, the suffix *kiṣyan* is applied.

The suffix *kiṣyan* is added after the roots *ruc* and *bhuj*. The meaning is that *kiṣyan* is added after these two: *ruc* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*) and *bhuj* in the sense of "protecting" (*pālanādau*). Regarding the form *ruciṣyam*: because of the *k*-marker, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*).
[The suffix] *ti* is added after the root *vas*.

*Vasastiḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *ti* is added to the root *vas* (to dwell). Regarding *vastir iti*, he states that it means *śāstiḥ*; this is due to *bāhulaka* (the principle of diversity). The suffix *ti* is added to the root *sās* (to instruct) [to form *śāsti*]. Regarding *agamaḥ*, the meaning is "a mountain. Now, how is this so?
In that case, since there would be an absence of *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels), he says: "The *śakandhvādi*-group [is mentioned].
The intention is that the *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent vowel) belonging to the *śakandhvādi* group sublates *savarṇadīrgha*.
[This applies to] *sāvasiḥ*.
The meaning is that when *sa* is the upapada, the suffix *tip* is applied to the root *as* (in the sense of "to be").

According to Amarasimha, "svasti" refers to blessings, well-being, merit, and so forth. Now, one might ask: "How is it then that the case-ending (*sup*) is not heard? To this he replies: "Because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*."
The suffix *vau* is applied after the root *tasi*.

*vau taseḥ*: When *va* is the prefix, the suffix *ati* occurs after the root *tasu* (to perish). Amara states: "A *vitasti* is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long, being the distance from the thumb to the little finger.
(*padiprathibhyāṃ nit*): [The suffix *iti*] occurs after the roots *pad* and *prath*.

The meaning is that the suffix *ti* is applied after the roots *pad* (to go) and *prath* (to become famous), and it is a *nit* (causing the *guṇa* substitution). Thus, *pati* [is formed]. According to Amarasimha: "A foot-soldier (*padāti*), a lord (*pati*), one who goes on foot (*padaga*), one who goes by foot (*pādātika*), and a foot-soldier (*padāti*) [are synonyms]. As for *prathiti*, it means fame. Now, regarding this term *prathiti*:

How is it that *iṭ* [is applied]? Since there is a prohibition by the rule "the augment *iṭ* is not applied after roots beginning with *val*, nor after those ending in *ti* or *tu*," he says: "because it is not among the roots beginning with *grah*" (*agrahādi*).
The intention is that this root *prath* belongs to the class of roots beginning with *grah*.
(From the root *dṛṇāti*, there is also the substitution of a short vowel.)

From the root *dṛ* (to split), there is the suffix *iti*, and the shortening of the root vowel. From *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing," the suffix *iti* occurs, and the root undergoes shortening. Thus: *dṛti*. Amara states: "A leather bag (*dṛti*), a parting of the hair (*sīmanta*), and green (*harita*).
[The suffix] *kīṭan* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *tṛ*, and *kṛp*.

The suffix *kīṭan* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *tṛ*, and *kṛp*. *Kṛ* means "to scatter," *tṛ* means "floating and crossing," and *kṛpū* means "capability. From these, *kīṭan* occurs. Thus, *kirīṭam* (a crown). Because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* strengthening of the root; however, by the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100), the substitution of *it* (short *i*) takes place. Amara states: "A *kirīṭa* is a crest, a garland, and cleansing."
The suffix *kitac* is applied after the roots *ruc*, *vac*, and *kuci*.

From *ruc*, *vac*, and *kuci*: the suffix *kitac* occurs after these roots—namely, *ruc* in the sense of shining and delighting, *vac* in the sense of speaking, and *kuc* in the sense of sound. *Rucitam* [is formed]; because of the *kit* designation, there is no *guṇa* substitution. *Ucitam*; because of the *kit* designation, there is *saṃprasāraṇa*. He says "kuṭitam" by virtue of *bāhulaka* (irregularity). In some places, however, it is in the sūtra itself.
The grammatical rule: From the roots *kuḍi* and *kuṣi*, the suffix *kmalan* is applied.
The suffix *kmalan* is added after the roots *kuḍi* and *kuṣ*. *Kuḍi* means "to burn," and *kuṣ* means "to extract"; the meaning is that *kmalan* is added after these two.
(There is also the rule: "And for *kuṣ*, there is the substitution of *l*."

"Kuṣe-laś-ca": the meaning is that after the previously mentioned root, the suffix *la* is substituted for the final letter. Regarding "kulmalam": due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), this is not mandatory; therefore, the previously mentioned form "kuṣmalam" is also valid.
(From all roots, the suffix *asun* [is applied]).
The suffix *asun* is applied after all verbal roots. Regarding the word *ceta*: it is derived from the root *citī* (meaning "to perceive") with the suffix *asun*.
[Likewise] from *sṛ* (meaning "to go"), *pīṅ* (meaning "to drink"), and *ṣadlṛ* (meaning "to perish," etc.). [From the root] *rap*, there is the substitution of *e* for the final vowel.
*raperata ecca*: from the root *rap* in the sense of "articulate speech," the suffix *asun* is applied, and the vowel *a* is replaced by *e*; this is the meaning.
(*aśerdeavane yuṭ ca*).

The suffix *yuṭ* is added after the root *aś* in the sense of "divine praise" (*devana*). From the root *aś*, meaning "to pervade," the suffix *asun* occurs, and there is the augment *yuṭ* for the verbal base. *Devana* means "praise.
After the root *ubj*, in the sense of "strength" (*bala*), there is the elision of the letter *b*.
*ubja-balopaś-ca*: [The suffix] *asun* occurs after the root *ubj* when "strength" (*bala*) is to be expressed, and there is the elision of the letter *ba*; this is the meaning.
(And there is vocalization of the vowel in the root) *śvi*.

"Śvas" [is derived] with vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). From the root *śvi* (meaning "to go" or "to increase"), the suffix *asun* is applied, and there is vocalization of the root; thus the form is "śvas. [Also,] from the root *śri*, when referring to one's own limb, the suffix *śiras* is applied, and it is also *kit*.
From the root *śri* [in the sense of] "one's own limb": from the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service," when one's own limb is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is applied;
the meaning is that the root is replaced by *śiras* and the suffix is *kit*.
From the root *ṛ*, there is also [the suffix *asun*], and [the vowel] becomes long (*u*).
From the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go," the suffix *asun* is added with the *kit* designation, and there is the substitution of *u* for the root vowel. Thus, *ura*.
By the rule of *rapara*, it becomes *uraḥ*.
(In the sense of) "disease," the augment *śuṭ* is also applied.

Regarding the rule *vyādhau śuṭ ca*: when the meaning "disease" (*vyādhi*) is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is applied to the root *ṛ*, and there is the augment *śuṭ*. Thus, the form is *arśas*. Amara states: "One who has the disease *arśas* is called *arśasaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *udake nuṭ ca*: [the suffix *asun* is applied to the root *ṛ*] with the augment *nuṭ* when the meaning "water" (*udaka*) is to be expressed.

The suffix *asun* is applied after the root *ṛ* when "water" (*udaka*) is to be expressed, and there is also the augment *nuṭ*. Thus, *arṇaḥ* ("water"). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām*. [Next, the sūtra:
*iṇa āgasi* ("after *iṇ*, when 'sin' [*āgas*] is to be expressed").
The suffix *asun* is applied after the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") when a sin (*pāpa*) is to be expressed;
furthermore, the augment *nuṭ* is added to it—this is the meaning.
After the root *ric*, the suffix *asun* is applied when wealth (*dhana*) is to be expressed, and it is also marked with the *ṅit* indicator.

*Rekṇas* [is derived] from the root *ric*, meaning "to leave" (*virecana*), in the sense of "wealth" (*dhana*). From this root, the suffix *asuṇ* is applied; it is marked with *k* (indicating the substitution of *guṇa*), and there is the augment *nuṭ*. Thus, it becomes *rekṇas*. By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, the change to *k* occurs, and by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*, the change to *ṇ* occurs.
And [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied after the root *cāyati*, with the vowel becoming short when preceded by *anna*.
Regarding the rule *cāyateranne hrasvaśca*: the root *cāyṛ* means "to honor" and "to observe. When the sense of "food" (*anna*) is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is applied after this root;
there is the augment *nuṭ* for that suffix, and the shortening of the vowel of the root. Thus, *cana*. By the rule *lopo vyorvali*, there is the elision of the *y*.
The suffix *puṭ* is added after the roots *vṛñ* and *śīṅ* when [respectively] a form (*rūpa*) and a limb of the body (*svāṅga*) are to be expressed.

[The suffix] *asun* is applied after the roots *vṛṅ* and *śīṅ*. *Vṛṅ* means "to gather" (*saṃbhakti*), and *śīṅ* means "to sleep" (*svapna*). When these two [roots] are to be expressed in the sense of "form" (*rūpa*) or "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*), *asun* occurs, and there is the augment *puṭ* for it. Regarding "it becomes *śepa*":
when *asun* is present with the *puṭ* augment, there is *guṇa* substitution.
After the [suffixes] *sru* and *rī*, there is also the augment *tuṭ*.

The suffix *asun* is applied after the roots *sru* (to flow) and *rīṅ* (to adhere), and there is the augment *tuṭ* for that [suffix]. The meaning is that *asun* is added to these two, and *tuṭ* is the augment for it. After the root *pā* (to protect), when meaning "strength," the suffix *juṭ* is applied.

After the root *pā* "to protect," when the word *bala* is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is applied, and there is the augment *juṭ*; [when *bala* is to be expressed, the suffix is *ṭi*. Also, when *udaka* is to be expressed, there is the augment *thuṭ*.

The suffix *asun* is applied after the root *pat* when "water" (*udaka*) is to be expressed, and there is the augment *thuṭ*; this means that *thuṭ* is added to it. Also [after *pat*] when "food" (*anna*) is to be expressed.

And [the suffix] *anne*. That is to say, even when *anna* is to be expressed, the suffix *pāti-asun* is applied and there is the augment *thuṭ*. (From the root) *ad-* etc., the augment *num* is applied before the suffix *dhak*.
And after the root *ad*, in the sense of eating, the suffix *asun* occurs; thus *andha*. As Amara says: "Bhissā, strī, bhakta, andha, and anna [are synonyms for food].
And after the root *skand*, when referring to one's own limb, [the suffix *asun* occurs].

And [the suffix *asun* is applied] after the root *skandi* when its own limb (*svāṅga*) is to be expressed. The root *skandi* means "to move" and "to dry up. From this root, when its own limb is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is applied, and the final letter of the root is replaced by *dh*. Thus, *skandhaḥ* ("shoulder").
(The suffix *ap* is applied) after [roots ending in *kṛ*, etc. when the action (*karman*) is to be expressed.

The word *āpas* is derived from the root *āplṛ* (meaning "to pervade") with the suffix *asuṇ* when expressing the object (*karman*). The meaning is that the vowel of the root is shortened and the augment *nuṭ* is optionally added to the suffix.
Regarding the term *bāhulakāt* (due to irregularity): it means that the shortening of the root vowel does not necessarily occur.
And [the suffix] *ju* occurs after the word *rūpa*.

*Juṭ ca*: When *rūpa* is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is added to the root *āp*, the vowel of the root is shortened, and the augment *juṭ* is added to the suffix; this is the meaning. Thus, *abja*. [In this form,] by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the letter *b* is changed to *j*.
(*udake num bhau ca*).

*udake num bhau ca*: when *udaka* is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is added to the root *āplṛ*, with the augment *num*, shortening of the vowel, and *bh* as the final substitute; this is the meaning. *naho divi bhaśca*.

And *nabhas* [is derived as follows]: from the root *ṇaha* "to bind," when the word *gagana* (sky) is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* is applied, and the letter *bha* is substituted for the final portion [of the root]. Thus, *nabhaḥ*. The letter *ha* is replaced by the letter *bha*.
