(*iṇ* is used in the sense of "coming" and "offense").

The suffix *asun* is applied after the root *iṇ* in the sense of "offense" (*aparādha*). When "offense" is to be expressed, the suffix *asun* occurs after the root *iṇ* meaning "to go," and the root undergoes the substitution *āg*. Amara states: "The word *āgaḥ* refers to sin and offense.
[Also: After the root *am*, the suffix *huḍ* is applied, and the augment *k* is added.
The root *am* is used in the sense of "going" and other such meanings; from this [root], the suffix *asun* is applied, and the augment *huk* should be added to the root.
According to Amarasimha, "ṭhaṃha" means "evil deed" (*durita*) or "misdeed" (*duṣkṛta*).
And [the suffix] *ra* is also applied.
And [the word] *rama*. From the root *ram* (in the sense of "to play" and so forth), the suffix *asun* is applied, and there is the augment *huk*; this is the meaning.
(In the case of a place-name, *ha* is also substituted.)
[The suffix] *asun* [is applied] after the root *ram*, provided that "direction" (*diś*) is to be expressed; furthermore, the letter *ha* is substituted for the final letter [of the root].
(Pāṇini 3.3.58) [The suffix] *asun* is applied after the roots *añc*, *añj*, *yuj*, and *bhṛj*, and the letter *ku* [is substituted for the final letter of the root]. (Pāṇini 3.3.59)

The meaning is that the suffix *asun* occurs after the roots *añcu*, *añj*, *yuji*, *bhṛji*, and so on; furthermore, the guttural class (*ka-varga*) is substituted for the final letter of these roots. [The roots are: *añcu* in the sense of "motion" and "worship"; *añjū* in the senses of "manifestation," "anointing," "splendor," and "motion"; *yujir* in the sense of "joining"; and *bhṛji* in the sense of "roasting. From these, the suffix *asun* is applied.
The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *bhū* and *rañj*.

The suffix *asun* is added after the roots *bhū* and *rañj*, and it is *kit*. *Bhū* means "to exist," and *rañj* means "to color. From these two, *asun* is applied. Regarding *bhuva*: because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution; instead, *uvaṅ* is applied. Regarding *raja*: by the rule *aniditām*, there is elision of the nasal (*n*).
After the root *vas*, the suffix *asun* is applied with the *ṇit* marker.
From the root *vas* (in the sense of "to cover"), the suffix *asuṇ* shall be added with the marker *ṇit*. Thus, *vāsaḥ* [is formed].

Because of the *ṇit* marker, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. As Amarasimha states: "Clothing for covering is *vastra*, *ācchādana*, or *vāsaḥ*. From the root *cand*, [the suffix *asuṇ* is added], and the initial *ca* is replaced by *cha*.

And for *cadi*, there is *ccha*. From the root *cadi* (to rejoice), the suffix *asun* is applied and the letter *ccha* is substituted [for the initial *ca*]. From the roots *paci* and *vac*, there is also the augment *suṭ*.

After the roots *pac* and *vac*, there is the suffix *asun* as well as the augment *suṭ*. [The root] *ḍupacaṣ* means "to cook," and *vaca* means "to speak"; after these two, the suffix *asun* occurs, and there is the augment *suṭ*. Thus, *pakṣa*. When *c* is changed to *k* (by *kutva*), *s* becomes *ṣ* (by *ṣatva*).
[Also, the suffix *asun* occurs] after the roots *vah*, *hā*, *dhā*, and *añ* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).

Regarding the rule *vahi-hā-dhā-ñbhyaś-chandasi*: from the roots *vah* (to carry), *hā* (to abandon), and *ḍudhāñ* (to hold, etc.), the suffix *asun* occurs in the Vedic language. Thus, *vakṣāḥ*. The lengthening of the vowel is by the rule *ṭha-santasya ca*.
The intention is that with the addition of *suṭ*, the *h* becomes *ḍh* by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, and then *ṣ* is substituted [for the *k*] by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. Thus say the ancients.

Thus [ends the explanation]. The word "prāñcaḥ" (easterners) is used to indicate a lack of consensus. For indeed, the examples mentioned are not seen in common worldly usage, since this sūtra applies only to Vedic literature; however, in the Veda, they are seen exactly according to the method stated by me. Thus he says: "In reality, however... [The suffix] *ṇit* is understood to follow from the rule "vaserṇiḥ."

Thus [it is said]: "The vṛddhi is for the upadhā. The intention is that this is because the suffix *asun* is marked with the *ṇit* indicator. He states the form when *yuk* is applied: *viśvo vihāyāḥ*. [Now follows: *iṇa āsiḥ*.
The suffix *asi* follows the root *iṇ*. From the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," the suffix *asi* occurs, as in *ayā*; the intention is that there is a substitution of the *guṇa* vowel.
In the case of a copulative compound (*mithuna*), the suffix *asi* applies, and everything else is as previously stated.

The suffix *asi* is used for the word *mithuna*. He states the meaning of the term *mithuna*: "A verbal root (*dhātu*) qualified by a prefix (*upasarga*) is a *mithuna*. Thus, the meaning is that the suffix *asi* is applied to the verbal root *asu* when it is accompanied by a prefix.
Regarding the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*): it means that the suffix *yuṭ* is applied to the root *aś* in the senses of eating and praising. [The example is] *suyaśāḥ*.
The root √han becomes *apavāda* when preceded by *asu*; furthermore, when the negative particle *nañ* precedes it, *han* becomes *eha*.

When the negative particle *nañ* is used as an upapada, the suffix *as* is applied after the root *han* (meaning "to kill" or "to go"), and the root vowel *ha* is replaced by *e*; this is the meaning. [Likewise,] when the root *dhā* (meaning "to place") is used, *vedha* is substituted for it.

*Vidhāñ* and *vedha*. The meaning is that from the root *dhā* preceded by *vi*—specifically from *ḍu dhāñ* in the sense of "holding and nourishing"—the suffix *asi* is applied, and there is the substitution of *vedhas*. This substitution applies to the verbal root when it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*). Thus, *vedhāḥ*; and as it is said: "In the sense of Viṣṇu, *vedhāḥ*; in the feminine, however, *āśīḥ*."
Thus says Amara:
"The suffix *nu* is added, and [the preceding consonant] becomes a *ghoṣavat* (voiced) sound."

*nuvo dhuṭ ca*: after the root *ṇu* (in the sense of "praise"), there shall be the suffix *asi*, and there is also the augment *dhuṭ*. Thus, *nodhāḥ*. [In this form,] there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel. Furthermore, when a prefix (*gati*), a kāraka, or a secondary word (*upapada*) precedes, the original accent of the first member [of the compound] is maintained.

There is also the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound when *gati* or a *kāraka* functions as the *upapada*. When a *gati* or a *kāraka* is the *upapada*, the suffix *asi* is applied after a verbal root. For example, *sutapāḥ*: here, *asi* is added to the root *tap* (meaning "to heat") with *su* as the *upapada*. Also, *jātavedāḥ*: here, *asi* is added to the root *vid* with the word *jāta* functioning as the object (*karmakāraka*) *upapada*.

From the word *jñāna*, the suffix *asi* is applied [by Pāṇini 5.2.127]. He states the purpose for prescribing the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [of the compound] by saying: "after a preverb (*gati*), a kāraka, or a subordinate word (*upapada*).
[In the case of] *candra*, [the suffix] *ma* is added with the marker *ḍit*.

Regarding *candre mo ḍit*: when the word *candra* is an upapada, the suffix *asi* is applied after the root *mā* (in the sense of measuring), and that [suffix] is marked with the indicator *ḍ*. The purpose of the *ḍit* marker is the elision of the *ṭi* portion (the final vowel and following consonant) in forms such as *candramasau*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.102: *vayasi dhāñaḥ*.

In the word *vayas*. Even when the word *vayas* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *as* is applied after the root *dhā* (in the sense of "holding" and "nourishing"). Thus, *vayodhāḥ* [is formed]; [here] the substitution of *ru* and *utva* etc., apply. Also [the suffix *as* is applied] after [the root *dhā*] when *payas* is the *upapada*.
And [the suffix] *asi* is applied after the root *dhā* when the word *payaḥ* is an upapada; furthermore, that [suffix] is marked with the indicator *ṭi*.
And [it is applied] when *puraḥ* is [an upapada].

And *purasi*: when the word *puras* is used as an upapada, the suffix *asip* is added to the root *dhā*, and that [suffix] is marked with the indicator *ḍit*. According to Amara, "The *purodhā* is the *purohita*. (Example: *purūravāḥ*.

The meaning is that *purūravas* is thus derived as an irregular form (*nipātana*). He states the irregularity itself: "of the word *puru*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "he cries out to many" (*puruṃ rauti*). From the root *ru*, meaning "to sound," the suffix *asi* is applied;
there is the substitution of *guṇa* and *āv* [for the vowel], and lengthening of the first member of the compound—this is the sense. The implication is that [the rule] *alo'ntyasya* applies.
"Ṭhu: Purūravas is the son of Budha and also a royal sage (rājarṣi)," according to Amara;
[the suffix] śit is applied extensively to the root *cakṣ*.

The suffix *asi* is frequently applied after the root *cakṣiṅ*, which means "to speak clearly. This means that the suffix *asi* occurs after this root, and it is frequently marked with the *śit* designation. Thus, in the word *nṛcakṣāḥ*: when the word *nṛ* is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the root *cakṣiṅ* takes the suffix *asi*. Because that suffix is marked with *śit*, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* affix; therefore, for the root *cakṣiṅ*— [the substitution of *khyā* does not take place].
In the case of *khyāñ*, there is no substitution by *khyāñ*;
[the suffix] *uṣ* is *kit*.

From the root *uṣ* (meaning "to burn"), the suffix *asi* occurs, and that [suffix] is marked with *k*. Thus, *uṣ-as*. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. As Amara states: "Pratyūṣa, ahar-mukha, kalya, uṣas, and pratyuṣas are synonyms for dawn.
From the root *dam*, the suffix *unas* occurs.
*Damunasiḥ*: the meaning is that the suffix *unasi* is added to the root *dam*, which signifies "to subdue" (*upaśame*).
Amara states: "The seven-rayed one, the subduer (*damunāḥ*), is Śukra. [The form] *aṃhasi* is derived from the root *aṅh* with the suffix *asi* and the augment *ir*.

Regarding *aṅgatiḥ*, there is the suffix *asi* and the augment *iruṭ*. This means that from the root *agi*, the suffix *asi* is applied along with the augment *iruṭ*. *Aṅgiras* is a particular sage (*ṛṣi*).
[Also,] from the root *sṛ* preceded by the prefix *apa*, the suffix *asi* is applied.

The suffix *asi* follows the root *sṛ* preceded by *ap*. The meaning is that the suffix *asi* is added to the root *sṛ* (meaning "to go") when preceded by *ap*. Thus, *apsarāḥ*; in the formation of this word, when the suffix *asi* is applied, there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowel of the root.
[The suffix *viśva* is added] after the roots *vid* and *bhuj*.

[The suffix] *asi* is applied after the roots *vid* and *bhuj* when the word *viśva* is used as an upapada. *Vid* means "to know," and *bhuj* means "to protect" and "to eat. When the word *viśva* is present as an upapada for these two roots, the suffix *asi* occurs. In the rule, because the word *viśve* refers to the specific form of the word itself and does not denote the general sense of "all," the substitution of *smin* for the locative ending does not take place. Thus, one who knows all (*viśvam vetti*) is called *viśvavedāḥ*.
The suffix *kanas* is applied after the root *vaś*.
The suffix *kanas* is applied after the root *vaś*. The meaning is that the suffix *kanas* is added to the root *vaś*, which means "to desire.

Regarding the term "vocalization" (*saṃprasāraṇa*): the intention is that it occurs because the suffix is marked with the letter *k* (indicating it is *kit*). Amara states: "Uśanas is the descendant of Bhṛgu, the sage.
Thus ends the fourth quarter in the *Uṇādi* [sūtras].
Now begins the fifth quarter:
*adi-bhuvo ḍutac*. (Pāṇini 3.2.174) [The suffix *ḍutac* is added after the verbal roots *ad* and *bhū* to form nouns denoting the agent.]

Now the fifth quarter. *Adi-bhuvo ḍutac*: the meaning is that from the root *bhū* (in the sense of "being") the suffix *ḍutac* is applied when the indeclinable *āt* (meaning "suddenly" or "unexpectedly") is the *upapada*. Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). Thus:
*adbhuta*.
The secret root.
*Gudherūmaḥ*: from the root *gudh* (to envelop), the suffix *ūma* is applied; thus, *godhūma*. Here, the *guṇa* substitution occurs because the penultimate vowel is light (*laghu*). *Maserūran*.
*Masūraṇ*: [The suffix] *uraṇ* is applied after the root *mas* in the sense of transformation (*pariṇāma*). The meaning is that the suffix *uraṇ* follows this [root].
Amara states: "The *masūraka*, *makuṣṭaka*, and *mayuṣṭaka* are synonyms for the lentil (*masūra*). (And [the suffix *uraṇ* is applied after the root] *sthā*, with the augment *kit*.)

The suffix *ki* is applied after the root *sthā* (meaning "to stop" or "to stand"). From this root, the suffix *kit* is added. Thus, *sthūra*. Because of the *kit* designation, there is elision of the final vowel (*ā*) of the root.
[Next: *ati* is added after the root *pāti*.
*pāter atiḥ*: the suffix *ati* occurs after the root *pā* (in the sense of "protection"). [The suffix] *ni* occurs after *vā*.
The suffix *ati* is applied after the root *vā*, meaning "to go" or "to smell," and it is marked with the *nit* designation;
this also applies to the root *ṛ*.
And from the root *ṛ* (meaning "to go"), the suffix *ati* is added, and it is marked as *nit*.
From the root *tṛh*, the suffix *kno* is added, and there is the elision of the *hal* (consonant).
From the root *tṛh* in the sense of "injuring," the suffix *kna* occurs, and there is the elision of the letter *h*. Thus, *tṛṇam* ("grass").
Because the suffix *kna* is marked with *k*, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening.
[The suffix] *ulac* occurs after the roots *vṛñ*, *luṭhi*, *tan*, and *taḍi*.

From the roots *vṛñ*, *luṭh*, *tan*, and *taḍ*, the suffix *ulac* is applied; the meaning is that after these roots, the root *taṇḍ* is substituted [for the original root]. (Regarding the rule *daṃseṣṭanau na ā ca*: from the root *daṃs*, the suffixes *ṭan* and *na* are applied, and the letter *ā* is substituted for the final letter).

The suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭana* are applied after the root *daṃś* (to bite), and there is also the substitution of *ā* for the *n* of the root. That is to say, from the root *daṃś*, which means "to serve" (*sevane*), the suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭana* occur, and the *n* of the root is replaced by *ā*. [This is the meaning of] *daṃśeśca*.
And from the root *daṃś* (to bite): from this root as well, the suffixes *ṭa* and *ṭan* may occur, and the letter *n* is replaced by *ā*.
Thus, *dāśa*. Amara states: "A fisherman is called *dāśa* or *dhīvara*. In both the preceding sūtra and this sūtra, the suffix *ṭan* is used so that the vowel of the root *vid* becomes udātta.
And thus ends the section on the sword.

The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied after the root *ciñ* (meaning "to collect") when *ud* is the upapada. Thus, [the form] *uccaiḥ*. Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*).
[The rule] *nau dīrghaśca* [states that] when *nau* is the upapada, there is also lengthening [of the vowel].

The word *nau* [is used] as an upapada, and there is lengthening of the vowel; the meaning is that when the root *ciñ* has *nau* as its upapada, the suffix *ḍṬasi* is applied, and there is lengthening of the vowel *i* situated in the prefix (*upasarga*).
Regarding *nīcaiḥ*: because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*).
After the root *ram*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of "restraint" (*dame*).

The meaning is: when *dama* (restraint) is to be expressed, the suffix *kta* occurs after the root *ram* (in the sense of "to sport") with *sa-* as the preceding word (*upapada*), and there is lengthening of the final vowel of the first member (*pūrvapada*). [The rule] begins with "kitvāt" (because of its being *kit*), according to the rule starting with "anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām."
The *pūñ* [augment] and also the short vowel [are inserted] after *ṇu*.

The word *puṇya* is derived from the root *pūñ*, meaning "to purify. From this root, the suffix *yat* is applied, the augment *ṇu* is inserted, and the vowel is shortened, resulting in *puṇyam*. According to Amara, "In the feminine, *puṇya* means *dharma* (merit/virtue).
Furthermore, from the root *sraṃs* (to fall), the suffix *śi* is applied, and the augment *kuṭ* is added, which is also treated as *kit*.

From the root *sraṃs* (in the sense of falling down), the suffix *śi* is applied, and *kuṭ* is added as an augment; *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu* mean "falling downwards. From this [root], the suffix *yat* is applied, and that is *kit*; *kuṭ* is its augment, and *śi* is the replacement for the entire verbal base (*sarvādeśa*). Thus, *śikyam*. Amarasimha states: "A carrying-pole and what hangs from it is called *śikya*; also *kāca* and *pādukā*."
The suffix *kyu* is applied after the root *ṛ*, and the vowel *u* is substituted for it.

*Arteḥ kyurucca*: The meaning is that for the root *ṛ* (in the sense of "going"), there is the suffix *kyu*, and the vowel *u* is substituted for the root's *ṛ*. Regarding *uraṇa*: there is the substitution of *u* (*utva*), followed by the replacement of *u* with *ra* (*raparatva*). Then, by the rule *ṭhyuvoranākāv*, the suffixes *-yu* and *-vu* are replaced by *-an* and *-aka* respectively; subsequently, by the rule *ṭhraṣābhyām*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs.
The rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2), however, serves as the justification for the application of this very sūtra;
[the roots] *hiṃs* (to injure) take the suffixes *īran*, *īrac*, and *u*.
*Hiṃs* forms *īrin* and *īrañ*. From the root *hiṃs* in the sense of "injury," the suffixes *īran* and *īrañ* occur;
there is a difference in accent.
*Udi dṛṇāte jalau* [is another rule].

The suffixes *ac* and *al* are applied after the root *dṛ* (meaning "to tear") when the prefix *ud-* is present; this means that the vowel *u* of the prefix *ud-* is elided. Thus, the form *udara* is derived. There is a difference between *ajalaḥ* and [the other forms] regarding the accent. Guṇa is substituted for the root vowel.
The augment *muṭ* is applied after a root ending in a *ḍit* suffix or the suffix *khan*.

The rule *ḍit-khaneḥ muṭ* follows from *aja-lā-v-iti*. The meaning is that for the root *khanu* (in the sense of "digging" or "tearing open"), the suffixes *ac* and *a* are applied, both of which are marked with the *ḍi*-diacritic (*ḍit*), and furthermore, the augment *muṭ* is added to the root. Regarding the word *mukham*: because the suffix is *ḍit*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*).
The suffix *san* follows the root *am*.

From the root *am*, meaning "to go" and so forth, the suffix *san* is applied; this is the meaning of *asa*. Regarding *asa*, Amarasimha states: "The shoulder is called *skandha*, *bhujaśiras*, or *as*; it is not feminine.
From the root *muh*, the suffix *kha* is applied, resulting in *mūrkha*.

From the root *muh*, [the suffix] *kha* is applied; for the root *muh* in the sense of "bewilderment," there is the suffix *kha* and the substitution of *mūr* for the root. From the root *nah*, there is the elision of the consonant *h*.
*naher halopaś ca*: from the root *ṇaha* (meaning "to bind"), there is the suffix *kha*, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ha*; this is the meaning. *śīṅo hrasvaś ca*.
The root *śīṅ* means "to sleep"; from this [root], the suffix *kha* is applied, and the meaning is that there is shortening of the verbal root. Thus, *śikhā*.
Because of the force of prescribing the short vowel, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
(*māṅ* with the suffix *ūkha*, and *may* is also substituted).
The suffix *ūkha* is applied after the root *māṅ* in the sense of measuring; the meaning is that the root undergoes the substitution of *maya*.
Regarding the term *mayūkha*, Amarasimha states: "The words *mayūkha*, *tviṣ*, *kiraṇa*, and *jvālā* denote rays, while *alī* and *bāṇa* denote bees and arrows, as well as *śilīmukha*."
The *phaga* [sign] is high for *kali* and *gali*.

The meaning is that after the roots *kala* (in the senses of counting or sound) and *gala* (in the sense of swallowing), the suffix *phak* is applied, and the vowel *a* is replaced by *u*. Regarding the word *gulpha*: Amarasimha states, "The two knots at its [the foot's] base are called *ghuṭikā* and *gulpha*."
After the root *spṛś*, the suffixes *svaṇ* and *śun* are applied, and there is also the substitution of *pṛ*.

From the root *spṛś* (meaning "to touch"), the suffixes *śvaṇ* and *śun* are applied, and the root is replaced by *pṛ*. Thus, from *spṛś* in the sense of contact, *śvaṇ* and *śun* occur, with the substitution of *pṛ* for the root. The word *pārśvam* ("side") is formed thus. Because *śvaṇ* has the marker *ṇ*, there is vṛddhi (vowel strengthening). From the root *śri* (meaning "to resort to" or "to serve"), the suffix *ḍuan* occurs before the word *śman*, which denotes the mouth. From *śriñ* in the sense of service, [the suffix *ḍuan* is applied] before the word *śman*.

The suffix *ḍu* is applied when [the word] *upapada* (an accompanying word) is present. Regarding *śmaśru*: there is elision of the *n* of *śman*, and because the suffix is marked with *ḍi*, there is elision of the vowel *i* of the root *śri*. As Amara states: "In its growth, *śmaśru* refers to the beard on a man's face.
Also, [the words] *aśva* and others [are formed similarly].
"And *aśva* and so forth" is the remainder [of the rule], meaning they are "irregularly formed" (*nipātyante*). Regarding *aśru*: from the root *aśū* (to pervade), the suffix *run* is applied.
[Also,] *janeṣṭan* with elision [of the final vowel].
The suffix *ṭan* is applied after the root *jan* (meaning "to appear" or "to be born"),
and there is elision (*lopa*) of the final *n* of the root. [By the rule] *ac*, the vowel *a* is substituted for that [final *n*], and the form becomes *jaṅghā*.
And [the suffix] *ac* is applied to that [root] *jan*, with the substitution of *jaṅghā*. He states the meaning of "to that" as "of *jan*" (*janeriti*).

The meaning is that the suffix *ac* is added to the root *jan*, and there is the substitution of *jaṅghā* for it. [The feminine suffix] *ṭāp* is applied by the rule "for roots beginning with *aj* and ending in *at*, *ṭāp*.
[The suffix *ac* is also applied] to the root *han* when referring to a part of the body, and there is reduplication.

Regarding the rule "after the root *han*, when a limb of the body is to be expressed": the meaning is that when a limb of the body is to be expressed, the suffix *ac* is added to the root *han*, and there is reduplication of the root. Thus, "jaghanam" [is formed]. The substitution of *gh* for *h* in *han* occurs by the rule "ṭhho hanteḥ," or alternatively by the rule "abhyāsācca. He states the definition from Amara: "the hindquarters are called *nitamba*."
The [suffix] *kli* and *raṇ* are added, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the letter *l*.

*kliśeran* [is formed] with *lopaśca*. The meaning is that from the root *kliśū* (in the sense of "to afflict"), the suffix *an* is applied and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *l*. *Phaleḥ* [is formed] with *it* and the substitution of *pa* for the initial [consonant].

"And for *phal* and *jā*, there is *pa*: the meaning is that after the root *phal* (in the sense of 'to bear fruit') when followed by the suffix *itac*, there is the substitution of the letter *pa* for the initial letter *pha*. Thus, *palitam*. According to Amara: 'Palita is the whiteness [of hair] due to old age.'"
The suffix *vun* is applied after [verbal roots] such as *kṛñ* when a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed.

*Vun* is added after *kṛñ* and other roots when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed. After roots such as *ḍukṛñ* (to do/make) in the sense of action, the suffix *vun* occurs when forming a name. Thus, *karakaḥ*. Here, the substitution of *ak* for the *yu* and *vu* suffixes applies (*ṭhyuvoranākāv*). According to Amarasimha, "A water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is also called *karaka*. [Similarly,] *kaṭakaḥ*: from the root *kaṭe* (in the sense of covering or protecting), this suffix *vun* is applied.

Regarding the term *kaṭaka*, Amara states: "The circle of the mountain slopes is called *kaṭaka*, and it is not feminine. Furthermore, there is a reversal of the initial and final sounds in the root *cīkayati*.

There is also the reversal of the initial and final [phonemes] of the root *cīk*. The meaning is that from the root *cīk*, used in the sense of "addressing" (*āmantraṇe*), the suffix *vun* occurs when forming a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*), and there is a reversal of the first and last letters of the verbal root. As Amara states: "Those bamboos which sound when stirred by the wind are called *kīcakas*. It also refers to a particular type of demon.
The final vowel of the word *cyoṣ* is replaced by *iC*, provided it is followed by a penultimate *u*.

[The suffix] *vun* is added after the roots *pac* (to cook) and *mac* (to grind), and there is the substitution of the vowel *i* for the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel. Thus, *pecaka*. When the vowel *i* is substituted for the penultimate, the form is established through the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel. [As it is said: "The word *pecaka* refers to an owl, the end of the trunk of an elephant, and the tip of its tail."
Thus says Amara:
"And after the root *jan*, [the suffix] *araṣṭha*."

And [the word] *jaṭhara*. From the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation," the suffix *ara* is applied, and the letter *ṭha* is substituted for the final part of the root. Amara states: "The word *jaṭhara* may also mean 'hard'.
[Furthermore, from the roots] *vac* and *man*, with the suffix *i* and the augment *cik*.
From the roots *vac* and *man*, with the suffix *ci*. From *vac* (meaning "to speak") and *man* (meaning "to know"), the suffix *ara-pratyaya* occurs, and that [suffix] is *cit*;
furthermore, the letter *ṭha* is substituted for the final [letter of the root].
(*ūrji dṛṇāter alacau pūrvapadāntalopaś ca*) [The suffixes] *ala* and *aca* occur after the root *dṛ* when preceded by *ūrj*, and there is elision of the final letter of the preceding member.

The suffix *lac* occurs after the roots *dṛṇāti* (in the sense of "strength") and *dṛ* (in the sense of "sound" and "tearing"), and there is elision of the final vowel of the preceding word. Thus, we have *ūrdara*. This form arises from the elision of the final vowel of the preceding word and the application of *guṇa* to the verbal root.
And *kṛdara* and others [are also irregular forms].

And *kṛdarādayaḥ*: these are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). Regarding *kṛdara*: it is the form derived from the root *dṛ* preceded by the indeclinable *kṛ*, with the suffix *āla*. Similarly, from the root *sṛ* preceded by *sṛ*, [the word] *sṛdara* is formed.
In the case of the root *han*, the letters at the beginning and end of the affixes *yu* and *na* are respectively treated as *gh* and *t*.

The suffix *yuan* occurs after the root *han*, which means "to kill" and "to go. From this root, *yuan* is added; and for the initial *ha* and the final *na*, there is a corresponding substitution of *gha* and *ra*, respectively.
(Also, the suffix *tun* occurs after the roots *krami*, *gami*, and *kṣami*, and there is a *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel.)
The suffix *tun* is added after the roots *kramu* (to step), *gamḷ* (to go), and *kṣamuṣ* (to endure),
and there is also *vṛddhi* [of the root vowel].
After the root *haryati*, the suffix *kan* is added with the augment *hirac*.

From the root *haryati* [is derived] *kanyan* with the suffix *hirac*. The meaning of *harya* is "motion" and "desire. From this [root], the suffix *kanyan* is applied, and the result is the meaning "gold" (*hiraca*). In the suffix *hirac*, the letter *c* is a *it*-marker (indicating that the preceding vowel is not subject to *guṇa*), and the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.
Thus, it becomes *hiraṇyam*. Because the suffix is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
The suffix *pāsa* is applied after the root *kṛ*.

The suffix *pāsa* is added after the root *kṛ*. The meaning is that the suffix *pāsa* is applied to the root *ḍukṛñ* (in the sense of "making"). Thus, *karpāsa* [is formed]; here, there is *guṇa* substitution for the verbal root. Furthermore, after the root *jan*, there is also the substitution of *ra*.

Regarding *jantu*: from the root *jan* (to be born), the suffix *tu* is applied and there is a substitution of the letter *ra* for the final [letter]. Thus, *jartu* is formed; here, the letter *na* is replaced by the letter *ra*. [From the root] *ūrṇoti*, [the suffix] *ḍa* is applied.

"From the root *ūrṇoti*, [the suffix] *ḍa* [is applied]. This means that the suffix *ḍap* is added to the root *ūrṇuñ* (meaning "to cover"). Because it is marked with the *ḍi*-indicator, there is elision of the suffix *ṭi*. According to Amara: "The word *ūrṇā* refers to the wool of sheep and the like, as well as to the curl between the eyebrows."
The suffix *ya* is applied after the root *dhā*, and there is also the augment *nuṭ*.

After the root *dhā*, the suffix *ya* is added, along with the augment *nuṭ*. [The root] *ḍudhāñ* means "to hold" and "to nourish"; from this root, the suffix *ya* is applied, and the augment *nuṭ* is added to it.
After the root *jṛ*, the suffix *krin* is added, and the letter *r* is replaced by *v*.

Regarding the rule *jīryateḥ krin raśca vaḥ*: the root *jṝ* (meaning "to decay" or "loss of vitality") takes the suffix *krin*, and the letter *r* of the root is replaced by *v*. Thus, the form *jivri* is derived; after applying the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the root according to *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*), and the substitution of *v* for *r*, this form is obtained. [Objection: But would not there be lengthening here by the rule *hali ca*?

Because [the objection] is difficult to ward off, he says: "by virtue of the rule *bāhulaka* (diversity). [The derivation is as follows: from the root *mavyati*, there is elision of *ya*, the substitution of *ma* for *m*, and the suffix *ap* with the augment *tuṭ*. Furthermore, the letter *l* is added.

Regarding *mavyate* with the suffix *yal*: the root *mavya*, meaning "to bind," takes the suffix *āla*; there is the augment *ap* and *tuṭ* for it, the elision (*lopa*) of *ya* from the root, and the substitution of *ma* for the final *va*—this is the meaning. Thus, the form *mamāpatāla* is produced.
The suffix *kīkin* is applied after the root *ṛji*.

The suffix *kīkan* is added after the root *ṛji*. From the root *ṛji* (meaning "to go"), the suffix *kīkan* occurs; thus we have *ṛjīka*. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. After the root *tan*, the suffix *ḍau* is added, and it is treated like *san* (the desiderative marker).

*Ḍauḥ* is added after *tan*, and it is treated like *san*. From the root *tan* (meaning "to expand"), the suffix *ḍau* is applied, and it functions as *san*. Thus, *titauḥ*. Because the suffix *ḍau* is treated like *san*, there is reduplication and the substitution of *i* for the abhyāsa vowel;
because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the *a* of the root. Guṇa is not applied due to the force of pronouncing the suffix separately as *ḍau*.
According to the Amarakośa: "Ṭhprasphoṭana, śūrpa, and cālanī are feminine; titau is masculine.
(The words) *arbhaka*, *pṛthuka*, and *pāka* denote [a child] in terms of age.
The words *arbhaka*, *pṛthuka*, and *pāka* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) in the sense of age. He explains the manner of their formation as follows:

from the root *ṛdh* (meaning "to increase"), the suffix *van* is applied; there is the substitution of *a* for the vowel, the change of *dh* to *bh*, and the *guṇa* strengthening of the light penultimate vowel. Regarding the word *pṛthuka*, he says: from the root *prath* (meaning "to spread" or "to become famous"). From *prath*, [the suffix *u* is added].

In *asmāt-kuk-aṇ*, the *ṛ* replaces the *r* by means of *saṃprasāraṇa*; because the suffix is *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. Regarding the word *pibateḥ*: the meaning is "from the root *pā* (to drink). Amara states: "A child (*pītaḥ*), *pākaḥ*, *arbhakaḥ*, and *ḍimbhaḥ* [are synonyms]; and *pṛthukaḥ* and *cipiṭa-arbhakaḥ* [are also synonyms]."
The words *avadya*, *avamādha*, *arvā*, and *repha* are used in the sense of "contemptible."

The words *avadya*, *avamādhama*, and *arvarepha* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*). He explains the very nature of these formations: [the word] *vader*. This means that from the root *vad* (to speak clearly), with the negative particle *nañ* as a prefix, the suffix *yat* is applied. [Regarding] *avateḥ*: [this refers to the root] *ava* (to protect, etc.). Regarding the word *adhama*, he says: "In the alternative where there is *va*, there is *dha*."

Regarding *arteriti*: the root *ṛ* means "to go. Regarding *riphateriti*: the root *ripha* is used in the sense of boasting and so forth; the meaning is that the suffix *apratyaya* is added to this. Amara states: "The words *nikṛṣṭa*, *pratikṛṣṭa*, *arvā*, *repha*, *yāpya*, *avama*, and *adhama* [all mean 'low']. Regarding *līrīṅ*: there is a short vowel and the suffix *puṭ* for the roots *lī* and *rī* in the senses of clinging and censuring, respectively. *Tau* (the suffixes *ta* and *ra*). *Śleṣaṇa* means "clinging" and *kutsana* means "censuring."

*līrīṅerhrasvaḥ*: from the roots *līṅ* (in the sense of "adhering") and *rīṅ* (in the sense of "flowing"), the suffixes *tap* and *rap* are respectively applied; there is the augment *puṭ* for that [suffix], and the root vowel becomes short—this is the meaning.
By the combination of the base and the suffix, [the forms] denote, respectively, "adhering" and "reproaching."

After the root *kliś*, when followed by the suffix *īyasun*, there is the substitution of *kan* for the penultimate vowel, the elision (*lopa*) of that vowel, and the substitution of *l* for the final consonant.

*kliśerīccopadhāyāḥ*: From the root *kliś* (meaning "to afflict"), the suffix *kan* is applied; there is the substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the elision of the letter *l*, and the augment *nām*. Thus, *kīnāśa*. Amara states: "In the masculine, *kīnāśa* refers to one who has reached the end of his actions. [The word] *cintyam* [is used here] precisely because of the force of the rule prescribing the substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel.
The meaning is that there will be no quality (*guṇa*).
[This is because] after the root *aś* (to reach), the suffix *varaṭ* is applied when the action is performed quickly.

Regarding the root *aś* in the sense of "quick action": from the root *aś* meaning "pervasion," the suffix *varaṭ* is applied, and there is the substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel, when a quick action is to be expressed. Thus, *īśvara*. For one who is entreated becomes capable of granting boons and the like quickly.
() They were fourfold.

From the root *cat*, meaning "to beg," the suffix *uran* is applied; the letter *a* in *uran* is for the sake of pronunciation, and the letter *n* is for the sake of the *it*-designation. Thus, we have *catvāraḥ*. [In this form,] the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *caturanaḍuhoḥ ām*.
[The suffix] *aran* occurs after *prātari*.

*Prātar* is derived from the root *at* with the prefix *pra*. From the root *at*, meaning "continuous movement," the suffix *aran* is applied. The vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. Thus, *prātar*. Because it is listed among the *svarādi* group, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
[Vārttika: After the word *amuṣya*, the augment *tuṭ* is also added.
And *ama* with the augment *tuṭ*. From the root *am*, meaning "to go" and so forth, the suffix *aran* shall be applied, and there shall be the augment *tuṭ* for that [suffix].
(From the root *dah*, there is elision of *go* and *da* becomes *na*).

*dahergo lopo daśca naḥ*: From the root *dah* (meaning "to reduce to ashes"), the suffix *g* is applied; the meaning is that there is elision of the final letter of the root, and the letter *d* is replaced by *n*. (*siceḥ saṃjñāyāṃ hanumau kaśca*): [The suffix *ka* is applied after the root *sic* when a name is being formed, and the letters *han* and *m* are substituted for it.]

After the root *sic* when used in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *kap* is added; for the root *ṣic*, meaning "to sprinkle," there shall be the substitution of *h* for its final letter, and the augment *num*.
After the root *ghrā*, preceded by *vi* or *āṅ*, the suffix *ci* is added in the sense of a genus (*jāti*).

The suffix *ka* is applied after the root *ghrā* (to smell) when the prefix *vi-āṅ* is present as an upasarga, provided that "a genus" (*jāti*) is to be expressed. Thus, from the root *ghrā* meaning "to perceive odor," the form *vyāghra* ("tiger") is derived. Because the suffix is *kit*, the rule *āto lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.64) applies, resulting in the elision of the long vowel *ā*.
And he struck Ghura.

*Ghura* and *ghora*. From the root *han*, meaning "to kill" or "to move," the suffix *ac* is applied, and the root is replaced by *ghur*. Regarding *ghoram*: the *guṇa* substitution occurs because the penultimate vowel is light (*laghu*).
[From the root] *kṣam*, there is also elision of the penultimate vowel.

*kṣamer upadhālopaś ca*: from the root *kṣamūṣ* (to endure), the suffix *ac* is applied, and there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root; such is the meaning. "Kṣmā, avanī, medinī, mahī" [are synonyms for earth], according to Amara. *tarateḥ ḍriḥ*.

From the root *tṛ* (meaning "to cross" or "to swim across"), the suffix *ḍri* is applied. Thus, *tri*. Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the *ṛ* vowel (*ṭilopa*). Since this [word] always ends in the plural number, he says: "three" (*trayaḥ*).
The absence of planets.

*Grahaṇī*. From the root *grah* (to seize), the suffix *ani* is applied, resulting in *grahaṇi*. The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *ṭhaṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi*. The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*.
Amara states: "Dysentery (*pravāhikā*) is *grahaṇī-ruj*."
The first chapter.
*Prathama*: From the root *pratha*, meaning "to become manifest," the suffix *amac* is applied; thus the form *prathama* is derived. Also from the root *cara*.

And [the suffix] *ara* after the root *car*. From the root *car*, meaning "to move" and "to eat," the suffix *amac* occurs. It would have been possible to formulate this as a single rule together with "after *prathi* and *car*" (*prathicaribhyām*).
[The suffix] *alac* after the root *maṅg*.

The root *magi* has the meaning "to go. The sense is that the suffix *alac* is applied to this root. Regarding the form *maṅgalam*: because the root is marked with the *it* indicatory letter (*idit*), the augment *num* is inserted. Amara states: "Śvaśreyasaṃ, śivam, bhadram, kalyāṇam, maṅgalam, and śubham [are synonyms for auspiciousness]. Thus ends the fifth section of the Uṇādi-sūtras.
Thus ends the section on the *uṇādi* suffixes in the *Bālamanoramā*.
Now, the section on secondary suffixes (*kṛdanta*).
(1) *uṇādayo bahulam* 3.3.1: The suffixes beginning with *uṇ* are applied diversely.

Now, the section on secondary suffixes (*kṛdanta*) is described. "The *uṇ* and other suffixes are applied diversely" (*uṇādayo bahulam*). This is the first rule of the third quarter of the third chapter. It begins with "in the sense of the present tense and when forming a name" (*vartamāne saṃjñāyāṃ ca*).

This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rules "the suffix *laṭ* is used for the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*) and "after the root *pu*, [the suffix *uṇ* is used] when forming a name" (*puvaḥ saṃjñāyām*).

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the word *anehas*, which is derived from the root *han* preceded by the negative particle *nañ* with the suffix *asi* and the substitution of *ah* for the root, refers exclusively to the present time.
Furthermore, in this context, the term "technical name" (*saṃjñā-śabda*) refers to conventional (*rūḍha*) words; this applies even to Vedic terms.

This is an illustration of words [formed by *uṇādi* suffixes]. For this very reason, the *vārttika*—"for that which arises from *naigama* and *rūḍhi* is truly correct"—and the *bhāṣya*—"Vedic words and *rūḍha* words are those ending in *uṇādi* suffixes"—are both consistent. And these *rūḍha* words, ending in *uṇādi* suffixes, are devoid of any meaning derived from their constituent parts (*avayavārtha*).

Generally, [words] are derived in the sense of the agent (kartari) by relying on the meaning of their constituent parts, even when such a meaning does not exist. Without stating "the *uṇādi* suffixes and others," he states the purpose of the mention of *bahulam* (in various ways): "some," etc. He explains that very point with "in names," and so forth. This verse is found in the Bhāṣya. In cases such as *ḍittha*, *ḍivittha*, and the like—
The forms of the verbal roots (*dhātu*) and their suffixes (*pratyaya*) should be inferred according to their occurrence.

One should recognize the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) by virtue of its function, such as the negation of the *guṇa* vowel substitution. In the word *anubandham*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "the prefix [ending in a short vowel] is lengthened before a suffix ending in *ghañ* when not referring to a human being. This refers to the *Uṇādi* treatise.
It must be taught. However, the meaning is that the rules beginning with *kṛ-vā-pā-jī-* in the sūtra are merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very mention of the word "optionally" (*bahulam*).
(2) They are also seen in the sense of the past (*bhūte*). 3.3.2.
They are also seen in the past tense; "the *tuṇ* suffixes and so forth" is the ellipsis. This mention of the past tense is made because the present tense is the governing topic (*adhikāra*).
The root *dṛś* (to see) is used for the sake of following actual usage. This sūtra is intended as an elaboration of the term *bahulam* (variously).

(3) *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* |3|3|3|. The meaning is that in the future tense, words such as *gamyā* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) with the suffix *ini*. Because of this irregular formation (*nipātana*), the augment *ṇit* does not apply here [in the case of *grāmaṃ gamī*].
The meaning is "about to go. *Prasthāyī* means "one who is about to set out" (*prasthāsyamāna*).

(4) *tumun-ṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* |3|3|10|. [The suffixes] *tumun* and *ṇvul* [are applied after a verbal root] when another action is intended as the purpose of that action. Regarding the phrase "when another action is intended": it refers to a verbal root whose activity has a subsequent action as its objective.

The meaning is "when [another word] follows as an *upapada*. The term "in the future" (*bhaviṣyati*) is understood from the previous context. In the case of the suffix *tumun*, the letter *n* is for the sake of pronunciation;

the letter *u* following the *m* is for the sake of articulation. In the case of the suffix *ṇvul*, the letters *ṇ* and *l* are elided. There is the substitution of *a* for the *v* of *vu*. Regarding the phrase "because it ends in *m*": because *tumun* ends in *m*, [the rule] "that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix having *e* or *ai* as its final vowel is indeclinable" (*kṛnmejantaḥ*) applies.

The meaning is that [the word *draṣṭum*] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Consequently, by the rule "the suffix *tumun* is used after an indeclinable to express the abstract action (*bhāva*)," the suffix *tumun* is applied here to denote the action. However, the suffix *ṇvul* is used only to denote the agent. Thus, in the phrase *kṛṣṇaṃ draṣṭum*, the genitive case is not applied by the rule "not [with words ending in] *loka*, indeclinables, etc. The meaning is: "going for the purpose of a future vision whose object is Kṛṣṇa. In this context...

The word *yāti* (he goes) is the subordinate element (*upapada*). Here, the fact that the act of seeing—the meaning of the verbal root to which the suffix *tumun* is attached—is not for its own sake (*anārthatva*) is either indicated (*dyotya*) or expressed (*vācya*) by the suffix *tumun*. Thus, "He goes as one who sees Kṛṣṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ darśako yāti*) means: "He goes for the purpose of seeing Kṛṣṇa, intending to see him."

In the case of *ṭhak* and *na*, the genitive case is not employed because of the rule "the sixth case is not used after a word ending in *ṭhak* or *na* when expressing the future or a debt. Now, one might object: "If the suffix *tumun* denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*), then even if suffixes such as *tṛc*—which are prescribed for the agent—are not applied in that context, why should suffixes like *tṛc* not apply to the agent in the domain of the suffix *ṇvul*? And it is not so.

It should be stated that by this *ṇvul* prescribed as a specific rule, *tṛc* and the other suffixes are superseded; however, because their supersession would be only optional according to the rule regarding "non-identical forms" (*vāsarūpa*), he says: "In this case.
Regarding the domain where a verb is used in the sense of an action [to express] another action, those [suffixes] which might optionally apply by the rule of non-identical forms—

The meaning is that the suffixes *tṛc* and others do not occur here. By the word "others" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of rules such as *nandi-grahi-pacādibhyo lyu-ṇi-nya-acah*. To the question "Why do *tṛc* and the others not occur here?", he says:
"Because of the mention of *ṇvul* again. This refers to the rule *ṇvul-tṛcau*, which applies to the agent in general time.

The meaning is this: since the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed when a verb denoting an action is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*) for the sake of another action, the fact that *ṇvul* is prescribed here once again indicates that other suffixes such as *tṛc* and so forth do not apply.
(5) *samānakartṛkeṣu tumun* 3.3.158. [This sūtra prescribes the suffix *tumun* after a verbal root when it denotes an action performed by the same agent as another action.]

Regarding the rule *samānakartṛkeṣu*: since the forms *tumun* and *ṇvul* are already established by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyām*, one might ask for what purpose this [present rule] exists. To this he says: "provided it does not denote an action" (*akriyārtha*). Regarding "in the case of verbs meaning 'to desire'" (*icchārtheṣu*): the intention is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "in the case of verbs meaning 'to desire,' the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ*" from a previous rule. Thus: *icchati bhoktum* ("he desires to eat"). Here...

In the expression *icchati*, although the desire (*icchā*), which is the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapada*), does not have "eating" as its intended object, the suffix *tumun* is still employed.
He states the purpose of including the term "meaning" (*artha*) in the rule *icchārtheṣu* by saying: "he desires (*vaṣṭi*) or he wishes (*vāñchati*).
Even though the root *vaś* is enumerated among the Vedic roots in the Dhātupāṭha, [the form] *vaṣṭi* is used according to the maxim "Bhāguri says *vaṣṭi*."
The sense is that because of the usage in the *vārttika*, there is also usage in common speech.

(6) *śakadhṛṣajñāglāghaṭarabhalabhakramasahārhāstyartheṣu tumun* [Pāṇini 3.4.65]. Regarding *śakadhṛṣa*: the rule *śakadhṛṣajña* is also for the purpose of cases where there is no verbal complement (*akriyopapada*). He is able (*śaknoti*).

Regarding "to eat" (*bhoktum*): here, the suffix *tumun* is used even though eating is not the intended purpose of the power (*śakti*). Similarly, examples such as "he dares," "he knows," "he is weary," "he exerts himself," "he begins," "he obtains," "he proceeds," "he strives," "he deserves," or "he is able to eat" (*dhṛṣṇoti*, *jānāti*, *glāyati*, *ghaṭate*, *ārabhate*, *labhate*, *kramate*, *utsahate*, *arhati*, *vā bhoktum*) should be cited. Regarding "only with the verb *as*" (*asti-naiva*): but not with others.
The meaning is "by means of Śaka and others. Why? To this he says: "Because of its immediate proximity" (*anantaratvāt*).
This means "because of its being contiguous" (*saṃnihitatvāt*).
(7) *Paryāpti-vacaneṣvalamartheṣu* |3|3|66|. [This sūtra applies] to words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*) in the sense of "being able to" (*alam*).

Regarding the term *paryāpta-vacane*: the explanation of *paryāpti* is "fullness" (*pūrṇatā*). The explanation of *alamartheṣu* is "in words expressing capability" (*sāmarthya-vacaneṣu*). The example is *paryāpto bhoktum*, which means "possessing no less than sufficient capability. He states the purpose of including the word *vacana* (word): [The result is that] the suffix does not apply in cases such as *paryāptam odanasya*, where the sense of fullness is understood from the context even without the use of a word expressing capability. Furthermore, the suffix does not apply when the word *paryāpta* itself is used in its primary sense of "one who has reached his limit," as in *paryāpto devadattaḥ śabdānuśāsane*, meaning "Devadatta has reached the limit [of his capacity] regarding the instruction on grammar. This is because the word *paryāpta* here denotes a person (*puruṣa*) rather than a word expressing capability. Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "equal to" (*tulya*), as in *paryāptaḥ kṣatriyo yoddhum*, meaning "the Kṣatriya is equal to fighting. This is because the word *paryāpta* here signifies equality (*tulyatva*) rather than capability. Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "sufficient for" (*alam-artha*), as in *paryāptam odanasya*, meaning "there is enough rice. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses sufficiency (*alam-artha*) rather than capability. Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "capable of" (*śakta*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is capable of killing Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses ability (*śakti*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "competent" (*kṣama*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is competent to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses competence (*kṣamatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "fit" (*ucita*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is fit to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses fitness (*ucitatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "proper" (*yukta*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is proper to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses propriety (*yuktatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "suitable" (*sadṛśa*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is suitable to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses suitability (*sādṛśya*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "appropriate" (*upayukta*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is appropriate to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses appropriateness (*upayuktatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "adequate" (*parimita*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is adequate to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses limitation (*parimitatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "measured" (*mātrā*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is measured [for the task] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses measurement (*mātrā*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "limited" (*paricchinna*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is limited [in capacity] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses limitation (*pariccheda*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "restricted" (*niyata*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is restricted [to this task] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses restriction (*niyatatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "fixed" (*sthira*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is fixed [in his resolve] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses fixity (*sthiratva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "certain" (*niścita*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is certain [to succeed] in killing Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses certainty (*niścitatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "ascertained" (*avadhārita*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is ascertained [to be able] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "determined" (*parikalpita*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is determined [to be able] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses determination (*parikalpana*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "conceived" (*saṃbhāvita*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is conceived [to be able] to kill Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses conception (*saṃbhāvanā*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "possible" (*śakya*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantuṃ yajñadattam*, meaning "Devadatta is possible [to kill] Yajñadatta. This is because the word *paryāpta* here expresses possibility (*śakyatva*) rather than capability (*sāmarthya*). Nor does it apply when the word *paryāpta* is used in the sense of "feasible" (*ghaṭamāna*), as in *paryāpto devadatto hantu

"Pravīṇa" and so forth; "alaṃ bhuktvā" (having eaten enough). Here, the sense is that *alam* has the meaning of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) and not the meaning of sufficiency (*paryāpti*). "Paryāptaṃ bhuṅkte" means he eats a great deal of food. Regarding "prabhūtatā," the word "of food" (*annasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

(8) *kāla-samaya-velāsu tumun* |3|4|167|. Regarding the rule *kāla-samaya-velāsu tumun*: this [sūtra] is intended to ensure the application [of the suffix] even when there is no verbal root (*akriyopapada*) as a subordinate element. Now, one might object: since only a few synonyms for "time" (*kāla*) are mentioned, would it not follow that in other cases—such as with words like *anehas* and so forth—the suffix would not apply? [The answer is: No, because the mention of these specific terms is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the suffix *tumun* is applied after verbal roots when used in connection with words signifying time, such as *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*. For example: *kālaḥ kartum*, *samayaḥ kartum*, *velā kartum*. This is taught so that the suffix may be applied even in the absence of a subordinate verb. However, since only a limited number of synonyms for time are explicitly listed, one might wonder whether it does not fail to apply to others, such as *anehas*. [This is not a fault, as the list is merely indicative. Thus ends the discussion.

Lest it be thought that [the suffix] would not occur when there is an *upapada*, he says: "the inclusion of synonyms. [The word] "it follows" means that it follows from the sūtra concerning *praiṣa* (command) and *atisarga* (permission). "The elements" refers to the five elements, earth and so forth;
"time cooks" means it brings about modifications such as increase and decrease—this is the report (*vārtā*).
The meaning is "the worldly course of events" (lokavṛtānta).

(9) *Bhāvavacanāś ca* | 3|3|11|. And those expressing a state (*bhāva*). [This refers to the rule] *kriyārthāyāṃ kriyāyām*, meaning "when there is an action for the sake of another action," as in "it will be."
And it follows [from the previous rule]. Since the formation would be established by the rule *bhāve ca* alone, he states the purpose of including the term *vacana* (mention):

"having taken over the heading *bhāve*. Having taken over the heading *bhāve*, those suffixes such as *ghañ* and others that are prescribed in a general manner will apply when there is a future time, provided that a verb denoting an action is present as an *upapada*.

The meaning is that [suffixes] are also combined with the *tumun* suffix even when it is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*). Nor should one suspect that this is established by the rule of "optionality of dissimilar forms" (*vāsarūpavidhi*), because it has been stated that "the rule of optionality of dissimilar forms does not apply in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and suffixes having the sense of *khala*. Now, [one might object] regarding the example "he goes for the sake of sacrifice" (*yāgāya yāti*):

Since the sacrifice (*yāga*) cannot be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), how can there be a dative case? Nor can it be a dative of purpose (*tādarthya-caturthī*), because that sense of "being for the sake of" is already obtained by the suffix itself. To this, he says: "After a word ending in a suffix having the sense of *tumun*... (Pāṇini 3.3.10). (10) *aṇ karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.12): [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a verbal root] when the object [of the action] is to be expressed.
And [the word] *akarmaṇi* (in the case of an intransitive verb). By the particle *ca*, [the phrase] *kriyārthāyāṃ kriyāyām* (when there is an action for the sake of another action) is conjoined.

Thus he says: "and when there is an action for the sake of another action. And so, according to the Bhāṣya, this [suffix] applies only when both conditions—namely, that there is an action for the sake of another action and that there is an object—are present, and not when either one alone is present.

This is clear. This suffix *aṇ* has the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "kṛt [suffixes] are used in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). Here, setting aside the rule "ṇvul and tṛc [are used after verbal roots]," the suffix *aṇ* is obtained by the general rule "uṇ is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇyuṇ*).
That [suffix *aṇ*] is [restricted] when a verb denoting an action performed for the sake of that [action] is present as an upapada.

The suffix *ṇvul* is prepared to set aside the rule "tumun-ṇvulau" (Pāṇini 3.3.10), which prescribes *ṇvul* as a specific injunction; however, it has already been stated that the rule of "non-similarity of form" (*asarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply here due to the force of the repeated prescription of *ṇvul*. This present rule for *aṇ* is intended to set aside that very *ṇvul*. Thus he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṇvul*."

The meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṇvul* suffix prescribed by the rule "ṭhtumunṇvulau". Thus, it is established that this prescription of *aṇ* serves as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the *aṇ* prescribed by "karmaṇyaṇ", which had been set aside by *ṇvul*.
Now, even if there is a counter-exception for the *aṇ* set aside by *ṇvul*, [one might ask] regarding the rule "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (*Pāṇini 3.2.3*).

The suffix *ka* would be unavoidable in the case of "kambalādayo vrajati," because the suffix *ka* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the object (*karman*), and because the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply due to their being similar in form. Nor should it be suspected that this specific rule for *aṇ* is also an exception to the suffix *ka*. It is not so.

This is not an original injunction (*apūrva-aṇ-vidhi*); rather, for the sake of brevity, the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* is here restated (*pratiprasūyate*). Furthermore, that *aṇ*—being prescribed as a general rule (*sāmānya-vihita*) by *karmaṇyaṇ*—is not an exception (*apavāda*) to the specific suffix *ka* prescribed by *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*; on the contrary, it is the suffix *ka* itself that is the exception to it.

Therefore, in the case of "kambhaladāyo vrajati" (one who goes to give a blanket), the suffix *ka* would apply, superseding both the *aṇ* prescribed for the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*) and the *ṇvul* prescribed by the rule "tumunṇvulau. To address this, he says:

"Because it is subsequent (*paratvāt*)," and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), examples such as "sāmago gurukulaṃ vrajati" (the singer of Sāman hymns goes to the teacher's house) are included.

The phrase "gāpoṣṭak" and so forth is a collective reference. The rule "aṇ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.2.1) recurs here. This consists of both a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) and a novel injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). Among these, by means of the counter-exception, the sublation of *aṇ* by *ṇvul* is removed. However, for the purpose of the novel injunction, [the sublation] of the *aṇ* belonging to the third pāda [is intended].

The meaning is that, because they are subsequent to the *kap* suffix situated in the second quarter [of the Pāṇinian system], the *ka*-type suffixes are superseded by this [rule regarding] *aṇ*. This is clear in the Bhāṣya. From here onwards—in the sūtras beginning with "ḷṛṭ śeṣe ca"—the phrase "when [another] action is for the sake of [that] action" (*kriyārthāyāṃ kriyāyām*) is no longer operative.
It should be understood that the phrase "it will be" (bhaviṣyati) follows [from the previous rule].
(11) *Pada-ruja-viśa-spṛśaḥ ghañ* | Pāṇini 3.3.16. [The roots] *pad*, *ruj*, *viś*, and *spṛś* take the suffix *ghañ*.

[The word] *pad* [is formed as] *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) only. [An example is] "he goes there" (*padyate'sau*). Here, because of the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) is also [intended as the agent].
The status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). From before the word *ajityataḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is governed.

(12) *sṛ sthire* [Pāṇini 3.3.17]. Regarding *sṛ sthire*: it is a form with an elided case-ending; that is to say, it has an elided ablative case (*luptapañcamīka*). In the sense of "stable" (*sthire*).

Regarding the term *kartarī*: the sense is that *sthire* is an adjective qualifying the agent (*kartṛ*), and not a subordinate word (*upapada*). Regarding *sarteḥ*: this includes both roots beginning with *bhū* (the first class) and those beginning with *hu* (the third class), and not only those beginning with *hu*, according to the explanation. Thus he says: "it flows," etc. Its masculine gender is due to its inclusion in the *ardharca* group.
And [the word] *klība* [is used]. For this very reason, *sthira* is not an upapada [in this context]. Regarding *vyādhi*:
the Vārttika is for the sake of expressing instability. Regarding *sāra* as strength: in the Bhāṣya, however, *khadirasāra* (the heartwood of the Khadira tree) is cited as an example of strength.

(13) *bhāve* |3|3|18|. Regarding *bhāve*: "Bhāva is bhāvanā, which is action (*kriyā*); and that [action], by virtue of being a verbal root (*dhātutvena*), is expressed by all verbal roots"—this is stated during the occasion of explaining the root text (*mūla*) beginning with these words. That which is expressed by all verbal roots...
Action in general and its specific instances, such as cooking and so forth, are denoted by verbal roots.

Among these, action in general is the meaning of the term *bhāva* (abstract state); it is expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), is incapable of connection with gender and number, and exists in a state of being accomplished (*sādhya*). However, that which is expressed by primary nominal suffixes (*kṛt*) is capable of connection with gender and number.

It has been explained at length that [the verbal root] enters the state of being accomplished (*siddhāvasthāpanna*), based on the Bhāṣya statement: "A state (*bhāva*) expressed by a *kṛt* suffix appears like a substance (*dravyavat*). He states this with the words beginning "having entered the state of being accomplished," and so forth. Regarding "the suffix *ghañ*":
the meaning is that this follows from the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] ending in "for *pada* and *ruj*."

(14) Regarding *raphuratisphulatyorghañi* [Pāṇini 6.1.47]: the phrase *ikaḥ kāśe* [6.1.48] applies because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *aluguttarapade* [6.3.1]. The word *dīrghaḥ* is understood from the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya* [6.3.111]. The word *upasargasya* [is understood from 6.3.122].

The word "in *ghañ*" is understood from the rule "when *ghañ* follows, provided it does not refer to a human being. Since the desired form is already established by that very rule, this [present rule] serves as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*). Thus he says: "only when ending in an *ik* vowel. The phrase "there would be lengthening" implies "in *ghañ*," which is the remainder of the context. Regarding the example *ācāmaḥ*: the point is that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "not after *ācam*" (*anācame*), there is no prohibition of *vṛddhi*.

Regarding the phrase *apāṇinīyam*: the sense is that the prohibition of *vṛddhi* [by Pāṇini 7.3.34], namely *nodātopadeśasya*, would apply. (15) *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.19). *Akartari* and *kārake* are specifications of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), and not an *upapada* (governing word), according to the commentary.
By the word *saṃjñā*, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is intended; by this, the example to be mentioned as "passion" (*rāga*) is consistent. (16) *Ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* | Pāṇini 6.4.27.

In the section on the elision of *n* under the rule *ṭhaniditām*, this sūtra follows after *rañjeśca*. Thus he says: "There shall be elision of *n* for the root *rañj*. This is a supplement to the sūtra. In the word *rāga*, the *j* is replaced by *g* according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*; once the elision of *n* has been performed, there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel.
The meaning is "the act of pleasing" or "the substance used for pleasing. Regarding the word *prāsa*:

from the root *asu* preceded by *pra*, meaning "to throw," the form *prāsa* is derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*) according to the rule *akartari ca*. Thus, *prāsa* is a specific type of weapon, so called because enemies are thrown down (*prāsyante*) or struck by it.
"Commonly" (*prāyika*)—this commentary is clear. Therefore, the intended meaning is that this *ghañ* suffix occurs even when not denoting a name (*asaṃjñāyām*) in certain instances.
He states this with the example "What is your gain? (*ko bhavataḥ*). Regarding "gain" (*lābha*), the *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The meaning is:
"What gain—that is, what acquisition in the form of obtaining gold and so forth—is obtained, i.e., has been accomplished? (*labdhaḥ* = *sampannaḥ*).
In the phrase *bhavate tv asya labdhaḥ*, because of the connection (*anvaya*) [of the word *asya*], there is a prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*.

Regarding the phrase *anuvartate*, the commentary itself is the only refuge [for clarification]. From the root *syandū* in the sense of "flowing," the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *akartari ca*; because of the absence of the markers *k* and *ṅ*, there is no elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti*.

It has been reached. Although the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is established there by the rule "syandeśca," nevertheless, once the elision of *n* has occurred, the *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*) would take place. To ensure both the elision of *n* and the absence of *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel, he says: "syadaḥ in the sense of speed. "Syadaḥ means velocity. This word is conventionally restricted (*rūḍha*) to the meaning of speed.

"Anywhere else" means in the word *prasravaṇa*. [The compound] *avoda-edha-udma* is a *dvandva* consisting of *avoda*, *edha*, *udma*, *praśratha*, and *himasratha*. Regarding *avoda*: the elision of the *n* is prescribed by rule (*nipātana*) when the suffix *ghañ* is applied. Once the elision of *n* has occurred, *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) applies; however, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not take place because of the rule "not when there is elision of a verbal root element" (*na dhātulope*).
Because of this prohibition [by Pāṇini]. Regarding *edha*: from the root *indhī* (meaning "to shine") with the suffix *ghañ*, there is the elision of *n*;

and setting aside the prohibition by the rule *na dhātulope*, *guṇa* is also applied as a *nipātana*. Regarding *odman*: from the root *und* with the *uṇādi* suffix *man*, the elision of *n* and *guṇa* are applied as *nipātanas*. Regarding *śrantheḥ*: [the same applies].
The remainder [of the rule] is: "after the root *sthā* preceded by *pra-* or *him-*, when the suffix *ghañ* is applied.

(17) *parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ* |3|3|20|. Regarding "when there is a designation of measure" (*parimāṇākhyāyām*): the word "*ghañ*" is supplied as the remainder. [This means that] after all verbal roots (*dhātu*), when not denoting the agent (*akartari*)...

The meaning is that when a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is to be expressed, the suffix *ghañ* occurs when the delimitation of the meaning of the suffix itself is to be understood. Now, one might ask:
since this is already established by the rule "after a root not ending in a consonant, provided the *kāraka* is other than the agent," for what purpose is this [present rule] stated?

To this he replies: "of *ac* and *ap*"—that is to say, for the purpose of setting aside the two suffixes *ac* and *ap* which will be taught in the rules "after *ther*, *ac*" and "after *ṛ* and *do*, *ap*."
The suffix *ghañ* [prescribed] by the rule "ṭhakartari ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.121) is superseded by those two [suffixes, *ap* and *a*,] because they are specifically prescribed for those cases;

or rather, the meaning is that the general rule of "non-identity of form" (*asarūpa*) does not apply here due to the identity of form. "A single *taṇḍulanicāya*"—it is called *nicāya* because it is gathered (*cīyate*) and collected (*saṅghīkriyate*) after being extracted (*niṣkṛṣya*); this refers to the object (*karman*) as the *kāraka*.

In the case of the word *vācya*, the suffix *ghañ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *thak*. The meaning is that a heap, which consists of an aggregate of rice-particles, is delimited as a single unit. Regarding the phrase "two *niṣpāva*s of winnowed rice":
a *niṣpāva* is a heap of rice and so forth, so called because it is "winnowed" (*niṣpūyate*), meaning it is purified by the removal of the husks.
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*); it is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for] *ap*. "Winnowing by means of a winnowing-basket" is *śūrpaniṣpāvaḥ*.

The compound is formed according to the rule "an agent or an instrument [is compounded] with a *kṛt*-suffix in various instances" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*). However, the duality [of the winnowing-baskets] relates to the act of winnowing only through the medium of the winnowing-basket; therefore, the duality of the winnowing-basket is implied (*ārthika*) rather than expressed (*śābda*), and thus the singular number is used.
This is without objection. He says this in the passage beginning with "śūrpeṣa" and so on. Regarding the two *kāra* suffixes:

that which is scattered (*kīryate*) or dispersed is a *kāra*, namely a heap of grain and the like. The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*), as an exception to [the rule for] *ap*.
Thus he says "here," etc. Nor is it the case that [the formation] is already established from any verbal root alone by virtue of the governing rule "dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.91).

One might suspect that the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is redundant; however, this is not so, because its purpose is to indicate that an exception (*apavāda*) based on the *prakṛti* (the base form) alone is sublated, whereas one based on the meaning (*artha*) is not. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *ekā tilocchratiḥ*.

[In this term,] *ucchritiḥ* means that which is raised (*ucchriyate*), i.e., made upright (*ūrdhvīkriyate*); it is a heap (*rāśi*) placed upwards (*ūrdhva*). This is used in the feminine gender in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The suffix *ktin* [is applied here]. And because it depends on the meaning (*arthāśrayatva*) and does not depend on the verbal root (*prakṛtyāśrayatva*), it is not superseded by this *ghañ*. However, it is clear in the *Bhāṣya* that the suffixes *ac* (from *therac*) and *ap* (from *ṭṛdora'p*)—which do depend on the verbal root—are indeed superseded. Regarding the rule *dārajārāv*: this is a *Vārttika*. [The roots are] *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*) and *jṛ*.

In the case of *vayohāni* (loss of youth), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to these two roots (*vayati* and *han*) when followed by the causative marker *ṇi*, in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The meaning is that the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇiluk*) takes precedence over the elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṇilopa*). Those who split (*dārayanti*) or cause the heart to melt (*vidrāyanti*) are called *dārāḥ*, i.e., wives. Amara states: "The word *dārāḥ* is used in the masculine and only in the plural. Here, *ghañ* is applied with the elision of *ṇi*, and the vowel increase (*vṛddhi*) dependent on the *ṇi*-affix occurs.
In the case of a *nivṛta* (non-causative) [denominative], the *vṛddhi* strengthening is based on the suffix *ghañ*. Thus it is said: "those who split are *dārāḥ*" (wives).
[The word] *jāraḥ* (an adulterer) means "one who ages" or "destroys the family. It is derived from the root *jṛ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by *ghañ*.
When *ṇic* is elided, because that elision is caused by what follows (*paranimittaka*), [the rule] "when there is something subsequent to an *ac*" (*acaḥ parasmin*) [applies].

Due to the status of being *sthānivadbhūta*, the *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening] dependent on the suffix *ghañ* would not occur. Nor should it be argued that the *vṛddhi* should simply be caused by the suffix *ṇi*; for if the suffix *ṇi* were applied according to the rule "the roots *janī*, *jṛṣ*, *knasu*, *rañj*, and those ending in *am* take *ṇi*," then by the rule "there is shortening of those [roots] marked with *mit*," a short vowel caused by *ṇi* would result. However, when there is *ṇilopa* (elision of *ṇi*), that [shortening] does not apply.

Because there is an absence of being caused by something else (*paranimittakatva*), there is an absence of the status of being "as if" (*sthānivadbhāva*); thus, there is no occasion for the short vowel (*hrasva*).

He says this: "one who causes to age is *jāra*" (*jarayati iti jāraḥ*). Regarding "paramour" (*upapati*): Amara states, "A paramour (*upapati*) and a lover (*jāra*) are synonyms. (18) [The rule] *iṅśca* 3.3.21.
"And *iṅ*. [The rule] "with the suffix *ghañ*" is a supplement to the previous rule. *Iṅ* means "to study," and it is invariably preceded by the prefix *adhi*.

The meaning is that from this root, when not denoting the agent (*akartari*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied. Since the result is already established by the rule "when not denoting the agent" (*akartari ca*), he says: "it is an exception to [the suffix] *ap*. This means it is an exception to the rule "after a vowel, *era*. [The word] "having approached" (*upetya*) means "having gone near."

The meaning is that one from whom [knowledge] is acquired and studied is an *upādhyāya*. The intention is that the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). The status of being an ablative is established by the rule "ākhyātopayoge" (Pāṇini 1.4.29). Regarding the term "āpāne":
the meaning is that there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the suffix *ghañ* after the root *iṅ* when the sense of the ablative case is to be expressed and the feminine gender is intended.

"Or, the suffix *ṅīṣ* may optionally follow that which ends in such [a word]"—this is a *vārttika*. The meaning is: "from a word ending in the suffix *ghañ* prescribed by the rule *ṭhapādāne striyām*. This very *vārttika*, which was read here, is presented in the root-text (*mūla*) under the section on feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), specifically in the rule *adhyāpikā yā tu svayameva tatra vā ṅīṣ*. Now, one might object:

If it is asked, "Since the rule *ṭh akartari ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.19) already establishes this, for what purpose is the prescription of *ghañ*?"— the answer is no; because of the statement in the Bhāṣya that "the sequential mention of *ṭha* and *ghañ* is for the sake of excluding the scope of *ac* and *ap*," the prescription of *ghañ* by *ṭh akartari ca* applies only when femininity (*strītva*) is to be expressed, as those two suffixes (*ac* and *ap*) would otherwise apply.

Regarding the rule *striyāṃ kti*n: since the suffix *ghañ* would not otherwise apply in the domain of *ktin* when feminine gender is intended, the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed by the rule *apādāne striyām*. The example *upādhyāyī* means "one from whose presence one studies after approaching.
Regarding *śṛ-vāyu-*, this is a Vārttika. The term *avibhaktikaḥ* means "having the fifth case ending elided."

The meaning is that the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *śṛ* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the wind (*vāyu*) and the object (*karman*) is color (*varṇa*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the suffix *ap*.
An example is "śāro vāyuḥ" (the wind that scatters). The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "those by which leaves, fruits, and so forth are scattered (*śīryante*).
