In *rūpakriyām*, the suffix *śa* is applied by the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca*. In *kṛtyām*, the suffix *kyap* is applied along with *tuk* by the word *ca* in the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca*.

In *kṛtim*, the suffix *ktin* is applied; it has already been stated that this is due to the word *ca* in the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca*. He provides examples for the sense of "narration" (*ākhyāna*)—namely, *sarvāṃ kārim* and so forth. Here too, [the same applies].

In the five [verses] beginning with "sarvāṃ kārīm," the words "sarvām" and "akārṣam" are to be construed together. Likewise for "gaṇim. Here too, the questions and answers—"Did you do it as you wished? and "I did it all"—are to be applied. From the root *gaṇ*, which ends in a short vowel, the suffix *ṇic* (of the curādi class) is added, followed by the suffix *iñ*.

There is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] because the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) takes the place of the elided portion (*allopasya*). Regarding *gaṇanām*: the suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "after roots ending in ṇi, ās, and śranth.

Here, however, the suffix *ktin* does not apply, because it is superseded by *yuc*. In *pacām*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied because the root is marked with *ṣ* (as in the rule "after roots marked with ṣ, bhī, etc."). In *ijyām*, the suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule "after *vraj* and *yaj*, in the sense of abstract state (*bhāve*)."
In *ṭhvacisvapī*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa*. In *iṣṭiḥ*, the suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *yaj*, and by the rule *vraśca*, the letter *ṣ* is substituted.
(104) *paryāyārhaṇotpattiṣu ṇvuc* [Pāṇini 3.3.111]. Regarding *paryāyārha*: the word *paryāya* is explained as *paripāṭī* (succession). Of that also...

The commentary says: "The sequence (*krama*). From the root *paṭ-* preceded by *pari-* in the sense of sequence, the suffix *iṇ* is applied in the feminine for the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *iṇajādibhyaḥ*. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. Regarding "worthy of honor" (*arhaṇam arhaḥ*), the intention is that the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). Regarding "among those things to be expressed" (*dyotyeṣu*), the intention is that the suffix is applied precisely in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).

Regarding the sequence, he gives the example *bhavata āsikā* ("your sitting"). The meaning is: first the act of sitting, then lying down, and then going ahead. Regarding what is due (*arha*), he gives the example *bhavān* ("you"). The rule *ṛṇeṭaḥ* indicates the example; the meaning is: "you owe the eating of sugarcane as a debt. [The rule] *utpatā*...

This indicates the example. Regarding "udapādi": the meaning is "it arose. [The form is derived] from the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *ut*, in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), in the *luṅ* tense; the suffix *ciṇ* is applied by the rule "after the root *pad*, when *ciṇ* follows in the *liṭ*, *luṅ*, and *lṛṅ* tenses" (*te padaḥ*).
(105) [The suffix] *ani* is used after the root *kruc* in the sense of reviling (*ākrośe*). Pāṇini 3.3.112.

In the case of *ākrośa* (insult), the suffix *ani* [is applied] with the negative particle *nañ*. The sense is that this is due to the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*). *Ajīvaniḥ* means "non-living" (*ajīvam*). *Aprayāṇiḥ* means "non-departure" (*aprayāṇam*). However, the suffix *ktin* does not occur here because it is superseded by *ani*; furthermore, there is no application of the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpa-vidhi*) for feminine nouns.
The intention is that, in certain instances following the *Vibhāṣā*, the suffix *kta* may occur. Thus ends the section on feminine formations (*stryadhikāra*).

*Kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*: The suffixes designated as *kṛtya*—namely those prescribed by the rule "the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-suffixes denote only those two [agent and object]" (*tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*)—are employed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). They are also used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The suffix *lyuṭ* is prescribed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Therefore, the meaning is that *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes may occur even in other senses.

[In the example] "snānīyaṃ cūrṇam" (powder for bathing), having taken it as established by the rule "the suffix *anīya* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*"), he gives an example with *lyuṭ*: "rājñā" (by the king). The intention is that here *lyuṭ* occurs in the sense of the object (*karmani*). [In the case of] "rājñaḥ," the suffix *kta* occurs in the neuter sense of an abstract action (*napuṃsake bhāve*).

This sūtra was already explained in the root [text] under the introduction to the sūtras as being "final" (*niṣṭhā*), by way of incidental discussion; however, it is presented here again because its turn has arrived. (106) *lyuṭ ca* 3.3.115.

"And *lyuṭ*. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), *kta* is also included. This applies only to the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Now, one might object: since the rule "in the neuter gender, in the sense of an abstract action, *kta* and *lyuṭ*" would already suffice, the division of the yoga (the separate rule) is useless. To this he says: "The yoga... [is for the sake of... The purpose is to ensure that only *lyuṭ* is carried forward into the subsequent sūtra, "also in the sense of the object when by means of which... (*karmaṇi ca yena*).

(107) And [the sixth case ending is used] for the object (*karman*) when, through contact with it, there is bodily pleasure for the agent. 3.3.116. "And for the object when [there is contact] by means of which": the word *saṃsparśa* ends in a *kṛt* suffix;

because of its connection with a *kṛt*-formed word, the sixth case ending is used for the object according to the rule "for the agent" (*kartuḥ*). The word *yena* takes the third case ending for the agent, because of the restrictive rule: "when both [agent and object] are eligible [to take the sixth case], [it is used] for the object."
"By which action" (yena karmaṇā): "of the body of the agent" (kartuḥ śarīrasya). The meaning is "of that which is delimited by a body.

Because the word *śarīra* belongs to the *ardharca* group, it can also be masculine; thus, the objection that "therefore it should have been [stated] as *kartṛṇām*" is refuted. "The suffix *lyuṭ* would occur": the remainder is "in the neuter, denoting the abstract state (*bhāve*)."

"By the preceding [rule]" means by the preceding sūtra, "lyuṭ ca. "Necessarily" means for the sake of forming an *upapada* compound; this is because that [compound] is obligatory. "The drinking of milk is happiness" means that it is the generator of happiness for one whose body is touched by the milk.

He states another example: "The eating of rice is happiness. He raises an objection: "In this case, it is from drinking," meaning that the happiness arises from drinking alone, and not from the act of touching;
the phrase "from eating" should also be understood in this way. Here he provides an illustration: "the anointing with sandalwood paste."

"By saying 'it is happiness'"—the sense is this: since there is no happiness in milk or rice by their very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), how can this serve as an example? He provides the resolution: "True. "Wherein there is contact"—wherein happiness exists by its very nature (*svarūpasat*).

The meaning is that there arises no perception of such an object characterized as contact (*saṃsparśa*). He states the conclusion with the words "where" (*yatra*): where there is pleasure through touch, such as the pleasure of sandalwood ointment;
or where there is pleasure from drinking preceded by contact, such as the drinking of milk.

In examples such as "sukham" (pleasure), the meaning is that this [suffix] applies in all such cases. [For instance: "The rising from the couch is pleasure. The point here is that there is no accompanying object (*karmopapada*). Regarding "of the fire-pit," the words "in the cold season" are to be supplied. In this case, there is no direct contact with the fire-pit.

The sense is that it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the suffix] *lyuṭ* being applied. Now, one might object: "In counter-examples such as ‘the rising of the cotton’ (*tūlakāyā utthānam*), the suffix *lyuṭ* would indeed be applicable by the preceding rule;
therefore, the mention of ‘in the objective case’ (*karmaṇi*) and so forth is redundant. To this, he says: "In the counter-examples... [This refers to cases where there is] no compound (*asamāsa*).
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that there is an absence of a *nitya* (obligatory) compound with an *upapada*. (108) *karaṇādhikaraṇayośca* | 3|3|117|.

"And in the case of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This is a specification of the meaning (*arthanirdeśa*), not an *upapada*, because of the [traditional] explanation (*vyākhyāna*).

Because it is subsequent, this [suffix] sublates *ajapa*. As it has been stated: "The suffixes *strī*, *khal*, and *na* [sublate] *ṭha* and *ac*; *khal* and *na* [sublate] the feminine suffix *striyāḥ* by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Regarding *idhmapravraścana*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of "that by which something is cut" (*pravṛścyate 'nena*).
The analysis (*vigraha*) is "the cutter of fuel-wood" (*idhmasya pravraścanaḥ*). Regarding *godohanī*: [it is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*].

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of "that in which something is milked" (*duhyate 'syām*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is "a cow-milking vessel" (*go-dohanī*). The phrase "the *khal* [suffix] comes before" is due to the [authoritative] commentary; this is the intended meaning.
(109) The suffix *gha* generally occurs when a masculine technical term (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed. Pāṇini 3.3.118.
In the masculine [the shortening occurs]. This applies specifically to the agent (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.

(110) *chāder ghe 'dvyupasargasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.96). [The sūtra is analyzed as: *chādeḥ ghe*, and *advyupasargasya* is a separate word. [The meaning is: "there shall be a short vowel. [This refers to] "there is shortening before *khac*" (*khaci hrasvaḥ*).

The meaning is that this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of that [rule]. The remainder [of the rule] is "of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root *chādi*, which is the base (*prakṛti*) of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)," because of the continued application of [the word] "of the penultimate *u*" (*ūdupadhāyāḥ*). By this, the view that the shortening applies only to the *ṇi* [suffix] and that its elision (*lopa*) does not occur due to the force of that [shortening] is refuted.

(111) *gocarasaṃcaravahavraja-vyajāpaṇanigamāśca* || 3|3|119 || [The word] *gocara*: Now, since [the formation of this word] is already established by the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.118), for what purpose is this [present rule]? To this he says: "of that which is to be stated [later] as *halaśca*" (Pāṇini 3.3.121). [The word] *ca* [in the sūtra] means "and *kaṣa*"; the intention is that this is based on the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
(112) *ave tṛstrorghañ* |3|3|120|. Regarding *ave tṛstror*: when the prefix *ava-* is present as an upapada, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *tṛ* and *stṛ*;

this generally occurs in the masculine gender when forming a technical name (*saṃjñā*). It is an exception to [the rule for] *ap*. This is because of the condition "in the masculine gender when forming a technical name."
The meaning is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to what has been prescribed by [the rule] *ghañ*.

(113) *halaśca* | 3.3.121 | *halaśca*. This is clear. [Examples: *adhyāya* [from the root *iṅ* preceded by *adhi*], *naya* [from the root *iṇ* preceded by *ni*], *utpāta* [from the root *pat* preceded by *ud*].

The roots *yudh* and *hṛ* preceded by *sam*, ending in the suffix *ghañ*, are irregularly formed (*nipātita*). This is an exception to the rule "in the masculine, when it is a technical name" (*puṃsi saṃjñāyām*) which prescribes the suffix *ap*. The meaning is that there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of this irregular formation to include *avahāra*, *ādhāra*, and *āvāya*, all of which end in *ghañ*.

(114) *udaṅko 'nudake* |3|3|123|. *udaṅkaḥ* [is formed] when not meaning "water. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *gha*. In *ghṛtodaṅkaḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* before the suffixes *ghi*, *ṇi*, and *yat* according to the rule *ṭhcajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*.

(115) *jālam ānāyaḥ* |3|3|124| The word *ānāyaḥ* [is derived from the root √*an*] when *jāla* (net) is to be expressed; that is to say, it is formed with the suffix *ghañ*. (116) *khano gha ca* |3|3|125| [The suffix *gha* is also applied after the root √*khan*].
"Khan-gha-ca: *gha* [is used] after the root *khan*; the meaning is that *ghañ* and *gha* [are the suffixes].

Now, one might object: "In this case, the designation *ghit* is useless, because since there is no *caj* (the letters *c* and *j*), the substitution of *kutva* cannot possibly occur. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The designation *ghit*... [as in] "from the root *bhaj*, *bhaga*."

The suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) because [the root] means "to be broken" (*bhajyate*). Regarding the word *pada*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that by which one goes" (*padyate gamyate anena*). Regarding the rule for the root *khan* (to dig): it is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of these four—*ḍa*, *ḍara*, *ika*, and *ikabaka*. *Ākha* is the form derived with the suffix *ḍa*; *ākhara* is the form derived with the suffix *ḍara*. In both cases, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs by virtue of the *ḍit* designation.
He gives an example with *ika*: *ākhanika*. He gives an example with *ikaka*: *ākhanikabaka*.
(117) *īṣadduḥsuṣukṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal* 3.3.126.

[The word] *īṣadduḥsuṣu* [is used]; [the word] *nivṛttam* [is understood]. The intention is that this is due to the explanatory commentary (*vyākhyāna*). In that case, [the suffix is applied] in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

Since the suffix *kṛt* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), he says: "of those two alone" (*tayoreva*). Here, *dur* connects only with the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*), whereas in the sense of non-difficulty (*akṛcchra*), *īṣat* and *su* connect [with it], by virtue of their semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).
He states this very point with the words beginning "in difficulty, difficult to perform," etc., ending with "it happens."

In the phrase "not in the world" (*ṭhna loke*), because the genitive case is prohibited, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent. Why [is it specified] "with difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) and so forth?

[Consider: *īṣatkāryam* ("an easy task"), which means "slight. Regarding *nimī-*: this refers to the roots *miñ* preceded by *ni*, the root *mīnāti*, and the root *līṅ*. [The rule applies] "optionally when *lyap* follows *mīnāti*, *minoti*, and *dīṅ*" (*mīnātiminotidīṅaṃ lyapi ca*).
The substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) that would otherwise apply by the rule "līyate" is prohibited in the case of the suffixes *khaL* and *niC*. He gives examples for *khaL*:
*īṣannimayaḥ*, etc. For the suffix *aN* (by the rule "herajaci"), he gives examples: *nimayaḥ*, etc.
(118) *upasargātkhal-ghañ-oḥ* | Pāṇini 7.1.67.

Regarding the rule *upasargāt khal-ghañ-oḥ*: the meaning is that the augment *num* is applied because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of both [the conditions] from *labheś-ca* and *idito num*. (119) *na sudurbhyāṃ kevalābhyām* | Pāṇini 7.1.68.

Regarding the rule *na sudurbhyām*: he explains the portion *ṭhkevalābhyām ṭam* as "when accompanied by another prefix" (*upasargāntarasahita*). In the examples *supralambhaḥ* and *atidurlambhaḥ*, because *su* and *dur* are accompanied by other prefixes, there is no prohibition of what was prescribed by the preceding rule. [The questioner asks: "How then [is the form *sudurlabhaḥ* derived]?"

The meaning is that because *sudūraḥ* is accompanied by another prefix (*upa*), the prohibition of *num* does not apply. He provides the solution: "when... (*yadā*). According to the rule "the word *su* is used in the sense of praise" (*svatī pūjāyām*), when these two are *karmapravacanīya*s in the sense of praise, they do not function as prefixes (*upasarga*s), and therefore [the prohibition of *num* does not apply].

The sense is that because [the word *su*] is accompanied by the prefix *dur*, there will be a prohibition [of the suffix]. It should also be understood that since *su* has the sense of "praise" (*pūjā*), it lacks the status of a prefix (*upasarga*); therefore, the application [of the rule] from the preceding sūtra does not occur there. [The sūtra] *kartṛkarmaṇośca* [is explained as follows]: *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* is in the locative case.

The term "upapadayoḥ" (in the case of two upapadas) is understood from the commentary. By the word "ca" (and), "īṣad-duḥ-su" is conjoined. In the expression "bhū-kṛñoḥ," the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. Thus he says:
"when the agent or the object, as well as words such as īṣat and others, are upapadas. In this regard:

The intended meaning is that both [the agent and the object] are combined as the governing condition (*upapada*) when either one of the two—agent or object—is present, along with any one of *īṣat*, *duḥ*, or *su*. It does not mean that each is a governing condition individually, according to the commentary (*vyākhyāna*) and because examples are given in the *Bhāṣya* in exactly that manner. "It is not desired" refers to the rule concerning the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*.
The meaning is that there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) between the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* and its application. Now, one might ask:

"When both a word denoting either the agent or the object and a word from the group beginning with *īṣat* are used as co-occurring adjuncts (*upapada*), how is their sequence determined? To this, he says: "the agent and the object."
"And so forth. The intention is that the examples are given in the Bhāṣya in exactly that manner. Regarding "cvyarthayoḥ" (in the two senses of cvi):

the meaning is "the state of becoming what one was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāva*). Regarding "bhūyate": this is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). Regarding "durāḍhyaṃbhavam": this is the suffix *khal* in the sense of the abstract action. Here, the word *dura*, as an upapada, is placed immediately before the root *bhū* without any intervening element.

The application [of the rule] is as follows: *durāḍhya-karaḥ* (one who makes difficult-to-wealthy). Here, *āḍhya* (wealthy) is the object (*karman*) serving as a subordinate word (*upapada*). The meaning is: "one who is made wealthy with difficulty. One should also infer examples such as *īṣadāḍhya-bhavaḥ* (becoming slightly wealthy). In this case, because *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su* are separated [from the following element], [the rule applies].
It should be understood that this [sūtra] is commenced because it was not obtained by the preceding sūtra.
(120) *āto yuc* | 3.3.128 | *āto yuc*. The phrase "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], because it is not marked with a svarita accent.

The meaning is that when words such as *īṣat* (slightly) and others, signifying difficulty (*kṛcchra*) or lack of difficulty (*akṛcchra*), are used as upapadas, the suffix *yuc* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ā*. The phrase "of those two alone" indicates that it occurs in both the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). The mention of *khal* is an exception (*apavāda*).
However, the rule of "optionality of dissimilar forms" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not apply here, because of the restriction: "In the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and the meanings of *khal*..."
Or rather, because it has been stated that "the rule of asarūpa [suffixes] does not apply. Regarding *duṣpāna*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ṭhidudupadheṣṭaḥ*.

Regarding "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*): this is a Vārtika following the rules *cchandasi gatyarthebhyaḥ* and *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*. It applies only after the prefixes *īṣat*, *dur*, and *su*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *khal*. Thus [it is said].

The suffixes [taught in this section] have the sense of *khal* (the *khal-artha* suffixes). (121) *Āvaśyaka-ādhamarṇyayoḥ ṇiniḥ* | Pāṇini 3.3.170. Regarding "necessity" (*āvaśyaka*) and "indebtedness" (*ādhamarṇya*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied. Since the rule *kartari kṛt* ("a *kṛt* suffix is used in the sense of the agent") still applies, [the suffix denotes the agent]. Thus, *avaśyaṃ-kārī* ("one who necessarily acts"). Here, *avaśyam* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
Regarding "śatandāyī": the genitive case is not used [here] because of the rule *ṭhakenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70).
(122) *kṛtyāśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.171): the phrase beginning with *kṛtyāśca* is clear.

(123) *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* ||3|3|174|| [The sūtra] *kticktau ca*. [The word] *āśiṣi* [is used]. The sense is that this is due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of [the condition] "in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi*) from the rule "*liṅloṭāv āśiṣi*" [Pāṇini 3.3.161]. [The example] *bhavatāt* is the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of benediction.
This is the explanation of the word *bhūti*. The suffix *ktic* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). [Regarding the rule] *na ktici dīrghaśca* 6.4.39:
"In *ktic*, there is no lengthening [of the vowel]. [The term] "of those that do not take *iṭ*" refers to [the rule] *anudāttopadeśa...* etc. (6.4.37).
The intention is that the rule from the *sūtra* [Pāṇini 1.2.18] applies here. Regarding the word *ranti*:

since the rule "śyukaḥ kitī" (Pāṇini 7.2.11) does not apply here, the augment *iṭ* is prohibited solely by the rule "titutre" (Pāṇini 7.2.9). However, in the case of *bhūti*, because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules], it is more appropriate that the rule "śyukaḥ kitī" itself applies.

(125) *sanaḥ ktici lopaścāsyānyatarasyām* | 6|4|45|. Regarding "of *san*" (*sanaḥ*): the meaning is that there is the substitution of long *ā* (*ātva*), because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyā't* [Pāṇini 6.4.41].

"And there is elision" (*lopaśca*). The remainder [of the rule] is "of the final *n*. He provides an example for the suffix *kta*: "The gods might give him" (*devā enaṃ deyāsuḥ*). This is the optative (*āśīr-liṅ*). "Devadatta" (*devadatta*)—here the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object by the rule "only of those two" (*tayoreva*). The prescription of *kta* is intended so that it may not be superseded by *ktic*; otherwise, the suffix *kta* would be set aside by the exception (*apavāda*) *ktic*.

[Otherwise, the rule] would be contradicted; however, it is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *praiṣātisarga* that the rule of non-identity of form (*asarūpavidhi*) applies only prior to [the rule] *striyāṃ ktin*.
(126) *alaṃkhalvoḥ pratiṣedhayoḥ prācāṃ ktvā* 3.4.18.

Regarding the rule *alaṃkhalvoḥ*: [it is stated] "the suffix *ktvā* should occur. This has the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), because of the statement "the indeclinable *kṛt*-suffixes denote the abstract action" (*avyayakṛto bhāve*).
And this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *tum-arthe seseṇa*. Now, one might object:
since the word "northerners" (*udīcām*) is mentioned in the subsequent rule *udīcāṃ māṅe vyatīhāre*, [does this not imply that the present rule does not apply to them?]

Since the requirement for [the suffix] *ni* is constant, the mention of "by the ancients" (*prācām*) would be redundant; therefore, he says: "The mention of 'by the ancients' is for the sake of honor. Nor should one suspect the application of the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vā'sarūpa*), because it has already been stated that this rule operates only prior to the sūtra "in the feminine, *ktin*" (*striyāṃ ktin*). As for the expression "enough with weeping," etc., however...
It is sufficient to say that [the objection] should be resolved by the inclusion of the word *bahula*. Having raised the doubt regarding the suffix *lyap* in a compound with an *upapada*, he says:

"By [the rule] *amaivāvyayena*. In the phrase "having given enough" (*alaṃ datvā*), the meaning is that there is nothing at all to be accomplished by giving. He causes one to remember the substitution of *ī* [for *ai*]: "by [the rule] *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām*. In the phrase "having indeed drunk" (*pītvā khalu*), [the sense is] by drinking.
The meaning is that there is no object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
(127) *udīcāṃ māṅe vyatīhāre* |3|4|19|.
[The word] *udīcām* [means] "of the Northerners"; *māṅe* [means] "after the root √mā"; *vyatīhāraḥ* is exchange, that is, mutual transfer. [This applies] when the agents are the same.
Having raised the objection regarding the establishment [of the rule] by the phrase "in the past time" (*pūrvakāle*), he says: "for the sake of [denoting] a time other than the past.
(128) *mayater id anyatarasyām* | 6|4|70|.
Regarding *mayater id anyatarasyām*: the word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over from the rule "optionally for another [root] beginning with a conjunct consonant" (*vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ*), and not...

The intention is that the term "lyapi" is understood as being carried over from the previous rule "lyapi. The example "apamitya yācate" (he asks for [it] after having borrowed) means that he asks for a cow in order to effect an exchange, thinking, "If you give me a cow, I will give you a buffalo. In this case, because the act of exchange does not precede the act of asking, [the rule does not apply].

The rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* does not apply here; on the contrary, since the act of begging (*yācanā*) occurs first, the suffix *ktvā* is applied after the root *yāc*. In a *gati-samāsa*, *ktvā* becomes *lyap*. [Thus we have] *itvam*, then *tuk*, resulting in *apamāya*. This is the form when *itvam* is absent. However, the substitution of *ī* by the rule *īdyati* does not occur, because of the prohibition [by *na*].
This is because of the prohibition [expressed by] "lyapi" (Pāṇini 6.1.41). Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of 'udīcām'":

by that [mention], the suffix *ktvā* after the root *meṅ* is obtained optionally; in its absence, since the root *yāc* denotes an action occurring prior in time, the suffix *ktvā* applies according to Pāṇini 3.4.21 (*samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*). This is the intended meaning.
(129) *parāvarayoge ca* |3|4|20|.

[The sūtra] *parāvarayoge ca*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "in the connection (*yoga*) of the remote (*para*) and the near (*avara*). The word *yoga* is connected with each [of the two]. Thus, it is understood that the suffix *ktvā* is used in the sense of connection with the remote and in the sense of connection with the near. With what is there a connection with the remote?

When there is an expectation as to what is joined [in the term] "yoga," it is understood that it is "of the lower" (avara). When there is an expectation as to with what the lower is joined, it is understood that it is "with the higher" (para). Thus he says: "by the higher, of the former";
this means "of the lower. For the words "higher" (para) and "lower" (avara) [are relative].

The suffix *ktvā* expresses that which occurs in a location either separated or not separated by a sequence [of time]. Since it is stated that "the indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes denote the abstract action (*bhāva*"), this suffix also has the sense of the abstract action alone.
He provides an example for its use with a word meaning "lower" (*avara*) in conjunction with another: *prāpya nadīṃ parvataḥ* ("having reached the river, the mountain").

This statement concerns the Vindhya mountain and the river Gaṅgā as they relate to one residing in the southern region from the Vindhya mountains. For the Gaṅgā lies precisely to the north of the Vindhya;
thus, for those situated in the southern region, the Gaṅgā is separated by the Vindhya unless they cross over it.

The connection of the Vindhya mountains—which are contiguous from the perspective of those in the southern region—with the Gaṅgā—which is separated from the perspective of those in the south—is understood. Thus it is said: "Here there is a connection with another river. Now, he provides an example of the connection of one thing with another by means of that which lies beyond: "Having crossed," etc.

The meaning is that for those of the South (Dākṣiṇātyas), the Gaṅgā stands as something to be reached only by crossing the Vindhya mountains, which act as an intervention. Here, the connection of the Gaṅgā—which is separated from the perspective of the Southerners—by the Vindhya, which itself is not separated [from them], is understood. Thus he says:

Regarding "avaraparvata" and so forth: here, since there is no state of standing on the Vindhya mountains prior to the act of crossing, the application of the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrva-kāle* (Pāṇini 3.4.21) is not obtained.
(130) *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* Pāṇini 3.4.21.

Regarding *samānakartṛkayoḥ*: the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). The phrase *pūrvakāle* means "in the sense of a verbal root whose action occurs at an earlier time. [The word] *vidyamānā* [is understood from the previous rule].

The remainder [of the rule] is "ktvā syāt" (the suffix *ktvā* should occur). Because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) formation, this [suffix] expresses the sense of an action (*bhāva*). In the example "having eaten, he goes" (*bhuktvā vrajati*), the meaning is that the act of going occurs at a later time than the prior act of eating.
Regarding the mention of "duality" (*dvitvam*), the intention is that the requirement of two actions having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) is not intended to be strictly observed here.

Regarding the word *snātvā*: it means walking after the time of bathing, eating, and drinking. Here, although bathing and the other acts precede walking, the suffix *ktvā* is used [to express the sequence];
this is clear from the Bhāṣya. However, in the case of "he eats first, then he walks,"...

Since the state of being prior (*pūrvatva*) is already understood by the word *pūrva* itself, the suffix *ktvā* is not used according to the maxim "that which has already expressed its meaning should not be employed. However, in the expression "having first eaten, he then goes," there is no priority or posteriority between two actions; rather, it refers only to the agent—namely, having eaten before other eaters.

The meaning is that it follows after other [roots] that take the *bhoktṛ* suffix. Regarding the form *āsyate bhoktum*, however, the detailed explanation in the Bhāṣya and other works is that the present tense marker (*laṭ*) is applied here by the rule of optional non-homogeneity (*vā’sarūpa-vidhi*). He states this with the suffix *ktvā* added to the root *nam*:
"anudātetī" [referring to Pāṇini 1.3.12]. [This applies to the roots] *svarati*, *sūti*, *sūyati*, and *dhūñ*.

Having raised the objection that the rule *svarati-sūti-sūyatīnām* would cause the optional insertion of *iṭ* (by overriding the prohibition *ktvā-pratyayasya ṛt-śyukaḥ kitī*), he says: "Of *svarati* and the others.
This refers to the section on the rules for the insertion of *iṭ* beginning with *ārddhadhātukasya iṭ*, prior to the rule *neḍ vaśi*.

The point is that, by virtue of the commencement of the rule beginning with *kṛti* which prohibits *iṇ*, one must here rely on a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior contradiction) so that only the prohibition of *iṇ* by the rule *ṛd-śy-ukaḥ kit-i* takes effect.

(131) *ktvi skandi-ndoḥ* | 6|4|31| The meaning is that after the suffix *ktvā*, in the case of the roots *skand* and *nad*, the elision of *n* does not occur. This is because the word "elision of *n*" (*nalopa*) is understood from the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* [6.4.23], and the word "not" (*na*) is understood from the rule *nāñceḥ pūjāyām* [6.4.29]. Thus, the term *ktvi* [is used].
The word *ktvā* is the locative singular form [of the suffix]. The elision of the final vowel (*ā*) occurs due to the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), which is split as a separate *yogavibhāga*.
Regarding *skantvā*: this is the form of the root *skandir*. Since it is taught with an *anudātta* accent, the augment *iṭ* does not apply.
Regarding the root *syandū* with the suffix *ktvā*, he says: "Because it is marked with *ū*, the augment *iṭ* is optional."

(132) *na ktvā seṭ* | 1.2.18. "Is it not [the case that the suffix] *ktvā* [is] *seṭ*?"—this is the question. The sense is that this is an exception to the prohibition [of *iṭ*] stated in the rule *na ktvā seṭ*.

(134) *nopadhātthaphāntādvā* | 1|2|23 | The analysis of the compound is: "that which has *th* and *ph* as its final elements" (*thaphau antau yasya*). Since the rule *na ktvā seḍ* prescribes a permanent prohibition [of the *iṭ* augment], this present rule provides an option. When the *kit* designation applies, there is the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). In its absence, [the nasal remains].

But thinking "no," he says: "having loosened," and so forth; "having rotted" (*kothitvā*) and "having boasted" (*rephitvā*). [The roots] *kuth* is used in the sense of becoming putrid, and *ripha* in the senses of boasting, fighting, harming, and giving. Here, even the optional rule (*vikalpa*) "of a root ending in *ṛ*, having *y* or *v* as a penultimate letter" (*ṭhralo vyupadhād iti*) does not apply, due to the force of the inclusion of the term "penultimate" (*nopadhagrahaṇa*).

(135) *vañci-luñcy-ṛtaś-ca* | 1|2|24 | [The suffix *ktvā*] after the roots *vañci*, *luñci*, and *ṛti* [is optionally *kit*]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *na ktvā seṭ*. Due to the optionality of its being *kit*, there is an optionality regarding the elision of the nasal (*n*). He gives an example for *ṛti*: *ṛtitvā* and *artitvā*.
However, due to the optionality of the *kit* designation, there is an optionality regarding the prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate vowel.

The root *ṛti* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "compassion. Since the rule *dhater īyaṅ* is optional in the domain of *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes, its absence allows for the optionality of the *kit* designation here.

(136) *tṛṣimṛṣikṛśeḥ kāśyapasya* | 1|2|25| [The suffixes] *san* and *ktvā* optionally take the augment *iṭ* after the roots *tṛṣ*, *mṛṣ*, and *kṛś*, according to the opinion of Kāśyapa. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *na ktvā seḍ*. Regarding the rule *ralaḥ*: after a root ending in a consonant (*hal*) that has either *u* or *i* as its penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), both *san* and *ktvā* optionally take the augment *iṭ* when they are *seṭ* (i.e., when they themselves have the augment *iṭ*).

The term *kit* has been explained previously. *Ral-pratyāhāraḥ* refers to the pratyāhāra consisting of the letters *r* and *l*. Regarding *vartitvā*: this is a form of the root *vṛt*, meaning "to turn" or "to exist. Regarding *eṣitvā*: this is a form of the root *iṣ*. Here, because the suffix begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), there is no optionality regarding its being *kit*; rather, by the rule *na ktvā seṭ*, it is invariably [not *kit*].

Because [the suffix] is marked with *k* (kit), there is no prohibition of the *guṇa* vowel. Since the roots *vas* and *kṣudh* are taught as having anudātta vowels, a prohibition of *iṭ* would have applied; therefore, he recalls the exception to that rule: "There is *iṭ* after *vas* and *kṣudh*" (*vasatikṣudhoriṭ*). Thus, we have *uṣitvā*; because [the suffix] is marked with *k* by the rule "after *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, etc. (*mṛḍamṛdeḥ kit*), [there is no *guṇa*].
In the case of *vañc*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vacisvapi-". In the case of *śās*, *vas*, etc., the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "śāsivasī-".
Regarding the root *añc*, since the option for the augment *iṭ* after a suffix with the marker *ud* would otherwise apply by the rule "udito vā", he states:
"of *añc* when meaning 'reverence'. However, in the sense of 'motion', because it is optionally augmented by *iṭ* according to the rule "udito vā," [the form *añcitvā* is established].

*Lubhitvā* and *lobhitvā*: the meaning is "having confounded. The root *lubh* [in the sense] of "deluding" belongs to the *tudādi* class. The commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "Deluding (*vimohana*) means confounding (*vyākulīkaraṇa*).
There is an option for the suffix *kit* by the rule *ralo vyupadhāt*. Regarding that, when there is an option for the suffix *iṅ* by the rule *tīṣasaheti*, he says:

Regarding the rule "lubho vimohane" (Pāṇini 7.2.54), the word "it" [referring to the augment *iṭ*] is understood from the preceding rule "nityam" (7.2.53). It has been explained previously that the augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *lubh* in the forms of the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā* when it means "delusion" (*vimohana*), but not when it means "greed" (*gārdhya*). As for the phrase "but in the case of non-delusion": when it means greed, since the augment *iṭ* is optional by the rule "tīṣasah" (7.2.48), the form *lubhitvā* also occurs.
The meaning is "desiring. The reading *lubdhvā* in the phrase *vimohane tu lubdhvā* is a corrupt reading.

(137) *jṛ-vraścyoḥ ktvi* | 6.4.18 | [The substitution of *īṭ* occurs] for the roots *jṛ* and *vraśc* before the suffix *ktvā*. Thus: *jarītvā*, *jaritvā*. [This is because of the rule] *ṛt-śyukaḥ kitī*.
When a prohibition would otherwise apply, this is a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Regarding *vṛtaḥ vā*, there is an optional lengthening of the *iṭ* augment.

In *vraścitvā*, although an option for *iṭ* arises because the root is marked with *ū*, the *iṭ* is obligatory. Due to the prohibition of the *kit* designation by the rule *na ktvā seṭ*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa*.

(138) *udito vā* | 7|2|56 | Regarding *udito vā*: the word *ktvaḥ* [is understood] because it is carried over from the preceding rule, *jṛvraścyoḥ*. This is an optional rule (*aprāptavibhāṣā*) concerning roots ending in *u*. He provides an example for the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is applied to the root *śam*:—

Regarding the form *śamitvā*: he states [the rule] for the absence of the augment *iṭ*—namely, *anunāsikasya...* [Pāṇini 6.4.15]. In the forms *dyaūtvā* and *devitvā*, because the root *div* is marked with the letter *u*, the augment *iṭ* is optional before the suffix *ktvā*. In the case where *iṭ* is absent, by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* [Pāṇini 6.4.19], the *v* is replaced by *ū*, and after the *i* is changed to a semivowel (*yaṇ*), the form *dyaūtvā* results. However, in the case where *iṭ* is present, by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* [Pāṇini 1.2.18], [the *k* of *ktvā* is not changed to *ṭ*].
The intention is that because *ktvā* is prohibited [from taking the augment *iṭ*], the *guṇa* substitution of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) applies.
(139) *kramaśca ktvi* | 6|4|18|.
The rule *kramaśca ktvi* [is explained as follows]: from the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*, the word *upadhāyāḥ* [is understood here].

The term *vibhāṣā* is carried over from the rule "ṭhtanotervibhāṣā," the term *dīrgha* (long vowel) from "ṭhḍhralope pūrvasya," and the mention of *jhal* from "ṭhanunāsika kvī. Thus he says: "of the penultimate [vowel] in *kram*, etc. Since the rule "anunāsikasya kvī" would otherwise apply invariably, this present rule provides an option.

Regarding *krāntvā*: since the root *kram* ends in the vowel *u*, there is an optional application of the augment *iṭ*. This is the form according to the alternative where the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is applied.

(140) *Jāntanaśāṃ vibhāṣā* [Pāṇini 6.4.32]: "Of those ending in *j*, *n*, and *naś*. From the rule *śrānnalopaḥ* [6.4.23], the phrase "elision of *n*" (*nalopaḥ*) is understood; and from the rule *ktvā*... [the context of the suffix *ktvā* follows].

The terms *skandi*, *syandi*, *arita*, and *ktvā* are understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of those ending in a *j*-sound," and so forth. *Bhaktvā*, *bhaṅktvā*: these are forms of the root *bhañj* (in the sense of "crushing"). *Raktvā*, *raṅktvā*: these are forms of the root *rañj* (in the sense of "coloring"). *Naṣṭvā*.

Regarding the word *naṣṭvā*, he says: *masji*. Regarding *tasya*: the meaning is that there is an optional elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* of the root *naś* by the rule *jāntanaśām*. Regarding *jhalādau*:
the meaning is that the optional elision of *n* according to the rule *jāntanaśāṃ vibhāṣā* applies when a *jhal* sound follows.

Regarding *añjitvā*: the sense is that because [the root] lacks the prefix *iṭ* and does not begin with a *jhal* consonant, there is no elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *jāntanaśām*. Regarding *pakṣe*: the meaning is that in the alternative case where *iṭ* is absent, there is the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel by the rule *janasanakhanām*, since [the root] begins with a *jhal* consonant. Regarding *ditvā*: this is from the root *do* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*).

*rūpam* (having become): this is the form of the root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarman*). *mitvā* (having measured): this is the form of the root *mā*. *sthitvā* (having stood): this is the form of the root *sthā*. Regarding the suffix *ktvā* after the root *dhā*, he says: *dadhāterhiḥ* ("for *dhā*, *hi*"). This refers to the substitution of *hi* for the root *hā* in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāga*) when followed by the suffix *ktvā*.
He demonstrates this: "And after the root *jahāti*, [the substitution of *hi* occurs] before the suffix *ktvā*. Thus, "having abandoned" (*hitvā*) means "having left" (*tyaktvā*).

Regarding the rule "after *jahāti*," since the form *jahāteḥ* is specified in the prescription for the substitution of *hi*, it refers to the root *o hāk tyāge* ("to abandon"), and not to *o hāṅ gatau* ("to go"). This is because of that [specific mention].

Regarding *bhṛñāmi*: because of the grammatical rule *jihāte*, there would be the substitution of *i* for *ā*. Regarding *jagdhvā*: when *jad-ktvā* is established, the substitution of *dha* occurs by the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*; then, by the rule *jharo jhari*, there is the optional elision of the original *dha*.

(141) *samāse 'nañpūrve ktvo lyap* [Pāṇini 7.1.37]. Regarding the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve*: since it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of compounds preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, it is understood that this refers to compounds where the preceding member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
Keeping this in mind, he says "indeclinable," etc. As for "the augment *tuG*": the intention is that it is applied by the rule *hrasvasya pitī* [Pāṇini 6.1.71].

Regarding *prakṛtyā*: the prefix *pra-* signifies excellence (*prakarṣe*). By the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, it forms a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) with a word ending in the suffix *ktvā*. In the example *paramakṛtvā*, the suffix *lyap* does not apply because there is no preceding indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the first member of the compound; this is the intended meaning. (142) *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.86.

"An operation caused by *ṣatva* or *tuk* is not established [with respect to what follows]. This sūtra was stated in the section on single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rules under the heading "ṭhekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ.
Consequently, the remainder of the phrase "asiddha" [in this context] refers to "ekādeśa. He states the resulting meaning:

"with respect to the rule for a single substitute (*ekādeśa-śāstrin*). Having rejected the non-establishment of the grammatical effect (*kāryāsiddhatva*), he maintains that it is indeed the non-establishment of the rule itself (*śāstrāsiddhatva*).

The intention is that this has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya. As for the form *osicat*: here, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is the *pūrvarūpa* [vowel] by the rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati. By the rule "the end and beginning are treated like the original," this substitute is considered to have the status of the latter part; thus, *osicat* becomes a word (*pada*). Consequently, because that *s* is not at the beginning of a word (*apadādi*), [the rule for doubling does not apply].
Since the prohibition by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* does not apply, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* would have occurred;

however, it does not take place because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). Due to this non-existence of the single substitute, in the form *ko 'sicat*, the *s* is separated from the *iṇ* [sound] by the vowel *a*.

Because of the absence of "otherness" (paratva). Thus he says: "In this case, there is no substitution of *ṣ*. Having provided an incidental example regarding the substitution of *ṣ*, where the status of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) as non-existent (*asiddha*) applies, he now provides an example regarding the application of the augment *tuk* after the root *lyap*:
"adhītya. The root √*iṅ* (meaning "study") is invariably preceded by the prefix *adhi*; from that [root], the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*.

Regarding the word *pretya*: from the root *i* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap*. Here, in both cases, because the substitution of a long vowel for two homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) and the substitution of *āṬ* for the *guṇa* vowel are considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules), the augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*. However, if the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) were not considered asiddha, there would be no short vowel [to trigger the rule], and thus the *tuk* would not occur. This is what he says:
Regarding the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71), there is the following: *vā lyapi* (6.4.38).
This [sūtra] follows after the rule *anudātopadeśavanatitanotyādīnām* (6.4.37).

The Sūtra says this: "anudāta... and so forth. The meaning is that for roots taught with an anudātta accent, such as *van* and *tan*, the elision of *na* (nalopa) may optionally occur before the suffix *lyap*, because they are designated as having an anudātta accent. The phrase "vyavasthitavibhāṣā" (restricted optionality) is used because of the [traditional] commentary; this is the intended sense.

"Of those ending in *m* or *n*, optionally" means that for the roots *gam*, *nam*, *ram*, and *yam*, the elision of *m* is optional. "Of those ending in *n*" means that for roots ending in *n*— specifically *man* and *han*, which are aniṭ (not taking the augment *iṭ*), as well as *van* and others—
the elision of *n* would be obligatory by the rule *ṭhān udāttopadeśe...* (Pāṇini 6.4.37).

The plural number in the rule *nāntā’niṭām* is intended to signify a multiplicity of applications. He provides examples of roots ending in *m*: *āgatya*. [This is derived from] *gam*, with the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) and the insertion of *tuk*.
*Praṇatya*. [This is derived from] *nam*, with the elision of the nasal in one alternative (*pakṣa*) and the insertion of *tuk*. *Vinamya*, *viratya*.

*Prayatya* and *prayaṃya* should also be cited as examples. He does not cite examples for the two ending in *-n*: *prahatya* and *pramatyeti*. In the case of the roots *han* and *man*, there is always elision of the nasal (*n*). *Pravatyeti*: in the root *van*, there is always elision of the nasal; then the *tuk* augment is added. *Vitatyeti*: in the root *tan*, there is always elision of the nasal; then the *tuk* augment is added. [As stated] in the Bhāṣya.
However, the sūtra "vā lyapi" is not seen [in the Aṣṭādhyāyī]. In the sūtra "anudātetaḥ," the vārtikas "anudātopadeśe 'nunāsikalopo lyapi ca" and "vā maḥ" are recited;
thus, when the suffix *lyap* follows, the elision of the nasal (n) occurs by the rule "anudātopadeśa... provided that the root is taught with an anudātta accent.

The meaning is "or" (*vā*) for those [roots] ending in the letter *m*. Now, keeping the example *prajagdhya* in mind, he recalls the rule for the substitution of *jagdhi*—namely, *ado jagdhir lyapi kiti*—"for the root *ad*, there is *jagdhi* when *lyap* follows, provided it is *kit*"—and states: *ado jagdhiḥ*. The vowel *i* is the substitute.

The purpose is for the sake of pronunciation. Now, one might object: in the form *vidhāya*, the substitution of *hi* [for *dhā*]—by the rule "of *dadhāti*, *hi*"—should apply. It cannot be argued that since that substitution is prescribed before an affix beginning with a *k*-sibilant (*kit*), how could it apply when the affix *lyap* is added, because the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not exist in a rule based on the letter *a*? [This objection is invalid.]
Even after [the substitution of] *lyap*,
it is difficult to prevent the occurrence of *dvirbhāva* (doubling) because it is *antaraṅga* (internal); likewise,
in the case of *pradāya*, the *it-tva* (the insertion of the augment *it*) prescribed for a *kit* suffix beginning with *t* would apply even after *lyap*.

Because it occurs earlier, it applies even before [the suffix] *lyap*. Similarly, in the case of *prakhanya*, the substitution of *ā*—governed by the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sanjhaloḥ*—which is conditioned by an affix beginning with a *jhal* sound, applies even before *lyap*.
Likewise, in the case of *dyatisyatimāsthām iti kitī*, the substitution of *i* applies even before *lyap*. And so on.

In the case of *āpṛcchya pradīvyet*, because [the root] begins with a consonant (*jhalādi*), the substitutions *śū* and *ūṭh* prescribed by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* would occur even before the substitution of *lyap*. Likewise, in the case of *pradīvyet*, the augment *iṭ* prescribed by the rule for roots beginning with a semivowel (*valādi*) would occur even before the substitution of *lyap*. Similarly, in the case of *pradīvyet*, the augment *iṭ* prescribed by the rule for roots beginning with a semivowel (*valādi*) would occur even before the substitution of *lyap*.
Anticipating the objection that [the substitution] would apply [too early], he says: "even the internal elements" (*antaraṅgān api*). To the question "Why is this so?", he replies:

"in the rule for *jagdhi*" (*jagdhividhau*). By the rule "for *ta* there is *jagdhi* when followed by a *kit* suffix," the substitution of *jagdhi* is already established even in the case of *prajagdhya*, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) prior to the application of the suffix *lyap*. Therefore, the mention of *lyap* [in the rule]...

This indicates the maxim: "An external rule (bahiraṅga) subverts even internal rules (antaraṅga). And thus, because the substitution of *lyap* is stronger than the internal substitution of *jha* (for *ghas*), once *lyap* has been applied, the condition of beginning with the letter *t*—which is the cause for the substitution of *jagdhi*—does not arise; therefore, in the rule prescribing *jagdhi*:

The intention is that the mention of *lyap* is purposeful. By the word "tena" (by that), the meaning is that [the following operations] do not occur when *lyap* follows: doubling (*dvitva*), substitution of *d* for *t*, substitution of *ā* for *i*, substitution of *i* for *u*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*), the substitution of *śū* and *ūṭh*, and the augment *iṭ*. (144) *na lyapi* 6.4.69.

The rule *na lyapi* applies; the phrase *ṭh-ghu-mā-sthā-gā-pā-jahāti-visām* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartate*), as is *idyati-īd-tyataḥ īt*. Thus he says: "when *lyap* follows," and so forth. *Dheḍ* is a demonstration of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). *Pradhāya*: the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti*. *Prapāya*: [from *pā*]; *nipīya* is from *pīṅ* in the sense of drinking.

The form *prasāya* is derived from the root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarman*). Regarding the root *lī*, he reminds us of the optional substitution of *ā* for the vowel before the suffix *lyap* (the gerundive suffix) by citing the rule:
*vibhāṣā līyateḥ*. As for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix:

from the root *ṛ* preceded by the prefix *ud*, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, there is Vṛddhi strengthening, followed by the replacement of the vowel with *ra* (*raparatva*), resulting in the form *utāri*.

The meaning is as follows: from the root *car* preceded by the prefix *vi*, with the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel, resulting in the form *vicārī*. From these two forms, after the suffix *ktvā* has been replaced by *lyap*, the *ṇi* is elided.
(Pāṇini 6.4.56): "When *lyap* follows, [the substitution of *guṇa* for the final vowel and the following vowel occurs] if the preceding syllable is light."

The word *lyapi* [is understood] from the rule *laghupūrvāt*; *ṇeḥ* is carried over from the rule *ṭhṇer aniṭi*, and *ayi* is carried over from the rule *ayāmanta-ālvāyyetviṣṇuṣu*. Thus he says: "from that which has a light (*laghu*) vowel as its predecessor. The analysis of the compound is: that from which a light vowel precedes.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision of *ṇi*. Regarding the form *vigaṇayya*: the root *gaṇ* meaning "to count" belongs to the *curādi* class; it is also listed in the *kathādi* group and ends in *a*. From this root, the suffix *ṇic* is added. By the rule *ato lopaḥ*, the final *a* is elided. When *lyap* replaces *ktvā*, the *ṇi* is replaced by *ay*. Regarding *prabebhidayya*: from the root *bhid*, the *yaṅ* suffix is added, followed by reduplication (*dvitva*). [The rule] *guṇo...* [applies].

When there is elision of *yaṅ*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by [Pāṇini 7.4.82]; then *jaś*-substitution; then elision of the *yakāra* by "the *hal* [portion] of *yasya*" [Pāṇini 6.4.49]; then elision of the *akāra* by "elision of *at*" [Pāṇini 6.4.48]; and when *lyap* replaces *ktvā*, the *ṇi*-affix is replaced by *ay*.
(146) *vibhāṣā''paḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.57].
*Vibhāṣā āpaḥ*. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) because the preceding [rule] does not apply due to the absence of a light vowel (*laghu*) preceding [the *āp*].
(147) *Kṣiyaḥ* | 6.4.59. *Kṣiyaḥ*. [The word] "in *lyap*" (*lyapi*) is supplied from the rule "after a root with a light vowel preceding it" (*lyapi laghupūrvāt*).
The word "dīrgha" (long vowel) also carries over from the rule "ṭhyupluvordīrghaśchandasī. Therefore, he says: "after the root kṣi, when the suffix lyap follows. (Pāṇini 6.1.41): *lyapi ca*.

Furthermore, the rule *veñaḥ* is understood [from the previous sūtra]. Also, from the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam*, the phrase *na saṃprasāraṇam* is understood. Thus he says: *veño lyapi*, etc.
In the form *pravāya*: [the root] *veñ* in the sense of "weaving" takes *lyap* in place of *ktvā*. [The rule] *ādeca...* [is applied].
In the case of *upadeśe*, there is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel]; here, however, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule *grahijyā*.
(149) *jaśca* | 6.1.42 | *jaśca*: the meaning is that there should be no *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root *jyā* when the suffix *lyap* follows. Thus, *prajyāya*. Here...
In the rule *ṭhgrahijyāvayīti*, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution).
[The word] *vyaḥ* [is understood]. The meaning is that there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* for the root *vyeñ* when followed by the suffix *lyap*. [As in] *upavyāya*. [This is from the root] *vyeñ*.

In the case of *saṃvaraṇa* (covering), when the suffix *lyap* follows the gerundive suffix *ktvā*, there is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel *u*] by the rule "ādeca upadeśe 'śiti. However, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel-contraction) does not occur here by the rule "grahijyāvayi.
(151) *Vibhāṣā pareḥ* | Pāṇini 6.1.44.

The rule *vibhāṣā pareḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.38) follows from *vyaḥ* (6.1.37), *lyapi* (6.1.39), and *saṃprasāraṇam* (6.1.15). Thus he says: *parervyeñaḥ*. When *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā* after the root *vyi* preceded by *pari*, and the semivowel *y* has undergone *saṃprasāraṇa* with the resulting *pūrvarūpa*, the form *pari vi ya* is established; regarding this, he says:

Regarding the word *tukam*: how so? At the very time of sleep there is the opening of the mouth, and at the very time of laughter there is the closing of the eyes. Thus, since the opening of the mouth and the closing of the eyes do not share the same temporal priority as sleep and laughter respectively, the objection is raised as to how the suffix *ktvā* can be applied here.

He explains: "In the case of yawning. Although yawning and closing the eyes occur at a time subsequent to sleep and laughter, and not prior to them, nevertheless, sleep and laughter [occur] both at a time subsequent to the arising of yawning and at a time subsequent to the arising of closing the eyes.
These two persist. In that regard,

although the opening of the eyes at the time of falling asleep and the closing of the eyes at the time of laughing lack the status of being preceded by sleep and laughter at that very same time, [they nevertheless occur].

The meaning is that the suffix *ktvā* is used because [the action of coming] occurs at a prior time relative to the laughter at one's own [previous] state, which persists until that [later] time. However, in passages such as "But having come to Me, O Kaunteya, there is no rebirth," the suffix is used so that the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) is not violated.
The word "of one who stands," etc., is to be supplied.
(152) *Ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.22):
"In the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), there is also the suffix *ṇamul*. This follows after [the rule] *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle*."

He states that [the suffix] *sūtam* [is used] in the following context: "In the preceding domain. Although the suffix *ktvā* is established by the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vā'sarūpa*), even under the view that this rule applies prior to the section on feminine formations—as was explained at length in the Bhāṣya on the *vā'sarūpa* sūtra regarding the prescription of *ktvā*—nevertheless...

In the rule *vibhāṣāgreprathame*, the particle *ca* is used to prescribe both [the *ktvā* suffix and the accusative case]. For in examples such as *agre bhojaṃ vrajati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta goes ahead to eat") and *agre bhuktvā* ("having eaten first"), the word *agra-* and so forth denote the priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*) of the eating performed by Devadatta in relation to the eating performed by Yajñadatta and others.
It is understood [as "having been awakened"], but not as having occurred prior to actions such as walking;

therefore, the suffix *ktvā*—governed by the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ*—"does not apply there. Nor is it appropriate to say that, by the rule *vibhāṣāgre*, an optional prescription applies there in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*).

"In the case of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), by means of the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), it is desired that only the rule *ṭhābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* (P. 3.4.22) should apply; this is the detailed explanation in the *Śabdenduśekhara*. Regarding 'reduplication' (*dvitva*): the remainder [of the sentence] is 'by means of the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*' (P. 8.1.4). Examples such as *smṛtvā-smṛtvā* [are formed]; [the suffix] *ṇamul* is applied."

The word "śivam" is supplied [from the previous context]. Regarding "pāyaṃpāyam": by the rule "āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ," the augment *yuk* is added; then, by the rule "vā dīrghaḥ," there is an option for lengthening. In the case of the root *gam* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) followed by the suffix *ṇamul*, when the shortening prescribed by "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" has been applied, there is an option for lengthening by the rule "ciṇṇamuloḥ. This is the meaning. As for the term "vyavasthita-": [it refers to a fixed or restricted application].
The intended meaning is "because of the explanation. Regarding the phrase "of that which is preceded by an upasarga," the meaning is "of that which has a prefix preceding it.
Anticipating the objection that there might be *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) in the root *jāgṛ* when followed by the suffix *ṇamul*, he says: "in *jāgra*.
[He further notes that] the same applies even to the causative (*ṇyanta*) form; thus, in the case of the root *jāgṛ* with the suffix *ṇiC*, the rule prevents *vṛddhi*.

The intention is that, by applying the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule "jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu" and by the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the form is simply "jāgara". (153) *na yadyanākāṅkṣe* 3.4.23.

"Not if there is no expectancy" means "if [the action] has been accomplished. This refers to the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul*. "In which" means: if that sentence in which the two verbal roots denoting the prior and posterior actions exist does not expect another sentence; that is, a sentence joined with two verbal roots denoting prior and posterior actions.

The phrase "if it does not require another sentence" means this much: regarding the word *yat*—which is an indeclinable (*avyaya*)—the meaning is "when he eats, after that he studies. The point is that this single sentence, consisting of the two verbal roots *bhuj* (to eat) and *paṭh* (to study), does not require another sentence.

The statement "that he goes after having eaten" consists of two verbal roots, *bhuj* (to eat) and *vraj* (to go). Therefore, it requires another sentence such as "he studies. The sense is that there is no prohibition [of the compound] in this case.

(154) *vibhāṣā'greprathamapūrveṣu* |3|4|24|. [The word] *vibhāṣā* [is used] with *agre*, *prathama*, and *pūrva*. *Agre*, *prathama*, and *pūrva*: this is a *dvandva* compound. *Agre* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), or it ends in *e* by virtue of a formal exception (*nipātana*). It does not carry over [from the previous rule]; this is clear from the *Bhāṣya*.

Regarding "firstly, eating": *prathamam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) [of the action]. Regarding "previously, eating": *pūrvam* is an adverbial modifier. Regarding "in the alternative" (*pakṣe*): since the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are indeclinables (*avyaya*), they denote the abstract action (*bhāva*). However, when there is a desire to express the agent (*kartṛvivakṣā*), then the *laṭ* (present) and other verbal suffixes are used.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Since the words *agra*, *prathama*, and *pūrva* serve as upapadas, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* would apply even in cases of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), because they are subsequent [in the order of rules]. To this he says: "By means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
The intention is that this is established through the traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).
(155) *karmaṇyākrośe kṛñaḥ khamuñ* [Pāṇini 3.4.25].

Regarding *karmaṇyākrośe*: considering that *karmaṇi* is the designation of the subordinate word (*upapada*) and *ākrośe* is the meaning to be expressed, he explains: "when *karman* is the subordinate word," and so forth. Since this is clear, it need not be further explained.

The sense is [the suffix *ṇamul*]. Regarding the form *coraṅkāram*: in this compound with an *upapada*, the augment *mum* is applied by the rule "after *ṛtu*, *dviṣat*, and those ending in a consonant" (*ṭharurdviṣajantasya*).

(156) *svādumi ṇamul* | Pāṇini 3.4.26. In the rule *svādumi ṇamul*, the term *svādumi* is taken as a reference to the meaning ("in the sense of 'tasting good'"), because of the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*). And thus:

In the rule *svādum-paryāye upapade*, the word *upapade* (as an upapada) is understood. From the preceding sūtra *karmaṇy-ākrośe*, the word *kṛñaḥ* (after the root *kṛ*) is carried over by *anuvṛtti*, but not *khamuñ*, because it is not *svarita*-accented. Consequently, from the rule *ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca*, the word *ṇamul* is carried over; [the phrase] *samānakartṛkayoḥ*...

And there is the rule *pūrvakālaṭa*. Regarding this, he says: "In the sense of 'delicious,' etc. Now, one might object that for the word *svādu*, the grammatical reference *svādau* alone would have been appropriate; to this he replies: "Of the word *svādu*. One might further object: why not let *khamuñ* alone be carried over here? And thus...

One might suspect that one should not even drink this [liquor] when it has become sweet (*svādu*). However, since the word ending in *cv-* (i.e., *svādu*) when applied to a feminine noun is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the suffix *mum* prescribed by the rule *ṭharurdviṣadajantasya mum* is difficult to obtain;

for in that rule prescribing *mum*, the term "not an indeclinable" (*an-avyayasya*) is understood from the preceding context. Consequently, one eats after having made what was not sweet into something sweet (*asvāduṃ svāduṃ kṛtvā bhuṅkte*).

In the case of *svāduṅkāraṃ bhuṅkte* as well, the suffix *mum* would not occur, because the *khi*-designation of *khamuñ* finds its scope in forms such as *coraṅkāram*. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening the vowel by the rule *ṭhcvau*. Therefore, the intention is that in the *ṇamul* suffix, the word *svādu* is prescribed with a final *m*.

He states the purpose of including the word *artha* [in the rule] as "for the sake of grasping the meaning of *svādu*," namely: *saṃpannaṅkāram*. Here, one should understand that the result of the nipātana (irregular formation) ending in *m* is the absence of the substitution of *ī* [for *u*], despite the existence of the rule *ṭhasya cvau*.
The phrase "synonyms of *svādu*" is used because such is seen in works such as the *Vṛtti*, etc.; this is the intended meaning.

"Or, by the rule of non-identity of form (vāsarūpa), there is also the suffix *ktvā*. Although it is established in the Bhāṣya that the rule of non-identity of form applies only prior to the rule "striyāṃ ktin," nevertheless, because there is a specific statement in that very Bhāṣya— "the mention of 'optionally' (*vāvacana*) regarding *ktvā*"— it follows that the rule of non-identity of form applies here specifically with respect to the *ktvā* suffix.

The meaning is that the suffix *ktvā* also occurs. Furthermore, another alternative view—that the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) applies both before and after the governing heading "in the feminine" (*striyām*)—is established in the *Bhāṣya* on that very point. On that view, the application of the *vāsarūpa* rule to *ktvā* is unimpeded; let this matter rest for now. Otherwise, it would be as follows.

Otherwise, [the forms] *evam*, *katham*, *ittham*—from this *dvandva* compound of these indeclinables, the locative plural is formed. The analysis of the term *siddhāprayoga* is: that *kṛñ* (the root √*kṛ*) for which there is non-usage (*aprayoga*), i.e., an absence of usage, is "one whose usage is established as non-existent" (*siddhāprayoga*). Thus he says: "in these, [the root] *kṛñ*," and so forth. Now, [an objection]:...
If the root *kṛ* (to do/make) is not employed, how is its meaning understood? And if there is no understanding of its meaning, for what purpose is its employment?
To this he says: "Because it would be purposeless" (*vyarthatvāt*). The sense is that it would be fruitless.
Even though the meaning is not intended to be expressed, its employment is for the sake of the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the suffix *ṇamul*.
The intention [of the author] is as follows: he shows that very point by stating, "the meaning is 'he eats in this manner'.

The intention is that [the rule] *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle* ("when two actions have the same agent, [the suffix -ktvā is used for the one occurring] at the earlier time") does not apply here because it is impossible [for the conditions to be met].
[The question] "Why [is it said] 'siddha'? means: what is the purpose of [the condition] "if there is non-usage of the established form"? [This is stated] in the Bhāṣya.

Having formulated it otherwise, the result is that the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to the root *kṛ* when these two words are used as upapadas, provided that *kṛ* is not actually employed [in its verbal form]. The analysis (*vigraha*) is "a reply characterized by envy" (*asūyayā prativacanam*). There is a compound according to the rule "the agent or instrument [is compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, diversely. Thus he says:
Regarding the word *asūyayā*:

(157) *karmaṇi dṛśividoḥ sākalye* |3|4|29|. [The commentary] says that *karmaṇi* is not an indication of meaning (*arthanirdeśa*), but rather [it means] "when *karman* is the upapada" (the subordinate word).

Thus, when a word denoting an object (*karman*) is used as an upapada, and the completeness (*sākalya*) of that object—which has become the object of the verbal root's meaning—is to be understood, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *dṛśi* and *vidi*; this is the established result. The rule "when two actions have the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the prior time" continues to apply here. Regarding the form *varayati*: the root *vṛ* (in the sense of *vara*) means "desire."

In the *cur*-class, the root *kath* ends in *a*. Due to the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel. Regarding *vid*: it means "he reveals," "he knows," "he obtains," or "he deliberates. [As the verse says: "In the sense of existence, one 'finds' (*vidyate*);
in the sense of knowledge, one 'discerns' (*vinde*); in the sense of deliberation, one 'discerns' (*vinde*); in the sense of attainment, one 'finds' (*vidante*) or 'obtains' (*vindati*)."

It was stated previously that "this [substitution] occurs respectively before the affixes śyan, luk, śnam, and śeṣ. In that context, the root *vid* meaning "to exist" is not included here, because it is intransitive; this is the intended sense. (158) *yāvati vindajīvoḥ* 3.4.30.

The meaning is that when the word *yāvat* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is added to the roots *vid* and *jīv*. The phrase "that which occurs here before [the action]" (*ya iha pūrvakālaḥ*) is not connected [to these roots], because it is inappropriate and because it is not perceived [as applicable]. The same applies elsewhere. For example: *yāvajjīvam adhīte* ("He studies for as long as he lives"), meaning "for whatever duration of time he lives."

The meaning is that one studies for such a length of time. Because of the rule "in connection with intransitive roots" (*akarmaka-dhātubhiḥ*), the accusative case is used after the word *yāvat* due to its being a measure of time (*kāla*).
(159) *carmodarayoḥ pūreḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.31).

Regarding "carmodarayoḥ pūreḥ": the meaning is that when *carman* (skin) or *udara* (belly) are the objects (*karma*) in composition with the root *pṛ* (to fill), the suffix *ṇamul* is applied. For example: *carmapūraṃ stṛṇāti*, which means "he covers while filling the skin. Regarding *goṣpadapram*: when *ṇamul* is added to *pṛ*, after the elision of the causative marker *ṇi*, there is the option of eliding the long *ū*.
And [the word] *rūpa*. Here, by the phrase "capable of filling a cow’s footprint," the smallness of the rain is understood.
[The question] "Why [is it said] *asya*? means: for what purpose is the word *asya* used after the root *pūri*? [The answer is:
if the word *asya* were not stated, there would be elision of the vowel *ū* even when a word ending in *u* (such as *mūṣika*) is the upapada, as in *mūṣikābilapra*.
The intended meaning is "it may be so.

(160) *cele knopeḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.33]. Regarding *cele knopeḥ*: the term *cela* is taken here as a reference to the meaning [of the word], because of the [traditional] commentary; this is the intended meaning. [The root is] *knūyī*.

The term "śabda" belongs to the *bhvādi* class [of roots]. Thus he says: "celaknopam. He clarifies the meaning of the word *knopa* by saying: "śabdāyayan. In order to clarify the measure of the rain, he says: "yathā varṣaṇa."

(161) *nimūla-samūlayoḥ kaṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.34. The meaning is that when *nimūla* or *samūla* are used as the object (*karman*) in proximity (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *kaṣ*. He will state [this] in the rule: "In the case of *kaṣa* and others, there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) according to the specific rule."

The meaning is that he will state the subsequent application (anuprayoga) of the verbal root that serves as the base for the *ṇamul* suffix. "It is not connected" means that it is because of unsuitability and because it is not perceived; this is the intended sense.
He avoids the redundancy between the base of the *ṇamul* suffix and the verb being subsequently applied:

"Of even one" (*ekasyāpi*): this refers to the fact that "mere eradication" (*kevalakaṣaṇa*) is distinct from "eradication with root and all" (*nimūlasamūlakaṣaṇa*), just as *Indra* is [distinct from] *Mahendra*; such is the intended meaning. "By that, [the term] 'general'" (*sāmānya*): the understanding is that "eradication" consists of both "eradication with root and all" and "mere eradication," just as in cases such as *Mahādeva* being [identical to] *Devā* and so forth; such is the intended meaning.
(162) *piṣaḥ* [is used] with *śuṣka*, *cūrṇa*, and *rūkṣa*. 3.4.35.
Regarding *śuṣka-cūrṇa-rūkṣeṣu piṣaḥ*: [the word] "with [these as] objects" (*karmasu*) is understood; the remainder is "when these are the attendant words" (*upapadeṣu*).
In this case, there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the root *piṣ*.

(163) *samūlākṛtajīveṣu han-kṛñ-grahaḥ* |3|4|36|. [The compound] *samūlākṛta* is a *dvandva* of *samūla*, *akṛta*, and *jīva*. [The rule applies] when the object (*karman*) is expressed; that is, when *samūla* and the others are used as objects (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇamul* is added after the roots *han*, *kṛñ*, and *grah*. This is the meaning.

In this context, the correspondence [of meanings] is accepted according to their respective order. If the word *jīva* were formed with the suffix *ghañ* denoting a state (*bhāva*), its meaning would be "that which sustains life" (*prāṇadhāraṇa*), and not "that which grasps one who is living. To prevent this, he says: "It is called *jīva* because it lives (*jīvati*). But [one might object]: "According to the rule *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*, [the suffix *ghañ* is used when the agent is not the subject and it forms a name... [The author continues: ...[this objection does not apply here]. Therefore, he states: "It is called *jīva* because it lives. This is intended to show that the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, the word *jīva* is derived from the root *jīv* with the suffix *ghañ*; thus, the meaning is "that which lives," and not "that which sustains life. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the rule *akartari ca kārake*. Thus, the meaning is established as "that which lives. Therefore, the word *jīva* refers to the individual soul (*pudgala*) because it possesses the quality of living. This concludes the explanation. Now, regarding the term *sattva*: the word *sattva* is derived from the root *as* (to be) with the suffix *tva*. Its meaning is "existence" (*astitva*). It is called *sattva* because it exists. Alternatively, it is called *sattva* because it is the locus (*āśraya*) of existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the nature (*svabhāva*) of existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the manifestation (*vyañjana*) of existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the support (*ālambana*) of existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) existence. Or, it is called *sattva* because it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) existence. To explain how the suffix *ghañ* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) through exclusion (*paryudāsa*), he says: "after a root ending in *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* [the suffix *ka* is added]" (Pāṇini 3.1.135). [Regarding the rule] "After the root *han*, when it denotes an instrument" (3.4.37): "After the root *han*, when it denotes an instrument. But surely, immediately following this, there is the rule: "And after roots meaning 'to injure' (*hiṃsā*) that have the same object [as the agent]. (3.4.48)
Since this [result] is already established by the sūtra that is about to be stated, for what purpose is this [present rule]? To this he says: "yathāvidhi" and so forth.

The meaning is that this undertaking is for the sake of ensuring the obligatory compounding (nityasamāsa) by the rule "upapadam atiṅ," and for the sake of the subsequent application (anuprayoga) according to the specific rules regarding the roots *kaṣ* and others. It is for the purpose of subsequent application.

This means that it refers to the sense of a permanent compound (*nitya-samāsa*). Furthermore, the rule *hiṃsārthānāṃ ca* is situated outside the *kaṣādi* group; if that rule were to apply here, there would be no subsequent application of the verb (*anuprayoga*). Moreover, the rule *hiṃsārthānāṃ ca* is recited after the rule *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām*.

The sense is that if this [rule] were not operative, there would be an optional compound with an *upapada* by virtue of the rule "tṛtīyaprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām" (P. 2.2.21). However, in the Bhāṣya, it is established that [the present rule] is for the sake of excluding the meaning of "injury" (*ahiṃsā*) and for the sake of making the compound obligatory (*nityasamāsa*). If so, what then is the scope of the rule "hisārthānāṃ ca" (P. 3.4.48)? To this he says:

The word *bhinne* means: when there is a connection with another verbal root (*dhātvantara*) in relation to the root *han*, which serves as the base for the suffix *ṇamul*, then—as in the examples "he drives the cows by striking them with a staff" (*daṇḍopaghātaṃ gāḥ kālayati*) and "by striking with a staff" (*daṇḍenopaghātam*)—the application of the rule *hiṃsārthānāṃ ca* will be explained; such is the meaning.

(165) *snehane piṣaḥ* | P. 3.4.38. Regarding "in the sense of moistening" (*snehane*) for the root *piṣ*: [the example is] *udapeṣam*. In the rule *peṣaṃvāsavānadhaniṣu ca*, the word *udaka* is replaced by *uda*.

(166) *haste vartigrahoḥ* |3|4|39|. The word *haste* [in the rule] is in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) where the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is intended. The mention of *hasta* is a reference to its meaning, according to the explanation.

Thus, it is understood as "that which has the meaning of *hasta*" (*hastārthaka*). Since the term *karaṇe* ("as an instrument") is understood from the previous context, he says: "in the sense of *hasta*."

Regarding the rule *karaṇe*: the meaning is that when a word synonymous with "hand"—acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*)—is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *vṛt* and *grah* when they take the causative marker (*ṇic*). (167) *sve puṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.40.

"Regarding *sve puṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.4.41], the mention of *artha* is because of the [traditional] commentary; this is the intended meaning.
