By that [mention], the sense is that *ṇamul* is applied when the word *sva* itself, synonyms of *sva* such as *dhana* (wealth), and specific words denoting particular types of *sva* such as *go* (cow) are used as *upapadas*. And this..."

This is clear in the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra "rūpam". There, he gives an example with a reflexive word (*sva-śabda*) as an attendant word (*upapada*): *svapoṣam*. The meaning is "he nourishes by means of his own wealth. He gives an example with a synonym (*paryāya*) as an attendant word: *dhanapoṣam*. He gives an example with a specific attribute of the self (*sva-viśeṣa*) as an attendant word: *gopoṣam*.

(168) *Adhikaraṇe bandhaḥ* |3|4|41|. When a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *bandh*. (169) *Saṃjñāyām* |3|4|42|. [The suffix *ṇamul* is applied when the resulting form is] a name (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the term *saṃjñāyām* (in the sense of a name): this rule is commenced to cover cases where it does not denote a location (*anadhikaraṇārtha*).

(170) *kartror jīvapuruṣayor naśivahoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.43). [The word] *kartroḥ* [is used]; in the expression *naśivahoḥ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. When the agent (*kartṛ*) *jīva* is the subordinate word (*upapada*), [the suffix *kvip* is applied].
The meaning is that the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *vah* when *naś* is the agent and *puruṣa* is the attendant word (*upapada*).
(171) *ūrdhve śuṣipūroḥ* |3|4|44|. [The rule states: "After *śuṣ* and *pūr*, when *ūrdhva* is the agent. That is, when *ūrdhva* is the attendant word for the roots *śuṣ* and *pūr*.
The word "namuḷ" is the remainder [of the rule].

(172) *upamāne karmaṇi ca* |3|4|45|. [The commentary explains: "In the case of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); and because of the word 'ca' [in the sūtra], it means 'and in the case of the agent (*kartṛ*)'. Thus, when the standard of comparison is used as an *upapada*, [the suffix *namuḷ* is applied] both in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*)."
The meaning is that the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after a verbal root (*dhātu*).
(173) *Kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.46).

Regarding "after *kaṣa*" and so forth: the word "from which" (*yasmāt*) refers back to the rule [3.4.45], and "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is the understood remainder. It is stated that this applies when *ṇamul* has been prescribed.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "by the sūtras beginning with *nimūlasamūlayoḥ kaṣaḥ* and ending with *upamāne karmaṇi ca*. Likewise, it has been illustrated; the ellipsis is: "in examples such as *nimūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati*. And thus, the sense is that it need not be illustrated separately here.

(174) *upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām* |3|4|47|. [The word] *upadaṃśaḥ* is connected [to the previous sūtra]. [This is understood] by means of "leaping like a frog" (*maṇḍūkapluti*). When a word ending in the third case is the *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is added to the root *daṃś* preceded by *upa*, provided that both [actions] have the same agent.

The meaning is "in former times. Anticipating the objection that this might be a compulsory *upapada* compound, he says: "starting with the third case" (*tṛtīyā-prabhṛtīni*). Now, in the example "he eats with radish as a side-dish" (*mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*), since the radish (*mūlaka*) is the object (*karman*) in relation to the act of eating (*upadaṃśana*), how can there be a third case (*tṛtīyā*) after *mūlaka*, or how...?
Regarding the rule *upadaṃśanāṇṇamul* [Pāṇini 3.4.47], he says: "of that which is being chewed," and so forth.

The intention is that [the compound is formed] because it conforms to the principal action and because of its subsequent position. Now, one might object: if the radish (*mūlaka*) is the instrument with respect to the act of eating, then a compound would be impossible due to a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) with the act of chewing (*upadaṃśana*).

He raises an objection with the words "yadyapi" (even though): the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the radish (*mūlaka*) as the object (*karman*) with the relisher (*upadaṃśin*) is not conveyed by the words (*śabdagamya*), because it has already been stated that its connection is as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of eating (*bhujikriyā*). He resolves this with "tathāpi" (nevertheless).

The meaning is that although the radish (*mūlaka*), by virtue of the grammatical convention (*śābdamaryādā*), is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of eating, it nevertheless possesses a syntactic connection (*ārthika*) as the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of nibbling (*upadaṃśana*);
for, in reality, the status of being an object does exist for the radish with respect to the act of nibbling.

[An objection is raised: "But how can there be an instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*), or the suffix *ṇamul*, or a compound, if one takes the connection with the objecthood (*karmatva*) to be merely implied (*ārthika*)? To this, he says: "By this much alone. Why is this so? To this, he says: "In the case of the instrumental," [meaning] "by the force of the specific rule (*vacanasāmarthyāt*). This is because if there were a verbal connection (*śābdānvaya*) with that which ends in the instrumental case...

The intention is that if this were what was intended to be expressed here, then he would have simply said "in the sense of an instrument" (*karaṇe*), just as in the rule *hanaḥ karaṇe*. The connection of the radish (*mūlaka*) with the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*) as an instrument is explicit (*śābda*), whereas its connection with the act of biting (*upadaṃśa*) as an object (*karman*) is implicit (*ārthika*); he explains this by saying, "and therefore, the meaning is as follows."

The verbal syntactical connection (*śābda-anvaya*) is "he eats with a radish" (*mūlakena bhuṅkte*), because the third case ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*) applies due to its priority and its conformity to the principal action; this is the intended meaning. As for the question "having done what?":
the sense is that when there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) such as "having done what does he eat with a radish?", the word "having served" (*upadaśya*) connects [to that expectancy].

Regarding the phrase "tadeva" (that very same): when there is an expectancy as to what [is the object], the meaning is that "that very same root-meaning" follows as the object by implication. (175) *hiṃsārthānāṃ ca samānakarmakāṇām* 3.4.48. [The affix *ṇamul* is used after verbs denoting injury when they have the same object as the principal verb.]

And [this applies] to roots meaning "to injure. For example: *daṇḍopaghātaṃ gāḥ kālayati* ("He drives the cows, striking them with a stick"). The root *kala* (in *kālayati*) belongs to the curādigaṇa and means "to scatter" (*vikṣepe*). In this context, the cows are the object (*karman*) both of the auxiliary verb *kālayati* and of the verb *upahanti* ("strikes"). Therefore, the sense is that the verb *upahanti* has the same object as the other verb. [The compound] *daṇḍenopaghātam* [is explained as follows].

The meaning is that the rule "ṭhtṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām" provides an option for the *upapada* compound. In the example *daṇḍatāḍam*, the root *taḍa* meaning "to strike" belongs to the *curādi* class. (176) *saptamyāṃ copapīḍarudhakarṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 2.1.49. The sense is that by the rule "ṭhtṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām," there is an option regarding the formation of an *upapada* compound. In the example *daṇḍatāḍam*, the root *taḍa* meaning "to strike" belongs to the *curādi* group. (176) *saptamyāṃ copapīḍarudhakarṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 2.1.49.

And with the seventh [case ending], *upapīḍa* is conjoined with [the rule] "not after the third. The form *karṣa* is an indication [of the root] from the root *kṛṣ* meaning "to scratch," which has undergone the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) before the *śap* suffix; therefore, this excludes the root belonging to the *tudādigaṇa*. Of these—*pīḍa*, *rudha*, and *karṣa*—...
The nominative case is used here in the sense of the ablative due to a collective dvandva compound; the masculine gender is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
The term *upapūrva* is a madhyamapadalopisamāsa (elliptical compound) meaning "preceded by *upa*" in the context of the roots *pīḍ*, *rudh*, and *karṣ*. Thus he says: "from those preceded by *upa*.
He states this while considering the optionality of the *upapadasamāsa* (compound with a prefix) according to the rule *tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām*.

Regarding the expression *pārśvayor upapīḍam*: from the root *kṛṣ* belonging to the *tudādi* class, only the suffix *ktvā* is applicable, and not *ṇamul*. As in the examples "having ploughed the field, he sows the seeds" (*kṣetre upakṛṣya bījāny āvapati*) and "having ploughed with a plough" (*halenopakṛṣya*). Although the *tudādi* root also has the meaning of "scratching," it nevertheless applies only to scratching that pertains to a field.
They say that this [suffix] occurs after that which expresses its occurrence.
(177) *Samāsatau* | 3|4|50|. Regarding *samāsatau*, he explains the word *pada*: "when proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) is understood."
"Proximity" (*saṃnikarṣa*) means conjunction (*saṃyoga*) without any intervening space. Regarding the expression "by seizing the hair":

this refers to extreme proximity; the meaning is that they fight while being extremely close to one another. Thus he says: "due to the intensity of the battle. By virtue of the extraordinary nature of the combat, the warriors [stand] extremely close to one another.
The meaning is that they are present.
(178) *pramāṇe ca* |3|4|51|. Regarding the rule *pramāṇe ca*: [the suffix *ka* is applied] only in this way when the word ending in the third case or the seventh case is the *upapada*.
The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after a verbal root when a measure (*pramāṇa*) is to be understood; this is the meaning. [The vowel] becomes short. *Khaṇḍa-*—*khaṇḍikā*.

Regarding "by two fingers" (*dvyaṅgulena*), the intention is that the suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*. (179) *apādāne parīpsāyām* 3.4.52. [The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after a root when there is a sense of haste (*parīpsā*) regarding the point of departure (*apādāna*).]

Regarding the term *apādāna*: when *apādāna* is present as a governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇamul* shall be applied after a verbal root, provided that haste is understood; this is the meaning. To demonstrate this haste, he says: "In such a manner," and so forth.

(180) And also when a word ending in the second case is present [as an upapada]. (Pāṇini 3.4.53). The meaning is that the suffix *ṇamul* is added to a verbal root when a word ending in the second case is present as an upapada.
(181) When it refers to a non-permanent part of one's own body. (Pāṇini 3.4.54).
Thinking that the split is "svāṅge'dhruve" and "adhruve," he says: "adhruva. Now, one might ask:
how can "śira utkṣipya" (having raised the head) be a counter-example, since the head is also non-permanent (*adhruva*)? To this he replies: "yenāṅgena... (by whichever limb...).

(182) *parikliśyamāne ca* |3|4|55|. [The rule applies] when there is the word *parikliśyamāna*. Regarding *urovidāram*: the meaning is "the entire chest. Regarding *praticaskare*: from the root *kṛ* (in the sense of "scattering") preceded by *prati*, the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used in the passive sense. [The augment] *suṭ* is placed before the initial consonant [of the suffix].

With the continuation of the rule "even when there is intervention by *ṭha* or *abhyāsa*," the augment *suṭ* is applied by the rules "in the sense of cutting, after *kṛ*" and "after *prati*, in the sense of injury. The meaning is "he struck with his nails. Now, one might object that in examples such as "urasi pratipeṣaḥ" (crushing against the chest), the result is already established by the previous rule [Pāṇini 6.1.62] simply because it involves a body part (*svāṅga*); to this, he says:

Regarding the phrase *dhruvārtham*: the sense is that since there can be no life without the chest (*uraḥ*), the chest is "fixed" (*dhruva*). (183) *viśi-pati-pad-i-skandām vyāpyamānā-sevyamānayoḥ* |3|4|56|. [The rule applies] to the roots *viś*, *pat*, *pad*, and *skand* when they denote being pervaded or being repeatedly performed. Regarding *gehādi-dravyāṇām*: thus, in the case of *gehānupraveśam āste* ("he sits while entering the house"), [the rule applies].

The meaning is either "having entered all houses" or "having entered the house again and again. In both cases, there is no duality; thus he says, "but duality does not exist. To the question "Why?", he says, "precisely by means of the compound. [An objection: But how can there be a description here by means of a compound?

To address the [objection] regarding "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) and "repetition" (*āsevana*), he says: "by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). Now, one might object: since this is already established by the rule *ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca*, the inclusion of the term *āsevana* here is redundant.
Nor should it be suspected that the purpose is to exclude the suffix *ktvā*, for the suffix *ktvā* is also desired in certain cases.
He raises an objection with "yadyapi" (even though). He provides the resolution with "tathāpi" (nevertheless).

The meaning is that [the mention of] the second case-ending is for the purpose of establishing the designation of "upapada. Now, one might ask: even in the absence of the mention of "repeated practice" (*āsevā*) here, why does the designation of "upapada" not apply by the rule "tatropapadam"? To this he says: "asati hi" (for if it were absent...).

Although the suffix *ṇamul* is established even in the absence of a specific rule for *ṇamul* in the sense of "practice" (*āsevā*)— by virtue of the rule "the suffix *ṇamul* [is used] in the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*)"— nevertheless, because the word ending in the second case is not included in the rule "the suffix *ṇamul* [is used] in the sense of frequency" due to its being specified there by the seventh case, it would not receive the technical designation of "governing word" (*upapada*).

And therefore, the sense is that the optional *upapada* compound governed by the rule *tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām* would not be possible. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of a non-compound": in the case of the suffix *ṇamul* used in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is a doubling because the house (*geha*) is what is being pervaded; however, in the case of the suffix *ṇamul* used in the sense of habitual practice (*āsevā*), it belongs to the element ending in *ṇamul*.
The sense is that duality [of the action] arises because repetition (*pāunaḥpunya*) alone constitutes the state of being practiced (*āsevā*).
(184) *asyatitṛṣoḥ kriyāntare kāleṣu* |3|4|57|. Regarding *asyatitṛṣoḥ*: "having passed two days" (*dvyahātyāsam*) means "having elapsed two days."
The suffix *ṇamul* is added after the root *as* preceded by *ati-pūrva*. The example is *dvyahatarṣam*, which means "having caused [them] to be thirsty for two days.
(185) Pāṇini 3.4.58: *nāmnyādiśigrahoḥ*.

Regarding the rule *nāmnyādiśigrahoḥ*: the analysis is *nāmni ādiśigrahorati* (with a break after *nāmni*). The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*). The meaning is that when the word *nāman* ending in the accusative (*dvitīyānte*) is the *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *diś* preceded by *āṅ* and after the root *grah*.

(186) *avyaye 'yathābhipretākhyāne kṛñaḥ ktvāṇamulau* |3|4|59|. Regarding the sūtra *avyaye 'yathābhi-*: "unintended" (*anabhipreta*) refers to the speaking of what is unpleasant in a low voice and the speaking of what is pleasant in a loud voice; this is what is intended (*abhipreta*). The opposite of that is "not intended" (*anabhipreta*). Thus it is said:

"An expression not as intended," and so forth. Considering the optional compounding (samāsa-vikalpa) according to the rule "ṭhṛtīyā-prabhṛtīny anyatarasyām," he says: "having made high" (*uccaiḥ kṛtya*) and "having made high" (*uccaiḥ kṛtvā*). The intention is that when there is a compound, the suffix *lyap* is used. As for "in the manner of high" (*uccaiḥ kāram*), in this case there is no distinction between the presence or absence of the compound.
A specific rule: (187) *tiryacyapavarge* |3|4|60|.
Regarding *tiryacyapavarge*: it ought to be *tiraścī*; this is a Vedic-style (sautra) designation.
Commentary: The explanation of the term "apavarge" is "samāpte" (upon completion). (188) *svāṅge tas-pratyaye kṛ-bhv-oh* | 3|4|61|.
[The word] "svāṅge tas-pratyaye" [is used]; this is a statement of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). The suffix "tas" [is added].

The word *yasmāt* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The meaning is that the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are added after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū* when a word ending in the suffix *tasi* is used as an *upapada* denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*). Here, there is no correspondence between the order of the elements (*yathāsaṅkhya*), because of the [authoritative] commentary.

(189) *nādhārthapratyaye cvyarthe* 3.4.62. [The suffix *ṇamul* is added after the root *kṛ* when a word ending in a suffix having the sense of *nañ* or *ā* is used as an *upapada*, provided it has the sense of the suffix *cvī*.]

In the rule *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau na-saha-iti*, the suffix *na* is prescribed after the prefixes *vi-* and *na-* when there is no sense of "endurance" (*asahatva*). In the rule *saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*, the suffix *dhā* is prescribed;
that which has this very meaning [of distribution] is called *dhārtha*. Thus, there is the suffix *na* and the suffixes having the sense of *dhā*.

The term *yasmāt* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. This is what he states: "not when ending in a suffix having the sense of *dhā*. The meaning is: "when the *upapada* ends in a suffix having the sense of *dhā*, or ends in the suffix *na*. The inclusion of the word *artha* (sense) applies specifically to the suffixes having the sense of *dhā*; by this, the suffix *dhamuñ* is also included. However, in the case of the suffix *na*, the inclusion of the word *artha* does not apply.

The meaning is: when a word ending in a suffix denoting "state" (*dhā*) or a suffix denoting "purpose" (*artha*), or one in the domain of the *cv*-suffix, is the *upapada*. For this very reason, the Bhāṣya asks: "What is the purpose of including the term 'artha'? and it simply states: "having made two parts, *dvaidhaṅkṛtya*.
(190) *tūṣṇīmi bhuvaḥ* | Pāṇini 3.4.63.

[The word] *tūṣṇīm* [is used as an example for the suffix] *bhuvaḥ*. Now, one might object: "Is not the mention of *bhū* redundant? For the desired form would be established simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *svāṅge tas-pratyaye kṛ-bhv-asti-yoge*. To this he replies: "[The mention of *bhū* is] for the purpose of excluding *kṛñ*."

(191) *anvacyānulomye* |3|4|64|. Regarding *anvacyānulomye*: it would have been more appropriate to state simply *anūcī*. This is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) formulation, similar to *tiryacyapavarge*. *Ānulomyam* means conformity or favorability. [The suffix *kvi* is applied] after *anvac* when meaning "behind" (*pṛṣṭhataḥ*).

The word "having become" (*bhūtvā*) [is used] because in examples such as "the Adhvaryu follows, with Agni at the head," the word *anvak* is well-known to mean "in the rear. Thus ends the section on secondary derivatives (*kṛdanta*).
Thus [ends the chapter].

By the Adhvaryu priest of the illustrious Ānandarāya, the sovereign among scholars and preeminent minister to the imperial lords of the earth—the illustrious Śāhajī, Śarabhajī, Tukkojī Bhosale, and the Chola king—who presides over a magnificent and boundless great sacrifice (mahādhvara) that shines with many virtues such as the form of the serpent, the tortoise, and the sixteen-spoked chariot-wheel, and who has been nourished by five generations of ancestors since his very childhood; [by him was this work composed].

By him—who had gratified the gods headed by Indra with sacrifices such as the Vājapeya, Sarvapṛṣṭha, and Aptoryāma, which were performed through the manifestation of immeasurable fires kindled by his compassion; who was a Brahmin who had reached the further shore of the ocean of grammar, logic, and epistemology; who had attained clarity of knowledge by performing the Vājapeya sacrifice for Viśveśvara; and who manifested his independence in all systems of thought through the composition of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti*—[this work was composed].

In the *Bālamanoramā*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntakaumudī* composed by the learned Vāsudevadīkṣita—who was born of the womb of mother Annapūrṇā and is the son of Mahādeva, a performer of the Vājapeya sacrifice who had mastered the *Kalpasūtras* and their commentaries of Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Satyāṣaḍha, Bhāradvāja, Kātyāyana, Āśvalāyana, Drāhyāyaṇa, and others—the section on *kṛdanta* (primary suffixes) is completed.
This *Bālamanoramā* is now finished. Now begins the section on the euphonic combination of the *visarga*.

The *visarjanīya* is replaced by *saḥ*. Although this was explained in the context of the analysis of consonant sandhi (*halsandhi*), it is presented again here in accordance with the current topic in order to demonstrate the continued application of the term *visarjanīya*. For example: *viṣṇustrātā*.

When the suffix *su* is added to the word *viṣṇu*, after the application of *rutva* and the subsequent *visarga*, we have *viṣṇuḥ*; in this state, [the rule] "trātā" being present, the substitution of *s* occurs by this [rule]. (148) *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.35.

The phrase "of the *visarjanīya*" (*ṭhvisarjanīyasya*) is understood from the previous rule. From the rule "before a *kha[r]* or at the end of a word" (*kharavasānayoḥ*), the term "*kha[r*]" is understood by means of a *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap) ellipsis. The compound *śarparaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi*: that after which a *śar* [consonant] follows. The word "*kha[r*]" is the qualifier. Thus he says: "before a *kha[r]* followed by a *śar*. [This applies] to the *visarga*.

Regarding the rule for *visarga*, he states the result: "but not otherwise. The intention is that the prescription of *visarga* is for the purpose of excluding (*parisaṅkhyāna*) anything other than that. To the question "What is that other [thing]? he says: "here.
The word *yathāsve* is a *nipāta* (irregular form) meaning *yathāyatham*. Its meaning is "as far as possible" (*yathāsambhavam*). [The question continues: "Who?"

The meaning is that in the word *tsaruḥ*, the substitution of *s* (satva) does not occur, and in the word *ghanāghanaḥ kṣobhaṇaḥ*, the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *visarga*-like sound before *k* and *p*)— by virtue of the rule *kupvoḥ*— does not occur. Thus, it is stated that this [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to both the rule for *satva* and the rule *kupvoḥ*.

(149) *vā śari* | Pāṇini 8.3.36. The words *visarjanīyasya* and *visarjanīyaḥ* are carried over [from previous rules]. The prescription of *visarga* for *visarjanīya* is for the purpose of excluding its change into *sa*.
And because of the inclusion of the word "or" (vā), the substitution of *s* (satva) is optional. Thus it is said: "when followed by *śar*" (*śari pare*).
For example: *hariḥ śete*. This is the form when the visarga is optionally replaced by the *visarjanīya*, and the substitution of *s* is applied.
Alternatively, when there is no rule for the visarga [to remain as such], and the substitution of *s* has occurred, then for the *s*:
The form [is derived] by the substitution of *ś* for *s*.
Regarding the term *kharpara*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which a *kha* or *ra* follows"; *śar* is the word being qualified.
The meaning is that when a *śar* (any sibilant) follows a *kharpara*, the optional elision (*lopa*) of the *visarga* should be stated.

In the alternative where there is no elision (*lopābhāvapakṣe*), the rule *vā śari* applies. Thus, in the case of *rāmasthātā*, when *rāmaḥ sthātā* is established, if the visarga is elided, the form consists of a single *s*. The same applies in the case of *hari sphurati*. In the alternative (*pakṣe*)—that is, in the alternative where there is no elision of the visarga—the rule *vā śari* applies.
When there is a *visarga*, the form is with *visarga* and a single *sakāra*; when both are absent but [the preceding vowel] is a *satva* (short *a*), the form has two *sakāras*.

Thus, there are two forms. Consequently, by adding the form with a single *sakāra* and no *visarga*—which is established under the alternative of elision (*lopa*)—there are three forms in total. This is the meaning.

*kupvoḥ* > *ikaḥ* > *ipau*. Although this has already been explained in the section on the euphonic combination of consonants (*halsandhi*), it is presented again here in accordance with the requirements of the present context. *kaḥ karoti* (who does? represents the alternative involving the *jihvāmūlīya* (the guttural spirant); *kaḥ karoti* represents the alternative involving the *visarga*. The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.
(150) *so'padādau* | 8|3|38|. The word *apadādau* follows from the previous rule [8.3.37] *kupvoḥ*. The term *apadādau* is a qualifier for that [word *saḥ*].
The use of the singular number (*apadādau*) in place of the dual (*apadādau*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*), or it is used in the singular with reference to each individual member.

The term *visarjanīyasya* (of the visarga) also carries over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "of the visarga. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *kupvoḥ*. [Examples include] *pāśakalpaka*. This vārttika was not adopted by the author of the treatise. [Another example is] *payaspāśam*.
The suffix *pāśap* is applied when the object (*ṭhyāpye*) is contemptible; thus, "contemptuous water" (*payaspāśam*) is the meaning. Regarding "yaśaskalpam":
the suffix *kalpap* is used for "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāptau*); thus, the meaning is "slightly incomplete fame. Regarding "yaśaskam":

the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "when unknown" (*ajñāte*) or "when contemptible" (*kutsite*), etc. [In the phrase] "yaśaskāmyati," [the suffix *kāmyac* is added to express] fame for oneself.
In the sense of "he desires thus" (*iccchati*), with the rule *supa ātmanaḥ* still in force, the suffix *kāmyac* is applied by the rule *kāmyac ca*.
Because of the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, these [forms ending in *kāmyac*] are verbal roots, and thus the *laṭ* (present) and other tenses are formed.
Regarding the phrase *anavyayasya*: the meaning is that the substitution of *s* [for *visarga*] by the rule *so 'padādau* does not apply to the *visarga* of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Regarding the term *prātaḥkalpam*: the suffix *-kalpa* is used in the sense of "slightly incomplete. Thus, the meaning is "the morning time that is slightly incomplete. Although the word *prātar*, when functioning as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), primarily denotes the power of the locus, its primary denotation of the possessor of that power (*śaktimat*) in the context of a compound is not contradictory; as in the examples *doṣābhūtam ahaḥ* ("the day that has become night") and *divābhūtā rātriḥ* ("the night that has become day").
It is like the word *rātriḥ*.

Regarding the rule *kāmye roḥ*: the meaning is that when the suffix *kāmya* follows, the operation prescribed by *so 'padādau* applies only to that *visarga* which stands in the place of *ru*. For example: *gīḥkāmyati*, meaning "he desires speech for himself."
The suffix *kāmyac* is used in the sense of "desiring.

From the root *gṛdh*, after the application of *kvip*, the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule "ṛta iddhatoḥ," followed by the replacement of *ṛ* with *r*. The *r* is then replaced by a visarga (*visarga*). Because this [visarga] is not in the place of a *ru*-substitute, the change to *s* (by the rule *kupvoḥ*) does not apply; rather, the rule *kupvoḥ* applies directly.
The meaning is "it becomes. (151) *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.39.
Regarding *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*: the word *iṇaḥ* is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*). The word *parasya* ("of what follows") is to be supplied [as the governing term].

The phrase "of the *visarjanīya*" (*ṭhvisarjanīyasya*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "following an *iṇ*. Regarding the phrase "in the aforementioned scope": the meaning is that here [the rules] "before *k* or *p*" (*kupvoḥ*), "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*), "not of an indeclinable" (*anavyayasya*), and "only for *r* before the suffix *kāmya*" (*kāmye roreva*) are connected [to this rule]. Consequently, [in the examples] *uccaiḥkalpam*, *doḥpāśam*, etc., [the *s* is substituted].

The intention is that there is no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in examples such as *gīḥ kāmayate*. In cases like *sarpiṣpāśam*, the suffixes *pāśa* and so forth are applied as in the previous rule.
(152) *namaspurasoḥ gatyoḥ* | Pāṇini 8.3.40.

Regarding *namas-purasoḥ*: from this point onward, the phrase "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) no longer applies. The rules *visarjanīyasya saḥ* and *kupvoḥ* continue to apply. This is understood through the rule *gati-saṃjñāyoḥ* and so forth. This [present rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *kupvoḥ*.

Regarding the form *namaskaroti*: when the *s* of *namaḥ* undergoes *ru*-substitution and subsequently a *visarga*, this rule [Pāṇini 8.3.115] effects the change to *s* (*satva*), overriding the rule [Pāṇini 8.4.2] concerning *k* and *p* sounds (*kupvoḥ*). Now, one might ask: since the word *namaḥ* is not listed among the *prādi* group, how can it possess the status of a *gati*? To this, he says: "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

Regarding the term *vibhāṣā*: the sense is that in the rule *sākṣātprabhṛtīni ca*, the word *vibhāṣā* is understood from the preceding rule *vibhāṣā kṛñi*. Regarding "in its absence": this means that in the alternative where it lacks the status of a *gati*, when the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *k* sound) occurs by the rule *kupvoḥ*, the form is *namaḥ karoti*.

In the word *puraḥ*, the sense is "to be entered first. From the root *pṛ* (in the meanings of protecting and filling), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *bhrājabhās...* etc. Then, by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, the vowel *u* is substituted for the root-final *r*. Next, by the rule *raparatvaṃ*, the letter *r* is substituted for that *u*. Consequently, when the case-ending *jas* is added, because it is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*), it lacks the status of a *gati*; therefore, the substitution of *s* [for the final *r*] does not occur. It is precisely to indicate its non-indeclinable nature that the forms *pūḥ* and *purau* are given.

Thus it has been stated. (153) *idudupadhasya cā’pratyayasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.41]. Regarding the term *idudupadhasya*: the word *visarjanīyasya* is understood to carry over [from the preceding rule]. The phrase *idudupadhasya* [means...]

That is its qualification. "Ṭhidutaupadhe" is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that which has ṭh, th, or t as its penultimate letter. The phrase "kupvoḥ" is also understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "ikāra-ukāra... (referring to the vowels i and u). Regarding the term "apratyayasya": it means "distinct from a part of an affix. If, however, the meaning were "of a visarga that is distinct from an affix," [then the following would apply].

In the case of *kavibhiḥ kṛtam*, the substitution of *ṣ* would also occur; for although *bhisaḥ* is a suffix (*pratyaya*) there, the visarga alone is not a suffix. Since the intended meaning—that the rule applies to the visarga following *i* or *u*—is already established here, the mention of *upadhā* (the penultimate vowel) need not be made.
It is established in the Bhāṣya on the *hayavaraṭ* sūtra: "The mention of *upadhā* will not be made;
rather, we shall specify that the *visarjanīya* which follows *i* and *u* [is meant].
Regarding the term *niṣpratyūham*: *pratyūha* means an obstacle (*vighna*); the absence of that is *niṣpratyūham*.

When there is an absence of meaning [between the members], an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed. Regarding the word *āviṣkṛtam*: Amarasimha states, "The words *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* are used in the sense of manifestation. Regarding the word *duṣkṛtam*: the particle *duḥ* is listed at the beginning of the section on prefixes as *duḥ*.
Among these, the substitution of *ṣ* for the first [particle] ending in *s* is beyond dispute; however, regarding that which ends in *r*—

According to an alternative view supported by the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *hayavaraṭ*, which states "the *visarjanīya* that follows a *sakāra* preceded by a long vowel or a short *u*," the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur;
this is because, in that case, the *visarjanīya* is not in the place of a *sakāra*. For example: *agniḥ karoti*.
The intention is that, by virtue of the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the *visarga* is considered a constituent part of the suffix.

Now, from the word *mātṛ*, the fifth case singular suffix *ṅsi* is applied. By the rule *ṛta ud*, there is a single substitute *ukāra* for both the *ṛkāra* and the *akāra*. Then, by the rule of *raparatva*, we have *mātuḥ s*. In this state, by the rule *rātsasya*...

[If it were so,] there would be the substitution of *ṣ* even in the case of *mātuḥ kṛpaḥ*. It must be stated that even though the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) *u* [in *mātṛ-u-ṛkāra*] is treated as part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), the *repha* [the *r* sound] is still a constituent of the suffix (*pratyayāvayava*).
This is because in the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, the term "beginning and end" (*ādyantau*) applies.

This is because, having accepted the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "end" (*anta*) from the rule *ṭakitāv antau*, the *Bhāṣya* establishes as its final position (*siddhānta*) that the substitution of the letter *r* constitutes the end of the single substitute (*ekādeśāntatā*). For this very reason, in the rules *ṭhra-dābhyām* and *ṭhthali ca seṭi*, it is stated: "the *guṇa* occurs," "the *vṛddhi* occurs."

The *Bhāṣya* states, "That which is designated as *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* arises with the letter *r* at its head," and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary is consistent with this, stating, "When an *aṇ* is applied in place of *u*, it is followed by *r*, and the *r* is a part of the preceding element. Furthermore,
since the term *ur* has the letter *t* following it (*paradit*), it possesses the status of being a constituent of the suffix.

It must be stated: for in this state, *mātṛ as*, because the vowel *a* lacks the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*) due to the proximity of the *s*, the substitute *thu* occurring in its place does not acquire the status of an affix, since the status of being an affix resides in the aggregate [of the base and the affix]. As for that which... [is applied] after [the substitution] has been made—

In the substitute *ur*, the *s* is not distinct [from its original form] and serves as the technical designation for the suffix; however, that [suffix] is indeed elided. Or, even if *ur* were a suffix by virtue of being "post-initial" (*parādi*), nevertheless, because it would be "prior-final" (*pūrvānta*), it would not be a suffix, and thus the substitution of *ṣ* for its visarga remains unimpeded. Nor does the status of being "final-like" (*antavat*) apply...

It should not be argued that because the substitution of *ṣ* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to what is to be performed, the rule of "treating as internal" (*antavad-bhāva*) does not apply there;

for by the statement "in regard to what is *asiddha* in the preceding [section], it is not like the original base" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*), it is permitted that other extended applications (*atideśa*) do indeed operate even within the final three chapters (*tripādī*). It is precisely for this reason that the substitution of *ī* and *ṇatva* are established in the example *amī kṣīrapeṇa*.

In that regard, since the status of being related to the word *adaḥ* in the rule *ekāre* and the status of having a monosyllabic subsequent member (*ekājuttarapadatva*) in the rule *ṭhpe* depend upon [the substitute] being "as if it were the final element" (*antavadbhāva*), [one might object]: if the form *uru-* were treated as a prior-final element (*pūrvānta*), then the substitution of *ṣ* in *mātuḥ kṛpā* would be unavoidable; therefore, he says: "by the single-substitute [rule]."

The sense is that, because the *visarga* has as its substituend a *repha* produced by a rule of single-substitution (*ekādeśa-śāstra*), it is not caused by a rule of single-substitution. Regarding the example *bhrātuṣputra*:
even though the *visarga* is caused by a rule of single-substitution, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) nevertheless takes effect.

The inclusion of the word *bhrātuṣputra* [in the list of *kaska*-type compounds] would be redundant; for its purpose there was to provide the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *kaskādiṣu ca*, yet since that *ṣ*-substitution is already established by this very [present rule], what need is there for it?

[The example is] *muhusaḥ*. The words "of the substitution of *ṣ*" (*ṭh-ṣatvasya*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the rule]. Here, a prohibition must be stated regarding the words *pum* and *muhus*.

Thus it is read in the Bhāṣya. In that context, the mention of the word *pum* (masculine) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), because its purpose is already served by the rule *saṃpuṃkānāṃ so vaktavyaḥ*. (154) *tiraso 'nyatarasyām* 8.3.22.

Regarding *tiras*: the word *sa* (the suffix *s*) is understood from the rule *so'padādau*; likewise, *kupvoḥ* and *visarjanīyasya* are understood. *ṭhiṇa* is excluded because it is impossible [in this context].
Due to its association with that, *ṭhṣa* is also excluded. Thus he says: *tiras*.
By the rule beginning with *visargasya* [Pāṇini 8.3.37], etc. Regarding the term *tiraskartā*: since the rule *kupvoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.37] would have applied, there is the substitution of *s*.
In its absence, the *jihvāmūlīya* and the *visarga* [would apply].
(155) *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* are used in the sense of frequency (*kṛtvas-artha*). [Pāṇini 5.4.18].

In the expression *dvi-tri-catur-iti*, the word *iti* is followed by the phrase *ṭhaśabdānām iti śeṣaḥ* (the suffix *ṭha* [i.e., *thuk*] is to be supplied after the words). The rules for *visarjanīya*, *kupvoḥ*, *anyatarasyām*, and *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* are understood as continuing (*anuvartate*). Furthermore, the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ kriyābhyāvṛttigaṇane kṛtvasuc* (the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is added to a numeral when counting the repetition of an action) is also understood.

The meaning of *kṛtvas* is "times" (*kṛtvo'rtha*). The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the rule applies] to the visarga of the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* when they occur in that sense. He states this with the words beginning "in the sense of *kṛtvas*" and so forth.
In the example *dviṣ karoti*, the suffix *suc* is applied in the sense of *kṛtvas* by the rule *dvitricaturbhyas suc*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [other examples are implied].

It is understood as "he makes three" (*triṣkaroti*) and "he makes four" (*catuṣkaroti*). Since the *visarga* is in every case a constituent part of the suffix, this rule provides an option (*vibhāṣā*) where the rule *idudupadhasya* would otherwise have applied. In the absence of *ṣatva*, the *jihvāmūlīya* and *visarga* are substituted by the rule *kupvoḥ*. As for the statement "the *visarga* which occurs in the sense of *kṛtvas*":

But this has not been explained [in that way], because if it were so, there would be non-application (*avyāpti*) in the case of *catuṣkaroti*; for in the word *catuṣ*, due to the elision of the final consonant of the *su*-suffix by the rule *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, the visarga is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
As in *catuṣpāla*: in the sense of "a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared in four potsherds (*kapāla*)."

When the suffix *aṇ* is intended [to derive] from the word *saṃskṛtam* in the sense of "food" (*bhakṣāḥ*), there is a compound by the rule *taddhitārthottarapada...*. Then, by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*. In this case, since the word *catur-* does not occur in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*), the optional substitution of *ṣ* for its visarga does not apply; rather—

In the rule *idudupadhasya*, the substitution of *ṣ* is indeed obligatory. Now, one might object: if that rule is explained as "belonging to something other than a portion of an affix," then since the visarga in *ṭh-cater-uran* (Pāṇini 4.1.109) is a portion of the Uṇādi affix *-uran*, how can there be the obligatory substitution of *ṣ* here by the rule *idudupadhasya*? Therefore, in that context, the rule must simply be explained as "belonging to something other than an affix."

The explanation is appropriate. If it is argued that, in this case, because the visarga of the word *catur* lacks the status of being a suffix (*pratyaya*), the obligatory substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *idudupadhasya* will remain unimpeded, this is not a valid objection. For, in order to prevent the substitution of *ṣ* in examples such as *kavibhiḥ kṛt*, [the rule requires the visarga to be followed by a vowel].
It is more appropriate to explain [the rule] as "of that which is distinct from the suffix and its components.

However, the word *catuṣ* is indeed an underived (avyutpanna) form; therefore, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "distinct from the suffix and its components" does not apply to the word *catuṣ*, by virtue of the evidence provided by such rules as *catuṣpādyo ḍhañ*.
Because that which is not subject to grammatical derivation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*) alone must be accepted. There is someone who is called "dvināmā" or "trināmā";
he acts twice (*dviḥ karoti*) or thrice (*triḥ karoti*). Even here, there is no substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*], because the word *kṛtvas* is excluded by the rule *avṛteḥ*.
(156) *isusoḥ sāmarthye* | 8|3|44| [In the case of the suffixes *isi* and *usu*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*).]
The words *isu-soḥ*, *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (from that [sūtra]), *kupvoḥ*, *visarjanīyasya*, and *anyatarasyām* are carried over [by anuvṛtti]. Therefore, he says: "of the visarga of *is* and *su*.
In the example *sarpiṣ karoti*, the visarga [is substituted] here according to the view of etymological derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*).

Since the rule *idudupadhasya* does not apply because [the word] is a member of a compound (*pratyayāvayavatvāt*), the statement of the option (*vibhāṣā*) is made. In the alternative where the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur, the *jihvāmūlīya* or the *visarga* is substituted by the rule *kupvoḥ*.
The same applies in the case of *dhanuṣkaroti*. Now, one might object: "But isn't *sāmarthya* (semantic capacity) characterized by *ekārthībhāva* (the formation of a single meaning)?"

It is clear from the *Mahābhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*, as well as from the works of Kaiyaṭa and others, that this [substitution] occurs only in a compound (*vṛtti*) and not in a sentence (*vākya*).
Thus, one might ask: how can there be this optional substitution of *ṣ* in sentences such as *sarpiṣkaroti* or *dhanuṣkaroti*?
To this, he says: "In this context, 'capacity' (*sāmarthya*) means mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). This refers to a specific kind of expectancy.

Vyapekṣā (mutual expectancy). That mutual connection of words which arises by virtue of their expectancy, semantic competency, and proximity is vyapekṣā. This, however, is the *sāmarthya* (semantic capacity) found in sentences, as in "the king's man and horse" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo'śvaśca*) or "the man of the king and Devadatta" (*rājño devadatasya ca puruṣaḥ*), and so forth. And thus...

In examples such as *sarpiṣkaroti* ("he makes [the pot] with ghee"), there exists such a capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*); thus, it serves as an illustration. The point is that the *Bhāṣya* cites *sarpiṣkaroti* precisely because it relies on this very capacity characterized by mutual expectancy. And [it is not the case that] "they cooked with wood" (*pecuḥ kāṣṭhaiḥ*).

In examples such as *sakhyuḥ kāmaḥ* and *kavibhiḥ kṛtam*, the occurrence of the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) might be suspected; however, this is not the case here because only the *i* and *u* that are constituents of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) are intended to be included. This is because, in the subsequent rule *nityaṃ samāse*, those two [stems] alone are possible in the cited examples, and thus one must rely on the governing context of the meaning.

And because of concomitance (*sāhacarya*). Regarding the example "tiṣṭhatu": "tiṣṭhatu sarpiḥ" is one sentence, and "pibatu udakam" is another. In that case, since there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the word *sarpiḥ* and the word *piba*, there is no semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). Therefore, this is not an instance of the optional application of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*), nor does the rule *idudupadhasya ca* apply here.

The substitution of *ṣ* is permanent because it is a constituent part of the suffix. For this very reason, the interpretation that "it applies to a *visarga* distinct from the suffix" has not been adopted. If that were the case, then in examples such as *tiṣṭhatu sarpiḥ* and *piba tvam udakam*, since the *visarga* is a portion of the suffix and thus distinct from the suffix [as a whole], [the rule would apply].
Because the substitution of *ṣ* would apply by the rule *idudupadhasya*.

(157) *nityaṃ samāse 'nutarapadasthasya* || 4.3.45 || The word *nityam* [is used] in the sense of "always" in a compound. The words *isu-soḥ*, *kupvoḥ*, and *visarjanīyasya* are understood [from the preceding rules]. Thus he says: "of *is* and *us*, etc. [The example is: *sarpiṣ-kuṇḍikā*.

The analysis (*vigraha*) is *sarpiṣaḥ kuṇḍikā*. Since the capacity (*sāmarthya*) characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) exists even in a compound, the rule "ṭhisusoḥ sāmarthye" would apply, resulting in an optional substitution of *ṣ* for *s*; this present statement [of the sūtra] is intended to prevent that.
In the case of *paramasarpiḥkuṇḍikā*, there is no substitution of *ṣ* because the visarga belongs to the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*).

The substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *idudupadhasya* does not apply here because the *visarga* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the suffix. However, if one were to explain the rule as applying to a *visarga* that is distinct from the suffix, then the substitution of *ṣ* by *idudupadhasya* would indeed apply here as well, since in this case the *visarga* is a constituent part of the suffix. [Objection: But surely [the desired form] is established by this very [rule].
The inclusion of the word *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā* in the list of *kaska*-type compounds is redundant; therefore, he says: "In the *kaska*-type compounds.

[He adds: "Even in the absence of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)," meaning in cases such as "the clarified butter remains" (*tiṣṭhati sarpiḥ*) or "look at the water-jar" (*paśya kuṇḍikām*). And here, because there is no compound, the rule "it is always a compound" (*nityaṃ samāsaḥ*) does not apply.

Because there is an absence of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the two [words], the rule *sāmarthye* does not apply. Furthermore, because it is a constituent part of a suffix, the rule *idudupadhasya* also does not apply. Therefore, the intention is that the word is included in the *kaskādi* group for the purpose of obtaining the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) in those cases. Regarding the phrase "in the case of syntactic expectancy" (*vyapekṣāyām*): [as in] "this *sarpiṣ-kaṇḍikā*."

The meaning is "in this case. The intention is that, since the option [of applying ṣatva] would otherwise apply there by the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye*, the word is read in the *kaskādi* group for the sake of making the ṣatva obligatory. (158) *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃśakumbhapātrakuśākarṇīṣvanavyayasya* 8.3.46.

Therefore, in the rule *kṛkami-ṭhaḥ*, the word *ṭhaḥ* is in the ablative case. The words *visarjanīyasya* and *nityaṃ samāse 'nutarapadasthasya* are understood to carry over [from previous rules]. Thus he says, beginning with "after the vowel *a*" (*akārāt*), and so forth.
In the example *ayaskāraḥ*, the substitution of *s* occurs, overriding the rule *kupvoḥ*. The same applies in the following cases as well.

Regarding *ayassahitā*: it is not stated that this means "a derivative of iron" (*ayasaḥ vikāraḥ*), because that would result in the suffix *ṅīṣ* by virtue of the rule beginning with *jānapada-* (Pāṇini 4.1.42). In the case of *ayaskarṇī*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose ears are like iron.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied here by the rule *nāsikodara-*.

(159) *adhaḥśirasī pade* | 8|3|47|. The form *adhaśśirasī* [is derived as follows]: in the rule *adhaḥśirasī*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. The words *visarjanīyasya* and *saḥ* are understood [from the previous rules]. Thus he says: "of these two. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *kupvoḥ*.
Regarding "adhaspadam": the analysis (*vigraha*) is "below the foot" (*padasyādhaḥ*). It is a compound by virtue of belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class.

Regarding "śiraspadam": the analysis is "the foot of the head" (*śirasaḥ padam*). Following the rule from the Sūtrapāṭha, he states again: "and in the *kaska*-class etc. Regarding "bhāskara": [the suffix] *ṭhak*... [is applied].

Thus, because of the inclusion of the *tapara* (long vowel marker), the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa...* does not apply; therefore, the intention is that the word *bhāskara* is listed in the *kaskādi* group for the purpose of ensuring the occurrence of *satva* (the substitution of *s*).
Thus ends the section on Visarga-sandhi in the *Bālamanoramā*.

Now begins the section on the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅntaprakriyā*). (Pāṇini 3.1.22): "The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after a root that consists of a single vowel and begins with a consonant, when there is an intensification of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).
Now, the formation of *yaṅ* is described. [The rule states: "after a root consisting of a single vowel" (*dhātor ekācaḥ*). [This means] "when that [intensive meaning] is to be indicated."

The point is that if [the suffix] were expressed [by the verbal root], then because that which is expressed by the suffix is primary, it would become the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the *saṃnanta* forms, just as desire (*icchā*) is in the case of the desiderative; this is the intended meaning.
(457) *guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.82.

The term *guṇa* [is applied] in the presence of *yaṅ* and *luk*. This is a locative case derived from the *dvandva* compound *yaṅ ca luk ca*. By means of the *ik-paribhāṣā*, it is understood that this applies to a stem ending in an *ik* vowel. Thus, we have *bobhūyate*. [In this formation,] there is reduplication by the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. Because *yaṅ* has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ū*. From the form *bobhūya*, when *laṭ* is added, followed by *tip* and *śap*...

The form of the subsequent word [is used]. As for the doubling [of the word] by the rule "when the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is to be expressed, the word is doubled," that does not apply here;

because that rule is restricted solely to the domain of the imperative (*loṭ*) endings prescribed by the rule "in the intensification of an action, the imperative. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "the imperative is used in the intensification of an action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ*), it is stated: "In the intensification of an action..."

It is read simply as: "The second person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*) has two forms when expressing repetition. However, in the case of the *yaṅ* suffix, there is no doubling [of the root] by the rule "the *yaṅ* occurs in the sense of frequency and pervasion" (*nityavīpsayoḥ*), because doubling of the imperative ending is prescribed for frequency by the rule "doubling occurs in the sense of intensification of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre dve*).
Since the repetition [of an action] is obtained from another source, there is no application of the word "twice" (*dvitva*) in the sūtra; this is what is being indicated, so enough of this.

Regarding the question "What is the purpose of mentioning *dhātu*?"—the question is: since the root (*dhātu*) is already obtained by the rule "in the sense of frequent repetition of an action" (*kriyāsamabhihāre*), for what purpose is the mention of *dhātu* made? Regarding the phrase "the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka*": [this would follow] if the word *dhātuḥ* were absent.

The sense is that the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix would not apply, because the status of being an *ārddhadhātuka* belongs only to those suffixes prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*). Regarding the example "brūva" (from *brū*), the sense is that the *yaṅ* suffix would [otherwise] have the status of an *ārddhadhātuka*.
Regarding "bhṛśam īkṣate" (he looks intensely), the sense is that the *yaṅ* suffix is not applied here because the meaning of intensity is already conveyed by the word "bhṛśam" itself.
It should be stated that [the meaning] will come to be; for intensity (*bhṛśatva*) is what is indicated (*dyotya*) by the *yaṅ* suffix, not its expressed meaning (*vācya*).

The point is that indication (*dyotana*) is possible even for that which has already been stated. "The *yaṅ* does not [apply]"—this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* because it is not denoted (*anabhidhānāt*). "In the case of repetition" (*paunaḥpunye*)—even when there is an accumulation (*samabhihāra*) of the word *punaḥpunaḥ*.
The meaning is that it is indeed so, because it is stated that [the suffix *kyaṅ*] does not express the sense of intensity (*bhṛśa*). Regarding "sūci-sūtrī":
this is a *dvandva* compound of *sūci*, *sūtri*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭi*, *arti*, *aśū*, and *ūrṇoti*.
[The roots are] *sūca* in the sense of "malicious speech" (*paiśunya*), *sūtra* in the sense of "weaving" (*veṣṭana*), and *mūtra* in the sense of "urinating" (*prasravaṇa*). These...

The first three roots in the *kathādi* sub-group are short-voweled (*adanta*). Since they consist of more than one syllable (*anekāc*), the application of *yaṅ* would not otherwise be obtained; thus he says, "the first three. For *aṭa* (to go), *ṛ* (to go), *aśa* (to eat), and *aśū* (to pervade), the rule does not apply because they do not begin with a consonant (*halādi*); however, for *ūrṇuñ*...
This statement is made because [the root] lacks the quality of beginning with *ha* and because it lacks the quality of having a single vowel (*ekāc*). Regarding the form *sosūcyate*:

after the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is *yaṅ*; upon the elision of *iṇ*, there is reduplication, and by the rule "guṇa for the *yaṅluṅ*" (*guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*), the guṇa substitution occurs in the reduplicated syllable.
He dispels the misconception that *sūci* is a root taught with an initial *ṣ* by stating "by virtue of having more than one vowel" (*anekāckatvena*). If it were taught with an initial *ṣ*...

The point is that once the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* has been made by the rule *dhātvādeḥ* (8.2.30), the subsequent portion [of the root] would undergo the substitution of *ṣ* because its initial sound is now *s*. When the form *sosūc-ya-ām* is established in the *liṭ* [perfect tense], [the following rule applies]:
(457) *yasya halaḥ* 6.4.49.
He dispels the misconception that the letter *a* [after the *ya*] is for the sake of pronunciation by stating "the mention of the aggregate" (*saṅghātagrahaṇam*).

This means [the rule applies to] the entire collection consisting of the letters *ya* and *a*. The word "of a consonant" (*halaḥ*) is in the ablative case. The term "in an ārdhadhātuka suffix" (*ārddhadhātuke*) is the governing heading (*adhikṛtam*).
From the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), the word "elision" (*lopaḥ*) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). Thus he says:

[The rule] "of what follows a consonant" (*halaḥ parasya*) and so forth [is applied]. Now, one might object that by the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*), there would be the elision of the letter *y* and the letter *d*;

therefore, he says: "of what follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*). The sense is that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "of the final [element]. [Regarding] "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*): when the cluster consisting of the letter *y* and the vowel *a* [is present], there is the elision of the letter *y*.

When there is the presence of the remaining letter *a* following the suffix *ṭha*, there is elision [of that *ṭha*]; this means the elision of *ṭ*. Now, one might object: "Let there be no mention of the entire cluster; let the elision here be prescribed for the letter *y* alone.
Once the elision of *ā* has occurred, the desired result will be achieved. This is not so, because when the root *īṣ* takes the suffix *tṛc*, [the form would be incorrect].
Enough of this discussion regarding the necessity of preventing the elision of the *yakāra* in the case of the root *īrṣya*.

Now, from the root *aṭ*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; by the rule "the second [syllable] beginning with *ṭh* or *j*" (*ṭhijāderdvitīyasya*), the syllable *ṭaḷ* (i.e., *aṭ-ya*) undergoes reduplication.
After the application of the *halādiśeṣa* rule, which eliminates the *yakāra* from the reduplicated portion, the form *aṭṭaḷ-te* is established.

(458) *dīrgho'kitaḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.83: "The long vowel [is substituted] for the non-kit [abhyāsa]. The meaning is that the word *abhyāsasya* ("of the reduplicated syllable") is understood here because it is carried over from the preceding rule, *lopo'bhyāsasya*. [The phrase] *yaṅ yiṅluki ca* means "also when there is elision of the *yaṅ* and *yiṅ* suffixes."

The intention is that [the term] *tad* (that) is understood from the rule "ṭh-guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ" (P. 1.1.3). However, the purpose of the rule "akitaḥ" (P. 1.1.5) will be explained in examples such as *yaṃyamyate*. When the suffix *yaṅ* is applied to the root *ṛ*, since it bears the marker *ṅ*, the prohibition of *guṇa* would otherwise apply; [therefore, the following is stated].

(459) Furthermore: *yaṅ ci* |7|4|30|. The rule *guṇo 'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ* is understood [from the previous sūtra], as well as *ṛtaḥ* from the rule *rīṅ ṛtaḥ*. Thus he says: "of *ṛti*, etc. Consequently, when the form *ṛ ya* is established...
When the vowel *ṛ* undergoes *guṇa* substitution resulting in *a*, and the rule *rapara* applies, the form *arya-* is established.

At this point, although the doubling of the *r* is prohibited by the rule *na ndrāḥ*, and the doubling of *ya* occurs, leading to the form *aryāyate*—where the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is applied by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ*—the author says: "of the *r* followed by *y*" (*yakārapararephasya*).

"From the example cited in the Bhāṣya": the remainder of the sentence is "in the rule *dhātorekācaḥ*. Regarding *arārat*: there is the elision of the *yakāra* by the rule *yasya halaḥ*. Regarding *aśāśita*:
from the root *aś*, after the application of *yaṅ*, when *śyi* is doubled and the *halādiśeṣa* has been applied to the reduplicated syllable...

When the *yakāra* is elided, by the rule "dīrgho'kitaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.53), the vowel is lengthened; then, by the rule "yasya halaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.49), the *yakāra* is dropped. Regarding the form *ūrṇonūyate*: when *ūrṇu-ya* is situated [in the derivation], by the rule "na ndrāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3), the doubling of the syllable *nu* occurs;

then, after the application of "halādiśeṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.60) and the guṇa substitution for the reduplicated syllable, the lengthening occurs by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.25). [Similarly,] *bebhid-yate*.
Thus, when *bhid-ya* remains, after doubling *mid* and applying *halādiśeṣa*, there is the guṇa of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsaguṇa*).

Now, one might object that in the case of *bebhidya*—derived from the intensive (*yaṅ*) stem with the suffix *luṭ*, the *tās* affix, the augment *iṭ*, the elision of *y*, and the elision of *at*—there would be the guṇa of the light penultimate vowel (*laghupadhaguṇa*) before the suffix *tās*. To this, he says: "of the elision of *at*" (*allopasya*).
Regarding the phrase "because of being like the original" (*sthānivadbhāvāt*):

[The rule] *nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau* (Pāṇini 3.1.23), "always [the suffix yaṅ is used] when there is crookedness in motion," [is applied]. The word *nityam* has the sense of "only" (*eva*), and it applies over the word *kauṭilye*.
It should be understood that the term *yaṅ* is supplied from the rule "dhātor ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.22). Thus he says:

"only when crookedness (*kauṭilya*) [is to be expressed] after a root meaning motion. The meaning of *yaṅ* is that it occurs after a root functioning in the sense of motion, solely when crookedness is to be indicated. He states what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*): "but not in the case of the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*)."
In the *Śabdenduśekhara*, however, it is explained in detail that the suffix *yaṅ* occurs after roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) when there is a repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

(461) *lupasadasacarajapabhadahadaśagṛbhyo bhāvagarhāyām* || 3.1.24 || [The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after the roots *lup*, *sad*, *car*, *jap*, *bhada*, *hada*, *daś*, and *gṛ* when there is censure of the action.]

*Lupasada*, *lupasada*, *cara*, *japa*, *jabha*, *daha*, *daśa*, and *gṛ*—this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The suffix *yaṅ* is understood from the previous rule. "Bhāva" (state) is the meaning of the verbal root; the censure directed toward that [meaning] is "censure of the state" (*bhāvagarhā*).
The word "nityam" (always), which is carried over [from the previous rule], has the sense of the particle *eva* (only). Thus he says: "from these," and so forth.
(462) *caraphalośca* | 7|4|87 | The words *caraphalośca* [are explained as follows]: from the rule *atra lopaḥ*, the phrase *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplicated syllable) is understood to carry over.
From the rule *nugato’nunāsikāntasya*, the word *nuk* is understood to carry over. [And] *guṇaḥ*... [is understood].
This is derived from the rules *yaṅ-lukoḥ* and *yaṅ-lukor*. Thus he says: "of the two others," and so forth.
In the augment *nuṭ*, the letter *k* is for the sake of marking (*it*), while the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the statement "it is characterized":
this refers to the previous rule, *nugato 'nunāsikāntasya*, [which applies] in cases such as *yaṃyamyate* and *raṃramyate*.
In such cases, for the sake of hearing the *anusvāra*, one must resort to the view that *nug* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *anusvāra*.

Otherwise, because the condition of being followed by a *jhal* consonant would be absent, the *anusvāra* prescribed by the rule "naśca" (Pāṇini 8.3.24) would be impossible, and thus only the letter *n* itself would be heard; so it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*.
The intention is that because this very [rule] continues here as well, the term *anusvāra* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [the rule concerning nasalization].

Regarding the phrase "as at the end of a word" (*padāntavat*), the intention is that this Vārttika from the preceding sūtra— "there is *nuk* after [a root] ending in a nasal" (*nugato'nunāsikāntasya*)— also continues to apply here.
(463) *utparasyā'taḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.88. Regarding *utparasyā'taḥ*: from the rule *atra lopaḥ*, the term *abhyāsasya* (of the reduplication) is carried over;
due to its connection with the word *para* (subsequent), it is transformed into the ablative case. [The remainder of the sūtra is: *guṇo...* [is substituted].
From the rule *yaṅlukor aḥ*, the phrase *yaṅlukor* is understood, as is *caraphaloḥ*.
Thus he says: "of *car* and *phal*" and so forth. Regarding the term "long" (*dīrgha*), the word "of the letter *u*" (*ukārasya*) is to be supplied.
In the example *cañcūryate*, the meaning is "he moves in a censurable manner. When the *yaṅ* suffix is doubled and the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant) has taken place...

When the *anusvāra* arises after the form *abhyāsākāra*, the rule "ṭh vā padāntasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.61) applies, whereby that [anusvāra] becomes a *ñakāra* through *parasavarṇa*. Then, when the vowel *a* in the subsequent portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) undergoes *utva*, it becomes long. Regarding the alternative case where *parasavarṇa* does not occur, he says: *cacūryate* and *pamphulyate*. Here...

The *anusvāra* becomes *makāra* when followed by a homogeneous sound. (464) [Pāṇini 8.3.23] *japa-jabha-daha-daśa-bhañja-paśām ca*. Regarding *japa-jabha*: everything that was carried over in the rule *caraphalośca* is also carried over here.

He says this with the words "of these" (*eṣām*) and so forth. Examples include: *jañjabhyate*, *dandahyate*, *dandaśyate*, *bambhajyate*, *pampaśyate*. Regarding the root *paś*, Mādhava states that it ends in a dental and is a Vedic (Sautra) root meaning "to go. The *Kāśikā* states that it ends in a palatal.

(465) *gro yaṅ* |8|2|20|. *gro yaṅ*: This is the genitive singular form of the root *gṛ*. From the rule *kṛpo ro laṭaḥ*, the phrase *ro la* is understood to carry over. Therefore, he says: "of the root *girati*" and so forth. *dā*, *pā*, *sā*— [Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a commentary on Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, specifically discussing the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* in the root *gṛ* under certain conditions.]
Regarding these, he states a specific rule: *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali* and so forth. As for the form *śośūyate*:

from the root *śvi*, there is the suffix *yaṅ*; by the rule "the substitution of semivowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the operation dependent upon it are stronger," first the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs, followed by the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), and then the doubling of the syllable *śu*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṭhakṛtsārvadhātukayor dīrghaḥ*. Regarding *sāsmaryate*: when *smṛ-ya* is established, because it begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the rule *ṭhyaṅ ca* applies; subsequently, by the rule for *guṇa*, the substitution of *ra* (for *ṛ*) occurs, followed by reduplication (*dvitva*), and finally the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ*. Regarding *cekrīyate*: when *kṛ-ya* is established...

Because the vowel *ṛ* is subsequent [to the augment], when *rīṅ* is substituted [for *ṛ*], there is the doubling of the syllable *ṭh-krī-* and the guṇa of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Regarding "suṭ":

it is by means of the rule "the augment *suṭ* is added before the root *kṛ* when preceded by *sam* or *pari* in the sense of ornamenting, and also in the sense of aggregation"—this is the remainder [of the explanation].
(466) *sico yaṅ* (Pāṇini 8.3.112).
Regarding *sicaḥ*: from the rule "ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ saḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the word "saḥ" is understood as a genitive case-form (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) by way of anuvṛtti.

The term "mūrdhanye" is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*). From the rule "na raparasṛpi" (Pāṇini 8.3.10), the word "na" is understood as anuvṛtti. Thus he says: "of *sic*" (*sicaḥ*). [The example is] "niṣiṣicyate."

By this [rule], the substitution of *ṣ* prescribed by the rules "after a prefix, in the case of *su*" (*upasargāt sunoti*) and "in the case of *sthā* and others, when followed by a reduplicated syllable" (*sthādiṣv abhyāsena*) is prohibited.
(467) [The suffix] *yaṅ* is not applied after the root *kavati*. 7.4.63.

Considering that "after *kavati*" [is understood] from the rule "there is elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*ṭhitra lopaḥ*), and that "the substitute *c* for *k* and *h*" (*ṭhkuhoścu*) is also carried over, he says: "of the reduplicated syllable of *kavati*.
Now, one might object: since the desired form is established by simply saying "after *ku* in *yaṅ*" (*koryaṅi*), the mention using the *śtip* affix (*nirdeśaḥ*) is redundant; to this he replies:

Regarding the phrase "kautakuvatyos tu": the mention of *kavati* is for the sake of indicating the presence of the *śap* suffix. By this, it is understood that both the root *ku* with the *luṅ-vikaraṇa* (i.e., *ku śabde*) and the root *kūṅ* with the *śap-vikaraṇa* (i.e., *kūṅ śabde*) are included; such is the intended meaning. Nor is there any issue even if [the rule] were stated simply as "koḥ," since [the substitution applies to] that which ends in a long vowel (*dīrghāntasya*).

It should not be suspected that there is the possibility of including [the root] with the suffix *śap*, because the reading of the short vowel in *ṭhkuṅ śabdaḥ* at the beginning of the *tud*-class is approved by the *Nyāsa*. In reality, however, the result of its non-application to this [root] belonging to the *tud*-class is precisely what is intended by the *Nyāsa*.

The meaning is that, according to the principle "between a [root] with a *luṅ*-suffix and one without a *luṅ*-suffix, only the one without the *luṅ*-suffix is taken," there is an exclusion of the inclusion of a root with a *luṅ*-suffix. Regarding the term *yaṅlukor*: it means "in the case of *yaṅ* and in the case of *yaṅ*-elision" (*yaṅluka*). "There is no long vowel": this refers to the state prior to the addition of the augment *nīk*.

The meaning is that [the substitution] has not been obtained despite the lengthening resulting from repetition (*abhyāsa*). The intention is that even though the *kit* status is yet to come into effect, it acts as an obstacle to the lengthening. "The elision of *n*" means that the *n* is elided by the rule *aniditām*. "And so forth" refers to forms such as *sanīsras-yate* and *danīdhvas-yate*.
*banībhrasyate*, *canīkasyate*, *panīpatyate*, *panīpadyate*, *canīskadyate*.

(468) *nugato 'nunāsikāntasya* |7|4|85|. The augment *nuK* is added after a root ending in a nasal (*anunāsika*). The term "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Here, [the rule] "elision" (*lopaḥ*) applies.

Therefore, "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*) is understood from the previous rule; and "of the *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk*" is understood from the rule "there is *guṇa* for the *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk*" (*guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*). Thus he says: "of that which ends in an *anunāsika*, etc. Now, one might object:

in the case of *yaṃyamyate*, how can there be [the application of the rule], since the *n* of the augment *nuK* is not at the end of a word (*apādanta*) and is followed by a non-jhal consonant (*ajhalpara*)?

Because of the rule "ṭhnaśca," there is an *anusvāra*; therefore, he says "nukā. Now, one might object: since a short vowel is prescribed for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), a long vowel cannot occur there; thus, in the rule for *nuk*, the use of the *tapara* marker (the lengthened *a*) would be redundant. To this he replies: "By virtue of the force of the *tapara* marker. This refers specifically to that short vowel *a* which is inherent [to the phoneme].

The intention is that the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with a following *p*) is used for the purpose of specifying the short *a* that results from the substitution of the long vowel, and not for the original short *a*. As for the example *bābhāmyate*: the meaning here is that the *nuk* augment does not apply to the *a* which has been produced by the rule for shortening in place of the *ā*. [This applies] to the *yaṅ* suffix of the root *jan*.
He recalls the optional substitution of *ā* for *na* with the rule *ye vibhāṣā*. Regarding the form *ghnī*:

although here, even in the rule prescribing the change to *hnī*, the substitution of *gh* for *h* is established by the rule *habhyāsācca*, nevertheless, because there is no reduction in effort and because it results in a simpler grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), the form is given as *ghnī*.
The intended meaning is the pronunciation of the syllable *gha*. Regarding the form *jeghnīyate*, it means that he strikes repeatedly or excessively.
Here, the locative case in *yaṅi* is a "locative of occasion" (*viṣayasaptamī*). This implies that the condition is when the *yaṅ* suffix is intended to be applied.
Consequently, it should be understood that the substitution of *ghnī* occurs even before reduplication, despite the latter's status as a subsequent operation.
"Jaṅghanyate" means "he goes to what is censurable.

(469) *rīgṛdupadhasya ca* | 7|4|10|. [The augment] *rīk* is added to a reduplicated syllable that has a short vowel (*ṛt*) as its penultimate letter; this is because the word "of the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsasya*) is understood here by virtue of its recurrence from the rule "there is elision" (*atra lopaḥ*).

The meaning is that [the rule] "guṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.82) follows from the subsequent application of that [rule]. Regarding *varīvṛtyate*: from the root *vṛt* (meaning "to turn"), there is the suffix *yaṅ*; after doubling and the substitution of *urat*, the *halādi-śeṣa* [remains], and then the *rīk* substitution occurs for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). In the case of *nirīnṛtyate* from the root *nṛt* with *yaṅ*: [the same process applies].

Anticipating the objection regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, he says: "There is no *ṇ* because [the root] belongs to the *kṣubh*-class. Regarding *jarīgṛhyate*: from the root *grah* (meaning "to take up") with the suffix *yaṅ*; after the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution), reduplication, the shortening of the vowel (*udaratva*), and the application of the *halādiśeṣa* rule, the substitute *rīk* is applied to the reduplicated syllable. Regarding *calīklṛpyate*: [this is formed] by the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*.

Thus, in the reduplication, the letter *l* replaces the *r*. This means that in the subsequent portion (*uttara-khaṇḍa*), the *r* which is a constituent part of the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by something similar to *l*. Now, one might ask: how is it that in the case of the root *vraśc* with the *yaṅ* suffix—as in *virīvṛścyate*—the reduplication becomes *rī*, given that the root has the letter *ś* as its penultimate?

Because there is no vowel with *ṛ* as its penultimate (*ṛdupadhā*), he says: "rīg for that which possesses *ṛ*" (*rīgṛtvataḥ*). The meaning is that in the rule *ṛdupadhasya*, the term *ṛdupadhasya* should be removed and replaced by *ṛtvataḥ*. That which has *ṛt* is called *ṛtvat*. Because of the designation *bha* in the rule *tasau matvarthe*, there is an absence of *padatva* (word-status), and thus no application of *jaśtva* (the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stops).

Regarding *parīpṛcchyate*: from the root *pracch*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; by the rule *grahijyā*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *r* into *ṛ*. Then, the formation of the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels (*pūrvarūpa*), reduplication, substitution of *r* for the semivowel (*raparatva*), and the retention of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*) result in *rī*.
Regarding *varīvṛścyate*: from the root *vraśc*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; with vocalization, reduplication, and so forth, as before.

(470) *svapisyamivyeñāṃ yaiṅ* [Pāṇini 6.1.19]. Regarding *svapisyam-*, the phrase "there shall be vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*)" is to be supplied as the remainder. This is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "vocalization for *ṣyaṅ*" [from 6.1.16]; such is the intention. Thus we have *soṣupyate*.

From the root *svap*, after the addition of *yaṅ* and the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *y* into *u*, followed by the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), reduplication, and the strengthening (*guṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in the subsequent portion; thus, *sesimyate*.
From the root *syam*, after the addition of *yaṅ*, the vocalization of *y* into *i*, the formation of the single substitute, reduplication, and so forth [the form is derived].

Because it is not taught with an *upadeśa* marker *ṣ*, there is no substitution of *ṣ*. Thus: *vevīyate*. From the root *vyen* (to cover), after the addition of *yaṅ*, the semivowel *y* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*, followed by the formation of the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*), reduplication, and so forth. Then, by the rule "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*) or "of the non-*kṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes" (*akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*), the long vowel occurs. Now, regarding the root *vaś* with *yaṅ*:
In the case of the form *uśyate*, since the substitution of semivowels for vowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) would have been required by the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), he reminds us of its prohibition:
(471) *na vaśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.20).
It is not *vaś*. It has already been stated that the Vedic nature (*chāndasatva*) of the root *vaś* is merely common (*prāyika*).

(472) Regarding *cāyaḥ kī*: the remainder is "after *ṭhyaṅ*" (*ṭhyaṅīti śeṣaḥ*). The intention is that this is due to the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*) of [the rule] "after *svapi*, *yam*, *vi*, and *vyeñ* in *yaṅ*" (*svapisyamivyeñāṃ yaṅī*). Thus, one forms *cekīyate* from the root *cāyṛ*.

[The suffix] *yaṅ* is applied after [the roots] *pūj* and *niśām* in the sense of repetition (*bhṛśa*) and observation (*darśana*). From this root, when the feminine suffix *kī* is added, there is reduplication (*dvitva*) and so forth.

(473) *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ* | Pāṇini 7.4.31. *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ*: *ghrā* and *dhmā*; this is the genitive dual from a dvandva compound of these two. The remainder of the rule is "*yaṅī*" (before the suffix *yaṅ* and before the feminine suffix *ī*).

And because of the recurrence of the word "ṭhy-aṅ ca" [from the previous rule], we have *jeghrīyate* and *dedhmīyate*. Once the substitution of *ī* has been applied, reduplication and so forth follow. Even though the rule "a short vowel is substituted for the *ik*" would have resulted in a short *i*, the long vowel is explicitly pronounced so that the rule "a long vowel is substituted for the penultimate vowel before a *ṭha*-affix and a sārvadhātuka suffix" may apply; this is also for the sake of the rule "the *ṭha* is substituted for the *ya* of *cvau*."
This is for the sake of what follows.

(474) *ayaṅ yi kṅiti* | Pāṇini 7.4.22. [The substitute] *ayaṅ* [replaces the final vowel of *śī*] before an affix beginning with *y* that has *k* or *ṅ* as its *it*. [The word] "before *y*" (*yi*) is in the locative case. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has *k* and *ṅ* as its *it*s."
The word *śīṅ* [is used]; the meaning is that this is because of its continued application from the rule "there is *guṇa* for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

In *ayaṅ*, the letter *ṅ* is for the sake of the designation *it*; the letters *ya* and *a* are for the sake of pronunciation. Because of the *ṅ*-designation, there is the substitution of *in*. Thus, when *śī* and *ya* remain, the *ī* is replaced by *ayaṅ*. Then, after reduplication:
